title: Majority of US voters link extreme weather to climate crisis, study finds
author: Dharna Noor with graphics by Andrew Witherspoon
summary: Top Democrat says findings show public ‘way ahead of the politicians’ as Trump dismisses global heating as ‘hoax’
body_text: Amid a summer of dangerous heat, drought and floods, a majority of Americans are connecting increasingly severe weather to the climate crisis, new polling shows, despite efforts by Donald Trump to dismiss global heating as a “con job” and a “hoax”. It’s a sign that attempts to suppress and polarize climate concerns may not be seeing full success, said Grace Adcox, senior climate strategist at Data for Progress. “We started with the question of ‘are extreme weather events increasing,’ because we thought [that] if we can find consensus on that, that can be an entry point to being able to have a more bipartisan conversation about climate and climate intervention,” she said. About 61% of likely American voters believe extreme weather events have become more frequent over the past five years, the survey from the progressive polling firm Data for Progress, shared exclusively with the Guardian, found. That includes 72% of Democrats, 63% of Independents, and nearly half – 46% – of all Republicans. Sheldon Whitehouse, the Rhode Island senator who has long criticized Democrats for quieting their talk of global warming – or “climate-hushing” – said the new data “adds to the mountain of evidence that the public is way ahead of the politicians on the dire consequences of climate change”. “Climate hushers who ignore this righteous fight should take note,” he told the Guardian. The researchers also asked participants about whether or not specific forms of extreme weather are being “worsened by climate change”. Majorities linked climate change to worsening wildfires (64%), droughts (63%), flooding and flash flooding (62%), hurricanes (59%), and severe thunderstorms and hailstorms (59%). But heatwaves topped the list, with 67% saying climate change is making them worse – including 48% of Republicans, the highest share for any of the extreme weather events surveyed. That could be because nearly everyone in the US has experienced unusually hot days or weeks in recent years, said Adcox. High temperatures kill more people annually in the US than hurricanes, tornadoes and floods combined. “There are regional differences across experiences with extreme weather,” said Adcox. “Extreme heat happens to have the biggest footprint in the American context compared to some of these other types of extreme weather.” The finding indicates that scorching conditions could provide an “interesting opening salvo” to speak about the climate crisis, she added. Anthony Leiserowitz, director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, said the new poll’s findings are “very consistent” with the conclusions researchers have drawn based on Yale’s surveys, which have shown Americans are increasingly linking extreme weather to the climate crisis and want to protect workers from heat. But Jennifer Marlon, a senior research scientist at Yale who also focuses on climate communications, said despite this, it’s not clear if most Americans understand why exactly the climate is changing. “This is probably the biggest misconception out there – many Americans still think the warming is due to some kind of natural cycle. But it isn’t,” she said, adding that a spring survey from Yale Program on Climate Change Communication found 27% of people think that the changes are mostly natural. The survey findings could help inform how to frame future conversations about the climate crisis with skeptical Americans, said Adcox. For instance, the data indicates heat may be the form of extreme weather that invites most conversation about climate. “You can say, hey, this extreme heat event is crazy, so let’s talk about it, let’s talk about why it’s happening,” she said. Another survey finding also indicates that even Americans who may not be convinced that the climate crisis is human caused – or even that it is happening – would support some climate justice-focused measures. Amid global and national rising temperatures, workers who labor outdoors – such as construction workers, farm workers and roofers – are among the populations most vulnerable to heat-related illness. In fact, extreme heat is a leading contributor to workplace injuries and deaths. Some indoor workers, including those in warehouses, commercial kitchens and manufacturing facilities, can also face severe heat risk due to a lack of air conditioning, poor ventilation, humidity and other factors. It’s a risk that the polling indicates most Americans think lawmakers should address. About 88% of participants in the Data for Progress survey said they favor policies in their own state requiring employers to provide heat protections like access to drinking water, shade, breaks, and air conditioning. Only 7% of likely voters said they oppose the policy, indicating broad support for the protections that previous Data for Progress polls have also shown. “These findings send a powerful message: protecting workers from dangerous heat isn’t a partisan issue,” said Jessica E Martinez, executive director of the National Council for Occupational Safety and Health, a network of two dozen local grassroots worker organizations. “When 88% of likely voters … support requiring employers to provide basic, lifesaving heat protections, it’s clear the public expects every worker to be protected.” She said the polling indicates the public would support the creation of a federal heat standard – something workers have demanded for years, but on which progress has stalled under Trump. The current administration this April also allowed the Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s nationwide enforcement initiative focused on protecting workers from heat illness, then later issued a revised but vastly weakened program. “Our hope in continuing to profile the broad and particularly strong support that we see across partisanship for extreme heat protections for workers is a way for us to illustrate what could it look like to take an approach to climate that puts working people first,” said Adcox.

title: Trump is invoking foreign election interference to justify his own
author: Jamil Smith
summary: The president no longer treats the people who defeated him as voters. He treats them as suspects
body_text: There is a version of this country in which Donald Trump tells Americans the truth he has been handed: that their elections are secure. Once, he apparently wanted to. The Atlantic reported after Thursday night’s address that a February 2020 election-security briefing pleased Trump so much he wanted to announce the news himself. The press conference never happened. The election did, and Trump lost it. More than six years later, he mocked the assurances he once wanted his name on, describing a system “so broken and so vulnerable that no one can possibly defend it”. The evidence hadn’t changed. Its usefulness had. Trump is dangerous twice over: in what he does and what he tells us to fear while doing it. Factcheckers agreed he proved nothing. Failing as evidence, his address succeeded as permission – for federal intervention already under way in Fulton county. In his speech, Trump assembled old intelligence, vulnerabilities and lies into a conspiracy: 220 million US voter records in Chinese hands, “extremely exposed” voting machines, 278,000 supposed noncitizens on the rolls and a deep-state burial of proof. Yet some documents he released contradicted him. A 2021 intelligence-community assessment distinguished foreign influence from interference with registration, ballot casting, tabulation or results, and found no indication that any foreign actor attempted the latter. A newly released document judged tabulation systems difficult to manipulate at election-changing scale; a report on Venezuelan voting never confirmed large-scale electronic fraud even there. The files instead documented a Russian influence campaign intended to defeat Joe Biden: allegations related to the Ukrainian gas company Burisma spread through American intermediaries, plans for a corruption scandal and fraud narratives involving mail ballots. Trump omitted the foreign influence that aided him and inflated vulnerabilities into interference that did not occur. Trump gave Bill Pulte – the loyalist installed as acting intelligence chief to investigate supposedly “rigged” elections – broad declassification authority. The conservative media figure John Solomon helped search government files for the speech. Yet after millions of documents were reviewed, a White House official told the Atlantic that no evidence showed a foreign power changed votes; Solomon conceded the same for 2020, 2022 and 2024. The speech named Michigan, but omitted Georgia. In January, FBI agents seized roughly 700 boxes of 2020 election materials from Fulton county, including about 150,000 mail ballots, 116,000 cast for Biden. The bureau redirected 260 analysts nationwide to work on an investigation into that year’s election. One day before Trump’s speech, ProPublica reported that the FBI had explored using artificial intelligence to re-examine ballot-envelope signatures, possibly against only one registration signature. Whoever builds such a system decides how much natural variation counts as suspicion. The predicate was never sound. The allegations behind the seizure had been found false; Georgia’s ballots were counted three times, once by hand. Yet an FBI source told ProPublica the hunt would continue “whether they find anything or not”. Signature-matching errors fall hardest on voters of color and other vulnerable groups. This is what Trump’s own interference means. He cannot alter a completed count. He can use federal power to place voters, workers and institutions under permanent suspicion, weakening the legitimacy of the next count before it begins. Fulton county was no random choice. Georgia is where Black opposition to Trump became governing power. Black voters made up about 29% of the 2020 electorate; nearly nine in 10 supported Biden. Fulton gave Biden an advantage approaching 243,000 votes in a state he won by 11,779. That coalition then elected Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff, transferring the Senate to Democrats. Trump’s falsehoods made targets of Ruby Freeman and Shaye Moss, two Black women who counted ballots; the federal project now extends suspicion to their county. Trump carried Georgia in 2024. That victory did not end his pursuit of Fulton. The racism of this project requires no window into his heart. It is visible in the jurisdiction selected, the method applied and the voters who will bear its errors. The president’s grievance is 2020, but his government is targeting 2026. His justice department has lost its first 15 district-court attempts to obtain states’ unredacted voter rolls, containing driver’s license numbers and partial social security numbers – more sensitive information than Trump showed China possessing. Having failed in court and struggled in Congress, he propagandized on television. His intelligence office identified voting-machine vulnerabilities but found no hacking. The White House shelved its report as the safe installation window closed, then emptied the agency supporting voting-system certification. The day before the speech, House Republicans attached Trump’s Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, or Save America Act, to a state department spending bill and passed it, 217–209. The bill would impose new identification requirements on mail voting, require documentary proof of citizenship to register and compel every state to send its complete federal voter list to the Department of Homeland Security within 30 days. Trump neither declared an emergency nor claimed control over state elections. But he ordered DHS to direct states to remove alleged noncitizens, and by Friday enforcement had arrived. A week earlier, the Department of Justice had warned election officials nationwide of criminal liability for knowingly retaining noncitizens or facilitating their votes. On Friday, the DHS secretary, Markwayne Mullin, claimed that a database known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements had identified more than 250,000 potential noncitizens registered in California, New Jersey, Nevada and Pennsylvania. His department offered no evidence and gave those four states two weeks to confirm cooperation. Mullin separately threatened election officials nationwide with criminal charges if they refused to run their rolls through the database. The database can misidentify naturalized citizens; last month, a federal judge blocked the revamped system from checking voter rolls, finding it less accurate and a threat to privacy and voting rights. The speech failed to prove an emergency. Yet within a day, Trump’s government was acting as though it had. Fulton was the laboratory. The Save Act is the architecture for taking it national. Trump can neither erase his loss nor the Black political power essential to it. So he no longer treats the people who defeated him as voters. He treats them as suspects. To this president, any election he loses is a crime scene. Jamil Smith is a Guardian US columnist

title: Trump’s rebranding of Palm Beach airport hasn’t taken off as he planned
author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
summary: Changes inside the Florida international airport are hardly evident as state and county hold back funds for full remodel
body_text: One of Donald Trump’s most grandiose vanity projects, a multimillion-dollar makeover of Florida’s Palm Beach international airport into a self-aggrandizing, gold-plated transportation hub, is running into turbulence, barely a week after the first plane’s wheels touched the runway. At first glance, the rebranding of the airport less than 5 miles from his opulent Mar-a-Lago resort appears to be complete. Its website bears the name and oversized logo of the President Donald J Trump international airport, and state transportation workers were quick to erect highway signs leaving drivers in no doubt where they were heading. Yet inside the terminals, at the ticket counters and baggage halls, the change is far less noticeable. Digital signage reflects the switch, but many physical signs and infrastructure still refer to its old name of Palm Beach International (PBI). There is no clear timeline of when, or even if, new signs will be installed and PBI fully becomes DJT, the three-letter airport code using the president’s initials that will be its formal aviation industry designation starting on 18 August. The issue is money. A state law signed in March by Ron DeSantis, Florida’s Republican governor and intermittent Trump ally, mandated the name change on a reluctant county commission, which voted 4-3 in May to approve a trademark deal with the Trump Organization as some members feared consequences if they did not. But Florida’s $117.6bn budget signed off by DeSantis last month contained only $2.75m to fund the switch, half of the estimated $5.5m overall cost. And Palm Beach county is refusing to make up the shortfall, with some commissioners insisting taxpayers cannot and should not be left on the hook. “We will be able to make the baseline, necessary changes to signage with the $2,750,000. But for the full extensive signage, we will be needing the other half of those funds from the state,” Joseph Abruzzo, the county administrator, told the Miami Herald. Abruzzo was speaking on 9 July, the official handover day when “Trump Force One” carrying the president’s son Eric landed just after 5am to become the first to do so under the airport’s new name. A statement on the airport’s website, meanwhile, says that, beyond the $2.75m received in state money: “The remaining costs will be funded through the [Palm Beach county] Department of Airports’ operating budget and capital improvement program.” It is an apparent contradiction to Abruzzo’s remarks to the media last week that no county money will be used, and has raised fears among some critics that funds earmarked for safety and other crucial improvements at the department’s four airports, which include Palm Beach international, will be siphoned off to support Trump’s glorification. Joel Flores, one of three county commissioners to vote against the unorthodox trademark and licensing agreement in May that critics say will further enrich the president and his family, said he would attempt to block any such move. “I will not personally be voting to utilize any operational funds towards this rebranding,” he said. “This should be solely on the state to be able to fund this. This is their initiative. This is their imposition, their rule over a local municipality over a local airport, so they should be responsible. “We’ve also heard that, federally, they might be sending some dollars down, but I have not seen any bills or budgets that address that. So until I see the money in the bank, I’m not going to count with it.” Flores said he agreed with Abruzzo’s assessment that the rebranding would move forward in phases, and stall until more funds were found. “That’s the kind of conversation I’ve had with our administrator,” he said. “If we don’t get to rebrand entirely, then that’s on them. I don’t feel that our dollars should be going to a rebrand that this board did not approve.” Rebeca Krogman, the public information officer for the Palm Beach department of airports, said a phased approach “ensures continued progress while aligning each step with available resources”. In a statement, she said: “As with any facility of this size, it would not be practical to list every individual sign or area that has or has not yet been updated. “We have begun updating all digital touchpoints, including the airport’s website, social media platforms, and digital signage within the terminal. Temporary signage is also being deployed across the campus pending installation of permanent signage, including the large welcome sign on Turnage Boulevard.” Krogman did not rule out drawing on the airports’ operating budget, but said it was not the department’s preference. “It is our intent to continue these improvements through the airport’s normal budgeting process, primarily utilizing available external funding sources, such as the recent state allocation for signage upgrades, while actively pursuing additional opportunities, including legislative appropriations and grant funding,” she said. The Florida department of transportation did not return a request for comment. Two lawsuits have also been filed to try to prevent the rebranding from advancing. One is by George Poncy, a retired pilot who said that changing the airport’s identifier from PBI, which has been embedded in air traffic control and aviation navigation and management software for decades, will cause confusion that could create a safety hazard. The other, by the trademark attorney Victoria Doyle, argues the state had no authority to impose the name change on a county-owned and -operated airport. Doyle, who is running for the Democratic nomination for a Palm Beach congressional seat in next month’s primary election, said her case has been granted a trial date next year. “Trump’s ego is going to demand upgrades to that airport as fast as possible,” she said. “He’s going to want it to be the best, most beautiful, most gold-laden airport on earth, and we could be on the hook. I am suspicious of all statements about funding and wouldn’t be surprised if the county ends up paying the money. “The airport is an extremely upsetting topic to many people here. We are a majority Democratic county, and we were not asked our opinion of this renaming. It was shoved down our throats from the state on high, and the money is a big part of why they’re so upset. Not only did we not want this rename, now we’re going to have to pay for it? It’s highly offensive to people who live here.”

title: When Maga’s power fades, we cannot abandon those ICE killed
author: Moira Donegan
summary: When this is all over, people will tell us to move on. But those who perpetrated this reign of terror must be held accountable
body_text: One day, when Maga is out of power and the conditions of political possibility have changed, there are going to be people who tell you that the best thing for the country is to move on. There are going to be people who tell you that attempts to hold the purveyors of Trumpism accountable are petty, vindictive, engaging in a kind of petulant recrimination and score-settling. There are going to be people who tell you that there must not be investigations, that it would be a waste of time to have trials. There are going to be people who tell you that it is not wise to change the law to allow for prosecutions and lawsuits; that too great an emphasis on the past will only divide the country, and keep us from looking toward the future. This argument was made after Watergate; it was made after the civil war. It was wrong back then, and it will be wrong again when it is delivered, with piety and smugness, after Trump. When Maga leaves power, all of the officers, bureaucrats and leaders of ICE – from the uniformed thugs in masks on the streets, to the contractors guarding concentration camps, to the suited vultures directing the operation in Washington and drafting legal memos to justify it – all of them must be held accountable. Their immunity from criminal prosecution and civil suits must be eradicated, and their liability must be made retroactive. They must be investigated, tried, fined, punished and ostracized. Needless to say, ICE must be abolished – attempts to merely reform it must be resisted as betrayals of democratic values. But it is not enough to abolish ICE. Those who are responsible for ICE must be driven from public life. This much is clear from a slew of recent deaths. Last Tuesday, a business owner and father of three named Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was shot dead in his car by an ICE agent in Houston while he was on his way to work. At 52, he had made an honorable and prosperous life for himself in Texas after immigrating from Mexico 35 years ago, at age 17. His three co-workers who were in the car – he had picked them up to give them a ride to work – survived the shooting, and were disappeared into ICE custody. Later, it turned out that the ICE agents had been looking for somebody else. Before Salgado’s body was even cold, ICE killed again. Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was a 25-year-old resident of Biddeford, Maine, who had been born in Colombia. According to his father, he had a work permit, a condition typical of asylum claimants. He worked two jobs – one as a food delivery driver, and another as a custodian at a veterinary office – to support his wife and three-year-old daughter. According to witnesses, his little girl witnessed the ICE agents ram into her father’s car, approach his driver’s side window and then shoot her father dead. The incident occurred at about 7am; the little girl was still in her Bluey pajamas. Angus King, a senator from Maine, was told by the DHS secretary, Markwayne Mullen, that ICE was looking for somebody else when they killed Durán, too. After the agents killed him, ICE proclaimed that Salgado had been trying to run them down with his car, a statement that witnesses have contested. It’s also exactly what ICE said about Renee Good, the mother of three they killed in Minneapolis early this year. Video quickly disproved ICE’s account of the Good killing; there is no reason to think that their account of Salgado’s death is true, either. What seems more likely: ICE, a group of reckless, trigger-happy bigots tasked with carrying out the president’s mass deportation and ethnic cleansing regime, is terrorizing communities, stalking disfavored populations, targeting innocent, hardworking people on the basis of their race, and often escalating their interactions to deadly violence. We have been here before. The needless, cold-blooded shootings of Salgado and Durán come months after ICE killed two US citizens in Minneapolis, first Good and then the Veterans Affairs hospital nurse Alex Pretti. Their deaths galvanized an already robust civilian anti-ICE resistance in Minneapolis, and sparked protests across the country against ICE’s kidnapping and ethnic cleansing operations. The bad PR clearly got to the president; Greg Bovino, the high-profile border patrol commander who became famous for his Nazi-like attire, lost his job, apparently as a concession to the unpopularity of the raids; Kristi Noem, the Homeland Security secretary who ran the department at the time, didn’t last long, either. But after a brief de-escalation, ICE has now resumed its raids with their former ostentatious cruelty, needless violence and terrorizing gore. “ICE hunts us like animals,” Maria Cervantes, a Mexican immigrant who lives in the Houston neighborhood where ICE killed Salgado, told the Guardian. “I can’t help but think, who’s next? Am I going to get a bullet to the head for being brown?” If we are to rebuild America as a new kind of country – if we are to make it fulfill its promise to be a free and pluralistic democracy of equals – then we have an obligation to make sure that no one ever has to ask that question again, and that those who do receive justice for the suffering, violence and indignity that this regime has inflicted on them. When this is all over, people will tell you to move on. What they will not tell you is that moving on requires forgetting about Salgado, and Durán, and about Good and Pretti, and about everyone else that ICE has killed and will kill. It will require you to leave the insult and injustice of their deaths unanswered. We must refuse to. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

title: ‘He’s a war criminal’: Mamdani exploring whether he can arrest Netanyahu if he visits New York
author: Lucy Campbell
summary: NYC mayor says in Times interview that’s he’s in ‘active conversation’ with city’s law department about the matter
body_text: New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, has said he is reviewing whether his administration could arrest Benjamin Netanyahu if as expected the Israeli prime minister visits the city for the UN general assembly in September. Mamdani’s comments on Saturday’s episode of the New York Times’s the Interview podcast echoed ones he had made to the publication as he successfully ran for mayor last fall. “I believe that prime minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague,” Mamdani said, referring to the Dutch city that is home to the international criminal court, which issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in November 2024 over alleged war crimes in Gaza. “He’s a war criminal who has been charged by the international criminal court, and what you will find is that is an opinion that is held by many, purely because of what his actions have wrought over these past many years.” Mamdani said it was unclear to him whether he has the legal authority to order the New York police department (NYPD), which he oversees, to detain a foreign leader like Netanyahu. But he said he was in “an active conversation” with the city’s law department about the matter. “Whatever the law allows me to do in New York City, that’s what we will do,” Mamdani added. “But we won’t be writing our own laws to that end.” The warrant which the ICC issued for the arrest of Netanyahu and other Israeli leaders accused them of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, including “starvation as a method of warfare, and … murder, persecution, and other inhumane acts”. During his mayoral campaign, Mamdani characterized Israel’s military actions in Gaza as a genocide and Netanyahu as a war criminal, telling the New York Times in September that he would order NYPD to arrest Netanyahu in the event he ever set foot there. He also condemned the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel as a “horrific war crime”. The Times report back then cited legal experts who judged that having Netanyahu arrested “would be a practical impossibility” for Mamdani – and could bring him into direct conflict with the US’s federal government. The US is not a party to the ICC and does not recognize its authority. And in February 2025, early in his presidency, Donald Trump ordered economic sanctions against the court, maintaining that it lacked jurisdiction over the US or Israel. Trumps’s US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, recently vowed to “dismantle” the court, accusing it of “waging a war against our country, not with bullets or missiles” but with “the force of so-called international law”. Netanyahu, who faces a tough re-election campaign in October, brushed off Mamdani’s arrest threats in a recent radio appearance, saying he was not concerned. Though Mamdani denies the accusation, Netanyahu also alleged Mamdani supports Hamas. “He’s with the terror actors,” Netanyahu told New York’s WABC. “And I think the problem is that he doesn’t recognize and he doesn’t care that those who hate the Jews and Israel ultimately hate America.” Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, accused Mamdani – New York’s first Muslim mayor – of failing to confront rising antisemitism in his city. Mamdani has countered such accusations by noting that he has increased funding for an office to combat hate crimes. “Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu will come to New York, address the United Nations General Assembly with pride, and stand before the world to state Israel’s truth and its unwavering right to defend its citizens,” Danon said. Trump’s ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, also dismissed Mamdani’s threat as “pure political theater”, saying the US was not a member of the ICC. World leaders from United Nations member-states are expected to travel to New York in September for the body’s annual session. Netanyahu has often participated in this event in previous years. “We’re not talking about a personal assessment of Benjamin Netanyahu,” Mamdani told the Times’ podcast. “We’re talking about the international criminal court and the fact that they have a warrant out for this prime minister’s arrest, and I think it’s important to talk about the weight that that has as a charge and that also, as the mayor of New York City, I’ll be following the laws of New York City.” Mamdani’s comments on Saturday came as his stance on Israel is becoming less fringe within the Democratic party. Close to half of US House Democrats on Wednesday voted to strip $3.3bn in military aid to Israel. It was not enough to pass the measure. But it signified a buckling of unconditional support for Israel, a shift that is also reflected in public opinion polling. Asked by the Times about the political weight he places on Israel and support for it by the US, Mamdani said ongoing war in Gaza was motivating voters throughout the country, including when his endorsed candidates swept House races in New York in June. “It is hard to find a more bankrupt policy approach than what our country has done to Gaza and to Palestine,” he said.

title: The Guardian view on perceptions of superpowers: the world isn’t Chinamaxxing, it’s America-avoidant
author: Editorial
summary: Editorial: Startling new research shows that in many countries – including old US allies – the public prefers Beijing to Washington
body_text: Earlier this year, a spate of western TikTok and Instagram creators announced that they were at “a very Chinese time in my life” – drinking hot water and wearing slippers around their homes. The Chinamaxxing phenomenon primarily reflected the constant need of influencers for novel content. But social media trends also reflect a growing fascination with China, as the economic historian Adam Tooze has noted. While it broods over China’s economic, military and technical advance, the Trump administration is accelerating Beijing’s diplomatic progress, as striking new polling by the Pew Research Center shows. For the first time, China and Xi Jinping are seen more favourably than the US and its president in most of the 36 major countries surveyed – including Canada, Mexico and Australia. Only in six countries did people rate the US more highly. While Beijing has seen significant improvements in some places, the slump in Washington’s standing is more dramatic. Across 20 countries, the median percentage with a favourable view of China rose from 32% to 46% between 2023 and this year; for the US, it fell from 58% to 36%. Views of China were much more positive in Latin America, Africa and parts of south and south-east Asia than in wealthier European and east Asian countries. On Thursday, Mr Trump accused China of interfering with the 2020 election – casting doubt on polls ahead of midterms that are forecast to hit Republicans hard. Never mind the lack of evidence; he offered Argentinians a $20bn economic incentive to vote in line with his preference last October. In nearly every country surveyed, more people thought the US interfered in other countries than thought China did so. Mr Trump’s demands to take over Greenland, the abduction of Venezuela’s then leader Nicolás Maduro and the illegal war on Iran have all left their mark. Even the World Cup, which should have been an easy US soft power win, has been tarred by his exclusion and bullying. Grave concerns about Beijing remain. Though it has dialled back displays of aggressive “wolf-warrior” diplomacy, it is forceful in its dealings. But it may benefit from lower expectations, and it looks predictable beside Trump-created turmoil. Famously, Beijing has just one ally: North Korea. Washington has more than 50 – but seems to accord them less respect than adversaries. Beijing detained two Canadian citizens for more than 1,000 days in retaliation for Ottawa’s arrest of the Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou due to a US warrant. But Mr Trump announced that Canada will be the 51st state. China is increasingly investing in overseas influence operations, including working with or amplifying local social media content creators. Content may range from paid-for Xinjiang travelogues intended to erase concerns about the persecution of Uyghurs, to softer material about food or technology. The Pew findings may further convince it of Washington’s hegemonic decline. China is keen to encourage the belief that it is leaping into a shiny new future of cyberpunk cities, while the west struggles with a declining standard of living – not least because it is useful in the face of domestic disillusionment. But public perceptions of other countries are often complex and volatile. US standing rebounded after dropping sharply over the Iraq war; China’s favourability ratings fell during the pandemic, reflecting its handling of the outbreak. The lasting lesson for both superpowers should surely be that presentation shapes opinion, but others will judge them on their actions – and respond accordingly.

title: Israel threatens ‘full force’ response if Iran fires missiles towards it
author: Andrew Roth in Jerusalem
summary: Return to all-out regional war grows increasingly likely as US and Iran trade strikes and Trump warns of escalation
body_text: Israel has warned it could retaliate against Iran with “full force” if Tehran’s missiles strike within its borders, threatening a return to an all-out regional war as the ceasefire brokered by Donald Trump collapses with a new round of missile strikes across the Middle East. On Sunday, Iran launched salvoes of ballistic missiles at US-allied Arab states, targeting a power and water desalination plant for the second time in two days in Kuwait, as well as sites in Jordan and Bahrain. Air-raid sirens sounded in Amman as Jordan said it shot down three Iranian missiles targeting the country. Israel said the strikes could spill across its borders, reigniting a direct regional conflict that had been restrained even as tensions between the Trump administration and Iran soared again in recent weeks. “If Iran fires missiles at Israel, we will attack them with full force,” said the Israeli defence minister, Israel Katz, on Sunday. The country was prepared for “both defensive and offensive” action, he added. The US is expected to send dozens of additional refuelling planes to Israel as part of a reinforcement of its force posture in the region, a US official told Reuters. The US and Iran expanded their strikes, with civilian infrastructure hit, as Trump told a US media outlet that he “couldn’t care less” about Iran’s repudiation of his ceasefire agreement to end the war and reopen the strait of Hormuz. But since April, direct attacks between Iran and Israel had grown less frequent, in large part because of Trump’s pressure to maintain a ceasefire needed to reopen the strait and resume the flow of oil through the key waterway. Now, however, Trump has moved to apply maximum pressure on Iran. “The gates of HELL have now been UNLEASHED like they never could have imagined or seen before,” the US president said in a social media post on Sunday. The escalation followed the deaths of two US soldiers in Iranian strikes on a Jordanian airbase on Friday that marked one of the deadliest days for US forces since the beginning of the war. US Central Command (Centcom) has said a third soldier is missing after Iran launched drone and missile strikes following days of US strikes on Iran meant to pressure Tehran into capitulating in talks over Iran’s nuclear programme. Trump also urged Republican allies in Congress to expand a sanctions bill targeting Russia to include Iran, saying it is what the late senator Lindsey Graham would have wanted. The bill would punish purchasers of Russian oil with high tariffs, probably targeting big importers such as India. Centcom said the US had concluded an eighth day of strikes on Sunday, targeting Iran’s “military coastal surveillance and air defence facilities, maritime capabilities, and missile and drone storage sites to continue degrading Iranian military capabilities”. It also sought to “swiftly punish” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for the deaths of the US military personnel. Since early in the war, Trump has threatened to target Iranian civilian infrastructure, including power plants and bridges, in what many observers have said would constitute a war crime. The US has denied targeting civilian infrastructure, but photos and videos have shown considerable destruction at civilian sites in the last few days. Tehran on Sunday said more than 40 people had died in attacks this month. Iran also accused the US of striking a nuclear power plant under construction in the south-western city of Darkhovin. The International Atomic Energy Agency said the site did not house any nuclear material but its director general, Rafael Grossi, urged “military restraint in the vicinity of all nuclear-related sites”. Iran has begun targeting crucial desalination plants in countries such as Kuwait, which are extremely arid and rely on the plants to produce potable water for the population. Kuwait said the Iranian strike had sparked a fire and damaged electricity generators at the plant, potentially disrupting power supplies. The Kuwaiti ⁠foreign ministry said the repeated targeting of civilian facilities amounted to a dangerous escalation and violated ‌international law, the UN charter and UN security council resolution 2817. It said Iran bore full legal and moral responsibility ‌for the attack on the plant and its consequences. Jordan summoned ⁠Iran’s ⁠chargé d’affaires in Amman ⁠over what ⁠it called “unjustified ‌and ‌blatant Iranian attacks” ‌and “provocative and inflammatory statements targeting the ‌kingdom’s territory”. Tehran has also increased pressure in the strait of Hormuz. Iran’s government-aligned Tasnim news agency said on Sunday that two ships had had an “accident” after attempting to traverse the waterway via an “unsafe route” not officially sanctioned by Tehran. “Vessels that are influenced by the words of the Americans and enter unsafe routes will certainly face accidents,” the IRGC said, adding that two other ships had turned back after the incident. In a statement on Saturday, Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, warned that the US would face “unforgettable lessons” if it continued its attacks.

title: Mission in Iran war has pivoted toward ensuring oil flow, Trump official says
author: Marina Dunbar
summary: Energy secretary grapples with mounting criticism over length of US war as Democrat calls conflict ‘war of choice’
body_text: A Trump administration official on Sunday grappled with mounting criticism over the length of the US war with Iran after months of promised diplomatic breakthroughs, short-lived ceasefires, and the deaths of three more American troops bringing the total number of American military members killed in the conflict to 17. Appearing on ABC’s This Week, the US energy secretary, Chris Wright, defended the Trump administration’s strategy after being confronted with his earlier claims that the war which began in February would have ended by now. Wright argued that the mission had since shifted toward ensuring oil shipments can move through the strait of Hormuz. “We did a pause to try to get an agreement with the Iranian people to allow oil to flow without them attacking it,” Wright said. “They’ve proven unwilling to do that, and we’ve pivoted. Now, what we’re doing is assuring that that oil and gas and other products can flow through the strait of Hormuz with or without Iranian cooperation, and we’ve continued to degrade their offensive military capabilities.” On the same program, a prominent Democrat continued his party’s sharp criticism of the Trump administration’s handling of the nearly five-month conflict. Senator Mark Warner of Virginia described the conflict as a “war of choice” that was launched without an imminent threat and argued the administration had failed to accomplish its previously stated objectives. “Regime change, how are we doing there? We got a worse crowd than before,” Warner said of Iran. He said the enriched uranium that the US wanted to get from Iran to prevent it from building a nuclear weapon was “still there”, adding: “Matter of fact, it would take a minimum of 15,000 troops on the ground for a week to try to take these canisters, which are quite volatile, out of their bunker.” Warner also remarked, “Getting rid of Iran’s missile and drone capability – obviously, we’ve not been successful there” because the conflict continued on Sunday. He said: “The continuation of this war, at this pace, will be a continuing disaster.” In addition to two deaths in Jordan on Friday, the US Central Command announced that another service member ‌was killed on Saturday “during a controlled detonation of ⁠unexploded ordnance” in northern Iraq. The unexploded ordnance ‌was ⁠from a “downed Iranian one-way attack drone”, Centcom said in a ⁠statement on social media on Sunday. The latest casualties in Iran for the US military came as a renewal of the campaign against Iran entered its second week, leading to intensified fighting around the strait of Hormuz. The US launched retaliatory strikes on Sunday against Iran’s Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) after the killings. After the deaths of the two US troops on Friday, Trump’s defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, vowed the military campaign in Iran would continue, writing on social media that the service members’ “sacrifice only stiffens our resolve”. Donald Trump himself also escalated pressure on Iran on Sunday, with the president urging Congress to include Iran in pending Russia sanctions legislation. The move would further weaken the memorandum of understanding between the two countries in June aimed at resolving the Iranian conflict that included an agreement to end sanctions for Iran. Alluding to the unexpected death on 11 July of the US senator Lindsey Graham, his ally, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, “Republicans should add Iran to the Russian Sanctions Bill. That’s what Lindsey wanted to do, and it was going to happen. IMPORTANT!!!”

title: Trump could ‘do something positive’ rather than fixate on 2020 loss, Fetterman says
author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
summary: Senator says Trump revisiting failed run against Biden ‘distracts from important things’ such as Iran war
body_text: Rather than continue fixating on the 2020 election defeat that ended his first presidency, Donald Trump could instead “do something positive”, including resolving the US war in Iran, the Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman said in an interview on Sunday. “I don’t know why the president is dragging up all this stuff,” Fetterman remarked on CNN’s State of the Union, three days after Trump dedicated a televised, primetime address to claims about Chinese meddling in the 2020 White House race that he lost to Joe Biden. “You’re the president. Do something positive – and you are talking about 2020; that’s been settled over six years ago. “It’s deeply unhelpful and that distracts [from] important things, especially like the Iranian war right now.” His comments to CNN came amid a stretch that could prove to be an inflection point in his political career. On Wednesday, he said he would consider leaving the Democratic party if ever it became “the anti-Israel party”, a comment that he delivered after more than 100 US House lawmakers voted in favor of halting Israeli military aid over incursions into Gaza and Lebanon. Fetterman has emerged as a prominent advocate of Israel among Democrats since he joined the Senate in 2023. He acknowledged some attempts by Republicans to convince him to defect to their party as some of his Democratic colleagues have backed away from their traditional support for Israel amid accusations that the government of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, committed genocide in Gaza. But he said he has no interest in such a switch because he disagrees with most policies favored by Republicans, who have been led by Trump across two Oval Office terms interrupted by Biden’s presidency. Trump for years has lied about his loss to Biden at the polls in 2020 by saying electoral fraudsters rigged the contest against him. Non-partisan voting experts have determined the election was secure. And as he successfully ran for a second presidency in 2024, Trump conceded on a podcast that he lost to Biden, arguing it was “by a whisker”. Yet Trump later asserted that statement was sarcastic. And on Thursday, Trump revisited his failed run against Biden by claiming China interfered in the race, prompting warnings from opponents that the president – who has grappled with low approval ratings – was poised to meddle in the forthcoming midterm elections. A 2021 US intelligence community assessment concluded that no foreign actor, including China, attempted to alter any technical aspect of the 2020 voting process. The assessment found that while Russia had conducted influence operations aimed at denigrating Biden’s campaign, China did not deploy any interference efforts intended to change the outcome of the election. American intelligence assessed that China did not see either Trump or Biden as advantageous to its ambitions – and it was therefore not worth the risk of damaging the US-Chinese relationship by interfering. Speaking to CNN host Jake Tapper on Sunday about Trump and the 2020 election, Fetterman said the results of that race – which saw Biden earn Pennsylvania’s electoral college votes – were “absolutely secure, fair and accurate”. “Pennsylvania … picked Joe Biden in 2020,” Fetterman, who was the state’s lieutenant governor at the time, added. “That’s a fact.”

title: House Democrats are finally shifting on Israel. Party leaders must listen
author: Norman Solomon
summary: More than 100 Democratic lawmakers voted against arms for Israel. They’re listening to the people – their bosses are behind
body_text: The Democratic party is in dire need of a mutiny. Top leaders at the party’s helm are unprepared to navigate the political sea change about Israel. Last week, nearly half of House Democrats voted to block $3.3bn in weaponry and other aid to that country. A recent New York Times poll found that 74% of Democratic voters “opposed providing additional economic and military support to Israel, including large majorities in all age groups”. Such polling numbers are not new. But the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, and his Senate counterpart, Chuck Schumer, still follow an old playbook of unwavering service to Israel. The moral bankruptcy amounts to political malpractice, as voters tend to bypass a party with leadership they see as lacking a moral compass. The day before 103 House Democrats ignored his guidance, Jeffries sent out a “dear colleague” letter filled with the kind of pro-Israel rhetoric that has worn transparently thin. The amendment to cut off aid, he claimed, “would restrict our country’s ability to confront Hamas, Hezbollah and other terrorist organizations in the region who are sworn enemies of both the United States and Israel”. But Nancy Pelosi’s vote for the weapons cutoff was a weathervane for how drastically the Democratic winds have swung away from Israel. Consider the former speaker’s remarkable words at an Israeli-American Council conference in 2018: “I have said to people when they ask me: if this Capitol crumbled to the ground, the one thing that would remain is our commitment to our aid, I don’t even call it aid – our cooperation – with Israel. That’s fundamental to who we are.” Fears of being slandered as antisemitic have routinely made automatic support for Israel seem safest. Now, while Aipac and other Israel-backing operations with deep pockets remain menacing, the dramatic shift in public attitudes toward Israel has notably reduced their intimidating power. Worries about alienating big donors have been palpable at the Democratic National Committee (DNC), where financial woes are a huge concern. The business model of courting megadonors has a grim logic when the party leadership is so uninspiring to grassroots Democrats. No one can make a credible case that Jeffries and Schumer, or the DNC chair, Ken Martin, for that matter, have been inspirational. A major factor in their inability to inspire has been failure to engage with the genuine moral anguish felt by so many Americans about their country’s complicity in genocide. Last month, a UN commission concluded that genocide is continuing, with Israeli forces intentionally targeting children in Gaza. “A significant body of research by legal and rights experts has concluded that Israel is intent on destroying Palestinians, including analyses by UN investigators, rights bodies such as Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, and genocide scholars worldwide,” the Guardian reported as this summer began. The incapacity of Jeffries, Schumer and Martin to meaningfully address such realities has mired the party deeper in its leadership crisis. That crisis could hamper turnout needed to win the midterm elections this fall, and very likely will come into full view by the time the presidential primary campaign begins in earnest early next year. In the near term, when the DNC convenes in mid-August for its last meeting before the midterms, the gathering is apt to be a scene of subdued discord about the party’s out-of-step leadership and Martin’s continual deep-sixing of the Israel issue within the committee. Its 450 members have maintained a long tradition of complying with the chair’s wishes. That the DNC’s culture is akin to the atmosphere of a corporation was just underscored by the news that DNC officials are being asked to sign nondisclosure agreements. A co-chair of the DNC’s national finance team described the move as “consistent with standard practice in the corporate world”. Defenders of the party leadership’s pro-Israel stance do not acknowledge the moral imperative of ending US support for what can fairly be called a genocidal state. But polling is clear that such denial won’t fly with the Democratic base. The timeworn verbiage being deployed by the party’s House and Senate leaders is functioning within a self-referential closed loop that has lost credibility with voters. Revulsion at Donald Trump might bring Democrats appreciable success in the midterm elections. But Israel apologism, continuing to stream out of the offices of the House and Senate minority leaders, is a wet blanket on a party that should be vibrant. Looking ahead at the field of likely contenders for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, all but a few have merely updated the standard political double-talk about Israel. The lane is now clearer than ever for a candidate to run with a full-throated anti-establishment campaign, dispensing with equivocation and mobilizing the progressive grassroots with positions that include an end to US support for genocide. Norman Solomon is the director of RootsAction and executive director of the Institute for Public Accuracy. His latest book is The Blue Road to Trump Hell: How Corporate Democrats Paved the Way for Autocracy

title: High school math teacher seeks to win US House seat in Minnesota by emphasizing affordability
author: Michael Sainato
summary: Democrat Jake Johnson is running against Brad Finstad, who has held his seat in Minnesota’s first district since 2022
body_text: High school math teacher Jake Johnson easily recalls the role government assistance played for his family in Stewartville, Minnesota, when he was growing up. His father was a garbage collector and his mother read meters for the local gas company. They relied on food stamps for groceries and Medicaid for healthcare. When it was time for Johnson to go to college, Pell grants and Stafford loans helped him pay the bill. “We were broke,” Johnson said. “I got to grow up living what I thought was an American dream, where you work hard and a lot of people invest in you.” It’s this upbringing that pushed Johnson to run for Congress, trying to take back a US House seat that hasn’t been held by a Democrat since 2018, when Tim Walz vacated it to run for governor. The congressional district is one of 44 across the country that Democrats say are “in play” in the midterms as the party seeks to gain a majority in Congress. And Johnson is one of a handful of Democratic candidates with a background in the labor movement who are trying to connect with workers frustrated with the economy. A former member of the bargaining team and a government relations coordinator with Education Minnesota, the state’s teacher union, Johnson said he’s advocated for increased benefits for teachers and fought to prevent school closures through his union. “To me, a lot of the great things that happen in public schools happen because of unions. We’re the ones fighting for smaller class sizes. We’re the ones fighting for reasonable wages,” Johnson said. “That’s happening because of teachers’ unions. We’re the ones that are raising the bar as far as teacher quality.” Johnson is running against incumbent Republican Brad Finstad, who has held the seat since 2022, and he is trying to convince voters that Finstad has supported policies that have hurt them. Trump’s tariffs have especially caused a surge in prices, Johnson said, in the predominantly rural district that he says is the ninth most agriculturally productive in the US. “A huge piece of affordability is ending the tariffs and rebuilding our export markets and lowering input costs for our farmers, small businesses and families,” Johnson said, adding that the Iran war has also increased fertilizer costs. “We’ve already got farmers who are planning ahead for the fall going, ‘I don’t know if I’m going to be able to get my fertilizer preordered for next season.’” He also argued healthcare cuts by the Trump administration, from cutting Medicare and Medicaid to slashing research, have greatly affected the district as it is home to the Mayo Clinic medical center. “Healthcare cuts have been particularly pronounced here. We have felt it acutely. We’ve had to close four clinics in our district alone,” he said. Johnson also criticized his Republican opponent for refusing to hold any in-person town halls, opting for virtual town halls. National Republicans have urged against holding in-person town halls amid protests at GOP events. “Finstad seems to have chosen his powerful political backers, his corporate donors over the people of this district,” Johnson said. “We want to make it very clear that that is who Brad works for, and I, who take no corporate Pac money, and am funded by the people of this district, am willing to meet with everyone to hear their concerns.” Finstad’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment. A February 2026 poll conducted by a Democratic polling firm found Finstad had a 35% approval rating in the district, with 38% disapproving. In a survey on the midterm election, Finstad led Johnson 44% to 41%, with 15% of voters undecided. According to the Cook Partisan Index, the district is a +6 in favor of Republicans. But Johnson argued that many of Trump’s policies have been deeply unpopular and provides an opening for Democrats in the district. “Finstad continues to hitch his wagon to policies that are very, very unpopular in this district, I think gives us an opening, gives us an opportunity to speak exactly to where folks are at,” Johnson said. “They want the war to end, they want the tariffs to end, they want their schools fully funded, they want opportunity again so that they can live their American dream.” • The subheading of this article was amended on 21 July 2026 to correct a misspelling of the surname of Tim Walz.

title: ‘Complete shock and dismay’: scientists unite against Trump’s $1tn grant attack
author: Jessica Glenza
summary: OMB proposal would upend entire grant-making system – and put vast sums into hands of political appointees
body_text: It was a late Friday afternoon in Boston when Harvard School of Public Health professor Nancy Krieger, a social epidemiologist, received an email that would reshape the next year of her life. It was from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) – her nearly $1m grant to study how discrimination affects population health was canceled. “I’m like, what? What does this mean? I don’t understand? My grant has another year in it. I immediately reached out to the office that helps with grants to find out what was going on, and it led to a flurry of emails over the weekend – just trying to even find out what was happening. “It was complete shock and dismay.” From that moment, she had three jobs. First, to continue her work as a professor. Second, to deal with the litigation that suddenly engulfed her work. Third, to patch up the tumult, crushed morale and chaos that weighed on the people whose careers depended on this funding. Krieger’s was one of the first R-01 grant cancellations in the country – one example of the chaos sown by the billionaire Elon Musk’s “department of government efficiency” as the group ripped apart federal grant-making infrastructure under the banner of ending “woke” research on gender, race, equity and a slate of other keywords the administration found objectionable. It would not be the last – and the list of delayed and canceled grants could, and probably will, fill books. Now Krieger is at the vanguard of scientists speaking out about a new proposal from the office of management and budget (OMB) that attempts to ensnare nearly the entire federal grant-making apparatus in this same tumult. This May, Trump’s OMB quietly proposed a more than 400-page overhaul of the federal grant-making process which would, if formalized, institutionalize much of the upheaval seen in federal funding scientists have experienced over the past nearly two years. The proposal would put nearly $1tn in grant-making into the hands of political appointees by October. “It’s the entirety of the federal grant-making process,” said Sara Rosenbaum, professor emerita of health law and policy at the Milken Institute School of Public Health at George Washington University. “Healthcare, education, social services, environmental protections – it’s way, way beyond just research.” The proposal has sparked outrage and consternation among a wide array of organizations, with a dramatic increase in support from individual scientists and scientific organizations, who have come together to oppose a rule that could affect an almost unimaginably vast swath of federal funding. Groups studying “the farthest reaches of the galaxy to the deepest depths of the sea to everything in between, including those of us who wander around predominantly on plants”, have come together, Krieger said. “That’s because, yes, we have experienced censorship. We have experience with blunt use of power to put forward the ideological agenda.” The proposal, now informally referred to as “the OMB rule”, has attracted almost half a million public comments – analyses show as much as 95% in opposition – and bipartisan criticism. “President Trump and [OMB director] Russell Vought are not only breaking the law, but they are also once again endangering the health and safety of Americans,” Tammy Baldwin, a Democratic senator of Wisconsin, said in a statement to the Guardian. “Americans expect their taxpayer dollars to be put to research that has the best chance at delivering a breakthrough or cure for a disease, not wielded like a cudgel to punish the president’s perceived enemies and score political points.” Of the potential $1tn affected, $150bn is typically invested in science and technology. To conceptualize the scope, consider the budget of the National Institutes of Health (NIH): at $47bn, the NIH is the world’s largest public funder of biomedical and behavioral research. “In the normal course of events, an administration faced with 500,000 comments – virtually all of which will be in opposition to the rule … would withdraw the rule,” said Rosenbaum. “I would say there’s a relatively low level of expectation that the administration will do the reasonable thing.” The proposal criticizes “woke” policies, would ban “DEI” (diversity, equity and inclusion programs), and prohibit undefined “anti-American values”. It would also discourage international collaboration between scientists, require demonstration of presidential “priorities”, and allow the government to consider, “an applicant’s affiliations with organizations engaged in activities that violate federal law, undermine public safety or national security, or advocate for the overthrow of the United States government”. It would also allow the federal government to cancel awards that are no longer in the federal government’s “interest”, a consideration that many researchers experienced first-hand in spring 2025, when federal research grants on disparate impacts and gender were summarily canceled. Already, 22 state attorneys general have come together to oppose the rule, and almost certainly are expecting to bring a suit. “The Trump administration is once again attempting to weaponize essential federal funding to advance its policy priorities. Except this time, it’s not just one agency, it’s almost all of them,” said California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, in a statement this week urging the OMB to withdraw the proposal. “This proposal aims to undermine practically every industry and public service supported by federal funding.” On social media, Vought, the OMB director, specifically targeted criticism of the rule from non-profits as a “freakout by those on the left”. The White House “fraud taskforce”, meanwhile, said the rule would ensure “American taxpayers will no longer be forced to fund woke NGOs with partisan agendas”. The rule is supported by the Heritage Foundation, the Washington DC thinktank that authored Project 2025. The administration allowed only 45 days for public comments, relatively brief in the scope of federal rule-making – which is typically 60 to 90 days. The public comment period closed this week. “Basically, in my mind, the notice and comment is just a subterfuge for moving ahead when they’re really not interested in what the comments say,” said Lawrence Gostin, a professor of global public health at Georgetown Law. Since the beginning of the second Trump term, funding fights have played out across the sciences – disrupting clinical trials, long-term research, laboratories and cutting short the careers of young scientists. If the proposal is enacted, as expected, how quickly the fight would move to the courts is an open question. Gostin argued that a grant may need to be denied before a plaintiff could find standing. Once that happens, he expects state attorneys general, institutions and perhaps even individual plaintiffs to initiate suits. “[It] seems to me one of the big questions is: would a lawsuit actually succeed?” said Gostin. “It’s not a 100% slam-dunk, although I do think there will be some trial judges, district court judges who will enjoin it.” Gostin said: “But as it goes though highly conservative courts of appeal and the conservative supreme court, the outcome is less certain. Whether the government attempts to mount an emergency appeal and get, ultimately, the supreme court moving forward is anybody’s guess.”

title: The trouble with Trump’s latest nominees lies in one word: integrity
author: Robert Reich
summary: As Todd Blanche, Erica Schwartz and Jay Clayton face the Senate, a fundamental disconnect becomes clear
body_text: There’s been a lot of discussion in America this week about the meaning of integrity. You didn’t hear the word used directly; it was alluded to indirectly – in wondering whether Lindsey Graham was an immoral opportunist or clever pragmatist; in suspecting Todd Blanche of being more loyal to Trump than to the nation; in distrusting Erica Schwartz, Trump’s latest pick to lead the CDC, when she said she would never compromise on the science; in doubting Jay Clayton, his pick for director of national intelligence, will tell Trump anything he doesn’t want to hear. The word integrity is rooted in the Latin word integer, meaning “whole” or “complete” – living by your principles, choosing honesty over opportunism, making ethical choices that may be inconvenient or unpopular, maintaining your moral compass. Graham’s public record of denouncing Trump on the Senate floor after 6 January 2021, and then becoming Trump’s most loyal Senate apologist revealed someone who traded honesty for influence – a person with little or no integrity. Blanche, in his hearing to be attorney general, said he wanted to bring trust back to the justice department but then accidentally referred to himself as Trump’s lawyer – before clarifying that he “was” – had been – Trump’s lawyer. Blanche’s momentary lapse revealed a deeper conflict, as evidenced by his unswerving loyalty to Trump. He lacks integrity. Schwartz, in her confirmation hearing, undercut her pledge to be guided by science in saying she believed Trump and the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, would not implement policies that hurt public health. That’s enough to cast doubt on her integrity. Clayton, in his confirmation hearing, repeatedly refused to say Biden won the 2020 election, causing Senator Jon Ossoff to ask: “You refuse to answer a basic question about who won a presidential election? But you ask to lead America’s intelligence community? Isn’t it humiliating to be unable to answer this question? To have to indulge the president’s delusions? We know, you know, everybody in this room knows the truthful answer to that question. Why can you not give it?” It is not possible to have integrity and be loyal to Trump. The two are in direct conflict. No one can be honest in a regime based on big lies. As the poet, philosopher and statesman Václav Havel put it: “If the main pillar of the system is living a lie, then it is not surprising that the fundamental threat to it is living in truth.” So a choice must be made – personal integrity or loyalty to Trump. In his book The Art of the Deal, Trump suggested he preferred loyalty to integrity – as epitomized by his mentor, Roy Cohn. History remembers Cohn for his ruthless bullying, profane braggadocio, opportunistic bigotry, lying and more lying. Like Trump, Cohn was utterly without principle and prioritized personal power that could be leveraged for wealth, influence and celebrity. In 1986, Cohn was disbarred in New York for unethical conduct after attempting to defraud a dying client by forcing him to sign a will amendment leaving Cohn his fortune. (Cohn died five weeks later.) Yet in his book Trump praised Cohn for his loyalty, contrasting him with “all the hundreds of ‘respectable’ guys who make careers out of boasting about their uncompromising integrity but have absolutely no loyalty … What I liked most about Roy Cohn was that he would do just the opposite.” It is not possible for Blanche or Schwartz or Clayton or anyone else in Trump’s orbit – nor was it possible for Graham – to be loyal to Trump and simultaneously maintain their own integrity. It must be one or the other. Yet integrity is more important than loyalty. As Trump demonstrates time and again, someone lacking integrity is inherently untrustworthy. Such a person cannot serve the people of the United States. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

title: Trump acknowledges that jet from Qatar lacks defensive systems of Air Force One
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: US president says $400m plane will be ‘maxed out’ with appropriate protections but doesn’t give further details
body_text: Donald Trump acknowledged on Sunday that the Boeing jet given to him by Qatar cannot match the defensive armor of a true presidential aircraft, telling reporters it will soon be grounded and “maxed out” with the protections it was never built with. The admission came as Trump touched down in Washington on the jet, fresh off a trip to MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where he handed the World Cup trophy to Spain alongside Gianni Infantino, the Fifa president, after the tournament’s climactic final. Asked by the reporter pool travelling with the president why he continues to fly on an aircraft that lacks anti-missile defenses, Trump explained that upgrades were coming soon. “Well, it has – it has a lot, and you know it has a lot of capability, but as I understand it, in about a month or so, they’re going to send it to have it be maxed out,” Trump said. “So they’re going to be sending it, and they’ll have it be maxed out. It’ll take about a month.” There was no clarification or further detail on the scope of the planned work. The comments follow reporting by the New York Times this month that found the roughly 14-year-old Boeing 747-8 – the “palace in the sky” donated by Qatar’s royal family and valued at close to $400m – lacks defensive systems fitted to the purpose-built Air Force One fleet, including infrared countermeasures to divert heat-seeking missiles and sensors to detect incoming launches. Unlike the decades-old VC-25A aircraft that have long served presidents, the Qatari jet was not built from the outset for hardening against electromagnetic pulses or equipped with the secure communications systems needed to run the government during a crisis. Officials have cast it as a stopgap while two newly ordered Boeing jets, delayed by roughly four years, are completed. Trump flew the jet to Turkey for a Nato summit earlier this month but switched to an older, more heavily defended aircraft for the return leg amid rising tensions with Iran, reportedly on the advice of the Secret Service. The disclosure has also inflamed a separate fight over press freedom. Days after the Times story ran, FBI agents showed up at the homes of several of its reporters to hand-deliver grand jury subpoenas, a case that would attempt to reveal the outlet’s sources for the story, though the Times has since moved to have the subpoenas thrown out. The jet’s acceptance has drawn scrutiny from ethics watchdogs and congressional Democrats, who argue that a foreign government’s gift of an aircraft Trump intends to keep for his presidential library after leaving office raises constitutional concerns under the emoluments clause. The justice department under Pam Bondi, the former attorney general, approved the arrangement in 2025. The air force has estimated retrofit costs at under $400m, though it remains unclear whether the further upgrades Trump referenced on Sunday fall within that figure or represent an additional phase of work.

title: Civil rights groups sue Trump administration over childcare funding restrictions
author: Michael Sainato
summary: HHS failed to respond to Foia request following claims of fraud against Somali childcare providers and Democrats
body_text: Civil rights groups have sued the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) after the agency failed to respond to a Freedom of Information Act request regarding the Trump administration’s restrictions on federal childcare and family assistance following claims of fraud against Somali childcare providers and Democratic state officials. The American Civil Liberties Union, the ACLU of Illinois, the ACLU of Colorado, the National Women’s Law Center and the National Center for Law and Economic Justice, are seeking correspondence between federal officials and far right social media influencer Nick Shirley. Shirley’s YouTube video posted in December 2025, where he showed up to 10 childcare centers in Minnesota and demanded proof of enrollment and attempted to enroll a fake child, and then claimed, without providing any evidence, that the centers were fraudulent. It went viral on Elon Musk’s X, as Musk boosted the video. “How do I know that [the allegations are] true?” Shirley responded when asked by CNN reporters following the video. “Well, we showed you guys what was happening, and then you guys can go ahead and make your own analysis.” Local reporters subsequently visited the childcare centers and debunked Shirley’s claims that there were no children at the centers. State investigators visited nine of the 10 centers following the video, as one center had been closed for years, and found normal operations and children at all but one, as it had not yet opened. The video was cited and credited by senior Trump administration officials as the basis for the restrictions and funding freezes. Minnesota Republicans worked with Shirley on the video. In January 2026, the Trump administration froze over $10bn in federal funds for California, Colorado, Illinois, Minnesota and New York. The three programs affected include the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF), the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), and the Social Service Block Grant (SSBG), programs that millions of Americans rely on annually for childcare, food, clothing and other social services. The states sued to block the freeze, and a court order stopping the freeze was granted by a federal judge on 9 January. In July 2026, the Trump administration moved to resolve the lawsuit after the freeze was withdrawn after being ordered by a court to produce unredacted emails from Trump administration officials regarding the freezing of funds for five states. The states added the office of management and budget to their lawsuit over the freeze as discovery showed the agency played an important role in the freeze, according to the lawsuit. In the lawsuit, the civil rights groups are seeking a court order to require the Department of Health and Human Services to promptly process and release all non-exempt records, including communications referencing “fraud” and “Somali” and other records related to statements and actions by Trump and administration officials over proclaimed justifications for the funding restrictions. The lawsuit alleges the funding restrictions and attempted freeze have caused panic and fear among families reliant on the programs, has resulted in delays in childcare funding. It also alleges Trump and Republicans in Congress have continued making unsubstantiated claims of widespread fraud in childcare funding “This lawsuit is really about demanding transparency and accountability from this administration, and really understanding what the true justifications for these attacks,” said Linda Morris, senior staff attorney at the ACLU Women’s Rights Project,. Morris added: “These attacks on childcare programs are fueled by racist rhetoric, including anti-Somali and anti-immigrant bias, and they’re also motivated by the administration’s desire to attack its political opponents.” The White House and Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
