title: Progressive frontrunner and Maine logger poised to replace Graham Platner in chaotic primary
author: Shrai Popat
summary: Troy Jackson is likely to be Democratic nominee after Platner ended Senate bid amid sexual assault allegations
body_text: Troy Jackson – a logger, longtime legislator and former president of the Maine senate – is now poised to become the Democratic nominee in Maine’s US Senate race. His rise comes after the party’s previous nominee, Graham Platner, abruptly ended his campaign earlier this month following allegations of sexual assault from a former partner. Platner’s withdrawal set off a frantic scramble inside the Maine Democratic party. Several contenders filed paperwork to be considered at a 25 July special convention of 601 delegates tasked with selecting a new nominee. But over the weekend, Jackson’s serious challengers dropped out one after another, clearing a swift and unobstructed path for him. Jackson, who lost the Democratic gubernatorial primary earlier this year, is now the presumptive choice. Among those who ended their bids was Jordan Wood, a former congressional staffer who ran unsuccessfully in the Democratic primary for Maine’s second district. Two other candidates who also fell short in this year’s gubernatorial primary – former Maine CDC director Nirav Shah and current secretary of state Shenna Bellows – likewise ended their campaigns. Dan Kleban, founder of Maine Beer Company, who briefly ran in the Senate primary against Platner before withdrawing months ago, also announced he would not stay in the race. Wood, Shah and Kleban have all endorsed Jackson, stressing the stakes of flipping the seat held for nearly three decades by Republican Susan Collins – the only GOP senator running for re-election in a state Kamala Harris carried in 2024. “This fight is bigger than any one person,” Wood said in a social media video. “There is too much at stake in our country, our democracy – our state is depending on us.” Maine is crucial to Democrats’ effort to net the four seats required to retake control of the Senate in November’s midterms. Over the weekend, all 16 counties elected 500 delegates who will vote in Bangor on Saturday, with the remaining 101 delegates coming from the state party’s central committee. Jackson, now the progressive frontrunner, once campaigned alongside Platner and received his endorsement during his gubernatorial run, where he finished third, which raised concerns that Jackson might be tainted in the breakneck process to replace the disgraced former nominee. Questions have also lingered about Jackson’s public speaking style and whether he could match the commanding presence that helped Platner build a statewide following for his populist platform. But Jackson has consolidated support from major unions, numerous state Democrats and national progressive groups – he also appears to have locked down broad backing from the newly selected delegates. While their commitments are not legally binding, a majority of the 601 delegates have now pledged to vote for him, according to Jackson’s campaign. “Those delegates were not handed to us. You know, we earned them because hundreds and hundreds of people organized their neighbors, made the calls, had the conversations,” Jackson said in Sanford. On Sunday, Jackson also told Politico it was “incredible” to see people “really concerned about making sure this momentum, this movement continues” as it became clear he would emerge as the presumptive nominee. His campaign said on Monday it was turning its “full focus” to defeating Collins after the weekend’s surge of delegate support. State Democrats have until 27 July to formally choose Platner’s replacement for the general election ballot. Jackson, 58, was first elected to the legislature in 2002 and became senate president in 2018. He left office in 2024 due to term limits.

title: Suspect in custody named following explosion at FBI building in New York
author: Richard Luscombe
summary: Three people reported injured after incendiary device allegedly thrown at building also housing ICE field office
body_text: Authorities in New York City are investigating an explosion on Monday morning outside an FBI building in lower Manhattan that reportedly injured three people. Investigators said a person who allegedly threw an incendiary device at the scene was taken into custody. The FBI later released the name in a press conference, identifying the suspect as Andrew Arrabaca. “Mr Arrabaca came armed with bad intentions,” said James Barnacle, the assistant director in charge of the FBI New York Field Office in a televised press conference. He then listed numerous weapons in his possession. The incident occurred at the bureau’s headquarters at 26 Federal Plaza, a building that the Reuters news agency reported also ⁠houses an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field office. Video posted on social media by an independent journalist showed white smoke billowing from just outside the building, and a number of armed law enforcement personnel in uniform emerging quickly from a doorway. A more detailed clip on CNN’s website appears to show the moment the device exploded, and a person on the ground surrounded by police officers or ICE personnel. According to the New York news channel PIX11, three people were injured, two of them requiring hospital treatment. The outlet cited officials who said a fire appeared to have been started by fireworks that were “loaded into a wagon bearing a sign that read ‘ICE out of our streets’”. In a statement, the FBI said: “This morning, an individual deployed an incendiary device outside 26 Federal Plaza. The individual has been taken into custody, and the FBI New York joint terrorism taskforce is investigating the incident.” NBC New York reported that Arrabaca “may have emotional issues” – and that he had previously served in the US army and the national guard. The top US House Democrat, Hakeem Jeffries, who represents a New York district, praised the quick response of authorities. “I am grateful to law enforcement for their swift actions to stop an attack at 26 Federal Plaza this morning, for successfully apprehending the suspect and for keeping the people of New York City safe,” he said in a statement. “Acts of terror and violence have no place in our city and will never be tolerated. The individual responsible for this must be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” Protests against ICE, and the Trump administration’s hardline approach to immigration, have proliferated in recent weeks and months as the number of deaths at the hands of federal immigration authorities has increased. Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero were killed during separate encounters earlier in July with officers attempting to conduct traffic stops in Texas and Maine. And on 13 July, Jesús Manuel Arenas-Silva, a 45-year-old Venezuelan man, became the 22nd person to die in ICE custody this year after he was found unresponsive at a detention center in Georgia. The Trump administration had appeared to step back from its policy of hardline immigration enforcement after the shooting deaths of two unarmed US citizens – Alex Pretti and Renee Good – by federal agents in Minneapolis in January. But the homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, denied on Friday that traffic stops by ICE and border patrol agents would be suspended in response to the most recent fatal shootings. And he promised that a surge of immigration arrests would continue. “We’re turning up the heat on the streets. We’re out there working harder than we ever have,” he said at a news conference.

title: Morning Mail: Online networks target children with ‘gamified’ violence, Seven’s Hanson pitch, Burnham takes power
author: Martin Farrer
summary: We reveal how organised networks are pushing youngsters into brutal and degrading acts
body_text: Good morning. Today we reveal how organised online networks are “gamifying” violence and encouraging self-harm, targeting children in games including Roblox and Minecraft. With cases before the courts in Australia and around the world, experts want parents to know the warning signs. We’re also reporting on how Seven pitched a Spotlight show about “uncontrolled immigration” to Pauline Hanson, Iran says it is in “full-scale war” with the US again, and Andy Burnham promises to be the UK “circuit-breaker” as he moves into No 10 and picks his new cabinet. Australia Hanson ‘pitch’ | A Seven producer urged Pauline Hanson to travel to Britain to meet Nigel Farage and film a Spotlight special highlighting so-called “uncontrolled immigration”, according to a pitch posted to social media by the One Nation leader. Tax system ‘rigged’ | A new tax rate for the highest income earners, introducing wealth and inheritance taxes and extracting more revenue from gas companies form part of a new leftwing manifesto circulating before the Labor party’s national conference. ‘One in 15 million’ | A 34-year-old woman from Brisbane has defied the odds and delivered naturally conceived, identical quadruplets in what is believed to be an Australian first. Exclusive | Australian researchers have found that antibiotic resistance – when bacteria are no longer killed by antimicrobial medicines – has increased in every region of the world. Down slope | Alpine ski resorts in New South Wales and Victoria saw climate records shattered on the weekend with maximum temperatures up to 12C above average. World ‘Circuit-breaker’ | After entering 10 Downing Street as Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham promised a “circuit-breaker” moment for the country, to restore hope to millions of people. His first pledge as prime minister was to end rough sleeping – here are six key takeaways from his speech. ‘Full-scale war’ | Iran’s president says the country is in a “full-scale war” after the US expanded its aerial campaign and Tehran struck Washington’s Gulf allies, even as diplomats said talks to de-escalate were continuing. India | Tens of thousands of “cockroach” protesters have defied police orders and descended on Delhi to demand the resignation of India’s education minister in one of the largest anti-government demonstrations in years. Ukraine rifts | Ukraine’s commander in chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi, is widely expected to lose his job amid signs that Volodymyr Zelenskyy has bowed to pressure from protesters and will reshuffle the army’s top leadership. Maine man | Troy Jackson – a former president of the Maine Senate – is now poised to become the Democratic nominee in the state’s US Senate race after the party’s previous nominee, Graham Platner, abruptly ended his campaign. Full Story How is online rage shaping our politics? Ed Coper, a political adviser and communications consultant who has studied online discourse, talks to Reged Ahmad about his new book, Angertainment: How Social Media Outrage Ruined Everything. In-depth In June, a Swedish teenager went on trial for dozens of offences – including allegedly encouraging someone to self-harm and the creation of child sexual abuse material – with alleged victims around the world, including in Australia. Guardian Australia has tracked this case, which is one of many before the courts in Sweden, the United States, Australia and around the world, to understand the spread of online networks that engage in sadistic sexual and violent extortion. This evolving and borderless online ecosystem is prompting growing concern from authorities, who warn that grooming and extortion can turn victims into perpetrators. “These are young people recruiting other young people,” one expert said. “It is a youth phenomenon.” Not the news In the latest iteration of our series about jobs that changed people’s lives, Rebecca Lowrey Boyd recalls how working in a photo shop gave her a working knowledge of photo chemistry, a comprehensive understanding of local penises and that the most ordinary jobs can be where you learn how to really look at people. Sport World Cup | Nearly 2 million Spaniards took to the streets to welcome the triumphant national team home. Jonathan Wilson pays tribute to Rodri, Spain’s midfield maestro who was player of the tournament. Spain’s media has hailed the country’s World Cup triumph as a “unique collective experience”, while the Argentinian press ignored the outrage over their team’s antics and said they were “beyond reproach”. Golf | Bryson DeChambeau has been accused of threatening to call Donald Trump during a row with senior R&A officials on Friday after the American golfer was handed a two-shot penalty at the Open. Football | Kevin Keegan, the former England captain and manager, has died aged 75. He was one of England’s greatest ever players but is also remembered for his rollercoaster reign as Newcastle manager. Media roundup Chris Bowen has set aside up to $4.2m of taxpayers’ money to secure accommodation for foreign bureaucrats in Fiji as part of his Cop president mission, according to the Australian. Qantas and Virgin are selling discounted flights to the Middle East despite the continuing conflict, the Telegraph reports. What’s happening today Courts | Former bishop of Broome on trial in Perth for alleged sexual offences in Aboriginal communities. Resources | Federal court case over approval of Woodside’s North West Shelf expansion begins. Media | Reuters’ editor-in-chief, Alessandra Galloni, to deliver Andrew Olle media lecture. title: Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham’s sister, to run for full Senate term
author: Shrai Popat
summary: Interim senator appointed after Lindsey Graham’s death endorsed by Trump ‘for the Good of our Nation’
body_text: Darline Graham, the South Carolina interim senator and sister of the late Lindsey Graham, said she plans to run for a full Senate term after Donald Trump endorsed her last week. In an interview with Sean Hannity that will air in full on Monday, Graham – who was appointed by Governor Henry McMaster to finish the remainder of her brother’s term – said she had “made a decision”. “I’m in,” she told the Fox News anchor. Graham, 62, made history as the first woman to represent South Carolina in the Senate when she was sworn in last week. Her brother, Lindsey died earlier this month, aged 71, after what his office called a “brief and sudden illness”. The chief medical examiner preliminarily ruled that he died of aortic dissection due to cardiovascular disease. On Friday, Trump said he had encouraged Darline Graham to run for a full six-year term representing South Carolina. “I asked Darline, for the Good of our Nation, to run for the U.S. Senate in the Special Republican Primary,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life and, should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement.” Because Lindsey Graham won the Republican nomination last month, the state will now hold a special primary to replace him on the ballot on 11 August.

title: Nicaragua’s president says country will not hold any more elections
author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
summary: Daniel Ortega, the 80-year-old authoritarian leader, says move will ‘build a wall’ against the opposition
body_text: Nicaragua’s long-serving president, Daniel Ortega, has said the country will hold no further elections to prevent the opposition from coming to power. The 80-year-old authoritarian leader, who has been in office since 2007, also said he would work with the congress he controls to pass new laws that would “build a wall” against the opposition. Ortega made the announcement on Sunday during the official ceremony marking the 47th anniversary of the 1979 Sandinista revolution, in which he helped overthrow the brutal dictatorship of Anastasio Somoza. Although his administration and that of his wife and “co-president”, Rosario Murillo, had already been marked by the steady erosion of democracy in the Central American country, many are describing his announcement as a significant rhetorical escalation. “With this decision, Ortega and Murillo have sealed the country’s transition to a full-fledged family dictatorship,” said Tiziano Breda, Latin America senior analyst at the NGO Armed Conflict Location and Event Data. During a speech in front of thousands of state employees who, according to local media, had been coerced into attending, Ortega said: “There will be no more elections here so that they [the opposition parties] can try to seize the government, seize power.” The president, who had not appeared in public for 61 days, added: “We will work with the National Assembly and the relevant institutions on laws, because we need laws that build a wall, a barrier, against the coup plotters and the traitors who sell out their country.” The elections were due to take place next year, but Ortega gave no details on whether they would be cancelled or whether the opposition would be barred from taking part – something that has already happened in practice. During the 2021 campaign, his regime outlawed parties and jailed all opposition presidential hopefuls. Breda said: “Ortega and Murillo are evidently afraid of the idea that the slightest political opening could create the conditions for dissent to manifest and threaten their grip on power, possibly suggesting that their already feeble domestic support is further falling. “Therefore, instead of staging a rigged election, they have opted to eliminate electoral competition altogether.” Last year, Ortega pushed through a series of constitutional reforms that included extending the presidential term from five to six years and promoting his wife, then vice-president, to the position of “co-president”. The US refers to their administration as the “Murillo-Ortega dictatorship”. During his speech, the Nicaraguan president criticised the US over the January operation that abducted the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro: “With all their power, they stormed the presidential palace, where Nicolás and his wife, Cilia [Flores], were. They killed the entire security detail there – most of them were Cubans – and took them away to imprison them in the US. It is monstrous.” The president said preventing the opposition from returning to power was necessary to protect the country from the “coup plotters” who, he claimed, had been behind the nationwide protests of 2018 – when, according to organisations including the UN, his regime carried out a violent crackdown that killed more than 350 people, wounded hundreds, jailed thousands and forced nearly 1 million Nicaraguans into exile. Recently, the UN, the US, human rights organisations and 30 former Ibero-American presidents have directly blamed Ortega and Murillo for the death of the Indigenous leader and four-term congressman Brooklyn Rivera, 73, who spent nearly three years “unjustly imprisoned” by the regime, the US state department said. According to organisations including Human Rights Watch, there are about 50 political prisoners in the country. The regime has stripped 546 people of their citizenship and shut down more than 5,600 non-governmental organisations, 29 universities and 58 media outlets.

title: ‘It needs to end now’: Democrats urge Trump to halt Iran war after US troop deaths
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: President accused of having ‘lost control of this war’ as deaths of trio in Iranian military strikes fuel rising concern
body_text: Democrats have seized on the deaths of three US troops killed in Iranian strikes to urge Donald Trump to urgently reverse his resumption of the war with Iran amid widespread anxiety over climbing casualties. Even as US forces launched a 10th consecutive wave of attacks against Iranian targets, concern over the deaths of American service personnel threatened to complicate moves to escalate the conflict, which has reignited after he last week walked away from a memorandum of understanding agreed with Iran in June. The Pentagon released the names of two soldiers killed in a strike on Muwaffaq Salti air base in Jordan on Friday. They were First Lieutenant Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii, and Private Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas. A third member of the armed forces was killed in northern Iraq on Saturday in what US Central Command called a “controlled detonation” of unexploded ordnance. The remains of a possible fourth dead service member were found over the weekend in Jordan. Chris Murphy, a Democratic senator for Connecticut, accused Trump of having “frighteningly lost control of this war”. “For those of us who pay attention to the hour-to-hour pace of the Iran War, things are getting very dark very quickly,” he wrote on social media. “The scale of attacks – and threats of escalation – are increasing rapidly.” The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, declared that the US would not be deterred by the casualties, writing: “Godspeed, heroes. Their sacrifice only stiffens our resolve.” Iran has vowed to carry out retaliatory strikes against US Gulf allies, which it has branded “collaborators” for providing logistical facilities for strikes on Iranian territory. In a brief telephone conversation with NewsNation, Trump called the deaths “a very sad thing” and said the service members had died “in service of our country”. But he faced a chorus of calls from Democrats to step back from his belligerent posture even as Republicans remained supportive. “The reckless and costly war of choice in Iran has been a disaster for the American people,” wrote Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader in the House of Representatives. “May God continue to watch over our troops who have needlessly been put into harm’s way.” Mark Warner, the vice-chair of the Senate intelligence committee and a Democrat from Virginia, said there were “hundreds of seriously wounded” US personnel, and added it was “remarkable” that casualty figures had not been higher. “This is what happens when you start a war of choice. And as a member of the Gang of Eight, I can say unequivocally there was no imminent threat from Iran,” he told CBS’s Face the Nation. Chris Van Hollen, a Democratic senator from Maryland who has introduced war powers resolutions aimed at ending the Iran campaign unless it receives congressional approval, posted: “This senseless war should never have been started and it needs to end NOW.” Jeanne Shaheen, the party’s ranking members of the Senate foreign relations committee, called for a return to diplomacy. “The President must negotiate an end to this disastrous war,” she wrote. And Ted Lieu, a California representative who has also vocally advocated reining in Trump through a war powers resolution, wrote: “We need Republicans to join us in passing the War Powers Resolution NOW.” The New York Times reported that Iranian forces carried out three strikes against US military targets in Jordan last week before Friday’s deadly attacks that were not disclosed by the Pentagon. The newspaper said the Pentagon also did not reveal “dozens” of casualties and damage inflicted by the earlier strikes. The latest casualties brought the number of US service members killed since the start of the war on 28 February to at least 17. More than 1,700 Iranian civilians are estimated to have been killed. The House and Senate have both passed war powers resolutions – requiring the president to ask for congressional approval after 60 days of hostilities – with the aim of restraining Trump. But the White House has contended that there has yet to be 60 days of continuous fighting because the clock stopped after an initial ceasefire in April, which held, shakily, for several weeks. Republicans, meanwhile, have remained publicly supportive of Trump – despite poll figures showing support for the war and the president’s conduct of it low and sliding. A Washington Post-Ipsos survey showed approval for Trump’s handling of the conflict at 29% – lower than the 33% backing his stewardship of the economy, which has been buffeted by soaring fuel prices caused by the war. A statement from New Mexico Republicans mourned the fresh casualties but accused Democrats of trying to exploit them for political reasons. “No matter how much Democrats try to politicize this, President Trump’s actions in Iran have made our country safer from a terrorist regime that has inflicted death and carnage on millions of innocent people around the world, including Americans,” the party said in a statement. James Comer, a representative from Kentucky and one of Trump’s staunchest supporters on Capitol Hill, told Fox News that a military response to the service members’ deaths was essential. “I don’t think anyone would prefer that we have any type of military conflict in Iran, but that’s the world that we live in,” he said. “We have to respond, and we have to respond swiftly and with full force, and that’s what President Trump’s doing.” Riley Moore, a West Virginia Republican, told Fox that the “precision” of the strikes on the Jordanian base suggested Iran was receiving targeting information from Russia or China. He called on the US’s Gulf allies on the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) to help. “Where do we go from here is also looking at how we’re going to work with those GCC partners in the region because this could tip over … into a regional destabilizing conflict,” he said.

title: ‘Front groups and fellow travelers’: state department attacks US left over Cuba
author: Maya Yang
summary: New report denounces Havana and claims ‘campaign of subversion’ has infiltrated highest levels of US government
body_text: As part of the Trump administration’s continuing attack on left-leaning groups, the US state department has listed several activists and organizations as “front groups and fellow travelers” for Cuba, including Hasan Piker and the Amazon Labor Union founder Chris Smalls. In a 100-page report released on Monday, the state department denounces Cuba as the “capital of 21st-century communism”, accusing the Cuban government of carrying out a “campaign of subversion” that has “infiltrated the highest reaches of the US government, recruited and cultivated generations of American activists [and] backed an unprecedented wave of leftwing terrorism on American soil”. The state department report alleges that the so-called campaign is “designed to turn America against itself” and singles out several left-leaning activists and organizations, including the Democratic Socialists of America, Isra Hirsi – the daughter of the Minnesota Democratic representative Ilhan Omar – the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and journalist Amy Goodman, citing their criticism of US policy toward Cuba or participation in Cuba solidarity movements. Describing the DSA, of which Mamdani is a member, the report says the organization “serves as a particularly potent illustration of the ideological victory of Cuba’s effort to position itself as the spiritual capital of Third Worldist radicalism”. It accuses the DSA of maintaining a “fierce, almost religious commitment to the cause of the Cuban regime – not because the group is controlled by Cuban agents, per se, but because that commitment is now simply the de facto policy orthodoxy on the American far left”. Trump has doubled down on similar messaging in recent days, using the term communism at political rallies and presidential engagements alike. For more than 60 years, the US has maintained a sweeping economic embargo on Cuba, in addition to crippling sanctions imposed by numerous administrations. Despite US claims that its policies are designed to pressure the Cuban government, Havana and many international critics including human rights organizations say they have severely hurt the island’s economy. The report comes just days after the state department, led by Marco Rubio – the son of Cuban immigrants and one of the US’s most outspoken critics of Cuba’s communist government – imposed further sanctions on the country, targeting its tourism ministry and several state-owned companies. The sanctions come as part of the Trump administration’s “comprehensive push to end the Cuban regime’s malign activities, both in Cuba and across our hemisphere”. Rubio has long advocated for “maximum pressure” toward Havana, arguing that easing US sanctions only strengthens Cuba’s communist government. Throughout his political career including his time as a senator, Rubio has backed tighter economic restrictions and repeatedly accused the Cuban authorities of repressing political dissent and fueling violence across the region. Earlier this month, Cuba suffered its third nationwide blackout in six months amid an oil blockade imposed by Trump on the island of 9.6 million people, prompting many residents to say that “living like this is agony”.

title: Donald Trump to impose 50% tariff on most Canadian goods, White House says
author: Mollie Reilly and agency
summary: Turmoil likely as Trump officials say Canada unfairly discriminated against US autos, alcohol and dairy products
body_text: Donald Trump is imposing 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods in response to the country retaliating against previous US tariffs, the White House announced on Monday, declaring Canada has unfairly discriminated against American cars, alcohol and dairy products. The tariffs will hit a wide range of products, the White House said, including wine, hockey sticks and cement. They also include goods previously protected from import taxes under the United States-Mexico-Canada (USMCA) agreement. The new tariffs will exclude energy products, fish, critical minerals and potash. They also exclude products already subject to tariffs aimed at protecting national security, such as steel and aluminum. The steep tariffs will probably unleash a new wave of economic chaos, with risks of higher inflation and further fraying of relations between two nations that had been closely woven together before Trump’s return to the White House. The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, said in a statement that his government had made comprehensive proposals ‌to resolve trade disputes with Washington, asserting that Trump’s past tariffs violated ‌a trade pact between the two countries. “This trade dispute has raised costs for families, particularly in the US,” he said. “Canada stands ready to engage intensively to address outstanding issues with the US to the mutual benefit of our citizens.” The White House said the tariffs will go into effect in 30 days, leaving time for possible negotiations between the two countries. Trump signed three proclamations to launch the tariffs under Section 338 of the 1930 Trade Act. Several Democratic lawmakers last year proposed repealing the section because they said Trump could use it to destabilize the economy. A White House fact sheet claims Trump is “taking action to hold Canada accountable for its continued discrimination against and unreasonable and unequal treatment of U.S. commerce that has burdened and disadvantaged hardworking Americans”. Trump claims in the proclamations that Canada discriminates against American automobiles, alcohol and cheese relative to other nations, but his argument rests in large part on retaliatory actions taken by Canada after the US president imposed tariffs on Canada under the pretext that it should do more to stop fentanyl smuggling into the US. Trump noted in his autos proclamation that Canada maintained, starting in April 2025, a 25% tariff on the imports of US motor vehicles that did not qualify for preferential treatment under the USMCA. The White House also cited all but two Canadian provinces and territories stopping the sale of US alcoholic beverages, while not imposing similar restrictions on other countries. Trump also objected to Canada’s treatment of US cheese, saying in his proclamation that Canada discriminates against the US compared with Europe on dairy products. Trump had threatened last week to impose tariffs due to smoke from devastating wildfires in Canada drifting across large portions of the US. “We are holding Canada responsible for the fact that they are not properly maintaining their Forests, and Brush therein, and the United States is being unnecessarily invaded by filthy, polluted, and unhealthy air, the quality of which is dangerous, and totally unacceptable!” he wrote on Truth Social. Trump watched Sunday’s World Cup final with Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister who has previously pushed back on the US president and won the premiership last year on a platform of promising to stand up for Canada. After the match, Trump told reporters he had raised the issue of wildfire smoke with Carney. “I told him, I mean, ‘You got to stop these fires from coming in and, you know, poisoning our air. Our air has been poisoned,’” Trump said of their conversation. A White House official who previewed the new tariffs to reporters said Trump had requested aides explore additional tariffs due to Canadian wildfires harming US air quality, the Associated Press reported. The Canadian federal government did not immediately comment on Trump’s action, but Doug Ford, the Ontario premier, said he would “never stop fighting to protect Ontario”. “If these tariffs proceed, Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar,” Ford posted on social media. Candace Laing, the CEO of the Canadian chamber of commerce, said the Trump administration’s moves were “regrettable” but the two countries needed to use the 30-day window before the tariffs start “to make meaningful progress in advancing formal talks”. The new taxes on Canadian imports could carry serious political and economic risks for Trump ahead of the November midterm elections for control of Congress. His so-called “liberation day” tariffs last year in April provoked a financial market meltdown over concerns about inflation and a recession, prompting him to walk back the rates for a period of negotiation. In a 6-3 decision in February, the supreme court ruled that Trump had illegally used emergency executive power to impose his global tariffs, causing the administration to find alternative ways to raise import taxes based on a series of legal authorities. The US has been forced to pay back $81bn in tariffs so far this fiscal year. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Almost 100 troops injured in recent weeks, Pentagon admits, as Iran launches reprisals on US allies
author: Guardian staff and agencies
summary: Iran has attacked a tanker in the strait of Hormuz, forcing its crew to abandon the ship, after the US launched a tenth consecutive night of strikes
body_text: Nearly 100 US service members have been injured over the last two weeks of escalating strikes on Iran, the Pentagon has said, as Tehran launched a wave of reprisals to the tenth consecutive night of attacks. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday they had targeted US military sites including air defence systems and a radar installation in Bahrain and Kuwait, while a tanker in the strait of Hormuz reported being ⁠struck by an unknown projectile, forcing its crew to abandon the vessel and board a lifeboat. Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan all said they had activated defences to repel the attacks, but the scale of US injuries at facilities across the region over recent week is likely to bring greater scrutiny to Iran’s reprisal attacks. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said the vast majority of those injured only experienced “minor concussions” and 96% had since returned to work. Parnell was responding to a New York Times report that the Pentagon has withheld information about troop injuries from Iranian strikes. He denied that the Pentagon was hiding data about injuries. In the last week three US soldiers have been killed in action in Jordan and Iraq. The 10 consecutive nights of US airstrikes haven’t compelled Tehran to loosen its grip on the strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of all crude oil and natural gas traded once passed in peacetime. Efforts to rein in the costs that the disruption is having on global trade and oil prices were complicated further on Monday, after Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthis announced they were imposing a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia. There were few details on how the embargo might work, but a Houthi official said that the Bab al-Mandeb strait – at the southern end of the Red Sea through which about 12% of the world’s trade usually passes – would be closed to the Saudis in response to the kingdom’s “unjust blockade on Yemenis for over 10 years”. The Houthis have demonstrated their ability to disrupt shipping in the past by targeting vessels over the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza. Saudi Arabia’s military said it would keep the waterway open, but the threat will put further pressure on the country’s oil exports, as it has increased shipping from Red Sea ports sue to the closure of the strait of Hormuz. Even as the US and Iran inch closer to all-out war again, Iran’s interior minister travelled to Pakistan, a key mediator in the conflict, for talks. However, it remains unclear just what new deal could be reached, after the interim deal signed last month that was meant to end the fighting crumbled. Shipping through the strait of Hormuz has largely stalled. And as fighting intensifies, both sides have targeted civilian infrastructure relied on by millions of people. The escalation has pushed oil prices higher in recent weeks. Benchmark Brent crude traded on Tuesday above $88 a barrel and regular petrol in the US climbed to an average of $4 a gallon, keeping pressure on Americans’ wallets ahead of midterm elections this November. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade ⁠Operations agency (UKMTO) said it had received multiple reports on Tuesday that a tanker had ⁠been hit by an unknown projectile. The incident was reported eight nautical miles east of Oman’s Limah. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards later claimed the attack, as well as two other attacks on ships Monday in the waterway. UKMTO said the tanker’s ⁠company security officer had reported that the crew had abandoned the vessel and were aboard a lifeboat and no environmental ‌impact had been reported. The route around Oman has been the one the US military has encouraged ships to travel to avoid Iran’s control. With Reuters and the Associated Press

title: Protests in Italy after death of Moroccan man under police restraint
author: Jon Henley Europe correspondent
summary: Teargas and water cannon used on protesters after Abderrahim ⁠Fakir died pleading for help from police
body_text: Police have clashed with demonstrators during a protest in the Italian city of Bologna after a Moroccan-born man died pleading for help under police restraint. Human rights campaigners and Italy’s opposition parties have demanded urgent answers over the death on Sunday of Abderrahim ⁠Fakir, 42, who had lived in Italy since he was five years old and ran a small removals and cleaning business. A video shared widely on Italian media shows Fakir, who reportedly had heart issues and asthma, repeatedly calling out “aiuto, aiuto, basta” (Help, help, that’s enough) as two officers sit on him and ambulance workers look on. After he stops moving, the police officers are seen binding his ankles together, only later checking his vital signs with the ambulance workers, the video shows. Prosecutors have opened an investigation and requested the officers’ body cam footage. “You can’t die like this,” Fakir’s sister, Khadija, told the Corriere della Sera newspaper. “The police have to protect us. If someone is agitated, you have to calm them down … not kill them like a dog.” Italian media reported that police had been called to the scene, in the north-eastern neighbourhood of Pilastro, shortly after noon on Sunday by local residents who were concerned by Fakir’s erratic and aggressive behaviour. The officers reportedly called emergency services soon after they arrived, and tried to calm Fakir before using pepper spray and holding him down while trying to handcuff ‌him. They told ambulance personnel that he was “having a psychiatric episode”. During the protests late on Monday, firecrackers were thrown near police buildings and police reacted using teargas and water cannon. A group of demonstrators also sat down in a square holding a photograph of Fakir, the Ansa news agency reported. The incident has been compared in Italy to George Floyd’s murder in the US six years ago, and also prompted comparisons with tactics used by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) under Donald Trump. However, Italy’s interior minister, Matteo Piantedosi, told public television: “Whoever makes insulting remarks against the police shows they have no trust in our law enforcement nor in our justice system [and] should look into what happened.” Tommaso Foti, the European ‌affairs minister, said: “The ‌chants of ‘police murderers’ and ‘the whole ‌world hates you’ shouted during a demonstration in Bologna … are disgraceful.” The far-right deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, also defended the police, while Galeazzo Bignami, head of prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party in parliament’s lower house, praised the officers’ “professional conduct”. Ilaria Cucchi, a senator whose brother died in custody in 2009, told Agence-France Presse she was sickened by the “solidarity and thanks” expressed to police after such an “inhumane act”. Cucchi, a member of the opposition Greens and Left alliance (AVS) party, criticised Meloni and her coalition government, saying their “policies seeped in hatred and racism” had fostered a climate of violence. Francesco Boccia, head of the centre-left Democratic party (PD) in the senate, told La Repubblica daily: “If the right wants to import the ICE model, this is the wrong country for it. We have democratic antibodies.” Barbara Spinelli, a lawyer, told Ansa she had met Fakir last year when he applied to renew his permit to stay. He had been “a very kind, well educated, respectful person” who was in Italy legally but worried about being expelled, she said. “I told him: ‘We are in Italy, a democratic country. Here the police respect the rules,’” she said. “I don’t know how I will ever again manage to tell someone they don’t need to be afraid.” Agence-France Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

title: First Thing: Trump urged to end Iran escalation as US deaths and injuries rise
author: Martin Belam
summary: Democrats call for end to war’s resumption amid widespread anxiety over casualties
body_text: Good morning. Democrats have seized on the killing of three US troops in Iranian strikes to urge Donald Trump to reverse his resumption of the war with Iran. Amid widespread anxiety over rising numbers of casualties, Chris Murphy, a Democratic senator for Connecticut, accused the president of having “frighteningly lost control of this war”. Even as US forces launched a 10th consecutive wave of attacks against Iranian targets, concern over the deaths of American service personnel threatened to complicate moves to escalate the conflict, which has reignited after Trump last week walked away from a memorandum of understanding agreed with Iran in June. How has Iran responded to continued US strikes? Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday they had targeted US military sites, including air defence systems and a radar installation in Bahrain and Kuwait, while the crew of a tanker in the strait of Hormuz reported being ⁠struck by an unknown projectile. Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan said they had activated defences to repel the attacks. How many people have been killed and injured in the war so far? The latest casualties brought the number of US service members killed since the start of the war on 28 February to at least 17. More than 1,700 Iranian civilians are estimated to have been killed. Nearly 100 US service members have been injured over the last two weeks of escalating strikes. Progressive frontrunner and Maine logger poised to replace Graham Platner in chaotic primary Troy Jackson – a logger, longtime legislator and former president of the Maine senate – is poised to become the Democratic nominee in Maine’s US Senate race. His rise comes after the party’s previous nominee, Graham Platner, abruptly ended his campaign this month following allegations of sexual assault from a former partner. Several contenders filed paperwork to be considered at a 25 July special convention tasked with selecting a new nominee. But over the weekend, Jackson’s serious challengers dropped out one after another, clearing a swift and unobstructed path for him. What is happening with Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat? Darline Graham, the South Carolina interim senator and sister of the late Lindsey Graham, said she plans to run for a full Senate term after Trump endorsed her last week. In an interview with Sean Hannity, Graham – who was appointed by Governor Henry McMaster to finish the remainder of her brother’s term – said she had “made a decision. I’m in”. Why are there fresh concerns about AI chatbots and elections? A European study, published by the civil liberties group Liberties and based on research during this year’s Hungarian parliamentary elections, has concluded that AI chatbots provide inaccurate, inconsistent and unreliable guidance to voters asking which party they should back. United Airlines says it will ‘look into’ worker’s threat to call ICE in viral video United Airlines is “looking into” a viral video showing a United Airlines employee threatening to call Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on a Mexican American man at San Francisco international airport last week. After three hours of waiting and a sour exchange with a United Airlines staffer while trying to correct an error made when entering his daughter’s name, the naturalized citizen Julio Varela pulled out his phone and demanded the woman identify herself so he could report her. The United staffer responded by pulling out her own phone and recording him. “Maybe we should call ICE on you,” the woman replied. “You don’t act like a citizen.” Suspect who sent anonymous tip to Alaska police charged with 1993 killing A Michigan man suspected of having murdered a co-worker in Fairbanks, Alaska, in 1993 was arrested recently after he called in what he intended to be an anonymous tip revealing where he had hidden the victim’s body, according to investigators. Christopher Popps, 54, faces charges of second-degree murder in the death of Patrick Dearth, Alaska state police said in a statement. title: Andy Burnham’s first Labour cabinet: who’s in and who’s out?
author: Rowena Mason and Peter Walker
summary: From the Treasury to the Home Office, we look at who will head up key departments in new PM’s government
body_text: Andy Burnham has appointed his first cabinet, with the new prime minister rewarding those who have been loyal to his takeover efforts. He had promised to pick his top team from all wings of the party in an effort to show he is trying to run a more inclusive administration. But at the same time, his decision to have a brutal clearout of Starmer allies resulted in many considered to be on the right of the party or close to the former prime minister losing their jobs. These are the key announcements so far: Who is in? John Healey Chancellor The former defence secretary who quit the government over a lack of funding for the defence investment plan is the surprise appointment to the Treasury. Healey, 66, is a steady and experienced force, having been an MP since 1997, and serving as a Treasury minister under Tony Blair. The job had been expected to go to Ed Miliband and then it was mooted for Shabana Mahmood. But one advantage of Healey is his longstanding history on Labour frontbenches for every faction of the party. He was a minister in the Blair-Brown years and a loyal member of the shadow cabinets of Miliband, Jeremy Corbyn and Starmer. Healey grew up in Wakefield, studied political science at Cambridge, and was a journalist, campaigns director at the Trades Union Congress and a disability rights campaigner before entering parliament. Unshowy and not part of the usual Westminster dramas or scandals, it was a shock when he resigned his role under Starmer, in what would be one of the fatal blows for his premiership. In the job, he will be expected to push for a fuller funding settlement for the Ministry of Defence, which was denied to him under the Treasury of Rachel Reeves. His other major shared interest with Burnham is reindustrialisation. His X bio describes him as “Husband and Dad. Proud Yorkshireman. Labour MP for Rawmarsh and Conisbrough and former secretary of state for defence”. He can now add chancellor to that list. Shabana Mahmood Home secretary Mahmood will keep her role in Burnham’s cabinet after being appointed home secretary by Keir Starmer last year and charged with driving through controversial immigration policies. She is considered to be on the Blue Labour right of the party, which is socially conservative and tough on crime. She grew up in Small Heath in inner-city Birmingham in the 1980s and 90s, where her father kept a cricket bat behind the till of the family shop to fend off would-be robbers. After going to the University of Oxford to study law, she worked as a barrister. The 45-year-old is an MP in Birmingham and ran Labour’s election campaign in 2024, before a stint as justice secretary overseeing an early release programme to ease overcrowding. She is viewed as steely and decisive. A cabinet colleague told the Guardian earlier this year that she “never wastes a word” in meetings, and last year warned that the government was still caught up in an opposition mindset and preoccupied with taking on the left instead of speaking to the concerns of the country more widely. She has also been a leading advocate for the UK to take a more pro-Palestinian stance, including on statehood. Ed Miliband Foreign secretary Miliband is a great survivor in the Labour party – almost as much so as Andy Burnham. A former cabinet minister under Gordon Brown, he led Labour to an election defeat in 2015 before serving in the shadow cabinet of Keir Starmer. He was a leading contender to be chancellor but there were fears his positioning on the soft left and as a firm defender of Britain’s net zero commitments would spook the financial markets. Having once made a speech pitching some companies as producers and others as predators, he is not a favourite politician of big business. Born in north London in a political family, his father was a Marxist academic. He studied PPE at Oxford and worked mostly in politics and research before joining his older brother, David, in the House of Commons as a Labour MP. They became the first brothers to both serve around the cabinet table since before the second world war, and their sibling relationship was put to the test when Ed beat David in the leadership contest to succeed Brown with the support of the trade union vote. As Labour leader, he led in the polls for many months against David Cameron and identified ahead of his time the public mood on the cost of living but was pilloried by some of the rightwing media as gaffe-prone and somewhat awkward. In Starmer’s cabinet he was viewed as one of the most successful cabinet ministers at driving through his priorities, including Great British Energy, and blocking more drilling in the North Sea – a policy expected to be partially overturned by Burnham. As foreign secretary, he will be expected to take international matters off Burnham’s hands as much as possible, take a more pro-Gaza stance and potentially set a path to restoring Britain’s aid commitments to 0.7% of national income. He replaces Yvette Cooper. Yvette Cooper Health secretary Among the Starmer-era big beasts who had been tipped to survive, Cooper is shifted from the Foreign Office to the vital domestic post of secretary of state for health and social care, the suffix especially important given Burnham’s stated mission to unlock the clogged adult care system. Cooper does, of course, have recent experience of a tricky UK-focused post, starting in Starmer’s government as home secretary, and she held several posts under Tony Blair and Gordon Brown. While still in her 50s, Cooper is approaching Labour “grandee” status, having been an MP since 1997 and getting her first taste of ministerial life at the tail end of the 20th century. When Labour’s 2015 leadership campaign began she was initially viewed as a favourite, but finished third behind Corbyn and a certain Andy Burnham. The daughter of a trade union leader, Cooper is a near-political lifer, having begun her career with then-shadow chancellor John Smith, although she did spend a period as a journalist before entering parliament. For a decade of her time in parliament, Cooper was part of a political double act with her husband, Ed Balls, who lost his seat in 2015 and later became a broadcaster. Pat McFadden Work and pensions secretary Some continuity had been expected with the new ministerial slate and it makes sense for this to happen with a department that could be central to Burnham’s political fortunes. McFadden, one of the more experienced operators in government, will be tasked with continuing to pilot through some sort of reform to social security, with the intention of limiting the costs without cuts or conditions of the sort that prompted a major backbench rebellion for Starmer. An MP since 2005, McFadden was soon propelled into the Blair and Brown frontbenches, and spent the buildup to the 2024 election as Starmer’s national campaigns coordinator, going on to take the Cabinet Office post at the centre of policymaking. A trusted voice on even the trickiest morning broadcast round, the child of two Irish speakers from County Donegal transplanted to Paisley, McFadden trod the traditional political path of researcher and policy adviser before winning his Wolverhampton South East seat. Louise Haigh Chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster, first secretary of state and Cabinet Office minister Haigh became a linchpin of Burnham’s byelection operation, so it is no surprise she is now his chief organiser in government and effectively his deputy as first secretary of state. As the most senior Cabinet Office minister, she will coordinate work across the government and oversee any changes to Whitehall. It marks a return to cabinet for the 38-year-old Haigh, who was sacked by Keir Starmer as transport secretary for not having told him fully about a fraud conviction over a missing mobile phone when she was in her 20s. She grew up in Sheffield and studied politics and government at LSE, then Nottingham University, before working in parliament, for Unite and later at the insurer Aviva. It was during her time at that company where she got in hot water over the phone, having reported it stolen but failed to update the police when it was found. She pleaded guilty to fraud, but it did not stop her political career. Elected in 2015, she was one of 36 Labour MPs to nominate Jeremy Corbyn for the Labour leadership that year and was given a frontbench role when he made her a shadow Cabinet Office minister at age 28. The MP for Sheffield Heeley rose through the junior ministerial ranks and was one of a handful of Corbyn’s frontbench to be appointed to Keir Starmer’s first cabinet when he took over. She became the shadow Northern Ireland secretary. Known for an engaging communication style, she retained her frontbench role even as Starmer moved his party to the right. As transport secretary, she oversaw the nationalisation of railways legislation until she was returned to the backbenches. She replaces Darren Jones. Wes Streeting Defence secretary Streeting is one of the only appointments to cabinet who is considered to be towards the right of the party. He is also one of the reasons Burnham is prime minister, after attempting unsuccessfully to challenge Starmer, kicking off the process of removing him. Having lost out on the top job, the role of defence secretary is still a substantial one. However, Streeting’s power is likely to be limited by the fact his predecessor, John Healey, is in the Treasury and will decide what kind of settlement the department gets for its investment plan. A former health secretary, the ambitious Streeting is likely to be pleased at getting an even bigger job, especially at such a crucial moment in the Ukraine war and during a time of warnings that Britain needs to rearm against global threats. Angela Eagle Environment secretary A first full cabinet role for the former security minister, but not much of a jump given Eagle is hugely experienced and, in a slightly unusual dual role, was a minister of state in the environment department along with her Home Office role. The twin of fellow Labour MP and minister Maria, Angela Eagle beat her sister into parliament by five years, winning her Wallasey seat for the first time in 1992 and getting her first shadow frontbench role as long ago as 1996. She held a series of junior ministerial roles under Blair and Brown, and was Jeremy Corbyn’s shadow business secretary before resigning and launching a brief attempt to challenge him for the leadership. Miatta Fahnbulleh Energy secretary Fahnbulleh is a rising star in the party who contributed heavily to Burnham’s policy ideas as he was preparing for government. She previously worked closely with Miliband so was a natural choice for the energy role and will have a crucial task in Burnham’s mission of cutting bills while sticking to commitments in net zero. Alex Norris Justice secretary The relatively low profile Alex Norris was a Home Office minister and an unexpected choice for justice secretary. A Nottingham MP, he was a trade union organiser for Unison and councillor before he entered parliament in 2017. Heidi Alexander Transport secretary Part of the relatively small continuity brigade in the Burnham cabinet, Alexander remains in the post she took over in November 2024 when the incumbent, a certain Louise Haigh, had to step down after admitting a past offence connected to a mobile phone. While not seen as especially cosy with the Burnham inner circle, Alexander is an effective operator who tends to not get distracted by factional matters, and will have an important role in helping a PM who places much store in decent public transport, not least buses. A south London MP from 2010, Alexander quit parliament in 2018 to become Sadiq Khan’s deputy mayor for transport in London. She returned to the Commons in 2024 in a Swindon seat, where she was born, and was soon in Starmer’s cabinet. Jonathan Reynolds Business secretary Reynolds returns to his former role after being shuffled sideways to the job of chief whip against his wishes. A fellow north-west MP, Reynolds has long been a friend of Burnham and has been given a crucial role in a beefed-up department that will cover science as well as his old portfolio. Burnham has stated he wants to be pro-business, as well as fighting for reindustrialisation and potentially overseeing the return of some utilities to more public control. Angela Rayner Housing secretary Rayner will be pleased to get back the job of housing secretary less than a year after she resigned over underpaid stamp duty on the purchase of a second property. She had been the subject of speculation that she would be health secretary but sources had suggested she would take some persuading when her main interest is devolution and housing. In this brief, she will be in charge of two of Burnham’s key priorities: spreading power to local government and embarking on a huge council house building programme. Lucy Powell Education secretary Powell is likely to be pleased with this substantive brief but Burnham has so far stopped short of making her deputy prime minister – despite her job as deputy leader of the party. Another Manchester area MP, Powell has long been an ally of Burnham and advocated for him to be allowed to run for parliament. She replaces Bridget Phillipson, her former rival in the race to be deputy leader, who is now minister for women and equalities in a stripped-back cabinet role. Lisa Nandy Culture secretary One of the few survivors of the original Starmer cabinet, Nandy stays in the same job. While some in Labour have grumbled about her occasionally low-key approach to the job, she is ideologically closer to Burnham than she was to Starmer, and her Wigan constituency adjoins his. She now gets to wrestle some more with a suite of challenges including the future of the BBC and the impact of social media. Earlier this month, Nandy announced that her department would stop using X as it “now favours abuse and misinformation over meaningful debate”. First entering the Commons in 2010, just before her 30th birthday, Nandy held a series of shadow cabinet posts under Corbyn and Starmer, including a stint as shadow foreign secretary. A confident and engaging media performer, Nandy stood in the 2020 Labour leadership election, coming third. Ellie Reeves Attorney general A bump up the ladder for the Reeves sister who remains in the cabinet – after nearly a year as solicitor general, she becomes attorney general, taking over from Richard Hermer. A change in personnel in the post was never in doubt, given Hermer is not only one of Starmer’s most loyal political allies, but also a close personal friend. For Reeves it is reward for her previous service in a series of important but largely backroom roles, such as party chair and deputy national campaigns coordinator. A lawyer by training, as is usual for the job, Reeves undertook a series of Labour party roles before winning her south London seat of Lewisham West and East Dulwich in 2017. Anneliese Midgley Chief whip Midgley, a former political director for Unite, had been instrumental in helping Burnham with his Makerfield campaign. She was thought to be a contender for party chair but instead Burnham is seeking to harness her talent for organising as chief whip. Emma Reynolds Chief secretary to the Treasury A cabinet survival – sort of, she will attend cabinet – for the former environment secretary who was very close to Starmer, and more associated with his centrist Labour politics than the views of Burnham. The rationale appears to be that Reynolds can be both an overtly pro-business voice in the Treasury, as well as being an experienced hand in such matters to assist Healey. After losing her Wolverhampton North East seat in 2019, Reynolds spent five years working for the financial services lobby group TheCityUK. On returning to the Commons in 2024, Starmer immediately put her in the Treasury, where she stayed until becoming environment secretary. Douglas Alexander Scotland secretary A continued stay in the cabinet for another Commons returnee, who has filled the role since Starmer’s September 2025 reshuffle. Being Scotland secretary was not new ground for Alexander – it was one of several cabinet roles he held under Blair. After losing his Paisley and Renfrewshire South seat to the SNP in 2015, Alexander was out of parliament until returning at the 2024 election. Chris Bryant Northern Ireland secretary Another cabinet debutant, although Bryant has held a series of other ministerial roles and was in the shadow cabinet in opposition. The Rhondda MP is known as a safe pair of hands, whether with a ministerial brief or a tricky morning broadcast round, and would be expected to relish the particular complexities and sensitivities of the Northern Ireland job. An MP since 2001, having studied theology and served briefly as a Church of England priest, Bryant is an expert in Commons procedures, and stood unsuccessfully in 2019 to become Commons speaker. Stephen Kinnock Wales secretary Also a first dip of the toe into cabinet waters for the former minister for care in the health department. The MP for Aberafan Maesteg in south Wales – Aberavon before the constituency boundaries were redrawn – Kinnock has been in the Commons since 2015, after an earlier career spent in part at the European parliament. He is, of course, the son of the former Labour leader Neil Kinnock, while his wife, Helle Thorning-Schmidt, spent four years as Denmark’s prime minister. Alan Campbell Leader of the Commons No change in this sometimes technical but highly important role, with Campbell tasked with piloting Burnham’s legislative agenda through the Commons. An MP since 1997 who had held various relatively junior roles, Campbell was called to the cabinet in 2025, when Starmer’s mass reshuffle removed Lucy Powell from the job and – for a period – kicked her out of the cabinet altogether. Who’s out? Rachel Reeves Former chancellor Reeves had always wanted the job of chancellor and was proud to be the UK’s first female holder of the office. She had worked hard to instil ironclad fiscal discipline on Labour, sticking broadly to her self-imposed fiscal rules and enforcing spending curbs across departments. However, some in Labour blamed early missteps from her Treasury for Starmer’s downfall, starting with the cut to the winter fuel payment, but also the rise in national insurance for employers that her critics in business claim stymied the jobs market and growth. Reeves can, however, claim a record of having started to turn the economy around. She made a valiant effort to stay in her job but ultimately was judged too close to the Starmer project to stay in the Treasury. She is believed to have turned down another senior position. A former child chess champion and Oxford economics graduate, Reeves had also faced criticisms from some newspapers for having exaggerated her credentials as an economist on her LinkedIn page, having allowed some plagiarism to creep into a book she wrote on female economists and having inadvertently failed to pay for a landlord’s licence. In her departing statement, she said: “It has been the privilege of my life to serve as the chancellor of the exchequer. The economy today is stronger, fairer and more resilient because of the choices we have taken as a Labour government over the past two years. “Stability restored, investment delivered and reform to our economy under way … I’m proud to say that they have. And to every young woman and girl let my time in office show there should be no ceilings on your ambitions, your hopes or your dreams.” David Lammy Former foreign secretary Lammy has been a longstanding frontbencher after serving as a minister in the last New Labour governments. A former lawyer, he served as foreign secretary for Keir Starmer and then won a promotion to deputy prime minister and justice secretary when Angela Rayner stood down. He has been at the former prime minister’s side for many of his toughest moments. Such is his experience and standing that there was some speculation he might stay on in a different ministerial role. In a post on X announcing his departure, Lammy made it plain he had been happy to stay on but was not wanted. He wrote: “I would have been proud to continue serving in cabinet. But a new prime minister is entitled to build his own team, and I wish Andy Burnham and the new cabinet every success.” Darren Jones Former chief secretary to the prime minister From the centre of No 10 operations to nothing. As Jones put it in a bluntly worded social media post: “Andy Burnham has called to tell me I won’t be a part of his new cabinet. I wish him and his team every success.” An MP since 2017, Jones’s fairly rapid rise to the top table began with well-reviewed performances as chair of the business and trade committee. It began with the tricky if powerful role of Reeves’s number two as chief secretary to the Treasury. There he was so central to spending negotiations, that when Starmer undertook one of his several organisational revamps, as part of the September 2025 reshuffle, Jones took on the new and somewhat artificial role of chief secretary to the prime minister, tasked with leading change from No 10. Vague hints that Jones might contest for the Labour leadership came to nothing, and while – as his tweet indicated – he would have been happy to do another role, this was also not on the cards. Steve Reed Former housing secretary Reed was one of most loyal cabinet ministers to the Starmer administration, although he had made a play to keep his job in recent weeks by highlighting his achievements. An old ally of Morgan McSweeney, Starmer’s former chief of staff, Reed was a veteran of south London local government before entering parliament in 2012. He served as environment secretary before his current job and will now return to the backbenches. His letter to Burnham after his departure from government was somewhat spiky, warning him not to disadvantage London and also sending his hopes that those who were not loyal to Starmer will be loyal to the new prime minister. Peter Kyle Former business secretary Kyle took on the job of business secretary last year in the emergency reshuffle prompted by the departure of Angela Rayner over her tax affairs. It meant he found himself on flights to the US and China at a moment’s notice at a critical time for negotiations over trade and tech companies. He previously served as science secretary – a role that is now likely to be folded into the business department. Kyle entered parliament in 2015 and has been open about his struggles to get there. He had difficulties at school owing to dyslexia and left, in his own words, “without any usable” qualifications. He made it to university in his 20s after several failed attempts. An ally of Wes Streeting and Starmer, Kyle appears to be departing from cabinet largely to make way for closer supporters of Burnham although he has also been criticised for a perception that he has been too open towards tech companies. Richard Hermer Former attorney general Hermer was probably Starmer’s closest friend in politics. A fellow human rights lawyer, he was made a peer so that he could join the prime minister’s first cabinet. However, he quickly became a bogeyman for the rightwing press, which disliked his role in signing over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and generally espousing views on the liberal left. His past legal work, including his representation of Gerry Adams and advice to Caribbean countries seeking reparations, has been raked over by Tories who have demanded that he publicly recuse himself from some areas. The criticism was not confined to the right. Maurice Glasman, the Blue Labour founder and associate of the US vice-president, JD Vance, called Hermer “an arrogant, progressive fool who thinks that law is a replacement for politics”. Starmer steadfastly stuck by him though, and Hermer has been an invaluable source of counsel and friendship through his final months as premier. He was also a bastion of progressive thought in a cabinet that many in the Labour party felt had veered too far away from core party values. Liz Kendall Former science and technology secretary Also to be filed under: no surprise here. Kendall has always been on the right of Labour and ideologically much closer to Starmer than to the new PM. An ever-present figure on Starmer’s frontbench, the Leicester West MP started as work and pensions secretary, the job she had shadowed in opposition, before moving to the science brief in the wholesale cabinet reshuffle of September last year. An MP from 2010, Kendall supported David Miliband in the Labour leadership election of that year. Five years later, she stood herself, coming last of the four candidates when Jeremy Corbyn became leader. In a tweeted letter, Kendall thanked Starmer and other cabinet colleagues, saying she was ready to support Burnham “in any way I can”. Jo Stevens Former Wales secretary Also not expected to stay on, the Cardiff East MP has been a fixture in the Wales office, filling the brief in opposition and then government since 2021, having previously been Starmer’s shadow culture secretary. A backer of Starmer when he stood to be Labour leader, Stevens had served as shadow Wales secretary under Corbyn, but resigned in opposition to Corbyn’s decision to back formal moves for the UK to leave the EU. Hilary Benn Former Northern Ireland secretary Some had speculated that Benn could be among ministers to stay in their job and provide continuity, given that he is not overtly partisan and was largely seen as doing a quietly good job in a sensitive brief. But Benn tweeted that he has gone. It is a return to the backbenches for a Labour grandee, in parliament for more than 25 years, who held a series of ministerial jobs under Blair and Brown.
