title: From Bernie to Mamdani, how the Occupy movement transformed American politics
author: Natasha Lennard
summary: Yotam Marom, who helped lead Occupy Wall Street, discusses why power must be built through movements, not simply through elected officials
body_text: Yotam Marom knows why the Occupy Wall Street movement fell apart 15 years ago. The New York-based organizer and author was a key participant in the nationwide constellation of encampments and rolling protests that brought tens of thousands of people into its fold. But the movement could not withstand police raids, evictions, a bitter winter and, as Marom sees it, an internal “politics of powerlessness”, which mistook a healthy distrust of institutional power for a failure to build a strong, coherent strategy for political change. Occupy splintered within a few short months and never seriously revived. As he recounts in his new book, For Louder Days: Reaching Beyond a Politics of Powerlessness, Marom has again and again seen similar dynamics weigh down social movements in his work as an organizer and facilitator. He founded the Wildfire Project, a training organization for grassroots groups, and has worked with organizations including the Sunrise Movement agitating against climate decimation, the abolitionist Dream Defenders fighting for racial justice, the Uncommitted movement to end Democratic party support for Israel’s war crimes, tenants unions battling landlords, and more. A lot has also shifted for the broader left and its relationship to power since 2011: a democratic socialist is mayor of New York City and a slate of serious leftwing candidates are challenging establishment Democrats for congressional seats. I first met Marom back in the heady days of Occupy. When we spoke recently, we discussed what movements have learned, what they must continue to learn, and why power must be built through movements, not simply through elected officials. We first met at Occupy Wall Street. That was a hugely politicizing and lesson-filled time for both of us, and many others. Beyond your personal experience, why do you think it might be important to look back on Occupy now? We’re in this moment in which we’re seeing some winning for the left, including winning actual governing power. I think there is a pretty direct through line from Occupy Wall Street to here. There are a bunch of ways in which we fell short, obviously. But Occupy brought thousands of people into the movement, trained hundreds of leaders, and led to the foundation of a bunch of different organizations. And it changed the public’s common sense around class in this country; it introduced the narrative of the 99% versus the 1%. It’s pretty hard to see how you get something like Bernie [Sanders]’s run in 2016 without that, and now this opening of mass socialist politics, with the elections of the Squad and Zohran [Mamdani] and a slate of DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] candidates in New York. Your key takeaway from Occupy, and from a lot of the organizing work you’ve done since, is the notion of the “politics of powerlessness” and how it harms movements. What is the politics of powerlessness, why is it a problem, and with that in mind, what do you mean by power? So, first of all, when I talk about power, I mean power to bring about a society whose institutions are geared toward people getting their material needs met and thriving. We want a powerful multiracial working-class movement that can bring about the world we all deserve. The politics of powerlessness is a set of ideas and behaviors that turn us inward, away from our opponent (the forces of capitalism and state violence) and the public, toward – and often against – one another. It often looks like a fear of leaders within the movement, a narrow and individualistic way of understanding identity like race and gender rather than a systemic one, and a kind of belonging that’s meant to protect our spaces and feel good to the people already in them rather than one that’s meant to welcome in the many millions of people our movements need if we hope to win. I think a lot of that stems from fear of our much more powerful opponent (billionaires, the far-right government, the police), and despair at the state of the world. I came up in a political generation that didn’t really believe leftwing political movements could win, and the natural thing to do, if you don’t believe you can win, is to abandon the risky and difficult work of building power and focus instead on being right, being surrounded by people who are like us, using our differences as weapons against each other. And then that creates unhealthy movements that people mostly don’t want to be a part of, and we lose. I do think we’re in a special moment of seeing in real-time some organizations intervening in that dynamic – most notably this electoral insurgency around the country and especially in New York with Zohran and this DSA slate – where they’re essentially saying, “No, we want power. We want to govern. We know it’s risky and complicated, but it’s the only way.” Organizations who take winning seriously do the hard work of crafting good strategy. They get over their ambivalence about leadership. They create structures and processes that let huge numbers of people feel that they belong and are part of the project. Is there a risk of overstating this moment of winning? We are still in the context of power concentrated with billionaires, a burning planet, authoritarian rule, our inability to stop Israel’s ongoing genocide, brutal border regimes; I could go on. For sure. In New York, where I live, we might be feeling on top of the world – Knicks in five! Zohran and the recent DSA sweep! And our movements are more mature than they were 15 years ago at Occupy. We have a lot more assets at our disposal now, and we’re a little more practiced at winning and building organizations that want to win, and that’s a huge deal. But, of course, we’re only at the beginning of this trajectory. And around the country, a lot of people don’t feel this way at all. The far right controls the federal government; they’re gutting the institutions that would make it possible to replace them. We’re facing the ticking timebomb of climate change. We’re up against some of the most powerful people who have ever walked the planet, who run some of the most violent institutions that humans have ever designed. We have a very long road ahead of us. When movements face serious barriers and real loss, we often feel the temptation to shrink – to narrow the playing field so that we can feel powerful in our tiny corner rather than powerless in the big wide world. I think that can happen here in New York, too. In your book you describe a particular moment on an organizing retreat with the organization CAAAV (Committee Against Anti-Asian Violence), and how the group shifted towards building a strong strategy, and the difficulty that can entail. The book is really full of stories, and one of my favorites is about CAAAV, a New York City community organization that organizes Chinese and Bengali tenants in Manhattan’s Chinatown and in Queens. In a strategy retreat years ago, they faced this hard moment of having to decide whether to continue doing what they’re doing, which is comfortable and known and righteous, or to choose to prioritize some things over others even though it was painful. They decided – against this enormous pressure that most groups have to maintain the status quo – to shut down a chunk of their organizing in Queens and reprioritize the people, time and money they had spent on a particular campaign in Chinatown, which they would probably have lost if they didn’t. But it was heartbreaking. It meant having to go back to the projects in Queens and say, “We’re going to close this campaign down. This isn’t a winnable campaign, and we’re not going to organize this building any more.” It meant that some of the people on staff who were hired for that work could lose their jobs. But there was this very powerful moment where they came to grips with this. In fact, a young woman at risk of losing her job said very bravely, “No, we have to do this. We have to make this choice.” Years later we can see that the choices they made there led to their sister organization, CAAAV Voice, being one of the early endorsers of Mamdani, and then playing a significant role in organizing a Chinese and Bengali base for his victory. But none of them knew at the time that that’s what it was going to be. The important thing then was telling the truth, being willing to be in conflict with each other and lose some things. That’s what leads to good strategy. It’s what leads to organizations healthy enough to carry it out. It’s also what leads to real transformation. Theorists like Anton Jäger have criticized the last 15 years of leftist movements and uprisings for failing to translate this work into mass politics and strong leftwing parties. What sort of structures – institutions, infrastructures – does the left need for power, in your view? In the same way as we’re not going to have real meaningful social transformation by hopping from one big movement moment to the next, we’re also not going to get it by hopping from one election to the next. That’s not going to happen. I also have fantasies of “the big party”, but I don’t feel qualified to say what exactly the form is. What would be wise for us to do is ask, “What would the big party be made up of?” We should build up those institutions and capacities with or without the umbrella. It’s made up of the capacity to mount an electoral challenge and govern. It’s the capacity to wage campaigns against a boss or a landlord and win concessions. The space to welcome people in and become politically educated and meet each other and have social relationships that are good and healthy. A compelling vision for this society. And a relationship between these different things, especially the non-electoral power-building slice of the movement and the electoral one, so that they really mutually support each other. Yotam Marom is an organizer, facilitator and writer based in Brooklyn, New York, with over 20 years of participation in movements and experience in facilitation, strategic planning, group dynamics and conflict work Natasha Lennard is a columnist for the Intercept and a professor of critical journalism at The New School in New York City. Her work has appeared in the Nation, Bookforum, Dissent and the New York Times, among others. She is the author of Being Numerous: Essays on Non-Fascist Life and the forthcoming On Un/Certainty

title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez should run for president
author: Bhaskar Sunkara
summary: The congresswoman can run a serious national campaign on the left and pull a movement in behind it. She should get in early
body_text: In the summer of 2018, almost no one thought Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez could beat Joe Crowley. Crowley was a 10-term incumbent, the fourth-ranking Democrat in the House, a man some thought would one day be speaker. A 28-year-old former bartender and democratic socialist was the longest of long shots to succeed him. But ever since she did, the political establishment has been trying to decide whether to take her seriously. For a while it decided not to. The Missouri representative Emanuel Cleaver said the Democratic caucus did not need her “sniping”, while the then senator Claire McCaskill dismissed her as a “bright and shiny new object”. Ocasio-Cortez seemed to enjoy the response. Asked on 60 Minutes whether she wanted people to underestimate her, she said: “Absolutely. That’s how I won my primary.” American socialism has produced dazzling individuals before. A little more than a century ago, Eugene Debs won nearly a million votes for president, while his socialist party sent Victor Berger to Congress, elected more than a thousand of its members to office and ran city halls from Schenectady to Milwaukee. Then it was gone, broken by wartime repression and its own splits, and eventually absorbed into a New Deal coalition that adopted parts of its program while denying it an independent political role. At best, it has been honored as a tradition of noble campaigners, a moral compass for the country rather than a contender for power. As Senator Ted Kennedy said of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) founder after his death in 1989: “Michael Harrington never believed that we could not do better and never stopped urging us to try harder.” Ocasio-Cortez never seemed content to be solely a voice of conscience, however. On Medicare for All and the Green New Deal, she made herself the most visible defender of the Berniecrat program and built a mass following among young Americans. In parts of Europe, the anger of a downwardly mobile generation hardened into support for the populist right. In the United States, Bernie Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez won a good part of that generation for the left instead. A majority of Americans under 35 and of Democrats overall now tell pollsters they view socialism favorably, and the DSA has grown to more than 120,000 members. Yet unlike the socialism of Debs, which was a movement of miners, garment workers and machinists, today’s socialism is built disproportionately by the young and the credentialed. Like the Democratic establishment they loathe, the left’s candidates have run strongest among college-educated professionals in cities and weakest among non-college, older and manual workers, especially those in more rural areas. It hasn’t always been clear that AOC could help broaden the left’s existing base rather than just deepen it. Her early trouble largely involved language and communication. Sanders moved people with plain talk about millionaires and billionaires. Ocasio-Cortez, despite being inspired by him, would sometimes drift into the dialect of the progressive non-profit and academic world, using terms more familiar in seminar rooms than union halls. In 2022, she scolded Democrats who objected to the use of “Latinx”, a term used by 3% of Hispanics. She offered “Latine” as an improvement, a fix to a problem most Latinos didn’t know they had. Or take the language of the Green New Deal resolution she introduced in an attempt to bridge the gap between environmentalism and the old producerist politics of the left. That resolution promised to repair the historic oppression of Indigenous peoples, communities of color, migrant communities, deindustrialized communities, depopulated rural communities, the poor, low-income workers, women, elderly people, unhoused people, people with disabilities, and youth. Of course, nobody on that list is un-wronged. But itemizing members of the same economic class as discrete interest groups was the opposite of how the 2016 Sanders campaign spoke, and of how the left traditionally has. It was the scholarly language of intersectionality, not the commonsense solidarity she was trying to inspire. Nor were her loyalties as fixed as her admirers assumed. Ryan Grim’s reporting in his book The Squad shows that in 2019 she gave consideration to Elizabeth Warren, who had courted her and believed her backing would settle the nomination. After Bernie Sanders’s heart attack, however, Ocasio-Cortez endorsed the ailing senator at his most perilous point and became the most effective surrogate he had. The left had sometimes faulted her for how she weighed confrontation against getting along inside the Democratic party. In that moment, it got the version of her it wanted. The direction she has traveled since has been encouraging. After Donald Trump’s victory in 2024, AOC went to dozens of her constituents who had voted for both her and Trump and asked them why. She wanted to understand them rather than lecture them. Their answers – that she and Trump both read as outsiders, that both sounded like they were on the side of working people – informed her politics in the months to come. Some of the people who once formed the base of the left had split their tickets or stayed home, and she was one of the Democrats willing to walk toward them instead of writing them off. In going to them, she was approaching one of the central questions of our era. In 1992, nearly two-thirds of working-class voters backed Bill Clinton for president. By 2024, the Democratic share of working-class voters was 45%, while among middle- and upper-class voters it had climbed to 68%. The lines crossed. The party of Roosevelt has become the party of the diploma, and its strategists have made peace with it, betting on affluent suburbanites and young professionals to sustain the party’s future. The math might work for those looking to win elections with 51% of the vote, but not for those looking to create a majority for sweeping change. In his long career and in his first run for president, Sanders offered a glimpse of how such a majority might be built. He held Vermont’s rather conservative Northeast Kingdom for decades and ran well ahead of his party among independents nationally in 2016, and a good deal of that rested on the sharp line he drew between himself and the Democratic establishment. Ocasio-Cortez will have to draw that same line despite being far more of a Democrat than Sanders ever was, more embedded in its caucus, and more implicated in its choices. The evolution of her rhetoric shows that she might be up for the challenge. On the “Fighting Oligarchy” tour with Sanders through 2025, she was talking to parts of the country the Democratic party had long since abandoned. More than 12,500 people turned out for a rally in Nampa, Idaho, a bigger crowd than the number of registered Democrats in the entire county. Twenty thousand came out in deep-red Utah. Whatever the tours’ ultimate efficacy, the US’s two most prominent leftists were showing their 50-state ambitions. Crowds are not a party, but Ocasio-Cortez has both. She is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, part of its socialists-in-office bloc, and that affiliation ties her to a concrete worldview, to an ideology and a history, even if she has at times seemed a less-than-enthusiastic member of an unruly organization. But DSA has plenty going for it, including thousands of talented organizers and a roster of hundreds of elected officials that includes the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani. There are other capable progressives weighing a run in 2028, such as the California congressman Ro Khanna. However, none of them can do the two things AOC can do at once: run a serious national campaign as one of the most recognized figures in the country, and pull an entire movement into being behind it. The last time the left had a standard-bearer with her reach, in Sanders, it expanded the largest socialist organization the country had seen in generations. A credible Ocasio-Cortez campaign would do more, and perhaps be a part of building a leftwing infrastructure rooted in working-class life and built to outlast any one candidate. The only thing left is for Ocasio-Cortez to announce her campaign, and to announce early. She should remember the lesson of 2015. Sanders got in as a protest candidate, with no national organization and no expectation of winning. He spent a year building what he needed to compete, and by the time he had it, Hillary Clinton had the nomination sewn up. Ocasio-Cortez should move decisively to consolidate the left behind her and ward off potential challengers. But consolidating the left is the easy part. To win, and to transform the country, she will have to speak to people’s anger and draw workers of every background into her coalition. That’s the longest of long shots, and it’s worth taking. Bhaskar Sunkara is a Guardian US columnist. He is the president of the Nation, the founding editor of Jacobin, and the author of The Socialist Manifesto: The Case for Radical Politics in an Era of Extreme Inequality

title: US claims of Cuba’s ‘unique threat’ jar with reality of hunger and blackouts
author: Ruaridh Nicoll in Havana
summary: State department’s 100-page report is latest push in Trump administration campaign to bring down government
body_text: The US government’s latest allegations that Cuba is behind “many of the most significant upheavals in recent American political history” and that its leaders pose “a unique threat to American homeland security” have come as startling revelations to those living under the six-month-long US oil blockade in Havana, where desperate people search through piles of uncollected rubbish for food, or else swelter at home in 24-hour-plus blackouts. The unsigned 100-page report, Cuba: Capital of 21st-Century Communism, published by the US state department on Monday, blames Havana for everything from “the George Floyd riots to the rise of antifa to the explosion of pro-terrorist activism on American college campuses”. It is the latest push in a maximum-pressure campaign to bring down the island’s government that began with the abduction of Nicolás Maduro, the president of Cuba’s ally Venezuela, on 3 January. Since then, Cuba has been brought to a standstill by the oil blockade, sanctions on foreign businesses and threats of a military intervention. It also seems to be an attempt to “other” those on the US left before November’s midterm elections. “Cuba’s assault on the United States was never, at root, a quarrel over economic policy or sovereignty or even ownership of a particular territory,” the report reads. “It was a revolution against western civilisation itself – waged, in part, via the novel and insidious method of persuading the children of the west to turn against their own inheritance.” “Fidel would have been quite proud of this,” said one amused Cuban as he read it. The US state department, run by the Cuban-American Marco Rubio, refused to name the author, but it is clearly someone who knows their history. “Almost immediately after taking Havana in January 1959, Castro began plotting armed assaults against neighbouring governments – launching expeditions against Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Nicaragua and Panama in just that year alone,” it reads. What it fails to mention is that Haiti was then run by François “Papa Doc” Duvalier, who killed an estimated 60,000 of his own people; the Dominican Republic by Rafael Trujillo, who launched the “parsley massacre”, killing between 20,000 to 35,000 Haitians; and Nicaragua by the Somoza family, who are credited with the murder of up to 50,000 Nicaraguans. Although the report provides no new evidence, there is a suspicious emphasis on race. The supposedly remarkable success of Cuban intelligence at infiltrating US institutions was due to a soft spot for “glamorous Latins”, it quotes an intelligence officer saying to the Miami Herald in 2002: “‘We’re much more open to Latins than we are to people with steel teeth and a Slavic accent.’” It also bemoans the ideological commitment of the spies Cuba recruited, while failing to mention either that several were inspired by the CIA’s attempts to assassinate Castro, or the shelter the US offered to the exiles Luis Posada Carriles and Orlando Bosch, who organised the bombing of Cubana flight 455 in 1976, killing 73 people. Most jarringly, the report groups together the US’s long internal struggle around civil rights and social reform and reframes it as a battle between the forces of foreign actors and “western civilisation”, lingering over groups such as the Black Panthers, which it credits to Cuba. While several black revolutionaries found sanctuary on the island, most famously Assata Shakur, who had a $2m price on her head for the killing of a New Jersey state trooper, the experience was not perhaps as conspiratorial as the author suggests. In interviews, Nehanda Abiodun, one of the mentioned fugitives, said her politics and revolutionary rage came from her experience growing up in 1970s New York, not out of any love for Cuba, whose government she came to resent for muzzling her in return for refuge. She used to say that the first thing that happened on landing was being racially profiled by the Cuban police. If she was part of a well-oiled international conspiracy, it didn’t show. For five years the Cuban government has not even been able to afford to feed its 9.5 million people, who mostly blame it for the crisis. But the report is ready for this: “To mistake Cuba’s poverty for harmlessness is to misunderstand the threat entirely. Its material weakness was never the measure of its danger.” It concludes: “Today, Cuban agents and operatives maintain a foothold in hundreds of front groups, activist organisations, solidarity centres, and ideological NGO and nonprofit networks. These groups collectively represent one of the single largest, most sophisticated and dangerous vectors for hostile foreign influence in modern American history.” In the run-up to the report’s release, Miguel Díaz-Canel, Cuba’s president, said the US had fallen prey to a “new and more dangerous version of McCarthyism”. But perhaps the more damning criticism came from a Cuban academic who preferred to remain nameless: “It reads just like a report Cuba’s state media might write about the United States.”

title: Hunter Biden for president? Stranger things have happened
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: Once Republicans’ favourite punchline, Joe Biden’s son is now building an online following by trolling JD Vance, taunting Trump and embracing the absurdity of US politics, writes Arwa Mahdawi
body_text: What sort of longshot candidate do we reckon is going to run for US president in 2028? The Rock? Kim Kardashian? Kermit the Frog? US politics has become so debased that being rich, famous and a natural-born citizen (sorry, Zohran Mamdani) now seem to be the only qualifications required for a job in the White House. Which is why you shouldn’t entirely write off murmurings that Hunter Biden might be interested in following in his daddy’s presidential footsteps. When asked by a Fox News reporter about Hunter’s 2028 odds last month, Donald Trump suggested Joe Biden’s prodigal son might “do well”. If other “basket case[s]” in the Democratic party could do well, Trump added, then Hunter probably had a shot. Various analysts appear to agree. “Could Hunter Biden run for office? Don’t rule it out,” a recent Times headline blared. The article quotes a Biden biographer saying: “With a character like Hunter Biden in a populist, social media-driven political environment, you have to never say never.” You would definitely have said “never” a couple of years ago: Hunter wasn’t exactly the US’s favourite person during his dad’s presidency. His various scandals made him a target for Maga and a headache for Democrats. But in recent months, Hunter has reinvented himself as a social-media star. Since reactivating his X account in May, the former first son has posted an average of 23 times a day – Elon Musk-levels of posting. Except while Elon is tweeting about how “whites are a rapidly dying minority”, Hunter is cracking self-deprecating jokes about drugs and gaining fans across the political spectrum, with some calling him the “Maga whisperer”. Writing on X in June, Biden said he’d gladly take the title. “Left, right, D or R we all want the same things,” Hunter added. “We’re being divided on purpose by the Epstein Elite Oligarch class because as long as we’re at each other’s throats, they get fat and rich off of our misery.” Amen to that. Still, despite his refreshing political commentary, I’m not sure we should be treating the man as a folk hero or a Maga whisperer quite yet. It seems to me Hunter’s comeback isn’t so much motivated by political ambitions as by his millions of dollars of debt. He’s always been good at capitalising on his last name, and I suspect he’s realised he can parlay being provocative online into monetisable opportunities. To that end, Hunter has been going on every podcast that will have him, including sitting down with the far-right conspiracy theorist Candace Owens and the white nationalist Nick Fuentes. He’s also launched a paid Substack called Where’s Hunter? (a reference to one of Trump’s favourite catchphrases) and joked about starting an OnlyFans. Look, if you’re going to milk your famous name, at least make sure you’re not boring. (Trump’s spawn have failed spectacularly in this regard.) And Hunter’s new Extremely Online persona may be occasionally unhinged, but it’s not boring. On Saturday, for example, Hunter went on the progressive commentator Jennifer Welch’s podcast and joked that America’s biggest problem wasn’t “oligarchy”, but “closetocracy”, or the angry “closeted gay mafia” of Republicans in DC. This is relevant, Hunter said, because he believes the “internal conflict creates so much vitriol inside a person that they take it out on the rest of the world”. Hunter added that while he didn’t get a “gaydar ping” from Senator Ted Cruz, the man definitely gave him a “really kinky weird” vibe. I don’t know that this particular conversation was big or clever, but I’m sure it annoyed Cruz, so there’s that. Speaking of things that aren’t big or clever, Hunter’s also been trolling JD Vance following the vice-president’s creepy comments about Biden’s “suggestive” ice-cream licking. (I’ll spare you JD’s thoughts on corn dogs.) On Sunday, which was National Ice Cream Day for those who celebrate, Hunter posted a photo of himself licking an ice-cream with the caption: “Hey @JDVance. I wish I knew how to quit you.” And Hunter hasn’t minced his words when it comes to Vance’s boss. In a recent interview, he said that if he were sitting next to Trump, he’d tell him to “go fuck his fucking self”. He then noted that he’d challenged Donald Trump Jr to a UFC fight “three times” but hadn’t heard back. He added: “That’s how I’m going to pay all my debt.” Good luck with that, mate. Hunter has zero chance of ever winning a presidential nomination, but I’d bet good money he’d beat Don Jr in a cage fight. The US may be divided, but that’s a Biden-Trump rematch I think everyone in the country could get behind. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: Senate committee advances nomination of Trump intelligence pick Jay Clayton
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Committee voted 9-8 to advance Clayton’s nomination to serve as intelligence chief despite Democratic opposition
body_text: The Senate intelligence committee on Tuesday advanced the nomination of Jay Clayton to serve as the US intelligence director, despite criticism from Democrats. Donald Trump had nominated Clayton, now the top federal prosecutor in the southern district of New York, for the role of the director of national intelligence (DNI) last month after the departure of Tulsi Gabbard. Intelligence committee members questioned Clayton at a hearing last week, and its Republican chair, Tom Cotton, announced that it had reported his nomination favorably by a 9-8 vote, teeing him up for a future vote on his confirmation by the full Senate. “Jay Clayton is a highly qualified nominee with a deep experience combatting a wide range of national security threats,” Cotton said in a statement. “I’m pleased that the Senate Intelligence Committee voted to advance his nomination to be Director of National Intelligence,” he added. Cotton did not provide a breakdown of how lawmakers voted. The committee is composed of nine Republicans and eight Democrats, and Mark Warner, a spokesperson for the Democratic vice-chair, said he had opposed the nomination. Democratic senator Ron Wyden released a statement announcing his no vote, accusing Clayton of “spreading conspiracies” about mail-in voting and denying Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election. “From start to finish, Mr Clayton has proven himself incapable of telling the truth or demonstrating an iota of independence from Donald Trump,” Wyden said. At his hearing last week, members of the Democratic minority criticized Clayton, a former Wall Street attorney who served as the chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), for previous statements he made echoing Trump’s claim that US elections have been marred by fraud. They also aired concerns about politicization at the office of the DNI, which serves to coordinate the nation’s intelligence agencies. It is unclear when his nomination will be voted on by the Senate. If confirmed, he would take over from Bill Pulte, a federal housing official who Trump appointed as acting DNI following Gabbard’s departure. Democrats strenuously objected to Pulte’s installation in that office, decrying him as a loyalist to the president who may try to use its powers to retaliate against his enemies. As director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency director, Pulte had last year referred several Democratic officeholders as well as the Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook for mortgage fraud. His predecessor, Gabbard, had raised similar concerns when she appeared alongside FBI agents who raided an election office in Georgia earlier this year. Administration officials later said she was running her own investigation of the 2020 election. Clayton’s confirmation may nonetheless clear a path for Congress to renew the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), a key spy tool that had its legal authorization expire last month in part due to a blockade by Democrats incensed by Trump’s appointment of Pulte. Since taking over as acting DNI, Pulte has reportedly fired dozens of staffers from the office. In his statement, Cotton signaled support for those purges, saying he looked forward to working with Clayton to “continue reforming the Office of Director of National Intelligence”.

title: Hegseth tells Senate war on Iran has so far cost $37.5bn at hearing to request more funds
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington and Lauren Gambino
summary: Defense secretary has asked Senate appropriations committee for nearly $88bn more to continue effort
body_text: The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth told the Senate on Tuesday that the US-Israel war on Iran had cost $37.5bn so far, as he faced lawmakers furious over the conflict’s soaring price tag and the deaths last week of three American service members. During an appearance before the Senate appropriations committee, Hegseth, whose opening remarks were repeatedly interrupted by protesters, provided an updated account of the war’s cost – up from previous estimates – and defended the Trump administration’s roughly $88bn supplemental funding request, calling it “urgent, necessary”. Alongside the chair of the joint chiefs, Gen Dan Caine, Hegseth argued that the Pentagon was running low on cash to keep the fight going. Of the total request, as much as $67.1bn is earmarked specifically to cover the costs of the Iran war effort. “Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls,” Hegseth told the Senate panel, warning that it would threaten the defense department’s ability to “pay our service members, rapidly replenish equipment and munitions, and sustain vital operations without disruption”. It was the defense secretary’s first sustained public questioning since a brief ceasefire collapsed and the war roared back to life. At least two US soldiers were killed in an Iranian attack on Friday, and another died in Iraq destroying an Iranian drone, pushing the American death toll since February to 17. Nearly 100 troops have been wounded in the conflict, officials confirm, though most injuries were minor. Patty Murray, the committee’s Democratic vice-chair, demanded Hegseth explain what the war had actually achieved, accusing the administration of shifting its rationale by the week and warning the conflict risked becoming “another forever war”. “We hear a different rationale for this war every few days,” Murray said in her opening remarks, noting the justification had moved from pre-empting threats that “did not exist” to regime change, then to dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme and navy, and now, she said, to simply reopening the strait of Hormuz, a waterway that was “fully open, toll-free, before this war began”. “Here we are, five months later”, she continued. “The strait is closed. The ceasefire hasn’t just disintegrated – this war is now spiraling out of control again.” Under questioning from lawmakers, Hegseth cast the funding request as the price of deterrence rather than admitting failure, and framed the Pentagon’s overhaul under the US president as a break from what he described as years of slow bureaucracy. “The best way to create peace is to prepare for war, to deter it,” Hegseth told the panel, arguing the department was “building a force so capable that it would be absurd for anyone to challenge it”. Hegseth said the $21bn readiness portion of the request would cover military pay, replace equipment used in recent operations and stabilize fuel shortfalls, while the $46bn capability portion would expand production of “solid rocket motors, Jdams [joint direct attack munitions], hypersonics and counter-drone capabilities”. Without the funds, he warned, the department faced “critical shortfalls” that threaten its ability to pay troops and replenish munitions, and he cautioned that failing to fund the Pentagon at $1.5tn was “the greatest threat that our nation faces”. Some Democrats, including Chris Coons of Delaware, plan to direct criticism at Russell Vought, director of office of management and budget, who is not testifying but who earlier told US Congress that the war’s running cost was about $30bn, a figure that is largely believed by experts to be a severe undercount. Hegseth and Caine faced potential threats from within their own party. Susan Collins of Maine, chair of the committee, and Alaska’s Lisa Murkowski, two prominent Republicans, have both crossed the aisle to back war-powers resolutions aimed at reining in the president’s authority over the conflict. Collins, who is facing a competitive re-election contest, has previously voiced frustration that the administration’s strategy for the war seems to shift almost daily. During the hearing, she asked Hegseth about the effect on military exercises if the supplemental funding is not provided. The defense secretary said that current and future training “would have to be curtailed” if the Pentagon does not get its budget needs met urgently. Senator John Kennedy, a Republican of Louisiana, pressed the panelists on the situation in the strait of Hormuz, asking if Iran will impose tolls on commercial vessels passing through the vital waterway which carried about a fifth of global oil and gas supplies before the war. “That’s a hypothetical question,” Caine replied, “and I don’t know the answer to that.” “Guys, we need straight answers,” Kennedy shot back. Both congressional chambers have passed a war-powers resolution urging the president to seek congressional authorization to continue military operations in Iran. Asked why the administration had not yet sought congressional approval for the war, Hegseth said it was the view of his department that “standalone Article II authorities exist for us to conduct this operation on behalf of the defense of the American people”. The defense secretary evaded the lawmaker’s question about whether he would use the approval of any supplemental funding as a “substitute for explicit congressional authorization”. House representatives have separately accused the Pentagon of stonewalling on basic figures: Betty McCollum, the top Democrat on the House defense appropriations panel, said the department has missed a deadline to detail war costs and has not disclosed how many precision munitions remain after the military burned through thousands of them in Iran.

title: House passes spending bill to head off government shutdown before midterms
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Measure authorizes spending until 4 December as Republicans seek to avoid volatile issue in election season
body_text: The US House of Representatives on Tuesday approved a stopgap measure to head off a government shutdown until early December, with its Republican leaders seeking to defuse a volatile issue in the run-up to the November midterm elections. The continuing resolution authorizing government spending until 4 December passed by a vote of 220-205, roughly along party lines. It next heads to the Senate, where it will need to win bipartisan support to clear the chamber. The government’s current spending authority expires on 30 September, but top Republicans had argued the measure’s passage was necessary to ensure that Democrats do not block government funding measures in the Senate. They did so last year for a record 43 days in protest against the expiration of tax credits that lowered some healthcare costs, and twice again this year, to push for reforms to immigration enforcement operations after the killings of two US citizens in Minneapolis. “Our conference refuses to let the obstruction and inaction of Senate Democrats trigger another manufactured shutdown at the end of September. That is why we are acting before a funding lapse crisis, not in response to it,” said Tom Cole, the House appropriations committee chair who spearheaded the resolution. Earlier on Tuesday, lawmakers agreed to move forward on the stopgap measure and a budget framework paving the way for a $95bn party-line package, in a 214-211 vote roughly along party lines. The constitution tasks Congress with authorizing government spending, and the Senate and House every year attempt to pass 12 appropriations measures granting those authorities. But lawmakers often miss those deadlines, forcing them to resort to passing continuing resolutions that extend governmental departments’ ability to operate. While the House has passed three appropriations measures for the 2027 fiscal year beginning on 1 October, the Senate – where the top Democrat and Republican say they remain far apart in government spending talks – has approved none, nor have any advanced through committees, a key procedural step. Republican leaders ‌in the chamber said they were negotiating with Senate Democrats on their own short-term funding bill. Rosa DeLauro, the Democratic ranking member on the House appropriations committee, denied that her party was seeking a shutdown, and called passage of a stopgap funding measure “necessary”. However, she opposed the Republican-backed measure, calling it “hastily” conceived and noting it appropriated funds for the border patrol without “substantial reforms” to the agency that plays a major role in Donald Trump’s crackdown on undocumented immigrants. “We are putting the cart before the horse by considering this legislation without understanding the full scope of what is needed to continue operations through December 4,” DeLauro said. Should the Senate fail to pass the measure, funding negotiations will intensify from September, when Congress returns to Washington DC after spending most of August in recess with the end-of-the-month deadline to prevent a shutdown near. Those talks could be complicated by the approaching midterm elections, in which Democrats hope they can retake control of the House and potentially the Senate, where they can only win a majority by picking up at least three seats in states that backed Trump two years ago.

title: Wednesday briefing: How Trump’s Iran gamble has produced a crisis reshaping the global order
author: Hettie O'Brien
summary: In today’s newsletter: ​A White House operating without expertise, strategy or restraint ​is stuck in a conflict with no easy way out, which is sending economic shockwaves far beyond its own borders
body_text: Good morning. Within two hours of entering No 10 on Monday afternoon, Andy Burnham had his first call with Donald Trump. After chit-chatting about the football (both agreed England had an “excellent tournament”) and Manchester (our new prime minister invited the president to visit the city Trump once described as a “town”), they got on to far trickier territory: the strait of Hormuz. The US has attacked Iran for the eleventh consecutive night, hitting aircraft hangars and drone storage sites across the country. It came after Iran launched retaliatory strikes on US air bases and neighbouring Gulf states, which have accused it of deliberately targeting desalination plants that are essential to life in the region. Each side now claims it is preventing the other from gaining control over the strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of the world’s oil was shipped before the war began. Vessels carrying crucial shipments of oil, gas and fertiliser remain at a standstill. “Operation Epic Fury” started with the aim of regime change. Since then, its objective has morphed into reopening the strait and undoing the damage caused by the US and Israel’s decision to start the war. The president drastically underestimated Iran’s capacity for enduring pain, and is now trying to bomb his way out of a conflict that he created. For today’s First Edition, I spoke to Vali Nasr, professor of International Affairs and Middle East Studies and author of Iran’s Grand Strategy, about the war over the world’s most critical bottleneck. That’s after the headlines. Five big stories UK politics | Andy Burnham is under mounting pressure to explain how he will pay for his policy pledges as he implored his new cabinet to examine “all possible ways” to tackle the cost of living crisis. UK news | A man has appeared in court charged with the murder of the former MP and Reform UK spokesperson Ann Widdecombe. Joshua Kerry, 28, is accused of killing the former Conservative minister at her home in Haytor, Devon, by hitting her on the head with a hammer 21 times. Middle East | The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, told the Senate the US-Israel war on Iran had cost $37.5bn so far, as he faced lawmakers furious over the conflict’s soaring price tag and the deaths last week of three American service members. Climate crisis | About 23 million people will be banned from using hosepipes by this weekend, as England and Wales moves closer to drought status. Ukraine | Volodymyr Zelenskyy has fired Ukraine’s commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi and offered a “prominent position” to the defence minister he sacked last week in a move that sparked nationwide protests. In depth: ‘In his mind, this was a legacy-building transformation’ “I’m not going to start wars,” Donald Trump told voters on election night in 2024. His decision to bomb Iran on 28 February in partnership with Benjamin Netanyahu was astonishing both in its aggression and its audacious break with this promise. Trump did nothing to prepare the US for war, gave seemingly no thought to the fact that Iran would inevitably hold the strait hostage if it came under attack, and resorted to contradictory explanations for his decision. In the war’s early days, he described “what we did in Venezuela” as a model for what he hoped to achieve. “He thought he would go down in history as the American president who had resolved the Iran problem,” Nasr told me. “In his mind, this was a legacy-building transformation that would be quick and cost-free.” That has proven a fatal miscalculation. Pete Hegseth, the US self-styled “secretary of war”, said the early US strikes that killed Iran’s Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, had “cut off the head of the snake.” But regime change is now a distant prospect. Trump underestimated the resilience of the Iranian regime and overestimated the power of protests against it. After just five months, his misadventure is as unpopular with American voters as the Vietnam war was six years in. It could yet escalate into a wider regional conflict, with the Houthis threatening a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia. Even Trump – whose private firm, The Trump Organization, is at work on a skyscraper in Dubai – won’t be insulated from the consequences of this violence. *** What happened to the ceasefire? The memorandum of understanding, a vague, short document that the US and Iran signed on 17 June, gave a brief respite from the strikes and (supposedly) initiated a 60-day negotiation period in which time both sides could reach permanent agreement on – among other things – the future of the strait. But it broke down when Iran fired on three commercial tankers that had used a shipping lane close to the shores of Oman, rather than a route off the Iranian coast approved by Tehran. “When ceasefires are violated, you have two options; either react to preserve the ceasefire, or use the violation as an excuse to end it,” Nasr says. Trump went with the latter option, calling Iran’s leaders “scum” and declaring the ceasefire “over” earlier this month. This week, the US energy secretary Chris Wright said the US mission had shifted towards ensuring oil shipments could move through the strait. It’s worth remembering that the strait had never been closed for an extended period. Before 28 February, ships had been sailing through it without obstruction. The US is now framing the potential of a return to this old status quo as a victory. Iran and the US are still negotiating, and Tehran has signalled its desire to permanently control the strait, including by charging tolls on passing vessels. “The US is now in a situation where it either has a long, protracted war, which would keep the strait closed, or keeps escalating to the next level with the hope of knocking Iran out,” Nasr says. *** A serious misjudgment There are signs that Trump and Netanyahu seriously misjudged the likelihood that Iran would seize control of the strait. In an interview earlier this year, Netanyahu admitted “the problem of the Hormuz strait became understood as the war went on.” As our diplomatic editor Patrick Wintour wrote at the time, in a piece suggesting the consequences of Trump’s excursion could prove greater than the Vietnam war, this was an “astonishing admission.” The closure of the strait is the type of doomsday scenario that previous administrations, and most Iran experts, would have considered. But the US government now has very few Iran experts, because Trump has instead chosen to surround himself with a royal court of loyalists. Nate Swanson, a former state department representative on Trump’s Iran negotiating team, was forced out earlier this year after far-right activist Laura Loomer accused him of disloyalty. “Folks who’ve watched this Iranian system … would have told [Trump]: ‘They’re not businessmen from New York. They’re made of a different type of DNA’,” Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute in Washington DC, recently told Guardian US political correspondent, Robert Tait. *** Consequences, consequences Inflation caused by rising oil prices is making everyday life more expensive and hiking the costs of borrowing for governments (including Burnham’s here in the UK). If there is no agreement until 2027, some are predicting global growth could fall by 1.3%, if not more. Europe may be uniquely exposed: since the Russia-Ukraine war, the continent has turned towards the Middle East for its gas, particularly to Qatar, which has had to slow production during the conflict. We could be facing a winter of shortages, bringing to mind the 1970s oil crisis, when the British government enforced power cuts to conserve energy supplies. *** Who’s in charge of the sea? Many of Trump’s proposed solutions to the conflict seem to have been thought up on the spot. He briefly suggested that the US could charge tolls on ships entering the strait in exchange for safe passage, despite European leaders and even Marco Rubio, his own secretary of state, having previously said these would be incompatible with international law. The fact the US and Iran have even proposed such tolls is a sign of the wilful disregard for international law that has become a defining feature of this conflict (notably, Iran, the US and Israel are among a small handful of nations that don’t ratify the UN convention on the laws of the sea). Freedom of navigation is a cornerstone of international law: without it, shipping starts to resemble a protection racket, where nations extract fees from passing vessels. Some experts now worry that other shipping routes could become more militarised, as coastal nations watching Iran use the strait as the ultimate bargaining chip try to take advantage of other important waterways. “A lot of other countries that feel they’re like Iran, and could use passageways as a deterrent” Nasr says. “If nations like the US and Israel can attack your country at any time, you’re going to resort to whatever you can in order to protect yourself.” What else we’ve been enjoying This thoughtful piece by Alice Lassman on how Gen Z has outsourced intimacy to AI reflects conversations I’ve been having with younger pals lately. Libby Ed Miliband was trying to start a green energy revolution in Britain. Now he’s at the Foreign Office, what happens to that agenda? I enjoyed reading this piece by Fiona Harvey, which has some answers. Hettie “It’s a crime that alters your whole reality.” Anna Moore on the impact of crime, here on the survivor-led campaign to end drug-facilitated sexual rape. Libby If (like me) you feel creeped out by reading about Meta’s new “smartglasses”, which allow wearers to film people without their consent, it’s worth reading this piece by Gaby Hinsliff. Hettie Herald writer Neil Mackay makes a powerful argument that the future health of the Scottish independence movement depends on Burnham’s success or failure in Westminster. Libby Sport Cycling | Remco Evenepoel took back-to-back stage wins in the Tour de France, and eroded some of Tadej Pogacar’s overall lead, with victory in the stage 16 time trial from Evian to Thonon-les-Bains. Tennis | The French Open has become the first grand slam tournament to offer players a share of the event’s revenue in a significant step forward in the row over prize money. Football | La Liga’s president, Javier Tebas, has accused Fifa of “destroying the football industry” and called for its president, Gianni Infantino, to quit. The front pages “Burnham implores cabinet to find ways to tackle cost of living crisis”, is the Guardian’s front page today, the Times writes “Burnham signals cuts to pay for spending pledges”, and the i Paper’s take is “Cost of living, cost of living, cost of living”. The Mail asks “Who’s going to pay the bill for Andy’s largesse?” and the FT has “Burnham backs away from rise in tax allowance ‘to show fiscal discipline’”. Elsewhere, the Telegraph leads on “Pc Harper’s killers set for early release”. The Mirror, Sun, Metro and Express all splash on details from court with variations of “Ann ‘hit 21 times with hammer’”. The Latest US soldiers killed: has Trump lost control of Iran war? The US has carried out a fresh round of strikes against Iran, after three US soldiers were killed in action. The Pentagon has also admitted that nearly 100 US service members have been injured over the last two weeks, as Tehran launched a wave of reprisals to the tenth consecutive nights of attacks, even as peace talks mediated by Pakistan continue. Lucy Hough speaks to senior international correspondent, Julian Borger. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Yotam Maron, a key organiser in the Occupy Wall Street movement which spawned a global network in 2011, has worked on multiple social movements since then. He identifies a “politics of powerlessness” which too often hobbles them, mistaking “a healthy distrust of institutional power for a failure to build a strong, coherent strategy for political change”. Since then, he founded the Wildfire Project, a training organisation for grassroots groups to counter that misplaced internal logic and argues now, even with Democrat socialists in the ascendancy across some parts of the US, that people power must continue to be built through movements not elected politicians. title: Americans far more likely to view politics as greatest threat to safety, study finds
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: New survey reveals one in 10 Americans identify politics as biggest risk they face in life – 10 times the global average
body_text: Americans are 10 times more likely than people elsewhere in the world to regard politics as the greatest threat to their personal safety, according to a global survey that suggests the country’s deep partisan divisions are poisoning everyday life. The latest Lloyd’s Register Foundation World Risk Poll found that one in 10 Americans identified politics as the biggest risk they face in their daily lives when asked an open-ended question. The figure is up from 6% in both 2021 and 2023 and well above the global average of 1% across 140 countries. Although Americans remain far more likely to cite road accidents and crime as the worst dangers they face, the survey found the US to be the only country in which more people named politics than personal health conditions as the biggest risk to their safety. “The US figure of 10% is unprecedented,” said Benedict Vigers, a senior global news writer at Gallup, which partnered on the research. “No other country ranked higher. It’s 10 times the global average. “It speaks to how charged the political environment is and has been for many years in the United States that people are now saying that the political situation is not just an issue nationally but is a seeable daily risk to their safety as they go about their normal lives.” The US has ranked among the countries most likely to cite politics as a personal safety risk in all three waves of the World Risk Poll but 2025 marks the first time it has reached the top of the global ranking. It was effectively tied with Hungary, which recorded 9%; polling was conducted months before the country’s recent election. Serbia, Latvia and Lithuania followed at 6% while Slovakia, Russia, Myanmar, Spain and Israel each recorded 5%. But the US in particular has witnessed a surge in political violence over the past decade, including three assassination attempts against Donald Trump, the 2025 killing of Charlie Kirk, the targeting of other national and state officials and a deadly insurrection at the US Capitol in January 6, 2021. There has been a rise in localised harassment, death threats against election administrators and the use of doxing and “swatting” to intimidate and silence political opposition. The concerns cut across demographic and ideological lines. There were no statistically significant differences by age, gender, education or political affiliation, with Republicans, Democrats and independents all similarly likely to identify politics as their greatest concern. Respondents often blamed the opposing political camp for creating an atmosphere of insecurity, while others pointed more broadly to the country’s increasingly fractured politics. “I would have to say the state of polarisation of the American people,” said one 54-year-old Republican man. A 42-year-old independent male respondent said: “I would say political extremism. I don’t have a lot of personal risk, but I do feel the biggest risk is people that are fanatical about their position and that they could be violent.” A 69-year-old Democratic woman added: “The political situation has a lot to do with the fact whether if I am safe or not. I am concerned where we’re going or might go.” Vigers said: “Almost all of the respondents who mention that politics is the top risk to safety mention or refer to polarisation whether directly or indirectly. It’s either Republicans saying the Democrats or it’s Democratic voters saying Trump and the Republicans are a big risk to my safety. “But we have several other people who call it out directly and say, the political environment makes me fearful for my safety or the heightened sense of polarisation makes me fear for my safety. It is quite a uniquely American phenomenon.” The findings echo other Gallup polling that has highlighted Americans’ growing disillusionment with politics. In 2025 a third of US adults identified politics and government as the country’s most important problem, well above the global median and exceeded only by respondents in the Philippines and Taiwan. In 2024, 5% of Americans named the US as its own greatest enemy, the highest figure on record. At the same time, confidence in government appears to have deteriorated. In 2025, 58% of Americans said the government does not care about them at all, the highest figure recorded and 11 percentage points higher than in 2021. Among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development member states, only Colombia and Greece recorded higher levels of public alienation from government.

title: The world is on fire, and who does Trump blame? The Canadians
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: The US president has been complaining about Canada’s ‘filthy, polluted and unhealthy air’. Maybe he should put all that energy into tackling the climate crisis, writes Arwa Mahdawi
body_text: Right, that’s it: we’ve got to do something about Canada. The country’s wildfires, which resulted in air quality alerts across more than 20 US states, ruined my weekend. On Friday the air in Philadelphia, where I live, was so unhealthy I couldn’t go outside without my eyes stinging. My kid’s preschool cancelled outdoor time, while the city suspended trash pickup and closed public pools. You know who did not suspend their regularly scheduled programming because of a bit of toxic smoke? The plot monitoring committee at my allotment. Despite the apocalyptic conditions, they were still busy ensuring the gardening bylaws were strictly adhered to. I realised this on Saturday when I got an official violation for too many weeds. Yes, I’d got a bit carried away with “chaos gardening” (all the rage these days) and I’d meant to clean things up on Friday, until the smoke got in the way. So, thanks for that Canada. Luckily, Donald Trump is on the case. On Friday he complained on Truth Social that the US had been “invaded” by “filthy, polluted, and unhealthy air”, and the situation was “totally unacceptable”. Then, on Sunday, the president said he’d spoken to the Canadian prime minister Mark Carney and told him “you got to stop these fires from coming in and, you know, poisoning our air”. He added: “Maybe they should pay some damages or something, or we should do some tariffs.” I’m surprised he didn’t order ICE to stamp out the fires. Carney, for his part, responded to Trump’s comments by referencing the climate crisis, and noting that this was everyone’s responsibility to address. But who wants to talk about an inconvenient fact like the human-caused climate crisis when it’s much easier to just blame Canadians? Maga certainly doesn’t. On Thursday the Republican senator Bernie Moreno from Ohio introduced a new bill that would sanction Canadian officials for wildfire smoke. Meanwhile, the geniuses on Fox News have been busy yelling about Canada while skirting around the root causes of the wildfires. Poor Canada isn’t just getting a lot of hot air directed at it from Trumpers, it’s now issued its own air quality warnings because of American fires to the south. It turns out that smoke doesn’t recognise border policies. And, as the weather becomes more extreme, things are only going to get worse: the world is literally on fire and the arsonists are fiddling with tariffs as it burns. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: First Thing: $37.5bn cost of Iran war revealed as senator warns of ‘another forever war’
author: Martin Belam
summary: Defense secretary Pete Hegseth reveals costs so far as Trump administration seeks more funding
body_text: Good morning. The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has told the Senate that the US-Israel war on Iran has cost $37.5bn so far, as he faced lawmakers furious over the conflict’s soaring price tag and the deaths last week of three American service members. He defended the Trump administration’s roughly $88bn supplemental funding request, calling it “urgent, necessary”. Patty Murray, a Democratic senator from Washington, demanded Hegseth explain what the war had actually achieved, accusing the administration of shifting its rationale by the week and warning that the conflict risked becoming “another forever war”. What is happening in Iran? The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has described how he was pulled from the rubble of a leadership compound after the US-Israeli airstrike that killed the country’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, on the first day of the war, and has survived since by constantly moving around Tehran by car. Deepa Parent, meanwhile, has reports from the ground with ordinary Iranians, who say “it’s truly hell here” as airstrikes, repression and water shortages become the “new normal”. What other developments have affected the region? Zohran Mamdani, New York’s mayor, has acknowledged he does not have the authority to arrest Benjamin Netanyahu, but urged US federal authorities to do so if the Israeli prime minister visits the US later this year. The White House has announced that American airline carriers will be able to resume direct flights to Lebanon more than 40 years after the US suspended the route. Saudis and US strike deal for kingdom to enrich uranium, reports say Donald Trump has approved an agreement with Saudi Arabia that could provide the kingdom with uranium enrichment capability for its civilian nuclear programme. The agreement may be announced as early as Wednesday. The deal is expected to last 30 years and is also expected to involve US firms in developing the program. It could allow for the building of a uranium enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia after a joint US-Saudi study. What is uranium enrichment? It is the process of increasing the presence of isotope uranium-235 so the substance can sustain a nuclear chain reaction. Enrichment is not an automatic path to a nuclear weapon, but could open the door to a Saudi Arabia weapons programme, something its de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, has not ruled out if Iran obtains an atomic bomb. US immigration agents arrested record number of people in June, data shows The Trump administration arrested a record number of immigrants last month, according to newly released government data that revealed how US immigration agents have been quietly but steadily increasing operations across the country. A Guardian analysis of the latest data published by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) found that federal immigration agents arrested 43,138 people in June – the highest number since Trump took office in January last year. ‘We were at their mercy’: inside the Amazon tactics that hiked prices across the internet Internal emails revealed in court and interviews with former employees describe how Amazon’s practices drove up prices for competitors such as Walmart and Target. Over the last decade, Amazon has suppressed the sales of some suppliers’ products or demanded millions of dollars in compensation from them because of the low prices of its retail rivals. The California attorney general, Rob Bonta, alleges that Amazon’s tactics have coerced suppliers into raising the prices of their products with its rivals. Amazon denies the price-fixing claims and says it works to lower costs for consumers. In other news … The actor Kaylee Hottle – who played a major role in Godzilla vs Kong – has died aged 18, following a car crash in Maryland. Canada has cancelled the joint opening celebrations of the Gordie Howe International Bridge with US amid trade tensions and Trump’s 50% tariff announcement. A new review by the Gates Foundation has found there were “roughly 30 meetings” between Jeffrey Epstein and foundation leaders and staff – including Bill Gates. OpenAI has revealed an autonomous AI agent went rogue and hacked a prominent startup by itself in an “unprecedented incident”. The Trump administration has sought phone records of several New York Times journalists in an unusually aggressive attempt to unmask the confidential sources of reporters Stat of the day: Two in five Americans believe stock market only serves the top 1% Two in five Americans believe the stock market isn’t for them and only benefits the top 1%, according to a Harris Poll poll exclusive to the Guardian. Meanwhile, almost 40% of respondents did not know that the economy and the stock market were not the same thing. In another stunning survey result, Americans are 10 times more likely than people elsewhere in the world to regard politics as the greatest threat to their personal safety, suggesting the country’s deep partisan divisions are poisoning everyday life. Well Actually: I’ve heard menopause hormone therapy fixes everything. Should I take it? For our Call the doctor series, Dr Keren Landman answers common medical questions. Here she says that timely treatment provides immense relief of menopause symptoms, and has the added benefit of lowering the risk of bone fractures. But ascribing all your ills to menopause and expecting treatment to fix them is a set-up for disappointment. Don’t miss this: ‘The bed you thought was safe, isn’t safe’ – surviving drug-facilitated rape In September 2024, Amanda Stanhope watched, transfixed, from her home in Manchester, England, as the Gisèle Pelicot case made headlines around the world. “Gisèle’s case was the first time I knew of somebody else who had been raped while they were drugged,” says Stanhope. “I remember feeling: ‘Thank God I’m not alone.’” Anna Moore speaks to survivors. … or this: Wreckage of 1952 Pan Am plane crash that changed air safety found near Puerto Rico A fascinating slice of aviation history has been rediscovered. The wreckage of a Pan Am flight that plunged into the ocean off Puerto Rico in 1952, in an accident that killed 52 people, has been found. The 17 people who survived told investigators everyone lived through the splashdown but panic set in as passengers struggled to find life vests. That directly led to the passenger safety briefings given on modern-day commercial flights. Climate check: Japan records its first ‘cruelly hot day’ as cities swelter in 40-degree heat Japan logged its first official kokushobi or “cruelly hot day” on Tuesday since the new term for when temperatures top 104F was introduced in April. The Japan Meteorological Agency coined the new designation to warn the public of the heat dangers of days that were once freak weather events but have now become more common. Last Thing: Why are fans wetting themselves to stand front row at concerts? I go to a lot of concerts, but I am yet – thankfully – to adopt the tactic of the “pit diaper”. Olivia Rodrigo, Noah Kahan and Morgan Wallen have all dealt with audience effluence in recent weeks – but that is only one part of a fearsome subculture that has built up around fandom, endurance and “getting barrier”, as Kate Solomon explains. title: Three speeches on a single day signaled a dying American democracy
author: Robert B Shpiner
summary: Stephen Miller warned of a leftwing ‘cancer’ threatening civilization. As a critical care doctor, I have a response to his diagnosis
body_text: The presumption that US elections are legitimate died last week in Washington. It was 237 years old. It did not die of one wound. It died of three, inflicted in a single day, in daylight, on the record. And the country, running to the loudest of them, never examined the one most likely to kill. In critical care we distinguish the mechanism of death from its cause. The mechanism was a Thursday. The cause was chronic, progressive and untreated. The morning belonged to the secretary of state. Before officials of more than 60 countries, he announced that the counterterrorism architecture of the free world, built over a generation against jihadist mass murder, should be rebuilt and aimed at the domestic left. He named a transnational enemy defined by hatred of the west, “a revolt of the worst against the best”. He tied it to Iran and to Cuba and offered no evidence for either link. He said the journalists and thinktanks who might check the claims often agree with the enemy’s goals. The move is old and reliable: discredit the second opinion in advance. Midday belonged to the White House deputy chief of staff. What he said deserves to be quoted rather than summarized, because summary is a mercy it has not earned. He called “leftwing political terrorism” a “fatal cancer of civilization”. He said that its politics, left to run its course, “always becomes a gulag”. He said antifa demonstrators are “all deformed in some way, in their appearance, in their dress, in their mannerism”, that “their outer appearance becomes a manifestation of their inner hatred”, and he asked why there is “not one normal-looking person among them”. He said that when the leftist protests that his rights are being violated, those appeals “must fall on deaf ears”. He urged the assembled governments to be “completely unflinching in the pursuit of justice against these enemies of civilization”. And he described the work already under way in six verbs: “disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest and prosecute”. I have been practicing medicine for four decades. Cancer is my vocabulary, not his. And I know what happened the last time a government borrowed it. The Nazi state’s central perversion was the medicalization of killing: the enemy as tumor, as bacillus, the nation as patient, extermination as cure. Robert Jay Lifton called it the biomedical vision. It recruited my profession first, and my profession answered willingly. When a government describes citizens as a cancer, it has written the first line of a treatment plan. On Thursday, the plan was read aloud, from a state department podium, in six verbs. One disclosure belongs in the chart. My family left Russia in 1917. My relatives left Germany in 1933. In both generations, leaving was called excessive; staying was the reasonable position. But an alarm that was right both times it sounded is not overcaution. On Thursday, it sounded a third time. The evening belonged to the president. In primetime he called the American election system indefensible, claimed a foreign power held 220 million voter files, declared mail voting inherently corrupt, accused his own intelligence services of concealment, and told Congress that the only reason to oppose his bill is the intent to cheat. That framework converts every future outcome into evidence. Pass the bill and win: the bill worked. Fail and lose: the cheaters blocked it. A presumption of legitimacy cannot survive inside a belief system engineered to be unfalsifiable. It was just a Thursday. Netflix’s forecast disappointed Wall Street. A rocket aborted on the pad. No sirens sounded, because this is not how they sound. Democracies do not die to soundtracks. They die on ordinary weekdays, between the earnings reports, while the country is at work. Then came the response, and the response was a triage error. Nearly all of it ran to the evening. The factcheckers parsed the voter files. The law professors graded the bombshells. Real work, spent on the loudest injury. The morning’s remarks, the ones that declared a class of Americans a cancer and read enmity on their bodies, drew the attention of an ordinary news cycle: straight coverage in the mainstream, horror at the margins, and in a portion of the press, open applause. I have watched teams run to the dramatic patient while the quiet one, the one not crying out, exsanguinates behind a curtain. The most dangerous words spoken in Washington on Thursday were not spoken in primetime. They were spoken before lunch, to more than 60 countries. The official transcript records the applause. The decedent is survived by the federal courts, still open. By 50 secretaries of state, still certifying. By a general election, still on the calendar, 108 days out. And by an electorate that has not yet been asked the only question that matters, which is whether it will accept a count its president has pre-declared corrupt, counted among citizens its government has pre-declared malignant. In 40 years of intensive care, I have pronounced death many times. The criteria are strict because the declaration is irreversible, and so we are taught to be certain before we speak. I have also, more than once, seen a rhythm return after the room had gone quiet, when someone refused to stop compressions on schedule. This notice is filed in the knowledge that pronouncements can be premature. It is filed in the fear that this one is not. Robert B Shpiner is a clinical professor of medicine in pulmonary and critical care at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA

title: Nicaragua’s congress announces ‘work plan’ to suspend elections
author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
summary: US secretary of state says international community should ‘join forces’ against authoritarian Ortega regime
body_text: Nicaragua’s congress, controlled by the country’s long-serving president, Daniel Ortega, has announced a “work plan” to implement the authoritarian leader’s order that the country should no longer hold elections. The UN and the US strongly condemned Sunday’s announcement by Ortega, who has been in power since 2007 and, after a controversial constitutional change last year, now governs alongside his wife, Rosario Murillo, as “co-president”. During the ceremony marking the 47th anniversary of the 1979 Sandinista revolution, in which he helped overthrow the brutal dictatorship of Anastasio Somoza García, Ortega said he would work with congress to pass new laws that would “build a wall” against the opposition. On Tuesday, the Ortega-controlled National Assembly issued a statement saying that, under the pretext of “ensuring peace, security, stability and the continuity of achievements in the fight against poverty”, it was “beginning the necessary analysis to draw up a work plan to implement the president’s directives”. Although the Ortega-Murillo regime has already overseen a profound erosion of democracy – marked by the violent suppression of protests, the imprisonment of thousands of people and the forced exile of nearly 1 million Nicaraguans – Sunday’s announcement marked a significant rhetorical escalation that is now being put into practice by congress. On Wednesday, the UN high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, called on the Nicaraguan authorities to “reopen civic space, and restore the rule of law. People of all political viewpoints must be allowed to vote and run for office, in line with the state’s international human rights obligations.” The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, who refers to the country’s government as the “Murillo-Ortega dictatorship”, said in a statement on Tuesday that “the Nicaraguan people have the right to choose their own leaders through democratic elections” and the US “calls on the international community to join forces” against the regime. Ortega’s uninterrupted period of almost 20 years in office is not his first spell in power. He led the junta that took office after the Sandinista revolution and, in 1984, was elected president, remaining in office until 1990. His current term, to which he was elected after he outlawed opposition parties and jailed all opposition presidential hopefuls before the 2021 election, had been due to end next November. However, last year’s constitutional changes extended the presidential term from five to six years. Despite the National Assembly’s announcement, it remains unclear whether the 2027 elections will be scrapped altogether or whether Ortega and Murillo will run unopposed.
