title: Brett Kavanaugh has become Trump’s chief enabler on the supreme court
author: Sidney Blumenthal
summary: The justice’s opinions have offered the president workarounds to enact his agenda despite clashes with the court
body_text: Of the conservative justices on the supreme court, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito have in the current session voted most consistently, at 89 and 88%, to support Donald Trump in his cases, according to the Wall Street Journal. Yet perhaps the most influential justice to advance key parts of Trump’s radical agenda has a slightly lower rating at 76%, and performed not so much by billowing lofty abstractions of originalism and textualism, but instead by contriving an assortment of glib schemes at justification. Mayhem in the city streets, violence, even killings, renewed rounds of Trump’s threats and shakedowns around the world through damaging tariffs, and chaos within the Congress around birthright citizenship, all of which helped fracture the divided Republican leadership on the eve of the midterm elections, have followed the opinions issued by Brett Kavanaugh. By the end of this session, he has clearly emerged as the chief enabler to operationalize Trump’s most salient political issues. Kavanaugh issued an unusual sole concurring opinion on 8 September 2025 in Noem v Vasquez Perdomo, staying a lower court’s temporary restraining order that had restricted ICE from targeting individuals based primarily on race, language or occupation. Kavanaugh stated that stopping people based on ethnic appearance, speaking Spanish and laboring at certain jobs was a “relevant factor” and “common sense” to establish “reasonable suspicion”. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, in a blistering dissent, accused the court of legitimizing “racial profiling on a massive scale”. She wrote prophetically: “We should not have to live in a country where the Government can seize anyone who looks Latino, speaks Spanish, and appears to work a low wage job.” Legal scholars were even more devastating in their analyses of Kavanaugh’s opinion. His “invocation” of “common sense” came “at the expense of facts and evidence”, Jennifer Chacón, professor and vice-dean at Stanford Law School, wrote. “Note the number of factual assertions … supported by nothing more than ‘common sense.’ I am not omitting his citations to evidence; there are no such citations.” Duncan Hosie, an academic fellow at Stanford Constitutional Law Center, described Kavanaugh’s claims as “factual revisionism” (ie, falsehoods), “a previously unrecognized form of precedent subversion that operates as a strategic tool to reshape legal doctrine while managing the Court’s dwindling sociological legitimacy”. “Almost every word of this is preposterous,” wrote Sherrilyn Ifill, professor at Howard Law School, about Kavanaugh’s opinion. “What we have seen repeatedly are not ‘stops.’ They are grabs and kidnapping.” Since Kavanaugh’s rationalization of what have become known as “Kavanaugh Stops”, within the first month more than 170 US citizens were detained, “dragged, tackled, beaten, tased and shot”, according to a ProPublica report, while through July of this year, 32 American children have been detained, 31 people have died at ICE detention camps, six people have been shot and killed, including two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, and in July 2026 two men who were not the actual targets ICE agents were seeking were killed. The sharp criticism of Kavanaugh’s opinion apparently embarrassed him. In an unrelated case, Trump v Illinois, in December 2025, Kavanaugh inserted a non sequitur as an obscure footnote repudiating his previous language. Now he wrote: “Officers must not make interior immigration stops or arrests based on race or ethnicity.” But Stephen Miller has paid no attention to the discreet footnote. The “Kavanaugh Stops” have continued, lately in Texas and Maine with fatal consequences. The method Kavanaugh applied to ICE abuses he also applied to Trump’s tariffs in the principal dissent on 20 February in Learning Resources, Inc v Trump, in which a six-to-three majority struck down Trump’s claim that he had the absolute power to impose tariffs at will under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). Trump angrily called those who ruled against him “fools” and “lap dogs”, but said of Kavanaugh: “I’m so proud of him.” Kavanaugh’s opinion again rested on factual revisionism, citing “history, and precedent” to justify Trump’s unilateral action, claiming it was “a traditional and common tool”, and appealing once more to “common sense”. Kavanaugh had in fact invented an imaginary historical pattern. No president before Trump had used IEEPA in its 49-year history to levy broad tariffs. Kavanaugh distorted the definition of a tariff, not as an import tax whose constitutional power to assert lies with the Congress, but rather a weapon of national security and foreign policy that belongs to the executive. Then Kavanaugh engaged in highly unusual and borderline improper speculation about other non-litigated economic and trade statutes that “might justify most (if not all) of the tariffs at issue in this case”, laying out a roadmap for Trump to skirt the court’s denial of his unconstitutional use of emergency powers. Trump announced within hours his workaround: a 10% global temporary import surcharge using section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which on 7 May the US court of international trade struck down as illegal. More recently, Trump has threatened further tariffs – a 25% tariff on Brazil, 100% tariffs on Britain and European nations that enforce digital services taxes against US tech companies, and a sudden punitive 50% tariff on most Canadian goods – all likely to be subject to new lawsuits if and when enforced. Then came Kavanaugh’s coup de grace of the session, his strange dissent in the birthright citizenship case on 30 June, Trump v Barbara, in which he stated that Trump’s executive order violated federal law but was not unconstitutional. His argument was a compound of “factual revisionism”, historical nonsense, sophistry, illogic and political consulting. His syllabus of errors was tightly scripted: First, significant illegal immigration into the United States is a new circumstance that was largely unknown as of 1868 and that the Framers of the Fourteenth Amendment could not have fully anticipated. And the Framers likely would not have anticipated (and presumably would not have intended) the odd result of granting a substantial birthright citizenship benefit to (i) those foreign citizens who violate U. S. immigration law and illegally enter or overstay and then have children in the United States over (ii) those foreign citizens who follow U. S. immigration law and have children in their home countries while seeking to lawfully immigrate to the United States … If Congress amends §1401(a) or otherwise enacts a statute creating new exceptions along the lines of the Executive Order for children born to foreign citizens unlawfully or temporarily in the country, such a statute, as I see it, would pass constitutional muster. While there was no “significant illegal immigration” as currently understood before 1868, chiefly because there were no federal legal restrictions, the Trump administration has invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 for its policy of mass deportation. And before the first major federal restriction laws – the Page Act of 1875 aimed at Chinese women and the more sweeping Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 – the colonies and then the states handled “illegal immigration”. The idea of illegal immigration was quite familiar to the framers of the 14th amendment, who openly discussed Chinese and other immigrants in connection to birthright citizenship. “If the 14th Amendment framers wanted to exclude the babies of temporary visitors (people not domiciled), children of unauthorized migration, or people who ‘owed allegiance’ to another country as the dissenters assert, they would have said so. They didn’t,” wrote Anna O Law, constitutional scholar at Cuny Brooklyn College, and author of Migration and the Origins of American Citizenship. Kavanaugh’s sheer speculation about what “the Framers likely would not have anticipated (and presumably would not have intended)” is mind reading in a time machine about a nonexistent legal category projected forward. Based on a fantastical fiction, he has reverse-engineered the originalist method into parody. His reasoning, such as it is, is an example of the well-known formal fallacy of arguing backwards from consequences, or “consequentialist” illogic. Kavanaugh piles on to this rubbish heap “the odd result of granting a substantial birthright citizenship benefit”, based on how he conjectures the 14th amendment’s framers would have reacted to their own constitutional creation. He guesses they would have shared his opinion and were already thinking about sorting out classes and castes of immigrants, even though they were deliberate and definitive in establishing a universal right. That they carved out two narrow exceptions, for children of foreign diplomats and of Native American tribes not taxed, showed the care they took. They purposely included, as a matter of constitutional rights, those very categories of immigrants Kavanaugh bizarrely speculates they would have excluded. Kavanaugh’s suggestion that Trump revive his executive order by a supporting act of Congress would not “pass constitutional muster” as he insists it would. It should be elementary that a legislative bill cannot void the 14th amendment as properly understood, even by a majority on the current court. But, predictably, within minutes, Trump hailed Kavanaugh’s idea. “We can easily make it up in legislation,” he said. “No long and unwieldy Constitutional Amendment is necessary!” The speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, instantly echoed Trump: “If there’s some legislative fix, we’ll advance that immediately,” he chimed in. And a bill was proposed that has no chance of ever being enacted by the Congress, but that if it were would be struck down under the recent court ruling. With his grab-bag of gambits, Kavanaugh mostly manages to avoid the more elaborate pretensions of other conservative justices, their conceits of originalism and textualism. He gets straight to the heart of achieving the desired political result. The conclusions of his opinions, after a bit of legal artifice, read like the political memos that they are. He offers a certain kind of cleverness that relies on sleight of hand, locates the cynical loophole, invents references if any at all, but which implodes to its hollow core upon examination. Kavanaugh’s controversial nomination in 2018 centered around allegations of high school sexual misconduct that he denied. In the uproar, his apprenticeship as a staffer was largely overlooked. He worked as an associate special counsel for Ken Starr, whom he convinced to launch an investigation into the suicide of Clinton White House deputy counsel Vince Foster, the subject of myriad rightwing conspiracy theories, after the previous special counsel had already issued a report attributing Foster’s death to his untreated clinical depression. That Starr report wound up affirming the original report, but in an effort overseen by Kavanaugh dragged out the bogus inquiry for three years of political exploitation. As one of the lawyers working for the George W Bush campaign in the Florida contest of 2000, along with the young John Roberts and Amy Coney Barrett, Kavanaugh advanced the notion that because counties counted votes differently, the vote count as a whole should be halted. This became the basis for the arbitrary Bush v Gore decision, an apotheosis of partisanship and blatant corruption of the 14th amendment’s guarantee of equal protection under the law – a ruling that even its author, Justice Antonin Scalia, later confessed was “a piece of shit”. Now, wearing the black robe, Kavanaugh charts roadmaps for Trump on how to work around adverse decisions and present ever more sly cases in the future. Kavanaugh acts as though he is in an ex-officio capacity to the administration’s legal staff writing option memos. The gamester has matured into the justice of the supreme court of counsel to Trump. That is something rarer to find, and far more powerful, than the next Roy Cohn. Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast

title: First Thing: US agrees Saudi uranium deal as strikes on Iran continue and Yemen’s Houthis hit tankers
author: Martin Belam
summary: Conflict continues across the region as White House announces nuclear technology agreement. Plus, the artist who flattened a Tesla with a tank
body_text: Good morning. The US has signed a landmark nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia that could allow the kingdom to enrich uranium in the future. The deal will be submitted to Congress for review, where it could face opposition among lawmakers who fear a lack of monitoring safeguards. In lengthy talks stretching over more than one administration, the US has feared that Riyadh would look elsewhere for nuclear technology if the US did not provide what it wanted. Saudi Arabia has long said that if it does not partner with the US, it could do so with China or Russia, which have different proliferation standards. Why is a uranium deal with Saudi Arabia controversial? The full details of the deal have yet to be released, but it comes as the US’s war with Iran is being fought in part to prevent Tehran enriching uranium domestically and make it near impossible for Iran to build a nuclear weapon. Saudi Arabia has in the past said it would need a nuclear weapon if Iran acquired one. Kenneth Roth has analysed why Trump would agree it right now. House Republicans to write $95bn bill to fund Iran war and aid farmers House Republicans have agreed to begin the process of writing a $95bn bill to fund the war with Iran as well as provide new aid to farmers, while making a long-shot attempt to impose new restrictions on voting nationwide. The resolution’s passage comes amid an intensification of the conflict with Iran, which Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, told the Senate on Tuesday had thus far cost $37.5bn. The Trump administration last month asked Congress to authorize approximately $88bn in supplemental funding, the majority of which – up to $67.1bn – will go to pay for the war. What are the latest developments in the war? The US military launched its 12th successive night of strikes, which have now widened to western and central Iran. In attacks lasting five hours, the US claims to have struck military targets including maritime capabilities, missile and ⁠drone storage facilities, coastal surveillance sites and air defense assets. Yemen’s ⁠Houthi militia also attacked two Saudi Arabian oil tankers, the Iran-aligned group said on Thursday, with a Saudi news agency later confirming one of the vessels was ablaze in the Red Sea. US senator wants urgent answers from Barclays over Jes Staley’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein The leading US senator Elizabeth Warren has called for urgent answers from Barclays over what she claimed was its “apparent failure to meaningfully investigate” ties between the bank’s former boss, Jes Staley, and the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. In a letter sent privately to the Barclays chair, Nigel Higgins, and seen by the Guardian, Warren – the most senior Democrat on the US senate banking committee – said it was “deeply unclear how Barclays, supposedly investigating Staley’s connection to Epstein, failed to uncover this decades-long relationship”. What other developments have there been in the Epstein case? A modelling scout who recruited women for the disgraced financier has been found dead at his home near Paris, French officials have said. Daniel Siad, 69, was under investigation by the prosecutors in France, accused of rape and other charges. He had not yet been questioned by investigators, but had denied the allegations, saying he wanted to give his version of events. His name appeared in more than 1,000 documents in the declassified US Department of Justice Epstein files. An investigation to determine the cause of death has been opened and an autopsy is to be carried out. In other news … Just days before trial, a US teen has dropped his Meta lawsuit blaming the firms’s platforms ⁠for his depression ⁠and anxiety, in a victory for the social media giant after an earlier landmark loss relating to social media addiction. Donald Trump has scoffed at the word “affordability” as he touted his economic policies in Georgia, describing it as a term concocted by Democratic political consultants. A police officer has fatally shot a man in Madison, Wisconsin, sparking protests. India’s prime minister has said he will set up “fast-track courts” to punish corrupt officials who leaked examination papers, as authorities seek to quell the youth-led Cockroach protest movement. Pride organisers have vowed to march in a Romanian city that has blocked the event four years in a row. Stat of the day: Google reports 12th consecutive quarter of strong revenue gains Google’s parent company, Alphabet, reported double-digit revenue growth for its second-quarter earnings on Wednesday. This is the tech giant’s 12th consecutive quarter of massive revenue gains. The Filter Recommends: 12 things our writers use to keep cool on hot, sticky days Portable fans, a “cooling necklace”, sun-protective hats and more products our writers reach for when the heat won’t quit. And once you have cooled down, here are seven screen-free activities that will help you survive summer indoors. Don’t miss this: Ken Turner, the 100-year-old artist who flattened a Tesla with a tank The British painter, sculptor and performance artist, who has devoted his life to making art available to the masses, discusses inequality, inspiration – and why despite being a centenarian he won’t be stopping any time soon. … or this: If you’ve heard that London is dystopian and dangerous – read this You will almost certainly have come across social media posts describing Britain’s capital, London, my home town, as a lawless mess – a “fact” that seems patently untrue every time I step outside my front door. My mayor, Sadiq Khan – the target of widespread racist abuse on the web – has now written for the Guardian that “If you’ve heard that London is dystopian and dangerous – read this. It just isn’t.” Climate check: Climate crisis-driven heat ‘sucking soils dry’ as extreme drought hits Europe Our environment editor, Damian Carrington, reports that extreme heat supercharged by the climate crisis is sucking Europe dry in summer and intensifying the drought hitting the continent. Researchers said the link between the human-caused climate crisis and the drying of European summers was strong. Last Thing: Orcas seen ramming prey so hard it explodes may be playing a game Orcas have been observed ramming into giant fish so hard that the prey explode, possibly as a form of gory entertainment. Dr Kathryn Ayres, a scientist at the non-profit organization Beneath the Waves, said: “We think this may help younger orcas feed more easily, or it could also just be for fun. Orcas are known for playing with their food.” Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. If you’re not already signed up, subscribe now. title: Republican-controlled committee refers former Trump prosecutor Jack Smith for criminal investigation
author: Richard Luscombe
summary: Committee accused of trying to ‘weaponize’ justice system via ‘laughably weak and vindictive criminal referral’
body_text: Democrats have accused the US House of Representatives judiciary committee of a “baseless” and “vindictive” attack on former special prosecutor Jack Smith after it referred him for criminal prosecution for allegedly lying to Congress over his investigation into Donald Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election. The committee chair, Jim Jordan, an Ohio Republican, wrote to the acting US attorney general, Todd Blanche, on Wednesday night, asserting Smith “made willfully and intentionally false statements of material fact” during testimony about obtaining phone records of a number of Republican lawmakers. Smith, Jordan claimed in the letter, falsely told the panel that his team had no access to privileged text messages when he testified in December that they had only “toll records” containing numbers, not content. US justice department documents presented to the panel on 14 July, Jordan said, showed that Smith’s investigators actually had access to the text messages of 44 members of Congress. “Based on this new information, there is cause for investigation to determine whether Mr Smith knowingly made false statements to obstruct the Committee’s oversight,” Jordan wrote. Smith’s lawyers Lanny Breuer and Peter Koski, in their own letter to Blanche, said their client “provided truthful, responsive answers” during closed-doors questioning by the panel in December, and again during an open session in January. “This referral reflects a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system by attacking a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law,” they wrote. “Mr Smith agreed to testify before the House Judiciary Committee fully cognizant of the risk that President Trump’s Justice Department would try to find something in his testimony to serve as the basis for a criminal charge. “This risk existed not because Mr Smith would make a false statement, but because President Trump has repeatedly ordered that Mr Smith be prosecuted and jailed.” Democratic members of the judiciary committee, meanwhile, called Jordan’s letter “a laughably weak and vindictive criminal referral” pandering to Trump’s frequent demands for retribution against the special prosecutor who investigated him. The Maryland Democrat Jamie Raskin, the panel’s ranking member, issued a lengthy statement saying Smith gave “clear and consistent” testimony, and that his statement about obtaining subpoenas for lawmakers’ toll records “was true when he said it, and it is true today”. Raskin wrote: “This referral deliberately distorts and misstates the facts, including what questions the Republicans actually asked at Mr Smith’s interview. “The Republicans fault Mr Smith for not reading the minds of congressional investigators and for not volunteering information they didn’t ask for. This is absurd. Mr Smith may be telegenic but he is not telepathic. “Wishing that you had asked different questions while you had the opportunity to examine a witness is not a proper basis for a referral of a witness for criminal prosecution.” Raskin added: “This referral, if ever brought before a judge, will get laughed out of court. It is meant to create a distraction so Republicans on [the] Senate Judiciary [committee] can feel just a little more comfortable confirming the architect of the Epstein cover-up and lawless Trump slush fund and super pardon, Todd Blanche, to the post of Attorney General. “We will not fall for this ludicrous distraction. Neither will the American people.” The US Senate panel is set to vote on Thursday morning whether to advance Blanche’s nomination to fill the role permanently. Blanche will ultimately decide whether to charge Smith, who led two investigations into Trump’s activities during and at the end of the president’s first term, including the hiding of classified documents at his Florida resort. The cases were dropped after Trump was elected to a second term. Previous efforts by the justice department to punish Trump’s political enemies have fallen flat. A federal judge in November threw out criminal charges against James Comey, the former FBI director, and Letitia James, New York’s attorney general, both vocal critics of the president. A justice department spokesperson told CBS News that it had received Jordan’s referral letter and said it “will investigate all evidence of criminal conduct”.

title: Two Russian men jailed in Angola for terrorism and spying
author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg and agencies
summary: The men were convicted over alleged plan to stage coup and organise deadly demonstrations over fuel prices last year
body_text: Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year. Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities. From 28-30 July 2025, a minibus taxi strike over fuel price hikes descended into riots and looting, in which 22 people were killed and more than 1,600 arrested according to official figures. Angola’s security forces were accused of firing live ammunition at protesters; the government said its “progressive” use of force was justified. Human Rights Watch had previously said Angola employed “excessive force” when it used rubber bullets and teargas to break up a peaceful protest against rising fuel prices on 12 July 2025. Angolan prosecutors said Lakshtanov and Ratchin wanted to influence next year’s presidential elections, including by funding Angola’s largest opposition party, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), or by forcing a leadership change within the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), which has ruled the country since independence from Portugal in 1975. Prosecutors also claimed the men were linked to Africa Politology, a Russian disinformation and propaganda network that emerged from the Wagner mercenary group. Africa Politology was taken over by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) after the death of the Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2023, according to an investigation by media outlets including Forbidden Stories. Wagner was rebranded as Africa Corps and absorbed by Russia’s military. Angola, whose economy is highly dependent on oil exports, has historically been close with Russia. During the cold war years of Angola’s 1975-2002 civil war, the Soviet Union and Cuba supported the MPLA, while the US and apartheid South Africa backed its opponents, including UNITA. However, Angola’s president, João Lourenço, has improved relations with the US and Europe since taking power in 2017. In the last decade, Russia has increased its presence in Africa. The Wagner group and then Africa Corps have provided security for the Central African Republic’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, since 2017. In 2021, Wagner forces arrived in Mali to support the military junta. Africa Corps also backs the military regimes in neighbouring Niger and Burkina Faso. Since 2023, Russian troops have also been deployed in Equatorial Guinea, Libya and Sudan, according to a US Congress report. Madagascar’s president, Michael Randrianirina, has also boosted ties with Russia since taking power in a coup in October 2025. There are Russians in his presidential guard and a weekly programme about Madagascar-Russia relations was launched earlier this month on national television. Two Angolans were also tried alongside the Russians. The sports journalist Carlos Tomé received a two-year suspended prison sentence. Francisco de Oliveira, the secretary-general of UNITA’s youth wing, was acquitted. Prosecutors have appealed against those sentences, according to the Portuguese news agency Lusa. Lakshtanov and Ratchin have also appealed against their sentences, but will remain in detention while the appeal is processed, according to Lusa. Russia’s embassy in Angola did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Agence France-Press contributed to this report

title: US House passes war powers resolution directing Trump to end Iran conflict
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Resolution, which follows similar one in June, is largely symbolic, as Democrats have few levers to force compliance
body_text: The US House of Representatives for the second time passed a war powers resolution directing Donald Trump to withdraw the US military from the conflict with Iran, amid renewed fighting that has driven oil prices to their highest levels in weeks and claimed four American lives. The resolution proposed by Democrat Pramila Jayapal passed by a 214-208 vote, largely along party lines. The same four Republicans who had helped pass a nearly identical resolution in June – Tom Barrett of Michigan, Warren Davidson of Ohio, Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania – joined with all Democrats in attendance to vote in favor. The war powers resolution passed last month was later approved by the Senate, in a significant bipartisan rebuke of the president’s decision to join Israel in attacking Iran in February and sparking a regional conflict that opinion polls have consistently shown is unpopular with the US public. “This is not a partisan issue,” Jayapal said following the vote. “Vast majorities of Americans, of all parties, believe that this is an unconstitutional, illegal war that needs to stop. It was not authorized by Congress, and it has cost us incredible tolls: [the] lives of 18 service members, millions who have been displaced and thousands who have been injured.” Later on Thursday, the Senate rejected a similar resolution proposed by Democrat Chris Van Hollen in a 47-49 vote, largely along party lines. The House measure’s passage is nonetheless largely symbolic, as the Trump administration has argued war powers resolutions are unconstitutional, and Democrats’ minority status in the House and Senate leaves them with few options to force compliance. In debate ahead of the vote, the top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, Greg Meeks, accused the president of violating the law. “Let me be clear: this body has already spoken. The war powers resolution passed with bipartisan support in the House and the Senate. The Trump administration was required to end its hostilities against Iran. It has not,” Meeks said. He later announced plans to introduce a resolution to compel Mike Johnson, the Republican House speaker, to bring a lawsuit against Trump to make him adhere to the resolutions. That proposal would face long odds, as Johnson is a close ally of Trump, as well as a lengthy wait, since the House is out of session through the majority of August. The resolution’s passage nonetheless underscore the continued ability of Democrats to seize on divisions among House Republicans – as well as their narrow majority in the chamber – to embarrass the president. Massie’s libertarian politics have brought him into conflict with Trump, and he lost his primary in May after Trump endorsed his opponent. Davidson harbors similar beliefs, while Barrett and Fitzpatrick represent swing districts and are top targets in November’s midterm elections. “If we want a war, or need one, we should apply the lessons from history and our Constitution,” Davidson said on social media following the vote, listing steps including “define the mission”, “declare/authorize the war” and “multiply allies, not enemies”. “Otherwise, avoid / exit the war with diplomacy or maneuver,” he said. The resolution’s passage offered a contrast to the day prior, when House Republicans had advanced both a $95bn budget blueprint that will chiefly be spent on military needs related to the Iran war, and a $1.15tn defense spending bill. The former is facing major delays in the Senate, while the latter is set to see major revisions, since it requires Democratic votes to pass and Johnson allowed the insertion of strict new regulations on voters that the minority party refuses to support. Fighting has meanwhile renewed in the Middle East, with Iran attacking US military bases around the region in recent days amid retaliatory American airstrikes. The Tehran-aligned Houthis in Yemen have threatened to halt Saudi oil shipments through the Red Sea, and announced on Thursday they had attacked two tankers, which drove crude prices upwards.

title: ‘Our system is in dire straits’: progressive Democrats hold Medicare for All hearing
author: Michael Sainato
summary: Congressional Progressive caucus say ‘healthcare should not be a privilege’ as they champions single payer system
body_text: The Congressional Progressive caucus (CPC) held a shadow hearing on Medicare for All on Wednesday, led by Pramila Jayapal and Debbie Dingell. The hearing comes as over half of the House Democratic caucus has co-sponsored Medicare for All legislation, and Senator Andy Kim introduced legislation on Tuesday that would enroll all children into Medicaid until the age of 26, while Republicans passed drastic healthcare cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including nearly $1n in cuts to Medicaid and allowing Affordable Care Act subsidies to expire. “I’m going to get this over the finish line before I die, and I don’t plan on dying soon. But I’d like to get it done,” Dingell said in an opening statement, citing her father-in-law, John D Dingell Sr, who drafted the universal healthcare legislation that laid the foundation for Medicare, and her late husband, John Dingell, who frequently introduced Medicare for All legislation in his decades-long career in Congress. “We spend twice as much per person on healthcare compared to other countries that have systems like Medicare for All, and we still have 28 million Americans without insurance, and an increase in the number of people uninsured since 2023,” she said. “We have worse outcomes, including low life expectancy and higher infant mortality rates. The only people benefiting are the corporations who are profiting while Americans are struggling.” National Nurses United, the largest union of nurses in the US, testified in support of Medicare for All, along with Public Citizen, Physicians for a National Health Plan, People’s Action Institute and other supporters of the policy. A study by Yale epidemiologists in 2020 found Medicare for All would save about 68,000 lives a year and about 13% in reducing US healthcare spending, about $450bn. “I do not exaggerate when I say our healthcare system is in dire straits. Every day in my clinic, I see patients struggling with the cost of healthcare,” said Dr Diljeet K Singh, president of Physicians for a National Health Plan, in her testimony at the hearing. “At least 35 cents of every healthcare dollar is wasted on insurance administration and corporate profit, not spent on patient care.” Jamie Brown RN, president of National Nurses United, described in her testimony the impact of healthcare employers prioritizing profits over healthcare, resulting in understaffed units and high patient loads that lead to worse health outcomes for patients. “The only way to transform our system for the better is to ensure that the profit motive is completely removed from the equation,” said Brown. The center-left Searchlight Institute has urged Democrats to refrain from supporting Medicare for All, citing a June poll by Tavern Research that found either a majority or plurality in support of single payer healthcare. Nevertheless the vast majority, 70% of those polled, preferred to keep their current health insurance – although the question did not account for the fact that 45% of respondents already received their insurance through Medicare or Medicaid. The thinktank has supported its Health Care Unity plan, which endorses incrementally expanding government’s role in healthcare such as negotiating drug prices and breaking up monopolies. In a separate poll conducted in November by the Medicare for All Pac, 52% of those polled were in favor of a Democratic candidate who supported the policy over 45% backing a Republican candidate supporting a standard Republican policy on healthcare. The poll found 90% support from Democratic voters for a universal healthcare policy. “Medicare for All remains, for the Progressive caucus, our number one priority for reforming our healthcare system, and we believe that it should be the number one priority for our Democratic party and for our country,” said Congressman Greg Casar at the hearing. He went on to cite the multimillion-dollar salaries of healthcare CEOs across the industry and the millions of dollars spent by healthcare corporations on lobbying in response to common criticisms from Republicans toward Medicare for All about the costs. “Healthcare should not be a privilege determined by your job, your income, or your zip code. Yet millions of Americans continue to delay or forgo care because they simply cannot afford it,” said Congressman Jesús “Chuy” García. Congresswoman Adelita Grijalva discussed her family growing up near a superfund site, having family members die of cancer, and requiring a hysterectomy at an early age. “We must address the underlying causes of this sickness of the system, not just treat the symptoms,” she said. “The symptoms of our current healthcare system are the highest out-of-pocket expenses for people in any high-income nation, the highest amount of medical bankruptcies, the highest national spending by far, worse health outcomes, delayed and denied care, and higher preventable deaths and lower life expectancies. The outcomes are especially terrible for people who are lower-income, people of color, and people who live in rural communities.” Congresswoman Melanie Stansbury cited the significant money spent on weapons and the US military in contrast with criticisms of the costs of universal healthcare system, as the Trump administration’s war on Iran has cost $37.5bn so far. “There is no person that should die because they’re afraid to go to the emergency room. There is no person that should live in a rural and tribal community in this country who can’t access basic care in their communities,” said Stansbury. “That is moral depravity. Healthcare is a human right.” In concluding the hearing, Jayapal emphasized healthcare for all as a cultural shift that would improve the lives of millions of Americans. “I think this is the moment where the current system has collapsed under the weight of for-profit insurance companies and all of the entities that stand to benefit,” she said. “It is going to be a fight to get there. But I believe the American people across party line are with us, and are looking for transformative system where everyone is in and nobody is out, and healthcare is truly a human right.”

title: Seth Meyers on Trump’s approval ratings: ‘Worse than Bush during the Iraq war’
author: Guardian staff
summary: Late-night host discussed Trump’s claims of a rigged 2020 election, push for voting changes and new Canadian tariffs
body_text: Last night, Seth Meyers focused on Donald Trump’s claims that China swayed the 2020 election, new tariffs on Canadian imports and his attempt to impose voting restrictions. Seth Meyers On Late Night with Seth Meyers, the host reacted to reports that Trump’s approval ratings in his second term are the worst of any 21st-century president, scoring lower than Barack Obama and George W Bush. “Trump is doing worse than Bush during the Iraq war – and remember, Bush had a pair of shoes thrown at him,” Meyers said. “That was the moment you could tell Bush played baseball. He reacted to [dodging] that first shoe like, ‘That’s inside.’ “Trump, on the other hand, has zero agility. If someone threw a shoe at him, he’d still have a mark. And the sole of the shoe would be a mess! Or just perfectly painted.” Meyers pointed out that Trump is unpopular with people with no party affiliation as well as those on the left. According to a Washington Post poll, he is scoring worse with independents than Richard Nixon during Watergate. Reacting to a CNN host who called the numbers “quite troubling”, Meyers laughed: “Quite troubling? I would say that’s a real fucking understatement. “That’s like if your doctor came into the exam room with an X-ray and said, ‘As you can see here, you have 27 Matchbox cars lodged in your rectum. Compounding the matter, you ate lettuce tainted with cyclospora, which means the cars are blocking the explosive diarrhea.’” In a speech last week, Trump accused China of illegally acquiring 220m US voter files in a pattern dating back to the 2020 election. “This happened in 2020, you say?” asked Meyers. “Man, whoever was president back then must feel like an idiot right now. “Also – I’ve never asked this of a president before – are you drunk, bro? You sound like you’re 10 beers deep at a frat party complaining about your girlfriend’s besties.” While Trump continues to insist that the 2020 election was rigged, Meyers pointed out that much of the voter data that he says China stole is in the public domain or available to be legally purchased from states for a small fee. “Yeah, of course you can – you can buy anything online,” said Meyers. “And by the way, not only is all that information already public, but Trump’s own team of cranks and nutjobs admitted after the speech there was still no proof of widespread election fraud.” This week Trump also announced plans for steep tariffs on Canadian imports with up to 50% fees on goods including cement and hockey sticks. “Hockey sticks?” asked Meyers. “So you’re just a total dick. You might as well slap a tariff on Molson, maple syrup and the concept of apologizing. That is such an insult to Canada. “It’s like Canada imposing a tariff on something that’s quintessentially American … like gambling on crypto while you sit on the toilet because you made the mistake of thinking it was safe to eat lettuce from Taco Bell.” Trump is also demanding that Congress pass a law that would require voters to show their passport or birth certificate at polling stations, in a move that would disenfranchise millions of people. “Who the hell knows where their birth certificate is?” asked Meyers. “I’m guessing mine’s in a manila folder somewhere between takeout menus and photos of my brother”.

title: Iran crisis is not solely a product of Trump’s rule
summary: Letters: Focusing on Donald Trump’s defects risks making war appear as an aberration rather than as a recurring feature of American power, writes David Eaton. Plus letters from Blaine Stothard and Harvey Gilbert
body_text: Simon Tisdall’s article (Trump, not Iran, is the world’s greatest danger. He’s a one-man weapon of mass destruction, 18 July) is a forceful polemic, but it risks turning a structural problem into a personal one. If Donald Trump is uniquely reckless, that deserves criticism. Yet the article implies that America’s present predicament is chiefly the consequence of his character, rather than asking why successive administrations, Republican and Democrat alike, have repeatedly resorted to military intervention in the Middle East. To focus on Trump’s defects risks making war itself appear as an aberration rather than as a recurring feature of American power. The same applies to the strait of Hormuz. Its strategic importance does not begin or end with one president. It reflects a global economic order that depends on secure energy supplies, trade routes and the projection of military power to guarantee them. That broader context is largely absent. The article also assumes that a more competent president, acting with Congress, allies and international law on side, would have avoided today’s crisis. History offers little comfort. We have been here before: the Iraq, Afghanistan and Libya conflicts were carried out under far more conventional presidencies. Trump may be the spectacle, but he is not the problem. The article focuses on the drama rather than the system that keeps producing it. David Eaton Sunderland • Simon Tisdall is right to identify the dangers to the world presented by the Trump administration and the president himself. Tisdall enumerates the recent damage, death and destruction that the Trump administration has presided over, seeing current excesses and abuses of power as dangers to the rest of us, as indeed they are. But the current excesses, overt and covert, can be seen as a continuation of American history and practice that not only has led to the 20th century being seen as the American century, but also as the century of US wars. Since the end of the first world war, we have seen the US initiate the war for oil, the war against communism, the war against drugs, the war against terror and the war against Islam. All continue to have negative impacts on the rest of the world, and perpetuate American foreign policy arrogance and belligerence. All these wars failed to achieve their supposed aims. They have also provided cover for other tyrannical governments to act in similar, if less universal, fashion. I’m not sure we should see Trump as an aberration – more as a more shameless manifestation of what has always been there. Blaine Stothard London • I agree wholeheartedly with Simon Tisdall, but he didn’t answer his own question: who will stop Donald Trump? The polls show his weakness, but the upcoming elections may not because the Democrats are so weak and Trump will inevitably confuse the results to his own benefit. The answer to the question must lie in the Republican party itself. Surely there are enough right-thinking Republicans to turn votes against him and force some control over his behaviour. It is beginning to happen. This may be the way to begin to bring him to heel, but it creates further issues before any real resolution. The immediate problem for the American people and the world is twofold. First, as the “wounded bear”, Trump will continue to do catastrophic damage before November’s elections. And second, Marco Rubio to take over? God save us all. Harvey Gilbert Milton Keynes • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Donald Trump says decision on ‘massive attack’ against Iran is close
author: Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent
summary: President’s remarks follow Houthi strikes on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and oil prices rising past $100 a barrel again
body_text: Donald Trump has said he is close to deciding whether to launch “a massive attack” against Iran, on a scale larger than strikes already witnessed during the months-long conflict with Tehran. Speaking to the Axios news site, the US president said: “I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before. I am close to making a decision. We are all set for it.” Trump made his remarks on Thursday as oil prices once again surged past the symbolic $100 for a barrel of Brent crude, the international benchmark, and amid indications the price could go higher still. He acknowledged that such a decision would have consequences but said he had not yet made a final determination. Israel “would join in two minutes if I ask them to”, he added, before saying: “We don’t need anybody.” Hours later the US carried out a 13th consecutive night of strikes on Iran lasting more ⁠than two hours. Iranian state media reported explosions along the strait of Hormuz in Qeshm and Bandar Abbas, as well as to the north-west of the country and in Tehran. The strikes however appeared to broadly match the scope and intensity of those the US has carried throughout the most recent escalation of violence. Trump’s comments on Thursday followed the earlier threat of “major military punishment” against Iran and the Houthis, after the Iran-backed Yemeni militia’s attacks on two Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea. Underlining the sense of a region increasingly approaching an abyss, the UN secretary general, António Guterres, told the security council that the Middle East was being pushed to the “edge of the unimaginable” amid mounting fears over the trajectory of the conflict. “The situation is getting out of control. It is teetering on the edge of the unimaginable. The region is being pulled into an ever-widening circle of confrontation. One crisis feeds another. One escalation triggers the next,” Guterres told a security council meeting. “As this dynamic spreads, the political objectives are becoming increasingly obscured by the confrontation itself.” The UK announced it was temporarily withdrawing diplomatic staff from Iran on Wednesday, and the German military announced on Thursday that it would withdraw two vessels from the Red Sea. And as Israeli cities opened bomb shelters, the US state department warned Americans living in the region that flights may be cancelled. In a separate development, Trump clarified on Thursday that an announced agreement that the US would help Saudi Arabia with its civilian nuclear programme would require the kingdom to normalise relations with Israel through the Abraham Accords, a move Saudi Arabia has long resisted until there is demonstrable movement on Palestinian rights and statehood. It emerged later that Trump had not spoken to Saudi Arabia about the new condition. The Houthi attacks threatened the safety of a second major maritime route connecting the Suez canal to the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. They also came amid reports that Iran had sent military advisers and drone parts to the Houthis 10 days ago. Quoting four sources, including two Iranians, Reuters reported on Thursday that Iran had transferred Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps personnel and military-related equipment on a flight from Tehran to Yemen on 13 July, as Tehran was calling for the Houthis to blockade the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Ships had begun turning back from sailing through the narrow strait this week after the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi ports, most notably the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which Riyadh has been using to ship oil to Asia during the conflict that has all but halted shipping through the strait of Hormuz. The maritime data and analysis firm Lloyd’s List Intelligence said the Houthi attacks put Saudi oil shipments from Yanbu at risk and presented a “double whammy” on top of the Hormuz disruptions, , adding that the Houthi threat “raises questions on the viability of this route”. Trump wrote on social media: “If [the Houthis] do this again, the US will hold Iran responsible, in that the Houthis are a Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran, and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves.” The Houthis’ Saba news agency said the rebels had struck two tankers, the Encelia and the Layla, causing fires on both. There were no reports of casualties in their first reported attack on a vessel since they announced the blockade of Saudi-linked shipping. The Bab el-Mandeb is a vital shipping chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. About 12% of the world’s trade, including a fourth of global container traffic, passes through there, moving between Europe and Asia via the Suez canal at the northern end of the Red Sea. Trump has been escalating his rhetoric against Iran in recent days, hinting the US is prepared to bomb an underground tunnel complex at the “Pickaxe mountain” site where Israel alleges Tehran has hidden centrifuges used in uranium enrichment. As Trump has struggled to get a grip on the spiralling crisis, during which Iran has occasionally launched lethal strikes against US bases and Washington’s Gulf allies, he appears to have been sucked into an “escalation trap”, threatening ever more violent retaliation. On Wednesday, Trump said the US would destroy one bridge or power plant every time Iran shot at a ship in the strait. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said Trump was seeking a “head for an eye” after the recent deaths of several US service members in an Iranian strike on the Muwaffaq Salti airbase in Jordan. However, speaking on the outskirts of the Asean conference in Manila, Rubio said Iran was “begging for a deal”, and insisted “they need to come to their senses” and that they will “pay a very heavy price for the things they are doing” – all claims US officials have made before. With Trump’s poll ratings in freefall, and his war against Iran deeply unpopular at home, the president and his administration are running short of time before the autumn midterm elections to find a resolution to the conflict on Washington’s terms. Underlining Trump’s growing political problems, the US House of Representatives narrowly passed a resolution on Thursday to halt US military action in Iran, the second such warning to the president.

title: The Hegseth budget: defense secretary’s $1.5tn ask reveals military-industrial chaos
author: Aram Roston in Washington
summary: The Pentagon head proposed a 44% increase – to second world war levels – while ‘woke’ programs are gutted
body_text: When the “department of government efficiency” was raging unchecked through the federal government in February 2025, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, ordered his subordinates to find cuts of 8% a year for the next five years, theoretically trimming a total of $340bn from the Pentagon budget. The disclosure briefly sent Palantir and defense stocks tanking – though soon the plan evaporated, as if it never existed. Instead, Hegseth is now demanding a $454bn increase for 2027 military spending, to a total of almost $1.5tn, in what he describes as a “generational investment”. Adjusted for inflation, that would for the first time match – and even exceed – US military spending at the height of the second world war during national mobilization, according to a chart prepared by the Center for Strategic and International Studies. The US defense budget is in what may be one of its messiest phases in recent memory. That’s because at the same time Donald Trump and Hegseth are making the push for the unprecedented increase in the defense budget – a 44% jump – they are also insisting on extracting emergency funding for the unpopular and disastrous war under way in Iran. The war needs to be funded separately from the main Pentagon budget, which is why Hegseth is running in essence a two-pronged campaign on Capitol Hill: on the one hand, to cajole and bully Republicans to fund, for the relatively short term, the Iran war, and, on the other hand, to pour a historic amount of financing into the already vast military enterprise he presides over with his deputy, the private equity tycoon Stephen Feinberg. $75bn in spare change Hegseth and chair of the joint chiefs of staff, Dan Caine, faced a skeptical Senate appropriations committee on Tuesday in a hearing that was intended to focus on the Iran war part of the military budget push. Hegseth is asking for $67bn in emergency defense funds for his department for 2026. The ranking Democrat on the committee, Patty Murray, pointed out how much of the spending the Trump administration is asking for as an emergency seems uncorrelated to the flailing operations in Iran. “$800m for the national guard to patrol DC even longer,” she listed. “Over $1bn for the army to patrol the southern border, which is [the Department of Homeland Security’s] job. $900m to support the administration’s illegal boat strikes in the Caribbean.” Hegseth answered by blaming his predecessors: “Why this kind of spending is needed is because of the gross negligence and neglect of the Biden administration.” It’s widely known inside and outside the Pentagon that because of the way the Iran war has been run, the US is running desperately short of what it needs in case of a new military crisis. But with extraordinary obstinacy, Hegseth appears to insist any shortages at all can be blamed solely on Joe Biden and past military leaders. The missiles fired and depleted during Iran, in this construct, are not his fault. There’s yet another kink that is making some senators wary: last year the Hegseth Department of Defense already received a $156bn bump under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. And half of that, about $75bn, is still unobligated – with no detailed plans for how it’s to be spent. By Pentagon standards, it’s spare change, but that’s nearly the value of the entire US Department of Education budget. Questioned about it in the hearing, Hegseth didn’t have any details about that $75bn, though he claimed there was actually a blueprint for where the money will go. “I’d have to get you the exact numbers,” he testified. The Iran war through 30 September Hegseth disclosed a new estimate about the cost of the Iran war – $37.5bn. But he was vague. He said that that would include expenditures up to the present “for certain aspects”, but hedged that the estimate included military pay, operations and maintenance, and other costs “through September 30”. Becca Wasser, a defense expert at the Center for New American Security, said Hegseth’s comments appear to be “a little bit of a signal that the war is still probably going to be going on by September 30”. Messy efforts to fund wars are not new: back during combat operations in Iraq and Afghanistan, the two Bush administrations, the two Obama administrations and the first Trump administration tagged the combat costs on to the defense budget under what were called “overseas contingency operations” (OCO) funds. Biden, Wasser said, shifted Ukraine spending to emergency supplemental requests rather than OCO funding, and Trump in his second term seems to be following that route on Iran. One huge break from the past: Trump defense department spending is being steered to so-called reconciliation – a legislative mechanism outside normal appropriations which strips the senators of the chance to filibuster a measure. Wasser of the Center for New American Security said: “That’s what makes it incredibly unique.” Late on Wednesday, the House passed a $1.15tn bill for a section of the White House request – which may move it forward, but experts say it’s still nowhere close to something that will clear the Senate. The real money, that $1.5tn, dwarfs the costs of the Iran war. While much of it is for the usual tanks and planes and hardware and training, there’s a good chunk for the pet projects of the tech bros and private equity financiers now running the department. The military’s head of research and engineering is the former Uber executive Emil Michael, who oversees artificial intelligence. As the Guardian reported earlier this year, Michael, while in his first months in office, made millions in profits, between 400% and 4,800%, just on his investment in Elon Musk’s xAI company. The Trump budget plans to steer $58.5bn to AI. About $20bn is targeted for the office of strategic capital, a defense department agency that functions as a private equity arm of the Pentagon. The powerful deputy secretary of defense, Stephen Feinberg, former head of Cerberus Capital, has a former employee of Cerberus presiding over the office. It’s the same agency that committed $620m last year to a mining company backed by a fund tied to Trump’s son Donald Jr. The Trump administration did nod in only one apparent way to fiscal constraints. Without apparent irony, the administration said it had identified $1.6bn in defense reductions related to DEI. “The budget,” the White House said earlier this year, “continues to eliminate millions of dollars in wasteful and egregious spending related to diversity, equity and inclusion and other ‘woke’ programs.” • This article was amended on 25 July 2026. The Pentagon originally aimed to trim $340bn from its budget, not $340m as originally stated in the article.

title: Trump says nearly 200 firms have signed pledge to protect Americans from costs arising from datacenters
author: Dharna Noor
summary: ‘Ratepayer Protection Pledge’ president has touted is non-binding as people continue to struggle with rising bills
body_text: Donald Trump has announced that about 200 entities have signed on to his non-binding “Ratepayer Protection Pledge”, expanding a voluntary commitment which claims to ensure US consumers will not bear the cost of the AI datacenter build-out. Trump delivered remarks on Thursday at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) headquarters, alongside Lee Zeldin, the agency’s administrator, and Chris Wright, the energy secretary. Other attenders included governors who signed on to the pledge, including Brian Kemp of Georgia, Mike DeWine of Ohio, Spencer Cox of Utah and Jeff Landry of Louisiana. The pledge, first announced in March, was initially signed by seven tech companies: Google, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, xAI, OpenAI and Amazon. It will now cover companies delivering 80% of all power to US homes and businesses, according to the White House. “We have kept rates down, way down,” said Trump. Twenty-three Republican governors have signed on to the scheme, Trump announced on Thursday, as have major utilities including Nextera and Duke Energy, datacenter developers and electricity cooperatives. “Electricity rates for 80% of the power distributed in America are now being kept in check by the plan,” Trump said at a press conference. The announcement came amid a growing backlash to the artificial intelligence boom and the datacenters powering it, as electricity bills rise ahead of November’s midterm elections. In June, utility prices were up 4% year-over-year, data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows. On Thursday, Trump said “radical left communists” are the ones who “want to shut down all new development, kill our most successful industries, destroy hundreds of thousands of jobs, and surrender the AI race to China”. Yet opposition to datacenters has become a bipartisan issue, with voters concerned about not only utility rates, but also the environmental and social impacts of AI. More than a dozen states have considered moratoria on datacenters, and New York became the first US state to enact a temporary ban this month. Senator Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a representative, have also proposed a national moratorium. And on Thursday, Greg Abbott, the Republican governor of Texas, called for a ban on datacenter development in rural Texas; he is now among the governors who signed on to the pledge. The pledge will “ensure everyone involved in building and powering data centers covers their own costs instead of passing them on to American families”, Taylor Rogers, a White House spokesperson, told the Guardian. “The President’s bold action is turning datacenters into engines of growth for local communities, while cementing America’s dominance in the global AI race,” Rogers said. Green groups are largely unimpressed with the non-binding pledge. “The American people don’t care about the weak pledges and empty promises; they need relief from soaring energy bills month after month and real action from these companies to pay their fair share and bring down high costs,” said Patrick Drupp, climate policy director at the national environmental advocacy organization Sierra Club. “Today’s pledge is a paper-thin commitment to families who are struggling to keep the lights on as bills soar. The companies signing on have done nothing to show their work on how they will lower costs.” Lena Moffitt, executive director of climate advocacy organization Evergreen Action, called Trump’s announcement a “photo op with big tech” that “won’t lower a single family’s electric bill”. “Trump promised again and again to cut Americans’ energy costs, but instead he’s letting the same corporations driving up demand write their own rules – a voluntary pledge with no teeth and no consequences if they break it,” she said.

title: Louisiana House candidate accused of rape says he hopes to again ‘earn’ Trump endorsement
author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
summary: Republican Blake Miguez is weighing what district to run in after state redrew map following supreme court decision
body_text: A congressional candidate from Louisiana who was the subject of a police report accusing him of rape – which he denies – says he is hoping to again “earn” Donald Trump’s endorsement as he considers precisely where to run amid redistricting. The candidate, Blake Miguez, is weighing running in one of two districts, neither of which he lives in but in which he is allowed to run. He has been mulling that choice after the supreme court’s landmark decision in Callais v Louisiana prompted the state to swiftly redraw its US House districts – and after he had secured the president’s backing under the previous congressional map. Approached on Wednesday after Miguez’s campaign website had become password protected and otherwise blank, a spokesperson said: “Blake was honored to have President Trump’s endorsement for [an] old … congressional district that no longer exists” after Callais, “and [he] hopes to earn it again after he announces a campaign under the new district lines.” A White House spokesperson clarified that Trump did not formally rescind his endorsement – but added that the president “will look at the candidate field after candidate [qualifying] if necessary”. “At this point, [Trump] has not made any changes nor does he have an intent to,” the spokesperson said. “If new information changes things, we will cross that bridge when we get to it.” The Republican Louisiana state senator secured the coveted backing of Trump in the race for a US House seat as he qualified to run in a 16 May primary for the post, which is safely held by their party. But that primary was postponed until the November midterms after the Callais decision. Miguez’s campaign has also had to grapple with an Atlantic report that he had not disclosed to Trump’s team the existence of a 2007 rape accusation reported to local law enforcement on the same day of the alleged assault. That police report – which the Guardian also independently obtained and reported on – never resulted in charges, and Miguez categorically denied the claim as false. But it reportedly raised concerns within the White House that Miguez “either wasn’t fully vetted or wasn’t forthcoming about discoverable documents from his past” while he successfully pursued Trump’s endorsement, as the Atlantic reported. The statements from Miguez’s campaign and the White House sparked verbal sparring from one of the candidate’s Republican rivals. Lionel Rainey, a spokesperson for a political action committee supporting another candidate in the postponed US House race, Rick Edmonds, said he found it “silly” to blame redistricting for evident uncertainty over Trump’s endorsement. “Nobody believes that,” Rainey said. Separate 12 March articles from the Guardian and the Atlantic reported on a woman who alleged being raped by Miguez in late August 2007 when he purportedly was her “live-in ex boyfriend”. A police report quoted the woman as saying the assault took place at the end of a night of drinking in Miguez’s home town of Erath, Louisiana. But the legal document said she did not want to press charges against Miguez – then in law school – because she did not want to get him into trouble. One of the ways the Miguez campaign responded to those claims was to link to an article from a Louisiana news outlet that followed up on the Atlantic and the Guardian’s reporting with quotes from family members of the accuser. Those family members questioned the accuser’s credibility while citing mental health and substance abuse problems. The campaign, meanwhile, also circulated an email attributed to her father that was sent to the state senator’s office which read in part: “Everything my daughter has reported about you were lies and she is a liar and has a drug problem.” The Guardian subsequently wrote to the woman offering her the opportunity to address her family member’s statements. She did not reply. In the months since the Miguez accuser’s claims, US House representatives Eric Swalwell and Tony Gonzales – a California Democrat and a Texas Republican, respectively – resigned under bipartisan pressure over allegations of sexual misconduct against both. Furthermore, on 10 July, the Democratic US Senate candidate Graham Platner of Maine withdrew his scandal-laden candidacy days after detailed sexual assault allegations were made against him. Miguez won election to Louisiana’s state senate in 2023 after more than eight years in its house of representatives. He signed up to contest for a seat that congresswoman Julia Letlow vacated when, with Trump’s backing, she victoriously ran in a Republican US Senate primary at the expense of incumbent Bill Cassidy. The boundaries of that seat – in Louisiana’s fifth congressional district – were outside Miguez’s Erath home when Trump endorsed him in February as a “warrior” of the president’s Maga movement. Miguez’s opponents seized on that to try to cast him as a political opportunist, and his campaign countered that he has also long kept a home as well as operated a business in the fifth district, which then included Baton Rouge, Louisiana’s capital, as the state’s Shreveport Times reported. Under the state’s post-Callais congressional map, Erath is still outside Louisiana’s fifth congressional district. The town is in Louisiana’s third district, which since 2017 has been represented by the Republican Clay Higgins. But the new sixth congressional district contains the Baton Rouge capital region. And on Thursday, the sixth district incumbent – the Democrat Cleo Fields – said that he would not seek re-election under the altered boundaries of the post-Callais map. The Times reported in June that Miguez opponents had sources telling them that he had asked Trump to let him carry the president’s fifth district endorsement over to the sixth. US House candidates are not required to run in their home districts. They only need to live in the same state as the congressional district in which they are running. Miguez’s campaign on Wednesday declined to say which Louisiana congressional district he may target when a three-day qualifying period opens on 5 August. • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html
