title: Trump seizes on New Jersey election error to boost misleading fraud claims
author: Sam Levine in New York
summary: Republicans have latched on to the announcement after Trump’s lie-laden speech, but experts say DHS’s data is ‘designed to create a false argument’
body_text: Donald Trump and his allies quickly seized on an announcement from Mikie Sherrill, the New Jersey governor, on Tuesday that 6,600 noncitizens had registered to vote because of a software error, and fewer than 400 of them voted, using the disclosure to escalate false claims that there are scores of noncitizens on the voter rolls. Trump seized on the news days after he said in a primetime speech that the Department of Homeland Security identified 278,000 noncitizens on the voter rolls in New Jersey and three other states. But a Guardian review of the letters the DHS sent the states shows the agency expressed less certainty about the number and has offered no explanation of its methodology. Since 2018, New Jersey has had automatic voter registration, which means that any time someone interacts with a motor vehicle office they are automatically registered to vote, unless they opt out. Between 2023 and 2024, some 6,600 people had indicated they were not citizens, yet nonetheless had been registered to vote. About 400 of those people cast a ballot, Sherrill said. Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the justice department’s civil rights division, sent a letter to Sherrill earlier this week requesting the names of those who were registered and voted and the department is reportedly mulling prosecutions. Sherrill suggested on Thursday the state wasn’t going to turn over the information on voters and said earlier in the week it would be unfair to prosecute them for an error that was the state’s fault. The number represents a small fraction of the more than 6.6 million registered voters in the state. But within hours of the announcement, Trump and other election deniers inflated the number of people who registered to vote because of the error, and held it up as yet another data point that “illegals” are stealing American elections on behalf of Democrats. Trump said in a post on Truth Social: “35,152 is the new number just released by Homeland Security of non-citizens registered to vote in New Jersey. These are just the ones that got caught. The real numbers will prove to be many times this amount. They are all Dumocrats!.” There were Democrats and Republicans erroneously registered, Sherrill said on Tuesday, with the majority unaffiliated with a party. The incident is far from proof of the widespread fraud that Republicans allege, experts say. “It’s not good, I don’t want to suggest otherwise. I don’t want to tell anyone that they’re stupid for thinking it’s less than perfectly optimal. But it’s not really an example of what they’re talking about,” said Stephen Richer, a Republican who oversaw elections in Maricopa county, Arizona, from 2021 to 2025. “These people were trying to do the right thing and acknowledge that they’re not citizens, and then the vast majority of them, even though registered and presumably [were] sent election mail materials, ignored that and didn’t vote.” The number of non-citizens the state says were registered represents a “minuscule fraction” of New Jersey’s active registered voters in 2024, said David Becker, an election administration expert and the executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research. “The number of potential ballots cast from those incorrect registrations would represent roughly 0.009% of all ballots cast in New Jersey’s 2024 general election, when Kamala Harris defeated President Trump by more than 250,000 votes. “While administrative errors such as New Jersey’s do infrequently occur, they are very rare and affect a very small fraction of voters. The states entrusted to run our elections are best positioned to detect and correct these errors, as they have access to substantially better data than the federal government,” he said. The firestorm over the New Jersey voter rolls came as Trump escalated his incendiary rhetoric about voting ahead of the midterm elections. Last week, in a primetime address from the White House, he offered what seemed to be an eye-popping statistic: the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) had found 278,000 non-citizens on the rolls in just four states – California, Nevada, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. That, too, is a misleading figure. In its letters to election officials in those four states DHS expressed less certainty about the 278,000 number, saying it was a ceiling of how many noncitizens could be on the rolls. The agency also offered little to no explanation of its methodology for identifying noncitizens on the rolls. It gave the states two weeks to respond. “It’s a laughable letter,” Becker said. “Imagine someone said to you: ‘Some of the items in your fridge are poisonous. Write us back in two weeks and tell us what you’re going to do about that.’” The first question one would ask, Becker said, is “which items?” “They’re not serious. They don’t want the states to even maintain their records correctly. If they did, they would be completely transparent, and they would have acted immediately and said we absolutely need you to do this,” he added. “This is designed to create a false argument post-election that the election was stolen. This has nothing to do with actually cleaning up the lists.” The noncitizen registration claim was part of a slew of misleading information Trump offered in a speech last week designed to weaken confidence in the US election system ahead of November midterm elections in which his party is expected to lose seats. It also comes as Republicans are pushing legislation that would impose new proof-of-citizenship requirements on voter registration, even though several studies have shown noncitizen voting is extremely rare. Last week, both Trump and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, cited the 278,000 number as evidence that states should share sensitive voter information with the federal government, with Mullin threatening potential prison time for those who don’t comply. At least one Republican has cited the number as a bona fide example of voter fraud. “We know there are roughly 278,000 noncitizens registered to vote. The last three presidential elections were decided by fewer votes,” Marsha Blackburn, a senator of Tennessee, said on Tuesday. “We can affirm that on its face, we refute these claims. These numbers are wildly speculative at best and the Department of Homeland Security hasn’t shared anything that backs it up,” said Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat serving as Nevada’s secretary of state. As of Wednesday afternoon, the DHS had not provided Nevada with a list of suspected noncitizens in the state. In a letter to New Jersey officials last week, the DHS said there may be as many as 35,152 noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls. The agency said it had matched 19,497 voter records to a noncitizen in its system, but did not offer an explanation for the rest. Sherrill said she had been informed of the voter registration issue in her state and begun investigating before Trump’s speech on Thursday evening. She said the DHS had provided no information to back up its claims. “We have asked them for any evidence of this, where they got that number, who this is. We’ve received nothing back yet,” she said on Tuesday. Understanding the methodology the DHS used is critical to assessing the veracity of its claims, experts say. Matching records across different databases is difficult, and the system the DHS uses to try and identify noncitizens – Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (Save) – is known to be error-prone. The DHS said it relied on publicly available voter information from the four states to try and identify noncitizens, information that probably lacks the level of detail needed to get a solid match between voter records and DHS data, Charles Stewart III, a professor at MIT and an expert in election administration, wrote in a post on Substack. “DHS likely lacked the identifiers needed for high-quality matching. Save checks generally require name, date of birth, and a unique immigration or Social Security identifier, and public voter files ordinarily do not contain the most sensitive identifiers,” he wrote. “Anyone with experience in these data-matching exercises should expect those numbers to melt as quickly as ice cream in a Phoenix August.” Even though the agency claimed there could be up to 278,000 noncitizens on their rolls, the DHS said in its letters to the states that it was able to match the name, date of birth, address and social security number to a noncitizen in its system for about 118,000 people. The agency offered no explanation for why it believed there were an additional 160,000 noncitizens on the rolls The DHS did not respond to multiple requests for comment on its methodology. “I am about as certain as I can be, without them coming up with some magical data technique that nobody has ever seen before, that these numbers cannot be even remotely credible,” Becker said. “What I can’t tell you is whether they just made them up. Because they have not been transparent about that. And it’s possible that they just made them up, because we just haven’t seen any methodology whatsoever.” Claims of widespread noncitizen registration and voting often start with a headline-grabbing statistic, and then the numbers often whittle down once election officials investigate. In 2019, for example, Texas announced it suspected there were nearly 100,000 noncitizens on its rolls, 58,000 of whom may have voted. The state later admitted the claim was based on bad data and agreed not to cancel anyone’s voter registration based on it.

title: Pentagon list of service members killed in Iran war removes most recent four
author: Robert Mackey
summary: New York Times reports that list of those killed changed from 18 on Wednesday to 14 on Thursday
body_text: The Pentagon’s official online list of service members killed in the ongoing Iran war does not include the four soldiers who died during renewed fighting over the weekend, despite the fact that their names were included in a Pentagon press release on the formal transfer of their remains back to the United States on Wednesday. A review of the current list on the Pentagon’s Defense Casualty Analysis System website shows that, despite having been last updated on Wednesday, the number of US military personnel killed during Operation Epic Fury, the Pentagon’s name for the US-Israeli war on Iran that Donald Trump launched on 28 February, remains at 14. A separate Names of Fallen list on the same Pentagon casualties site currently includes just 13 service members. According to a New York Times report, the Pentagon website listed 18 American service members as having been killed during the war on Iran on Wednesday, but was changed on Thursday to exclude three service members killed last Friday, Saturday and Sunday as Iran retaliated for new US strikes with an attack on a base used by US forces in Jordan. The list also excluded a fourth soldier who was killed during a controlled detonation of an Iranian drone at Erbil airbase in Iraq. By Thursday, the defense department had lowered that number, reporting that 14 American troops had been killed in the war. Three military officials told the Times that “one reason behind the change was that the Trump administration decided to remove four service members killed this past weekend from the list … because their deaths occurred after President Trump declared a cease-fire in the war in April”. A Pentagon spokesperson disputed that contention, telling the Times that the decreased total of service members killed was due to “temporary data disruptions” that would be quickly fixed. The Pentagon did not immediately return the Guardian’s request for comment. The reported removal of the recent service members killed from the Pentagon list comes one day after Trump traveled to Dover air force base in Delaware to salute the remains of the four soldiers killed in the past week and as he continues to demand credit for the number of people killed being so much lower than in years-long conflicts like the US wars in Korea, Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan. On Wednesday, Trump posted a chart on his social media platform comparing the death toll of 18 in his Iran war with those previous wars, which misstated the number of people killed in Iraq and Afghanistan, with the caption: “These are the real facts. REPORT THEM!” Speaking to reporters on Thursday, on his way to what the Pentagon calls the “dignified transfer” of the service members’ remains, Trump claimed that the dead soldiers had supported his claim that the war on Iran is necessary to prevent that country from developing a nuclear weapons – an effort US intelligence assessed Iran abandoned in 2003. “We’re going to Dover,” Trump said, “to honor our heroes, and they’re indeed great heroes. All of them said, very strongly, that we can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.” At an event on Thursday, Trump again argued that the death toll from his war on Iran was low compared with that of Vietnam, the war he did not serve in as a young man. “You know, we were in Vietnam for 20 years, lost thousands and hundreds of thousands of lives,” Trump said, inflating the actual death toll among US troops of 58,220. “We were in Afghanistan for years. We were in all these wars that you heard about for years and years,” Trump added. “Well, we’re in for four months and we – I had a very sad day yesterday. I went to Dover, four great American patriots killed. That’s 18 … and one is too many, but it’s 18. Whereas in Vietnam, we lost 200,000.” Thomas Massie, a Republican congressman of Kentucky, suggested that the reason the Pentagon death toll for the Iran war excludes the four soldiers killed in the past week is that the Trump administration claims that the war technically ended in June, when Trump signed a temporary ceasefire with Iran over dinner at the palace of Versailles. “Let me explain this absurd ruse: The Pentagon is pretending there have been two Iran wars separated by a brief cease-fire,” Massie wrote on social media. “The reality: By going more than 90 days without congressional authorization,” the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, “IS BREAKING THE LAW and must be held accountable”.

title: What to know about Trump’s new tariffs on more than 80 countries
author: Gaya Gupta
summary: Tariffs ranging from 10%-12.5%, taking effect on Friday, are US president’s latest effort to circumvent Congress
body_text: Just before a temporary levy on global imports was set to expire, the Trump administration issued a fresh wave of tariffs on more than 80 countries late on Thursday, ranging from 10% to 12.5%. The new tariffs take effect on Friday morning. It’s Donald Trump’s latest effort to continue imposing global levies without congressional approval, despite the supreme court ruling in February that found the US president had illegally used his executive power to implement his global trade policies. Trump has long maintained that the US has been paying more than its fair share in tariffs, and that increased duties are necessary to boost American manufacturing and jobs. Here’s what to know about Trump’s latest round of tariffs. Which countries are affected? The US’s largest trading partners, including Canada, Mexico and China, were included among the more than 80 countries that will face the latest tariffs. The United Kingdom, Australia, India and the 27 countries that make up the European Union will also be affected. All of these countries were investigated for their labor practices, according to the office of the US trade representative, who apparently determined whether they were effectively blocking goods that had been produced with forced labor from being imported to the US. How much will they have to pay? These countries will be subject to either a 10% or 12.5% duty. The trading partners that will be subject to a 10% tariff are those who “have made commitments to adopt, and effectively enforce, forced labor import prohibitions”, said the US trade representative. This includes Canada, the European Union, India, Mexico and the United Kingdom. Those that have “failed to adopt a forced labor import prohibition”, including Australia, Brazil, China and Japan, will be subject to a 12.5% tariff rate. What did the supreme court decide on tariffs? In February, the supreme court ruled 6-3 that the 1977 law that Trump had invoked a year earlier was not a sufficient legal justification for the president’s “Liberation Day” tariffs. The law was designed to grant the president greater authority during a national emergency to regulate international trade, but the court said that the power to enact during times of peace belongs solely to Congress. “And they gave Congress ‘alone … access to the pockets of the people’,” the majority opinion reads. “The Framers did not vest any part of the taxing power in the executive branch.” Are the latest tariffs legal? Even after the supreme court found that many of Trump’s tariffs were illegal, the administration had signaled it was determined to find an alternate solution to make tariffs permanent. Trump immediately issued a 150-day 10% global tariff under section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 after the court’s ruling, scheduled to expire at 12.01am, on 24 July. The latest tariffs fall under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which had been used sparingly before Trump’s presidency. It allows the president to impose tariffs if the US trade representative has conducted the required investigations and found sufficient evidence of unfair labor practices that affect American commerce. It is likely that the latest tariffs will be challenged in court. Alan Wolff, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics and the former deputy director-general of the World Trade Organization, wrote in an analysis on Thursday that the “new tariffs would represent another case of presidential overreach”. “If they were challenged in court, the supreme court would likely overturn them,” he added. How have tariffs affected Americans? The New York Federal Reserve estimated that 90% of the economic burden imposed by tariffs was passed on to US consumers and businesses, even though Trump’s administration has maintained they have benefited Americans. Tariff policy has also proved unpopular among many Americans, including Republicans. A recent survey from Harris Poll found that 72% of Americans believe tariffs have had a negative impact on consumers, including 64% of Republican voters. For some American small businesses, however, tariffs have become a non-issue compared with other pressing concerns about the economy, including higher costs and artificial intelligence. Since the February supreme court ruling, the government has also paid companies back tens of billions of tariff revenue.

title: Ireland urged to put pressure on Germany over pro-Palestinian activist’s trial
author: Deborah Cole Berlin correspondent
summary: Irish politicians concerned about Daniel Tatlow-Devally’s treatment in jail want Micheál Martin to send observers to Ulm 5 trial
body_text: A cross-party delegation of Irish politicians has urged Dublin to send observers to a high-security trial of pro-Palestinian activists in Germany and to raise concerns about the Irish defendant’s detention when the German chancellor visits next week. Mairéad Farrell of Sinn Féin, a member of the seven-member delegation, said she and her colleagues had attended the hearing in Stuttgart on Wednesday of the so-called Ulm 5 activists, who are facing charges over an attack on an Israeli arms company. Farrell and two other members of the delegation visited Daniel Tatlow-Devally, the Irish defendant being tried as part of the group, in prison. “I was quite shocked by the treatment that he is receiving. He is 23 hours a day in his cell,” Farrell said, calling on the Irish prime minister, Micheál Martin, to discuss the issue with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, when he visits on Tuesday. Farrell said: “His cell, from what I understand, is 5x2 metres. He doesn’t have much in his cell, so he’s stuck there for 23 hours a day. He only has an hour of visitation per month, which is obviously incredibly short. “It just seems that there’s very harsh conditions that seem unwarranted for the scale of the fact that these people haven’t harmed people.” German prosecutors say Tatlow-Devally was part of a group of five activists who trespassed on to a site owned by Israel’s Elbit Systems last September in the southern city of Ulm, shouting pro-Palestinian slogans as they destroyed equipment and smashed windows. They allegedly caused about €1m (£850,000) in damage. The activists posted videos online in which they claimed responsibility for the attack, saying it was aimed at drawing attention to Germany’s support for Israel and its actions in Gaza. Germany is the second biggest supplier of arms to Israel, after the US. The defendants have remained defiant throughout the proceedings, with Tatlow-Devally telling the court in May that the group was motivated by “urgent humanitarian concerns” and sought to “make a fuss … in the hope to at least interrupt” Elbit’s deliveries to Israel. Last month, a British judge imposed lengthy custodial sentences on four Palestine Action activists who smashed up drones and other equipment at an Elbit Systems UK factory, after ruling that there was a “terrorist connection” to their offending. Farrell said German authorities had not allowed the Irish delegation to discuss the case with Tatlow-Devally. “That felt, I suppose, quite unusual for us,” she said. The politicians also found fault with the trial itself. The defendants, Farrell said, “are basically in a glass cage or behind a glass wall, unable to communicate with their lawyers in … a kind of free manner”. She said: “One of the accused said that they felt that they couldn’t really participate fully in the trial … because of these barriers that have been put in place.” Lawyers for the defendants, Berlin-based activists who are British, Irish, German and Spanish citizens, have repeatedly raised the issue of the glass wall with the court, saying it hinders their clients’ right to representation. The five activists have been charged with trespassing, destruction of property and membership of a criminal organisation – Palestine Action Germany – under section 129 of the German criminal code. That charge means authorities consider the accused a threat to society, allowing them to deny bail, even after the six-month limit of pre-trial detention had passed. If found guilty, they face up to five years in prison. Court representatives have said the conditions of the defendants’ detention are warranted based on the severity of the charges against them. Before the trial began in April, Stuttgart’s higher regional court ordered the continuation of pre-trial detention for all defendants based on “a risk of flight, which would not be sufficiently mitigated even by the posting of bail”. Farrell said it was “absolutely crucial” for the Irish government to send envoys to regularly attend hearings until a verdict was delivered. “That was something that couldn’t have been clearer coming out of that trial yesterday: that there is a need for observers,” she said. Farrell urged Martin to bring up the Ulm 5 case when Merz visits for talks focused on Dublin’s six-month presidency of the EU, which began on 1 July. She said the Irish prime minister needed to raise concerns expressed by the defendant, his family and the delegation related to his treatment in prison and “his access in terms of legal representation as part of the trial”. The delegation included the MPs Richard Boyd Barrett and Ruth Coppinger, both of the People Before Profit-Solidarity party, Barry Ward of Fine Gael and Duncan Smith of Labour, as well as senator Patricia Stephenson of the Social Democrats and MEP Lynn Boylan of Sinn Féin. Farrell said the group aimed to return to Germany before the trial wrapped up, probably in January: “This isn’t the end for us. We will be keeping an eye on this trial.”

title: Trump imposes fresh tariffs on UK, EU and dozens of other trading partners
author: Gaya Gupta and Shrai Popat
summary: New tariffs will replace 10% global duty and come after US supreme court declared many of the earlier levies illegal
body_text: Donald Trump has imposed a fresh round of tariffs on more than 80 countries to replace a 10% global duty that was due to expire, provoking a wave of criticism and protests from US allies and major trading partners. In the latest attempt to instate aggressive trade policies despite challenges from the US supreme court, the president has imposed tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% on dozens of countries, including the UK, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, China and the 27 countries that make up the European Union. It in effect replaces the blanket 10% tariff that Trump imposed in February, right after the supreme court declared many of his earlier tariffs were illegal. The newest levies, announced late on Thursday by the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, would fall under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which is aimed against countries that engage in forced labor. Trump had said his administration would investigate unfair trading practices to impose permanent tariffs as soon as the February supreme court decision was announced. “The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” Greer said in a statement. “I am encouraged by the trading partners who have moved quickly to adopt forced labor import prohibitions, and look forward to ensuring their effective enforcement.” Australia and Brazil described the new tariffs as unjustified and said they would seek to have them removed, while Norway’s foreign minister said there was no basis for the new tariffs. The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said the bloc would seek clarification from Washington, adding that it had honoured commitments under a transatlantic trade agreement reached last year and viewed ⁠the new tariffs as a shock. Canada, one of America’s largest trading partners, immediately responded that it “should not be targeted”, adding it was a leader against the practice of importing goods produced with forced labor. “If the intent is truly to address forced labour, the focus should be a coordinated approach through a multilateral mechanism,” Matthew Holmes, executive vice-president of the Canadian chamber of commerce, said in a statement. “The timing of this is somewhat suspect as previous rounds of tariffs sunset.” Trump had long viewed tariffs – border taxes levied on imports – as a core tool to protect American jobs and manufacturing, reduce trade deficits and reverse what he sees as “unfair” practices by US trading partners. Tariff, he has said many times, is “the most beautiful word in the dictionary”. Only Congress has the authority under the constitution to levy taxes. But last April, on what he declared was “liberation day”, Trump announced a baseline 10% tariff under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, a trade law that grants the president the authority to regulate international transactions during a national emergency. That policy, however, suffered a damaging blow in February when the US supreme court ruled 6-3 that the ability to enact tariffs during peacetime still belongs to Congress. Trump immediately announced another 10% tariff regime under another trade law that had never been used before, which limited the tariffs to a period of 150 days. Those tariffs expired a minute past midnight on Friday morning US eastern time. The latest round of tariffs invoke section 301, which has long proved controversial and so far been used sparingly, according to a Brookings analysis of the law in March. Alan Wolff, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics and the former deputy director-general of the World Trade Organization, wrote in an analysis on Thursday that the latest tariffs “again raise the question of whether the president has the legal authority to determine and implement US tariff policy – an authority that the constitution vests in Congress”. “The answer is no: Congress did not delegate authority of such breadth to the president. It cannot constitutionally do so,” he said. “These new tariffs would represent another case of presidential overreach. If they were challenged in court, the supreme court would likely overturn them.” Outside courtroom setbacks, Trump’s tariffs have also proved unpopular among Americans, potentially presenting a threat to Republicans at the midterms this November. A Harris Poll survey, conducted exclusively for the Guardian, found earlier this year that seven in 10 Americans said they paid higher prices because of Trump’s tariffs, and 72% of voters believe the tariffs have had a negative rather than a positive impact on consumers. This belief persisted even among Republican voters: 64% agreed that Trump’s tariffs had led to higher prices, and 60% said tariffs had had a negative impact. American consumers have also been pummeled by the effects of the war in the Middle East, which have sent energy costs and gas prices soaring. The rise in energy prices has also led to a surge in inflation, which jumped to a three-year high this May. Trump and his administration, however, are adamant that his policies have only improved the lives of American consumers. During a heated exchange before US senators on Wednesday, Greer appeared to claim Trump’s policies had not driven prices higher. Asked by the Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren if the tariffs had increased prices for American families, Greer said: “No.” “Core inflation fell to 2.6% year on year, much better than in January 2025,” he added. Core inflation excludes food and energy. Overall inflation is slightly higher than it was when Joe Biden left office.

title: Trump says he will dismantle the ICC ‘brick by brick’. It could be his most chilling move of all
author: Steve Bloomfield
summary: The US is aligning itself with dictators and autocrats to prevent those accused of genocide, ethnic cleansing and war crimes from ever facing justice, says Steve Bloomfield, former international editor of the Observer
body_text: Barely a month appears to go by without Donald Trump making a fresh attempt to destroy the international rules-based order. The US has pulled funding from dozens of international institutions, shut down USAID and withdrawn from the Paris climate agreement. Nato may survive on paper, but Trump has made clear that he has little interest in coming to the aid of any ally that is attacked. The Board of Peace is clearly an attempt to sideline the United Nations. But the state department’s announcement last week that it wishes to dismantle the international criminal court “brick by brick” could be Trump’s most frightening move of all. This is not an idle social media post sent out late at night; there is no chance that the next person to speak to Trump might change his mind. It is now official US policy to destroy the ICC, and the administration is prepared to go to extraordinary lengths to do so. Nations that do not fall into line will be punished. The state department has promised “increased scrutiny of nations that refuse to reject the ICC’s false authority while relying on US assistance”, particularly targeting those countries that “enjoy the benefits of the US security umbrella”. That will include the UK, a country that contributes just over £15m a year to the ICC, making it the fourth largest donor after Japan, Germany and France. Travel and sanctions bans have already been imposed on judges and senior officials; now more will be targeted. As one of those previously threatened with sanctions told me, it can result in individuals being completely cut off from modern life. Personal bank accounts are shut down, while a whole host of US apps and websites, from Uber to booking.com, are off-limits. Email accounts can be blocked – Microsoft and Google are US companies. For the court itself, it means backing up evidence previously held on Microsoft systems. The state department campaign also includes working with other nations that are not part of the ICC, suggesting that the US could ally itself with Russia and China. Make no mistake, this is an existential crisis not just for the ICC but the very idea of international justice. The most powerful nation on Earth and the supposed leader of the democratic west is aligning itself with dictators and autocrats to prevent those accused of genocide, ethnic cleansing and war crimes from ever facing justice. The US has had a complicated history with international justice. It was integral in the establishment of the post-second world war Nuremberg trials but was reluctant to ratify the genocide convention, only doing so in 1988, four decades after it was passed by the UN general assembly. The issue was always one of self-preservation, rather than principle. For generations of US politicians, mainly Republicans but including some Democrats, the very idea that judges in other countries could hold American citizens to account was a non-starter. Until now, successive US presidents have generally accepted the idea of international justice even if, hypocritically, they did not want it to apply to them. The US refused to sign the Rome statute that created the ICC in 2002, but it did not use its power to prevent its birth. In 2005, at the height of the Darfur genocide, it allowed the UN security council to pass a resolution authorising the ICC to investigate, and if necessary prosecute, those accused of war crimes in Sudan. Under Joe Biden’s presidency, it also encouraged the ICC to prosecute Vladimir Putin for alleged war crimes committed in Ukraine. For Trump, though, the ICC has always been a threat. He imposed sanctions on court officials during his first term, following an investigation into alleged war crimes committed by US troops in Afghanistan. The campaign against the court ratcheted up after his return to office last year. The ICC’s chief prosecutor, Karim Khan, had issued an arrest warrant for Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of committing war crimes in Gaza. In response, Trump imposed fresh sanctions on ICC officials including Khan. The threats to the ICC are not just coming from its enemies – many of them are self-inflicted. Two women, one a staffer at the ICC, have accused Khan of sexual abuse. The executive committee of the ICC’s governing body last month voted to suspend Khan, who denies any wrongdoing, after concluding that he had committed serious misconduct. The court’s 125 member states will, this Friday, vote on whether to remove him from office. Staff in The Hague say the ICC has become an increasingly high-pressure place to work, with one former senior official describing the atmosphere as toxic. There are also concerns from international law and human rights experts over its record. It has botched many of its big cases, including against Uhuru Kenyatta and William Ruto, two opposing politicians who were both accused of fomenting Kenya’s post-election violence in 2007-8. As the ICC dithered, witnesses disappeared and the two men joined forces to run for election. Their election as president and vice-president in 2012 eventually led to the case collapsing. The question now is what the “rest of the west” will do in response to Trump’s attacks. The court’s biggest donors need to stay strong and not give in to intimidation. It will be an early test for Ed Miliband, who said upon his appointment as foreign secretary on Monday that “we face a time of greater instability and threat to international law … than at any time since the second world war”. The ICC’s imperfections undoubtedly make it a harder institution to defend. Those weaknesses can be magnified and targeted, making the court’s natural defenders reluctant to man the barricades. Yet that is exactly what needs to happen. Even when it is badly run or cases are poorly constructed, the ICC’s very existence can have an impact. Netanyahu and Putin will for ever be referred to as men indicted for war crimes. Their worlds have shrunk thanks to the threat of arrest. The Philippines’ former president, Rodrigo Duterte, is on trial, accused of crimes against humanity during his “war on drugs”. This is why Trump is so determined to shut it down, argues Luis Moreno Ocampo, the court’s first chief prosecutor. “Trump knows he could be a target after he leaves office,” he told me. “The ICC is a huge obstacle for him.” And that’s another reason why it’s so important the ICC is saved. Actions need to have consequences. After the midterm elections in the US, a Democrat-led Congress is likely to hold hearings and open investigations into a whole host of Trump’s actions, from his murky dealings to his use of paramilitaries against his own citizens. But the rest of the world needs to hold him accountable too – whether it’s for bombing boats in the Caribbean, striking a school in Iran or indeed any fresh horror he commits in the next two and a half years. Just as Putin and Netanyahu will live out the rest of their days knowing the threat of arrest could lie just around the corner, Trump fears this might be his fate. He cannot be allowed to escape it. Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prize

title: Donald Trump hits Australian exports to US with new higher trade tariff over claims of ‘forced labour’
author: Josh Butler and Sarah Basford Canales
summary: Australia’s trade minister, Don Farrell, says tariff regime is unjustified and inconsistent with free trade agreement with US
body_text: Donald Trump has hit Australian exports with new trade tariffs, claiming the country is not doing enough to combat forced labour, but the Albanese government has demanded he remove them immediately. The United States announced on Friday morning (AEST) that many Australian exports now attract a new 12.5% tariff as part of a broader regime affecting dozens of countries. However the Albanese government says Australia’s three largest export categories – including beef and gold – will avoid the tariff hit. In a statement, the US trade department said Australia was on a list of 54 economies it deemed as having “failed to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor”. Other countries facing a 12.5% tariff include Brazil, China, Egypt, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, Russia and Singapore. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Economies on a separate list – including the UK, India, Indonesia, Canada and Mexico – will be subject to a lower 10% tariff after the US claimed they had only failed to “enforce” forced labour prohibitions. Friday’s news followed through on an earlier threat from the Trump administration to level such tariffs, which came after the US supreme court earlier this year struck down Trump’s 10% global tariffs. Trump had responded to that court ruling by immediately announcing temporary trade sanctions, which were due to expire today. Australian government sources had previously told Guardian Australia they believed the forced labour-related tariffs had been levelled as a replacement for the tariffs struck down by the courts. US congresswoman Linda Sánchez, a California Democrat, has denounced the pretext for the new tariffs as a sham. “President Trump isn’t serious about combating forced labor. He’s trying to make an end-run around the Supreme Court and Congress to reimpose his illegal tariffs,” Sánchez wrote on social media. The American trade action document claims “the United States is the only country in the world to adopt, and effectively enforce, a ban on imports made with forced labor”. “President Trump is asking all trading partners to join the United States in eliminating forced labor from global supply chains.” In total the tariffs apply “to the top 60 U.S. trade partners covering 99.4% of U.S. imports”, according to a trade department statement. The Australian trade minister, Don Farrell, immediately called for the US to change course. “These tariffs are unjustified, inconsistent with our free-trade agreement and should be removed,” Farrell said. “Australia’s measures to combat forced labour and modern slavery are among the strongest in the world and we are recognised globally, including in the US, for our leadership.” On the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing program, Farrell said has previously had “acrimonious” talks with the US trade chief, Jamieson Greer, over tariffs. “The idea that the Americans should impose this tariff … is just crazy to be honest with you,” he said. “And the idea that India or Pakistan has a better regime, in terms of modern slavery, than Australia is simply incorrect.” The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, told ABC radio the US actions “make no sense”. “Forced labour is definitely something which needs to be combated around the world, so we support that objective,” he said. “But we have laws, which are amongst the strongest in the world, and we’ve been making that point to the Trump administration.” The US trade action document that sets out the new tariffs includes exemptions for a range of goods including beef; agricultural products such as vegetables and fruits; aircraft parts; certain coal, oil, mineral and chemical products; some metal and steel products; timber products; and machinery. The shadow trade minister, Matt Canavan, claimed the Albanese government had “failed” exporters by not securing lower tariffs, like the UK or Canada. “Australia is subject to a 12.5% tariff rate, the same rate as Russia, China and Venezuela,” the Nationals’ leader said. Canavan said the government had “failed to take meaningful action against forced labour in international supply chains, despite years of warnings”. The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s chief executive, Andrew McKellar, described the move as a “ludicrous decision” and “completely unjustified”. The Business Council of Australia’s head, Bran Black, said the US trade chief’s finding rests on a “narrow claim” without “identifying a single company, enforcement failure, or quantified trade impact”. The National Farmers’ Federation’s chief, Michael Guerin, said the industry was “profoundly disappointed”. “Rather than moving back towards the free and fair trading arrangements that have served both our countries well for two decades, the United States has chosen to further increase barriers to trade, despite Australia’s longstanding record of high standards and responsible trade,” he said. The action, as it pertains to Australia specifically, states that after an investigation, “the Trade Representative has determined to impose 12.5 percent tariffs on products of Australia” except for a limited number of exemptions.

title: ‘Forced labour’ rationale for Trump tariffs met with bewilderment
author: Mark Sweney and agencies
summary: Measures effectively replace blanket 10% tariffs Trump imposed in February that were struck down by US supreme court
body_text: Donald Trump has once again inspired anger and confusion in US allies and trading partners as he imposed a wave of tariffs on more than 80 countries, replacing an expiring global duty introduced earlier this year. The new measures effectively replace blanket 10% tariffs that Trump imposed in February. The US supreme court ruled many of those were illegal. The new levies come in at between 10% and 12.5% on countries including the UK, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, China and the 27 countries that make up the EU. They are imposed under section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974, and the Trump administration has said the new measures are due to the dozens of countries failing to enforce bans on goods produced by forced labour. The imposition of the new tariffs led to Asian stock markets taking a hammering overnight. The Japanese Nikkei 225 fell 3.1%, while the Chinese SSE Composite dropped 1.4%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index was the most heavily hit, down 11.4%, while the South Korean Kospi, which is dominated by its major semiconductor companies, slumped 6.2%. It was more of a mixed picture in Europe as trading began on Friday, with the Stoxx 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, dropping 0.7% before steadying to a fall of 0.1%. France’s Cac 40 initially fell almost 1% before moving into positive territory, up 0.12%. Similarly, Germany’s Dax fell 8% before erasing losses to climb 0.51%. In the UK the FTSE 100 index rose 0.28% in early trading. For many officials digesting the news on Friday, the US rationale was hard to swallow. “You can’t say that ⁠for the European Union,” its foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said on the sidelines ‌of the Asean ‌meeting in Manila. “If you compare our ‌labour laws to the ones of the United States, I mean, we have paid vacations, we have very good labour conditions for our employees, so ‌it’s not really grounded.” Kallas said the EU would seek clarification from Washington, adding that the bloc had honoured commitments under a transatlantic trade agreement reached in 2025 and viewed ⁠the new tariffs as a shock. “We had a deal with America, and we have kept to that deal, that ‌side of the deal,” she said. “That’s why this is a negative surprise that this agreement is not kept.” Australia and Brazil described the new tariffs as unjustified and said they would seek to have them removed. Norway’s foreign minister said there was no basis for the tariff against Norway because the country already had “clear rules that are intended to prevent trade in goods produced using forced labour”. The Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said: “We oppose all forms of unilateral tariff measures. Tariff wars and trade wars are not in the interests of any party.” New Zealand’s prime minister, Christopher Luxon, called them “extremely disappointing” and said the US had not provided “meaningful evidence to support claims in relation to forced labour”. On announcing the tariffs on Thursday, the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, said the US had rigorously policed its own forced labour import ban for almost a century, adding: “It’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same.” However, critics argued the measure was an effort by the Trump administration to rebuild the president’s tariff wall after the supreme court struck down many of his duties in February. “Today’s forced labour justification is too convenient to be taken seriously,” said Richard Neal, the top Democrat on the US House ways and means committee. “Forced labour is a real and pervasive problem in our supply chains and demands serious enforcement. It should never be cheapened into a pretext for a tariff policy built on dubious legal theories and personal grievances.’’ The Trump administration had been hunting for options that would allow it to aggressively deploy tariffs, the former US trade official Ryan Majerus said. The new measures were planned after months of investigation and are considered more resistant to legal challenges. Under Thursday’s announcement, countries that have implemented a forced labour import prohibition or committed to do so were hit with the lower 10% rate – among them Canada, the EU, India and the UK. A UK government spokesperson said that the tariff situation with the US remained unchanged by the latest move from the White House. “There is no change to the tariff rate facing UK businesses as a result of this announcement,” the spokesperson said. “The UK remains on a 10% tariff rate and the preferential access secured under our agreement with the United States remains in place.” He added: “We take forced labour very seriously and ensure that in global supply chains UK businesses are not complicit in forced labour and human rights violations. “The US has recognised the steps the UK is taking, which is why there are no additional tariffs for the UK under this announcement.” China, Japan, South Korea and dozens of others were deemed to deserve the higher 12.5% tariff. Japan’s chief government spokesperson, Minoru Kihara, said the country’s industry and trade were “conducted in accordance with international rules”, adding that Tokyo regretted the new US measures. In the Canadian province of Ontario, officials were getting ready to open a new bridge to the US over the Detroit River, which is expected to enhance trade on both sides of the border. A celebration with officials from both countries was to be held but Canada rejected the joint gathering after Trump this week suddenly announced a 50% tariff on Canadian goods entering the US. Government officials issued a muted response to the latest news, saying it was “not unexpected”. Friday’s measure is unlikely to be the last word from the White House on tariffs. Washington is separately investigating 16 economies for alleged excess industrial capacity – which experts warn will probably lead to additional duties. With Associated Press, Reuters and Agence France-Presse

title: Scientists decry Trump’s ‘blame game’ after he claims Canada ‘poisoning’ US air
author: Oliver Milman
summary: Trump told Mark Carney ‘you got to stop these fires from coming in’ as experts say wildfires symptom of climate crisis
body_text: Scientists have reacted with incredulity after Donald Trump accused Canada of “poisoning” the US’s air with smoke billowing from a slew of forest fires and threatened sanctions upon the country’s northern neighbor. The US president has said that he raised the issue of smoke wafting into the US from nearly 1,000 Canadian wildfires with Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, at the weekend’s World Cup final. “I told him, you got to stop these fires from coming in and poisoning our air,” Trump said. “If we can help them, we’ll help them. But maybe they should pay us some damages or something, or we should do some tariffs.” Trump, who has previously advocated the “raking” and “cleaning” of forests to prevent major conflagrations, this week announced 50% tariffs upon Canada, a long-term US ally that he has previously threatened with annexation. The US is being “unnecessarily invaded by filthy, polluted and unhealthy air”, Trump claimed last week. With palls of wildfire smoke causing unhealthy, hazy skies in cities including New York, Washington DC, Detroit and Toronto in recent weeks, some Republicans in Congress have issued further threats against Canada. Bernie Moreno, a Republican senator from Ohio, said he will introduce legislation to sanction Canada for the “atrocity” of not managing its forests properly. Such threats have been met with shock in Canada, where thousands of people have been evacuated from fires that have badly burned remote towns. More than 8.1m acres (3.3m hectares) have been consumed by fires across Canada’s vast, mostly unpopulated boreal forests, a steep increase on the long-term average. Such fierce wildfires are a symptom of the climate crisis rather than a lack of management, experts warn, with the current blazes worsened by the recent severe heat dome that expanded from the US into Canada. The world is rapidly heating up due to the burning of fossil fuels, a process that Trump has actively sought to accelerate. “This is like crashing into the car in front of you because you were speeding and tailgating, and then demanding they pay for the damage to your headlights,” said Michael Mann, a climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, of Trump’s comments. “It’s victim-blaming by the assailant. “The policies of Trump and the GOP are worsening the problem by doubling down in fossil fuel production and doing their best to obstruct the clean energy transition while the rest of the world moves on,” Mann added. While Trump has falsely dismissed established climate science as “crap”, there is robust evidence linking prolonged hot, dry weather with fire-prone conditions. Elevated temperatures caused by the climate crisis more than doubled the likelihood of severe fire conditions when Canada was last engulfed by major wildfires in 2023, a previous analysis found. “The main cause of worsening fires in Canada is not mismanagement – most Canadian forests are remote and haven’t been managed at all, unlike the US – but instead a warming climate that has made large and extreme wildfires more common,” said Marshall Burke, an environmental policy expert at Stanford University. “These fires are not the result of Canadian action nor inaction, but instead largely the result of forces outside their control. So, punishment here would do nothing.” Attacking Canada over the fires is “unfounded, uninformed and even insensitive to people losing homes and firefighters putting their lives on the line”, said Lori Daniels, an ecologist and wildfire expert at the University of British Columbia. “It’s weak leadership to blame someone else when disasters are happening. It’s not helpful, [Trump] is not contributing to real solutions by playing the blame game.” Daniels said that while some densely thicketed woodland in North America could benefit from “thinning” to reduce the amount of potential fire fuel in them, thereby restoring the small, targeted fires used by Indigenous people before European settlement, such an approach would be futile in Canada’s boreal forests. These forests are dominated by spruce and fir trees that sit within soils topped by spongy mosses that are usually sodden with water. In hot, dry conditions like now, however, the forest floor itself becomes highly flammable, sometimes nourishing fires non-stop for extended periods. Clearing – or “raking” as Trump puts it – this organic material would only hasten fires, Daniels said. Such an endeavor would be logistically difficult regardless, with many of the current fires located in highly remote areas lacking roads and nearby firefighting resources. Canada has more than a quarter of the world’s boreal forests, spanning about 1.2bn acres of the country. “It would be physically impossible to do what Donald Trump has suggested, even with all the money and firefighters in the world,” said Daniels. “Some of the rhetoric from political leaders in the US is almost laughable, they don’t understand the ecosystem or the scope of the problem. This is a climate change-driven disaster and of course the Trump administration are climate deniers so they won’t take responsibility for US contributions to greenhouse gases. This is about deflecting attention from the cause of this.” Smoke from wildfires can trigger severe respiratory and heart problems for people living many miles away, with plumes of smoke eroding long-term improvements in air quality for Americans in recent years. But climate change-fueled wildfires is a global problem, including in the US, where smoke from fires in the west of the country has routinely spread into Canada. Huge blazes in Colorado and Utah have recently scorched 235,000 acres, sparking evacuations and causing the death of Nicholas Dale, a Canadian pilot who was helping fight the fires. “We crossed a tipping point in the last decade, just think of the shocking fires we’ve seen in the Amazon, Australia, Europe, the US and Canada,” said Daniels. “The smoke goes both ways across borders. Unless we address climate change we will continue to see this around the world, so that has to be our priority. “We can’t manage all these fires in Canada but we can triage and manage for safety and shift forest management,” Daniels said, adding that a range of methods, such as planting different tree species and fuel reduction could be suitable. For those in the path of wildfire smoke, air conditioning and filtration when indoors will be important. “We will have to try to adapt because we are in a new climate now,” she said. “Canada is warming twice as fast as the global average so this is the canary in the coalmine for the rest of the world. This is what happens when we heat the planet – we change the ecosystems and we get catastrophic disasters.”

title: Trump administration drive to seize election powers sparking ‘chaos’ despite pushback
author: Peter Stone in Washington
summary: US courts, state officials and Democrats warn that moves are endangering voting rights and the rule of law
body_text: The Trump administration continues to expand its authoritarian and radical drive to revamp voting rules and seize state election powers, though it faces growing resistance from US courts, state officials and Democrats, who warn the moves are sparking “chaos” and endangering voting rights and the rule of law. Donald Trump’s unprecedented drive to change election rules, which states legally set, is fueled by his obsession with his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden, which he falsely attributes to voting fraud, coupled with his fear that Democrats will “find a reason to impeach me” if they take control of the House in November’s midterms elections, say former election officials and legal experts. Given Trump’s dark mindset, his administration has used justice department legal moves and threats, FBI raids and investigations, and other federal agencies to coerce states to change voting rules in key ways, including curtailing voting by mail and machines that Trump and Maga allies have vilified, baselessly, as riddled with fraud. Legal experts say the administration is intimidating election workers and voters before the November elections, and laying the groundwork for potentially challenging election results where Republican candidates lose to ensure the GOP keeps control of Congress. In a conspiratorial 25-minute televised talk on 16 July, Trump presented a hodgepodge of selective intelligence and misleading allegations about Chinese efforts to influence the 2020 elections to hurt him, plus debunked claims of increased voting by noncitizens, flawed voting machines and other threats, to argue that the US elections system needs drastic changes. Trump asserted without hard evidence that American elections were rife with “hacking, manipulation and corruption. Great damage has been done to our country.” In a sharp rebuttal, the nation’s 24 Democratic governors said: “It’s deeply alarming that President Trump continues to try to undermine free and fair elections. No amount of lies and conspiracy theories can change the fact that our country’s elections have repeatedly been proven to be safe and secure.” Trump’s goal, say critics, is to instill fear in voters’ minds, and push for radical measures pre-election including congressional passage of the Save America Act, which would sharply limit voting by mail and require voters to present proof of US citizenship. It lacks the votes in the Senate to pass. Over the past few months, for example, the Department of Justice has demanded that 30 US states provide unredacted voter lists, which contain personal and sensitive information. In July, top justice department official Harmeet Dhillon threatened state election officials with criminal investigations and prosecutions if they knowingly permitted noncitizens to register to vote. The FBI has taken extraordinary steps to again investigate the Georgia election results in 2020 that Trump bitterly contested after his loss there: early in 2026, the FBI seized hundreds of boxes of 2020 ballots from Fulton county, and in July sent 200 agents there to investigate the 2020 results and election workers. The administration’s hardball tactics have sparked strong criticism from experts, and resistance including legal rebuffs from courts nationwide as well as state officials and Democrats. Voting rights advocates and former election officials point out that courts have overwhelmingly rebuked justice department lawyers for their claims seeking to justify administration moves to obtain unredacted voting lists from the states and information about election workers in Georgia and other states. Eileen O’Connor, who spent eight years as an attorney in the justice department’s voting section in the civil rights division and is now with the Brennan Center for Justice, said: “[The] DoJ has had case after case seeking unredacted voter rolls from the states rejected by judges. The DoJ has filed 30 of these cases and has now lost 15 of them.” In another election-related matter where the Department of Justice sought detailed information on every election worker in Fulton county, Georgia, in the 2020 election, O’Connor noted the judge “openly excoriated the DoJ” and called the subpoena an “arbitrary fishing expedition”. Although the justice department is not winning in courts, O’Connor stressed, “they’re injecting chaos” into this year’s elections. More broadly, O’Connor said, the administration’s strategy was “to decrease confidence in the elections and possibly lay the groundwork for possible challenges” post-election. Former election officials are also raising red flags about Trump’s multiple moves to undermine confidence in the fall elections and intimidate voters and election workers. “Trump is trying to intimidate state election officials and threatening actions aimed at suppressing the Democratic vote,” said Larry Noble, a former general counsel at the Federal Election Commission who teaches law at the American University. “It’s also likely he thinks he’s laying the groundwork to claim that any Republican loss is due to fraud.” Noble said several of Trump’s recent actions – including his “firing the members of the non-partisan Election Assistance Commission, and suggesting he is open to possibly sending ICE agents and national guard troops to polling places” – were “a continuation of his efforts to exert control over the midterm elections”. He added: “It’s not clear what, if any, limits he has on how far he will go to prevent Democrats from gaining back power. I fear it’s even possible he will order actions to try to disrupt voting or vote counting during the election to avoid Republican losses.” Democratic and Republican election officials and congressional Democrats have been pushing back hard on the Trump administration’s multifront fight to change election rules. In a social media post, for instance, Deidre Henderson, Utah’s top election official and lieutenant governor, condemned the tone and tactics used by Dhillon in her threatening letter to states. “Got another love letter this morning from the DoJ, sprinkled throughout with threats of criminal prosecution,” Henderson wrote. “This is truly bizarre behavior by the federal agency that is supposed to be protecting civil rights.” In another pressure move, Dhillon told Michigan officials this month that the justice department plans to send federal monitors to three cities, including Lansing, that are Democratic-leaning while the state’s 4 August primaries are held. Likewise, the Federal Emergency Management Agency promulgated new rules late last month that demand states change how they conduct elections to avoid losing federal counter-terrorism funding from the Department of Homeland Security, Fema’s parent agency. Markwayne Mullin, in a press briefing the day after Trump’s speech, upped the ante by threatening local election officials with jail time if they failed to comply with the administration’s moves to change election policies. The DHS secretary reiterated several of Trump’s unsubstantiated assertions about the security of American elections. Voting experts and former justice department officials say the administration’s multifaceted blitz to overhaul voting rules is a dangerous political exercise aimed at boosting Trump’s powers and keeping the GOP in control of Congress. “Six years after the 2020 election, after audits, recounts, litigation and now internal investigation, Donald Trump has failed to produce any evidence of election tampering that changed votes,” said Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney who teaches law at the University of Michigan. “While foreign adversaries have conducted propaganda campaigns to influence public opinion, those operations have favored Trump as much as his opponents. Reducing foreign influence in our elections is a valid goal, but stopping voting by mail will not advance that goal. With an estimated one in four Democrats and one in five Republicans voting by mail, ending voting by mail has only one effect, and that is to favor Republican candidates.” McQuade added: “Trump’s speech revealed no new evidence and merely served to lay the groundwork for baseless claims of election fraud in November, when election outcomes will almost certainly be disastrous for a president with a dismal 37% approval rating.” Justin Levitt, a professor at Loyola Law School and a former top official in the justice department’s civil rights division, said: “The administration is trying desperately to project power that it simply doesn’t have. That includes trying to intimidate state and local officials who aren’t going to be intimidated.” Still, that intimidation drive is especially acute in the FBI’s efforts in Georgia. “The assignment of hundreds of FBI personnel to look at the 2020 election is doing nothing more than allowing a puppet FBI director to be dangled about by the president,” said Michael Moore, a former US attorney in Georgia. Some Republicans also worry that Trump’s obsession with his 2020 loss and his non-stop attacks on election rules and voting rights will backfire and hurt GOP candidates. “Trump simply has an unhealthy obsession with the 2020 election that he lost,” said Charlie Dent, the former Republican House member of Pennsylvania. “He’s using the levers of the federal government to investigate an election that’s already been well investigated. “Trump seems very determined to prevent losing congressional control by the GOP. But he’s doing so much that makes it difficult for the GOP to win.” In historical terms, some voting rights experts say the Trump administration’s attacks on voting rules are unprecedented and foresee other dangerous moves ahead. “The Trump administration is doing everything they can to stack the deck in their favor. This is the most hostile administration towards voting rights and democracy we’ve seen in our lifetimes,” said Jonathan Diaz, director of voting advocacy at the non-partisan Campaign Legal Center. Looking ahead, Diaz warned: “We have very real concerns that they’ll try to weaponize law enforcement either to disrupt or interfere with the elections while they’re in progress, or after ballots have been cast before they’re certified.”

title: Digested week: History shrugs off Keir and makes room for brilliant Kerr
author: John Crace
summary: A low-key PM leaves the stage briskly, while a breathtaking athlete misses out on the attention he deserves
body_text: Monday And so it was over. You normally get a bit more notice when a prime minister is about to deliver their resignation speech outside No 10. The buildup. The sense of occasion. Keir Starmer did things differently. No sooner had “Hot Podium Guy” set up the lectern in Downing Street than Keir was out the front door. As if he couldn’t wait for it all to be over. His speech was done in little more than five minutes. There was no David Cameron confected nonchalance. No tears as there were with Theresa May. No unconcealed bitterness and resentment like Boris Johnson. No bewilderment at the speed of the ending like Liz Truss. And no symbolic rainstorm as with Rish Sunak. Keir said he was going with good grace and he looked as though he meant it. He may still feel angry at the way some of his cabinet turned on him, but it was no longer consuming his every waking minute. What was done was done. He would miss the attention but could see the upside of no longer being the bloke who got woken up at 4am to be told of Donald Trump’s latest efforts to start world war three. Despite the rapid turnover of prime ministers in the last 10 years, there is still something quite poignant about these moments. To see the very public end of a frontline political career. Keir did his best to cement his legacy by saying he had left the country in a better place than he had found it. Which was probably true. He just hadn’t changed the country enough. Or given us a reason to believe in him. And now it was like watching him being airbrushed out of history. From now on, anything that goes wrong for Andy will be Keir’s fault. And anything that goes right, Andy will take the credit for. It was always thus. Tuesday We’re going to have to reset the clock. Coming in to the World Cup, all the talk was of ending “60 years of hurt”. Now we’re going to have to up that to “64 years of hurt” for the next tournament in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. I feel like I really should know better, but this time round I did allow myself to believe that this might be the year when we got to the final and maybe even win it. A team that seemed to be able to play as a team and a manager with the nous to be able to find a way to win matches that we appeared to be losing. Then came the Argentina semi-final. It was like watching Spurs again. Mind you, I knew the game was up when we took the lead. It was far too early in the second half. Far too much time to think about all the ways they could screw it up. The only way we were ever going to win that game was to keep the score at 0-0 until injury time and then go for the winner. Whose idea it was to try and defend for the last 40 minutes is still not clear. I was just screaming at the TV for England to carry on playing in the way that had got them the lead and had kept Lionel Messi relatively quiet. Desperate for someone on the pitch to realise that another way to have won the game was to score a second goal. Still, we did get to participate in the most entertaining match of the whole World Cup when we took on France in the third-place playoff. Not that we should read too much into the 6-4 scoreline other than that it was a joy to watch what was basically a friendly between two teams that were demob happy. And we did get to miss out on Trump making a fool of himself by trying to gatecrash the celebrations. Swings and roundabouts. Wednesday This time last year, Reform was setting the political agenda. While Labour and the Tories seemed to have shut up shop, having decided the public must have been as fed up with politics as they were, Nigel Farage and co were dominating the headlines with new policy announcements every week. Now it seems that the two main parties are trying not to make the same mistake again. Andy Burnham’s government is dripping us a new policy every day while Kemi Badenoch has become desperate to get television airtime at every opportunity. The latest is to tell us that she doesn’t really trust Andy. Who would have guessed? As for Reform, it appears to have stalled somewhat. From leading the polls it now finds itself neck and neck with Labour in many samples and it feels more and more as if Nige can’t stand the level of scrutiny he is coming under with regard to his own finances. Ever since the Guardian revealed he had received a £5m gift from the Thai crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, Nige has rather gone to ground. Refusing to do regular press conferences, taking no questions from the media and reduced to posting videos on social media from the middle of random fields. Moreover, his financial affairs are becoming more opaque the more he tries to explain them. First the £5m was to pay for his security, then a gift. Now it is alleged it was a downpayment on his demand for £1m a year to stand as an MP for Clacton. All this before we get to the donations both in kind and cash from the convicted fraudster George Cottrell and his mum, Fiona. It’s not very Man of the People. Also, despite protestations to the contrary, it becomes more and more clear that Reform is really a one-man band. Dicky Tice is a halfwit, Robert Jenrick a liability and Zia Yusuf so dislikable that even Reform constituency associations don’t want him to stand as their MP. All of which seems to be getting to Nige. This week he turned up at a rally – if you can call it that – in Norfolk and appeared as bored as the 200 people in the audience. Just a rehash of some of his favourite lines that we’ve all heard before. Nothing new to say. Just a need for some attention. And no questions from anyone. He’s desperate for all the talk about his finances to go away but the more he deflects, the greater the interest. The Reform bubble might just be bursting. Thursday Regular readers of this column will have realised that I was away two weeks ago while visiting my daughter in Minneapolis. At least that was the plan. But a couple of days before we were due to fly, my wife tripped on an uneven pavement and broke her shoulder. So we had to stay at home. Chemo can make the bones more brittle, so that’s another thing to blame cancer for. The charge sheet gets ever longer. It was meant as a short trip – I was going for four days, my wife for eight – but I was still gutted. This was the second trip to the US we have had to cancel in the past year and we are yet to see Anna’s new house – she moved in the middle of last year – or to meet her new dog, Pearl. I have also yet to discover whether I will actually be allowed into the US or if I will be put on the first return flight home. Fingers crossed that border security have better things to do than read satirical sketches about the president in the Guardian. We are now planning/hoping/not counting our chickens that we can get to Minnesota for Christmas. So I guess I will find out then. Maybe Trump will still be too moany about the midterm election results to bother with the odd UK journalist. Talking of dogs, we have also had a massive disappointment. We had made it down to the last two to rehome a six-year-old cockapoo called Tinka whose owner had died unexpectedly. We did get to meet Tinka once and take her for a walk. She was very different to Herbie, much more nervy and insecure. But we had fallen in love with her on the spot and had dared to look forward to making her a part of our lives. But it was not to be. So the hunt goes on. If any of you knows of a house-trained cockapoo that is in need of a home or even a cockapoo puppy that nobody wants, then please do get in touch. We are both feeling very much dog deprived. The last year has been unremittingly shit. We are due a break. Friday Maybe it was the excitement of the third place playoff and the buildup to the World Cup final. Maybe it’s just that the UK no longer cares that much about athletics. The Commonwealth Games start today and they barely register on the public consciousness. Ticket sales are sluggish and they aren’t even being broadcast on terrestrial TV. When I was young they were almost as big a deal as the Olympics. Probably because it was the one Games back then when we won a shedload of medals. But even so, I can’t help feeling that Josh Kerr hasn’t got quite the credit he deserves for breaking the world record for the mile at the London Stadium last Saturday. A remarkable achievement by any standard, but all the more so because he beat the record set by Hicham El Guerrouj in 1999 by nearly half a second. A breathtaking piece of running that had been more than a year in the planning. Kerr had dedicated his whole season – he called it Project 222 because that’s the precise number of seconds he needed to run to finish in 3.42 – to this one race. From March this year, he was telling the world what he planned to do. The time and place he would achieve sporting immortality. And yet … While most papers covered the world record on the night, Kerr seems to have rather slipped out of the British public’s mind since. As if, everyone was thinking, “That’s nice”, before forgetting about it. The US media seem far more impressed, with the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times both having written in-depth analysis of how Kerr did it. All very different from the late 70s and early 80s when Steve Ovett and Sebastian Coe were regularly swapping the mile record. Back then almost everyone had a favourite – mine was Ovett; I found Coe unbearably smug. Still do, in fact – and their races didn’t just lead the sports pages, they made front-page news as well. They were both personalities as well as athletics greats. Instantly recognisable. Josh Kerr could walk into a pub and there’s a fair chance no one would know who he was. So let’s hear it for Josh. I’m biased, of course. I used to run myself. Though my best 10K time was 10 minutes outside the world record. Call this the start of a campaign for Josh to win this year’s sports personality of the year. Let’s face it. No other athlete is going to come close to achieving what he has.
