title: New York Chinatown fears impact of $8bn casino development, calling it ‘predatory project’
author: Katie McQue in New York
summary: Residents warn project could worsen gambling addiction and raise rents, while developers promise jobs
body_text: On Main Street in Flushing’s Chinatown, shoppers weave between fruit stands, restaurants and family-run businesses that have served the New York City neighborhood for decades. But behind the bustle, many residents fear the working-class immigrant community is under threat from an $8bn casino development that could displace thousands of renters and force small businesses to close. “A predatory project is being dumped in our community that disproportionately harms our people,” said Jack Hu, 35, a Flushing resident and member of the No Casino in Flushing Meadows Corona Park campaign. “This community is really upset about this project and how it was pushed through without our consent.” Metropolitan Park is a casino and entertainment project backed by the New York Mets owner, Steve Cohen, and Hard Rock International through Queens Future LLC. The development would turn parking lots next to Citi Field at Willets Point into a casino, hotel, restaurants, an entertainment district and a public park between the Flushing and Corona neighborhoods. Chinese immigrant communities have higher rates of problem gambling than the general population, studies have found. This is due to a number of issues, including cultural beliefs around luck and fortune, immigration-related stresses and isolation, barriers to accessing mental healthcare, and casino marketing targeting Chinese-speaking clients. In Flushing, the community is already burdened by gambling addiction, and a casino on its doorstep could make things worse, especially among its elderly populations, said some residents. “This is a working-class community and the Metropolitan Park casino is also going to extract wealth from the most vulnerable,” said Hu, who says his father has a gambling addiction, which he developed soon after immigrating to the US. “Casino operators use things like meal coupons, free bus vouchers, free gambling vouchers to lure working-class Asians into casinos so that they can take their money.” In a statement to the Guardian, a spokesperson for Metropolitan Park said: “We take our responsibility to be a good neighbor and a good partner seriously. Metropolitan Park includes over $1bn in community benefits. This includes a community impact fund and specific funding for responsible gaming, addiction and mental health services.” The project has also signed memorandums of understanding with local organizations such Elmcor Youth & Adult Activities; Hamilton-Madison House, which provinces clinical mental health services; Korean Community Services; and the Korean American Family Service Center to create “culturally sensitive and community-adapted addiction services”, the spokesperson said. According to the Urban Institute, a DC-based thinktank focused on economic and social policy research, the Metropolitan Park proposal could displace almost 16,000 renters who spend more than half of their income on housing in Corona and Flushing due to rising rents. “It will make the whole town worse. Gambling is not a good thing, people get addicted to it,” said Xiang, an employee of a bakery who moved to Queens from China seven years ago. “Tourists might bring money, but the casino could also bring trouble here.” The Metropolitan Park spokesperson said: “A comprehensive environmental impact study (EIS) was conducted, finding that Metropolitan Park will not directly displace any existing businesses or residents. This study was reviewed and accepted by the city planning commission.” Many business owners in the community have recently been affected by the Trump administration’s sanctions against China, making imported goods more expensive. If commercial rents were to rise as a result of the casino, many of these businesses could also be displaced, said some residents. Residents also said they were skeptical that casino visitors would patronize Flushing’s independent businesses, noting that the resort will have its own restaurants and amenities. As evidence, they pointed to the limited spillover from nearby Citi Field and the US Open, which they said have brought few sports fans into the neighborhood. “If you look around here, you’ll see just locals,” said Hu. “There’s nobody that comes here and drops a load of money at a local restaurant. These events do not pull business into Flushing.” A new poll, shared exclusively with the Guardian, found that 61% of likely Democratic voters in New York’s sixth congressional district oppose the project, compared with 20% who support it. The remaining 19% were undecided. The poll was conducted by Public Policy Polling in June. It was commissioned by the Democratic congressional candidate Chuck Park as part of a broader survey conducted during his campaign for the Democratic nomination to challenge Grace Meng, the incumbent representative in New York’s sixth congressional district primary, in June. Park ultimately lost the nomination to Meng, who has represented the district in Congress since 2013. Separately, Park said he knocked on the doors of 6,000 residents during his campaign, many of whom raised their objections to the casino with him. “We heard over and over and over again that people did not want the casino. This spanned from really socially conservative first-generation immigrants who thought that the casino would bring crime, human trafficking, and lead to major quality-of-life concerns,” said Park. “We also heard from young progressive leftist activists that this casino is a giveaway of public land to a billionaire who just wants to make himself even richer.” During the project’s public approval process in March 2025, the casino’s backers told the New York City council that Metropolitan Park had “actively engaged with community leaders” and that community involvement had been central to the proposal. The project won one of New York’s three downstate casino licenses in December 2025. “With nearly four years of community engagement, over 30 public meetings and approvals from six community boards, the city council, the state legislature, the community advisory committee and the gaming commission, Metropolitan Park has undergone one of the most rigorous and transparent public reviews of any project. The community has been heard, and their message is clear: they want Metropolitan Park,” said a spokesperson for the project. “Metropolitan Park will be an economic gamechanger for the local community, bringing over 23,000 new jobs, a dedicated Queens vendor food hall and over $100m in anticipated local spending annually.” The casino developers highlight they have adopted a “community-first” approach on the Metropolitan Park project’s website, and claim the project will provide jobs, green space and entertainment for residents. “Casinos are the worst form of regressive tax,” said Park. “They lure in low-income members of local communities. They get them addicted to gambling, and then they just milk money.” The casino project received a major boost from the state senator John Liu, who introduced Senate Bill S7121A, known as the “parkland alienation” bill, last year, which allows a local government to sell or repurpose public parkland for non-park uses. Without the legislation being signed into law, Cohen’s project may never have been realized, critics say. Liu was able to introduce the bill because a small area of the proposed project falls in the 16th senate district he represents. In exchange for the parkland alienation bill, Cohen pledged to build a bridge, similar to Manhattan’s High Line, connecting downtown Flushing to Willets Point, which Liu has called “Flushing Skypark”. “Given the inevitability of three casinos in NYC resulting from the 2012 state referendum, all within a stone’s throw of Senator Liu’s district, he appropriately turned his focus toward mitigating potential harms and maximizing public benefits to his constituents,” said Liu’s spokesperson. “Senator Liu appreciates the passion with which some advocates oppose the casino, but he has received far greater demand to allow the bid to be submitted for consideration by the gaming commission.” Public campaign finance records show that Liu received a $5,000 donation from the New York Hotel and Motel Trades Council committee on political education political action group in 2025. The Pac receives the majority of its funding from the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council (HTC) labor union. “Senator Liu has been proud to receive substantial support for over two decades from a union that has been particularly successful in fighting for record-breaking wage and benefit increases for its members, mostly immigrant women of color,” said his spokesperson. Liu’s move was met with backlash, including protests from the community. In 2024, one year earlier, Liu penned an op-ed in Daily News, stating the three New York casino projects would exact “disproportionate harm” on “this historically marginalized and increasingly vulnerable community”. “It’s clear they have Asian-Americans squarely in their sights,” Liu said of the casino developers in the article. The spokesperson for Liu said: “Senator Liu has been clear about his opposition to casinos and gambling in general anywhere, but if they are in fact going to be sited downstate (a decision made by voter referendum in 2012), the maximum amount of public benefit must be provided. That is what Senator Liu negotiated, under the assumption that casinos will be sited downstate – whether at the Mets site or the others, which are all in close proximity to the Asian community.” Having watched his father struggle with gambling for more than three decades, Hu fears that a casino in his neighborhood will deepen his father’s addiction. “He wants to retain a little bit of hope to become wealthy,” said Hu, whose parents moved to Flushing from Guangzhou in the 1980s. “It’s like you’ve grown up your entire life with nothing. You come here seeking to build a better life for yourself and for your family, and it’s these types of people that fall victim to these predatory businesses that tell you that you can get wealthy quickly.”

title: Maga influencer Laura Loomer reverses course on Ukraine after Kyiv visit
author: Luke Harding in Kyiv and agencies
summary: Rightwing provocateur meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who says he expects to meet Donald Trump in Washington next week
body_text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy will meet Donald Trump in Washington next week, according to the rightwing US influencer Laura Loomer, amid signs the White House’s traditional hostility towards Ukraine is beginning to crumble. In an interview with Loomer, the Ukraine president said he will probably attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham and hold talks with Trump, which will take place as the latest version of the Russian sanctions bill makes its way through Congress. Loomer interviewed Zelenskyy in the garden of the presidential palace in Kyiv – a remarkable move for the online provocateur who has previously minimised Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and amplified Kremlin propaganda to her nearly 2 million followers on social media. This week, however, she performed a stunning about-turn. “Just experienced my first air raid in Ukraine. Sirens blaring. This is every day for every Ukrainian,” Loomer wrote on X. “I often said I don’t care. Looking back, that wasn’t very nice of me to say. We need to have moral clarity.” Loomer posted a photo of her one-on-one meeting with Zelenskyy as well as a clip from her interview with him in which she asks about his infamous confrontation last year with Trump and the US vice-president, JD Vance, in the Oval Office. No questions were off limits, she said. In the clip, Zelenskyy said his relationship with Trump had significantly improved and describes their brief conversation in the Vatican in April 2025 as a “historic moment”. “We changed the relations during 15, 20 minutes,” Zelenskyy added. Writing on Truth Social, Trump praised Loomer’s interview, calling it “Very good!!!!”. The White House later confirmed that the two leaders were scheduled to meet on Tuesday, while commentators in Kyiv said Trump’s message confirmed his administration’s once negative view of Kyiv was changing at a time when Ukrainian long-range drones are pummelling Russia. Russia has continued to strike Ukraine, with a daytime ballistic missile attack on Friday killing 10 people in the Kyiv region and injuring nearly 100 more. Another five people died when an air bomb hit the eastern city of Sloviansk. Expressing support for US sanctions on Russia, Loomer said the Kremlin was a close ally of the Iranian regime. “Russia is funding Iran and providing them with explosives to murder US soldiers as Iran has called for President Trump’s assassination,” she wrote, arguing: “The United States needs to break Russia’s economy until they submit to peace.” Loomer’s comments are a reversal for a woman who has spent years criticising US support for Ukraine’s defence, declaring it “a country full of Nazi apologists” – a claim used by Russia to justify its full-scale 2022 invasion – and “led by a Jihadi apologist”. Her scepticism towards Kyiv has been shared by other major conservative influencers, including Tucker Carlson, a former Fox News host. The issue became a big point of contention between more traditional Republicans, such as Mike Pence, a former vice-president, and Trump’s Maga base. Anton Gerashchenko, a popular blogger and former Ukrainian government adviser, described Loomer’s interview with Zelenskyy as “important and necessary”. “It records a public break with Russian narratives and propaganda by part of the Maga movement. We are seeing a shift in rhetoric regarding Russian aggression,” he said. “It is really important that @LauraLoomer is in Ukraine and sees things with her own eyes as they are,” Zelenskyy’s office added this week. “It takes courage to come to Ukraine and not be deterred by Russian propaganda or air raid sirens. Thank you, Laura.” Loomer also visited the Dormition Cathedral of Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, one of the country’s most significant religious landmarks, which came under Russian drone attack in June. In a video recorded from inside the church, she accused Vladimir Putin of hypocrisy by portraying Russia as a pro-Christian nation – a perspective many US evangelicals appear to share. “I just don’t think that you should be allowed to say that you’re protecting Christianity if you’re trying to drone strike Jesus Christ,” Loomer remarked. Loomer also met Ukraine’s chief rabbi, Moshe Reuven Azman, and toured a branch of McDonald’s hit repeatedly by Russian missiles. Loomer ordered a cheeseburger and sat demonstratively on an outside table in front of a wrecked building, in Kyiv’s much-bombed Lukianivka district. On Friday, the chief rabbi wrote: “I had the honour of welcoming @LauraLoomer – whose views have a significant influence on the U.S. audience and who is well known for her close ties to President Donald Trump – to the Central Synagogue of Ukraine. “The conversation was candid. I told her the truth about this terrible war – about the daily Russian shelling, the children and civilians killed, the destroyed cities and villages, and the pain that Ukrainian families endure every day.”

title: Poland’s main rightwing opposition splits after loyalty pledge ultimatum
author: Jakub Krupa
summary: Former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki and allies say they were forced out over factional disagreements
body_text: Poland’s main opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party has split, after former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki and his allies said they were forced out over factional disagreements on policy direction ahead of next year’s parliamentary election. Speaking at a press conference, the party’s longtime leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, said dozens of members of parliament effectively left the party after refusing to sign a loyalty oath. All those who refused to sign the pledge were deemed by Kaczyński to have effectively resigned from the party. The rebel MPs insisted they did not intend to leave, but conceded they may be formally expelled at a party leadership meeting on Tuesday. “Everyone knew what they were signing, and at the same time everyone knew what the consequences of not signing would be … it’s all done,” Kaczyński said, adding that the decision will be formally processed on Tuesday. Law and Justice is one of Poland’s two most successful political parties since 1989, having ruled the country for 10 years in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023, with its candidates winning four out of eight presidential elections. Despite losing to a coalition of pro-European parties led by former European Council president Donald Tusk and going into opposition at the last election in 2023, PiS remained the largest party in the Polish parliament – a status it could lose as a result of the split. The resignations come after months of increasingly bitter disagreements in Poland’s main opposition party as it lost its grip on the Polish right. Over the past two years, it struggled to respond to the emerging libertarian-right Confederation and the far-right ethno-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown, splitting the conservative vote into three. In April, Morawiecki, who served as Poland’s prime minister between 2017 and 2023, set up a growth-oriented policy group in a bid to broaden the party’s electoral appeal on the centre-right. It is planning to host its inaugural public event later this month. But the move was harshly criticised by Kaczyński and his allies, who questioned the former prime minister’s loyalty amid rumours of his growing disenchantment with the party’s drift towards the nationalist right and interests of the older electorate. After tense talks behind closed doors, Kaczyński told all MPs to sign a loyalty pledge committing them not to work with any other political groups or face expulsion, with the deadline set for midnight on Thursday. Speaking to reporters on Friday, Morawiecki said his group “until the very last moment fought for the unity of the party” as it wanted PiS to follow “a strategy of two lungs” to mobilise younger centre-right voters and entrepreneurs to boost its electoral prospects in 2027. Morawiecki blamed a circle of “plotters” around Kaczyński for leading the party into the crisis and issuing the loyalty ultimatum. He confirmed the splinter group includes 40 MPs, three members of the European parliament and one senator. “The situation emerging on the Polish right is that … there is no single dominant force, it comprises many different factions,” he said. “For me and for us, these disputes within the right are like squabbles within a family, but in fact we will be directing the brunt of our attack at this very bad government by Donald Tusk.” He declined to speculate on whether the group will form a new party, and instead urged PiS leaders to “take a step back”. Morawiecki, a former senior banker and one-time economic adviser to Tusk, remains one of the most recognisable leaders on the right. But he is also the face of the highly divisive eight years of Law and Justice’s last term in power, seen by critics through the prism of democratic backsliding, conflicts with the European Union and alleged irregularities and abuses of power. He is also the leader of the European Conservatives and Reformists party in the European parliament, a grouping of like-minded parties in Europe, including Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy. His departure is likely to further splinter the vote on the right. Hypothetical polls including a new party had it polling at about 6%. The next parliamentary election is scheduled for October 2027.

title: Justice Elena Kagan decries idea that US supreme court ‘rubber-stamps’ Trump’s agenda
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Kagan rejects notion that high court ‘does whatever the administration wants’, pointing to tariffs ruling and more
body_text: The liberal justice Elena Kagan has said it was “wrong” to accuse the US supreme court of becoming a rubber stamp for Donald Trump in his second term, amid criticism of its authorization of some of the president’s most controversial actions. Pointing to rulings against the president on key issues such as tariffs, Kagan – one of three liberals on a court that has in recent years been defined by rulings authored by members of its six-justice conservative majority – defended it at an annual gathering of attorneys and judges for the ninth judicial circuit in Bellevue, Washington, on Thursday. “Is this a really conservative court? The answer is yes. The second question is: is this a court that does whatever the current administration wants? The answer is no,” Kagan said. It comes after the court allowed Trump to have his way on a string of issues. These include on immigration policy, where they upheld his effort to end temporary deportation protections for Haitians and Syrians, and also issued an order on the shadow docket that strips Venezuelans of those same protections. Conservatives have also recently allowed Trump and future presidents to fire the heads of independent agencies, while boosting his Republican allies’ chances of keeping control of the House of Representatives by weakening the Voting Rights Act. Three members of the court’s conservative majority were appointed by Trump during his first term. But Kagan pointed to the court’s February ruling, in which she and the liberals joined three conservative justices to strike down Trump’s use of executive authority to impose tariffs on a host of countries. “Tariffs is probably the key policy issue for this president,” said Kagan, who joined the court in 2010 after being appointed by Democratic president Barack Obama. “I don’t think that there are all that many decisions in recent times where a court strikes down such an important policy to a sitting president.” Beyond trade policy, the supreme court has also scuppered Trump’s attempt to fire the Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, and blocked his administration’s effort to end birthright citizenship. Kagan added: “I don’t see this as a court that is … going to rubber-stamp what the current administration does. You know, quite the opposite. I actually think that there are significant times with respect to very significant issues where the court has checked the executive branch.”

title: Seth Meyers on Elon Musk’s AI Odyssey movie: ‘I can’t wait for that to suck’
author: Guardian staff
summary: The late-night host ridiculed the right’s ‘alternate reality’ where Christopher Nolan’s film is a flop and the Iran war is over
body_text: Seth Meyers took aim at Elon Musk and the right over their inconsequential attempts to bring down Christopher Nolan’s hit adventure The Odyssey. On Late Night, Meyers said that with the second presidency of Donald Trump, it had been pushed that “the era of woke was over”, with those on the right gloating over what they felt was coming. Ever since casting was announced for Nolan’s big-budget epic, the right had dismissed it as a “commie woke-fest” due to its diversity. “How dare you cast popular actors in fictional roles in a movie adaptation of a poem written 2,700 years ago,” Meyers said. Much of the anger was aimed at Oscar winner Lupita Nyong’o who had been cast as Helen of Troy, a character who “hatched from an egg that was the result of Zeus turning into a swan who had sex with a goddess”, or as Meyers joked “white lady stuff”. The host joked that Maga pundits had suddenly become “poem cops”. But the right’s favourite saying “you go woke, you go broke” was once again proven wrong when The Odyssey opened to a massive $264m box office haul worldwide last weekend. Meyers said it meant that “woke is back” and also that the right’s inability to predict a hit was because “most of them haven’t seen a movie in theatres since Fast and Furious”. One of the film’s most vocal critics was Elon Musk, the world’s richest and “weirdest” man who has now claimed he will make a “historically accurate” version of the film with his AI tool Grok. “I can’t wait for that to suck,” Meyers said. He also added: “It’s a myth! Are you also making a historically accurate version of The Santa Clause?” Meyers said the right were not to be trusted on film as “they also said the Iran war would be a huge success” yet it was “definitely not over” and was “spiralling further out of control” despite what they might claim. This week saw Trump asked by a journalist about Iran showing no signs that they are willing to stop fighting and he responded by asking if she knew something he didn’t. “I don’t think he’s being sarcastic, I think he’s genuinely asking,” he said. Many of them “declared premature victory” but it’s “only getting worse”, something that was raised by the Democratic senator Jon Ossoff this week. He asked the Pentagon chief, Pete Hegseth, why he would say on day 14 of the war that Iran’s military had been destroyed when that’s clearly not the case. Hegseth avoided answering yet Ossoff kept repeating the question “like the fucking Terminator”. This angered Trump who used a “very, very weird line of attack” at a rally in calling Ossoff Pinky Herman. “Do you mean Peewee Herman?” Meyers said, before saying that the inside of Trump’s brain “looks like Peewee’s Playhouse”. He finished by saying the right “live in a bubble” and “an alternate reality”.

title: Trump accused of using forced labor as ‘convenient’ justification for tariffs
author: Gaya Gupta and Chris Stein in Washington
summary: US president faced criticism from Democrats after tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% imposed on more than 80 countries
body_text: Donald Trump has been accused of using forced labor as “a pretext” to impose a fresh wave of tariffs on dozens of countries, as critics warned of higher prices for Americans. The US president faced swift criticism from Democrats after his officials presented their latest effort to make his signature economic policy permanent following a string of high-profile legal setbacks. Some Republicans also expressed concern. Hours before a temporary US duty of 10% on many countries was due to expire on Friday, the Trump administration announced new tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% on more than 80 countries, including the UK, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, China and European Union members. The new tariffs are being implemented under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the president to bypass Congress to instate tariffs designed to punish countries using forced labor to export goods to the US. Trump “recognizes that decades of moral suasion have not eradicated forced labor from global supply chains”, said Jamieson Greer, his US trade representative, on Thursday, adding it was “well past time” that countries across the world eradicated the practice. But as the US president continues to face questions over his controversial focus on tariffs, and the threat of higher prices, leading Democrats accused his administration of using forced labor to prop up their strategy. “Today’s forced labor justification is too convenient to be taken seriously,” said Richard Neal, the top Democrat on the US House ways and means committee. “Forced labor is a real and pervasive problem in our supply chains and demands serious enforcement. It should never be cheapened into a pretext for a tariff policy built on dubious legal theories and personal grievances.’’ Linda Sánchez, a California Democrat who also serves on the tax-writing committee, noted that Trump had gutted funding to combat forced labor at the Bureau of International Labor Affairs and rolled back worker protections domestically “while encouraging companies to profit off some of the world’s worst forced labor abusers through his proposed US-China Board of Trade”. “If he was serious, he would not be applying the same tariff rate to China, one of the worst forced labor abusers in the world, as he does to countries like Australia,” wrote Sánchez. “Then again, unlike China, Australia, doesn’t manufacture any Trump corporation products.” Trump’s trade strategy suffered a damaging blow in February when the US supreme court ruled 6-3 that many of his tariffs had been imposed illegally. His officials immediately announced another 10% tariff regime under another trade law that had never been used before, although these duties could only be imposed for up to 150 days – and expired after midnight EST on Friday. This latest wave of tariffs is designed to replace the 10% regime. Democrats said the levies would accomplish little besides increasing costs for Americans amid inflation that has climbed to a three-year high – a message they have pushed again and again in the run-up to November’s midterm elections, in which they seek to regain control of Congress. “Trump has bled the inflation-battered American people dry with his tariffs. Now he’s coming back for more,” the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, said. He urged Republicans “to finally grow a backbone – work with Democrats to reject this tax and bring down costs for the American people”. Brendan Boyle, the top Democrat on the House budget committee, cited an estimate by the Congressional Joint Economic Committee that US families have had to pay $3,500 more under Trump’s policies, adding that new tariffs would only cost them more. “Federal courts have repeatedly struck down President Trump’s illegal and costly tariff taxes,” he said. “These new tariffs are more of the same: a nationwide sales tax that will make life even harder for families already struggling under the costs of Trump’s reckless war in Iran.” A Harris Poll survey for the Guardian found earlier this year that 70% of Americans have reported paying more due to tariffs, and a majority of voters, including 60% of Republicans, say tariffs have had a negative effect on consumers. All signs pointed to the latest tariffs being as divisive among Republicans as previous rounds, as they drew mixed responses from Trump’s allies in Congress. “True to its word, the Trump administration is fighting for American families, farmers and small businesses – as well as American values – when it comes to our trading relationships,” said the House ways and means committee chair, Jason Smith. “Holding accountable those countries that are not doing nearly enough to rid their supply chains of goods produced with forced labor is appropriate to address unfair trading practices that put American workers at a competitive disadvantage.” But John Cornyn, a Republican senator from Texas, raised concern about the effect of the tariffs on Americans. Cornyn is leaving the US Senate at this end of this term, after his Trump-endorsed rival, Ken Paxton, won the Republican nomination for his seat. “There’s no question that tariffs on imports raise prices on American products,” Cornyn told the Hill. “So yeah, I’m concerned about that.”

title: Democrats move to keep South Carolina as first state to vote in 2028 presidential primaries
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: DNC move aims to better represent views of party’s racially diverse voter base ahead of next presidential cycle
body_text: Democrats moved to keep South Carolina as the first state to vote in their party’s 2028 presidential primary process, while moving up several other states, in an effort to better represent the views of the party’s racially diverse voter base. At a meeting in Washington DC of the Democratic National Committee’s (DNC) rules and bylaws committee on Friday, South Carolina received a slim majority of votes to take the first spot, scheduled for 22 January 2028, with Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia set to follow, in that order. The selections must still be confirmed by the full DNC at a meeting set for next month. Minyon Moore and James Roosevelt Jr, who co-chair the committee, called the proposal “a rigorous, fair, and efficient calendar that will win Democrats back the White House in 2028”. South Carolina was the state whose primary voters revitalized Joe Biden’s presidential campaign in 2020, and as president he returned the favor by encouraging the DNC to make the state the first to vote in the 2024 nominating calendar. That supplanted New Hampshire, the site for decades of the first primary for both parties, as well as Iowa, which holds caucuses that have traditionally been the first nominating contest of presidential election years. However, both states are overwhelmingly white, and with Democrats increasingly relying on Black, Latino and other minority voters to elect their candidates, the party has sought to move states with larger populations of those groups towards the front of the nominating calendar, where they can play a crucial role in selecting the presidential frontrunners. Making the case for South Carolina, the long-serving congressman James Clyburn said in a statement ahead of the meeting: “We have a record that all of us can point to and be proud of. It’s a relatively small state. It has four distinct cultures, a relatively cheap media market, and demographics that reflect what our voter population needs to be in order for our candidates to be successful in the general election.” During the meeting, the Nevada Democratic chair, Daniele Monroe-Moreno, argued that her state offers the ideal racial mix and nodded to Donald Trump’s success there in 2024, when he became the first Republican in two decades to win its electoral votes. “When we go into the next presidential cycle, my state, the state of Nevada, is that coalition that we need to win back,” she said. The new early voting states are either presidential battlegrounds or home to hotly contested US Senate races and House districts. They also have substantially more Black and Latino voters than the states that led the 2020 nominating calendar, as well as larger populations of voters in unions or without college degrees, both constituencies with which many Democratic candidates have struggled to win in recent elections.

title: Paramount agrees to pause $110bn Warner Bros merger as case plays out
author: Guardian staff and agencies
summary: Twelve states led by California had obtained temporary restraining order blocking merger from closing for 28 days
body_text: Paramount ⁠Skydance ⁠has agreed to pause its $110bn acquisition ⁠of Warner ‌Bros ‌Discovery until a ‌ruling on several states’ challenge ‌to the deal, or until 1 June ⁠2027, according to court papers filed on Friday. A group of 12 US states headed by California obtained a temporary restraining order this week that blocked the merger from closing for 28 days, pending the outcome of a motion for a preliminary injunction. The states allege that the deal should be blocked because it will reduce competition in the cable and theatrical markets. A Warner-Paramount merger would bring together two of the five last legacy studios in Hollywood, as well as a host of TV networks, titles filling streaming libraries and news operations. That would include Warner’s HBO Max and CNN coming under the same roof of Paramount-owned CBS, movies including Top Gun and the Paramount+ streaming service. The ⁠delay could cost Paramount Skydance, controlled by the Ellison family, about $7m a ‌day in fees ‌it agreed to pay Warner Bros ‌shareholders if the merger does not close by 30 September. Similar merger challenges have taken an average ‌of eight months for a judge to rule on, a Reuters review of recent cases found. Journalists at CBS News and CNN have expressed concerns about the possibility of the networks being merged and the likely resulting job losses. Press freedom groups have also voiced fears over political influence around the deal. David Ellison and his father, Larry, a longtime Trump associate, have reoriented the CBS network in an editorial direction more favorable to the president, especially under the leadership of CBS News’s embattled editor-in-chief, Bari Weiss. However, David Ellison pledged in March that CNN’s editorial independence would be protected amid speculation that he could put Bari Weiss in charge of the cable network. At the time the deal was approved by the Trump administration in June, Elizabeth Warren, the progressive Democratic senator, said in a social media post that the development was “terrible news for every American who doesn’t want Trump-aligned billionaires to control what they watch and how much they pay”, adding that the merger “has reeked of corruption and influence-peddling”. In a statement, Paramount said: “Today’s agreement is a significant win because the result is exactly what we have sought from the outset: a direct path to a trial based on the evidence.” It added: “This is the fastest and clearest way to prove that this transaction is good for competition, good for consumers and good for creators – a conclusion dozens of competition authorities around the world have already reached … We look forward to proving our case at trial.”

title: Trump administration admits canceling clean energy grants to Democratic states
author: Lucy Campbell
summary: Court fillings show grants denied to states if they didn’t back Trump’s re-election, but administration claims it’s a ‘misrepresentation’
body_text: The Trump administration has admitted scrapping more than $7.5bn in federal grants for clean energy projects to states “based solely” on whether they backed Donald Trump in the 2024 election. US federal officials appeared to acknowledge in court documents last week that they had terminated the funding last October “based solely” on political criteria, targeting projects in states that were represented by Democrats and had voted for Kamala Harris. The administration previously framed the move as safeguarding taxpayer dollars from “waste” and continues to insist it was not politically motivated. “[The Department of Energy] accepts that neither the inclusion of the ARCHES grant nor any other grants in the October notice tranche was based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor,” government lawyers said in the filing. “[The Department of Energy] accepts that the inclusion of grants in the October notice tranche was based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state, ie, whether the recipient’s location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State. “[The Department of Energy] will not contend that it looked beyond the prime grantee(s) to consider the political identity or geographic distribution of downstream beneficiaries of the grant funds.” The apparent admission was first reported by the New York Times. In a statement on Friday, a spokesperson for the US energy department said of the report: “That is a misrepresentation of the court filing. None of the termination decisions were based on political considerations.” The acknowledgment of political considerations “was referring to the timing of the announcement, not of the decisions themselves”, the spokesperson claimed. The filings stem from a lawsuit, filed last June, by a group of six University of California faculty and other researchers challenging various federal agencies that halted Biden-era funding. The plaintiffs said in a press release at the time that the abrupt cancellations of already-awarded grants had been a part of a “political ‘cost-cutting’ agenda and ideological purity campaign” waged by the administration. It comes as the White House seeks to exert even greater control over billions of dollars in annual federal grants, aiming to have Trump’s political appointees review all federal grants, with the power to block or revoke vast amounts of funding if they did not conform to or align with Trump’s priorities. According to a 400-page proposed rule for federal financial assistance published on 29 May, “Discretionary awards must, where applicable, demonstrably advance the President’s policy priorities.” They must also adhere to further standards set out by the White House, including not promoting “anti-American values”, the denial of “the sex binary in humans” and the use of “racial preferences” in selection criterion. Per last week’s court filing, the energy department had reviewed its financial assistance awards and created a list last September that recommended canceling more than 600 grants awarded by the Biden administration for a wide range of clean energy projects in states represented by both Republicans and Democrats. However, in October, the White House budget office, led by Russell Vought, terminated only 284 of those grants. Vought announced on X: “Nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left’s climate agenda is being canceled. The projects are in the following states: CA, CO, CT, DE, HI, IL, MD, MA, MN, NH, NJ, NM, NY, OR, VT, WA.” Last week, federal officials appeared to concede that the decision had been purely informed by politics. “With one exception, the 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing Senators (“Blue State” grants),” the court filing says. Meanwhile, the energy department left in place hundreds of other energy grants in state represented by Republicans and that had voted for Trump in 2024 – despite the department having also recommended that they too be scrapped. Last month, Trump’s energy secretary, Chris Wright, appeared before the House science, space and technology committee to defend his department’s fiscal 2027 budget request. “No decisions were made on politics,” he insisted. The Guardian has reached out to the White House.

title: Trump escalates Smithsonian attack with order for signs outside history museum
author: Roque Planas
summary: President directs interior department to display signs outside museum that accuse institution of inaccuracy
body_text: Donald Trump on Friday ordered the interior department to display signs in front of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History that accuse the institution of inaccuracy. The order escalates the Trump’s attacks against the Smithsonian, which he and his allies accuse of politicizing the institution by focusing too much on injustices in American history, instead of more triumphant moments such as the signing of the Declaration of Independence. The order directs interior secretary Doug Burgum to huddle with the National Park Service and assistant to the president for domestic policy Vince Haley to come up with some temporary signs to install along the National Parks Service-maintained sidewalks and walkways leading into the museum. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for more details about what these signs would say. The order says the signs “shall notify visitors that the museum exhibits should be renovated consistent with the findings in the report”. The signs should direct the public to other places where they can get better American history information, the order says. The same group will also have to produce signs for the public criticizing the Smithsonian for not commemorating sufficiently the Declaration of Independence during the 250th anniversary of its adoption. The American Historical Association, a group composed of professional historians, praised the Smithsonian Institution’s “commitment to scholarship and accuracy” in a statement earlier this month. “Historians practice our craft with scholarly integrity according to established standards of evidence, historical inquiry, and professional practice,” the AHA statement reads. “Political interference in professional museum work threatens the accuracy of historical interpretation and erodes public trust in one of our nation’s most important institutions.” The National Museum of American History declined to comment. But the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, defended the institution’s interpretations in a pair of congressional hearings earlier this month, where Republican representatives fumed about “some overtly sexual things up there” and accused Hartig of encouraging “self-loathing”. “We honor the declaration, the revolution, the constitution, our national symbols,” Hartig responded, according to the New York Times. “And we tell the truth about the times that the country fell short of its own founding ideals. Telling our story fully is a form of respect for the American people and a commitment to constantly being in pursuit of a more perfect union.” A recent report prepared by the White House’s domestic policy council called “Saving America’s Story” accused the museum’s leadership of “ideological capture”. The Smithsonian “explicitly adopted an ideological framework that no longer treats the American story as a shared national inheritance to be taught or celebrated, but as a political instrument to divide, dispirit, and discourage our citizens”, the report says.

title: Insults, potshots and quip about a third term: Trump’s rambling gala address
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: President mocks opponents and journalists in mostly lighthearted speech at White House correspondents’ dinner
body_text: Donald Trump joked around with the room of journalists whom he again accused of producing “fake news” as he hurled insults at his political enemies in a speech at the White House correspondents’ dinner. A day after the Trump administration abandoned, for now, an extraordinary bid to subpoena reporters over their coverage, the US president attended the rescheduled White House correspondents’ dinner – an annual celebration of press freedom – in Washington on Friday evening. It came three months after the original event was scrapped in April when a man fired a shotgun at a security checkpoint outside the ballroom. The president’s hour-long speech was mostly lighthearted and sarcastic, with occasional swipes at the news media, a profession he eventually said he respected, praising journalists for doing an “amazing job”. Later in the speech, Trump, who has regularly attacked the press over its coverage of his presidency, insisted his war on Iran was going “extremely well”. He told a room full of journalists: “Don’t believe the fake news.” Trump and his officials joined hundreds of reporters at the Waldorf Astoria, a smaller venue than the vast Washington Hilton ballroom that was evacuated when shots were fired in April, in a suspected targeting of the president and his administration. The speech included a handful of scripted jokes, one at the expense of Robert F Kennedy Jr, his health secretary, whom he quipped had personally run over the cow that became the evening’s “very delicious beef tenderloin”. Kennedy has championed the health benefits of beef tallow and animal protein. Trump also mocked the weight of Chris Christie, the former New Jersey governor, and Jerry Nadler, the New York congressman, imagining the two wrestling over a piece of cheesecake. He ridiculed the appearance of his critics, including Bruce Springsteen, whom he said “looks like hell”, and took aim at CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, who had been honored earlier for her White House coverage, saying she does not smile enough. Trump said he “hated” Adam Schiff, a Democratic California senator, and one of his most prominent congressional critics, while mocking the size of his head and neck. At one point, after a joke about term limits fell flat, Trump broke the fourth wall, asking the audience whether anyone understood “this whole freakin stupid speech that they wrote”. Trump ended his remarks with a joke that landed awkwardly, declaring that he planned to run and win a fourth election – a reference both to his false claim he won the 2020 election and to his repeated suggestion that he could seek a third term, despite the constitution’s two-term limit. “I won three times, now I’m going to do it again,” the president said, sarcastically, placing a red “Trump 2028” hat on his head. Oz Pearlman, a world-renowned mentalist, dazzled as the entertainment for the night, in place of a comedian who typically fills the role at the gala. Before Trump spoke on Friday, a series of journalists who published revealing stories on the president and his administration – including the team behind the Wall Street Journal story alleging he had sent a “bawdy” letter to the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2003 – received awards on stage. Trump has sued the Journal over its reporting. Weija Jiang, outgoing president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, had sought to underline the importance of duty – both for those in the White House, and the people who cover them. “No matter how complicated or tense the relationship is between the press and the presidency, what we share is far more important than anything else and that is our duty: to serve the American people,” Jiang told the dinner. Beginning his remarks, Trump claimed the speech he had originally prepared was “gonna be a doozy”, suggesting he would pare back his attacks at the rescheduled event: “Just like my presidency, the second time is always better – and the third time will be better yet … I’m only kidding.” The usually celebratory dinner was dedicated in part to Victor Gonzales, a Secret Service officer who was shot and wounded at the original correspondents’ dinner in April while helping stop the gunman, and hotel staff who helped guests during the attack. The man charged for the shooting, Cole Allen, has pleaded not guilty to attempting to assassinate the president. An advance team spent weeks putting together a security plan for the new venue, and Sean Curran, the US Secret Service director, told reporters this week that agents were braced for trouble even at the black-tie dinner. While it is customary for presidents to address the annual White House correspondents’ dinner, Friday’s speech is the first Trump has made at the event in either of his two terms. He boycotted the dinner throughout his first term, and has long attacked the press corps, including many of the journalists in the room. “It matters that you came here tonight,” Jonathan Karl, chief Washington correspondent at ABC News, told the president on stage. Trump has sued multiple news organizations over their coverage of him, and routinely dismisses unfavorable stories as “fake news”. Trump’s administration has gone further still, barring the Associated Press from the White House press pool and limiting other journalists’ access to the Pentagon. Missing from the affair this time: Melania Trump, the US first lady; JD Vance, the vice-president; and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. All had been present in April. • This article was amended on 25 July 2026 to correct the spelling of Oz Pearlman’s surname.

title: Trump forced to play good sport at correspondents’ dinner – but it couldn’t last
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: President’s speech started well enough but quickly moved to the usual insults, taunts, jokes and grievances
body_text: This time, at least, everyone got to finish their dinner. And any urge to hide under the table was driven not by the barking commands of Secret Service agents on alert against a marauding gunman, but by a desire to escape the tedium of a meandering speech from Donald Trump that strayed quickly and wildly from the matter at hand into the weeds of his normal stump addresses. For more than two hours at Friday’s rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, Trump was forced to play the good sport; smiling and applauding while awards were bestowed on journalistic foes he berates daily as purveyors of “fake news” and plaudits heaped on past presidents he loathes. But eventually something had to give. Trump had to be Trump, insults had to be hurled, some of them stale and familiar, a few of them funny, all of them grievously petty. As often happens with his stump speeches these days, the president lost his audience. Phones were gazed at, silence ensued. Never more so than when he embarked on a tiresome bigoted diatribe against the Democratic representative from Minnesota, Ilhan Omar, one of his frequent targets. Trump was finally getting to deliver his maiden speech as president to the association’s annual marquee gathering that a alleged would-be assassin had denied him by trying to storm the original event in April, before being foiled by Secret Service agents. Both the association and Trump had decreed such an act of political violence could not be accepted as the final word. So a rescheduled dinner was arranged – but with significant adjustments. Instead of the vast auditorium at the Washington Hilton – the dinner’s venue for several decades and once the site of an attempt on the life of Ronald Reagan – the Astoria Waldorf was chosen to stage a drastically scaled-down dinner, with just 700 guests attending, compared with the 2,600 who were at the original event in April. Given the upheaval that unfolded then, the greater visibility of armed security personnel – even for a much smaller guest list – was unsurprising. Weijia Jiang, the outgoing WHCA president, vowed in advance that the restaged dinner would be “more intimate”. Trump, when he spoke – after being forcibly humbled by the dishing out of awards to a succession of journalists for their unflattering portrayal of his presidency – quickly established that humility would not feature strongly in his speech. His first comment on the changed venue was to observe that he had once owned it, when it was the Trump International Hotel. “This has not been an easy evening. All these awards. Do I have a say?” he asked. “But it’s great to be back at a place that I know very well because I built it, and I’m very proud of it because I built it for $2.9bn less than the Federal Reserve Building, which is a lot smaller, by the way.” To his credit, he quickly entered the intended spirit by invoking the episode that had caused everyone to be there in the first place. “Tonight we come back together to answer that heinous attack with unwavering resolve, and every one of us here this evening to show that in America we do not yield to political violence,” Trump said to applause. “So in this country, we believe in freedom of speech. We settle our differences not with bullets, but with open and vigorous debate.” It seemed an apt response to Jiang’s appeal, based on the event’s theme of “celebrating the first amendment”, to respect and honor the media’s place in American life. “Many founders [of the US constitution] couldn’t stand the press … but they understood our access is restricted,” she said. “If the media faces government pressure or censorship, it’s the people who end up knowing less. There is a difference, though, an existential difference between criticizing the press and trying to undermine it.” But that was as high-minded and worthy as Trump was willing to allow. From there, it was on to the insults, taunts, jokes – and grievances. Some of it was amusing and drew laughter, notably when he jested at the expense of the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr. “I hope that everyone finally got to enjoy their entire, very delicious beef tenderloins, very special beef,” he said. “And I want you all to know that Bobby Kennedy, who’s right here, personally ran over the cow and he cut it up, and he brought it here for you to eat tonight. Bobby also suggested appetizer featuring his favorite cut of male raccoon roadkill, but we drew the line at that.” Adam Schiff, the Democratic senator for California and a particular Trump bete noire, was mocked as “watermelon head because he has the largest head I’ve ever seen with the smallest pencil neck”. Jimmy Kimmel, Jimmy Fallon and Stephen Colbert, all comedians who have mocked Trump unceasingly, were derided as “people without talent”. Trump said the speech was much more generous than the one he had planned to give in April before the gunman and would-be alleged assassin, Cole Tomas Allen, stole his thunder. But what could have been going through his mind as Wolf Blitzer, the veteran CNN anchor who famously witnessed the shooting scenes at the original dinner, announced that the Katharine Graham award for courage and accountability was going to a Wall Street Journal team who had reported on the president’s past relationship with Jeffrey Epstein. In the event, Trump shook hands with the team’s members, including one journalist whose home address had been disclosed in a $20bn suit he filed against the paper, forcing the reporter’s family to have to move home. “I hope you all know that I believe in the free press more than anyone in this room,” Trump told the gathering later, overlooking the fact that his administration had filed subpoenas for several New York Times reporters and their relatives after the paper had reported on security breaches on the new Air Force One jet, gifted by Qatar. “You people have no idea how lucky you are. When I’m gone, you’re all going to be broke. There’s not going to be anybody to report on.” As he wound up, the sound system blared out YMCA by the Village People. By then, Trump had been talking for 65 minutes, paeans of praise to the founding fathers and journalistic bravery had been forgotten – and there seemed little doubt about whose event it really was.

title: ‘Proxy for Trump’ Milei tours Latin America to meet far-right leaders
author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
summary: Tour comes amid Argentinian president’s declining popularity and far-right victories across Latin America
body_text: Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, is not particularly fond of travelling to multilateral forums – it is not unusual for him to skip Mercosur summits, as he did a few weeks ago. But on Saturday he begins a tour of Latin America to meet far-right leaders, starting in Brazil with the launch of Senator Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidential campaign against the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, ahead of October’s election. Milei will then attend Keiko Fujimori’s inauguration in Peru on Tuesday, followed by Abelardo de la Espriella’s inauguration in Colombia on 7 August, from where he will travel to Ecuador to meet president Daniel Noboa. The self-styled libertarian has justified the trips as those of “a president willing to open up to the world, seeking to triple the country’s trade”. But analysts point to the timing: amid his declining popularity at home, the tour comes in the wake of a wave of far-right victories in presidential elections across Latin America. “As someone who has been in power for a little longer, Milei is trying to establish himself as a leader of that group,” said Cristóbal Rovira Kaltwasser, a researcher and professor at the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. “I’ve never seen Milei take much interest in official visits to other countries,” said Juan Gabriel Tokatlian, a sociologist and professor at Universidad Torcuato Di Tella in Buenos Aires. “What interests him are figures from the world of big tech and the far right, but in neither case is there any real interest in opening trade negotiations,” he added. Benjamin Gedan, a senior fellow and director of the Stimson Center’s Latin America programme, said a constant in Milei’s trips has been his effort to remain “deferential to the US president, Donald Trump, and never trying to upstage him”. When Trump took office in January 2025, Milei faced relatively little competition for his affection in Latin America, where fewer than a dozen other far-right presidents were in office, most notably El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. Trump described Milei as his “favourite president”. Since then, however, rightwing or far-right candidates have won all seven presidential elections held in the region, with the US president accused of attempting to influence some of them. Almost all of the winners also interacted with Milei during their campaigns through public exchanges of praise or video calls but, according to Tokatlian, there is no doubt about whom they were really trying to please. “All these rightwing leaders see Milei as a kind of proxy for Trump, who is the one who is really in charge. They don’t want to be under any kind of Argentine leadership. It’s Milei who’s trying, but there’s no great eagerness for him,” he said. Tokatlian believes that any contest for Trump’s favour, if one exists at all, will be decided by “whoever gives the US the most on drug trafficking, migration, military cooperation and containing China’s influence”. The US has signed a series of military cooperation agreements with countries across the region. In March, Trump launched the Shield of the Americas, a “counter-cartel coalition” made up exclusively of far-right leaders aligned with him. Notably absent were key countries for drug production and trafficking in the region – Mexico, Brazil and Colombia – all of which are governed by leftwing administrations. After being elected, De la Espriella said that Colombia would join the initiative and establish a local Shield of the Americas office in Medellín. Ariel Goldstein, a researcher and professor at the University of Buenos Aires, believes Milei nonetheless remains ahead of the others in the race for Trump’s attention. “He has already spent the past two or three years building an intense relationship of friendship and subordination with the US,” he said. When Trump was re-elected, Milei travelled to Palm Beach to become the first foreign leader to meet him after his victory. The Argentinian president has also emulated a number of policies from his US counterpart, including withdrawing from the World Health Organization and tightening immigration policies. Last year, Trump offered a $40bn US bailout that was widely seen as crucial to the libertarian party’s victory in Argentina’s midterm elections. However, Milei’s path to re-election next year is far from looking smooth: although inflation has fallen, purchasing power has also declined, while unemployment and informality have risen and his administration has been hit by corruption scandals. Meanwhile, Goldstein believes that Milei and Trump are now heavily invested in winning the next major prize on the electoral calendar: Latin America’s largest country, Brazil. Besides attending the launch of Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign, the Argentinian president had hoped to visit the senator’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest after being convicted over an attempted coup, but the request was denied by a justice. Milei has never held a bilateral meeting with Lula. “A Bolsonaro victory would be hugely important to Milei and Trump because it would allow them to reorganise the whole region around an axis of subordination to the US,” said Goldstein.

title: What’s behind Maga influencer Laura Loomer’s about-face on Ukraine?
author: James Risen
summary: After a Kyiv visit, rightwing firebrand now supports Ukraine – but perhaps it’s just because Trump favors a winner
body_text: Laura Loomer, the online Maga provocateur, has never worked in the White House or anywhere else in the government, but her sudden conversion to the Ukrainian cause this week is significant because her social media posts often have real policy implications in the second Trump administration. The rightwing commentator has spent the last few days in Kyiv, where she announced a newfound sympathy for Ukraine in its long war with Russia, and admitted that she had previously fallen for Russian propaganda. Loomer – who has previously echoed Kremlin talking points to her 2 million followers on social media – has enjoyed direct access to Trump since the 2024 presidential campaign. During the early months after Trump returned to office, Loomer used her online presence to push for ideological purges of government personnel, including many in the national security arena. For a time, her power to break careers among foreign policy officials made her seem as if she were Trump’s de facto national security adviser. It is unclear whether she still has that kind of pull inside the White House, but Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, certainly took her seriously when she arrived this week, holding a private meeting with her on Thursday. Three days earlier, Loomer posted about experiencing her first air raid, as Russian missiles pounded the Ukrainian capital “This is everyday for every Ukrainian,” she posting, adding she felt that she had been “an asshole for minimizing the struggle of Ukrainians for the last 5 years”. “I often said I don’t care. Looking back, that wasn’t very nice of me to say. There are people in Ukraine who have to run to a bomb shelter everyday and some of us had the audacity to say Russia wasn’t wrong because we believed the lie that Ukraine is a country full of Nazi sympathizers. We have been so propagandized by Russia and we don’t even realize it.” Before their meeting on Thursday, Zelenskyy’s office posted a statement saying: “It is really important that @LauraLoomer is in Ukraine and sees things with her own eyes as they are.” Loomer’s change of heart is potentially important not only because she is close to Trump, but also because she has long served as a reliable barometer of Maga attitudes. Loomer has long been disdainful of Ukraine, adopting what could only be described as a pro-Russian perspective. Many in Maga circles have for years held positive views of the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, thanks to Russian propaganda that portrayed him as a bulwark against homosexuality and a defender of fundamentalist Christianity. They became convinced that the Russia-Ukraine war was a proxy fight between Russia’s fundamentalist Christianity and the EU’s western secularism. Loomer’s shift comes at a critical moment for Ukraine, which recently lost one of its strongest supporters in Washington with the death this month of Lindsey Graham, the Republican senator from South Carolina who had consistently pushed for increased sanctions on Russia to punish Moscow for its invasion of Ukraine. But Loomer’s change also coincides with what appears to be an important recent shift in Trump’s own views on Ukraine. Trump returned to office openly hating Ukraine, at least in part because of the 2019 impeachment over his attempt to hold up aid to Ukraine in exchange for dirt on Joe Biden. Early in his second term, Trump humiliated Zelenskyy in an Oval Office meeting, cut off direct the supply of US weapons and forced Ukraine’s European allies to buy American weapons for Kyiv instead. But Trump likes winners, and even without full support from Washington, Ukraine has been able to slow Russia’s advance. Kyiv has become a global leader in drone technology, and it has taken the war to Russia itself with long-range missile attacks on the country’s oil infrastructure, leading to an energy crisis in one of the world’s biggest oil-producing nations. Clearly impressed with Ukraine’s performance, Trump announced at the Nato summit in Turkey earlier this month that the US would license Patriot missile technology to Ukraine, allowing Kyiv to produce the advanced air defense missiles on its own. At the same time, Trump also supported a move in Congress, which had been backed by Graham, to impose new sanctions on Russia, while also seeming to back off an earlier insistence that Ukraine would have to agree to give up large swaths of territory in exchange for any US-brokered peace deal with Russia. Trump’s policy shifts were modest, but significant; it is possible that Loomer changed her position simply in order to stay in lockstep with Trump. But her about-face could be even more politically significant if it represents a broader thawing of Maga attitudes towards Ukraine and an awakening to the dangers of Russian propaganda.

title: ‘I’m over the moon’: New York’s small business owners rejoice as Mamdani cuts red tape
author: Christopher Mathias in New York
summary: Initiatives including cutting permits just to serve ice-cream amount to a sweeping program of deregulation
body_text: Red Scare? The democratic socialist mayor of New York City spent this week talking about red tape. On Tuesday, Zohran Mamdani – the politician at the center of a revived rightwing panic about socialists and purported communists winning elections across America - posted a video on X of himself putting a sheet of paper with the phrase “RED TAPE” into a paper shredder. Other pieces of paper, with phrases such as “cumbersome fees and fines” and “a permit you need just to serve ice-cream”, were shredded too. The video, set to Wu Tang Clan’s If Time Is Money, shows Mamdani joining a handful of city officials and small business owners throwing the resulting paper shreds into the air like confetti. “New York’s small business owners have said it over and over: endless paperwork and the uncertainty of dealing with City government has made getting their stores up and running too difficult,” Mamdani wrote on X, announcing a package of 50 policy changes aimed at easing the financial burden of fines, fees and regulations on mom-and-pop shops across the five boroughs. At a press conference in the Bronx, Mamdani listed some of the onerous policies getting the axe. Bodega owners will no longer need a separate license to sell the same products outside the store – such as fruit and flowers – as inside. Restaurants will no longer need a “superfluous” frozen dessert permit to sell ice-cream on top of the permit already required to sell food. Barber shops will no longer have to renew their permit every year, instead doing so every three years. Street fair vendor permit fees will be reduced, restaurant inspections will be sped up, and equipment registration fees will be eliminated for a year. A corresponding executive order signed by Mamdani on Monday will also expand the NYC Best program, assigning each of the city’s 180,000 small businesses – which employ an estimated 1 million people – a case worker to help owners navigate the Big Apple’s sometimes byzantine bureaucracy. “I’m over the moon,” Dawn Kelly, the owner of the Nourish Spot in Jamaica, Queens, told the Guardian about the new reforms. She launched her business in 2016 with the help of Best. Her case worker, she said, “held my hand from the idea to cutting the ribbon”, and she’s thrilled more businesses will now have the opportunity to use the program. Over the last decade, Kelly says her business has faced challenges. Her staff, for example, would have to travel from the outer-reaches of Queens all the way to the Upper West Side to take a three-day course to get a required food-handling certificate as the course is offered at only one location in the whole city. A member of the city’s Small Business Advisory Commission, Kelly relayed this problem to the mayor’s office. She says she got “emotional” this week watching Mamdani’s press conference. Julie Su, deputy mayor for economic justice, called out Kelly by name when announcing that the city will now offer the food-handling course at multiple locations. “These people are serious. They really care about small businesses,” said Kelly, adding: “They get shit done.” Such reforms by the mayor, who took office in January, come during a trying time for small businesses, which often survive on the slimmest of margins. A recent study conducted by the city found that while 3,540 businesses opened in the second quarter of 2025, another 8,400 similar-sized businesses closed, amounting to the lowest ebb of new business formation in five years. The reforms are also at odds with the hysterical caricature of Mamdani being manufactured by Donald Trump, the Republican party, and rightwing media. The right has repeatedly depicted the mayor, and a wave of his fellow electeds from the Democratic Socialists of America, as raging anti-business radicals. Appearing on Fox News in May, Bruce Blakeman, the Republican nominee for New York governor, alleged that if “you own… a “small business, a grocery store, a bodega, Zohran Mamdani wants to take your property.” “THE LEFT’S PLAN: CONTROL AND CONFISCATE,” read the Fox News chyron beneath Blakeman. The small business initiatives Mamdani announced this week, however, amount to a sweeping program of deregulation – a term most often associated with free-market conservatives. Some of Mamdani’s opponents couldn’t help but praise him. “Mamdani is clearly no libertarian icon,” the libertarian magazine Reason noted. “He has proposed opening government-run grocery stores, pushed for freezing the rent, and has called for higher taxes on the city’s top contributors. Mamdani’s free-market critics are well justified in opposing these policies. But if Mamdani’s critics are principled, they will welcome these pro-small business reforms.” But for JW Mason, an associate professor of economics at John Jay College at the City University of New York, Mamdani’s reforms are “completely consistent with a democratic socialist approach to governance”. “I think the reality is that when we talk about ‘pro-business government’, historically we almost always mean government that caters to large, politically connected businesses,” said Mason. “Governments that call themselves pro-business don’t particularly serve the interests of these smaller businesses that New York depends on … In some sense a lot of what being a socialist mayor, a socialist in office, means is making government simply work better.” At High Beam Coffee Roastery in Red Hook, Brooklyn, co-owner Vicki Forshee said it always feels like big businesses including Amazon – which operates multiple warehouses in the neighborhood – often seem to operate with more tax breaks, and less oversight or regulation, than small businesses like hers which “have to climb a crazy mountain just to survive”. Selina Ullrich, the cafe’s other co-owner and a veteran of the city’s food industry, pointed to how health department inspections always feel like shakedowns, prioritizing penalizing restaurants over violating obscure regulations, as opposed to just ensuring food safety. “There’s rules where nobody can explain why the rule exists,” she said. “It’s a rule that is impossible to comply with, but we all just agree that we just have to deal with it.” She’s excited the mayor is starting a process to change that: “It seems like he wants to accomplish things versus just talking about accomplishing things.” Mason, the economist, believes such an approach could pay political dividends for Mamdani, overcoming the efforts to depict him as some kind of extremist. “I think the reality is that people who are political professionals, people in the media, have this very strong kind of view that politics is all on a sort of left-right axis, and if you’re a socialist, you’re on the left … I don’t think most people see it that way. I think most people have a much more diffuse view of politics, and they like some things and they don’t like other things, and they don’t necessarily rearrange everything in the same sort of left-right way that we do in elite conversations. I think for most people, they perceive Zohran as somebody who’s come in, who’s made promises and is delivering on those promises, who can point to concrete things he’s done that make people’s lives better.” Kelly, the owner of the Nourish Spot in Jamaica, Queens, was a longtime fan of former mayor Eric Adams, the centrist Democrat who left office plagued by scandals. She now considers herself a fan of Mamdani. “I don’t really care about those labels nowadays,” Kelly said, when asked about Mamdani being a socialist. “I like that he stands for making sure nobody seems to feel marginalized, like we’re all in this together, we all win together. “If that’s what socialism is,” she added, “I’m all for it!” • This article was amended on 26 July 2026 to correct the name of the Nourish Spot.
