title: Staff turnover is rampant under Trump 2.0 – with insidious results
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: A new report shows more Senate-confirmed staffers have left their jobs this time around than in his first term
body_text: Donald Trump loves a construction project. He’s building a ballroom, revamping a reflecting pool, and overseeing the construction of a skyline-altering arch in Washington DC. For his next real estate scheme, may I suggest a giant revolving door in the White House? It would certainly get a lot of use: senior officials are leaving Trump’s second administration at record rates. According to a new report called Quiet Chaos by the nonpartisan Partnership for Public Service, 27 Senate-confirmed officials have left their positions within cabinet departments to date. That’s nearly 150% higher than the 11 departures in the first 18 months of Trump’s first administration. Per the report, it is also “nearly two and a half times as many as Trump’s first administration (11) and over six times as many as the average between the George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations (4.3)”. High-profile departures, like that of homeland security secretary Kristi Noem’s, have had a lot of media coverage. But as the Partnership for Public Service note in their report, there has been “remarkably little public attention” when it comes to overall departures in Trump 2.0. Indeed, the narrative has largely been that while Trump’s first term was a chaotic mess marked by constant personnel changes, his second presidency has been far more stable. And that narrative isn’t entirely wrong. In Trump’s first term the rapid turnover was a sign that the reality TV host and real estate nepo baby had no idea what he was doing. In Trump 2.0, however, the departures point to something far more insidious. Rather than signaling incompetence, they are fueling a power grab by a president who seems to think of himself as a king. “Turnover on this scale does not just thin the government’s leadership ranks – it concentrates power in the president,” Chris Piper from the Partnership for Public Service writes in a blog post. “Each seat left to an acting official is one the president can fill on his own terms without the Senate’s advice and consent: no vetting, no confirmation hearing, no vote.” Trump himself has said he likes acting officials because the temporary nature of the position gives him more control. “And so, Acting gives you much greater flexibility,” the president said in his first term. “A lot easier to do things.” Last month Trump similarly told the Wall Street Journal that he thought the non-permanent status of Bill Pulte, his incoming acting director of national intelligence and a man sometimes referred to as “Little Trump”, was an asset. “You’re less shackled,” he said. “It sort of gives you more power, you know, for a somewhat limited period of time.” Power, and the rapid accretion of it in the executive branch, is the overwhelming theme of Trump’s second term. The conservative supermajority in the supreme court, which Trump helped create, has been invaluable to him in this regard. In July 2024, the court ruled that former presidents are entitled to some degree of immunity from criminal prosecution, nullifying the chance of an election subversion case against him before the election. Then, last month, the supreme court gave the president another gift: the power to fire leaders of independent agencies or commissions. The decision in Trump v Slaughter overturned Humphrey’s Executor, a 1935 ruling that the US constitution did not grant “illimitable power of removal” to the president. Trump doesn’t quite have carte blanche to remove whomever he likes. On the same day as that decision, the supreme court ruled in Trump v Cook that the Federal Reserve was an exception to Trump’s power. Nevertheless, it is hard to overstate the significance of the Slaughter ruling, which upended almost a century of well-settled law curbing executive power. “Today, the court discards that democratic regime in favor of one that distorts the structure of government to fit the majority’s theory of unitary, total executive control. The result is a president who emerges with far greater power than ever before,” justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote in her dissent. Trump, meanwhile, wrote on Truth Social that it was “the Greatest Increase in Presidential Power in the last 100 years”. I highly doubt that Trump has spent significant portions of his life thinking about the constitutionality of the Humphrey’s Executor decision. But do you know who has? The people at the Heritage Foundation, who are behind Project 2025, which is widely seen as the playbook for Trump’s second term. Overturning Humphrey’s Executor is right there on page 560 of Project 2025. Also in that playbook are steps to interfere with election administration and weaponize the Department of Justice against election officials who make decisions the Trump administration disagrees with. In other words: a strategy for influencing the upcoming election. Make no mistake: the masterminds behind Trump’s second term haven’t overseen “the Greatest Increase in Presidential Power in the last 100 years” just to easily cede that power to a Democratic president at the next election. A bunch of losers are still complaining that the Odyssey isn’t white enough Elon Musk has been whining about Christopher Nolan casting Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy for months now. This week, following rave reviews of the Odyssey, Musk announced that his AI image and video generator Grok Imagine would create its own “historically accurate” version of the film. Perhaps Musk should listen to Colman Domingo, who recently said on Jimmy Kimmel Live that he has a message for everyone upset about diversity in The Odyssey: “If you want to see a film with a cast of all white people who are cursed by the gods, the ‘Melania’ movie is currently streaming.” Record 384 World Cup-linked reports of domestic abuse in England and Wales The data was collected as part of a strategy to better understand the link between football tournaments and domestic abuse. A police chief cited extended pub opening hours as one of the factors in the surge in violence. AOC is leading Kamala Harris in a new 2028 presidential poll by a long way A University of New Hampshire poll has AOC leading the field with 22% support while Pete Buttigieg has 21%. Harris only has 5%. Model scout for Jeffrey Epstein found dead at his home near Paris Daniel Siad, who was found dead at his home on Monday, compared his work trying to source women with fishing. “In This busyness I feel like fisherman some time I cache (sic) quick, some time no fish,” he wrote in an email to Epstein in 2014. Australian politician Pauline Hanson thinks domestic violence is a ‘two-way street’ The senator also suggested women experiencing abuse should simply “not put up with it”. Israeli rights groups warn of ‘mass pogroms’ in occupied West Bank While violence by Arabs is called “terrorism”, the media tends to downplay attacks by Jewish settlers in Israel by characterizing it as “settler violence”. This violence, enabled by the Israeli military and ignored by many in the US, has been intensifying. Following a deadly settler attack on Friday, Israeli-Palestinian human rights group B’Tselem and 19 other Israeli human rights organisations condemned the international community’s “silence and inaction” and called for “immediate action to stop Israel’s violence and prevent pogroms by settler militias”. Why middle-aged women are raving Women are putting the internalized ageism aside and realizing you’re never too old to go out clubbing. People are watching porn based on ICE raids Rule 34 of the internet is that if something exists, there is porn of it. The dystopian machinations of the Trump administration are no exception. Wired has a disturbing piece on the rise of Maga-themed porn. The week in pawtriarchy Meet Jimothy, who appears to be the internet’s new favourite racoon. Seattle-based Jimothy hasn’t won hearts and minds by passing out drunk in a Virginia liquor store like some of his compatriots. Rather, he has gone viral because of his distinctive body shape, which may be the result of a rare genetic condition called short spine syndrome. He looks a bit like a furry goblin, basically. I reckon Jimothy’s lack of a well-functioning backbone means he has a promising political career ahead of him. Perhaps Trump could make him Secretary of Trashury. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: Troy Jackson: the Maine lumberjack Democrats believe can beat Susan Collins
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: Jackson, a prominent workers’ rights advocate and a leading progressive voice, replaces the scandal-plagued Graham Platner
body_text: As cinemagoers flock to The Odyssey, Democrats in Maine are hoping that their long and perilous quest for a political hero ends in Troy. They have nominated lumberjack Troy Jackson this weekend as their candidate to challenge Susan Collins, a veteran Republican in the US Senate, after the implosion of the party’s original candidate left them scrambling for a replacement less than four months before the midterm elections. Jackson, a former president of the Democratic-controlled Maine senate, i secured the nomination at a special party convention in Bangor on Saturday. He inherits a race transformed by the abrupt withdrawal of the primary winner, Graham Platner, following allegations of sexual assault made by a former girlfriend, accusations he has denied. While Kamala Harris infamously had only 107 days to build a presidential campaign in 2024, Jackson would have even less time for a battle that could decide control of the 100-member Senate. The fifth-generation logger from Aroostook county in northern Maine combines an unusual political biography with an unapologetically progressive platform. He first came to prominence in the late 1990s when he led a week-long blockade by Maine loggers protesting the employment of Canadian workers, whom they accused of depressing wages. The demonstration ended with police escorting him away but established his reputation as a champion of rural workers, which would continue into his time as a legislator. Jackson initially ran as a Republican in 2000 when he sought a seat in Maine’s house of representatives. He lost but won two years later when he ran as an independent. He switched to the Democratic party in 2004 and went on to serve three terms in the house before being elected to the state senate, where he was president from 2018 until 2024. In contrast to Platner, the biggest scandal attached to him so far is that he displayed flashes of temper such as cursing, shouting and throwing a water bottle in a meeting when he could not persuade someone to vote his way, according to a Washington Post report based on interviews with more than two dozen people. Jackson’s political views have shifted significantly over the years. Earlier in his career he opposed abortion rights and same-sex marriage, positions he has since abandoned. He has emerged as one of Maine’s leading progressives, backing policies such as Medicare for All and calling for the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). For those seeking an economic populist and working-class champion, he appears to fit the bill. Tim Fullerton, a Democratic strategist from the southern part of the state, recently spent time with him and came away impressed. “Troy is as Maine as they come, Maine through and through,” he said. “He shoots from the hip. He says what he thinks which in this particular case, running against a very calculated and polished politician, is a striking difference because if you just were to meet him you wouldn’t think that he was a politician at all. “He also has the best Maine accent of any of them by far, which is nice. He’s salt of the earth. I feel like I know 50 guys who are just like him.” Fullerton distinguished Jackson’s approach from the slicker, poll-tested aesthetics typical of modern political campaigns. “I don’t think he could fake it if he wanted to, to be honest. I’ve only met him once but he told me right off the bat what he thought about everything, which was quite refreshing compared to a lot of these people. They’ve been in DC for a million years and learn a certain language that doesn’t always translate at home.” Still, Jackson’s ties to the left extend beyond Maine. He chaired Bernie Sanders’ successful 2016 presidential caucus campaign in the state and remains a close political ally of the Vermont independent senator. Yet the sudden pivot from Platner, who survived various scandals including a tattoo resembling a Nazi symbol until finally stepping down, to Jackson brings plenty of anxieties. The oysterman was a charismatic firebrand capable of whipping up crowds and capturing more than 150,000 votes in the primary. Jackson, by his own admission, is a more plain-spoken and less polished orator. Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of the progressive organisation Our Revolution – which backed Platner and has now thrown its weight behind Jackson – dismisses the notion that a lack of traditional charisma is a fatal flaw. “He strikes me as a regular working class person, a regular dude,” he said. “That’s my gut-check vibe on him, having numerous interactions with him over the years. Does Graham Platner have a certain dynamism and charisma? Yes, but I think Troy counters that with a true authenticity, and that is reflected in his background and should not be discounted.” Geevarghese dismissed sniping that Democratic consultants were merely ticking demographic boxes, deliberately swapping an oyster farmer for a lumberjack to simulate working-class appeal. “He represents who we are and want to be as a party,” he insisted. “He is not somebody that was designed by a marketing agency or created by political consultants. Troy Jackson is the real deal, and there’s nothing manufactured here. This is what the electorate wants and why not give it to them?” Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, echoed this sentiment, arguing that Jackson embodies the rural working-class man challenging both the political and corporate establishment. He said: “My prediction is that if he comes across on a debate stage as a normal working-class dude who happens to be stepping up to run for political office, that reinforces his core message as opposed to taking away from his power as a messenger. “Running someone who’s a little less polished, but having that actually accentuate his biggest strength, which is that he’s a rural working class guy is not a bad thing, especially when up against an establishment insider and corporate ally like Susan Collins.” Nevertheless, the contest against Collins is sure to be hard fought. Both politicians hail from Aroostook county – called simply “the county” within the state – a sparsely populated, heavily Republican region best known for its potato farming and strong support for Donald Trump in recent presidential elections. Financially, Collins, who has held the seat for three decades, begins the race with a commanding advantage. Federal campaign filings show she has raised more than $16m, while Jackson’s campaign says it has brought in just over $1m. Jackson has framed Collins – viewed as one of her party’s most vulnerable figures in the 2026 cycle – as an enabler of Trump, accusing her of siding with Republicans and corporate interests at decisive moments, including over Trump’s war in Iran. Collins has sought to portray Jackson as an ideological extremist. Speaking to the Associated Press this week, she described his political evolution as that of a “Bernie bro”, arguing that his record placed him firmly on the socialist wing of American politics. Republicans have also attacked the circumstances of Jackson’s expected nomination. Jim Deyermond, chair of the Maine Republican party, criticised Democrats for selecting a long-serving political insider after insisting the replacement process would be open following Platner’s withdrawal. The Platner saga left Democrats pointing fingers at each other and tarnished the party’s brand. But they cling to the hope that, with inflation and the Iran war driving down Trump’s approval rating, Collins could be swept aside in a blue wave. And a lot can happen between now and November. Earlier this month, for example, a 26-year-old Colombian national, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, was shot dead by an ICE officer in Biddeford, Maine. The Department of Homeland Security claimed that Guerrero was fleeing and threatened “public safety”. Jackson condemned ICE as a “rogue agency that goes around doing things that they’re being told to on high”. Fullerton, who is also cofounder and chief executive of Find Out Media, commented: “The situation with ICE and Biddeford has changed the game for Mainers. You heard from Susan Collins: oh, they need to be reformed, and she was pretty mealy about it. Troy and the rest of the Democrats were rightly angry and very direct. External factors are going to weigh more heavily into that than Graham leaving and Troy stepping in.” Corbin Trent, a cofounder of Justice Democrats and former communications director for Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, praised Jackson’s unflinching stance on the issue. “He gets that ICE cannot exist in its current form,” he said. “That’s the kind of candidate people are looking for: one that says things that are quite clear, quite obvious, but also not the easiest thing to convince people of. That moral clarity is something that’s going to carry forward.” There is also an optimistic sense among progressives that the movement built over the past year is entirely separate from the flawed man who previously led it. Trent frames it very differently from the rightwing populism of the Republican party. “Whether it’s reforming our entire immigration system and getting rid of a paramilitary force like ICE, whether it’s Medicare for all, whether its building millions of houses across this country and hundreds of thousands across Maine, I don’t think these ideas died with finding out that we had a shitty candidate,” he said. “In fact, these ideas are still very popular, there’s still passion behind doing the job and that’s what people are excited about. Luckily, we’re not building a cult of personality like Maga, one where you wonder, how does this go beyond Trump? It’s a great asset that we’re building around ideas and not individuals.”

title: Troy Jackson secures Democratic nomination for Maine Senate seat after chaotic primary race
author: Shrai Popat in Bangor, Maine
summary: Progressive former state senate president gains nomination after Graham Platner dropped out over sexual assault allegations
body_text: In a race defined by scandal, withdrawals and a frantic hunt for a replacement candidate, Maine Democrats hit reset on their chaotic Senate primary on Saturday as Troy Jackson officially secured the party’s nomination. He took the stage at the Cross Insurance Center in Bangor to rapturous applause, a standing ovation and Noah Kahan’s Northern Attitude blaring over the speakers. “This is the absolute honor of my life,” Jackson said. “If you’ve ever been ignored, underestimated, pushed around or told that you have to wait your turn while the rich cut the line, I’m asking you to stand with us in this campaign.” Jackson’s win amounted to a coronation for the progressive fifth‑generation logger and former state senate president, who faced no real opposition at the special convention after every major rival stepped aside. Their exits cleared the path for Jackson to replace Graham Platner, the oysterman and marine veteran who ended his campaign amid mounting controversies that culminated in a sexual assault allegation he has denied. Platner dropped out days after Politico first reported that a woman he dated five years ago said he forced her to have sex despite repeated objections. His withdrawal triggered a breakneck scramble inside the Maine Democratic party to devise a process for selecting a new nominee before the state’s 27 July deadline to select a replacement for the general‑election ballot. “I know many of you poured your hearts into building this movement way before I ever entered this race,” Jackson said on Saturday before the official vote. “But the hope that you built never belonged to anyone campaigning. It belongs to every Mainer who knows that healthcare is a human right, belongs to every worker fighting for a union, a living wage and a dignified environment.” Jackson, who finished third in the ranked‑choice gubernatorial primary, won the snap convention by a vote of 566-5 on Saturday. But his victory was all but assured once a majority of Mainers who won county‑level delegate elections last weekend pledged to back him before the convention. The remaining delegates come from the state party committee. By Sunday, as Jackson’s nomination became inevitable, all of his major challengers bowed out of the hastily assembled contest. That included fellow gubernatorial contenders – former Maine CDC director Nirav Shah and the Maine secretary of state, Shenna Bellows – as well as Jordan Wood, the former congressional candidate who ran unsuccessfully in the Democratic primary for Maine’s second district. “The easy solution”, said Charlie Dingman, the Maine Democratic party chair, would be to let the state committee select the new nominee. “Instead, we responded to the growing grassroots movement in our state to build power for ordinary working people,” he said. However, some Democratic voters said the convention process was still not representative of the more than 200,000 voters who turned out in the June primary, which Platner won. Jackson will now face Susan Collins, the five‑term Republican incumbent, in one of the most closely watched races of the midterm cycle – for a seat Democrats view as central to their audacious plan to retake the Senate. They need four pickups nationwide in November, and Maine is integral to that strategy. Collins is also the only Republican in the upper chamber seeking re-election in a state that Kamala Harris won in 2024. “For 30 years, she’s told us that she’s ‘concerned’. But look, concern is not courage,” Jackson said on Saturday, as supporters waved “Retire Susan” placards in the audience. “What she says in Maine does not erase what she does down in Washington.” Preliminary polling from the University of New Hampshire shows Jackson with a slight edge over Collins, a moderate GOP senator who has been politically untouchable for the past three decades. And while Jackson is well-known in Maine political circles, his nascent campaign will have to accelerate quickly to match Collins’s fundraising lead and the momentum Platner built after months of statewide travel, town halls and a grassroots surge strong enough to force the term‑limited governor, Janet Mills, out of the Democratic primary in April. Collins’ camp was quick to cast Jackson’s nomination as undemocratic. “A 24-year Augusta insider was appointed to run for the Senate by fewer than three-tenths of one percent of its primary voters,” said campaign spokesperson Shawn Roderick. “Troy came in third in the Democratic primary for governor. Now he will run for Senate as the third choice of his party insiders.” Jackson, who began his political career as a Republican and once opposed abortion and gay marriage, is now staunchly progressive and campaigned alongside Platner’s economic‑populist platform, even earning Platner’s endorsement during his own unsuccessful run for governor. Both points are likely to feature prominently in the efforts by Collins and conservative groups to undermine his political acumen in the months ahead. Shortly after Platner exited the race, Jackson tried to distance himself from the turmoil – telling MS Now that Platner assured him there was “nothing in his past that I had to worry about”. “He lied to me. And he lied to a lot of us,” Jackson said in an interview after Platner posted an 11‑minute video announcing his withdrawal. In Bangor on Saturday, the new nominee insisted the chaos that has consumed the Democratic race was in the rearview mirror without naming Platner. “Today we turn the page. Today this becomes a general election campaign, and today we begin the work of defeating Susan Collins in November,” Jackson said. A number of delegates said that Jackson’s proximity to Platner’s messaging shouldn’t be off-putting. “It never was about the person, but about the policies,” said Lydia Stone, 31, who lives in North Yarmouth and works for a company that sells forestry supplies. “I think what Graham said he was, I think Troy Jackson actually is.” Many people in Bangor noted that it was crucial for Jackson to be meeting voters as much as possible in the 101 days until the election. “It’s going to be difficult because there’s a short window window of time, but I would say to get out there as much as he can into especially those rural communities like where he’s from, and actually be there,” said Lisa Marin, 69, who lives in Jonesport and chairs the Washington county Democratic committee. Marin added: “That was one of the things in the Platner campaign that I think was really helpful for Graham – he was out there and really meeting people where they are. And I know Troy wants to do that, and as much as he can, I feel like that’s what he needs to do.”

title: More than 1 million children lost access to food benefits after Trump bill passed
author: Marina Dunbar
summary: Analysis finds more than 4 million Americans lost Snap benefits, or food stamps, from July 2025 to March 2026
body_text: More than a million children across the US have lost access to Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap) food benefits since Congress approved the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, according to a new report from the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (CBPP). The analysis found that more than 4 millions Americans were removed from Snap from July 2025 to March 2026, marking a significant decline in participation in the federal food assistance program. Arizona recorded the largest drop in enrollment after the bill became law. The legislation tightened eligibility rules for food assistance and increased state screening requirements. State data through May shows that more than 450,000 Arizonans have come off Snap, cutting overall participation within the state in half. According to the CBPP analysis, children make up a significant portion of those losing benefits, with more than 1 million children across the 19 states studied no longer receiving Snap assistance. In Louisiana, nearly one in four children receiving Snap benefits lost assistance. Massachusetts and Texas each saw close to one-fifth of children enrolled in the program removed from Snap. The report comes as participation in the program continues to fall nationwide following major reductions to the federal food assistance program under the Trump administration. Snap, commonly referred to as food stamps, provides monthly benefits to low-income and no-income households to help pay for groceries and remains the country’s largest food assistance program. The report says the steep decline in participation is likely tied in large part to the 2025 Republican reconciliation law, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which shifted a substantial share of Snap benefit costs to states based on their payment error rates. The CBPP warned that the situation would continue to deteriorate unless Congress intervenes. “Without immediate congressional action to delay this cost shift for all states, the unfolding emergency will only worsen as more children are cut off from the food assistance their families need to afford nutritious food,” the CBPP said. Representative Ilhan Omar, a progressive Democrat from Minnesota, pointed to the outcomes during a speech on the House floor earlier this month. Omar had introduced an amendment aimed at reversing the Snap cuts, but the proposal was rejected by the Republican majority. The latest figures also prompted action from the US Conference of Mayors. On Monday, the nonpartisan organization representing cities with populations of at least 30,000 sent a letter to the Senate signed by more than 200 mayors calling for lawmakers to reverse the Snap cuts amid the US’s “deepening food security crisis”. “Snap remains the nation’s most effective and efficient anti-hunger program. It reduces poverty, supports local economies, and provides an automatic stabilizer during economic downturns,” the letter said. “Hunger is not a partisan issue, and efforts to address food insecurity should rise above political divisions.”

title: Like Trump, Pauline Hanson plays the media and attacks the media simultaneously. Who’s using who?
author: Zoe Daniel
summary: One Nation is borrowing heavily from the Maga playbook. But constant claims of being misquoted predate the US president’s
body_text: Time to call a spade a spade. One Nation’s rise is the media’s fault. And Pauline Hanson being misunderstood is also the media’s fault. Elements of the media have amplified the rise of One Nation over three decades, with outsized coverage normalising what is now a populist machine. At the same time, Hanson treats the media as her enemy. Can both things be true? The first is a deliberately provocative statement. The second is an observation. Both lead to questions about the media’s role and responsibility in an era of information manipulation. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The phrases “fake news” and “enemy of the people” come to mind in these times when it appears that whatever the question is for Hanson, Donald Trump is the answer. The latest example relates to her comments about violence against women in which she makes excuses for violent men. “It is wrong, but it’s also a two-way street,” she told the Brisbane radio station 4BC. “I’m not saying that it’s just men, women can lose their cool as well. Society is under so much pressure … Everyone is under so much pressure, and it’s really hard.” The facts are that intimate partner violence is overwhelmingly perpetrated by men. She went on to say that women who are being abused should just leave: “If these women are getting abused by men out there, then don’t put up with it.” The data also shows that leaving is the most dangerous time for women and children. The remarks have caused an outcry, which has provoked Hanson to again claim that her comments have been misrepresented. “Here’s exactly what I said on 4BC about domestic violence, so you don’t get it twisted by the media or the Labor Party,” she posted on social media. “There is a concerted effort by some in the media to constantly take my comments out of context.” It could not be more Trumpian as she plays the media and attacks the media, simultaneously. In 2016, Trump was estimated to have received as much as US$5.9bn in free media coverage, more than doubling Hillary Clinton’s presence in the press, while underspending her official campaign on his way to victory in the 2016 presidential election. At the same time, he dominated social media, simultaneously vilifying and bypassing the mainstream media to build an audience he could communicate with directly, while sucking the legacy media into chasing the ratings he could command. Sound familiar? When I was the US bureau chief for the ABC in 2016, US television networks hung on Trump’s every word, broadcasting hours of live, unchecked diatribes. By the time the factcheckers properly mobilised, it was too late. The post-truth era was already upon us. Factchecking no longer landed with the average person. Trump had become all but untouchable. The media had become the enemy of the people, and anything remotely critical was labelled fake news. Eroding trust in the media was crucial to his strategy. One Nation is now borrowing heavily from this playbook. Hanson’s gaslighting over the White Australia policy, “no good Muslims”, paid parental leave and now violence against women mirrors Trump’s tactics; making statements then walking them back or denying she made them at all. While she’s taken the predictable approach of arguing that the “left-wing media” has twisted her words in “false clickbait stories”, it’s not true. Her recent remarks follow a long pattern of behaviour. In her maiden parliamentary speech in 1996 she said: “I believe we are in danger of being swamped by Asians.” That was before she told the Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi to “pack your bags and piss off back to Pakistan”, which led to a federal court finding of unlawful racial discrimination and vilification under the Racial Discrimination Act. Yet parts of the media continue to facilitate her rise, while appearing surprised and disturbed that it’s happening. Channel Seven’s Spotlight program was snookered by Hanson’s team when it either participated in or helped organise her trip around Europe, in which she met rightwingers and hung out in Italy with Gina Rinehart. Seven denies arranging the meetings while, surprise, surprise, Hanson has accused the program of misrepresenting its intentions. That said, the network got the ratings. Conspiracy theorists might suspect that the argy-bargy was confected to achieve that. Who knows? The mainstream media is losing influence as consumers increasingly get their news from social media, which is forcing legacy organisations to feed the algorithm to survive. But the more Hanson is freely platformed as clickbait rather than properly scrutinised, the more likely it is that One Nation will find its way to power. And who will take responsibility for that? Zoe Daniel is a three-time ABC foreign correspondent and the former independent member for Goldstein

title: Trump revives old tropes as he pushes warnings of ‘communist menace’
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: President harks back to red scare of his childhood to attack US left – but will such language resonate beyond Maga base?
body_text: Perhaps above all else, Donald Trump is a child of the cold war. Three months before the US president was born, Winston Churchill delivered a historic speech in Fulton, Missouri, that ushered in a generations-long existential struggle between western capitalism and Soviet communism. Lamenting the spread of Soviet communism across eastern Europe following the allied victory in the second world war, Churchill – by then no longer British prime minister – warned his audience on 5 March 1946 that “an iron curtain has descended across the continent”. It was the prelude to a nuclear-armed standoff between Washington and Moscow that triggered a hysteria-driven “red scare” in the US – leading to the execution of convicted spies and exemplified by witch-hunts instigated by the Republican senator Joe McCarthy, who claimed he had obtained lists of communist agents working in the state department and other key areas of American life. The hunt for communists would have been a ubiquitous theme of Trump’s early childhood. Strikingly, Roy Cohn – McCarthy’s chief counsel, who had masterminded the federal prosecution of the convicted Soviet spies, Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, subsequently executed for treason – became Trump’s mentor in later decades, as he rose in the New York real-estate world. “For many years, communism and communists were the major enemy of the United States,” said Harvey Klehr, an emeritus professor at Emory University and an expert in the US’s history with communism. “There were obviously times it might have gotten exaggerated or or got out of hand, but there was a darn good reason for people to be alarmed about it.” Paranoia waned in relative terms after McCarthy was censured by the Senate in 1954, but only abated after the collapse of eastern European communist regimes in 1989 and the dissolution of the Soviet Union two years later. Now, 37 years after the fall of the Berlin Wall and the end of the cold war, Trump is reviving it. In a series of high-profile addresses, Trump has identified an ideology that millions of Americans are too young to recall as the US’s biggest threat. “A generation after we fought and won the cold war against the menace of communism, there is now a resurgence of the communist menace in our land, including from newcomers to our country who embrace ideas totally opposed to our way of life and our great success,” he said in a speech at Mount Rushmore on 3 July, on the eve of the US’s 250th birthday. He vowed to “vanquish communists quickly” and “send them into exile”. That the topic was no one-off was confirmed by a new 100-page report from the state department published this week, titled Cuba: the Capital of 21st Century Communism. “For nearly seven decades, the Cuban regime has waged a sustained campaign of subversion against the United States,” states the report, claiming that the “highest reaches” of the US government have been “infiltrated”. “Today, that network continues to maintain ties to powerful leftist nonprofits, anti-ICE collectives, socialist groups, and Marxist militant organizations across the United States.” The rebirth of anti-communist animus has been fueled by the recent success of Democratic candidates identifying as “democratic socialists” – most notably the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani. A succession of leftwing candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have followed Mamdani’s triumph by winning Democratic primaries, including Darializa Avila Chevalier, who ousted the veteran New York representative, Adriano Espaillat, in June. Chevalier has drawn scrutiny over a now deleted Twitter account that praised Marxist ideology and historical communist figures, such as Vladimir Lenin. Several high-profile Democrats and liberal-leaning figures have ridiculed Trump’s attacks for falsely conflating socialism – a term which can describe democratic governments in several European countries – with Soviet-style communism. “Not subtle: new party line is to associate Communists with every crime, every offense,” wrote Ruth Ben-Ghiat, a historian of fascism, on X. “Create a sense of Communist threat to justify a rightwing crackdown. Old playbook used with coups and Fascist takeovers.” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the Democratic representative for New York and a member of the DSA, called the communist label “very silly”. “They want to call it communist because they don’t want you to know that Germany, Italy, the UK, Canada – everybody else – has it better than us, and we spend the most money for the worst care in the developed world,” she told reporters. Cara Tobe, a spokesperson for the DSA – asked whether the association’s membership included communists – said: “Our organization’s dues-paying members range in political beliefs, but we are all united under the banner of democratic socialism. “It’s concerning but not surprising that Donald Trump would like to send his opponents into exile, because it’s increasingly evident our ideas win with the American people: socialism beats fascism.” Yet some commentators say Trump’s charge is not baseless. “The communist issue is not entirely a bugaboo,” said Klehr, who said the DSA had a “very significant communist component”. Formed by Michael Harrington, the leftwing activist and writer, in 1982, the DSA was founded under a constitution that excluded members of “democratic centralists” organizations – code for Soviet-style communist parties founded on Lenin’s model. Klehr said that provision had been repealed – resulting in an influx of radical new members that he compared to the “entryist” infiltration of Britain’s Labour party by the Trotskyite Militant tendency in the early 1980s, which resulted in the adoption of leftwing policies and led to an overwhelming election defeat at the hands of Margaret Thatcher’s Conservatives. The faction was expelled in 1985 by Labour’s then leader, Neil Kinnock. “The DSA has changed, and a significant number of people who unapologetically call themselves Marxist-Leninists or communists have moved into DSA and attained some significant positions,” said Klehr. Bill Galston, a fellow at the Brookings Institution and a former White House domestic policy adviser under Bill Clinton, said: “There are people who’ve been in the DSA for decades and can remember the struggle between the democratic and the undemocratic left, and in particular between communists and socialists, and so they are definite. “They are responding to the perception that there are various communist or communist-adjacent factions that have joined the DSA, and that they don’t want to be part of that.” Two recent articles in the Atlantic have highlighted the fierce debate over the credentials of DSA candidates and their potential to be catalysts for an ideological shift within the Democratic party. However, Galston – a self-proclaimed “red diaper baby” whose grandfather stood multiple times as a communist candidate in New York – questioned the ability of Trump’s “communist” tag to resonate beyond his Maga base. He cited a recent Economist/YouGov poll asking voters how much of a threat communism posed to the US. Some 18% termed it a “major threat” and another 25% a “minor threat”, while 33% said it was “not a threat”. “Trump is 80 years old, and for him, the epithet ‘communist’ rolls off his lips quite naturally, because it was part of the conflict with internal communism and the Soviet Union as an external communist foe that was part of his formation,” said Galston. “Older Americans, those who do have a memory of the cold war, are more responsive to this alleged threat than are younger Americans. He’s speaking to a political party that is disproportionately supported by older Americans. “So one way of looking at this is as part of Trump’s overall strategy of base mobilization. He’s preaching to the choir here and he knows intuitively who makes up that choir.” Galston also attributed the resurgence of fears of communism to an age-old popular American failure to make fine distinctions in political terminology – a confusion Trump’s critics say applies to him. But Klehr argued that the trend signaled a broader threat to democracy and liberal values that he said emanated from the extreme left and far right. “Donald Trump wouldn’t know a communist from a democratic socialist from a Martian, but there are other very smart people that do understand the difference, and the significance,” he said. “It’s the same sort of thing that occurred on the political right not that many years ago, when various kinds of rightwing lunatics, neo-Nazis and racists began to move into the Republican party, they won some primaries, they established a beachhead and they’re still there. “I think some of that is happening in the Democratic party, and it’s dangerous on both counts. It raises serious concerns for the health of a democratic society. “The memory of communism is fading, and yet … some of the things they call for, it’s like they’ve forgotten the history.”

title: Republicans head home for the summer after a string of losses in Congress
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: GOP legislative priorities could be at odds with voters as midterms come into view and Democrats attempt a resurgence
body_text: When the chief Republican budget writer took to the floor of the House of Representatives this week to tout a plan to spend tens of billions of dollars on the war with Iran, he avoided using the words “war”, “conflict” or even “Iran”. “Just baseline battlefield readiness” is what Jodey Arrington said the money in the $95bn budget blueprint would be used for. “Bullets and bombs to finish the job and come home safely and victoriously, strengthen our food supply, and ultimately safeguard the integrity of our elections.” It was a rosy depiction of a risky proposition for House Republicans three months before they face voters in November’s midterm elections amid sticky inflation, signs of a Democratic resurgence , and poor approval ratings both for the war with Iran and Donald Trump’s presidency in general. Under the leadership of the speaker, Mike Johnson, House Republicans in their final week of work before a long summer recess opted not to alter course. In addition to passing the war spending plan along party lines, they approved a super-sized military budget and made multiple attempts to forge new restrictions on voting nationwide. “Many of you like to say that major legislating can’t happen in an election year. We just proved you wrong,” Johnson told reporters on Wednesday, after the votes. Not 24 hours later came a reminder of how Democrats can leverage divisions within the House GOP’s historically small majority, when four dissident Republicans joined with the minority to pass a symbolic war powers resolution that would mandate Trump withdraw troops from combat against Iran. “You’re about to have hundreds of members of Congress go home to their constituents, and a lot of folks are about to get crushed, rightfully so, by their constituents,” the Democratic congressman Jason Crow told reporters following that vote in an articulation of the affordability agenda his party is counting on to return it to power. “They’re going to hear that people are losing healthcare, they’re losing their homes, they’re losing their farms, they’re losing their small businesses. And why the hell are you supporting $100bn for another endless war in Iran that’s not making us safer, and contributing to the woes of the American people?” The Thursday vote amounted to an embarrassing defeat for Johnson, but the bigger issue for the speaker was that his legislative barrage landed with a thud among his own party in the Senate. As they have done twice prior since Trump returned to office, the House had written the budget blueprint to comply with the reconciliation procedure, which can circumvent Democrats’ use of the filibuster in the Senate and pass with a simple majority. But senior Republicans have shown little enthusiasm for a third such bill, and before the House even approved the budget blueprint, the Republican Senate majority leader, John Thune, said he would put it on “hold” in case he needed the measure as leverage over the Democrats in negotiations to continue government funding beyond its 30 September expiration. That raised the likelihood that the question of how much to spend on the Iran conflict will remain undecided in September. And while the House’s passage of the annual Pentagon budget, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), is typically a major accomplishment, Johnson complicated its chances in the Senate by bowing to pressure from rightwing lawmakers and merging it with the Save America Act. A fixation of Trump, the legislation would ban mail-in ballots and impose new identification requirements on voters when they register and cast ballots. But that’s not the only headwind the defense budget faces: Democrats have objected to its $1.15tn cost, and earlier this month they halted the advancement of the Senate’s version of the bill, in protest of the renewed hostilities with Iran. As they departed the Capitol for the five-week recess, House Republicans nonetheless believed they had a credible case to make for why the opposition should stay in the minority for the final two years of Trump’s presidency. “Joe Biden and the Democrats are the ones that ran this country into the ditch, and we’re on a rescue mission to save it. And we passed some really good policies that are actually working, and so we got a great story to tell to the voters,” said Richard Hudson, who chairs the National Republican Congressional Committee, the party’s House campaign arm. Nodding to the party’s victories in the redistricting battle, Hudson said: “If you look at the seats that are up for grabs, it’s a majority of Democrats in Trump seats. For the Democrats to pick up the majority, they would have to win a lot of Trump seats, and that’s just not going to happen.” Glossing over the collapse of peace talks and the return of fighting with Tehran, Ralph Norman, a rightwing stalwart from South Carolina who is vying to replace the late Lindsey Graham in the Senate, predicted that Trump “is at the cusp of ending this thing with Iran, and he’s doing the right thing”. “The American people’s opinion is to end it quick. I think he will do that,” he added. Nebraska’s Don Bacon, one of the few Republicans representing a district Kamala Harris won two years ago, offered muted criticism of Trump’s approach to the war, saying the president would benefit from trying to work more with the Democrats. “The go-it-alone approach fails us in the end,” said Bacon, who is not seeking re-election. “But we need their help,” he said of Democrats, “and so I think he should lean in to working across the aisle more.” However large the problems of House Republicans may be, they appear to be no solution for the Democrats’ own woes. The party’s own supporters remain sour in the wake of Harris’s defeat, and earlier this week a Washington Post-Ipsos poll found that while the most highly motivated voters are eager to back the Democrats in the midterms, they have a scant advantage over the GOP in the wider electorate. “I think a lot of people aren’t sure, depending on where you’re from, what it means to be a Democrat,” the progressive congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said when asked about the party’s quandary. She saw hope in the party’s primary process, which this year has been defined by further showdowns between centrist and leftwing candidates and passionate debates over how to manage the US relationship with Israel. “I think that’s part of why this primary process has been so active this year, because we’re having much deeper substantive conversations than just … what is the color next to the box on your name,” Ocasio-Cortez said.

title: RFK Jr urges Alzheimer’s screening but blunts key panel that could drive research
author: Jessica Glenza
summary: Experts say evidence for cognitive screening desired by health secretary ‘not great’ as taskforce idle since last year
body_text: The US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, has called for better Alzheimer’s screening – but a critical federal panel that might have helped researchers find practical ways to do that has been prevented from meeting for more than a year. The panel, formally called the US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), had planned to issue a recommendation on screening for cognitive decline this year, alongside 13 other topics as varied as autism screening and food allergy prevention. “The evidence for cognitive screening for dementia is not great,” said John Ruiz, a professor of clinical psychology at the University of Arizona and a recent member of the panel. The taskforce is a group of expert volunteers who assess preventive services for health insurance coverage. The Trump administration has prevented the taskforce from meeting since March 2025, a political appointee fired two panel chairs, and the administration has so far failed to appoint new members. Ruiz rotated off the taskforce in January. “You get 10 neurologists, you get 10 approaches on how they’re going to assess that – there’s no consensus. The evidence is mixed at best,” said Ruiz. “The taskforce’s response has been to say, ‘Put more funding into building the evidence, allow researchers to do screening studies to find out – what does the evidence say about screening tools?’” The USPSTF recommendations can help inform future research, said Ruiz, as their draft recommendations are open for public comment and frequently receive substantial input from research communities. Alzheimer’s researchers also reported their work has been “slowed” by the health department’s policies, including funding disruptions. In April, Kennedy criticized the panel and called for better Alzheimer’s screening in the same breath. “Screening for prevention is absolutely critical,” said Kennedy in congressional testimony, responding to a question from Republican House member Vern Buchanan of Florida. “We are forming now the USPSTF, which is the committee that decides on new procedures and interventions that need to get [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid] compensation. And that committee has been lackadaisical and negligent for 20 years,” Kennedy said, adding later: “We’re making huge investments at NIH and elsewhere, and doing the kind of science that we need to do better screening for Alzheimer’s.” At the time Kennedy made the statement, the health department had prevented the USPSTF from meeting for more than a year and failed to fill at least eight vacancies (the panel usually has 16 members). A month later, a political appointee, director of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality Dr Roger Klein, fired two taskforce chairs. Emily Hilliard, a health and human services department (HHS) spokesperson, said: “HHS remains committed to advancing research in Alzheimer’s disease and other serious health conditions. [National Institutes of Health] remains the federal government’s largest funder of Alzheimer’s research, CMS is expanding access to coordinated dementia care through the nationwide ‘Guide’ model, [the Food and Drug Administration] continues to oversee new Alzheimer’s therapies and diagnostics.” She added that other federal agencies “are carrying out programs focused on prevention, workforce development, caregiver support and dementia-capable communities”. An estimated 7.4 million Americans 65 and older live with Alzheimer’s, the most common form of dementia. Although older people account for the vast majority of cases, it is not considered a normal part of aging. About 200,000 Americans in middle age are also diagnosed with the disease, according to the Alzheimer’s Association. Alzheimer’s screening typically relies on the appearance of symptoms. Patients are then subjected to cognitive testing, such as recall of words or phrases over the course of a conversation, and referral to a neurologist and potentially imaging, such as with an MRI, to reach a diagnosis. There is no major treatment for Alzheimer’s. That makes the search for reliable screening urgent, since it could lead people to undertake health lifestyle changes to delay the onset of cognitive decline. “There’s not like where you might go get a mammogram for breast cancer screening – there’s nothing like that set up for Alzheimer’s disease or cognitive impairment,” said Allison Aiello, a professor of health longevity and epidemiology at Columbia University, whose population studies are seeking biomarkers and cognitive tests that could detect cognitive changes as early as 24 to 44. Kennedy’s criticism of the USPSTF was not his only promotion of Alzheimer’s screening. Also in April, Kennedy told the House energy and commerce subcommittee: “It’s almost regulatory malpractice that we do not have early screening already.” Kennedy did not refer to a specific test, but some researchers believe Kennedy might be speaking about a new blood biomarker test for P-Tau217, a diagnostic tool approved in May last year. It is cleared for people older than 50 experiencing signs and symptoms of Alzheimer’s – not screening. The Alzheimer’s Association has promoted the blood tests as a “mammogram moment”, but researchers have urged caution. “I disagree with [Kennedy’s] assertion we should be rolling those out broadly,” said University of Pittsburgh Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center co-director Ann D Cohen, also an associate professor of psychiatry. “They have very good diagnostic – not prognostic – value.” Further, one study suggested the tests could be subject to many false-positive results in the real world. Importantly, Cohen’s own work advancing screening tools for Alzheimer’s Disease was spiked because of other Trump administration policies. The Guardian reported in March 2025 that 14 of the US’s 35 Alzheimer’s disease research centers (ADRC) nationally were impacted by funding freezes, making it difficult to hang on to staff and even clinical trial patients. One of those centers was Cohen’s – her funding did not clear until the “end of last summer”, which forced her to use “several hundred thousand dollars” in philanthropic funds once earmarked to advance blood biomarker tests. “We had to cancel that because we had to use those funds to keep our clinic open,” said Cohen, who added: “There’s no way around the fact that science has been slowed down.” Aiello also made a distinction between the emergence of tests and rolling them out broadly – the kinds of questions typically considered by the USPSTF. “If we can measure these kinds of things we know are associated with cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s in older age, we might be able to find small nuanced changes that characterize patterns that lead to change in older life,” said Aiello, citing the potential positive impact. “Should we be doing that at every primary care visit? That’s a whole other question – and that’d be something you’d have to talk to a policy person about.”

title: Loyal to the look: why Zohran Mamdani wears a suit in all seasons
author: Adam Gabbatt in New York
summary: Around town, on the pitch and even in the pool, the New York mayor keeps his suit on – what do his sartorial choices tell us?
body_text: Playing football. Playing in the sand. Dancing on a stage with Alicia Keys and the entire New York Knicks roster. Swimming in a swimming pool. Swimming in the ocean. Traditionally, a suit and tie would be considered inappropriate attire for each of these activities. Yet over the past year Zohran Mamdani has seemingly been on a one-man crusade to prove otherwise: to convince people that a formal suit is, actually, suitable for all activities. That’s because the New York mayor hardly ever wears anything but a suit: frequently purchased from Suit Supply, almost always in a dark colour and worn with a formal tie, mostly paired with smart black boots. He’s hardly the first male politician to embrace the suit – it’s the de facto uniform, after all, of those seeking to project seriousness and solemnity – but few, if any, have been quite as wedded to the formal blazer and matching trousers. Cheering on the Knicks at Madison Square Garden in May, Mamdani stood out for his decision to wear a dark suit and tie. After the Knicks won, he took the unusual decision to wear the team’s jersey over his shirt and tie, but under his suit jacket. In June, he wore a navy suit, white shirt, and blue striped tie for a press opportunity with children at the beach. Those aren’t even the most unusual examples. On New Year’s Day 2025, while running for mayor, he wore a suit to take part in the Polar Bear Club plunge, a New York tradition whereby people go swimming in the frigid Atlantic. “I’m freezing … your rent as the next mayor of New York City,” Mamdani said in an accompanying TikTok video, a message that was rather on the nose, but won him lots of press coverage. Water proved again to be no obstacle when Mamdani leaped, fully suited, into a swimming pool in Harlem last month, to announce the opening of the city’s pools for summer. (Mamdani “broke the rules in the process”, the rightwing New York Post reported, “which requires all swimmers to wear bathing suits in the water”.) The mayor is trapped, it seems, in a wool or possibly wool-blend prison of his own making. But why? Mamdani’s most recent predecessors weren’t as tied to the suit. Bill De Blasio was keen on shorts – although, in a furore that won’t have gone unnoticed by Mamdani, the former mayor was mercilessly ridiculed for wearing the cargo variety – while Eric Adams was partial to a polo shirt, and sometimes a woolly cardigan. “I think Mamdani wants to double down on appearing as a working mayor, as someone who is always on the job and on the clock,” said Ella Devi, a fashion commentator and, like Mamdani, Democratic Socialists of America member whose (typically negative) assessments of Republicans’ style have made her a target for conservatives. “I think that he kind of wants to convey that he is committed to the job, through his sartorial choices. I think that is reflected in his attachment to the suiting.” Devi added: “It’s also that he’s a young, Muslim, socialist.” It seems likely that Mamdani, the repeated focus of rightwing media, is held to a higher bar than white centrist politicians. It’s an issue Hasan Piker, the Turkish American leftwing streamer, brought up recently, when he said conservatives are “more receptive to what I have to say” when he dresses smartly. “I used to wear T-shirts all the time,” he told Dazed. “But then I figured I should start wearing a suit and a tie because there are a lot of adults watching on Fox News [the rightwing channel frequently airs clips of Piker speaking] – if they see me saying something in the clips, they’ll be more receptive to what I have to say if I’m in a more appealing format.” The mayor’s office declined to comment on Mamdani’s wardrobe, but he addressed his penchant for suit-wearing in a recent interview with CNN. Asked about his decision to jump into a swimming pool wearing a suit, the mayor said: “I think I misunderstood the term swimsuit. I do also have to say thank you, though, to Goodwill [a charity known for its shops that sell used clothing], because I got that suit for 30 bucks, because you can’t go ruining the other suits that you have. But I’m clearly learning that there might be a different way to dress when it’s 100-degree weather.” Leftists have not always been known for formal dresswear. That remains true in some cases – the disgraced Maine senatorial candidate Graham Platner wore sweaters and T-shirts during his campaign; John Fetterman, the Democratic senator from Pennsylvania, has a passionate commitment to wearing basketball shorts – but that might be changing. “If there’s a visual language that connotes credibility and authority, why not take advantage of it?” Nathan Robinson, the editor of the leftwing Current Affairs magazine wrote this month. “You might see someone in a suit as serious, professional, ready to do business. You might think they belong in the Senate or a boardroom. That’s certainly what Mamdani is trying to convey with his suits. He understands that socialists face a challenge: we’re considered fringe. People think we don’t belong among those making important decisions. The suits are a subtle way of asserting the legitimacy and authority of socialist ideas.” Mamdani has taken the concept further than most. A keen football player, he wore a black suit with a grey tie while doing keep-ups with a football in July, and when he played in a game that same month, Mamdani simply threw a football shirt over his suit – although he did ditch the jacket. It was not always thus. A source who played for the same team as Mamdani before his election said that he did not play in a suit and tie, although they added: “He always showed up in a suit, or at least suit pants, and his famous boots, and would change on the pitch because he was also always running late.” The source, who asked not to be named, but who now plays for a football team with the author of this article, continued, “But he never missed a tackle” – a remark which was possibly aimed at this writer. The source said Mamdani used to play in “black shorts”. Asked if a suit would be appropriate attire for a football match, they said it would not. They explained: “Limited stretch in the materials, restricted range of motion, you get sweaty and probably don’t want to have to dry-clean a suit as often for cost and longevity purposes, likelihood of it getting grass stains or torn up during play, excessive wear from friction which would also compromise longevity of a likely costly piece of clothing less easily replaced, too hot to play in (comfortably).” Having become so intertwined with the suit, the question might be: can Mamdani ever wear anything else? Can the mayor ditch the formalwear? “I think that now he’s kind of trapped in the suit, and he knows that he’s trapped in the suit, because he’s made it his thing to always wear the suit,” Devi said. “He has to stick with the bit, the suit bit. If he wears jeans, then the New York Post is just going to write about that for the next three weeks.” With temperatures in New York recently hitting 38C (100F), Mamdani might be wishing he could wear something else – although Devi had a suggestion should the heat become too unbearable. “He would never go for this, because it would not be seen as very socialist, but Thom Browne does some very good suit shorts for the future heatwaves. So that’s my advice to Mayor Mamdani,” she said. It’s a fine idea, except according to Thom Browne’s website, those shorts retail at about $1,300, which might raise questions over Mamdani’s socialist credentials. It seems that, at least for now, Mamdani is stuck in the suit.

title: Readers reply: Some people want to break up the EU. Why not break up the US?
summary: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions looks at secessionary movements on both sides of the pond
body_text: If it’s wrong, as some would say, for European countries to come together as a fully federal European Union, rather than individual states, why is it right for the US to be a federation rather than separate states? It always strikes me that the EU gets unfairly criticised for a system that was established over the Atlantic many years back. The US hasn’t looked back, but has become powerful as a result of being an umbrella for smaller entities. Just imagine if each state needed its own army, air force and currency, with its own customs and border controls not to mention trade tariffs! There’d be no White House and no Congress. Why is it so wrong for European countries to want similar strength, coming together as a union? Howard Phillips, Lisbon Send new questions to nq@theguardian.com. Readers reply There’s no nostalgic past for US states to hark back to. What the US achieved it did as a union. That’s the difference which prevents would-be secessionists from causing the harm they have done in Europe. John_Brown1955 The US absolutely needs a secession amendment to the constitution. Based on the lessons of Brexit and limited to five states every 20 years. Each departing state should be able to take non-fixed assets in proportion to their net contribution to the federal budget over 20 years. That would mean the states that would like to leave – Alabama, Arkansas, Kansas, Oklahoma – would take nothing, while California and New York could take the cake. Politicians would be motivated to pander to the left. Elliot, by email Language? English unites the US but divides the EU. jno50 I’m very much in favour of collaboration between European countries and the integration of resources, but I’m also very much against the EU. After decades of staring into its navel and failing to resolve petty problems with its single market, continental Europe has found itself to be totally insignificant in the contemporary geopolitical turmoil. This despite having a larger population than the US and a greater GDP than China. Discussions on the future of Europe are characterised by two opposing teams of ignorant players hurling soundbites at each other. This lack of informed Europe-wide democratic debate is, perhaps, at the heart of the problem. Roger Irwin, Italy In a word: history. Too many wars over the centuries based on nationalism in Europe among the Indigenous populations mean that small differences can be exaggerated for political gain, which prior to the EU led to military conflict. In America, the main target of military intervention by Europeans was the Indigenous populations, while violence also had an outlet when taken out on those that they had transported there against their will. Although the latter in the guise of slavery led to a civil war, the former helped to bind the American states together. Dr Peter Davis, Bristol The US has had its share of growing pains. Can the EU become the US without its own civil war? Is abandoning the veto power, because pro-Russians and populists abuse it, so that we can finally have a unified defence force, a good idea, keeping that part of history to mind? I find that reforming veto power is needed, but let’s keep it for things where lack of unanimity threatens our existential principles. I wouldn’t want to see European troops marching in Budapest in 2056. Luca, by email First, the US was put together 200 years ago. Second, they sort of speak one language, not 20 different ones. Last, no one has even bothered asking European citizens if a federal Europe is something they would like, mostly because they are afraid of the answer. We already have a situation where people in smaller countries have a disproportionate amount of say over EU laws. David Michaels, by email I suppose you suggested the strongest answer yourself: “The US … has become powerful as a result of being an umbrella for smaller entities.” Vanished “customs and border controls, not to mention trade tariffs”. Who doesn’t want the EU strong? Economic competitors. Forces that see their global dominance waning. Separatists seeking salvation in the past. All that speaks for a strong EU. And for countries on the European continent to join, rather than to leave. Erik A Sevapiragasam, by email The US was born under a sense of honesty and togetherness. The founding fathers thought hard as how to serve the best interests of the people. The EU was born out of deceit and divisiveness. To hide the fact that its aim was always political union, populations were fed the “common market” ploy and not informed of its ultimate goal. The EU is fundamentally undemocratic. In the US, the president is elected by the eligible voters of the 50 states. In the EU, the president is elected by some 700 council members and, in many cases, not in a competitive ballot. Chris Zisimides, by email I think the same forces that try to break the EU up are also trying to do the same to the US – they are just doing it more covertly. Regardless of whether these are state actors like Russia, large corporate entities or tech billionaires, they all would rather have smaller political units to deal with, if any at all. The only big difference is that there are now people inside the US government who want to break the EU up, while the reverse is not the case. anda_skoa If you watch the TV show How the States Got Their Shapes, you will see that the US federal project was not predicted to work. Narrow necks of land join states to waterways or the sea. They didn’t trust their neighbours. Early consolidation was the result of conflict alliances for independence. Later it was federal colonisation of Native American land or conquest of Spanish territory. Why not break it up? It might still happen. Windyday All empires fall eventually. GrannieSal The civil war. There have always been movements to break up the US, and even today there are lots of Americans who like to talk about how the country can’t survive, or how it’s really made up of numerous different regions. But the civil war addressed that very question. The south said the states could leave at any time, the north said no you can’t, and the north won. Carnthebombers I’m surprised by the question. I’ve never considered the EU breaking up – well, not so much until Brexit. And why not break up the US? From my view over here is that the European Union has succeeded at so much that the United States has not, especially now with our wavering on those truths we hold to be self-evident. dallastxhollywood Because EU is more recent. Everyone is just used to US being one country, with some internal separations, more organisational than existential. Most of the states and territories became part of it long before anyone currently alive. But Europe has never been unified in any way. Except for geographical proximity, there’s virtually nothing European countries have in common. And unlike the US, the EU is still relatively new, making it a change. Change is something that terrifies many people, and is far easier to undo than something that no one remembers being any different. GrumpyMat As a US citizen, I have no right to an opinion about the EU. As a student of history, I am profoundly grateful that the EU exists. Other than Russia’s horrible invasion of Ukraine, this is the longest period of peace among European nations since the Roman empire. AnneinMaryland Russia feels threatened by a united Europe, hence the need to encourage as much disunity as possible. It is less affected by a united US. It’s not just the US that offers a model of successful unification. Germany was only unified into one country in 1871. TobermoryNightlife I think the US is already broken. eibhear Well, I sincerely hope that European states are discreetly stirring various secessionist pots in the US in response to the Trump administration’s blatant attempts to destabilise/break up the EU. Sauce for the goose. And I’m sure that Russia is. DaBishop In reply: The stirring they do is a measurement of the fear felt of a cohesive EU. Onward towards unity increased, I say. Time for the UK to start the process to rejoin as a committed equal member. Also time to get serious and talk to the Canadians about some sort of associate membership. ErasmusVanBaltimore Is the US truly unified? There have always been cultural and political differences between the states, and some of these seem only to be widening. Are there not real secessionist movements in California and Texas? kingscrosscowboy In reply: I don’t know about Texas, but the California secession “movement” or “Calexit” is fake, the product of Russian meddling. There’s also the more popular “Cascadia” idea where California, Oregon, and Washington secede together, but that’s not going to happen either. You’re right about the illusion of “unity”. The only time the US was anything close to unified was during the second world war. Didn’t last. fantod A group of nations that have evolved over 2,000 or more years, frequently at war with each other, with differing governing systems, are coming together via trade and an understanding that war is futile. Negotiations are more careful and considerate as a result, and more often a compromise. The US, on the other hand, came together as a nation building its own, modern identity, and the first to do away with inherited monarchy. In what was felt to be an “empty” continent, this made sense. It sticks together today, through a shared sense of independence and “freedom”. It’s like comparing apples with elephants. GrasmereGardens Since many of the people investing money and effort in breaking up the EU are in the US, while no people in the EU have made corresponding efforts to break up the US, it might just be down to relative levels of malice. CharlieApples It’s a good question. I suspect one historical reason, in addition to what has anyway been mentioned, is language. The US white population is, of course 100% immigrant (which makes the current anti immigrant rhetoric all the more depressing). But the lingua franca is English (for now, at least). My understanding is that this wasn’t a given – there was a very significant German- speaking minority in the early days, and that could have changed things. But they voted to have a single, common language. I like the level of integration the EU has – I would not want to see everyone speaking a single language as their mother tongue – it enriches us all, and maintains cultural diversity (a good thing). I have no doubt there are state-level differences, beyond different political and religious preferences/biases in the US. But from the outside, the difference looks to be more pronounced at the individual person level than at the state level. scobie27 I don’t think it’s an easy binary of “deeper integration good/bad”. Broadly speaking, deeper integration can give you efficiencies of scale, the more frictionless existence that comes with uniformity, and a more powerful whole, but it also (pretty much by definition) reduces the ability of the component parts to do their own thing even if they want to. The US is one level of integration (but states still have, say, their own laws, agencies and taxes); the EU is another, less integrated one. There are lots of possible levels, and people may favour different ones under different circumstances. One obvious reason people might be more in favour of doing things at the nation-state level in EU countries is they have been doing so for much longer – all but two states have been part of the US for over a century now, and many pre-joining were fairly new, low-population territories, rather than countries with centuries of acting as such. Jebedee
