title: Meet the South Carolina Democrat looking to flip Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat
author: David Smith in Columbia, South Carolina
summary: Dr Annie Andrews says her ‘mission remains the same’ as she now aims to unseat Darline Graham, sister of the late Republican senator
body_text: It was early Sunday morning and Dr Annie Andrews was far from the political fray, dropping her youngest daughter off at a summer camp, when she heard the news. “It was shocking and unbelievable,” she says of the death of Lindsey Graham, a Republican senator who defined South Carolina politics for a generation aged 71. “It’s a profound moment for the whole state of South Carolina.” For more than a year Andrews, a Democrat, had been building a formidable grassroots campaign designed to unseat Graham in the midterm elections. The 45-year-old paediatrician had pitched herself as the antithesis of the veteran senator she never met – an outsider running a campaign “powered by people, not Pacs [political action committees]”. Now Andrews, who had been aiming to become South Carolina’s first female senator, has seen the honour bestowed instead on Graham’s sister, Darline, who was appointed to serve out the remainder of his term and will compete in a primary next month to decide the Republican nominee in November. So everything has changed – and yet nothing has changed. “The problems that South Carolinians are facing did not change over that weekend,” Andrews says by phone from her base in Mount Pleasant. “My opponent will change but my mission remains the same and that’s what I’m staying focused on.” That mission was galvanised by the two decades that Andrews spent on the frontlines of what she describes as America’s “broken” public healthcare system, including 15 years at a children’s hospital in Charleston. The experience ultimately compelled her out of the medical ward and into the political arena. “Over those years, I started to understand that the problems my patients and their families were facing were policy problems. These were systemic problems with systemic solutions and what we needed to do was start electing people who inherently care about South Carolina’s kids and families and care about solving those problems.” Her initial foray into politics – a 2022 congressional run against Republican representative Nancy Mace – ended in a 14-point defeat. After that loss, Andrews stepped away from her practice at the Medical University of South Carolina and founded a political organisation focused on the climate crisis, gun violence and childhood poverty. But it was the darkness of Trump’s second term that pulled her back on to the ballot for the Senate, in particular the nomination of Robert F Kennedy Jr to lead the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). She recalls: “In the aftermath of Trump being re-elected, the day that I decided to consider this seriously was the day RFK Jr was nominated to lead HHS because, as a paediatrician, that’s the worst-case scenario for America’s public health system.” For Andrews, the elevation of Kennedy – who spent decades amplifying baseless anti-vaccine views – is not merely a political affront but a direct threat to the lives of the children she treats. “Doctors are trained, when they take a history from a patient, to ask if their immunisations are up to date. Twenty years ago, when I started asking that question, the answer was almost universally yes. “Now when I ask that question, I brace myself for the response because bad actors like RFK Jr, grifters and conspiracy theorists have been peddling in these anti-vaccine conspiracy theories for decades and it has seeped into the consciousness of many parents in America who now don’t know who they can trust for solid evidence-based medical information about decisions for their children’s health and it’s deeply frustrating to watch as this has evolved.” The consequences are brutal. Measles cases in the US have hit a 35-year high, according to data from Johns Hopkins University, with more than 90% of reported infections occurring among the unvaccinated or those whose vaccination status is unknown. Andrews adds: “It is pervasive across sociodemographic groups now. People do not know who they can trust and sadly right now, when I talk to patients, I say: ‘You cannot necessarily trust the health information that we are receiving from the federal government.’” The Covid-19 pandemic, she believes, acted as “kerosene on the fire”, catalysing an anti-science movement that has now fully entrenched itself within the Republican party. Indeed, for Andrews, the triage urgently required in Washington is clear. She views the impending Medicaid budget cuts signed into law by Trump as a devastating threat to rural South Carolinians. She advocates for defending Medicare, lowering prescription drug costs through federal negotiating power, and gradually introducing a public option to force private insurers into offering more competitive, less profit-driven plans. And her definition of the public health emergency extends to gun violence. She speaks with the authority of a doctor who has “cared for children with bullet holes in them” and “stood at the bedside of a child who has been shot and held the parent’s hand, understanding that these are preventable injuries, these are policy choices that have been made by our lawmakers”. While acknowledging that gun control may not be the primary issue driving voters to the polls in 2026, she insists: “I will not stand on the sidelines as gun violence continues to be the leading cause of death for kids in South Carolina and kids all across this country. But the good news is the vast majority of Americans agree with me. Over 90% of Americans believe we need commonsense solutions like universal background checks.” Andrews views the broader landscape of Trump’s second term with profound alarm. She sees a state and a country buckling under the weight of “chaotic” economic and social policies. “I’m deeply concerned about the direction this country is moving in,” she says. “Gas prices are high. Grocery prices are high. There’s an affordability crisis in housing and in childcare. We don’t have jobs to meet the needs of folks who are graduating from technical colleges or from four-year universities and, on top of that, we’re witnessing unprecedented corruption in the federal government.” Her proposed remedies to break the fever include ending partisan gerrymandering, implementing term limits, banning members of Congress from trading stocks or becoming lobbyists and overturning the Citizens United supreme court ruling to purge dark money from politics. Andrews has spent a year building a statewide campaign apparatus, raising funds and recruiting more than 2,000 volunteers. This week, she gained the endorsement of Her Bold Move, a national support network for women running for political office. But even in the absence of Lindsey Graham, a close Trump ally who served four terms, she faces a monumental structural disadvantage. South Carolina is a stronghold for Republicans with state elections historically decided by double-digit margins. In 2020, the Democratic challenger Jaime Harrison shattered national fundraising records, amassing a war chest of more than $100m, yet still lost to Graham by a crushing 10 percentage points. “I’m used to fighting fights that are uphill battles,” Andrews admits. “That does not make the fight any less important and what I’ve seen over the past year is a growing sentiment that everyone on both sides of the aisle recognises that Washington DC is broken.”

title: India’s Cockroach Janta party protest victory signals trouble ahead for Modi
author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
summary: Ally forced to resign, with opposition parties reinvigorated and strongman leader’s grip over media channels rocked
body_text: Even the night before Narendra Modi accepted the resignation of his education minister, India’s prime minister appeared confident that the largest mass uprising to take place in his 12 years in power would do little to rattle his government. Addressing his “young friends” in a late-night Instagram selfie reel on Friday, he thanked the people – who were mobilised en masse across the country, shouting anti-government slogans – for their “thoughtful suggestions”. Less than 24 hours later, Modi, who has fiercely cultivated his strongman image for years, had bowed to public pressure and accepted the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan. It was, say analysts, the remarkable humbling of a government that has ruled with almost untouchable impunity since 2014. Over that past week, a gen Z movement that called itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) mobilised unprecedented protests in the name of justice for millions of young people, after the leaking of a crucial exam paper forced 2 million students to resit the test and was blamed for more than a dozen suicides. The resignation of Pradhan, Modi’s loyal political ally, remained their first and foremost demand for accountability, even as the protests expanded into a wider fight for democracy. Yet Pradhan went unmentioned by Modi in his Instagram address. On Saturday morning, more people than ever were pouring into Delhi’s historic Jantar Mantar site – the centre of the protests – and unrest was spreading fast to other cities, including states ruled by Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). It was not only physical space that had been captured by the cockroach movement. Since coming to power, the BJP has proved enormously effective at capturing the online narrative, deploying its powerful, highly organised IT cell to mobilise and attack any perceived criticism of the government, whether it came from citizens, politicians or journalists. But this proved no match for the millions of gen Z memes and reels that began to flood Instagram over this past week, fearlessly insulting Modi and pillorying the government, each more creative and incendiary than the next. Modi’s last-ditch attempts to speak directly to the youth on Instagram were simply met with more ridicule and spin-off memes. Modi had also lost another medium critical to the BJP’s domination over the national narrative – the mainstream TV news channels widely acknowledged to have been co-opted by the BJP government over the past 12 years and turned into mouthpieces for its rightwing Hindu nationalist ideology. Initially, the channels ignored the protests, and when they did cover them it was to suggest the protesters were being bankrolled by sinister foreign forces and Pakistani terror groups. In response, the protesters turned on the channels, using social media to expose their “lies”. When the protests escalated, Modi remained conspicuously absent from the airwaves. Pradhan’s resignation came as it appeared that all other options for the government had gone. The option of a ruthless crackdown appeared untenable given the mass outcry to the police violence that had hit protesters on Monday. “The online space was totally conquered by the protesters and regime-loving media was seriously delegitimised,” said Ashutosh Varshney, a professor of international studies at Brown University in Rhode Island. “The anger was so comprehensive there was no option left but for Pradhan to go.” But this was more than the loss of a minister, Varshney said, it was also the first time in 12 years that the Modi government had lost control of the political narrative. “This is a repressive government,” he said. “It wants obedience, it wants no critical discussion and it generates fear. But now the climate of fear has collapsed.” Analysts say the resignation of Pradhan could also have implications for Modi’s power over his own cabinet. Pradhan was one of Modi’s most loyal ministers and ideological footsoldiers, and had implemented policies exactly as senior party figures had wanted. He had also helped the BJP win Odisha state for the first time in the general election, bringing in crucial seats. “Modi knows once you start firing your most loyal ministers, it sets up the incentives for defections in other ministers as well,” said the political columnist Pratap Bhanu Mehta. “If your own cabinet starts to hedge for a future where they may not be backed by your own government, that’s when you are in trouble.” Prior to this week’s unrest, Modi had been riding high on a string of important state electoral victories, in particular the BJP’s first triumph in West Bengal, a politically important state that had long pushed back against its Hindu nationalist politics. The BJP appeared to have fully bounced back from the blow in the 2024 elections, when the party failed to win an outright parliamentary majority and had to scramble together a large enough alliance to take power. At the same time, the much-beleaguered opposition had continued to lose countless state elections and their allegations of voting impropriety by the BJP fell mostly on deaf ears. Yet the emergence of the cockroaches has reinvigorated not only India’s youth, but its political opposition parties as well. Jumping on the bandwagon, the opposition Congress party has had its best week in years as it mobilised protests and shut down parliament. The party’s leader, Rahul Gandhi, was dramatically dragged away by police outside Modi’s house in support of students. Analysts say that dissent, which had been systematically crushed over the past 12 years, has now been re-galvanised as an effective tool to hold the government – and in particular the prime minister – to account. “After a long time, there’s an assertion of political agency across different sections of society,” said Mehta. “And the minute you see that agency out in the street, it empowers lots of other agents.” The next big test of the electoral implications of the CJP movement will come early next year, when India’s largest and most politically important state holds its state elections. Holding on to power in Uttar Pradesh, the BJP’s political heartland, is seen as crucial for the party and would have major implications for the next general election in 2029. The grievances of India’s newly-politicised youth are extensive, including a chronic lack of graduate jobs and stagnant wages. Just how the CJP intends to politically mobilise after its striking victory on Saturday remains to be seen. Leaders and supporters insist this is just the “beginning”, particularly in their push for education reform. Their founder, Abhijeet Dipke, has some past experience as a political party organiser, but has not made his own ambitions known. Yet analysts said that one of the most crucial impacts of the CJP had been to reopen a rapidly closing democratic space and make it seem possible that a new kind of political opposition could emerge, one reflective of the voices heard on the streets of India this week. Saurav Das, a CJP spokesperson, said it was encouraging people involved in the movement to go into politics. “This is one of our goals,” he said. “We need to increase youth participation in politics, because right now it’s controlled by uncles and aunties who are only interested in looking after their own lifestyles and don’t understand the needs of our generation. The answer also has to be political.”

title: Katy Perry ‘deeply appalled’ over White House using her song in Iran war video
author: Marina Dunbar
summary: Singer rebukes Trump administration after it uses her song Firework over footage of missile striking Iranian naval ship
body_text: Pop star Katy Perry has condemned the Trump White House after it used her hit song Firework in a TikTok video showing US military strikes on Iranian targets, saying she never approved the use of her music. The White House video, which featured Firework playing over footage of a missile striking an Iranian naval ship, has amassed more than 6 million views. The post was captioned: “Iran has been warned.” Perry responded on Saturday with a statement on X criticizing what she called the unauthorized use of the song. “I am deeply appalled and angry to see ‘Firework’ used on the White House TikTok account as a backing track for video footage of military strikes,” the singer said. “I did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it.” Perry continued: “I wrote this song to be an anthem of hope, healing, and inner strength for people going through their darkest personal moments. To see a message of self-worth and upliftment weaponized to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for. My music is for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare.” The White House launched its TikTok account in August 2025, when Donald Trump threatened to ban the platform months into his second presidency. Perry is among a number of artists to criticize the Trump administration over the unauthorized use of music in government social media posts, with the president picking fights with several – mostly female – pop singers. Olivia Rodrigo previously criticized the administration after one of her songs appeared in a government video promoting deportation efforts. Beyoncé also blocked Trump from using her song Freedom after it was featured in a campaign video on social media. The track had served as the central campaign song for former vice-president Kamala Harris, who lost the 2024 White House election to Trump. In March, Kesha condemned the White House’s use of her song Blow in a military-promotional TikTok video, calling it a “show of blatant disregard for human life”. Sabrina Carpenter spoke out after her hit song Juno was used in a Trump-posted video showing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers making arrests. Carpenter called the video “evil and disgusting” and told the administration: “Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.” In June, Ariana Grande also rebuked the White House for using her song Bye in a social media post promoting US immigration arrests, describing the video as “barbaric”. Singer Jess Glynne also objected after the White House used her song Hold My Hand in a post on X promoting ICE deportations. Glynne said she felt “sick” that her music was being used to spread “division and hate”. It was revealed in December that Perry is in a relationship with the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, who is familiar himself with Trump’s trolling. He has repeatedly been targeted by Trump, who has continually threatened to impose tariffs on Canada and has even suggested the US should annex the country, referring to Trudeau as the “governor” of the “Great State of Canada”. The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) lists the official death toll for the US-Iran conflict at 14 service members, with 420 total personnel wounded in action. Those official metrics, however, have been subject to ongoing controversy due to a sudden drop from the 18 deaths and 482 wounded recorded days earlier. The collapse of the ceasefire with Iran and the subsequent resumption of near-daily airstrikes starting on 6 July have sparked debate over how casualties are counted. Analysts and officials have questioned whether victims from the two weeks since should be tracked in a separate tally, a move that would be unprecedented. The Trump administration is attempting to have the latest resumed strikes in Iran be treated as a separate campaign from Operation Epic Fury, the US military’s official name for the Iran conflict. The separate casualty count beginning 7 July stems from that. The US House member Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, responded to the updated numbers in an X post, writing, “Let me explain this absurd ruse: The Pentagon is pretending there have been two Iran wars separated by a brief cease-fire. “The reality: By going more than 90 days without congressional authorization,” the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, “IS BREAKING THE LAW and must be held accountable”.

title: Trump ‘border czar’ says ICE officer in Maine killing should not have cleared vetting
author: Maya Yang
summary: Tom Homan comments on officer’s eligibility to serve after reports that agent’s two ex-wives had accused him of abuse
body_text: Tom Homan, the Trump administration “border czar”, on Sunday said he did not believe the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer at the center of a recent fatal shooting in Maine “should have ever cleared vetting”. Speaking to CNN’s State of the Union, Homan was asked by host Dana Bash about the officer’s eligibility to serve following reports that two of his ex-wives had accused him of abuse. “Should someone with those issues be an ICE agent?” Bash asked. “No, if those … are facts … I don’t think he should ever have cleared vetting,” Homan replied. Homan also said part of an ongoing investigation into the 13 July shooting death Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero is determining “how … did the vetting process fail”. “When they hire somebody, they put them through a vetting process and look at all that stuff. So I know, based on that information – that’s part of the ongoing investigation,” Homan said. “How … did the vetting process fail? Was that information not available? Did they not know?” He added: “So there’s a separate administrative investigation on what happened here. Did we have that information? Did we not have that information? But the vetting process … if that was factual, he would have an almost impossible time to pass vetting.” The officer involved in the killing of Durán, a 25-year-old Colombian man in Biddeford, Maine, has since been identified by news outlets as David Brouillette. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, has not publicly confirmed Brouillette’s identity. Since the shooting, two of Brouillette’s ex-wives have publicly described alleged abuse during their relationships with him. One, Lucinda Brouillette, alleged her ex-husband engaged in a “persistent pattern of abuse, intimidation, manipulation, fear and control”. “If you were to ask me whether I believe David Brouillette is capable of this level of violence, my answer is unequivocally yes,” she said in a statement to NPR. Although Homan declined to comment directly on this particular case, describing it as “a rare instance”, he said: “If this person had that type of history, it would have been a vetting issue, and it should have been brought to the attention of those who make those decisions.” He added, in part: “We will see. It’s all being reviewed. We will see where it lies.” The shooting has prompted renewed scrutiny of ICE’s hiring practices. Democrats have called for reviews of the agency’s vetting process. For instance, the Mississippi congressman Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the US House homeland security committee, said that Brouillette’s alleged abusive past “directly call[s] into question the supposed vetting and training ICE does of its recruits”. Neither the fatal shooting in Maine nor another one involving an ICE officer in Texas earlier in July yielded body-camera footage from officers. That prompted Homan to announce that the agency would require officers to wear body cameras during vehicle stops. In the Texas case, which resulted in the killing of Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the Harris county district attorney Sean Teare said in a statement that lab results of a white substance found in a van at the center of a case tested negative for narcotics or illicit drugs – despite an FBI search warrant application that maintained a bag with the substance in question was consistent with methamphetamine. Salgado’s family had said the substance was a salt mixture that he and his construction crew colleagues used as electrolytes to stay hydrated in extremely hot temperatures. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Morning Mail: Israeli siblings owed Australian protection; Europe’s tough wildfire fight; swimmers win gold in Glasgow
author: Paul Gallagher
summary: Trio able to seek protection over Gaza fears; authorities battle massive blazes in France and Spain; swimmers boost Commonwealth Games medal haul
body_text: Good morning. Today we reveal that three Israeli citizens can reapply for protection visas in Australia after officials accepted they held a genuine fear they would be forced to break international humanitarian law in Gaza. And we shed light on a One Nation senator’s claims that his party wants to deport at least 200,000 people from Australia. Overseas, firefighters are in a desperate battle with a huge wildfire near the major French city of Bordeaux. And: Australia’s Commonwealth Games medal haul is growing as swimmers make a splash in Glasgow. Australia ‘Get rid of them’ | Senator Malcolm Roberts has repeatedly referenced the far-right concept of “remigration” in interviews and speeches to niche platforms, saying in two recent podcasts that One Nation wanted to deport 100,000 temporary residents as well as 100,000 international students. Exclusive | A government tribunal has accepted three Israeli siblings could face “persecution” for refusing conscription into the Israel Defense Forces due to their political opinion on the war in Gaza and granted them the right to reapply for protection visas in Australia. ‘What counts matters’ | Next month’s census will for the first time include questions about sexual orientation, sex at birth and gender. Is it the “most progressive” census Australia has ever seen? Christian Ellis | A key figure at the centre of an anti-corruption inquiry involving the New South Wales Liberal party has moved to the UK and is not expected to give evidence during public hearings. Lost knowledge | What happens when the AI bubble bursts? Cory Doctorow, a science fiction author and journalist, believes humans will take their jobs back – but it will take a “really long time” to restore their skills. World Wildfire fight | Windy conditions are hampering firefighters’ efforts to contain a huge wildfire near Bordeaux in France that has consumed an area of land four times the size of Paris as Spain’s PM, Pedro Sánchez, warns Spain and the Iberian peninsula are suffering the effects of the climate emergency. Berlin Pride attack | A man suspected of a driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival then going on a knife rampage in an Islamist terror attack has been shot dead by German police. Middle East crisis | As Donald Trump’s military chiefs warn of dwindling munitions stockpiles, the US has paused its strikes on Iran for a second night while diplomatic negotiations continue. Russia-Ukraine war | Romania has said it is summoning Russia’s ambassador over “repeated violations” after the Nato member’s military shot down a third drone in as many days. India protests | The victory achieved by the Cockroach Janta party’s protest movement signals trouble ahead for India’s strongman leader, Narendra Modi, Hannah Ellis-Petersen writes. Unesco recognition | Mount Olympus, the mythical home of the ancient Greek gods, has been inducted into a hall of more modern fame as Unesco updates its world heritage list. Full Story Inside the violent online network coercing children to self-harm This year the FBI issued urgent warnings to parents about 764, a global online community where children are manipulated into acts of violence. Groups like 764 are accused of using coercion to turn vulnerable minors into victims and, in some cases, predators. Nour Haydar speaks with Ariel Bogle about the dangers these networks pose to children. In-depth One Nation is pushing a vision of a “monocultural” Australia alongside an anti-immigration agenda. But in the NSW electorate of Barnaby Joyce, an entirely different story is playing out. Almost a decade ago, Joyce backed a campaign to make the city of Armidale a refugee resettlement site; now, many who settled there are wondering how his track record squares with the policies of the rightwing party he defected to. Not the news In the latest in our Kindness of strangers series, we hear from a reader who recalls a terrifying and stressful time as a young child when a blood vessel burst in her mother’s brain on a family holiday in France. Learning of their plight, the owners of a hotel gave her and her siblings a priceless sense of safety, comfort and warmth. Sport Commonwealth Games | Australia’s swimmers are adding to their medal tally in Glasgow, including golds for Iona Anderson and Tim Hodge – look back on the latest action from day three. Meanwhile, Australia dispatched England with ease in a clash between fierce netball rivals. Cycling | A relentless Tadej Pogacar has won a record-equalling fifth Tour de France – and warns his rivals he is still “improving a lot”. AFL | Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera has taken down the Kangaroos – a year since he dismantled the Demons, Jonathan Horn writes. Motorsport | Lando Norris took out the F1 Hungarian Grand Prix for his first victory of the season, as Oscar Piastri retired after gearbox failure. Boxing | Tim Tszyu won a battle of broken soldiers as Errol Spence Jr headed into the sunset, Owen Lewis writes. Media roundup Victoria’s premier, Jacinta Allan, may face a leadership challenge just four months out from the state election, the Age suggests. Forensic testing has revealed dozens of tomato products which claim to be from Australia or Italy are actually from China, ABC News reports. And the Sydney Morning Herald is lifting the lid on the secretive work of the AFL’s integrity and security unit. What’s happening today Sport | Australians are in action as the Commonwealth Games continue in Glasgow. NSW | Hearings in the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion continue in Sydney. QLD | A public hearing is scheduled in Brisbane in the inquiry into the Support at Home program. Warning! | A nationwide test of the new AusAlert emergency warning system is due to take place this afternoon. title: Pentagon reports more than 600 Iran war casualties in quiet database update
author: Marina Dunbar
summary: Figures are source of dispute as US defense department days ago reduced record of troops killed and wounded
body_text: The Pentagon updated its official war casualty database over the weekend, adding more than 140 wounded service members. The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) also introduced a new casualty category labeled “Overseas Operations” for personnel killed and wounded “starting July 7”. According to the updated database, the official toll for the earlier phase of the US-Iran war, known as Operation Epic Fury, now stands at 14 service members killed and more than 400 wounded in action. These figures have been a point of contention after the Pentagon previously reduced the totals from 18 deaths and 482 wounded that had been recorded just days earlier. The dispute comes after the collapse of the ceasefire with Iran and the resumption of near-daily airstrikes beginning on 6 July. Analysts and officials have questioned whether casualties from the renewed fighting should be counted separately from Operation Epic Fury, a move that would be unprecedented. The Trump administration is seeking to classify the renewed military campaign as separate from Operation Epic Fury, the US military’s official name for the Iran conflict. The change is tied to the War Powers Act of 1973, which requires the president to end military operations within 60 days unless Congress authorizes an extension. The Trump administration has argued that the April ceasefire with Iran paused the clock on 1 May for the conflict’s initial period. The separate casualty count beginning on 7 July follows that interpretation. The shift became apparent earlier this week when the Pentagon’s official online list of service members killed in the ongoing Iran war did not include the four soldiers who died during renewed fighting over the weekend. Their names, however, were included in a Pentagon press release announcing the formal transfer of their remains back to the US on Wednesday. Combined with the updated Operation Epic Fury totals, the new Pentagon figures show that 18 US troops have been killed and 624 wounded since the US launched its war against Iran on 28 February. Lawmakers from both parties have challenged the administration’s interpretation of the War Powers Act timeline. Thomas Massie, a Republican House member from Kentucky, responded to the updated numbers in an X post, writing: “Let me explain this absurd ruse: The Pentagon is pretending there have been two Iran wars separated by a brief cease-fire. “The reality: By going more than 90 days without congressional authorization,” the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, “IS BREAKING THE LAW and must be held accountable”.

title: ‘My mother was 4ft 11in and scared the hell out of people’ – Sean Astin on child stardom, The Lord of the Rings and surviving 45 years in Hollywood
author: Steve Rose
summary: His mother was an Oscar-winning actor who had been exploited from a young age; Astin appeared in The Goonies at just 13. Now, he has followed in his mother’s footsteps again as a union leader. He talks Stranger Things, AI and why playing Samwise Gamgee cost him his house
body_text: Sean Astin is showing me around his new office. There’s framed movie prints on the walls, piles of paperwork and a stack of boxes of Stranger Things Funko Pops. “If you were here, you could look out this window and see a 10-storey building with our iconic Sag-Aftra logo on it,” he says proudly on video call, gesturing out of the window to the Los Angeles skyline. “But you just have to trust me that it’s there.” He shows me a framed photo of his mother, Patty Duke, aged 16, with the best supporting actress Oscar she won in 1963 (for playing Helen Keller in The Miracle Worker), and even more proudly, a framed copy of Duke’s business card from when she was president of the Screen Actors Guild in the mid-80s – the role he now occupies (Sag merged with the American Federation of Television and Radio Artists in 2012). The 10 months of his presidency “has been a whirlwind”, he says. It’s still slightly jarring to see Astin in a suit and tie, lanyard around his neck. We’re more accustomed to seeing him in the handwoven cloak and hairy feet of Samwise Gamgee, loyally accompanying mister Frodo into Mordor in The Lord of the Rings. Or as Winona Ryder’s short-lived partner in Stranger Things (before a Demodog got to him). Or as never-say-die college football underdog “Rudy” Ruettiger in the 1993 biopic. Or, for viewers of his own vintage, as plucky leader Mikey in The Goonies. Astin has been a member of the union he now represents for 45 of his 55 years, but he seems to have survived the perils of child stardom and a Hollywood upbringing remarkably unscathed. In fact, you could see it all as preparation for the role. He certainly honed his negotiating skills early. “I learned at a very young age, how to speak different languages. I could speak the language of my mother, I could speak the language of father and my brothers and I had a peacemaker role in our five-boy family.” But there’s also an overlap between Astin’s roles on screen and off. “The parts I get are the ‘working man’ parts,” he says. “Rudy comes from a steel mill, Samwise is a gardener, he’s hands in the soil. There’s just something physically about me. I don’t know whether it’s my height and weight or whatever my internal life became with my parents and my wife and children and everything, but I’m just appropriate for those parts.” This was his pitch to Sag-Aftra’s 160,000 members – not just actors but also dancers, stunt performers, broadcast journalists and DJs: “I said I want to lean into the parts of my personality that are depicted in The Goonies and Rudy and Stranger Things and The Lord of the Rings, on behalf of the members.” He was elected last September with nearly 80% of the vote. Astin was born into what some might term “Hollywood royalty”, though on paper it sounds less like a head-start than a curse. Duke, his mother, was groomed as a child star and acquired considerable commercial clout, including her own TV show, which ran for three years in the 60s. But she suffered the worst of the industry in the process. She was taken into the care of talent agents John and Ethel Ross when she was eight, given drugs and alcohol and exploited and abused, sexually and financially. As well as eating disorders there were “suicide attempts, violent outbursts, and long stretches of depression,” Astin says. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in 1982. When Duke became pregnant with Sean in 1970, aged 23, it was not clear who his father was. She had been in a relationship with 17-year-old Desi Arnaz Jr (which apparently infuriated his mother, the comedian and actor Lucille Ball). Duke then fled to Las Vegas and hastily married Michael Tell, a rock promoter (the marriage lasted 13 days), then a year after Astin was born, she married the actor John Astin, best known for portraying Gomez in the original Addams Family television series. John and Duke were married until 1985, and he became Sean’s adoptive father, although a DNA test in 1994 revealed that Tell, who died last year, was his biological father. Astin maintained good relationships with all of these men, he says, including his stepfather, Duke’s fourth husband, Michael Pearce. He calls Arnaz Jr his “godfather”. Astin senior is now 96 and happily retired. Sean credits him for somehow making this complicated, potentially traumatic setup work: “He always wanted to do the right thing, and for him the right thing was humanity, and to put yourself in the other guy’s shoes, and two wrongs don’t make a right.” The same goes for his mother, who died in 2016. To classify her as a casualty of the entertainment industry is too reductive, Astin suggests, “because she was so smart. She was brilliant. My dad had all this academic training, but if you watch the gameshows that they were on in the 70s and 80s, she’d wipe the floor … so I feel like it’s a trope to lean into the melodrama and the pop culture.” Still, Duke’s level of child stardom cannot have been healthy, he acknowledges, “when you have money and that level of impact on other people, it can be destabilising for everyone involved.” His parents never discouraged Astin from following the same path, although his mother was fiercely protective of him. He hesitates to psychoanalyse her, but says, “I think she wanted to rectify the pain and trauma of her childhood by raising a child who could have a similar experience absent that trauma.” He remembers a time as a teenage actor when she was on set, and a sound engineer made a disparaging comment about his braces. “He mumbled something about ‘the kid’s got fucking marbles in his mouth.’ And my mom flipped out. Her upset was way more traumatic than me not having even heard this mildly disparaging thing that this guy had whispered to himself. But that is the level of mama-bear protection that she had. She was only 4ft 11in, but she scared the shit out of people.” For similar reasons, Duke was also a formidable union leader. “She was, from everything I’ve heard, a beloved figure.” Being a child star in the 80s certainly had its dangers. Astin was 13 when he starred in The Goonies. His co-star Corey Feldman, and Feldman’s friend Corey Haim, both later alleged childhood sexual abuse within the industry – and struggled with substance abuse and other issues in adulthood (Haim died in 2010). His near-contemporary Drew Barrymore was in rehab by the time she was 13. Astin remembers meeting her in a nightclub around that time. “I saw her and gave her a big hug. We kind of liked each other … But I remember thinking: ‘Boy, is it OK that she’s in that experience?’” Astin didn’t do that kind of stuff, he says. “I was never interested in drugs and alcohol or like wild promiscuity or those kinds of things. I got married very young, at 21. We just had our 34th wedding anniversary.” If there was one time the industry started to get to him, it was during The Lord of the Rings movies, in the early 00s. Astin was a key member of the huge cast, arguably the story’s moral centre, but “I was not prepared for that level of visibility and access,” he says. “And there was a disconnect between the attention that I was getting and how much money we had. It was not a lot of money! In fact, I had to sell my house because I negotiated such a small amount on the trilogy.” He’s “very comfortable financially now”, he says. He has also had the very 21st-century experience of seeing Samwise Gamgee as the subject of erotic fan fiction, endless memes and now AI-generated fan slop, where his character meets his older or younger self, or dies and has a funeral, or does things with Frodo that would make Tolkien turn in his grave. “So far I haven’t been bothered by it,” he says, “but what happens when it truly is indistinguishable from yourself?” He still sees his fellow hobbits – Elijah Wood, Billy Boyd and Dominic Monaghan – regularly, at conventions all over the world. “We have a great time. We go to fancy dinners together. We really enjoy the fellowship. We’ve probably done a dozen of them, we’ve got more planned.” And a return to Middle-earth is still possible. Andy Serkis is now in New Zealand filming in-between movie The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum, with Wood and Ian “Gandalf” McKellen reprising their roles. And director Peter Jackson recently announced another project after that, co-written by Tolkien superfan Stephen Colbert. It’s very early days, says Astin, who has spoken to Colbert about it, but he could see himself returning. “I don’t think anybody is opposed to it. We’d all love to connect to those characters, particularly if it’s done with such sensitivity as we heard.” And better paid this time? “Goddam right.” For the time being, though, acting is not really the priority. There’s no shortage of issues in Astin’s in-tray, uppermost of which is the looming spectre of artificial intelligence. Under his predecessor, Fran Drescher, Sag-Aftra went on strike in 2023 for 118 days, partly over studios’ use of AI-created “digital doubles” of performers, but also over residual fees from streaming services. Deepfakes and other AI image technology have become more sophisticated and widely available since. Sag-Aftra has been campaigning for the past three years to pass the No Fakes Act, alongside a coalition of politicians, and tech and media companies such as Disney and Google. “The premise of this law is, it’s going to establish for the first time an individual intellectual property right in name and likeness. So this is the silver-bullet fix,” Astin says. Earlier this month he warned the House judiciary committee of the threat, but he did not dismiss the technology wholesale: “We don’t want to stop progress, we need to civilise it.” There are myriad complications to this issue. He was a month into the job when AI-generated actor Tilly Norwood arrived on the scene, for example. Big tech is moving in on Hollywood, as with the Paramount-Warner Bros merger, bankrolled by the Oracle-owning Ellison family, which threatens further job losses on top of a downturn in US film and TV production of as much as 40% in recent years (Sag-Aftra recently announced its opposition to the merger). At the same time, elder statesmen such as Martin Scorsese and George Lucas have openly embraced AI, and urged the industry to do likewise. Astin gives a measured response: “I would ask these legends in the industry to speak thoughtfully and carefully about this technology. I get the sense sometimes that some of the commentary is not well thought-out. And I think that audiences really need their leadership in navigating this space.” If Astin seems comfortable in the role, it’s partly because he has been a local Sag-Aftra delegate and sat on its committees for several years now. He’s still learning, he says, but he seems to relish it. “I gotta say, it’s a much more enjoyable existence than feeling buffeted by the winds of a trillion-dollar industry that has just foisted itself on the public without any real concern for the safety and wellbeing of people who are going to use this technology.” His career has had ups and downs. “I’ve been number one on the call sheet and I’ve been number 247,” he says. “Even at the height of any of these movies, including Lord of the Rings, I’ve never been on the A-list.” He’s always had a steady stream of work, but he’s been turning down offers recently because he doesn’t want to step out of Sag-Aftra negotiations, he says. Given that past presidents of Sag include Ronald Reagan, I wonder if he has considered getting into politics. He has supported Democrat politicians in the past, including Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. Well-known and liked, scandal-free, diplomatic, a family man, with a record of standing up for the little guy and vanquishing evil (on film at least) – it feels as if he’s got all the attributes. “I appreciate that,” he replies. “I certainly have the interest, but my wife and I have talked a lot about the porch with the rocking chairs …” She has been very patient through his various exploits, he says. Not just acting and union work, he’s also done a master’s degree (in public administration and policy), completed an Iron Man triathlon, hosted a podcast … he’s always busy. “So at a certain point, it’s just not very courteous to not honour the family.” So he has thought about it? “Well, I’ve always fantasised about it. You know, actors love politics. We want to play congressmen and senators and presidents.” He deflects, pointing out that thanks to social media, everyone has a platform these days, not just actors and celebrities, and that we should all be participating in the political process and making our voices heard, especially given the threat big tech poses, not just to Hollywood, but to all of us. But Astin is also smart enough, and modest enough, not to get ahead of himself. “I’m a straight shooter and I’m honest. There are certain things about my value system that are unimpeachable. But I’m also, you know, a fuck-up sometimes,” he says. Being president of the actors union is plenty enough for now. “I feel equal to the task of accepting the responsibility of this job and the constitutional requirements that come with it … I don’t expect that anyone would look at me and think he’s, you know, unflappably perfect, but I like the idea that people would look at me and go: ‘Wow, he sort of put his shit together.’ That’s pretty good.” • This article was amended on 27 July 2026. An earlier version said Sag-Aftra had not taken a position on the Paramount-Warner Bros merger; in fact, they announced its opposition on Saturday.

title: He’s commander-in-chief of chaos. Now we’re all victims of Trump’s wars
author: Nesrine Malik
summary: New tariffs, gas price rises, the deaths of thousands, insecurity … We’re living at the whim of one capricious, vain, easily bored man and his gang of stooges, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
body_text: You would be forgiven, as the US and Iran traded strikes over the past few days, for thinking that it was only last month that the two signed the Islamabad Memorandum, which formalised the process of ending the war and established a 60-day period to negotiate the final terms of a deal. That’s because it was only last month. But there has been so much talk and bluster and strike and turn tail that the conflict feels like it has started and ended several times already. The whole war is only five months old but is already settling into a sort of permanent feature of life, one that is all repetitive theatre now, each act indistinguishable from the one before it to all but the most plugged-in observers. The war is over. The war is at its peak. The Iranians are brave people. The Iranians are scum, not least their leaders. The Iranians don’t want a ceasefire. The Iranians are begging for one. The strait of Hormuz is open, it is shut, it is partly open. To recap, where we are now in the war that was only supposed to last a few weeks but is now entering its sixth month is that the US has expanded airstrikes on Iran in a “major military punishment”. Iran has once again struck US base targets located across the region. The Houthis have claimed their own blockade over a second shipping chokepoint – the war now extends from the Gulf to the Red Sea. Trump can’t get out. Iran now understands the powerful leverage of the strait and its geographical, and therefore military, advantage in controlling it. Trump cannot end the war with that bargaining chip in its hands and the Iranians will not end the war without it. He can’t withdraw on terms that merely restore the prewar status quo. And Trump can’t go all in. Boots on the ground would be an extended bloody campaign that would claim many lives. In the US, the deaths of 18 troops so far and how the Pentagon appears to be trying to undercount that number has triggered outrage. So what now? A sunk-cost logic that will continue to throw more money, and more bodies, into the quagmire. The war has already cost the US almost $40bn. And the Pentagon is asking for another $67bn. The White House’s request for Congress for the fiscal year is a colossal $1.5tn. The implications of this profligacy for the US are the choking of domestic spending. “We’re fighting wars,” Trump said earlier this year. “It’s not possible for us to take care of daycare, Medicaid, Medicare … We have to take care of one thing: military protection.” For what? A war that the US itself launched, that nobody asked for, that has no defensive features at all, and which is run by a frat house of bullies and lickspittles. Everything into the furnace for Trump’s adventures: Iranian children and civilians and infrastructure; Gulf countries’ economies and political stability and even their drinking water, as Iran strikes desalination plants upon which several are heavily dependent. And almost every household in the world. Oil broke $100 a barrel last week and energy prices are higher across the board. Brent oil prices are now almost 40% higher than before the war. A gallon of gasoline in the US now also costs 37% more than it did and diesel is 40% higher. Gas prices have soared again in the UK, up nearly 50% just this month, and the lag between the new raised oil prices and what you pay at the pump will show up in a fortnight. And the story is replicated all over the world, slamming energy consumption and government budgets. These are not just statistics: together they constitute nothing short of a global energy re-configuration as the Iran war beds in. One that heaps pressure on economies all over the world in various states of distress, whether it is wealthy capitalist ones creaking under the weight of privatisation, price gouging and profiteering, or poorer ones where governments cannot absorb more pain for already stressed consumers. Protests over rising costs and fuel prices have flared up and paralysed transport from Ireland to Kenya. Which makes this volatile moment a perfect time to pass some stabilising measures and increase confidence in economic stewardship. Something, perhaps, like a swap of Trump’s tariff regime, which expired last week, with a new one, imposed on the grounds that countries were not doing enough to “tackle forced labour”. If you think that this is a risible excuse, and that the Trump administration does not harbour a deep moral concern about poor working conditions across the world, then this is sadly a symptom of Trump derangement syndrome. You should get that looked at. There is no amelioration of the cumulative impacts of this vandalism, no subsidy or cap that can soak up a colossal shock at the heart of global energy transit channels and oil production. We are all held hostage by a regime in the US that has pressed its military and economic prowess in service of ego and ignorance; tethered to an administration that runs the country as it runs in the world, in pursuit of point-scoring in a game where no play is too small or too big. Whether it is adding warning signs outside the Smithsonian to alert that exhibits are “inaccurate”, initiating crude tariff policies, or dragging a whole region into war because he thought it would be easy and look cool, Trump is wildly casual, cavalier, one moment bored and the other vexed. As if the whole world were a plaything to be toyed with and discarded, then picked up again and shaken and prodded. And it all shows no signs of abating. Yoked to US hegemony, we all count the pennies, the bodies, the ever-escalating tithes of the election of a single man and the willingness of careerists and cowards who enable and support him. The more it carries on, the more these costs will be recounted in a sort of background noise to our existence and what was previously unthinkable will become the new normal, again and again. The Iran war is the most hazardous manifestation of this. Phantom breakthroughs, threats of final decisive escalations, all have given way to a chilling reality. An exorbitant war that is with each day rearranging geopolitics, domestic budgets and household ones, is once again, a new normal. Trump is stuck. Unable to swallow the unpalatable price of peace. And everyone else pays the cost. Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

title: Monday briefing: ​How the Cockroach ​protests ​have expose​d the ​cracks in ​India’s government
author: Hettie O'Brien
summary: In today’s newsletter: Across ​the country, a ​younger generation is turning private disillusionment into public defiance​ against a government that once felt untouchable
body_text: Good morning. As flames engulfed parts of France and Spain this weekend, in India, the prime minister, Narendra Modi, was trying to put out a very different kind of fire. Thousands of people arrived in Delhi on Saturday to demand the resignation of his education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. When he stepped down in the early afternoon, the protests turned into a triumphant block party. But the Cockroach protests that have swept through India this summer are about much more than a single minister. They have humiliated Modi and undermined the indomitable power of his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) that has ruled India for the past 12 years. They’re also a lesson in using humour to political advantage. Modi likes to present himself as an infallible messiah, but young people have mocked the prime minister online and in the streets, calling him a “56-inch monkey” (a reference to Modi boasting about his ample 56-inch chest), and parodied his social media addresses. “Hating Modi is cool on the internet now, after years of criminalising dissent,” one told a reporter. Now the protesters have secured a victory, will their calls for revolution continue? For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to our south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen, who has been reporting on the “Cockroaches” in Delhi, about what their anger stems from and what it means for the BJP. That’s after a roundup of the biggest stories of the weekend. Weekend roundup Wild fires | Authorities in France battled to contain a huge wildfire near Bordeaux in the south-west as Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, warned Spain and the Iberian peninsula were suffering the effects of the climate emergency. Germany | A man suspected of driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival then going on a knife rampage in an Islamist terror attack has been shot dead by police, German officials have said. Iran | The US has paused strikes on Iran for a second night as top military officials advised Donald Trump to halt his bombing campaign, and diplomatic negotiations have continued to avoid a return to all-out war. UK politics | Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is to indicate he will put the climate crisis and overseas development at the heart of UK international relations by taking up the country’s seat on the board at the World Bank. UK news | Five Palestine Action activists face being sentenced as terrorists for breaking windows and throwing red paint at a branch of Barclays Bank in Lancashire. In depth: ‘What if all cockroaches come together?’ It started as a sardonic joke. On 16 May, Abhijeet Dipke, an Indian student at Boston University, posted on X: “What if all cockroaches come together?” It was a tongue-in-cheek response to India’s chief justice, who had called unemployed young Indians “cockroaches”. Online, thousands of people responded to Dipke’s message. Realising he had tapped into something big, Dipke flew to Delhi on 6 June and went to Jantar Mantar, its famous protest ground. The protests drew young people from across the country, and the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) – a play on the BJP’s name – created a website listing their demands, including reform of India’s education system. India has a young population who are better educated than ever before, but it has proven a weak point for the BJP, with the country’s universities crumbling and its economy failing to provide jobs for many graduates. Millions of young people spend years prepping for gruelling public exams in the hope of securing a decent job, and their parents go into debt or sell their land to fund these studies. To make matters worse, these exam papers are routinely leaked and sold to the highest bidder. “Anyone rich enough can buy the answers,” Hannah tells me. This is devastating for millions of young people, forcing them to retake tests for which they’ve already studied. After a medical entrance exam was leaked in May, at least 12 students took their own lives; some left notes behind saying they could not bear the thought of resitting the test. The leaks are a potent symbol of institutional corruption, inflaming the anger that young people feel towards a political system that is failing them. *** Thief, thief Sonam Wangchuk, an engineer and education reformer from Ladakh, joined the protest on 28 June and declared he would go on indefinite hunger strike until the education minister resigned. “The idea of a hunger strike has a particularly powerful resonance in India,” says Hannah. “Gandhi put his life on the line several times with his hunger strikes for independence.” Delhi police forcibly removed Wangchuk from Jantar Mantar on 18 July and took him to hospital, supposedly for the sake of his health. Footage of his hospital stay went viral, and the Cockroach party called for a march on parliament. On Monday, tens of thousands of people started to fill Delhi’s streets. “In my whole time covering India, I’ve never seen so many people turning out,” Hannah says. The mood was jubilant, but by the afternoon, things had turned violent as the police began firing teargas and using batons on the protesters. Despite that, many of the protesters stayed put, and Hannah went back to Jantar Mantar in the following days. “It was the place to be in India,” she says. “There were people camping out, delivery guys bringing pizza and biryani, people cooking food. It had become about more than just the education minister resigning. More, even than education.” The protesters’ very public displays of contempt – graffiti of Modi’s name under the image of a urinating dog; people stamping on a poster of his face and chanting “thief, thief” – would have seemed unimaginable just two weeks ago. “People were just revelling in the opportunity to speak their mind,” Rahul Bhatia, a writer and author of The New India, who attended the protests on Saturday, tells me. “It was delightful. It made people think: things are possible.” *** Modi lost control of the narrative Pradhan’s resignation is a major victory for the Cockroach protesters. He is a Modi loyalist and former organiser for the RSS, the Hindu supremacist group closely affiliated with the BJP (for more on its sinister ideology, it’s worth reading this fascinating 2020 piece by Samanth Subramanian). “It creates a crack in the BJP’s armour,” Hannah says. Modi has projected an image of total authority, but this is one of the first instances where he has bent to popular will. He demands unflinching loyalty from his ministers. They may now be questioning whether their positions are quite as secure as they thought. India has taken a sharp turn towards autocracy under the BJP. Its main media channels are controlled by (or intensely favourable to) the government, and most of them gave minimal coverage to the protests, so young people resorted to sharing information and anti-government memes on social media. The party is no stranger to social media (its “troll army” is adept at smearing digital opponents, and the government tried to shut down the Cockroach party’s X account in early July), but it has lost control of the narrative. Modi’s last-ditch attempt to engage protesters with two reels he posted to his then 101 million Instagram followers on Thursday night (after which he gained over 1 million more, an impressive number, though still fewer than Beyoncé’s 299 million) seemed contrived and stilted. “He has been crucified online for those videos,” Hannah says. *** Is this the start of something bigger? It’s tempting to compare the Cockroach protests to other youth uprisings that have led to regime change in south Asia. But “a quick look at the outcome of people’s movements in India is not encouraging,” the novelist Arundhati Roy wrote in a recent piece for Equator magazine. “Revenge is surely being planned and will be visited on those [the government] sees as the main instigators.” After people took to the streets in 2019 to protest against the BJP’s controversial new citizenship act, the government swiftly outlawed gatherings in several places and detained protesters. The real test of the BJP’s power will come at election time. It is one of the world’s richest and most formidable parties, and has attempted to capture India’s electoral machinery, pushing for reforms to its voting map that would tilt power further in Modi’s favour. In West Bengal, a state the BJP had never won before, it “revised” the electoral roll and excluded more than 9.1 million voters from the register, securing a decisive victory earlier this year. “It seems like the BJP has much less support than people actually think,” Bhatia says. But after these protests, Modi will be doing all that he can to maintain his party’s grip on power. The week to come Monday | Andrew and Tristan Tate are due back in the Florida court where they’re fighting their extradition to the UK, to face rape and sex-trafficking charges. Tuesday | Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy are expected to be among those attending the Washington DC memorial service for the late South Carolina senator and Trump ally Lindsey Graham. Thursday | People will go to the polls to elect the next mayor of Greater Manchester, who will replace Andy Burnham. What else we’ve been enjoying To enshittification, we can now add the idea of decadence without pleasure: “For anyone with an Internet connection and a little discretionary income, the contemporary moment offers a superabundance of seductive distractions. Why then the pervasive mood of emptiness?” Truly, what a time to be alive. Toby Moses, head of newsletters The world is approaching “plutocratic collapse”. That’s the view of the French economist Gabriel Zucman, and I’m inclined to agree. I enjoyed Will Dunn’s recent profile of him in the New Statesman (£). Hettie Add shingles to the long list of things millennial women need to worry about – Emily Retter has looked at why the excruciating disease is on the rise. Toby Sport Tour de France | Tadej Pogacar took a record-equalling fifth win in the Tour de France on Sunday, joining the all-time greats, as Mathieu van der Poel won a frantic final stage in Paris. Commonwealth Games | Adam Ramsay-Peaty is ready to bounce back after his 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games. He said: “The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind, but I’m really happy with that.” Formula One | Lando Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix with an assured drive for McLaren at the Hungaroring, his and the team’s first victory of the year. The front pages “Miliband vows to give UK ‘global leadership’ role on climate crisis”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Times says “Teen anxiety pays more than job”, and the Telegraph also has “PM to crack down on youth benefits”. Still on politics, The Mail goes with “Streeting: I will quit if defence plan falls short”, the i Paper says “Council tax and stamp duty to be scrapped under Burnham plans”, and the Express splashes “Police ‘waste’ millions on diversity schemes”. The FT splashes “Biggest defence companies home in on start-ups for nimbler military tech”, and the Mirror leads with its water safety campaign, saying “No child should die for a day at the seaside”. Lastly, Metro splashes “Fly and dry” on Gatwick’s water outage. Today in Focus How Palantir got into the NHS Investigative journalist, Lucas Amin, reports on how the tech company Palantir won a £330m contract with the NHS … and what happened once its software was introduced. Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Restricting eating to a nine‑hour window and avoiding food for four hours before sleep may improve cognitive health in older adults. In a six‑month trial of 47 women who were considered overweight or obese, both groups lost similar weight, but those following time‑restricted eating performed better on spatial planning and problem‑solving tests, with hints of improved memory. Researchers suggest circadian rhythms, metabolism and inflammation may play a role. Experts stress the findings are preliminary and require larger, peer‑reviewed studies. Prof Wendy Hall, the head of nutritional sciences at King’s College London, said: “Time-restricted eating is a plausible approach to supporting cognitive health in midlife”. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. title: Republicans have ‘nothing to run on’ in midterms after Trump failures, Jeffries says
author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
summary: Top House Democrat says US president ‘failed to deliver’ on campaign promises to lower costs and avoid overseas wars
body_text: Donald Trump’s Republican party has “nothing to run on” for the congressional midterm elections after the president broke promises to lower costs and avoid starting war overseas, the US House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, has said. The New York congressman made those comments on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday, exactly 100 days from the 3 November midterms, when Jeffries and his fellow Democrats are aiming to take control of the US House and Senate from their Republican opponents. Asked to discuss the elections, Jeffries alluded to how Trump and other Republicans quickly seized on a 21 July announcement from the Democratic New Jersey governor, Mikie Sherrill, that 6,600 noncitizens in the state had registered to vote because of a software error. Fewer than 400 of them voted before the identification and correction of the error. But the president and his allies nonetheless used the disclosure to boost false claims that there are scores of noncitizens on voter rolls who could compromise the integrity of the midterms, during which Republicans are predicted to lose seats. Jeffries on Sunday argued that was because it is a more comfortable strategy to adopt rather than confront how the US and Israeli militaries began warring with Iran in February after Trump won a second presidency in 2024 having promised “not to start … endless wars in the Middle East”. The costs of the war have included the deaths of 18 US service members as of Sunday, along with injuries to hundreds more. Gas and grocery prices have also soared amid the conflict, leaving 95% of Americans believing that the US is suffering an affordability crisis, according to exclusive polling conducted for the Guardian. Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, on Sunday acknowledged there was an affordability crisis in the US – but argued the blame for that fell on Democrats and Joe Biden’s presidency. “All these things will only get better if given two more years with a Republican Congress” in November, Leavitt said on Fox News. Speaking to State of the Union host Dana Bash, Jeffries said, “Republicans … have failed to actually deliver on making life more affordable for the American people.” He continued, “It was Donald Trump who promised to lower costs on day one. But we know that costs haven’t gone down in this country. Costs have gone up. “It was Donald Trump … who said that he was elected not to start wars, endless wars in the Middle East, but to stop them – and then turned around and has gotten us involved in this reckless war of choice in Iran that has skyrocketed gas prices on the American people.” Jeffries then referred to how Republicans a year earlier cut more than $1tn from Medicaid, the public health insurance program for people in the US who are low-income and disabled, adding: “They have nothing to run on. We’re going to run on fighting for an affordable America. “Too many people are working hard – they’re playing by the rules, but they can’t thrive,” Jeffries also said. “And they can barely survive, not enough food on the table, not enough gas in the tank, unable to actually regularly and consistently afford to pay the rent or pay the mortgage.” A recent analysis from Decision Desk HQ forecasts that Democrats are likely to win a majority in the House – and that Republicans are narrowly favored to retain control of the US Senate.

title: Blanche-led DoJ likely to derail Epstein survivors’ pursuit of justice, experts say
author: Victoria Bekiempis
summary: Lawyers predict ‘more suppression and no active investigations’ but victims’ groups determined to continue fight
body_text: As Donald Trump’s former defense lawyer Todd Blanche appears poised for confirmation as attorney general, numerous Jeffrey Epstein survivors have sounded the alarm that a US justice department helmed by him would derail their pursuit of justice. In a letter urging Republican senators Thom Tillis and John Cornyn to reject his nomination, these survivors said that Blanche’s handling of the Epstein case as acting attorney general was characterized by misstep after misstep. Blanche, who reportedly led the disclosure of documents as required by the bipartisan Epstein Files Transparency Act, allowed the disclosure of survivors’ names, photos and identifying information – but omitted the names of accused abusers and enablers, they said. While more than 1,000 teenage girls and women were abused, not a single person other than Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell faced charges, they noted. And in a recent sit-down with survivors at Tillis’s urging, survivors “received an hour of deflection, interruption and gaslighting”, they said. These survivors’ concerns about Blanche by no means exist in a vacuum, and have only fanned the flames of a controversy that has dogged Trump since he again took office. While campaigning, Trump promised to release all Epstein files – playing into his supporters’ belief that there was a global sex-trafficking cabal involving high-profile business and political figures. But Trump’s justice department only released dribs and drabs of information until Congress forced its hand following a series of embarrassing disclosures that renewed attention on Trump’s former friendship with Epstein. Trump has denied all wrongdoing including in relation to Epstein. Blanche’s meeting with Maxwell in prison last summer, which was followed by her transfer to a lower-security facility, further heightened outrage over the DoJ’s underwhelming disclosures. The constellation of circumstances has raised the question: what would a Blanche-directed justice department mean for Epstein survivors’ search for justice? Legal veterans told the Guardian that a Blanche-led DoJ would likely derail survivors’ efforts for accountability. Several survivors’ advocates said that all hope was not lost, noting that roadblocks likely under Blanche did not portend a permanent impediment to justice. Bryan Sullivan, a partner with Early Sullivan Wright Gizer & McRae, said that based on what he has read and seen in Blanche’s testimony before the judiciary committee, he thinks a confirmation would mean “more suppression and no active investigations” into Epstein’s sex trafficking. “I think it’s because that’s what Trump wants. He wants this to go away,” Sullivan said. “And that’s one of the reasons he fired [former attorney general Pam] Bondi, because she didn’t make it go away, in my opinion.” Ron Kuby, a renowned defense lawyer with a focus on civil rights, voiced similar sentiments about a Blanche confirmation. “It means that no other perpetrators will be held criminally liable for their misconduct,” he said. “That’s no different from the way it’s been throughout the Trump administration and the Biden administration.” “All the millionaires and billionaires and hangers-on and others in Epstein’s orbit who, you know, enabled him have not been brought to justice,” Kuby said. “And they’re not going to be.” Carl Tobias, the Williams chair in law at the University of Richmond School of Law, said that even if Blanche were not confirmed, he could serve as acting attorney general for the rest of Trump’s term, meaning he would have continued control over the Epstein case. “He’ll have more power, of course, if he’s formally confirmed by the Senate … but he’ll have plenty of power even if he’s not,” Tobias said. “So I can’t be very optimistic about what he might do – if anything – about the Epstein files, or to give much comfort to the survivors.” While there are some legal avenues for survivors to seek justice outside an allegedly recalcitrant DoJ, attorneys cautioned that success would be an uphill battle. “You could bombard them with [public records] requests, and then file a lawsuit for them not providing responses to the Foia [Freedom of Information Act] requests, but that alone is a long process,” Sullivan said. “Bluntly, the problem with all of this is [that] all of it takes time.” “Courts are grossly underfunded [and] understaffed,” he said. “It will take quite a while to go through that sort of legal process.” There has been litigation against federal authorities over their handling of the Epstein investigation, alleging that their failure to act years ago enabled more abuse. Those kinds of cases “are exceptionally difficult to win”, Kuby said. “It’s always true that had the government done something differently, a different outcome would have ensued,” Kuby explained of the legal intricacies. “There’s no generalized duty to protect specific individuals outside of a special relationship with the victims.” “I’m certainly sympathetic to those claims, but the government historically is not.” Tobias similarly described the possibility of winning litigation against the DoJ as “difficult”. Neither reps for Tillis or Cornyn responded to requests for comment. Asked for comment on survivors’ concerns, White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson said: “Todd Blanche has done an excellent job as acting attorney general and will continue doing so as attorney general.” A justice department spokesperson said in a statement that Blanche, senior DoJ officials, FBI agents and victims services representatives “met with Epstein victims last week and had a productive, initial discussion”. The spokesperson said Blanche “answered questions and walked through what is needed for investigations to proceed”. “While some victims said that they had not reached out to the FBI under this administration, he encouraged victims to meet with FBI investigators as the next step, and attendees spoke with agents after the meeting about scheduling interviews. The justice department is determined to bring justice for all victims of human trafficking and sex crimes.” Gretchen Carlson and Julie Roginsky, who filed sexual harassment lawsuits against Roger Ailes, the former Fox News CEO, and co-launched the non-profit survivors advocacy organization Lift Our Voices, expressed hope that survivors could still find justice one day even if faced with more setbacks. Carlson said she was disappointed in Republicans poised to let Blanche’s nomination go through, noting that Trump went on the attack against Cornyn and Tillis. “They have the ability not to allow this,” Carlson said, explaining that not everything should be on their shoulders, as “everyone should have questions about Todd Blanche being attorney general, just about the Epstein issues”. That said, there are midterm elections coming up. “I’ve learned, in all the work I’ve done on the Hill in trying to get bills passed, that you never know who you might get, first of all, to be on your side,” Carlson said. “So you never judge it before you actually try.” “I feel the same way about this,” she said. “We don’t know who’s going to potentially step up to the plate and say, ‘You know what, I’m going to take over the work that [Republican congressman] Tom Massie was doing on this. “We can’t do this work with any kind of a negative lens. And although it feels like we’re in a little bit of a setback if Todd Blanche is confirmed, I think there’s always a way to find victory.” Roginsky expressed similar views. While a possible Blanche confirmation represented a “slap in the face to anybody who’s ever fought … a system that is already rigged very much against survivors”, she advised survivors and advocates to keep pushing for justice. “If you think about how far our movement has come just in the last decade, we’ve seen tremendous advances,” Roginsky said of Lift Our Voices’ successful advocacy for federal legislation against non-disclosure agreements and forced arbitration related to workplace sexual misconduct. “We’ve seen some setbacks, but ultimately the advances will always outweigh the setbacks.”
