title: Why are Democrats so quiet about the Tate brothers?
author: Moira Donegan
summary: The party’s silence shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategists
body_text: It’s not exactly strange that elements of the Magaverse have embraced Andrew Tate. What’s strange is that the Democrats do not seem interested in holding the Trump movement to account for it. Andrew Tate, the misogynist influencer who is accused by numerous women around the world and now by British prosecutors of rape and strangulation, as well as assault, sex trafficking, possession of child abuse images and extreme pornography, and various other forms of gender violence and exploitation, was arrested in Miami last week, along with Tristan, his brother and sidekick. Or I should say, they were rearrested: the men were previously charged in Romania, where they were under house arrest until, following some conveniently timed diplomatic moves from the Trump administration, they were allowed to leave the country and resettled in the US. When asked if the Trump administration had secured their release from Romania back then, the Tates’ lawyer said: “Do the math. These guys are on the plane.” Now, finally, they are awaiting extradition to the UK, where they are dual citizens. The Tate brothers have long made their living by making provocative, contemptuous statements about women online. But in June, the New Yorker’s Heidi Blake published a long investigation that centered not on what the Tates have said, but on what they’re said to have done – detailing a long and documented history of alleged sex trafficking, violence and sexual assault along with a disturbing pattern of police mismanagement, incompetence and indifference that allowed the men to go free. The Tates denied wrongdoing in that piece; their lawyer called the new British charges against them “garbage”. But if anyone thought the Tates’ misogynistic influencer career was mere bluster, the Blake investigation offered a formidable bit of counterevidence: she painted a picture of the men acting exactly the way that they talked. In a world where people take misogyny as seriously as they claim to, the Tates would long ago have been ostracized, and condemned, for their hatefully sexist rhetoric and alleged violence against women. In this world, they got rich, and ingratiated themselves to powerful figures in the Republican party. Tate is a natural fit on a Maga right that has served to unite its many different factions – from Christian conservatives to Silicon Valley eugenicists, to beer-chugging barstool denizens, conspiracy mongers, and the male hosts of multi-hour podcasts – around a foundation of male supremacy. Contempt for women is the uniting force on the American right, more uniform across the competing styles within the movement even than the hatred of immigration or devotion to the prerogatives of capital. Donald Trump cemented the presidency, after all, when he was revealed to have bragged about “grab[bing]” women “by the pussy” and still maintained his base of support. In the decade that followed, his domineering, narcissistic, vulgar style of masculinity, and the alternately belittling and hateful treatment of women that accompanies it, have come to be seen on the right as a feature, not a bug. Other men within the Maga movement now imitate Trump’s style of misogyny with a gleeful competitiveness; the coalition welcomes men who collect harems of women to breed their children, those who have been multiply accused of sexual abuse and those who decry our right to vote. Andrew Tate, in this milieu, is not an exception. He is the rule. But just because Tate’s style of masculinity is popular on the right – in which sex is seen to elevate men’s status at women’s expense, in which women’s aspirations to education, skilled work, dignity, public participation, or even mere decency are mocked; and in which men’s mistreatment of women is the key way for them to gain the esteem of other men – does not mean that it is popular with the public. Tate’s version of vulgar, avowed, preening misogyny has a constituency of Republican politicians and unlikable teenage boys; it does not have a constituency among the majority of the American public. Why are Democrats not making the Tates into symbols of Maga’s hateful and bizarre cultural project, of Trump’s personal alleged affinity for sexual misconduct, or of the antisocial, anti-democratic and anti-equality stances of the Maga movement? Rape, after all, might be the most quintessentially anti-democracy act: a violent refusal of equality in the most intimate terms. One could imagine an opposition to Trumpism that built from anti-rape principles into pro-democracy ones; less ambitiously, one could imagine an opposition to Trumpism that merely drew a link between Trump’s pathetic narcissism and that of the sleazeball Tates and their manosphere ilk. It seems like an easy win. That the Democratic party is not taking it shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategists, and how anathema even the most basic and remedial feminist claims are now understood to be by those same forces. Because one explanation for why the Democrats are not taking advantage of the Tates’ links to Trump is as simple as it is dark: they do not want to alienate the Tates’ base of manosphere content consumers. It is by now a cliche to say that Democrats are losing men, a demographic reality that is treated as a much greater emergency than the GOP’s parallel loss of women. Sects within the Democratic consultant class have made the recruitment of manly men candidates into their singular mission. Following the 2024 election, major party players fundraised a massive $20m for a “Speaking with American Men” project, meant to lure men back to the party; the California governor, Gavin Newsom, a likely 2028 presidential candidate, has forged his own podcast project, in which he has taken to embracing some rightwing cultural positions on things like trans rights. The party is running white male candidates who say cartoonish things like it’s OK “to be a manly man” – as if anyone was confused. It is this desperate and frantic effort to re-masculinize the party at any cost that led to the recruitment of Graham Platner, the ex-marine who dropped out of the Maine Senate race earlier this month after being accused of rape (he has denied the allegations). Major players in the Democratic party did the right thing in that case, calling on Platner to drop out en masse. But many of them still believe in the strategy that elevated him in the first place: that of prizing men over women, of coveting men’s votes and men’s support as somehow more legitimate, more valuable, than women’s. In this sense, there is another reason that some in the Democratic party won’t seize upon the Tate issue: even if they don’t condone his alleged violence, on his most fundamental principle – that men are better and more important than women are – they may not entirely disagree. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

title: ‘Our country is the mission’: more than 100 ex-Nasa astronauts launch new voting campaign
author: Richard Luscombe
summary: Astronauts for America liken effort to instill trust and faith back in constitution’s principles and democratic institutions to ‘making a course correction’
body_text: Orbiting 250 miles above the US in the international space station, astronaut Cady Coleman did not look down and see red or blue states, sanctuary cities or communities occupied by thousands of federal immigration enforcement agents in camouflage uniforms and automatic weapons. What she saw was a single land, from Pacific to Atlantic, no borders or partitions, just a united America, and a population valuing its equality while convinced that what brought them together was far greater than anything that divided them. It is that unique perspective, witnessed only by a few hundred people in history, that led Coleman and dozens of other retired Nasa colleagues to form Astronauts for America, a non-partisan advocacy group of fellow space explorers. Launched, pun intended, to coincide with the 2026 semiquincentennial of the US, the out-of-this-world alliance wants to restore faith in, and support of, the country’s constitutional democracy. It seeks to encourage politicians and the public to commit to the principles of the constitution itself, something its members believe has fallen into a sort of a black hole in recent months and years. Or, as Coleman puts it, “being willing to speak out when we know something isn’t right”. She said: “All 108 of us, we’re very different people from each other. Some of us have very different politics and we certainly each have our own opinions about the current administration, about past administrations. “But during my spaceflights, in looking at all the patches and the names on my astronaut jacket, I literally didn’t know and never asked about their politics. It was just not part of the mission. “The fact is now we’re all together, and what we’re fighting for is something that’s common to all of us, we’re fighting for our country, for our democracy, and for decision making, and restoring the faith in our institutions.” Coleman, 65, who flew two space shuttle missions and spent a total of 180 days in space, including a lengthy tour of duty on the ISS between 2010 and 2011, will join colleagues on Astronauts for America’s Vote for Freedom campaign this summer and fall. Ahead of November’s midterm elections, they plan to tour about 60 college and university campuses, many in swing states, talking to young and first-time voters and encouraging them to exert their right to be part of the country’s democracy. “Every one of these voters can change the course of our nation, it’s like making a course correction in space,” she said. “My astronaut colleague Ron Garan gives this example, a small adjustment now is a large distance later, like getting to the moon or not. A small course correction now can really mean big things as the ship continues on its course.” The who’s who of Astronauts for America includes some standout names. There are dozens of space shuttle crew members from that program’s 135 missions, including Charles Bolden and Bill Nelson, who both went on to become Nasa administrators, and in Nelson’s case, a US senator. The oldest is Rusty Schweickart, 90, who flew on Apollo 9 in March 1969, four months before the first moon landing. Bolden, a retired marine corps major general who flew four shuttle missions between 1986 and 1994, is one of the most outspoken of the group, having served as head of Nasa for both of Barack Obama’s terms of office to January 2017. “All of us have been kind of watching the deterioration in the US over the last few decades,” he said. “It seems like every president issues more and more executive orders because they can’t get action out of Congress, or they don’t want action out of Congress. “I was upset when President Obama started relying on executive orders. I understood the reason, I was in the administration and saw the incalcitrance of Congress and their desire not to give him any wins, so I could understand where he was coming from. “But still, that’s not in accordance with the constitution.” Bolden said that “failure to adhere to the constitution the way we think the framers intended it” placed the country in peril, as well as more recent assaults on democratic norms by the Trump administration. “We may not make it if we don’t do something now,” he said. “We may not have another presidential term to try to make a difference.” Linda Godwin, a scientist whose four shuttle missions spanned 10 years and 38 days in space, and two space walks between 1991 and 2001, is on the group’s steering committee plotting its strategy, which includes plans to “grade” midterm congressional candidates on their commitment to constitutional principles. “As astronauts, perhaps we would have a voice,” she said. “Not that we’re necessarily more knowledgable or smarter or anything like that, but we have a background in which we participated in big missions that depended on truth and accountability, and evidence, and trust. “We worked with people who have many different opinions on different things, and we know how to work together to get the mission done. And we kind of felt like, you know, right now, we think our country is the mission.” The astronauts met on 20 July at the California Science Center to launch their Freedom to Vote campaign, a rare gathering of many of the nation’s space pioneers on the 57th anniversary of the 20 July 1969 Apollo 11 moon landing. The occasion and date were full of poignancy for those present, turning their inspirational past experiences into a message of hope for the future, with a meticulously planned checklist to try to achieve it, just like the scores of missions they once flew. “It’s important to speak up when things are happening in our country that are moving us away from the democratic society that we all grew up with, and that we all supported as government employees as well,” said Ellen Ochoa, another four-time shuttle flier who was the first Latina in space in 1993, and the first person to play the flute there. “One reason we’re reaching out at college campuses is that for a lot of the students this might be their first opportunity to vote, or they may not be in the habit of voting and not thought too much about exercising this right. “The message is it’s really important to vote. That’s the most important right you have in a democracy. And it’s also not only a right, but I feel it’s really a responsibility. A democracy depends on the people actively participating, and this is the single most important thing that people can do.” The assembled astronauts agreed on Monday on a single, space-themed statement all of them could use to encapsulate the purpose of their voting campaign. They did not disappoint: “Going to the polls is one small step for you, and one giant leap for our country.”

title: First Thing: Trump continues pause on Iran strikes as Pentagon reveals higher US casualty figures
author: Martin Belam
summary: Eighteen American troops have been killed and 624 wounded since White House launched war on Tehran. Plus, International Cowboy Day in Kenya
body_text: Good morning. The US has paused strikes on Iran for a third night as top military officials advised Donald Trump to halt his bombing campaign, and diplomatic negotiations have continued to avoid a return to all-out war. Oil prices fell on Monday as markets responded to the pause in combat. Tehran said on Sunday it would pause what it called “retaliatory” attacks against US allies in the region. Trump is said to be weighing up diplomatic and military options in the nearly five-month-old conflict. Axios reported on Sunday that Adm Bradley Cooper, the top US military commander in the region, had told Trump the US military campaign had reached the limits of its effectiveness. How many US service personnel have been killed and injured in Trump’s Iran war? The Pentagon updated its official war casualty database over the weekend, adding more than 140 wounded service members. The new figures show that 18 US troops have been killed and 624 wounded since the US launched its war against Iran on 28 February. How has Katy Perry become embroiled in debate over the war? The pop star has condemned the White House after it used her hit song Firework in a TikTok video showing US military strikes on Iranian targets, saying: “I did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it. I wrote this song to be an anthem of hope, healing, and inner strength … my music is for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare.” Netanyahu accuses Mamdani of ‘fomenting hate’ in calls for PM’s arrest Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday that Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, was “fomenting hate” by calling the Israeli prime minister a war criminal who should be arrested over Israel’s war in Gaza if he visits the city for the United Nations general assembly. “He’s supposed to be the mayor of all New Yorkers – Jews, Christians, Muslims, everyone,” Netanyahu said, adding: “But he’s trying to turn one group against the other.” What has the international court accused Netanyahu of? The court, based in The Hague in the Netherlands, issued a warrant accusing the Israeli prime minister of being “allegedly responsible for the war crimes of starvation as a method of warfare and of intentionally directing an attack against the civilian population; and the crimes against humanity of murder, persecution, and other inhumane acts”. Police have shot dead Berlin Pride van and knife rampage suspect, officials say A man suspected of driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival then going on a knife rampage in an Islamist terror attack has been shot dead by police, German officials have said. One woman was killed on Saturday evening and 29 others were injured in an attack that took place in the Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate at about 10pm local time on Saturday, close to one of Europe’s biggest LGBTQ+ celebrations. Police confirmed on Sunday evening that the chief suspect had been shot dead. Two dead in shootings at Bite of Seattle food festival, say authorities Two people were killed and five others wounded in a shooting on Sunday evening during a food festival at an events complex near the Space Needle in Seattle, a city fire department spokesperson said. Susan Gregg from the Harborview medical center said it had admitted four victims including a toddler, a 23-year-old man and two women. One patient was in a critical condition, she said. In other news … An Oklahoma woman known for posting on social media about parenting her children was fatally shot in an apparent murder-suicide by her husband a short time after she published a clip alluding to allegations he had molested a minor. It was “not standard” for Taylor Farms to ask the White House to delay a cyclospora-related recall, an ex-FDA head has said. The top House Democrat, Hakeem Jeffries, has said Trump’s Republican party has “nothing to run on” for the congressional midterm elections, after the president broke promises to lower costs and avoid starting war overseas. Slovenia’s Tadej Pogacar joined the small club of five-time Tour de France champions in the final stage of this year’s race in Paris at the weekend. Misleading TikTok health claims online pose a “huge danger to public safety”, experts have warned, after research has shown that AI-generated doctors are gaining millions of views by spreading dubious health advice. Stat of the day: Uganda begins emergency food handouts after 19 die from hunger Uganda has launched emergency food relief distribution after at least 19 deaths from hunger were reported in an area of prolonged drought in the east of the country. Health facilities report treating hundreds of children for severe malnutrition. Experts attribute the region’s recurring food insecurity and vulnerability to climate crisis shocks, environmental degradation such as deforestation and overgrazing, as well as poverty and low agricultural productivity. Building Power: From Bernie to Mamdani, how the Occupy movement transformed American politics Yotam Marom, who helped lead Occupy Wall Street, discusses its legacy, 15 years after the movement fell apart. Don’t miss this: How Trump could undermine the midterms George Chidi says while the president really has no power over elections in the US, that hasn’t stopped Trump from laying the groundwork to challenge results he doesn’t like in November. … or this: ‘I thought it didn’t stand a cat’s chance in hell’: Andrew Ridgeley on Wham’s surreal trip to China I miss George Michael. Four decades after they became the first western pop act to tour China, Michael’s bandmate Andrew Ridgeley recalls silent gigs and awkward embassy receptions as a new documentary with footage of the tour is released. Climate check: US heatwave stretches on with millions still under warnings At least 40 million people were under extreme heat warnings across central and southern parts of the United States on Sunday as high temperatures and severe humidity gripped large swaths of the country for a second straight day. Meanwhile, Europe is suffering a spate of dangerous wildfires. Kate Lamb explains what a “fire cloud” is, and how the unprecedented phenomenon – pyrocumulonimbus – could exacerbate the effects of the blazes. Last Thing: International Cowboy Day celebrations in Nairobi – in pictures Who knew that they celebrated International Cowboy Day in Nairobi, Kenya? Certainly not me. Here is a spectacular set of photos from the event. Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. If you’re not already signed up, subscribe now. title: Tariffs are Trump’s favorite plaything – and his justifications are absurd
author: Steven Greenhouse
summary: The president is using forced labor as a pretext to slap tariffs on countries around the world
body_text: With the midterm elections less than four months away, it’s a precarious time for Donald Trump and Republicans: Trump’s war against Iran is going badly, his approval ratings are in the toilet, gas prices are soaring and pushing up inflation, and nation after nation is furious about Trump’s insults, bullying and ugly American unilateralism. So amid all this mess, what does Trump do? He turns to his favorite economic plaything: tariffs. On Monday, Trump signed orders to slap a 50% tariff on many Canadian goods, and four days later, he imposed across-the-board 10% or 12.5% tariffs on goods from more than 80 countries. Trump was no doubt thumping his chest, while millions of people overseas were dumping on him for yet another unnecessary, hostile act. Too bad for Republicans, and most Americans, though, because Trump’s fixation on tariffs will only worsen their troubles. Trump’s new tariffs will push up prices – let’s not forget that tariffs are taxes on imports, and US consumers will pay those taxes. A corollary of that: Trump’s tariffs will worsen Americans No 1 economic concern: affordability. In bad news for typical Americans, the Yale Budget Lab estimates that Trump’s tariffs will increase costs for the average US household by $1,100 each year. The tariffs are also likely to push Trump’s approval ratings deeper into the sewer. If Trump thinks these tariffs are going to distract Americans from thinking about the Epstein files or the disastrous mess he’s made with his Iran “excursion”, he’s deluding himself. The American people aren’t going to forget those things. It’s hard to tell whether Trump’s repeated use of tariffs is a fixation or an addiction. Emperor Donald I evidently loves tariffs because he can use them to clobber other countries whenever he wants. They’re a powerful cudgel he won’t let go of. Trump imposed his new tariffs on more than 80 countries on the very day that another set of tariffs he slapped on dozens of countries was due to expire. To paraphrase the actor Charlton Heston, I can imagine Trump saying: “I’ll give up tariffs when you take them from my cold, dead hands.” With these new tariffs, Trump is again engaged in his delusional, destructive tariff tomfoolery. They’ll push up prices, squeeze Americans’ wallets and anger other countries. Trump said his tariffs would boost US manufacturing, but the US has lost 75,000 factory jobs since he returned to office, with many executives complaining about all the herky-jerky uncertainty Trump has wrought. Assessing Trump’s effects on the economy, Atsi Sheth, the chief credit officer for Moody’s Ratings, told the New York Times :“Volatility and unpredictability is the new normal.” Like so much that Trump does, his new tariffs are clearly based on pique and false premises with lots of shamelessness and absurdity thrown in. After the US supreme court overturned Trump’s me-against-the-whole-world tariffs in February, Trump, refusing to let go of his tariff toy, turned to other strategies. To justify his new 50% tariffs against Canada – which are piled atop numerous other tariffs he’s imposed on a country that was long the US’s closest ally – Trump relied on a never before used provision of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, a widely derided 1930 law that greatly worsened the Great Depression of a century ago. With this new tariff, placed on hockey sticks, paper, plywood, dairy products and many other Canadian goods, Trump invoked a Smoot-Hawley provision that allows retaliation against countries that engage in trade discrimination against the US. In making that case, Trump’s exhibit No 1 is something rather preposterous, or should I say rather shameless? After Trump imposed high, punitive tariffs on Canada last year, 11 of Canada’s 13 provinces and territories halted liquor imports from the US because they were so irate about those tariffs along with Trump’s outlandish and belittling statements that he wanted to make Canada the 51st state. The White House called this ban on US liquor illegal discrimination, while Canadians view it as a type of traditional trade retaliation that countries engage in when another country – here the US – slaps tariffs on them, a situation made worse by the fact that Trump’s tariffs against Canada are an egregious violation of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. Trump also insists that Canada has improperly discriminated against the US because Canada imposed a 25% tariff on select US-made cars after Trump slapped a 25% tariff on Canadian-made cars. He is essentially telling Canada: I have a right to punch you in the nose whenever I want. But if you punch me back, that’s illegal discrimination against the US. That’s the logic of America’s leading stable genius, who also offered another far-fetched justification for his decision: “We’re going to put a big tariff on Canada because of the smoke,” he told reporters on Friday, referring to wildfire smoke that has crossed the US border. Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, isn’t happy about Trump’s painful, new 50% tariff. “We won’t back down,” he said on social media. “The fastest and only way to get US alcohol back on Ontario shelves is for the U.S. to drop its illegal tariffs on Canada.” As for the new tariffs hitting more than 80 countries, Trump, who over the years has shown next to no concern about worker exploitation, turned rather surprisingly to the issue of forced labor to slap on those tariffs. After the supreme court overturned his Liberation Day tariffs, Trump hit dozens of nations with a replacement tariff that would expire after 150 days. Eager to follow the boss’s wishes and impose a new tariff as soon as that one expired, Trump’s toadies uncovered a trade law provision that lets Washington punish countries that fail to take enough action against forced labor. No surprise here: Trump’s US trade representative issued a report that made the boss happy. That report found that dozens of countries, including Canada, the UK, Australia, Norway, Japan and China, plus the European Union, were not doing enough to enforce a prohibition against forced labor. That report pointed to forced labor in producing rice in Myanmar, tobacco in Malawi, and cotton and polysilicon in China. It’s deeply perplexing that Trump is punishing some of these trading partners. Norway has pioneered laws to crack down on forced labor in overseas supply chains, while the European Union’s new ban on goods produced with forced labor will take effect in December 2027. Canada already bans imports made with forced labor, and is moving to strengthen that prohibition. It’s not as if Trump has shown much concern before about worker exploitation or forced labor. In 1998, Trump agreed to pay $1.375m to settle a lawsuit brought by undocumented Polish workers who said they were underpaid for their work demolishing a department store to make way for Trump Tower in New York. Some trade experts criticize Trump for slamming all these longtime allies about forced labor even as he is pushing vigorously to improve ties with China, which the Biden administration found to have serious forced labor problems in its Xinjiang region. Trump’s newfound concern about forced labor rings especially hollow considering that his administration chopped more than $500m from the labor department’s efforts to investigate and fight against forced labor, child labor and human trafficking. “This was a completely indiscriminate meat ax that was taken to these projects, and workers will suffer,” said Thea Lee, who served as the labor department’s deputy undersecretary for international labor affairs under Biden. Bemoaning that $500m-plus in cuts, Kelly Fay Rodriguez, who was Biden’s special representative for international labor affairs, told Equal Times. “Unfortunately, it is extremely likely that child labor and forced labor practices will increase. We know these problems are endemic but … we’ve wiped out the resources and the prioritization for fighting them.” Imagine a world where Donald Trump truly cared about worker exploitation and forced labor. He would be pushing to raise the absurdly low $7.25-an-hour federal minimum wage – something he has never lifted a finger to do. He would be increasing, rather than cutting, the number of safety inspectors for mines and factories. He would be pushing to strengthen – instead of repeatedly moving to weaken – the nation’s labor unions, long the most effective voice in fighting against worker exploitation. He would be pressuring China’s President Xi Jinping to stop all the forced labor in his country. But that would be a make-believe Donald Trump – he cares far more about what’s good for billionaires than what’s good for workers. Bottom line: there remains far too much forced labor in the world – more than 27 million children, women and men are in forced labor, according to the International Labor Organization. It would be great if Donald Trump sincerely seized on that issue rather than used it as an insincere pretext to clobber other nations with tariffs. Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

title: Netanyahu and Zelenskyy to arrive in Washington for Lindsey Graham funeral
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: Both men scheduled to meet Trump at time where US policy towards wars in Iran and Ukraine in state of flux
body_text: Benjamin Netanyahu and Volodymyr Zelenskyy are set to arrive in Washington simultaneously with the goal of winning the ear of Donald Trump at pivotal moments in wars affecting their respective countries. Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, and Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, will attend Tuesday’s funeral of Lindsey Graham, the former Republican senator for South Carolina, who died suddenly on 11 July and was a close ally of both leaders. Both men are scheduled to meet the president at a time when US policy towards the wars in Iran and Ukraine is in a state of flux. The meeting between Trump and Netanyahu will be the first between the two leaders since February, when they were in lockstep preparing for strikes against Iran that began on 28 February. Since then, tensions between the pair have risen as the war has drifted inconclusively, with Trump calling the Israeli premier “crazy” and declaring: “Without me, there would be no Israel.” Fueling the tensions between the pair is continuing uncertainty over Trump’s zigzagging approach to the regime in Tehran, which he once openly supported toppling – in line with the stance of Netanyahu, who has long plotted its overthrow. Last month, the US signed a memorandum of understanding that was meant to institute a 60-day ceasefire in the conflict, during which Iran would reopen the strategically vital strait of Hormuz and negotiations would begin over the country’s nuclear program. Netanyahu is not believed to have been consulted on the deal, which some analysts say took little account of Israel’s interests. Trump this month publicly repudiated the agreement as Iran continued to attack commercial ships in the strait. US forces struck Iranian targets for 13 consecutive nights as Trump threatened to escalate further by hitting civilian infrastructure. In recent days, however, the conflict has been paused once again amid reports that negotiations have resumed and Pentagon concerns that US missile stocks are running low. Axios reported that Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, had recommended stopping the bombing campaign because it had reached the limits of effectiveness. Netanyahu is also believed to be unhappy over a deal announced last week between the US and Saudi Arabia allowing for a civil Saudi nuclear program. Zelenskyy’s presence is equally significant as it coincides with signs of a dramatic change of Trump administration posture in Ukraine’s war with Russia – with the White House appearing more supportive of Kyiv’s position than at any time since Trump’s return to office. The rightwing social media influencer Laura Loomer gave the latest signal of a sea change in Washington’s position when she met Zelenskyy in the Ukrainian capital last week, before publicly recanting her previous support for Russia. Trump and Zelenskyy had a cordial meeting at this month’s Nato summit in Ankara that contrasted starkly with last year’s bitter confrontation in the White House, when Trump openly berated his Ukrainian counterpart and told him: “You don’t have the cards.” Trump has long been open in voicing his preference for Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin. Zelenskyy posted on social media at the weekend that he had instructed Ukraine’s intelligence services to share information on Russia’s support for Iran in the conflict with the US. He wrote on X that Ukraine had recorded Russian satellite surveillance of US military facilities in the Gulf, and that of Washington’s allies in the region. Graham – a hawkish supporter of Israel and fierce critic of Iran’s Islamic regime – met Zelenskyy in Kyiv, the day before his death, and had been in the process of advancing a Senate bill to strengthen sanctions on Russia.

title: Fauci expressed disillusionment with ‘rambling, crazy’ Trump in journal
author: Martin Pengelly
summary: Former top US health official wrote about challenging interactions with publicity-fixated Trump during Covid
body_text: Diary entries released by a Republican senator in an attempt to damage Anthony Fauci also show the former top US government science adviser’s growing disillusionment with Donald Trump in the first year of the Covid-19 pandemic, branding the president “rambling”, “crazy”, “desperate”, “bumbling”, “incompetent”, “an idiot”, “a true embarrassment”, “totally nuts” and “truly an obnoxious adolescent”. From the earliest days of the crisis six years ago, Fauci noted in his journal challenging interactions with the publicity-fixated Trump. On 27 February 2020, amid the first stirrings of public alarm, he wrote of a surprise late-night call, in which the US president “wanted to chat about the coronavirus situation in general”. For “about 20-25 minutes”, Fauci wrote, he “encouraged [Trump] not to underplay the seriousness of the situation since if it turns out bad, it would look like he is covering up. I even spoke to him from a political standpoint that his chances for re-election might be more damaged if he downplayed the potential spread of virus in the USA than if he said we may face serious problems and even if the Stock Market goes down further, he was at least honest and the country would respect him for it. “I thought that he heard what I said, but the next day, he again underplayed it.” By 14 March, in the thick of the first Covid shutdowns, Fauci is bemoaning Trump’s fixation on “the fluff of ratings and publicity. And so he wants us to do 2 press conferences/day – one in AM and one in PM … We now will have no time to do work.” ‘A true embarrassment’ On 22 May, Fauci wrote that Trump is “getting out of control in pushing to open up the country and get the economy back before election day. He is desparate [sic]. This is all about re-election.” That proved correct. In October 2020, Fauci wrote: “As the [presidential] election nears, the cases increase and surges are inevitable as we enter cooler weather. Trump is on the campaign trail spewing nonsense. He is really out of control. A true embarrassment.” By March 2021, having watched Trump attempt to retain power despite electoral defeat in a way that reminds him “historically of Hitler”, Fauci writes: “He is truly an obnoxious adolescent.” Fauci’s diary entries read as raw source material for reporting on the pandemic and its politics. He admitted to being a source himself, and worried about being suspected as a leaker, but wrote in late May 2020: “Had long conversation on ‘background’ with [Washington Post reporter] Bob Woodward who is writing a book on the early response to Covid in the USA. I provided him with some history of our response in early January and into February. Will tlak [sic] more with him tomorow [sic].” The release of Fauci’s diaries was orchestrated by Rand Paul, the Republican senator from Kentucky, who has long voiced skepticism about the Covid-19 response Fauci led, accusing him of needlessly shutting down the country while covering the supposed truth that the virus was human-made, and that US-funded research contributed to its creation. Fauci has consistently said the virus originated in animal-to-human transmission, the generally accepted theory. The two men have clashed before. At a hearing in January 2022, for example, Fauci told Paul his attacks put him in danger, “kindl[ing] the crazies out there and I have threats upon my life, harassment of my family and my children with obscene phone calls because people are lying about me”. Fauci also charged: “You are making a catastrophic epidemic for your political gain.” Paul and Fauci will square off again on Wednesday, at a hearing for which Fauci, 85, was compelled to appear. Paul has said he will “make sure Fauci answers for his dangerous decisions and the consequences they had for millions”. In the rightwing press, coverage of the Fauci diaries has focused on his notes about his rise to global fame amid the Covid response, particularly about meeting celebrities or appearing on TV and in the press. The singer Joan Baez and actors Julia Roberts and Sean Penn are among names prominently noted. Fauci does seem to have been proud of his newfound celebrity. On 13 July 2020, his relationship with Trump rapidly souring, he turned to his diary. “Major, Major show of support for me for multiple and varied sectors,” he writes. “Most peo[p]le expressing outrage that the trump administration woud [sic] be so bumbling and incompetent to try to discredit the most credible scientist in the world.”

title: Oil prices fall as US pauses strikes on Iran over strait of Hormuz
author: Jasper Jolly
summary: Brent crude drops 9% to below $88 a barrel, prompting UK government bond yields to fall
body_text: Oil prices have dropped sharply as traders bet that a pause in US attacks on Iran could prevent an escalation in the conflict that would further restrict global supply. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, initially fell 9% to below $88 a barrel on Monday after climbing to $100 last week, when the Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea. An attempted recovery later in the day was halted by comments from Donald Trump that the US was having “good talks” with Iran, pushing Brent back down about 8%. The retreat from the short-lived return to more than $100 a barrel came as the US and Iran paused hostilities after 13 days of fighting, amid Trump’s comments suggesting that talks to end the conflict had resumed. Iran said it had stopped “retaliatory” attacks after two nights without American missiles, after the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, told journalists on Sunday that Trump had decided to pause the attacks to allow more time for diplomacy. Separate reports claimed that US military officials had told Trump that the bombing campaign had reached the limits of its effectiveness and warned of dwindling stocks of munitions. The comments raised hopes that a renewed focus on diplomatic solutions could de-escalate the regional conflict, which since the end of February has disrupted flows of oil and gas from Gulf states via the strait of Hormuz, and in recent weeks has interrupted vessels leaving the Red Sea via the Bab al-Mandab strait, too. However, the brief reprieve from rising oil prices was met with scepticism by some market observers. “We’ve been here multiple times since March,” said Ole Hvalbye, an analyst at SEB Research. “And each rally on a leak has faded as substance failed to materialise.” John Evans, an analyst at PVM, said he expected oil prices would only be able to fall further if there was a meaningful decline in demand, “not questionable mini-ceasefires”. He said: “The market seems to be forever seeking good news from an arena that really is not providing any. A stay of military strikes might seem an improvement, but it does not come with any guarantees that oil will soon flow from the area.” Analysts at Deutsche Bank led by Jim Reid said the 10% increase in Brent crude prices last week had “added to fears that the global economy was facing a prolonged inflation shock, and that the Fed might need to hike rates more aggressively in response”. The expectation of higher inflation caused by rising global energy costs has put pressure on central banks to raise interest rates. In recent weeks that has pushed up sovereign bond yields, which move inversely to prices. However, the oil price drop on Monday prompted yields to fall. The yield on UK 10-year government debt dropped below 5%, down 0.05 percentage points during the day. The rate-sensitive two-year yield fell 0.06 percentage points to 4.35%. Higher oil prices could harm Trump politically, with many members of the Republican party nervous of the effects of inflation on their prospects at midterm elections in November. Some Federal Reserve policymakers may feel the need to raise interest rates to try to counteract price increases, a move that could slow the US economy – despite Trump’s wish for lower rates.

title: Mitch McConnell still not cleared to resume Senate duties, office says
author: Anna Betts
summary: Kentucky senator has been absent and not seen in public since mid-June after he was hospitalized due to a fall
body_text: US senator Mitch McConnell is still not cleared to return to work, his office confirmed on Monday, six weeks after he was hospitalized after a fall at his home. An update released alongside a new photograph of the Republican lawmaker – one of the highest-profile figures in Congress, as a former Senate majority leader – said he was undergoing “intense physical therapy” and is “working hard” to get back to his duties. “I’m still working hard to get back to my full schedule of work in the Senate and in Kentucky, keeping up with intense physical therapy per my doctors’ orders,” McConnell, of Kentucky, said in a statement released by his office on Monday. In the statement, he said that he wouldn’t be able to make it to Kentucky this coming weekend for an annual Fancy Farm picnic. “There’s no place I’d rather be on the first Saturday in August than with the good people of western Kentucky, feasting on pork and mutton,” said McConnell, 84. “I hate that I’ll miss the fun this year, but I’m sending my best wishes to the St Jerome community for a successful picnic,” he said. “As always, I appreciate all of your continued well wishes, and I’m looking forward to getting back to the Senate and to Kentucky soon.” McConnell has been absent from the Senate and not seen in public since mid-June, when his office said he was hospitalized and recovering, but did not elaborate on his condition. After weeks of silence, and mounting speculation about his health, McConnell’s office provided an update on 12 July, where they said that he was recovering at a rehabilitation center after having been admitted to the hospital on 14 June after suffering a fall at his home that left him “briefly unconscious”. In the 12 July statement, the senator also disclosed that he had also been dealing with “a mild case of pneumonia” and explained the long silence about his condition by saying that “folks of my generation often hesitate to share the vulnerability that comes with growing older”. McConnell has missed 38 Senate votes since he was hospitalized. He said last year that he would not seek re-election, and is set to retire from the Senate at the end of his term, in January. McConnell’s office also released an image of the senator with his wife, Elaine Chao, which the caption states was from 26 July. Along with the statement and photograph, McConnell’s office also released a statement from the office of the attending physician (OAP) in US Congress. “OAP physicians visit with the Senator every day, discussing all aspects of his rehabilitation care,” the OAP statement said. “Since his discharge from hospital care, he has maintained a strenuous course of physical therapy and rehabilitation, including multiple sessions a day designed to rebuild strength and reduce the risk of future falls.” “His bout with childhood polio continues to be a significant factor in his mobility,” it added. “He is not yet medically cleared to leave the rehab facility and return to the office.”

title: Fifa president Gianni Infantino called to appear before Congress over Trump ties
author: Ella Brockway
summary: Democrat Jamie Raskin pushes Fifa to release records of contact with Trump, administration and family business
body_text: Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, has launched an investigation into the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, seeking documents that would detail the ties between soccer’s governing body and Donald Trump and his administration. In a Sunday letter, Raskin wrote to Infantino and called for Fifa to provide any documents and communications related to gifts, payments or benefits provided to Trump and his associates, as well as the visitor logs for Fifa’s office space in Trump Tower, which it acquired last year. The committee also requested that Infantino sit for a transcribed interview. Infantino’s relationship with Trump came under scrutiny in the lead-up to this summer’s World Cup. In December, at the World Cup draw in Washington, Trump was awarded a newly created “Fifa peace prize” at the Kennedy Center, where renovations were allegedly “rushed” on the administration’s orders to prepare for the event. Fifa opened its office in Trump Tower in midtown Manhattan last July. Such scrutiny intensified during the World Cup. Trump made several calls to Infantino to lobby for a review of the US striker Folarin Balogun’s controversial red-card suspension before the Americans’ last-16 match against Belgium. Fifa did reverse Balogun’s ban, but the political circus cast a pall over the US team and drew the ire of other teams and associations from around the world. Alongside the leaders of Canada and Mexico, Trump joined Infantino for the World Cup trophy presentation after Spain beat Argentina in the final. The pair, who watched the final together in a glassed-in section of luxury seats, were met with boos from the New York New Jersey Stadium crowd when they took the field. Raskin’s letter references the Department of Justice’s decision to “dismiss the indictments” of defendants in US government investigations into corruption in global soccer, including the 2015 prosecution of more than 20 high-level Fifa officials and sports-marketing executives. “[Y]our election as Fifa president was supposed to mark a red-card break from a decades-long culture of corruption and scandals that dressed down world soccer’s reputation,” Raskin wrote to Infantino in the letter. “Instead, at the start of your tenure, you dismantled Fifa’s ethical guardrails and disabled the organization’s ethics committee by pushing out most of its members. This lack of transparency and oversight has since paved the way for you to ingratiate yourself with the Trump administration via tactics that a New York University law professor and one of your former ethics committeemen described as ‘legal bribery’.” The letter also addresses Fifa’s World Cup ticketing policy, which is already the subject of investigations by several attorneys general in the United States. The use of dynamic pricing drew much criticism during the tournament, leading to big surges and pricing out many fans from attending games. “The most recent quid pro quo that Fifa and President Trump orchestrated is not a victimless crime. It hurts Americans. Fifa has taken its newfound favored status in the Trump administration as a sign that it may rip off its consumers, most notably, by employing illegal price-gouging and fraudulent sales tactics for the World Cup,” Raskin said in the letter. The letter gives a deadline of 9 August to provide the requested documents and schedule the interview. Raskin does not have the power to compel Infantino to appear, given that Democrats do not hold the majority in the House, unless he garners Republican support. Fifa’s interactions with the US government did not end with this summer’s World Cup. The US is expected to be the primary host of the Women’s World Cup in 2031, and the success of this year’s tournament has led many to speculate that the 2038 men’s World Cup could be hosted by the US. Fifa has been approached for comment. Earlier on Monday, Infantino used a 15-part message on Instagram to denounce his critics, accusing them of spreading hate and false narratives. He touted the World Cup as a success. More than 200 Fifa members have endorsed Infantino ahead of the presidential election in March, but some associations have stood in opposition. The Norwegian football federation is planning to submit a formal complaint to Fifa ethics investigations over Trump’s role in the reversal of Balogun’s ban.

title: Trump administration’s revision of Iran war casualties ‘huge disrespect’, say veterans
author: George Chidi
summary: Defense department updated database of casualties to list four service members deceased in ‘Overseas Operations’
body_text: A controversial move by the Pentagon to reclassify casualties in the Iran war is being taken by US military veterans as a sign of disrespect for the dead. “It’s such a huge disrespect for the families,” said Michael E Smith, a retired US rear admiral and the founder of National Security Leaders for America. “To claim that they weren’t killed as a result of the war – oh, it was just overseas operations – is just ludicrous.” In a quiet weekend update to the Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), a military database for displaying casualties, the US Department of Defense – renamed the Department of War under Donald Trump – added more than 140 wounded service members. They also introduced a new casualty category labeled “Overseas Operations” for personnel killed and wounded “starting July 7” which splits the count from the beginning of the US-Israel war on Iran. Four US service members killed in action by Iranian forces fall under that category: 1st Lt Tyler James Feehan, Pvt Isabella Gonzales, Sgt Angel S Rampersad and Sgt Michael Emmanuel Swinton. “I definitely think that this isn’t an issue just about numbers, but also about accountability,” said Tristeza Ordex, a US Marine Corps veteran and the national organizer of partnerships and engagement at VoteVets. “When I was deployed to Afghanistan, I remember attending ramp ceremonies,” she said, referring to an airfield memorial honoring a fallen service member before their casket is loaded on to an aircraft and returned home. Gonzales, 19, was from Carrollton, Texas, near Ordex’s home near Dallas. Gonzales was not yet born when Ordex first enlisted in 2004. “Thinking about it now makes me emotional, to think about how we have people coming home now … 19 years old,” she said. “I think about people like her that were excluded. Not only are Latinos being excluded from so much more and being targeted: we have this person that paid the ultimate sacrifice for this country who isn’t even being recognized as a casualty of this war, so it feels like erasure.” The War Powers Act of 1973 requires the president to end military operations within 60 days unless Congress authorizes an extension, which it has not. The Trump administration has argued that the April ceasefire with Iran paused the clock on 1 May for the conflict’s initial period. The separate casualty count beginning on 7 July follows that interpretation. Smith, who completed combat tours in Iraq, Bosnia and Kosovo, likened the administrative change to the manipulation of Pentagon casualty data last seen in the Vietnam war. “It’s so disrespectful to our service members who gave their lives, and the only reason they died was because Donald Trump decided to do this illegal war,” Smith said. “I mean, clearly the president is very sensitive about the deaths. You know, he is comparing it to Korea and Vietnam. “Obviously their boss doesn’t want to hear about deaths. OK, well, here’s one way we can make it look like there’s not as many deaths.” Joel Valdez, acting Pentagon press secretary, said: “The classification of Iran conflict casualties under Overseas Operations is grounded strictly in a factual basis, not commentary or narrative. We honor our fallen service members forever and always.” The department’s reclassification of Iran war casualties has faced criticism in Washington, including from Thomas Massie, a Republican House member from Kentucky, ousted in a primary earlier this year after repeatedly breaking with the president. “Let me explain this absurd ruse: The Pentagon is pretending there have been two Iran wars separated by a brief cease-fire,” Massie wrote on X on Friday. “The reality: By going more than 90 days without congressional authorization,” the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, “IS BREAKING THE LAW and must be held accountable”. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, a Democrat on the armed services committee, added: “Americans deserve the truth about the human cost of President Trump’s Iran war, and I will not stop fighting until this administration gives our military members and their families the transparency and accountability they deserve.”

title: DNC chair faces growing scrutiny amid financial pressure and internal turmoil
author: Lucy Campbell and Lauren Gambino
summary: Fraught time for Ken Martin as new reporting details cashflow problem and divisions over party’s direction
body_text: Mounting financial pressures and growing internal turmoil at the Democratic National Committee (DNC) have intensified scrutiny of the chair, Ken Martin, as new reporting detailed a deepening cashflow problem, management concerns and widening divisions over the party’s direction less than 100 days before the November midterm elections. The latest reporting has underscored both the committee’s financial distress and the toll it has taken on Martin personally. The New York Times reported that the embattled DNC chair, who took the helm last year, became the subject of an internal HR inquiry after throwing his phone in the direction of a junior aide’s desk during a heated exchange in early July, prompting a formal complaint. The Times, citing people familiar with the matter, also reported that the incident nearly cost him his job and has contributed to growing isolation with the party as the committee grapples with mounting financial strain. The latest revelations include that the DNC put its physical Washington DC headquarters up for collateral last year in order to obtain a $15m line of credit to help invest in off-year elections, Notus reported, citing Washington DC deed records. The New York Times separately reported that the DNC is about $2m in debt, compared with roughly $130m cash on hand held by the Republican National Committee. The committee argued that the arrangement was “not new” and that it had done so to secure loans previously. However, one DNC member told the outlet: “Ken is gaslighting us about the DNC’s finances and not being transparent about the financial situation makes us doubt if he can oversee the DNC during the most important primary of our lifetime.” Another Democrat close to Martin told Notus he had struggled to convince donors to maximize their contributions, which had contributed to the small cash-on-hand total. Adding to the party’s financial woes, the Times reported that the DNC had asked vendors not to send invoices until after the midterm elections in November. Roger Lau, the executive director of the DNC, told the Times in a statement that the bill-deferral discussions were “nothing more than standard negotiations with vendors over contracts and payment processes”. It is an increasingly fraught time for Martin, whose tenure has been marked by turbulence almost since the start, when he became embroiled in a public spat with then vice-chair David Hogg. Their philosophical disagreement proved irreconcilable and Hogg eventually quit. Faith in Martin’s leadership had eroded further following his botched handling of a long-promised autopsy of the 2024 election that ultimately failed to address what actually went wrong for the party – from Gaza to the Biden-Harris transition. The release in May prompted a round of calls for Martin’s resignation. Last week, Martin defended the state of the DNC’s finances in an op-ed on Substack, writing that the committee had made the “conscious decision” to spend the cash it raises on “electoral assets” rather than stockpiling resources. He said the DNC had “done exceptionally better with high-net worth donors”, citing an increase of donations from major donors relative to comparable years. “We must measure success by power built, not simply dollars retained,” he added. But some veteran Democratic fundraisers remain unconvinced. In a Substack essay published on Monday, the former Democratic finance chair and former US ambassador Rufus Gifford argued the party’s financial problems stem from a broader collapse in donor confidence. “I think there is no saving Martin’s chairmanship,” Gifford wrote, arguing that the “two main jobs” of the DNC chair were to “raise money and message relentlessly on every form of media”. The committee, he warned, was at risk of becoming “irrelevant” unless it found a way to restore donor trust and rebuild its national fundraising operation before the 2028 presidential campaign. The reports renewed calls for Martin to step aside, which he has firmly resisted. “Ken Martin must resign,” Congressman Sam Liccardo, a California Democrat, wrote on X. “As Democrats, we have become too captured by failing strategies. We must fail forward, and pivot. The urgency of this moment will not reward – and our children will not forgive – torpidity.” But at a campaign event in Pennsylvania on Sunday, Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, expressed confidence in Martin, telling reporters covering the rally that the DNC chair had his “full support”.

title: Michigan progressive Abdul El-Sayed says ‘ogre’ remark not directed at rival
author: Robert Mackey and Lauren Gambino
summary: El-Sayed says in TV debate ‘ogre on a pike’ Zoom comment was in reference to John Fetterman, not Haley Stevens
body_text: The Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said his comments that progressives need to put the head of an “ogre” on a pike was in reference to the Senator John Fetterman – not his opponent, Representative Haley Stevens. In a televised debate on Monday, the final head-to-head before the state’s 4 August primary, the moderator asked El-Sayed whether he regretted his comments made in a Zoom meeting, in which, according to leaked audio published by Politico, he suggested that if “you put one ogre on a pike, and then everyone else gets the message”. The comments drew immediate backlash from several high-profile Democrats and charges of sexism by those who believed the remark was a reference to Stevens. “Many people took offense to that,” the debate moderator, Roop Raj, noted. “Do you regret any of the comments that you’ve made?” El-Sayed did not reply directly, but said he had been speaking of supporting a primary challenge to Fetterman, the towering Pennsylvania Democrat who campaigned as a progressive but has moved to the right since taking office. “I was referring to a guy named John Fetterman, who’s a senator from Pennsylvania who has done terrible things, got elected on a set of values, and is now completely throwing those values in the mud,” El-Sayed said in the debate. Fetterman and El-Sayed have clashed mightily over the senator’s increasingly robust support for Israel, and in recent weeks Fetterman has said he would consider leaving the Democratic party if it became “anti-Israel” . During the hour-long debate, El-Sayed pushed back on criticism that he had failed to foster a spirit of political civility as candidate, noting that he recently chided his supporters for mocking Stevens’s accent. “Look, I took to Twitter last week and said that the tone in which people talk about my opponent is unkind, and I asked anybody who supported me to not talk about her that way,” he said. Before the moderator moved on, Stevens quipped: “Thank you for clarifying that you didn’t call me an ogre.” The expensive and increasingly bitter Democratic primary to replace retiring senator Gary Peters has evolved into a proxy fight over the party’s future, pitting the establishment-backed moderate Stevens against El-Sayed, a progressive former Detroit health director. The candidates have split sharply on the issue of Israel, with Stevens identifying as a “proud pro-Israel Democrat” and accepting substantial support from American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). By contrast, El-Sayed has called Israel’s campaign in Gaza a “genocide” and has denounced US arms support for Israel. Last week, Stevens picked up the endorsement of Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer, who El-Sayed challenged unsuccessfully in the 2018 gubernatorial primary. El-Sayed has rallied the party’s left flank, and has been endorsed by the independent senator Bernie Sanders and New York congressmember Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. The dueling coalitions have turned Michigan’s closely watched Senate contest into a clear test of whether the twin forces of anti-Washington sentiment and progressive energy can overcome broad institutional support in a presidential battleground state. Asked about whether he would call himself a progressive or a democratic socialist, El-Sayed replied: “I’m not a socialist. I’m just a capitalist who understands how capitalism works. The biggest threat to capitalism was never the idea of government regulation. It was always monopoly.” The contest – one of the few open-seat races this cycle – is widely viewed as central to the battle for Senate control. Donald Trump won Michigan in 2024, making it among Republicans’ most promising pick-up opportunities. Former congressman Mike Rogers, who narrowly lost Michigan’s 2024 Senate race to Elissa Slotkin, cleared the Republican field early and has spent months preparing for the general election. Earlier on Monday, Rogers appeared on stage with Trump at a rally in Milford, Michigan, where he promised to help the president enact his agenda, if elected.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Disastrous drone expo’s organiser appears in Kyiv court
author: Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies
summary: Russian attack killed 11 at publicly promoted event attended by military and state officials; Zelenskyy heads for Washington. What we know on day 1,616
body_text: A Ukrainian court remanded in custody the organiser of a weapons exhibition that was struck by Russia in an attack that killed at least 11 people. Prosecutors brought a case against Vasyl Goncharuk, head of the Armada weapons industry association, accusing him of negligence leading to loss of life after the Russian ballistic missile strike on a shooting range outside Kyiv on Friday. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it “certainly should not have been taking place there”. Russia’s defence ministry confirmed it hit the site during “a demonstration of Ukrainian and foreign-made” drones. Goncharuk appeared at the Kyiv court limping and said he sustained light injuries in the attack. Prosecutors have said the weapons association invited more than 300 people including military personnel, state representatives and business figures without official authorisation, providing only a small shelter. The event was even promoted on social media. Agence France-Presse said its reporters saw homes in ruins and victims in body bags after the attack. Previous incidents of Russian attacks on openly held Ukrainian military gatherings have also triggered outcry and resignations. A Wildberries warehouse in the Koledino district of Moscow was reportedly on fire on Tuesday morning after being hit by drones as the Russian capital came under attack. The distribution complex for the Amazon-like chain had been targeted previously. A steel factory in Chekhnov, Moscow oblast, was also hit, the Kyiv Independent reported. The Russian regional governor, ‌Andrei Vorobyov, said an apartment ⁠building in Chekhov was damaged. Drones targeted other areas including Podolsk, ‌Domodedovo and Kolomna. The Pentagon official tasked with building ⁠a domestic drone industry said on Monday the US was still far behind Ukraine’s production capabilities. Travis Metz, chief operating officer of the Defense Innovation Unit, told Reuters that Ukraine would produce 6m-7m small first-person-view attack drones this year – roughly 500,000 a month. By comparison, the ‌Pentagon’s $1.1bn programme will have ordered ‌just under 200,000 altogether by February. But the US would catch up and lead the sector, he predicted. The Pentagon is insisting military drones must be made with US parts to foster “a wholly domestic” supply chain. None of the drones from the 19 companies competing an August test event may contain banned parts like Chinese-made motors or battery packs. “It’s an increasingly difficult thing,” Metz said. Ukrainian companies competing in the test, called Gauntlet II, are being required to localise production in the US as a condition of future orders. All ⁠100 members of the US Senate have been invited to ⁠a meeting ⁠on Tuesday evening with Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Ukraine’s president will be in Washington for the funeral of the late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who was a strong and influential supporter of Ukraine. A Senate aide said voting might also begin during Zelenskyy’s visit on a bill to impose sanctions on Russia that was championed by Graham. Zelenskyy is due to meet on Tuesday with Donald Trump. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, the war in Ukraine has changed dramatically. The Guardian’s Luke Harding looks at who has the advantage in the war now and how Zelenskyy’s strategy has shifted. Andy Burnham welcomed Zelenskyy in his first meeting with another world leader since becoming the UK prime minister, writes Pippa Crerar. “It is intended to send a very clear message,” Burnham told him. “We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.” Burnham said Britain was providing new jamming technology to Ukraine that would “help them to hit their targets and help save Ukrainian lives”. The system is known as Stone Cloak. Zelenskyy posted that he was “grateful” to Britain for “today’s decision to provide Ukraine with electronic warfare technologies” that would “certainly be useful on the battlefield”. Romania’s ⁠foreign ministry ⁠said it had expelled a ⁠diplomat at Russia’s embassy after repeated violations of ⁠its national airspace by drones. Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots have shot down three drones in as many days. The Russian ambassador was shown drone fragments that Romanian authorities identified as a Russian “Shahed model”. Two people were hurt in May when a drone smashed into an apartment building in the Romanian city of Galati near the border with Ukraine. Ukraine ⁠struck a Russian export ⁠terminal in ⁠the Rostov region, as well ⁠as oil facilities in ⁠the Yaroslavl and Udmurtia ‌regions, Zelenskyy said on Monday. “Last night, our long-range sanctions were effective in the Rostov region. An export terminal approximately 250km (155 miles) from the frontline was hit,” he posted. “Deep strikes also targeted oil facilities in the Yaroslavl region and the Udmurt Republic, which is 1,300km from Ukraine’s state border.” Five people were reported killed in Russia’s Rostov region bordering Ukraine. Russian ⁠forces meanwhile struck three Ukrainian ports, including ⁠fuel ⁠loading and storage facilities at the port ⁠of Odesa, the defence ‌ministry in Moscow said ‌on Monday. Russian strikes on frontline localities in eastern Ukraine killed ⁠seven people and ⁠injured more than 20 on Monday, officials said. Prosecutors in the Donetsk region said three people died ⁠in two areas near the contested city of Kostiantynivka. A fourth person was killed near Kramatorsk, a heavily defended “fortress” city considered critical to Ukraine’s defences. Prosecutors said a total of 18 people were ‌injured throughout Donetsk region. In Ukraine’s adjacent Dnipropetrovsk region, the governor, Oleksandr Hanzha, said three people were killed and six wounded in more than 50 drone and artillery attacks on five districts. Two people died near the town of Nikopol and one person was killed near the town of Syneklykove. Over the border in Russia’s Belgorod region, a Ukrainian drone struck a building, killing one person and injuring two. Donald Trump’s administration has told members ⁠of Congress it will not finish spending $400m in aid to Ukraine until fiscal year 2029, even as Kyiv runs critically low on weapons. Democrats and some of Trump’s fellow Republicans have criticised the Pentagon for sitting on aid for Kyiv that members of both parties pushed through last year. In May, the Pentagon sent a letter to lawmakers outlining its spending ⁠plan. It covers $200m for weapons, ammunition and explosives, $99.9m for vehicles, spares and equipment and $100m for services such as transportation of defence articles to Ukraine. The funds still have not been put to use.

title: Who is Ben Carroll, the man who has become Victoria’s new premier?
author: Benita Kolovos and Stephanie Convery
summary: Carroll, who was elected to parliament in 2012 and says he has always been ambitious, has been sworn in as premier after Jacinta Allan resigned
body_text: In 2023, when then-public transport minister Ben Carroll failed in his surprising bid to secure the leadership of the Victorian Labor party, he told a press conference: “I was always very keen to rise.” The premier Daniel Andrews had resigned, believing he had locked in his succession plan: his loyal deputy Jacinta Allan as premier, and treasurer Tim Pallas as deputy. But Carroll, a relatively little-known junior minister from Labor’s diminished right faction, refused to fall into line. What was meant to be a short, box-ticking caucus meeting turned into a marathon debate, with Carroll threatening to challenge Allan for the leadership unless he was made deputy. The standoff reportedly provoked an expletive-laden outburst from Andrews, but Carroll got his way – and the job. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Asked about the meeting just hours later, Carroll replied that he’d always wanted to rise up the party’s ranks. “I’ve had 14 portfolios over six years … and I’m always looking to see how I can continue to increase my contribution to this outstanding Labor government,” he said. Less than three years on, he become premier, just four months out from a state election. It came after Allan stepped down as premier on Tuesday morning, and said Carroll had her ‘unqualified support’. Carroll, 51, was elected to parliament in 2012 as the member for Niddrie in Melbourne’s west, encompassing Essendon West, Keilor East, and Airport West, where he grew up and still lives with his wife, Fiona, and daughter, Madeliene. It was in his home suburb that he got his first job, at Kmart, joining the Shop Distributive and Allied Employees Association (SDA) and being introduced to unionism. Carroll has claimed his journey into politics truly began in 1996, when he was offered a tour around Canberra by Simon Crean, then federal member for Hotham, at the same time that Bill Clinton was in town. He shook the US president’s hand, and joined the Niddrie Labor branch the same year. After graduating university, Carroll became a solicitor and worked in insurance, before the Bracks government came to power in 1999. He worked for then-senator Stephen Conroy in cabinet before being preselected over Jaclyn Symes to stand in Niddrie in a 2012 byelection. After entering state parliament, he held numerous portfolios including industry, roads, employment, youth justice and corrections, until Andrews’ resignation in 2023. Under Allan’s cabinet reshuffle after her elevation, Carroll was given his choice of portfolio – as is tradition – but the new premier showed her mistrust by excluding him from the expenditure review committee, cabinet’s most senior decision-making body. Carroll took on the education portfolio. During his tenure, Victoria had its best ever Naplan results, ranking first or second in 18 of 20 measures in 2025, with the highest number of students performing at “strong” or above. He also oversaw the state’s introduction of mandatory phonics classes in schools, a method that is divisive among academics and the powerful Australian Education Union, but that some teachers claim has a remarkable effect on children’s reading. But he’s also been at the helm for some serious errors, such as the discovery of mistakes in VCE maths and chemistry exams in 2023, and the 2024 “cheat sheet” bungle, when exam content for 65 subjects was accidentally published and circulated widely weeks before students sat the tests. A review into the incident led to Carroll sacking the entire board of the curriculum authority. Most recently, he’s been overseeing protracted negotiations between the government and the state’s teachers, with AEU Victoria members taking industrial action for the first time in 13 years in March, and again just last week. Carroll’s name has been associated with a possible leadership spill in the Labor party for months, with momentum building before parliament rose for a winter break in June. Poor polling and Allan’s weak personal approval ratings, rising support for One Nation and concerns about Allan’s response to organised crime infiltrating the state’s Big Build, via the construction union, all contributed. At a press conference at that time, Carroll repeatedly dismissed suggestions he was positioning himself as a challenger, telling reporters: “I’ve got the job that I want.” “We have a premier, and she’s working harder than anyone every day. I want to serve Jacinta Allan. I’ve got a young daughter at home, and I couldn’t be more proud to make sure she grows up knowing that I supported Jacinta Allan to be a world-class premier and get re-elected in her own right,” he said. He would not be asking Allan to step aside the next day, he said, before turning to the premier and saying: “I can look her in the eye and say that.” A spill did not eventuate at the party room meeting the next day. However, Carroll emerged from the meeting as he did in 2023, perhaps revealing a little more than he intended, declaring himself a “marathon runner” when asked if he had missed his chance to launch a challenge. Carroll is understood to be in favour of calling for a royal commission into Big Build corruption allegations, also believing he’d be better able to resolve the pay dispute between the government and public school teachers, and improve the party’s economic credentials and supporting businesses.
