title: Javier Milei accuses US Democrats of financing ‘anti-Argentina campaign’ at World Cup
author: Facundo Iglesia in Buenos Aires and Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
summary: President also blames Brazil and Mexico and says online critics ‘do not want the ideas of freedom to succeed’
body_text: More than a week has passed since Ferran Torres scored the extra-time goal that gave Spain its second World Cup, but – at least for Argentina’s president – the tournament is not over. Javier Milei has claimed that a coordinated “anti-Argentina campaign” was behind criticism of the country’s team, accusations of racism among its fans and conspiracy theories alleging that Lionel Messi’s side was secretly being favoured by Fifa. Now, the far-right president has taken the narrative a step further, alleging that the supposed campaign was financed by the US Democratic party and the governments of Brazil and Mexico. “It was the work of progressive minds who do not want the ideas of freedom to succeed,” claimed the self-styled libertarian in an interview with a local radio station on Sunday. He went on to claim that the “government of Brazil”, led by the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, had allegedly provided the largest share of the funding. Analysts in Argentina said Milei had embraced the narrative as a distraction from his plummeting popularity, while others argued that the “real anti-Argentina campaign” was the one the president was waging “with his chainsaw” austerity plan. Yet the narrative has gained traction, even reaching people who do not support Milei. Pablo Torres, a 52-year-old bookseller from Buenos Aires who “never voted for him and never would”, said there had been a social media “bombardment” against the country that left him feeling “outrage” and “disgust”. He said some of the accusations of racism had come from “great colonial powers that enslaved people, trafficked enslaved people and decimated populations”, adding: “They denied the existence of the black population in Argentina, and ignored our idiosyncrasies and our history … We are a welcoming home for all nations.” During the tournament, incidents involving racist behaviour by some Argentine supporters drew widespread attention. Hours before the final, the US actor Samuel L Jackson posted an Instagram story that said: “Dear black people, please do not cheer or root for Argentina to win the Fifa World Cup. Argentina has historically been one of, if not the most, racist countries in the world.” The post prompted reactions even from human rights organisations such as Amnesty International Argentina, which acknowledged racism in the country but criticised “reducing the country to a stereotype”. Milei, meanwhile, posted that the criticism could be attributed to Argentina’s opposition, which had “validated the woke movement that is now accusing us of being racist”. Over the weekend, he also decided to blame Brazil – while on Brazilian soil. On Saturday, the Argentinian president attended the launch of the presidential campaign of the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro and Lula’s main challenger in October’s presidential election. In his speech, as well as calling Lula a “thief” and a “prisoner” – prompting a strong reaction from the Brazilian government – Milei said: “If you examine the data from the recent anti-Argentina campaign, the place from which the most attacks came was Brazil.” He reinforced the claim on Sunday, this time adding Mexico and the US Democratic party. The digital anthropologist Mercedes Máspero analysed more than 2m posts on social media and wrote that she had found “some undeniable patterns” of orchestration such as the repeated use of variations of “disgusting human beings” in different languages. Even so, it was “a tough call” to describe it as a coordinated campaign “because the narrative is incredibly widespread”, she wrote. Natalia Aruguete, a researcher at Argentina’s National Scientific and Technical Research Council who specialises in social media and political agendas, said she had seen “no evidence of a large-scale coordinated operation”, despite the existence of “a hostile, widespread and transnational conversation centred on Argentina”. “Brazil had a significant presence [in those messages],” she added, “particularly in the conversation about racism, but … Milei’s accusation of alleged Brazilian involvement was not backed up by any public evidence.” Some critics said that the last time the idea of such a campaign was propagated by the state was during the brutal 1976–83 dictatorship, whose crimes Milei has repeatedly downplayed. During the 1978 World Cup, hosted by Argentina, the military junta claimed that criticism of the regime’s human rights violations was part of an “anti-Argentina campaign”. Aruguete said Milei had turned a “diverse online conversation” into a political conflict that fits his narrative of a “culture war” against the left, at a time when his administration is facing “internal deterioration”: inflation appears to be under control, but rising unemployment and corruption scandals have driven the president’s popularity to its lowest point since taking office. The narrative that suggests Argentinians are all victims of a supposedly orchestrated campaign by leftwing foreign governments “allows Milei to shift the focus of the debate away from his own governance issues and on to an external adversary”, said Aruguete.

title: Mary Beth Barone on provocative jokes, Palestine and manosphere misogyny: ‘It’s hard to stomach that those are my co-workers’
author: Owen Myers
summary: The comedian and actor’s new Netflix special is a gleefully absurd take on politics and potty-mouthed humor
body_text: Mary Beth Barone knows exactly who will be offended by her new Netflix special. “JK Rowling, Republicans, establishment Democrats, the British, the Irish and Zionists,” she tells me, reading a list from her Notes app. Then there’s “Katy Kats – which is what Katy Perry calls her fans – and male comedians and one specific girl named Tatiana”. When informed that this encompasses over half of the population of the US, she beams. Barone’s comedy is a delicate balance between sweetness and cynicism. In her standup she’ll adopt a ditzy pose while she tears down morally bankrupt politicians, sends up cis male entitlement or implores her audience to have sex with moderates in the hope of bringing them over to the left. In the past five years, she has edged her way closer to the mainstream with a Comedy Central web-series, a couple of standup spots on Jimmy Fallon’s late-night show, and a podcast co-hosted with her friend Benito Skinner that is so popular it has its own merch line. The past 12 months have seen her career go into overdrive: now she is the co-lead of a wildly popular TV show (Overcompensating, created by Skinner), chats to the A-list on the Golden Globes’ red carpet and sits front row at New York fashion week. She says that her Netflix special, Galaxy Brain, is one of the most meaningful milestones yet. “So many of the goalposts have changed [for comedians] with the internet, but the one constant is the hour-long special with an esteemed network or streamer,” Barone says, tucking into a plate of scrambled eggs at a Brooklyn cafe. “With the special, it feels like you’ve achieved something pretty rare and they’re betting on you.” Galaxy Brain is a riot, 55 minutes of whip-smart laughs that tackle all the no-nos of polite dinner party conversation – sex and politics, bad men and good girls – with gusto. Barone describes the Israel-Palestine conflict as a “genocide” twice (“just in case you didn’t hear it the first time”), and later invites the audience to cheer if they like doggy style. In the most outrageous tonal shift, she caps off a critique of Maga amorality by conceding that the Trump-aligned draconian Project 2025 was at least focused in its aim to take from the poor and give to the rich. “That shit was airtight,” she says. “That shit was like a pussy in a denim romper.” She then launches into a manic impression of a vagina with its air supply cut off, clawing at fabric and screaming to be let out. “It sounds cheesy to be like, ‘I want to make people think,’” she says. “But I feel that’s one of the core tenets of being a comedian. With the special it was like, ‘How can we look at darker, heavier themes in the dumbest way possible?’ The goal was that it’s so dumb that it comes back around to being smart.” Her approach wasn’t so different when hosting the Golden Globes official red carpet live stream this year. Dressed to the nines, Barone teased out a looser side to celebrities with absurd questions that cut through media-trained platitudes. It felt like many A-listers’ realest red carpet interview in memory: The Rock offered to pick up Barone with one arm, Tessa Thompson gamely played “pork, marry, kill” with fellow nominees – both human and Na’vi – and Hudson Williams of Heated Rivalry was forced to ponder whether it was tougher to be a gay male hockey player or a straight male flight attendant. “I wanted to make everyone feel comfortable and feel like they didn’t have to do the hard work,” says Barone, who worked on the jokes with the comedian George Civeris. “I’ve been on the other side of it where I’ve been asked questions and everything I’ve ever known has escaped my brain and I can’t form a sentence … So I did not want to make people feel that way.” Backlash was slight. “We got a couple of people whose publicists were like, ‘We don’t want that out there.’ I don’t want to say who, but if you walk me to my spray tan I’ll tell you off the record.” (Sadly, I can’t make it.) She also made a last-minute edit to a moment in Galaxy Brain to avoid a moment that could be viewed as punching down, in a section where she discusses her personal battle with an eating disorder. “I had this joke where I said my goal weight is 1.5 Ariana Grandes,” Barone says. “And I go on to say that 1.5 Ariana Grandes is one Bella Hadid or two Troye Sivans. That’s really a joke about me and my mental illness. But I didn’t want people to hear it and think I was making a joke about Ariana Grande.” Barone brings a similar thoughtfulness to her role in Overcompensating. As Grace, the uptight older sister to Skinner’s character of Benny, she adds a touching depth to a character that could be a caricature. After becoming a hit with both viewers and critics, it became one of the few recent LGBTQ+-focused shows to be renewed for a second season. How did it feel for her first big acting gig to be so warmly received? “I could get chills just thinking about it,” Barone says, running her hands up and down her bare arms. *** Barone has been grinding in New York since she dropped out of Boston College and moved to the city in 2011. While working at a startup, she took classes at the local improv-focused group Upright Citizens Brigade and soon after quit her job to focus on comedy full-time. “I’ve been in this industry for 10 years now, so it was a slow start,” she says. Ride, Barone’s podcast with Skinner, shares space in the upper reaches of the comedy podcast chart with right-leaning shows from Joe Rogan, Theo Von and Andrew Schulz, hosts whose brashness and casual misogyny has led them to be grouped in with the manosphere. “Comedy has become increasingly polarised,” Barone says. “There’s people who want to make a cash grab and there’s nothing they could do that would make their audience turn against them. It’s genius if you think about it. It’s creating a space where you can say anything and do anything and you’ll never be held accountable.” She is particularly horrified by the rise of Schulz, the self-styled everyman doofus whose Flagrant podcast series cultivates a machismo-fueled atmosphere of casual racism and sexist views, and who invited Trump on for a cosy chat ahead of the 2024 election. “I would always see him at [New York’s] Comedy Cellar when I was starting out,” she says. “He was so funny – I literally thought he was hot. I think I slid into his DMs one time,” she recalls with a shudder. “I’ve watched him create this space where I’m like, ‘You just want to perpetuate the bigotry and the systems that have benefited people that look like you for all of time.’ I guess if money is the most important thing to you, that makes sense,” she says tartly. “But I have integrity, so I could never do something like that. It’s just hard to stomach that those are my co-workers, technically.” Audiences on the left do not give their entertainers the same freedom, she thinks, and especially not to women. “I love comedy,” she told the audience in her 2024 YouTube special Thought Provoking. “And being a woman in comedy is so fun because the goal is to get so successful that you become the most hated person on the planet.” I think of Lena Dunham, who somehow became the most hated woman in America after the success of her hit TV show Girls. “And it goes back as far as Lucille Ball – she was accused of being a communist!” Barone adds, before reeling off a list of female comedians who have faced vicious backlash for minor perceived missteps. “Kathy Griffin, Amy Schumer, Mindy Kaling, Tiffany Haddish … Tina Fey ate cake on SNL and people were mad. “Pursuing [comedy] as a career is such a funny choice because I’m sort of setting myself up for that,” she says. “Unfortunately it is a sign that things are going pretty well when people start to turn on you.” Not that it has stopped Barone from sticking her neck out for what she believes in. In early 2025, she DMed Zohran Mamdani and asked if he would guest at her standup show as part of a segment called Politics for Hot People. On stage at Brooklyn’s the Bell House, she grilled New York’s future mayor about his policies, saying: “Politicians are liars, so how can we trust these things are achievable?” That takes guts, I say. “Maybe there’s something in my brain where I don’t even know when things are socially unacceptable,” she replies. “I just asked him questions that I wanted to know the answers to! It’s the same with my jokes. Sometimes I’ll say things on stage and people will be like, ‘I can’t believe you said that.’ And I’m like, ‘But it’s true.’” Comedy isn’t the only way to change people’s minds, but laughter can sure make politics feel like less of a black box. To celebrate the special, Barone is planning a series of fun release-week events including a pool party at a Brooklyn spa and the Galaxy Brain Ball, a party co-hosted with Skinner at a local queer club. “I really wanted to do events with the people I made this special for,” she says. It’s tough to picture Barone’s down-to-earth qualities changing as more eyes turn towards her. “It’s hard to know how much to continue to say,” she says. “But I want to write about what’s going on in my life. And even though that can be really vulnerable and personal, it is what I want to talk about. I just can’t help it.” Mary Beth Barone: Galaxy Brain is on Netflix now

title: First Thing: Pentagon accused of disrespecting war dead as Trump threatens to resume Iran war
author: Martin Belam
summary: Controversial move to classify Iran war as two separate campaigns criticised as attempt to minimise casualty figures. Plus, the man who started an animal shelter after a dog saved his life
body_text: Good morning. A controversial move by the Pentagon to reclassify casualties in the Iran war as being killed in “overseas 0perations” is being taken by US military veterans as a sign of disrespect for the dead. Michael E Smith, a retired US rear admiral who completed combat tours in Iraq, Bosnia and Kosovo, said: “It’s such a huge disrespect for the families. To claim that they weren’t killed as a result of the war – oh, it was just overseas operations – is just ludicrous.” The change came as Donald Trump once again warned that the US would return to “strong military action” against Iran if diplomatic efforts did not bring a rapid resolution to the crisis in the Middle East. “We are in very deep talks with Iran. If they don’t work out, we will go back to very strong military action,” the US president told Axios on Monday. Asked for how long he would allow the talks to proceed, he answered: “Not much time. Either it goes fast or not at all.” What changes did the Department of Defense make? The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), a military database for displaying casualties, introduced a new casualty category labeled “Overseas Operations” for personnel killed and wounded “starting July 7”. That splits the count from the beginning of the US-Israel war on Iran into effectively two different campaigns. How is the administration justifying the change? The War Powers Act of 1973 requires the president to end military operations within 60 days unless Congress authorizes an extension, which it has not. The Trump administration has argued that the April ceasefire with Iran paused the clock on 1 May for the conflict’s initial period. The separate casualty count beginning on 7 July follows that interpretation. Michigan progressive Abdul El-Sayed says ‘ogre’ remark not directed at rival The Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said his comments that progressives need to put the head of an “ogre” on a pike was in reference to the US senator John Fetterman – not his opponent, representative Haley Stevens. The comments drew immediate backlash from several high-profile Democrats and charges of sexism by those who believed the remark was a reference to Stevens. El-Sayed claimed he had been speaking of supporting a primary challenge to Fetterman, the Pennsylvania Democrat who campaigned as a progressive but has moved to the right since taking office. “I was referring to a guy named John Fetterman, who’s a senator from Pennsylvania who has done terrible things, got elected on a set of values, and is now completely throwing those values in the mud.” US airman accused of ‘spree’ of rapes on sleeping women in England avoided UK courts A US airman accused of a “spree” of rapes and sexual assaults in England, drugging some women and breaking into the homes of others, was able to avoid English justice after local police handed over part of the case to the American military. Two British women went to Suffolk police in August 2019 to allege that James Loubeau and another US airman had drugged and raped them. Less than two weeks later, Suffolk police allowed the US air force to take responsibility for investigating the two alleged rapes. It has since emerged that Loubeau, 38, allegedly attacked a total of six women in East Anglia over a four-month period in 2019, in what US prosecutors described as a “frightening and dangerous” pattern of assaults. DoJ urges supreme court to allow Trump order targeting mail-in voting The Trump administration has asked the supreme court to clear the way for an executive order from Donald Trump that could dramatically change mail-in voting. The emergency appeal comes after an appeals court upheld a ruling blocking the president’s order in nearly half the country ahead of November’s midterm elections. What is the president attempting to do? Trump ordered the government in March to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters and deliver mail ballots only to those people on that list. The legal challenge says the constitution gives states and Congress the authority to set election rules, not the president. Trump promoted the proposed changes as safeguards to keep non-US citizens from voting, which has been shown to be rare. In other news … Andrew and Tristan Tate will remain in jail until their next extradition hearing as they fight being sent to the UK where they face rape, sexual assault and other allegations, which they deny. Betye Saar, a pioneering figure of the Black arts movement, has died at the age of 99. She was best known for reclaiming Jim Crow era memorabilia and recasting them as images of Black liberation. Cracker Barrel CEO, Julie Masino, is to step down after overseeing the logo redesign backlash last year. The musician Carly Simon has revealed that she has Parkinson’s disease. Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, has been called to appear before Congress over his ties to the Trump administration. Stat of the day: Johnson & Johnson to pay $5.5bn settlement in talc cancer lawsuit Johnson & Johnson said it would pay an estimated $5.5bn to resolve tens of thousands of lawsuits alleging its baby ⁠powder and other talc products caused ⁠ovarian cancer, in a landmark deal that could end a contentious, decade-long legal battle. Culture Pick: Furious – a proper grownup thriller that’s powered by sheer female rage Dropping this week on Hulu in the US, Lucy Mangan says Furious is possibly the birth of a new post-Epstein files sub-genre of television drama. She says it asks how individuals survive such predators and how society survives the knowledge of the depth and breadth of his network of suppliers, enablers and willing (rich, male) participants. Don’t miss this: Odyssey translator Emily Wilson attacks Nolan blockbuster It might be raking it in at the box office, but Emily Wilson, a classicist whose 2017 translation of Homer’s epic was praised by director Christopher Nolan, said his film was grandiose and superficial with “nothing convincing to say”. Ouch. … or this: A dog saved Houssein Hamze from a bomb. When war returned, he stayed to care for Lebanon’s animals Soon after his near-death experience, Houssein Hamze founded the Mashala shelter in the village of Zefta, south Lebanon, to take care of animals in the area. In normal times he takes in strays, and in wartime he is the only lifeline for animals in the area. Climate check: France and Spain race to contain huge wildfires before fresh heatwave begins Wildfires have forced about 375,000 people to leave their homes in France and Spain. These tourists have been caught up in the unfolding disaster as firefighters struggle to regain control amid a warning the fires could burn until November. Last Thing: Motorbikes and mountains – photographing the 2026 Tour de France I adore the Tour de France, and this picture essay by Pete Goding, who has been photographing it for 20 years, gives an insight into what it’s been like to document this year’s race. title: How close is the Trump administration to the toxic Tate brothers? Let’s ask the president’s son Barron …
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: The 20-year-old crypto bro likes to keep a low profile. He could still be forced to testify before the House oversight committee, writes Arwa Mahdawi
body_text: Unlike his garrulous father, Barron Trump seems to be a man of few words. The president’s youngest son has been busy flogging energy drinks and making millions from cryptocurrency schemes, but he’s not big on public speaking. Indeed, the best-known clip of him talking is probably from when he was four years old and said “I like my suitcase” in a Slovenian accent. Still, while 20-year-old Barron Trump might prefer to stay behind the scenes, he may find himself hauled in front of Congress and forced to answer some difficult questions. Last week, Yassamin Ansari, a Democratic congresswoman and a member of the House oversight committee, called for Barron to testify about his alleged connections to the toxic influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate. The Tate brothers, who have become household names by monetising misogyny, were recently arrested in Miami, just before Andrew was due to co-host a bare-knuckle boxing event. They’re now fighting extradition to the UK, and face allegations of rape, assault, trafficking and offences relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography”. They deny these charges. What’s Barron got to do with all this? Over the years, the Trumps and the Tates seem to have forged a mutually beneficial alliance. Donald Trump Jr has been friendly with Andrew since 2016 and, while I wouldn’t go so far as to call Barron and Andrew besties, the New York Times has reported that a teenage Barron admired the influencer and had a Zoom call with him. According to the New Yorker, Barron also spent a lot of time with Justin Waller, who has called himself the Tates’ “third brother”, and gave Barron dating advice. Barron, in turn, gave his dad a political steer: he is widely credited, including by the president himself, for pushing Trump to tap into manosphere influencers such as Tate during the 2024 election in order to mobilise young male voters. In return for their help with the election, the Tates got friends in high places. “The Tates will be free, Trump is the president,” Andrew posted after the inauguration. And that prediction was partly correct: it has been widely reported that the Trump administration intervened in 2025 to get the Romanian government to lift travel restrictions on the Tates, who were under house arrest in the country for trafficking charges. (Romania’s foreign minister has said he did not face any pressure from the US regarding the Tates. The Trump administration has said it had no insight into the matter.) Will the Trump administration help the brothers when it comes to this new extradition request? Press secretary Karoline Leavitt has said the White House won’t get involved. Secretary of state Marco Rubio has also dismissed the idea. Whether you should believe this is debatable, but it’s certainly possible the Tates have outlived their usefulness to the ever-transactional Trumps. Still, the Trump family can’t sever ties with the Tate brothers that easily. As congresswoman Ansari notes, there are plenty of questions that remain unanswered about the Tate-Trump relationship. In a letter to the House oversight committee chair, Ansari said: “The committee must investigate whether back-channel communications between the Tate brothers, presidential advisors, and members of the First Family such as Barron Trump influenced official actions or administration policy regarding criminal prosecution and investigation of the brothers or international law enforcement cooperation.” The letter specifically recommends a subpoena for Barron to see if he had “any involvement” in relation to the Tate brothers’ alleged crimes. Over the weekend, Ansari reiterated her calls for an investigation on the MeidasTouch podcast, noting that Barron “is a full-blown adult, and he is very influential in the Trump White House orbit”. Republicans have a slight majority in the House, so it’s highly unlikely that Ansari’s request will go anywhere. I don’t need to tell you that we still don’t have real answers about Trump’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein. Nor do I need to tell you that Trump is an adjudicated sexual abuser. This isn’t an administration that takes violence against women seriously. That said, if the Democrats win the House in the midterms, as they are expected to do, the situation might shift and Barron might find himself with some explaining to do. And if the US government won’t demand answers from Barron, then the media should. As Ansari notes, Barron is very much an adult now. He may not have chosen to be born a Trump but he has chosen to profit from his name and connections. He’s not some little kid who needs protecting. But there are a lot of vulnerable young kids out there who do need protecting from the bigotry and hate that men like the Tates peddle. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Ex-FCC officials warn agency sending ‘chilling message’ with ABC license review
author: Jeremy Barr
summary: Ex-officials ask FCC to reject petitions to deny renewal of broadcast licenses for eight stations owned by ABC
body_text: A group of prominent former Federal Communications Commission (FCC) officials, including key staffers and commissioners appointed by both Democratic and Republican presidents, issued a filing on Tuesday that warns the agency is trying to send a “chilling message” to broadcasters after it received petitions to deny ABC license renewals for eight of its local television stations. The network’s licenses are up for early renewal after an extremely unusual order from the Brendan Carr-led FCC in late April, following criticism of ABC by Donald Trump and Melania Trump. The group behind the filing includes Mark S Fowler, who served as FCC chair during Ronald Reagan’s presidency; Alfred C Sikes, who served as FCC chair during George HW Bush’s presidency; Thomas E Wheeler, who served as FCC chair during Barack Obama’s presidency; and several high-ranking lawyers and advisers to past commissioners. “This early license renewal proceeding is unprecedented in the history of the Federal Communications Commission and a grave violation of both the Communications Act and the Constitution,” the coalition wrote in the filing. “Through this proceeding, the FCC seeks to censor Disney’s and ABC’s speech and send a chilling message to all broadcasters: carry speech we don’t like at your peril.” Seeking to put the ABC license challenge into context, the group called the order “the latest attack in a sustained campaign by Chairman Carr and the Trump administration of threatening legal sanctions against licensees whose speech President Trump dislikes”. The filing is a response to petitions to deny ABC’s license renewals submitted by conservative media watchdog the Media Research Center (MRC) and the Center for American Rights (CAR), a conservative legal organization that is closely aligned with Carr and has initiated several complaints against television networks premised on accusations of liberal bias. CAR’s petition to deny ABC’s license renewal accused the network of “[ignoring] long-standing Commission precedents and principles protecting the integrity of the news” and “[engaging] in explicit racial and gender discrimination”. The coalition said in its Tuesday filing that the petitions should be denied because they ask the FCC to wade into “content and viewpoint regulation” and accusations of bias by punishing a network for their editorial decision-making – “a stunning – and plainly unconstitutional – expansion of the Commission’s role”. “As former Chairs, Commissioners, Chiefs of Staff, General Counsels and Bureau Chiefs, we call on the Commission to respect the constitutional and congressional prohibitions on its ‘power of censorship’ and terminate this proceeding,” the group wrote. Interested parties have until 5 August to reply to petitions to deny ABC’s licenses. After that time, the FCC could either grant the extension requests, a prospect that seems unlikely, or schedule hearings on the matter. The process has no clear timetable, leaving ABC and its eight local television stations mired in a cloud of uncertainty about their ability to continue broadcasting long-term.

title: Lindsey Graham’s funeral ceremonies to begin with Netanyahu and Zelenskyy in attendance
author: Martin Pengelly
summary: Memorials for the Republican senator to start in US Capitol as the Israeli and Ukrainian leaders meet with Trump
body_text: Two days of funeral ceremonies for Lindsey Graham, the late South Carolina Republican senator, will begin in Washington on Tuesday, with mourners set to include the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Both leaders are also meeting Donald Trump at the White House. A longtime foreign policy hawk, Graham was working on a new Russia sanctions bill when he met Zelenskyy in Kyiv earlier this month, dying shortly after returning to Washington from a heart condition aged 71. On Sunday, the Wall Street Journal released footage shot by a documentary team in February, showing Graham’s delight over the Iran war and eager support for Netanyahu and Israel. Memorial events on Tuesday will begin on Capitol Hill, where Graham, a former US air force lawyer, was a member of the House for eight years and a senator for 23. From the Capitol Rotunda, the casket will be taken to the Washington National Cathedral for an afternoon service, with Trump – who Graham once called a “jackass” and a “race-baiting bigot” before switching to support him – among the scheduled speakers. On Wednesday, in Graham’s home state, ceremonies will begin with services and an F-16 flyover at the South Carolina state house in Columbia, followed by a procession to First Baptist church for a public service. A private family burial will take place in Pickens county, home to Central, the small town where Graham and his younger sister and Senate successor, Darline, were born. Back in Washington on Tuesday, the Israeli and Ukrainian leaders will each head for high-stakes White House meetings. The behind-the-scenes footage of Graham released by the Wall Street Journal was shot on the first day of US-Israeli strikes on Iran, a move long urged by Netanyahu and eagerly embraced by Trump. “I almost cried,” Graham said. “I mean, like, how long have we been pushing this? It’s here. I talked with Trump this morning. Holy Jack. It’s here. It’s the best thing I’ve ever done. He loves blowing stuff up.” At least 175 people, most of them schoolchildren, were killed in the Iranian city of Minab in those first strikes, in all likelihood by US missiles in a controversial “double tap” strike. Another clip released on Sunday showed Graham predicting that it would take “about three or four weeks” for attacks on Iran to cause the regime in Tehran to “start losing control of some cities” and for the US-Israeli effort to achieve “almost irreversible momentum”. That has not happened. Nor has the US joined Israeli attacks on Lebanon, as Graham was shown advocating to Netanyahu. In the footage, Graham also said: “Trump and Bibi [Netanyahu] are like Roosevelt and Churchill. They’re the right two guys to confront this evil.” As it turns out, Netanyahu and Trump’s relationship has been placed under considerable stress, with reports of angry confrontations. Zelenskyy, meanwhile, will hope for a more constructive Oval Office meeting than the now-famous occasion in February 2025, when he was upbraided by Trump and JD Vance, including for not wearing a suit. Relations between Kyiv and Washington have remained strained, even as Ukraine has gained the upper hand in its long fight against Russian invaders.

title: Trump administration needs to stop ‘public harassment’ of Fauci and scientists, open letter says
author: Anna Betts
summary: Letter, published before Anthony Fauci will appear before Congress, accuses Republicans of ‘waging a war on individual scientists’
body_text: More than 155 scientists, physicians and public health advocates have called for an end to what they describe as the “vilification and harassment of many American scientists” by the Trump administration and its allies. In an open letter published one day before Anthony Fauci, the former top US government science adviser, is scheduled to appear at a high-profile hearing in US Congress, after the Republican-controlled Senate homeland security and governmental affairs committee compelled him to testify, the scientists and physicians dismissed allegations against the ex-National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (Niaid) director as “baseless”. Fauci, 85, who helped guide the country’s response to the Covid-19 pandemic as director of the Niaid, is set to testify under subpoena before the committee on Wednesday as a part of its investigation into the origins of the virus and whether US federal officials, including Fauci, misled the public and Congress about the source of the outbreak, a claim that has been made by Senator Rand Paul, a Republican of Kentucky who chairs the committee, for years. The letter signed by the group of scientists and public health advocates alleges that the Trump administration and its congressional allies are “waging a war on individual scientists, through public harassment, arrests, criminal indictment and ongoing threats of prosecution”. The letter states that several scientists have come under scrutiny under this administration, but the signatories argue that “the most prominent target of the administration and its allies” is Fauci, who left the federal government in 2022 after leading the Niaid for 38 years. “The charges against Dr Fauci are baseless, suggesting he covered up the origins of Covid, that he bribed or persuaded other scientists to join his cover-up, that Niaid-funded research sparked the pandemic, that he personally holds patents on the virus, and that he’s working with intelligence agencies to suppress the true story of the pandemic,” the letter states. “No credible evidence has been produced to support these absurd charges.” The letter adds that the allegations and accusations about Fauci have led to “five-year period of harassment and threats of violence directed at Dr Fauci and his family”. “Now, this month, he is being subpoenaed by Congress once again,” it continues. “In over 60 years of public service, Dr Fauci has led the United States through epidemics of HIV and Covid, through outbreaks of Ebola and Sars 1, and through the 2001 anthrax attacks. He has worked tirelessly to advance science and protect the public’s health. “As the congressional hearings targeting Dr Fauci approach, we are urging our elected representatives in Congress stop these witch-hunts and support good public health and scientific practices so that America’s leadership in innovation remains secure,” the letter concludes. Ahead of Wednesday’s hearing, Paul, the Republican who chairs the committee, released thousands of pages of Fauci’s diary entries from during the Covid-19 pandemic, which showed Fauci’s efforts to manage and address the pandemic, navigate his relationship with Donald Trump, and reflect on his public profile and media image. Fauci left the government at the end of 2022 and has said over the years that research has “strongly suggested” that coronavirus most likely emerged through natural origins, probably from animal-to-human transmission. But he has insisted he keeps a “completely open mind” about other possibilities, including the theory that the virus may have leaked from a lab in China in 2019, and has denied allegations by some Republican lawmakers, including Paul, that he sought to suppress that theory. Before Trump returned to office last year, Joe Biden issued a pre-emptive pardon to Fauci and other senior officials. But despite the pardon, Paul has referred Fauci to the Department of Justice for “potential criminal prosecution”.

title: The Guardian view on India’s gen Z revolt: the cockroaches are coming together
author: Editorial
summary: Editorial: A youth movement born from exam leaks and online mockery has pierced Narendra Modi’s aura of invincibility and may yet reshape Indian politics
body_text: “What if all cockroaches come together?” was the question that humbled India’s strongman prime minister, Narendra Modi. It was posted on X by Abhijeet Dipke, an Indian student in the US with a master’s in public relations. Enraged that India’s top judge likened unemployed youths to insects and “parasites”, and that millions saw medical exams compromised by leaks, Mr Dipke lit a fuse. For India’s nearly 400 million gen Z, public exams are often the only ladder to a secure future. When papers leak or tests are cancelled, that ladder is kicked away. By June, young people were protesting peacefully in Delhi as the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), a parody of Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). They demanded the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. This weekend, Mr Pradhan became the first senior minister in Mr Modi’s 12 years in power to be forced from office by a mass-protest movement. It came after credible reports suggested police officers attacked protesters marching to parliament. Security sources say it was they who were attacked. This may be just the beginning. The concession has taught the Cockroach movement’s leadership that pressure works. They could have declared victory and gone home. Instead they have accused the government of breaching the terms of the settlement offered by Mr Modi’s government. The CJP claims at least 100 people have been arrested, many on non-bailable charges. Its leaders are now demanding the release of detainees and threatening to remobilise nationally. Mr Modi has built an authoritarian order which rested upon Hindu majoritarianism and demonising Muslims. Education in the country has been subordinated to ideology and political patronage. But corruption in public exams cannot be divided so easily along religious lines. A Hindu graduate in northern India and a Muslim graduate in its southern cone experience the same anger over leaked papers and worthless qualifications. The grievance, crucially, creates an economic identity that cuts across the BJP’s preferred religious cleavage. Until Mr Pradhan’s resignation, ministerial accountability to public protest had all but disappeared; loyalty to Mr Modi’s ideological project had mattered more. The CJP has also broken the spell of fear that has dominated the public square. The movement’s leadership were not requesting generosity; they were asserting a claim to clean administration, fair exams and ministerial accountability. Writing in the Guardian, the historian Mukul Kesavan says the CJP’s social-media dexterity is crucial. Like New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, they combine eloquence, message discipline and composure, making Mr Modi look leaden. Their victory may have produced not merely a protest movement, but a new generation of political leaders. A similar kind of unrest during an anti-corruption movement in 2011 paved the way for Mr Modi to wrest power from the ruling Congress coalition 12 years ago. The next general election is in 2029 and predicting its outcome today is not a worthwhile exercise. But the political scientist Christophe Jaffrelot argues that the CJP represents a much deeper revolt than just anger over exam leaks. It has, he says, become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Many Indians are either cockroaches now or in the process of becoming them. If they were to come together in a meaningful political way then Mr Modi may be in much bigger trouble than he is in today. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Rising Zelenskyy and falling Netanyahu cross paths in chaotic White House
author: Julian Borger
summary: Ukrainian and Israeli leaders converge on Washington with criss-crossing fortunes, but knowing they can count on little from US counterpart
body_text: The converging visits of Benjamin Netanyahu and Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Washington offer an unusually eloquent snapshot of a world in turmoil, unmoored from decades-old certainties. Some things remain the same. The US is still an almighty military and economic power and for both foreign visitors, a White House encounter with Donald Trump is critical to their governments and the wars they are fighting. The imperial presidency Trump has tried to forge is in decline, however, in large part as a result of his own erratic leadership. He may see his visitors as client-potentates flying in from the edges of empire to kiss his ring. But they will be as aware of Trump’s weaknesses as they are of their own. Netanyahu and Zelenskyy arrive in Washington on opposite trajectories. The Israeli prime minister’s star has declined dramatically since he persuaded Trump to join him in an ill-conceived war on Iran five months ago, on the groundless promise that the Tehran regime would quickly collapse. Since then, a viscerally disappointed president has publicly scolded Netanyahu and insisted Netanyahu would ultimately do his bidding, while the White House has liberally leaked Trump’s foul-mouthed tirades belittling him. Israel has been left out of negotiations with Iran, and its views were ignored when it came to selling F-35 stealth fighter planes to Turkey, or making a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia. An Economist/YouGov survey found that nearly half of Americans polled thought that Netanyahu should be arrested on arrival for war crimes. By contrast, Zelenskyy arrived in Washington in the ascendant. Ukraine has defied the US administration’s predictions of inevitable defeat to Russia’s might, his country is now a world leader in drone warfare, and parts of the Magaverse are now warming to the accidental war leader they once scorned as a loser. In traditional administrations, both men and the countries they represent would be natural allies and both could be sure of solid welcome in the Oval Office. It is telling that the occasion of their coinciding visits was the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican hawk of the old school who could be relied on for wholehearted promotion of the Israeli and Ukrainian war efforts. In that respect, he was one of a dying breed. But this is no normal administration, led by a president who rules on a whim, and neither visitor can predict how he will be received. Neither wanted cameras in the room. Trump began his presidency by throwing all-in support behind Netanyahu and his wars, dropping even the pretence of concern for the lives of Palestinians or the people of southern Lebanon that had tempered backing for Israel from earlier presidents. Facing a hostile electorate, the president is trying to extricate himself from the region, but in doing so is finding Israel the most recalcitrant party on every front. In Ukraine, Trump threw out the American foreign policy handbook altogether, proposing peace deals that often echoed Moscow’s talking points, rewarding aggression with territory Russia had not even won on the battlefield. Rather than capitulate, Ukraine showed it could fight on despite drastic cuts in US military aid, relying more on Europe and its own hard-won improvised expertise. Now Zelenskyy finds himself the unlikely darling of far-right Maga influencers such as Lara Loomer, formerly an apologist for the Russian invasion, who interviewed the Ukrainian president in his garden last week, and called for “moral clarity” in Kyiv’s support. Zelenskyy’s recent ascent may mirror Netanyahu’s simultaneous decline, but that does not mean they came to Washington with comparable status. When it comes to the Trump administration, they arrive from very different starting positions. Just about anything would count as an upgrade for Zelenskyy compared with his infamous White House ambush in February 2025 by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, who tried to humiliate the Ukrainian visitor in front of the cameras, demanding gratitude and acceptance of defeat with “no cards” left to play. Zelenskyy does have cards this time but well short of a winning hand without US support. The Ukrainian’s immediate aim is modest: for Trump to honour Senator Graham by backing a Russia sanctions bill he was pushing at the time of his death. He knows that direct US military aid to Ukraine is not likely to return in meaningful quantities any time soon. The Patriot interceptors and other weapons Ukraine once counted on for its defence have been used up wholesale in the Middle East, many of them to protect Israel. It will take years for the US to rebuild its own stocks. Netanyahu may be out of favour in the current White House, but the US is committed to Israel’s defence in a manner and on a scale of which Ukraine can only dream. Netanyahu and Zelenskyy came to Washington on different paths and footings but they do at least share an awareness that their relationship with the administration can be upended with scant notice, without any clear reasons, in a matter of mere seconds in the court of the irascible, flagging would-be emperor.

title: Trump reportedly pushing RFK Jr to cut vaccines more aggressively
author: Melody Schreiber
summary: White House has halted changing vaccine schedule as it is unpopular, but anti-vaxx Trump set on ‘alleviating autism’
body_text: Donald Trump is pushing the longtime vaccine opponent and current health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr to be more aggressive on cutting vaccines in the US, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal. Trump has a long record of anti-vaccine statements, but the White House recently put a hold on vaccine changes after polling indicated they were a losing issue in the midterm elections. Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services, recently slashed the routine childhood immunization schedule in an unprecedented move. Trump reportedly asked Kennedy at his northern Virginia golf course in May if the health secretary had the “yips”, according to the Journal. Trump wasn’t talking about a sudden inability to make putts. Kennedy wasn’t making enough cuts to the US vaccination schedule, Trump reportedly said. The US president hopes to make “alleviating autism” a component of his legacy, the Journal reported – and he has taken issue with Kennedy’s less aggressive changes to vaccination recommendations in recent months. “Donald Trump has been anti-vaccine at least since 2015,” said Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center and an infectious diseases physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. At the Republican primary debate that year, Trump said that autism had gotten “totally out of control” and vaccines should be in “smaller doses over a longer period of time”. Trump regularly posted on social media about debunked links between vaccination and autism as early as 2014, and his posts on Truth Social have recently advocated for breaking up shots into individual components and delaying some childhood vaccines for more than a decade. Tony Fabrizio, a top pollster for Trump, found that anti-vaccine moves are unpopular with voters in key districts, concluding in a December memo that “skepticism toward vaccine requirements is politically risky for both parties”. Susie Wiles gave HHS the deadline of New Year’s Eve to make vaccine changes, to allow vaccines to fall into the background with the midterms looming, according to reporting by the Rolling Stone. But Trump’s priorities appear to lie elsewhere. He issued a memo, two days after Fabrizio’s poll results, directing HHS to align with “peer” nations on vaccination recommendations, even though the US was already making similar recommendations to other countries. A month later, Kennedy slashed vaccine recommendations by one-third, from 17 to 11. A federal judge ordered a halt to these changes following a lawsuit in March from the American Academy of Pediatrics. The judge also paused the work of the advisory committee on immunization practices (ACIP), which was illegally formed under Kennedy, he said. Kennedy has not made any significant changes to the vaccine schedule since then, though he has continued speaking about autism and its potential causes, and the US government is appealing the judge’s stay on vaccine changes. Kennedy also sought to divert $5bn in funding – more than 10% of the entire National Institutes of Health budget – toward research on vaccines and autism, according to reporting by Reuters. Decades of research into the causes of autism point overwhelmingly to genetics, and dozens of studies have indicated no link between vaccines and autism. Even so, Trump issued an executive order in May urging HHS to change vaccine recommendations. Kush Desai, a spokesperson for the White House, did not dispute the details reported by the Journal and others in a statement to the Guardian. He instead pointed to parents of autistic children – but not to autistic people themselves – with “questions and concerns” who “have long been ignored if not mocked”. The Trump administration was “committed to leaving no stone unturned” to address those concerns, Desai added. Kennedy and Trump are “aligned in their commitment” to confront the “chronic disease epidemic affecting America’s children”, said Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, in an apparent reference to autism. HHS would “continue to pursue evidence-based research to identify the root causes of autism and other chronic diseases”, she added. “I think Donald Trump has a fixed, immutable belief that vaccines cause autism,” Offit said. That makes Trump the most powerful anti-vaxxer in the world, Offit said – and it means he is unlikely to fire Kennedy, even as rumors have swirled that the health secretary is on his way out. The abrupt rise of measles and other deadly diseases are more likely to be Trump’s legacy than advances in understanding autism, Offit said. As top leaders have downplayed the safety and importance of vaccines, measles has surged to its highest rate in 30 years, and the nation has suffered a rise in deaths from whooping cough, flu and tetanus in recent years. “And our commander in chief, our vaccine guy in chief, is our president. He’s fine with this. Just as RFK Jr is fine with this,” Offit said. “Trump has become the president of Measles Land,” Offit added. “That should bother him.”

title: Lindsey Graham remembered as ‘true American original’ at Capitol memorial
author: Lucy Campbell and Guardian staff in Washington
summary: ‘He died doing the work he was born to do,’ Trump says as political leaders honor Republican US senator
body_text: Donald Trump and other political leaders convened in Washington for the memorial of the long-serving US senator Lindsey Graham on Tuesday afternoon, remembering the “swashbuckling” South Carolina Republican as “a true American original” whose embrace of “America first” never softened his advocacy for a staunch interventionist US foreign policy. Graham, a polarizing figure and one-time rival turned stalwart ally of Trump, was known for championing the US-Israel war on Iran and was a prominent voice in the anti-abortion movement and an unwavering supporter of Israel, serving as one of Capitol Hill’s most outspoken foreign policy hawks. “He died doing the work he was born to do. He was truly a great politician, serving the country he loved to serve so deeply,” Trump said of Graham in his eulogy at the National Cathedral. “He went out at the peak of his career, the top of his game as a legend that every one of us, many of us here today, blessed to know him and a friend that none of us will ever forget,” he added. Trump took the opportunity to reiterate his support for Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to the late senator’s seat for the remainder of his term. And he focused on Graham’s foreign policy record as a war hawk. “I will tell you, he never saw a war that he didn’t like. Only his true friends would understand that. But he wanted it for the good of our country,” he said. The president, who ran against Graham in the 2016 presidential election, admitted that “Lindsey and I did not exactly get off to the best of starts”. Recalling his leaking of Graham’s phone number to the public after Graham called him a “jackass” during the presidential race, Trump said: “It was Lindsey who had the last laugh because while I blew up his phone all for one day, we became great friends, and Lindsey did not stop calling me for the next 10 years. It was not easy.” Other speakers included the Fox News host Sean Hannity, who said Graham would have been honored by the presence of Benjamin Netanyahu and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who held meetings with Trump earlier in the day. The television host also turned to flattery with Trump in the pews. “Lindsey, Mr President, I would argue in my mind probably has a heavenly version of Mar-a-Lago. It may even be a little bigger … Because he would want to obviously duplicate his dearest friend in life. You, Mr President,” he said. Speaking during a ceremony earlier on Tuesday inside the Capitol Rotunda, the US Senate majority leader, John Thune, hailed Graham as a “fierce defender of Ukraine”, following its full-scale invasion by Russia in 2022, and a “powerful voice for the [anti-abortion] movement”. “I feel his absence every day, and I know my colleagues do as well,” Thune continued, growing emotional. “I look forward to the days when you make us laugh again.” Darline Graham, who was sworn in earlier this month, attended both services. She is running in the Republican primary to permanently succeed her brother. Graham died suddenly earlier this month, aged 71, shortly after returning to Washington from a trip to Kyiv. The Ukrainian president and the Israeli prime minister are due to attend an afternoon service for Graham at Washington National Cathedral. JD Vance, the US vice-president, credited Graham with the successful confirmation of Brett Kavanaugh to the US supreme court in 2018, which helped conservatives secure a supermajority on the bench within two years. “I believe that he saved that nomination,” Vance said. “I choose to remember Lindsey Graham as a person who could fight with you on one issue, but fight for you on another issue,” the US vice-president said. “I remember Lindsey Graham as a man who loved people, and because he loved people, he was willing to reason with them, to respect them and ultimately to persuade them.” “May God rest the soul of Senator Lindsey Graham, a true American original,” he said. A former air force lawyer who served in the air force reserve while in Congress, Graham was elected to the House of Representatives in 1994 and served as a manager during Bill Clinton’s 1999 impeachment trial before winning a Senate seat in 2002. Weeks before his death, Graham defeated a field of challengers to win the Republican nomination in his bid for a fifth term. On Wednesday, in Graham’s home state, ceremonies will begin with services and an F-16 flyover at the South Carolina statehouse in Columbia, followed by a procession to First Baptist church for a public service. A private family burial will take place in Pickens county, home to Central, the small town where Graham and his younger sister and Senate successor, Darline, were born.

title: Trump pausing Iran attacks shows US military power is not enough on its own
author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
summary: Tehran has not been bombed into submission, leaving America unable to enforce its demands without a ground war that it does not want
body_text: Has Iran won a war it didn’t start against the United States? It is not a victory in any conventional military sense: about 3,500 Iranians have been reported killed and the US-led bombing has caused anywhere between $150bn and $270bn of damage. Yet Donald Trump’s decision to pause, rather than intensify, the 13-night summer bombing campaign in effect represents a degree of recognition that the US cannot achieve its stated goals by military power alone. “Iran’s initial standard for victory was simply to survive,” said HA Hellyer, a Middle East expert with the Royal United Services Institute. “If anything, that’s been raised. The regime has demonstrated it is not going anywhere, and Tehran has changed the calculus on the strait of Hormuz”. The past five months are a clear demonstration of how an asymmetric conflict can flip the tables. All Iran, helped by its extensive and mountainous geography, has needed to do is maintain enough of a missile and drone capability to scare merchant shipping from using the strait of Hormuz. It is a low bar Iran’s military is still clearing. Two tankers were attacked sailing north of Oman last week. One of them caught fire in the engine room and had to be evacuated, before being towed to Oman, one of a handful of serious attacks on merchant shipping that took place during the nearly two-week July escalation of fighting. The US, meanwhile, has spent at least $38bn and used more than 1,000 Tomahawk and 1,100 Jassm $2.6m cruise missiles, according to estimates by the CSIS thinktank, to bomb targets in Iran, a third and a quarter of total stockpiles. The Tomahawks, which cost up to $3.6m each, might not be replaced until 2031. It is surprising that the US has allowed key munitions to be run down at such speed. On Monday, Trump tried in part to blame Ukraine, arguing that “so much was given” to Kyiv in military aid – though the reality is that Ukraine was never given long-range cruise missiles, only Patriot air defence systems. Patriot missile interceptors were more heavily depleted, by 1,000 or so, or 50% of the total US stockpile, raising questions as to how well the US can continue to defend its bases in the Gulf. More were used during the 38 days of heavy fighting in the spring than the 600 or so that Ukraine has said it had received during four years of war. A fresh escalation in the Red Sea by the Houthis, Iran’s allies in Yemen, complicates the picture further. The rebel group kept out of the first phase of the US-Iran war in the spring but, as Saudi Arabia seeks to redirect oil traffic through the Red Sea, they have stepped up attacks, targeting a refinery in the Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday. The US’s stated central war aim, meanwhile, may have repeatedly shifted but it has always been maximalist – whether it was regime change (as demonstrated by the killing of Ali Khamenei), destroying Iran’s entire missile programme or, as most frequently stated, preventing the country from having a nuclear weapon. Yet the US has no means of enforcing this level of demand without committing ground forces in numbers to occupy Tehran – an unlikely move that the US has not shown signs of preparing for. Donald Trump’s previous threats to bomb Iranian power plants to try to force the regime’s capitulation have raised concerns they would amount to war crimes, and he dropped them in April and again last week. “I don’t think the Iranians can be bombed into accepting US terms,” said Peter Ricketts, a former UK national security adviser. “Until the US accepts it can’t get its way by bombing, Iran has effective leverage. Tehran can absorb the pain, and they know they can close the strait with the economic impact it has on the US.” The resulting situation is what Ricketts calls an “escalation dominance” that he says favours Iran. Tehran, faced with US pressure to abandon its nuclear programme, can string out peace negotiations, wait for the White House to get impatient and restart bombing, then close Hormuz until the US has to stop attacking because the oil price is tto high for too long. The question then becomes who gains as unstable equilibrium endures. Tehran may well believe it has leverage as the US heads towards midterm elections in November, given how unpopular the war is. Just a third of all Americans support the war, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey out on Tuesday, though that rises to 71% of Republicans. Laurel Rapp, from the Chatham House thinktank, said that “a resumed ceasefire and promise of future talks is the least bad option for Washington” – though whether that is attractive to US ally Israel, whose prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu has his own election to fight in October, is another source of uncertainty. But if Tehran may have short or medium-term leverage, any idea that it has won the war is exaggerated. Hellyer argues that Iran, long struggling under western sanctions, cannot afford to rebuild without an agreement with the US: “Ultimately this isn’t sustainable for Iran, because its economy isn’t going to be able to survive”.

title: Senate confirms Trump ally Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence
author: Sam Levine
summary: At confirmation hearing, Clayton sidestepped questions about 2020 election and declined to say Trump lost
body_text: The US Senate voted to confirm Jay Clayton as the director of national intelligence on Tuesday, giving Trump another key ally directing the nation’s intelligence apparatus. The tally, 51-47, fell along party lines, with all Republicans supporting his nomination and all Democrats opposing it. Clayton, currently the US attorney for the southern district of New York, will replace Bill Pulte, a staunch Trump loyalist who had been temporarily serving in the role since June. Trump’s first director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, resigned earlier this year. Clayton served as the chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) during Trump’s first term. During his confirmation hearing on 15 July, Clayton sidestepped several questions about the 2020 election and declined to say that Trump lost it. During an interview on CNBC in June, Clayton also suggested there was something amiss about the long period California takes to count ballots. “We had a problem, a deep problem with voting in America,” he said on the network. “On the integrity side, we’re doing an absolutely terrible job, and the American people are right to question it.” Clayton also would not say during his confirmation hearing whether voter fraud was a problem in American elections, even though several studies have shown it is exceedingly rare. His office also issued widely criticized subpoenas to New York Times journalists over their reporting on security concerns around Trump’s Air Force One airplane that was a gift from Qatar. The government abruptly withdrew those subpoenas during a court hearing in which a federal judge pressed an attorney from Clayton’s office about errors and irregularities in the subpoenas. While Democrats saw Clayton as a more preferable pick than Pulte, who has assisted in executing some of Trump’s sloppy and ugly acts of political retribution, including the criminal prosecution of Letitia James and a ham-handed effort to remove Lisa Cook from the Federal Reserve board of governors, Pulte was also leading the office of the director of national intelligence earlier this month when Trump declassified and released intelligence in support of false claims about the 2020 election. Pulte oversaw several rounds of layoffs at the agency. But Clayton’s contentious hearing earlier this month cost him bipartisan backing. Before the vote, the senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, spoke in opposition to the nomination, warning that Clayton was unqualified and would act as the president’s “election conspiracy win”.

title: White House teleprompter operator accused over Trump bets no longer in job, official says
author: Roque Planas and agencies
summary: Official declines to say whether Gabriel Perez, who allegedly bet on prediction market Kalshi, resigned or was fired
body_text: A White House teleprompter operator who reportedly used inside knowledge to make bets about Donald Trump’s speeches on the online prediction market Kalshi is no longer in his post, according to a White House official. The official, who was not authorized to comment publicly about the personnel matter and spoke on condition of anonymity, said on Tuesday that Gabriel Perez “no longer works in the federal government”. The official would not say whether Perez resigned or was fired. The White House confirmed earlier this month that Perez had been placed on unpaid leave after ABC News reported he had used his inside knowledge to win more than $100,000 betting on what the president would say in big speeches, including his State of the Union address earlier this year. That figure is more than half the $175,000 salary he earned for his teleprompter work, according to White House personnel records. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt had described the reports of the insider trading as “deeply unfortunate and, frankly, a disgrace”. Robert Denault, Kalshi’s lawyer and head of enforcement, said on X following the ABC News report that the “Kalshi surveillance team promptly flagged, investigated and referred these trades” to the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the body that has regulatory authority over such matters. His statement did not name Perez, who has operated Trump’s teleprompter since 2016. The ABC report described suspicious activity on Kalshi’s “Mentions” market, in which users can place bets on phrases and specific words that might be used in public speeches. Kalshi recently began requiring users to disclose their place of employment, and the platform’s policy prohibits betting based on information that users gain because of their job. Prediction markets, which allow users to place speculative bets on a seemingly endless list of public events and trends, have exploded recently. Trading volume on Kalshi, one of the two largest prediction market trading platforms, soared from $100m last year to $3bn today, according to an estimate cited by CNBC. Kalshi recently said it would allow users to bet on drug trial results. The rise in prediction markets has created a major new incentive for insider trading. In April, federal prosecutors indicted Gannon Ken Van Dyke for allegedly betting on the whether former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro would be deposed. Prosecutors say Van Dyke, a US soldier who worked on the operation to remove and extradite Maduro, walked away with $400,000 in earnings. That same month, Kalshi said it had fined three political candidates who placed bets on their own races. In one case, Mark Moran placed a small bet on whether he would run for office before announcing his bid for a US Senate seat in Virginia as an independent. The industry’s proponents describe prediction markets as a form of derivatives, a type of contract that allows parties to make bets on the future value of an asset or commodity. Critics, however, have raised concerns from state authorities who view the industry as little more than unregulated gambling. Minnesota became the first state to ban prediction markets entirely in May, but a federal judge temporarily blocked the law before it went into effect. Trump has defended the prediction markets industry, saying that states should avoid regulating them, leaving the job instead to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

title: Trump praises back-to-back meetings with Zelenskyy and Netanyahu
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: US president makes positive posts as Ukraine seeks more firepower and Israeli PM seeks to repair relationship
body_text: Donald Trump hosted back-to-back White House meetings with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday, as Ukraine seeks more firepower for its air defenses and the Israeli prime minister tries to repair his strained relationship with the US president. Trump described both meetings in positive terms on social media on Tuesday evening, remaining vague about what was discussed. “Had a very good meeting!” Trump said of his sit-down with Netanyahu. “Obviously, many important subjects were discussed.” He posted a similar statement about his time with Zelenskyy, writing the “meeting went very well!” It was Netanyahu’s first visit to the Oval Office since he and Trump launched their joint military campaign against Iran on 28 February. Netanyahu’s relationship with Trump has been complicated in recent weeks by his push to keep fighting Iran and Hezbollah in Lebanon, even as Trump pursued a diplomatic opening with Tehran. Tensions between the pair have risen as the war has drifted inconclusively, with Trump calling the Israeli premier “crazy” and declaring: “Without me, there would be no Israel.” The two men are each facing pressure at home, with Netanyahu in a tough re-election fight, and Trump under pressure to end an unpopular war that has pushed up prices before November’s midterms. Trump signaled some of that friction beforehand. Asked on Fox & Friends on Tuesday morning about reports that Netanyahu planned to brief him on intelligence about Iranian activity at Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site Trump has threatened to bomb, he said he knew “exactly what’s going on at Pickaxe”, adding that Netanyahu raises it because “he wants me to stay involved”. Far outside the White House, behind the fences, protesters chanted: “Netanyahu, you’re a tyrant” and “Bibi, you’re not welcome here” on Tuesday. The closed-door meeting, which lasted about an hour, was expected to cover Iran, a framework deal the US and Israel signed with Lebanon, and a possible expansion of the Abraham accords, according to a White House official. Netanyahu also faces the task of reassuring Trump he will not obstruct US-led diplomacy in Gaza and Lebanon, as support for Israel among the US public has slipped, with a new AP-Norc poll showing a sharp decline amid accusations, denied by Israel, that its conduct in Gaza amounts to genocide. In a statement, Zelenskyy said he had discussed licensing arrangements to let Ukraine manufacture its own interceptors for Patriot missile systems. “We also spoke about diplomacy – it’s important that the diplomatic process be reinvigorated,” said Zelenskyy. “Our teams will arrange the details of their further communication. I am grateful to the United States for its firm support.” He opened by offering condolences over the death of the US senator Lindsey Graham, calling the late foreign policy hawk “a true friend of Ukraine”. Graham died suddenly earlier this month, aged 71, shortly after returning to Washington from a trip to Kyiv. Later on Tuesday, with Zelenskyy watching from the Senate gallery, the chamber advanced a sweeping Russia sanctions bill in tribute to Graham. The bill, renamed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, easily cleared a procedural hurdle, 86 to 12, hours after Graham’s funeral in Washington, where the late senator was hailed as a “fierce defender of Ukraine”.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Wildberries attacks shake Russian economy and banking
author: Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies
summary: Kremlin and state bank VTB may be forced to prop up online retailer amid crippling Ukrainian attacks; Kyiv prosecutors may target Lukashenko. What we know on day 1,617
body_text: The Kremlin has acknowledged it may have to prop up online retailer Wildberries – which has lost 10% of its warehousing capacity and huge amounts of stock in Ukrainian drone attacks. Kyiv has said its forces are attacking “Russia’s Amazon” because of its role in supplying Moscow’s army. The Kremlin acknowledged the government had discussed possible support for Wildberries. A senior industry source told Reuters that Wildberries was in a difficult situation and might have to seek government support, most likely through state-controlled banks, in order to maintain operations. An ‌executive at Ukraine’s leading arms producer Fire Point has said Wildberries is being targeted by Ukraine partly because of its partnership with state-controlled bank VTB. Denys Shtilerman, Fire Point’s co-founder and chief designer, in an interview posted on 27 July with the Ukrainian journalist Dmitry Gordon, described Wildberries as the largest borrower in Russia and said its demise would lead to the collapse of a large number of banks, including VTB. Wildberries and its rival Ozon are central to the Russian government’s plans to spur economic growth as Moscow faces mounting budget pressures from increased military spending and a broader economic slowdown. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov lavished praise on Wildberries for providing assistance to third-party sellers whose goods were stored in damaged warehouses. Those sellers have been clamouring for support. One of them, Marina Gorshkova, told her Instagram audience of 1.3 million people that she was appealing to “the country’s leadership” and there were a million registered users on Wildberries who needed help. Wildberries said that ⁠it had ⁠so far paid out 40 million roubles (US$508,582) to ⁠the families of those killed or those ⁠injured in Ukrainian drone attacks ‌on its ‌warehouses. Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s office has asked Ukraine’s top prosecutor to consider launching criminal proceedings against Alexander Lukashenko, the Belarusian dictator, according to a ⁠letter made public on Tuesday. Lukashenko allowed Vladimir Putin to use Belarus as a launchpad for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The Ukrainian ⁠president’s office said an exiled opposition group, the Belarus Democratic Forum, had asked Kyiv to prosecute Lukashenko ⁠for war crimes, genocide and “state terror”. Lukashenko’s administration did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. There is no current ‌prospect of Lukashenko appearing before a Ukrainian court, but Dmitry Bolkunets, secretary general of the Belarus Democratic Forum, said a prosecution would “significantly increase the personal legal and security risks faced by Lukashenko” and would be an act of historical justice. “It could have a profound impact inside Belarus, because Lukashenko would take it very personally and be deeply concerned about the consequences.” Ukraine and Iran’s foreign ministers spoke on Tuesday, Kyiv said, adding it wants to avoid an “escalation” after a Ukrainian attack on an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea. Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday said Kyiv had carried out long-range strikes in the Caspian Sea against vessels carrying military cargo involving Iran. Andriy Sybiga said he reiterated to his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, that “all of Ukraine’s actions are aimed solely at defending our country from Russian aggression and never intended to target civilian vessels or people”. Araghchi claimed that Sybiga had assured him the attack was “unintentional and Ukraine seeks no escalation”. However, Ukraine did not appear to publicly characterise the attack as unintentional, and Sybiga said he emphasised to Iran the need to “end any support for Russia’s war against Ukraine”. Ukraine suffers much damage and many casualties in Russian attacks that use Shahed drones either bought from Iran or built to its designs. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after meeting Donald Trump at the White House: “We talked ‌with the president about licences for producing interceptors for the Patriots and other ideas that could help.” Zelenskyy said he had met with officials from Lockheed Martin – one of the companies that produces Patriot interceptors – and teams were working “to move to co-production as quickly as possible”. “We also talked about diplomacy [with Trump] – it is important to step up the diplomatic process,” Zelenskyy said, referring to the lack of peace talks with Russia. Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have agreed to visit Ukraine for the first time, two sources familiar with the conversations told Reuters. The US Senate took the first steps toward passage of a sweeping Russian sanctions bill on Tuesday. The legislation would penalise countries that continue to buy Russian oil, gas and other exports. The bipartisan 86-12 procedural vote came hours after a funeral for Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, the bill’s chief negotiator. Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with senators just before the vote. The bill provides exceptions for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and are taking steps to reduce those imports. Some Democrats are hesitant that it might give Trump additional powers to recklessly impose tariffs elsewhere and on other countries.
