title: Wednesday briefing: Will Zelenskyy’s domestic struggles harm his reputation on the global stage?
author: Michael Segalov
summary: In today’s newsletter: A recent government reshuffle has exposed deep fractures within Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s wartime cabinet
body_text: Good morning. Another week, another diplomatic success for Volodymyr Zelenskyy. On Monday, his first meeting with Andy Burnham as PM confirmed continuity in the UK’s steadfast support for Ukraine. “We’ve got your back,” Burnham said as the pair spoke in Portsmouth. Yesterday, in Washington DC, after attending the funeral of Lindsey Graham – a once supportive Republican senator – Zelenskyy and Trump held a “positive and productive” meeting, as per the White House. Overnight, the US Senate advanced a sweeping Russian sanctions bill. Save for that somewhat shaky start in the early days of Donald 2.0, these well-executed global stage set-pieces have come to define Zelenskyy’s wartime leadership. The hundreds of billions he has secured in military, financial and humanitarian aid from the US, Europe, the UK and beyond during a period of global economic unease is remarkable. At home, however, Zelenskyy’s grasp of statecraft appears less comprehensive. Today, he returns to Kyiv to face another political crisis, with daily protests continuing in Ukraine, after the dismissal of popular defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov. And it’s not the first time one of his domestic decisions appears to have involved serious miscalculation. For today’s First Edition, we explore the challenges facing Zelenskyy on the home front and the battlefield, as Luke Harding, the Guardian’s senior international correspondent, shares the latest from Ukraine. Before that, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories UK news | Young people will be expected to engage with new support to find work, Pat McFadden has said. World news | At least 13 people have been killed after a 6.8 magnitude earthquake struck southern Japan, injuring hundreds and knocking out power and water to tens of thousands. Europe news | Nearly 4,000 people have been evacuated from tourist sites on France’s Atlantic coast as the return of winds and extreme heat jeopardises firefighters’ battles to contain wildfires raging in France and Spain. US news | Donald Trump hosted back-to-back White House meetings with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday, as Ukraine seeks more firepower for its air defences and the Israeli prime minister tries to repair his strained relationship with the US president. UK news | Led By Donkeys has received compensation after a giant banner it displayed in Parliament Square saying “Yes It’s A Genocide” was seized by officials and destroyed. In depth: ‘There’s a standoff between Zelenskyy, Fedorov and civil society’ Since taking up the Ukrainian defence brief in January this year, Fedorov proved himself effective. The 35-year-old former digital transformation minister and deputy PM hit the ground running. “Fedorov is seen as a young, modernising tech-savvy reformist,” Luke tells me, from his apartment in Kyiv. “Here in Ukraine, Fedorov is believed to have cleaned up a defence ministry plagued by Soviet era practices and alleged corruption.” Fedorov upped pay and modernised contracts for infantry, and introduced more transparent processes for procurement. There have been reports he identified significant murky military overspend. He messaged Elon Musk on X to request Starlink be switched off for Russian soldiers, and Musk obliged. It was a coup for Ukraine, and massively impactful on the battlefield. And despite his short tenure, Fedorov achieved change on the frontline too. He is a proponent of data-driven, hi-tech warfare – an approach which has shifted fighting to Ukraine’s advantage. Vibes-wise, at least, the contrast between Fedorov and Oleksandr Syrskyi – Ukraine’s 61-year-old erstwhile old school army chief – couldn’t be starker. “The culture around Syrskyi was extremely deferential and rather Soviet,” Luke says. “His reputation is that of a micromanager who hadn’t adapted to the changing nature of the war, fighting with infantry in the traditional way which comes with heavy losses.” While the details remain unclear, Fedorov and Syrskyi clashed. Earlier this month, Zelenskyy announced a government reshuffle. Among the top tier changes was the removal of Fedorov, while Syrskyi remained in post. It was a curious choice. He may be popular, but Fedorov appeared (previously, at least) to pose no political threat to Zelenskyy. He was a key ally and former aide to the president, a Zelenskyy loyalist. “He’s not someone who previously had independent political ambitions,” says Luke. Now, he is emerging as a potential successor. Polling found 72% of respondents were against Fedorov’s dismissal, with only 5% for. Last week, under mounting public pressure, Zelenskyy attempted to change course. Syrskyi was sacked, and Fedorov invited back into government. It appeared the crisis was averted. Only, Fedorov has since turned down alternative senior ministerial posts, while Zelenskyy is yet to re-offer him the defence gig. “Only three positions in the state … determine the course of the war: president, defence minister and commander-in-chief,” Fedorov said in a statement. “There’s a standoff between Zelenskyy, Fedorov and civil society,” says Luke, “and it shows no signs of resolving.” *** Reforms, not scams It’s not the first time Zelenskyy – a highly skilful diplomatic operator – has made what appears to be impulsive, certainly unpopular, personnel decisions. In July 2025, a wave of protests erupted in Kyiv and other major cities, in response to the Ukrainian government’s proposals to strip two major anti-corruption bodies of their independence. Despite these demonstrations, Zelenskyy signed the bill into law, before eventually backtracking under public pressure a few months later. “It was an enormously unpopular move,” Luke says, “and a bizarre decision to make.” One of these organisations (NABU – the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine) subsequently investigated Zelenskyy’s chief of staff Andriy Yermak who was widely understood to have been pushing for the reforms. It led to his abrupt resignation. One year on, protesters in Kyiv have been returning to the very same spot to again voice concerns about Zelenskyy’s judgment. “Initially, they were chanting ‘Syrskyi out, Fedorov back’.” Syrski’s subsequent departure, and Zelenskyy’s appointment of a younger, highly rated new commander-in-chief failed to placate protesters. Last Friday, Luke joined them at the Ivan Franko Square – connected to Bankova Street, home of the Presidential office. “The message had shifted,” Luke observed. “They still sang the national anthem and want Zelenskyy to succeed, but now they’re chanting ‘reforms not scams’, and ‘the people are the power’.” *** A path to victory This comes at a significant juncture for Ukraine. Wartime martial law bans elections, so Zelenskyy has been in power since 2019, when he won a stonking majority. Despite pressure from Putin (and at times Trump) to call a fresh election, polling shows appetite is low for a pre-peacetime vote, with six million Ukrainians now based abroad, and indiscriminate Russian airstrikes posing a risk to any public gatherings. Still, reports suggest the government had explored options for holding a (ceasefire dependent) election as soon as this year, with Zelenskyy apparently negotiating with his rivals. Fedorov’s trust rating has climbed in recent weeks, overtaking Zelenskyy; it’s a trajectory worth tracking. Meanwhile, the war is rapidly changing shape. Fedorov (and Syrskyi, who created Ukraine’s standalone drone department) have shifted focus from ground to sky. Luke has just returned from meeting one drone unit, which claims to have “destroyed the majority of Russia’s air defences” with their homemade kit. “What was once Russia’s great strength – its size and strategic depth – is turning into a liability,” says Luke. “Ukraine has regained the initiative.” Russia continues to slowly advance, but at a price of 30,000 dead and wounded troops per month. “I wouldn’t say Ukraine is winning,” cautions Luke, “but it’s taking a path to victory that is more convincing than anything we’ve seen since 2022.” *** Power struggle A difficult decision now sits at the top of Zelenskyy’s in-tray: reinstate Fedorov and take the politically embarrassing hit; or stand his ground, and hope the protests peter out. “There’s a suggestion that lots of vested interests don’t want Fedorov back as it’ll hurt them financially,” says Luke. “The protesters I spoke to believe that certain people around Zelenskyy are benefiting from the old system that Fedorov was challenging. That can’t be proven, but it’s what many Ukrainians think.” Last year’s (botched) attempts to change those anti-corruption bodies adds to this suspicion. Whatever motivated the initial reshuffle, to many the Fedorov/Syrskyi debacle represents something existential. “It’s a struggle for Ukraine’s soul,” Luke says, “between a younger western, progressive and inclusive generation who want Ukraine to be in the European mould, and the Soviet-inflected, insider-oriented older guard who operate in deals and handshakes and yes, some corruption.” There is, of course, an alternative read on the public outpouring of frustration. The protests have been policed with a distinctly light-touch. Even as Russia’s violent assault continues, with UN figures showing last month as the deadliest for Ukraine’s civilians in four years, civic life continues. “It shows people understand all this isn’t just about beating Russia,” says Luke, “but constructing a decent, fair, modern, forward-looking society after victory.” What else we’ve been enjoying “Put me through to real person” is something I often find myself typing when faced with an AI customer chatbot. I was heartened to read this letter from a reader who feels the same way. Hettie The Nigel Farage soap opera continues in Clacton, ahead of next month’s vanity project byelection. For this in-depth piece, Tim Burrows spent a few days in this coastal Essex corner, perfectly capturing the mood there. Michael Elisabeth Zerofsky has written a fascinating piece for the New York Times Magazine about the ideological war consuming the Heritage Foundation, and how it got sidelined by the second Trump administration. Hettie If you, like Thomas, by email have a less-than-perfect success rate when it comes to fresh pasta rolling, these tips from professional chefs will prove invaluable. It’s all about egg-size, apparently. Michael After reading Gardiner Harris’s book No More Tears, a blistering exposé of Johnson & Johnson, I’ll never look at talcum powder in the same way. The company has been ordered to pay $5.5bn to resolve thousands of lawsuits alleging that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer. Hettie Sport Commonwealth Games | Amy Hunt settles for 100m silver, after New Zealand sprinter Zoe Hobbs won the women’s 100m in a personal best of 10.93sec, while Emmanuel Eseme surged to the men’s 100m title in 9.83. Football | The roads around the French football federation headquarters in Paris were closed off for Zinédine Zidane’s unveiling as head coach for France. Golf | As she heads to Royal Lytham as a guest of the R&A for Thursday’s start of the Women’s Open, the inaugural winner Jenny Lee Smith gives us an interview. The front pages “Burnham calls for consensus on ‘urgent’ fix for social care crisis”, is the Guardian’s top headline today. On the same issue, the Telegraph writes “Workers face new tax to fund social care”, the Times has “Shake-up of social care to lock out private firms” and the Express says “2m missing out on social care they need”. Still on politics, the Mail runs with “Burnham benefits ‘bribe’ for parents of apprentices”, the FT has “Burnham to seek private sector deals in growth push”, and Metro writes “£4k if you let your children learn a trade”. Elsewhere, the i Paper says “Fury over Fifa plan to sell off World Cup”, and on the same news the Sun writes “For sale”. The Latest Labour overtake Farage’s Reform UK in polls Labour has overtaken Reform UK this week for the first time since March last year, according to multiple polls. The ‘Burnham bounce’ comes two weeks into Andy Burnham’s tenure in No 10, during which he has made major announcements on the cost of living and localised education to reduce youth unemployment, and an announcement on social care is expected soon. Is this a turning point for the beleaguered Labour government – or simply a honeymoon for the new PM? Lucy Hough speaks to senior political correspondent, Peter Walker. Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Matthew Myerscough came to fossil hunting after he was caught in an avalanche. Revisiting his old hobby as a boy was a way to cope with stubborn memories of the accident, and the enduring panic he faced. Now, it’s opened up a world of treasures, including a dinosaur footprint and, spectacularly, a sea dragon – a marine reptile from the Jurassic period, washed up on Lavernock beach in south Wales. His recent book details his “star finds”, and illuminates the strange, underground world of fossil hunting which gave him refuge in a moment of darkness. “There’s this mindful, almost meditative state that I get into because I’m forgetting about all the other stresses and worries in life. I’m so focused on what I’m doing in that moment.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? title: US joins forces with Saudis to strike Tehran-backed militias in Iraq
author: Guardian staff and agencies
summary: Oil price spikes after flare-up of fighting and claimed Iranian attacks on three tankers in strait of Hormuz
body_text: The US military said it knocked down an Iranian missile barrage and worked with Saudi Arabia forces to strike sites in Iraq that Tehran-backed militias have used to launch attacks in recent days. The strikes on Wednesday killed at least 20 members of a former paramilitary alliance that includes pro-Iran groups. In what Washington cast ⁠as “an attempted surprise ⁠attack” by Tehran, Iran had launched multiple ballistic missiles at US forces in the Middle East, shattering a brief pause in fighting. Iran’s target was a US base in Jordan, Axios cited a US official as saying. US Central Command (Centcom) said all Iranian missiles launched on Tuesday were intercepted, and the US warned any further attacks on American troops or Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure would trigger retaliatory strikes. The joint US-Saudi strikes on targets in Iraq killed at least 20 members of Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces and wounded others. The PMF is an Iraqi state security service that Iran has infiltrated. In a further sign that the lull in fighting could be over, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed on Wednesday to have struck and halted three “violating” oil tankers sailing an “illegal” route in the strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported. The price of Brent crude oil rose after news of the flare-up, hovering around $88 a barrel. Both sides had held fire over the weekend, after nearly two weeks of nightly strikes by the US on Iran, and repeated missile and drone salvoes by Tehran targeting Washington’s allies around the Gulf. Oil prices had plummeted after the weekend lull and Donald Trump said there was a “good chance” of progress in negotiations to end the war. The US and Saudi warplanes carried out strikes on Iran-backed militants in Iraq after accusing them of launching drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities in recent days. On Tuesday, the Iraqi prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, ordered security agencies to investigate the alleged attacks by militant groups, saying his country was committed to “preventing Iraqi territory from being used as a route or launching point for any attack targeting brotherly or friendly countries.” The Iraqi militias have denied any role in the drone attacks. The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed armed groups, called the Saudi claims “fabrications” and implied that Monday’s attacks were carried out by the Houthis, who had themselves claimed to have attacked Saudi oil facilities. The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen claimed to have forced a Saudi oil tanker to turn around as part of their self-styled blockade. Last week, they announced a blockade of Saudi shipping, putting another key Middle Eastern waterway – through the Bab el-Mandeb strait leading to the Red Sea – at risk. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center said a tanker reported hearing explosions while travelling in the southern Red Sea. It did not name the tanker but said the crew and vessel were safe. The Houthis also fired on at least one Saudi tanker in the Red Sea last week. Iran’s surprise attack came as the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, visited Washington. Israel has been notably absent from the recent fighting with Iran. Netanyahu said he had an “excellent” meeting with Trump at the White House, their first sit-down since launching the war, which offered Netanyahu a chance to smooth out strains in their relationship. The closed-door meeting lasted nearly an hour and a half and was “positive and productive”, the White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said. It comes as both leaders face growing pressures at home. Netanyahu is up for re-election and is embattled in part because of his deteriorating relationship with Trump. Trump is under pressure to end an unpopular war that has wreaked economic havoc and driven prices higher ahead of midterm elections this November. With the Associated Press and Agence France-Presse • This article was amended on 30 July 2026 to remove an image that was not editorially relevant.

title: Welcome to America, where you’re never quite sure if your senator is dead or not
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: Is it normal for a sitting senator to have to routinely submit proofs of life to a public who suspect he might be braindead? Just asking for 340 million friends
body_text: Is it normal for a sitting senator to have to routinely submit proofs of life to a public who suspect he might be braindead? Just asking for 340 million friends in the US. Mitch McConnell was hospitalized for a medical event on 14 June and we are now in week six of What on Earth Is Going on With Mitch? – a mystery that has riveted the nation. According to McConnell’s team there isn’t actually a mystery at all. The 84-year-old is doing great, they want us to know. So great that they have now released two photos to prove it. The first was made public on Sunday 12 July, almost a month after McConnell’s hospitalization and appears to have been prompted in part by Trump ally and far-right agent of chaos Laura Loomer’s claim that Mitch was “officially brain dead”. Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, had also just sent a letter to McConnell asking him to be transparent and put an end to the speculation about his health. Funnily enough, the day before that photo came out, I’d published a column with the headline “Is Mitch McConnell secretly deceased?” Rarely is a question answered so quickly. Perhaps, as my next offering to the mischievous headline gods, I’ll put out a piece titled: “Is Benjamin Netanyahu going to escape accountability forever?” But back to that photo, which we’ll call Proof of Life One (POL1). Mitch, I’ll be honest, looked pretty good. He was wearing a nice pink shirt and his wife was standing next to him with her mouth stretched into something resembling a human smile. I wouldn’t say she was caressing him exactly, but she had a hand under his arm. Mitch was also holding a copy of the day’s Washington Post Sports section so we could all see that he was not secretly deceased. Very normal stuff! Our tech overlords have ushered in a world where no one can be ever sure that visual evidence is real and POL1 immediately set off rabid speculation that the photo was AI. There is, I should note, no evidence whatsoever that the photo was AI. But there is also no evidence that McConnell had any idea what was going on in that photo, or that he is in a fit state to continue serving his constituents. His office put out a statement saying he’d had a fall in his home and had subsequently been treated for pneumonia, but we still haven’t actually heard directly from the senator. All of which is why POL1 did not put an end to the speculation that McConnell’s office is hiding details about the senator’s condition from the public. So, on Monday, to try and quell a new round of speculation, his office released a new photo dated 26 July, which we’ll call Proof of Life Two (POL2). This photo is pretty similar to the first one, except the senator is in a blue shirt. His office also put out a statement saying the senator is out of hospital, but still having “intense physical therapy” and wouldn’t be able to travel to the annual Fancy Farm picnic in western Kentucky. The statement did not say when he might be expected back in the Senate, which is scheduled to break for a month on 7 August. He has already missed 38 votes. Once again, this photo of an apparently living, breathing Mitch has not put an end to the questions around McConnell’s health. If the issue is his mobility rather than his mental capacity, why can’t McConnell come into the Senate in a wheelchair to do his job? That’s what happened last year, after all, after he suffered a fall and then was seen using a wheelchair at the Capitol. Demanding more transparency from a public servant who is collecting a taxpayer-funded salary to represent his constituents is not unreasonable. Indeed, if McConnell were in perfect health and a Democratic senator were in this position, McConnell would be leading the charge to ensure they resigned. The man has never been interested in empathy or civility, just power. It looks like Kentucky’s governor hasn’t been reassured by POL2 either. On Monday, Beshear renewed his calls for transparency, asking the senator to directly address Kentuckians about his health or resign. “As Governor of the state you serve, I am calling on you to directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky and provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign,” Beshear wrote in a letter. “If you are unwilling to voluntarily show that you still have the capacity to serve, I will insist Leader Thune fully investigate your condition, report to the American people, and begin the process [to fill your Senate seat] if warranted.” Is this letter finally going to lead to answers? I don’t know. But I do know that it’s highly likely that a situation like this is going to happen again. Regardless of where they are on the political spectrum, US lawmakers seem determined to cling to power until they die at their desks. Earlier this month, Senator Lindsey Graham became the fourth member of the US Senate since 2013 to have died while in office and the sixth member of Congress to have died while serving in the 119th Congress. Because the US is the greatest democracy in the world, Graham has now been replaced in the Senate by his sister Darline. And if lawmakers aren’t dying in office, then they’re vanishing from their responsibilities without feeling the need to be transparent with their constituents. In 2024, for example, a reporter discovered that Kay Granger, a Republican congresswoman from Texas, who hadn’t cast a vote in months, was dealing with “dementia issues” at a senior living facility. Her office hadn’t felt the need to disclose this to the public. There was also some speculation that House Republican leaders had been aware of the situation and deliberately chose to keep the information quiet to maintain their majority. And earlier this year Tom Kean Jr, a Republican, went off the radar for almost four months. He missed more than 100 votes but continued to collect his salary. Eventually he resurfaced and said he’d been to inpatient treatment for depression and hadn’t wanted to explain because he was a private person. Which is fair enough. But then may I suggest that a job in public office isn’t for you? It’s funny, isn’t it? There are millions of Americans who are never going to have the funds to retire. Who are going to be forced to work for minimum wage until they keel over on the job. Our lawmakers, however, have excellent salaries and an array of taxpayer-funded health benefits. They can retire early if they choose to do so. It’s a tragedy for our democracy that more of them don’t. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist and the author of Strong Female Lead

title: How free childcare started winning US elections: ‘Overnight, people realized how essential it was’
author: Sunny Patel
summary: Francesca Hong, a candidate for Wisconsin governor, is part of a wave of democratic socialists finding traction with an old idea
body_text: In a matter of weeks, Francesca Hong, an unlikely candidate for governor in one of the country’s most heated battleground states, will test a message that is at once radical and, to many, incredibly practical: the government should help pay for childcare. “When we talk about free childcare, you can connect to folks whether it’s on an economic argument or just purely that it’s the right thing to do for our kids,” said Hong, a democratic socialist running in Wisconsin’s Democratic primary on 11 August. “I always like to remind folks: if we don’t take care of our kids, who’s going to take care of us?” For 50 years, US childcare policy lived in the welfare drawer with programs such as Head Start, a free early learning initiative for low-income families, and subsidies focused on keeping poor mothers in the workforce. Anything broader was often shut down by conservatives advocating for families’ “personal choice” over government-run childcare. And while Democratic lawmakers, often women, campaigned on the need for affordable childcare – presidential hopefuls Hillary Clinton, Elizabeth Warren and Kamala Harris made it central to their platforms – they had little success. Then something shifted as the cost of care surpassed college tuition and a pandemic hangover pushed caregivers, and their wallets, to their limits: childcare became a middle-class problem that could no longer be ignored. In November, Zohran Mamdani made universal childcare a cornerstone of his New York mayoral campaign, and two centrists, Abigail Spanberger and Mikie Sherrill, won the governorships in Virginia and New Jersey, respectively, running on the same plank. In March, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare for all. In the nation’s capital, Janeese Lewis-George won the mayoral primary this summer with universal childcare among her top priorities. “We’re in an era of real affordability issues,” said Deb Haaland, former secretary of the interior who is currently running for governor of New Mexico. “Universal childcare is good for our economy – it creates jobs, it helps parents go to work without worrying about their children.” Behind these wins, though, are decades of painstaking organizing. Compounding crises, coupled with organizers’ longstanding work, have catapulted childcare from the sidelines to a kitchen-table issue as politically potent as the price of eggs or a grocery bill. Now, candidates vying for office in the midterm elections are seizing the moment to build on half a century of advocacy and win contests to give families some relief. Georgetown professor Joan Lombardi, who has advocated for early childhood policy across presidential administrations, distilled the moment into three parts: “First, for more parents today, childcare is their everyday reality. Second, affordability is driving it. And third, we have new innovations coming out of states and communities that can help inform policy decisions.” From radioactive policy to winning platform The US almost had a federally funded childcare system more than 50 years ago: Congress passed the Comprehensive Child Development Act, but Richard Nixon refused to sign it, fearing the alienation of his conservative base. At the time, one-third of women with children under age six worked. In the aftermath of the veto, the veteran civil rights activist Marian Wright Edelman founded the Children’s Defense Fund, which kept the vision of universal childcare alive, laying the groundwork for politicians’ childcare policy platforms since the 1970s and other legislative wins, such as the 1990 Child Care and Development Block Grant, which gave low-income families a voucher to pay for childcare. As more working mothers joined the halls of Congress, so did the push for federal childcare policy. Patty Murray, a senator from Washington state and former preschool teacher with two children, introduced the Child Care for Working Families Act in every Congress since 2017, but it took the pandemic to accelerate her cause: the bipartisan American Rescue Plan in 2021 infused $39bn into childcare – the first time Washington DC paid providers directly for operating costs rather than subsidizing individual slots. “Childcare facilities shut down, so our nurses couldn’t work, our essential employees couldn’t work,” she said. “And almost overnight, people realized how essential it was.” Solutions to affordability issues – the high costs of rent, groceries and childcare – have only continued to resonate with voters over the past year. In a sign of the times, the political action committee Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy is pouring $50m into races this midterm cycle. Even the Senate Democratic leadership is making childcare a pillar of their affordability agenda. “It’s not something people plan for the way they plan for buying a first home – suddenly it falls on their shoulders and they’re figuring it out alone,” Sondra Goldschein, executive director for Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy, said about childcare. “This appeals to people who are older and younger, Democrats and Republicans, people in cities and in suburban and rural areas. It’s just top of mind.” Universal childcare in the midterms While there is still no federal law that supports childcare for all families who need it, organizers are pushing states – and running candidates in those states – to fill the vacuum. In Wisconsin, Hong, a leading candidate for governor, has made a payroll-funded universal childcare guarantee a key part of her platform – a message that particularly resonates after $110m in pandemic-era childcare funding ran out last month. “We have not seen childcare, paid leave, elder care as part of infrastructure,” Hong said. “It is the care economy that allows us to have communities.” Hong’s plan would provide free childcare up to 400% of the federal poverty level, a 7% cap on childcare spending for all families and loan-forgiveness programs for early educators. “We cannot have a sustainable workforce without affordable childcare for working families,” Hong said. In DC, parents and childcare providers protested after outgoing mayor Muriel Bowser cut early childhood educators’ pay and initiated an enrollment freeze in the city’s childcare-subsidy program for low-income families. “We coordinated the largest-ever day of early learning program closures in March – ‘a day without childcare’ – culminating in about 150 people rallying in subzero temperatures,” said Travis Ballie, executive director of the Under 3 DC coalition. “We did all that because this was existential – not just to preserve what we’d won, but because losing it would set us back.” Lewis George, the democratic socialist who won the Democratic primary for DC mayor in June, has heard voters’ concerns and promised to take a different tack. Her platform for “childcare for all” would build a subsidy toward universal affordable care on top of universal pre-K for all three- and four-year-olds in the district. “People don’t want to hear what government can’t do – they want to hear what government can do, how government will solve their problems,” said Lewis George. How one state won childcare for all New Mexico is perhaps the most-cited example of where the vision of universal childcare has been realized – and it took more than a decade of organizing to make happen. Before Javier Martinez was the speaker of the house in New Mexico, he was a community organizer helping immigrant families obtain driver’s licenses. “We’d look at this room full of little kids, and the parents themselves were saying: ‘It’s impossible to find childcare,’” he said. Immigration advocacy groups, such as New Mexico Voices for Children and Olé, led the charge for the state to pay for universal childcare in an innovative way: through a land grant funded by oil and gas revenue. In session after session, the legislature refused to hold a hearing on the issue, said Martinez. “I got to the point where, looking from the outside in, I thought: ‘Is this the best we can do as a legislature, as Democrats especially?’” he said. That’s when he decided to run for office in 2014. When the childcare plan remained stymied by three fiscally conservative Democratic state senators, organizers targeted their re-election in 2020. “Our coalition pushed hard and ran good people,” said Martinez. “Once those three people were out of the equation, this thing flew right by.” In 2022, organizers successfully put a state constitutional amendment on the ballot establishing a right to early childhood education funded by the land grant. A state law established universal early childcare earlier this year. Martinez said that New Mexico’s circumstances were sometimes viewed as exceptional: “Some people have pooh-poohed our idea because they say: ‘Well, not everybody has oil and gas.’ No, but everybody has poor people. You [need to] organize poor people in genuine ways.” Not all pro-universal childcare candidates are winning their races in the midterms. In Colorado and California, progressive candidates lost their primaries to incumbents and longtime local politicians. In New York, the lieutenant governor, Antonio Delgado, laid out a clear universal childcare vision for the state but lost to his competitor, incumbent Kathy Hochul, who had adopted a version of his plan after seeing Mamdani become New York City mayor on a similar platform. For organizers, affordable childcare is more than a winning platform and a goal in the current midterm cycle. “Childcare is having a moment,” said Helene Stebbins, executive director for the early childhood advocacy group Alliance for Early Success. “Let’s build it. Let’s solidify it. But let’s recognize that that’s not the solution, or the end, for building that infrastructure.”

title: Jordan Klepper on Trump being heckled: ‘That’s President Pedophile Protector’
author: Guardian staff
summary: Late-night hosts speak about Trump’s trip to Michigan, where a local again shouted the same name at him
body_text: Late-night hosts spoke about Donald Trump’s recent Michigan visit and his attendance at Lindsey Graham’s funeral. Jordan Klepper On The Daily Show, Jordan Klepper took viewers through Trump’s recent visit to the General Motors facility in Michigan, showing footage of him walking past cars and knocking on one of them. “Knocking on the car hood is probably the most normal thing he’s ever done,” Klepper said, comparing it to standard dad behaviour. When Trump last visited Michigan in January, a heckler called him a “pedophile protector” during his visit and once again, during a speech, he was called the same thing. “Show some respect for the office,” he said. “That’s President Pedophile Protector.” He continued: “Why does this keep happening? Is it the same guy? Is it something in the water? Is it because Trump withheld millions of Epstein files and no one has been held accountable for it? We’ll never know!” Trump responded by calling the heckler a communist with Klepper said is the “opposite of pedophile” joking that “we all remember Karl Marx hosting To Catch a Predator”. Klepper also said to the heckler directly: “Don’t shout crazy shit at him, he was elected to shout crazy shit at us.” This week also saw the opening of a new trade route from Michigan to Ontario clouded in controversy after Trump imposed a 50% tariff on Canada which led to a joint ribbon-cutting ceremony being cancelled. Klepper said it was “so heartbreaking to see mum and dad fighting like this” but said that Trump was “beefing with the entire rest of the world” as well. The president was “losing his war on drugs” after it was revealed that a long-term boat-targeted operation has not reduced the amount or purity of cocaine and has instead encouraged drug lords to find new ways to smuggle goods in. Klepper said that the “same people who found a way to sneak in a powder using your butt” are “pretty good at problem-solving”. Seth Meyers On Late Night, Seth Meyers spoke about Trump’s speech at Graham’s funeral which he said would have the president claiming the late senator would want to point out the “2020 election had massive voting irregularities and Trump barely knew Jeffrey Epstein”. This week has also seen a report showing that the beleaguered Taylor Farms tried to delay an FDA recall announcement after it was alleged the recent explosive diarrhea outbreak originated there. “If I understand correctly, cyclospora makes it very hard to delay anything,” he joked. The American Museum of National History has also started to display a replica of the New York Knicks championship trophy, leading Meyers to quip: “You can also see a Mets trophy at Ripley’s Believe It or Not.” Kids in New Jersey recently fell ill after eating chocolate laced with mushrooms, which had Meyers saying that it was also “the day they all learned how to make a campfire with their minds”. Canada has been issuing warnings that people need to stop dumping goldfish, which had Meyers joking that things are going well if “their biggest problem is loose goldfish”. Starbucks has also entered into a new deal with Delta Air Lines, which plans to reward members with one sky mile for every dollar spent. “Do you know how much coffee you’d have to drink to get a free trip?” he said. “You wouldn’t need a plane.”

title: Trump officials turned to AI and a mafia killer to bolster case, Comey lawyers allege
author: Sam Levine in New York
summary: James Comey’s lawyers say Secret Service illegally tracked him to develop case around his ‘8647’ seashell post
body_text: Lawyers for former FBI director James Comey alleged on Tuesday that US Secret Service agents illegally surveilled Comey, Donald Trump requested regular updates into the investigation, and law enforcement turned to ChatGPT and a known mafia killer as they scrambled to find justification for criminally charging Comey for posting a picture of seashells that spelled out “8647”. The claims were laid out in a motion to dismiss a criminal case the US Department of Justice filed against Comey in April, in which it said the post by Comey – whom Trump fired in his first term – was a threat on the US president’s life. In the motion filed on Tuesday in federal court in North Carolina, Comey’s lawyers said the case should be dismissed for vindictive and selective prosecution. “The government had initially investigated Mr Comey’s seashells post, but that investigation appeared to be going nowhere until Mr [Todd] Blanche and US attorney Ellis Boyle reinvigorated it,” Comey’s lawyers wrote. “The ensuing indictment is not based on a good-faith application of the law to the facts; instead, it effectuates a years-long campaign by the president to use the criminal process to punish Mr Comey for his protected speech and because of the president’s deep-seated animosity.” Comey filed a separate motion earlier this week, seeking dismissal of the case on grounds that the post was protected speech and not a “true threat” against the president. Trump has long fumed over the way Comey handled the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election while director of the FBI. Comey has also been an outspoken critic of Trump. The justice department indicted Comey last year in a separate case, claiming he had lied to US Congress. Those charges, which were seen as thin, were tossed out after a judge ruled the prosecutor handling them had been unlawfully appointed. Comey told investigators he came across the formation of shells while on vacation with his wife in eastern North Carolina in May 2025. The phrase “86” is often used as shorthand to get rid of something, while Trump is currently serving as the 47th US president, and Comey posted the photo to Instagram. Comey later deleted the photo, saying he didn’t know it could be interpreted as a violent threat. “It never occurred to me, but I oppose violence of any kind so I took the post down.” Comey and his wife, Patrice, voluntarily spoke with Secret Service investigators after the incident. Internal Secret Service documents show that Trump was requesting updates on the investigation as it was ongoing. Even though Comey agreed to a voluntary interview in Washington, a Secret Service supervisor was asked about the possibility of tracking Comey’s phone on his drive back from Washington to North Carolina through an “exigency” request without a warrant. The supervisor said it was a “bad idea”, according to their notes that were attached to the motion. “To declare an exigency exemption, we needed to believe that there is an imminent threat to life or limb,” the supervisor wrote. “At that time we did not believe that anyone’s life was in immediate danger and legally it was a bad idea to ping the phone.” The supervisor wrote another agent agreed with him, but said the Secret Service might do it anyway. The next day, the supervisor wrote a note saying the “#3 guy at DOJ” wanted to ping the cellphone with an exigency request. The notes do not say the name of the official. Comey’s phone ultimately was tracked and the couple was also followed as they drove back from North Carolina, Patrick Fitzgerald, his attorney, said in a sworn affidavit. Documents included in the filing also lay out how law enforcement officials were unable to confirm that the term “86” was one that implied violence. Secret Service agents interviewed an unidentified person who knew the Comeys, but said they had not talked to them in several years and hoped the former FBI director went to jail. After telling agents they initially believed the term “86” meant something on a menu, they came to believe it was a violent threat after hearing Rudy Giuliani claim Comey had worked on cases where the term “86” meant kill. The FBI searched records related to the federal case against mobster John Gambino, which Comey handled when he was a federal prosecutor for references to “86”, according to the motion. There were no references to it. The FBI also conducted a broader search of all of its records going back decades for the term and the results were inconclusive. After the indictment was filed against Comey in April, Comey’s lawyers said, law enforcement officials were still hunting for evidence that Comey would have understood the term “86” to be a violent one. They interviewed two former FBI agents who worked on mafia cases, who said they were familiar with the term, but could not say definitively that it would have been used violently by the mafia. Agents also turned to ChatGPT and Google AI to search for meanings of the term “86”. Neither returned definitive results. Officials also interviewed Salvatore “Sammy The Bull” Gravano, a one-time underboss in the Gambino crime family, who confessed to nearly 20 murders, to try to build a case against Comey, the filing says. Gravano was a cooperating witness in the Gambino case Comey prosecuted. He told agents that while he believed it meant “to get rid of someone” he did not recall ever discussing the term with Comey, Comey’s lawyers said. Gravano, a podcaster who has praised Trump, told investigators that he interpreted Comey’s photo to mean “let’s kill Trump,” but he did not take it to mean Comey personally was going to kill Trump, Comey’s lawyers wrote.

title: Fauci invokes fifth amendment and declines to testify in Senate Covid hearing
author: Jessica Glenza
summary: Adviser to Trump and Biden for pandemic says Republican senator has ‘unhinged obsession’ with him
body_text: Dr Anthony Fauci refused to answer questions at a high-profile Senate committee hearing on the origins of Covid-19 and accused the Republican senator leading questioning of having an “unhinged obsession” with him. Fauci, the veteran former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (Niaid), served as a key adviser to Donald Trump and Joe Biden during the Covid-19 pandemic. The hearing was called by Kentucky senator Rand Paul, who has investigated Fauci for years. Fauci said Paul’s goal was “embarrassing and intimidating me”, and ultimately landing him “behind bars”. “Therefore, although it pains me to do so, because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys I will invoke my right under the fifth amendment of the constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” Fauci said in his opening statement. Paul, frustrated, later told reporters that he would hold a vote to hold Fauci in contempt of US Congress next week, and described the question of whether the fifth amendment could shield him as “a question for the courts”. Fauci, 85, served under seven US presidents and through numerous health crises, including the HIV crisis, Ebola outbreaks and the first coronavirus outbreak, called Sars-CoV-1. He became a household name overnight when the Covid-19 pandemic halted social life in 2020. Quickly after opening statements, the hearing became a back-and-forth between Paul and Fauci. Paul grew visibly agitated as Fauci refused to answer, threatened the scientists with “repercussions”, and then tossed one of Fauci’s attorneys from the hearing room. “Did the [National Institutes of Health] ever fund gain-of-function [research] on monkeypox?” Paul asked, in reference to research that manipulates viruses to make them more effective to shed light on how outbreaks happen. “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution,” said Fauci. After another description of research Paul found unacceptable: “Dr Fauci, did the NIH ever conduct research for or in coordination with any element of the intelligence community, CIA, [Office of the Director of National Intelligence]?” Fauci responded: “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution.” Paul pressed on: “Dr Fauci, would you at least like to answer this one question for us today, and let us know whether or not you have changed your mind on whether or not the benefits of gain-of-function [research] outweigh the risks?” Fauci replied: “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution.” A visibly frustrated Paul soon scolded Fauci: “There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.” Soon, an attorney for Fauci attempted to join him at the table, and Paul demanded the attorney move. “This is not a game with his lawyers,” said Paul, to the attorney who was apparently trying to speak, but could not be heard for lack of a microphone. “The attorneys were not recognized.” “There’s a row behind you, sir,” said Paul. “This is the way Anthony Fauci wants to be remembered – for a lawyer not recognizing the rules … Security please remove him from the room,” Paul said. The attorney patted Fauci on the shoulder and voluntarily left, alongside a guard. Members of the audience, which conspicuously included rightwing media figure Laura Ingraham, applauded. In part, Paul’s frustration at the hearing stemmed from a presidential pardon Fauci received from Biden, which in turn implicates the fifth amendment. There is debate among experts about how far the fifth amendment extends. Some argue that once a person accepts a presidential pardon, they cannot invoke the fifth amendment for federal crimes. Without that right, Congress could hold a witness in contempt, which can lead to fines or – in the extreme – jail time. Others have argued that the right extends as long as there is a valid threat of prosecution, particularly by states. “You don’t have any rights under the fifth amendment,” claimed Josh Hawley, a Republican senator of Missouri, in a line of accusatory questioning. “This is about contempt – contempt for this body, and contempt for the American people.” Democrats, meanwhile, defended Fauci. Paul is “single-mindedly fixated on seeing Dr Fauci prosecuted for imaginary crimes, and you are so invested in that outcome you have created a personal brand around it”, Fauci’s attorneys argued in a statement read aloud by the Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal, of Connecticut. Ahead of the hearing, Republicans characterized their work as investigating “the origins of Covid-19 and risky taxpayer-funded life science research”, while scientists have characterized the investigation as “vilification and harassment” of Fauci, who led Niaid for 38 years before retiring in 2022. Indeed, Republican senator Bernie Moreno took the opportunity to demand Fauci apologize for a military policy that required service members to take the Covid-19 vaccine, to Americans who lost businesses during the pandemic and to a single Ohio mother who was arrested for not wearing a mask during an outdoor football game early in the pandemic. The senator called Fauci a “total and complete disgrace”. Ron Johnson, a Republican senator of Wisconsin, used the hearing to call the Covid-19 vaccine, credited by scientists with saving millions of lives, an “experimental gene therapy”. He also accused Fauci of “lying” to his own diary, which elicited a smirk from Fauci. The hearing was a continuation of Paul’s years-long support of the “lab leak” theory, or the idea that the Covid-19 pandemic began as a release from the Wuhan Institute of Virology, a theory many virologists contend is improbable. “For years, Americans were told a lab origin wasn’t just unlikely – it was dismissed outright by the very people funding and reviewing this research,” Paul, who chairs the Senate committee on homeland security and governmental affairs, where Fauci testified, said last week. Paul has argued that Fauci lied about the origins of the pandemic to shield his own culpability, because the NIH funded the lab in Wuhan through a sub-grant. Paul argued Fauci lied about the origins of the pandemic because, as Paul later hypothesized to reporters: “Holy you know what – if it came from the lab, If I funded the lab, I could be responsible for this entire pandemic.” The “lab leak” theory has gained significant traction in Republican circles since political opinion on the pandemic began to fracture. In just one example, the White House published a treatise on the theory in April 2025 that served as a rationale for defunding the National Institutes of Health (NIH). The theory in part impugns gain-of-function research, in which scientists seek to develop better vaccines by working with potentially dangerous pathogens. A 2024 survey of virologists from the Global Catastrophic Risk Institute found that most believed the pandemic began as a so-called spillover event, or a virus jumping from an infected animal to a human. Similarly, a group of virologists argued in the Journal of Virology that the “preponderance” of evidence points to a natural origin, that the “lab leak” theory received outsized attention and that, ultimately, the origin may never be known. Gain-of-function research, meanwhile, has split the scientific community for years. The scheduled hearing comes just days after Paul released what he described as Fauci’s “diary”, a more than 1,100-page document characterized as revealing Fauci’s inner conflicts about the lab leak theory. Scientists have said this is a normal part of scientific debate. The diary also contained entries about Trump, who he advised closely during the early days of the pandemic. He described the president as “rambling”, “crazy”, “desperate”, “bumbling”, “incompetent”, “an idiot”, “a true embarrassment”, “totally nuts” and “truly an obnoxious adolescent”. Gary Peters, a Democratic senator of Michigan, described the hearing as damaging to science and ignoring ongoing public health threats, such as the outbreak of the food-borne parasite cyclospora and measles, both at record highs. “It’s attempting to turn one person into a scapegoat for a crisis that hundreds of officials across the Biden and Trump administrations were responsible for handling,” said Peters, who did not ask Fauci any questions. “This is only going to deter other scientific experts from public service.”

title: Anthony Fauci’s high-profile Senate hearing: what we learned
author: Jessica Glenza
summary: Six years on from Covid crisis, Republicans still politicizing science – and Fauci remains a political punching bag
body_text: A US Senate committee hearing featuring Dr Anthony Fauci revealed at least one certainty: six years after the pandemic, politicizing science remains a vital political tactic. The high-profile hearing was pitched by its Republican chair, Rand Paul of Kentucky, as an investigation into the origins of the Covid pandemic. It quickly became a forum for recrimination of a once-leading US government scientist by Republican senators. Fauci, a career civil servant who spent 38 years at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (Niaid), declined throughout the hearing to answer questions. Here are five takeaways from Wednesday’s hearing. Rand Paul’s ‘unhinged obsession’ with Fauci The hearing was centered around an assertion Paul has promoted for years: that the Covid pandemic began in 2020 as a “leak” from the Wuhan Institute of Virology, even as virologists see a natural jump from animals to humans as more likely. This belief underpinned Paul’s argument for bringing Fauci before the committee. If the pandemic was indeed started by a “lab leak”, Fauci “could be responsible for this entire pandemic” because the National Institutes of Health (NIH) provided the institute with a sub-grant, he later told reporters. His only witness was Fauci, who served as a key adviser to Trump and Joe Biden during the pandemic, and has become a political punching bag on the right. Paul has interrogated Fauci in the past. Fauci appeared at Senate hearings at least a dozen times, according to his attorneys, and answered lawmakers’ questions. Fauci described Paul’s investigation as an “unhinged obsession” with seeing him “behind bars”, and one that had led to starkly different advice from his attorneys this time around. “Although it pains me to do so, because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys I will invoke my right under the fifth amendment of the constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” said Fauci. Paul appeared to know Fauci would do this. The senator had a copy of a law which he claimed compelled Fauci to testify ready to hand to him. Criticism of scientists continues Scientists have not witnessed Fauci’s compelled testimony – he only appeared on Capitol Hill on Wednesday under subpoena – without dissent. A group of 155 scientists wrote an open letter calling for the government to stop the “vilification and harassment of many American scientists”. “The charges against Dr Fauci are baseless, suggesting he covered up the origins of Covid, that he bribed or persuaded other scientists to join his cover-up, that Niaid-funded research sparked the pandemic, that he personally holds patents on the virus, and that he’s working with intelligence agencies to suppress the true story of the pandemic,” the letter stated. “No credible evidence has been produced to support these absurd charges.” Paul’s frustration with fifth amendment Whether or not Fauci can successfully invoke the fifth amendment of the US constitution – which allows Americans to decline to answer questions that could incriminate them, without repercussions – became a part of the hearing itself. Fauci received a presidential pardon before Biden left office. Recent presidential pardons from Trump and Biden have led to renewed debate about whether the amendment can be invoked when a witness appears before federal lawmakers post-pardon. Visibly frustrated by Fauci’s assertions, Paul told him: “There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.” Later, Paul told reporters he intends to call a vote for contempt of Congress next week, in the committee on homeland security and security and governmental affairs where Fauci appeared. His Republican colleague, Josh Hawley of Missouri, later joined in. “You don’t have any rights under the fifth amendment,” he said. “This is about contempt: contempt for this body and contempt for the American people.” Republican criticism of Fauci wide-ranging Republicans lined up to attack Fauci. The Wisconsin senator Ron Johnson accused him of covering up unfavorable information about Covid vaccines, which he described as “experimental gene therapy”, even after scientists credited them with saving millions of lives. The Republican senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio demanded Fauci apologize for a military policy that required service members to take the Covid vaccine, to Americans who lost businesses during the pandemic, and to a single Ohio mother who was arrested for not wearing a mask during an outdoor football game early in the pandemic. The senator called Fauci a “total and complete disgrace”. The Republican Joni Ernst of Iowa criticized use of aborted fetal tissue in research. The Democratic senator Gary Peters of Michigan argued the hearing was an attempt to “turn one person into a scapegoat for a crisis that hundreds of officials across the Biden and Trump administrations’ were responsible for handling”, warning: “This is only going to deter other scientific experts from public service.” Criticizing science important for Republicans The Trump administration has invoked the “lab leak” theory to criticize past pandemic policies – even as the party has asserted that the end of the pandemic justified cutting $11.4bn state and local health department funding. Disruptions to government funding that imperiled critical research into cancer and Alzheimer’s are justified as ridding the government of a focus on diversity, equity and inclusion. Canceling grants based on political priorities, trialled at the National Institutes of Health in 2025, are now the basis of a proposed rule that would bring the $1tn entire federal grant-making apparatus under the control of political appointees. Wednesday’s hearing was another example of how criticizing scientists has become an important outlet for the party – and where relitigating the Covid crisis justifies skepticism of a broad range of science. “For the past 18 months, the Trump administration has been engaged in a campaign to rewrite this history,” said Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat of Connecticut, about the darkest days of the pandemic, when hospitals overflowed and researchers worked on hyper-speed to understand the virus. “Today’s proceeding, I fear, is part of that effort.”

title: Trump announces $22bn plan to rebuild Dulles international airport
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Planned overhaul forms part of president’s broader pattern of directing changes in Washington after arch and ballroom
body_text: Donald Trump announced on Wednesday a $22bn plan to rebuild Washington’s Dulles international airport on Wednesday after the US president personally weighed in on the design of the capital’s main international gateway. “In the end, you can end up with – I think – maybe the best airport, and one of the biggest airports, anywhere in the world, and it’s going to be a great thing for Washington DC,” the president said during an announcement at the Oval Office on Wednesday. He was flanked by Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, Scott Kirby, United Airlines CEO, and Jack Potter, president of Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority (MWAA), which operates the airport under a 50-year lease from Congress. Jensen Huang, the Nvidia CEO, was also off-camera in the Oval Office. The news followed reporting from CBS News that Trump had scrutinized 3D models from contractors competing to carry out the overhaul at the White House, and offered proposed changes. The planned overhaul of Dulles forms part of a broader pattern of Trump personally directing changes to Washington, from a proposed White House ballroom to a planned 250ft arch. Unlike some of those projects, the president’s push to remake Dulles has drawn a more tepid response, given longstanding complaints about the airport’s distance from the city, its jet-fuel-scented concourses, and its reliance on ageing shuttle vehicles. Trump said he wanted a parking garage large enough to hold roughly 32,000 cars, boasting: “That’ll be a world record, and very convenient.” He said passengers would move through the site via a new spine running straight through the terminal into “massive, massive ports”, adding that the goal was for planes to load without doubling back. “It’s going to be amazing,” he said. The scheme is also expected to include five new terminals to replace the airport’s existing four, with the underground train system expanded so passengers no longer need Dulles’s much-maligned “mobile lounges” – the slow-moving shuttles that ferry travelers across the tarmac to their gates. A new underground pedestrian tunnel and additional moving walkways are also planned. People briefed on the proposal said the approved design leans on glass and gold, including gold-mirrored ceilings throughout the terminals. Trump explained how he was displeased with the airport he inherited. “Right now, this is not a very good airport. We’re going to make it a great airport,” he said, later adding that the current set-up, split between trams and elevated shuttles, was “a real mess” that leaves “nobody” sure what’s going on. He also framed the project as part of a wider ambition to reclaim American airport-building bragging rights, noting the country hasn’t opened a major airport since Denver in 1995, and arguing: “It’s time to ensure that the United States has the greatest airports anywhere in the world.” The final design was distilled from a competitive field, according to Trump, who claimed there were “over 30 architects and 30 different designs” to choose from. Duffy, who has publicly championed the overhaul, described the existing Dulles as “dark, it is dated, a little dank maybe”, and said the redesign would strip out the airport’s much-mocked elevated shuttles – which he compared to something “from Star Wars” – in favor of a horseshoe train line and a direct walkway running the length of the terminal. He credited Trump personally with shaping the final concept, telling him “you actually did it”, and predicted the finished airport would be “the premier airport in our country”. Duffy also cast the project as a rare point of consensus in Washington, saying frustration with Dulles cuts across party lines: “Whether you’re Republican or Democrat, you hate the way [Dulles] operates.” United, which handles roughly 70% of traffic at Dulles, has agreed to help finance the project, which is expected to take years and cost more than $20bn, according to the Washington Post. MWAA is expected to fund much of the work through new bond issuances, and had already approved a separate $7bn capital plan for the airport in 2025. Complaints about Dulles sharpened last November when a mobile lounge collided with a concourse dock, injuring at least 18 people. A Trump-appointed MWAA board member later cited the crash as further reason to retire the shuttles. Dulles handled a record 29 million passengers in 2025, up 6.4% on the previous year, and is set to open a new 14-gate concourse for United this autumn.

title: Morning Mail: headwinds for green revolution, Football Australia’s Fifa deadline, Fauci takes the fifth
author: Martin Farrer
summary: Anti-wind campaigns eat into popular support for renewable power sources; federation must decide whether or not to join World Cup selloff
body_text: Morning everyone. Despite Australians’ enthusiasm for installing home solar panels and batteries, a survey shows today that anti-wind power campaigns are undermining wider popular support for the transition to green energy. We have analysis on how the revelations at the NSW Icac are pushing the Liberals into dangerous territory, Anthony Fauci declining to give evidence to the US Senate, and “Clicky Ponting” suspended amid a local cricket scandal in the UK. Australia Bat signal | A sudden decline in critically endangered bats is troubling experts, who recorded about 5,000 fewer southern bent-wing bats than usual at Naracoorte’s “bat cave” in South Australia this summer. Electric shock | Organised campaigns against wind and solar energy have proved “extremely effective” in undermining support for renewable energy but enthusiasm for electric vehicles has jumped after Donald Trump’s attack on Iran, according to a snapshot of attitudes to the clean energy transition. AI spending ‘cap’ | Software firm Atlassian has sought to tighten tracking of its staff’s AI spending by introducing “wallets” with monthly caps of up to $2,000 for each employee amid an explosion in costs at other tech companies. Flu spread | Scientists have confirmed that bird flu is being spread locally in Australia but what does it mean for wildlife, what can be done to stop it, and how bad will it get? ‘Shit sheet’ fight | The NSW Icac hit pay dirt yesterday, Anne Davies writes, with the revelation that a faction of rightwing Liberals compiled “shit sheets” of potentially damaging material to use against their factional political opponents. World Wildfires crunch | The next 12 hours will be “decisive” for a large wildfire burning near Madrid, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said, as blazes rage across southern Europe and three firefighters died in Crete. Half of England is officially in drought, with July set to be the driest on record while hot summers are endangering hydrangeas in the south of the country. Fauci fifth | Anthony Fauci, who served as a key adviser to Trump and Joe Biden during the Covid-19 pandemic, has refused to answer questions at a high-profile congressional Covid hearing, accusing a Republican senator of having an “unhinged obsession” with him. Actor accused | The actor and singer Jared Leto has been accused in a BBC documentary of criminal sexual conduct by four women, with the alleged offences taking place when the women were teenagers. ‘Uncharted territory’ | US-Saudi strikes on Iran-backed militia in Iraq on Wednesday have pushed the region into “uncharted territory”, analysts have warned. ‘Clicky’ suspended | Saltburn, the cricket club at the heart of the “Clicky Ponting” row, have said they are treating allegations of cheating very seriously and have suspended the player at the centre of the controversy. Full Story Will Peter Falconio’s body ever be found? Twenty-five years ago, on a desolate stretch of Australian highway, Bradley John Murdoch flagged down British backpackers Falconio and Joanne Lees. Falconio was never seen again. One former British government expert says he knows the “most likely” place Falconio’s body was hidden. Queensland correspondent Ben Smee joins Reged Ahmad as police try to finally close the case. In-depth “I refuse to allow this cynical outlook of politics to infect our country,” Cheek Media co-founder Hannah Ferguson writes, explaining why she is running as an independent in Anthony Albanese’s seat of Grayndler at the next election. She argues the prime minister represents a closed political system that does not deliver change – and which has allowed the rise of Pauline Hanson. Not the news Australians consume more chicken than any other meat but packaging can be confusing. Check out this explainer as experts break down the difference between free-range, organic and “hormone-free”. Sport Commonwealth Games | Australian runner Olli Hoare has clarified he did not witness a murder in Glasgow as he had the good news that he has been reinstated in the men’s 1500m. Former Australian track cyclist Matt Richardson has pulled out of the Games because of injury, depriving crowds of a much-anticipated showdown with his former teammates. World Cup | Fifa member associations – including Football Australia – have been given a deadline of 19 September to decide whether to apply for an initial payment of about A$30m from the proceeds of Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors. Cricket | Justin Langer has said he has had no contact from the England about coaching the men’s Test team, but suggested he could be tempted. The Indian Premier League’s value has surged to an estimated A$30bn, with only the NFL having a higher per-match value. Media roundup Victorian Labor is braced for Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan to give evidence at the newly established royal commission into the Big Build, the Australian claims. The ABC reports that AstraZeneca will provide a breast cancer and endometriosis treatment drug to eligible women indefinitely and free of charge. And also on the ABC, Neil the seal’s damage bill in Tasmania has passed $45,000. What’s happening today Courts | A federal court decision that found the government does not have a legal duty of care to protect Torres Strait people from climate harm is being appealed. Art | The Archibald prize announces its people’s choice-winning portrait at 11am. title: Senate unanimously passes resolution opposing pardon for Ghislaine Maxwell
author: Anna Betts
summary: Longtime Epstein associate serving 20-year sentence for sex-trafficking crimes has exhausted series of appeals
body_text: The US Senate on Wednesday unanimously passed a resolution declaring its opposition to any presidential pardon for Ghislaine Maxwell, the longtime Jeffrey Epstein associate who is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence for sex-trafficking crimes. Introduced by Senator Jacky Rosen, a Democrat of Nevada, the resolution states that Maxwell “should not be granted a Presidential pardon or any form of clemency for her crimes with Jeffrey Epstein relating to the sexual exploitation and abuse of minors”. Although Senate resolutions like these are non-binding and symbolic, Rosen’s office noted in a news release in February when she introduced the measure that the resolution was “designed to put the Senate on record opposing the prospect” of Donald Trump of granting a pardon or clemency to Maxwell. “It’s frankly horrifying that Trump would entertain the idea of clemency for even a second for a convicted sex trafficker,” Rosen said in a floor speech on Wednesday. The resolution was brought on Wednesday, as the Senate weighed Trump’s nomination of Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, to stay in the role permanently. Rosen said its unanimous passage sent a clear message to the White House and Blanche that “there should be NO special treatment for Ghislaine Maxwell”. A representative for Maxwell did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. By refusing to object, Republicans agreed to the resolution, which states that granting Maxwell “a pardon, commutation, or any other form of executive clemency” would be “inconsistent with the interests of justice and accountability for crimes involving the sexual exploitation of children”. The resolution also states that “the President should not grant a pardon, commutation, or any other form of executive clemency” to Maxwell. “The Senate stands with the victims of sexual exploitation and trafficking and affirms its commitment to justice, accountability, and the protection of children,” it adds. The resolution comes as Maxwell has exhausted a series of appeals of her conviction, with the US supreme court declining to hear her petition last October. Earlier this year, in February, Maxwell appeared via video for a congressional deposition before the House committee on oversight and government reform as part of its investigation into Epstein, but refused to answer questions and invoked her fifth amendment right. Her attorney told lawmakers that she would only speak if granted clemency. In April, reports emerged that members of the congressional committee were divided over whether Trump should consider pardoning Maxwell in exchange for her cooperation in the panel’s Epstein investigation. Last year, after the supreme court declined to hear Maxwell’s appeal, Trump was asked directly whether he would consider pardoning her. “You know, I haven’t heard the name in so long,” he said at the time. “I can say this: that I’d have to take a look at it. I would have to take a look.” He added: “I wouldn’t consider it or not consider – I don’t know anything about it. I will speak to the DoJ.” In May of this year Blanche told lawmakers during a hearing that he would not recommend a pardon for Maxwell. During the same hearing, he was questioned about the interview he conducted with Maxwell last summer, as part of the justice department’s Epstein investigation, and the fact that shortly after she was transferred from a federal prison in Florida to a minimum-security prison camp in Texas – a move which experts described at the time as “unprecedented”. During the hearing Blanche denied that Trump personally sent him to interview Maxwell, and also claimed that he didn’t know whether Maxwell was receiving preferential treatment at her new facility. The prospect of clemency for Maxwell has long outraged survivors of Epstein’s abuse. Earlier this year, in May, an attorney who has represented numerous Epstein survivors, told the Guardian that “any talk of clemency for Ghislaine Maxwell in exchange for testimony turns justice on its head – it risks rewarding the very person who helped enable the abuse”.

title: Trump’s pick for US attorney general Todd Blanche in jeopardy as vote postponed
author: Sam Levine
summary: Republican John Cornyn says he will not back nomination without written confirmation $1.8bn slush fund is dead
body_text: Todd Blanche’s hopes of becoming US attorney general seemed to be in jeopardy on Wednesday after the Department of Justice did not provide written assurances to a key Republican senator that a $1.8bn slush fund was dead. The US Senate judiciary committee postponed a vote scheduled for Thursday on whether to advance Blanche’s nomination. “Chairman [Chuck] Grassley works to set President Trump’s nominees up for success in committee, not failure. Senators [John] Cornyn and [Thom] Tillis want written assurances from the Department of Justice regarding the Trump-IRS settlement,” a committee spokesperson said in a Wednesday statement. “Tomorrow’s markup is postponed as work continues to secure sufficient support in committee to favorably report Attorney General-nominee Todd Blanche, who is highly qualified for the job.” Blanche, Trump’s former personal lawyer, is already serving as acting US attorney general. He needs the vote of every Republican on the Senate judiciary panel to advance his nomination to land the role on a permanent basis. But a swing vote on the committee, John Cornyn of Texas, told reporters on Wednesday he would not support Blanche’s nomination until he received written confirmation that the fund was not moving ahead. Cornyn also wants to clarify that a provision giving the president, his sons and related businesses blanket immunity from tax audits for all matters up until this year could not be applied to future matters, or to people who were not parties to the settlement. “Maybe they think I’m just going to give up or, you know, go along, but they’re mistaken,” said Cornyn, a four-term Republican senator who lost a re-election bid earlier this year to a Trump-endorsed rival. “We actually sent them a red-line strikeout of what we need, and they just need to make a decision. And if they do, then we’ll proceed with the markup tomorrow.” The US federal government reached the agreement to resolve a $10bn lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS over the unauthorized leak of his tax returns. The deal created a $1.8bn loosely controlled fund to compensate people who say they are victims of government weaponization and gave Trump, his family and businesses blanket immunity from audits for anything filed until the agreement was reached. The agreement immediately faced bipartisan scrutiny and outrage. The justice department did not make any effort to defend itself from the lawsuit, prompting a federal judge overseeing the case to conclude the case was brought with an “improper purpose”. Under pressure, Blanche announced in June that the department was scrapping the “anti-weaponization” fund, but has repeatedly declined to say so in writing. Pressed by Cornyn during his confirmation hearing, Blanche acknowledged that Trump or the other plaintiffs in the case could try to enforce the settlement agreement. He also did not say the tax immunity provision was dead.
