title: Anthony Fauci’s diaries take aim at News Corp journalist Sharri Markson’s ‘nonsense’ Covid-19 investigation
author: Caitlin Cassidy
summary: US former top health official, who was subpoenaed to appear at a Senate hearing into Covid-19, says Markson’s reporting about virus’s origin ‘does not make any sense’
body_text: Dr Anthony Fauci, the US’s chief medical adviser at the start of the pandemic, has described a book by News Corp investigative journalist Sharri Markson backing the “lab leak” theory of Covid-19’s origins as a “bunch of nonsense” in his newly released diaries. This week, Fauci, 85, was subpoenaed by the Republican senator Rand Paul to appear at a Senate hearing into Covid-19 and his handling of the pandemic. The physician and veteran former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, who retired in 2022, accused Paul of an “unhinged” campaign lobbying for his imprisonment and refused to answer questions at Wednesday’s hearing. The hearing was a continuation of Paul’s years-long support of the lab leak theory, or the idea that the Covid-19 pandemic began as a release from the Wuhan Institute of Virology. Ahead of his appearance, Paul published 1,141 pages of Fauci’s pandemic-era journal entries. In the entries, Fauci criticised reporting in The Australian newspaper and a book by Markson that claimed a facility in Wuhan was “immersed in genetically manipulating bat-coronaviruses in perilous experiments”. On 7 May 2021, Markson reported in The Australian that Chinese military scientists “discussed the weaponisation of Sars coronaviruses five years before the Covid-19 pandemic” and predicted a third world war would be fought with biological weapons. Fauci, who served under seven US presidents but became a household name overnight in 2020, wrote in his private diary that the article “does not make any sense”. “Why would someone want to make an agent that could equally infect your own population. Something is wrong with this report. I will have to follow up on it,” he wrote. Guardian Australia later found the “chilling” document produced by Chinese military scientists in the article was based on a discredited 2015 book containing conspiracy theories about biological warfare which is freely available on the internet. Markson’s story was criticised as misleading and alarmist by China analysts. A deputy editor of Foreign Policy magazine and China expert, James Palmer, said the article had links to conspiracy theories about the origins of the coronavirus which are popular with the political right. The story was published to promote Markson’s debut book, What Really Happened in Wuhan, which argued there was “no scientific consensus that Covid-19 has a natural origin” and that China had conspired to cover up the truth. Fauci also took aim at Markson’s book, writing in his diary that “the same old crap is going on with the far right continuing to attack me”. “The latest written by an Australian person who says I’m the father of gain of function research quotes from the infamous Richard Ebright saying that I’m a liar and I have misled everybody about gain of function,” he wrote. “What a bunch of nonsense! The far right continues to try and discredit me.” Ebright is an American molecular biologist and proponent of the lab leak theory. Markson told Guardian Australia “the majority of the intelligence community now concludes that Covid-19 likely originated in a Wuhan laboratory”. “I led the way internationally exposing the role of Anthony Fauci’s agency funding 65 projects at the Wuhan Institute of Virology, funnelling the money through EcoHealth Alliance,” she said on Thursday. The origins of the Covid-19 pandemic remain the subject of intense debate among scientists and the wider public. There are two competing theories – the natural-origins hypotheses, which suggests the pandemic began when a close relative of Sars-CoV-2 jumped from a wild animal to a human through the wildlife trade, and lab leak theories, which argue that the virus emerged when Chinese scientists became infected through research-associated activities. News Corp was approached for comment.

title: Afternoon Update: Fauci takes aim at News Corp journalist; Bikram Lama’s body returns home; and what to do about cultural collapse
author: Kat Wong
summary: Journal entries of US’s former chief medical adviser, released by Rand Paul, contain criticism of journalist Sharri Markson’s reporting
body_text: Good afternoon. Dr Anthony Fauci, the pandemic-era US chief medical adviser, has described a book by News Corp investigative journalist Sharri Markson backing the “lab leak” theory of Covid-19’s origins as a “bunch of nonsense” in his newly released diaries. This week, Fauci, 85, was subpoenaed by the Republican senator Rand Paul to appear at a Senate hearing on the origins of Covid-19, where he refused to answer questions, invoking the fifth amendment and accusing Paul of having an “unhinged obsession” with him. Ahead of Fauci’s appearance, Paul published 1,141 pages of Fauci’s pandemic-era journal entries, Caitlin Cassidy reports. In the entries, Fauci criticised reporting in The Australian newspaper and a book by Markson that claimed a facility in Wuhan was “immersed in genetically manipulating bat-coronaviruses in perilous experiments”. Fauci, who served under seven US presidents but became a household name in 2020, wrote in his private diary that Markson’s reporting “does not make any sense”. But Markson backed her work, saying she “led the way internationally exposing the role of Anthony Fauci’s agency funding 65 projects at the Wuhan Institute of Virology, funnelling the money through EcoHealth Alliance”. title: ‘Warring kingdoms’: cofounder of religious Reformers compares NSW Liberal party factionalism to Braveheart
author: Penry Buckley and Jack Larkin
summary: Robert Assaf tells Icac that Angus Taylor wasn’t ‘that involved’ but the federal opposition leader ‘definitely wasn’t opposed’ to work of conservative group
body_text: A member of a group of young conservative Liberal power brokers being investigated for allegedly soliciting illegal donations has compared their factional work to Mel Gibson’s Braveheart – and said they “didn’t think the law applied to us” when it came to political funding. The Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Thursday heard from Robert Assaf, the first witness from the conservative right Liberal factional group the Reformers to give evidence. Icac is investigating whether Liberal figures, including Assaf, “solicited or accepted” donations, including from prohibited donors, in amounts which were undeclared or exceeded caps, to recruit or renew members to the party – a practice known as “branch-stacking”. The Reformers allegedly wanted more conservative policies on issues including same-sex marriage, transgender rights, abortion and euthanasia. Assaf, 30, who admitted to being one of two founding members of the Reformers in 2017, said the group was started in the context of a factional split in the Liberal party between the religious conservative hard right and the centre-right. “My observations at the time were, the right faction was like – I’m not sure if you’ve seen Braveheart – but like these warring kingdoms, and they would slaughter each other, and then every now and then they’d come together for a big fight,” Assaf said. While branch-stacking is not of itself illegal, Icac is investigating whether the alleged conduct of the Reformers involved possible offences under NSW’s Electoral Funding Act. Asked about his knowledge of the laws governing donations, Assaf told Icac that the group “didn’t think the law applied to us”. “Because it was an electoral law, we’re not campaigning in elections in that sense,” he told counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC. “We’re internal Liberal party machinations. My understanding the whole way through was, until very recently … was it’s internal. It doesn’t count as anything to do with electoral laws or any other law.” He defended the Reformers, which includes members being investigated over a second allegation: that they took $2m in payments from the fugitive property developer Jean Nassif in exchange for outcomes sought by Nassif. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “The Reformers sound really spooky in the media right now, but it was just a bunch of 20-year-old people trying to figure things out,” Assaf said. Assaf appeared after two days of evidence from former Liberal staffer Dylan Whitelaw, who was associated with the group but has not been named in allegations against the Reformers. After being mentioned during Whitelaw’s examination on Tuesday and Wednesday, the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, dodged further questions on Thursday after denying he had ever donated to the Reformers. “I’ve answered these questions yesterday. I’m not going to give a running commentary on it,” Taylor said. The federal Liberal leader is not accused of wrongdoing. On Thursday, Assaf claimed Taylor was one of several state and federal Liberal politicians who were aware of and supported the Reformers’ work. “Angus was around it, but I don’t think he was really that involved,” Assaf said. “He definitely wasn’t opposed.” He said the former NSW Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet, whose brothers Jean-Claude and Charles Perrottet are named in the Icac allegations, was “pretty absent in the whole thing, but supportive from what I understood”. Dominic Perrottet is not accused of wrongdoing. The commission heard Assaf went to the same independent Catholic schoolas Jean-Claude and Charles Perrottet, as well as another member of the Reformers, Jeremy Greenwood. After spending a year in a Catholic seminary, Assaf later worked in federal parliament for various ministers, senators and MPs, including Tony Abbott, who the commission heard gave talks at recruitment events hosted by the Reformers. He described having an “icky feeling” about getting involved in politics, but said he was convinced to join the Liberal party after attending a 2015 talk at the Sydney University Liberal club by NSW upper house member Damien Tudehope, against the Safe Schools program, whose stated aim was to keep gay and transgender students safe. Assaf, who described Tudehope as “a warrior for the values that he cared about”, said the politician subsequently gave numerous talks at events hosted by the Reformers. Tudehope, who is not accused of wrongdoing, stepped aside from his role as shadow attorney general and Liberal upper house leader after being called as a witness by Icac. The inquiry heard that Assaf and fellow Reformer, Christian Ellis, started the group in 2017, after forming a strong friendship while working together on the No campaign for the same-sex marriage plebiscite. The inquiry heard that adopting the model that had seen Assaf recruited, the group began to organise talks on conservative issues, aiming to sign up new members afterwards. Dwyer on Thursday showed Assaf a draft document sent to him by Ellis which detailed a plan to recruit 5,000 Christian conservative members to the party to take control of the NSW division of the Liberal party, which had 4,000 members at the time. Assaf said the main aim of the Reformers was “policy change” but increasing the number of members in the Liberal party was “certainly part of the process”. Asked about a stated aim “to take over left-wing branches through stealth”, Assaf said “ideally, we would not want to take branches through stealth”. “I prefer to be a front stabber than a back stabber,” he added, stating the group’s intention was to create a “broad church” within the party. Assaf said they wanted to “change the terrible situation of factionalism”. “Christians obviously don’t like lying,” he said. “But there was a strategy to it, and some people needed to be more comfortable with that than others.” The inquiry heard the Reformers expanded to include members such as Jean-Claude Perrottet and Greenwood and began to have success taking over branches. “Great news. God’s granted us a victory. We’ve officially taken the Coffs Harbor branch away from the left wing,” wrote Assaf in one email. But the inquiry heard Assaf became concerned that some Reformers were paying for the cost of new memberships, a practice which under Liberal party rules would see branches frozen. Under questioning from Dwyer, Assaf said this included Jean-Claude Perrottet, while his brother Dominic Perrottet was serving as a NSW MP. “Anything [Jean-]Claude did at that time, noting his brother’s position, I was sensitive to,” he said. Jean-Claude Perrottet has previously denied any wrongdoing. Assaf occasionally clashed with Dwyer over his ability to remember details about the Reformers, including an agreement with prohibited donor Michael O’Hara. On Monday, O’Hara admitted to a fake arrangement in which he paid registered lobbyist Beckington, founded by Christian Ellis, for “strategic wealth strategy investment advice” when in fact he understood he was paying to “get my conservative values into the Liberal Party”. But he disputed whether the payments to the Reformers were to the NSW Liberals or should be considered political donations. At one point on Thursday, Dwyer asked Assaf, “Can I suggest to you that in fact you were aware of this arrangement, whether your memory is being refreshed or not?” Assaf said: “You can suggest it, but the problem is … my memory is my memory.” But Assaf, who admitted to the bogus arrangement with O’Hara, said the Reformers later became concerned that Ellis was “getting rich” on the money rather than using it for factional work. O’Hara told Ellis he would end the arrangement. “Ellis might have to cancel the upgrade to his fifth Land Cruiser, ha ha ha ha,” Assaf wrote in a message to Greenwood and Jean-Claude Perrottet. The inquiry heard that Assaf, Greenwood and Jean-Claude Perrottet were able to salvage the arrangement with O’Hara directing the money to another vehicle not controlled by Ellis. Jean-Claude Perrottet wrote in a message: ‘O’Hara saved”, to which Greenwood replied “Good work. How’s your mouth taste.” “That sounds like a crass reference,” Assaf told the inquiry. Icac’s inquiry continues.

title: Fifa wants more money for its members but that does not guarantee investment
author: John Duerden
summary: Asia and Africa are bastions of support for Gianni Infantino but Fifa’s money has not always been well spent in the regions
body_text: Fifa’s justification for its proposed plans to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors is about giving the 211 member associations more money to develop football. It’s safe to say that in the past, funds have done more developing in some places than in others, with millions either going missing or not being used for their original purpose and Fifa too often shutting the stable door after the horse, laden with cash, has ambled out. The reaction has been swift. Uefa has declared its outrage, Concacaf – the North, Central American and Caribbean governing body – has gone for concern and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) is disappointed at the lack of consultation. From the Confederation of African Football (Caf), there is, as yet, no word. Asia and Africa have over the years provided Gianni Infantino with steadfast support. There were murmurs over the Fifa president’s close relationship with Donald Trump during the World Cup, especially during the Folarin Balogun affair, but extra cash may help prevent anything louder coming out of Kuala Lumpur or Cairo. The sums on offer are significant – with promises of “over $10bn” (£7.5bn) being redistributed – and could do significant good, especially in countries that lack the infrastructure and facilities the big powers have. In the past, however, there has often been too little oversight too late when checking if the money that flows down from Switzerland actually trickles into all the necessary places around the world. This may not be surprising given that, according to reports, only about a fifth of federations actually return audited accounts detailing how the money is spent. For example, between 2015 and 2025, the Nigerian Football Federation (NFF), is believed to have received more than $20m in development grants from Fifa and Caf. In 2024, the chairman of the Professional Footballers Association of Nigeria task force, Harrison Jalla, demanded that the NFF account for the money. “What happened to these funds from Fifa and Caf?” he asked. “All these funds disappeared into thin air and translated into huge debts.” In October, it was announced that the Nigerian parliament was to launch an investigation into the federation’s activities. Behind the motion was the lawmaker Adedayo Adesola. “There has been a significant absence of visible improvement or grassroots growth in Nigerian football, despite these massive financial interventions,” he said. “There is a need to take decisive action to stop further misuse of public funds by the leadership of NFF.” Last week, the senate committee on sports criticised the federation for repeatedly failing to honour invitations to account for expenditure. In March, Jean-Guy Blaise Mayolas, president of Congo-Brazzaville’s football federation (Fecofoot) was convicted on charges of embezzling $1.3m of Fifa funds. It was claimed that Mayolas had misappropriated much of the money that was expected to be used to fund a training centre, women’s football and Covid relief. In 2019, Fifa banned the Caf executive committee member Musa Bility for a decade for “having misappropriated Fifa funds”. In Asia, there have been plenty of issues too. In June, Fifa suspended Nepal’s FA due to third-party interference but football in the Himalayan nation had been in turmoil for years. It had funds cut off by Fifa in 2021 after financial irregularities were discovered. In 2014, the then FA president, Ganesh Thapa, was investigated by Nepal’s anti-corruption agency, the commission for investigation of abuse of authority, but this was put on hold the next year. In 2015, however, he was banned by Fifa for 10 years after it ruled he had “committed various acts of misconduct over several years”. In neighbouring India in 2024, Nilanjan Bhattacharjee, the legal head of the All Indian Football Federation, accused the president, Kaylan Chaubey, of corruption and a lack of transparency in using federation funds, charges the latter strongly denied. The AFC asked Bhattacharjee, who was fired for his comments, to submit any evidence. He said he had done so, but so far, there has been no official response from the AFC or the football federation. In Bangladesh, more than $7m was allocated between 2016 and 2022 for football projects but only about $620,000 was reportedly used. In 2023, Fifa published a report detailing the financial irregularities it had found. Abu Nayeem Shohag, general secretary of the Bangladesh Football Federation, was banned from the sport. Fifa said: “Specifically, it is alleged that Mr Shohag – whilst maintaining his position as General Secretary – participated in procurement and payment processes (within the BFF) which were supported with falsified quotations/documentation and subsequently paid for, or expected to be paid for, with FIFA Forward funds.” Shohag, who denied the accusations, appealed and took the case to the court of arbitration for sport but the original decision was upheld in 2024. Whatever happens, more transparency on how such cash – which is, after all, generated by football – is used and more oversight can only be a positive. That’s because history shows that more money given to federations does not automatically equate to investment in football, regardless of what Fifa says. • This article was amended on 30 July 2026. An earlier version said that Jean-Guy Blaise Mayolas was president of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s football federation; he is president of Congo-Brazzaville’s federation.

title: Republican disenfranchisement bid drives Black voters to polls, study finds
author: Adria R Walker
summary: Black voters in south motivated to turn out by Republican push to redraw maps after supreme court ruling
body_text: A new analysis of Black voters in the south indicates that Republican attempts to dilute their political power is driving them to the polls in larger numbers and shifting their counties further left. After the supreme court effectively gutted section 2 of the Voting Rights Act protections in late April, Republican legislatures across the south rapidly pushed to disenfranchise Black voters by redrawing congressional maps. Louisiana, Florida, Tennessee and Alabama all immediately worked to pass new maps, while the Mississippi governor has said that he wants legislators to redraw maps before the upcoming midterm elections. The analysis by VoteHub, a data-focused election organization, indicates that the efforts have only motivated Black voters in the 78 Black belt counties it tracked. All but one shifted left in partisan turnout compared with 2024. Further, majority-Black counties that voted after Louisiana v Callais, the landmark supreme court decision that triggered the Republican-led redistricting efforts, had a surge in voter participation. The trend was clear earlier this year when Louisiana, South Carolina, Alabama and Georgia held primaries after the supreme court ruling. Louisiana, from which the Callais decision stemmed, disregarded votes that had already been cast until the state was able to redraw congressional maps, while nearby Alabama quickly split its majority-Black districts. South Carolina and Georgia moved to dilute Black political power in the state by redrawing maps, though neither state ultimately did so. Alabama produced one of the strongest shifts of all, with one of the largest positive turnout differentials and a significant partisan turnout that indicates increased Black voter mobilization in states with substantial Republican redistricting efforts. Alabama’s Greene county surpassed 50% turnout in the primary election, a positive turnout differential of 27.6 percentage points. Bullock, Lowndes, Macon and Montgomery counties, all of which are in Alabama’s second congressional district that was targeted by Republican legislators, also experienced significant turnout. Bullock county, which is more than 70% Black, had the third-largest turnout in the state. In nearby Louisiana, Black voters made up 35.7% of the primary electorate, despite making up only 32.1% of the population. The state experienced increased voter turnout across partisan groups and race, but 30.9% of Black voters cast ballots in the primary election – 3.2 points more than white voters. In contrast, Mississippi and North Carolina held their primaries before the Callais decision. In those states, turnout in majority-Black counties only outpaced statewide averages by 1.1 points on average.

title: First Thing: US government borrowing costs hit new high as strikes on Iran resume
author: Martin Belam
summary: Federal Reserve votes to hold its key interest rate steady, sending stocks tumbling. Plus: the origins of Coca-Cola may have been found
body_text: Good morning. US government borrowing costs have hit their highest level since 2007 after the Federal Reserve voted to hold its key interest rate steady, feeding fears it may not move fast enough to tame a rise in inflation. Kevin Warsh, the central bank’s chair, said the Fed would “not waver” in its commitment to tackling rising prices. The decision to leave rates on hold has spooked investors, who are worried about the US economy’s ability to absorb a rise inflation, caused by Donald Trump’s war in Iran. US inflation cooled to an annual rate of 3.5% in June after Washington and Tehran agreed a brief ceasefire – but this has since ended. US stocks fell sharply on Wednesday, with the blue chip S&P 500 index closing down 1.5%. The Dow Jones industrial average fell 2.2% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq was down 1.7%. US launches fresh strikes on Iran after days-long pause, amid fears war is widening The US military has launched strikes on Iranian targets in response to Tehran’s attack on American forces in Jordan on Wednesday, risking a return to all-out-war in the region. The latest round of strikes were launched hours after President Donald Trump vowed to hit Iran “very hard” after it targeted a base in Jordan that hosts US troops, and comes after a days-long pause in violence between the two sides. US central command said in a social media post that over the span of two hours they had struck “dozens” of targets belonging to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corp. The barrage came after the US partnered with Saudi Arabia to strike Iran-backed militias in neighboring Iraq on Wednesday, killing at least 20 fighters and six Iranian advisers. The renewed hostilities sent oil prices soaring. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 7.3% to more than $88 a barrel. Fauci invokes fifth amendment and declines to testify in Senate Covid hearing Dr Anthony Fauci refused to answer questions at a high-profile Senate committee hearing on the origins of Covid-19 and accused the Republican senator leading questioning of having an “unhinged obsession” with him. The hearing was called by the Kentucky senator, Rand Paul, who has investigated Fauci for years. Fauci said Paul’s goal was “embarrassing and intimidating me”, and ultimately landing him “behind bars”. Gary Peters, the Democratic senator of Michigan, described the hearing as damaging to science and ignoring continuing public health threats, such as the outbreak of the food-borne parasite cyclospora and measles, both at record highs. “It’s attempting to turn one person into a scapegoat for a crisis that hundreds of officials across the Biden and Trump administrations were responsible for handling,” said Peters. “This is only going to deter other scientific experts from public service.” What did we learn from the hearing? Jessica Glenza has analysed the hearing, and reports that six years on from the Covid crisis, Republicans are still politicizing science – and Dr Fauci remains a political punching bag. Wednesday’s hearing, she says, was another example of how criticizing scientists has become an important outlet for the party – and where re-litigating the Covid crisis justifies skepticism of a broad range of science. UK government reviews why police ceding criminal cases to US military The UK government and police chiefs are reviewing the process through which US military personnel accused of committing serious crimes on UK soil are avoiding the British justice system. The effort, involving multiple government departments, is examining why UK police forces, which have primary responsibility for investigating such cases, have been ceding jurisdiction to US military investigators. Survivors of sexual attacks by US military personnel that would meet a common definition of rape in the UK are finding that perpetrators are instead being prosecuted for lesser offences. In other news … The death toll from the powerful earthquake that hit Japan on Tuesday has risen to 30, as the search for survivors trapped in a badly damaged shopping mall, paper mill and collapsed homes across the south-west of the country continues. The US Senate judiciary committee postponed a vote scheduled for Thursday on whether to advance Trump’s pick for US attorney general, Todd Blanche, after the Department of Justice did not provide written assurances to a Republican senator that a $1.8bn slush fund was dead. Russian airstrikes killed at least 13 people in Ukraine on Thursday, as attacks that extended as far ⁠as the western city of Lviv caused neighboring Poland to scramble fighter jets to secure its airspace, and a missile landed in a field in Poland. Elon Musk’s company xAI has sued Minnesota over the state’s first-in-the-nation law banning “nudification” technology on websites and apps. European football authorities have called an emergency meeting over Fifa’s plan to sell a stake in future men’s soccer World Cups to private investors. Stat of the day: Hollywood producer charged with seven counts of wire fraud in $100m scheme A federal grand jury in Chicago has charged the Hollywood producer Jason Cloth with seven counts of wire fraud for allegedly defrauding investors of $100m, according to federal authorities. The Filter Recommends: Can’t hear what’s playing on TV? These affordable soundbars can help Ryan Waniata offers his advice on what to buy so you can get rid of the subtitles to hear what movies and TV shows are supposed to sound like – for as little as $130. Don’t miss this: How author Michael Thomas lost 20 years to mania, depression and more The Broken King, the new memoir by Michael Thomas, is “an extraordinary read” according to Steve Rose in this interview. Deeply personal and intimate, it covers what Thomas describes as the “perfect storm of conditions” – poverty, parental abandonment, racism, alcoholism, sexual violence, self-sabotage and mental illness – that has led to its release being two decades after his breakthrough debut novel, Man Gone Down. Climate check: Three firefighters killed in Greece as Europe battles wildfires Wildfires fueled by the climate crisis continue to burn across Europe, forming an arc from the Atlantic coast to the eastern Mediterranean and from the Highlands of Scotland to southern Spain. Three firefighters have died after tackling wildfires on the Greek island of Crete. Meanwhile, temperatures climbed to 100F in Bordeaux on Wednesday, where French firefighters stopped a huge blaze in nearby pine forests from reaching the suburbs. Last Thing: Was Florentine friars’ fatigue-fighting elixir a precursor to Coca-Cola? An Italian friar has unearthed a document from the pharmacy archives of an ancient convent in Florence describing a medicinal potion made from Bolivian coca leaves and kola nuts, prompting suggestions it could have been a precursor to the famous US soft drink, Coca-Cola. title: Fifa’s sale of the century: how Kushners and Trump are at centre of a tangled web
author: Rob Draper
summary: Joshua Kushner is now the kingpin in driving the sale of the World Cup to investors and family ties are tight around the project
body_text: It isn’t just football fans and Uefa executives who want to give Gianni Infantino the red card for his plan to sell off 20% of the World Cup to a privately backed commercial enterprise. The Fifa president is also in the crosshairs of the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee in Washington and ranking Democrat member Jamie Raskin. The reason? Infantino’s plan, which is backed by Joshua Kushner’s investment fund, has, for some observers, president Trump’s sticky fingers all over it. Raskin told Politico that Fifa was “going directly into business with the Trump family”, before making reference to the peace prize Infantino awarded the president in December and Fifa’s use of office space in Trump Tower, New York. “Apparently the fake Peace Prize and giant lease with Trump Tower weren’t enough – now Infantino performs a kickback hat-trick by pursuing a multibillion-dollar deal with Jared Kushner’s brother to sell ownership stakes in the World Cup to private investors.” As is often the case with Trump, the Kushner family is at the centre of any tangled web he weaves. Jared and Joshua’s father, Charles Kushner, convicted of tax evasion, witness tampering, illegal campaign contributions and sentenced to two years in prison, is Trump’s ambassador to France though he speaks no French. He was pardoned by Trump in 2020. Jared, married to Trump’s daughter Ivanka, is a Special Envoy for Peace and helped negotiate the Islamabad Memorandum ceasefire with Iran, which has now seemingly collapsed. He was also the man charged with fulfilling Trump’s pledge of bringing the Russia-Ukraine war to an end within 24 hours of him assuming the presidency. But at the heart of this and once again keeping influence very much within the family is Jared’s younger brother, Joshua, 41, who has established various private investment funds including Thrive Eternal, who will be lead investor in Fifa Forward Enterprise, the commercial spin-off Infantino is proposing to sell shares in. With Jared having divested his shares in Thrive Capital (the parent company of Thrive Eternal) in 2017 when taking on a role in Trump’s first administration, the familial ties seem especially tight around this project, as intimated by Raskin, who has already summoned Infantino to attend the House judiciary committee. He has also requested Fifa documents related to any gifts and benefits provided to Trump and details of the visitor logs for Fifa’s office space in Trump Tower. Given Trump’s boasting that his direct line to Infantino persuaded Fifa to suspend the USA’s Folarin Balogun’s red card for the World Cup last-16 game against Belgium – the USA lost 4-1 – it is an unfortunate look for Infantino that the extended Trump family, through marriage, will be leading the sale of the century, the handing over of substantial control of the World Cup. Some critics say even a 20% minority stake will in effect be a controlling stake if Infantino remains in charge without accountability. Joshua, though, is only following in the footsteps of his older brother Jared in his incredible capacity for dealmaking. Six months after the end of the first Trump presidency and after having being involved in US negotiations with Saudi Arabia during Trump’s first term, Jared managed to secure £2bn worth of funding for his own investment vehicle, Affinity Fund Management, from the Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF), which is chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto ruler of the kingdom. The New York Times reported that PIF advisers raised objections about the deal reeling to “the inexperience of the Affinity Fund management” and that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia seemed to bear “the bulk of the investment and risk” but the PIF board, chaired by the crown prince, overruled those warning to approve the money. Coincidentally, Saudi Arabia will be hosting the 2034 World Cup in a bid driven by Prince Mohammed. The PIF, also owner of Newcastle United and Aramco, the oil company which is 81% owned by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, is Fifa’s newest World Cup sponsor, with deals reportedly worth around $100m a year. Kushner has always defended the tie-up with the PIF, challenging critics to “point to a single decision we made that wasn’t in the interest of America”. Prince Mohammed was implicated in the murder of US citizen Jamal Khashoggi in Istanbul in 2018, with the United Nations concluding that the state of Saudi Arabia was responsible while a US intelligence report, that was released by the former president Joe Biden, concluded that Prince Mohammed “approved an operation … to capture or kill” the Saudi dissident. The Saudi government rejected both reports, calling them “inaccurate”. US-Saudi relationships have been much warmer in both Trump’s terms compared with the Biden interim and last week the US agreed a landmark deal to cooperate with Saudi Arabia to develop civilian nuclear power, while the two nations coordinated airstrikes on Iran-backed militias in Iraq this week. However, it is a different Kushner brother from an unrelated investment fund who is now the kingpin in driving the sale of the World Cup to investors. It is, however, reported by Politico that Joshua will be approaching sovereign wealth funds “to build a globally diversified investment base”. Perhaps his brother Jared will be able to help with some contact numbers to get the ball rolling?

title: US economy grows sluggish 1.5% in second quarter as inflation tops Fed target
author: Gaya Gupta and agencies
summary: Consumer spending remained resilient even as policymakers kept interest rates on hold
body_text: The US economy expanded at a sluggish 1.5% pace from April through June as rising imports weighed on growth. But consumer spending rose. And the Federal Reserve’s favored measure of inflation grew more slowly last month despite remaining above the central bank’s 2% target. The commerce department reported on Thursday that growth in US gross domestic product (GDP) – the nation’s output of goods and services – decelerated from 2.1% in the first three months of 2026 and came in below economists’ expectations. The commerce department also said on Thursday that its personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the measure of inflation favored by the Fed, rose 3.7% last month from June 2025 , down from a 4.1% year-over-year increase in May. Excluding volatile food and energy prices, so-called core consumer prices were up 3.3% from a year earlier, little changed from a 3.4% increase in May. The latest data paints a clearer picture of the effects the war in the Middle East has had on the economy after increasing energy prices and pushing inflation higher. The first GDP reading of this year captured the effects of just a month of war, but indicated that consumer spending was starting to slow as prices started to creep up. Oil prices have come down from their wartime high, and took a sharp downturn when the US and Iran announced a peace deal. But when that deal collapsed and the two countries began trading strikes again, oil prices climbed and still remain much higher than prewar levels. The pressure is growing within the Fed to raise interest rates in order to combat heightened inflation, which Kevin Warsh, the central bank’s chair, has acknowledged has remained too high for years. Though the Fed on Wednesday chose to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged for the fifth straight meeting, three regional Fed presidents dissented, saying they wanted to raise rates to combat elevated inflation. It was the first time in a decade so many Fed officials had dissented in the same direction over a policy vote. Higher costs have frustrated Americans ahead of November’s midterm elections, which will determine whether Donald Trump’s Republicans keep full control of Congress. Two-thirds of Americans, including 49% of Republicans, say they have little faith the federal government will address the high prices they face, according to a Harris Poll survey released earlier this month. Still, the US economy has proven surprisingly resilient in the face of the Iran war and the spike in energy prices it caused. The job market has bounced back this year from a lackluster 2025, giving consumers the wherewithal to spend. Employers are adding an average 92,000 jobs a month this year, compared with fewer than 10,000 a month in 2025 when high interest rates and Trump’s erratic use of tariffs discouraged businesses from hiring. Thursday’s GDP report was the first of three commerce department estimates of second quarter economic growth. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Mayor of St Paul reportedly under investigation for sexual harassment
author: Richard Luscombe
summary: Democrat Kaohly Her, Minnesota’s city’s first female mayor, allegedly sent inappropriate messages to employees
body_text: The first female mayor of St Paul, Kaohly Her, is reportedly under investigation for sexual harassment following a complaint filed by the Minnesota city’s police chief. City leaders have contracted an outside law firm to conduct an independent inquiry into the allegations that Her, a Democrat who was elected in November, sent inappropriate messages to employees, including several members of the police department, the New York Times and NBC News said. The outlets obtained a 1 April letter to the city attorney, Irene Kao, written by Chris Madel, a lawyer representing St Paul’s police chief, Axel Henry, claiming that Her, a former state congresswoman and a Hmong refugee born in Laos, engaged in a prolonged campaign of harassment against a number of workers “using one or more mobile phones”. Henry, police chief since 2022, decided to “step forward as a formal complainant against the mayor after becoming aware that the mayor’s conduct has extended beyond isolated incidents and has included sexual harassment of subordinate city employees, including members of the Saint Paul Police Department”, the letter said. It contains a screenshot of one message allegedly sent by Her to an employee, wishing them a “Happy Weiner Wednesday”, a redacted image, laughing emojis, and the caption “when she wraps you up in her blanket after you gave her a good weinering”, a misspelt reference to sexual intercourse. An investigation by Cally Kjellberg-Nelson, an employment law expert at the law firm Resolute Law, was already under way, the Times said, citing records it had obtained. The newspaper said Kjellberg-Nelson did not respond to an email seeking further information. The Guardian has contacted Mayor Her’s office for comment. In a written statement to NBC on Wednesday, Her said she had cooperated with the investigation and believed the “full facts will come to light”. The statement said: “As Mayor, I take my responsibility to treat every employee with professionalism and respect very seriously. I recognize that some of my attempts at humor fell short of the standard I expect of myself.” In an emailed statement to the Times, Matt Wagenius, a spokesperson for the mayor, said he could not answer questions about the ongoing investigation. “The mayor has deep respect for city employees and regrets any unintended impact her actions may have had,” he said. Asked if the investigation report would be made public, he said: “We will honor all applicable laws when making the determination.” Madel told the Times that Henry would not be giving media interviews, but “will do everything to ensure that appropriate conduct is modeled and followed in the St Paul police department”. The letter said Henry made “a thoughtful, deliberate decision” to file a formal complaint against Her because he wanted to protect city and police department employees. “Recognizing both the seriousness of that misconduct and the vulnerability of those directly affected, he is concerned that, absent a formal complaint, the behavior will continue unchecked and may expose others to retaliation for speaking out,” it said. Her served in the Minnesota house of representatives for six years before ousting the incumbent mayor, Melvin Carter, in a close, two-round election in 2025. The 53-year-old came to the US aged three as part of a resettlement program following the Vietnam war, which she told the Guardian in January gave her a unique perspective as a vocal opponent of federal immigration raids in the twin cities of Minneapolis and St Paul that resulted in the deaths of two unarmed US citizen protesters. Henry has also spoken out against the surge of Immigration and Customs enforcement (ICE) and border patrol agents ordered by Donald Trump, telling the Times in January that residents were “scared to death” and “afraid to go outside”.

title: Three-quarters of Americans think Trump isn’t focusing on top US issues – poll
author: Richard Luscombe
summary: Trump’s overall approval rating slumps to 34%, according to new CNN poll, as midterms testing Republican power loom
body_text: Three-quarters of Americans believe Donald Trump is not paying enough attention to the country’s most important problems, and two-thirds think he places himself above the needs of the US, according to a new poll. The CNN survey, conducted by the market research company SSRS, comes less than 100 days before November’s midterm elections in which the president’s Republican party is widely expected to lose control of one or both chambers of Congress. Trump’s overall approval rating has slumped to 34%, the poll found, matching his previous lowest immediately following the 6 January 2021 insurrection he incited trying to cling on to power after losing the 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden. The figure reflects growing dismay at the ongoing war in Iran – only 28% approve of Trump’s actions there, and even fewer, 25%, say the conflict has been worth it in terms of cost and American lives lost; meanwhile, the war’s effects at home are also causing disquiet, with 74% saying rising gas prices have caused at least some hardship, up from 63% in March. In the parallel poll a year ago, 58% of respondents said Trump had not gone far enough in trying to reduce the price of everyday goods, a figure that has climbed to 71% this week. Even Trump’s hardline immigration policies, previously a bright spot for his approval ratings, are dragging the president down. Only 39% believe he is doing a good job, and 54% say he has gone too far in mass deporting undocumented immigrants. Overwhelmingly, Americans are outraged by Trump stamping his personality on the presidency. His pursuit of a taxpayer-funded White House ballroom, botched renovation of the Washington DC reflecting pool, and plans for a self-aggrandizing ceremonial arch, have left only 17% feeling positive. In direct contrast, asked if Trump was in touch with problems Americans face in their everyday lives, 73% said no. Only 38% of those polled consider him to be an effective world leader; and 57% say the 80-year-old president lacks the stamina and sharpness to serve effectively.

title: Democrats demand answers over treatment of wounded US troops after Iran strike
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Lawmakers question delays in medical care, casualty figures and Pentagon’s handling of drone attack in Kuwait
body_text: The Trump administration is facing growing demands to explain why wounded US soldiers went more than a week without adequate hospital care after a March drone strike in Kuwait, just days into the US-Israel war on Iran. In a letter to the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, congressional Democrats urged the Pentagon to answer their questions – which include why the Pentagon’s public casualty count for the war with Iran briefly changed – by 12 August. The letter, sent on Wednesday and led by the US senator Elizabeth Warren and the representative Pat Ryan, poses 23 questions to Hegseth over the 1 March strike on a US logistics hub at the port of Shuaiba, south of Kuwait City. It was first reported by the Washington Post. A single Iranian drone evaded air defenses and hit the relocated operations center of the US army’s 103rd sustainment command, killing six reservists from Des Moines, Iowa, and wounding dozens more – the first US combat deaths of Operation Epic Fury, the war Donald Trump launched, alongside Israel, against Iran on 28 February. The unit had asked for more medical staff and supplies before the strike and been turned down, according to reporting by the Washington Post and CBS News cited in the letter. There was no doctor on site afterward, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance, with some of the wounded driving themselves to a hospital in Kuwait City, according to the reports. It took nine days before roughly two dozen soldiers, some still unscreened for brain injuries, were flown to the US military hospital at Landstuhl in Germany. “Doctors told them that because they hadn’t been recorded as medical evacuees on the flight’s manifest or as seriously injured in [the defense department’s] casualty-processing database, they could only get limited treatment and had to wait in nearby barracks because the hospital was unable to admit them,” the letter states. Soldiers later sent to Fort Hood, Texas, are said to have gone weeks without seeing a doctor able to diagnose traumatic brain injury, despite repeatedly failing post-blast cognitive tests, and families have told CBS News the US army downplayed the severity of individual wounds. The Pentagon declined to comment on the letter. The letter also presses Hegseth on the Pentagon’s official count of how many US service members have been killed in the war on Iran, which dropped from 18 to 14 on 23 July. The department blamed a data problem, but the lawmakers cite reporting that officials privately said four service members – three killed in Jordan and one in northern Iraq on 17 and 18 July – were dropped because their deaths came after Trump’s declared ceasefire in April, even though they died well after Trump had told Congress on 7 July that strikes on Iran had resumed. Those four deaths, plus more than 200 wounded, have since been filed under a new “Overseas Operations” category, rather than be counted as part of Epic Fury, following an earlier episode in which about 100 troops injured in strikes on Jordan went undisclosed until reporters asked questions. The letter also questions the independence of the US army’s internal review. One of the unit’s commanders initially assigned a mid-career officer under his own command to the inquiry, before a senior officer and US army central took over; soldiers questioned in the process came away with the impression that, as one put it, “we are investigating ourselves and found no wrongdoing”, according to the Washington Post. It is the second time in a week that a US senator has pressed the Pentagon over the way it has conducted the war on Iran. On 24 July, Tim Kaine, a Democratic senator from Virginia, demanded answers by 14 August about the pre-selected target lists used in the war’s opening strikes, after a 28 February strike on a school in Minab, Iran, killed more than 150 civilians, most of them children. Kaine said he was “deeply concerned about the inclusion of a school in Minab, Iran, on the lists of verified targets”. In the latest letter, led by Warren and Ryan, the lawmakers point out to Hegseth that at least 18 service members have been killed and more than 620 wounded in the war overall since it began in February. “As you and President Trump continue to risk the lives of service members in this reckless war, the American people deserve answers on whether you were adequately prepared to protect service members from Iranian attacks and get them the care they needed,” the lawmakers wrote, “and whether you will be prepared to do so if the war continues and escalates even further.”

title: Trump says he may ‘temporarily’ drop bid to make Blanche US attorney general
author: Sam Levine
summary: President’s former lawyer has been struggling to persuade some Republican senators to back his nomination
body_text: Donald Trump said on Thursday he may “temporarily” pull the nomination of Todd Blanche to serve as attorney general, but would keep him in the role in an acting capacity until two Republican senators objecting to his confirmation leave office next year – an extraordinary escalation of an intra-party fight over an agreement to create a $1.8bn slush fund and give the president tax immunity. Two Republican senators – John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina – have refused to back Blanche’s nomination until they receive written confirmation from the justice department that it is not moving forward with a widely criticized agreement creating a $1.8bn fund to compensate people claiming they were targets of political weaponization and granting the president, his family and business entities broad immunity from past tax investigations. Blanche has already said publicly that the payout fund to compensate victims of so-called government weaponization is not moving forward amid bipartisan backlash. But Cornyn and Tillis had sought assurances in writing, something Blanche has refused to do. Cornyn also sought to clarify the terms of the tax immunity portion of the agreement. The Senate judiciary committee canceled a vote on Blanche’s confirmation scheduled for Thursday when it became clear he did not have the votes to advance. The two senators – who are both leaving Congress in January – appeared to be negotiating language with the justice department on Wednesday. On Thursday, Trump blasted Cornyn and Tillis and vowed that he would instead keep Blanche, the president’s former personal lawyer, as the acting attorney general – a role he has held since April, when Trump fired Pam Bondi. Federal law allows the deputy attorney general – Blanche’s role under Bondi – to serve indefinitely as the acting attorney general until a successor is confirmed. “John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting. “I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office,” Trump posted. Cornyn, who lost his re-election bid to a Trump-endorsed rival, responded by saying: “POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis.” The fate of Blanche’s possible confirmation remains unclear. Cornyn met with Blanche on Thursday, according to a source familiar with the matter. The Texas senator and Tillis were reportedly close to a deal to advance Blanche’s nomination. Tillis, who is not seeking re-election after repeated clashes with Trump, told reporters on Capitol Hill: “It makes no sense to me. This is not popular.” “The president’s not winning on this issue,” he continued. “It is killing some of our candidates because they can’t explain it. And now it looks like they weren’t being honest when they said it was inoperative.” Earlier on Thursday, both Cornyn and Tillis had expressed a willingness to vote for Blanche. “If this were just between me and Todd Blanche, we would have worked this out, but, apparently, he’s getting some pushback from higher-ups at the White House. I don’t know who, but it doesn’t need to be this hard,” Cornyn said on Capitol Hill. The agreement was reached as part of a settlement in a lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS over the unauthorized leak of his tax returns. A federal judge who oversaw the lawsuit blasted the arrangement, noting that the justice department did not make a good faith effort to defend the government and that it appeared to be a collusive effort to engineer a beneficial result on behalf of the president. Blanche needs the vote of every Republican on the Senate judiciary committee, including Cornyn and Tillis, to advance his nomination to land the role on a permanent basis. Anna Betts contributed reporting

title: Fifa could draw US Congress inquiry over ‘smash-and-grab scam’, top Democrat warns
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Jamie Raskin targets football body’s proposed commercial sell-off and links to Trump administration
body_text: Fifa could face a sweeping US congressional investigation into its expanding financial and political ties to Donald Trump and his family if Democrats reclaim the House of Representatives in November, a senior party figure has warned. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, accused global football’s governing body of a “smash-and-grab scam of colossal proportions” after it proposed a multibillion-dollar privatization of its commercial operations. Raskin, a Democratic representative of Maryland, would become the judiciary committee’s chair under a Democratic House majority, vowed to make Fifa an early target of scrutiny – and accused the organization of embedding itself in what he described as a pattern of corruption surrounding Trump’s second administration and the Kushner family. “Over the last few weeks, Fifa’s cozy relationship to Donald Trump has been floating to the top of the swamp of quid pro quo corruption in which the Trump Administration is swimming,” Raskin said in a statement to the Guardian. “But now we see where all the bribes, kickbacks and sweetheart deals have been leading.” Raskin’s comments follow plans of the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, to pursue a spin-off of the organization’s commercial business into a standalone company, reportedly valued at about $20bn. JPMorgan Chase is leading the fundraising effort, with Thrive Eternal, an investment vehicle linked to the Thrive Capital founder, Joshua Kushner, among the prospective investors. Joshua Kushner is the brother of Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a high-level White House adviser. The proposal has sparked an immediate backlash across world football, and beyond. Uefa, the European football governing body, has warned that “none of us are the owners of football”, and on Thursday voted to boycott the World Cup if Fifa presses ahead. The inquiry also follows a series of similarly scandalous controversies surrounding Fifa’s relationship with the Trump administration. The organization invented its first-ever “peace prize”, which they awarded to Trump in December, weeks after he publicly complained about missing out on the Nobel peace prize. During this summer’s World Cup, Uefa accused Fifa of undermining the tournament’s integrity after officials reversed a red card issued to the US forward Folarin Balogun following a call from Trump to Infantino. Separately, the US Department of Justice dropped the long-running bribery and money-laundering cases tied to the Fifa corruption scandal after prosecutors said they no longer fit the administration’s enforcement priorities. Should Democrats – who lack the legal power to demand that witnesses appear under the current Republican House majority – win control of the chamber in November’s US midterm elections, Raskin would have the authority to compel testimony and documents from Fifa, JPMorgan and entities connected to the Kushner family’s investment vehicles. “Fifa needs to cooperate in good faith now,” he added. “If and when Democrats take the House, this Committee will have the tools we need to get answers, expose corruption, protect sports fans against exorbitant and fraudulent charges and block this attempt to turn world soccer into a global financial shakedown.” The White House has previously dismissed similar allegations as politically motivated. Fifa did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The judiciary committee minority under Raskin has already requested records from Fifa, including documents related to gifts provided to Trump, communications with the justice department, and visitor logs for Fifa’s Miami headquarters and its Trump Tower office. “Fifa appears to have struck a several hundred-billion-dollar deal orchestrated by Jared Kushner’s brother and JPMorgan to privatize Fifa’s business operations so private equity, hedge funds, autocrats, kleptocrats and large investors can come to own and control the world’s most beautiful game,” Raskin said. “The United States is set to host the Women’s World Cup in 2031, and we have a responsibility to ensure Fifa will not again bring its own brand of corrupt pay-to-play politics and exploitation onto our soil,” he added.

title: Republican congressman Max Miller faces backlash over domestic abuse allegations
author: Maya Yang
summary: Republican congressman is accused by his ex-wife and ex-girlfriend of abuse as he campaigns for re-election
body_text: The Ohio representative Max Miller is facing growing pressure to resign over a series of domestic abuse allegations made by his ex-wife and former girlfriend. The Republican congressman, 37, who represents Ohio’s seventh congressional district, has denied accusations made by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and former girlfriend Stephanie Grisham, as he campaigns for re-election. Moreno, a conservative policy adviser, shares a two-year-old daughter with Miller. The pair have been engaged in a legal battle over custody of their child since 2024. In one alleged incident, Miller “took hot water from a pan he had just cooked eggs in and threw it at me”, Moreno testified earlier this year amid a defamation lawsuit Miller filed against her. Moreno has also accused Miller of holding a gun to her head, the New York Times reported. The pair married in 2022. In addition, Moreno alleged that Miller “regularly speaks to me in an inappropriate, aggressive and demeaning manner, which is not in the best interest of our child”. A prominent anti-gun-violence group has called for Miller’s resignation after Moreno alleged he had held a gun to her head. Responding to Moreno’s allegations, Miller told Spectrum News in June: “They’re false allegations. Our divorce was finalized on December 18 in 2025. No police reports were ever filed.” In May, Miller also claimed on X that Moreno’s father, the Republican US senator for Ohio Bernie Moreno, “continues to fund and enable his daughter’s malicious campaign to ruin my life despite his knowledge of her mental health issues”, adding: “These antics harm your own grandchild.” In a statement to the Guardian, a spokesperson for Bernie Moreno said: “Senator Moreno’s top priority is the safety and well-being of his daughter and granddaughter … While he will not litigate these matters in the media or respond to baseless public attacks, he will do whatever it takes to ensure a just outcome for his family.” Separately, Miller’s former girlfriend Grisham, who served as White House press secretary during Donald Trump’s first administration, has also accused him of abuse, an allegation he has denied. Grisham and Miller dated from 2019 to 2020. In a 2021 Washington Post op-ed, Grisham – without naming Miller – wrote about a relationship that “turned abusive”, and of a former partner who was “physical” with her. Although she did not identify Miller in the article, he said it was widely understood that the op-ed referred to him. She later confirmed she was talking about Miller, according to the Times. Miller subsequently sued Grisham for defamation before later dropping the lawsuit as part of a confidential settlement agreement. Grisham has since filed a new lawsuit against Miller, alleging that he violated the confidential settlement through comments he made to Spectrum News. In his June interview with Spectrum News, Miller said: “What should be noted is [Grisham’s] allegation came out on the same day as somebody’s book launch. And the other part, what I would like to discuss, is my ex-wife was with me every single day during that time of my life in that election, and she, in her own words, will tell you that I never did any of those things.” The Guardian has reached out to Miller’s campaign and office for comment. Miller himself described a New York Times reporter as “disgusting” when approached for comment earlier this month. In a statement to the New York Times, Miller’s Democratic rival for Ohio’s seventh congressional district, Brian Poindexter, said: “If the allegations prove to be true … Miller should be in jail, not worried about retaining a seat in Congress.” The Guardian has reached out to Poindexter for additional comment. He trailed Miller by a single point in a June survey. Giffords, the national gun violence prevention group founded by former House representative Gabrielle Giffords, called on Wednesday for Miller’s resignation. “Congress is no place for violent abusers who attack their family and hold a gun to their wife’s head. Max Miller needs to resign now – and if he refuses, the House should expel him,” the group’s executive director, Emma Brown, said of the allegations. Brown continued: “If Republicans in Congress use their power to shield dangerous abusers from consequences, it will give voters yet another reason to take away their majority this November.”

title: US Senate rejects bid to rein in Trump’s authority over Iran war
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Measure fails 49-50 as US launches new retaliatory attacks in Iran and lawmakers question the prolonged conflict
body_text: The US Senate on Thursday rejected a largely symbolic effort to limit Donald Trump’s authority to wage war in Iran, amid rising regional tensions after the US conducted a “heavy wave” of retaliatory airstrikes. The war powers resolution failed in a 49-50 vote, marking the second time in two weeks the chamber has taken up legislation aimed at forcing Trump to end hostilities. The US military said it launched a fresh wave of airstrikes in Iran on Wednesday, in retaliation for an Iranian missile attack targeting a US base in Jordan. The exchange marked an escalation in the Iran war, following the collapse of a ceasefire between Washington and Tehran. The Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman voted with Republicans to sink the measure, the only Democrat to do so. The Republican senators Susan Collins, of Maine, Lisa Murkowski, of Alaska, and Rand Paul, of Kentucky, crossed the aisle to vote in favor of the motion, which would have directed Trump to withdraw US forces from hostilities with Iran absent explicit congressional authorization. Mitch McConnell was absent for the vote as he continues to recover from a fall in June and has not received medical clearance to return to work. The vote is the latest sign of eroding patience with a conflict that has now stretched more than five months, far beyond the “four to five weeks” Trump predicted when he co-launched the war with Israel against Iran on 28 February, killing the country’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei. The often twisty aim has been to prevent Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and to curb its support for militant proxies across the Middle East, though under its new leadership the regime seems more inclined to pursue a bomb than ever before. Iran responded by striking US bases and allied targets across the Gulf region and by disrupting oil traffic through the strait of Hormuz, triggering a global energy shock. A ceasefire brokered in June collapsed within weeks, and fighting resumed with a nearly two-week escalation in July before a renewed pause. At least 18 US service members have so far been killed in the conflict and more than 450 wounded, according to Pentagon figures, which Democratic lawmakers have questioned over a lack of transparency. Four of those deaths came within a 48-hour span in mid-July, when service members were killed in an attack at Muwaffaq Salti air base in Jordan. Thousands of Iranian civilians and combatants are estimated to have died. The Pentagon has told Congress it needs roughly $80bn more to sustain the war effort, on top of the more than $37bn already spent. The Senate approved a war powers resolution for the first time in late June, in a 50-48 vote that saw Collins, Paul, Murkowski and Louisiana’s Bill Cassidy break with their party. Trump confronted the defecting Republicans at the Capitol the next day, and Paul and Cassidy both reversed their votes within 24 hours, allowing the Senate to kill a nearly identical measure by a similarly narrow margin. Since then, the chamber has rejected the legislation repeatedly. The Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, noted after one earlier defeat that a growing number of Republicans had nonetheless broken ranks over the course of the war. The House, unlike the Senate, has twice passed its own symbolic resolution calling on Trump to end the war, most recently by 214-208 in late July, with a handful of Republicans joining Democrats. Because the House measure is a concurrent resolution rather than a joint one, it does not carry the force of law and would not go to Trump’s desk even if the Senate followed suit. The Trump administration has separately argued that the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which set out Congress’s authority to check presidential military action, is itself unconstitutional. The scale of the political problem for Trump was underscored by a new poll from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, released on Thursday. About two-thirds of US adults said the war has not been worthwhile, versus 33% who said it was worth fighting. That includes the vast majority of Democrats and independents, as well as roughly 37% of Republicans. Ahead of Thursday’s vote, the senator Kirsten Gillibrand, of New York, urged colleagues to back the resolution, arguing that the war was straining household budgets and that Congress held the constitutional authority to end it immediately. “This reckless war is driving up monthly bills and making everyday life harder for working families,” she said. “Under the constitution, we have the power to end the war today – let’s use it!”

title: Trump’s tax immunity scheme hoists president by his own petard on Blanche AG nomination
author: Sam Levine
summary: Republican senators sought written limits on settlement, but president held firm despite risk to attorney general pick
body_text: Donald Trump’s refusal to officially end a hugely controversial agreement giving him broad tax immunity and creating a $1.8bn slush fund underscored how the US president’s own self-interest takes precedence above all else in his government. For weeks, Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, has said that the slush fund portion of the agreement was dead. And for a few brief hours on Wednesday, it seemed that the president might agree to a relatively modest request from two Republican senators to put in writing that there were certain limits on an extraordinary tax immunity deal. After all, it seemed like a small price to pay in exchange for getting Blanche, a staunch Trump loyalist who previously served as his personal lawyer, confirmed permanently as the US attorney general. The agreement was part of a deal between Trump and the government to end a lawsuit seeking $10bn in damages for the unauthorized disclosure of the president’s tax records. A federal judge overseeing the case harshly criticized the government earlier this month, noting the government did not make a serious attempt to defend itself in the case and it seemed to be an effort to engineer a favorable result for the president. As negotiations wore into Thursday, the two Republican holdouts, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, signaled they were ready to support Blanche. “If this were just between me and Todd Blanche, we would have worked this out, but, apparently, he’s getting some pushback from higher-ups at the White House. I don’t know who, but it doesn’t need to be this hard,” Cornyn said on Capitol Hill. “I don’t know who it is – I’m just trying to get them out of the way so we can get the president his AG,” Tillis told Punchbowl News. But as reports of negotiations continued into the morning, Trump left little doubt who the one holding up the negotiations was. “John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting,” Trump posted on Truth Social a little before noon on Thursday. “Remember, both Cornyn and Tillis voted for Merrick Garland, and others, too numerous to mention. I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office.” It was not immediately clear if a confirmation vote for Blanche was off the table. Both Cornyn and Tillis met with Blanche late on Thursday afternoon and were reportedly close to reaching a resolution. In the immediate future, there is no penalty for Trump or Blanche in blowing up the negotiations. Under federal law, Blanche, who was confirmed by the Senate to be the deputy attorney general, can continue serving as the acting attorney general indefinitely. In some sense, the episode was a vindication of the power of Congress and an illustration of the immense sway even one or two Republicans can have when they push back on the president. Trump’s ultimate position also underscored how unwilling he is to concede anything to political rivals – he has openly feuded with Cornyn and Tillis – even if it means sacrificing a political achievement. The White House declined to comment. “Refer you to the TRUTH,” a spokesperson said. One does not have to look very far to understand why Trump would be unwilling to cede any ground on the agreement. One IRS audit could have cost the president $100m, according to the New York Times. So it’s easy to understand why Trump would want the tax provision in the agreement – which grants him, his family, and businesses or related entities immunity from audits for any matter until the agreement was reached. Cornyn reportedly sought to get Blanche to put in writing the agreement that clarified the exemption only applied to the named plaintiffs in the case, exclusively applied to the IRS, and was only about past tax returns. Even under those conditions, Trump still could have benefited tremendously. Under the settlement agreement, Trump and his sons were prohibited from making a claim on the slush fund. Blanche has been publicly adamant that the fund is not moving forward, though he conceded during his confirmation hearing that the plaintiffs in the case could theoretically try and push to enforce it. Trump’s refusal to formalize the end of the fund leaves open the possibility he could try to do it. Trump also seemed to be making a gamble that any resistance to confirming Blanche would disappear after the midterm elections. Cornyn suggested on Thursday that was not going to happen. “POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis,” he posted on X. Anna Betts contributed reporting

title: Mandela Barnes drops out of high-stakes Wisconsin governor’s race
author: Lauren Gambino
summary: Former lieutenant governor says path to Democratic nomination no longer viable as democratic socialist rival surges ahead
body_text: Mandela Barnes, the former lieutenant governor of Wisconsin, dropped out of the Democratic primary for governor on Thursday, upending the high-stakes contest less than two weeks before the 11 August election. Barnes announced the decision in a video posted on social media, saying he no longer saw a viable path to the nomination, as democratic socialist Francesca Hong surged ahead with a commanding lead. “It’s become very clear who our nominee is going to be,” Barnes, 39, said. A Marquette Law School poll showed Hong significantly ahead of Barnes in a distant second place, with 38% compared to his 16%, having consolidated liberal support, especially among young voters, although about a third of primary voters remained undecided. Soon after Barnes’s withdrawal, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported it had sent questions to the candidate about past allegations of inappropriate behavior that had been anonymously submitted to the Wisconsin Democratic party, local party officials and others. According to the Journal Sentinel, the state party hired a law firm in 2025 to investigate the claims sent in a letter that Barnes had used his position in the party to pursue inappropriate relationships with “young adult women”. The party’s internal review and outside investigation found no actionable evidence because the claims were “anonymous and unspecific”, the Journal Sentinel reported, citing an unnamed person familiar with the matter. Barnes’s campaign denied any wrongdoing. “There are no allegations of misconduct or wrongdoing against Mandela,” it said in a statement. His departure adds another twist in the Democratic primary for governor in Wisconsin, a perennial presidential battleground that has also been at the center of national disputes over election administration since the 2020 election. He is the third Democrat to exit the race, following lieutenant governor Sara Rodriguez, who withdrew two weeks ago amid a campaign finance scandal. After Rodriguez’s exit, Milwaukee county executive David Crowley re-entered the race with the endorsement of Governor Tony Evers, who is not seeking re-election. Earlier this summer, Missy Hughes, a former state economic development director, ended her campaign. On Wednesday, a judge rejected an effort backed by the Democratic party to let voters who had already cast absentee ballots void their initial vote and vote again, over concerns that many early ballots had been cast for candidates who were no longer in the race. Crowley moved quickly to appeal to Barnes’s supporters: “There’s a place for you in what we’re building.” Evers told reporters he was surprised by Barnes’s decision to withdraw but reiterated his support for Crowley, saying he believed Crowley was the strongest candidate “even if Mandela was in”, the Associated Press reported. The Democratic gubernatorial nominee in Wisconsin is expected to face Republican US congressman Tom Tiffany, who is backed by Donald Trump. Barnes was once viewed as a rising star in Democratic politics. In 2022, rather than seek re-election as lieutenant governor, he ran for the US Senate, narrowly losing the race to incumbent Republican Ron Johnson. Rachel Leingang contributed reporting
