title: After teargas, protests and legal strife, Turkey has a new opposition party. Is this the man who can defeat Erdoğan?
author: Kaya Genç
summary: Under Özgür Özel, the CHP became Turkey’s most popular party. Now his Yeni (New) movement is growing fast, says the Istanbul-based novelist Kaya Genç
body_text: In May this year, police in Ankara stormed the headquarters of the Republican People’s party (CHP), the oldest political party in Turkey. Officers used teargas to enforce a controversial appeal court decision that reinstated the CHP’s 77-year-old former leader Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu – seen as less of a threat to the ruling Justice and Development party (AKP). CHP members aligned with Kılıçdaroğlu’s successor, Özgür Özel, placed furniture at the building’s entrance, creating a barrier to prevent police from entering. It didn’t work. Hours later, party members loyal to Özel were physically removed from the premises. Entering the offices of Turkey’s leading opposition party in such a fashion was a spectacular act with historic consequences. Last Friday, Özel and 90 CHP deputies resigned from their party and declared the founding of the New (Yeni) party. The CHP had served as Turkey’s main opposition since 2002. But not any longer: with the exodus of members to the New party, the CHP is reduced to just 44 legislators in the 600-seat parliament, its third smallest party out of seven. Over the past week, Turkey’s new main opposition, with its 91 legislators, enjoyed strong winds in its sails. Throughout Turkish political history, those who have suffered legal injustices have gone on to benefit from them at the ballot box. In 1999, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan himself spent four months in prison. Four years later, he was prime minister. If managed well, the ousting of Özel from the CHP will probably boost the popularity of Turkey’s progressives overall. But what of the CHP itself? This is the party Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded in 1923, which played a crucial role in establishing the modern republic of Turkey. In the past 18 months, it has witnessed a stunning reversal of fortunes. At Turkey’s nationwide local elections in March 2024, the CHP was Turkey’s most popular political party. Özel’s leadership engineered that success: the CHP won 37.8% of the vote, beating Erdoğan’s AKP on 35.4%. This was the first national election since the AKP’s establishment in 2001 in which it wasn’t the largest party – a decisive moment in Turkish politics and one with worrying implications for Erdoğan in the run-up to 2028’s presidential elections. The CHP victory, on a platform of municipal socialism, has raised the profile of a generation of young, charismatic leftwing mayors who, like Zohran Mamdani in New York, won office in Turkey’s wealthiest and most populous cities: Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir. Their proximity to power must have raised concerns among the country’s ruling elites, who have profited from an economic order that prioritises the construction, defence and tourism industries. Three weeks after he announced his candidacy for the presidential elections, in March last year, Istanbul’s CHP mayor, Ekrem İmamoğlu, was removed from office. He has been accused of 142 offences, including accepting bribes, unlawfully obtaining personal data, racketeering, leading a criminal organisation, interfering with public tenders and aiding the outlawed Kurdistan Workers’ party (PKK). His charges could lead to 2,430 years behind bars, and it looks extremely unlikely that he will be able to run for president in 2028. Writing in this newspaper from jail last September, İmamoğlu claimed Erdoğan was “weaponising the courts against the democratic opposition”. (The government has denied putting pressure on the courts to prosecute CHP mayors.) Since İmamoğlu’s arrest, a different CHP city or district mayor has been arrested almost every month. One after another, politicians have been sent to jail or threatened with prosecution. Several detained CHP mayors have since been released, including İnan Güney, the suspended mayor of Istanbul’s touristic hub, Beyoğlu. Over time these developments led to apathy among opposition supporters: for months, it felt almost impossible to keep up with CHP’s legal troubles, which dominated the Turkish media. When İmamoğlu was arrested in March 2025, it triggered nationwide protests, the largest in Turkey in more than a decade. But since then, court cases against the CHP have largely been met with silence. In April, I went to follow İmamoğlu’s case in a courtroom in Silivri, 83km (52 miles) away from Istanbul’s city centre; I saw no supporters inside or outside the courtroom. The cab driver who took me to the court that day said he wished to see the CHP mayor of Silivri in jail next. While holidaying on Büyükada island off the coast of Istanbul two months later, I heard of the Silivri mayor’s arrest. By the end of June, Büyükada’s CHP mayor had been jailed too. After his reinstatement as party leader, Kılıçdaroğlu implied, in a public statement, that those CHP mayors could indeed be guilty. Likening the CHP to a tree, he said: “The shade of this mighty tree can never, ever be a refuge for the forbidden and the polluted. When necessary, it knows how to purify itself and conduct its inner accounting.” Kılıçdaroğlu’s call for purification has led to fury among opposition supporters, protests and an exodus of party members. Despite the excitement over Özel’s New party, it faces challenges: it lacks CHP’s resources, personnel, history and financial support from Turkey’s treasury. Breakaway parties have often suffered defeat in Turkish politics: the Good party, established in 2017 by disgruntled Turkish nationalists, has little support among the electorate. The Future party and the Democracy and Progress party (DEVA), founded by former AKP leaders in 2019 and 2020, fared poorly in elections, failing to distinguish themselves from the AKP. The CHP is a similar colossus, with an unsurpassable brand name in Turkish politics. It is the Republic of Turkey’s founding party, the party of Atatürk, and its history carries a lot of weight. Özel has defined the New party as “social democrat”, and the party programme acknowledges Turkey’s different religions, ethnicities and languages. It also references gender and sexual orientation, terms that have become taboo in Turkey in recent years. The New party embraces full membership of the EU and promises to increase Turkey’s role at the Council of Europe and Nato. If Özel can position his party as not just another splinter party but the new CHP, that would be an attractive proposition. A century ago, the CHP implemented a flurry of social, cultural and political reforms across Turkey, from the abolition of the caliphate to significant advancements in women’s rights. In the 1960s and 1970s it found support from students, the underprivileged and the marginalised with its leftist turn. The New party should promise an equally bold and progressive agenda. That way it won’t just emerge as the victor of the 2028 elections but will be in a position to truly transform Turkey. Kaya Genç is a novelist and essayist from Istanbul, and the author of The Lion and the Nightingale: A Journey Through Modern Turkey

title: Senators accuse Republican ‘gelatinous blobs’ of caving to Trump on Iran war
author: Rachel Leingang in Davison, Michigan
summary: Democrats Warren and Van Hollen attack Republican ‘rubber stamps’ in Congress for ceding authority to Trump
body_text: Senior Democrats accused Republicans in the US Congress of becoming “gelatinous blobs” who won’t stand up to Donald Trump and “rubber stamps” for his war on Iran. Elizabeth Warren, a US senator for Massachusetts, and Chris Van Hollen, a US senator for Maryland, argued that the Republican-controlled Congress had surrendered its constitutional authority to the president. In interviews with the Guardian, the senators urged their Republican colleagues to stand with Democrats and assert Congress’s authority as a separate branch of the federal government – with power over declaring war. “The Republicans have all had their spines surgically removed,” Warren said in Michigan, while stumping for the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. “I mean, they’re just gelatinous blobs that kind of make it through the United States Senate.” The constitution sets up three separate branches of government to hold one another accountable, Warren noted – and the assumption was that each of the three branches would “jealously guard its own powers”. “But with Donald Trump in the White House, and a bunch of weak-kneed Republicans in the House [of Representatives] and the Senate, all of a sudden, we’ve lost the whole game,” she said. The US-Israel war on Iran, launched in February, has cost the US tens of billions of dollars. Hundreds of US service members have been wounded and 18 have been killed since the start of the operation. A tentative peace deal fractured in recent weeks. The latest congressional bid to rein in Trump’s attacks on the Middle East failed on Thursday, when a war powers resolution failed by 49 votes to 50 in the Senate. The controversial conflict rumbles on, as Trump faces a crucial political test with November’s US midterm elections. Democrats could win back power in the House, which is currently controlled by Republicans, and are also vying to retake control of the Senate. If there is a Democratic majority, Warren suggested that, coupled with the groundswell of opposition to the war among voters, could enable Congress to serve as a proper check on Trump. If that happens, “I think we are able to rein in Donald Trump and [defense secretary] Pete Hegseth, even if they have gallons of testosterone”, said Warren. Earlier this month, the House passed a war powers resolution for the second time that directed Trump to withdraw the US military from Iran – this time on a 214-208 vote, with four Republicans joining all Democrats in voting in favor. But in the Senate, the resolution failed 47-49. In June, a similar war powers resolution passed the Senate. The resolution directs the US military be removed from Iran without explicit approval from Congress. Van Hollen, who introduced the war powers resolution, said the situation in Iran was a “senseless war” that “should never have started”. “Ultimately, Congress will have to turn off the funding spigot for this war,” Van Hollen, also in Michigan to support El-Sayed, said. “And I will not vote for a dime for this illegal war,” adding that he wouldn’t support Hegseth’s request for more funding, delivered to the appropriations committee earlier this month. “At some point, these Republican senators are going to have to explain to their constituents why they’ve contracted out their constitutional responsibilities to Donald Trump, because that’s what they’re doing,” said Van Hollen. “So long as you have a majority of senators who are turning over their constitutional responsibilities to Donald Trump, then they’re just rubber stamps for Donald Trump’s illegal war.” Van Hollen said Democrats should continue to press for votes on the war powers resolution, to hold Republican senators accountable. The war is unpopular in the US, with 29% of Americans approving of Trump’s handling of the situation with Iran, and 69% disapproving, according to a Washington Post-Ipsos poll earlier this month. “I would rather see Republicans assert their constitutional duties and help us end the war now,” added Van Hollen. “But, you know, maybe they’ll get the message from their constituents.”

title: McCarthyism has returned to the United States – and this time it’s even more dangerous
author: Judith Levine
summary: Trump’s campaign of repression echoes the red scare. But now the government has bigger ambitions and more powerful tools
body_text: There are many parallels between the first McCarthy era, roughly 1946 to 1956, and Trump’s campaign of political repression, his own updated McCarthyism. Both regimes crafted a monster of quasi-facts and innuendo and fed it with fear: an enemy within, well-organized and financed, secretive and violent, allied with evil foreigners and bent on overthrowing capitalism, democracy and Christian morality. Both used flagrantly unconstitutional means to cleanse the nation of the spectral menace. Each time, federal employees were targeted first. President Harry S Truman’s Federal Loyalty Program screened 5 million workers for communist affiliation; 2,700 lost their jobs, 12,000 resigned. Schools, unions and Hollywood fell in line; blacklists outlasted their makers. The Trump administration purged the federal agencies of his equivalent of the cold war communist, the “woke”. Applicants for civil service jobs were asked to identify their favorite administration policies and explain how they would advance them if hired. The federal employees’ union correctly called this request a “loyalty question”. Then as now, law firms quailed, media companies capitulated, universities collaborated. Artists and performers – Zero Mostel, Jimmy Kimmel – were exiled from film and television. In the 1940s and 50s, the attorney general compiled lists of supposedly subversive organizations, which, along with communists and socialists, included groups from the National Negro League to the Nature Friends of America. Trump’s justice department is investigating progressive non-profits, including ActBlue, a chief funding source for Democratic candidates, the Southern Poverty Law Center, and the Open Society Foundations, funded by George Soros, best known for supporting democracy movements in the former Soviet Union. In both eras, the standard bearers were full of ideological passion. “Can there be anyone who fails to realize that ... this is the time for the showdown between the democratic Christian world and the communist atheistic world?” McCarthy thundered to the Senate in 1950. Trump believes in nothing but himself. But like McCarthy and his confederates, the intellectuals behind this repression are true believers. “When the leftist – who does not believe in freedom, who does not believe in civil rights, who does not believe in any ordinary notion of justice – protests that we are violating his rights, understand that he is lying to try to persuade people who are not closely following the political scene that some injustice has perpetrated against him,” Trump’s policy adviser Stephen Miller said in a speech. “We must stay the course and be completely unflinching in the pursuit of justice against these enemies of civilization.” McCarthy and his more powerful and enduring co-conspirator, the FBI director J Edgar Hoover, ruined countless lives and crippled progressive movements. But the scope of this administration’s ambitions; its armies of enforcers inside a gargantuan carceral state; the technological and legal tools at its disposal; and the dearth of principled government actors to obstruct it make this McCarthyism far more dangerous. Global ambitions While McCarthy claimed that American communists were puppets of the Soviet Union, and the CIA conspired to undermine progressive organizing in Europe, today’s attempt to enlist foreign governments in a coordinated fight against “far-left terrorism” potentially extends the administration’s repressive reach around the globe. On 22 September 2025, Trump issued an executive order designating the non-organization “antifa” a “domestic terrorist organization”. Three days later it issued National Security Presidential Memo-7 on “countering domestic terrorism and organized political violence”. Invoking Charlie Kirk’s murder, the assassination attempts against Trump and the supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, and “riots in Los Angeles and Portland” – but not the January 6 insurrection or the 2019 El Paso, Texas, massacre of 23 Chicano shoppers by a young white supremacist – the memo is as much manifesto as battle plan. “This political violence,” it says, “is a culmination of sophisticated, organized campaigns of targeted intimidation, radicalization, threats, and violence designed to silence opposing speech, limit political activity, change or direct policy outcomes, and prevent the functioning of a democratic society. A new law enforcement strategy that investigates all participants in these criminal and terroristic conspiracies – including the organized structures, networks, entities, organizations, funding sources, and predicate actions behind them – is required.” But if a war on the US left inside US borders were not enough, on 16 July the White House announced a “global campaign to crush radical left terrorism”. The secretary of state, Marco Rubio, invited representatives of more than 60 countries to a “summit”, where he named four European “far-left terrorist organizations” and offered $10m for information on their financing. He promised: “There will be more [terrorist] designations soon.” At the same time, the US implemented new visa restrictions targeting people who have allegedly “supported or incited acts of terrorism”. Europe has expressed skepticism that leftwing terrorism is a big problem. Still, some countries are cooperating. The US requested the extradition from Spain of a wealthy American who has donated to humanitarian aid efforts in Palestine – which the administration views as support for Hamas. Spanish authorities are detaining him while they decide whether to send him home or release him. Unlike the US criminal code on domestic terrorism, the laws on combatting foreign terrorism offer “many more tools” to pursue not just people planning or committing violent acts, but also those within “two to three degrees of separation” from the act, Mike German, a former FBI special agent, told Democracy Now. The purpose of the 16 July summit, he said, was “to reframe the discussion around domestic terrorism to imagine that it has these foreign connections that justify the use of these much more aggressive tools”. Laws passed since 11 September 2001, make this sleight of hand easier. The 1947 National Security Act created a wall between the CIA and the FBI, between international and domestic intelligence gathering. But the USA Patriot Act, written and signed hastily after al-Qaida’s attacks on US soil, broke down that wall. Civil libertarians have long argued – and whistleblower Edward Snowden proved in 2013 – that the collection of communications to, from or about a foreign target can sweep up tons of private information about Americans. “The most acute danger” of “uncontrolled sharing of criminal investigative information with intelligence agencies”, argued the ACLU at a 2005 congressional hearing, “is that federal prosecutors and law enforcement agents … concerned with preventing and punishing criminal activities” will become “a domestic spy network directed at unpopular religious and political organizations”. In fact, after September 11, that is what happened. George W Bush’s administration maligned and shut down US Muslim and Arab charities and non-profits under the suspicion that they were supporting a vaguely defined foreign terrorist enemy. German continued, citing current investigations into progressive non-profits like the Southern Poverty Law Center: “This effort to designate left-wing groups as foreign terrorists … using these broad terms like ‘antifa’ will allow them to go after people who are not committing violence, but who are simply engaging in the political process.” Extreme policing In June, the administration circulated a press release boasting of the blows it had delivered the “violent anarchist network” antifa. It cited crackdowns from coast to coast – from Spokane, Washington, where “multiple Antifa insurgents were convicted on federal conspiracy charges for their roles in a violent attack at [an] ICE facility”, to Newark, New Jersey, where “Antifa thugs violently laid siege” to an immigrant detention center, “resulting in dozens of arrests and federal charges”. For the record, the Spokane protesters blocked an ICE van. The New Jersey public defender has filed a motion to dismiss the charges against 40 protesters, which “contain nearly identical, generalized allegations and fail to identify the specific conduct attributed to each individual”. It makes sense that an administration that criminalizes immigration and sends federal agents to detain and deport law-abiding gardeners, shopkeepers, mothers and toddlers will use the same tactics to suppress protest against that brutality. A carceral system that locks up millions and imposes extraordinarily harsh sentences functions in concert with these enforcement tactics to intimidate would-be dissenters and punish those who openly dissent. The charges often don’t stick. The New York Times reviewed hundreds of cases involving charges of assaulting or impeding federal immigration officers and found that most of them unraveled, due to federal agents’ “extensive misconduct”, from “attacking protesters” to “misrepresenting facts in court”. But when they stick, the damage can be devastating. Case in point: the trial and conviction of nine participants in a 4 July 2025, action outside ICE’s Prairieland detention facility in Alvarado, Texas. Some brought guns, which is legal in Texas. Benjamin Song fired at a police officer – he said he aimed at the ground – who was injured. Others scrawled graffiti on cars and shot off fireworks. Song was convicted of attempted murder, the other eight on charges of riot and explosives (the fireworks) and material support for terrorism; the prosecution presented a claim that their black clothing and use of Signal are antifa tactics. Daniel Sanchez-Estrada, who was not there, was convicted of conspiracy to conceal documents for moving a box of zines. The prison sentences they received were extreme by any measure: 100 years for Song, 30 for Sanchez-Estrada; 50 to 70 years for the others. The justice department proudly broadcast the total: 450 years for a “terrorist attack” on an ICE facility. The woman who attempted to assassinate supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh got eight years. By comparison, between 1941 and 1957 hundreds of communists and others were prosecuted under the Smith Act, which made it a crime to “advocate, abet, advise or teach the … desirability or propriety of overthrowing the Government of the United States or of any State by force or violence” – all constitutionally protected speech. Eleven leaders of the Communist party convicted in one major trial were sentenced to three to five years. Techno-surveillance At the counter-terrorism summit, Miller described efforts to “disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest and prosecute these political terrorists that are operating in our country”. Aided by technology and undeterred by watchdogs, they can do it. McCarthy relied on wiretapping, spies, informants and human bureaucrats digging through paper files to identify his targets. He managed to find thousands. But late 21st-century technology, including artificial intelligence, which enables the state to conduct surveillance on millions and collate data from government agencies at all levels, makes Hoover’s witch-hunt look like a game of hide-and-seek. The examples are myriad. ICE has a new $25m-a-year contract with a subsidiary of the data broker Thomson Reuters to provide “continuous monitoring” of such things as potential government fraud and the arrival of unaccompanied immigrant minors. It also does “academic risk flagging”, whatever that is. The agriculture department has contracted with Palantir to provide an AI-empowered return-to-office tracking tool, which critics say can be used for other kinds of employee surveillance. The White House has mandated the installation of an app on federal workers’ phones that “gives all Americans direct access” to administration news alerts, social media posts and policy announcements. A “text President Trump” option pre-populates a message praising him. What happens to the worker who wants to criticize him? Those antiterrorist visa restrictions are determined through the ideological vetting of travelers by pulling social media content into government databases using AI-powered monitoring tools; the process continues after the person enters the country. Trump’s friendly relations with tech companies that amass mountains of customer data constitute an incalculable asset to the repressive regime. Submissive Washington On 2 December 1954, the Senate, led by three Republicans, censured Joe McCarthy. Its resolution described the senator’s hunt for suspected communists in the federal government as “contrary to senatorial traditions”. Quaint as that sounds, it initiated his undoing. Throughout the 1950s, Chief Justice Earl Warren’s supreme court dismantled the tools of McCarthyism piece by piece, fortifying the fifth amendment against self-incrimination and reining in Congress’s power to call witnesses when testifying would “unjustifiably” abridge their right to privacy or “liberty of speech, press, religion or assembly”. Now, cowed by their vengeful and fickle commander-in-chief, the Republican Congress has relinquished its powers – of appropriation and regulation, declaration of war or removal of a corrupt, incompetent or emotionally unstable president. While the lower federal judiciary has ruled frequently against Trump, the supreme court’s majority has upheld the president’s prerogative to reshape the federal government according to his whim. The recent ruling that allowed his no-cause dismissal of the Federal Trade commissioner Rebecca Slaughter – and overturned a 91-year-old decision limiting such executive authority – reverberates throughout the federal workforce, politicizing the public sector and reopening the door to the ruinous inquests of the McCarthy era. What will be the next frontier of political repression? Will the postal inspector be deputized to open packages in search of abortion pills bound for red states? Will Trump send ICE or the national guard to intimidate voters at the polls? A president without a moral compass and advisers whose true north is the extreme right, helming a government with unparalleled legal, technological and financial resources, can implement a regime of political repression that Joe McCarthy – or even Big Brother – could not have dreamt of. Judith Levine is a Brooklyn-based journalist and frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

title: Uefa has formed a rare but fragile united front against Fifa in battle for football’s future
author: Nick Ames and Matt Hughes
summary: Emerging from this week with unity over Fifa’s World Cup sell off was quite an acheivement but Europe cannot rest on its laurels
body_text: It was a phrase not always heard when Europe’s football associations discuss a pressing issue. “Touchingly unanimous,” was the assessment of a senior Uefa executive within moments of Thursday afternoon’s seismic decision to boycott Fifa tournaments unless Gianni Infantino scraps his private investment plan. United fronts on this scale are vanishingly rare and there is now a narrow window in which to make it count. Fifa doubled down on its proposal overnight with “clarifications”, which blamed the media for disrupting the “consultation process” of a scheme that had been constructed under cloak and dagger. There was no suggestion that it would shift from its 19 September deadline to in effect ram the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal through. Anyone would be forgiven for asking what the rush was but Uefa and its allies must not allow the next seven weeks to drag. The European stance is a triumph for Uefa and its president, Aleksander Ceferin, whose eventful reign may have reached a high. Associates often cast the Slovene as a “no bullshit” operator, and tough rhetoric has been matched with action in facing down Infantino. But neither Ceferin nor his entourage will be preparing a victory march. Events will move rapidly and it is essential the accord between Uefa’s 55 members holds firm. Infantino and his emissaries will be probing for weaknesses. It took an intensive lobbying effort to ensure Uefa could gather behind a common cause. One mid-sized federation, tempted by the riches Fifa has dangled, was brought into line after that country’s biggest club was deployed to talk the FA president round. A smaller nation was left surprised when two others, who it had believed shared its interest in Infantino’s offer, changed tack late on. Another had hoped for more time in Thursday’s two-hour meeting to air its view. None of this is unusual; it is simply politics. European football has plenty of internecine struggles to resolve when left to its own devices. It was no small achievement to emerge from the meeting with sources at all levels proclaiming unity. Only 48 hours had passed since news of Fifa’s plan broke and, particularly after looking through a hurriedly dispatched sales deck that many found insulting, everyone could at least agree they had been crudely sidelined by global football’s governing body. There was astonishment at Fifa’s timing given the Folarin Balogun affair, a mere three weeks previously, had sharpened appetites within Uefa to oppose Infantino. A number of western European FAs are understood to have been mobilising their peers ever since Donald Trump revealed he had repeatedly called Infantino asking him to overturn the USA striker’s suspension for their last-16 tie against Belgium. Balogun was ultimately handed a reprieve. While only the German and Norwegian FAs publicly backed Belgium’s subsequent complaints, others including the English FA were involved in discussions behind the scenes. “Balogun was the moment everything changed,” a European FA chief said. “We have been working together since then, and this week has accelerated matters.” They will need to quicken further if Infantino is to be deposed or, as a minimum, his investment plan is to be scuppered. The less economically fortunate could yet be seduced if Fifa is given the oxygen of time. Some countries privately note the irony of bigger states seeking their support when it has not always been forthcoming in the other direction. Perhaps more money can be rustled up for waverers. Uefa is encouraged by positive discussions with individual states in Asia, many of whom have expressed dissatisfaction with Infantino. It felt a significant intervention when, on Friday morning, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said in a strong statement that it believes “the proposed FFE cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward”. There is also evidence of a widespread loss of confidence in Infantino within Concacaf, the North, Central American and Caribbean confederation. But Concacaf and the AFC have stopped short of Uefa’s threatened boycott; their public pronouncements have focused on serious concerns over governance, a lack of consultation and the expedited timeline, rather than the substance of Fifa’s proposals. Concacaf did, however, point to Fifa’s $4bn (£2.97bn) cash reserves as a ready source of added funding. What next? Anyone hoping an unprecedented level of opposition may force Infantino to resign is likely to be kept waiting. There are parallels with his previous attempt to alter the structure of world football five years ago, when he proposed the World Cup should become a biennial event. Uefa killed that scheme off but Infantino emerged from the wreckage with his position enhanced. Less than 12 months later he had secured support to expand the World Cup to 48 teams. If Fifa’s mid-September cutoff looms like a before-and-after moment for the global sport, the de facto deadline may lie two weeks sooner. The Under-20 Women’s World Cup begins on 5 September and, as things stand, it would be the first test of resolve for those promising a boycott. It is in all parties’ interests, not to mention those of players caught in the middle, to find a clear resolution by then. Infantino’s opponents would have the numbers to call an Fifa extraordinary congress, where a no-confidence vote could be triggered. Only 43 countries would have to formally request that step. But sources close to Uefa have cautioned that this would be hard to organise, not least because Fifa can wait as long as three months before convening such an event. An extraordinary congress is already scheduled for 23 November, when the 2031 and 2035 Women’s World Cup hosts will be rubber-stamped. Meanwhile, rumblings within Europe regarding a potential candidate to rival Infantino at next year’s election grow louder. Nasser al-Khelaifi, the Paris Saint-Germain president and the chair of the European Football Clubs organisation, has proponents but has given no suggestion he is willing to run, even if history shows the Qatari has a pattern of taking key roles with apparent reluctance. Any serious contender would realistically need the backing of Europe and at least one other confederation, but there are more immediate priorities. Those involve harnessing the momentum Uefa has built, quickly stopping Infantino’s project and preventing football from plunging into terminal disarray. Nobody involved can rest on their laurels. As one FA president put it after Ceferin’s rallying effort: “The game has started now.”

title: First Thing: Top Democrats accuse Republicans of becoming ‘gelatinous blobs’ on Iran war
author: Nicola Slawson
summary: Senators Warren and Van Hollen attack Republican ‘rubber stamps’ in Congress for surrendering authority to Trump. Plus, could AI take your job? Some workers in China already know the answer
body_text: Good morning. Senior Democrats accused Republicans in the US Congress of becoming “gelatinous blobs” who will not stand up to Donald Trump and “rubber stamps” for his war on Iran. The Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren and the Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen argued that the Republican-controlled Congress had surrendered its constitutional authority to the president. In interviews with the Guardian, the senators urged their Republican colleagues to stand with Democrats and assert Congress’s authority as a separate branch of the federal government – with power over declaring war. What else is happening in Washington? Trump has said a deal has been reached for Hamas to disarm and for Israel to withdraw its forces from Gaza. However, briefings from both sides exposed disputes over its implementation that could prove difficult to overcome. Trump says he may ‘temporarily’ drop attempt to make Blanche US attorney general Donald Trump said yesterday he may “temporarily” pull the nomination of Todd Blanche to serve as attorney general, but would keep him in the role in an acting capacity until two Republican senators objecting to his confirmation leave office next year – an extraordinary escalation of an intra-party fight over an agreement to create a $1.8bn slush fund and give the president tax immunity. Two Republican senators – John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina – have refused to back Blanche’s nomination until they receive written confirmation from the justice department that it is not moving forward with a widely criticized agreement creating a $1.8bn fund to compensate people claiming they were targets of political weaponization and granting the president, his family and business entities broad immunity from past tax investigations. What has Blanche said? Blanche has already said publicly that the payout fund to compensate victims of so-called government weaponization is not moving forward amid bipartisan backlash. But Cornyn and Tillis had sought assurances in writing, something Blanche has refused to do. Cornyn also sought to clarify the terms of the tax immunity portion of the agreement. At least 34 die as 49,000 cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco At least 34 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, after about 49,000 migrants breached the border with Morocco and poured into the tiny territory. Spain sent military and police reinforcements to Ceuta on Thursday after people crossed by land and sea. Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, was expected to join the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, on a visit to Ceuta on Friday. Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers’ association representing civil guard officers, described the situation as a “serious humanitarian crisis”. He said: “People are still entering. The reinforcements that have arrived are only helping the injured and other humanitarian efforts.” How did the people die? Many drowned but some were killed in a crush to cross the breakwater fence at Tarajal beach, Sbihi said. Why have so many breached the border at the same time? It was not immediately clear what prompted so many people to cross to Ceuta. In other news … Seattle’s police chief has resigned amid criticism of the city’s response to a fatal shootout at a food festival last weekend, Katie Wilson, the mayor, said last night. The announcement followed hours of speculation about whether Shon Barnes would step down. Anthropic ⁠said on Thursday its AI Claude model hacked ⁠systems of ⁠three organizations during testing, days after its rival OpenAI ⁠revealed a rogue agent had gone on a days-long ⁠hacking spree at another AI firm, Hugging ‌Face. George and Amal Clooney have been forced to evacuate their home in south-eastern France as a wildfire burned nearby, the actor’s agent confirmed to Associated Press on Thursday. In a letter to the local mayor, the actor said that “whatever happens, they remain fully part of this community” and would “contribute to its rebuilding”. Culture pick: Spider-Man: Brand New Day review – Zendaya saves Tom Holland’s semi-Cronenberg-style superhero In the new instalment of the Spider-Man franchise, Peter is back where he started, adored by New Yorkers for crime-fighting as Spider-Man, living in a scuzzy single room with all his screens and tech gear, his secret identity a secret once more, but pining for the people he loves. And he’s not getting any younger. How much of a “brand new day” is this? Stat of the day: All 55 Uefa members agree to boycott Fifa competitions if World Cup sell-off plans proceed European countries have agreed to boycott all Fifa competitions if Gianni Infantino pushes forward with his proposals to sell chunks of the World Cup to US-based private investment. In an extraordinary development, all 55 Uefa members resolved not to participate in future World Cups or other Fifa-run events, saying in a statement that they “unanimously and unequivocally reject” the proposals. Don’t miss this: Could AI take your job? Some workers in China already know the answer In China, the deployment of AI is being encouraged at a scale unseen in the west. Across the country, workers are fearful about the impact of AI on their livelihoods as the technology is rolled out at a staggering rate in an increasingly precarious labour market. Climate check: Europe is burning – and if Trump’s war on the climate is not met with sanctions, things will only get worse “Are we understanding it yet?,” writes Alexander Hurst for Guardian Opinion “As Europe burns in the west, the south and the north, are we grasping the fact that our economies, food systems, political stability and even our ability to plan for the future, will all be charred in a world on fire? Meanwhile, the White House seems committed to ecocide.” Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. If you’re not already signed up, subscribe now. title: Seth Meyers on Trump’s unpopularity: ‘Madam Web has a higher audience rating’
author: Guardian staff
summary: The late-night host poked fun at the president’s record-low approval rating as he gets rich while Americans struggle
body_text: Seth Meyers examined Donald Trump’s lowest approval rating yet as Americans struggle to afford gas and groceries. The Late Night host started by taking aim at Trump’s recent justification for attacking Iran after the president said “it’s our turn”. Meyers said it was “not a good enough reason to keep a war going” and that “it’s a military conflict and not Othello”, referring to the board game. This week also saw Trump saying he would change the grass in Washington DC parks, comparing it to humans as it has a life also. “Does that mean grass can also get dementia?” Meyers quipped. With Anthony Fauci facing a Senate hearing this week. Trump has claimed that Joe Biden called him to tell him he was no good. Meyers said this was obviously a lie because “if you called Joe Biden, you’d still be on the phone right now”. Fauci has been testifying about the origins of Covid, which Meyers joked has Taylor Farms saying “please don’t be us”. Meyers also expressed frustration towards Republicans trying to blame Fauci as “your boss literally told us to drink bleach”. Trump’s approval rating has hit a new all-time low as, despite claiming during his campaign rallies that he would make America affordable again on day one, prices have instead gone way up. Meyers said that the day one claim “should have been an obvious red flag” as “what was the plan for day two?” Trump has since attacked the press for asking him about affordability and high prices as he claims they’re not his fault. “You’re the president!” he said. “Of course they’re asking you why prices are so high!” While Americans are struggling, Trump raked in $2bn last year and Meyers spoke about the double standards with rightwing pundits. “Obama wore a tan suit once and Republicans lost their minds,” he said. The same people also “relentlessly” accused the Biden family of corruption and various crimes despite Joe looking “like a guy that was just about to get pickpocketed”. Trump is now the least popular he’s ever been and that includes after January 6 with an approval rating of 32%. “Madam Web has a higher audience rating on Rotten Tomatoes,” Meyers said. He added that “most Americans oppose the Iran war and want it to end” and Trump’s back-and-forth on what is happening has been “erratic and insane”.

title: Iran strikes tankers under US escort in Hormuz strait as Trump gathers cabinet to discuss war
author: William Christou in Beirut
summary: Energy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle East
body_text: Iran has said it struck two tankers trying to pass through the strait of Hormuz under the escort of the US military as Donald Trump gathered his cabinet to discuss the stalling war and rising prices as midterm elections in the US loom. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Friday that the “non-compliant oil tankers … were struck and brought to a halt, while four other oil tankers quickly changed course and returned to their previous positions”. The military body said the ships had tried to pass through the strait via an “undeclared route” and under US aerial escort. Iran and the US have said ships should pass through the strait via two competing routes, with Iran bombing ships that take the southern route, close to the coast of Oman, and the US bombing ships that violate its blockade of Iranian ships and ports. The strait has been almost completely closed to traffic since Iran and the US returned to fighting two weeks ago, sending energy prices soaring. On Thursday, the price of crude oil pushed past $90 a barrel when the US struck Iran in retaliation for its targeting of US bases in Jordan. Fighting continued on Friday, with the Kuwaiti defence ministry reporting that it had shot down Iranian drones targeting “vital and military facilities” without any casualties. In Lebanon, the Israeli military carried out a huge detonation overnight near the ancient Beaufort Castle. It said it was targeting Hezbollah tunnels and infrastructure. The explosion was heard across south Lebanon and covered nearby towns in ash, while photos showed the affected area levelled by the force of the blast. Lebanese officials accused Israel of violating the ceasefire by carrying out the detonation. The Israeli military said it was ensuring the security of its northern residents. Trump has tried to open the strait of Hormuz by force, but increasingly intense US strikes on Iran have yielded few results. The price of gas and groceries remain high in the US as a result of the energy disruption, complicating Republicans’ chances at the ballot box in November’s midterm elections. On Friday, Trump brought his cabinet together at the Camp David retreat in Maryland to try to chart a path forward for the war. The White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said at a briefing last week that the cabinet meeting would be “a lot of fun and something different for the cabinet to experience together”. Top of the agenda will be the Iran war, which Trump promised would last a few weeks but has now dragged on for five months. A Reuters-Ipsos poll this week found that one in three Americans support the war, the lowest polling since the war began. Support in Congress is also waning, with the US Senate narrowly rejecting a symbolic vote to express disapproval of the war. The war powers resolution asking the president to stop the war failed in a 49-50 vote. Inflation caused by the war is a boon for Democrats, who are hoping to wrest control of the house from the Republicans. Energy companies have posted record profits as a result of the conflict, with ExxonMobil’s profits doubling and Chevron reporting more than five times its profits in the same time period last year.

title: Trump defends $1.8bn slush fund that is holding up Todd Blanche confirmation
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: President calls for former personal defense lawyer to be ‘immediately approved’ as attorney general
body_text: Donald Trump has defended controversial plans for a $1.8bn slush fund even as they threaten to derail the nomination of his former personal lawyer Todd Blanche for US attorney general. Blanche “should be immediately approved” by the US Senate, the president declared in a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday morning, defending the payout scheme proposed by his officials in the Department of Justice as it holds up Blanche’s confirmation. Blanche, who has been serving as acting attorney general since Trump fired Pam Bondi in April, has been lined up to take the job permanently. Under agreements to resolve a long-shot $10bn lawsuit filed by Trump against the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) over the leak of his tax returns, the justice department proposed the creation of a secretive fund – to be awarded with no restrictions to allies of the president – and barred the IRS from auditing his tax returns. Democrats and some government watchdogs, however, are calling it a slush fund, and have warned it could end up paying out to defendants convicted over their role in the January 6 Capitol riot. While Blanche later said the slush fund was dead after an extraordinary backlash, two Republicans on the Senate judiciary committee – John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina – have demanded assurances in writing that the fund will never be activated before they back his confirmation as attorney general. Blanche has not given them that assurance, and the committee’s vote to advance his nomination was postponed this week as a result. “I felt that they should be given compensation for what has been done to them,” Trump wrote of his supporters, whom he described as “a group of people treated so badly in our Nation’s history”, adding: “I gave up any payments for myself, which would have been substantial … I will always feel that these victims of government abuse should be paid back for what they were forced to endure, their lives have been ruined! “John Cornyn never had a problem with the so called ‘Fund’ … until after I decided to Endorse and Support his Republican Primary opponent,” Trump wrote. That opponent, the Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton, beat Cornyn by roughly 28 points in May, ending Cornyn’s Senate career and making him the first Texas Republican senator to lose a renomination bid. Blanche was previously Trump’s personal defense lawyer, representing him in the New York hush-money case and other criminal matters, before joining the justice department as Bondi’s deputy. Responding to Trump’s post on Friday, Tillis said the president had made clear the fund was “still alive”. He said Blanche had been “forthright, thoughtful and patient” throughout the course of negotiations. “It’s a shame his confirmation has hit a snag only because an incompetent personal advisor to the President refuses to amend the bogus settlement,” Tillis wrote on X, without naming the advisor. “I will continue working in good faith to put an end this legal and political albatross and prevent any potential misallocation of taxpayer dollars.” Judiciary committee Democrats have said Blanche privately told the senator Dick Durbin that pushing for the fund had been a mistake. He has also faced questions over his firm’s past payments from a Trump-aligned political action committee and his handling of the Epstein files. The Senate majority leader, John Thune, has said he expects the nomination to come back for a vote once Cornyn and Tillis are satisfied. Trump has said he is willing to pull Blanche’s name temporarily and resubmit it later, once Cornyn and Tillis are “out of office”, while keeping Blanche on as acting attorney general in the meantime.

title: Infantino under huge pressure after plan for World Cup sell-off sparks resignation and rebuke
author: Nick Ames and Matt Hughes
summary: The walls started closing in on Gianni Infantino after another dramatic day that saw one of his senior advisoers resign and brought a scathing rebuke from Fifa’s own chief operating officer
body_text: The walls started closing in on Gianni Infantino after another dramatic day that saw one of his senior advisers resign and brought a scathing rebuke from Fifa’s own chief operating officer. Infantino is under huge pressure after his plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors met a tide of opposition from around the globe. European countries have already promised to boycott Fifa competitions if he does not shelve the scheme but Friday’s developments, which led to two key members of his inner circle distancing themselves from him, may prove equally damaging to any prospects of salvaging his presidency. Meanwhile Uefa and other confederations are actively seeking candidates to run against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, in which he had been expected to comfortably win a fourth term. The pressure that has built since this week’s revelations casts doubt on whether the previously unassailable Swiss, who has doubled down on the proposals, will be able to cling on for that long. The resignation of Carlos Cordeiro, one of Infantino’s senior advisers since 2021, struck a fresh blow upon Infantino hours after Uefa’s 55 members had unanimously threatened a boycott. Cordeiro, a former US Soccer chief, said Infantino had proposed “a bad deal for Fifa’s member associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game”. He questioned the lack of transparency in Fifa’s process and pointed out that the governing body is sitting on vast debt-free reserves that could be used to fund development. “Why this deal?” he asked. “Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?” But an extraordinary statement later in the day by Kevin Lamour, Fifa’s current chief operating officer, may have inflicted a more serious wound. Lamour, a close associate of Infantino at Fifa and during their previous spells at Uefa, said staff and other stakeholders had been “deceived” by the president and said he would tolerate being sacked for expressing his views. “What has been announced in recent days and what has been happening behind the scenes in recent months defies belief and imagination,” Lamour said. “To put it very clearly and directly: the project that has sparked so much controversy and debate is not a Fifa project. It is even less a project of Fifa’s administration. It is the project of one person. “The Fifa vice-presidents, the members of the Fifa Council, the confederations, the federations, the players, the leagues, the clubs, and the fans were not the only ones who were ignored. Fifa’s own administration was also deceived. “This lie by omission over many months and this unilateral exercise of power are not trivial. They are indicative of a lack of trust, a lack of transparency, a lack of discernment, a lack of good governance. And a serious lack of respect.” Lamour said Fifa’s mission is “not to serve the personal interests of a person who, unfortunately, believes he embodies Fifa when he is supposed to be at its service”. He stated that his colleagues “deserve better than contempt and intimidation”, adding: “My feeling is that we all want to be proud to work for Fifa, and today, unfortunately, it seems that is no longer the case for many of us.” Infantino appears to be shedding allies and there was no succour to be taken from a strongly worded statement from the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), which backed Uefa and Concacaf in their opposition to the privately funded Fifa Forward Enterprise plan. The AFC stopped short of matching Uefa’s boycott but was clear in saying the proposal should be scrapped. “The fact that the situation has reached the point where the real possibility of a Fifa World Cup boycott has entered public discourse should concern everyone who cares about the future of our game,” it said. “The AFC believes that the proposed FFE cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward.” It called upon Fifa to “undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework”, echoing its peers’ complaints about a lack of consultation regarding key decisions such as World Cup hosting arrangements. A further revelation on Friday that Fifa has opened a tender for research companies to assess the economic benefits of expanding the World Cup to 64 teams, demanding a hugely accelerated timescale, has only increased such concerns in football’s corridors of power. Uefa is minded to play a waiting game after securing a united front in opposing Infantino’s plan. It will assess how Fifa reacts, although early signs suggest little change of tack. Overnight Fifa had attempted to blame media reporting for such widespread opposition, claiming its commitment to “an open and democratic consultation”, although that intervention has cut no ice among its opponents. It is unlikely any mechanism to depose Infantino will be triggered immediately although in theory an extraordinary Fifa Congress, and subsequent vote of confidence, could be convened if 43 countries make such a request. The priority around Uefa and beyond is to see off the FFE plan before taking further steps. Any Europe-backed candidate for the Fifa presidency election in March is likely to hail from a different continent, with the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, and AFC president, Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa, among possible contenders. The latter lost narrowly to Infantino in the 2016 election. Fifa continues to lobby federations to accept their project and have stuck by the 19 September deadline originally given for those who wish to sign up. Late on Friday night the South American soccer body ⁠Conmebol said it had ⁠requested further ⁠information from Fifa on its proposal to ⁠sell a stake in its tournament business, including ⁠the World Cup, and launched ‌a consultation ‌process with its member ‌associations. Conmebol said it had requested further information and clarifications from Fifa on the proposal’s scope, structure, ‌governance and potential effects, and would continue to analyse it before taking a position. “We recognise that the development ⁠of football requires commercial and financial decisions. However, such decisions must always serve ‌football and never take precedence over its very essence,” Conmebol said in a statement.

title: EU relations, climate crisis and Gaza: why Ed Miliband is fired up by Foreign Office challenges
author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
summary: Labour veteran is said to relish role that requires careful negotiation of Trump and impending G20 leadership
body_text: Extraordinarily, given the importance of geopolitics, the office of foreign secretary has sometimes appeared a consolation prize in British politics, perhaps reflecting the transfer of responsibility to Downing Street or the Cabinet Office. That is not how Ed Miliband views the job. His allies say suggestions that he nurses resentment after he was deprived of the chance to be chancellor misunderstand his grasp of the policy challenges ahead. “Ed has an immense appetite to get things done and is relishing being in this job,” one says. “Ed will be a policy-driven foreign secretary.” To that end, he is preparing a distinct agenda on relations with the EU over the next decade, Britain’s chairing of the G20 next year and the climate crisis. Miliband is also determined to contribute to some of the big debates about shaping the international order of the future – debates that may take him into difficult territory given the volatility of the US alliance. Palestine may take longer to address, partly owing to the Israeli elections and the sudden glimmer of progress over Hamas disarmament, but his instincts are clear. In 2014, as Labour leader, he urged his MPs to vote to recognise Palestine. Acutely conscious that he is the tenth foreign secretary since William Hague stood aside in 2014, Miliband also arrives without a Foreign Office permanent secretary after the sacking of Olly Robbins, and with some staff on a rolling strike over the large job cuts that Robbins had announced he would impose. But Miliband, working with the new Europe minister based in the Foreign Office, Hamish Falconer, intends to be closely involved in talks on the UK’s relations with the EU since he regards a successful solution to that relationship as the single biggest question facing the UK. His personal involvement will give the Foreign Office greater influence in the Europe debate than under Keir Starmer’s leadership, when the Cabinet Office was the sole proprietors of negotiations with the EU. Miliband represents a Eurosceptic constituency and remains bound by Labour’s manifesto red lines not to enter the single market or customs union in this parliament. But that does not prevent him from seeking to influence Andy Burnham’s longer-term thinking about where the UK’s relationship with the EU should be in 10 or 15 years. Burnham, Miliband’s aides argue, has shown an openness to ideas on social care and the same openness may apply to issues such as European defence. “Having a closer relationship with Europe is a key foreign policy priority to protect our national security and grow our economy,” an ally said. “Ed will be working in lockstep with No 10 and Hamish Falconer to make this happen. He sees Europe as at the heart of this agenda.” Friends also said Miliband wants to find a way to revive the ailing G20, a largely economic multilateral body that has been steadily declining in influence since 2008, when the UK played a major role coordinating the response to the financial crash during Gordon Brown’s premiership. In the latter days of his own tenure at No 10, Starmer appointed Brown to act as his special envoy on global finance and cooperation in advance of the G20, and Brown will retain the role, working alongside Miliband who was one of his advisers while chancellor. Lord Wood, who acted as a foreign policy adviser during the Brown premiership, has also been appointed to the Foreign Office as a minister in the Lords, and will bring experience and intellect to the role. With the UK due to chair the postponed illicit finance summit in December in advance of taking over the G20, ideas such as a global wealth tax and greater transparency in overseas financial holdings are all being promoted. But the secrecy of Britain’s overseas territories has for a decade been a millstone in the UK’s call to combat corruption. Kirsty McNeill, the new international development minister and a former executive director at Save the Children, has been asked to wrestle with the impact of massive aid cuts. She has previously said the UK will not regain credibility on aid unless it sets out a path for returning aid spending to 0.7% of GDP. Aid will fall to 0.3% next year and Burnham’s £2 bus fare cap is being funded by a raid on the aid budget. The G20 at least provides a creative way for her to build alliances to tackle unjust debts and illicit financial flows. A global wealth tax was proposed during the Brazilian presidency of the G20 in 2024 after a study commissioned from the French economist Gabriel Zucman. “There is overwhelming public support for this idea,” Zucman said at the report’s launch. “Ten years ago, nobody believed 130 countries would support a minimum tax on multinationals. It was thought of as utopian.” The report said billionaires were paying an average of 0.3% tax on their wealth – less than the rates paid by workers. Zucman said the average wealth of the top 0.0001% of individuals had grown by 7.1% a year on average between 1987 and 2024, increasing the share of global wealth held by billionaires from 3% to 14%. Trump’s own G20 summit is due in Miami in December, by which time he could be diminished by a reverse in the midterm congressional elections. There has been a slow drop-off in world leaders attending the G20 partly owing to geopolitical rifts over Ukraine and questions over its value, but by next year the economic fallout from the war in Iran may require economic and political coordination. Miliband is not, meanwhile, expected to act quickly on Burnham’s admission that Labour needed to “do better” on Gaza. Burnham suggested action on trade with illegal Israeli settlements was on his agenda, but Foreign Office diplomats have questioned the enforceability of such a ban. A debate is under way as to whether European states would best help the political parties opposed to the Israeli prime minister in the October elections by imposing fresh sanctions, underlining Benjamin Netanyahu’s diplomatic isolation, or whether he would use international disapproval to his domestic advantage. The pressure from the Labour backbenches for a more robust policy that treats international law with the same seriousness in the Middle East as the UK does in Ukraine is intense. A letter from 80 parliamentarians coordinated by the MP Kim Johnson called on Burnham to impose comprehensive sanctions on Israel and recognise the findings of the UN commission of inquiry that Israel is committing genocide. Burnham has said it is for the international courts to make such determinations. But a consequential question will be how Miliband retains his progressive credibility and yet remains on good terms with the US state department under Trump. Wood, a sceptic about past UK foreign military interventions, strongly opposed the US military attack on Iran. But the need to retain a modicum of US support for Ukraine has, ever since Trump’s election, been seen as an essential UK foreign policy priority, one that has required compromises and often involved working with the recently deceased Republican senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine. That is unlikely to change in the short term.

title: Laura Loomer, Lindsey Graham and the deepening Iran crisis: what’s behind Trump’s reset with Zelenskyy?
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: The US administration has struck a warmer tone of late as Ukraine has shown its value as an ally in the Middle East
body_text: As leadership pairings go, Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy is not a match made in heaven. It is a far cry from the warm rapport and kindred spiritedness that defined Ronald Reagan’s relationship with Margaret Thatcher, or even the guarded pragmatic friendliness Reagan forged with Mikhail Gorbachev to effectively end the cold war. Yet from a calamitous start that saw Trump publicly ambush and then virtually expel Zelenskyy from the White House after an explosive meeting in February 2025, relations between the US president and his Ukrainian counterpart have taken an unexpectedly warm turn. The thaw has coincided with the US-Israeli war with Iran – and appears to have accelerated as Trump has struggled to end the conflict. A memorandum of understanding, signed in June and designed to institute a 60-day ceasefire, has been rendered moot as hostilities have resumed over the status of the strait of Hormuz, the strategically vital waterway that Iran has effectively closed from the start of the war – threatening the stability of the global economy. “There’s no question that he’s warmed up to Zelenskyy,” said Charles Kupchan, a senior fellow at the Council of Foreign Relations and a former White House adviser on European affairs. “We’ve gone from a phase in which he was throwing Zelenskyy out of the Oval Office, and turning his back on him, to a situation today where they seem to have a reasonably good relationship, and where there have now been a succession of meetings that have gone well.” This week, the pair met once more at the White House after Zelenskyy travelled to Washington for the funeral of Lindsey Graham, the Republican senator who had staunchly backed Ukraine in its war with Russia, even as Trump and his Maga movement all but threw in their lot with the Russian president, Vladimir Putin. The encounter followed another at last month’s Nato summit in Ankara, when Trump strikingly praised Zelenskyy – whom he had once labelled a “dictator” – and said he would grant licenses for Ukraine to develop its own Patriot missile interceptors, although he cast doubt on that promise at a cabinet meeting on Friday. It also came on the heels of an arguably even more remarkable occurrence: the meeting in Kyiv between Zelenskyy and Laura Loomer, the far-right social media influencer known to have sway with Trump, and who has previously vocally supported Russia. After meeting the Ukrainian leader, Loomer said she had been “bamboozled” by Russian propaganda and admitted having believed “a lot of untrue things” about Ukraine. She also said she had followed the meeting with a phone call to Trump and that her change of view was affecting sentiment across the Maga movement. This sea change may have several causes, from Trump’s mercurial nature and preference for backing a winner to Putin’s stubborn refusal to accept several favorable peace deals after Trump vowed to settle the conflict “on day one” of his second presidency. Yet one potential factor stands out among all others. While administration officials have offered no explanation, the accelerating thaw between Trump and Zelenskyy has coincided with the US’s deepening difficulties in concluding the war with Iran’s hardline Islamic regime that Trump launched, along with Israel, on 28 February. “At a moment when he is stuck in a war, faced with bad military options, and suddenly the Ukrainians are approaching him no longer asking for American charity but offering help, I find it quite plausible that that could be a reason, amongst many probably, as to why Trump’s attitude appears to have shifted in a rather strong way,” said Trita Parsi, an Iranian analyst who is vice-president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. Tehran’s retaliation with drone attacks on US military bases and infrastructure in allied Gulf kingdoms has served to illustrate the shared interest between Kyiv and Washington. Ukraine, too, came under sustained attack from Iranian Shahed drones after Tehran supplied them to Moscow in the early stages of Russia’s invasion of the country in 2022. Ukraine has since responded by becoming a world leader in defensive drone technology, an innovation it has trumpeted to the US and its Gulf allies since they came under fire from the weapons as Iran responded to the military onslaught on its territory. Zelenskyy told UK MPs in March that 200 Ukrainian military experts had been dispatched to 11 countries across the Gulf – including the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait – to advise on how to combat Shahed drones. Not just a taker, but a giver Last weekend, Ukraine was accused of trying to merge the two conflicts after it struck an Iranian commercial vessel on the Caspian Sea. Kyiv justified the strike by saying that the ship was being used to transport arms to Russia. Iran said the strike had killed an Iranian sailor and threatened retaliation. Preparing to meet Trump in Washington, Zelenskyy said Iran had “attacked” Ukraine by supplying weaponry to Russia. “What do you expect, if Iran transferred new technologies to Russia from the first year of the war,” he told Sky News. “These were Shahed drones. They transferred thousands of these drones in the first year of the war. Then they issued licenses. What did they do? Did they attack us? I think so.” Zelenskyy also vowed to share Ukrainian intelligence that he said showed Russia giving Tehran help to hit US targets. “Since the beginning of July, we have recorded active Russian satellite surveillance of the Gulf states and US military facilities located there,” he posted on X. “These images subsequently appear in Iran … There is clear correlation between Russia’s satellite imagery of these sites and Iranian strikes – both before the attacks, in preparation for them, and afterward, to assess the damage.” Kupchan, of the Council of Foreign Relations, said Zelenskyy was being a “good salesman” in persuading Trump that Ukraine was an ally worth supporting, by contributing help that the US needs – thus appealing to the US president’s transactional instincts. “Zelensky has done a very good job of communicating to Trump that he is going to help him on Iran,” said Kupchan. “He travelled in the Gulf and said, ‘I’m going to help you deal with Iran and drones, because we’ve been there and done that.’ “It’s an investment in his relationships with Trump, and with Europe, because he’s demonstrating Ukraine’s value as an ally. And I think Trump, who is endlessly transactional, might actually agree to help Ukraine a bit more because Ukraine has stepped up when America’s chips are down in the war with Iran. “The case for helping Ukraine is even stronger now, because Ukraine has demonstrated that it is not just a taker, but a giver.” However, the US president’s apparent vacillation over his Patriot missile pledge shows that cultivating Trump is always at the mercy of his mercurial nature. Some analysts warn that Ukraine risks turning two local localized wars into a global conflict by “merging the battlefields” - thereby inviting Tehran to widen the scope of any retaliatory measures. Sina Toossi, a fellow at the Center for International Policy, said Ukraine’s intervention bolstered the view in Tehran that the Russia-Ukraine war, and Iran’s confrontation with the US, are becoming a single, interconnected conflict. “Trump’s apparent warming toward Zelensky only strengthens this perception,” he said. “The likely implication is not an immediate missile strike on Ukraine, but a broader expansion of where Tehran believes it can legitimately impose costs.” Recognition of such dangers appeared to spur Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s acting foreign minister, to call his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, immediately after Zelenskyy’s latest meeting with Trump. “I stressed that our goal is to avoid unnecessary escalation,” Sybiha wrote on social media. “All of Ukraine’s actions are aimed solely at defending our country from Russian aggression and never intended to target civilian vessels or people.” Parsi said Ukraine’s involvement could have the effect of “reframing” the Iran war, so that it would no longer be perceived merely as serving an agenda set by Israel, but as helping to defend Ukraine. That might appeal to European countries, and Democrats in the US, who have broadly opposed the Iran war, but supported Ukraine. Yet, even with Loomer’s belated conversion to the Ukrainian cause, it seems far less likely to impress Trump’s base. “The centre of gravity in the Maga movement is still skeptical of foreign wars, and of sending large amounts of money to Ukraine, and I don’t see that changing,” said Kupchan. Matt Duss, vice-president of the Center for International Policy, warned that Zelenskyy’s efforts to help Trump with Iran risked undermining support for Ukraine. “Trying to draw closer to Israel in the war on Iran really undermines a lot of Ukraine’s case, because Israel is effectively trying to do to the Palestinians precisely what Russia has been trying to do to Ukraine, which is to erase them as a people,” said Duss, a former foreign policy adviser to Bernie Sanders. “That could potentially diminish what has been up until now pretty good bipartisan support for Ukraine.”

title: DoJ appears to ignore New Mexico deadline for key Epstein ranch files
author: Richard Luscombe
summary: State attorney general set 31 July deadline for documents relating to abuse of girls at Epstein-owned Zorro ranch
body_text: The US Department of Justice (DoJ) appeared to ignore a Friday deadline set by Raúl Torrez, the attorney general of New Mexico, to share information about the abuse of girls at a remote ranch formerly owned by the disgraced financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Torrez’s office asked the DoJ in February for unredacted files after he reopened a dormant criminal investigation into activities at Zorro ranch, a remote 10,000-acre property in desert scrub outside New Mexico. It set a 31 July deadline for the department to share relevant records. As it approached on Friday, the justice department did not respond to a request for comment. The Guardian reported in February that recent releases of the so-called Epstein files included thousands of mentions of the ranch, and numerous photographs of men and young girls there. A succession of survivors had previously given testimony about abuse they were subjected to. However, unlike other properties prominent in Epstein’s sex-trafficking conspiracy in Palm Beach, New York, and his private Caribbean island, no federal search of the ranch was ever confirmed to have taken place. Torrez set a deadline of Friday for federal prosecutors from the justice department, and the US attorney’s office for the southern district of New York (SDNY), which led the original Epstein investigation, to allow access to whatever documents they had. Despite promises of cooperation from Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, and Jay Clayton, former US attorney for the SDNY, now director designate of national intelligence, Torrez said only 31 pages were ever handed over. They were mostly old news clippings and heavily redacted pages of little use to state investigators, he said. Torrez said in a 14 July letter to Blanche he would “pursue all available legal remedies without further notice” if the 31 July deadline passed, having made “repeated, documented, good-faith efforts to obtain the unredacted investigative records in the USDOJ’s custody”. The same week, in an interview with Albuquerque ABC News affiliate KOAT, Torrez said: “I’m not taking anything off the table. I’m not ruling out a lawsuit.” Epstein died in jail in New York in August 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex trafficking charges. The fight for documents relating to his activities at Zorro ranch, which he bought in 1993 from the estate of the Democratic former New Mexico governor Bruce King, became something of a cat and mouse affair after Torrez’s reopening of an inquiry first launched by his predecessor Hector Balderas in February 2019. According to the attorney general, the southern district of New York called him in July to announce that it would not cooperate. But Clayton, in his confirmation hearing in the US Senate last month, told Martin Heinrich, Democratic senator for New Mexico: “My folks, I think as we speak, are seeking dialogue with the attorney general to see if we can reach an accommodation”. Clayton noted that the documents were subject to certain “protective orders”, namely redactions to hide the identities of victims. Blanche, accused in February by Democrats of a “full-blown cover-up” of the Epstein files, told his own confirmation hearing last month that he was “continuing to work” with the New Mexico department of justice. But Torrez said he had heard nothing further, either from Blanche, or the SDNY. Meanwhile, the US attorney’s office for the district of New Mexico, in a statement to the Guardian, said it had “substantively responded” to Torrez’s request on 30 June by emailing the 31 documents. Some, a spokesperson said, were communications directing Torrez to the SDNY. The New Mexico US attorney’s office “did not lead or handle the Zorro Ranch investigation and therefore neither collected nor retained any investigative materials”, the statement said. Torrez did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian on Friday. He told MS Now’s the Briefing with Jen Psaki on 23 July that he was annoyed by months of stonewalling from Blanche, Donald Trump’s pick for attorney general, whose confirmation is in peril. “It appears that the administration has been really focused on the management of communications around the Epstein case, rather than acting in a way that demonstrates a commitment to getting to the truth and getting to accountability,” said Torrez. Especially frustrating, he told MS Now, was the conduct of the SDNY after the first, Balderas-ordered investigation was shelved. Torrez said: “We stood down that investigation at the explicit request of the southern district of New York, and so to have them fail to honor their agreement and then not give us access to this file is extremely unusual, and it’s complicating our ability to advance this criminal investigation.” Blanche “has the authority right now, with the stroke of a pen, to grant us this access, to let us, our investigators and prosecutors, come and take a look at the files, identify co-conspirators, witnesses, corroborating evidence, identify new potential leads,” Torrez added. “Every day that goes by that that doesn’t happen is another day that we’ve delayed delivering justice for the survivors.”
