title: Gianni Infantino ‘has lost Uefa’s confidence’ after Fifa chief scraps World Cup sell-off plan
author: Matt Hughes and Nick Ames
summary: Gianni Infantino ‘has lost the confidence’ of Uefa following his aborted project to sell off the World Cup to private investors, European football’s governing body has said
body_text: Uefa has warned Gianni Infantino that his style of leadership cannot continue in demanding a thorough and fundamental review of Fifa’s governance. In a strongly worded statement that referred to “secret schemes”, “shabby backroom deals” and “faceless individuals”, the Uefa leadership made clear it wants change at the top of Fifa, despite the world governing body’s overnight U-turn in abandoning Infantino’s plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup and other competitions. While stopping short of calling for Infantino to resign, Uefa’s leadership is understood to be determined that he should not be permitted to survive a crisis of his own making, a view that is shared by many of the biggest football governing bodies across the world. Leading European officials are already understood to have begun the process of identifying a candidate to stand against Infantino in next year’s Fifa presidential election, which will continue over the next few days. Uefa’s statement made clear that under the leadership of its president, Aleksander Ceferin, who succeeded in getting all 55 member associations to support a World Cup boycott last Thursday, it will continue to push for change. “We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game,” the statement read. “We must identify those responsible and hold them to account. “It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, Uefa will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again. That review should be thorough and fundamental. No option should be off the table. The current Fifa leadership has not only lost Uefa’s confidence, but also that of many other members of the football family.” Uefa went on to criticise Infantino directly, saying he has failed to deliver on pledges he made to be transparent and accountable before he was first elected president in 2016. The Football Association backed Uefa and, in a statement, said: “We fully support Uefa’s position. It is time for a full and robust review of Fifa’s leadership and governance to ensure that the global game is run transparently, for the benefit of all 211 member nations and with the long-term stewardship of football at its heart!” Speaking in Manchester on Saturday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was the right decision for Fifa to back down. It comes after he previously called the plans “outrageous” and said bringing them forward made it clear that Infantino was “the wrong man to lead the organisation”. Elsewhere in Europe, the Dutch FA said the withdrawal of Infantino’s proposal was not the end of the issue, adding: “The matter is ⁠not settled for the KNVB. The way this process has unfolded has led to a fundamental breach of trust in the leadership of Fifa president Gianni Infantino. The KNVB no longer has ⁠confidence in his leadership.” Bernd Neuendorf, president of Germany’s DFB, said: “The events surrounding this project initiated by Gianni Infantino must now be fully investigated. The Fifa president acted unilaterally, opaquely and ultimately irresponsibly in the best interests ⁠of football.” Infantino had been expected to be re-elected unopposed for a third full term at next March’s Fifa congress in Rabat, but while he is determined to stay on the 56-year-old could now face a challenger. While he has already secured more than 200 letters of support from member associations endorsing his re-election campaign they can be withdrawn, and the deadline for other candidates to announce an intention to stand is not until 18 November. The Paris Saint-Germain president, Nasser Al-Khelaifi, is favoured by many in Europe, but appears reluctant to stand and is also chair of the powerful lobby group European Football Clubs. Other potential candidates include Victor Montagliani, the Canadian who is the president of North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, Concacaf, and the Asian Football Confederation president, Salman al-Khalifa, who lost narrowly to Infantino in the 2016 Fifa election. Uefa’s statement used Infantino’s own words from his initial election campaign 10 years ago against him. “When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of Fifa’s member associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said: ‘Of course we have to be transparent. I have been this in the last 15 years of my life in Uefa. You will have to play a part every day in the life of Fifa,’ before telling the assembled stakeholders: ‘The money of Fifa is your money. It’s not the money of the Fifa president. It’s your money. You are the national associations, and the money of Fifa has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.’ On both these promises, he has failed to deliver. The shabby, backroom, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through were anything but transparent. And with reserves standing at over $5bn, he has also failed to use associations’ money for the benefit of the game.” Uefa also called for an immediate overhaul of Fifa’s system of financial distribution, the Fifa Forward programme in which all 211 member associations receive the same central payment from Fifa over each four-year cycle. Infantino had claimed that selling 20% of a new commercial company – Fifa Forward Enterprise – to private investors would enable them to increase the Fifa Forward payments from $8m over the next four-year cycle to $20m, as well as a one-off $20m bonus for signing up to the scheme. Handing out millions of dollars to tiny nations has been widely criticised as a system of patronage designed to keep Infantino in office, while the $20m bonus on offer for associations who signed up by a deadline of 19 September was condemned. “Uefa will begin work immediately with partners and stakeholders all over the world and right across the game to propose a new way of distributing resources through the existing Fifa Forward programme,” its statement continued. “We must start to use some of that money that is sat idle in Fifa’s bank account to deliver the kickstart that the grassroots and the wider game need in each of the 211 countries of Fifa. But we don’t need to sell off the family silver to pay for it. “This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story. The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in Fifa has only just begun.” Concacaf later echoed Uefa’s call for a review of Fifa’s leadership in a similarly powerful statement. “A proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident,” Concacaf said. “It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first. This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A full review of this leadership must now take place. “This concern is not Concacaf’s alone. It is shared across many confederations, Member Associations and those who serve and love the game. When people entrusted with protecting the game conclude they can no longer do so from within, the football family is entitled to ask how such a proposal was allowed to proceed, and who bears responsibility for it. “Fifa is not a private enterprise. It is a body held in trust for the game and its members. Those appointed to serve it carry a fiduciary duty, a duty of service over power. Where that duty is not upheld, accountability cannot be optional. “The unity demonstrated by our member associations this week has reaffirmed that when guided by courage, integrity, and sound governance the game will remain where it belongs: in the hands of football - not a single individual.” There was one positive for Infantino, though, as the Qatar FA issued a statement supporting his leadership. Its president, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa bin Ahmed al-Thani, said: “We welcome Fifa President Gianni Infantino’s decision to withdraw the Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal in the interest of the global football community. While the proposal had merit, we applaud the wisdom behind prioritising unity among member associations. “The Qatar Football Association fully supports President Infantino’s efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game globally.”

title: Biohacker Bryan Johnson is keeping his girlfriend’s menstrual blood in his freezer
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: The longevity influencer and his girlfriend, Kate Tolo, say they’re studying women’s health – a worthy goal, but perhaps some skepticism is in order
body_text: The tech entrepreneur Bryan Johnson has devoted his life to dodging death. The 48-year-old is obsessed with becoming the healthiest person in the world and is on a quixotic quest to reverse his biological age and live forever. As such, Johnson is disciplined about what he eats, takes dozens of supplements a day, and measures every single biomarker possible, boasting that he is “certainly the most biologically measured person ever”. In short: good luck finding any ice cream in his freezer. But you know what you will find? His girlfriend’s menstrual blood. On Thursday, Johnson, a chronic oversharer, posted a photo of his 30-year-old girlfriend, Kate Tolo, on X with the caption: “Kate’s period blood is in my -80 °C freezer. Around 10 mL.” This isn’t the first time Johnson has collected a loved one’s bodily fluids: a few years ago he boasted about infusing himself with a liter of his “blood boy’s” plasma. What in God’s name is a blood boy? Oh, that’s just what Johnson calls his son Talmage, who was 17 at the time. Johnson also donated a liter of his own blood to his own father. This also isn’t the first time Johnson has taken it upon himself to share personal information about his loved ones on the internet. Last year, he posted data comparing his and his teenage son’s nocturnal erection metrics. “Nighttime erection data from my 19-year-old son ... and me,” he wrote on X, tagging Talmage. “His duration is two minutes longer than mine. Raise children to stand tall, be firm, and be upright.” Once we’ve all taken a moment to recover from that, we can move on to the menstrual blood in the freezer. What is Johnson planning to do with it? Study it, apparently. “Menstrual blood is valuable and underutilized … It’s a non-invasive look into the uterus,” Johnson explained on X. Tolo and Johnson intend to examine the blood for everything from endocrine disruptors to microplastics. “I like that Kate is a science experiment with me,” he added. OK. But does she like it? Well, she hasn’t said she doesn’t. Rather she replied to his post with a message saying: “Thanks for looking after me bby.” Tolo hasn’t just given a one-off blood sample. Johnson has said that she is collecting “14 million data points on her menstrual cycle”, which he touts as a “world first for female health”. Her protocol involves “100+ tasks a day” and “50+ devices”, all of which is being monitored by a “12 person medical team”. Tolo has to take regular urine samples, swallow a temperature pill, and blow into a metabolism tracker. At exactly 9.42 pm, he writes, she has to “insert techno tampon device”. When the Independent asked for more information about the techno tampon, Johnson said: “We will be sharing more on that soon.” Tolo has done some sharing of her own. In mid-July, she was featured in a Wall Street Journal piece titled: “Bryan Johnson’s girlfriend wants to share her body with the world,” where she explained that she’s doing all this data-tracking for the good of womankind. “I’m really doing it because I think that this is our path toward women being understood in the world and being seen,” Tolo told the Journal. On a personal level, Tolo has said she has polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, and is hoping to find treatments that might help her symptoms. Helping her out with that is the famous techno tampon: the Journal’s piece features a photo of Tolo looking very intently at a small tampon-shaped device which will track her blood-flow variations. As Johnson has said: “Women are not well understood medically.” It wasn’t until 1993, when US Congress passed a law requiring that women and minorities be included in clinical research, that we began to be properly represented in medical trials. Menstruation has also been understudied. Indeed, until 2023 there hadn’t been a published study testing period products like tampons using human blood. They’d used saline solution instead. This sort of “medical misogyny” has impacted the quality of care that women get, and resulted in women’s pain not being taken as seriously as men’s. In many ways, then, Johnson and Tolo’s new women’s health initiative is to be applauded. It’s helping break down the stigma attached to menstruation, and it’s raising awareness about women’s health. All that said, I think a smidgen of skepticism is warranted. It’s important to remember that Tolo (who has a background in fashion) and Johnson (whose background is in tech) are not exactly highly credentialled medical researchers. They own a company called Immortals that sells supplements. And guess what? According to the Journal: “The company is on the verge of launching products for women.” Which makes all of this feel a lot like a marketing campaign. I don’t know if the techno tampon will end up being a giant step forward for womankind, but it might well provide a healthy boost to the Immortals balance sheet. Elon Musk’s xAI is challenging Minnesota over its ban on ‘nudification’ technology Minnesota is implementing a first-in-the-nation law to ban apps and software that allow someone to “nudify” an image or video. Guess who isn’t excited about this? Musk’s AI company. xAI sued to block the new law on Monday, arguing that its definition of “intimate part” is too broad and the statute “imposes an overbroad, content-based ban on free speech”. A good time to remember that Musk is the world’s biggest free speech hypocrite and only seems to care about free speech when it enriches him. We are entering a terrifying new era of genocide-as-a-business-model The genocide scholar Omer Bartov has a powerful piece in the New York Times about how: “If the plans that are being elaborated for Gaza go forward, genocide may come to be seen by some nations as the legitimate and lucrative extension of politics by other means.” Majority of Maga voters would support GOP candidate accused of sexual assault Per a Politico poll: “Two-thirds of self-identified MAGA Trump voters say they would continue supporting a GOP candidate accused of sexual assault” by a former partner. That’s “13 percentage points higher than the share of Trump 2024 voters writ large, which include those who do not identify as MAGA”. These numbers don’t really make sense considering that 100% of Trump voters voted for a man accused of sexual misconduct by multiple women, and found liable for abuse in the E Jean Carroll case. Republican congressman Max Miller accused by ex-wife and ex-girlfriend of abuse Seems like a very common theme in the party of family values! As for whether this will impact Miller’s career, see the poll above. US government map of Africa mislabels every country at global conference The map was apparently made with OpenAI tools. Schools are adding pepper-spraying drones to help combat active shooters Per the Washington Post, at least nine schools in three states (Florida, Georgia, Colorado) have bought drones “that can zoom through halls, smash windows and pepper-spray active shooters if teachers report a threat”. Nearly 400,000 students have experienced gun violence at school since the 1999 attack at Colorado’s Columbine High School. Instead of sparking gun reform, it’s spawned a multibillion-dollar security industry focused on campus shootings. Senate unanimously passes resolution opposing pardon for Ghislaine Maxwell Resolutions like this are largely symbolic, so a possible pardon isn’t completely out of the question. Matt Damon’s stunt double in The Odyssey is a 4ft 6in woman called Devyn Dalton Dalton is getting a lot of buzz after an interviewer congratulated Damon on his biceps in the Odyssey and the actor explained that his double was a female stunt performer who had “the greatest arms I have ever seen”. I have investigated further and can confirm they are elite arms. The week in pawtriarchy The Trump administration has slashed environmental research funding, meaning cash-strapped scientists are having to get creative. Enter an OnlyFans account called OnlyMarms, promising “unfiltered yellow-bellied marmot content from the Rockies!” While OnlyFans is known for risqué content, you’ll be glad to hear this is G-rated. “We’re not trying to sexualize marmots,” the marmot researcher Daniel Blumstein said. “Although I was just at an international conference and three people came up to me and said: ‘Oh, you have to have more pictures of Marmot feet.’” So far the site has only raised about $3,000, but let’s hope it builds marmentum. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: Trump’s favorite cable news channel is pushing back against his war on Iran
author: Jeremy Barr
summary: Prominent Fox News hosts have expressed concern, bewilderment and frustration over US objectives in Iran
body_text: Throughout his two presidencies, Donald Trump has leaned on reliable support from the conservative opinion wing of his favorite cable news channel, Fox News. But, like a broad swathe of the American public, several traditionally supportive commentators on the channel have recently expressed concerns about whether the war on Iran is succeeding, suggesting that Trump is on increasingly dicey footing in the conservative media world he relies on for backing. While he isn’t close to losing the support of hosts such as Sean Hannity or Jesse Watters, Trump has received scrutiny from one of the network’s top personalities, Laura Ingraham, who has regularly questioned whether the US has achieved the tactical wins it has claimed in Iran. He has also faced reliable skepticism from one of the network’s most prominent commentators about the armed forces, Johnny “Joey” Jones, a contributor and retired Marine Corps staff sergeant who lost both his legs in combat in Afghanistan. Jones’ commentary is particularly salient because he is close to Pete Hegseth, his former Fox colleague who is now the defense secretary and who oversaw Jones’ recent re-enlistment in the Marine Corps reserve. That’s not to mention the network’s military commentators, such as retired Lt Gen Keith Kellogg, who said on Fox on Wednesday that Trump needs to “change” his strategy. “I don’t think we’re close, in that regard of finishing the job, if we are just depending on bombing,” said Kellogg, who left his perch at Fox for a short-lived stint in Trump’s second administration as his envoy focused on Ukraine. “Bombing is not going to get the job done.” On her 24 July show, Ingraham acknowledged a New York Times report that Trump faced threats that forced him to use an alternative plane to Air Force One and suggested claims that the US has demolished Iran’s military seem inaccurate. “If Iran can credibly threaten Air Force One overseas, we didn’t decimate their military capabilities, obviously,” she said. “They’re still capable of a lot of harm.” She made a similar point in June, telling viewers: “We keep hearing their military is destroyed. But if they’re destroyed, how are they continuing to hit us?” Back in March, Ingraham called for the US to precipitously investigate and “address head-on” what she called a “horrible unintended tragedy of this war”, the killing of 175 civilians – mostly children – in an errant attack on a school in Iran. Later that month, Ingraham questioned whether Trump understood the “complexity” of the war in Iran, suggesting that he had not properly been briefed. “Was the president fully briefed about the risks of all of this from the beginning?” she asked on 30 March. “And was he then able to take it all in and understand the complexity of this, how complex it could actually get, and further possibilities of casualties or other damage, the difficulty of dealing with these people? Or was he told this would be relatively quick in and out?” From the beginning of the war, Jones on his weekend show sought to emphasize the stakes of the conflict after multiple American service-members were killed in a counter-attack in Kuwait. “It’s important and it’s okay for any Americans who are saying: ‘Wait just a minute. Tell me more. Tell me why we are at war. Explain to me why this was imminent,’” he said. “I don’t think that questions your patronage to the American government or even if you’re Maga or what have you. It doesn’t question president Trump’s wisdom in this.” On 18 July, after reports that two American service members had been killed in Jordan, he questioned whether the US strategy was working. “I often say that president Trump [should] speak loudly and carry a big stick,” he said on air. “Right now might be the time that the big stick part of it matters most, because simply dropping bombs from the air isn’t stopping them from doing what they want to do.” While he mentioned some potential options the US could take, he noted that they would take time, “and time is not on our side”. A few days later, Brit Hume, a Fox News analyst, connected the quagmire to Trump’s political promises to voters. “He promised to keep us out of endless wars or unsatisfactory wars, and now he’s in one, and it’s not at all clear how it’s gonna end. So, he’s vulnerable on this point, and in political terms, he does need to get this over with.” In June, John Roberts, a Fox News anchor, said he was “a little puzzled” about Trump’s Iran negotiation strategy. Even Watters, a reliable Trump booster, seemed skeptical about his ever-changing timelines for reaching a deal with Iran to end the war. “He keeps saying: ‘We’re very close. We’re days away.’ And I don’t know what that means. We’ve heard that for a very long time,” he said in June. Hosts on the network’s business channel have also regularly questioned the rising price of oil and the impact on American consumers, particularly ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. As Stuart Varney, a Fox Business Network anchor, put it in March: “Houston, we have a problem.”

title: Democrats’ ‘climate hushing’ prompts activists to turn up the volume
author: Dharna Noor
summary: Nationwide actions seek to counter view that talking about climate crisis distracts from affordability messaging
body_text: This summer, torrential rains have washed away Texas neighborhoods, dangerous heat has blanketed swaths of the country, and smoke from Canadian wildfires has choked communities as far south as Florida. Research makes clear that global warming is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe. Yet the climate crisis has largely disappeared from the political agenda, with many Democrats who once described it as an existential threat now shying away from talking about it. Now US activists are pushing back against this trend of “climate hushing”, arguing it is misguided. During the summer’s federal recess, during which lawmakers leave the nation’s capital to work directly within their home states or districts, demonstrators organized by the environmental advocacy coalition Climate Action Campaign are calling on representatives to put climate back on the political agenda. “The long history of the climate movement proves that we move fastest when there’s real pressure from the grassroots,” said Bill McKibben, the environmental author and activist who co-founded climate non-profit 350.org, “All the evidence shows those grassroots are as worried about [the] climate crisis as they ever were.” The events, set to take place over the next month in at least 20 states during the House and Senate recess periods, will mobilize members of groups including local Sierra Club chapters, the senior citizen-led climate organization Third Act, which McKibben founded, and local affiliates of the racial justice group the NAACP. “It’s the broadest brush that we are working with,” said Margie Alt, director of the Climate Action Campaign. “The message is, talk about climate, climate can’t wait, and we want to see action.” Actions began on Thursday and will take a variety of forms. In Michigan, participants will demonstrate against the Republican representative Bill Huizenga who voted for Trump’s so-called big beautiful bill, which boosted planet-heating fossil fuels. In Arizona, young activists will meet with the Democratic representative Adelita Shirley Grijalva, a climate champion, and encourage her to continue talking about global warming. In other districts, organizers have circulated petitions calling on the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, and Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, to prioritize climate issues or plan to call on their representatives to connect the climate crisis to recent heatwaves. The activists’ campaign comes as new polling challenges the need for “climate hushing”, a trend that took off as some policy wonks argued that talking about global warming could alienate voters and distract from the message of affordability. July research from the University of California, Santa Barbara found that emphasizing climate change was neutral to beneficial for Democratic candidates, suggesting that talking more about the issue does not alienate voters and can even increase support in competitive races. Though the Trump administration frequently derides climate policy as a “scam” and a “hoax”, polling indicates most Americans are not onboard with that view. Another July poll from Data for Progress found that 61% of likely voters believe extreme weather has become more frequent over the past five years, including nearly half of Republicans. And one month earlier, a Yale survey found that roughly two-thirds of Americans are worried about global warming. “Smart politicians will grab on this issue,” said McKibben. “There’s perhaps no other question where the gulf between Maga and the general public is higher.” Alt said she saw climate-hushing as “the climate denial of 2026”. “I don’t think that ignoring the climate crisis is smart politics,” she said. “I think that it is dropping the ball on the biggest threat the US and the world faces.”

title: Trump vows to push $1.8bn slush fund as Senate committee set to reconsider AG nomination
author: Edward Helmore
summary: After declaring ‘anti-weaponization’ fund ‘dead’, Trump reverses and says he’ll revive it despite Senate opposition
body_text: The US Senate judiciary committee has scheduled a meeting early next week to consider Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general, as Donald Trump promised to revive the controversial $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” fund. The meeting, set for Tuesday, comes as Blanche’s confirmation has stalled over a dispute between the president and outgoing Republican senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, who are seeking written confirmation that the justice department would not establish the proposed fund. A spokesperson for the committee said in a statement that Chuck Grassley, committee chair and Iowa Republican, “wants Todd Blanche’s nomination to be successful”. “Grassley would like to see Blanche confirmed before the August recess as he has an excellent record restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe,” the statement added. Opponents of the president consider it a slush fund to compensate political allies for political lawfare; supporters say it is a vehicle to compensate individuals who claim they were wrongfully targeted by the government more broadly. “It is dead, but I wish ⁠it weren’t, to be honest with you. I think people were horribly treated, horribly abused,” Trump had said during a cabinet meeting on Friday. “I’d like to ⁠see them compensated for the pain.” At the cabinet meeting on Friday, Trump urged Republican senators to confirm Blanche and warned that they “will never get anybody like him” and repeated a claim that Cornyn was blocking Blanche because Trump had endorsed Cornyn’s Republican primary challenger Ken Paxton. “I’d be upset also,” ‌Trump said. “I fully understand it. He shouldn’t be that way. I shouldn’t be that way.“ Trump then slammed Cornyn and Tillis in a post on Truth Social on Saturday, claiming that both were upset because he had not endorsed them. Trump threatened to withdraw Blanche’s nomination, keep him on as acting attorney general and “push hard” for anti-weaponization bill. “Todd Blanche was a voice of reason!” Trump wrote. “It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done.” Blanche, Trump’s former personal attorney, has told senators that the fund was dead, but has so far not agreed to put that in writing. The “anti-weaponization” fund was crafted as part of a ⁠legal settlement between Trump and the justice department to resolve his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS over allegedly mishandling his tax records. Trump wrote that the fund “will not benefit me, but rather the great American Patriots who were hunted down like dogs and whose lives were unfairly and illegally destroyed”. Tillis has said those who attacked law enforcement during the 6 January 2021 riots should still be in prison and should not get a check from the federal government. Cornyn and Tillis also object to an IRS deal that would prevent tax audits of Trump and his associates. Tillis responded on Saturday, saying that despite Trump’s comments that the fund is dead, the president “clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against”. “It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal,” he said on X. “Hopefully, we can resolve this by Tuesday.” The back-and-forth over Blanche’s nomination, which is vigorously opposed by victims of Jeffrey Epstein over his handling of investigative files related to the late sex trafficker, now likely lies with backroom negotiations over the weekend. The same controversy dogged Trump’s original second-term attorney general, Pam Bondi, before she resigned. Cornyn and Tillis were reported to be close to backing Blanche as recently as Thursday. But with just more than two years left in Trump’s second term, Blanche may not need formal Senate confirmation to serve so long as his nomination is pending and not formally rejected or withdrawn.

title: Trump offering early access to online posts in move seen as corruption
author: Marina Dunbar
summary: Truth Social, where Trump’s account is by far the largest, to offer users early access for up to $100,000 per month
body_text: Donald Trump is now offering early access to his Truth Social posts in a move that has been seen as corruption benefitting a sitting president. Trump Media and Technology Group officially rolled out its new subscription-based data service on Saturday, giving paying customers faster, real-time access to Truth Social posts from Trump and other high-profile accounts. Called Truth API, the application programming interface is intended to provide businesses with “a direct, licensed, real-time feed of the platform’s most market-moving Truths”, interim CEO Kevin McGurn said in a release announcing the launch. Trading firms and other paying subscribers can now access the posts earlier than other users – for a fee of up to $100,000 per month. The new offering mirrors similar paid data services available on competing social media platforms, though with a particularly steep price tag. However, Truth Social stands apart because its most influential user is Trump, who is also the largest shareholder of the publicly traded parent company, meaning he could personally benefit from the service. Although the announcement does not specifically mention Trump, his @realDonaldTrump account is by far the platform’s largest. He frequently uses it to announce major policy decisions before making them elsewhere. As of Saturday, the account had 13 million followers. Critics argue the service is blatant evidence of market manipulation and insider trading. Trump has repeatedly used Truth Social to reveal significant policy moves with the potential to shift financial markets, including posts involving tariffs and the Iran war. The launch comes just days after Democratic senators Adam Schiff and Elizabeth Warren called on the Securities and Exchange Commission to examine the new service. In a letter dated Tuesday and sent to SEC chair Paul Atkins, the lawmakers urged the agency to investigate whether the company was breaking the law. “This appears to be an outrageous abuse of the President’s office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets, while enriching Wall Street and other wealthy insiders,” they wrote. Last year, Trump published more than 100 Truth Social posts in a single day while global stock markets tumbled amid concerns that his economic agenda could trigger a “Trumpcession” in the US. His posts about Iran have drawn particular attention because investors remain concerned that rising oil prices could keep inflation elevated and potentially lead the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates. Trump Media’s stock has fallen by more than 70% since the president took office last year, wiping out roughly $6bn (£4.4bn) in shareholder value. Those losses, combined with billions more in investor losses connected to new Trump family cryptocurrency ventures, have come under increased scrutiny after Trump’s annual financial disclosure showed he generated more than $1 billion in revenue last year from the same companies and offerings. On Friday, one day before Truth API’s debut, shares of Trump Media climbed 5.5% to $10.39 shortly before the market closed, reported Forbes. The president’s company has primarily depended on advertising revenue, but the new API service could expand its revenue sources if it proves successful.

title: Upheaval in Maine and another 100-day campaign – can Democrats pull it off?
author: Shrai Popat in Bangor, Maine
summary: Troy Jackson gained the party nomination for Senate, but now he needs to consolidate support to take on Susan Collins
body_text: Troy Jackson is ready to move on. In fewer than 100 days, the new Democratic nominee has to convince Maine voters to send him to the US Senate – and he’s trying to do it without dwelling on Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race after accusations of rape, which he denies. “The movement represented in this room did not just begin two weeks ago,” said Jackson, a progressive lumberjack and former state lawmaker who won nearly all the delegates at a hastily organized special convention last Saturday. “I’ve always known that your trust has to be earned.” On stage, no one mentioned Platner by name, but the fallout from the oyster farmer’s campaign collapse hung over the room. He had ridden an anti‑establishment wave before crashing under a series of scandals – which included problematic online posts, a tattoo resembling a Nazi symbol and allegations of abusive behavior in past relationships. Jackson, who previously launched an unsuccessful bid for governor this year, now faces a compressed timeline to build the same momentum his predecessor generated against Susan Collins, the moderate Republican who has weathered every challenger during her three decades in the Senate. Maine is central to Democrats’ effort to pick up the four seats they need to regain control of the upper chamber in the midterms. But some in the party worry that Jackson faces a steep climb in a short window. “He won an interparty fight – which is nothing like the fight he’s got ahead of him,” said Lynn Bromley, a former Democratic state senator. “He’s going to have to build a statewide coalition. That’s a whole different process.” “I would say Jackson has momentum, but I would also say momentum isn’t the same thing as trust,” she added. Who Jackson needs to win Jackson quickly emerged as the natural heir to Platner’s anti‑oligarchy message. More than 17,000 voters turned out for the county‑level delegate elections, and by the time the roughly 500 selected delegates arrived in Bangor, most had already pledged to support Jackson. In a Tuesday interview on political talkshow Morning Joe, Jackson acknowledged that Platner was the more compelling orator, but said his focus now is making sure voters understand the election is about “the movement”, not any one candidate. To win in November, he still has to consolidate Democratic support and reach voters outside Platner’s core supporters. The most crucial demographic for Jackson is 2020 ticket‑splitters in Maine – those who backed Susan Collins for Senate and Joe Biden for president. Back then, Collins ultimately won by nine points, defeating Democrat Sara Gideon, the former state house speaker, despite trailing in most public polls. A Guardian review shows that more municipalities voted for both Biden and Collins than they did for a straight Democratic ticket that year. One of those voters is Wendy Tooth, a physiotherapist in Manchester, who’s been “disappointed” with Collins since her 2020 vote for the incumbent, and particularly since Donald Trump’s re-election. “I wasn’t really a Graham Platner fan,” Tooth, 58, said. “[Collins] doesn’t seem as centrist as she used to be. She seems to go along with a lot of Trump’s policies, which I don’t agree with.” Part of the unenrolled bloc that makes up about a third of voters in the Pine Tree state, Tooth says she needs to see Jackson “work across party lines” – and Collins take firmer positions against the war in Iran and the deadly federal immigration crackdown across the country – before making her decision. Democrats such as Alan Blake of Thomaston say the party must now rally behind Jackson regardless of any concerns about the chaos that has plagued the race so far. “We’re just going to carry Jackson in there because we absolutely need the policies he stands for,” Blake, 74, added. “It’s not drastic to say we’re trying to save democracy here.” And Ellie Gunnoe, 39, a psychiatric nurse practitioner and registered Democrat in New Gloucester, said Jackson – a fifth‑generation logger from Aroostook county – can reach voters across the state as a “working‑class Mainer”. “We just need someone fighting in our corner,” Gunnoe added, noting that the fatal shooting of 26-year-old Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, by an ICE agent in Biddeford, is one of the key motivators pushing her to the ballot box this year. “My husband is Mexican American and is the exact same age and brown, and so it’s just been feeling increasingly unsafe for people like us,” she added. A slice of moderate Democrats who voted for Janet Mills, Maine’s term-limited governor, in the June primary – after she had suspended her campaign but remained on the ballot – are also in play. One of them, Brenda Garrand, 69, of Rockland, said she plans to vote for Jackson even though she doesn’t consider herself a progressive. “I don’t think he’s the best and brightest, I don’t think he is Senate material,” she said. “But we’ve got to have a Senate majority.” Mills, for her part, told a local ABC affiliate this week that Collins is “vulnerable” and “should be defeated”, but did not endorse Jackson directly. Jackson’s run could be buoyed by the anti-Trump animus that’s grown since the financial fallout of the ongoing war. According to a recent New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll, only 39% of likely Maine voters approved of the president’s job performance since he returned to the White House. “Susan Collins keeps telling us everything is just fine. And you know they act like you know we’re idiots. We know it isn’t. We all have eyes,” Jackson said in Bangor. He used his victory to highlight Collins’ votes to confirm the supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh and advance the president’s $70bn bill to guarantee funding for federal immigration enforcement. “Who has she served?” Jackson asked the audience. “She has served Donald Trump. She voted with them 96% of the time.” Meanwhile, Collins has sought to brand Jackson a “Bernie bro”, pointing to his long relationship with Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, and his role leading Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign in Maine. Ronald Schmidt, a politics professor at the University of Southern Maine, said that attack puts the onus on Jackson to “flip that playbook” of being affiliated with an outsider and “link [Collins] to Trump”. But some local Republicans counter that Jackson’s more than two decades as a state legislator, and a failed run for Congress in 2014, mean he lacks Platner’s outsider profile. “He is Maine’s establishment,” said Chuck Ellis, chair of the Cumberland county GOP. “All the appeal of Platner being anti‑establishment is lost when you replace him with a career politician.” The long road ahead, paved with attack ads An ad offensive from conservative Pacs has begun painting Jackson as an extension of Platner, often using footage from their time on the campaign trail when they endorsed each other. After Jackson clinched the nomination on Saturday, the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) even pushed out an AI video of Platner morphing into Jackson with the caption: “No tattoo, same crazy.” James Blair, a former White House adviser now leading Trump’s midterm operation, wrote that Jackson carried “all the baggage” of Platner “without the ‘rizz”. And the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) – the top Senate GOP Super Pac, which has pledged more than $40m to the race – is highlighting the many scandals that plagued the unvetted Platner, alongside reporting about Jackson’s alleged fiery temper during his time in the state legislature. “Jackson is like Graham Platner but worse,” the voiceover in a video says. Meanwhile, the Republican National Committee (RNC) quickly cast Jackson’s nomination as illegitimate, drawing a parallel to the 2024 Democratic convention, where Harris became the nominee after delegates originally pledged to Biden backed her following his withdrawal from the race. “This coronation is proof that Democrats are willing to shove socialism down the throats of Maine voters,” spokesperson Kristen Cianci said. Collins told reporters in Casco last weekend that her challenger’s platform economic populism – which includes many of Platner’s policies such as Medicare for All and taxing the ultra-wealthy – is untenable. “It is disturbing for me to hear Troy say that everything should be free, when in fact it’s going to be middle- and low-income taxpayers who are going to be paying the bill,” she said. Jackson’s ground game is also in need of a significant financial boost to compete with Collins’ war chest of more than $11m cash on hand, according to her latest disclosures. As of now, Jackson’s campaign reports he has amassed $2m since he won the nomination. That’s on top of the $1m he raised since he formally entered the Senate race in early July. Perhaps more daunting than the attacks or the finances, however, is the support Collins has built over five terms, and a record of political survival that has been impossible to beat – even when the odds appear to be against her. “She’s an intimidating political presence, and I think people underestimate that,” said Matt Gorman, a Republican strategist. Collins has spent much of the race, and the years leading up to it, underscoring the millions of dollars in federal funding she’s steered to Maine as chair of the powerful Senate appropriations committee. Her campaign spokesperson, Shawn McRoderick, said the senator looks forward to “waging a vigorous, issues‑oriented campaign that will distinguish her record of accomplishment against Troy’s angry soundbites”. In a small state, tangible results are hard to ignore. “I was speaking to a town official from upstate who was able to get fire department money to improve the local volunteer fire department with the help of Collins’ office,” Schmidt recalled. “People who’ve directly been helped by her staff probably will vote for her again in this election, regardless of their party ID.” While antipathy toward the gerontocracy may color many midterm races this year, Collins’ seniority in Congress – despite serving alongside an administration many Mainers can’t stomach – may be her strongest asset. “With Collins you actually have serious influence that can successfully make progress at cooling off the Trump administration when she feels like that’s necessary and that’s appropriate,” said Ellis. “To lose that, you would have to be able to say that we have a substantial upgrade that’s going to do so much better for us.” Andrew Witherspoon contributed reporting

title: California announces minimum wage increase as governor taunts Trump
author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
summary: Gavin Newsom says new pay floor of $17.40, set to become highest of any US state, will go into effect on 1 January
body_text: Governor Gavin Newsom of California announced that the state’s minimum wage will rise to $17.40 next year, a pay floor set to become the highest of any US state. The pay bump will go into effect starting 1 January, Newsom announced on Friday. The state’s current minimum rate is $16.90. In a news release, Newsom touted the move as a salve for working families amid high living costs and took a jab at the Trump administration. “For years, Donald Trump and Republicans have blocked efforts to raise the federal minimum wage while handing tax breaks to billionaires and big corporations,” Newsom said. The federal minimum wage was last increased during George W Bush’s presidency, when it rose from $6.55 to $7.25. Opponents of a federal increase fear adverse effects to the labor market such as job losses. “California has chosen a different path – one that rewards work, grows the economy and puts working families first. We believe if you work hard, you deserve a decent paycheck. They think $7.25 an hour is enough. We don’t,” Newsom said. Thirty states in addition to Washington DC have set wage rates above the federal minimum. The state of Washington will trail close behind California in 2027 with a minimum wage of $17.13, according to data from the Department of Labor. In New York City and three nearby counties, the minimum wage is $17. Since Newsom took the gubernatorial seat in 2019, the state’s minimum wage has grown from $12, according to his office. Still, for a family of two working adults and two children in California, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) estimate each adult must earn $36.38 to cover food, childcare, healthcare, housing and transportation, among other basic necessities. Cost-of-living concerns have been at the forefront of the upcoming midterm elections. The Trump administration has faced blowback over the protracted war with Iran that has led to a surge in gas prices across the nation. In California, a state that relies on a reduced emission type of gasoline, fuel prices topped $6 a gallon in recent months.

title: Gianni Infantino could face leadership challenge as Fifa council members rebel
author: Exclusive by Matt Hughes
summary: Gianni Infantino is facing a rebellion from members of the Fifa council who are attempting to force an extraordinary general meeting that could develop into a leadership challenge
body_text: Gianni Infantino is facing a rebellion from members of the Fifa council who are attempting to force an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) that could develop into a full-blown leadership challenge. The Guardian has learned that moves to call an EGM were already under way before the emergence of Infantino’s abortive plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup, with council members demanding an independent review into the unprecedented decision to lift Folarin Balogun’s suspension during the World Cup, which involved multiple phone calls from Donald Trump. The Fifa council is the world governing body’s main decision-making forum composed of 28 representatives of the six confederations, eight vice-presidents and Infantino. Under Fifa rules a motion from 50% or 19 of the 37 council members can trigger an EGM. It is understood that the rebels had already reached double figures before it emerged that Infantino had secretly proposed to sell 20% of a new World Cup operating company to Thrive Capital, an investment company founded by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. The unhappy council members had been planning on calling for Infantino to resign if he refused to sanction an independent review of the Balogun affair, which led to the Norwegian FA filing an official complaint to the International Olympic Committee alleging Fifa had breached rules on political neutrality by bowing to pressure from Trump. Fifa has insisted all along that it followed due process, with the decision taken independently by its ethics committee, but has yet to publish a written report on the hearing. The rebels are likely to have been emboldened by Infantino’s U-turn over the World Cup sell-off debacle, with the plan abandoned in a statement from Fifa in the early hours of Saturday morning after Uefa, Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – and the Asian Football Confederation denounced it. Uefa and Concacaf both issued further statements condemning Infantino and calling for a thorough review of Fifa’s governance on Saturday, but it is unclear if they have sufficient support from the rest of the world to oust him. The Confederation of African Football and the South American Conmebol remain fully behind Infantino, while the Qatar Football Association issued a statement yesterday backing him to stay as president. Of the 37 council members 14 are from Europe and North America so support from Asia will be required to put real pressure on Infantino. The Fifa council is not due to meet until November with the rebels attempting to move quickly to force an EGM, where Infantino would be asked to explain himself. A refusal to commission an external review into Balogun would lead to more active attempts to oust Infantino, with alternative presidential candidates already being sounded out. Qatar’s stance has definitely ruled out a presidential bid from Paris Saint-Germain’s president, Nasser Al-Khelaifi, and much will depend on whether Victor Montagliani, the Canadian who is president of Concacaf, has the appetite to take on Infantino. A campaign from the AFC president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, who lost narrowly to Infantino in the 2016 Fifa election, would be difficult without his own confederation’s support. Infantino has already secured more than 200 letters of support endorsing his re-election campaign, but they can be withdrawn and the deadline for other candidates to announce an intention to stand is not until 18 November. Another potential vehicle for removing Infantino would be an emergency Fifa congress to trigger a vote of no confidence in the president, which can be called if letters are submitted by 43 associations.

title: Democrats face most contentious – and crucial – test yet with Michigan primary
author: Rachel Leingang in Davison, Michigan
summary: Voters are faced with the thorny question of electability: who can win this purple state in November and potentially push Democrats toward a US Senate majority?
body_text: At Chad Green’s house in Davison, Michigan, a brood of baby chicks roamed around the idyllic green lawn as US senators pitched a couple of dozen voters on why they should turn out for the hopeful one, Abdul El-Sayed. Green, a retired federal firefighter, hosted a similar small gathering for Mallory McMorrow, who was running for the US Senate before she dropped out of the race in early July, narrowing the contest to El-Sayed, a progressive insurgent campaigning for universal healthcare, and US representative Haley Stevens, who has branded herself as a workhorse. Green, 54, sees himself as a more moderate Democrat, and originally aligned with McMorrow. After she dropped out, he looked into El-Sayed and Stevens, and resonated more with El-Sayed’s policies. “I’ve never seen people more excited about a candidate,” Green said. “I feel like there’s not going to be excitement for the Republicans to vote. And I feel like there is excitement for Democrats to vote for Abdul.” The Michigan primary is, perhaps, the most contentious Democratic primary this year – and a test for the party’s future. Voters are weighing the policies and personalities of the candidates as they once again consider the thorny question of electability: who can win this purple state in November, and potentially push the party towards a majority in the Senate? Recent surveys have shown El-Sayed pulling ahead. A non-partisan Emerson poll this week of likely Democratic voters found 54% intended to vote for El-Sayed compared with 39% for Stevens, with a stark age divide. Voters under 50 broke for El-Sayed by 42 percentage points, while voters over 60 preferred Stevens by a 14-point margin, it showed. Independents were siding with El-Sayed by a 27-point margin. Stevens, 43, has represented Michigan’s 11th House district since 2019, after flipping the seat. She has been endorsed by the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, the Michigan governor, Gretchen Whitmer, and Gary Peters, the retiring senator who holds the seat she and El-Sayed, 41, are now running for. El-Sayed, an epidemiologist who served in health director roles in Detroit and its county, counts leading progressive officials among his supporters, including the US senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Van Hollen, who rallied with him in Michigan last weekend alongside a host of representatives and former elected officials. The winner of Tuesday’s Democratic primary will face Mike Rogers, a former congressman from the state who was also the Republican nominee for US Senate in 2024, when he lost to Elissa Slotkin. El-Sayed, often mentioned alongside democratic socialists who have won a string of party primaries ahead of this year’s US midterm elections, is not himself a democratic socialist: he says he is a “capitalist who understands how capitalism works”, and wants to regulate monopolies and oligopolies. But the race has become a key focal point in the rise of the left flank of the Democratic party, and its potential limits – especially after a wave of wins in solidly blue districts across the country. More than $40m has poured into the race from outside groups supporting Stevens or attacking El-Sayed, including from groups associated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), a pro-Israel lobby. AdImpact shows more than $60m in ad reservations and spending to benefit Stevens. Misleading ads have attacked El-Sayed for “disrespecting women” while tying Stevens to Barack Obama, who has not endorsed in the race, but previously praised Stevens’ work on the auto industry rescue plan. The Obama connection sits prominently in the minds of some Black voters in Michigan, who cite Stevens’ work with the former US president as key to their vote in the primary. El-Sayed has seized on the major outside spending against him and turned it into a central line of attack against Stevens. Stevens points to an A-rating from End Citizens United, a group dedicated to getting money out of politics, and says she feels “very strongly” about campaign finance reform. While talking to reporters outside Plymouth United Church of Christ in Detroit last Sunday, Stevens held up a note passed to her during the church service from a member of the congregation. “Had I known that you would be at church today, I would have brought my checkbook,” the letter said, according to Stevens, who added that most of her direct campaign contributions come from small donors. In the waning days of the primary, Stevens attacked El-Sayed for not releasing his full financial disclosures, which he subsequently did. She also often accuses El-Sayed of seeking fame, pointing to his previous podcast, which he co-hosted for Crooked Media, his book, and a website purchase for El-Sayed for president. El-Sayed said he purchased URLs for various offices as a defensive maneuver so others couldn’t snap up the websites and use them against him, and said he didn’t understand the line of attack on podcasts or books: “I would think that you’d want to send a nominee who’s comfortable doing podcasts.” The campaign has grown increasingly tense in its final weeks. Earlier this month, El-Sayed faced backlash over remarks that he later clarified were in reference to the Democratic senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania – not his primary rival. El-Sayed had said a leftwing victory over Fetterman – who campaigned as a progressive but has moved sharply to the right in office, particularly on Israel – would be akin to putting an “ogre on a pike”. Stevens responded: “Thank you for clarifying that you didn’t call me an ogre.” And in a Twitter post this week, Stevens criticized a video where El-Sayed criticized Aipac, with Stevens saying: “Everyone in America understands you want to blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans.” Stevens said she wasn’t campaigning on “false promises” or “slogans”, a nod to El-Sayed’s central issue of the Medicare for All proposal of universal healthcare. “I am offering a path to win, to make sure that Mike Rogers goes back to Florida for a second time, so that he doesn’t get to go into the Senate and return nothing for us, just rubber-stamping Donald Trump,” she told reporters last weekend. El-Sayed contends that universal healthcare requires fundamentally changing Congress – by electing politicians who will fight for it. “If you don’t fight for certain things, you’re never going to get them,” he told the Guardian. Where the voters go Stevens stood in front of Black congregations on a recent Sunday morning, joining in worship services before telling the churchgoers who she was, and what she could deliver. Black voters – who make up about 20% of the Democratic primary electorate – have expressed some skepticism of El-Sayed. Black voters in the state have tended to side with more moderate candidates in primaries. Polls of the race show Black voters overall siding with Stevens. At Hartford Memorial Baptist church in Detroit, Stevens mentions Obama and Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic minority leader in the US House of Representatives. She says she prayed for her parents. Her dad, she said, always told her: “Do not be the smartest person in any room; be the hardest working.” Later, at Plymouth United Church of Christ, she told the congregation that she “could have stayed comfortable” in her House seat. Scott Benson, a Detroit city councilman and a deacon at Plymouth, said he had been a longtime supporter of Stevens because of her focus on “kitchen-table issues”. He worked with El-Sayed when he was the city’s health director, he added, but El-Sayed’s politics don’t align with his. “I am very pragmatic. I’m very kitchen table. I’m about jobs,” Benson said. “Other issues just really don’t align with mine and so, great guy, but Haley Stevens’ policies align with mine, and her effectiveness as a legislator is also a very big deal to me.” After services ended at Plymouth, people stopped to get photos with Stevens and tell her she had their vote . One woman said she had seen Stevens’ actions, including the work she did under Obama. “I know that there was hope then,” she said. “There’s more hope for us now in Michigan.” Willie Goston, 71, of Redford, said he and his wife filled out their ballots two weeks ago – two votes for Stevens. He knew he would vote for Stevens right away, citing her work with Obama, and her connection with James Clyburn, a longtime South Carolina congressman. “She’s an amazing politician, and she seems like she’s honest, seems like she’s not going to go back behind and do no underhanded stuff,” said Goston. On Sunday afternoon, in Rouge Park in Detroit, volunteers and supporters of El-Sayed rallied, getting egg rolls and ice-cream from food trucks as they listened to elected officials and activists talk about the candidate, frequently calling on his central slogan: “Money out of politics, money in your pockets, Medicare for All.” El-Sayed has hosted rallies and door-knocking launches throughout the campaign, his ground game aided by groups like the Working Families party, the United Auto Workers and the progressive activist network Indivisible. His campaign has more than 10,000 volunteers and is knocking on nearly 10,000 doors a day, he said. Justin Daniels, 45, who attended the park event, said the dividing line in the race was establishment versus non-establishment. Daniels, who is Black, said if younger Black voters tune into the primary, they would probably lean toward El-Sayed, while for older Black voters it’s more of a toss-up. But he thinks El-Sayed can win in November. “I see him winning over Republicans, because what a lot of people don’t understand is they’re getting their benefits cut just as well,” Daniels said. El-Sayed said he believed his campaign would do well with a number of different subsets of Democratic voters, including the Black community. “My relationship with the Black community isn’t built on photo ops and all of a sudden crossing 8 mile because somebody told you that’s what you need to do,” he said. “My public service is built in the city and county, and I’ve been building these relationships for a very long time.” The electability question El-Sayed, who is of Egyptian descent and Muslim, said the electability argument was often a coded way of questioning his name and religion. He has been “Abdul in Michigan” his whole life, including as a high school student after September 11, and still was voted captain of the football team the next year. “Michiganders are open-minded. They’re big-hearted people,” he told voters at Green’s house. “And the funny thing is, when they say I’m unelectable … that’s not a comment on me. You know what that’s a comment on? It’s on you. They’re trying to say that you all, Michiganders, who I know to be open-hearted, kind, thoughtful people, are not big enough to see past my name. And I’m betting otherwise, because I’ve been betting otherwise my whole life.” Voters have shown a strong anti-incumbent bias in recent polls. A recent CNN poll found that a majority of voters think US Congress would be better off if most sitting members were unseated in the midterms. El-Sayed said he regularly has people attend his town halls who tell him they voted for Trump, and now would for him. He is trying to both inspire people who haven’t been voting to come out and back his campaign, and win over people who voted for Trump, but feel betrayed by the administration’s actions. “Why did it go for Bernie, then Trump, then Biden, then Trump?” El-Sayed asked the group at Green’s house of Michigan’s recent voting history. “And either it’s because we can’t make up our minds – which, y’all been in Michigan long enough to know, we know what our minds are – or it’s because we keep going to the buffet, and not finding what we really want. So what happens if you give an alternative that is actually against the system, the corruption on both sides of the aisle, that’s also not a megalomaniacal, narcissistic billionaire asshole?” Stevens points to her record of winning over Republican voters in a tight congressional district. She notes that she has beaten Maga four times. When she and El-Sayed both ran (in separate races) in 2018, Stevens won a six-way House primary. She is the first Democrat to hold the 11th district seat for a full term since the moon landing, she said. As to which of the two candidates is better placed to win in November, “I think the Republicans have answered that for us”, Stevens said, pointing to a leaked phone call where Rogers said he had a better shot at flipping the seat if El-Sayed won the primary. Videos of Stevens’ heavy Michigan accent, where she said she was going to fight with “a little bit of stick it to ’em”, have circulated widely online in the final weeks of the campaign. Stevens has moved to embrace the phrase, putting it on campaign signs, though also suggested its virality was driven by “cool kids on the internet doing the cool kid chatter”, some of whom “might be the coastal elites”. Both Stevens and El-Sayed were born in Rochester Hills, a suburb of Detroit. El-Sayed told his supporters not to “make fun” of Stevens, calling it “unkind and unhelpful”. “I’m going to run through anything and anyone to cut the best deal for Michigan,” Stevens told reporters at an event in Detroit last weekend. “So yeah, they can make fun of my voice, but I sure as damn well am going to make sure we’re heard in the halls of power.” Benson, the Detroit councilman, said he believed El-Sayed’s positions were too far to the left for a purple state. Trump won Michigan in 2024, after Joe Biden won it in 2020. “I believe in the centrist Democrats,” he said. “So I’m a centrist Dem, I’m moderate Dem, and I’m proud of that fact. I just believe it’s what we need to be competitive in the state of Michigan. Those views, his views, they are very well accepted in other places. But when you have a purple state, I’m not sure that’s going to play well here.” Robin Evans, a 75-year-old registered Democrat who attended the gathering at Green’s house with her two siblings, said she would be voting for El-Sayed. His background in public health, and focus on healthcare, appealed to her. “They’re trying to sell the fact that he’s not electable, but I’m not doing that,” she said. “I’m voting for whom I feel is right, not for electability.” Why this race is so closely watched Some of El-Sayed’s potential future colleagues are betting that a win for him, and other progressive wins this cycle, will change the tenor of what Democrats in the Senate are willing to stand for. The US senators Elizabeth Warren, of Massachusetts, and Chris Van Hollen, of Maryland, rallied with El-Sayed in Michigan last weekend, saying they wanted fighters like him to work alongside. Voters want people who have courage and aren’t afraid to stand up to Trump, but also aren’t afraid of losing their seat, Warren told the Guardian, so they’re committed to making meaningful change. “Remember, the Senate is actually a pretty small place. For Democrats to be in the majority, shoot, there’d only be 51 of us,” she said. “You bring us just a few more progressive fighters, and the whole tone of that place changes. We’re in the fight now. We’re pulling people over. It’s shifting, but bring us some new blood. Bring us some fighters. Bring us more energy into this. And watch what we can do.” El-Sayed is tapping into deep-seated anger among the electorate, like dysfunction in the healthcare system that allows insurers or AI programs to say whether a doctor-ordered test or medication could be covered, Warren said. “I think that’s going to connect with people who aren’t even part of the Democratic primary.” Van Hollen, the Maryland senator, said he thinks El-Sayed has a better chance of winning the general election because of his ability to mobilize and motivate voters, who see his campaign as not a simple test of left versus right, but about uniting against political corruption and concentrated economic power, a “much more universal” message. Washington is in a bubble, Van Hollen said, and too caught up in pundit-class chatter, but the general public is “way ahead” of Washington on upending politics as usual. The pre-Trump status quo wasn’t working either, he said. “Voters don’t vote for a convicted felon unless they’re really frustrated with the way things are,” Van Hollen said of Trump. “And he has changed the status quo in all the worst ways. We need to change the status quo in all of the best ways.” El-Sayed told the crowd at Green’s house that they all know how important they are as Michigan voters. Campaigns come to court them every other year, knowing that their status as swing-state voters gives them a coveted spot in deciding the direction not just of their state, but the country. And this election is no different. Think of what it would say to the country, to Congress, to other politicians, he said, if a campaign like his wins, “if a politics that opposes corporations, that takes on their power, that opposes sending our money elsewhere” wins in a place like Michigan. “Every single person thinking about running for president is going to be watching on November 3,” he said.

title: Republican senator calls for Max Miller to quit Congress amid abuse allegations
author: Marina Dunbar
summary: Senator Bernie Moreno says congressman and former son-in-law should step down after ex-wife’s allegations
body_text: The Republican senator Bernie Moreno on Sunday publicly called for Representative Max Miller, his ex son-in-law, to step down from Congress amid allegations of domestic and child abuse. As recently as Friday, the Ohio senator had avoided giving his opinion directly on accusations made by his daughter, Emily Moreno, against the congressman. “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them. He should not serve in the House of Representatives,” the Ohio senator wrote in a post on X on Sunday. “I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake. I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does.” Moreno also said he had hoped the situation would remain private but added that Miller’s “increasingly erratic and dangerous behavior has made that impossible”. The senator’s statement came hours after Miller released a live stream on Sunday morning denying allegations of domestic and child abuse and insisting he would remain in the race for re-election. The public appearance came ahead of Wednesday’s deadline to replace him on the ballot. “Just want to be clear: no court, no agency has ever substantiated any allegation of abuse against me. No criminal charge has ever been filed against me,” Miller said on the live stream. “Every single one of these allegations were already investigated, and I cooperated fully every single time because I had nothing to hide and I have nothing to hide now.” The statement follows allegations that Miller poured hot water on Emily Moreno, held a gun to her head and broke their toddler daughter’s collarbone. The accusations have intensified scrutiny of Ohio’s seventh congressional district race, with Democrats viewing the seat as a possible pickup while Republicans have largely remained silent so far. When asked on Friday by Notus whether Miller should continue his re-election campaign, Moreno responded, “I don’t know,” according to the outlet. Miller, 37, has denied allegations made by both his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and former girlfriend Stephanie Grisham, the former White House press secretary, as he continues his re-election campaign. Emily Moreno, a conservative policy adviser, shares a two-year-old daughter with Miller. The former couple has been involved in a custody dispute over their child since 2024. In his Sunday statement, Bernie Moreno said it had been “horrific” to witness the situation unfold in view of the public “all while knowing an innocent two-year-old girl is caught in the middle”. Among the allegations, Emily Moreno testified earlier this year in connection with a defamation lawsuit filed against her by Miller that he “took hot water from a pan he had just cooked eggs in and threw it at me”. She has also accused Miller of holding a gun to her head, according to the New York Times. The couple married in 2022.

title: RFK Jr tells US families to vaccinate children against measles amid outbreak
author: Ed Pilkington in New York
summary: Health secretary, longtime vaccination skeptic, spent years boosting misinformation about vaccines including MMR
body_text: Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, on Sunday told American parents that they should get their children vaccinated against measles, as the surge in infections has reached numbers not seen in the past 35 years. Kennedy, a leading vaccination skeptic who has spent years amplifying misinformation about vaccines, including the shot that protects against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), made his call in the course of a contentious interview with CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday morning. His remark came as the incidence of measles crossed a milestone – the US has now officially recorded 2,371 confirmed infections so far this year, surpassing 2025’s total tally of 2,289. Taken together, the past two years have seen more measles infections in the US than the rest of the 21st century combined. The last time a greater number of measles cases were recorded in a single year was in 1991. Kennedy’s statement was extracted from him by Dana Bash, CNN’s host, who invited him to use his “bully pulpit” to talk directly to parents as the new school year approached. She urged him to tell families that they should vaccinate for measles “because it is safe and it will help them save their children’s lives”. The health secretary replied: “Parents should get their children vaccinated for measles. A measles vaccine is effective, it stops measles in about 97% of the cases. People should get vaccinated.” Later in the interview he added that people should also get the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, the main protection against the disease that has been a particular target of the anti-vaccination movement. The health secretary’s call for parents to vaccinate their children for measles contrasts starkly with the many years in which Kennedy has been a leading proponent of misinformation questioning the efficacy and safety of vaccinations. Even since he became the country’s top health official, he has depicted a measles vaccination as a personal choice and claimed inaccurately that the power of the inoculation is waning. The call also comes late in the day, given the rate at which measles is spreading in the US. The 37 new measles outbreaks that have already been recorded this year are putting the US in danger of losing the measles elimination status that it has held since 2000. Kennedy continues to shrug off criticism that his work as a prominent vaccine skeptic, both before and after he entered the Trump administration, has exacerbated the problem. Asked whether he took any responsibility for the measles surge, he said: “Absolutely not.” He went on to blame the outbreaks on religious communities who eschew vaccines and on global health conditions. Any hope that Kennedy’s measles statement might indicate a change of heart were dashed in the rest of the CNN interview in which he turned combative. Batting off questions from Bash, the health secretary responded with personal attacks. He accused the CNN host of “saying nonsense”, “repeating like a parrot” and “making assertions you can’t support”. In one especially demeaning remark he said Bash had become “flustered”. “I’m not flustered at all,” she asserted in a calm voice. “I am frustrated because you are the HHS secretary and you are talking about things that lead to vaccine hesitancy in this country.” In a further comment dripping with condescension, Kennedy told Bash “you probably don’t understand this because you’re not a scientist”. The journalist riposted: “But you’re not, either.” The health secretary’s belligerent approach, in which he at times appeared red-faced while frequently poking his finger towards Bash, attracted the attention of commentators. The journalist Aaron Rupar described the performance as “RFK Jr’s epic CNN crashout” and said in a post on X that Kennedy’s “yelling” sounded like “a rabid dog barking”. Andy Kim, the Democratic US senator from New Jersey, took from Kennedy’s comments that he and Donald Trump had no plans to prepare for a possible next pandemic. “The only thing they have a plan for is trying to distract you from the fact that they’ve taken away healthcare from millions,” Kim said. Kennedy used the CNN exchange to spread further misinformation about other aspects of public health. He claimed that both respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) that is a major cause of infant mortality and Lyme disease were caused by manipulation of germs in laboratories. The suggestion has been contradicted by decades of scientific evidence that suggest they both have natural roots. RSV was initially identified in the 1950s, two decades before such experimentation, known as “gain-of-function” research, started. During the interview, Kennedy repeated unfounded claims that there was a link between Tylenol use during pregnancy and autism, and poured doubt on the efficacy of vaccines to protect children against Covid-19. Speaking to CNN’s State of the Union later in the show, Ashish Jha, who advised Joe Biden’s White House on its Covid response, said he was heartened to hear Kennedy say that “every kid in America should be getting the MMR vaccine”. But he added that much else of what the health secretary had said “just isn’t true”. Jha said that the dramatic rise in measles cases on Kennedy’s watch was not coincidental. “The administration has not done enough to promote vaccines. It has not done enough to highlight the harms that come from measles.”
