title: One Nation names eight Victorian election candidates as Hanson bars ABC and Guardian from press conferences
author: Benita Kolovos Victorian state correspondent
summary: Former Liberal, ‘anti-woke’ film animator and councillor who says he used to work on Daniel Andrews’ security team among lineup for November’s state poll
body_text: One Nation has named its first candidates for the upcoming Victorian state election, as the party leader, Pauline Hanson, has vowed to ban the ABC and the Guardian from attending her press conferences during the campaign. Guardian Australia understands reporters from the ABC and the Age were refused entry to Hanson’s press conference on Monday, where she announced seven of the eight candidates who will lead One Nation’s upper house tickets. The Age has been contacted for comment while the ABC declined to. Reporters from the ABC, the Age and the Guardian were not told the time or location of the event in advance. One Nation has previously said the ABC and the Guardian were not welcome at the party’s events and press conferences. Asked whether all media should have access to press conferences in a democracy, particularly given her ambition to form government in Victoria, Hanson replied: “Democracy doesn’t happen on the ABC at all.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email She said it was not the first time she had excluded the national broadcaster, claiming she denied ABC journalists access to her events for “eight months” in 1996. “The same will go with the Guardian,” she added. “I’m not putting up with the spin, gotcha moments, wanting to have a go at me … [and they] treat us totally different to what you do the other major political parties. Enough is enough.” In a later follow-up question, another reporter asked: “Aren’t you cutting off your nose to spite your face here? Don’t you need your message to get out to regional Victoria in particular, and you need the ABC, the national broadcaster to be able to carry it?” To which Hanson responded: “We’ve got Rebel News here, I am happy with them.” Rebel News Australia is run by Avi Yemini, a former Israeli soldier and self-styled investigative journalist. Warren Pickering, One Nation’s Victorian president, said the party “expect and invite a healthy amount of scrutiny of our candidates and our policy positions”. “However, any blatant character assassination attempts based on fabrications of our candidates will be met with swift legal action,” he told reporters. A Guardian spokesperson said it was “disappointing that One Nation continues to prevent the Guardian and other news outlets from reporting on its press conferences”. “Holding public figures to account is the role of a free press and an essential part of the democratic process,” they said. “Journalists should be able to ask questions in the public interest and not be deterred from doing their job.” They added that the Guardian has published important public interest journalism about Hanson and her party, which it stands by. Candidates announced In a media release prior to Monday’s press conference, Hanson announced Pickering would lead the party’s campaign and run as its candidate for the eastern Victoria region in the upper house. But at the event she said he would instead be running in the lower house seat of Pakenham, an ultra-marginal electorate southeast of Melbourne where One Nation has set up an office. Pickering ran One Nation’s campaign in the 2022 election, where it won 0.22% of first-preference votes in the lower house and 2% in the upper house. He also unsuccessfully contested a Victorian Senate seat for One Nation at last year’s federal election. But since then, the party has surged in the polls, with latest figures showing between 19 and 27% of Victorians are considering voting for One Nation. Colleen Harkin, a former member of the Liberal party’s administrative committee, will contest the south-eastern metropolitan region. Harkin quit the Liberal party in June to join One Nation. Harkin, who is the director of education at the conservative thinktank the Institute of Public Affairs, has been a vocal supporter of Moira Deeming and led a supreme court challenge against the Liberals’ decision to grant John Pesutto a $1.5m loan after he lost a defamation case against the MP. She drew controversy during the 2022 federal election campaign as the Liberal candidate for Macnamara when she said describing global warming as a climate emergency was “almost” child abuse. She also sought Liberal preselection for the neighbouring seat of Goldstein in 2024 but lost to Tim Wilson. Mark Nicholson, co-founder of animation house Stepmates Studios – which creates Hanson’s cartoon web series Please Explain and her satirical, “anti-woke” movie – will stand in the northern metropolitan region, while Geelong councillor and former police officer, Chris Burson, will contest western Victoria. Burson, who also has served with the Australian Defence Force, ran unsuccessfully for the Angry Victorians Party at the 2022 state election and the Australian Values party at the 2022 federal election. He told a podcast in June he worked with the close personal protection team guarding then premier Daniel Andrews and his wife, Catherine, as they faced increased threats during the pandemic. “We’d be sitting there kitted up, ready to go in case there was an attack. You’d have your guns ready, you were in your vest,” Burson said. “You’d be like, ‘how do we have six [counter-terrorism officers] looking after him and two people looking after the city of Melbourne?” One Nation’s only current MP, Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell, will seek re-election in northern Victoria, while Fiona Lopez, Aaron Sandford and Natalie Adams will head the party’s tickets in the western metropolitan, southern metropolitan and north eastern metropolitan regions. With Pickering running in the lower house, it remains unclear who will contest the eastern Victoria region for the party. Monday’s announcement comes after new Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, introduced legislation to parliament last week that will scrap group voting tickets (GVTs). The change means if One Nation maintains its current polling, the upper house candidates in the number one spot on each ticket are the party’s most likely prospects to win seats. But Hanson said One Nation will be fielding candidates in every seat at the election, with the party to release policies in coming weeks. She also said Yemini should “take credit” for the decision to scrap GVTs, after he registered the“Free Palestine party” earlier this year, with the intention to funnel votes to conservative parties.

title: Are Trump’s most blatant authoritarian moves backfiring?
author: Jan-Werner Müller
summary: The president’s methods, from ‘flooding the zone’ with scandals to prioritizing loyalty over competence, could ultimately weaken rather than strengthen him
body_text: The pattern is by now all too familiar: with every power grab Trump tries – from a fraudulent speech about voter fraud to appeals to his supreme court to let him rig the midterms – a debate kicks off about whether these moves are signs of strength or of desperation. Maybe we keep getting caught in this debate because the question is badly posed. So much of what is distinctive about Trump’s governance during his second term can serve the consolidation of an autocratic regime and at the same time create particular vulnerabilities for the regime. We have to become better at identifying these weaknesses, as opposed to being shellshocked by Trump’s brazenness every single time. Aspiring autocrats operate differently in the 21st century; in previous eras, they had little hesitation about unleashing violence and committing massive human rights violations. Today, they try to fool both domestic and international audiences into thinking that democracy and the rule of law still exist. The recently deposed Hungarian prime minister, Viktor Orbán, was a master of this technique; he spent many years performing what he called “the peacock dance” to convince the European Commission (and Chancellor Angela Merkel) that he wasn’t creating a kleptocratic autocracy. This contrast between what the social scientists Serguei Guriev and Daniel Treisman have called “fear dictatorships” on the one hand and “spin dictatorships” on the other is empirically proven: there really is less violence, according to Guriev and Treisman, than in the 20th century. But elaborate efforts to fake democracy do not change the fact that violence is always kept in reserve: Putin dropped the mask entirely in 2022 and now has no hesitation to be seen as the violence-prone dictator who in one sense he always was. It is crucial to understand how Trump differs from these patterns: unlike Orbán, for instance, he was never constrained by international institutions and other powerful capitals (let alone “international public opinion” – even mentioning the term in as self-centered a country as the US seems faintly ridiculous). What’s more, his own modus operandi, from his early days as a New York real estate investor onwards, has always been to simply do things that everyone can see are illegal – the point is to create facts on the ground (think of the demolition of the East Wing) and hope that the other side will settle out of court or just live with a fait accompli. This method (strategy might be too big of a word) of illegality – and hope for impunity – now characterizes almost the entire administration. More particularly, the Trumpists have figured out that a scandal per year can spell political death, while 10 scandals a day elicit hardly a shrug, because no one, it seems, can keep up. This “flooding the zone” with scandals is in itself a means of generating power – but it also creates vulnerabilities. One never knows whether one scandal – even a relatively harmless one like the reflecting pool disaster, combining grift and incompetence – might not focus the public’s attention after all and become a symbol for the corruption of the regime as a whole, the way that one child abuse scandal – an Orbán ally pardoned a man convicted of covering up abuse – became the symbol of everything wrong with Orbán’s rule. Every aspiring autocrat faces a trade-off between loyalty and competence. It is no secret where Trumpists have tended to be placed on the spectrum. That total devotion to the leader – including the willingness to lie shamelessly, or at least engage in election denial, as a de facto loyalty oath to Trump sworn in public – can consolidate power. But it also creates a distinct vulnerability, as, sooner or later, the egregiously incompetent will produce terrible outcomes, plain for all to see (at least if an effective opposition party manages to make them plain to see). Contrary to the tendency of today’s dictators shying away from violence – so as not needlessly to invoke memories of 20th-century authoritarianism and provoke resistance – Trumpists have made a spectacle of cruelty. Again, this can contribute to consolidating power – after all, the glaring impunity apparently enjoyed by the men who killed Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero sends a signal that loyalists can count themselves above the law. The spectacle might also please a Maga audience. But the fact is that, in the end, the ostentatious displays of cruelty have not been popular with the public at large. For now, the administration increases its power by effectively telling people “We can do whatever we want, and you can’t do anything!” But making cruelty a priority also creates images that can be turned against it. And the shameless corruption? Again, the shamelessness might easily generate a sense of hopelessness on the part of Americans watching unprecedented acts of malfeasance. But, unlike with other aspiring autocrats, the Trumpists are not really creating a coherent system of self-enrichment (the way Orbán did with what came to be called his mafia state – where tricks with public procurement were disguised well enough for many years). Under Trump, everyone just grabs whatever they can as quickly as they can. That inability to build a system is ultimately a sign of weakness; the Trumpists themselves do not really seem to believe that their rule will last, and what Mike Johnson, in a revealing moment, called the Republicans’ “protection program” – the majority in Congress – might be gone this year. Self-confident creators of autocratic kleptocracy would have stayed silent on the point – and been smarter in their approach altogether. To be sure, that is no consolation for victims of cruelty. Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton University

title: Will Missouri be the next primary win for a democratic socialist challenger?
author: Chris Stein in St Louis, Missouri
summary: Voters face a choice of progressive ex-congresswoman Cori Bush or pro-Israel incumbent Wesley Bell on Tuesday
body_text: The pastor of a historically Black church on St Louis’s north side, Rodrick Burton, has watched with bewilderment as the congressional race in his district has drawn national attention not about the bloodshed in his community, but rather in Gaza. “As a pastor who’s had eight members murdered, violence over there is terrible,” Burton said of the conflict in the Middle East. “We have to deal with the problems right in our metropolitan area,” Burton added. “While there’s kinship and stuff … you’re talking about blood overseas, blood on the TV. We got blood right here in our metropolitan area.” In Tuesday’s Democratic congressional primary, voters in Missouri’s deep-blue first congressional district will decide whether to give pro-Israel incumbent Wesley Bell a second term, or replace him with Cori Bush, a former progressive congresswoman who accuses Israel of perpetrating genocide in Gaza. Along with a heated primary in Michigan, the contest has become a proxy battle over the Democratic party’s role in supporting Israel’s military before the November midterm elections, which will determine which party holds the majority in both chambers of Congress. After losing to Bell two years ago, Bush, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, is vying for her seat back, and a Super Pac linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) has so far spent more than $3m to try to keep her out. In recent weeks, Democratic voters in New York City and Denver ousted incumbents in favor of candidates who promised they would take a hard line against support for Israel. In Congress, large shares of Democrats have voted for unsuccessful efforts to block arms sales to the country’s security forces, and progressives hope that a win by Bush will underscore their movement’s momentum. “I think her victory this cycle would be monumental,” said Usamah Andrabi, a spokesperson for Justice Democrats, which has long supported Bush and backed several of the other insurgents who ousted Democrats in recent primaries, though it is not channeling funds into the campaign this year. “We haven’t had a lot of cycles to try this out, but this would be the first time that we would be able to take a seat back from Aipac after they bought one and deliver it back to working-class people.” African Americans make up about half of the district’s population, and Burton said some draw parallels between their history in the United States, and how Palestinians have been treated in Israel. Others’ views have been affected by conflicts with Palestinian shopowners in predominantly Black neighborhoods, said Burton, who hopes that whoever wins does not forget the community’s needs. “It’s caused a level of divisiveness that really we don’t need in our community, in the light of what the African American community is dealing with, with the Trump administration and the various policies. We really don’t need these type of hard divisions and bitter feelings,” Burton said. Ubiquitous ads Elected in 2020 after beating long-serving incumbent William Lacy Clay, Bush was a member of “the Squad”, the informal grouping of progressive lawmakers of color that also included congresswomen Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar. Following the 7 October attack, Bush was one of the earliest and most forceful objectors in Congress against Israel’s counterattack in Gaza, staking positions on which many other Democrats were hesitant to join even as it became clear that Joe Biden’s support for Israel was complicating both his and, later, Kamala Harris’s campaign to keep Donald Trump out of power. It also put her in the crosshairs of Aipac, with the group and its allies spending heavily to unseat both Bush and New York Democratic congressman Jamaal Bowman. In an interview, Bush said their defeats changed how her party thought about Israel, and how they voted on issues like the Massie amendment, a recent proposal in the House of Representatives to block some military aid to Israel that failed, but only after receiving votes from nearly half of the Democratic caucus. “If Jamaal and I would still be in Congress, we’d still be voting no on some of these bills, and … people would just be going on as if Aipac was not still influencing elections,” Bush said. “I credit the fact that we didn’t stop, that we grew the coalition, and then having the loss grew the coalition even more.” Bell and Bush can both trace their political journeys to the unrest in the St Louis suburb of Ferguson following the 2014 police killing of Michael Brown. Bush was an activist in the protests that followed, while Bell unseated the longtime St Louis county prosecutor after promising voters he would reopen the case of the police officer who killed Brown, but ultimately decided not to charge him. “The people in St Louis, they want someone that cares,” said Maria Miller, a Democratic candidate for state legislature who met Bush during the protests in Ferguson. “And once you betray them from that trust, it becomes like a war, because they’re very combative, and I just don’t feel that Wesley Bell’s earned that trust.” Though international conflict overshadows the race, both candidates have made prominent campaign promises to counter Trump, help the city and county recover from a deadly tornado last year and reverse years of divestment and high crime. While polling in the race is scarce, Bell is the clear leader in fundraising, having brought in $3.5m, for his own campaign in addition to the support from the Aipac-linked Super Pac United Democracy Project. Ads from his campaign and his supporters are ubiquitous in the district, with Bell making his case that Bush was an ineffective lawmaker, citing her no vote on Biden’s 2021 infrastructure legislation, as well as a comment where she appeared to accuse both Biden and Harris of “fascism”. Bush has responded that she voted against the infrastructure bill because it did not include additional social spending Biden had promised voters, and that the “fascism” comment was taken out of context. Each candidate has accused the other of corruption, with Bush noting protesters arrested at a town hall the congressman held last year have sued him and his security guards for allegedly assaulting them. Bell has seized on reports that Bush is paying her husband with campaign funds to provide security, and noted the justice department investigated her while she was in Congress. She has denied any wrongdoing. In an interview, Bell emphasized he could not coordinate or control the spending by outside Pacs. He describes Israel as an ally worth supporting alongside Ukraine, Taiwan and western Europe, and said he opposed the Massie amendment as “more of a show, as opposed to serious public policy”. “I’m not a fan of Netanyahu, but I think it’s important to stand with all of our allies,” he said. Bell rejected the idea that the trends that unseated 30-year incumbent Diana DeGette in Denver, or Adriano Espaillat in New York, chair of the congressional Hispanic caucus, would oust him next: “What happens in New York is not the same as what’s on the ground in Texas, is not the same as what’s happening in Wisconsin, and it’s not the same in St Louis.” Sean Fauss, the chair of St Louis City Democrats, acknowledged the potency of concerns about Israel, but said Bush had made significant errors during her two terms. “I have my differences with Congressman Bell on that very issue,” Fauss said of the congressman’s views on Israel. “But I’m not going to support a candidate who made speaker Pelosi have to count on Republican votes in order to get President Biden’s infrastructure bill across the line, and that’s what Cori Bush did.” Russell Gunn, a Democratic former state lawmaker who is supporting neither candidate, warned that the Aipac-linked spending was “a liability” for Bell because of the controversy surrounding it. “But I don’t think it’s a big enough liability that he’s going to lose the election,” he said. “It helps him in some areas, and it hurts him in others.” ‘Because of Trump’ Bush’s campaign has raised a comparatively small $1.3m, and is going without the assistance of Justice Democrats’ Pac, which spent $2m trying to keep her in office in 2024. Andrabi said the group’s “limited set of resources” and long list of candidates it is backing has kept it from spending on Bush. On an uncomfortably hot afternoon, 22-year-old Alec Martirez joined a small group of volunteers for Bush who went knocking at the doors of voters in the leafy suburb of Maplewood, which had only recently been added to the district after Missouri’s Republican leaders redrew their maps to oust the state’s only other House Democrat. A former co-chair of the Young Democratic Socialists of America at the University of Missouri, Martirez had hosted Bush on the campus, and was drawn to her views on Israel after watching the invasion of Gaza play out over social media. “I just thought that was unacceptable that somewhere halfway across the world there was a genocide taking place with money that I was giving my federal government here,” he said. A few days prior, Bush and Bell had met for a combative debate on St Louis Public Radio, where Bell had pressed his challenger on the allegations of financial mismanagement. When Martirez knocked on the door of a white brick home, the woman who answered said she’d watched the encounter hoping to hear an explanation from Bush. “She didn’t satisfy my concerns and I’m pretty sensitive about that right now because of Trump,” said the woman, who did not want to give her name but said she had cast an early ballot for Bell. The views were reversed further down the block, when Katie Davies, 44, emerged on to her porch and declared she was ready to vote for Bush, saying she didn’t feel Bell had done enough to help the city recover from the tornado and found Aipac’s involvement in the district’s politics unseemly. “Blind support for Aipac candidates is not leading us to anything,” she said. As he walked away, Martirez pulled up an app on his phone that allowed him to track which houses he had visited and how they were leaning. “I think I’ll mark her down as a supporter,” he said.

title: First Thing: Trump promises new Iran talks as Tehran touts Hormuz shipping deal with Oman
author: Martin Belam
summary: US president says he called off another US attack on Iran as part of a push for an agreement. Plus why Pokémon Go is still bring global joy 10 years on
body_text: Good morning. Donald Trump said talks with Iran would happen on Monday but declined to set a deadline for an agreement, after earlier saying he had called ⁠off an imminent attack. For its part, Iran said it was nearing a deal with Oman over a new route through the strait of Hormuz, and it had no plans to receive a delegation or send an Iranian one to any talks. On Saturday night, Trump claimed on social media that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for time to complete a deal ⁠that would lead to “the immediate, complete and total” reopening of the strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”. He added that Tehran must “rapidly make a deal”. What has Iran said about the strait? The Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baqaei, told state television on Sunday that a deal was close with Oman over a new route through the waterway. “We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides – neither the northern route nor the southern route – but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security,” he said in an interview. RFK Jr tells US families to vaccinate children against measles amid outbreak Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, on Sunday told American parents that they should get their children vaccinated against measles, as the surge in infections has reached numbers not seen in the past 35 years. Kennedy, a leading vaccination skeptic who has spent years amplifying misinformation about vaccines, including the shot that protects against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), made his call in the course of a contentious interview with CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday morning. How many measles cases has the US seen? His remark came as the incidence of measles crossed a milestone – the US has officially recorded 2,371 confirmed infections so far this year, surpassing the total tally in 2025 of 2,289. Taken together, in the past two years there have been more measles infections in the US than in the rest of the 21st century combined. The last time a greater number of measles cases was recorded in a single year was in 1991. Republican calls for Max Miller to resign from Congress after abuse allegations The Republican senator Bernie Moreno on Sunday publicly called for Representative Max Miller, his former son-in-law, to step down from Congress amid allegations of domestic and child abuse. As recently as Friday, the Ohio senator had avoided giving his opinion directly on accusations made by his daughter Emily Moreno against the congressman. The senator’s statement came hours after Miller gave a live stream Sunday morning denying allegations of domestic and child abuse and insisting he would remain in the race for re-election. The public appearance came before Wednesday’s deadline to replace him on the ballot. “Just want to be clear: no court, no agency has ever substantiated any allegation of abuse against me. No criminal charge has ever been filed against me,” Miller said on the live stream. Family to sue after woman released from ICE custody froze to death The family of a Haitian immigrant who froze to death in early March at a bus shelter in Pittsburgh after she was dropped off in the city by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is poised to file a lawsuit this month against the US and “multiple other governmental and non-governmental entities”, the Guardian has learned. Daphy Michel, 31, had been in county jail for six months after a reported mental health crisis and street incident, and then was arrested by ICE before being released with an ankle monitor. In other news … Eastern Washington fires have destroyed 600 structures and forced 60,000 people to evacuate, stretching the ability of federal and local agencies to fight the blazes. The chaos of a mass border crossing has given way to limbo for Moroccans on the streets of Ceuta, the Spanish colonial enclave in northern Africa. Marcy Kaptur is being treated ⁠for non-life-threatening injuries after a car crash in Toledo, ⁠Ohio, on Sunday, ⁠the Democratic US representative’s office said. The suspect in an Idaho restaurant shooting that killed three people died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound, police said. Pressure on the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, to step down has increased as members of Europe’s footballing authority Uefa prepare to oppose his re-election. Stat of the day: Spider-Man: Brand New Day makes debut to $927m box office The Marvel Studios president, Kevin Feige, has hailed the movie’s “phenomenal” opening – the second biggest opening weekend in history – which followed a box office already buoyed up by The Odyssey and Toy Story 5. Building Power: How free childcare started winning US elections Sunny Patel reports for the Guardian’s Building Power series on Francesca Hong, a candidate for Wisconsin governor, who is part of a wave of democratic socialists finding traction with an old idea. Don’t miss this: ‘The language of Pokémon is universal’: why fans are still catching ‘em all I originally started playing Pokémon Go as a going out activity with my children. Ten years later, they have (mostly) put away childish things, but I still play it every day without fail. In this lovely piece, Sammy Gecsoyler speaks to devoted players who explain how the game has created a vibrant intergenerational community spanning the globe. … or this: Hide the Pain Harold and Rubik’s Cube creator among social media’s picks for Hungarian president Péter Magyar and his newly elected Tisza party asked the public to put forward names for the next president of Hungary, which is resetting its politics after years of being dominated by the rightwing populist Viktor Orbán. The suggestions have ranged from the sensible to the downright bizarre. Climate check: ‘Stop all outdoor activities’ – South Korea records its highest ever temperature South Korea has registered its highest temperature since records began more than a century ago, at 42.5C, as authorities warned people to immediately stop all outdoor activities in affected areas. London’s Kew Gardens has gone without rain for a whole month for the first time in history, as Europe continues to battle a heatwave. Two firefighting helicopters have collided west of Athens, killing the two-person crew of one of the aircraft, as efforts to control a massive wildfire barrelling towards the outskirts of the Greek capital intensified. Last Thing: ‘The greatest arms I’ve ever seen’: Matt Damon’s muscular female stunt double Devyn Dalton A 35-year-old stuntwoman is one of the great unsung heroes of Christopher Nolan’s new blockbuster The Odyssey – standing in for Matt Damon and displaying what the actor called “the greatest arms I’ve ever seen”. Canadian Devyn Dalton was the Hollywood star’s stunt double in a pivotal scene. Olivia Bowden spoke to her. Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. title: Lawmakers push for a more robust Epstein Files Transparency Act – but would Trump sign it?
author: Victoria Bekiempis
summary: After the justice department botched file rollout under the original act, lawmakers now want legislation with teeth
body_text: As Jeffrey Epstein survivors and their supporters continue searching for justice and transparency in the US, a bipartisan group of politicians is trying to rework legislation that heralded the release of long-hidden investigative files on the scandal. While the Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA), signed into law by Donald Trump on 19 November, mandated that the justice department release all investigative files within 30 days with limited exceptions, survivors and their supporters have repeatedly grappled with missed deadlines and what they say are incomplete disclosures. They have also accused the justice department of disclosing survivors’ personal information while withholding names of men involved in Epstein’s sexual abuse of teenage girls and young women. So now politicians from the Senate and the House and both main political parties announced on 15 July the introduction of the Epstein Files Transparency Act II (EFTA II). The planned law addresses what legal observers and public records advocates have described as shortfalls in the original EFTA – namely, the lack of a robust enforcement mechanism. Under the EFTA II, state attorneys general, local district attorneys, Epstein survivors and Congress members would have standing to fight the justice department in court if it doesn’t release files as required. If the proposed legislation becomes law, survivors would also have the right to “full, unredacted records concerning themselves or the harm they suffered”, including transcripts of FBI interviews. The justice department would also have to provide “state and local prosecutors with unredacted records needed for investigations, prosecutions and judicial proceedings, including secure access to classified materials”. The EFTA II would also “enforce compliance with the existing law by subjecting [justice department] and FBI officials to existing federal criminal penalties for knowingly concealing, destroying, falsifying, withholding or misrepresenting files”, supporters said. Legal veterans say this proposed law does have the potential to foster transparency, but noted that practical issues remain. Not only does this bill face political hurdles to actually pass into law, but – if it does – record seekers would also have to deal with the same justice department necessitating it in the first place. Oleg Nekritin, an attorney with the Law Offices of Robert J De Groot, said that the EFTA was a “pretty robust bill” enabling state attorneys general to get records they demand. “Under the first Epstein Files Transparency Act, people were permitted to search for various records, but people criticized those specific records, because a lot of them were redacted, they were difficult to read, and critics said they didn’t even disclose individuals who may have been involved … in various criminal acts,” Nekritin said. This bill, Nekritin explained, grants state attorneys general access to unredacted records. “If they aren’t provided access by the US attorney’s office, they’re permitted to file actions.” Nekritin noted that many state attorneys general think that the Trump administration has acted unlawfully in a variety of areas. With Epstein, “they may believe that the United States government isn’t taking sufficient steps to investigate or prosecute obscene crimes”. So if state attorneys general can get all records, “they may do their own investigations, follow leads, etc”. He also noted that survivors will have access to records that involve them. “If passed, it will be a gamechanger for individuals who want to investigate further or learn more about Epstein or individuals associated with them.” Carl Tobias, Williams chair in law at the University of Richmond School of Law, said his “first thought” was: “Can it pass?” “Can they move it in the House or maybe even more difficult, in the Senate?” Tobias said that if House members can convince their colleagues to greenlight the bill, there would still need to be 60 Senate votes. Then the question remains: would Trump sign it? Tobias noted many of the lawmakers publicly behind the bill have long been committed to transparency and describe its intent as a good idea. They include the Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie, California Democrat Ro Khanna, New Mexico Democrat Teresa Leger Fernández, Oregon Democrat Jeff Merkley and New Mexico Democrat Ben Ray Luján “They’re very dissatisfied with what happened at [the justice department], and so I think they want to provide avenues for victims and for state attorneys general to bring [the justice department] into court and try to bring more transparency.” Roy Gutterman, director of the Newhouse School’s Tully Center for Free Speech at Syracuse University, said: “This bill amends the existing law and has more teeth with authorizing a state attorney general and victims to litigate for release of the materials. “It has specific terms, definitions and expectations that the US attorney general, upon request from a state AG or victim, would turn over the wealth of materials that have remained withheld for more than a year,” he also said. But Gutterman warned: “If the [justice department] drags its feet or refuses to turn over the unredacted materials, I am not sure another law will dramatically change delays or outright refusals we’ve seen for the past year.” The news website Radar Online, which has long been pursuing a public records lawsuit over access to investigative files, called this effort “a step in the right direction”. But a Radar spokesperson said: “The entire American public already has a private right of action: Foia” – the Freedom of Information Act. “The fastest way to achieve true transparency would be to support Radar Online’s nine-year quest for the Epstein Files.” Backers of this bill are confident that it will force the justice department to comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act. This bill “strengthens the enforcement of the original law, which is only necessary because Trump’s Department of Justice refuses to comply with it”, Merkley said. “No one is above the law, and EFTA II ensures that even Trump and his crony, acting attorney general Todd Blanche, can’t stop the truth from coming to light. And if Blanche continues to side with the Epstein class instead of the victims of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes, then he has no business serving as our nation’s chief law enforcement officer,” Merkley said in a statement. Luján voiced similar sentiments. In a statement he said: “With the Trump Department of Justice refusing to comply [with] the law, we must empower state attorneys general and victims to challenge this Department of Justice for failing to provide the transparency and accountability that Epstein’s victims deserve.” The Department of Justice did not respond to a request for comment on the bill or criticism over disclosures. Trump, who made releasing the Epstein files a key tenet of his campaign, has defended his administration’s handling of the issue. Trump has denied any and all wrongdoing in relation to Epstein. “Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein,” a White House spokesperson, Abigail Jackson, said in a statement. “And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House oversight committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him.”

title: The right’s exploitation of the Ceuta migrant ‘crisis’ almost guarantees that it will happen again
author: Ruben Andersson
summary: The EU’s panic and the lack of solidarity emboldens smugglers and the far right – and makes Spain even more vulnerable, says Ruben Andersson, professor of social anthropology
body_text: For the European hard right and the White House, it seemed almost too good to be true: left-liberal Spain punished with a migration crisis of its own making. The histrionics came right on cue. As thousands of mainly Moroccan citizens streamed into the tiny Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the tip of north Africa, Spain’s far-right party Vox decried a migrant “invasion”, blaming Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s regularisation and leftist politics. The Trump administration did the same. A senior Israeli diplomat goaded Madrid over its “colonial” territories while Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area. Denmark and Finland backed Italy’s move and, by the weekend, 22 EU leaders had penned a letter pointing an implicit finger at Madrid over its presumed failure to “relentlessly combat illegal migration”. But what these self-ascribed doyens of border control don’t want to understand is that it’s their panic and politicking over migration that has brought us here. Ceuta is hardly a poster-child for Spain’s otherwise liberal migration policy. Rather, since the 1990s it has been the prototype for Europe’s relentless border security battle. Drones, heat detectors, motion sensors, digital watchtowers, Moroccan Auxiliary Forces: Ceuta’s border is so thoroughly militarised that it puts even Trump’s barrier-building – let alone that of Greece, Poland or Finland – to shame. The paradox, as civil guards told me when I last visited in 2023, was that this militarisation had involved ceding control. “Rabat knows it can destabilise Spain with migration,” one chief said, as he reflected on the mass entry of Moroccans in 2021, after Madrid had angered its partner by taking in Brahim Ghali, the leader of Western Sahara’s Polisario movement, for urgent healthcare. The heavily guarded fences have become a perfect foil for staging a migration crisis. While Morocco is usually tight-lipped about its intentions, at times its ministers have bluntly said it won’t play the “gendarme” of Europe unless its partners support its economic and political aims. The quiet at the border since 2021 had little to do with the aggressive security hardware, and everything to do with Madrid’s 2022 endorsement of Rabat’s plan for occupied Western Sahara. So why the latest crisis? While the facts and motives are still being established, it’s unlikely to be a coincidence that, only recently, Sánchez announced a “new phase” in relations with Algeria – Rabat’s arch-rival and supporter of Polisario. Sánchez blames the mass entry on people smugglers and misinformation about a recent Spanish supreme court ruling that prevents authorities from summarily expelling migrants who attempt to swim by sea to Spain’s territories in Africa. The official line from Morocco’s government is that the surge was due to “criminal organisations” and that cooperation with Spain is still “exemplary”. Yet blaming criminal organisations makes little sense: most of those who made it across were quietly returned within the day – unthinkable, if they had lost their life savings to pay smugglers. The social media rumour mill did mobilise people to cross; but crucially – according to Spanish intelligence – Moroccan law enforcement stopped controlling the border while its intelligence services failed to notify Spain about the online campaigns. Video clips and accounts from border crossers in numerous media outlets further suggest that law enforcement actively encouraged people to cross. It’s clear to anyone who knows the Ceuta border that nothing dramatic happens there without the Moroccan authorities letting it happen. Yet Spain is unable to call out Morocco as it desperately depends on it. Instead, both Madrid and Brussels showered Rabat with praise this past week. This is the corner the EU has painted itself into: dependent on repressive and often undemocratic regimes that use migration threats for their own purposes. This has been a favoured tactic for years across the external EU borders, from Muammar Gaddafi’s threats to Ankara’s antics. And it’s all the more attractive to them thanks to the European obsession about unwanted migration – the higher the stakes, the bigger the rewards. The geopolitics are looking unfavourable to the EU. Since the Abraham accords were signed in 2020, Morocco has strengthened its hand internationally through close alliances with the Trump and Netanyahu administrations. And those two governments see Spain as their arch-foe in Europe. This January, Rabat deepened its military cooperation with Israel. In April, a US House of Representatives committee stated that Ceuta and the other Spanish enclave of Melilla were “in Moroccan territory”. Israeli and Republican figures have made increasingly frequent noises of this kind. Recently, Morocco named a highway through Western Sahara after Trump. What all this points to is not necessarily some grand conspiracy. Rabat may well have sought to benefit opportunistically and then lost control of events. But it does suggest that what occurred in Ceuta was a geopolitical game with people as its pawns, leaving more than 70 dead. European leaders have become so obsessed with “security” that they can’t see their own best interests clearly. Notably, one of the governments waving the threat of Schengen suspension was Denmark, which should know something about geopolitical blackmail against Europe. Coercive migration pressure, evidence shows, works best when destination regions are politically divided and prone to slanging matches. This is exactly what the far right and government leaders are now indulging as they nervously blame Spain and raise the spectre of another 2015 migration crisis. Having shown their hand to “partner” states and unfriendly regimes alike, these leaders will know exactly which button to push for maximum impact. Through their reaction, EU politicians are not only undermining European solidarity – they are actively encouraging more crisis-generation, while abetting the anti-European forces in the White House and further afield. We need a different kind of migration politics that de-escalates panic instead of inviting it, that prioritises frank diplomacy over one-eyed “combat”, and that weakens the hand of hardmen and smugglers. European leaders could make a start on shifting this dynamic by not turning themselves into useful idiots at the first opportunity. • Ruben Andersson is professor of social anthropology at the University of Oxford and author of Age of Security: The Rise of a Global Obsession (William Collins) out 13th August Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here.

title: Kay Granger, first Texas Republican woman elected to House, dies aged 83
author: Richard Luscombe and agencies
summary: Representative who did not seek re-election in 2024 died of Alzheimer’s disease, her son said
body_text: Kay Granger, who served in the US House for almost three decades as the first elected Republican woman from Texas, died on Sunday, her family said. She was 83. The cause of death, according to her son JD Granger, was Alzheimer’s disease. It was revealed in 2024 after questions about a prolonged absence from Washington DC that Granger had “dementia issues” and was living in a care home – a development her office did not disclose for months, the New York Times reported. Mike Johnson, the Republican US House speaker, posted a tribute to the veteran lawmaker on X on Sunday, recalling “her extraordinary life of service and lasting legacy” and describing her as a dear friend. “Kay Granger devoted her life to serving her Fort Worth, Texas, community,” Johnson wrote. “Throughout her career, she broke barriers for women in public service,” Johnson said, before highlighting how she “was the first woman to serve as mayor of Fort Worth, the first Republican woman elected to represent Texas in the House of Representatives, and the first Republican woman to chair the House appropriations committee”. Born in January 1943, Norvell Kay Granger was a high school teacher and businesswoman before entering politics. She was mayor of Fort Worth from 1991 to 1995 and was elected to the House in Texas’s 12th congressional district the following year. She was the ranking member of the powerful House appropriations committee until her party won back control of the chamber in 2022 – then served as its chair until April 2024. In all, she won 14 successive elections in her district, winning 92% of the votes in 2002. She did not seek re-election in 2024 and, according to her office, experienced worsening “health challenges” during and after her final months in Congress. After casting her final vote in July 2024, Granger largely disappeared from the public eye. A reporter with the Dallas Express began to dig into where Granger was after finding calls to her offices redirected to voicemail – and found few signs of a physical presence at her constituency office. The reporter, Carlos Turcios, eventually received a tip from a local resident that Granger had moved into an assisted living center specializing in memory care. The revelation forced her office to release a statement in December 2024 that said she had been navigating “unforeseen health challenges that have progressed since September and made travel to DC difficult”. In an interview with the Hill in 2008, Granger said her separation and eventual divorce from her husband reshaped her pathway and helped strengthen her into an advocate for women. “I was a high school teacher with three children, a two-year-old and six-month-old twins, and my husband left,” she said. “It’s the reason I talk so much to working mothers. “You just fight your way through the day.” As Fort Worth mayor, she introduced citizen patrol initiatives that halved a rampant crime rate. She also secured partnerships with the private sector that drew major businesses to the city. Her resuscitation of Fort Worth’s flagging economic fortunes drew national attention. In 1996, she was recruited by both parties to run for the House under their banner, and she won as a Republican. Upon entering Congress, she was named to an advisory board to the then House speaker, Newt Gingrich. She also received seats on three committees: budget, oversight, and transportation and infrastructure. She resigned from those assignments when she accepted a seat on the appropriations committee. As chair, she sought to enact steeper non-defense spending cuts than the top-line numbers agreed to between another former Republican speaker, Kevin McCarthy, and then-president Joe Biden as part of a plan to avoid a government default. Granger was originally a vocal critic of Donald Trump, demanding he step down as a Republican candidate for the 2016 presidential election that vaulted him to his first presidency. She called his comments against women “disgusting”. By 2020, she had a change of heart, endorsing Trump for re-election and earning his endorsement in return The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Author of Democrats’ 2024 election autopsy report says chapter was left out
author: Edward Helmore
summary: Paul Rivera says missing section included questions on Biden’s decision to run for re-election, the Times reports
body_text: The author of an infamous internal Democratic party report on the 2024 presidential election loss has claimed that an entire section that included a discussion of generational wealth established by high-ranking elected officials was cut from the draft version leaked and later released earlier this summer. Paul Rivera, the author of the autopsy, told the New York Times that a section titled “What Happened in 2024” was missing from the published version but had been included in the version he personally handed to embattled party chairman, Ken Martin, in January. The Democratic National Committee has previously claimed the autopsy had been released “in its entirety”. Rivera said that elements of the report that were excised included questions about Joe Biden’s decision to run for re-election and the policy influence of Democratic party operatives who had become “generationally wealthy off politics”. While the chapter did not name those who had become enriched he wrote that Democrats seeking change “keep banging their heads up against a system proven to be inflexible and self-enriching. “Whether that was a conscious decision on their part to bury the section for the purposes of hiding a paragraph, I don’t know,” Rivera told the Times. “That’s a them question. What I can tell you is they had it, and they made a decision not to release it.” Martin disputed that account in statement to the paper, saying “this alleged report section was not in any binder I reviewed”. Had it been included, he added, “we would have released it with the rest of the report.” The report was released in May to resounding disappointment that it had failed to address why the party, or its two presidential candidates, Biden and later Vice-President Kamala Harris, had failed to gain sufficient traction to win against Donald Trump. The missing chapter, provided by Rivera and published in full by the Times, states that Democratic wins before the election led the party “to believe they were stronger than they actually were. President Biden, seeing those results, made the consequential decision to seek re-election even when Americans were already sending a very strong signal: they were unhappy with the status quo.” The report said that Democrats had failed to do enough to convince voters that Trump was an unacceptable candidate and made wrong assumptions about Latino and male voters. It pointed to successful Democratic candidates in swing states who concentrated on economic and cost-of-living messaging more than identity politics. The Democratic party now heads into the midterm elections in November and the 2028 presidential election with a significant $2m cash deficit while the Republican party nationally reports a positive balance over $128m. A recent supreme court decision indicates that the cash gap could widen. Among the topics Rivera attempted to address in the disputed “What Happened” chapter were entries about Biden’s decision to seek re-election; a loss of support among Hispanic, Black, Asian American and Native American voters; and the issue of party officials and consultants being insulated or divorced from voters’ concerns by wealth. “It is therefore possible the people ‘in the room’ at the highest levels of 2024 decision making misunderstood the mood and practicalities facing everyday America,” Rivera wrote, according to the missing section. “They missed important signals about why people were frustrated with Democrats, who seemed not to appreciate or understand their situation.” The Times report may now set off a new round of questions about its direction as Democratic primary voters head to the polls in Michigan on Tuesday to choose between moderate and progressive Senate candidates Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed. Martin said the party would have released the disputed or missing chapter “that went after self-enriching consultants” if it had had them and that he personally had campaigned for the party chairmanship “to hold the consultant-industrial complex accountable and ensure the party only pays for work that actually helps us win”. Rivera said he was now going public with the claim, along with his own 564-page review of the election loss. “It’s coming from a place of hope and, honestly, a little bit of desperation,” he told the outlet. “I think that we need some disruption here to force change.”

title: Republican holdouts say they will back Todd Blanche for attorney general
author: Shrai Popat and Guardian staff in Washington
summary: Move comes after Blanche gives senators written assurance he will drop Trump’s $1.8bn anti-weaponization fund
body_text: Two Republican senators who threatened to block Todd Blanche’s bid to permanently become US attorney general announced they will advance his nomination after he said in writing that a planned $1.8bn slush fund for Donald Trump’s allies was dead. The US Senate judiciary committee is due to vote on Tuesday on whether to approve the nomination of Blanche, who is already acting attorney general, and send it to the wider Senate for a vote. Outgoing lawmakers John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, two key holdouts on the committee who have repeatedly clashed with Trump over the past year, said their concerns were resolved after a “successful negotiation of a legally enforceable document”, which was released by Blanche late on Sunday. The document formally ends the $1.8bn “anti‑weaponization fund”, and makes clear that Trump and his family will not receive indefinite protection from audits of future tax filings. Both controversial prospects arose from an agreement reached as part of a settlement in a lawsuit Trump filed against the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) over the unauthorized leak of his tax returns. A US federal judge who oversaw the lawsuit blasted the arrangement, noting that the US Department of Justice did not make a good faith effort to defend the government, and that it appeared to be a collusive effort to engineer a beneficial result on behalf of the president. Both the fund and the scope of Trump’s immunity from tax audits became dealbreakers for Cornyn and Tillis. “We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund,” the senators said in a joint statement. “Additionally, the department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share. “We look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate judiciary committee soon.” Just this weekend, Trump had defended the fund, and threatened to “push hard” to legislate for it. The fund would “immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done” if senators fail to approve Blanche’s nomination, the president wrote on social media.

title: Trump meets his obstinate match in Iran’s hardball regime
author: Andrew Roth
summary: US president reduced to bemoaning Tehran’s ‘unbelievable duplicity’ as he struggles to find solid negotiating ground
body_text: The Donald Trump doctrine has always contained a tenuous relationship with the truth. It was his mentor, the infamous New York lawyer Roy Cohn, who taught the young real estate mogul always to claim victory and never to admit defeat. Unfortunately for Trump, in Iran the US president has found a counterpart just as stubborn as himself. As Trump claims new negotiations are to begin with Tehran this week, Iran has shown it can also reignite the conflict by lobbing ballistic missiles at US bases in the region and maintaining a stranglehold on the strait of Hormuz, effectively taking initiative in the stalled peace process. And time is of the essence for Trump as the clock ticks toward a global energy crisis and a painful midterm elections for him and his Republican party. But as soon as his latest attempt to hammer out a peace deal was announced, it was denied by Iran and the US president was left fuming once again. “Iranian Leadership is unbelievably duplicitous!” he posted to his social media site, Truth Social, saying that Iran had begged for a meeting and talks had already begun. “Nothing gets through to Iran, unless we want it to, and nothing will get through, unless a Deal, or Total Surrender, is accomplished.” Trump has suggested dozens of times since the beginning of the war that a deal with Iran is imminent, and his latest claim that new negotiations could produce a peace deal within days has shown the administration’s desperation to reopen the strait and find a road map out of the crisis. After promising to hit Iran “very hard”, Trump made a U-turn on Sunday and claimed that talks would continue and that the “perimeters of a deal” for the opening of Hormuz and the “denuclearization of Iran” had been agreed. Unfortunately, the Iranians don’t agree. In a statement on Monday, an Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson denied any peace negotiations were taking place. “We are not currently negotiating with the United States,” said Esmaeil Baqaei. “Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the strait of Hormuz.” That may result in an agreement. But that will not result in the return of the strait of Hormuz to its prewar status, Baqaei added, in effect keeping the waterway a political football for the foreseeable future. “We must ensure that the strait of Hormuz cannot be misused by parties that have committed aggression against Iran,” said Baqaei. Little has changed since the last round of negotiations. Iran remains capable of closing the strait of Hormuz and stifling shipping – including a fifth of global oil supply – through the crucial waterway. The US remains capable of inflicting devastating strikes on Iran – despite a shortage of key munitions that could be needed for a war against key rivals like China – but has a lack of meaningful targets that could force Iran to change its policy. The Trump administration has been signalling a desire to end the conflict since April and three ceasefires have come and collapsed since then. With just over three months left until the US midterm elections, in which the Republicans are expected to lose the House and possibly even the Senate, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll last week showed that fewer than a third of Americans support the war in Iran, and 69% believe that Trump has not “clearly explained the goals of US military involvement in Iran”. For Iran, the strategic unpredictability has become a new weapon in a war that has counterintuitively strengthened its negotiating position, giving the regime new tools in slowing global oil supply and in attacking regional US allies in the Gulf. Iran has concluded that its best strategy is to “maximise the pain that they can impose on the United States and its partners in the region”, said Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute and an expert on Middle East security issues with a focus on Iran, during the institute’s podcast last week. The view there was that Trump “is not really yet ready for a deal with Iran, not a deal that would work for the Iranians anyway”. Iran is also facing a time crunch with a US blockade in effect halting trade out of the country. “They are now at a point where they don’t think just sitting back and having one round after another of diplomatic talks is the best way forward,” he added. “They’re trying to shake things up to try get Trump’s attention and see if they can get a different result.”

title: More European countries’ FAs withdraw support for Infantino as pressure intensifies
author: Nick Ames and Matt Hughes
summary: The English FA and Serbia’s have followed Wales’s and Finland’s in dropping support for Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid as Fifa president
body_text: European countries began turning their backs on Gianni Infantino as moves intensified across the globe to end his crisis-hit tenure as Fifa president. The Football Association was the highest-profile of several Uefa member associations to drop its support for Infantino’s proposed re-election next year. It will write to Fifa confirming it no longer endorses Infantino for a fourth term in charge after the intense controversy surrounding his failed plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors. Wales and Serbia publicly confirmed that they had withdrawn their backing, following a lead taken by Finland last week. Along with the FA, those federations had all previously written letters in favour of Infantino prolonging his tenure but patience has run out across the continent. The Swedish Football Association, which was one of five European FAs not to write letters of support, issued a statement confirming it would oppose his candidature in the election in March. The FA had previously fallen into line behind Infantino, who will helm an extraordinary Fifa congress confirming the United Kingdom’s hosting of the 2035 Women’s World Cup in November if he is still in position. But it has been consistent in condemning his doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, publicly and in private representations. On Saturday it called for a “full and robust review of Fifa’s leadership and governance”, and its latest move is a further escalation. It is joined by the Football Association of Wales, which said in a statement: “The Football Association of Wales hereby confirms its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr Gianni Infantino for re-election as Fifa president for the 2027-2031 term. “The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgment have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football. Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.” Striking a similar tone, the Football Association of Serbia explained recent events had “seriously damaged the reputation and credibility of both Fifa and its president”, saying a withdrawal was “the only logical and rational step”. In a sign that consensus may not be easy to achieve, the Swiss Football Association stopped short of abandoning its countryman. Instead it asked for “another personal exchange of views with the Fifa president” and said it would “continue to review the developments surrounding Fifa” before the leadership election. More countries are, however, expected to withdraw their support for Infantino in what amounts to a vote of no confidence. The intended effect is for the embattled president to resign although some insiders are braced for a drawn-out process. While the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Concacaf, which runs the sport in North and Central America, have both strongly criticised Infantino there has been no move by any of their individual federations to call back letters in favour of his re-election. Ensuring they do so may be critical to the ongoing efforts to remove Infantino quickly. There is acknowledgement in some parts of Europe that other continents should be seen taking the lead if enough of a groundswell for his departure is to be reached. Only 15 countries have publicly supported Infantino since he shelved the FFE project on Saturday but there is an appetite to form a broad coalition against his re-election quickly. The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, is a contender to take over if Infantino is deposed. Montagliani is understood to be in consensus with the Uefa and AFC hierarchies that new leadership is needed at Fifa. In another blow to Infantino, lawyers acting for Uefa have ordered him and other staff to identify, locate and preserve all documents related to the FFE scheme. Their letter includes Arsène Wenger, the Fifa chief of global football development, among those obliged to comply with its order. It says Uefa is “actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints ... arising out of and in connection with the FFE plan”. Thrive Eternal, the investment firm that had been expected to lead a group taking a 20% stake in FFE, is believed to have been sent a similar letter. JP Morgan, which was enlisted for an advisory role in the scheme, is also understood to have received an order related to FFE. On Monday afternoon the US State Department denied reports that Infantino had been scheduled to meet Marco Rubio, the United States secretary of state, in a bid to stoke up support for his continued reign as president.

title: US House ethics panel recommends censure for Republican Chuck Edwards
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: North Carolina congressman’s campaign rejects committee finding that Edwards ‘engaged in sexual harassment’
body_text: The US House of Representatives ethics committee on Monday recommended that Chuck Edwards, a Republican congressman, face censure after determining he “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on two young female staffers. The bipartisan panel began investigating the second-term North Carolina congressman earlier this year, after receiving complaints about his conduct. In a report approved by Democratic and Republican committee members, they determined there “was substantial reason to believe” Edwards broke House rules by singling out the two unidentified aides for special treatment that made them uncomfortable and harmed relations with other employees. While the investigation uncovered no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it, his behavior likely violated provisions in the House code of conduct that prohibit sexual harassment and unwanted advances. The congressman “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate”, but “has not acknowledged or taken responsibility for the harm he caused”, the committee wrote in its report. “A member of Congress should not single out a staffer and isolate them from other staff, make frequent comments regarding that person’s appearance and weight, send messages in the middle of the night, text staff deeply personal and seemingly romantic thoughts, intrude on personal occasions without invitation, pay for personal vacations, and spend thousands of dollars on gifts for staffers,” they continued. Edwards’s re-election campaign criticized the report, arguing its findings “completely exonerate” the congressman while saying ethics committee staff “have taken it upon themselves to write their own rules based upon an interpretation that is inconsistent with the written rule of law or House rules”. “Representative Edwards looks forward to having his name cleared and will work to ensure that the full light of day is brought on this process and that every member of Congress and the public can see the attempt to harm the congressman who has brought no harm to others,” the campaign said in a statement. If the House agrees to censure Edwards, he would have to stand in the well of the chamber while the text of a resolution rebuking him is read aloud. The congressman was already viewed as vulnerable to losing re-election to his western North Carolina district in the November midterm elections. Last week election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball announced it was rating his race a “toss-up” in a sign of improving Democratic chances. “My heart goes out to the young women who took these roles to serve our community,” Jamie Ager, his Democratic opponent, said following the report’s release. “We deserve leaders with the moral character western North Carolina can be proud of.” Elected in 2022 after ousting the scandal-plagued Madison Cawthorn in the Republican primary, Edwards, a former state senator, left most of the hiring for his new office up to his chief of staff, but insisted on bringing “three young women” into his operation, according to the report. This group included a woman who was still in college and identified by the committee as “Staffer 1” and a second woman in her early 20s, identified as “Staffer 2”. “Both young women were subject to increasingly unusual attention from the congressman while they worked for him, creating an environment where both they and their coworkers felt uncomfortable,” the committee found. These behaviors included Edwards bringing Staffer 1 to a White House event without telling the rest of his staff, buying her flowers and texting her in advance that he was “so excited about tonight” and wanted it to be “perfect”. After the event, the staffer said Edwards tried to “pressure” her into continuing the night together, which the congressman told the committee he did not recall. He invited both staffers to private dinners, and at one point told Staffer 2 to ensure the event was not put on his calendar by his office scheduler. He would also send both “personal texts” later in the evening about planning events together or expressing “personal sentiments”, the committee found. Edwards also planned lengthy and elaborate trips with the two staffers either together or individually, at one point suggesting to Staffer 2 that they “go to Annapolis for lunch, meditate by its water, stroll about town, find a day spa, see a movie, or wipe out the casino”. “I’m probably over thinking being impulsive but I really want you to enjoy our time together nearly as much as [I] know [I] will,” he wrote in a text message to the staffer released by the committee. His actions made the two staff members uncomfortable, and when a senior employee of his office spoke to Edwards on their behalf, that staffer told the committee the congressman “got very angry” and said she “didn’t understand the unique relationship” he had with the two women. Both staffers later resigned because of his behavior, but gave Edwards other reasons why when they departed. The behavior affected the morale of his office, the committee found, with one senior aide telling investigators Edwards “lashes out at everyone on the team except” the two women. The congressman denied yelling at his staff. Another staffer said they had told Edwards that an “unfair standard existed” in his office, which he said was caused by employees being “jealous”. Even after she left his employment, Staffer 2 agreed to a trip to Las Vegas with Edwards, saying she felt pressured to do so in part because he had influence over her being hired for another job in civil service. He paid for her flights, accommodation at the Bellagio hotel and a show at the Sphere. After receiving a bouquet of flowers upon arrival, Staffer 2 texted Edwards: “I’m almost ready and just got the flowers – they’re very pretty. Thank you! I did want to flag that the message made me uncomfortable. Just want to make sure this trip isn’t meant to be anything it’s not?” “Understood, and agree. I’m sorry it made you uncomfortable. Nothing was meant by it, other than what was intended to be a cute play on the name of the arrangement,” Edwards responded.
