title: ‘Completely hollow’: critics denounce Blanche deal to halt Trump slush fund
author: Sam Levine and Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Democrats say agreement – which clears way for Blanche’s confirmation – makes promises president can easily reverse
body_text: A compromise between Todd Blanche and two Republican senators that potentially cleared the way for Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general is weak, Democrats and several experts said, as it makes promises Donald Trump can easily reverse. Blanche, the acting attorney general, posted two documents on Sunday evening showing he was withdrawing an 18 May order allowing for the creation of a $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” fund and clarifying that broad tax immunity the justice department granted to Trump only applied retroactively to the president, his sons, and businesses. The agreement stemmed from a deal worked out with John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, two Republican senators who had threatened to block Blanche’s nomination. Cornyn and Tillis said on Monday they would support Blanche when his vote comes up for the Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday. “We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund,” Cornyn and Tillis said. “Additionally, the department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share.” But legal experts and Democrats said what Blanche announced on Sunday was far from ironclad and left room for Trump to resurrect the fund. “These assurances are not worth the paper they’re written on,” Brandon DeBot, the policy director at the Tax Law Center at NYU, said in a statement. “They don’t pull back on the ongoing attempts to give the president, his family, and his affiliates unauthorized immunity from tax audits. They don’t do anything new to stop the president from trying to bring back the fund, as he threatened to this weekend. It’s abundantly clear we need congressional action.” Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal, a member of the judiciary committee, said: “Cornyn and Tillis seem to have gotten nothing. The tax immunity deal is still unlimited in terms of tax control liability, and the slush fund, or the thug fund, as I call it, is still alive and well so far as Donald Trump is concerned.” The documents Blanche released only say the prior justice department order creating the anti-weaponization fund is rescinded. It does not modify the original settlement agreement creating the fund, reached as the result of a Trump lawsuit seeking billions in damages for the unauthorized release of his tax returns. In brief comments to reporters, Tillis defended his and Cornyn’s deals, saying the anti-weaponization fund is “rescinded to death” and that the Texas senator had assured him “it would be very difficult for anybody to construe it as some sort of get out of audit free for any kind of future matter”. “That’s enough for me,” Tillis said. Blanche acknowledged during his confirmation hearing that Trump or his sons – the plaintiffs in the case – could theoretically sue to enforce the agreement. Trump spent the weekend praising the slush fund, and even threatened to revive it. Trump again praised the fund on Monday, saying: “These people were treated so horribly, and this fund could’ve given them some solace.” He added that he had not seen Blanche’s agreement. “I don’t know what they agreed to,” he said. Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrat on the House judiciary committee, said Blanche’s announcement does nothing to prevent the justice department and Trump from creating the anti-weaponization fund under a different name. Raskin said: “These hollow words are an affront to the American people, Congress and the courts, and are clearly designed to lull Senators Cornyn and Tillis into a false sense that their legitimate concerns have been addressed while leaving Blanche’s corrupt scheme fully intact.” Even if the department does not move ahead with the fund, there is another path for January 6 defendants to receive a payout from the federal government. A once-obscure process under the Federal Tort Claims Act allows anyone to seek damages from the federal government, first by filing a claim and then through a lawsuit. The justice department has wide discretion over whether to settle those lawsuits and some January 6 defendants are already moving through the process with claims for millions of dollars. “This supposed ‘deal’ doesn’t prevent payouts to violent insurrectionists in the future,” Adam Schiff, a California Democrat and member of the Senate judiciary committee, said in a post on X. “It doesn’t prevent the admin from bringing the slush fund back from the dead next week or using DOJ’s Judgment Fund for the same illicit purpose.” Republicans and Democrats have harshly criticized the anti-weaponization fund and the tax immunity deal ever since they were announced in mid-May. Both arose out of a $10bn lawsuit Trump, his sons and business filed against the government for damages over the unauthorized release of his tax returns. The justice department did not even attempt to defend the government in the lawsuit. A federal judge later said it was a “bad-faith” suit designed to engineer a beneficial result for Trump. The New York Times reported in May that the tax immunity could potentially free Trump of a $100m penalty related to past audits of his tax returns. “Can you believe the guy, or did he and Trump announce the $1.9bn Trump justice fund in a month, and now we’re back where we started?” asked Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic senator and another judiciary committee member. “Or did they open the drive-up window at the Department of Justice for free Federal Tort Claims Act giveaways to any Maga person who asks?” Referring to Cornyn and Tillis, Whitehouse said: “It doesn’t look to me like they’ve actually pinned down the result they claim to have achieved.” The fund would have been run by five commissioners, four of whom would have been appointed by the attorney general (the fifth would have been named in consultation with congressional leadership). The fund was not required to disclose how much money it paid and to whom and aside from Trump and his sons, there were no restrictions on who could apply. The agreement Blanche announced is “completely hollow”, said Virginia Canter, chief counsel and director of ethics and anti-corruption at Democracy Defenders Action. “Nothing changes the terms of the actual settlement agreement, which cannot be modified without all parties’ consent. As a result, Blanche could reverse course tomorrow if he wanted.” Lawyers for the watchdog group Democracy Forward, which sued over the fund and secured a court order stopping it, sent a letter to the justice department on Monday noting Blanche had still declined to say under oath that the fund was not moving forward. The organization also asked the justice department whether it would seek to amend the underlying settlement agreement. “The DoJ and Acting Attorney General Blanche appear to want to have their cake and eat it too,” Skye Perryman, the group’s president, said in a statement. “They ask members of the United States Senate to believe the anti-weaponization fund is dead while they seek to preserve favor with the president through refusing to make real commitments backed up in court regarding the operation and future of the fund.” Even some Trump allies appeared unpersuaded that Blanche’s announcement amounted to the death of the fund. Mike Howell, an ally of Trump and director of the Oversight Project, a conservative watchdog group, posted a picture of Blanche’s documents on X and said they “can be undone after Tuesday. The anti-weaponization fund is great.” Asked about the possibility of Blanche going back on his promises to the Republican senators after being confirmed, Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Senate judiciary committee, said: “Knowing how Trump works … I wouldn’t be surprised.” • This article was amended on 4 August 2026. An earlier version referred to the anti-weaponization fund as a “weaponization fund”.

title: Trump accuses oil companies of ‘making too much money’ from his war on Iran
author: Jillian Ambrose
summary: US president hits out at ExxonMobil and Chevron, saying they should ‘give some of that back to the public’
body_text: Donald Trump has criticised oil companies for “making too much money” from the global energy market disruption caused by his war on Iran. Brent crude had been trading at about $70 (£52) a barrel before the first US-Israeli strikes at the end of February, but by the end of April it had soared as high as $126 and is now trading at about $85 a barrel. The US president took aim at the windfall profits revealed last week by ExxonMobil and Chevron, and said the companies would “give some of that back to the public”. “They’re making too much money based on a shortage,” he told reporters at the White House on Monday evening. “I don’t like it.” Trump was speaking just hours before BP reported its profits had doubled in the last quarter, to $5.7bn. The US oil companies made profits totalling more than $26bn for the three months to the end of June by taking advantage of the energy market disruption triggered by the US-Israeli war on Iran. Chevron reported its highest ever quarterly profit of $12.2bn, a fivefold increase on the same period last year. ExxonMobil reported a profit of $14.5bn in the second quarter, double what it made in the same period a year ago and its highest quarterly profit since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. “Chevron: too much money. ExxonMobil: too much money,” Trump said. “They’re going to give some of that back to the public and they better cut the retail price, the consumer price.” Asked about Trump’s comments, the BP chief executive, Meg O’Neill, told CNBC that she understood the pressures on households. “The reality is, we produce a global commodity, and the product we sell hangs off that global commodity price,” she added. Climate campaigners have also attacked big oil’s bumper quarterly earnings, condemning them as “obscene”. Clémence Dubois, a campaigns director at 350.org, an international environmental group, said: “Chevron and Exxon are profiteering from a model of distraction, leaving ordinary people to pay the price with higher bills and devastating impacts such as these fires. These profits feel almost criminal.” Trump criticised oil company profits weeks after warning energy retailers to cut their prices as he nears the November midterm elections with flagging approval ratings. He also ordered the US justice department to investigate potential price gouging in the retail energy sector. “Gasoline Retailers must get their Prices down, IMMEDIATELY,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform in late June. “If Retailers don’t do this, big problems lie ahead!” The president told journalists that the fall in oil and gas prices during the administration’s June peace talks with Iran should have caused petrol prices to fall to $2.25 a gallon. “Oil prices have come down so much and we are not seeing anything at the pump by comparison the way they should be,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. US gasoline prices currently average $4.11 a gallon, according to data from the AAA motoring group. The Trump administration has repeatedly said it has no plans to introduce an export ban on oil or petroleum products, but some analysts say this could be revisited if prices at the pump continue to rise.

title: Michigan votes in key Senate primary as Democrats battle over party’s future
author: Rachel Leingang
summary: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed leads in polls against centrist Haley Stevens as party looks to regain control of US Senate
body_text: The Democratic party faces a crucial test of its direction on Tuesday as voters in the midwestern swing state of Michigan decide whether to nominate for US Senate a progressive candidate advocating for universal healthcare or an-establishment-backed moderate. The state’s Democratic primary is the latest high-profile battle over the party’s future, as it seeks to chart a course back to power in Washington following Donald Trump’s victory in 2024. Leftwing candidates have surged in Democratic primaries in solidly blue areas across the country in recent months. Some congressional primary races in Michigan will also offer a sense of where the party is headed as it looks to take back control of US Congress from the Republicans. Progressive Abdul El-Sayed, a 41-year-old former public health official, has led in recent polls against his moderate rival, Haley Stevens, the 43-year-old US representative who first came to Congress after flipping a red seat. A flood of more than $40m in outside spending has come into the race to support Stevens or attack El-Sayed, including from groups associated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), a pro-Israel lobby. The winner of Tuesday’s Democratic primary will face Mike Rogers, a former congressman from the state who was also the Republican nominee for US Senate in 2024 when he lost to Elissa Slotkin. The Michigan US Senate seat is critical for Democrats in their dark-horse quest to retake the upper chamber, where Republicans currently hold 53 of the 100 seats. Michigan is not the only state with primaries on Tuesday. In Missouri, voters will weigh whether to nominate Cori Bush, the former US representative who is running to return to the chamber against Wesley Bell, in a race punctuated by the war in Gaza and outside spending by pro-Israel groups. And in Washington state, voters will decide which two candidates to elevate in the third congressional district, where blue-dog Democratic representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is seeking re-election amid challengers from both sides of the aisle. Congressional seats, including one in Slotkin’s former district, are also in the mix in Michigan, with further tests of progressives’ rise. The progressive US senator Bernie Sanders has boosted El-Sayed and two progressive challengers in congressional races. In the Lansing-area seventh district, Sanders backed William Lawrence, a community organizer who co-founded the Sunrise Movement, over the former US ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink and Matt Maasdam, a former US Navy Seal. Maasdam received Slotkin’s endorsement in the race for the purple district, currently held by Republican Tom Barrett. In the 13th district, Sanders boosted the state representative Donavan McKinney, who is running against the incumbent Democratic representative Shri Thanedar in the Detroit-area district. On the right, Republicans will figure out if they want to nominate John James, a US representative with Donald Trump’s endorsement, or businessman Perry Johnson to face Jocelyn Benson, the secretary of state and likely Democratic nominee for the governorship. James has led in polls, but late grassroots energy has given Johnson some momentum. Governor Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, served for eight years and faced term limits, preventing another run for the high office.

author: Martin Belam
summary: US president takes aim at profits as oil companies worldwide benefit from US-Iran conflict

The US president took aim at the windfall profits revealed last week by ExxonMobil and Chevron, and claimed the companies would “give some of that back to the public”. The US oil companies made profits totalling more than $26bn for the three months to the end of June. Chevron reported its highest ever quarterly profit of $12.2bn, a fivefold increase on the same period last year. ExxonMobil reported a profit of $14.5bn in the second quarter, double what it made in the same period a year ago. Is it just US oil companies profiting from Trump’s war? Europe’s largest oil company, Shell, doubled its net profit to almost $10bn in the three months to June. The crisis helped the Saudi ⁠oil company Aramco to a ⁠44% rise in net profits, to $32.69bn, in the same period, despite disruption in ‌the strait of Hormuz. BP has reported its highest quarterly profits since the first year of Russia’s war on Ukraine, though its new chief executive, Meg O’Neill, said there was “more to do” because BP was “not making the most” of its potential. What is happening with Trump’s new trade tariffs? A coalition of 25 US states sued the Trump administration on Monday over new tariffs pegged at 10%-12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, calling them a pretext for replacing import taxes that were struck down by the supreme court in February. According to the states involved in the action, tariffs on 59 countries and the European Union imposed last month cover 99.4% of US imports. Immigrant death at Delaney Hall marks 22nd in ICE custody this year An immigrant being held at a New Jersey ICE detention center died on 1 August, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced on Monday. Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, 41, is the 22nd person to die in ICE custody this year, according to agency data. Lopez-Cornejo, who is originally from El Salvador and first came to the US in 2006, was arrested by ICE agents in Plainfield, New Jersey, on 18 June and sent to Delaney Hall detention facility to await deportation. Less than two months later he had an unspecified “medical emergency” and was later pronounced dead by University Hospital in Newark, New Jersey, ICE said. Trump accuses Jeanine Pirro of ‘folding’ by dropping reflecting pool charges Donald Trump accused the US attorney Jeanine Pirro of having “folded like an umbrella”, amid reports he was considering removing her from her post. Trump criticized Pirro on Monday after she dropped vandalism charges against a former Olympian accused of damaging the recently renovated Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. title: Asking Anthony Fauci for medical advice then calling for him to be jailed? Katie Miller is the latest Maga hypocrite
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: The vocal vaccine sceptic and wife of Trump’s deputy chief of staff turned to the former US science adviser when she was worried about Covid. Now, she’s claiming it was a cunning plan, writes Arwa Mahdawi
body_text: You should keep your friends close, your enemies closer, and Stephen and Katie Miller as far away from your general vicinity as humanly possible. Many people will not need to be told this. Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, is famous for masterminding the first Trump administration’s family separation policy and Muslim ban. His wife, Katie, is similarly enthusiastic about mass deportation and has reportedly said she didn’t feel compassion for families separated at the border. Stephen met Katie when they were both working in government, but she has since left politics to start a podcast. Now she asks guests such as JD Vance important questions such as: is a hotdog a sandwich? While I may not need to inform you that the Millers are bad news, it seems Dr Anthony Fauci is only just getting the memo. The former top US government science adviser, who helped guide the country’s Covid-19 response, was forced to appear at a US Senate committee hearing last week. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky framed the hearing as an investigation into the origins of the pandemic. Really, however, it was an opportunity for Republicans to harass Fauci, who is widely loathed among the Maga base. He has become such a target of vitriol that Biden preemptively pardoned Fauci before leaving office in case he was prosecuted by the Trump administration. While the Millers were not directly involved in the Fauci hearing, they did make an interesting cameo. Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci’s diary from 2019 to 2022, which revealed that Fauci regularly talked to Katie, then a communications aide to vice-president Mike Pence, about her health concerns. “I am calling katie frequently to check on her couple time per day,” Fauci wrote in notes dated 9 May 2020. “She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant. Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone.” Fauci seemed to like Katie, who he described as “tough, smart, but great”, and she seemed on good terms with him. Fauci also sent the Millers a baby gift and, per his diary, the couple called him to say thank you. “We had a nice discussion about life after Trump,” he wrote in December 2020. I don’t think any more gifts are going to be exchanged, however, because Katie has thrown Fauci under the bus. It’s very embarrassing for a Maga bigwig like her – someone who has amplified vaccine-sceptic views and publicly called for Fauci to be jailed – to be revealed as having privately asked him for medical advice. Katie has tried to explain away the relationship by insisting that she had simply been feigning friendship as part of a cunning plan. Katie told the political news website Notus that she’d been cordial with Fauci so that he “did not leak against me or my husband”. She added that she understood “how to manage somebody like him”. Some of the information about her seems to have been redacted. Notus reports that the original Fauci journal entries released “mentioned Katie Miller 56 times, while the redacted document mentioned her 37 times”. After the diary entries became public, Katie attacked Fauci on social media and accused him of being fame-hungry. “Every man who has a journal is a narcissist,” she wrote on X on Thursday. “Dr Fauci was neither my friend nor my doctor, but a work colleague who weaponised my pregnancy and child for his gain to aggrandise himself. As they say, keep your friends close and your enemies closer … this man should be in prison.” Katie isn’t entirely wrong about Fauci enjoying fame. His journal entries contain cringeworthy details about flattering press coverage and celebs fawning over him. Julia Roberts, he wrote, “said that every time she sees me her throat gets dry and she gets nervous”. Barbra Streisand apparently also chatted to Fauci about vaccines. “Had great call with Barbra Streisand,” he wrote in February 2021. “I told her that I work listening to her songs on Alexa. She really did not know what Alexa was. I accidentally butt called her later in the evening …” Still, this was a private journal, and we’ve all been embarrassing in private haven’t we? Plus, if Roberts was gasping over me, you best believe I’d be telling dear diary. Fauci getting carried away by his sudden fame is understandable; there is no vaccine for being cringe. One day, however, I hope there will be a cure for the harm people like the Millers have inflicted on the body politic. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: US federal judge blocks New York’s ban on ICE officers wearing masks
author: Edward Helmore
summary: Judge puts hold on mask ban while allowing state law prohibiting cooperation between police and ICE to stand
body_text: A New York law banning US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from wearing face coverings and requiring that they wear visible identification has been put on hold by a federal judge. But a state law prohibiting cooperation between local police departments and ICE has been allowed to stand. The mask ruling comes after federal judges have blocked similar laws in California, Virginia and Pennsylvania that sought to ban federal immigration agents from covering their faces. They are still required to wear agency identification badges and badge numbers. The US district judge Mae D’Agostino of the federal court in Albany, New York, wrote that while the state “appears to be well-intentioned in its pursuit of transparent policing”, her decision was made on constitutional arguments rather than “transparency or preferable policy decisions”. D’Agostino said that New York officials “may be correct that federal immigration officers wearing masks and not displaying viable identification creates certain dangerous situations that the face covering and identification acts remedy”. She wrote that the Trump administration nonetheless has shown a likelihood that the measures go against the supremacy clause of the US constitution, which bars state governments from regulating federal law enforcement. The preliminary ruling means local police officers are blocked from arresting ICE agents for covering their faces in public settings. “The United States has demonstrated a likelihood that it will succeed on its claim that [New York’s] face covering and identification acts directly regulate federal officers in violation of the supremacy clause,” D’Agostino wrote. “Whether federal law enforcement agencies have chosen to carry out such operations in a sufficiently transparent manner is an important question. But that question is not for this court to answer at the present time.” New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, signed the restrictions known as the “New York mask law” in late May in response to federal immigration enforcement tactics during Donald Trump’s second presidency. Members of the president’s Republican party argue that a mask ban undermines public safety. On the issue of whether local law enforcement can cooperate with federal agents, D’Agostino’s 51-page preliminary ruling said New York’s ban on 287(g) cooperation agreements – which comes into effect later in August – should stand because it is an “appropriate means of furthering New York’s legitimate interests in protecting public welfare and choosing how state and local resources are expended”. Brandon Neuman, a US justice department lawyer, argued in July that both the mask and cooperation bans in New York are invalid because states can’t make laws that regulate the actions of federal agencies. “The key harm here is to the sovereign function of the United States,” he said. James Percival, a general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees immigration enforcement agencies, reacted to D’Agostino’s ruling by saying on X that Democratic-led states “continue to stack losses as they try to pass unconstitutional bans on ICE officers wearing masks”. Hochul and New York’s attorney general, Letitia James, said the ruling allowing the 287(g) ban to remain in effect shows the law “is legal and will keep our communities safe”. “Local law enforcement should be focused on local matters, and New York taxpayers should not have to foot the bill for any collaboration with ICE,” they said in a joint statement. “While the court enjoined enforcement of New York’s mask ban, we stand firm in our belief that masked agents do not make New York safer.” The statement alluded to the New York government’s ability to appeal D’Agostino’s ruling, saying: “Our offices are reviewing all legal options at this time.” ICE cooperation has become a campaign issue in Hochul’s bid for re-election in November. She is facing Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau county executive, who supports ICE tactics and opposes the prohibition of cooperation with the agency.

title: Pauline Hanson has knocked another brick out of our creaky political system. It’s not good for anybody
author: Peter Greste
summary: By deciding who gets to ask questions and who is barred, the One Nation leader is upending the democratic role that journalists are supposed to occupy
body_text: Democracy’s lifeblood is information. But like any bloodstream, the more gunk that flows through it, the less healthy the system. For public debate to work, we all need reliable information grounded in facts and ethics, and the way we’ve done that for almost two centuries is through good journalism. The system isn’t always perfect – and sometimes it can look downright unedifying – but it has generally helped deliver one of the world’s most stable and successful political systems. We mess with it at our peril. For the most part, social media just doesn’t cut it. Nor do the media releases and videos published by our politicians. It is important that we hear from them, of course, but the whole point of having journalists in the room is to interrogate, challenge and question those statements. If that sounds obvious, Pauline Hanson seems to have missed the memo. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email At the event to launch her party’s campaign for the Victorian state election, reporters she deemed “unfriendly” were stopped from getting in. “The ABC were denied entry into here, and the Guardian,” she said. “I’m not putting up with their rubbish. I’m not putting up with their spin, their lies whatsoever.” Her staff also stopped a journalist from the Age. This should not come as a surprise. In her speech to the National Press Club in June, the One Nation leader warned she would bar media outlets she didn’t like, and singled out the ABC, the Guardian and SBS. Earlier this year, ABC journalists were removed from a One Nation campaign event in the Farrer byelection. But if she has a problem with the media, there are mechanisms for complaint. The Australian Press Council oversees print publications, while the Australian Media and Communications Authority handles broadcasters (both radio and TV). The ABC has its own ombudsman, and the Guardian has its own dedicated readers’ editor. All those institutions have clear sets of standards and ethics designed to hold news organisations within the bounds of responsible journalism. All have been criticised for being weak and ineffectual, but they remain the port of call for complaints about ethical breaches. In each case, the regulators measure complaints against their codes, and if a story has fallen short, they exercise their powers of sanction. Let the regulators do their job. By deciding who gets to ask questions and who is barred, Hanson is claiming that power for herself, and in a world already struggling with trust, that is indisputably bad for democracy. But there is an additional problem. Picking and choosing between news outlets and journalists also poses serious challenges for all the journalists covering One Nation. If Hanson is deciding between those she likes and those she doesn’t, between publications branded “friendly” and those marked “hostile”, between “good media” and “bad”, it risks tarnishing those who are allowed inside the One Nation tent as being on “their side”. In an instant, she has wiped out the neutral position that journalists so jealously guard. This is not to suggest those who remain “in the tent” are compromised, but it creates an awkward image for the media outlets who continue to cover her events. They are, after all, the ones permitted through the door. It also creates an incentive to keep delivering soft stories. That might have been Hanson’s intention, but it doesn’t make for robust scrutiny of her policies or her party, and it certainly doesn’t help public debate. As for those journalists who’ve been shut out, if they are ever allowed back in, there will always be questions around whether they got permission by ingratiating themselves, or whether One Nation recognised its mistake. Either way, by upending the independent democratic role that journalists are supposed to occupy, Hanson has knocked another brick out of our creaky system, and that can’t be good for anybody. Peter Greste is professor of journalism at Macquarie University and the executive director of the Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom

title: David Ellison claims opposition to his mega-merger stems from potential CNN control
author: Jeremy Barr
summary: With $111bn deal to acquire cable network’s parent company stalled in courts, Ellison courts public
body_text: Speaking out on the lawsuit against the big merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros Discovery (WBD), Paramount’s CEO, David Ellison, said that the legal backlash against the deal is “not really about market share” but rather stems from political motivations. Noting in a New York Times guest essay published on Tuesday that the deal had “been reviewed and approved by regulators reflecting 65 countries, including the United States”, Ellison played down the competitive concerns raised by the state coalition and Writers Guild of America West and Writers Guild of America East, which also sued to block the deal, and said he believed the reaction came from a “plainer worry”. “The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN. There has been speculation about my politics, my loyalties, my intentions,” Ellison wrote. “Unfortunately, I can’t give anyone a view into my heart and mind, but I can share this: I have regularly voted for candidates of both parties; I hold some views that would be called conservative and others that would be called liberal, just like most Americans.” Reporting has showed that Ellison and his father have made promises to the Trump administration about swaying the network in a more favorable direction, purportedly to encourage federal regulators to approve the merger, prompting backlash from Democrats such as Senator Elizabeth Warren. Backlash against Ellison, son of the tech mogul Larry Ellison, one of the wealthiest people in the world, as a media owner began last summer after after his company, Skydance Media, went through an $8.4bn merger with Paramount Global. As the deal was closing, CBS abruptly announced it was canceling The Late Show With Stephen Colbert, which aired its last episode in May. Once the merger was completed, Ellison appointed the heterodox opinion writer Bari Weiss to run CBS News, a controversial move that has led to layoffs and editorial tensions at the network. Without directly addressing any of the controversies around CBS News, Ellison wrote that he was committed to the independence that is at the core of the “founding principles” of CNN and CBS News. “I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views. I believe that news should be based on facts and truth,” Ellison wrote. “Great news organizations like CNN and CBS News are here to tell it straight down the middle. That requires newsrooms that reflect the whole world, not one side of it. And it requires independence. Our journalists will continue to answer to the facts and to all the people they serve – not to any party or cause. “These were founding principles for both CNN and CBS News,” Ellison continued. “For legends like Ted Turner and Edward R. Murrow, and it is exactly that kind of independence that has always fueled the greatness of ‘60 Minutes.’” Ellison’s essay (“The Critics Are Wrong About My Politics”) comes at a pivotal time for his $111bn merger agreement to buy WBD, which is currently held up in a California court after a 12-state coalition sued to block the deal on anti-competitive grounds. After district judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín agreed to temporarily block the deal, Paramount made the unusual decision to bypass the temporary injunction stage and hold up the merger until the case can go to trial – or until June 2027. The parties have both made proposals for when the case should reach trial, with Paramount asking for a November trial and the state coalition asking for a date in April 2027.

title: Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination will advance to full US Senate vote
author: Joseph Gedeon and Sam Levine
summary: Blanche, formerly Trump’s personal lawyer, confirmed in writing that $1.8bn slush fund for president’s allies was dead
body_text: The US Senate judiciary committee voted along party lines to advance Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general after he confirmed in writing that a planned $1.8bn slush fund for Donald Trump’s allies was dead. Experts say, however, that Trump could easily reverse the deal. His nomination will now proceed to the full Senate, where it will probably face intense skepticism from Democrats. Ahead of the vote on Tuesday, every Democrat on the committee railed against Blanche’s nomination, saying he was unfit for the role and would do the president’s bidding. They emphasized his work defending the controversial fund, his mishandling of the files related to Jeffrey Epstein, the murder of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, and prosecutions of protesters and Trump’s political rivals. “We are going to advance out of this committee probably the most discreditable person ever to seek the office of attorney general of the United States,” said Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic senator from Rhode Island. Blanche, one of Trump’s most trusted legal aides and formerly his personal defense lawyer, has faced questions over his suitability to lead the Department of Justice, which is supposed to operate independently of the White House. He signed an order scrapping the so-called “anti-weaponization” fund – a roughly $1.8bn pool of money created in May as part of a settlement ending Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service – in an attempt to defuse a Republican rebellion over his nomination. The lawsuit came after the leak of the US president’s confidential tax records by a former IRS contractor, who has been serving a prison sentence since 2024. Trump had cast the fund as compensation for people he claimed were unfairly targeted by politically driven investigations, and defended it as recently as this weekend. Critics said it risked becoming a taxpayer-funded payout to Trump loyalists, including some defendants from the January 6 Capitol riot. The most consequential criticism stemmed from two Republican members of the judiciary committee, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina. Blanche’s nomination required their support. But both outgoing senators have turned on Trump, recently telling party leaders they would not let Blanche’s confirmation move without firm guarantees that the fund would be shelved for good. Speaking ahead of the vote on Tuesday, both Cornyn and Tillis said their concerns had been satisfied. Tillis described the anti-weaponization fund as a “payout pot for punks”, but said he was satisfied it would not be moving forward. “I’ve never liked this 1776 fund. It made no sense to me, and I thought it was an insult to the police officers and the people that defended us on January the sixth. It’s done. It’s been rescinded, and I am satisfied,” he said. Despite saying he would vote for Blanche, Tillis lamented the politicization of the justice department under Blanche’s leadership. He criticized the department’s ongoing prosecution of the former FBI director James Comey in eastern North Carolina over a picture Comey posted with seashells arranged saying “86 47” – shorthand for getting rid of Trump. “Some bonehead in North Carolina thinks that that’s a crime. Well, they better damn sure have information to back it up because if all it is is a picture, that person should lose his job, his or her job,” Tillis said. Cornyn and Tillis faced public criticism from Trump over the weekend for pushing Blanche to put in writing that the anti-weaponization fund was dead and the scope of the tax immunity was limited. Cornyn defended the push on Tuesday. “While this may sound like nitpicking to some, it’s critically important not only to me but to other members of the Senate,” Cornyn said. “Given this agreement with Mr Blanche, I expect the department to live up to to this in future litigation.” Echoing the concerns of many other Democrats, Cory Booker, a Democratic senator from New Jersey, said the agreement with Blanche offered little assurance the justice department could not reverse itself and go ahead with the fund anyway. “I’ve been here 14 years. I have not seen something as farcical as what I’ve witnessed over the last few weeks,” Booker said. “I’m going to say it very clear: this is all hat and no cattle.” In his order, released on Sunday, Blanche stressed that the fund had never actually been operational: no board had been appointed, no money moved, and no claims filed or paid. While there was concern that the settlement also provided broad immunity for Trump and members of his family from tax audits, the US Department of Justice separately clarified the IRS-related order was limited to the plaintiffs in the original settlement, and did not amount to blanket protection from future audits. Both Cornyn and Tillis later confirmed they would vote to advance Blanche’s nomination. Because the underlying settlement still references the fund, a future attorney general – or Trump himself, with Congress’s help – could try to revive it. Trump added to that uncertainty over the weekend, saying that if Blanche’s confirmation stalled, he would simply keep him on in an acting capacity and push lawmakers to create the fund through legislation instead.

title: Vivek Ramaswamy is struggling to connect with voters. Can Ohio’s Indian community help?
author: Stephen Starr in Beavercreek, Ohio
summary: Ohioans of Indian heritage will see one of their own take center stage in the race for governor, but their support amid a rocky campaign is not guaranteed
body_text: At the Hindu temple of Dayton in south-west Ohio, there’s no little pride for gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy – he and his parents have been coming here to pray for decades. On a quiet recent Tuesday afternoon, a priest lights incense sticks at the altar of the temple. Outside, a group of first-time visitors take a relaxed walk around the grounds. “I remember him coming here with his parents when he was a little child,” says Ashwani Kumar, a priest from India’s Himachal Pradesh state who has served at the temple since the early 1990s, and says he intends to vote for Ramaswamy in November’s election. “We are citizens, so we always support our [vote]. Real Hindu people believe in goodness,” he says. “Peace and goodness.” Making up the largest immigrant group in the state, Ohioans of Indian heritage are set to see one of their own in Ramaswamy take center political stage ahead of the gubernatorial election this November. But their support for Ramaswamy, amid a rocky campaign, is not a guarantee. For one, Indian Americans tend to lean Democratic. As of 2024, Pew Research Center found that 68% of the group identified as such. But a smaller poll released in February by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace found that support slipping, with the number of people identifying as Democrats declining from what they say was 52% in 2020 to 46% this year. And more Indian Americans have appeared in the rightwing sphere, including in Donald Trump’s administration. Harvard- and Yale-educated Ramaswamy, whose parents immigrated from Kerala before he was born in Cincinnati in 1985, himself received Trump’s much-coveted endorsement for Ohio governor in February 2025 – nearly two years before the election – to the shock of many in Ohio’s Republican establishment circles. Ramaswamy, who had run an unsuccessful campaign for president himself in 2024, then met little opposition in the Republican primary election last May, winning 82% of the vote. But for a host of reasons ranging from xenophobia and outright racism from the right (a recent report found that Ohio’s classrooms are among the most segregated in the country) to accusations that he is a rich opportunist from the left, Ramaswamy, who made billions of dollars as a biotech entrepreneur, has struggled so far to connect with voters. His difficulties have now led to pollsters at the Cook Political Report shifting the Ohio gubernatorial race from “leans Republican” to a “toss-up” this month, despite the state not electing a Democrat to the role for two decades and Trump winning Ohio by more than 11 points in 2024. Ramaswamy created a major stir in December 2024 when appearing to criticize American workers, writing on X that, “Our American culture has venerated mediocrity over excellence for way too long … A culture that celebrates the prom queen over the math olympiad champ, or the jock over the valedictorian, will not produce the best engineers.” His Hindu faith has also become a flashpoint on the trail. In a widely circulated clip from a Turning Point USA event last year, he attempted to answer a student who asked how he could represent a largely Christian state, while another asked him why he chose to “masquerade as a Christian”. Ramaswamy answered with an explanation of Hinduism and attempted to bridge the divide, calling himself an “ethical monotheist”. In May, he struggled to offer a straight answer when asked by a television reporter in Youngstown to name his favorite place to stop by at in the city, responding: “I love long drives.” More recently, Ramaswamy was criticized for spending part of the Fourth of July holiday weekend in Paris. “I think that Vivek, unfortunately, is out of touch from the struggles and concerns of the community – both the Indian American community, and the majority of Ohioans,” says Priya Tamilarasan, an attorney and Democrat based in the metro Columbus area whose parents immigrated from the state of Tamil Nadu in southern India decades ago. “I think it’s very telling that, especially during the campaign cycle, especially during America 250 that he chose to focus on his own lavish lifestyle [by traveling to France]. Connection with and trusting the candidate requires deeper bonds than just someone that looks like you, or speaks the same language as you, or who has a name like you,” says Tamilarasan. In January, an Ohio-based security person who worked for Ramaswamy was arrested on drug-trafficking charges. Ramaswamy’s campaign team fired the security company that employed the bodyguard shortly thereafter. Ramaswamy has little political experience, failing in his 2024 bid before quickly becoming a staunch backer of Trump, the eventual winner. He was briefly appointed to work with Elon Musk in creating the controversial “Department of Government Efficiency” but left just weeks in. This November, Ramaswamy is running against a fellow political novice, Democrat Amy Acton, who led Ohio’s response to the Covid-19 pandemic for several months in 2020. Still, his national profile and entrepreneurial success have seen some among Ohio’s Indian community gravitate towards him. Last November, the Ohio chapter of Americans4Hindus, a small political action committee (Pac), was formed and immediately endorsed Ramaswamy. “The Indian American community in Columbus and across Ohio is strongly supportive – I’d say in the range of 70% to 80%. People are excited. They see Vivek as someone who understands both our cultural roots and the American Dream,” says Neil Patel, the Pac’s president. “He’s a proud Ohioan, a successful entrepreneur, and a father who wants the same opportunities for every child that he and his family have been blessed with. There’s a real sense of pride and optimism in the community about what he can do for the state. “He has a clear, practical plan that speaks to what Ohio families actually care about – putting more money in people’s pockets and giving kids a world-class education,” says Patel. An estimated 18,000 Indian immigrants live in metro Columbus, many who are students or faculty at Ohio State University, whose current president, Ravi Bellamkonda, is from Telangana in southern India. In the wealthy suburb of Dublin situated north-west of Columbus, the 6,000-strong Indian American community is so prominent that local movie theaters show Bollywood films throughout the day. The Dublin Cricket Club has about 100 players, says Himavanth Ganta, a club board member who moved from Hyderabad to the US for college in 2012. “It’s the sport that every Indian boy plays; it’s my passion,” he says. “We got our own cricket ground in 2016. Close to 70% to 80% of our members are people of Indian heritage.” For him, when it comes to choosing a good political candidate, the character of the person outweighs their personal background. “My friends say that [Ramaswamy] is someone to be proud of, being Indian,” says Ganta, who works in software for a large banking institution. “I really don’t care what the candidate’s origin is. They have to do the right things for the people. Our priority is not to have an Indian as a governor; instead, we want them to take care of the people of Ohio.”

title: Washington state Democrat who flipped pro-Trump district faces tough primary
author: Lok Darjee in Vancouver, Washington
summary: Incumbent Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a moderate who owns an auto repair shop, hopes to retain congressional seat
body_text: The two-term Democratic congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is heading into one of the country’s most closely watched contests on Tuesday after national recognition for flipping a Republican seat in 2022. Representing Washington state’s third district, Gluesenkamp Perez finds herself squeezed between the Democrat and progressive Brent Hennrich and the Republican state senator John Braun on her right. There are six other candidates on a single crowded ballot and the top two finishers will advance to the November general election regardless of party. Democrats are favored to win the House of Representatives in November’s midterm election, but highly contested seats such as Gluesenkamp Perez’s will be crucial to securing a majority, and expanding the margin. Republican Jaime Herrera Beutler won Washington’s third district in 2010 and held it for six terms, until Gluesenkamp Perez narrowly beat Trump-endorsed Joe Kent in 2022. Trump has carried the district in all three of his presidential runs, most recently by about three points, and yet in 2024 Gluesenkamp Perez ran roughly seven points ahead of her party’s presidential nominee. Logging, mills, agriculture, shipping and manufacturing still shape daily life in much of the area and Gluesenkamp Perez’s success has stemmed from her appeal to moderates and rural voters. An auto repair shop owner, she won over many in south-west Washington, including Republicans who considered Kent too extreme. “We like her a lot,” said Laura Oltmann, 41, a resident and supporter who describes herself as a conservative. Kent did not embody conservatism, Oltmann said. But through Gluesenkamp Perez’s two terms, frustration has built among her own party, growing when Democrats saw her siding with Republicans on major legislation. Hennrich, who is challenging her in the primary, ran for the same seat in 2022 before standing down, but decided to run again. “I stepped out of this race to unify Democrats to help get Marie through, so we could get rid of our six-term incumbent, Jaime Herrera Beutler,” he said. “[Gluesenkamp Perez] has turned out to be just an absolute epic failure for Democrats.” Hennrich is not alone. Several local Democratic organizations inside the district have broken with her. “She ran as a Democrat and inspired a lot of people, and she won, and we thought she was going to be what we wanted her to be. But everybody’s disappointed,” said LaDonna Kirkpatrick, chair of the 18th legislative district Democrats, speaking in a personal capacity. Kirkpatrick traces that disappointment to Gluesenkamp Perez’s votes for the Save Act, Trump’s effort to overhaul elections, as well as for a bill restricting how public schools address gender identity, and federal funding tied to the war in Iran. She claims the congresswoman has also stopped talking to her own party’s local officers. Thea Zahn, the chair of the 20th legislative district, agreed. “What majority are you going for?” she said. “Are you going for a majority that believes in Democratic values, or a majority that will fail over and over again when it comes down to it, when you really need people to stand up and say this is what we believe in?” Asked if she would vote for the congresswoman if she is on the ballot in November, Zahn said: “I won’t vote for Marie. I will never vote for Marie Perez again.” The congresswoman’s defenders make a different argument: that the district’s partisan lean leaves her little room, and that the seat matters more than any single vote. “The reality is we live in a Republican district. It is Republican,” said Terri Niles, who chairs the 17th legislative district Democrats and spoke in a personal capacity. “I’ve knocked on tens of thousands of doors.” Niles argues that none of Gluesenkamp Perez’s contentious votes actually resulted in legislation passing, and that the calculation for Democrats is simpler than her critics allow. “The most important thing everybody should keep in mind is that flipping the House is our goal,” she said. “That should be the most important thing for every Democrat out there.” The Democratic infighting comes at a precarious moment. An Emerson College poll conducted in mid-July for the Northwest Progressive Institute found Gluesenkamp Perez and Republican Braun tied. Braun, the Republican leader in the Washington senate, has become one of the GOP’s top congressional recruits, earning Donald Trump’s endorsement in April and the backing of the National Republican Congressional Committee. “We could hand a truly 100% Maga candidate a congressional seat for life,” said Tim Probst, a local Democratic party leader. “Because once he gets in there, he’s not getting out.”

title: Jay Clayton sworn in as US director of national intelligence
author: David Smith
summary: After a bumpy confirmation hearing, Clayton replaces acting director Bill Pulte to head US intelligence agencies
body_text: Jay Clayton has been sworn in as the US’s top spy after a contentious Senate confirmation hearing during which ⁠he refused to directly ⁠acknowledge that Donald Trump lost the 2020 presidential election. The oath of office was administered to Clayton on Tuesday by the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, in the Oval Office as the president looked on and applauded. He becomes the ninth director of national intelligence, replacing Tulsi Gabbard, who stepped down in June. Clayton, a former US attorney for the southern district of New York and chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), will oversee 18 US intelligence agencies. His appointment follows a turbulent two months in which the intelligence apparatus was temporarily led by Bill Pulte, the housing regulator whom Trump installed as acting director after Gabbard’s departure. Pulte’s appointment had unsettled some Republicans because of his lack of national security experience. During his brief tenure, however, he became involved in the administration’s increasingly prominent campaign to raise concerns about the integrity of US elections. Shortly before Clayton’s confirmation, Pulte released intelligence community documents from 2020 describing China’s capacity to interfere in US politics and vulnerabilities in the election system. The material was largely previously known but its release came as Trump has made “election security” a central political issue ahead of November’s midterm elections. Trump has continued to promote false claims that the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden, was stolen. During Pulte’s tenure, he also released classified material that he said supported his arguments. Clayton’s own confirmation was overshadowed by the same issue. Democrats condemned his refusal to state that Biden had won the election, while Republicans ultimately confirmed him along party lines. The controversy has raised questions about how the intelligence community will operate under a president who has repeatedly accused federal agencies of being “weaponised” against him. In his first statement as director, Clayton sought to address those concerns, promising to protect the intelligence community from political interference. “The safety and security of the ‌American people will be ‌our North Star, and we will work to make sure the ‌American people have complete confidence in the [intelligence community] through proper oversight, transparency and accountability,” Clayton said in a press release from the office of the director of national intelligence. “This includes ensuring the vital work of our [intelligence community] is never weaponized for political motives,” he added, echoing language frequently used by Trump and his allies to describe their claims that previous administrations abused federal power to target the president. Clayton brings substantial experience in law enforcement and government to the job. As US attorney in Manhattan, he oversaw prosecutions involving terrorism, international drug trafficking and organised crime. Before that, he chaired the SEC from 2017 to 2020, where the administration says he oversaw more than 2,300 enforcement actions resulting in more than $10bn in penalties and disgorgement. He has also held senior positions in business and law, including at Apollo Global Management and Sullivan & Cromwell, and has taught at the University of Pennsylvania and Wharton. Republican senators have pointed to that record as evidence that Clayton is qualified to lead the intelligence community. John Thune, the Senate majority leader, has called him a “proven leader” whose record inspired confidence. Tom Cotton, the chair of the Senate intelligence committee, said Clayton had deep experience in national security threats. Other Republican supporters highlighted his previous bipartisan confirmation as SEC chair. Senator Katie Britt of Alabama added via X on Tuesday: “Congratulations to our Director of National Intelligence, Jay Clayton! I look forward to seeing him lead our intelligence community and keep our nation safe from threats.” Clayton now inherits an intelligence community that has already endured a succession of upheavals under Trump. Gabbard’s tenure was marked by clashes with congressional Democrats, who accused her of advancing the president’s political agenda and promoting debunked election claims. Pulte’s temporary appointment then raised fresh concerns about the politicisation of the intelligence agencies. Clayton said his aim was to create an intelligence organisation that was “streamlined, agile, team-oriented and mission-focused”. He added: “I look forward to making sure the men and women of the [intelligence community] have the resources they need to carry out our critical mission.” With just more than three months left before midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, Trump has escalated efforts ‌to make “election security” a central issue, despite established findings that voter fraud is rare.
