title: The Fifa family: which confederations could support Infantino or turn against him?
author: Nick Ames, John Duerden, Alexander Abnos, Osasu Obayiuwana and Marcela Mora y Araujo
summary: The president is under increasing scrutiny following his World Cup sell-off plan. We look at each confederation’s relationship with the governing body
body_text: The pressure is growing on the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, with many countries withdrawing their support following the bungled World Cup sell-off. However, how key is Infantino’s relationship with each confederation and is it likely that an election contest will actually happen? We look at the key considerations, confederation by confederation. 1) How does each confederation view Infantino’s re-election? Uefa (Europe) has firmly led the moves under way to achieve Infantino’s removal. The threat last week to boycott all Fifa competitions if the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme was not scrapped contributed hugely to its failure. In a scathing statement on Saturday, Uefa said the current Fifa leadership had “not only lost Uefa’s confidence, but also that of many other members of the football family”, and pledged to push for change. Some Uefa member associations, including the English and Welsh FAs, have withdrawn their letters of support for Infantino’s re‑election and efforts are continuing to ensure others follow suit in a bid to weaken his position irretrievably. Nick Ames Reports of AFC (Asia) support for Uefa are premature; the confederation is divided. The AFC has spoken out, strongly in relative terms compared to its usual pronouncements, against the proposed World Cup deal and has called for reform of Fifa. The AFC has been a staunch supporter in the past but if it looks as if Infantino is in trouble the AFC leadership, which was genuinely angry at how the proposal was made (probably more so than the actual details of the deal), could switch sides, which would probably confirm Infantino’s downfall if Uefa and Concacaf oppose but it is not a foregone conclusion – some in Asia are not convinced that Uefa has the numbers. The big problem is that, while the AFC leadership may want Infantino out, most individual Asian federations do not want him to be replaced. The AFC president, Sheikh Salman, has ambitions of his own and has been historically successful at preserving AFC unity but this will be tricky especially as west Asian nations such as Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia support Infantino and are influential in Asia. It could be that the only way to ensure Asian unity is to have an Asian candidate. Jordan’s Prince Ali bin Hussein’s claim of “blackmail” could prove a significant moment, however. John Duerden Concacaf (North and Central America, and the Caribbean) is among the confederations that have come out strongly against Infantino and his FFE proposal, first directly rejecting it and then releasing a statement after it was withdrawn that took direct aim at Infantino. A release speaking on behalf of Concacaf’s 41 member associations called the plan “a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first”, and a “unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership” and said that “a comprehensive reckoning with this presidency is imperative”. That is about as direct a call for no confidence in Infantino as you are likely to get outside of an election itself. It should be noted, of course, that the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, is also a Fifa vice-president and would be a leading candidate to run for president should there be a united desire among confederations to oust Infantino. Montagliani has kept silent on the subject when asked in the past but this statement, which speaks for him, shows at the very least he is not immune to the idea of going against Infantino. Alexander Abnos Patrice Motsepe, president of the Confederation of African Football, has said the 54 member associations are in unanimous support of Infantino’s re-election in Morocco next year. Osasu Obayiuwana Since the rumpus over Infantino’s proposed FFE broke and died, the South American confederation, Conmebol, has been notably silent. Its president, Alejandro Domínguez, has been posting birthday wishes to individuals, clubs and institutions from Uruguay where he is visiting ahead of the 2030 centenary of the first World Cup. Unlike Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC, which publicly opposed Fifa’s aborted FFE proposal, Conmebol took several days before issuing a fence-sitting statement stressing football first, and requesting further information and clarification. That was the only official response at all, and there has been absolute silence since. “Conmebol’s current position is best described as cautious support rather than open confrontation,” says Marina Mendez, a director of AD Sporting Industry Professionals and a friend of Conmebol who consults on football in the region. “The distinction is politically significant. It suggests Conmebol wants to preserve its institutional relationship with Fifa and maintain room for negotiation, rather than join a public campaign against Infantino. This should not necessarily be interpreted as unconditional personal loyalty. Conmebol’s approach is pragmatic: it is protecting South American football’s access, influence and negotiating position within Fifa while assessing how the international balance of power develops.” Brazil and Argentina are the main countries, and Domínguez looks after the relationship with both, with most of the other countries expected to follow suit. “They are not federations likely to confront Infantino directly because they will always prefer to be on the right side of the non-Europeans,” says an industry insider who does not wish to be named. Marcela Mora y Araujo It remains to be seen what the 11 Oceania Football Confederation member associations will do. New Zealand, the leading member of the confederation, was quick to come out against the World Cup proposal – though the reaction of the OFC itself was noncommittal – and there is still support for Infantino among the other federations. John Duerden 2) What are the historical links to Infantino? Uefa The parties go back a long way. Infantino was Uefa’s secretary general from 2009 until 2016 and it backed him strongly when he first ran for the Fifa presidency. But there has long been push and pull between the global governing body and that of football’s most powerful continent. Relations have deteriorated in recent years, Uefa fending off Infantino-led initiatives such as a biennial staging of the World Cup and a proposed investment in 2018 by SoftBank. Things appeared to reach a head in May 2025 when delegates from several European federations walked out of Fifa’s annual congress in protest at Infantino’s late arrival. They accused him of pursuing “private political interests”. That turned out to be the tip of the iceberg. The past year’s near-interminable list of Fifa-related controversies have further ensured that the differences between the two are irreconcilable. NA AFC It has been a close relationship, Salman and AFC have backed Infantino since he beat Salman in the 2016 election. It is not just about money either, though this is of course important. He is seen as approachable, available and open. Fifa has historically been seen as a European (and to a lesser extent South American) institution in Asia, and while Infantino is from Uefa, he is seen as a leader who gives equal weight to all. One president said to me that in the past, conversations with Fifa were like receiving decrees from above but now there is a genuine dialogue. World Cup expansion has gone down well, 64 teams would be welcomed too, and there are more tournaments held in Asia these days. Infantino has already been reminding Asia about this. JD Concacaf Infantino’s most direct relationship has been as the president under whom the World Cup was awarded to the US, Mexico and Canada, after a bid from the US lost out to Qatar for the 2022 hosting rights. Aside from that, there was not much of a direct, historic relationship between Infantino and Concacaf – at least, not until the letter released by the confederation over the weekend. AA CAF Infantino’s association with African football began in 2016, when he backed Ahmad Ahmad of Madagascar to topple the late Issa Hayatou as CAF president in March 2017. Being an eyewitness to that election, at the African Union HQ in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, I recall the anger with which Hayatou confronted Infantino and Fatma Samoura, then Fifa secretary general, over their involvement in an election. Infantino, under Ahmad’s ill-fated four-year tenure between 2017 and 2021 – which ended in his untimely removal from office over ethics violations – got Fifa to take over the daily administration of the CAF from August to December 2019, with Samoura going to Egypt to take charge of the organisation. Many in African football saw this as a neo-colonial act and a direct violation of the CAF’s autonomy and independence. Infantino was involved in the ascension of Motsepe to the presidency in March 2021. OO Conmebol Along comes Infantino, the Uefa salvation who promises an anti-corruption ticket. After Julio Grondona’s death, an AFA (Argentina Football Association) election found more votes than members and Fifa intervened, naming a committee of industry insiders to oversee a cleansing of the house. Infantino was present in the AFA headquarters at its inaugural press conference. Imagine Infantino launching an English FA governance intervention. In 2018, in Buenos Aires for a Libertadores final to be played by two clubs from the same city for the first time in Argentina’s history (policing was a mess and fan violence before the second leg led to its suspension and eventual move to Madrid) Infantino was invited by the then president of Argentina, Mauricio Macri, to be guest of honour at the G20 held in the city later that week. Infantino, as we know him today is created then, photographed gifting football shirts to the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman and Donald Trump, POTUS at the time. “Yes, that G20 was key for Infantino, because he’d inherited a corruption scandal. He needed to instil the belief that football would cease to be a mafia, that he would achieve this. And he managed,” Macri, now president of the Fifa Foundation, told the Guardian: “From an ethical point of view he is impeccable. There is nothing odd in Fifa today, Fifa manages fortunes, more than ever, because Infantino is successful; he organises competitions that are more and more profitable, and it’s all above board. I should say the same applies to Conmebol.” The Conmebol president, Nicolás Leoz, fell in the same Fifagate swoop, although he had left office in 2013. A series of interim and short-lived presidencies ensued until January 2016 when current president Domínguez took his post. Unanimously voted in by the 10 member associations, he pushed for every professional club to have a female team and introduced “hydration” breaks before this World Cup, albeit less structured ones. Infantino has also maintained a functional and stable relationship with the AFA president, Claudio “Chiqu” Tapia. “This relationship is politically relevant because Macri has been an opponent of “Chiqui” Tapia,” Mendez says. “This demonstrates Infantino’s ability to maintain links with both sides of Argentine football’s internal power structure.” Tapia was approached for comment. MMA OFC Like Asia, Infantino has worked hard to build relationships both of the personal and financial kind. It is common to hear officials describe him as a friend. The expansion of the World Cup to 48 teams finally gave Oceania an automatic World Cup spot – something that Fifa had promised in the past but never delivered. And the idea of having more spots in a 64-team competition was also attractive. Under Infantino, New Zealand co-hosted the Women’s World Cup with Australia. Fifa also supported the establishment of the Oceania Professional League that kicked off in January to provide much-needed pro club football for the region. JD 3) How financially dependent is the confederation on Infantino and Fifa? Uefa Not at all. While the World Cup is Fifa’s most essential driver of revenue, Uefa can lay claim, among other things, to the highly lucrative Champions League and the vast sums that it attracts on an annual basis. Expanding its tournaments and staging them more often is one of the only ways available for Fifa to keep pace. Private investment would not harm its cause, either. Uefa’s annual revenues have recently totalled around double those of Fifa; as things stand football’s powerhouse can cope perfectly well on its own. NA AFC Like always in Asia, it varies. There are rich federations on either side of the continent but in between there are some that are almost completely dependent on Fifa money. Bhutan, for example, gets $1.5m a year, which makes up the majority of its budget. Even Australia, which has reached the knockout stages of the past two World Cups, has lost around $17m over the past two years, which may explain its rather vague statement calling for more time when the plan was first heard. JD Concacaf This is a very top‑heavy confederation, perhaps more so than any other in the world. The US and Mexico have been regional powers for most of the past 30‑40 years, and recently Canada has shown signs it can compete on the field and is addressing business issues off of it. Just below them is a middle class consisting of Panama, Jamaica, Costa Rica and Honduras. The remaining 33 Concacaf nations are fairly small by comparison, and thus naturally more reliant on funding from Fifa via the forward programme and other initiatives. The fact that smaller Caribbean nations feel empowered to join with the big dogs says a lot about how at risk they feel they may be without Infantino at Fifa’s helm. AA CAF The confederation funds activities from its own commercial revenue, so it is not dependent on Fifa and Infantino in that sense. But the majority of CAF’s 54 member associations are financially challenged and are dependent on the annual grants that the world governing body gives them to meet their operating costs. OO Conmebol It represents only 10 nation members. Variations among them notwithstanding, the federations are self-sufficient economically and their local leagues are attractive and profitable. Their national teams are the No 1 sporting attraction, pulling in vast numbers of fans who are emotionally attached to their heroes, who in turn love to play for their country. The main sources of revenue for clubs are TV rights, marketing and the sale of players. For this, the top market is the Premier League (which operates entirely outside the FA and therefore Fifa) and the other European leagues, which are also largely independent of their FAs. Montevideo has produced more World Cup players than any other city in history, so even a financially struggling association such as Uruguay’s continues to rely more on the income from the development of youth talent than Fifa aid. There were six Argentinian managers with extensive international trajectories at this World Cup. Exporting home‑grown talent, of which there is plenty, is a bigger source of revenue than Fifa project distribution funds. Two of the most colourful stories of the World Cup, the Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha and the New Zealand defender Tim Payne, transferred to Chilean and Paraguayan clubs respectively following their popularity during the tournament. Popularity due in no small part to the efforts of streamers and influencers from Argentina and Brazil. MMA OFC Oceania is made up of small federations that tend to be reliant on what Fifa gives them. So the recent World Cup proposal would, had it gone through, have made a huge difference financially. JD 4) Would a breakaway cause an existential threat? Uefa Europe has the strongest club and international teams in the world. Parting ways from Infantino and Fifa would be unlikely to cause serious damage, although it could cause issues with clubs who have been looking to expand their global reach through the revamped Club World Cup. It is plausible that bigger teams from other continents would seek to join forces with Uefa and compete in new tournaments given the kudos and financial opportunities available when competing with the majority of the sport’s giants. NA AFC It is a generalisation but, in Asia, Fifa as an institution does not make the headlines that it does in western Europe. Usually, interest in a country comes when they are affected specifically by a decision, as when bidding for a tournament. In my experience, there just isn’t the same interest in the day‑to‑day running of the organisation. Breaking with Infantino would not be a massive threat to Asia but there is some concern about a return to a more Europe‑dominated Fifa, if that were to materialise. While pretty much everyone has supported Infantino from 2016 until the past few days, Asian federations that have done so are seen in some quarters as being corrupt and/or greedy but the Europeans, who did exactly the same, are now trying to paint themselves as the moral guardians of the sport. JD Concacaf If a breakaway would cause an existential threat, then Concacaf is living it right now. One could certainly read it as a principled stand, but it’s hard to separate the confederation’s statement with Montagliani’s current position as Infantino’s most likely successor, should the latter need to stand down. AA CAF The relationship between Infantino and Africa’s 54 national associations is largely seen as a “master-servant” one, in which he basically tells the FA/federation heads, through Fifa officials, to do his bidding. Those who do not toe the political line of Zurich, as decided by Infantino, may well end up having their books audited over how they have spent their Fifa grants. Many FA/federation presidents faced Fifa ethics proceedings and subsequent bans as a result. OO Conmebol “There’s no morality involved, just politics,” the industry insider says. Mendez concurs: “It’s not a simple case of morality, it’s a power struggle and a rupture in perspectives about football in general and the business of football in particular. Today, Eurocentrism is dominating, and things like sponsored hydration breaks and Super Bowl-style half-time shows impose a North American regard hitherto unseen.” MMA OFC Oceania welcomed the fact that Infantino had a “global” mentality and went out of his way to engage with smaller nations far from the centre of global football power. If the confederation does break away, it would want something similar in the opposition candidate and not a return to the old days when the confederation was an afterthought in the corridors of power. JD 5) How important is the current and historical relationship? A strong relationship between Uefa and Fifa would make for a far more harmonious global football scene but, as described above, there is huge work to do before that can be repaired. NA It’s very important – barring some new organisation stepping in to run world football in a better way, Fifa is Concacaf’s best link to the traditional power centres of world football. The US, Mexico and Canada derive a lot of their value as federations from how they’ve been able to perform at men’s and women’s World Cups – that’s not something they’ll want to give up lightly, which is perhaps why they did not threaten a boycott the way Uefa did. AA CAF Africa’s political power within Fifa began to rise in 1974, when João Havelange successfully courted the continent as a block and made it an important pillar of his electoral victory over Sir Stanley Rous in Germany, becoming the first and only non-European, to date, to be Fifa president. Sepp Blatter, Havelange’s successor in 1998, also leveraged Africa’s support in a similar fashion to defeat the Uefa president Lennart Johansson. Delivering on his promise to the continent that it would host a World Cup during his presidency, which South Africa did in 2010, bolstered his popularity and support base on the continent. But the last 10 years of the Infantino presidency have made many resent the undue influence of the world governing body in Africa’s affairs. OO Conmebol Fifa as we know it was essentially invented, developed and moulded by the Brazil and Argentina federation presidents Havelange and Grondona respectively. They specifically wanted to break Europe’s stronghold. Initially, they started funding grassroots via “partnerships” with big brands, which benefited from reaching wider markets. A vivid example is the giant sign with a Coca-Cola bottle on every corner of the pitch, seen in places such as Russia and China where advertising was otherwise prohibited, every single time a corner kick was awarded. After Havelange’s time at the helm was up, Blatter took the lead. Blatter kept Grondona close by, his right-hand man, while the business venture grew and grew, and places for other confederations increased. When Fifagate blew up, most leaders close to the top faced trials and disgrace; Grondona was saved by death. Infantino’s reign was a continuation of keeping Conmebol as a key ally. The historic power derived from on-the-pitch success in the region, and the crown jewel that is Lionel Messi, have contributed to keeping the small confederation big. “The relationship is neither purely personal nor purely institutional. It is built on mutual strategic value,” says Mendez. “The coming election will be Uefa versus footballistic populism,” the industry source said. “Conmebol owns Fifa.” MMA

title: Man charged in Washington state with starting largest wildfire in the area
author: Richard Luscombe
summary: Suspect had a prior conviction for shooting his father in Arizona, reportedly after he told his son to do the dishes
body_text: Authorities on Monday charged a man in Washington state with starting a wildfire that has consumed almost 4,000 acres and forced tens of thousands from their homes. Aaron Farinacci, 37, of Spokane, was arrested and charged with first-degree arson for setting the Old Trails fire, the largest of three devastating wildfires burning through the region. He was found in possession of waterproof matches and a butane lighter – and was identified by witnesses who spotted him kneeling in grass close to where the blaze began over the weekend. At a press conference on Monday night, John Nowels, the Spokane county sheriff, said Farinacci had been apprehended quickly. “As it happens in so many critical cases, it was citizens who were paying attention to their surroundings, being aware and willing to step up and say something that led to the relatively quick apprehension of Mr Farinacci,” Nowels said. “This was fantastic, very quick work by everybody involved.” Nowels also offered details of the suspect, including that he had a prior conviction in Arizona for manslaughter. According to the Phoenix New Times, the victim was Farinacci’s father, who was shot and killed at their Mesa home in 2010, reportedly after telling his son to do the dishes. Farinacci was later found injured by a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Farinacci, then aged 21, pleaded guilty in 2012 to manslaughter and aggravated assault. A judge found he was mentally fit to assist in his own defense, though defense lawyer Jose Colon continued to raise questions about his mental health and said that he had been hospitalized multiple times for psychiatric treatment, court records show. Beth Farinacci, who had married Aaron Farinacci’s father, said second-degree murder, not manslaughter, would have been a more appropriate way to resolve that case. “Manslaughter is for when someone accidentally kills another person. It is not for someone who intentionally points a loaded gun at their father and shoots him in his face and back,” she wrote in a letter to the judge. It was also reported that Aaron Farinacci had been contacted by police twice before during fire investigations. Spokane police responded to reports of several fires on 8 July 2025, near Farinacci’s apartment. The area near the Spokane River involved several “bus-sized” fires and prompted a significant emergency response, according to a police record. The Washington state patrol made contact with Farinacci the following month while pursuing a suspect in a wildfire at Riverside state park. They found him on a park bench, “seemingly out of breath from possibly running”. They took photos of him. He was wearing a green T-shirt just like the one he was seen wearing on Saturday, the document says. Farinacci was expected to make his first court appearance Tuesday, Nowels said, as crews continued to battle the fires that have expanded across the county. The Old Trails fire started on Saturday north-west of downtown Spokane. The blaze jumped the Spokane River and ripped through neighborhoods that some residents were able to return to on Monday. “There’s nothing to save,” said Miriam Sim, 76, as she and her husband, Daniel Sim, surveyed the ruined home where they had lived since 2005. In one Spokane neighborhood, blackened vehicles, a boat twisted by the heat and melted plastic recycling bins remained. Across the street, lawns were still green and houses were spared, as residents continued to run hoses or sprinklers to water their properties. More than 67,000 people were told to evacuate the three fires – Old Trail, Autumn Lane and Fairview – that by early Tuesday had burned about 16 sq miles (41 sq km) of Spokane, although orders in some areas were downgraded late on Monday. Elsewhere across the state, where extreme high temperatures and a fourth year of drought conditions have taken hold, at least 15 wildfires were burning, covering at least 390 sq miles. Washington state’s entire congressional delegation wrote to Donald Trump on Monday urging the president to approve an expedited emergency declaration. Bob Ferguson, the state’s Democratic governor, said he spoke to the White House over the weekend after making his own emergency declaration. “Hundreds of people have completely lost their homes and farms, and many are prohibited from returning to their homes or neighborhoods as crews continue to extinguish smoldering embers,” the politicians’ letter said. No deaths or major injuries have been reported, although Cpl Mark Gregory, a spokesperson for the Spokane sheriff’s office, said on Monday that 14 remained unaccounted for. They were, he said, probably people who had not been in contact since evacuating and were not truly missing or in danger. More than 1,000 firefighters, many from out of state, arrived by Monday to help tackle the blazes, a number expected to double in the coming days, authorities said. Crews continued to fight the fires by land and air, with Nowels warning the public during the Monday press conference not to interfere with aerial operations by using drones. A bulletin issued by the National Weather Service (NWS)’s Spokane office on Tuesday morning warned that challenging conditions would persist through the remainder of the week. “Extensive amounts of smoke will continue over the region, maintaining unhealthy air quality,” it said. “Dry conditions and breezy winds increase Friday and Saturday across portions of central Washington, bringing elevated fire weather conditions.” Hundreds of homes, businesses, and other structures have been destroyed in what Dave Upthegrove, Washington’s commissioner of public lands, called “an extraordinary wildfire season across the Pacific north-west”. The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Ohio Republican Max Miller faces growing calls to resign over domestic abuse allegations
author: Robert Tait in Washington and Coral Murphy Marcos
summary: Miller calls women accusing him liars as Republican senator Bernie Moreno says former son-in-law unfit for Congress
body_text: Max Miller, the beleaguered US Republican representative from Ohio, has vowed to defy a rising groundswell of resignation calls from his own party over domestic abuse allegations after his ex-father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, a GOP senator, said he was unfit to serve in Congress. In a combative interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper, Miller turned the tables by attacking Moreno, accused three women – including his ex-wife – of lying by saying he had been violent towards them, and invoked Donald Trump in insisting that he would not resign. As a deadline loomed for party leaders to choose a potential replacement, Miller, a former White House aide, took an unapologetic stand a day after Trump himself brought pressure to bear by calling him and reportedly telling him “things aren’t looking good” for his re-election campaign against his Democratic opponent, Brian Poindexter. The congressional ethics committee launched an investigation into allegations that Miller “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use in violation of the code of official conduct or any other applicable standard of conduct”, it said on Tuesday. Earlier in the day, Miller said he would request an ethics investigation into himself “to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family”, adding: “I have absolutely nothing to hide.” Pleas for Miller to step down intensified after Moreno – the father of Miller’s former wife, Emily Moreno – broke his silence after months of refraining from comment on allegations concerning the alleged abuse of his daughter. “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” Moreno, an ally of Trump, posted on Sunday. “He should not serve in the House of Representatives.” Addressing reporters on Tuesday, Moreno described the dispute between his daughter and Miller as “truly the seventh level of hell”, adding: “This has been a horrific experience for my entire family. “This has been brutal beyond comprehension, and if there’s any minimum standard for being an elected official, as I said, he fails to meet that minimum basic standard.” Moreno said he had to handle the pickup of his granddaughter at a police station this weekend because he didn’t “want my daughter interacting with this man”. “I don’t know what this guy’s capable of,” he said. Moreno’s comments came after Miller posted a livestream video defending himself against the abuse accusations and saying his former wife had “significant mental-health challenges”. The senator also accused Miller of withholding a blue bunny from his small daughter that he said helped the toddler go to sleep – an allegation that drew a belligerent response from Miller when Tapper asked on The Lead if he had been guilty of “emotionally abusive behavior”. “I would agree that if that were true, that would be incredibly disturbing, and that the senator would be right,” Miller said. “However, he has taken two years to publicly acknowledge for me to resign from my seat. Why is that?” After a prolonged back-and-forth, Miller gave an unambiguous response when asked if Emily Moreno and two other women – including Stephanie Grisham, a former White House spokesperson in Trump’s first presidency – had lied in accusing him of treating them violently. “Yes, it’s very easy … Every single time, and people have asked me, what are you going to do? Are you going to drop out of this race? Are you going to resign? Are you going to get out before the deadline? And my answer to you, Jake, is no, and I can tell you why. “In 2016, when President Donald J Trump faced the most extreme allegations in the world that hit him day after day after day, and people in the media, very much like yourself and others, said that he would have no shot at winning, that he should not be the president of the United States. But guess what? He stayed in, and he was resilient. “So for no second am I going to sit here and continue to be debased by false and baseless allegations, and be pushed out of the seat I have worked so hard to represent and done a terrific job for our community.” Yet a series of public statements from Moreno’s fellow Republican senators indicate that their sympathies are with him. “[Miller] should resign. He should quit,” Roger Marshall, a senator from Kansas, told Politico. “I don’t know Mr Miller’s story, but I trust Bernie [Moreno] so much as a good friend, and his family has such high values.” The West Virginia senator Shelley Moore Capito said: “I don’t know [Miller]. I haven’t read a whole lot about him, but if [Moreno] thinks he ought to resign, I’m supportive of that.” Lisa Murkowski, a Republican senator from Alaska, said: “The accusations are very serious, and if there is truth to them, I am one who says that our elected officials need to be held to high standards. “And certainly, when it comes to allegations of domestic abuse, child abuse, that’s not what we want in our lawmakers.” Three other senators, Rick Scott of Florida, West Virginia’s Jim Justice and Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, also gave public backing to Moreno against Miller. “I don’t know enough about the allegations, but like Bernie said, it sounds like he thinks he needs psychological help,” said Scott. “I trust Bernie.” Miller – who married Emily Moreno at Trump’s club in Bedminster, New Jersey, in 2022 – has been accused of holding a gun to her head and scalding her with boiling water. Their toddler daughter, who was born in 2023, is also said to have suffered a broken collarbone due to his actions. Miller denies allegations of abuse and has filed a defamation case against his wife over the claims. The couple divorced in 2025. Axios reported that Trump called Miller on Monday amid concerns that the situation threatened Republican chances of holding the congressional seat in November’s midterms, when the party already faces an uphill challenge to keep its wafer-thin majority in the House of Representatives. But the president avoided taking sides when asked about the issue by reporters in the White House. “I know Max, he’s a good person. I mean, I always thought he was a very good person. And I’m going to let the families figure that out,” he said. Miller has resisted calls for him to withdraw from the race and told the Wall Street Journal that Trump “was supportive of me over the phone” on Monday’s call. “He said he had a poll with no detail, and I pushed back with our poll that has us winning by 9 with our message out there,” Miller told the newspaper. “He kept on reiterating it’s going to be tough, and it’s going to be a really hard one for you.” If Miller were to remove his name from the ballot before the close of business on Tuesday, a special Republican primary would be held to replace him. If he were to withdraw after that, the party would still need to replace him by 10 August, but would need to give two days’ notice beforehand to hold a meeting to choose a substitute candidate. • In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.

title: US revokes Brazil ambassador’s visa in escalation of diplomatic feud
author: David Smith Washington bureau chief
summary: Move is retaliation for Lula’s government refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília
body_text: Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US in a sharp escalation of a diplomatic feud with the country’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The US state department said Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti’s visa had been cancelled in retaliation for Brazil’s refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília and its decision last month to deny visas to two US diplomats seeking to visit ahead of an October election. The Trump administration stopped short of expelling Viotti, a former senior United Nations official. But Washington warned that further diplomatic action remains possible if Brasília continues to withhold its approval for would-be ambassador Daniel Perez, a Florida Republican and close ally of the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio. “We communicated continually with the Brazilian government for weeks and have given the Brazilian government every opportunity to do the right thing, yet they have continually delayed and obfuscated,” a state department spokesperson said. The ambassador’s visa could be restored if Brazil accepts Perez’s appointment. “This is a reciprocal action,” the spokesperson said. “Should the ambassador leave the country, she would need to reapply for a visa.” The dispute has become entangled with Brazil’s increasingly bitter election campaign, in which Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, and a close political ally of Trump. Brasília swiftly condemned the US action as part of a deliberate campaign to influence the election. Lula’s office said: “Today’s decision is not an isolated incident. It is part of a deliberate escalation of hostile measures against Brazil, motivated by ideological reasons.” Brazil also accused the US of breaching diplomatic norms by announcing Perez’s nomination before seeking Brasília’s consent. The Brazilian government said its consideration of the appointment was still under way, and that it had been made clear no decision would be taken before the first round of the election, on 4 October. The Trump administration argues that Brazil has no right to interfere with the president’s choice of US ambassador to the country. “President Trump has the right to determine who represents the American people and interests around the world,” the state department said. “We reject any effort by foreign countries to interfere in our domestic processes.” The latest confrontation follows Brazil’s refusal last month to issue visas to Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, and one of his senior aides. The US officials had planned to visit Brasília from 27 to 30 July for meetings with government officials, religious leaders and others about election integrity, religious freedom and freedom of expression. Washington described the trip as routine, and rejected Brazilian claims that it was intended to interfere in the election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” the state department said at the time. Brasília has stood by its decision, saying the officials intended to cast doubt on the integrity of Brazil’s electronic voting system in what it called an “unacceptable attempt to interfere in the national political process”. The row is particularly sensitive because Jair Bolsonaro and his supporters have spent years alleging, without evidence, that Brazil’s electronic voting system is vulnerable to fraud. He has been barred from standing for office and was convicted over a plot to overturn his defeat in the 2022 election. The diplomatic confrontation is the latest in a series of clashes between Trump and Lula, whose governments have sharply diverged over Latin American politics, Venezuela, Cuba and the role of the US in the region. Trump has repeatedly intervened in political contests across Latin America, while Lula has made national sovereignty a central theme of his campaign. The Brazilian president has blamed Rubio for some of the administration’s actions against his government, although he has sought to avoid a direct personal confrontation with Trump, and has said the two men got on well when they first met. Economic pressure has added to the tensions. The Trump administration has imposed tariffs of up to 37.5% on thousands of Brazilian exports, citing what it says are unfair trade practices and failures to prevent forced labour. Lula’s government has rejected the allegations, and accused Trump’s administration of trying to help Bolsonaro’s political family. The US has also classified Brazil’s two biggest drug-trafficking organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, a move opposed by Lula’s government. Yet the state department insists that it still wants to restore a normal relationship with Brasília. “We want to be back in a situation where we have a normal, productive, transparent relationship with our colleagues,” a senior US official said.

title: Wesley Bell wins Missouri House primary as Cori Bush comeback bid fails
author: Chris Stein
summary: Democratic incumbent wins in St Louis rematch dominated by Israel-Palestine issue
body_text: The Democratic congressman Wesley Bell won his primary in the St Louis area on Tuesday, ending the progressive former representative Cori Bush’s bid for a comeback and blunting the momentum pro-Palestinian candidates have shown in recent elections. Bell unseated Bush, a democratic socialist who opposes aid to the US ally and accuses it of committing a genocide in Gaza, in the Democratic congressional primary two years ago with the help of millions of dollars in spending from pro-Israel groups. Their rematch this year came amid a spate of primary defeats of Democratic incumbents at the hands of progressive outsiders. On Tuesday, according to the Associated Press, Bell prevailed in the heavily Democratic district, making him the favorite to win a second term in the November election. “St Louis is up against a president that is coming after our healthcare, our due process and the paychecks of working families,” he said, vowing to “keep standing up to this reckless and cruel administration every single day”. Amid a wave of anti-establishment sentiment, Bell’s victory bucks the trend, notching a win for moderate and pro-Israel Democrats. “Tonight’s result is another clear victory for Democrats who are focused on delivering results,” said the New Democrat Majority, a political action committee (Pac) that supports the centrist New Democrat Coalition, which invested $1m in the contest to defeat Bush. “Wesley Bell is focused on fighting to deliver for Missouri families, not fighting his own party.” Bush was first elected to the House in 2020 and served two terms as a member of “the Squad” of progressive lawmakers of color. The former congresswoman had sought to make the race a referendum on Bell’s support for US aid to Israel, working to channel progressive fury over pro-Israel spending on her opponent’s behalf. The United Democracy Project, a Super Pac aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), poured about $3m into helping Bell’s campaign overwhelm Bush on the airwaves. In a post on X, Aipac congratulated Bell on his victory. Bell was also backed by House Democratic leadership and the Congressional Black caucus, while Bush drew support from the Democratic Socialists of America and other progressive groups. The two candidates had squared off over who would better stand up to Donald Trump and spur growth in the St Louis region, which is managing the aftermath of a deadly tornado last year. On the campaign trail, Bell, a former county prosecutor, criticized Bush for voting against Joe Biden’s 2021 infrastructure bill, and for a comment in which she appeared to link both Biden and Kamala Harris to “fascism”. Bush said she opposed the infrastructure bill only because it did not contain spending on social services that Biden had promised, and that her words about the former president and vice-president were taken out of context. Bush hit back by accusing Bell of having his seat bought for him by Aipac. The congressman has said he is in favor of supporting Israel while opposing Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, and insisted that the group’s spending was not dictating his policy positions.

title: ‘Won’t happen’: One Nation Victoria leader’s comments raise questions about Hanson’s mass deportations policy
author: Josh Butler and Benita Kolovos
summary: Exclusive: Warren Pickering told 2025 podcast mass deportations ‘not a reality’ in Australia and suggested politicians over 55 should ‘handball it to the next generation’
body_text: One Nation’s Victorian leader has previously said mass deportations in Australia are “not a reality” and “won’t happen”, in newly unearthed comments which raise further questions about Pauline Hanson’s signature policy to deport 75,000 people she says have overstayed visas. Warren Pickering, on Monday unveiled as the party’s leader for Victoria’s November state election, also previously conceded in niche podcast interviews that the party ran so-called “ghost candidates” who didn’t actively campaign in order to harvest more Senate votes. Pickering, whose party’s federal leader Hanson is aged 72, also suggested politicians over age 55 were no longer the “finger on the pulse demographic” and should “handball it to the next generation”. “People have had a gutful of these dinosaurs, these 70-year-old elites in the major political parties that are still pulling the strings,” Pickering told the Carly Unfiltered podcast in April 2025. Pickering, a former federal Senate candidate for One Nation and the party’s state president, will run for the ultra-marginal seat of Pakenham. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email In comments which raise further questions about One Nation’s federal immigration policy, Pickering told another podcast in April 2025 that while he supported the party’s goals to “abolish multiculturalism” and deport 75,000 people, he believed mass deportations would not occur. “I’ve heard people talk about remigration and and things like that,” Pickering told conservative podcast WilmsFront, connected to rightwing nationalist website The Unshackled. The host interjected “mass deportations”, to which Pickering responded: “Look, it’s just not a reality. “You’re not going to see it in any western country. You can advocate for it all you like, but it won’t happen,” he said. “The reality is we don’t need to isolate those people, that are new Australians, from our communities. If you want them to ultimately to assimilate to the Australian culture and the Australian way of life, you can’t isolate them.” Pickering went on to say One Nation would “not discriminate against people that are already Australian citizens”. Hanson’s office and Pickering were contacted for comment and clarification of the party’s policy. Guardian Australia last week revealed One Nation senator Malcolm Roberts has repeatedly advocated for “remigration” of international students and people overstaying visas. In one interview, Roberts said of visa overstayers: “That’s 100,000 we would deport, remigrate. Call it what you want.” Asked in a recent Channel Seven interview about the concept of mass deportation, Hanson said: “I love it.” However One Nation has consistently declined to detail how it would enact such a policy. In the same WilmsFront episode, and a separate 2022 interview with the podcast, Pickering admits One Nation ran some “ghost candidates” in election campaigns – which he described as “non-active candidates” – in a bid to boost its upper house votes. As Guardian Australia has reported, One Nation is known to run “ghost candidates” in many seats to secure the public funding entitlement. While these candidates are real people – usually taken from the party’s membership base – they are largely invisible on the hustings. “The more lower house representatives you can sport, the more likely you are to pick up Senate votes … we had quite a few electorates where for one reason or another, nobody either stepped forward or the person that stepped forward decided it was probably not worth them taking the time off work and coughing up the money to to potentially not get those funds back,” Pickering said in 2022. The host said media described this tactic as “the ghost candidate”, to which Pickering replied: “This is what I’m alluding to.” In the 2025 interview, Pickering claimed “most parties do run non-active candidates in certain seats”. He said while the party had grown its candidate ranks since the 2022 poll, they were “running as many physical candidates as we possibly can”. “We do have a couple of seats that there isn’t an active candidate,” Pickering said in 2025, saying the tactic “ultimately it does helps us achieve our our upper house bid”. During the Carly Unfiltered interview, in a discussion about social demographics, Pickering said older politicians should “handball” to younger representatives. “I’m not saying you can’t add value, what I’m saying is that I think people need to get involved in politics a lot younger, carry the baton for a few years, and once you get to sort of that 55 and above [age] it’s probably then time to start thinking about training the next generation, which we’ve had made a conscious effort to do at One Nation,” he said. “We need people to get involved much younger, carry the baton for seven to 10 years or whatnot, and then train up the next generation and hand it over before you fall outside of that demographic.” Hanson is 72 years old. Her Senate colleague Roberts is 71, Barnaby Joyce is 59 and newly elected David Farley is 69. Hanson has been in the Senate since 2016, after first being elected to the lower house in 1996. Roberts was first elected to the Senate in 2016, and has served eight years after being disqualified partway through his first term then being re-elected in 2019. Joyce has served in parliament since 2005. Pickering was among eight candidates unveiled by Hanson at a press conference on Monday. One Nation banned the ABC, the Age and the Guardian from attending the event, with Pickering threatening to sue media organisations that published “blatant character assassination attempts” of candidates. While a press release initially said Pickering would lead the party’s upper house ticket in eastern Victoria, it was later confirmed the position will be filled by Greg Hansford, who ran for One Nation at the 2025 federal election. Hansford stood at the 2022 federal election in May for One Nation and at the state election in November for the Freedom party, which ran on an anti-lockdown and anti-vaccine mandate platform.

title: Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez survives Washington’s crowded primary
author: Lauren Gambino
summary: Two-term Democrat faced attacks from the left and right while defending a House seat in a territory Trump won
body_text: The Democratic representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez secured one of two spots in Washington state’s crowded all-party primary, overcoming criticism from both the left and the right to advance in one of November’s most closely watched US congressional races. The two-term Democrat – known for bucking her party on key issues – heads into the general election as she seeks to defend a district carried by Donald Trump in 2024 and a seat that remains central to the battle for control of the House of Representatives. She will face the Republican state senator John Braun in November. Gluesenkamp Perez faced competing ideological pressures in a sprawling field that included Braun, a navy veteran backed by Trump, and progressive Democrat Brent Hennrich, who mounted a challenge from the left, arguing the US congresswoman had drifted too far from the Democratic party. Six other candidates also appeared on the primary ballot. Under Washington’s primary system, the top two finishers advance regardless of party. “Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is an authentic, independent leader who is fiercely loyal to south-west Washington,” the Washington representative Suzan DelBene, chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said in a statement. “Marie is focused on the issues that matter most to her community, like lowering costs for families, revitalizing Washington’s timber economy, and investing in rural schools and infrastructure.” Gluesenkamp Perez, who has carved out a distinctive political profile, is viewed as one of the most vulnerable House Democrats. Since flipping the Republican-held seat in 2022, she has built support among moderates, independents and some Republican voters, often emphasizing her background as the co-owner of an auto repair shop and breaking with her party on high-profile issues such as immigration, transgender rights and Trump’s elections overhaul bill, known as the Save Act. That approach, however, increasingly alienated parts of her own party. Progressive critics argued she has too often sided with the president and Republicans, while supporters countered that her willingness to stake out opposing views reflected the realities of a district that has consistently backed Trump for president, most recently by about three points. They argue that ideological purity is less important than maintaining a foothold in Trump territory – and a seat that could ultimately help deliver Democrats the House majority in November. In 2024, Gluesenkamp Perez ran roughly seven points ahead of Kamala Harris, her party’s presidential nominee. Democrats hope Trump’s poor approval ratings, and frustration with the economy and the US-Israel war on Iran, will help propel them to power in Congress by winning control of the House and possibly even the Senate. But Republicans see the seat as one of their top pickup opportunities. “John Braun is a navy veteran and job creator, and in November south-west Washington will send Perez’s sputtering political career straight to the scrapyard,” Christian Martinez, a spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said in a statement.

title: El-Sayed holds narrow lead in Michigan Senate primary but race too close to call
author: Rachel Leingang and Joseph Gedeon in Detroit
summary: Abdul El-Sayed and his opponent Haley Stevens were both optimistic late in the evening
body_text: The marquee race for the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan remained too close to call on Tuesday night, with Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, holding a narrow lead over congresswoman Haley Stevens. The battleground state is crucial to the party’s hopes of winning back control of the Senate in November’s midterm elections. The winner of Tuesday’s Democratic primary will face the Republican nominee, former representative Mike Rogers, in November, to succeed the retiring Democratic senator Gary Peters. As ballot counting continued into the early hours of Wednesday morning, hundreds of restless El-Sayed supporters remained at the election watch party at the Majestic Theater in Detroit, as his lead over Stevens remained at a few percentage points. At about 4am local time, El-Sayed had 48.7% of the vote and Stevens 47.3%, with 95% counted, according to the Associated Press. In remarks to supporters, El-Sayed turned his attention from the contentious primary against Stevens to the Republican nominee. He called for the party to unite against Rogers, who he assailed as a “corporate sellout” who “should never see the inside of the US senate”. “We’re going to have to wait a little longer to see the outcome of this race,” El-Sayed said, “but as I look in front of me, I already see the outcome.” Hasan Piker, the streamer and new Democratic kingmaker, as well as the Democratic nominee for Philadelphia’s third district, Chris Rabb, and the Democratic nominee for Colorado’s 1st district, Melat Kiros, were among the crowd listening to El-Sayed speak at length about his American story as the son of Egyptian immigrants. With 13 weeks left before November, El-Sayed argued that however much his supporters may disagree with his Democratic opponent, there was more uniting the left than dividing it. “However we might feel about the campaign we’ve just come through, I want you to understand that it pales in comparison to the cynicism, in comparison to the corporatism, in comparison to the lies that Mike Rogers and Donald Trump are going to tell,” he said. Nearby, at the Hotel Saint Regis, an upbeat Stevens told supporters at her election night event that results may not come until later Wednesday morning. “We knew that this was going to be a close race, and that’s exactly what we’ve got,” she said. “But friends,” she said to loud cheers from the room, “I am feeling good about this race.” El-Sayed, 41, built a grassroots campaign statewide on a message of universal healthcare and getting money out of politics. Stevens, 43, cast herself as a pragmatic problem-solver, and saw her campaign boosted by tens of millions of dollars in outside spending, including from groups affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), the pro-Israel lobbying organization. Rogers, a former Michigan congressman who was also the Republican nominee for Senate in 2024 when he lost to Elissa Slotkin, ran unopposed in the Republican primary. Mallory McMorrow, a Democrat who dropped out of Michigan’s Democratic primary race in July, said it was vital for the party to come together after a bruising campaign to help the ticket win in November. “I voted for great Democrats up and down the ballot, and I made a commitment that whoever wins the Senate race tonight, I will be endorsing as soon as that race is called,” she told CNN. “I will be headed to their election night party to show we all come together after whatever happens tonight, so that we can be a team as we head in November.” McMorrow later endorsed El-Sayed. “Abdul has my full endorsement and support,” she wrote on social media. “This was a brutal primary (believe me, I know). And Trump and Mike Rogers are counting on us staying divided. Let’s prove them wrong by beating Mike Rogers and taking our country back.” With ballots still being counted, the results in Michigan – and in four other states holding elections, including Kansas, Missouri, Virginia and Washington state – were coming into focus. Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic secretary of state, will face John James, a Donald Trump-endorsed congressman, in the state’s open governor’s race after Gretchen Whitmer faced term limits. James has denied the results of the 2020 election where Joe Biden won; most recently, alongside Trump at a rally, James claimed Trump had won Michigan “three times”. In Michigan’s seventh congressional district, progressive organizer William Lawrence beat out two more moderate candidates, former US ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink and Matt Maasdam, a former US Navy Seal. Lawrence secured an endorsement from Bernie Sanders, the progressive Vermont senator. A challenge to the incumbent representative Shri Thanedar in Michigan’s 13th district by Detroit state representative Donavan McKinney remained too close to call. In Missouri and Washington state, the Democratic establishment struck back, blunting a string of progressive victories. In Missouri’s first congressional district, the Democratic congressman Wesley Bell defeated the progressive former representative Cori Bush in a rematch for the St Louis-based seat. Bush had sought to make the contest a referendum on pro-Israel spending and the war in Gaza. “When we think about all of the division that we hear, I think it is important that we focus on what this place can be,” Bell said after his race was called. Meanwhile, in Washington’s third congressional district, blue dog representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez fended off a progressive challenger in her battleground district, prevailing in a crowded all-party primary. She will face Republican John Braun in November. Missouri voters also rejected an amendment that would have required citizens’ initiatives to pass in all congressional districts rather than by a simple statewide majority. In Kansas, state senator Cindy Holscher won the Democratic nomination in the gubernatorial race, beating two other politicians to advance to the general election. And in Virginia, Shannon Taylor won in the first congressional district and Elaine Luria won in the second congressional district, in wins for moderate Democrats.

title: Afternoon Update: Labor plans migration cuts; extent of bird flu disaster revealed; and the secret of immortality
author: Miles Herbert
summary: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here, and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter.
body_text: Good afternoon. Tony Burke was all set to speak at the National Press Club tomorrow – until he wasn’t. The home affairs minister’s address, which would have touched on “managing the migration program”, has now been delayed, reportedly amid political considerations inside the Albanese government. Despite this, the Guardian understands Labor will push ahead with new rules to cut net overseas migration and push temporary residents to leave Australia (figures last month showed net overseas migration numbers were at their lowest since 2022). It is believed the rescheduling of the address will allow Anthony Albanese to help sell any changes as the government seeks to push back on criticism of its record on migration by One Nation and the Coalition. A Labor spokesperson told Guardian Australia the address would probably take place in the next fortnight and “deal with the migration system as a whole”. title: Daniel Andrews defends actions as opposition labels Labor ‘a gangster government’ after Ibac report released
author: Benita Kolovos Victorian state correspondent
summary: Victorian corruption watchdog finds ‘serious and concerning’ conduct by senior Andrews government members in dealings with union boss
body_text: Former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews has defended the actions of senior members of his government, whom the state’s anti-corruption watchdog found engaged in “serious and concerning” conduct in their dealings with the leader of the firefighters’ union. A long-awaited report by the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission, tabled in parliament on Wednesday, stopped short of making any findings of corrupt conduct. But it found senior members of the Andrews government engaged in “serious and concerning” conduct in their dealings with Peter Marshall – the secretary of the United Firefighters Union (UFU) – when negotiating pay deals for the Country Fire Authority (CFA) and Metropolitan Fire Brigade (MFB), and their later amalgamation into Fire Services Victoria (FSV). This included “actions contrary to policy, procedure and codes of conduct, deliberate attempts to conceal and mislead, and the misuse of information”. The findings led the Victorian opposition to claim the state is being led by a “gangster government”. The Operation Richmond report said the investigation began in 2018 following a tip-off that Marshall “blackmailed or otherwise compromised” Andrews “to change his position on the CFA EBA”. But Ibac found no evidence of blackmail and did not substantiate the allegation, which both Andrews and Marshall denied. In a rare public statement on Wednesday afternoon, Andrews said the report found “no evidence whatsoever to to support the false and completely outrageous claims that I had been blackmailed to force a favourable outcome” for the UFU and its members. “These claims were baseless when they were made almost a decade ago, and they remain baseless today,” he said. Andrews said he acted in the public interest to resolve the “spiteful and dysfunctional enterprise bargaining dispute” that had “dragged on for years” between the CFA and the UFU. “Fire chiefs were spending more time in the Fair Work Commission than running their organisations. That was not acceptable to me or to the government when community safety was on the line,” he said. Andrews also defended the amalgamation of the fire services, saying it was done in the “best interest of community safety”. ‘Extraordinary influence’ The report largely centres upon the Andrews government’s first term, following its election win in 2014. During the election, the UFU campaigned heavily against the then-Coalition government over pay and conditions. In February 2015, Labor began negotiations for a new enterprise bargaining agreement (EBA) for the CFA, which the then Brunswick MP, Jane Garrett, oversaw as emergency services minister. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email But the Ibac report said by the end of 2015, negotiations had “reached an impasse” and the UFU had begun industrial action. Efforts to resolve the industrial dispute through Fair Work Commission conciliation and external mediation failed and in early 2016, negotiations broke down completely. Andrews told Ibac the relationship between Garrett and the union had become so ‘“dysfunctional” and that he considered “she could play … no useful role in resolving this matter”, so he asked his special minister of state, Gavin Jennings, to take over. The head of the Department of Premier and Cabinet, Chris Eccles, asked his deputy, Tony Bates, to assist Jennings. “At some point I’ve said to [Jennings], ‘You need to go and fix this. This needs to get fixed’,” Andrews told Ibac during an examination. Ibac’s report said Jennings, Bates and Marshall, accompanied by a small team of UFU negotiators, held negotiations over four days in April, “with the first sessions held at a rented meeting space, and the final session on 12 April held in a hotel meeting room”. An unnamed federal Labor senator also attended as an intermediary. On 12 April, Ibac said Jennings sent a text to Andrews that read: “Handshake has occurred – it’s done!”, to which he responded, “Very good”. Ibac said photographs were also taken of the unnamed senator “with full champagne glasses in hand and sparkling wine bottles on the table, toasting towards the camera” with three UFU negotiators. A day later, Marshall met Andrews at 1 Treasury Place with a new “UFU proposal”. Bates told Ibac he had led the development of the draft agreement, which led the anti-corruption watchdog to form the view the meeting was “not genuine but staged”. Ibac found Garrett and some cabinet members, who signed off on the EBA proceeding through to the next step of the bargaining process, were not told of Jennings’s negotiations. In a lawfully intercepted phone call in March 2019, Marshall gave an account of the origin of the EBA to a ministerial adviser: “This agreement was negotiated with fuckin’ Jennings in a back room. It was endorsed by fuckin’ Andrews and cabinet.” Garrett resigned from the ministry as she did not want to back an EBA she was opposed to. She died from cancer in 2022. The CFA board, which Ibac said was also unaware of the deal, was dismissed after they failed to endorse the EBA. Ibac said new board was appointed through an “opaque and non-competitive process.” Ibac found the undisclosed deal allowed Marshall to “exert extraordinary influence over the negotiations” and later on the MFB EBA, which ended up with many of the same terms. Ibac’s report also raised concerns about the way the 2019 bill that amalgamated the MFP and paid parts of the CFA into the FRV passed parliament. It found Marshall had sought to secure the support of a crossbench MP by hiring their relative days before it was due for a vote in the upper house. In another intercepted phone call in June 2019, Marshall told a friend the MP was “100 per cent behind us … just to make sure we just employed [their relative].” Marshall, meanwhile, was also granted “privileged access” to MPs, Ibac found, and “sensitive or confidential information” was provided to him once by an MFB board member and twice by Bates,who has since been appointed the secretary of the Department of Education. In a statement on Wednesday, Marshall said Operation Richmond was Ibac’s second report into “myself and the UFU that has concluded no corrupt conduct”. “I feel vindicated by both outcomes, but very disappointed by the damage to my reputation caused by this failed investigation and the constant leaks arising from it.” Victoria has a higher threshold for what constitutes corrupt conduct than in NSW, with Ibac requiring that the conduct would constitute a relevant criminal offence. Ibac “did not establish that the conduct investigated met all required elements to make findings of corrupt conduct”, the report said. The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, called on the premier, Ben Carroll, to sack Bates. “This report today demonstrates that this is a gangster government. Corruption is in Labor’s DNA, and Victorians have had enough,” she said. Carroll told reporters on Tuesday morning Bates had taken a leave of absence. He said the report was “10 years in the making” and he was “not in the cabinet when all of these matters began”. While he said he was yet to read the report, the behaviour described was both “poor” and “intolerable”. “I will take action. I will accept the recommendations and get on with implementing them,” Carroll said. The release of the report comes after years of legal attempts by the UFU to keep it secret, including a high court challenge.
