title: ‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon Valley
author: Steve Rose
summary: As Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and their peers have grown richer and more influential, Gil Durán argues they have all but abandoned democracy – and found the perfect government to enable them
body_text: In April, Gil Durán was permanently banned from Elon Musk’s X for posting just two words. Durán was responding to a post from the tech company Palantir outlining its 22‑point “technological manifesto”, which praised American “hard power”, western culture and AI weapons, denounced inclusivity and called for compulsory national service. Durán responded: “TLDR: Fascism” (TLDR is short for “too long, didn’t read”). Durán didn’t break any of X’s written rules, he points out over a video call from San Francisco – so much for Musk’s “free-speech absolutism”. His ban might just have had something to do with his preceding tweet, showing the cover of his new book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy. The book’s central argument is that big tech is no longer our friend, as many of its billionaire owners have seized economic and political control and are steering the fate of the planet towards their own bizarre, apocalyptic visions. Fascism is no exaggeration, Durán asserts. He researched multiple definitions – by Umberto Eco, Robert Paxton, Jason Stanley – and decided that Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement ticks all the boxes. “It’s a cult of grievance that seeks to purge its enemies by demonising them through absurd and surreal propaganda that exploits fears over law and order and gender and sexuality in order to seize power and install a permanent hierarchy that fascists consider the moral order of the world and the universe. In addition, you also have this sort of nationalistic, militaristic vibe.” By extension, he says, Silicon Valley is fascist “because they have wholly aligned with a fascist movement. That’s their vehicle for gaining power.” Few could dispute this alignment after seeing the bosses of Meta, Google, Apple, Amazon and OpenAI line up behind Trump at his second inauguration, or Musk’s now shuttered “department of government efficiency” (Doge) being given free rein to conduct mass firings of federal employees, or Palantir’s AI-driven surveillance technology enabling deportations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It’s a cosy relationship, Durán says: the tech titans have helped Trump and his family become billionaires through cryptocurrency and have been given government contracts and freedom from regulation or oversight. In addition, Durán believes, “Silicon Valley has gone fascist because they have adopted an extreme ideology of tech supremacy.” While Maga promises a return to a mythical glorious past, he says, the “technofascists” are promising a mythical glorious future: “We’re going to be in the stars. We’re going to be in space. And all we need is to get rid of anybody who stands in our way as we seek to accelerate technology toward this speedy, violent, God-like transcendence that we will achieve if we can only burn enough energy and enough compute to bring our boom loop into existence.” It sounds almost like a conspiracy theory, but Durán is not short of evidence. Musk making an apparent Nazi salute and describing empathy as “the fundamental weakness of western civilisation”. Palantir’s Peter Thiel writing in 2009 that “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible” and giving a lecture series suggesting Greta Thunberg could be the antichrist. Marc Andreessen, the CEO of the tech investment company Andreessen Horowitz, paraphrasing Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, the co-author of Mussolini’s Fascist Manifesto, in his “Techno-Optimist Manifesto”: “Technology must be a violent assault on the forces of the unknown, to force them to bow before man.” Durán, a journalist and former political adviser, lays out the narrative in exacting detail, outlining the connections between these men (and it is all men) and the origins of their often deeply weird beliefs, many of which view everyone outside their circle or opposed to their agenda as expendable. Unpacking all their overlapping philosophies would take some time, but TLDR: “It’s the idea that what matters more is the billions or trillions of people yet unborn in the future. And the only way they’re going to get to be born is if this elite group of white tech figures and gazillionaires makes the right decisions to make the human race transhuman and multiplanetary through AI and technology,” says Durán. “By becoming a billionaire, they all have this idea that they’re superior to everyone else. They are susceptible to this kind of thinking.” Durán, 50, is almost the opposite: the son of working-class Mexican immigrants in California. He was the first in his family to go to college, having grown up in relative poverty: “It made me tough and gave me an unyielding loyalty to regular people over the many rich and powerful people I’ve spent a lot of my time around.” Durán’s book traces the roots of this movement to two important sources. One is the 1997 book The Sovereign Individual, written by the American investor James Dale Davidson and William Rees-Mogg, the former Times editor and BBC grandee (and father of Jacob). Their book prophesied how digital tools such as the internet and cryptocurrency would pave the way for a privatised, corporatised, unregulated, post-democratic future ruled by rich, powerful, unaccountable individuals. Two decades later, this led to the idea of “network states” – digital realms beyond the jurisdiction of nation states – as popularised by Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at Andreessen Horowitz. The other source is Curtis Yarvin, a former software developer and armchair philosopher with a penchant for psychedelics, sometimes referred to as the godfather of the “dark enlightenment”. In pseudonymous blogs in the late 2000s, Yarvin outlined a worldview in which liberal democracy had failed to deliver progress, partly because institutions such as education and the media had been captured by what he called “the Cathedral”. His proposed solution was a mass firing of government employees (he coined the acronym “Rage”, “retire all government employees”) and the installation of a “national CEO, [or] what’s called a dictator”. Yarvin also mused about a “humane alternative to genocide” to deal with unproductive citizens and has had to deny accusations that he is a white supremacist or supports racist ideologies. Scratch the surface, Durán suggests, and Yarvin’s ideas have much in common with Nazi ideologies, “but updated as rightwing dogma for the blogging age”. Both of these sources might have languished in obscurity had it not been for Thiel, the man at the heart of Silicon Valley’s rightward lurch. He has amassed enormous wealth through a series of investments in tech startups – first PayPal, then Facebook, Spotify, LinkedIn, Palantir and OpenAI, among others. He was the first major tech figure to back Donald Trump, in July 2016, and persuaded others to follow, including Andreessen, who said he spent half his time at Mar-a-Lago in the month after Trump won the 2024 election. Thiel liked The Sovereign Individual so much that he wrote a new introduction when it was reprinted in 2020. He has also made steps to found his own network state – first via the ill-fated “seasteading” movement (establishing floating countries in international waters) then via Próspera, a “special economic zone” on an island in Honduras. Incorporated in 2017 with permission from the Honduran government and reportedly co-funded by Srinivasan, Andreessen and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Próspera has sought to attract digital startups with loose regulations (appealing to longevity researchers), low taxes and a crypto-friendly economy. Other similar projects have sprung up. In 2021, the president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, hailed the mooted creation of a “Bitcoin City”. In 2023, Trump announced plans to build 10 “Freedom Cities” on government land across the US, with input from Próspera representatives. In 2024, Srinivasan founded a “Network School” in Johor, Malaysia. Thiel also began to absorb Yarvin’s theories about how the political order was preventing progress. In the 2009 essay in which Thiel declared the incompatibility of freedom and democracy, he also said “the vast increase in welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the franchise to women” made capitalist democracy impossible, which did not win him many mainstream supporters. But Yarvin backed up Thiel and the two became friends and allies. “While The Sovereign Individual provided the foundation for the billionaire’s political vision, Yarvin created a blueprint for turning that vision into reality,” Durán writes. Thiel was instrumental in injecting these ideas, and people, into the US government – not least JD Vance, whom Durán describes as “almost entirely a creation of Peter Thiel”. It was Thiel who set up Vance as a venture capitalist, giving him a role at his firm Mithril Capital, then investing in Vance’s own fund, Narya Capital (Tolkien-derived names are a theme with these people). It was Thiel who backed Vance’s move into politics, where he went from condemning Trump as “America’s Hitler” to supporting him and parroting Yarvin’s ideas. “I think that what Trump should do, if I was giving him one piece of advice: fire every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state, replace them with our people,” Vance told the podcaster Jack Murphy in 2021. Durán had observed this Silicon Valley takeover developing and began writing about it in 2024. “I thought this would be a problem in five to 10 years, but when JD Vance got on the ticket, it suddenly took on a new urgency,” he says. Now, it almost feels too late. In 2025, Bloomberg reported that at least 16 men connected to Thiel and his companies occupied positions of power in the Trump administration, including David Sacks, who is now a special adviser for AI and crypto. Musk’s Doge has swung its chainsaw at the government, crypto and AI regulation has all but disappeared, the Trump family are now billionaires and the tech oligarchs have become the Republicans’ largest donors. At the same time, they have become substantial beneficiaries of the very government they once sought to dismantle. Palantir has an estimated $13.7bn in US government contracts; last year, its stock price rose more than 90% in six months. Andreessen is backing dozens of defence companies scooping up government contracts and recently joined the Pentagon’s advisory board. Last week, Musk’s SpaceX received a $1.6bn contract to supply rockets to the US Space Force – on the same day he pledged at least $100m to help Republicans in November’s midterm elections. “It’s a severe cautionary tale about the hazards of privatisation,” says Durán. “The government created these men, especially Elon Musk. And now these welfare kings want to pull up the ladder, want to destroy the very system that made them. This is a massive failure by the US intelligence apparatus – to not see this threat forming from the inside.” Durán, who worked in communications for Kamala Harris when she was California’s attorney general, as well as for the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, blames the Democrats as much as the Republicans. “They have failed tremendously to stand up to billionaire power because the only people as addicted to billionaire money in American politics as the Republicans are the Democrats,” he says. He singles out the California governor, Gavin Newsom, as a prime example of a “Silicon Valley Democrat”: “You don’t see him criticising these guys. He only goes after Trump, Trump, Trump and Vance, Vance, Vance … You want some viral content? Why don’t you go off on Peter Thiel’s weird antichrist obsession?” Even if the Democrats take control after the midterms or the 2028 presidential election, Durán is worried that “these tech fascists will win … because Democrats will not hold them accountable”. On the plus side, the Silicon Valley takeover has not been going that well lately. Network states around the world are losing ground. In 2021, Próspera’s special economic status was repealed by the new president, Xiomara Castro (it is suing the Honduran government for $10.8bn). Two weeks ago, Srinivasan’s Network School was ordered to close (Srinivasan says he is moving it to Kazakhstan). Trump’s Freedom Cities remain unbuilt. One saving grace, says Durán, is that “a lot of these people don’t really have a great grasp of on-the-ground realities”. Nobody really wants to live in a soulless network state, he says: “Why would you be in Kazakhstan instead of San Francisco, which is the global capital of tech?” On the other hand, he points out, the tech billionaires have effectively turned the US into a de facto network state. But they may well have overplayed their hand. “Silicon Valley oligarchs are really vulnerable right now,” says Durán. “People don’t like them. People are starting to rise up against data centres and this vision of an AI apocalypse that kills all the jobs and potentially kills all of humanity. You’re scaring the hell out of people and now they don’t like you. Into that could step a politician to take advantage of that trend and come up with a message that speaks to the concerns of people and against the dark fantasies of the oligarchs.” The question now, he says, “is how we turn the momentum in our favour and against the billionaires. Because they have a plan to win. They think they’re going to succeed.” This could be a radicalising moment: “In fighting against billionaire power, we find the key to all of our problems. Every moment is an important opportunity to wake people up and to start to fight back.” If not, he says, we’ll find ourselves in a situation where “we don’t have democracy, we don’t have an economy and we don’t have a future. If that doesn’t radicalise people, then we deserve what we’re going to get.” • The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy is published on 18 August (Simon & Schuster, £25). title: Let’s call Trump’s approach to Iran what it is: kindergarten diplomacy
author: Moustafa Bayoumi
summary: Amid stop-and-start threats and with a divided staff, it’s clear Trump has no idea how to end a war that shouldn’t have begun
body_text: On Thursday, 23 July, after weeks of escalating attacks between the US and Iran, Donald Trump told a reporter that Iran hadn’t received “enough pain yet”, and he leveled a threat. “I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before,” he warned. “I am close to making a decision.” Then, on Monday 27 July, he called it off. A few days later, on Friday 31 July, Trump said: “We’ll be hitting them very hard. At some point, they’re going to say: ‘We just can’t take it any more.’” This time, it took him just one day to back down. Here we go again. Ever since the US and Israel launched their latest war on Iran on 28 February, the people of the planet have been subjected to Donald Trump’s on-again off-again relationship with raining down catastrophic destruction on the nation. It started on 21 March, when Trump promised to hit Iranian power plants (a war crime, incidentally) unless Iran opened the strait of Hormuz. He delayed that plan for five days, and then another 10 days, before issuing his next threat. That was on 7 April, when he wrote: “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again.” A mere 10 hours later, he walked back that (genocidal) threat. On 17 May, he wrote: “For Iran, the Clock is Ticking, and they better get moving, FAST, or there won’t be anything left of them. TIME IS OF THE ESSENCE!” On 18 May, he wrote that he had been asked by Gulf leaders to “hold off on our planned Military attack of the Islamic Republic of Iran, which was scheduled for tomorrow”. The approach seems as tedious as it does childish, constantly threatening one thing only to back down in a cringey, face-saving effort shortly thereafter. Let’s call it what it is: kindergarten diplomacy. From appearances, it would seem that Trump considers this a strategy. One can only assume he holds out hope that it will achieve an end to this catastrophic conflagration he and Benjamin Netanyahu began. The war is a massive failure, plunging his popularity along with American regional dominance in the Middle East. What’s clear is that Trump hasn’t a clue about how to exit a war he never should have started in the first place. Leadership is needed when difficult decisions must be made, but Trump is not capable of such resolve. Instead, he seems primarily driven to make pronouncements based on the last person he talked to. When Netanyahu visited him in the Oval Office on 21 July, the Israeli prime minister discussed three options for the war with Trump, according to reports: “a (negotiated) deal, continuing the blockade and economic pressures, and a massive strike”, is how a senior Israeli official described the meeting to Reuters. (Let’s not forget that Netanyahu helped convince Trump to start this war back in February.) Two days later, Trump threatened a massive strike (then called it off, then threatened it again). When the president’s threat reappeared, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump on 1 August to argue for de-escalation. Guess what? To no one’s surprise, Trump backed down again. Nixon had his madman theory, in which he sought to project an image of himself as unhinged and irrational to frighten the Soviet Union into concessions. Trump, whether he knows it or not, is turning indecision into his own presidential doctrine. Such indecision is probably in part a reflection of Trump’s unflagging desire to please influential people around him. Trump’s deep-seated need to be liked by those he perceives to be powerful or popular (see: Trump’s meeting with Zohran Mamdani) is, I think, often underappreciated. But there is more behind Trump’s indecision as well. This administration cannot make any of the necessary decisions on Iran because it, along with Trump’s Maga base and the larger Republican party, has been split, as if by a lightning bolt, by the question. Vice-President JD Vance has been the most skeptical in the president’s inner circle of the war. Ever aware of the political winds, the vice-president is said to be carefully watching the rising rightwing criticism of Israel, due in part to this war. Vance went on the popular podcast The Joe Rogan Experience in mid-July and claimed that there was an Israeli government campaign to shape popular opinion in the US about the war. “There are some people within their system, we know beyond a shadow of a doubt, who are manipulating and trying to change American public opinion to keep the war going on indefinitely,” he said. “Not toward any objective, but just indefinitely.” Ever the faithful lieutenant to Trump, Marco Rubio, on the other hand, told Lara Trump on Fox News that the Iranian regime “has never faced a president like President Trump, which is someone that actually takes action”. Trump’s son-in-law and US negotiator Jared Kushner (along with Vance and their fellow negotiator Steve Witkoff) favors reducing the conflict, thereby lowering gas prices and limiting the danger to US armed forces, but just until after the midterm elections, when the war could potentially be ramped up again, according to Israel Hayom. The chairperson of the joint chiefs of staff, Gen Dan Caine, who counseled the president against the war in the first place, is now warning that stockpiles for air defense interceptors are dangerously low due to the war in Iran, putting the men and women in the US military at greater risk. Meanwhile, the Memorandum of Understanding that the US signed with Iran in June has been the subject of fierce Republican opposition, with the Louisiana Republican senator Bill Cassidy calling it “the worst foreign policy blunder in decades”. Even Trump loyalists such as the Texas senator Ted Cruz criticized the memorandum, saying: “The president is receiving some very poor advice on this deal.” And the Maga faithful have grown cold on the war, with only about a third of its voters believing the war is worth the economic cost, according to a Politico poll. Add to this the fact that CNN is now reporting that US military leadership is basically out of ideas about how to proceed with Iran at this point and is soliciting, via a crowdsourcing-type email sent to a group of military analysts, “new creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran”. The report also explains that Trump “has been considering strikes akin to a ‘fireworks’ display’”, which would suggest “a symbolic victory that would allow him to exit the war without actually accomplishing one of his initial aims: ridding Iran of its nuclear program”. Charting a course through the stormy winds of political decision making is what presidents must do all the time. A debacle like the war in Iran, begun with a terrible decision and bringing much unnecessary harm to the people of the region, must eventually be followed by a brave one, however painful it is to this nation or its leadership. A responsible president would make such a choice, even when difficult, and explain the reasoning to the nation. We, unfortunately, do not have serious leaders. And so we are left with kindergarten diplomacy. Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel To Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnist

title: First Thing: Michigan Democratic race in the balance with El-Sayed holding narrow lead
author: Martin Belam
summary: Congresswoman Haley Stevens trails intensely Senate primary as counting continues
body_text: Good morning. A Democratic Senate primary in Michigan remains too close to call, with Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, holding a narrow lead over the establishment-backed congresswoman Haley Stevens. The battleground state is crucial to the party’s hopes of winning back control of the Senate in November. At about 4am local time, El-Sayed had 48.7% of the vote and Stevens 47.3%, with 95% of votes counted, according to the Associated Press. In remarks to supporters, El-Sayed said: “We’re going to have to wait a little longer to see the outcome of this race, but as I look in front of me, I already see [it].” In Missouri, the Democratic congressman Wesley Bell won his primary, ending the progressive former representative Cori Bush’s comeback attempt and blunting the momentum that pro-Palestinian candidates have shown in recent elections. Who won in the crowded primary in Washington state? The Democratic representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez secured one of two spots in the all-party primary, overcoming criticism from both the left and the right. She will face the Republican state senator John Braun in November. Why are citizens being denied a voice in Missouri? The state’s top election official has rejected a petition seeking a statewide referendum on redistricting. Hundreds of thousands of petition signatures had been submitted in an effort to force a vote on whether to use a new US House map approved by the Republican-led state legislature. The Republican secretary of state, Denny Hoskins, said the number submitted did not matter because challenging a congressional map was unconstitutional under Missouri law. US revokes Brazil ambassador’s visa in escalation of diplomatic feud Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US, in a sharp escalation of a diplomatic feud with the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The administration stopped short of expelling Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti. The confrontation is the latest in a series of clashes between Trump and Lula, with their governments sharply diverging over Latin American politics, Venezuela, Cuba and the role of the US in the region. Trump has repeatedly intervened in political contests across Latin America, while Lula has made national sovereignty a central theme of his campaign. What is the dispute about? The US Department of State said Viotti’s visa had been cancelled in retaliation for Brasília’s refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Brazil and its decision last month to deny visas to two US diplomats. Brasília swiftly condemned the decision, calling it part of a deliberate campaign to influence the outcome of the presidential election in Brazil this October. Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term against Flávio Bolsonaro, the senator son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro and a close political ally of Trump. OpenAI pays $3.2m to settle claims it discriminated against US workers OpenAI and a subsidiary will pay $3.2m to settle US government claims they ⁠favored foreign workers with temporary employment visas and discriminated against US job applicants in recruiting and hiring, the justice department has said. The assistant attorney general Harmeet Dhillon said: “This substantial settlement ensures that OpenAI redresses harm and changes its recruitment practices so US workers receive a fair opportunity for highly sought-after technology positions.” OpenAI did ‌not immediately respond to ‌a request for comment. The company denied wrongdoing in the settlement agreement. El Niño could push 50m people into acute hunger before end of 2027 About 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger before the end of next year by the rapidly developing El Niño weather system, according to forecasting. This is in addition to the hundreds of millions of people already facing dangerous levels of hunger, owing to years of drought in parts of Africa and pressure on food prices caused by the Iran war. Even if the forecasted El Niño is less strong than some models predict, it will tip many countries over the edge, adding more than a fifth to the 225 million people in 45 countries in acute food insecurity, the UN’s World Food Programme said on Wednesday. In other news … A Russian attack on Kyiv has killed at least 17 people after Ukraine was unable to shoot down any incoming missiles. The intensifying attacks have prompted Kyiv to plead for more US-made Patriot interceptors. The celebrity blogger Perez Hilton has been hospitalised after apparently livestreaming acts of self-harm on TikTok. The Trump ally Mike Lindell is leaving his role with the MyPillow company to focus on his campaign to become the next governor of Minnesota. Lindell has spent millions of dollars trying to prove the 2020 election was rife with fraud. An armed man has been arrested at Trump’s California golf course. Jeanine John Taele allegedly took photos and videos of the property days before the president’s visit. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reportedly expanded the scope of the largest known cyclosporiasis outbreak in the US to 15 states. Arkansas, Iowa, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire and North Carolina are now said to be affected. Stat of the day: UFC’s White House spectacle led to losses of about $30m, company reveals Freedom 250 at the White House garnered 8.2 million viewers domestically and about 34 million worldwide, making it one of the most-watched mixed martial events of all-time, but led to losses of about $30m, the company’s owners announced. Well Actually: Skip the run – here are six joint-friendly cardio alternatives suggested by experts Whether you’re nursing a joint, have a condition or just don’t feel like running, Rae Witte suggests these exercises to help still get your cardio in. And hobbies can improve your health – Julia Hotz has four tips for choosing one. Don’t miss this: The ‘Cockroach Lord’ who names new species after Tolkien and Pokémon characters The invertebrate of the year 2026 competition is running, and Rebecca Ratcliffe has spoken to Cristian Lucañas, who has discovered multiple species of cockroach in the Philippines. He believes there is far more to the much-maligned insect than meets the eye. Here are six mind-bendingly amazing facts about invertebrates to intrigue you, but in my book this “immortal” jellyfish is going to take some beating. … or this: Protesters occupy 200-year-old tree at US-Mexico border to stop its destruction Protesters are staging a “tree sit” in a tiny Arizona town to prevent the destruction of a grove of ancient cottonwood trees as federal contractors race to build a row of two 30ft walls along the border with Sonora, Mexico. Climate check: Three lions die of suspected heatstroke at Tokyo zoo as Japan swelters Three lions from a Tokyo zoo have died from suspected heatstroke as Japan swelters. Japan experienced its hottest summer on record last year, and in recent weeks parts of the country have hit 40C, qualifying for the new “cruelly hot day” designation. Last Thing: AI-generated stories rated better quality than human-written ones, study finds In a development that sounds rather worrying for people who write for a living – yours truly, for example – a study has found participants who read an AI-generated story rated it as more absorbing and of higher quality than those who read a human-written one. title: Republican Chuck Edwards drops bid for re-election after report finding sexual harassment of staffers
author: Guardian staff
summary: Congressional ethics panel had recommended Edwards face censure over its findings on ‘hostile work environment’
body_text: Chuck Edwards announced he would not run for re-election after the US House of Representatives ethics committee determined the US congressman “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on two young female staffers. Edwards, a Republican for North Carolina, said he would complete his current term, which is due to end in January. In a statement posted on social media early on Wednesday morning, Edwards said: “After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign. I will complete my current term. Serving western North Carolina has been the honor of my life. Thank you for your trust, prayers, and support.” The bipartisan congressional ethics panel recommended on Monday that Edwards face censure over its findings. Should the House agree, he will have to stand in the well of the chamber while the text of a resolution rebuking him is read aloud. The ethics committee launched an investigation into Edwards earlier this year, after receiving complaints about his conduct. In a report approved by Democratic and Republican committee members, it said there was “substantial reason to believe” that Edwards had broken House rules by singling out the two unidentified aides for special treatment that made them uncomfortable and harmed relations with other employees. While the investigation uncovered no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it, his behavior probably violated provisions in the House code of conduct that prohibit sexual harassment and unwanted advances. The congressman “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate”, but “has not acknowledged or taken responsibility for the harm he caused”, the committee wrote in its report. Edwards was already viewed as vulnerable to losing re-election to his western North Carolina district in the November midterm elections. Last week the election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball announced it was rating his race a “toss-up”, in a sign of improving Democratic chances.

title: The Democratic party chair is a handy scapegoat. But the party’s problems are much bigger
author: Norman Solomon
summary: Much of the criticism of Ken Martin is deserved. But his actions are symptomatic of a party that fails to listen to the grassroots
body_text: Ken Martin is now a convenient scapegoat. As chair of the Democratic National Committee, he has stumbled into disrepute as a dubious fundraiser and bad-tempered boss who bungled an autopsy report on the 2024 election disaster. Much of the criticism is justified. But Martin is just a symptom of what deeply ails a party that does not live up to its name. As the Democratic party’s governing body, the Democratic National Committee has long operated as a fortress for party elites who expect to get their way. Martin seemed to offer a bit of a departure when, as Minnesota party chair, he won the committee leadership election last year in part because of his close ties with other state party chairs. They remain among his strongest supporters. That’s one reason why Martin is very well-positioned to fend off any challenge to his hold on power when the full committee meets next week in Austin. But a more basic dynamic protecting Martin is the committee’s internal culture of conformity. Most of its 450 members would not dream of publicly challenging the chair, despite the recent torrent of bad press. News media have hammered on the fact that the DNC is $2.2m in debt while the Republican National Committee reports $128m in cash on hand. Yet depictions of the DNC’s financial woes have given short shrift to some relevant factors. For instance, after Kamala Harris spent $1.5bn during her short presidential campaign in 2024, the DNC took on about $22m in debts that she left behind. Martin has fulfilled his promise to send more money to state parties. In April 2025, the DNC announced: “Each state party will receive a baseline of $17,500 a month, a $5,000 per month increase over the last agreement, and Republican-controlled states will receive an additional investment of $5,000 a month.” What happens to that no-strings money, however, is a whole other question. “When we’re talking about giving tens of thousands of dollars away on a monthly basis, we need to know that it’s going towards real, grassroots organizing,” Chris Davis, the president of Colorado Young Democrats, told me. “Money received by each state party from the DNC needs to be tied to deliverables that will directly grow the party, such as direct voter engagement through canvassing, having a presence in community spaces like tabling on college campuses or large community gatherings, or building the party’s following through organic social media engagement. Otherwise, the money could be going to consultants, for all we know.” The prevailing criticism is that Martin has failed to take full advantage of the party’s biggest donors and fundraisers. The emphasis on the importance of well-heeled patrons is telling. It says a lot about prevailing assumptions that the party should be largely dependent on – and responsive to – the rich. The DNC’s business model involves catering to – and relying on – big donors. A current somber refrain from news media and some party operatives is that Martin has lost the confidence of party backers who can write big checks. His response, in an essay posted on 20 July, underlines the problem. Martin trumpeted success with “grassroots donors” – whom he defined as people giving “under $10,000”. And he touted an upsurge in funding from the super wealthy during the last year and a half, writing: “The current DNC secured contributions of $100,000 or more from 67 donors.” Rarely mentioned is the truth that he and other party leaders have lost the confidence of countless small-dollar donors, who’ve shown ample capacity to provide fully adequate national funding hauls if inspired, as during the 2016 and 2020 Bernie Sanders presidential campaigns. But it would be hard to find more uninspiring Democratic leaders than the party’s most visible and powerful ones, Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries. Although Schumer and Jeffries did not support Martin’s run for DNC chair in early 2025, the three share a top-down approach that sticks to the party’s standard positions on key issues, even when those positions are in sync with only a minority of Democrats or voters overall. Party leaders are hardly in a good position to effectively raise money from the Democratic base while continuing to flagrantly oppose what polls show the base overwhelmingly wants, such as major tax hikes on the wealthy and an arms embargo on Israel. Journalists have been vastly more fascinated by Martin reportedly throwing a cellphone at a DNC employee’s desk than how he has blocked any DNC resolution for halting US arms shipments to Israel that enable deadly attacks on Palestinian civilians in Gaza. The ingrained habit of deferring to a DNC chair makes a course correction unlikely in the next few months. But all bets are off after the midterm elections in early November. Conjecture is already widespread about who might replace Martin next winter. One of the names cropping up as a possibility in mainstream media is Donna Brazile, whose second stint as interim chair of the committee began in mid-2016. Later that year, she was fired as a CNN commentator after the revelation that she had shared debate questions with Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign to aid her performance against Sanders. In a Washington Post op-ed last week, Brazile argued that Martin “should keep his job”. The piece was ostensibly focused on unifying her party to defeat Republicans this fall, but Brazile slipped in a battle cry on behalf of the corporate Democrats circling Martin’s blood in the political water. “Democrats can win control of both houses of Congress in the midterms by rallying around what unites them,” Brazile wrote. “By advocating for pragmatic policies that most Americans support to make our country more affordable, rather than extremist socialist policies that most voters oppose.” But the momentum of democratic socialists and other progressives in primary elections this year offers real possibilities for transforming the party from the grassroots up – to end the reign of unaccountable authority from the top down. Norman Solomon is the director of RootsAction and executive director of the Institute for Public Accuracy. His latest book is The Blue Road to Trump Hell: How Corporate Democrats Paved the Way for Autocracy

title: Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate primary in defining race for Democrats
author: Rachel Leingang and Joseph Gedeon in Detroit, Michigan
summary: Progressive candidate will face Republican Mike Rogers in race to represent midwestern purple state in the Senate
body_text: Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan, becoming the latest leftwing candidate to capture the party’s nomination ahead of November’s midterm elections. El-Sayed, a progressive, beat Haley Stevens, a moderate US representative backed by the party’s establishment. He will now face Republican Mike Rogers in the race to represent the midwestern purple state in the Senate. The Associated Press called the race on Wednesday morning, moments after Stevens’s campaign said she had called El-Sayed to concede. El-Sayed succeeded by a relatively close margin, in a sign that battleground state voters are still grappling over the direction of the Democratic party. Michigan voters also delivered victories for other progressive candidates, nominating climate activist William Lawrence and Donavan McKinney, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, both of whom are backed by Bernie Sanders in their bids for seats in the House of Representatives. Donald Trump won Michigan in 2016 and 2024, though Joe Biden won it in 2020. Both the state’s current senators are Democrats and retaining the seat remains critical to Democrats’ hopes of winning back the US Senate this year, and a crucial part of the map for the 2028 presidential election. El-Sayed, 41, is a former public health official who centered his run on the Medicare for All model of universal healthcare, while confronting heavy outside spending against him, which became another theme of the race. Stevens, meanwhile, touted her work on the US auto rescue taskforce, where she served as chief of staff. Rogers, a former congressman from the state, was also the Republican nominee for US Senate in 2024, when he lost to the senator Elissa Slotkin. Should he win in November, and beat Rogers in the general election in Michigan, El-Sayed could become the first Muslim US senator. While he is not a democratic socialist, his primary win came amid a wave of wins by democratic socialist candidates elsewhere in the country. He has said he is a “capitalist who understands how capitalism works”, and who wants to regulate monopolies. “They spent an unprecedented amount of money to beat us,” El-Sayed said at a press conference on Wednesday, referring to the tens of millions of dollars in spending against him. “But it turns out the commercials are the part of the television show most people don’t want to watch. “We took on a machine. You’re not supposed to be able to beat $70m of outside spending, a record amount of money spent in a campaign against a Democrat in a primary, in any campaign. You’re not supposed to be able to beat that. And what we showed is that the power of our many is greater than the power of their money.” Stevens saw the backing of establishment Democrats, including Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, while El-Sayed received endorsements from prominent progressives such as Sanders. In a statement on Wednesday, Stevens said: “I love Michigan and am so proud to have put up my hand to serve. I spoke with Abdul a few moments ago to offer him my full support as we work to defeat Mike Rogers this November.” Until earlier this summer, the race was a three-way race with Mallory McMorrow, a state senator who eventually dropped out. Early Wednesday, McMorrow threw her support behind El-Sayed. “I’m proud to give Abdul my full endorsement and support as we head to November together as a unified party,” she said in a statement. The role of Black voters in the Democratic primary came into focus in the final weeks of campaigning, with both candidates seeking to turn out the vote in Black communities, which make up about one-fifth of the Democratic primary electorate, via events at churches and festivals. More than $40m poured into the race from outside groups supporting Stevens or attacking El-Sayed, including from groups associated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), a pro-Israel lobby. Some ads elevated Stevens’s connection to Barack Obama on the auto rescue, which voters have seen as a quasi-endorsement, despite Obama not formally endorsing in the race. Trump celebrated El-Sayed’s victory on Tuesday, claiming it was “great news” for Republicans in a post on his Truth Social platform. The president went on to call El-Sayed a “communist loser who hates Jews and Israel”, despite the Democratic nominee’s frequent denunciations of antisemitism. “Now, the Dumocrats crazy policies will only get worse!” Trump wrote. Shortly after 1am, when the race remained too close to call, El-Sayed took the stage at Detroit’s Majestic Theater to Tupac Shakur’s Changes, telling hundreds of supporters to stay patient as the votes were being counted. Instead, he cast his contest with Stevens as proof that a grassroots campaign could compete against unprecedented outside spending. “We’re still standing,” he told the raucous crowd, arguing Michigan voters were motivated less by ideological divides than by the rising cost of rent, groceries and healthcare. The political streamer Hasan Piker, the democratic nominee for Philadelphia’s third district, Chris Rabb, and Colorado Democratic nominee, Melat Kiros, were in the room. Rabb said he believed El-Sayed’s campaign reflected a broader shift inside the Democratic party, pointing to recent victories by progressive candidates including Zohran Mamdani in New York and Adam Hamawy in New Jersey. “This is not just among coastal elites,” Rabb said. “That’s something that could benefit Democrats if they have the collective wisdom to move us forward, not left or right. Because if they don’t learn this lesson, it’ll be through all of our defeats.” More than 1.2 million Michiganders cast ballots before election day, including nearly 139,000 who voted during the state’s nine-day early in-person voting period, a number that doubles 2024’s primary, according to the Michigan department of state. Rabb argued that unusually strong early turnout suggested the campaign was expanding the Democratic coalition rather than simply energizing existing voters. He said voters were turning out “because they believe in this brother”, adding that Democrats should see the result as evidence that “our base is radically expanding to folks who have not been seen, heard, or respected”. During his speech in the early hours of Wednesday, El-Sayed sought to lower the temperature of the bitter primary, calling on his supporters to unite behind the eventual Democratic nominee against Rogers. “Tomorrow we begin to mend fences,” he said. “There is so much more that unites us than divides us.”

title: Abdul El-Sayed’s win proves change is possible for Democrats. His next fight may determine their future
author: Joseph Gedeon and Rachel Leingang
summary: If the progressive wins Michigan’s general election, it could redefine the 2028 presidential contest. If he fails, the establishment will call him a cautionary tale
body_text: In the final stretch of the state’s Democratic primary for US Senate, Abdul El-Sayed challenged voters at a small event in rural Michigan to think about the message they could send the rest of the country when they cast their ballots. “Who are we? Who do we want to be?” El-Sayed said. “Do we want a state that’s defined by how much money corporations brought in to tell us what we couldn’t have? Or do we want to be a state where we demonstrate to the rest of the country what’s possible when you build a movement of, by and for the people?” On Tuesday, El-Sayed’s vision cleared its first hurdle: he won the primary over moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens, who was backed by the party’s establishment, and tens of millions of dollars in outside spending. His rise, and victory, could serve as a revision to how the political establishment views swing-state politics – not requiring candidates to run from the center, but articulating how you will materially improve people’s lives as the working and middle classes struggle with affordability and rising healthcare costs. A contentious general election, in a battleground state, awaits. El-Sayed led by 48.5% to 47.5% over Stevens when the race was called. The narrow margin, in addition to more than 60,000 votes for a candidate who dropped out altogether, suggest he will have to unite the party, and convince more independent and even right-leaning voters in a swing state, to beat Republican Mike Rogers. But the race solidified a growing anti-establishment sentiment on the party’s left, where activists and supporters have sought a proactive vision that doesn’t rely on the pre-Trump status quo, apparent in a string of wins for insurgent candidates. There’s a sense that systems were already broken before Trump’s rise, and a return to those norms won’t serve everyday Americans. They’re looking for politicians who can call out their own party’s orthodoxies, and challenge the big money that haunts US politics. Michigan voters found it in El-Sayed, who centered his campaign around universal healthcare, and wasn’t shy about calling the war in Gaza a genocide. “It doesn’t limit us to just what we think is possible, but it changes what we think is possible,” said David Sernick, a voter in Detroit who supported El-Sayed. El-Sayed first ran for office in 2018, losing to Gretchen Whitmer, now the governor of Michigan, in a Democratic primary. This time, he built a grassroots machine, barnstorming the state with in-person rallies while delivering clippable moments for social media feeds. His campaign knocked on more than 200,000 doors and made more than 1m phone calls, aided by leftwing groups such as the Working Families party and Indivisible chapters. El-Sayed held more than 500 campaign events and visited 150 churches. People like Racquel Garcia, who voted for El-Sayed in Dearborn, Michigan, said his willingness to show up underpinned their vote. El-Sayed worked as a public health official in Detroit and in Wayne county, and would show up at permit hearings and represent the people, she said. “Every time we meet with the city of Detroit officials, we’re like, ‘we need you to be like him’,” said Garcia. “You’re here to protect us, not to protect industry. So we’ve been wanting him in office. We were happy that he’s real.” Andy Levin, a former congressman from Michigan who lost to Stevens in 2022 after their districts were redrawn, said the moment rejected a “static notion of electability” that stems from a politics of anxiety and fear. “They want authenticity, they want truth telling and they want brave policy, not just proposals but action, so they can breathe in their lives,” Levin told Democracy Now. “This is a movement of Americans who are saying, enough of politics as usual.” Roy Harris, who voted in Detroit on Tuesday but wouldn’t say for whom, detailed how it was time for a change. “First-time homebuyers can’t buy a house – $400,000, first time you going out, nobody can afford that,” he said. “I’m tired of paying $4 for gas, and I am looking for a change. And I hope the new regime coming in brings that to us.” In Washington, El-Sayed’s effort to win the US Senate race in Michigan is critical for Democrats’ ambitious hopes of retaking control of the upper chamber, and will be closely watched by all factions of the left as a bellwether for the party’s future. Michigan voted for Trump, then Biden, and then Trump, in presidential elections. It is firmly a swing state. If El-Sayed, an unabashed progressive who frequently notes he has a “funny name”, can win a statewide general election, it could remake the contours of the 2028 presidential contest. If he fails, the establishment and pundit class will call him, and his ideas, too extreme – a cautionary tale for play-it-safe politics. In other parts of the country, moderates won their Democratic primaries, including blue-dog Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez in a purple district in Washington state, who staved off a progressive challenge, and Wesley Bell, who saw off a challenge from Cori Bush, a former representative. Chris Rabb, a progressive who won a contested primary for a US congressional seat in Pennsylvania, recently noted the high bar people from his branch of the party face as they seek to challenge moderates. “Nobody asks ‘centrist’ Dems to explain their losses,” Rabb wrote on X. “They lose purple districts every cycle & Beltway pundits call it ‘a tough map’. Progressives lose one major race & Dem operatives call us electoral pariahs. It’s a specious double standard.” Meanwhile, the attack lines from the right have already been drawn. Rogers posted an AI-generated video of El-Sayed, depicting him as Odysseus among other prominent Democrats inside a Trojan horse, and saying “don’t let communism into Michigan”. A Republican has not won a US Senate seat in Michigan since 1994. The Republican National Committee called El-Sayed “Michigan’s Mamdani” and said the race “pits common sense against crazy”. El-Sayed himself remains confident. In November, he is counting on turning out people who normally turn off from politics because they’re cynical, or believe the system cannot change in a way that would make their lives better. “The goal now is not to dunk on anybody, the goal now is to come together so we can all collectively dunk on Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said.

title: Progressive climate organizer William Lawrence wins Michigan Democratic House primary
author: Dharna Noor
summary: Activist who rallied around a datacenter moratorium will face incumbent Republican Tom Barrett in November
body_text: William Lawrence, a prominent environmental organizer who foregrounded his support for a datacenter moratorium, has won the Democratic primary in Michigan’s seventh congressional district in a victory for progressives. Lawrence was a co-founder of the youth-led climate justice organization the Sunrise Movement, the group that in 2018 mainstreamed calls for a Green New Deal to battle economic injustice while rapidly phasing out planet-warming fossil fuels. The 36-year-old defeated Bridget Brink, a former US ambassador to Ukraine and Slovakia, and Matt Maasdam, a former US Navy Seal and military aide to Barack Obama. In the November general election, Lawrence will face off with incumbent Republican Tom Barrett. Lawrence secured endorsements from Senator Bernie Sanders, as well as Representative Rashida Tlaib and progressive US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed,. On the campaign trail, he highlighted his support for universal healthcare, boosting taxes on billionaires and ending the war in Iran and arms sales to Israel. But his biggest focus may have been his opposition to the unchecked build-out of AI datacenters; he focused on the issue in his first television ad. “Will made opposing datacenter development a core part of this campaign and it helped power him to victory all across the district, including massive margins in small towns where DC insiders didn’t expect him to compete,” Stevie O’Hanlon, Lawrence’s campaign manager, said. “In Mason, where one datacenter is being proposed, Will won with 49% of the vote in a three-way race.” In May, Lawrence said “datacenters put a tremendous, unprecedented and unexpected burden on the grid to increase overall demand” and that there is “no plan to do that in a clean way”. Survey research conducted by the left-learning polling firm Data for Progress found that 63% of US voters, including 66% of independents and 47% of Republicans, were more likely to support a candidate calling for pausing datacenter construction. “Tonight the people of Michigan’s 7th district sent a clear message: They are tired of Silicon Valley billionaires and D.C. insiders determining the future of our towns and our country,” he said in a Tuesday night statement. “They want an unbought representative who isn’t afraid to stand up to leaders of both parties and fight for working people.” Lawrence’s district in central Michigan is one of just 18 House seats that the Cook Political Report called “toss-ups”. Barrett has often voted with Trump. “Tom Barrett may have the high-powered DC consultants and corporate CEOs in his corner, but our movement is made up of real Michiganders, coming together across political differences,” Lawrence said in his election night statement.

title: What we learned from midterm primary elections in five key states
author: Chris Stein
summary: Elections underscored that momentum of progressive candidates remains strong but not unstoppable
body_text: Tuesday’s primary elections in five states will be looked back on as a marquee moment ahead of November’s midterm elections, as voters in Michigan, Washington, Virginia, Kansas and Missouri selected candidates for races that could decide which party wins control of Congress. Here’s a rundown of what we learned from the results: Progressives thought their Michigan Senate candidate would be a shoo-in – but his victory was narrow Michigan was the site of a bitterly contested Democratic Senate primary in which the moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens faced former public health official Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, in a state that Donald Trump won two years ago. Ahead of Tuesday’s vote, polls showed El-Sayed with a firm lead over Stevens, who had the backing of Governor Gretchen Whitmer as well as the top Senate Democrat, Chuck Schumer, and his campaign projected confidence accordingly. But the election turned out to be a squeaker, with El-Sayed winning 48.5% of the vote to Stevens’s 47.5%, the Associated Press reports, far from the blowout polling appeared to show. Republicans nominated former congressman Mike Rogers, who narrowly lost the race for the state’s other Senate seat two years ago. The left’s momentum remains strong … El-Sayed’s victory underscored the continued momentum of progressive candidates, who have been on a roll in primaries in New York and Colorado as they harnessed discontent among Democrats with party leadership and their traditional support for Israel. Adding to the movement’s trophies was William Lawrence, the co-founder of the climate change activist group the Sunrise Movement, who clinched the Democratic nomination for the battleground seventh congressional district in central Michigan. In Detroit, progressive Donavan McKinney succeeded in ousting Congressman Shri Thanedar, who had been backed by groups aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). … but not unstoppable Leftwing challengers did not triumph everywhere. In Missouri, voters in the St Louis area rejected former congresswoman Cori Bush’s attempt at a political comeback and renominated the incumbent Wesley Bell, who unseated her two years ago with the help of spending from pro-Israel groups. Bush, a progressive who believes the US ally committed a genocide in Gaza, attempted to harness dislike of Israel among primary voters to her advantage against Bell, who received heavy backing from an Aipac-linked Super Pac. But she lost badly, receiving not even 40% of the vote. In Washington, Congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, one of the few Democrats holding on to a district that Trump won two years ago, clinched her primary against a crowded field that included a challenger to her left. Republicans asked too much of their own voters Missouri’s Republican leaders had backed a ballot initiative that would have made it more difficult for state constitutional amendments to pass, after their voters in recent years approved abortion protections, paid sick leave and cannabis legalization at the ballot box. That measure was rejected by a whopping 80% vote, as was an attempt to phase out the state income tax, by a similarly huge margin. And four years after voters in heavily Republican Kansas approved abortion protections in the state constitution, they turned back a GOP-backed attempt to have state supreme court judges popularly elected rather than appointed by the governor. The current bench had attracted Republican ire for issuing rulings against the party’s interests, including on abortion rights. Democrats in battleground Michigan are split all kinds of ways Michigan’s Democratic voters chose their fighters in Tuesday’s primary for a Senate race that could determine whether the party returns to the majority in the chamber, as well as for vital House races. But the primaries also underscored sharp divides among their backers over which brand of the Democratic party works best for them. Stevens’s strong primary performance shows El-Sayed has work to do to win over the centrist voters she courted, as well as those who preferred her views on Israel. The task is much the same for Lawrence, who triumphed over a divided field of moderate Democrats but now must convince voters to get on board with his progressive politics in a district that’s one of the most narrowly divided in the country.

title: Abdul El-Sayed offers a template for Democrats to defeat Trumpism
author: Peter Beinart
summary: The candidate has crafted a progressive nationalism and shown his party how to turn Republicans’ financial advantage against them
body_text: Every now and then, a Senate race sets the direction for an entire party. In 1991, a state official named Harris Wofford – advised by a foul-mouthed Cajun named James Carville – upset his far better-known Republican opponent to win a special election in Pennsylvania. He did it by promising to expand access to healthcare – and thus created a template for Bill Clinton’s presidential campaign the following year. If Abdul El-Sayed can follow up his victory in last night’s Democratic Senate primary by winning the general election in Michigan this fall, he will have created a template of his own. Despite his closer-than-expected margin of victory, his campaign offers a model for how Democrats across the country can answer the political challenge posed by Donald Trump. By casting the Michigan Senate primary as yet another battle between progressive insurgents and establishment centrists, media coverage of El-Sayed’s campaign has tended to overlook what is innovative about it. Like Zohran Mamdani and the democratic socialists who have won House races in New York, Pennsylvania and Colorado, El-Sayed wants to end unconditional US military support for Israel. But while Mamdani sometimes discusses Israel purely through the language of human rights and international law – as he did in his recent video arguing that Benjamin Netanyahu should be arrested as a war criminal – El-Sayed’s message is more nationalistic. He rarely discusses the Jewish state without linking it to Washington’s failure to address problems at home. In a recent interview, the New Yorker editor, David Remnick, asked El-Sayed whether he supports one or two states in Israel-Palestine. El-Sayed did not take the bait. He replied that his focus was less on “what’s happening there rather than what’s happening here”. His primary concern, he explained, was that the US was allocating money for Israeli weapons that it could be spending on schools in Michigan. While acknowledging: “I believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination, for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike,” he said: “It is not my job as an American policymaker to decide what the ultimate peace should be. But it is my job to make sure that our resources are stewarded correctly for the people I’m responsible for: those kids going to those broken schools.” In relentlessly linking US military aid to Israel to unmet needs in the United States, El-Sayed is crafting a progressive version of America First. In 2016, Donald Trump exploited the resentment many Americans felt after a decade and a half of failed wars in the Middle East. Now, in the wake of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and Trump’s war in Iran, El-Sayed is turning the tables. The difference is that Trump fused nationalism and imperialism: he said that the Iraq war was a mistake because the US sought to “make western democracies out of countries that had no experience or interests in becoming a western democracy”; the US, he said, should have taken Iraq’s oil. El-Sayed, by contrast, is fusing nationalism with progressivism. He’s not attacking the humanitarian assistance once offered by USAID. He’s condemning military aid to Israel (and also to Egypt, where his father was born) because it both violates human rights overseas and denies resources to Americans at home. This isn’t a message that only resonates with the American left. Last summer, the late rightwing activist Charlie Kirk tweeted that young conservatives “are skeptical about the state of America’s current relationship” with Israel “and they want to be confident America’s leaders are putting their own country first”. A poll in May by the Institute for Middle East Understanding found that by a margin of almost two-to-one, Republicans under the age of 45 prefer candidates who support reducing taxpayer-funded weapons sales to the Jewish state. But El-Sayed’s campaign offers Democrats another lesson as well. He isn’t only showing them how to reclaim nationalism from the GOP. He’s also showing them how to turn the Republican party’s financial advantage against it. In the last five weeks of El-Sayed’s primary campaign, outside Super Pacs supporting his opponent, representative Haley Stevens, spent more than 12 times as much on television ads as did those supporting him. Most candidates can’t overcome that kind of disparity. But El-Sayed made it a source of strength. Again and again, he used Stevens’s financial support from the pro-Israel lobbying group Aipac – which contributed the bulk of the outside money on her behalf – against her. He also linked her to other unpopular special interests. His supporters ran a television ad highlighting the contributions she had received from the Michigan utility, DTE Energy, which is widely disliked for charging high rates and allowing recurring power outages. El-Sayed’s relentless focus on the source of Stevens’s donations turned her financial advantage into an electoral albatross. When the Bulwark’s Sarah Longwell asked a Michigan focus group why they didn’t like Stevens, “voters repeatedly brought up Aipac and the appearance of corporate influence.” El-Sayed performed this political jujitsu against a fellow Democrat. But this fall, and probably again in 2028, Democrats across the country will be badly outspent by Republicans. Donald Trump has turned the federal government into a cash cow for corporations and billionaires who profit massively from his administration and return the favor by writing campaign checks. Elon Musk alone recently announced that he will spend at least $100m supporting Republican candidates this fall. Overall, reported MS Now late last month, the Republican National Committee, the Republican House and Senate campaign committees and GOP-aligned Super Pacs have raised almost $600m more than their Democratic counterparts. El-Sayed’s campaign offers a template for how Democrats can respond: make the money the issue. El-Sayed drew a connection between Stevens’s backing from AIipac and her support for US military aid to Israel. But other Democrats can brand their Republican opponents as lackeys not just of Aipac, but of Elon Musk, big oil, big pharma or AI – and highlight the connection between their campaign funds and their support for policies that hurt ordinary people. This strategy requires Democrats to eschew corporate and special interest funding and run campaigns that rely primarily on small donors. There’s no guarantee this will work. Not all Democrats can deliver a populist message as effectively as El-Sayed. But the staggering corruption of Trump’s presidency, and the obscene wealth gap that his policies have helped create, presents them with an opportunity. Which means that El-Sayed’s model could prove effective far beyond Michigan. There are many reasons Democrats have struggled to defeat the Trump-era GOP. But among them are these: Republicans have owned nationalism and populism. If Abdul El-Sayed can win this fall, he’ll have handed his party a roadmap for how to reclaim both. Democrats across the country should be taking notes. Peter Beinart is a contributing opinion writer at the New York Times, editor at large at Jewish Currents, a professor at the Newmark School of Journalism at the City University of New York, and the author of The Beinart Notebook, a weekly newsletter. His most recent book is Being Jewish After the Destruction of Gaza

title: Michigan nominates first trans woman for state legislature
author: David Smith Washington bureau chief
summary: Joanna Whaley, ex-megachurch pastor who endured years of conversion practices, comfortably bested her opponents
body_text: A former megachurch pastor who endured 15 years of conversion practices is set to become the first transgender member of Michigan’s state legislature after winning a Democratic primary election on Tuesday. Joanna Whaley comfortably defeated Frank Liberati, a former state representative, and Gary Schlack in the primary for the second district of the Michigan statehouse, a Democratic stronghold. Earlier this year Liberati sought to have Whaley disqualified from the ballot over her name change but the Wayne county clerk’s office dismissed the challenge, finding that Whaley’s candidate affidavit was legal and proper. Sarah McBride, the first openly transgender member of the US Congress, posted on X on Wednesday: “So proud of my friend, Joanna Whaley! She faced indignities from her opponent, channeled the energy into knocking on doors, doubled down on her economic agenda, and she defeated that former Dem legislator (who took the low road against her) by 30+%! Way to go, Joanna!” Whaley, 38, who grew up in a Catholic family, previously spent nearly two decades working as a pastor at an evangelical megachurch. As she wrestled with her gender identity, the church forced her to undergo Christian conversion therapy with four different therapists over 15 years. In 2022 she was forced to quit when the church’s leaders discovered she was contemplating a gender transition. Whaley went to work for a more progressive church, shared her story on social media and launched a podcast. She also found work as a hospital chaplain in emergency rooms, intensive care units and hospice. Since deciding to run for state office, she has had some unusual meetings with potential campaign donors. She told the LGBTQ Nation website in April: “Some of those conversations go weird. We have a semi-pro hockey team in the area, and I was sitting down with one of the directors. In the middle of the conversation, he says, ‘So do you have a brother? I went to high school with someone named blah blah blah,’ and they said my dead name. I’m like, ‘That’s me.’ And they’re like, ‘Whoa, what?’” Whaley added: “It happens all the time. I’m honored by it, but at the same time, it does turn into some really weird and uncomfortable conversations, especially with some of my old Christian friends who then try to save my soul and tell me that I’m living in sin.” But in a separate interview with the Detroit Free Press newspaper, Whaley noted that some voters appreciate her historic candidacy: “It hits me when I’m talking to trans folks across the state. I’ll get in that conversation with someone across the state who just comes up and says, ‘Thank you,’ and I’m, ‘What are you thanking me for?’ “I understand in this moment in politics what it would mean to elect a trans woman could be monumental. I don’t take that responsibility lightly at all. I take it very seriously.” Whaley has earned endorsements from groups including the LGBTQ Victory Fund, Run for Something, Her Bold Move and Families United for Trans Rights. She will run against Republican Ronald Kokinda to replace Liberati’s brother, Tullio Liberati, in the statehouse in the 3 November general election.

title: Trump is pioneering the role of commentator-in-chief when issues grow thorny
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: The president is constantly assigning motives, identifying heroes and villains, and telling his audience what to think
body_text: From Charles Barkley to Thierry Henry to John McEnroe, the path from the arena to the commentary box is well trodden, and plenty of politicians have made the transition from elected office to the TV studio. One man, however, insists on doing both at the same time. Donald Trump is the US president, empowered to kill terrorists, grant pardons, sign and veto bills, and represent the nation on the world stage. But when issues become thorny, as they have of late, he is wont to embrace an alternative role as commentator-in-chief. The president has become his own talking head, offering a running voiceover on everything from crime and immigration to the Iran war and his own administration’s scandals. His off-the-cuff remarks are typically peppered with phrases such as “people are saying”, “I hear” and “some people think”, rather than “I have decided”. Take the sorry saga of the algae-afflicted Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. On Saturday, Trump used his Truth Social platform to paint a colourful – and fictitious – picture, posting: “Look for yourselves at the VANDALISM that took place at The Reflecting Pool. The material is being cut with a knife or a box cutter, for all to see!” On Monday he opined that US attorney Jeanine Pirro “choked” and “folded like an umbrella” in moving to drop charges against a former Olympian accused of vandalising the pool. Sitting in the Oval Office, he launched a tirade worthy of the extras in the Trump presidency DVD boxed set. Of course it included exaggerated accusations against some of his favorite targets. “Biden spent $58m. Barack Hussein Obama spent much more than that. He said, ‘I have an idea. Let’s take the river from, let’s take the water from the Potomac.’ So they took the water from the Potomac and it was putrid. It was putrid. It was a disaster,” the president said. Perhaps Trump’s past life as a reality TV host has something to do with his steady stream of commentary. He is constantly assigning motives, identifying heroes (he regularly uses “from central casting” as a descriptor) and villains, and telling his audience what they should think. When things get awkward, he has an instinct to fill the silence and supply the talking point of the day. He is subject, narrator and critic all in one. When, for example, pressure mounted over his administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files, Trump did not simply maintain a dignified silence and let the justice department answer questions, as his predecessors might have done. He put himself front and centre of the news cycle – attacking critics, dismissing the matters, sympathising with people who “innocently met” the convicted paedophile and telling supporters to move on. More recently, when his attorney general nominee Todd Blanche said he would abandon Trump’s controversial $1.8bn “anti-weaponisation fund” to secure the support of Republican senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, the president made clear that it was not his decision – but he had plenty of thoughts. “All I know is that Todd Blanche is great,” he told reporters, sounding like a guest analyst lamenting a policy he had no power over. Yet he still insisted that his supporters should get compensation from the justice department. “These people were treated horribly, and this fund could have given them some solace. “But, you know, it happens to be very popular among many quarters. And I don’t participate in that fund. I was certainly treated badly. I don’t participate, but I thought it would be very fair for people that spent years in prison, people that were treated so badly for, in many cases, people that did absolutely nothing wrong.” These informal exchanges with reporters in the Oval Office and on Air Force One are an exercise in postmodern punditry. Trump frequently breaks the fourth wall by interrupting questions to “correct” the premise, insult the reporter (“piggy”, “very nasty person”, “very obnoxious person”) or their network and offer an alternative interpretation of the day’s news. He does not want their narratives to get in the way of his own. There is a paradox here. During an interview with New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan for their book Regime Change, Trump showed off a document asserting that he is the most powerful person to ever walk the earth, ranking above despots such as Attila the Hun, Genghis Khan, Napoleon, Stalin, Mao and Hitler. Yet his constant commentaries in response to actions taken by Iran, the courts or his own government departments are evidence of impotence, an admission reminiscent of the Vicomte de Valmont in the play Les Liaisons Dangereuses: “It’s beyond my control.’” When supreme court justices ruled against him on tariffs, Trump lamented: “They were appointed by me, and yet have hurt our Country so badly!” Like sports professionals, the president’s time is finite. He continues to tease an unconstitutional third term. If that doesn’t happen, he will surely commentate on his own succession, leaving JD Vance, Marco Rubio and other potential contenders facing the unenviable prospect of the White House occupant delivering his snap verdict on their every move. And then: Trump as host on Fox & Friends? Trump firing off ornery letters to the New York Times? Trump as crank caller on C-Span’s phone-in shows? The words will continue to flow – but it is less certain whether they will still be good for ratings. Elsewhere on the Guardian ... Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate primary in defining race for Democrats Trump administration targets children amid push to ‘deport at all costs’ ‘They’re selling the safety of the traveling public’: TSA workers decry Trump privatization push

title: Republican who withdrew last month beats Trump-backed rival in Michigan
author: George Chidi
summary: Thomas Smith, whose name remained on ballot, beats Republican rivals in primary contest for eighth district
body_text: Thomas Smith withdrew from the Republican primary contest for Michigan’s eighth district last month. On Tuesday, he won the nomination. Unofficial results show Smith with more than 50% of the vote, according to the Associated Press, defeating the man he endorsed, anti-abortion activist Al Lemmo, and the man Donald Trump endorsed, former federal law enforcement officer Amir Hassan. In a statement on Wednesday, Smith said he was “humbled and honored that Republicans have chosen me to take the fight to Kristen McDonald Rivet”, the Democratic incumbent in the battleground House district. “I look forward to working with Speaker [Mike] Johnson and the entire Republican team to expand our House majority and advance President Trump’s ‘America first’ agenda to lower costs for working families and make America affordable again,” he added. In June, Trump endorsed Hassan, an African American navy veteran who worked for the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security and Transportation. The president also appeared with Hassan at a campaign event in Michigan. Hassan said during his campaign that he had recently converted to Christianity from Islam. Nonetheless, social media commentary suggests Republican voters did not view Hassan’s conversion as authentic and were apprehensive about nominating a Muslim candidate. “It was a tough race, but over the last year I’ve had some incredible dealings with people across the entire district,” Hassan said in a video posted to X and Facebook. “The biggest conservative value is that we don’t make excuses.” In a statement, Joe Gruters, the chair of the Republican National Committee, congratulated Smith on a “hard-fought, well-earned primary victory”. Smith, who did little campaigning, posted on social media in July to endorse Lemmo, describing Hassan as a crypto-Republican. In Michigan, a US House candidate must withdraw their candidacy before 24 April for election officials to have enough time to remove their name from ballots. The Federal Election Commission has no electronic campaign finance filings from Smith. It does have a handwritten letter dated 12 July declaring $1,850 in fundraising. “I could not file this electronically because I have had no success logging in and have not been able to get a response from the helpdesk,” Smith wrote in a postscript on the letter. The Flint native and retired General Motors engineer made a brief appearance at a Republican unity event hosted in Macomb county by Mike Rogers, the party’s newly minted Senate candidate. Smith said he intended to “unseat communist comrade Rivet”. Though the victory on Tuesday of Abdul El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary has drawn national attention to progressive politics in Michigan, Rivet has signaled her relative moderation as one of 10 House Democrats to join Promise to America, a congressional initiative led by US representatives Tom Suozzi of New York and Adam Gray of California explicitly embracing capitalism and rejecting socialism. The congressional district along Michigan’s Saginaw River, connecting Flint to the Saginaw Bay, was one of 13 districts nationwide that voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election while also electing a Democratic representative to Congress.
