title: Senate confirms Trump pick Erica Schwartz as new CDC director
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Schwartz, president’s third pick to lead top US public health agency, confirmed in 51-44 Senate vote
body_text: Dr Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a rare win for the Trump administration after a string of failed attempts to fill senior health posts. Schwartz was confirmed by a ⁠51-44 vote that broke largely along party lines, with Tim Kaine of Virginia the sole Democrat to support her nomination. Donald Trump’s third pick to run the CDC, Schwartz is set to take the reins of the agency after a tumultuous period of leadership turnover, and amid public concern over an outbreak of cyclosporiasis and Robert F Kennedy Jr’s hesitancy towards vaccines. At her confirmation hearing last month, senators pressed Schwartz on whether she would stand firm against any attempts by the health secretary to erode the scientific consensus around vaccines. She replied that she “will never betray the science” but generally deflected questions about how she would manage the relationship with Kennedy. “We need a CDC director that will ⁠actually stand up to crazy, stupid things being said that undermine faith in immunization,” said Bill Cassidy, the committee’s Republican chair and a physician. Schwartz replied that Kennedy “will absolutely allow me to be CDC director”, and Cassidy later announced his support for her nomination. “There are challenges facing Americans’ health today. I will work with her to face those challenges and regain trust in the CDC,” Cassidy said after the Senate confirmed her. A navy veteran, Schwartz served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term, after positions in the United States Public Health Service where she was detailed to the Coast Guard, eventually becoming the force’s chief medical officer. Trump’s first nominee to lead the CDC, David Weldon, a former Florida congressman, was withdrawn by the White House in March 2025 just before his confirmation hearing. Schwartz will be the first permanent CDC director since Susan Monarez, Trump’s second pick, who was fired by Kennedy last year after less than a month over a clash on vaccine policy.

title: Morning Mail: First home buyers’ scheme twist; explosive drone scare at German airport; butterflies on the move
author: Paul Gallagher
summary: Homes bought under 5% deposit scheme turned into investments; drone carrying explosives found in Leipzig
body_text: Good morning. Nearly 1,500 properties bought using the government’s first home buyers’ 5% deposit scheme have ended up being converted into investments: we dig into the data to find out more. A drone carrying explosives was found at a German airport. Meanwhile, Ukraine is pleading with its allies for more air defences after Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles. Scientists are excited by new pictures of the sun, but worried by the migration of butterflies. And a poll has placed Cathy Freeman at the top of a list of Australia’s most admired sportspeople. Australia Operation Richmond | A new report has highlighted how – via a “staged” meeting and a secret deal – a union boss exerted “extraordinary influence” on the Daniel Andrews government in Victoria. ‘It shouldn’t benefit the wealthy’ | The government’s 5% deposit scheme for first home buyers has enabled the purchase of almost 1,500 properties that were turned into investments, data shows. ‘Easy cash grab’ | Jetstar’s new carry-on luggage charge means the airline has joined a growing number monetising basic services in the sky. And: what’s one more humiliating ritual for the masses, James Colley asks. Analysis | Ex-NSW premier Dominic Perrottet’s brother Jean-Claude was the star witness at the Icac hearings yesterday. It won’t be the last we hear from his family, Anne Davies writes. Datacentre stoush | The energy minister, Chris Bowen, has vowed to override states opposing national rules that new AI datacentres are to be powered by renewable energy and not fuelled by gas. World Russia-Ukraine war | Volodymyr Zelenskyy has blamed allies for not delivering air defences fast enough after Ukraine failed to shoot down a single Russian missile in a deadly overnight attack. Drone scare | German police deployed a bomb disposal robot after a drone carrying explosives was found at Leipzig airport, causing alarm and the diversion of several flights; the Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for Europe, Dan Sabbagh writes. A defining race? | Abdul El-Sayed has won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan; top Democrats are now setting aside their qualms to embrace the progressive leftwing candidate. Middle East crisis | Iran says it has agreed the coordinates of a shipping route through the strait of Hormuz with Oman. An Israeli airstrike in south Lebanon has killed one person and injured 11. Science | Butterflies around the world are on the move, and their migration reveals the impact of climate change. In other news, scientists are very excited by new high-res photos of the sun. Full Story Decoding America: are the Democrats having their own Maga moment? In our weekly US politics podcast, Jonathan Yerushalmy and Reged Ahmad look at how the Michigan Senate primaries could decide the future of the Democrats. The race has revealed the civil war raging inside the party, as some seek to take it further to the left. Will this schism be the Democrats’ Maga moment, or could it cost them in the midterms? In-depth The Reserve Bank governor, Michele Bullock, says rate rises don’t really increase living costs. But the latest data is clear – they very much do. Economics and finance are purposefully confusing but, Greg Jericho writes, people are well aware of how rate hikes affect them. Not the news For her new book, It’s Not For You, the Camp Cope bassist Kelly-Dawn Hellmrich interviewed 18 women and gender-diverse artists who have changed the Australian music industry on their own terms, including Amy Taylor, Marcia Hines and Courtney Barnett. The book opens up topics such as motherhood, abuse and respect – and is intended, she says, “for every artist who felt pushed away, or talked over”. Sport Sporting poll | Cathy Freeman leads a trio of women at the top of a list of Australia’s most admired sportspeople, with Ash Barty and Sam Kerr coming joint second. Rugby league | The UK Super League is closing in on a gamechanging investment from Australia’s NRL. Football | “Fifa Super League”: Gianni Infantino discussed having the governing body’s name on an ill-fated European breakaway; why has football taken so long to rebel against Fifa, Jonathan Liew asks. And: Mohamed Salah has landed in Turkey to sign for Trabzonspor. Cycling | Demi Vollering was victorious on stage five of the Tour de France Femmes as Pauline Ferrand-Prévot’s defence unravelled. Golf | LIV Golf says it has secured a “lead investor” until 2030 – but the future of star names still remains uncertain. Media roundup Crew members on Carnival cruise ships have made “horrifying” allegations about their working conditions in an ABC News investigation. Kidnapping has emerged as a major escalation of the violence used in the so-called tobacco war, the Age reports. Documents reveal that taxpayers shelled out for a $50,000-a-year Tasmanian electorate office that nobody ever used, the Mercury reports. What’s happening today WA | A public hearing is scheduled in the inquiry into the NDIS amendment bill in Perth. NSW | The trial of Alan Jones continues in Sydney. NSW | Public hearings in the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion continue in Sydney. ABS | The Australian Bureau of Statistics is scheduled to release its latest international trade in goods figures. title: Top Democrats set aside qualms and embrace progressive Abdul El-Sayed
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Democrats are ‘united by a common purpose,’ Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand say in joint statement
body_text: Leading Democrats quickly papered over whatever qualms they had about progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed after his win in the Michigan Senate primary was confirmed on Wednesday, instead welcoming the former public health official as their champion against the Republican nominee, Mike Rogers. The state is now key to Democrats’s hopes of retaking control of the chamber in November’s midterm elections. Winning in Michigan would put them on the path to snarling Donald Trump’s legislative agenda and blocking his judicial nominees for the final two years of his presidency, while defeat could undermine their prospects of gaining a majority in the chamber for years to come. Rogers lost a Senate race in Michigan two years ago by a slim margin to Democrat Elissa Slotkin. “Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate. We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November,” the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and Kirsten Gillibrand, who chairs the Democratic Senate campaign arm, said in a joint statement. Schumer was among a long list of Democratic establishment figures who had rallied behind Stevens in the weeks before the vote, as polls showed her trailing El-Sayed. He ultimately prevailed but by a far slimmer margin than data indicated, winning by 48.5% to Stevens’s 47.5%. “There’s a lot of passion and energy in these primaries, and that’s a good thing. Democrats are ready to beat Republicans across the state,” said Governor Gretchen Whitmer, who had endorsed Stevens. “We’re all united by our shared goal of getting things done for the people in Michigan.” The easiest path for Democrats to win back the Senate – which Republicans control with 53 lawmakers to their 47 – requires holding on to their seats in Michigan and Georgia while ousting Republicans from blue state Maine as well as three other red states. Democratic leaders believe they have the right candidates to pull that off in North Carolina, Ohio and Alaska, but it will nonetheless be a tall order, given that all three states backed Trump in 2024, and the latter two by double-digit margins. Michigan’s Democratic senator Gary Peters, whose decision not to seek re-election had sparked the primary for his seat, backed Stevens as his replacement but quickly endorsed El-Sayed after his primary. “Both candidates ran strong campaigns focused on improving the lives of all Michiganders. But now it’s time to come together as a party and rally around our nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, to make sure Mike Rogers never sees the floor of the US Senate,” Peters said. In a statement released following her loss, Stevens congratulated El-Sayed but did not outright endorse him, instead indicating she was ready to campaign for him as well as Democrats vying to win swing districts in Michigan. “This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic party – and that is why we have primaries. I am proud to have put up my hand to serve, and prouder to continue to work together to make sure this Senate seat remains blue, that we flip the United States Senate and continue the work for Michigan,” Stevens said. Republicans meanwhile pounced on El-Sayed’s views to paint him as too far left for voters in Michigan, a state that backed Trump in 2016 and again in 2024. “The choice this November is simple: common sense or complete insanity,” Rogers said. The former congressman blamed Democrats – who have held both of Michigan’s Senate seats since 2001 – for job losses in manufacturing, while saying El-Sayed “doesn’t represent a vision for the future. He’s leading a movement grounded in ideological fanaticism.” The question of aid to Israel animated the primary, with Stevens arguing Democrats should continue backing the US’s top ally in the Middle East and El-Sayed calling for an end to military support in response to its actions in Gaza and the West Bank. The United Democracy Project, a Super Pac connected to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), spent more than $30m in the race to support Stevens and oppose El-Sayed, to no avail, and he now joins others in Denver, New York City, New Jersey and Philadelphia in having wooed Democratic voters in part by vowing to stand up for Palestinian rights. “Abdul’s victory is a win for everyone who supports equality, justice, and a thriving future for all,” said the IfNotNow Movement, a Jewish organization opposed to Israel’s policy towards Palestinians. “We urge those who see Abdul’s support for Palestinian human rights and blocking weapons to Israel as a threat to our community to reconsider. It is incredibly dangerous to conflate Jewish safety with support for Aipac or Israel’s military.” Brian Romick, president of the Democratic Majority for Israel Pac, called El-Sayed’s victory an indicator that “there is clearly strong anti-establishment energy this cycle, but no one should count pro-Israel Democrats out”. “While El-Sayed’s razor-thin victory in Michigan is disappointing, it was hardly the sweeping triumph he predicted or a mandate for his views,” Romick said, noting that Stevens lost only narrowly.

title: Thursday briefing: ​Is this the final whistle for Gianni Infantino at Fifa?
author: Michael Segalov
summary: In today’s newsletter: Global football’s governance crisis is exposing ​a​ long history structural flaws, ​and as federations revolt and officials resign the sport faces a reckoning at the highest level
body_text: Good morning. In every pub where I watched this summer’s World Cup unfold, two motifs were shared by supporters. Yes, football was coming home, and also the (frankly more firmly held belief) that Gianni Infantino was a wrong’un. As in matchday stadiums, boos would routinely erupt when cameras cut to the Fifa boss; a proper panto villain. Regardless, he looked poised to cruise to victory in next year’s vote for Fifa president, despite this competition’s controversies – Fifa’s jaw-dropping, unprecedented overturning of US striker Folarin Balogun’s red card after Donald Trump’s lobbying chief among them. Undeterred, more than 200 of Fifa’s 211 member associations still backed his fourth term. Then last week, his Fifa Forward Enterprise plans were revealed: Infantino’s scheme to flog a stake in Fifa competitions to profit-seeking investors. World football has reacted with revolt, resignations and strongly worded statements. A growing chorus wants Infantino out. Yesterday, he gathered Fifa bigwigs for crisis management. But how did the gatekeeper of the beautiful game make things so ugly? That’s the topic for today’s First Edition, answered with the help of Guardian reporter Paul MacInnes, who has closely followed Infantino’s tenure. First, this morning’s headlines: Five big stories UK news | A woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in Covent Garden, central London, police said. Education | Jason Arday, the Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, has resigned after the university announced he was to face new investigations into his qualifications and career. Ukraine | Nato is working to get Ukraine the air defences it “urgently needs”, its secretary general has said, after Kyiv failed to shoot down a single Russian missile in an attack on Wednesday. Middle East crisis | Iran and Oman have reached an understanding on ⁠the geographic coordinates for a shipping route through the strait of Hormuz, and ⁠a joint announcement ⁠is being finalised provided certain third parties do not interfere, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said. US news | Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan, becoming the latest leftwing candidate to capture the party’s nomination ahead of November’s midterm elections. In depth: ‘It’s hard to dispute that football’s legitimacy is being undermined’ Barely two days after details of Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) emerged, came Infantino’s first major blow. Last Thursday, European football’s governing body Uefa announced its members had unanimously voted to boycott all Fifa competitions until FFE was scrapped. Of the six regional federations, two others soon expressed disdain at the proposals. Carlos Cordeiro, a senior Infantino adviser, announced he was quitting. Fifa chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff had been “deceived”. Pressure mounted until the weekend, when Fifa relented and scrapped the proposal. This backtracking hasn’t dispelled dissent. Uefa says it’s lost confidence in Infantino. Legendary Arsenal manager Arsène Wenger – a key Infantino hire at Fifa – said abandoning FFE was “absolutely necessary and beyond question”. Meanwhile Fifa’s secretary general wrote of “a sad and reproachable series of events” and that individuals “come and go” in a leaked internal memo. Jordan’s football chief has accused Infantino’s administration of “blackmail”. Portugal icon Luís Figo didn’t hold back, labelling Infantino’s actions “the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed”. At least four countries have now withdrawn their support for his reelection, with England set to follow suit, and more expected. “Many would like him to resign on principle,” says Paul, “but that hasn’t happened.” Yesterday, after a meeting in Morocco, Fifa confirmed that Infantino will remain as president. In a statement, which also revealed that Infantino has sent written apologies to the Fifa council and the member associations for failing to consult them over the World Cup sell-off, the world governing body said that he retains the full support of his leadership team. “Currently, it feels like the pressure has dropped slightly,” Paul tells me. “There’ll be discussions about how the ante is upped again. If he doesn’t fall quickly, nations might assume he won’t go, cut their losses and stick with him. Without a well-established rival and widespread withdrawal of support, he’ll likely win re-election.” Because, despite the sleaze, when it comes to cold hard cash, Infantino has proven effective. This year’s World Cup generated $15bn – a tripling under his leadership. “Infantino has proven himself an elite executive when it comes to his priority: generating more revenue,” says Paul. In his rhetoric, at least, Infantino talks of boosting funds to footballing nations. And for the lesser-resourced, non-European football associations, this extra cash is gamechanging, even if Infantino’s $40m offer to those who backed his plans looked remarkably bribe-like. *** The clean-up candidate It’s hard to believe that Infantino was elected as a clean-up candidate. In 2015, after the US Department of Justice indicted 14 Fifa figures for racketeering conspiracy and corruption, Fifa’s last president, Sepp Blatter, announced his resignation. Blatter had been caught up in a long-running corruption case, alongside Uefa boss Michel Platini. The pair were accused (then acquitted, twice) of misappropriating £1.7m of Fifa cash. All of this, and the highly controversial awarding of the 2018 and 2022 World Cups to Russia and Qatar respectively, made Blatter’s position untenable. There was a gap at the top of world football and with Platini out, no obvious European successor. (Of Fifa’s nine permanent presidents, eight have been European). Enter Infantino, then second-in-command at Uefa. Central to his pitch was World Cup expansion. He had a message to world football, Paul says. “It’s not our money, it’s yours. And Fifa will make more for you.” It marked a rhetorical shift, with “a sense post-Blatter that execs had been lining their own pockets.” Looking to Europe, he offered another promise. “We’re going to clean the stables,” Paul recalls, “introduce new governance structures.” Infantino was perceived as a strait-laced Swiss bureaucrat – an image he projected. On his victory in 2016, he spoke of change. “Fifa has gone through sad times, moments of crisis. But those times are over,” he said. “We enter now a new era. We’ll restore the image of Fifa and make sure everybody will be happy with what we do.” *** A quick backlash Scandal came thick and fast. His election campaign first: Infantino declared spending €500,000 of Uefa funds to drum up support, but sources suggested the figure was closer to €1m. Fifa’s ethics committee began to investigate; Infantino organised the removal of its chair and members. Weeks after taking office, he was named in the Panama Papers, pulled into his own corruption scandal. There was a criminal probe after “indications of criminal conduct” in Switzerland. Swiss prosecutors subsequently closed their investigations, satisfied that suspicions against Infantino had been “invalidated”. “These stories have been endless,” says Paul. Take the Qatar World Cup, which Infantino inherited. Infantino committed to protecting human rights and remedying failures. These were widely documented, but no compensation fund was created. Fifa refused to act on fan safety in Qatar, where same-sex sexual acts are criminalised. Meanwhile Infantino goaded critics with that monologue: “Today I feel Qatari, today I feel Arab, today I feel African, today I feel gay, today I feel disabled, today [like] a migrant worker.” “That’s where it properly kicked off,” says Paul. “He became a real antagonist in the eyes of football fans.” Infantino’s awarding of the 2034 World Cup to Saudi Arabia was widely criticised. His 2022 proposal to make the World Cup biennial (which, he claimed, could stop migrants from finding “death in the sea”) was botched. He invented a Trump-placating peace prize. In fact, he’d even attempted an FFE style ploy before. His 2018 proposal to fatten up the Club World Cup with private investor cash was “sprung on people with no consultation and little notice,” says Paul, adding that it “saw huge backlash before Infantino backed down.” *** The future of Fifa What incentivised Infantino to try to push through FFE has caused speculation. His multimillion pound salary and ample perks, already come with status that offers him access to the world’s most powerful figures. There were reports that Infantino might have eventually headed up FFE at a basic salary of $30m but Fifa have denied discussions on this have taken place. But this mess isn’t exclusively of Infantino’s (or Blatter’s) making. Paul has been speaking to academics, lawyers and football officials. “There’s a shared view reform is needed.” Many point to the need to break Fifa up: “Organising the biggest football tournament, while also regulating it, is untenable,” says Paul. Others see this as a chance to address inequality and elitism in the game. And European figures are also manoeuvring to push for external Fifa regulation. When doping scandals threatened to delegitimize sport, national governments and governance bodies founded the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada). “It’s hard to dispute that football’s legitimacy is being undermined,” says Paul. “Wada proves sporting organisations needn’t mark their own homework.” There are suggestions that the EU, OECD or even the UN should play a role, to “create a body outside football to handle complaints when they arise. So many complaints against Infantino have just disappeared. Someone needs to be able to hold Fifa accountable.” What else we’ve been enjoying I thought Symeon Brown was excellent in yesterday’s Long Wave newsletter, on Britain’s booming Black bourgeois class and why Brits just can’t seem to acknowledge it. This explainer from Chris Stein on the Guardian’s US politics team helped me get a grip on the results. Michael I enjoyed Arwa Mahdawi’s take on the Trump officials who won’t just … focus on their actual jobs. Poppy My boyfriend is a real anchovy-head, and cans of surplus fishy oil often float in our fridge for days before eventual binning. No longer, with this salsa verde recipe from Tom Hunt I’m making as I type. Michael I was also thoroughly ruffled by our profile on the Phillipines’ so-called “Cockroach Lord”. Poppy Sport Cycling | Race favourite Demi Vollering won a three-way sprint to claim stage five at the Tour de France Femmes. title: Afternoon Update: Gina Rinehart gets apology from ABC; Angus Taylor mentioned again at Icac; and a forbidden novel
author: Miles Herbert
summary: Broadcaster’s managing director Hugh Marks says film has been edited on the ABC’s platforms to remove the material in question
body_text: Good afternoon. The ABC’s managing director, Hugh Marks, has issued an apology to Gina Rinehart after she threatened the public broadcaster with legal action over crude comments aired in its Race Around the World program. The show featured a short work by film-maker Kate McGuinness which included crude and offensive comments about Rinehart. Marks said the film had been edited on the ABC’s platforms to remove the material in question, and the broadcaster will now change its policies after Hancock Prospecting said the crude joke posed “serious risks” to Rinehart. McGuinness also issued an apology last Thursday, saying it wasn’t her intention to promote violence: “My writing is cartoonish and always satirical. Unfortunately, jokes do not land with everyone. Its purpose was never to be taken literally,” she said in a statement uploaded to the ABC’s website. title: ‘Morocco feels emboldened’: Trump’s influence in spotlight after Ceuta disaster
author: Ashifa Kassam in Madrid
summary: Washington-Rabat ties under scrutiny as questions swirl over what led to deadly influx into tiny Spanish territory
body_text: The cosy relationship between Washington and Rabat has long been flaunted by both sides, from Morocco’s announcement this year that it would be the first African state to join Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to the congratulatory message recently sent by Trump to mark King Mohammed VI’s 27 years in power. The latest example landed this week. As Spain grappled with the aftermath of the sudden influx – and swift return – of more than 70,000 people into Ceuta, Morocco’s monarch confirmed he had named a $1bn highway flanking the disputed territory of Western Sahara after Trump. The deepening ties have come under renewed scrutiny as questions continue to swirl over what exactly led to the deadly mass border crossing into the tiny Spanish territory in north Africa. “I think there’s enough evidence to hypothesise or claim that Morocco is behind this,” said Riccardo Fabiani, the north Africa project director for the International Crisis Group. “But there was no clear trigger for this, and this is what is puzzling for everyone.” Observers have suggested Spain’s recent rapprochement with Rabat’s archrival, Algeria, could have set off Morocco. But another, perhaps more plausible explanation pointed towards the US, said Fabiani. “It’s obviously impossible to demonstrate,” he said. “But in terms of plausibility, I don’t think it’s impossible to imagine that Morocco might have done something to earn brownie points with its allies, given that Morocco and this particular administration in Washington do have a very close, excellent relationship.” While Morocco had probably not “masterminded” the surge into Ceuta, he said, its relationship with the Trump administration – along with the Moroccan king’s desire to keep its claim to Ceuta in the spotlight – may have affected how it responded to fast-spreading online rumours about the Spanish border being thrown open. “For sure the Moroccan security forces were monitoring those conversations,” said Fabiani. “They saw that and there was probably some conversation where they decided to do nothing and see where this goes.” What followed made headlines across the globe as tens of thousands of people swam or waded across one of the EU’s two land borders with Africa. As Spain scrambled to cope, far-right voices seized on the images. In the US, the vice-president, JD Vance, and the state department blamed the influx on the Socialist-led government of Spain, while Trump warned that electing Democrats would make what happened in Spain “look small-time”. At no point did any of them mention Morocco or the potential role it might have played. Trump and his administration have long been open about the deep antipathy they feel for Pedro Sánchez, the Spanish prime minister, whose refusal to allow the US to use its airbases during the Iran war, rejection of the 5% defence spending target and vociferous criticism of Israel’s actions in Gaza have arguably made Spain the administration’s least favourite EU country. The American response seemed to be a triumph for Rabat, whose relationship with the US president traces back to his first term, when Morocco agreed to normalise ties with Israel in exchange for Trump’s recognition of its sovereignty claim over the disputed territory of Western Sahara. Since then, Morocco’s all-powerful monarch had doubled down on outreach efforts, said Fabiani. “The Moroccans have really made extra efforts to cultivate every single major decision-maker within the administration, including the president himself, to make sure that this administration will support, until the end, the Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara.” A hint that the relationship could help Morocco lay claim to more than Western Sahara came in a recent US congressional report that appeared to be sympathetic to Morocco’s refusal to recognise Ceuta as Spanish territory, describing it as “Spanish-administered” rather than a part of Spain, as it has been since 1580. Days after the influx, interest in Ceuta remained heightened among those close to both Trump and the Israeli government, said Haizam Amirah-Fernández, the director of the Madrid-based Centre for Contemporary Arab Studies. “They haven’t stopped talking about Ceuta for several days in a row, which is quite striking.” What had been laid bare was Rabat’s willingness to use “hybrid tactics to achieve political objectives”, said Amirah-Fernández, drawing a parallel with May 2021 when Rabat loosened border controls to allow more than 8,000 people to cross into Ceuta in a show of anger over Madrid’s decision to allow a Western Sahara pro-independence leader to travel to Spain to be treated for Covid-19. This time around, as nearly 10 times more people crossed into Ceuta, it set off a bout of finger-pointing across the EU rather than any kind of concerted effort to push back using the bloc’s status as Morocco’s largest trading partner and largest foreign investor. “The reaction of several governments in the EU was, in the end, what the White House was looking for – the erosion of solidarity between European partners,” said Amirah-Fernández. Senior officials in Morocco have pushed back against accusations it was in any way complicit. At the Rabat-based Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis, there was little doubt that relations between Morocco and the US were in their “golden era”. Even so, the country’s approach to the Trump administration remained pragmatic, said Said Saddiki, a senior fellow at the institute. “Moroccan policymakers are well aware of President Trump’s transactional style and have sought to preserve Morocco’s strategic autonomy,” Saddiki said in an email, citing efforts to maintain partnerships with the EU, China and the Gulf states, among others. “The relationship with the Trump administration has strengthened Morocco’s international position, but so far it has not come at the expense of its relations with Spain or the European Union.” For Fabiani, the events in Ceuta served to underscore the perils of Europe’s reliance on north African states to control migration flows. “This has made Europe entirely vulnerable and dependent on the goodwill of a country like Morocco,” he said. “Morocco is a partner, but at the same time it has its own interests. This vulnerability was on show.” This weakness could become more of an issue as time passed, given Morocco’s perception that the issue of Ceuta remained unsettled, Fabiani warned. “And Morocco feels emboldened, and there is an administration in Washington that is willing to back it up,” he said. “I don’t think Europe is ready for what comes next because it could get much more complicated.”

title: Top Democrats accuse Trump officials over Israeli settlers’ ‘unbridled violence’
author: David Smith Washington bureau chief
summary: Letter says lifting of sanctions sent ‘clear message’ settlers can use deadly force in West Bank without consequences
body_text: Senior Democrats have accused Donald Trump’s administration of giving a green light to violent Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, warning that its policies created “a climate of impunity and unbridled violence” that endangers both Palestinians and US citizens. In a letter seen by the Guardian, a group of 19 Democratic senators and representatives call for the restoration of sanctions against extremist settlers and demand independent US investigations into the deaths of nine US citizens killed in the West Bank since 2022. The letter, signed by the Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren among others, is addressed to Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, and Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary. It argues that Trump’s promise last year that “I will not allow Israel to annex the West Bank” has been undermined by events on the ground. “In practice,” the Democrats write, “violent settlers and the [Benjamin] Netanyahu government have proceeded to rapidly extend Israeli control over civilian populations in the region.” They urge the administration to use “all the diplomatic and economic tools at its disposal, including restoring sanctions, to end this violence and expansion of settlements”. The Democrats argue that Trump’s decision on his first day back in office to rescind sanctions imposed on more than 30 settlers and organisations linked to violence has had profound consequences. “Ending sanctions against those individuals and entities associated with West Bank extremism sent a clear message,” they write. “Settlers can use violent and deadly force with impunity against Palestinians and Americans while seizing land … and no one will face consequences.” The letter cites UN figures showing 1,835 attacks on Palestinian communities and property during 2025, the highest number since records began, and says the UN has reported that the pace of settler attacks this year is higher than in any year on record. It highlights repeated attacks on Turmus Ayya, a Palestinian town where the majority of residents are US citizens, including the burning of a family home belonging to Americans from Massachusetts and Washington state. The elected officials also focus on what they say has become an increasingly dangerous environment for Americans. Since Trump returned to office, they write, four US citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in the West Bank, bringing the total since 2022 to nine. The victims include the Palestinian American journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, 14-year-old Amer Mohammed Rabea, 17-year-olds Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Ahmed Mohammad Khdour and 20-year-old Sayfollah Musallet, as well as Omar Assad, a 78-year-old Palestinian American, and the Turkish American activist Aysenur Ezgi Eygi. The letter says the justice department “has the authority to independently investigate the killing of Americans abroad” but “has reportedly not opened investigations into any of the killings since 2025. Israel has yet to indict a single person involved in these incidents.” The Democrats also express concern over the detention of US citizens by the Israeli military including 20-year-old Sama Safi, whose access to vital medication was allegedly interrupted after her arrest, and Mohammed Ibrahim, who they say was detained for nine months while aged 15. They urge the administration to secure Safi’s immediate release and “push for the end of unjust and arbitrary detentions in the territory”. The senators and representatives argue that the violence extends beyond Palestinian communities, pointing to repeated attacks on Taybeh, described in the letter as “the last entirely Christian village in the West Bank”. Although the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, described an earlier attack there as “an act of terror” and pledged that those responsible would be prosecuted, the senators and representatives note that “no one has been arrested in connection with these crimes”. Huckabee is an evangelical Christian who has supported Jewish claims on the occupied land that settlers call Judea and Samaria. The letter is signed by Warren, Ed Markey, Jeff Merkley, Patty Murray, Jack Reed, Bernie Sanders, Brian Schatz, Adam Schiff, Chris Van Hollen, Peter Welch and Ron Wyden. The House of Representatives signatories are Katherine Clark, Richard Neal, Jim McGovern, Seth Moulton, Ayanna Pressley, Jake Auchincloss, Stephen Lynch and Lori Trahan. It concludes that Israeli security forces and settlers have attacked and displaced Palestinians in the West Bank “at an unprecedented rate” since the Trump administration took office and argues that Washington’s “deference to the Netanyahu government has contributed to a climate of impunity and unbridled violence towards civilian populations and religious minorities”. It demands answers by 17 August on investigations into attacks on Americans, the lifting of sanctions and the treatment of US citizens detained by the Israeli military.

title: US senators urge crackdown on wildfire betting amid warnings of arson risk
author: Sophie Sullivan
summary: Experts say growing trend on prediction markets could motivate people to start fires to win money
body_text: A group of US lawmakers is sounding the alarm over prediction market platforms that allow users to bet on wildfires, as experts warn the emerging trend could raise the risk of arson. Democratic senators from six states sent a letter this week to the chair of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), an independent government agency that regulates platforms such as Polymarket, urging it to rein in the practice. “As the United States faces yet another record-breaking fire season this year, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) cannot allow these prediction markets to offer unrestricted betting on wildfires,” said the lawmakers, who included the Oregon senator Jeff Merkley, California senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla, and Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada. They said such bets posed a risk that “individuals could be tempted to commit arson in order to make sure their bets are successful”. Concerns about money placed on wildfire predictions specifically stem mostly from Polymarket’s offerings during the 2025 Los Angeles fires. Kalshi, a main competitor, has not offered wildfire markets because “it creates perverse incentives”, the company’s head of communications, Elisabeth Diana, told the Guardian after publication. As the Palisades and Eaton fires devastated LA in early 2025, Polymarket gave users the chance to bet on questions such as when the wildfires would be contained, whether flames would spread to certain neighborhoods by a particular date, and how many acres of land would burn. The amounts wagered on the LA fires totalled more than $1.2m, according to Jamie L Pietruska, a historian at Rutgers University who followed those predictions. And this summer, a site called Wyldfyre, purported to be the “first prediction market for California wildfire” exclusively, has offered trades on “what fire does next”. Lawmakers’ concerns come as the US faces another brutal wildfire season. Huge fires in Washington state and Oregon have burned more than 2m acres and forced tens of thousands to evacuate. Ann Skeet, the senior director of leadership ethics at Santa Clara University’s Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, commended the senators’ demands of the CFTC, and said offering bets on how a wildfire spreads could incentivize people to commit arson. “Somebody could place a bet and then be motivated to actually start a fire,” Skeet said. “There’s just the practical reality of what it is you might be motivating people to do.” Pietruska said she was glad to see the senators’ call to regulate prediction markets, but that the demand was “year and a half late” after the Polymarket bets on the Los Angeles fires. “Gambling on the weather is not new. People have been betting informally on temperature and precipitation around the world for centuries,” Pietruska said. But it’s the “speed and scale” at which prediction markets work in a “climate-changed world” that concerns Pietruska, noting police investigations into an incident at Charles de Gaulle airport in Paris, where unusual temperature readings on weather forecasting equipment coincided with suspicious winning Polymarket bets. Neither Polymarket nor the CFTC responded to Guardian requests for comment. The US government has already launched several investigations into Polymarket, the world’s largest prediction market. The Wall Street Journal first reported in June that the agency had begun investigating Polymarket earlier this year, an investigation not publicly detailed but which is the CFTC’s third inquiry into the platform in recent years. In 2022, Polymarket was fined $1.4m for operating in the US without a license. The senators’ letter urged the CFTC to consider whether betting on wildfires was in the “public interest” and gave the agency until 14 August to respond to a list of questions. “The CFTC must lead the charge to rein in these contracts in the US and offshore and put in place commonsense guardrails to prevent people from profiting as wildfires threaten communities,” the letter demanded. • This article was amended on 12 August 2026. An earlier version incorrectly implied that Kalshi offered betting on wildfires; it does not.

title: Why making Anthony Fauci the enemy will harm US public health for years
author: Melody Schreiber
summary: Republicans are trying to scapegoat the infectious disease expert, even as they have gutted healthcare amid outbreaks of measles, cyclosporiasis and Ebola
body_text: Katie Miller, an erstwhile Trump administration official and wife of Stephen Miller, once relied on Dr Anthony Fauci to get through Covid. Now, she’s calling for his imprisonment – a reversal that illuminates the politicization of Fauci and of public health writ large, a trend that could have major repercussions for America’s preparedness for future crises. A US Senate committee will vote on Thursday morning over whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress after the physician and former public health official invoked his fifth amendment rights during a Senate hearing last week focused on Fauci’s actions during the Covid pandemic. The invocation of the worst days of the Covid pandemic comes as midterms loom and the administration struggles to address several infectious outbreaks, including cyclosporiasis and Ebola. Rand Paul, a senator, released contemporaneous notes that Fauci took during his time in public office, which Paul called Fauci’s diary, that reveal the confusion and fear of the time and illuminate the private episodes of a man who became known as America’s doctor. “By focusing entirely on one human being and by calling him all sorts of names, including ‘evil’, and by calling for him to be jailed, it abdicates Republicans’ own responsibility in the US response to the pandemic, which was under President Trump,” said Gavin Yamey, director of the Center for Policy Impact in Global Health at Duke University. “I think that this is all aimed at riling up the base ahead of the midterms and at washing their hands of any culpability themselves in the mass death event of Covid.” And it comes after substantial cuts to the public health infrastructure; misinformation has spread at the highest levels of the government, and growing outbreaks of measles, whooping cough, cyclosporiasis, Ebola and more. “This is an extraordinarily good way to distract people from the very deliberate destruction of the US public health system,” Yamey said. Like most Americans, Miller turned to Fauci for advice during the pandemic. As communications director for then-vice president Mike Pence, she was involved in the White House Covid-19 response. Fauci, who served as the director of the National Institute for Allergies and Infectious Diseases (Niaid), was also the chief medical adviser to seven presidents over three decades. Fauci described Miller warmly, writing that she was “great (tough, smart, but great)” on 25 March 2020, and that they “laugh at each other” in the Situation Room on 6 May 2020. When Miller tested positive for Covid, Fauci called to check on her several times a day. “She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant. Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone,” Fauci wrote on 9 May 2020. Later, Fauci wrote that he had directly contacted Miller’s pediatricians to discuss the baby’s care. It is perhaps not surprising that Miller would turn to Fauci, as many others in the country also relied on his advice and insight during a deeply uncertain and terrifying time. But her actions contrast with the intensity and speed at which Covid was politicized – and the extent to which Fauci would draw conservatives’ ire, even years later. In February and March 2020, Miller was reassessing communications from the Covid taskforce, and Fauci was told to stand down on media appearances until he received clearance again. “That’s the episode that got tagged ‘muzzling Fauci’,” said Céline Gounder, editor-at-large for public health at KFF Health News and a member of the Covid transition team under Biden. Soon after “deciding how much of Dr Fauci the public gets”, Miller was getting regular check-ins from Fauci on her own health, Gounder pointed out. “The same expertise: she’s rationing public access, but it’s available to her in private.” By April 2020, the pandemic was already being heavily politicized. The administration released plans for states to reopen, and President Trump posted a series of tweets encouraging supporters to “LIBERATE” blue states such as Minnesota, Michigan and Virginia. In late April, nearly half of Republicans (47%) surveyed by Pew Research Center said the pandemic was “made a bigger deal than it really is”. By June, that figure was 63%, and it rose to 66% in September. Republican attention to pandemic coverage went from 48% in March to 43% in late April to 35% by early June, while Democrats did not see any such changes. Spring 2020 looked similar across America; schools, for instance, were closed at about the same rate in red and blue states. But that changed by the fall, when “local partisanship predicted which districts would remain remote better than local Covid incidence did”, Gounder said. Those decisions were made not by Fauci, as he has been accused, but by about 13,349 public school districts, she pointed out in her newsletter, Underlying Conditions. “The more interesting story to me is who had private access to federal scientific expertise, what that access was worth in 2020, and what those same people have said about that expertise since,” Gounder said. She also pointed to early access to experimental treatments for Covid for Trump and his inner circle, nearly two months before they were available to the public. “A president publicly minimized a virus he was privately treated for with a drug the public couldn’t get,” Gounder said. Even after conservatives began publicly opposing his recommendations, the Millers still turned to Fauci for support. Fauci recounted speaking with Miller multiple times in October 2020, after her husband tested positive for Covid and she was traveling. “Spoke to her at Houston airport and after she landed,” he wrote on 6 October 2020. “Am on phone frequently with Katie and Stephen,” Fauci wrote on 31 December 2020. Katie Miller has since come out forcefully against Fauci. On the Covid taskforce, “Fauci cared more about virtue signaling than science,” Miller wrote in September 2025 in an apparent reference to wearing a face mask. In June, she said “he should be in jail”. After Fauci’s notes were made public, Miller claimed Fauci used the pandemic to “maximize his popularity”, and she endorsed calls to prosecute him. She told Notus she kept Fauci close so that he “did not leak against me or my husband”, though she didn’t specify what Fauci might leak. “Dr. Fauci was neither my friend nor my doctor, but a work colleague who weaponized my pregnancy and child for his gain to aggrandize himself,” Miller posted on Thursday, adding that “this man should be in prison”. Fauci has led the US through epidemics and pandemics over the decades: anthrax attacks in 2001, HIV, Sars, Ebola, Covid-19 and more, and he co-authored one of the most esteemed internal medicine textbooks. “We lose a lot when we see Republicans vilify Tony Fauci,” Yamey said. The US wasn’t unsafe because of Fauci’s leadership, Gounder said. “It wasn’t safe to leave home because a novel airborne virus was circulating in a population with no immunity, no vaccine, and no treatment.” And the Trump administration’s politicization and mismanagement “raised the toll”, she added. The trials facing Fauci make it less likely that others will step forward to guide public health, now or during a crisis. There were 1,499 harassment events across 583 local health departments between March 2020 and January 2021, and 222 officials left the field because of the targeting, Gounder pointed out. About 71% of the public health workforce reported at least one symptom of burnout and 20% reported near-constant symptoms in a 2024 survey. Three senior CDC leaders resigned last August over politicization of the agency, and one was fired for refusing to “rubber-stamp” Robert F Kennedy Jr’s anti-vaccine policies. The same month, a man fired more than 180 rounds into the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) campus because of misinformation about the Covid vaccine. He killed a police officer, David Rose. “If you’re 40 and choosing between US government service and industry, that’s now part of the math, not just the vast differences in compensation,” Gounder said. Yamey said he worried “that’s going to put future public health leaders off”. And there is an overwhelming amount of work to be done in addressing current public health crises and decades of repair to come. “But we will get there,” Yamey said. “We will all roll up our sleeves and build back, and hopefully build back better.”

title: The real meaning of Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan
author: Robert Reich
summary: We’re seeing America wake up to the tyranny that’s engulfed us
body_text: With the victory of progressive Abdul El-Sayed over representative Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic primary, prepare yourself to hear enormous quantities of bullshit about the Democratic party now being “taken over” by the “left” or by “democratic socialists”. Or as the reliably establishment New York Times put it: “Can an insurgent candidate, with unabashedly liberal positions, win a general election in a moderate state?” Oh, p-l-e-a-s-e. Michigan Democrats didn’t choose El-Sayed because he’s “unabashedly liberal”. Or because he’s a democratic socialist (in fact, he’s not). They chose him because he’s a fighter – at a time when America needs fighters willing to stand up to the worst tyrant who has ever occupied the Oval Office. Corporate Democrats – such as Haley Stevens, along with Rahm Emanuel, Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries – aren’t up to the task because they won’t bite the corporate hands that feed them campaign money. They won’t criticize the billionaire class. They refuse to talk about how big money has corrupted America. Yet it’s big corporations and the billionaire class that are supporting Trump’s authoritarianism. They’ve sucked up to Trump for corporate welfare, giant tax cuts, tariff exemptions, antitrust acquiescence and war contracts. They’ve given Trump hundreds of millions for his inauguration, his ballroom, his 250th birthday, his Super Pac. Jamie Dimon and his cronies on Wall Street; Elon Musk and his billionaire bros; Brad Carp and his corporate lawyers; Peter Thiel, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg and the Ellisons – all have sold their integrity for huge profits. They’ve created media empires that won’t criticize Trump, financial empires that feed Trump’s crypto, energy empires that feed off Trump’s war, and legal empires that allow Trump to ride roughshod over the rule of law. Which is why the US desperately needs people in Congress who will fight against Trump and his sycophants. The Democratic party isn’t being taken over by “the left” or by democratic socialists. There’s no civil war between progressives and moderates. We aren’t witnessing an ideological battle between the “left” and the “center”. We’re seeing the US wake up to the tyranny that’s engulfed us, and to a crisis of affordability that’s causing most Americans to struggle financially while fueling the biggest stock market rally in history. Trump’s tyranny and America’s affordability crisis are related. When corporate America and Wall Street are unleashed – when the president of the United States has made an implicit deal with the moneyed interests to back him and his authoritarian regime in exchange for tax cuts, deregulation, monopolization and pay-to-play corruption – of course prices soar and wages stagnate. Tyranny is the handmaiden of the moneyed interests. The Democratic party’s mega-donor class may be horrified by the rising tide of progressive populism overtaking more than a few primaries this cycle. After all, it spent tens of million of dollars on Stevens – making the Michigan primary one of the most expensive in US history. Too bad. It’s time that the Democratic party’s mega-donor class recognizes that its real choice is between democracy and tyranny, between an economy that works for all or one that works for a small sliver at the top. If the mega-donor class chooses the latter, it may be acting in its narrow self-interest, but it will also be acting against the future of this nation. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

title: The American left is making strides. But can they win in November?
author: Ben Davis
summary: The left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party. But it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of beating Republicans
body_text: The ideological struggle within the Democratic party continued on Tuesday night with primaries in Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, Virginia and Washington. The results showed an increasingly intense conflict within the party, with high Democratic primary turnout and bruising ideological battles up and down the ballot. The Democratic electorate is shifting, becoming more progressive and more willing to challenge party leadership, but not as quickly or uniformly as many assumed. Progressives and socialists scored another round of victories, most notably Abdul El-Sayed for Senate, but also downballot with Donavan McKinney and Will Lawrence in congressional races, and in state legislative seats such as Chris Gilmer-Hill in Detroit. But the scale and breadth of those victories fell short of the expectations created by polling and media coverage. A few key lessons have emerged. First, building a mass left in the United States is a slow and bruising process, and there is no single tipping point at which the party and its voters suddenly become committed leftwing partisans. Second, the left is nonetheless growing rapidly, able to win beyond young, deep-blue urban areas where concerns about general-election viability against Republicans are relatively limited, and across an entire statewide Democratic primary electorate in a swing state. This is a major step in the left’s development as an electoral force. Third, the left’s next and most important challenge is winning swing states and competitive seats against Republicans. The left has enjoyed a string of notable electoral victories during the second Trump administration, beginning with Zohran Mamdani’s primary win in New York City, and continuing up through the 2026 primaries. The Democratic electorate’s attitudes are changing: party leadership has grown less popular, while democratic socialism has gained support. The left has quickly gone from an extremely marginal force, with just a handful of members of Congress, largely confined to deep-blue urban districts and a small number of favorable constituencies, to a driving force in the party. Much of the media coverage has portrayed the party as being overtaken by an ascendant left. That broader narrative, reinforced by favorable polling, created an expectation that El-Sayed would win resoundingly. In practice, the recent wave means that a meaningful additional share of Democratic primary voters, perhaps 10-15%, is now willing to consistently support left candidates, on top of the existing leftwing base. It does not mean that every candidate backed by the DSA or the broader progressive movement will automatically win, or every Democrat backed by Aipac will lose. The actual campaign still matters tremendously; a large share of Democratic voters remain moderate, cross-pressured or primarily candidate-driven. Politics just doesn’t move that fast. The project of building a leftwing base and turning it into a durable majority, even within the Democratic party, is still a long-term one. El-Sayed’s narrow victory has been described as disappointing, because of favorable polling and the expectations created by the recent wave of leftwing victories. It is anything but. The polling miss has distorted how the result is being interpreted. Viewed against Michigan’s demographics, the left’s previous statewide performance, spending disparities, endorsements and comparable results elsewhere in the country, the victory was historically significant. The left has not previously won a genuinely competitive statewide Democratic primary of this kind, nor has a left candidate previously assembled a winning primary coalition extending this far beyond the movement’s urban base, especially in a swing state where voters are likely to weigh general-election viability. The left’s strategy over the past decade has been one of patience, winning seats in friendly areas, knocking doors and slowly building a base. It began by winning city council and state legislative victories and expanded more recently into successful mayoral and congressional races, all in deep blue areas. This is the first time the left has real proof of concept that beyond urban cores with friendly demographics, it can win over a majority of Democratic voters. It also offers early evidence that a left candidate could compete seriously in a Democratic presidential primary in 2028. The next test is November. The left has been battle-tested in primaries against moderate candidates, party institutions and well-funded outside groups such as Aipac and the crypto lobby. But a general election in a swing state is a different and less hospitable terrain. El-Sayed, along with Francesca Hong if she advances in Wisconsin, needs to demonstrate the left can win not only a winning Democratic primary coalition, but a broad enough general-election coalition to prevail outside deep-blue territory. This matters in the near term, for Democrats to win the Senate and retain governorships; in the medium term, because presidential primary voters in 2028 will want evidence that left candidates can win competitive general elections; and in the long term, because the leftwing political project rests on being able to twin and govern with durable electoral majorities. On Tuesday, the left continued its string of victories, activating young voters and bringing Arab and Muslim voters back into the Democratic fold. But these victories do not resolve the movement’s central challenges. Every primary remains a brutal fight, highly contingent on candidates, organization, spending and local conditions. And the movement must now prepare for the more difficult terrain of November. The left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party, but it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of defeating Republicans. Ben Davis works in political data in Washington DC. He worked on the data team for the Bernie Sanders 2020 campaign and is an active member of the Democratic Socialists of America

title: Exclusive: Major Republican fundraiser winning contracts from Trump administration, emails reveal
author: Aram Roston in Washington
summary: Palmer Luckey has donated $5.9m to Republicans and bundled more, while reaping billions in Pentagon contracts
body_text: Wealthy Republicans on the west coast received an emailed invitation in July to an upcoming fundraiser titled “Keep the Senate”. The email, obtained by the Guardian, described the event as a “private roundtable and dinner with the National Republican Senatorial Committee” where donors can pledge $50,000 for seats at the head table, and mingle with legislative heavy hitters from Capitol Hill including the Senator majority leader, John Thune, and Mike Rogers, who is running for Senate in Michigan with Donald Trump’s endorsement. One of the organizers listed on the invite was the defense industry tycoon Palmer Luckey, the 33-year-old co-founder of sprawling weapons manufacturer Anduril Industries. The invitation is one of dozens of emails obtained by the Guardian that unravel Luckey’s vast Maga political fundraising over the last seven years. A longtime GOP donor and activist who spoke on condition he not be identified in order to preserve his political relationships said Luckey was now the “godfather of Republican fundraising on the west coast”. “If you’re raising campaign money in California, you have to go to Palmer Luckey,” he said. “Luckey is the top tier. There are others who are important below him but no one at his level.” Anduril, launched just nine years ago, has emerged as a major military contractor for the Trump administration, working on contracts for everything from drones to autonomous jet fighters to space-based interceptors. In March, the US army awarded a $20bn sole-source contract to Anduril for a variety of drones it sells, though it is not clear which of its weapons systems are operational or have been deployed for combat in US operations. Anduril, though it is not widely known as a space contractor, announced in May it would work, with a team of other companies, on what may be the mother of all contracting opportunities offered by the Trump administration, the so-called “Golden Dome” anti-missile space-based interceptor effort. Estimates for the Golden Dome range between $185bn and $1.2tn. Much of Anduril’s PR sparkle comes from Luckey. He’s a media darling, profiled on 60 Minutes and in the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times, which called him the “It Guy of the booming defense-technology industry”. His offbeat, relaxed attire – colorful Hawaiian shirts, a chin puff goatee, cargo shorts and flip-flops – counterintuitively makes him seem more credible. Luckey is treated by many in the defense industry as a technology prophet and futurist who often holds forth on what he believes to be the true nature of warfare. For example, he told Axios that future wars will be fought in a “subterranean domain”, under the earth’s crust, in underground conflicts. Anduril’s success in winning huge contracts has blossomed with little attention paid to the central role Luckey plays as a donor and fundraising “bundler” for the Republican party. Bundlers hold large fundraisers for candidates or campaign committees and political action groups, and curate high-dollar invitation lists for those events. The emails obtained by the Guardian shed light on Palmer Luckey’s vast GOP political fundraising efforts and activism over the last 10 years. Palmer declined an interview for this piece, writing, “I am not going to help you guys make money,” and did not respond to a detailed list of questions. Rising influence OpenSecrets, a non-profit that tracks campaign donations, says Federal Election Commission (FEC) records show that Luckey has donated $5.9m to Republicans since 2017. While that is a tremendous amount of money for one person to give to politicians, it does not put him in the order of, say, Miriam Adelson, the widow of Sheldon Adelson, who has forked over $100m to Trump’s campaign in 2024. Luckey doesn’t have her wealth. His real value to GOP politicians exceeds his own donations. He hosts and organizes fundraising events and campaigns for Republicans from the president all the way down to state races. “If you become a bundler, it just multiplies your influence,” said Brendan Glavin of OpenSecrets. “It makes you a more important person. You’re bringing in not just your money. You’re bringing other people’s money. It integrates you in the campaign and makes you more important to the candidate than just a donor.” Behind the scenes, Luckey has reached a position in campaign finance and politics that rivals his influence in military contracting, according to two GOP fundraising figures. The emails, which are a partial list of invitations, show that Luckey has held fundraisers over the last seven years for at least 20 Republican politicians, ranging from Trump to a California attorney general candidate. Just as Luckey has emerged as a major fundraiser on the right, his co-founder, Anduril’s CEO, Palantir veteran Brian Schimpf, became a major donor to Democratic causes, albeit on a far smaller scale. So, in time-honored tradition, Anduril’s management ends up donating to both sides of the political aisle, though the vast majority goes towards the GOP. FEC records show Schimpf’s donations at $1.16m over the same period that Luckey gave $5.9m. An Anduril official emailed the Guardian: “It shouldn’t surprise anyone that two executives at the same company have different political views. Like millions of Americans, Brian and Palmer don’t share identical political views.” A fundraising dam breaks Luckey first became famous in tech before he could legally drink. At 20, in 2012, he launched a Kickstarter that raised more than $2m for a virtual reality gaming headset he said he was building first in his parents’ garage. It was a Silicon Valley Cinderella narrative. Two years later, Facebook became the prince at the ball and paid him $2bn for the company. In 2016, after four years of hype, the first Oculus Rift headset started getting shipped to consumers. And then, quickly, Luckey seemed to flame out in scandal. The Daily Beast revealed he’d been secretly funding a group dedicated to “shitposting” negative memes about Hillary Clinton. “We know Hillary Clinton is corrupt, a warmonger, a freedom-stripper. Not the good kind you see dancing in bikinis on Independence Day, the bad kind that strips freedom from citizens and grants it to donors,” Luckey had written, under the pseudonym Nimblerichman, on Reddit. The disclosure had an immense impact, at least for a time. Eight months later Luckey left Facebook, and he later portrayed himself in interviews as simply being canceled for giving money to Republicans, ignoring the main criticisms over the group’s crude and underhanded tactics. Luckey left Facebook with immense wealth, and in April 2017, just four months after Trump’s first inauguration, he founded Anduril. His partners in the venture came from the Peter Thiel-backed Palantir, a company that had long had success in federal contracting through major lobbying and PR battles. In June of 2017, his company just two months old, Luckey gave his first ever actual campaign finance donation, to Ted Cruz, the senator from Texas. Looking at his subsequent donations, it appears that the dam broke for him. Palmer gave 25 more times to political committees and legislators that year alone, FEC records show, and he has donated on more than a thousand occasions, or, on average, about 100 times every year. In the emails shared with the Guardian, the very first fundraising event Luckey co-hosted took place in August of 2017, two months after his donation to Ted Cruz. It was a major effort, and would include GOP House members such as Ken Calvert, Duncan Hunter, Darrell Issa, Devin Nunes, Dana Rohrabacher and Kevin McCarthy. Then in November, in a separate email chain, Palmer’s name came up again, for the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC). A congressional aide named Jason Pitkin wrote to a party official: “we are going to be asking people for $33,900 for the NRCC and then after the first of the year we can ask them for $101,700.” Pitkin noted that congressman Rohrabacher had introduced Luckey to Kevin McCarthy, then the powerful House majority leader, “at a Private meeting”. “As you can see by the attached invitation,” Pitkin said, “Palmer is hosting an event for Dana [Rohrabacher] On December 15th. Our understanding is that Palmer was going to contribute $100,000 for the CA Victory event. Please let us know how much more Palmer can give to the NRCC.” Pitkin did not respond to emailed questions. In July of 2020, just three years after its creation, Anduril won its first mammoth contract from the first Trump administration. Customs and Border Protection awarded the young company a contract estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars for surveillance towers on the border. And in that period it was clear that Luckey had hit the most senior levels of political access. On 6 October, the emails show, Luckey and his wife hosted Trump himself at a lunch at their waterfront mansion. The stakes were high and so were the tickets. Donors were told that $150,000 would get access to the round table, a VIP reception and event, and a photo op with the president. During the Biden years, Anduril still maintained its business efforts targeting US national security, and still won contracts. It went on a major acquisition binge, buying up drone companies across the country. And Luckey’s fundraising for the GOP continued. The records obtained by the Guardian show that after 2021, Luckey hosted fundraisers for key figures including Tom Cotton, the head of the Senate intelligence committee; Rick Scott, the Republican senator from Florida; Ken Calvert, then the influential ranking member of the House’s defense appropriations subcommittee; and Mike Waltz, now Trump’s UN ambassador and briefly his national security adviser. Luckey also hosted another event for a future Trump official: a $50,000-a-plate fundraiser in June 2022 for Mehmet Oz, who would later join the Trump administration. That event became scandalous when Jezebel reported the fundraiser incorporated a speech by Oz in front of a car that once belonged to Adolf Hitler. Jezebel pointed out that Luckey’s sister is married to Maga firebrand Matt Gaetz, then a congressman from Florida. Now that Trump is president, Anduril appears to be taking its turn at the table of the major contractors, amid Lockheed Martin, Raytheon and General Dynamics. Certainly it has raised extraordinary money. In the latest round, led by Thrive Capital, controlled by Jared Kushner’s brother Joshua, it raised $5bn in venture capital. Anduril says in Trump’s first year in office it doubled its revenue – a growth rate of 100%, but still only reached $2.2bn for 2025, which is barely a blip in the Pentagon’s trillion-dollar budget. Still, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has twice toured Anduril factories. “Palmer and everyone, thank you so much,” he said last December as he visited Anduril’s factory in Costa Mesa, California, at a giant former industrial site where the Los Angeles Times was once printed. The Anduril factory was “foundational” to the new Pentagon, Hegseth said. On that tour, Hegseth donned a special helmet designed by Anduril. A soldier wearing the helmet would be able to see the outside world not through his eyes but through sensors, as a kind of virtual or “augmented” reality, just like the old Oculus Rift headset Palmer Luckey made his fortune on. In his speech, Hegseth referred to “that cool helmet I just saw that the army might be wearing eventually”.

title: First Thing: Democrats look forward after progressive El-Sayed victory in Michigan
author: Vivian Ho
summary: Abdul El-Sayed is latest leftwing candidate to capture nomination for November’s midterm elections. Plus: gender parity in Latin America’s city of cycling
body_text: Good morning. The progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed has won the Democratic primary for the US Senate in Michigan. Despite many backing his opponent, Haley Stevens, in the race, leading Democrats are now uniting behind the former public health official with the goal of retaking control of the chamber in November’s midterm elections. “Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate. We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November,” the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and Kirsten Gillibrand, who chairs the Democratic Senate campaign arm, said in a joint statement. What does El-Sayed’s victory mean for the Democratic party? Though a contentious general election, in a battleground state, awaits, his rise could serve as a revision to the political establishment’s prior playbook of requiring candidates to run from the center in swing-state politics. What do the Democrats need to retake the Senate? Republicans currently control the chamber with 53 lawmakers. The easiest path for Democrats to take back the Senate requires holding on to their seats in Michigan and Georgia while ousting Republicans from blue state Maine as well as three other red states. Senate confirms Trump pick Erica Schwartz as new CDC director In a rare win for the Trump administration after a string of failed attempts to fill senior health posts, Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). As Donald Trump’s third pick to run the CDC, Schwartz will take the reins of the agency amid public concern over an outbreak of cyclosporiasis and Robert F Kennedy Jr’s hesitancy towards vaccines. What was the vote? Schwartz was confirmed by a ⁠51-44 vote that broke largely along party lines, with Tim Kaine of Virginia the sole Democrat to support her nomination. Israeli strike that killed journalist in Lebanon was war crime, say rights groups Investigations from Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Legal Agenda have determined that Israel deliberately and directly attacked the Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil and her colleague Zeinab Faraj in April, with apparent knowledge that they were civilians. Deliberate attacks on civilians is a war crime. Khalil, 42, was killed while Faraj, 21, was injured. What has Israel said about the attack? Israel said it “regrets any harm caused to journalists” and that the journalists were killed “as part of a series of events” during which two Hezbollah military operatives were killed. How many journalists have been killed in this conflict? Israel has killed at least 15 journalists in Lebanon and 210 in Gaza since 2023, according to the UN human rights office. In other news … Senior Democrats have accused Donald Trump’s administration of giving a green light to violent Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank with policies that began with Trump rescinding sanctions on his first day in office. Nato is working to get Ukraine the air defences it “urgently needs”, its secretary general has said, after Kyiv failed to shoot down a single Russian missile in an attack on Wednesday. Donald Trump’s legal team is pushing to block a court order that would grant the BBC access to the president’s financial records, as part of his multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the British broadcaster. The Cambridge professor Jason Arday, accused of plagiarism and embellishment, has resigned after the university announced he was to face new investigations into his qualifications and career. Stat of the day: 90% of US adults listed groceries and food costs as their top cost-of-living concern A new survey found that a majority of Americans agree that the rising cost of living is a significant barrier to achieving a better life. According to a new survey of more than 30,000 adults from across the country spanning generations and economic classes, 60% of respondents said they wanted greater financial security but 40% described themselves as either “getting by but financially vulnerable” or “struggling to meet basic needs”. The Filter recommends: 32 things worth buying from Nordstrom’s anniversary sale Nordstrom’s annual sale, which runs until 9 August, includes more than 22,000 items across home, fashion, beauty, travel and more. The Filter crew has sifted through all of them to find the 32 deals they endorse, on top brands ranging from Le Creuset to Ray-Ban. Don’t miss this: Black college gymnasts in a divided South Gymnast Nyla Aquino is one of the University of Georgia’s brightest stars, leading her team to a resurgent sixth-place finish at the 2026 NCAA championships. But she and other Black athletes competing in the Southeastern Conference are striving to make their mark in a region of historical anti-Black prejudices, in a time when diversity, equity and inclusion programs and voting rights are under attack. “No matter how well I do, someone’s going to be racist,” she said. …or this: Achieving gender parity in Latin America’s city of cycling While Bogotá records nearly 900,000 bicycle trips each day – more than any other city in Latin America – less than a third of cycling journeys are taken by women. City officials are looking to change that. “Many older women come here because they were never allowed to ride a bicycle as girls,” said Sergio Prieto, who helps to oversee Bogotá’s Bike School. “They were told bikes were for men, that women shouldn’t be riding them. Here, those barriers and stereotypes are left behind.” Climate check: How the human-driven climate crisis fuels Canada’s deadly wildfires A new study conducted by World Weather Attribution found that the human-driven climate crisis amplified the conditions that led to fires blazing across Canada. Burning coal, oil and gas has overheated the planet and caused climate-influenced conditions to occur every two to six years in the Northwest Territories and every six to 15 years in Ontario. There are 700 fires burning in Canada at present. Last Thing: How well do you know the latest dating terms? Fresh dating trends seem to emerge every week in this age of app-based romance. Some terms such as “ghosting” or “catfishing” have become part of the modern parlance. But how familiar are you with other dating trends? Take this quiz and find out.
