title: Senate committee says it has copy of Fauci’s phone as it weighs holding him in contempt
author: Edward Helmore
summary: Veteran US health official invoked fifth amendment right amid hostile questioning from Republicans last week
body_text: A US Senate committee says it obtained a backup copy of Anthony Fauci’s iPhone as it weighed whether to hold the veteran government health official in contempt of Congress for refusing to answer Republicans’ questions amid a hostile inquisition last week. The phone was used by Fauci during his time as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, including his time fronting the first Trump administration’s response to the Covid pandemic in 2020. Senator Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, chair of the Senate homeland security permanent subcommittee on investigations, said he had obtained a copy of the phone. “Hopefully, this device will address many of the questions he refused to answer at last week’s hearing,” Johnson wrote on social media. The Wall Street Journal reported that the copy was transferred by the US Department of Health and Human Services, led by Fauci critic Robert F Kennedy Jr. Last week, Fauci invoked his fifth amendment right not to testify dozens of times, and accused the Republican senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, who chairs the Senate homeland security and government affairs committee, of having an “unhinged obsession” with him. Before the hearing, excerpts from Fauci’s journals were released to the public. They showed his growing disillusionment with Trump in the first year of the Covid-19 pandemic, when he called the president “a true embarrassment”, “totally nuts” and “truly an obnoxious adolescent”. Johnson and Paul have sought to increase pressure on Fauci in recent days to answer questions related to pandemic health measures and the origins of Covid-19. Last week’s hearing was a continuation of Paul’s years-long support of the “lab leak” theory, or the idea that the Covid-19 pandemic began as a release from the Wuhan Institute of Virology, a theory many virologists contend is improbable. Paul has argued Fauci’s constitutional protections did not apply during the hearing, since Fauci had received a pardon from Joe Biden. Fauci, 85, has said he fears criminal charges because Paul was trying “to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars’”.

title: ‘He should resign’: unease in Republican Max Miller’s Ohio district amid domestic abuse allegations
author: Stephen Starr in Wooster, Ohio
summary: Voters in the red district are concerned with congressman’s alleged behavior and political future ahead of the midterms
body_text: David Griffith was a registered Republican for years. But on Sunday evening, he watched the Ohio congressman Max Miller stumble through an 18-minute statement in which the lawmaker attempted to defend himself against allegations of domestic abuse against his ex-wife and infant child. What Griffith saw and heard, he said, was a person that bore no resemblance to the Republican party he once supported. “What I saw was a person who needs help,” said Griffith, seated at a bench in a community park in Wooster, a quiet town of 26,000 people situated at the southern end of the beleaguered Miller’s congressional district. Though he has been critical of Donald Trump for years, last May Griffith ended his formal affiliation with the Republican party. “At this [midterm] election, I’m voting a straight Democratic ticket,” he said. “I’ve never done that before.” Across Miller’s largely red district, Republicans are deeply concerned with their representative’s alleged behavior and political future. Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, the daughter of the Republican Ohio senator Bernie Moreno, has accused Miller of pointing a gun at her head, pouring hot water on her and potentially breaking their two-year-old daughter’s collarbone. Emily Moreno has also alleged Miller physically attacked her attorney and another legal representative, and filed for a restraining order on her lawyer’s behalf. Emily Moreno and Miller are now locked in a bitter custody battle. On Sunday, Bernie Moreno called for Miller to resign in an X post after years of silence on the issue: “He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter.” Miller, who faces an election this November, has denied any allegations of domestic abuse. In his statement on Sunday, he blamed the so-called leftwing media and his former wife for initiating a campaign to sully his name. On Tuesday, he attempted to defend himself further on Jake Tapper’s evening show on CNN, likening his fight to that of Trump’s when the president also faced sexual assault allegations. “The police are not investigating it; ask yourself, why aren’t they investigating these things?” he said. Before specific details of the allegations against Miller were recently made public and before Senator Moreno’s calls, Miller was expected to easily retain his seat, with pollsters suggesting in June the district leans Republican by five points. Miller, 37, who had previously served as a presidential aide during Trump’s first administration, was endorsed by Trump in 2021 during his first campaign. But this week, reports emerged that the president’s support for Miller may be waning. The final day the Ohio Republican party could replace Miller with another candidate, if it decides to do so, is 12 August. Bill Heck, vice-chair of the Republican party of Medina county, which lies inside Miller’s district, wouldn’t say if he thinks the congressman should resign. “There is so much stuff flying around that we have not been able to decipher what’s real and what’s not. What we’re trying to determine right now is how much of this is credible and how much he can refute and recover from,” he said. But he did concede that Republican voters in Miller’s district are worried. “I think a lot of our members and our steadfast Republicans are concerned,” he said. “I’m sure the president does not want to lose that seat. With 92 days left [to the election] it’s going to be really difficult for anybody to come in and take over the position – if appointed.” A host of other Republican party county organizations and groups across Miller’s district, including the women’s branch of the Republican party of Cuyahoga county, asking if they thought the congressman should resign, did not respond to requests for comment on the situation. While Miller as the incumbent won his 2024 congressional election by a 15% margin, a Democrat and an independent candidate split the vote between them. In November, Miller faces Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker from Brook Park, a Cleveland suburb. “The district leans Republican, but it is not so overwhelmingly Republican that a Democrat could never win,” says Justin Buchler, an associate professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland. “If you combine a midterm election moving everything nationwide towards the Democrats with a weak Republican candidate, that could be enough for the seventh district to flip. Miller is weakened at the moment, so if he tries to stay in the race, that helps Poindexter, and if Miller withdraws, then without a strong replacement, that still helps Poindexter.” ‘He hasn’t engaged with our community’ A former Marine Corps reserve, Miller, who is seeking a third congressional term, has a long history of allegations of violence towards women, including from the former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham, who accused him of pushing her against a wall and slapping her when the two were dating. (Miller has denied the allegation.) In north-eastern Ohio, the Miller family is known as one of the most powerful and respected in the region. Max’s grandfather, Sam, who died in 2019, was an esteemed Cleveland real estate mogul and philanthropist. Sixty miles south of Cleveland, Wooster, the county seat of largely rural Wayne county, was once a heartbeat of the industrial midwest. The collapse of the local jobs market in the early 2000s and accompanying economic decline that followed over the past two decades has fueled resentment locally that Trump has long since tapped into. In the 2024 presidential election, Trump won 70% of the vote in Wayne county. Wooster hasn’t elected a Democratic mayor for decades. “If the [Republican] party followed the standards we did, then I’d say he should resign,” says Bill Bailey, a former judge and the chair of the Wayne county Democratic party. “In my view, the Republican party is more concerned about retaining votes than they are about enforcing any kind of standards.” He says he doesn’t believe Miller’s claims of innocence, nor do many typically Republican voters. In Wayne county’s primary elections held last May, Bailey says about 1,600 registered Republican voters chose independent candidates and another 500 Republicans picked Democrats. “He hasn’t engaged with our community,” says Bailey of Miller. “I doubt that the average person would recognize him on the street.” For Griffith, who runs a local Facebook group called Defending Democracy and believes that the Republican party should support the US’s allies overseas, Miller represents everything that’s gone wrong with the party. “I have to believe that people get involved in public service because they want to do good, regardless of party,” he says. “Max Miller is not one of those people.”

title: US Senate panel votes to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress over Covid hearing
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: Anthony Fauci’s lawyer condemned the vote from the Republican-controlled committee as a ‘crude political stunt’
body_text: A Republican-controlled US Senate committee voted to hold Dr Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after the veteran public health official repeatedly pleaded the fifth amendment to parry a hostile inquisition into his stewardship of the response to the Covid-19 pandemic. Fauci, the former director of National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (Niaid), who led the agency for 38 years before retiring in 2022, gave the same response to dozens of questions while refusing to give clarifying answers during a tense hearing last week, citing his constitutional protections. The Senate homeland security and government affairs committee voted in favor of referring a potential criminal case against Fauci to the US Department of Justice. The vote was condemned as “shameful” and a “crude political stunt” by Fauci’s lawyer, David Schertler, who was forcibly ejected from last week’s hearing when he tried to speak on behalf of his client. The committee is chaired by the Republican Kentucky senator Rand Paul, whom Fauci last week accused of having an “unhinged obsession” with him as he refused to answer questions at the hearing. Paul insisted on Thursday that he wasn’t trying to entrap Fauci. “He had no liability if he told the truth,” Paul said. “The chair directed Anthony Fauci to answer. He refused,” Paul said in his opening statement. “That is what we are voting on today – not his opinions, not his policies, not anything he said from the podium six years ago. “We are voting on whether a witness who has received the benefit of a sweeping federal pardon can be ordered by this committee to answer questions and then defy that order without consequence.” But top Democrats criticized the Republican-led process. The Michigan senator Gary Peters, the ranking Democrat on the Senate panel, argued that the drive to subpoena Fauci, and now to hold him in contempt, accomplished nothing to advance public health. Paul’s work amounted to “a one-sided investigation and a rushed process … that could harm our ability to conduct future investigations”, said Peters. While a contempt referral must typically be approved by the full Senate after a congressional committee, this would probably require a 60-vote majority – requiring Democratic support. Paul acknowledged this standard path on Wednesday, but said he did not “want to waste time” moving the matter to a vote of the full Senate. He previously suggested during a Fox News interview that he could send the referral directly to the justice department, with a legal brief. Peters warned that bypassing a full Senate vote might not be legally valid and said punishing Fauci for exercising his fifth amendment rights could deter future witnesses from giving congressional testimony. “Future witnesses will argue that appearing before Congress exposes them to punishment regardless of whether they comply with a subpoena and invoke a constitutional protection,” he said. The fifth amendment is enshrined in the US constitution as a protective measure intended to save individuals from being forced to incriminate themselves when under investigation or asked to provide testimony. The evening before the vote, it emerged that the US Department of Health and Human Services had provided a copy of Fauci’s phone to a Senate subcommittee. “Hopefully, this device will address many of the questions he refused to answer at last week’s hearing,” Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, the subcommittee’s Republican chair, wrote on social media. Fauci, 85, who was pardoned by Joe Biden at the end of his presidency, declined to answer questions after accusing Paul of harboring a goal of “embarrassing and intimidating me” and of putting him “behind bars” because of his leading role in urging widespread restrictions, including masking and social distancing, to combat the pandemic. The senator has long accused Fauci of deliberately downplaying the possibility that the virus originated from a research laboratory in the Chinese city of Wuhan, rather than jumping from an animal to humans in a wet market, as most scientists believe. “Although it pains me to do so, because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys I will invoke my right under the fifth amendment of the constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” Fauci said during the hearing. Thereafter, he warded off all subsequent questions with identical answers that invoked the fifth amendment, enraging his Republican critics. “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution,” he said, in an undeviating answer to different questions. Paul – who had subpoenaed Fauci to appear – warned him during the hearing that his stance would have “repercussions”. Later, he told him: “Because you refuse to answer, citing a privilege that is unsupported because of your pardon, and after being denied to do so, this committee has scheduled a vote next week on a resolution certifying your contempt.” It is unclear whether a vote in favor of contempt will have legal force. According to the constitution, the fifth amendment guarantees that no individual “shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself, nor be deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law”. The US supreme court has confirmed in several decisions since 1955 that witnesses can invoke it in congressional investigations, according to the Library of Congress. “Although the [Fifth] amendment’s protection expressly refers to criminal cases[s], the Court has nevertheless found the privilege against self-incrimination to be available to a witness appearing before a congressional committee,” the library’s annotated interpretation of the constitution states. Paul has insisted Fauci is precluded from pleading the fifth, however, on the grounds that the pre-emptive pardon Biden granted him means he cannot be prosecuted for any of the matters senators were asking him about. Paul argued that Fauci’s refusal to answer could lead to criminal prosecution for contempt of Congress or obstructing a congressional proceeding. Federal law makes it a crime for witnesses to “willfully” refuse to answer questions when called to give congressional testimony. A separate law makes it illegal to obstruct an investigation by a congressional committee. Fauci’s lawyers have argued that he is on unassailable legal grounds by pleading the amendment. “For years, Senator Paul has proclaimed to anyone who would listen that Dr Fauci should be prosecuted and put in prison,” Schertler, Fauci’s legal counsel, said on Thursday. “Dr Fauci has committed no crime – and Senator Paul knows it. “Today’s resolution is a continuation of Senator Paul’s personal vendetta against Dr Fauci, who spent 50 years in public health and has saved countless lives. It is shameful and wrong that Senator Paul is abusing his power by trying to weaponize the justice department against an honorable public servant.” Robert Mackey contributed reporting

title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon
body_text: The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China. The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada. The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants. More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association. Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China. “China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee. “The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places where China is present?” The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism in Canada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods. Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital. Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC the closure could harm US interests. “I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto. “It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.” A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.” China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island of Grenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”. A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time. “We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.” In a later statement, issued after this story was first published, a department spokesperson countered the assertion that the closures would benefit China. “Claims that China is filling a diplomatic vacuum is [sic] inherently false and we recommend that individuals who subscribe to this propaganda take a look at the so-called help China had in the recent earthquakes in Venezuela or to address the Ebola outbreak,” the spokesperson said. The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions. Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.

title: FCC scraps limit on local TV ownership in win for media conglomerates
author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
summary: The 2-1 vote along party lines repealed ‘national cap’ that served as a key check on consolidation of the TV industry
body_text: In a historic vote on Thursday morning, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) voted along party lines to overturn a key check against the consolidation of the television industry, throwing out a rule that prevented any one company from owning stations that collectively reach more than 39% of all US TV households. The vote is a win for television conglomerates that aim to expand their reach across the country, particularly conservative-leaning companies like Sinclair Broadcast Group and Nexstar. In a presentation endorsing the move, the FCC’s media bureau told commissioners on Thursday that the cap was no longer necessary in the current media environment, and that instead of promoting competition, it “constrains” local television networks from increasing their scale. The initiative was supported by the FCC chair, Brendan Carr, and Trump-appointed commissioner Olivia Trusty, who said she did not see it as a “silver bullet” to address all issues with competition – but viewed it as a meaningful step to help broadcasters. Carr argued that repealing the cap would serve to benefit local broadcasters, although large media conglomerates will most immediately benefit from the decision. “The FCC has the authority to modify the cap as we did today, and it is the right policy answer [if] you care about the future of trusted local news,” he said. “It’s time to restore balance to the broadcast airwaves. Repealing the national cap will provide essential relief for local broadcasters by restoring a healthy counterbalance for the growing leverage and power of national programmers.” The 39% “national cap”, as it is called, came out of a 2003 compromise hammered out by congressional negotiators. Anna M Gomez, the lone Democrat on the FCC, voted against overturning the cap, an action she said was “unlawful” and would hurt local journalism. “Today’s decision to eliminate the 39% national audience reach cap is unlawful on its face and a profound departure from both statutory boundaries and longstanding broadcast policy,” she said. “Congress set this cap in federal law, and only Congress can change it. I cannot support an action that so plainly violates the law and exceeds the Commission’s authority while simultaneously overlooking the real-world consequences for the public we serve.” While the $6.2bn merger of mega-broadcasters Nexstar and Tegna is now on ice after a California judge issued a temporary injunction holding it up, the FCC in March granted a waiver of the ownership cap to approve the deal, arguing that the commission had the “authority” to do so. Nexstar, in particular, has seemed to take steps to stay in Carr’s good graces. Nexstar was one of two major owners of local television stations that acted quickly to pre-empt broadcasts of Jimmy Kimmel’s late-night show after it drew Carr’s ire in September 2025. Chris Ripley, the chief executive of Sinclair, said on an earnings call on Wednesday that he “couldn’t be happier” about the overturn of the cap. The 2-1 vote drew heavy criticism from groups that advocate for press freedom and media pluralism. A group of protesters demonstrated outside the FCC building in Washington, holding out photos of Carr’s face with the word “shame” on it. “Changing this limit requires congressional action, but Carr doesn’t care,” said Matt Wood, vice-president of policy and general counsel of Free Press, an advocacy organization that aims to promote free speech, in a statement. “He’ll do whatever it takes to clear the way for Trump-aligned billionaires to swallow up stations wherever and whenever they please. The result would be just one or two dominant broadcasters in every market, deep job cuts for journalists and an influx of bargain-basement content disguised as local news. This spells disaster for the local communities that broadcasters are supposed to serve.” Clayton Weimers, executive director of Reporters Without Borders North America, said the move was not just deregulation, but also a “consolidation in the interest of the powerful”. “The FCC has abandoned one of the last significant safeguards against excessive concentration of media ownership in the United States,” Weimers said. “Americans are already confronting the collapse of local news, rising political pressure on independent media and an increasingly toxic online information space. Rather than strengthening media pluralism, the FCC is accelerating its erosion.” Free Press said after the vote that the group and its “allies” would challenge the decision in court. In a press conference after the FCC’s monthly meeting, Carr said: “If it goes to the courts, it goes to the courts. And we’ll litigate it and see where it goes.”

title: Trump denies US low on key munitions in war with Iran after reports of shortages
author: David Smith Washington bureau chief
summary: President’s comment come after report he had demanded answers from Pete Hegseth over alleged shortages
body_text: Donald Trump has lashed out at reports that the US is running short of key munitions in its war with Iran, threatening long prison sentences for officials who leak information about the military’s weapons stocks. The US president claimed on Thursday that the US had “massive amounts” of ammunition and said more was being manufactured and shipped to the region, as his frustration over the conflict spilled into a public attack on the media. “Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, without providing evidence or details about the specific weapons in question. His remarks came after a report that he had demanded answers from his defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, over alleged shortages at a cabinet meeting last Friday at Camp David, the US presidential retreat in Maryland. Trump told Hegseth he felt misled because he believed the problem “had been fixed”, according to the Washington Post newspaper, citing two unnamed sources familiar with the exchange. Hegseth defended himself and sought to shift blame to his deputy, Stephen Feinberg, the Post reported. The president responded angrily on Thursday, accusing the media of spreading “treasonous statements” and warning that those responsible would be pursued. “The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down,” he wrote. “Long term jail sentences will be sought!” The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump had ordered investigations into the disclosures about US munitions stockpiles. CNN separately reported that shortages of long-range guided missiles and air defence interceptors had begun to constrain Trump’s strategy in the conflict. The US military had “nearly exhausted 80%” of its stock of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (Thaad) interceptors, the network said. The Washington Post also reported that concerns over dwindling supplies had contributed to Trump calling off further strikes against Iran, despite his repeated threats to hit the Islamic Republic “very hard”. The White House and Pentagon rejected the claims. Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, described the account of the Camp David exchange as “FAKE NEWS!” on X. She wrote: “I was at Camp David with President Trump and Secretary Hegseth. This literally never happened.” Seeking to quash speculation about Hegseth’s future, Leavitt insisted that “the President loves the Secretary and thinks he’s doing a tremendous job”. Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, dismissed both the reports of a confrontation between Trump and Hegseth and claims of weapons shortages as “equally fictional”. Parnell added: “Secretary Hegseth isn’t going anywhere and he’s going to continue to work side by side with Deputy Secretary Feinberg to execute President Trump’s agenda, strengthen America’s defense industrial base, and ensure our warfighters have every capability they need to deter and defeat any adversary.” Trump himself weighed in later on Thursday. “I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing,” the president said on social media, accusing outlets reporting otherwise of “spreading false and completely unfounded rumors”. The increasingly public dispute comes as Trump seeks to project confidence over the course of the war. On Sunday he claimed he had ordered and subsequently called off “the biggest attack since” the second world war, in the light of fresh negotiations over the strait of Hormuz. Iran’s foreign ministry denied that talks were taking place, despite Trump’s claim that Tehran was eager to reach a deal. The Pentagon has faced criticism for manipulating US casualty figures and failing to hold regular press briefings about the war. Hegseth, a former Fox News host who styles himself as the secretary of war, last month announced a screening programme for “testosterone deficiency” among US troops. Joe Scarborough, an MS Now host and former Republican congressman, posted on X: “When Hegseth attacks media questions on this extreme munitions shortage as ‘fake news’, he makes this unforgivable blunder worse. Congress needs to take action. Americans need the truth. Hegseth can’t give it. He needs to go.”

title: Aipac-linked Super Pacs spend millions in California to thwart progressive candidate
author: Dani Anguiano
summary: More than $5m in recent weeks have been spent in ads targeting Aisha Wahab and in support of Melissa Hernandez
body_text: Super Pacs tied to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) have spent millions in a California congressional race to keep a progressive Democrat from winning Eric Swalwell’s former seat. Aisha Wahab, a state senator who has been endorsed by the California Democratic party, is widely considered the frontrunner in the special election for the district covering a swathe of the East Bay. Swalwell had been in office for more than a decade when he resigned earlier this year following multiple allegations of sexual assault. Wahab, who was the first Muslim woman and Afghan American elected to the state legislature, has had a significant lead in the contest to represent one of California’s most diverse congressional districts. Wahab outpaced her closest competitor, Melissa Hernandez, the president of the board of directors for the Bay Area Rapid Transit (Bart) agency and a former Dublin mayor, in a June primary as well as a special election to complete the remainder of Swalwell’s term, by more than 20 points. They are set to face off against each other in a runoff election later this month, and then again in November. Super Pacs are pouring money into the race, dropping more than $5m in recent weeks and supporting pro-Hernandez ads and Wahab attack ads, Politico reported on Thursday. The spending includes $1.2m from United Democracy Project, which is backed by Aipac, and $2.1m from Bold America Pac, which has received significant financial backing from the United Democracy Project, according to the outlet. Track Aipac, which tracks the group’s funding of US politicians, reported that the lobby had spent more than $4.4m to support Hernandez in the race. Wahab said there had been a barrage of attack ads against her in the last month that had misrepresented her record, particularly as it relates to public safety issues. She described the Super Pacs’ involvement as election interference. “You have to ask yourself, why? Aipac is clearly not interested in having diverse voices at the table, they are not interested in supporting the Jewish community and a peaceful dialogue,” she argued. “They want a puppet they can control.” The ads had generated outrage among her constituents, she said, adding that her campaign fields calls and emails daily from people “disgusted by the ads”. People were familiar with her record, Wahab added, and her personal history. Her father was murdered when she was a child, and Wahab grew up in the foster care system. As a state lawmaker, she has prioritized victims, she said, and supported legislation to make human trafficking a serious felony and a bill of rights for sexual assault survivors. Aipac, which is one of the largest Super Pacs and the most powerful pro-Israel lobby organization in the US, has significantly expanded its political spending in recent years. The New York Times reported earlier this week that Aipac had doubled its spending, largely in Democratic primaries, to $67.2m. The organization spent millions to support moderate Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. The progressive Abdul El-Sayed ultimately won the primary race in what has been described as a defining contest for the party. Wahab pointed to her record and wide-ranging support, including endorsements from the organization Our Revolution to state and local officials including the attorney general, Rob Bonta, and the Alameda county sheriff, Yesenia Sanchez. In a statement to the Guardian, Ajay Mohan, campaign manager for Hernandez, said: “Melissa does not control independent expenditures. No candidate does. That is the law, and she sees those ads when you see them. “Melissa remains laser focused on lowering the costs of housing and healthcare, and supporting strong public safety - just as she did as Mayor,” Mohan added. The Guardian has contacted Aipac for comment.

title: Mitch McConnell announces discharge from rehabilitation center
author: Shrai Popat in Washington
summary: Republican, 84, absent from Senate after fall that led to hospital stay, says he will continue recovery at home
body_text: The Republican US senator Mitch McConnell has been discharged from a rehabilitation center following the fall that left him hospitalized, he announced on Thursday. McConnell, 84, whose weeks‑long absence from Capitol Hill fueled mounting speculation about his health, said he will continue his recovery at home. While the Senate is set to wrap up legislative business this week, before a five‑week recess, several agenda items remain – including a vote to confirm Todd Blanche as US attorney general. McConnell’s absence further narrows Republicans’ already tight path to approving Donald Trump’s former personal attorney as head of the Department of Justice. McConnell is one of the highest-profile figures in Congress, as a former Senate majority leader. He has been absent from the Senate and not seen in public since mid-June, although his office has released several photos of him. “On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period,” McConnell said in a Thursday statement. “And I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business.” His 53‑day absence has drawn scrutiny from lawmakers in both parties. Last month, Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, publicly urged McConnell to release more information about his health, writing: “Kentuckians have grown increasingly concerned about the current state of your health and wellbeing, and ability to hold office.” McConnell was admitted to hospital on 14 June. His office initially offered few details, saying only that he was “continuing to improve”. A month later, McConnell disclosed that a fall at his home and a “mild case of pneumonia” had prompted the hospitalization and his extended time away. In late July, his office said he still had not been cleared to return to work.

title: Trump’s birthright citizenship attack the latest effort in obsessive campaign
author: Robert Mackey
summary: For more than a decade, president has been fixated on trying to undermine a key constitutional right
body_text: With a pair of executive orders on Thursday, Donald Trump has tried – once again – to undermine the guarantee of birthright citizenship, a right enshrined in the US constitution and reaffirmed by the supreme court just five weeks ago. The orders attempt to broaden the categories of children who would be ineligible for automatic US citizenship and ban so-called “birth tourism”, which the president claimed is practiced by “hundreds of thousands” of people. That estimate appears to be wildly inflated. According to the non-partisan Migration Policy Institute, the highest census-based estimate “puts birth tourism at 22,000 to 26,000 babies born annually on US soil, although government data show just 9,600 births to mothers with foreign addresses in 2024”. It was the latest attack in a quixotic campaign that the US president has waged for more than a decade. At a Republican presidential primary campaign event in Orlando, Florida, in November 2015, Trump hinted that he had a plan to end what he called the scourge of “anchor babies”, a derogatory term for the US-citizen children of undocumented immigrants. “You can’t come into the country – you’re illegal, you come down, you sit down, you have your baby, and we take care of the baby for the next 85 years!” Trump said. “Everybody says, ‘Well, you need a constitutional amendment, it’ll take 15 years, it’ll never happen’. You don’t, you don’t. You need a simple act of Congress. You might not even need that.” If elected, Trump promised the crowd at a resort near Disney World, “the anchor baby, birthright citizenship, it’s over.” Three years later, as president, Trump said in a televised interview just before the 2018 midterms that he planned to issue an executive order to instruct federal agencies that children born in the United States to non-citizens were not entitled to US citizenship at birth. “It was always told to me that you needed a constitutional amendment. Guess what? You don’t,” Trump told the interviewer Jonathan Swan. “You can definitely do it with an act of Congress,” Trump added, incorrectly, “but now they’re saying I can do it just with an executive order.” As Swan reported at the time, Trump’s claim that he could undo the birthright citizenship guaranteed by the 14th amendment to the constitution was a minority view among legal scholars, but was supported by a then-obscure figure: John Eastman, a former law clerk to the supreme court justice Clarence Thomas who had argued for decades that the amendment granting citizenship to “All persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof,” should be read to exclude the children of people who are not US citizens when their child is born. Eastman later claimed in a 2020 Newsweek op-ed that Kamala Harris was ineligible for the vice-presidency because she had no right to US citizenship at birth, since she was born in Oakland, California, in 1964 to non-citizen parents who were, “subject to the jurisdiction” of their native lands of India and Jamaica. In the 2018 interview, Trump called birthright citizenship “ridiculous”, and falsely asserted that the US is “the only country in the world where a person comes in and has a baby, and the baby is essentially a citizen.” In fact, 32 other nations grant citizenship this way. He also claimed then that an executive order was in the process of being drafted. Although that order did not materialize until the start of Trump’s second term, and was struck down in June by the supreme court, his obsession with casting doubt on the citizenship of children born in the US to foreign parents has had an overtly political element from the start. Trump’s original rise to political prominence was tied to his false claim that Barack Obama, born to an American mother and a Kenyan father in Honolulu, just two years after Hawaii became a state, might have been born outside the US. Then, after Joe Biden picked Harris as his running mate in 2020, Trump repeatedly refused to confirm that she was eligible for an elected office open only to “a natural-born citizen”. Instead, Trump called the question Eastman raised about Harris’s citizenship at birth in his Newsweek op-ed “very serious” and a potential “problem” for her. He also praised Eastman as “a very highly qualified, very talented lawyer” and called him “brilliant”. Eastman, who went on to devise the fake electors scheme designed to keep Trump in office after he lost the 2020 election, and gave an inflammatory speech before the Capitol riot on 6 January 2021, was finally disbarred by the California supreme court in April, based on “clear and convincing evidence that he advanced false claims about the 2020 presidential election to mislead courts, public officials, and the American public”. While asserting the right to deny citizenship to some children of non-citizens is clearly still a priority for Trump, it remains to be seen if his latest attempts to curtail the right will succeed. The two new orders are likely to face legal challenges, and come just weeks after the US supreme court struck down Trump’s previous order denying citizenship to the children of non-citizens, issued on the first day of his second term. In the court’s June decision, Chief Justice John Roberts said Trump’s first order violated the 14th amendment of the US constitution. “Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights – to freely participate in our political community,” he wrote. “The framers of the 14th amendment extended that promise to ‘every free-born person in this land’. We keep that promise today.”

title: Mexico and Argentina line up behind Infantino to deepen football’s civil war
author: Matt Hughes
summary: The Mexican and Argentinian football federations have issued their public backing for beleaguered Fifa president Gianni Infantino in a move that has deepened world football’s civil war
body_text: Mexico’s football federation has broken ranks with the rest of Concacaf by publicly backing the beleaguered Gianni Infantino in a move that has deepened world football’s civil war. Concacaf has called for a thorough review of Fifa’s governance in the light of the World Cup sell-off debacle, and is backing Uefa’s demands for meaningful change, although has yet to follow its European counterparts by threatening to boycott tournaments if they do not achieve their objectives. In a statement issued on Thursday night, the FMF went some way towards explaining Concacaf’s reticence, as its second-biggest member after the US was unequivocal in its support for the Fifa president. In a Fifa statement released under Infantino’s name on Wednesday, the world governing body had called for its institutional practices to be respected, a coded way of condemning any leadership challenge before next March’s scheduled presidential election, which the FMF endorsed. “The Mexican Football Federation is convinced that football is its fundamental value and that its best defence lies in institutional integrity and respect for the governance and processes that safeguard it,” the FMF said. “Therefore, the FMF will not recognise or approve any process convened outside of this institutional framework, and it embraces the call issued by president Infantino on 5 August 2026 to collectively continue developing football for the benefit of its 211 member associations. “The FMF supports president Infantino’s leadership in continuing to promote the development of football through institutional strengthening.” The Argentina Football Association (AFA) followed Mexico’s lead by backing Infantino in a gushing tribute and expressing support for his leadership over the past decade. Unlike Concacaf, South America’s Conmebol appears united behind Infantino, while in an intriguing subplot there is growing speculation that Mexico would like to switch confederations to join the latter. “In relation to the recent events that are public knowledge, we must recognise the decision of the administration to withdraw a project that generated, within the football family and from its inception, many more uncertainties than certainties,” the AFA statement read. “That is why it is worth highlighting the acceptance of the errors made in this process and the apology expressed in the heartfelt message displayed to the 211 member associations of Fifa. Prioritising governance standards is a fundamental pillar for strengthening good relations between Fifa, its member associations and the confederations. “In the same way, and as we have already expressed, you are leading a management that led to a profound transformation of Fifa, which opened the doors of the organisation to all member associations and confederations, so that with a frank and direct dialogue, we can, together, continue to promote football at all levels and disciplines. “This transformation was based on a model of transparent governance, respect for statutory structures and the monitoring of democratic procedures, essential principles for the football family to be united, firm and working to continue generating improvements in sports and institutions, which have an impact on a better quality of life for millions of human beings who practise our beloved sport. “Accordingly, with the upcoming Fifa congress approaching, the association that we proudly preside over firmly believes and reaffirms that the way forward is to continue to work under your leadership, so that we can continue to develop better and even more inclusive football.” Earlier on Thursday, the Confederation of African Football had reaffirmed its support for Infantino, providing him with further allies as he fights to extend his 10-year reign.

title: With their assault on science, Trumpists aren’t just harming America – they’re harming themselves
author: Jan-Werner Müller
summary: The administration is subjugating science to political imperatives, a major blow to US soft power and technological progress
body_text: The Trump administration is waging an unprecedented war on institutions devoted to research and higher learning. While plenty of countries have harmed universities by imposing neoliberal logics on academia – creating artificial markets in the name of spurring professors to be more productive – the Trumpist subjugation of all science to political imperatives has no equivalent in a democracy; if anything, it is reminiscent of Stalin’s Soviet Union. The assault now also targets foreign students and any kind of international collaboration – a major blow to US soft power. Why are Trumpists engaging in what can only be described as an act of wanton self-injury? Project 2025’s Russell Vought, the director of the office of management and budget, initiated the rule change that would make any federal grant subject to review by political appointees – including funds for science that so far have been allocated through judgment by first-rate fellow scientists. This measure would furnish Trumpists with a new weapon to threaten universities along the lines of: “Nice medical school you have there – pity if something were to happen to it because your administration had failed to come into alignment with the president’s priorities.” Then there is the strategy recently presented by Trump’s science adviser, a former employee of Peter Thiel, with the unique distinction of having no relevant experience in research whatsoever. Michael Kratsios wants to shift decision-making from experts in universities to private corporations, which, helped by AI, are supposedly better positioned to spot potential breakthroughs. This constitutes a major break with the enormously successful approach the US took after the second world war: pour taxpayer money into basic, open-ended science which no private company would risk sponsoring – but with both citizens and American capital eventually benefiting from the inventions that came out of fundamental research. Kratsios wishes the government to adopt “the intentionality of a serious investor” in order to usher in a new “golden age of science” (declaring something “golden” seems enough to succeed in Trump-world). De facto, as critics have rightly pointed out, this seems a strategy to take money from what Trumpists perceive as their political enemies – universities – and shovel it to their allies in tech. Meanwhile, the more directly ideological assault on universities continues. Having failed to tempt select institutions of higher learning with a “compact” to receive preferential federal treatment last year, Linda McMahon, the fake-wrestling-executive-turned-anti-education secretary, is now asking university presidents to pledge allegiance to the administration through statements on their websites: among other things, they are supposed to explain how they will increase “intellectual pluralism” (read: affirmative action for conservatives); deal with campus protest (read: police student speech the Trump administration does not like); and make education more provincial (serving America first) and instrumental (only immediate employability and vocational credentialism count) – and less critical of “our civilizational inheritance”. In the spirit of Stephen Miller-type nativism, international donors are targeted no less than international collaboration in general; visas for PhD students are now limited to four years (an unrealistic time frame for many academic subjects), with possible extensions if students spend time and money on appealing to the Department of Homeland security (instead of doing actual research). The fact that many researchers in the past have stayed in the US after obtaining their doctorates, contributing to national wealth (just like America Firsters would presumably want) or went back to their countries with good feelings to the US – all that counts for nothing. What explains such self-harm? Rightwing hostility to higher education is nothing new: from intellectuals supposedly being communist eggheads in the 1950s, to moral panics about “political correctness” in the 1990s and “wokeness” in recent years, there is the basic stance made explicit by JD Vance in 2021: “Universities are the enemy.” But Trump’s rule has brought together a novel coalition, one divided by many issues but united in their desire to destroy universities as we know them. Among them: the Maga hardcore with its traditional anti-intellectualism and nativism; the Silicon Valley oligarchs who imagine their companies replacing (and monetizing) university functions; and conservatives in name, but radicals in practice who want to take over higher education, but, failing that, would like to burn the whole system down. Also novel, in the wake of Covid, is the commitment of so many on the right to the idea that, somehow, science and freedom are opposites, that not having ever to listen to people who know something better than you do is the essence of personal liberation. If that emotional fuel for the new anti-intellectualism were not powerful enough, there is a highly flammable desire for revenge – amply on display in the endless attacks on Anthony Fauci. To be sure, Congress has not gone along with some of the major funding cuts for science Trump keeps requesting; even Republican politicians quietly resist when monies would stop flowing to their districts. And the new OMB rule, it seems, is being blocked in a funding deal reached in the Senate this week. But one cannot rely on such occasional pushback by one Republican or another, because none of them has offered a principled defense of the postwar model (in fact, given the conduct of the likes of the senators Thom Tillis and John Cornyn this week, it seems fair to say that “principled Republican” is fast becoming a contradiction in terms). University leaders and prominent scientists have to hold the line in opposing possible “deals” with the Trump administration; everyone could have learned by now that Trumpists will not stick to their end of the bargain. More importantly, those seeing things wrong with peer review, for instance, or too much administrative busywork for researchers – and some of these problems are real – have to realize that Trumpists are the last who can be trusted to solve them. Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton University

title: Iran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in war
author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
summary: By dragging out talks, Tehran aims to damage the US president politically – but some fear a bruised and weakened Trump could lash back
body_text: Tehran has set out a protracted negotiating timetable designed to keep Donald Trump embroiled in the Iran conflict until the midterm elections, in the hope of inflicting the same ruinous blow on his presidency as Jimmy Carter suffered over the 1979-81 US embassy hostage crisis. For many inside Iran, inflicting meaningful revenge on Trump is a legitimate and self-standing war aim, reflected in the mood of those attending the funeral of the supreme leader Ali Khamenei where demands for retribution were ubiquitous. While Iranian officials since the 1979 Islamic revolution have never trusted the US, that animus is now also directed personally towards Trump. He not only tore up the painfully negotiated nuclear deal in 2018, but he sanctioned the assassination of the military leader Qassem Suleimani and twice involved Iran in negotiations on its nuclear programme only to launch wars against it. He shows no remorse for the killing of the country’s supreme leader, or for the attempt on the life of Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian. As the countdown to November’s midterms begins, what could be Trump’s political demise has become a subject of obsessive speculation in Tehran. Iranian media track the US president’s waning ratings, attributing the decline to the war’s unpopularity and high oil prices. The changing politics of the Democrats is minutely examined. But the focus on the midterms became more obvious this week when the deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, told the official IRNA news agency that after agreeing a route for commercial shipping through the strait of Hormuz, it would take two to four months to reach the second phase of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme. The original plan – to commence the nuclear phase of the talks within 30 days of signing June’s memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the US – had been jettisoned by the Trump administration, Gharibabadi said. To get to that second stage, he laid out an obstacle course including the lifting of sanctions, the end of the US blockade of Iranian ports, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and new commitments on non-belligerence in a process that could last well beyond the midterms. If Tehran gets its way on this timetable, Trump will be going to the polls with no Iranian commitment on nuclear weapons, only a hefty economic bill for a failed war. “This raises the very likely scenario of continued cycles of conflict between the US and Tehran over the strait,” said Jason Brodsky from United against a Nuclear Iran, an advocate of the war. “There won’t be any true quiet before the midterm elections – Tehran has no interest in giving this to the Trump administration … It will continue to play games.” Mehr News, an agency close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, published a piece saying Iran had given Trump a major dilemma. “Continuing the war could increase political and economic pressure on the government and exacerbate the decline in his popularity. On the other hand, backing down, or moving towards reducing tensions, could also be interpreted by some of Trump’s supporters as a retreat from his campaign slogans,” it said. From this perspective, the outcome of this war will not be played out on the battlefield, but at the ballot box. The agency suggested the outcome could affect the course of American domestic and foreign policy for years to come. Few in Iran take Trump’s statements at face value. But his denials that the midterms affect his Iran strategy are treated with special scepticism. Iranian media point to comments from Marc Zell, chair of Republicans Overseas Israel, who has said: “It’s all about the midterms … the American public simply is tired of war and the administration is navigating the pre-election waters adroitly in order to avoid a Democratic takeover of Congress.” Such remarks fuel the debate inside Iran about how much the midterms should be part of Iran’s calculus. Some believe the loss of Congress will inhibit Trump or lead to his impeachment; at the very least, it may mark the end of the war’s funding. Mostafa Zahrani, a former Iranian diplomat, argued electoral defeat “will make it inevitable that Trump will not be able to go back to war and will take the negotiations seriously”. Others such as Nasser Hadian, a professor of international relations at Tehran University, disagree, advocating cashing in on Iran’s victories now rather than waiting for Trump to become weaker. “If he loses, he’ll have less incentive to reach an agreement with Iran, because in that case he’ll be weakened, and Israel and others will find it much easier to attack him – something they don’t dare do now,” he said. “Those who say we should wait for the midterm elections have no understanding of politics in America.” Iran’s pleasure in seeing Trump defeated would indeed be reduced if he felt he had nothing left to lose, but its diplomats overall believe the US president’s freedom to act will be constrained by the unpopularity of more conflict and by Republican presidential candidates’ anxiety to wrap this up. Trump would also be at risk of seeing his whole second term consumed by a disastrous war. The bigger question is what Iran itself wants to achieve. Agreeing to keep the dispute simmering until November is not an answer to that question – one that Iranians are better at debating than resolving. Pezeshkian, working in alliance with Mohammad Ghalibaf, the chief negotiator, repeatedly says he does not want endless war, and insists that almost all the supreme national security council concur. He still has faith in the MoU, saying it should be the cornerstone of Iran’s foreign policy. But the conservative newspaper Kayhan describes the memorandum as worthless since the US always breaks its commitments. “Accordingly, officials should know that the strait of Hormuz is not a bargaining chip and should not be opened as a passage for America,” it said. Both hardliners and moderates envision the war leading to a new regional security architecture. But the hardliners put the emphasis on America’s expulsion and see this as something less to be negotiated and more to be enforced using control of the entry points to the strait of Hormuz as a lever to close US bases. Pezeshkian says he sees a place for legitimate US investment in Iran, while the former foreign minister Javad Zarif, in an essay this week, argued Iran in “a post-polar era would benefit from not depending solely on Russia and China in future”. If Iran developed “a balanced and multifaceted foreign policy”, Tehran would not be forced into relationships based on necessity, he wrote. “Continuing uncontrolled tensions with the United States not only imposes direct costs on Iran, but also makes it more difficult for other countries, even close partners such as China and Russia, to cooperate with Iran.” Just as Trump cannot resolve from one sentence to the next what he thinks of Iran, nor can Iran agree what it thinks it can get from America.

title: Trump is laying waste to the agency that keeps hospital patients safe
author: Robert B Shpiner
summary: Few have heard of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, but it has saved tens of thousands of lives and billions of dollars
body_text: When I started my training in 1980, we accepted an arithmetic that would now be indefensible. Central lines, the catheters we threaded into the great veins of the critically ill, became infected, and some of those patients died. We recorded the deaths as complications. Almost no one thought of them as preventable, because no one had yet done the slow work of proving they were. That work got done, and federal money paid for it. Beginning in 2008, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, a small arm of the health department, funded a national effort in more than a thousand adult intensive care units: a checklist, a sterile insertion protocol, and a unit culture in which a nurse could stop a surgeon. Central-line bloodstream infections fell by 41%, from 1.915 to 1.133 per 1,000 catheter days. The agency estimates that effort alone averted between 290 and 605 deaths. Across its wider work on hospital-acquired harm, AHRQ’s own accounting credits 20,500 deaths prevented and $7.7bn saved in the four years from 2014 to 2017. Hardly any of my patients have heard of the agency. That was always rather the point. On 15 July, AHRQ sent researchers around the country nearly identical letters ending at least 104 grants, most of them aimed at making care safer. Congress appropriated $345m for the agency this fiscal year. It has spent under $15m on grants and has not issued a new one in more than a year. About three-quarters of the staff have been fired or have quit since Donald Trump took office, and the office that ran grant review was eliminated last summer. An agency with no grant managers cannot make grants, which tells you how long the closure is meant to last. Senator Tammy Baldwin, the ranking Democrat on the appropriations subcommittee that funds AHRQ, counts 150 awards cut off, worth $94m. If you have spent a night in a US hospital in the past 20 years, this agency was working on your behalf whether you knew it or not. It built the patient-experience surveys Medicare uses to help set what hospitals are paid. The quality indicators regulators rely on to spot a hospital that is harming people are its work. With the defense department, it produced the team-communication training now standard in operating rooms and emergency departments. The scientist who spent three decades building those Medicare surveys learned her funding was gone from an email that arrived around 5pm. Among the other grants killed this month: training for physicians, nurses and paramedics managing high-risk pregnancies, in a country where rural women die of pregnancy-related causes at two to three times the rate of women elsewhere; a study of how to spare children in community emergency rooms from unnecessary CT scans and the radiation dose that comes with them; work on catching lung cancer earlier; and telehealth projects serving rural patients. The stated rationale does not hold. AHRQ’s director, Roger Klein, told grantees the agency was redirecting resources toward patient safety, antibiotic resistance, overmedication of children and measurable health outcomes. When KFF Health News examined about 20 of the cancelled grants, nearly all of them pursued those objectives. One of the cancelled grants studied antibiotic resistance. The Michigan pediatrician who lost the last two years of her award said none of it makes any sense, and her field studies exactly what Robert F Kennedy Jr’s “Make America healthy again” agenda claims to champion. Klein has held no agency-wide meetings and published no plan. He has said little in public since January, when he co-wrote an essay in Newsweek arguing that “scientific neutrality” had given way to “moral signaling”. He has reportedly told staff that artificial intelligence can replace much of what his scientists do. A White House science report released on 22 July urged the government to back individual scientists over legacy institutions, to move past slow consensus peer review and to build the future on AI. I use AI tools daily. They are gifted assistants, and they have never placed a central line. I wrote this week in the Annals of Internal Medicine about patients who arrive holding a chatbot’s answer. The models are fluent and often correct, but they have no way of knowing what they were never told. That limit scales. A language model can summarize everything ever published about catheter infections. Someone still had to stand in the unit at three in the morning and notice that the nurses were quietly working around the protocol. Someone still had to design the study that found out why. None of that knowledge existed until people went and got it. Then there is the money. Congress decides how public funds are spent, a principle written into statute after Richard Nixon tried withholding appropriations he disliked. The Society of General Internal Medicine and the North American Primary Care Research Group sued Kennedy and Klein last August over the frozen grant-making, and the case is pending in Maryland. The Government Accountability Office is examining whether the agency’s conduct amounts to an unlawful impoundment. On 17 July a federal judge in Boston held that agencies may not cancel awards over priorities they adopted after making them. Now consider what the health department says about the AHRQ letters: nothing was terminated, and the grants were merely “not awarded continued funding”. That phrasing is doing work. It is an attempt to walk through the one door the court left open. After 45 years in medicine, I know this much about safety. When it works, no one notices. No patient wakes up grateful for the bloodstream infection she did not get, or for the dose a pharmacist’s protocol caught before it reached her line. AHRQ costs each American about a dollar a year, roughly 0.3% of the health department’s discretionary spending, and it is being dismantled in the confidence that the people it protects will never learn what they were spared. The deaths will arrive one at a time, in different hospitals, unlabeled. No letter from Washington will claim them. In 1980 we did not know how to prevent those deaths. We know now. That knowledge took 30 years and public money to build, and it is being discarded by people who have not said why. Robert B Shpiner is an internist and clinical professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. He has practiced and taught intensive care medicine for more than 40 years

title: First Thing: Soaring oil profits from US-Iran conflict drive calls for windfall tax
author: Martin Belam
summary: Environmentalists and activists furious as Trump’s policies raise costs for Americans
body_text: Good morning. Donald Trump’s statement that oil companies have made “too much money” from the Iran war has angered environmentalists, who say his policies were designed to benefit those very corporations. Americans have paid more than $78bn more at the pump since the start of the Iran war, according to a Brown University tracker. A recent analysis from the environmental advocacy group Climate Power and the Center for American Progress Action Fund, a liberal thinktank, found that Trump’s policies had cost the average American family $285 more when filling up their cars. As oil companies have reaped billions from the Iran war’s impact on fossil fuel prices, the Rhode Island senator Sheldon Whitehouse and the California congressman Ro Khanna have proposed taxing big oil’s windfall profits from the crisis, and said proceeds from that tax should go to American families who are paying more for fuel. What policies has Trump enacted to help the oil industry? Since re-entering the White House last year, he has eased dozens of restrictions and regulations on fossil fuel expansion, exempted fossil fuel producers from environmental rules, and signed an executive order last year directing the attorney general to prioritize blocking climate lawsuits targeting oil majors. Trump has also personally invested in major oil companies. Trump signs new orders targeting birthright citizenship Donald Trump has made a second attempt to restrict the constitutional guarantee of birthright citizenship, just weeks after the US supreme court rejected his initial, more sweeping attempt to deny automatic citizenship to children born to undocumented immigrants and temporary foreign residents. Trump on Thursday signed two executive orders that seek to broaden the categories of children ineligible for automatic US citizenship and ban so-called “birth tourism”. The directives are expected to face legal challenges. Trump’s obsession with casting doubt on the citizenship of children born in the US to foreign parents has had an overtly political element from the start – his original rise to political prominence was tied to his false claims about Barack Obama’s eligibility for office, something he repeated when facing Kamala Harris as an electoral opponent. What did the supreme court previously rule? In the court’s June decision, the chief justice, John Roberts, said Trump’s first order violated the 14th amendment of the US constitution. “Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights – to freely participate in our political community,” he wrote. “The framers of the 14th amendment extended that promise to ‘every free-born person in this land’. We keep that promise today.” US law enforcement gave false information in case against woman charged in anti-ICE protest Law enforcement officials provided false information to federal judges as they sought to build a criminal case against the independent journalist Georgia Fort in connection with a January protest, her lawyers said in court filings on Thursday asking that the charges against her be dismissed. Fort was one of nearly 40 people charged after demonstrators interrupted a service at Cities church in St Paul, Minnesota, after they learned that an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) official was a pastor there. Trump administration officials vowed to arrest anyone involved in the protest. How has the Trump administration expanded the tracking of immigrants? The US is tracking nearly 54,000 immigrants through GPS-enabled ankle monitors as part of an ICE electronic surveillance program, according to The Geo Group, a private prison corporation. Early last year, just 17,000 immigrants were wearing the devices. Executives said a large number of participants had been shifted from less intensive forms of surveillance, such as phone check-ins, to ankle monitors. Why have airports become an increased target for ICE enforcement? With a goal of 2,000 daily immigration arrests, ICE has started detaining people – many of whom have overstayed visas after coming to the US legally and have pending applications for immigration relief – in public places far from security checkpoints, whether at ticket counters or near gates. Authorities have generally avoided immigration enforcement at airports so as not to disrupt domestic travel. In other news … A Thai teenager killed two of his grandparents before opening fire at his school, where he shot five people dead and took his own life, police have said, in an attack that has shaken a country struggling to deal with gun violence. Donald Trump has doubled down on his criticism of Jeanine Pirro after the US attorney for the District of Columbia publicly challenged his claims that vandals had damaged the recently renovated Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. The FCC has scrapped the limit on local TV ownership, in a win for major media conglomerates. Donald Trump has ordered a new 15% tariff on imported products made of polysilicon, a key material for solar panels and microchips that is primarily produced by China. The Republican US senator Mitch McConnell has been discharged from a rehabilitation center after a fall that left him hospitalized. Stat of the day: New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567m over harms to children’s mental health A New Mexico court has ordered Meta, the parent company of Facebook, to pay $567m into a fund aimed at redressing adverse mental health impacts from the social media firm’s platforms. The ruling comes as a part of the second phase of a landmark trial that the company lost in March. title: US unexpectedly lost 23,000 jobs in July as slump in growth continues
author: Michael Sainato and Gaya Gupta
summary: Estimates for previous two months were revised down sharply but unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%
body_text: US employers unexpectedly lost 23,000 jobs in July and gains for the previous two months were revised down sharply by a combined 103,000 jobs, painting a weaker picture of the labor market than past data indicated. The unemployment rate, however, held steady at 4.1%. Economists had projected an unchanged unemployment rate and 83,000 new jobs for the month. The latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics illustrates the continued summer slump in job growth amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Pressure has been mounting within the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to combat persistently high inflation, but July’s job report and its latest revisions may cool those expectations at the central bank’s next meeting. July’s job losses were concentrated in local government education, with 50,000 jobs lost, and retail, which lost 19,000. The private sector, however, gained 30,000 jobs, with growth focused once again in healthcare. Hourly earnings of all employees changed little over the past year, increasing by 3.2% compared to last year. Next week’s consumer pricing data will reveal whether these gains have kept pace with inflation. Figures for May were revised to 63,000 jobs added, down from an initially reported 129,000 jobs, while figures for June dropped 37,000, to 20,000 jobs added. In total, job figures for May and June were revised down 103,000 jobs. In June, the US added 57,000 jobs, about half of what economists had predicted, with most of the growth concentrated in healthcare and social assistance. The unemployment rate had also dropped to 4.2% in June, down from 4.3% in May, driven by 720,000 people leaving the workforce. Other data had pointed toward a slowdown in July. Private employers added 44,000 jobs in July, according to the payroll firm ADP, a significant drop from the 98,000 jobs added in June recorded by the firm. Job openings decreased by 178,000 to 7.4m in June, according to the latest Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey. Job openings in healthcare and social assistance, key areas of job growth, declined by 147,000 in June, the largest decline since July 2025. Economists have long said the US labor market is in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, and recent data from outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas found that layoffs in July plunged compared with last year. US-based employers announced about 33,500 job cuts in July, the lowest month in two years. Though consumer spending has remained resilient, increasing by 0.3% in June 2026, the personal savings rate for Americans in June 2026 hit a four-year low at 2.7%, the lowest rate since June 2022, according to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis. “With immigration having largely been stopped – and possibly now a net negative – the labor force is growing very slowly,” wrote Dean Baker, economist and co-founder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, in a post on what to expect from the July jobs report. “However, slower wage growth, even in the face of rising inflation, indicates it is not a very good labor market for most workers. That story does not seem likely to change any time soon.” Economists are closely watching the labor market and inflation as officials at Fed have become divided on whether to raise interest rates or leave them unchanged. Though the Fed held rates steady last month, officials indicated that they expect at least one rate hike before the end of the year to combat price increases. The annualized inflation rate in June was 3.5% – 0.8% higher than a year prior. Inflation data scheduled to be released next week will probably be “the deciding factor” for the next rate meeting, Ellen Zentner, chief economic strategist at Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, said in a statement. “If those numbers come in hotter than expected, a cooler labor market may not be enough to quiet the calls for hikes inside the Fed, or lower expectations outside of it,” she said. Democrats are already criticizing Donald Trump for the worse-than-expected report. In a statement on Friday morning, the Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren said: “President Trump’s failing economic agenda is weakening the labor market. “Job growth in May and June was revised down by more than 100,000 jobs, job openings have fallen and more people are out of the labor force than at any time on record. And wage growth slowed, straining families’ paychecks even more as they struggle to keep up with Trump’s inflation,” Warren added.
