title: Trump’s attorney general pick Todd Blanche appears to clear last hurdle for confirmation
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Bill Cassidy, Republican seen as a decisive holdout, said he is prepared to back Trump’s former personal lawyer
body_text: Bill Cassidy, the US Republican senator seen as the decisive holdout on Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general, announced on Friday that he will support the pick, setting the stage for a major win for Donald Trump. Confirmation that Cassidy, of Louisiana, is prepared to back Blanche – Trump’s former personal lawyer, and a loyal ally of the president – appeared to clear the last hurdle of his confirmation process, which had been challenged by the defections of the Republican senators Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins. Blanche is already serving as acting attorney general. “I will vote for Mr Blanche,” Cassidy said in a US Senate floor speech on Friday morning. “Mr Blanche is not perfect, and he will tell you this, but the choice is not between perfection and Mr Blanche; it is between Mr Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump, and who indeed may not be as good as Mr Blanche.” With Cassidy now on board, Blanche is expected to be confirmed by a narrow margin, probably along party lines, as the Senate works through a final vote series before senators leave for the five-week August recess that starts this weekend. Cassidy, who lost his Louisiana primary in May after facing two challengers, including one backed by Trump, had faced weeks of pressure from the White House and had voiced concerns about “lawfare” at the justice department before announcing his decision. Murkowski, Alaska’s moderate Republican senator, had announced earlier on Friday that she would not vote for Blanche’s confirmation, leaving his path to the job down to a single Republican vote. Murkowski’s announcement came a day after Trump, speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday, was asked about his fraying relationships with Republican critics including Murkowski and Cassidy and whether the president would reach out to either Republican senator to save the vote. “I’ll reach out to whoever I have to, but anybody voting against [Blanche] would be doing a great disservice to the country,” Trump told reporters. “People have such unbelievable respect” for Blanche, he claimed, expressing hope that reaching out to those lawmakers “won’t be necessary”. Maine’s Susan Collins had already said she will oppose Blanche’s confirmation over concerns about the independence of the US Department of Justice, and with Murkowski’s opposition now confirmed, Cassidy had been the last undecided Republican vote standing between Blanche and confirmation. Murkowski and Cassidy were among the handful of Republicans who voted to convict Trump after his 2021 impeachment over the January 6 Capitol riot. After the Oval Office meeting, Trump acknowledged the political toll his feuds with GOP holdouts have taken. “Look, I don’t regret it. You do what you have to do,” Trump told Punchbowl News. “And just so you understand, they voted to impeach me … In all fairness, you think that I’m going to support somebody that voted to impeach me?” She took her stance even though Blanche confirmed in writing the controversial fund was dead. Experts say Trump could easily reverse it. Murkowski said the Senate only currently has leverage over the fund because Blanche’s nomination to head the Department of Justice is pending necessary confirmation by the upper congressional chamber. Blanche had persuaded the Senate judiciary committee in a 12-10 vote in his favor earlier this week only because he promised Republican holdouts that he would not pursue the payout fund. Blanche issued a formal order late on Sunday terminating Trump’s $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” slush fund designed to compensate political allies who had been “targeted” by the justice department, including prosecutions of January 6 insurrectionists. That move followed weeks of negotiations with two Republican senators who were blocking his nomination to become attorney general – Thom Tillis and John Cornyn, who were eventually swayed by Blanche. Murkowski posted on X on Friday, praising Blanche but then saying “ultimately” she would oppose his nomination, a position she took on Tuesday and is now sticking with. “The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration. I hope Mr Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case,” she wrote, as part of a much longer post on the topic. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, but Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, who was just released from the hospital, is not attending sessions because of his health.

title: Mike Lindell faces legal complaint over pillow giveaway amid run for Minnesota governor
author: Edward Helmore
summary: Judge finds probable cause to believe the MyPillow founder violated campaign law by handing out free pillows at event
body_text: An administrative law judge in Minnesota has found probable cause to believe Mike Lindell, candidate for Minnesota governor and the MyPillow founder, violated campaign finance law by handing out free pillows at a public event last month. In a four-page ruling issued on Thursday, Judge Nicholas Lienesch found that a complaint against Lindell had enough to move on to an evidentiary hearing in front of a three-judge administrative panel. “There is probable cause to believe that the pillows in this case were a thing of monetary value and were not explicitly exempted by any provision of the statute,” Lienesch wrote. “There is probable cause to believe that the pillows were distributed in order to induce a voter to vote in a particular way at an election.” Lindell, one of Donald Trump’s most reliable political allies and a US pillow advertising fixture, is running for Minnesota governor against six Republican rivals, including Minnesota’s house speaker, Lisa Demuth, and state GOP-endorsed candidate Kendall Qualls, and seven Democrats, including the Minnesota senator Amy Klobuchar. The candidates face a primary election next week to tease out who will go head-to-head in November. Reached for comment on Friday, Lindell argued the pillow giveaway complaint was “complete nonsense”. “It’s been a nonstop campaign since President Trump endorsed me three weeks ago,” he said, claiming that he had checked out the pillow giveaway ahead of time with Minnesota’s campaign finance board. “We got everything completely OKed. This a just a catch-up right before the primary to put doubt in people’s heads. We did everything right. There was no law broken, period. “It’s just an attack,”Lindell added. “It’s disgusting.” On Tuesday, Lindell said he was stepping down as MyPillow CEO to focus his “time and energy” on his run for governor, calling it “one of the biggest decisions” of his life. The complaint against Lindell was brought by Dan Fiskum, a Democrat running for state senate, saying that Lindell threw free pillows from the company he started at an event at a Fourth of July parade in Delano, Minnesota. Under Minnesota law, it is impermissible to give away or promise something of monetary value to induce a voter to vote in a particular way or refrain from voting. Food and beverages valued at less than $5 are exempted. Lindell has said that the pillows he threw were bought wholesale for $4.90 each. Thursday’s ruling does not say Lindell broke the law with the pillow distribution, but Lienesch wrote that he was determining whether “sufficient facts exist in the record to believe that a violation of the law has occurred”. Lindell’s MyPillow fortune, once valued at $300m, has diminished in recent years and he has faced defamation lawsuits and financial judgments over his claims that the 2020 US presidential election was rigged. The candidate said at a hearing on Monday that he could not see a difference between the pillows, which came with campaign literature, and typical campaign trinkets like buttons and keychains. Lindell compared the pillow giveaway to his campaign purchasing his memoir – titled What Are the Odds? From Crack Addict to CEO – and handing it out free at campaign events. The Minnesota Star Tribune reported that he was asked what the pillow was worth to people who got one. Lindell responded that most of the pillows went to kids and “those little kids, they like a good night’s sleep and hug that pillow”, but acknowledged that sleep patterns “would be subjective between each individual”. For the adults who received a pillow, Lindell said: “The gift of sleep, I don’t know, it’s all subjective. I don’t think any one of them said: ‘Oh I’m getting a value of $10 and I’m getting it for free.’”

title: Appeals court halts construction of Trump’s $400m White House ballroom
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: Ruling put on hold for two weeks, allowing administration to appeal to US supreme court
body_text: A US federal appeals court has ordered the Trump administration to halt construction of the US president’s $400m White House ballroom, in a fresh blow to the controversial project. Donald Trump, who demolished the historic East Wing of the White House last year to make way for planned ballroom, has repeatedly touted it as “a gift” to the US people. But in a major setback in a case testing ⁠his presidential authority, the Washington-based US ⁠court of appeals for the District of Columbia circuit upheld a preliminary injunction in a divided 2-1 order on Friday. The appeals court put ⁠its ruling on hold for two weeks, allowing the administration to appeal to the US supreme court. Writing on social media, Trump described the ruling as “totally wrong” and said an appeal would be filed. Explaining their majority decision, Judges Patricia Millet and Bradley Garcia wrote: “Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence.” The judges also said it was for US Congress to determine whether the ballroom could ultimately be built. “Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help,” they wrote. “This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy,” the judges added. “This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom. “What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorization, as the constitution and laws require.” Trump criticized the decision, which he argued “severely jeopardizes the lives and welfare of the people who work, and will be working”, at the White House. “This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety.” A third judge on the panel, Neomi Rao, who was appointed by Trump, dissented and sided with the president’s assertion that the ballroom project was within his authority. Her position earned praised from the president in his social media statement on Friday. The injunction was won by the National Trust for Historic ⁠Preservation, which sued last year after the Trump administration tore down the East Wing and began building a 90,000 sq ft (8,360 sq meter) ballroom without seeking authorization from Congress. The latest decision supports an earlier ruling issued by a US federal judge in April, which limited the construction project only to the undergound part of the project deemed necessary on national security grounds while blocking the hospitality facility envisioned by Trump for entertaining guests. At the time, Trump lambasted that decision, by Judge Richard Leon – appointed to the bench during George W Bush’s presidency – as the work of a “Trump Hating” judge who he alleged had “gone out of his way to undermine National Security, and to make sure that this Great Gift to America gets delayed, or doesn’t get built”.

title: US Senate passes Russia sanctions bill championed by Lindsey Graham
author: Chris Stein
summary: Late senator spent final days of his life working to advance bill that will now head to the House after 86-11 Senate vote
body_text: By a large, bipartisan margin, the US Senate on Friday approved a bill intended to punish Russia and countries that buy its petroleum exports over the invasion of Ukraine, capping a legislative push that was spurred by the death of its champion, the Republican senator Lindsey Graham. The measure, renamed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act in honor of the late senator’s work on the issue, was approved by an 86-11 vote. Rand Paul of Kentucky was the sole Republican to oppose the legislation, together with 10 Democrats. The bill would impose new sanctions and visa bans on Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and top military commanders, as well as put tariffs of up to 500% on the country’s exports. It would also allow Donald Trump to impose levies of up to 100% on goods from countries that are the top five importers of Russian oil and gas. The proposal was a top priority for Graham, a Republican senator from South Carolina who spent the final days of his life working to advance it. But the effort had became mired in months of negotiations between the White House and Senate leadership. After Graham’s sudden death last month at the age of 71 following a trip to Kyiv, party leaders announced an agreement to get the bill through the chamber and honor his legacy as an ally of Ukraine. The Senate took the first step toward advancing it last month, on the day of Graham’s funeral, with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, watching from the chamber. “This bill forces those primary countries keeping Russia’s economy afloat to make a simple yet critical choice – a choice between doing business with America or buying cheap Russian energy,” said Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who was appointed to his seat after his death. Graham, who presided over the Senate and announced the bill’s passage, added: “This legislation tells Russia’s customers that the United States of America will not sit by while they fund Putin’s assault.” The measure was a relatively rare bipartisan accomplishment ahead of November’s midterm elections, where Democrats hope to channel voter sentiment against Trump to regain control of Congress. “By imposing steep sanctions that will further drain the Kremlin’s war chest, Congress is delivering an important reminder to Putin and his allies that this is a losing war and authoritarianism will never go unchallenged,” said Chuck Schumer, the minority leader. “I urge Trump to use these sanctions to hit Putin where it hurts. Continuing to appease Putin won’t work.” After the vote, Zelenskyy thanked the US Senate, writing on X that the bill’s advancement “certainly helps increase pressure ⁠on the aggressor to bring this insane Russian war against our ‌independence and our people to an end”. Ursula ⁠von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, also cheered the Senate’s action. “Together, let us drain Russia’s means to continue a war it cannot win,” she wrote on X. “With hard-hitting, complementary ⁠sanctions, Europe and the United States can once again show what historic partners can ‌achieve when we act together.” The measure now heads to the House of Representatives, which may consider once it returns from recess at the end of August. Some Democrats have warned that the bill would give Trump new tariff powers at a time when he has put such levies at the center of his trade policy. Paul and Democratic senator Ron Wyden had offered an amendment that would have stripped some of the new tariff authority from the text, but the Senate rejected it by a 32-64 vote. “This bill gives him so much discretion that Trump can ultimately decide what countries to tariff, or what countries to exempt. And he can modify tariffs at his will,” said Wyden, who voted against the bill. “Trump can pick and choose even more countries to tariff every 180 days, but there is no mechanism in this bill for Congress to roll back these tariffs,” he continued. “If Congress passes this bill, members will be condoning the tariff chaos of the last year and a half – and inviting more.” Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, and Don Beyer, the senior Democrat on the joint economic committee, criticized the legislation for creating “sweeping new tariff authorities that the president could weaponize with abandon, as he has repeatedly done in the past”. Noting that Trump just weeks ago imposed new 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods, the two Democrats said: “We welcome our Senate colleagues’ urgent effort to support Ukraine and punish Russia for its continued illegal war, but this bill would not achieve those goals. Instead, it would allow President Trump to dodge holding Russia accountable and impose yet more tariffs in his destructive trade wars, leaving Americans to foot the bill.”

title: David Brat bound for Australia as diplomat confirmed as next US ambassador
author: Josh Taylor
summary: Former Republican state congressman, who once argued Christianity and capitalism should merge, confirmed by US Senate to fill long-vacant role
body_text: Former Virginia congressman David Brat has been confirmed by the US Senate to be the next US ambassador to Australia, after the role had been left vacant for 18 months. Brat’s confirmation was among more than 70 votes pushed through the Senate by Republicans on Friday, Washington time, before the summer recess. Brat was nominated by Donald Trump in April. The 61-year-old served two terms in Congress until 2018, when he was defeated by a Democrat, and was vice-president of business relations at Virginia’s Liberty University. The ambassador role had been vacant since November 2024, when Joe Biden’s ambassador, Caroline Kennedy, left the post. Anthony Albanese in April said he would work with anyone Trump nominated, when asked to respond to Brat’s earlier claims that US intelligence agencies conspired to remove Trump from office. “We respect the sovereignty of countries to put forward ambassadors just like we expect our choices to be endorsed,” he said at the time. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, welcomed Brat’s appointment in a statement on Saturday. “He will find Australia to be a warm host and a good friend,” she said. “We share his priorities of critical minerals, defence cooperation and partnership in the Indo-Pacific. Together we will strengthen the alliance in the interests of both our countries.” The climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, told reporters on Saturday it was important to have the position now filled. “The bilateral relationship is of course a deeply important one and we welcome the appointment of the new ambassador.” Brat was described by Time magazine in 2010 as a “Tea Party professor” and an enthusiast of the author Ayn Rand. In a 2011 paper, he argued that capitalism and Christianity should merge, writing: “If we all did the right thing and had the guts to spread the word, we would not need the government to backstop every action we take.” Brat was swept into Congress in 2014 when he defeated the then House of Representatives majority leader, Eric Cantor, in a primary. He lost his seat in 2018 to Democrat Abigail Spanberger, who is now the governor of Virginia. The confirmation comes amid tense US-Australia relations, with Trump levelling 12.5% tariffs on many Australian exports in July. Australia was on a list of 54 economies hit with the tariffs due to what the US claimed was a failure “to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor”. At the time, the trade minister, Don Farrell, called for the tariffs to be removed, saying they were inconsistent with Australia’s free-trade agreement with the US. Brat’s arrival in Australia will coincide with the 75th anniversary of the Anzus treaty, a security pact over defence of the Pacific, and comes after the Albanese government announced in May it would instead buy three second-hand American nuclear submarines as part of the $370bn Aukus deal, instead of two second-hand and one new as originally intended. While the Albanese government has remained supportive of Aukus, there has been growing disquiet from some within Labor about the plan. Former cabinet minister Ed Husic said in June that the change meant “we are not going to get the deal that was promised to us”. The former defence secretary Greg Moriarty has been Australia’s representative in Washington since taking over from former prime minister Kevin Rudd in April. • This article was amended on 9 August 2026. An earlier version incorrectly stated David Brat entered the US Senate in 2014; he was elected to the House of Representatives.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Wildberries warehouse struck by Kyiv’s drones more than 2,000km from Russian border
author: Guardian staff and agencies
summary: Depot hit in city of Ekaterinburg and hundreds evacuated in latest attack on Russian online retail giant. What we know on day 1,627
body_text: Ukrainian long-range drones hit a warehouse beloning to Russia’s biggest online retailer in the Ural Mountains, more than 2,000km (1,200 miles) from the two countries’ border, local officials and the company said on Friday. Wildberries said its warehouse in Ekaterinburg, Russia’s fourth-largest city, was set ablaze in the attack. Most merchandise was not damaged, the company said. More than a dozen other Wildberries depots struck by Ukraine in recent weeks have burned down. The regional governor, Denis Pasler, said three drones hit the warehouse’s roof. The Kremlin’s representative in the region, Artyom Zhoga, said 800 people were evacuated from the warehouse and nobody was hurt. Vladimir Putin chaired a meeting of Russia’s security council on Friday and said in televised opening remarks that the meeting would focus on additional measures to “strengthen … protection of infrastructure facilities” but gave no further details. Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked the ⁠US Senate ⁠on Friday for passing ⁠a bill backing sweeping energy sanctions on ⁠Russia, saying it helped increase pressure on Moscow. The European Commission president, Ursula ⁠von der Leyen, also welcomed the vote, saying it came on the back on the EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia and showed that with complementary ⁠sanctions “Europe and the United States can once again show what historic partners can ‌achieve when we act together”. The US bill, intending to punish Russia and countries that buy its petroleum exports, advances a long-delayed measure backed ⁠by the late senator Lindsey Graham. Russian strikes killed three people – including a child – in a district north-east of the Ukrainian capital, a regional military official said on Saturday. Three people were also wounded in the strikes on the Brovary district, Kyiv’s regional military administration chief, Tymur Tkachenko, said on Telegram. In the capital, four people were wounded from overnight attacks, the administration said, with mayor Vitali Klitschko saying fires were reported in two districts. On Friday Russian strikes on ⁠Ukraine’s south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region killed ⁠two people and injured six, regional ⁠governor Oleksandr Hanzha said, amid nearly 50 ‌attacks. Two people were killed ‌near the town of Nikopol on the western bank of the Dnipro River, opposite ⁠the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant. Russia’s defence ministry said its forces struck two ⁠more cargo vessels in ⁠the Black Sea being ‌used in the Ukrainian military’s interests. In Russian-occupied Crimea, two people ⁠were ⁠killed after a ⁠Ukrainian drone struck ⁠an apartment ‌building ‌in ‌Kerch on Friday, ‌said the peninsula’s Russia-installed governor, ⁠Sergei Aksyonov. A ⁠fire broke out at the ⁠Ilsky ⁠oil refinery and five people were wounded ⁠in Russia’s Krasnodar region after a ⁠Ukrainian drone attack, ‌local authorities said ‌on Saturday. Separately, drones ‌targeted an industrial facility in Russia’s Samara region, the regional governor said, ‌without identifying the enterprise. Zelenskyy on Friday began his first official visit to Serbia to discuss security with a European country still closely allied with Moscow. Welcomed at Belgrade airport by the energy minister, the Ukrainian president had dinner with his Serbian counterpart, Aleksandar Vučić. Zelenskyy said on X: “We will discuss expanding economic ties between our countries, relations with the European Union, other areas that can benefit our nations, and security issues.” Vučić and Zelenskyy are to hold official talks on Saturday at the presidential palace and make a statement to the press, according to the Serbian presidency. A senior Ukrainian official told AFP ahead of the trip it was an attempt to “pull the Serbs away from Russia’s side”, but Vučić has insisted his decision not to sanction Moscow will not change. Chancellor Friedrich Merz convened Germany’s national security council on Friday to discuss an explosive-laden drone found near a Ukrainian cargo plane and the midair collision of another aircraft with an unidentified object this week. Germany has not blamed anyone for the incident at Leipzig-Halle airport early on Wednesday, but the Russian embassy in Berlin on Friday claimed the discovery of a “fabricated provocation” was set up to blame Moscow. German interior minister Alexander Dobrindt has called the discovery “a hybrid attack” that spelled “a new level of danger”. Russia’s supreme court said on Friday it would consider a lawsuit to bar Yabloko, the only officially registered party that opposes Moscow’s war in Ukraine, from contesting parliamentary elections in September. The ⁠suit was filed by Rodina (⁠or Motherland), a small pro-Kremlin nationalist party whose leader, Alexei Zhuravlev, denounced Yabloko as a western-backed movement bent on discrediting the elections and Russia itself. Yabloko accused Zhuravlev of making defamatory statements against it and said it would launch its own ‌suit to protect its reputation.

title: US promises $1bn in security aid to Colombia as new rightwing president pledges drugs crackdown
author: Guardian staff and agencies
summary: Trump ally Abelardo De La ‌Espriella vows to start ‘profound transformation’ of country’s destiny as he is sworn in
body_text: The Trump administration plans to provide $1bn in security assistance to the ⁠government of Colombia’s new rightwing ‌president, the US state department announced, soon after Abelardo De La ‌Espriella was sworn in and used his inaugural speech to pledge a vigorous fight against drug trafficking, as well as austerity measures to restore confidence in the economy. De La Espriella, 48, won June’s runoff election with ⁠promises to crack down on armed groups, shrink ⁠the state by as much as 40% and revive the oil and gas sector. “I have come to close a long chapter of national resignation and, together with the people, embark on the most profound transformation ⁠of our destiny,” De La Espriella said at the Pichincha Battalion military base in Cali after being sworn in on Friday. “I send a firm message to the Colombian people: the time has come to restore order, authority and freedom,” said De La Espriella, who received the endorsement of Donald Trump before his runoff election. “Members of criminal gangs and narco-terrorist groups have two choices: submit to the ⁠rule of law or face the determined response of the Colombian state and its security forces,” the new president told assembled troops at the base during a 75-minute speech, adding the option of peace talks with armed groups had been “completely exhausted”. The US ⁠state department said in a statement on Friday: ⁠“As a cornerstone of this renewed partnership, the United States, working with Congress, ‌intends to announce $1 billion in assistance as part of a security package to support ⁠President de la Espriella’s Administration in achieving our shared goals.” De La Espriella’s election is part of a rightward shift rippling across Latin America. In Peru, Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Bolivia and Panama, weak ‌economies and rising crime have reshaped voter priorities, allowing once-fringe ‌hard-right candidates to gain traction by promising crackdowns amid a global rise of rightwing nationalism. De La Espriella could push through some of his policies via decree, but analysts say many of his proposals will require backing from a divided congress and could ‌be watered down in negotiations. The new president vowed to “definitively eradicate the scourge of illicit crops”, saying he would use aerial herbicides that did not harm human health or the environment to destroy coca, the plant used to make cocaine. In one of his first acts as president, Colombia would join the Shield of the Americas program founded by Trump, he said. Before his inauguration, he held bilateral meetings with the king of Spain and the presidents of Argentina, Ecuador, Chile, Paraguay and Panama. Also attending was Gianni Infantino, the embattled head of Fifa, football’s world governing body, while the US sent a delegation headed by the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche. De La Espriella has blamed former president Gustavo Petro, who has not recognised the new president’s victory, for an expansion of armed groups, and narrowly defeated leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda – a Petro ally – in the runoff. Cepeda led a morning march on Friday in Barranquilla, where he told demonstrators that the country’s opposition would work to defend democracy and called for peaceful civil disobedience. With Reuters

title: Two weeks that rocked Fifa: how Gianni Infantino unravelled, day by day
author: David Hills
summary: A fortnight ago the Fifa president looked untouchable. Now he is fighting for survival, accused of overseeing a ‘smash-and-grab scam of colossal proportions’
body_text: Monday 27 July A swipe at fake news Gianni Infantino marks the end of the World Cup by taking to Instagram with a 15-page post calling out the media for trying to sully it. He says it was a month of “joy and happiness”, and “those sitting behind their pens and papers, behind their screens, spreading hate and false rumours” about greed and his relationship with Donald Trump had let themselves down – “while we at Fifa are on the frontlines, working hard”. He says journalists should step back and instead “take a moment to reflect, meditate, pray or watch a match”. Tuesday 28 July Advice not taken Hours later, a report in the Times exposes Infantino’s secret £3.1bn plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors, potentially earning him tens of millions of pounds. The deal involves the brother of Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Politicians and football figures attack it – including a surprise intervention from the former Fifa president Sepp Blatter. He tweets his discomfort that “the financial dimension is deeply damaging football”. Wednesday 29 July First response As outrage spreads, Infantino tries to cool the mood, admitting the scheme is real but saying it is also just a “proposal, an offer … part of a democratic process, a consultation”. It later emerges that Fifa has given its 211 member associations a deadline of 19 September to back it or lose their £15m cut. Concacaf says it was “only made aware of this matter through media reports”, while Uefa accuses Fifa officials of “using our sport to enrich themselves and their friends”. Thursday 30 July Uefa bares teeth After the Guardian exposes the full details of the plan drawn up by Fifa and the US bank JP Morgan – which calls Fifa “undermonetized” – Uefa holds an emergency meeting. All 55 members agree to boycott Fifa competitions if the plan goes ahead. Other football bodies join the backlash, while, in the US, a senior Democrat warns Fifa could face a congressional investigation. Jamie Raskin calls it “a smash-and-grab scam of colossal proportions”. Friday 31 July Potus puts some distance Hours after Fifa’s own chief operating officer slates the proposal, Andy Burnham becomes the first head of a major nation to call on Infantino to resign. Trump, meanwhile, says he has nothing to do with it: “I never spoke to him.” In response to the global coverage, Fifa condemns journalists: “Our planned consultation process was disrupted by incorrect media reports. We will proceed with this consultation … Nobody is selling football.” Saturday 1 August On second thoughts Fifa doesn’t proceed with the consultation. Infantino instead issues a new statement, withdrawing the plan “having listened carefully to all the views”. But Uefa still ups the pressure on him, saying the Fifa leadership has “lost our confidence … We must identify those responsible and hold them to account … No option should be off the table.” There is one voice of support, though. Qatar’s FA says it “fully supports president Infantino’s efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game”. Sunday 2 August Trump won’t pick up A rebellion appears to begin among members of the Fifa council, while European countries discuss withdrawing longstanding letters of support for Infantino’s re-election. Elsewhere, the New York Post claims Infantino has “repeatedly tried” to call Trump for help, but Trump isn’t answering. And @SeppBlatter posts another disappointed tweet: “Money matters, but it must never become everything. #GianniInfantino” Monday 3 August Lawyers send letters The coordinated withdrawal of support begins. England, Wales and Serbia join Finland and Sweden in demanding change at the top. Meanwhile, lawyers acting for Uefa order Infantino and his staff to preserve all documents related to the collapsed scheme, saying Uefa is “considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints”. The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, emerges as a leading contender to challenge for the job. Tuesday 4 August Mattias turns More key allies distance themselves from the Fifa president, including his No 2, Mattias Grafström, who calls the plan a “sad and reproachable series of events” in a leaked email to staff. Greece pulls support from Infantino, while Jordan’s Prince Ali bin al-Hussein accuses Infantino’s administration of “blackmail”, alleging that Fifa threatened to withhold financial assistance from his federation if it refused to back the president’s bid for re-election. Wednesday 5 August Wagons circle Infantino reacts, calling a Fifa staff crisis meeting in Morocco. Fifa then issues a statement saying staff gave him their unanimous backing while also putting his critics on notice: “It was agreed that Fifa will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity.” The former Portugal star Luís Figo, meanwhile, writes in the Daily Mail that “Infantino has lied, deceived and tried to feather his own nest … It is too late to save his dignity but it is not too late to save football. He should go. Now.” Thursday 6 August Having none of it Responding to the Fifa statement about its staff meeting, Uefa doubles down on its boycott threat. It adds: “Yesterday’s announcement that some people employed by the Fifa president (and whose careers depend on his favour) agree with him changes nothing.” The global players’ union, Fifpro, meanwhile, says that while Infantino’s scheme is gone, “the abuse of power that produced it is not … Reforms, not a cover-up, are urgently needed.” Friday 7 August Battle lines drawn Allies begin to surface as Mexico and Argentina follow Africa’s governing body in rallying round – but others join the backlash. Norway’s FA calls for him to go and makes a new ethics complaint against Infantino on multiple fronts, including over his alleged breaches of Fifa’s rules on political neutrality. Infantino, meanwhile, takes a mini- break, arriving in Colombia for the inauguration of the hard-right president Abelardo de la Espriella, a key Trump ally. Infantino tells an audience there: “It is a joy to be here today. Football is joy, football is happiness, football is unity.”

title: Senate passes funding bill to prevent shutdown through US midterms
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Bill must still be approved by House but would keep government running at current funding levels
body_text: The US Senate on Friday passed a government funding bill that will prevent a shutdown through the midterm elections, though it still must be approved by the House of Representatives. The continuing resolution (CR) passed by a 90-6 vote will keep the government running at its current funding levels until 11 December, more than a month past the midterms in which Democrats are hoping to regain control of Congress and block Donald Trump’s legislative agenda for the final two years of his presidency. The measure’s passage signals a recognition by both parties that they would prefer to avoid a messy battle over federal spending in the weeks leading up to the 3 November vote. The government will shut down after 30 September if new funding is not approved, and the Republican Senate appropriations committee chair, Susan Collins, called the CR “a major step toward averting a damaging shutdown that only harms vital programs and federal workers”, and noted it makes no major changes to funding levels. The House had last month approved a different CR that would continue funding until 4 December. It is unclear which bill will ultimately be adopted – the House is on recess until the end of the month, and senators were expected to leave Washington DC for their break following the vote. Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the Senate appropriations committee, said the House’s bill had “several major issues” that the Senate’s version addressed. It would block until 11 December a new rule by the White House office of management and budget that Democrats fear would allow the Trump administration to cancel grants at any time for any reason. The Senate CR also closes what Murray called a “loophole” in the House bill that would have allowed the White House to take money meant for other purposes and give it to the border patrol. “Today’s CR gives us the breathing room necessary to work out a budget that helps make life more affordable to working families and reins in Trump’s rampant chaos, his rampant corruption,” the Democratic minority leader, Chuck Schumer, said ahead of the vote. Democrats instigated a government shutdown last year when they refused to approve funding bills without an agreement to extend subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans. That led to the longest funding lapse in US history, but ultimately no agreement to keep the cost offsets going after the shutdown ended 43 days later. Some government agencies shut down again briefly earlier this year after Democrats held up a funding bill for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in protest of the killings by federal agents of two US citizens in Minneapolis during an intensive immigration enforcement drive. While an agreement was reached to resolve that blockade, the two parties did not agree on funding DHS for weeks, as Democrats held out for reforms to immigration enforcement operations. A bipartisan agreement was reached to fund the department operations exclusive of the agencies involved in Trump’s mass deportation push, then Republicans passed a party-line bill that allocated funding to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection for the duration of Trump’s presidency, with no reforms to immigration enforcement.

title: Trump loyalist Todd Blanche confirmed by Senate as US attorney general
author: Sam Levine
summary: Major win for president as former personal lawyer wins approval despite outcry over $1.8bn slush fund
body_text: The US Senate voted to narrowly confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general in a major win for Donald Trump, who will now have his one-time personal attorney sitting atop the nation’s law enforcement apparatus. Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana cast the deciding vote in Blanche’s favor after two other Republicans – Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska – voted against him. Every Democrat rejected Blanche’s nomination as the Republican-led Senate voted 50-49. Blanche had already been leading the department in an acting capacity, and the vote came after his nomination had been in limbo for weeks. He faced pushback from Republican senators over the department’s deal to create a $1.8bn so-called “anti-weaponization fund” and to give the president, his sons and his businesses tax immunity. “Mr Blanche is not perfect, and he will tell you this, but the choice is not between perfection and Mr Blanche,” Cassidy said Friday on the Senate floor announcing his decision. “It is between Mr Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump and who indeed may not be as good as Mr Blanche.” The Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, said Senate Republicans have “handed Trump an excuse on a silver platter” to continue his “pervasive, breathtaking corruption” by confirming Todd Blanche as attorney general. “If you want to wipe out corruption, you can’t have the president’s personal attorney as the attorney general. You don’t need a PhD in political science to know that,” he wrote in a post on X. “Todd Blanche has no intention of stopping Trump’s corruption. He advanced his career enabling it. Every senator who voted to confirm him has now branded themselves as an enabler, too.” Blanche said on social media that he was “deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me”, adding that he was “grateful” to senators for working late to confirm him. Concern around the “anti-weaponization fund” appears to have cost Blanche among at least some GOP senators who opposed his nomination, including Murkowski. “I am also keenly aware that the Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund – which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters – is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage. Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds,” Murkowski said in a post on X on Friday, announcing she was voting against Blanche. But John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina successfully pushed Blanche to put in writing that the fund was not moving forward and to clarify the scope of the IRS deal. Even though experts said the assurances were far from ironclad, Cornyn and Tillis wound up supporting Blanche, allowing his nomination to narrowly clear the Senate judiciary committee. Blanche also faced heavy criticism for the department’s sloppy rollout of files related to Jeffrey Epstein, which redacted information that should not have been redacted and left unredacted the names of victims that should have been kept private. During his confirmation hearing, Blanche refused to personally meet with Epstein victims, then agreed to do so. The survivors said they received few answers from Blanche during the meeting. Blanche, who left a lucrative partnership to represent Trump in 2023, has been at the center of the president’s attempt to bend the federal government to his will. Scores of career justice department attorneys have left the agency under his leadership. Department lawyers have been rebuked by judges across the US for making misrepresentations to the court. Blanche has also been at the center of Trump’s efforts to use the justice department to punish political rivals. During his tenure as both the deputy attorney general and acting attorney general, the department has indicted former FBI director James Comey twice; the New York attorney general, Letitia James; and the non-profit Southern Poverty Law Center – all in cases that exerts see as thin. It has also tried to bring criminal charges against two Democratic senators, Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Mark Kelly of Arizona, and used its investigative powers to try and get leverage over Jerome Powell, the former chairman of the Federal Reserve. “The Attorney General should serve the American people, not the president’s wish list,” Kelly said in a statement on Saturday in which he also noted that Blanche “met with Ghislane Maxwell in secret” before the convicted Epstein accomplice was transferred to a minimum-security prison camp. Blanche, Kelly added “is defined by his loyalty to Trump”. As his nomination was pending, Blanche also promised anti-abortion advocates the department would make the Dobbs decision permanent in every state, according to Politico. “While I believe Mr Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political,” Collins, who is running for re-election in Maine, said earlier this week. “Mr Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation.” Earlier this year, Blanche spoke about how he would feel if someone else was named attorney general. “As to whether or not I want this job, I did not ask for this job. I love working for President Trump, it’s the greatest honor of a lifetime,” he said in April, shortly after being named the acting attorney general. “If he chooses to nominate somebody else and asks me to go do something else, I will say, ‘Thank you very much. I love you, sir.’ I don’t have any goals or aspirations beyond that.”

title: Fifa defends Gianni Infantino and launches attack after ‘effort to undermine’ president
author: Matt Hughes
summary: Fifa has issued a new statement alleging there is a ‘concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president’ as pressure increases on Gianni Infantino
body_text: Fifa last night issued a thinly-veiled attack on Uefa and other leading figures in European football in a statement which alleged there is a “concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president,” as football’s civil war escalated further. Uefa has made it clear they regard Infantino’s continued leadership of world football as untenable following his role in the World Cup sell-off plans, while the Guardian revealed on Friday the Norwegian Football Federation has publicly called on him to resign, with Fifa responding by accusing them of attempting to subvert the organisation’s democratic processes. Fifa’s latest defence of Infantino followed Uefa’s confirmation on Saturday that a “departure payment” was made to a female employee who is alleged to have been in a relationship with Fifa president while he was the organisation’s general secretary over a decade ago. The Daily Telegraph had reported on Friday night that the woman received a six-figure sum following the alleged relationship with Infantino, allegations Fifa dismissed as “categorically untrue.” Fifa went further last night by accusing Infantino’s critics of attempting to remove him from office before next March’s presidential election. As previously reported by the Guardian, Uefa is seeking support from other confederations to call an Emergency Fifa Congress to trigger a vote of no confidence in the president, but their own members can provide the 43 votes to call a meeting it is unclear whether they would reach the threshold of 106 of the 211 Fifa members required to unseat Infantino. North American confederation Concacaf are aligned with Uefa, while there is some support amongst the Asian Football Confederation, but the Confederation of African Football and South American confederation Conmebol have both publicly announced their backing for Infantino. “Echoing the recent statements of Conmebol and CAF, as well as discussions with Fifa Member Associations and Confederations from around the world, Fifa will not support, facilitate or tolerate any process concerning the election of the Fifa President that is inconsistent with Fifa’s Statutes, democratic procedures and established governance framework,” a Fifa spokesperson said. “The Fifa President was democratically elected by Fifa’s Member Associations and continues to serve with their mandate. “The Fifa president was democratically elected by Fifa’s member associations and continues to serve with their mandate. Those who do not have the support of Fifa’s member associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa’s established democratic processes.” Uefa had responded to Fifa’s proposal to sell 20% of a new company controlling the World Cup’s commercial assets with a threat backed by all 55 European countries to boycott their tournaments unless the plans were abandoned, which they were less than 48 hours later. Significantly however, Uefa released a new statement last Thursday after Fifa had confirmed that Infantino retained the organisation’s “full support” following a crisis meeting of their management board in Rabat the previous day, saying that nothing had changed and that the boycott threat remained in place. Fifa is now convinced that Uefa is behind coordinated attempts to remove Infantino. It is unclear what further concessions Uefa is demanding to cancel the boycott, which faces its first test next month at the Under-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland. Fifa’s statement last night also included a new attack on the media, a well-worn tactic used by Infantino. “Recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning Fifa and its president,” a spokesperson said. “Speculation and insinuation should not be presented as fact, and repetition does not make an allegation true. “Fifa welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to distort facts, amplify unsubstantiated allegations or manufacture distractions designed to undermine progress. “Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading, Fifa will challenge it directly and vigorously. Fifa’s responsibility is to its 211 member associations and to football around the world. We will not be distracted or diverted from strengthening the organisation, delivering for our member associations and continuing the work of making football truly global.”

title: The Democratic party needs to do more than represent wealthy progressives
author: Dustin Guastella
summary: New research shows that a class gap on the left threatens any winning coalition – but there are ways to address it
body_text: Debates on the left are typically framed as a division between moderates and progressives, with the two sides wrestling over how best to form a governing coalition. Yet, in many ways, this divide obscures a much bigger fault line: the class divide. The fact is, many of the Democratic party’s ideological factions consist almost exclusively of college-educated professionals. As a result, the priorities of this class tend to dominate the party’s appeals. The priorities of working-class voters, meanwhile, are an afterthought. A new report from Jared Abbott, the director of the Center for Working Class Politics, and Joan Williams, author of Outclassed: How the Left Lost the Working Class and How to Win Them Back, looks at ways to bridge the yawning class divide that threatens the possibility of forming a winning coalition. They developed an original survey to explore the various attitude “gaps” between the broad working class (defined as non-college educated, middle-income workers) and the liberal upper middle class (Democratic-leaning college graduates with a household income in the top 25%). The resulting report, titled The Left’s Coalition Crisis: Understanding the Massive Divide Between Working Class and College Educated Voters, and How to Bridge it, is, according to the authors, “the most comprehensive review available to date” of class-based political attitudes across a number of issue areas. The first thing to note about the gaps between the educated upper middle class and the working class is that the latter overwhelmingly prioritize economic issues, while the former lean toward cultural ones. Of the top 12 political priorities listed by working-class respondents, 11 are economic concerns. The only non-economic issue prized by the working class was a desire to lower the crime rate. Meanwhile, educated upper-income respondents rated cultural and symbolic issues over economic concerns. Of their top 12 priorities, only six were economic. They also rate abstract ideals over concrete, material ones. Educated voters prioritized “resisting authoritarianism” above “protecting social security” and “ending racism” above “protecting Medicaid”. On an issue-by-issue basis, the largest gaps that Abbott and Williams found were along culture, climate, crime and immigration issues. That is, the very issues many college-educated liberals have built their political identities around. Maybe that wouldn’t be such a problem if these issues were largely downplayed by Democratic party leaders, in favor of shared economic grievances. But that’s hardly the case. Not only do the cultural priorities of the privileged fail to speak to working-class voters’ economic frustrations, but, because Democratic party primaries are dominated by educated upper-income voters, these appeals have come to define liberalism itself. No doubt, the surest way to get a huge cheer at a liberal political rally is to simply mention racism or authoritarianism. Bonus points if you bravely proclaim your unwillingness to “throw X group under the bus”. Such rhetorical gestures have the added benefit of committing candidates to nothing in particular, and thus never threaten potential rich donors. You might say, so what? Who cares if candidates say some throwaway lines about the “marginalized” at a campaign rally; what’s the harm? As Abbott and Williams demonstrate, signaling allegiance to such political priorities is far from costless. Embracing the values and slogans of the privileged tells working-class voters that you are either aloof to, or ignorant of, their priorities. And worse, that you don’t respect working people as political actors. As the authors note, college graduates in Europe and the United States “are more biased against the less-educated than any other stigmatized group”, including racial, religious and sexual minorities. Blue-collar workers can sense liberal condescension in smarmy injunctions to “be kind”, and they resent what they perceive as upper-class attempts to morally re-educate them. It gets worse. Even if upper-income progressives steer clear of cultural condescension, their economic priorities are also class-bound. While working-class voters prioritize jobs, wages and economic growth, the educated knowledge workers are mainly concerned with high costs. This, too, is a function of the latter’s relatively privileged class position. Despite recent wage erosion, the college-educated set still make much more than their non-college educated counterparts – between 60% and 80% more on average. This wage premium, combined with our K-shaped economy, means that the well-educated and well-heeled, those in the top 20% of the income hierarchy, now drive nearly 60% of all consumer spending. For many educated, upper-income voters – especially those in corporate careers – the defining feature of their economic lives is consuming, not producing. As such, they are extremely sensitive to price increases. Working-class voters are too, but for very different reasons. It’s the devaluing of work that drives their frustrations. As the authors point out, for the working class, and especially for blue-collar workers, it’s work, not consumption, that defines their lives. But long-term wage stagnation, and the disappearance of good stable jobs, has meant that essential goods have become even more difficult to afford. Here, globalization plays a major role. And, on that issue, the data shows yet another chasm between the popular classes. While some liberal appeals to “affordability” emphasize the need to scrap tariffs and embrace more liberal immigration rules in order to broaden consumer demand (and lower the agricultural wage-bill), working-class voters are rightly skeptical of these solutions. Restrictions on trade and immigration represent efforts to address the long-neglected problems of wage stagnation. Free trade has devastated the working class, shuttering thousands of factories and sinking many into drug-addiction and despair. At the same time, mass migration has eroded the wage packet for manual workers. For them, addressing affordability must mean policies that speak to the essentially place-bound character of blue-collar life. While professional-class status is portable – effectively equivalent in London, New York, Paris or Washington DC – working-class status is not so liquid. Seniority in a job or trade is not typically a transferrable credential. For these reasons place-loyalty matters a great deal to working-class people. On the other hand, globalization and the growth of “knowledge work” has supercharged select high-income metro areas, where many professionals live and where progressives thrive. Democrats now represent nine of the top 10 highest-income congressional districts in the country. The truth is, educated upper-income voters, be they progressive or moderate, largely benefit from low-wage immigrant labor and cheap foreign goods. Contrary to the place-based loyalty of blue-collar workers, they prize their status as global-citizens and cosmopolitan consumers. Navigating these tensions isn’t easy, but Abbott and Williams did find a number of issues that could serve as a foundation for a progressive program of popular-class unity. Getting it right means addressing both the wage and the price side of the affordability equation, downgrading the cultural priorities of the privileged (including on abortion and transgender issues), and grappling with the tension between globalist affinities and local loyalty. By focusing only on those issues that win more than two-thirds of support from both working-class and educated upper-middle-class respondents, they propose a political program with the following planks: allow Medicare to negotiate lower prescription drug prices, protect and improve social security, spend $150bn on infrastructure, expand Medicaid, ratchet up education spending and raise the minimum wage. That’s a great start. But it could be improved by an even greater emphasis on working-class priorities. We need new trade rules, revitalized national industry and real pro-labor immigration reform that can help right the wrongs of globalism. We ought to advocate expansive and generous policies that emphasize the importance of family life. Why not make giving birth entirely free, implement national paid-parental leave, and provide affordable childcare? And finally, we need to make expanding and improving badly underfunded local police and fire departments a national priority in order to make every neighborhood and community safe. Such priorities speak directly to felt needs and they signal a genuine political attempt at reorganizing politics around working-class demands, rather than the preferences of the professionals. Putting working-class priorities first will no doubt result in political tensions. Flashpoints around gender, immigration and even class itself, will break out. Getting through those fights will be necessary if progressives ever hope to expand their coalition by reaching into the working class. Plus, who knows, maybe professional-class progressives could learn a thing or two from their working-class counterparts. Dustin Guastella is a research associate at the Center for Working Class Politics and the director of operations for Teamsters Local 623. He is a Guardian US columnist

title: As AI guzzles water and energy, we are already facing a choice: datacentres or homes?
author: John Harris
summary: Whitehall wants to triple their number in the UK. Yet in Slough, I saw the impact they’re having on communities, says Guardian columnist John Harris
body_text: Amid headlines about the UK’s drought, Europe’s wildfires and impossible global temperatures, it was 28C when I arrived in Slough last Monday. I was there to look around Slough Trading Estate, a place that might once have conjured up images of the TV comedy The Office, many of whose laughs came at the expense of this overgrown patch of suburbia, 20-odd miles west of London. But these days, this area of town – an incongruous mixture of old-school businesses such as Mr Clutch and Angling Direct, and vast, metal-clad leviathans that look like something pulled from JG Ballard – has become a byword for the constant expansion of datacentres, those hulking symbols of the vast computing power that big tech now requires, not least because of the ever-more complex workings of artificial intelligence. In many people’s minds, datacentres are also a byword for the two totemic issues of yet another searing summer: heat and water. Across the world, the huge amounts of electricity they demand, mostly generated using fossil fuels, indelibly connects them to the climate emergency. The constant machinations of their crammed-in servers require cooling processes that also use vast amounts of water. So it is that the 21st century’s dominant means of communication intensifies our era’s most terrifying threats. The first building I loitered around was a datacentre owned by the California-based company Equinix. There were 100 or so cars in its “visitor” and “staff” spaces, no corporate branding to be seen – and, up close, the constant sound of a low industrial whirr. On the other side of the street, poetically enough, was a set of offices occupied by Thames Water, a few of whose employees were taking a break outside. I pointed across the road: did they know what the building contained? “There’s loads of AI bits in there,” said a twentysomething woman called Louise. “I saw something about it on Instagram: all the water they use.” She rolled her eyes. “It’s ridiculous. Loads and loads of water because of all the AI.” On her phone, she found one of the posts she had seen. “Slough is quietly running Britain’s AI boom but there’s a problem,” it said. “When a heatwave hits, the machines get thirsty too. Cooling systems work overtime in hot weather, spiking demand for power and water.” Someone suggested I make the five-minute journey to nearby Britwell, a housing estate built for bombed-out Londoners after the second world war. The first person I encountered was a mum from the area called Sheryl. “You notice the noise at night: like a whirring, buzzing sound,” she said. “And since we’ve had all these [new] ones up here, there seems to be more heat round here.” Early research, including a recent preprint of a paper authored by researchers at Cambridge University earlier this year, does suggest that datacentres can have a “heat island” effect, pushing up temperatures in their immediate vicinity by an average of 2C, and as much as 9C. Last month, the trading estate’s corporate owners said they had “not seen conclusive evidence demonstrating that datacentre operations on Slough Trading Estate are causing increases in local temperatures”. Slough has the densest cluster of datacentres in western Europe: as many as 40, with more to come. What has happened here is bound up with the trading estate’s recent history as a partly deregulated “simplified planning zone”, the town’s proximity to London (the faster that digital financial transactions can happen, the better), and the apparently flukish fact that Slough sits atop the cables that connect Britain to the US and Ireland. The datacentres the town hosts are owned and maintained by companies that are far from being household names – Equinix, Digital Realty, Iron Mountain – but serve famous customers including Amazon, Google, Oracle and Microsoft. Fierce arguments about datacentres are a big part of the discourse surrounding the upcoming US midterm elections, with Donald Trump taking a predictable position: “You have to convince your community how great these things [are] … You can’t fight it.” But actually, you can. Resistance is now pouring into the US political mainstream: midway through last month, New York became the first state to impose a one-year pause on new “hyperscale” datacentres, and, as litigation is fought out across the country, there is mounting pressure for other parts of the US to follow suit. The leftist insurgent Abdul El-Sayed, who last week won a Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, has crisply captured the mood: “People really effing hate datacentres,” he says. Even the Republican governor of Texas has called for a ban on their development in rural areas, and last week ordered that new centres won’t join the state’s power grid until regulators have reviewed their use of water and energy. Increasing numbers of US facilities have their own dedicated gas turbines; in the UK, high-ups at the energy regulator Ofgem say that 100 planned centres here aim to do the same. US sites are putting added pressure on existing power grids that also use coal and oil, and backup generators powered by diesel are a standard industry feature. Green datacentres are attracting growing interest, but many insiders insist that renewables simply don’t cut it: “Our datacentres have to run 100% of the time so we can’t even consider using [renewables] as a primary source,” one industry kingpin told the Financial Times last year. With good reason, not many people are minded to listen to private water companies. But only a fortnight ago, Water UK, the organisation that represents firms in the four nations, said that the government’s existing water forecasts were “fatally flawed” and “explicitly exclude” datacentres, which can use up to 5m gallons a day, equivalent to the consumption of up to 50,000 people. What that omission says about our readiness for more datacentres – and what will happen during inevitable future droughts – is an interesting question. Would the public be expected to stoically limit their use of water while datacentres carried on guzzling it? All sorts of tensions could soon explode. For all Andy Burnham’s talk of local decision-making, Whitehall’s official aim is still to triple the UK’s number of datacentres by 2030, which could be aided by the fact that they are now classed as critical national infrastructure. In December, a report by the London assembly revealed that datacentres’ electricity requirements had led to stalled housebuilding in the capital; last week brought news of the returned housing secretary, Angela Rayner, approving a redevelopment of the old Truman Brewery site in east London that had been called in by her predecessor, Steve Reed. It will include a datacentre handling transactions in the City, offices and 44 homes, in contrast to plans supported by the local council centred on 350 new dwellings. Whatever that represents, it doesn’t sound like what the new PM calls “good growth in every postcode”. There may, in fact, be a stark choice lurking in such stories that politicians will soon have to face: homes or servers? On my way out of Britwell, I had a chat with a woman called Jodie, on her way home from Lidl. “My brother said he saw something on TikTok that said if there was a war, Slough would be a target because of the datacentres,” she said. I grimly laughed: “Come friendly bombs and fall on Slough”, and all that? “Let’s hope not,” she said. In the middle distance, the increasingly gigantic datacentres whirred on, and I thought of a few lines from another of John Betjeman’s poems: “And over all the land, instead of trees / Clean poles and wire will whisper in the breeze / We’ll keep one ancient village just to show / What England once was when the times were slow.” John Harris is a Guardian columnist

title: Top Democrats simulate election threats as Trump continues assault on voting
author: George Chidi
summary: Chuck Schumer and other senators took part in exercises in which legal experts laid out election disruption scenarios
body_text: In a Washington DC conference room last month, some of the most senior Democrats in the US Senate gathered to plan for a prospect that only recently would have felt more akin to science fiction: they started to wargame democracy. Chuck Schumer, the US Senate minority leader, and senators including Alex Padilla, Adam Schiff, Mark Warner, Elissa Slotkin and Raphael Warnock were among those in the room as a team of legal experts offered scenarios. The first: realistic deepfake videos, created with artificial intelligence, showing “evidence” of widespread election fraud, spreading through social media a few weeks before voting begins. Forensic experts discredit the videos quickly as synthetic in the given scenario, but rightwing media – and the US president – amplify the claims, nonetheless. Election workers begin receiving death threats. Armed men start appearing at polls. If you’re a Democratic senator, what would you do? “These tabletop exercises are a standard planning tool for experts and stakeholders to prepare for potential scenarios. We’re not predicting exactly what would happen,” said Justin Vail, who leads the DC office of the non-partisan advocacy group Protect Democracy. “But we do want to create a realistic context that can help us identify gaps, test our assumptions, and strengthen coordination, and then ultimately develop some recommendations to increase our preparedness.” Senate Democrats have held two election disruption exercises this year. Voting rights and legal groups like Protect Democracy have also participated, along with election attorney Marc Elias, former attorney general Eric Holder, election law expert Norman Eisen and members of the left-leaning non-profit Democracy Forward. Skye Perryman, CEO of Democracy Forward, expressed confidence in the resilience of the foundations of US democracy, pointing to the legal system and the distributed nature of American elections, which she said builds a defense against crass political interference, even from the US president. “The president can try to imagine whatever he may wish to imagine,” Perryman said. “He can’t imagine a new constitution, and the constitution, frankly, is quite clear in no uncertain terms; there’s not a role for the president in election administration in this country.” Nonetheless, Donald Trump’s continuous false claims about a stolen election in 2020, and his increasingly strident demand for the US Congress to pass a package of federalized oversights of elections, have raised concerns among progressive voters that the administration may mar November’s midterms with misinformation, or worse. The administration billed Trump’s primetime TV address last month as a presentation of new evidence that the 2020 election was illegitimate, and that his administration had uncovered new findings about vulnerabilities in the US election system. Instead, Trump claimed China had illicitly acquired voter information on 220 million Americans, and that China had undermined his 2020 campaign in other unspecified ways, arguing that intelligence officials had suppressed this information. Trump’s claims fell apart under scrutiny. His own intelligence officials had already concluded that China refrained from interfering in the US election out of concern for potential political blowback if caught. Trump threatened the broadcast licenses of networks that refused to carry the address live. In his speech, he again implored Congress to pass the Save America Act, which would ban mail-in ballots nationwide and impose new identification requirements on voters when they register and report to polls. Republican senators refuse to dispense with the 60-vote filibuster threshold to pass the law. Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, representing a swing state that is a favored rhetorical target of the president, described Trump’s address as “signaling his unmistakable intent to attack these elections and our voting rights, just as he tried to throw out our votes and seize the presidency in 2020”. Voting rights advocates pointed toward Trump’s July primetime address as indicative of the president’s intentions – rhetorical attacks on the integrity of voting machines and elections offices, potentially escalating into more direct interference. Trump’s public commentary, and the actions of agencies under his supervision, shaped the scenario building as Democratic leaders plan their possible responses. Senators were asked at their recent session to contemplate how to react to a threat to withhold Office of Management and Budget (OMB) funding for states that don’t submit their voter rolls for federal oversight. They also considered a threat of Federal Communications Commission (FCC) action against news outlets covering deepfakes. “The development of AI will only add to the complexity and could create confusion among voters in our fragmented media landscape,” said Vail. “Unfortunately, that confusion can be to the benefit of the administration’s strategy.” FCC enforcement actions seem relatively mild compared to more extreme scenarios, like planning a response to armed vigilantes in tactical gear at ballot drop boxes – which was not a hypothetical problem in Arizona during the 2022 midterms. Senators were asked to plan responses for online license-plate doxxing, a midnight firebombing of an early voting site and a last-minute unilateral deployment of Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents and the national guard to polling stations. The main lesson of the exercise “is that this is an all-hands-on-deck moment, and it is an all-hands-on-deck response”, said Perryman. “And so what that means is that, we’re not looking at any one silver bullet to be able to fully protect elections. It’s going to take all of us.”

title: Moderate Democrat Ed Case defies progressive challenge in Hawaii primary
author: Guardian staff and agencies
summary: Case, who has represented island state’s first district in US Congress since 2019, beat state senator Jarrett Keohokalole
body_text: The moderate Democratic representative Ed Case has seen off a progressive challenge to retain his party’s nomination for the US House of Representatives election in Hawaii’s first congressional district. Case, who has represented the district in Washington DC since 2019, prevailed in Saturday’s primary over Jarrett Keohokalole, the state senator. A wave of leftwing candidates has swept through a series of high-profile Democratic primaries in recent months, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan this week. Focus will turn next week to Wisconsin, where the democratic socialist Francesca Hong is leading the party’s chaotic gubernatorial primary. Keohokalole, 43, had argued during the campaign in Hawaii that the time had come for a new generation of political leadership in the state. With 91% of votes counted, Case had won 60% of the vote, according to the Associated Press. Keohokalole, in second place, had 36.1%. “I feel very grateful that the voters want me to continue in office,” Case, 73, told Hawaii Public Radio on Saturday. He will now face Adriel Lam, the Republican who ran unopposed in the party’s primary, in the general election. “The voters decided, and we respect the results,” Keohokalole told KHON2. “The seats don’t belong to any individual. You have to earn them, and so the voters spoke.” Case had faced criticism from Democrats including Keohokalole after voting last year for Donald Trump’s Save Act, which would require US voters to prove their citizenship when registering for federal elections. More recently, Case stressed that he no longer supported the legislation, after an option for voters to attest in writing that they are a citizen was removed. But he used his former vote as an example of his independence. “I’m not 100% voter with my party,” Case told HawaiiNewsNow. “Never have been, never will be.” Case holds a senior position on a key spending committee and had argued that Hawaii would attract fewer federal dollars if he was not re-elected. Keohokalole highlighted Case’s campaign donations from businesses to argue he has lost touch with voters. Hawaii is divided into two US congressional districts. The first, represented by Case, covers the urban center of Honolulu. The second, represented by Jill Tokuda, covers the rest of the state. Tokuda also won the Democratic primary for the second congressional district. According to AP, with 90% of votes counted, she had won 91.6%. Josh Green, the Hawaii governor who has led the state since 2022, also defeated several challengers for the Democratic nomination. Reuters contributed reporting

title: Taylor Swift songs removed from Trump and White House’s social media posts
author: Eric Berger
summary: Rage-baiting efforts of Trump accounts silenced after posts such as a video linking her Red album to Republicans
body_text: Some of Taylor Swift’s songs have been removed from videos posted on social media by Donald Trump’s campaign and the White House, silencing efforts to mock the pop star. A video posted on 3 August featuring the US president and the first lady, Melania Trump, watching fireworks was posted this month on TikTok with Swift’s song August. “I’m sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song! #taylorswift #maga #august,” the accompanying text states. Trump’s campaign later published another post, needling Swift over the title of her 2012 album, Red. “Did you know Taylor Swift wrote a whole album about the color of the Republican party?” it said, suggesting parody track titles. Both videos are now silent. Trump-related social media accounts have used Swift’s music in other campaign videos, too, but several of those also no longer have sound. As the text with the August video suggests, Trump’s social media accounts have used pop stars’ songs as rage bait. They have featured music from artists including Ariana Grande, Katy Perry, Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo and Kenny Loggins, all of whom publicly objected to the use of their music. “Please do not use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense,” Grande posted after the White House posted her music over a montage of ICE agents handcuffing and detaining people. When Trump’s White House used one of Carpenter’s songs to soundtrack a video of immigration raids in 2025, the singer wrote: “This video is evil and disgusting. Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.” In this latest case, Swift has not commented. Trump had previously attacked Swift, who endorsed then Democratic vice-president Kamala Harris during the 2024 election. “I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!” Trump declared at the time. Last year he wrote: “Has anyone noticed that, since I said ‘I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT,’ she’s no longer ‘HOT?’” Swift’s Eras tour was the the highest-grossing tour of all time, according to Pollstar, generating about $2.2bn worldwide. Her album The Life of a Showgirl became the most pre-saved album ever on Spotify ahead of its October 2025 release.
