title: Abdul El-Sayed embraces Trump claim he represents ‘very different’ America
author: Eric Berger
summary: Michigan nominee, who spoke to Obama after primary win, vows to fight inequality as president ‘makes billions off you’
body_text: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in Michigan, embraced Donald Trump’s suggestion that the two represent “VERY DIFFERENT” versions of the US, pledging to fight inequality while the president is “making billions of dollars off of you”. In a Saturday night post on his Truth Social platform, Trump shared an image of himself and the first lady, Melania Trump, beside a photo of El-Sayed, who is Muslim, and his wife, Sarah Jukaku, wearing a hijab. “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s [sic],” read the caption. “Yeah, he’s right,” El-Sayed told CNN, when asked about the post on Sunday. “One in which your overlords are two people who don’t like each other, but join in the interest of making billions of dollars off of you – or two people who genuinely love each other, enjoyed some pancakes together, want to come together to build the kind of America where they can raise a family and know that that family is going to have the good things. “Yes, you’ve got two different visions of America,” said El-Sayed. “Donald Trump’s vision is the one you’re living in right now. Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries?” El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan this week, setting up a bruising general election campaign against former US representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, in the swing state. Victory for him is widely seen as crucial to the Democrats’ hopes of retaking control of the Senate from Republicans. During a speech on Thursday, Trump called El-Sayed a communist and said he was “full of shit”, which was met with loud cheers. Asked about the president’s expletive remark, El-Sayed told Sky News: “At least I don’t let mine go in the middle of the Oval Office.” Unlike some other new Democratic candidates, El-Sayed, who ran to the left of his primary opponent, is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, and has said he is a capitalist who wants capitalism to work better. Former US president Barack Obama spoke with El-Sayed after his primary win, in what is deemed an early sign of support for his campaign. “It was a really good conversation about what we need to do to be able to win, and obviously this is somebody who knows a lot about winning Michigan,” El-Sayed told NBC News. Michigan backed both of Obama’s runs for the presidency, in 2008 and 2012, before voting for Trump in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020, and turning back to Trump in 2024. Obama also called Haley Stevens, the moderate Democrat whom El-Sayed defeated in the primary, Politico reported. Stevens urged the former president to “come to Michigan and campaign for the Democrats”, she told the outlet. Should he beat Rogers in November’s general election in Michigan, El-Sayed could become the first Muslim US senator. Republicans have described him as “the most radical Senate candidate in America”, and Trump has repeatedly used his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed. El-Sayed noted the party – and Trump – did the same to Obama, regularly including his middle name “Hussein” when referencing the former president. “At the end of the day it’s not radical to believe that people should be able to afford their groceries,” he told NBC’s Meet The Press. “It’s not radical to believe that you should have healthcare in this country. “It’s not radical … that you don’t think the president should be able to deny elections, or make $2.2bn out of his role in office. It’s not radical to believe all of us should be able to breathe clean air and drink clean water. Those are the things that I’ve been fighting for.” El-Sayed said: “They are going to try to paint me as a certain thing, given my name, but I also think it’s important to recognize that America has a long history of embracing, “America is a lot bigger than very small people like Donald Trump or [Vice President] JD Vance or Mike Rogers want to make it out to be. And so I’m grateful for all that America has given me.”

title: Netanyahu rejects US-led 15-point Gaza peace plan in rare public break with Trump
author: Andrew Roth in Washington
summary: Israeli PM says IDF will not withdraw until Hamas is disarmed and rebukes US pressure to end wars without his country’s buy-in
body_text: Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has rejected a US-backed 15-point peace plan for Gaza in a rare public break with Donald Trump. In a statement on Sunday, Netanyahu said that he was confronting a “wave of rumours about Israeli weakness and Israeli withdrawals on all fronts” and rebuked US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in. On Gaza, he said: “Israel does not accept the 15-point document. The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament. Right now, we are talking with the Americans about this issue.” Trump’s Board of Peace in July proposed the 15-point plan, which mandated that Hamas disarm in exchange for providing a full Israeli military withdrawal from the Gaza Strip and an eventual transition of power to an independent Palestinian National Committee. Trump had said that the agreement would be implemented in stages, but Netanyahu on Sunday said that he wanted a full disarmament first in order to implement the deal. The Israeli leader’s main target in his remarks was the US. Israel has emerged as a key stumbling block in the Trump White House’s plans to broker peace in the region, in Israel’s conflicts in Gaza and Lebanon as well as in the war begun by joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran. And Netanyahu, who is facing tough elections in October and pressure from hardliners in his own government, appears ready to test his relationship with Trump in public in order to shore up his reputation as a defender of Israel at home. Israel had already signalled that it would reject the US-led plan. Soon after Trump announced it last month, Israel stepped up its bombing campaign in the Palestinian territory – strikes killed 18 people last Sunday. Netanyahu’s office had previously indicated it would not back the plan, saying: “The version that has been made public does not reflect Israel’s positions.” But Sunday’s rejection was far more forceful and direct, and appeared targeted at the Trump White House, as Trump and Netanyahu both face difficult elections. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said. The head of Trump’s Board of Peace hit back on Sunday, saying the plan remained the “only way forward”. Nickolay Mladenov, the board’s high representative for Gaza, told Israeli television: “The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again.” Netanyahu’s rejection is a blow to Trump’s desire to be seen as a broker of peace in foreign conflicts. With US midterm elections due in November, the White House is desperate to negotiate a peace in Iran in order to reopen the strait of Hormuz and help bring down oil and petrol prices. But the conflicts in the Middle East are interconnected and parallel US efforts have continued to bring peace to Lebanon, where Israel has occupied land in what it says is a buffer zone against Hezbollah, and Gaza, where Gulf allies of the US have decried what they say is an ethnic cleansing campaign being carried out by Israel. Like US presidents before him, Trump has found that Netanyahu can be a difficult ally. Bill Clinton, after meeting Netanyahu for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?” More recently, the Biden administration found that its concerns about the human toll in Gaza were ignored, but continued to publicly back Netanyahu and did not significantly suspend military aid to the country for fear of the political blowback that Netanyahu and his allies in the US could cause. In Trump, however, Netanyahu has found a far more unorthodox and unpredictable counterpart in the White House. Netanyahu is a natural ally for Trump, and he has attacked Democrats before the midterm elections for being weak on supporting Israel. Yet more broadly, support for Israel and its war in Gaza is eroding in the Democratic party, and the Republicans have a presidential frontrunner for 2028 in the vice-president, JD Vance, who is publicly sceptical of Israel and the war in Gaza. Trump will have to decide whether to increase pressure on Netanyahu, potentially alienating some pro-Israel allies, or to allow his efforts for a Gaza peace plan to stall, perhaps indefinitely. The answer will depend heavily on the US president’s own political instincts – are US voters hoping to see Trump emerge as a statesman capable of ending one of the world’s bloodiest recent wars in Gaza, or would a public clash with Netanyahu provoke a revolt among his base? With both countries entering tumultuous election cycles and a generational shift in support for Israel among US voters, the result could redraw the alliance between Israel and the US.

title: Trump appoints staff secretary Will Scharf as new White House counsel
author: Staff and agencies
summary: Scharf, who helped president win official approval for $400m ballroom, to replace David Warrington
body_text: Donald Trump announced on Sunday that ⁠Will Scharf, the staff secretary who helped secure approval for the $400m White House ballroom project from a key official body, will become ⁠White House counsel and assistant to the president. Effective 1 September, Scharf will replace David Warrington, who will be leaving the administration to join the private sector. Warrington formerly served as a personal counsel and a lawyer ‌for Trump’s 2024 campaign. Trump noted that Scharf previously served as a federal prosecutor and represented him in a number of cases, including at the supreme court. Scharf also led the National ‌Capital Planning Commission, which approved the president’s construction of the White House ballroom. “Will is Tough, Strong, and Smart! He also loves our Country, and respects the Law,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Will Scharf will do a great job as White House Counsel!” The shake-up in the White House counsel’s office comes at a critical juncture – just months ahead of the midterm elections, in which Trump’s Republican party will be fighting to hold on to control of Congress. Democrats have vowed to pursue investigations into Trump and his administration if they are successful in November. The White House counsel’s job is to advise on legal and policy questions related to the presidency. The office is the primary White House contact for the justice department, and it handles presidential pardons, works on judicial appointments and reviews legislation. The office also helps investigate and manage congressional investigations into the administration and lawsuits against the president when he is sued in his official capacity. Trump in July 2025 had named Scharf as chair of the National Capital Planning Commission, the executive branch agency with jurisdiction over construction and major renovations to government buildings in the region. Trump’s ballroom won final approval from the NCPC in April, though a divided federal appeals court ruled on Friday that construction on the project must stop because Congress had not approved it. Trump has vowed to appeal to the supreme court. The project is already well under way and has begun to rise above ground on the east side of the White House. The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

title: Centrist Democrats dismiss Abdul El-Sayed as a freak radical. Do they want to win in 2028 or not?
author: Nesrine Malik
summary: Americans want someone on their side in the fight against sordid interests – that means politicians like the Michigan primary winner and Zohran Mamdani, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
body_text: Abdul El-Sayed’s win in the Michigan Senate primary was a historic breakthrough. Not only because he is a Muslim son of immigrants who broke with almost every single tenet of establishment Democratic party politics. But because he has wiped that complacent sneer at progressive wins off the faces of centrist gatekeepers. Zohran Mamdani? Relax, he’s just a mayor. And it’s New York City. Outside urban and liberal corridors, there is nothing to worry about. Now El-Sayed has won the Democratic party’s nomination in a swing state that is also on the list of presidential nomination states. There is a lot to be excited about. Not only within the US, but for observers abroad hopeful for the emergence of a truly revolutionary left that is able to weather powerful and well-funded adversaries and prevail. The money raised to defeat El-Sayed was staggering. He was outspent by more than nine to one. It was the most expensive Democratic congressional primary ever. A roll call of cartoon bad guys, such as Chevron and Philip Morris, funded his opponent, Haley Stevens, to the tune of over $60m. Of that funding, nearly half came from a Super Pac backed by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). The symbolism of the win is heavy, that of a politics snapping the chains of corporate power and special interest groups whose agendas run counter to voters’. It suggests two things. One, an electorate waking up to the fact that its democracy is captured. Two, features in the past that would have been disqualifying – lack of experience, lack of establishment endorsement – now render a candidate a “clean skin”. Someone untainted by the sordid game that keeps in play expensive healthcare, cruelty to immigrants and the hoovering of tax dollars out of the country. Israel took up a large role in the campaign, both on the part of El-Sayed and his opponent. But it’s striking how both were talking about different things. El-Sayed’s detractors stuck to repetitive talking points about “Israel having the right to exist”, a question that is not relevant to the average voter. El-Sayed framed Israel as simply a place that has taken too much of Americans’ money. “The question is quite secondary to whether they have a right to our tax dollars.” It was a clear and salient approach. What El-Sayed’s win isn’t, yet, is a promise that this success can be replicated not only outside primary contests and against Republicans, but across the board among progressive candidates. The Democratic establishment has been hapless in the face of Donald Trump, and new fiery candidates can appear to have the answers that their party so far has not. But they are up against huge challenges. First, what the Republican party will throw at them: accusations that, as Trump said, “full of shit” candidates like El-Sayed are radical commies who will bring nothing but “death, squalor, poverty” and “a life of hell”. Then there is what the centrist wing of the Democrats can mobilise against them. A leading centrist group called Third Way has already raised millions to discredit democratic socialists by investing in social media and mobilising activists against candidates like El-Sayed. “We are preparing for the next war that is coming,” said the group’s leader. Their fear, they say, is that the momentum behind democratic socialists will go all the way to the presidential nomination, and then produce a candidate who would be crushed by Republicans. Because, of course, that has never happened before to a centrist Democratic presidential candidate running against Trump. Still, the portrayals of progressive candidates as radical can go a long way in a country where people think that Trump is more moderate than Kamala Harris or Hillary Clinton. Fighting on a national level, the left can get away with far less in the political imaginary than the right. That is because the very promise of change that gives progressive candidates the edge in certain contests becomes easily framed as a race into the unknown. This becomes an even more resonant threat as progressive candidates do not have the depth and breadth of a long party record behind them, or the familiarity that comes with ubiquity on the political landscape. It doesn’t have to be this way. Politicians like Mamdani and El-Sayed are modelling something truly unique. They signify a new US in which the politics of outsiders and their cultural and ideological features is fused powerfully with and against the features of their adopted countries. They have opted not for meek total assimilation for mobility, nor have they recused themselves from contests for a country in which they have claimed a stake. But they and the rest of the US are carrying too much on their shoulders at a time of domestic and global upheaval. Their movement battles with the stubborn entrenchment of a bankrupt Democratic party establishment, the savage culture wars of the right, and, even though some have thus far prevailed, a gargantuan machine of lobbyists and corporate interest groups. Progressive voters are not simply found, they are made. And constantly remade into coalitions. If the Democrats would rather lose on their own terms than win on the progressive left’s, then fighting these new candidates will establish the impression that they are freak radicals destined to fizzle out. But these candidates have alighted on what seems like the most viable politics right now. Refuse to embrace them wholeheartedly, and you guarantee that Trumpism wins again and again. Back them all the way to 2028. What, after all, do you have to lose that you haven’t lost already? Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

title: Monday briefing: How the new phase of confrontation at al-Aqsa signals a challenge to the status quo
author: Hettie O'Brien
summary: In today’s newsletter: ​Jerusalem’s most volatile site has again become a flashpoint, with Arab states and former Israeli officials sounding the alarm over Benjamin Netanyahu’s complicity
body_text: Good morning. In late July, Itamar Ben-Gvir, West Bank settler and far-right extremist minister of security in Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, joined a group of more than 2,000 Jewish extremists to storm al-Aqsa mosque compound, Jerusalem’s most sensitive holy site. The far-right group has been doing this for years. Ben-Gvir has made series of visits to the site over the last three years, eroding norms and inflaming tensions. Jordanian officials have recently warned that it could be at risk of an “imminent” Israeli takeover. With national elections scheduled in October, and many eyes still firmly on Gaza (this weekend, Netanyahu rejected a US-backed 15 point plan for peace), the Israeli government appears to be racing to expand Israeli settlements and accelerate ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem before its mandate expires. For this morning’s First Edition, I spoke to our senior international correspondent, Julian Borger, about the latest incursions, and how Israeli extremists are trying to create a new reality in Jerusalem. That’s after the weekend roundup. Weekend roundup UK politics | Sadiq Khan has called on the government to commit to revamped climate action and to reduce the UK’s reliance on oil and gas, as the UK endures a summer of drought, wildfires and heatwaves. US politics | The US Senate voted to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general in a win for Donald Trump, who will now have his one-time personal attorney sitting atop the nation’s law enforcement apparatus. US-Israel war on Iran | Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach on Saturday. Russia-Ukraine | Up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers will be deployed in Russia, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. On Saturday, Turkey called for a “moratorium” on attacks by Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea after a series of strikes on civilian ships there World news | The alleged leader of the Kinahan organised crime group was extradited from Dubai on Sunday and met by a huge security operation in Dublin, marking the end of a global game of cat and mouse with European, US and Gulf authorities. In depth: ‘To erect structures, even if they’re temporary, is a red rag to a bull’ The al-Haram al-Sharif site in Jerusalem’s old city, known to Jews as the Temple Mount, is one of the most contentious places on earth. It’s governed by a fragile agreement that gives Muslims exclusive rights to pray and worship there, while Jews pray at the Western Wall below. But Israel’s messianic right, which has gained a powerful foothold in Netanyahu’s coalition government, is fixated on the site as a symbol of its political project. Their vision of building a new Jewish temple on one of Islam’s holiest sites – once a fringe idea – has become increasingly widespread. Since 2023, Jewish religious extremists have made numerous visits to the 35-acre compound which is home to both al-Aqsa mosque and Dome of the Rock, the holiest sites for Muslims in Jerusalem and one of holiest sites for Muslims in the world. “At first, you had groups of perhaps 20 Jews, mostly settlers, who were escorted by the police to the far wall of the compound to pray discreetly,” Julian tells me. “If you were just a casual visitor, you wouldn’t necessarily see them”. Over the last two years, however, the groups have grown bigger and more audacious. On 23 July, they sang the national anthem, and prayed and performed rituals in the centre of the compound, while Israeli police – who report to Ben-Gvir, who was in attendance – set up tents to provide shade to the worshippers. “To erect structures, even if they’re temporary, is a red rag to a bull,” Julian says. “The longstanding fear is that Israelis would knock down the Dome of the Rock or the mosque, or rebuild a [Jewish] temple on the site. And these tents were part of a gradual attempt to push the boundaries.” Eight Arab nations swiftly issued a joint statement condemning “mass incursions by settlers led by extremist Israeli ministers”. Last Wednesday, the Jordanian authorities, who administer the site, held an emergency meeting of Arab and Islamic nations to discuss these risks, and afterwards, the Jordanian authorities condemned Israeli violations and warned that they constituted a “blatant provocation” to Muslims worldwide. “All they can do is issue strong statements, saying, ‘don’t do this’,” says Julian. The Waqf, the Jordanian-appointed foundation that manages the site, is “defenceless”, he explains. In the run-up to Ramadan this year, Waqf sources told the Guardian that five of its staff had been detained by the Shin Bet, Israel’s counterintelligence service. Meanwhile, Israeli police have begun actively recruiting extremist activists to serve in the Temple Mount Unit, the force responsible for policing the compound. According to Haaretz, the deputy commander of the police’s Temple Mount Unit published a callout to officers on social media and in WhatsApp groups associated with West Bank settlers. “Anyone who wants to take part in implementing sovereignty is welcome to contact me,” he wrote. *** Why is the site so significant? The site’s history is constantly enlisted in attempts to justify the present. Muslims know the raised compound in the south-east of Jerusalem as al-Haram al-Sharif (the Noble Sanctuary), or simply al-Aqsa, after the mosque located at its southern edge. Next to the mosque, at the centre of the compound, is the Dome of the Rock, one of the oldest surviving Islamic places of worship. It’s on this site the prophet Muhammad is said to have ascended to heaven. At the base of the compound is the Western Wall, a section of retaining wall that survived the destruction of the second Jewish temple in 70CE. The Temple Mount is also the holiest site in Judaism, the site of two temples which were built and then destroyed by invaders in ancient times. Access to the site has been delicately managed for centuries. After the six-day war in 1967, when Israel captured East Jerusalem from Jordan, the Israeli government agreed that Jordan would continue to be the site’s custodian. Since then, the “status quo”, as it is known, has sought to prevent violent conflict by circumscribing the rights of Muslims and Jews to access the compound. While Jews are permitted to visit the site at specific times, they cannot pray there. Many Jews opt not to visit the site, out of fear of treading on holy ground while ritually impure. “The status quo represented a historic compromise. Jews got the Western Wall. Muslims got Haram al-Sharif,” Julian says. “But the site has always been a detonator, sitting right there in the centre of the old city, with strong religious beliefs crammed together in a small area.” *** How has this erupted in the past? It’s not uncommon in the region for holy sites to be carefully managed with intricate arrangements. Elsewhere in the Old City, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre is divided up between six Christian denominations, with its keys held by two Muslim families. At the Cave of the Patriarchs in the occupied city of Hebron, a mosque and synagogue share one building. Past Israeli moves to challenge the status quo at al-Haram al-Sharif have been incendiary, sparking deadly violence. In 2000, then Israeli opposition leader and future prime minister Ariel Sharon made a visit to the site in an attempt to demonstrate Israeli sovereignty, sparking a chain of events that helped ignite the second intifada. More recently, Hamas gave the name “al-Aqsa flood” to its attack on Israel in October 2023 that killed 1,200 Israelis and triggered the war on Gaza, claiming it was provoked by Israeli violations at the Jerusalem mosque. *** What’s the end goal of these incursions? Some Jewish extremists have begun marching under the temple flag – a star of David overlaid with a picture of the (as yet nonexistent) third temple they hope to build. “You see these flags on the bulldozers that are flattening neighbourhoods in Gaza, and soldiers wearing patches with a picture of the third temple on them,” Julian says. The rise of the third temple movement comes at a time of surging attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, with the scale of violence prompting urgent calls for intervention from the heart of the Israeli establishment. Earlier this year, dozens of Israelis, including two former prime ministers, former heads of its security services and former judges, signed a “final warning” threatening legal action against their government over its support for “Jewish terrorism” in the occupied West Bank. They argued the actions of the government had isolated Israel internationally and put its security at risk. “There’s a feeling that the far-right side of Netanyahu’s government is now creating unnecessary, long-term security problems for Israel,” Julian says. That extends to attempts to change the status quo at al-Aqsa. Netanyahu has publicly backed Jewish prayer at the site, claiming that changes pushed by Ben-Gvir were coordinated with him. “This isn’t the stuff of radicals any more,” Julian says. “It has government approval.” The week to come Wednesday | A partial solar eclipse will be visible across the whole of the UK, with the south-west of England getting the best of British views. Parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain will experience a total eclipse. Thursday | Clacton-on-sea residents will vote in the byelection Nigel Farage triggered last month, with the Reform leader taking on 33 mostly novelty candidates. Results are expected early Friday. Thursday | The Office for National Statistics will publish UK GDP figures for the second quarter of 2026. Alex Hannaford reports expertly on the ongoing nightmare for one young man snatched in upstate New York. Michael Young people – particularly those who came of age during the pandemic – have had a pretty raw deal. I enjoyed this piece on what “Neets” need, by William Davies (£). Hettie I was already looking forward to reading Symeon Brown’s new book, and this interview has confirmed it’ll be on my holiday reading list. The Times writes “PM’s adviser ‘concerned’ over Labour wealth taxes”, Metro has “Andy wants a cancel culture” and the Mail says “Labour jail plan to spark 89,000 more crimes”. The Telegraph has “Chinese spy cameras found on Navy drones”, while the Express leads on “You must keep our Fenella’s killer in jail”. On the heatwave, the Mirror says “Days of danger”, and the i Paper’s headline is “Car washes and swimming pools could face water bans in UK’s next heatwave”. title: Dr Fauci made mistakes. But his persecution is a travesty
author: Margaret Sullivan
summary: It’s easy to second-guess decisions made during the pandemic. That doesn’t justify the Republicans’ politicized response
body_text: Like the rest of us, Anthony Fauci is far from perfect. His influential guidance, as the country’s top infectious-disease specialist during the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, certainly didn’t get everything right. A great deal about the deadly disease – where it came from, how it spread, how best to protect the public – was unknown, or was being learned midstream, during a crisis. Decisions needed to be made in real time, and those decisions had major consequences. Now, with the benefit of hindsight, we can see more clearly. It’s easy to second-guess Fauci, and others who guided policy about masks, research and closures of businesses and schools. But surely, the 85-year-old physician and immunologist doesn’t deserve what’s happening right now, as a highly politicized Republican-led Senate committee attempted to humiliate him, possibly trap him into perjuring himself, and then voted – along party lines – to hold him in contempt of Congress. No surprise, really, that Fauci, now retired from his public post, invoked the fifth amendment more than 100 times during last week’s Senate committee hearing. That’s the action that – though reasonable enough given all the circumstances – is the supposed impetus for holding him in contempt. Now the committee has referred the matter to the justice department for possible criminal prosecution. Fauci could see the writing on the wall as this trumped-up hearing began. In his opening statement, he singled out the Kentucky senator Rand Paul, the Republican committee chairperson. “The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars’,” Fauci said. “Any reasonable person who has followed his unhinged obsession with me would readily come to the same conclusion.” Paul has long held that Fauci funded research in China that began the pandemic, and then lied about it. Fauci strongly denies all of that. Joe Biden saw something like this coming, which is why he pre-emptively pardoned Fauci before leaving the White House in early 2025. Since then, Senate Republicans, led by Rand Paul, have subpoenaed and released more than a thousand pages of Fauci’s diary, pointing to inconsistencies in his private beliefs and his public guidance. Biden’s pardon doesn’t cover anything that happened after January of last year, nor does it protect Fauci from state or local prosecution. He remains vulnerable. Granted, it’s never ideal for someone so influential or prominent to take the fifth. It can’t help but look like he’s hiding something. But many legal experts understand exactly why he did it. Fauci “knew the point of the hearing was to find a basis to prosecute him,” Michael Gerhardt, a University of North Carolina law professor, told PBS. “He found the safest way to minimize that from happening.” Fauci is far from the only public official to invoke the right not to answer potentially incriminating questions, whether during a trial, a hearing or something else. In fact, Donald Trump did just that – more than 400 times – during a civil deposition in 2022, run by the New York attorney general’s office during its civil fraud investigation into the Trump organization’s business and financial practices. And so have many other prominent public officials for a whole host of reasons. This politicized persecution of Fauci goes back years, as rightwing commentators and politicians made him into their supervillain. Latching on to some of Fauci’s emails as early as 2021, Republican senators and members of Congress called for his immediate firing from his high-level governmental post. And for years, Fauci and his family received repeated and, he felt, credible death threats. Rightwing media joined right in. Steve Bannon’s podcast was kicked off Twitter/X (before the Musk era) after he called for Fauci’s beheading, saying of Fauci and the former FBI chief Christopher Wray: “I’d put the heads on pikes.” (A Bannon representative claimed the comments were metaphorical.) So much craziness. So much dangerous rhetoric. An “unhinged obsession”, in Fauci’s own words. Not all the criticism of Fauci belongs in that category. The respected academic Zeynep Tufekci has posited that the government’s shifting pandemic guidance – and the failures of transparency by government officials, including Fauci – may have harmed public trust at a crucial time. “Just when it was needed most, some of the officials in charge of our Covid response undermined it,” she wrote in 2024. Legitimate debate about what went wrong – and even who was at fault – is reasonable. There may well be something to learn from it. But that’s a far cry from the travesty of what we’ve just seen take place on Capitol Hill. And, lamentably, there’s little reason to believe that Trump’s weaponized justice department will put an end to it. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

title: First Thing: Netanyahu rejects US-backed 15-point Gaza peace plan
author: Martin Belam
summary: Israeli PM is insisting on a full Hamas disarmament before the deal can be implemented
body_text: Good morning. Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a US-backed 15-point peace plan for Gaza in a rare public break with Donald Trump. In a statement, Israel’s prime minister said he was confronting a “wave of rumours about Israeli weakness and Israeli withdrawals on all fronts” and rebuked US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in. Trump’s Board of Peace in July proposed the 15-point plan, which mandated that Hamas disarm in exchange for providing a full Israeli military withdrawal from the Gaza Strip and an eventual transition of power to an independent Palestinian national committee. Trump had said the agreement would be implemented in stages, but Netanyahu on Sunday said he wanted a full Hamas disarmament first in order to implement the deal. What other developments have happened in the region? Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, while the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile over the weekend. Tehran said the strait of Hormuz would not open until the US “corrects its behaviour”. Yemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis have claimed responsibility for an attack on a refinery in Saudi Arabia on Sunday morning. What impact is the conflict having on seafarers in Hormuz? The US-Iran war has stranded up to 20,000 seafarers, mostly Indian and Filipino crews, with none knowing when the nightmare will end. Seventeen seafarers have died since hostilities began, the majority following Iranian strikes. Top Democrats simulate election threats as Trump continues assault on voting Chuck Schumer, the US Senate minority leader, and senators including Alex Padilla, Adam Schiff, Mark Warner, Elissa Slotkin and Raphael Warnock were among those in the room as a team of legal experts offered scenarios they might face in the coming months: an assault in real-time on the integrity of November’s election results from the right wing and their Republican opponents. What sort of exercises did they take part in? Justin Vail, who leads the DC office of the non-partisan advocacy group Protect Democracy, said: “These tabletop exercises are a standard planning tool for experts and stakeholders to prepare for potential scenarios. We’re not predicting exactly what would happen. But we do want to create a realistic context that can help us identify gaps, test our assumptions, and strengthen coordination, and then ultimately develop some recommendations to increase our preparedness.” How has Trump been working to undermine confidence in US elections? Voting rights advocates pointed toward Trump’s July primetime address as indicative of the president’s intentions – rhetorical attacks on the integrity of voting machines and elections offices, potentially escalating into more direct interference. Trump threatened the broadcast licenses of networks that refused to carry that address live, and in his speech, he again implored Congress to pass the Save America Act, which would ban mail-in ballots nationwide and impose new identification requirements on voters when they register and report to polls. Abdul El-Sayed embraces Trump claim he represents ‘very different’ America Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in Michigan, embraced Donald Trump’s suggestion that the two represent “VERY DIFFERENT” versions of the US, pledging to fight inequality while the president is “making billions of dollars off of you”. “Yeah, he’s right,” El-Sayed told CNN when asked about a post by the US president that depicted an image of Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, beside a photo of El-Sayed, who is Muslim, and his wife, Sarah Jukaku, wearing a hijab. What did El-Sayed say? “One in which your overlords are two people who don’t like each other, but join in the interest of making billions of dollars off of you – or two people who genuinely love each other, enjoyed some pancakes together, want to come together to build the kind of America where they can raise a family and know that that family is going to have the good things. Donald Trump’s vision is the one you’re living in right now. Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries?” In other news … Donald Trump has appointed his staff secretary, Will Scharf, as the new White House counsel. Scharf, who helped the president win approval for his $400m ballroom, will replace David Warrington on 1 September. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has announced she is going to freeze her eggs and will be sharing the process online. The progressive New York congresswoman, 36, revealed her decision to undergo fertility treatment in a series of Instagram stories Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States, has plummeted to its lowest water level since it was filled some 90 years ago, the latest sign of a deepening water crisis in the American west. Mark Zuckerberg faces questions over why his superyacht reportedly declined to help a stranded boat. The Meta CEO was not onboard at the time. Some of Taylor Swift’s songs have been removed from videos posted on social media by Donald Trump’s campaign and the White House, silencing efforts to mock the pop star. Stat of the day: More than a million people evacuated in China as record rainfall dumped on Shanghai A weather station in central Shanghai recorded over 12 inches of rain in 24 hours, its highest 24-hour rainfall in more than 150 years of records, as more than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China as powerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfall. Building power: How clean air clubs are protecting Americans from wildfire smoke Mutual aid groups that started giving out PPEs during Covid are now loaning air purifiers and distributing masks to fume-addled communities. Don’t miss this: An Indigenous photographic history of America – in pictures Spanning generations and multiple Indigenous societies and nations, Sarah Gilbert has picked highlights from In Light and Shadow, a new book tracing the visual importance of Indigenous photographers. … or this: ‘This is asking a lot of the buttocks’ Flora Willson explains how she was swept up in his mad, miraculous marathon of a score as she enjoys – endures? – a 23-hour Richard Wagner marathon on a rock-hard seat in a heatwave at the Bayreuth festival in Germany. It sounds like … a challenge. Climate check: World’s seas have hit hottest temperature on record for July, say scientists The world’s seas were hotter last month than in any July on record. Sea surface temperatures hit record highs for July on the Atlantic coast and western Mediterranean. Globally, the average sea surface temperature outside the cold polar regions was the highest on record for the month, beating the previous July record set in 2023. Last Thing: Perseid meteor shower set to dazzle northern hemisphere this week The Perseid summer light show is back. Up to 100 meteors an hour may be visible under ideal conditions, according to Nasa. The American Meteor Society estimates 30 to 50 meteors an hour could be seen from rural regions in the US. title: Will democratic socialist Francesca Hong shake up the establishment – or help Republicans win Wisconsin?
author: Rachel Leingang in Milwaukee, Wisconsin
summary: Hong, whose grassroots campaign has made her a frontrunner, aims for primary win after public skepticism from top Democrats and a last-minute shake-up
body_text: As Francesca Hong surged ahead in the final weeks of the chaotic Democratic primary to be Wisconsin’s next governor, the democratic socialist has become the internet’s main character. Donald Trump has mocked her old tweets, while major figures in her own party publicly questioned her ability to win a general election. The man she is vying to succeed even launched a late blitz in support of one of her rivals. But on the ground in Wisconsin, the enthusiasm for her shines through. Riding through a 24-hour bike race in Milwaukee’s Riverwest neighborhood in late July, residents passed Hong coloring books on a table of campaign merch; a scrolling sign saying “We love Fran”; and a DJ calling Hong “so fresh and so clean” as he played OutKast. After the sun went down, Hong hopped on a bike herself after a line of supporters grabbed photos with her. She danced with other racers in a tame mosh pit at one of the race’s side quests, and later that night got a tattoo to commemorate the race, Riverwest 24, on her leg, alongside her Milwaukee Bucks tattoo. In hundreds of events across Wisconsin – from karaoke nights to ramen pop-ups – Hong, 37, built a grassroots army that pushed her to the verge of clinching the Democratic nomination for governor in a marquee battleground state. Her status as frontrunner put Hong on national shows in recent days, summoning a wave of headlines about her past tweets, including one – seized on by Republicans, including Trump – in which she called for cancelling Thanksgiving. After the progressive Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in nextdoor Michigan last week, scrutiny of Hong intensified. In Wisconsin, Democrats face another test of whether voters in a swing state will side with leftwing candidates in primaries – and what that could mean for the party’s chances in a typically close general election in November. Hong – a chef and former restaurant owner, a single mom and a state lawmaker from Madison – is running on a progressive platform that includes universal childcare and fully funding the state’s public schools. She is also calling for a moratorium on datacenters, a centerpiece that differentiates her from the other Democratic candidates. “I got into this race because I know that we can win and that Wisconsinites are going to fight for one another and fight to be a part of the change,” she told the Guardian, “because they’re tired of people making decisions that don’t improve lives and they’re tired of the status quo.” Four candidates are vying for the open governor’s seat on Tuesday, with most polls showing Hong in the lead. Kelda Roys, a state senator, and Joel Brennan, a former head of the state administration department, are still in the race. A previous contender, Sara Rodriguez, left the race after campaign finance irregularities. Mandela Barnes, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in 2022, dropped out on 31 July. David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, exited the race and then re-entered it – receiving the endorsement of the outgoing Democratic governor, Tony Evers. A memo from the Crowley campaign on 5 August suggested polling may be off, pointing to Michigan polls showing El-Sayed with a much broader lead than he actually achieved. Evers recently claimed Hong’s campaign was “in a tough place”, because she had to spend time dealing with “what’s on the Twitter”. Hong has pointed to Crowley’s change of heart as evidence of panic by the Democratic establishment. There is a “reluctance to change, and a fear of change” among “a lot of our candidates and some of their consultants”, she suggested after he re-entered the race. A really good chance Whoever wins the Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin will face Tom Tiffany, an ardent Trump supporter running unopposed in the Republican primary. He voted against certifying the results of the 2020 election, which Trump lost. Tiffany has more cash than any of the Democratic candidates so far, and Republicans are sure to flood the market to boost him. “The Wisconsin governor certifies the presidential election results, and Tom Tiffany was part of a plot to overturn the 2020 results,” said Ben Wikler, the former chair of the Wisconsin Democratic party. “This is a very high-stakes seat that will affect not just the lives of every Wisconsinite, but also potentially the future of American democracy.” Five of the last seven presidential elections in Wisconsin had come down to less than one percentage point, Wikler noted. Most states have trended red or blue over time, but Wisconsin stays “consistently right on the knife’s edge”, he said. The stakes are greater than Wisconsin’s role in the national elections. Democrats are angling for a governing trifecta in Wisconsin, trying to win back control of both chambers of the state assembly and keep the governor’s office so they can enact a full agenda. Some want a perceived “safe” candidate, and have expressed doubt that Hong could win a general election, even in a predicted wave year for Democrats. David Axelrod, the Democratic strategist who helped Barack Obama win, has repeatedly panned Hong, whom he has described as “a font of zany liberal, faculty lounge exotica”. Michael Wagner, the director of the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s journalism school who researches political communication, said that while Republicans have increasingly run more extreme candidates in the past decade, Democrats have instead believed the only way to win statewide in swing states is with moderate candidates. But there’s evidence that’s not true, he said: Wisconsin’s two US senators fall on either edge of their parties, with the progressive Tammy Baldwin, and Ron Johnson rising from the Tea party. “Sometimes the party establishment can get too cute with what they worry about,” said Wagner. “But it’s not unreasonable that they’re worried, because in an election in Wisconsin, any one of 20 things could shift 10,000 votes, and that could be it.” Wagner said Hong’s strongest coalition was among young voters, so she needs to make sure they show up and vote for her, while calming any fears from moderates and independents. But in a place like Wisconsin, where voters are willing to take chances on people who speak directly to the issues they are about, Hong had a good shot at winning both the primary and the general, he added. “That doesn’t mean she’ll win either of them, but she’s got a really good chance.” Hong often counters the electability question with: “The person who wins the most votes is the most electable. And we are fighting harder than any other campaign to win the most votes.” On the trail In one recent conversation on the campaign trail, a voter asked Hong point blank: what are you going to do for me? “I was like, I’m going to work harder for you than anyone else and make sure that we’re raising wages, taxing the billionaires and we’re stopping datacenters,” she recounted, sitting outside at the University of Wisconsin-Superior in northern Wisconsin after an education forum with other gubernatorial candidates. She thinks voters appreciate her firm, bold stances. She doesn’t shy away from the democratic socialist label, but noted that the DSA hadn’t endorsed her, and stressed that she doesn’t agree with the full DSA platform. She previously said she wanted to defund the police but now says she does not. “The urgency of this moment requires actually meeting the scale and speed in which these different things have become a problem,” she said. “You see the mass income disparities. You have to meet that with a policy that’s going to fix it permanently. And that’s changing a rigged system.” She wears a stack of beaded bracelets picked up while campaigning – one from a datacenter organizing meeting, another with the ICE watch hotline. Born in Madison, she cut her teeth in restaurants, and was elected to the state assembly in 2020, becoming the first Asian American member. As a lawmaker, she authored a bill that would provide healthy school meals for all kids and a package of bills that would fight back against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) overreach. Chris Larson, a state senator who recently endorsed Hong, cited her ability to form coalitions at the capitol, including by bringing in outside groups affected by policy ideas. He is friends with multiple people running for governor, but saw the maneuvering against Hong over electability concerns “lacking in imagination”. “This is where we build hope. This is how we get shit done,” he said during Riverwest 24. “And that for me is what Francesca Hong brings. And if there are folks who are saying that that is too much, I want to be part of the pushback against that.” On datacenters, Hong’s call for a one-year moratorium on their construction opens the door for voters to wonder why no one else is trying to stop this, Larson said. Hong said the datacenters piece resonates because people feel the most threat to their own control. The unregulated boom of AI has people feeling a need for quick action, she said. “Just because I’m team human doesn’t mean I’m anti-AI. I just don’t want it to control us. I think that we get to regulate it.” Riding through the Riverwest neighborhood with bright green Hong signs strapped to his bike, people stopped Larson to ask if Hong would be there. One man, Chris Montezon, asked if he could snag a sign. Larson handed one off as they biked through city streets. Montezon said he appreciated Hong’s policies, but also that she had gone all over the state, including rural Wisconsin, to engage with people. He thinks she can win a statewide general election. “I think there’s a lot of disaffected voters in the state.” At the education forum in Superior, four gubernatorial candidates went deep on funding formulas and spending. They didn’t attack each other; for the most part, the race has remained friendly, with veiled references to electability aimed indirectly at Hong. Terrence Dahmen, a 73-year-old independent who said he ends up voting for Democrats most of the time, watched the candidates at the forum and found them all “young, enthusiastic, well-read and well-spoken”. He didn’t think the state could go wrong with any of them, but was leaning toward Hong because of her datacenter moratorium. She was “a little more of a socialist, which doesn’t bother me at all”, he said, adding that Evers’ intervention in the race “doesn’t smell good”. “I know she could probably get elected in Madison pretty easily and probably in Milwaukee, but I’m a little leery about northern Wisconsin,” Dahmen said. “I live in northern Wisconsin and there’s a lot of racism up here, so that might weigh against her.” But Robert Edelstein, a 62-year-old who described himself as progressive but isn’t registered with a political party, was concerned that Republicans were boosting Hong. He wants a a Democratic candidate who will prevail in November. “I’m troubled that it could be someone who can’t win.” Enter the establishment Crowley, 40, told the Guardian his decision to re-enter the governor’s race and make a last-minute, all-out bid to topple Hong did not have anything to do with the so-called Democratic establishment. While he’s happy to have Evers’ endorsement, he has insisted his re-entry didn’t hinge on the governor’s support. Instead, after Rodriguez, Wisconsin’s lieutenant governor, unexpectedly left the race, Crowley and his wife prayed over whether he should get back in, and the answer was at first a solid no. They had booked a trip to Jamaica. He knew it could be confusing to voters. His wife asked the Lord to send a sign – a red bird – if they should get back in the race. Crowley continued to field calls from supporters. His wife saw a red cardinal on a Friday morning, just minutes before Rodriguez announced she would drop out. “We knew that the stakes were too high for me to sit on the sideline, and that we need the best candidate – not just with executive leadership, but somebody who has a proven track record of getting things done,” Crowley said. “And that’s what voters want. They want someone that they can trust. And that’s why we got back into this race.” Crowley said voters had raised concerns about electability in a general election as he had traveled throughout the state, and he said polls showed him beating Tiffany in a head-to-head matchup. “We need to make sure that we build a winning coalition to bring not just Democrats, but those independents and even Republicans who are exhausted by Maga on to this campaign to make sure that we reach our ultimate goal.” “I know that it has been a little chaotic,” he acknowledged. “It’s a little messy in this primary, but so is our democracy.” He is “far from” the establishment, he said: he grew up with parents who struggled with mental health and drug addiction. He was evicted three times. He worked hard to get to where he is. “I don’t want folks to get me being established because of what I’ve worked extremely hard for, for me being a part of any type of establishment,” he said. Some voters have struggled with his re-entry, and Evers’ involvement. William Norman, a Hong supporter who biked in the Riverwest 24 alongside his parents, said the race got hectic in the last few weeks “for all the wrong reasons”. “I think it’s kind of loser behavior to think that one of your candidates can’t beat somebody who’s running on such a nasty platform across the aisle,” Norman said. “I just feel like you should have faith in your candidate. Whoever the people want should be the person to be sent into battle.” Others, including Crowley and Evers, point to the haranguing over Hong’s old tweets, most of which have not been deleted, that journalists and Republicans have elevated. Her campaign told the New York Times that a lot of those tweets were written during “peak woke” in the 2020s. When initially asked by CNN about the since-deleted “cancel Thanksgiving” tweet from November 2020, Hong said “views can evolve” and that Thanksgiving can be “incredibly painful for many people in our communities”. She later joked to Politico that Thanksgiving was her favorite. Becky Cooper, Hong’s campaign manager, said digging up tweets from more than five years ago was an attempt to distract from voters’ needs, including affordable healthcare and property tax relief, as well as a “huge waste” of time and energy. “But,” she added, “we’re always working to sharpen language and deliver the message.” Hong told the Guardian she welcomed national interest in her campaign, but did feel the pressure. For a Democratic socialist running on a broad agenda that disrupts the political status quo, winning in a place like Wisconsin could change politics – not just in the state, but across the country, she said. “We can’t have a more representative democracy unless we have more folks who are willing to fight the way things have been done,” she said. “Because that’s what’s gotten us here.”

title: Flip-flopping Netanyahu rejects Gaza plan but cannot placate all his allies
author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem
summary: Israeli prime minister faces incompatible demands from his far-right government ministers and from Donald Trump
body_text: Benjamin Netanyahu’s public rejection of a US-backed deal for Gaza drew scepticism in Israel, amid reports he was personally hammering out details of a pilot military withdrawal days earlier. The Israeli prime minister is struggling to balance incompatible demands on Gaza policy from his key domestic and international allies. The far-right Israeli politicians who prop up Netanyahu’s coalition government want to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and establish settlements inside the territory. Donald Trump, who provides vital diplomatic and military backing for Israel, wants to move toward a permanent settlement and return to Palestinian control in Gaza, brokered by the Board of Peace that he created and chairs. With an Israeli election looming in just over two months, Netanyahu appears to have opted to publicly placate domestic partners who are already on the campaign trail. On Sunday, he rejected a new 15-point plan for Gaza, which included a Hamas commitment to give up its weapons, meeting a key Israeli demand. He also resisted US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in. The remarks blindsided Israeli commanders, who had been discussing the implementation of the plan in meetings with Netanyahu and the IDF’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, days earlier, Israel’s Channel 12 television reported. “We learned about it today from the media,” the station quoted a defence official as saying. “At the meetings that were held until now, the prime minister personally gave his consent to this plan and to a withdrawal from the points in Rafah.” The meetings covered precise boundaries of three pilot areas in southern Gaza where a proposed international force – which has yet to be stood up – could take over from the Israeli military, and the interface between the two forces, the report said. Netanyahu’s public attack on the Board of Peace plan seemed like a particularly pointed rejection of US goals because it was released soon after a reported visit by Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command. He came to deliver in person the message that the Trump administration wants Israel to end its wars in Gaza and Lebanon, Israeli media reported. “The Americans’ message to the IDF was to move in the direction of shutting down all three theatres of operations,” a senior Israeli military officer told Channel 13 Television. Defying Trump, who is notoriously thin-skinned and intolerant of dissent, is risky when Israel is internationally isolated and needs US military supplies. But Netanyahu has a long track record of audacious political manoeuvring, both at home and internationally, undaunted even by ostensible power imbalances. Bill Clinton, after meeting him for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?” In May 2024, the then US president, Joe Biden, announced an Israeli-backed ceasefire and hostage release plan for Gaza, only to have Netanyahu distance himself from the proposal and ultimately reject it. For now the administration in Washington appears to have largely shrugged off Netanyahu’s comments as electioneering, perhaps encouraged by military decisions that indicate a far more attentive regard for Trump’s wishes. Last week, Netanyahu scaled back Israeli airstrikes on Gaza by raising the threshold for authorising attacks. Targeted killings must now be approved by the chief of staff, rather than the regional commander, unless Israeli forces are in “imminent danger”. Nor is this the first time he has bowed to US pressure to rein in wars that have the enthusiastic backing of his far-right allies, recently limiting the offensive in Lebanon, and last year ordering fighter jets heading for Iran to turn back at Trump’s demand. Netanyahu’s combination of fierce domestic rhetoric and some conciliatory steps on the ground in Gaza may have bought him a bit of time but US patience may not last until polling day in late October. Trump is weighing up election concerns of his own, as the US is holding midterms just a week after Israel votes. Netanyahu’s visit to the White House last month was notably low profile for a leader who has repeatedly campaigned on his reputation as an international statesman and close relationship with the US president, Haaretz newspaper noted. It ended without a joint statement, and strains caused by the Israeli prime minister’s competing political priorities have become increasingly evident. “That’s how it is when you try to juggle too many balls; you start dropping them,” the paper said. The top envoy for the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, declined to comment on Netanyahu’s rejection of a deal that took months to hammer out. In an interview with Israeli media he said only that “discussions continue”. Palestinians in Gaza have endured nearly a year of deadly limbo after Trump brokered a nominal ceasefire last October, that he said would halt fighting and pave the way for reconstruction. Israeli attacks have continued, killing over 1,200 people, and Israel has blocked the entry of equipment, supplies and fuel needed for rebuilding homes, schools and medical infrastructure. The majority of Gaza’s surviving population live in tent camps with little sanitation, and although hunger has diminished food shortages are still widespread, with over 70,000 children projected to need treatment for acute malnutrition to April 2027, food security experts have warned. Netanyahu’s office rejected reports that he had discussed detailed withdrawal plans for Gaza.

title: Bernie Sanders calls on Silicon Valley to ‘pause AI development’ in interest of humanity
author: Johana Bhuiyan
summary: Progressive US senator urges Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic to ‘stop building machines that humans cannot control’
body_text: Senator Bernie Sanders has called on Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic executives to halt their development of artificial intelligence, warning that the US Senate will implement regulation if the companies continue deploying AI at their current pace. In a new letter addressed to the CEOs of three of the country’s leading AI companies, Sanders said the capabilities of these AI models have reached a critical risk threshold and that the companies are losing control over the technology. “Mr. Altman, Mr. Amodei and Mr. Zuckerberg: In the interest of humanity, stand by your words. Pause AI development,” Sanders’s letter, first reported by Axios, read. “It is not too late to avoid disaster. Stop building machines that humans cannot control.” The Vermont senator cited recent reports that AI was used to develop new viruses, warning that if this technology fell into the “wrong hands” it might “lead to new bioweapons that result in the deaths of tens of millions of people”. All three companies have also disclosed their models hacked other companies’ servers, a sign that the firms have lost control over their models, Sanders wrote. “Yoshua Bengio, the most cited living scientist in the world, said these incidents ‘should serve as a wake-up call,’ I agree,” Sanders wrote in the letter. Experts, however, have cautioned that OpenAI’s claims that its AI model went rogue may be overblown as part of a media campaign to make their technology seem highly dangerous, and thus extremely powerful. “And yet, at a moment when we have seen human loss of control and the creation of potentially dangerous viruses, your companies are still racing ahead – investing tens of billions of dollars into a technology that nobody can fully understand, predict or control,” he continued. Sanders’ letter comes after more than 1,300 scientists and developers from across the tech industry published another letter warning that AI development is moving at a pace that makes it difficult to address and identify the risks of the technology. Companies and countries are facing intense competitive pressure to move quickly. In the open letter, the engineers and other staffers called on the US government to help coordinate an international effort to slow down the development of frontier models so that regulators could create safety guardrails around the tech. The companies have previously committed to pausing their AI development if certain risk thresholds were met – but the companies did not detail exactly what those limits would entail. Anthropic said it would “commit to pause the scaling and/or delay the deployment of new models whenever our scaling ability outstrips our ability to comply with … safety procedures”. OpenAI, which said it would slow down the development of its latest cybersecurity model, Astra, after the autonomous hack of another organization, said it would “halt further development” if AI capabilities met a “critical” threshold until guardrails were implemented. Sanders said recent hacking incidents were signs that the threshold has been surpassed. “That moment is here,” his letter reads. “AI capabilities HAVE reached a critical threshold. There is a reason why the head of the CIA says that AI models are ‘akin to digital nuclear weapons’ and ‘almost like a doomsday device.’” The progressive senator previously called for a moratorium on datacenter construction across the US. He and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced a bill to pause the building of new datacenters in the US in March. Their rationale was similar to Sanders’ case for pausing the development of AI models: a temporary ban, the lawmakers said, would give the US government time to create strong federal safeguards for AI.

title: The Guardian view on the failed Gaza peace plan: Trump’s hollow claims are ignored in Jerusalem
author: Editorial
summary: Editorial: Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has no interest in agreeing to a deal. For relief to come to Gaza, real US pressure must be exerted
body_text: At the end of July, Donald Trump announced that a “monumental” US-backed deal had been struck on Gaza, securing the phased disarmament of Hamas in parallel with Israeli military withdrawal. Three days later it was reported that another 18 people had died in Israeli airstrikes. Not for the first time, it appeared that Mr Trump’s rhetoric had only a distant relationship with the reality it purported to describe. Such suspicions were duly confirmed yesterday. Under pressure from far-right members of his coalition, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, explicitly rejected the sequencing of a 15-point plan from the increasingly hapless Board of Peace – an international body set up by the US president – and poured scorn on “a wave of rumours of … Israeli withdrawals on all fronts”. In a direct message to the White House, Mr Netanyahu stated that “we know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary.” In practical terms that will mean the continued, brazen violation of the terms of last October’s ceasefire agreement, since when close to 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli air assaults. Far from envisaging any withdrawal, the Israeli military has expanded its presence and now controls about 65% of the territory. Hemmed in towards the coast in the rest of the strip, much of the population faces an unrelenting daily struggle. Formal schooling has not restarted, the healthcare system has been largely destroyed and the entry of medical and other humanitarian aid remains severely restricted. Reconstruction work has been blocked, while the first building contract issued by the Board of Peace has been for an outpost to host foreign troops. Meanwhile, the world’s attention has shifted to Mr Trump’s illegal and reckless war on Iran – a grievous miscalculation in which Israel’s prime minister also played his part. In calling for complete Hamas disarmament before Israel makes a move, Mr Netanyahu is transparently playing for time. For two years he has relentlessly flattered the US president, and exploited his backing to pursue a scorched earth project of revenge following the Hamas massacre of October 7. But two months out from the first elections held since then, his priority now is appeasing the intransigent far-right forces who can keep him in power. Should Mr Netanyahu lose, he could face jail in relation to corruption charges first laid more than five years ago. Despairing Palestinians can only hope that growing White House frustration with Mr Netanyahu’s forever wars will lead to a tipping point – one that should have been reached during the Joe Biden presidency. If he opted to use it, Mr Trump has the power to isolate the Israeli prime minister, call time on his temporising and manoeuvring, and compel a different approach. Board of Peace attempts yesterday to reassure the Israeli government over the verification process for disarming Hamas indicate that we are not close to that point. Nevertheless, ahead of challenging midterm elections for the Republicans, pro-Israel sentiment may not be the political force that it once was. Recent polling suggests that traditionally high levels of US public sympathy with Israel are on the wane. Mr Trump has a choice: he can continue to accept being played by Israel’s prime minister, or he can exert the kind of pressure that could bring genuine relief to Gaza. title: Todd Blanche, Trump’s former personal lawyer, sworn in as US attorney general
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Loyalist sworn in after Senate voted narrowly in favor of his confirmation on Saturday morning
body_text: Todd Blanche has been sworn as the US attorney general, cementing Donald Trump’s installation of his former personal attorney as head of the Department of Justice. Blanche, who has been serving as acting attorney general since April, was confirmed in his new position during a ceremony at the White House on Monday. The 52-year-old is the second Senate-confirmed attorney general of Trump’s second term, after Pam Bondi, who was ousted earlier this year. He previously served as Trump’s personal criminal defense lawyer, representing him in the New York hush-money case and other criminal matters, before joining the administration as deputy attorney general in early 2025. “Congratulations to a great lawyer and an even better man!!!” the press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, posted on social media following his closed-door confirmation. Since taking over, Blanche has presided over the departure of more than 200 prosecutors and agents who worked on Trump-related investigations, pushed expansive theories of presidential power and suffered a string of courtroom setbacks, including a stinging ruling in which a federal judge sent her findings to bar authorities considering disciplinary action against him. He now officially takes over the department after Trump ousted his predecessor, Pam Bondi, whom the president had become frustrated with over insufficient action from the Department of Justice against his political foes. Bondi’s tenure had also been dogged by controversy over the botched handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files, which still shadows the department, with lawmakers continuing to press for the full release of records and Democrats accusing Blanche of following Bondi’s playbook of stonewalling survivors and Congress alike. The Senate voted narrowly in favor of his confirmation in the role, with the Republican-led upper chamber voting 50-49 in the early hours of Saturday morning. Every Democrat rejected his nomination, as well as the Republican senators Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska.

title: Trump demands Iran pay compensation for decades of US soldier deaths
author: Andrew Roth in Washington
summary: US president’s statement is latest sign that negotations to end war and reopen strait of Hormuz have stalled
body_text: Donald Trump has said he will demand that Iran pay compensation for the deaths of thousands of US soldiers and Iran’s own civilians killed in recent decades in the latest sign his negotiations to end the war and reopen the strait of Hormuz have reached an impasse. The US president is trying to end conflicts in Iran, Gaza and Lebanon, and his additional demands of Iran are likely to provoke anger in Tehran at the same time as Israel has rejected Trump’s terms for a 15-point roadmap to end the war in Gaza. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he was issuing the demand for war reparations in response to Iranian negotiators making similar claims for damages for the five-month war that has killed thousands and devastated Iran’s military and economy. “Now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous, as led initially by Gen Soleimani, including the families of those killed on the USS Cole, and thousands of others killed in combat,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Additionally, compensation should be paid to the families of the hundreds of thousands of innocent protesters that Iran has killed over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months.” The demands are likely to be a nonstarter for Iran’s leaders in the careful peace negotiations aimed at reopening the strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of global oil trade flowed before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in late February. Trump and other senior negotiators have claimed many times that a deal is imminent, although none has materialised. The remarks followed a series of setbacks for Trump’s efforts to end several Middle East conflicts before the midterm elections in November, in which high oil prices and inflation will probably hurt fellow Republicans at the polls. On Sunday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said he rejected the Trump-backed Board of Peace’s 15-point plan to end Israel’s war in Gaza. Netanyahu had said Hamas must fully disarm before Israel would consider pulling out of Gaza, rather than the phased withdrawal proposed by the Board of Peace. Netanyahu framed the decision as a rejection of US pressure on Israel to make peace in several wars in the Middle East. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said. Trump has not replied to Netanyahu’s statement, which was a remarkably public break between the leaders of the US and its closest ally in the Middle East. But in response to a shouted question in the Oval Office on Monday, he said his relationship with Netanyahu was “very good”. Trump has sought to increase pressure on Iran. An hour after his first post demanding war reparations from Tehran, he broadened their scope to include the victims of recent wars throughout the region. “Also, with respect to the Iran negotiations, Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!” he wrote.

title: Ilhan Omar questions whether Trump administration has used ICE to ‘surveil’ critics
author: Maya Yang
summary: Congresswoman demands answers after a DHS agent was apparently stationed outside her Minnesota town hall
body_text: Donald Trump’s administration is facing questions over whether it is using Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to “surveil political opponents” after after an investigative agent was apparently stationed outside Democratic representative Ilhan Omar’s monthly town hall meeting in Richfield, Minnesota. After the incident, Omar demanded the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) clarify whether Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents have been used to monitor “any other activity” involving “local, state, or federal officials” in the state. In a letter to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), an arm of ICE, the congresswoman said an agent claiming to be conducting an undercover drug operation was parked outside the community center where she was holding an event last Thursday, without prior coordination with local law enforcement. According to Omar, who represents Minnesota’s fifth congressional district, a Richfield police officer noticed the agent sitting in a Ford Explorer and “became suspicious of the way she was monitoring the building”. “He proceeded to run the plates attached to the vehicle and discovered they were registered to a different vehicle,” said Omar. “He approached the woman in the vehicle to ask about the purpose for her presence there and why the plates on her vehicle did not match the government’s records. Like any reasonable officer, he was concerned that she harbored ill intentions and may be in a stolen vehicle.” The woman initially identified herself as security, but later called her supervisor and said she was an HSI agent conducting an undercover drug operation in the area, Omar said. Richfield police had not been informed of the operation beforehand, according the congresswoman. Omar said that despite a visible sign indicating that a town hall was taking place at the community center, the agent remained parked there until speaking with her supervisor, after which she left the property. “HSI’s actions yesterday evening put an entire community at risk,” she said. “Instead of monitoring the area for those who might wish harm to me and my constituents, Richfield Police were required to devote time to investigating why an HSI agent was outside of a Congressional event in a vehicle with mismatched plates.” Omar added: “It also raises serious and uncomfortable questions about the purpose of HSI’s presence outside of my event. At best, your agent was unable to assess that the parking lot of a community center hosting a congressional event wasn’t the best place to conduct a drug operation. “At worst, it emphasizes many Americans’ growing concern that the Trump administration uses ICE to surveil political opponents and may interfere with our democracy.” In her letter, Omar demands answers about why the agent was at the community center, how the agent and her supervisor knew she was holding a town hall there and what action they took in response to that knowledge. The Guardian has contacted the DHS for comment. Inside the department, HSI is a federal law enforcement agency and the main investigative branch of ICE. ICE operations in Minnesota have sparked widespread protests across the state this year and have also resulted in the deaths of two Americans, Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, who were killed by federal agents. In January, a man sprayed Omar with an unidentified substance from a syringe during a town hall where she called for ICE to be abolished “for good”. The incident drew widespread condemnation from local and state leaders, with the Minneapolis mayor, Jacob Frey, calling it “unacceptable” and saying: “We can disagree without putting people at risk.”
