title: Tennessee set to execute man despite botched attempt on another prisoner
author: Sam Levin
summary: Darrell Hines’s lawyers ask supreme court to intervene, arguing he could face fate similar to failed execution in May
body_text: Tennessee is scheduled to execute a man this week despite bipartisan backlash after the state botched its previous lethal injection, which dragged on for more than an hour before it was canceled. Darrell Hines, who was convicted of the 1985 murder of Catherine Jean Jackson Jenkins, a motel maid and mother of four, is due to be put to death on Thursday. Hines’s lawyers have asked the US supreme court to intervene, arguing that he could face a fate similar to Tony Carruthers, who endured a prolonged, failed execution in May. Hines is one of three people slated to be executed on Thursday across the US as a handful of states continue to aggressively pursue capital punishment. Hines has maintained his innocence. Jenkins’s family has called on the execution to proceed. Tennessee’s execution procedures are shrouded in secrecy. It is unclear how the state acquires, maintains and administers its lethal injection drugs, and attorneys have long warned the lack of oversight could result in protracted, agonizing killings and botched procedures. On 21 May, during the failed execution of Carruthers, an IV team and a physician spent roughly an hour and 15 minutes struggling to establish an IV line to inject Carruthers with the lethal drugs, Maria DeLiberato, Carruthers’s attorney, said in a court declaration. The IV team pierced Carruthers all over his body more than a dozen times, causing him to groan in pain, said DeLiberato, senior counsel with the ACLU’s capital punishment project. In a declaration, DeLiberato recalled her client being strapped to an execution gurney as the doctor and others on the IV team tried and failed to locate veins in his arms, hands, feet and shoulder, and then could not establish a central line in his jugular. A warden eventually paused the execution, and Tennessee’s Republican governor, Bill Lee, granted Carruthers a one-year reprieve. When DeLiberato was able to see her client after the botched execution, she said, he was “sweaty, pale, tearful, and he seemed to be in shock and pain”. Hines is 66 years old, very thin, has suffered significant muscular atrophy after recent strokes and has stiffness in his arm that causes his hand to remain clenched in a fist – all factors that would make it challenging to establish an IV line, according to medical declarations filed by his lawyers. Kit Thomas, one of Hines’s attorneys, noted her client was generally bed-bound or in a wheelchair: “It’s grotesque. It’s particularly horrifying to think of them lifting a partially paralyzed man from his hospital bed, which he’s lived in for the last eight months, then strapping him to a gurney, while executioners attempt to establish IV access.” The names of officials carrying out executions are kept secret by state law, but the identity of a physician involved in Carruthers’s execution became public when a warden inadvertently disclosed it following another prisoner’s execution last year. That physician, Dr Mark Fowler, was subsequently deposed by death row attorneys. Under questioning, Fowler said the last time he had placed a central IV line was around 2013, the Guardian recently reported. The Tennessee supreme court recently denied Hines’s request to force the state to confirm whether Fowler would be involved in his execution. Fowler has objected to claims made by Hines’s attorneys that he was “unqualified” to perform executions. He declined to answer detailed questions from the Guardian, including about Carruthers’s execution, saying this was “a private situation. The inmate is entitled to privacy. The lawyers are churning up a lot of nonsense, and I don’t want to discuss it.” Hines’s attorneys have also raised concerns about the management by Frank Strada of Tennessee’s department of correction, which oversees executions. Strada previously served as a deputy director of Arizona’s corrections department. Arizona conducted three executions during Strada’s tenure, which Hines’s lawyers said in a statement to reporters were all “marked by prolonged and problematic attempts to establish IV access”. The attorneys have pointed to a 2023 court declaration from Ryan Thornell, Arizona’s corrections director, who said his review of execution procedures identified “several critical issues”, including “inadequate knowledge and expertise” of staff involved in executions, concerns about the efficacy of the lethal injection drugs and concerns about the IV team’s procedures. In Arizona, Strada oversaw prison operations and supervised the assistant director managing executions, according to the Tennessean newspaper. One of the three executions took 40 minutes, according to the man’s attorney, and in two of the killings, staff cut open the prisoners’ groins to insert catheters after they failed to insert IVs into their arms. In June, nine Republican state senators in Tennessee who support the death penalty wrote to the governor condemning Carruthers’s botched execution. They urged an independent review of what went wrong, including an accounting of whether staff were qualified to perform the procedures and “independent testing” of the execution drugs, saying deficiencies should be corrected before the state attempted another execution. Lee, the governor, has declined to pause executions and has denied Hines’s clemency petition. Hines’s attorneys have also asked Tennessee corrections officials whether staff have confirmed the execution drugs to be used Thursday were not expired, and whether officials had done quality-control testing and ensured the drugs were properly stored and handled. The state has not responded to the lawyers’ questions. Spokespeople for the governor, Tennessee’s corrections department and attorney general’s office did not respond to inquiries about Strada, Fowler and the other concerns raised by Hines’s lawyers. Thomas said she was worried about the “pain, suffering and [humiliation]” Hines could endure through another prolonged, botched execution: “The trauma that such an event will inflict on everyone in the execution chamber is really unimaginable.” On Thursday, executions are scheduled in Oklahoma and Alabama.

title: David Crowley wins Democratic primary for Wisconsin’s governor in upset over progressive Francesca Hong
author: Rachel Leingang
summary: Crowley pulls off last-minute victory in tight race after polls had shown Hong as the clear Democratic frontrunner
body_text: David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, won the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor after beating the democratic socialist Francesca Hong in a tight contest. Crowley pulled off a last-minute victory in the critical swing state after re-entering the campaign and snagging an endorsement from Tony Evers, the outgoing governor. With most votes counted, Crowley had 39.8% of the vote, ahead of Hong’s 39.4%, according to the Associated Press: a lead of just more than 3,000 votes. The race came down to the wire, with Hong and Crowley running close to each other as each batch of results came in. Polls had shown Hong as a clear frontrunner during the campaign, but with large chunks of voters still undecided and an ever-changing field of candidates, polling was difficult. Polls in Michigan had similarly shown the progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed with a more sizable lead than he ended up with in his victory in the Democratic primary for US Senate. Hong, a chef and former restaurant owner from Madison, ran on a platform that included childcare for all, free school meals and a one-year moratorium on the construction of new datacenters, which differentiated her from her Democratic colleagues in the governor’s race. Crowley welcomed those who voted for Hong in Tuesday’s primary to join him in the lead-up to November’s general election. “I look forward to earning their support,” he told reporters. While the messy Democratic primary has been branded as a “battle between the left and the center”, Crowley argued this was an inaccurate characterization. “We may not agree on every policy,” he said. “We may not use the same labels, but we all want safe communities, strong schools, affordable healthcare, good-paying jobs, and a brighter future for all of our children. “Every one of us has something much bigger to unite around, and that is keeping Maga extremism from bringing the chaos we see in Washington into our neighborhoods right here in the state of Wisconsin,” said Crowley. Evers, a Democrat who has served as Wisconsin’s governor since 2019, did not seek re-election. He endorsed Crowley, who re-entered the race after leaving it earlier in the cycle. Evers hailed Crowley as “the future of our Party” in a social media post overnight. “For now, we polka,” he said. “Tomorrow, we’re back at work to win.” In a statement on Wednesday morning, Hong congratulated Crowley and said she would support him in the general election. “The last 11 months have been one of the greatest joys of my life. Traveling the state, meeting people in churches and dive bars and bike races and dance parties and in their homes, and hearing about what matters most to them informed every decision we made on the trail,” she said. “It will continue to inform the work we do – and ask our supporters to do – moving forward. “This campaign was not about getting one person into office. It is about a building movement for permanent affordability and a government that puts working people first. Our movement is strong and the work isn’t done. I am overwhelmingly proud of our team and the work they have done to achieve that goal.” Crowley’s pitch to voters in the waning weeks of the campaign was electability: he felt he was more poised to win against Tom Tiffany, a Republican congressman and ardent Trump supporter who ran unopposed in the Republican primary. Tiffany voted against certifying the results of the 2020 election, which Trump lost. Crowley previously told the Guardian: “We knew that the stakes were too high for me to sit on the sideline, and that we need the best candidate, not just with executive leadership, but somebody who has a proven track record of getting things done. And that’s what voters want. They want someone they can trust. And that’s why we got back into this race.” Hong’s previous statements had dragged her down in recent days, including past support for defunding the police and a tweet calling to cancel Thanksgiving, which she had since retracted. She had previously vowed to use her grassroots network built during the primary to aid whoever won. Kelda Roys, a state senator, and Joel Brennan, who previously led the Wisconsin department of administration, rounded out the Democratic field. There were entries and exits from the chaotic race in recent weeks. A previous top contender, Sara Rodriguez, left the race after campaign finance irregularities, after which Crowley re-entered the race, with Evers’ backing. Mandela Barnes, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in 2022, dropped out on 31 July. The Wisconsin governor’s race became the latest test of the progressive wing of the party’s durability with Democratic voters in the midwest, after Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan last week. Next door, Minnesota voters were also weighing a US Senate primary between a moderate and a progressive. Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, won the Democratic primary for Senate over Congresswoman Angie Craig. The midwest primaries came after a wave of wins of progressives and Democratic socialists in solidly blue parts of the country. Democrats in Wisconsin are angling for a governing trifecta, trying to win back control of both chambers of the state assembly and keep the governor’s office so they can enact a full agenda. The governor’s race is expected to draw huge money and attention – Wisconsin is a close state for most statewide elections, and its voters are known to swing in either direction depending on the candidate or platform. Elsewhere in Wisconsin, voters in the western part of the state chose Rebecca Cooke, a blue dog Democrat, to advance and face the Republican Derrick Van Orden in the third congressional district, a key pickup opportunity for Democrats. Cooke previously ran for the seat in 2022 and 2024, coming close to Van Orden. Emily Berge, a former Eau Claire city council president, ran against Cooke. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee endorsed Cooke, which angered some local Democrats who saw it as interfering in a primary. Berge’s momentum, amid a wave of anti-establishment sentiment, had other national groups spending to boost Cooke, who they believe is better placed to win the district.

title: Trump sued over $100,000-a-month early-access offer to Truth Social posts
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Suit alleges subscription offer aims to sell privileged access to information generated in president’s official capacity
body_text: Donald Trump has been sued after a subscription service charging up to $100,000 a month for early access to his posts on his Truth Social platform sparked allegations of corruption. The lawsuit, filed in the US district court for the southern district of New York, was brought by the Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation against Trump, two of his aides and the executive office of the president. It targets “Truth API”, a paid data feed launched on 1 August by the Trump Media & Technology Group, the company behind Truth Social. The complaint calls the arrangement “extraordinary, corrupt and unconstitutional”. The service gives paying subscribers faster access than the general public to posts from 10 of the platform’s highest-profile accounts, including Trump’s own account, as well as those of the vice-president, JD Vance; press secretary, Karoline Leavitt; and other senior officials. Subscribers pay $100,000 a month, or $60,000 a month for a three-year commitment. The White House and Trump Media did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit. Trump has a history of using Truth Social to disclose market-sensitive news, including posts on tariffs and the war on Iran, which have triggered swings in stock and oil prices. Trump Media’s interim chief executive, Kevin McGurn, has even promoted the service as a way to give businesses fast access to the platform’s “most market-moving” posts. He has described it as a “high-margin” product meant to provide a “meaningful, ongoing source of revenue”. The launch followed criticism from the Democratic senators Adam Schiff and Elizabeth Warren, who had urged the Securities and Exchange Commission to examine whether the service amounted to market manipulation benefiting insiders at ordinary investors’ expense. According to the complaint, Trump Media disclosed on 10 August that it already had more than 10 subscribers, reportedly including financial news outlets and high-frequency trading firms, and was exploring licensing the data to prediction markets while working to block third-party tools that let outside groups scrape and archive Trump’s posts. The plaintiffs argue that the president, who remains Trump Media’s largest shareholder, with a stake worth roughly $1bn, stands to personally profit from selling privileged access to information generated in his official capacity. The suit also raises concerns about the historical record. Truth API subscribers get access to an archive of posts stretching back to 2022, including ones later deleted or altered, while McGurn has said the company intends “to create a lot of friction for those folks that aren’t coming to us directly”. The plaintiffs are asking the court to declare the arrangement unlawful and to bar the administration from relying on Truth Social as the exclusive venue for official announcements while it sells preferential access to that information.

title: What can we learn from Francesca Hong’s loss in Wisconsin?
author: Ben Davis
summary: A fairly overtly radical socialist winning about 40% of the vote in a primary like this was unthinkable even a few years ago
body_text: The left’s insurgency against the Democratic party establishment has hit its first serious bump in the road in Wisconsin. Democratic socialist Francesca Hong entered Tuesday up by big margins in the polls, the huge betting favorite. She left it just a few thousand votes short of the Democratic nomination. What happened, and how, offers extremely important lessons for both the left and the Democratic establishment. The first is that the party still matters. Its institutions and leaders matter. We saw that power in Democratic primaries in 2020. After Bernie Sanders won the Nevada caucuses and emerged as the frontrunner, party leaders rapidly consolidated around Joe Biden. Pete Buttigieg and Amy Klobuchar dropped out and endorsed him, and within days Biden went from trailing badly to winning majorities of the Democratic vote across much of the country. It was a stunning demonstration of the power of the party, its institutions and its elites to signal to voters who the party’s candidate was and rapidly consolidate support around him. The same basic thing happened here. For all the talk of the party’s discredited and elderly establishment, the party can still move enormous numbers of voters. Sure, it has lost some legitimacy in the eyes of Democratic voters. But a majority of Democrats in most places still like the Democratic party and trust many of its leaders. This is how, in the span of a month, David Crowley went from licking his wounds after dropping out of the race to being the Democratic nominee for governor of Wisconsin. Governor Tony Evers and other party leaders were able to send a strong signal to voters who trust them and the institutions they represent that Crowley was the party’s candidate and the best vehicle for continuing Democratic governance in the state. Years of organizing and ground game, and even a well-developed socialist base, were enough to bring Hong within a few thousand votes of winning statewide. But they were not enough by themselves to withstand a rapid consolidation among Democratic voters outside the left’s organized base. The Democratic party establishment is not as hollow and desiccated as it sometimes may appear. It is still one of the strongest political forces in the country. Second, the left needs to address the problem of scale. It has built powerful political machines in many urban quarters, built on door-knocking and tight social connections. But that is not enough to win at a statewide scale. This form of organizing has built a deep base for the left, but still a narrow one. To win across an entire state, especially a swing state, the left needs to learn statewide mass communication. Many on the left scoff at TV ads and other traditional political strategies they view as padding the pockets of consultants and forgoing the base-building, on-the-ground, roll-up-your-sleeves hard work that builds political organization. But these tactics are used because they work. They reach voters outside community networks and social media, including hundreds of thousands of voters who may have little connection to organized politics at all. To win these races, the left has to build its own knowledge and expertise in television, paid digital, earned media, opposition research, rapid response and message discipline. The left also needs to reckon with the fact that it is now taken seriously as a threat. Candidates and organizers used to operating at a local level are now facing national scrutiny, opposition research, hostile interviews and an unforgiving media ecosystem. The left may take some of these attacks as bad faith, the product of a media apparatus that defaults to the status quo. This may be true, but it is an obstacle that cannot be avoided. The left needs to be better at communicating through a hostile media ecosystem and at translating principle into concrete, defensible policy. The tactics and rhetoric that work with the left’s social base do not necessarily translate to the median voter, even the median Democratic primary voter. Hong’s defeat may have been shocking and disappointing, but it still represents a meaningful gain for the growing left. If, when Hong announced her campaign as a virtually unknown state legislator, an observer had been told that she would get about 40% of the vote in the gubernatorial primary, most would have seen that as a surprisingly positive result against many better-known and better-funded rivals. The left has built a social base among a rising class fraction at the heart of the postindustrial economy: teachers, nurses, social workers, researchers, public and non-profit workers, and other skilled wage earners who possess substantial education and organizational capacity but lack capital, accumulated wealth or authority over other workers. Many earn decent salaries but remain renters deep into adulthood, carry substantial debt and find themselves unable to accumulate the property and economic security once associated with professional employment. They are workers central to the institutions and industries that increasingly organize American economic life, and an increasingly central part of the Democratic coalition itself. Over the past decade, these shared conditions have helped make democratic socialism one increasingly coherent political expression of this class fraction. And the left has also grown beyond this base, winning over segments of other classes. But it still does not command a majority of the Democratic party, just a substantial stratum within it. The traditional institutions of the party – elected officials, editorial boards, churches, unions, non-profits and more – still retain credence with broad sections of the Democratic electorate whom the socialist left does not yet organize, even as many of those institutions have slowly hollowed out and lost power. But the establishment should not rest on its laurels. The left continues to grow and advance, and represents a growing segment of the electorate and a key strategic segment of the economy. The voters who first voted for Bernie in their 20s now have kids and are moving into their 30s and 40s without necessarily leaving their politics behind. A fairly overtly radical socialist winning about 40% of the vote in a primary like this was unthinkable even a few years ago. Even as Hong lost, in neighboring Minnesota, progressive Peggy Flanagan won the nomination for Senate by a wide margin over a much better-funded opponent. The left is still a minoritarian force even within the Democratic electorate. As its ambitions have grown, so have its losses. There are many lessons yet to learn if the left wants to turn a substantial minority into a democratic majority for egalitarian governance. Ben Davis works in political data in Washington DC. He worked on the data team for the Bernie Sanders 2020 campaign and is an active member of the Democratic Socialists of America

title: Karoline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary, Trump says
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: US president announced departure on social media, saying Leavitt was leaving to ‘spend more time’ with family
body_text: Karoline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary at the end of August, Donald Trump announced. The US president revealed her departure on social media, saying Leavitt was leaving “so she can spend more time” with her family. The 28-year-old gave birth to a daughter, Viviana, in May, and returned from maternity leave last month. The departure of Trump’s most prominent spokesperson comes with his approval rating at a historic low as voters express discontent over rising prices and a war in Iran that has no end in sight. Trump said Leavitt, who became the youngest person to serve as White House press secretary on his return to office in January 2025, “will now be one of my top outside advisors” in a post on his Truth Social platform. Leavitt wrote on X: “The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary – and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life.” Leavitt served Trump as a press aide during his first term in the White House. She ran for Congress in 2022 as the Republican nominee for New Hampshire’s first congressional district but lost the race. She joined Trump’s 2024 campaign and was transition spokeswoman before Trump selected her to ‌be White House press secretary. At 27 she was younger than Ronald Ziegler, who was 29 when he was Richard Nixon’s spokesperson. A devout Christian, Leavitt, wearing a cross necklace, and her team would hold a short group prayer before she walked into the briefing room to face reporters. The briefings rarely strayed off message or made headlines but did keep factcheckers occupied. For example, her claim that “tariffs are a tax cut for the American people,” was rated false by Politifact. In a smooth delivery with few verbal stumbles, Leavitt zealously defended the president while berating Democrats and the “fake news” media. In her first appearance on the podium, she described Trump as “the hardest-working man in politics” with “wildly popular” policies responsible for a new “golden age”. Leavitt was cordial with reporters behind the scenes but could be combative in front of the camera. In January this year, when a journalist raised the killing of Renee Good by an ICE agent in Minneapolis, Leavitt demanded to know why Good had been killed. The reporter answered: “Because an ICE agent acted recklessly and killed her unjustifiably.” Leavitt, jabbing her finger, snapped: “You’re a leftwing hack. You’re not a reporter. You’re posing in the room as a journalist … You shouldn’t even be sitting in that seat.” Trump often praised Leavitt as an effective communicator and drawing attention to her appearance. He once told the Newsmax network: “She’s become a star. It’s that face, it’s that brain, it’s those lips – the way they move, they move like she’s a machine gun.” On Wednesday the president’s allies joined the acclaim. Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, tweeted: “Karoline Leavitt has served President Trump and the American people with courage and conviction. She’s a great colleague, a fearless voice for the President’s agenda and a true professional.” Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, added: “Karoline Leavitt has been the most successful Press Secretary in history. Always strong, clear and right to the point … We are all Karoline Leavitt fans!” Democrats, however, took a different view. Adam Schiff, a senator for California, posted: “Karoline Leavitt is leaving the White House to spend a little more time … with the truth.” Trump did not outline plans for who might succeed her. He had four press secretaries during his first term. Sean Spicer is now a political commentator and podcaster; Sarah Huckabee Sanders is now the governor of Arkansas; Stephanie Grisham is now a fierce critic of Trump who spoke at the 2024 Democratic national convention; Kayleigh McEnany is a host on Fox News.

title: Wisconsin Democrats chose a middle path – will it lead to victory in November?
author: Rachel Leingang
summary: Democratic socialist Francesca Hong fell just short as David Crowley strives for unity for the general election
body_text: Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, was on course to win the party’s nomination for Wisconsin governor on Wednesday by a clear margin, according to the polls – presaging the latest in an extraordinary wave of leftwing victories across the country, challenging the party’s establishment. It was not to be. In a photo finish after a messy campaign, David Crowley eked out a win by a few thousand votes over Hong, raising questions over the limits of the progressive movement that has swept through Democratic contests in recent months. Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, had exited the race in early July, only to re-enter late in the month, with the backing of the outgoing Democratic governor, Tony Evers. The two barnstormed the state, consolidating support from a more moderate chunk of undecided voters, many of whom believed Crowley would more easily win November’s general election over Tom Tiffany, the Republican. The stakes for the governor’s race are high, both locally and nationally. Tiffany voted against certifying the 2020 election, and Wisconsin is a key part of the presidential electoral map. And Democrats want a governing trifecta after years of a split government so they can enact a more expansive agenda. Those high stakes resonated with voters in a place where statewide elections are frequently decided by decimal points. Hong was seen as more of a gamble – and it didn’t help that when some voters just started paying attention, they found headlines focused on old tweets about canceling Thanksgiving or defunding the police, putting Hong on the defensive. “So those were the first things some people learned about her, while the first thing they learned about Crowley was that Governor Evers endorsed him,” said Michael Wagner, the director of the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s journalism school, who researches political communication. “I don’t think it was a huge effect, but it didn’t need to be.” Crowley, 40, became the first Black person to hold the role of Milwaukee county executive in 2020, just a decade after conservative Scott Walker, who would go on to become governor and dismantle workers’ rights, held the same role. “Now that this primary has come to a close, allow me to reintroduce myself,” Crowley told a cheering crowd after his win on Wednesday morning. “My name is David Crowley. I am a son of Milwaukee. I’m a community organizer by heart who has just happened to find themselves in the halls of the state capitol building, at the head of Milwaukee county government for the last six years.” ‘We have to take these people seriously’ While the results of a single race should not be overread, Hong’s loss is not an outright rebuke of a growing progressive movement, but more a sign that a democratic socialist can mount a serious race – even in a midwestern swing state. In prior years, she might have finished in third or fourth place, rather than become the clear frontrunner. “If folks overlook the growing power of people like Hong supporters, they will be doing a disservice to themselves and to the work ahead,” said Joe Zepecki, the Wisconsin Democratic consultant. “And we have to take these people seriously. We have to find space for them in the pro-democracy movement and in Democratic campaigns. It is the only way to build an enduring majority.” Hong threw her support behind Crowley on Wednesday morning. She had previously vowed to use the grassroots movement she grew statewide to help whoever won the Democratic nomination. The Democratic gubernatorial candidates had brunch together, in a show of unity. Their work now shifts to November, and defeating Tiffany, who quickly tried to tie Crowley to Hong and her “socialist agenda”. There were strong paths to victory in a general for both Hong and Crowley, Zepecki said. For Hong, it was turning out younger voters or those disaffected by the Democratic party. For Crowley, it’s more about reaching independents and moderate Republicans, while bringing in Hong’s enthusiastic primary voters. But the headwinds against Republicans are strong, and Tiffany’s lockstep alignment with the Trump administration will probably haunt him on the campaign trail. Crowley, although backed by figures in the Democratic establishment, has bristled at the suggestion that he is an establishment candidate. “He’s just somebody who’s going to win people over once you meet him in the room,” said Dan Shafer, a Wisconsin journalist who runs the local publication the Recombobulation Area. “And I think once he was actually able to get out and do that a little bit more, he found some real success with it.” Polls of the race showed Hong with a runaway lead. They failed to detect Crowley’s surge back into the race. Chaz Nuttycombe, a pollster and executive director of State Navigate, which polled on the Wisconsin race, said he talked to a number of people in the polling industry after polls in Michigan overestimated the margins for Abdul El-Sayed. He said Hong voters were more enthusiastic about responding to the polls, and such a response bias was impossible to correct. Hong, a democratic socialist, finished half a percentage point away from winning a Democratic primary in a battleground state. Time will tell whether this was the high-water mark of progressive performance in Wisconsin – or the precursor to a future victory. In neighboring Michigan, El-Sayed’s victory in last week’s Democratic primary for US Senate came eight years after his defeat in the race for state governor. “This is a minor setback for DSA,” said Robert Lasica, the communications coordinator for the Madison Area Democratic Socialists of America. “But we have a lot of good momentum coming out of this, and we have a lot of good debriefing to do going forward.” The Madison chapter has seen its numbers grow with Hong’s campaign, and her race was the biggest project it had undertaken, he said. Her razor-thin loss shows that people want “big, significant changes” to the status quo, because it isn’t working for most people, Lasica said. ‘This is going to be a tough fight’ For now, Lasica said, most of Hong’s supporters are likely to support Crowley in the general, knowing the value a Democratic trifecta in state government could bring for material improvements in people’s lives. Election prognosticators adjusted their ratings after Crowley’s victory. Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved it from a tossup race to lean Democratic. Shafer, though, cautioned that the governor’s race will probably be close, as they often are in Wisconsin. “This is going to be a tough fight for David Crowley. It would have been a tough fight for Francesca Hong,” he said. “I get the whole national environment, the generic ballot, polling, all of those different things. But Wisconsin is always going to be a close race in a fall election.” Crowley was at work on Wednesday morning to define Tiffany as a Maga extremist who did not care about the people of Wisconsin. The framing of the primary election – as between the left and center, or progressives and the establishment – missed the point, he said, as people struggle to afford childcare, run their small businesses and grapple with wages lagging the cost of living. “From the very first day that I announced this campaign, I said the real threat wasn’t any of my primary opponents,” said Crowley. “The real opponent has always been Tom Tiffany. That remains true today.”

title: Australia’s largest aluminium smelter to run on renewables by 2033 after Rio Tinto strikes $2.5bn taxpayer bailout deal
author: Adam Morton
summary: Rio Tinto makes power supply deal with federal and NSW government to cut emissions and decarbonise, preventing potential closure
body_text: Resources giant Rio Tinto says Australia’s largest aluminium smelter will run entirely on renewable energy by 2033 after it struck a $2.5bn subsidy deal with the federal and New South Wales governments to prevent a potential closure. The deal – announced by Anthony Albanese and the NSW premier, Chris Minns, at the Tomago smelter near Newcastle on Thursday – is for a 10-year below-market power supply guarantee that begins after the facility’s existing coal-focused electricity contract with AGL ends in December 2028. The governments said the deal would underpin nearly 3,000 megawatts of new renewable and “firming” capacity in the state, more than a giant coal station. Rio Tinto, a joint owner of the smelter, said it meant by 2033 the smelter would run on clean energy only and cut its annual greenhouse gas emissions by 7.1m tonnes a year, equivalent to 1.5% of Australia’s annual climate pollution. In a statement, Rio Tinto Aluminium and Lithium’s chief executive, Jérôme Pécresse, said the smelter had a pathway to “long-term, cost-competitive, low-carbon power”. The deal is the latest in a series of Albanese government bailout packages meant to ensure major industries keep operating. Other commitments include $2bn for Rio Tinto’s Boyne aluminium smelter in Queensland and $2.4bn for steelworks in the South Australian town of Whyalla. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Aluminium production is particularly vulnerable to rising power prices due to its huge electricity use, and the Australian industry has for decades relied on cheap long-term supply deals. Tomago is the country’s largest single electricity user, taking more than 10% of total generation in NSW. It directly employs about 1,000 people, and is claimed to indirectly support about 5,000 more. The smelter’s owners committed to invest $1.1bn in Tomago over the next 12 years, including $100m for “decarbonisation activities”, as part of the deal. The federal climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, said Tomago Aluminium had told the governments that the smelter could no longer rely on coal-fired power and did not have confidence that enough renewable energy was being built to keep it operating. “We agreed … and so we worked on a very innovative arrangement together with New South Wales, working with our government agencies, Clean Energy Finance Corporation and Snowy Hydro, to bring on that renewable energy,” he said. Bowen said the renewable energy developments would not all be in the Hunter Valley, and would be “spread predominantly out through New South Wales”. “It will take projects which have been worked on in the pipeline that maybe have already received environmental approval, but haven’t reached final investment decision,” he said. “Some will be windfarms, others will be solar backed by batteries.” Minns said the deal was vital to the local and broader economy. “The truth of the matter is we couldn’t have a situation where that level of economic stimulus is withdrawn from an economy like that,” he said. “If you look at the Liberals in South Australia or the Democrats in Michigan, they presided over the deindustrialisation of those regions. We are never going to do that for the Hunter.” The federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said he did not oppose the deal, but its cost was a “$2.5bn admission of failure on energy policy” caused by “Labor’s net zero wrecking ball” pushing up electricity prices. Analysts say the increases in power bills in recent years have largely been due to external events, including Russia’s invasion of Ukraine pushing up the cost of fossil fuels globally, not the 2050 national net zero emissions target introduced by the Morrison Coalition government and continued under Labor. They say firmed renewable energy is the cheapest generation available to replace the ageing coal-fired power grid, but have expressed concern about delays in building windfarms and transmission lines. The independent MP Nicolette Boele blamed the cost of the deal on the failure of successive governments to act over the past decade, despite knowing Tomago’s power contract ended in 2028. She said evidence showed aluminium production succeeded “where clean power is cheap and steady”, citing Canada, Norway and Iceland as countries that run smelters on hydro and geothermal energy and were winning market share because of it. “Australia has better sun and wind than any of them and yet we are buying our way out of a shortage instead of selling into a strength,” Boele said. The Greens senator Penny Allman-Payne said the government should have taken a stake in Tomago as part of the deal to ensure Australians “share in the wealth from our own resources and give workers the security they deserve”.

title: Trump administration accused of ‘bullying’ union leader at consumer protection agency
author: Michael Sainato
summary: Critic of Consumer Financial Protection Bureau leadership was put under investigation and suspended from job
body_text: The Trump administration has been accused of “bullying and intimidation” after a labor union leader and critic was put under investigation and suspended from his job at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). Stephen Wheeler, a data scientist at the agency since 2022 and chair of the CFPB union organizing committee, was placed on administrative leave effective immediately earlier this month. The union said it was not provided with any specific violations or given any details of the investigation. The CFPB – conceived by the Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren to protect consumers after the 2008 financial crisis – has long been a target of Republicans. When Donald Trump appointed Russell Vought, architect of the rightwing manifesto Project 2025, to oversee the agency last February, Elon Musk posted, “CFPB RIP,” on X. The labor union representing workers at the agency, the National Treasury Employees Union Chapter 335, noted that Wheeler had been a vocal presence at union pickets, sitting behind Vought during his testimony in Congress in July, and had recently spoken with NPR about the forced relocation of staff at the agency. Workers have viewed the relocation and return-to-office mandates at the agency as a means to force resignations, after an appeals court blocked attempted mass firings at the agency by the Trump administration in June 2026. “An investigation with no stated scope or scale is no investigation – it’s a fishing expedition,” Wheeler said. “I have nothing to hide, and when the facts are examined this will be seen for what it is: bullying and intimidation for union activity and protected speech.” Another union member and worker, Alexis Goldstein, was also put on administrative leave in February 2025 before she was fired in February 2026 after she confronted staff with Elon Musk’s so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge), questioning their credentials in accessing data at the agency and recording their actions. “CFPB is illegally retaliating against me for trying to do my job. I acted to protect the sensitive data of Americans and the trade secrets of some of the nation’s largest banks and financial institutions from being accessed by individuals from Doge without CFPB credentials and required training,” Goldstein said in a statement after her firing in February. The union filed a grievance over her firing and is awaiting arbitration to begin, which has been delayed, according to the union, by the CFPB, which told the union the delay is due to an agency official who is on leave. The Trump administration has attempted to dismantle the CFPB since the beginning of Trump’s second term. The office of management and budget director, Vought, called for the abolition of the agency. He halted most the work there in February 2025. The agency deleted nearly 4,000 webpages on its website earlier this year, including all press releases issued by the agency before February 2025. The union has noted that for every $1 spent on the agency, it returns $2.80 to consumers, reimbursing at least $21bn since 2010 to consumers ripped off by corporate scammers. Other workers at the CFPB criticized the investigation of Wheeler, alleging it was retaliatory and an intimidation tactic. “Our union will not be cowed by these bush league tactics to silence us,” said Doug Wilson, a member of the union and employee at the agency, in a statement. “If this administration thinks that mysterious investigations into public servants and union leaders like Steve [Wheeler] will intimidate the rest of us into silence, they clearly underestimated us once again,” added Tyler Creighton, another union member and employee at the agency, in a statement. Ravisha Kumar, a third union member, added in a statement: “Yet again, here’s a poorly executed attempt by this administration to silence us through intimidation. Yet again, we’ll just get louder.” The CFPB did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

title: AOC and Mamdani wanted to defund the police. Their backtracking puts organizers at risk
author: Derecka Purnell
summary: Progressive and democratic socialist politicians are recanting pandemic-era statements on police and prison abolition
body_text: The north may not remember, but 9 August this year marked the 12th anniversary of the police killing of Michael Brown Jr in Ferguson, Missouri. That day, the US representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez reassured an ABC news anchor that she, like other progressive politicians and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates, had “moved away” from statements they made during the pandemic, particularly on police and prison abolition. Questioned further, she explained: “I have a local city councilman that has this saying: ‘Woke 1 was crazy’… especially during Covid, I think that the doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place. And I actually think that the discussions that were had in that time were quite fruitful. I think that when we talk about crime today, it’s fundamentally different than the way that we talked about crime in bringing crime down. And I think that we all share in the goals of having as low a crime rate as possible. I think that, you know, during lockdown, of course, rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today. And I’m grateful that these candidates have the opportunity to present who they are to their electorate and what they’re campaigning on in this moment.” A few days later, on Wednesday, Zohran Mamdani, the progressive New York mayor, who has previously stated that his pandemic-era tweets supporting the defund movement were “out of step” with where he is now, chimed in on Ocasio-Cortez’s comments, saying: “Sometimes what you believe in can change. I know there are some for whom they still believe in that. I’ve made very clear that I do not believe in defunding the police and that to me, delivering critical public safety also looks like working with our police department alongside many other partners.” The New York City councilman to whom Ocasio-Cortez was referring, Chi Ossé, was actually inspired by the abolition movement to run for office. But earlier this week, he was quick to proudly claim coinage of the term “woke 1”, which has been used by people who seek to minimize statements they made in the aftermath of George Floyd’s murder by police in May 2020. In one sense, these politicians are absolutely correct. If “woke 1” represents a political baptism in shallow waters, then I have met many who were swept up in an emotional online conversion toward the radical, romantic rhetoric of “defund the police”. I know the power of the feeling of being connected to an idea that can offer relief and salvation. Ocasio-Cortez, Mamdani and Ossé appeared at an altar of abolition during a global movement that condemned policing. It was a vibe. Sure, they may have even been earnest at the time. But as the abolitionist Mariame Kaba has said about centuries of organizing: abolition is not about your feelings or how you identify. It’s what you do. During the pandemic, I was a couple of years off from an ongoing campaign to close a jail and about to enter a campaign to prevent another one from opening. I wrote my book, Becoming Abolitionists, in that time partially because of how quickly some conversions happened – through charismatic check-marked profiles and inspirational protests, rather than through an organization or collective. Many people were just beginning to understand how abolition was connected to other movements, including those against capitalism, imperialism, racism and ableism. I wanted to focus on centuries of abolitionist resistance that gave rise to contemporary abolitionist demands. “Defund” wasn’t simply a new idea about removing dollars from a budget (though we’d take it!) and leaving everything in society the same. Rather, it was and is a personal and political commitment and strategy to eliminate carceral, communal, colonial, capitalist and climate-based violence while building the people, practices and institutions to help us thrive. This fact is what makes Ocasio-Cortez’s comments additionally troublesome. Even by her own logic, “crime” is largely a product of exploitative, unequal social relations, such as economic inequality, and democratic socialism would produce more equal social relationships and reduce crime. So if democratic socialism is effective, then why keep funding the New York police department at $11bn? And why dismiss taking money away as “rhetoric”? Because: the police were not created for public safety. They were created to keep property owners and slaveowners safe. The abolitionist geographer Ruth Wilson Gilmore writes in Geographies of Global Change that “the best estimate for crime as a driving force of prison expansion shows it to account for little more than 10 percent of the increase. Rather, it is a greater propensity to lock people up, as opposed to people’s greater propensity to do old or new illegal things, that accounts for about 90 percent of US prison and jail growth since 1980.” The rhetoric of public safety obscures this history and protects the institution as a heavily unionized, violent jobs program. This does not mean the police never show up when someone needs help, or that people become cops because they only want to hurt others. What it does mean is that historically, cities are willing to rely on the poverty that capitalism creates to fill its carceral ranks with people looking to enter the middle class. Seeing progressive politicians move away from their earlier feelings poses a question about what they’re moving toward. Ossé and AOC did not introduce any “woke 1” legislation or resolutions that they now have to retract. Mamdani actually attempted the opposite: the racial justice working group of DSA, among others, successfully pressured him to reverse his commitment to add almost 600 more officers and $70m to the NYPD, against his campaign promise to maintain the headcount of the force. He was positioning this move while boasting historic lows for crime in the city. So unlike the students, artists, congregants and organizers I met and know, the politicians prioritized political office over political homes. Because these figures represent more than their political ideas, I understand. But the dismissal is the problem. The ideas rooted in the defund movement that got them the spotlight were not polling well by the time their volunteers were canvassing for their political campaigns. As a result, they dismissed those ideas as something to grow and learn from, not to publicly explore and explain. By contrast, for example, upon receiving pushback from the “defund” framing, activists in North Carolina chose “refund Raleigh” instead as an organizing campaign strategy to explain abolition to the community, develop a public services investment strategy and secure policies that decouple public safety and police. Even decades before abolition entered a mainstream branding debate, Wilson Gilmore said that she and others organizing through Californians United for a Responsible Budget chose a “deliberately bland name” to attract community members to the campaign. Still, other organizers chose more explicit “defund” campaign names as clear sites of struggle, sacrificing public palatability for political clarity. These efforts are equally important: people, politicians and corporations weaponized the ambiguity of “Black lives matter” toward everything, including more police funding and hires. So whether explicit in naming “defund” or not, abolitionist organizers across the country have been spearheading electoral campaigns, mutual aid efforts, disaster recovery, anti-immigrant detention networks, stopping jails and more. It is not always successful and apparent, but the commitment remains because the struggle continues. Right now, DSA members like AOC, Ossé and Mamdani feel refreshing because electoral politics have been captured for so long by Democrats and Republicans. And the state has done such a horribly impressive job at exhausting, shackling, killing and exiling actual revolutionaries that politicians who repeat the slightest radical rhetoric can start to feel like revolutionaries. What remains, though, is that the very movements producing that rhetoric, from abolition to Free Palestine, also produced the possibilities of their elections. And downplaying those movements puts organizers who continue this work at risk, especially right now. What time is it when politicians across the political spectrum, from AOC and Ossé to Marco Rubio and Donald Trump, suggest that progressive and left organizers are “woke” and “crazy”? It is the time when those who have not yet realized that the demonization of people, organizations and ideas about justice – regardless of where they come from – leads to targeting, surveillance, deportation, imprisonment and death. If leaders of DSA, an organization of which I am also a member, want to continue to grow as an electoral political home for people who believe these ideas are not only possible, but also worth pursuing, they must know that they are subject to the same lessons they are teaching establishment Democrats right now: do not laugh off the political demands of those who put you in office. For all of what their constituents, canvassers and staffers did as part of a fight on our behalf, is it worth treating years-long radical, Black and multiracial pursuits of freedom as mere pandemic pandemonium? No, it’s not. But more than what we are called by any of them is what we continue to call ourselves. Our own histories, convictions and clarity, not politicians, lead the way.

title: Trump has amassed staggering wealth in ‘most openly corrupt’ presidency
author: Peter Stone in Washington
summary: Ethics experts and Democrats express alarm as Trump uses office to grow his personal fortune to ‘unprecedented’ level
body_text: Donald Trump’s use of his second presidency to grow his personal fortune has alarmed legal and ethics experts and congressional Democrats as he has reaped an “unprecedented” $2.2bn in 2025 revenues by amassing big cryptocurrency holdings, benefiting from wealthy foreign interests, expanding his Truth Social business and more, while federal oversight of his actions has waned. Trump last year raked in at least $1.4bn from his crypto ventures according to financial disclosure forms he filed in June. Simultaneously, about one million investors in a Trump crypto scheme suffered almost $3.8bn in losses as their volatile crypto holdings tanked in value. Monetizing his presidency further this summer, Trump’s Truth Social media business is pushing a new scheme that offers wealthy buyers special early access to his posts for a fee of $100,000 a month, which top Democrats and public interest groups say pose serious conflict of interest and corruption issues. Mark Warner, the Democratic senator of Virginia, in July wrote to six major Wall Street financial trade groups urging them to reject a new Truth Social product, dubbed Truth API, that would enrich Trump by giving big investors early looks at Trump’s postings. Warner’s letter urged that they “not legitimize an arrangement that sells privileged access to market-moving presidential communications, especially for the president’s personal financial benefit”. On another monetization front, critics raised red flags about how Trump tapped his justice department to forge a potentially lucrative and sketchy deal to settle a $10bn lawsuit by Trump against the IRS about a leak of his tax returns that gives him and his family immunity from IRS audits of prior tax returns and could save him $100m. Likewise some analysts are troubled by how Trump has circumvented the constitution’s prohibition on foreign emoluments by accepting a $400m plane as a gift from Qatar, and how other wealthy foreigners have backed some Trump family hotel and golf deals abroad. Beyond his personal enrichment, Trump’s monetizing his office and transactional governing style has proved lucrative to his sons, some top advisers, billionaire buddies, big donors and other allies, say critics. A CNN poll in late July buttressed criticism of Trump’s monetizing his second term: the poll revealed that 66% of 1,225 respondents said Trump doesn’t put the good of the country over his personal gain and only 34% said he does. Former federal officials, historians and other experts have raised “corruption” concerns and other red flags as Trump has monetized his presidency for personal gain in ways that far exceed any other president’s tenure. “Trump has figured out a way to monetize the presidency, political power and public policy in ways no other president has achieved,” Princeton historian Julian Zelizer told the Guardian. “In the first term, he created the thinnest of firewalls between his business and policy. In the second term, he didn’t put up any firewall and smashed all guardrails that existed. “The precedent is dangerous in general, as we are moving to a virtually unregulated era where there will be unending opportunities for corruption.” Former election officials concur that Trump is cashing in on his presidency to an unprecedented level. “Trump has openly rejected restraints on presidential conflicts of interests and is using the powers of the presidency, both real and imagined, to financially benefit his and his family’s business interests on an unprecedented level,” said Larry Noble, a former general counsel at the Federal Election Commission who now teaches law at American University. “In just the first year of this term, he reported his business holdings earned over $2bn.” Noble added: “While Trump’s second term is less than half over, it already looks like the most openly corrupt administration in our history. “Whether you’re a foreign country, a company or an individual who wants the government to approve a business deal, stop an investigation or just be a friend when you need a favor, the message is that this is a pay to play administration.” Other legal experts offer equally strong critiques. “I think the biggest concern is not simply that the president is making money from his office, but the potential for corruption,” said Barbara McQuade, a former federal prosecutor for eastern Michigan who now teaches at the University of Michigan law school. “Trump’s settlement of his lawsuit against the IRS typifies his self-dealing. The judge assigned to the case later found that because Trump controlled both sides of the case, there was no adversity of parties to provide the court with jurisdiction. Instead, Trump used the court to legitimize what was essentially a gift to him at taxpayer expense.” Since his second term began, Trump has dismissed concerns about conflicts of interests, boasting to the New York Times in January that he has a “very honest family” and that he had never taken his presidential salary. Unlike prior presidents, though, Trump has declined to put his assets in a completely blind trust or divest from his businesses, although ethics experts have urged him to do so. Despite Trump’s protestations, Trump’s crypto earnings in 2025 are eye-popping – especially in contrast to the dismal returns for many investors and given Trump’s warnings in 2021 that crypto was a “scam”, and a “disaster waiting to happen”. Trump’s strong embrace of crypto came after the industry poured millions of dollars into his 2024 campaign, and he pledged to make the US “the crypto capital of the world” with less regulation. For instance, the crypto venture World Liberty Financial, which Trump and his sons launched in the fall of 2024 with the family of Steve Witkoff, who now is Trump’s special Middle East envoy, brought in $799m in 2025 for Trump, according to public filings. Last year too, Trump earned another $636m from his novelty memecoin $Trump which Trump began marketing just days before his inauguration in 2025. The Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Adam Schiff of California this year wrote a tough letter to the Trump-allied memecoin marketing firm Fight Fight Fight as Trump was poised to host an April event for buyers of $Trump at Mar-a-Lago similar to one Trump hosted at his Virginia golf club last year. “We have previously raised concerns with President Trump’s willingness to use the presidency for personal profit,” the lawmakers noted in their letter to the marketing firm for $Trump. The letter stressed that “not all $TRUMP holders have benefited from their investment”, and cited a February industry report that $TRUMP – and the first lady’s memecoin, $MELANIA – “erased an estimated $4.3 billion in retail wealth in recent months, with 2 million holders currently underwater”. In stark contrast, the same report found that 45 other crypto wallets that were early holders of $Trump coins had profited by about $1.2bn. After Trump’s memecoin bash in 2025 prompted conflict of interest questions and charges of corruption , the press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said Trump was “abiding by all conflict-of-interest laws that are applicable to the president”. But legal critics and experts say Trump’s monetization of his presidency has given short shrift to conflict of interest concerns, as his regulators have eased oversight and Trump has used his office to reward an array of wealthy allies in crypto and other fields. The Cornell economist Eswar Prasad faults the Trump administration’s regulatory laxness for some of the scandals and legal headaches that have plagued the crypto industry. “The Trump administration has clearly shifted the priorities and focus of the government’s regulatory apparatus to look past any and all sins of the crypto industry, thereby directly benefiting the Trump family’s financial interests,” Prasad said. A case in point, say critics, has been the weak oversight of Binance, the world’s biggest crypto exchange that has benefited Trump’s World Liberty Financial. WLF was tapped to play a central role in a $2bn investment by the Abu Dhabi financial fund MGX that is backed by the United Arab Emirates in Binance. As part of the deal, the Abu Dhabi fund bought $2bn of a WLF stablecoin, dubbed USD1, to invest in Binance. Stablecoins are a popular type of cryptocurrency that are often pegged to the dollar. The WLF deal came after Binance in 2023 pleaded guilty to violating US money-laundering laws and other violations and the justice department fined it a whopping $4.3bn. Furthermore, Binance’s ex-CEO and founder, Changpeng Zhao, pleaded guilty in the US to violating the Bank Secrecy Act and failing to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program. Zhao, who still owns 90% of Binance, served a four-month jail term in 2024 and last year received a pardon from Trump. Despite Binance pledges to crack down on crime, internal investigators last year found that about $1.7bn in crypto reportedly moved through Binance to Iranian entities linked to terrorism. Similarly, watchdog groups are sharply critical of Truth Social’s offer to sell Wall Street advance looks at Trump’s Truth Social posts for $100,000 per month. “Using the presidency to channel non-public information to his media company’s major institutional customers for profit is not simply Trump’s newest act in self-dealing,” said Virginia Canter, the chief counsel for ethics and anti-corruption with Democracy Defenders Action. “It is a significant escalation in exploiting and monetizing the presidency for his personal private gain. Providing Trump Media high-speed access to official non-public information is a step towards normalizing insider trading and public corruption, disregarding the damage it may cause to regular investors who will not have the same access as his wealthy institutional customers.” Canter added that “Trump is increasingly dependent on the presidency to generate business profits since his media company has been losing money over the past several quarters.” Trump Media & Technology, the company behind the Truth Social platform, on 10 August announced it lost a whopping $238m in the three months through June as it branched out into new businesses including crypto. Top Democrats echo these critiques. In a July letter to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Senators Schiff and Warren called the new Truth Social deal “an outrageous abuse of the President’s office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets, while enriching Wall Street and other wealthy insiders”. Looking forward, McQuade urged “new rules and new consequences to protect the public from a president willing to put his own financial benefit ahead of the public interest”.

title: Hegseth criticized for locking Democrats out of closed-door defense budget talks
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Republican lawmakers express concern after US defense secretary repeatedly excluded Democrats from briefings
body_text: Republican senators have criticized the Pentagon for locking Democrats out of classified briefings on defense spending, warning that Pete Hegseth’s approach could jeopardize passage of Donald Trump’s record $1.5tn military budget increase. The US defense secretary has made at least two trips to Capitol Hill in recent weeks to pitch the budget, but has repeatedly excluded Democrats from the closed-door sessions, according to lawmakers from both parties. Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, argued that Hegseth was undermining his own case. “He calls himself the secretary of war, but ironically, he doesn’t want to go to war and win the argument with nearly half the members of the Senate,” Tillis told Politico. “You got to engage.” Much of next year’s defense budget will still require Democratic votes to pass, even if Republicans push part of the package through, under the party-line reconciliation process. Senate Democrats have threatened to boycott the funding bills altogether, meaning Hegseth’s exclusion of the party’s congressional representatives could backfire on the administration’s own spending priorities this fall. “The Department of War remains fully committed to working with Congress to ensure our warfighters have the resources necessary to execute their mission,” said Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson. “Secretary Hegseth and senior department leadership regularly engage with lawmakers to discuss the defense budget, readiness, and national security priorities.” Mike Rounds, a Republican senator of South Dakota, said he had personally raised the issue of engaging Democrats with defense department officials. “The Democrat members need to be brought up to speed,” Rounds told Politico, adding that Pentagon officials feared classified material would leak. Lisa Murkowski, a senator of Alaska, also called for a bipartisan approach to the briefings. “I know that sometimes you want to have smaller groups, but I think it needs to be bipartisan,” she told the website. The dispute follows comments Hegseth made in April, when he told the US House of Representatives armed services committee that congressional Democrats were among the “biggest impediment” to stopping Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. “The biggest adversary we face at this point are the reckless, feckless and defeatist words of congressional Democrats and some Republicans,” he said.

title: Max Miller’s ex-wife sues him for sharing image of daughter as part of custody battle
author: Shrai Popat in Washington
summary: Republican congressman publicly shared links to evidence his team compiled in response to domestic abuse allegations
body_text: Emily Moreno, the ex-wife of Max Miller, has sued the embattled Republican congressman and his lawyer for uploading a picture of their infant daughter to a publicly accessible Dropbox folder as part of their custody battle. The complaint argues that Miller “recklessly published and disclosed to the world a nude image” of their daughter. The photos in the lawsuit were part of a tranche of evidence that Miller’s team compiled in response to the domestic abuse allegations the lawmaker is facing following his divorce. Those allegations include holding a gun to Moreno’s head, pouring boiling water on her, and actions that resulted in his two-year-old daughter’s collarbone being broken, all of which Miller denies. Miller, who is seeking re-election in Ohio, has faced a wave of calls to resign, including from members of his own party and his father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, a Republican senator. However, Donald Trump has remained largely supportive of the congressman, who represents a conservative district, and there are reports that the White House squashed efforts to replace him on the ballot in November’s midterm election. The suit alleges that Miller “so desperately wanted to salvage his political job” that he “recklessly and intentionally” provided his lawyer (Aaron Minc) with “a trove of documents and photos, indifferent about what they contained or how they were used”. Miller then shared the link to the files online after he went live on social media to deny the allegations against him on 2 August. Moreno’s lawyers note that “more than 400,000 people saw or interacted with” Miller’s posts containing the Dropbox folder. The lawsuit – filed in US district court for the northern district of Ohio – demands the court award $150,000 in damages for “every time someone accessed, transferred, distributed, published, or downloaded the image” of their daughter. At the time, Minc had accepted sole responsibility for inadvertently releasing the unredacted image of Moreno and Miller’s daughter in the files. The Guardian has approached both Miller and Minc for their response to the latest lawsuit. Brian Poindexter, the Democrat running against Miller in November, has ramped up attacks on his opponent. “No one credibly accused of holding a gun to his wife’s head and breaking their two-year-old daughter’s collarbone belongs in the halls of power,” he said recently on X. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has also seized on the moment to add Poindexter to the “Red to Blue” program, which identifies districts the party thinks can be flipped from Republicans to the party for congressional control. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.

title: Tesla paid Elon Musk 2.5m times more as CEO than its average worker in 2025
author: Michael Sainato
summary: Tech billionaire’s $158.3bn deal an outlier in report showing widening gap of CEO to worker pay at top companies
body_text: Elon Musk received over 2.5m times as much compensation at Tesla as the company’s average worker, according to a new report on the growing gap between top corporate executives and their workers. Musk’s $158.3bn pay deal was an outlier but came as the gap between CEO and worker pay continued to grow. Excluding Musk, last year the average ratio of CEO to worker pay for the top S&P 500 companies was 312 to 1, up from a 285:1 ratio in 2024. With Musk, the average pay ratio was 5,387:1, according to the executive pay watch report released this week by the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US. “In 2025, Elon Musk received the median Tesla worker’s pay every 4.23 seconds – less time than it takes to read this sentence,” states the report. “A majority of S&P 500 CEOs made more in one day than the median US worker made in one year.” Average CEO pay, excluding Musk, was $22.8m in 2025, up from $18.9m in 2024. With Tesla accounted for, the average increases to $340.1m. The report notes workers’ share of US national income has fallen to the lowest level since the second world war. The report also looks at Donald Trump’s income in 2025. At $2.2bn, largely from his crypto holdings, Trump’s income rose nearly 254% from 2024. The median US worker would require 43,154 years to earn what Trump received in 2025. “This is political grift unlike what we have ever seen in our lifetimes, perhaps ever, but it only tells part of the story of how CEOs and the Trump administration has rigged our economy to enrich themselves at the expense of working people,” said Fred Redmond, AFL-CIO’s secretary-treasurer. “Trump’s radical budget bill that Republicans rammed through Congress last year, it made drastic cuts to healthcare, food assistance for children and families in order to give massive tax cuts for corporations and the wealthy.” The report cited data demonstrating the economic struggles of most Americans; 33% of US adults have no retirement savings, 37% of adults do not have enough money to cover a $400 emergency expense, 26% of US adults have skipped medical care due to costs, and 23% of renters in the US have fallen behind on rent over the past year. Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report. “As President Trump said, he has a lot of assets because he was a massively successful businessman prior to becoming President, which was why he was elected to office in the first place,” said a White House spokesperson in an email. “All of the President’s assets are in held in fully discretionary accounts managed by independent third-party financial institutions. There are no conflicts of interest.”

title: Third person dies at New Jersey immigration detention center
author: Marina Dunbar
summary: José Chajón-Raxón experienced ‘seizure-like activity’ at Delaney Hall and later died after being hospitalized
body_text: A Guatemalan immigrant detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at a Newark, New Jersey, facility suffered a medical emergency and later died after being hospitalized, according to the Trump administration. José Chajón-Raxón is the third immigrant to die after being held at Delaney Hall, an ICE detention center that reopened in May 2025 amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. A nurse responded when Chajón-Raxón experienced a medical emergency and “witnessed Chajón-Raxón experiencing seizure-like activity”, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Medical personnel were called, and he was transported to a hospital, the DHS said in a statement shared with the Guardian. ICE agents had arrested Chajón-Raxón before bringing him to Delaney Hall on 18 July, the agency said. Four days later, Chajón-Raxón was “released from ICE custody on July 22”, according to the agency, which did not provide further details about the circumstances of his release. Key questions about what happened next remain unanswered in the DHS account. The department did not say what occurred after Chajón-Raxón arrived at the hospital, whether he left the hospital before his death or exactly when he died. “Per ICE policy, when an individual is no longer in ICE custody then ICE will no longer be responsible for monitoring or reviewing deaths that may occur. This is common sense,” the DHS statement said. The case comes after a policy shift announced earlier this year under which the agency stopped reporting deaths occurring within 30 days after a person is released from custody. That change reversed a policy put in place by the Biden administration in 2021. US representative Rob Menendez, a New Jersey Democrat who has regularly visited Delaney Hall, has sharply criticized the change. Menendez told the Associated Press that it creates a “loophole” allowing the agency to release someone from custody and then “claim it has no responsibility to investigate their death or inform Congress and the public”. Chajón-Raxón’s death did not become publicly known until Menendez disclosed it last week in the aftermath of another death connected to the facility. Delaney Hall has already faced scrutiny from human rights advocates and Democrats over two other deaths involving immigrants detained there. Edwin López-Cornejo, a man from El Salvador, died earlier this month after experiencing a medical emergency while in ICE detention. Jean Wilson Brutus, a Haitian man who had also been detained at Delaney Hall, died in December. The latest disclosure adds to broader concerns surrounding deaths in immigration detention. More than 50 people have died in ICE custody nationwide since Donald Trump took office, while rights groups have repeatedly raised alarms about medical care and conditions inside detention facilities. Delaney Hall itself has increasingly drawn national attention. In recent months, protests have followed allegations of problems including physical abuse by guards and spoiled food. Those concerns escalated in late May, when at least 300 detainees organized a hunger and labor strike. Weeks after that action began, women housed in a separate unit at Delaney Hall launched a hunger strike of their own. Their demands include improvements at the facility as well as calls for ICE to release women younger than 21, women with medical conditions and mothers. ICE maintains that detainees receive appropriate medical care.
