title: Donald Trump doesn’t just love billionaires, he loves multimillionaires too
author: Eduardo Porter
summary: US tax policy deprives the government of revenue and overwhelmingly serves the interests of the rich
body_text: After the House passed its version of Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) last year – the one that paired a $5tn-plus tax cut with $1tn-plus of cuts from food stamps and Medicaid – the House speaker, Mike Johnson, explained that “this is not giving tax cuts to the millionaires”. The beneficiaries, he said, were “small business owners” that “provide the jobs in every community in America”. Johnson was playing to the myth of the modest, sturdy Main Street job creator. It is an appealing story. It’s also the most consequential piece of BS distorting American policy that deprives the government of tax revenue, stunts American capitalism, twists regulations, thwarts competition and overwhelmingly serves millionaires’ interests. The speaker was specifically talking about “pass through” businesses. About 95% of businesses in the country take this form. They employ half of all workers and generate more than half the nation’s business income. These creatures of the tax code are freed from paying the corporate income tax rate. Instead, their untaxed profits are distributed to their owners, who generally face lower individual tax rates, saving them billions. Republicans have consistently gone to bat for pass throughs. In 2017 Ron Johnson, the Republican senator from Wisconsin, threatened not to vote for Trump’s Tax Cut and Jobs Act, relenting only after the Senate increased a tax deduction for pass-through business income from 17% to 20%. “I just have it in my heart a real affinity for these owner-operated pass-throughs,” Johnson said at the time. That deduction, made permanent in the ”big beautiful bill” last year, will cost the budget $820bn over a 10-year period, almost as much as was cut from the Medicaid budget. About 57% of the $1.3tn in pass-through income in 2022 went to 890,000 people in the richest 1% of the population, according to the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center. A study by economists at the Department of the Treasury, the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis and Dartmouth University found that 35% of the total deductions in the year after the 2017 tax cut, a cold $54bn, flowed to taxpayers with income of at least $1m. Johnson and Johnson know this. Senator Ron owned a stake in a pass-through, a plastics maker in Oshkosh, which he sold in 2020 for between $5 and $25m and upon which he built a fortune worth about $40m in 2018, making him the sixth-richest senator at the time. Speaker Mike, a man of “modest means”, lives in a $3.7m townhouse steps from the US Capitol owned by the millionaire Republican donor Lee Beaman, who made his fortune from a string of car dealerships. Next month, economists Owen Zidar from Princeton and Eric Zwick from the University of Chicago will publish a panoramic profile of these “everywhere millionaires”. They are your dentist and doctor, the car dealer and the insurance salesman, the lawyer and the real estate developer, the accountant, the consultant and the building equipment contractor. They have largely organized themselves as pass-throughs. Many are amazingly rich. Zidar and Zwick estimate that for every billionaire in the Forbes 400 list, there are more than 4,000 Main Street millionaires worth at least $10m. Their net worth adds up to $46.7tn, nearly 12 times as much as that of the Forbes plutocrats. The political system is at their mercy. Consider Trump’s ”big beautiful” tax cut last year. The 20% deduction granted to pass-through profits means that the top income tax rate for their rich owners is only 29.6%. For people who earn wages, the top marginal rate is 37%. Concern over the political power of the plutocracy has focused on billionaires. But Main Street millionaires flying under the radar might be more influential. Political action committees (Pacs) run by the National Association of Realtors, the National Beer Wholesalers Association and the National Automobile Dealers Association were among the top 10 by donations in the 2023-24 cycle. And Main Street millionaires play in politics themselves, at the federal, state and local level. Car dealership millionaires Don Beyer from Virginia, Vern Buchanan from Florida and Mike Kelly from Pennsylvania sit on the House ways and means committee. They are probably not unhappy about the pass-through deduction, nor about the deduction for new auto loan interest that also made it into the OBBBA, which Zidar and Zwick estimate will cost the budget $5bn to $10bn a year for four years. Though tax breaks may be their top concern, the damage to the republic runs deeper. In 1997, doctors got the federal government to freeze the number of residency positions funded by Medicare, a neat way to limit the availability of new doctors. That helps explain why there are only 2.7 doctors per 1,000 people in the US, compared with 3.7 across the other OECD countries, and why 26% of American doctors fit in the richest 1% of the population, compared with only 5% in Sweden, despite Americans’ comparatively tenuous hold on life. Let’s not just pour hate on the doctors, though. Car dealers in 50 states benefit from franchise laws that prevent automakers from closing them down and stop new dealers from entering their turf. In 17 states they also benefit from a ban on direct sales by automakers. The income of real estate brokers is protected by privileged access to listing information and exorbitant, monopolistic fees of dubious legality that they extract from homeowners. Beer distributors have lobbied hard to prevent breweries from selling directly to retailers and to get ironclad territorial rights. This is not the page to pity billionaires. But it’s worth pointing to the privileges of the rich below that status. Trump may love Elon Musk. But his signature bill – which stripped the EV subsidies turbocharging Tesla’s sales – shows much more love for the car dealers and the doctors and the real estate developers living a few floors below Elon but well within the 1%. Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

title: Where healthcare could sway voters, organizers ramp up an old tactic: talking to people
author: Rachel Leingang with photographs by Eric Ruby
summary: In Wisconsin, voters weigh candidates who backed cuts to Medicaid, and those who want to expand it
body_text: Going door to door in western Wisconsin multiple times per week, Bill Hogseth tells strangers about his seizure. Hogseth, the co-executive director and lead organizer of the nonpartisan group GrassRoots Organizing Western Wisconsin (Groww), tells them about waking up in an ambulance, and the impact of the seizure on his ability to drive and work. Usually standing on their doorsteps, he asks to hear their stories too – about ambulance rides, hospital bills, broken bones. Hogseth’s vulnerability encourages others to share. It’s a concept called “deep canvassing”, a long discussion, usually about 15-20 minutes, with a neighbor at their door about a political issue not tied to a specific candidate. It’s designed to assess a person’s support for a policy at the start of the conversation, then see if it changes by the end of it. Open minds are key to Hogseth’s work in western Wisconsin’s third congressional district, where a heated season is ramping up as Democrats are trying to unseat Republican representative Derrick Van Orden. A host of national Republican figures have visited the area in recent months, including Trump himself, who came to Chippewa Falls in June to talk about farming, a sign of the area’s prominence on the electoral map. Healthcare has become a critical issue in the state, and system failures have become a political liability. Democrats are reminding voters that Van Orden voted for Trump’s so-called big beautiful bill, which will deliver $1tn in healthcare cuts over the next decade, starting in January. Two hospitals in western Wisconsin closed permanently in 2024, and researchers have identified others at risk of closure or service reductions. Rebecca Cooke, who won the Democratic primary to face Van Orden in November, lists “healing our healthcare system” first on her website’s priorities list. Cooke told the Guardian earlier this summer that she not only frequently heard about healthcare concerns from voters, but shared them herself. “I’ve actually canceled my own insurance through the ACA because it’s increased so much and I can’t afford it,” Cooke said in June. “There’s a lot of people that I know that are doing the same.” The people who open their doors to Hogseth and his colleagues often share stories of how the US healthcare system has failed them. There’s the man who drove himself to the hospital while passing a kidney stone to avoid a costly ambulance ride and the mom who wants to stay home with her kids but needs her job to cover health insurance. There’s the cancer care, the surgeries, the peculiarities of medical billing, the lapses in insurance coverage, the people who see the state’s Medicaid program as a lifeline for their family members. Groww is conducting these deep canvasses throughout western Wisconsin on healthcare, specifically on potentially expanding access to BadgerCare. That’s the state’s Medicaid program, which provides insurance for low-income families. The group wants to have 4,000 conversations in the northern part of the third congressional district from May to November, Hogseth said. About 40 trained deep canvassers are out in the field three times a week throughout the region. In addition to the congressional race, Wisconsin voters in November will also decide on key state legislative races and an open governor’s race that could make expanding BadgerCare a reality. Estimates show more than 276,000 Wisconsinites could lose healthcare coverage as the cuts roll out. Wisconsin is also one of 10 states that did not expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act (ACA). “Regardless of who people vote for, [the issue of healthcare] is cutting into people’s anger,” Hogseth said. At the doors in western Wisconsin’s small towns, people show a willingness to slow down and talk, even to a stranger. Most say they don’t think anyone in Washington understands their struggles with healthcare. By the end of the conversations, many people move up in support of expanding access to BadgerCare. In some instances, they say they don’t support the issue at all, then fully support it and want to get involved by the end. Studies have shown these deep canvasses can lead to reduced prejudice and decreased exclusionary attitudes. One study, commissioned by a group called People’s Action in 2020, showed that the method can change voting behavior. At a July protest in Taylor county, one of the reddest areas of the state, a decommissioned ambulance and gurney sat outside a picnic shelter right next to a Republican picnic where Tom Tiffany, a Republican congressman who is the state’s gubernatorial nominee, was set to speak. The Medford, Wisconsin, protest, led by Taylor county’s Indivisible chapter and attended by allies from other parts of western Wisconsin, was so close to the Republican picnic that attendees of both could look each other in the eyes. When protesters chanted against Tiffany’s support for Trump’s budget bill and its healthcare cuts, they were a few dozen feet away from Tiffany himself. When someone at the protest mentioned Tiffany’s support for healthcare cuts, some at the Republican picnic cheered. The county is outside the competitive third district, but similar protests have plagued Van Orden’s events and Wisconsin visits from prominent Republicans, including JD Vance. Van Orden has countered the protests by claiming the upcoming cuts, which leave people uninsured partly through work requirements and other barriers, are not cuts at all. “There has been no cuts to Medicare and Medicaid. There’s not going to be cuts to Medicare and Medicaid,” Van Orden said. “What’s going to end, though, is the rampant waste, fraud and abuse present.” Sally Rasmussen, part of the Taylor county group, said participants came together during this year’s winter mostly in response to the immigration enforcement surge in Minneapolis, a few hours away. The group holds a weekly protest. They sometimes get middle fingers and obscenities, she said, but the balance has felt tipped since the start of the war with Iran. “Now we get more positives than negatives,” she said. “And I think that a lot of people that want to be Republican just say, I can’t. It was a step too far for them.” At these ambulance protests, people share their experiences of getting cut off from Medicaid or seeing their premiums rise, and healthcare providers talk about the crises they’re seeing at work. “People also are not realizing that the cuts to Medicare and Medicaid are going to eventually affect them, even if they’re not on Medicare and Medicaid,” said Teresa Kriese, a voter who lives in the third congressional district and who has spoken about her experience with a cancer clinical trial. “Because hospitals and clinics do a lot of treatments that are funded by those coverages, and if they lose that money, they’re not going to be able to survive and they’re going to close.” Kriese, 61, has lung cancer that’s spread to her brain, and there’s no approved treatment option. But she has stayed alive beyond her doctor’s initial predictions due to a clinical trial in Chicago, which was defunded in January 2024. The drug she takes is still available, so she’s still able to take it – for now. “It’s the only thing that’s kept me alive for the past three years,” she said of the trial. If she loses access to the drug, she will have to seek out another trial in a scarcer environment as Trump administration cuts to scientific research have disrupted clinical trials. Kriese felt a responsibility to share the plight of people in clinical trials, so she spoke at the Eau Claire rally against the healthcare cuts. “Clinical trials are there for everybody,” she said. “It’s not just cancer that clinical trials work for. Every single drug that you take, over-the-counter or prescription, at some point was in a clinical trial. You don’t get drugs for any other condition without clinical trials. So if we’re not funding them, that to me says this entire administration doesn’t care if we live or die.” Mark Steigerwald, a 54-year-old colon cancer survivor from Eau Claire, saw his monthly health insurance premiums nearly triple this year after Congress allowed Covid-era subsidies to run out. For the small-business owner and his wife, the monthly cost is now more than $2,700. Steigerwald recently spoke publicly about his experience at a similar Eau Claire rally against the healthcare cuts. He felt it was time to speak up because he felt “we’re crossing some lines here that we shouldn’t be”. He’s started working more hours to cover the price hike. He called private insurers to see if he could get a better price, but none would cover him due to his pre-existing condition, leaving him with the ACA marketplace. His current plan has a $13,000 deductible for him and his wife. “If you’ve ever had an illness like cancer, you’ll never be without health insurance,” he said. “That illness cost over $1m to deal with, and that was a good outcome.” A political independent, Steigerwald ranks healthcare among his top three issues when casting his vote this year. Van Orden voted to extend the subsidies, he acknowledged, but the US Senate has not taken up a vote on the extension. While the Democrats fit more with his values now, he thinks they’re struggling to come up with a platform. He’d love to see a groundswell of independents challenge the two-party system. “They’ve both been around for all this time,” he said of the Democrats and Republicans. “And all these problems are still around, and they won’t face them. Almost everybody’s responsible who’s ever been in power before. “I just want to see better responsibility for humanity.” Elsewhere in the third congressional district, deep canvassers hit the doors in Menomonie, a politically mixed town of about 17,000, where most people readily agreed to talk. One older woman said people in Washington don’t know what life is like for everyday people like her. “They don’t shop for their own groceries,” she said. A man at a different house pointed out that he sees health insurance company logos on Nascar racecars. Groww filtered out strong Democrats and strong Republicans, seeking to talk to people in the political middle, Hogseth said. The script helps show why decisions made by Congress are personally relevant to the people at the doors. Canvassers also invite locals to a summit on the topic, hoping to find people interested in organizing together long term. People don’t always move up in support for expanding BadgerCare; canvassers said they sometimes talk to people who start with zero support for expanding BadgerCare and stay there at the end. Some mention concerns over fraud in the system or believe people are taking advantage of it. Even in those tough conversations, canvassers feel they’ve planted a seed or found some places for common ground. One canvasser said the conversations renewed her hope in humanity. Another said the conversations show that people have contradictions in their views, a sign they can change their minds. “There’s a lot of people who are with us on the issue, who are either hopeless or cynical,” Hogseth said. “And they’re like, the only way things will change is if there’s a major crisis or if I move to another country. Part of what I think we need to break through with people on is their cynicism and hopelessness.”

title: US navy veterans and military health experts express concern over USS Abraham Lincoln sailors
author: Anna Betts
summary: Prolonged deployment is coupled with reports of water shortages, plumbing issues and attempts to jump overboard
body_text: US navy veterans and military health experts are expressing concerns about the strain on sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has spent nearly nine months at sea supporting US operations in the Middle East, amid reports of poor living conditions and worsening mental health among its crew. The San Diego-based aircraft carrier left port on 21 November, originally bound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East as the US-Israel war with Iran began. It has now spent more than 250 consecutive days at sea without a significant port visit, with its deployment repeatedly extended. On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the US military was preparing to replace the Lincoln with the USS George Washington, as concerns mount over the conditions aboard the Lincoln. Reports by the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes this week described shortages of supplies and water as well as plumbing problems, low morale and deteriorating mental health among the Lincoln’s roughly 5,000 sailors, and further reported that there had been multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard. The reports prompted several Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon. In response to the reports, a navy official told the Guardian this week that they were aware that “extended deployments place a significant strain on our service members and their families, and we are grateful for the resilience and sacrifices they make” and said that the health and wellbeing of every Lincoln sailor was a priority. “Based on information available to the command, we have not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship,” they said, adding that religious, medical and mental health professionals were available as part of a “comprehensive support network” that included “onboard deployment-resilience counselors and chaplains”. The official recognized that the war had disrupted traditional supply hubs, but added that “current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional AC and healthy meal options”. On Thursday, Pete Hegseth claimed that the conditions aboard the Lincoln had been “completely misrepresented”. “We make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” the US defense secretary told reporters. “Some deployments are longer than others, and ⁠I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody.” Military experts said on Friday that prolonged deployments, particularly without coming ashore, can place increased strain on both the crew and the ship itself, and noted that extensions can also take a psychological toll by leaving sailors uncertain about when they will return home. Armen Kurdian, a retired US navy captain, who served aboard the Lincoln in 2005, described the carrier as a “giant floating city” with about 5,000 people aboard. “You’re feeding people 15,000 meals per day, you’ve got TV stations, communications,” he said. During his deployment, he said, he took a graduate-level business class remotely, while other sailors found different ways to occupy their downtime. “There’s always something to do,” he said, although he added that life aboard was “certainly high-ops tempo and highly stressful at times”. Sailors live in close quarters, he said, with junior enlisted personnel sleeping in open bay barracks. Kurdian recalled some plumbing problems, including broken toilets, during his deployment, and said that things becoming rusty, dirty or broken can have a “kind of depressing impact on you”. “Things break on a ship,” he said. “You’re in the middle of the Gulf, you’re operating, you’ve got aircraft smacking down on decks repeatedly, hundreds of times per day, and that rattles the ship. There’s never a time when you’re on the ship and everything’s going to be working perfectly. But the question is, [is] it happening a lot?” Kurdian said that what surprised him about the Lincoln’s current deployment was not its length, but the amount of time the crew had gone without a significant port visit. “That will take a toll on people when you don’t get to stand on dry land for a while,” he said. Robert Murrett, a retired US navy vice-admiral, said that a typical aircraft-carrier deployment is closer to six months and normally includes port visits that allow sailors to rest and spend some time away from the ship. The Lincoln, Murrett said, “has had none of that since they left San Diego last November”. “They’ve been under way for that very, very long period of time, approaching nine months, and they’ve also been under combat conditions for much [of it] because of their time in the Middle East,” he said. “That’s very, very tough on a crew.” Murrett described life aboard an aircraft carrier as “tough”, calling it a “huge, compressed environment”, where there is “a lot of stress” and it can be a “very dangerous environment”. Earlier this year, the USS Gerald R Ford aircraft carrier returned home after a 326-day deployment, marking the longest US carrier deployment since the Vietnam war. That deployment had reports of a fire and complaints about food shortages. Nancy Lacore, a retired navy rear admiral who served in the navy for 35 years, said in a statement that during her first deployment, she was “operating in that same region as the USS Abraham Lincoln”. “Just like those sailors, when we left our home port on deployment, we knew when we were supposed to come home,” said Lacore, who was ousted by Hegseth in August during his purge of senior US military officials and who is now running for Congress in South Carolina. “We had an end date, and we were counting down to it.” “Then something changed in the region and just as we thought we were heading home, our ship turned around and went back to the Gulf,” she said. “I still remember how mentally crushing it was to realize the date you’ve been holding onto is gone.” People aboard the Lincoln, she said, have “experienced that uncertainty repeatedly”. “Our Sailors are tough and resilient,” she added. “But their resilience shouldn’t be taken for granted or used as an excuse to keep asking more of them without a clear end in sight.” Terri Tanielian, a senior behavioral scientist who has studied deployments and their impact on troops and families, said that prolonged separations are difficult, but that uncertainty over when a deployment will end can make the strain worse. “When families know what they’re planning for, or when an individual knows what they’re planning for … then that is an expectation that they can set themselves up to manage,” she said. But when those expectations change unexpectedly, she said, “like we saw, for example, in 2008, 2009 and 2010 timeframes, and with the deployments there, where we had to keep people for longer, we also saw some increases in the mental strain that the units were facing”, referring to both troops and their families. Responding to the reports about the conditions aboard the Lincoln, Tanielian said it was “heartbreaking to think about the struggles that folks are facing and to feel that they’re kind of feeling that desperate and isolated and perhaps not supported”. Support, she said, needs to extend beyond just ensuring access to psychological support: “It’s also about, are they getting enough sleep? Are they getting reset opportunities? Are they getting the opportunity to exercise? How are we helping them maintain their overall wellbeing?”

title: ‘He had magnetism’: Lula returns to site of political origins to launch fourth-term campaign
author: Tom Phillips in São Bernardo do Campo
summary: Brazil’s president was union chief who led metalworkers’ strikes of 1979-80 that paved the way for return of democracy
body_text: Day after day, tens of thousands of metalworkers would cram on to the football pitch in São Paulo’s industrial suburbs to demand higher wages and, perhaps unwittingly, transform the destiny of Brazil. “You weren’t just documenting a fact – you were documenting history,” said photographer Jesus Carlos, who immortalised the now legendary strikes of 1979 and 1980 with his 24mm lens. As Carlos snapped the sea of downtrodden but tenacious labourers, he remembers sensing the momentous nature of their challenge to Brazil’s military dictatorship, whose foot soldiers would surround the Vila Euclides stadium wielding truncheons and guns. “I was a photographer – but before being a photographer I was a leftie,” recalled the former Communist party activist, now 75. “So I was fully aware what all it meant … [and] that the whole situation would be really important for the future.” Carlos’s instincts were right. The strikes in the industrial city of São Bernardo do Campo – a bold act of defiance against a regime that ruled with an iron fist – were subsequently credited with helping to pave the way for Brazil’s 1985 return to democracy and spawning one of the most influential and enduring politicians in modern Latin American history. For one of the key architects of those walkouts was Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a bushy-bearded, heavy-smoking 33-year-old union chief who became a household name in Brazil and a global icon as a result. The New York Times hailed him as “the continent’s leading working-class hero” and “a Brazilian equivalent of Poland’s Lech Walesa”, the activist who became the European country’s first democratically elected president after the fall of communism. In 1980, Lula helped found what became one of Latin America’s biggest leftwing political movements, the Workers’ party (PT), and in 2002, he was finally elected Brazil’s first working-class president after three unsuccessful attempts. The former lathe operator was re-elected in 2006 and won a historic third term in 2022, helping thwart an attempted coup led by his far-right opponent, the outgoing president Jair Bolsonaro. João de Deus Martinez, a metalworker who came to know Lula during the São Bernardo strikes, said his leadership potential had been obvious to those who saw him charm the throng in Vila Euclides. “There was no one who could beat him up there on the podium … He had this magnetism. People cried [when he spoke] – tears of hope,” recalled the scraggly haired 85-year-old whom Lula calls “Cabeludo” (Shaggy). Nearly 50 years after the São Bernardo strikes catapulted him to fame, Lula, now 80, is preparing to make an emotional return to Vila Euclides to launch the seventh – and final – presidential campaign of a storied life that began in rural poverty and took him to the highest job in the land. On Sunday, thousands of PT supporters are expected to fill the football ground in the city where Lula’s astonishing rise began to watch him fire the starting gun on October’s election. “Vila Euclides is more than a stadium. It’s a symbol of democracy. A cradle of change,” reads the invitation urging party activists to travel to “where it all began” to make their voices heard. Like 2022’s election, when Lula beat Bolsonaro by a whisker, this year’s contest is expected to be tight. Bolsonaro cannot run, after receiving a 27-year jail sentence for plotting to stop Lula taking power. His senator son, Flávio Bolsonaro, will stand in his place, with polls giving Lula a modest lead. “I don’t think it’s going to be a walkaway,” said Lula’s American biographer, John D French, who has charted the leftist’s trajectory since first visiting the ABC Paulista – the industrial region of which São Bernardo is part – in 1980. French called the factory strikes “a unique effervescence” of disgruntlement against worker exploitation and the “ignorant military men” who seized power in 1964 but suddenly found themselves on the back foot. “Nobody knew what was going to happen, which is what made it dramatic, because there were a number of moments when it could have turned into a massacre,” recalled the academic, whose next book focuses on the reporters and photojournalists who chronicled the workers’ rebellion in the heartlands of Brazil’s automotive industry. Memories of that mobilisation, in which famous musicians, intellectuals, film-makers and politicians flocked to the region to champion the metalworkers and demand democracy, remain fresh to this day. “There was an awakening,” said Fernando Ferreira, 67, another photographer who covered the Vila Euclides assemblies. “Brazil is only what it is today because of the ABC.” Ademir Medici, a former newspaper editor who often interviewed Lula for the regional Diário do Grande ABC, said: “It was more exciting than a local derby between Corinthians and Palmeiras. It was thrilling. You thought: can this really be happening in my city? It gave you goose bumps.” Back then, Medici said the buzz around Lula was such that locals would boast of ties to the union boss, however tenuous. “It was cool to go around saying: ‘I’m Lula’s friend! I know Lula! I used to play football with Lula!’” Lula’s newfound fame even earned him a flattering profile in the Brazilian edition of Playboy, in which the interviewer asked the union leader if he would consider posing nude. (Lula declined.) But the ABC has changed dramatically since those heady days of people power, amid factory closures, sociodemographic shifts, union splits, public anger at PT corruption scandals, and a lurch to the right driven by social media and the evangelical church. Once known as the “red belt” – Brazil’s version of the Labour party’s “red wall” in the UK, or a smaller version of the US Democratic party’s “blue wall” – much of the region backed Bolsonaro when he won power in 2018. Today, only one of the seven cities in the ABC has a PT mayor. São Paulo state is governed by Tarcísio de Freitas, a close Bolsonaro ally who looks likely to be re-elected. “If Lula turned up on Marechal Deodoro [São Bernardo’s main street] he’d be booed,” Medici claimed. Dalila Teles Veras, a PT-voting poet and cultural activist who also witnessed the strikes, lamented the rightward drift of an area so crucial to the history of Brazil’s left. “Today, the sons of those [1979] union leaders are grown men who subscribe to fascist ideas,” she said of their support for the Bolsonaros. “How do you switch sides just like that? I keep thinking about those old workers. What if they were still around? They’d die of heartbreak, no doubt.” Veras, 80, had kept faith with Lula, calling him the “kind of leader [who] only comes along once every 100 years or more – if that”. She feared Brazil was facing its “most dangerous year” because of Donald Trump’s efforts to swing the election in favour of Flávio Bolsonaro, by slapping tariffs on Brazilian imports, revoking the visa of Brazil’s US ambassador and championing Lula’s rival as “a smart young man who loves his country”. But Veras was trying to remain upbeat, insisting: “We have to believe – otherwise we’d go mad.” Martinez was also sticking with Lula, despite feeling frustrated that his octogenarian union comrade had failed to nurture an heir. “Lula has one flaw: he never bloody wants anyone to upstage him,” the former Volkswagen factory employee grumbled. As he prepared to return to Vila Euclides’ yellow and black stands on Sunday to witness another historic day, Martinez vowed to vote for Lula, almost certainly for the last time. “I can’t betray my way of thinking,” he said. “He showed us the path.”

title: Alaska candidate for US Senate rejects Kamala Harris’s unsolicited support
author: Adam Gabbatt
summary: Former VP sent fundraising appeal for Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign – with half of donations going to Harris’s organization
body_text: Alaska US Senate candidate Mary Peltola has rejected the support of Kamala Harris, her fellow Democrat, after the 2024 presidential candidate sent out a seemingly unsolicited fundraising appeal on Peltola’s behalf. Harris, who lost Alaska – typically a Republican-voting state – by 13 points during her unsuccessful White House run, on Wednesday sent an email from her political organization to supporters of Peltola, a former US House member. “If there’s anyone who can flip Alaska and secure the Senate majority for Democrats – it’s Mary,” the email, which was signed “Kamala Harris”, said. “But she cannot do it alone.” It asked recipients to donate to Fight for the People Pac, which Harris set up last year. Donations would be split between Harris’s organization and Peltola, the email said. It was a fairly innocuous message and didn’t explicitly endorse Peltola. But the unwanted help was swiftly batted away by the Alaskan’s campaign. “Mary isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 – her focus is and always will be Alaska,” a Peltola spokesperson said in a statement to KTUU that invoked a term for the contiguous US. “That’s why she’s proud to have the endorsement of [the American Federation of Government Employees], the Alaska [American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations], the Alaska [International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers] Local 1547 and more than 10,000 Alaskans who have signed up to volunteer with the campaign.” The campaign was right to be concerned because Peltola’s Republican opponent almost immediately used the email to try to tie Peltola – a moderate Democrat whose campaign has focused on Alaskan issues rather than party politics – to Harris. “Kamala Harris supported the Biden administration’s disastrous anti-Alaska agenda, which is why Alaskans rejected her by double digits,” Nate Adams, a spokesperson for the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, said in a statement. “Alaskans can see exactly whose team Mary Peltola and Kamala Harris are on, and it isn’t Alaska’s.” The episode suggests Harris remains a divisive figure within the Democratic party, even as the former vice-president weighs another run for president. Earlier this year, Harris, who also ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020, left the door open when asked about her future ambitions. “Listen, I might, I might. I’m thinking about it, I’m thinking about it,” Harris said, when US civil rights leader Al Sharpton asked if she was planning to run again. Harris replaced Joe Biden as the Democratic 2024 presidential candidate after questions and concerns about Biden’s fitness as he initially ran for re-election became inescapable. With only 107 days to run her campaign, she lost the electoral college and the popular vote to Donald Trump to hand him a second presidency.

title: Marco Rubio has unique power to promote peace, but he hasn’t. He is almost as bad for the world as Trump
author: Simon Tisdall
summary: As chief US diplomat, Rubio could do great good. His pandering and neglect are a disgrace we shouldn’t ignore, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
body_text: Viewed from the state department in Washington DC, the world is on fire – but record heatwaves are not to blame. The unresolved Iran war has badly burned Donald Trump. His military campaign conclusively failed, energy and food prices are still rising, and a Republican rout in November’s midterm elections looms. Humiliatingly, Israel this week flatly rejected his latest Gaza peace proposals, days after Trump congratulated himself on a “historic breakthrough”. In Europe, Russia’s attacks on Nato allies grow increasingly brazen, threatening a wider escalation. The Ukraine war, which Trump vowed to end, is now well into its fifth year, with civilians on both sides caught in the killing fields. And these are just the bigger firestorms. There are plenty more. Rarely has the need for effective, professional diplomacy been more pressing. So step forward Marco Rubio, US secretary of state and chief American diplomat. These are challenges that, if successfully tackled, could propel the 55-year-old son of Cuban immigrants and the former US senator for Florida into pole position in the 2028 Republican presidential nomination race. Here is a chance for Rubio to defy critics who dismiss him as a lickspittle and Trump dogsbody, and transform himself into respected global statesman. His boss mocked him as “little Marco” and a “loser” when they were election rivals in 2016. (Rubio called him a conman.) Now is Rubio’s opportunity to go big, be brave and prove he’s a winner. Or maybe not. Rubio is unlike recent US secretaries of state – heavyweights such as Hillary Clinton and Antony Blinken, or John Kerry, famed for his high-energy shuttle diplomacy. Rubio has little time for “peace processes”. Instead, he projects brute US power to impose take-it-or-leave-it “solutions” that advance US interests, as defined by Trump. It’s a modern form of imperialism. Target countries have a choice: become client states, like Venezuela and, prospectively, Cuba and Greenland, or be crushed. In Iran, the policy is not regime change, let alone democratic renewal. It’s regime compliance. Rubio behaves less like a peace-broker, more like a pith-helmeted colonial viceroy demanding fealty from obsequious satraps. Speaking in Munich in February, Rubio aired his hawkishly retro doctrine of US primacy. He lamented the decline of “the great western empires … accelerated by godless communist revolutions and anti-colonial uprisings” and warned Europe faced “civilisational erasure”. The US didn’t want milksop allies “shackled by guilt and shame” about their imperial past, he said. “We want allies who are proud of their culture and heritage … and who, together with us, are willing and able to defend it.” Here was a familiar assertion of US hegemony, but one stripped of bogus altruism and pretence. It sounded a death knell for diplomacy. Trump has attacked eight countries in the past year. Cuba, Rubio’s obsession, could be next. Rubio’s reluctance to get personally involved in peacemaking may be partly explained by his other, contradictory role, as Trump’s national security adviser. He has accepted the White House’s outsourcing of negotiations over Ukraine and Palestine to amateur envoys of limited ability – namely Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and business crony Steve Witkoff. Broadly speaking, Rubio has steered clear of direct involvement in the Iran talks, too, leaving JD Vance, the vice-president and his main potential rival in 2028, to take the flak. Rubio’s arm’s length approach smacks of calculation. Or maybe he’s just out of his depth. Maybe he has no clear idea what he, Marco, really thinks about any of these issues and simply does Trump’s erratic bidding. This perception of a political chameleon lacking firm principles, consistent opinions and a strong moral compass is reinforced by his record. His biographer, Manuel Roig-Franzia, believes Rubio’s personal and political slipperiness – he once became a Mormon, then reverted to Catholicism – is rooted in a childhood need to belong, to be on the winning side, no matter the price. Senator Rubio was a China hawk. Now he toes Trump’s ingratiating line on Beijing. He used to castigate Russia; now he’s an appeaser. He championed overseas assistance but, in office, has gutted USAID and seeks to dismantle the international criminal court, a keystone of global order. He blasted Barack Obama’s Iran nuclear deal. Now he backs an accord that would offer additional concessions to Tehran. Accused by the Vatican of waging an immoral, unjust war, he travelled to Rome and set the pope straight. The irony, or tragedy, of the Rubio conundrum is he has the power to do great good, if only he would stand up and be counted. Russia’s Vladimir Putin, losing on the battlefield and at home, is weaker than at any time since 2022. Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy is short of missile interceptors, soldiers and political support. A ceasefire deal freezing the conflict is there for the making by the only country – the US – that can meaningfully squeeze both sides. Likewise, in Israel, the architect of the Gaza genocide and disastrous wars with Hamas, Iran and Hezbollah – Benjamin Netanyahu – faces defeat in October’s elections. Here’s a rare opportunity to quietly shelve Trump’s Board of Peace idiocies, halt Jewish settler violence in the West Bank and make a fresh, inclusive start based on UN resolutions. Rubio could also do the Middle East, the global economy, American consumers and himself a power of good by taking charge of moribund peace talks with Iran and resuscitating the June memorandum of understanding that Tehran insists is the only route out of the strait of Hormuz logjam. In doing so, Rubio would have the enthusiastic backing of most Americans, European and Gulf state governments, energy producers and businesses, and Maga supporters who rightly fear Trump has dragged the US into another forever war. Even Trump may be grateful. He knows he’s in a hole. He needs someone to dig him out. The fact that Rubio, despite his ostensibly uniquely powerful position, is unlikely to do any of the above marks him out as the most dangerous man in the US administration after Trump himself. He is dangerous because he enables and facilitates Trump’s worst instincts – and neglects his duty. He is dangerous because he provides pseudo-intellectual respectability to far-right fantasies about unfettered US supremacy. More so than the impetuous Vance, indulging in puerile name-calling on social media, and the “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth, a ranting ultra-nationalist, Rubio is dangerous because he can look and sound reasonable. He stands a fair chance of becoming Trump’s chosen successor and heir to the Maga brand. Maybe, before that happens, he will change again. Maybe he will rediscover a few principles, find a diplomatic backbone, extinguish a few fires. He has shown repeatedly that his views are infinitely fungible. Rubio could yet do great things. Or he could become a problem as great or greater than Trump. Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

title: Trump’s midterm malaise: endless war and high prices could spell doom for Republicans in November
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: ‘Complete unraveling’ of Trump and Republican project reflects attitude of not caring at all about governance
body_text: He was always one step ahead. Donald Trump won the US presidency as a wildly unlikely outsider in 2016 and staged an astonishing comeback to win it again in 2024. Even his foes grudgingly called him a political savant with an intuition for exploiting grievances that left so-called experts floundering. But now they are asking if the dark genius has lost his touch. Trump is trapped in the quagmire of an unpopular war, obsessing over monuments in Washington and looking for a new spokesperson after his White House press secretary quit. If the 80-year-old was deliberately trying to sabotage his Republican party in November’s midterm elections, it is not clear what he would do differently. “He’s always had a reptilian political instinct for public opinion that has served him well,” said Charlie Sykes, a conservative author and broadcaster. “You’re not seeing that much any more. You’re not seeing his ability to read the room. He seems tone-deaf on issues like the cost of living, the war, and the optics of gilding everything in sight and enshittifying Washington and he doesn’t care.” Trump campaigned on promises to lower prices and keep the US out of foreign entanglements and forever wars. The opposite has happened. Voters say they are suffering a cost of living crisis, exacerbated by Trump’s sweeping tariffs. Buying food to eat at home has become 33% more expensive in US cities since the beginning of 2019, according to government figures. Gas prices are at a record high for this time of year, in part thanks to the US war in Iran, which drags on with no end in sight. While Trump claims to have destroyed Iran’s military capabilities, it emerged this week that he was forced to hide in a catering truck and secretly swap planes after a Nato summit in Turkey because of a possible Iranian assassination plot. The administration’s entanglement has metastasised into a gruelling, daily haemorrhage of resources, currently costing the taxpayer an estimated $1bn a day. Critics argue the administration has strengthened Iran’s resolve and provided it with global leverage, specifically over the strait of Hormuz. They see it as betrayal of the noninterventionist posture that fuelled Trump’s rise to power and attracted a generation of disaffected voters. Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, said: “What we’re watching right now is the complete unraveling of everything that Donald Trump, Maga and Republicans said they were about. They were against endless conflicts in the Middle East and they started a conflict in the Middle East without an exit strategy. They were supposed to be about no more spending American dollars abroad; we’re spending a billion dollars a day on this war without an end.” Yet the president appears to have other, more aesthetic concerns. Since returning to power last year, the longtime property developer has invested much time and energy in construction projects across Washington, including a White House ballroom and helipad, a triumphal arch and an ill-fated makeover of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. Bardella added: “As he continues this misadventure in the Middle East that has resulted in the cost of living going up, and continues to pour resources into putting his name on shit and building ballrooms and monuments to himself, the American people are going: what the fuck? That’s the only realistic reaction you could have when you objectively look at the circumstances.” Trump’s second term has been defined by thinking big – Greenland, Venezuela, Iran – and thinking small. The board he appointed to the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts added his name to the complex, only for a judge to order that it be removed; this week the board voted to add “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump” beneath the main sign. According to Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump, written by New York Times journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, the president has been seen with a tube of super glue trying to stick golden decorations to the marble fireplace in the Oval Office. Haberman estimates that Trump now devotes 70% of his mental space to renovation projects and “monuments to self”. She told Axios’s Behind the Curtain video series that she and Swan visited Trump in the Oval Office in March. “You would think that on the 17th day of the war that he would have maps of the Middle East or maps of troop deployments – who knows,” she said. “He picks up these pictures, and [they’re] of maple trees, and he says: ‘I am choosing maple trees for the White House. I am good at picking trees.’ I’m paraphrasing here, but that is pretty much what he said.” The president’s preoccupation with whether columns for his ballroom are more evocative of Athens or Rome, and with other efforts to preserve his legacy in marble, come as little surprise to Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill and longtime Trump critic. She said: “Donald Trump has been an egomaniac, a narcissist his entire life. Even in the private sector he has slapped his name on buildings and a multitude of failed branding businesses from Trump steaks to Trump airline to Trump University to Trump water to Trump wine. Why is anyone surprised that he would take that same type of narcissism and bring it over to his role in his second-term as president when he’s spending other people’s money to do it? “The problem has been that the Republican party has enabled him to get away with this and to their own detriment, which is why more and more people in his inner circle are concerned about how this is going to impact the midterms and control of Congress.” Indeed, Republicans are said to be quietly panicking about Trump costing them the House of Representatives and putting even the Senate in jeopardy. A national Quinnipiac University Poll released late last month showed his job approval rating dropping to an all-time low of 32%, with 58% disapproval. It found six in 10 Americans oppose the US military action in Iran. Past presidents such as George W Bush in 2006 and Barack Obama in 2010 have faced challenging midterms but worked with their parties in an effort to at least stem the losses. Rick Wilson, co-founder of the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, said: “In both those cases their efforts were not successful, but it’s nightmarish to think what that would have been if Barack Obama had been saying, ‘I’m going to build a basketball arena at the White House,’ or George Bush had said, ‘I’m gonna build a golf course.’ “Instead you’ve got a very different visual from this White House and that visual is 'we don’t care about anything else except for the ballroom and the arch and all the throw-away ephemera that he wants to focus on. It’s a terrible political look and it’s quite dangerous for the party because they have nothing to run on right now.” The sense of malaise deepened this week when Karoline Leavitt, the youngest person ever to serve as White House press secretary, announced that she will be stepping down at the end of the month. The official explanation was that the 28-year-old wants to spend more time with her young family but the timing was unfortunate for an administration struggling to spin its way out of one crisis after another. For a president whose entire self-image is built on winning, the realisation that he is facing electoral defeat at home and humiliation abroad could be cause for an existential crisis. Sykes observed that, while Trump’s historical literacy is notoriously thin, he has begun to obsess over the ghosts of presidencies ruined by foreign blunders. “It’s awfully interesting that in the Maggie Haberman book he’s comparing himself to Napoleon and Alexander the Great and Caesar but his deepest fear right now is that he’s going to be Herbert Hoover or Jimmy Carter,” he said. Trump’s cloud does have a golden lining, however. He made an estimated $2.2bn during the first year of his second term thanks to cryptocurrency holdings, foreign interests and his Truth Social business. Sykes added: “He hasn’t lowered the cost of living, he hasn’t made America more respected, he hasn’t won the war but he has succeeded in making himself a billionaire many times over by abusing his office.”

title: US law to investigate foodborne illness outbreaks has been delayed for 15 years
author: Jessica Glenza
summary: Law was set to go into effect in January, months before cyclosporiasis outbreak, but now is set for 2028
body_text: Congress passed a law to help federal agencies investigate outbreaks of foodborne illness – a regulation experts said could have stopped the US’s largest cyclosporiasis outbreak much sooner. The only problem? The rule has been delayed – for 15 years, including most recently amid lobbying in 2025. It was set to go into effect in January 2026, months before the single-celled parasite sickened more than 24,000 people and killed two in the midwest. Now, it won’t go into effect until 2028. “Congress recognized this issue in 2010 and asked [the Food and Drug Administration, or FDA] to develop solutions,” said Sara Sorscher, an attorney who specializes in food safety at the Center for Science in the Public Interest, a consumer advocacy group. “We are now 16 years in, and we still don’t have enforcement of this rule that’s meant to deal with exactly this type of situation.” Often called the “traceability rule”, the regulation comes from the Food Safety and Modernization Act (FSMA) of 2011, passed during the Obama administration. The regulation requires enhanced record-keeping for high-risk foods – namely, those which have a history of making people sick, such as soft cheese, leafy greens, eggs and peanut butter – “for persons who manufacture, process, pack, or hold foods”. The promise of the traceability rule is to allow the FDA to more quickly and accurately pinpoint where tainted food came from, all the way down to the farm. However, the rule has raised the hackles of some in the food supply chain, and retailers and food manufacturers have been particularly vocal about their concerns, lobbying reports show. “It’s pretty crazy,” said Jennifer McIntire, founder of the food safety consulting firm Food Strategy, about the lengthy implementation of the rule. Earlier this month, a group of 11 consumer, public health and labor advocates called on Congress to speed up implementation of the rule in a letter to lawmakers – arguing this summer’s cyclospora outbreak caused a “crisis in consumer confidence”. “It’s probably getting close to 30,000 people – 95% of all the illnesses occur in the 15 states that have Taco Bell and Taylor Farms,” said Bill Marler, a leading food safety attorney, about the cyclosporiasis outbreak. He is representing more than 400 people sickened in the outbreak, and has publicly said he supports the groups’ letter. The heart of uncovering the culprit in a foodborne illness outbreak is the “traceback”. Local health departments are the first line of defense – they find out who ate what and where – a restaurant, a bagged salad, a carton of eggs. Then federal agencies, including the FDA, find out where potentially contaminated food came from by following the supply chain back from a restaurant or grocer to distributors, packing operations and farms. “For example, let’s do packaged salad – lettuce and greens,” said David Lennarz, who co-founded Registrar Corp, a supply chain company that helps businesses comply with federal food safety regulations. “Some of the products you can buy are multiple types of greens – you could have radicchio, spinach, you could have lettuce. Those could be coming from completely different sources and then are all packaged up.” The current tracking system in the US derives from the Bioterrorism Act of 2003, according to Jennifer McEntire, founder of the food safety consulting firm Food Strategy. In the years following September 11, 2001, and amid the anthrax threats sent to senior US officials in its aftermath, “it was recognized that food was a critical infrastructure, and that FDA had no idea – no authority – to know what food facilities even existed in the United States. And that was a loophole that was closed through the Bioterrorism Act,” said McEntire. That left the US with its current system, often called, “one up, one back” – meaning a restaurant or retailer needs to document where they bought something, and a distributor or manufacturer needs to know where they sold something. Still, this system left food traceback incredibly difficult. “I think FDA does a pretty darn good job, but tracebacks are very, very challenging,” said Lennarz. Determining where individual greens came from is hard because, per a group representing US farmers, data related to where the crop originated is often lost at the point where cases from farms are combined into pallets, which are then loaded on to trucks. “Since a field of leafy greens can go to multiple restaurants or multiple homes, we want to be able to find any lettuce that is offending and gather it and pull it back as quickly as possible,” said De Ann Davis, vice-president of science for the Western Growers Association, which represents farmers and supports the traceability rule. The stakes are high for farmers – the price of lettuce dropped more than 16% in July, according to government inflation data, as consumers dropped lettuces. Davis said farmers have collected data on where cases of their produce goes for more than a decade as part of a voluntary initiative called the Produce Traceability Initiative. “If post-when-we-ship it is not traced well, or tracked well, there is very little our grower can do about it,” said Davis. The government’s traceability rule would require manufacturers and sellers to retain that information, so that it can be provided to the FDA in the case of contamination. Even as food safety advocates and growers promote traceability, some of the most intense lobbying has come from retailers and food industry groups. The Food Industry Association (FMI) described traceability as “the most complex regulation the food industry has ever faced” in a recent statement, and retailers made their “concerns” about the regulation known to lawmakers and regulators, lobbying reports show. In 2024, the Reagan-Udall Foundation for the FDA, a private nonprofit created by Congress during the Bush-era, held a roundtable with representatives of the food industry, from behemoths to influential restaurant groups. Among the attendees were Chipotle, Kellogg Company, the midwestern convenience store chain Kwik Trip, the National Restaurant Association, the National Grocers Association and McDonald’s. In a summary of the event published by Reagan-Udall, industry representatives argued traceability would “potentially require significant increases in labor, equipment, and space, with significant associated costs”, according to a 2024 industry roundtable with an FDA-affiliated nonprofit. From 2024 to 2025, lobbyists for FMI, the southern giant Publix Super Markets, the National Retail Federation and the International Food Service Distributors Association all lobbied on the traceability rule. The National Retail Federation (NRF), whose board of directors includes food heavyweights such as Albertson’s, Walmart and Target said in lobbying disclosure reports that it was “requesting inclusion of language in FY24 Agriculture Appropriations bill to require FDA to work collaboratively with industry to address concerns with FMSA 204 traceability rule”, and that it was “seeking support” for a bill that would relax food traceability requirements, introduced by a House Republican from Florida. NRF also expressed “concerns with FMSA 204 traceability rule” to the House, Senate, FDA and CDC, according to lobbying reports. After all this lobbying, the industry got part of what it wanted – another delay. In March 2025, the FDA announced a 30-month delay in enforcement of the traceability rule. In November 2025, Congress ended a historic 43-day government shutdown with a budget bill. Buried in the massive appropriations act was an important provision for food safety: Congress prohibited enforcement of the traceability rule until July 2028 – the same provision that consumer groups asked lawmakers to rescind in a letter this month. In a statement, FMI said: “The food industry shares FDA’s commitment to strengthening food traceability, protecting public health and assisting with foodborne illness investigations to quickly identify and remove potentially contaminated products from commerce. FMI and our member companies have put in a tremendous amount of time, effort and resources over the last four years to understand and implement the FDA Food Traceability Rule.” FMI continued: “It is extraordinarily complex and requires unprecedented coordination among growers, manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers, retailers and foodservice operators. Having adequate time is essential for addressing operational realities and developing practical, workable solutions across the entire food supply chain without increasing costs or disrupting the flow of goods. We look forward to continuing to work with FDA to ensure that the rule reflects the goals of the 2011 Food Safety Modernization Act and that food companies of all sizes are able to comply.” The Guardian also contacted NRF and Publix Super Markets for comment, but did not receive a response. But for some advocates like Marler, whose law firm handles cases of victims who may be severely injured or even killed by food contamination, the delays are nothing short of inconceivable. The traceability rule “allows product to get off the market faster so less people get sick – all of those things are good for industry, whose product is being besmirched by one entity”, said Marler. “These grown white men who run these organizations are acting like 2-year-olds… They just don’t want to be told what to do.”

title: California law would force companies to disclose toxic chemicals in disposable diapers
author: Tom Perkins
summary: Legislation requiring disclosure of chemicals in diapers passed assembly and will go before state senate soon
body_text: New California legislation would require manufacturers to disclose the “mystery cocktail” of toxic chemicals used in disposable diapers. Diapers often contain among the most toxic substances – phthalates, lead, Pfas, quats, arsenic, a range of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and “fragrance”, which can include any number of 1,200 compounds thought to be hazardous to human health. The risk is especially high because diapers press against an infant’s skin almost continuously for several years and babies’ skin is thinner than adult skin and prone to absorbing dangerous substances. Many of the chemicals, like phthalates, attack the endocrine system, potentially causing hormones that are essential for brain and reproductive development to misfire. While manufacturers are not required to fully disclose materials and ingredients in any state but New York, the California law goes further. It passed the California assembly 68-1 and is expected to go before the state senate in coming weeks. Advocates say the passage would be powerful because it would put tremendous market pressure on diaper manufacturers to use less toxic ingredients. “Parents deserve better than a guessing game, especially when it comes to a product that will be touching their babies’ skin for every minute of every day for the first two or three years of their lives,” said the California assembly member Marc Berman, who authored the bill. It is supported by a coalition of at least 150 public health groups. The bill would require companies by 2028 to disclose on a publicly accessible webpage a list of all intentionally added ingredients, and each ingredient’s specific function or purpose in the diaper. By 1 January 2029, diaper manufacturers have to include that information on the packaging. Toxic chemicals are often added to diapers to provide a range of functions. Pfas are used as a moisture barrier, formaldehyde could be added as a preservative and phthalates are added to make plastic flexible. Lead or other heavy metals may be added to inks and dyes. Testing commissioned by the Mamavation public health advocacy site found Pfas in a range of popular brands. French regulators detected widespread use of chemicals like formaldehyde, pesticides and dioxins, while other peer-reviewed research identified numerous VOCs in disposable hygiene products and diapers. However, there is a dearth of research on how these steady exposures affect babies. A small 2025 study in China checked diapers and urine samples in 66 babies for several phthalates, finding correlation for some of the compounds. The study also found markers of DNA damage in the urine, and the researchers estimated that absorption of the phthalates likely accounted for major portions of the phthalate levels. The study, however, does not establish that wearing diapers causes DNA damage or other disease, but points to a risk. “California parents shouldn’t need a chemistry degree to buy a diaper,” said Susan Little of the Environmental Working Group, which helped develop the legislation. They deserve to know exactly what is touching their child’s skin.” The Center for Baby and Adult Hygiene Products, a trade group representing many top manufacturers, previously said: “Diapers are designed and manufactured to meet strict safety standards, and decades of real-world use support their safety for infants and children.” Advocates said industry has claimed the ingredients are covered by confidential business information laws that protect companies’ formulas in products from being shared with competitors. Advocates say the laws do not cover diaper ingredients. The bill’s sponsors stop short of a ban of any chemicals because industry pressure would probably kill any such legislation. California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, who has indicated he is running for the Democratic nomination for president, also has a history of vetoing strong chemical legislation that is opposed by industry or his donors. This legislation has a real shot at passing and is important because it would create tremendous public pressure on companies to act while also boosting nontoxic brands, advocates say. “Transparency laws can move the marketplace,” said Oriene Shin, safety advocacy manager with the Consumer Reports non-profit, which has performed testing that identified toxic chemicals in diapers. “When a customer can compare ingredients, manufacturers have an incentive to follow what the consumer wants, instead of deciding what to do based on internal analyses,” she added. Other states often follow California’s lead on environmental and consumer protection laws, so it could create even more market pressure, as similar laws around toxic chemicals previously have. New York now requires some labeling, but the new legislation goes further. There are plenty of concrete, easy things parents can do to protect their kids – like choosing fragrance-free diapers. Cloth diapers are typically better options, though they are not always chemical-free as dyes, detergents, waterproofing agents and other components can still include toxic compounds. The Environmental Working Group’s safe diaper guide evaluates diaper ingredients, and the non-profit also provides recommendations for products that meet its standards, though companies pay for the EWG-certified label. Mamavation provides a list of which diapers it tested do or do not contain Pfas. Parents should be skeptical of claims like “natural”, “plant-based” and “eco-friendly”, which have no legal definition and do not necessarily mean the diapers are nontoxic. Parents can also contact diaper manufacturers and ask whether they use Pfas, phthalates, heavy metals or other substances.

title: ‘Outrageous’ handcuffing of New Orleans journalist sends ‘chilling message,’ says media group
author: Ramon Antonio Vargas in New Orleans
summary: Danny Monteverde had been protesting the closure of a courtroom during indictment of state attorney general
body_text: The “outrageous” handcuffing of a New Orleans journalist covering the indictment in July of Louisiana’s attorney general – a case that ultimately was dismissed – conveyed “a chilling message to members of the press and the public” for which there is no excuse, according to a prominent media rights advocacy organization. An attorney for the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (RCFP) made those assertions in a recent letter to the New Orleans criminal district courthouse where deputies temporarily detained WWL Louisiana investigative producer Danny Monteverde and outlet lawyer Elana Beiser in the course of their duties in early July. Beiser and Monteverde, whose station is a Guardian reporting partner, were trying to object to judge Leon Roche’s closure of the courtroom where a grand jury had handed up an indictment against state attorney general, Liz Murrill, on accusations that she had threatened the jobs of Democratic New Orleans officials who fought a Republican-led overhaul. A 5 August letter from RCFP attorney Virginia Hamrick to New Orleans criminal court chief judge contended that there were “no findings justifying closure” and urged the courthouse to “properly hear and consider objections of the public and the press before any … proceedings are closed”. “Refrain from detaining reporters (or their counsel) who are simply exercising their constitutional rights,” which include the access to court proceedings, Hamrick’s letter continued. The missive added that such “outrageous actions send a chilling message to members of the press and the public who may seek to object to closure in the future”. “Members of the public – including journalists – should not fear being hauled away in handcuffs merely for asserting these basic rights,” Hamrick went on, saying open access to court proceedings “informs the public, ensures an accurate portrayal of proceedings and promotes government accountability”. The letter alluded to arguments from Roche that he closed the courtroom where the indictment had been handed up – and outside which Monteverde and Beiser were handcuffed – in order “to protect grand jurors’ safety and anonymity”. “But such concerns do not warrant the closure of a courtroom without hearing objections to such closure,” Hamrick’s letter said. “Moreover, there is no excuse for deputies to handcuff reporters and counsel asking to be heard.” Hamrick’s letter also offered the New Orleans criminal courthouse “comprehensive and collaborative training regarding the importance and legality of access to judicial proceedings” from the RCFP, whose steering committee members include highly regarded former Washington Post editor-in-chief Marty Baron and Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg. The Guardian reached out to Lombard, Roche and WWL for comment. Prior to Monteverde and Beiser’s handcuffing, there had been months of political tensions between Louisiana Republicans and New Orleans Democrats over a law that eliminated a court clerk position won in an election by Calvin Duncan, who spent nearly three decades in prison in connection to a murder that he was exonerated of having committed. New Orleans leaders opposed the elimination of that office, which was consolidated with another post. And they unsuccessfully attempted to schedule an election that would have given Duncan a chance to win the consolidated clerk job. Amid that politicking, Murrill issued letters to New Orleans officials warning them that their offices could be taken from them as well for purportedly violating state “usurper” laws, which prohibit supporting an unauthorized officeholder. A New Orleans grand jury then voted to return an indictment against Murrill charging her with intimidation and malfeasance. Louisiana law requires grand jury returns to be made in open court. So when Roche tried to clear out and close the courtroom where Murrill’s indictment would be returned on 2 July, Monteverde and Beiser protested. The courtroom was nonetheless emptied and closed. Deputies then ordered Monteverde and Beiser to leave the courthouse – a public building – entirely, and temporarily handcuffed the pair after they protested again. A statement issued on 3 July by WWL said “no … journalist should be detained for seeking transparency or asking questions about access to a courtroom, particularly when state law provides for proceedings to occur in open court”. Roche later indicated in court filings that he never instructed deputies to “detain any members of the media”. The sheriff’s office, which provides courthouse security, for its part said that its deputies “acted in accordance with the directives they received” to protect grand jurors and other proceeding participants. Louisiana’s state supreme court put the case against Murrill on hold almost immediately, ruling that procedures surrounding the indictment had not been properly followed. A special prosecutor brought in to handle the case then dismissed the case against Murrill on 22 July – a day after she was urged to do so by a letter from New Orleans district attorney Jason Williams, mayor Helena Moreno and five city council members. Murrill reacted to the dismissal of the case by saying: “What I did was not a crime – it was never a crime. I think this was a malicious prosecution.” Meanwhile, the letter from Williams, Moreno (herself a former broadcast journalist) and the others said: “The people of New Orleans are not served by this prosecution, which continues to alienate the city from the rest of the state and distract from the important work we have ahead.” The Associated Press contributed reporting
