title: Why cancer, not cost of living, may be the biggest issue in Iowa’s midterm elections
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: A broad group of diseases in the agricultural powerhouse is top of mind for the midterm elections
body_text: In Iowa, one of the key battleground states in November’s midterm elections, just about every political candidate agrees on one thing: something must be done about the state’s rising rates of cancer. The midwestern state has the second-highest rate of cancer nationwide and, together with Utah and West Virginia, is one of only three states where the incidence of the disease is rising, according to cancer rate monitoring from the National Institute on Minority Health and Health Disparities. Promises to address the issue are now top of mind for candidates ahead of the 3 November elections, in which Iowa may play an important role in deciding control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s term. Republicans hoping to preserve their party’s dominance of the state and Democrats who believe conditions are right for them to win key races have pledged to make fighting the disease a priority. Where they differ is in their views over the degree to which the state’s powerhouse farm economy has contributed to making Iowans sick, and what to do about it. “I think state leadership and industrial agriculture are very hesitant to have those conversations, but I think the Iowa public is calling and demanding action and conversation and answers in a way that both parties are needing to respond, and [that’s] why it has become the campaign issue of this upcoming election,” said Sarah Green, executive director of the Iowa Environmental Council, a non-partisan group whose research into the disease’s prevalence has helped fuel public awareness of the crisis. Iowa’s cancer rates followed national trends until 2012, when they began climbing upwards for reasons that Green said remain unclear. Cancer includes a broad group of diseases, and many aspects of life, from stress to food to environment, can modify someone’s risk. What’s plain is the importance to voters – one survey has cancer ranked as the top issue facing the state, eclipsing even the cost of living. In the race for the state’s open US Senate seat, Democrat Josh Turek whose spina bifida he attributes to his father’s exposure to Agent Orange during the Vietnam war, has brought up his sister’s struggle with breast cancer, while his opponent, the Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson, has emphasized her attempts to reform health policy in Washington. Candidates of both parties vying for the state’s four Republican-held US House districts have battled over who would be better suited to channel federal resources to the state’s needs. In the race to replace the incumbent governor, Kim Reynolds, Zach Lahn won an upset victory in the Republican primary with the support of a Pac connected to the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, and both he and his Democratic opponent, Rob Sand, have unveiled lengthy plans to curb rates of the disease. “The road I live on, I think there’s only one family that has not dealt with some kind of cancer,” said Seth Watkins, a longtime farmer in south-west Iowa who sees the emphasis on fighting the disease – and potentially changing the state’s approach to agriculture – as long overdue. “We have a farm policy that has resulted in less soil, less biodiversity in wild species, more cancer, fewer farmers and fewer opportunities. I mean, at some point, wouldn’t people just look at that data and say, you know, maybe we should do something different?” ‘Taboo’ conversations Iowa is the top producer of corn and pork in the US and one of the largest growers of soy, and agriculture generates a third of the state’s economic output and a fifth of its jobs. But that immense productivity comes at a cost: Iowa’s farmers use more fertilizer than those of any other state, and it also leads in the number of concentrated animal feeding operations (Cafos), which are part of the meat processing supply chain and generate runoff. Green pointed out that Iowa also had relatively few regulations intended to keep pesticides and farm runoff, which can be heavy with cancer-linked nitrates, away from people and out of water supplies. In 2022, Iowa’s overall rate of cancer was approximately 506 cases per 100,000 people, higher than the national average of 442 per 100,000 people, according to National Institutes of Health data. It also has elevated rates of non-Hodgkin lymphoma and acute myeloid leukemia, two cancers that some studies have found may be linked to glyphosate, the herbicide marketed as Roundup that is the most used in the state. Agriculture’s impact on Iowans has recently become pronounced, even for people that have nothing to do with farming. Some Iowa waterways are among the most polluted by nitrates in the US, and last year the water utility serving Des Moines, the state’s capital and largest city, announced its first-ever lawn watering ban because levels of the compounds in the rivers from which it draws its water supply had hit near-record levels. The utility ordered water rationed again this summer. When the Iowa Environmental Council last year dispatched researchers across the midwestern state to learn more about how cancer was affecting its residents, Green said talking about the link with agriculture was often regarded as a “taboo”. “Iowans knew there were issues, but felt like they were not supported by their state and by elected officials in, one, hearing their stories, and then two, addressing and recognizing real challenges that Iowans are experiencing a health crisis,” said Green, whose group convened the 16 listening sessions together with the Iowa Farmers Union and Drake University’s Harkin Institute, a public policy thinktank. There are other factors connected to cancer diagnoses in Iowa – its residents face a higher risk of exposure to naturally occurring radon, and this year the state legislature approved a law mandating that mitigation systems be installed in new homes. Under Reynolds, the state has also sought to curb alcohol and tobacco use, and in June the GOP-dominated legislature approved a $320m investment in water quality. But Green said that measure offered relatively little new funding and “doesn’t address pollution at the source”. The gubernatorial candidates Lahn and Sand came out against a June supreme court ruling making it more difficult for people who believe they contracted cancer from exposure to Roundup to sue its manufacturer. The Republican Lahn’s campaign platform has largely focused on incentivizing farmers to change their ways to prevent water pollution, while accusing major chemical manufacturers of misleading Iowans about their products’ safety. “We all know something is terribly wrong, but too many politicians from Washington DC to Des Moines have had their heads stuck in the sand while big ag and big pharma printed money. This will not go on when I’m governor,” Lahn said after winning the nomination in June. His Democratic opponent, Sand, has called cancer “the top issue on everyone’s mind no matter what part of the state I’m in, and rightfully so”, and proposed measures to better manage farmers’ use of manure, test for radon and help farms enroll in conservation programs. Neither has as aggressive a platform as Chris Jones, the Democratic candidate for state agriculture secretary. A former University of Iowa researcher, he wrote a popular blog that explored the state’s water quality issues, but stopped writing it after, he told the Iowa Capital Dispatch, two Republican state senators threatened the university’s funding over his writings. One of the lawmakers denied the allegations, and Jones later left the school. Jones is proposing a wholesale transformation of the state’s approach to farming to reduce its impact on water quality. His platform includes zoning changes to address the environmental effects of Cafos and a “strategic retreat” from growing corn for ethanol, a top cash crop for the state’s farmers. “We know radon is a driver of lung cancer here. Well, guess what? We have policies to help reduce exposure to radon,” Jone said. “The same could be said for nitrate and drinking water. Let’s develop policies that reduce that risk.” The incumbent agriculture secretary, Mike Naig, a Republican and former lobbyist for Monsanto, the manufacturer of Roundup that’s now part of Bayer, did not respond to an interview request sent to his campaign. ‘The Lobe Rangers’ Some farmers aren’t waiting for the election results to change their agricultural practices. Last March, three farmers in north-central Iowa announced themselves as “the Lobe Rangers”, unveiling a website complete with a logo of a masked man standing amid the corn in which they made their case for how it is possible to farm profitably without harming themselves or the environment.. “This has been boiling underneath the surface for me for 15 years, and the reason I think we launched is that we just kind of had enough. We saw the inaction of the political class and the ag lobbying leadership class of putting up the same nonsense,” said Zack Smith, a corn and soybean farmer who is one of the rangers. The group – which took its name from a particularly fertile part of the state called the Des Moines lobe – follows the state’s nutrient-reduction strategy, a blueprint to keep nitrates out of the state’s waterways and the far-off Gulf of Mexico that’s only voluntary, but which the rangers insist works. Watkins, who works land his great-grandfather first cultivated in 1848, has in recent years downsized what was once a 4,000-acre (1,600-hectare) farm, helping younger farmers grow diversified crops on smaller plots of land. The change in tack follows more than three decades of Watkins farming at scale and growing more disillusioned by an industry that depends heavily on federal subsidies while exacting a worsening toll on the environment. “I feel like we’re mining instead of practicing agriculture. And, you know, show me an area, whether it’s the oil industry or mining or any of that, where when the resources are gone, the people are better off,” Watkins said. Watching the state’s political class focus on cancer, and by extension, water quality, had been a curious experience, since it had been a concern of theirs for more than a decade, said Smith. While the group – which has not endorsed any candidates – doubt any single election can reverse Iowa’s frightening health trajectory, it can at least make a step in the right direction. “It’s definitely not gonna be solved by what’s gonna happen in the election in 2026,” said Smith. “We’ll maybe start making some steps in the right direction, but this is going to be something that is going to take a lot of change at a lot of different levels.” • This article was amended on 16 August 2026. An earlier version referred to glyphosate as a fertilizer; it is an herbicide.

title: Todd Blanche declines to pledge independence from White House
author: Michael Sainato
summary: US attorney general says no one in his role ‘should ever’ make this vow amid concern over Trump steering DoJ
body_text: US attorney general Todd Blanche on Sunday declined to assure that the federal justice department he helms would always act independently of the White House and Donald Trump. “No, I’m not going to pledge that,” he said when asked about the topic by NBC’s Meet the Press host, Kristen Welker. “And no attorney general should ever pledge that.” Blanche also claimed Trump would never ask him to do something that crosses an ethical or legal line – after the president dismissed his predecessor, Pam Bondi, having become frustrated over insufficient action from the justice department against Trump’s political foes. “The president will never ask me to do something unethical or legal or illegal,” Blanche told Welker. “He never has. He never will. And no, I have – I swore to the constitution of the United States, like every cabinet secretary has done, and like every attorney general before me has done. “And so, this narrative that’s mostly pushed by the left and pushed by the media that the president’s going to pull me aside and ask me to do something illegal is completely a false narrative, not true, will not happen and hasn’t happened.” In response to his demurring on the questions of always acting independently of the White House, Barb McQuade, a University of Michigan law professor, wrote on social media that Blanche’s stated position was “an appalling departure” from the justice department’s mission after the Watergate scandal that prompted Richard Nixon to resign from the presidency in 1974. The justice department, “as we once knew it, is no more”, McQuade wrote. “Blanche has turned it into Trump’s private law firm. What a complete disgrace.” Blanche’s comments to Welker on Sunday came days after he was only narrowly confirmed by the US Senate in a 50-49 vote to succeed Bondi, with all Democrats voting against him. He previously served as Trump’s criminal defense lawyer when a New York state jury convicted Trump between his two presidencies of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in connection with payments to adult film star Stormy Daniels. In April, Blanche said he would tell Trump, “I love you, sir,” if the president decided to fire him and nominate someone else to replace Bondi. Blanche, meanwhile, in December defended moving Ghislaine Maxwell, the convicted child sexual trafficker and Jeffrey Epstein associate, to a minimum-security prison. And Blanche has also continued facing scrutiny over his handling of the so-called Epstein files and his treatment of those victimized by the sex-trafficking network built by Epstein. While speaking with Welker on Sunday, Blanche also defended Trump’s pardoning of 1,500 supporters who were convicted of attacking the US Capitol toward the end of his first presidency in early 2021. “I’m not opining or in any way saying what President Trump did was wrong,” Blanche said when asked about the pardons, which included more than 170 people who pleaded guilty to assaulting police officers. “That is the president’s right.” Blanche declined to say whether any of the pardoned attackers might still receive settlements from the federal government – though they attorney general also claimed a $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” fund for allies whom Trump considered to be unfairly prosecuted was dead. “Well, anybody can file a claim against the federal government, not just anybody associated with [the Capitol attack],” Blanche said. “I’m not going to sit here and say on a news program whether a litigation that may or may not happen will result in money. I can’t do that.” He also affirmed the justice department would not drop “election integrity” efforts despite more than 20 consecutive court defeats connected to efforts to try to force states to turn over voter rolls ahead of the midterm elections in November, when the president’s Republican party is projected to lose seats in Congress and favored to lose the majority in the US House.

title: Democrats demand answers from Trump on USS Abraham Lincoln conditions
author: Marina Dunbar
summary: Senator Ruben Gallego calls carrier’s months-long deployment a ‘deep problem’ as wellbeing concerns mount
body_text: Democrats on Sunday intensified their demands for answers from the Trump administration over conditions onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln as the aircraft carrier’s nearly nine-month deployment continued fueling concern over crew morale, mental health and living conditions. Ruben Gallego, a Democratic senator from Arizona, said on Sunday that problems onboard the Lincoln had kept mounting – and he blamed the carrier’s prolonged deployment on the unresolved war that Donald Trump started in February with Iran as well as lackluster leadership in general from the Republican president’s administration. “I was just speaking to a [Lincoln crew member’s] spouse just about three days ago, and this is the current problem right now,” Gallego said on ABC News’s This Week. “The deep, deep, deep problem here is that this administration did not plan for this war, did not plan how to get out of this war, [and] did not really understand how this war was going to escalate.” Gallego, a retired US marine, also warned that comments from the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and Trump dismissing Lincoln concerns could discourage service members from staying in the military. Those remarks from Gallego came amid growing scrutiny over the Lincoln’s extended mission in the Middle East. The navy aircraft carrier has been at sea for nearly nine months and has gone more than 200 days without a port call. That has prompted Democratic lawmakers to call for an investigation into conditions onboard the carrier, citing reports of low morale among its 5,000 navy sailors and marines as they endure a record-breaking deployment at sea. Hegseth has rejected those reports as “completely misrepresented”. Trump, meanwhile, has minimized the duration of the deployment, saying it is “not nearly long enough”. The Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, two leading publications specializing in the US military, have reported multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard as poor conditions and mental stresses aboard the Lincoln reach a breaking point during its ninth months at sea. The carrier has been supporting the US war against Iran. And several Democratic lawmakers are pressing the Pentagon to take accountability for conditions facing its crew. Wes Moore, Maryland’s Democratic governor and a military veteran, on Sunday also sharply criticized Trump’s response to concerns about the mental health and living conditions of those onboard the Lincoln. Appearing on CNN’s State of the Union, Moore said: “The response of the president of United States pisses me off. And it should piss all of us off.” Moore continued by alluding to the fact that Trump did not serve in the US military beside becoming its commander-in-chief during his two presidencies. “I would have hoped that, since he’s never been forward deployed, since he’s never put on the uniform and sacrificed for this country, that he would have more compassion for the people who are willing to, that he would have more compassion for their family members who are willing to offer their loved ones to this country because they love this country so much,” Moore said. Moore added that “nobody understands” the Iran war, which “all of us are paying for”. The Lincoln recently received a visit from the US Central Command commander, Adm Brad Cooper, who said in a statement on Saturday that its crew “is a strong team of high-achieving Americans standing tall with immense, justified pride in everything they accomplished”. “History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era,” Cooper’s statement added. Cooper – who oversees the war with Iran – made the visit during a 10-day trip that also took him to Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, his statement said. That statement came one day after Trump downplayed concerns about what the Lincoln crew was enduring during its record-setting deployment. “That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it’s being replaced with another very similar ship,” Trump said when questioned about the lengthy deployment. Asked whether family members were worried about the situation, Trump responded: “No, they’re not.” The Guardian on Sunday reported on naval families who denounced Trump and Hegseth for dismissing their loved ones’ experiences, including onboard the Lincoln. Retired Adm Mike Mullen, a former chair of the joint chiefs of staff, pushed back on Trump’s comments during his own appearance on Sunday on This Week, saying such lengthy deployments take a toll on crews. Mullen said he spoke with Cooper on Saturday evening and was told that poor conditions onboard the Lincoln had been addressed. He also said morale among the crew improved after Cooper told the sailors they would be going home. An exact date for the Lincoln’s return has not been announced.

title: Brazil’s Lula launches historic fourth term bid – but son of jailed Bolsonaro stands in his way
author: Tom Phillips in São Bernardo do Campo
summary: President, 80, vows to keep far-right from power as Flávio Bolsonaro tells supporters he will ‘fight this system’
body_text: Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has launched his campaign for a historic fourth term and vowed that as long as he lived he would not allow the “shameless” right to return to power. Addressing a sea of supporters in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his political career began nearly half a century ago, the 80-year-old politician reminded voters of the chaos and violence that unfolded during the 2018-22 presidency of his far-right predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro, whose son Flávio Bolsonaro will face Lula in October’s presidential election. Lula recalled how hundreds of thousands of citizens died during a Covid outbreak Jair Bolsonaro was accused of bungling with his anti-science policies. Gun ownership soared as laws were relaxed, allowing criminal groups to expand their arsenals. “They handed out … more than a million weapons,” Lula said, promising to dedicate a fourth term to improving education and healthcare as well as developing Brazil’s rare-earth deposits, the world’s second largest after China’s. Lula also said he would improve security by targeting the rich organised crime bosses who lived in luxury apartments. “It’s easy to kill a crook in a favela. But the guy running the show lives in a penthouse … and we need to stop this,” Lula said. He also told his far-right rivals to “show some shame”. Lula was speaking at the Vila Euclides football stadium, where his astonishing rise to the presidency began in 1979 when, as 33-year-old union leader, he spearheaded two historic strikes that helped end the military dictatorship. Those strikes made Lula a household name and in 2002, after three failed attempts, he won a landslide victory to become his country’s first working-class president. During Lula’s first two-terms, from 2002 until 2010, he was credited with fighting hunger, dramatically expanding social welfare programmes and access to higher education, and improving Brazil’s global standing, although his administration was blighted by corruption scandals. His successor, Dilma Rousseff, became Brazil’s first female president but led the country into a severe economic recession before being controversially impeached in 2016. In 2018, Lula was jailed for alleged corruption and he spent 580 days in prison before the supreme court quashed his conviction. Lula’s imprisonment allowed Bolsonaro to win that year’s election, ushering in four years of environmental destruction and international isolation. In 2022 Lula won his third term, defeating Bolsonaro by a razor-thin margin and vowing to rescue the country from “one of the worst periods in Brazilian history”. “This nightmare is over,” Lula declared at his January 2023 inauguration. A week later, far-right radicals rampaged through the capital, Brasília, in a botched attempt to bring Bolsonaro back. Bolsonaro was jailed in 2025 for 27 years for plotting that failed post-election power grab. Flávio Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator, launched his campaign on Sunday with an event on Rio’s Copacabana beach, previously the scene of huge rallies in support of his father. “I am going to be Brazil’s next president because I’m going to fight this system,” Bolsonaro, who wore a bullet-proof vest under a yellow Brazil shirt, told a crowd far smaller than those his father used to attract. Polls suggest Lula holds a slender advantage over Bolsonaro, with 43% of intended votes to his rival’s 40% in a run-off which will take place on 25 October if, as expected, no candidate secures 50% of the vote in the 4 October first round. André Pagliarini, the author of a book about Lula called A People’s President and the Fight for Brazil’s Future, said the showdown would be “the single most important electoral contest this year in the world”. Pagliarini said he believed a Bolsonaro victory would be a significant boost for the pro-Trump “reactionary bloc” that has won elections across Latin America, from Argentina and Chile to Colombia, where the far-right lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella recently took office. Donald Trump’s administration has repeatedly asserted its leadership over the region, launching deadly military operations against alleged “narco-terrorists” in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific, threatening to “take back” the Panama canal and, in January, abducting Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro. Last week, the US state department published an incendiary video declaring that “American dominance in the western hemisphere will never be questioned again”. In recent months Trump has turned up the heat on Brazil, designating its two biggest organised crime groups, the Red Command and the PCC, as terrorist organisations. That has kindled fears of a US military intervention on Brazilian soil or interference in Brazil’s presidential election. During a visit to a jungle training camp in Panama on Friday, Trump’s defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, said Washington planned to use the military to “ruthlessly” pursue Latin American drug traffickers, “just like [they did with] Isis and al-Qaida” during the “war on terror”. The idea, Hegseth said, was to “do bad things to bad people – because for too long, bad people did bad things to good people inside the United States of America and across Central and South America”. There was anger at the US outside Lula’s campaign launch on Sunday, where some activists handed out stickers that read: “Fuck Trump.” Seixas Alves, a 33-year-old Lula supporter, said he worried the decision to classify Brazilian drug factions as terrorist groups could be used as a pretext for a US attack. “Just like they [did with] Saddam Hussein,” Alves added, referring to the Iraqi dictator’s supposed development of weapons of mass destruction. In Rio, Flávio Bolsonaro praised Trump’s decision to target the Brazilian crime groups and said he was the only politician capable of “sitting down with the US”. In Vila Euclides, Simone Tebet, a centrist Lula ally, urged voters to do everything they could to stop Brazil falling back into the hands of far-right politicians who wanted “to kill Brazilian democracy” and create “a country of hate”.

title: Republican senator denounces Trump’s ‘crazy, stupid’ claims about MMR vaccine safety
author: Robert Mackey
summary: Outgoing Louisiana senator Bill Cassidy, a medical doctor, voted to confirm anti-vaccine activist Robert F Kennedy as health secretary before speaking out
body_text: The Republican senator Bill Cassidy – a medical doctor who voted to confirm anti-vaccine activist Robert F Kennedy as federal health secretary in early 2025 – on Sunday denounced Donald Trump’s “crazy, stupid” claims about the safety of the combined MMR vaccine for undermining faith in immunization. When Trump recently ordered changes to the recommended childhood vaccination schedule, with Kennedy by his side, the president called for two shots of the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to be scrapped in favor of two doses of three separate vaccines, claiming that the MMR shots are “sort of like a nuclear weapon” that could be “quite lethal”. Cassidy, whose re-election bid ended in defeat to a Trump-backed challenger in a Republican primary in Louisiana, has been on the president’s enemies list since 2021, when the senator voted to convict him of “incitement of insurrection” in connection with the US Capitol attack carried out by Trump supporters toward the end of his first presidency. Asked about Trump’s comment that “nothing bad can happen” from advising parents to get six separate shots for their children, instead of two, Cassidy told CNN on Sunday: “If it wasn’t so potentially tragic, you would break out laughing at a comment like that. “Let’s just take it from the perspective of the parent: now instead of going to the doctor twice to get their child vaccinated, they have to go six times. Instead of the child getting two jabs, they get six jabs,” he continued. “Instead of the insurance company paying for two doctor’s visits, they’re paying for six, which is going to ultimately drive up premiums … “So the president is wrong; there’s a lot of bad things that will come out of this.” Cassidy’s critics have lambasted the outgoing senator for expressing misgivings about Trump’s actions, including a recent shouting match over the ongoing Iran war – but continuing to cast crucial votes to confirm the president’s nominees. He cast the decisive vote on 8 August that allowed Todd Blanche – a former criminal defense lawyer for Trump – to secure Senate confirmation as US attorney general. When Cassidy, the chair of the Senate health committee, previously announced that he would vote to confirm Kennedy as health secretary, he acknowledged that “the most notable opponents of Mr Kennedy were pediatricians on the frontlines of our children’s health who regularly have to combat misinformation; combating vaccine skepticism with correct information – correct information that comes from their education, training and experience as physicians.” Cassidy also revealed that he had extracted a promise from Kennedy, who has pushed the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism for decades, that “CDC will not remove statements on their website pointing out that vaccines do not cause autism”. After Kennedy became health secretary, however, the “Autism and Vaccines” page on the CDC website was altered to undermine that scientific consensus. An asterisk was added to the headline “Vaccines do not cause Autism”, which leads to a footnote pointing out that “the root causes of autism” remain unknown. Text was also added to the top of the same page, so that anyone who searches for CDC guidance on autism and vaccines is now presented with two “key points” that further appease vaccine skeptics and conspiracy theorists. “The claim ‘vaccines do not cause autism’ is not an evidence-based claim because studies have not ruled out the possibility that infant vaccines cause autism,” the first key point reads. The second addition, since one of the nation’s leading anti-vaccine activists took charge, suggests that the lack of evidence for a link between vaccines and autism could be the result of a conspiracy. “Studies supporting a link have been ignored by health authorities,” the CDC site now claims. Cassidy on Sunday told CNN that Trump’s MMR commentary “will do nothing” to address the discredited link between vaccine and autism stemming from a single paper that was ultimately retracted.

title: Who is Hasan Piker – and why are some Australian conservatives outraged about his return to the ABC?
author: Nick Visser
summary: The leftwing commentator has been invited to appear on the Planet America program on Monday night
body_text: The ABC is set to air the return of its Planet America program on Monday night as the US midterm elections gain steam, with a new episode featuring the leftwing commentator Hasan Piker. Host John Barron said the episode will focus on the “rise of Democratic socialists and the populist left”, with Piker speaking about “what it’s like in the eye of a political storm”. But the appearance quickly sparked the ire of conservatives in Australia. News Corp’s News24 host James Morrow was deeply critical of the interview on Friday, wondering if there was “something in the water at the ABC’s Ultimo HQ that makes them think they are immune to consequences”. “If the ABC wants to have this clown on their network, that’s their business, but let them do it without our tax dollars,” he challenged last week. Barron has urged critics to watch the appearance before casting judgment, saying he’s not surprised that “some of the usual suspects are outraged, OUTRAGED, that we would even speak to Piker”. “Like it or not, he’s a central figure in the 2026 US election,” Barron wrote on X. “I was prepared to talk to Piker about his role in this election just as I was prepared to talk to @seanhannity about his role in the 2012 election … relevance.” So who is Hasan Piker, and why does he have some in a tailspin? Streaming to millions Piker, 35, is an extremely popular figure in left-leaning politics in the US, with more than 3 million followers on Twitch and millions more on YouTube and Instagram. He streams on the internet nearly every day, sometimes for eight hours at a time, and has been heralded as a modern-day kingmaker for progressive Democrats. He has built a legion of fans – many whom are young men – with regular discourse about American foreign policy, capitalism, his support for LGBTQ+ rights and for a willingness to heap criticism on the Democratic establishment. He’s described himself as a “megaphone”, amplifying frustrations with “establishment liberalism”, not as a change maker himself. His readiness to champion progressive challengers over established figures has angered some top Democrats. He’s also become a frequent target of the Murdoch empire in the US, with Fox News publishing running criticism of his commentary. Piker’s opinions are unfiltered and, at times, extreme. In 2019, as part of a broader critique of American foreign policy, he said the US “deserved” the September 11 terrorist attacks (he later apologised for the remark). He’s also a frequent and vocal critic of Israel’s leadership and claimed he would “vote for Hamas over Israel every single time”. He maintains he’s not antisemitic, but strongly against Zionism and the country’s policy on the war in Gaza and Palestinians. “I have no issues getting vilified by people on the right. I love when my enemies hate me,” he told the Guardian in December. “It is what it is: they talk shit; what are you gonna do?” But Piker’s comments have landed him in hot water. The British government banned him from entering the country for a speaking engagement in June, saying at the time his presence “may not be conducive to the public good”. Complaints to ABC Piker was last on the ABC in September to speak about the assassination of the conservative activist Charlie Kirk. The streamer spoke to Sarah Ferguson for 7.30, saying he was “horrified” at the killing, which came just weeks before the pair were set to debate each other. The appearance prompted 68 complaints to the ABC, with viewers suggesting the national broadcaster should not have platformed Piker “as he is a far-left extremist” and had made “unsupported adverse claims about Mr Kirk’s past remarks”. The ombudsman determined the appearance did not breach the ABC’s editorial standards. Ferguson also interviewed Trump kingmaker Steve Bannon during the US president’s first administration, which prompted its own criticism. The ABC did not have an ombudsman at the time. Morrow wondered if Piker’s latest appearance could lead to a similar outcome, pointing to the ABC bowing to criticism in recent weeks. The network’s managing director, Hugh Marks, apologised to Gina Rinehart after airing a short documentary for its Race Around the World program that included crude and offensive comments about the mining billionaire. While the ABC ombudsman found it did not breach any editorial policies, Marks said it had fallen “short of community expectations” and that the ABC would change its editorial guidance. ‘It makes sense to hear from him’ Barron has defended the interview on X in recent days, saying Piker’s position in American politics is more relevant than ever due to the surge in progressive Democrats. “He’s become a central figure in this year’s election, it makes sense to hear from him,” Barron wrote to a critic about Piker. Barron said he had also interviewed Roger Stone, a longtime friend and ally of Trump who was sentenced to three years in prison in 2020 before he was granted clemency by the president. “If you watch, I’ll be interested to know if it confirms your concerns or overcomes them,” he went on. “Either way, we choose guests of all stripes based on interest and relevance.”

title: Trump’s tough-guy image has been undone by his own actions
author: Mohamad Bazzi
summary: The president was forced to hide in a catering truck amid the Iran war, in an encapsulation of the conflict’s failures
body_text: For decades, Donald Trump cultivated a public image based on strength and dominance. He was a brash New York real estate mogul; a reality TV star who deployed his signature phrase: “You’re fired!” to eliminate contestants from The Apprentice; and eventually US president and undisputed leader of the Republican party. In recent months, Trump has taken his boastfulness to an extreme, reportedly telling confidants that he’s “the most powerful person to ever live” and comparing himself with some of history’s most feared leaders, including Genghis Khan, Napoleon, Hitler, Stalin and Mao. But recent revelations have threatened to shatter Trump’s image as a strongman: the US president departed on a secret military flight out of Turkey after attending a Nato summit, while the White House told the public he was flying onboard Air Force One. The operation involved an elaborate ruse in which Trump boarded his jumbo jet in view of TV cameras, and then was hustled out by the Secret Service through an airport catering truck. Trump was taken to an alternate military aircraft, which flew him to Britain – all unbeknown to journalists and several White House staff members who stayed on Air Force One and thought they were on the same plane as the president. The embarrassing necessity was a result of Trump’s unnecessary war against Iran. US officials used such levels of subterfuge because they were worried about an Iranian assassination attempt against Trump, according to reports in the Washington Post and New York Times. On 11 August, Trump confirmed that he had secretly switched planes in Turkey, and attributed the decision to his protective detail and military advisers. “I go by Secret Service and the military,” Trump told reporters who asked why US officials had used such an intricate ploy and kept the public in the dark about it until the story was leaked. “They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane. Equal safety. But they wanted me to do it, so I do it. I do what they say.” Trump tried to evade criticism that the decision left several cabinet members and senior White House officials – including Marco Rubio, the secretary of state; Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary; Stephen Miller, Trump’s top domestic adviser; and Steven Cheung, the White House communications director – on Air Force One to serve as decoys, along with other Trump staffers and journalists. To deflect more questions, Trump claimed, without providing evidence, that the secret military plane he flew on was actually at “greater risk” than the Air Force One jet that the world saw him board after the Nato summit. “I think it was at greater risk because that would be the plane I think that they would be more likely to go for,” he said. It’s easy to see why Trump and his administration did not want to publicly share details of the ruse after the danger had passed, as past presidents had done when they used subterfuge to visit war zones and other hazardous locations. The image of Trump hiding in an airport catering container to avoid a potential Iranian assassination attempt is a stark contrast to the tough guy brand he spent years cultivating. It’s also an antithesis to the image Trump projected after he survived an assassination attempt at a presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. In a series of photos captured by news photographers at the scene, Trump raised his fist in the air and mouthed the words: “Fight, fight, fight” to supporters as he was rushed off stage by Secret Service agents, bleeding from his ear. One image in particular, showing a bloodied Trump pumping his fist with a US flag in the background, became iconic – and his campaign quickly tried to monetize it by using the photo on the cover of a book and to sell $299 Trump-branded sneakers. Beyond the dueling imagery, the fact that Trump took refuge in a catering truck has deeper political implications. It encapsulates Trump’s failure in his war on Iran: a president who constantly boasts about US military prowess and tries to project personal strength instead appears weak in front of the world as he hides from the consequences of his own actions. Nearly six months ago, Trump launched his reckless war against Iran as an act of imperial hubris – and a culmination of a series of lawless acts since he returned to office in 2025. With little resistance from the Republican-controlled Congress or the US supreme court, Trump was able to gut government agencies, use federal law enforcement to target his political enemies, appoint his loyalists as top prosecutors, deploy national guard troops into US cities, and weaken decades-old anti-corruption laws designed to constrain presidential power after the Watergate scandal. He also steamrolled over Congress and its authority to declare war. In late February, when the US and Israel launched a series of devastating airstrikes against Iran, Trump had expansive goals: to destroy Tehran’s military capabilities and nuclear program, and to topple Iran’s theocratic regime by decimating its leadership and instigating a popular uprising. In the war’s early days, the US and Israel assassinated more than 30 senior Iranian military and political officials, including the supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. But the Iranian system proved resilient and it quickly replaced those officials, partly by appointing Khamenei’s son, Mojtaba, as the new supreme leader, to ensure continuity. Iran also turned its proximity to the strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway through which more than a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed each day, into an effective economic weapon. Tehran closed the passageway at the start of the war, increasing energy prices and disrupting the global economy. Since then, Trump has struggled to reach a deal with Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz and prevent the war from spiraling into a regional conflict that could cause severe economic damage. For months, Trump has tried to negotiate a face-saving agreement that would allow him to declare victory and shift US public attention away from the war before midterm elections in November that could see Republicans lose control of Congress. Iran’s leaders and Trump both say they don’t trust the other side to abide by any agreement – and a memorandum of understanding reached in mid-June, which included reopening the strait of Hormuz and lifting a US naval blockade against Iranian ships in the region, has collapsed. Since then, tit-for-tat attacks by Iran and the US have rekindled fears of another all-out war. Not surprisingly, Iranian officials and state media are reveling in the extensive media attention over Trump secretly switching planes in Turkey – and especially the detail about him being ushered into an airport catering truck. A presenter on Iranian state TV called it a “scandal stemming from fear of Iran’s military power”, and described the incident as a source of “humiliation” for the US president. It will take time for Trump to undo the damage this ruse has done to his self-proclaimed image as a strong and dominant world leader. More importantly, his disastrous decision to launch a war against Iran will shape his legacy long after he leaves office. Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York University

title: A tale of two Dan Sullivans: Republicans with same name contest Alaska primary
author: Chris Stein
summary: Democrat Mary Peltola, who won the red state’s House seat twice, is also running to unseat the incumbent senator
body_text: Dan J Sullivan is a retired schoolteacher and US Forest Service employee living in the town of Petersburg in south-eastern Alaska, who is running as a Republican for the US Senate. Dan S Sullivan is a Republican US senator, who has represented Alaska since 2015. Both candidates will appear on the ballot, one name after the other, when Alaskans vote in primary elections this week – a complicated quirk of the contest that has drawn howls from Republicans. But the incumbent senator’s real threat, Alaska politics watchers say, is Mary Peltola, a Democrat who managed to twice win election to the state’s seat in the US House of Representatives, and is now vying tobeat him in November’s midterm elections in the US Senate. The Tuesday vote in the non-partisan primary will see four candidates advance to the general election for the seat in November. Though no Democrat has been elected to the US Senate from Alaska since 2008, the party believes Peltola is the right candidate to flip the seat, and her victory would put Democrats well on their way to retaking control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. “The reason Mary Peltola has a chance is not because, necessarily, Democrats are surging in Alaska,” said Scott Kendall, an election law attorney who has worked for candidates of both parties, including the senator Sullivan. “It’s that Mary Peltola, you know, she’s very pro-oil and gas development. She’s good on issues that matter to Alaskans’ pocketbooks, and that makes her just a bit of a unicorn.” The largest state in the union but physically separated from the lower 48, Alaska has unique politics. With an economy heavily reliant on oil and gas production, the state’s Democrats tend to advocate for expanded production, in contrast with their counterparts elsewhere, who are concerned about fossil fuels’ role in driving the climate crisis. While Alaska has only once voted for a Democrat in a presidential election – Lyndon B Johnson, in 1964 – power has oscillated between the two parties at the state level, and bipartisan coalitions today control both the state house and senate. Independents make up two-thirds of registered voters and Republicans about 23%, while fewer than 12% of Alaskans are Democrats. Sullivan won election in 2014 after beating the first-term Democratic senator Mark Begich, and has been a reliable Republican vote in his two terms, hewing much closer to his party’s agenda than the state’s senior Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski, who has grown prominent nationwide for repeatedly bucking Trump. Peltola cracked the GOP’s dominance of the state’s federal delegation in 2022 when Don Young, the Republican who had represented the state’s at-large US House district since 1973, died suddenly. She triumphed in the special election to finish his term, becoming the first Alaska Native ever to serve in Congress, and won a full term later that year. In 2024, Republican Nick Begich III narrowly defeated her bid for re-election. Alaska voted for Trump by more than 13 percentage points that year, but Peltola is viewed as Democrats’ best bet for the Senate race in one of a handful of red states the party is targeting to win back a majority in the upper chamber. Seeking to prove that she can better advocate for the state’s specific interests and needs in Washington, Peltola has put her moderate brand of politics at the center of her campaign. Her slogan “fish, family, freedom” is a nod both to the cultural importance of fishing in Alaska – and especially to its native communities, which form a potent political bloc – and to the issue of bycatch, whereby trawlers pick up valuable catches like crab and salmon in their nets, harming sport and commercial fishers alike. “Fish has always been, really, a passion issue in Alaska,” said Joelle Hall, president of the Alaska AFL-CIO, which has endorsed Peltola. Hall credited the former congresswoman with making the issue of bycatch and the health of the fishing industry in general more prominent in the state’s politics. During her time in the House of Representatives, Peltola advocated for Joe Biden to approve Willow, one of the biggest oil and gas developments in decades. The decision raised the hackles of environmentalists for its potential to drive global heating, but Hall describes it as huge for unionized workers. “We are also in the middle of a little bit of an oil and gas boom in Alaska,” said Hall. “That’s because Mary Peltola brought us the Willow project with the Biden administration.” Peltola may be further boosted by national trends breaking in Democrats’ favor. Trump’s approval ratings are low in the state as they are nationwide, while gas prices in Alaska have shot up since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, and are now among the highest nationwide. Polls have recently found the two candidates neck-and-neck before the November election, and major election forecasters view Sullivan’s re-election bid as a toss-up. A former marine who served as the state’s attorney general and natural resources commissioner, Dan S Sullivan has emphasized his focus on military affairs in a state with a large number of bases and veterans, as well as his own efforts to preserve the state’s fisheries. Steve Frank, a Republican former state senator, said that despite Peltola’s efforts to see Willow approved, he believed Sullivan would be a more reliable advocate for the state’s economically vital oil industry, especially with the presidential administration set to change in another two years. “The federal government views us kind of like a colony, and they forget that we’re American citizens trying to earn a living up here,” said Frank, referencing moves by the Biden administration to protect tracts of Alaska land and water from oil drilling. “And so they tend to want to lock us up, keep us from developing our resources, and so he’s pushing back against that.” The race has seen major spending, with the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund announcing it will put $17m towards helping Sullivan, while the Democrats’ Senate Majority Pac invested $12m into backing Peltola. Federal Election Commission filings until the end of July show Peltola has outraised Sullivan, bringing in $18.5m to his $11.7m, with $4.6m on hand compared with the Republican’s $7.3m. Meanwhile, OpenSecrets, a non-profit that tracks campaign donations, reported that two Super Pacs (political action committees) have spent a combined nearly $2m in Alaska recently to back other candidates who could syphon votes from both Peltola and Sullivan. Also on the ballot in Tuesday’s election will be Nick Begich III, who is vying for a second term against independent Bill Hill, the main challenger for the House seat after Democrat Matt Schultz dropped out and endorsed him. Alaskans will also select candidates to replace governor Mike Dunleavy, the Republican incumbent who is barred by term limits from seeking re-election. Dan J Sullivan of Petersburg, Alaska, who did not respond to a request for comment, is listed just above the senator among the 16 names running for Senate, though Dan S Sullivan has “registered Republican” and “incumbent” next to his name. The GOP went to court to boot Dan J Sullivan from the race, arguing that he was a “sham” contender propped up by Democrats to confuse voters and undermine Senator Sullivan, but were unsuccessful. Though it’s a marquee race of this year’s US Senate elections, when it comes to Alaska-specific issues, Kendall predicted there may wind up being less daylight than would be expected between Peltola and Sullivan on Alaska-specific issues. “I think she would probably frustrate a lot of Democrats, if I’m being honest. I think she would be, to national Democrats, what Lisa Murkowski is to national Republicans,” said Kendall. “There’ll be a moment where a Democratic president says something like: ‘Well, I want to turn this huge swath of Alaska into a wilderness preserve, no hunting, no fishing, no development,’” he suggested. “She’s going to balk at that.”

title: New Mexico’s attorney general pushes new social media safety laws after $900m court victory over Meta
author: Katie McQue
summary: Exclusive: Raúl Torrez is drafting two bills with state lawmakers to bolster consumer protections and child safety online, building on state’s landmark case against Meta
body_text: New Mexico’s attorney general is mounting a full-court press against technology companies to improve their child safety measures, capitalizing on a landmark win in court against Meta earlier this year. Raúl Torrez is working with state lawmakers to draft two new bills he says will strengthen consumer protections and child safety online. The legislation, expected to be announced in the coming weeks, will build on the state’s case against the parent company of Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram. A jury found in March that the company misled its users about the safety of its platforms and enabled harm, including child sexual exploitation. The social media giant was fined nearly $1bn as a result of the case. The trial was the first to hold Meta liable for harmful acts committed on its platforms. It followed a 2023 Guardian investigation that exposed how Facebook and Instagram had become marketplaces for child sex trafficking. Torrez is pursuing additional lawsuits, including a second case against Meta and one against an AI company whose chatbot has become a source of emotional attachment for children. In an interview with the Guardian, the state’s top legal official said the proposed laws would go beyond social media, creating a broader consumer protection framework for emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence and chatbots. He has also had preliminary discussions about the legislation with Deb Haaland, the former US interior secretary and Democratic nominee for New Mexico governor, who expressed support for his efforts. “I think there’s a lot of momentum coming out of our victory in court, and the idea is to build on that momentum,” said Torrez, who is running for re-election this year. A Meta spokesperson said: “We have strict, longstanding rules against child exploitation and have invested billions to fight it, both through proactive detection technology and safety features designed to prevent harm.” The company cited its record on sharing the amount of child sexual exploitation content it removes, including 36m pieces from Facebook and Instagram in 2025. The spokesperson added that Meta had spent the last decade working to support young people using its apps, in particular through the introduction of “teen accounts”. New suits, new bills Earlier this month, a judge ordered the company to pay $567m as part of the second phase of a case brought by the state. The money will primarily fund youth mental health treatment, with the remainder directed toward awareness, prevention and screening services. The court also imposed a series of reforms that will remain in effect for five years, including age verification, enhanced safeguards against child sexual exploitation, overnight limits on push notifications and mandatory time-use limits for users under 18. The judge’s ruling followed a seven-week trial earlier this year in which a jury found that Meta knowingly harmed children’s mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms. The jury imposed the maximum penalty available under state law, a $375m fine, bringing Meta’s total liability across the two phases of the lawsuit to $942m. “We disagree with the ruling and will appeal,” said a Meta spokesperson. His office is also pursuing another case against Meta, with a trial involving data privacy and civic harms expected to begin in September. The attorney general’s office is also filing a lawsuit against an AI company over a chatbot that children have been known to form bonds with, Torrez said, describing the case as likely to be filed in the “relatively near future”. ‘The pervasiveness of child sexual exploitation’ Reflecting on the first phase of the trial, which ran from February to March, Torrez said the evidence that most shocked him was “the depth of what they knew about not only the mental health problems that were occurring on the platform, but also the pervasiveness of child sexual exploitation”. The evidence came in part from internal emails obtained by the state during the discovery process, he said. “A lot of times, when we are dealing with corporate misconduct and we start investigating, we rarely see that kind of history of and depth of knowledge that was apparent in Meta’s case,” he said. Meta fought hard to prevent the disclosure of the emails, bringing “nearly 50 lawyers”, Torrez said. The legal battle also briefly raised the prospect of Meta withdrawing its services from New Mexico. In April, ahead of the second phase of the trial, Meta threatened to block access to Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp in New Mexico – a move that would have been unprecedented in the US. Torrez said he dismissed the threat as a negotiating tactic. “It seemed to me at the time to be a bluff that was intended to either shape the court’s determination or to bully the state of New Mexico,” he said. Potential legal blueprint for other states The New Mexico lawsuit was the first of several the company faces. In March 2026, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube liable for designing intentionally addictive products that harmed a young user. Meta is now facing a separate federal trial in Oakland, California, as part of a 29-state multidistrict lawsuit filed in 2023. The trial involves California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey, while eight other states, including Tennessee, have brought separate cases in state courts. Torrez said the New Mexico case has generated interest from other potential plaintiffs. “There is substantial interest, not only in with state attorney generals, but in smaller municipalities, school districts, private plaintiffs and others to look at the work that we’ve done here and to try and replicate it,” said Torrez. The potential damages in the broader state attorneys general litigation could exceed $1.4tn, according to a July court filing by Meta, putting the lawsuits on a scale that could potentially pose an existential threat to the company. A Meta spokesperson said: “The State AGs may call this a landmark case, but their limited claims are unsubstantiated and their financial demands are vastly disproportionate. The AGs offer no proof anyone in their states was misled, claim benign features such as having an additional Instagram account somehow harmed their residents, and attempt to penalize Meta for industry-wide challenges like age verification.” Despite the victory, the New Mexico ruling did not grant all of the remedies sought by the state. New Mexico had sought $3.7bn as part of an abatement plan to fund child mental health services. The judge declined several of the state’s requested measures, including proposals to de-encrypt children’s messages and appoint a child safety monitor to oversee Meta for five years, finding that some of those measures were more appropriately considered by the legislative branch. One of the bills state legislators are writing would remove caps on penalties for violating consumer protection laws in New Mexico, Torrez said. “And so, what we are going to do is, continue to lobby Congress for that, but also to work at the state level to try and build not only a comprehensive social media safety bill, but also to reform and update our consumer protection laws,” he said. He believes the issue ultimately requires federal legislation, but argues that states cannot wait for Congress to act. “There hasn’t been any willingness by Speaker [Mike] Johnson to really put forward a forceful piece of legislation, a strong piece of legislation that would protect kids online,” said Torrez. “I think it’s a pretty straightforward case of the lobbying power of big tech on Capitol Hill.” State’s push for stronger age checks For phase two of the New Mexico trial, the state proposed a number of actions Meta could take, which it said would “remedy the harms the company has created for users under 18”. The state sought to require Meta to deploy technologically feasible age-verification tools for all users, permanently delete any personal identifying information collected during the verification process, block children under 13 from using its platforms and delete their accounts and associated data, and require all users under 18 to have an associated guardian account. Requiring age verification for social media platforms is controversial, as it raises significant privacy, data security and free-speech concerns, particularly if companies are required to collect sensitive personal information to verify users’ ages. “The judge did not go as far as we would have liked on age verification,” said Torrez, who concedes that concerns about data privacy are valid. “My instinct is that this will be a process that evolves over time because it’s a five-year period that Meta is under the court’s jurisdiction in terms of compliance, and obviously we have to wait for the appellate process to play out before all of those terms are fully in effect,” said Torrez.

title: First Thing: Trump cuts US-South Korea military drills citing ‘good relationship with Kim Jong-un’
author: Martin Belam
summary: President said he was ‘not happy’ with plans for large-scale joint exercises he described as ‘inappropriate and hostile’
body_text: Good morning. Donald Trump has said he is scaling back joint US military drills with South Korea aimed at deterring North Korea, despite military officials from both countries warning that Kim Jong-un’s regime is learning new battlefield tactics from the Ukraine war. The president said he was “not happy” with US participation “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong-un”. He added that the drills were costly and “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a country that, as long as Donald J Trump has been president, has been unthreatening and respectful”. Trump added that it was too late to cancel the drills so he had ordered the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, to “substantially reduce” them. Why are there continuing concerns about USS Abraham Lincoln? Democrats have intensified their demands for answers from the Trump administration over conditions onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln amid concern over crew morale, mental health and living conditions. Ruben Gallego, a Democratic senator from Arizona, said he blamed the carrier’s prolonged deployment on the unresolved war that Donald Trump started in February with Iran as well as lackluster leadership in general from the Republican president’s administration. Jared Kushner meets Hamas leader before talks with Netanyahu on Gaza Donald Trump’s son-in-law and envoy, Jared Kushner, held a rare meeting with Hamas’s political chief on Sunday in Egypt, in a new diplomatic effort to make progress on the stalled Gaza ceasefire. On Monday, Kushner will meet Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, who is under pressure after rejecting the new 15-point, US-backed roadmap. The roadmap involves Hamas gradually giving up its weapons while Israeli forces halt attacks and begin withdrawing from Gaza. Netanyahu says Israel will not retreat from any position in Gaza until Hamas has been completely disarmed. Israel has killed more than 1,200 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded more than 4,100 since agreeing to the ceasefire on 10 October 2025, according to Gaza’s health ministry. Todd Blanche declines to pledge independence from White House The US attorney general, Todd Blanche, on Sunday declined to assure that the federal justice department he helms would always act independently of the White House and Donald Trump. “No attorney general should ever pledge that,” he said on NBC. Blanche also claimed Trump would never ask him to do something that crossed an ethical or legal line. Blanche added: “I swore to the constitution of the United States, like every cabinet secretary has done, and like every attorney general before me has done. And so this narrative that’s mostly pushed by the left and pushed by the media that the president’s going to pull me aside and ask me to do something illegal is completely a false narrative, not true, will not happen and hasn’t happened.” Republican senator denounces Trump’s ‘crazy, stupid’ claims about MMR vaccine safety The Republican senator Bill Cassidy, a medical doctor who voted to confirm the anti-vaccine activist Robert F Kennedy as federal health secretary in early 2025, on Sunday denounced Donald Trump’s “crazy, stupid” claims about the safety of the combined MMR vaccine for undermining faith in immunization. Asked about Trump’s comment that “nothing bad can happen” from advising parents to get six separate shots for their children instead of two, Cassidy told CNN on Sunday: “If it wasn’t so potentially tragic, you would break out laughing at a comment like that.” In other news … Hayden Panettiere, the actor known for her roles in television shows such as Heroes and Nashville, has died at the age of 36. Her father, Skip Panettiere, asked for privacy “as our family takes time to process this unimaginable loss”. Kyiv could hit Russia with its own domestic ballistic missiles in months, a former defense minister has said. Wildlife groups in Florida are celebrating record numbers of sea turtle nests this season, but experts warn Donald Trump’s recent gutting of the Endangered Species Act could reverse decades of their recovery. Tommy John, synonymous with a ligament-replacement surgery that paved a path to recovery for injured baseball players, has died. He was 83. The left-hander was 31 years old when he tore the ulnar collateral ligament in his pitching elbow and had it replaced with a tendon from his right forearm. The University of Cambridge has defended its mental health support for the academic Jason Arday. Arday was pronounced dead on Friday, weeks after he resigned from his post as professor of sociology of education, following widespread press coverage of accusations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements. Stat of the day: At least six people dead from days of storms and record flooding in Indiana A four-year-old boy, two men and three women were among those who died since storms began on 11 August in Indiana, the state’s homeland security department spokesperson, Liz Woods, said. Building power: Teenagers demand more support after US schools ban phones More students are advocating for their own digital wellbeing and developing programs to thrive in tech-free learning environments. Don’t miss this: Why cancer, not cost of living, may be the biggest issue in Iowa’s midterm elections The midwestern state of Iowa has the second highest rate of cancer nationwide and is one of only three states where incidents of the disease are rising. Promises to address the issue are now top of mind for candidates ahead of the 3 November elections, in which Iowa may play an important role in deciding control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s term. … or this: The Fair Hill Five, horse racing’s bizarre transatlantic betting coup, explained Someone, somewhere, appears to have made a lot of money by betting on a series of unfancied horses who all unexpectedly came good. Bryan Armen Graham looks at what could be a sensational stroke of luck … or something more sinister. Climate check: Spotlight on UN desertification summit as it mulls how to spend $12bn war chest Environment editor Fiona Harvey reports that as swathes of the northern hemisphere bake in what could be the hottest year on record, with wildfires blazing across North America and Europe and heatwaves afflicting millions across Asia, the UN’s biannual talks on desertification have assumed much greater importance – and have started attracting more money. title: Jon Ossoff calls Trump’s handling of Iran war ‘uniquely despicable’ in excoriating speech
author: George Chidi in Atlanta
summary: Georgia Democratic senator has stoked speculation for 2028 presidency bid by delivering stinging attacks on Trump
body_text: Democratic senator Jon Ossoff has attacked Donald Trump’s “uniquely despicable” handling of the US-Israel war on Iran, accusing the US president of “re-rigging” a corrupt system for himself in an excoriating speech. Ossoff, who is running for re-election in Georgia in November, has repeatedly stoked speculation that he is laying the ground for a bid for the US presidency in 2028 by delivering a series of stinging attacks on Trump and his administration. “They made you pay more for everything, and took us to war on lies, and spent most of last year trying to cover up for the world’s most famous pedophile while the crook president and his crook family raked in billions while your tax dollars were put to work backing Trump’s businesses,” Ossoff said at a rally in midtown Atlanta on Sunday afternoon. He pointed to the US sailors enduring a record-setting deployment of nearly nine months onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, amid mounting concern over conditions and mental health issues onboard the aircraft carrier, whom Trump suggested last week had not been deployed “nearly long enough”. “While the sailors on the Lincoln fight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings,” Ossoff said. “He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the amir of Qatar.” Ossoff appears to have been referring to Natalie Harp, Trump’s executive assistant, who has drawn scrutiny on social media for her perceived closeness to the US president. It emerged last week that Harp accompanied the president when he left Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent and other key officials on a decoy plane as they left Turkey under threat of Iranian attack in July. Stump speeches like the one he delivered on Sunday, with plain, sharp language well-tailored for social media, have become a staple of Ossoff’s campaign. “They’ve lied non-stop about this war like they lie about everything. And they know they’re lying, but they lie and they keep lying anyway because in this White House, they view persistence in deceit as a virtue,” the senator said. “And there’s something uniquely despicable about lying a nation into war, treating citizens as fools and those who serve as pawns.” Early voting begins in eight weeks in Georgia, and Ossoff has maintained a lead well above the margins for error in polling above the Republican nominee, US representative Mike Collins. But Ossoff has framed his campaign as something more than a referendum on his term in office, raising broader questions about Americans’ tolerance for corruption. “Corruption in American politics runs a lot deeper than Donald Trump,” Ossoff said, pointing to what he called the “coin-operated” politics of political action committees. “Trump promised to attack a broken system. I get it. Right target. Yes, the system is really rigged. But he’s not unrigging it. He’s re-rigging it for himself.” Ossoff’s personal wealth is held in a blind trust. He has pursued a ban on stock trading by members of US Congress and their families as a signature political issue. The Ending Trading and Holdings In Congressional Stocks Act passed out of the preliminary committee stage in July 2024, but has not been put to a vote in the Republican-controlled US Senate. Ossoff also highlighted the vast increase in Trump’s personal wealth since he returned to office in January 2025. “When he first announced the tariffs, you remember that? He called it liberation day and it crashed the markets because it was clown policy,” Ossoff said, noting how the president then purchased stock a week after the markets fell. “And then the very next morning, April 9th, he posts on Truth Social. ‘This is a great time to buy.’ Three exclamation marks. “OK, now listen to this. Three hours and 41 minutes after that post, one day after he bought millions in stock, he cancelled the tariffs and triggered one of the biggest same day rebound rallies in market history. He’s trying to get money.” Trump launched a subscription service on 1 August charging up to $100,000 a month for early access to his posts on his Truth Social platform. The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation have launched a suit against Trump, two of his aides and the executive office of the president over the service. Ossoff attacked the president over the offering. “Just understand what’s for sale here,” he said. “The sitting president’s pronouncements on war and peace and economic policy delivered first to paying customers. What an absolute crook.”

title: Trump’s move to gut South Korea alliance is ‘inane, haphazard decision’, lawmakers say
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: US president’s abrupt order to scale back joint exercises with Seoul is meant to ‘flatter’ North Korea’s dictator, top Democrat says
body_text: Donald Trump’s move to gut Washington’s 73-year-old military alliance with Seoul has been called “inane” and “shortsighted” as lawmakers warned it risked strengthening Russia’s hand in Ukraine. The US president abruptly ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint exercises with South Korea just days after North Korea test-fired ballistic missiles, justifying the decision by citing his “very good relationship” with Kim Jong-un, the nuclear-armed dictator such exercises exist to deter. Trump announced the order on social media, directing the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, to scale back Ulchi Freedom Shield, an 11-day exercise due to run from 17 to 27 August involving about 18,000 South Korean troops rehearsing scenarios including missile strikes, drone incursions and cyber-attacks. Trump framed the decision as a courtesy to Kim, writing that the drills “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to a country he described as “unthreatening and respectful”, despite North Korea’s continued missile testing and its expanding nuclear arsenal. Democrats in Congress said the move handed Kim a propaganda win for nothing, while an ally was left paying the price for a war in the Middle East it never agreed to fight. Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate armed services committee, called it “another inane, haphazard decision by President Trump and his chaotic administration”. “When President Trump cuts military exercises to flatter a dictator or punishes South Korea for declining to join a war he started, all of our allies – and adversaries – think that America’s commitments are negotiable,” Reed said in a statement, describing the move as punishing Korea “for no reason beyond Trump’s ego”. Reed’s warning was echoed by Mark Kelly of Arizona, who sits on the same committee, and argued that the drills were not symbolic but the basis of the alliance’s ability to function in a crisis. “North and South Korea are still technically at war,” Kelly said. “Our ability to help defend our ally against the North Koreans is because our forces are well trained and able to coordinate with the South Koreans. Hollowing out these joint exercises is shortsighted and a mistake.” In the Oval Office on Monday, Trump claimed Kim had responded to his overtures, but did not provide details. “I understand him,” the president said. “He understands me.” The alliance Trump is now unwinding dates to the 1953 Mutual Defense Treaty signed after the Korean war armistice. Roughly 28,500 American troops remain stationed in South Korea, backed by a combined US-South Korean command structure and Washington’s pledge to extend its nuclear umbrella over Seoul. Despite Trump calling North Korea “unthreatening”, his own administration’s 2026 Annual Threat Assessment describes an “increasingly confident North Korean regime”, warning that its weapons of mass destruction, conventional forces and cyber operations threaten the US, South Korea and Japan. His former director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, testified in March that “North Korea’s ICBMs [intercontinental ballistic missiles] can already reach US soil”. Trump also tied his decision to the Iran war, saying he was unhappy that Seoul had declined to join the US military campaign against Iran, a campaign that has drained US missile stockpiles and, after Tehran shut the strait of Hormuz, helped push up prices at home. He acknowledged the two issues had little to do with one another, even as he punished Seoul over both. “While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks’!” Trump wrote. Andy Kim, the New Jersey senator who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, said linking the exercises to that refusal exposed a troubling attitude toward a key partner. “Our alliance with the Republic of Korea is critical for US security and prosperity – and I am concerned that President Trump’s post today suggests a disregard for this relationship,” Kim said. “South Korea is an essential partner in peace and security in a part of the world filled with risk; we should treat them that way instead of venting frustration on social media.” It is not the first time Trump has treated the drills as a bargaining chip. After his 2018 summit with Kim in Singapore, he suspended major exercises outright, calling them costly and provocative, before they were quietly restored once nuclear diplomacy with Pyongyang broke down. The dispute comes as Seoul has spent much of the past year charting its own path on the Middle East. In February, South Korea’s government said it had “grave concern” over Israeli measures expanding control in the occupied West Bank and urged Israel to “reverse its decisions immediately”. In April, Seoul’s ambassador to the United Nations told the security council that any unilateral annexation of Palestinian territory “should be revoked”. Lee Jae Myung, the president of South Korea, has twice clashed publicly with Israel: in April over remarks he made comparing footage of an Israeli soldier’s treatment of a Palestinian man’s body to the Holocaust, and in May after two South Korean activists were detained on a Gaza-bound aid mission. Thom Tillis, the outgoing Republican senator from North Carolina, chimed in making the point that the butterfly effect of Trump’s decision would inadvertently benefit Russia. “South Korea has been a solid military ally for over 70 years that possesses exquisite military capabilities,” Tillis wrote on social media. “Reducing joint exercises with South Korea does nothing more than free up thousands of North Korea’s troops to support Putin’s systematic kidnapping, torture, rape and murder of innocent Ukrainian citizens.”
