title: Trump administration pauses border construction in Big Bend national park
author: Cecilia Nowell and agency
summary: Controversial project has faced bipartisan opposition by critics who say it mars pristine environmental area in Texas
body_text: Construction on a US-Mexico border project in Big Bend national park has halted, the Trump administration said Monday, as Customs and Border Protection (CBP) evaluates the controversial project in Texas. “CBP is pausing all construction activity in Big Bend National Park while I visit and conduct a personal, on-the-ground evaluation,” CBP’s head, Rodney Scott, wrote in a social media post. Footage of bulldozers ploughing through the 800,000-acre (325,000-hectare) Chihuahuan desert national park emerged earlier this month, after the Trump administration did not announce and initially denied construction on a multibillion-dollar “smart wall” expansion in the park. Last year, Congress approved $46.5bn for a border wall expansion in the “big, beautiful” spending bill Donald Trump signed into law on 4 July 2025. News of construction in Texas’s largest and most-visited national park sparked concern from environmental groups. “They’re bulldozing a brand new road through the most beloved stretch of the park,” said Laiken Jordahl, a public lands advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. Although many Texas Republicans have remained silent about the construction, outgoing senator John Cornyn sent a letter to Markwayne Mullin, the US homeland security secretary, asking him to halt construction on the wall. “My constituents believe that the 1,000-foot riverbank cliffs and remote Big Bend terrain offers its own sources of deterrence for any illegal migrants crossing into the United States,” Cornyn wrote. Scott, the CBP chief, has said that he expects the agency will build the first layer of the wall by the end of next year. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: US navy destroyer adrift in South China Sea for four days after losing power
author: Edward Helmore
summary: USS Benfold lost power after ‘engineering casualty’ leaving sailors without galley services, toilets and air conditioning
body_text: A US guided-missile destroyer reportedly spent four days adrift and without power in the South China Sea in July, furthering concerns about strain being placed on deployed military members. The USS Benfold, an Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer which had been sailing with the George Washington carrier strike group, was reported to have been towed to Subic Bay in the Philippines, according to the US Naval Institute News, an independent military publication. The 10,000-ton destroyer lost power after what a spokesperson with the US seventh fleet called “an engineering casualty involving its generators”, resulting in a loss of power. That loss of power meant sailors were without galley services, toilets and air conditioning, Commander Matthew Comer told USNI News in a statement. Another vessel, USS Robert Smalls, the cruiser attached to the strike group, had to help provide meals for the crew. Comer said that Benfold lost power on 24 July and was towed on 28 July. Power was restored two days later. “There were no injuries to the crew, who demonstrated resilience, grit, professionalism and unwavering steadiness in their response,” Comer’s statement to USNI News said. The Guardian has approached theseventh fleet for comment. Separately, the Pentagon was ordered to scale back annual joint military exercises with South Korea as his war against Iran stretches the limits of US aircraft carriers. Trump said on Sunday that he had instructed Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, to “substantially reduce” the joint military exercises with South Korea. The USS George Washington strike group on Monday was headed to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, a carrier that in recent days was subject to reports by the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes of multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard after more than 200 days without a port call. Trump told reporters on Monday the carrier had been at sea for a “good period of time” and said he had spoken with a retired admiral over the weekend who recounted being on ships for “much longer”. Trump said the admiral assured him that the Lincoln was “beautifully maintained and beautifully taken care of”. Reports of poor morale prompted Democratic lawmakers and military families to demand that the Trump administration answer questions about low morale, mental health challenges and living conditions for crew members. Senator Ruben Gallego, an Arizona Democrat and retired marine, said on ABC News on Sunday that the problems arose from the Iran war that the Trump administration started in February but has not been able to resolve. The Lincoln originally deployed to the Indo-Pacific before being ordered to sail to the Middle East in January. “The deep, deep, deep problem here is that this administration did not plan for this war, did not plan how to get out of this war, and did not really understand how this war was going to escalate,” he said. Hegseth has rejected the accounts, calling them “completely misrepresented”. “We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” he told Newsmax, adding that sailors in “austere conditions with less port calls” were doing “incredible” work. The navy, meanwhile, has said: “Based on information available to the command, we have not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship.” Navy officials said in a statement obtained by Task & Purpose: “We know that extended deployments place a significant strain on our service members and their families, and we are grateful for the resilience and sacrifices they make in support of our nation’s security.” In an opinion piece published by the Wall Street Journal on Sunday, Adm Brad Cooper, commander of US Central Command, said he had been onboard the Lincoln in the Arabian Gulf a day earlier and addressed the sailors. Cooper said he had made the trip to “see how its 4,000-plus service members are doing and thank them for their extraordinary resilience in the face of constant pressure” and called it “an amazing visit”. He acknowledged the media reports on the ships “operational tempo, crew morale and the realities facing our deployed forces” and said what he found “is that many elements of those stories are old news”. “The crew is tired, but they continue to fire on all cylinders,” he wrote. “History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era.” In a post on X Monday, Cooper said that of the navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers, the Lincoln has among the lowest number of cases related to mental health. “This doesn’t mean all is perfect,” he wrote. “Find any of the nearly 4 million Navy veterans today and they will likely tell you that service at sea for long periods isn’t for everyone. It’s uniquely challenging and tough, and every single one of us, including me, reacts to stressors in different ways.” The Guardian on Sunday reported on families who have had loved ones deployed for months on US warships amid the Iran war and were furious with the Trump administration’s dismissal of their concerns about the pressures and conditions at issue. “It’s a feeling of betrayal,” the sister of a Lincoln crew member said in that report. “These are frustrating, false and careless comments, and they are going to have a lot of consequences for my brother.”

title: Election denier Tina Peters to be hired as elections consultant in conservative California county
author: Dani Anguiano in Chico, California, and Sam Levine in New York
summary: Shasta county, center of US election denialism movement, set to appoint ex-Colorado clerk who served prison term
body_text: A northern California county that has become a hotbed of activism for those who sow doubts about the reliability of voting machines plans to hire Tina Peters, the prominent Colorado election denier recently released from prison, to work on elections. Clint Curtis, the top election official in Shasta county, told the Guardian he plans to hire Peters as a consultant to replace Brent Turner, his top deputy, who has been on medical leave. He said Peters would not have access to the county’s voting system and did not directly respond when asked what her responsibilities would be. Plans to hire Peters, who is still on parole and must receive permission to travel outside Colorado, were first reported by Action News Now. Shasta county, a conservative region home to 182,000 people, has emerged as a center of the US election denialism movement in recent years. In 2023, the county’s governing body unsuccessfully sought to remake the voting process by cutting ties with the voting machine company Dominion Voting Systems and implementing a hand-count system that experts warned would be costly and far less accurate. The former MyPillow CEO, Mike Lindell, one of the leading promoters of falsehoods about election fraud in the US, said he would support the county’s effort. The state ultimately blocked Shasta’s plans. In addition, several candidates who lost their race for local office have embraced baseless conspiracy theories about election fraud and sued to overturn results. Last year, the Shasta county board of supervisors appointed Curtis, a Florida-based attorney who had never before overseen an elections office, to serve as the county clerk and registrar of voters. Curtis, who opposes the use of voting machines and has long argued US elections are being manipulated, vowed to overhaul the elections and set an example for the rest of the US. But his tenure has been controversial. Earlier this year investigative reports conducted by the county and an outside body concluded that he had created a hostile work environment and made violent threats against workers. Curtis has denied those claims. Last week, the same board that appointed Curtis censured him, and denounced what it described as his “ongoing and flagrant violations” of county personnel rules, pointing to policies preventing elected officials from “making unfounded allegations that have not been investigated”. Curtis accused staff of “sabotaging elections” and said he planned to sue the county, telling the Guardian: “Everything the old staff accused me of is a lie, and we will be able to prove it in court.” Peters, the former top election official in Mesa county, Colorado, was convicted of four felonies and three misdemeanors in 2024 after she allowed an activist affiliated with Lindell to impersonate a county employee and attend an upgrade of the county’s Dominion voting software. The Gateway Pundit, the far-right news website, subsequently published screenshots of sensitive county information after that breach. Peters was released from prison in June after Colorado’s governor, Jared Polis, a Democrat, commuted her nine-year prison sentence. The hiring of Peters was alarming, said Matt Crane, the executive director of the Colorado county clerk’s association. “Tina Peters and others in the election-denial movement appear to have found another weak link in the chain in California,” he said. “The idea that anyone would bring Tina Peters in as an election expert is almost beyond parody. Maybe she’s an expert on leaving ballots sitting in a ballot box for months after an election. Maybe she’s an expert on committing crimes in the process of trying, and completely failing, to prove election fraud. “When it comes to actually administering secure, lawful elections, Tina Peters is the last person anyone should be looking to for expertise,” he added. Jena Griswold, Colorado’s secretary of state, said in a statement: “Peters was convicted of four felonies and three misdemeanors related to breaching her own voting equipment while county clerk. It is troubling that she would be in a position to have direct influence on election administration.” Securing the release of Peters from prison was a celebrated cause on the right. Even as Donald Trump pardoned those involved with the January 6 attack on the US Capitol and the fake elector scheme in 2020, he could not help Peters because she was only convicted of a state crime. Polis, facing mounting pressure from the federal government to free Peters, eventually commuted her sentence in May, saying it was unfairly harsh. Polis overrode recommendations from his own clemency board in doing so, according to the New York Times, and has been rebuked by the Colorado Democratic party. The California senator Alex Padilla, a Democrat, also criticized the plan to hire Peters. “This should be stopped immediately: Shasta County Registrar Clint Curtis is trying to hire election-denier Tina Peters to collude with the Trump Administration’s election mischief,” he posted on X. “Americans – and Californians – deserve nothing but safe, secure, and free elections – without political interference and partisan loyalists beholden to Trump.” Since being released from prison, Peters has hit the Maga media circuit and continued to try to undermine faith in American elections. She continues to assert, falsely, that votes were flipped in 2020, and has urged Trump to declare a national emergency ahead of the 2026 midterms, according to the Atlantic. A copy of Peters’s clemency petition, obtained by the Atlantic, said she would not have the ability to commit similar crimes to the ones she was convicted of because she is no longer a clerk. Curtis’s move to hire Peters comes in the final months of his time in office. In June, voters ousted Curtis in favor of Joanna Francescut, a longtime employee of the Shasta county elections office who was serving as the assistant registrar when Curtis fired her after taking over the office. In the same election, Shasta voters backed a measure to require elections to be held in person on a single day and effectively ending vote by mail while also mandating photo ID and a hand-count. The state quickly sued the county and a judge has temporarily blocked the implementation of the measure.

title: Trump reportedly casts mail-in ballot in Florida Republican primary
author: Cecilia Nowell
summary: President, who has decried mail-in ballots amid false claims of election fraud, issued March order to curb voting by mail
body_text: Donald Trump voted by mail in Florida’s Republican primary, Politico reports, citing Palm Beach county voting records. The White House has confirmed the president’s mail-in vote, according to the New York Times, which added that this was at least the third time the president has mailed his ballot. In March, the president signed an executive ⁠order restricting the use of mail-in ballots ahead of the November midterm elections that will decide control of US Congress. Trump has repeatedly criticized mail-in voting, calling for restrictions on the policy for years and falsely claiming that his 2020 election defeat was the result of widespread voter fraud. In a post on Truth Social on Monday, Trump continued his years-long false claims of election fraud in the United States – including by implying that mail-in voting is insecure. “Earlier this month, India’s Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, asked our Administration – How can you have Elections in the U.S. without a valid Photo ID? India’s last Election had 646,000,000 Voters! Less than 1% voted by mail, and every single Voter had to have a VALID Photo Identity Document. We need to pass THE SAVE AMERICA ACT, now!” Trump wrote. A federal judge has blocked ⁠the US Postal ⁠Service from implementing part of the executive order, although Trump’s administration has asked the supreme court to intervene. After Politico reported on the president’s ballot on Monday afternoon, citing local voting records, the New York Times reported that it “could not access these records through the Palm Beach county supervisor of elections website, which said that Mr Trump’s voting record was ‘protected from public disclosure’”. However, a White House spokeswoman later confirmed to the newspaper that Trump voted by mail, saying: “As everyone knows, the president is a resident of Palm Beach and participates in Florida elections, but he obviously primarily lives at the White House in Washington DC.” Trump first registered to vote in Palm Beach county in 2019. Since then, he has voted by mail in 2020, during a special election for statehouse earlier this year and last week, when he mailed his ballot on 13 August.

title: White House launches personal attack on CNN reporter over question to Trump
author: Sam Levin
summary: CNN says attack ‘beneath the office’ after Kristen Holmes asked president about Jon Ossoff’s comments on key aide
body_text: The White House launched a personal attack against a CNN reporter on Monday with a social media post that mentioned her children and accused her of asking a “disgusting and inhumane question”. A White House post targeted Kristen Holmes, a senior White House correspondent for the network, after she asked Donald Trump to respond to a widely shared comment by the Democratic senator Jon Ossoff in a speech on Sunday. The Georgia senator told a crowd that Trump “doesn’t want to do the job” and instead “wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar”. The comment was an apparent reference to Natalie Harp, the president’s executive assistant, fueling scrutiny of her perceived closeness to Trump. When Holmes asked Trump in the Oval Office to respond to Ossoff’s remark, the president dismissed her, calling the senator a “Pee-wee Herman lookalike”. The White House’s “rapid response” social media account posted a clip of the exchange and tagged Holmes, calling her a “disgraceful, humiliating embarrassment to her alleged profession”. The post went on to criticize her for taking a “cheap shot” at a staffer, adding: “These scumbags are the lowest of the low.” The White House later sent out another post criticizing Holmes, writing: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive. It’s quite troubling.” Trump also directly criticized Holmes during the Oval Office event, at one point telling her: “Quiet, quiet, quiet. You’re very disrespectful.” After she told him she worked for CNN, he responded: “Fake news, you’re fake news, you’re a loud boisterous person. You’re fake news. Be quiet. Be quiet. You’re a fake reporter and you report fake news.” He talked over her as she tried to ask a question. CNN defended Holmes in a statement, calling her “one of the most respected and accomplished journalists covering the White House”. The network said she had asked Trump a “tough, relevant, and newsworthy question on behalf of the American people”, writing: “Public officials are free to challenge reporting they disagree with, but personal attacks on journalists for asking questions are beneath the office and inconsistent with the principles of a free press.” Earlier, the White House director of communications also posted a series of insults targeting Ossoff in response to the senator’s speech, writing: “Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics.” Trump has a long history of aggressively attacking and insulting women in the press corps who ask tough questions, including saying, “Quiet, piggy” to a Bloomberg reporter, calling another CNN journalist “corrupt”, and storming out of NBC’s Meet the Press after calling the moderator “crooked or stupid”. Other journalists condemned the White House’s personal attack against Holmes, with one of her colleagues at CNN saying: “Kristen is an incredible reporter, person and, above all, mother. I don’t understand such a reaction to a journalist asking the president for his response to something a Democratic senator has leveled against him.”

title: Top Democrats tussle in Florida primary but progressive liberalism not on menu
author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
summary: Politics that worked for Democratic candidates in New York, Minnesota, Michigan won’t cut it in red Florida, analysts say
body_text: If primary elections elsewhere this summer were tussles between progressives and moderates for the direction of the Democratic party’s political future, Tuesday’s contests in Florida could not be more different. In a former swing state that has in recent years become reliably red, moderate Democratic candidates Alex Vindman and David Jolly are heavily favored to become the party’s nominees for November’s Senate and governor’s race, respectively. Analysts say the brand of progressive liberalism that worked so well for Democratic candidates in Minnesota, Michigan and New York, won’t cut it with voters in conservative Florida, and neither are Vindman, frontrunner for the Senate nomination to challenge Republican incumbent Ashley Moody, or Jolly, vying to succeed Ron DeSantis as governor, trying to sell it. “There is a lot of curiosity about me from more traditional, pre-Trump-era Republicans that feel homeless,” Vindman said in March as he weighed the broad coalition of voters he will need to topple Moody, appointed by Republican DeSantis in January 2025 to replace Marco Rubio after his elevation to secretary of state. “I’m running here as a kind of a different kind of Democrat, I’ve got my handguns, a concealed carry permit, not the standard fare.” Florida has closed primaries, meaning only those voters who have declared party affiliation can choose its nominees. But Vindman and Jolly are already looking to court independents and disgruntled Republicans beyond Tuesday. Vindman, a retired army lt col, and an impeachment witness against Trump during the president’s first term of office, is polling clear of state representative Angie Nixon in the Democratic primary. He has run a “Florida First” campaign that leans heavily on establishment values – the economy, social security stability for seniors, and tackling corruption in Washington. “My race is entirely focused on my opponent, I’m not focused on anything besides Ashley Moody,” he said. “I feel a huge amount of support and kind of a new hope for a balanced politics in this state.” Jolly, a former Republican congressman who became a Democrat last year, and is the most prominent name in a crowded field for the party’s governor’s nomination, also believes his moderate credentials are an asset. In an interview with the Associated Press last week, Jolly stated he had no plans to try to reverse DeSantis’s ban on transgender girls and women athletes playing on female teams at public schools and universities. “I don’t think we should have biologically born men playing in competitive sports,” he said in comments starkly at odds with pro-diversity positions taken by progressive victors elsewhere, such as Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, who promised to be “a lion” for LGBTQ+ rights if elected to the Senate. Even so, the likely Republican candidate for governor has been declared to be a “radical liberal” by Byron Donalds, the Trump-aligned congressman who is the clear favorite for the Republican nomination. In attack ads prevalent on Florida’s television screens in recent days, Donalds has painted Jolly as a fervent supporter of the transgender community, attempted insults Jolly has shrugged off by challenging Donalds on issues he said matter more to “regular” Floridians, such as soaring costs for property, insurance, gas and groceries, instead of focusing on culture war issues. The man of the people approach is also a theme for Jay Collins, DeSantis’s lieutenant governor, and one of three Republicans challenging Donalds for the nomination. “I mow my own yard. I gas up my own truck. I live the same Florida life that working families live,” Collins, a former Green Beret, told reporters in a press conference Thursday that portrayed Donalds, a congressman since 2021, as an absentee Washington elite. “We won’t win with vibes. We’re certainly not going to win with celebrity.” Other Republicans in the governor’s race are James Fishback, a far-right extremist who has endured a bumpy primary campaign, and Paul Renner, the former speaker of the Florida house and legislative ally of DeSantis, who has declined to make a primary endorsement. Polling shows Donalds close to 50%, with his rivals at 15% or below. Political analysts see voter dissatisfaction in Florida with Trump, and the soon-to-be termed-out DeSantis to a degree, but nothing likely to spark a wholesale ideological swing. “Going back many decades, if you look at Florida’s political culture, it’s moderate to conservative,” said Aubrey Jewett, professor of political science at the University of Central Florida. “Roughly 40% of Floridians say they’re moderate, 40% say they’re conservative, and only about 20% say they’re liberal. It’s been steady for decades, and one way of saying there’s just not as many progressives, or liberals, or socialists, in Florida as apparently there are in some other places currently. “Unlike some of the big battles we’ve seen nationwide between the progressive socialist wing of the Democratic party and the moderate wing, I don’t think that’s going to be the case in Florida. The voters will sort it out but from a Democratic perspective it would be good for them if they got the more moderate candidates, and I think that’s what most Democrats feel.” Nikki Fried, the chair of the Florida Democratic party, and its most recent winner of statewide election when she became agriculture commissioner in 2018, largely sees the middle ground as the key to reversing years of disappointment. “The coalition that makes up Florida is different. Every demographic inside the Democratic party is more conservative than the demographics outside of our state,” she said. “And a coalition here that has to be built is very unique to Florida, candidates running up and down the ticket from first responders to veterans, Teach for America alumni, and just everyday Floridians who are frustrated with the state affairs here. “All of them have been at the doors, on the phones, talking to voters for the better part of the last year and a half, and really listening, listening to concerns from Floridians. And it’s a pretty consistent drumbeat.” Fried said she expected a voter backlash to DeSantis’s partisan gerrymandering of congressional districts, which was intended to reduce Democrats’ share of the state’s 28 seats from eight to four. It forced some candidates to switch districts mid-campaign, and set up rancorous primary races elsewhere between leftist hopefuls and established Congress members. Fried said DeSantis’s move could backfire. “Right now, the Republicans have a nasty primary for governor that is going to decrease their motivation to turn out in November,” she said. “You have a president who is significantly underwater, and a state where for 30 years one party has had control and people can’t afford to live here. So the enthusiasm on the Republican side to turn out is going to be significantly diminished. “One-third of our state is independent and what we have seen since the last 18 months since President Trump took a second term is that that independent block has been breaking for Democrats in record numbers. An energized Democratic base, independents breaking with us 60, 70%, and a diminished Republican turnout in energy … that’s a winning equation.” Jewett, meanwhile, said DeSantis’s eight years as a hardline governor might prompt chunks of the electorate to seek something different. “When you talk about some very specific policies, sometimes Floridians actually have more progressive views than you might think, it’s just that most of them don’t want to call themselves progressive or socialists, even if they agreed,” he said. “You know, we voted to increase the minimum wage to $15 an hour over time. We voted for medical marijuana. So there are some particular issues that Floridians may be a little bit more progressive on, but most don’t think of it like that. “That label still has a negative connotation to a lot of voters.”

title: First Thing: Meta’s treatment of children on social media in spotlight as landmark trial set to begin
author: Martin Belam
summary: Multiple US states have accused Instagram and Facebook’s parent company of deliberately causing young people harm with its products
body_text: Good morning. More than half of the states in the US have joined together in an unprecedented lawsuit against Meta that goes to trial on Tuesday, accusing the parent company of Instagram and Facebook of deliberately designing addictive products that lured in young people and caused them harm. The sweeping legal proceedings could have profound consequences for the company. The attorneys general say that if Meta is found liable, damages could be as high as $200bn – equivalent to the company’s 2025 annual revenue. The lawmakers are also asking that Meta be compelled to change the design of its products to make them safer for children, which may have longer-term effects than a fine. What is Meta accused of? The 233-page lawsuit, first filed in October 2023, alleges that Meta regularly collects data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission. The lawmakers claim in court documents that Meta “refuses to abandon its use of known harmful features” and that its motives are based solely on profit. How has Meta responded? Meta denies all allegations and says: “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout. The state AGs may call this a landmark case, but their limited claims are unsubstantiated and their financial demands are vastly disproportionate.” Trump dismisses USS Lincoln criticism and snaps at CNN reporter to ‘be quiet’ Donald Trump claimed he had third-hand reports that the USS Abraham Lincoln is “beautifully maintained” despite extensive accounts of deteriorating living conditions during its lengthy deployment in the strait of Hormuz. The Navy Times and Stars and Stripes – the latter notably under increased control of the Pentagon as a defense publication – have largely confirmed reports of the Lincoln’s conditions. The publications described shortages of supplies and water and plumbing problems. Several sailors have attempted to leap from the ship according to their reports, prompting Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon. At the White House the president berated CNN reporter Kristen Holmes insisting that she “be quiet” and describing the reporting as fake news. The White House also attacked Holmes in social media posts, calling her “callous and vindictive”. Why have conditions onboard the ship become contentious? The Lincoln, a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier left port from San Diego on 21 November 2025 and has now set a modern record for the longest time at sea without a port call. It has been more than 250 days since it has touched land. What else is causing concern with US navy ships? A US guided-missile destroyer reportedly spent four days adrift and without power in the South China Sea in July. The USS Benfold was reported to have been towed to Subic Bay in the Philippines. South Korea president calls for military independence in wake of Trump call to cut joint drills South Korea’s president ⁠has renewed his push to regain independent control of the military from the US in the event of war and urged faster progress in acquiring nuclear-powered submarines after Donald Trump’s order to cut joint drills. Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that Seoul should proceed without disruption with ‌the planned transfer, during his term, of ‌wartime operational control of South Korean forces from the US – a goal he and the government have long held. Why does the US have operational control of South Korea’s forces? The issue dates back to the Korean war, which ended without a formal peace treaty in 1953, meaning the two Koreas remain technically at war. The authority to direct South Korean forces if fighting resumes still rests with the US. Seoul regained peacetime control of its own military in 1994, but wartime authority has become a potent symbol of national sovereignty. Luigi Mangione New York murder trial postponed after guilty plea in federal case A New York state ⁠judge ⁠effectively postponed Luigi Mangione’s trial on murder and weapons charges over ⁠the 2024 killing of a health insurance company CEO, after Mangione pleaded ⁠guilty last week to separate federal charges. The trial had ‌previously been ‌scheduled to begin on 8 September. Mangione ‌has pleaded not guilty to the state charges. Mangione’s lawyers on Friday asked New York state justice Gregory Carro ‌to dismiss the charges. They argued that Mangione should not have to be punished for the same conduct twice. In other news … Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party has compared the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, to the leaders of Iran and Hezbollah on a campaign billboard in Tel Aviv which says “They want Netanyahu to lose, don’t let them win”. Donald Trump voted by mail in Florida’s Republican primary despite his nationwide moves to restrict mail-in voting. Construction on a controversial US-Mexico border project in Big Bend national park has halted, the Trump administration said. News of construction in Texas’s largest and most-visited national park had sparked concern from environmental groups. Democratic senator Jon Ossoff has attacked Donald Trump’s “uniquely despicable” handling of the US-Israel war on Iran, accusing the US president of “re-rigging” a corrupt system for himself. Stat of the day: Tens of thousands pay tribute to Jason Arday at Trafalgar Square vigil An estimated 30,000 mourners gathered in London for a vigil honoring Jason Arday. Friends, campaigners, and lawmakers paid tribute to the 41-year-old former Cambridge professor, who was pronounced dead on Friday. He had recently resigned his sociology of education post following disputed allegations of plagiarism and career inaccuracies. Culture Pick: Hollywood continues to fail child stars and Hayden Panettiere is the latest casualty Jesse Hassenger writes that the untimely death of the Heroes and Scream star was a tragic ending to a life filled with darkness in an industry that still lets its younger stars down. Don’t miss this: Visual effects maestro Rick Baker on a monstrously good career Rick Baker helped define Hollywood’s creature features with his wild makeup effects skills. Here he talks about Gremlins, his love of simians – and why AI will never replace expert design. … or this: What we know about Tupac Shakur’s death and what to expect from murder trial Nearly 30 years after Tupac Shakur was killed in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas, the only man ever charged in connection with the rapper’s death is now on trial. Here is what we can expect. Climate check: Extreme heat more dangerous for people 60 and over than previously thought Older adults will bear the brunt of increasingly frequent sustained spells of extreme heat globally. Research has found that people aged 60 and over face dangers to their health from exposure to heat at much lower temperatures than previously thought. Last Thing: Nuns fight Italian town’s plans to take away their beach club A group of Italian nuns is fighting local council plans to take their beach club away from them. The nuns have been managing the resort since 1946. Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. If you’re not already signed up, subscribe now. title: Israel withdraws support for embattled Fifa president Gianni Infantino
author: Matt Hughes and Nick Ames
summary: The Israel Football Association blamed an ‘unprecedented crisis of confidence’ and lack of ‘proper vision’ in retracting its backing for Fifa’s Gianni Infantino
body_text: Gianni Infantino’s decision to sack his chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, after the Frenchman’s criticism of the World Cup sell-off plan has hardened some opposition to the Fifa president, with the efforts to force him out expected to intensify over the next few days. On Tuesday Israel became the latest Fifa member to officially withdraw their support for Infantino’s re-election in a letter sent by the head of the Israel Football Association (IFA), Moshe Zuares. The move is not a surprise as the IFA has been a member of Uefa since 1994 and Zuares sits on the European governing body’s executive committee, but it remains another blow to Infantino, who has invested significant political capital in attempting to improve sporting relations with Palestine. At Fifa’s congress in April Infantino tried to stage a photo involving the two delegations in Vancouver, but the Palestinian Football Federation president, Jibril Rajoub, refused to stand alongside IFA ⁠vice-president, Basim Sheikh ⁠Suliman. Undeterred by this setback, Infantino wants Israel and Palestine to compete in the first match of a new under-15 tournament in the United States next month, as reported by the Guardian in June. In his letter, which has been seen by the Guardian, Zuares says recent events have triggered an “unprecedented crisis of confidence” between the visions of Uefa and Fifa when it comes to global governance, adding that the rift is “profound, substantive, and principled, and compelling all stakeholders to reconsider the path forward”. In a decision he described as being taken unanimously after a meeting of the IFA’s board, Zuares confirmed: “We have no choice but to retract our previous letter of support, in the sincere hope that fruitful dialogue among all parties will eventually restore a shared, proper vision and direction for world football.” Israeli’s intervention echoes the withdrawal of support from other Uefa members including England, Wales, Scotland and the Republic of Ireland, and followed confirmation on Monday night that Lamour had left Fifa, having been deeply critical of Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. “If that means I lose my job, then so be it,” he said prophetically in a statement on 31 July. “I will understand and respect that decision. At least I’ll sleep well tonight.” Another Uefa executive committee member, the former Wales Women international Laura McAllister, said the decision to sack Lamour “sends a deeply troubling message” and casts serious doubt over any efforts by the global governing body to recalibrate after the FFE scandal. McAllister, who is one of five Uefa vice-presidents and worked there with Lamour before his move to Fifa in 2024, praised her former colleague for standing up to Infantino’s doomed scheme. “During the shabby events of the past weeks, he showed himself to be a courageous advocate for the most important stakeholders in football,” she said in a statement. “Kevin’s sacking seriously weakens Fifa’s administration, while undermining this unique opportunity to shift the culture at Fifa and to reset the organisation on sporting values, not simply commercial and financial ones. “Fifa is not the president, it is the whole football family. As I have said repeatedly, world football needs strong, principled, independent leaders who are prepared to speak up, challenge when necessary, and stand firmly by their values and those of the global game. Instead, the loss of a leader of Kevin’s calibre sends a deeply troubling message to all of us seeking change.” Meanwhile, Richard Masters, the Premier League chief executive, told the BBC that Infantino pressed the “self-destruct button” over his botched plan to bring private investment into the World Cup. “This is a problem of Fifa’s making,” Masters said. “This is a self-inflicted wound. The organisation has pressed the self-destruct button, and the consequences of that flow now into the solutions that need to be found. “I don’t think Fifa should be ever contemplating selling off a stake in the World Cup. They’re a not-for-profit organisation. They should really be holding that competition in trust for the future of football.”

title: US senator Jon Ossoff condemns Trump as ‘draft-dodging, crook president’
author: Cecilia Nowell
summary: Potential presidential hopeful running for re-election in Georgia intensifies White House feud after remarks about ‘Natalie’ drew ire of president and allies
body_text: The Democratic senator Jon Ossoff called Donald Trump a “draft-dodging, crook president” while defending the senator Mark Kelly as a hero during a Tuesday campaign appearance in Georgia, escalating his public feud with the US president. “I don’t think anything illustrates the times more aptly than that the draft-dodging, crook president, who has plunged our nation recklessly into a war he knows not how to end or to win, tried to imprison this man, who embodies American heroism,” Ossoff said while appearing alongside Kelly and his wife, the former Arizona congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords. Kelly, a former navy captain, and five other Democratic lawmakers were attacked by Trump last year after they released a social media video saying troops are not required to carry out illegal commands. Trump called for the lawmakers’ arrests, accusing them of “SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!” Ossoff, who is currently running for re-election to his Senate seat in Georgia and is widely speculated to be eyeing a 2028 presidential run, has received viral attention on social media for his sharp criticism of Trump. On Sunday, during a campaign appearance in Atlanta, Ossoff similarly attacked Trump’s handling of the US-Israel war on Iran. “While the sailors on the Lincoln fight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings,” Ossoff said. “He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the amir of Qatar.” Ossoff appears to have been referring to Natalie Harp, Trump’s executive assistant, who has drawn scrutiny for her closeness to the US president. The White House quickly criticized Ossoff on Monday, with the president calling him “Pee-wee Herman” and the White House communications director, Steven Cheung, writing on social media that Ossoff is “a radical, extremist Dumocrat”.

title: Trump-backed Byron Donalds to face Democrat David Jolly in race to succeed Florida governor DeSantis
author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
summary: Congressman had pledged to implement president’s agenda if he gained governor’s seat
body_text: Byron Donalds, a congressman backed by Donald Trump, won the Republican nomination for governor on Tuesday in the race to succeed Ron DeSantis. Donalds, who has represented south-west Florida since 2021, trounced three reasonably prominent Republican rivals, including Jay Collins, DeSantis’s handpicked lieutenant governor. If he wins the November election, as he is expected to do in the conservative stronghold, Donalds would become only the second elected Black governor in any southern US state. So confident was Donalds of victory that his television advertisements in the weeks leading to the primary ignored his Republican challengers and focused on former Republican congressman David Jolly, who secured the Democratic party’s nomination on Tuesday. He continued that message on Tuesday evening. “I am grateful to my family, my team, my volunteers, and every Floridian who powered us to this victory,” he wrote on X. “My Democrat opponent would raise taxes, make life more expensive, and bring the Democrats’ radical left agenda to the Sunshine State – Florida cannot afford Liberal David Jolly. David Jolly has lost before, and he will lose again on November 3. United, we will win the Governor’s mansion in 77 days and ensure that Florida remains the best state in this great country.” In his victory speech, Jolly addressed political division and the economy before placing blame on Donalds for the state’s rising costs. “To my Democratic friends, thank you for welcoming me into the party. We have built friendships, we have found common ground,” he said. He added: “Byron Donalds has sold the governor’s mansion to the highest bidder and the special interests across the state have been happy to play ball.” DeSantis did not make an endorsement in the race, but Trump did, backing Donalds and his conservative credentials, with support that could prove decisive in Florida, arguably the heart of Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, and home to his Mar-a-Lago Palm Beach estate. DeSantis was largely considered dead in the water in his own campaign to become governor in 2018, before Trump’s endorsement turned things around. Republican voters roundly rejected the credentials of Collins, an army special forces veteran who called Donalds part of a Washington elite; Paul Renner, the former Florida house speaker; and extremist James Fishback. Instead, they favored Donalds, who at times polled close to 50% and is, according to his campaign website, “committed to implementing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Great Again”. A vocal Trump ally who was reportedly considered for the 2024 vice-president pick that ultimately went to JD Vance, Donalds made affordability and reducing property taxes and insurance costs a central plank of his campaign, which some have seen as a dig at DeSantis’s obsession with culture war issues during his eight-year tenure. Jolly, a former Republican congressman and lawyer, became an independent, then switched parties last year. He ran a much more moderate campaign than the ones that worked well for progressive Democrats in other states’ primaries this summer, although that did not stop Donalds assailing him as “a radical liberal” who he claimed was an advocate for gender-reassignment surgery who supports transgender males in girls’ and women’s sports. Jolly easily fended off a challenge from five other Democrats, including state representative Dotie Joseph and Dayna Marie Foster, a former high school educator who was endorsed by the Florida Democratic Progressive caucus. Jolly faces an uphill battle in November, however. No Democrat has won a Florida governor’s election since Lawton Chiles in 1994; and no Democrat has won a statewide election in Florida since Nikki Fried, the current chair of the Florida Democratic party, was elected agriculture commissioner in 2018. • This article was amended on 19 August 2026. Owing to an editing error, an earlier version incorrectly said Byron Donalds would become, if elected, the first Black governor of any southern US state.

title: First Nations MP resigns from NT parliament, accusing government of passing laws which are ‘dehumanising, oppressing and destroying’ Indigenous people
author: Douglas Smith Indigenous affairs reporter
summary: Yolngu independent Yiŋiya Guyula accused the CLP of ‘contributing to the breakdown of our culture and people, in what is becoming a slow genocide’
body_text: A First Nations MP from the Northern Territory has resigned from parliament, accusing the ruling Country Liberal party of introducing laws that are “dehumanising, oppressing and destroying our communities and our people”, and contributing to a breakdown of culture that he says is “becoming a slow genocide”. Yiŋiya Guyula, a Yolngu man from the Djambarrpuyŋu clan in east Arnhem Land, was elected as the independent member for Nhulunbuy, now known as Mulka, in 2016. In a statement on Wednesday, Guyula said he could no longer “sit opposite a government who are not willing to listen or form partnerships”, and accused the Finocchiaro government of not being willing to work with First Nations people. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “I have been sent by my people to work with the government but their answer has always been, ‘we know what is best for you’, rather than working in partnership with us,” he said. “What I have discovered is that Aboriginal communities are the political football that gets passed around with no real intention of working with our people to bring positive change for our communities.” He specifically criticised the passage of new child protection laws which had been widely criticised by communities and peak Indigenous bodies, and prompted the resignation last month of the NT children’s commissioner, Shahleena Musk. Guyula said the Territory government changed the laws “with no consultation with our communities” and ignored an appeal he made to withdraw the bill. “Since their election, the CLP have introduced too many laws that are dehumanising, oppressing and destroying our communities and our people,” he said. “They have significantly failed Aboriginal people and their ongoing actions are contributing to the breakdown of our culture and people, in what is now becoming a slow genocide. “I no longer feel that I can be a part of the NT parliament and sit opposite a government who are not willing to listen or form partnerships. We are sovereign people and the only way things will improve is when the government recognise that and come and sit with us respectfully. We are kindly offering partnership, but instead of diplomacy the government are walking all over us. “This is very serious business because people are dying. I buried a younger brother earlier this month and on Friday the funeral for my older brother will begin. We have people dying avoidable deaths every day. We are physically, mentally and spiritually struggling because of the frequent loss of family members as we move from one funeral to the next.” The minister for Indigenous Australians, Malarndirri McCarthy, said Guyula was a “man of great strength and leadership” who had a “deeply held sense of justice he carried with him in the Northern Territory parliament”. “He is a man of many firsts. A commercial pilot, a bilingual educator and the Member for Mulka,” she said. “I know his story is not done with his retirement. He will continue to fight for homelands, for justice and against racism.” The independent senator for Victoria, Lidia Thorpe, also issued a statement in solidarity with Guyula and said it was “heartbreaking” to hear of his resignation. “His election as an Independent three times was historic. He showed that Aboriginal people can represent their communities on their own terms, accountable directly to their people rather than to any political party. He has shown how important Blak Sovereign voices in politics are, and his leadership will be missed,” Thorpe said. A byelection will be held for the seat of Mulka, with a date yet to be announced. An NT government spokesperson said the CLP acknowledged the “resignation of the Member of Mulka and wishes him all the best”, and that it would continue to focus on the “economic future of Nhulunbuy and region”. “Engagement with local Yolngu leadership will continue through the assistant minister for Nhulunbuy transition, Oly Carlson MLA,” they said.

title: Who is Natalie Harp? Trump’s closest and most devoted aide is in the spotlight
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: Speculation about US president’s executive assistant sparks furious backlash from White House
body_text: Wearing shoulder-length blond hair, gold earrings and a red dress, cancer survivor Natalie Harp introduced herself to the 2020 Republican national convention as “a formerly forgotten American from California” and compared Donald Trump to George Bailey, the everyman hero played by James Stewart in the classic film It’s a Wonderful Life. “George Bailey’s father was right,” smiled Harp, her voice echoing in the Andrew W Mellon auditorium in pandemic-hit Washington. “All you can take with you is that which you’ve given away. Mr President, that makes you the richest man in the world.” Six years later, Harp is now one of Trump’s closest and most devoted aides. Her official job title is special assistant to the president and executive assistant to the president on an annual salary of $150,000. Her unofficial job title is the “human printer” for supplying him with print-outs of information. And for years she has only been a minor character in the Trump Cinematic Universe. But all that changed this week when Jon Ossoff, a Democratic senator and possible 2028 presidential contender, accused Trump in a campaign speech of wanting to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie” instead of doing his job. The remark triggered a tsunami of online speculation about the precise nature of the relationship and a furious backlash. On Monday Trump lashed out at the CNN reporter Kristen Holmes after she asked a question about Ossoff’s comments, while the White House’s anonymous “Rapid Response” team posted at Holmes: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question.” Far from dousing the flames, the White House had in fact poured kerosene on them, inadvertently enhancing Ossoff’s national standing among Democrats and inviting millions of people to ask the same question. Who is Natalie Harp? The 35-year-old Californian graduated from Point Loma Nazarene University, a Christian liberal arts college in San Diego, in 2012. Three years later, she earned an MBA from Liberty University, an evangelical college founded by Jerry Falwell in Lynchburg, Virginia. Four years later, as Trump was mounting a bid for re-election, Harp wrote a post on LinkedIn entitled: “I’m Living Proof – the Party of Healthcare is Trump’s.” Recalling her experience with bone cancer, it explained: “On November 9, 2015 – a year to the day Donald Trump would win the presidency – a nurse mixed up my IV with the deadly substance of sterile water leaving me housebound and searching for care. “Instead of studying my symptoms to diagnose my condition, my Democrat-controlled state and country offered me opioids, barbiturates, medical marijuana, disability, Do-Not-Resuscitate orders, and yes, Death With Dignity. Before one appointment, I was even instructed in the voluntary stopping of eating and drinking (VSED).” Harp praised Trump’s signing of the 2018 Right to Try Act for giving her the opportunity to access experimental treatments that proved successful. “My oncologist didn’t tell me I had other options,” she said. “Donald Trump did … Now my numbers are stabilizing and so is my pain.” The LinkedIn post caught the eye of Rupert Murdoch’s conservative Fox News network, which invited Harp on air to talk about it. Trump responded on social media: “Natalie Harp, fighting Stage 2 Cancer and doing really well, was a GREAT guest on @foxandfriends. Right To Try is producing some truly spectacular results. Proud of Natalie!” That led to Harp’s speech in praise of Trump at the Republican national convention, a month after the death of her father. She managed to take a swipe at Britain’s National Health Service (NHS) after offering a message to Trump: “I wouldn’t be alive today if it wasn’t for you.” But a Washington Post article cast doubt on the claim, noting that experts point out that “Harp’s description of the treatment she received and her timeline for receiving it make it unlikely Trump had any effect on her case.” ‘Human printer’ Still, Harp and her mother quit California and moved into an 18th-floor apartment in West Palm Beach, Florida, three miles from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate. In 2020 Harp joined the far-right One America News Network (OANN), where as a presenter she amplified Trump’s “big lie” that the presidential election had been stolen by Joe Biden. Harp left OANN in 2022 and began working for Trump, then a former president facing criminal cases and mounting a seemingly unlikely bid to return to the White House. She fed him a diet of good news on the election campaign trail. The New York Times reported in 2024: “She has no official title, but during the campaign, colleagues referred to her as the ‘human printer’ because she followed Mr Trump around with a portable printer and a battery pack to charge it, so she could hand him information in hard copy, as he prefers.” Now that Trump has returned to the Oval Office, Harp is frequently seen at his side and has become an indispensable aide. Last month, when the president was forced to secretly swap planes in Turkey because of an alleged Iranian assassination threat, she was one of the few people to join him on a military plane while other staff and journalists remained on a decoy Air Force One. One acquaintance of Harp, who did not wish to be named, said on Tuesday: “Nobody questioned [deputy chief of staff] Dan Scavino being on the military plane but frankly Natalie is a lot more capable than Dan Scavino in a lot of areas. She is beautiful by any definition and because of that people don’t understand how intelligent, articulate, loyal, trustworthy and engaged she is with politics.” ‘Guardian and Protector’ Harp also plays an outsized role in shaping both Trump’s worldview and his output. She reportedly shows him proposed Truth Social posts – often containing recycled content – then logs into his account to publish them. These have included a racist video depicting Barack and Michelle Obama as apes and an AI-generated image portraying Trump as Jesus Christ, according to the Wall Street Journal. In the book Regime Change published this year, New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan wrote that Harp’s loyalty extended to writing Trump “adoring letters” including one that read: “You are all that matters to me.” In one she wrote: “I want to bring you joy, to feel like we can get through a day without ever having to talk ‘work.’” In another she said, “I don’t ever want to let you down” and described Trump as her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”. Haberman and Swan also described a typical scene: “Harp was generally on a chair off to the side, her laptop open, head cocked, listening but never contributing unless ordered to by Trump. She fulfilled, in a flash, any request, whether a ‘Trump 2028’ that needed to be fetched from the merchandise room, a quick Google search, or producing the latest story from rightwing websites like Breitbart or Gateway Pundit.” Harp’s devotion to Trump does not sit well with her estranged brother, Preston Harp, who lives in Nicaragua’s capital, Managua. He told the Daily Beast website last month: “I think that she does see Trump as a kind of father figure because he embodies the doctrine of American exceptionalism.” Meanwhile the administration’s furious response to Ossoff’s speech implies that he touched a raw nerve and looks set to invite further scrutiny of Harp and her role in Trump’s life. Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, said: “It does invoke the famous line, ‘Methinks he doth protest too much’. You made this a bigger thing. “There’s something in life called a proportional response and what we saw from the White House was a massive response, which only further encourages questions and intrigue. It’s like, ‘Oh, there must be a there there for you to react so violently.’ If their thought process was this will tamp down speculation and gossip, whoever thought that is a moron.”

title: Activist forced out of US after criticising Trump-aligned Colombian politician
author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
summary: Beto Coral held up banners in Florida warning fellow Colombians to not vote for Abelardo de la Espriella
body_text: In the week before Colombia’s presidential election, Beto Coral, a well-known activist living in the United States, travelled to Florida to persuade fellow Colombians not to vote for the far-right candidate Abelardo de la Espriella. Coral held banners outside polling stations in Miami warning that the millionaire lawyer, whose candidacy was endorsed by Donald Trump, would “help deport all of you”. The following morning the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, issued a memo to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) alleging that the activist had used his presence in the country “to conduct political activity” against a Colombian presidential candidate, and that DHS could take steps to “facilitate his departure”. Hours later, Coral was arrested. He said that, over the following 30 days in DHS detention, he was assaulted, deprived of food and water, and held in solitary confinement before securing his voluntary departure back to Colombia in mid-July, after more than 10 years living in the US. Although other immigrants have previously been detained in the US over their political activism – most notably the Palestinian student Mahmoud Khalil for protesting against the war in Gaza – Coral’s case is being seen as the first involving remarks about a foreign election. “They detained me simply because I protested against a Trump-backed candidate,” said the 40-year-old activist, whose full name is Franklin Humberto Coral Garrido. Coral, who has no criminal record, alleges that his detention resulted from a request by De la Espriella, who went on to win the election and was sworn in earlier this month to replace the leftwing president Gustavo Petro, with whom Trump had repeatedly clashed. In early June the US deputy secretary of state, Christopher Landau, wrote on social media about Colombia’s election that those “tempted to undermine or manipulate the democratic process” were putting their visas at risk. “That’s why they call me El Quitavisas (the visa taker)”, he added. De la Espriella replied: “I have the list, dear deputy secretary.” On the morning of 16 June, the same day Rubio issued the memo, De la Espriella posted: “There will be good news for Colombia and for patriotic Colombians abroad,” alongside an AI-generated image of “El Quitavisas” projected into the sky. That afternoon, Coral was arrested. “De la Espriella knew that I was going to be arrested and announced it on X,” said Coral. The US state department and De la Espriella did not respond to requests for comment. Colombia’s new president already knew the activist from his years as a lawyer. De la Espriella represented the former president Álvaro Uribe Vélez in a defamation lawsuit filed in Florida against Coral after the activist accused him of leading paramilitary groups. Coral lost the case and was ordered to issue a public apology. Last May, Coral filed a complaint with the FBI alleging that De la Espriella had secretly recorded a telephone conversation between them and attempted to blackmail him with it. In his memo, Rubio cited the activist’s alleged “use of US courts to target a Colombian presidential candidate” as one of the political activities he claimed Coral had carried out “on behalf of the Petro government”. Coral entered the US on a tourist visa in December 2015 and applied for political asylum in March 2016, saying he had received death threats in Colombia after investigating the death of his father, Humberto Coral Caballero. A police captain who took part in the US-backed operation that brought down the notorious drug lord Pablo Escobar in 1993, Caballero was murdered months later. “I had been waiting for a decision on my asylum application since 2016, but I always had legal status and a work permit,” said Coral, who, besides his work as an activist and YouTuber, held “the kinds of jobs immigrants usually have in the US: I drove for Uber, worked in construction, was a cook, a waiter, a baker”. On the day of his arrest, he was returning from the supermarket with his 12-year-old son. He was later transferred six times between detention facilities across four states. “Those journeys were extremely long, and the agents wouldn’t give me water or food,” said Coral, who estimates that he spent “24 of the 30 days” in solitary confinement. “ICE officers shoved me, threw me against the wall and kicked me in the legs,” he added. A DHS spokesperson did not respond to questions about the mistreatment Coral said he suffered, instead sending a statement describing him as “an illegal alien” who “in violation of our nation’s laws, overstayed his visa for 10 years”. Nine Democratic members of Congress sent Rubio a letter on 23 June demanding Coral’s immediate release, arguing that the US government had violated his human rights, including his right to free speech. He was released only after his lawyer, Elizabeth Shaw, secured an agreement allowing him to leave the country voluntarily. In her filing, Shaw argued that Coral had been detained despite facing no immigration charges. She sought his release before De la Espriella’s inauguration, arguing that the incoming government posed “an open, real, and substantial threat” to his life. After briefly returning to Colombia – where he warned Petro that “he could be the next” to be arrested by the US – Coral has since left the country. He said he does not know where he will live next, but even though in theory he could still try to return to the US, as he was not deported, it will not be there – because it is “the worst place in the world for any immigrant”. “I find it paradoxical that Rubio is a Latino, the son of immigrants who came from Cuba in search of a better future for him, and now he persecutes, mistreats, detains and deports an immigrant who entered the country legally,” he said.

title: Why are progressives winning across the United States? It’s not complicated
author: Bernie Sanders
summary: Poll after poll shows the same thing. The American people know that the current economic system is rigged
body_text: The media pundits have written article after article desperately trying to understand why progressive candidates, despite being heavily outspent, keep defeating establishment Democrats in primaries around the country. Well, the answer is not complicated. Whether it is a corrupt campaign finance system, unprecedented income and wealth inequality, a broken and wildly expensive healthcare system, the enormous threats posed by AI or an immoral and destructive foreign policy, progressives are talking about the real issues facing working families. And they are providing real solutions. Establishment Democrats are not. Poll after poll shows the same thing. The American people know that the current economic system is rigged. The very rich get richer, while working families struggle. Today, while 60% of Americans live paycheck to paycheck, the billionaire class has never ever had it so good. We now have more income and wealth inequality than at any time in American history. The top 1% now own more wealth than the bottom 93% and one man, Elon Musk, owns more wealth than the bottom 50% of US households. Not surprisingly, working families are tired of status quo politics and the same old, same old establishment policies that have failed them for years. They want change, real change – and are supporting progressive candidates who are fighting for that change. In the richest country in the history of the world, Americans do not want to have to struggle every single day just to pay the bills. Working-class people do not want to die years younger than they should because of illnesses caused by the never-ending stress they experience just to survive. And, like past generations, they do not want their kids to have a lower standard of living than they do. Establishment politicians and the establishment media have described the agenda that progressive candidates are winning elections on as “radical”, “far left”, “extremist” or, in the words of Donald Trump, “communist” . All that is nonsense. On major issue after major issue, the progressive agenda is reflecting exactly what a strong majority of the American people need and want. Let me take this opportunity to share with you some of the major proposals that most progressives support. And you tell me how “extreme” they are. Campaign finance reform Progressives believe that our current campaign finance system is corrupt and is undermining democracy. It is absurd that one man, Mr Musk, can spend $290m to help elect Donald Trump as president and that billionaires in both parties can spend unlimited amounts of money in campaigns through their Super Pacs. We believe that we must end the disastrous US supreme court decision on Citizens United, ban Super Pacs and move to the public funding of elections. We believe that democracy means one person one vote, not billionaires buying elections. Healthcare Progressives believe that our current healthcare system is broken, dysfunctional and wildly expensive. We believe that it is immoral and fiscally irresponsible for us to spend roughly twice as much per capita on healthcare as do the people of other major countries, while 85 million Americans remain uninsured or underinsured. At the same time, we pay, by far, the highest prices in the world for prescription drugs. Progressives believe that healthcare is a human right and that we should do what all other major countries on Earth do, guarantee healthcare to all people. We agree with the 64% of Americans who want a Medicare for all single payer system. Protecting American workers Progressives believe that all Americans are entitled to a decent standard of living. We regard it as outrageous that in the year 2026 millions of workers continue to earn starvation wages and that the federal minimum wage remains at a disgraceful $7.25 an hour. We believe that the federal minimum wage should be raised to a living wage of at least $20 per hour. We also believe that employers should no longer be able to deny workers their constitutional right to join unions through illegal actions. Progressives support the passage of the Pro Act which will make it easier for workers to join unions and negotiate contracts that will provide them with better wages, benefits and working conditions. Tax the rich Progressives believe that, at a time of unprecedented income and wealth inequality, the wealthiest people in this country must start paying their fair share of taxes. At a time when we have the highest rate of childhood poverty of any major country on Earth and when one-third of our senior citizens are struggling economically, it is absurd that billionaires have an effective tax rate lower than truck drivers or nurses. The wealthiest people in this country and large profitable corporations must start paying their fair share of taxes so that we can adequately fund the needs of working families, the children and the elderly. Regulation of AI Progressives believe that AI and robotics, developed and pushed by the wealthiest people on Earth, are the most transformational technologies in the history of humanity and that they will impact every man, woman and child in our country. At a time when AI is threatening to displace millions of workers, eviscerate our privacy, harm our environment, undermine our democracy and negatively impact the mental health of our children, we believe that the government must play a decisive role in making sure that these revolutionary technologies are used to benefit all Americans, and not just make the big tech oligarchs even richer. Climate change Progressives believe that Trump’s assertion that climate change is a “hoax” is not only extraordinarily ignorant, but is a real danger to the planet. The last 11 years have been the hottest 11 years on record and the last three years have been the hottest three years on record. This past year the United States and countries throughout the world have seen major heatwaves, flash floods, increased drought and horrific forest fires – and scientists tell us the worst is yet to come. Progressives believe that we must forcefully take on the greed of the fossil fuel industry. The truth is that we can create millions of good-paying union jobs by transforming our energy systems away from fossil fuels and into energy efficiency and sustainable energy. For the sake of our kids, future generations and the habitability of the planet that is what we must do. Foreign policy Progressives believe that we need to fundamentally reform our foreign and military policies. The war in Vietnam was based on a lie. The war in Iraq was based on a lie. The current war in Iran is based on a lie. We do not need to spend $1.5tn a year on the Pentagon fighting endless wars and propping up dictatorships around the world. We certainly do not have to invest tens of billions supporting the extremist Netanyahu government in Israel, which has killed 73,000 Palestinians and wounded over 173,000 more – the vast majority of them women, children and the elderly. Despite what the media will have you believe, progressives are winning across this country for a simple reason: the ideas they are running on are extremely popular. It’s time for the political establishment to stop telling the American people what they should believe and start listening to what they actually want. Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. He represents the state of Vermont and is the longest-serving independent in the history of Congress
