title: By disparaging 2020 protests as ‘Woke 1’, liberals are following the rightwing’s lead
author: Andre Gee
summary: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s co-opting of conservative language to discuss a movement against state-sanctioned killings of Black people is damning
body_text: August has brought us a referendum on “Woke 1” – a term that reductively brands 2020’s social justice movement – as prominent liberal voices reflect on that time period with disappointing hindsight. During a recent appearance on ABC’s This Week, when asked about 2020-era demands to abolish prisons and police, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the US congresswoman from New York, abandoned her previous support of the “defund the police” movement, and instead joked: “Woke 1 was crazyyyyy.” Ocasio-Cortez, a democratic socialist, implied that the still-resounding calls for municipalities to reduce police budgets and to divert aid to poor communities were worth advocating for during the 2020 uprising, but are now “crazyyyyy”. In 2020, she noted that “a lot of people cannot fathom what an abolitionist America looks like. Tell them it looks like a suburb. Affluent white communities already live in a world where they choose to fund youth, health, housing more than they fund police.” But she has since backtracked on that idea. On 9 August, she told This Week co-host Jonathan Karl: “We all share the goals of having as low a crime rate as possible [but] rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today.” Days later, Zohran Mamdani, the progressive New York mayor, echoed her sentiment by surmising: “Sometimes, what you believe can change and develop.” But their reversing course on abolition isn’t development; it’s a devolution. The backlash to Ocasio-Cortez’s comments was widespread from leftists who felt as if her disavowal of the abolition and “defund the police” movements was an attempt to appease the Democratic establishment at their expense. Others, however, agreed with the assertion that “Woke 1” was defined by overly rigid radicalism, much of which occurred on social media, as with Chi Ossé’s 2021 post on Twitter declaring that “a cis white man should not be the next speaker of the council”. Ossé, a New York City council member, coined the term “Woke 1” after being confronted this past May with his old tweet. While everyone weighed in on “Woke 1”, though, I was more concerned with why the hell we were using branding co-opted by conservatives to discuss a movement against state-sanctioned killings of Black people. “Woke” has long shifted from Black America’s prideful adjective to a mocking noun that has been weaponized to ridicule Black liberation movements. Progressive liberals now adopting that dismissive language while placing confines on the movement for Black lives is damning. The term “woke” originated in Black American communities, and was popularized by a 2008 Erykah Badu lyric: “Even though you go through struggle and strife / To keep a healthy life, I stay woke.” The term became popular parlance in the 2010s; to “stay woke” meant you understood the components of white supremacy enough to identify them anywhere, whether in a work of art or a politician’s dog-whistling comments. But, as with other terms that originated in Black culture (“Blexit”, “Black fatigue”), the phrase was co-opted by rightwingers who claimed that calls for progressive policy were divisive and reactionary. By 2020, as the police killings of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor sparked a worldwide uprising, the burning of Minnesota’s third precinct, and widespread calls for radical change, conservatives pushed back by vilifying the word “woke”. In 2022, Ron DeSantis, the Florida governor, introduced the Stop Woke Act (Stop Wrongs to Our Kids and Employees Act), which tried to restrict schools and businesses from discussing critical race theory, misogyny and other oppressive dynamics. The then minority leader in the Senate, Mitch McConnell, warned that corporations should stop listening to our calls for equity lest they become “a woke parallel government”. The conservative commentator Ben Shapiro held live events to discuss “how wokeness is destroying America”. And a Santa Barbara Independent op-ed lauded the late far-right podcaster Charlie Kirk for “going into the lion’s den of woke”. So Ocasio-Cortez and Ossé evoking “woke” with the same pretense as these sectarian conservatives is cringeworthy. And when they do it to scoff at a movement against the police system’s predation of Black people, it’s dangerous. These comments come at the same time that Maga-world is engaged in a full-scale assault on Black people’s past, present and future, including the rollback of diversity measures leading to mass layoffs of Black employees, the systematic erasure of Black history from schools and attempts to repeal our voting rights. The phrase “Woke 1” is also off-putting because it’s dismissive of the work that abolition advocates and social justice organizations have been doing before and after 2020. What happened at the start of the decade wasn’t momentary advocacy; it’s in lockstep with what freedom fighters have been seeking since the inception of this country. It behooves some Democrats to realize the vitality of grassroots movement work isn’t dependent on photo ops and national headlines. The truest advocates are still on the frontlines, even if the masses have decided it’s no longer trendy. When Ocasio-Cortez was elected to Congress in 2018, the New Yorker characterized her as “the embodiment of anti-corporate politics”. There was hope she could help shake the party out of its moderate malaise. She initially advocated for like-minded candidates such as Cori Bush. People were excited by Ocasio-Cortez’s people-first platform: Medicare for all, raising the minimum wage to $15, the Green New Deal to mitigate the climate crisis and abolishing ICE (a stance she still holds). But some of her politics have retreated toward party orthodoxy. Today, she no longer wants to defund the police and controversially endorsed Joe Biden for president in 2024, despite him having a 42% average approval rating at the time and aiding Israel’s genocide in Palestine. And while Ocasio-Cortez still supports certain progressive candidates, she has also stopped endorsing candidates running against Democratic incumbents, helping stagnate any chance of a progressive insurgency. She’s sought to assimilate within the Democratic establishment, where the status quo outnumbers progressive voices. Some surmise that she is being pragmatic to garner more support for a 2028 White House run. But her need to do so exemplifies the hopelessness of electing progressive candidates who have to dilute themselves to rise in the party. There’s an oft-expressed belief that genuine liberation for Black people can’t come under the two-party system, with the Democratic party fixated on centrist consensus instead of radical policies that will offer marginalized groups a better material reality. For the first time in my lifetime in 2020, however brief, it seemed like Democrats understood that Black people wanted a genuinely equitable country. Officials such as Ocasio-Cortez aligned with these movements because the social current carried everyone in that direction. What happened to Floyd, Taylor and many others was too heartbreaking, too unjust to ignore. But years later, once swimming upstream became more difficult and supporting radical policy wasn’t good careerism, our demands became a “woke” fever dream to Ocasio-Cortez. I implore her and the rest of the Democrats not to find it “crazyyyyy” when droves of leftists once again express apathy toward the party in 2028.

title: First Thing: Trump in Canada tariff backdown after ‘substantial progress’ made on trade deal
author: Martin Belam
summary: US president cancelled planned tariff imposition just hours before it was to come into force
body_text: Good morning. Donald Trump has paused his threatened punitive tariff on Canada just hours before it was due to come into effect. After Trump’s announcement, the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, said “substantial progress” had been made towards a trade deal, but more work was needed. Tuesday’s 11th-hour backdown comes after a contentious year for the two countries, with the longstanding alliance strained by tit-for-tat tariffs and online broadsides in which Trump has mused about wanting to turn Canada into a US state. In February 2025, the White House hit Canada with a 25% tariff, citing what it regarded as inadequate progress in curbing cross-border illegal immigration and drug trafficking. In retaliation, Canada announced a reciprocal levy, calling the US’s actions “unwarranted and unreasonable”. How much trade do the two countries do? Historically, Canada and the US have been strong trading partners. In 2024, trade between the countries was estimated to be roughly $909bn, according to the office of the US trade representative. Democratic socialist Angie Nixon clinches surprise primary win in Florida US Senate race In an upset for the Democratic establishment, the progressive Angie Nixon won the party’s US Senate primary in Florida, beating the former army intelligence officer Alexander Vindman. Nixon, a state representative and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, had significantly less funding going into the primary. Vindman served on the national security council in Trump’s first term and became a well-known whistleblower and witness in the president’s first impeachment. What else happened in Florida’s elections? Byron Donalds, a congressman backed by Trump, won the Republican nomination for governor in the race to succeed Ron DeSantis. Donalds trounced three reasonably prominent Republican rivals, including Jay Collins, DeSantis’s handpicked lieutenant governor. If he wins the November election, as he is expected to do in the conservative stronghold, Donalds would become the first Black governor in any southern US state. OpenAI announces slowing pace of development after hack by rogue agent OpenAI said it had slowed down the ⁠pace of ⁠its AI development while it overhauled its ⁠research and training systems. The company’s researchers were ⁠caught unaware last month when an ‌AI agent ‌under testing hacked another AI ‌firm, Hugging Face. The AI research lab behind ChatGPT said its new measures included pausing its model testing for two ‌weeks and investing more in adding other systems to monitor the activities of AI agents in testing. Some of ⁠the company’s largest planned training runs remained on hold, it said. Pentagon threatens to cut federal funding to 30 universities over foreign academic partnerships Thirty US universities could lose federal funding unless they review and cut foreign academic partnerships the Pentagon considers a national security risk within the next two weeks, under a Pentagon directive aimed largely at ties to Chinese institutions. Harvard, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Johns Hopkins, Georgetown and Cornell are among the institutions ordered to conduct and report the reviews – and end partnerships deemed problematic – by 31 August, according to a US official who provided the full list to the Guardian. “The ‘Department of War’ has zero tolerance for academic partnerships that compromise our national security,” Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s chief technology officer, said in a news release. In other news … Harvard University has agreed to pay a $53m settlement to resolve civil lawsuits stemming from the illegal theft and sale of human remains that had been donated to its medical school for scientific research. A man accused of attacking two people at New York City synagogue on Friday has been charged with federal hate crimes. The ZZ Top drummer Frank Beard has died at the age of 77. The National Trust for Historic Preservation has urged the US supreme court to suspend Trump’s $400m White House ballroom project while it considers whether the work can continue. Engineers from Elon Musk’s SpaceX are on their way to a remote Australian island to retrieve part of a Starship that dived into the Indian Ocean. Stat of the day: Shares in humanoid robot firm Unitree surge 600% on Chinese stock market debut Unitree’s robots have gained global fame via videos of them performing martial arts and as dancers for pop stars. The company, which was founded in 2016, shipped more than 5,500 humanoid robots last year. Well Actually: Iceberg, romaine, kale – which salad greens are healthiest? “Eat your greens!” was a constant refrain in my childhood, and a mantra I found myself repeating as a parent. Adrienne Matei has everything you need to know about why it is important and how to get the best bang for your buck in terms of nutrition. Don’t miss this: Brain-breaking sex, bad boys in leather and queer glory – why TV vampires are so intoxicating My vampires of choice will always be Spike and Angel. Here Kayleigh Dray explores why everybody loves a bad boy – or girl – blood-sucker on TV. Why we are so hooked? Because, Kayleigh says, vampires embody absolute freedom, power, immortality, beauty and often forbidden love. … or this: Sonic the Hedgehog at 35 – from 2D to 3D to a billion-dollar film franchise I probably spent more time at college playing Sonic than I did studying. Keith Stuart looks back at the history of the world’s fastest blue hedgehog, while thankfully ignoring the unnervingly human teeth that he briefly had in that dreadful initial movie trailer. Climate check: Carbon pollution has fuelled ‘massive expansion’ of marine heatwaves in Europe, study finds The hottest fortnights of this year would have been “virtually impossible” in a preindustrial climate in three of the four sea regions studied, according to analysis by World Weather Attribution, while in the Celtic region, which covers much of the water around the British Isles, heat hit levels that used to strike just once a century. title: Democratic socialist Angie Nixon scores surprise win in Florida US Senate primary
author: Sam Levin and Richard Luscombe
summary: Nixon bested Alexander Vindman to win Democratic nomination and now faces Republican Ashley Moody in November
body_text: In an upset for the Democratic establishment, progressive Angie Nixon won the party’s US Senate primary in Florida, beating former army intelligence officer Alexander Vindman. Nixon, a state representative and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, had significantly less funding going into the primary – with $975,000 to Vindman’s $16.3m at the end of July, according to Florida Politics. But she won by a clear margin. Nixon received 56.1% of the vote, according to the Associated Press, ahead of Vindman’s 43.9%. Vindman served on the national security council in Donald Trump’s first term and became a well-known whistleblower and witness in the US president’s first impeachment, centered on Trump pressuring Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, to investigate Joe Biden. Democrats have their sights set on upsetting Republican Ashley Moody in the US Senate general election. Moody, picked by DeSantis to replace Marco Rubio when he became secretary of state last year, won what was almost a token primary election to run in November to serve the remaining two years of Rubio’s term. Nixon, who was born in Jacksonville, has aggressively opposed DeSantis’s policies, including with a sit-in at the governor’s office this spring to protest against Republican redistricting, the Miami Herald reported. That demonstration resulted in her facing misdemeanor charges of trespassing and resisting, which she is fighting in court. Vindman’s campaign had been focused on Moody, not his primary opponent, and he did not agree to debate Nixon, despite her public calls for him to take the stage with her. “Floridians don’t want the establishment in Washington DC deciding who their Democratic nominee and US senator is going to be,” Nixon told the Tampa Bay Times in an earlier interview. “I’m someone who’s willing to debate. He’s not. I’m someone who doesn’t have to be briefed on the issues Floridians are facing because I’ve been fighting the attacks alongside them for nearly two decades.” Vindman praised Nixon in a post on Tuesday night after the race was called, saying she “ran a strong campaign”. “I will be standing by her side in the fight against Ashley Moody. I hope you’ll join me,” he wrote, adding: “Who would’ve ever thought that a Jewish refugee would make it to the US Army, to the White House, and to becoming a candidate for the US Senate. Only in America is that possible.” Vindman had been expected to win the primary given his huge fundraising advantage. Nixon’s supporters had pointed to one poll suggesting that she would perform better against Moody in November than Vindman, though that poll projected the Republican incumbent would win against either Democrat. “We did it ya’ll,” Nixon posted on Tuesday night. “Thank you to every person that put their heart into this campaign.” National Democratic leaders praised Nixon’s victory, with Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, and Kirsten Gillibrand, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee chair, releasing a statement noting her background as a former union organizer, saying she had “dedicated her career to fighting for Florida”. Nixon’s victory follows a series of primary wins for Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates across the country, including in primaries in Philadelphia, Colorado, Michigan and New York City. But establishment Democrats prevailed in other Florida races this week, in the first election in the state after redistricting. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, an 11-term congresswoman and former chair of the Democratic National Committee, defeated Elijah Manley, a 27-year-old substitute teacher who was endorsed by a progressive group. Wasserman Schultz had faced criticisms for running in a district that has a plurality of Black voters and has long been represented by a Black Democrat. Wasserman Schultz’s previous district was broken up by Republicans’ gerrymandered congressional maps, and she chose not to run in the district where she lives, but in a newly drawn one that was solidly blue. Jared Moskowitz, a two-term congressman and centrist Democrat, defeated a democratic socialist challenger, running in a new coastal seat extending from Delray Beach to Miami Beach. Moskowitz was up against Oliver Larkin, a 34-year-old who called for universal healthcare and free tuition at public universities and has supported abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Moskowitz was the first congressional Democrat to back Trump’s “department of government efficiency” (Doge) initiative, which dismantled the US Agency for International Development. Moskowitz also faced criticism from Larkin over his support for a Republican-backed law that expanded ICE’s detention authority. The centrist congressman has also been a staunch supporter of Israel and voted against a resolution to restrict US military involvement in Iran.

title: Trump is full speed ahead in making money off being the US president
author: Margaret Sullivan
summary: Some restraint on Trump’s excesses might be accomplished if November’s midterm elections give Democrats more power
body_text: Donald Trump is essentially unrestrained when it comes to enriching himself during his second term, with no sign of stopping. If anything, he’s ramping things up. The numbers so far are astonishing. He amassed $2.2bn in 2025 revenues, the Guardian and other news outlets have reported. And despite widespread criticism of this astonishing fact, very little is standing in the way of his reaping even more. “The Congress has decided not to commit oversight to this topic, and that’s just the fact of the matter at this point,” Eric Lipton, an investigative reporter for the New York Times, told National Public Radio recently. While his actions appall historians, academics and millions of ordinary Americans, they may be within legal boundaries. Moral or ethical boundaries? Not so much. “While Trump’s second term is less than half over, it already looks like the most openly corrupt administration in our history,” Larry Noble, a law professor and former general counsel at the Federal Election Commission, told the Guardian’s Peter Stone. Despite his loyal base of followers, much of the American public isn’t happy about it. Two-thirds of Americans polled by CNN said that this president doesn’t put the good of the United States over his personal gain. His overall approval ratings have tanked to 33% – the lowest level of his presidency – with a disapproval rating at 64%, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll. Startling as the details of his enrichment may be, his mindset – full speed ahead, don’t bother me with past practices – reflects his behavior in other realms. He glories in knowing no restraints or boundaries, and shrugs off criticism. His power is held back only by his “own morality”, he told the New York Times in January. “It’s the only thing that can stop me.” He was speaking specifically about being restrained on the international stage – his freedom to use any military, economic or political power for what he sees as American supremacy. But it’s a mentality he apparently brings into feathering his and his family’s own nest. As Lipton told NPR, queries about apparent conflicts of interest are brushed off, and the party line is that the Trump family’s extracurricular businesses are building the US economy. In earlier presidencies, his actions surely would have political consequences, perhaps impeachment. (He was impeached twice, but not convicted, first in 2019 for abuse of power and obstruction of Congress, then for incitement of the violent insurrection at the US Capitol on 6 January 2021.) Trump has amassed at least $1.4bn last year from his cryptocurrency ventures alone, the Guardian reported, noting that others fared less well; about a million investors in one of his crypto projects suffered nearly $4bn in losses as the value of their holdings cratered. Then there are the wealthy foreigners who have invested in the Trump family’s hotel and golf-resort projects, creating potential conflicts of interest. His media company, Truth Social, has been another major source of wealth. Now there’s a new plan to offer early access to his posts for a fee of $100,000. Those posts, of course, have the power to move markets. It’s come under heavy criticism – and prompted lawsuits from media organizations and advocacy groups such as the Freedom of the Press Foundation that argue it’s unconstitutional. But, to date, as with so much of what Trump does, it’s proceeding brazenly. Every once in a while, the courts step in to provide some restraints. Trump tried to use his already weaponized federal justice department to settle his $10bn lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service. The initial result was to provide him and his family immunity from earlier audits of their tax returns, which might save the Trumps about $100m. But in a rare bit of accountability, a federal judge – one appointed by Barack Obama – nullified major parts of the agreement. The legal status is still being contested, and the stakes are high. All of this has the power to shock those paying attention to news reports. But there, too, Trump has given himself a form of protection by constantly playing on citizens’ mistrust of legacy media and to brand such investigations as “fake news”. The result, as author and journalist Craig Unger put it recently on Substack, is that nothing “moves the needle”. Not that long ago, he wrote, the press could “root out corruption, topple presidents, and end wars”. But now, even the biggest scoops and the most dramatic revelations seem to have little impact, Unger argues; that’s because the national citizenry doesn’t share an agreed-upon set of facts as it used to do. Trump’s low approval ratings do seem to tell a different story, however, and voters will get a chance to make their voices heard soon. At the very least, some restraint on Trump’s excesses might be accomplished if November’s midterm elections give Democrats more power with a majority in one or both chambers of Congress. Many forecasters think the Democrats may well regain the House of Representatives but that their getting a majority of Senate seats is quite a bit less likely. For now, Trump continues to take full advantage of a situation that has so greatly benefited his personal wealth, if not his reputation or legacy. Like a greedy toddler, he keeps sticking his hand in the presidential cookie jar. And no one, so far, seems able to yank it out. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

title: Florida governor suspends former close ally over child sexual abuse charges
author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
summary: Michael Caruso, once praised by Ron DeSantis, removed from Palm Beach county civic official roles after arrest
body_text: Florida’s Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, has suspended a former close ally and senior civic official who was arrested on felony child sexual abuse charges. Michael Caruso, who was removed as clerk of court and comptroller for Palm Beach county on Tuesday, was a vocal supporter of a law signed by DeSantis in 2023 that allowed the death penalty for anybody convicted of the sexual battery of a child under 12. The governor previously called Caruso “a legend” for his support of hardline legislation while he was a Republican state representative from 2018 until last year. Caruso, 67, a married father of seven children, was denied bond during his first court appearance on Wednesday in West Palm Beach on five felony charges of kidnapping, child molestation, lewd exhibition, luring or enticing a child and child abuse causing mental injury. Court documents said the alleged victim, who is a male relative of Caruso, is under the age of 12, and was molested multiple times during 2024 and 2025 during holidays and on family trips, including a Caribbean cruise. Caruso’s arrest was announced on Tuesday in a social media post by James Uthmeier, Florida’s attorney general. “Early this morning, with substantial assistance from FDLE [Florida department of law enforcement] and local law enforcement, Palm Beach County Clerk of Court Michael Caruso was arrested on charges related to child sexual abuse,” the post said. “The investigation is ongoing, and we will provide more information to the public at the appropriate time.” DeSantis was asked about Caruso’s arrest at a later press conference, and said he acted immediately on hearing of it to suspend him from office. “It was a very easy decision for me to yank him from that position,” DeSantis told reporters in Sarasota. The governor’s office later posted to its website a three-page order of suspension, accompanied by an arrest affidavit with details of the allegations. Caruso, DeSantis said at the press conference, was “well regarded in the community”. He coached little league baseball for decades and was a volunteer with boy scouts. But, DeSantis said, he “is going to be in a world of hurt” if he is convicted. The governor replied “of course not” when asked if he or anybody in his administration was aware of any allegations against Caruso. However, the Miami Herald reported that Caruso’s personal life was “marked with ugly flare-ups and at least one previous allegation of sexually assaulting a child”, documented in Palm Beach court records the newspaper said it had reviewed. In a 2013 divorce filing from his ex-wife, the Herald said, Caruso claimed she had orchestrated “a false sex abuse case” against him, which was the subject of a 2012 investigation by local and state authorities. DeSantis and Caruso recently enjoyed a close working relationship, with the governor frequently praising his ally for supporting hardline causes in the Florida legislature. According to the Herald, DeSantis called Caruso “my representative” after he was the sole backer of controversial immigration legislation, then appointed him as Palm Beach clerk of court in August 2025 shortly before he was termed out of the Florida ouse. Additionally, the Herald reported, DeSantis gave several plum appointments to Caruso’s wife, Tracy Stein Caruso, to the board of Palm Beach county’s healthcare district, and as chair of its housing and finance authority. She is shortly to take up a third DeSantis appointment, on the Palm Beach State College trustees board, subject to Florida senate approval, the newspaper said. Michael Caruso was most recently state representative for Florida’s 87th house district, a seat including Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort that was captured by Democrat Emily Gregory in an upset March election. The Guardian has contacted Caruso’s attorney, Jason Weiss, for comment. In a statement to the NBC affiliate WPTV on Wednesday, Weiss said: “Mr Caruso is innocent of these allegations and intends to vigorously defend himself against these charges. “We look forward to his expeditious transfer to Orange County so that appropriate bond conditions can be set.” • In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453 or visit their website for more resources and to report child abuse or DM for help. For adult survivors of child abuse, help is available at ascasupport.org. In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helplines International

title: US justice department defends prosecution of James Comey over ‘8647’ seashell post
author: Anna Betts
summary: Justice department claims there’s ‘no dispute’ over whether ex-FBI head’s post could be read as a threat against Trump
body_text: The US Department of Justice has defended its prosecution of former FBI director James Comey, claiming in new court documents there is “no serious dispute” that his social media post last year featuring a photo of seashells arranged to read “8647” could be interpreted as a threat against Donald Trump. “There is no serious dispute that an objective viewer of Comey’s post could read it to mean ‘Kill President Trump’,” prosecutors wrote in a document filed on Tuesday in response to Comey’s efforts to have the case dismissed. Comey was indicted in April after a grand jury in North Carolina charged him with making a threat against the US president and transmitting that threat, via social media, across state lines, over an image he posted on Instagram while vacationing in North Carolina last May. In the photo, the seashells were arranged to read “8647”, which the president’s allies and supporters quickly denounced as a threat against Trump. The number “86” is often used as shorthand to mean to get rid of or remove something, while Trump is the 47th US president. Comey deleted the photo after the uproar, saying he didn’t know that it could be interpreted as a violent threat. “It never occurred to me, but I oppose violence of any kind so I took the post down,” he said. In the court documents filed earlier this week, prosecutors with the eastern district of North Carolina continued to argue the post was a “coded message to his followers meaning ‘kill’ or ‘get rid of’ President Trump”. Comey has denied the charges against him and his lawyers have asked the judge to dismiss the case, arguing that the post was protected speech and did not amount to a “true threat” against the president. “The indictment alleges that Mr Comey’s ‘86 47’ post constitutes a ‘true threat; on the President’s life,” Comey’s lawyers wrote in a filing last month. “That claim is contradicted by every possible source of meaning: dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense. ‘86’ simply means ‘get rid of’ or ‘eject’ and has no violent connotation except in the most uncommon usages.” Comey’s lawyers have argued that “in this context, no reasonable observer would understand the phrase ‘86 47’ to connote violence at all – let alone to threaten that Mr Comey personally would commit violence against the President”. Comey’s lawyers have also said the case should be dismissed for “vindictive and selective prosecution” and have said the indictment is “not based on a goodfaith application of the law to the facts; instead, it effectuates a yearslong campaign by the President to use the criminal process to punish Mr Comey for his protected speech and because of the President’s deep-seated animosity”. Trump has long feuded with Comey since his handling of the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election while he was FBI director. Last year, the justice department also indicted Comey in a separate case, alleging that he had lied to Congress. But those charges were later thrown out after a judge ruled the prosecutor handling the case was unlawfully appointed.

title: Lindsey Graham’s sister and fill-in senator says she’s ‘not that informed on national security’
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: She made the statement during a debate when asked about potential threats to US national security in South China Sea
body_text: Asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea threaten US national security, Republican fill-in senator Darline Graham hesitated. “I’m just going to be honest here,” she told Tuesday night’s debate audience. “I’m – not that informed on national security, so – but I do support the military.” Gasps, and boos, rolled through the opera house hosting the only debate before next week’s Republican runoff – a race to succeed her brother, Lindsey Graham, who was one of the Senate’s most committed rightwing foreign policy hawks before his sudden passing in July. She did not retreat. “I’m not a polished politician up here,” she added. “National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military.” Her opponent, the ultra-conservative representative Ralph Norman, who once advocated for martial law to keep Joe Biden from the presidency after his election win in 2020, needed no such disclaimer. He walked through Taiwan’s economic ties to the US and made the case that it was worth protecting from Chinese aggression. Graham, endorsed by Donald Trump and leaning on her outsider credentials, recovered later in the evening, describing her family’s reliance on social security survivor benefits after her parents died, and accusing Norman of being unable to decide whether he wants to work in South Carolina or Washington, citing his gubernatorial loss just this year. Norman, who backed his state’s former governor Nikki Haley over Trump in 2024, used the debate to distance himself from the president over the war with Iran, saying Trump “is going to have to tell the American people what it’s going to take” if the strait of Hormuz remains under the control of a country the administration has claimed to have decimated. Since 1979, the US has stuck to what’s called “strategic ambiguity” on Taiwan: refusing to say whether it would actually send troops if China invaded, on the theory that being vague keeps the peace. Trump has largely kept up that dodge, but with his own twist. At his May summit with Xi Jinping in Beijing, the US president said he wasn’t looking to fight a war “9,500 miles” away and wanted “China to cool down”, and put a pending $14bn Taiwan arms package on hold, calling it a “very good negotiating chip”. Xi, meanwhile, told him mishandling the Taiwan issue could lead to “clashes and even conflicts”. Last August, Trump said Xi had personally told him China wouldn’t invade Taiwan while he’s in office – a claim Beijing brushed off, reaffirming its commitment to “reunification”. In South Carolina, early voting begins on Wednesday, ahead of the 25 August primary.

title: A democratic socialist win and losses for Trump allies: takeaways from primaries in three key states
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Elections in Florida, Alaska and Wyoming provide a sense of how voters are feeling ahead of November’s midterms
body_text: Primaries in Florida, Alaska and Wyoming held on Tuesday provided the latest view into how voters are feeling ahead of November’s US midterm elections. One candidate aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) netted an extraordinary win while another was defeated handily. Donald Trump’s handpicked candidates received a mixed reception from voters. In Alaska, voters chose their fighters for one of the year’s marquee US Senate races, and in Florida, extremism remained alive and well among Republicans. Here’s what we learned from the results: Democratic socialists win their first statewide victory In a shocking upset, state representative Angie Nixon beat Alexander Vindman for the Democratic nomination in Florida’s US Senate race, becoming the first member of the DSA to win a statewide primary, although the group did not endorse her. Her odds of victory in November against Republican Ashley Moody appear long, but Nixon’s win was the latest sign that Democratic voters are willing to buck the preferences of their party’s establishment in favor of candidates whose policies and personalities they prefer. Vindman, known for his role as a whistleblower during Trump’s first term, had a significant cash advantage and backing from leading Democrats, yet lost by a wide margin. The US Senate battle is set in Alaska As expected, the Republican senator Dan Sullivan won his primary in Alaska, and former congresswoman Mary Peltola won the Democratic nomination to take him on in what will be one of the top US Senate contests of the year. The state conducts non-partisan primaries in which the top four vote-getters advance, and while counting is not complete, the Associated Press reports that another Republican candidate named Dan Sullivan and Democrat David B Leslie are in the lead to appear on the November ballot. In what may be a troubling sign for Sullivan in the midterms, Peltola led him in the primary, winning 48% of the vote to the Republican senator’s 42.8%. No clear answers for progressives Progressives did not win everywhere. In south Florida, the Democratic congressman Jared Moskowitz won his primary, easily beating DSA-endorsed challenger Oliver Larkin. In the hours that followed, the congressman harshly criticized the DSA and the popular streamer Hasan Piker for campaigning against his renomination, arguing that because his district has been gerrymandered by Florida’s legislature to be more easily winnable for Republicans, he’s the best candidate to keep it in Democrats’ hands in the US midterm elections. Democrats continue to show strength down the ballot A handful of local and special elections offered further evidence that Democratic voters were fired up this year. Pennsylvania statehouse candidate Brandon Dukes won a special election against his Republican opponent Scott Timko, in a seat Trump carried by 18 percentage points in 2024. And though Florida has become increasingly conservative and Republican in the past decade, Democrats ousted a Moms for Liberty board member in Sarasota and won an at-large city council seat in Jacksonville. Extremism in the Republican party was on display The primary elections included several extremist candidates. Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback, backed by neo-Nazi influencer Nick Fuentes, lost badly in the Republican primary, but still picked up support in precincts around college campuses. Election denier Chuck Gray won his bid for the at-large US House seat in Wyoming. Congressman Randy Fine, who has been criticized for Islamophobic and homophobic statements, survived a primary challenge from antisemitic and transphobic influencer and businessman Dan Bilzerian. Trump endorsees lose Several candidates Trump had endorsed were not to voters’ tastes. The president had backed state superintendent of public instruction Megan Degenfelder in Wyoming’s Republican gubernatorial primary, but she lost to state senator Eric Barlow. Congressman Cory Mills lost his primary in Florida to former TV reporter Ryan Elijah, while a former official from Trump’s first term, Catalina Lauf, failed in a bid for a nomination to the US House. House GOP solves a problem named Cory Mills Mills’s primary loss is notable also because it solves a problem for House Republicans without dealing further damage to their razor-thin majority. The second-term congressman had been under investigation by the House ethics committee for a range of misconduct, and has faced allegations of domestic assault and fraud. While some House lawmakers had hinted that he should resign, as three other lawmakers facing similar allegations did earlier this year, Mills’s departure could have jeopardized the GOP’s control of the chamber. Instead, two of his Republican colleagues endorsed his successful primary challenger, and Mills’s time in the House will end at the start of next year.

title: Unhinged White House response shows senator’s ‘Natalie’ barb struck a nerve
author: Adam Gabbatt
summary: Senator Jon Ossoff, who is up for re-election, came up with arguably the standout line of the midterm elections so far
body_text: Jon Ossoff really struck a nerve. That much is clear. The US senator for Georgia, running for re-election in November, came up with arguably the standout line of the midterm elections campaign so far when discussing Donald Trump at a rally on Sunday. “While the sailors on the [USS Abraham] Lincoln fight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings. He golfs and trades stocks,” said Ossoff. “See, he doesn’t want to do the job. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.” Not only did the remark enter into national consciousness the existence of “Natalie” – Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old aide to Trump who rarely leaves the president’s side – Ossoff’s riff also succeeded in upsetting Steven Cheung, Trump’s director of communications. “Jon Jackoff,” Cheung wrote on X on Monday, misspelling, perhaps deliberately, the name “Ossoff”, “has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics. Instead of denigrating hard working people serving their country, Jon should look deep into his soul and ask himself why he’s a miserable person who hates this country. It’s because he’s a radical, extremist Dumocrat.” Even for someone in Trump’s orbit, where outbursts against political opponents are commonplace, this plumbed new lows. What could possibly have triggered Trump’s stoutly built, middle-aged communications guru into attacking Ossoff, the handsome, athletic, 39-year-old senator? It’s hard to be sure. But, apropos of nothing, this essay by Dana Schwartz, from 2016, examined why rightwing men are obsessed with calling people “cucks”: “‘Cuck’ is a concept borne [sic] out of insecurity: a fear that one is inadequate, sexually or otherwise, and that inadequacy will lead to the loss of the things that are important to him,” Schwartz wrote. In any case, Trump wasn’t far behind Cheung, calling Ossoff a “Pee-wee Herman lookalike” – a reference to a TV and film character whose popularity peaked 40 years ago. (Trump has also called Ossoff “Pinky Herman”, which is neither a character nor a thing.) The anonymous White House Rapid Response X account joined in too, branding a CNN reporter who had asked Trump about Ossoff a “disgraceful, humiliating embarrassment to her alleged profession”, and later posting: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive. It’s quite troubling.” It’s hard to really be shocked by any of this any more, with daily attacks on the media from the president and his most senior aides, but an official White House account, with 2.2 million followers, invoking a reporter’s children prompted widespread criticism. In truth the rhetoric from Trump and his acolytes, always bellicose, has been getting worse for a while – and people who dare to publicly question Trump’s narrative that he is a successful, popular president, seem to particularly trigger those on the right. Take James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Texas, who is running neck and neck against Ken Paxton, whom Trump picked for the Republican side. Talarico’s popularity in a traditionally red state has seen Republicans come out swinging. Trump dubbed the Democrat “Talafreako” in July; earlier US senator Bernie Moreno had called Talarico, “a far left freak”, while a Texas congressman falsely claiming Talarico “daydreams about trans kids”. (There was also Trump branding a reporter “piggy” after she asked him a question onboard Air Force One.) Perhaps the fury is prompted whenever something, or someone, succeeds in puncturing the alternate reality that Republicans have created for themselves: a reality where the GOP is not predicted to suffer heavy losses in November’s midterms, and one where Trump is a spry, capable president. When someone points out that Trump is an 80-year-old, easily distracted man who is overseeing an ill-defined, meandering war in Iran, while doing little as prices soar at home, it appears to bring out the particularly vulgar insults. Ossoff did all this on Sunday – and sparked fresh speculation about the president’s relationship with a close aide. With Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, stepping down, there is some jostling taking place in Trump’s circle to replace her, perhaps explaining the amped up language as each potential successor seeks to be more pugnacious than the last. And given Democrats in Congress will be running on Trump’s unpopularity this November, there’ll be plenty of opportunity for bellicose responses from the White House. We should brace ourselves for plenty more of this sort of thing.

title: Epstein client Leon Black threatened with contempt by House panel chair
author: Stephanie Kirchgaessner in Washington
summary: Republican James Comer writes to private equity investor demanding full cooperation with investigation
body_text: The Republican chairman of the House oversight committee has threatened to hold the private equity investor Leon Black in contempt if he does not fully cooperate with the panel’s ongoing investigation into Jeffrey Epstein, amid accusations that the billionaire is purposely delaying and disrupting the panel’s inquiry. A letter released by Representative James Comer’s office on Tuesday, which was addressed to Black’s lawyer, revealed new details about the high-stakes clash between the powerful Kentucky congressman and Black, the co-founder of Apollo Asset Management who was Epstein’s friend and former client and paid Epstein tens of millions of dollars in fees. “If Mr Black refuses to provide the Committee with responsive documents or refuses to appear for his scheduled deposition on September 3, 2026, the Committee will use all tools at its disposal, including contempt,” Comer said. Susan Estrich, Black’s lawyer, rejected Comer’s assertions in a statement released on Tuesday night, saying the letter was misrepresenting the facts, and that Black was being targeted in a “political witch hunt”. Black voluntarily agreed to be questioned by the House panel in June as part of the committee’s broad investigation into Epstein, which the panel has said includes an examination of the alleged mismanagement of the federal government’s investigation into the late sexual predator; the operation of sex-trafficking rings; and the ways in which Epstein and his companion Ghislaine Maxwell “sought to curry favor” to protect their “illegal activities”. But Black’s appearance ended abruptly – after just one hour of questioning – after members of both parties said Black was refusing to answer questions about non-disclosure agreements (NDAs). Comer, in his capacity as committee chairman, issued two subpoenas on that day in response to Black’s alleged lack of cooperation: one demanding that Black produce “all non-disclosure agreements to which he is a party” and another demanding he appear before the committee for a deposition. The fight between the congressional oversight panel and Black is now centered on the scope of the oversight committee’s investigation. Black has so far handed over one NDA to the committee for review and – according to this week’s letter – has indicated he is willing to provide one additional NDA. But in return, according to Comer, Black’s attorneys are seeking a promise that Black will not be held in contempt. They are also seeking to change the planned deposition subpoena to a voluntary transcribed interview. Black’s attorneys, Comer said, were also seeking to limit the scope of questions about confidentiality agreements to the two NDAs he was willing to provide. Black’s team was also seeking to delay the interview from 3 September to early October. “At no point has Mr Black sought a reasonable accommodation from the Committee, but rather he has consistently sought to dictate to the Committee the scope of its investigation,” Comer wrote. One of the points of contention appears centered on the timing of NDAs that Black may have entered. According to Comer’s letter, Black defended his decision to provide a single NDA because “to the extent any more such confidentiality agreements exist, they would have been negotiated … well after Epstein’s death” in 2019. In response, Comer said Black did not have “the right to decide what documents are responsive” to his subpoena, and that any agreements signed after Epstein’s death “could still involve [Epstein’s] victims”. Estrich, Black’s lawyer, said: “Mr Black provided the Committee with the only confidentiality agreement that pre-dated Epstein’s death and the only one of which Epstein was aware.” She added: “Congress has no right to invade private lives as part of a fishing expedition especially where the parties to a confidentiality agreement do not want their identities revealed in a circus-like atmosphere and especially when Epstein had nothing do with any agreement.” According to a report commissioned by Apollo several years ago, Epstein provided financial services to Black between 2012 and 2017. After Epstein pleaded guilty to Florida state prostitution charges in 2008, including procuring a minor, Black became Epstein’s largest client, paying him a total of roughly $170m in fees, according to an investigation by the Senate finance committee’s ranking member, Ron Wyden. Black has described his work for Epstein as tax and estate-planning services. In his statement before the oversight committee in June, Black wrote: “I did not know about this nefarious activity until Epstein was charged with trafficking in July 2019.” But Black acknowledged that he did know about Epstein pleading guilty in “2008 to state charges relating to prostitution involving a minor”. • This article was amended on 19 August 2026. An earlier version said that the investigation into Jeffrey Epstein’s finances was carried out by the Senate finance committee. In fact, it was done by Ron Wyden, the ranking member of that committee.

title: Trump nominates abortion opponent Heidi Overton to be head of FDA
author: Jessica Glenza
summary: Overton has said that Congress should strictly regulate abortion drug mifepristone ‘to protect women and children’
body_text: Donald Trump nominated Dr Heidi Overton – an abortion opponent who stood next to the president as he made false claims about vaccines – to be commissioner of the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). “Today I am honored to nominate the wonderful Dr. Heidi Overton, MD, PhD, as our next FDA Commissioner. Dr. Heidi has been a ROCKSTAR in my Administration, where she has worked directly with Secretary Kennedy, Dr. Oz, and team, to deliver on the MOST TRANSFORMATIVE Health Agenda in History. She is known to take on the HARDEST issues, and bring me solutions that work best for the Country,” the president wrote on Truth Social on Wednesday. He continued: “She is SMART and RESPECTED by all! Dr. Heidi will work with Secretary Kennedy and Dr. Oz to RAPIDLY deliver on my priorities of FASTER Cures, INCREASED American Innovation, MAJOR Clinical Trial Reforms, LOWER Drug Prices, and even more MAHA WINS!” The FDA, which regulates the nation’s drugs, medical devices and much of its food supply, has spent the bulk of the second Trump administration in tumult following widespread job cuts and disease outbreaks. Overton would also take the reins of an agency tasked with regulating medication abortions, specifically the drug mifepristone, which has become an important piece of abortion access for the 23 million women living in states with bans. In a 2023 policy brief, Overton has previously described mifepristone as “teleabortion” and “abortion-on-demand”, which Congress should work to strictly regulate “to protect women and children”. More recently, Overton appeared with Trump during a press conference for an executive order to split up the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate shots. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) described the order as “not only disheartening but dangerous”. The executive order has been widely cited by health experts as sowing confusion about vaccinations even as the US is in the midst of the worst measles outbreak in 30 years. “We do still recommend the measles vaccine for all children, but we want parents to be informed about the timing and to have the option to separate them out,” Overton said. “So, Mr President, this is a historic action. We are going to be working directly with states so that we’re not reliant on the court case to resolve.” Trump repeatedly claimed, without evidence, that the change would improve autism rates, even though studies have found no connection between autism and vaccines. “So you are saying, especially to states that are willing, take a look at this scientific assessment, these are the gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations,” said Overton. She also criticized “blue states” for following the guidance from the AAP, and not the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), whose expert advisory panel on vaccines was fired by the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, a vaccine opponent. She is reportedly Trump’s third pick for the FDA position. NBC News reported that Trump initially tapped Kyle Diamantas, the acting FDA commissioner and a former corporate lawyer, and then the Ohio Republican Bret Wenstrup.

title: Republican senator Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola advance in Alaska Senate primary
author: Chris Stein
summary: Result tees up marquee race in US midterm elections, which could decide if Republicans or Democrats control Senate
body_text: Incumbent Dan S Sullivan, the US senator, advanced in Alaska’s non-partisan primary race for his seat on Tuesday alongside Mary Peltola, a former Democratic congresswoman. With the top four candidates moving forward from Alaska’s open primaries to the general election, the Associated Press reported that Sullivan and Peltola had qualified for November’s general election. Another Dan Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher and US Forest Service employee who infuriated his namesake senator by running as a long-shot Republican candidate, was in a distant third place, although his qualification had yet to be confirmed. David B Leslie, a Democrat from Fairbanks, Alaska, is currently in fourth place. He appears to have raised no money for his campaign, and has reportedly said he has no idea why a Super Pac (political action committee) named the American Democracy Project spent about $300,000 supporting his candidacy. After 80% of votes were counted, Peltola led the primary, at 48%, while Sullivan, the senator, had 42.8%. The result tees up one of the marquee races of this year’s US midterm elections, which could determine whether Republicans or Democrats control the Senate for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. First elected in 2014, Sullivan easily won re-election in 2020, but this year faces what is expected to be a stiff challenge from Peltola. She is the first Alaska Native ever to serve in the US House of Representatives, and won a special election for the state’s at-large congressional district in 2022, then a full term later that year. In 2024, Peltola lost her re-election bid to Republican Nick Begich III, but is nonetheless viewed as a top-tier Democratic recruit to take on Sullivan in the Senate race. Both candidates are champions of Alaska’s oil and gas industry – a major employer and economic driver – but Peltola has sought to distinguish herself through her advocacy for the state’s fisheries and opposition to Trump’s economic policies. Sullivan has meanwhile described himself as a reliable advocate both for the state’s oil needs and its military installations, while championing more popular aspects of the president’s agenda such as the tax cut extensions included in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. But Sullivan’s path to retaining his seat in the US Senate has been complicated by the emergence of Dan J Sullivan, his namesake rival, who is also running as a Republican. Alaska Republicans have condemned him as a “sham” candidate who is backed by Democrats and running solely to confuse voters, but their efforts to disqualify him from the race were unsuccessful. Alaska figures prominently in Democrats’ ambitious plans to retake the US Senate, which would require flipping at least three Republican-held seats in states that voted for Trump in 2024. The party is hoping to see its candidates elected in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio and elsewhere, but is also defending seats in Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire. Peltola, who recently replaced her longtime campaign manager, has raised more than $18.5m this election cycle, with upwards of $4.6m on hand. Sullivan has brought in more than $11.7m, with nearly $7.3m on hand. In the primary for Alaska’s sole US House district, Begich advanced to the general election, alongside his main challenger, independent Bill Hill. Alaskans in November will also elect a successor to the incumbent Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, who is barred by term limits from seeking re-election. In a crowded field of 17 candidates, Democrats Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich advanced to the November election. Two more nominations remain open, with 80% of votes counted.

title: Another democratic socialist victory – Angie Nixon in Florida – sends shock waves through party establishment
author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
summary: ‘They call us extreme, they call us radical,’ the progressive Senate candidate said. ‘But I think people see through that’
body_text: It wasn’t supposed to be this way. In conservative Florida, Alex Vindman – a retired army intelligence officer who blew this whistle on Donald Trump in his first term – appeared set to carry the Democratic establishment banner as the party staged a long-shot bid to topple a Republican US senator. Florida’s Democratic voters had other ideas. Democratic socialist Angie Nixon emerged a surprise victor in the US Senate primary on Tuesday, after a campaign in which she was outfunded and outspent by Vindman at a ratio of more than 10 to one. Her triumph sent shock waves through the Democratic party machine as it prepares to mount a challenge to the incumbent Republican senator, Ashley Moody, in November’s US midterm elections. Nixon, a tenacious leftwing fighter and former union organizer who has represented Jacksonville in the Florida house since 2020, raised $975,000 in her campaign, as against Vindman’s $16.3m, but garnered more than 750,000 votes to her opponent’s 550,000 – an overwhelming victory that left his campaign scratching its head as to where it all went wrong. “The reason that we all collectively thought that he was the favorite was because he had that national name recognition, and especially because he was able to raise so much money,” said Aubrey Jewett, professor of political science at the University of Central Florida. She noted, however, that polling largely focused on how Nixon and Vindman would respectively fare against Moody in a general election, rather than whether Democratic voters preferred Nixon or Vindman as their party’s candidate. “Is Florida ready for a democratic socialist candidate in a general election? I still don’t know the answer,” added Jewett. “But what this primary showed was that, within the Democratic party base, there is a strong majority of progressive social Democrats in Florida – just like there apparently is across the country.” Nixon’s victory followed a series of primary wins for progressive candidates this summer, including in Philadelphia, Colorado, Michigan and New York City. She only recently joined the Democratic Socialists of America, and was not endorsed by them. She is also set to face trial next month – charged with trespassing and resisting an officer without violence – after a sit-in protest at the office of the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, in May. It remains to be seen how attractive Nixon will be to Florida’s wider electorate in November. As Jewett notes, Florida is heavily populated by Hispanic communities, and Moody is certain to try to affix the “socialist” label to Nixon’s campaign that has long proven toxic at the ballot box for such voter groups. The conservative commentator Noah Rothman, writing in National Review on Wednesday, went one step further, characterizing Nixon as “communist-curious”. “Even if the race for Senate in Florida is now a foregone conclusion, this race will still feature prominently in the national conversation,” he argued. “Why? Because it demonstrates that Republicans are right when they warn that the socialist phenomenon is coming to a town near you.” Pollsters already appear to have concluded that Nixon’s primary victory has limited Democrats’ chances of taking the seat. Within hours of her fiery victory speech on Tuesday night, Sabato’s Crystal Ball, the respected analytical wing of the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics, moved the Florida Senate race from “likely Republican” to “safe Republican”. It also leaves Democratic leaders in the US Senate, who publicly warmly welcomed Nixon’s win, in something of a quandary. While their path to reclaiming control of the upper chamber from Republicans was never predicated on success in Florida, Vindman, as a moderate, was considered to have at least an outside shot of an upset. Accordingly, the party’s hierarchy was preparing to send dollars and resources to bolster his campaign. Now, with Nixon on the ticket, analysts expect a rethink. “The Democratic establishment was more comfortable with Vindman,” Jewett said. “He had a demonstrated track record of being able to raise money, and Nixon does not.” Florida has about 1.5 million more registered Republican voters than Democrats, she noted. “Nixon is really going to have her work cut out for her to show that she can raise money, or if she can’t, to show that somehow they can recreate the success of the grassroots campaign that brought her victory here,” Jewett added. Her supporters are certain that will be possible. Among a flood of tributes to her on Tuesday night and through Wednesday were calls for unity, including from Vindman himself, who said: “I will be standing by her side in the fight against Ashley Moody. I hope you’ll join me.” Some of the messages were also critical of Vindman, and those in Democratic circles who bet on the wrong horse. “Angie Nixon’s win sent shock waves through the Democratic establishment who got too comfortable behind corporate donors and moderate candidates,” said Hayley Margolis, an organizer with Jewish Voice for Peace South Florida. “Her votes were hard earned through heartfelt grassroots conversations with the working class across the state of Florida.” Nixon, who was reprimanded for using a bullhorn on the Florida house floor earlier this year, does not care for internal party wrangling. And she made one thing clear: she is unlikely to change tack as she presents herself to the wider statewide electorate before November. “They look at this movement and they call us extreme, they call us radical, but I think people see through that. I won’t let them define me and I know you will always know where I stand,” she told supporters on Tuesday night. “If believing a mom shouldn’t have to work three jobs to keep a roof over her head is extreme, call me extreme. Ashley Moody can call me whatever she wants, but in November she’ll be calling me senator.”

title: Morning Mail: Holes in Labor’s gambling law, IDF rejects criminal investigation into Frankcom death, Meta and child safety in spotlight
author: Martin Farrer
summary: Recovering addict says new laws will not prevent companies using inducements; Meta chief ‘misled’ regulators, whistleblower says
body_text: Good morning. Free booze, free footy and even free bets. These are the kinds of inducements used by gambling companies to keep addicts hooked, according to one recovering addict who says Labor’s reforms won’t stop the practice. The Israeli military has cleared itself over the 2024 airstrikes that hit a World Central Kitchen convoy, killing seven aid workers including Zomi Frankcom. Plus, our columnist Greg Jericho notes the disparity between falling real wages and plump corporate profits. Australia ‘Huge mistake’ | The former Wimbledon finalist Nick Kyrgios says he has made a “huge mistake” after being suspended from tennis after testing positive for cocaine while playing at an ATP event in Mallorca in June. Gambling bust | Labor’s gambling reforms have passed parliament but do not pass muster, according to the husband of the late Labor MP Peta Murphy. Plus, a recovering addict who was given $43,700 in betting inducements has “no confidence” that Labor’s crackdown “would have made my experience any different or any easier”. Roblox pledge | Roblox has committed to making changes to its online gaming platform after Australia’s eSafety commissioner discovered adults were still able to see child accounts and send connection requests without parental consent. Rent research | Critics of the government’s tax changes have latched on to research purporting to show that rents will rise up to 30%. But will they really? Luca Ittimani and Jonathan Barrett investigate. Exclusive | Almost one-fifth of older Australians who contested their Support at Home funding allocation determined by an algorithm had a higher level of support or higher priority allocated once a human reviewed the decision. World Mark Zuckerberg | A former Meta safety engineer has told a jury that the boss of the tech company, Mark Zuckerberg, “created a false and misleading impression of Facebook’s commitment to young people” and that the company was aware of the harm its products could cause children. IDF strikes | The Israeli military has decided not to open a criminal investigation into the 2024 strike on an aid convoy that killed Australian Zomi Frankcom and six others. But it admitted its troops had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, and ordered a criminal investigation into that killing. Ukraine intrigue | Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has fired a senior aide amid a fresh corruption investigation – one day after a former defence minister warned the country was facing “a crisis of governance” and needed to hold a wartime presidential election. Progressives progress | Progressive Democrat Angie Nixon has upset the party establishment by winning the US Senate primary in Florida, beating former army intelligence officer Alexander Vindman. Dog doubt | A British dog food brand has recalled all of its fresh meals after reports that a recipe change may have caused some animals to go blind. Full Story Decoding America: Why Maga vaccine scepticism might be catching Reged Ahmad and Jonathan Yerushalmy discuss what the USS Lincoln crisis says about whether the US military is stretched too thin as the war on Iran drags on. In-depth Greg Jericho has consistently argued that the RBA’s concerns about pay rises fuelling inflation are misplaced. In today’s column he highlights the crisis caused by the “pathetic” level of wage growth. Not the news Luke Buckmaster gives four stars to Sweet Milk Lake, the story of a trans man who return to who returns to his home town to see his terminally ill estranged father and in which Harvey Zielinski excels as director, writer and star of his feature debut. Cricket | England reached 112-2 at stumps on the first day of the First Test against Pakistan after Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue each took five wickets to dismiss the visitors for 171. Football | Gianni Infantino has lost the support of another one of Fifa’s vice-presidents with the Hungarian federation chief criticising the president’s “professional judgment, ethical standards and leadership”. title: Trump shows off White House renovations and ornate new helipad
author: Robert Mackey
summary: Former real estate developer leads press corps on tour of grounds and says ‘one thing I know how to do is build’
body_text: As the US national debt climbed past $40tn for the first time on Wednesday, and the war with Iran that Donald Trump started nearly six months ago dragged on, forcing Americans already struggling to pay the bills to spend more on fuel, the US president led the press corps on a tour of the extensive remodeling of the White House grounds he is personally overseeing in his role as the self-styled “builder-in-chief”. The tour, during which Trump showed off upgrades such as a new granite driveway and refurbished columns, and expounded at length on newly laid grass, culminated in Trump autographing the back of a stone, inscribed with his name, to go in the center of the ornate new helipad he insists he needs. All in all, the 40-minute diversion from the work of being US president, which seemed at times like a lost episode of the 1980s TV show Lifestyles of the Rich and Famous, did little to help Trump beat the charge laid against him by senator Jon Ossoff, the Georgia Democrat who said earlier this week that the former real estate developer is not really that interested in the work of leading the nation. While US service members “fight his war” on Iran, Ossoff said, “the president sleeps through his meetings. He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom” and travel with his close aide Natalie Harp on the luxury jet gifted to him by the emir of Qatar. At one point in the tour, after Trump boasted about the “flawless granite” he replaced the asphalt driveway with, he told his captive audience of reporters: “We get the best stuff; one thing I know how to do is build.” “It’s ridiculous the way this place was taken care of,” he said. “Nobody, including other presidents, they didn’t see it. But I see it because I was very good at real estate, like maybe the best in a lot of ways.” Drawing attention to the newly laid sod around the helipad, golf course owner Trump repeated one of his favorite lines. “You know, grass has a life like humans have a life,” he said, for at least the 10th time in public remarks in the past year. “It’s all been top-soiled. In other words, we put top soil, brand new earth on top. Very, you know, very – a lot of good ingredients in that earth for grass. If you’re grass, you’re very happy,” the president said. He then pivoted to something like a product placement. “This grass is the highest quality. It was given free of charge by Scotts Miracle-Gro. Scotts. And Scotts is a great a great company. They actually contributed to my campaign,” he said. “They said to me, ‘Sir, we’d like to replace the grass at the White House with the highest quality grass and do a real job.’ So, Scotts, I want to thank Scotts Miracle-Gro,” Trump went on. “It’s a very, I think the biggest grass company in the world, somebody said, but it’s very big and very good.” Trump first made his observation that “grass has a life” during remarks last August to the federal forces he deployed to police Washington DC. “I know more about grass than any human being I think anywhere in the world,” the president claimed on that occasion. He made the observation again in the Oval Office the following month, while announcing his rebrand of the defense department as the Department of War, and has repeated it multiple times since, including: during a cabinet meeting; while meeting with the Nato secretary general; while signing an executive order on trade; and as he unveiled plans for a renovation of Dulles airport. The president also suggested that his new helipad will be dual use, also serving as a second patio. “They can have events on it. They can have people go there for cocktails and then walk to the ballroom after that’s finished,” he said. Before he was done with the tour on Wednesday, the president also reminded the press pack that he had donated the two huge flag poles now flanking the White House, and made a point of saying that those poles were of the highest quality. “This is a great pole,” Trump said. “This is the top of the line. It’s tapered. Great. I’m very good at flagpoles.”

title: Trump threatens Iran’s trade partners, as military strikes make way for economic pressure
author: Jonathan Yerushalmy
summary: US president pivots towards ‘crushing’ economic operation against Iran and its trading partners as military strikes fail to bring Tehran to the table
body_text: Donald Trump has announced a new campaign to isolate Iran’s economy, threatening “tremendous economic consequences” on any country that helps or does business with Tehran, a move that could set up a fresh confrontation with China if implemented. “Today, I am announcing the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face tremendous economic consequences.” His announcement however contained no detail on what actions would be taken or which countries could be affected, and comes as the war nears its six-month mark, with the president facing pressure over the cost of the conflict as the US midterm elections approach. Last month the US president paused attacks on Iran, after a fortnight of nightly strikes that had failed to bring officials in Tehran back to the negotiating table and reports that the war has run down US stockpiles of key munitions. Pentagon advisers reportedly told Trump last month that the US had nearly exhausted its list of targets in Iran and the military campaign had reached the limits of its effectiveness. The White House has signalled in recent weeks a shift in strategy to tightening pressure on Iran economically. US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said last week the US would begin ramping up efforts to isolating Iran economically. The US treasury has for months been carrying out an effort, called Operation Economic Fury, aiming to cut off Iran’s funding with targeted sanctions, while a naval blockade in the strait of Hormuz has sought to block Iranian ports from exporting oil vital to keeping the country’s economy afloat. Iran’s economy already faces a punishing array of US and western sanctions that have ground down the economy over years and curtailed its ability to sell oil. But experts say the country’s leaders have learned to adapt to the measures, including by exporting oil through a sophisticated network of shadow tankers. In his announcement on Wednesday, Trump listed several activities that he said needed to stop immediately, including “oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies”. The wording of the president’s announcement suggested that he could be threatening secondary sanctions on countries that buy Iranian oil, but experts say such a move could lead to direct confrontation with China – Iran’s biggest trading partner – at a time when the US is trying to establish a new trading relationship with Beijing. “Whatever new economic measures the US can use will need to be directed at Iran’s trading partners,” said Gregory Brew, a senior analyst at theEurasia Group, adding that it will be “hard for the US to direct such actions at China, the country that matters most to Iran’s economic future.” Chinese leader Xi Jinping is also expected to visit the US next month, further complicating any efforts to target Beijing’s imports of Iranian oil. Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, said on Tuesday that military pressure and sanctions would not break Iran’s resolve. He added that Iran remained open to dialogue ⁠with the US, but would not confuse negotiations with surrender, according to the semi-official Fars news agency. On Tuesday, the United Arab Emirates, announced it would suspend all trade activities, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran, after it said it had detected two missiles launched from the country. Tehran dismissed the reports as baseless. Prior to the war, the UAE was one of Iran’s biggest trade partners, providing more than 30% of its imports. Earlier on Wednesday, Trump also claimed that vessels from Gulf countries allied with the US were continuing to move through the strait of Hormuz, despite the Iranian threat to shipping in the waterway. The president said the US military was aiding ships in the strait, saying “right now, a lot of boats are coming through.” Axios reported that US forces were facilitating the transit of 15 to 20 ships in and out of the Hormuz each night in recent weeks – carrying “roughly half the prewar volume” of daily oil shipments – while also continuing to blockade Iranian exports. Those volumes were disputed by some, with ship tracking data ‌from Kpler showing transits remained low. Referring to the Axios report, Danny Citrinowicz, the former head of the Iran branch of Israeli military intelligence, said it was an important operational development, but questioned how long the US government would be able to sustain such an operation. “More importantly, this will not force Iran to surrender or fundamentally change its negotiating position,” said Citrinowicz.
