title: Progressive Aisha Wahab wins California special election to fill Eric Swalwell seat
author: Dani Anguiano
summary: State senator beats rival Melissa Hernandez and will replace US congressman who quit amid sexual misconduct claims
body_text: Progressive Aisha Wahab has been elected to Congress in a special election following a bitter intra-party battle over the seat formerly held by Eric Swalwell, who resigned in April after facing sexual misconduct allegations. Swalwell has denied the allegations. Wahab, a state senator, was widely considered the frontrunner in the district in California’s East Bay and had the backing of the state Democratic party as well as Our Revolution, labor unions, local officials and the state’s attorney general, Rob Bonta. She won the primary for the special election for the final months of Swalwell’s term by more than 20 points over Melissa Hernandez, the president of the board of directors for the Bay Area Rapid Transit (Bart) agency. “I will fight for this district that raised me,” Wahab said in a statement on Thursday. “From foster care to Congress, this journey shows the possibility of the American Dream.” While Wahab held a major lead throughout the race, Hernandez’s campaign received a significant boost as Super Pacs connected to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) poured money into the race. With 95% of votes counted on Thursday afternoon, Wahab led Hernandez by just over six points in Tuesday’s election to fill the remainder of Swalwell’s term – a much closer race than expected. Earlier this month, it emerged that Super Pacs had spent more than $5m in a matter of weeks on pro-Hernandez ads and Wahab attack ads. Track Aipac, which monitors the group’s funding of US politicians, recently reported that the lobby had spent nearly $6.4m to support Hernandez. Wahab, the first Muslim woman and Afghan American elected to the California legislature, told the Guardian there had been a sudden surge of critical ads that had misrepresented her record. She described the Super Pacs’ involvement as election interference, and said they were attempting to buy the seat. The race further intensified in recent days after the congresswoman Zoe Lofgren, chair of California’s Democratic delegation, endorsed Hernandez. Lofgren said Wahab did not back an effort to elect a caretaker candidate in order to fill Swalwell’s seat as quickly as possible. But the progressive wing of the party strongly supported Wahab, with a former chair of the progressive caucus of the California Democratic party, Amar Shergill, telling Politico that Lofgren’s actions were “astounding”, and continued backing Wahab amid the upheaval in the race in recent weeks. Hernandez, in a statement, said she was proud of her showing against Wahab. “I’ve been a fighter my whole life, and when I promised the residents of CA-14 I would fight for them, I never gave up,” she said.

The Plymouth Brethren Christian Church has denied it secretly paid far-right influencers to stage stunts targeting Anthony Albanese and other politicians during an appearance at a parliamentary inquiry into the 2025 election. title: Voting rights experts skeptical over Trump pledge of 1,000 election monitors
author: Rachel Leingang in Minneapolis and Sam Levine in New York
summary: Department of Justice plan raises questions over its ability to recruit so many people – and what they would do
body_text: Former officials and voting rights experts have expressed skepticism over a pledge by the Trump administration to dispatch 1,000 monitors across the country to scrutinize November’s US midterm elections. While the Department of Justice (DoJ) has expressed hope that the operation will be the largest in its history, its plan raised questions over its ability to recruit so many people – and what they would do. The US president has repeatedly denied the results of election defeats, including his 2020 loss in the presidential election to Joe Biden, and in recent months has escalated concerns that he will seek to meddle in November’s elections. Harmeet Dhillon, who leads the justice department’s civil rights section, told Bloomberg News of the plan to send out 1,000 election monitors earlier this week, which she claimed was “probably going to be a historic number for a Republican administration”. But experts suggested the justice department’s target should not spark alarm. “This DoJ has amply earned the public’s distrust, but this announcement isn’t reason to freak out,” said Justin Levitt, a professor at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles who has worked on voting rights issues at the justice department and White House. “I’m skeptical they’ll actually get to 1,000. Even if they did, that wouldn’t be so different from the number in prior years; that’s a national number suitable for observing but not nearly enough to disrupt; and local election officials can, and will, toss anyone who makes trouble,” said Levitt. “As in the primaries, the most anyone should expect from this group is a handful of suits standing quietly in the back of the room.” Observing elections is a routine part of the department’s work, but the discourse around such activity has caused unease during the second Trump administration. The justice department has taken an adversarial position, suing some states in a bid to access private voter data, and some state officials have said they don’t feel the federal government is a partner in protecting elections. The president has said he wants the federal government to take over elections, and issued executive orders to exert such power, which the courts have largely curtailed. Still, state and local election officials around the country who had federal election monitors observe their areas in the last year said they did not know of any instances in which the monitors caused concerns, though several also declined to comment. “For decades, DoJ has sent hundreds of monitors and attorneys to polling places during each federal election,” said a former DoJ official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to avoid professional repercussions. “In the last year, DoJ has sent monitors to off-cycle and primary elections, and they have done little to nothing. “DoJ may try to send 1,000 monitors into the field this November, but they probably won’t be able to coordinate a deployment of that size. Even if they manage the logistics, 1,000 DoJ monitors will only give us more videos of lawyers standing around with clipboards, following instructions from poll workers and being ignored by voters.” Monitoring the monitors The justice department has long sent personnel to monitor elections across the country to ensure compliance with federal voting laws and court orders in certain jurisdictions. CBS News reported that the DoJ sent 289 monitors in 2022, during the last midterm election. During the last presidential election, in 2024, the department sent 714 people. This time around, the justice department said: “We hope to have the largest monitoring effort in the department’s history.” It’s not yet clear where the DoJ intends to send the monitors in November, or whether it will be able to achieve its goal – especially after scores of personnel have left the justice department’s civil rights division under Trump. Its monitors will be spread across the country’s tens of thousands of polling places. So far this election cycle, the department says it has sent 75 monitors to more than 200 polling locations across five states. Those include Minnesota, Michigan and Arizona earlier this cycle, with more going to Florida and Wyoming this week for those state’s primaries. Several California jurisdictions and a New Jersey county saw federal monitors during special elections late last year. When monitors were sent to Minnesota – which saw an immigration enforcement surge earlier this year where two people were killed and thousands deported, leaving a deep distrust of federal authorities – during the state’s primaries earlier this month, state officials decided to monitor the monitors. Steve Simon, Minnesota’s secretary of state, estimated there were six or seven teams of two to three federal monitors across its Hennepin and Ramsey counties, where Minneapolis and St Paul are located, on primary day. The federal monitors provided real-time updates to the state attorney general’s office on where they were going, he said. They stayed a short time at each precinct. He estimated they visited more than 50 precincts out of thousands throughout the state. “There was no cat-and-mouse game. They were very straightforward about that,” Simon said. “And there were no major disruptions or obstructions.” There were a couple instances of reports where observers were inside a 100ft boundary, as captured in a video from a local news outlet, and were asked to move further out. They did, Simon said. Monitors need permission from local jurisdictions to enter polling places. In this year’s Minnesota primaries, Hennepin and Ramsey counties declined to allow the justice department to observe inside the polling places. This meant the observers needed to stay outside a 100ft boundary, as any member of the public not actively voting would be required to do. Local residents had been concerned “about safety and the presence of federal officials in their communities”, Joshua Yetman, a Hennepin county spokesperson, said. “Although we have had no issues with previous DoJ election monitoring, we determined that prioritizing a safe, orderly and welcoming environment for voters was necessary this year.” The monitors were present in three cities within the county, remaining outside the 100ft boundary, and there were no disruptions to voting, Yetman said. No concerns so far Other election officials around the country said the monitors seemed routine. The justice department sent one monitor to Orange county, California, during a statewide special election in November 2025, the county’s registrar of voters, Bob Page, said via email. “There were no concerns about the USDOJ monitor in 2025. He observed our vote-by-mail ballot processing operation over portions of three days. He was treated and allowed observation access the same as any member of the public when he visited our office.” The California secretary of state’s office noted that election observation is “standard practice for every statewide election” and said that the secretary of state and California attorney general collaborate to ensure election laws are enforced. In a press release after the justice department announced its 2025 plan to send monitors, California’s secretary of state, Shirley N Weber, said the department had not provided a justification for sending the monitors to five counties in a non-federal special election. “We will not permit tactics masquerading as oversight to erode voter confidence or intimidate Californians,” Weber said at the time. “Our voters have earned the right to cast their ballots free from surveillance or interference – from anyone. In California, election integrity is not a talking point; it’s a practice built on decades of professionalism and public trust. We intend to keep it that way.” In Arizona’s Maricopa county, home to the state capital of Phoenix, elections officials said they had no issues. “We have monitors during most large elections,” said Jennifer Liewer, the deputy elections director for communications in the county’s elections department. In Pima county, where Tucson is located, monitors also came for the July primaries, and “the voters and poll workers did not report any concerns”, said Constance Hargrove, the county’s elections director. After Dhillon cited “problems” in Arizona’s elections as the basis for sending monitors to three counties for July’s primary, the Democratic secretary of state, Adrian Fontes, filed a records request and wrote a letter to the department. “We do not know what the Department considers those problems to be, in which jurisdictions they are alleged to have occurred, or what evidence supports them,” he wrote. Should monitors return to Minnesota, Simon, its secretary of state, described his expected response as a “situation of trust, but verify” in November. “They say they’re here for a specific purpose. They have in the past been here for that exact same purpose. The purpose that they’re here for is a good one under the law,” he said. “So we hope and expect that they will, if they come here at all, continue to abide by the rules and laws.”

title: First Thing: US aircraft carrier arrives to relieve USS Lincoln amid reports of poor living conditions
author: Jem Bartholomew
summary: The USS George Washington has arrived in the Middle East. Plus, an investigation into the add-on utility fees that can lead to evictions
body_text: Good morning. The USS George Washington aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln from its record deployment, amid concerns about poor living conditions and morale. US Central Command announced on Thursday that the Washington arrived in the area on Wednesday, and posted an image of sailors working on the flight deck as the ship transited the Arabian Sea. According to the New York Times, which cited a US official, the Lincoln began its home journey to San Diego on Thursday. Recent reports have rung alarm bells about conditions on the Lincoln. “I just don’t really think they’re treating them like people. I think they’re treating them like a uniform, like a pawn on a chessboard,” the wife of a sailor onboard told the Guardian’s Anna Betts this week. What are conditions like on the Lincoln? The ship has spent more than 250 days at sea supporting US operations against Iran without a significant port visit or date to return home for the 5,000 sailors and marines onboard. Reports from families of crew members published in the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes military newspapers described food and water shortages, disrupted mail services, plumbing problems, low morale and worsening mental health, prompting Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon. ‘It kept adding up’: Investigation reveals how add-on utility fees can lead to eviction for tenants An investigation co-published by the Guardian and the Economic Hardship Reporting Project, a journalism non-profit that supports stories about inequality and poverty in the US, has revealed a problem emerging nationwide: fees charged on top of rent known as “ratio utility billing system” fees – or Rubs. Rubs, unlike standard utility bills, where tenants owe money to the utility company, are owed to the landlord and often paid through a third-party billing company. Many leases that include Rubs are written so tenants can be evicted for not paying utilities, even if they have paid their rent. For working-class and low-income tenants such as Constance Soule, an 81-year-old disabled Alzheimer’s patient, falling behind on these utility charges can lead to eviction notices, Tracie McMillan reports. “It just kept adding up,” Margot Jones, Soule’s sister, said. Tenants in Los Angeles and Seattle have launched “Rubs strikes”, refusing to pay utilities until landlords agree to reduce charges that can approach $300 a month per apartment. How are people fighting back? At least 13 lawsuits have challenged Rubs since the start of 2025 across five states – including a case in California that led to a nearly $500,000 settlement last fall with a national property manager. “Some California landlords have tried to get away with illegal rent increases by shifting utilities and other fees to tenants and pretending those new charges are not ‘rent’” under state law, Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, said when announcing the settlement. Efforts to limit or ban add-on utility fees are also gaining momentum across several cities. In other news … Israel’s national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has been condemned for posting a gloating video of the construction of a gallows complex where Palestinians convicted of terror offences – but not Jewish extremists accused of similar crimes – will be hanged. It comes after the minister sparked a backlash a few days ago for saying there should be “30 to 40 targeted assassinations per night” in Gaza. Progressive Aisha Wahab has been elected to Congress in a special election, following a bitter intraparty battle over the seat formerly held by Eric Swalwell. North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea on Thursday, South Korea’s military said. It comes after Donald Trump’s order earlier this week to scale back US military drills with South Korea. Fans’ groups worldwide have launched a petition calling for the resignation of Gianni Infantino, the Fifa president, and for wholesale reform of soccer’s international governing organization. Stat of the day: US deports 20 people to Liberia, the first of 1,200 migrants under Trump deal Twenty deportees from the US arrived in Liberia on Thursday, as part of a new agreement in which the west African country will receive as many as 1,200 people under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The Liberian information minister, Jerolinmek Piah, said the 1,200 deportees will include African nationals as well as nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean. Culture pick: It Ends review – gripping micro-budget horror ranks among the year’s best A crew of aimless twentysomethings take a late-night drive to get food, but their GPS leads them deeper and deeper into a desolate forest. “It Ends often reaches the quality of high-concept cult horror classics while also nodding to our uniquely modern malaise,” writes Owen Myers in his four-star review. Don’t miss this: How to get back into reading books – podcast For Today in Focus, the Guardian convenes a specialist panel on which books may help you put your phone away and get reading again. “I think we’re all bored of talking about ChatGPT at parties, and really interested in getting back to things that feel human,” Rebecca Liu, acting Saturday culture editor and a Booker prize judge, says. Climate check: How one American couple ditched their lawn and created a wildlife haven – and you could too Novice gardeners James Reed McGuire and Crystal Fritz wanted to try something new when they moved from Chicago out to the suburb of Highland Park, Illinois. They set about rewilding their garden. “It brings us a lot of peace and tranquility in a very troubled world,” McGuire says. Read their story – and see tips for how to rewild a lawn. Last Thing: The Guardian reveals 2026’s Invertebrate of the year – the leaf sheep The winner of the global ballot for Invertebrate of the year has now been revealed: the leaf sheep (Costasiella kuroshimae). The leaf sheep, which lives in tropical waters around Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines and feeds on algae, has inspired at least one Pokémon character. title: With ICC sanctions, Trump wants to make the world safe for war criminals
author: Kenneth Roth
summary: The US is engaged in a lawless quest to protect American and Israeli officials
body_text: The Trump administration has taken another step in its crusade against the international criminal court by imposing sanctions on two more senior ICC officials. The growing number of sanctioned jurists – now 13 – does not change the lawless nature of this quest. Donald Trump and his henchman, Marco Rubio, want to make the world safe for US and Israeli war criminals. No one should let them. The latest victims of Trump’s vendetta are the ICC president – its chief judge, Tomoko Akane of Japan – and Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, a senior ICC trial lawyer, evidently for his role advancing the prosecution of Israeli officials. Yet the real victims are not these particular individuals, but people worldwide who look to the court as one of the few avenues of recourse against unscrupulous leaders who commit mass atrocities such as fighting wars by targeting civilians. We should never let Trump normalize these sanctions. Their main effect is to deprive the target of the ability to use the international financial system – no credit cards, no access to banks, extreme difficulty navigating a modern economy. That is a tool once reserved for corrupt or violent officials who were otherwise beyond the law. Trump is using them to attack the public officials who would bring such heinous individuals to justice. Rubio, the secretary of state, dressed up the sanctions with high-sounding rhetoric about the ICC threatening “America sovereignty”. That is true only if Americans (and Israelis) have a sovereign right to commit war crimes wherever they want. Even Rubio cannot get himself to spell out what King Trump’s campaign is really about. Rubio’s main articulated complaint is that the ICC can “investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction”. That is true, but it is wrong only if one adopts a conveniently (for Washington and the Israeli government) narrow sense of how the court should obtain jurisdiction for a crime. On the one hand, when a country joins the ICC, it accepts the court’s jurisdiction over its citizens. That might be called jurisdiction by virtue of nationality. The US government accepts that route to jurisdiction because it never joined the court. But when a country becomes a court member, it also confers jurisdiction over crimes on its territory, even when committed by a foreigner. That is hardly controversial. A hallmark of sovereignty is the ability to enforce the law on a country’s own territory. Even the Trump administration would not dare object to, say, the British government prosecuting an American for a crime committed in London. But the administration claims it is somehow an outrage if a country confers that same territorial jurisdiction on the ICC for war crimes and similar atrocities committed by foreigners on its territory – a major purpose of the court. The US government objected to such territorial jurisdiction when the court’s treaty was adopted at a major diplomatic conference in Rome in 1998 – and lost overwhelmingly, by a vote of 120 to seven. Since then, even the US government has accepted territorial jurisdiction when convenient. After the ICC used it to prosecute Vladimir Putin (Russia never joined the court) for the kidnapping of children from Ukraine (a member), Joe Biden called the prosecution “justified”. The late senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican leader on foreign policy, orchestrated a unanimous Senate resolution in support. But for Trump, territorial jurisdiction suddenly became toxic again when it was used to charge Benjamin Netanyahu and the former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant with deliberately starving and depriving Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Israel is not a member of the ICC, but Palestine, where the alleged crimes took place, is. Territorial jurisdiction can also be used to charge foreigners from non-member states with aiding and abetting crimes in a state where the ICC has jurisdiction. For example, the court might charge United Arab Emirates officials with aiding and abetting genocide in the Darfur region of Sudan by sending arms and mercenaries to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, Rwandan officials with aiding and abetting war crimes in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo by arming and supporting the M23 rebel group, or US officials (Trump’s real concern) with aiding and abetting Israel’s genocide in Gaza by supplying arms and military aid. Indeed, territorial jurisdiction means that the sanctions themselves could lead to prosecution of Trump and Rubio. Article 70 of the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty, codifies the crime of obstructing justice when someone retaliates “against an official of the Court on account of duties performed”. That’s exactly what the Trump-Rubio sanctions do. The court would have jurisdiction because the sanctions relate to the prosecution of Israeli officials for crimes committed on Palestinian territory. Rubio has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick, if necessary”, announcing: “We expect more countries to join our campaign by ending their funding and participation in this politicized and unaccountable court.” Yet that bombast so far has produced few results among the court’s 125 members. Venezuela, which has become a US vassal state since Trump’s seizure of Nicolás Maduro, has announced its withdrawal. So has Chad, which announced its departure after a call from a state department official. But Chadian officials have their own reasons to worry about the court because they allowed their territory to be used by the UAE to arm the RSF in Sudan. (Separately from Trump’s campaign, three military juntas in the Sahel have also announced their exit from the ICC: Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso.) Yet if the response to the Trump administration’s call to leave the court so far has been tepid, the defense of the court by its supposed closest defenders has not exactly been vigorous. The European Union has what is known as a “blocking statute”, legislation designed to negate the application of US sanctions in Europe by prohibiting European banks from complying. But while the EU says it “deeply regrets” these new sanctions on the ICC, it has not invoked the blocking statute to protect court personnel. One reason appears to be fear among banks, particularly in the Netherlands, of retaliation from Trump. The ICC is located in the Hague, also the Dutch seat of government. In other words, as European officials see it, fighting genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity is important. Trump’s efforts to allow Americans and Israelis to commit these crimes with impunity is disgraceful. But if defending the rule of law might put Dutch banks in Trump’s crosshairs, justice can wait. The EU can do better than that. Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

title: Andrew Hastie is effective in attacking One Nation, unlike his Liberal colleagues. So why won’t they use him?
author: Tom McIlroy
summary: The member for Canning has stood up to Pauline Hanson, risked the wrath of Gina Rinehart, criticised WA opposition tactics and sat quietly behind Angus Taylor for months
body_text: Amid the sometimes raucous scenes of question time in federal parliament this week, Andrew Hastie maintained a dignified silence. The Liberal frontbencher barely spoke, even as his colleagues pursued Labor over Australia’s newly minted $1tn national debt, controversial caps on veterans’ healthcare funding, and rising rental prices around the country. So evident was Hastie’s silence, day after day, that even Anthony Albanese motioned to the shadow minister for industry and sovereign capability at one point, asking what was going on. “When are you going to get a question? It’s been six months,” the prime minister was heard to say across the chamber to Hastie. The former soldier sits just behind the opposition leader – and his putative leadership rival – Angus Taylor. But, despite his silence in question time, Hastie has a bit going on. He has spoken regularly about the threat of Pauline Hanson’s surging popularity to the Liberal party, and will be closely watching the results in the upcoming byelection in the Western Australian state seat of Secret Harbour. One Nation wants to win the seat from Labor next weekend, and then come for Hastie’s own federal electorate of Canning, which shares much of the same territory. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email There is little love lost between Hanson’s supporters and Hastie, who some hate because he gave evidence against the Victoria Cross recipient Ben Roberts-Smith in a mammoth defamation trial against Nine newspapers. Hanson and her billionaire benefactor Gina Rinehart have publicly supported Roberts-Smith and are using their money and political muscle in WA to go after Hastie as a result. It’s always hard to understand internecine power dynamics in Perth from the east coast, but the current turf war, including in local media coverage, is particularly bitter. Hastie has talked about the many threats made by others to his safety and the moves by the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, to offer additional security for his home and electorate office. In interviews with News24, formerly Sky News, this week, Hastie said he and his wife were shielding their young family from online abuse and vitriol, and even revealed an unnamed One Nation official had told him he should prepare for a deluge of personal attacks after campaigning in the Farrer byelection earlier this year. In another interview, Hastie said Hanson’s closest adviser and One Nation strategist, James Ashby, was “coming for me”. Hastie insisted he would run at the 2028 election, and hold Canning for the Liberals. Unlike many of his colleagues, Hastie has correctly identified a weakness in One Nation’s political offering. He said this week that Hanson’s problem “is that she is Maga first”, even when Australian voters suffer the economic consequences from the US president Donald Trump’s backwards and misguided political project. Just like Labor successfully hung Trump around Peter Dutton’s neck at the last election, painting Hanson as the unpopular president’s best friend in Australia could be a smart strategy to dent her support. The result of all this – and Hastie’s position as likely alternative if Taylor cannot turn around dire opposition polling in time for the next election – means he hasn’t been used well by the Liberals. Hastie surely would have done a better job pursuing the veterans’ affairs minister, Matt Keogh, over the government’s cap on allied health services costs and anger from ex-servicemen and women who accused Keogh of disrespecting them in a meeting, even claiming he rolled his eyes at one point. Liberal Phil Thompson overreached in question time on Thursday when he told Albanese that one Afghanistan veteran had said he would prefer to deal with the Taliban than talk with Keogh. The prime minister might have pointed out the Taliban are fundamentalist thugs and backers of international terrorism, determined to ruin lives and destroy personal liberties. Hastie is a thoughtful and policy-oriented MP. This week, alongside colleagues Aaron Violi and Jonno Duniam, he helped secure support from Labor for the creation of a new standing committee on artificial intelligence. Hastie wants the joint House and Senate panel to consider the effect AI is set to bring to Australia’s national security, political system and institutions. He identified the race for control of AI as a key part of a fight for dominance between the US and China, but also a fight over quality of life in Australia’s suburbs and towns. As well as the energy, planning and security ramifications, Hastie argued in a speech that Australia’s education system needed to quickly plan for success in an AI-led world. He said Australian students needed to be better equipped to build future AI models, not be “slaves” to those developed overseas. That starts with improving reading and writing competencies, lifting Naplan scores and better fostering curiosity in young minds. “Policymakers have a moral obligation to hammer out a new political and economic settlement that ensures that AI serves all Australians, not just a few,” Hastie said. “We can’t let Big Tech reshape our nation without democratic oversight and accountability.” Politically too, Hastie might be ahead of some of his Liberal colleagues. He risked attracting the ire of the WA branch in an interview with the Australian Financial Review on Tuesday, criticising the Liberals’ campaign activities and messaging in Secret Harbour under the state leader, Basil Zempilas. “If you’re on the ground in a byelection, then you run to win, not to help someone else win the seat,” Hastie said, in a reference to One Nation. “We should never, ever indicate to voters that we are not fully committed to the fight.” Labor’s strong political position and Hanson’s surge in support will likely mean things will remain tough for the Liberals for some time yet, but sidelining serious assets like Hastie won’t help matters at all. • Tom McIlroy is Guardian Australia’s political editor

title: JD Vance reportedly mocks Carney for trying to ‘out-tough’ Trump on trade
author: Olivia Bowden in Toronto
summary: Audio recording of US vice-president apparently made at New York fundraiser and shared with Canadian Press
body_text: Leaked audio from a private event has reportedly captured the US vice-president, JD Vance, mocking Canada for apparently capitulating in a trade deal and taunting the prime minister, Mark Carney, for trying to “out-tough” Donald Trump. The recording, which was reportedly made at a fundraiser and shared with the Canadian Press, comes in the last stretch of a difficult negotiation in which the US president has threatened to impose 50% tariffs on Canada. According to the Canadian Press, Vance is heard in the audio telling a room of supporters in Southampton, New York, that Carney is a “very sweet guy” and that he gets along with him well. But he also says Carney “comes in and puffs his chest out and says: ‘I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.’” Vance says: “It’s hilarious because Carney presents this as some victory for Canada when fundamentally, like, they climb down on a lot of issues.” The audio is unlikely to help relations between the two delegations at a crucial time. Canadian officials have said a deal is close that is likely to include Canada again allowing US alcohol sales across the country in exchange for avoiding the worst of Trump’s tariffs. Trump first said he would apply the tariffs from 19 August, but on Tuesday he backed down and announced a three-day pause. The White House said in July that the 50% tariffs were in retaliation for “discriminatory treatment” by Canada that included bans on the sale of US alcohol in eight out of 10 provinces and all three territories – a response in early 2025 to Trump’s first threats of tariffs against Canada. US producers of wine, beer and spirits have said the boycott has significantly affected their sales. Canadian imports of US alcohol are down about 81% year on year, according to the White House. The premier of Manitoba, Wab Kinew, and his Nova Scotia counterpart, Tim Houston, confirmed this week that Carney had asked the provinces to return US alcohol to shelves. “I wouldn’t say [Carney] was begging us, but what is a step before begging?” Kinew said on Thursday. Kinew encouraged Canadians to continue their boycott of US products regardless. “If we put the booze back on the shelves, don’t buy it … Buy the Canadian stuff instead,” he said. “We’ve done an amazing job of sticking together in the face of Donald Trump’s tariff threats and I think we should continue to do that.” Kinew said he respected Carney for taking on Trump and believed Canada should stand firm in the negotiations. “I think Donald Trump is weak. America is weaker around the world today than it was a year ago, and he’s about to get slaughtered in the midterms,” he said. “Very wise people have said you can’t get a good deal with a bad person, and I think that rule applies here, so I think we should fight.”

title: Trump faces backlash over reports US navy carrier could be named after him instead of Black war hero
author: George Chidi
summary: Sources say US navy is working to rename carrier originally planned to honor second world war sailor Doris Miller
body_text: The Trump administration has been accused of delivering a “slap in the face” to US military veterans after reports that a navy aircraft carrier set to honor a Black war hero may, instead, be named after Donald Trump. The US navy had previously announced that the carrier under construction would be called the USS Doris Miller, in tribute to a sailor celebrated for his heroism during the attack on Pearl Harbor in the second world war. But the navy is now working to rename the carrier, CNN reported, citing three sources familiar with internal discussions. Two of those sources said there have been conversations about renaming it to honor Trump, according to the network. “This is a slap in the face to every war hero and every service member who has worn the uniform,” said Derrick Johnson, president of the NAACP civil rights group. “Doris Miller earned his place in American history through courage, sacrifice, and service,” added Johnson. “Donald Trump only wants to serve himself.” The US navy declined to comment. When contacted for comment, the White House referred the Guardian to the Department of Defense, which declined to comment. Doris “Dorie” Miller, a navy cook, reportedly shot down four to six Japanese bombers at Pearl Harbor in 1941, despite no formal training on the weapons system he used. He died at sea, in 1943, with two-thirds of the crew lost to a Japanese torpedo aboard the Liscome Bay. Cuba Gooding Jr portrayed him in the 2001 film Pearl Harbor. He was awarded the Navy Cross for his actions at Pearl Harbor. The citation reads: “While at the side of his Captain on the bridge of the battleship U.S.S. WEST VIRGINIA, Mess Attendant First Class Doris Miller, despite enemy strafing and bombing and in the face of a serious fire, assisted in moving his Captain, who had been mortally wounded, to a place of greater safety, and later manned and operated a machine gun directed at enemy Japanese attacking aircraft until ordered to leave the bridge.” His family has long advocated for his award to be upgraded to a Medal of Honor. No carrier in the US navy has ever been named for a sitting president, and reports of the plan to name this one after Trump prompted heavy criticism on Friday. “It’s beyond comprehension for a president to want his own name on a Navy ship while our armed forces are living in deteriorating conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln,” Johnson, of the NAACP, said. “For generations, millions of Black women and men have proudly served in the United States military, defending freedoms that too often were not even afforded to them, their families, or their communities. “Donald Trump is making a mockery of that legacy by treating military service as another opportunity for personal branding. Our brave service members signed up to defend the nation, not the fragile ego of one man. America deserves better than this.” Mark Kelly, a Democratic US senator of Arizona and a retired navy officer, wrote on X: “Dorie Miller’s bravery at Pearl Harbor is legendary and resulted in him being awarded the Navy Cross. This aircraft carrier shouldn’t be renamed at all, let alone for Donald Trump, who has denigrated servicemembers like Dorie Miller who have paid the ultimate price.”

title: US supreme court lets Trump continue work on White House ballroom for now
author: Marina Dunbar
summary: Chief justice signs temporary order to permit work while court considers emergency appeal from administration
body_text: The US supreme court has allowed Donald Trump to continue construction of his controversial White House ballroom for now, temporarily pausing a lower court order that would halt much of the project. Supreme court chief justice John Roberts signed a temporary order on Friday, permitting work to continue on the planned White House addition – a top priority of the president – while the court considers an emergency appeal from Trump’s administration. Democrats accused the supreme court, which is controlled by a conservative super-majority, of “rubber stamping Trump’s vanity-driven, gilded corruption”. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, said: “As costs skyrocket, the administration is wasting money on an endless and illegal war, corporate giveaways and Trump’s pet projects.” The president swiftly welcomed the order, which puts the Friday deadline from the appeals court on pause. That court had ordered construction to stop while a legal challenge proceeded, after concluding earlier this month that the ballroom project probably requires congressional approval before work can continue. The Trump administration then turned to the supreme court, arguing that construction of the structure was critical to national security and the safety of the US president. On Tuesday, the National Trust for Historic Preservation had urged the supreme court to suspend the ballroom project following an earlier lawsuit seeking to block construction. The massive 90,000sq-ft (8,400 sq meters) ballroom project part of the president’s sprawling plans to reshape the nation’s capital, has already involved the demolition of the White House East Wing. Construction also includes an underground military facility that the administration says is needed to protect the president. The underground military bunker would be a five-story complex that will include shelters, a hospital and other features designed to protect the president and senior officials during an emergency. The total cost of the project is expected to exceed $400m. “It is something that Presidents have wanted for 150 years, and that the Military has been seeking for the last 100 years,” Trump claimed in a social media post on Friday. “Their wish will soon be fulfilled! Construction is under budget and ahead of schedule.” Administration officials say the ballroom itself will be reinforced with missile-resistant columns and a drone-proof roof, allowing the structure to serve as a shield for both the underground military complex and the wider White House. Construction on the ballroom has been under way for 10 months with the administration saying the project is now approximately 65% complete. The administration has argued that authority over White House renovations is held by the president, not Congress or the courts. The justice department also argued that leaving the site in its current condition, effectively an open construction zone, makes protecting the White House more difficult.

title: US Postal Service rule tightens mail-in voting despite court orders blocking changes
author: Robert Mackey
summary: Rule would require states to provide federal government with information on voters in return for delivering ballots
body_text: The US Postal Service prepared to publish a final ⁠rule late ⁠on Friday to impose new requirements on states to provide the federal government with information on voters before the November ⁠midterm congressional elections, despite a pair of court ‌orders ‌that currently block the ‌changes from taking effect. The USPS acknowledged in the text of the final rule posted online Friday, which is scheduled to be published in the Federal Register next week, that two injunctions issued by federal courts in California and Massachusetts currently bar it from moving ahead with the changes to comply with a March executive order signed by Donald Trump. In accordance with the order, the postal service would ‌require states to give the US Department of Homeland Security and other agencies access to lists of voters and to adopt new balloting procedures before the mail agency would make deliveries. If states did not comply, the USPS would refuse to deliver the ballots. The federal government has sued 30 states and Washington DC for refusing to hand over lists of eligible voters. Despite the injunctions, the Trump administration is pressing ahead with plans to disrupt votes cast by mail. According to the text posted online Friday, the USPS is ready to implement the new restrictions on mail-in voting if the court injunctions are lifted. “If the government obtains timely relief from the injunctions, implementation immediately thereafter will provide election officials as much time as possible before the next election to comply with the rule’s preparation standards for Federal Ballot Mail envelopes, and to prepare to submit data to the Federal Ballot Mail Portal (‘Portal’), before the mail-in and absentee ballots subject to this rule are mailed (which generally occurs in September or thereafter, as determined by state law),” the rule reads. “The Portal will become active (along with the verification process that relies on Portal data) at the time of the publication of the system of records (‘SOR’) governing the Portal.” Nearly one in three Americans voted by mail in 2024, but Trump, who wants to restrict the number of voters by limiting ballots cast by mail, signed an executive order in March that prohibits the USPS from delivering ballots to any voters not on a federal list of citizens deemed eligible to vote in each state by the Department of Homeland Security. The USPS proposal to implement this order seeks to require states to give the postal service the names and barcodes tied to mail-in ballots for federal elections. The service said it received more than 200,000 responses to its proposed rule change during a public comment period. Trump himself voted by mail in Florida’s Republican primary this year, which was at least the third time the president has mailed in his ballot.

title: Trump’s new attorney general poses a huge threat to abortion rights
author: Moira Donegan
summary: A call revealing Todd Blanche’s plans to crack down on mifepristone lays bare the danger
body_text: The abortion pill is a miracle. Mifepristone, then called RU-486, was synthesized by a French lab in the 1980s; in combination with misoprostol, commonly used as ulcer medication, it cuts off the body’s supply of progesterone, halts the development of a pregnancy, and incites contractions, which empty the uterus. The drug allows pregnancies to be terminated with a shocking degree of reliability and ease. Gone are the concoctions of ergot and Spanish Fly dispensed by 19th century midwives, which only sometimes worked to induce a miscarriage; gone are the backroom procedures of the pre-Roe US, when drunk, lascivious, incompetent or cruel providers wielded bent coat hangers in dirty rooms. The abortion pill is safe, effective and cheaper than ever. And since Dobbs, it’s everywhere: even if you live in a state with an abortion ban, you can get the pills shipped to your house in the mail. Since Roe was overturned, there has not been a return to the terror of mass death that marked the pre-Roe era of septic abortion wards, where women routinely found themselves maimed, sickened or killed. There’s exactly one reason why: because illegal abortions were largely unsafe without the pill, and they are extremely safe with it. So of course, the Trump administration and their allies on the American right are trying to get rid of it. And this month, they gained a powerful new ally when Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer and an anti-abortion zealot, was confirmed as attorney general. The vote, in which Blanche was confirmed by a margin of one along party lines, was conducted in the wee hours of the morning on 8 August. Maybe that’s because the Republicans who confirmed him didn’t want anyone to see what they were doing. Blanche has, after all, been shockingly subservient to Donald Trump, and seems poised to complete the president’s long-brewing transformation of the country’s chief law enforcement agency into a vehicle for score settling, personal vendettas, distributing favors to the administration’s friends and suppressing dissent from its political enemies. But perhaps most incendiary is what Blanche has said, publicly and privately, about how he intends to use the justice department and its vast array of oversight powers, legal prerogatives, and investigatory purview to curtail abortion access nationwide – and to shut down the life-saving distribution of mifepristone, in particular. In a call facilitated by the White House faith office just days before he was confirmed, Blanche reportedly told Christian conservative leaders that as attorney general, he would move more aggressively than his predecessor Pam Bondi to outlaw the mailing of mifepristone across state lines, and target the Democratic-controlled states that have protected abortion most effectively. Blanche, who was then the acting AG, told the religious group Intercessors for America that the justice department was working “so that the Dobbs decision becomes permanent in every single state.” “We don’t have complete victory yet,” Blanche said, “but we will have victory, and victory will be soon, and, and, and it will be permanent.” Exactly how Blanche intends to secure his victory over women’s freedom is unclear. But as AG, he has several paths at his disposal. His comments on the call prompted widespread speculation that Blanche could call for enforcement of the Comstock Act, a long-dormant law from 1873 that has been unenforced for years and has been partially repealed in the past. Anti-choice advocates say it could be used to legally ban the mailing of abortion pills, thus cutting off access for many women who live in states with bans. In 2022, the Biden justice department declared that medical providers could not be prosecuted under the Comstock Act for mailing abortion pills; as the attorney general, Blanche would have the power to reverse that decision. The Comstock Act’s application would be particularly significant, as it could be used to halt virtually all commercial traffic in abortion pills – not only mifepristone, but also misoprostol, the second drug, which has sometimes been used to induce abortion on its own. Such a move would reverse the miracle of the pills, pushing many desperate women towards methods that are less effective and can carry grave dangers. Another path that Blanche could take to restrict abortion access would be to sue the states that seek to protect it. On the call, Blanche explained his reasoning: “If states have said, ‘We are going to protect the unborn and we’re going to protect every life from the moment of conception,’ we’re putting practices and policies in place so that other states and other organizations can’t attack that. They can’t do things like they’re doing with mailing in mail-order drugs.” Here, Blanche appeared to be referencing shield laws, legislation passed in a number of Democratic-controlled states that prohibits state authorities from participating in other states’ abortion-related investigations and prosecutions. The laws mean that doctors operating out of states like New York or Washington can prescribe and ship abortion drugs to people living in places such as Texas or Arkansas, safe in the knowledge that their own state police will not come knocking at their door to serve another state’s warrant or extradition order. Blanche’s comments suggest that his Department of Justice might sue to have the shield laws declared illegal, thus significantly curtailing liberal states’ rights to choose their own law enforcement priorities and granting conservative states the power to enforce their own laws even beyond their borders. Blanche also appeared to indicate that he would seek to restrict abortion access using other agencies’ powers. On his call with leaders of the Christian right, he said his department was “working hand in hand” with health agencies to make Dobbs permanent. The FDA, which expanded access to mifepristone in 2021 under the Biden administration and made the change permanent in 2023, has been under intense pressure from anti-choice allies in the Maga coalition to revise that guidance, making the drug ineligible for telehealth prescriptions and requiring patients to retrieve it from providers in person, a regulatory move that would also serve to cut off access in Republican controlled states. But the anti-abortion movement is pushing the FDA even further: it has succeeded in getting the agency to initiate a “review” of mifepristone’s safety (though the safety of the drug has been proven by nearly four decades of use worldwide and hundreds of studies), which is widely seen as a pathway for the FDA to create a pretext to remove mifepristone from the market. That’s not fast enough for some on the misogynist right: Louisiana has sued the FDA, asking it to forbid mifepristone from being prescribed via telehealth, in a case that is set to be heard by the ultraconservative fifth circuit next month. So far, the justice department has supported the drug’s online availability in court. Under Blanche, it could reverse that stance. Trump has been gunshy about pursuing the agenda of his antiabortion allies since returning to office. He appears to have been spooked by the political reaction to Dobbs, which was credited for the Democrats’ better-than-expected showing in the 2022 midterms, as well as with a slew of pro-choice victories in special elections in the years that immediately followed the decision. The anti-choice movement has even been angry with Trump for the slow pace of his anti-abortion agenda since his return to power in 2025. Which is not to say that the Trump administration has given the movement nothing: enforcement of the Face Act, a federal law meant to stop anti-choice protestors from physically blocking clinic entrances, has been all but abandoned since Trump returned to the White House; some who were prosecuted under the law have even been pardoned and remunerated by Trump, at taxpayer expense. But until now, Trump has faced a looming threat that seems to have slowed the pace of his anti-abortion policymaking: the 2026 midterms. Soon, that obstacle will be removed. The appointment of Todd Blanche is a dark signal for women’s rights: more abortion restrictions can be expected in 2027. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

title: A mosque in Ohio was attacked for the third time. Members doubt Trump’s FBI will call it a hate crime
author: Stephen Starr in Cincinnati, Ohio
summary: Latest attack happened amid Islamophobic blowback against Arab and Muslim Americans running for office
body_text: Nashid Shakir describes how assailants used wire cutters to break into the Westwood Islamic Community Center in the early hours of 3 August. “They cut the wire and broke the window to get in. They broke into the office, too. It was total disarray,” says Shakir, a board member, and member, at the community center since the 1960s. Just as troubling is the smashed glass – still evident – on two posters containing lines in Arabic from the Quran hanging on one of the center’s walls. He shows where valuables including a surveillance camera and television monitors were stolen and where swear words including the word “die” and other profanity were written on a whiteboard. The leaders of the center, which houses a mosque and food pantry and is situated in an underserved, majority-Black neighborhood in west Cincinnati, and local Muslim community members have called the incident a hate crime. It’s the third time the center has been broken into in the past seven years, with the previous incident seeing racist comments graffitied on the center’s walls. “The police came out and they checked the boxes for making a report. But we haven’t had any follow-through,” says Shakir. The attack happened against the backdrop of a rise in Arab and Muslim American politicians running for political office in the US, and a series of shocking Islamophobic comments that have followed from Republican politicians and far-right figures. In Michigan, Democratic senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed has been targeted by conservative and rightwing voices following his primary win on 4 August. El-Sayed, an epidemiologist who has called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and for an end to US military funding for Israel, has been repeatedly targeted by Donald Trump. A report by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH), a Washington DC-based thinktank, found that the targeting of El-Sayed increased twentyfold since the election earlier this month. On 10 August, Trump told reporters from the Oval Office that “we have jihadists being elected all over the place”, echoing rhetoric that noted extremists have used in their attacks on Muslim Americans in recent weeks and months. In March, the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair) reported an unprecedented rise in the number of Islamophobic incidents and discrimination nationwide last year. In May, three people were killed by two attackers at a mosque in San Diego. “What we are seeing right now is a very organized and coordinated campaign to generate fear and hysteria about Muslims for electoral gain, to justify domestic policies, and build support for foreign wars,” says Raqib Naik, executive director of the CSOH. “The idea that Muslims are coming to ‘take over’ America is more mainstream. It is a continuation of post-9/11 Islamophobia, but in many ways, it has become uglier and more blatant. We are now at a point where 65 members of Congress have formed a so-called ‘Sharia-Free America caucus.’” Formed last December by the Texas Republican representatives Keith Self and Chip Roy, the so-called caucus has representatives from 17 states. “What is particularly worrying is that bigotry once largely confined to fringe anti-Muslim groups is now being repeated and amplified from the highest office in the country, by elected officials, billionaires and major political influencers,” says Naik. In Ohio, Somali Americans in particular have been subjected to Trump-fueled violence and immigration crackdowns. Last winter, ICE agents, rightwing influencers and other provocateurs descended on childcare and other facilities run by Somali Americans in Columbus following false claims from Trump that members of the community were “ripping off the country”. Amid this climate, religious and community leaders in Ohio say there is little doubt whether federal law enforcement would do anything to help. Muslim leaders say that no suspects in the Westwood Islamic Community Center attack have yet been apprehended. Tala Ali, a community organizer at Cair-Ohio and a Cincinnati resident, says she does not intend to approach the FBI to ask them to investigate the community center attack as a hate crime. “I don’t have trust in authorities to find who’s behind this. We have had incidents where the largest mosque in Cincinnati was bombed,” she says. In December 2005, two pipe bombs exploded outside Cincinnati’s Clifton mosque, resulting in significant damage to a door and windows. The explosions happened just two hours after worshippers had gathered to pray. No one has ever been charged with the attack. “Our focus now is to get local authorities just to acknowledge it and condemn it and any acts of bias, intimidation [or] violation against the Muslim community and the Black community,” she says. “I think that this was an identity-motivated targeting, so by definition because of that [it’s a hate crime].” With about 25 people gathering to pray at the center’s mosque on most Fridays, now the local Muslim community is working to find support to improve security at houses of worship around Cincinnati, including at the community center, which at the time of the attack had no security cameras. Shakir says he has been surprised by the positive response from the wider Cincinnati community but not by the rhetoric emanating from the White House. “I take what [Trump] says with a grain of salt even though I know there’s a part of the country that takes what he says as gospel,” he says. Ali says the local Muslim community would like to apply for federally funded grants through the Federal Emergency Management Agency that specifically tailor to non-profits in need of security assistance. But because of who’s in government, she says, locals aren’t sure about seeking that out. “Look at the culture and the environment that we live in. Do you want to bring that into your house [of worship]?” she says. “Because, will these people really protect you, or will they use it, as they have historically used it, to access what we do in our community?”

title: It’s a miracle: Natalie Harp has turned Republicans into feminists
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: A Democrat’s remarks have resulted in impassioned defenses of the Trump aide. The right has discovered misogyny
body_text: Jon Ossoff is quite the miracle worker. Perhaps the Democratic senator can’t turn water into wine, but he has managed to turn whining conservatives into impassioned feminists. During a rally last Sunday, the Georgia senator delivered a takedown of Donald Trump, which included a reference to his aide Natalie Harp. “He doesn’t want to do the job,” Ossoff said of the president. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.” Those three words – travel with Natalie – were deliberately loaded. Harp was in the spotlight at the time because of the decoy plane story. The 35-year-old was one of a handful of people Trump had taken onto a different plane via a catering truck when he was worried about a potential assassination attack targeting Air Force One. Intrigue as to the exact nature of the relationship between Harp and Trump was heightened by the fact that Melania Trump, the president’s third wife, hadn’t been seen in public for weeks at the time. (Funnily enough, she magically reappeared on Thursday, a few days after Ossoff’s comments, for a press conference where she lovingly held hands with Trump. Very cute.) Ossoff’s remarks about “Natalie” might have been something of a cheap shot, but it’s hilarious to watch the right discover misogyny and decry the remarks as sexist. Suddenly, everyone from Fox News to prominent conservatives are very worried about a professional woman not being taken seriously. The former House speaker Newt Gingrich, for example, said on Twitter/X that Ossoff owes Harp an apology. “If a conservative Republican had attacked a liberal Democrat working professional woman the way Ossoff smeared Natalie Harp there would be cries to kick them off the ticket and reject this kind of misogynistic language diminishing and smearing someone who is simply doing their job.” The conservative commentator Scott Jennings, who is rumoured to be a potential replacement for Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary, was also appalled. “[Ossoff] unleashed a comment so vile against a young Republican woman working in politics that every woman in this country, no matter your ideology, ought to listen carefully and never forget it,” Jennings said on his podcast. Meghan McCain also clutched her pearls at the coverage Ossoff’s comments sparked. “The egregious sexist attacks on Natalie Harp are absolutely insane – and they’re coming from prestigious journalists,” she wrote on X. “What is wrong with everyone?! Every president has close aides and sometimes they are females. Like what year is this?!” It’s 2026, Meghan. And in the year 2026 I think the masses have generally understood that simply criticizing a woman is not in itself misogynistic. I’m not saying there hasn’t been any misogyny in the Harp coverage, but the main reason there has been so much attention on the story is because the White House has had a completely unhinged response to Ossoff’s comments and kept it in the news. More importantly, the reason so many people aren’t taking the Trump aide seriously isn’t because she’s a woman; it’s because she’s not a serious person. And I’m being diplomatic with that choice of language. After all, we’re talking about someone whose nickname is “the human printer” because, while working on Trump’s re-election campaign, she reportedly ran around after him with a portable printer, handing him hard copies of flattering coverage. You could write that off as a canny career move from someone who understands flattery gets you everywhere with Trump, but that’s also one of the least weird things Harp has done. Per a CNN report, which has pictures of the incident, back in 2023, Harp jumped in the trunk of an SUV because she wanted to be close to Trump and there was no room in his motorcade. Once Trump won re-election and Harp joined him in the White House, she apparently worked for a year without security clearance. According to reporting by MS NOW, she declined to complete the clearance process for unknown reasons. And then there are the “adoring letters” Harp sent Trump, first mentioned in the book Regime Change, by the New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. Two were later published in the Daily Beast. “You are all that matters to me,” she wrote in one letter. Other memorable lines included “I want to bring you joy, to feel like we can get through a day without ever having to talk ‘work’”; she also called Trump her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”. To state the obvious: these are deeply weird things to say to your boss. (It’s also weird that Harp shares Trump’s unconventional approach to capitalization.) I should note that Harp, who says she is a cancer survivor, seems to believe that Trump saved her life by signing legislation that gave her access to experimental bone cancer treatment when she was younger. While that might make her obsession with Trump more understandable, it does not make her general conduct any more professional. So spare me all the lectures from the right about sexism, please. If you’re worried about how women in politics are treated, you should probably focus your attention on the adjudicated sexual abuser who is president. Donald Trump attacks another female journalist Trump can’t seem to stand it when a woman doesn’t fawn over him and has a history of attacking female journalists. The latest object of his ire is the CNN reporter Kristen Holmes, who asked the president about Ossoff’s comments regarding Natalie Harp. Trump called Holmes a “loud boisterous person” and instructed her to be “quiet”. Meanwhile, the White House’s social media account posted about Holmes multiple times. In one post they wrote: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive.” New York gives parents a ‘night out’ New York mayor Zohran Mamdani hosted the city’s first Parents’ Night Out. The city provided free childcare for nearly 300 kids so parents could have a little time off. This is what “family values” and being pro-life actually look like: supporting parents, not forcing women to give birth. Sudan’s humanitarian crisis grows, with 200,000 newly displaced people Increased fighting in the Kordofan region and flooding has made one of the world’s largest displacement crises even worse. Chanel has made pricey ‘barefoot sandals’ for the well-heeled Margaret Qualley was spotted stepping out in the sole-less shoes. Somehow I do not think I will be wearing these around the filthy streets of Philadelphia. ‘Heated Rivalry’ author donates $300,000 to rural libraries facing closure “I had to do it because I don’t know what the point is of being a successful author in Nova Scotia if you’re not going to use it for good,” Rachel Reid told CBC News. Wouldn’t it be nice if Elon Musk thought like that? Israel launches an ‘investigation’ into killing of Hind Rajab In January 2024, 335 bullets were fired into a car containing five-year-old Hind and six of her family members in Gaza. When paramedics came to help, they were killed too. IDF vehemently denied responsibility for this atrocity, despite investigations making it obvious that its military was responsible. This week, Israel finally admitted its troops fired into the car and said there would be an investigation. Which is not particularly reassuring: Israel’s investigations into itself rarely result in any sort of accountability. Wesam Hamada, Hind’s mother, is demanding an independent inquiry, which is the least Hind deserves. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: Free speech group calls foul play at prosecutors using Comey novel in case against him
author: Edward Helmore
summary: PEN America condemns lawyers using passage from thriller to bolster claim ex-FBI director intended to harm Trump
body_text: A leading US free-expression group has hit out at federal prosecutors’ use of a novel written by former FBI director James Comey in their case accusing him of threatening to kill Donald Trump. “Citing a novel to save an indictment that is constitutionally dubious is a desperate Hail Mary and should be rejected,” said a statement posted on Friday by Mara Gassmann, legal director of PEN America, using a term for a last-second heave in American football. Prosecutors with the Trump administration-led justice department had argued in a filing days earlier that Comey sent coded messages to his followers suggesting they kill an enemy of his citing the fictional protagonist – a federal prosecutor – in his novel FDR Drive. The book’s main character tries to take down a far-right media personality, Sam Buchanan. The filing quotes passages from the book and a Publishers Weekly book review that described a prosecutor who “believes Buchanan went far beyond the protection of the first amendment” of the US constitution, which provides the right to free expression, “when he singled out his enemies by name and suggested ‘something should be done’ about them”. The citation is part of an legal effort to sustain its prosecution of Comey on charges that he made a threat against the US president and transmitted that threat across state lines through social media – over an image he posted on Instagram while vacationing in North Carolina five days before the publication of FDR Drive. Prosecutors in new court documents maintain there is “no serious dispute” that Comey’s May 2025 social media post featuring a photo of seashells arranged to read “8647” could be interpreted as a threat against Trump, who according to authorities has been the target of multiple assassination attempts. The number “86” is often used as shorthand to mean to get rid of or remove something (particularly in the restaurant service industry, to which Comey once belonged). Trump, meanwhile, is the 47th US president. Those documents were filed on Tuesday in response to Comey’s efforts to have the case against him dismissed. Comey, who has denied the charges, has said it “never occurred to me, but I oppose violence of any kind so I took the post down”. Trump’s feud with Comey – the FBI’s director for four years beginning in 2013 – dates back to his handling of an investigation into Russian interference during the 2016 election that led to Trump’s first presidency. That investigation found that Russia interfered “in sweeping and systematic fashion”. But it did not establish that members of the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with Moscow’s election interference activities. The government’s filing also claims that Comey had an “apparent financial incentive to stir up controversy”, suggesting the seashell photo was shared in an effort to juice sales for his “eerily on-the-nose novel”. Comey’s novel has sold 6,471 copies, according to Circana BookScan. In PEN America’s statement, Gassmann said: “A political message, expressed through a photo of seashells, is no true threat; now, the government’s use of Comey’s work of fiction to support this prosecution compounds the first amendment concerns.” Her statement added: “Extreme caution should be taken any time creative works are used to support criminal charges to protect the free expression rights of us all.” In arguing that the case should be dismissed, Comey’s lawyers say that the post was protected speech and did not amount to a “true threat” against the president. “In this context, no reasonable observer would understand the phrase ‘86 47’ to connote violence at all – let alone to threaten that Mr Comey personally would commit violence against the president,” they contend. Comey’s attorneys say their client is being subjected to “vindictive and selective prosecution” and have said the indictment is “not based on a good faith application of the law to the facts”. “Instead,” Comey’s lawyers say, “it effectuates a years-long campaign by the president to use the criminal process to punish Mr Comey for his protected speech and because of the president’s deep-seated animosity.”

title: The major parties had several chances to meet the moment. Instead they chose to safeguard their collective mediocrity
author: Zoe Daniel
summary: Labor and the Coalition united three times to defy the expressed desire of the voters; on gambling, on disability and on the power of the tech companies
body_text: If you need any more evidence that the two-party system is cooked, look no further than the not-so-grand coalition that came together to preference power over people in the federal parliament last week. These days the Liberal and National parties have taken to condemning modern Labor as “socialist” and some of its policy “communist”. Meanwhile, the prime minister has labelled the three parties of the right the “Noalition” as the Liberals and Nationals increasingly align with Pauline Hanson’s One Nation. They hate each other. Yet apparently, needs must. And in plain sight this last week, we have seen a more profound and perhaps permanent realignment as both government and opposition prioritise political survival over community concern. They could choose to better collaborate to meet the moment. Instead, they choose to swallow their hatred of each other to safeguard their collective mediocrity. In at least three instances Labor and the Coalition united to defy the clearly expressed desire of voters; on gambling, on disability and on the power of the digital companies. On the recommendations of the Murphy report, on the NDIS and on media diversity, Anthony Albanese chose to deal in the dark with Labor’s nominal “enemy” rather than with a crossbench that had proposals better reflecting what the public want and could have provided an alternative pathway to a majority in the Senate. On gambling, Labor purports to have done more than any other government before it. Spare me. You don’t get to skite about something being better than nothing. Voters across the spectrum remain sickened at the literal death toll from gambling harm, the women and children hurt, the money sucked out of their communities into the coffers of largely multinational gambling companies, big sport and big broadcasting. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email They know this deal made between the major parties provides a half arsed ‘solution’. What we are witnessing, as the vote share of the major parties continues to decline, is the emergence of a new political pragmatism that could ultimately compound the very loss of trust – and voter support that the legacy parties are trying to subvert. It is the uniting of the parties of an establishment that is increasingly out of touch with and alienated from the electorate. As they play a game of whack-a-mole on thorny problems that communities want solved; gambling ads, gas taxes, the money and power behind big tech, combining their numbers to neutralise the niggles is a neat albeit short-term solution. In the case of gambling, the Coalition claims that it “strengthened” the reform package with its tweaks, which are even less ambitious than those Peter Dutton proposed before the last election. The government gets to claim some level of groundbreaking bipartisanship to help it sleep at night. It is a not-so-grand coalition of right and “left” along the lines of what we have seen on and off for decades in Germany, for example, but now struggling to satisfy that country’s voters and to fend off the AfD rise from the extreme right. There may be a warning here: “Dance with the one that brung you” is a phrase borrowed by Ronald Reagan and others from American slang for sticking with those who helped you achieve your goals. Remaining Labor voters are unlikely to be impressed with their elected representatives conspiring with political opponents they are repeatedly told are the enemy of the interests of working Australians in defiance of their expressed wishes. Likewise, disappointed Liberal voters, dissatisfied with the direction, behaviour and record of a party they had supported habitually are likely to be further disenchanted as they see them lining up with their opposition to defeat their wishes. Such a coalition of convenience will reinforce the sentiment that the “system” has nothing for them any more; the big end of parliament lining up with the big end of town conspiring with each other rather than working for them. It is the ultimate display of self-interest. No wonder support for the majors is down to about 50% in total; no wonder some everyday Australians are choosing anger, in the form that One Nation represents. Others, seeking representation free from vested interests are leaning independent to provide the transparency and accountability that they’re looking for. Labor also likes to make big claims about transparency, and yes, it is crystal clear what is going on here. If democracy is in essence a contract between people and power, that contract is broken. We will all wear the consequences. Zoe Daniel is a three-time ABC foreign correspondent and the former independent member for Goldstein
