title: Peter Malinauskas grabbed headlines by announcing a royal commission into AI. How genuine are his ‘nation-leading’ moves?
author: Tory Shepherd
summary: The South Australian premier says his choices, including on AI and the social media ban, are powered by the need to turn the state’s smaller size into agility
body_text: It is a tale oft told that Labor kingmaker Don Farrell spotted Peter Malinauskas’s potential when Malinauskas was a shelf-stacker at Woolies. Thirty years on, the South Australian premier is garnering a reputation for audacious “nation-leading” moves, and Farrell, an SA senator, is still singing his praises. “He’s the standout politician of his generation,” Farrell says. The at-times effusive praise for Malinauskas comes not just from his own side, but also from industry organisations and even from former Liberal leader Peter Dutton, who once described him on Sky News before the last federal election as “the most honest of the Labor premiers”. The hosts of podcast The Rest is Politics, Alastair Campbell and Rory Stewart, have sung his praises multiple times, particularly for his role in Australia’s social media ban. The 45-year-old’s most recent headline-grabber was the announcement of a royal commission into artificial intelligence. That move prompted ABC state political reporter Thomas Kelsall to dig through his inbox where he found more than 50 government media releases using the phrase “nation-leading” in the past year and a half. Being constantly “nation-leading” is not a specific strategy, the premier says, but a function of being a more nimble state. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “We have to turn our smaller size, our relative size, into a source of agility, which we can make a strength,” he says. “The state’s always had a bit of a history in trying to seize a first-mover advantage where we can … and if we can translate that into economic opportunity and better living standards, then that’s the main game.” ‘Forward-looking’ inquiry In June, Malinauskas released a plan to cash in on the datacentre boom. This month he made a flying visit to the United States, where he met with Apple’s chief executive, Tim Cook, and Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown and signed a memorandum of understanding with OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman. He announced the royal commission upon his return, saying the two-day trip merely confirmed his thinking that there are “pretty essential questions that AI raises that no one seems to be answering”. The inquiry will be tasked with examining the risks and benefits of AI in health, the public service, the workplace and the energy grid. But it is the use of AI in education that is front of the premier’s mind, and the wicked problem of how to teach children to use AI without letting them use it to do their homework. However, the commission won’t look at the role of datacentres, which the premier describes as the “mines of the future”. The datacentre boom is a source of contention because of their environmental impact. Malinauskas says it’s also because they’re a “physical manifestation” of AI. But he also says he sees them as a ready-made “customer” for the state’s prolific renewable energy generation. “By the end of next year, we’re going to be 100% net renewables,” he says. “The only reason a lot more renewables aren’t being developed in SA is because there’s no customer, there’s no demand. Datacentres provide our source of demand.” It is the third time Malinauskus has called a “forward-looking” royal commission to propose policy rather than investigate specific incidents, following on from the royal commission into early childhood education and care – led by former prime minister Julia Gillard – in 2023 and the royal commission into domestic, family and sexual violence – led by former Democrats leader Natasha Stott Despoja – in 2024. The royal commission framework allows them to appoint expert commissioners, rather than having parliamentarians interview witnesses; allocates extra resources to the inquiry; and gives them the power to potentially compel witnesses such as tech companies. High and low Malinauskas has not got where he is now without some scuffles. He faced strident backlash for his commentary on the Adelaide Writers’ Week plans to include author Randa Abdel-Fattah. In June, Malinauskas voted alongside the opposition leader, Ashton Hurn, and four One Nation MPs to restrict abortion access. The move was defeated by 36 votes to nine. His government has also come under fire for its handling of the devastating algal bloom, an ecological crisis that is set to be exacerbated by the arrival of bird flu that has begun rapidly spreading among SA’s coastal colonies. And an election promise to “fix” the hospital ramping crisis has not eventuated. Plans to redevelop a public golf course in Adelaide’s famous parklands and to host the MotoGP, which would require the removal of hundreds of trees, sparked furious “stop the chop” protests. His popularity has led critics to accuse him of arrogance. At a leaders’ debate before the March state election, Hurn asked: “Do you even think you need to try at this election?” In all these cases, Malinauskas says he thinks “ad nauseam” about the right thing to do. He adds that he “overwhelmingly” votes on what would be considered the progressive side, and laments that the nuance in so many issues is lost in the increasingly polarised world. Rob Manwaring, a political scientist at Flinders University, says criticism over issues like the MotoGP is unlikely to take off too much paint. Much of Labor’s core constituency is in favour of these sorts of sporting events, Manwaring says, while describing Malinauskas as both thoughtful and “genuinely concerned about populism and democracy”. “He’s got that Hawke thing where he can do highbrow and lowbrow at the same time,” he says. The government’s enormous majority helps keep the peace between Labor’s left and right factions, Manwaring says, which in turn tends to plug up any damaging leaks. “There’s a sort of ‘Teflon-ness’ to him,” he says. Another key part of his success – and of some progressives’ disquiet – is that the business sector likes him. In November last year, the Business Council of Australia named SA as the best place to do business for the third time running. And it doesn’t hurt that the state has well and truly recovered from the 1991 state bank disaster and the collapse of the car industry, which culminated in Holden’s closure in 2017. The SA economy is the fastest-growing in the nation, Malinauskas says – though critics point to the burgeoning state debt. In 2014, the then defence minister, David Johnston, said he would not trust shipbuilder ASC to build a canoe. But thanks to Aukus and other defence projects, development at the Osborne shipyard is continuing apace. Renewable energy, advanced technologies including in the space sector, major events and a booming copper industry are all playing a part in bolstering Malinauskas’s economic credentials – even if he can’t claim all the credit. In February, on the cusp of the state election that gave Labor a whopping 34-seat majority in the lower house (the Liberal party won five, One Nation four, and independents four), the Australian Financial Review described the “cult of Malinauskas” and referred to “the rampant speculation of his eventual move to federal politics”. He has consistently said he has no intention of going to Canberra. “Everyone always assumes that the main game is in federal parliament,” Malinauskas says. “But that discounts or misunderstands the amount of things that you can do at a state level.” It’s also personal. The premier has four children – the oldest is 11, and the youngest is just two – and his wife, Annabel West, works full-time as a lawyer. Canberra would mean more than 20 weeks a year away from home. “This is enough,” he says.

title: ‘I hate Democrats, but I love Abdul’: voters who left over Gaza return for progressive push
author: Minnah Arshad in Dearborn
summary: Michigan Senate nominee and others have re-energized one-time Democratic voters who abandoned party under Biden
body_text: Two years ago, Zainab Bibi Ahmed thought she had turned her back on the Democrats for good. Now, she is volunteering for the party’s US Senate nominee in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed. Ahmed was one of 100,000 people to vote uncommitted in the February 2024 Democratic Michigan primary, in a bid to send a message to then US president Joe Biden about his support for Israel, as people watched what Amnesty International later called a “live-streamed genocide” in Gaza on their screens. That November, Ahmed – a resident of Troy, Michigan, and an academic staffer at Wayne State University – opted to vote for the Green party’s Jill Stein amid calls to punish Democrats over the administration’s support for Israel. “I did not think I would come back to the Democratic party after 2024. I really didn’t. But then when I saw [New York City mayor] Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed, of course, and Shereef Akeel and Amir Makled,” Ahmed said, referencing two university regent candidates in the state, “I was like, OK, I cannot not support these gentlemen just because they’re Democrats.” A wave of progressive victories since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 has ruptured the Democratic party, from the unlikely victory last year of Mamdani to Peggy Flanagan’s nomination for Senate in Minnesota last week. In Michigan, El-Sayed was joined by a slate of other progressives who secured the Democratic nomination at every level of government, including attorney general hopeful Eli Savit, US House nominees Will Lawrence and Donavan McKinney, state House nominee Chris Gilmer-Hill, and Ann Arbor mayoral candidate Yousef Rabhi. This month, 2.5 million people voted in Michigan’s primary election – a significant jump from the 2 million who turned out for the 2024 state primary election. It’s a sign, some supporters hope, that El-Sayed’s progressive, pro-Palestinian politics will help bring back reluctant and disenchanted Democrats. “If we keep going on this trajectory, I believe that the Democratic party will actually gain back a lot of support,” Ahmed said. Reluctant and former Democrats backing El-Sayed Like Ahmed, Waqas Sarwar, a Dearborn resident, voted for Stein in 2024, but he was excited to cast his primary ballot for Democrats El-Sayed and Representative Rashida Tlaib this month. “I hate Democrats, but I love Abdul,” Sarwar said. Sarwar believes that the party needs to bring “fresh blood” like El-Sayed and that it should pivot on Israel and Aipac to align with young voters. Polling shows a majority of Democrats oppose military aid to Israel, a position that has slowly gained some traction in Washington. A similar majority of roughly 75% supports the Medicare for All proposed system of universal healthcare and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), three positions shared by El-Sayed. Meanwhile, the Democratic party’s approval rating has reached historic lows, at times sinking lower than Trump’s favorability. “The party is totally lost right now,” Sarwar said. Not everyone has been persuaded to return. Some, like Amin Hashmi, have pivoted to Trump. Hashmi, 63, a Pakistani American Muslim engineer in Troy, Michigan, described himself as a “solid Democrat” until 2024. “I voted for Trump out of nowhere,” he said. “It was a desperate attempt for survival because I knew that Green party will not be a useful vote.” Hashmi said he was angry at Biden over Israel and initially hoped then US vice-president Kamala Harris would be different. But Hashmi said Harris did not seem to differentiate herself on foreign policy, nor did she make a substantive effort to reach out to Arabs and Muslims. In this month’s primary, Hashmi opted to vote on the Democratic side of the primary ballot and support El-Sayed over Haley Stevens, whose campaign was heavily backed by Aipac, the pro-Israel lobbying group. But in the general election, Hashmi said he remained undecided. A Republican precinct delegate, Hashmi said he’s leaning toward the GOP nominee, former representative Mike Rogers, who ran unopposed in the party’s primary. But, Hashmi said, if the Trump-backed candidate aligns with Stevens on Aipac and foreign policy, and he does not have a plan for affordability or local issues like data centers, he could vote for El-Sayed. “Mike [has] to offer better than what Abdul is doing,” he said. Hashmi also voted for Aisha Farooqi, a progressive Democrat in the 11th district who was running against a pro-Israel candidate, Jeremy Moss, to succeed Stevens in the House. Farooqi lost the primary, but Hashmi said he would have voted for her in the general had she won. “Being an old Democrat, the love is still there, but it’s kind of reluctant,” Hashmi said, who now calls himself a “reluctant Republican and a dejected Democrat”. Samraa Luqman, a Yemeni American political activist in Dearborn who similarly voted for Trump and El-Sayed, said it’s not the first time Muslim and Arab Americans have changed parties over war. Luqman said Muslims and Arabs used to vote Republican because of their alignment on social, and for some, financial, conservative stances. But former President George W Bush’s invasion of Iraq in 2003 – a military offensive that eventually killed over half a million Iraqi people – prompted a seismic shift, she said, pointing to the “neoconism” and “warhawks that came out of the Republican party”. In 2024, some Arabs and Muslims voted Republican after more than two decades of backing the Democratic party, again over foreign wars. In Dearborn alone, Trump was the first Republican presidential candidate to win since Bush in 2000. For Luqman, US support for Israel has pushed her to support the Republican party after previously calling herself a “staunch Democrat” until 2024. “The Democrats became the George Bush of Gaza,” Luqman said. But in November’s US Senate race in Michigan, Luqman said she is returning to the Democrats, to back El-Sayed. On top of foreign policy, Luqman said he appeals to her because he is “worried about Americans at home, and that to me is America first”. Luqman said Israel policy was the top issue for her, and if the Republican candidate in this race had a similar anti-war stance as El-Sayed, then “I think it would have been a tougher decision for me in November”. Dorian Sdunek, a resident of Howell, Michigan, who recently graduated high school, said he liked El-Sayed because of his commitment to campaign finance reform, a defining feature of the Democratic nominee’s platform. Sdunek, 18, said he would have supported the uncommitted movement in the 2024 primary if he had been old enough to vote then. But for the general election, Sdunek would rather help elect someone who had “a chance of listening to us”, he said, rather than a conservative who is going to “blow the whole place to the ground”. Sdunek said he was glad to see progressives such as El-Sayed gain momentum. Rima Mohammad, an uncommitted delegate at the 2024 Democratic national convention and the co-founder of the People’s Coalition, said she ultimately supported Harris in the general election out of fear of another Trump presidency. But efforts to convince others were futile. “I would try to explain why it’s important to support her at that point, but there was no saving that,” she said. “Even after seeing what Trump was doing, it was still hard to get people back engaged with the party, and back engaged with politics.” Shortly after Trump’s victory, Mohammad co-founded the coalition to organize progressive and marginalized Democrats in Michigan. But she struggled to re-engage community members, including pro-Palestinian supporters, progressives, and, most of all, young people, who she said had “lost hope”. This time around, Mohammad said El-Sayed’s candidacy has energized people, and she has received messages from community members asking for guidance on their ballots. “There were brand new primary voters. They didn’t know what to do, but they came because Abdul was on the top of the ticket, and they would say: well, who else?” From uncommitted to Abdul for Senate The outrage over Gaza, which manifested in nationwide protests and boycotts, ignited a debate among some Democratic voters over whether they would support Biden a second time. Uncommitted, a national protest vote movement, sprang up from Michigan in 2024. Biden was running largely uncontested in the primary, and pro-Palestine advocates used the otherwise inconsequential election to register their anger with the administration. The movement garnered about 13% of the Democratic primary vote in Michigan. In Dearborn, more people voted uncommitted than they did Biden, after he handily won the Arab-majority city four years earlier. Lexis Zeidan, co-founder of the uncommitted movement and the director of engagement at Arab Americans for Progress, said the coalition “made it very clear that we were organizing under the Democratic tent”. “We were trying to save Palestinian lives, while also trying to save the Democratic party against the Trump election.” Ultimately, the uncommitted group declined to formally endorse Harris but implicitly encouraged people to vote for her. The leaders said in September 2024 to “vote against” Trump and “avoid” third-party candidates. Zeidan, who is Palestinian Christian American, said the effort to make pro-Palestinian voices heard “fell on deaf ears at the time”, but candidates appear to be responding to the message now. A separate group called Abandon Biden, which morphed into Abandon Harris when she became the nominee, urged people to oppose the Democratic candidate in an effort to punish the party over its support of Israel. El-Sayed, for his part, backed uncommitted in the 2024 primary, then endorsed Harris in the general election the day after she announced her campaign. But Stevens and Aipac attack ads used his support for uncommitted against him. Zeidan called the effort “clear propaganda” used to disinform everyday voters. (After his primary win this month, Harris formally endorsed El-Sayed.) She added that the uncommitted voting bloc was “incredibly diverse”, and young people in college towns made up a majority of the supporters. Mohammad of the People’s Coalition said Gaza has become a litmus test in US politics. “Palestine was like the moral compass,” Mohammad said. “If you were not with the people in Gaza … If you’re pro-war, you’re OK with the war, what else do you stand for?”

title: Trump’s continued distrust in election integrity has experts eyeing his next move
author: George Chidi
summary: President’s speech, declassification of documents and heightened claims of noncitizen voting have experts concerned
body_text: A series of moves by Donald Trump’s administration to sow doubt in the integrity of US elections has intensified concern among voting experts – and sparked hope among election deniers – that it could declare a national emergency. The White House and US federal agencies have released a string of documents this summer – including disputed analyses of alleged voting by noncitzens and historical intelligence memos – stoking expectations that the US president could move to exert greater control over November’s US midterm elections. Trump used a primetime television address in July to claim – again – that US elections were vulnerable to foreign manipulation, and repeat the lie that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to Joe Biden, was stolen. Trump’s speech prompted Steve Bannon, his former political strategist, to predict the US president will declare a state of emergency on national security grounds to “protect” elections. “Take your No 2 pencil out,” Bannon, a rightwing commentator, said on his War Room video podcast on 29 July. “It’s coming. It’s coming. Just block the last week of August out. It’s coming.” While Trump and his allies could try to use a national emergency declaration to delegitimize results of November’s results, experts say such a declaration would not supersede the constitutional restrictions on executive power on election administration. No president has ever attempted to invoke an emergency to assert control over voting. Asked earlier this month by Wayne Allyn Root, a rightwing broadcaster, if he would “declare a national security emergency for elections”, Trump notably did not shoot down the idea. “Let me just say, stranger things have happened, OK?” the president told Real America’s Voice, a rightwing cable channel. “I’ll leave it at that.” The administration is “trying to lay the groundwork to declare some sort of emergency to nationalize elections”, said Aria Branch, a partner at the Elias Law Group, who led a lawsuit blocking Trump’s previous executive orders on election administration. “I think the president is looking for any opportunity to do that.” ‘We need to be prepared for everything’ “I mean, listen, I think it is quite obvious that the man is losing his grip in reality, so I think we need to be prepared for everything,” said Santiago Mayer, president of Voters of Tomorrow, a gen Z-led voter advocacy organization. “We have spent a long time thinking and preparing for any eventuality and anything that he might attempt. I think our focus at the end of the day is to turn out enough voters where, no matter what he pulls, it won’t succeed.” Democratic members of US congress have been wargaming strategies to respond to executive provocations in recent months, considering scenarios such as AI-generated disinformation videos and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents being dispatched to polls. Progressive organizations in the democracy space have also been preparing for something to happen before the election. The presence of Tulsi Gabbard, Trump’s former director of national intelligence, at an FBI raid in Fulton county, Georgia, raised questions earlier this year. Gabbard later testified before Congress that she had been leading an investigation into claims of foreign interference in US elections. Gabbard’s team was involved in the seizure and examination of voting equipment in Puerto Rico, and spent months scrutinizing potential vulnerabilities in voting machines and the possibility of foreign interference. When Gabbard resigned on 30 June, Trump named his longstanding ally Bill Pulte as her acting replacement, a widely criticized move by members of both parties, who pointed to Pulte’s lack of intelligence experience. While Jay Clayton later took up the post permanently, Pulte is said to have pushed the election interference narrative in a less-visible role. “This is why Pulte is so important,” Bannon said in July. “So, ah, Jay has got to – Clayton – has big shoes to fill. Every day we’re going to be dogging him on, like, where’s the next release on this.” On the night of Trump’s July address, Bannon texted CNN: “We need a National Security Emergency about the midterm elections immediately – this is a powerful predicate for that.” Ty Cobb, a former White House attorney, now a sharp Trump critic, warned of the same while speaking to PBS following the president’s July TV address. “Well, I think tonight’s speech is intended to add the predicate that he needs to declare an emergency at or about the time of the elections,” he said. ICE agents at polls is “a virtual certainty”, said Cobb, who questioned whether National Guard officers would also be presented. “Anything to intimidate minority voters, particularly immigrant voters, and also I think anything that allows them to try to seize voting machines, as Trump wanted to do in 2020, but [then-attorney general] Bill Barr explained to him there was just no basis for it.” ‘Noncitizen voting … is just not a widespread problem’ After Trump’s TV address, a White House “Government Transparency Task Force” – composed of members of the office of the director of national intelligence, the National Security Agency, the Central Intelligence Agency and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) – began releasing declassified “election integrity” documents on the White House website. The first tranche included declassified intelligence memos which described electronic voting machine vulnerabilities, foreign access to state voter registration data and foreign digital manipulation strategies. Much of the material was already known to the public and amounted to a US intelligence assessment that found no evidence Beijing altered the 2020 vote, which Trump lost. A week later, Trump and his allies quickly seized on an announcement from Mikie Sherrill, the New Jersey governor, that 6,600 non-citizens had registered to vote because of a software error. While fewer than 400 of them voted, the disclosure was used to escalate false claims that there are scores of noncitizens on the voter rolls. On 31 July, DHS released a public notice arguing that New Jersey’s administrative errors demonstrated a need for standardized federal oversight. The taskforce also declassified documents in a Michigan case where the FBI investigated suspected fraudulent voter registrations by a get-out-the-vote organization, in which no criminal charges were filed, and investigative material related to a data scrape of voter information in Maricopa county, Arizona. The pace of releases has been accelerating. On Monday, the taskforce declassified and released investigative files related to an investigation into Chinese intelligence, which disclosed how disgraced former Democratic US representative Eric Swalwell had told FBI agents how he had “occasionally hooked up” with Christine Fang, a Chinese national allegedly engaged in a political influence campaign. On Tuesday, the US Census Bureau released a brief claiming it had identified 24,000 noncitizens voting in the 2020 election in a preliminary match of 128m records. It did not reveal its methodology and was sharply criticized by democracy advocates. “This alleged analysis based on census data fails the laugh test,” said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research. “The administration does not provide a sufficient explanation of how it arrived at these numbers – and for good reason.” Branch, of Elias Law Group, suggested the Trump administration is “searching for” the legal basis for an executive order. “I think they believe there may be one. I think such a document just doesn’t exist, because the fact is our elections are secure,” she said. “Noncitizen voting in our elections is just not a widespread problem … All of the fear and narrative around that issue is just completely unfounded, and it’s really just to stoke fear and lay the groundwork for future action.” In July, DHS also released an analysis arguing that 278,000 noncitizens are registered to vote in federal elections. It did not reveal its methodology for identifying the noncitizens, either, or disclose how confident its officials were in their assessment. The tool it used to flag noncitizens on voter rolls is known to be inaccurate. ‘The founders recognized the risk of centralizing power’ Asked about the possibility of an executive order declaring a national emergency on elections, the White House did not rule it out, refusing to comment on hypotheticals. “Extreme liberal Democrats are keeping Americans from having full confidence in their elections by refusing to vote for the Save America Act,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, referring to legislation that would enforce a crackdown on voting. “The American people overwhelmingly support this commonsense legislation that ensures Americans, and Americans only, decide our elections. President Trump is absolutely right: we fix this now, or we lose our country.” The Save America Act would require states to submit their voter rolls to federal inspection, effectively give DHS the power to de-register anyone it deemed ineligible to vote. The act would also sharply curtail mail-in voting – a practice Trump repeatedly criticized, but has reportedly done himself as recently as in this week’s Florida Republican primary – and require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote and a narrow set of photo IDs to cast a ballot. “I mean, we’ve been closely monitoring what the administration is saying,” said Branch, who sees the rhetoric itself as an act of intimidation. “The constitution is extremely clear on this, and the founders recognized the risk of centralizing power over elections in the executive branch,” she added. “Very helpful, in terms of litigation to push back on these types of efforts.”

title: Artemis II crew to receive top US space medal for historic lunar journey
author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
summary: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen broke record for farthest distance traveled from Earth
body_text: The crew of the historic Artemis II lunar flyby mission have earned the US’s top space medal, officials have announced. Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen are set to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on 28 August, the US space agency Nasa said. Nasa’s website indicates that only 30 astronauts have gained the honor – among them Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon, and John Glenn, who was the first American to orbit Earth and then served four terms in the US Senate. Wiseman, Glover, Koch and Hansen were selected for the medal, despite its name, by Donald Trump after the Nasa administrator, Jared Isaacman, recommended them to the president. The Artemis II crew broke Apollo 13’s record for farthest distance traveled from Earth during their 10-day mission, which began on 1 April. They reached 252,756 miles (406,771km) as they swung above the lunar surface, surpassing the 1970 record of 248,655 miles as part of US plans to again land on the moon – then eventually reach Mars. Furthermore, Hansen – who is from Canada – became the first non-US citizen to fly to the moon. “This was not easy,” Wiseman said to reporters after the Artemis II mission safely ended with a textbook splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. “Before you launch, it feels like it’s the greatest dream on Earth. And when you’re out there, you just want to get back to your families and your friends. It’s a special thing to be a human, and it’s a special thing to be on planet Earth.” The medal ceremony scheduled for Wiseman and his colleagues at the Johnson Space Center in Houston comes four months after Trump hosted the Artemis II crew at the White House. The occasion was marked in part by the president, who turned 80 in June, telling the astronauts: “I would have had no trouble making it – I’m physically very, very good.” Nasa listed an 11am Eastern start time for the ceremony, with a video live stream of the event available at www.nasa.gov/live. Trump has sought to embrace the Artemis II crew’s achievements despite his administration’s proposal to cut Nasa’s budget by 23%, including a 46% reduction for space science initiatives, for the 2027 fiscal year beginning on 1 October. A House commerce, justice and science subcommittee led by Trump’s Republican party responded by advancing its own Nasa budget proposal that would maintain the science projects the president has been aiming to eliminate. Beside Armstrong and Glenn, previous Congressional Space Medal of Honor recipients include astronauts who were killed in the Apollo I fire as well as the explosions of the Challenger and Columbia space shuttles. Douglas Hurley and Robert Behnken were the last astronauts to have been chosen for the medal before the Artemis II crew. Hurley and Behnken in 2020 became the first to launch into orbit on a commercial spacecraft, and they accepted the medal in 2023 during Joe Biden’s presidency. • This article was amended on 23 August 2026. John Glenn was the first American to orbit the Earth, but not the first person as an earlier version said.

title: Natalie Harp reportedly posted 150 pro-Trump tweets on day of Capitol riot
author: Marina Dunbar
summary: Devoted Trump aide flooded her now-disabled profile urging people to ‘never concede’ on 6 January 2021
body_text: The Donald Trump aide Natalie Harp flooded a since-disabled social media account with pro-Trump posts on the day that the president’s supporters attacked the US Capitol in early 2021, years before she went to work for him and developed an extraordinary close relationship with him, a new report has revealed. CNN on Saturday reported that a deactivated account which Harp had on what is now known as X was packed with fiercely pro-Trump messages on the day of the January 6 Capitol attack in Washington DC, including posts repeating his lies that the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden toward the end of his first presidency, had been stolen from by fraudsters. “FIGHT FOR TRUMP!” Harp wrote 12 times in one of more than 150 posts that day alone. She followed that with a post declaring: “Today, DC is TRUMP COUNTRY!” Among her other posts was the declaration “today we STOP THE STEAL!’”. And as Trump delivered a speech that day, Harp wrote: “We will never give up. We will never concede!” CNN’s reporting on those posts come as the US news media have put a spotlight on Harp, 35, and her near-constant presence at the side of Trump, 80, during his second presidency. The scrutiny has been fueled by intensely affectionate letters from Harp to Trump, including one in which she called him her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”; claims from her estranged brother that her relationship with the president is “unhealthy”; and a recent speech from Jon Ossoff, a Democratic senator from Georgia, who contended that one of the few things Trump wants to do is “travel with Natalie”. The social media account that CNN reported on, opened by Harp in 2016, also contained posts in which she compared Trump to a biblical figure, according to messages unearthed by the Daily Beast. “We all know the story of the Good Samaritan,” Harp wrote as she went on to recount her claim that an intervention by Trump had saved her life while she grappled with cancer. “But what you don’t know is I was that forgotten person on the side of the road – left to die of medical error and cancer. The Political Establishment passed me by. But @realDonaldTrump didn’t. Meet my Good Samaritan!” she wrote in the 2019 message. The X account now appears to be suspended. It remains unclear when it was taken down or whether Harp or the platform was responsible for removing the posts. Harp’s official roles are special assistant to the president and executive assistant to the president – positions that come with an annual salary of $150,000. Inside Trump’s orbit, she has also earned the unofficial title of “human printer” – a reference to her role supplying the president with printed information. CNN’s report on Saturday also indicated that Harp’s embrace of Trump’s election-fraud narrative began well before the day of the Capitol insurrection. In the weeks leading up to the attack, she told followers: “We will never give up – for TRUTH is on our side. January 6th is coming!!” Her posts immediately following the election that ended Trump’s first presidency were similarly emphatic. “WE LOVE YOU! WE LOVE YOU! WE LOVE YOU!” Harp wrote days after the election results. Then, on 14 December 2020, as she denounced Biden’s victory, Harp posted: “THIS IS A COUP.” The resurfaced social media posts are not the only written materials now fueling scrutiny of Harp’s devotion to Trump. The Daily Beast published two intimate letters on Thursday written by the Trump aide in 2023. Beside calling him her “Guardian and Protector”, she wrote in one letter: “You are all that matters to me.” She also wrote: “I want to bring you joy, to feel like we can get through a day without ever having to talk ‘work.’”

title: Tim Scott defends Darline Graham’s ‘national security is not my thing’ comment
author: Sam Levine
summary: Republican senator tries to assuage concerns but does not offer details of Graham’s national security experience
body_text: Tim Scott defended fellow US South Carolina Republican senator Darline Graham’s knowledge of national security issues ahead of their state’s runoff election on Tuesday. Graham, who was appointed to fill the Senate seat held by her brother Lindsey Graham after his sudden death in July, is in a Republican primary runoff against South Carolina congressman Ralph Norman. During a debate between the two on Tuesday night, Graham struggled to answer a question about US national security interests in Taiwan and the South China Sea. “I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not that informed on national security,” she said during the debate. She added: “National security is not my thing.” Scott tried to assuage concerns about her experience on Sunday when he was asked about Graham’s qualifications – and whether a US senator should have an understanding of national security issues. “Well, the answer is yes. And she does,” he said during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press. He went on to give an answer that did not detail any of her national security experience. “The question we’re asking ourselves today is whether or not she is prepared to serve in the United States Senate and represent the people of South Carolina on the issues that are germane to the moment, with all the issues of the moment,” he said. “And is she prepared to hit those issues? She hits those issues spot-on.” Graham held various public policy jobs in South Carolina – but never had run for or held public office before she was appointed to the Senate. Beside Scott, Donald Trump has endorsed Graham – and he traveled to South Carolina on Friday to rally for her. The president also brushed off Graham’s answer on Friday. “I watched that,” he said. “I thought it was a very honest answer, actually.”

title: Democrats incredulous over Hakeem Jeffries and Jared Kushner meeting
author: Sam Levine
summary: Critics include Senator Chris van Hollen, ex-aide to Obama Tommy Vietor and ex-Republican congressman Adam Kinzinger
body_text: Democrats and other Donald Trump critics reacted incredulously to a New York Times report on Sunday that House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries met with Jared Kushner, the president’s influential son-in-law, to discuss possible areas of collaboration. The reported meeting comes months ahead of the November midterm elections in which Democrats are favored to retake the US House, a development that would make Jeffries speaker. If they are in the majority, Democrats are expected to use their oversight power to aggressively investigate the Trump administration, including self-enrichment by the president and his family. There are longstanding conflict-of-interest concerns about the way Kushner has continued to make money from foreign nations as he works on foreign affairs, including conflicts in Ukraine, Iran and Gaza. Asked about the reported meeting, Jeffries said in a statement: “Throughout this Congress, Republicans have adopted a my-way-or-the-highway approach to governing that has failed the American people. To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition. “The American people want bold change and that’s what House Democrats will deliver. In every conversation that we have with the Trump administration, we will continue to make it explicitly clear that the affordability crisis is not a hoax and nothing short of transformational policy change is acceptable. We are fighting for an affordable America. The question is whether Republicans will join us.” Nonetheless, among some who lamented the reported gathering was Tommy Vietor, previously an aide to former president Barack Obama and now a co-host of the left-leaning podcast Pod Save America. “Jared Kushner has no actual government job he just uses his family connections to get money from gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals. The only way [Jeffries] should work with him is with demands for documents and subpoenas,” Vietor posted. In April, Democrats on the House judiciary committee opened an investigation into Kushner’s financial conflict of interest. The investigation is focused on the way Kushner’s private business has raised money from Gulf nations while Kushner served as a special envoy for peace for the government. “You cannot both be a diplomat and a financial pawn of the Saudi monarchy at the same time; you cannot faithfully represent the United States with billions of dollars in Saudi and Emirati cash burning a hole in every pocket of every suit you own,” Maryland congressman Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, wrote in an April letter to Kushner. The reaction to the meeting underscores the appetite that Democrats have to bring a no-holds barred approach to investigating Trump during the final two years of his second presidency, should they have the opportunity. Not all Democrats have taken such a pugilistic approach to Trump. The Michigan governor, Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, for example, has taken a more collaborative approach to working with Trump in his second term. Asked whether he supported the meeting during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Senator Chris van Hollen – a Maryland Democrat – said: “I’m in favor of people meeting with whoever they want to discuss ideas. But it’s one thing to have a meeting. It’s another thing to see something real come out of that.” Adam Kinzinger, a former Republican congressman from Illinois who is an outspoken Trump critic and served on a House committee that investigated the Capitol attack, posted in reference to the meeting, “Make this make sense,” while tagging Jeffries. Appearing on Sunday on Fox News, Mike Johnson, the US House speaker and a Louisiana Republican, asserted Kushner was “not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House”. “I don’t know what that’s about,” Johnson said of Kushner’s reported meeting with Jeffries. “I know Jared has interests and lots of other things going on.”

title: ‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade war
author: Lauren Almeida
summary: PM Mark Carney says ‘we got attacked’ as tariffs come into force on items from hockey sticks to tongue depressors
body_text: Donald Trump has hit back at Canada after a breakdown in negotiations plunged the two countries into a trade war. In his first public comments since negotiations collapsed on Friday in Washington, the US president wrote on social media: “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!” “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” he added. “No more!!!” His comments came after the US imposed 50% tariffs on $20bn (£14.6bn) worth of Canadian goods, while Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, has vowed to match them “dollar for dollar”. The US tariffs came into force on Saturday, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Trade experts have predicted that the tariffs could result in some job losses, but the biggest impact is expected to be political, triggering fresh tension between the neighbours. Both sides blamed the other for the breakdown in talks on Friday. Carney told Canadian journalists that the country was “at war” over trade with the US, after Trump “miscalculated” by escalating his tariff attack. “You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” the Canadian prime minister told reporters in Ottawa. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered and we will not give what they’ve asked.” Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, has said the US was compelled to act after a year of retaliatory measures by Canada. He told Fox & Friends Weekend: “We’ve said enough and so we’ve taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains.” Dan Kelly, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, estimated that 40% of small Canadian exporters will be directly hit by the US tariffs, and that nearly one-third expect their revenues will drop by 50% or more as a result. The escalation was also met with anger by Democratic lawmakers and governors from US states that border Canada including Minnesota, New York and Washington. New York governor Kathy Hochul posted on X: “Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That’s Trump’s economic policy in a nutshell.” Minnesota senator Amy Klobuchar, said the new tariffs meant “higher costs for small businesses, farmers, and all Minnesota families.” She wrote on X: “Canada is Minnesota’s #1 trading partner. Minnesotans are paying for Trump’s chaos.” Carney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England, was elected as Canada’s prime minister last year after campaigning to lead a fightback against Trump, who has suggested he wants to make Canada a 51st state with “economic force”. Carney’s “dollar for dollar” tariffs are expected to take effect from 8 September, with new levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. The escalation has also called into question the future of the North American trade pact between the US, Canada and Mexico, known as USMCA. The pact, which was signed by Trump during his first term, governs about $2tn annually in goods and services between the three countries. Trump refused to renew the USMCA this summer after Canada and Mexico formally requested for it to be renewed for another 16 years. When asked how the US-Canadian collapse in trade talks would affect the USMCA, Carney said it was “certainly not good news”. Increasingly aggressive rhetoric and trade policy from the Trump administration has damaged US-Canadian relations, with tourism also suffering – there was a 21% drop in Canadians entering New York state in 2025 and 3m fewer visits compared with the previous year. Furthermore, a petition to expel the US ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, from the country has gathered about 248,000 signatures since late July, according to the Associated Press. This year a poll by Globe and Mail newspaper found that only 9% of Canadians agreed that the US was a “trustworthy ally”, and that 51% of those polled had cancelled American trips in reaction to comments by Trump.

title: Morning Mail: anger over gambling logos ban delay; Canada and US plunge into trade war; classroom digital detox debate
author: Paul Gallagher
summary: Betting logos to remain on jerseys until 2032; war of words in US-Canada trade dispute; rethink urged over screen time in classrooms
body_text: Good morning. The Labor government has banned gambling logos on sports jerseys – but there’s a catch. A long transition period allows teams’ betting sponsorships to remain on full view until 2032, and those who argued for the ban are unimpressed. Property investors are stepping back as rising interest rates and tax changes make their impact felt, but new data suggests first home buyers are spying an opportunity to get off the sidelines. Elsewhere, a fractious new trade war is brewing between Canada and the United States. And we weigh up the arguments for whether Australia’s school kids need to take a digital detox. Australia Exclusive | Amid interest rate rises and tax changes, first home buyers are still taking out a large number of loans – even as investors step back from Australia’s property market. Meanwhile, a new analysis shows renting the median apartment in some cities would be too much of a stretch for someone earning the median wage. ‘Absurd situation’ | Children across Australia will continue to see gambling logos on professional sport jerseys until up to 2032, despite Labor’s pledge to weaken the link between sport and betting. ‘Unique and distinct’ | Leading marine scientists are urging the government for stronger protections for marine ecosystems as a once-in-a-decade review of marine parks gets under way. In pictures | Once the economic lifeblood of the region, Latrobe Valley’s coal industry is in terminal decline. Jesse Thompson’s photographic project examines its legacy. ‘A mismatch’ | Halloween: The Game has been banned in Australia due to “incentivised drug use” rather than its gruesome depictions of violence: academics say this highlights incoherent standards. World Trade war | Donald Trump has hit back at Canada after a breakdown in negotiations plunged the two countries into a trade war – with Mark Carney vowing to match US tariffs “dollar for dollar”. The lesson from Canada’s collapsed trade talks with the US? Negotiation may be futile, Olivia Bowden writes. Poll warnings | A series of moves by the Trump administration to sow doubt in the integrity of US elections have intensified concern among voting experts that it could declare a national emergency. Russia-Ukraine war | Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said holding elections in Ukraine during wartime would risk splitting the country at a time when Russia is amassing new stocks of ballistic missiles. Middle East crisis | Iran’s foreign minister has dismissed the threat of new US economic sanctions as a “desperate” ploy, even as its president admits that Iranians face “many problems”. Marriage vow | Andy Burnham has surprised Manchester newlyweds with a video message confirming some good news: the new British PM would not come to their wedding. Full Story Who is Natalie Harp? Trump’s most devoted aide is in the spotlight Natalie Harp is President Donald Trump’s most devoted aide: she travels the world with him, types Trump’s Truth Social posts, and even pens him “adoring” letters. David Smith speaks with Reged Ahmad about Harp’s journey into Trump’s inner circle – and how one Democrat senator put her in the global spotlight. In-depth More than 15 years after laptops were marched into schools across Australia, many teachers and parent groups think it may be time to rethink screen time in classrooms. Is it time that schools had a digital detox? Not the news In the latest of our Kindness of strangers series, we hear from a reader who found themselves facing an increasingly aggressive taxi driver. Two men stepped in to help and began a friendship that would last for years. title: Start your engines! Trump completes fast and furious takeover of Washington with IndyCar race
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: US president, pushing on with Freedom 250 festivities, makes over nation’s capital for Trump rally on wheels
body_text: He got the wrong end of the stick. Donald Trump couldn’t figure out how to hold the green flag until his wife, Melania Trump, and Command Sgt Maj Matt Williams set him right. Then the US president waved the flag fast and furious like an excited schoolboy. The race was under way – and his conquest of Washington DC was complete. Since returning to Washington, Trump has deployed the national guard, wrecked the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, demolished the East Wing of the White House and run the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts into the ground. His face adorns the Department of Justice, and he still has grand plans for a triumphal arch worthy of a Roman emperor. On Sunday he made the nation’s capital tremble with fast, flashy cars brazenly roaring around a 1.7-mile (2.7km) street circuit in IndyCar’s Freedom ⁠250 Grand Prix, the capstone of his Maga-flavoured celebration of the 250th anniversary of US independence. Washington was not built for a Trump rally on wheels and had to make accommodations, like a party host bracing for a noisy and obnoxious guest. More than 200 manhole covers were welded down around the course so they would not be sucked up by cars thundering over them. The National Gallery of Art studied how vibrations from the vehicles might affect its exhibits and shielded some outdoor sculptures. Indeed, as the vehicles whizzed by the National Archives, home to the US’s desperately fragile founding documents, and the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum, where Neil Armstrong’s spacesuit requires constant vigilance, it was not hard to imagine anxious curators twitching at every rattle of crockery or spillage of tea. Not that the president seemed to be sweating it. While officially the Grand Prix was open to everyone – and DC’s Democratic mayor, Muriel Bowser, declared, “Drivers, to your cars!” – the event had a distinctly Trumpian flavour reminiscent of June’s Ultimate Fighting Championship bouts on the White House South Lawn. The UFC impresario Dana White, testosterone avenger Pete Hegseth and “human printer” Natalie Harp, who would wait for Trump as ardently as Penelope did for Odysseus, were among the guests. Democratic socialists were less in evidence. IndyCar is neither Woke 1 nor Woke 2. Wearing a dark blue suit, white shirt and red tie, Trump gave fist pumps and shook hands with the IndyCar drivers. They posed for photographers, Trump giving his signature thumbs-up, as the sun gleamed off the US Capitol dome beyond. The president gave a perfunctory TV interview to the Fox network. Why was it important for him to bring IndyCars to the streets of DC? The reply was very Trumpian: “Well, Roger [Penske, a billionaire who owns the IndyCar series] told me they’ve been trying to do it for 20 years, and he’d come down; I think he said he was down 211 times to try and get it done. And when he came to see Trump, it got done in about 15 minutes, and it’s turned out to be much bigger than we ever even thought possible.” Translation: every previous administration and mayor thought this plan was madness, and told Penske where to go. Note also the characteristic reference to “Trump” in the third person, and the boast that only he could fix it, and in 15 minutes. (If only ending the Ukraine war were so easy.) A ceremonial trundle True to form, the president also bragged about the crowd size and, as he has done since UFC night, insisted that he knows better than the meteorologists. “You know, I was hearing about rain all week long. ‘It’s gonna rain, it’s gonna rain.’ I said: ‘No, it’s not.’ And this is as nice today as I’ve seen in Washington in a long time.” Trump climbed into his armoured limousine, the Beast, mounted with flags and flashing blue and red lights, and trundled a ceremonial lap of the track. Was that Harp sprinting after him? Or hiding in the trunk? No, but we did get the Qatari-gifted plane that Trump has used as Air Force One flying overhead, escorted by four fighter jets. Then Christopher Macchio, one of Trump’s favourite singers, performed The Star-Spangled Banner as Trump saluted and Melania, wearing a white blouse, stood with hand on heart in the presidential box, a temporary white, air-conditioned structure with a clear front. A trained bald eagle was released near the start line, swooping and flying overhead before returning to its handler. There were flyovers of military aircraft including a B-2 stealth bomber. Officials paused air traffic at Washington’s Ronald Reagan National airport for three hours to accommodate them. It fell to another stalwart ally, interior secretary Doug Burgum, sporting sunglasses, to bellow: “Gentlemen, start your engines!” The race began, with drivers completing 147 laps covering roughly 250 miles (400km), and produced an American winner in Kyle Kirkwood. It was the latest chapter of a sporting summer in which Trump inserted himself into the UFC fights, the football World Cup final and the Patriot Games, a cross between a game show and athletics meet for high schoolers. Never slow to demonstrate his fealty to Trump, Mike Johnson, the Republican speaker of the House of Representatives, told Fox News that he wants to bring the IndyCar Grand Prix back next year and make it an annual event. By then, one hopes, Trump will have figured out how to hold and wave a green flag. Or as they say in Iran, a white flag.

title: Ex-mayor Dan Sullivan supports incumbent Dan Sullivan’s Senate bid against third Dan Sullivan
author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
summary: Endorsement of Republican incumbent over challenger with same name adds twist to unusual campaign in Alaska
body_text: Dan Sullivan supports Dan Sullivan against Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s US Senate election, says a former Alaskan mayor who recently backed the race’s Republican incumbent over a challenger sharing their name. That development provided another of multiple absurd elements to Dan S Sullivan’s campaign for a third term in the US Senate, which – beside Mary Peltola, a former Alaska Democratic congresswoman – has drawn opposition from Dan J Sullivan. Dan J Sullivan emerged from an 18 August primary to join a four-candidate field rounded out by Dan S Sullivan, Peltola and one other contender. His presence in the field for the general election during the 3 November midterms has prompted accusations that he is a Democratic plant aiming to draw enough votes away from Dan J Sullivan – whose name was positioned consecutively to him on the primary ballot – so that Peltola can win. Donald Trump’s Republican party is projected to lose congressional seats during the midterms, and the president wrote on social media on the day of the primary, “ALASKA: Be careful. VOTE FOR THE REAL DAN SULLIVAN TODAY. “The Dumocrats know how good he is and have put up an imposter of the same name.” Trump, though, was not the only Republican politico to come out swinging for Dan S Sullivan’s re-election bid on the day of the primary, in which Peltola finished first. Another who came out in favor of the incumbent was Dan A Sullivan, the mayor of Anchorage, Alaska, for six years beginning in 2009. “As the OG Dan Sullivan, I urge Alaskans to vote for [Senator] Daniel S Sullivan,” he also wrote. “He’s been great for Alaska.” Dan A Sullivan’s statement of support for Dan S Sullivan, the senator, at the expense of Dan J Sullivan invoked a colloquial term meaning original. It was unclear if he staked the claim of being the original because, at 75, he was older than Dan S Sullivan, 61, and Dan J Sullivan, 70, a retired schoolteacher and US Forest Service employee with no prior political experience. He also entered his first elected office before Dan S Sullivan – on Anchorage’s governing assembly, where he served from 1999 to 2008. The Republican party unsuccessfully went to court to try to prevent Dan J Sullivan from running in the primary, maintaining that his campaign was a Democratic-engineered sham trying to confuse voters into selecting him rather than Alaska’s junior US senator since 2015. Dan J Sullivan – who appeared on the primary ballot with no party affiliation – has denied running at the behest of the Democratic party, which has not held a Senate seat in Alaska since 2008. “This is my choice,” he said to the Associated Press in June. Adding that he was displeased with the state of affairs in the US, he told the outlet: “I have every right to run.”

title: From Arizona to Wisconsin, election deniers are vying for office nationwide
author: Rachel Leingang
summary: Republicans who deny Joe Biden won the 2020 election are running for governor and secretary of state across the US
body_text: Election deniers are back on the ballot. In most swing states, at least one major Republican candidate has questioned or outright denied the results of the 2020 US presidential election, which Donald Trump lost to Joe Biden. While voters in swing states have previously largely rejected candidates who denied election results, Republicans running for statewide offices across much of the country are trying again. In Arizona, gubernatorial candidate and US representative Andy Biggs voted against certifying his own state’s election results. In Wisconsin, Republican gubernatorial hopeful Tom Tiffany similarly voted against certifying the 2020 results as a US representative for his state. Candidates for governor in Pennsylvania and Michigan have cast doubt on the validity of the 2020 results. And some swing state Republican candidates for secretary of state have questioned or denied election results. Governors sign off on state election results, issuing certificates to the presidential electors of whichever candidate wins. They can call for investigations or special sessions, and use their bully pulpit to cast doubt on election results. Secretaries of state are meanwhile the chief election officials in most US states, overseeing voting systems and advising the local jurisdictions that run elections. They usually play a role in certifying election results, too. In 2020, Trump pressured governors and secretaries of state, alongside a host of state and local officials in several swing states, to withhold their signatures in a broad campaign to overturn his loss. Swing state governors and secretaries of state refused to stall or impede their states’ results. But if election deniers or skeptics are elected to these key statewide roles, they would be in office in 2028, raising apprehension that they may refuse to sign off on results, or succumb to pressure from Trump and his allies, should Republicans lose. None of the candidates mentioned below responded to inquiries from the Guardian about who they currently believe won the 2020 election, or whether they would certify the 2028 results. Arizona Governor candidate: Andy Biggs Biggs, a former state lawmaker elected to the US Congress in 2016, still has not straightforwardly acknowledged Biden’s 2020 victory. That year, he pressured Arizona Republicans, including the speaker of the statehouse, not to certify the valid election results. He has repeatedly claimed, without evidence, that there is widespread voter fraud and cast doubt on voting machines. On 6 January 2021, Biggs voted against accepting the electoral votes in his home state of Arizona, and in Pennsylvania. In prepared remarks, he called for an audit of the results in Arizona. The eventual audit by the Arizona senate affirmed Biden’s win. The Arizona senate president who launched the audit, Warren Petersen, is the Republican nominee for attorney general this year. “The debate as to the legitimacy of the 2020 presidential election has been suppressed by the left and its propogandists [sic] in the media….until today,” Biggs said in his prepared remarks. He reportedly sought a presidential pardon for his role in seeking to overturn the election results. He faces incumbent Democratic governor Katie Hobbs in November. Secretary of state candidate: Alex Kolodin Kolodin, a state representative and attorney, served as legal counsel on lawsuits seeking to overturn the 2020 results in Arizona. He has also represented some of the fake electors in the state, who were charged for their roles by attorney general Kris Mayes, though the case was dismissed earlier this year. Kolodin was disciplined by the state bar of Arizona, including a period of probation and required ethics courses. Kolodin dismissed the complaints as made by “radical left-wing activists”. Kolodin faces Democratic incumbent Adrian Fontes in November. Georgia Governor candidate: Rick Jackson Jackson, a rich healthcare executive, attacked Georgia’s current Republican secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, calling him a “Judas” in his campaign ads. Raffensperger refused to give in to pressure from Trump to question and overturn the state’s results. Raffensperger lost in the primary, where Jackson and Burt Jones, who was one of Georgia’s fake electors, made it to a runoff. Jackson won the runoff. Per Politico, Jackson has said: “That was totally ridiculous what happened in 2020 and our people really let us down.” Jackson’s campaign told CNN that Jackson “acknowledges both Biden’s win and that there were issues in the 2020 election that needed to be resolved in order to ensure Georgians have faith in our electoral system”. He faces Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, in November. Michigan Governor candidate: John James James, who has served in the US House of Representatives since 2023, initially refused to concede his own 2020 loss for a US Senate seat, and cast doubt on the results of the race. While running for governor this year, James has said the 2020 election was “rigged” and claimed Trump won Michigan three times (he lost it in 2020). In 2022, though, James told PBS News Hour that Biden had been duly elected as president. He faces the Democratic secretary of state, Jocelyn Benson, in the November general election. James has claimed without evidence that Benson “rigged and manipulated the election process to defeat me and President Trump” in 2020. Nevada Secretary of state candidate: Jim Marchant Marchant, a far-right state lawmaker and prominent election denier, previously sought the secretary of state’s office in 2022, losing to Democrat Cisco Aguilar, whom he will face again this November. That year, he was part of a coalition of Republican secretary of state candidates in swing states who supported Trump’s lie that the 2020 election had been stolen. Marchant also lost a 2020 bid for a US House seat, then sued over his loss and tried, unsuccessfully, to redo the election. He supported the fake elector scheme in 2020 and told the Guardian in 2022 that it was “very possible” he would be prepared to do the same in 2024, if he won his race for secretary of state. He believes a host of conspiracy theories central to the election denial movement, including that voting machines are manipulated and that judges were “bought off” when they sided against lawsuits seeking to overturn election results, he told the Guardian in 2022. Pennsylvania Governor candidate: Stacy Garrity Garrity, the state’s treasurer, spoke at a Pennsylvania rally on 5 January 2021 that called for decertifying the 2020 presidential election results, though her 2024 re-election campaign claimed she spoke specifically about a state senate race at that time. She also appeared with Trump and Mehmet Oz at a rally in 2022 and said of Trump’s 2020 race: “We know that he won.” Garrity herself was on the ballot in 2020, and won her bid for state treasurer. She told a local news outlet earlier this year that there were “irregularities” in the 2020 election, though she said she couldn’t say “to what extent”. “But the president seems, you know, he’s very convinced that there was a lot there. And it seems like more information comes out all the time. But I’d rather look forward,” she said. Garrity told CNN this month: “As I have said repeatedly since the 2020 election, I am painfully aware that Joe Biden was elected president.” She is running against Democratic incumbent governor Josh Shapiro in November. Wisconsin Governor candidate: Tom Tiffany Tiffany, a US representative first elected to Congress in 2020, voted against accepting the votes from Arizona and Pennsylvania. He has said he would have objected to Wisconsin’s results as well if given the chance to vote directly on them. He has said, without evidence, that “illegal votes” were cast and counted that year. As recently as May 2026, Tiffany would not say whether Biden had won the 2020 election in Wisconsin fairly, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. He also supported the FBI’s questioning of election workers in the state earlier this year, the paper reported. “The problem with the 2020 election was the improprieties that happened,” Tiffany said in May 2026, the Journal Sentinel reported. While his campaign did not respond to the Guardian, CNN reported this month that Tiffany said Biden won in 2020, and committed to certifying the vote in 2028. He faces Milwaukee county executive David Crowley in November.
