title: Trump’s border wall construction threatens rock art as old as the pyramids: ‘The ancestors are still here’
author: Roque Planas in Comstock, Texas
summary: The president’s border wall plan could damage or destroy ‘the oldest-known books in North America’
body_text: On an overcast summer morning, Carolyn Boyd, an archeologist at Texas State University, stood at the foot of a cave in west Texas, looking up toward a series of towering murals painted on a rock wall. Three massive human-like figures soared toward an overhang that had sheltered the painting from the elements since they were drawn here perhaps 4,000 years ago. An artist herself, Boyd knows how hard it would have been to paint these long, crisp lines. Before starting, the bands of Indigenous hunter-gatherers who lived in this west Texas valley, where the Pecos River empties into the Rio Grande, would have spent weeks pulverizing gypsum, hematite, limonite and manganese to make paint. They would have gathered massive quantities of sotol stalks to fold its fibers into scaffolding. The painting itself would have required teamwork and precision, with people at the bottom guiding artists on the wall as they painted figures stretching up to 30ft tall. “As a muralist, I can tell you that just maintaining a straight line on an even surface is a challenge,” said Boyd. She’s spent 35 years analyzing these sites, some of which are older than the pyramids, and she describes them as a sprawling and still largely unreadable library storing some of humanity’s earliest stories. “Look how perfect this line goes down and tapers,” she said, dragging a green laser pointer along its length. “It’s just stunning. I’ve brought fine artists, painters out here and they scratch their heads.” The Trump administration is now dealing these rare treasures a potentially fatal blow. Last year, Republicans in Congress heaped a whopping $46.5bn for border wall expansion into Trump’s “big, beautiful” spending bill. The longest remaining unwalled stretch of the US-Mexico border lies in west Texas, a remote region that includes some of the state’s most-visited public lands, including the Big Bend national park. Since February, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has indicated it will use that massive war chest here to expand what it calls its “smart wall” – a mix of steel bollard fencing, vehicle barriers and hi-tech surveillance. The area has remained unwalled until now, partly because geography already impedes most illegal crossings. Large ranches dominate the Mexican side, which contains no major cities and only few large towns to attract would-be migrants. Steep cliffs abound. But with such vast sums on the table, CBP is pushing forward at breakneck pace with its plans – riding roughshod over virtually universal opposition from locals, business leaders and a growing number of political leaders from both parties. Most of that tension has focused on the controversy over CBP’s plans to mar the wilderness of the Big Bend national park, which the agency halted last week after activists publicized videos of bulldozers plowing up ground at the park’s famed Santa Elena Canyon. The impending construction also threatens to mar or destroy an untold number of these millennia-old rock art murals that stand in the coming wall’s path. The slated construction includes 165 miles (266km) of four-to-six-foot-tall vehicle barriers and patrol roads starting a few miles outside the Big Bend national park and ending at Lake Amistad. It runs straight through the Seminole Canyon state park, which is home to 27 murals, including the Fate Bell Shelter where Boyd stood. Boyd has emerged as perhaps the most prominent voice defending the region’s ancient heritage. One day, she hopes, archeologists teaming up with Indigenous communities who have preserved stories by word of mouth through the millennia will learn to decipher the murals the way we can now read the hieroglyphics of ancient Egypt or Mayan pictographs. “These are world-class masterworks,” Boyd said. “These are sacred sites. They’re the oldest-known books in North America. We need to protect them.” Heritage threatened by border wall expansion Boyd, 68, wore tiger-print framed glasses and a red bandana around her neck, and her tightly braided silver hair was covered with a green felt hat to shield her fair skin from the desert sun. She fell fast in love with rock art murals after first encountering them on a trip to the Lower Pecos region in 1989. Back then, she says, most scholars viewed the murals as little more than ancient graffiti – images that early humans haphazardly scrawled on the wall. That seemed implausible to Boyd. Not only did the murals require great skill and teamwork to paint, they also demanded precious materials. Muralists used marrow from deer bones to make what amounted to an ancient variety of oil paint. In a region with few reliable sources of fat, hunter-gatherers depended heavily on marrow for calories. “It’s not just a bunch of painted figures on the wall,” Boyd said. “They sacrificed food off their plates.” Her husband, a 74-year-old archeobotanist named Phil Dering, shares her enthusiasm. They went on their first date at the Seminole Canyon state park back in 1992. They married a few months later. After completing her dissertation, the couple settled in the town of Comstock in 2003, so Boyd could study the murals full-time. They founded a non-profit, the Shumla Archaeological Research and Education Center, that has since educated about 13,000 students on the region’s rock art heritage and documented more than 250 rock art sites. Boyd has befriended local landowners, who have facilitated access to researchers, students and pilgrims to murals found on their properties. She has forged relationships with Indigenous communities on both sides of the border to share knowledge about the images and their meanings. Boyd’s perpetual state of curiosity has collided head-on with the Trump administration’s single-minded fixation on wall-building. The smart wall’s proposed path runs dangerously close to known murals and may cut through yet-to-be-discovered ones. Surveying for rock art is an arduous task, often requiring the skills of a rock climber and the knowledge of a graduate-level anthropologist. Covering a few miles in rough country takes weeks. The expanded wall doesn’t have to touch the murals to damage them. A close look at Fate Bell Shelter reveals a string of superficial pockmarks ranging in size from that of a golf ball to a pancake. Limestone, which served as the early muralists’ canvas, is a porous rock that allows water to seep in. Daily and seasonal temperature swings cause changes in limestone’s internal pressure, leading bits and pieces of the rock face to flake off over time – a natural process called “spalling”. But the vibrations from construction, which will probably include dynamite blasting and excavation with heavy machinery, threaten to supercharge this spalling, chipping away chunks of painted limestone up to several hundred yards away. In Boyd’s nightmare scenario, entire panels could come crashing down – including from previously undocumented murals. Even if the rock art makes it through the process relatively unscathed, the new border barrier would leave at least 80 known murals on the southern side of the new fence, raising questions about access for the researchers who study them and Indigenous people who visit them as sacred ancestral sites. “Many of those messages will be destroyed or damaged to the point where we cannot decipher them, work with them, or go to them for help or inspiration,” said Maria Rocha, 78, a member of the Miakan-Garza tribe of the Coahuiltecan people who has visited Lower Pecos rock art sites for spiritual reasons. “But deeper than that, we have a connection to those paintings for our creation stories.” Attempts to buy out landowners One of the murals that Boyd worries about the most is called Painted Shelter, which lies on a private sheep ranch owned for more than a century by the Zuberbueler family. Painted in a series of installments by different peoples over a period spanning about five millennia, it contains several different styles that flourished in this area over the years. It’s also something of a historical record, containing images of people wielding the atlatl spear-hurling device, a traditionally shaped bow and a more modern, recurve-style bow. The current smart wall map shows the vehicle barrier running very close to Painted Shelter, despite the fact that it is a Texas-designated historic landmark. Fisher Sand and Gravel Co received a $2.7bn contract to build the barrier – a cost of about $16.5m a mile. To expedite construction, the Department of Homeland Security has waived dozens of federal laws that would normally require surveys, environmental reviews and damage mitigation plans to protect historical treasures. Like other local landowners, Patrick Zuberbueler began receiving letters in February offering $5,000 to cede portions of the family’s ranch land for construction, without going through the eminent domain process. So far, the family has refused. Still, Fisher Sand and Gravel Co has pushed forward with its construction plans, asking the family for access to millions of gallons of water for its proposed operations. With the ranch’s undulating terrain and rocky ground, Zuberbueler expects the company to blast extensively. “It’s almost like [they’re saying,] ‘We don’t even really care what you think,’” Zuberbueler said. Painted Shelter already suffers from significant spalling, with fallen shards as large as basketballs marring what is otherwise a remarkably well-preserved painting, naturally shielded by the overhanging cliff. “Vibrations from blasting and heavy equipment will be devastating to the site,” Boyd said. “There’s no question.” Even more frustrating to Boyd is the fact there’s little logical reason to guard this area from vehicle crossings. There are no paved roads along the Zuberbueler ranch, just shrubby landscape strewn with boulders. Even if the land were easily navigable on four wheels, getting from the Mexican side into the United States requires plunging over oak- and laurel-studded cliffs at least 30ft high, fording the Rio Grande and then climbing back over equally steep precipices on the other side. Anyone who managed to accomplish that feat and make it to a paved road would then have to evade border patrol agents cruising the roads and pass undetected through one of the many checkpoints that dot the highways within 100 miles (160km) of the southern border. CBP did not answer specific questions about the vehicle barrier’s potential impact on ancient rock art, nor the need for a locally opposed vehicle barrier in an area rarely crossed by car. But the agency said that it would conduct its own reviews. “Even with the use of a waiver, CBP remains committed to environmental and cultural stewardship,” an agency spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement. “Prior to border barrier construction activities, CBP conducts environmental and cultural reviews, seeks public input, and collaborates with state and federal agencies to minimize impacts and balance operational needs with responsible land stewardship.” Fisher Sand and Gravel Co did not respond to a request for comment. Raymond Skiles, a former wildlife biologist for the Big Bend national park, shares Boyd and Zuberbueler’s sense of frustration. He inherited a property that his grandparents bought for the scenic views overlooking the canyons and the Rio Grande. But Skiles also started getting letters from CBP offering money to avoid an eminent domain fight back in February, followed by inquiries from Fisher Sand and Gravel Co. “My first response was ‘Can’t you find a job doing something that’s not hurting people and wrecking places?’” The part of Skiles’s property outside the town of Langtry that CBP wants to seal off with a vehicle barrier is even more treacherous than the Zuberbueler ranch. Cliffs soar 130ft over a dry canyon that leads into the Rio Grande. Two separate murals lie about midway up the canyon walls. Skiles expects heavy blasting both to level terrain and break through rock, raising fears of damage to the rock art. “You can’t do anything without blasting,” Skiles said. “My grandpa put in a little bit of fencing and a jeep road, and it was all dynamite.” In all the time that Skiles, 71, has spent on the property, he has personally seen a total of eight people crossing illegally, all on foot. Six of them wanted to be found, he said. “It ain’t an issue,” Skiles said. Imperiled messages from the past Damage to the murals wouldn’t be the only tragedy, said Boyd. It’s also the loss of a long-term, deeply human goal: to understand the artists’ stories and messages from the past. Even a very clear mural can keep a scholar occupied for decades. One of the best-preserved examples is White Shaman, a roughly 100ft panel tucked into a cave perched above the Pecos River. The muralists used four colors derived from pulverized rocks – black, red, yellow and white. One of the mural’s central images is a headless white figure with outstretched arms that Boyd says represents the Moon Goddess, a central deity for the Nahua and Wixárika peoples. The painting faces west. As the sun sets on the lunar solstice, it moves up the wall, illuminating the painting and stops right at the Moon Goddess’s neck, visually “decapitating” her. “Every time I look at it, I see more,” Boyd said. “This is a panel that just keeps on giving.” On a recent morning, she hiked with trekking poles up a steep set of stairs toward the panel. At the entrance, which was surrounded by ocotillos flowering from the recent rains, she announced the arrival of our group – herself; her husband, Phil; the site’s director, Aimée Spana; and this reporter. With a broad smile, she waited for a moment before proceeding. “The ancestors are still here,” Boyd said. “We need to respect them.” The story is co-published with Public Domain, an investigative newsroom co-founded by Roque Planas that covers public lands, wildlife and government

title: Why does the New York Times keep calling the left ‘divisive’?
author: Dana Frank
summary: The newspaper often uses the word to describe elections with progressive contenders, implying a previous whole destroyed by the left
body_text: “El-Sayed and Stevens Project Party Unity After Divisive Race,” announced the New York Times on 5 August, the day the progressive Abdul El-Sayed beat out his centrist Democratic rival, Haley Stevens, in the Michigan senatorial primary. “Divisive” is now the Times’s favorite attack word, deployed repeatedly to disparage and try to undermine the astonishing recent advances by progressive candidates. Four days after that first story, the Times again landed “divisive” under “Obama and El-Sayed Discuss Unity After Ugly Michigan Primary.” El-Sayed, it asserted, had “narrowly prevailed in a divisive primary after campaigning on a progressive and anti-establishment platform”. On 12 August, the Times reported that David Crowley, who narrowly beat out Democratic socialist Francesca Hong in the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, “promised to leave behind the divisive Democratic primary and focus on Mr. Tiffany”, his Republican opponent. Other stories slip it in more subtly. That same day, in a piece about representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez allegedly distancing herself from “Woke 1.0”, the Times cited Middlebury College professor Erik Bleich, who “pointed to the calls to defund the police as a divisive goal”. “Polarizing”, a close cousin to “divisive”, appears regularly, too. The Times especially likes to apply it to New York mayor Zohran Mamdani. A reporter insisted in October 2025, for example: “As Mamdani’s campaign upends New York politics, no single stance has polarized New Yorkers as passionately as his pro-Palestinian activism and caustic criticism of Israel.” Perhaps most outrageous was the Times’s choice of headline for a recent review of David Zirin’s new book about Howard Zinn: “America’s Most Divisive Historian Gets a New Biography.” How, exactly, was Zinn “divisive”? And who are those other historians who are also divisive, just not as bad? Neither Adam Hochschild, in his review, nor Zirin, in his biography, nor any discussion of I’ve ever seen in 40 years as a practicing US historian (and co-author, along with Robin DG Kelley, of a book with Zinn), talk about Zinn that way. The Times’s choice to cast Zinn as divisive out of the blue, on top of its repeated usage of the word since the midwest primaries, suggests there’s a conscious campaign underway to utilize the concept however it can. Overall, the Times’ repeated charge of “divisive”, along with “polarizing”, implies a previous and virtuous whole that is currently being destroyed by the left. It assumes voters agree that in the face of deep fear of Trump and his allies, we have to stick together, and that progressive candidates can’t beat Republicans in the midterms. But the Times’s mythical unified country never existed. The United States has always been riven by race, class, gender, religion, immigration status and much more. And vigorous debate has always been at the core of truly democratic politics. For the Times, “unity” is a stand-in for the powers-that-be in the Democratic party and “their preferred strategy of running moderate campaigns that won’t offend aging incumbents, never-Trump Republicans, and the multimillionaire-and-up donor class,” as the editors of Hammer & Hope Magazine recently put it. The mealy-mouthed, centrist candidates the party’s leadership has chosen in the name of unity have repeatedly alienated or failed to energize voters, especially African Americans. The Times does on occasion employ “divisive” to describe far-right Republicans, such as with Florida governor Ron DeSantis. But that, in turn, colors its usage against the left, which, implicitly, is behaving fanatically and dangerously, too. As the paper claimed on 16 August, after the midwest primaries, “Democrats Face a Potential Tea Party Moment.” Note, moreover, the recent actions by “moderate” Democrats the New York Times has apparently not deemed divisive: James Carville, the political consultant, who called Democratic socialists “a pack of fools” on Fox News, or Abigail Spanberger, the governor of Virginia, who in May vetoed a bill granting collective bargaining rights to public workers, betraying the union base that had elected her. In Michigan, it’s Islamophobia that’s in fact “divisive”, not the Muslim candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who, along with many of the other candidates the Times calls divisive, is not coincidentally a person of color. By charging progressives – and especially democratic socialists – with divisiveness, the New York Times is doing everything it can to shore up a fantasized unity in which corporate powers, Wall Street, and billionaires control the Democratic party, and the rest of us fall into line to vote however they like. But it’s the Times that’s trying to divide us, as we form ever broader, ever more dynamic and ever more effective coalitions to challenge the masters it serves. Dana Frank is professor of history emerita at the University of California, Santa Cruz. Her newest book, Balancing Acts: How a Japanese Immigrant Built a Life in the Face of Racial Danger – Until Federal Agents Arrived, will be out from Beacon Press in April 2027 • This article was amended on 24 August 2026. An earlier version incorrectly referred to Abdul El-Sayed as a democratic socialist.

title: US supreme court rules Trump can proceed with crackdown on mail-in voting
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: Justices’ ruling comes after lower courts had blocked president’s election order ahead of November midterms
body_text: The US supreme court sided with Donald Trump on Monday in his effort to crack down on mail-in voting, though it remains unclear if his administration can take action ahead of the midterm elections in November. Justices on the court voted 6-3 along ideological lines to lift an injunction from June that a judge in Massachusetts placed on an executive order issued by the president. But a second injunction remains in place and the ruling leaves room for legal challenges. “The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful,” the majority wrote in an unsigned order. “On that score, time will tell.” The three liberal justices dissented. In a blistering dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the decision “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections”. Trump has repeatedly likened voting by mail to cheating, despite his own use of it and overwhelming evidence that the system is secure. In March he ordered the government to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters, requiring that mail-in ballots only be delivered to people on that list. He also directed the justice department to prioritise investigations and prosecutions of state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote in federal elections. Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia sued over Trump’s March order, saying the US constitution gives states and Congress the authority to set election rules, not the president. They argued that imposing sweeping changes so close to the election risked disenfranchising voters and disrupting preparations already under way. A judge in Massachusetts, Indira Talwani, sided with the plaintiff states – nearly half the country – and ruled that Trump lacked authority to dictate how states administer federal elections. She also questioned whether federal agencies could compile accurate citizenship lists. An appeals court upheld her decision. Talwani later issued a second injunction with nationwide effect. The justice department had argued that the states’ lawsuit was premature because the administration had not yet taken concrete actions that harmed them and they therefore lacked legal standing to sue. The administration said the Massachusetts injunction prevented it from finalising and implementing policies intended to promote “election integrity” before November. Republican-led states backed the administration before the supreme court, arguing that states would have an opportunity to provide input on the final lists of eligible voters. The supreme court’s conservative majority has now lifted the first injunction, allowing the administration to move forward while litigation continues. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic minority leader in the House of Representatives, said: “The sycophantic Supreme Court majority’s decision in the vote-by-mail case is sowing chaos in service to Donald Trump’s effort to undermine our free and fair elections. The Trump-aligned justices on the supreme court did not and cannot give the President the power to decide how states run elections or who gets to vote by mail.” Jeffries added: “The legal fight against Donald Trump’s unlawful executive order is not over, the order does not override the Constitution and the power to regulate elections remains with states and the Congress.” Letitia James, New York’s attorney general, called the court’s decision a “painful setback” but said her office was exploring all legal options. “It won’t be the final word,” she said. Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, said his state is also planning a legal challenge. “The Supreme Court just let the Trump administration move ahead (for now) with its plan to disenfranchise voters across the country,” Newsom said in a statement. “California will be suing AGAIN to block these Orwellian rules from being implemented.” Voting right activists condemned the ruling. Derrick Johnson, the president of the NAACP, said: “Let this ruling be a reminder that democracy is never, ever, guaranteed. We have to fight for it, we have to fight to keep it, and we have to protect the rights we do have within it. “Those in power know full well that they are unpopular and will lose in a free and fair election, and so they are trying to do everything they possibly can to make it difficult for you to vote. Trump’s order has nothing to do with election integrity. It has everything to do with maintaining power at all costs.” The wrangling over how US voters can cast their ballots comes less than 100 days until November’s midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in the US Senate and House of Representatives. Democratic voters are deemed more likely to cast their ballots by mail than Republicans: about one in four registered Democrats did so in 2024, according to the States United Democracy Center, alongside one in five registered Republicans. About 30% of all ballots were cast by mail in the 2024 presidential election, according to federal data. A 2025 Brookings Institution study found roughly four cases of fraud for every 10m mail ballots cast. Trump’s executive order forms part of a wider effort to reshape the electoral system. He has repeatedly made false claims of widespread fraud in American elections, including his defeat by Joe Biden in 2020, and has pressed the Republican-controlled Congress to pass the Save America Act, a contentious package of voting restrictions.

title: I once saw Enes Kanter speak truth to power. Now he only punches down
author: Bryan Armen Graham
summary: Nearly a decade after I watched him defy Erdoğan at great personal cost, Kanter is using his hard-won freedom to turn transgender people into a national punchline
body_text: Nine years ago, I watched Enes Kanter ask America to take him in. It was May 2017, inside the National Basketball Players Association’s offices in midtown Manhattan. Kanter had just returned from a frightening detention at Bucharest airport, where Romanian border police told him Turkey had canceled his passport. He’d just turned 25, an NBA center with a green card and no country he could safely call home. “I’m open for adoption,” he joked from the head of a table in a nondescript conference room, addressing a dozen reporters hastily summoned by his manager. Then he turned serious: “My next move is to just become an American citizen.” The previous 48 hours had unfolded like a John le Carré thriller. Kanter said his manager woke him at 2.30am in Jakarta where he’d been hosting a basketball clinic because Indonesian security forces were looking for him. He hurried to Singapore, then Frankfurt, only to be stopped in Romania. He feared being sent to Turkey, where he had grown up and whose national team he had represented. There, he said, no one might hear from him again. Department of Homeland Security officials and lawyers for the Oklahoma City Thunder and the players’ union helped get him back to the United States. Sitting in that room that Monday morning, I saw someone who had already paid a steep cost for the right to speak truth to power. Kanter called Recep Tayyip Erdoğan the “Hitler of our century”. He recounted daily death threats, a family placed in jeopardy by his opposition to Erdoğan and support for the president’s exiled rival, Fethullah Gülen, and parents he had stopped calling because he feared the government was tapping their phones. He said his father, Mehmet, a university professor, had been spat on at a supermarket. “I try to be the voice of those innocent people,” he told us. The reprisals only widened. Turkey issued warrants for Kanter and later sought an Interpol Red Notice and his extradition. He skipped NBA trips abroad, including a Knicks game in London, because he feared detention or assassination. His father was dismissed, detained and charged with membership in a terrorist organization before his eventual acquittal in 2020. In 2021, Kanter finally became an American citizen and legally added Freedom to his name. You didn’t have to squint hard to make out the symbolism. The dissident Turkey tried to render voiceless and stateless had found both an adopted home and a protected platform. On Sunday night, I found myself thinking about the young man from that news conference – and wondering what became of him. Back then, he used attention to protect vulnerable people. Now he uses vulnerable people to attract attention. Kanter was sitting courtside at the Chicago Sky’s game against the Indiana Fever in a shirt reading: “WOMAN noun. adult human female.” He had joined a rally outside the arena in support of Sophie Cunningham, the Fever guard who opposes transgender participation in women’s sports. In recent weeks, Kanter had also declared himself eligible for the 2027 WNBA draft, claiming to identify as a woman and posting workout videos about beginning his “transition”. (League sources have since said he is not eligible to play and dismissed his declaration as a publicity stunt the WNBA would not “give oxygen” to.) The crudity of the attempted reductio ad absurdum was matched only by the breathlessness of the response across the Maga right, where Kanter’s stunt was greeted as an intellectual masterstroke: BRILLIANT, GOT ‘EM, CHECKMATE. Fox News has not merely covered Kanter’s bit uncritically; it has plainly participated in the mockery. Take the premise of transgender inclusion, distort it into the spectacle of a former NBA player treating womanhood as a debating prop, and wait for the audience to laugh. Yet Kanter exposed no contradiction. The punchline was simply the existence of transgender people. No player assigned male at birth has ever competed in the WNBA. Whatever legitimate questions exist about eligibility rules, competitive balance and the place of biology in elite sport can be discussed without reducing them to a spectacle designed to humiliate those at the center of the debate. Kanter’s stunt depends on the idea that gender identity is inherently fraudulent and that trans women are simply opportunistic men waiting to invade women’s spaces. It has done nothing to clarify policy. It has merely turned a vulnerable minority into content – including many trans fans who have long regarded the 30-year-old league as one of the few places in professional sport where they belong. At a moment when ESPN’s WNBA coverage is averaging 1.4 million viewers, up 16% from the same point last season, Kanter’s stunt has hijacked a feelgood story about the league’s growth and made a phantom threat the focus instead. The invasion rhetoric carries a bitter irony. The WNBA is not being overrun by trans women but by straight men who cannot let women have a flourishing league of their own without mocking it, manufacturing controversy and making themselves the story. Some of loudest voices posing as defenders of female athletes openly ridicule and try to humiliate them for laughs, in some cases through sexualized stunts. There is something almost pitiable about men squandering their energy and influence on belittling women whose discipline, sacrifice and extraordinary achievement have carried them to the highest level of their profession. Misogyny has simply put on the costume of concern. In Kanter’s case, this was not simply a lone provocateur wandering into an arena. According to Talking Points Memo, the Trump-aligned America First Policy Institute (AFPI) promoted Kanter’s arrival, circulated footage of his ejection and began selling a $45 “Let Freedom Play” sweatshirt featuring him in a mock-up of the WNBA logo. An AFPI executive was seated a few rows behind him, although the organization did not answer questions about whether it bought his courtside seat. Kanter, who attended the 2024 State of the Union as House speaker Mike Johnson’s guest and has said he plans to run for Congress in 2028, has political ambitions of his own. Whether or not there is a formal arrangement, the transaction is visible enough: Kanter lends the campaign the credibility of an 11-year NBA veteran and supplies a spectacle in which transgender people are the bait, while an organization embedded in Trump’s political network converts those assets into attention, merchandise and political capital. If it keeps voters staring at a nonexistent threat to the WNBA instead of the breathtaking corruption engulfing the administration in the run-up to the November midterms, the stunt has done its real work. Late in the third quarter of Sunday’s contest, Natasha Cloud, one of the most uncompromising athlete-activists of her generation, finally took the rage bait. The Sky guard approached Kanter, yelling and pointing in his direction. Kanter stood, spread his arms and stepped on to the court before security intervened. As he was escorted away, he stopped near the basket to argue his case, then stretched out his shirt and tried to draw a response from the crowd. He had arrived ready to provoke and left performing martyrdom. Kanter did not suddenly discover the uses of spectacle on Sunday. In 2020, after marching with Black Lives Matter protesters in Boston, he told the Guardian that athletes should use their platforms “to spread good, and to spread the truth”. He had long understood publicity as a political tool, and with good reason: he believed international pressure helped secure his father’s acquittal. The difference is what the performance now serves. None of this diminishes the courage Kanter showed in opposing Erdoğan. The offer of US citizenship is not a contract for ideological obedience. Human rights are not a prize withdrawn when their beneficiary later behaves immorally, nor does surviving persecution bind anyone to a prescribed worldview. But suffering does not automatically make a person generous, either. And Kanter, more than most, should understand the mechanics of dehumanization: how a powerful movement marks a minority as dangerous, treats its identity as illegitimate and converts real human beings into totems of social decay. The scale of Erdoğan’s repression and an American culture-war stunt are not equivalent. The moral reflex behind them – identifying people with less power and making public sport of their vulnerability – should have been instantly recognizable to him. The least cynical reading, perhaps charitable to a fault, is that Kanter can recognize this kind of othering only when he is its target. US citizenship gave Kanter what he asked for in that Manhattan conference room: safety, a home and the freedom to speak without Erdoğan deciding the consequences. That freedom includes the right to make a cruel spectacle of himself, but it does not exempt the spectacle from judgment. “I try to be the voice of those innocent people,” Kanter said in 2017. I believed him then. On Sunday, he used that voice to make other innocent people feel smaller. What a waste.

title: Darline Graham and Ralph Norman head to South Carolina’s Senate runoff
author: George Chidi in Conway, South Carolina
summary: Republican nominee to face Democrat Annie Andrews in midterm after rushed campaigns for Lindsey Graham’s seat
body_text: Reese Boyd, the chair of the Horry county Republican party marveled on Monday afternoon at how little time Senator Darline Graham and Representative Ralph Norman have had to campaign for the Senate primary: “This is not the normal way of things.” “This is something that usually lasts at least, you know, the better part of a year,” he said. “People normally spend the better part of 18 months getting ready for it. Who knows? This may be the right way to do it? Who knows.” On Tuesday, Graham and Norman will conclude a 45-day campaign sprint that began with the unexpected death of Lindsey Graham in July. Henry McMaster, the state’s Republican governor, appointed Graham’s sister, Darline, to serve out the remainder of his term. Because Lindsey Graham had won the Republican primary, state law required a fresh election to replace him on the ballot in November. The winner will face Annie Andrews, a pediatrician and the Democratic candidate, in a state where Democrats haven’t won statewide in two decades. Many observers had expected Darline Graham to serve in a caretaker role while South Carolina’s political leadership staged a political knife fight for a rare shot at a US Senate seat. Instead, the political newcomer – a career civil servant who led the state’s commission for the blind – surprised the political establishment and announced her decision to stand for a full term – with the encouragement and backing of Donald Trump. Graham overcame concerns about her lack of legislative experience earlier this month, claiming the top spot to advance to the 25 August runoff, from a sprawling, 10-candidate Republican field. “I have said many times I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician,” Graham said recently, referring to a well-publicized gaffe in a debate last week with Norman, where she responded to a question about defense policy by saying that military stuff “is not my thing”. Norman has pounced on her comment, highlighting it as an example of her unreadiness for the role. “Imagine if I went to [head football coach] Dabo Swinney at Clemson and any of the coaches and said: ‘Look, I got a prospect I want you to look at, and I want them to,” Norman said to the Associated Press. “‘They can start. I want you to sign them up. They can start for the next six years.’ ‘What’s the qualifications?’ ‘They’re kin to Tom Brady.’ Tell me how that analogy doesn’t work here.” Lindsey Graham had built a reputation as a foreign policy hawk, who championed the US war against Iran and rallied support for Ukraine in its defense against the Russian invasion. Darline Graham has framed her candidacy as a way to “carry my brother Lindsey’s legacy”. Since being sworn in as his successor last month, she has voted along party lines, but little else is known about her politics. Norman, who has been called the most conservative member of the US House, is running billboard advertisements on South Carolina highways that say “Voting for Ralph Norman is MAGA” as an answer to Trump’s endorsement of Graham. Trump framed his support for Darline Graham as the repayment of a favor to his late friend, Lindsey Graham. “I asked her to do this,” Trump said on Friday in a campaign stop in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. “I said, ‘Darline, you gotta do it.’ ‘Cause everyone loves her, everyone respects her. I’ve known her, through Lindsey … I think Lindsey respected Darline more than any other person he knows, including me. That does not make me happy. I’m not happy about that.” But by elevating a relative political unknown whose primary appeal to voters is her promise to follow the president’s lead, Trump has offered one more high-profile test of his influence over Republican voters before the midterm elections in 10 weeks, a point he made explicit at the rally on Friday. “The problem that we have is, they say that Trump does great when he’s on the ballot, but when he’s not on the ballot, his people don’t come and they don’t vote for senators, congressmen and other Republicans,” the president said. “And that these people, they’re running, they’re great. But Trump isn’t actually on the ballot. So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote.”

title: Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932. Will that change in November?
author: Chris Stein
summary: Adam Hamilton, a liberal megachurch pastor, is challenging incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall in this year’s midterm election
body_text: In one of the first ads of his campaign to represent Kansas in the US Senate, the Democrat Adam Hamilton stands grilling steaks at a barbecue and attacks his opponent, Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican, for supporting “tariffs and war”. If history is any guide, it is Hamilton who is set to get cooked. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and more than half a century has passed since one of their nominees even came close. But he and his supporters believe circumstances have conspired to end this streak – and potentially deliver Democrats control of the Senate. “When it comes to tariffs, healthcare, immigration, when it comes to the war in Iran, these are all things that are having a negative impact on people in Kansas,” Hamilton, 62, said in an interview. “That makes this a particularly vulnerable time for Roger Marshall. Then, I think I’m a particularly strong candidate. I wouldn’t have got in the race if I didn’t.” The founder of the largest Methodist congregation in the US, Hamilton won 35% of the vote in the 11-candidate Democratic primary earlier this month. His campaign recently announced he had broken a quarterly fundraising record in the state, and two major election forecasters say the Senate race has grown more competitive since Hamilton won his party’s primary, though Marshall is still favored to win. For national Democratic leaders, the possibility of a close Senate race in Kansas is enticing. Their path to retaking Congress’s upper chamber involves winning at least three seats in states that Donald Trump carried two years ago, and they’ve named Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Iowa as among their best bets to do so. The US president’s slumping approval ratings and the Iran war’s impact on prices for gasoline and other staples are seen as boosting Democrats’ chances in those states, but Kansas is a bit redder. Trump carried it two years ago by a 16 percentage point margin. This week, Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer told Punchbowl News that if the November elections wind up producing a “blue wave” of Democratic victories, Hamilton may well win. Asked what he thought of Schumer’s prediction, Hamilton said: “I don’t agree with that. I think there will be a blue wave, but I’m telling you, here in Kansas, we have a real chance to win. I don’t care what else happens across the country.” No Kansas Democrat has won a full term in the US Senate since attorney George McGill in 1932, the longest streak of any state. In 1974, Senator Bob Dole, who would go on to become the chamber’s Republican leader and run unsuccessfully against President Bill Clinton in 1996, nearly lost his bid for a second term, but Republicans have wiped out their opponents ever since. Democrats and their causes have had better luck at the state level. The governor’s mansion has seesawed between the two parties since the late 1950s, and the race this year to replace outgoing Democratic governor Laura Kelly is viewed as a toss-up. After the supreme court overturned Roe v Wade, Kansans have on two occasions rejected Republican-backed attempts to curb abortion access in the state. “Kansas voters, the majority anyway, there’s something about the Senate where, especially those moderate Republicans, still won’t pull the trigger in terms of enough of them voting for a Democrat, where they will for governor,” said Bob Beatty, a longtime state politics watcher who chairs the political science department at Washburn University in Topeka. But Hamilton’s experience in leading a church gives him a unique skill set that Beatty predicts will make for “a very competitive race” against Marshall. “What Hamilton has going for him is the communication side. He’s been giving sermons, AKA speeches, to crowds of thousands for years,” he said. Marshall is an OB/GYN who represented western Kansas in the US House of Representatives, then won election to the Senate in 2020 and embraced Trump’s debunked claims of fraud in that year’s presidential vote. He has been an ally of Trump in Congress, and last year left a town hall early after attendees pressed him about the Trump administration’s funding cuts and layoffs of federal employees. A spokesperson for the senator did not respond to a request for comment. Hamilton said he decided to jump into the Senate race ahead of Easter, as he prepared to preach the sermon on the mount at his Church of the Resurrection outside Kansas City, which boasts around 24,000 congregants. He mulled running as an independent, but ultimately filed as a Democrat, saying he was concerned that he’d split the vote if he wasn’t in a party and agreed with its views on “healthcare, education [and] social safety nets”. “Those are things that matter a lot to me, and my faith leads in that direction,” he said. A self-described “moderate or independent-minded Democrat”, his campaign recently released an ad where Hamilton likens Kansas’s position in the middle of the country to his own approach to the politics that would await him in Washington DC. Hamilton has criticized Marshall for being “a spokesperson for Washington and Donald Trump instead of representing the people of Kansas”, and accused the senator of spending most of his time in Florida. Marshall has acknowledged owning a property in that state, but recently told reporters it was destroyed by a hurricane. Earlier this month, the Topeka Capital-Journal reported he’d put the Sarasota property on the market for $1.45m. The senator recently called his opponent a “megachurch pastor that’s too woke for Kansas”, the Capital-Journal reported. Main Street Fund, a Massachusetts-based Super Pac that lists its treasurer a consultant who has worked for Republican campaigns, spent more than $600,000 this month to air ads in Kansas, making a similar accusation against Hamilton that the Kansas City Star found relied on snippets from his sermons that were taken out of context. Like so much in his career, Hamilton’s chances may come down to faith. Jim Slattery, a Democratic former congressman from the state who supports Hamilton, described him as “a known quantity in the Methodist world in Kansas” and among Christians in the Kansas City area who may win if he gains the support of right-leaning Catholic voters opposed to the war with Iran. “The reason Hamilton is a compelling candidate is because he can, and he has the ability to, dramatically expand the audience for a Democrat candidate in Kansas,” Slattery said. “It’s the bottom line.” • This article was amended on 26 August 2026. A previous version described Adam Hamilton as the founder of the largest Methodist denomination in the US. He is the founder of the largest United Methodist congregation in the US.

title: US building twice as much gas-fired capacity as China in AI boom, analysis finds
author: Oliver Milman
summary: There has been a 76% increase in under-construction gas-fired projects amid ‘frenzy’ to build more datacenters
body_text: The US has surged ahead of China in the building of new gas-fired power generation, largely to feed a boom in artificial intelligence (AI) that is adding vast amounts of planet-heating emissions, a new analysis has found. For decades, China’s rapid economic growth has seen it outpace the US in the addition of new gas power generation but a recent “frenzy” in datacenter construction for AI has reversed this, said Global Energy Monitor (Gem) in its new report. The US is now building twice as much gas-fired capacity as China, and more than any other country in the world, after a stunning 76% increase in under-construction projects in the first half of this year. When adding announced and pre-construction projects, the US is building nearly three times as much as its fellow global economic powerhouse. Since January, gas power capacity in overall development in the US has ballooned by 50%, rising from 252GW to 378GW – a third of the global total. If all of these projects are ultimately built, the US will increase its gas fleet by about two-thirds at a capital cost of more than $647bn, Gem found. Around half of the new capacity is directly tied to a rash of upcoming datacenters that require a huge amount of electricity to handle the increased demand from AI. Using gas, a fossil fuel that is dangerously overheating our planet, rather than renewables to power this glut of new datacenters threatens to increase US power emissions by as much as 20%, according to one estimate. “Six months ago, China had more gas plants under construction but that has now flipped,” said Jenny Martos, a project manager at Global Energy Monitor. “There has been an enormous surge in datacenter proposals powered by gas in the past year and the climate implications of that is huge. Building all of this gas for AI locks in decades of pollution and it is also locking in dependence on a volatile fuel cost, which will get passed down to rate payers.” Donald Trump and others in his administration have repeatedly claimed that China, the world’s largest carbon polluter, is expanding its fossil fuel use so much that any emissions cuts by the US would be futile. The president has said of China that “their air is dirty, and it drifts over to us”. But the rush of new infrastructure for AI, along with the Trump administration’s demolition of environmental regulations and China’s rapid adoption of clean energy, is changing this equation. US spending on power plants fueled by coal and gas will outstrip that of China for the first time in decades, the International Energy Agency has forecast. The stampede by tech companies, such as Google, Open AI and Amazon, to build datacenters has contributed to a backlog of the most efficient gas turbines used for accompanying power plants. This has led several companies, including Elon Musk’s xAI, to quickly switch to smaller, less efficient turbines which are more heavily polluting. Concerns over the climate crisis, rising power bills, tax breaks for AI companies and water shortages – two-thirds of more than 800 planned datacenters are located in drought-stricken areas – has fueled mounting local opposition to data center construction. A recent poll by Heatmap found that three-quarters of Americans do not want to live next to a datacenter, a huge increase in opposition in the past year. Dozens of cities and counties have placed restrictions on new datacenters, with New York in July becoming the first state to enact a temporary ban on new hyper-scale datacenter permitting and construction. Despite this backlash, which could well hurt Republicans in the November midterm elections, the Trump administration has championed the building of new datacenters and eliminated environmental reviews in order to speed them up. Trump said this month that “data centers could be bigger than oil” and state governors should cut taxes to encourage them. “Frankly, communities that don’t take a datacenter, they’re making a mistake because there’s plenty of communities that want them,” Trump said in separate remarks to his former lawyer Michael Cohen last week. “Because it means jobs, and it means tremendous tax revenue coming into the towns and cities that take them.”

title: Meta goes on trial as Silicon Valley faces a growing backlash
author: Blake Montgomery
summary: Also: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressed his surprising sympathy over the construction of datacenters across the country
body_text: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you from a sunny park in New York City, which was supposed to endure rain all weekend but in fact delivered the best weather of the year. Why Meta’s big American backlash happened in court A blockbuster case against Meta went to trial a week ago in Oakland, California, just north of the US tech company’s headquarters in Silicon Valley. California and 28 other US states are suing the £1tn ($1.36tn) company for allegedly designing products that are addictive for children, and hiding that information from the public. The courtroom has already seen minor fireworks. On the witness stand, a whistleblower who worked extensively with Mark Zuckerberg accused the CEO of lying to the public about his commitment to child safety. The prosecutor who opened the case framed her argument around four words that start with the letter H: Meta “hooks” in users, “holds” them on its platforms for as long as possible, “harvests” their data and then “hides” the truth from the public. She contended that this business model “worked especially well for kids”. More pyrotechnics are expected. Zuckerberg himself is expected to face tough questions on the stand, as is the CEO of Instagram. Meta has denied all allegations. Liza Crenshaw, a spokesperson for the company, said: “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout.” The trial presents a major challenge for Meta, not in the least, because in the United States, it’s proceedings like these that regulate the tech industry. China regulates tech by crackdown; the UK and Europe regulate the industry with legislation – Brussels’ prescriptive stipulations have become global defaults. But in the US, it’s mostly the courts that set the boundaries. They move much faster and with the vindictive authority that Americans often crave in response to harms. The slow wheels of democratic debate and bill drafting feel ill-suited to respond to Zuckerberg’s mantra of “move fast and break things”. Read more: Hook, hold, harvest and hide: Meta’s alleged strategy laid out in first week of landmark trial Meanwhile, US regulators have famously, obviously, and avowedly had difficulty keeping pace with the innovations that arise from Silicon Valley. As one Republican representative told a quantum computing expert during a 2018 hearing on Capitol Hill: “I can understand about 50% of the things you say.” Members of Congress would undoubtedly say the same about AI today. “Courts have the ability to force these changes much quicker than legislation. Courts have this authority to say, ‘Look, you either comply with these orders … or you stop doing business in our state’. States have the ability to enforce that. I think for these companies this is a real point of reckoning,” said Laura Marquez-Garrett, an attorney with the Social Media Victims Law Center, which is representing individual plaintiffs suing Meta and other social media companies in thousands of cases in California. Her organization was deeply involved in Meta’s first loss of a social media addiction trial in March in Los Angeles. Will this trial bring Meta’s moment of accountability? Maybe. Other tech companies have faced significant government lawsuits in recent years, and come away only stronger. Google faced perhaps the most significant antitrust litigation of the 2020s, losing its antitrust case against the US Department of Justice last year. The penalty was not divesting the Chrome browser but a “slap on the wrist”, critics said. But in the 1990s, a coalition of US states sued tobacco companies and secured a settlement that banned a laundry list of marketing tactics, including advertising on transit or anywhere outdoors, paid product placement for cigarettes, cartoon mascots, branded apparel and nearly all free distribution of cigarettes. You’d never see a tobacco company’s name on a US sports stadium today. Like those tobacco suits, the states’ suit against Meta may force the company to operate its social networks in less harmful ways and to keep them out of the hands of children. The states are explicitly asking the court that Meta be forced to change the design of its products to make them safer for children. “These AGs have a real chance at fixing the product,” said Marquez-Garrett. Read more: ‘I always considered social media evil’: big tobacco whistleblower on tech’s addictive products OpenAI makes safety moves ‘We are hitting a different chapter’: OpenAI leader warns of threat of ‘persistent’ AI cyber-attacks OpenAI announces slowing pace of development after hack by rogue agent OpenAI launches ChatGPT for Teens with stronger safeguards The week the US data center backlash reached a fever pitch The political champions of datacenters in the US are turn coatings to detractors. It’s knives out in the US datacenter backlash. Democrats who fast-tracked the development of these gargantuan fortresses of AI are now implementing restrictions on them. Republicans who trumpeted calls for their unrestricted construction are hastily rolling out plans to constrain them. Josh Shapiro, Democratic governor of Pennsylvania, rolled out restrictions for large datacenters last week. Just two months ago, the Guardian reported on how he was fast-tracking them and cutting red tape. Greg Abbott, Republican governor of Texas, said this weekend that the datacenter industry has “dug its own grave”. In November 2025, he called his state the “epicenter of AI development”. A Republican running for a contested Senate seat in Texas, Ken Paxton, debuted an anti-AI action plan over the weekend, though it was marked as “made with AI” on X. Read more: How the fight over US datacenters is scrambling this state’s politics: ‘We don’t want it’ It’s no wonder: more than 70% of Americans oppose the construction of datacenters in their cities, per a poll released by Gallup three months ago. In just one year, the percentage of respondents saying they “strongly oppose” a datacenter being built near their homes more than doubled, according to polling by the climate news group Heatmap. Conservative media in the US has likewise taken notice. Fox News on Thursday: “Silicon Valley is losing the datacenter fight, risking a repeat of a classic failure.” The Daily Wire, often a bellwether for young Republicans’ opinions, on Monday: “Silicon Valley created the datacenter backlash.” Donald Trump, always liable to turn on an ally and usually an extremely adept reader of political winds, is standing by the tech industry’s multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout. “Communities that don’t take a datacenter, they’re making a mistake,” the US president said in an interview with his former fixer and once-mortal nemesis Michael Cohen last week. Silicon Valley is extremely worried. The tech industry is all-in on AI, so much so that the entire US economy is as well, and the success of AI is predicated on access to enough computing power. No datacenters, no chips, no computing power, no AI, no profit, no economy. What to do when faced with a spiraling political threat? Some companies are playing nice. They’re sponsoring community celebrations or pledging major community investments. They’re hosting listening sessions and making promises about how many jobs their projects will guarantee. Running de facto political campaigns for infrastructure projects is a big change for an industry accustomed to moving at the speed of bytes. Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, expressed some surprising empathy on a podcast last month. His company has a range of partnerships across the US for hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of datacenter construction. “I understand emotionally why people don’t want datacenters in their back yard in the same way that I don’t really want a nuclear power plant next to my house, even though I know it’s a super safe thing,” he said. Other Silicon Valley insiders are feeling hostile. Garry Tan, CEO of the influential startup incubator Y Combinator, wrote on X this weekend, “Reminder: the datacenter discourse is a documented psyop and they’re winning.” Alexis Ohanian, tech investor and co-founder of Reddit, wrote of the discourse: “It’s been brilliantly executed ngl [not gonna lie]. Facts are not gonna win this, esp at this point, it’s gotta be on emotional appeal.” In July, entrepreneur and Shark Tank host Kevin O’Leary accused opponents of his planned Utah datacenter of acting on behalf of the Chinese government. He later said he had “no evidence” for the claim and apologized for it, as did Fox News’ own hosts. The US’ adversaries have taken note of the heated debate and fanned the flames of fury. OpenAI disclosed in early July that Chinese and Russian propagandists, including state-owned media, had used its tools to create materials circulated on X, including a cartoon tycoon holding bags of cash and smoking a cigar, encouraging pushback against datacenters. title: First Thing: Supreme court threatens midterms mail-in voting as it backs Trump plan
author: Martin Belam
summary: US president has been obsessed with restricting the ability to vote by mail, despite using it himself
body_text: Good morning. The US supreme court has sided with Donald Trump in his effort to crack down on mail-in voting, though it is unclear whether or not his administration will be able to take action before the midterm elections in November. The court’s justices voted 6-3 along ideological lines to lift an injunction that a judge in Massachusetts had placed in June on an executive order issued by the president. But a second injunction remains in place, and the ruling leaves room for legal challenges. Trump has repeatedly likened voting by mail to cheating, despite his own use of it and overwhelming evidence that the system is secure. In March he ordered the government to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters, requiring that mail-in ballots only be delivered to people on that list. He also directed the justice department to prioritise investigations and prosecutions of state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote in federal elections. What did the dissenting judges say? In a blistering dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the decision “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections”. How have rights organisations reacted? The president of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, Derrick Johnson, said: “Let this ruling be a reminder that democracy is never, ever guaranteed. We have to fight for it, we have to fight to keep it and we have to protect the rights we do have within it … they are trying to do everything they possibly can to make it difficult for you to vote.” Trump announces new 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and steel Donald Trump has announced a new 50% tariff on automobiles and crucial raw materials from Canada, the latest deterioration in trade relations between the two neighbours with traditionally strong economic ties. The US president said Canada had been “ripping off” the US for years and that it was “among the worst Nations in the World to deal with”. How has Canada reacted? The country’s prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters that Trump’s announcement was largely expected. “It’s not a surprise for us that the US would take some form of reprisal to our response to their unjustified tariff,” he said. Carney has vowed to match the American tariffs “dollar for dollar”, and said Canada could not accept any proposed trade deal that would weaken French language protections. US strikes vessel in eastern Pacific, killing two people in first attack in months The US military has struck a vessel in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of drug trafficking. US Southern Command (SouthCom) said it had “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific”. SouthCom did not provide evidence of the vessel’s alleged involvement in drug trafficking. Monday’s strike marks the latest in a series since the Trump administration launched what it described as a campaign targeting “narco-terrorists” smuggling drugs into the US. Numerous reports, however, indicate the strikes have done little to stem the flow of drugs into the country. US threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to Iran The US has threatened to impose severe sanctions against any country or entity maintaining economic ties with Iran, hoping to achieve with economic measures what military means have so far failed to do. It is unclear, however, how far the Trump administration is prepared to go in confronting China, Iran’s biggest trading partner, which has signalled its resistance to US economic pressure to cut off links with an ally. Iran vowed retaliation against any country that takes part in the US-led isolation campaign. Launching what he called Operation Economic Outcast, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called it an unprecedented campaign and compared it with the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war. In other news … Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has announced a crackdown on immigrants. The country continues to deal with the aftermath of a 7.4-magnitude earthquake that killed more than 300 people and destroyed more than 30,000 homes. US healthcare officials said a food-poisoning outbreak tied to alfalfa sprouts had sickened people in at least 15 states. Target has pulled a controversial Halloween costume off its shelves after criticism across social media that it resembled a racist caricature. A mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husband was found dead six days after she disappeared from her Massachusetts home, authorities said. An independent arbitrator has ordered the Washington Post to rehire the high-profile opinion columnist Karen Attiah, who was fired abruptly last September over social media comments about Charlie Kirk. Stat of the day: Trump administration plans to revoke 200,000 asylum seekers’ visas A Department of State spokesperson said it was coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security “to identify and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently”. Associated Press put the number of people potentially involved at as many as 200,000, which would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history. Culture pick: Seam me up, Scotty! After 60 years, Star Trek has had a muppet takeover The creators of Strange New Worlds talk about boldly sewing where no one has sewn before. Don’t miss this: Australia has just 12,000 sea lions left – and ‘carnage’ may await them as bird flu takes hold Everybody loves seals and sea lions – the dogs of the ocean – but in Australia there are fears that bird flu has jumped species and could endanger them. Lisa Cox investigates. … or this: Why we’re still so fascinated by Meg White Recent incorrect attempts to reveal the White Stripes star’s whereabouts reflect how much we’re still obsessed with the one-of-a-kind drummer who did things her own way. Climate check: Nevada files lawsuit challenging federal plan for Colorado River revival Nevada has filed a federal lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s plan for the imperilled Colorado River, which threatens to cut roughly 20% of the water supplied to lower basin states – Nevada, Arizona and California – over the next two years. It could become the first of many court battles over the waterway that supplies 40 million people, dozens of tribes and 5.5m acres of farmland across the American west. Last Thing: Toddler invades pitch during Minnesota’s MLS win over San Jose A toddler interrupted a Major League Soccer match between Minnesota United and San Jose Earthquakes at the weekend by invading the pitch – a bizarre scene punctuated by an on-air analyst saying: “There’s a baby on the field.” There’s an adorable video of it to enjoy. title: Sex sells and wins votes – and the Democrats know it
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: Wonder why they’re posting flirty photos and wearing tight T-shirts? It’s a thirst trap strategy in motion, writes Arwa Mahdawi
body_text: Despite being a card-carrying member of the International Order of Confirmed Homosexuals, I have spent quite a lot of time lately thinking about Abdul El-Sayed’s biceps. I mean, have you seen them? The progressive Michigan senate nominee is jacked and he knows it. He almost always wears a tight black T-shirt to show off his muscles and incorporates a lot of fitness content in his campaign. I’m not the only one who has noticed El-Sayed’s prominent muscles. They have had a lot of coverage, and are seen as part of a wider attempt to rebrand the Democratic party. Which, I don’t need to tell you, has a serious image problem; a poll in March found that the party is looked on even less favourably than the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. So, to make it look less like a party that is full of out-of-touch technocrats who sound as if they are reading from a 500-page PowerPoint presentation every time they try to explain anything, Democrats seem to be trying to up the sex appeal. “Democrats enter their thirst trap era,” News website Axios recently declared, summing up the phenomenon. The piece observed that the Democrats’ main TikTok page has given “the thirst trap treatment” to big names including El-Sayed, Zohran Mamdani and senator Jon Ossoff (“nicknamed ‘Senator My Boo’ by internet fans”), by posting flirty photos and videos. Axios quotes a political analyst who explains that while female Democrats such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have had their share of screen time, the Dems’ TikTok page has made a “very intentional choice to feature the most attractive male members”. Fox News would appear to reluctantly agree with the assessment that Democrats are leaning into good looks to win the midterms. “El-Sayed is out in these tight T-shirts,” Fox News host Ainsley Earhardt said in a discussion last week. “AOC with her pretty smile. She’s beautiful. She’s got the red lipstick. You have Mamdani, always smiling … It doesn’t make their philosophy any less dangerous, right?… even with a tight T-shirt, it’s still socialism and it fails.” Over on CNN there was a little more jubilation about the Democrats’ vibe shift. “Dems are hot again,” strategist Yemisi Egbewole proclaimed. “They’re coming out of the closet as hot people and I’m so excited.” Egbewole added that it wasn’t just about physical attractiveness: “I think they’re learning from Trump. Entertainment really sells.” Sex sells too: it’s well established that voters around the world prefer good-looking candidates. But, while we may all be shallow deep down, some of us are shallower than others. A 2016 study found that rightwing politicians in Europe, the US and Australia tended to be more attractive than their progressive counterparts. That’s partly because “low-information” conservative voters are particularly prone to choosing attractive candidates. “In low-information city elections, a beauty increase of one standard deviation attracts about 20% more votes for the average candidate on the right and about 8% more votes for the average candidate on the left,” an analysis of the study by the Washington Post noted. Which raises the question: if looks really are so important to low-information rightwing voters, how did we end up with Donald Trump as president? (Woke 1.0 is over, haven’t you heard? It’s OK to say things like this now.) Social media may have brought a new visual element to politics, but the most famous anecdote about how looks can sway an election is almost 70 years old. In September 1960, 70 million Americans watched Richard Nixon debate John F Kennedy in the first nationally televised debate between presidential candidates. Nixon had been the favourite going in but he had just been in hospital for a couple of weeks and looked terrible. JFK, on the other hand, was tanned and rested and had good stage makeup. You can quibble with the conventional wisdom that Nixon lost that election on looks, but it certainly played a part. In his memoir, Nixon wrote: “What hurt me the most in the first debate was not the substance of the encounter between Kennedy and me, but the disadvantageous contrast in our appearances. After the program ended, callers, including my mother, wanted to know if anything was wrong, because I did not look well.” In short: if thirst traps are what it takes to get the US on a better path, then so be it. Jacked candidates in tight T-shirts may seem like a cheap trick, but even Nixon’s mother would agree that it’s a sound political strategy. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: One Nation’s Malcolm Roberts ‘in two minds’ about whether gay people should be equal
author: Tory Shepherd
summary: Footage shows senator on stage at the Church and State conference responding to question about party’s director James Ashby
body_text: One Nation’s Malcolm Roberts told a conference earlier this year that he was in “two minds” about whether gay people should have equal rights. In footage from June’s Church and State conference, released on Sunday, the senator can be seen responding to a question about James Ashby, the party’s director, who is gay. Both Roberts and the One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, appeared at the conservative Christian conference. In the footage, Roberts described Ashby as bright, honest and straight. “Well, straight in one way,” he joked. An audience member then asked Roberts what Christians should think about Ashby. Roberts responded by referring to the late American bishop and gay rights advocate John Shelby Spong, citing him as saying that after women and black people were no longer recognised as “inferior”, gay people were next. “Now I’m in two minds about that,” Roberts said. “So I haven’t got a firm position on it myself other than I don’t, I’m not homosexual and I can’t, I can’t understand it. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “But there have been a number of homosexuals who are very, very prominent in many, many fields throughout history. So all I know is that in this environment, James is not morally sound. But from what I’ve seen of him, his honesty, his integrity, his ability, he is sound. “So if you pardon me, I haven’t made up my mind, but there are a number of people in society in very prominent positions in the arts, sports, science, business, politics, who are homosexual. “And I don’t think we can afford to ban them. So it’s difficult.” The chief executive of Equality Australia, Anna Brown, said it was “genuinely shocking” that a One Nation senator would talk about “banning” people. “As though something so incompatible with a democratic society could be an acceptable option,” she said. “The idea that One Nation or its senators think that this could be an idea that’s on the table, or even a matter of legitimate debate, is incredibly chilling. “And perhaps it’s worth reminding the senator that being gay and a person of deep faith are not mutually exclusive, and neither makes someone any more or less morally sound.” The organiser of the conference, Dave Pellowe, said in the same forum that “loud, screaming activists” had held American medical health professions to ransom “until they capitulated to delisting same-sex attraction as something that needed treatment, as an illness”. Roberts is also seen in the footage vowing to push for the party to adopt a blanket abortion ban, contradicting Hanson’s position. He also said he would push for the party to claim that life begins at conception. In an Instagram post from earlier this year, also from the conference, Hanson can be seen saying she “had to have a conversation” with the Farrer MP, David Farley, after he commented that the current immigration intake of 306,000 was “probably not” too much. As leader she sometimes had to “call the shots”, she said in the latest footage. Since Farley’s migration comments, there have been multiple contradictions and changes in the anti-immigration party’s policy. Church and State describes itself as a “Christian political education ministry” teaching people to look at political issues and candidates through the lens of Scripture. One Nation representatives have made frequent comments about homosexuality on other occasions. Earlier this month, the MP Barnaby Joyce described One Nation as “one of the gayest parties in Australia” after its failed candidate Parminder Singh described homosexuality as a mental illness. Hanson then said she didn’t like Mardi Gras and that “your own personal sexuality should be kept behind closed doors”. Ashby has said as a “gay bloke” he doesn’t like the rainbow flag. Jason Virgo, who is gay, was elected as a One Nation MP in the South Australian election in March, while his newly elected colleague in the upper house, Cory Bernardi, said he stood by his 2012 comments linking same-sex marriage to polygamy and bestiality. In the Church and State footage, Roberts also discussed various conspiracy theories and said family law changes made since 1975 – including the introduction of no-fault divorce – were “tearing apart this country”. “It’s deliberate because they’re after the family. They’re after anything that can stand up to communism,” he said. Malcolm Roberts, James Ashby and One Nation did not respond to a request for comment.
