title: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on wide range of US goods
author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
summary: Ottawa’s ‘focused response’ to levies imposed by Donald Trump on Canadian products comes after trade talks collapsed last week
body_text: Canada has announced it will impose tariffs on a wide range of key American industries including cosmetics, dairy, wood products and outdoor equipment in the coming weeks, as it retaliates roughly “dollar for dollar” against levies imposed by the US. In a strong Canadian countermove to tariffs levied by Donald Trump, which took effect on Saturday after trade talks collapsed the day before, Canada’s finance and industry ministers on Tuesday called the measure a “focused response” to what they see as unfair trade practices. The White House claimed it was using section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to protest against “discriminatory” trade policies by Canada, including provincial bans on US alcohol – a ban that was only implemented in protest against tariffs imposed on Canadian goods last year. The prime minister, Mark Carney, had previously pledged a “dollar-for-dollar” response from his government after roughly 5% of exports to the US were singled out by the White House. The retaliatory Canadian measures will cover C$27.6bn ($19.9bn) in imports and are meant to target key industries including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper. The list from Ottawa has more than 700 items, ranging from from hockey sticks to ornamental fish and toilet paper to smoked lobster, with most of the tariffs set at 25% or 50%. A small group of items, including air conditioning units and tool parts, will face a lower 15% tariff. The levies will be effective starting 8 September and only apply to goods originating from the US. In announcing the retaliatory measures, the finance minister, François-Philippe Champagne, said the country was united in its fight against the US, telling attenders that Canada remained “masters of our own home”. The industry minister, Mélanie Joly, called on businesses and consumers to buy Canadian goods as part of a broader “resistance” movement in the trade war. “You have power,” she said. The government also announced more than C$7bn in support for businesses affected by the latest tariffs, adding to more than C$20bn in support announced over the past 18 months. Canada’s decision to retaliate means both countries have doubled down on a trade war that could cost billions. Earlier on Tuesday, Trump said he was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” – reminiscent of his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Others pointed out that Ontario, Canada’s most populous province, was named after the lake, not the other way around. Trump’s frustration with Ontario in particular stems from his feud with the province’s premier, Doug Ford, who called the president a “loser” and the “king of bankruptcies” and told the US president to “kiss my ass”. He also threatened to cut electricity and rare earth metal exports to the US. Trump called Ford a “flunky” of “Governor Carney” and warned “these clowns to ‘fall in line’ or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!” Trump later alluded to revelations that his trade negotiators had looked to weaken French language rules, saying he would “never interfere” with Canadians speaking French, calling it a “lie … made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support”. Trump later added: “I love French Canadians!”

title: Trump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: The Republican Senate candidate announced the plan with a graphic flagged as ‘Made with AI’
body_text: Ken Paxton, a Republican candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has unveiled plans to tackle the “negative impact” of datacenters amid a growing backlash across the political spectrum. Paxton, endorsed by Donald Trump but facing a close contest against Democrat James Talarico, posted a “Texas first” datacenter plan on X with a graphic that the social media network flagged as “Made with AI”. Republicans have been struggling to keep up with a shift in public opinion fueled by concerns that power- and water-hungry datacenters will push up energy costs and harm the environment. Some fear the issue could prove costly in November’s US midterm elections. An Annenberg Public Policy Center survey last month found that 61% of Americans now oppose the building of a new datacenter in their area, an increase from 49% in March. This includes 69% of Democrats, 54% of Republicans and 53% of independents. Last year Greg Abbott, the governor of Texas, dubbed his state the “epicenter of AI development”, but on Sunday he told ABC’s This Week program that tech companies “basically dug their own grave for the problem that’s been caused for them and that’s why they got the backlash they deserve”. On Monday his ally Paxton, currently the state attorney general in Texas, outlined a four-point plan that includes banning Chinese technology to power US datacenters, holding companies criminally liable if AI chatbots undermine children’s safety and cutting red tape to ensure datacenters do not raise Texans’ electricity bills. He also pledged to support Abbott’s state plan to ban new datacenters from rural neighborhoods, repeal sales tax exemptions and ensure they are adding to Texas’s electricity capacity rather than taking from it. Paxton said in a statement: “Texans deserve a fighter to lead and represent them as we address the growing presence of datacenters in Texas and stop their negative impact on our neighborhoods. “This plan will ensure that happens while putting Texas first, protecting our culture and land, and safeguarding our families and communities. My plan will also work to ensure that datacenters are not utilized to power Al platforms that endanger our children.” The move signals an effort by Paxton, a rightwing populist who defeated the incumbent US senator John Cornyn in a Republican primary runoff, to blunt attacks on what could be a potential electoral issue. His rival Talarico has urged tighter regulations on datacenter development and an end to sweetheart tax deals for big tech companies. Talarico accused Paxton of trying to erase his history giving datacenter tax handouts. He said in a statement: “Ken Paxton has taken nearly half a million dollars from the datacenter industry, voted to flood Texas with datacenters by giving them billions in tax handouts, and has refused to use his power as attorney general to respond to Texans’ requests to block datacenter development in their communities. “Now he’s scared his ties to big datacenter companies will lose him the election, so he’s making a sad attempt to reverse course by releasing a plan he literally used AI to make.” The race is tight in what is traditionally a Republican stronghold. A Fox News poll in late July showed Talarico leading 51% to 48%. The Cook Political Report describes the election as a toss-up. Paxton is struggling to overcome a series of political scandals. He was impeached in 2023 after being accused of corruption and later acquitted in a trial in the Texas senate. He was also indicted on charges of felony securities fraud but the case was dismissed after a 2024 pretrial diversion agreement. Last year his wife of 38 years, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce “on biblical grounds”, citing adultery. Politicians are scrambling to adjust to the backlash against AI datacenters, which consume huge quantities of electricity and water, threaten to alter the landscape of local communities, and create relatively few jobs. Josh Shapiro, the Democratic governor of Pennsylvania, last year championed a $20bn investment by Amazon but last week signed an executive order he said imposes the “strictest guardrails in the nation”. Bernie Sanders, an independent senator for Vermont, has urged big tech leaders to pause AI development. The Axios website reported that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned leading AI companies that voter discontent with the centers is endangering the party’s chances of defending a Senate seat in Ohio. Trump, however, remains supportive of the industry. He told Punchbowl News recently: “I saw Texas the other day sort of is against datacenters. I think it’s a mistake. And I’m not taking positions, I just think it’s a mistake, because there are other communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community.”

title: Hakeem Jeffries defends his meeting with Trump envoy Jared Kushner
author: Edward Helmore
summary: House minority leader is under attack from his own party for ‘affordability crisis’ meeting with president’s son-in-law
body_text: Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic minority leader in the US House of Representatives, has defended his meeting with Jared Kushner and claimed it was arranged at the request of Donald Trump’s son-in-law. Jeffries, who has come under attack from Democrats since the New York Times reported on Sunday that the two met privately to discuss common ground on issues like housing, immigration and the high cost of living, said he agreed to the meeting “to discuss the affordability crisis” in the US. In an X post on Monday, Jeffries insisted: “No one from the Trump cartel is getting a pass.” “I shouldn’t have to say it, but I am. No one is going to get a pass,” he said. “We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law and be guided by the constitution beginning on day one. And hold the crooks accountable.” Jeffries appeared to be referring to actions planned by Democrats should they retake control of US Congress in November’s midterm elections. But in meeting with Kushner – who serves as an envoy for the Trump administration, working on conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran – Jeffries provoked a response from Democrats and Republicans alike. Tommy Vietor, a former Obama aide and co-host of Pod Save America, criticized Kushner, noting that he had “no actual government job” and claiming he “just uses his family connections to get money from Gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals”. Former Clinton strategist James Carville said in an “urgent message to Hakeem Jeffries” that the House minority leader had no business meeting with Kushner. A more appropriate response than meeting to discuss affordability, Carville suggested, would be to “drag his ass” before a congressional committee and grill him on his “backdoor-dealing” with other figures in Trump’s orbit. The Trump administration, family members and cronies “have no idea what they’re doing”, Carville added. “They’re making every backdoor bullshit deal they can. And we don’t meet with them. Don’t meet with them.” New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, who opposed a primary challenge to Jeffries’ Brooklyn seat by the city councilman Chi Ossé, was asked if he would still support the representative as House majority leader if Democrats take back the House in November. “I continue to support Congressman Jeffries and his bid to become the leader,” Mamdani said. Republicans have mostly been more circumspect about the meeting. “I don’t know what that’s about,” the House speaker, Mike Johnson, told Fox News’s Peter Doocy on Sunday. “I know Jared has interest in lots of other things going on.” “He’s not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House,” Johnson added. In an earlier response to news of the meeting, Jeffries said that he was looking “to stop the madness”, adding that Democrats “have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition”.

title: Trump faces backlash from Republicans over plan to lift tariffs on beef imports
author: Shrai Popat in Washington
summary: Alarm as Republicans warn that ‘flooding’ stores with 300,000 metric tons of beef imports will hit US farmers
body_text: Donald Trump is facing growing criticism from within his own party over his decision to temporarily pause US tariffs on foreign beef in a bid to bring down grocery prices. The president’s announcement that the US will import up to 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef without charging higher tariffs has alarmed some senior Republicans, who warn that “flooding” stores with imports will hit US ranchers. This comes as the US faces a 75-year low in cattle inventory. Trump claimed his administration had secured a commitment that the imported would be sold at 25% below “current market prices” on Friday, adding: “This deal will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again.” But many GOP members are apprehensive and issued rare rebukes of the new policy. “Americans want US beef on the table – not foreign imports,” John Barrasso, a Republican senator from Wyoming and the majority whip, wrote in a post on X. “Wyoming ranchers produce the highest quality beef in the world. Our ranchers don’t ask for special treatment. They simply want a fair marketplace. It needs to be easier – not harder – for Wyoming ranchers to feed America.” On Tuesday, Brooke Rollins, the agriculture secretary, defended the president’s move as an attempt to mitigate prices for consumers. “This is a very short-term fix from the president’s perspective, that he believed necessary to get lower cost beef on to American plates,” Rollins said in an interview with Spectrum News. However, the agriculture secretary said that she did not yet know where the beef would be imported from, noting that it was part of US trade representative Jamieson Greer’s remit. “I am actually not part of any of those conversations, so I am not sure what that looks like. I think we’ll know very soon,” Rollins said. This comes after a cascade of criticism from Republican lawmakers last week. “I absolutely want to see those prices come down,” said congresswoman Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee in a competitive race for a US Senate seat in Iowa. “But I think this isn’t the way to do that.” In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, Hinson added: “I think we need to focus on letting our cattle men grow their herd … it takes some time and it takes some resources, and so I think we should be letting market conditions to do what they do – demand for beef is still really high.” Other Republicans in states with sizeable cattle farming industries also criticized the president’s recent decision. “Short term policy shifts do not equal long term solutions,” said Pete Ricketts, a Republican senator from Nebraska and prominent ally of Trump. “Flooding the market with lower quality beef compromises Nebraska farmers and ranchers. They should be enabled to grow herd sizes and meet consumer demand.” Another Trump loyalist, Senator Tim Sheehy of Montana, said that he had advised the president “against this course of action for a year”. Sheehy added that while Trump’s “heart is in the right place on wanting lower prices for the American people”, the action would actually make it more difficult for American ranchers to rebuild their herd. Most of whom, he said, are “Maga Republicans”.

title: Trump administration threatens to demolish Kennedy Center if $250m renovation not done
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: US president’s lawyers in court filing say Washington arts complex must undergo repairs or risk demolition
body_text: The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts could be demolished if repairs are not carried out, the Trump administration warned in a court filing on Monday. Lawyers for the US president said the national arts complex in Washington DC must undergo a $250m renovation or risk facing the wrecking ball. “Without those efforts, the ⁠Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years,” they argued. The warning came as Donald Trump leaves a trail of destruction in Washington, demolishing the East Wing of the White House to make way for a $600m ballroom and ordering a renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool that resulted in algae blooms and a peeling liner. The court filing represented the first time that Trump’s allies have raised the prospect of knocking down the Kennedy Center – a 100ft-high complex with a concert hall, opera house and theatre – as the dire alternative to closing it for two years of improvements. Such an aggressive move would be sure to face legal challenges, protests and an outcry from historic preservation groups. The threat emerged on Monday as the administration urged a federal judge to reject a fresh legal challenge to Trump’s efforts to put his name on the Kennedy Center. The dispute has become part of a months-long battle over the president’s attempt to alter the memorial created by Congress in honour of John F Kennedy, the 35th US president, who was assassinated in 1963. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. A federal judge ruled in May that only Congress has the power to change the Kennedy Center’s name. But the centre’s board, now largely made up of Trump appointees, voted 20-3 on 13 August to change the building’s signage to read “The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump”. It also voted to name the grounds the “President Donald J Trump Plaza”. The administration argued the latest proposal did not breach the court’s injunction because the building would still formally be called the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. The words “Restored and Renovated by” merely acknowledge Trump’s role, lawyers said, comparing the inscription to acknowledgments of major donors at other cultural institutions. The filing was made in response to a request by Joyce Beatty, a Democratic congresswoman from Ohio and a member of the Kennedy Center board by virtue of her position in Congress, to stop Trump’s name being restored to the facade. Beatty sued last year after the centre altered its white marble facade to read “The Donald J Trump and John F Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts”. In May, Judge Christopher Cooper ordered Trump’s name removed, ruling that the venue “must be named for, and is meant to honor, President Kennedy alone”. Cooper added: “Congress named the Kennedy Center and only Congress can change it.” Trump’s name was removed from the facade in June and a big tarpaulin has covered the affected section of the building since then. An appeals court last month rejected the administration’s request to keep the name in place while it challenges Cooper’s ruling. Nathaniel Zelinsky, a lawyer for Beatty, described Monday’s filing as legally baseless and said it “reads like it was written personally by Donald Trump”. Judge Cooper is due to hear Beatty’s request for an injunction at a hearing in federal court in Washington on Thursday. The Kennedy Center was established by Congress as a living memorial to Kennedy and opened in 1971. It has hosted stars ranging from Frank Sinatra and Beyoncé to Robert De Niro and Lin-Manuel Miranda. It has been limping artistically and commercially since Trump took over last year, culling staff and declaring war on “woke” programming. On Tuesday, the Washington Post reported that ticket sales, already down since Trump seized control, plummeted further after his board of trustees voted in December to rename the complex after him and put his name on its marble facade. Norm Eisen, a former White House “ethics czar” and co-founder of the nonpartisan group Democracy Defenders Action, posted on social media that “the administration is now threatening in federal court to LEVEL the Kennedy Center if Trump does not get his way. His path of destruction knows no bounds & he will answer for it in court.” John Larson, a Democratic congressman from Connecticut, condemned Trump’s threat. “No one is surprised that someone with an ego as big as Donald Trump’s believes their name should be above John F Kennedy’s on our beloved former president’s living memorial,” said Larson. “I wish President Trump were more focused on ending the illegal war he launched in Iran than he is on destroying the Kennedy Center and building his taxpayer-funded ballroom.” Hands Off the Arts, a group of more than 2,800 activists opposed to government censorship of the arts, said in a statement: “President Trump today issued the judge and American people a threat: ‘Allow me to hijack JFK’s memorial or I will turn it into a crater.’ As Americans, we have already watched in anger the obliteration of the East Wing to satisfy Trump’s vanity – we won’t let it happen again to the Kennedy Center. This is the people’s memorial to honor JFK, and we refuse to let it be desecrated or demolished.”

title: From Hasan Piker to Jesse Watters, El-Sayed seeks to focus on affordability amid scrutiny from both sides
author: Rachel Leingang
summary: Democratic Senate candidate for Michigan distances himself from Twitch streamer and debates Fox News host
body_text: The Democratic candidate for Senate in the swing state of Michigan has spent the week trying to keep his affordability message front and center as scrutiny mounts from both ends of the political spectrum. In the span of two days, Abdul El-Sayed distanced himself from leftwing streamer Hasan Piker, spoke out against rightwing hate directed at the Muslim community, and debated Fox News host Jesse Watters on taxing billionaires. The clip circulating most from the Fox interview, though, focused on circumcision - specifically, El-Sayed asking Watters whether he circumcised, in a retort to Watters’ question about gender-affirming care. In each instance, El-Sayed tried relentlessly to stay on message. On Fox, he called opponent Mike Rogers a “beta” and took a jab at Pete Hegseth in a response to a question about the federal deficit, saying Watters didn’t seem concerned that the defense secretary, “the guy who used to work on your channel”, wanted to increase the military budget to $1.5tn. “Why, so we could fight a war we don’t know how to get out of, to raise our gas prices $5 a gallon?” El-Sayed said. At a press conference condemning Islamaphobic agitator and January 6 rioter Jake Lang on Tuesday morning, El-Sayed emphasized a religious unity message in Michigan, then brought it back to Rogers and the cost of groceries. Perhaps the most heated dialogue this week has been between centrist Democrats and the left wing of the party about controversial political streamer Piker. In the most recent dustup, Piker called out Jeremy Moss, who is Jewish and running for Congress in Michigan’s 11th district, for not endorsing El-Sayed. Moss has said he’s not ready to endorse El-Sayed because of their differing views on Israel. “If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews,” Piker said in a stream. “I don’t know how people don’t recognize how dangerous this predicament is, how dangerous this is for Jews.” The comments were met with online anger from some prominent Democrats, including the House speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, who didn’t mention Piker by name but called the comments “dangerous and antisemitic”. Politico reported that Representative Hillary Scholten, a Democrat, does not want to put her name on campaign literature with El-Sayed due to his association with Piker. Others defended Piker, saying he did not call for violence, but that Israel’s actions had dangerous effects on the safety of Jews. El-Sayed campaigned with Piker during the Democratic primary, which his Democratic opponents at the time took issue with because of the Twitch streamer’s comments on Israel. “If Abdul El-Sayed had any courage at all, he would call this out and disavow Hasan Piker once and for all. We’re waiting, Abdul …,” Rogers said, calling Piker the candidate’s “running mate”. El-Sayed did put out a statement, saying his “commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters” and calling antisemitism a “scourge”, though he did not say Piker was antisemitic. It was a rare step for El-Sayed to distance himself from the Twitch streamer and drew condemnation from some who said it was playing into efforts to conflate Israel and Jewish people. The move came at a time when El-Sayed works to win over Jewish voters, some of whom have expressed concerns over his comments or positions on Israel. “I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk,” El-Sayed said. “But I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople.” But like all of his responses to attacks in recent days, he brought it back to the same note: the cost of living. “While politicians and pundits try to make this race about a Twitch streamer, we’re going to be talking about gas, groceries, good schools, and healthcare,” he said. “Because that’s what Michiganders keep asking about. It’s why I’m fighting to get money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for All.” Piker said on a stream in response to El-Sayed’s statement: “There are going to be a lot of people who are already questioning Abdul El-Sayed’s sincerity on these issues that will then turn around and say, ‘he’s moderating his position on Israel!’ I don’t think he is. I will say this: I am literally the person that is being dangled and I’m going to tell you once again; he’s not moderating on his perspective on Israel or anything like that.” In the anti-hate press conference on Tuesday, El-Sayed told reporters he has had ongoing conversations with Moss “about what it looks like to come together agreeably across our disagreements”. He said he was grateful to Judaism and the Jewish community, who he called “a light unto the world, and said the Jewish faith was a “beautiful faith that rhymes with so much of my own”. “I think all of us agree that the things that divide us are so much smaller than the things that unite us against somebody like Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said. According to Semafor, Moss was in talks to endorse El-Sayed before the Piker comments. Moss said in a statement late Monday that he has been in “continual dialogue” with El-Sayed over their disagreements, which he said he was grateful for. “But provocateurs are exploiting this moment to create further divisions,” he said. “I will not be lectured by a California podcaster about what Oakland County, Michigan’s Jewish community should and shouldn’t believe.”

title: South Carolina chooses Darline Graham as Republican nominee for US Senate
author: George Chidi in Columbia, South Carolina
summary: Darline Graham, sister of late Lindsey Graham and backed by Trump, overcomes concern about lack of experience
body_text: South Carolina voters have chosen Darline Graham as the Republican nominee for US Senate, the seat formerly held by her late brother, Lindsey, on November’s ballot. Darline Graham, with Donald Trump’s full-throated support, overcame concern about her lack of legislative experience to beat the five-term congressman Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s Republican special primary runoff. With nearly all of the ballots counted, Graham had received 52.5% of the vote, according to the Associated Press, ahead of Norman’s 47.6%. Lindsey Graham, a US senator for more than two decades, won the party’s primary in June, but died the next month. Days later, Darline Graham was appointed to serve out the remainder of her brother’s Senate term. “The critics say I shouldn’t run for the Senate,” she told a rally audience on Friday. “They say I’m not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged.” Graham will face Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee and a Charleston-area pediatrician, in November. Andrews faces steep historical odds; the last Democrat to win a statewide race in South Carolina was state superintendent Jim Rex in 2006. Trump recommended the appointment of Darline Graham, a career civil servant who was head of South Carolina’s Commission for the Blind, then encouraged her to run for a full term – upending a Republican scramble to select a new Senate nominee. She advanced to the runoff election after emerging as the top vote-getter in a 10-candidate field that included two congressmen and a former South Carolina governor. “What I really want you to do is pretend – please – that I’m on the ballot,” Trump said at a rally in Myrtle Beach on Friday. “Just come and vote.” Trump’s Maga Inc Super Pac spent more than $800,000 in support of Graham during the campaign. Graham spent the last week of the unusually short campaign digging out from a gaffe made at a debate. Asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues, she replied that she was “not that informed on national security … but I do support the military”. Some Republican voters saw that as evidence that she was not prepared for the role. Others dismissed the perceived effect as media spin. “Who is going to back Trump?” said Bill Bullard of Conway who, along with his wife, Linda, voted for Graham on Tuesday. “Who is going to support Trump? It’s just that simple.” Horry county, home to Myrtle Beach, proved decisive in the race. Though Norman won the northernmost counties of South Carolina – his political base – he did not win them by enough to counter the strength of Myrtle Beach and the coastal communities that have been surging in population and have less political loyalty to the state’s political apparatus than they have to Trump. Norman, a member of the far-right House Freedom caucus, is ranked by Heritage Action and other conservative organizations as one of Congress’s most conservative members. In the days following the January 6 riot at the US Capitol, Norman texted Trump’s chief of staff, urging Trump to declare martial law to prevent Joe Biden from taking office. In the whirlwind campaign to replace Graham, Norman leaned into hard-right themes on the Senate campaign trail, calling for Anthony Fauci, the former National Institutes of Health director, to be jailed. His campaign sought to cast Graham as a creation of the Washington elite and himself as the true heir to South Carolina’s Maga legacy. But many of Trump’s most ardent supporters in South Carolina remember that in 2023, Norman endorsed Nikki Haley, the former South Carolina governor, over Trump in her candidacy for the Republican presidential nomination. A deluge – by South Carolinian standards – of negative advertising suggested that Norman had bucked Trump on border security votes, a charge he says mischaracterized his long holdout on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to strip subsidies for electric cars and renewable energy. “I would do that over again,” he said in a debate. “I don’t apologize.”

title: Dan Sullivan v Dan Sullivan: officials confirm challenger will join senator on Alaska midterms ballot
author: Chris Stein
summary: The incumbent senator Dan S Sullivan has condemned ex-school teacher Dan J Sullivan, claiming he is running at the behest of Democrats to confuse supporters
body_text: Dan S Sullivan, the Republican senator, will be joined on the November ballot in Alaska by a challenger with a nearly identical name from the same party, election officials confirmed on Tuesday, adding a twist to what is expected to be one of the most hotly contested races of the midterms. The Republican senator is running for a third term against Democrat Mary Peltola, a former US House representative whom polls show is neck-and-neck with him in a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 2008. Alaska holds nonpartisan primaries in which the top four vote-getters advance to the general election. The Associated Press reported that with 85% of the ballots counted, Dan J Sullivan, a retired school teacher and US Forest Service employee running as a Republican, would appear on the ballot alongside incumbent Dan S Sullivan and Peltola, with a fourth candidate yet to be announced. The other Sullivan entered the race earlier this year, with the incumbent senator condemning him as a “sham” candidate who is running at the behest of Democrats to confuse his supporters and split their votes. In June, Alaska election officials disqualified the other Sullivan from the election, but the state supreme court ordered him restored. The two were listed next to each other among the 16 candidates on primary ballots, but the senator had “registered Republican” and “incumbent” next to his name, while his similarly named challenger was unadorned. It’s unclear how much of a threat the other Sullivan may pose to the senator’s chances of winning re-election. His 2.5% of the vote is much less than the more than 48% received by Peltola and almost 43% senator Sullivan won in last week’s primary. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting for general elections for congressional offices, raising the possibility that residents who want to vote for the senator but are confused by the similar names can rank both, with their votes likely to wind up going to the incumbent. In addition to Alaska, Democratic leaders are seeking to win Senate seats from Republicans in North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Iowa, all of which voted for Donald Trump in 2024. They also hope to pick up a seat in blue state Maine, while defending Democratic-held seats in Michigan, Georgia and New Hampshire.

title: Wednesday briefing: How Canada has turned a trade dispute into a defence of its sovereignty
author: Libby Brooks
summary: In today’s newsletter: A collapsing trade deal has united Canadians more than ever, in an existential confrontation with the US president
body_text: Good morning. When the Guardian asked Canadian readers whether they planned to boycott US products after dramatic escalations in the ongoing DC/Ottawa trade war, we received more than 2,000 responses within 12 hours. This inundation is perhaps evidence of the existential crisis many Canadians feel they now face, something often lost in the granular reporting of trade negotiations: this is about so much more than the price of lumber. Assailed by a US president who has repeatedly expressed a desire to consume Canada into a supersized 51st state, the country has felt perpetually on the brink of war – albeit an economic one – since Donald Trump’s early second-term tariff salvo in February 2025. This culminated in Canada’s finance minister announcing tit-for-tat tariffs on key American industries yesterday, further incensing the US president. Canadian PM Mark Carney has emerged as a leader whose refusal to be dominated by Trump is underpinned by an ambition to reorder global politics. For today’s First Edition, I spoke to the Guardian’s Canada correspondent Leyland Cecco about trade narratives, Carney’s grand plan and the price of fruit in his local grocery store. But first, the headlines. Five big stories US news | Dolly Parton, one of the greatest singer-songwriters in country music who was also much cherished for her philanthropy, has died aged 80. UK news | UK citizens will be told to stock up on tinned food and take steps to ensure they are prepared for national emergencies as part of a new government campaign to improve the nation’s resilience. UK politics | Andy Burnham will face an immediate test of his backing for electoral reform in his first week in parliament as prime minister, with almost 100 Labour MPs supporting a bid for a new national commission. Ukraine | A man from South Yorkshire is believed to be the first British citizen to die fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine. Climate crisis | The carbon emissions from just two planned datacentres in England will exceed all of the fossil fuel company ExxonMobil’s UK emissions, analysis has revealed. In depth: ‘If we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu’ The United States and Canada have enjoyed one of the strongest bilateral relationships in recent history. They share the longest unprotected border in the world, along with deep trading, security and cultural ties. But the second Trump presidency has brought about a fundamental breach in the shared values and understanding that once united the two nations. Trump has repeatedly threatened to annex Canada, as he yearns to access its critical minerals. Carney, a former Governor of the Bank of England, was sworn in as prime minister last year in the midst of Trump’s tariff wars, having never held elected public office before. He has since become the first western leader to openly acknowledge the hazard Trump poses to the global order. In a high-profile January speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, he urged “middle powers” like Canada to “act together, because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu.” Tariffs appear to have become a proxy for this political rupture. The ongoing US/Canada trade war began in February 2025, when Trump then (briefly) imposed tariffs of 25% on almost all imports from Canada and Mexico. Canada retaliated in kind, and the bitter dispute had just been rumbling on. Against this backdrop, Leyland tells me, reporters like him are “trying to figure out the magnitude of what’s happened.” *** What’s the latest? Last Tuesday, in a late night Truth Social post (is there any other kind?) Trump declared a “DEAL” with Canada was in its final stages. Trump delayed for three days the swingeing import taxes he was threatening to impose, which would have affected everything from anoraks to Christmas ornaments. The White House said in July that these 50% tariffs were in retaliation for “discriminatory treatment” by Canada. Still with me? On Friday, Canadian officials agreed a deal was still close, yet 24 hours later the whole thing fell apart. Canada walked out of negotiations hours before the 50% tariffs on roughly $20bn (£14.6bn) of Canadian goods kicked in on Saturday, with Carney accusing the US of using “economic integration as a weapon”. Yesterday, Canada pledged to roll out “dollar-for-dollar” retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of US goods next month, prompting Trump to denounce the nation as “difficult and unreasonable”. Precisely how this all unravelled depends on whose narrative you follow. Carney’s position was that the US was breaching a red line on French language protection. Currently, Canadian rules require companies operating in Quebec, its predominantly Francophone province, to provide French-language goods and services to help protect its cultural identity. These stipulations have frustrated US negotiators. There’s also a counter narrative, that Canada’s negotiators were conceding so much – for example, accepting tariffs on the auto sector, steel and aluminium – that a number of senior Canadian politicians had urged Carney to harden his resolve. Meanwhile, US officials accused Canada of collapsing the deal by seeking additional last minute concessions. In the concurrent war of communications, Carney emerges the winner, says Leyland, “because he can defend the decision to walk way to Canadians”, while the US is hampered both by Trump’s ego and top officials pushing their own agendas. *** How Carney won this round Polling over the weekend found strong majority support for Carney’s stance in every Canadian province, and a mood of steadfast defiance can be read across Canada’s media. “The coming period will be hard and the damage may be awful but no one should ignore what is at stake. A free Canada is worth the sacrifice,” declared an editorial in the Globe and Mail. “What we see now is near uniform support for the prime minister ,” says Leyland, “and immense feelings of national unity”. This even extends to successionist Quebec, where support for independence from the rest of Canada is at its lowest level in decades. Carney – who has consolidated support for his previously ailing Liberals – is enjoying “a key political win” Leyland says, defending totemic language rights that are seen as integral to Canada’s cultural fabric. But his refusal to bow to US demands is part of a broader strategy. “What we’re seeing right now is the logical extension of that [Davos] speech, which was a warning and also laying the groundwork for how Canada would conduct itself”. For now, Carney is strengthening trade ties with China and the EU, to the chagrin of US negotiators. “The message is that Canada has long enjoyed a very beneficial relationship with the US and that’s over,” says Leyland. “Now we will walk away from the table if there is any erosion of our sovereignty.” Compare this Canadian unity with the domestic reaction south of the border: with the midterms looming, Trump is reportedly heading for a tariff-shaped clash with Senate Republicans. As venerable economist Paul Krugman pointed out yesterday: “The US is far more dependent on Canadian goods than most Americans realise.” *** The mood in Canada “There’s an asymmetric aim in this war,” says Leyland, “which is that Canada is fighting for its sovereignty, its national identity.” The US, meanwhile, is just “fighting for cheaper goods”. This perhaps explains why boycotting US goods has such visceral and consistent support among Canadians. A grassroots boycott has emerged as a consumer-driven response to the tariff war, with supermarket scanning apps like Maple Scan springing up to help users buy Canadian. Leyland is a parent of two young kids who like to eat berries – now he analyses every package in the grocery aisle to work out where they were grown. “I remember there was a period when US berries were on the steepest discount because they just weren’t selling.” And the decline of cross-border tourism has had a fairly devastating effect on American businesses. After Canadian visitor numbers fell by 26% in 2025, New York state launched a “NY loves Canada” promotional campaign this month to woo back its northern neighbours. “Every Canadian knows that this is not a fight that they want to be in”, says Leyland “but right now they believe it’s a fight worth having”. Weekend polling revealed a public who feel “frustrated”, “angry” and “exhausted” after 18 months of tariff turmoil. But, like their premier, they have no intention of backing down. title: With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition
author: Rafael Behr
summary: Everyone can see that the Iran war has been a strategic disaster for the US, while a failing president pretends he is winning, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
body_text: Now is the twilight of Donald Trump’s supremacy. The US is still the richest and most heavily armed nation on Earth. That status is secure. The current president, contemptuous of law and indulged in lawlessness by a supine Congress, enjoys even greater power than the constitution allows. With those advantages it takes a special talent for incompetence to look as thwarted and impotent as Trump does with more than two years of his second term still to run. History will record the war against Iran as a turning point in the fortunes of the current US administration and a grievous wound to national prestige. Pumped with hubris after the audacious military operation to kidnap Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, Trump believed an equally brisk triumph was available in the Middle East. The Tehran regime would be decapitated. The country’s hydrocarbon resources would then be available for US exploitation. Six months later, Iran is controlled by a new generation of hardliners. Emboldened by resilience under US and Israeli bombardment, they demand financial concessions from Washington as the price for peace – reparations and a right to toll the strait of Hormuz. The war is not over, it has just turned cold. Trump believes Iran’s fragile economy is close to collapse. He threatens to push it over the brink with “D-day” sanctions. The metaphor of second world war amphibious assault is supposed to make yet another round of financial coercion succeed where past embargos have failed. It is true that ordinary Iranians are suffering terrible privations, but repression limits their capacity to translate discontent into demands for political change. By contrast, US consumers, aggrieved by the inflationary consequences of the war, and confused about its purpose, get to express their unhappiness in midterm elections in November. The calculation in Tehran is that American tolerance for economic pain is low enough that Trump will be forced to blink first. It is a reasonable assumption: the need to declare mission accomplished to a domestic audience – even on terms that amount to defeat by any objective measure – drives an impatient president’s actions more than long-term strategy. If sanctions fail, diplomatic climbdown is the only remaining move. The Pentagon couldn’t revert to the all-out military option even if Trump ordered it, because Operation Epic Fury burned too much of the national munitions stockpile. This is where an asymmetry of cost and capability comes into play. Iran can frighten ships out of the Gulf with a few mines. It can harry neighbouring states with drones knocked together for less than $50,000 and dispatched from mobile launchers that are hard to target. The Patriot interceptors that protect US forces and their allies in the region cost $4-5m apiece. (More than 1,500 Patriots are thought have been fired in the war so far, leaving fewer than 830 in the US inventory.) That depletion has global repercussions, most pressingly in Ukraine where top-end US interceptors are essential for shielding civilians from Russia’s most sophisticated ballistic missiles. Trump’s attitude to that conflict has evolved from craven pro-Kremlin partisanship and an assumption of inevitable Russian victory to grudging respect for Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s fortitude and ingenuity in proving that assumption wrong. But the shift is not stable. It depends on undertakings by Nato’s European members to cover the cost of arming Kyiv. If Trump had used normal diplomacy to cajole European democracies into financing the defence of their eastern flank, it would count as a foreign policy success – rebalancing the relationship to both sides’ benefit. But he did it with credulous admiration for Vladimir Putin and deranged demands for territory in Greenland. As a result, the European drive to autonomy looks less like burden-sharing and more like a hedge against American perfidy. It isn’t just Europe where US allies feel burned. Gulf states that found themselves on the frontline of Iranian retaliation in a war they didn’t start or want, expected a more reliable umbrella of protection. They feel unrewarded for their decades of service, hosting US military bases and functioning as proxies for American interests in the region. Last week Trump abruptly cut short a joint military exercise with South Korea – a loyal Asian partner to the US. A rational explanation, and the one preferred by Seoul, was that US forces were overstretched by their Middle Eastern entanglement. Trump framed it instead as an amicable gesture towards North Korean tyrant Kim Jong-un, whose regime he judged to be “unthreatening and respectful”. Such civility, lavished on a monstrous dictatorship, is withheld from Canada, a benign democracy. Trump dismisses his northern neighbour as an economic freeloader, barely even a proper country; a mislabelled territory that should be the 51st US state. Unsurprisingly, that attitude sours relations. Canadian prime minister Mark Carney pulled out of trade talks last weekend, citing unreasonable last-minute demands from US negotiators. Trump responded with punitive tariffs, to which the Canadians promise “dollar-for-dollar” retaliation. The smaller economy is likely to suffer more from a trade war. But for Carney the cost in reduced commerce had to be weighed against the political damage he may incur if seen to capitulate to Trump’s bullying. He knows the US president takes concessions as an invitation to come back with yet more demands. He also knows that November’s midterm elections are likely to flip the House of Representatives to Democratic party control, and possibly the Senate too. Trump cannot be chastened by unwelcome election results. He would rather deny their validity. But irrefutable evidence of failure at the ballot box may at least stir some Republicans out of stupefied obedience to a commander-in-chief whose way of governing has made their party less popular and left their country friendless. Even if the constitutional mechanisms that are supposed to keep a president in check are only partly rehabilitated, the spell of impunity is broken. The cult of personality that once made Trump look like an irrepressible force of nature has shrunk to a sycophantic sect. An administration that styled itself as a national revolution looks more like a kleptocratic junta, using the privileges of office to pilfer what it can as the clock runs down. The president still has followers across the country. A hardcore bring unshakable devotion to the cause. But even some of them can surely sense the decay of purpose and whiff of panic in a man running out of ammunition. Trump’s reign is far from over. With his hands on the levers of American power he can still do a lot of damage. But the rest of the world has learned to read his lurches, anticipate his spasms, manoeuvre around him. The phase of deference is past. Now is the time of planning for whatever comes next in the dimming light of a waning star. Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

title: Abortion rights group endorses Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Maine Senate race
author: Shrai Popat in Washington
summary: Reproductive Freedom for All – one of the country’s oldest pro-choice groups – backs Jackson in his fight against Republican Susan Collins
body_text: One of the oldest abortion rights groups in the US is endorsing Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee in Maine’s critical US Senate race, according to details first shared with the Guardian. Reproductive Freedom for All is supporting Jackson, the former state senate president, in challenging Susan Collins – the five‑term Republican incumbent who has been dogged on the campaign trail for her role in overturning abortion access in the US. Collins voted in 2018 to confirm conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh to the supreme court. In 2022, Kavanaugh joined the majority opinion overturning Roe v Wade, a landmark abortion rights protection. In the aftermath, more than a dozen states enacted near‑total abortion bans. This year’s midterm elections mark the first time Collins is on the ballot since the decision. “Flipping the Maine Senate race is a critical path to winning a Senate majority, and we do not restore a federal right to abortion without flipping the Senate majority,” said Mini Timmaraju, the group’s president. Timmaraju will join Jackson on Wednesday in Brunswick for the launch of the campaign’s Women for Troy coalition. Jackson, a former logger who began his political career as a Republican, once cast votes restricting abortion access before reversing course years later. He has expressed regret for his record and his earlier belief that abortion should “never be legal”. In a July interview with MS Now, Jackson said he recognized he had been “wrong”. “Early on, I wasn’t real clear on reproductive rights. But I had a lot of conversations over time. A lot of conversations with women, doctors, community members, just people that I came to trust,” he said. “And it became more and more clear to me that abortion access was healthcare.” Since 2017, Jackson has held a 100% rating from Planned Parenthood and has become one of Maine’s most consistently pro‑choice Democrats. In 2023, the year after the supreme court overturned Roe v Wade, he co‑sponsored legislation expanding abortion access to include medically necessary procedures after fetal viability. His evolution has extended beyond reproductive rights: Jackson has also shifted his positions on marriage equality and other social and economic issues, emerging as one of the Pine Tree State’s leading progressives during his time in the legislature. “[Jackson] in many ways reflects the reality of a majority of independents and Republicans in this country who now support abortion rights, but might personally have felt conflicted in the past,” Timmaraju told the Guardian. “Having someone like Troy in the Senate who can talk to his Republican colleagues and talk to some of those moderate Democratic colleagues who don’t have the same courage that he has is actually going to be a huge value add for our movement.” In June, Collins – who has long cast herself as a moderate Republican supportive of abortion access – said she did “not regret that vote” for Kavanaugh. Jackson’s campaign has seized on the remark to tie her to the Trump administration’s anti‑abortion agenda. “She can defend that vote all she wants. I’m running for Senate to restore and expand the federal right to abortion and make damn sure politicians never again get to take this freedom away from Mainers,” Jackson said in a statement. Planned Parenthood’s Super Pac announced this month it would spend more than $600,000 on ads criticizing Collins’s record on abortion in Maine. But strategists in both parties note that Collins’s seniority in Congress – and the millions of federal dollars she has steered back to Maine over the years – has historically proven difficult to beat. In a midterm shaped by record inflation, affordability concerns, and the military conflict with Iran, they argue her vote to confirm Kavanaugh may not be top of mind for many Mainers weighing their choices at the ballot box. Jackson – who mounted an unsuccessful bid for governor earlier this year – secured the Democratic nomination in July at a snap convention. He replaced Graham Platner, the oyster farmer who exited the race after facing allegations of sexual assault, which he denies. The turmoil around the race “gave us pause”, Timmaraju said, explaining the group’s decision to wait before endorsing Jackson. “We needed a little bit of time to regroup. We needed to follow the lead of people on the ground in Maine.”

title: Wiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with Canada
author: Lauren Aratani in New York
summary: Paper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimated
body_text: Using the bathroom or having a cry is about to become more expensive for North Americans as the US and Canada enter a full-fledged trade war that threatens to flush away decades of peaceful trading between the two nations. After trade negotiations broke down between the two countries last weekend, Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, vowed to match US tariffs “dollar for dollar” and unveiled a list of nearly 900 American goods that will face 25% to 50% tariffs starting on 8 September. Paper products are among the hardest-hit sectors, with Canada threatening to put tariffs of between 25% and 50% on “toilet paper or face tissue stock” from 8 September in retaliation for a 50% hike from Washington DC. Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, they heavily rely on lumber-rich Canada for raw materials. Procter & Gamble, the owner of Charmin toilet paper, said last year that it would have to increase prices amid tariffs that were in place at the time. The US imported $328m worth of toilet paper from Canada in 2024, according to the World Bank, making it by far the largest exporter of the product to the US. Retailers including Costco source much of their paper products from the country. The US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population. The average American uses 141 rolls of toilet paper per year, making them No 1 for No 2s globally, just ahead of Germans, each using an average of 134 rolls annually. It’s not just paper products that could rise in price. The trade war highlights the deep economic ties shared between the two countries as consumers continue to worry about inflation on both sides of the border. US tariffs are specifically affecting Canadian liquor, including popular whiskey brands Crown Royal and Canadian Club, which are currently under a 50% tariff. While Canada has not introduced a tariff on American liquor, most Canadian provinces have introduced their own bans on American alcohol, in retaliation for earlier tariffs on Canadian products. Donald Trump used these province-wide bans on American alcohol as part of his legal justification for his new tariffs against Canada. Carney has asked province leaders to consider putting American liquor back on the shelves, though as the Nova Scotia premier Tim Houston told CBC News: “Whether Nova Scotians or Canadians will actually buy it when it’s back on the shelves, that’s a whole other discussion.” Trump also said that his new tariffs are in retaliation for Canadian levies against the American dairy industry. He introduced a 50% tariff on nearly all Canadian dairy products, with the exception of Canadian cheese. In response, Canada has a 50% tariff on American dairy products, along with a 25% tariff on American cheese. Canada also took a swing at the US fishing industry, with a 25% tariff on American fish and seafood, including frozen lobster. The move prompted Republican senator Susan Collins, facing a tough re-election battle in lobster-capital Maine, to call Trump’s latest move “a mistake”. A 25% tariff on Canadian cars and auto parts is set to affect the American auto industry, which relies heavily on Canadian parts for manufacturing. Trump has threatened to double the tariff to 50% if a deal isn’t made by 1 January 2027. With negotiations down the drain, it’s unclear if or when the tariffs will be lifted. But the Trump administration is adamant that “there’s no possible way” the trade dispute with Canada will affect US consumers, according to Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative. “The fundamentals are good,” he said. “I don’t think this is going to affect anything.”

title: Goodbye to the Soviet Union – archive, 1991
author: Compiled by Richard Nelsson
summary: On 2 September 1991, the Congress of People’s Deputies voted for the dissolution of the Soviet Union, allowing its republics to opt for independence
body_text: Deputies stunned by plan for a la carte USSR By Jonathan Steele in Moscow 3 September 1991 The USSR’s supreme legislative body voted overwhelmingly yesterday to bury the existing union of 15 Soviet republics, allow the Baltic republics and any others that wish it to go free, and prepare for an economic confederation in its place. In a move which is no less dramatic than the suspension of the Soviet Communist party 10 days ago, the Congress of People’s Deputies adopted a new structure of power which gives radically new rights to the republics. They acted after hearing a report on the crisis meeting held in the Kremlin yesterday between President Gorbachev and the representatives of 11 republics. The Kazakh president, Nursultan Nazarbayev, read the report, which stunned deputies. It turned the present system of Soviet power upside down by proposing three new bodies in place of the present parliament and union government. There would be a state council, consisting of President Gorbachev and the leaders of the other republics which sign the union treaty, to handle foreign and domestic policy. An inter-republican economic council would manage the economy and bring in reforms. In place of the parliament would be a kind of senate consisting of 20 representatives from each republic. Republics would be offered a Soviet Union a la carte. Each could join a political union by signing a union treaty, but would be free to decide later on full or associate membership. Alternatively, it could go free, in which case the congress would be asked to support its application for membership of the United Nations. All 15 republics, even if they opted for independence, would be eligible to join an economic union aimed at maintaining a ‘single free economic space’. They would also be invited to sign an agreement on ‘collective security’ with the aim of maintaining a single army and a single ‘military-strategic space’. Continue reading. Editorial: Mikhail signs, but Boris calls the shots 3 September 1991 The Soviet map was transformed yesterday with such devastating effect that it can never be undone. The hand which holds the pen may be that of the Soviet President. But Mr Gorbachev was being firmly guided from behind, by a coalition of interested republics among whom the Russian President Boris Yeltsin wields the most effective grip. George Bush’s heavily trailed announcement that he would recognise the three Baltic states has by contrast lost all power to amaze. The new proposal grants by implication the right for any republic to secede. It appears to be an entirely facultative exercise in which only those republics ‘which wish to’ will sign the Union Treaty. This has been changed from previous drafts out of all recognition. It is up to each signing republic to decide for itself the form of participation in the Union. In theory the Baltic states too could sign, while deciding on a ‘form’ which was effectively non-participatory. Politically the new proposal is a brilliant sleight of hand for the newly reconstituted Gorbachev-Yeltsin alliance. Mr Gorbachev salvages a Union cleansed from everything which made it objectionable. He survives as a useful lightning conductor at home and abroad, patronised in both senses of the word. Continue reading. Soviets tuck in a la carte 6 September 1991 After three days of intense argument, the Soviet Union’s Congress of People’s Deputies approved President Mikhail Gorbachev’s plan to replace the centralised Soviet Union with a loose confederation of sovereign states. The a la carte plan envisages a multi-tier structure which will allow republics to decide the extent of their relations with central government while retaining the armed forces under a single military command. The confederation plan was drafted in overnight negotiations on Monday between President Gorbachev and the representatives of Russia, Ukraine, Armenia, Byelorussia and six other republics. The Baltic states and Moldova refused to take part in the discussions, while Georgia attended with observer status. The confederation plan caused great suspicion and disagreement in the Congress, with representatives of several republics and nationalities objecting to aspects of the proposals and many deputies opposing their own reduced role. After warnings from President Gorbachev that a decision had to be made quickly, the Congress passed a law suspending parts of the Soviet constitution and substituting a three-part interim government structure: a parliament, a State Council made up of President Gorbachev and the leaders of participating republics, and an Inter-Republican Economic Committee. Prospects of independence for the Baltic states increased rapidly during the week when the United States announced its recognition. The three states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – applied for membership of the United Nations. Meanwhile Azerbaijan declared its independence from the Soviet Union. Russians in Moldova – which declared its independence last month – set up a separate republic of the Dniester. Serbian rebels and Yugoslav government troops captured most of the eastern Croatian region of Slavonia, in which many Serbs live. The Slavonian capital, Osijek, was the centre of heavy fighting in which at least 16 people were killed. Seven more deaths were reported from Pretinje, south of Zagreb. Road and rail links between Croatia and Serbia were completely severed.

title: This is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this November
author: Robert Reich
summary: They should ask the question Reagan asked at the end of his debate against Jimmy Carter: ‘Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?’
body_text: The midterm elections are already upon us, and every Democrat and independent running against a Republican should ask voters the question Ronald Reagan asked on 28 October 1980, at the end of his televised debate against Jimmy Carter: “Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?” Unless you’re very, very rich, the answer is obviously: “No, I’m worse off.” Start with his tariffs, which are costing every American household an average of $1,100 annually, according to the Yale Budget Lab. (If you don’t trust Yale, the conservative Tax Foundation estimated last year’s tab to be $1,000 a household.) Even cleaning supplies and toilet paper are up at least 5%. Household furnishings, up at least 8%. Clothing, up at least 14%. Trump’s tariffs have also increased the costs of big-ticket items such as cars and made it more expensive to build new homes. Other studies find that the tariffs have added as much as 0.7 and 0.5 percentage points to the consumer price index and the personal consumption expenditures price index, respectively. Then there’s Trump’s war in Iran, which is driving up energy and food prices, as oil tankers remain stranded in the strait of Hormuz. The war is costing more at the gas pump – about $670 more a household since the war began. Americans face what the Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers describe as “a worsening utility debt crisis”. The groups wrote in an analysis published last month: Energy bills have increased three times faster than the rate of inflation while Trump has been president. The national average monthly utility bill reached $280 in early 2026, a 12% increase since the end of 2024, just before the second Trump administration took office. What’s the Republican response to soaring energy utility prices? Eliminate billions in clean energy subsidies and tilt the scales toward costlier, dirtier fossil fuels. Also driving up the cost of electricity are AI datacenters. They’re also using up huge amounts of water and creating noise pollution. And who’s been pushing these datacenters? Trump and, before recent backlash, many Republicans. Trump’s war and the blockage of the strait are also causing fertilizer shortages, which are sending food prices upward. Millions of Americans are now struggling to afford groceries. Meanwhile, Trump’s huge tax cuts – which mostly benefited big corporations and the super-wealthy – are being paid for, in part, by Republican cuts to Medicaid and Medicare. Trump announced last month that he is ending Medicare subsidies that have kept drug prices low for seniors; Republican cuts to the Affordable Care Act have deprived millions of Americans of health insurance. Hell, even Trump’s executive order to divide the measles, mumps, rubella vaccine into three shots instead of one is adding burdens to the typical American family. As the Republican senator Bill Cassidy said on ABC’s This Week: “This is why the president’s poll numbers are down, because you’ve lost sight of affordability for the parent. You’ve lost sight of the convenience for the American family. You’ve lost sight of that which is driving higher costs in healthcare – for example, more doctor’s visits … for something which has no rationale in science.” Trump’s obsession with gutting the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has denied Americans billions in foregone rebates and settlements. The regime spent $464m of taxpayer dollars in a no-bid contract for a special fleet of jets intended to deport immigrants. The planes have almost never been used. On and on it goes. Trump says the US economy is “doing unbelievably from the standpoint of Wall Street”. Maybe, but most Americans live on Main Street and own few if any shares of stock. The richest 1% holds more than half of the value of stocks listed on US stock exchanges; the richest 10%, 92%. Even including retirement accounts, only 16% of adult Americans have assets exceeding $100,000. The stock market boom reflects a boom in corporate profits. The pharmaceutical industry, big oil, and other sectors are posting banner earnings. Second quarter earnings for S&P 500 companies are on pace to rise a remarkable 50% year over year, the highest growth rate since the second quarter of 2021. But average working Americans are struggling to keep their heads above water. Trump’s comments about the roaring stock market came the same day that new data showed US consumer sentiment dropped in August. Americans’ outlook on the country’s economic conditions have worsened among Republicans as well as among Democrats. The July jobs report showed the US economy shedding 23,000 jobs, wage growth slowing, and the unemployment rate falling because more people left the workforce. My humble advice to Democratic candidates in the midterms: don’t be distracted. Don’t take the bait and discuss socialism, “wokeism”, or anything else. Just ask this simple question: are you better off now than you were before this presidency? And explain how badly Trump and congressional Republicans have shafted average working people. You’re better off than you were before the start of this presidency only if you’re a major investor in the stock market, a top corporate executive or a beneficiary of Trump’s largesse to his billionaire backers. But if you’re an average working American, you’re indubitably worse off. Hopefully, you’ll vote your economic interests on 3 November and deposit Trump’s congressional lapdogs into the dustbin of history. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK
