title: ‘A Bible-sized blind spot’: congressman sounds alarm on rising Christian nationalism
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: In his new book, congressman Jared Huffman argues that theocratic insurgency has only grown more powerful after Donald Trump returned to the White House
body_text: Crosses, shofars and “Appeal to Heaven” flags. Rioters praying with their hands aloft as police officers are brutalised. January 6 2021 is widely remembered as a deadly insurrection by supporters of Donald Trump; but for Congressman Jared Huffman, who was locked down alone in his office that day, something else stands out. It was a very Christian coup. “This Christian nationalist movement that I had seen growing so much stronger and more militant during my time in Congress erupted in plain view,” Huffman, 62, says by phone from his home in Marin county, California. “I truly believed January 6 would be the wake-up call our country needed to confront this movement to understand it and to hold it to account. “Unfortunately, the country went back to sleep and many of my own colleagues who the mob wanted to kill that day didn’t even seem to notice the religious elements of the group that was trying to kill them.” That is a big part of why Huffman is now deciding to sound an alarm of his own with a new book, No Prophets: The Fight to Save Democracy from Christian Nationalism. Contending that the US has a “Bible-sized blind spot”, it argues that the theocratic insurgency has only grown more powerful after Trump’s return to power and is now the country’s most dangerous political movement – a greater threat to science, education and freedom than most people realise. No one is better qualified to make this case than Huffman, the only current member of Congress to admit he does not believe in God. He grew up in Independence, Missouri – the home of former president Harry Truman and historic headquarters of the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (now the Community of Christ), an offshoot of Mormonism. A devout Christian, Huffman was ordained into its priesthood. The first crack in his faith occurred during his sophomore year of college at UC Santa Barbara. The sudden death of his father triggered some questioning. “The bottom line is the supernatural tenets of my faith, the God belief, the notion of heaven and hell and miracles and so forth, no longer worked for me. That’s a hard thing when you lose your faith. “It took me years of reflecting and thinking about it to determine that the things I liked about my religious upbringing, the universal values that are very much part of the Christian gospel, are available in all sorts of faith perspectives, including non-belief. They’re things that good people often innately do and think.” Huffman settled on the label humanist. “The reason I prefer that to atheist is because atheist is a negative statement about what you don’t believe. That feels like it reduces me. Humanism is a much more affirmative expression of what you do believe, and humanists believe we have a duty to lead moral and ethical lives based on science and facts and reason. You choose to be a good person not because of some sky god or some inducement of an afterlife or fear of hell.” For decades, Huffman kept his secular worldview private. In 2013, on his first day in Congress, he stood sheepishly before House speaker John Boehner, who asked, “Alright, who’s going to hold the Bible?” for the swearing-in photo-op. Huffman’s devout mother was beaming in the background. Caught off guard, Huffman put his hand on a Bible, a moment that left him feeling “sullied and hypocritical”. The turning point came in 2017. Huffman’s mother had died, removing the fear of breaking her heart, and Trump had entered the White House, opening the floodgates of religious extremism. But when Huffman decided to go public as a non-believer, his wife, brother, senior staff and political advisers warned him it was “a terrible, career-wrecking idea”. He explains: “They were giving me good advice because the polling to this day shows that the worst label you could attach to a candidate for public office in the United States is ‘atheist’. I appreciated them trying to protect me, but I also knew that I felt increasingly uncomfortable hiding my moral framework and ducking these questions about religion. I felt increasingly drawn into the fight against all of these encroachments of religious extremism into our government. I was on a collision course with ‘coming out’, if you will, and I decided to do it against that advice.” Huffman received support from individuals including House of Representatives minority leader Nancy Pelosi, congressman Jamie Raskin, with whom he founded the Congressional Freethought Caucus, and House chaplain Father Pat Conroy, a guitar-playing priest who jammed with Huffman after hours. Conroy told Huffman that he wished more members of Congress would be honest about what they believed. Huffman says: “I’m very glad I did it, but have I encountered some harsh judgments and prejudices? Absolutely. I’ve been called every name in the book. I have Democratic colleagues who are devout Christians who seem to take some offence at my public existence as a non-believer. “They seem to feel that threatens or insults them as Christians, which is baffling, of course, because I don’t have a quarrel with Christianity or Christians, but it does speak to the privileged status of Christians not just within the Republican party, where Christian nationalism has become a defining feature, but even among my fellow Democrats.” He defines “Christian privilege” as a deeply ingrained cultural taboo that protects home-grown religious radicalism from the same state and media scrutiny instantly applied to minority or foreign faiths. That Christian privilege was manifested in the January 6 attack on the US Capitol, Huffman argues, when many fellow members of Congress did not even seem to notice the religious elements of the group trying to kill them. It was evident again, he asserts, in one of the most consequential political cover-ups in recent history: the deliberate erasure of Christian nationalism from the final report of the House January 6 select committee. As the committee raced toward its deadline at the end of 2022, its staff split into colour-coded drafting teams. The “Purple Team” was tasked with investigating rightwing radicalism, and they meticulously documented the role of charismatic evangelical networks, particularly the New Apostolic Reformation (NAR), in radicalising and mobilising the shock troops of the insurrection. Chairman Bennie Thompson told Huffman: “We asked the Purple Team to look into the role of religion in what happened, and they came back with a report that shows those people, rightwing Christian extremists, actually had a lot to do with it.” But then came a veto. Liz Cheney, the committee’s formidable vice-chair, demanded the entire section be excised. She argued that focusing on Christian nationalism would “distract” from Trump’s personal culpability and alienate conservative Christian voters. Cheney’s argument prevailed. Huffman says: “I give her huge credit for standing up to Trump at a time when almost no other Republicans would do it. That courage was very real, but she also did the country a huge disservice with her Christian privilege.” If the attackers had worn hijabs or carried Qurans, he contends, the select committee report would have dissected their religious connections with “surgical precision”. Against this backdrop, Huffman argues that modern Christian nationalism is not a monolith but a temporary coalition of three distinct, volatile and historically hostile religious subcultures, held together by the glue of Trump. The biggest and politically most potent is NAR, a decentralised network of self-declared “apostles” and “prophets” who reject traditional denominational authority in favour of direct revelation. NAR prophets such as Paula White-Cain and Lance Wallnau cast Trump as a modern King Cyrus – a flawed, pagan ruler anointed by God to save his chosen people – to provide a divine permission structure for millions of evangelicals to overlook Trump’s moral failings. On the Catholic flank are the “Rad Trads”, a small but highly influential subculture that resent the liberalising Vatican II reforms of the 1960s and believes that Catholic moral authority should govern the state. Sympathisers include vice-president JD Vance and political strategist Steve Bannon. Neo-nazi agitator Nick Fuentes openly calls for a “Catholic monarchy” to replace the US constitution. Perhaps the most sophisticated and economically formidable faction is the “Theobros”, a network of Protestant Reconstructionists led by Pastor Doug Wilson of Moscow, Idaho. Wilson advocates for “Mere Christendom”, a system where the Apostle’s Creed is codified into the US constitution, women and non-Christians are stripped of voting rights. The Theobros have forged a powerful “Theo-tech bromance” with Silicon Valley venture capitalists such as Peter Thiel. The ultimate Theobro is Pete Hegseth, Trump’s self-styled “secretary of war”, whose body is adorned with Crusader tattoos – including “Deus vult” (God wills it) and the Jerusalem cross – and who hosts a workday “Secretary of Defense Christian Prayer & Worship Service” in the Pentagon auditorium, broadcast live on internal networks. Huffman comments: “The nicest thing I can say about Pete Hegseth is to thank him for his lack of subtlety. He is so cartoonish in his Christian nationalism that he provides a great case study. “If anybody wants to know what Christian nationalism looks like in its most strident militant form, he embodies it literally in the tattoos on his own body but certainly in the rampant proselytising that he does and these overt power plays to institutionalise his version of Christianity in Pentagon prayer services once a month with radical hate preachers brought in as honoured guests.” Nowhere is the advance of Christian nationalism more striking than inside the Capitol itself, which Huffman describes as a “shadow theocracy”. Visitors on official tours see Statuary Hall and hear speeches on the separation of powers; they do not see the sprawling, tax-subsidised “ministry-industrial complex” operating under the dome. Pastors lurk like lobbyists in the Capitol hallways, Huffman writes. The most influential is Ralph Drollinger’s Capitol Ministries, which hosts weekly Bible studies for members of the House, Senate and White House cabinet. Drollinger, a 7’2” former basketball player, teaches a “free-market gospel” that frames environmentalism as a sin against God’s dominion mandate and instructs cabinet members on how to inject biblical literalism into federal policy. More than a hundred years have passed since Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution was debated in the “Scopes monkey trial” in Dayton, Tennessee. But ideas long taken for granted are once again under attack. Huffman warns that Christian nationalism’s ultimate target is Enlightenment values that date back to Thomas Jefferson and the founding of the US in 1776. In a chapter entitled “The Dumbing of America”, he quotes Voltaire: “Those who can make you believe absurdities can make you commit atrocities.” He also profiles Mary Miller of Illinois, who began her congressional career in 2021 by quoting Adolf Hitler to a Moms for America rally: “Hitler was right, whoever has the youth has the future.” In June last year, Miller had a moral panic when a Sikh cleric, Giani Surinder Singh, delivered a guest prayer in the House chamber. Assuming Singh was a Muslim, Miller tweeted: “America was founded as a Christian nation, and I believe our government should reflect that truth ... May God have mercy!” On climate science, Miller is equally blunt, dismissing solar panels because God “controls the sun, and the sun controls the weather”. Huffman reflects: “This is potentially the unravelling of a 250-year truce between fundamentalist Christians and the Enlightenment. The stakes are much higher now than even in Jefferson’s time because then it was just about the form of government and individual liberty and protecting us against religious tyranny. But today, it’s about whether we cure the next disease or pandemic and whether we can survive the climate crisis. We look to these institutions of research and science and knowledge to allow us to keep living on this planet at a time when we’ve created some terrible threats to our own existence.” Huffman insists the fight is still winnable but will require a broad coalition that includes moderate Christians, non-Christians and secular Americans. “We need to reckon with our Christian privilege problem, our Bible-sized blind spot when it comes to just speaking without fear or favour about this movement that poses as Christian. We’ve got to get more comfortable working across different faith perspectives in a pro-democracy coalition.” But he also offers a warning from history: “I am thinking a lot these days about the final unraveling of the Weimar Republic in the early 1930s. From what I have read and studied about that, Hitler and his National Socialist party were a small minority that could easily have been stopped right up to the end had the centrist parties and the left been able to overcome their differences and work together. “They couldn’t do it, and so they left the lane wide open for Hitler to become chancellor, and the rest is a very grim part of our history. That’s absolutely how the United States could unravel and evolve into fascism – and Christo-fascism in our case.”

title: First Thing: Pause on US immigrant visa leaves thousands of applicants in limbo
author: Martin Belam
summary: All US immigrant visa applications halted as state department moves to tighten restrictions and limit access. Plus tributes pour in for Dolly Parton
body_text: Good morning. All US immigrant visa applications have been paused by the Trump administration as the state department moves to tighten restrictions and limit access to applicants whom they deem could need US assistance. The agency launched the initiative at all embassies and consulates in early August. Applicants with scheduled interviews were sent emails that their appointments had been canceled. Agency officials claim this will ensure visa applicants will not end up relying on US public benefits. This week the Trump administration also announced plans to revoke visas from asylum seekers who had initially entered the US for tourism or business. Up to 200,000 people seeking asylum could be affected. Is the move lawful? “The court made clear that immigration laws cannot be used to justify discrimination,” Joanna Cuevas Ingram, a senior staff attorney at the National Immigration Law Center, said. In February, a federal judge overturned the president’s attempt to suspend the US refugee system entirely. Instagram CEO denies company hid low use of teen safety feature in Meta trial Adam Mosseri, the first senior Meta executive to testify in a historic lawsuit brought by 29 US states, disputed allegations by US prosecutors that his company hid negative information from the public in a court in California. Questioned over touting a feature called Take a Break, meant to encourage teens to close Instagram if they had been scrolling for a while, Mosseri was asked about not disclosing low user numbers for features geared toward teen safety. He brushed the concerns aside, saying: “We don’t publish every single stat. I’ve definitely said publicly that the opt-in rates are low. I don’t know if I’ve said numbers.” Just 1.8% of teens signed up for the feature. Why are the states suing Meta? The lawsuit centers on the allegations that Meta deliberately designed addictive products that hooked young people, leading to mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and suicide. Meta has denied all allegations, saying the states are chasing an “outlandish payout”. At least 14 newborn babies die in fire at Pakistan hospital’s maternity ward At least 14 newborn babies have died in a fire that broke out in the maternity ward at one of Pakistan’s most prominent state hospitals. The blaze began in the early hours of Wednesday and engulfed the ward at Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, the biggest state hospital in Islamabad. Dr Aneza Jalil, a hospital spokesperson, said 15 babies were on the ward at the time and that “one baby was saved by a doctor”. Women who had just given birth were forced to run down several flights of stairs to evacuate. Investigators were still at the scene and authorities have not confirmed the cause. How have authorities responded? The prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, directed authorities to conduct an immediate investigation. “Such a situation involving children is irreparable,” said Sharif. “Those responsible should be identified and the strictest action should be taken.” Trump threatens to demolish Kennedy Center if $250m renovation not done The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts could be demolished if repairs are not carried out, the Trump administration has warned in a court filing. Lawyers for the US president said the national arts complex in Washington DC must undergo a $250m renovation or risk facing the wrecking ball. The threat emerged on Monday as the administration urged a federal judge to reject a fresh legal challenge to Trump’s efforts to put his name on the Kennedy Center. The dispute has become part of a months-long battle over the president’s attempt to alter the memorial created by Congress in honor of John F Kennedy. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. What other changes has Trump already made in Washington DC? Trump has demolished the East Wing of the White House to make way for a $600m ballroom and ordered a renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool that resulted in algae blooms and a peeling liner. The Kennedy Center board has voted to change the building’s signage to read: “The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump.” It also voted to name the grounds the “President Donald J Trump Plaza”. In other news … South Carolina voters have chosen Darline Graham as the Republican nominee for US Senate. She overcame concern about her lack of legislative experience to beat the five-term congressman Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s Republican special primary runoff. An Ecuadorian mother and daughter were arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at a hospital after a car crash in central Florida. A polygamous sect leader serving a 50-year federal sentence for orchestrating sex involving children was given another 24 years in prison on separate state convictions for child abuse. The father of a US navy sailor who has been deployed on the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier has been released from immigration detention, according to his family. Stat of the day: At least 47 killed and dozens kidnapped in gang attack near Haiti capital At least 47 people were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped when armed men attacked a once peaceful community near Haiti’s capital. A gang leader has threatened to kill hostages if authorities kill any gang member, piercing the belief that security in the Caribbean country was improving. Well Actually: 11 gym dos and don’ts from fitness experts Hogging weights? Loud grunting? Sweaty benches? Here’s what professionals have to say about good workout etiquette, from using equipment to being on your phone. Don’t miss this: Dolly Parton, country star, actor and philanthropist, remembered The world feels a little dimmer today without Dolly in it after her death was announced by her nephew Bryan Seaver on Instagram. We have lots of coverage worth spending a little time with – an appreciation of her music by critic Alexis Petridis, a wonderful gallery of her life in pictures, a selection of her greatest quotes, Hannah Marriott writing on Parton’s unique fashion style, and a list of her 10 best recordings. You can share your tributes and memories of the country music icon with us too. Rest well, Dolly. Climate check: Record-breaking heat dome expected to bring dangerous temperatures to US south-west Surging temperatures are expected to broil more than 45 million people as a heat dome settles across the south-western US through the end of August and into early September, according to the National Weather Service. Last Thing: Call to ban marmot hunting in France as campaigners say they are ‘killed for fun’ Animal rights campaigners are gearing up for protests and petitions aimed at persuading the French government to ban the hunting of Alpine marmots. Although the marmot is not a threatened species, its numbers are reportedly declining as a result of the climate emergency. Campaigners say they are opposed to them being hunted for fun. title: Texas law banning drag shows where children may be present struck down again
author: Edward Helmore
summary: ‘This is a profoundly flawed decision that endangers our children and is an affront to Texas values,’ Ken Paxton says
body_text: A federal judge has, for a second time, struck down a Texas state law banning drag performances in settings where children may be present. In a ruling issued on Tuesday, US district judge David Hittner said Texas cannot enforce its drag show ban. He said that the measure improperly restricts speech and violates the first amendment of the US constitution. The Texas ban, known as Senate bill 12, was passed in March 2023 and bans drag performers from dancing suggestively or wearing certain prosthetics on public property or in front of children, or “sexually-oriented performance” presented on the premises in the presence of an individual younger than 18 years of age. Advocacy groups sued the state after the bill’s passage, arguing the ban on “sexually oriented performance” infringed on constitutional rights. Texas’s move was just one across several states in 2023, driven by a right-wing backlash to increasing queer and transgender rights and equality. Hittner initially declared the ban unconstitutional in September 2023, but it was unblocked by the 5th US circuit court of appeals in 2025, which returned the case to the judge. That allowed Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton, who is locked in a race for a US Senate seat against Democrat James Talarico, to resume enforcing the law earlier this year. The new ruling prevents Paxton from enforcing the law. Paxton said he would appeal the decision. “This is a profoundly flawed decision that endangers our children and is an affront to Texas values,” Paxton on X. In his ruling, Hittner advised anyone “who find such activities as described in this case offensive” to “just don’t go”. The ruling mentioned Dolly Parton, who died on Tuesday, when it critiqued the law’s definition of banning performances that “appeal to the prurient interest”. Hittner cited people who would chastise Parton “as a voluptuous sex symbol because of her big hair, flamboyant clothes and breast exposure”. “There are ‘erotic’ elements in countless popular performances that could be subject to both civil and criminal penalties under SB 12,” Hittner wrote. Hittner said the terms used in the legislation were so broad they could block performers like Lady Gaga or Miley Cyrus from performing in the state. “Even if S.B. 12 were somehow content-neutral (an argument the Attorney General has never advanced), it still prohibits huge swaths of constitutionally protected performances. Because the term ‘prurient interest in sex’ is open-ended, SB 12 can be used to cherry-pick particular aspects of performances that might be ‘in some sense erotic’,” Hittner wrote. He said that because the law was very broad it caused some everyday activities, including “cheerleading, dancing, live theater, and other common public occurrences” to be regarded as civil or criminal violations. He also said that the law was vague on its face and that it failed “to give a reasonable person notice of what is prohibited”. Civil liberties groups welcomed the ruling. “Drag has a rich history as a refuge of joy and liberation for countless Texans, and it’s not going anywhere,” said the Texas chapter of the ACLU in a statement. “All Texans – no matter our gender or background – are guaranteed the right to free expression,” it added. Brigitte Bandit, a plaintiff in the case who impersonates Parton, celebrated the ruling on social media. “Drag is free speech, b----.” She announced she would also perform as Parton, who gave her a rhinestone guitar as a gift in 2023, at an Austin bar Saturday in her honor.

title: Three pro-Israel Democrats given key roles on House foreign affairs panel
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: Debbie Wasserman Schultz and Wesley Bell to join as Jared Moskowitz becomes ranking member on subcommittee
body_text: Three pro-Israel Democrats have been given key roles on a powerful congressional body overseeing US foreign policy in a move running sharply counter to popular sentiment within the party and likely to anger leftwing activists. The appointments to the US House of Representatives foreign affairs committee follow a succession of wins in party primaries for progressive candidates who put criticism of Israel and its actions in Gaza at the core of their campaign messages. In an apparent effort to stem the anti-Israeli tide, Debbie Wasserman Schultz, a representative from Florida, and the Missouri representative Wesley Bell will join the committee, while Jared Moskowitz, also from Florida, becomes the Democrats’ ranking member on the subcommittee for the Middle East and North Africa. All three recently defeated primary challengers who targeted them for their pro-Israel positions. Mark Pocan, a progressive Democrat from Wisconsin who has vocally criticised the powerful American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or Aipac, also joins the committee. Moskowitz, who last week defeated an anti-Zionist democratic socialist challenger, Oliver Larkin, vowed to use his new position to advance support for Israel. “At a moment of enormous change across the region, I’ll work to strengthen America’s relationships with Israel and our Gulf allies, expand regional peace, advance American diplomacy, and ensure our foreign policy is grounded in strength, security, and reality. I’m ready to get to work,” he posted on social media. He predicted his position would become vital if the Democrats retake the House in November’s midterm elections, as many polls indicate. “If Democrats take control of the House, I’ll be in a position to help steer US policy on Israel and the Middle East,” Moskowitz told Axios. In a statement on Wednesday, the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair) expressed “deep concern” with the appointments of three Democrats whom it described as being among “the Israeli government’s most committed and consistent enablers”. Their elevation was an “insult to American voters and a desperate attempt to shield the Israeli government from accountability”, said Edward Ahmed Mitchell, the group’s national deputy director. “These decisions must not stand.” In this month’s primary campaign, Moskowitz accused Larkin, his opponent, of antisemitism and refused to debate him. One rabbi reportedly urged Republican congregants to register as Democrats in order to vote for Moskowitz. Wasserman Schultz won her primary after her congressional district was heavily redrawn, beating her main challenger, 27-year-old Elijah Manley, who also criticised her support for Israel and acceptance of financial donations from Aipac. Bell won a rematch poll against the former Democratic representative Cori Bush, who he defeated in a 2024 primary. Bush was a vocal critic of Israel’s military offensive in Gaza. Polls consistently show a loss of support for Israel among a US electorate that once staunchly backed it. The drop in support is particularly pronounced among younger voters, with older Republicans and white evangelicals being the only groups showing majorities holding favorable views of Israel, according to a Pew Poll in April. A leftwing Democrat, Angie Nixon – a vocal critic of Israel – last week won a special election to become the party’s Senate candidate in Florida in November.

title: Should Kamala Harris run for president again? ‘Nope,’ says Iowa Democrat
author: Rachel Leingang
summary: ‘We need some new leadership,’ says the Democratic nominee for governor in Iowa, Rob Sand
body_text: The Democratic nominee for governor in Iowa bluntly answered a question that scores of national Democrats have thus far refused to respond to. Asked by Politico whether the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee, Kamala Harris, should run for president again, Rob Sand responded: “Nope.” Sand, who Democrats hope can flip the midwestern state back to their control this year, also said he would not want former president Joe Biden or Harris to campaign for him in the state, where he will need to win over independent and Republican voters to win in November. “Can he even do that right now?” Sand responded when asked by the Politico columnist Jonathan Martin whether he would want Biden to campaign for him in Iowa. When asked whether he would want Harris to campaign for him in Iowa, he said: “No thanks.” “We need some new leadership,” he added. Prominent national Democrats have often dodged the question when asked directly, saying it is Harris’s choice or that the 2028 presidential field is too far away for them to opine. Harris, the former US vice-president who lost the 2024 presidential election to Donald Trump, has not said whether she would seek another run for president – only saying she has “not made a decision”. Mary Peltola, a Democrat running in Alaska who similarly needs to win over non-Democrats to flip a US Senate seat, rejected support from Harris, who sent a fundraising email on Peltola’s behalf that appeared to be unsolicited by the candidate. Peltola’s campaign said she “isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 – her focus is and always will be Alaska”. Sand, expanding on his thoughts, noted to Politico that he is the state auditor of Iowa and running to be governor, so his focus is on his own state and the issues that affect its people and differentiate him from his opponent, Republican Zach Lahn. He also gave a blunt “no” when asked if he would one day run for president, or be open to being tapped as a vice-presidential candidate. “You’re asking a guy who was a registered independent first,” Sand said. “I don’t tend to like the party politics stuff. I think that we have a fundamentally broken two-choice political system. I don’t think that either the Democratic or the Republican parties are solving enough problems or deserve special legal privileges in order to force us to pick between the lesser of two evils. My inclination is that I want it to be shaken up.”

title: How to lose Trump’s trade war: test Canada’s resolve with threats to hockey sticks
author: Adam Gabbatt
summary: The US president expected Ottawa to bow to tariff demands, but Canada is striking back – and it could cost Americans
body_text: Earlier this year, a survey found that Canada, along with Switzerland, was the best-liked country in the world. We all know this kind of polling is about as scientific as a high school popularity contest, but at least anecdotally, Canadians have a reputation for being friendly and welcoming, respectful and polite. Many people would find it difficult to dislike Canadians. But not Donald Trump, who in a “hold my beer” moment this week demonstrated that he, at least, finds it easy to resent Canadians. The US president called the country “difficult and unreasonable”, and in a particularly hysterical moment, threatened to rename a lake, after trade talks collapsed. Days earlier, Trump had claimed a deal with Canada was imminent, which would avoid the new taxes. But, in a development that surely galled the Art of the Deal author, there was no agreement. Instead, Trump and his team demonstrated the art of collapsing the deal, as trade talks fell apart due to what Canada said were unreasonable, last-minute demands from the US side. It meant that the US tariffs duly came in on Saturday, applied to various Canadian exports including hockey sticks and tongue depressors, but if Trump expected Canada to bow to his demands – the president was seeking more favorable terms on things like steel and aluminum – he was disappointed. Instead, Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister who has emerged as a rare world leader willing to stand up to Trump, said Canada had been “attacked”, and announced retaliatory tariffs on about $20bn worth of US goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment. All this means US consumers are seeing surging prices on all kinds of products – including toilet paper. My colleague Lauren Aratani reports that “the US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population”. And this outsize usage has grown more expensive. “Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, they heavily rely on lumber-rich Canada for raw materials,” she writes. It’s fair to say that Canada’s retaliation upset Trump, who famously loves to win. On Tuesday, he claimed the US “is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer” – we’ll see how that goes – and has dubbed Canadian negotiators “clowns”. Earlier this week, Trump compared Doug Ford, the premier of Ontario, unfavorably to his deceased brother Rob, the scandal-plagued former mayor of Toronto, whose time in office saw him admit to smoking crack cocaine and being “hammered” in public. And while Trump was flailing about, JD Vance was doing his best Scrappy-Doo, “lemme at ’em” impression, lobbing insults at Canada from the safety of a Republican rally in Maine. Vance claimed that Canada and China are “the two worst countries when it comes to trade policy anywhere in the world”. He added: “We have to remember, Canada is a state. Sorry. Freudian slip. That was actually an accident.” The satisfied look on his face didn’t make it seem like one. Vance went on to add that Canada “quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America”. It was an interesting take, given the only country that has mused about invading Canada is the US – as recently as last year Trump was threatening to annex the nation. So in a nutshell: Donald Trump has led the US into an unsavory spat against the world’s most popular country, a scrap that could result in Americans – less than three months out from crucial midterm elections in which Republicans face an uphill battle – struggle to pay for a roll of toilet paper. Win!

title: Federal appeals court declines to dismiss criminal charges against US congresswoman
author: Rachel Leingang
summary: LaMonica McIver, a Democrat from New Jersey, was charged with interfering with an arrest in May 2025 at ICE facility
body_text: A federal appeals court has declined to dismiss criminal charges against a sitting US congresswoman who visited an immigration facility as part of congressional oversight. LaMonica McIver, a Democrat who represents New Jersey’s 10th congressional district, was charged with interfering with an arrest in May 2025 outside Delaney Hall, an immigration detention facility that has drawn protests over poor conditions inside. Criticizing a decision that she said “emboldens” Donald Trump’s officials to pursue people who seek to hold the administration accountable, McIver said she would “not fold” to pressure. McIver has pleaded not guilty and argued she is immune from prosecution under the US constitution’s speech and debate clause because she was doing her job. She has argued that she has been selectively prosecuted by the Trump administration, and sought to have the case thrown out. McIver, a mother of one who is expecting her second child this fall, previously told the Guardian the Trump administration is trying to make an “example” of her by charging her. She is the only member of Congress whom Trump’s Department of Justice has indicted. A lower court ruled against dismissing the charges, which she appealed to the third circuit court of appeals. In a 2-1 ruling, the appellate court wrote that McIver’s actions outside Delaney Hall were “non-legislative”, meaning they would not make her immune from prosecution because she was fulfilling her job duties. It ruled against dismissing two of the three counts, and sent a third, broader count back to the lower court for more fact-finding. One of the counts in question “neither charges Congresswoman McIver for an act that is legislative in nature nor requires that she answer for any legislative act”, Judge Cindy Chung wrote. “I fundamentally believe that the court got it wrong here. To protect the people, their elected representatives must be authorized to conduct oversight of the executive branch without fear of retaliation,” McIver said in a statement. “Today’s decision chills that authority and emboldens the Trump administration to continue persecuting our most vulnerable communities, those who try to defend them, and anyone who dares hold the president or his lackeys accountable. “I will not fold to this administration. We are exploring every possible option. The administration will not stop me from doing my job or standing for what is right. This is not over.” On the 9 May 2025 visit to Delaney Hall, McIver joined other elected officials in an inspection of the facility, a task given to members of Congress that the Trump administration has sought to limit. Ras Baraka, the Newark mayor, who joined the officials, was asked to leave because he was not a member of the US Congress, and he was arrested for trespassing. Charges against Baraka were subsequently dropped, but McIver was charged with assaulting, impeding and interfering with an arrest. The charges carry up to 17 years in prison. Charging documents noted that people, including members of Congress, surrounded Baraka to prevent his arrest and alleged that McIver shouted “hell, no” repeatedly. The Washington Post, after analyzing video from many angles, said McIver “made contact with at least two agents” in the scuffle, but that it was “difficult to discern the force of the contact and to what extent it was intentional or the result of the chaotic moment”. Paul Fishman, McIver’s attorney, said after Wednesday’s decision: “As we argued before the court, it is too dangerous if the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security are able to thwart members of Congress from inspecting an ICE detention facility, create chaos, and then prosecute those members and pretend it was their fault.”

title: Morning Mail: Australians among hundreds caught in deadly Nepal floods, Meta settles landmark lawsuit, Tim Curry dies
author: Martin Farrer
summary: At least 157 dead in Himalayan disaster; residents in Tasmania angry at planned AI datacentre
body_text: Good morning. More than 150 people are dead and hundreds more are missing – including a reported 34 Australian tourists – after a flash flood swept away houses, roads and bridges on the Nepal-Tibet border. Residents in Tasmania are angry at the planning process around a datacentre, while our economics columnist wonders if it’s worth building them at all, and could they cost Donald Trump the midterms? Plus: Meta settles a landmark lawsuit with US states over harm to children, and the Rocky Horror star Tim Curry has died. Australia Icac denial | The sister-in-law of former Liberal NSW premier Dominic Perrottet has told the state Icac hearing that she rejected the suggestion that she had been put in an “impossible situation” and lied under oath to cover illegal donations to her husband, an inquiry has heard. Datacentre debate | As Anthony Albanese endured a tough day wrangling the issue of datacentres at national cabinet, people in northern Tasmania were still seething after their local council approved a new facility that they say threatens to use excessive water and energy. Health saving | Removing the higher private health insurance rebate for people aged 65 and over is good policy that is unlikely to place additional pressure on public hospitals, according to health economists. Comic cut | The Egyptian-American comedian Bassem Youssef has announced his imminent Australian tour has been postponed after he was asked to provide background checks as part of his visa application. Royal commission | From the initial rumpus over Dennis Richardson to victims sharing their anguish, Ben Doherty picks key moments from the four months of the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion. World Himalayan disaster | At least 157 people have died and hundreds are missing after flash floods ⁠hit the Himalayan border areas of ⁠Nepal and Tibet. Many of the missing are overseas tourists, including at least 33 Britons and 34 Australians (by one early estimate). Meta settles | Meta reached an agreement of up to US$18bn to settle a landmark case brought by states across the US that accused the tech giant of addicting and harming children with dangerous products, according to a court filing. Dementia clue | Women using hormone replacement therapy are at lower risk of dementia, a new study suggests, with scientists finding those who had used HRT were 10% less likely to be diagnosed with the condition. ‘Escape wizard’ | Police in Spain have arrested a dangerous Albanian criminal nicknamed the “escape wizard” who has managed to break out of four jails in Italy and Belgium. Tim Curry tributes | Tim Curry, the versatile performer of screen and stage, who made his name as the flamboyant Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Show, has died aged 80. Our chief film critic pays tribute to Curry’s subversive blast of fun. Full Story Decoding America: Could datacentres lose Trump the midterms? Co-hosts Jonathan Yerushalmy and Reged Ahmad explore why datacentres in the US have provoked such anger – and whether that could harm Republicans in the midterms. In-depth The millions of dollars being invested in datacentres does not impress Greg Jericho. He explains in his column why it’s unlikely to lift living standards for Australians, isn’t showing up as any meaningful construction industry boost, and could also provoke another rate rise. Meanwhile fears are rising that the Reserve Bank will hit millions of mortgage holders with a fourth rate hike this year due to stubbornly high inflation. Not the news Does anyone need to spend $1,000 on a pillow? Thaslima Begum went in search of the perfect sleep and found that slumbering bliss comes at a price. Sport Tennis | On the eve of what she hopes will be a US Open challenge, Amanda Anisimova talks about learning to cope with the stresses of the tour and bouncing back. Football | Uefa is poised to drop its threatened boycott of Fifa competitions after receiving guarantees that the global governing body will never attempt a repeat of Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup. A winner of that tournament, Emiliano Martínez, could be leaving Aston Villa for Chelsea, and there’s Carabao Cup action in England this morning. Cricket | Joe Root’s “robust conversation” with the England Test squad at Lord’s this week has finally ended any uncertainty about the conduct expected of them, according to fast bowler Josh Tongue. Media roundup The Australian claims that Labor will soon reveal its plans for immigration levels, with restrictions expected on international students and onshore visa applications. The WA government is appealing the landmark Yindjibarndi compensation ruling, WAtoday reports, seeking “clarity” on the $150m judgment. The Broncos star Reece Walsh faces sanction by the club after liking a post that criticised the coach, the Courier Mail reports. What’s happening today Business | Wesfarmers, Star Entertainment Group and Qantas release full year results. Sydney | Full federal court appeal hearing by retired judge Walter Sofronoff over finding of corrupt conduct in Bruce Lehrmann inquiry. Darwin | Reforms to legalise voluntary assistant dying expected to be debated in the Northern Territory parliament. title: No more UK energy bills support likely before price cap rise
author: Jessica Elgot and Jillian Ambrose
summary: Andy Burnham stops short of pledging further help as gas and electricity prices due to increase by 4% in October
body_text: Households are unlikely to receive further energy bills support before the October price cap, though more targeted measures could be looked at if there is a further shock in January, government sources said. Gas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from October under the new cap. The government has already removed VAT from domestic electricity bills to save average households £45 a year, a move announced in Andy Burnham’s first week in office. Prices had climbed by 13% at the start of July to take account of global energy market price rises caused by the US war on Iran and the closure of the strait of Hormuz. Burnham said on Wednesday that rising energy bills were “difficult for people and I recognise that” but he stopped short of promising intervention beyond the VAT cut, saying the government “would continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term”. Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said bills were being driven up by the Iran war and the government would “keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills”. The chancellor, John Healey, said the government would look again towards the end of the year at whether more support was needed. “No government can stop the squeeze felt by families and businesses with a global shock of this magnitude. It’s being felt around the world. But we can keep close watch as we move towards the new year, and we remain focused on giving families a bit of breathing space with the cost of living,” he told the Sun. “We’re a government that will look for practical action – working to put our country on a more resilient footing so we can better weather these shocks in future.” Burnham will continue his summer tour of the UK on Thursday with a stop in south Wales, promising to win back the trust of voters after historic losses for Labour in the May Senedd elections. “The answers to the UK’s challenges will not come from an echo chamber. They will come from the places that know their own strengths, and from a government willing to listen and then act,” he said ahead of the visit. The prime minister will spend the morning speaking to workers and apprentices, including about the cost of living and reindustrialisation, and the cost of energy is likely to be a key part of discussions. The Resolution Foundation thinktank, which has close ties to the government, suggested there should be targeted support designed, costed and ready to switch on if needed from January, when bills have been forecast to rise again by up to 9%. It said this should go beyond those on benefits and target those earning less than £24,000 a year, reaching about 40% of households, with potential savings of £175 on average. The thinktank’s chief executive, Ruth Curtice, said: “The rise in energy bills in October has been tempered but not avoided by the government’s decision to reduce electricity bills for everyone through a VAT cut. With wholesale gas prices hitting new post-Iran highs in the past week, there is a real risk of further rises in January. Given the acute pressure on both family and government budgets, we need a better mechanism for targeted support ready to activate if needed.” The Trades Union Congress renewed its call for a windfall tax on bank profits to pay for a cut to bills. Its general secretary, Paul Nowak, said the government should be looking at ways now to fund more support for households this winter. “The government is going to have to keep going on measures to boost living standards – starting with a tax on banks’ enormous profits to cut energy bills for the majority of households,” he said. “It’s the right thing to do. Banks are raking it in while many up and down the country are struggling to get by – they can well afford to pay more tax.” Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, was preparing targeted support for energy bills before Burnham became prime minister. She told the Commons in March she wanted to “ensure that we are in a position in the autumn to have a targeted approach”. Government sources suggested that any further support would be costed in the budget and officials would wait to see how the conflict in the Gulf developed over the coming months, including whether the strait of Hormuz could be reopened. Burnham has suggested he is open to allowing more drilling sites in the North Sea if a quasi-judicial process approves exploration of the Jackdaw and Rosebank fossil fuel sites. That is likely to cause a backlash from some Labour MPs, but in a interview with the FT Burnham pointed to the “pragmatic approach” taken by the green energy entrepreneur and climate campaigner Dale Vince, who recently backed both schemes on the BBC’s Newsnight programme. Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary and now foreign secretary, once called the Rosebank proposal “climate vandalism”, and climate experts have warned that the environmental damage caused by developing the oil and gas fields would destroy any economic benefits.

title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez rejoins DSA after membership lapse of seven years
author: Maya Yang
summary: Then House candidate joined Democratic Socialists of America in 2018 but didn’t renew membership after a year
body_text: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has rejoined the Democratic Socialists of America after not renewing her membership for seven years, amid speculation that she might run for president in 2028. The 36-year-old New York representative and one of the country’s most prominent democratic socialists renewed her membership in the group’s national organization after reports emerged earlier this month that it had lapsed. Ocasio-Cortez initially joined the group in 2018. In a statement on Tuesday night, the DSA announced: “Democratic Socialists of America confirms Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is a member in good standing of our organization, having recently rejoined in August 2026,” according to a report in City & State New York. It added: “Previously, the representative joined DSA in 2018 with a one-year membership, which DSA’s national leadership recently noticed had lapsed, in 2019. She has since renewed her membership as of this month.” DSA said it decided to disclose Ocasio-Cortez’s membership details amid reports that she could run for president in the next election cycle. Interest in the congresswoman’s status comes as the organization has seen its ranks grow exponentially across the country, following a string of election victories from New York to Florida. “While it is atypical for DSA to address the membership status of individuals, ongoing discussions about the 2028 presidential campaign have prompted this release … With chapters and members campaigning to draft Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as a potential Presidential Primary candidate, we believe that the status of her membership is essential information for members to have in their deliberations and discussions,” the statement said, as City & State New York reported. The Guardian reached out to the DSA for additional comment, but the organization declined. The Guardian has also contacted Ocasio-Cortez’s office. According to City & State New York, annual DSA membership cost $60 when Ocasio-Cortez joined in 2018, with members required to manually renew their dues each year. The organization has since moved to automatic renewals and introduced a range of monthly membership options, with dues ranging from $5 to $50. Despite Ocasio-Cortez having been a lapsed member of the DSA over the last seven years, in November 2020 the DSA offered its “congratulations to DSA member AOC on officially being re-elected to Congress” on X. Similarly, in March 2024, the DSA wrote on X: “We commend DSA members Rep @CoriBush and Rep @AOC for upholding our democratic values by voting against this authoritarian legislation,” referring to the now-former Missouri representative Cori Bush and Ocasio-Cortez voting against a TikTok ban. Earlier this month, in an interview on ABC, host Jonathan Karl asked Ocasio-Cortez whether she was still a member of DSA. She responded: “Of the New York City chapter.” “Not the national chapter?” Karl asked, to which Ocasio-Cortez replied: “No.” Asked to elaborate on the distinction, Ocasio-Cortez said: “Every DSA chapter is formed locally. And so the New York City DSA chapter, those are folks that you know, it’s kind of like your local union chapter.” In July 2024, DSA withdrew its endorsement of Ocasio-Cortez at the request of NYC-DSA, according to the organization, citing her decision to vote for a House resolution that described “denial of Israel’s right to exist” as an example of antisemitism, as well as her participation in a recent panel discussion on antisemitism. “A national DSA endorsement comes with a serious commitment to the movement for Palestine and our collective socialist project … To build a socialist movement that’s capable of defeating capitalism, we must demand more from leaders in our movement,” DSA said at the time. It added: “AOC recently hosted a public panel with leaders from the Jewish Council for Public Affairs, lobbyists for the [International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance] definition of antisemitism. On this panel, anti-Zionism and antisemitism were conflated and boycotting Zionist institutions was condemned. This sponsorship is a deep betrayal to all those who’ve risked their welfare to fight Israeli apartheid and genocide through political and direct action in recent months, and in decades past.”

title: Jon Ossoff went low on Natalie Harp. The plan worked
author: Moira Donegan
summary: The senator’s remarks reflect a turning point in Democrats’ attacks on the president. What should we make of them?
body_text: Apparently, he likes to say her name with a French accent. “Na-tah-lee!” the president cries out, in that affected tone of faux-formality that one might use with a person they love but do not quite respect, and she comes running, her thin legs teetering on her heels. Natalie Harp, Trump’s 35-year-old “executive assistant”, was an odd recurring character in the latest blockbuster Trump administration book, Regime Change, by the New York Times’ Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. In the book, Harp features like a silent sentinel, ever present but eerily quiet as Trump rants and raves. It’s not exactly clear what the scope of her responsibilities is; though, as Jamelle Bouie points out, the fact that she evidently helps run the president’s social media accounts, which can sway markets and influence his foreign counterparts, makes her one of the most powerful people in the federal government. But the dignity of Harp’s character does not often seem to equal the gravity of her influence: once, she was caught on video sprinting across a golf course on foot, chasing the golf cart that was speeding the president away to the next hole. For a while, she was called the “human printer” among Trump aides, in reference to the portable printer that Harp carries around with her: one of the primary ways she spends her time appears to be searching for flattering news stories and social media commentary about the president online, and printing it out to nourish his self-regard. But from Haberman and Swan’s reporting, it was not always clear exactly what Harp was thinking. Though many Trumpworld insiders are clearly identifiable as off-the-record sources in their book, Harp does not seem to be among them. But recently, more of Harp’s own words have come to light. The Daily Beast published the full text of two letters from Harp to Trump, whose existence had previously been reported by Haberman and Swan. In the letters, Harp is rapturously worshipful, sycophantic, almost slavish. “You are all that matters to me,” she wrote to Trump. She called him her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”. (The capitalization is in the original.) It’s long been known that Trump prizes devotion among his underlings, that he seeks out flattering commentary about himself, and that he is surrounded, particularly in his second term, exclusively by the kind of people who will never tell him anything that he does not want to hear. Still, the spectacle of Harp’s obsequiousness – her willingness to debase herself for an 80-year-old man whose vulgarity, misogyny, racism, narcissism and impulsiveness have damaged her country in ways it will probably never recover from – is disturbing and grotesque. Still, Harp herself might be less unsettling than the near certainty that there are others like her – White House staffers and federal bureaucrats and petty functionaries of the Maga machine – who have made flattery of Trump a large portion, if not the entirety, of their jobs. Probably, few Americans would ever have heard of Harp if it were not for Jon Ossoff, the Democratic Georgia senator running for re-election and widely assumed to be mulling a presidential bid, who mentioned Harp in a pointed barb in a campaign stump speech in Atlanta. Trump, Ossoff said, doesn’t want to do the job of president; he wants, instead, to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie”. We do not need to be stupid: it strains credulity, and discredits the considerable savvy of Ossoff’s team, to claim that this remark was not meant to arouse salacious suspicion about the nature of Harp’s relationship with the president, and speculation that it might be sexual. Ossoff’s wording retained plausible deniability; still, I think he knew exactly what he was doing. Ossoff, in his campaign, has styled himself as firm-minded, resolute and morally ambitious – an inheritor to Barack Obama. But in this remark, he diverged noticeably from Michelle Obama’s famous mantra “when they go low, we go high,” which has long been a shibboleth for the kind of Democratic politicians who have preferred dignity over effectiveness in the Trump era. Ossoff was going low. It is shocking how well it worked. The evocation of Harp in Ossoff’s speech triggered a slew of news stories about the aide, delivered by White House reporters who seemed almost giddy to be able to cite as newsworthy something that before had been merely creepy. Asked about Harp on television, Haberman referred to her as Trump’s “binky” and “comfort blanket”, infantilizing him in humiliating terms. Trump surrogates were dispatched to defend Harp with a ferocity and insistence that couldn’t help but suggest that the president himself was angered. Ossoff, it seemed, had struck a nerve. At the beginning of Trump’s rise to power, many in politics gawked at his seemingly sui generis ability to dictate the news cycle: to say outrageous things, or make bizarre provocations, and send reporters, commentators, surrogates and his opponents into a frenzy trying to respond to them. The effect was that Trump determined the subject of discourse; everyone else responded to him. Ossoff turned the tables, and he made it look easy. One of the allegations that Trump’s aides spewed in their responses to the remark was that in insinuating that something inappropriate was afoot between Trump and Harp, Ossoff was being sexist. Those on the left rushed to discount this: no one, after all, really believes that Donald Trump, he of “grab ’em by the pussy”, is leading a movement that has serious or sincere concerns for women’s dignity. But to say that Ossoff’s remark contained no misogyny would be naive, if not dishonest: if his suggestion was made deliberately, then he was using Harp’s gender to undermine her professionalism, and to evoke a sex scandal. Of course there is misogyny in this gesture, the suggestion that a young woman is not entirely serious. That Harp’s character and conduct suggest this much more than her sex does need not force us to pretend not to see things that we do. What is the moral consequence of this kind of sexism, the kind that Ossoff evoked – obliquely, subtly, but definitely – with his remark? For my part, I do not see any equivalence between the misogyny imposed on American women by the Trump regime – or, for that matter, the misogyny imposed on American women by Trump personally – and the minor distastefulness of Ossoff. It’s like comparing a dropper of water to the Pacific Ocean. Every woman, every feminist, knows that she has accepted things out of necessity or convenience that the most stringent adherence to principle would require her to reject. And I confess, I am more encouraged by Ossoff’s pugnaciousness than I am put off by the gendered undertones of the remark. After all, it is a grim reality of our gendered world that wherever there is a straight man who esteems himself to be godlike and extraordinary, there will be a straight woman somewhere not far behind who inexplicably believes him. We must work on building a world where this is not true. The first step might be getting this guy out of the White House. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

title: In a Pennsylvania congressional swing district, a Republican incumbent faces allegations over embellishing résumé
author: Michael Sainato
summary: Ryan Mackenzie, running for re-election, is accused of ‘fabricating’ a career in the real estate industry
body_text: The Republican congressman Ryan Mackenzie has been accused of embellishing his résumé with private sector experience in real estate sales amid an acrimonious showdown over his Pennsylvania seat. Mackenzie, who has previously been accused of lying about his age on Tinder, “was a real estate salesperson licensed in PA”, according to his LinkedIn profile, and biographies have consistently listed it has his former profession. In a statement to the Guardian, however, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) accused the congressman of having “fabricated a career … that never existed”. His campaign would not comment on whether he ever used his real estate license, or made any sales. His office also did not respond to multiple requests for comment on the Tinder allegations, or reports of a staffer scrubbing the story from Wikipedia. Mackenzie is attempting to keep his seat in a Pennsylvania’s seventh congressional district, where he won his first term in 2024 by 1% of the vote. Trump won Pennsylvania in the US presidential election two years ago, after losing the state to Joe Biden in 2020. Mackenzie is running for his seat against Democrat Bob Brooks, former president of the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association – and has called his opponent a “fraud”, a “conman”, a “lobbyist”, a “dumpster fire candidate” and a “union boss”. Mackenzie’s campaign manager claimed Brooks has “all the hallmarks of a common criminal”. Ahead of the US midterm election in the battleground district, the DCCC has characterized Mackenzie as a career politician who has supported both Trump and policies pursued by the Trump administration that have resulted in increased costs for Americans – including tariffs and the war in Iran. As Mackenzie attacks Brooks, the DCCC has alleged Mackenzie has embellished his résumé, and pointed to misleading citations of “licensed real estate sales”. Mackenzie’s state representative campaign told Patch.com in 2012 he had “private sector experience as a real estate salesperson”. Mackenzie has cited holding a real estate license, which he received in 2006 in Pennsylvania, but did not renew when it expired in 2008. During this same period, he worked for the Republican Federal Committee of Pennsylvania and the US Department of Labor. “Ryan Mackenzie was already disgustingly caught lying about his age on his Tinder profile by nearly 10 years. Now it looks like Mackenzie and his allies have embellished his résumé and fabricated a career in real estate that never existed,” said Eli Cousin, a DCCC spokesperson, in a statement. “The truth is that Mackenzie is a career politician who has seemingly never worked a day in his life outside of politics and straight up does not understand the challenges that working Pennsylvanians are facing.” In 2024, it emerged that Mackenzie had claimed on his Tinder dating profile in 2020 that he was 29 years old when he was actually 37. His office did not deny the allegations at the time. For a 2025 Harvard Business School talk featuring the congressman, Mackenzie would “reflect on his career path from the real estate sector to public service at both the state and federal level”, according to the event’s web listing. A LinkedIn post for the event stated “discussions ranged from how Rep Mackenzie transitioned to and built a career in politics”. Harvard Business School did not respond to multiple requests for comment. A 2025 voter guide by Boeing’s political action committee stated: “Mackenzie worked in real estate.” In Mackenzie’s Pennsylvania state house biography, as part of his professional career history, he cites “licensed real estate sales”. “I was an employee at the US Department of Labor and also I used to hold my real estate salesperson’s license,” Mackenzie told a local Pennsylvania news outlet in 2012 while recounting his job experience. His congressional representative webpage bio cites the license, stating: “He worked on a number of political campaigns and earned his real estate sales license before entering public service.” A spokesperson for Mackenzie, Arnaud Armstrong, would not comment on whether Mackenzie ever used his real estate license or made any sales, and dismissed the touting of the credential as a career profession as “passing mentions, mostly from third parties”.

title: We surveyed 6,000 Americans. Here is the winning message for Democrats
author: Dustin Guastella and Erica Etelson
summary: It’s about ‘kitchen-table populism’: focusing on Americans’ day-to-day economic struggles
body_text: This year’s Democratic primaries look and sound a lot more populist than usual. Brian Poindexter, a union iron worker running on a “workers first” message, won a House primary outside Cleveland. Sherrod Brown is mounting a Senate comeback in Ohio on the same “rigged system” message that has allowed him to outshine other Democrats in Ohio. Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger who built his career fighting corporate landowners, is the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine. And Josh Turek, a self-described “prairie populist”, is on the Senate ballot in Iowa. In fact, according to research we’ve conducted through the Center for Working-Class Politics (CWCP), more than 70% of 2026 Democratic candidates now rely on populist rhetoric in their campaigns, laying the blame for our broken system on rich elites of one kind or another. It seems after decades of bleeding working-class support, Democrats are converging on a solution to win them back: run populists. The real question, then, is not whether Democrats should embrace populism, but rather what kind of populism they should embrace. To settle that argument, CWCP teamed up with the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative (RUBI) to conduct a new survey. In polling conducted by Verasight between late June and early July, we asked more than 6,000 Americans to rate 13 different kinds of messages commonly deployed by Democratic candidates to see which pitch would draw the strongest support. We also randomly presented each respondent with one of two Republican attack messages modeled on actual Republican campaign rhetoric in order to see how well Democratic messages hold up under attack. The top-performing messages we tested have a simple formula. They focus on Americans’ day-to-day struggles to pay for rent and groceries, and the widespread frustration with prices that rise faster than working-class wages. They insist that working people should be able to give their kids a better shot. They promise to bring costs down, make the biggest corporations pay their fair share, and crack down on the people who game the system. Ultimately, they tell a simple story: hard work should pay off. We call this winning combination “kitchen-table populism”. None of the plausible alternatives to this kind of messaging performed nearly as well. Consider what we call the “divide-and-conquer playbook” messaging popular with certain progressive campaign consultants. One prominent proponent of this style is the Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico. Talarico strikes a populist posture, emphasizing that economic elites keep working people divided over race, immigration, and cultural issues so that no one sees that they’re all getting fleeced. It sounds good, and Talarico is holding his own in red Texas, but this tactic is not the slam dunk against the culture war that some progressives think it is. In fact, in our survey, it was not all that effective, severely underperforming the pure kitchen-table messages we tested. The weakest variant of the divide-and-conquer narrative is the one that tells voters they’ve been tricked into blaming scapegoats. These “race-class narrative” appeals, so popular in progressives circles, finished at the bottom of the field. Why? Because telling people they’ve been duped comes off more like a condescending sermon than an invitation. Unlike kitchen-table populist messages that meet voters where they’re at, the race-class narrative strays from voters’ concrete economic woes to expound a more abstract theory of political gamesmanship. These messages trailed our top kitchen-table populist pitches with every group, including non-white voters and Democrats. Another alternative to populist messaging is a big-tent anti-Trumpism, pushed by some establishment liberals. The argument here is that candidates could unite all those Never-Trump Republicans, anti-Trump independents, and Resistance Democrats with a simple opposition message – one that steers clear of divisions over policy or ideology. Again, the theory makes sense. The trouble is that messaging focused on attacking Trump performed poorly across the board. We fielded the strongest-testing anti-Trump message we know, one that ties his attacks on democratic norms directly to pocketbook pain, and even this steelman version was a net negative with rural voters and Trump waverers. It wasn’t all roses for populism either. We found that anti-elite messages varied in their efficacy. While naming corruption, and promising to end it, was a powerful way to convey anti-elite sentiments – especially with Republicans, where adding an anti-corruption pledge to a plain cost-of-living pitch lifted support by 18 points – messages that leaned too stridently into class war turned off these same voters. Republicans swung 25 points against messages that blamed “big corporations” and “the wealthy few”. We also tested a progressive-coded anti-plutocrat message that railed against oligarchs and fascists: it trailed kitchen-table populism by about 14 points among Democrats and by huge margins among working-class, rural and swing voters. To be clear, this shouldn’t be understood as a plea for centrism or moderation. While it may seem like Democratic candidates are forced into a trade-off – either you opt to fire up the progressive base with ultra-liberal anti-Trump bromides or you aim to persuade Trump-voting working-class voters with a more conservative pitch – our results show that this is a false choice. The winning messages do neither; instead, they name a rigged system, call out the people rigging it, and promise to rebalance the economy in favor of those who work for a living. But they also avoid moral high-handedness and the preachy activist rhetoric that turns off many working-class, rural and swing voters. These are the lessons Democrats must internalize if they want to win back the working class, including some of the 59% of working-class white voters who, according to a March poll by Catalist, still plan to vote Republican in 2026. Some of the strongest-performing Democrats have already shown the power of kitchen-table populism in tough districts. Pat Ryan rode what he calls “patriotic populism” to a 14-point win in a Hudson Valley swing district in 2024, naming greedy corporations and corrupt politicians as the villains while casting working people as heroes. And Gabe Vasquez has won one of the country’s toughest seats in rural New Mexico twice with a similar pitch: Vasquez points the finger at corporate landlords, elites in Washington DC, and price-gouging investors who get rich by bending the rules, while praising hard-working blue-collar families that are struggling to stay afloat. That’s the winning formula, one we hope to see more Democrats and independents deploy. Dustin “Dino” Guastella is director of operations for Teamsters Local 623 in Philadelphia and sits on the board of the Center for Working-Class Politics Erica Etelson is president of the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative

title: Unlike needy Keir, trash-talking Andy speaks a language Trump understands
author: John Crace
summary: Burnham has nothing to hide as he prepares to meet president he once called poisonous. It may actually win him more respect
body_text: It makes a pleasant change. Not so long ago, Keir Starmer was falling over himself in his efforts to keep things sweet with Donald Trump. Offering the US president a second state visit within minutes of meeting him. Everyone knows you should never put out on the first date: it only makes the other person think you’re a pushover. Sure enough, The Donald banked the marching bands and the Windsor silver service, made polite conversation for three days and then went back to trash-talking him. Yet still, Starmer just sat there and took it. As if one word of criticism would be too much. Wittering on about the “special relationship” as if Trump gave a moment’s thought to the UK before he did anything. The rest of us wouldn’t have put money on the US president even being able to locate Britain on a map. It was only latterly, when The Donald chose to bomb Iran, that the penny finally dropped for Keir. And even then he looked pained by the apparent betrayal, as he resisted the calls of Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage to join in the war. No such misgivings for Andy Burnham. This week, the prime minister was reminded that when he had been mayor of Greater Manchester, he had said The Donald wouldn’t be welcome in his city and that he could take his poisonous politics elsewhere. Words that had been loudly cheered at the time by many in Britain who had had enough of all the toadying. After all, it wasn’t as if the Trump-whispering had made any difference. If anything, it had only added to his contempt for us. You’ll never get any thanks from a narcissist. Nor did Andy have any regrets now that he was prime minister and was likely to meet Trump in person for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York at the end of next month. Far from it. “Shit happens” was pretty much his precis of what had gone down. He wasn’t going to apologise to The Donald for what he had said. Not least because he had meant every word. This was the real world. Politicians say stuff. Trump had said all sorts of things about him, too. That he had been mayor of “some town”. To be fair to Agent Orange, it’s quite likely he had never heard of Manchester before. Neither geography nor an interest in other people have ever been his strongest suits. All he had known about Andy was that he was “extremely liberal”. Which in Maga language is the same as saying he’s a “Commy bastard”. So here was Burnham’s deal. He wasn’t planning to go out of his way to insult the US president, but neither would he be offering unexpurgated sycophancy. Instead, we would be getting a very British type of pragmatism. He would do what was necessary in the UK’s interest but not much more. They would be polite and try not to accentuate their differences, but there would be no pretence of any lasting friendship. Just stick to the matters in hand and get the hell out. After New York, Andy wouldn’t be sending weekly WhatsApps. Out of sight, out of mind. Weirdly, this performative show of an ersatz friendship – the US and UK are meant to be more or less on the same side, after all – is likely to be far more effective than Keir’s more needy approach. Because this is the type of language The Donald understands. Although he craves the fawning, he has no respect for those who offer it. He takes it as a sign of weakness. Equally, no amount of flattery is ever enough. There is a hole in Trump’s psyche that can never be filled. With Burnham, there is going to be more a meeting of equals. Two world leaders who are doing what it takes to get along with each other. It’s as close to respect as a sociopath like Trump can get. Andy hasn’t taken a backward step, or attempted to deny his previous comments. More that that was then and this was now. Just get used to it. You can say one thing one day and the opposite the next. It’s up to the other person to work out which one was the truth. Or maybe neither, or maybe both. After all, that’s precisely what The Donald does. Contradiction is his modus operandi. And it’s got him to the White House. So if it works for Trump, why not for Burnham? Sincerity can be an overrated virtue for a world leader. You don’t always need a Love, Actually moment to make your feelings known. “So I’m looking forward, actually, to my first meeting [with Trump],” said Andy. And he probably is. His cards are on the table and he has nothing to hide. Plus, he has a sense of humour and self-deprecation, which also might confuse the US president, who has neither. It also feels as if there’s less at stake with this meeting than there was with many of Starmer’s. Back in the early days of Trump’s presidency, it was as if much of the world was holding its breath for what he might do next. Now, not so much. We’ve all learned to adapt to The Donald. Even to his never-ending war with Iran, which has jacked up the cost of living. All his bad habits are now priced in. And suddenly he looks more vulnerable. A man who has found the world doesn’t automatically bend to his will. A man who is under pressure on the domestic front, with many Americans fed up with his foreign wars and angry at the cost of petrol (never get between an American and their car). A president facing tricky midterm elections and in danger of becoming a lame duck. For Burnham, it’s also the home front that is occupying most of his attention. Good vibes are a decent start, but sooner or later he has to do something different to Starmer while boxing himself in with the same fiscal rules. So who knows? The meeting between Andy and The Donald may be less tricky than first imagined. A welcome distraction for both of them.
