title: US Postal Service says new mail ballot rules tied to Trump order are in effect
author: George Chidi
summary: Move from USPS comes amid Trump administration’s efforts to restrict mail-in voting in November’s midterms
body_text: The US Postal Service (USPS) said on Thursday ‌that ‌new ‌requirements for mail-in ‌voting are now ⁠in effect as Donald Trump seeks to crack down on the practice. The move is expected to trigger a new round of legal challenges. The Trump administration has sought to impose new rules requiring state election leaders to submit their voter rolls for inspection as part of a broader bid to increase federal government oversight over voting and elections. The post office requirements stem from an executive order issued by Trump earlier this year, requiring the post office to refrain from delivering ballots for mail-in voting to registered voters deemed ineligible when compared to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and other federal records. The USPS posted a final rule on ballot delivery on Friday. On Thursday, the service said it would be implemented immediately, applying to ballots for November’s US midterm elections. The US supreme court ruled on Monday that an injunction by a lower court should be lifted, at least until the post office had begun implementing the rule. The procedural ruling did not address the legality, or constitutionality, of the rule. The constitution confers control over elections to states and Congress, not the executive. US district judge Indira Talwani on Wednesday then lifted her nationwide block on the implementation of the postal service change, citing the supreme court’s decision. Two dozen states and the District of Columbia filed a fresh lawsuit on Wednesday to block the executive order restricting mail voting in this year’s midterm elections. The states said that the USPS policy is part of “a broader effort” by the administration “to rewrite federal election law and usurp the authority of the states and Congress”.

title: Georgia senator Jon Ossoff slams racist posts allegedly from Republican opponent’s ex-staffer
author: Lucy Campbell
summary: Representative Mike Collins has been dogged by associations to white nationalism and antisemitism
body_text: The US senator for Georgia Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, has slammed a “disgraceful and disqualifying” report that a former staffer for his Trump-backed Republican challenger Mike Collins shared images online of a swastika and depicting himself in Ku Klux Klan robes. It is the latest instance of someone in Collins’s orbit facing scrutiny over racist or white nationalist conduct. Ossoff called the report “stunning” and said it “should shock the conscience of every Georgian”. The report “confirmed yet more extensive ties between Congressman Mike Collins and white nationalism, and Congressman Mike Collins and neo-Nazi ideology”, said Ossoff. “Mike Collins needs to hold a press conference this afternoon, and he needs to release all the communications between his office and these white supremacists.” Meyer Siegfried, a spokesperson for Collins, said: “Preston Parra has no affiliation with Mike Collins’ office or campaign. The posts are vile, completely unhinged, and Mike Collins unequivocally condemns them.” Siegfried also attempted to highlight other cases of extremism, claiming there had been a “rise in antisemitism and hate among younger Americans” and “Jon Ossoff’s allies”, and describing this as “equally abhorrent”. On Thursday, the Washington Post reported that an ex-staffer for Collins, Preston Parra, who has described himself as a “twink fascist” on his X account, shared images in June and July of a swastika and one that depicts himself in Ku Klux Klan robes. The posts are still there, along with others in which Parra repeatedly casually uses the N-word, quotes Nazi song lyrics and uses the phrase “White Power”. Reached for comment, Parra responded with a racial slur. According to the Post, Parra, 24, interned for Collins for two months in 2024 before working as a contractor for his leadership political action committee the next year. He was paid $7,700 for fundraising consulting in May 2025, according to Federal Election Commission filings, and in an interview with the Post said he worked for the group for several months, shortly before Collins announced his US Senate bid. Responding to the Post’s reporting, Parra told the paper that many of his posts – including the KKK one, which he said he made using Grok AI – were “satirical”. He also said he was not a white supremacist, but added: “I do think that the white race contributes more to the world.” According to Parra, Collins was not aware of Parra’s personal X account when he worked for him because he had made it private. It is just the latest episode in an ever-growing scandal that has embroiled Collins’s bid in the high-stakes Georgia race, which will be critical to control of the Senate. Last month, CNN revealed that Collins’s son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, is a white nationalist and social media influencer with a history of sharing antisemitic material and sentiment and Nazi imagery on the internet. Among them are posts from the neofascist, white supremacist hate group Patriot Front, which descended on Washington DC this Fourth of July wearing white masks and brandishing the Confederate flag. Scheer is registered to vote at a Collins-owned property in Georgia, has been featured in Collins’s campaign photos and was at Collins’s victory party after the candidate won the Republican primary in June, according to CNN’s report. Collins, a trucking executive, has been the GOP representative for Georgia’s 10th congressional district since 2023. In that time he has been plagued by a string of such controversies, drawing scrutiny over his associations with far-right and extremist figures, incendiary social media activity and accusations of antisemitism, which he has denied. Having won the Republican nomination in June, Collins faces rising Democratic star Ossoff in November’s midterm elections. Several Georgia Republicans told the Post that they were increasingly worried about what they see as a pattern of troubling associations and behavior from Collins. “In the south, we have a saying: You lay down with dogs, you get up with fleas,” Debbie Dooley, a prominent conservative activist in Georgia and one of the original Tea Party founders who backed Collins’s rival in the primary, told the paper. “Well, Mike Collins has got a lot of fleas on him.”

title: Florida grand jury finds DeSantis administration ‘misappropriated’ funds from Medicaid settlement
author: Anna Betts
summary: Grand jury declined to indict anyone but said there was a ‘sophisticated scheme’ to use funds for political activity
body_text: A Florida grand jury has found that the administration of the governor, Ron DeSantis, “misappropriated” $10m in taxpayer money from a Medicaid settlement into the Hope Florida Foundation, a charity with ties to DeSantis’s wife, before the money was reportedly “funneled” into “two political action committees”. In the grand jury report, which remains sealed but was obtained and published by CBS News Miami on Wednesday, the grand jurors wrote that “we conclude that these funds were misappropriated as part of a sophisticated scheme to fund political activities” but said that they found “insufficient evidence to charge anyone criminally”. The grand jury report, dated 28 January 2026, states that in 2024, the Hope Florida Foundation received $10m from a Medicaid settlement between the state and Centene, a contractor for the government health insurance program for low-income Americans and children. The report goes on to say that after the money was transferred to Hope Florida, it was “quickly funneled” from there into two political action committees, and that the money was then reportedly used to lobby against a ballot measure that would have legalized marijuana in Florida, and was sent to the Republican party of Florida. In the report, the jurors write that “nobody will take responsibility for deciding the $10 million of taxpayer money would go to Hope Florida” and “this decision was the original misappropriation, and no witness would take responsibility for making the decision or had any memory of who made it”. “While we can’t prove who is responsible, we can plainly see that taxpayer money was misused for political purposes and we would like to see changes made to prevent this from happening again,” the report concludes. When asked by a reporter about the report on Thursday, DeSantis said that the only crime that was “apparent was whoever leaked the grand jury report”. He described the settlement as “legally sound” and “appropriate” and that it “advanced the interest of state”. “There was no diversion of any Medicaid funds” he said. “That was a private settlement where a company made a private contribution with one of the state agencies. “The whole reason people tried to make hay of this, was they were trying to use it to smear the first lady of Florida, my wife, and what has come out? Oh, she wasn’t involved in anything,” he said. “She wasn’t involved in any of this.” (The report only has one mention of Casey DeSantis, in which it refers to Hope Florida as an initiative “championed by the First Lady of Florida, Casey DeSantis”.) In the report, the grand jurors also wrote that they found that the Florida attorney general, James Uthmeier, who was DeSantis’s chief of staff at the time and is currently running for election for a full four-year term, was in a “position of authority over those involved in settling with Centene” and that testimony identified him as “having involvement in directing the money after it went to Hopе Florida”. The grand jurors wrote that no witness admitted or identified who directed the money to go to Hope Florida and noted that testimony also revealed that Uthmeier’s political action committee, Keep Florida Clean, was the “prime recipient of the majority” of the $10m. The jurors also noted that the office of Ashley Moody, then Florida’s attorney general who is currently serving her second year in the Senate and is up for re-election, knew of the payment, and that her chief deputy signed the agreement “without conducting his due diligence to ensure the proper appropriation of taxpayer funds”. Both Moody and Uthmeier have denied any wrongdoing. On Thursday, at an event at the Villages in Florida, Uthmeier was asked about the report, to which he said that under Florida law, he was not allowed to comment on it. “I can’t say if it’s true or not,” he said. But he added that “if it is indeed true” it shows that “there was no probable cause found that anybody did anything wrong”. He also said, without evidence, that Democrats had been behind the report, and called it a “hoax that has been debunked time and time and time again”. “Nobody did anything wrong here,” he added. In a statement to the New York Times on Wednesday, a spokesperson for Moody said that “the reports confirm what we have said all along”, that “neither the Department of Legal Affairs nor the former attorney general had knowledge of how the settlement money would be spent. Attempts to characterize this any other way are disingenuous.” In the report, the jury recommended that the Florida legislature “enact a law to prevent this situation from occurring”. They suggest enacting “a law that says any monies received by the state from any source must be deposited into General Revenue, and there should be real consequences for anyone violating this law”. On Thursday, the Democratic nominee for governor in Florida, David Jolly, said that if elected, he would “reopen an investigation” into the incident and challenged the Republican nominee for governor, Byron Donalds, to do the same.

title: Democrats to investigate ‘miraculous’ rise of Trump Jr’s investment firm
author: Shrai Popat in Washington
summary: Congressman Jamie Raskin asks president’s son to detail firm’s recent success after he joined 1789 Capital as partner
body_text: Democrats on a powerful US congressional committee have launched an investigation into a venture capital firm which has thrived since recruiting Donald Trump’s son. Donald Trump Jr joined 1789 Capital as a partner just days after his father won a second term in office in November 2024. Congressman Jamie Raskin, ranking member of the US House of Representatives judiciary committee, has asked the president’s son to detail the firm’s recent success. The Guardian previously reported that after Trump Jr joined 1789 Capital, its assets under management ballooned: going from a reported $150m in 2024, to $1bn last August, to $2.7bn at year’s end, to a reported $3.5bn by May, according to SEC filings. A significant proportion of that capital came from foreign investors, according to CNN reporting and the Guardian’s review of SEC filings. Forty per cent of assets under management were from overseas investors. In a letter to the US president’s son, and the founders of the firm – Omeed Malik and Christopher Buskirk – judiciary committee Democrats have asked for records that include companies that have received investments from the firm and any communications with any US elected official or federal government officials by 9 September. However, in the minority, Democrats have little subpoena power without Republican support for their cause. “Two years ago,” Raskin wrote, 1789 Capital was “a struggling venture capital firm that earned consistently disappointing results by serially investing in total market flops” but has since undergone a “miraculous transformation”. “With Don Jr’s new leadership role, 1789 Capital has developed an uncanny ability to identify companies that are about to receive massive influxes of cash from the Trump administration or to benefit from significant changes in federal policies and regulations,” the top Democrat wrote. “They say there is no such thing as a sure thing in investing, but this is about as close as you can get.” In a statement to the Guardian, AJ Merton, counsel for 1789 Capital, called the allegations leveled by Democrats “unsubstantiated talking points”. “Repackaging press clippings on congressional letterhead does not turn news headlines into evidence,” he added. “And that practice is a hallmark of partisan stunts and politically motivated harassment, not oversight.” Raskin also argued “it is now impossible to believe” that the firm’s “astonishing growth and success are due to anything other than insider political influence and thoroughgoing corruption”. The ranking member outlined a series of reports of recent investments by 1789 Capital that include millions of dollars in Vulcan Elements, a rare earth company, in August 2025. Before this, the manufacturer had reportedly touted several government contracts they had secured months prior. Raskin then notes that the Pentagon announced a $620m direct loan to Vulcan Elements in November last year. At the same time, the Department of Commerce (DoC) provided the company with a $50m grant under the Chips and Science Act – legislation signed by former president Joe Biden. “This was an amazing turn of events when the Trump Administration decided to pump over half a billion dollars into an unproven startup company,” Raskin wrote. He also pointed to a recent July interview with CNBC in which the US president said that his children have “inside information” due to the fact his policies touch nearly every part of the economy. “I tell my kids, ‘stay away,’” Trump said at the time. “But they also have a life. You know, they were doing business long before I ever thought of running for president.” In an interview with the New York Times last month, Trump Jr said he only talks to his father, the president, “every few weeks”, and never discusses business with him and – as a private citizen – holds “no policy position and no role within the administration whatsoever”. Raskin’s letter also cites reporting from the Guardian that Anduril Inudstries, a major military contractor founded by Trump ally and donor Palmer Luckey, has received billions in government contracts over the last year. 1789 Capital, the judiciary Democrats note, has acquired a stake in the company. Anduril says in Trump’s first year in office it doubled its revenue – a growth rate of 100%. Earlier this month, the Guardian also reported that two appointments to the Defense Policy Board, a key Pentagon advisory body, include two men with ties to 1789 Capital. Andreessen Horowitz, one of Silicon Valley’s largest venture capital firms, co-invests in three defense contractors alongside Trump Jr’s firm. The other appointee, Blake Masters, also sits on the boards of three ventures tied to 1789 Capital. Both men now advise the Pentagon on the defense-technology sector those companies operate in.

title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?
author: Aisha Down
summary: Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands
body_text: In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war. For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address. Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”. Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.” On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”. But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered. For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage. For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn. For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US. None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people. Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question. The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant. It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump. Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this. In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make some changes to this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads. But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily have personalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies. Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.” It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle. In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year. Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.” In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries. Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.” The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”. That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm. It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere. Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe. Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia. Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”

title: Dolly Parton brought divided Americans together. What can we learn from her?
author: Margaret Sullivan
summary: The singer had a serendipitous mixture of humor, humility and humanity. We could all stand to channel it a bit more
body_text: The moment that the world found out that Dolly Parton had died, I was in a hair salon in the reddest congressional district in New York state. The neighborhood on the shore of Lake Erie where I move every summer voted solidly for Donald Trump in 2024. I often pass a lawn sign that has something misogynistic to say about New York’s Democratic governor, Kathy Hochul, and the mere mention of Kamala Harris’s name can bring derisive jokes. Of course, there certainly are liberals and independents to be found, but on balance the area leans right. On my errands around town, I’ve heard scornful comments about transgender people, and the local Catholic church where I sometimes attend mass has a priest who, during a homily this summer, praised Trump for his war in Iran. A lot of the people I’ve chatted with around town are outspoken about being anti-vaccine. But when cellphones started pinging with the news about Dolly, it’s not overstating things to say that everybody was devastated. Stylists and customers alike seemed to feel a personal connection – to her music, to her philanthropy, to her sheer goodness. How did Dolly, a rags-to-riches country music superstar with a Tennessee twang and bedazzled everything, manage to endear herself to Americans of every political stripe? What was her secret – and does it hold some wisdom for the those who seek unity in this divided nation, who appreciate civility, who believe there’s an American ethos that transcends our ugly politics? Some of it, surely, was that she had a gift for poking fun at herself, and joining in the laughter, as when she would say she didn’t mind being called a dumb blonde because she knew, after all, that she wasn’t dumb – and that she wasn’t a blonde. After her illness made headlines last year, she took to social media to make a simple point: “I ain’t dead yet.” She called herself a “Backwoods Barbie” in a song of that name. Then there was her remarkable generosity. Her organization, Imagination Library, gave more than 330m books to children around the world. She founded it, in part, she said, because her father couldn’t read or write. She never forgot where she came from, as she raised money for a new hospital in her home country in Tennessee, or offered $500 awards to local teenagers when they graduated from high school. Still, how did she manage not to alienate the Maga world when she promoted the Covid-19 vaccine (the research for which she had helped fund)? Again, the humor helped, as when she changed the words of one of her most famous songs, Jolene to something that rhymed, and sang “vaccine, vaccine” in promotional videos. You had to smile, and maybe decide to get the jab, or at least to tolerate those who did. And she never made it political. “She practiced a unique brand of radical acceptance,” wrote Jad Abumrad in a New York Times essay this week. “No one would ever be thrown out of the Big Dolly Tent.” And, though she is being mourned as something of an angel on earth, she was a razor-sharp businessperson. She was smart and savvy about it all, as befitted the superstar who chalked up 25 No 1 country singles over the years. As Abumrad learned while interviewing and observing her at length as he created the podcast Dolly Parton’s America, she always told her own story. “If a male talkshow host made a joke about her figure, she’d make an ever better joke about it. She was always two steps ahead of you. She never allowed herself to be a part of a story of which she was not the author.” Can what Dolly Parton did be bottled somehow? Can her serendipitous mixture of humor, humility and humanity be sprinkled over our troubled waters to calm and soothe them? Probably not – there is only one Dolly Parton – but that doesn’t mean we can’t learn something from this rare individual. The rest of us might channel Dolly a bit more, and remember that a self-deprecating joke goes a long way toward easing tensions. We might recognize that financial success need not turn into ego glorification or arrogance. And most of all, we might keep in mind that genuine generosity – if it comes from the heart – has the power to transcend politics. Dolly Parton’s legacy, of course, resides in her wonderful songs, from Coat of Many Colors to 9 to 5. That’s what she would want. But I don’t think she’d object if we also kept in mind her authentic kindness, her disarming wit – and the “radical acceptance” that fueled it all. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

title: Trump’s midterm campaign theme is unrequited love
author: Sidney Blumenthal
summary: The president senses a crisis in his cult of personality. He believes the path to victory is through unwavering devotion
body_text: Donald Trump has framed his theme for the midterm elections. It has come to him as naturally and inevitably as staring into the mirror, beyond any logic or argument, his definitive answer to no specific issue, providing no understanding of any particular problem, but transcending all of them. His political theme is more primal than programmatic, more instinctive than analytical, a heartfelt expression to protect his greatest romantic attachment, his obsessive fixation, his idealized object: himself. Trump’s campaign theme is unrequited love. Unlike the pollsters, media consultants and pundits, he alone has grasped the magnitude and the source of the existential crisis threatening his politics. He has identified the problem for the Republicans as the faltering measure of complete devotion to him. His demand has nothing to do with mutual affection. It is a ploy to reassert his slipping control, a manipulative test to prove loyalty to him, or else. There can be no absolute rule without an absolute ruler; no absolute ruler without absolute submission; no absolute submission without the expression of absolute love. His sadness at its fading gives way to anger, paranoia and greater acts of retribution. He equates the fear he instills as a form of love. Trump accepts subservience, from whatever motive, as affection or its closest equivalent. He cares nothing about sincerity, so it’s all in the show. The less love displayed, the more fear required. Yet there is no rebound, but only deeper rejection. Trump is heading toward the floor for presidential unpopularity – Nixon during Watergate on the eve of his resignation, Truman late in his second term at the depth of the Korean war, and George W Bush at the 2008 financial crash. But Trump’s breakdown differs uniquely from theirs. His decline has come earlier in his term, been more sustained, and his disintegration has not stabilized but is accelerating. He is being crushed by the accumulation of catastrophic events of his own making to which his impulsive response is to double down in each and every area. Stalemated in his reckless Iran war, he has now launched a heedless trade war against Canada that will devastate Republican candidates in the northern tier of states. His latest vanity project is gestural retribution to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America”, a watery ballroom. Admission of error for Trump would be the denial of self-love. Trump began his campaign on his unrequited love theme on 16 August during a Fox News interview in which he discussed his press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, leaving her job after just having a baby. He had held her up as meeting his highest criterion in remarks last December: “Isn’t she great? Is Karoline great? … She gets up there with that beautiful face and those lips that don’t stop, ba ba ba like a little machine gun.” Now, he tried to make a joke of her departure that expressed resentment at abandonment. “In fact, she likes her children more than she likes Trump. I’m very concerned about that,” he said. Then he repeated his unfunny “joke” at a campaign rally in South Carolina on 21 August: “I just learned she loves the baby more than she loves Donald Trump, and I’m very angry …” Trump’s lame attempt at humor was a rare instance of his truth-telling and self-revelation, a contemporary illustration of Freud’s Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious. Trump was in South Carolina to campaign for his chosen candidate in the Republican primary, Darline Graham, who he had insisted be appointed to the Senate seat of her brother Lindsey Graham after he died on 11 July. Darline Graham confessed to cluelessness when asked in a debate about her position on Taiwan. “National security is not my thing,” she answered. “I’m not … that informed on national security.” But she was fully informed on the necessity of obedience to Trump. “You saved our country, and I want to thank you for that,” she said at the rally. Trump praised his worshipper: “She’s got a good gene pool.” She was born to love him. She stood in stark contrast to the immigrants he had described as “poisoning the blood of our country”. Then Trump called on the crowd to embrace his new theme. “So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot … So just say that I’m on the ballot one more time. You got to say it.” He wishes every candidate to sound like Darline Graham in proclaiming him the national savior. He insists he is beloved, and if those who revere him turn out the Republicans must win. In fact, though he is not on the ballot in the midterm elections, Trump is the central issue. Voters do not have to “pretend, please”. Trump intuitively comprehends that the midterm elections are about him in a way that makes this midterm unlike any other. In the marrow of his bones, he senses it is a crisis of his cult of personality. Trump’s Maga was never a new party structure, but constructed on his wreckage of the old Republican party. In its place, every particle of the replacement is connected to the leader to advance his supremacy and self-enrichment. Everything flows upward, all heads tilted, all knees bent. Maga has always been Maga Inc of, by and for one man. The movement is the man. When charisma fails, the movement implodes. If the leader is not worshipped, his uber-principle – the leader principle – collapses: no fuhrerprinzip, no Führer. Trump’s plea for their unconditional love – “pretend, please” – defies gravity. He is running against Isaac Newton, and Newton always prevails. Intensity is gauged by “strongly approve” and “strongly disapprove” poll numbers. More than the general statistics of approval or disapproval, these provide insight into the motivation of voters that determine the contour of elections. Trump now stands at 13% “strongly approve” in the most recent Reuters-Ipsos Poll. His “strongly disapprove” rating is at 49%. His total approval is at 33%, while disapproval is at 65%. Those in the “somewhat approve” category include low propensity soft voters especially inclined to skip midterm elections. And this poll was taken before his declaration of trade war against Canada. All along, the Republicans have been Trump’s indispensable accomplices. Even if they were disposed to object, they could do nothing to draw him back from his “pretend, please” campaign. His anxiety to rescue his invincible image from the reality he’s created makes him more inescapable than ever. Any effort to restrict him will provoke his rage. He will not diminish himself for the sake of the party or even his own future. He plans to spend millions from his Maga Inc political action committee to tell the voters that they have never had it so good – “the greatest economy we’ve ever had, by far”, he says. He has mocked the suggestion that “affordability” might be a problem for many – it’s “a word they”, the media, “devised”, he has said. Trump intends to stage a mini convention in Dallas on 9 September, featuring Donald Trump to “celebrate … our achievements”. Republicans are locked almost uniformly into blind support, with the Maine senator Susan Collins venturing hollow criticism of the Canadian tariffs that makes her seem powerless and infuriates the remaining Maga base. Just as Trump has trapped himself, he has trapped the Republicans. The expenditure of tens of millions to depict his dire consequences as paradise on earth will have the unintended effect of supercharging the already motivated “strongly disapprove” voters and disillusion those who cannot help but be aware of the actual conditions of their own lives. The sudden surfacing of Natalie Harp as a meme at this particular moment propitiously coincides with the wobbling of Trump’s cult. The 35-year-old is his model of the perfect staffer, perfect companion and perfect American citizen. If unrequited love is the problem, she is the solution. In Trump’s hierarchy of need, his pyramid of status, love and self-actualization, she is at the apex. Harp is his “binky”, as Maggie Haberman of the New York Times has called her, his comfort blanket, his plush bunny rabbit. The “human printer” who trails after him, pressing the button to churn out an endless stream of adulatory articles, conspiracy theories and “alternative facts”, has become an extension of his nervous system. The former anchor at the fringe far-right One America News Network serves as Trump’s personal anchor. Harp broadcasts around the clock to an audience of one. She is the connector to the neurons of the far right, serving as a conduit to dodgy characters such as Laura Loomer with her lists of national security officials who were supposedly disloyal. Harp is Trump’s neurotransmitter who distributes a steady supply of dopamine and delusion. Harp’s self-abasing devotion to Trump, expressed in her letters to him, serves as a kind of inadvertent political manifesto for the cult, a template for followers. Harp tellingly muddles a line from Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice – Mr Bennet blessing his strong-willed daughter Elizabeth in her engagement to Darcy – to demean herself and offer subservience to Trump: “To modify a classic, ‘I could not have parted with you, to anyone less worthy’ – And, I will add, it is I who is unworthy.” In another letter, after self-disparaging apologies, Harp writes: “You are all that matters to me. I don’t want to ever let you down. Thank you for being my Guardian and Protector in this Life … With all my Heart.” As public opinion curdles on Trump, no longer able to “pretend, please”, Harp has not come to the wisdom of Conway Twitty in his 1959 rockabilly hit: My only prayer will be Someday you’ll care for me But it’s only make believe Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast

title: A conservative strategist called for ‘getting rid of Trump’ three years ago. Could he be his next press secretary?
author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
summary: Scott Jennings has pivoted from his early critiques and caught the White House’s eye with pro-Trump commentary on CNN
body_text: In 2016, a month before the presidential election that Donald Trump would win, the longtime Republican strategist Scott Jennings described him as “a vulgar, crude, braggadocious, desperate-to-impress playboy who tends to view most everything through a sexual lens”. After Trump’s loss in the 2020 election, Jennings excoriated Trump’s conduct during the January 6 Capitol insurrection, saying he “clearly violated his oath of office to preserve, protect and defend the constitution to the best of [his] ability”. When Trump was in the political wilderness in 2022, Jennings said the party “[needs] a new nominee”, later encouraging the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, to launch a primary challenge. “There’s only one strategy for getting rid of Trump: it’s to beat his ass,” he said the following year. So why exactly is the 48-year-old conservative TV pundit being considered “an early favorite” to serve as Trump’s top spokesperson, replacing the departing Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary? The answer can be traced to Jennings’s virtuosic ability to pivot (or shape-shift, as some critics might suggest) to land on the right political side. As soon as it became clear that Trump would in fact win the Republican nomination, in early 2024, Jennings became a bigger supporter than ever. And over the last few years, Jennings has emerged as a star in his own right: CNN’s in-house Maga gladiator who is always game to appear on television and beat up any liberals that challenge him. Highlighting his transformation, Jennings appeared onstage with Trump in 2025, telling a rally crowd: “Michigan, we were flying in here today and I said: ‘Look at these farms. I got to get a farm in Michigan, because when you own as many libs as I do, you gotta [get] a place to put them all.” Jennings’s bombastic performances have made him a target of hatred for Democrats but won him praise – and, most importantly, attention – from conservatives, including those in Trump’s circles, even as the president still reportedly holds some reservations about picking him as press secretary. ‘It’s an important job,’ Jennings says Ben Ferguson, who served as a conservative contributor on CNN for many years and still occasionally appears as a guest, said Jennings was uniquely talented as an on-air pugilist – and that he could use that experience to serve him well as Trump’s press secretary. “The more reps you get, the more fights you have, then the better you are, and the better you can serve the president,” he said in an interview. It would also help that Jennings is already well-acquainted with the CNN journalists who cover the administration, he added. Some longtime politics reporters have vouched for Jennings, who became a known quantity to beltway journalists as a staffer in George W Bush’s administration and a longtime adviser to Senator Mitch McConnell from his home state of Kentucky. “Not that my opinion matters here, but Jennings would be great in this role,” Rachael Bade, a former Washington Post and Politico journalist, wrote on X last week. “Most reporters in this town have known him for years from his time in McConnell Land – WELL before he was a CNN celeb. He’s also just a nice & fair guy – tho maybe not so nice if you’re on the other end of his slap-down.” But Jennings has plenty of detractors. During a May 2024 segment on CNN, Jennings clashed with George Conway, the conservative attorney who had been married to the Trump counselor Kellyanne Conway, after a New York jury found the then ex-president guilty on 34 felony counts. “You’re lying. You’re lying, Scott. You’re lying about the law,” Conway told Jennings, drawing the objection of a CNN anchor when he asked “why this network is paying Scott to say those lies.” Conway, who later claimed that he was temporarily “shadow-banned” by CNN after the segment, wrote on X last week that Jennings would be perfect for the job as press secretary. Asked by the Guardian to explain why he was seemingly endorsing his former sparring partner, Conway responded: “Because it’s a terrible job for a terrible boss and he’s a terrible guy! All around, a great fit.” Mark Feldstein, a former CNN and ABC News journalist who teaches broadcast journalism at the University of Maryland, noted that Jennings’s background “is mostly as an establishment Republican rather than Maga fanatic, so in that sense he may seem a bit more credible than one of the more obsequious Trump toadies from the rightwing mediasphere”. “But,” he added, “I don’t think he, or any press secretary for the Trump White House, will carry much credibility with the mainstream Washington press corps because anyone appointed to that position will be expected to defend the indefensible and convey Trump’s habitual lies to the news media. It’s an inherently credibility-diminishing job.” Jennings’s reputation for embodying a certain kind of folksy charm faced scrutiny this spring, when he told Adam Mockler, a 23-year-old progressive commentator, to “get your fucking hand out of my face” during a contentious segment about Trump’s war on Iran. Despite calls for CNN to punish what former network contributor Keith Boykin called a fireable offense, there is no evidence that he faced any punishment from the network, which has struggled in the past to find credible Trump defenders. While he’s never expressed interest in working for the Trump administration, he has also never said no – though he told a McClatchy reporter for a 2024 profile that he was not auditioning for the job by taking on the president’s critics on CNN. “It would be a major life upheaval,” he said for the story, which was headlined: “KY’s Scott Jennings is CNN’s breakout pundit. Could he be Trump’s White House press secretary?” Jennings has continued playing coy in the days since his name was first floated as Leavitt’s potential successor, even when asked directly about it on CNN. (The White House did not respond to a request for comment.) “I don’t have any comment about that, but it’s an important job, because that person has to represent the most powerful person in the world, and the entire US government,” Jennings told the CNN anchor Abby Phillip, who hosts the evening show that he most regularly appears on. “And what they say matters … whoever gets it, it’s a big responsibility.” (When asked if he would take the job, Jennings replied: “I’m not going to answer that.”) When asked about the rumors by the CNN anchor and chief White House correspondent, Kaitlan Collins, Jennings said: “I don’t really have anything to say about it, other than, I would get to see you every day, and I would think you’d be happy about this.” (“I already see you every day. … We already work together, Scott,” Collins responded.) Highlighting the irony of a CNN contributor being the subject of CNN reporting, a recent story about Jennings’s prospects noted that “CNN has reached out to Jennings” for comment. Some have accused Jennings of using his perch on CNN to lobby for the job, particularly in his recent vociferous defenses of the Trump aide Natalie Harp. A CNN spokesperson declined to comment on Jennings’s potential appointment, but noted that he had been asked about it on air several times. Were Jennings to take the job, it would leave CNN without its most high-profile and prolific conservative commentator, and it would take a reliable Trump defender off one of the president’s most-hated networks. But, Ferguson, the conservative former CNN contributor, said: “I think Scott can serve the president in an even better way being his press secretary than he does being at CNN.”

title: Trump official faces inquiry over claims he diverted wildfire resources to his own property
author: Anna Betts
summary: Exclusive: Michael Boren, a senior official overseeing the US Forest Service, is accused by Democratic senators of ‘inappropriate interference’
body_text: Donald Trump’s administration is facing calls to launch an investigation into allegations that Michael Boren, a senior official who oversees the US Forest Service, pressed agency staff to deploy additional resources to fight a fire burning near his Idaho ranch. Three Democratic senators accused Boren of “inappropriate interference” in a letter seen by the Guardian, demanding answers from Brooke Rollins, the US agriculture secretary. Boren serves as undersecretary of agriculture for natural resources and environment. Senators Ron Wyden, Amy Klobuchar and Martin Heinrich expressed “serious concern” over reports that Boren used his federal government position in July to remove firefighting personnel and resources from active fires elsewhere to tackle a fire near his private ranch in Idaho. “We request a full investigation into the nature and extent of Boren’s involvement in response to the Cabin Creek Fire and a detailed accounting of the safeguards the agency has implemented or plans to implement to prevent political interference and conflicts of interest in wildfire response,” they wrote. Their letter follows a report from the Washington Post earlier this month, in which several forest service officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said that Boren – who reportedly owns a 480-acre ranch in the Sawtooth national recreation area – contacted forest service officials multiple times in mid-July to question why more aircraft were not being used to fight the Cabin Creek fire in Idaho, which spread across several acres in Idaho’s Sawtooth national forest. The fire began on 12 July, as a result of an unattended campfire and was 100% contained by 15 July. It reportedly ultimately burned seven acres. Six current and former forest service officials described the response to the fire to the Post as greater than would typically be expected for a fire of that size, which posed no significant threat to life or property. Communications reviewed by the Post also reportedly confirmed that Boren personally contacted forest service staff about the fire. When asked for comment on the senators’ letter, a spokesperson for the USDA said: “We will respond to the Senators’ request through the proper channels.” In a statement last month to the Guardian responding to the initial report, a USDA spokesperson said Boren “is expected to have regular contact with the agencies he oversees” and the “fact that a senior government official would be monitoring and communicating with other government officials about an event he oversees is a non-story”. “Undersecretary Boren did report a fire that was near property he owns, just as one would hope any citizen in an area under threats from wildfires would do,” they said. “However, at no point did he pressure leadership or order more resources to fight this or any other fire.” In the letter from the Democratic senators, sent on Thursday, they wrote that “during this record setting fire season, fires of much larger size have not received even a fraction of the same commitment of resources”. “The personal interests of political employees should not be a factor that influences the allocation of wildfire resources to communities threatened with devastation,” they added. They argued that Boren’s reported “actions constitute potentially a misuse of taxpayer funds and put American families at further risk by diverting scarce resources from high-priority wildfires threatening communities elsewhere in the region and country”. “Political interference in wildfire response jeopardizes lives, property and federal resources,” they wrote. “We request that you respond by September 10th detailing how the Department will prevent this type of inappropriate interference, or even the appearance of it, in wildfire response going forward.”

title: ‘It’s all you can hear’: New Jersey lawsuit takes on datacenter’s noise pollution
author: Jessica Glenza
summary: Lawsuit alleges sound is nuisance for up to one mile around datacenter as residents experience noises from DataOne
body_text: It’s a sound Steve Brown, a 63-year-old Vineland, New Jersey resident, literally hears in his sleep: BGRRRRRRRRRRR. It drones, oscillates, growls – these are machines at industrial scale. Are they generators? Pumps? Fans? Brown does not know what equipment causes the sound or why. He only knows two things: he’s tired of it, and it’s coming from DataOne – a 350MW datacenter under construction a little more than a mile from his home of 25 years. “It woke me up probably around, I don’t know, somewhere around 2 o’clock in the morning,” said Brown, who was weary by mid-afternoon. “I couldn’t get back to sleep, because once you hear it, it’s all you can hear.” Of all the concerns Americans have raised about datacenters – including mind-boggling electricity demands, water use and emissions – sound pollution ranks high among them, according to attorneys, experts and the people whose homes are nearby. Now, Brown and two of his neighbors are the named plaintiffs in a lawsuit that alleges the sound is a nuisance for up to one mile around the datacenter, which is seeking class-action status. They are represented by a seasoned environmental pollution law firm in Michigan: Liddle Sheets PC. “We have four cases that are being litigated in court against datacenters for noise, and we’re gearing up to file quite a few more,” said Laura Sheets, attorney for the class. “This is one of several.” Opposition to datacenters across the country has led to raucous town halls, protests and now potential election consequences. Republicans recently told AI companies they were concerned backlash could swing elections. Democrats appear to have also smelled blood in the water: a challenger for Vineland’s very red congressional seat hired a truck outfitted with digital billboards reading: “No datacenter here.” The Vineland datacenter, at 2.4m sq ft, represents both the scale and speed with which many facilities are coming to American communities. As recently as October 2024, the site was a brand new nine-hole public golf course. By March 2025, Amsterdam-based Nebius, a spin-off of Russian search-engine Yandex, had contracted with DataOne. Since spring, permit meetings and town halls about the datacenter have packed the Landis Theater, a music venue in town. DataOne executives have sought to quell the backlash with a town hall of their own and a “microsite” dedicated to questions about the datacenter. The company even promised, “weekly baskets of organic, non-GMO fruits and vegetables” to “underprivileged residents of Vineland”. “What I say is that there’s really four problems here: three are given a great deal of attention – energy consumption, water use and contamination,” said Jamie Banks, president of Quiet Communities Inc, a non-profit advocacy group. “The forgotten stepchild is noise.” The dangers of noise to public health have been recognized since at least 1968, when then US surgeon general, William H Stewart, attended the first meeting of the American Speech and Hearing Association in Washington DC. “Aside from hearing, it has been demonstrated that noise can cause physiological changes,” Stewart said in a keynote address. “These include cardiovascular, glandular and respiratory effects reflective of the generalized stress reaction,” which can occur “under sustained high level, or even moderately high noise conditions”. Congress tasked the EPA in 1972 with regulating sound and funded regional noise centers. They got to work regulating consumer goods such as motorcycles – and people can still appreciate the relics of this work on EPA-stamped-and-approved mufflers. However, when the Reagan administration defunded noise pollution offices in 1982, regional centers closed, and the EPA has done no appreciable research or enforcement since. Noise pollution, as a priority for federal government enforcement, was all but forgotten. Except by people like Bank. As class actions scrutinizing the sound of datacenters ramp up, Quiet Communities won an important legal victory – they sued the EPA for failing to regulate sound. In July, they won. Now, there is just one EPA regional noise center still in operation: the Rutgers University Noise Technical Assistance Center in New Jersey. Eric Zwerling, its director, kept the center alive by turning it into the training center for every noise control officer in the state. “It’s 50 years since then – there’s been a lot more research on the impacts of low frequency,” said Zwerling. “My personal opinion – not that of Rutgers and the center, [is] the permissible sound levels for sources such as this need to be re-evaluated according to the correct state of knowledge on the impact.” He continued: “If [datacenters] are designed and properly built, they can be relatively quiet. On the other hand, if there is no consideration to the sound emissions from the facility, the facility can have impacts that are virtually catastrophic to the people nearby.” Volume is measured in decibels, a logarithmic scale based on human hearing. It begins at the edge of auditory perception – zero. If a whisper is 30 decibels and a normal conversation is 60 decibels, it means the typical conversation is 1,000 times louder than the whisper. A rock band, at 100 decibels, is 1,000 times louder than the conversation. A second dynamic of sound is its disruption of atmospheric pressure as it moves in waves. The frequency with which those waves cycle through the atmosphere per second is measured in hertz. Experts describe this as important for people living with the thrum of a nearby industrial facility, because low frequencies are known to travel long distances and can be experienced as vibration. “Effects like hum, whooshing, whistling,” occur in “very narrow frequency bands in the low frequency range”, said Banks. “That noise … is coming right into people’s homes.” Another plaintiff in the Vineland suit, Michael Gentile, 63, said he “found out it was a datacenter after I began to hear the noise”. He estimates he has called the county health department, responsible for enforcing noise ordinances, about “20 times”. “I said, ‘I know you guys are testing for sound, but what about vibration?’ I said, ‘Can you feel that?’ I could feel it on my porch,” he said. “They don’t have any tools to do that. I said, ‘Well that doesn’t help me now.’” In a statement to the Guardian, a DataOne spokesperson, Naomi Race, said the company was working to mitigate sound. The company, built “a northerly wall … as an additional layer to mitigate any sound from the construction site”; adjusted construction timing, said it would be using “quiet fuel cells to power the facility” and that it “retained the services of a sound mitigation specialist to assess the project site”. Race said the company was unable to comment on litigation, but that it was “committed to constructive dialogue, regulatory compliance, and being a valuable and responsible long-term member of the community”. Nebius echoed DataOne. “In Vineland, we are working with DataOne to minimize impact, including measures to minimize noise and water use and ensure local residents don’t pay more for electricity … We remain committed to engaging openly with the Vineland community and being a responsible long-term partner,” the vice-president of public affairs, John Sutter, said in a statement. title: Detroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes city
author: Tom Perkins in Detroit
summary: Unpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan races
body_text: Every day $1bn worth of goods crosses the river dividing Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, two largely blue-collar US and Canadian cities that have come to act as one in the creation of North America’s auto industry. News this week of Donald Trump’s escalating trade spat with Canada has everyone worried. Political and economic leaders and observers labeled the move an act of “hubris” , blamed Trump’s “ego”, and called the escalation “insanity”. “We don’t need Canada, they need us,” Trump declared. But many are hoping that Trump’s imposition of 50% tariffs on Canadian goods this week will not last long, with the upcoming midterm elections as a pivotal reason the plan may be scrapped. Control of the US Congress hangs in the balance and will almost certainly be decided by several close Michigan races. It also comes just two months after polling highlighted Michiganders’ fatigue with and opposition to the president’s unprecedented tariff program. By a 63%-31% margin, residents here oppose tariffs on Canadian goods, according to a June Epic-MRA poll, including 35% of Republicans. Meanwhile, nearly 75% of Michiganders said the tariffs are fueling high prices. Trump doubling down on an unpopular policy deep into election season is viewed by many observers as a gift to Democrats, and there is a real possibility that it contributes to a midterm loss for the Republicans. Meanwhile, there seems to be little upside for Trump. “I don’t understand what Trump is thinking,” the Epic-MRA pollster Bernie Porn said. Regardless, Michiganders have already suffered disproportionately as they pay on average over $3,200 annually for tariffs, or about 142% more than the rest of the country, because of the state’s shared border with Canada. The Canadian economy would also take a major hit if the tariffs are imposed, said Patrick Anderson, a Michigan-based economist with the Anderson Economic Group. “Both will suffer – there are no two ways about it,” Anderson added. This critical upper midwest swing state has picked the presidential winner in five consecutive elections, going from Barack Obama to Trump to Joe Biden and back to Trump. Democrats’ chances to retake the Senate rest heavily on the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed beating Trump ally Mike Rogers in the 3 November general election race. Rogers has supported the tariffs, but so far has been silent on the latest escalation. The tariffs and the unpopular Iran war’s contribution to inflation represent a “double hit” for Republicans, Porn said, and Trump is handing ammo to a particularly adept candidate in El-Sayed. He has energized people with his anti-establishment, populist political vision, and a no-holds-barred delivery. “El-Sayed has proven to be very, very articulate on a number of issues,” Porn added. “I think that he is going to try and just throw bombs at Rogers [in an upcoming debate] because Rogers supports these tariffs and trade war. Trump’s low popularity is an anchor around Rogers’ neck.” In a statement, El-Sayed hammered Trump and Rogers, saying that the president “cares more about his ego and saber-rattling than addressing the affordability crisis. “Donald Trump is launching this trade war for his own vanity, and he’s asking Michigan families to pay the price,” El-Sayed said. “Trump has been failing Michigan through these chaotic tariffs and bad trade deals for far too long, and Mike Rogers won’t do anything but rubber-stamp them.” El-Sayed said he would push for “real, fair trade deals that create good-paying jobs”. Rogers’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment. The United Auto Workers (UAW), which has 350,000 members in Michigan and is often a political kingmaker here, has supported some of Trump’s targeted tariffs, but said in a statement it “rejects” the latest escalation. “If we’re going to increase tariffs anywhere, it should be on countries where automakers continue to offshore jobs because they can pay workers $3 an hour, force them to work in unsafe conditions, and crack down on independent unions,” the UAW president, Shawn Fain, said. Canada has strong unions, and the UAW supports those. “Tariffs work, but only if they are deployed intentionally to protect workers and grow our manufacturing communities, and it’s time to permanently end offshoring and the race to the bottom,” Fain added. Mexico and Canada currently face 25% US tariffs on autos, though partial exemptions in the nations’ free trade agreement make the effective rate much lower, overall. Anderson estimated tariffs cost US auto companies about $12.5bn in 2025. The Canadian government has announced it will impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of goods starting 8 September. The actions leading to the latest blow-up have been “rife with miscalculations, overreactions, and hubris”, Anderson said. He read through the list of goods on which tariffs would be imposed – feathers, sweaters, girls’ dresses, lobster. “This is not a trade war. This is an annoyance list. Chest pounding,” Anderson said. The North American auto industry over the last 60 years has integrated across the continent, and auto parts cross a border an average of six times before they land in a final product. That means there would be shared pain, Anderson said, and it would reverberate across the upper midwest, where bigger manufacturing cities are typically powered by industries that are often reliant on international trade. But the Canadian economy is smaller, and Ontario’s economy is so concentrated that it would hit harder north of the border, Anderson added. Ultimately, the real threat is that “these two countries go pell-mell into it” and impose tariffs on oil, energy and commodities that hit harder than lobster. The dialogue has devolved into the usual petty antagonism that is a hallmark of Trump’s beefs. Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Thursday, and Vice-President JD Vance referred to Canada as the 51st state. “Let me say with great understatement that this is not helpful,” Anderson added. Indeed, the Windsor mayor, Drew Dilkens, took exception to that particular comment. In an interview, he expressed deep frustration over Trump’s moves, and labeled justifications Trump has used for issuing tariffs, including framing them as a response to illegal immigration on the northern border, “nonsense”. The latest escalation “is an aggressive move, one that could not be ignored by our country”, added Dilkens, who leads the city of 230,000 people. “It’s just offensive that he launches these attacks at Canada, who is your largest trading partner, your closest ally, and your neighbor.” The chaos has cooled investment in Windsor, and prices remain high on both sides of the border. He pointed out how much more US consumers are paying not just for automobiles, but for beef, which in part stems from tariffs on Canadian beef. “What is really crazy is that he is willing to throw his own citizens under the bus to pursue his tariff agenda,” Dilkens said. “They have Donald Trump to thank.” Highlighting the tension among the president and some in his base, the Michigan chamber of commerce, a trade organization that lobbies on behalf of the state’s largest corporations, normally vocally supports the president on economic issues. It has not made a public statement, and did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. However, the typically pro-Trump Detroit chamber of commerce did not mince words. “Escalating tensions and tariffs will only cause economic pain on both sides of the border, especially in Michigan and the binational Detroit-Windsor region,” the chamber said in a press statement, adding that global competitors like China benefited most. “Our economies are intertwined, interconnected, and stronger together; the sooner normalcy is restored the better.” • This article was amended on 28 August 2026. An earlier version gave incorrect commencement dates for the US and Canadian tariffs.

title: Dolly Parton was the polar opposite of our bullying president
author: Robert Reich
summary: Terrified of being seen as a loser, Donald Trump is nonsensically lashing out – even against our old friend Canada
body_text: I’m still grieving Dolly Parton. I never met her and always wanted to. She was almost exactly my age and my height and had values I deeply admired. Her death leaves a hole in the firmament. Which brings me to the person whose values are as far from Dolly Parton’s as any human could possibly be and still claim to be human. I’m referring, of course, to the current occupant of the Oval Office. “I knew her a little bit,” Trump boasted about Parton on Glenn Beck’s radio show. “She really liked me, I will tell you!” at which Beck laughed out loud. Trump has become mad as a hatter. Loonier than looney tunes. Totally nuts. An enraged, engorged child who’s frightened to death of being seen as a loser. He’s losing his war in Iran – the war he decided to start without consulting Congress, without even telling the American people his goal or exit strategy. Now he’s trapped there – with a stronger and more extreme group in control of Iran than before his attack, probably more intent on making a nuclear bomb, blocking the strait of Hormuz (it was open before Trump attacked), causing oil prices to rise again. His current attempt to stop other countries from dealing with Iran is a bad joke. Iran is becoming the dominant power in the Gulf, having demonstrated its ability to damage the oil and gas infrastructure of its neighbors. Besides, China can supply almost everything Iran needs and has a strong incentive to do so. So – now clearly revealed as a loser – what does Trump do? Like any bully, he lashes out. If the courts won’t allow him to put his name on the Kennedy Center, he’ll demolish it. If they say he doesn’t have authority to build his ballroom, he’ll fight to build it anyway. If his blue paint on the reflecting pool is peeling and the green algae are back and his US attorney won’t prosecute “vandals” for causing the problem, he’ll stick to his story and blame vandals anyway. It’s all going so badly for Trump that his lizard brain is compelled to show he can bully someone. So who does Trump choose? Our old neighbor and friend Canada, who has always gone along with whatever the American colossus ever wanted. Trump imposed 50% tariffs on all cars, trucks, auto parts and steel coming from Canada. Why? Because, he says: “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years. On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!” In other words, we’re in a trade war with Canada because, well, Trump wants one. A trade war with Canada probably seemed easier to win than a hot war with Iran. And he had to save face somehow, right? Even though the supreme court found his attempt to use emergency powers for his last round of tariffs to be unconstitutional, he’s now using the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 – which, not incidentally, worsened the Great Depression. But maybe a trade war with Canada won’t be all that easy to win. Canada has now retaliated with its own tariffs of up to 50% against about 700 American products. As the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, noted on Saturday: “Last spring, I warned that America is trying to break us so they can own us, and I promised that will never, ever happen. We are keeping that promise.” Carney is now a hero in Canada with approval ratings in the 60s, while Trump’s have sunk to the low 30s. Humiliation upon humiliation for the man who can’t stand to be humiliated. It gets worse by the day. Netanyahu has rejected Trump’s plan for Gaza. Congressional Republicans are blasting him for increasing imports of ground beef. Universities are rejecting his latest directives. ABC has sued his regime for threatening its broadcast licenses. Even the bond market won’t be cowed. It’s in open revolt against his bonkers fiscal policies. Thank goodness for him that Darline Graham won South Carolina’s special election Republican runoff to replace her brother. Trump had made her race all about himself – of course – telling supporters that her opponents were “only fighting Darline because they want me to lose”. I’m sure that’s what he’s telling himself about his many losses and humiliations – that they’re all due to his opponents plotting and scheming against him. (Hopefully, he’s about to lose Congress, too.) That’s an easier story for Trump to accept than the truth: that his carefully cultivated aura of invincibility has just about disappeared. The would-be emperor has no clothes. Almost everybody now sees the thin-skinned, peevish, petty, incompetent, corrupt, naked infant who’s been parading around in presidential garb. And they’re not going to obey him any more. Dolly Parton was a huge winner, bless her soul. Trump is the biggest loser on the planet. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

title: First Thing: Rescue efforts continue as death toll rises in Nepal-Tibet flood
author: Vivian Ho
summary: More than 1,300 people are missing in Nepal and in Tibet after catastrophic flash floods. Plus: Six months of the war in Iran
body_text: Good morning. Rescue operations have resumed in Nepal and Tibet after a pause when a lake at the border began to overflow. The lake was formed when a wall of mud and debris hit the hub of Gyirong in Tibet on Wednesday, causing catastrophic flash floods that thundered down valleys and obliterated villages. More than 1,300 people are missing, with the death toll reaching 469 on Friday. More than 500 foreign citizens were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials have said, with Chinese state media reporting that at least 260 of the 558 missing people on the Tibet side of the border were foreign nationals. What could have caused this deadly flash floods? Satellite imagery suggests a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas was the primary cause, raising concerns that the climate crisis is destabilizing the geology of mountain and polar regions. This is a developing story. Follow our live coverage here. Senator calls for criminal investigation of RFK Jr after Guardian report A senior Democratic senator has called for a criminal investigation into Robert F Kennedy Jr after reporting by the Guardian that indicated he lied during Senate confirmation hearings last year. Ron Wyden said in a statement: “RFK’s platform is built on lies and grifts that leave a trail of dead children in their wake. There are consequences for lying to Congress.” What did Kennedy purportedly lie about? A Guardian analysis of newly obtained documents found that the US health secretary had lied when he told lawmakers who held the key to his confirmation that a 2019 visit to Samoa had “nothing to do with vaccines”. South Korea to re-examine 310,000 missing person cases after fake record scandal South Korean police will re-examine about 310,000 missing persons cases closed over the past three years after an officer was arrested on suspicion of falsifying records to close files on two people who were later found dead. President Lee Jae Myung has ordered an investigation into the police handling of adult missing persons and told the force to draw up a reform plan. How many people have been reported missing? More than 70,000 were reported missing last year, with 99.7% of cases closed without a full-scale search. Of those, 931 people were found dead. Why were so many missing persons cases closed? Only children, autistic people, and people with dementia or mental disabilities are formally treated as missing under missing law. Everyone else is classified as a runaway, with none of those tools automatically available. In other news … King Harald V of Norway, Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, died on Friday at the age of 89. He will be succeeded by his son King Haakon VIII. Seven people charged with vandalising Donald Trump’s Turnberry golf course in Scotland have been accused of malicious damage and “having a terrorist connection”. Three journalists who were fired by the Pentagon from a US government-funded news outlet have sued the Department of Defense and are arguing that their dismissals were illegal and violated their first-amendment rights to free speech. A federal judge on Thursday placed a 14-day hold on attempts to implement Trump’s executive order limiting mail voting in a case that could head back to the supreme court. Stat of the day: $1bn worth of goods cross into Detroit from Windsor, Canada every day Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, are two largely blue-collar US and Canadian cities that have come to act as one in the creation of North America’s auto industry. With an estimated $1bn in goods crossing the river that divides the two cities each day, Trump’s bluster this week about imposing 50% tariffs on Canadian goods has many in the two cities worried. Culture Pick: Tim Curry’s best screen roles The world lost an acting legend this week with the death of Tim Curry. Here’s a look back at some of his most memorable screen roles, from the campy menace that was Dr Frank-N-Furter to the terrifying Pennywise the Clown. Don’t miss this: The man leading the DRC’s Ebola fight Prof Pierre Akilimali heads the Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which is in the midst of the largest outbreak in its history. There have been more than 5,650 confirmed cases and more than 2,710 deaths. “Rest is not an easy thing for the Ebola workers to find,” the doctor said. “What carries me and the team is the simple knowledge that every contact followed, every family supported, is a life where the worst was avoided.” … or this: Six months of the Iran war Today marks the six-month anniversary of when the US and Israel began launching large-scale strikes on Iran, plunging the region into a conflict that upended global trade. The Guardian’s visuals team has put together a timeline documenting six months of strikes, public threats, failed diplomacy and wild swings in the price of oil. Climate check: The burning of fossil fuels may have supercharged El Niño climatic patterns, study finds El Niño – a naturally occurring phenomenon when the waters of the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean heat up, causing a cascade of effects around the world – typically brings a surge of global heat that further amplifies the escalating climate crisis. But new research has established that the reverse is also true – that human-caused global heating is making El Niño more intense when it does arrive. Last Thing: Erykah Badu on defying definition Erykah Badu sat down with the Guardian before the release of her newest album, Before the World Blows: The Abi and Alan Experiment. A collaborative record with the famed underground producer the Alchemist, it will be her first album in 11 years. “Procrastinating and living, learning and stuff – that gives you stuff to write about,” she said. “It’s important to gather the data, upload as much as I can. I don’t have a choice. But when the thing gets kind of full, I download it through writing music.” Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday.
