title: Vaccine misinformation spreads as RFK Jr suggests two measles deaths were ‘fabricated’
author: Melody Schreiber
summary: Anti-vaxxers are spreading conspiracy theories after two recent measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania
body_text: Anti-vaccine activists are trying to track down the families of two people, including at least one newborn, who died after contracting measles in Pennsylvania, as Governor Josh Shapiro tangles with Robert F Kennedy Jr over his “inaccurate and misleading claims”. Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), suggested late on Wednesday that the deaths in the state may have been “fabricated” after a Republican coroner – an elected political office in Lancaster county – claimed one of the measles-associated deaths was unrelated to the virus, although the given cause would be consistent with measles. Brian Hooker at Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine organization that until recently was led by Kennedy, said in a recent video that the organization is “trying to get boots on the ground” and “do outreach” in Pennsylvania. Kennedy is “an anti-vaccine activist in the role of the most powerful public health person in this country”, said Paul Offit, an infectious diseases physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “It’s like the world’s turned upside down.” It would be helpful to know the deceased patients’ ages and more information about their deaths, he added. “By not having that information, it allows fertile ground for the kind of conspiracy theory that RFK Jr puts out there, where he said in some posts that these weren’t measles deaths.” The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said in a Thursday post on X that it was “working to determine what actually occurred”, including “whether the two reported deaths were caused by measles”. The HHS did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about whether Kennedy recommends the vaccine or whether the newly confirmed CDC director, Erica Schwartz, would make a statement about the outbreak and the need for vaccination. About 424 Pennsylvanians have confirmed measles cases, and 73 have been hospitalized. None of the sickened people are fully vaccinated. The two deaths were in unvaccinated patients in Lancaster county, Pennsylvania, which is home to large Amish and Mennonite communities. While these communities do not have religious objections to vaccines, they eschew many parts of modern life, and thus are relatively disconnected from modern healthcare. Few other details have been released about the patients, fueling a firestorm of misinformation from anti-vaccine activists spreading conspiracy theories about vaccines, which are 97% effective at preventing measles. The anti-vaccine activists are attempting to figure out who died so they can reach the families, as they did in Texas when a six-year-old girl died last year, Hooker said. They filmed a misinformation-filled interview with the Mennonite parents in a rare media appearance after their daughter’s death. Hooker also speculated that the Pennsylvania announcement was a political ploy in advance of the US midterm elections, claiming it was “a strategic move” to “get measles deaths on the tip of everybody’s tongue, to get in the forefront”. The Trump administration has at times attempted to downplay its anti-vaccine moves because they are not popular with voters, according to internal polling. When Shapiro first announced the deaths, he pointed to the inaccurate claims from the highest levels of the US government, saying at a press conference: “There’s real-life consequences to spreading misinformation.” Kennedy responded on X with debunked myths about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Shapiro called those claims “inaccurate and misleading” in his own X post. When Kennedy offered to help after the announcement of the two deaths, Shapiro asked him to encourage vaccination and stop spreading misinformation, the governor said in the post. The health secretary responded by repeating vaccine misinformation and saying “it would be better if we went back to ‘natural measles’,” Shapiro wrote. “Secretary Kennedy has stoked confusion amongst parents and others – and the result has been less protection from measles and more cases,” Shapiro added. In 2021, for instance, Kennedy gave a speech praising Amish parents in Lancaster county for not vaccinating their children. “The cure for measles is chicken soup and vitamin A,” he said. There is no cure for measles, only supportive care. A few hours after Shapiro’s response, Kennedy posted to X wondering whether the deaths had been “fabricated” and alleging that Pennsylvania was refusing to share information with the CDC. But Pennsylvania notified the CDC of the deaths early on Tuesday morning, before making the public announcement, Dr Debra Bogen, the state’s secretary of health, said in a statement. “I have thoroughly reviewed the case investigation information and sadly can confirm that there were two recent measles-associated deaths in Lancaster County,” she said. The cases were also thoroughly investigated by the state’s epidemiology team, and both individuals tested positive for measles, she added. One of the deaths was in a newborn who tested positive for measles, the department of health said on Facebook. Stephen Diamantoni, the coroner for Lancaster county, told the Philadelphia Inquirer that a test on the baby’s lung tissue after death indicated a measles infection acquired before birth. He believes the baby died shortly after birth because of a lacerated spleen. Spleen issues are a known complication of measles infection. Having an enlarged spleen from measles “was not uncommon actually in the pre-vaccine era”, Offit said. The scientific literature includes doctors’ observations of enlarged spleens, which can lead to rupture. “If you have an enlarged spleen and you’re infected with measles virus, the measles virus caused your enlarged spleen. If you then have a splenic rupture which kills you, you die from measles,” Offit said. Anti-vaccine activists have been successful in driving down vaccination rates, Offit said. The ensuing outbreak “isn’t a good look” for them, he said. Children’s Health Defense appeared to want to downplay its role and put out “the same kind of bad information” after the children died in Texas, Offit said. “It’s very easy to convince those parents – very easy – that this wasn’t their fault, because otherwise, they would have to take on the responsibility or the notion that they could have prevented their child’s death.” Hooker complained on Wednesday that the scant details released about the patients made it difficult to reach them. He also noted that his organization was unable to contact the family of a measles-positive adult who died in New Mexico last year, because the state did not release more public information. “The more information that they release regarding these particular deaths, the more that we would be able to dig in and contact family members, get access to medical records and see exactly what happened,” said Hooker. Children’s Health Defense has claimed that one of the child deaths in Texas last year was due to medical error, not measles, despite findings from officials on measles. Measles deaths have become rare in the US because of vaccination, but between one and three people usually die with every 1,000 infections. The US is now experiencing its worst outbreak of measles in three decades. It is unusual for measles to spread in summer months like this – and now children are heading back to school, potentially amplifying transmission, Offit said. “You’re just going to see, I think, an explosion of measles.” Infants under the age of six months are too young to be vaccinated against measles, which is a large reason why it is important to vaccinate pregnant parents and others in the community, Offit said. More than 35,000 Pennsylvanians got vaccinated against measles last month – an increase of 10,000 compared to typical months.

title: Pauline Hanson courts wealthy donors with $2,000 ‘exclusive’ Melbourne lunch, but where are the receipts?
author: Henry Belot and Benita Kolovos
summary: One Nation hopes to raise $36,000 from the lunch but the state party has disclosed just one donation this financial year
body_text: On Tuesday at 9am, a hand-picked group of business leaders in Melbourne will be texted the address of one of the city’s “most prestigious and exclusive venues”. Pauline Hanson will be waiting for them. Over a three-course lunch, One Nation Victoria will provide “a unique opportunity to meet senator Hanson” and engage in an “open, candid discussion” about economic issues. In return, the party hopes to raise at least $36,000. Details of this “deliberately small” gathering in Melbourne’s CBD are being closely guarded by the party’s state branch. It is eager to protect those paying a $2,000 entry fee from protesters who have already targeted two high-profile fundraisers in June and August. Hanson will have just returned from a separate fundraising dinner on Monday with the Victorian party’s leader, Warren Pickering, in the regional town of Sale. The pair are also hosting a barbecue in Melbourne’s outer suburbs a day earlier. Despite their significant fundraising efforts in recent months, One Nation Victoria had not disclosed a single donation above the $1,290 threshold since 1 July until late this week, after being contacted by Guardian Australia. Last financial year, the state branch disclosed less than $20,000. So far this year, with an election in November, it has disclosed just one $5,000 donation. All donations must be reported to the state electoral commission within 21 days. Meanwhile, Labor’s well-oiled fundraising vehicle has secured 217 donations worth $634,000 since 1 July and the Liberals have disclosed 65 donations worth $220,000. The rush for cash The federal party claims to have raised millions of dollars from its “fire the liar” campaign targeting the prime minister, Anthony Albanese. Multiple Victorian Liberal sources have told Guardian Australia that some of its traditionally loyal donors are also supporting One Nation. But in Victoria, money donated to federal parties cannot be used to finance state election campaigns. Local candidates must raise the money themselves. This has led to state candidates, government ministers and opposition leaders attending fundraising dinners across the state. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “They know there is no such thing as a free meal,” said one person involved in organising fundraising dinners. According to the Victorian Electoral Commission, One Nation Victoria did not disclose a single donation in July. In June, it received three donations worth $7,970. It also disclosed one donation in May of $2,000. After being contacted by Guardian Australia on Wednesday, One Nation disclosed a $5,000 donation that was received on Thursday last week. The total of that donation has not yet been confirmed by the donor – a requirement of the commission. One Nation updates invites Politicians dining with donors behind closed doors in return for money is nothing new. Almost every party does it, from the prime minister down, despite routine criticism from transparency experts who warn it’s harming trust in democracy. But One Nation’s invites to fundraisers have differed from the approach taken by Labor and Liberal campaigns, which clearly state which branch money will go to and how it will be used. An invitation to Tuesday’s “private lunch” did not carry a formal authorisation message, which tells potential donors which party is ultimately responsible for the political content and the event. University of Melbourne law professor Joo-Cheong Tham, an expert in electoral integrity, said the invitations should have been authorised. The Victorian Electoral Commission did not comment directly on the invitation, but said “all electoral material produced by a registered political party must be authorised”. When contacted by Guardian Australia with these comments, One Nation Victoria did not respond but updated its invitations to include authorisation from the state party. This matches the authorisation for Monday’s dinner fundraiser with Hanson and a local candidate, Greg Hansford. But a third fundraising dinner with Hanson in Melbourne, scheduled for less than a month before the November election, contains an authorisation message from the federal party registered in Queensland. It also carries One Nation’s federal logo. This “senator’s circle” dinner specifically mentions the state campaign and tells donors that “we look forward to sharing the evening with you as we prepare for an important period ahead in Victoria”. “With the Victorian election approaching, this dinner provides a unique opportunity to hear from our representatives, connect with fellow supporters and help strengthen One Nation’s efforts across the state,” the invite said. ‘Donors risk exceeding the cap’ None of the three One Nation invitations to dinner seen by Guardian Australia outline disclosure obligations or a donation cap. Labor invitations to fundraisers seen by Guardian Australia include an overview of the donation cap and disclosure threshold, authorisation by the state party, and details on which branch receives the money and what it will be used for. An invite to a “cocktail evening” on Wednesday with the Liberal candidate for Hawthorn, Amelia Hamer, said all donations would go to the state campaign but carried no formal authorisation. This was corrected by the Liberal party on Friday, after being contacted by Guardian Australia. The lack of detail about donation rules on One Nation invitations has concerned one senior Liberal party figure, who was not authorised to comment publicly. “Donors are at very high risk of inadvertently exceeding Victoria’s strict donation caps because One Nation is not even bothering to tell them about them when soliciting contributions,” the source said. A senior Labor source also raised concerns about the lack of detail on invitations and said “every political party and candidate should be subject to the same level of scrutiny and accountability”. But the Victorian Electoral Commission said there was no “obligation to provide this information to donors before the donation has been given”. “For example, it may be provided in a receipt once the political donation has been given,” the spokesperson said. The spokesperson said it would “look at any material raised with us and compare it against the requirements of the [electoral act]”. “When in doubt, authorise.” One Nation Victoria did not respond to questions from Guardian Australia.

title: Labor wrestles with migration figures but opponents struggle to find the target
author: Sarah Basford Canales, Krishani Dhanji and Tom McIlroy
summary: By focusing on the net overseas migration number, Labor risks making a ‘silly mistake’ experts say
body_text: Anyone looking for an indication of just how hot the politics of immigration are running inside federal Labor need only consider what happened on Thursday. Morning newspaper reports confirmed that Labor would cut Australia’s annual refugee intake, with numbers dropping from 20,000 arrivals to 13,750 from next financial year. Under intense pressure from One Nation, and facing public concern that the rate of overseas arrivals are adding to infrastructure pressures and housing shortages, the government had already flagged plans for a major immigration policy reset. The cut to humanitarian places had been settled separately and was simply the end of a temporary increase from 13,750 places, announced in 2023. But the news quickly roiled Labor MPs. Some believed the increased allocation had been extended, others believed that decision was a fait accompli at next year’s budget. Appearing at a summit in Dubbo mid-morning, Albanese sought to dismiss the reports but did not say they were wrong. By late afternoon, he overruled the decision and confirmed in a statement that the cut would not proceed. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email One Labor MP was frank about the chaos. The party would be at war if the cuts went ahead, they said. Members of Labor’s left faction were “pretty outraged”, and said caucus had not been consulted. More than a few MPs went straight to the offices of Albanese and the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, seeking an explanation. One Labor source said that Burke told MPs no decision had been made on cutting the intake. Labor for Refugees, a rank and file group, said in a statement released on Friday that it was “grateful” for the prime minister’s intervention in “ensuring Australia’s humanity hasn’t been forgotten”. This latest incident only adds to the growing expectations on the broader reset, expected to be announced soon. Originally due earlier this month, Burke’s timing was delayed by Labor’s internal deliberations. Now more than three years on from the end of pandemic border closures, just how did Australia get here and how important will the politics of immigration be at the next election? A difficult migration target to achieve Quickly after Labor’s 2022 election victory, effective management of overseas arrivals became a policy and political challenge for the new government. Ahead of the 2023 federal budget, the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said the halt on immigration for four quarters during the pandemic would result in a reactive surge – an expected catchup, he suggested. Net overseas migration (Nom), the overall gain or loss of total population through long-term arrivals and departures, would become a familiar term. Nom measures people coming into or leaving the country for a period of at least 12 months over 16 months, including leaving and returning Australian citizens. The 2023 federal budget forecast a Nom of 400,000 in 2022–23, dropping to 260,000 in 2024-25. Chalmers said at the time Australia wanted students in the economy and tourists to support communities and industries. “Those are good things, but we need to find places for people to live,” he said on ABC’s Q+A program. The 2024-25 Nom ended up reaching 301,000, which was 50,000 off the 2023 budget forecast but within 6,000 of the next budget’s revised forecast. Still, the Albanese government’s adversaries have pointed to the figures as evidence of policy failures. The former deputy immigration department secretary, Abul Rizvi, said the first problem was focusing the debate on a Nom figure as a strict cap to be adhered to. Rizvi said governments should set a range to achieve in line with policy goals because predicting the Nom was extremely difficult. “If the Nom falls outside your target, then you have to ask, ‘well, what policy change do we need to make to get it back in the target?’” he said. The challenge is a high or unpredictable Nom makes budget and policy planning, and service provision for governments very difficult. So, what can Labor do? Senior ministers have been discussing how to find a sensible middle ground on immigration without serious negative ripple effects. It hasn’t been easy. From a numbers perspective, the number of temporary migrants has soared in recent years due to an easing of restrictions under the Morrison government when the country faced a labour shortage in addition to economic challenges. While overseas arrivals are on par with, or even below in some quarters, pre-Covid figures, the surge in Nom has been mostly affected by fewer migrants leaving, Rizvi said. “The first and biggest factor driving Nom is the labour market,” Rizvi said. “A strong labour market makes pushing Nom down hard because everything is acting against you. A weak labour market makes pushing Nom down a lot easier because you’re sailing with the wind.” When the labour market isn’t on side, migration policy tweaks are required. One response is slowing the rate of backpacker visa approvals, which the government has already ordered. It has also told the home affairs department to prioritise skilled foreign workers already in Australia for visa approvals, rather than allow more overseas arrivals. On Thursday, Albanese said tight control of arrivals would be a bedrock of Labor’s new plans, complemented by removing visa holders who had lost their right to live in Australia. The changes could include tougher restrictions on international students, tougher rules for their family members seeking to come to Australia and efforts to stop visa category changes for those enrolled in higher education. New enforcement options are being discussed, as well as rules restricting people in the country already being able to lodge new applications. Visa periods could be reduced to six months for tourists and some businesspeople, and appeal rights for rejections further curtailed. Other plans to bring down the Nom continue to be developed, with Burke charged with overseeing a drop from the current rate of more than 300,000 to the forecast included in the May federal budget of 245,000 this financial year. From there, it would drop to 225,000 in 2027-28. Critically, according to Rizvi, is a new requirement for the minister to report to cabinet every quarter on progress in achieving the Nom forecasts. For other migration experts, like Alan Gamlen, a social scientist at the Australian National University, the conversation is focusing on the wrong figures. “If we talk about Nom, we’re inviting imprecision. We’re not targeting the parts of migration that actually need to be addressed in order to properly address the concerns that people have,” he said. “What we are doing is having a debate about a number that nobody understands, in a way that isn’t connected to the problems people are experiencing, and has zero chance of being successful at addressing those problems.” Nom focus could force ‘silly’ mistakes The Nom has fallen in seven consecutive quarters since September 2023. It is forecast to fall further lower than pre-Covid levels by 2027-28. What hasn’t fallen is the number of temporary visa holders. For the 2024-25 financial year, there were 568,370 overseas arrivals, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics data. The figure includes Australian and New Zealand citizens, as well as permanent visa holders. Still, 363,090, or 64%, were temporary visa holders. During the same period, 147,930 temporary visa holders departed. It’s a major talking point of conservative populist politicians but Gamlen said there are some issues. Australia’s permanent migration program has remained consistently stable over the decade with the exception of the pandemic travel bans. Many are international students looking for ways to stay and work in Australia. Gamlen said the temporary migration population could be controlled efficiently by stemming the demand-driven process. Simply, instead of letting anyone apply directly for visas, it could be done on an invitation basis through prospective visa applicants filling out expression of interest forms. That can prevent those being denied visas – due to not fulfilling the visa criteria – appealing through the Administrative Review Tribunal. “The danger is that by constantly barking on about net overseas migration the government will feel pressured to do something that is silly, and regulate types of migration that shouldn’t be regulated simply in order to hit an arbitrary Nom target,” Gamlen said. “There’s a very simple rule that that the government needs to be aware of – the size of the temporary population stabilises if you have an equal number of net temporary arrivals and conversions from temporary to permanent status. “If there’s too few temporary to permanent conversions, you’ll get a growing temporary population, and if there’s too few temporary arrivals, you get a shrinking temporary population.” No one has a clear policy While Labor’s position remains unclear, its political rivals have less sense of what their own migration numbers should be. One Nation has struggled to explain its own plans, with neither Pauline Hanson nor her parliamentary colleague David Farley seeming to understand what the Nom is. Both have claimed Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (Palm) scheme workers and backpackers working on farms would not be counted in their 130,000 Nom target. The Coalition quickly separated itself from shadow housing minister Andrew Bragg’s suggestion that the Nom should drop to under 180,000 but on Friday left the door open to cutting refugee intake. “What is clear though is we are a very generous country but charity starts at home and we have got to do the right thing by Australians first,” the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told News24. Earlier, the shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, said Australia had a responsibility to “look after those less fortunate”. The party says firmer commitments will come closer to the election. As for Labor’s approach, Albanese and Burke will announce the new policy within weeks. “We’re worried about trying to get numbers right,” the prime minister said. “We’re responding to national needs.” This story was amended on 29 August 2026. An earlier version misspelt Abul Rizvi’s first name.

title: Labour rejects Zack Polanski’s call to ‘slam brakes’ on building AI datacentres
author: Robert Booth UK technology editor
summary: Government says Green leader’s proposed moratorium on ‘energy-guzzling’ AI projects would be disaster for economy
body_text: Labour has rejected calls to pause construction of major AI infrastructure in Britain after the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said it was time to “slam the brakes on these energy-guzzling, water-guzzling datacentres”. The government hit back at the opposition party’s proposal of a “moratorium other than [for] local-scale datacentres for the local community”, saying it “would be a disaster for jobs and national security”. The Greens’ call for a pause comes amid one of the UK’s worst droughts in years and predictions that datacentres’ electricity use, now standing at about 2.5% of the UK’s supply, will rise fourfold by 2030. Datacentres contain the processing chips that power billions of AI prompts every day and Labour has designated them as critical national infrastructure, a decision Polanski called “outrageous”. “To most people critical infrastructure means hospitals, water, electricity,” he said. “It doesn’t mean artificial intelligence.” He added: “Right now the government is putting our communities, our water security and our climate ambitions second to the demands of tech giants.” A spokesperson for the government said: “A pause on building new datacentres would simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on overseas computing for the processing of sensitive health and defence data.” They said critical national infrastructure status did not give datacentres priority access to water or electricity, nor did it automatically put them ahead of households during shortages, and that in England datacentres’ water usage represented less than 1% of non-household water consumption. The row comes amid increasing signs that datacentre policy, already a major political issue in the US midterm elections, is rising up the agenda in Britain. In energy- and water-rich Scotland, the Scottish National party government appears to be “inching towards a moratorium” amid voter pressure, while local disputes have erupted from Devon to Buckinghamshire and Cardiff to Fife where residents have raised fears about noise, heat, traffic and the visual impact of datacentres affecting house prices. The AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, has linked the need for more AI datacentres to strong defence and this month claimed the British public “doesn’t just want foreign billionaires to own things that matter to our lives. If we’re being true to those British values, it is impossible to achieve that without building a sovereign level of datacentre capacity.” The government spokesperson said its refusal to pause development “does not mean a blank cheque for big tech or that every datacentre should be approved”. They said developers should “prioritise clean power, use water responsibly, create British jobs and supply chains, and provide investment to the communities in which they are built”. The tech equity campaign group Foxglove warned that with some datacentre developers seeking to mitigate long waits to connect to the energy grid by planning their own gas-fired power stations, there was a risk of a “deeply alarming backward step on climate action”. Rosa Curling, its co-executive director, said: “It’s good to hear that the government thinks there shouldn’t be a ‘blank cheque’ for big tech’s datacentres. But without urgent action, that’s exactly what will happen – the public and the planet will be left to foot the bill for the environmental and social costs of these energy-hungry giants.”

title: Trump pledges to allow cattle ranchers to process own food amid beef imports backlash
author: Shrai Popat in Washington
summary: President faces criticism over plan to import up to 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef without charging higher tariffs
body_text: Donald Trump has pledged to allow cattle ranchers and farmers to process their own food amid a backlash from the US agricultural sector over his decision to pause US tariffs on foreign beef. The US president has been sharply criticized, including from members of his own party, since announcing the US will temporarily import up to 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef without charging higher tariffs in an effort to bring down prices. Republican lawmakers have warned in recent days that “flooding” stores with imports will hit US ranchers, suggesting that the move is a short-term solution that will hinder cattle farmers from building out their herd, amid a 75-year low. In a statement on Friday, Trump praised farmers and ranchers – describing them as “smart, efficient, and immaculately CLEAN” on social media – and claimed the agricultural sector had “always been a number one priority for me”. “For years I have heard that they have had a tremendous problem with the Big Processors, who many say are a nasty Monopoly,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, referring to food processing companies. “There are, essentially, 4 of them, a very non competitive number, and they make life miserable for our wonderful Farmers and Ranchers, and I can’t let that happen, can I? “So, in order to break this powerful monopoly, with much of its ownership based outside of the U.S., I am authorizing legal documents to be drawn in order to allow Farmers and Ranchers to be given the right to PROCESS THEIR OWN FOOD. This should move quickly.” It comes after Trump’s interview with the conservative commentator Glenn Beck earlier this week, during which the radio host and ranch owner implored Trump to “look at” the “meat processing cartel” and suggested easing regulations for ranchers to slaughter their own cattle and sell. Brooke Rollins, Trump’s agriculture secretary said there would be “big announcements” next week to facilitate the president’s plan to allow ranchers and farmers the ability to process their own food. Rollins said it was a “matter of national security” that the US was able to “feed and fuel ourselves”. She outlined that her department would waive “red tape in processing” and expand ranchers ability to “sell across state lines”, as well as other measures. However, it is not clear what authority the administration has to enact these changes, since there are strict regulatory requirements in place, and a bill that would ease US Department of Agriculture (USDA) inspections for small ranches and farmers to sell meat directly to consumers is now stalled in Congress. Thomas Massie, a Republican congressman from Kentucky and one of the bipartisan sponsors of the bill, said the president’s action was “great” but “it should be a law, not just an executive order”.

title: Trump administration pushing to hand parcel of Yosemite land to private developer – report
author: Dani Anguiano
summary: Nevada-based Kingsbarn Realty Capital seeks to acquire land to construct private road to development outside park
body_text: The Trump administration is reportedly pushing to give a parcel of land inside Yosemite, one of the country’s most popular national parks, to a Nevada-based private developer. Staff with the National Park Service have been exploring how the agency can give a quarter-mile parcel to a company operated by Kingsbarn Realty Capital, the news outlet Notus reported on Friday, citing agency documents and unnamed sources “directly familiar with discussions”. The company already owns an 83-acre (34-hectare) plot of undeveloped land immediately outside the park. The previous owner of that land had hoped to create a resort and unsuccessfully lobbied the federal government for decades to allow him to construct a private road in the park, the outlet reported. The current access road to the land, which Kingsbarn bought in 2024, is more than 10 miles (16km) from the nearest park entrance and would require travelers to take a longer, indirect route to reach popular park attractions. Jeff Pori, the company’s CEO, wants to construct a short road to connect the parcel to a central Yosemite route, according to Notus. Administration officials have proposed that the park service give up the land in exchange for equally valuable land elsewhere in California, the outlet reported. The interior department’s top political leaders support the proposal, according to sources cited by Notus, and the situation has created tension inside the park service. In a statement to the Guardian, Aubrie Spady, an interior department spokesperson, rejected the reporting, arguing there “has been no political pressure to reach a predetermined outcome”, and said “suggesting the Department is secretly working to hand over National Park Service land to a private developer [is] false.” The report has sparked outrage among National Park Service supporters and environmental advocates. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for Save Our Parks, described it as part of a “push to sell off public lands and privatize America’s national parks” by the US interior secretary, Doug Burgum. “If mismanaging parks and stealing entrance fees for Trump’s DC vanity projects wasn’t enough, now Americans find out Doug Burgum and his cronies spent a year secretly negotiating to hand a piece of Yosemite national park over to a well-connected developer, all while lying to us about protecting them,” O’Neill said. “National parks belong to the American people, not monied developers who are part of Trump’s donor class.” Both of California’s senators have expressed their opposition to efforts to develop the road, as has Jared Huffman, the Democratic California congressman representing the state’s north coast. “Our parks belong to all of us. These places should be protected for every generation, not sold off to Trump’s ultra-wealthy friends to profit off of,” Huffman said. “I will fight this, both for Yosemite and for every treasured park that would be up for grabs if this domino falls.” The interior department said no final decisions had been reached and that any land exchange or access proposal would be “subject to all applicable federal laws, regulations and Departmental policies, including required environmental review and public notification processes”. • This article was amended on 29 August 2026. Yellowstone was the first US national park, not Yosemite as the original version stated.

title: Los Angeles fire survivors face record wait for federal disaster aid under Trump
author: Gabrielle Canon
summary: Nearly 600 days after the devastating 2025 fires, thousands of Los Angeles residents are still waiting for more than $15bn in federal funds to rebuild their communities
body_text: As thousands of residents in Spokane, Washington, begin to grapple with a long recovery after a destructive set of blazes that consumed hundreds of homes in the state’s second most populated city this month, victims of the Los Angeles firestorm broke a grim record – they have faced the longest delay in modern history for federal aid. Nearly 600 days since a historic firestorm roared into communities across Los Angeles, reducing more than 16,000 structures to ash and toxic debris, the Trump administration has failed to appropriate more than $15bn in long-term recovery funds that are crucial to rebuilding. The delay in supplying the badly needed funds is months longer than the last record set when victims of the Maui fires had to wait 500 days to receive the support, LAist noted this week. Recoveries from large-scale disasters like these have long stretched across years. But there are concerns that lags or lapses in support from the federal role will add new challenges to already complex rebuilding efforts in devastated areas across the US. Donald Trump has repeatedly been accused of politicizing disasters, to the detriment of communities left in limbo. “Spokane has joined a rapidly growing list of our communities that have been devastated by these climate-exaggerated fires,” Jay Inslee, the former Washington state governor said, adding that he had recently visited Altadena, one of the areas of Los Angeles decimated by the fires. It has just been absolutely ripped open and has not been able to recover yet,” he said. “Donald Trump has strangled these communities by refusing to give emergency assistance.” Along with withholding funds, the president has also imposed “unlawful” conditions on states requesting federal grants for disaster response and preparedness, according to attorneys general from 25 Democratic-led states that sued the administration in July. The group, which was led by California’s Rob Bonta, claimed the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) have used a “campaign of coercion”, leveraging the needed disaster support in an attempt to force states to implement voting and immigration policies pushed by the president. Trump has rejected disaster aid for Democratic-run states far more often than his predecessors, approving only 23% of their requests compared with 89% of requests from states largely represented by Republicans, Politico reported in March. The president also initially threatened to attach political conditions to federal aid he said would go to Los Angeles fire victims. Meanwhile, recovery there has been painful and slow. The fires, which erupted in the parched southern California hillsides and cascaded into the surrounding suburbs with shocking ferocity in January 2025, left behind unprecedented levels of destruction in the city and county of Los Angeles. Thirty-one people were killed directly by the disaster. Homes, businesses, churches and schools were leveled in the aftermath, with thousands more structures left uninhabitable or damaged from smoke and surrounding toxic debris. “Eighteen months after the Eaton and Palisades fires, the challenges facing impacted communities continue to grow more urgent,” the Department of Angels, a non-profit founded to support recovery efforts in the immediate aftermath of the fire, wrote in its latest report, which noted that LA had experienced the longest wait for major disaster funding from the federal government in modern history. With the second anniversary of the fires just months away, scores of Angelenos remain in limbo. Roughly two-thirds of survivors were still displaced as of late July, according to a report from the Department of Angels. In their sixth survey done with more than 2,000 fire victims, the group found that all forms of financial assistance had decreased in recent months, while homeowners typically face a roughly $500,000 gap in trying to rebuild. Close to half of those affected had to take on debt to stay afloat and 20% have had to delay rebuilding or repairs due to financial constraints. “Recovery has stalled while families wait for the federal resources that have long helped communities rebuild after disasters,” they wrote. While it can take years for federal funds to be allocated in the aftermath of a complex disaster, the Trump administration has yet to begin the long process. State officials have accused the president of politicizing the disaster, which affected a county that largely votes Democratic. “Donald Trump’s desire to punish Los Angeles and the state of California for not voting for him, means once again that thousands of Angelenos are left watching this administration fight for anything but them, their businesses, and their communities,” the California Democratic senators, Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff said in a joint statement issued in June, after the president’s $87.6bn budget request focused on military funding for the war in Iran omitted funds for disasters. California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, has reportedly made several additional requests to Trump over the last 18 months, urging immediate action to support victims of the fire. These requests had yet to be approved as of early August, according to the governor. In March, the state issued an updated accounting of what’s needed from the federal government, which includes roughly $10.5bn in Community Development Block Grants to help with rebuilding both housing and infrastructure, $179m in economic development administration business grants and $3bn for public assistance projects meant to replace damaged or destroyed schools, senior centers, libraries and parks. The governor has also requested support to restore damaged water systems and improve affected streets and sidewalks. Newsom called on Trump to make good on his pledge to provide the support while the president was visiting LA earlier this month. The trip, however, has come and gone. Advocates and officials in Washington are also urging Trump to take urgent action to support the fire recovery just beginning there. “There is a major effort to put pressure on this president to do his job, which is to help these families and communities – and he hasn’t done that,” Inslee said. In 2020, while Inslee was governor, Trump neglected to issue a disaster declaration that would help victims in the rural town of Malden, Washington, after a fire destroyed roughly 80% of the homes there, due to a political feud between the two politicians. The order came a year later, after Biden took office. “We’re hoping that that does not happen again in the Spokane fires,” Inslee said. “We’re hoping that he will have an epiphany to understand what his job is, which is to help all Americans, no matter who they voted for.”

title: Trump announces new US oil agreement with Venezuela
author: Guardian staff and agencies
summary: US president says US will have ‘majority’ control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves
body_text: Donald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez, saying the US will have “majority” control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves. The terms of the agreement remain to be seen, but the US president said on his social-media platform that it had been brokered “through a partnership with ⁠private business” by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. The administration, Trump wrote, has “secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 BILLION ‌BARRELS of proven Oil ‌Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the ‌American Taxpayer”. Trump said the agreement would more than double American oil reserves. “This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people,” Rubio wrote on social media. Trump’s announcement provided few details on the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved, or how the US would exercise majority control over the ⁠reserves. Venezuela has an estimated 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves, the world’s largest. Since the US captured and removed former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro from power in January, Washington has been trying ‌to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude oil for US refineries while promoting American investment into the Opec country’s deteriorated energy industry, which produces 1.25m barrels per day of crude. Trump is under pressure before November’s midterm elections over rising gasoline prices, which could be eased through cheaper oil supplies and expanded output. The US also has ‌been looking for solutions to replenish its strategic petroleum reserve, the oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude swaps with US producers. Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was “in advanced talks with Venezuela for the U.S. to take a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields that house nearly one-third of the country’s massive energy reserves”. Axios also reported on the negotiations, quoting a US official who claimed the deal would be “massive”. The discussion was reportedly over a US stake in Venezuela’s most promising oil-and-gasfields, with some 90bn barrels of proven reserves. The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro. “It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticizing the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States.” The announcement comes as Chevron and other US energy companies are expected to sign a deal next week investing billions in Venezuela’s oil fields, according to the Journal. Tom Phillips and Reuters contributed reporting

title: ‘I don’t want to be a backseat driver’: Gordon Brown on Burnham, billionaires – and his vision for a better Britain
author: Charlotte Edwardes
summary: The former UK prime minister is still shaping politics (even if he doesn’t want to interfere). He talks about keeping his temper, staying fit – and why he won’t pay £90 for a Scotland football shirt
body_text: It’s a Monday in August and as England burns in dystopian heat, Gordon Brown and I are in his office at the top of his house in North Queensferry, overlooking the moody waters of the Firth of Forth. It’s hard to recall the top of my own sauna-like house in London as we stand here in the cool, wearing wool suits and necessary socks, my coat slung over the back of a chair. “I was watching Raith Rovers – the local football team – on Saturday,” Brown says, “and it was really cold. There was a wind blowing in from the sea.” He asks if I’ve heard the famous joke – “Scotland’s only got two seasons: July and winter”– then chuckles. It’s one of his favourites. (I’ll hear him tell it three times today.) That’s not to say Fife has been untouched by the multiple heatwaves. They had a few sunny days. One hit 24C – “a shock”, Brown says, July temperatures typically being 15-17C. He stood in his kitchen and considered the modest patch of grass at the back of the house. “I never imagined being out in the garden in the summer. I never imagined it because it’s either raining or too cold.” Once out, he found himself battling a “very dangerous” nest of wasps. One family member was stung, then there was the rigmarole of specialists in thick gloves and protective suits undertaking its removal. By the time that was done, the sun had gone in. Climate is something we will discuss today, it being something of a wasps’ nest. Also: Donald Trump, Europe, Andy Burnham and the Labour party. The former prime minister (2007-2010) and longest-serving chancellor of the exchequer in modern history (1997-2007) will touch on Iraq, the financial crisis and Scottish independence. He will give his diagnosis of the current state of global politics, the focus of his new book, The Future Starts With Us. What’s telling is how much people still want to hear his views – arguably far more than any of the six broken PMs since (tickets for his forthcoming book events in Bath and Edinburgh sold out in minutes). Many feel we didn’t know how lucky we were with Brown and his old-school sense of duty. At the time we saw him as a brooding toad, a hangdog, grizzled pessimist, instead of prizing his gratitude and prudence. His father’s booming refrain was “Be thankful for what you have; you can cope with a lot less!” so perhaps it wasn’t surprising Brown did not cash in when he left No 10. Did not take a fat job in banking, a knighthood, or even the prime ministerial pension to which he’s entitled. He’s aware that, as a political heavyweight, his views on Labour still count and that he has a reputation for micromanagement, so initially he’s careful when I ask about Burnham. “I don’t want to be a backseat driver,” he says, settling into a tub chair next to a wall of books (political biographies, political philosophy, a first edition Keynes). But can he help himself? No, he cannot. A second later he’s saying he “hopes” Burnham will heed a report he did for Keir Starmer recommending abolishing the House of Lords and replacing it with an elected chamber “representative of all the regions and nations of the country, which fits in with Andy’s idea that the regions and the nations are going to have a bigger voice”. He reminds me the Lords is an unelected chamber of about 800, “the second largest legislature in the world after China”. It’s packed to the Pugin rafters with lobbyists. The problem will be persuading them to vote to cut their own throats. “But something’s got to change.” Brown calls Burnham “Andy”. He has known him a long time. Burnham’s first cabinet job was under Brown as chief secretary to the Treasury (later, he was health secretary in Brown’s government). Brown’s official role under Burnham is as an adviser overseeing the G20, which Britain hosts next year. He was brought in to do it by Starmer (remember the photo op of him going in to No 10 with Harriet Harman?), along with an overhaul of defence spending. Brown doesn’t deny that Burnham sought his advice before appointing Brown’s friend and former parliamentary private secretary John Healey as chancellor, but says, “My advice would’ve been not to take my advice.” (It’s the same line he used when journalists asked if he’d been advising Rachel Reeves.) Not that he doesn’t have plenty of advice to give: “Look, the British economy was growing about 2.5% a year when I was chancellor, and now it’s growing about 1% a year. So I do believe, as I said to Andy, that the focus on Britain as an innovation nation is an important part of the solution to this growth deficit.” Someone brings me a tea and Brown a glass of still water. He hasn’t had caffeine since he overdid it during the financial crisis in 2008, and recently gave up sparkling for “reasons of health”. (No joke, his rider for book events is tap water. An adviser adds, “And maybe a banana.”) * * * Since leaving office, Brown has popped his head above the parapet on specific issues: Brexit, antisemitism, universal credit. He is gravely concerned about the far right, more popular in Europe now than before fascists seized power in the 1930s. The number of truly liberal democracies has dropped to its lowest level in three decades – 29, he writes in his book. “Some fear we are approaching a moment comparable to the run-up to the second world war.” Part of the issue is that the postwar rules-based order no longer exists. We have moved from a “unipolar” to a “multipolar” world in which leaders promote a sort of zero fucks nationalism – America First, Italy First, Russia First. “Putin feels he can ignore the rule of law with impunity,” Brown says. “Netanyahu feels the same. In my book, I’ve got quotes from each explicitly saying it’s all about power now. If you’ve got the power, you use it. It doesn’t matter what the morality of what you’re doing is. I’ve got Trump saying, ‘I decide what my morality is. I don’t take moral lectures from anybody.’” This posturing is behind Putin and Netanyahu’s indiscriminate bloody slaughters in Ukraine, Gaza and Lebanon, behind America’s devastating attacks on Iran (“hospitals and schools should never be subject to bombing in any war”). But also, Brown says, “America was not able to stop the invasion of Ukraine, even though they knew about it in advance. And the Americans are not telling the Israelis actually to respect the idea that Palestine should have sovereignty. When I was prime minister and Israel invaded Gaza in 2009, the Americans told them to get out and they left.” Brown met Netanyahu a few times when the Israeli leader was finance minister and he was chancellor. “He’s changed dramatically,” Brown says, then corrects himself, because “he’s always been obsessed with Iran. For 20 years it’s been the country that he wanted to neutralise or destabilise. So I’m not surprised that he persuaded Trump to [bomb].” But were seeds of these violations not sown with the Iraq war, which he supported with Tony Blair in 2003? “To some extent, the interventions in the years from 2000. You can go back to the Vietnam war, to be honest.” He has long admitted he made a “mistake” with Iraq. He felt “misled” when he learned, through a document he saw after he left government, that the US knew Saddam Hussein did not have weapons of mass destruction in 2002. Had he known, would he have resigned? “Yes. I would not have been able to support the government.” Blair now sits on Trump’s Board of Peace. While it’s promoted as an alternative peacekeeping agency, Brown sees it as essentially a corporate exercise. Its founding document, Brown argues, is closer “to an international property developer under the guise of making peace”. I begin a question and he interrupts: “I know what you’re going to ask.” What? “About Tony Blair. I don’t want to talk about Tony Blair.” In his book, Brown writes that the US “may” have a new president in 2028. Why “may” and not “will”, given the two-term limit? Does he believe there won’t be an election? “No, Trump’s never been against elections. He’s just against results he doesn’t like.” What might this mean for the UK-US relationship? “The thing about that is, no matter what you think of any individual, you’ve got to try and make it work. Keir Starmer, to his credit, tried. Andy Burnham will try. Nobody’s saying they are going to be soulmates. You want to make it work without the abandonment of any principle.” Brown’s suggestion for dealing with the spiralling global chaos is to get back to a rules-based world ASAP, with an “updated” commitment to “the rule of law, democratic accountability, respect for human rights, freedom of assembly, international cooperation, humanitarian aid, environmental stewardship. People are angry,” he continues. “Rightly so, because things they took for granted have somehow been undermined.” But he skates over the role played by social media in the darkening of the political discourse, except to say it’s a “shouting match without an umpire”. Tech bros are the pied pipers of our children’s attention, I say. He points to a local Facebook group, Love Kirkcaldy! which, to him, exemplifies the positive way people come together online. He stresses – and this is a big theme of his book – one answer to tackling issues in national politics and international geopolitics lies at home. We need to refocus on our local communities: “Stronger communities will give us a stronger resistance to extremism.” The book is dedicated to the people of Kirkcaldy, where Brown is an active force. We visit the Cottage Family Centre, a charity of which he is patron that helps under-16s and their families. During Covid I visited one of the charity’s two sites. A volunteer said that, on hearing about two children who were sleeping on the floor, Brown had gone home and dismantled his sons’ bunkbed, returning to present it to her along with sheets. (She also said he attempted to make the beds, but bodged this so comprehensively that his protection team had to take over.) Then there’s the local multibank charity he set up: warehouses that take donations of goods from 90 companies, including Amazon, then redistribute them to the poor. I ask if he feels conflicted, given Amazon is a notoriously appalling employer with no unions. It’s the only time he’s a little gruff with me. “My first priority is to see if we can alleviate poverty. If Amazon is prepared to help, we will work with Amazon. If other companies are prepared to help, we will work with them. Poverty has been really severe here.” He says they’ve probably turned over £250m worth of goods to people who really need them. “So for a small charity just starting off … ” There’s also his work as a UN special envoy for global education. He tells me about going to see Gianni Infantino, the controversial president of Fifa, four years ago at the organisation’s HQ in Zurich with proposals of how to raise a billion dollars for global education through donations. “And you know the boardroom table is gold. There is a lot of conspicuous consumption on display. “My only worry is we are not talking enough about my book,” Brown says when we are back in his protection team’s Range Rover. We are talking about the book, I stress. In fact, trying to get the interview back on track when Brown talks about the book is like wrestling a ball off Lionel Messi when he has the goal in sight. Brown builds the book’s central argument on the idea of empathy (and there’s a certain irony in that Blair famously accused Brown of lacking emotional intelligence). “Empathy is a term that comes from Adam Smith, from The Theory of Moral Sentiments,” he says. “Smith called it sympathy, but now you’d call it empathy, which is to put yourself in other people’s shoes.” Smith recognises that loyalties to family are strongest, but “unlike JD Vance in his spat with the Pope, Smith would have said, ‘It is possible to have loyalties and feel sympathy towards people in difficult situations in any part of the world.’” He points out of the window towards the church where his father, the Rev John Brown, was minister. There are more churches in Kirkcaldy than you can shake a stick at. “There was a disruption,” Brown says, “so churches broke away from each other. My father was one of the dissenters.” Gordon and his two brothers, John and Andrew, grew up in the draughty old manse. There was no central heating until they were teenagers. “It was quite cold.” How cold? “You got used to it.” His mother, Jessie, had a huge influence on him, too, he says. “She always asked whether I really wanted to do the things I was doing. She made you question what you were doing.” The porridge-every-morning Calvinist upbringing was “quite strict”. He pauses. “She was quite appalled one day. She said, ‘I’ve heard a terrible story about you. I’ve heard you sometimes swear.’” (The only exclamation I hear him use is a forceful “gee whizz”.) When the Beatles came to Kirkcaldy, the Brown boys “didn’t get to go”. Because the Fab Four encouraged loose morals? “We were told we were too young. People in my class were going, but I wasn’t.” He laughs deeply. “Luckily, I have met Paul McCartney since.” He tells me the Beatles had links with the town because John Lennon had “an aunt or someone” who lived here. Kirkcaldy was where Brown’s prodigious intelligence was first recognised. He excelled in everything. Academically, he was fast-tracked to the University of Edinburgh at the age of 16. He was the Kirkcaldy boys’ tennis champion, a sprinter, an excellent rugby flanker. It was while playing rugby that he sustained a detached retina, an injury so serious he spent three months lying in a hospital bed, eyes bandaged, unable to move. He lost the sight in his left eye, and nearly in his right eye, too. The disability stopped him doing the thing he really wanted to do – sport – and he was forced to rethink his ambitions. “I think that’s what made me want to do something more active in the community.” On the back seat of the car are the copious notes Brown makes while people talk to him, large letters in black felt tip, stuffed in a transparent folder. Biographers say he was an introverted child. Still now, there’s a voice in his head before he stands to give a speech, saying, “Am I really wanting to do this?” But another says, “Yes, you really have to.” “I don’t get up in the morning wanting to be on the radio or television or in front of a crowd. You do things out of obligation.” When he was young, hierarchy expected deference, he says. The students of his generation protested, pushing “for greater individual freedom”. Photos of Brown show a serious student with long hair in a severe side-parting (unlike his beer-drinking contemporaries, he is wearing a tie). He admits he may have been more leftwing then than in his New Labour days. “But what happened in a way was that the balance between individual freedom and social obligation, between self-expression and your sense of being part of a community, got out of sync. So we threw out the baby with the bathwater. We threw out this idea that we’re a part of a society. And I think that’s the reason why commercialisation, consumerism, the amassing of wealth, inequality has become so prevalent. Because we’ve lost that sense of social obligation to each other, this sense that we’re part of one community.” While we’re on the subject of protest (and empathy), I ask about Labour’s treatment of peaceful Palestine Action protesters, thrown into police vans for holding placards in support of activists who raided an Israeli drone manufacturer based in the UK. “I think you’ll find most people in the Labour party did not intend this to be the outcome,” he says. “And I have always defended the freedom to assemble and protest peacefully.” We pass a disused linoleum factory, and he points it out for me, as an important part of the industrial history of the town. “They lost out to fitted carpets,” he explains. Being with Brown is like being with a particularly feverish member of the Scottish tourist board. Did I know there’s an exhibition of Scottish colourists in Perth (even he “hadn’t realised how many there were”)? Did I know the current one-mile world record holder is a Scot called Josh Kerr? Did I hear Scottish football fans were feted in Boston during the World Cup because they were so well behaved (though “obviously they drank the place dry”)? Do I know about famous Fife emigres, such as Andrew Carnegie? Don’t get him started on the Scottish Enlightenment philosophers. Did I know that three tenets of the US Declaration of Independence come from Scotland? Did I know Barack Obama has Scottish ancestry? But he’s also self-deprecating, saying that when he fought the Scottish National party in the 2014 independence referendum, “I always had this line: ‘I’m Scottish through and through.’ But we did this DNA test and before 1700 we’re actually from Sweden!” Bearing in mind his ardour for Scotland and the rise of English nationalism, does he now feel that swooping in on the side of no was a mistake? “That’s not in the book,” he says. Pressed, he recognises that the present status quo is not satisfactory and probably half the country want independence. At the same time, he says, “Scotland’s got to find a way of living in cooperation with other countries, and independence would not be the right way forward. We’re geographically, economically, socially, culturally linked to the rest of the United Kingdom, whether it’s Wales, England or parts of Ireland.” Surely, that “part” of Ireland is geographically linked with the other part of Ireland, so, by this reasoning should Ireland be united? “Yes. Well, of course, in the long term, Ireland will be united.” Wait, what? Brown, who was heavily involved in the peace talks that followed the Good Friday agreement in 1998, has always been pro-union. He says that a united Ireland will be “a long process where people have got to come together and find a way of agreeing. Basically, that is the issue: whether people can actually agree.” * * * The climate debate is raging, we are frying in record temperatures, phones are squawking with government wildfire warnings. There’s fierce criticism of Burnham for his support of drilling in the North Sea. I know Brown supports this, too, justifying it on the grounds it creates jobs in Scotland – but surely, we need to do something now? “The debate, Charlotte, seems to be divided between those who support North Sea development and those who support renewables. But I don’t think that’s the conflict.” Like Burnham, he argues that the same skills and infrastructure used for the development of the North Sea for oil and gas can also be used for the future development of renewables. “So the future of the North Sea is not that it dies when oil and gas run out but moves in a transitional way to hydrogen, wind and carbon capture. Thousands of jobs still can be based on the North Sea, but they will gradually move through to being jobs based on renewables.” Many might feel this is quintessential New Labour triangulation that fails to recognise the urgency of the moment. A touch of après moi, le deluge? Brown has written a lot about what he got right and what he got wrong in government. (Does this self-reflection help him? “No.”) “One of my faults was I wasn’t as good at communicating as I should have been,” he says now. He knows it would be worse in the world of social media, that no politician would “survive” without cringey TikToks and Reels. Would he have coped? “I don’t know how good I would have been. It depends on your willingness to open yourself up to different things. But Andy would be the first to tell you that it’s not just your ability to communicate; you’ve got to have the right policies.” Unwittingly, he became a TikTok star while in the queue to the Scotland game at the World Cup (he’d promised his younger son they’d go if Scotland qualified). There he was, smiling among the fans in tartan tam o’shanters, incongruous in a smart blue shirt. Was he the only fan not in a Scotland jersey? “No, no!” he scoffs. “Not everybody can afford £100 for a jersey, as I told my son. A hundred pounds! Actually, they were charging £90, I think. I wasn’t in a kilt, either, but I was wearing a blue shirt and Scotland plays in blue.” Does he have a kilt? “No, no! The last time I wore a kilt, I was eight or 10.” His parents forced him into one for church on Sundays. “I didn’t like it.” Football is Brown’s great love, his “best relaxation” in No 10 and still now it’s how he unwinds – on the edge of an armchair in his sitting room, shouting and pumping his fist at a screen the size of a wall, the green reflection perhaps visible to passing ships. He saw Scotland in the World Cups of 1982 and 1990, too. In 1998, as the newly appointed chancellor after the New Labour landslide of 97, he watched them play Brazil in Paris, standing behind the Duke of Edinburgh, who was furious when the unofficial national anthem, Flower of Scotland, was played, spitting with incredulity, “‘What is that?’” Brown says. “He thought it was going to be God Save the Queen and was very annoyed. It was really funny.” (Later, I ask his adviser if Brown is a republican and she tells me firmly I am not to ask.) “The book … ” he urges. Yes! The book. To write it he rose at 5am, ascending to this office and bashing at his keyboard for four hours straight. He has breakfast, scrambled egg and tomato, or smoked salmon and toast (you can tell when his wife, Sarah, is not at home because the kitchen looks like something out of The Young Ones), then “gets on” with the day job. Brown married late, at 49 – his single status was once used against him as a candidate for high office – to Sarah’s 36. Their first child, a daughter called Jennifer, was born prematurely in 2001 and died in Brown’s arms at 10 days old. He has said he didn’t want to go back into politics after her death, that he wanted to “stay away”. “For the first few months, I couldn’t really smile or anything. I couldn’t listen to music. It was a very difficult period. But you do decide that something good has got to come out of a tragedy, and that’s what we – Sarah in particular – tried to do.” They founded the Jennifer Brown Research Laboratory, to better understand premature births. Sarah also runs the charity Theirworld; among other places, they helped schoolgirls in Afghanistan and organised “pop-up” Sure Start centres in Gaza. Brown has said he cannot bear to think of children suffering, that the needless deaths of children all over the world makes him angry. In the past, he worried that his two sons, John, 22, and Fraser, 20, found him “old”. That he’d done them a “disservice” with the age gap. Today he’s feeling spry. At the house, Sarah comes in to say hi with a small dog struggling with excitement in her arms. He’s said that she was a great sounding board on women’s issues and equality. (Does he have a theory of why there still hasn’t been a female leader of Labour? “Timing.”) The boys don’t remember much of Downing Street. Brown has joked about how they’d occasionally burst into meetings (memorably, one with the US general David Petraeus and Northern Ireland first minister Ian Paisley, at whom one son shouted, “Teach me how to march!”). All were affected by the pernicious savaging by the Murdoch press, who he says printed “complete lies” and used “black arts” to snoop bank accounts and medical records. “I don’t think people understand just how much damage the Murdoch press did,” Brown says, “how much they tried to control British political life for years. They were operating hand in glove with the Conservative party attempting to control British politics – for commercial gain, as well as for political influence. They were only stopped by exposure.” Examples he gives include the Remembrance service where he bowed his head in prayer and the Sun claimed he’d fallen asleep. “It’s difficult to understand how they can talk about a free press when they actually wanted a press that dictated events regardless of truth,” he says. In 2024, with new information, Brown made a submission to the Metropolitan police. Have they formally opened an investigation? “I’ll have to come back to you on that.” Brown speaks in swathes of sentences with multiple clauses, and reads multiple books at a time. Currently, one on the Cambridge spies, which he thinks should be made into a film – “It really makes you very worried about the damage spies can do.” Another, Shattered Dreams, Infinite Hope, is a “reinterpretation” of the civil rights movement. Another is a history of the 1960s by David Kynaston. Plus he just finished Lyse Doucet’s The Finest Hotel in Kabul. To each review, he brings an unfiltered enthusiasm. What will he take on his summer holidays? “Ha! If I could get a summer holiday.” He listens to podcasts and participates in philosophical discussion. His jokes are highbrow and niche. There’s one about 1960s Labour party entryism, another about Austrian economists, and one about 1970s rock bands I didn’t understand. I notice he has a slightly seesawing walk as we return from the charity, but remarkable stamina given we haven’t had lunch (he demolished a Tunnock’s teacake, scrunching the foil into his pocket). How does he keep going at this pace at 75? “You’ve got to try harder to stay fit.” How? “Lots of walking, a bit of treadmill, a bit of these machines.” Machines? He admits Sarah bought a Pilates reformer years ago which “maybe” he uses, too. How often? “Four days a week.” Are there any aspects of ageing that he’s found hard? Memory fade, creaky joints? “You don’t want to go grey,” he says, “and I’m sorry I have. I always had very dark hair. But that’s life.” When he smiles, it’s like the sun bursting through cloud, so I ask about his famed temper. He says he doesn’t recognise the characterisation. “Look, we all get angry. We all respond to certain situations in a way that sometimes you would prefer not to. But I don’t see myself as someone who regularly loses their temper.” Perhaps the formidable Brown, once known for his fierce glare, basso profondo and intolerance of the ridiculous, has mellowed? “Look, I’m still working as hard as I did 20 years ago. I don’t think I’ve let up.” • The Future Starts With Us by Gordon Brown is published by Simon & Schuster on 1 September at £25. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. He will also be speaking at the University of Glasgow on 2 September, tickets available here.
