title: Was it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms?
author: Daniela Díaz in Valle del Guamuez and Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
summary: Fighters in legal limbo after accepting ‘total peace’ plan of Petro government just days before hardliner Abelardo De la Espriella took over
body_text: In mid-June, 99 guerrilla fighters were flown by helicopter to a small settlement in a rural area of southern Colombia where they lined up and, one by one, handed their weapons to government officials: rifles, pistols, machine guns and grenade launchers. They also stripped off their heavy tactical vests, field packs and camouflage uniforms, which were each piled into a bonfire to mark the beginning of a new life away from an armed conflict that has claimed nearly half a million lives in the last six decades. That was precisely what the former president Gustavo Petro’s “total peace” plan had sought to achieve: negotiating with and disarming all of Colombia’s criminal groups, which are estimated to have nearly 30,000 members. But the group of just 99 people was the only one to disarm, and did so just three days before the presidential runoff, which was won by the far-right millionaire lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who had campaigned on a promise to end “total peace” and return to a full-on strategy of jailing or killing criminals. Now, several weeks after the new president took office – and amid efforts to deal with the aftermath of the 7.4-magnitude earthquake, as his government has already begun the promised airstrikes against criminal groups – the 99 do not know what will happen to them. “We’re in limbo,” said Natalia Bríñez, 29, one of 13 women among the group staying in the temporary location zone, or ZUT by its Spanish initials, a government-controlled zone where, under surveillance and unable to leave, they were supposed to make the transition to civilian life over the following months. The former guerrillas are housed in beige brick buildings decorated with drawings they painted themselves, including doves of peace, with a communal dining hall where three meals a day are served. No weapons are allowed inside and soldiers guard the ZUT from a perimeter less than a mile away. One former combatant built a makeshift gym with weights made from metal pipes and tins filled with cement and sand, and there is an improvised football pitch, but most of them spend their days on their phones. De la Espriella has repeatedly said his government will no longer negotiate peace agreements and has yet to announce what he intends to do regarding the people at the ZUT. The president has not responded to requests for comment. In theory, any arrest warrants against the group are suspended, and they remain under state protection until 25 December, when Petro’s decree establishing the ZUT expires. But De la Espriella could revoke the decree at any time. Armando Novoa, the former government official who led peace negotiations with the group, said “the worst-case scenario would be for the new government to close the ZUT, launch a military operation and try to capture or kill them. That would be a crime against humanity, because these people are unarmed.” Between 2 and 4 August, days before De la Espriella’s inauguration, Novoa led journalists including the Guardian through the ZUT. The Office of the High Commissioner for Peace, where he worked, has since been absorbed into the newly created National Security Commission – a move expected to result in more than 200 job losses – and Novoa has resigned. For now, at least, the ZUT remains in operation and has a small library run by Bríñez, who has a phoenix tattoo on her left shoulder as a symbol of her rebirth away from the armed conflict. “The hardest thing for me has been being away from my children,” said Bríñez, who has a seven-year-old daughter and a 10-year-old son and speaks to them on video calls, but will only be able to see them in person once her “transition” is complete, a process that includes vocational training and psychosocial support. They were also supposed to receive financial support of about £425 a month, which had not yet been paid. In the meantime, some of them were planning to start a chicken-rearing business. The 99 made up a small part of a group of about 1,000 combatants called Commandos of the Frontier – most of whom remain armed – and are part of the National Coordinator of the Bolivarian Army (CNEB), a former dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) with about 2,500 members which controls the border with Ecuador. The Petro administration said negotiations were also under way with other members of the CNEB, who published an open letter addressed to De la Espriella saying they were willing to continue talks with him. It is not known whether the president responded. The CNEB’s chief “peace negotiator”, Geovany Andrés Rojas, known as “Araña” (Spider), had been in custody since February under a US extradition request for drug trafficking, which Petro had delayed. Last Wednesday, De la Espriella ordered extradition. Although such groups emerged in the 1960s as leftwing rebels fighting government abuses and seeking revolution – followed soon afterwards by far-right paramilitary groups – ideology has long since been overtaken for most of them by economic interests, above all drug trafficking (Colombia is the world’s largest producer of cocaine) and illegal mining. “Here in the ZUT, the vast majority were not in the group because of any ideological commitment, but for economic reasons,” said Novoa. “It even surprised us that most of them simply called the group ‘the company’.” Petro repeatedly tried to negotiate peace agreements with larger groups. The armed factions took advantage of temporary ceasefires to continue expanding, a process that had already begun before he took office. They also clashed among themselves for control of territory and illicit economies, which many security experts say contributed to a rise in homicides, kidnappings and massacres. “Total peace” was an attempt to address what the landmark 2016 peace deal between the government and the Farc failed to resolve, as other armed groups and Farc dissidents remained active. Petro’s administration failed to reduce violence, which instead reached its worst levels in a decade, and to reach the disarmament stage with any of the gangs, apart from the 99 former combatants – who handed over their weapons only on the eve of an election that every poll indicated the government-backed candidate would lose. “They [the government] told us: ‘If this works, you’re opening the door for other groups and will set an example,’” said Bríñez. Some security experts saw the agreement as rushed. “It was a somewhat irresponsible decision,” said Paula Tobo, a senior researcher at the thinktank Ideas for Peace Foundation, which published an extensive report on why Total Peace failed. Tobo said the 99 were now in a “legal limbo” because their protection rested on decrees that could be revoked and there is no legal framework for their transition to civilian life. All of the Petro administration’s proposals to regulate surrenders failed in Congress and, under current law, anyone who has committed crimes such as kidnapping or drug trafficking is not eligible for amnesty. “It’s positive that these people wanted to lay down their arms, but it really wasn’t the right time for the government to take that decision … The previous administration clearly put them at risk of this government suddenly deciding to abolish the ZUT and arrest them,” said Tobo. The group wrote a letter to De la Espriella reaffirming its “irreversible decision to commit to peace” and inviting him to visit the ZUT. At the time of publication it had received no response. The youngest member of the group, a 19-year-old who asked to be identified only as Adrián, said they wanted “to have a home, a family”. However, he knows what he will do if things do not go according to plan. “Honestly, I’d take up arms again, because we’re keeping our side of the bargain and the government should do the same, shouldn’t it?” he said. Daniela Díaz travelled to Valle del Guamuez at the invitation of the Colombian government’s former Office of the High Commissioner for Peace.

title: Democrats ignored the uncommitted movement for Gaza in 2024. Now, it’s winning elections
author: Tracie McMillan in Michigan
summary: By linking progressive politics with nominally Arab American issues, organizers are building winning coalitions
body_text: Abbas Alawieh initially thought the uncommitted movement of 2024 had failed. The insurgent group, which he helped co-found, had gotten more than 700,000 Democrats to vote “uncommitted” on their 2024 presidential primary ballots to pressure the US government to call for a ceasefire in Gaza. But when the group pushed for the Democratic party to add an embargo on arms to Israel in its platform, it didn’t happen. And when they asked to have a Palestinian American speaker address the Democratic national convention, it was also a no-go. Those failures, said Alawieh, prompted a new solution – one, observers say, that has been shaping Democratic primaries across the country. “I decided: ‘Oh, actually, the only fix here is we have to take power away from those leaders who are misusing it,” said Alawieh over Yemeni coffee in Dearborn, a city neighboring Detroit that has the highest share of Arab immigrants in the country. In August, Alawieh won the Democratic nomination for Dearborn’s state senate seat, which is safely Democratic. He is expected to win in November. Alawieh is one example of a larger trend that’s emerged across multiple Democratic primaries, including the marquee victory of progressive Abdul El-Sayed, who won the Democratic nomination for Michigan’s open US Senate seat: by linking nominally Arab American concerns, like the war in Gaza, to progressive politics, organizers and campaigns are building winning coalitions. “We’ve seen a lot of leadership from the Arab American community [and] Muslim American community,” said Amirah Sequeira, director of federal affairs for the Working Families Party, which organizes for progressive change within and outside of the Democratic party. It has been “extraordinarily important” to the progressive victories across the 2026 primaries, she said. Arab American votes became ‘up for grabs’ Organizing Michigan’s Arab American voters has taken on increasing importance in recent years, as the longstanding community has grown and election margins have tightened. The number of Arab residents grew by 75% from 2010 to 2020, and the group now represents roughly 4% of the state’s electorate, mostly concentrated in metropolitan Detroit, according to data from the Arab American Institute (AAI), a research, policy and civic engagement group. Until the genocide in Gaza, the Arab community’s growth had primarily benefited Democratic presidential candidates, which had drawn the majority of Arab votes since the mid-2000s, according to AAI data. But in 2024, as the Democratic party refused to change course on the genocide in Gaza, Arab voters shifted away from the Democratic ticket. This shift was especially pronounced in Michigan. The high concentration of Arab voters in certain pockets of the state made it easy for campaigns to target ads and candidate visits, said Maya Berry, executive director of the AAI. While this was something Democrats failed to do, Trump and third-party candidate Jill Stein made campaign stops in Dearborn in 2024, and Republicans blasted mailboxes with literature opposing the war, she said. “It was a lack of leadership from the [Democratic] campaign to not engage at the level of the candidate when the other guy was showing up to have meals with people,” Berry said. It “was a night-and-day difference”. The Democratic party’s absence in Arab communities was exactly what uncommitted had hoped to change, said Andy Levin, a former congressman and mentor to Alawieh. Anti-genocide Democratic party activists launched “Listen to Michigan” in the lead-up to that state’s late February primary. They organized primary voters to use the ballot’s “uncommitted” option to indicate support for a ceasefire in hopes that it could get the White House to change course – a tactic that quickly spread to other states. Beyond the moral issue, said Levin, there was a real political issue as well. “Our point was, President Biden, wake up. We need you to win re-election. We can’t have Donald Trump anywhere near the White House ever again,” said Levin. “And we just can’t see how you can win Michigan if you don’t change course on Gaza.” On election day, Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris took just 31% of the vote across Michigan precincts with majority Arab voters, compared with 47% of Arab voters nationally in the 2024 presidential election, according to AAI. Much of the Arab vote shifted to third-party candidates, who took 20% of the vote in the same Michigan precincts, significantly more than the 8% nationally. The 2024 presidential election showed that Arab American votes “are up for grabs”, said Branden Snyder, Michigan state director for the Working Families Party. The war in Gaza, and Democrats’ reluctance to oppose it, galvanized not just Arab American voters, but young and progressive voters across backgrounds. Uncommitted’s organizers, who had feet in both worlds, saw themselves fighting a moral battle that had a pragmatic angle: money spent on war meant less for social programs at home. In the process, the genocide became politically entwined with the broader progressive movement. ‘Muslim issues are American issues’ Uncommitted’s strategy of linking what were traditionally considered Arab American issues to broader progressive politics has turned into electoral work and support across many of this year’s primary upsets. “The genocide in Gaza has obviously exponentially increased involvement in politics” for Arab voters, as well as for progressives and young people, said WFP’s Sequeira. But “issues of affordability, housing, healthcare are central to those communities as well”, she said. Two other uncommitted co-founders, Layla Elabed and Lexis Zeidan, have since founded Arab Americans for Progress in metropolitan Detroit. The group runs a fellowship program to train Arab Americans for leadership and helps organize grassroots efforts like door-knocking and mailers for candidates, which it did for Alawieh, said Elabed. The group has also prioritized building relationships with Black residents through a recurring discussion group and events like an iftar solidarity dinner during Ramadan. Other organizations have also bridged a common cause between progressive groups and Arab voters. This includes the work of Emgage Action, which lobbies Congress and endorses candidates addressing concerns for Arab Muslim voters. In 2026, their endorsements stretched across 14 states, including Michigan, Texas, Florida, New York and New Jersey. Although the group is bipartisan, the Islamophobia pushed by Republican officials has led Emgage to endorse progressive Democratic candidates, said Nada Al-Hanooti, the group’s national deputy organizing director. That has been especially pronounced since December, said Al-Hanooti, after Republican representatives from Texas launched the anti-Muslim “Sharia-Free America” congressional caucus in the US House of Representatives. Emgage has organized canvassers to knock on doors, coordinated mailers and sent text messages for some of the year’s most notable progressive wins across the country. In Michigan, that included Arab Muslim candidates Alawieh and El-Sayed, as well as white progressive Will Lawrence and the Michigan state representative Donavan McKinney, a Black Detroiter who bested the incumbent US representative Shri Thanedar in a safely Democratic district. In Florida, Emgage backed upset candidate Angie Nixon, who bested a former national security official to win the Democratic nomination for Senate by 12 points. As a state lawmaker, Nixon had been the lone backer of a ceasefire resolution in Florida’s house in November 2023. In New Jersey, Emgage turned out canvassers, developed mailings and reached out to Muslim voters by text to increase support for Adam Hamawy, a Palestinian American doctor. In a field of 13 candidates, Hamawy won the Democratic nomination for the state’s 12th congressional district. Emgage’s strategy has been to endorse candidates aligned with the group on policy, not identity alone, said Al-Hanooti. “Muslim issues are American issues,” she said. “We’re here to prove that you need our vote in order to win, and you need to start visiting our communities.” All of it is a sign that Arab and Muslim Americans are building real power, said Razi Jafri, a journalist who covered the uncommitted movement in a documentary of the same name. “What’s fascinating about Abbas [Alawieh] is that his trajectory embodies this evolution,” from representation alone to shaping politics and coalitions, said Jafri. Alawieh and El-Sayed have even fielded calls and meetings with Kamala Harris recently. “That transition from protest to power building is really incredible,” Jafri said.

title: ‘Inept, incompetent, craven’: Scott Bessent struggles to clean up the president’s mess
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: There’s little optimism about treasury secretary’s ability to handle Trump’s tariffs, Iran sanctions and colossal US debt
body_text: History remembers Gen Dwight Eisenhower, the supreme commander of the allied forces in Europe during the second world war, for his role in the D-day invasion of Normandy. Whether Scott Bessent will achieve similar posterity as the face of the “economic D-day” in Iran remains to be seen. The US treasury secretary, already trying to manage a $40tn national debt pile, this week took charge of Donald Trump’s effort to reverse-engineer his war of choice. Whereas the US would typically take on an adversary with diplomacy, sanctions and military force, in that order, the US president started with a six-month bombing campaign and now hopes that economic isolation can finish the job. The effort shines a harsh spotlight on Bessent, a billionaire hedge fund manager and former Democratic donor who the president likes to say is “central casting” but critics warn is dangerously out of his depth. The coming months could reveal whether Bessent serves as a constraint on Trump’s worst impulses – or, in fact, enables them beneath a veneer of respectability. “He is, bar none, the worst treasury secretary in the history of the United States,” said Steve Schmidt, a former political strategist for President George W Bush and the John McCain presidential campaign. “Because the first treasury secretary was a true genius, the distance between Alexander Hamilton and Bessent in evolutionary scale is the difference between a flea and a human being. He is inept, he is incompetent, he is dishonest, he is smug, he is craven.” Scott Kenneth Homer Bessent is an unlikely avatar of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement. Born in South Carolina, he made his way to Yale and graduated in 1984. Openly gay, in 2015 he told the Yale Alumni magazine: “If you had told me in 1984, when we graduated, and people were dying of Aids, that 30 years later I’d be legally married and we would have two children via surrogacy, I wouldn’t have believed you.” Bessent went on to play an influential role in the liberal philanthropist George Soros’s London investment operations, including his famous 1992 bet against the pound, which generated huge profits on “Black Wednesday”, when the pound was delinked from European currencies. He also donated to various Democratic causes in the early 2000s, notably Al Gore’s presidential run, but eventually drifted toward the Republican fold, transforming into an adviser and intellectual defender of Trump’s economic nationalism. He championed spending cuts while vigorously advocating for the extension of the tax cuts approved by Congress in Trump’s first term. Still, in a cabinet of questionable qualifications, there were hopes that Bessent – an advocate for deficit reduction and deregulation – would prove a moderating influence on Trump. Last year the Senate confirmed him as treasury secretary by a vote of 68 to 29, with those in favour including some Democrats and independents. Bessent was hailed as the first openly gay treasury secretary in US history. It has been far from smooth sailing. With the national debt ticking past $40tn, the bond markets have begun to rebel. Yields on long-dated treasury bonds have soared to heights not seen in nearly 20 years, dramatically escalating the cost of servicing the nation’s debt. Earlier this month, Bessent carried out the first joint intervention in the Japanese yen in 15 years to support currency stability. Then, last week, he surprised global investors by announcing that the treasury would double the size of its quarterly buybacks of longer-dated bonds – boosting the repurchases of 10-to-30-year securities to at least $4bn per operation. Bessent claimed that his objective was to support liquidity in a thinly traded August market. The market intervention achieved its goal, but only fleetingly. Yields dropped briefly before retracing nearly all of those losses by the end of the week. The core problem remained: Bessent has not identified the funding source for the buybacks, leading analysts to assume he will tap the Treasury General Account (TGA) at the Federal Reserve. Perceptions of Bessent’s competence were shaken by the move. Charlie McElligott, a cross-asset strategist at Nomura, told the Financial Times newspaper that it was a “band-aid on a bullet hole” and would “not be enough to placate market forces”. Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, summed it up: “The long bond buyback was perceived as somewhat farcical by the financial community, and when he went on to opine that we could grow our way out of the debt, I’m sure he knows better than that. I don’t think he’s thrown away his reputation but as headlines in the past 24 hours have been indicating, Wall Street, like Queen Victoria, is not amused.” Then there was Iran. With a six month-bombing campaign having failed to break Tehran’s will, and the US running low on the defensive weapons it would need to repel a counterattack, Trump handed Bessent the unenviable task of finding another way. The upshot was “Operation Economic Outcast”, designed to isolate Iran from the global financial system. Galston observed: “The president has decided on a strategy of maximum economic pressure. Bessent has no choice but to devise the best plan possible. Now, it does matter what he’s telling the president behind the scenes.” At a press conference on Monday, Bessent’s rhetoric about “economic asphyxiation” was sweeping, but the reality was far more tentative: a series of warnings rather than the immediate imposition of secondary sanctions on Iran’s major trading partners. If Bessent were to enforce secondary sanctions fully, he would have to target major Chinese state-owned banks. This could spark a catastrophic trade war between the world’s two biggest economies, shattering the fragile trade truce that Trump has spent the last year trying to maintain. “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” the secretary reasoned. But to observers the lack of concrete penalties suggested a bluff. Larry Jacobs, director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, said: “His effort on the economic D-day appears to have been mostly rhetorical, not breaking any major new ground. At its core, what Bessent announced is an attempt to create an out for Donald Trump from the war he created and the mess that has resulted.” He added: “Bessent is in the unenviable position of trying to make Trump’s whimsical preferences become reality and is repeatedly failing or making the situation worse.” Meanwhile the president continues to be fixated on tariffs, which he often describes as his “favourite word”. Trump announced 50% tariffs on $20bn worth of Canadian goods over the weekend, after talks between the countries broke down. Canada retaliated by imposing retaliatory tariffs on $20bn worth of American goods including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment. There is little evidence that Bessent disapproves, or has sought to rein Trump in. Although he wrote an investor letter in 2024 arguing that tariffs were inflationary, Bessent said last year: “I’ve evolved on this. The president has been right.” He has also described tariffs as “a useful tool for achieving the president’s foreign policy objectives”, claiming that Hamilton was their original proponent. Such remarks suggest that the former Democratic supporter now feels the zeal of the convert, and has become a true believer in Trump. Jacobs is not so sure. “We shouldn’t dismiss the possibility that it’s the attraction to power,” he said. “He’s got vast wealth but he’s now got a global standing that he’s never enjoyed before. But now that he is into the thick of a job you can see how ill prepared he is for a complicated situation with an out-of-control president.” The price to pay, however, could be Bessent’s reputation. Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, commented: “Bessent has zero credibility on the global stage and appears in over his head. On interest rates, the national debt, inflation, tariffs, he has mismanaged expectation and appears to be more preoccupied with being a yes-man to Trump than actually protecting the full faith and credit of the United States. At this point, the United States would be better off with an AI-bot running the treasury department than this blowhard.”

title: Is Donald Trump’s bid to brand Democrats as ‘radical’ communists working?
author: George Chidi in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina
summary: In deep red South Carolina, the president helped stoke apprehension of a deeper red surge ahead of November’s US midterm elections
body_text: After casting his vote in South Carolina, a man who introduced himself as Chestnut was unwilling to give his full name. “You don’t have a need to know,” the air force veteran declared. He was, however, happy to share his views. “I’m a true American. I believe in the USA,” said the man, outside Christ the Servant Lutheran church in Conway. “And I don’t believe in communism or socialism.” Several hundred thousand South Carolinians took part in a Republican special runoff on Tuesday, selecting the party’s nominee for US Senate after the sudden death of the veteran lawmaker Lindsey Graham. Darline, his sister, prevailed – in a victory for Donald Trump. The US president had traveled down to South Carolina days before the vote, reaching for a familiar theme as he rallied supporters to get behind his handpicked candidate. Also on the ballot was a message that Trump has been ramping up in recent months. “So the Democrats hate our country. They’re communists,” Trump declared at a rally in Myrtle Beach. During the speech, he mentioned communists or communism no fewer than 13 times. “They’re radical left lunatics.” As Democrats have looked left in some primaries, nominating socialists to represent the party in November’s US midterm elections, Trump has increasingly – erroneously – claimed the party has been overrun by communists. “You can be a communist or you can be a patriot,” he said in the shadow of Mount Rushmore during the US 250th birthday celebrations this summer. “You cannot be both.” As Trump seeks to galvanize his base ahead of November’s US midterm elections, the thoughts of voters in South Carolina, and fears of an ascendant “Communist party” on the left, offer a window into how his efforts are faring. Chestnut was not the only voter with whom such warnings appeared to resonate. In deep red South Carolina, where no Democrat has won statewide in 20 years, there is apprehension of a deeper red surge in US politics. “I don’t like the DSA,” Charles Rogers said, referring to the Democratic Socialists of America, as he left a polling station at Marion intermediate school. “I don’t like how the Democrats want to back them. Democrats used to be for the working man, but something’s changed … I do not agree with the DSA, and more Democrats are backing them with crazy ideas.” While DSA members would adamantly describe themselves as standing for working people, fears of communism coming for America – fanned by Trump – were on the mind of Republican voters contemplating their choices on Tuesday, and in November. Lee and Donna Criswell voted on Tuesday afternoon at the Lamar library in Darlington county, South Carolina. Asked what issues they viewed as politically important, Lee replied: “We’re concerned about the socialism thing going on in some parts of the country. I don’t think we have an issue regardless of whether you’re Republican or Democrat here in South Carolina, but I don’t know where it’s going, you know, in other areas.” “We want to maintain our freedoms,” Donna added. As Trump continues to level allegations of political “extremism” at the feet of the Democrats, his own extreme actions – from persistent election denial to the pursuit of his political enemies – continue to cause alarm in much of the country. Such concerns were not raised by Republicans in South Carolina who spoke to the Guardian this week. Zachary Cogan, a retired army engineer voting in Lamar, called himself a transplant from the “communist state” of New York. He said he was looking for responsiveness and accountability from conservative political leaders, saying: “We’re not importing [New York City mayor Zohran] Mamdani voters into South Carolina. South Carolina has no danger of turning purple.” Cogan thought about the political environment he left behind, and laughed. “I mean, when you have to say [US Senate minority leader] Chuck Schumer is the more moderate of the Democrats, that’s going the wrong way. OK? But why – why are the Democrats … well, you’ve got the Communist party now that is so pro-intifada.” The victories of Mamdani in New York City, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s US Senate primary and now Angie Nixon in Florida’s US Senate primary have been heralded by American progressives as a sign of renewed vigor for the left in Democratic politics amid the provocations of Trump’s administration. But they have also become daily fodder for conservative cable news channels like Newsmax or Fox News, and social media accounts on Facebook and X. The fear of communism has become a driving rhetorical force on the right. Fox and other media outlets catering to a conservative audience have been amplifying the anticommunist rhetoric of Trump, according to Brian Leiter, a law professor and director of the Center for Law, Philosophy & Human Values at the University of Chicago. Leiter co-authored a book on Karl Marx and is a keen observer of America’s history with red-baiting politics. “Trump and Fox News work in tandem on these things. They’re mutually reinforcing,” Leiter said. “Trump understands red-baiting better than anyone, because who was his mentor? Roy Cohn. And Roy Cohn was, of course, legal counsel to Joseph McCarthy in the original purge and political persecution.” The words “socialist” or “socialism” have been mentioned almost 6,000 times in Fox News programming since 1 January, according to a search of the Internet Archive’s database of show transcripts. The word “communist” appeared more than 1,700 times. In each case, mentions spiked sharply in May and have steadily increased, occurring about five times as often in August as they did in April. Often, Leiter said, Fox invites on its shows members of the DSA who – unlike media-savvy Democrats like Mamdani or congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez – look and sound like progressive caricatures, espousing fringe views within the Democratic party, unwilling or unable to articulate the difference between the beliefs of a democratic socialist and a committed communist. “I gather they have been doing a lot on democratic socialism on the theory that it’ll help the Republican party,” Leiter said. “Communism has always been a bogeyman in American politics in a way it’s not in Europe, say, and it’s not helped by the fact that every self-proclaimed communist government was a disaster … None of these people – Zohran Mamdani, Bernie Sanders, AOC – none of them are communists. They’re not even close.” But those distinctions do not seem to have generally filtered down to rank-and-file Republican voters of South Carolina. Trump’s rhetoric has landed.

title: Ex-White House teleprompter operator fined $172,000 for Trump speech bets
author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
summary: Commodity Futures Trading Commission said Gabriel Perez wagered on Kalshi about words president used in speeches
body_text: A White House teleprompter operator who left his post amid accusations that he used inside knowledge to make bets on Donald Trump’s speeches on an online prediction market has been fined $172,000, according to federal regulators. Gabriel Perez illicitly exploited “material, nonpublic information” that he gathered through his work for the president in order to place wagers on the Kalshi platform “for his personal benefit”, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) maintained in a news release on Friday. The CFTC ordered Perez to both “disgorge the profits he made from his unlawful [conduct]” totaling $107,539.02 and to pay a civil penalty of $65,000, the agency’s news release said. Such amounts represented “a substantial discount”, the CFTC added, attributing that to what the agency called “Perez’s exemplary cooperation” with its investigation into him. According to the CFTC, from December to February while working as a White House teleprompter operator, Perez made bets on Kalshi tied to words or phrases that Trump might make during his speeches. Perez’s White House role gave him access to those speeches before the president delivered them, and he “misappropriated that information” to profit, breaching “his duty of trust and confidence”, the CFTC asserted. Perez – besides being fined – “agreed to cease and desist from further violations” of federal laws prohibiting market manipulation and CFTC regulations, the CFTC said. He was also handed a three-year trading ban. The CFTC issued its news release about Perez on Friday, about a month after the White House said he no longer had his job there. It was unclear whether Perez resigned or was fired. Yet his departure came after he was reportedly put on unpaid leave amid an investigation into whether he had used his inside knowledge to win more than $100,000 betting on what Trump would say on big occasions, including his State of the Union address in February. The White House press secretary at the time, Karoline Leavitt, had described the reports of insider trading by Perez as “deeply unfortunate and, frankly, a disgrace”. Perez earned an annual salary of $175,000 for his teleprompter work, according to White House personnel records. The case centering on Perez was only the latest to illustrate the continued proliferation of online prediction markets, which allow users to place speculative bets on public events and trends. That has evidently incentivized insider trading. For instance, about four months before Perez’s fine, federal prosecutors indicted US soldier Gannon Ken Van Dyke for allegedly making a $400,000 bet on Kalshi rival platform Polymarket about whether Nicolás Maduro would be removed from Venezuela’s presidency. Van Dyke had worked on the operation to remove Maduro and extradite him to the US on drug-trafficking charges, according to prosecutors. Furthermore, Kalshi in April also announced fines against three political candidates who bet on their own elections, including one who wagered on whether he would run for office before announcing an independent campaign for a US Senate seat in Virginia. Trump has defended the prediction market industry, to which his family has business ties. He has advocated against individual US states regulating those markets and has argued that the CFTC should instead carry out that function. In its news release on Perez’s fine, meanwhile, the CFTC made it a point to thank Kalshi for its “assistance … in this matter”.

title: Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers says he saw Bin Laden’s body with his ‘own eyes’. He did not
author: Robert Mackey
summary: Ex-House intel committee chair, now running against Abdul El-Sayed, instead saw photo of Osama bin Laden’s body
body_text: In a recent fundraising email, the Republican candidate for Michigan’s open US Senate seat, former congressman Mike Rogers, appeared to mislead supporters about his past by suggesting that he had played an active role in the killing of Osama bin Laden, the leader of al-Qaida who was shot and killed in an American military raid on his compound in Pakistan in 2011. “When I served as a US army officer and an FBI special agent, I swore a sacred oath to defend the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic,” Rogers wrote, according to a screenshot of the email shared online by Azi Paybarah, a former Washington Post reporter now with Straight Arrow News. “I dedicated my life to keeping our families safe – working in the shadows, hunting down terrorists, and standing on the frontlines of our national security.” He then added, in a section of the email highlighted in bold type: “I saw the dead body of Osama bin Laden with my own eyes, knowing that together, we had delivered justice for America.” Rogers, however, was not in Abbottabad, Pakistan, on 1 May 2011, when Bin Laden was shot and killed – nor was he in the White House Situation Room, where then president Barack Obama and senior administration officials at the time, including Joe Biden and Hillary Clinton, followed the raid in real time. Instead, as Rogers told reporters the next day, and recounts in a campaign video, he was at home in Washington DC – where, as the chair of the House intelligence committee at the time, he was informed about the raid in a phone call from Obama’s CIA director, Leon Panetta. While the Rogers campaign did not respond to requests to explain what the former congressman meant by his claim, Paybarah, who first reported the fundraising email sent by Rogers on Sunday, suggested that Rogers must have been referring to the fact that he was one of a select few US officials to have seen a photograph of Bin Laden’s dead body. Rogers said – days after the raid – that the photograph he’d seen made it clear that Bin Laden was dead. But he said he supported Obama’s decision to not make the graphic images of the raid public. “The risks of release outweigh the benefits,” Rogers said in a statement at the time. “Conspiracy theorists around the world will just claim the photos are doctored anyway, and there is a real risk that releasing the photos will only serve to inflame public opinion in the Middle East.” In the years since, though, Rogers has frequently referred to his role as a congressman who helped provide funds for US intelligence agencies in vague terms that seemed to exaggerate his role. Since Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim doctor and former public health official, became his opponent in the Senate race, Rogers has repeatedly cited his own role in the US war on Islamist terrorism in his campaign statements. “Abdul doesn’t represent a vision for the future. He’s leading a movement grounded in ideological fanaticism,” Rogers said the night that El-Sayed won the Democratic nomination. “I spent years hunting terrorists and bringing Osama bin Laden to justice. Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11.” A New York Times factcheck pointed out that the second part of Rogers’s “incendiary statement” was false: it was not El-Sayed, but one of his supporters, the Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who once said that the US deserved 9/11, before retracting and apologizing for that statement seven years before he endorsed El-Sayed. For his part, El-Sayed has clearly denounced the 9/11 attacks for years. In a recollection of that day written in 2021, El-Sayed wrote: “I watched terrorists with names like mine attack my country in the name of my faith. Three thousand of my fellow Americans were killed in the craven terrorist attacks in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania. The attack devastated me.”

title: Trump’s ‘economic D-day’ against Iran risks driving the stakes even higher
author: Sina Toossi
summary: As with its approach to Hormuz, the US has mistaken applying pressure for an actual strategy. But Tehran has chips of its own to play, says Sina Toossi of the Center for International Policy
body_text: Donald Trump has found a new way to promise victory over Iran. After months of war have failed to force Iran’s capitulation or collapse, his administration has unveiled what the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, calls Operation Economic Outcast: an effort to cut it off from what remains of the global economy and threaten foreign governments, banks and companies with sanctions if they continue doing business with Tehran. There is no question that Iran is vulnerable. Its economy has been battered by years of sanctions, war and a months-long US naval blockade. Iranian officials acknowledge that oil exports and access to foreign currency have been severely constrained. Ordinary Iranians are already enduring high inflation, currency depreciation and worsening living standards. Further economic strangulation will inflict significant additional hardship. Iran also wants an end to the war. Its president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has said it should seek peace while it can still negotiate from a position of “power and dignity”. But Iran needing a deal is not the same as Iran preparing to surrender. That distinction has repeatedly eluded Trump in formulating his Iran policy: ramping up pressure is not the same as having a strategy. Iran gets a move too. Indeed, Iranian officials increasingly suggest this strategy has the opposite effect than what was intended. Each successive escalation, in their telling, demonstrates why Iran relinquishing its remaining leverage would simply leave it vulnerable to the next round of US pressure. The emerging strategy therefore appears to combine bargaining with endurance: seek an agreement while demonstrating that it can withstand the pressure without capitulating or abandoning its core terms. This is why recent Iranian rhetoric deserves more attention than it has received. Mohsen Rezaei, the new head of Iran’s supreme national security council, has called participation in Washington’s economic campaign an “act of war”. He says Tehran will first try to persuade neighbouring states not to participate, but has threatened their interests if they do. He has even warned that Iran could prevent Gulf oil exports through routes designed to bypass Hormuz. These statements should not simply be dismissed as declarations of defiance for an audience in Iran. They reflect a consistent strategic logic: Iran cannot defeat the US economically, but it can try to make the economic strangulation of Iran prohibitively expensive for Washington and the countries it needs to enforce it. That could mean tightening pressure on Hormuz, threatening infrastructure that enables alternative oil-export routes or putting greater pressure on US interests across the region. None of this would help ordinary Iranians. Escalation would compound their suffering. But that is precisely why Washington should think beyond the first-order effects of its own actions. There is another weakness in Trump’s plan. For Bessent’s threat to work, Washington must persuade or coerce much of the world into participating, especially China, the principal buyer of Iranian oil. Yet Beijing is moving in the opposite direction. It has ordered firms not to comply with US sanctions targeting Chinese buyers of Iranian oil, while its top court recently highlighted a ruling penalising a Singaporean company for complying with US sanctions. Beijing has now warned it will take “all necessary measures” if Chinese interests are targeted. Washington therefore faces an uncomfortable choice: tolerate continued trade between Iran and China, its neighbours and other partners, or dramatically escalate coercion of the governments, banks and companies that keep those channels open. That risks multiplying the US’s economic confrontations at a moment when it needs international cooperation to isolate Tehran. Bessent acknowledged the danger when asked why Washington was not immediately imposing its most sweeping secondary sanctions. “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he responded. That is quite an admission for an operation advertised as “economic D-day”. With the midterms approaching, the White House has strong incentives to avoid another major escalation that could further disrupt Gulf energy flows and send fuel prices soaring. Tehran knows this. Its gamble is that it can endure and reroute enough commerce while imposing enough costs that Washington and its partners eventually prefer a settlement to continued confrontation. That makes this a dangerous contest of endurance. Washington is betting Iran’s economy completely breaks first. Tehran is betting the US’s tolerance for the war and its mounting economic costs breaks first. This has been the recurring flaw in Trump’s approach. In 2018, he left the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran, in an attempt to secure more favourable terms. Iran instead expanded its nuclear programme. Military conflict was supposed to force Tehran to accept US terms. Instead, the war expanded and Hormuz became a central source of Iranian leverage. Now intensified economic strangulation is supposed to accomplish what military power could not. Unless Trump starts thinking several moves ahead, his latest attempt to force Iran into submission could leave the US with even higher energy prices, an even more confrontational adversary and yet another escalation it never counted on. Sina Toossi is a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, where his work focuses on US-Iran relations, US policy toward the Middle East and nuclear issues

title: ‘Grassroots will beat big money every day’: can a DSA member flip a Republican Senate seat?
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: Angie Nixon won one of the biggest upsets in US midterm primaries – and if elected, the Democrat would be the first African American senator in Florida history
body_text: The Democratic establishment had the money, the machinery and the candidate with national name recognition. Angie Nixon had a bookshop called Café Resistance and a grassroots campaign for the Senate. On primary election night in Florida, Nixon won in arguably the biggest upset of the primary season. But at least one person was not shocked: Angie Nixon herself. “We weren’t surprised,” the 42-year-old reflects after overcoming a vast fundraising disadvantage to defeat Alex Vindman, a combat veteran who testified against Donald Trump during his first impeachment. “We actually knew we were going to win; we just didn’t know that we were going to win by that much. We put in the work and so super excited about the outcome. It shows that good old-fashioned grassroots organising will beat big money each and every day.” Nixon won 56.1% of the vote to Vindman’s 43.9%. The result stirred tensions within the Democratic party in a year defined by the struggle between moderates and economic populists. In Florida – a state that has trended increasingly Republican in recent years and is now Trump’s home state – Democrats have now nominated a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) who speaks openly about class war. If elected, Nixon would be the first African American senator in Florida history. She has already cleared numerous barriers to get here, she says by phone. “Money. Racism. People saying I can’t win in the state because I’m a Black woman. People regurgitating talking points. All the things.” Nixon was born and raised in Jacksonville, primarily by a single mother who worked two jobs to put food on the table. Her father, an army veteran, was not always present. “None of my parents were involved in politics,” she recalls. “My mom, though, was a union member and so that’s where I learned about the power of organising. “I remember my mom telling me she was on strike and I overheard her conversations talking about scabs in the union and people crossing the picket line. I am someone who grew up knowing the importance of solidarity with your fellow workers and people who were being oppressed and whatnot.” Nixon’s youth was shaped by the systemic failures of public institutions. She was bussed across town to elementary school because her predominantly Black neighbourhood school lacked resources. Later her family suffered a devastating tragedy when her favourite cousin was killed by gun violence. After graduating from the University of Florida in 2007, Nixon became a union organiser with the Service Employees International Union. What she witnessed convinced her that the professional political class is fundamentally out of touch with ordinary Americans. Nixon says: “Working families are getting the short end of the stick. They are oftentimes being exploited and they’re the ones that actually make the profits and drive the economy. Meanwhile the billionaires and the corporations and the CEOs get all the credit.” In 2020 she was elected to the Florida house of representatives, where she has pushed for expanding childcare and stopping a major grocery chain from gouging their prices. In May this year she protested against the Republican-controlled legislature’s redistricting of the state’s congressional maps by shouting through a megaphone on the house floor, earning a reprimand from an ethics committee. After Governor Ron DeSantis approved the gerrymander, she staged a sit-in at his office and was arrested. Nixon also sued the state after being denied access to the south Florida migrant detention centre known as “Alligator Alcatraz”, and introduced legislation that would require Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and other US law enforcement agents to unmask and identify themselves on the job. Why did she decide to take the fight to the national stage? “Because people are struggling, people are snapping, people are losing their minds, people are taking their lives. People can’t even enjoy just being alive any more. They’re just working to live.” In her Senate campaign Nixon proposes fixes such as the Medicare for All universal healthcare plan, universal childcare, a national rent freeze and moratorium on evictions, stronger union protections and a federal minimum wage of $25 an hour. She proposes higher taxes on billionaires, driving big money out of politics and reining in tech companies and datacentres. In June Nixon joined the DSA, whose more than 100,000 members include Zohran Mamdani, elected mayor of New York City last year. Candidates associated with the DSA have pulled off notable wins in recent House of Representatives primaries. Nixon explains: “They are an organisation that was pushing and fighting for the same things that I was fighting for. I don’t agree with everything that they agree with, but they’re fighting hard to ensure we have access to universal healthcare, access to free college and fully funded public schools. “Unfortunately, the Democratic party isn’t fighting as hard as they should, at least those elected officials, and so I decided to join them because I’ve been on the frontlines fighting as well and I want people who are actually going to get to work.” Nixon believes that, even if she had not joined the DSA, she would have won the election anyway – pointing out that the DSA did not endorse her, and that she also joined the progressive Working Families party. But would she describe herself as a democratic socialist? “I would describe myself as a former single mama who is putting my family and my community first. I am a Democrat. I’ve always been a lifelong Democrat but I’m more of social democrat who believes in strong safety nets.” While Nixon performed strongly in working-class, majority-Black counties, she was notably weaker in south Florida’s Latino communities, where historical experiences with leftwing authoritarian regimes make the socialist label highly polarising. Nixon resists being put in a political box. She comments: “We can argue about labels each and every day but I care about people’s needs and I’ve never been able to fit in one box but, as I do more research, I see that I’m aligned with what folks have referred to as ‘the FDR [Franklin Delano Roosevelt] Democrats’. He’s someone who believes in social programmes and I believe in social programmes, especially if the current economy isn’t working for everyone.” But Democratic establishment figures are worried that nominating a DSA member will backfire in conservative Florida. The internal friction was laid bare shortly after Nixon’s victory when reports emerged of a heated, shouting phone call between her and the Florida Democratic party chair, Nikki Fried. At one point Nixon yelled, “Stop gaslighting me!”, a source told the Axios news site. Nixon does not deny the incident, describing the tension as a natural feature of a broad coalition. “Sometimes you argue with your siblings because you want to do things a certain way and they may want to do things a certain way and at the end of the day you are all going to move in the direction to help benefit your family. Our family is the community of Florida and so she and I are together. There’s no ill will among us. We are going to do what we need to do to make this state and country better.” Nixon’s populist economic message faces an uphill battle in November, when she goes head-to-head with the Republican senator Ashley Moody, a former state attorney general appointed by DeSantis to fill Marco Rubio’s vacant Senate seat. Whereas active registered Democrats outnumbered Republicans in the state in 2020, there are now 1.5 million more Republicans than Democrats. Republicans have already begun framing Nixon’s victory as a gift. Congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna told Fox News that Nixon’s nomination “will bring Republicans out to vote specifically against her because of the fact they don’t want her radical policies”. Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina called the Democratic left wing “dangerous, radical and, frankly, weird”. Progressives, however, argue that a bold, authentic economic message is the only way to reverse the party’s decline in the state. They point to the recent Miami mayoral race, where Eileen Higgins campaigned openly as a Democrat despite the race being officially nonpartisan and defeated Trump-backed Emilio Gonzalez, marking the first Democratic mayoral victory in Miami in nearly 30 years. No political campaign in Florida is fought outside the shadow of Trump, whose Mar-a-Lago estate is in Palm Beach. The president gleefully celebrated Vindman’s defeat, calling him a “treasonous creep” and predicting “certain defeat” for “Radical Left Lunatic” Nixon in November. In her eyes, Trump’s influence represents a clear and present danger to democracy. “I’m concerned with whether this country is still going to be standing because we have someone who does not want to leave the White House. We have someone who is creating a paramilitary force and creating basically an underground ballroom-bunker type situation. “I’m concerned about that and I want to go to Washington DC to put a check on his corruption and his power to let him know that he is not a king. We did not appoint him to be a king.”

title: Documents leaked by Trump official to bolster a conspiracy show ‘absolutely nothing’
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Inside the US state department, critics are still attacking a shuttered office established to counter foreign propaganda. Now, some of its work is also being resumed
body_text: A botched leak of purportedly explosive government files to a prominent conservative online personality was supposed to offer proof of what the Trump administration and its allies have long alleged: that a little-known office inside the US state department, created to fight foreign propaganda, had secretly become a tool for domestic censorship. Two former high-ranking officials at the Global Engagement Center (GEC), a target of Republican ire that lost its funding in 2024 and was disbanded after Donald Trump’s return to office in 2025, say the documents show nothing of the kind. Instead, they argue, the files are a symptom of a protracted and bitter political fight over an office that spent nearly a decade tracking and countering foreign influence operations, particularly from Russia, China and Iran. And the state department is now resuming some of this work in other parts of its operation, including plans – laid out in a proposal reviewed by the Guardian – to pay social media influencers across south-east Asia as part of an $11m campaign to counter Chinese propaganda. Sarah Rogers, the state department’s undersecretary for public diplomacy, provided the so-called “GEC files” to Jennica Pounds, a rightwing online data analyst known as DataRepublican – only for Pounds to claim earlier this month she was leaked the documents as part of a bid to “entrap” her. Rogers, who denied this claim, then published the files herself, claiming officials inside the center “betrayed their stated mission”. The files included a 2022 GEC report on “gendered disinformation”, a flashpoint in the culture wars. “These guys have consistently misrepresented what the GEC did, and this was a great example of that,” said Daniel Kimmage, who served as the center’s principal deputy coordinator and acting coordinator from its founding in 2017 until its complete dissolution in 2025. His own congressional testimony was included in the leaked files. Kimmage and Carrie Goux, a Joe Biden appointee and the center’s former acting deputy coordinator, say nothing in the material shows the GEC, whose mandate was explicitly foreign-facing, ever turned its tools on Americans. “If the smoking gun was a gendered disinformation report, that feels like they came up short,” Goux said. “There seems to be absolutely nothing here.” Weaponization The dispute is the latest chapter in a years-long campaign by conservatives to portray the GEC as part of a broader effort by the US government and technology companies to suppress rightwing speech. Republican congressmen including Michael McCaul, former chair of the House foreign affairs committee, argued in a July 2024 letter that the GEC was “at best indifferent to, and at worst complicit in” stretching the definition of disinformation to “censor” conservative speech in the US. Trump’s return to the presidency drew this view into the heart of the federal government. The center was abolished in 2025, and what remained of its work scattered across the state department. Much of that Republican-led campaign centered on how the GEC had funded the Global Disinformation Index (GDI), a UK-based non-profit that rates media outlets by how likely they are to spread disinformation, to help monitor propaganda in Asia. But in 2022 the GDI separately published its own study of the US media market that rated several conservative outlets, including Newsmax, One America News and the New York Post, as high-risk – a finding its critics have cited ever since as evidence that a foreign-facing office had funded a group meddling in domestic politics. The question raised by the files leaked this month is narrower, however: whether they show the GEC itself ran a domestic censorship operation. Kimmage and Goux insist they do not. Kimmage said his own congressional testimony, which Rogers included in the leak, had been selectively read. “If you look at the transcript, [the question was], ‘Does GEC take positions on US outlets?’ And I said, ‘No, it didn’t,’” he said. Rogers “tried to twist that into something that it wasn’t”, according to Kimmage. “For people who talk a lot about weaponization of government, this seems a lot closer to the weaponization of government and psy-opping of the American people than anything that the emails from the Global Engagement Center show.” ‘False’ allegations Pounds, the rightwing analyst, is not a neutral bystander. Days after the documents were released, she disclosed that she had been quietly working since July as a special government employee for the defense department. On Friday, Pounds released a database to track US citizens in the Democratic Socialists of America. The Pentagon did not respond when asked whether the database is included in her scope of government work. Both former senior officials, Kimmage and Goux, draw a sharp line between the accusations made by critics of the GEC and what the center actually did. “We were not ever looking at Americans,” Goux said. “We were looking at the foreign actors and what their [tactics, techniques and procedures] … are doing overseas.” The GEC “did what its congressional mandate charged it to do, which is to fight foreign [misinformation and] disinformation”, added Kimmage. “This allegation that it’s censoring Americans is false.” During its almost decade-long existence, the center published eight detailed public reports on Russian and Chinese information operations and ran four major exposures of Russian disinformation campaigns – in Latin America, Africa and Moldova, and on the Kremlin-linked network RT. Its largest such operation traced a Kremlin-backed effort called the “African Initiative”, which the center said had recruited local journalists, bloggers and public figures to spread conspiracy theories about US-funded health programs across the continent. In January 2024, the GEC helped broker an international pact on countering foreign state disinformation that eventually drew more than two dozen government signatories, among them Moldova, Spain, Estonia, Poland and Finland – a framework its backers hoped other countries would use to build their own version of the office. A 2022 inspector general review found the GEC “generally effective” at supporting counter-disinformation programs overall, while flagging weaknesses in its internal controls, contractor oversight and strategic planning. That record was enough to sustain bipartisan support: senators Rob Portman, a Republican, and Chris Murphy, a Democrat, repeatedly pushed to fund and strengthen the center, and its authorization survived multiple renewal fights before House Republicans, increasingly focused on the domestic-speech question, declined to extend it again in 2024. That mandate cost roughly $61m per year. The GEC employed about 120 people before Congress declined to reauthorize it, letting the office lapse at the end of 2024. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, later folded what remained of its work into a new counter foreign information manipulation and interference office, framing the closure as an end to wasteful, censorious government overreach. Trust exercise Now, less than a year after the GEC shut down, a proposal reviewed by the Guardian shows the state department preparing to pay up to 30 online influencers across 11 countries in south-east Asia $2,500 apiece as part of an $11m, multi-year campaign to counter Chinese propaganda. The project, which would be operated by the US Mission to ASEAN, has three parts: a $5m messaging campaign, a $3m program training influencers and journalists to counter Chinese propaganda, and a $3m trip bringing about 180 participants to studios in Washington and Houston “for intensive collaboration, studio production and first-hand engagement with US institutions and creators”. The proposal’s planning materials describe the ideal recruit as starting from a “welcoming” position of what one document calls the “rejecting-affirming continuum”: someone not yet sold on the US, but not hostile either. As participants move through the accelerator, the materials say, exposure to evidence of US commitment in the region and training in spotting propaganda from China (which has reportedly invested billions of dollars in disinformation efforts globally) is meant to carry them toward the “affirming” end of that scale, publicly backing closer ties with Washington on trade, tech standards and the South China Sea. The document cited the rightwing analyst and new Pentagon special government employee, Jennica Pounds, the DataRepublican, as an ideal model to seek out in other recruits abroad. Contacted for comment, the state department declined to directly address questions about the documents released by Rogers, the influencer proposal, the department’s current foreign influence programs and whether other regions are being targeted as well. A state department official said: “Undersecretary Rogers has been clear that the department will continue to confront censorship, anti-American propaganda and coercive influence directly while demonstrating the enduring advantages of freedom, accountability and open communication.” Meanwhile, the office of policy, planning and resources for public diplomacy (R/PPR) was separately shopping for commercial help with a similar mission this spring. A government filing from May 2026 shows the R/PPR requesting information from vendors on software that can mine open-source data, map “adversarial propaganda influence networks” and detect deepfakes. That apparent contradiction is not lost on the GEC’s former staff. “Are they trying to re-create it? Probably,” Goux said. “But now they’re spending a lot more tax dollars doing that, trying to get contractors to do some of the stuff that we were doing.” Goux put the broader cost in plainer terms still. “The US has lost their seat at the table to do that, and that’s unfortunate,” she said. “I hope we can gain it back, but we’re losing trust too, and that’s significant.”

title: Flooding devastated swathes of Indiana but response is hampered by politics
author: Stephen Starr in Cambridge City, Indiana
summary: Record inundations wrecked homes and took seven lives but Trump has not approved emergency aid and state has cut funds for environmental agencies
body_text: It’s been 10 days since the floodwater receded from Cambridge City’s main street and yet signs of disaster are all around. Abandoned cars, toilets and bathtubs are strewn across parks and side streets on a recent visit to the city. Garages have been lifted from their foundations and moved by the rushing water. Dumpsters up and down the street are overflowing with people’s belongings, with red paint sprayed on homes indicating which houses have been cleared by water rescue teams. Flooding from the Crietz Creek, a tributary of the Whitewater River, has damaged one-third, or about 250, of all houses in this quiet town of 1,700 people in south-east Indiana. About 175 of those homes have experienced significant damage. “At first, earlier in the morning the water was coming into the basement from the west, and we were fighting it with a pump. We were good. But then, as the river swelled, it started to come back up the opposite direction,” recalls Rick Keasling of what happened on the morning of 12 August. By the time about 10in of rain had fallen by mid-morning – three times the average amount for the entire month of August for the town – the flood waters had risen almost 5ft inside his home. He, his wife and dog fled shortly before. “The dog had to swim to the truck. We’ve lost everything on the first floor and in the basement. All the big appliances,” he says. “We’ve had some water in the basement [in the past] but nothing like this, not even close.” Record flooding across swathes of central and eastern Indiana have destroyed critical infrastructure, made more than 1,000 people homeless and taken seven lives. In the north-west part of Indiana, hundreds of thousands of people in Gary, the only majority-Black city in the state, were left without electricity for more than two weeks following a derecho storm that pummeled the region on 11 August. A section of Interstate-70, one of the most important regional highways connecting the populated eastern US with the midwest, was washed away a few miles north of Cambridge City. All the while, Indiana’s state legislature, where Republicans hold a supermajority, have repeatedly refused to fund climate-related initiatives in the state. While Indiana cut state funding for state environmental agencies by 19% between 2010 and 2024, neighboring Ohio and Michigan increased resources in their states by 19% and 78% respectively. Twice in recent years Indiana’s senate environmental affairs committee has refused to consider legislation for a climate solutions taskforce for the state. The state’s disaster relief fund stood at just $2m before the flooding (it has since been raised to $5m) and, according to the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, Indiana is one of 18 states with no climate action plan. “Climate change played a role in the intensity of the event since the warmer atmosphere would have allowed for more vapor to ultimately condense and fall as rain,” says Beth Hall, the director of the Indiana state climate office. “Additionally, the warmer temperatures may have caused the heat dome to be the large size it was and to stick around longer than normal.” Donald Trump has approved Federal Emergency Management Agency disaster aid for more than 50 counties around Indiana, but with that capped at just $5m, many say it doesn’t go far enough: the cost of this month’s storms and flooding is estimated by state leaders at about $5bn. Fema, too, has come in for criticism. Indiana’s governor, Mike Braun, submitted a disaster declaration to the federal agency on 21 August, which would allow for the release of millions of dollars in federal support to flood victims, but no response has been received. Fema under the current Trump administration has turned down more than 30 disaster declarations and is taking longer to approve requests when it grants approval. Meanwhile, Cambridge City has only a moderate risk from flooding, according to First Street, a flood risk non-profit. But nearly all the properties affected by flooding in the town are located in a Fema flood zone AE, which signifies a high-risk flood area where there is a 1% or greater chance of flooding in a particular year. According to Fema mapping, many buildings, including a former elementary school, are located in a “regulatory floodway”. In a town where the median household income is about 60% of the national level, many residents have been forced to go without flood insurance due to prohibitively high premiums and deductible charges. In the aftermath of the flooding, while small businesses can apply for a county grant of up to $5,000, the few that have been able to open their doors are struggling. “We’ve had some people [come in] but it’s not normal,” says Tami Hall, who runs Vinton House Antiques on Cambridge City’s main street, and which lost most of its basement equipment, including its HVAC system in the flooding. “I think people think that everything’s closed.” Sitting on a bench inside the antiques store, Tom Saunders, who serves on the town board in the neighboring community of Lewisville, which was also hit by flooding, says that smaller villages in particular are struggling in the flood’s aftermath. “I have a gentleman, he’s 69 years old, he lost his mobile home, his four cars, everything. He’s living with me right now. We’re past a week of this and we still don’t know anything,” he says. “There’s nobody to help.” Ten days since disaster struck Cambridge City, volunteers are staffing a food truck that serves hotdogs, chips and drinks to about 70 people each day. Residents have had to deal with looting and Keasling says that while he had some flood insurance coverage, it won’t come close to covering the damage incurred. “There’s so many people displaced,” he says, as the sound of industrial dehumidifiers whirls through the ground floor of his home, where nothing but the wooden structural studs and floor are left. “Down in Connersville, they’re tearing down houses today.”

title: Why is ‘vegan’ suddenly being used as a slur?
author: Emma Beddington
summary: US republicans are tarnishing their plant-eating opponents at every opportunity. Yet vegans are perfectly suited to hold power – let me count the ways, writes Emma Beddington
body_text: Cool news, fellow soy boys and girls – we’ve been promoted from feeble, tofu-eating wokerati to dangerous radicals unfit for public office. Politico reports that US Republicans have started throwing “vegan” around as a tactic to tarnish their political opponents. “He’s a vegan,” Trump warned of Democratic Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico in May, while Talarico’s opponent, state attorney-general Ken Paxton, is trying to get the nickname “Tofu Talarico” to stick. Paxton also called him “a vegan who thinks God is non-binary”, which I find hilarious as a political put-down – give the man a Netflix special. (Sidenote: I investigated, and according to the Catholic catechism, God is “neither man nor woman”.) Republicans have also been digging up past pro-plant-based statements from Colorado congressional candidate Manny Rutinel: a campaign committee press secretary described him on X as “a far-left vegan activist who wants to end animal agriculture”, posting an old pic of Rutinel bare-chested and wearing a Peta anti-meat banner. Other Dems have also been accused of, erm, liking animals and eating plants: Arizona congressional candidate Amish Shah has been attacked for his “wacky liberal agenda pushing vegan policies” and Lindsay James in Iowa drew heat for merely supporting the idea of “meatless May”. It’s ridiculous but also depressing. Because hang on: does America actually think veganism disqualifies a person for political responsibilities? Apparently, when you look at how these candidates reacted. A Talarico spokesperson issued an official response to “vegan accusations” (“accusations” – the word you’d use for say, corruption or sexual assault): a picture of him wrapping his face around a giant hunk of meat. The candidate himself joked, spicily, “I’ve been eating barbecue since before Ken Paxton’s first indictment” (despite many years of legal issues, Paxton has never been found guilty of any crime). Rutinel, meanwhile, clarified he’s not vegan now, saying he needs to “enjoy the delicious products that Colorado ranchers make”. His Reddit posts supporting animal rights, he said, were “the views of a 22-year-old kid,” giving the impression his veganism was youthful folly, like taking a puff of a joint in college – he tried a tempeh wrap, but he didn’t finish it! A spokesperson for James said she has “always sided with Iowa farmers”. Obviously harbouring vegan sympathies plays badly in agricultural communities (claiming your opponent is a seitan worshipper is a canny strategy when you’re appealing to ranchers), so I understand the emphatic denials. But rather than playing into this notion that vegans are extreme-left fantasists who can’t be trusted, I wish someone would defend the idea that they’re actually perfectly well qualified for political office. Why wouldn’t they be? Sure, people think we’re pleased with ourselves and boring (guilty), but that never excluded other politicians from power. We’re not so weakly undernourished that we couldn’t survive the rigours of the job, either – these days, plant proteins are thrust at us from every angle. And actually, there are plenty of reasons why vegans can make great public servants. For a start, anyone who has gone vegan for planetary or animal welfare reasons is OK with a spot of self-denial for the greater good. You think we’ve forgotten how delicious butter is? Believe me, I remember. I’m not suggesting vegans live heroic lives of self-sacrifice (there are vegan pistachio croissants now!), or that not eating animals makes us better people. But any politician with a sense that there are things more important than their own gratification is welcome. Vegans are used to ridicule, and being the target of people’s strongly voiced opinions – that’s always handy in politics. We’re also – and apologies for veering into classic vegan self-righteousness – basically right, no? Talarico’s 2022 comment, that reducing meat consumption to fight climate change is an “existential” matter, has been weaponised against him, but meat production alone accounts for nearly 60% of agriculture’s greenhouse gas emissions. Thomas Poore, lead author of the landmark 2018 study on the environmental impact of agriculture from which that statistic comes, concluded that excluding meat and dairy from your diet is “the single biggest way to reduce your impact on planet Earth”. Politicians who think individuals can make a difference, and that collectively we can mitigate the worst impacts of climate breakdown and stop things getting even worse, are exactly who I want to see in power. Because they give us something even better than a plant milk that doesn’t curdle in hot tea: hope. • Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
