title: Ghislaine Maxwell has virtually run out of legal routes to overturn conviction, experts say
author: Victoria Bekiempis in New York
summary: The Jeffrey Epstein associate’s apparent last hope would be a Hail Mary from Donald Trump – a presidential pardon
body_text: Ghislaine Maxwell seems to be all but guaranteed to have run out of legal avenues to challenge her conviction for her involvement in Jeffrey Epstein’s abuse of girls and young women with perhaps her lingering hopes of freedom resting on a pardon from the Trump administration. Paul Engelmayer, a Manhattan federal court judge, last week rejected Maxwell’s contention that her constitutional rights were violated at trial and sentencing for her crimes. “Maxwell’s claims are all meritless and all or almost all are frivolous,” Engelmayer wrote in his ruling on the former British socialite’s legal gambit. Engelmayer also rejected Maxwell’s claim that new evidence, which she said came to light during Epstein Files Transparency Act disclosures, did not support her allegations of constitutional violations. “On the contrary, to the extent it is relevant, far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings,” he ruled. Maxwell’s family said in a statement that Engelmayer’s ruling was “marked by a tone of sarcasm and disdain that, in our view, undermines the appearance of impartiality and invites scrutiny of the judge’s conduct”. They also said Maxwell “will continue to pursue every available legal avenue” for relief. Legal veterans said, however, that Maxwell had virtually exhausted all her court-based routes. With Maxwell apparently running out of legal pathways, many have wondered whether Donald Trump will at some point deliver a Hail Mary – a presidential pardon. “She’s exhausted her direct appeals. Now she’s trying to collaterally attack the conviction, which is very difficult to do,” said Neama Rahmani, a former federal prosecutor who founded the law firm West Coast Trial Lawyers. “I don’t know what world she lives in,” Rahmani also said. “Her only chance of ever seeing the light of day before her sentence runs is a presidential pardon.” Rahmani explained Maxwell’s recent rejected request was different from her supreme court effort – which was based on claims that a decades-old non-prosecution agreement with south Florida federal authorities shielded her from prosecution. The supreme court bid failed when the justices declined to review that appeal. Maxwell could ask the second circuit court of appeals to review Engelmayer’s ruling, but that is a request, not a surefire opportunity to be heard, said Mark Chutkow, a former federal prosecutor now practicing white-collar defense at the firm Dykema. “Ordinarily, you either have to get a certificate of appealability from the trial court that denies your motion or your petition, or you can get it from the appellate court,” he said, noting Engelmayer did not grant such a certificate. “I would assume what she’s going to do is seek a certificate of appealability [from] the second circuit.” The second circuit, however, will see Engelmayer’s decision and his denial of this certificate. “It seems unlikely that she is going to get a certificate of appealability from the second circuit court of appeals meaning that in essence, her legal avenues are going to be dead,” Chutkow said “This decision should bring Ghislaine Maxwell’s campaign to escape accountability to a final close. A jury heard the evidence and convicted her. The court of appeals affirmed her conviction. The supreme court declined to intervene,” said Spencer Kuvin, an attorney at Goldlaw who has represented dozens of Epstein survivors. “Now, after thoroughly reviewing her latest claims, Judge Engelmayer has found that the evidence of her guilt was overwhelming and that her arguments were largely frivolous, procedurally barred, and based upon speculation, distortions and outright falsehoods.” Given that Engelmayer’s ruling virtually shuts the door on future efforts per longtime attorneys, attention has once again shifted to a presidential pardon or commutation from Trump, who has been saddled with ongoing Epstein and Maxwell controversies since taking office again. ‘Politically, a pardon would be catastrophic’ Trump vowed while campaigning that his administration would release all Epstein documents, but his justice department repeatedly missed congressionally mandated disclosure deadlines, and some allege that some files remain secret. Trump, who socialized with Epstein before the latter’s Florida state court soliciting conviction, has maintained that he never engaged in inappropriate conduct. The White House, when asked for comment on the pardon issue, pointed to two statements. When Trump was asked if he had ruled out a pardon, he said: “I haven’t even thought about it, I mean, I haven’t thought about it for months.” “Maybe I haven’t thought about it at all,” Trump also said. “But I don’t talk about that. I don’t rule it in or out, I don’t even think about it.” “Politically, I think it would be catastrophic,” said Brittany Martinez, a Republican strategist who is the executive director of Principles First. “You run on releasing the Epstein files. Then when documents are released, they’re limited and heavily redacted. Then you turn around and call the entire controversy a hoax. And after all of that, you pardon Jeffrey Epstein’s closest associate? While claiming to be the president who protects women and children? “That would be incredibly difficult to defend,” she added. Rahmani explained that there is a formal pardon process. A request would go to the justice department’s pardon attorney who, in turn, makes a recommendation. That said, “the president sort of marches to the beat of his own drum,” Rahmani said – Trump could just grant it. “There is a very, very, very slim chance it happens at all,” Rahmani added. If it did, however, Rahmani said he would expect it to happen when Trump’s presidency wraps, not before the midterms. “Even though the president is very unpredictable, I just can’t see it … It would be career suicide. But again, he obviously doesn’t care.” Maxwell’s family said legal routes must be exhausted before making a pardon application. They said to the best of their knowledge, there isn’t an application to the Trump administration. For advocates, presidential clemency would deal an immense blow to survivors. Lauren Hersh, a former prosecutor who is the CEO of the non-profit World Without Exploitation, said: “After listening to so many survivors and hearing the devastating harm caused by Ghislaine Maxwell, I can’t imagine anybody would give the idea of a pardon a moment’s thought. It would be totally egregious.” Asked about a pardon, Thomas Massie, a Republican Kentucky congressman who co-sponsored the bipartisan Epstein Files Transparency Act, said in a statement: “I’m adamantly opposed to it. [Todd] Blanche already inexplicably and inappropriately moved her to a country club prison with no new information or indictments of coconspirators.” Julie Roginsky, who filed sexual harassment lawsuits against Roger Ailes, the former Fox News CEO, and co-founded the survivors advocacy non-profit Lift Our Voices, said an act of clemency would be a “monumental slap in the face” for survivors. But she did not rule it out. “She already got a sweetheart deal by being moved not just into Club Fed, but by being given privileges that nobody else in her position would be given,” Roginsky said, referring to Maxwell’s controversial transfer to a low-security prison. Roginsky also pointed to Blanche’s interview of Maxwell, which the now attorney general conducted while he was the justice department’s second-ranking official. “I think we already understand that the fix is in for her, and I don’t know whether she had some sort of guarantee that once the president is on his way out, as one of his last acts of commutation, he will commute her sentence or just give her a full pardon,” Roginsky said. “Nothing would surprise me.”

title: Barack Obama, JFK and … Josh Frydenberg: what can a memoir do for an ambitious politician?
author: Joshua Black
summary: The former treasurer’s new book will hit shelves soon, but he may learn that memoirs can be blunt instruments for political renewal. Just ask Peter Costello
body_text: Former treasurer Josh Frydenberg’s new memoir, marketed as a coming-of-age story, family history and pandemic retrospective rolled into one, is due to hit shelves soon. Publisher HarperCollins Australia promises it will be a reflection “on what political power can and cannot achieve, on the cost of public life in an increasingly divided world, and on the unique promise and potential of Australia”. The press release promises an account of how Australia achieved “one of the strongest economic and health recoveries in the world” in the wake of the pandemic and a rumination on Frydenberg’s many ways to lead: “In his inspiring advocacy against antisemitism and hate in the aftermath of Australia’s deadliest domestic terrorist attack at Bondi, he found the words many were searching for.” Some observers see it as the latest tactic in a larger strategy to help position Frydenberg – who lost his seat to independent Monique Ryan in 2022 – for a potential comeback. If the pundits are correct and Frydenberg’s midlife memoir is part of a tilt, it would suggest the former treasurer has yet to learn from the fable of so many predecessors. Labouring under American illusions Book-length political myth-making is not new to today’s politicians. It’s a tried and tested tool in American presidential candidacies, from John F Kennedy through to Joe Biden. Presidential hopeful Barack Obama showed what a well-timed book could do for an up-and-coming leader. In the 20th century, Labor partisans languishing in opposition were the ones most likely to emulate the Americans. A growing local publishing industry urged them on. But the men who published in the 1960s, such as opposition leader Arthur Calwell and senior left figure Jim Cairns, quickly found that they were, to borrow Lloyd Bentsen’s immortal words, “no Jack Kennedy”. Labor parliamentarians such as Lindsay Tanner and Wayne Swan published more political musings during the Howard years. Sales were rarely stellar and just one, an up-and-coming western Sydney MP named Mark Latham, found that his densely cerebral book, Civilising Global Capital (1998), marked him out as a possible leader. In any case, observers such as Michelle Grattan knew that “Labor books” tended to become “Liberal weapons” before long. Liberal literature Liberals have more recently turned to this version of performance politics, curating personas and sculpting personal backstories in service of a larger ambition. The crisis of authority within the Liberal party post Howard has seen bitter conflict between factions, leaders and ideological traditions. Owning one’s own history, and that of the party generally, has in that context become a more important feature of conservative politicking. Tony Abbott’s mid-career memoir, Battlelines, helped make him leader. That book began as a project to help Abbott recover from what colleagues called a “political funk”. It gave him a larger public platform and a series of controversial policy ideas (ranging from carbon charges and a referendum for greater commonwealth constitutional power, through to age pension reforms and a special “covenant” form of marriage) to debate with his interviewers. It culminated in a promotional tour that showed he still had communicative skills – and a little charisma. Abbott’s book events conveniently became dialogues with increasingly disillusioned Liberal members who loathed the then Rudd government’s emissions reduction policy. Earlier inclined to concede the issue, Abbott was emboldened to pick a fight with Labor and, in the first instance, with climate-conscious opposition leader Malcolm Turnbull, whose job he secured by a single vote in a party room on 1 December 2009. But Battlelines was the exception, not the norm. In 2011, Liberal frontbencher Andrew Robb published a very decent book, Black Dog Daze, describing his suffering and treatment for diurnal variation (serious morning depressions). It was an honest and brave account of a sensitive personal topic. But it too was shaped by leadership aspirations that would go unfulfilled. In government, Christopher Pyne published a book called A Letter to My Children, explaining his approach to public service and the inspiration of his father, the late ophthalmologist Remington Pyne. The book and its marketing softened his reputation as a parliamentary antagonist and would-be deregulator of higher education fees. But that hardly placed him in the “winner’s circle”, as it were. The cautionary tale of Costello But perhaps the best cautionary fable for Frydenberg is the story of former treasurer Peter Costello. John Howard’s longsuffering deputy shocked Liberals by declining the leadership after the 2007 election. Returning to the backbench, he knuckled down to work with his father-in-law – conservative intellectual Peter Coleman – on the book that became The Costello Memoirs: The Age of Prosperity. From go to whoa, that book was synonymous with leadership speculation. Costello joked with his publishers that the book could be called “The story so far”. He told reporters he would not be a leadership candidate in the future, but Coleman told the same reporters there was still “a crack in the door”. Journalists initially mused that a successful memoir might make Costello leader. But by the time the book was published in October 2008, life (and the media) had moved on. There was leadership churn already, and a global financial meltdown under way. The book sold well, but even that was initially unclear. It was reportedly beaten in its first few weeks by a children’s fantasy book (Christopher Paolini’s third Eragon novel) and the follow-up sequel of a book of recipes using no more than four ingredients (4 Ingredients 2). It must have all been rather anticlimactic. Costello left parliament the following year. Performance politics There are good reasons for serving politicians to publish books. They can command attention, stimulate debate and, occasionally, make for engaging reading. Jim Cairns helped modernise Labor politics with his ambitious – if dense – tomes on Australia’s future as a social democratic society in the Asian region. Abbott and Costello both made a contribution to Liberal debates about the future. Today ambitious politicians recognise that growing disaffection with the political class and declining attachment to the major parties mean they need to present themselves in increasingly personal, autobiographical terms. But these books are imperfect vehicles for political revival. Even if there are still enough Liberal party members to fill a book launch in Kooyong, Frydenberg cannot assume there’s a long line of readers, voters and parliamentary backers to usher him to high office, no matter how many glowing endorsements appear on the back of his book. • Performance Politics by Joshua Black is out through New South Press on 1 September ($39.99)

title: Trump says NBC’s Kristen ‌Welker should face ‘punishment’ from FCC
author: Edward Helmore
summary: Trump’s threat comes after host described success record of candidates whom president had endorsed as ‘mixed’
body_text: Donald Trump ⁠on Sunday said NBC’s Kristen ‌Welker – host of Meet the Press – should face “rebuke or punishment” from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). Welker, during a live segment for a local Washington DC affiliate, described the success record of political candidates whom the president had endorsed as “mixed”. The segment aired before Sunday’s edition of Meet the Press. Trump “is going to loom large over these midterms”, Welker remarked on that live shot. “He, of course, has endorsed a slate of candidates in the primaries. He’s had some mixed results.” But Welker went on to mention Trump’s endorsement of the appointed interim US senator Darline Graham, sister of her late predecessor Lindsey Graham, who was successful in her primary battle. Nonetheless, the president then took verbal aim at Welker with a social media post deriding her as the “Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of … Meet the Fake Press,” accused her of “purposeful inaccuracy” and warned that she would “be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment”. The post also said that Trump hoped his appointed FCC chair, Brendan Carr – and Carr’s colleagues on the commission – “take this Threat to our Country very seriously”. Once Meet the Press actually started on Sunday, a guest analyst on the show said “the single most important factor in who the Republican nominee will be in [the presidential election of] 2028 will be who Donald Trump endorses”. Trump is estimated to have made more than 300 endorsements that resulted in the recipient winning. In the election cycle leading up to November’s midterms, 214 of the 218 House candidates he endorsed winning their primaries, including all 24 Republican Senate primaries. Meanwhile, in gubernatorial primaries, five of the 21 candidates he endorsed lost their primaries, among them Mike Lindell – who finished a distant second in Minnesota to the state house speaker, Lisa Demuth. The state’s supreme court on Saturday effectively confirmed Lindell’s 11-percentage-point defeat by rejecting his bid for a recount. “My Endorsements are stronger than ever,” Trump nonetheless maintained in a 23 August social media post. “There has never been anything close!” When taking aim at Welker on Sunday, beside touting Darline Graham’s victory, he mentioned the Oklahoma gubernatorial hopeful Mike Mazzei’s Republican primary win. He had said days earlier that any of his endorsed candidates who lost were already faced with “impossible” races – but they had earned his support “out of loyalty”. How much power Trump’s endorsement carries has been a touchy issue for the president. On Friday, the HBO Max talkshow host Bill Maher apologized to Trump for claiming that the president was winning “almost none of” his endorsements. Trump had sent Maher statistics making the president’s case that the talkshow host was wrong. Welker and Trump have a contentious relationship. In June, he walked out of an hour-long interview with the host after being asked, among other unpleasant topics for him, about having pledged “no new wars” during his successful run for a second presidency. He started a war in Iran in late February alongside Israel, and Trump denied guaranteeing there would no wars if he were returned to the Oval Office. “You’re a one-sided crooked network,” Trump said at the time. “Let’s call it quits because I’ve had enough. Thank you, darling. Have a good time.” He added: “You ought to straighten out your press. A country can never be great with a dishonest press.” NBC on Sunday issued a statement saying: “Kristen is one of the best in the business, and we stand by her.” NBC News on 19 August had published an article examining Trump’s endorsement record, saying in the story’s headline that the president’s “endorsement record takes a hit at the end of primary season”. Trump’s comments on Sunday about Welker were only the latest instance of him or his administration seeking to bring the weight of the FCC down on media outlets with whom he has become cross. In September 2025, Carr – appointed by Trump – reportedly put pressure on television station groups to pre-empt Jimmy Kimmel’s show as punishment for a comment that the ABC host, a frequent critic of the president, made in the wake of the assassination of the conservative influencer Charlie Kirk. Two conservative-friendly broadcast groups, Sinclair and Nexstar, did so. And ABC opted to “indefinitely” pull Kimmel’s show before he ultimately returned to the air a week later. Trump has also won private settlements from ABC and CBS totaling more than $30m during his second presidency. Earlier in August, ABC sued the FCC, arguing that it was being illegally targeted by the regulator after being forced to apply early to renew its eight local broadcast licenses. Among Republicans’ complaints about ABC are that its candidates are not given equal airtime on the daytime talkshow The View. “Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts,” the network said in its lawsuit. NBC is licensed by the FCC to directly operate 11 local stations. Involving itself in broadcast outlets’ editorial decisions and constitutionally protected speech is beyond the mandate of the FCC, which was established in 1934. The CNN media reporter and commentator Brian Stelter, who on Sunday first found the clip of Welker mentioning Trump’s “mixed record”, wrote that the FCC “can’t punish Welker” because it has “limited power … by design”. But Stelter noted that Carr had been “responsive” to Trump in the past – and “it’s reasonable to think NBC will be targeted next”.

title: Trump’s plan to hand over a part of Yosemite is what oligarchy looks like
author: Rebecca Solnit
summary: Public lands belong to all of us. No one should plunder those lands
body_text: Do people still say a car was “sold for parts”? Because the US is being sold for parts or just handed over to the oligarchy. It’s a fire sale, a bankruptcy auction, it’s a planned dismantling of everything from its military to its institutions of higher education to its scientific research to its public lands. And while the threat to give part of Yosemite national park is about a quarter-mile parcel on the park’s edge, Yosemite is a crown jewel in the national park system and, arguably, the world’s first national park. To let any bit of it be traded for the benefit of a corporation’s planned development on the park’s western border would compromise the inviolability of national parks and sacrifice public good for the sake of private profit. This is of course the ongoing agenda of the Trump administration. Public lands belong to all of us, a gift from the past because people worked hard to protect these forests, mountains, canyons, and a trust for the future, because the public should include everyone in this country alive now and everyone yet to come. The Trump administration’s ruthless efforts to turn over public lands for mining and logging and fossil fuel exploitation while it also dismantles the US Forest Service and National Park Service is about turning long-term wellbeing for the many, human and more than human, into short-term profit for an elite. These public lands have many kinds of value – the trees and grasslands are sequestering carbon as part of a natural climate amelioration, the mountains are watersheds, and most of these natural places now are key to rural tourism and outdoor recreation economies. White people first entered Yosemite valley in the early 1850s, on a military campaign to punish, displace, or exterminate the Indigenous people there who were interfering with another era’s environmental destruction: the Gold Rush, whose miners were hunting out the game, cutting down the trees, polluting the rivers, and massacring the region’s original inhabitants. Some of the early visitors recognized Yosemite’s extraordinary scenic beauty of its oak grasslands, high canyon walls, waterfalls. By the 1860s, photographers such as Carleton Watkins and Eadweard Muybridge had made images of Yosemite that were shown internationally. The place became iconic before many white people had visited it. In the spring of 1864, Abraham Lincoln signed into law a bill establishing that “Yosemite Valley’s premises shall be held for public use, resort, and recreation; shall be inalienable for all time.” It was originally managed by the state of California, since the federal government had little presence in the west and was busy fighting the civil war. Yellowstone national park, on the other hand, was set aside eight years later as a federally managed preserve because Wyoming and Montana were not yet states and is usually recognized as the first national park. The document Ulysses S Grant signed said the place was to be “reserved and withdrawn from settlement, occupancy, or sale under the laws of the United States, and dedicated and set apart as a public park or pleasuring-ground for the benefit and enjoyment of the people.” There was always a lie in the foundation of Yosemite, Yellowstone, Death Valley, the Grand Canyon and many other parks, in that they were Indigenous peoples’ ancestral homelands long before Columbus set sail or Lewis and Clark headed west. In Yosemite, those wrongs have been addressed over the past 30 years by changes in signage, representations of the place’s history, and opening to the traditional usage and ceremony of the original inhabitants’ descendants. The flawed premise of national parks matters, but so does the fact that the system kept these places from being privatized, developed and destroyed. But that is what is now happening to the park service as a whole: Trump has been funneling Park Service money meant to be spread across the country to his pet projects at the White House and in Washington DC including gilding statues and the incompetent $16m painting of the reflecting pool. Michael Scherer reports in the Atlantic that there’s a fast-track approval process for funding Trump projects out of park service funds, while the National Park Service as a whole is being starved. He notes there’s “a decrease of $854m, or 68%, in spending on projects in park regions outside the Washington area in the first eight and a half months of fiscal year 2026, compared with the full prior fiscal year. During that same period, spending around Washington increased by about $100 million.” The Trump administration proposes to further slash the number of park service employees, who had already been reduced by 24% in 2025. To give up a piece of land is one form of harm to the parks, to take away the park’s workers, whose labors protect endangered species, waterways and land, prevent fires and provide public services from search and rescue operations to education to clean restrooms is another. To open up the ancient sacred site of Chaco Canyon in New Mexico to fracking is yet another form of destruction by the Trump administration under way. The same is true of the 90% reduction of Bears Ears and Escalante in Utah. As the Associated Press reported earlier this month that this radical shrinkage undoes “protections established by his Democratic predecessors on public lands that are sacred among many Native Americans. Trump administration officials and congressional Republicans have sought to expand drilling, mining and logging on public lands, while removing protections for imperiled species and rolling back rules for conservation.” Yosemite was first established as protected land during one civil war. Another is under way about whether the federal government exists to serve the good of the many or the profiteering of the few. A small parcel in Yosemite is nevertheless a big indicator of who this country belongs to and whose rights and interests matter. Rebecca Solnit is a Guardian US columnist. She is the author of Orwell’s Roses and co-editor with Thelma Young Lutunatabua of the climate anthology Not Too Late: Changing the Climate Story from Despair to Possibility

title: As US-Canada tensions flare, who’s calling the shots in Trump’s trade team?
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: US trade representative Jamieson Greer has a level-headed reputation but commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House adviser Peter Navarro also have key roles
body_text: Having reportedly read Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables, in French, during a military tour of duty in Iraq, Jamieson Greer considered himself an unlikely target for accusations of francophobia. But Donald Trump’s US trade representative, hitherto one of the president’s less high-profile cabinet members, found himself in that uncomfortable position amid the acrimonious collapse of bilateral trade talks with Canada that now threatens to degenerate into an all-out trade war between the two close trading partners whose economies are tightly intertwined. An apparent pending deal between Washington and Ottawa aimed at avoiding damaging tit-for-tat tariffs broke down at the last minute, with Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, claiming his country had come “under attack” from the US. Among the multiple and complex points of disagreement was a Canadian accusation that US negotiators had pressed for a weakening of legal protections for the French language, which is most heavily spoken in the province of Quebec. Canadian provisions include legislation that mandates streaming and online video companies to invest in and promote Canadian content and promote the French language. Carney cast US objections to such regulations as a deal-breaker, and said they amounted to “threats to French language and culture”. For Greer, a fluent French speaker who once served as a Mormon missionary in Belgium, France and Luxembourg, the charge was too much. “I speak French, too,” he told CNBC, dismissing the claims as “a funny, fake story”. “My kids speak French,” he said. “One of my kids was born in Paris. So I like the Québécois, and I like that they speak French. What we don’t like is a situation where Canada, the federal government, forces American tech companies to take their earnings and give a percentage to their competitors in Canada.” The controversy may be the closest glimpse the public will see of Greer being rattled. By Thursday, in what was being being seen by some Canadian officials as a potential olive branch, he was peddling a softer line on the language issue. “President Trump, myself and the US government recognizes the importance and sensitivity of the French language in Canada,” he told CBC, the Canadian broadcaster. “We know that this is quite sensitive and quite important, and we actually champion the use of French.” The impact was undermined hours later, however, when Trump publicly signed a retributive executive order supposedly changing the name of Lake Ontario – one of the Great Lakes which has shores on both countries – to Lake America. Petty as the act was, it seemed to graphically illustrate the limited freedom of manoeuvre held by anyone representing a president so preoccupied with trade. And Greer is not the only official seeking to steer the president’s aggressive agenda on trade – raising questions over who is really in control. Moving the goalposts Those who have met and worked with Greer describe the 46-year-old – who served as a military lawyer in Iraq, where he is reported to have read Hugo’s classic novel between bombardments – as a model of calm and expertise. “I have high respect for him. He been pretty creative in terms of trying to thread the needle with other countries as he tries to promote Trump’s trade policies,” said Wendy Cutler, a former US trade representative’s negotiator who has met Greer several times. “From a professional viewpoint, he’s extremely impressive. His reputation as being very level-headed, a very calm demeanor, and not someone who loses his temper or who grandstands.” It is not known if Greer retained his sang-froid in private as the talks with Canada unravelled, just days after Trump himself publicly declared a deal was at hand. According to reports, the agreement was derailed after Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary, objected to the scale of proposed tariffs reductions on imports of Canadian steel, aluminium and cars, sectors falling under his responsibility after Trump declared them areas of national security under the 1962 Trade Expansion Act. Carney, explaining why Canada decided to abandon the talks, pointed to disunity among the US negotiators. The White House has denied claims of division between Greer and Lutnick, but seasoned commentators are skeptical. “Lutnick viewed all this as his turf, and here is Greer, who is the designated guy to be effectively the trade minister, if you think about it in the context of other countries, conducting the negotiations,” said William Reinsch, a senior adviser to the Center for Strategic and International Studies and a former undersecretary for commerce. “It appears Greer was willing to go farther than Lutnick was. “From the Canadian point of view, this was a disagreement that developed late in the day and led the Canadians to believe that the United States was moving the goalposts.” Cutler, who served Republican and Democratic administrations during a 27-year stint as a US trade negotiator, said tensions within negotiating teams were not unprecedented, but were normally ironed out before talks reached the critical stage. “I think the challenge under this administration is that you have Greer in charge of the trade portfolio, but Lutnick’s in charge of section 232 investigations [restricting foreign import on national security grounds] and that’s where a lot of the sensitive issues are,” said Cutler, now vice-president of the Asia Society Policy Institute. ‘Trump whisperer’ Greer cut his trade negotiating teeth as chief of staff to Robert Lighthizer, US trade representative in Trump’s first presidency, who played the leading role in renegotiating Washington’s economic ties with Mexico and Canada, and the former North America Free Trade Agreement (Nafta), which was replaced with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) in 2020. He was chosen for the position when Lighthizer apparently indicated he did not wish to be considered for the post a second time. “Greer plays the same role that Lighthizer played,” said Reinsch, who noted, however, that Greer lacked his former boss’s intimate understanding of Congress. “He figures out legal ways to do what Trump wants to do, and to get as much of Trump’s objectives accomplished as is possible within the framework that he has to operate in,” added Reinsch. “So that allows him to come back to Trump on occasion and say, ‘there’s a better way to get what you want than what you’ve employed so far.” Another complicating element may be Peter Navarro, the president’s senior counsellor for trade and manufacturing. He is reckoned by analysts to be a “Trump whisperer” on Canada, despite a belief that his influence has been marginalized compared with the first Trump presidency, when it was widely joked, according to Reinsch, that Lighthizer was reluctant to travel outside Washington for fear that Navarro would persuade the president to adopt impractical trade policies in his absence. Navarro, who went to jail for contempt of Congress after refusing to comply with a subpoena from the committee investigating the 6 January 2021 insurrection, vented in an appearance on the C-Span network last week. Asked to respond to an article in the Guardian by the Canadian writer Jen Gerson, who wrote that US retaliation should be taken as a warning by other western allies, Navarro said: “Madam, your country screws us. You’re in bed with the Chinese and playing games with us. “Look in the mirror at your tariffs codes. You are the problem.” Blame game Navarro has voiced concern that Canada has allowed the import of nearly 50,000 Chinese-manufactured electric vehicles under a most favoured nation agreement, which he fears will ultimately end up crossing the border to be sold in the US. “Navarro’s worried that the whole USMCA negotiation is really about how do we prevent Canada and Mexico from being a backdoor to Chinese stuff,” Reinsch said. “He would probably have argued last week that the deal wasn’t any good because it wouldn’t shut down Chinese imports in the United States.” Yet the focus on Trump’s advisers cannot obscure the president’s own fixation with tariffs. Carney referred to agreements being “signed in pencil”, suggesting that Trump would try to change terms even after the details had been hammered out. “The larger Canadian objection was not due to interagency American disagreement,” Reinsch said. “Trump has very strong fixed views on trade. He thinks tariffs are good. So if you’re going to blame somebody, don’t blame Lutnick or Greer. Blame Trump, because I’m quite confident he had the last word on this.” Regardless of where blame is apportioned, the consequences of Carney’s defiance will reverberate beyond Canada, analysts say, as other countries forced to confront Trump’s threats of tariffs reassess and recalibrate how they should respond. “Other countries are watching the developments with Canada very closely,” said Cutler. “Some of our other trading partners have expressed similar frustrations [to the Canadians] to me privately, and so we could be at a turning point. “It is possible that what we’re experiencing with Canada now spreads to other countries.”

title: First Thing: Desperate rescue attempts continue in Nepal to reach hundreds thought to be trapped
author: Martin Belam
summary: Death toll from unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris now stands at more than 900. Plus, was it a mistake to take away Pluto’s planet status?
body_text: Good morning. Rescue teams are working to reach hundreds of people feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of half a dozen hydropower projects in Nepal as more than 900 workers were reported missing after the devastating flash floods. The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris that crashed through valleys of Nepal on Wednesday last week has risen to 903 people, with 16 reported dead on the Tibet side of the border. More than 4,000 are missing in Nepal, with another 500 in Tibet. Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, have been buried in shallow graves. How large is the rescue operation? Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations, besides civilian workers and volunteers. China’s state-run CCTV reported that Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers. The Red Cross has ‌estimated that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster, which China and some experts linked to the effects of the climate crisis. Why has the disaster sparked a racism row in Australia? A slew of racist social media comments have been made towards missing Australians. Most of them were on pilgrimages, including to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Mainstream media outlets including News Corp, Channel 7, Channel 10 and Nine have been hit with highly offensive and discriminatory comments on Facebook articles identifying the missing Australians. US strikes Iranian launchers in strait of Hormuz, sparking reprisal attack on airbases in Jordan and UAE Iran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates after the US attacked Iranian rocket launchers in the strait of Hormuz, the first such hostilities in a month. The last known ‌US strikes on Iran were in late July and the war has reached a stalemate in recent weeks. The latest exchange of fire was sparked late on Sunday by a US attack on the island of Larak in the strait. Iran’s ⁠Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said the US attack killed and wounded several soldiers and citizens and would be met with “punishment” from ‌Tehran. What has Donald Trump claimed US forces are doing? Hours after the attacks, the US president, Donald Trump, claimed in a social media post that Iran’s energy hub of Kharg Island was being “blown to smithereens” but gave no further details. The White House and ⁠the US defense department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Attacking Kharg, which handled 90% of ⁠Iran’s oil exports before the war, would severely disrupt the Islamic republic’s energy trade and put huge pressure on its economy. Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalates Donald Trump and Canada continued a verbal duel at the weekend over the US government’s administrative renaming of Lake Ontario, with the Ontario premier erecting a giant sign saying “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” – and the American president posting an AI video depicting him tearing down an avatar of that sign, erecting a replacement saying Lake America, and dancing to YMCA. The Wendat Nation grand chief, Pierre Picard, called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history. “I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said. Trump ‘border czar’ denies Milo Yiannopoulos was deported quickly to spare him from ICE detention The White House “border czar”, Tom Homan, denied on Sunday that deporting the British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos just a day after being arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) amounted to preferential treatment. Homan said it was his understanding Yiannopoulos, 41, had overstayed what he believed to be a visitor visa, had not appeared at an immigration hearing and was issued a final order of removal on 22 July. He added: “He had his due process, ordered removed by a federal judge, and ICE removed him. It’s that simple.” In other news … Donald Trump ⁠said NBC’s Kristen ‌Welker should face “rebuke or punishment” from the FCC after she described the success record of political candidates whom the president had endorsed as “mixed”. Ghislaine Maxwell has virtually run out of legal routes to overturn her conviction for her involvement in Jeffrey Epstein’s abuse of girls and young women, experts say, bar a presidential pardon. At least eight people have died off the coast of Turkish-occupied northern Cyprus after a ferry capsized. Nearly 20 people are still missing. The Trump administration is shuttering ⁠two of the three US Department of Agriculture research projects studying cyclospora after the foodborne parasite has ⁠sickened tens of thousands of Americans during the summer. Michigan’s Democratic US senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed apologized to the state’s Jewish Democratic Caucus for comments he made after an attack on a synagogue in March, which he tied to Israel’s actions in the Middle East. Stat of the day: Discount gas stations praised by Trump sold $4m of stolen fuel, lawsuit claims Mansfield Oil Company of Gainesville is suing KRSM and its president, Syed Kazmi, for allegedly picking up nearly $4m of fuel and not paying for it. KRSM sold some of the fuel to stations that are part of the Freedom Fuel Network, promoted by the Trump administration when drivers were facing higher oil prices amid the war with Iran. Building Power: How two Indiana tribes drove out a mining company in one week At the sacred prairie of Pe’ Sla in South Dakota, Indigenous and environmental groups banded together to halt drilling. “We’re just not used to winning,” said Dr Valeriah Big Eagle, who directs the Black Hills work of NDN Collective, an Indigenous-led advocacy nonprofit based in Rapid City. “We’re people used to being screwed over by the government at every level.” Don’t miss this: The sadistic online groomers targeting victims around the world This is an incredibly harrowing read about one woman’s attempts to keep her daughter safe from an online predator with ties to the extortion group known as 764. He has been sentenced to decades in prison. We also have this guide to five warning signs for parents about sadistic online exploitation. … or this: Was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake? Pluto will always be a planet to me. Tim Dowling explores the debate about its status that continues two decades after it was demoted to being a “dwarf planet”. Climate check: ‘Breakthrough’ as Turkmenistan starts fixing ‘mindboggling’ methane mega-leaks The secretive state has begun repairs on ageing facilities after being revealed as the worst country for leaks of the potent greenhouse gas. Last Thing: ‘Humongous’ marmot crowned winner in inaugural Fat Marmot Week contest Dawn was crowned the winner of the inaugural Fat Marmot Week after securing back-to-back victories in both the mass-gain and popular-vote competitions. The contest was started by researchers who previously turned to OnlyFans to help save a decades-long research project. Go, Dawn! title: In a town in the heart of the US, Israeli settler violence in West Bank hits close to home
author: Stephen Starr in Toledo, Ohio
summary: War on Gaza and violence in West Bank is playing out in the streets of Toledo, Ohio, where the Arab American community has flourished
body_text: From his office outside Toledo, Ohio, Thamin Tim Ridi opens his phone to livestream the scene outside the besieged house of his brother, Loui, thousands of miles away in the occupied West Bank. This month, with his property at risk of being destroyed by Israeli settlers, Loui traveled from Ohio to his ancestral home in Qusra, south of Nablus, where his mother and other family members have been living in constant fear of attack. In Qusra, settlers have besieged a number of Palestinian properties and homes, preventing members of the Ridi family from leaving, as their food and water supplies dwindled. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, took to X on 13 August to describe the settlers’ actions as those of “terrorists”. While the Trump administration has offered broad support to Israel and its illegal settlement building over the years, recent comments from JD Vance, the vice-president, and Donald Trump himself indicate a change of tone. Regardless, for Loui’s extended family in Ohio, it’s created a world of concern. “This building has been taken by settlers; that one up there by the soldiers,” Ridi said, pointing at the outline of buildings further up the hill from his brother’s home that are barely visible on his phone. “I’m extremely worried about them,” he said, his eyes fixed on the security camera footage that’s coming through his phone. One of the first things Loui did upon arriving at his home in Qusra, said Ridi, was plant an American flag on his property. For decades, the war in the Middle East had been a distant headline, something that appeared briefly on the evening news, for residents of Toledo in north-west Ohio. But decades of migration to small cities in the American heartland, combined with the war on Gaza and recent rise in settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, are bringing the conflict into the streets and homes of places such as Toledo. Last October, five people were arrested in downtown Toledo for protesting outside the office of Jon Husted, an Ohio Republican senator, who at the time had voted to send aid to Israel. “There’s been demonstrations, petitions and the city council passed a resolution calling for a ceasefire not long after October 7 [2023]. There’s a palpable difference of opinion regarding what Israel is doing and that the US is funding it,” said Mike Ferner, a US navy veteran and one of those arrested in Toledo. Ferner said he began speaking out against America’s support for Israel after the war on Gaza began. “It just comes to a point where you have to ask: is this what I want my country paying for?” Israel’s military assault has largely destroyed the Gaza Strip and killed more than 76,000 people while being condemned by a United Nations body as a genocide. It has prompted Ferner to travel to New York City and organize a 40-day fast in front of the United Nations building last year. “We made our point as best we could that this is something dreadful and the US has got no business participating in it,” he says. Ferner’s position is illustrative of a widening gap between American public opinion and the US government’s support for Israel. While Americans broadly supported Israel in the past, a Pew Research Center poll released in April found that six in 10 participants had an unfavorable view of the country – an increase of 7% in just a year. The reason is partly explained by mounting anger with the actions of pro-Israel groups such as American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), which have spent billions of dollars over a period of decades helping to elect American politicians who are supportive of Israel. This year, many of its high-profile candidates have been defeated in primary elections, despite an outlay of tens of millions of dollars. Arab American communities have grown particularly in the midwest, where job opportunities and a comparatively affordable cost of living have attracted many immigrants to start out. Aside from English and Spanish, Arabic is the most popular primary language spoken in Ohio. Drawn to the region’s growing manufacturing industry in the early 20th century, Toledo once had its own “Little Syria” district, located in the Old North End neighborhood. “Since the late 1800s, people would come here, work at Cooper Tire and then retire back in Lebanon; my great-grandparents did that, everyone did it,” says Nabil Shaheen, who as a child emigrated from Lebanon with his mother, brother and sister in 1979, and also worked in manufacturing. “There are at least 300 families from Sultan Yacub [Shaheen’s village in Lebanon] here. We even have a Sultan Yacub club, which for every occasion we meet there.” Today, he and his family run a sign manufacturing company west of downtown Toledo. “This used to be a church, then it was empty, and we came in. There’s a variety of [Arab American] businesses that are contributing to the city of Toledo,” he says from his office, which has wall-to-wall paraphernalia of the Cincinnati Bengals NFL team. Today, many Arab Americans in the area have moved to suburban Sylvania west of Toledo, where eastern Orthodox churches, a mosque and an Islamic school have opened in recent decades. In these communities, away from the conflict, dialogue between Arab and Jewish Americans has flourished. “As a Jewish community, we believe deeply in the importance of a shared society: one grounded in respect for diversity, the dignity and rights of every individual,” says Roy Büchler of the Jewish Federation of Greater Toledo. “Loui [Ridi] and his brother have built successful businesses, created jobs, paid taxes, supported numerous philanthropic causes, and worked to build bridges among people of different backgrounds throughout our community.” However, the federation declined to comment on the settler violence. Founded in 1999, the Ridi family’s chain of supermarkets, car washes and gas stations stretch out across north-west Ohio, Michigan and Indiana after several of the brothers came to the US to attend university during the 1990s. The company, which employs hundreds of people, forms the cornerstone of Toledo’s bustling Palestinian American community and donates hundreds of thousands of dollars every year to charities and non-profits. Ridi said he typically visits Qusra three times a year, taking his children, but the war on Gaza and violence in the occupied West Bank have made that harder in recent years. Still, he is not without hope for change. “I was so surprised by [US ambassador] Huckabee’s comments, calling the settlers Israeli terrorists,” he said. “Maybe something is changing.”

title: AI is hurting US politics. Here’s how candidates could use it for good
author: Bruce Schneier and Nathan E Sanders
summary: The technology can help candidates listen more deeply to voters, as examples from Japan and Scotland show
body_text: There are plenty of signs that AI will make all of our experiences of the US midterm elections worse. Voters have anxiety about AI’s impacts on the country. Politicos are using AI deepfakes to spread lies. The White House is posting slopaganda. Meanwhile, candidates are missing a real opportunity to use AI to make campaigning better. The technology can help candidates listen more deeply to voters’ concerns, engage constituents more inclusively, and formulate policy platforms that are more responsive to our input. There are vanishingly few examples of this in US politics, but groups in Japan, Scotland and the US’s own academic and private institutions show how that could change. The problem with American campaigns’ current use of AI is that it’s not very different from the web ads of 30 years ago, or television ads before that: they are all about inundating voters with the candidate’s message. This one-to-many broadcasting is an uninspiring way to campaign, but not the only way. AI can help candidates connect one-to-one with as many people as possible. Or it can facilitate many-to-many connections, engaging voters in deliberation about issues at scale. One of the most promising applications of AI being developed by pro-democracy innovators around the world is broad listening. These tools can collect public input in a format much richer than checkboxes on a survey form. For example, the newly founded Japanese political party Team Mirai has built a foundation for eliciting public input from voters at scale, in depth, and across the breadth of legislative policy issues. It has developed an AI interviewer to cultivate constituent input on policy. Through extended conversations with this chatbot, voters explore and share their perspectives on specific policy issues. And the party has scaled this across a wide array of policy issues by integrating this functionality with an AI-powered portal for exploring bills. Team Mirai describes itself as a “utility party”, developing tools for any Japanese political party to use to connect with voters. You might question whether Americans would willingly talk to a political AI. So far, Japanese voters have exchanged more than 300,000 messages across 16,000 AI interviews. Team Mirai grew adoption by providing a real incentive to engage: that talking to their AI interviewer does more than just posting on a platform such as Twitter/X or, equivalently, shouting into a void. Users see evidence that the party is actually listening and might take action on their behalf. Team Mirai party members have directly cited AI interviews from constituents during legislative committee hearings, published a synthesis of that input back for voters, and even amended their policy platform based on user input. The party has rapidly risen to win 12 seats in the Diet, and is explicitly following in the footsteps of the civic hackers in Taiwan’s “gov zero” movement, who won political influence in their fight for transparency. Other civic technologists are developing AI tools for scaling many-to-many conversations. CrownShy, a company funded in part by the Scottish government, is building a platform to bring the Platonic ideal of the town hall debate into the digital age. Their Comhairle tool integrates AI interviewing tools like the ones described above with software for synthesizing diverse viewpoints, holding virtual assemblies, and sharing video testimonials to help legislatures – or campaigners – organize digital consultations of their constituents en masse. One thing the AI-powered software of Team Mirai and CrownShy have in common is that they are open-source, meant for anyone to use. Even though they are projects funded by political parties – the upstart party in Japan and the ruling party in Scotland – they are built to make democratic processes better, not necessarily for partisan political advantage. For interested candidates, there is a wealth of tools available, many of them US-grown. The Stanford-affiliated deliberation.io uses AI to facilitate structured dialogues among thousands of participants and has been piloted for public listening sessions by the city of Washington DC. The MIT-affiliated Cortico project provides tools that surface under-heard community perspectives from recorded conversations, and is now organizing listening sessions at libraries across the country. The US non-profit-built Talk to the City uses AI to analyze large datasets of stakeholder input. The US startup Remesh has a commercial offering that uses AI to generate recommendations from dialogue, which has been tested in policy development scenarios. There is a long and proud tradition of this sort of “civic technology” in the United States. Two decades ago, the spirit of innovation to develop software for better politics and civic engagement was so strong in organizations like Code for America and the Obama 2008 campaign that Congress funded a new executive agency to bring these ideas to government: the US Digital Service. (The Trump administration repurposed the USDS to become the US Doge Service in 2025.) One signal that candidates and political parties may start adopting these kinds of tools came this spring from Higher Ground Labs. The Democratic-aligned campaign tech investment firm launched a new fund targeting, in part, “AI-Native Campaign Systems” and “community-Led Messaging Platforms that surface authentic, bottom-up insights from real conversations”. AI is a multifaceted issue that deserves to be on the table in the midterms. So far, the powerful force of polarization in US politics seems to be separating the parties into the AI skeptics versus the AI boosters. We urge both voters and politicians to separate the technology of AI from its profiteers. We want big tech money out of politics, holding the AI companies accountable for the harm their models cause, taxing their revenues, and maybe even nationalizing them if the AI bubble bursts. But we also think congressional candidates in the US midterms seeking authentic connection with voters, and seeking to differentiate themselves from their opponents, should be looking to use AI responsibly in their campaigning. The broad listening and deliberation tools pioneered by others around the world could make US politics more transparent, responsive and community-driven. The impact of AI on campaigning doesn’t have to be all bad. Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School and the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs & Public Policy Nathan E Sanders is a data scientist affiliated with the Berkman Klein Center of Harvard University and co-author, with Bruce Schneier, of the book Rewiring Democracy: How AI Will Transform Our Politics, Government, and Citizenship • This article was amended on 31 August 2026. An earlier version incorrectly described CrownShy as a non-profit.

title: A pediatrician is running for Senate. Can doctors change the political debate over health and science?
author: Melody Schreiber
summary: After Lindsey Graham’s death, Democrat Annie Andrews finds herself in a closely watched race as she seeks to flip his Republican seat
body_text: Annie Andrews was a dark horse Democrat challenging a five-term Republican in the US Senate when 314 Action, a political action fund devoted to electing scientists and doctors, first backed her. Now, after the unexpected death of Senator Lindsey Graham, Andrews finds herself in a closely watched race. Donald Trump persuaded South Carolina voters last week to select Graham’s sister, Darline, as the new Republican candidate. They will face off in November in an election still heavily favored to keep the seat in Republican hands in the conservative state. Andrews, a pediatrician for 20 years, has made public health and science a central part of her campaign, highlighting the importance of vaccines as measles spread through South Carolina – and so have the other candidates supported by 314 Action. Last year, 314 laid out an ambitious goal: elect at least 100 doctors to state and federal office by 2030. The group had an initial fundraising target of $25m, which it reached in August, to help establish Democratic doctors in state legislatures, governorships, and federal offices – “building that pipeline of talent to higher office”, said Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action. Headlines in 2026 have been dominated by outbreaks of infectious diseases and foodborne illnesses, the biggest cuts to Medicaid in its history, the gutting of scientific research, immigration raids in hospitals, and more, making health and science salient issues in the US midterm elections. Doctors and experts are “on the frontlines of this”, Andrews said. “I don’t think there’s ever been a more important time to elect scientists and medical doctors to all levels of our government.” In the 2018 midterm elections, record numbers of people – nearly 200 – with backgrounds in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (Stem) ran for House and Senate seats. But only about 12% of the candidates won, according to research by Matthew Motta, assistant professor at Boston University’s School of Public Health. “So to say that you want to get 100 physicians to not just run but to actually be elected to public office is quite a tall order,” he said. Endorsement and financial support from 314 Action do increase the likelihood that Stem candidates will win, according to his research. But the goal of 100 wins in the next four years is ambitious, Motta said. In fact, candidates with Stem backgrounds were less likely to win than non-Stem peers in 2018, according to an analysis co-authored by Meredith Conroy, political science professor at California State University, San Bernardino. They probably didn’t lose because of their science background, Conroy said, adding: “I just don’t think it was a salient enough identity at the time to suggest it made or broke their campaign.” But recent events are changing that, making health and science a top-of-mind concern for voters, Conroy and Motta pointed out. “It’s really important then, if we want to defend science from politicized attacks on its daily operation, that those who actually do science and who do medicine are elected to Congress,” Motta said. State-level leadership on health will also be key as national health agencies falter and as states consider restrictive laws on issues like vaccination and reproductive health, Motta said. Josh Green, the governor of Hawaii and an emergency physician, is the only doctor-governor in the United States right now. But he wants to feel less alone. “We want to create a bench of people” who are better-qualified and could be appointed to positions like these, Green said. He is mentoring candidates through 314 on how to engage with constituents and “how to message in a way that political people have to master”. There are 20 physicians in the House and Senate right now, but only six of the House representatives are Democrats, and there are no Democratic doctors in the Senate. Running for office takes deep pockets, which means doctors who are already wealthy – a group that tends to skew conservative – are more likely to be elected. Some of these doctors, like Rand Paul, have contributed to misinformation on vaccines and other health issues. That partisan divide is increasingly evident when it comes to health, Motta noted: “Just because somebody has a scientific background does not necessarily mean that they’re going to fight for science.” Yet electing more physicians could help repair trust in science, Naughton said, as “most people do trust their physicians and they bring a lot of credibility.” Doctor-politicians aren’t just important for opposing harmful laws or misinformation, Naughton added. They also have a fact-based approach to problem solving. Scientists and doctors frequently go into debt for their education, making it difficult for them to leave their fields for politics, Green pointed out. He was only able to do it because he qualified for student loan forgiveness through the National Health Service Corps. “Had I had $300,000 or $400,000 of debt, like a lot of my colleagues from medical school, I could never have run for the state house. There’s no way,” he said. “If we can seed their campaigns with enough money to get off the ground,” Green said of new candidates, “they’ll stand a chance.” When Barbara Bollier, an anesthesiologist and a Republican-turned-Democratic state lawmaker in Kansas, decided to run for the Senate in 2020, she knew the odds were long. Kansas hadn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. Even though Bollier lost that race, she still feels victorious. “I moved the ball down the field,” she said. She received more votes than any Democrat in the history of the state, she said, and when the next big health issue arose in Kansas, the state shocked the country by voting to protect abortion rights. There’s a persistent belief that medicine and science are above politics, Naughton said, pointing out “that approach has failed us … We need folks to go beyond just signing polite letters and waiting to be tapped as scientific advisers, and actually step up and claim the seat at the table.” And the stakes are high: “The hard truth of it is, people are going to die if we don’t follow science,” Green said. Running for office “was not something I ever, in a million years, thought I would be doing with my life”, Andrews said. At the age of four, she told her preschool teacher she would be a doctor one day, and she never wavered from that plan. But “it became clear to me that the most effective and efficient way to solve the problems my patients and their families were facing was through politics, by changing who actually has the power, by electing people who inherently care about America’s children,” she said. It would take decades to counter the misinformation and damage from officials currently in power, Andrews said. But she is in it for the long haul. “I’m just so happy to be a part of this movement of physicians all across the country raising their hands, stepping up to run for office,” she said.

title: James Clyburn says supporting Clarence Thomas for supreme court ‘was mistake’
author: Richard Luscombe
summary: Congressman says Thomas abandoned his principles to become an extremist, hard-right member of bench
body_text: The senior Democratic congressman James Clyburn said his decision to support Clarence Thomas for a US supreme court seat “was a mistake” and called for the expansion of the nation’s highest legal panel to 13 justices. Clyburn, of South Carolina, spoke up for Thomas at his fiery 1991 confirmation hearings, calling him “a personal and professional friend” who would use their shared experiences lifting minorities and advancing civil rights to become a respected and accomplished jurist. Instead, Clyburn told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Thomas abandoned his principles to become an extremist, hard-right member of a bench that has delivered some stunning legal reversals in recent years, including the overturning of federal protections for abortion and ending affirmative action in higher education. Asked by host Kristen Welker if he regretted standing up for Thomas, Clyburn replied: “I have made mistakes in my life, and that’s one that I made. And I will own up to that mistake. “I had no idea that Clarence Thomas would rebel the way he has against his own background and experiences. He was raised by his grandfather, and he has shown very little sensitivity to the environment his grandfather grew up down in Pin Point, Georgia.” Before joining Congress in 1993, Clyburn was South Carolina’s human affairs commissioner for 18 years beginning in 1974. He said Thomas’s tenure as chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission from 1982 until 1990, a time in which it vigorously pursued anti-discrimination legal actions, had assured him that Thomas “believed in precedents, the law”. He told Welker: “I had faith and confidence in the fact that his background and experiences would instruct him in his professionalism, especially sitting on the bench. I thought, sure, that he would be here upholding those precedents set down in 1954 in the Brown v Board of Education decision” that declared racial segregation in public schools was illegal. But Thomas, whose later years on the bench have been mired in allegations of corruption, turned his back on civil rights, Clyburn suggested, notably in the 2024 decision on ideological grounds that ruled affirmative action in college admissions unconstitutional. “That was a mistake on my part,” Clyburn said of his past support for Thomas. “And I own up to it.” Clyburn spoke as the prospect of increasing the number of US supreme court justices, a popular rallying cry for sections of the Democratic party as it attempts to retake the House in November’s midterms, returned to public discourse. Former Democratic vice-president Kamala Harris in July called for the expansion of the bench from nine to 13, a proposal Clyburn said he would support. “Thirteen is a pretty good number,” he said. “A baker’s dozen would be a good number to have on the court. “And I would hope we would get people on the court who will follow the constitutional underpinnings of this great nation of ours. I had hoped that Clarence Thomas would follow the underpinnings of that constitution of ours, but he has not done so. “In fact, he’s decided to go all the way from an angry leftist, to a very angry rightist.” Clyburn, however, said Democrats’ immediate priorities after November should not be either supreme court expansion or impeachment of Donald Trump for what would be a third time across his two presidencies. “If the Democrats were to take back the House, and I feel confident that we will, our first order of business ought to be developing an accessible and affordable campaign effort that will yield what I will call making this country, its greatness, accessible and affordable for all of its citizens,” he said.

title: Trump attacks datacenter backlash, claiming communities pushing back risk becoming ‘backwards and poor’
author: Maya Yang
summary: Three-quarters of Americans said in a recent poll that they oppose datacenters being built next to their homes
body_text: Donald Trump has criticized communities pushing back against datacenter projects across the US amid a growing backlash, warning those that reject them risk becoming “backwards and poor”. As controversy surrounding local datacenter plans continues to swirl around election campaigns nationwide ahead of November’s midterm elections, the US president declared Americans “will only have yourselves to blame” if they are canceled. Bipartisan opposition to datacenter expansion has intensified across the US, particularly in states with ample land, low-cost power and generous tax incentives, as local communities raise concerns over environmental impacts, soaring utility costs and noise pollution. According to a recent poll, three-quarters of Americans said they would oppose a datacenter being built next to their homes, while more than six in 10 Americans said they would strongly oppose such a proposal. In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump wrote: “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign. “The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame. China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement. Actually, they can’t believe it is happening!” Responding to Trump’s statement on Monday, JD Vance told reporters that datacenters were an “important part of the AI economy”, adding: “When people build them, they have to build the power plants along with the datacenters. I think probably 99% of the backlash to datacenters has come in areas where building a datacenter means higher utility and higher electricity for the people on the ground. “I think what these companies have to do is take advantage of some of the federal deregulatory efforts that we’ve undertaken,” the US vice-president added. “If you build a datacenter, you should be putting power back into the grid, not taking it out. And if that is happening, I don’t think the datacenters are that controversial. It’s when the utility bills get so much higher that’s when it’s a real problem.” However, several users replied to Trump’s post on his own Truth Social platform, voicing their concerns about datacenters. “Mr. President: Think about farm land and about water resources, and a man as intelligent as you will see that the absolute position you are taking is flawed,” one user wrote. “What use is being rich if you cannot get access to water and food?” As opposition to datacenters grows, the research group Data Center Watch found that grassroots groups blocked or delayed at least 75 datacenter projects worth approximately $130bn in the first three months of 2026. Monterey Park, a small city east of Los Angeles, is among the local communities that have pushed back against datacenters and won. Other communities successful in their resistance include Prince William county, Virginia, as well as Wake county, North Carolina. Environmental groups have also weighed in, with a coalition of more than 230 organizations urging members of Congress last year to halt the development of new datacenters amid the climate crisis, worsening droughts in already water-stressed areas, and rising electricity bills.

title: Congressional nominee Brad Lander heckled over Israel stance at New York protest
author: Lucy Campbell
summary: Lander screamed at and verbally abused as he protested against Hindu nationalist rally in Madison Square Garden
body_text: The New York Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander was screamed at and verbally abused by protesters over his stance on Israel as he protested against a Hindu nationalist politician speaking outside Madison Square Garden. As Lander attended a demonstration on Saturday against the event, organized by the Hindu nationalist RSS movement and where Mohan Bhagwat, leader of Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh was speaking, he was confronted by several protesters demanding that he leave the rally. “We don’t want no Zionists here. Get the fuck out!” one man yelled at Lander in a video circulating online. “You say you’re a liberal but we know how you act.” Another shouted: “You’re a Zionist, we don’t need you. We don’t need your help!” Other protesters welcomed Lander’s presence at the event and defended him against the heckling. “Thank you for coming, thank you for standing in solidarity with us,” one man told Lander, shaking his hand. Lander, who is Jewish and an outspoken critic of the Israeli government, describes himself as a liberal Zionist – stating that he believes in the vision of Israel as a safe, Jewish home, but argues that it cannot ever be a true democracy while it continues to occupy Palestinian land and deny Palestinians their human rights and freedom. He condemns Israel’s continued occupation of the West Bank and Gaza, supported the restriction of US military aid to Israel, and believes that Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks amounts to genocide. An ally of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and a former comptroller for the city, Lander is the progressive candidate for the US House of Representatives New York’s 10th congressional district. His critical approach to Israel was a key factor in his thumping primary victory in June against fellow Jew and Zionist Dan Goldman, a prominent supporter of Israel. Lander appeared undeterred by the abuse and determined to remain at the rally, to which he had been invited, on Saturday. In one exchange, he calmly responded, “Bring it on,” when a protester wearing a face mask and sunglasses shouted in his face that he was a “Zionist ball sack”. Addressing the incident in a video message on X on Monday, Lander said: “The event was dedicated to standing up against the persecution of religious minorities in India. I was honored to be invited and glad to participate. “I won’t stop joining rallies against hate – in India, in Israel and Palestine, or in New York City – because of a couple of loud numbskulls.” Lander went on: “I was proud to attend. As a Jewish New Yorker, I protest when I believe people are perverting Judaism to justify ethnic cleansing and exclusion, and I feel solidarity for Muslims who are doing the same.” He reiterated his critical stance on Israel’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon, and noted that he gets “criticized frequently by centrist and rightwing Jews. And as someone who nonetheless believes in the vision and the possibility of a Jewish and democratic Israel, alongside a free Palestine, once decades of occupation and apartheid end, I get criticized by leftwingers who oppose Zionism.” He stressed the importance of people coming together, even when they don’t always agree on everything. “A few loud numbskulls must not deter us from building multi-faith, multi-racial coalitions for justice,” he said. He also thanked the Hindu and Muslim groups that had leapt to his defense on Sunday. The Indian American Muslim Council said on X: “The individuals responsible were not part of IAMC or our coalition and did not speak for us. Our fight … requires building strong coalitions, respecting differences, and working together wherever we share common ground. Insulting or silencing allies undermines that work and is unacceptable. We offer Brad Lander our sincere apologies for the treatment he received.” Hindus for Human Rights said on X: “Brad Lander is a Jewish leader who has vocally disavowed the genocide in Palestine and is a rare progressive voice against the RSS. Multiple organizations invited Brad to the protest as a longtime ally who understands the majority’s role in combating hate in their communities.” The confrontations Lander experienced are telling of tensions within the United States over Israel. Public opinion in the US has shifted against the country over its actions in Gaza in a historic way, while a wave of progressive candidates have swept to victory amid pro-Palestinian sentiment and criticism of the Israeli government. The incident has also tapped into an aspect of the debate where the lines between anti-Zionism and antisemitism are often blurred, with some commentary on social media suggesting that people hurled abuse at Lander because he is Jewish. But in a video shared on Substack, the liberal commentator Peter Beinart argued that the people harassing Lander “are rude, obnoxious, self-righteous, they’re really kind of acting like assholes. But they’re not saying anything antisemitic.” Highlighting that the protesters explicitly took issue with Lander’s self-declared Zionism, not his Jewishness, Beinart added: “The term antisemite should be reserved for clear cases in which people have an animus towards Jews as Jews.”
