title: Kalshi bans ex-congressman George Santos from prediction platform for life
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Santos was accused of profiting from bets tied to his attendance at Trump’s State of the Union address
body_text: George Santos, the former Republican congressman whose political career collapsed under a mountain of lies, has become the first person ever handed a lifetime ban by the prediction-market platform Kalshi. The company announced the permanent suspension on Monday, along with a $71,356 fine, after federal regulators accused Santos of profiting from bets tied to his own attendance at Donald Trump’s State of the Union address earlier this year. A Kalshi spokeswoman said Santos’s refusal to cooperate fully with the platform’s internal investigation was what pushed the penalty from temporary to permanent. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) alleges that Santos exploited stormy weather forecasts that threatened to disrupt his travel to Washington in February. According to the agency, he bought Kalshi contracts betting he would miss the speech, then posted social media updates suggesting he planned to attend after all, driving up the value of contracts he held on the opposite outcome and allowing him to cash out at a profit. Regulators concluded he had improperly traded on an event whose outcome he had some power to influence himself. Santos responded on X, thanking Kalshi for the ban. “Let’s see how much longer you guys are around for,” he said. Santos was expelled from the House in December 2023 after the ethics committee found substantial evidence he had defrauded donors, lied about his finances and fabricated much of his biography. He later pleaded guilty to federal wire fraud and identity theft charges and was sentenced to more than seven years in prison, serving less than three months before Trump commuted the sentence. Santos agreed in July to pay more than $35,000 to settle the CFTC’s case, without admitting wrongdoing, according to his attorney. That settlement also barred him from trading on any platform for three years, a far lighter penalty than the lifetime ban Kalshi has now added on top. The disgraced representative was not the only person disciplined by Kalshi on Monday. Laurie Buckhout, a Trump-endorsed Republican congressional candidate in North Carolina, was banned for three years and fined $2,590 after wagering under $1,000 on her own campaign, calling it a mistake she moved to fix as soon as she noticed it. The former Planet Fitness president Ben Midgley was banned for three years and fined $5,434.30 over bets on his unsuccessful bid in Maine’s Republican gubernatorial primary, and Diamond Resorts founder Stephen Cloobeck received a three-year ban and roughly $31,770 fine for wagering around $10,000 on his own abandoned run for California governor. The action follows a separate CFTC penalty last week against Gabriel Perez, a White House teleprompter operator accused of trading on inside information, who agreed to pay $65,000 and forfeit more than $107,000 in winnings. The ban arrives as Santos has been working to rebuild his public profile and finances. He is set to appear this month on the latest season of Fox’s endurance competition “Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test”, and has been supplementing his income through paid video shout-outs on Cameo, whose price has reportedly dropped from $300 to $100 as he works to pay down campaign debts once estimated above $800,000. He has said he does not plan to seek public office again for at least a decade.

title: US military has no plans to send troops to midterm polling sites, Dan Caine says
author: Shrai Popat and agencies
summary: Letter from chair of joint chiefs of staff addresses concerns over Trump officials using military to interfere with vote
body_text: The highest‑ranking US military officer says there are no plans to deploy troops to polling places during the November midterm elections – responding to Senator Elissa Slotkin’s request for information amid concerns about whether the Trump administration might send service members to election sites. In a letter obtained by the Guardian, first reported by the Associated Press, Gen Dan Caine, chair of the joint chiefs of staff, told Slotkin “the Joint Force has no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections”. He added that there were also “no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election‑related material”. Slotkin – a Democrat who serves on the Senate armed services and homeland security committees – sought confirmation from Caine and the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, after Donald Trump urged Republicans to “nationalize” elections and said he had not ruled out sending guard members or immigration enforcement agents to the polls. In his letter, Caine added: “I have neither received nor anticipate receiving any unlawful order concerning the role of the Joint Force in the upcoming November 2026 midterm elections.” Slotkin’s office had not yet received a reply from Hegseth, said Sonja Thrasher, her press secretary. The senator had asked both men to respond by 28 August. Anxiety among Democrats that the Trump administration could try to meddle in the midterm elections has grown, particularly after the president deployed federal agents in Democratic-led states over the objections of local leaders. Slotkin told the AP earlier in August that Trump had been laying the groundwork to claim the elections were stolen. She noted that Trump contemplated using the military to seize voting machines after his loss in 2020 and had deployed the national guard to cities against the wishes of Democratic leaders. He also deployed active-duty marines to Los Angeles during his immigration crackdown in 2025. Federal law prohibits the deployment of armed federal forces to election locations unless “necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States”. If any element of the military were to get involved, it would probably be the national guard under state control. Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, denied in a Vanity Fair interview last year that Trump would use the military to suppress voting in the midterms. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to an email from the Guardian asking for the status of Hegseth’s response to Slotkin. Slotkin asked Hegseth during an April congressional hearing if he would follow orders to seize ballots. Hegseth called the question a “gotcha hypothetical”, but said: “I’ve never been ordered to do anything illegal, and I won’t.” In 2020, Gen Mark Milley, then chair of the joint chiefs of staff, responded to a similar letter from Slotkin, a congresswoman at the time. “I believe deeply in the principle of an apolitical U.S. military,” Milley wrote. “In the event of a dispute over some aspect of the elections, by law U.S. courts and the U.S. Congress are required to resolve any disputes, not the U.S. military.”

title: US supreme court allows Trump to keep building $400m White House ballroom
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Justices’ 5-4 ruling permits Trump administration appeal to block lower court order halting above-ground work
body_text: A divided US supreme court has permitted Donald Trump to continue building his controversial $400m White House ballroom despite legal challenges, raising the likelihood it will be completed. In a 5-4 ruling, the justices permitted the Trump administration’s request to ⁠block a lower court order that had halted above-ground construction of the project while a lawsuit by a historic preservation group seeks to block it. The US president, who demolished the historic East Wing of the White House last year to make way for planned ballroom, has repeatedly touted it as “a gift” to the US people. Monday’s decision from the supreme court comes after the court’s conservative chief justice, John Roberts, issued a temporary order that had enabled work to continue. However, Roberts joined the court’s three liberal justices in dissenting from the majority’s decision and wrote that the construction was “likely unlawful”. The court’s decision may allow Trump to bring to fruition a project that is at the center of his ambition to remake the US capital in his image. Since taking office, he has ordered the National Mall’s reflecting pool covered in blue liner, proposed a $250m renovation to the Kennedy Center performing arts center that would see his name emblazoned on its side, and is pursuing plans to renovate a golf course and build a massive arch. While some projects have hit legal roadblocks, such as when a judge ordered Trump’s name removed from the Kennedy Center, or descended into farce, like when the reflecting pool line began falling off, the supreme court’s decision today is a victory for the president. Trump celebrated Monday’s ruling in a post on Truth Social, boasting that the White House complex would be “one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington DC”, with construction to be completed by the summer of 2028. In an unsigned opinion, the five conservative justices said the National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States lacked standing to bring a lawsuit against the project. The trust had centered its argument on the declaration of a board member, the architectural historian Alison Hoagland, who said the ballroom was an “aesthetic, cultural and historical” affront because of its design, and that she would suffer “injuries” when viewing it in Washington DC. “The government is likely to prevail in showing that the Trust lacks standing to challenge the East Wing project,” the majority opinion read. “This court has not found standing in circumstances like these before. To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury.” The justices also agreed that the government would suffer “irreparable harm” if construction is stopped, or only allowed to continue on a military installation set to be built underneath the ballroom while the above-ground portion remains unfinished. The majority ultimately side stepped the question of whether the president’s decision to tear down a chunk of a building that rotates between presidential officeholders was actually legal. “Today, we do not pass upon the legality of the government’s East Wing project,” they wrote. The dissenting justices – Roberts, together with Democratic-appointed justices Elena Kagan, Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson – argued that the project is unlawful because Congress has not approved it. In his opinion, Roberts wrote that the construction is a “likely infringement of the legislature’s power of the purse and authority to regulate federal property in the District of Columbia to continue”, and says the majority’s ruling “is no victory for the separation of powers”. “The ballroom is a building or structure being erected on federal park grounds – President’s Park – in the District of Columbia. Yet Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’ for the executive’s construction of it,” the chief writes. He also disagreed that the potential injuries to Hoagland are insufficient for the historic trust to sue, saying she was “deeply committed to the preservation of such historic American buildings” through her work with the association. “Hoagland’s injury suffices for standing,” Roberts wrote, likening the impact of the White House’s transformation on her to how “an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys”.

title: US army secretary Dan Driscoll resigns over reported friction with Pete Hegseth
author: Guardian staff and agencies
summary: Resignation comes after months of turmoil at Pentagon, from leaked investigation to ousting of senior officials
body_text: The army secretary, Dan Driscoll, has handed his resignation to Donald Trump, the White House said on Monday, becoming the latest high-profile figure to depart the defense department. The army official, who is second in line to the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, had reportedly been eyeing an exit from the Pentagon amid apparent friction with the secretary. “Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” a White House spokesperson, Anna Kelly, said in a statement to the Associated Press. “The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added. The news was first reported by the Wall Street Journal. The resignation comes after months of turmoil at the defense department, which has seen numerous incidents, from leak investigations and budget issues to the ousting of several senior officials including the army chief of staff, Randy George, in April. In June, the army’s commander of its forces in Europe and Africa, Gen Christopher Donahue, unexpectedly stepped down. Driscoll was a George ally, and lamented his departure, as did Republican and Democratic lawmakers. Driscoll told Congress in April that he and his family drove to George’s house following his resignation “and we all gave him a hug”. “That being said, the civilian leadership, the design of our system, is that they get to pick the leaders that they want,” Driscoll added. Driscoll is an Iraq war veteran, tech investor and former adviser to JD Vance, whom Driscoll met at Yale law school. When nominating Driscoll in 2024, Trump called him “a disruptor and change agent”. As army secretary, Driscoll was tapped for the unusual role of key negotiator to try to end the war between Russia and Ukraine. He was also a major force behind trying to cut the red tape for military contractors to quickly develop more drones and counter-drone capabilities as warfare rapidly changes around the world. The Senate confirmed him in February 2025, voting 66-28, following an armed services committee hearing that was largely non-confrontational and focused on how the army could modernize its systems, improve recruiting and beef up the military industrial base.

title: Afternoon Update: Australian missing in Nepal-Tibet floods found alive; Ray Hadley takes stand at Alan Jones trial; and the Kākāpō bounces back
author: Miles Herbert
summary: Foreign minister ‘incredibly thankful’ another Australian has been found and says they have spoken with their family
body_text: Good afternoon. An Australian believed to be missing after floods ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border last week has been found alive. The person made contact with officials from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) on Tuesday from Tibet. “We’re incredibly thankful another Australian, who had been unaccounted for, has now been found,” the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said. They are receiving support from Australian consular officers and have spoken with their family. This brings down the number of Australians missing in the flash floods from 43 to 42 and comes after another Australian, 25-year-old Cara Severino, was safely located on the weekend. title: Trump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland Islands
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: Comments signal president prepared to use dispute to push UK to raise defence spending and Nato contributions
body_text: Donald Trump has suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, in a move likely to strain the “special relationship” between Washington and London. “I always review every position – that’s just one of many,” the US president told reporters in the White House, in response to a question about whether he was reviewing the US’s position over the South Atlantic islands, an archipelago whose status has long been disputed by Argentina, which claims sovereignty. Officially, the US takes a neutral position on who has rightful sovereignty over the islands, which Britain first claimed in the late 17th century and has held almost continually since 1833. In practice, it recognizes British administration over the territory, which was the subject of an Argentinian invasion and subsequent military conflict with Britain in 1982. Trump’s remarks were the clearest sign yet that the administration is prepared to use the dispute as leverage to pressure the government of the new British prime minister, Andy Burnham, to raise defence spending and contributions to Nato. A spokesperson for Burnham said on Tuesday that the UK’s position on the Falkands was “crystal clear”. “The Falkland islanders are British with a right to determine their own future. The islanders have expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory, and our commitment to them is unwavering,” he said. “The prime minister was clear on his first day in office that we’ll meet our international commitments to our allies on defence spending, and he hasn’t wavered from that.” Trump’s comments came after an unnamed US official told the Telegraph last week that Washington could change its position over the islands if Britain failed to meet its defence spending commitments. That followed reports that John Healey, the UK chancellor, was preparing to drop Britain’s prior commitment to devote 3% of its GDP to defence spending by 2030 when he delivers his first budget on 28 October. Trump has made a priority of pressuring the US’s allies into boosting defence budgets and raising their Nato contributions during both his presidencies, accusing other countries of “freeloading”. At a summit in The Hague last year, allies committed to spending 5% of GDP on defence and security-related expenditures by 2035. Speculation about a US switch of allegiance over the islands has been swirling for months. In April, a leaked Pentagon email suggested reviewing Britain’s claim in response to its lack of support for Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. A switch of US position would represent a psychological blow to Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands. After Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, the decision by Margaret Thatcher’s government to dispatch a naval taskforce that eventually resulted in their recovery was bolstered by staunch diplomatic support from Ronald Reagan, who came down on Britain’s side, even though Washington was also an ally of the Argentinian ruling military junta. A total of 649 Argentinian and 255 British personnel died in fighting before Argentina’s forces surrendered in June 1982. The episode played a central role in cementing the bond between Thatcher and Reagan, who were political allies and ideological kindred spirits. In recent times, Trump has become close to Argentina’s populist president, Javier Milei, who attended his second inauguration in January last year. Last year, Trump authorized a $20bn financial lifeline to Argentina to help it navigate a financial crisis, but made the funds contingent on Milei’s party winning subsequent congressional elections. Milei’s La Libertad Avanza party duly won the election, confounding pollsters’ forecasts. Trump later authorized the importation of Argentinian beef in an effort to reduce US grocery prices. Milei has vocally supported Argentina’s claim to the islands. In a 2013 poll, 1,513 out of 1,517 Falklands residents who cast a ballot said they wanted the territory remain a part of the UK. Feelings over the islands surfaced after Argentina’s 2-1 victory over England in the semi-final of the World Cup in July, when celebrating Argentinian players unfurled a banner reading “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” – the Falklands are Argentinian. The Argentinian football association was subsequently fined $235,000 by Fifa for violating its rules on non-sporting demonstrations.

title: Nepal’s glacial collapse foreshadowed a future of climate disaster
author: Michael Mann
summary: The deluge capped a summer of extreme climate events, from deadly heatwaves to wildfires. We must take action now
body_text: For millennia, the high peaks of the Himalayas were held together by an invisible, frozen cement – permafrost and glacial ice that bound ancient rock into seemingly unshakable fortresses. But as the planet continues to warm, this alpine glue is liquefying. The glacial collapse and deluge in Nepal and Tibet was not a freak weather event; it was the structural failure of a mountain itself, nature’s latest commentary on the deadly consequences of human-caused planetary warming. And it was the exclamation point on a summer of extremes, illustrating with a sole unnatural disaster the apocalyptic future that lies in store if we fail to take dramatic climate action. As the death toll continues to mount – the latest count showed more than 900 dead and more than 4,400 individuals missing – this event has crystalized the climate crisis for many. One reason is undoubtedly the sheer horror of what unfolded here. Chilling surveillance and eyewitness footage captured the horrific moment a 40mph wall of “liquid concrete” violently overtook fleeing crowds, instantly swallowing entire families and burying them beneath feet of thick, red-soaked silt. Another reason, however, is that the connection with climate change was unassailable in this case. The torrent was the direct result of warming-induced glacial collapse, which dumped millions of tons of rock, unleashing a high-velocity wave of mud and debris. The new reality in the era of human-caused climate change, a CNN headline put it, is that “living downstream from a glacier has become a deadly liability”. The impact of climate change on extreme weather, by contrast, is usually established though a statistical, rather than direct causal, connection. Through what is known as attribution science, climate scientists demonstrate the influence of climate change on the characteristics of an extreme weather event. It is analogous to how epidemiologists establish a linkage between cause (eg smoking cigarettes) and effect (lung cancer), through massive statistical evidence. In the case of climate attribution, scientists run parallel climate model simulations, including a “control” simulation that represents a counterfactual world without human impact, and a “treatment” simulation where human drivers – primarily the increase in greenhouse gas concentrations – are included. They then compare how often a particular event happens in the two cases. If there is a substantial increase in occurrence of a particular event in the “treatment” simulation relative to the “control” simulation, then the extremeness of the event – and its human, societal or environmental impacts – can be “attributed” to climate change. Critics might say that the connection here is merely statistical – almost circumstantial. But much as we are willing to attribute causality when a lifetime smoker contracts lung cancer because they were as much as 30 times more likely to do so because of their use of tobacco products, the extreme characteristics (unusually massive precipitation totals, high temperatures or destructive winds) of the weather event can be attributed to human-caused warming. While the tragic and deadly Tibetan flood might have been the most prominent climate change-induced disaster this summer, it followed an unprecedented series of deadly, destructive and dangerous extreme weather events that can be connected to rising carbon pollution and the warming of our planet. This summer of extremes began early. It started out with a March “heat dome” in the south-western US that yielded extremes of heat we only expect to see in mid-summer. The unprecedented extreme March heat was found by climate scientists to have been “virtually impossible” in the absence of human-caused warming. Then came a midsummer-like May heat dome in the eastern US that smashed temperature records in my home city of Philadelphia. And within weeks, a European heat dome brought deadly triple-digit temperatures to large parts of France leading to the deaths of more than 3,000 people in Paris and nearly 6,000 for all of France. That was just the first of four record-breaking, back-to-back heatwaves in Europe that, by summer’s end, has cost the lives of more than 35,000 people. And yes, the deadly heat was attributed to climate change. The record July heat combined with extreme dryness over large parts of western Europe – particularly France and Spain – to generate catastrophic wildfires that dominated the headlines for weeks, along with a viral photo of vacationers calmly lounging under a colorful umbrella while apocalyptic wildfire smoke billows in the background. The fires forced the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people from their homes. And at the risk of sounding like a broken record: yes, it was formally attributed to human-caused warming. Back in the US, we had our own wildfire problems. A combination of very hot and dry conditions over southern Ontario and the upper midwest led to huge wildfires generating plumes of smoke that choked the east coast for weeks. Air quality was rated hazardous in my home city of Philadelphia. And yes, these wildfires – and indeed, the Canadian wildfires we now see summer after summer – can be attributed to climate change. The summer of extreme weather disasters wasn’t done with us yet. In mid-August a historic “derecho” (a very wide, fast-moving line of severe thunderstorms associated typically with destructive, hurricane-strength straight-line destructive winds) struck the midwestern US with winds exceeding 100mph and devastating flooding, the better part of a million people from Illinois to Virginia were left without power. While it is a challenge to apply attribution methods to these rare events, there is emerging evidence that climate change is making them more frequent and more damaging. This past summer’s collective extreme weather disasters were an unmistakable consequence of the continued warming of our planet. The current administration’s policies – which were written by polluters themselves – are making things worse. Donald Trump and enabling congressional Republicans continue to double down on policies favoring fossil fuel extraction and dependence at the very time we need to be moving even more quickly away from fossil fuels toward clean energy. These extreme events underscore the urgency of taking action now, and – while there are many things we can do – one of the greatest opportunities Americans will have to affect climate policy is the upcoming midterm election. You can make support for urgent and dramatic climate action a litmus test issue as you go to the voting booth. Michael Mann is presidential distinguished professor and director of the Penn Center for Science, Sustainability and the Media at the University of Pennsylvania, and co-author with Peter Hotez, of the recent book Science Under Siege

title: Life after Maga: the group offering an ‘exit ramp’ for rightwingers questioning Trumpism
author: Fabiola Cineas
summary: The non-profit Leaving Maga is built on the premise that abandoning the Trump-built movement is like fighting a disease or breaking an addiction
body_text: Stephania Messina kept birthing boys. In the Quiverfull conservative Christian church she belonged to outside Detroit, Michigan, that made her a community celebrity. Your quiver, as the church taught it, is your womb, meant to be filled with as many arrows – a metaphor for children – as you can shoot unto the Lord. She shot five. “They treated me like I was Mother Mary, like I was this gift to the church,” she said. But while she was quickly pushed into leading worship and Bible study groups for women and children, she wasn’t permitted to talk about politics. “It wasn’t my job to vote or to know who to vote for. I was just supposed to submit to my husband and do what he thought was necessary,” Messina said. “I was being indoctrinated into Christian nationalism.” Messina quit her job, yielded to household voting, and took on home schooling and homesteading in a farmhouse, as part of an early 2010s precursor to the “Make America healthy again” (Maha) movement. When Donald Trump launched his first presidential campaign, he was suddenly “God’s chosen one” in the church, she said. Though Messina was never a “red-hat wearing” Maga supporter, she didn’t start questioning the movement until the early days of the Covid pandemic. Trained as a respiratory therapist, she watched Trump reverse course daily – from claiming the Covid vaccine was good to questioning its effectiveness. Meanwhile, her pastor preached that Covid lockdowns were a “demonic deep-state attempt to keep people out of church”. After a few other instances left her with doubts, she expanded her news sources beyond the church’s approved media, and then, she said: “The dam broke.” She sought mental health support and began to understand her years inside Maga as what she calls “a religious psychosis” built on fear, isolation and control. When she finally turned away from the church in 2021, she was cast as an outsider but felt the need to proclaim her Maga exit on social media: “I started speaking out to spread awareness. I was in so deep.” She felt alone. A few years later, she connected with the group Leaving Maga. “Leaving Maga is about normalizing leaving,” said Messina. “And it’s especially important now, since I think the Maga [bubble] is bursting.” Many Americans, like Messina, have drifted away from Trump in the past decade, but have done so quietly. Leaving Maga offers an exit ramp from Trump’s rightwing movement that has reshaped the Republican party and platformed political extremism. Launched in 2024, the movement turned non-profit is built on the premise that abandoning the Maga identity – and the community surrounding it – functions less like changing one’s mind and more like leaving a high-control religious group, fighting a disease or breaking an addiction. It requires not just rejecting a set of beliefs but rebuilding an entire structure of belonging and identity. Leaving Maga has touched thousands, operating on multiple fronts: weekly support meetings for the friends and family of people still inside Maga, monthly in-person meet-ups for those who have already left, a nationwide billboard campaign built around invitation rather than confrontation and a budding media literacy program meant to help people recognize disinformation. The goal isn’t to start or win a debate – it’s to give people somewhere to land once they’re ready to leave on their own. “There are more people than ever who are in Maga who are starting to have doubts and confusion,” said Rich Logis, who founded the group. “We’re trying to counter the toxicity of the Maga community by providing an exit ramp and a community where people can become what I call ‘a born-again human being’ and can reclaim their individuality, their empathy and their agency.” How Leaving Maga works Logis was drawn to Trump’s “burn it all down” energy in 2016, voting for him that year and in 2020. He spent nearly a decade as one of Maga’s most committed foot soldiers, writing part of the campaign’s call script for the first presidential election, helping register new voters for Trump, donating money and appearing on Fox News as a Maga pundit. But his decisive break from the movement came after the Uvalde school shooting in 2022 – he could no longer square his own values with the response he knew was coming from Trump supporters. Months after the Texas shooting that claimed the lives of 19 children and two teachers, Logis published a public apology online for supporting Trump and hurting people with his actions and rhetoric. The response was overwhelming – people commended him and criticized him – leading him to start the movement. He figured others had also left Maga and wanted to repair the damage they caused. “I had to go through a reckoning and acknowledge to myself that I had been culpable and complicit in assisting the president in dividing our country and amplifying conspiracy theories that resulted in unnecessary death, suffering and trauma,” Logis said. He built Leaving Maga the way he poured into Maga years prior – by writing countless online posts, speaking out on social media and reaching out to others. On any given day, Logis is on Instagram Live explaining how and why he left and how others can do the same. Maga leaders have defined the movement as one that calls for economic nationalism, secure borders, “America first” foreign policy and traditional conservative values, said Laura K Field, a political theorist and author of the book Furious Minds: The Making of the Maga New Right. “But an element of Maga that gets underestimated is its community-building dimension,” she said. “There’s a kind of appeal – a fascist and contrarian element, a deep religiosity to it – that unifies different parts of Maga, including the ordinary voters who aren’t DC beltway types, the elites, the high-powered Catholic intellectuals, or those in the manosphere, for example.” Logis was one of those people who saw Maga as a community more than a political ideology. “I think that it’s where people find vindication and validation,” he said. “It’s where they feel seen and heard and respected and appreciated.” But the glue holding the community together was “lies and falsehoods” and an “addiction to fear and rage” fueled by misinformation and disinformation, he said. “[In Maga], I had a dangerous belief in a ‘they’. A ‘they’ who were trying to abridge my rights and indoctrinate my children and take my guns and replace white people with brown people and foreigners.” Logis argues that leaving Maga requires more than distancing yourself from the president; you have to actively renounce Maga’s underlying conspiracy theories and also commit to building democracy that understands “we as Americans agree on important issues more than we disagree.” Logis and Messina describe leaving as a project of rebuilding empathy that Maga has deliberately suppressed. “As I began to listen to the people I had been told not to – the feminists, the people who they called ‘race baiters’, trans creators – my empathy came back,” Messina said. Logis put it similarly: leaving means you “no longer need to dehumanize and vilify and demonize those with whom we once disagreed”. They also don’t try to change the minds of Maga supporters. The idea is to let those who are already questioning it know there is support on the other side. “It is my philosophy that I do not engage in debates with people who are in Maga,” Logis said. “I don’t try to bombard and inundate people with facts and with policy.” Instead, he and other representatives for the organization spread the word through Instagram live streams and TikToks that receive thousands of likes. They go on cable news programs to speak out against the movement that once dominated their lives. One of the most effective methods is billboarding. Nearly 40 billboards have gone up in 27 states this year, with a simple message: “Having doubts? You’re not alone.” Logis said more than half a million visited the group’s website last year, and just as many have visited so far this year. Through the website, people can sign up for a newsletter that shares testimonies about people’s journeys out of Maga, access a guide on how to talk to family members and friends still engaged in Trumpism and join online group chats and monthly meet-ups with others who have left. Carter Brown, a former self-proclaimed tradwife who voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024, said Leaving Maga had helped her realize she needed to do more than just speak out online after leaving; she needed to help rebuild. “It has taken deconstructing my religion and the dogma of western theology and realizing that I wasn’t even living like Jesus,” Brown said. She has changed her views on women’s rights, LGBTQ+ rights, capitalism and immigration. Brown said she now votes according to her new beliefs, volunteers with groups she harmed with her votes and has conversations with people she harmed. She also seeks friendship with people who have different lived experiences than her own. Leaving Maga is growing, Logis said, as polls show Trump’s increasing unpopularity. In recent months, Logis has spoken with people who left after being fired during “department of government efficiency” (Doge) cuts. Others have been turned off by Trump’s broken promises on foreign policy and rising costs. Messina said the people she had met in Leaving Maga came from all kinds of backgrounds. “We got into Maga for different reasons and got out for different reasons,” said Messina. “This is a space to learn other people’s stories and reckon with our own. Though the right knew how to capture us in its algorithms, I feel like the tide is turning.” How the group supports friends and family of Maga supporters Leaving Maga’s weekly online support group isn’t for people in Maga – it’s for the people who love them. That includes spouses, adult children, parents, siblings, friends and extended family who have watched someone close to them become “not the person who they once were”, said facilitator Julianna Forlano. Forlano, a therapist, has worked with families of people with narcissistic personality disorder and in addiction recovery, and said the ruptures she sees every week aren’t really about ideology. “What’s happening in families and in marriages, and between mothers and daughters and fathers and sons has to do with behavior,” she said. Forlano and her group borrow a framework used in addiction and recovery circles, treating the psychological grip of constant fear-based media and conspiracies like a disease. The mechanism is neurobiological, she said: people who consume a steady diet of fear narratives become fearful in general, adopt a “with us or against us” mentality and start treating loved ones as threats. “The mind is functioning as a dopamine seeker,” she said, craving the next piece of alarming news the way an addicted brain craves its next hit. Forlano is careful to note that holding certain political beliefs doesn’t make someone diseased; the compulsive, threat-seeking pattern layered on top of those beliefs is what the group tries to address. The stories members share reflect how the rupture disrupts daily life. One member married into a Latino family with her parents’ blessing, only to watch those same parents tell guests to “speak English” at her child’s birthday party and use slurs about mixed-race people; she has since decided her parents can no longer be part of their lives. Forlano said even conversations that start out ordinary can snap into political conflict without warning. “You could say something as simple as: ‘The tomatoes in my garden aren’t growing,’ and that person will respond by saying: ‘Well, climate change is a hoax,’” she said. Instead of encouraging members to cut ties, or to keep engaging in the kind of fact-based debate Forlano believes is useless, the group teaches patience and creates a space for members to see they aren’t alone. Members are coached to “hold the door open”, staying present in case a loved one ever starts to notice cracks in what they have been told, without continuing to push, argue or send articles that only further entrench the divide. The first step, Forlano said, was admitting that everything they have already tried hasn’t worked and to stop warring. Conflict often de-escalates once one party stops pushing back, she said. From there, the work isn’t about holding out hope that loved ones will turn on Trump and the movement he built; it’s about grief – mourning the relationship as it was, finding solidarity with others living through the same struggle and rebuilding a sense of self. Members stay in touch through group chats between sessions, trading techniques and support in real time. “The supportive nature of the community has been healing,” Forlano said. “It helps people find their footing again.” What life after Maga looks like Coming out on “the other side” is different for each person leaving Maga. Logis now supports Democrats. Messina has gone further. “I consider myself a democratic socialist now 100%,” she said. “I’m a member of the DSA. So is my son.” She has become an outspoken supporter of Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan, and describes watching her husband and her 20-year-old son’s friend group all turn decisively against Trump within the past two years. But that doesn’t mean everyone in her family has left Maga. Her mother, 64, voted for Trump twice and still struggles to fully let go of messaging that casts Democrats as enemies. However, Messina has slowly had influence. She has talked to her mom about misogyny, intersectionality and the privilege that white women in Maga wield. “Now we’re working on Islamophobia because she can’t say Abdul El-Sayed without cringing because of these deeply ingrained biases,” Messina said. Their arguments used to end in screaming matches, but Messina has learned, slowly, not to cut her mother off. “Cutting them off completely just furthers the divides,” she said. The group continues to grapple with questions about forgiveness and grace. How much grace does the rest of the country owe people who spent years amplifying conspiracy theories before denouncing Maga? Logis said Leaving Maga regularly receives hostile messages from people who see forgiveness as unearned. Logis understands the anger, he said, but argues that a movement built entirely around punishing defection offers no incentive for anyone else to leave. “I am not asking anyone to like me. I’m not even asking for forgiveness,” said Messina. “I just hope that you’ll take what I have to say and believe it because I don’t have anything to gain except to hope that we can make a change.” • This story was amended on 1 September 2026. A previous version quoted Julianna Forlano as saying the mind functions as a “dope” seeker; in fact, Forlano said the mind functions as a “dopamine” seeker.

title: Progressive Ed Markey, 80, faces generational test in Massachusetts Senate primary
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: Markey, looking to clinch another Senate term, leads younger rival Seth Moulton in blue state’s primary poll
body_text: Democrats have spent the summer ousting long-serving incumbents in primaries across the country. On Tuesday, Massachusetts voters will decide whether that generational revolt extends to the 80-year-old Ed Markey, whose younger Democratic rival has argued that the incumbent is simply too old to serve another term. But the Senate primary in this heavily Democratic state flips a central dynamic of previous contests, where youthful progressive insurgents have targeted – and in several cases, toppled – older incumbents they derided as avatars of an outmoded cautious establishment. In something of a role reversal, it is the long-serving Markey who is positioned as the voice of the progressive left, while 47-year-old Seth Moulton, a member of the House of Representatives, has moved some of his more moderate positions closer to those of his older rival in an effort to win over a younger voting cohort. Polls indicate that Markey – who was first elected to Congress in 1976, before Moulton was born – is poised to confound concerns over his age by winning election for a third full term, at the end of which he would be 86. Markey’s leftwing credentials have been burnished by endorsements from other high-profile progressives, including Bernie Sanders, the leftwing independent senator from Vermont, and Elizabeth Warren, his fellow Massachusetts senator. In a recent televised debate, Markey, who became a senator in a 2013 special election to replace John Kerry, when he resigned to become US secretary of state, attempted to tackle the age issue head on. “I think everyone watching this debate can see that I’m more energized than I’ve ever been before in my life. I am crisscrossing the state. I’m fighting for families,” the senator said. “Congressman Moulton has a hard time keeping up with me in the course of this campaign.” Moulton – a former marine who later ran a private health company after military service in Iraq – called for age limits to serve in Congress and contrasted Markey’s campaign performance with his own. “I’ve done over 50 town halls. You’ve done a couple,” he told Markey. “You’ve missed three candidate forums just in the past week. It’s a lot of work to represent this entire state.” But it was when the debate turned to technology and the candidates’ personal use of artificial intelligence that the age question appeared to sharpen. Asked whether the senator used AI platforms such as ChatGPT in his work, Markey replied that he uses “whatever is inside of my iPhone and my iPad – whatever comes up”. Moulton seized on that response as evidence that the incumbent did not fully understand the latest technology and how it was poised to transform every sector of society. “Senator,” he said, “if you don’t even know what you’re using on your phone or your iPad, this is why we need a new generation of leaders to regulate these technologies to make sure that they are safe.” Moulton, who entered the House of Representatives in 2015, has embraced more moderate positions than Markey, namely on healthcare – on which he stopped short of advocating the single-payer system advocated by his opponent – and on transgender athletes. He apologized at a recent debate for previously saying in the fallout of Kamala Harris’s loss to Trump in 2024 that he did not want his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete”. He has said he would not vote for the Democrats’ current leader in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, if elected. Schumer, 75, has been portrayed as a symbol of what critics say is an out-of-touch and ageing establishment leadership that has left younger and left-leaning voters disenchanted. In blue Massachusetts, the Democratic primary often decides who wins office. An Emerson College Polling survey released on Sunday, suggested voters are willing to look past Markey’s age. In the survey, Markey led Moulton 60% to 33%, a dramatic increase from its May poll, when the senator held a five-point edge over the congressman. “If these numbers hold, this race will mirror Markey’s successful ‘peak-late’ approach to winning in 2020,” Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling, said, referring to the senator’s defeat of then congressman Joe Kennedy III, a scion of the state’s best-known political dynasty. Despite Kennedy’s youth – he was 39 at the time – young progressives rallied behind Markey, painting the incumbent as the leader most willing to take on the party’s establishment. Markey’s re-election would contradict the trend of a growing backlash against elderly leaders that critics have labelled a gerontocracy. Joe Biden was forced to drop his presidential re-election bid in 2024 amid concerns over his mental acuity after a disastrous presidential election debate in Atlanta against Donald Trump. Trump, who won the subsequent election against Biden’s replacement, Kamala Harris, is himself 80 and has been the subject of increasing age-related concerns about his health and ability to serve. Mitch McConnell, 84, the former Republican Senate majority leader, has been absent from Congress for months following a fall and hospitalization that has fueled fevered speculation about his health. On the campaign trail, Markey sought to cast his age as experience. “I’ve been standing up to the bosses for a long time, so I know no one gives it to you,” he says in one of his most prominent ads, featuring Warren and Sanders. “We have to fight for it.”

title: The media’s Hasan Piker obsession is letting Republican Mike Rogers off the hook
author: Mehdi Hasan
summary: Mike Rogers isn’t merely campaigning alongside a controversial supporter. His campaign put an extremist on its faith leadership team
body_text: Hasan Piker. Turn on cable news. Pick up a newspaper. Log on to Twitter. It doesn’t seem to matter where you get your political news: for the past month, the leftist Twitch streamer has become one of the dominant subjects of coverage, conversation and controversy surrounding the crucial Michigan Senate race between the Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and the Republican Mike Rogers. “I can’t stop talking about him,” the conservative pundit Hugh Hewitt recently admitted on Fox, the rightwing network that also can’t stop talking about Piker, day after day, from morning until night. And it isn’t just Fox. The media analysis platform Ground News aggregated 242 separate stories mentioning Piker from across the political spectrum over the past three months – almost three stories a day. Think about that. Piker doesn’t live in Michigan. He isn’t running for office. He isn’t a member of El-Sayed’s campaign. Most Americans have probably never heard of him. Yet the political press is obsessed. The incessant, relentless coverage of him is bad enough. Worse is the gaslighting – including from Democrats and liberal commentators – over why Piker has attracted so much attention, and why El-Sayed is apparently expected to spend his campaign answering for every provocative thing the streamer has ever said. “You can’t deploy Hasan Piker aggressively in factional primaries and then turn around after you win and say ‘why is everyone talking about Hasan Piker,’” influential liberal pundit Matt Yglesias posted on Twitter/X. “If you don’t want people to talk about him, don’t campaign with him!!” There is just one rather large problem with that argument. Mike Rogers isn’t merely campaigning alongside a controversial supporter. His campaign gave a Michigan-based extremist and religious bigot a leadership title in its faith outreach operation. His name is Lorenzo Sewell. And you’ve probably never heard of him. Sewell, a former gang leader and Black evangelical pastor in Detroit who spoke at Donald Trump’s second inauguration in January 2025, was unveiled by the Rogers campaign last year as one of seven members of the “senior leadership team” of “Faith Leaders for Mike Rogers”. And Sewell’s views are not exactly difficult to discover. He has publicly and proudly described Islam as a “conquering religion” and a “death cult”. He has called El-Sayed an “Islamic jihadist” who wants to impose “Sharia law all over this land”. The United States, he insists, is “not a nation of Muslims. We are a nation of Christians.” Imagine, for a moment, that a senior member of El-Sayed’s campaign had described Judaism as a “death cult”. Imagine that he had accused Rogers of being a white nationalist terrorist. Imagine the headlines. Imagine the cable-news panels. Imagine the demands – from Republicans, Democrats and journalists alike – that El-Sayed denounce him, disavow him, fire him. But Sewell’s vile rhetoric is only part of the story. On 18 August, the pastor co-organized the “Christian Crusader March on Dearborn City Council Meeting” with the far-right anti-Muslim agitator Jake Lang. Lang was charged with assaulting police officers with a deadly weapon over his actions on 6 January 2021, before receiving a pardon from Trump. He also says he doesn’t believe the Holocaust happened “at that level” and has used the N-word and was arrested in Texas in June on a charge of making a terroristic threat. The Dearborn “Crusader” rally co-organized by Sewell and Lang attracted neo-Nazis waving a swastika flag and wearing Nazi armbands. There were also reports of pro-KKK material being distributed during and after the event. Dearborn police made 22 arrests that day. Again: imagine the reaction if a senior faith leader affiliated with El-Sayed’s campaign had co-organized an event that drew people wearing Nazi armbands and waving a swastika flag, and that ended with a bunch of arrests? Would we ever hear the end of it? And unlike El-Sayed and Piker, who first campaigned together in April this year, Rogers and Sewell’s relationship goes back much further, to the former’s previous Senate run in 2024. Rogers spoke alongside Sewell at multiple events during the final weeks of that campaign. So you might assume that the Republican candidate has faced a barrage of questions about his political relationship with Sewell. You might assume that the same reporters demanding answers from El-Sayed about a Twitch streamer would be demanding answers from Rogers about a man his own campaign identified as part of a “senior leadership team”. You would be wrong. I searched the websites of the New York Times, the Washington Post and CNN. Not one of them appears to have mentioned Sewell in its coverage in 2026. The Times covered the “Christian Crusader” rally in Dearborn, including Jake Lang’s role in it, but made no mention of Sewell – or of Sewell’s connection to Rogers. To be clear: this isn’t whataboutism. I am not asking anyone to excuse anything Piker has said, or saying journalists shouldn’t scrutinize him. Nor am I saying they shouldn’t question El-Sayed’s decision to appear with him. What I am asking for is that our so-called liberal media simply apply the same standard to both candidates. If 242 stories about Piker are justified because El-Sayed campaigned with him, how many stories are justified about Sewell, whom Rogers’s own campaign named to a senior leadership team? If El-Sayed keeps getting asked about Piker’s rhetoric, why shouldn’t Rogers have to answer for Sewell’s? Why aren’t reporters asking Rogers whether he disavows Sewell’s description of Islam as a “death cult”? Why aren’t they asking whether he agrees that El-Sayed is an “Islamic jihadist” trying to impose sharia law on Michigan? Why aren’t they asking him to condemn Nazi flags at a “Christian Crusader” rally organized by a senior faith leader on his campaign? Oh, and why aren’t top Democrats also asking those same questions, and demanding answers for them? The near-erasure of Sewell, Lang, and those Nazi flags from the media coverage of the Michigan Senate race, combined with the silence from so many Democratic party leaders about Mike Rogers’ extremist ties, tells us something important. Three things, in fact. First, this was never really about antisemitism. Otherwise, why aren’t literal Nazi flags at an event organized by a Rogers ally a much bigger story than any of Piker’s remarks? Second, anti-Muslim bigotry continues to be seen and treated as a lesser offense in American public life. Calling Islam a “death cult” doesn’t apparently merit a single panel discussion on primetime cable news. And third, Republicans and Democrats continue to be held to radically different rules. If you’re a Democratic candidate, you have to repeatedly answer for the views of someone who isn’t even on your campaign team. If you’re a Republican candidate, your campaign can put someone on its faith leadership team who has a long record of brazenly bigoted rhetoric and never have to worry about any kind of media backlash. That is the real scandal here. Not that Abdul El-Sayed has been asked endless questions about a controversial ally. But that Mike Rogers has been asked none. Mehdi Hasan is the founder, CEO, and editor-in-chief of Zeteo

title: House Republicans ramp up labor union investigations before midterms
author: Michael Sainato
summary: Inquiries come after conservative thinktanks claim unions are using member dues to support Democratic causes
body_text: House Republicans are investigating several US labor unions based on claims from far-right non-profits alleging union dues are being used for illegal political funding. Republicans on the House’s education and workforce committee opened the investigation this summer after multiple reports from the conservative thinktanks targeted unions and their spending, claiming that unions are using member dues to support Democratic causes. While unions are allowed to advocate for political causes, they are prohibited from using union dues to directly fund specific candidates or political action committees (Pacs). Union members can voluntarily donate to labor unions’ political action committees. The unions under investigation include the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), United Auto Workers, United Steelworkers, Smart Transportation Division (Smart-TD), Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen (BLET), and the Brotherhood of Maintenance of Way Employees Division (BMWED). The allegations come from research reports by the American Accountability Foundation (AAF), a “dark money” non-profit that counts Project 2025 architect the Heritage Foundation as a donor, and the Freedom Foundation, a conservative thinktank whose chair once protested against Labor Day, claiming: “I can’t think of a problem in society that can’t be traced in some way back to the abuses of organized labor.” Among the AAF’s allegations against labor unions are that the BLET supported a lawsuit filed by the UAW to halt the Trump administration’s attempt to end collective bargaining. It also highlighted the BLET’s criticism of Project 2025, which advocates for several policies that would weaken labor unions and collective bargaining rights. “The industrial unions the [House] committee is investigating have become glorified political arms of the Democrat Party,” said Tom Jones, president of the American Accountability Foundation in a statement. “When these unions care more about their friends in Congress than their members in the factories and railroads, it becomes clear they’re not serving the working men and women of America!” In a statement, a spokesperson for United Steelworkers said the group is “working diligently on fully addressing the committee’s request”. “Our union values transparency and annually reports our spending with the Department of Labor,” the spokesperson said. As a part of their union investigations, House Republicans are also investigating AFT president Randi Weingarten after the Freedom Foundation claimed, using speculation around the union’s annual financial filing, that union member dues funded her 2025 book, Why Fascists Fear Teachers: Public Education and the Future of Democracy. “Perhaps Weingarten’s next book should be entitled, Why Teachers Fear Teachers Unions,” the analysis claimed. In a letter responding to the allegations, Michael Bromwich, an attorney representing Weingarten and the AFT, called the Freedom Foundation’s report “a partisan attack masquerading as investigative journalism”. “Its claims are premised on factual inaccuracies, misleading characterizations, and a willful disregard for the complete record,” Bromwich wrote. “The documents produced to the House committee refute these allegations and demonstrate that the book project was lawfully and ethically undertaken to advance AFT’s mission, with appropriate oversight and transparent financial arrangements.” The Freedom Foundation and House Republicans on the investigating committee did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The House investigations follow reports that the Trump administration conducted surveillance of labor unions in Minnesota during a mass anti-immigration enforcement operation earlier this year, including the CWA and the SEIU. Cathy Creighton, director of Cornell University’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations Buffalo Co-Lab, said that union finances are strictly controlled, with disclosure requirements on how money is spent – which is how the conservative groups got the information for their reports. Most union members vote Democrat, because the party “has a platform that supports the labor movement, the right to organize [and] the right to bargain”, Creighton said. “The labor movement is allowed to spend money on political actions, and they do,” she said, noting that the motivation behind the reports seemed political. “The Trump administration has been trying to eliminate bargaining rights and unions, full stop.” A 2024 poll by Gallup found that 62% of Americans say the Democratic party best serves the interest of union members compared with 27% who said the same about the Republican party. US labor unions have historically supported Democrats over Republicans since Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s administration passed the National Labor Relations Act in 1935. But Republican presidents, up until Ronald Reagan in the 1980s, refrained from taking hostile positions toward labor unions and collective bargaining. In 1976, Republican Gerald Ford’s presidential campaign stated “free collective bargaining remains the best way to insure that American workers receive a fair price for their labors”. But under Reagan, the Republican party began to emphasize so-called “right to work” laws over collective bargaining and adopted more hostile, pro-business stances toward labor unions. Under Trump’s second term, he issued an executive order to rescind collective bargaining rights from more than 1 million federal workers and made cuts to federal agencies tasked with enforcing labor laws.

title: Once again, Trump wants the FCC to put a bandage on his thin skin
author: Tom Wheeler
summary: The president is lashing out at an NBC host. As the agency’s former chair, I can only hope it stands up for free speech
body_text: Will the FCC chairperson again abuse his authority over broadcast licenses to put a Band-Aid on Donald Trump’s thin skin? Since the opening days of the Trump presidency, Brendan Carr has acted as the president’s attack dog to coerce broadcasters to say things that please his client. Only days after taking office in January 2025, Carr revived a previously dismissed complaint against CBS for the editing of 60 Minutes that tracked candidate Trump’s specious lawsuit on the matter. At the time, the FCC was considering the transfer of CBS licenses to Skydance, a decision that did not come until after CBS agreed to pay $16m to settle with Trump. In September, after Jimmy Kimmel’s remarks about Charlie Kirk, Carr urged broadcasters to take action, saying “we can do this the easy way or the hard way” – an attack even the senator Ted Cruz said sounded “right out of Goodfellas”. In March 2026, he threatened broadcasters over their coverage of the Iran war after the president complained on Truth Social. In April, he ordered Disney’s eight ABC-owned television stations to submit their licenses for premature review, even though most aren’t even halfway through their license term (Disney, ABC and the stations are suing). On Sunday, as the morning talkshows aired, the president posted on Truth Social that Kristen Welker, the host of NBC’s Meet the Press, “will be reported” for her claim that his primary endorsements yielded “mixed results”. “I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” the post instructed. NBC is owned by Comcast, a company that has long been in the president’s crosshairs. Putting aside the question of whether an interpretation of primary results is a “Threat to our Country”, as a former FCC chair, I almost feel sorry for Brendan Carr. Once again, the president has said “jump”, and Carr will be judged by his audience of one on how high he goes. The FCC was created by Congress as an independent commission. Early in his term, Trump issued an executive order that brought the FCC and other formerly independent agencies under White House supervision. Now, before taking any significant action, the agency must get approval from the White House. It appears that also includes following White House orders to initiate action. Enforcing his total control, in March, the president fired both Democratic commissioners (whose positions were mandated by Congress) from another formerly independent agency, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). When the commissioner, Rebecca Slaughter, sued, the supreme court sided with the president. For almost a century, the FCC has followed the statute that the five-member commission have a 3-2 majority in favor of the president’s party. Today there are two Republicans and only one Democrat on the FCC, Anna Gomez, because Trump won’t appoint another. Trump has nominated another Republican to the commission. Many fear that as soon as that appointment is confirmed by the Senate, the president will be able to fire Gomez and eliminate her effective voice while maintaining the required three-person quorum. There is a parallelism here. Trump wants the FCC to control what broadcasters say, while he controls what it can do. As chair of the FCC, Brendan Carr has immense authority to set the agenda and the decisions of the agency. Thus far he has wielded that power against journalism the president dislikes. The first amendment, however, does not have an exception for Donald Trump’s thin skin. Carr’s 2019 comments as a sitting commissioner should be his answer to what President Trump is asking him to do. At that time he took a firm stand: “The FCC does not have a roving mandate to police speech in the name of the ‘public interest’.” Hopefully, the chairperson will tire of doing the opposite and once again stand for the principle of free speech. Tom Wheeler was chairperson of the Federal Communications Commission from 2013 to 2017

title: Forest Service chief faces scrutiny over logging ties as Trump plans to scrap protections
author: Dharna Noor
summary: Rollback of ‘roadless rule’ expected to benefit companies US Forest Service chief, Tom Schultz, previously lobbied for
body_text: Donald Trump this month announced plans to rescind a landmark rule that has protected old-growth forests in the US for 25 years. If finalized, the rollback is expected to benefit the companies that Tom Schultz, chief of the US Forest Service, represented in his previous roles as a timber industry lobbyist and executive, according to research by consumer advocacy non-profit Public Citizen. The Roadless Area Conservation Rule, more commonly known as the “roadless rule”, was adopted in 2001 to limit development in roughly 45m acres of national forest. Industry interests and Republican representatives have long lobbied for the rule’s rescission, which would open up those swaths of untouched land to road construction, drilling and logging. In a statement, Schultz described the move as “the best way to restore the balance, reduce wildfire risk, and secure the long-term health of our forests and neighboring communities”. But studies suggest it could put 400 threatened and endangered species at risk and imperil ecosystems. Industry interests will be the main beneficiaries of the change, advocates fear. In an emailed statement, a Forest Service spokesperson, who did not provide their name, noted that Schultz had also held positions in Idaho and Montana government. “Chief Schultz’s appointment reflects the administration’s recognition that the Forest Service’s current challenges require leadership with broad federal land management experience, not just internal tenure,” the person said. Schultz is the first-ever Forest Service chief who did not previously work within the agency itself. Before Trump tapped him for the job, he served as president of the Federal Forest Resource Coalition, a trade association representing companies that purchase timber from the federal government, and was also vice-president of resources and government affairs at Idaho Forest Group, a major lumber manufacturer. He is one of dozens of former extractive industry insiders Trump has placed in key environmental positions. Energy secretary Chris Wright was CEO of fracking company Liberty Energy, while interior official Tyler Hassen was an oil executive. Forty-three former fossil-fuel employees and 29 former corporate executives held administration positions, an October analysis from Public Citizen and corporate watchdog Revolving Door Project found. Schultz has long been critical of the roadless rule. As it was being considered in 2000, he said: “It’s going to be very difficult to actually generate revenue from state trust lands that could be encompassed within a roadless designation.” The American Forest Resource Council (AFRC), a timber industry trade association on the west coast that includes the Idaho Forest Group, has recently directly advocated for the rescission of the roadless rule. In comments to the federal government last year, the lobbying group said the “one-size-fits-all” policy unnecessarily prevents “active forest management” – intentionally thinning forests through practices including logging – which it says is the best way to mitigate wildfire risk. Since his appointment, Schultz has echoed these calls. “Active forest management is not an option. It’s essential,” he said in the announcement of the proposal to rescind the roadless rule, which also referred to the policy as “one-size-fits-all”. “Active forest management is central to the Forest Service’s multi-use mission – not an industry agenda,” the Forest Service spokesperson said. In a statement, Nick Smith, spokesperson for the AFRC, said: “There is broad bipartisan support for increasing forest health treatments – thinning, prescribed fire, and even logging – to reduce the size and severity of wildfires and make forests more resilient to climate change.” A recent analysis of the Forest Service’s own data found that wildfires were nearly three times as likely to start near roads, raising questions about the administration’s claim that expanding road access will reduce wildfire risk, said Lois Parshley, climate research director at Public Citizen. “But from the industry’s perspective, it will also open up new possibilities for logging,” she said. Asked about Parshley’s concern, the Forest Service spokesperson said that repealing the roadless rule “allows safer use and maintenance of existing roads that first responders have long said they need to reach fires quickly”. “Forest‑treatment science is clear: thinning plus prescribed fire reduces wildfire severity by more than 60% – and up to 72% compared to untreated areas,” they said. “Access enables treatment; without access, prevention and response suffer. Gates and seasonal closures can be used to manage public traffic while preserving routes that firefighters and forest managers may need.” The AFRC’s comments say that “strategically placed and maintained roads are essential for safe and effective wildfire response”, and that in “nearly every major wildfire over the past 15–20 years”, the Forest Service has identified a lack of road access as a key barrier to effective response, Parshley said. That argument also appears in Schultz’s rationale for repealing the rule, she noted. In the administration’s announcement, he said the roadless rule “has frustrated land managers and served as a barrier to action – prohibiting road construction, which has limited wildfire suppression and active forest management”. Smith of the AFRC said that “millions of roadless acres have burned across the west since the rule’s adoption in 2001.” “Federal lands are far more likely to burn than private lands, which typically have far more roads,” he said. “According to the congressional budget office, a wildfire on federal land is on average five times the size of one on nonfederal land nearby.” Critics dispute the logic that the roadless rule is good for wildfire management, arguing that roads can increase the risk of human-caused fires. Since Schultz came into the Forest Service in February 2025, the American Forest Resource Council has spent more than $210,000 advocating to expand harvesting in national forests, lobbying records show. Meanwhile, the Idaho Forest Group increased its spending on lobbying in 2026 and reported advocating to support “efforts to advance forest management”, including with the agency now run by its former executive, Parshley found. Smith of the AFRC claimed that “the amount of money AFRC spends lobbying Congress and federal agencies in support of policies to improve the health of federal forests and nearby rural communities is dwarfed in comparison to the many anti-forestry NGOs.” Idaho is exempt from the roadless rule; it has its own regulations on roadless areas developed with the federal government. But the proposal to kill the roadless rule is just one industry-backed change to forestry that the Trump administration has put forth. As the head of the Federal Forest Resource Coalition, Schultz in July 2022 delivered testimony before Congress in which he suggested roadless areas were limiting the industry, saying: “nearly half of the National Forest System [is] off limits to management.” Though he did not call to overturn the policy specifically, he advocated allowing states to manage more Forest Service timber sales, expanding exemptions from environmental review processes, and changing stewardship contracting rules to support logging and wood-processing infrastructure. The Trump administration has since adopted or advanced each of those proposals, Parshley found in a report earlier this year. And Schultz has directly helped implement them, she found. For instance, in December 2025 he personally signed an agreement with Idaho’s governor to double federal timber sales from the state’s national forests. “That directly benefits his former employer the Idaho Forest Group”, she said. Idaho Forest Group has been contacted for comment. Under Schultz, the Forest Service has ramped up timber sales. In June, he told senators that the agency had exceeded its timber-sale target. He has also overseen a historic and widely criticized structural reorganization of his agency, moving the agency’s headquarters from the nation’s capital to Salt Lake City, eliminating regional offices and staff and shifting authority over forests to states. Schultz has made it clear that he aims to weaken regulations. In April, he told Congress that he is “trying to cut through regulation”. In a company earnings call after Schultz was confirmed, lumber company PotlatchDeltic CEO Eric Cremers confirmed that industry executives maintain direct familiarity with Schultz in his new role, saying: “We know the new Forest Service chief.” “It’s pretty clear that the industry was excited by their reactions to Schultz’s nomination and then confirmation,” said Parshley.
