title: The man who shaped Trump: book sheds fresh light on ruthless Roy Cohn
author: Martin Pengelly in Washington
summary: American Scoundrel tells story of McCarthy attack dog, mob lawyer and Trump mentor – will the president be thumbing its pages?
body_text: Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark have written a book Trumpworld doesn’t want you to read. Published on Tuesday, American Scoundrel is a propulsive, horrifying biography of Roy Cohn, the New York mob lawyer whose extraordinary life charted, as the book’s subtitle has it, a “Dark Journey from Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump”. “I told my publicist to reach out to any of the Fox News hosts and reporters, to Joe Rogan, Steve Bannon,” Bird said. “We haven’t gotten a peep, other than Joe Rogan. He said he looked at the galleys, and he got back to my publicist and said, ‘I’m not interested.’ I’m kind of surprised. This is a serious biography of the president’s mentor, whom he publicly admires and says he still misses.” From the mid-70s to the mid-80s, Cohn guided Trump through the cutthroat world of New York real estate. Everything brutal about Trump, in business and politics, he probably learned from Cohn. How to profit from ties to organized crime? Check. How to stay a step ahead of the law? Check. How to remorselessly lie and never admit wrong or defeat? Check. Small wonder that in 2017, amid scandal over links to Russia that aides couldn’t master, Trump memorably demanded: “Where’s my Roy Cohn?” Trump does know about American Scoundrel, because Bird called him four times on his personal number. “The interviews were eight, nine, 10 minutes,” Bird said. “He told some stories. They were of use to me. I asked, ‘Well, how did you first meet Roy Cohn?’ And I was expecting what he had said before in The Art of the Deal and in interviews, and instead he flipped the story all the way upside down. Instead of him going up to the older man, recognizing the powerful lawyer sitting at a nearby table at Le Club in Manhattan [in 1973], he said, ‘Oh, Roy Cohn recognized me. I was making a name for myself as a young developer in Manhattan.’” Another lesson from Cohn: tell the story however the hell you want. Describing his final Trump call, Bird said: “It’s so weird. You cold-call him, and he picks up. This time, instead of politely listening to my questions, he says, ‘Oh, I can’t do this. I don’t have time for this. You shouldn’t be using this number. I’m the president. I have Russia calling. I have China calling.’ And I say, ‘OK, I understand, Mr President, but I just have two questions.’ “And I ask, ‘Did you know that Roy Cohn in 1976 voted for Jimmy Carter?’ And he says, ‘Ah, that’s unbelievable. Why would he do that?’ And I said, ‘Well, Roy was kind of fed up and impatient with the old guard Republican party symbolized by Gerald Ford, and he thought Jimmy Carter was a fresh face.’ And Trump said, ‘Oh, I can understand that. That makes sense.’ You know his frustrations with the Republican party establishment. So that must have resonated with him. “Then I said, ‘Well, Cohn quickly got disillusioned with Carter, particularly over the Panama canal treaty, and of course Trump jumped in and said, ‘Yeah, that was a terrible deal. What a terrible deal!’ He’s trying to get off the phone, and I say, ‘Well, I just want you to know this book is coming out in the autumn, and he says, ‘Oh, terrific, maybe I can promote it. Anything I promote goes to number one.’ And then there’s a pause, and he says, ‘Of course, it would have to be fair.’” American Scoundrel is certainly fair. Bird won a Pulitzer prize for American Prometheus, a life of the nuclear scientist J Robert Oppenheimer co-written with Martin J Sherwin and the basis for Christopher Nolan’s Oscar-winning biopic. Bird’s last subject was Carter. Cohn kept cropping up, so Bird and Goldmark (his wife, “director of research” and “muse”) got down to work. Then Trump was re-elected. Cohn was current again. “At 27, Cohn was on the cover of Time magazine,” Bird said, pointing to a rise that saw Cohn graduate from Columbia Law School at 20, prosecute Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, executed for spying for Russia, then become the GOP senator Joe McCarthy’s aide in the Red Scare, the brutal 1950s witch-hunt of liberals and homosexuals. “Joe McCarthy is a much less complicated and driven kind of figure than Roy Cohn,” Bird said. “Joe McCarthy was a populist senator from Wisconsin who was simply looking to generate some headlines, and he kind of stumbled on the idea of communists and the government.” Cohn was “the ideologue. He’s the svengali, the real brain, who tells Joe McCarthy how he can take advantage of this issue. He runs the hearings, actually conducts the interrogations of these witnesses and is driven out of ideological certainty that there is a danger to the nation from internal communism, and a desire as a Jewish American – this is, I think, important to his identity – to prove his own loyalty, to prove not all Jews are leftwing.” Cohn’s rightwing credentials were impeccable: he was close to Rupert Murdoch, Ronald Reagan and other major reactionary figures. As the horrors of McCarthyism now echo in Trump’s extralegal war on “woke”, so do inquisitors’ unenforced errors. The Army-McCarthy hearings, which brought McCarthy down in 1954, were spawned by Cohn’s attempts to get another young inquisitor, G David Schine, out of overseas service. Senators insinuated Cohn and Shine were lovers. Cohn was certainly gay but never came out of the closet. He was also, Bird said, “quite definitely attracted to Donald Trump. When he met him, Trump was 27 years old. He was tall, blonde, blue-eyed. Wealthy, somewhat. So he was Roy’s type. I don’t think anything sexual went on between them but there was a dynamic, and a pattern to Roy’s friendships.” Cohn could be generous. Bird considers the case of Gary Belis, who dated Cohn, 25 years his senior, but didn’t sleep with him and remained fond. But that story is told in a chapter titled “Predator”, which also contains the horrific story of Richard Kerr, a Northern Irish boy abused in care then trafficked around the world, including to Roy Cohn. “He could be very charming with someone like Gary Belis and sort of decent,” Bird said. “He courted him, gave him favors as Roy would, but he backed off when Gary indicated he couldn’t go down that path. And yet Cohn was a sexual addict, and he had these ‘boy toys’” – teen hustlers paid for sex. Cohn is an American villain. He features in Angels in America, Tony Kushner’s stage epic of the Aids crisis. In 2024, Jeremy Strong played him in The Apprentice, Ali Abbasi’s Trump biopic. A portion of his archive is owned by Michael Stipe of REM, author of the song Exhuming McCarthy. He died in 1986, aged 59, from Aids. As he always denied his sexuality, so he denied his final illness, claiming liver cancer even as he received experimental Aids treatment thanks to Washington connections. Not long before he died, he was disbarred for unethical conduct, three indictments having failed to bring him down. (He still had 36 character witnesses, among them Trump, William F Buckley Jr and the TV host Barbara Walters, once Cohn’s “beard”, or fake romantic interest.) In extremis, Trump is commonly said to have abandoned Cohn, causing him to say: “Donald pisses ice water.” Bird said: “That’s not entirely true. “I quote the switchboard operator Chris Seymour at Cohn’s New York townhouse law firm. He said that when Trump recognized that Roy was dying of Aids, he began to keep his distance. He didn’t rely on him as much, as his lawyer. The calls were fewer. But that didn’t mean he cut him off. He did invite him down to his new estate in Mar-a-Lago for this fabulous dinner, March 86, so just five months before he dies. And it was a touching farewell dinner, with many toasts.” Cohn’s memorial service was held in midtown Manhattan. A witness saw Trump weeping. American Scoundrel is out now

title: What should we do with Trump’s monstrous architectural legacy?
author: Jan-Werner Müller
summary: Questions over Trump’s ballroom and other structures might not feel urgent. But when his reign ends, Trumpism must be repudiated
body_text: On Monday, a majority on the supreme court found a technical way to overrule a lower court’s imperative to stop work, while not taking a stance on whether the whole enterprise might be illegal to begin with. Preservationists, the majority held, appear to lack legal grounds for filing a suit blocking Trump’s ballroom; that means construction will proceed, even if none other than John Roberts, in a dissent, held that “those responsible” were breaking the rules in deciding “what to build up at the People’s House”. The solicitor general, John Sauer, is on record claiming that 65% of the project is completed (of course, he might have exaggerated – such things are known to have happened in Trump administrations). Either way, it is thus likely that there will be a massive structure next to the original White House; and, given that the ruling will embolden the president dramatically to change Washington DC’s landscape by spending money never approved by Congress, we might be cursed with a triumphal arch as well. All of which raises the question: what to do with a monstrous architectural legacy in post-Trump America? Some might dismiss the question as a bit of a luxury problem. After all, a war that also demonstrates the ongoing disempowerment of Congress keeps dragging on; ICE continues its cruel day-to-day work; Trump is trying every tactic to make the midterms go his way. But the built environment, and especially the civic landscape of a capital, is never just an afterthought. Buildings and monuments make values visible, as the philosopher Susan Neiman once put it. And the decision to leave Trump’s structures in place as if his reign had just been another normal era in US history is not neutral – just like leaving Confederate monuments in place is not neutral. For those who dismiss talk of civic values made visible as all too idealistic, there is another, hard-nosed argument to consider: after all, for anyone around the globe ever to trust a US government again, Trumpism will need to be thoroughly repudiated. Without a clear distancing from his toxic reign – during which the whims and obsessions of one evidently incompetent conman wreaked havoc with old alliances – other countries might well conclude that the US has failed to learn any lessons. And the built environment is a prime candidate for making that distancing visible to the outside world. The ballroom in particular has become a central symbol of Trump 2.0, as it combines core features of Trump’s governance: the shameless corruption, as private companies are invited to “donate” for the project; the sheer destructiveness, as the East Wing was brutally torn down without discussion, let alone permission – something that Trumpists might try to repeat with the Kennedy Center, as Howard Lutnick and others are threatening that it will have to be demolished unless Trump gets to “renovate” and have his name on it (notice the abuser’s logic of “if I cannot have it, no one can have it”). Democrats, noticing the symbolic importance of the structure, have started to weigh in on its future: Gavin Newsom, the California governor, affirming that “we have to be builders” and not destroyers, would just leave things alone; Senator Chris Murphy has suggested that all “dirty” – which seems to mean: corrupt – projects under Trump might need to go; meanwhile, Senator Ruben Gallego wants to sell the ballroom off “piece by piece” (it is unclear whether that would be some sort of political performance art, intended as a comment on corruption, or an act of symbolic catharsis, copying the way people demolished the Berlin wall piece by piece). The prior, fundamental question is whether a structure honors a particular person or at least affirms a set of political values. This was always the strongest reason why monuments of those defending slavery could simply not be left standing; as Neiman also pointed out, there was no way a Germany that still had Hitler street names – let alone Hitler statues – could have regained the trust of anyone. So, as painful as it might be for members of the Maga cult, no official building should bear Trump’s name, and no publicly funded statues of him must ever be erected – unless the country decides that we should honor a man bent on establishing autocracy in the US. Then again, some republics have precisely not erased all traces of a tyrannical ruler because they wanted such traces to serve as a warning to future generations. Visitors to Venice’s most famous palace can marvel at portraits of all the doges, except one that is painted over with a black shroud; here the dishonor of the person – Doge Marino Faliero, who attempted a coup – is immortalized, and the moral meaning of history unmistakably clarified. Political iconoclasm wants to leave remnants of an image in place to remind people why iconoclasm had been necessary in the first place. That is why some have suggested that problematic monuments should ideally not be removed at all, but come with explicit statements, such as plaques that disavow their initial political message – or even be legitimately vandalized, such that both original and acts of vandalism remain clearly visible. Contextualization has a pedagogical impulse similar to that of museums; hence, there is something coherent about the congressman Jamie Raskin and the progressive politician Saikrat Chakrabarti suggesting the ballroom should at least partly be turned into exhibition spaces documenting corruption, autocracy and what Raskin described as attempts to “undermine and thwart popular democracy in American life” (though, as Raskin seeks to keep a space for dining, too, guests might end up awkwardly sipping champagne next to depictions of January 6). Perhaps there is a more straightforward approach: the edifice could be named after Renee Good and Alex Pretti, the way some places in the south ended up testifying to those who fought injustice. This could teach a history lesson in a way that, for instance, turning the ballroom into a soup kitchen, as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has suggested, might not – worthy as that idea might also appear. Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton University

title: Echoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian election
author: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro
summary: Claims that Trump and Rubio are trying to influence result have parallels with CIA intervention 64 years ago
body_text: The year was 1962 and the Kennedy administration was desperate to swing Brazil’s congressional elections against its leftwing president, João Goulart, as a way of countering the supposed communist threat sweeping a region the US considered its back yard. Historians say that in the lead-up to the vote, the CIA and the Department of State secretly channelled millions of dollars to opposition candidates and a group tasked with spreading rightwing propaganda and stirring up unrest. “There was a very heavy-handed intervention here by the US government,” said Chico Rubens Paiva, a political activist whose congressman grandfather Rubens Paiva investigated Washington’s meddling during a 1963 parliamentary inquiry into the conspiracy. More than six decades later, Paiva, whose grandfather was murdered by the US-backed dictatorship that seized power in 1964, is among those who fear history is repeating itself on the eve of Brazil’s 2026 presidential election. October’s vote will pit the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Donald Trump ally who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a military coup. Polls suggest a tight race and Trump and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, have been accused of trying to tip the scales in Bolsonaro’s favour by launching an overt campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure against Lula. The US measures include imposing 25% tariffs on most Brazilian imports and designating Brazil’s biggest crime groups – Rio’s Red Command and São Paulo’s First Command of the Capital – as foreign terrorist organisations. Brazilian officials suspect this is partly designed to boost Bolsonaro by making Lula look soft on crime. In July, Lula said two Trump officials had been denied entry visas because they planned “to meddle in Brazil’s elections”. Brazilian officials believe the pair, who reportedly planned to meet Flávio Bolsonaro, intended to sow doubt about the reliability of Brazil’s internationally respected voting system – something the Bolsonaros have sought to do repeatedly. Soon after, the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington was revoked. Celso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist and podcast pundit, voiced bewilderment that US interference – which he considered the election’s most urgent theme – was not getting more coverage in mainstream media. “The greatest superpower in human history is explicitly backing a candidate in our election and is strangling the Brazilian economy in order to help him [win],” Barros claimed. “We cannot pretend that this isn’t happening and treat this like a normal election … the Brazilian economy is under attack.” Trump’s tactics have echoes of Washington’s cold war-era attempt to manipulate Brazilian politics in the lead-up to the 1964 coup, which ushered in two decades of authoritarian rule in which hundreds of people were killed or disappeared. Back then, the CIA helped finance the Brazilian Institute for Democratic Action, which, according to the historians Lilia Schwarcz and Heloisa Starling, illegally poured money into the campaigns of hundreds of lawmakers and eight gubernatorial candidates. “The objective was strategic: to create a strong opposition in congress, block government initiatives and prepare the way for a coup d’état,” Schwarcz and Starling argued in their book Brazil: A Biography. Another US-funded group, the Research and Social Studies Institute, was used to disrupt Goulart’s government by bankrolling anti-communist propaganda and anti-government protests. James N Green, a Brown University historian who has written a book about the period, said: “The intention [was] getting rid of Goulart [and] opening the door to the military coming to power.” Green sees parallels between Trump’s use of tariffs to sabotage Lula’s campaign and how in the early 60s Washington sought to enfeeble Goulart’s government by funding his opponents and cutting off loans. Then, as now, the US government was “bent on doing everything possible to weaken the government” in Brazil. But Barros sees one key difference between the two US gambits. “[The 1962 campaign] was done covertly, precisely because the CIA knew there would be real public anger in Brazil if people knew the US was bankrolling candidates. So they did it secretly,” he said. “Today, this is being done openly – and on an incomparably larger scale.” The Department of State rejected claims the US was seeking to meddle in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” an official said in a statement. “We respect the Brazilian people and whatever government that they choose freely through free and fair elections in Brazil. We’ve respected and dealt with governments from both sides of the spectrum in Brazil, and had very successful relationships with them.” Last year Trump was accused of meddling in the politics of neighbouring Argentina after he threw his weight behind its rightwing president, Javier Milei, on the eve of crucial midterm elections. Milei recently attended Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign launch in Brazil, using his speech to lambaste Lula as a “thief”. Green believes two strategic objectives lie behind the Brazilian pressure campaign being waged by Trump and by Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, who has made toppling Cuba’s communist government a personal project. Firstly, it is designed to weaken and delegitimise Lula’s government, making it harder for Brazil, Latin America’s largest democracy, to challenge the US economic asphyxiation campaign against Cuba. Secondly, it is about “neutralising” leftwing forces in Latin America more generally and boosting the right in the hope of helping to elect even more Trump-aligned leaders. Since 2023, a succession of radical rightwing populists have won power in Argentina and Chile, Costa Rica and Colombia. In reference to Trump’s tangerine complexion, this has been nicknamed Latin America’s “orange wave”. Paiva, 38, believes US interference is intended to have a similar effect to the abduction of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro – strengthening “American dominance” in a region it considers a US sphere of influence. Maduro’s removal in January allowed the US to impose a pliant successor, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has started opening up the South American country to US oil and mining firms. Paiva believes Bolsonaro’s election will “serve the same purpose: putting people into power who will serve their interests”. He fears that as election day draws near, US social media companies could enter the fray, potentially giving Bolsonaro another lift. “Any kind of change to the algorithm has a brutal impact in the way information reaches people,” warned Paiva, who is running for a seat in congress in the election for the centre-left Brazilian Socialist party. He highlighted “the scary lurch the Silicon Valley bros” had taken into Trump’s camp during his second term. Barros is convinced the US aims to help elect Flávio Bolsonaro, “because Flávio will give them everything they want”, he said. “Flávio will make a rare earths deal no other president would. Flávio will let American big techs do whatever they like in Brazil. Flávio will reduce economic relations with China as much as he can.” He noted that Bolsonaro supporters attended rallies carrying US flags. Barros believes the campaign’s real driving force is not Trump but Rubio, who hopes to bolster a possible 2028 presidential run by showing voters he has “delivered the whole of Latin America to American interests”. “The fact is, this is an election between Lula and Marco Rubio,” Barros said.

title: New system for screening mail-in ballots risks denying entire batches, says whistleblower
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: US senator says that project, a key part of Trump’s voting restrictions, is ‘perilously rushed and potentially unlawful’
body_text: A new system to screen millions of mail-in ballots for this November’s US midterm elections was thrown together so hastily, and tested so little, that a single scanning glitch could see entire batches of ballots turned away, a whistleblower has told Congress. The project – a key part of Donald Trump’s new restrictions on voting – is “perilously rushed and potentially unlawful”, according to the US senator Richard Blumenthal, who disclosed the warning in a letter to David Steiner, the postmaster general, on Tuesday. Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the US Senate’s permanent subcommittee on investigations, said the account he had received made clear the US Postal Service “lacks the technical or operational capability” to roll it out safely before ballots go out to voters. The system stems from a March executive order by Trump tightening federal control over mail-in voting, directing USPS to check ballots against a federally approved voter list before sending them – a break from its usual role of simply delivering whatever is handed over by states. Courts have blocked and unblocked parts of the order repeatedly since, amid lawsuits arguing it oversteps into territory the constitution leaves to states. USPS calls the result the “Federal Ballot Mail Portal”. Officials upload voter and barcode data in advance; clerks then scan a sample of arriving ballots – 15 to 400, depending on batch size – against that list. According to the whistleblower’s disclosure, the system runs on a “zero percent failure rate”: one mismatched scan rejects the entire batch, even if it holds tens of thousands of ballots. USPS was contacted for comment. Engineers had roughly three months, including a court-ordered pause, for work the whistleblower says would normally take close to a year. The full system was not even assembled for testing until about 24 August, the disclosure says, leaving only a handful of working days to catch problems before launch. By the final week, officials were reportedly calling the effort “a shit show”, and one worker who raised concerns about the lack of testing time was told simply: “We cannot fail.” About a third of voters cast ballots by mail in 2024. The whistleblower’s prediction of mass disruption remains unconfirmed – the system had not gone live as of this week. “The whistleblower’s allegations make clear that USPS lacks the technical or operational capability needed to effectively implement the EO’s [executive order’s] provisions in a way that safeguards every citizen’s right to vote in the upcoming midterm elections,” Blumenthal wrote. “Despite this, the Trump Administration appears intent on USPS moving forward with its flawed plans, no matter the chaos they may create.” Blumenthal’s letter also alleges USPS kept building the portal under active court orders to stop, including one issued on 27 August that remains in force. “USPS should have ceased all work on the Portal on June 25, 2026,” he wrote. Blumenthal has given USPS until 4 September to answer questions, including who ordered the work to begin and resume, and until 8 September to hand over internal records. USPS has not disclosed an expected rejection rate, which the whistleblower says was withheld because it would expose how shaky the rollout is. The representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, said his panel had received similar reports. “This new secret tracking system at the US Postal Service is faulty, untested, and threatens to totally disrupt ballot delivery for millions of American citizens,” Garcia said, calling the policy an “unconstitutional and dangerous power grab”.

title: US lawmakers demand investigation into Trump administration’s secret surveillance of Americans
author: Sam Levine in New York
summary: Exclusive: Two congressmembers respond to revelations of government snooping on journalists, non-profits and unions
body_text: Two congressional Democrats asked a government watchdog on Tuesday to investigate the Trump administration’s use of an obscure law to secretly collect records on journalists, non-profits and unions without judicial oversight. The request from the Oregon senator Ron Wyden and the representative Pramila Jayapal of Washington seen by the Guardian comes amid mounting scrutiny over the way the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) recently used its power to issue administrative summonses related to customs matters to make extraordinary unilateral demands for information. They sent their request to the government accountability office (GAO), the non-partisan congressional watchdog. The Guardian reported this week that Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of the DHS, has used the summonses to secretly obtain six months’ worth of telephone records for Georgia Fort, a Minneapolis journalist. In one particularly stunning episode, it issued an administrative summons to Google requesting information on the YouTube accounts of Fort and Don Lemon after a judge had twice rejected a search warrant application for the information, telling the government Fort and Lemon needed to have a chance to contest the request. HSI sought the records after federal prosecutors charged Fort and Lemon with civil rights crimes in connection with a protest at a Saint Paul, Minnestoa, church in January that they were covering. Both have pleaded not guilty. The DHS has used administrative summonses to successfully obtain financial information on labor unions and Venmo transactions for a non-profit group. The DHS has also issued a slew of administrative subpoenas to tech giants such as Meta, X and Reddit to try to unmask anonymous DHS critics. Wyden and Jayapal asked the GAO to investigate the way that the DHS was using the summonses outside of customs matters. It also asked the GAO to investigate language in each summons requesting that the recipients of the summons not notify the user of its existence because it would “impede the investigation and thereby interfere with the enforcement of federal law”. Privacy experts say that language is not legally binding and the companies can ignore it. “Crucially, the recipients of these subpoenas – often third-party companies and service providers – maintain a First Amendment right to notify their customers of the demand, allowing the actual targets of the subpoenas the opportunity to assert their own legal rights or challenge the demand in court,” they added. “We request an audit of HSI’s use of non-disclosure language in immigration subpoenas and customs summonses, as well as the circumstances under which HSI has used customs summonses unrelated to import violations or customs duties.” A GAO spokesperson confirmed the office received the request and was examining it. Wyden and Jayapal also raised concerns about how the Department of Justice and the US Drug Enforcement Administration have used language in subpoenas that pressure companies into keeping a request subpoena private when, in many cases, the law does not prevent notifying the customer about the inquiry. “Although large technology firms with sophisticated counsel sometimes ignore these extra-legal requests, many other businesses in heavily-regulated sectors – such as telecommunications, pharmaceuticals, automotive manufacturing, and banking – often comply out of fear of regulatory retaliation,” they wrote. “Indeed, companies like AT&T and CVS have explicitly cited these extra-legal government demands to Congress to justify their failure to notify customers when their private records are turned over to the government.” Wyden and Jayapal also asked the GAO to identify any changes the DHS made to its policies around administrative summonses after a 2017 DHS inspector general report found they were being used improperly. Wyden and Jayapal additionally asked the judicial conference, the group that oversees policies for the federal courts, to amend the template for a grand jury or trial subpoena to make it clear that recipients are allowed to disclose their existence unless there is a court order prohibiting that. “These steps will help ensure that agencies do not abuse their subpoena authorities at the expense of privacy and free speech rights,” they wrote.

title: House passes funding bill to avoid shutdown before midterms
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Continuing resolution to approve government spending until 11 December passes 370-48 and will now go to Trump
body_text: The US House of Representatives on Tuesday approved legislation to prevent a government shutdown through the midterms, as both parties opted to defuse a volatile dispute before the November elections that will decide the balance of power in Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. A continuing resolution (CR) authorizing government spending until 11 December passed the House by a 370-48 vote, with only 19 Republicans and 29 Democrats in opposition. Had it not passed, lawmakers would have had until the end of September to approve new funding or face a government shutdown. The measure, which keeps federal spending at their current levels until the CR expires, now heads to Trump’s desk, after the Senate approved it last month by an overwhelming margin. In July, the House passed its own CR that would have authorized government spending until 4 December, but most Democrats rejected it for funding immigration enforcement agencies without including new guardrails on their conduct that they had demanded, and the Senate never took it up. The relatively uneventful end to the annual government funding debate comes as lawmakers step up their campaigning before the 3 November elections, in which most forecasters believe Democratic candidates have an edge in retaking the majority in the House of Representatives. There are mounting signs that the minority may also be able to regain control of the Senate by winning seats in at least three states that voted for Trump two years ago, as the president struggles with approval ratings driven lower by persistent inflation and the war with Iran. In the run-up to the vote, top House Democrats said they were ready to support the Senate measure, noting it included policy tweaks that the party supported. Among those was a delay until 11 December on a new rule by the White House office of management and budget that Democrats feared would allow the Trump administration to cancel grants at any time for any reason. “Given that the objectives that we had were met, I think that there’s going to be broad bipartisan support,” Pete Aguilar, the Democratic caucus chair, told reporters before the vote. Tensions flared among House Democrats later on Tuesday, when representatives Jared Golden of Maine and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington unexpectedly joined Republicans to help House speaker Mike Johnson pass a procedural rule governing debate on a suite of GOP-backed bills. The Democrats’ votes effectively salvaged Johnson’s agenda in the face of a conservative revolt that risked tanking Republicans’ legislative priorities. While Golden, who is retiring at the end of his term, and Gluesenkamp Perez, who is running for re-election in a district Trump won in 2024, often buck their party, the move was highly unusual and prompted a sharp rebuke from Democratic leadership. In a joint statement, Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, whip Katherine Clark and Aguilar said the two lawmakers had “blindside[d] the entire House Democratic Caucus” and called their actions a “significant breach of trust”. “It is an action that necessitates a serious response, and we have asked the Committee on Caucus Rules to take this up in short order,” they said. Passage of the rule paved the way on Tuesday for a vote on a resolution denouncing socialism in “all its forms”, which passed the divided chamber with the support of Republicans and eight Democrats. Tuesday’s floor action was a reminder of the deep divisions within the Democratic ranks after losing control of both houses of Congress in the 2024 elections. Without power in Congress, they have used the Senate’s filibuster to force the government closed and push the Republican majority into compromising over their preferred policies. Last year, Senate Democrats instigated a government shutdown by refusing to vote for any spending bill that did not extend subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans. That led to the longest funding lapse in US history, but ultimately no agreement to keep the cost offsets going after the shutdown ended 43 days later. Some government agencies shut down again briefly earlier this year after Democrats held up a funding bill for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in protest of the killings by federal agents of two US citizens in Minneapolis during an intensive immigration enforcement drive. While an agreement was reached to resolve that blockade, the two parties did not agree on funding the DHS for weeks, as Democrats held out for reforms to immigration enforcement operations. A bipartisan agreement was reached to fund the department operations exclusive of the agencies involved in Trump’s mass deportation push; then Republicans passed a party-line bill that allocated funding to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection for the duration of Trump’s presidency, with no reforms to immigration enforcement.

title: Republican calls Leon Black and David Copperfield co-conspirators of Epstein
author: Stephanie Kirchgaessner
summary: Outgoing congressman Thomas Massie urges justice department to launch immediate investigation
body_text: An outgoing Republican congressman accused the billionaire Leon Black and David Copperfield, the illusionist, of being co-conspirators of the late accused sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein, and repeated a call for the Department of Justice to launch an immediate investigation into the men, among others. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who recently lost his primary to a challenger backed by Donald Trump, named several friends and associates of Epstein on the floor of the House in his bid to “shame” the Department of Justice to investigate a group of men and one woman who Massie called “perpetrators” of Epstein’s crimes. He also noted that, nearly one year after Trump signed the Epstein Transparency Act, which led to the release of millions of so-called “Epstein files”, millions more have yet to be publicly disclosed. “The government continues to withhold over three million files” Massie said on Monday. “That’s why we’ve introduced the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, to bring the fight to the state courts, accountability to the Department of Justice and closure for survivors. “We want perpetrators of these crimes to be investigated and prosecuted” he added. Massie called the individuals “co-conspirators” on his Instagram account. Black, the New York private equity investor who paid Epstein tens of millions of dollars in fees, is separately facing a threat of being held in contempt of Congress because of an ongoing standoff over demands that he appear to testify before the House oversight committee later this week, on 3 September. Black has not yet confirmed his appearance before the committee, according to a person familiar with the matter. Black’s spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the scheduled hearing or Massie’s comments. Black has described his work for Epstein as tax and estate-planning services. In a previous statement before the oversight committee in June, Black wrote of his relationship with Epstein: “I did not know about this nefarious activity until Epstein was charged with trafficking in July 2019.” But Black acknowledged that he did know about Epstein pleading guilty in “2008 to state charges relating to prostitution involving a minor”. The chairman of the House oversight committee, the Republican James Comer, has previously said he would hold Black in contempt if he did not fully cooperate with his panel’s ongoing investigation into Epstein, including by handing over subpoenaed documents. Susan Estrich, Black’s lawyer, has rejected Comer’s assertions that Black has not been cooperative and has said that Black was being targeted in a “political witch-hunt”. Epstein’s former lawyer, Alan Dershowitz, has also not yet confirmed his appearance before the oversight committee, according to a person familiar with the matter. Dershowitz’s appearance was scheduled to take place on Wednesday. Dershowitz told the Guardian on Tuesday that he was “working on a date”. FBI agents investigating Copperfield in 2007 said that “a clear connection” existed between the famous illusionist and Epstein, according to documents released by the Department of Justice earlier this year. Copperfield’s lawyers have previously denied he was friends with Epstein. Lawyers for the illusionist did not respond to a request for comment on Massie’s comments, accusing Copperfield of being an Epstein co-conspirator. In a post on X on Tuesday morning, Massie said that he, along with Representatives Ro Khanna and Teresa Leger Fernández had launched a “discharge petition to collect 218 signatures” to force a vote on the new Act. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Additional reporting by Anna Betts

title: Democratic contender Abdul El-Sayed hits back at JD Vance over ‘evil’ taunt
author: Rachel Leingang
summary: Michigan Senate candidate accuses vice-president of ‘dog whistle’ and says Republican policies are true evil
body_text: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic US Senate candidate in Michigan, has hit back at JD Vance’s onslaught against him, saying it is “evil” to deprive people of healthcare and affordable groceries. The Republican vice-president, in a Monday speech that railed against undocumented immigrants, cast El-Sayed as representative of “terrible evil” and as someone who fights for “one group at the expense of others”. El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim US senator if he wins in November, accused Vance of a “dog whistle” at the Islamophobic attacks he has faced throughout his campaign. While Vance did not directly invoke El-Sayed’s religion during his speech in Sterling Heights, Michigan, the vice-president warned: “There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil. And on the rise in the United States of America today.” El-Sayed retorted in a statement: “Evil is ripping healthcare away from working people in exchange for tax breaks for billionaires. Evil is making people pay more for groceries and gas while pushing for trade wars and actual war. Evil is dividing people for your own gain. Evil is selling out your morals for a little bit of power.” In his speech, Vance repeatedly claimed that El-Sayed prioritized his ethnic group over others, and called attention to comments El-Sayed made after the attack on Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Michigan, earlier this year, where a man rammed a truck filled with gas and fireworks into a synagogue with families inside. As part of his initial response to the attack, El-Sayed noted the attacker had lost family members in an airstrike in Lebanon, saying “hurt people hurt people”. El-Sayed recently said he “made a mistake” and should have issued a statement that solely condemned the attack. Vance said in his speech: “When you have people who start to say my ethnic group deserves something and yours doesn’t, or that ethnic group is good and this other ethnic group is bad, that is how you erode the very foundations of commonality and common citizenship that we need to continue to have the United States be the most powerful and prosperous nation anywhere in the world.” Vance also told El-Sayed to “keep my wife’s name the hell out of your mouth, because she’s way out of your league”. The jab was in response to comments El-Sayed had made about Vance’s family, after the vice-president said in an Ohio speech he would struggle to go back in time and explain the modern Democratic party to his late grandfather, whom he called “Papaw”. In those remarks, Vance baselessly accused El-Sayed of wanting to impose sharia law. After Vance’s comments about Papaw, El- Sayed wrote on X: “So do we think JD is taking [his wife] Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no?” Rightwing commentators called the post racist, and said it was out of bounds to bring up spouses. Usha Vance, who is Indian American, told Fox News that although she had not met her husband’s grandparents, she said Vance’s family was loving to her, and she believed his grandparents would have been loving toward her as well. El-Sayed told CNN on Monday night he would “rather not talk about spouses at all”. But he said he brought up Usha Vance because JD Vance’s political philosophy relies on an idea that some people are “more American” than others. He asked why Vance would invoke his grandfather unless it was to hark back to a time when people like El-Sayed were “less than normal” in American politics. Last month, Trump posted a photo of El-Sayed and his wife alongside one of Trump and his wife, which El-Sayed said was an attempt “to highlight the fact that my wife wears a hijab, as if to make an argument that that’s somehow less American”. Trump used El-Sayed’s full name, which Republicans have done to call attention to his ethnicity and religion, and wrote “two VERY DIFFERENT America’s [sic]”. El-Sayed told CNN: “I believe in an America where any of us – me, his wife, any of us with different color skin or who pray different ways – can be just as American as JD and his Papaw, but he’s not making that argument. “He [Vance] likes to dog-whistle about these things, but when you actually call him out on it, he acts like he would never bring anything like that into our political conversation, despite him and his boss doing that every single day.” The escalating attacks come as Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee, seeks to appeal to moderate Democrats and Jewish Americans following a bruising primary that saw El-Sayed narrowly defeat the pro-Israel congresswoman Haley Stevens. In closing his speech, Vance called on Michigan voters to “reject” El-Sayed, saying he “defends literal terrorism”. Vance urged people to vote for Rogers. “I’m asking you to send the crazy people to the curb, send a message to the elected leadership of the Democratic party that if you want us to vote for you, you’ve got to stop sending us crazy people to represent your party,” Vance said. El-Sayed referred to Vance and Rogers as “sock puppets from Ohio and Florida”, a reference to Vance’s home state and Rogers’ residence in Florida. He said: “We understand what’s at stake, and Michiganders will show you at the ballot box this November when we send Mike Rogers packing.”

title: Democrats warn of ‘hollowed out’ leadership after army chief resigns amid clashes with Hegseth
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Sudden departure of Daniel Driscoll comes after Pentagon chief removed senior officers and blocked promotions, prompting warnings of a leadership crisis
body_text: A senior Senate Democrat accused Pentagon secretary Pete Hegseth of having “hollowed out” the army’s senior ranks after its top civilian leader resigned after months of internal clashes with Hegseth. No official reason was given for army secretary Daniel Driscoll’s departure after 18 months on the job, while thousands of US soldiers are deployed in the Middle East. In a statement on Monday night, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said Driscoll had been “highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda”, citing his work on “readiness and lethality” and his role in Russia-Ukraine negotiations. Democrats and Republicans alike praised Driscoll’s leadership, and, in a statement, the Democratic senator Jack Reed, the ranking member on the Senate armed services committee, said he did “not welcome” Driscoll’s resignation. “It is far past time for President Trump to recognize the lasting harm that Pete Hegseth is inflicting on the Department of Defense,” Reed said. “In the Army alone, he has fired and blocked the promotions of dozens of senior officers without explanation, including Army Chief of Staff General Randy George and half of all four-star generals. “Secretary Hegseth is cultivating a culture where dissent is punished and competence is secondary to personal allegiance.” An army official told CBS News that Driscoll spoke with Trump about the “current state” of the army before submitting his resignation. NBC News, citing a source familiar with the matter, reported that in that conversation Driscoll raised concerns about the army’s transformation and readiness and about Hegseth’s blocking those efforts by firing the generals responsible for them. The public rupture traces back to April, when Hegseth forced out the army’s chief of staff, Gen Randy George, along with two other senior officers. George had worked with Driscoll on the army transformation initiative, an effort to shift the service toward drones and faster weapons acquisition based on lessons from the war in Ukraine. Driscoll later told Congress he considered George “a transformational leader” and said he went to George’s house the day he learned of the firing. Driscoll sought the help of JD Vance, a friend since law school, as tensions with Hegseth deteriorated, the Washington Post reported. Driscoll also told the Post then that he had no plans to leave his post. “I have no plans to depart or resign as the secretary of the army,” he said. Since George’s departure, the army has moved to scale back a drone unit he and Driscoll had championed, returning it to a conventional infantry role, CBS has reported. Hegseth also removed four army colonels from consideration for promotion to brigadier general, over objections from Driscoll and George. Driscoll’s exit adds to a string of senior departures under Hegseth, including navy secretary John Phelan, Southern Command chief Adm Alvin Holsey, and Gen Chris Donahue, who commanded US army forces in Europe and Africa. Sean Parnell, Hegseth’s chief spokesperson, had privately expressed interest in the army secretary post before it became vacant, the Hill has reported, and is among those reportedly under consideration to succeed Driscoll. “The Pentagon right now is in some cases rudderless, without leadership at the senior rungs of the uniform offices and even in the civilian offices,” Representative Jason Crow, a Democrat and former army ranger who serves on the House armed services committee, told reporters. “I’m gravely concerned about it.” Driscoll, an Iraq war veteran who worked in finance and technology before joining the administration, also served as a Trump-appointed negotiator in talks to end the Russian war on Ukraine. Neither the White House nor the Pentagon has said what Driscoll told Trump in their final conversation or how the president responded.

title: Trump homeland security chief says ICE agents could be sent to polling places
author: Maya Yang
summary: Markwayne Mullin says officers could be deployed ‘if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant’
body_text: The US homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, on Tuesday said that federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers could be deployed to polling sites across the country. Speaking to reporters in New York, Mullin said: “ICE isn’t there to patrol the polling places. We’re there to enforce specific threats.” For months, Democrats and voting rights groups have warned that the Trump administration might attempt to deploy federal agents to polling locations in an effort to intimidate voters and depress turnout ahead of the November midterm elections. Although the White House has downplayed such suggestions, Donald Trump has declined to rule it out while continuing to sow doubt about the integrity of past – and future – US elections. “The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said. “ICE’s job is immigration, customs enforcement. That’s their job … if we’re serving a warrant we will be where we need to be.” Federal law prohibits military personnel or other “armed” agents from being “at any place where a general or special election is held”. In a separate statement to Politico, the homeland security department said: “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.” The Guardian has contacted the DHS for additional comment. Mullin’s latest comments follow statements he made in July, when he threatened to withhold federal aid from states that refused to comply with homeland security election directives as part of the administration’s crackdown on what it alleges is widespread voter fraud. “We will scrub all election records, looking for illegal aliens and those who are ineligible to vote, including those that somehow voted, yet they were deceased,” Mullin said earlier this summer, adding: “If states want the grant funding, to recap, they must secure the election.” Yet experts say the administration has failed to offer any proof for its claims of non-citizen voting. In one instance, the DHS officials claimed that there may have been as many as 16,000 non-citizens registered to vote in Nevada, but later admitted they could confirm that only 185 of those people were actually non-citizens, according to records obtained by the Guardian. Meanwhile, Dan Caine, chair of the joint chiefs of staff, recently wrote in a letter that the US military had no plans to deploy troops to polling sites during the upcoming November midterm elections. Caine’s letter came in response to a request for information from Senator Elissa Slotkin amid concerns that the Trump administration could send US military personnel to patrol polling sites. In his letter to Slotkin, Caine said: “The joint force has no plans to send federal military personnel or federalized members of the national guard to polling places during the 2026 elections.” He added that there were “no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material”.

title: Senator Ed Markey wins Massachusetts Democratic primary
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Incumbent, 80, beats back challenge from Seth Moulton, who argued Markey was too old to be effective at his job
body_text: Senator Ed Markey won the Democratic primary in Massachusetts on Tuesday, beating back a challenge from Seth Moulton, a congressman who tried to unseat him by arguing to voters his opponent was too old to be effective at his job. Massachusetts is heavily Democratic, making the senator favored to win a third full term in the November general election, where he faces the Republican nominee, John Deaton. The 80-year-old incumbent, according to the Associated Press, easily defeated his 47-year-old rival, at a moment when Democratic voters agonize over the age of some lawmakers, a concern that was amplified by Joe Biden’s disastrous re-election bid in 2024, and Kamala Harris’s subsequent failure to keep Donald Trump from returning to the White House. In primaries elsewhere in the country this year, Democratic voters unseated a handful of long-serving incumbents in favor of younger, progressive challengers who vowed to break from the party orthodoxy on issues like support for Israel. But the dynamics in Massachusetts were somewhat of a reversal, with Markey being a longtime advocate for progressive causes and Moulton, who was born after Markey was first elected to the House in 1976, staking out more moderate positions on certain issues. The senator is a champion of proposals to create a universal single-payer healthcare system and enact sweeping clean energy policies known as the “Green New Deal”, and had the backing of top congressional progressives, including the Vermont independent senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren, also of Massachusetts. Moulton, who first won election to a north-eastern Massachusetts district in 2014, has not endorsed single-payer healthcare proposals, and shortly before Tuesday’s primary election apologized for saying that he did not want his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete” – comments made after Trump beat Harris in the 2024 election in part by vowing to curb transgender rights. The question of when a lawmaker is too old to continue serving loomed large when the candidates met for a debate in August. “I think everyone watching this debate can see that I’m more energized than I’ve ever been before in my life. I am crisscrossing the state. I’m fighting for families,” the senator said. Moulton said his opponent had spent less time holding town halls and candidate forums, and pounced when the senator replied to a question about what AI tools he used by answering “whatever is inside of my iPhone and my iPad – whatever comes up”. “Senator, if you don’t even know what you’re using on your phone or your iPad, this is why we need a new generation of leaders to regulate these technologies to make sure that they are safe,” Moulton said. In the days before the primary, polls showed Markey with a sizable lead over Moulton. In 2020, the senator had fended off a challenge from congressman Joe Kennedy III, a member of the state’s best-known political dynasty.

title: ‘If he can make money in a tyranny, that’s fine by him’: Francis Fukuyama on Trump, democracy – and changing his mind
author: Jonathan Freedland
summary: The political thinker became famous for declaring the triumph of liberal democracy. Thirty-seven years on, he explains what he really meant and why he made the rare journey from right to left
body_text: There are not many public intellectuals who can say they’ve been cited by Capt James T Kirk of the Starship Enterprise, but Francis Fukuyama is one of them. In Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country, William Shatner’s character is in a reflective mood, and speaks to the Klingon chancellor. “Some people think the future means the end of history,” Kirk muses. “Well, we haven’t run out of history quite yet.” When the film came out in 1991 and in the years that followed, you’d often hear comments like that. They were nods to a thesis so famous it hardly needed spelling out. It debuted in a 15-page essay written by Fukuyama, then a 36-year-old thinktanker, which was published in the National Interest, a right-leaning journal of US foreign policy, in the summer of 1989. There was a question mark in the title: it was called The End of History?. In book form three years later, it became The End of History and the Last Man. But these were subtleties that, as we shall see, got lost. The essay made its author internationally renowned and helped power a career as a political scientist, philosopher and analyst, specialising in foreign policy and political economy. Fukuyama’s counsel was sought by governments and boardrooms worldwide, from the C-suite of Ford to the tent of the Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi. But, as is clear from his new memoir – which is less a conventional autobiography than the story of a life in ideas, one that revisits intellectual shifts and academic schisms and which, by contrast, scarcely mentions the author’s 40-year marriage – it also became something of a millstone. I ask how he feels about that article. Perhaps the way the Beatles might have come to regard their breakthrough hit She Loves You: grateful for the success, but tired of having to replay it, again and again. “Well, a little bit of both,” Fukuyama, now 73, says on a video call from California, via a computer which, incidentally, he built himself. “I certainly think that I would not have gotten the attention that I did if I’d used a different title. So that made a difference.” But there has been a downside. “You know, I get these ridiculous comments, on the internet. If I post a picture of my grandkids, they say, ‘Oh, I thought it was the end of grandkids.’” The problem, as Fukuyama sees it, is a 37-year-old misunderstanding – one that took root as soon as the essay was published. Thanks to that simple, memorable phrase – “the end of history” – people assumed that Fukuyama was arguing that, with the cold war winding down and the Berlin Wall about to fall, human conflict, even human events, were drawing to a close. That all the big arguments had been settled, there would be no more war, and the entire world was about to live under US-style liberal democracy. As he puts it in his new book, In the Realm of the Last Man, it was taken to be an expression of “naive liberal triumphalism, and I have been asked several times a week over the past three decades whether I wished to recant my argument. I have written thousands of words and given dozens of interviews seeking to answer this question.” Indeed, he tells me, that was “one of the reasons for writing the memoir: to finally get down in a very clear way what I was intending and the ways I was wrong, and the ways I believe I’m still right.” The book makes clear his argument was a subtle one, drawn from Hegelian thought and inspired by an earlier interpreter of Hegel, Alexandre Kojève, from whom Fukuyama borrowed that all-important title. According to Kojève, the end of history was the moment when a principle or set of ideas emerged that could not be bettered, in terms of their ability to satisfy the human beings who lived in a system shaped by them. Kojève himself had playfully proposed the year 1806 as the end of history, since that was the moment when, thanks to his defeat of the Prussian monarchy in the Battle of Jena-Auerstedt, Napoleon brought the code that bore his name to the heart of old Europe, the legal framework that emerged from the French Revolution. As Fukuyama writes, the revolution of 1789 “established the underlying principles of a modern liberal order, namely, the two principles of liberty and equality, or the equality of liberty”. Of course, those principles were not immediately or fully implemented: even as Napoleon was advancing in central Europe, the French colonial authorities were putting down a slave revolt in Haiti. “But Kojève’s point was that once the idea of universal freedom got out, it was only a matter of time before those principles became accepted and practised around the world.” Even if the time it took was measured in centuries, with plenty of events – including two world wars – along the way. This was the nature of the argument Fukuyama was making for 1989. Not that liberal democracy was perfect or that it had been achieved everywhere and that all conflict was over. But rather that the evidence had become compelling that there was no better guiding principle or system. And Fukuyama still maintains that view. “For the last 30-odd years, I’ve been saying that I’m looking for an alternative system that purports to be more humanly satisfying than liberal democracy. And a number of candidates have come along. Some of them, I think, are very implausible.” He cites Iranian-style theocracy as one such candidate. The Chinese model is a more serious contender. As an authoritarian system, he says, it can make decisions more efficiently than liberal democracy. “So the question for me is: is this also a sustainable system? Are we going to see this [replicated] in other places in 30 years? And that is still an open question.” If, over the next generation or so, China turns out to be much more successful than the US, with an exportable model that satisfies human needs, then Fukuyama promises he will be “perfectly happy to concede that I was wrong on the fundamental premise”. He also accepts that the current consensus on liberal democracy is far from universal, and that the “liberal” part of that idea – the belief in constraints and checks on elected power – is especially vulnerable. He writes that is in part because support for those constraints has often been contingent on a collective memory of how dangerous the world can become without them. A younger generation who have known only peace and prosperity, and for whom the tyrannies of the mid-20th century are ancient history, will only be dimly aware of the perils of unrestrained, illiberal rule. But surely Donald Trump, born just one year after the defeat of nazism, is living proof that proximity to that dark history hardly entails respect for the guardrails imposed by liberal democracy? How do we explain the US president’s disregard for that danger? “You know, that is one of the great psychological questions that future historians are going to have to answer. He has had this weird attraction not just to the current Russia and Vladimir Putin but, all the way back in the 1980s, he visited Moscow. He took out these full-page ads attacking Nato way back then, when we were still in the middle of the cold war. I mean, it somehow has to do with his lack of any kind of moral compass beyond his own self-interest. He basically worries about whether he can make money, and if you can make money in a tyranny, that’s fine with him.” It’s worth getting to the bottom of what Fukuyama meant all those years ago because, once you’re there, you find an idea more interesting than the soundbite versions of his thesis ever allowed. The final paragraph of his original essay declared: “The end of history will be a very sad time.” With the fundamental question of politics essentially resolved, even if far from realised, “the worldwide ideological struggle that called forth daring, courage, imagination and idealism, will be replaced by economic calculation, the endless solving of technical problems, environmental concerns, and the satisfaction of sophisticated consumer demands.” As Fukuyama writes now: “The being who emerges at the end of history is typically someone stripped of struggle, risk and ambition, someone whom the philosopher Nietzsche labeled the ‘Last Man’. We have been living in the realm of the Last Man for some time now.” Once this notion is unpacked, even those who dispute Fukuyama’s reading of 1989 will concede that he had an uncanny inkling of what was to come. For what he was anticipating was that liberal democratic societies might prove adept at delivering stability and relative material comfort, but that would still leave something profound missing. He cites Socrates’ notion of thymos, or spiritedness: that part of the soul which desires the respect or esteem of other human beings. The last man might have his basic economic needs met, but he would become angry if he believed he was not receiving the recognition that was his due. It amounts to the simple craving for one’s equal dignity to be respected. Reading those passages, it’s hard not to think of the worldwide surge of nationalist populism and the Maga movement in particular. “The mass of the people that come to Donald Trump’s rallies feel that the liberal elites have not been respecting them,” says Fukuyama. “One of the things that propelled Trump to the top of the American political system is his recognition that they were being disrespected, and he found a way of talking to them in a manner that didn’t show that kind of contempt. He doesn’t use big words. He tells stupid stories that they think are very funny, and you know, educated people are appalled by.” This, he says, is a key challenge for Democrats. “If you really want to solve this problem of equally distributed respect … it’s about both listening and talking. I think a lot of elite politicians actually don’t listen to people that are not like themselves. They don’t necessarily listen to ordinary people, and they also don’t know how to speak to ordinary people.” He notes the desperation of Democrats “looking for working-class candidates that they can push” in the November midterm elections, but says the “equal distribution of respect requires both policies that distribute actual material benefits more equally and a different kind of political discourse”. In that context, he likes the look of former Chicago mayor and potential 2028 presidential candidate Rahm Emanuel, a man with a streetfighter’s manner who is also, says Fukuyama, “very funny”. The other defining trait of the last man is the hunger for a cause, for a life-or-death struggle that might give his life meaning. In 1989, Fukuyama anticipated “a powerful nostalgia” for the age when such battles raged, and that too reads like a premonition of our own era. “Fundamentally we’re living in a really weird time,” he says now. He looks back to Germany of the 1930s. “They’d just lost a horrendous war, millions of casualties. Then hyperinflation. Everybody’s savings get wiped out. You have instability on the streets of the Weimar Republic, and so – it’s not an excuse – but you can kind of understand why people would be drawn to extremist ideologies at that point. But that’s not the world we’re living in in 2026. You know, we’re actually pretty stable, peaceful. And yet you find people on both the left and the right that are saying, ‘This is the worst possible world.’ In America we have the Maga right that says that America is dying. It’s being killed by the other side. And it’s very hard to understand how they can argue that with any kind of historical awareness.” For the left, at least, hasn’t the climate crisis played a part in contributing to that mood of existential doom? Fukuyama doubts it. “I am sitting in California. It’s a comfortable 70 degrees [21C]. You know, I’m not burning up like you in Europe, so maybe it’s just my personal situation. But I think that climate still remains a rather abstract thing for many people.” He points the finger in a different direction. “Social media and the internet in general have permitted this vast disconnect between actual material lived reality and what people experience online.” He cites the legions of young men in the manosphere, gaming the days away, simultaneously fed a falsely bleak picture of the world and longing for a cause worth dying for, as an illustration of the phenomenon he warned of in the very last sentence of the 1989 essay: “Perhaps this very prospect of centuries of boredom at the end of history will serve to get history started once again.” There’s a chapter in the new book whose title hints at the other story the memoir tells: On Changing Your Mind. Fukuyama has made the relatively rare political journey from right to left. A former official in the Reagan and Bush administrations, he tells of his time as a disciple of the noted conservative scholar Allan Bloom and as part of the neoconservative gang of thinkers who prepared the intellectual ground for the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Fukuyama renounced his support for that war in February 2004. In the book, he candidly admits that what prevented him from making the break earlier was, in part, less ideological than social and human: he didn’t want to end friendships he had cherished. Still, his departure from the right was not solely in the sphere of foreign policy. While his former colleagues could only see government as an obstacle to be cleared out of the way, his own studies of societies around the world led him to regard a capable state as essential. As if to confirm how far he has travelled, one chapter of the book is titled Learning to Love Bureaucrats. I ask whether his perspective on the world might have differed from other Republicans and conservatives because of his Japanese-American roots, which are detailed affectingly in the book. It tells of his grandmother, a “picture bride” who left Japan at 21 when she was put on a “steamer to Los Angeles all alone, where she was to marry a stranger 10 years older than herself”, and of an uncle left “penniless” after the store he built was effectively confiscated when he, like all Japanese-Americans on the west coast, was interned during the second world war. Did he see things differently because he was a member of an ethnic minority that had suffered a bitter history of exclusion? “No, I don’t think so,” he says immediately. “I’ve tried to avoid thinking of myself as an Asian-American my whole life, because I just don’t like that sort of identity politics. It’s true that, after 11 September, you had certain rightwing people in the United States saying, ‘Well, we ought to put Arab-Americans in camps.’ And, yeah, of course, I felt that that was really wrong based on my family history, but I don’t think that made me especially sensitive to those sorts of issues.” What changed his mind was a changing world. Even if he still thinks the big question has been resolved, events matter. The Iraq war and the crash of 2008 upended his worldview. As he puts it, “If you’re an intellectual and you believe certain things about the use of military force in foreign policy and about unregulated markets in economics, and both of them lead to big disasters, you ought to rethink some of those assumptions.” For Francis Fukuyama, an end to history never meant an end to thinking. • In the Realm of the Last Man by Francis Fukuyama is published by Profile Books (£20) and is out on 8 September. title: The deportation of Milo Yiannopoulos signals a rupture within Maga
author: Moira Donegan
summary: The far-right provocateur helped galvanize a movement that no longer needs him. Now his imitators are claiming victory
body_text: It’s been a long, slow decline for Milo Yiannopoulos. From the vantage point of 2026, it’s easy to forget that he was once a big deal. The British-born far-right provocateur, who was arrested by ICE in Louisiana and deported from the US this week, was among the first media figures to ride the “gamergate” controversy and ensuing rightwing populist wave that brought Donald Trump to office in 2016. An editor of the then ascendant Breitbart News from 2014 to 2017, Yiannopoulous was an early adopter of the media strategy of algorithm-optimized outrage bait, trawling the internet and consulting a large network of well-placed sources in search of stories he could use to fan the flames of online culture war discourses. He would write a story mocking a feminist, or fire off a tweet saying something racist about Muslims, and the ensuing firestorm of controversy would result in online arguments, media coverage, and his own promptly and decisively rising star. Rinse, repeat. Back then, at the start of the Trump era, Yiannopoulous was something of a novelty. Rightwing provocation peddlers had not previously come in his millennial, digitally savvy mold; few others had adopted a fey, gregarious kind of gay male humor for the increasingly theatrical right. But soon, Yiannopoulous was overrun with competitors. The rightwing influencer field became crowded, then saturated. He has spent the past few years at the fringe of the fringe, working for and hobnobbing with a hodgepodge of odious figures who aim to critique Donald Trump from the right, such as the former congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, the white nationalist streamer Nick Fuentes, and the antisemitic rapper who now goes by Ye. In a particularly pathetic bid for relevance, he once declared himself “ex-gay” and set about promoting conversion therapy. His downfall had been a long time coming. Yiannopoulous, often willing to say in vulgar terms what many parts of the American right were only willing to allude to in polite ones, often found himself overstepping. He was banned from Twitter, then from Facebook; he was banned from Australia. In 2017, he resigned from Breitbart and lost a book deal with Simon and Schuster after comments resurfaced in which he claimed that sexual abuse of children by adults could be consensual and “hugely positive experiences”. Yiannopoulous’s comments, which he later apologized for, are not so far out of line from what some on the far right have said about child marriage, or the need to encourage childbirth among teen girls. But Yiannopoulous was talking about boys, not girls, and by then the Maga movement he had helped to galvanize no longer needed him. There were already plenty of Milo imitators, eager to see a rival deposed and ready to fill his grotesque niche. Several of those imitators are now claiming victory, declaring themselves responsible for Yiannopoulous’s recent deportation. Laura Loomer, a far-right influencer, provocateur and conspiracist in Yiannopoulous’s mold, who has become a confidante of Donald Trump, quickly claimed to have orchestrated Yiannopoulous’s arrest. “I reported him to ICE and the FBI,” Loomer posted. “I told you all that Milo was an illegal alien.” As Anna Merlan of Mother Jones reported, two other far-right influencers – who, unlike Yiannopoulous, are still in good standing with the Maga regime – also claimed to have advance knowledge of the DHS’s plans to remove and deport their enemy: Raheem Kassam, a onetime Breitbart UK editor and current Washington DC restaurateur, and Benny Johnson, a Maga-aligned writer and social media personality. There’s reason to take at least Loomer seriously: last year, Trump fired several high-ranking national security officials after their names appeared on a list of alleged enemies that Loomer presented to him in the Oval Office. If these figures’ boasts are true, this would mean, at best, that at least some figures within the DHS are leaking information about what are supposed to be confidential proceedings to online grifters and grievance peddlers, so that those influencers can get in a bit of satisfying mockery online. At worst, it would mean that the country’s massive federal security apparatus is being deployed to settle internet feuds among crackpot influencers. There’s always a bit of schadenfreude to witnessing these incidents, watching the Trump camp dissolve into infighting and treachery, and seeing the amorality, bigotry or cynical opportunism of those who once sided with Trump be punished with a blow to something those actors actually care about: their own status and careers. By now, there have been so many purges and abrupt reversals of fortune for the once-ascendant members of the Maga coalition that it is hardly worth enumerating them all: Trump, it turns out, has done his purging more frequently and unexpectedly, less a single Night of the Long Knives and more a recurring series of Afternoons of the Mean Tweets. But Yiannoupoulous’s downfall is more than just another case of the Maga revolution eating its children. His abrupt arrest and deportation seems, instead, like the product of a bigger rupture within the Trump movement, wherein the isolationist, anti-Zionist, and increasingly antisemitic faction is in revolt against Trump and the neoconservative, expansionist and pro-Israel and pro-military adventurism wing that persuaded him to go to war with Iran. As the unpopular, unwinnable war drags on, sending prices soaring and making it seem more likely that irate voters will look to punish the Republicans in the November midterms, fingers are pointing within the Maga coalition, as major players look to dilute their own responsibility and find someone else to blame. Milo’s deportation might be just one instance in the much uglier fight to come as these figures seek to throw one another under the bus. If they were honorable people, after all, they wouldn’t be in the Trump camp in the first place. Those of us hoping for a sizable Democratic victory might understandably welcome this outcome. Let them fight; let them tear each other to pieces; let them destroy themselves, and nothing of value will be lost. But there is something gruesome, too, about seeing the government deployed this way. It is humiliating to be ruled over by such people – conspiracists and bigots and idiots, people without virtue or competence or even dignity to match their power. They’re all going to suffer in the ugly infighting that’s coming. But we’re all suffering, too. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist
