title: Trump’s threat against an NBC journalist is an attack on reality
author: Margaret Sullivan
summary: The president’s call for the FCC to scrutinize Kristen Welker’s innocuous remarks is a sign of desperation
body_text: With his approval ratings tanking, the crucial midterm elections looming, and his war with Iran turning into a quagmire, Donald Trump has entered full freak-out mode. It’s not hard to tell. Just look at what happened this week when he lashed out at Kristen Welker, the well-respected host of NBC’s Meet the Press, and one of the best-known journalists in the nation. Welker observed recently that Trump – while having significant influence – has a “mixed record” on making successful endorsements this year. An innocuous statement, made in advance of the Sunday show during her analytical comments to a network affiliate station in Washington. But not harmless in Trump’s opinion. Furious, he called on the Federal Communications Commission to go after Welker, saying she “will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment”. In fact, as the Hill newspaper reported this week, while Trump “boasts a 100 percent record in Senate Republican primary contests this election cycle, several of his high-profile gubernatorial picks have lost”. That sounds like a mixed record, doesn’t it? Not to Trump, who called Welker’s comments “purposeful inaccuracy”. “The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation, and I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” he wrote on Truth Social. He later added: “FCC to the rescue.” The threat is absurd. It would seem even more so if Trump had not already been using the agency as a weapon in his long-running campaign against the reality-based press. Carr is a partisan, fully devoted to Trump’s mission, and he has shown himself more than willing to do the bidding of the president who appointed him during this second presidential term. The FCC is intended to be bipartisan and independent but under Trump, it has skewed heavily Maga – and clearly political. Carr himself seems to embrace without embarrassment the role of Trump’s media attack dog. He has warned that he would use the FCC’s power to issue broadcast licenses to go after what he and his boss call “fake news”. The skirmishes are widespread. ABC has sued the FCC, charging that the agency’s early review of eight local broadcast licenses violates the first amendment. The FCC is supposed to adhere to first amendment restrictions in dealing with broadcast licenses or in any punitive measures at all. “While the FCC has the limited ability to revoke stations’ broadcast licenses, it has not done so in over 40 years and its powers do not include revoking licenses because of a disagreement over a viewpoint expressed on the station,” the Washington Post noted this week. It’s no surprise that Trump has singled out Welker for this unwarranted attack. He has a long and shameful history of going after female journalists and seems to particularly relish criticizing female journalists of color. In his first term, his targets included Yamiche Alcindor, then of PBS, April Ryan of American Urban Radio and Abby Phillip of CNN. In one particularly vicious moment, he went after Welker herself during an interview earlier this year, saying: “You’re either crooked or you’re stupid.” This new attack on Welker brings together some of his favorite techniques – trashing a Black female journalist, cracking down on free speech in apparent violation of first amendment protections and using what should be an independent government body (including, of course, the justice department) to carry out his retaliation efforts. Although this new chapter is part of a well-established pattern, it feels especially desperate when seen in context. In recent days, Trump’s efforts to control the media through threats and punishment have ramped up. The administration has barred reporters from three major news organizations from covering the G20 meetings, even as top journalists at Stars and Stripes, the military newspaper with a long history of independence, have been fired. Trump’s reality has turned sour, so he certainly doesn’t want that reality reflected in the news media. Threatening Kristen Welker – like so much of what he’s doing – is obvious over-reach. If the FCC does somehow attempt to punish her or her network, there’s a solid first amendment case to be made in response. NBC, which has staunchly defended Welker, is likely to make it. Welker did nothing wrong, not in terms of the facts and not in terms of her journalistic role. As for Trump, his attacks against the mainstream media will continue. Pointless and misguided as his media revenge tour is, it seems to be all he knows how to do. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

title: Teamsters union leaders support Republicans despite members endorsing Democrats
author: Michael Sainato
summary: Sean O’Brien, president of 1.3 million-strong union, was also first to speak at the Republican national convention in 2024
body_text: The powerful Teamsters union is backing Republican candidates in the 2026 election cycle even after members have voted to support their Democratic opponents. The 1.3 million-strong union’s president, Sean O’Brien, angered many members and union leaders in 2024 when he became the first union president to speak at the Republican national convention (RNC). The latest moves by the union’s leadership are further stoking tensions within the union. “The Republicans have done nothing but take a gun to our head at every turn. And why we think that we can somehow change their behavior, I don’t understand it. It’s not a logical argument,” said John Palmer, who was elected on O’Brien’s slate in 2021 as an at-large vice-president on the Teamsters executive board, but who broke ranks in criticizing O’Brien’s RNC appearance in 2024. “I live in Texas. I’m a moderate guy, but I know when somebody’s trying to cut my throat.” The national union declined to make an endorsement in the 2024 presidential election for the first time since 1996, claiming a majority of members supported Trump after they supported Biden in 2020, though Teamsters locals and councils representing 1 million members at the union independently endorsed Harris. So far this election cycle, O’Brien has made two personal contributions – both to Republicans. O’Brien donated $1,000 to the Republican US Senate campaign of Scott Brown in New Hampshire on 19 February 2026. Brown appeared on O’Brien’s podcast, Better Bad Ideas, on 25 February. The only Teamsters’ local in New Hampshire, Teamsters Local 633, endorsed Brown’s Democratic rival Chris Pappas for the Senate race in April 2025. Teamsters Local 633 did not respond to multiple requests for comment. O’Brien also made a $1,000 donation in May 2025 to another Republican, Markwayne Mullin, now Trump’s secretary of the Department of Homeland Security. The two have clashed spectacularly in the past. During a US Senate hearing in November 2023, Mullin challenged O’Brien to a fight while reading aloud social media posts made by O’Brien that were critical of Mullin. After Trump’s 2024 election win, Mullin and O’Brien publicly made amends during Lori Chavez Deremer’s confirmation hearings for secretary of labor in February 2025. Teamsters local members and the Teamsters leadership are differing on endorsements in several key races. In April, the Pennsylvania Conference of Teamsters voted by voice to endorse Paige Cognetti, Scranton’s Democratic mayor, in her congressional race in Pennsylvania’s eighth congressional district. “As mayor, Paige has taken on special interests and fought for reform. She turned down a [city-issued] car, eliminated cash payments and cut costs, leading to budget surpluses and a credit rating that went from junk to investment-grade,” Bill Hamilton, president of the Pennsylvania Conference of Teamsters, said at the state union’s annual meeting where they endorsed Cognetti. But the Teamsters’ political action committee (Pac) subsequently endorsed Rob Bresnahan, a Republican congressman, following a $5,000 donation to his campaign in May 2026. Bresnahan appeared on O’Brien’s podcast in January 2026. Following the endorsement, Hamilton released a statement backing Bresnahan. “Rep Bresnahan has always had our backs, particularly when he played a critical role in the successful bipartisan push to pass the Faster Labor Contracts Act in the House of Representatives,” Hamilton said in a statement in June 2026, which did not address his conflicting endorsement of Cognetti. “The Teamsters support candidates who support us regardless of their party affiliation, and for that reason Robert Bresnahan has our unwavering endorsement.” Hamilton did not respond to multiple requests for comment. In August, O’Brien visited the congressional district and added an endorsement of his own for Bresnahan. In June, O’Brien announced the Teamsters were endorsing Chris Swanson for governor of Michigan. He lost easily in the Democratic primary to Jocelyn Benson, who had received endorsements from Teamsters Locals 283, 406, 243, 1038, 247 and 337 in Michigan, the majority of the union’s locals in the state. The Teamsters have also thrown their weight behind Max Miller, Ohio’s beleaguered Republican congressman. Miller has faced resignation calls from his own party over domestic abuse allegations and has argued in court filings that allegations made by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, daughter of the Republican US senator Bernie Moreno, have cost him union support in his re-election bid against ironworker Brian Poindexter. Miller was among 16 congressional Republicans who met with O’Brien at a roundtable discussion in November 2024, as the Teamsters under O’Brien have refrained from criticizing actions by the Trump administration that have been opposed by the majority of the largest labor unions in the US. In July 2026, the Ohio Conference of Teamsters announced its endorsements, which included Miller, citing his vote for the union-backed Faster Labor Contracts Act, though Miller’s lifetime voting score on labor issues is rated at 14% by the AFL-CIO. The Ohio Conference of Teamsters did not respond to multiple requests for comment. O’Brien’s 2024 appearance at the RNC marked a shift from his rhetoric when he ran to lead the union in 2021, when he called Trump “our enemy” and criticized the previous Teamsters leadership for not doing enough to stand up to Trump’s first administration. O’Brien defended the appearance at the RNC as the union has since shifted toward supporting more Republicans, even as the Trump administration has taken several actions undermining labor unions and collective bargaining rights, including an ongoing attempt to eliminate collective bargaining rights for more than 1 million federal workers. O’Brien faced an attempted challenge to his leadership earlier this year, but the slate of candidates failed to receive the 5% of delegates required to make the ballot. O’Brien’s slate was then re-elected, unopposed, to another five-year term. O’Brien and the Teamsters did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

title: First Thing: US-Iran hostilities resume amid concerns at Hegseth’s military leadership
author: Martin Belam
summary: Leading Democrat accuses secretary of defense of causing ‘lasting harm’ to US forces
body_text: Good morning. The US has launched more airstrikes on Iranian targets, prompting counterstrikes by Tehran targeting American interests in Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan and Iraq. The six-month conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before this weekend’s strikes, but recent promises by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly the conflict could spill back into military action. The Iranian Red Crescent said four people, including a child, were killed and more than 50 were injured when shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a home where a wedding celebration was taking place in the city of Kuhestak. The US central command spokesperson Capt Tim Hawkins said: “The US military never targets civilians.” Why are there concerns about US military leadership? A senior Democrat accused Pete Hegseth of having “hollowed out” the army’s senior ranks after its top civilian leader, Daniel Driscoll, resigned. Senator Jack Reed said: “It is far past time for Trump to recognize the lasting harm Pete Hegseth is inflicting on the Department of Defense … cultivating a culture where dissent is punished and competence is secondary to personal allegiance.” How do officials appear to have profited from AI stocks? Emil Michael, a Pentagon official who is overseeing military artificial intelligence policy, reaped profits this year of up to $24m by selling his private investment in Elon Musk’s AI company. He has now sold his holdings in another AI company for between $5m and $25m, according to records seen by the Guardian. Trump homeland security chief says ICE agents could be sent to polling places In another move that threatens to intimidate voters at November’s midterms, the US homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, on Tuesday said that federal immigration and customs enforcement (ICE) officers could be deployed to polling sites across the country. Mullin said: “ICE’s job is immigration, customs enforcement. If we’re serving a warrant we will be where we need to be.” In a separate statement, the department said: “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.” Federal law prohibits military personnel or other “armed” agents from being “at any place where a general or special election is held”. What has a whistleblower identified as a risk to mail-in ballots? A new system to screen millions of mail-in ballots for the midterms was thrown together so hastily, and tested so little, that a single scanning glitch could mean entire batches of ballots are turned away, a whistleblower has told Congress. Tucson police investigate deadly shooting outside gay bar as hate crime Authorities in Tucson, Arizona, are investigating a shooting outside a gay bar that left three people dead as a possible hate crime. Police said: “Initial evidence suggests the suspect confronted the victims in the parking lot. The suspect was in possession of a note with several LGBTQIA+ associated businesses written on it. The department is currently investigating this homicide as a hate crime.” What is the latest legal setback to the Trump administration’s attack on LGBT+ rights? A federal judge has dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit challenging California’s policy of allowing transgender youth to play on sports teams. The justice department had been fighting for a year to force California to ban trans girls from women’s sports, with the president directly singling out one trans track and field athlete in online attacks. US officials defend Venezuela oil deal amid questions over rebuilding plan Trump administration officials have defended a highly contentious deal giving the US control of a significant chunk of Venezuelan oil reserves. Last week, Donald Trump announced a deal that would give the US “majority” control over 65bn barrels – roughly one-fifth – of Venezuela’s oil reserves. US officials said the agreement would create a stable economic platform to restore Venezuelan democracy after nearly three decades of autocratic rule, but the pact has provoked outrage among Venezuela’s opposition, already furious that democracy has yet to return to the country eight months after the removal of Nicolás Maduro by US special forces. In other news … The accused in the killing of Charlie Kirk, Tyler Robinson, must stand trial and is eligible for the death penalty, a judge has ruled. The Democratic contender Abdul El-Sayed has hit back at JD Vance after the vice-president described him as representative of “terrible evil”. The incumbent senator Ed Markey, 80, has won the Massachusetts Democratic primary despite his opponent claiming he was too old to be effective. Tiger Woods is set to change his not guilty plea in the DUI case stemming from a crash in Florida this year. A federal judge dismissed the remaining claims against Lizzo’s production company, declaring the case brought by her former wardrobe stylist could not proceed. Stat of the day: USS Abraham Lincoln arrives at Thai port after gruelling 270 days at sea The US aircraft carrier at the center of a row over conditions on board after months at sea as part of Trump’s war against Iran has finally arrived at a Thai port. Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health on the vessel have made headlines around the world. Well Actually: How do you define good health – and achieve it – in a broken US medical system? Elle Hunt speaks to Dr Lucy McBride, whose new book aims to help people navigate US healthcare – and to tread carefully in the wellness industry. Don’t miss this: As Nepal’s morgues fill, Parkrit hopes her DNA can be used to find her mother Cait Kelly has been in Kathmandu in the aftermath of the devastating floods in Nepal. A week on from the disaster, she reports how authorities are urging relatives of the thousands of missing and dead to provide blood samples. … or this: Modern Family’s Mitch and Cam on their hilarious and groundbreaking love The on-screen love between Mitchell (Jesse Tyler Ferguson) and Cameron (Eric Stonestreet) in Modern Family was a rare example of a gay couple raising a child on TV. Hannah Verdier has spoken to the two actors whose chemistry made them one of the most adored on-screen couples of the era. Climate check: Global heating will hit at least 1.8C, UN warns, and there are ‘no good outcomes’ A report by the UN Environment Programme has confirmed overshooting the 1.5C goal inscribed in the Paris agreement is now “unavoidable”. It said the best hope to limit the impact was to adopt an “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway, but that human health, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure and economies could all be severely damaged, and some losses would be irreversible. Last Thing: Australian police investigate after 5,500 sheep stolen from farm It sounds like a heist at an incredible scale. Queensland police are investigating after about 5,500 Dorper sheep worth more than $1.2m USD were allegedly stolen from a farm in western Queensland. title: Trump’s ridiculous bullying of Canada is backfiring
author: Robert Reich
summary: The US president’s need to assert dominance is igniting patriotism abroad and a backlash at home
body_text: What do bullies do when someone stands up to their bullying and punches them in the face? They look for someone weaker to bully who won’t punch back. Presumably that’s why Donald Trump has now taken on Canada, after Iran punched back so hard in the cage match the US president began more than six months ago as to leave him humiliated and baffled. Trump wants to be the bully who humiliates others and forces them into submission. Needing to assert his dominance, Trump has now started a trade war with our northern neighbor, friend, second-largest trading partner (after Mexico) and, at least until now, reliable ally. He’s hammering Canada on his Truth Social and in media appearances, saying Canada has “ripped off” the US for years, and signing an order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”. This is pure bunk, of course – more empty Trump bravado and ignorant belligerence. Canada? Really? If Mel Brooks were still making movies, this would be a comedy. But as all else with Trump, it’s no laughing matter. Trump apparently assumed that Canada would quickly surrender because it had more to lose. The tariffs Trump has imposed on Canada – along with those he’s threatening if Canada retaliates – affect a tiny portion of the US’s total imports but a huge portion of Canada’s total exports. Jamieson Greer, Trump’s US trade representative, says the duties are too small to pose a problem for the US and are “more [Canada’s] emergency than ours”. But bullies like Trump rarely think about the effects of their bullying on the thinking and attitudes of their targets. Trump’s bullying of Iran has not only reinforced its hardline regime but shown them that control over the strait of Hormuz is an effective means of gaining concessions from other Gulf states as well as the US, and likely strengthened their resolve to build a nuclear weapon. Trump’s bullying of Canada, meanwhile, is igniting a patriotism that has often eluded that nation, which separatist factions have long threatened to pull apart. Mark Carney’s decision to stand up to Trump – through “dollar for dollar” retaliation on goods coming from key industries in states including Ohio and Texas with competitive Senate elections – has led to a surge of support for the prime minister’s Liberal party. Liberals won three special by-elections on Monday. Trump’s trade war with Canada has also dimmed the prospects of Canada’s separatist movements, at least in the short term. A candidate from Carney’s Liberal party edged out a Quebec separatist in one of Monday’s special by-elections, in a district hit hard by US tariffs. This is a good omen for Canada before 5 October’s vote in Quebec on whether the province’s secessionist party, Parti Québécois, gains additional seats in the province’s legislative body, and 19 October’s vote in Alberta on whether to hold a referendum to secede from the rest of Canada. Trump may also have underestimated the negative reactions to his trade war at home. According to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll, 57% of Americans ‌oppose Trump’s moves to impose tariffs on Canadian imports. About 63% oppose his peevish order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”. Only 20% support the higher tariffs on Canadian goods. The negative response is especially pronounced in border states whose economies are tightly interconnected with Canada. In Michigan, for example, where overwhelming majorities oppose Trump’s tariffs on Canada, Democrats have launched new attack ads on the Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers for refusing to denounce the tariffs. The Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed called Trump an “asshole” for launching the trade war. There’s still time for the US and Canada to avoid the worst of the economic and political fallout from this. Carney’s “dollar for dollar” retaliation goes into effect on 8 September but Trump’s counter-counter measure – threatened 50% tariffs on autos and auto parts – won’t go into effect until New Year’s Day. Still, no one should expect an easy resolution to what may go down in history as the stupidest of all the stupid foreign policies Trump has initiated. And given the extent of Trump’s dumb international moves, that is saying something. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK • This article was amended on 2 September 2026. An earlier version said the provincial election in Quebec is on 8 October, but it will be on 5 October.

title: Taxing the banks: what Europe’s windfall levies brought in as Burnham eyes his next move
author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
summary: Ahead of a crucial budget, four countries’ experiments offer a mixed verdict on how to tax bumper profits
body_text: The countdown is on. Two months out from Andy Burnham’s inaugural autumn budget, bank executives are wringing their hands over whether the government will target their bumper profits with fresh taxes. The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly considering a windfall tax on both banks and oil companies in the late October Westminster setpiece. The UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group – have generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years, largely off the back of rising interest rates. They are now in the crosshairs of campaigners – including the Trades Union Congress (TUC) and campaign group Positive Money – who say a tax increase could help cover rising household bills as part of Burnham’s drive to tackle the cost of living. The TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, who has been pushing hard for a new bank tax said: “Britain’s largest banks are making a fortune. Not because they’ve suddenly become more competitive or improved their services to customers, but because high interest rates mean that, right now, they can sit back and watch the money roll in. Inflated mortgages are fuelling record bonus pots. “With energy bills edging towards record highs this winter, the government is going to need to provide more support for households – and taxing banks’ windfall profits is the obvious way to pay for it.” Any move in the UK would echo similar efforts in mainland Europe to make lenders pay more tax to help offset surging living costs and higher defence spending. Here are some of the tools different governments used, as well as the benefits and pitfalls of targeting the profits of some of the world’s largest banks. Spain: taxed and undeterred Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, revealed plans for a windfall tax in 2022 that would raise €3bn from banks over the following two years to help alleviate cost-of-living pressures. It spooked investors, wiping more than €5bn off the value of Spanish-listed bank stocks, but politicians pushed ahead: putting a 4.8% “solidarity tax” on the domestic revenue of banks whose income passed €800m. That included fees and net interest income, – the amount of money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits. The €800m threshold and the focus on domestic revenues meant it broadly excluded small local banks and most foreign lenders’ Spanish operations. Big banks and lobby groups filed legal challenges over the tax, while the European Central Bank (ECB) warned that Spain risked disrupting monetary policy, and damaging lenders’ capital positions, which help to cushion the blow of economic shocks. Politicians eventually decided to extend the levy a further three years to 2027, after successfully raising €1.3bn in the first year, and €1.7bn in 2024. Banks now face a sliding tax rate of between 1% and 7%, with the highest rate hitting lenders such as Banco Santander whose annual revenue from interest and fees surpassed €5bn. The extension triggered a fresh spate of legal challenges by banks and lobbyists, and criticism from both the International Monetary Fund and ECB, which warned it could hit bank profits, push up borrowing costs for low-income households, and make Spain’s banks less competitive on the international stage. Lithuania: a defence spending boost Lithuania’s government decided to roll out its own windfall tax on banks in 2023, after forecasts showed lenders were due to rake in €1.3bn in net profits that year. That was three times higher than 2022, following a surge in interest rates sparked by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The 60% tax, which applied to any net interest income that was 50% higher than the previous four-year average, was used to fund infrastructure projects and boost defence spending amid Russian threats. Politicians agreed to exclude income from any newly agreed loans, to prevent a situation where banks stopped issuing mortgages and business loans to avoid paying tax. The levy helped raise about €250m in 2023 and €247m in 2024, representing 0.3% of the country’s annual GDP, before being extended by an extra year. The European Commission appeared to support the move, saying it helped cut public debt at a time of regional security threats. But the tax is said to have spooked foreign firms, with the central bank having repeatedly tried to lure new lenders “with no significant success”, according to an EU report. The banking sector said it also disadvantaged lenders serving local customers, while letting others such as Revolut, which is registered in the country but serves mostly non-residents, off the hook. Czechia: ‘unrealistic expectations’ Czechia announced its own three-year windfall tax on banks to help cover consumers’ soaring electricity and gas prices in 2022. The temporary measure, lasting from 2023 to 2025, involved a 60% tax on any profits that were more than double (120%) the previous four-year average. Deeply unpopular with businesses, the tax also caused friction within the far-right ODC civic democratic party, which said it was interfering with the free market and contradicted core conservative values. Czech finance minister, Zbyněk Stanjura, talked about scrapping the tax a year earlier than planned, but later admitted the levy had not yet covered state costs linked to the energy crisis. While the finance ministry originally hoped to collect more than 30bn Czech koruna from the country’s six largest banks, it quickly became clear they would fall short of those targets. “It is unclear whether this was due to unrealistic expectations driven by a vision of easy extra revenue and convenient scapegoating of big corporations, or whether the delayed implementation of the tax (from 2022 to 2023) and the behavioural responses by businesses were not duly considered,” the law firm A&O Shearman said in a 2024 report. The country ended up raising just 1bn Czech koruna, months before the tax expired in December 2025, according to figures reported by local broadcaster Ct24. Italy: a tax that fell flat While plans for a windfall tax by prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s rightwing government gained international attention, it was one of the least effective levies. Meloni’s team shocked markets in August 2023 after revealing plans for a 40% tax on banks’ net interest margin. The move drew the ire of banking lobby groups and wiped €10bn off shares in financial services companies, forcing politicians to water down the proposal a day later with a cap that halved the estimated tax takings to €2.5bn, from €4.9bn. The rules eventually came into force in October that year, but not before being diluted further. Banks – which are already subject to higher corporation and regional taxes in Italy – were allowed to choose one of two options: pay a tax equivalent to 0.26% of the risky assets on their balance sheets – ensuring those with safer loans paid less – or keeping the money on their balance sheets but putting aside two-and-a-half times that amount into their own reserves to cushion the blow of any economic shock. Unsurprisingly, all banks chose to put the money in reserve, scuppering original hopes that extra funds could help support mortgage holders and cut taxes. However, Italy’s deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, has now revived plans for a new tax three-year levy, that would involve a 5% tax on the profits of Italy’s 10 largest banks. What if the UK followed suit? If current trends continue, the UK’s four largest banks will rake in £60bn in profits for 2026. Windfall taxes have been used on banks in the UK before, notably in the early 1980s when Margaret Thatcher’s then chancellor, Geoffrey Howe, accused high street banks of escaping the recession and in the 1990s by Labour chancellor Gordon Brown to generate extra revenue. Calculations by campaign group Positive Money suggest that the UK could raise up to £10.9bn this year from adopting Czechia’s model; up to £6.95bn by following Spain’s sliding tax scale; and £2.2bn by following in Lithuania’s footsteps. “Plenty of countries have successfully taxed banks’ windfall profits,” the TUC’s Nowak said. “We’re calling for an increase in the bank surcharge to raise billions for the Treasury to cut bills across the country. This is an easy win for government – and the chancellor should ask the banks to pay a fairer share”. The world’s most powerful banker, JP Morgan boss, Jamie Dimon, has repeatedly warned the UK government against increasing taxes on banks. The chief executive of lobby group UK Finance, David Postings, said the banking sector “is a major contributor to the public finances, paying over £43bn in tax last year,” a figure which includes income tax payouts on staff salaries. “Banks based here already pay a corporation tax surcharge and the bank levy, giving them a higher total tax rate than in other major financial centres. Increasing sector‑specific taxes would risk damaging the UK’s international competitiveness and make it harder to attract investment.”

title: What’s really behind Trump’s deference to Putin?
author: Luke Harding
summary: Whether or not US president fits the definition of a Russian asset, his actions align closely with the Kremlin’s interests
body_text: Could Donald Trump be a Russian asset? The headline on a review in the Guardian of my new book Betrayal has provoked heated international debate. Written by the historian Lawrence Freedman, the piece generated thousands of comments from across Europe and beyond on social media. Many people responded with a single word: “Duh!” Trump’s relationship with Vladimir Putin is the biggest mystery in international politics. In 2017 I wrote a book called Collusion, which set out Moscow’s operation to support and cultivate Trump, going back decades. The US president, of course, denies links with Russia. But in his second term, his behaviour towards Putin has been as weird and perplexing as during his first. For example, at the Alaska summit last year the US president applauded his Russian counterpart, meeting him at Anchorage airport and rolling out a red carpet. Trump seemed uncharacteristically nervous, as he waited for Putin to emerge from his plane. At their joint press conference after talks, he allowed the Russian president to speak first. It was a bizarre act of deference. Why? There are, I think, overlapping reasons for Trump’s submissive behaviour. I explore them in Betrayal, (which is published this week in Denmark by Politikens Forlag, with Italian, Finnish and Ukrainian language editions to follow.) As I mentioned in a Q&A with Guardian readers, one factor is ideological: Trump’s Maga supporters see Russia as an “anti-woke” kindred state. Putin leans into this idea, positioning himself as a defender of conservative values, under threat from a decadent and godless Europe. High-profile Trump supporters have travelled to Moscow. Erstwhile Maga cheerleader and former Fox News host Tucker Carlson even absurdly praised the Russian capital’s well-stocked supermarkets. Another explanation – advanced by Fiona Hill, the former White House adviser – is strongman envy. Trump would like Putin’s freedom of action, when it comes to making money and crushing opponents. It is evident the US president prefers the company of autocrats. By contrast he frequently badmouths European democrats, among them the former British PM Keir Starmer (“no Churchill”), and Giorgia Meloni (“I felt sorry for her”.) A third theory is kompromat, a KGB term to describe potential compromising material. We know from declassified records that the Czechoslovakia secret police began spying on Trump in the 1970s, when he married a woman from behind the iron curtain. He visited Moscow in 1987, on a trip organised by a Soviet state agency, and subsequently made many visits to Russia including in 2013 for the Miss Universe beauty pageant. What exactly happened on these excursions is unclear. But I know from my own experience in Moscow – I was the Guardian’s bureau chief from 2007 to 2011 – that Russia’s intelligence agencies are adept at surveillance operations. Shortly after I arrived, the FSB broke into the apartment I shared with my wife and our two children. They left clues, busting open the window in my son’s bedroom, with a perilous drop to the courtyard below. The British embassy advised us our home was bugged. Possibly, Putin’s ghost-like spies had installed video cameras too, we were told. Over the next four years we experienced on-off harassment from a shadowy and paranoid state. There were mysterious break-ins, veiled threats from foreign ministry officials, and a summons to visit Lefortovo, the FSB’s infamous pre-detention centre and gloomy prison. Undoubtedly, the KGB and FSB will have spied on Trump too, as well as on other high-profile foreign guests. A 2020 report by the US Senate intelligence committee alleged that the FSB has secret cameras inside the Ritz-Carlton hotel, where Trump stayed during his 2013 trip. There will be tapes. They may be innocuous. But Putin knows what they show, and Trump knows that Putin knows. *** Consequences remain the same Does this make Trump an asset? My conclusion is that the terminology doesn’t much matter. As the chess champion Garry Kasparov notes, if Trump were an asset, or an agent of influence, what exactly would he do differently? Since 2025 he has stopped direct US military aid to Kyiv, humiliated Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Oval Office, and repeated Kremlin lies and disinformation. The US president’s Russia-friendly actions have consequences. I have been visiting Kyiv for nearly two decades, and have spent much of the past five years reporting from Ukraine and the frontline. I was in the capital in February 2022 when Putin tried to seize it. Since then, the conflict has evolved. It is no longer fought with armoured vehicles and tanks, and has become instead a hi-tech aerial battle. Most nights, Russia bombards Kyiv with kamikaze drones and ballistic missiles. Ukraine, meanwhile, carries out its own long-range strikes. It has the world’s most innovative drone and counter-drone industry. But Kyiv badly lacks US-made Patriot interceptors – the only system capable of shooting down fast-moving ballistic missiles. Trump refuses to send Patriots or allow Kyiv to develop its own version under licence. And so civilians die – families, elderly couples, teenagers – entombed under the ruins of pulverised apartment blocks. At night you hear explosions, a moped-like growl from enemy drones, and booms from Ukrainian air defence. Asset or not, Trump is doing little to make this horror stop. Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest, is published in the UK by Guardian Faber. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. title: Pete Hegseth criticized for body-shaming Canadian cadets: ‘Literally they’re kids’
author: Richard Luscombe
summary: US defense secretary faces backlash for attempting to mock Canada’s armed forces amid trade war
body_text: A social media post by Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, body-shaming female members of a Canadian youth development program remained online on Wednesday despite a furious backlash on both sides of the border. On Monday night, Hegseth posted on X a photograph of two people in uniform with a Canadian flag and the caption “this is real”, an apparent attempt at mocking the country’s armed forces amid the Trump administration’s trade spat with its northern neighbor. However, the photograph was reproduced from an Instagram post by the Vernon Cadet Training Centre in British Columbia, which hosted a summer camp in July for teenagers learning adult skills on the military base. Its subjects are not members of Canada’s frontline military, and the person whose appearance Hegseth was attempting to ridicule is likely a volunteer instructor, critics said. The girl receiving a medal is a teenager no older than 18. The post, widely seen as part of a Trump administration “bullying campaign” over the trade war, was immediately condemned by officials in Canada and in the US. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, called it “beneath the office” of the secretary of defense. Responding on Tuesday to attacks on his country by US government officials, including Donald Trump’s attempt to rename Lake Ontario by executive order, Carney told reporters it was time for Washington to “start being serious” about efforts to de-escalate trade tensions. “When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” he said. David Eby, the premier of British Columbia, echoed Carney’s sentiment. “It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to,” he said. The civilian Army Cadet League of Canada accused Hegseth of online harassment. “Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable,” the group said in a statement. Adam Kinzinger, the former Republican US congressman and a military veteran, was even more outspoken in a post on X. “Literally they’re kids. This is a cadet program and our ass hat of a Secdef is making fun of children,” he wrote. “MAGA [Make America Great Again] males are betas who have to punch down to feel big.” Ruben Gallego, the Democratic Arizona senator and a former marine, called the post “stupid” and “disrespectful”. Danny O’Regan, a Canadian veteran writing on X, also criticized the post. “The Secretary of Defence is body shaming cadet groups,” he said. “This is not a military unit. They are kids looking for adventure, test themselves and align themselves with the values of service. Don’t be a Pete.” The Pentagon, meanwhile, defended Hegseth. On Tuesday, Jacob Bliss, the defense department’s deputy press secretary, said: “The X post speaks for itself.” The incident comes as Hegseth faces increasing pressure on several fronts. The US army chief Dan Driscoll resigned this week, reportedly after months of internal clashes with Hegseth. Democrats have accused the defense secretary of having “hollowed out” the military’s senior ranks. On Wednesday, Iran accused the US of a “war crime” after four people were killed, including a four-year-old child, and dozens injured in a reported missile strike on a wedding at a home in the south of the country. The ongoing Iran war has also left the US with a “beyond critical” shortage of missile interceptors, the Associated Press reported, sparking fears among Nato allies of increasing vulnerability to a potential Russian military attack. Hegseth has previously been critical of body shapes in the US military, telling senior commanders in Virginia last year that “fat troops are tiring to look at”. Ordering military officials to crack down on a lack of physical fitness, he said: “It’s tiring to look out at combat formations, or really any formation, and see fat troops.”

title: ‘He’s a good man’: George Clooney defends Mark Ruffalo in Paramount-Warner Bros merger row
author: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent
summary: ‘I worry whenever big companies are consolidating,’ Clooney said at Venice film festival, supporting Ruffalo’s right to criticise the deal amid antisemitism accusations
body_text: George Clooney has defended Mark Ruffalo’s right to criticise the proposed $111bn Paramount takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, saying he is concerned about the consequences of further consolidation in Hollywood. Speaking in Venice ahead of receiving the festival’s Golden Lion for lifetime achievement, Clooney said he supported Ruffalo’s “ability to speak freely” about the proposed merger, while expressing his own doubts about the deal. “I worry when a big company swallows up another company,” Clooney said. “I always worry whenever big companies are consolidating because it means a lot of people are going to lose their jobs.” Ruffalo has emerged as one of the most outspoken opponents of the Paramount-Warner Bros deal. In a social media post last month, the Marvel star attacked the proposed merger over its potential consequences for Hollywood, while also turning his criticism on the family behind Paramount. David Ellison, the company’s chief executive, is the son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, and Ruffalo accused the Ellison family of being complicit the “genocide” of Palestinians, arguing that it was “built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle”. Ruffalo highlighted Oracle’s ties to the Israeli military, sharing a video of the company’s executive vice-chair and Paramount board member Safra Catz discussing technologies Oracle had used after the 7 October Hamas attack on Israel. His comments prompted a backlash from Paramount, which accused him of invoking antisemitic tropes. Ruffalo rejected the accusation and has continued to defend his criticism of the deal and of Oracle’s business ties to Israel. More than 170 Jewish artists, academics and public figures subsequently signed an open letter defending the actor and warning against attempts to silence criticism of Israel or the proposed merger. “I support Mark Ruffalo’s ability to speak freely,” Clooney said. “I think that that’s ridiculous. We’re not going to ban speech. I believe in free speech even when I completely disagree with it. That’s important, right? In fact, it’s part of how a democracy works. “There are going to be people tonight in the room that are going to disagree with most everything I say or stand for. Fair enough. That’s how it’s supposed to be. We’re supposed to argue these things out and come to a conclusion based on the information that we take in … I will always support Mark Ruffalo’s ability to speak freely. I like him. He’s a good man.” Clooney said he did not believe the Paramount-Warner deal necessarily made financial sense. “I don’t know how this goes through. There are so many issues involved,” he said. Clooney also warned that artificial intelligence will become “a very big part of this industry” but will “hurt us in a lot of ways”. He joked: “I would like to avoid being in a tampon commercial 20 years after I’m dead.” The prominent Trump critic said the US midterm elections in November “should be a check and balance”, adding that in 2028 “with any luck, we’ll have some restoration into normalcy”. He also raised concerns about the concentration of media ownership among the world’s wealthiest people. Asked about the state of journalism, he pointed to Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, owner of the Washington Post, and Elon Musk, owner of X. Clooney will accept the lifetime achievement award on Wednesday evening. It is a striking case of life imitating art: last year, he attended the festival for Noah Baumbach’s Jay Kelly, in which he played an ageing Hollywood star travelling to Italy to receive a lifetime achievement honour. Clooney will now undergo the same ritual in real life, with Laura Dern – his Jay Kelly co-star – presenting the award. The honour caps a relationship with Venice stretching back almost three decades. Clooney first appeared at the festival with Out of Sight in 1998 and has returned with films including Good Night, and Good Luck, Michael Clayton and Gravity.

title: Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding
author: William Christou in Beirut
summary: Blast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilities
body_text: Iran has accused the US of a war crime after a missile blast killed at least four people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikes prompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities. Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people. Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi. “It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride, told Mehr News. A video of the aftermath shows colourful wedding streamers and decorations strewn across the ground, and shoes abandoned in the rush to escape the attack. “You wicked people have attacked people’s homes and turned their wedding ceremony into a funeral,” said a man filming the aftermath of the strike, shared by Fars news agency. The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”. The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”. “If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X. The US attacks followed strikes on Sunday, ending a month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran, and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets, including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets. Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devastating” retaliation. Videos of the aftermath of the strike show a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watching as injured children were being treated. “When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency. A woman with her hands decorated in henna for the nuptials posted a video on Instagram after the attack, saying “my hands and feet are still shaking”. A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”. In February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation. Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to show the internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst, identified some of the remnants as belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missile touted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate”. It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footage captured at least six strikes in the area within a minute. A separate strike appeared to hit a communications tower about 150 metres away from the home. Authorities said that several “telecommunications and internet towers and sites were also seriously damaged in the latest strikes”. The US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply. Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board. In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.

title: Democratic party infighting engulfs center-right over House rules vote
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: While leaders focused on Hasan Piker, two of the party’s more conservative members salvaged a GOP measure that was poised to fail
body_text: House Democratic leaders have spent the past few weeks waging a bitter campaign against their own left flank over a leftwing streamer. On Tuesday, it was the party’s center-right who blindsided them. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, announced late on Tuesday that he had asked the Democratic caucus’s committee on caucus rules to consider punishing the retiring Jared Golden of Maine and Blue Dog Coalition leader Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington after the pair sided with Republicans on a procedural vote that had appeared doomed. “The decision by two of our colleagues to blindside the entire House Democratic caucus and join with the Republican majority to pass a procedural rule on the brink of failing represents a significant breach of trust,” Jeffries said in a joint statement issued with the Democratic whip, Katherine Clark, and the caucus chair, Pete Aguilar. “It necessitates a serious response, and we have asked the committee on caucus rules to take this up in short order.” The rebellion lands at an awkward moment for Jeffries. For much of the past few weeks, he and other senior Democrats have trained their fire on the party’s left, repeatedly condemning Hasan Piker, a leftwing streamer, over remarks about antisemitism and the 11 September attacks that he says were taken out of context. That campaign has drawn accusations from progressives that leadership is picking an unwinnable fight with a Twitch personality while ignoring bigger political threats. On Tuesday, the bigger threat to comity turned out to come from the party’s center-right instead. The vote in question was a routine procedural measure known as a “rule”, which the House majority must pass before it can bring legislation to the floor. Five Republican hardliners had planned to vote it down, in a dispute unrelated to its substance, which would have handed the speaker, Mike Johnson, an embarrassing defeat and potentially disrupted the House’s legislative calendar for the rest of the month. Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez supplied the votes that let the rule pass, 210 to 208. Under House rules, a tied vote is treated as a defeat, meaning their support was decisive. It is highly unusual for members of the minority party to back the majority’s procedural rules, which typically pass on party-line votes and are treated by leadership as a basic marker of caucus discipline. Neither Golden nor Gluesenkamp Perez gave Democratic leaders advance notice, according to House Democratic leadership. Clark told reporters shortly after the vote that the move “came as a surprise”. Jeffries later told reporters that the two Democrats “blindsided the entire caucus and created a significant breach of trust”. The rule cleared the way for a package of Republican-favored bills to reach the floor, including a GOP resolution condemning socialism and the Democratic Socialists of America, a measure Republicans are expected to use against Democrats in midterm campaign messaging. That resolution also included a poison pill in the form of a statement of support for Donald Trump’s restrictive voting legislation, Save Act. The stunt was designed to force House Democrats to choose between voting against the resolution in what Republicans would portray as tacit support for socialism, or vote in favor of it and lend a (non-binding) blessing to legislation that experts say could stop millions of Americans from voting. The rule also advanced a bipartisan bill, co-authored by Golden, to shield Maine’s lobster industry from federal whale-protection regulations the fishing industry says could put smaller operators out of business. Golden said that bill was his reason for breaking ranks. “I voted for the rule for one simple reason: it paved the way for a vote on my bill to protect Maine lobstermen from costly, burdensome new regulations that would put them out of business,” he said in a statement. Gluesenkamp Perez, who leads the conservative Democratic Blue Dog Coalition, cited similar concerns for working waterfront communities in her south-west Washington district, jabbing on social media that “what the DC bubble doesn’t get is that working waterfronts require working people”. Golden, who is retiring at the end of this Congress, has also indicated he had lined up other Democratic votes for the rule beforehand, suggesting the move was deliberate rather than a last-minute miscalculation. The episode has exposed deeper strains inside a Democratic caucus that has struggled to project unity since its losses in the 2024 elections. Asked whether the two lawmakers would face consequences, Jeffries told reporters on Tuesday that the matter was “under discussion”. By the evening, he, Clark and Aguilar had escalated that to a formal referral. Axios has reported that stripping Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez of committee assignments was among the options being discussed by frustrated members as a way to “make an example” of the pair, though no decision has been made and it remains unclear what disciplinary powers the committee on caucus rules can actually exercise. Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez, both first elected in swing or Republican-leaning districts, have each broken with their party before, including on past government funding bills and an earlier version of a Republican voter-fraud measure. Golden co-chaired the centrist Blue Dog Coalition until Gluesenkamp Perez succeeded him in the role. Johnson, for his part, told reporters after the vote that critics who had predicted his majority would fail to pass the rule “were wrong”. “The rule has passed,” Johnson said. “Many of you thought that would not happen today, but we passed a rule to continue business this week. Republicans are here to work.”

title: The $1 Trump coin: legal tender, depending on what you mean by legal
author: Adam Gabbatt
summary: Various laws and 250 years of tradition prevent the likeness of living people from appearing on currency. Donald Trump and Scott Bessent don’t want you to worry about that
body_text: Two hallmarks of Donald Trump’s second-term: the president’s enthusiasm for putting his name and face on things, and his cavalier approach to established law. Today the president is once again combining both those interests, as the government releases a $1 coin bearing his image, an item of currency that scholars say should be illegal, but which is happening anyway. How many times have you heard that in the last 18 months? The US has had a long tradition of not putting living people on US currencybeginning in the late 1700s when the US Mint, which manufactures and distributes currency, wanted to put an image of George Washington on US money. Washington declined, saying it would be too much like a monarchy putting its rulers on money. In 1866, Congress passed an amendment barring the “portrait or likeness” of living people from appearing on currency. That doesn’t appear to have bothered Trump. His scowling face dominates the new $1 coin, which is legal tender, and looks gold but is actually made from zinc, manganese, nickel and copper. It costs $61 to buy 25 one-dollar coins – you do the math – and about 9m of the coins are being made. They will, according to the US Mint, “honor 250 years of great American heritage”. That all sounds great, if you’re into that sort of thing, but what about the law?. Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, has argued that during the 150th celebration of America’s “birthday”, the face of then president Calvin Coolidge appeared on a coin, so during the 250th, the Trump coin is fine. The main problem seems to be that there’s a hodge-podge of laws which govern what can and cannot go on a coin. The 1866 ban on featuring living people arose from an impressively creative act of vanity. An incoming five-cent note was supposed to feature an image of the deceased explorer William Clark, but a treasury official called Spencer M Clark took advantage of the pair sharing a last name to instead print his own face on the note. The problem was that members of Congress a) noticed and b) were unamused. They passed an amendment which ruled that US money can only feature dead individuals – but it only applied to paper money. “For me, I would consider it illegal,” Gabriel Mathy, an associate professor of economics at American University who has studied American currency, said of the Trump coin. “But the United States has all these laws, which really are norms because they’re not really enforceable.” The coin hasn’t been produced without a fight. In May, a group of Democratic members of Congress wrote to the treasury department in May, urging them to desist with the coin, pointing to a 2005 law which further restricted which presidents could appear on coins. And in March, James Rickher, a retired attorney in Portland, filed a request to block the coin, arguing it was illegal, but in June a federal judge denied that motion, writing that Rickher had “failed to present evidence that clearly shows he will personally suffer concrete harm from issuance of the challenged coin”, Fox 12 reported. The judge noted, however, that his ruling did not determine whether the coin is illegal or legal. And so today, Americans will be able to honor 250 years of great American heritage by buying a questionably legal one-dollar coin for roughly $2.44. If you’d like to know who came up with such a brilliant plan, just look at the coin.

title: MMA fight in Florida condemned after fighter’s antisemitic comments
author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
summary: Paul Miller, an openly racist fighter, derided Ben Azoulay, and a spectator was ejected for waving a swastika flag
body_text: Democrats in Florida have condemned a professional mixed martial arts event in Orlando at which an openly racist fighter derided his beaten opponent as “a short little fucking Jew prick”, and a spectator was ejected for waving a giant swastika flag. Anna Eskamani, a Democratic state representative running to become the city’s mayor, said Saturday’s event, and the assertion by city officials that they were compelled to host it, were unacceptable. “This is another reminder of how prevalent extremism is in our society, and of the responsibility every one of us carries to combat antisemitism, racism, white supremacy and hate in all its forms,” she said in a statement to the Guardian. “It is also a reason for the Kia Center, and all public venues, to re-evaluate their rules. The first amendment is broad, and I take it seriously, but conduct that invites and incites violence is a different question, and every angle should be explored to prevent this from happening again.” The Duel Arena kickboxing event at the downtown venue featured a headline fight between Paul Miller, a convicted felon and self-professed antisemite who served prison time for weapons offenses, and Ben Azoulay, a Jewish “manosphere” influencer who has a conviction for the sexual assault of a 15-year-old girl. After the fight was over, several brawls broke out in the crowd. Miller, who goes by the nickname of the gypsy crusader, assailed Azoulay over the arena’s loudspeaker system using the racial epithet and appeared to give at least two Nazi salutes from the ring. On Tuesday, Orlando Venues, a division of the city’s government that runs the 18,500-seat arena, released a statement claiming that it was compelled to host the controversial event and defending what it said was the participants’ constitutionally protected right of expression. The city’s statement, posted on the X account of the Kia Center, said in part: “As operators of public venues, the City is bound by the First Amendment. This means we cannot deny access because we disagree with the political ideology, opinion, or perspective, irrespective of the message.” It added that the views of the participants “do not reflect the views of Orlando Venues, the City or Orlando, or our staff” and added that it took community concerns seriously. But it said it would continue to review its event policies only “while respecting the Constitution”. The City of Orlando, and Orlando Venues, did not address further questions from the Guardian about the event, including how a person with a large swastika flag was able to gain access to the arena in contravention of the Kia Center’s strict admittance policies. Buddy Dyer, the Orlando mayor, said in a statement that the city rejected the messaging of the fighters. “Symbols of hate, including the Nazi flag, were brought to Kia Center this weekend. But hate will never be welcome here,” he said. “Our community will continue to stand against antisemitism and all forms of hate to ensure that Orlando is a place where every person is valued and respected.” Kia, in a statement, also condemned the incident. “As Kia America is the naming rights partner of the Kia Center, we are not involved in its operations or security protocols,” a spokesperson said. “However, we appreciate the prompt action taken by venue personnel to address the situation. Such behaviors are in stark contrast to the values of respect and dignity that we, and our employees, fully support and promote.” Rick Scott, a Florida Republican US senator and former governor, said in a post on X that Saturday’s events were “extremely disturbing”. He said: “Antisemitism has no place in Florida.” Miller, according to the Anti-Defamation League, is a far-right extremist and white supremacist who used the gypsy crusader moniker on inflammatory social media posts long before his transformation into a mixed martial arts fighter. In 2021, the US attorney’s office for the southern district of Florida noted he had called for a race-based civil war before his 41-month prison sentence for illegal possession of firearms by a convicted felon. He did not respond to a request for comment. Azoulay, meanwhile, has his own controversial past. In February, California’s Beverly Hills unified school district apologized for allowing him to address a Jewish student club at the city’s high school. Azoulay was convicted in 2011 in relation to the rape of a minor, and maintains an Instagram account with more than half a million followers. His misogynistic social media commentary has included advice for women to “keep a man’s belly full and his balls empty” in order to keep him. “Some of the views espoused by this man which I’ve seen on social [media] are abhorrent,” Alex Cherniss, the district’s superintendent, said in a statement at the time. “Had the principal or district known ahead of time, he would have never been approved to speak to this student club.” Several school board members further apologized at a heated subsequent meeting in April.

title: Epstein survivors urge billionaire Leon Black to cooperate with House panel
author: Marina Dunbar
summary: Black called on to comply with subpoenas and appear as required to clarify connections to convicted sex offender
body_text: More than a dozen survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s abuse have called on the billionaire Leon Black to appear before the House oversight committee in order to clarify his connections to the late disgraced financier and convicted sex offender. In a letter released on Wednesday, the survivors urged Black to comply with congressional subpoenas ahead of Thursday’s deposition before the House oversight committee. “We are survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s abuse and exploitation, and we are calling on Leon Black to appear as required before the House oversight committee on Thursday,” the statement said. “We are also calling on Black to fully comply with the committee’s subpoenas, including its demand that he produce all responsive nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) in his possession.” Black, the New York private equity investor, paid Epstein tens of millions of dollars in fees during work he has described as tax and estate-planning services. He has already faced accusations of purposely delaying and disrupting the panel’s inquiry. The letter further stated that “Black’s use of NDAs underscores why Congress must scrutinize the agreements in his possession and determine whether they shed light on his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and others in Epstein’s orbit”. “If Black continues to withhold responsive records or refuses to comply with the committee’s demands, Congress should use every tool available to enforce its subpoenas.” Last week, the Republican chairman of the House oversight committee, James Comer, threatened to hold Black in contempt if he fails to fully cooperate with the panel’s investigation into Epstein. Black had not yet confirmed his appearance before the committee as of Tuesday, a person familiar with the matter had told the Guardian. In a previous statement before the oversight committee in June, Black denied knowledge of Epstein’s crimes, writing: “I did not know about this nefarious activity until Epstein was charged with trafficking in July 2019.” However, Black acknowledged that he was aware that Epstein had pleaded guilty in 2008 “to state charges relating to prostitution involving a minor”. In a speech from the House floor this week, Thomas Massie, the Kentucky Republican who recently lost his primary to a challenger backed by Donald Trump, read aloud the names of several friends and associates of Epstein, including Black. Massie called on the Department of Justice to investigate the group of men and women whom the representative referred to as “perpetrators” of Epstein’s crimes. Massie also emphasized that despite the fact it has been nearly a year since Trump signed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, millions of the Epstein files remain unreleased.

title: Trump ranks himself the greatest US president ever. Historians beg to differ
author: Adam Gabbatt
summary: Donald Trump posted his own presidential rankings to Truth Social last week, separating past US presidents into six categories from ‘greatest’ to ‘failures’
body_text: Donald Trump has declared himself to be the “greatest” US president ever, sharing a post on social media last week which graded him above the likes of Abraham Lincoln, Franklin D Roosevelt and George Washington. Experts take a different view. Few presidential historians have previously suggested Trump holds such a place in the history books. After all, neither Lincoln, nor Roosevelt, nor Washington – the three leaders typically seen as America’s best – orchestrated an insurrection. None were impeached. And none of them were convicted of felonies over hush-money payments to a pornstar-turned-ghost hunter. Trump has made clear how he feels about his performance. Does the president’s self-assessment match reality? “It’s not consistent with the findings of the surveys we’ve conducted,” said Justin Vaughn, a political science professor at Coastal Carolina University and the co-creator of the Presidential Greatness Project, which polls experts to rank US presidents. “It’s also not consistent with other surveys that have been conducted over the last several years.” Trump posted his presidential rankings last Thursday. It separated US presidents into six categories, from “greatest” to “failures”: he stands alone in the “greatest” grouping. The image in his post appears to have been adapted from a 1948 article in Life magazine, in which the historian Arthur M Schlesinger Jr muses about “what makes a president great or a failure” – that publication date would explain why certain presidents, including Ronald Reagan, Richard Nixon and both Bushes, are missing. The original image didn’t have a “greatest” category – someone has retrospectively created that – while Joe Biden, Jimmy Carter and Barack Obama have all been inserted in the “failures” category. Bill Clinton, perhaps surprisingly given the years Trump has spent attacking him, was deemed to be “average”. Yet the most recent Presidential Greatness Project survey, which asked 154 academics about presidents, had rather different findings. It saw Trump ranked dead last, below even James Buchanan, who is frequently blamed for not averting the civil war. The survey asked academics to rank each of the 45 presidents from 0 to 100, with 0 being “failure” and 100 meaning “great”. Lincoln was No 1, with an average rating of 93.87. Trump got a rating of 10.92. Trump performed slightly better in a Siena University poll of 141 presidential scholars in 2022. In that study, he was ranked only third-to-last, besting Buchanan and Andrew Johnson, who succeeded Lincoln, but opposed federal protections that would guarantee enslaved people’s rights to citizenship. The Siena study also asked academics to rank presidents in various categories including “background”, “executive ability” and “leadership ability”. Trump was ranked 45th, out of 45, in the “integrity” and “intelligence” categories. Trump might find some solace, however, in the fact that he has managed to unite academics on both the left and right of the political spectrum. “We break down our results between self-identified Democrats or self-identified conservatives or Republicans,” Vaughn said. “When you look at the statistics of the Republican respondents versus the Democratic respondents, the Republicans also view Trump very poorly.” Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said: “President Trump is solely focused on fighting every day to deliver the strong, safe, and prosperous country that we all deserve. The only legacy President Trump is concerned with is making America greater than ever before. “But when all is said and done, this President will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in modern American history.” Whether this prediction will come to pass will depend on how history treats Trump. Americans “have a kind of a golden glow about most ex-presidents”, said Barbara Perry, a professor in presidential studies at the University of Virginia, who noted that leaders have shifted in rankings over the decades, as their tenures are reassessed. In any case, Trump’s personal rankings offered an insight into the presidents he admires. The “greatest” category included only Trump; under “great” came Lincoln, Roosevelt and Washington. “Near great” included Theodore Roosevelt and Grover Cleveland, who like Trump, served nonconsecutive terms as president. Unfortunately Perry, as with Vaughn, took issue with Trump’s ranking. “In no universe of scholars, I believe, would Donald Trump be in the ‘great’ category, the ‘greatest’ category, ‘near great’ category,” she said. “My view as a scholar and a constitutional historian would be that his promotion of the insurrection of January 6, and his continuation of perpetuating this view that Joe Biden stole the election: that is undermining the American constitutional system, the rule of law,” added Perry. “Not to mention the racism and the bias against anybody who’s not a white Anglo-Saxon Protestant. So all those things will work against him, I believe, throughout history.”

title: Working-class ER nurse seeks to flip battleground Wisconsin House seat
author: Michael Sainato
summary: Mitchell Berman is among Democrats the party hopes can flip a Republican-leaning district in November’s midterms
body_text: Democrats are targeting vulnerable seats this midterm election with working-class candidates they hope will resonate with voters exhausted by the economy. Some candidates are new to politics, and many have backgrounds as union members and leaders, which the party hopes will give them an edge over Republican incumbents as people have grown weary of Washington and the higher cost of living. One of these new candidates is Mitchell Berman, an emergency room nurse who Democrats hope will flip a Wisconsin House seat by emphasizing his experience as a worker. “Being a nurse working in the emergency room, we don’t have the luxury of standing around and not delivering for our patients. We have to make sure that we are addressing concerns in the immediate, making sure that when our patients come in, they leave the emergency department in better condition than they arrive,” Berman said. “That is not happening for folks here in our district.” Berman is running in a swing district that polling shows is leaning Republican for the House race. It’s the same district that former House speaker Paul Ryan represented from 2015 until he left office in 2019, when he was replaced by Bryan Steil, a corporate attorney and former Ryan aide. Berman is trying to convince voters that Steil has been out of touch with voters who are seeing costs rise because of White House policies. The campaign is paralleling Steil with Berman, who has worked in healthcare for more than 20 years. “Coming from a working-class background, understanding what folks are going through [and] having walked a mile in my neighbor’s shoes gives me the ability to look at legislation from the perspective of having some empathy and understanding for what people are dealing with,” Berman said. He recalled when Scott Walker, the state’s former Republican governor, passed Act 10 in Wisconsin, which stripped collective bargaining rights from most public sector workers in the state, and the negative impact it had on workers. Berman specifically cites his membership in unions as helping him understand how workers have to fight for fair pay and benefits. “Just seeing the benefits packages, seeing the work-life balance that was afforded to us because of that union was just incredible,” Berman said, adding that workers getting a seat at the table is “the only way they’re going to be able to have a voice when it comes to making sure they get treated fairly”. In Wisconsin and throughout the midwest, the decline of manufacturing has also hit the region hard as offshoring and trade policies have decimated the industry. Manufacturing jobs in the state declined from 560,000 in 2001 to 460,000 in 2025, with healthcare jobs surpassing manufacturing in the state for the first time. From January 2025 to January 2026, the state lost 9,500 manufacturing jobs. Tariffs have led to the loss of 3,910 jobs in Wisconsin, and they are also costing households in the state an additional $1,095 a year, according to a July 2026 report by the Midwest Economic Policy Institute and the University of Illinois Project for Middle Class Renewal. Trump has continued to push widespread tariffs, with claims they would bring US factories “roaring back”. Berman noted that his opponent has defended tariffs, despite the higher costs they bring to voters. While he is not against targeted tariffs, the current tariffs have created “an atmosphere and an economy that makes it difficult for manufacturing jobs to survive”. “Right now people in the district feel betrayed by Bryan Steil because he had made promises to bring costs down, but things have only gotten worse here for people, and I think that’s because of policy positions he’s championed, allowed and abdicated to Donald Trump,” Berman said. “People are starting to recognize that a lot of the woes that they are feeling, when it comes to looking at their bank account at the end of the month, are because of poor decisions made by my opponent.” Steil’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
