title: In 2016, Trump pledged to erase the federal debt. It just hit $40tn
author: Steven Greenhouse
summary: The trillions in tax cuts going to the rich and corporations could have instead been used to address the affordability crisis
body_text: Dear reader, I recognize that your eyes might glaze over at any mention of the nation’s $40tn federal debt. But your reaction to this mind-boggling number shouldn’t be ennui; it should be outrage and dismay. Outrage is in order because the nation’s debt has climbed to more than $40tn under Donald Trump, even though back in 2016, when the debt was less than half what it is today, candidate Trump insisted that he’d totally eliminate the debt within eight years. That was yet another example of the Demagogue-in-Chief’s willingness to say anything, no matter how insincere or untrue, to woo voters. Not only has Trump failed to reduce the debt, he has spectacularly increased it. Take Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” and the huge tax cuts it lavished upon the very rich and corporations. That legislation is expected to increase the nation’s debt by a whopping $3.4tn over the next decade. Worse, during Trump’s time as president, including his first term, the federal debt has climbed by a colossal $11.6tn. Outrage is also in order because the trillions in tax cuts going to the rich and corporations could have instead been used to address the affordability crisis that is squeezing so many Americans. Those trillions could have gone to creating more affordable childcare for every family or increasing subsidies to hold down soaring healthcare premiums or expanding government aid to make college more affordable. Trump’s tax cuts for the rich and the $40tn debt have worsened the affordability crisis in one important and painful way. They have helped push up long-term interest rates to their highest level in nearly two decades, and that has pushed up mortgage rates, too. The unhappy result: housing has become less affordable, when housing affordability has already been a big problem for young Americans. Higher mortgage rates often mean that homebuyers have to pay several hundred dollars more in interest each month. Interest rates have climbed not only because investors are dismayed that the national debt has hit a record, but also because Trump’s tariffs and war against Iran have fueled inflation and because investors are unsettled by all the chaos Trump has created at home and abroad. Outrage is also called for because of the way Trump and his Republican yes-men in Congress jumped to enact giant tax cuts when their super-wealthy donors and friends said jump. In a move that shows how rigged the system is, Trump and the GOP legislated these tax cuts for the rich and corporations even though the wealthy and corporations were already doing perfectly well and would continue doing just fine, with their mansions, yachts and private jets, even without those tax cuts. Of the $4.4tn in tax cuts in the “big, beautiful bill”, nearly half go to the richest 5% of Americans. If any further evidence is needed to show that Republicans in Congress have sold their souls to billionaires, millionaires and corporations, the increased debt caused by the big, unbeautiful bill’s tax cuts will be a burden on our children and grandchildren for decades to come. By the mid-2030s, the nation will have to pay more than $2tn in interest payments each year to finance the federal debt. That’s double the $1tn a year we are paying now – $1tn is slightly less than what the government spends on Medicare, is higher than this year’s Pentagon budget and is more than five times what the federal government spends on education each year. All this is maddening for another reason. In recent decades, Republicans held themselves out as the party of “fiscal responsibility”. But they’ve really become the party of fiscal irresponsibility. During George W Bush’s two terms, with his tax cuts tilted toward the wealthy and his expensive, ill-fated war against Iraq, the federal debt ballooned by 85% (by $4.9tn). In Trump’s first term, the debt soared by $7.8tn (a 39% increase), stemming from his initial big tax cuts for the rich as well as increased Pentagon spending – and then there was more than $2tn in emergency spending to stabilize the economy during the first year of the Covid-19 pandemic. During Trump’s second term, the debt is likely to soar by nearly $8tn once again. Trump is pushing for a record $1.5tn annual defense budget, far higher than any previous year, even though it will send our country’s debt further into the stratosphere. Some of that money will go to redesigning aircraft carriers merely because Trump dislikes how the current ones look. Bill Clinton was the last president to have an annual budget surplus, but Democratic presidents have also pushed up the federal debt. During Biden’s four years as president, the debt rose $8.4tn, partly because of the annual budget deficits he inherited from Trump and partly because of his $2tn-plus pandemic-era emergency spending package to stabilize families’ finances and ensure the US didn’t sink into a deep economic downturn. The federal debt has grown even larger than the country’s overall gross domestic product. Indeed, the ratio of the debt to GDP will soon be higher than the record 106% where it stood when the second world war ended. Franklin D Roosevelt ran up huge debts for an urgent reason: to defeat Nazi Germany and its allies. In sharp contrast, under Trump, the US is running big deficits, of approximately $2tn a year, for the opposite of urgent reasons: to finance a disastrous war in Iran and to give big tax giveaways to two powerful groups that were already prospering, eg the ultra-wealthy and corporations. It would be a very different thing if Trump were borrowing money to build a better future, as people do to build a new house or pay for college. But Trump is not jacking up the country’s debt to improve our future; he’s not spending to improve education, childcare or our country’s infrastructure or to fix the housing crisis. I am not a fiscal conservative and nor are many Democrats, but it is a real concern that for the first time in US history, other countries and many investors seem truly worried about the record size of the federal debt. Those worries have spooked financial markets and pushed up interest rates. As the midterm elections heat up, the Democrats should attack Trump and the Republicans over the huge, fast-growing federal debt. Democrats need to make clear that Republicans have become the party of fiscal irresponsibility. We can agree that the $40tn debt isn’t a sexy issue, but the Democrats can and should turn it into a hard-hitting and winning campaign issue that they can use to hammer Trump and the Republicans, along with the affordability crisis and Trump’s calamitous war against Iran. Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

title: Leon Black fails to appear for US House deposition about Epstein ties
author: Victoria Bekiempis and Anna Betts
summary: Billionaire financier, who previously walked out of a deposition, instead launches lawsuit against the committee
body_text: The billionaire financier Leon Black did not appear on Thursday in front of the House oversight committee for a scheduled deposition about his ties to Jeffrey Epstein, and has instead launched a lawsuit against the committee arguing that it does not have the authority to compel him to turn over non-disclosure agreements. Black was a top Epstein client over several years, and the committee is investigating the men’s relationship as well as the existence of any NDAs to which Black is a party. Black’s name has come up repeatedly in the Epstein files. He has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and has said that he regrets dealing with Epstein. Black’s lawyers said in a statement on Thursday morning announcing the lawsuit: “The Committee is on a fishing expedition that oversteps its authority and completely ignores its responsibility. This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr Black. We were left with no choice but to file this lawsuit in response to an abuse of Congressional power.” The lawsuit, filed in the US district court for the District of Columbia, seeks to stop the committee from enforcing its subpoenas. In the statement, they added: “We want to reiterate that Mr Black had no awareness of the criminal activities that led to Epstein’s arrest in 2019. “Mr Black never abused a woman,” they said. “He never was with an underage woman. He never engaged in sex trafficking. He never paid Epstein for access to women. He was never blackmailed by Epstein.” In a statement on Thursday, Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the oversight committee, called for Black to be held in contempt after his refusal to appear. “By refusing to testify today, Leon Black is now defying two congressional subpoenas,” said Garcia. “His connections to Epstein and his unwillingness to cooperate are unacceptable,” Garcia added. “We must hold him in contempt immediately.” The new development on Thursday, comes as Black first appeared before the committee in June for a transcribed interview, but the testimony ended abruptly after members from both parties said that Black refused to answer questions about NDAs. That day, James Comer, the Republican who chairs the committee, issued two subpoenas to Black, one demanding he produce “all non-disclosure agreements to which he is a party”, and another to appear before the committee again. In August, in a letter to Black’s attorney, Comer threatened to hold Black in contempt if he refused to comply with the committee’s subpoenas or refused to appear for his deposition, which had been scheduled for 3 September. On Thursday morning, Comer criticized Black in a statement, though stopped short of signalling a contempt vote. “It’s a shame Leon Black is hiding behind litigation rather than provide answers to the American people,” Comer said. “Our deposition is moving forward this morning for the record and there will be an empty chair for Mr Black. I will speak with our members about next steps.” Earlier this week, ahead of Black’s scheduled deposition, over a dozen survivors of Epstein’s abuse urged Black to comply with congressional subpoenas. “Black’s use of NDAs underscores why Congress must scrutinize the agreements in his possession and determine whether they shed light on his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and others in Epstein’s orbit” the survivors wrote. “If Black continues to withhold responsive records or refuses to comply with the committee’s demands, Congress should use every tool available to enforce its subpoenas,” they added. Black’s lawsuit alleges that the two subpoenas issued to him are “invalid to the extent they exceed” the committee’s “delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection to OGR’s legislative purpose”. “Additionally, the subpoenas would also expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it, and who have no ability to protect themselves and their privacy before the Committee,” the suit says.

title: Iran targets US bases as Israel warns sanctions could drive Tehran to ‘desperate steps’
author: Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent
summary: Air bases used by US in UAE and Kuwait hit as Israeli defence chief says Iran’s regime fears collapse due to economic pressures
body_text: Iran has continued to demonstrate an ability to target bases in the Gulf used by the US despite six months of war and a new sanctions regime described by the Trump administration as an “economic D-day”. As Iran’s military targeted US bases in the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait, despite threats of further strikes by the US president, Israel’s defence chief warned that economic pressures from the sanctions could lead Tehran to escalate to more “extreme measures”. “This morning, the army hit the satellite communication systems, equipment depots and fighter aircraft hangars of the terrorist US army at the Ahmad al-Jaber air base in Kuwait with missiles and drones,” the Iranian military said on Thursday in a statement carried by state television. The “location of forces and radar systems of the child-killing US army at the Al Minhad air base in the UAE were also attacked by missiles and drones of the army”, it added. In a post on X, Kuwait’s ministry of defence said its air defences had intercepted missile and drone attacks during a “blatant Iranian aggression”. The Kuwaiti statement came after the US allies Bahrain and Jordan said their air defence systems intercepted several Iranian air attacks on Wednesday. Fighting between the US and Iran has increased this week after the US hit Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz on Sunday, claiming that Iran was planning to use them to shoot mines into the waterway. The latest flare-up in the conflict comes amid little evidence that the Trump administration is succeeding in advancing its nebulous war aims either on the battlefield or via mediation, despite the US president’s repeated claims to have opened the strait of Hormuz to oil traffic. Instead, traffic through the key maritime passageway remains far below prewar levels, with oil prices remaining stubbornly elevated ahead of US midterm elections. Oil prices jumped again on Thursday after the Iranian strikes. Among the weapons Iran has used this week is its Kheibar Shekan medium-range ballistic missile system. The cheap and accurate missile can be launched within minutes and has become a staple of Iranian strikes. The rocket’s solid fuel motor means it does not require lengthy fuelling. It can be deployed very quickly to avoid detection and can be armed with a powered and steerable final stage to help beat anti-missile systems. Despite claims by the Trump administration that Tehran is running out of rockets, Iran continues to fire missiles that are considerably cheaper to produce than the US interceptors used to shoot them down. Iran has claimed as recently as the end of August that it maintained both missiles stockpiles and the ability to manufacture them. “Initially, some believed that Iran had only a limited number of missiles and that its stockpiles would eventually be depleted as the war continued,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Brig Gen Hossein Mohebbi said. “However, that assumption proved incorrect, as Iran’s missile capability has remained sustained and its missile production has continued.” Mohebbi’s characterisation of Iranian missile stockpiles could not be verified. The continued strikes came as Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said that while the new US economic sanctions appeared to be effective, the increased pressure could lead Tehran into extreme measures. “We see signs indicating that the heavy economic pressure they are under, and the fear of an uprising and the collapse of the regime, may push them to desperate steps,” Katz said at a ceremony for defence ministry employees. The hawkish minister reiterated the threats against the Islamic Republic that he has made in recent months. “An Iranian attack on Israel will free Israel from any existing constraint,” he said. “We will strike all of Iran’s national military and civilian infrastructure – including energy infrastructure – and push Iran deep back into the stone age.”

title: US House passes bill penalizing universities that participate in boycott of Israel
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: GOP-backed bill mandates institutions receiving federal funds not impose restrictions on programs related to Israel
body_text: The US House of Representatives on Thursday passed a Republican-backed bill that would penalize universities that participate in boycotts of Israel, or attempt to prevent students from taking part in exchange programs with the country. The Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act passed by a 237-169 vote, with 33 Democrats breaking with the rest of their party to vote in favor, and only two Republicans opposed. It now goes to the Senate for consideration. The measure would require that colleges and universities who participate in federal student aid programs not participate in boycotts of Israel and also mandates that institutions receiving federal funding for international study and foreign language programs certify annually that they do not impose restrictions on their students participating in programs in Israel, or on students from Israel participating in programs on their campuses. House Republican leaders had brought the measure to the floor as they attempt to exploit divisions among Democrats over hot-button issues ahead of the midterm elections, in which voters will decide control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s term. “This legislation is about a simple principle: our colleges and universities should not discriminate against Israel, Israeli institutions or Israeli students, and federal taxpayer dollars should never support institutions that engage in such discrimination,” said Tim Walberg, the Republican chair of the House education committee. After the 7 October attack and Israel’s invasion of Gaza, student and faculty groups at some universities intensified calls for administrators to participate in the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against the country, but were largely unsuccessful. Bobby Scott, the top Democrat on the education committee, criticized the bill as unnecessary and potentially in conflict with first amendment protections of protest. “No college or university has embraced the BDS movement anyway. So, we should combat antisemitism wherever it occurs, but we should not do so by punishing protected speech or conflating a student’s view with university policies,” he said. Democrats who voted for the bill typically face tough re-election contests in November, or are supporters of Israel. Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey congressman who co-sponsored the legislation with Republican Virginia Foxx, described the proposal as “narrow and tailored” and necessary to combat antisemitism. “No student, no professor should be shut out of research, study abroad opportunities, or academic partnerships or feel unwelcome in the classroom because of where they are from or what religion they practice. Yet that’s exactly what the boycott-divest-sanction movement seeks to do – targeting one country and one religion: Israel and Judaism,” he said. The question of support for Israel has divided House Democrats in recent months. In July, more than 100 House Democrats supported a bill cutting off some military aid to the US ally amid accusations its military’s actions in Gaza constituted a genocide.

title: Hillary Clinton leads tributes to Gloria Steinem: ‘Her activism was rooted in optimism’
author: Richard Luscombe
summary: Former secretary of state joins Nancy Pelosi, Jill Biden, Roxane Gay and others in heralding groundbreaking feminist
body_text: Leading figures from politics, entertainment and wider society led glowing tributes to Gloria Steinem on Thursday, with Hillary Clinton hailing the American feminist icon who died at 92 at home in New York City as “one of the architects of the entire structure of women’s equality”. Clinton, a former US secretary of state, presidential candidate and first lady, was among the first to jump in with praise early on Thursday when she appeared on the CBS Mornings TV show to share her respect and gratitude for Steinem. Clinton urged younger generations to use Steinem as a role model in supporting each other in promoting the causes she championed. “I’m hoping that young women realize that the fight is worth it,” she said. “It is exhilarating.” Kamala Harris, the former US vice-president, hailed Steinem as a “trailblazing activist, organizer, and journalist – an icon in so many ways”, in a post on X. “To know her as a person is to know someone who was kind, sharp, and witty. She was invested in young women and keeping the door open for the next generation of leaders,” Harris wrote. “I will always be grateful for her encouragement and support in my campaign for the presidency. A campaign that was made possible, in no small part, because of her activism and so many other giants upon whose shoulders we stand.” Others who eulogized Steinem included Nancy Pelosi, the Democratic former House speaker, who called her “a fearless trailblazer who transformed the fight for equality in America”. Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex, added her voice to call Steinem her “friend and mentor”, while the music icon Patti Smith referred to her as “the greatest”. Broadcaster Oprah Winfrey called Steinem a “formidable reformer who shaped American thought and culture”. And Billie Jean King, the athlete who led the fight for equality for female tennis players, said in a Facebook post that “the world has lost a true giant and a dynamic voice”. “She lit a torch many years ago. It is now our responsibility to keep it lifted into the future. May she rest in power,” King wrote. Jill Biden, another former first lady, released a statement in which she said she and former US president Joe Biden “are holding Gloria’s loved ones in our hearts”. Biden wrote: “Gloria Steinem understood that women’s equality begins with the freedom to make decisions about our own bodies, health, and futures. For decades, she fought to make that freedom real for generations of women and girls. “She spoke up when it was difficult, listened to those whose voices too often went unheard, and never stopped pushing our country forward. Her voice changed our country, and her courage will continue to inspire us to keep fighting for the freedoms she spent her life defending.” Steinem had supported Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential campaign as the Democratic nominee running against Republican Donald Trump, which was ultimately unsuccessful as Trump prevailed in an election that would have given the United States its first female president. Clinton said on Thursday she was “heartsick” at news of the death of her feminist friend and ally. “Everyone who not only knew her but followed her, was inspired and challenged by her,” she said. “I think back to my first awareness of Gloria way back in the 1960s into the 70s, when all of a sudden this incredibly smart, beautiful, talented woman began talking about how women should have equal opportunity, how we should aim for the stars, be able to pursue our own dreams. “I knew there were, back when I was a young woman, schools that wouldn’t take women, jobs that wouldn’t take women, scholarships that weren’t open to women. I lived it. “But the lived experience became much more real and applicable to our entire society when Gloria began to point it out.” Clinton noted Steinem’s distaste at what politics had become in recent years, and said she had “the most incredible conversation” with her during a visit to Steinem’s home last year. “Even though we’re facing some challenges and pushback here in this country and around the world to women’s full participation and equality, Gloria was at heart an optimist,” she said. “Her activism was rooted in optimism, and that’s a moral choice, and she made it every day.” Pelosi paid tribute in a post on X that said: “Gloria Steinem was a fearless trailblazer who transformed the fight for equality in America and inspired generations of women to know their power. “Her voice, courage and relentless advocacy helped break down barriers and open doors once firmly closed to women. May it be a comfort to all of us who loved Gloria that her extraordinary legacy will live on in every generation that carries her fight forward.” Markle posted her memories on Instagram. “Celebrating the life and legacy of my friend and mentor, and also grateful to know that in these last few weeks and days she knew exactly how loved and admired she was,” she wrote. “My very favorite story about GLO is when she was out one day in NY, and a woman approached her in absolute awe and said she wanted to introduce her young daughter to her (though she was embarrassed to say the young girl may not know who she was).” The post continued: “Gloria replied: ‘It doesn’t matter if she knows who I am. What matters is that she knows who SHE is’. Rest in peace, and rest in pride.” Smith, who shared a similar path to Steinem as a cultural revolutionary icon emerging from New York in the 1960s and 70s, posted a brief tribute on Instagram. “This is the greatest Gloria. All are grateful for her revolutionary spirit; a lifetime of service,” she wrote. The Oscar-winning actor Julianne Moore played Steinem in the 2020 biopic The Glorias. She said on Instagram: “The time I spent studying Gloria in order to play her was one of the most edifying of my life. “Everything I watched, everything I read, everything I observed about her gave me a template for how I wanted to behave. Her honesty, her tolerance, her patience, and her insistence on humanism and inclusion as she moved through the world offers us all a moral roadmap.” Others who paid tribute on Thursday also recalled Steinem’s trailblazing. “Gloria was one of a kind. Genuine, generous, curious, thoughtful. She lived a staggering life and her passing is a staggering loss tempered only by the ferocity of her legacy,” Roxane Gay, the prominent social commentator and author of Bad Feminist, commented on the Instagram post announcing Steinem’s death. Winfrey, on her own Oprah Daily website, said Steinem “challenged a culture that often told us who we could be, what we could do, and how much space we were allowed to take up, and then spent her life making that space wider for all of us”. Alongside a picture of Winfrey and Steinem together, the TV host added: “She never wanted the movement to be about her. She understood that real change happens when one woman finds her voice and then uses it to help another woman find hers.”

title: ‘This could just be the beginning’: minorities fear first far-right win in German state election
author: Ashifa Kassam in Magdeburg
summary: As polls point to victory in Saxony-Anhalt for AfD party promising deportations, people face agonising choice: stay or go
body_text: As the Bible study session wrapped up, leaving worshippers to mingle over cake and coffee, Fatemeh, 44, fought back tears as the conversation turned to Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt. “I worry about it every day,” she said. “I can’t stop thinking about my son and what might happen to us.” Three years ago she fled Iran with her son after he was stopped by police during a protest over the death in police custody of Mahsa Amini. They ended up in Saxony-Anhalt, where, as they await a final decision on their asylum claim, she has watched him blossom into a gifted athlete and develop a knack for repairing vehicles. Fatemeh worries about what might happen after the elections. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian Looming over their lives, however, are the politics of Saxony-Anhalt. Polls have suggested that the election on Sunday could yield Germany’s first-ever state government led by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), shattering a postwar taboo and leaving Fatemeh and her son’s fate in the hands of a party that has promised to launch deportations “from day one”. That possibility has left her racked with worry. “They might send us back to Iran,” she said. “As a converted Christian, that could mean the death penalty for me.” It was a glimpse of the stakes at play in the election. Polls suggest the state’s AfD, whose antisemitic, anti-Islam and anti-migrant discourse has contributed to authorities classifying the party as “firmly rightwing extremist”, is poised to win the most votes. The square in the centre of Magdeburg where the Christmas market attack took place on 20 December 2024. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian A strong showing in the election could allow it to govern Saxony-Anhalt, turning the eastern state into Germany’s first testing ground for the AfD’s long-running hostility towards migrants, including refugees, Muslims and the LGBTQ+ community. “We’ve never seen emotions run so high over an election,” said Undra Dreßler of Lamsa, an umbrella group for migrant organisations in the state. Calls were coming in daily, she said, as people wrestled with whether the time had come to pack up their lives and start over again somewhere else. “People are really worried and scared,” said Dreßler. “For those with migrant backgrounds, it feels like this vote is about their right to exist and their security.” The pages-long manifesto for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt promises a “complete, 180-degree” overhaul of the approach to migration, from educating refugee children separately to redirecting funds earmarked for integration to a unit focused on remigration, and calling on federal officials to stop recognising Ukrainians as war refugees. In June, Dreßler’s organisation appealed to Germany’s 15 other states, calling on them to prepare to take in refugees from Saxony-Anhalt after the election. “It’s a precautionary measure,” she said. “The social climate here is already extremely heated. We don’t know what will happen after the elections.” Left: A billboard in Magdeburg shows the AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund and the slogan ‘everything is possible’. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian. Right: Siegmund addresses delegates at the federal congress of Generation Germany, the party’s youth organisation. Photograph: Jens Schluter/AFP/Getty Tensions have run high in Saxony-Anhalt since late 2024 when a Saudi man drove his car into a crowded Christmas market in Magdeburg, killing six people and injuring hundreds more. Authorities described the attacker as an anti-Islam activist who was sympathetic to the far right. Even so, rightwing voices seized on the moment to scapegoat migrants and minorities for the ills of a state long ravaged by deindustrialisation and depopulation. In the aftermath of the attack, reports of racist attacks soared as migrants and people of colour told of being spat on, threatened and, in some cases, physically attacked. “By mid-2025, we had received as many reports of racist insults and attacks as we did in all of 2024,” said Dreßler. “As forces on the right become stronger, everyday racism and discrimination have become part of everyday life.” On the streets of Magdeburg, many shared their own brushes with overt racism. “When you’re on the street, some people harass you verbally,” said Kirti, 27, a student from India. “They show you the middle finger.” An AfD billboard reads ‘All for our children’. The party has promised to educate refugee children in the state separately. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian Kirti moved to Magdeburg just over a year ago to study for a master’s degree, becoming part of a cohort of foreign students for whom reports of racism were all too familiar. “I heard of one incident where a student was travelling on a train and people were throwing stones at the door, but the door was closed,” he said. “So people are more concerned about going out. They go out with fear, rather than feeling safe.” A recent survey suggested that as many as 80% of people with a migration background in Saxony-Anhalt are considering leaving, said Ketevan Asatiani-Hermann, who leads the board of the Advisory Council for Integration and Migration in Magdeburg. As questions swirl over what the AfD could realistically do if the party garners enough votes to govern alone, a chorus of voices has begun to warn of the fallout. Saxony-Anhalt is a rapidly depopulating state where the average age of 48.2 ranks as the highest in Germany. “So the fear is that we lose people because of what happens on 6 September,” said Asatiani-Hermann. “And Saxony-Anhalt is dependent on migrants, so it’s absolutely necessary that they stay here.” Ketevan Asatiani-Hermann says Saxony-Anhalt is dependent on migrants and it is ‘absolutely necessary’ they stay. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian Foreign nationals account for about 9% of the state’s population – compared with approximately 15% nationwide – with many playing a critical role in sectors such as hospitality and care for elderly people. In May, the state medical association said that more than one in four doctors working in Saxony-Anhalt’s hospitals, or 27.1%, do not hold a German passport. “In many regions of the state – especially in rural areas – comprehensive healthcare coverage would no longer be possible without foreign colleagues,” it said, citing the possibility of longer waiting times or facility closures if some of these doctors were to leave. “Migrants make up a huge part of healthcare. If you were to take them out, the whole system would collapse,” said Hamid, 41, a paramedic originally from Iran. “So it’s like if you have a bus and you take off all the tyres. You cannot move.” Hamid, a paramedic originally from Iran, says without migrants in Magdeburg, the ‘whole system would collapse’. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian At Magdeburg’s synagogue – whose light-filled foyer includes a mural showing one of the few remaining photographs of the original synagogue that was destroyed in a 1938 pogrom – people listed their concerns about an AfD majority, from whether it would affect the funding they receive, to what the party’s plans for a “remigration offensive” would mean for the Ukrainian refugees who had joined their congregation after Russia’s full-scale invasion. The far-right party has also promised to make changes to the school curriculum, in what one party member described as “more Bismarck, less Hitler”. The underlying assumption was that the focus on the rise of National Socialism and the Holocaust – as opposed to the unification of Germany by Otto von Bismarck – had shifted the guilt over what had happened to the current generation, said Igor Mendel Itkin, the synagogue’s rabbi. “They think: ‘If we get rid of this, we will feel free.’ But I think it will be the other way around,” he said. “You cannot get rid of this ghost; you can pacify it, but you cannot get rid of it. If people don’t learn about it, then something like this could happen again, maybe not with the Jewish people, but maybe with the Muslims.” He pointed to Saxony-Anhalt’s AfD manifesto, which makes no mention of the Jewish community but includes promises to “exhaust all legal means to restrict the influence” of Islam, even as it notes that Muslims account for just 2-3% of the 2 million people in the state. Rabbi Igor Mendel Itkin with Maria Schubert at the Magdeburg synagogue say an AfD win is ‘unimaginable’. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian An AfD win would put Jewish people in a complicated position, said Maria Schubert from the Synagogue Community of Magdeburg. “If they win, we don’t know how we will act with them. For me, it’s unimaginable,” she said. She worried that it could also be a dilemma faced by others if Sunday’s election turned out to be a bellwether of shifting political forces rather than an outlier. “I see it as a threat, in that this could just be the beginning. In other German states, many are looking at Saxony-Anhalt to kick things off,” she said. “I mean, at the beginning, nobody took Hitler seriously.” The AfD was approached for comment. With contribution from Niclas Boenki

title: Private equity faces existential crisis in US as unsold companies pile up
author: Heather Timmons
summary: Private equity firms and the companies they own employ over 13 million, from startups to rural hospitals and large retailers, but experts’ concerns of collapse are growing
body_text: Retail stalwarts Saks and Eddie Bauer filed for bankruptcy. Kmart and JoAnn Fabrics are gone for good, a trail of layoffs and disappointed customers in their wake. Hospital giant Steward Health Care collapsed, costing thousands of jobs and leaving several communities without a local hospital. These once-trusted US companies have one thing in common: they were owned by private equity investors, who load companies with debt when they buy them and squeeze out profits as they restructure. The business model is now facing an existential crisis that may have profound ramifications across the US. Once fringe financial players, private equity investors have bought up vast swathes of US, UK, European and Australian industry, from local dentists to shopping mall anchors and fast-food chains and even the video games company EA. In the US, these firms and the companies they own, employ more than 13 million people in everything from quirky startups like Dave’s Hot Chicken, Two Men and a Truck and School of Rock (all owned by Roark Capital) to the US’s largest pet retailer PetSmart (BC Partners) and classics Birkenstock (purchased by L Catterton in 2021) and Pyrex (owned by Centre Lane Partners). Private equity investors also bought thousands of healthcare facilities in the US in recent years, including non-profit hospice care, rural hospitals and small-town dentists’ offices. But this wave of buyouts is running smack into a wall of persistently high interest rates, rising buyout prices and pressure over moribund returns. Private equity funds are sitting on a “record number of unsold companies, many of which they’ve been unable to sell … or at least unable to sell at the prices that they’re looking for”, said Jim Baker, the executive director of the Private Equity Stakeholder Project, an industry watchdog. The US’s over 13,500 unsold companies in private equity portfolios include 2,563 consumer products and services companies, PitchBook data shows, and 1,536 healthcare companies. Hundreds of these have been sitting in PE portfolios for years longer than funds historically like to keep their investments. A growing concern is that “eventually, the companies that have accumulated this much debt are going to collapse”, said Audrey Stienon, Industrial Policy Program Manager at Open Markets, an anti-monopoly thinktank that is examining private equity’s role in the greater economy. And often, what private equity buys up “are really, really important businesses”, Stienon said, providing jobs or vital services to local communities. “When they go down, either you need to bail them out, or you need to find someone to save them, or else you’re just stuck with fewer options for consumers down the line.” Executives in the industry argue their deep pockets will help businesses weather any upcoming crisis. “Private equity-backed businesses face the same higher interest rates and economic pressures as other companies, but they also have committed investment partners that can provide additional capital and keep investing through difficult periods,” Will Dunham, the president and CEO of American Investment Council, an industry trade group, said in a statement. “Ultimately, private equity only succeeds when the businesses it invests in succeed over the long term,” he said. High rates, more competition Think of private equity deals like buying a home, explains Brad Lipton, director of corporate power and financial regulation at the Roosevelt Institute. Investors buy the company with a hefty loan, like a mortgage, but plan to sell in a matter of years. But unlike with a mortgage, the company is on the hook for making payments, not the buyer, and the buyer almost always plans to sell in a few years. “Interest rates being unexpectedly high may have complicated exit strategies,” Lipton said. Private equity firms promise investors higher returns than the stock market, in exchange for holding on to their money for a longer time period, generally 10 years, a business model that’s been the same for decades. “What has changed is that the price of buying a target company has gone through the roof,” as the number of private equity funds increased, explains Rosemary Batt, a Cornell University management and labor professor who studies the industry’s impacts on workers and companies. Healthcare companies that once sold at 11 times EBITDA, a measure of enterprise value, are now priced at 18 times or more, for example. That makes exiting the investment for a profit even more difficult on investors – and on customers and employees. The higher prices for buyouts are “putting even more pressure on PE firms to squeeze the juice out of their portfolio companies”, Batt said, at a time when there’s almost no regulation governing how they do that. “They can engage in financial engineering or just slash and burn on the operating side,” Batt said. “And it takes years for anyone to really see it.” As they hold the company, these investors generally channel free cashflow to “creditors and equityholders, often constraining capital expenditures, worker training, and safety investments”, the University of Chicago’s Business Law Review warns. Tightening macroeconomic conditions can result in forced restructurings “that are costly and value‑destroying for the going concern”. One vulnerable area is rural hospitals and other health provider chains which could face cashflow issues, making debt payments even more difficult, as the Trump administration’s cuts to the Affordable Care Act tax credits and Medicaid bite, warns Pablo Willis, spokesman for the Americans for Tax Fairness, which is advocating for changes to how private equity managers compensation and the firms overall are taxed. “There’s bound to be a very negative effect,” he said. A lack of financial transparency means it is hard to predict where or when, though. Companies owned by private equity generally don’t disclose their debt levels or other financials unless they go public or issue bonds themselves. “By design, the industry takes place in the shadows,” Lipton said, so “everything has to begin with the thought that we don’t have a lot of clarity.” More bankruptcies ahead In a hint of the turmoil to come, private equity-backed companies have accounted for the lion’s share of big corporate bankruptcies in 2025 and the first half of 2026, research from the Private Equity Stakeholder Project shows. The biggest determinant of whether or not a company will go bankrupt is leverage – the amount of borrowed money explains Edith Hotchkiss, a finance professor at Boston College. Private equity-backed companies are no more likely to default than other similarly leveraged firms, but their business models mean they have more debt. They carry debt of about 50% of their enterprise value, recent studies show. US consumers have felt private equity’s impact through the deteriorating quality of some fast-food outlets and disappearing stores as brands under PE ownership go broke. Other industries have been hit too. More than 60% of big manufacturing bankruptcies in the US last year were private equity-backed, Baker said, as were an outsized number of healthcare bankruptcies. Still, the number of PE-backed companies entering bankruptcy declined in 2025 from the year before, even as overall bankruptcies climbed, S&P found, as more companies pursued out-of-court settlements. The entire process is disruptive by nature. “By definition there is not enough money to go around to pay” a company’s debts, Roosevelt’s Lipton said. “Someone is going to lose out and all too often that can be workers” who are owed pensions. “It is a cause of concern for workers and consumers left holding the bag,” said Lipton. New rules ahead Private equity operates without the rules and regulatory oversight of publicly traded companies. The industry has long argued that because it caters to sophisticated, high-net worth investors, it doesn’t need the same scrutiny. But tens of thousands of layoffs, high bankruptcy rates, and the soaring wealth of dozens of private equity billionaires has created bipartisan momentum for more oversight, even before the current interest rate crisis. And Donald Trump’s push to allow everyday Americans to invest in the sector through their retirement plans has raised new concerns. Congress’s June housing bill curbs private equity investments in single-family homes. November’s midterm elections, which are widely expected to deliver one or both houses of Congress to Democrats, could see a sea change for the industry in Washington, while several states are pursuing their own regulation. “For private equity, the question increasingly is not whether Congress will investigate private equity firms and their practices, but rather where the scrutiny will turn to next,” corporate law firm Holland and Knight warned this month. Multiple bills are circulating on Capitol Hill that would regulate how private equity is taxed, how it can invest in certain industries and how fund managers and investors can take profits. States’ bills would limit private equity in healthcare, scrutinize deals more closely and put caps on debt. The “Let Kids Play” Act seeks to ban private equity from youth community sports, now a “$40bn industry dominated by private equity, with the singular goal of extracting as much profit as possible from families”, it contends. The Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren, one of the industry’s most vocal critics in Washington, is leading a healthcare bill that seeks criminal penalties for “executives who loot health care entities like nursing homes and hospitals if that looting results in a patient’s death” and clawbacks of PE compensation. Whether US consumers see some relief could depend on what state they live in, or what other issues Congress takes up in the fall. “Even Democrats will be very hard pressed to do much,” if they have any clout in Congress, Batt predicts, because they have so much on their plate. “The best opportunities right now are for local and state level initiatives,” she said.

title: It’s time for Mark Zuckerberg to resign from Meta
author: Joan Donovan
summary: The CEO is the throughline in a history of billion-dollar blunders that have caused real harm, culminating in last week’s settlement
body_text: Last week, Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook, agreed to a settlement of up to $18bn after dozens of US states accused it of harming children with addictive products. The settlement’s regulatory implications for social media will affect every user, far beyond teens. But if Meta is truly interested in prioritizing the safety of users, the board should request the resignation of Mark Zuckerberg and restructure to put safety above profit. The settlement does little to resolve the scientific question about the degree to which social media is addictive, but instead is the culmination of a battle launched by journalists and independent researchers in 2016 that focused on the digital design of disinformation campaigns powering Brexit in the UK and the US presidential election. Zuckerberg is the one throughline in Meta’s history of billion-dollar blunders that have hurt real people. For the past 15 years, I have studied how science and technology produces social change, for better and worse. As the founder of The Critical Internet Studies Institute, I lead a team investigating harms caused by emerging technologies. We educate practitioners and professionals about the manifest and latent features of new technologies, warts and all. In 2020, I testified to Congress about misinformation as “secondhand smoke”. My comments came weeks after testimony from Facebook’s former director of monetization, who likened the design process of making Meta’s engagement optimization algorithms to the ways tobacco companies made cigarettes more addictive. In a series of op-eds, congressional briefings and research papers, I extended the tobacco case study to show how cultural attitudes about smoking as a personal luxury were upended by concepts such as secondhand smoke, and scientific confirmation that tobacco increases risk of cancer, whose true costs were passed on to families, insurance companies, and employers who lost time and resources to combatting smoking. The public health solution did not go as far as to ban smoking, but limited the areas where smoking was allowed, set an age limit for possession, made companies pay for public education campaigns on the hazards of the product, and most importantly, put products behind grumpy cashiers who validate IDs to purchase. Public health campaigns and warning labels were also important strategies. Similarly, social media companies make all kinds of critical decisions about how to deliver content to your feed. Some of those features are algorithmically engineered to increase the likelihood of users remaining on the app. The settlement comes with design restrictions; teen accounts are limited to two hours per day, no access from midnight to 6am, and no notifications from school bell to bell. Teen accounts must be linked to a parent’s accounts, amid stronger age verification. It’s still unclear how that will be implemented, but it promises to become a privacy nightmare. While these interventions limit time for 13-18 year olds, they do little to address contentious content, such as how drugs, sex and gambling end up algorithmically recommended. It is clear that this latest settlement is the harbinger of a punishing future ahead for Zuckerberg’s businesses. Meta has litigated a number of issues, while avoiding any serious regulation on content moderation (cost center) or advertising (profit center). Enforcing these new rules for teens will increase costs. Meta has faced billions in settlements or fines for harms ranging from failing to protect user privacy to a 2018 security breach to abhorrent outcomes for young people’s mental health. Meta has also caused unremunerated harms to other groups, including amplifying hate speech against Rohingya in Myanmar and hosting and algorithmically promoting rampant medical misinformation and conspiracy theories leading to toxic poisoning and vaccine hesitancy that the World Health Organization labelled an “infodemic”. Zuckerberg’s leadership failures directly led to well-documented damage to civic life, democracy, and global mental and physical health and wellbeing, especially that of young people. Since founding Facebook in 2004, Zuckerberg has been in constant litigation over a number of issues related to ownership and stock early on, which is where he first started to employ a PR strategy to delay, deny and deflect any issues that arise from executives’ decisions to put profit over users’ health. Meta executives lined their pockets off of the tragic and devastating amplification of hate, harassment and incitement. Meanwhile, it has produced a cadre of whistleblowers, with more to come now that it’s clear these executives’ choices led to “real-world harm”, a Silicon Valley term of art that separates cyberspace from meatspace. The settlement comes on the heels of last week’s damning hearings, where one of those whistleblowers, Arturo Béjar, boldly stated: “You just cannot trust Mark Zuckerberg with kids.” Béjar was a lead on safety at Instagram when his teen daughter was the victim of unwanted sexist harassment and profanity on Instagram. Because of his role at Meta, he had real data for accurate measurements of harms on Instagram including the effectiveness of different algorithmic interventions on growth, engagement and user experience. Béjar estimated he had met with Zuckerberg more than 100 times before becoming a whistleblower. Many whistleblowers’ stories begin with an ardent attempt to fix the problems through the correct channels and a refusal from higher-ups to tackle the issue. Ironically, whistleblowers tend to be rule followers who become increasingly indignant as their concerns are met with a workplace culture of ambivalence or advance compliance. In December 2023, I experienced intense professional blowback in academia after obtaining documents culled from another whistleblower, Frances Haugen, which I intended to publish in a publicly accessible database. I acquired the documents legally and used my expertise to help tech insiders, journalists, researchers and Washington DC staffers understand what the Haugen documents did, and importantly did not, say about Meta’s liability and knowledge of product problems. But the message was clear: Meta, then called Facebook, knew of the damage Instagram caused to teenage girls. And yet, through every scandal, Zuckerberg’s net worth has climbed to nearly $200bn, according to Forbes. Fines mean nothing to those with wealth like his, so the first step to safeguard society is to give Meta a fresh start without Zuckerberg’s influence on future products. His vision for “a future for everyone” is an incredibly facile utopia, where AI agents run your life and you just slop your way through it. Beyond the courts, Meta could triage the situation by calling for Zuckerberg to voluntarily resign. Ushering in hope for the future of technology requires changing Meta’s leadership now, so that the future is collectively imagined and built upon a new reputation and commitment. Zuckerberg does not deserve another chance simply because he can afford it. We as a society ultimately pay for his mistakes. Now is the time for shareholders to speak up and push back on Zuckerberg’s dominance and control. Joan Donovan is an assistant professor of journalism at Boston University who studies how technology impacts society. She is the founder of the Critical Internet Studies Institute, where she leads a project on political violence and social movements • This article was amended on 4 September 2026. An earlier version described Facebook’s former director of monetization as an executive.

title: First Thing: JD Vance accused of ‘gaslighting’ after saying he is skeptical US struck Iranian wedding
author: Martin Belam
summary: Vice-president’s claim US-Iran conflict is not war draws ridicule from Democrat Ro Khanna. Plus, iconic feminist Gloria Steinem dies at 92
body_text: Good morning. The US vice-president, JD Vance, has responded to claims that an American strike was responsible for killing four people, including a child, at a wedding celebration in southern Iran by saying that “sometimes things happen”. The deaths were reported by the Iranian Red Crescent, which operates independently of Tehran and is treated by most international monitors as a credible source on casualty figures. In a further comment, described by the congressman Ro Khanna, a Democrat from California, as “gaslighting”, the vice-president said the conflict between the US and Iran, which has stretched into a seventh month and caused the deaths of 18 US service members, was not presently “a war”. Iranian authorities have put the overall death toll from US and Israeli strikes in the thousands, figures outside observers, including US-based monitoring groups, have broadly corroborated. What did Vance say? At a White House press briefing he said: “I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far, so I’m extremely skeptical of this. What I can say with 100% confidence is that, unlike the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the US never targets civilians in combat. We never will do that. We never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen”. Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to blow up Iran’s civilian infrastructure. What is happening with US military leadership? Trump on Thursday named Adam Telle as the acting army secretary after the departure of Daniel Driscoll amid widespread reports of tensions with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. Telle is currently the assistant secretary of the army for civil works. Far-right Israeli minister outlines plan to remove all Palestinians from Gaza Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has outlined a plan for the illegal forced expulsion of all Palestinians from Gaza, with the intention of sending them abroad. The forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva conventions, but as a tightly fought election approaches in Israel, political figures have competed over the harshness of their visions for the strip. Ben-Gvir’s comments follow those of the defence minister, Israel Katz, who said Israel was seeking the Trump administration’s approval to displace Palestinians from Gaza, which he said was still under discussion after being “frozen” by the US president. Katz said Israel would facilitate the emigration “by any means”, implying a policy of coercion. What has the House decided about university boycotts of Israel? The House has passed a Republican-backed bill that would penalize universities that participate in boycotts of Israel. “This legislation is about a simple principle: our colleges and universities should not discriminate against Israel,” said Tim Walberg, the Republican chair of the House education committee. Thirty three Democrats broke with the rest of their party to vote in favor. It now goes to the Senate for consideration. Two workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after Nepal-Tibet flood Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after being trapped by deadly flash floods that buried the project in deep mud. The workers were rescued during a continuing operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel in one of the areas worst affected by last week’s deadly Nepal floods. Officials said the men had been flown to a hospital in Kathmandu. Nepal’s communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, said officials still hoped more workers would be rescued. At least 1,287 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 are missing, Nepal’s disaster management agency said. Missouri supreme court throws out new congressional maps backed by Trump The Missouri supreme court has unanimously blocked new congressional districts backed by Trump from being used in the November election, and ordered a statewide vote on whether to uphold or reject the new map. The decision on Thursday marks a rare setback for Republicans in a national redistricting battle. Missouri’s new districts were used in the August primaries. The state supreme court said they cannot be used in the November general election – or ever again – unless voters first uphold the new districts, after citizens submitted petition signatures seeking a referendum. In other news … The UN general assembly will vote today on a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favor of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size. The deadlocked jury in the Lindsay Clancy trial went home without a verdict Thursday after a dramatic sixth day of deliberations. The billionaire financier Leon Black failed to appear for a US House deposition about his Epstein ties, instead launching a lawsuit against the committee. Excavation work on Trump’s towering, gilded Washington arch is to begin in the next two weeks, despite the plan facing a lawsuit. Fox News Media has abruptly ousted Maria Bartiromo, one of its most well-known hosts and anchors, without explanation. Stat of the day: Thieves steal more than 70,000 pints’ worth of Guinness from depot in England Two trucks were driven into an industrial estate in Runcorn, north-west England, on Monday. They were attached to trailers that were already holding about 800 barrels – or $155,000 worth – of the famous Irish drink, and made off with them. Culture Pick: Turning Point – Generation 9/11 The US will soon cross the point at which half its population were born after 11 September 2001 or were too young to remember the attack. David Smith looks at a new Netflix documentary about those events and their global impact, as memory begins to give way to history. Don’t miss this: Gloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist, dies aged 92 Hillary Clinton was among those remembering Gloria Steinem yesterday, hailing the American feminist icon who died at 92 at home in New York City as “one of the architects of the entire structure of women’s equality”. We have a gallery of Steinem’s life in pictures, a review of the activist’s forthcoming memoir, which now stands as a posthumous testament to her remarkable life, and a selection of her wit and wisdom in her greatest quotes. In a column, Moira Donegan says Steinem personified America’s feminist movement, and we would also like to hear your tributes and memories. … or this: Art Garfunkel on a rich, restless life A beautiful interview with Art Garfunkel, one of the purest voices in the rock/pop canon. And yes, his relationship with Paul Simon does get a mention or two. Climate check: Strongest El Niño on record forecast Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology is the latest body to issue a warning over El Niño, saying it has already broken records, with Pacific Ocean temperature change exceeding 3.6F in six months. Last Thing: I didn’t know I was pregnant until I gave birth Aubrie Morris recounts what must one of the strangest surprises anyone can have – unexpectedly delivering a baby you did not know you were carrying. title: Reform officials ‘plotted to break law on foreign donations’ in undercover film
author: Rowena Mason Whitehall editor
summary: Investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News shows man posing as ‘impermissible donor’ paying for polling that helped Reform
body_text: Nigel Farage is facing fresh criticism on the eve of the Reform UK party conference after some of his team were filmed appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations in an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News. A group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party. The polling was not attributed to Reform, and was reported in the Telegraph and the Times without those newspapers knowing that it was commissioned by the party and paid for by the US donor. The benefit in kind was also not reported to the Electoral Commission. In footage of another meeting, a senior adviser to Farage, Dan Jukes, appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son. When the possible structure was explained to Farage, footage of a meeting between him and the fake donors shows him saying: “Thank you both.” The investigation will reopen intense scrutiny of Reform’s approach to donations and its finances, which are already the subject of a standards inquiry and police investigation. Reform said it had been “the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded climate-change activists posing as would-be party donors” and the party denied any wrongdoing. In Channel 4 News’ investigation, broadcast on Thursday night, footage shows that the fake UK-based supporter also had conversations with Reform UK’s head of policy, James Orr, who talked about commissioning polling that would be paid for by the US-based father. In the film, Orr can be heard saying of the arrangement that Farage “doesn’t know, won’t know” and it was the kind of thing he would “rather not know”. At one point the footage shows him saying it was “totally legit” and with “nothing untowards about it at all”. Farage was subsequently caught on camera in a meeting with the fake US donor in Clacton where he appears to be celebrating the success of the poll, saying it was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”, adding: “It worked. Boom.” Jukes, a close aide to Farage, was also filmed meeting the fake donor, and at a Reform UK reception where in one conversation he appeared to introduce the undercover operative as “key donor for off-the-book project”. In footage of a meeting with the fake US donor, he is heard describing the polling as “clandestine” and “hugely important”. The polling, conducted by JL Partners, made headlines before the local elections in May. The foreign source of funding and its links to Reform were not publicly disclosed, and the Telegraph said it had now suspended the articles about the polling, while the Times said it was not aware of the relationship with Reform. After Channel 4 News’ broadcast, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said the “scandal goes right to the top of Reform UK”. She added: “Nigel Farage needs to urgently prove today that his top team haven’t broken the law and secretly plotted to undermine our democracy.” Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, called on the police and the Electoral Commission to investigate. A Reform spokesperson said: “Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission. The hoaxers are ‘Verbatim Investigations’; a new company, incorporated in July 2026 in an attempt to mask their true identity: the Centre for Climate Reporting.” The party claimed the group’s methods had previously been “rebuked by members of the United States Congress” for “videos [that] appear to be substantially edited, creating an incomplete record of the conversation”. The investigation is likely to create a serious problem for Farage as he attempts to turn the page on Reform’s summer of funding scandals, with his party conference speech scheduled for Friday. In the speech, he will boast of record donations compared with the other parties, including £4m from a crypto billionaire pardoned by Donald Trump in the last quarter. The Reform UK leader will tell the annual Birmingham gathering that the party is “much stronger than we were last year”, saying that it has the highest number of members and has brought in the most donations. Farage will also seek to look to the future by claiming he would declare a “national emergency” in order to pass legislation day and night if made prime minister, insisting he believes Reform UK will win the next election. The party outperformed Labour and the Conservatives with donations of more than £5m in the second quarter of this year, new figures from the Electoral Commission show. However, it remains reliant on a handful of mega-donors who have been based abroad and could be caught by the government’s new £100,000 annual cap on overseas funders which requires donors to have been a UK resident for 12 months. The biggest donation in the last few months was the £4m from Ben Delo, a crypto entrepreneur who has been based in Hong Kong in recent years but in April said he was moving back to the UK. Delo, who was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money-laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business, before being pardoned by Trump, has previously given Reform £4m. Party sources said it was “very confident” that none of Delo’s latest £4m would need to be returned due to the cap when the legislation is passed. The government has said donors would have to have been on the UK electoral register for at least 12 months and meet a residency test showing that they are “genuinely resident at a UK address”. Any gifts over the £100,000 cap from an overseas-based donor would have to be handed back once the new legislation is passed if deemed to be impermissible under the new law. Reform’s confidence in the donation would suggest Delo has been on the UK domestic electoral register and believes he could meet the residency test when the donations were made in April and May. Delo did not respond to a request for comment. Christopher Harborne, the Thailand-based billionaire who has given the party £15m and £5m to Farage personally, did not give any cash after the cap was introduced in March. The £5m gift to Farage from before the last election is under investigation by the standards commissioner, and Reform has slid in the polls since the amount was first revealed by the Guardian.

title: North Carolina becomes first state to send out mail-in ballots for US midterms
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: State decides to proceed hours after Trump administration asks supreme court to let it carry out proposed crackdown
body_text: North Carolina became the first state to start sending out mail-in ballots for November’s US midterm elections on Friday, as Donald Trump’s administration fights to impose sweeping restrictions on the practice before millions of Americans cast their votes. The state’s decision to proceed – hours after Trump’s officials asked the supreme court to let the administration press ahead with its proposed crackdown – comes amid deep uncertainty over whether new federal rules governing mail ballots will be allowed to take effect, and whether the US Postal Service can implement the changes in time. North Carolina is first out of the gate because its state statute requires county boards to begin sending absentee ballots 60 days before a general election – one of the earliest start dates in the country. Other states set their own timelines, ranging from a few weeks before election day to, in a handful of cases, similarly early starts, meaning most will follow in the coming days and weeks. The Trump administration asked the supreme court on Thursday to let it revive a rule barring the postal service from delivering ballots in states that don’t share voter data with the federal government, and requiring ballot envelopes to be screened against new standards before delivery. D John Sauer, the US solicitor general, told the justices that a lower court’s freeze on the plan was causing “serious irreparable harm” to the government, states and voters. It is the second time in weeks the administration has turned to the court over the plan, part of an executive order Trump signed in March directing agencies to compile citizen lists for use in screening mail ballots. A federal judge in Massachusetts, Indira Talwani, blocked the plan in June, ruling that it encroached on states’ constitutional authority over elections. The supreme court’s conservative majority sided with Trump in August but called the challenge premature, leaving the door open for further litigation once the plan was finalized. Talwani froze key parts of it again on 27 August. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, who oversees emergency applications from the region, has not granted the administration’s request for an immediate stay. Instead, she has given challengers until Tuesday to respond, a timeline that leaves little room for the postal service to act before ballots need to be in voters’ hands nationwide. Underscoring how tight the window has become with barely two months left before polls open, a postal service official told the Massachusetts court this week that the agency was still refining its screening system and expected to make it available to states on a voluntary basis “sometime next week”.

title: How much does Donald Trump care about winning the midterms? Apparently, not much at all
author: Jonathan Freedland
summary: Such is the US president’s narcissism that he would see a Democratic victory as proof that he’s indispensable – meanwhile, his every decision spells calamity for voters, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
body_text: What is Donald Trump playing at? If it’s true that the best way of understanding the behaviour of an organisation is to assume it’s controlled by a secret cabal of its enemies, perhaps that same logic extends to the current conduct of the president of the United States. Maybe he secretly wants Republicans to lose the looming midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in the US for the next two years and for which the first postal ballots were sent out today. That’s not as mad a theory as it sounds. Indeed, there are at least two reasons why Trump might either be unbothered by Republican defeat in November or even covertly desire it. We’ll come to those, but let’s start with a pattern of behaviour that is hard to explain as anything other than calculated self-sabotage. At the centre of it is the single act that is already defining Trump’s second term: his reckless, failed war of choice against Iran. No matter how many times he declares mission accomplished or claims to have destroyed the Iranian military or to have reopened the strait of Hormuz, the facts keep telling a different story. In the past week, the two sides shifted from an economic standoff back to a shooting war, with the US firing on Iranian targets that included a wedding party, killing four, and Tehran striking out all over the neighbourhood, hitting Iraq, Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain. The impact on US voters is severe, felt most directly through rising petrol prices and grocery bills. But look at the graph measuring the cost the US government must pay to borrow money: it’s been a steep upward climb since 28 February, the day the war began, hitting a fresh high on Tuesday. For consumers, that rise translates into an expected jump in interest rates. It means that many of those casting ballots are likely to be doing so just as they start paying more on their credit card bills and mortgages. Given that Trump was elected in November 2024 on a promise to bring down inflation, it’s hard to think of a worse environment for a governing party about to face the voters’ verdict. And that’s before you consider the disenchantment of the Maga faithful, who thought the whole point of Trump was an end to forever wars in the Middle East. And yet, Iran may not even be the most electorally damaging of Trump’s foreign adventures. He is, and it would once have been absurd to write this sentence, leading his country into a state of war with … Canada. It’s easy to laugh at the petty gestures, such as Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario as Lake America, a move shamefully followed, and therefore endorsed, by Apple and Google in their map apps. But the economic confrontation is serious – and seriously damaging to Republicans’ electoral prospects. For which US states are hit hardest by Canada’s “dollar-for-dollar” response to Trump’s tariffs? Why, it’s Michigan, Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Texas, all of which just happen to have key senate contests this year. Republican candidates in those states now have to explain why a crucial and previously friendly export market – Canada takes nearly a third of Iowa’s exports, for example – has suddenly turned icy. What’s odd is that Trump’s trade wars are also wars of choice, and they are hurting especially badly what should be a reliable Republican constituency: farmers. Take Iowa: Democrats have not won a senate seat in that farming state for nearly 20 years, yet now, thanks to Trump’s tariffs, they have a genuine shot. Still, perhaps the most egregious illustration of Trump’s apparent determination to ruin Republican chances in the midterms is his support for datacentres. Few issues have seen their salience rise so quickly and in such a clear direction: almost overnight, they have become objects of fear and loathing across the country and across the political spectrum, with seven in 10 Americans saying they would not want one anywhere near where they live. Even among Republicans, there is deep concern over their environmental impact, energy consumption and water use. For others, datacentres have become a lightning rod for a broader anxiety over AI and what it may do to our jobs and our lives. Either way, they are kryptonite to voters. So where does Trump stand? “The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want data centres is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” the president posted on Monday. In that remark, he not only put himself at odds with most US voters, he insulted them too. It’s almost a talent, this ability of Trump’s to land on the wrong side of so-called 80/20 issues, siding with one-fifth of the electorate against the rest. Likewise, strong majorities oppose his vanity projects, whether demolishing the East Wing of the White House to build a ballroom or putting his signature on the dollar bill, yet he persists not only in doing them but in talking about them constantly. And all the while, he has hobbled his party by endorsing radioactively unpopular candidates. Few politicians in the US are more tainted than Ken Paxton, who as attorney general of Texas was impeached by his fellow Republicans on a long list of charges that included bribery and abuse of public trust. Yet who did Trump back as the Republicans’ senate choice in Texas? As a result, now even that red-state stronghold is shaky. Put it all together, and these look like the actions of a man who has no fear of the blue wave that seems to be coming and who could not care less if it sweeps away the Republicans’ current majorities in Congress. That’s curious, given how useful it has been for Trump to have Capitol Hill serve as a rubber stamp that, combined with a largely pliant supreme court, has allowed him to rule with the scarcely fettered power of a would-be autocrat. What could explain the insouciance? One answer is that Congress’s most potent weapon – the power of subpoena and investigation – holds no terror for Trump because he knows that the House and Senate have no means to enforce their will. They have no police or troops at their command. They can issue their writs and summonses, and he will simply ignore them – comforted by the near-blanket immunity he has already been granted by the supreme court. If Congress goes after his aides and advisers, he will instruct them to follow his lead, on the promise of a comprehensive presidential pardon protecting them from any and all legal consequences. The only real weapon Congress has – impeachment and removal from office – he knows they will never use. If senate Republicans could acquit him after the 6 January insurrection, as they did, he knows they will never vote to convict him of anything, no matter how great the crime. But that only goes so far. It explains why Trump does not fear Republican defeat in November, but not why he would actively seek it. For that, one has to look into the abyss that passes for the president’s soul. The bestselling new book Regime Change, by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, spells it out: “If Republicans were wiped out in the 2026 midterm elections, or in 2028, he could simply boast that they couldn’t win without him” on the ballot paper. Such is Trump’s narcissism, he will take an epic Republican defeat in two months’ time not as a repudiation, but as a compliment. And, it seems, he is doing all he can to earn it. Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist
