title: US judge extends block on Trump order to restrict mail-in voting
author: Dara Kerr and agencies
summary: Indira Talwani’s ruling presents major setback for president as first states begin to send out mail ballots for midterms
body_text: A federal judge on Friday again blocked Donald Trump’s executive order to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in voting, the latest in a legal back-and-forth playing out less than two months before election day. US district court judge Indira Talwani initially placed a temporary order blocking the president’s mandate and has now extended that prohibition with a stronger preliminary injunction. The ruling comes hours after North Carolina became the first state to start sending out mail-in ballots for the 3 November midterm elections. Talwani referred to the tight timeline in her ruling. “Plaintiff States are required under state law to mail millions of ballots to voters on a prescribed timeframe. As detailed below, they are unable to pivot this late in the election cycle, nearly guaranteeing significant disenfranchisement for eligible voters,” the judge wrote in her ruling. Trump signed an executive order in March that would create a nationwide list of verified eligible voters, compelling the US Postal Service (USPS) to work with states to establish lists of mail-in voters before elections. The result would mean a limited ballot delivery only to voters on those lists. The Trump administration had already appealed against her temporary block to the supreme court, and it appeared the justices were likely to have a final say on the matter. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but the administration quickly appealed Friday’s ruling. The USPS has said in recent court filings that the technology needed to administer the order isn’t even available. Earlier this week, a USPS whistleblower came forward and warned of “potentially catastrophic problems” if the agency were to try to carry out the order. After Trump signed the order, a coalition of 24 state attorneys general sued the USPS to challenge the rule. They also filed a motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction as litigation was ongoing. Oral argument on the coalition’s request for a preliminary injunction was held on Thursday. “We’ve now secured longer-term relief that will keep the USPS changes blocked while our case moves forward,” said Rob Bonta, the attorney general of California, who co-led the state coalition. “We will continue to take all steps to stop the Trump Administration from trampling on voting rights and restricting mail voting.” The order allows states to voluntarily use the new system. To date, not a single state has announced that it will do so. A coalition of voter service and civic groups, plaintiffs represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) in the lawsuit, issued a statement: “Today’s ruling makes it crystal clear: The US Postal Service must deliver all election mail. USPS has no authority in the Constitution or federal law over how states administer mail voting. And the President cannot order the Postal Service to create a disruptive new bureaucracy that will throw the election into chaos and disenfranchise untold numbers of voters.” Trump has long sought to limit mail voting, even though he himself often uses that method to cast his own ballot. He has falsely blamed mail balloting for his 2020 election loss, spreading baseless claims of fraud, but has so far been unable to change the longstanding voting procedure. An initial executive order Trump issued last year to change election rules, including a requirement for people to show documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote, was halted by federal judges. They ruled that the constitution gives states and, in some cases, Congress the power to set voting procedures, not the president. After Trump issued his mail voting executive order in March, Democrats and voting rights groups filed several lawsuits. Two ended up before Talwani, who placed an initial hold on the order in June, prohibiting its implementation until after November. But the supreme court late last month overturned that order. Its conservative majority pointedly did not say Trump’s move was legal but found the lawsuits were filed prematurely before the US Postal Service issued its rule on how it would implement the order. The rule came out just before the supreme court released its ruling, and the plaintiffs refiled their suits.

title: Leftist insurgents are storming the midterms – just don’t call them all democratic socialists
author: Alice Speri
summary: Progressive candidates navigate their ties to the DSA as the group faces historic growth and mounting pressure
body_text: Days before he won the Democratic primary for a US Senate seat in Michigan, insurgent newcomer Abdul El-Sayed was asked whether he was concerned about being labeled a “socialist”. “I’d rather think of myself as a capitalist who has actually read about capitalism,” El-Sayed told CBS News anchor Ed O’Keefe. “I’m not a socialist.” While El-Sayed might take pains to distance himself from the label in the swing state of Michigan, O’Keefe noted that the candidate has been linked to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the ascendant leftist group whose meteoric rise has captured the enthusiasm of voters desperate for bold change and whose recent wins have stoked the anxieties of both conservatives and the party’s establishment. “I’m not DSA,” El-Sayed stressed in the interview, though he made clear there is room for the DSA in the “big tent” he said he’s seeking to build. El-Sayed is just one of a number of progressive candidates and elected officials across the country who are navigating their relationship and differences with the DSA, which has come under increasing pressure as its candidates have won one race after the other in Democratic primaries mostly in blue states. But as other progressive candidates to the left of the Democratic establishment have mounted bids for office, there has at times been confusion about who is a “DSA candidate” – a confusion some Republicans have been eager to exploit. Some, like El-Sayed, espouse many of the group’s political priorities – fighting fascism, instating universal healthcare, getting money out of politics and boosting labor rights, to name a few – but are not members, nor have they been endorsed by the DSA. Others, like New York’s Claire Valdez, have been organizing with the group for years. Then there are those like Colorado’s Melat Kiros and Pennsylvania’s Chris Rabb who have long identified as socialists but only recently joined the organization. (All three are DSA-endorsed.) Brad Lander was once a member but left the group over its response to the 7 October 2023 attacks in Israel. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the national figure most often associated with the DSA, rejoined the New York City chapter last month after letting her membership lapse for seven years, as speculation mounts about her intention to run for president. But DSA membership doesn’t guarantee endorsement, and intense debates have roiled the organization in recent months about which candidates to endorse and how to best ride the current momentum. In Los Angeles, for example, the local DSA chapter voted to endorse mayoral candidate Nithya Raman this week after weeks of discussions on whether she was too centrist to earn their backing. Pragmatism v purism A decade into Trumpism and the Democrats’ failure to stop it, and buoyed up by the popularity of longtime member Zohran Mamdani, the DSA has helped popularize positions once viewed as radical – from taxing the rich to ending support for Israel. The DSA has become a “shorthand for this rebellion against Democratic party leadership”, said Peter Sterne, an editor at City & State New York who has extensively covered the DSA and a former member of the group. In recent months, the group has seen its membership soar to 120,000, its leaders are getting prime time on cable news and a recent poll found that one-third of Democrats now openly identify as “socialist”, a term not long ago viewed as a slur. The backlash has been swift. After DSA candidates won nine out of 10 races in which the group had fielded candidates in New York City in June, party establishment figures issued a string of hostile statements. Third Way, a centrist Democratic group, announced a $15m effort to go to “war” against them. DSA leaders and members have become tabloid fodder. And this week, House Republicans – joined by eight Democrats – adopted a resolution condemning “socialism” and specifically naming the DSA. The organization’s critics point to some of its more radical stances, from eliminating the Senate to abolishing borders and defunding the police, as a sign of its unseriousness. But many DSA members view those as aspirational and consistent with the group’s fundamental values, while calling for a more realistic approach. Even some more moderate Democrats recognize that the DSA’s message is resonating because the rest of the party has failed to present a satisfying vision of its own. “You can’t beat something with nothing,” said Bill Galston, a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington. “The more moderate wing of the Democratic party is going to have to raise its game substantially.” The DSA’s popularity and campaigning capacity on the one hand, and the animosity from more conservative corners on the other, has left some candidates, particularly in swing states, navigating a balancing act. In Florida, Angie Nixon, who recently won the Democratic Senate primary in one of the biggest upsets of the primary season, joined the DSA only in June but has not been endorsed by the group. When asked whether she identified as a democratic socialist, she equivocated. “I don’t agree with everything that they agree with, but they’re fighting hard to ensure we have access to universal healthcare, access to free college and fully funded public schools,” she said in an interview with the Guardian. “I’ve always been a lifelong Democrat but I’m more of [a] social democrat who believes in strong safety nets.” Some of the most popular politicians associated with the DSA have broken with the group on some issues. The group has for months been debating how to respond to a possible presidential run by Ocasio-Cortez. Some factions, and particularly many NYC-DSA members, have openly encouraged it, while others are suspicious of what they view as her willingness to compromise on DSA priorities. Mamdani has also broken with the group over policing. Ultimately, the decision will be made democratically – DSA members report often excruciatingly deliberative processes and stress that the “democratic” element of the group’s identity is just as fundamental as its socialist one. Endorsements, Sterne noted, can power a campaign with an “army” of canvassers and phone bank volunteers – the DSA’s New York City chapter says that its 50,000 volunteers knocked on doors 1.6m times in support of Mamdani’s candidacy. But the “DSA doesn’t just want to help get people into office and then let them do whatever they want”, he added, noting that there was some concern within the organization that candidates may opportunistically hitch their wagon to the group but not work with it after getting elected. The tension between the pragmatists and the purists, he argued, is healthy, and a sign of the organization’s strength. “More people are joining,” he said. “More people are identifying as socialists, which was once seen as a taboo term.”

title: ‘Sinn Féin traitors!’: how far-right rhetoric derailed party’s path to power in Ireland
author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
summary: Party insider reveals how election campaign was blindsided by rise of anti-immigrant feeling in new book
body_text: For Siobhán Fenton, the dream of Sinn Féin winning power and leading a progressive leftwing government evaporated the day she was canvassing in Dublin and felt a cold, sharp sting on her neck. She was in the passageway of a block of flats in the inner city, knocking on doors, and looked around for the source. Fenton, a media adviser to the party leader, Mary Lou McDonald, felt another sting on her shoulder, then another on her forearm. They were coins, thrown from a balcony above, where a man’s voice was shouting. “Sinn Féin traitors!” he roared. “Mary Lou Mohammad! Ireland is full!” It was May 2024, and instead of steaming towards victory in local and European elections – widely deemed a foregone conclusion, to be followed by a historic triumph in a general election – the party was experiencing a backlash fuelled by anti-immigrant sentiment in what was usually a bastion of working-class support. The coins left Fenton with gashes and bruises that augured an electoral hammering. “By the time the party realised how bad things had gotten it was almost too late,” she said. “The far right had infiltrated lots of Sinn Féin strongholds and we hadn’t picked up on it.” In a rupture to the party’s reputation for secrecy and discipline, Fenton has written a rare insider’s account, titled Ourselves Alone: Sinn Féin Behind Closed Doors. It lifts the lid on a debacle that ambushed the party on the path to power. Instead of winning a general election and turbo-charging the campaign for Irish unification by ratcheting up pressure for a referendum, the party stumbled and today remains in opposition. It is a cautionary tale for progressive movements across Europe and elsewhere that struggle to reconcile tolerance for immigrants and refugees with clamours for crackdowns on new arrivals. A surge in xenophobia among grassroots supporters had blind-sided and, for a time, paralysed party leaders, Fenton said in an interview. “There was a moment of genuine sheer panic and just not knowing what to do. We were struggling to adapt because it was a sense that things had started to spiral out of control.” The book, published this week, depicts a largely well-intentioned but hapless party, and is also an account from a member of an organisation that many perceive as secretive and still in thrall to former IRA leaders on both sides of the Irish border, a perception Fenton disputes. Fenton, 34, was an atypical “Shinner”, the informal name for party adherents. She came from a middle-class Belfast family that abhorred the violence of the Troubles and favoured constitutional nationalism, not flinty republicanism. Fenton briefly worked for the Social Democratic and Labour party (SDLP) before studying English literature at Oxford, researching gender-based violence at Cambridge and becoming a London-based journalist for the Independent before returning to Northern Ireland in 2016, where she freelanced for the BBC and other outlets, including the Guardian, and wrote a book on the Good Friday agreement. In early 2020, Sinn Féin offered Fenton a job in Dublin. The party was on a high. It had just won 24.5% of first preference votes in the Irish general election, overtaking Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael, two centrist parties that had alternated in power for a century. As successor to Gerry Adams, McDonald, a Dubliner universally known as Mary Lou, offered a fresh alternative, especially to young voters who blamed the political establishment for a housing crisis. Sinn Féin had run too few candidates to capitalise on the breakthrough, so Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael mustered enough seats to form a coalition, leaving Sinn Féin in opposition. Analysts expected it to win power after the next election. After Sinn Féin became the biggest party in Northern Ireland in 2022, which paved the way for Michelle O’Neill to become first minister at Stormont, the onus was on the party’s southern branch to ensure McDonald became taoiseach at Leinster House. “Don’t fuck it up,” a Belfast colleague half-jokingly told Fenton. For three years, Fenton, having relocated to Dublin, experienced the giddy nervousness of a party soaring in the polls while the ruling coalition slumped. The republican mantra – “tiocfaidh ár lá”, our day will come – seemed apt. A section titled “the long fall” chronicles the unravelling amid missteps and a volatile public mood. McDonald appeared to blame police for a riot that rocked Dublin in November 2023, and alarmed middle-class property owners by suggesting average Dublin house prices should fall to €300,000. More damagingly, the party failed to navigate growing xenophobia, the result of a housing shortage, a cost of living crisis, an influx of migrants and refugees, and far-right activism on social media and the streets. “It was a blind spot,” said Fenton. Covid-19 restrictions and a focus on the parliamentary party withered grassroots networking, leaving leaders unaware of the extent to which conspiracy theories and hostility to Muslims had taken hold, she said. The party should have tried to combat racist narratives by peeling people away from smartphones and having “really difficult conversations”, said Fenton. “Go door to door, talk about community concerns but be very, very clear that scapegoating immigrants and refugees is the wrong response.” Instead of gains in the May 2024 local and European elections, the cascade of coins on to Fenton foretold haemorrhaging support, especially in working-class strongholds that branded McDonald a “traitor” for not seeking greater curbs on migration. Months later the party limped into a general election that kept Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael in power. Fenton’s contract was not renewed and she returned to her native Belfast, where she now works as a writer and analyst. She is no longer a member of Sinn Féin. Immigration remains a fraught issue for a party squeezed between those wanting a harder line and those who favour solidarity, said Fenton. Leaders may be tempted to sidestep the issue until the next election, then take a stance, she said. “It will be dependent on what the political environment looks like then.”

title: ‘It cost me many friendships’: former Brazil military chief reveals inside struggle to stop Bolsonaro’s coup
author: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
summary: Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior describes 2022 meeting in new book as ex-leader’s son vies with Lula for presidency
body_text: The far-right populist Jair Bolsonaro was in his final days as Brazil’s president when, six weeks after losing the election and still refusing to recognise the result, he summoned the heads of the armed forces to a meeting. The defence minister, Gen Paulo Sérgio Nogueira de Oliveira, took out a document from a plastic folder and handed copies to the commanders of the navy, army and air force. It was a draft decree proposing to invalidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s election in October 2022 and keep Bolsonaro in power. “The draft coup decree – which some people still insist to this day never existed – was there, awaiting approval or rejection; consensus or a majority,” writes the then head of the air force, Lt Brig Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior, in a new book coming out this month. After learning that the document would prevent Lula from taking office, Baptista Júnior told the defence minister he refused even to receive it: “The air force will not take part in this.” He then stood up and left the room. The extensive investigation and trial that convicted Bolsonaro of attempting a coup concluded that the plot failed to move forward mainly because the heads of two of the three armed forces – Baptista Júnior and the army commander, Gen Marco Antônio Freire Gomes – refused to take part. The navy commander, Adm Almir Garnier Santos, was convicted, as was Nogueira. Both are serving their sentences at military facilities, while Bolsonaro is under house arrest. Freire Gomes has kept a low profile, but Baptista Júnior, speaking to the Guardian by video call, said he had decided to write a book to help prevent history from repeating itself. In the book, the 65-year-old former fighter pilot gives a detailed, first-hand account of the various ways in which Bolsonaro tried to cling to power. Baptista Júnior said he was motivated by the fact that, despite the abundance of evidence presented during the former president’s trial, opinion polls still showed that about a third of the population did not believe there had been an attempted coup. “Keeping in power someone who lost an election is a coup d’état,” he said, speaking from his home in Brasília, where he was dressed in civilian clothes – having recently retired – and about to pick up his grandson from school. The book, the Portuguese title of which translates as I Said No! – An Anti-Coup Bulwark, is due to be published on 15 September, about two weeks before the first round of the presidential election, in which Lula will face one of Bolsonaro’s sons, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro. Some Bolsonaro supporters have accused Baptista Júnior of trying to influence the vote, although he makes clear that he will vote for neither Lula nor Flávio, and criticises both in the book. He said the timing of the book was simply the result of the writing and editing process. Despite writing that he voted for the far-right populist in the 2018 and 2022 elections, and even recounting a lighthearted moment at a barbecue when he saw the first lady reprimand the president for drinking beer, Baptista Júnior is critical of Bolsonaro, a former army captain who spent 30 largely undistinguished years as a city councillor and then congressman before reaching the presidency. He describes his former boss as someone with “significant limitations in political, institutional and administrative experience” and an “almost total imperviousness to outside opinions or information that did not conform to the ‘truths’ he had already established as his own” – citing his refusal to accept facts such as the scientific evidence supporting Covid-19 vaccination. During the election, Bolsonaro became “entirely consumed by his own efforts to remain in office”, writes Baptista Júnior. After repeatedly casting doubt on the vote, the president ordered the armed forces to investigate the electronic voting system, but refused to accept their reports when they found no irregularities. “He may still not believe the election result even today. Whether that is a matter of character, personality or something pathological, I don’t know,” said Baptista Júnior. The book touches on, but does not go into detail about, one of the most shocking revelations from the coup investigation: a plan drawn up by army special forces to kidnap or assassinate Lula, the newly elected vice-president and a supreme court justice. Baptista Júnior writes that he was not summoned to those meetings and only learned about them through the press. He does, however, recount more than a dozen meetings in which Bolsonaro summoned the heads of the armed forces to discuss ways to remain in power. At one of them, he witnessed the army chief tell the president, after hearing a proposal for an institutional rupture: “If you do that, I’ll have to arrest you.” Baptista Júnior had already given that account in testimony, and during the trial both Freire Gomes and Bolsonaro denied it. But he stands by his account in the book, writing that it was not something anyone present would forget. Saying no to the coup cost the pilot “many friendships”, he said. Even some military personnel still call him a “traitor” or a “watermelon”, a slur for soldiers seen as green on the outside because of their uniforms, but communist red within. The attacks started soon after the air force chief refused to join the plot, when the army general Walter Souza Braga Netto, whom Baptista Júnior considered a friend, ordered other military officers to attack him on social media and “make his life and his family’s hell”. Braga Netto, Bolsonaro’s running mate, was also convicted over the attempted coup. Most of Baptista Júnior’s revelations in the book initially emerged in 2024, when he was summoned to testify to federal police and only then, more than a year after leaving office, revealed that he had witnessed an attempted coup. Juliano da Silva Cortinhas, who worked on the civilian side of the defence ministry between 2013 and 2016, before the Bolsonaro administration, said: “It’s positive that he [Baptista Júnior] and the army chief said no to the coup, but as a matter of duty they should have reported it to the police as soon as it happened.” Cortinhas, who heads a security research group at the University of Brasília, said the armed forces could not present themselves as the “saviours” of democracy because that would be like “tripping society up and then holding out a hand to help it back to its feet”. “It was the commanders who allowed active-duty officers to take part in politics,” he said, noting that the Bolsonaro administration had by far the largest number of military personnel serving in civilian posts since the end of the brutal 1964–85 military dictatorship. Cortinhas sees as positive the fact that high-ranking officers were convicted of an attempted coup for the first time, but noted that others involved in the plot escaped justice, and many were not even identified. “The risk of a new coup is even greater today,” he said. The new factor, he said, was the US president, Donald Trump, who has sought to influence elections across Latin America in support of far-right candidates such as Flávio Bolsonaro. In 2022, when Joe Biden was in the White House, Bolsonaro’s vice-president acknowledged that attempting a coup would leave Brazil in a “difficult position before the international community”. Cortinhas said he feared that if Lula was re-elected and Trump refused to recognise the result, some members of Brazil’s military could feel emboldened. “Coup-supporting groups remain within the armed forces,” he said. Baptista Júnior confirmed that, although it was difficult to know how many, there remained active-duty military personnel who believed a coup d’état would be justified under certain circumstances. “That’s why eternal vigilance is the best path,” he said.

title: Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US military
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: The US defense secretary faces internal dissent and discord at the Pentagon, accused of focusing on culture war issues and his own political ambitions as the Iran war drags on
body_text: In a different Washington, under a different president, a return to the well-worn playbook of all-out sanctions to counter Iran might have been the signal for a publicity-hungry US secretary of defense to adopt a lower profile. But these are no ordinary times. And Pete Hegseth is no ordinary defense secretary. Barely a week after the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, unleashed a supposed “economic D-day” aimed at crushing the regime in Tehran under the weight of commercial pressures, Hegseth once again returned to the limelight – and the center of controversy. The former Fox News host usurped Bessent from center stage as the conflict with Iran reverted to open warfare and discontent at the Pentagon was laid bare once more. Turf wars within Hegseth’s own fiefdom resurfaced with the resignation of the army secretary, fresh revelations of blocked promotions and leaked disclosures of resistance from military top brass of extended deployments to the Middle East. While the Pentagon insists that any suggestion the defense department is in disarray under Hegseth is “completely baseless”, alarm over his conduct in the role – and the implications – has not merely been expressed by Hegseth’s political opponents. “The secretary of defense is a clear and present danger to the national security of the United States and the world,” said Randy Manner, a retired major general in the US national guard – in which Hegseth also served – and member of National Security Leaders for America (NSL4A), a group of former military leaders. “He has done more harm to the national security of the United States than any secretary of defense since the country was created.” Thom Tillis, the Republican senator from North Carolina, who is stepping down from the US Senate after clashes with Donald Trump, bluntly urged the US president this week to fire his defense secretary. “I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis wrote on social media. “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and wellbeing of our fighting force.” After a month-long lull, the resumption of strikes on Iranian targets near the strait of Hormuz meanwhile renewed questions over just what the US wants to achieve in its war with the Islamic regime, which Trump and his defense secretary once loudly vowed to topple. The strikes, on mainland Iran as well as Iranian islands in the Gulf, caused multiple casualties. In one incident, Iranian media reported that five people, including a six-year-old child, were killed in the southern city of Kuhestak when a missile struck a wedding party. Iranian authorities labelled the deaths a war crime. The episode had echoes of strikes in the city of Minab on the first day of the war on 28 February, when more than 150 people, including 120 children, were killed when missiles hit an elementary school. The US has not formally admitted responsibility, although officials have said the incident is under military investigation. The latest strikes were quickly followed by disclosures that Hegseth had extended military deployments in the Middle East, where the US currently maintains 50,000 troops and 19 warships – partly to enforce a naval blockade on Iran – into the middle of next year. The extensions were ordered even after several commanders in other sectors voiced objections, formally known as “non-concurs”, to the deployments, arguing that they could leave the US at risk of being unable to meet its commitments in other areas, while subjecting forces to the additional strain of being at sea for too long. The non-concurs were recorded in the Secretary of Defense Orders Book of 14 August, a classified document whose contents were leaked and reported by the Washington Post. The Pentagon reached out to the Guardian after publication of this story. Hegseth “has been a transformative leader for the Department of War and, at President Trump’s direction, has ushered in a new era of Peace Through Strength”, press secretary Kingsley Wilson said in a statement. “Standards and merit are back, our arsenal is stronger than ever before, and morale and recruitment across every service are at all time highs. “Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way. The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first.” ‘The past six months has failed’ “I’m not sure what the strategy is here,” Kevin Carroll, a former army colonel and military intelligence officer who served in the offices of the defense secretary and joint chiefs of staff, said of the war on Iran. “What’s the enemy’s center of gravity that we’re going after? “We tried decapitating their leadership. That didn’t work. We tried going after their missile program. We were not able to destroy it. Tried sinking the navy, but they still maintain a mining capability. “We could easily take out their energy infrastructure. But that would drive the price of oil much, much higher, and lead to retaliatory attacks on the energy infrastructure of our Gulf allies. It’s not clear what this target set is intended to do.” Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former White House and state department adviser on Iran, said Hegseth’s long-term deployment orders reflected the administration’s decision to embrace a policy of long-term economic blockade. “It’s a recognition of the fact that the past six months has failed, but they don’t know what to do,” argued Swanson, who suggested that Trump was attracted by the idea of abandoning the conflict, but wanted to do so in way that enabled him to project strength. As the war drags on, Hegseth stands accused of being insufficiently engaged with such grave policy matters, preferring instead to focus on “cultural” issues – sacrificing the careers of talented career officers in the process – and his future political ambitions. The defense secretary, who has evaded awkward questions or scrutiny by not holding a formal Pentagon briefing since 5 May, has reportedly told associates that he is considering a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. In the midst of a burgeoning trade war between the US and Canada, Hegseth – who has previously railed against “fat” generals and instituted testosterone tests for service personnel – found time to wade in by apparently “body shaming” two Canadian female teenage cadets. The social media post attracted a storm of criticism. In a podcast, Joe Walsh, a former Republican congressman who is now a Democrat, accused Hegseth of “fucking online harassment” and denounced the defense secretary as a “punk”. Tensions over Hegseth’s priorities reached a head this week when the army secretary, Dan Driscoll – a friend and ally of Vice-President JD Vance – resigned after repeatedly clashing with Hegseth over blocked promotions and purges of senior commanders on flimsy pretexts. A large proportion of those blocked or fired have been black or female, in line with Hegseth’s vocal crusade against “woke” DEI (diversity, equity and inclusiveness) initiatives. In the latest of a series of purges, the New York Times reported that Hegseth had blocked the promotions of seven officers to the two-star general rank. In submitting his resignation, Driscoll – who has spearheaded efforts to modernize the army, including through embracing drone warfare – voiced concerns “surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible”, a source told CNN. Driscoll’s departure – and the reasons for it – aroused anger even among Republicans, most notably Tillis, the outgoing GOP senator. “Dan was the right man at the right moment to lead our Soldiers and Army civilians,” wrote Tillis. The withering verdict is seconded by some retired generals, who say misgivings over Hegseth’s leadership are quietly shared by many serving officers who remain. Manner said Hegseth was depriving other parts of the armed forces to fund the Iran war out of “readiness accounts”. “These are for training the rest of the force,” he said. “So the rest of the force is losing training hours, equipment and money for maintenance and operations. The rest of the military is significantly degraded.” Manner also said his conversations with serving officers bore out the leaked concerns voiced in the Secretary of Defence’s Orders Book. “I have firsthand knowledge of people who are serving on active duty who echo the exact same concerns that we are headed to a situation where we can no longer defend Taiwan, that we are very unlikely to be able to defend even, quite frankly, South Korea,” he said. ‘Infinitely worse’ than Rumsfeld Hegseth, who has drawn accusations of war crimes for ordering a succession of strikes on alleged drug-ferrying boats off the coasts of South America, is not the first US defense secretary to come under a harsh spotlight over the conduct of a far-off American war. Robert McNamara, defense secretary under Lyndon Johnson, became a lightning rod for criticism during the Vietnam war before eventually undergoing a crisis of conscience and being moved to a new role as head of the World Bank. During George W Bush’s administration, Donald Rumsfeld became the target of fierce criticism after failing as defense secretary to plan adequately for the occupation of Iraq after the initial invasion to topple Saddam Hussein. But Paul Eaton, a retired major general who trained Iraqi troops after the invasion and is now an adviser to VoteVets – an advocacy group for progressive military veterans – said Rumsfeld’s failings paled in comparison with Hegseth. “Rumsfeld had ‘next war-itis’, which was a contributing factor to Bush firing him after the shellacking that the Republican party had in the [2006] midterms,” Eaton said. “All this sounds faintly familiar with what we’re going through right now. “But this is infinitely worse because we had a lot of other very smart people to corral the bad ideas coming out of Rumsfeld. [This time] we’ve had the whole removal of seasoned men and women who have learned things the hard way most of the time in combat. “If you fail to plan, plan to fail, and what we’re seeing in the Iran war is just evidence. The frustration is, we’re better than this in the uniformed military but we got handed a terrible set of guidance from our civilian leadership.” Michael O’Hanlon, a defense and strategy expert at the Brookings Institution, argued that the armed forces had enough “bench strength” to survive Hegseth’s purges without imminent collapse, but lamented the loss of certain key individuals who could not be easily replaced. He singled out Gen Chris Donahue, who recently stepped down from his post as head of the US land command in Europe and Africa. “We haven’t had a TV talkshow star with a strong partisan and cultural agenda wind up as secretary of defense,” said O’Hanlon. “There may be some echoes of previous secretaries, but the political and culture stuff is Pete Hegseth through and through.” Hegseth was “not going to wind up leaving a major mark”, O’Hanlon predicted. “He’s going to wind up being known as the guy who fought Trump’s culture wars for him – and maybe failed to help Trump stay out of trouble in the Iran war, depending on how bad that gets.” • This article was amended on 5 September 2026. An earlier version erred in saying that Robert McNamara became head of the International Monetary Fund; he was head (as its president from 1968 to 1981) of the World Bank, the IMF’s sister organization. • This article was amended on 6 September 2026 to include a statement from the Pentagon.

title: Even in safe-haven Massachusetts, trans care is at risk. Young people are fighting to protect it
author: Lex McMenamin in Boston
summary: Activists are calling on the state attorney general to take action against hospitals that have ended gender-affirming care programs after Trump retook office
body_text: A group of trans activists from across Massachusetts brought their needles, hormone gels, pills and sharps containers to Boston on Wednesday to send a message to state attorney general Andrea Campbell. Organizers with the youth-led group Protect Trans Futures (PTF) took their hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in the lobby of her office building, then occupied the space, refusing to leave without a commitment to protect civil rights for trans kids. While Massachusetts is considered one of the legally “safest” places for trans people, some local hospitals are still dropping youth gender-affirming care and canceling surgery appointments amid an expansive legal fight across the US. Gender-affirming care remains legal for all in Massachusetts, but the Trump administration’s attempt to undermine state laws has still created barriers to care, and a chilling effect. So organizers came asking Campbell to order those hospitals to reinstate care, or investigate or launch litigation against them for failing to do so. Some advocates – who share Protect Trans Futures’ outrage at the hospitals for pre-emptively complying with Donald Trump’s agenda – fear undermining a sympathetic attorney general and eventually ending up with a less friendly replacement. But many trans organizers see the action as simply holding the government to its own standards. “Massachusetts politicians at the local, state and federal level are very naive in thinking and hoping that there’s not this massive loss of care, but that’s not the reality of patients and families,” said Teddy Walker, a 21-year-old with Protect Trans Futures. “The Trump administration’s policies are working exactly as intended.” A majority of American medical experts support access to trans youth care, which demonstrably reduces suicide and mental health risks. Nonetheless, in 27 states, such as Texas and Missouri, youth gender-affirming care is now restricted or banned; in some, doctors can be prosecuted for providing it, and parents have been investigated for seeking it out for their children. Fifty percent of trans youth ages 13 to 17 live in one of those states. Even hospitals in blue states, like New York’s NYU Langone, which ended care last year, have been subpoenaed for the medical records of their former minor clients. After the state attorney general’s building had closed for the day, organizers were handed a phone: An assistant attorney general offered them a meeting – a step organizers had taken months before, with no results. So they refused. After a few hours, nine organizers, including Walker, were arrested by state troopers. (The attorney general’s office told the Guardian they were not involved in the decision to arrest the protesters.) He screamed a message to supporters witnessing his arrest – a chant from LGBTQ+ activists who held die-ins and other protests to force a change in the Aids epidemic: “Act up! Fight back!” The ‘trans great migration’ Over the last few years, hundreds of thousands of trans people and families with trans kids have fled home states with anti-trans laws, relocating to states like Massachusetts in hopes of maintaining access to gender-affirming care and other trans civil rights. Massachusetts is one of a handful of US states with shield laws to protect LGBTQ+ residents from lawsuits and penalties from states where gender affirming care is criminalized. In addition, elected officials in the state are vocal supporters of their trans constituents, including Gov Maura Healey, the state’s first woman and lesbian governor, and Senator Edward Markey, who won the Democratic primary this week in a race that was largely defined by trans rights. But the Trump administration attacked these state-level protections for trans youth healthcare soon after taking office in January 2025. In the first weeks of his second term, the president signed an executive order threatening to cut off federal funding for hospitals that provide gender-affirming medical care to trans youth. Later that year, health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr sought to target Medicaid funding to hospitals providing youth gender affirming care. Many of those efforts have been tossed; there are no reports of hospitals losing federal funding for providing this care. Still, in response to the administration’s directives, at least three local hospitals or healthcare systems in Massachusetts have ended gender-affirming care programs for patients under 19. (This means that 18-year-olds, who are legally adults, are impacted.) A fourth Massachusetts hospital canceled all appointments for a gender-affirming surgery for adult trans women, even though adults aren’t the subject of Trump’s executive order. Initially, organizers protested outside these hospitals in an effort to pressure them to reinstate the care. They later shifted their focus to pressuring state officials to enforce existing civil rights laws. In April, Campbell’s office met with a group of trans youth advocates after some hospitals ended care for youth. She has repeatedly expressed support for trans youth, saying that trans healthcare “remains legal and protected” in Massachusetts, and warning hospitals that ending youth gender-affirming care “may amount to discrimination” under state law. And on 2 September, the same day as the protest at her office, Campbell joined 21 other state attorneys general in suing the Trump administration over its attempt to block Medicaid coverage for youth gender affirming care. In August, Walker publicly confronted Campbell at an event at the Boston public library over her inaction. She stated she will not litigate against hospitals that have ended care, and has not ordered them to reinstate it, as attorneys general in blue states like New York and California, as well as Colorado’s supreme court, have done. After Wednesday’s protest, the attorney general’s office shared with the Guardian the email it sent to Protect Trans Futures. In it, the attorney general’s office argued that what’s been done in California and New York were imperfect comparisons and would not result in care being reinstated in Massachusetts. The office reiterated that youth gender affirming care remains legal in the state, and wrote, “The cessation of gender-affirming care for minors by Fenway Health, Outer Cape Health Services and Baystate Health has not resulted in a wave of hospitals or clinics ceasing to provide care in the Commonwealth.” The email added, “The AGO and PTF share a common goal: maintaining access to gender-affirming care.” Campbell’s office has said it is unaware of any youth who has lost care, but Walker, of the group Protect Trans Futures, says he knows dozens of youth and their families who have. In its email, the attorney general’s office asked PTF to connect with those families. Walker said that the group has previously brought those families to meetings with the office, but nothing came of it. Shattered trust Last October, Fenway Health, Massachusetts’ largest LGBTQ+ healthcare provider, stopped providing youth hormone care and puberty blockers, routine medical care to prevent the major physical changes that come during puberty. Fenway was a particular blow: from its founding as a community health drop-in location in the early 1970s, it centered gay clients and made the first Aids diagnosis in New England. Other providers, including Outer Cape Health Services, which runs three facilities on Cape Cod, and Baystate Health, which services western Massachusetts, followed suit. Other hospitals and clinics have taken in those who’ve lost care. Transhealth in Northampton, the country’s only independent clinic focused solely on trans and gender-nonconforming patients, has shouldered an avalanche of referrals. Josh, who asked to use a pseudonym for privacy reasons, 18, was born at Fenway to lesbian parents, and still sees his primary care physician there. Following the typical medical routine for youth who transition in childhood, he started going to Fenway for hormone replacement therapy in middle school. After two years on puberty blockers, he then started taking testosterone. That process is intentionally slow, requiring letters from therapists and evaluations, often taking at least a year. When Fenway halted care last year, Josh was able to get a referral to Boston Children’s hospital, which has vocally refused to close its trans healthcare program. Restarting the intake process, however, took over a year, he said. It shattered his trust that his home state would be able to protect him. He’s just one case of young people abruptly stripped of care. Safara Malone, a senior at Harvard University, moved to Massachusetts from Texas, which has extreme anti-trans laws, in 2024. Malone was a strident advocate for trans rights in her home state and intentionally chose a college where she would face fewer barriers and find more explicit support. But with graduation less than a year away, Malone says she’s not sure where she’ll feel safe living next, amid what she called the trans “great migration”. It was difficult for her to realize that had she arrived in Boston just one year later – after the changes at Fenway – she would have been refused her care. Malone is now considering leaving the country. Fighting for change Now, trans people of all ages are fighting to protect the very civil rights that brought many of them to Massachusetts in the first place. Fenway’s cessation of care spurred the creation of Protect Trans Futures, a group of trans youth that has been fighting the state government and hospitals themselves to reinstate care. PTF has held a series of actions this summer pushing Campbell to consider their demands, including coordinating a letter campaign which now has more than 3,000 signatures. After Baystate cut off youth gender affirming care, another group, Western Massachusetts Trans Alliance (WMTA), emerged to push back. These nascent grassroots efforts join the existing fabric of LGBTQ+ and trans advocacy organizations across the state, including the Massachusetts Transgender Political Coalition. Other organizations like the Boston chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America have signed on to PTF’s efforts. Many of these groups, as well as the national Gender Liberation Movement, joined PTF outside Campbell’s offices. A grassroots group of parents and other adults from western Massachusetts also came in to support and set up a large banner depicting a blue bus labeled “Baystate Health”. Around the banner, people held smaller signs that read “throws trans kids under the bus”. Under the banner, fabric legs with children’s sneakers poked out. “Unlike Boston, western Mass does not have as many choices for healthcare,” Ali Wicks-Lim, one of the grassroots organizers protesting Baystate, said outside the attorney general’s office Wednesday. “So for them to end this gender-affirming care means that people have to travel further, and search harder, to find any kind of gender affirming care for their youth.” Wicks-Lim says that they’ve heard of many families who have not been able to find another provider. “Once we let the government start making decisions about what we do with our bodies, and what our children are able to do with our bodies, and the decisions that parents and grandparents and caregivers need to be able to make for their children”, they said, “we’re in a really dangerous territory.”

title: Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash
author: Thor Benson
summary: Politicians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the tech
body_text: Growing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda. The bipartisan backlash against Flock Safety cameras resembles nationwide rage toward the construction of large datacenters that power artificial intelligence. Polling shows roughly 75% of Americans oppose new datacenter construction in their areas. Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans per month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who have used them to stalk ex-lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequently utilized by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Data and polling from the Washington Post show that social media posts about Flock have increased since July, and about 46% of Americans oppose ALPRs being used in their community – up 13 points from the previous year. Vigilantes are posting videos of themselves destroying the cameras to digital applause. According to privacy and surveillance experts, hatred of Flock cameras has become bipartisan. “In my 20-plus years at the ACLU, I’ve never really seen such a grassroots uprising against surveillance technology like this,” said Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). “On the left, there’s a historical memory of law enforcement spying on and interfering with advocates for social change … On the right, there’s a long tradition of ‘don’t tread on me’ – keep the government out of my life, keep it from looking over my shoulder.” Both liberal and conservative politicians are pushing back against Flock cameras. Greg Abbott, Texas’s Republican governor, blocked state agencies from procuring Flock products. On the other side of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator, is promising to introduce legislation to restrict the use of Flock cameras. Republican senator Josh Hawley has launched an investigation into potential Flock privacy abuses, and Democratic congressman Ro Khanna is cosponsoring a bill with Republican congressman Thomas Massie to prevent federal funds from being used to purchase Flock cameras. Municipal leaders of all political stripes are dropping contracts with Flock, though sometimes they replace the license plate readers with another brand of camera and continue the surveillance. We reached out to Flock Safety for a statement and did not receive a response before publishing. Surveillance hasn’t always been a unifying topic in US politics. Debates over the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), the Patriot Act and other surveillance issues have often been divisive. This appears to be an unusual case where politicians are getting on the same side of a hot-button issue. “Privacy, to some extent, is bipartisan,” said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “When you put up these cameras, they last longer than the current administration. You might trust the people in power now who put them up – but are you going to trust the next people who get access to that equipment?” Americans have been showing up at town hall meetings by the dozen over the past six months or so, and there have been numerous protests to show opposition to Flock surveillance cameras around the country. More than 100 jurisdictions have canceled their contracts so far, according to data from the non-profit Institute for Justice. An organization called DeFlock, founded in 2024, hopes to increase the numbers by compiling a map of the cameras’ locations. While ALPRs aren’t new, Flock, founded in 2017, has made them far more prevalent than they used to be. The company’s software allows disparate law enforcement agencies to share data with one another, meaning a license plate scan by a police department in one state could easily and quickly be used in another. “Flock represents tech companies in bed with governments, doing the exact stuff people have become distrustful of and resentful about for the past few decades. It feels like it’s finally hit the boiling-over point,” said Woodrow Hartzog, a professor of law and computer science at Boston University. Hartzog predicts the actions against Flock Safety will continue at the state and local level amid this growing popular outrage. He expects people are going to stay angry about the issue, and politicians will have to respond. “The pushback we’re seeing against Flock cameras is one of the most vivid illustrations I can think of that surveillance is not inevitable – that these tools aren’t inevitable,” Hartzog says. “It’s up to all of us to stop them.”

title: Judge orders Trump administration to reveal who set up $1.8bn ‘anti-weaponization fund’
author: Edward Helmore
summary: Judge issues order as part of discovery process in lawsuit brought by non-profit into now defunct compensation fund
body_text: A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to reveal who set up the structure of a controversial $1.8bn “anti-weaponization fund” to recompense victims of so-called political lawfare that was reportedly dropped by the justice department last month. Ivan Davis, the US magistrate judge for the eastern district of Virginia, issued the order compelling discovery materials from the government as part of a lawsuit brought by the Democracy Forward non-profit on behalf of plaintiffs including a fired prosecutor and a college professor acquitted of assaulting federal agents at a protest against an immigration raid in California. “Today’s order granting discovery is a significant step in getting to the bottom of the slush fund,” said Aman George, senior counsel at the non-profit. “We will continue to meet the government in court until our investigation is complete and the slush fund is permanently halted.” Last month, Todd Blanche said the fund he proposed before he was confirmed “is dead”. The US attorney general told Fox News Sunday: “The fund is dead or whatever word you want to use. It never started. So, it’s not as if the fund is coming back.” Democrats maintain that the proposed fund would have been used to compensate prosecuted and since-pardoned January 6 rioters, among others. Blanche said that Trump “believes the justice department was weaponized against a lot of Americans” under the Biden administration, adding: “It really hurt them financially.” The proposed compensation scheme was set up as part of the settlement Trump reached with the IRS regarding a lawsuit over the leak of his tax returns. The agreement shielded the president and his family from future tax audits. In July, another federal judge found that the parties had never truly been in conflict and Trump’s $10bn lawsuit against the IRS had only ever been a pretense for setting up the fund. “There was never adverseness between the parties; there was never a case or controversy; and there was never a question as to who would prevail,” the US district judge Kathleen Williams said in a ruling, adding that the lawsuit had been brought “for an improper purpose – to gain the imprimatur of judicial legitimacy for a ‘settlement’ that had no viable basis in law or fact”. The proposed fund drew bipartisan criticism in Washington, including opposition from two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and it put Blanche’s confirmation for attorney general at risk. Critics of the program have noted that the document demanded by lawmakers did not include signatories to the initial agreement, suggesting that it could be revived. Blanche has said that “there were never commissioners” in charge of the “payout pot”. But Senate Democrat Cory Booker said the agreement guaranteed “nothing … no guarantees whatsoever that this slush fund still can’t go forward”. Trump has rued the abandonment of the fund and has not ruled out another avenue to compensation. “It is dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t,” he said of the fund at a cabinet meeting in July. “To be honest with you, I think people were horribly treated, horribly abused.”

title: Big tobacco is back in town as cigarette tax fight lights up Australian politics
author: Henry Belot and Tom McIlroy
summary: The industry has been pushing for cuts to excise for decades. With the explosion in illegal cigarette sales, those calls have grown louder
body_text: Anti-smoking campaigners had been on the lookout for weeks. While in Canberra for hearings about the booming illicit trade in Australia in May, longtime observers of the tobacco industry suspected its lobbyists were working in the background to influence events. Then, on the same day public health groups were lined up to give evidence to a parliamentary inquiry, they watched as executives from Philip Morris were ushered into a private hearing at Parliament House. The move, orchestrated by a committee led by the Liberal Leah Blyth, was a break with decades of bipartisan practice by Australian policymakers, who have followed international practice to only deal with cigarette manufacturers in a transparent way. The tobacco industry’s influence campaign burst back into the headlines this week as the politics of smoking emerged as a key fight in the next election. On Thursday, a couple of weeks after Pauline Hanson pledged a 75% cut to tobacco excise, the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, one-upped her with a promised 80% cut. The Coalition has also pledged $200m for tougher law enforcement against organised crime. Big tobacco companies have been pushing for major cuts to excise, the federal tax and policy tool used to push down smoking rates, for decades. Those calls have grown louder in response to the explosion in illegal cigarette sales around the country. This illicit trade now accounts for 80% of tobacco consumption. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email In short, the manufacturers, long shut out of policy debates in Canberra and subject to increasingly tough plain packaging standards, were given a window of opportunity for the first time in years. Becky Freeman, a leading public health expert at the University of Sydney, tells Guardian Australia the industry took its shot. “If you were a tobacco industry executive this morning, I’m sure you’d be thinking ‘Fantastic, I hope the Coalition wins government as it will prop up our business and help our bottom line,’” she says. ‘You scratch my back, I’ll scratch yours’ Freeman is a long-term observer of the tobacco industry and one of its fiercest critics. For years, she has warned the industry is using a combination of political donations, well-connected lobbyists and third-party groups in an effort to influence government policy. Two of the world’s biggest tobacco giants continue to donate to the Nationals, which is the only major party to still accept their money. The Liberals stopped accepting tobacco donations in 2013, when Tony Abbott was opposition leader. Labor stopped in 2004. In 2024-25, the Nationals received $225,500 from two large manufacturers. British American Tobacco donated $55,000 to the Nationals in 2022-23 for the first time in more than a decade. A year later, it sent the party $88,000. The Nationals deny this money has influenced their policy positions and the party’s long-held advocacy on vapes. Leader Matt Canavan tells Guardian Australia tobacco companies are legal businesses and are free to donate to the political parties of their choice. “I am proud of the role the Nationals have played in developing a more reasonable approach to cigarette excise and vaping regulation,” he says. “The lack of engagement with the legal tobacco industry is one of the reasons why we have one of the greatest public policy failures in history.” He has called on Labor to drop its opposition to an excise cut, telling the government to “get its head out of the sand”. But Freeman is unconvinced. “I know how political quid pro quo works,” she says. “You scratch my back, I’ll scratch yours.” Simon Chapman, who has researched the tactics employed by tobacco lobbyists for more than 50 years, says he recognises the same talking points he heard early in his career. “I cannot remember a time in my career where they have not been calling for a reduction in tax. “The tobacco industry is just a pathetic shadow of what it used to be and yet here we are, two major political parties are effectively doing their bidding,” Chapman says. Lobbying ‘front and centre’ Tobacco executives appearing in closed-door hearings of a parliamentary inquiry, without cameras, was unusual because it signalled a change in how the industry has been operating over the past decade. Much of this lobbying has been done indirectly. The World Health Organization has for years accused tobacco companies of funding scientists and third-party groups to produce biased research and to lobby for outcomes to benefit their bottom line. Five years ago, the Australian Retailers Association cancelled a contract with the public relations firm Burson Cohn and Wolfe to lobby for vapes to be legalised. According to media reports, the money from the firm was actually sourced from Philip Morris International. Two other lobby groups, the Australasian Association of Convenience Stores and Master Grocers Australia, have long supported the tobacco industry’s campaign against plain packaging reforms. Their corporate members include tobacco companies. In 2023, both groups declined to tell a Senate inquiry how much money they received in tobacco and vaping industry funding, saying the information was “commercial in confidence”. That same year, an academic study found almost half of internal tobacco company lobbyists held positions in state, territory or federal government before or after working in the tobacco industry. Freeman says that traditionally the tobacco industry would much rather operate behind the scenes and “avoid being questioned and examined”. “Once the plain packaging debate quietened down, after Australia won, I saw the industry go quiet and back under cover,” Freeman says. “But in the last couple of years, it has become increasingly clear to me that the industry is becoming more front and centre.” Freeman points to a recent podcast hosted by British American Tobacco’s chief corporate officer, Kingsley Wheaton, who interviewed Abbott on 2 April. The former prime minister had been elected federal president of the Liberal party just days earlier, on 30 May. ‘It is extremely disappointing’ David Hill is another anti-tobacco campaigner who has devoted his entire career to public health research. He says cutting the excise won’t make a substantial difference to organised crime, despite the Coalition’s assurances. Hill also argues the cut will ultimately benefit tobacco companies, whose profits have been smashed by people turning to cheaper illicit cigarettes. “At first glance, it may look plausible,” Hill says. “This idea that if the legal price of cigarettes drops enough then you’ll successfully compete in a business sense with the illicit market and it will go away. “But the price of making these illegal cigarettes is so trivial. If you can get them for 4c a stick in Cambodia, there’s a huge scope for crooks to just drop their price and still make a profit.” The Coalition’s changes do have some significant support. On Thursday, the economist Richard Holden and former deputy chief medical officer Nick Coatsworth wrote to the prime minister urging him to support the excise cut. So too did the former border force official Rohan Pike, who has advised nicotine industry-linked organisations. But most health groups are alarmed. The Public Health Association of Australia says the change could risk an increase in daily smoking prevalence, which fell to 5.6% in 2025. The Cancer Council and the Australian Medical Association believe it could lead to a new generation of nicotine addiction. On Friday, the World Health Organization, which does not comment on specific policies, reaffirmed its position that affordability reduces demand for tobacco products. “From a public health perspective, taxes should be set with the aim of continually reducing affordability and demand,” says Benn McGrady, the head of WHO’s fiscal and legal measures unit. After almost 50 years of hard-fought wins, Hill is worried the tide may be turning. “It is extremely disappointing,” he says. “But I am also optimistic that when people really roll up their sleeves and look at this, the current excise will be retained.”

title: More voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves Republican
author: Roque Planas
summary: Latest data from Gallup, showing 49% leaning Democrat and 39% Republican, marks sharp reversal from 2024
body_text: More voters are identifying as Democrats and shying away from calling themselves Republican, according to the latest quarterly data published by Gallup. Some 49% of voters surveyed leaned Democrat, including independent voters asked to pick one party or the other. Only 39% of respondents leaned Republican. That 10-point spread marks a sharp reversal from the four-point advantage that Republicans held over Democrats in the fourth quarter of 2024, when voters sent Donald Trump back to the White House and Republicans swept both houses of Congress. Democrats are seeing their most sizable advantage since 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president, according to the New York Times. The data offers the latest evidence that Trump’s second term has proved unpopular with voters, driving a potential backlash. Trump’s approval rating stood at 52% at the time of his second inauguration in January of 2025, according to an average of polls published by the New York Times. But his popularity dwindled immediately, as he cleaved the federal workforce, imposed price-inflating tariffs, passed a profligate spending bill and launched a rudderless war with Iran. Some 58% of voters now disapprove of his performance, with only 38% approving, according to the Times. Democrats are hoping to take advantage of Trump’s tanking popularity. Liberals are likely to retake the US House of Representatives in midterm elections this November. The party is much less certain to retake the US Senate, though polling is giving Democrats reasons to feel optimistic. A growing share of American voters have not identified with either party in recent years. Back in 2002, roughly a third of voters surveyed by Gallup identified as either Republican, Democrat or independent. By last year, 45% of respondents called themselves independents, with only 27% identifying as either Democrat or Republican.

title: Trump’s pique with UK could lead to favor to acolyte Milei over Falklands
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: US president suggests he might support his Argentinian ally’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands
body_text: Donald Trump has long embraced vengeance. “I am your retribution,” he declared to an admiring audience at the 2023 Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) as he commenced his march back to the White House. It is unlikely Argentina, and far-flung holdovers of the former British empire, were on the US president’s mind at the time. But the tide of international events in the past three and a half years have turned Trump’s vindictive mindset to the advantage of Javier Milei, the boisterous rightwing Argentinian president. Trump’s notorious fixation with payback was almost entirely the trigger for Milei’s televised address to his fellow Argentinians on Thursday, as he stated his intention to reopen his country’s claim to a set of windswept islands in the south Atlantic – known to Britain as the Falklands, and to Argentina as the Malvinas. The centuries-old dispute over the islands’ sovereignty has lain dormant since 1982, when the two countries fought a brief, but bloody, conflict that began after Argentina’s ruling military dictatorship invaded the territory. Britain reclaimed it after troops in a naval taskforce dispatched by the then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher – ironically lionized by Milei as a political exemplar and inspiration – stormed the territory and eventually forced Argentina’s surrender. An uneasy peace has reigned in the generation since, although Argentina, which returned to democracy the year after the conflict, has never renounced its claim to the isles – despite the adamant insistence of their fewer than 2,000 inhabitants that they remain British. This week, however, Trump suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands. Why would the president go out on a limb to threaten this fragile peace? And why now? Milei jumped on Trump’s comment that he was “reviewing” the US’s longstanding neutral stance on the territory’s sovereignty, which amounts to a de facto recognition of Britain’s control. Fueling Trump’s animus is grievance that Britain, under former prime minister Keir Starmer, declined to support the US president’s decision to go to war on Iran, another irony given that country’s deep-rooted suspicions of Britain and its imperial past. The president’s obsession that allies declined to help him in a war he never consulted them on runs deep and wide – from Westminster to Seoul – and has the potential to upend US relationships around the globe, if unchecked. And Milei’s attempt to capitalize on Trump’s vengeance underlines the potential for ripple effects of this war to reach waters far beyond the Gulf. In what has become a repetitive refrain, Trump laid bare his sense of wounded affront in an interview with a rightwing British cable channel on Thursday. “Your country was not there to help me,” he told GB News. “We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader: ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said: ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.” Milei’s opportunism could also be used by Trump as a bargaining chip – to lever more money from the cash-strapped UK treasury for defense spending and Nato contributions, after the new British chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, recently suggested that it might not reach increased spending targets. It is a sorry pass for the “special relationship”, fostered through alliances in two worlds wars and deepened during the cold war and subsequent conflicts. Yet Britain is hardly alone in feeling the heat of a wrathful Trump. Vengeance has been targeted in recent months at numerous other allies, now regarded with more hostility by the White House than traditional adversaries such as Russia and China. Annual joint military exercises with South Korea – a vital ally of Washington since the Korean war broke out in 1950 – were suddenly scaled down and cut short by six days last month, on Trump’s orders, because of his irritation that the Seoul government declined to join the fight against Iran. He has repeatedly threatened to bomb or “blow up” the tiny Gulf kingdom of Oman, which has had friendly ties with the US for 200 years, if it impedes his efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz, which Iran has closed to most commercial shipping. The White House also announced the withdrawal of 5,000 US troops from Germany after the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, rebuffed pressure to get involved in the Iran conflict and said Trump had been “humiliated” in the conflict. Threats of retribution have also been aimed at Spain, which has resisted pressure to boost defense spending, and Italy, whose prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, was a former Trump ally. Turbulence under Trump But Milei, a self-styled “anarcho-capitalist” who has paraded with a chainsaw to signify his attitude to public spending and attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration, remains on the US president’s good side. Last year, the administration extended his troubled government a $20bn loan guarantee to stabilize the infamously shaky Argentinian economy – but premised the money on Milei’s party defeating the leftist opposition in forthcoming congressional elections, which it duly did. This time there are no guarantees, other than that of never-ending turbulence at the hands of Trump. Such rough currents may be the “winds of change” Milei referenced in Thursday’s speech, delivered – Trump-style – with his cabinet members flanking him. But he may have been aware the phrase had other, historical connotations – evoking the words of a famous speech in 1960 by then British prime minister Harold Macmillan in Cape Town, heralding independence for Britain’s former colonial possession in Africa. “The wind of change is blowing through this continent,” Macmillan said then. “Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.” In his address, Milei suggested the sun was setting on Britain, just as it once did on its empire, citing multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. “It is clear that they are on a path of decline,” he pronounced. He did not mention his own falling political popularity – a factor that may also have played a key role in the former military junta’s decision to seize the islands in 1982, as opposition grew against the backdrop of mass disappearances of political dissidents and multiple human rights abuses. Then, too, Britain was grappling with tensions over immigration and race riots, soaring unemployment and long-term economic decline that Thatcher had been elected pledging to reverse. In the late winter of 1982, there was little sign that she was capable of doing so – until the Falklands conflict sparked a sudden upturn in her political fortunes. But she had the solid backing of the special relationship, and her ideological soulmate, Ronald Reagan, in the White House. Andy Burnham, Britain’s newly installed Labour prime minister, must contend with the chill wind emanating from the menacing and destabilizing presence of Trump.
