title: Legal veterans lead fightback against Trump’s ‘full-out assault on democracy’
author: Peter Stone in Washington
summary: Advocacy groups expand legal challenges and condemn president’s ‘self-serving attempts to take over midterms’
body_text: A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and ex-judges have expanded legal challenges to Donald Trump’s authoritarian executive orders on voting and other presidential actions they see as a “war” on the rule of law in the US. Heavy legal opposition to Trump’s two executive orders on elections to curb voting rights and supplant the authority of states on election matters has come from the Democracy Defenders Fund, the Campaign Legal Center, the American Civil Liberties Union and kindred groups. These legal outfits and like-minded allies have won key lawsuits on election issues, plus litigation thwarting Trump’s moves to end birthright citizenship and a $1.8bn slush fund that could have paid money to allies including January 6 rioters he deemed were unjustly charged. Since Trump returned to power, for instance, Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center have jointly filed lawsuits against Trump’s 2025 and 2026 executive orders on voting, challenging their constitutionality to set new voting rules that by law are run by the states. Key legal briefs they filed together include an August one on behalf of several voting rights groups and local officials in two states to block Trump’s March 2026 executive order that would restrict voting by mail and authorize the US Postal Service to implement rules to that end. Other groups that have accelerated their legal challenges to Trump’s moves to thwart voting rights and expand his executive powers in other ways, include the Brennan Center for Justice, Democracy Forward, members of the Democratic Attorneys General Association and the Washington Litigation Group. Last month, for instance, 24 Democratic attorneys general and other plaintiffs filed suit to block USPS from moving forward with rules to curb mail voting and in late August won a temporary 14-day restraining order from federal judge Indira Talwani in Massachusetts. In response, the justice department’s solicitor general, John Sauer, on Thursday appealed to the supreme court to lift the injunction, arguing in heated words that the freeze would create “serious, irreparable harm on the federal government, the states themselves, and the voting public”. On 4 September Talwani made her injunction permanent, writing that implementing Trump’s order so close to the election “threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail”. She also stressed that “the record includes no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting to support the rushed implementation.” Sauer on 6 September responded with another emergency appeal to the high court urging it permit the new USPS rules to go into effect, claiming that it “does not seize control of states’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail”. In a related twist, a detailed whistleblower complaint that the Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut released last week alleged that the USPS had been proceeding with a “secretive, rushed” effort to implement Trump’s order that could lead to “catastrophic failure” with this year’s mail-in voting. About 50 million Americans, the majority of whom are Democrats, vote by mail, according to reports. With the elections about two months away, the legal groups are stepping up efforts to thwart “self-serving attempts to take over the midterms”, said a former justice department lawyer, which experts fear may create chaos and disenfranchise millions of voters. Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at the Campaign Legal Center, told the Guardian: “The CLC and the DDF have worked closely together on two ongoing lawsuits challenging the president’s unlawful voting executive orders that attempt to dictate election rules. We’ve teamed up in the supreme court on a brief filed by former state and federal judges, including noted conservative judges, that emphasized just how unlawful and dangerous the president’s efforts to dictate election rules are.” Baldwin, who spent 14 years in the justice department’s civil rights division, said the CLC and the DDF have also “worked together in federal cases filed in Oregon and California to make sure that the DoJ isn’t able to seize voters’ sensitive data by making false claims about non-citizen voting. In cases around the country, the Campaign Legal Center is pushing back on the DoJ’s lawless efforts to vacuum up and aggregate sensitive data to create a national voter file of some sort.” Further, former ambassador Norm Eisen, the executive chair of the Democracy Defenders Fund, which he co-founded in 2023, told the Guardian that since its inception the DDF has been involved in more than 300 legal cases and matters in three primary areas: elections, the rule of law and anti-corruption. Eisen said the group, whose board boasts former federal judge and conservative stalwart J Michael Luttig and liberal-leaning ex-federal judge Nancy Gertner, likes to work in conjunction on cases with other ideologically diverse and non-partisan groups like the CLC and the WLG because “they both have strong bipartisan credibility. It’s a big-tent approach we’ve taken with our election work.” Eisen said Luttig and Gertner were instrumental in helping recruit dozens of former judges with bipartisan credentials to file amicus briefs on multiple matters including an August one to the supreme court opposing Trump’s 2026 executive order to curb mail voting. For its part, the WLG this summer hired about half a dozen new lawyers to handle election-related litigation. “As the midterms approach with growing concerns about potential federal interference in elections, we’ve brought on more attorneys to be even more prepared to litigate sensitive matters under acute time pressure,” said James Pearce, a principal with the WLG. Elsewhere, Sophia Lin Lakin, who leads the ACLU Voting Rights Project, said the group had been “pushing back” on administration efforts to seize personal voting data from states, and said the ACLU had been involved in 26 of 30 legal challenges to the administration on the issue. To date, the administration has lost 23 cases where rulings have been made. Critics say Trump, the justice department, the USPS and the Department of Homeland Security seem to be laying the groundwork for further attacks on the nation’s election rules, citing Trump’s false claims about election fraud and his radical plans to change voting rules. In July in a televised speech, Trump falsely portrayed the nation’s voting system as riddled with fraud and condemned voting by mail and non-citizen voting. “Mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt,” Trump claimed without evidence, even though he voted twice by mail this year. Trump, who continues to blame voting fraud for his 2020 loss to Joe Biden, also charged that non-citizen voting, which is illegal and historically minuscule, poses a “crisis of election security”. Trump’s fixation on noncitizen voting is belied by a database from the rightwing Heritage Foundation that only cites 100 cases over a quarter-century. But according to documents reviewed by the New York Times, hundreds of DHS agents have been engaged in a hunt to find noncitizens among registered voters. The chief of the DHS has said ICE agents could be sent to polling places “if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant”. The justice department has helped to amplify Trump’s bogus election claims with legal threats and actions. In July, Harmeet Dhillon, who runs the department’s civil rights division, wrote to officials in 50 states warning that “any election officer, including the chief election officer of the state, who knowingly retains noncitizens on the state’s [voter list] or facilitates noncitizens in receiving and casting ballots could be subject to criminal liability”. In August, the justice department announced plans to send a larger-than-usual contingent of 1,000 lawyers to monitor voting nationwide, raising concerns that such large efforts could lead to voter intimidation. And in a harbinger of coming legal fights, Trump announced on his Truth Social platform last month that the justice department’s Ed Martin, a key election denialist in charge of pardons, was leaving to handle election-related litigation. Former justice department lawyers say administration threats to voting rights make opposition from legal advocates crucial. Stacey Young, a lawyer who left the department at the start of 2025 after 18 years to found Justice Connection, a group of more than 3,000 ex-justice department lawyers and other alumni, denounced Trump’s moves “to interfere” with elections. “The constitution makes clear that the president has no authority over the administration of our elections, but that hasn’t stopped this president, or those he put in power at the justice department, from trying to interfere,” Young said in a statement. “We’re taking these threats seriously and leveraging our collective strengths to protect election integrity, which is key to maintaining a functioning democracy.” Justice Connection is working with experts in its alumni network to engage with the media, Congress and the public to highlight the justice department’s traditional role in election security and ensuring compliance with federal voting laws. Other justice department alumni agree that opposition to Trump’s election agenda is critical. “These organizations are doing critical work in protecting the ability of people to vote and make their voices heard – a cornerstone of democracy,” said Michael Bromwich, a former Department of Justice inspector general. “The full-out assault on democracy must be addressed through the courts because Congress has proven itself unwilling and unable to check the undemocratic steps taken by the administration.” Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney for eastern Michigan who now teaches law at the University of Michigan, said: “Large law firms sent armies of young attorneys to our nation’s airports to represent individuals caught up in Trump’s travel ban. That is not happening any more because of the ‘deals’ they negotiated with the Trump administration in his second term to support his pet causes. “Thank goodness for groups like the Democracy Defenders Fund, which are attracting top legal talent and challenging some of Trump’s lawless activities. Their work is protecting the rights of all Americans.” Further, Nick Brown, Washington state’s attorney general, who chairs an election protection group for the Democratic Attorneys General Association, said it had teamed up with some legal advocacy groups such as the Brennan Center, States United and the DDF to hold “strategy sessions” to prepare for potential disruptive moves by the Trump administration in the November elections. Brown also attacked the administration’s appeal to the supreme court to move forward with Trump’s executive order on voting by mail, despite Judge Talwani’s strong concerns and litigation against it by Democratic attorneys general. He said: “As the court said, states’ compliance with this illegal order would be ‘practically impossible’ before the November elections given the unprecedented demands it would put on state and local elections officials. The chaos that would cause is exactly what Trump wants. That’s why we continue to fight for a fair and properly administered election.” Baldwin too raised strong concerns about the justice department’s push to get the supreme court to issue a ruling that would expedite Trump’s executive order on voting by mail. She said: “The DoJ’s slapdash effort at getting the supreme court’s blessing to turn the USPS into a gatekeeper for mail would be a farce, if it didn’t put our fundamental right to vote in the crosshairs. Given the importance of what is at stake, the DoJ’s continued efforts are nothing more than an attempt to foist chaos on the electoral process. But they will fail.” Other lawyers engaged in key election legal battles and other litigation voice optimism they will prevail. Tianna Mays, the legal director of the DDF, said: “The Trump administration has declared war on the rule of law, yet our democratic guardrails are still holding. We refuse to stand by idly while this administration flouts the constitution and attempts to eviscerate our institutions.” This article was updated on 7 September 2026 to reflect that members of the Democratic Attorneys General Association have filed suit, not the Daga itself.

title: Morning Mail: Labor group’s alarm at US military in Australia; food price warnings amid El Niño; and Radiohead return
author: Paul Gallagher
summary: Labor Against War reacts to US military’s presence in Australia; El Niño could push up food prices for Australian families; alarm at far-right win in German state election
body_text: Good morning. While the government has defended the growing presence of the US military in Australia, the Labor Against War group is urging it to chart a foreign policy independent “from the American war machine”. There are warnings the impacts of the predicted record-strength El Niño weather event could spill into supermarket aisles by increasing food prices for Australian households already struggling to make ends meet. Overseas, the alleged killers of Australian surfers Jake and Callum Robinson have gone on trial in Mexico. And shock waves from the far-right’s victory in a German state election are being felt across Europe. Australia ‘Chart a new course’ | After revelations US military and weapons manufacturers control or have access to more than 100 bases across Australia, Labor Against War is urging the government to move its foreign policy away from “fading guarantees of the past”. El Niño impacts | The most severe El Niño weather event on record threatens to push food prices higher this year, experts say, piling pressure on households already grappling with a cost-of-living crisis. Baja trial | The alleged killers of Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, at a Mexican surfing hotspot in 2024 have gone on trial in Baja California. Stolen Generations | Indigenous Australians who were forcibly removed under assimilation policies have far greater physical and health challenges than the wider Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations, a report reveals. Parliamentary scrutiny | Top bureaucrats want the government to ban video footage from parliamentary hearings being edited and shared on social media, in a bid to stop online ridicule and abuse. Everything in its right place | British band Radiohead will return to Australia to play a series of 16 shows in Perth, Melbourne and Sydney next year, marking the band’s first tour of the country in 15 years. World ‘Grave moment’ | Politicians around Europe have expressed alarm after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland swept to a historic state election victory in Germany; the German chancellor has vowed to stay in office despite the AfD win; and Europe’s centre fears a nationalist wave after the AfD victory but only has itself to blame, Jon Henley writes. ‘Butcher of Bosnia’ | Thousands of mourners gathered in Belgrade for the funeral of Ratko Mladić, a Serbian general convicted for his role in the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war. Middle East crisis | The UK government looks set to announce a tougher stance in its relations with Israel – including a ban on the trade in goods and some services from illegal Israeli settlements. Going nuclear | A nuclear reactor built secretly during the rule of Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad could have been used for nuclear weapons if completed, the UN nuclear watchdog has revealed. A pour return | French vineyards hit by severe drought and heatwaves are expected to report a 30-year low in wine production after the country’s hottest ever recorded summer. Full Story How much control should we have over the algorithm? As the federal government prepares to introduce digital duty of care laws, social media users could soon be given the option to turn off their recommendation algorithms entirely. But with the Coalition warning of internet censorship and big tech relying on these feeds for revenue, would an opt-out switch actually make platforms safer? Josh Taylor joins Reged Ahmad to unpack Labor’s proposed crackdown on algorithms. In-depth The excitement around such “GLP-1s” such as Ozempic and Wegovy has been difficult to miss: the medications have grabbed headlines around the world, with clinical trials suggesting they can help participants lose an average of 15% to 20% of their body weight. GLP-1 medications have been a gamechanger in the fight against obesity. But for a minority of patients, their impact is negligible. Researchers are now trying to work out why. Not the news For most bands, releasing a new album is cause for celebration. For Brisbane band Bugs, the moment is much more bittersweet. Jordan Brunoli, their bass guitarist, is in palliative care for colorectal cancer. While he may have just weeks to live, there’s still the new album – Head Noise – and two live shows to play. The band reflects on their friendship, facing terminal illness, and making the most of their time together. Sport Tennis | Zheng Qinwen had an epic comeback against Iga Świątek and Mirra Andreeva beat Anastasia Potapova in the latest action at the US Open at Flushing Meadows. Olympics | There has been a warning over the future of the Olympic Games if the Brisbane 2032 program is not modernised. Football | Fitter, happier, more productive: Arsenal could hardly have started the new season better, Jonathan Wilson writes. Chelsea’s midfield is proving a headache for Xabi Alonso, Jacob Steinberg writes. Cricket | Pakistan have launched an investigation into “discipline and conduct” during their highly dysfunctional tour of England. Rugby union | The Wallabies’ Carter Gordon is set for a stint on the sidelines after breaking his leg. Media roundup More than 60 people in New South Wales have been diagnosed with early-stage lung cancer before they developed a single symptom via a new screening program, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. Leaked messages have revealed details of a new $1bn treaty Anthony Albanese wants to strike with his Solomon Islands counterpart to combat Beijing’s Pacific reach, the Age reports. Tasmanian officials are being urged to launch an immediate investigation into claims of alleged animal welfare breaches within the state’s Atlantic salmon farming industry, ABC News reports. Hundreds of jobs at the Whyalla steelworks remain on the line despite more than $1bn of taxpayer funding, the Advertiser reports. title: Donald Trump’s midterm strategy? Make it all about him
author: Robert Reich
summary: The president apparently plans to focus on the person he most admires – himself – even if Republicans would rather he didn’t
body_text: With the midterm races officially beginning this week, a big question hanging over the Republican party is how Trump will allocate his giant stash of Super Pac money. As of 31 July, Maga Inc had more than $400m on hand, larger than the cash reserves of any of the major party committees. But he’s barely spent any of it yet. Why not? Is he waiting to see where his stash can do the most good for Republicans during the peak campaign season, starting in a few weeks? On Friday, he said he would personally weigh where to direct support, including toward Republican candidates he believes can win competitive races. But this seems doubtful. He’s already missed the chance to lock in airtime at lower, advance rates and define candidates before attitudes harden. Is he using his stash as a means of silencing criticism in the Republican ranks, or holding back support until a candidate lavishes praise on him? Also doubtful. Republican candidates who believe they need to criticize his war or his economic policies to stay viable won’t restrain themselves because of his possible campaign cash. Maybe he’s conserving the money to discipline Republican candidates in the 2028 primaries and general election, when he’ll use the stash to penalize disloyalty and reward loyalty? Possibly, but he’s already practically a lame duck. Is he conserving the cash to pass it on to his chosen presidential successor – either Vance or Rubio or a third selection as yet unknown? Probably not. That’s a long way off. None of these theories holds water because they don’t figure in Trump’s giant, towering, malignant narcissism. It seems he’ll be putting money behind his favorite politician – the person he most admires, who represents everything he believes in, who he considers the single most important and talented living person in the entire flaming firmament of the known universe. Himself. He’s going to use campaign cash to make himself look good, or at least far better than he looks now. Multiple polls show Trump’s approval rating now mired in the mid-30% range – at or near historic lows for a president facing a midterm election. So he’ll launch a campaign to regain the adulation he’s lost, to recast himself as the hero he believes he is, to reclaim the mantle of savior to which he thinks he’s entitled. In other words, it will be a campaign to promote, glorify and exalt Donald J Trump. The non-profit arm of Trump’s political operation, Securing American Greatness, has already spent about $1m on its first midterm ads set to air nationwide, featuring video clips of Trump talking about tax breaks in his domestic spending legislation and lower prices for eggs and prescription drugs. In early August, according to the Atlantic, Trump told advisers that they should follow the same strategy as the Democrats: making the election about him. But as Karl Rove, who was senior adviser and deputy chief of staff for George W Bush, notes in the Wall Street Journal, given Trump’s unpopularity, making the election even more about him only helps the Democrats. Trump also plans to travel all over the country, holding rallies like he did during his presidential elections. As Rove notes, Fox News’s senior White House correspondent, Peter Doocy, reports hearing “whispers of a ton of Trump travel in October, possibly as much as a Trump rally a day” in competitive states and districts. But Rove also warns: “Trump is never disciplined. He’ll have no script, saying whatever comes to mind. His crazy comments will dominate the news, locally and nationally. Republican candidates will constantly have to fend off questions about whether they agree with his latest insult or half-baked idea. The narrative won’t be on anything positive about them or the GOP.” Presumably this is why some battleground Republicans told Trump’s staff that they would prefer he not visit their districts ahead of November, according to four Republican operatives involved in the conversations, as reported by Politico. Meanwhile, Republican pollsters have told candidates in tight races to limit their references to him. “We’ve told them he cannot come,” one senior Republican, involved in a district where Trump won by double digits in the last election, told Politico. “Candidly, he would not be helpful here … I do not believe they would send him without our OK. And if they did, we probably wouldn’t campaign with him.” Rove and other Republican functionaries are urging Trump to “act more presidential” by using his Super Pacs’ $403m to support Republican candidates rather than support a campaign about himself. But they’re yelling into the wind of Trump’s ballroom-sized ego. The truth is, Trump doesn’t give a damn about the midterm elections except insofar as Republican losses make him look bad. He probably figures if he backs a candidate with his Pac money and they lose, he’ll look even worse. So better to spend it on boosting himself. As almost everyone in the world knows by now, Trump cares only about himself. That’s been his MO for ever. Bad news for Republicans in the midterms and good news for Democrats. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

title: New Hampshire voters head to polls in race crucial to Democrats’ Senate hopes
author: Shrai Popat
summary: Centrist Chris Pappas faces progressive primary challenger Karishma Manzur while Republicans eye chance to flip seat
body_text: New Hampshire voters head to the polls Tuesday for primaries that will set up a closely watched Senate contest – a vulnerable open seat Democrats must defend if they are to have any shot at reclaiming the upper chamber. The race opened when Jeanne Shaheen, 79, the state’s three‑term incumbent Democratic senator, announced her retirement. Congressman Chris Pappas, who represents New Hampshire’s first district, is seeking the nomination and enters the final stretch with a clear financial edge: more than $4m cash on hand, according to his latest filings. But his main challenger, Dr Karishma Manzur – a scientist and progressive activist with no experience holding public office – has gained ground. If he wins the primary, Pappas, 46, is likely to face the Donald Trump-endorsed former senator John E Sununu, who is seeking a return to the seat he once held and is part of a political dynasty that includes his father and brother, both former governors. “This is the kind of place where you can’t just run a bunch of TV ads and expect to win,” Pappas said. “You’ve got to meet people where they are. We’re finding support in corners you might not expect – including from people who voted for Trump last time but are open to a conversation about moving the country forward.” A popular centrist, Pappas has served in the House since 2019 and has crossed the aisle at various points. He calls himself “battle‑tested” and has consolidated establishment backing, earning endorsements from leading Democratic lawmakers and former vice‑president Kamala Harris. His family’s name also carries weight in New Hampshire: the Pappases own the Puritan Backroom, the century‑old Manchester restaurant famed for allegedly inventing the chicken tender and long embedded in the state’s retail‑politics circuit. Sununu, 61, is the clear frontrunner in the GOP primary, though he faces Scott Brown – another former senator who represented Massachusetts, later moved to New Hampshire, and served as US ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during Donald Trump’s first term. The president threw his support behind Sununu earlier this year despite the former lawmaker’s past criticism of the president, including a 2024 op‑ed in which Sununu called Trump a “loser” and backed Nikki Haley in the Republican presidential primary. On the trail, Sununu has tried to show daylight between himself and the administration, criticizing Trump’s tariff policy, urging Congress to rein in executive power and questioning the decision to launch military action in Iran. He told New Hampshire Public Radio it was “a tactical mistake” to go to war “without having a plan for protecting the strait of Hormuz”. That posture may matter in a state where Trump’s approval rating sits at 38%. Sununu and Brown did not respond to the Guardian’s interview requests. Kristen Cianci, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said that Sununu was a “strong candidate” who was “well-positioned to beat out Pappas” in a general election. “While Democrats have been consumed by infighting, Republicans have been laser-focused on real issues like affordability and security,” she added in a statement. Some Democrats worry New Hampshire could become a sleeper risk – a state where Republicans control the legislature but haven’t won a Senate race since 2010, when Kelly Ayotte, the now-governor, captured a seat. Pappas insists he’s not taking anything for granted, and is running like he’s “10 votes behind” at all times – especially in a midterm cycle where progressive challengers have scored surprise primary wins across the country. This, however, hasn’t fazed Pappas, who says he is running as a “New Hampshire Democrat” who knows his state. But Manzur, who supports Medicare for All and higher taxes on mega‑corporations and the ultra‑wealthy, has repeatedly highlighted the money Pappas has received from donors aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). She casts him as milquetoast and ineffective. “I was tired of choosing between the lesser of two evils and still seeing so much pain and suffering right here in my state,” she said, calling both Pappas and Sununu “corporate politicians”. “One has a ‘D’ after their name. One has an ‘R’ after their name … neither of them have been able to address the real needs of the people,” Manzur added. Pappas, for his part, has long backed US aid to Israel but said that Benjamin Netanyahu was “not a trustworthy ally of the US” and said he hoped the Israeli prime minister was ousted in his country’s October election. Pappas noted he had rejected corporate Pac money in this race but did not directly address his support from pro‑Israel donors, instead pointing to a “broad‑based effort” of individual contributors that have supported his Senate bid. Pappas said he would support the Democratic nominee if he loses. “We need a big tent and new voices in the party to win tough elections,” he said at last week’s Democratic debate. Manzur declined to make the same commitment. “I’m focused on winning,” she said. “I’m not going to get into these discussions – they’re intentionally distracting from the people’s movement.” Further down the ballot, the Democratic primary for Pappas’s House seat has drawn eight candidates, with Stefany Shaheen – daughter of the outgoing senator – and Maura Sullivan, a former Obama administration official, leading the field. The district, long purple, has been reliably blue since 2017. Republicans now see it as flippable, and Trump has endorsed Anthony DiLorenzo, a businessman who owns several car dealerships, in the GOP race.

title: Trump’s approval rating is plummeting – as his fortune grows and grows
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: The US president says criticising his soaring investment portfolio is ‘very unfair’. Tell that to the millions of Americans struggling with the cost of living, writes Arwa Mahdawi
body_text: If I had a dollar for every time Donald Trump said something inane, I would be a very rich woman. But even with an income that steady, I could never hope to be as flush as the president. A Forbes calculation from March puts his net worth at about $6.5bn – and it’s growing rapidly. Trump made $2.2bn in 2025 via business interests that ranged from selling cryptocurrency and Trump Bibles to offering early access to his (often market-moving) Truth Social posts. To be fair, Trump isn’t making all this money just so he can buy golf clubs and gold toilets. No, he’s amassing these billions for the good of the little people; it’s altruism, not avarice! “I do this for our Country, not myself,” the president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday night alongside an AI-generated picture of him trading Intel stock. “I’ve made Hundreds of Billions of Dollars on Stocks, and many other type Holdings, for the U.S.A., not myself, and all I do is get criticized by the Radical Left Dumocrats. Very unfair, but what can you do!” Oh, I have some ideas about what you can do, Mr President. Unfortunately, I can’t print most of them. I also can’t explain why Trump said he’s made hundreds of billions, apart from pointing to his propensity for exaggeration. It seems his post was referring to the fact that the US government took a 9.9% stake in Intel last year. That stake was worth $8.9bn at the time and as of Friday is worth nearly five times as much. According to the Trump administration, this is a win for everyone. In May, the White House released a statement calling Intel’s surging stock price “a direct windfall for American taxpayers”. Weirdly, I seem to have missed my portion of that windfall. Intel’s stock price has had little impact on my life. What is having an impact is the soaring cost of necessities such as electricity and groceries. But I shouldn’t be grumpy, should I? I should be grateful that our intrepid president is balancing the demands of the day job with stock trading for the good of the country. According to Trump’s latest government disclosure, he made more than 1,000 equity trades in June. And his picks are doing very well: a report published in August by Democrats on Congress’s joint economic committee argued that Trump’s holdings in oil and gas stocks had risen by nearly $16m because of the war with Iran. “Experts on government ethics have flagged how rare it is for presidents to hold and trade stocks in individual companies, especially since Trump’s war in Iran and his other favors to the oil industry have all pushed up the value of Big Oil stocks,” the report read. Trump’s shamelessness may be rare, but he isn’t the only politician with serious conflicts of interest issues apropos stock market dealings. A 2022 New York Times investigation found that, from 2019 to 2021, 97 lawmakers or their family members traded financial assets in industries that could be affected by their legislative committee work. In 2020, for example, the wife of the now retired Democratic congressman Alan Lowenthal sold her Boeing shares a day before a House committee on which Lowenthal sat released a damning report about the company. Lowenthal told the Times that he was not involved in this trade at all, so I imagine it was just a funny coincidence. Still, these sorts of funny coincidences don’t do much to build up trust in the US government, do they? A majority of Americans support commonsense legislation to stop lawmakers and their family members from trading individual stocks. After a lot of resistance, a bill to this effect is winding its way through Congress. The bill does not affect the president or the vice-president, however. Money can’t buy you everything, of course: while the president’s stock portfolio is rising, his personal stock is plummeting. According to an FT poll this week, Trump’s approval rating has hit a record low, with only 33% of registered voters saying they approve of his performance. But don’t take that as a sign that the US is coming to its senses or that Republicans are cognisant that dear leader’s war is bleeding the country dry: the same poll found that 72% of Republicans still approve of the president. That figure is down from 82% in May, but it’s still an awful lot of people. Either these Trump loyalists are bigoted fools or they are getting the Intel windfall checks that I’m missing. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk film
author: Philip Oltermann in Venice
summary: Alex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering children
body_text: Veteran documentarian Alex Gibney’s film about the richest broligarch on the planet has been one of the most eagerly anticipated films at the Venice film festival this year. The Oscar-winning 72-year-old, who has in previous films taken on the US military, the Catholic church, Vladimir Putin and Scientology, has been investigating the tech tycoon’s ascent and speaking to people in his orbit since late 2022, before his Maga turn and Trump 2.0. The result clocks in at just under four hours and presents a comprehensive answer to how on earth one man managed to amass so much money and political influence. It is shocking less for any individual new pieces of information Gibney has unearthed than for its totality. Here are six things the film tells us: Musk is a genius – at tricking the government into giving him assistance At Maga rallies, Musk has been introduced as “America’s biggest capitalist”, but Gibney reminds us that he’s always been more than happy to go begging to the state for handouts – such as by cosying up to Obama to gain government contracts for SpaceX to launch satellites for Nasa and the military. The film zooms in on a Tesla press event in June 2013, where Musk unveiled a new “battery swap” system that promised to remove and replace the drained battery pack of a Model S with a fully charged one in just 90 seconds. As it turns out, the technology was never rolled out, and interviewees tell Gibney that a demonstration site at Harris Ranch was barely used for the process. Instead, the film-maker suggests that Musk’s over-promise allowed Tesla to get more ZEV credits from the Californian government, which are awarded to electric car makers based on range and which Musk could then sell to more polluting manufacturers. In spite of everything, there was something admirable about Musk once Gibney’s film serves as a reminder that Musk has never been in possession of charm or charisma – the petulant perma-poster retweeting praise is not far from the self-regarding twentysomething start-up bro. But what he did with the funds he earned from selling shares of his first software companies, Zip2, X.com and PayPal, was unusual, Gibney concedes. Where others turned to venture capital, Musk turned to engineering. It’s partially an act, we learn from his ex-wife Justine when she recalls how self-consciously he picked his wardrobe, telling her “I can’t look cool or hip, because I need to look like an engineer”. But in footage of Musk biting his nails with fellow engineers during SpaceX rocket launches his enthusiasm and emotional investment is genuine, and at times infectious. Musk’s procreation drive is motivated by a fear of civilisational breakdown Musk has 14 publicly known children, and sources tell Gibney that there are probably more. Some of them were conceived in romantic relationships but more recently the circumstances of their birth seem to have been entirely transactional, via sperm donations to employees of his companies. In a text message to one of his ex-partners, influencer Ashley St Clair, Musk said his desire to have “a legion of children” was driven by a fear of “civil war”. The documentary mostly places the roots of that fear in his South African childhood (in one scene, his father Errol Musk talks with no visible remorse of shooting three intruders in their home). “It’s no doubt he had a traumatic childhood,” Gibney said at a press conference in Venice. “He’s now playing out the trauma on the rest of us.” But, oddly for a man who was long a prominent atheist, the film also hints at a religious dimension to his vision of the apocalypse. The sordid business of negotiating disbursements and NDAs with the mothers of Musk’s children are handled by his right-hand man Jared Birchall, a devout Mormon whom St Clair calls his “henchman” and “demon”. To Musk, empathy is good in principle but not in action Recently, Musk has held forth at length about his view that “suicidal empathy” – people who have more empathy for criminals than the victims of criminals, in his view – is behind the decline of western civilisation. Empathy isn’t bad, he says in the doc, it’s just that it’s become too shallow. But interviews in the film raise the question of whether Musk is capable of empathy at all. This is a man who tells his wife that “if you were my employee, I would fire you”, and urges her to tell his estranged trans-daughter Jenna that “I’ll always love her” – and then cuts off her health insurance the next day. Musk knew with a disconcerting degree of certainty that Trump would re-elected In the film, St Clair describes the events of Trump’s election in November 2024. Musk, she tells Gibney, had a “degree of certainty” about the results before they came in that “I had never seen before”. He told her that he would “unleash the anomaly in the matrix” and that “we have 10,000 lasers in space”. Gibney leaves that comment hanging. The godfather of AI is worried Musk might rig the next election Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-winning British-Canadian computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, used to be friendly with Musk, but the pair fell out after Hinton declined his offer to join the xAI board. In the film, he makes clear that he does not trust Musk to weigh up the risks and benefits of AI responsibly, and there’s more. “It’s fairly clear to me that Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections,” Hinton says onscreen. “If you wanted to corrupt those midterm elections and you wanted to use AI, all you needed to do was get detailed information on US citizens. And what Doge did looked like just what you would do.”

title: Trump’s call to rename New Mexico ‘New America’ is a distraction tactic, Democrats say
author: Shrai Popat in Washington
summary: Amid unpopular Iran war and persistent inflation, governor says state has had its name since before US existed
body_text: Democrats have hit back against Donald Trump’s suggestion that the state of New Mexico should be renamed “New America”, accusing the US president of trying to distract from his war on Iran and rising prices. The administration moved to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” hours after Trump’s return to office in January 2025. In August, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, it moved to do the same with Lake Ontario, moving to rename it as “Lake America”. The president spent Labor Day posting memes on social media platform in support ⁠of changing the ⁠name of the state of New Mexico to “New America” as tense trade negotiations ⁠with Mexico ramp up. On Sunday Trump claimed that ‌he had received suggestions to change the name ‌of the state and that he liked the idea. “So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform. “Wow, I Love It!!!” The US federal government has no authority to change a state’s name. Any renaming would require New Mexico voters to approve an amendment to the state constitution through a ballot measure. The state ⁠is currently governed by Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat. She has been in the job since 1 January 2019, and was re-elected ‌in 2022. The governor said in a post on X: “New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate – it’s been ours since before the United States existed.” “While the President tries to distract Americans from his disastrous war in Iran, gas prices keep soaring,” she wrote. “Americans are also spending more at the grocery store, losing access to health care and wondering if they’ll ever be able to afford a home.” New Mexico’s senior senator, Martin Heinrich, blasted the president’s recent efforts to rename bodies of water via executive order. “Three things I will always call by their actual names,” Heinrich wrote. “The Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario, New Mexico.” His colleague in the Senate, Ben Ray Luján, echoed the sentiment. “It’s New Mexico, always has been and always will be,” he said, adding that Trump will “always be a sinvergüenza” – a spanish word for scoundrel – and “corrupt”. Melanie Stansbury, one New Mexico’s Democratic US House representatives, was also resolute. “WE ARE NOT CHANGING OUR NAME!” she said in a video, standing on the banks of the Rio Grande, which runs through the state. “New Mexico is New Mexico. We are fiercely proud of our name, our people, and our places, including this river.” Even Greg Hull, the Republican nominee running to replace Grisham, who is term-limited, denounced the president’s suggestion. “New Mexico does not need a new name. This state carries the history of Native nations and Spanish explorers who named this land nearly five hundred years ago, and generations of families who built New Mexico into what it is today. That identity is not up for negotiation,” Hull said in a statement to Santa Fe Public Radio.

title: Mass polygraphs at the Pentagon show Hegseth’s weakness
author: Margaret Sullivan
summary: The more defense secretary Pete Hegseth tries to flex his manly strength, the wimpier he looks
body_text: The more the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, tries to flex his manly strength, the wimpier he looks. The former Fox News host has attempted to seize control of what the public is allowed to know, but bad news keeps creeping out from the Pentagon. Shortages of key weapons, deteriorating conditions onboard a US aircraft carrier, and no end in sight for President Trump’s misguided war – all a very bad look for the boss. But what to do? Hegseth has restricted reporters’ access at the Pentagon, fired journalists at the military newspaper Stars and Stripes, and installed “influencers” to spread pro-Trump propaganda. He hasn’t held a Pentagon news briefing on the war since early May. But none of it seems to work. Now, trying to root out the problem at the source, he’s chasing down leakers by giving polygraph tests to about 50 military officers and civilian officials – something never done before in such a widespread way, according to New York Times reporting. The boss, of course, heartily approves. “The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down!” Trump crowed on Truth Social, his favorite venue for venting rage and threatening retribution. “Long term jail sentences will be sought!” Granted, the ubiquitous news reports about shortages of American weapons, including long-range missiles, are a particularly bad look for Trump’s war effort, which seems more every day like a costly and directionless flop. And a huge political liability. The war’s unpopularity has driven down the president’s approval ratings, and that’s a real worry as the midterm elections approach in early November. Trump himself is not on the ballot, of course, but control of Congress certainly is. Democratic control of one or both houses, now in Republican hands, could put some unwelcome restraints on this president’s unbounded malfeasance and endless self-dealing. Such control might even restore long-missing checks and balances. That is a nightmare scenario for this out-of-control president. No wonder he and his allies are trying every method to seize control of journalists and their sources. The weaponized justice department even went so far as to subpoena several New York Times reporters over their stories on security problems with a Qatari-donated plane that’s been repurposed as the new Air Force One. Instead of addressing underlying problems, it’s all about seeking revenge. Since the media’s reporting is (largely) protected by the first amendment, the leakers themselves must seem like fair game. Hegseth has played the polygraph card before. Furious last year after press leaks about plans to give Elon Musk a Pentagon briefing on China, the defense secretary yelled at Christopher Grady, then the acting joint chiefs chairman, accusing him of leaking, the Wall Street Journal reported. “I’ll hook you up to a f---ing polygraph!” Hegseth reportedly shouted at Grady. But poorly led organizations, like Hegseth’s Pentagon, will always leak. Chaos and dysfunction need a steam valve. And the truth will out. Inevitably, facts come to the surface when insiders have information that they want exposed and when journalists are doing their jobs. What politicians never admit is that leaks often serve an important and positive purpose. “Without leaks, we’d be left in the dark about vital information involving government, corporations, and powerful individuals, who often act in secret,” notes the Freedom of the Press Foundation, which also downplays the constant warnings of threats to national security. “We should be skeptical of claims that leaks cause harm and of broad leak investigations that can lead to the surveillance of journalists and sources and the chilling of reporting.” Don’t try telling that to Hegseth and Trump, who vastly prefer pro-war propaganda to uncomfortable facts. And who are always looking for someone to blame and punish. Some military officials may be scared off by this witch-hunt and decide to keep their lips sealed. But others, if they trust journalists to provide protective anonymity, will take their chances and expose the truth. Some, at least, do this out of old-fashioned patriotism, allowing cleansing sunlight into the dark corners of government and the military. Call such truth-telling another form of lie detection, one that is a far cry from Trump’s charges of treason. And in terms of democracy, a far more effective one. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist

title: Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer urges Trump to consider pardon after mistrial
author: Oliver Milman
summary: Attorney hopes Trump would consider clemency given ‘the type of person she is’ and ‘what she has been through’
body_text: The lawyer of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her three young children, has said he hopes Donald Trump will pardon his client after her trial recently ended with a deadlocked jury. Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, made the appeal on a televised interview on the ABC show Good Morning America on Tuesday. The plea comes to Trump after a judge on Friday declared a mistrial after the jury in the Clancy case could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was guilty or not guilty. Reddington said he hoped that the president would “consider a pardon” for Clancy given “the type of person she is” and “what she has been through”. “Mr President, I would hope that you would consider this young lady,” said Reddington, who also alluded to how Trump on Friday called the case a “tragedy”. Trump’s pardon powers are applicable in the federal justice system in the US, and Clancy was tried in Massachusetts’ state criminal justice system. But in June in Colorado, Tina Peters – the former clerk convicted in state court of participating in a plot to chase election conspiracy theories boosted by Trump – was released early from a nine-year prison after the Democratic governor, Jared Polis, succumbed to pressure to do so from the Republican president. Clancy, who is 36, was charged with fatally strangling her three children – Cora, five; Dawson, three; and Callan, eight months old – in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. She had also thrown herself out of her bedroom window in an apparent suicide attempt, which left her paralyzed. Prosecutors argued that Clancy was aware of her actions and had “coldly and efficiently executed” the children after planning to do so, including ensuring her husband was out of the house. But her defense, led by Reddington, claimed that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis which compelled her to carry out the killings and therefore was not legally culpable. During the trial, Reddington called a forensic psychiatrist, Dr Phillip Resnick, to testify that Clancy had “severe depression” and a history of anxiety, which increased after the birth of her children to the point that she “felt she couldn’t function”. “At the time of the crime … Ms Clancy was frankly psychotic,” Resnick said. “She was clearly psychotic on that day.” Jurors in Plymouth state court spent more than 38 hours in deliberations over the charges, which sparked a broader national debate over maternal mental health issues that can occur postpartum. Ultimately, Reddington has said the 12-person jury, made up of nine women and three men, was split 11 to one in favor of a not guilty verdict. The lack of a unanimous verdict led to the judge declaring a mistrial, opening the way for another trial. Trump was asked about the trial by reporters on Friday, with the president calling the case “a shame” and a “horrible tragedy”. “I think the judge has said it’s going to be a mistrial, so there’s going to be another trial,” he said. “It’s a terrible situation. Look, she did a horrible, horrible thing. “Can’t be worse. But you’ll find out what the price to pay is. There’ll be a price. It’s going to be mental institution or jail or something, but I guess they’re going to go through another trial.” In the US, the national maternal mental health hotline is 1-833-852-6262. In the UK, the Pandas foundation offers support via Whatsapp on 07903 508334. In Australia, the national maternal and perinatal mental health hotline is 1300 726 306

title: Smithsonian Institution secretary to retire amid Trump attacks on museum independence
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: ‘I have to be honest, it has been stressful,’ says Lonnie Bunch III
body_text: The Smithsonian Institution’s secretary, Lonnie Bunch III, will retire at the end of the year amid Donald Trump’s attacks on the museum’s content and independence. Bunch, who was appointed in 2019 as the first African American to lead the museums, cited personal reasons for departing, while acknowledging the pressure that the president’s attacks on the Smithsonian’s depictions of US history had taken. “There is no place like the Smithsonian – it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together,” Bunch, 73, said in a statement. “I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.” “It was really just saying, now’s the time,” Bunch, 73, told the New York Times. He added: “I have to be honest, it has been stressful. And at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.” Trump largely left the Smithsonian alone during his first term, but sought to align its content with his administration’s policies shortly after returning to the White House. In March 2025, the US president signed an executive order accusing the museum of coming “under the influence of a divisive, race-centered ideology”, and outlining steps to “restore the Smithsonian Institution to its rightful place as a symbol of inspiration and American greatness”. Two months later, he tried to fire Kim Sajet as director of the National Portrait Gallery, calling her “a highly partisan person” and a “strong supporter” of the diversity and equity programs his administration was seeking to ban. Bunch pushed back, and the Smithsonian issued a statement affirming that the power to hire and fire lay with him, but Sajet nonetheless resigned in June 2025. Trump has kept up his pressure campaign in recent months, and in July ordered the National Museum of American History to display signs that accuse it of inaccuracy, though those have yet to appear. A historian who previously led the creation of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, Bunch acknowledged to the Times that he had to choose his battles in the job. “My goal has been to win, not to make me feel good,” he said. “To win – to protect the Smithsonian – there were times I would fight, make clear what the red lines were. And there were other times I let things go.” Bunch’s replacement will be selected by the Smithsonian’s 17-member board of regents, which is led by John Roberts, the chief justice of the supreme court. The panel also includes JD Vance, three Democratic members of Congress and three Republicans, as well as nine private citizens. Three of those citizens’ terms expired recently, however, and the Trump administration has not yet announced replacements. Roberts praised Bunch for having “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story”, adding: “The Regents, and the Smithsonian, have benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership. We look forward to working with him in the coming months to ensure a smooth transition for his successor.” News of Bunch’s departure drew mixed reactions from Capitol Hill. Bunch was a frequent target of conservative critics, and Republicans celebrated his decision to step down. “Good riddance,” wrote Josh Hawley, a Republican senator from Missouri. The lawmaker and staunch Trump ally said that Bunch “should return his salary to the American people”. Democrats, meanwhile, praised Bunch for his steady leadership in the face of constant pressure from the president and his administration. Senator Alex Padilla of California, the ranking Democrat on the Senate rules and administration committee, which has oversight of the Smithsonian Institution, applauded Bunch for “putting truth and accuracy over politics”. Senator Catherine Cortez Masto, a Democrat from Nevada, who serves on the Smithsonian’s 17-member board and will be responsible to selecting his replacement, echoed the sentiment, heralding Bunch as a “student of history who has devoted his life to telling America’s full history”. She added: “I look forward to working with Secretary Bunch over these next few months to ensure his successor exhibits the same commitment to the arts, culture, science and history that he did.”

title: Will UK sanctions have any impact on Israel’s ‘settler terrorists’ in West Bank?
author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem
summary: A look at whether Ed Miliband’s plans will be effective and what they signal for future Israel-UK relations
body_text: The British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has announced plans for an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in occupied Palestine and sanctions for companies that “finance or facilitate” the construction, infrastructure and marketing of illegal settlements. He also said “settler terrorists” were perpetrating ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank, while the government turned a blind eye and some members supported it. Britain’s argument was with the government of Israel, not its people, Miliband said. The new measures would target only the expansion and entrenchment of Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestine, not Israel inside the green line – the 1949 armistice boundary, once seen as a possible template for Israel’s border with a future Palestinian state. The measures were prompted in part by Israel’s decision to press ahead with a vast new settlement in the heart of the West Bank, in an area known as E1. The project is designed to “bury the idea of a Palestinian state”, the far-right Israeli minister Bezalel Smotrich has said, and Miliband described the issuing of construction tenders in August as a “red line”. He told parliament of his family ties to Israel, including joyful childhood memories of visiting his grandmother, who found a home there after Nazis murdered her husband and 60 other relatives. By acting against ethnic cleansing and settlement expansion, Britain was standing up for its core values, including “rule of law, freedom and self-determination”, and the future of both Israelis and Palestinians, he said, adding that the new measures were designed to “salvage the only course for peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians, the two-state solution”. Why is going after E1 settlement financing a big deal? The trade in goods grown or produced in settlements is a relatively small part of Israel’s export economy, although its exact scale is obscured by a lack of Israeli statistics. Miliband highlighted that the Israeli settler population in occupied Palestine had almost tripled over the past three decades, from 270,000 in 1993 to 770,000 today. That expansion is underpinned by large government subsidies. A trade ban alone would be unlikely to have much impact on the viability of construction that is a government priority, or on the broader Israeli economy. However, plans to place sanctions on any company that finances or facilitates settlement expansion could force Israel’s main banks and insurance companies to chose between their business interests in the UK and those in occupied Palestine. Miliband has not provided details of the new measures, which he said would take between six and nine months to put in place. But they have the potential to slow or stop construction. The activist Yehuda Shaul wrote in a social media post about new building projects: “Companies that bid for tenders on government-led projects, including settlement expansion, must have a financial guarantor. Without the backing of Israeli financial institutions, these projects cannot occur.” What is the status of Israeli settlements and the settler economy? Miliband said Britain recognised Israel’s occupation of Palestine as unlawful, in line with a landmark 2024 ruling from the UN’s international court of justice (ICJ). The UK had previously recognised settlements as illegal, but remained silent on the occupation overall. The ICJ ordered Israel to end its occupation “as rapidly as possible” and make full reparations for its “internationally wrongful acts”. Israeli supporters of the UK measures say they redraw the line between Israel proper and illegally occupied territory, and are a much-needed response to Israeli government policies that are undermining the country. Michael Sfard, one of Israel’s leading human rights lawyers, said the measures were “enormously important”. “It redraws the green line and provides a recommitment to international law. Every cent that goes from the UK or other countries to support the economy of settlements is a cent that allows violation of international law,” he said. The former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert, whom Miliband quoted in his speech, said: “The British government decision became unavoidable as a result of a continuous effort of ethnic cleansing perpetrated by a large group of Jewish terrorists in the West Bank … Sanctions are directed against the terrorists, not against Israel, and as such they are unavoidable.” What does Miliband’s intervention mean for UK-Israel relations? Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, responded rapidly with a series of measures, including closing the UK the consulate in East Jerusalem, Britain’s diplomatic mission to occupied Palestine. There was fierce condemnation from other Israeli politicians. The far-right minister Ben Gvir called for Israel to recognise Argentinian sovereignty over the Falklands – even before Miliband made his speech. However, Israel holds elections in six weeks, and for months polls have shown Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition stuck below the threshold needed to form a new government. Although none of the leading candidates to replace him oppose the occupation, there has been growing condemnation of violence in the West Bank. A new government would mean a chance to reset ties. Israel may be seeking to deter others from following the UK’s lead, but a dozen countries have already said they are planning similar restrictions on settlement trade, among them Israel’s historical allies Canada and France. A joint statement from the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham; the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney; and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said the action marked “a further turning point in our approach to protecting the two-state solution”. Netanyahu’s policies have already pushed Israel into a position of unprecedented international isolation, and taking similar punitive action against all these countries would only deepen that. What other pressure could be applied? The measures unveiled by Miliband mark the most serious step yet to impose a political and economic price on Israel for settlement expansion. The Israeli government’s furious response belies growing support both inside Israel, and among some of the country’s staunchest supporters abroad, for stronger action to halt violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. This summer dozens of Israelis from the country’s security, political and cultural elite threatened legal action against their government over support for “Jewish terrorism” and an “ideology of ethnic cleansing” in the occupied West Bank. Trump’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, and some Republicans in Congress attacked Miliband before his speech. But the US also has elections this autumn. The Democrat Rahm Emanuel, a former Chicago mayor whose father fought in the Israeli military, used a speech in Tel Aviv to call for broad sanctions on Israel’s financial sector to stop violence against Palestinians. Pressed on the implications of placing sanctions on banks with branches in settlements – which is all of Israel’s major institutions – he told the Jerusalem Post: “America uses its tools to achieve its policy goals. We believe in a two-state solution. You want to pursue a greater Israel? You pay full price for it. Everything. That’s a choice you make.”

title: Missouri congressional maps thrown into chaos after conflicting court rulings
author: Dani Anguiano and Uwa Ede-Osifo
summary: Tug of war as federal judge says old maps cannot be used in November, hours after supreme court blocked new maps backed by Trump
body_text: Clashing court rulings plunged Missouri’s congressional elections into uncertainty on Tuesday, the latest in a legal tug-of-war that comes less than two months before the November midterms that will decide which party controls a closely divided Congress. First, the conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh denied the emergency request from Missouri officials to use a congressional map in November that was redrawn with Donald Trump’s support to give Republicans an edge in the midterms. Then, shortly thereafter, a ruling by a federal judge in Missouri temporarily prevented the state from using its old congressional maps in the November elections. The temporary restraining order, known as a TRO, was issued by US district judge Stephen Clark and ordered Missouri to use the newly drawn districts that favor Republicans, which the state had used in its August primary elections. “Using a different map for the general election would wreak havoc on the fairness and orderliness of Missouri’s congressional elections, calling into question the candidacy of those nominated in the primaries and the votes of those who voted in the primaries. Widespread voter confusion would inevitably follow,” Clark, who was appointed by the president, wrote. “The public interest factor thus weighs in favor of a TRO.” That order was swiftly appealed to the eighth US circuit court of appeals. Tuesday’s legal action came after the Missouri supreme court ruled that the map must go before voters to approve or reject the new districts, meaning it cannot be used in the November election. The president and Republicans had fumed over the decision, with Trump calling it “horrible, ridiculous, and unConstitutional”. The state’s attorney general argued the decision would disenfranchise Missouri voters and thrust the state into a “full‑fledged constitutional crisis”. Trump set in motion a national redistricting battle last year as a way to give Republicans an advantage in the midterm elections, in which the party that controls the White House has historically lost seats. But with Trump plagued by low approval ratings and an unpopular war against Iran, Republicans are bracing for potentially major losses in the House and possibly even control of the Senate. Failure to cement the Republican redistricting effort in Missouri would be a rare setback for the party that has largely succeeded in redrawing congressional lines. Missouri was the second Republican state to act in response to the president’s push to redraw congressional maps to favor Republicans. Mike Kehoe, the state’s governor, called the legislature into a special session last year to create new boundaries ahead of the US midterm elections. The revised map targeted the fifth congressional district, held by longtime Democratic representative Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City. It reassigned portions of Kansas City to two neighboring districts represented by Republicans and stretched the remainder of Cleaver’s district far eastward into rural Republican areas. Cleaver was unopposed in the Democratic primary. State senator Rick Brattin won the Republican primary in the reshaped district. Kehoe backed the temporary block of the old congressional maps on Tuesday, saying it provided “clarity” in the election process. “With today marking the deadline for changes to the November ballot, the Missouri First Map will be used in the general election. Voters and candidates deserve consistency, certainty, and not to have the rules changed between elections,” Kehoe wrote on X. While Republicans in the state celebrated the latest legal twist in their favor, Chuck Hatfield, an attorney for People Not Politicians, an advocacy group that sponsored the referendum petition, said the decision from the state’s supreme court remains in effect. “An individual federal judge cannot overrule the Missouri supreme court,” he said. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Congressman Chris Pappas wins New Hampshire Democratic Senate primary
author: Shrai Popat
summary: Pappas fends off challenge from progressive Karishma Manzur in seat to be vacated by retiring Jeanne Shaheen
body_text: Congressman Chris Pappas beat back progressive challenger Karishma Manzur in the Democratic primary for US Senate in New Hampshire on Tuesday, advancing as most observers expected to what will be a closely watched general election that is critical to Democratic hopes of flipping the upper chamber. The two were competing for the nomination that opened up after Jeanne Shaheen, 79, the state’s three‑term incumbent Democratic senator, announced her retirement. Pappas, a popular centrist, has served in the House since 2019 and has crossed the aisle at various points. He calls himself “battle‑tested” and has consolidated establishment backing, earning endorsements from leading Democratic lawmakers and former vice‑president Kamala Harris. His family’s name also carries weight in New Hampshire: the Pappases own the Puritan Backroom, the century‑old Manchester restaurant famed for allegedly inventing the chicken tender and long embedded in the state’s retail‑politics circuit. Support for Israel played a large role in the primary, as it has in many intraparty contests this year. Manzur, who supports Medicare for All and higher taxes on mega‑corporations and the ultra‑wealthy, has repeatedly highlighted the money Pappas has received from donors aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). She casts him as milquetoast and ineffective. “I was tired of choosing between the lesser of two evils and still seeing so much pain and suffering right here in my state,” she said. Pappas has long backed US aid to Israel but told the Guardian that Benjamin Netanyahu was “not a trustworthy ally of the US” and said he hoped the Israeli prime minister would be ousted in the country’s October election. Pappas noted he has rejected corporate Pac money in this race but did not directly address his support from pro‑Israel donors, instead pointing to a “broad‑based effort” of individual contributors that have supported his Senate bid. Pappas will face the Donald Trump-endorsed former senator John E Sununu, who is seeking a return to the seat he once held and is part of a political dynasty that includes his father and brother, both former governors. Some Democrats worry New Hampshire could become a sleeper risk – a state where Republicans control the legislature but have not won a Senate race since 2010, when Kelly Ayotte, now the governor, captured a seat.

title: Trump-backed John Sununu wins New Hampshire Republican Senate primary
author: Shrai Popat
summary: Frontrunner Sununu beats Scott Brown to earn Republican nod in closely watched race in November
body_text: Former senator John E Sununu triumphed on Tuesday in the New Hampshire Republican Senate primary over Scott Brown, earning the GOP nod in what will probably be a must-win race if Democrats hope to seize the upper chamber. Sununu, 61, was the clear frontrunner in the GOP primary. He served one term in the Senate from 2003 to 2009. Brown represented Massachusetts, later moved to New Hampshire, and served as US ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during Donald Trump’s first term. The US president threw his support behind Sununu earlier this year, despite the former lawmaker’s past criticism of Trump, including a 2024 op‑ed in which Sununu called Trump a “loser” and backed Nikki Haley in the Republican presidential primary. On the trail, Sununu has tried to show daylight between himself and the administration, criticizing Trump’s tariff policy, urging Congress to rein in executive power, and questioning the decision to launch military action in Iran. He told New Hampshire Public Radio it was “a tactical mistake” to go to war “without having a plan for protecting the strait of Hormuz”. That posture may matter in a state where Trump’s approval rating sits at 38%. Sununu and Brown did not respond to the Guardian’s interview requests. Kristen Cianci, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said Sununu was a “strong candidate” who was “well positioned to beat out Pappas” in a general election. “While Democrats have been consumed by infighting, Republicans have been laser-focused on real issues like affordability and security,” she added in a statement. Sununu will face congressman Chris Pappas, who beat back a progressive challenger in the Democratic primary, advancing as most observers expected to what will be a closely watched general election that is critical to Democratic hopes of flipping the upper chamber. Some Democrats, however, worry New Hampshire could become a sleeper risk – a state where Republicans control the legislature but haven’t won a Senate race since 2010, when Kelly Ayotte, now the governor, captured a seat.
