title: Democrat John Fetterman makes surprise appearance at Republican convention
author: Shrai Popat in Washington and Adam Gabbatt in Dallas
summary: Senator praises ‘great friend’ Dave McCormick and says he will help him and Trump to support steel in Pennsylvania
body_text: The Democratic senator John Fetterman made a surprise virtual appearance at the Republican midterm convention, delivering a video address supporting Dave McCormick, a Republican senator in Pennsylvania. Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his party since his election in 2022, said in the video that he would always reject “extremes and socialism”, repeating an oft-used Republican critique of the Democratic party’s increasingly popular left wing. The video message will do little to dampen speculation that the renegade senator, who is now more popular among Republican voters in Pennsylvania than the Democrats who helped elect him, is preparing to switch political parties. Fetterman has repeatedly said that is not his plan, though he recently suggested he would be forced to formally break with the Democratic party if it ever became “the anti-Israel party”. Democrats currently hold 47 seats in the US Senate. Despite the long odds, Democrats believe discontent with the economy and Trump’s low approval ratings have given them a rare opportunity to retake control of the upper chamber. A defection would jeopardize their already narrow path to a majority. Yet if Fetterman remains a Democrat, he would hold outsized influence, effectively wielding veto power in a 51-49 majority. In the roughly one-minute video, Fetterman, wearing his trademark black hoodie, stood outside the Mon Valley Works – a processing plant operated by US Steel in Pittsburgh. In a stunning display of support for a Republican colleague in the Senate, Fetterman called McCormick his “great friend”, and said that he would work with him and Donald Trump “to fight and defend the steel way of life”. “Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I’m a commonsense Democrat. I’m always going to stand with America,” the Pennsylvania lawmaker said in the pre-recorded message. “I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life. Dave McCormick is the kind of senator that gets the job done, and he’s going to fight for Pennsylvania.” At the convention center in Dallas, attenders welcomed the senator’s rightward march. “I actually think it’s really awesome that he’s come around,” Tracy Smith, an attender from Maryland, said. “He’s more commonsense, and even though he’s a Democrat, he can see both sides. You have to get along. It’s like a seesaw. You know, not right or left, but in the middle. And I think he realized that, and it’s actually amazing.” Asked if she thought Fetterman could switch to the Republican party, Smith said: “I actually do. I think he’s leaning that way right here. It would be great. I think it would be awesome.” Eric Torrison, who traveled from Arizona to attend the convention, was also laudatory. “There is no way on God’s green Earth that I would have supported Fetterman when he ran for the Senate, and [was] aghast when he got elected,” said Eric Torrison, who lives in Arizona. “But it’s really interesting. He seems to have held to his beliefs, and not run to the left, and he seems to be, from a conservative standpoint, from a Republican standpoint, the only sensible Democrat there.” Fetterman’s fellow Democrats were far less charitable. “John Fetterman is the laziest Benedict Arnold America has ever seen. He didn’t even have it in him to get off his couch in his million-dollar penthouse to kiss Donald Trump’s ring in person. He phoned it in, just as he has every day as our senator. John should do his job or resign,” the Pennsylvania state representative Malcolm Kenyatta said in a statement. Fetterman has been in the limelight after reports from current and former staff that he was avoiding constituent events, behaving erratically and cozying up to conservative media. In the past week, the senator has attempted to defend himself after an account on X, which claims to be run by former staffers, gained traction.

title: Rhode Island’s Democratic governor loses primary amid anger over bridge
author: Lauren Gambino
summary: Helena Foulkes beats incumbent Dan McKee after criticizing handling of Providence’s Washington bridge, now expected to be completed in 2028
body_text: Rhode Island’s Dan McKee became the first sitting governor to lose a primary in nearly a decade, bested not by a more progressive challenger or a more youthful upset but by frustration over a bridge. McKee lost his Democratic primary to Helena Foulkes, a former longtime executive with the Rhode Island-based retail pharmacy CVS, the Associated Press said on Wednesday. “Tonight, we may have won the Democratic primary for governor, but let me be clear about what happens next: you will have a governor for everyone,” Foulkes said during her victory speech in the state’s capital, Providence. “Because there is so much work that needs to be done, and we need to do this together.” It is rare for a sitting governor to lose a primary election. It hasn’t happened in Rhode Island since 1994. In his concession speech, also in Providence, McKee promised to work with Foulkes to ensure she is elected in November. “This is something that I think is difficult to deal with,” McKee said, “but we just got to hold our heads high.” Several Democratic incumbents have been toppled this cycle, in a wave of anti-establishment anger that has elevated young and progressive insurgents. But this contest was different. On the campaign trail, Foulkes criticized McKee’s handling of repair work on Providence’s Washington bridge, a major east-west traffic artery that carries roughly 100,000 vehicles a day. She accused him of bungling those repairs, which have dragged on longer than originally planned. McKee closed the bridge in December 2023, after inspectors uncovered serious structural problems. By March 2024, officials had concluded that repairing the structure was not feasible and that it would have to be rebuilt. State officials initially estimated that the bridge would be reopened to traffic this year, but the project’s completion date has since been delayed to November 2028. The primary contest was something of a rematch from four years ago, when Foulkes, who is the niece of former Democratic Senator Chris Dodd of Connecticut, came in a close second behind McKee in a five-way contest. McKee went on to easily win the general election in 2022, after having assumed the role from then-governor Gina Raimondo, who stepped down to become Joe Biden’s US commerce secretary in 2021. Election prognosticators rate the seat as strongly Democratic, and therefore the winner of Wednesday’s primary is seen as having a major advantage in the November general election. McKee’s defeat was not the only electoral upset on Wednesday. In Providence, David Morales, a 27-year-old Democratic socialist defeated Mayor Brett Smiley in the Democratic primary, ending the incumbent’s bid for a second term. Morales’s campaign was backed by progressive stalwarts, including Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and several labor unions.

title: ‘Fundamentally unfair’: Burnham must overhaul migration reforms, says TUC general secretary
author: Heather Stewart
summary: Paul Nowak says changes to immigration rules risk overstretching social care and fuelling far-right sentiment
body_text: Andy Burnham must overhaul Shabana Mahmood’s migration reforms or risk overstretching social care and fuelling far-right sentiment, the TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, has warned. Speaking ahead of the TUC’s annual congress in Brighton next week, Nowak welcomed the “sense of optimism” around Burnham’s fledgling government, but he urged the PM to act in a series of areas, including migration and the cost of living. Burnham reappointed Mahmood as home secretary when he became prime minister in July. Her department is consulting on proposals that would force more than 300,000 low-paid workers to wait 15 years for the legal right to remain in the UK. These include many carers who came to the UK to fill vacancies after the Covid pandemic, and were told they could apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years. “I think it is fundamentally unfair to change the rules when people came to this country with one set of expectations,” Nowak said. “I hope we can think again on that.” He added: “There are 111,000 staff vacancies in social care at the moment. I want us to train up as many Brits as possible to do those jobs. But I suspect in a growing economy with an ageing population, we are still going to need people to come and live and work in the UK and work in sectors like social care.” As well as criticising the backward-looking changes, Nowak also condemned the idea of applying a 10- or 15-year wait to many new arrivals, as the Home Office has proposed. “Both my granddads came to this country after the second world war – one came from Hong Kong, one came from Poland. Both raised their families here. The idea that you could be here for the next 10, 15 years and you’d still have no legal right to remain in the country … how the hell do you plan? Can you buy a house? What does that mean for your employment? Do you have kids? Do you send them to school? I mean, it cuts across any effort to integrate at all.” Labour politicians supportive of the changes see them partly as a way of assuaging public concerns about migration, and neutralising the appeal of populist parties, including Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. But Nowak suggested that by significantly lengthening the time before people can consider themselves settled in the UK, the approach could ultimately fuel far-right sentiment. “I tell you where you end up: you end up with Reform claiming that a woman who was born in Somalia and has lived here for most of her life and worked hard and contributed to our society, somehow isn’t fit to hold elected office in this country.” Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, was recently accused of “straightforward racism” by Labour after he suggested the party’s frontrunner to replace Keir Starmer in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, former child refugee Sagal Abdi-Wali, was not British. Nowak acknowledged that many TUC members will have backed Reform in recent local elections, but suggested the party’s appeal may be waning. “Our members are a broad cross section of the British public. Of course, large numbers of them voted Reform, like other people did. But certainly the evidence that we’re getting fed back from unions is that just like the British public, the more they see of Nigel Farage, the less keen they are.” Nowak claimed there was a “direct line” from the rhetoric of Farage and his allies, to what he called the “proto-fascism” of the balaclava-clad vigilantes who blocked infrastructure in Dover and tried to stop migrants arriving in Portsmouth last weekend. He suggested Labour should focus on cost-of-living issues to combat Reform’s populist appeal – including offering voters more help with rising energy bills. “The most important thing that Andy Burnham can do is to deliver the change that people voted for back in July 2024. If people feel that the government is taking the stuff that matters to them seriously and is delivering on it, I think it cuts the legs from underneath that rightwing populism.” Ahead of the budget on 28 October, Nowak called for a “social tariff” to cut energy bills for lower paid users, funded by a windfall tax on the banks. “As well as delivering a boost to hundreds of thousands of households up and down the country, it will help bear down on the cost of inflation,” he said. “The public bailed the banks out in 2008. For those families who are worried about turning on the heating this year, asking the banks to pay their fair share isn’t unreasonable.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “last November, we set out reforms to double the standard qualifying period for settlement to 10 years for most migrants, with shorter routes for those who contribute most to the UK. “A consultation on elements of those reforms has now closed, and we will set out our response in due course.”

title: US citizens will receive $5,000 if Republicans win midterms, Trump claims in lengthy convention speech
author: Adam Gabbatt in Dallas
summary: President makes offer that would cost US over $1tn and asks voters to ‘pretend that I’m on the ballot’ despite being deeply unpopular among electorate
body_text: Donald Trump pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections, during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which the president assailed Democrats as “radical” and defended his unpopular war in Iran. The outlandish proposal, which would cost over $1tn, immediately raised ethical concerns. But it laid bare the extent of the Republicans’ concern about their prospects in the pivotal November elections. “If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump told a roaring crowd, during a nearly two-hour speech in which he also urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot” – despite his historic unpopularity causing many vulnerable Republican politicians to avoid the event. Surrounded by supporters waving American flag placards, Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”, but devoted much of his speech to fearmongering about what would happen should Democrats win the House or the Senate for the final two years of his presidency. “There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country,” Trump said. “We will defeat communism in America.” The president and Republicans are gambling that throwing a midterm convention – the first the GOP has ever held – can buoy the party, which is predicted to lose control of the House. Yet, Trump’s deep unpopularity among Americans – his approval rating is hovering at about 38% – meant many Republican candidates running in competitive races skipped the two-day confab entirely. Even so, Trump’s speech made it clear he thinks he will be the deciding factor in November. Noting that the party which holds the White House traditionally struggles in the midterm elections, Trump said: “We’ve got to change that, because we have something going that’s so good. “If we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth. Our country is going through hell – we will be going through hell, just like we did, just two years ago,” he said. The buildup to the midterm convention had somewhat of a chaotic air. Trump was initially scheduled to speak on the second night, before the Republican National Committee announced that he would deliver the keynote on Wednesday, and instead give closing remarks on Thursday after his vice-president, JD Vance, speaks. Trump made several references to the war in Iran, warning Tehran “not to get cute” or the US “will have to hit them very hard”. But he also appeared to acknowledge the economic pain caused by the soaring price of oil. Trump re-enacted the way he told his economic advisers that the US needed to start the conflict because Iran was “two, maybe three weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”. “I hate to do this to you,” he said he told them, noting the economy had been doing well. At the convention center, there were signs of middling enthusiasm among the rank and file. Compared with the four-day traditional convention in Milwaukee two years ago, the first day felt muted. There were no long queues to enter, no eternal waits for food or bathrooms. Swathes of empty seats were visible throughout Trump’s speech. Visible, except to Trump, who claimed, wrongly, that the arena was full. “Not only is this packed but you have an equal number of people standing outside,” Trump declared. This was not observed by Guardian reporters. The RNC had announced in mid-August that Americans could apply for tickets to attend the event, suggesting that applicants would enter a lottery and only a lucky few would be granted access. Yet on Wednesday, with the convention under way, applications for tickets were instantly being granted on an RNC sign-up page. Trump himself, however, appeared energized in his call to action on the first night, cracking jokes, including at the expense of Ken Paxton, his handpicked candidate for Senate in Texas who won a primary against the incumbent John Cornyn earlier this year. “He may not dress right. He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said of Paxton. “But you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America.” Trump spent several minutes attacking Democrats, including Paxton’s opponent, James Talarico, who Trump mocked as a “weird-looking dude”; the former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper, who is now running for Senate; and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan. In a statement, Ken Martin, the chair of the Democratic National Committee, accused Republicans of holding a “bizarre dog-and-pony show” to placate the president’s “fragile ego”. “Tonight only confirmed that the president is a lame duck failure who is dragging his party toward defeat,” Martin said. The Republicans’ unusual midterm convention features 12 hours of programming across two nights. On Wednesday, the speaker lineup featured Trump loyalists and candidates, but showmanship remained at the center of the agenda. Byron Donalds, a rising star in the party who is running for governor of Florida, and Mehmet Oz and Scott Bessent, two of Trump’s cabinet secretaries, were among those to take the stage, yet the president, a UFC fan, decided he would be introduced by two fighters, the middleweight Bo Nickal and Justin “The Highlight” Gaethje, a lightweight. Most speakers only got five minutes. Nickal and Gaethje, who both fought at the UFC 250 event on the White House Lawn in June, got 10. Gaethje told the crowd he had earned his “Highlight” nickname when he knocked out his first opponent very quickly in 2016, before linking himself to the 80-year-old Trump. “One mistake I’ve made in my career was becoming complacent while I was on a winning streak and forgetting how unforgiving my sport would be,” Gaethje said. “If we are not just as passionate about voting and winning in these midterms as we were in the last presidential election, then we risk being knocked out and losing all the momentum we have been fighting for.” Earlier, Republicans said the focus would be on “lowering costs, securing our border, making our communities safer, and putting American workers and families first”. Yet speaker after speaker instead attacked Democrats on alleged support for transgender rights, in particular, suggesting the Republican party intends to put culture wars towards the front as November approaches. Trump will speak again on Thursday, but said his address would be much briefer. “I gave you a lot of material,” he said, capping his remarks on Wednesday, before pleading one more time with voters to “please pretend that I’m running”. • This article was amended on 10 September 2026. An earlier version incorrectly described Roy Cooper as a Republican.

title: ABC and the Guardian call on One Nation to reverse media ban amid censorship concerns
author: Caitlin Cassidy
summary: News outlets raise alarm after being barred from media events and condemn offensive comments made by party director James Ashby
body_text: The ABC and the Guardian have called on One Nation to reverse its ban on select media outlets from press conferences amid warnings the party is practising censorship and actively avoiding public scrutiny. On Tuesday both outlets were asked to leave a One Nation press conference in Victoria. During the event, the state’s party leader, Warren Pickering, admitted to illegal drug use and drink driving. Reporters from Guardian Australia and the ABC were escorted to the media appearance at Crown Melbourne by hotel staff, but were asked to leave by One Nation’s national party director, James Ashby, and ushered out by security after identifying who they worked for. The interaction was recorded by both the ABC and the Herald Sun, with the latter immediately posting about it on social media. The Age, owned by Nine Entertainment, has also been rejected from previous press events. The Australian, which broke the Pickering story, was not barred from attendance but was denied entry to a One Nation event in Sale, Victoria, last month. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here In August, Pauline Hanson blocked the ABC, the Age and the Guardian from the announcement of her party’s Victorian election candidates in a tense press conference where she claimed the ABC didn’t provide “fair” reporting. At that press conference Hanson said “we’ve got Rebel News here, I’m happy with them,” in reference to the rightwing website led by Avi Yemini, who was in attendance. The ABC’s managing director, Hugh Marks, said the exclusion of the ABC and the Guardian “hinders the legitimate right of Australians to information about a party and its nominees who are seeking election to public office”. He pointed to comments made by Ashby on Wednesday when he compared One Nation’s relationship with the ABC to one of “domestic violence”. Appearing on the Today show, Ashby was asked about the party’s refusal to allow journalists to attend its press appearances. He said One Nation didn’t want “morally bankrupt or corrupt media organisations coming into a room”. “With the ABC, it’s like going back to some domestic violence relationship and just getting beaten every time they come through the door,” he said. Marks said Ashby’s comments were “inappropriate and offensive on so many levels, especially to victim-survivors”. “Ashby’s exclusion of the ABC and the Guardian from One Nation press conferences and events hinders the legitimate right of Australians to information about a party and its nominees who are seeking election to public office,” he said. “It can only be seen as an attempt to avoid scrutiny, control the media and influence the information available to voters. The ban should be removed immediately.” Guardian Australia’s editor, David Munk, said the Guardian supported the ABC in condemning the “offensive comments” from Ashby. “The Australian public deserve better from our elected politicians and their representatives,” he said. “The job of covering politics the world over is one that will by its nature often bring journalists into conflict with politicians and their parties. But One Nation’s ongoing refusal to admit reporters from the Guardian and the ABC to its press conferences and events is a very concerning departure from the norm. “Journalism plays a vital role in maintaining a healthy democracy, we must be able to ask questions of politicians so that the public has accurate and trusted information.” The Guardian has reported extensively on One Nation’s internal finances, party governance and political relationships and substantial financial backing from Australia’s richest person, Gina Rinehart. After Pauline Hanson’s National Press Club address in June, she attacked Guardian Australia senior correspondent Sarah Martin for asking about her daughter, Lee Hanson, who is employed as a senior adviser to the New South Wales One Nation senator Sean Bell, despite living and working in Tasmania. In May the Guardian and the ABC were barred from the party’s election night party on the day of the Farrer byelection, when One Nation’s David Farley took the seat vacated by longtime Liberal member Sussan Ley. Local ABC reporters were also rejected from a One Nation media event ahead of the byelection. The Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom executive director, Peter Greste, said Australia’s democracy hinged on the press being able to interrogate politicians on behalf of voters. “When Warren Pickering said he would rather ban a media outlet than face greater scrutiny, he directly threatened to weaken our democratic system and our right as voters to know what is going on,” he said in a statement. “Any politician deciding who gets to scrutinise them is practicing censorship, and in a democracy, that’s something we should never accept.” • This article was amended on 10 September 2026. A previous version incorrectly stated that David Farley ousted Sussan Ley in the Farrer byelection. In fact, Ley resigned.

title: Thursday briefing: 68 facts about the Bayeux tapestry as it goes on display
author: Hettie O'Brien
summary: In today’s newsletter: No Bayeux ticket? Everything you need to know about the sold-out exhibition – from its epic journey to London to a Game of Thrones likeness
body_text: Good morning. If you live in the UK, you have probably heard about the Bayeux tapestry exhibition, which opens today, and you probably haven’t got a ticket. The digital queue was nine-hours long when they first went on sale in July, and the exhibition has already broken the British Museum’s record for the number of tickets sold in a single day. Some lucky individuals, including King Charles and aspiring overlord Peter Thiel, have been treated to early previews of the medieval tapestry. Guests staying at One Aldwych, a hotel where rooms go for £1,000 a night, can partake in the “Bayeux experience” with a themed cocktail (mead spritzer, anyone?), a full English breakfast and preferential access to tickets. In a break from our regular programming, this morning’s newsletter brings you 68 facts about the Bayeux tapestry for anyone who hasn’t been able to see the real thing. That’s one fact for each of its 68 metres (bonus fact: it’s 68.3m long). If that’s not your vibe, just be glad I didn’t manage to find 1066 facts. First, here are the headlines. Five big stories Reform | The Met police will investigate allegations that Reform UK broke electoral law relating to overseas donations as part of a wider inquiry. UK- Israel | Prominent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end. Technology | Just a day after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, US politicians have begun lashing out about the risks of the burgeoning technology. UK news | Protesters who gathered outside a Portsmouth hotel mistook Pakistan’s under-19 cricket team for asylum seekers. US news | Donald Trump pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections, during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas. In depth: From nudity, a save from the Nazis and its restoration, a buffet of Bayeux facts 1. First of all, as the exhibition’s curator Michael Lewis points out in his book, the Bayeux tapestry isn’t really a tapestry. It’s “more accurately described as an embroidery”, Lewis writes. (Nobody actually calls it an embroidery, though, so we’ll stick with tapestry). 2. The embroidery tapestry tells the story of the events that culminated in the Battle of Hastings in 1066, when William the Conquerer defeated King Harold. 3. It was supposedly commissioned by Bishop Odo, William the Conquerer’s half-brother, for his newly built cathedral in Bayeux in 1077. He was prone to “self-aggrandisement” (in Lewis’s words), which is why he gave himself a starring role in the tapestry. 4. But it wasn’t made in Bayeux. Researchers think it was probably made in England, near Canterbury. 5. It’s embroidered on linen, with 10 colours of woollen thread likely dyed with woad, madder and indigo. 6. Its nine panels were embroidered separately, and then stitched together to form a continuous picture. 7. It features 623 men, 190 horses, 35 dogs, 37 buildings (including Mont-Saint-Michel) and 41 ships. 8. It may have had a single master designer who plotted its narrative, but … 9. The embroidery was almost certainly stitched by multiple women (William of Poitiers cited English women as skilled embroiderers). 10. It’s unclear how long it took them – one estimate reckons the stitching took between two and four years. 11. Yet, only three women actually feature in the tapestry. None of them are having a good time: one is weeping at her husband’s deathbed, another is fleeing a burning building and a third is being assaulted by a priest. 12. This third figure is Ælfgyva (meaning elf-gift), the only named woman in the tapestry. Scholars think that she could be Emma of Normandy, who was accused of having an affair with the Bishop of Winchester. 13. The tapestry conveniently doesn’t mention Edgar Ætheling, who had a stronger hereditary claim to the English throne in 1066 than either William or Harold. 14. The borders tell their own stories. They’re filled with fantastical beasts, creating what the Guardian’s art critic Jonathan Jones described as a “marginal world of monsters and myths”. 15. The upper border features one of the first depictions of Haley’s Comet. 16. The tapestry also shows a figure with the name Harold, depicting the famous (and probably apocryphal) moment he was struck in the eye by an arrow. Most scholars think Harold was actually hacked to death. 17. It was possibly designed to be interpreted by a live storyteller in front of an audience, much like an epic poem. 18. It’s damaged at the end, and incomplete. Nobody knows what scene would have finished the tapestry (some think it could have been a depiction of William’s coronation at Westminster Abbey in 1066). 19. It survived at least three fires in Bayeux Cathedral. 20. The first recorded reference to the tapestry was in the 1476 inventory of Bayeux cathedral, which described a “very long and narrow hanging of linen, embroidered with figures and inscriptions representing the Conquest of England.” 21. The tapestry hasn’t always been well looked after. For centuries it was rolled out for cathedral visitors. One visiting English antiquary observed in the early 1800s that it was “much rubbed at the beginning, torn towards the end.” 22. In 1792, during the French Revolution, the tapestry was nearly used to cover a wagon (it was saved at the last minute by an official who swapped it for a piece of canvas). 23. In 1794, an proposal was briefly floated to cut the tapestry into strips to decorate a festival float. 24. A 19th-century British artist secretly snipped off two fragments that ended up in a London museum (these were eventually returned to Bayeux). 25. In 1803, Napoleon had the tapestry temporarily moved from Bayeux to Paris, where it hung on display at the Louvre, to rally support for his planned invasion of Britain. 26. The first full photographic copy of the tapestry was made for the South Kensington Museum in 1872 (now the V&A museum). 27. A group of women in Staffordshire created the largest Bayeux reproduction in 1885, which is displayed in Reading Museum. It took them 18 months. 28. They removed 93 penises from their reproduction, 88 belonging to horses and five to men. 29. The Nazis saw the tapestry as a propaganda tool, and wanted to establish that Normans were actually the descendants of Viking settlers. 30. They appointed a professor of Viking archaeology as the leader of “Special Assignment Bayeaux” to study it. 31. Heinrich Himmler tasked two SS officers in 1944 to seize the Bayeaux tapestry from the basement of the Louvre, where it was being stored. 32. A group of local resistance fighters tipped off by code breakers at Bletchley Park managed to intercept the officers and protect the tapestry. 33. Since 1983, the tapestry has been displayed at the Bayeux museum, in a 17th-century seminary near Bayeux’s medieval town centre. 34. When the tapestry arrived at the Bayeux museum in the 1980s, photos show that it appeared to have been folded and hoisted up a stairwell. 35. It’s incredibly fragile, and liable to fray. A 2020 study found the tapestry had “24,204 stains, 16,445 wrinkles, 9,646 gaps in the cloth or the embroidery” and “30 non-stabilised tears.” 36. The first request for the Bayeux tapestry to be loaned to Britain was in 1953, for Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation. The French refused. 37. Another request was made in 1966, to mark the 900th anniversary of the Battle of Hastings. The French refused, again. 38. In 2013, a committee was formed to advise on how the tapestry could be redisplayed. It raised the prospect of a loan to the UK (“I did sort of bang on about it,” Lewis, a committee member, later recalled, “until I was a bit like a broken record”). 39. The Bayeux museum was scheduled to be closed for refurbishment, creating an opportunity for the tapestry to travel on loan. 40. In January 2018, Emmanuel Macron announced at a summit with Theresa May that the French had agreed to loan the tapestry. Although France had “found the best experts of the world to explain in perfect detail” why the loan “was impossible”, Macron said that the French government had “decided” otherwise. 41. Many people insist it should never have been moved. Arts journalist Didier Rykner started a petition against the loan that gained more than 70,000 signatures. 42. The late David Hockney agreed, described the loan as “madness,” and said “some things are too precious to take a risk with.” 43. And two expert reports in 2021 and 2022 advised Macron against the transportation of the tapestry. 44. The loan specified the tapestry had to be stored lying flat, and couldn’t be subject to tremors any greater than two millimetres per second during its transportation. 45. A team of conservators and experts, including a German vibration technology scientist, were involved with its relocation. They designed a meticulous solution for transporting the tapestry involving a “paravent”, a hinged folding screen on wheels. 46. The paravent was designed so it could be closed into a rectangular block with the tapestry inside, effectively folded 28 times. 47. It took ninety people in blue latex gloves seven hours working to extract the tapestry from its case and transfer it to the paravent. 48. It then had to be stored in a specially manufactured crate for shipping. The art logistics firm Hizikia built two nesting crates, with an outer aluminium crate designed to reduce the impact of movement. 49. The firm also provided a customised reinforced truck to dampen vibrations. 50. Experts carried out two dry runs, one with a replica tapestry transported across the channel that made its way to an art warehouse in south London. 51. Data from these dry-runs showed that French roads are smoother than British roads. 52. The tapestry has been insured by the Treasury’s indemnity scheme for £800m, which is more than twice the value of the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction (Salvator Mundi, a painting of Jesus attributed to Leonardo da Vinci). 53. Two threads were reportedly broken when the tapestry arrived in London. 54. At the British Museum, it will be housed in a custom-made case, believed to be the longest ever constructed, and will be exposed to a limited number of light hours per day. 55. When the lights are switched on, they’ll be dimmed to 50 lux, the international museum standard for sensitive materials. 56. Andy Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and King Charles viewed the tapestry last Wednesday. 57. It will be displayed at the British Museum until July 2027, before it returns to a newly built museum in Normandy that will open later next year. 58. Nicholas Cullinan, director of the British Museum, has said he hopes the Bayeux loan could revive the prospect for a loan of the Parthenon marbles. 59. The tapestry has inspired numerous copycats, including the Bloody Sunday Tapestry created by the artist Darren Cullen in 2013. 60. There’s also a Game of Thrones Tapestry at the Ulster Museum in Belfast. 61. The Sun newspaper commissioned a “Bye-EU” tapestry in 2018 to commemorate the Brexit vote, which depicted Boris Johnson in chain mail and Theresa May surrounded by the decapitated corpses of Brussels bureaucrats. 62. A helmet from Sutton Hoo, and the Lewis chess pieces, were both loaned to Normandy museums as part of the Bayeux loan. 63. My favourite bit of any trip to the British Museum is the gift shop (eds: does this count as a fact?), where you can now buy a replica Norman helmet and bottle of Bayeux mead with your Tutankhamun pencil tin. 64. Speaking of Bayeux tat, Nigel Farage sported a Bayeux-themed tie during the 2014 Rochester byelection, a reminder of “the last time we were invaded and taken over”. 65. Radio 4 has devoted a special day of broadcasts to mark the arrival of the tapestry. 66. And the museum’s videos about the tapestry’s arrival are narrated by the Traitors presenter Claudia Winkleman. 67. Philippe Bélavel, Macron’s former culture adviser, has said “such a loan will only happen once and never again.” 68. The next wave of public tickets for the tapestry, which cost £33, will go on sale on 21 October at 10am. Best of luck getting yours. What else we’ve been enjoying I loved Micha Frazer-Carroll’s brilliant newsletter exploring how and why generations of Black athletes have become style icons. Sign up to receive the Long Wave in your inbox here. Michael Segalov, newsletters team J Oliver Conroy’s long piece on what happened to Turning Point USA in the year after the killing of Charlie Kirk is a compelling, frightening read on the future of the American right. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team Among all the tributes, I found these reflections on Gloria Steinem’s legacy from a host of contemporary feminist writers to be a particularly powerful homage. Michael Resident sex expert Alix Fox hosted this riveting reader Q&A yesterday, fielding your queries on making time for intimacy in parenthood, the rise of audio erotica, and why trendy sex toys are apparently shaped like fruit now. Charlie I watched the trailer for Andrew Garfield’s new film The Uprising while at the cinema last weekend (the Odyssey; quite long?), and Peter Bradhsaw’s cutting review confirmed my initial instinct to steer well clear. Michael Sport Cricket | England lead Pakistan by 23 runs at Edgbaston, after 14 wickets tumbled on the opening day of the third Test. Tennis | Elena Rybakina will become the No 1 woman in the world for the first time after orchestrating a supreme recovery to reach the semi-finals of the US Open with a 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 win over the Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen. Cycling | Matthew Brennan claimed a fifth stage victory on Wednesday as the young British rider edged a bunch sprint in Seville to win the 17th stage. The front pages “Police launch inquiry into alleged overseas donations to Reform UK”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Times says “Farage faces Met inquiry over Reform donations”, the i Paper also has “Police set to interview Farage over Reform UK donations”, and the Mirror writes “Farage faces cop quiz on donors”. The FT has “US spy chief to take stronger role in stalled Ukraine talks”, the Mail writes “Burnham: National security can’t come at the expense of social security”, and the Express leads with “The King has spoken with Harry since return”. The Telegraph splashes “Labour’s new tax assault on hospitality”, and on air traffic chaos, Metro has “Ready for departure?” Today in Focus: The Latest Why is Trump silent on UK sanctions against Israeli West Bank settlements? The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is facing a backlash over the government’s sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank after the chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, said the safety of British Jews could be at risk. Miliband has rejected the warnings, emphasising that ministers can confront the actions of Benjamin Netanyahu’s government while also fighting antisemitism. US president Donald Trump, however, has failed to comment on the UK government’s action. Lucy Hough speaks to diplomatic editor Patrick Wintour. title: As the midterms loom, Trump returns to his happy place: on stage in the theatre of the absurd
author: David Smith in Dallas
summary: President’s quest in self-mythology stops off in Dallas for a Republican convention where fans indulged his lies and revelled in his jokes
body_text: Kim Il-sung of North Korea reportedly sought transfusions of blood from young men; Mao Zedong of China believed sex with young women could prolong his life; Muammar Gaddafi underwent fat injections and hair transplantation to make himself look younger. But for Donald Trump, the secret of eternal youth lies in nights like this. The occasion of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas was enough to get the 80-year-old US president’s juices flowing. An arena with thousands of fanatical supporters indulging his lies, laughing at his jokes and burnishing his fantasies of greatness is Trump’s happy place. It certainly beats stuffy Washington. “State of the Union, you have to be very staid,” he said, feigning stiffness and a dreary voice: “Ladies and gentlemen, it’s an honour to be your president.” The crowd laughed. Trump continued: “You do that for about an hour and then everybody’s falling asleep. This is a much harder routine, let me tell you. We’re also out here to have a little bit of fun.” The crowd roared. Trump’s second term has been a quest in self-mythology. It is there in the dramatic foreign policy aimed at reshaping the world. It is there in the monuments and renovations in the capital, Washington DC. It is there in the barrage of social media posts and AI slop in which Trump appears as a young and virile all-conquering hero. It was also there on Wednesday night as Trump milked the adulation of his fanbase, the Make America Great Again diehards who, in some cases, have followed him for more than a decade. He was visibly gratified to see the “front row Joes” from his rallies, including Blake Marnell, who wears a brick-patterned suit resembling his brick wall. The president spoke for an hour and 44 minutes, surpassing his own record length convention speech set in Milwaukee two years ago. He never stopped to sip water, though the adrenaline shot of this crowd, as devoted as his aide Natalie Harp, likely could have kept him going much longer. Anyone who suspected that this unconventional convention would be a “Trump-a-palooza” had the view reinforced when Lee Greenwood sang (somewhat shakily) “God Bless the USA”, the familiar intro to Trump campaign rallies. A giant video screen with the US flag slowly rose to reveal dozens of mainly female Trump fans, waving little flags and smiling exuberantly. Trump, wearing a navy blue suit, white shirt and blue tie, walked slowly across the shiny black stage, trimmed with gold. Chants of “USA! USA!” erupted as the song finished. “Welcome to the first ever midterm convention of any party,” Trump said, conveniently ignoring three that the Democrats held in the 1970s and 1980s. He soon told another lie. “Not only is this packed, but you have an equal number of people standing outside. If anybody would like to give up their seat!” In fact there were dozens of empty seats in the stadium, with the “nosebleeds” in the upper tier mostly unfilled. Making the dubious boast that no one had left the arena after 80 minutes, the president said: “It’s a great tribute to Trump … Everybody loves me and I love everybody!” But the most grievous lie came when he falsely claimed to have won three presidential elections, and declared, also falsely, that “people on the other side are actually admitting it”. The crowd cheered and shouted: “Four more years!” This was political theatre of the absurd with many bizarre Trumpian riffs, ranging from bad sporting trades involving the Dallas Mavericks and Babe Ruth to how Trump had to sacrifice hygiene for his political career so he could shake hands (“I’m a very clean person”). In trying to champion Texas attorney general Ken Paxton for the US Senate, he said: “He may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly and he may not be the best looking guy I’ve ever seen but you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America and he deserves to be your next senator. I’m sorry, Ken. Where the hell is he? He’ll never speak to me again but that’s OK.” There were language games. He spoke as if his big idea of changing “Democrats” to “Dumocrats” was a piece of marketing genius or political artistry worthy of Lee Atwater. (“Nobody knows that dumb has a B at the end of it – most people think it’s ‘D-U-M’”.) Most reasonable people would look at him and think this poor elderly person is in need of an intervention. But this audience, of course, lapped it up and encouraged him. So he revelled in his name changes. He mentioned the “Gulf of America” and earned cheers and chants of “USA! USA!” He said, “Lake Ontario, you know we’re going to call that Lake America” – more cheers. “We did come up with one the other day which we think is appropriate. You have a neighbouring state, New Mexico. We think it should be called ‘New America.’” Turning to the Iran war and strait of Hormuz, he said: “Ladies and gentlemen, I’ll have an announcement, we’ll call it the ‘Trump Strait’ and I’m sure the Iranian leadership will be thrilled with that.” Speaking of Iran, the war would be seen as a liability by any normal president in an election year and it is a subject many Republicans would rather avoid. But Trump, true to form, bulldozed straight ahead. He also advised Iran “not to get cute” and asked the crowd: “Does anybody here think that Iran should have a nuclear weapon?” There was a huge shout of, “No!” Trump even speculated what would have happened if Iran obtained a nuclear weapon and subjugated the US. “If they had a nuclear weapon, I’d be calling the Supreme Leader and I’d be saying, ‘Mr Supreme Leader, how are you, sir? Is there anything we can do for you?’ – as opposed to bombing the crap out of him.” Somewhere in all this mess, Trump talked about the midterms. He asked voters to “pretend” that he is on the ballot and promised $5,000 to every adult US citizen if Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate. It was the old Trumpian trick: flaunt your bribery in public so blatantly that enough people assume it can’t be corrupt. He railed against Democratic “communists” and declared: “They have more bullshit than any human beings on the planet.” His supporters went wild. Such a witty putdown, sir! Trump castigated James Talarico, the Democrats’ candidate for the Senate in Texas, as “Talafreako” and claimed: “He ran a campaign to ‘beat meat.’ He called it ‘beat meat.’ I don’t know what the hell he meant by that … he wants to ‘beat meat?” … I’m getting myself in trouble. He was recently seen having a barbecue and eating a lot of meat.” All this and so much more. It went on and on, looping back on itself, zigzagging across the map, bamboozling any outside observer but somehow here, in the arena of Maga, making a warped kind of sense. “I love the weave,” Trump mused, gesticulating wildly. “You know what the weave is? You talk about something, then you bring in a ballroom, or you bring in an aeroplane, or you bring in Air Force One – but you notice I always get right back to the same topic. Some day there’ll be a time when I do the weave, weave, weave; some day there’ll be a time when I don’t get back to the original subject.” Pointing his finger in the air, Trump said: “And then you can say: he’s had it.”

title: Trump’s comments on the Falkland Islands reflect a fractured US-UK relationship
author: Ted Widmer
summary: President suggested US might not help UK if Argentina tried to seize Falklands – a new low for UK-US ‘special relationship’
body_text: Last week, Donald Trump suggested in an interview with the British TV channel GB News that he might not help the UK if Argentina tried again to seize the Falkland Islands. It was a new low for UK-US relations. The “special relationship” (Winston Churchill’s phrase) was never perfect, but the UK helped the US on countless occasions, from Korea to Iraq to Afghanistan. The US often stood by the UK as well – although not during the Suez Crisis of 1956, but Ronald Reagan’s government provided significant intelligence and logistics support to Britain during the dust-up over the Falklands in 1982. That relationship is fading fast. Trump characteristically turned the conversation toward a grievance, and his disappointment with the UK’s initial reluctance to provide support for the Iran war launched on 28 February by Israel and the United States. That reluctance was fairly easy to understand at the time, given that the White House refused to consult Nato allies as it planned its sneak attack, and the goals of the war were (and remain) imprecise and inconsistent. It should be added that Nato is a defensive alliance, designed to resist a Russian invasion from the east, not support a US invasion from the west, to seize Greenland from a Nato ally. Further, Nato has no business in the Middle East. The words “North Atlantic” inside “North Atlantic Treaty Organization” make it clear that Nato is all about Europe, bringing North American troops (including both Canadians and Americans) into an interlocking defense structure with European partners. That includes roughly 80,000 US troops stationed in Europe, a strategic fact of the highest order, one that would suggest careful vetting of remarks about a Nato ally like the United Kingdom. Roughly 10,000 of those troops are based in the UK, in fact. Emboldened by Trump’s careless remarks, the president of Argentina, Javier Milei (a fan of Margaret Thatcher), delivered a windy speech about “the winds of change”, designed to shore up his sinking popularity, approximately 37% in July. He hinted that the US would back Argentina if it were to renew its territorial ambitions, and called the UK a nation “in decline”. Those tremors deepened early this week, as the UK’s announcement of sanctions on Israeli settlers released a predictable explosion from the Trump administration, and Israeli threats to recognize Argentinean sovereignty in the Falklands. The UK will survive Milei’s speech, which stemmed from Trump’s unfocused complaints, and the surreal fabrications that get so much attention yet contribute so little knowledge. The diplomatic flare-up will fade, but memories will linger of Trump’s poorly chosen words, and the ease with which he chose to abandon Britain – on British television, no less. It’s also another stark reminder of how foreign the themes of democratic aspiration are to the 47th president. Were Argentina to seize the Falklands, it would overturn the result of a very democratic election, the 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islanders chose to remain connected to the UK. More than 90% voted; of 1,517 votes cast, a whopping 1,513 were for remain. That’s the voice of the people speaking. Democratic presidents have never had a problem talking about democracy. Similarly, most Republican presidents have understood this language. Nixon was not gifted in this way, and George W Bush got many things wrong – Iraq above all – but he seemed to mean it when he spoke of the yearnings of peoples to be free. Ronald Reagan could achieve poetry at times, as he spoke of those suffering behind the Iron Curtain, and in other autocracies, and meditated on how the US had historically given hope to the world’s disenfranchised. In his 1989 farewell address, he argued: “She’s still a beacon, still a magnet for all who must have freedom, for all the pilgrims from all the lost places who are hurtling through the darkness, toward home.” It’s impossible to imagine these words being spoken from today’s Oval Office, just as it would be difficult to find a president more alienated from the goals of genuine self-determination. In 1941, Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt articulated the shared UK-US values in their famous Atlantic charter – a statement about their commitment to democracy, free trade and peace. A year later, they issued an anniversary statement about their shared goals and values. It offers wistful reading at a time when the language of great ideals appears to be woefully dated: “When victory comes, we shall stand shoulder-to-shoulder in seeking to nourish the great ideals for which we fight. It is a worthwhile battle. It will be so recognised through all the ages, even amid the unfortunate peoples who follow false gods today. We reaffirm our principles. They will bring us to a happier world.” Ted Widmer is a former White House speechwriter, and the author of an anthology, American Speeches. His most recent book is The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text (Library of America)

title: First Thing: Trump makes highly unusual promise of $5,000 for all if Republicans win midterms
author: Martin Belam
summary: Speaking in Dallas, the president raised ethical concerns with an apparent $1tn offer to the electorate
body_text: Good morning. Donald Trump has pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections. The outlandish proposal, which would cost over $1tn, immediately raised ethical concerns. Trump made the promise during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which he assailed Democrats as “radical”, defended his unpopular war in Iran, and urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot”. Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”. In a statement, Ken Martin, the chair of the Democratic National Committee, accused Republicans of holding a “bizarre dog-and-pony show” to placate the president’s “fragile ego”. “Tonight only confirmed that the president is a lame duck failure who is dragging his party toward defeat,” Martin said. Why did the Republicans hold a midterm convention? Republicans are gambling that the GOP’s first midterm convention can salvage their threatened House majority. However, Trump’s dismal approval rating drove many competitive candidates to skip the two-day event entirely. What has Trump said about the former attorney Michael Cohen? The US president has said he would consider pardoning Michael Cohen, the former fixer whom he once branded a “rat” for testifying against him. Cohen was Trump’s personal lawyer, but flipped in 2018, and pleaded guilty to federal crimes including facilitating a hush payment to the pornography star Stormy Daniels and lying under oath to Congress. Rubio says US will work with allies to stop drug-trafficking as three killed in latest boat strike The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the Trump administration was focused on working with allied countries and aligning with their laws but insisted the military would “still blow up ships if need be”. The statement comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters. “I think it’s an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito. “The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended”. How many people has the US killed in its campaign? Late Wednesday, US Southern Command announced the latest strike in the Caribbean Sea, saying it killed three people. That brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the US military to at least 230 in 69 strikes. What has the US announced about Ecuador’s gangs? The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang as a terrorist organisation. Rubio said the gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists. “We are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said. Apple unveils folding iPhone Duo … and its new CEO Apple has unveiled the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable phone and the most significant change to the iPhone since its 2007 introduction. title: Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast
author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
summary: Iran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widens
body_text: Houthi forces in Yemen are making a concerted drive to take over the country’s Red Sea coast fully, claiming control of the key port of Mocha in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years, bringing the Iran-aligned group closer to full control of a key shipping route. Seizure of the coast and some of the islands in the sea would be a strategic disaster for Saudi Arabia and the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two choke points for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandab at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by the Houthis to open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz. Baraa Shiban, the Royal United Services Institute’s (Rusi) Yemen specialist, a London-based security thinktank, said the situation in the country was spiralling out of control, adding that the UN-recognised Yemeni government was opening new fronts against the Houthis in the hope of putting more pressure on their forces than they could withstand. But in the past 48 hours the Houthis had major advances south, down Yemen’s west coast, taking them closer to the high ground overlooking the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait. The fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. The pact is designed to be defensive in nature and believed unlikely to apply to Saudi military activities in Yemen. By taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to use a new lever to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf. Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged he did not expect the war with Iran to end before the US midterm elections at the start of November. The latest phase in the escalation began when Houthis attacked energy installations and southern cities in Saudi Arabia using drones and ballistic missiles. In response, the kingdom’s military forces launched at least 15 strikes between 3 and 7 September. The conflict data monitor Acled estimated there were 276 fatalities over the five-day period alone. The fighting has continued, with the Houthis claiming control of Mocha in Taiz province, as well as the inland city of Hays and the Khalid ibn al-Walid camp, the largest military base in the region. One Houthi-linked estimate suggested its forces had gained control of more than 2,320 sq miles (6,000 sq km) of land. The commander of the Yemeni government forces, Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, admitted he had organised a strategic retreat south of Mocha in order to regroup in a secure location. “The armed forces in the western coast paid a heavy price – martyrs and wounded – over the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack planned by Iran, and supported by it,” he said. Analysts claimed that the effectiveness of Yemen’s government forces was weakened by internal divisions, as well as external pressure from Saudi Arabia. The latter, meanwhile, continues to take advantage of its air superiority to attack Houthi positions, though government sources acknowledged Houthi ground advances along the coast and their missile strikes on the strategic Red Sea islands of Zuqar and Hanish. The clashes have raged across Yemen, including Ad Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwah, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, and Taiz. In the initial days of the renewed conflict the Houthis were forced back in some areas as battles on multiple fronts overstretched their resources and fighter numbers. The Houthis will be hoping political divisions inside the Yemeni government, reflected in a lack of an integrated military, will slowly give them the upper hand. The United Arab Emirates, previously a powerful player in southern Yemen where it backed the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council, withdrew its financial and military support at the turn of the year. The southern forces have refused to fight outside their own region. “A reduction in hostilities anytime soon seems unlikely, as both sides continue to escalate with the goal of inflicting enough damage to the other side to force a compromise,” said Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst for Acled. “In terms of military capability, both sides are more equal compared to the immediate period prior to the 2022 ceasefire when the Houthis had the upper hand.” He added: “Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in Hodeidah and Taiz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-Yemen government have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab al-Mandab.” The head of the Houthis’ national delegating negotiating team, Muhammad Abdul Salam, insisted non-Saudi commercial shipping would not be attacked. The fighting has contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80. The escalation to this week’s all-out violence has been a slow process. It began after a senior delegation of the Houthi group, which has long been in a complex alliance with Iran, flew to Tehran for the funeral of the Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in July, returning in an Iranian plane that the Saudis refused to land in rebel-controlled Sana’a. The Saudis instead bombed the runway, leading the Houthis to announce a Red Sea naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in what the Yemeni group described as a blockade for a blockade. The 20 July announcement of the blockade was followed by a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on 25 July and on a tanker off Yanbu on 24 August. Saudi Arabia has become reliant on the Red Sea route for trade after Iran throttled shipping through the strait of Hormuz as a result of US-Israeli attacks.

title: American democracy depends on the census. Trump is undermining it
author: danah boyd
summary: The very mechanisms that allow the census bureau to resist partisan interference are coming undone. And Congress is silent
body_text: When the constitutional architects of the United States got together, they came up with a crazy plan: “What if we count everyone in the country and allocate political representation that way?” It was a radical act. Until then, censuses had been used by kings to levy taxes and conscript men into war. With the penning of article 1, section 2 of the US constitution, being counted ensured that states would get financial resources and political representatives. Congress was tasked with building the processes to anchor representation to the population. People wanted to be counted. And politicians wanted their people to be counted more. For more than a century, professionals at the US Census Bureau have built protocols and established norms to resist partisan interference. Scientists and other experts work together to make the best data possible so that democracy can function. But many of their systems are being upended and challenged by “Jenga politics”. In the game of Jenga, players take turns pulling out planks and adding more pressure to the top, hoping someone else will be blamed for making the tower collapse. This is what’s happening to our government. Few politicians publicly admit that they are trying to dismantle our administrative state – although some do – but it’s teetering on the brink. Meanwhile, oft-maligned civil servants are running around with duct tape trying to keep the whole tower from falling. The public pays little attention to the census. The census involves math. It is wonky. Eyes glaze over when government officials start talking about statistical methods and esoteric policies for governing data. It’s hard to convince most people – perhaps including you? – to care about the census. This has created a vulnerability that weakens the American republic. Politicians understand the power of the census. And since the beginning, they have schemed different ways to shape the data to their advantage. Congress has responded by building rules around both the construction of data and its use. Courts have reinforced these rules by constructing guardrails to ensure that the public is counted and that Congress gets final say over how the data are made. In modern times, politicians have focused their energies on using census data to best one another in the political sport of redistricting. However irritating gerrymandering is, using rigorously produced data in political games is fundamentally different from directly manipulating the underlying infrastructure of data-making in the country. This summer, we’ve seen the latter. The very mechanisms that allow the Census Bureau to resist partisan interference are coming undone. And Congress is silent. After having forcibly retired thousands of dedicated civil servants who held a gobsmacking amount of institutional knowledge, the Trump administration has increasingly made impossible demands of those who remain. In June, they ordered the Census Bureau to stop using the most sophisticated techniques available to protect the confidentiality of the public’s responses when publishing data. Government scientists were told that they must return to the statistical dark ages and use methods that horrify their peers. By micromanaging the tools that experts can use, politicians are forcing civil servants to choose between publishing unusable data, risking the privacy of Americans’ data, or simply not publishing data. In August,another controversy roiled the Census Bureau. Partisan data geeks leveraged a program designed to help the government recruit talent. Once there, they obtained access to government data and leveraged the bureau’s brand to publish a report arguing that numerous non-citizens voted in the 2020 election, reinforcing Trump’s conspiracy theory that he did not lose the election fair and square. This report is anomalous in countless ways: it’s unsigned, lacking methodological detail, devoid of error metrics, and rushed through without oversight by the bureau’s experts. But it doesn’t matter how bad the report was (and it’s truly abysmally bad). The reputational damage was done. Economists and advocates from across the partisan spectrum were outraged at this blatant politicization of the Census Bureau. The Trump administration doubled down. Days later, the commerce department eliminated the language that prohibited political interference from the agency’s official scientific integrity policy. This week, the Trump administration released a new bombshell. In outlining how it will govern the 2030 decennial census, the Census Bureau has indicated that it plans to stop collecting data about race and only count a subset of the population, contrary to what the constitution requires. This is part of the “residence rules” that the Census Bureau produces in the middle of the decade to finalize its operational plan. While purportedly intended to make the census “colorblind” and to protect the privacy of respondents, these proposed changes to the residence rules will ensure that anti-discrimination laws – such as the Voting Rights Act – that are anchored to the census data can’t be enforced. These incidents collectively reveal that well-honed norms and protocols that uphold the Census Bureau are being battered, even as the Trump administration chooses to use other standard procedures. Taken together, these upheavals undermine the legitimacy of our institutions and directly harm the data. If we don’t trust democracy’s data, we can’t have a functioning democracy. Civil servants will do their best to do “the impossible”, as they put it, but they can only do so much without the support of Congress and the public. If neither understand nor appreciate what our civil servants do, we cannot prevent the Jenga tower from falling. Congress is constitutionally responsible for the census. They have final say over what questions are asked, who is to be counted, and what methods are acceptable. Whether they know it or not, the Congress that is elected this November will make critical decisions that will irrevocably determine how the next census unfolds. They could take an active role in governing the census, as the constitution asks of them, or they could allow the Trump administration to weaponize the process. While most members of the public won’t pay much attention to the census until 2030, all the key systems will be locked and loaded by 2028. The operational plan will be finalized, the questions will be decided, and the staffing capacity will be locked in. Congress has the power and responsibility to ensure that the census is both functional and legitimate. By not taking this responsibility seriously and allowing the census to be politicized by the executive branch, both parties are driving a stake through the heart of the American project. danah boyd is the Geri Gay professor of communication at Cornell University and the author of Data Are Made, Not Found: A Story of Politics, Power, and the Civil Servants Who Saved the US Census

title: Kimmel says interview with Talarico won’t air on TV after threats from Trump’s FCC
author: Anna Betts
summary: Host says he’s interviewing Senate candidate ‘under unusual circumstances’ and it will be posted on YouTube
body_text: Late-night TV host Jimmy Kimmel has said an upcoming interview with the Democratic Senate candidate from Texas James Talarico will not air on ABC, the US network that broadcasts his show, after the federal media regulator “threatened” his show, ABC and its local affiliates. “Tomorrow night I’ll be interviewing James Talarico under unusual circumstances,” Kimmel said during his opening monologue on Jimmy Kimmel Live! on Wednesday. Kimmel said that since the show began over 20 years ago, he has interviewed “Americans who are running for office with no problem at all”, noting that this ranged “from Hillary Clinton to Ted Cruz to Donald Trump himself”. “I interviewed Donald Trump when he was running for president in 2015,” Kimmel said. Trump came back for another interview, just before he became the Republican nominee in 2016. “But for some reason, and I can’t seem to figure out what that reason is, something has changed,” Kimmel continued. “Now that he is president, his FCC [Federal Communications Commission] has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations based on simple traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don’t like. “And so out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas, who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television,” he said. “It will be posted on YouTube instead.” The FCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Kimmel’s remarks. Talarico is running for US Senate in Texas against Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate and state attorney general. Kimmel’s announcement on Wednesday came amid increased scrutiny of broadcast television by the FCC under the Trump administration. In January, the agency issued guidance warning that daytime and late-night talkshows would be expected to comply with rules requiring broadcasters to give equal airtime to candidates running for the same office. According to the Hollywood Reporter, in general, talkshows have qualified for exemptions from those rules, ever since the FCC granted such an exemption to Jay Leno’s Tonight Show in 1996. Earlier this year, in February, Stephen Colbert, said Talarico was set to appear on an episode of The Late Show, which ran on CBS, until the network controversially canceled the series. But, Colbert said: “We were told in no uncertain terms by our network’s lawyers, who called us directly, that we could not have him on the broadcast.” That interview also ran on YouTube. Last year, following unusual pressure from the FCC, ABC temporarily suspended Kimmel’s late-night show for nearly a week over a monologue he delivered about the fatal shooting of the conservative activist Charlie Kirk. Last month, ABC and its parent company, Disney, sued the FCC, accusing the agency of violating the first amendment in ordering an unusual early review of the network’s local station broadcast licenses. “Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts,” the complaint alleges. In an interview with the New York Times in August, the FCC chairman, Brendan Carr, called the lawsuit “meritless” and denied that the agency was violating free speech rights. “Holding a broadcaster accountable to their public interest obligations and statutory obligations is not a violation of their first amendment rights,” he said, “and that is what the FCC is doing.” Last week, the FCC asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit.

title: Jimmy Kimmel on RNC convention: ‘They’re very nervous about the midterms, and rightly so’
author: Guardian staff
summary: Late-night hosts recapped the Republican event in Dallas and calls to ban Zohran Mamdani from 9/11 ceremonies
body_text: Late-night hosts roasted the Republican National Committee’s underattended “midterm convention” and attempts to ban the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, from 9/11 remembrances. Jimmy Kimmel On Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host opened with the news that financial disclosures revealed how Donald Trump gave his aide and “least secret admirer” Natalie Harp a $45,000 cash gift for the holidays last December. Harp “is the woman who praises him, shows him his iPad, keeps him distracted, and in return he gave her a wad of cash – like you do a babysitter, like you do when a neighbor girl comes over and does a diaper change,” Kimmel quipped. Trump also gave similarly sized cash gifts to two other young female staffers. “But I just want to say, before you rush to any judgment, there’s absolutely nothing unusual about an 80-year-old billionaire president giving the three young attractive women in his office 45,000 bucks each,” said Kimmel. “You’re the weird one for even thinking that, and shame on you.” Kimmel then turned to the Republican National Committee’s unusual “midterm convention”, a two-day affair in Dallas aimed at convincing Americans to vote for a party led by a deeply unpopular president who has led the US into an increasingly unpopular war. “They never had a midterm convention before, but Trump wanted one and so they’re having it,” Kimmel said. “The president, he’s hyping this. He’s saying it’s ‘the greatest rally of them all’. He said it’s ‘really hot’, it’s ‘totally sold out’, which is funny because the RNC had to hand out a bunch of free tickets to this sold-out event.” A large number of Republican lawmakers have also opted out of the convention due to “scheduling conflicts” and “not wanting to be anywhere near him right now”, Kimmel noted. “They’re very nervous about the midterms and rightly so. They are in serious danger of losing bigly.” They’re in danger, in fact, of losing a Senate seat in Texas to the Democratic candidate James Talarico, whom Kimmel will interview on YouTube this week “under unusual circumstances” after a Trump-appointed federal regulator “threatened” his show. The Daily Show On the Daily Show, Michael Kosta also checked in on the RNC’s rare “midterm convention”. “Everyone is going to be there,” he said before several clips of Republican lawmakers claiming they would in fact not be in attendance, for excuses up to an including a Wednesday night high school football game, “stuff” that was already planned and a “can’t miss dove-hunting event”. “Yeah, you can’t miss dove hunting!” Kosta quipped. “Eat lead, symbol of peace!” In other tough news for Republicans, JD Vance told a crowd this week that the country was about to “celebrate” 25 years since the terrorist attacks on 9/11. “Well, we’re not going to celebrate it, JD,” said Kosta. “‘Happy 9/11, everyone! I brought Rice Krispy towers!’ “We’re not going to celebrate 9/11, but we are going to commemorate 9/11,” he continued, “and one thing I always think about is how in the days after the attacks, President Bush made a genuine effort to defend Islam.” Kosta played a clip from 2001 in which Bush reminded: “These acts of violence against innocents violate the fundamental tenets of the Islamic faith, and it’s important for my fellow Americans to understand that. Islam is peace.” “Boy, we really didn’t understand how good we had it, did we?” Kosta added. “I mean, I’m not saying this man was perfect, but that was a full, coherent, non-racist sentence. Hindsight, huh? “The point is, back in 2001, President Bush was imploring the country not to lump all Muslims in with the terrorists who committed 9/11. Now it’s 25 years later, so how’s that going?” Kosta then cut to a news clip about a petition to ban the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, a Muslim, from the city’s 9/11 ceremony, while Sean Hannity and Fox News’s Laura Ingraham criticized his signing of a proclamation declaring 11 September a city-wide day of remembrance. “Look, I know nothing I say is going to convince the Mamdani haters, but if you ask me, the idea that 9/11 is about Muslims v America isn’t just wrong, it’s accepting Osama bin Laden’s vision of the world,” Kosta concluded. “And the fact that 25 years after 9/11, we have a New York-grown, Muslim mayor leading our remembrance proves to the world that al-Qaida didn’t win. New York won. “So yes, everyone is welcome at the New York ceremony, and I would be there … but I’m going dove-hunting and it’s can’t-miss.”
