title: Trump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’
author: George Chidi
summary: Critics react to bid for Republican votes with incredulity and point to potential $1.2tn cost atop existing national debt
body_text: Donald Trump’s promise of a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery. “If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000,” Trump said during the unprecedented Republican midterm convention in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump dividend.” It comes amid extreme concern over the US national debt, which exceeded $40tn for the first time in August. Speaking to Politico, Chip Roy, the Republican US representative from Texas, sounded skeptical. “Well – I would like to know how they would plan to pay for … back of envelope … well over $1tn,” he said. In the moments after Trump made the announcement, Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget wrote on X that “this would cost about $1.2 TRILLION in just one year. That’s more than ALL THREE ROUNDS of COVID relief checks, despite no recessions. The result would be a huge spike in the deficit, and almost certainly in the inflation rate.” The US has roughly 240 million adult citizens, suggesting the cost of $1.2tn. The federal government spent about $7tn in fiscal year 2025, with about $2tn taken on as debt. “The 10-year [treasury bond is] approaching 5%,” Goldwein said on Thursday morning. “Inflation is not under control. We spend more on interest than we spend on defense or on Medicare at this point. Social security is six years from insolvency. Just about the last thing we need is to borrow another trillion dollars to send checks to everybody.” Spending like this risked an economic sugar high followed by a recessionary crash, he said. But Goldwein was most concerned about what might happen if Trump’s gambit is effective. “If this works, the lesson for every future politician is going to be: if you want to win an election, promise a trillion dollars. And multiply a trillion dollars times the number of elections we have coming up, that is a recipe for bankruptcy.” Democratic political leaders reacted with blunt condemnation. “After making you sicker and poorer with his war, Donald Trump now wants to buy your vote with $5,000 in taxpayer-funded blood money,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said. “The most corrupt man ever to occupy the Oval Office.” The Democratic National Committee (DNC) pointed to Trump’s record on similar pledges, from $5,000 stimulus checks as a result of the work of the so-called department of government efficiency (Doge) to $2,000 stimulus checks from revenue from tariffs. “Donald Trump and Republicans are once again offering empty promises to Americans,” said Kendall Witmer, the committee’s rapid response director. “The only people reaping the benefits of Trump’s economy are himself, his family, and his ultra-rich elite donors. Meanwhile, working families get nothing except sky-high receipts at the grocery store and the pump, unaffordable healthcare premiums, and wages that aren’t keeping up with inflation.” The Bipartisan Policy Center has been tracking tariff revenue since Trump began raising rates in 2025. As of 8 September, the US has collected about $210bn in tariff and excise tax revenue in 2026. At a rate of $21bn a month, the US federal government would have to collect tariffs for nearly five years to cover a $5,000 payment, assuming every dollar of tariff revenue went to the payment, and discounting tariff payments refunded to retailers in legal challenges. Peter Schiff, chief economist for Euro Pacific Asset Management, said that Trump’s pledge had already begun rippling through financial markets. “Even though bond investors know that, even in the unlikely event Republicans retain control of the House, Trump’s promise to borrow over $1 trillion more to buy votes won’t be kept,” Schiff wrote in a post on X. “The promise itself is so reckless that they’re dumping Treasuries, sending yields to new highs … “Making his promise even worse, Trump referred to his $5,000 bribes as ‘dividends’, as if his policies had been so successful that the US now has surpluses to share. Instead, his reckless policies have produced massive deficits. Trump needs to send Americans bills, not checks.” JD Vance appeared to walk back Trump’s pledge, suggesting that the benefit would be means-tested. But the US senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, promised support for Trump’s idea. “I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” Moreno wrote on X.

title: French FA accuses Infantino of ‘seriously damaging’ football as it withdraws support
author: Raphaël Jucobin in Paris
summary: The French Football Federation’s president, Philippe Diallo, has strongly criticised his Fifa counterpart, saying ‘trust has been broken’
body_text: The French Football Federation’s president, Philippe Diallo, said Gianni Infantino had “seriously damaged the image and the unity of football” as he announced the end of France’s support for the Fifa president’s re-election. The FFF’s executive committee unanimously voted on Thursday to withdraw its backing, which had been formalised at the end of June. Diallo referred to “events during the World Cup” which had “flagrantly gone against the way we believe our sport should be run” and to Infantino’s World Cup sell-off plan, which was revealed in July and scrapped after a widespread backlash. During the World Cup the suspension of the US forward Folarin Balogun was overturned by Fifa after lobbying from Donald Trump. The US president said he called Infantino to recommend that Balogun be allowed to play. Fifa has said the decision taken by its disciplinary committee was “a balanced measure” and “based on an explicit provision of the applicable regulations”. Diallo outlined the reasons for the loss in confidence: “From July onwards, the conditions which led to us to support his candidacy had been disrupted. Does the withdrawal of the [sell-off] project solve the issue? I don’t think so. His initiatives during and after the World Cup have seriously damaged the image and the unity of football. As a result, we believe that trust has been broken.” Diallo said of the initial decision to support Infantino: “It would be wrong to say that certain developments in football were not made under his mandate.” But he added: “When you are making changes to the game itself, in a unilateral and opaque fashion to sell our shared asset, that changes our appreciation. “France is one of the founding members of Fifa, and as such we have a historical legitimacy to intervene when we feel that Fifa and its president are deviating from our vision of how world football should be run. We also have sporting legitimacy, as one of the top three teams in the world rankings over the last 10 years. We wanted to make it clear that we refuse to go in a direction which does not correspond to the general interest of our sport.” When reports of the sell-off project came to light, the FFF expressed “doubts and deep concerns”. Uefa threatened a boycott of Fifa competitions and several European countries, including Wales and England, withdrew their support for Infantino but the FFF had not until Thursday publicly disavowed him. Diallo indicated France would play an active part in Uefa’s search for an alternative candidate for the Fifa presidency before the 18 November deadline. The election will take place in March during Fifa’s next congress. Before then, Diallo said, the FFF would reach out to figures it considers experts in “transparency and good governance” in football and beyond as part of France’s “contribution to the debate”, as it pushes for “far-reaching reform” of Fifa. He cited Kevin Lamour, the former Fifa chief operating officer who was dismissed after criticising the sell-off plan, as one of the people the FFF would look to consult. Fifa was approached for comment.

title: Democratic socialist clinches Rhode Island nomination amid party victories
author: Lucy Campbell
summary: David Morales wins Democratic primary for Providence mayor, unseating the incumbent mayor, Brett Smiley
body_text: In the latest in a string of victories by progressives across parts of the US, the democratic socialist David Morales won the Democratic primary for mayor in Providence, Rhode Island, on Wednesday night, unseating the incumbent mayor, Brett Smiley. The Rhode Island state representative, who was endorsed by the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders as well as the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), is now the favorite to secure the mayoralty in the deep blue city’s November general election against the Republican nominee, 77-year-old David Talan. If he wins, Morales, at 27, will be the youngest mayor Providence has ever had. “Few believed that a 27-year-old democratic socialist could ever, few believed that we could ever take on big money, corporate real estate interests and endless attack ads – and we took them on and we won,” Morales said in his victory speech, which he delivered partly in Spanish. “The same way that we campaigned, we are going to govern – in coalition, side by side with our neighbors,” he added. Morales ran on a progressive platform pledging sweeping changes including capping annual rent hikes, building more affordable housing and raising taxes on corporate polluters and landlords. Rent stabilization was a key factor in the race, with Smiley, now ousted after one term, having vetoed a rent-stabilization ordinance back in April that had been passed by the city council. “When working people are getting priced out of the city that they love, then we must cap rent increases at 4% every single year,” Morales said. “We put housing justice on the ballot.” Morales, the son of a Mexican immigrant single mother, also took a hardline stance on making Providence an official sanctuary city and standing up to Donald Trump’s aggressive anti-immigrant agenda. “The city of Providence must use every tool that we have at our disposal to defend our immigrant community and protect us from the fascist ICE agents,” he said in his primary victory speech. In his tenure as mayor, Smiley had also faced scrutiny for implementing the city’s largest property tax increase in a decade, and for his continued support for Israel. Morales, by contrast, has accused the Israeli government of committing genocide in Gaza, and is a fierce proponent of Palestinian freedom. Born in Soledad, California, Morales became the youngest graduate in the history of the Brown University public administration master’s program. And when he was elected to the Rhode Island house of representatives at age 22, he became the youngest Latino ever elected to a US state legislature. He is also a part-time professional wrestler. A victory for Morales in November would follow a surge of democratic socialist victories in US cities this year, following the groundbreaking election of Zohran Mamdani as mayor of New York City last November. Since then, the Seattle mayor, Katie Wilson, has also taken office, with Janeese Lewis George set to follow in Washington DC, and the movement secured a string of summer wins in Democratic primaries in places including Michigan, Florida, Colorado, New York and Pennsylvania. As momentum around leftwing challengers to more established incumbents continues to grow, focus will turn to Los Angeles over the coming months, where another member of the DSA, Nithya Raman, will attempt to continue this winning streak against the current mayor, Karen Bass.

title: Steve Hilton vows to abolish California DMV if elected governor
author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
summary: Republican calls department of motor vehicles a ‘bloated bureaucracy’ as he seeks to boost his longshot campaign
body_text: The longshot California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton pledged this week to abolish the state’s department of motor vehicles if he is elected, promising to shutter the oft-criticized department for good and set a flat $73 annual registration fee per car. Hilton, a Trump-backed former conservative pundit running in reliably blue California, called the state’s DMV a “bloated bureaucracy”, during a Tuesday campaign event, echoing the Trump administration’s efforts to slash the federal workforce. “The plan for buildings like this is to turn them into something that’s actually useful for California,” he said, standing in front of the DMV in West Hollywood. “We’re going to turn DMV offices into after-school clubs.” A California DMV spokesperson declined to comment on Hilton’s remarks. For many US motorists, updating their license at the DMV can be a herculean feat with lengthy wait times. And vehicle registration fees, which California motorists must pay annually, are steep: typically several hundred dollars a year. However, it is unlikely the state’s DMV could be abolished. The California legislature, in which Democrats hold a supermajority in both the state assembly and senate, would need to pass Hilton’s proposed legislation. Hilton also faces an uphill battle in the gubernatorial race. A Republican has not been elected to a statewide position in 20 years, and Hilton is trailing well behind his Democratic rival, Xavier Becerra, in recent polls. In a news release expanding on the idea, Hilton took aim at the cost of running the state’s offices – the legislature allocated $1.46bn to the DMV for the 2025-26 fiscal year – and the fees drivers pay for services at the DMV. He proposed transferring some functions of the DMV online and punting routine car title and plate transactions to local county offices. Becerra’s campaign, meanwhile, suggested his proposal would risk driver safety. “Nothing says ‘safer roads’ like outsourcing driver safety checks to the lowest bidder,” spokesperson Jonathan Underland said in a statement.

title: Does Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ count as a bribe if we never get the money?
author: Adam Gabbatt
summary: Trump’s promise to pay $5,000 to every adult US citizen if the Republicans win in November was only one questionable moment in a nearly two-hour speech
body_text: Hello, from the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, where on Wednesday night Trump definitely, definitely, did not try to bribe the American public into voting for his party in November. Speaking for almost two hours at the American Airlines Center, Trump promised to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections. The speech felt very much like a desperate last pitch to voters: the electoral equivalent of a dumped boyfriend offering to take his estranged girlfriend on a mini-break to Venice. It’s very important that even if the $5,000 offer might sound like a bribe – “if you do this for me, I will give you this money” – it is not a bribe; instead serving as a “dividend”, paid because of what Trump says is his administration’s “tremendous economic success”. The $5,000 non-bribe – inducement, perhaps – was the headline of Trump’s speech, during which the president was the liveliest he’s appeared in months. There were no surreptitious naps here as Trump rattled through some of his greatest hits (Sleepy Joe, Barack Hussein, Crooked Hillary) to the delight, initially, of the crowd. I say “initially” because this was evidence that you can have too much of a good thing. Even your favorite entertainer can go on too long. That was the case here, as an arena that wasn’t even full to begin with began to quietly empty after an hour and a half as Trump, becoming visibly drained by this point, leaned on his lectern and called Democrats “communist” for the 11th time. Earlier there had been energy from the audience, with the Maga base cheering and laughing in the way a crowd might will on a comedian who is fondly regarded, but way past his prime. They went wild for Trump’s bizarre character assassination of Ken Paxton, his handpicked candidate for Senate, who was the butt of a joke. Trump has invested a lot of political capital in Paxton – a flawed candidate who is running neck-and-neck with the Democrat James Talarico – so you might have thought the president would spend his time here lavishing praise. But this is Trump, who a) is just odd, and b) can never resist an opportunity to put another person down. “He may not dress right. He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said of Paxton. He wasn’t wrong, but it’s not the kind of thing that will convince people to vote for the guy, although Trump rounded off the remarks with the claim that Paxton “is the greatest attorney general in America”. That statement is worth a fact check, and we should be skeptical, too, about whether Americans will ever get that $5,000. As the Bulwark’s Catherine Rampell pointed out, Trump has previously discussed paying Americans: a “Doge dividend”; $2,000 tariff dividends; and checks from Obamacare rebates. Those payments also were not bribes, but neither did they ever come to pass. title: Global bond sell-off resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflation
author: Heather Stewart and Phillip Inman
summary: Crude jumps above $107 a barrel amid concerns over Middle East conflict and out-of-control government borrowing
body_text: Nervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation. The cost of a barrel of oil jumped 6% to above $107 on Thursday amid concerns that advances by Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coast in Yemen could choke off Saudi crude exports. The global bond sell-off that has rocked markets in recent weeks resumed in response to the news from the Middle East – which came against a backdrop of escalating concern about out-of-control government borrowing. Higher oil prices, which had already climbed since hostilities resumed in the Iran war, are expected to drive up inflation, prompting central banks to raise interest rates and putting the brakes on economic growth. Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that the conflict with Iran could continue until “immediately after” November’s US midterm elections, at which point he claimed oil prices would be “tumbling downward”. The European Central Bank (ECB) raised its main interest rate to 2.5% on Thursday, with its president, Christine Lagarde, saying: “We believe inflation will be longer lasting than we had anticipated.” “The conflict in the Middle East continues to ⁠generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an ⁠extended period,” she added. As Thursday’s sell-off gathered pace in London, the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds surged above 5.37% – the highest cost of borrowing since 2007 – creating a fresh headache for the new chancellor, John Healey. With less than seven weeks to go until Healey’s first budget on 28 October, higher interest rates on the UK’s debt-pile will raise the cost of future investment projects and eat into the Treasury’s fiscal headroom. At the same time, the prospect of higher energy bills as oil and gas prices rise is likely to intensify pressure on the government to help consumers to weather the winter. Unleaded petrol prices have already risen by 6p a litre since the start of September, according to the motoring organisation the RAC, while the prospect of higher inflation has prompted some banks to raise their mortgage rates. Healey has promised to provide a “breathing space” for UK households while also addressing the cost of doing business. In a speech on Monday, however, he also sought to tame bond market fears by committing himself to “controlling borrowing to bear down on inflation, and reducing long-term pressures on our public finances”. In the US, where Trump has promised to write a $5,000 (£3,700) cheque for every adult citizen if the Republicans win the midterms, Thursday’s sell-off pushed up the yield on 10-year borrowing to 4.92% – the highest since 2023. The cost of longer-term borrowing also continued to surge, with 30-year yields hitting the highest level since 2007, despite the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, intervening directly in debt markets on Wednesday. Bessent hoped to bring down yields by buying back $6bn worth of government debt; but investors appeared to respond by deepening the sell-off. Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at the broker Capital.com, said: “Ultimately, a sustained drop in long-end yields can only be achieved by genuine shifts in macroeconomic policy: either the US government pulling back on spending or the Fed lifting rates.” Policymakers at the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, will meet under its new chair, Kevin Warsh, to set interest rates next week. Markets are expecting a rise – potentially enraging Trump, who has repeatedly demanded rate cuts. In a TruthSocial post last week, the president said: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.” A plethora of UK data to be published over the next week, including on inflation, jobs and growth, will give an updated snapshot of how resilient the British economy has been in the face of the Iran war. In the first six months of the year, UK growth was the strongest among the G7 economies. This was despite higher-than-expected oil prices and the absence of hoped-for rate cuts. Bank of England policymakers will also meet next week, but are expected to leave the UK’s key interest rate on hold at 3.75% for the time being as they continue to monitor the impact of higher oil prices.

title: ‘It was all hands on deck’: how the CIA responded to 9/11
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: Veterans recall chaos and confusion as the attacks unfolded – followed by a ‘war on terror’ that left agency with a tarnished reputation
body_text: A generation of spies had lost an enemy but not yet found a role. Then came 9/11. A decade after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, al-Qaida’s devastating attacks on New York and Washington on 11 September 2001 announced to the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) that the long era of battling communism, for which it had been founded, was officially at an end. It was to be replaced by a no-holds-barred “war on terror” that would leave the CIA with a soiled reputation over falsified intelligence that led to the invasion and occupation of Iraq, and an extraordinary rendition program in which suspects were subjected to “enhanced interrogations” at secret sites that official US inquiries subsequently defined as torture. The US intelligence community was dramatically transformed after two planes flew into the World Trade Center, a third smashed into the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed in the Pennsylvania countryside after passengers overcame the hijackers. Accounts of what unfolded inside the CIA’s headquarters in Langley, Virginia, suggests an organization unprepared for the drastically changed world the attacks ushered in, despite an awareness among some in the intelligence community that al-Qaida and its leader, Osama bin Laden, represented a clear and present danger. Margaret Henoch, then a counter-intelligence officer with little knowledge of terrorism, recalls confusion, chaos and an initial lack of direction from senior leadership as staff struggled to process what seemed like a bolt from a clear blue sky on that balmy late summer day. “One of my officers came in and said to me: ‘A plane just ran into the World Trade Center,’” she said. To this day, Henoch – who had previously been stationed in Vienna, where she focused on the International Atomic Energy Agency and nuclear threats – is haunted by the apparent vacuum that followed. About 40 minutes after the first attack, with no clear direction from the top of CIA, she decided to go up to the seventh floor, which accommodated the agency’s senior figures, including its then director, George Tenet. To her surprise, the area was deserted, apart from three assistants. “It was reasonable that they would have moved those guys someplace else,” said Henoch. “What was unreasonable, in my humble opinion, was that no one thought about all those people sitting in that building. Because if the Pentagon was hit, there was a chance that we, too, were a target – and it would be nice to believe that the people who left the building rapidly had a thought for all those who worked for them. “It was not clear that they did.” The Guardian contacted Tenet, now working in the private sector, for comment. In an emailed response, Bill Harlow, the CIA’s public affairs director at the time of the attacks, cited details in the 2007 memoir, At the Center of the Storm, which he co-wrote with Tenet, and said orders were issued for the majority of the staff to leave the building at “about 10am” – nearly an hour after the second plane struck at 9.03am. Harlow added: “We were aware at the time of intelligence gathered around 1995-96 of terrorist desires to attack CIA HQ with an airplane. “Director Tenet and the senior leadership moved to another building on the compound that presented a lower profile and would have a greater chance of survival if we were hit by a plane. “Notably, a decision was made that the personnel of the counter-terrorism center remained in the original headquarters building throughout that day … accepting the risk. The senior leadership team returned to the headquarters in the middle of the afternoon on 9/11.” ‘I had a briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was’ Some time afterwards, an order was given for the thousands of personnel in the building to evacuate. Some, including Henoch, were told to relocate to alternative sites to address the emergency. But by the time of that instruction, nearby roads were choked with traffic as commuters returned home from Washington DC after being released from work early. That prevented agency staff from departing, and triggered fears that they could be sitting ducks for the doomed fourth plane, which was already known to be in the air. “Large segments of the CIA operating staff were trapped,” Henoch said. “One guy, who was senior to me, was standing next to me in the car park and he said, ‘I have served in multiple war zones. I was a combat soldier in Vietnam and I’m going to die in the parking lot of the CIA.’” The dysfunctional scene was soon replaced by one of much greater conviction – leading to permanent changes in US intelligence. “I just remember loads of cable traffic coming in that said: it’s got to be al-Qaida,” said Henoch. “It wasn’t my world, so I had to have a quick briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was, because I just didn’t know anything about it. “The change was immediate. The next morning, everybody at the Central Intelligence Agency had to know who they were, and how it intersected with everything you were doing.” Steven Cash, a former CIA counter-terrorism officer who had left the agency to join the staff of the US Senate intelligence committee six months beforehand, faults the CIA’s pre-9/11 terrorism strategy as being too narrowly focused “looking to find bad guys” while neglecting the “political dimension”. “There was an emphasis on looking at terrorists as if they were a motorcycle gang,” said Cash, who had specialized on the Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah, a close ally of Iran. “A decision was made in the first [George HW] Bush administration to take terrorism away from the people who looked at geographic areas and separate it out. [It was] illustrative of a mistaken way of looking at the world, because terrorists don’t exist in a vacuum.” Cash moved on to focus on the Balkans before leaving the agency, but still harboured guilt after the attacks. “Was this our fault? Did we fail? That kind of guilt felt, at least for me, really personal.” Cash had been on Capitol Hill, attending a committee meeting, when news of the attacks filtered through. “Somebody said, put on the TV and we saw the second plane hit,” he said. “And then they started evacuating the building. “It was a mess. People were in the hall screaming, running around. The third plane had hit the Pentagon by that point, because we could see smoke across the National Mall.” The following day, Cash and his then boss, the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, visited CIA headquarters and found a mood of determined resolve. “It was all hands on deck. The people I knew were getting deployed very quickly to Afghanistan,” he recalled. “These people are pros. They didn’t care whether they were blamed or not. They wanted to do something. “I have a little bit of survivor guilt here. Maybe I should have been shipped out to Afghanistan.” Political pressure On their visit to CIA headquarters on 12 September, senators asked agency operatives what legislation and resources they would need to respond to the attacks of the previous day, according to Cash. Two early – and controversial – results were the USA Patriot Act of 2001, which expanded law enforcement and surveillance powers, and the Homeland Security Act of the following year, creating the US Department of Homeland Security, which houses agencies including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Later changes established the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, with the goal of coordinating 18 different intelligence bodies and eliminating the lack of coordination widely held to blame for warning signs of the 9/11 plot going unheeded. “DNI was formed to make sure that we actually share everything with everybody. We don’t just keep it inside CIA,” said Susan Miller, a retired CIA counter-intelligence officer. “What’s really cool is we’ve changed how we do things across the board, not just for terrorism. It’s really improved things. There was no coordination before.” Yet the reaction to the attacks changed intelligence in another way – by making it more susceptible to political pressure, as President George W Bush’s administration searched for information that could be used to justify an invasion of Iraq to topple Saddam Hussein. In September 2002, Henoch – who had previously studied Russian weapons capabilities working at the Stanford Research Institute – was asked to assess intelligence provided by an Iraqi defector codenamed Curveball, who had sought asylum in Germany, and provided its intelligence agency with what he said was proof of Saddam’s biological weapons program. She quickly concluded the claims were fabricated, and passed her conclusions up the chain of command. They were not well received. When Colin Powell, the then US secretary of state, visited the CIA months later to review the agency’s intelligence on Iraq, Henoch and her fellow doubters were not informed. Powell’s subsequent speech to the United Nations security council in February 2003, in which he made the case for war, relied heavily on Curveball’s testimony – despite Henoch’s insistence when the address was checked with her and other officers beforehand that his assertions were not credible. “We took a look at the Powell speech and I said: ‘You can’t use this. We think this is garbage,” she said. “I did write somewhere – I can’t remember on what page – ‘How can you send someone to die for something like this? No one ever answered that for me. “The next thing I heard was, ‘Well, when we get in there, we’ll find something.’” After the invasion, inspectors found no evidence of biological weapons. Curveball was later debunked as a fraud. Miller, too, encountered the administration’s zeal for intelligence that could justify invading Iraq when she was posted to Prague as CIA station chief in 2002. Czech intelligence had investigated – and, initially, tentatively confirmed – a claim that one of the 9/11 ringleaders, Mohammed Atta, had travelled to Prague the previous year and met an Iraqi embassy official, Ahmad Samir al-Ani, months before the attacks. The report was seized on by the hawkish US vice-president, Dick Cheney, as evidence of Saddam’s possible links to the attacks, thus providing another justification for war. But Czech intelligence officials retreated from their earlier stance, and the CIA concluded there was no evidence that the meeting happened. Nevertheless, Donald Rumsfeld, then the US defense secretary, brazenly tried to revive it when Miller briefed him – along with George W Bush and Condoleezza Rice, the national security adviser – when they visited the Czech capital for a Nato summit in 2002. “‘Young lady, you forgot about this other thing’,” Rumsfeld told Miller, she said. “I played dumb and said: ‘What other thing?’ He replied: ‘Mohammed Atta was here in Prague meeting the Iraqi consul.’ “Bush was looking really uncomfortable and Condi was looking straight ahead. I simply said, ‘Mr President, Madam Secretary, and Mr Rumsfeld, the CIA, the Czech service and I don’t make things up. We give you the facts, and the fact is that he was not here.’ “Bush and Rice nodded in acceptance and the ambassador supported me. But Rumsfeld threw his pen down in disgust.” The invasion the neocons craved Whether the supposed meeting happened or not, Rumsfeld and his neoconservative allies got the invasion they craved – leading to a protracted conflict that tarnished the CIA’s reputation and whose length, along with the coinciding US-led military campaign in Afghanistan, spurred popular opposition to “forever wars”. Despite the blow to the agency’s standing, Cash insisted that its intelligence-gathering and functioning radically improved, thanks to the changes instituted after the attacks. “We have improved our intelligence capabilities significantly from what they were before 9/11,” he said, citing the success in preventing repeat attacks on US soil. But with the Trump administration now engaged in a war with Iran, roiling the Middle East, such security could no longer be guaranteed, he believes. “I’m not saying it was a great time,” Cash said, of the CIA’s record in the months and years after September 2001. “But the sense of purpose of being at a place in history where we – as a group, as a society – can do something, was pretty intoxicating. “I was very proud to have been part of it. It sucked – but proud to have been part of it. And I think everything we’re seeing now is the antithesis of that.”

title: James Talarico accuses Ken Paxton of ‘ignoring’ Epstein survivors
author: Adam Gabbatt and David Smith in Dallas, Texas
summary: Democrats are targeting Trump’s relationship with Epstein as part of strategy ahead of midterm elections
body_text: James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Texas, accused his rival Ken Paxton of “ignoring” survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s sexual abuse, as Democrats seek to increase pressure on Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections. Speaking in Dallas, where Republicans are holding a midterm convention this week, Talarico appeared alongside one of Epstein’s victims at an exhibit that featured about 3.5m pages of Department of Justice’s files related to Epstein. “When did pedophilia become a partisan issue? When did holding sexual abusers accountable become controversial?” Talarico said. Talarico, who has emerged as one of the Democrats’ best hopes of winning one of the Republican Senate seats they need for a majority in the chamber, is among several members of his party appearing in Dallas this week, seeking to counter the Donald Trump-led convention. Democrats have made it clear in recent days that highlighting Trump’s longtime friendship with Epstein, a convicted sex offender, will be part of their strategy ahead of the midterms, and Talarico sought to loop Paxton into the attack. Talarico said survivors of Epstein’s abuse had requested to meet with Paxton, the Texas attorney general, but he had refused. “Our attorney general here in Texas has the power to get justice for these survivors, and he’s refusing to do so,” Talarico said. He added: “Ken Paxton has two choices: he can stand with these survivors and get justice, or he can continue to cover up Jeffrey Epstein’s abuse. The choice is entirely his.” The Epstein exhibit, which has previously been shown in New York, features row upon row of shelves holding all the files released so far related to Epstein. Critics say some of the documents released by the government revealed victim’s names, and that some material has been withheld. Speaking in Dallas, Sharlene Rochard, a survivor of Epstein’s abuse, said: “Questions remain about what hasn’t been released and why. Releasing only half of the documents is not transparency, and it cannot be where accountability ends. “I urge people to read the files, to follow the evidence, no matter where they lead. And when those leads reach someone wealthy, famous, politically connected, Republican or Democrat, keep following them, because justice that stops when it reaches power is not justice.” On Wednesday Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running against the Texas governor, Greg Abbott, visited the same exhibit, reinforcing that the focus on Trump’s relationship with Epstein will not go away. “It’s really incredible that we live in a country where the justice system is so broken at every level that there has not been accountability of what we know was extensive sexual abuse, exploitation that happened for decades,” Hinojosa said, according to Associated Press. “And that powerful people who run this country are still living their lives without having been held to account.” Elsewhere Democrats condemned Trump’s Wednesday night speech promising a $5,000 “dividend” to all US adults if Republicans win the House of Representatives and Senate in November. Beto O’Rourke, former US congressman and presidential candidate, told a roundtable hosted by Bloomberg News in Dallas: “I think people will take it for what it is – it’s a gimmick, it’s a bribe. It’s another promise that the president will be unable to fulfill … It adds to the stink of desperation that is emanating from that convention centre.” At a press conference in a hotel near the convention centre, Robert Garcia, a Democratic congressman from California, told reporters: “Donald Trump is a known liar. This is the biggest liar to ever serve in government, period. And look, the dividend is not happening. He promised a dividend on tariffs; that didn’t happen. He promised the dividend on Doge; that didn’t happen. He promised some strange dividend from Air Force One six months ago; that never happened. “There’s no one in the country that thinks somehow this new dividend is actually going to happen. What the American people want is the president to actually focus on lowering the costs of gas, groceries and expand healthcare. The president has done the opposite. He’s made everything more expensive, and so he needs to stop lying and actually get to work.” Madeleine Dean, a congresswoman from Pennsylvania, described Republicans’ first midterm convention as a failure. “I think you can take a look at the arena last night, you can see the empty seats,” she said. “He is weak. His approval rating has plummeted. His numbers on the economy: a disaster. His numbers on this war: a disaster. His numbers of the personal economy for everyday Americans: a disaster. This is a spectacle really laced with fear.” The Democrats also faced questions about their colleague Senator John Fetterman’s surprise appearance in a video at the Republican convention. Dean said she has known Fetterman and his family for years “but what we have seen in his service as a senator is something very different than what I got know around John. You can see in his work ethic that he’s just not present.” The congresswoman said she held a one-to-one meeting with Fetterman in his office a couple of months ago, but it was “a disappointing conversation” and “he was not listening to me”. She added: “I am gravely disappointed with John and that stunt … I will tell you from the ground from suburban Philadelphia, my constituents are livid. Those who went out and knocked doors for him are absolutely livid.”

title: US appeals court rejects Trump’s bid to restrict mail-in voting before midterms
author: Lucy Campbell
summary: Court declined to ⁠put on hold ⁠injunction preventing the USPS from tightening rules around postal voting
body_text: A US appeals court has rejected Donald Trump’s attempt to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in voting before November’s high-stakes midterm elections, dealing a fresh blow to the president’s attempted crackdown. The Boston-based first US circuit court of appeals declined on Thursday to ⁠put on hold an ⁠injunction issued by a lower court judge last week, preventing the US Postal Service (USPS) from tightening rules around postal voting. The panel of three judges, nominated by Joe Biden, agreed with the plaintiffs that the president does not have the power to regulate states’ election policy. “Appellants have not made a strong showing that the district court erred in determining that the Final Rule is likely unlawful,” they wrote, making reference to a rule published by the USPS to implement Trump’s order. It comes as the US supreme court also considers Trump’s efforts to introduce new requirements curtailing the practice, which the US president has frequently criticized despite doing it himself. Back in March, Trump signed an executive order seeking to prohibit the USPS from delivering ballots to any voters not on a nationwide list of eligible voters in each state created by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The result would mean a limited delivery of ballots to only the voters on those approved lists. Democratic states and voting rights groups swiftly filed several lawsuits, arguing that Trump’s ordered changes are unconstitutional. Meanwhile, state election officials who run the elections have said there is not enough time to overhaul their systems to meet the new federal directives. Indeed, with the midterms less than two months out, some states have already started sending out ballots. The Trump administration has called its plans to limit mail-in ballots “commonsense measures” aimed at protecting voting security. Trump has called the order blocking those plans “unreasoned and unlawful”. Trump has repeatedly sought to restrict voting by mail, despite doing it twice himself this year alone in his resident state of Florida. He has falsely blamed mail voting for his 2020 election loss to Biden, while promoting baseless claims of fraud. The president’s order allows states to voluntarily use the new system. But as yet, none have announced they will do so. The USPS, for its part, has said it stands ready to implement Trump’s new restrictions, which would require states to give the postal service the names and barcodes tied to mail-in ballots for federal elections, if the court injunctions are lifted. However, it has also said in recent court filings that the technology needed to administer the president’s order is not even available. And earlier this month, a USPS whistleblower warned of “potentially catastrophic problems” if the agency were to try to carry out the order.

title: US supreme court again rejects Missouri maps drawn to boost Republicans in midterms
author: George Chidi
summary: Latest decision appears to set the stage for the state to use its old electoral maps this year
body_text: The US supreme court again rejected a push backed by Donald Trump to overhaul Missouri’s congressional maps in an effort to hand Republicans an edge in November’s midterm elections. Its latest ruling, after days of confusion, comes less than two months before the pivotal midterm elections in which control of the narrowly divided US House of Representatives could be determined by a handful of seats. Following conflicting decisions that spanned four courts, Wednesday’s ruling appeared to set the stage for the state to use its old electoral maps this year. The end result does not completely end confusion for Missouri’s voters, who cast ballots in primary elections using the new map, butwill vote in November on the older map. “The state, the election apparatus, had no business going forward with the primaries under that bill, under that circumstance,” said David F Walbert, a storied voting rights attorney in Georgia, who has argued voting rights cases before the US supreme court. “The problem that we’re dealing with today is 100% the result of the state machinery that created this.” At the behest of the president, Missouri’s Republican-dominated legislature redrew district lines last year to net one additional seat for Republicans in the US House of Representatives. The new maps carve up a district representing Kansas City, long held by Emanuel Cleaver, a Democrat. After Missouri’s governor, Mike Kehoe, signed new congressional district boundaries into law in September 2025, the legislation faced immediate challenges, including a push by People Not Politicians, a campaign group, which gathered more than 300,000 signatures to force a statewide referendum on whether to keep or repeal the new map. But Missouri’s secretary of state, Denny Hoskins, a Republican, sought to use the new map anyway. The Missouri supreme court certified the referendum for the ballot on 3 September over Hoskins’s objections, ruling the new district lines would not take effect until 2027 – after the referendum vote – and that the 2025 redistricting did not comply with the law. The legal argument over redistricting pitted Missouri’s court, which is “not exactly full of foreigners that are some kind of wild liberals from California or New York”, Walbert said, against state leaders auditioning for the president’s attention. The court’s unanimous decision speaks to the clarity of state law on referendums. The law “suspends completely the effective date of the law that has been subjected to the referendum”, Walbert said. The state attorney general, Catherine Hanaway, also a Republican, immediately appealed this decision. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who oversees emergency hearings from the eighth circuit, refused to stay the Missouri supreme court ruling on Tuesday. But federal district judge Stephen Clark made a ruling only minutes later, in a separate federal case, requiring Hoskins to use the new Republican-friendly map – compounding confusion over November’s elections. Hoskins then said he would follow Clark’s order, and a federal appeals court panel declined to block that order. On Thursday morning, Kavanaugh again ordered the state to comply with the Missouri supreme court ruling, blocking the new maps. “Today’s decision ensures Missouri voters will not be forced to vote under a gerrymandered map pushed through by the state legislature last year and then cynically imposed on voters by the secretary of state, in violation of the state constitution,” said Mark Gaber, senior director of redistricting at Campaign Legal Center. “Voters deserve to have their voices heard and to have fair representation in Congress. The Missouri supreme court unanimously affirmed that principle, and now, so has the US supreme court.” The Missouri supreme court meanwhile ruled on Thursday afternoon that Hoskins, the secretary of state, had been in contempt of court after continuing to use new maps that the judges had ruled invalid. But chief justice W Brent Powell also noted that Hoskins had purged himself of the contempt after declaring that the order by Kavanaugh had ended the controversy over which map to use in November elections, and would direct local election officials to use the 2022 map.

title: Morning Mail: Woolworths increased prices during ‘freeze’; Abbott weighs in on Hastie cartoon; and turning the algorithm off
author: Guardian staff
summary: Cost of chicken fillets, potatoes and donuts rose during supermarket giant’s three-month promotion; former PM calls on One Nation to remove ‘offensive’ animated series; Caitlin Cassidy tries to travel back to 2012
body_text: Good morning. Woolworths raised prices for popular items – including a 33% mark-up on chicken fillets – within days of promising to freeze prices on 300 “family staples” for three months to help customers with the cost of living. Tony Abbott has joined in widespread condemnation of an “offensive” cartoon posted on social media by One Nation. And our reporter Caitlin Cassidy explores what it’s like to turn the algorithm off. Australia Brain freeze: The southern hemisphere’s only cryonics facility, Southern Cryonics, is selling people “a chance of life extension” for more than $200,000. Experts say there’s no way it will work. Woolies counter: Pricing data compiled by CW Scanner and provided to Guardian Australia shows the supermarket chain increasing the prices of at least four key products after starting its three-month “Price Freeze” promotion. Hastie takedown: The former prime minister Tony Abbott has called on One Nation to remove a cartoon labelling the Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie a “traitor” or accept that it’s playing a double standard. Granted: Anthony Albanese is under fire after an invite-only grant program allocated millions to marginal Labor seats and his old local golf club. What went wrong – and is this sports rorts all over again? World 9/11 remembered: CIA veterans recalled the chaos and confusion as the attacks unfolded – followed by a “war on terror” that left the agency with a tarnished reputation. Global bond sell-off: Nervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation. Trump bucks: Donald Trump’s promise of a US$5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery. Gaza documentary: Testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders on the secret systems used in the war on Gaza has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians. Full Story Alan Jones on Trial: Fierce loyalty, fiery texts and a parade of witnesses | Week 6 After a slow start to the week, the criminal trial of Alan Jones accelerated with a swift succession of witnesses taking the stand. Through a former politician, close friends and loyal associates, the court heard details of alleged indecent touching, scornful text messages and declarations of an “unbreakable bond” with Jones. Nour Haydar speaks to media correspondent Amanda Meade to unpack the cross-examinations, key testimonies and courtroom revelations. In-depth On the edge of the main highway winding from Hobart to Tasmania’s west coast, the concrete shell of the Royal Hotel stands like a spacecraft lingering on otherworldly terrain. One of the few official ruins in Tasmania, the old building is roofless, weathered by the elements – and has just sold for $300,000. Located in the ghost town of Linda, near Gormanston, the historic property was snapped up sight unseen by a Perth chef, Naiche, and his partner. Not the news Would Hollywood have brought Practical Magic back from the dead if the intervening 28 years looked more visible on Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman? An awkward question, as it risks subjecting their faces to the invasive scrutiny older female actors already endure. Their return as leads in their late 50s and early 60s should count as progress. Yet it reveals a condition of female stardom: age can increase a female actor’s nostalgic value, provided it does not show too clearly on her face. Sport AFL| Fremantle frenzy has turned to fear as the AFL finals straight-sets exit draws nearer. Cricket | England has batted Pakistan out of third Test with Ollie Robinson taking two wickets in the first over. Football | Benjamin Sesko has soared as Manchester United surged past Sabah Baku in a Champions League return. Media roundup The NSW premier, Chris Minns, is hoping to avoid a 2027 state election fought over law and order as frustration grows within Labor at escalating gangland violence in Sydney, the Sydney Morning Herald says. Labor’s flagship $75m anti-extremism program is failing to reform the vast majority of participants, The Australian says. A prominent disability advocate is furious with Qantas after a battle over compensation for a wheelchair that was broken on one of its flights, the ABC reports. What’s happening today NSW | The LA Rams will play the San Francisco 49ers at the MCG in Melbourne. title: JD Vance pitches himself as Trump’s political heir on day two of Republican midterm convention
author: Adam Gabbatt in Dallas
summary: Vice-president dog-whistled, exaggerated claims of success and echoed Trump talking points to excited audience
body_text: JD Vance made a clear pitch that he should be the heir to Donald Trump on Thursday night, closing out the Republicans’ midterm convention with a blistering speech that featured exaggerated claims of success, criticism of Democrats as “lunatics” and an aggressive dismissal of a protester waving a Mexican flag. Speaking in Dallas, the vice-president showed he could channel the basest instincts of his boss, filling his remarks with dog whistles and echoing Trump’s false claims that Democrats “cheered” the 7 October massacre of Israelis. Vance had been met with chants of “JD, JD,” as he walked on to the stage: the liveliest response anyone besides Trump received across the two-day convention, with some shouting that he should be the nominee in 2028. “We gotta take care of business this November, then we’ll worry about what comes next,” the vice-president responded with a smile. Vance began the speech by running through a list of Republican grievances, channeling Trump’s pugnacious attitude toward immigration as he told the crowd that two years ago “we were tired of being called racist for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer and less safe and less prosperous”. The Make America Great Again (Maga) crowd inside the arena liked that line, but the loudest cheer of the night came when Vance responded to a protester who briefly interrupted his speech. Vance claimed the protester was waving a Mexican flag, and adopted a fiery tone as he said: “Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there – I’ll buy you the plane ticket.” The applause was rapturous. The vice-president had to walk a tightrope coming into the speech, arguably the most important address of his short political career. He had to present his own case to the Republican base, without breaking too much from the notoriously sensitive Trump. Vance praised Trump as “the toughest SOB in American politics”, and paused repeatedly as the crowd lavished him with cheers and applause. He also invoked the recent birth of a fourth child, saying he had been looking at “the future of this country through the eyes of the future of my son” and “the birthright of this newest of Americans”. Addressing Democratic “radicals”, whom he accused of wanting to destroy the nuclear American family, he boomed: “Stay the hell away from our kids.” But it was also a speech aimed squarely at rallying the Maga faithful: attacking transgender rights, extolling the importance of American manufacturing and religious freedom, and accusing Democrats of “doubling down on the crazy”. Vance showed a penchant, too, for Trump’s baseless statements, claiming that some Democrats in New York “cheered on” the slaughter of Jewish people on 7 October, and suggesting that a “new generation” of Democrats seek to defund the police and “abolish the border”. “What is it that drives this new generation of radical Democrats? It’s not new policies. They’ll say the same stuff: defund the police, abolish the border, the green new scam. We’ve heard all this stuff before,” Vance said. He then tried out a new line: “I think that what’s new about them is what motivates them is a new type of hardcore hatred.” Vance won applause, too, for his praise of Charlie Kirk, the far-right activist who was assassinated in Utah exactly one year ago. Addressing Kirk’s children, who were not in the arena, Vance said: “History will record that your father was a great man. “Those of us who loved your dad, we know him as something even better than a great man – he was a good man,” he added of Kirk, a man who, among other things, endorsed Trump’s stolen-election lies and the racist great replacement theory. One problem Vance could face should he run in 2028 is his attachment to the deeply unpopular Iran war, and foreign policy was conspicuous by its absence in his speech. Last week he rejected the use of the word “war”, but said he wouldn’t set “artificial lines” regarding an end to the conflict. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Trump’s advisers have raised the prospect that the war could drag on through the rest of his term. Vance did not address the war directly. But in an oblique reference he invoked Kirk’s disdain for conflict. “Charlie hated war,” Vance said, before pleading with undecided voters to not abandon the party over policy differences. “What I’m asking you to do is do what Charlie did: do not throw the baby out with the bathwater,” he said. “Don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.” A poll found Vance was the favorite choice among likely Republican primary voters, with 43% saying they wanted him to be the nominee in 2028. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, got 21%; Donald Trump Jr was at 7%. Vance will hope those numbers stick, but he wasn’t the only one auditioning in Dallas. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the health secretary who switched parties to support Trump in 2024, praised the president and attacked the Democratic party during a well-received speech earlier on Thursday, while Ted Cruz, the Texas senator, received a rousing response in his home state. “They hate Christians, they hate Jews, they hate the ‌capitalism, they hate ⁠the constitution and they hate America,” Cruz said of Democrats, offering no evidence for his claims, but very much tapping into the theme of the two-day convention. Rubio did not speak at the convention, instead taking part in a tour of South America. Both he and Cruz ran against Trump in 2016. During that contest, Trump dubbed Rubio “Little Marco” and suggested Cruz’s father was involved in the assassination of John F Kennedy. Vance, by contrast, has never publicly attracted Trump’s ire, and he will want to keep it that way as he seeks to take on leadership of the party in two years’ time. That was probably the thinking as the vice-president ended his speech, shouting over jubilant applause that Trump was the “greatest president” before relinquishing the stage for his boss to bring the convention to a close.

title: ‘I’m on the ticket’: Trump implores Republicans to vote in November at unusual midterm convention
author: David Smith in Dallas, Texas
summary: The president demonised Democrats in an attempt to wangle votes in midterms despite backlash over Iran war
body_text: With his approval rating at a historic low, Donald Trump has brought down the curtain on the Republicans’ first ever midterm convention by pleading with supporters to do him “the biggest favour” and “pretend” they are voting for him in November’s US elections. The president is facing a growing backlash over rising prices and the war in Iran. Sweeping losses for the Republican party could effectively turn Trump into a lame duck for his final two years in the White House. Sensing political danger, Trump wrapped up the novel two-day event in Dallas, Texas, on Thursday with a pitch that critics are likely to say smacked of desperation: “You gotta do me the biggest favour you’ve ever done me. You’ve gotta do this for me. You’ve got to pretend I’m on the ticket. I’m on the ticket! I’m on the ticket! He’s on the ticket! Pretend I’m on the ticket because this is going to turn out to be one of the most important elections.” In an improvised pledge of allegiance to himself, Trump directed the crowd of about 20,000 to raise their right hands and repeat: “I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States, that loves us so much he can’t even breathe, that I will go out with my family, my friends, I’ll do it any way – I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going to try to cheat like hell like they do.” The convention had been aimed at turning around Republicans’ fortunes. Opinion polls suggest they are on course to lose the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate. In what was effectively an abridged version of his rambling keynote address on Wednesday, the president reiterated his promise of “Trump dividend” of $5,000 for every US adult if Republicans win both chambers of Congress. Democrats have dismissed the pledge as a bribe while economists have warned it would cost more than $1tn. Trump also hammered the theme of the convention: drawing a contrast between his own accomplishments and what he argues amounts to a threat posed by Democrats. “Less than two years ago, the American people gave us a mandate to save America – and in 19 months, I’ve delivered on every single promise I made,” he claimed. “They gave us wide open borders with 25 million people pouring in from all over the globe. They turned our cities into scenes of death and misery, murder, poverty and destruction, and made America a laughingstock all over world. “But we took that dark age of America and turned it into the golden age of America.” The reduction of prescription drug prices alone “should get us a big victory in our midterms”, he suggested, before he turned the microphone over to the opera performer Christopher Macchio, who belted out a soaring rendition of America the Beautiful as red, white, blue and golden balloons cascaded down from the ceiling of the basketball arena. The convention resembled a Trump mega-rally more than a traditional party meeting, with no nominations or formal business and more than 50 speakers or presentations each night. Supporters wore “Make America Great Again” regalia and waved signs displaying the Stars and Stripes. Republicans believe it has been successful in galvanising the party’s base in the face of stiff electoral headwinds. Earlier on Thursday, speaker after speaker sought to champion Trump’s accomplishments while constantly branding the Democratic party as extremist and communist. The president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, delivered a fiery address setting Republican “common sense” against a “dystopian hellscape” of leftwing ideology. “As we speak, Democrat candidates across the country are openly embracing the radical ideology of democratic socialism,” suggested Trump Jr. “They claim that their socialism is for the people, but that’s the exact same story we’ve heard from every communist in human history.” Describing childhood memories of his grandparents in communist Czechoslovakia, he warned of bread lines and rationing. “Communism is on the march and it’s up to us to stop it in its tracks,” he said. Trump Jr framed the Republican platform, including pledges to end taxes on tips, overtime and social security, as a direct response to a “war on the working people” by Democrats. “The choice is clear,” he said. “Don’t let these radicals gaslight you into thinking common sense is extreme, and extreme is somehow common sense. Don’t let them convince you that caring about this country makes you a villain.” Senator Ted Cruz meanwhile warned of a “red-green alliance” between “communists and Islamists” who “hate Christians, hate Jews and hate capitalism”. Invoking his father’s escape from Cuban communism, Cruz declared that “sharia law has no place in America” and was “fundamentally inconsistent with the constitution”. The House speaker, Mike Johnson, echoed the conspiratorial tone, suggesting the nation was being “attacked from within”. The Democratic party is now beholden to radicals, he claimed, warning: “They’re the ones who have let the barbarians inside the gate, and next year the communists will be in Congress. That’s what’s so frightening.” Johnson added that, while big names like Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed are known entities, the bigger threat comes from “Democrats in the swing seats who say one thing, and then join forces and vote with the socialists that they’re afraid of”. The US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, took the stage to champion the “Make America Healthy Again” (Maha) platform. The son of a former US attorney general and nephew of John F Kennedy said the “irony of my presence here is inescapable”. He continued: “The Democrats of that era stood with labour and working people and the American middle class. Nearly every cop and firefighter was a Democrat … The Democratic party, in short, lost its way.” Speaking less than a mile from the spot where his uncle was assassinated in 1963, Kennedy claimed it was a “fact” that “neither my father, nor my uncle, would recognise the Democratic party of today”. JD Vance, the vice-president, gave the keynote address of the night. He said: “The Democrats are the party of hatred. They’re the party that despises America and the people who built it … America belongs to those who love it – not those who hate it.” The political attacks were briefly paused for two sombre interludes. A tribute marked one year since the assassination of the rightwing provocateur and organiser Charlie Kirk. Lucas Miles, a Turning Point USA vice-president, said that while “they could take the man, they could not take the mission”. Chants of “Charlie, Charlie” filled the air. The arena was plunged into darkness as Macchio performed Ave Maria on the eve of the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks. Two beams of light stretched upward from the arena floor, reminiscent of the twin towers in New York, as the crowd held up mobile phone lights. A video narration accompanying the tribute urged the audience to: “Say their names. Honour their sacrifice. Defend Freedom. Never forget September 11.” Democrats have dismissed the Republican event as a stunt. At a press conference in Dallas, Robert Garcia, a California congressman, told reporters: “What’s happening right now is Donald Trump is throwing a two-day party to celebrate himself, so that JD Vance can give a speech, and so his donors, some of whom have paid $800,000 a pop for these ticket packages, can spend two days celebrating themselves. “This is happening as the American public is struggling. So as Donald Trump and JD Vance party away for two days, the average American family can’t afford groceries, the cost of the rent’s going up, they’re looking at their gas prices skyrocketing and they’re making difficult choices at the dinner table. But Donald Trump does not care about the average American family or about affordability.”

title: Friday briefing: Would a wealth tax save our public services or be billionaire repellent?
author: Libby Brooks
summary: In today’s newsletter: Some think taxing the super-rich is a moral obligation, others say it drives cash away from the country. The truth may be somewhere in the middle
body_text: Morning pals, and let’s join in a heartfelt ευχαριστώ (thank you) to hedge fund billionaire Chris Rokos for the estimated £330m he paid to the UK Treasury last year, and sadly won’t be contributing in future as he’s relocating to Greece. The publicity shy tycoon (and former Tory donor) has not made explicit his reasons for leaving the UK: so one can only speculate Rokos may be drawn by the noted health benefits of the Mediterranean diet, or the Greek government’s attractive €100,000 flat tax for overseas investors. Predictably, one man’s decision is now being framed by some as a dire warning to government to halt taxes on wealth in the UK. Conversely, campaigners are arguing ever more stridently for a specific wealth tax. With taxes already at their highest level since the second world war, could this be the goose to lay the cure-all golden egg and fix our crumbling public services? I spoke to our senior economics commentator, Aditya Chakrabortty, whose response might not be what you first expect it to be. And, yes, we get into goose-plucking too. Five big stories UK politics | Ministers are facing a backlash from the hospitality industry after they announced mayors in England would be given sweeping powers to levy taxes on holiday accommodation such as hotels and Airbnbs. Economy | Nervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation. US news | JD Vance made a clear pitch that he should be the heir to Donald Trump, closing out the Republicans’ midterm convention with a blistering speech that featured exaggerated claims of success. Israel | Testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders on the secret systems used in the war on Gaza has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians. UK news | Consumers will pay higher energy bills unless the UK government speeds up work on a vast programme of upgrades to the electricity grid to enable the switch to renewables, the public spending watchdog has warned. In depth: We need to think about what wealth actually means Taxes are at record highs; satisfaction with public services at rock bottom. It’s a dichotomy familiar to us all from our own private focus groups, be that the street WhatsApp community or the bowling club. Alongside this, wealth is rising exponentially while wages are not: from 2000 to 2025, for example, average weekly earning rose just over 100% while property prices went up by about 240%. According to the British Social Attitudes Survey, the segment of the public who say the government should further increase taxes to spend more on health, education and welfare is at its lowest level in over a decade, at 36%. Aditya offers me a quote from Jean-Baptiste Colbert, the minister of finances under King Louis XIV of France: “The art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing.” “This has become harder to do as the tax burden has got higher,” Aditya tells me. “And so wealth taxes have really emerged as an attractive option to people in government, and to campaigners, not just here, but around western Europe and in America too.” *** What is a wealth tax and how would it work? Most advocates, when they talk about a wealth tax, mean an annual tax on assets over a certain threshold. The Green party of England and Wales, for example, proposes an annual tax of 1% on assets above £10m and 2% on those above £1bn, estimating it could raise almost £15bn a year. The campaign group Patriotic Millionaires – a bunch of likable sorts including Gary Lineker, Brian Eno and Val McDermid – suggests a 2% annual tax on total net wealth exceeding £10m, projecting revenue of £24bn a year. Oxfam, which is campaigning alongside them, says this rate would affect 20,000 people – about 0.04% of the UK population – and highlights polling carried out this May by YouGov, which found 76% of the public support “this fair wealth tax”. Campaigners present this as a slam dunk – minimal hissing for maximum feather. But dig into that polling a wee bit further and you’ll find the YouGov tracker poll, which instead indicates that Britons, over the past seven years, have a baseline preference for taxing income, rather than assets. It seems that, while the public are attracted to the concept of a wealth tax, they’re pretty selective about how wealth is defined. *** Why not start plucking? Critics of a wealth tax, in the right-of-centre thinktanks and the publications that report on them, argue that taxing the same wealth every year would penalise saving and investment; that a specific wealth tax would require expensive and unwieldy new administrative apparatus to value wealth; that focusing on the super-rich to raise revenue would make the UK a less attractive place for those people to work and invest. Aditya may not share their ideology, but he has his own reasons for being sceptical about current wealth tax campaigning, which he argues “offers apparently easy solutions, which will always affect someone else and never me”. Crucially, he says, if you’re running the government, the money raised by an annual wealth tax doesn’t make much dent in your bills, relatively speaking. The highest estimate is less than a third of the £80bn the UK government is planning to spend on defence annually by the end of the decade. And, once a tax is in place, so the dodges begin. “The one thing that the wealthy have in droves are advisers to show you how to avoid taxes.” “It doesn’t mean you shouldn’t do it,” he adds, “just don’t oversell it as a magic bullet.” *** What’s this about a one-off wealth tax? So with that bubble burst, Aditya points us to what he considers the most substantial piece of work done on wealth taxes in the UK to date. A couple of academics and a tax barrister came together during Covid lockdown, when the rest of us were struggling with the recipe for banana bread, to form the independent Wealth Tax Commission. They propose a one-off wealth tax, arguing that its fairer because it targets people with the most ability to pay, is very difficult to avoid and wouldn’t distort behaviour because it’s one-time only. Accounting for behavioural responses and admin costs, they estimate this would raise a total of £260bn at a rate of 5% over £500,000 per individual, payable at 1% per year over five years. To be clear: this would be paid by individuals whose total wealth after mortgages and other debts, and after splitting the value of shared assets such as a jointly owned family homes, exceeded the tax threshold, and only on the value of wealth above that threshold. For example, a wealth tax levied at 1% above £500,000 would require a couple to have net wealth of more than £1m before any wealth tax would be payable. This is where Aditya gets excited: “£260bn is more than we get from income tax in a year. It would be transformative – you could put it in a sovereign wealth fund and invest in renewables. Or you could put it directly into the NHS and schools.” It would, however, affect a very different tranche of the population – those de facto millionaires with property in desirable parts of Edinburgh or Manchester or London. And that’s where the hissing starts up again. *** Are there other ways to tax wealth? We’ve heard it many times before over other proposed taxes on wealth: Rachel Reeves reversed her plans to end inheritance tax breaks for farmers after lobbyists drove tractors up to the doors of parliament and drowned out speeches with their horns. When Ed Miliband proposed a mansion tax on properties valued over £2m, to raise £1.2bn annually for the NHS, in his 2015 manifesto, he was eviscerated by the rightwing media, party critics and Myleene Klass, who confronted him in a TV debate, arguing the tax wouldn’t just touch the super-rich but would devastate “little grannies” who bought modest London homes that had simply skyrocketed in value over the decades. But times change, don’t they? And Reeves was able to avoid a similar backlash when she introduced a similar council tax surcharge on properties worth £2m or more at the last budget. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has argued consistently that, rather than introduce a new wealth tax, the government should sort out the mess of current capital and property taxes. In May, Wes Streeting received a mixed reception when he proposed equalising capital gains with income tax, as part of his brief tilt at Labour leadership, describing it as a “wealth tax that works”. And of course, HMRC could get better at collecting tax from the super-rich: its own estimates suggest that at least £2.1bn extra could be raised from closing the wealthy tax gap. The trouble with getting more granular on wealth taxation, Aditya says, is that many of the groups affected – whether that’s farmers, lawyers or GPs in partnerships – are also very well-networked and good at making a noise about the specific unfairness of targeting them as opposed to others. Which takes us back to the more subtle point about burden-sharing and democracy that underlies his arguments: by focusing on the billionaires in the corner, we avoid looking at the millionaires in the mirror – and having an honest conversation about what wealth is and how sophisticated those who have it are at lobbying against further taxes on it. An annual wealth tax has so much support right now because “it’s very politically palatable”, Aditya says. “It will poll brilliantly for you, because everyone will say that won’t affect them”. His advice is to pivot, philosophically: “Forget about the wealthy. Think about wealth.” We want to hear from you Remember the Makerfield test? Andy Burnham promised it would be at the heart of his decision-making: whether policy worked for areas, such as his constituency, that feel overlooked by Westminster. Ahead of the Labour party conference I’ll be asking experts which of the prime minister’s decisions have passed or failed that test.
