title: Australian fuel prices set to rise by 30c as global markets react to ‘deadly cocktail’
author: Patrick Commins Economics editor
summary: Global oil price at its highest since May while investors dump stocks and bonds after Donald Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ promise
body_text: Fuel prices are on track to climb a further 20-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, after the escalating Middle East conflict pushed the global oil price to its highest since mid-May. As investors dumped stocks and bonds in an increasingly febrile environment, Donald Trump’s promise to give every US adult citizen a US$5,000 “dividend” after the November midterms if Republicans win added to alarm around the parlous state of the country’s finances. Investors pushed US bond yields towards 5% for the first time since 2007 as the prospect of higher energy costs firmed up expectations that the US Federal Reserve would need to hike rates again. That dragged Australia’s 10-year rate up to 5.38% and to fresh 15-year highs. The international oil benchmark, Brent crude, pushed towards US$110 a barrel, before settling at above US$108 in late Friday trade. Steve Miller, an investment strategist at fund manager GSFM, said bonds were reacting to a “deadly cocktail” of high oil prices, American fiscal irresponsibility, and worries around the independence of the Fed. “The $5,000 promise is a great example of Trump’s unwillingness to tackle the deficit, and even to make it worse for short-term political expediency. No wonder bond markets are sketchy,” Miller said. Tai Hui, chief market strategist for Asia-Pacific at JP Morgan Asset Management, said rising long-term borrowing rates would normally undermine stock valuations, as investors rethink the relative trade-off between the riskier sharemarket and climbing yields on safe bonds. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Evidence of this was clear on the ASX this week, where the benchmark S&P/ASX 200 index was on track to end the week down 3% and below the level it was this time last year. But Hui said ongoing optimism about the state of the global economy and, especially, the titanic boom in artificial intelligence investment was providing a tailwind for sharemarkets around the world, and especially on Wall Street. Since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran at the end of February, the US benchmark S&P 500 sharemarket index is up about 10%, against a 5% fall for the ASX 200. But the Hong Kong-based Hui said the increasingly debated question among investors was at what point the steady march higher in yields begins to drive a broader and deeper switch out of stocks and into bonds. “We are approaching a crossroad,” he said. As economists warned of a new post-Covid era of structurally higher interest rates, financial markets upped their bets that the Reserve Bank of Australia would deliver a fourth rate hike on 29 September, pricing in an 80% chance. Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said the RBA would have to respond to recent evidence that inflationary pressures were not easing as hoped, even as the economy proved resilient. “I think they [the RBA] will go in September,” Kearns said. The former top RBA official said the central bank’s inflation-fighting credentials were increasingly at stake. “They need to get inflation to 2.5%, and that’s not forecast to happen until early 2028; that then becomes almost a seven-year inflationary episode.” The prospect of higher mortgage costs comes as Vivek Dhar, CBA’s head of commodities research, warned that diesel prices could climb by 10-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, from over $2.50 per litre today. Unleaded petrol prices could push from about $2.10 a litre in major east coast cities to about $2.30 over the next couple of weeks, according to a rough rule of thumb that says every US$1 increase in the crude oil benchmark translates to a 10c increase at the pump. Dhar, who is based in Singapore, said meetings with energy producers and traders on the sidelines of a major energy conference over recent days revealed a deep sense of uncertainty about how the next six to 12 months will play out. Dhar said he expected Brent crude to swing between US$70 and US$100 a barrel for the foreseeable future, until eventually the world becomes comfortable with the supply workarounds to a restricted strait of Hormuz. But the more pressing worries were around the supply of refined products, particularly diesel. “Everyone pays attention to oil, but it’s the refined product that hits the economy and feeds through to inflation. And that is what everyone is worried about, because there isn’t any workaround; we just need disruptions to stop.”

title: 9/11 entrenched Islamophobia in US politics. But it doesn’t work the way you think
author: Moustafa Bayoumi
summary: Anti-Muslim sentiment is used as a political weapon. Meanwhile, Muslim American leaders are making a difference for all
body_text: It’s been 25 years since the terrorist attacks of September 11, and during this time Muslim Americans have learned how to live in that dangerous space between other Americans’ fears and their ignorance. The fear was clear from the beginning. Immediately following 9/11, Muslim Americans faced what Human Rights Watch called “a severe wave of backlash violence”. A tide of hate rose up against ordinary Muslims and those who appeared to be Muslim, including at least three murders in the immediate backlash after the attacks. The federal government, for its part, began targeting Muslim immigrants in a massive surge of repression that legal experts soon compared to the Palmer Raids of the 1920s. The ignorance was just as evident. Even Oprah Winfrey did her part to allay it, dedicating an episode of her show in October 2001 to “Islam 101”. The Qur’an leapt on to the New York Times bestseller list that fall. Yet despite these early efforts at education, most Americans still learned little about Islam and Muslims. One 2006 study found that only a third of those polled realized that Muslims worship the same God as Christians and Jews do. Close to 10% of respondents thought Muslims worship a “moon god”. Much of this fear and ignorance has continued unevenly over the last quarter century, with negative attitudes towards Muslim Americans softening at times and hardening, sometimes into deadly violence, at other times. What’s interesting is when expressions of these attitudes happen. It turns out that predicting when animosity to Muslims will rise and fall may not be quite what you think. Researchers who study Islamophobia discovered several years ago that anti-Muslim outbreaks in the United States don’t follow highly publicized acts of terrorism. Rather, Islamophobic incidents tend to cluster more routinely around our election cycles. That’s what the New American Foundation found in 2018. That’s what the researcher Dalia Mogahed discovered earlier. And that’s partly what the Brookings Institution’s Shibley Telhami was referencing when he wrote, in 2024, that there was “strong suggestive evidence” that presidential messaging and crisis rhetoric can considerably sway American public attitudes toward Muslims. Islamophobia, in other words, is better understood not as an irrational fear of a religious other but rather as an increasingly instrumentalized part of our politics, one that is most often activated around our elections. (Needless to say, when Islamophobia is deployed, it’s at the expense of the American Muslim community’s wellbeing.) And since we’re also closing in on a fiercely contested midterm election season, we should take note of the sky-high levels of Islamophobic rhetoric we’re witnessing today from the (mostly Republican) politician class. Consider Laura Loomer, the far-right activist and Donald Trump’s close confidante. “Ban Muslims from holding office in America,” she posted on Twitter/X in July. Then there’s the South Carolina representative Nancy Mace, who wrote: “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic. We refuse to be silent.” The Florida representative Randy Fine, who has called for the deportation of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, believes: “We need more Islamophobia, not less. Fear of Islam is rational.” And the senator Tommy Tuberville recently stated: “Michigan Democrats just voted to send a TERRORIST to the Senate. Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed is a RADICAL ISLAMIST who will do everything he can to destroy America.” In a thinly veiled Islamophobic comment, JD Vance recently said: “There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil. And on the rise in the United States of America today.” In Texas, the levels of Islamophobia are now stratospheric. Lone Star politicians loudly trumpet anti-Muslim messages and repeatedly introduce versions of anti-Muslim legislation, seeking to forbid everything from sharia courts, which don’t actually exist in Texas, to real estate developments by Muslims. Must be election season. The Texas governor Greg Abbott, who is up for re-election, has designated the country’s largest Muslim civil rights organization, the Council on American Islamic Relations (Cair), a foreign terrorist organization. This is ludicrous, of course, but as a Muslim organization, Cair’s an easy mark. As the Knight First Amendment Institute points out, “the domestic targeting of dissent starts with groups that those in power deem to be attractive political targets, but it never ends there. Without further opposition to these orders, CAIR is likely only the first of many groups to be in the crosshairs of politically motivated governors.” And that’s the larger point. Muslim Americans have been weathering these kinds of attacks for decades now, but what we also know is that attacks on Muslims won’t end as attacks on Muslims. For 25 years, we have known what it means to live under a national security state. We have known what warrantless surveillance feels like. We have known what politicized immigration enforcement looks like (remember the Muslim ban?). We have known what it means when our dissenting voices are silenced, especially when advocating for Palestine. And so, we recognize when those same tools are used by the National Security Agency to spy on ordinary Americans (as revealed by the whistleblower Edward Snowden) or when today’s mass deportations carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement resemble the immigration crackdown on Muslim immigrants decades earlier. Republicans worry loudly about their made-up fantasy of “creeping sharia”, but what all of us should really be concerned about is the reality of this creeping authoritarianism. Muslim Americans have hardly been silent when facing this repression. Instead, we’ve organized ourselves to oppose it. If the political culture of the United States is poised to deny us our legitimate rights, then the response must be preserving those rights for everybody, not just for Muslim Americans. That’s exactly what we’re witnessing today. Muslim Americans are more present in the American political scene than ever before. According to a recent study, a record 255 Muslims now serve in elected positions across the country, including 11 mayors, 18 judges and four members of the US House of Representatives. Muslim women account for more than 43% of the total. Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed are probably today’s most visible Muslim American politicians. What makes them noteworthy is not just their obvious communication skills, but their deliberate attention to policies that enhance the public good for all. El-Sayed, for example, prioritizes universal access to healthcare and clean water, eliminating medical debt and banning corporate money in politics. Mamdani, for his part, has delivered a pilot program delivering taxpayer-funded childcare for two-year-olds, a rent freeze on rent-stabilized apartments, and a parents’ night out program, where children spend supervised time at city recreation centers so parents can have time for themselves. These Muslim politicians have discovered a simple, timeless truth: Democracy’s best defense is ensuring that everyone lives well. For the last 25 years, a bevy of political forces have routinely mobilized fear and ignorance against Muslim Americans to peddle the fiction that Muslims will take over the country. Their message has always been that Muslim Americans don’t belong in the United States. But you know what? We’re paying less attention to them by the hour. Muslim Americans have too much work to do preserving our democracy. The truth is that, while the Islamophobes waste everyone’s time with the ludicrous charge that Muslims and Americans are irreconcilably different, Muslim Americans are just too busy making a difference. For everyone’s sake. Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel to Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnist

title: Trump’s clash with Canada is his latest imperialistic embarrassment
author: Sidney Blumenthal
summary: The president’s chaotic schemes of aggrandizement, from Venezuela to Iran, have no larger rationale
body_text: Trumpism is the lowest stage of imperialism. “We’re not going to invade Greenland. We’re going to buy it,” Donald Trump reportedly told the annual black-tie dinner on 1 February of the private Alfalfa Club, an assemblage of prominent Washington figures, a number of whom he had publicly humiliated, and others he was investigating or suing. “It’s never been my intention to make Greenland the 51st state. I want to make Canada the 51st state. Greenland will be the 52nd state. Venezuela can be 53rd.” The room greeted several of his remarks with dead silence. His cosplay as the Pirate King was not received as a good-humored takeoff from a Gilbert and Sullivan opera. He went on. “So many people in the room I hate,” he said in a display of honesty. “Most of you I like,” he claimed. Then, at his peak euphoria, he flew off to Mar-a-Lago to plan his attack on Iran, which took place 27 days later. Trump’s imperialism of piracy and plunder is less of a system even than that of the earliest imperialism of 17th-century privateers raiding the Spanish Main, the divine right of kings, and monarchs dividing up the spoils as favors to create their lords and earls. His schemes of aggrandizement operating by threat and force are justified by no larger rationale, nothing as exalted as “the white man’s burden”, marauding wherever and however he can to seize resources. Describing his actions as some version of colonialism grants him a more orderly and coherent method than he possesses. His pillaging bears not the slightest resemblance to the highly organized administration of Queen Victoria’s British empire. Trump’s predation is calculated to wreck the long-established arrangements of international trade, law and cooperation created after the second world war and the fall of colonial empires, whose guidelines he sees as obstructing his own profit and power. Obsessed with his fortune hunting, he couldn’t care less about the political consequences for ill-fated Republican candidates in the midterm elections who must face the music for the harm he is doing to their states. They are the least of his collateral damage. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, offered the most succinct critique of Trump’s intent to usurp the sovereignty of countries in order to make them turn over their wealth to him. Carney said: “Canada is a sovereign, independent nation. We are not a target to be bullied, nor are we a client state to be subordinated … We will not sign an agreement that sacrifices our basic sovereignty, undermines our legal system, or cedes control over our foreign trade to Washington.” He called Trump’s demands a “last-minute power play intended to reduce Canada to an economic subsidiary”. Trump’s ultimatum abrogated the legal foundation of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which he himself had signed in 2020. He had previously demeaned Carney as the “governor” of Canada. Now, adopting his characteristic pose as victim, Trump claimed Canada had been “ripping off the United States for years” and were among “worst” nations to “deal with”.. “They feel entitled and will be entitled no longer … It’s time to teach Canada you can’t do this anymore…. Someone should get these clowns to fall in line.” Carney replied that Canada was “at war” and would adopt “counter-measures”, tariffs of its own. “America,” he said, “has changed … If Washington wants to trade, they must come to the table as equals.” Trump’s answer was to issue an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America”, the reflexive branding of the real estate operator. The White House put out AI-generated videos of Trump kicking over a sign reading “Lake Ontario” and replacing it with a new one, “Lake America”, and another with a squadron of ducks all with Trump’s hairdo and armed with machine guns patrolling the shore of “Lake America” to the theme music of Hawaii Five-O. The implied invocation of the Marx brothers’ farce of the ludicrous country of Freedonia nonsensically going to war, Duck Soup, seems lost on the busy beavers of Trump’s slop. Trump’s method has been consistent since he leveraged a mineral resource deal out of Ukraine in April 2025 at a weak point in its conflict with Russia. Rather than pressure Putin, Trump’s agents disguised as diplomats, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and real estate pal Steve Witkoff, the Rosencrantz and Guildenstern of Trump’s imperialism, stand by to negotiate post-sanctions deals on his behalf. Venezuela became Trump’s template for his piratical adventures. After swooping in on 3 January to capture its strongman, Nicolás Maduro, Trump promised a transition to democratic elections and that the US would play a custodial role over Venezuelan oil for the benefit of its people. Not long after Trump grabbed Maduro, he declared he needed to acquire Greenland and threatened a tariff war against Denmark and European allies to “get Greenland, including right, title and ownership”. “We probably won’t get anything unless I decide to use excessive strength and force, where we would be frankly unstoppable. But I won’t do that,” Trump said, adding, “I don’t have to use force,” and “I don’t want to use force.” He relented momentarily on 21 January after he claimed he had reached a “framework” agreement to negotiate over natural resources, though he subsequently sent preposterous agents into Greenland to stir up a quixotic annexation movement to no avail. A month later, he bombed Iran. Trump stated that his true inspiration for the Iran war was the Venezuelan model in a post on 11 June: “At some point in the not too distant future, we will … assume total control of their Oil and Gas Markets, much like we have with Venezuela, which is working out brilliantly for both Venezuela and the United States of America.” On 31 August, Trump announced that the US would take a stake in 17 oilfields in partnership with North American Blue Energy Partners, controlled by a Venezuelan oilman, Alejandro Betancourt. Betancourt was briefly detained in Britain, which was reportedly linked to a Swiss warrant on suspicion of money laundering. Betancourt has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with any offenses. The Swiss warrant was withdrawn in May and he became a Trump associate. The Trump administration has already claimed to have received proceeds of $500m from oil sales, initially deposited in an account in Qatar. When the congressman Sean Casten of Illinois and the senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland wrote a letter requesting information, the administration shifted the money to an opaque account managed by the treasury department. In an article published in June by the Council on Foreign Relations, “The U.S. Took Over Venezuela’s Oil Industry. Where Has All the Money Gone?”, Roxana Vigil, a former treasury department expert, observed that in dealing with the “same corrupt regime, different leader … the Trump administration has provided almost no information on the system it has established to sell Venezuelan oil, collect the revenue, and use the funds”. The countries whose sovereignty, self-interest and rule of law Trump has struck include the United States. His assault on Canada has sent a shock through the whole US economy. The state most affected economically, Michigan, shares with Canada one of the most integrated industrial relationships in the world. More than 38% of Michigan’s exports go to Canada, the Detroit-Windsor corridor handles 25% of all US-Canada trade, and Trump’s tariffs immediately threaten 260,000 jobs with an immensely damaging multiplier effect. As of March, his tariffs had already caused estimated losses of $35bn to automakers. The average cost per Michigan household is estimated to be $5,619 in added expenses due to tariff-induced price increases. Trump’s tariffs have effectively hamstrung the Republican candidate for the Senate in Michigan, Mike Rogers, leaving him with the Hobson’s choice of either inciting Trump’s rage or submitting to his whim. Rogers has decided to take the latter course. He has called Trump’s economic policies “masterful”. When JD Vance came to the state, Rogers praised the administration. “The impact you have had on our state is phenomenal,” he said. Rogers hurls language about “extremism” against the Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed that substitutes for discussing Trump’s economic fiasco. Rogers is performing the kind of self-abasing fealty to Trump that Trump wishes he would receive from Carney. If only Rogers were the prime minister of Canada, there would be no trouble about “independence”. Vladimir Lenin, in his 1917 tract, Imperialism: The Highest Stage of Capitalism, argued in his dogmatic and overdetermined style that imperialism at the turn of the 20th century represented the integration of monopoly, finance and industrial capital, with the great powers dividing the world into colonies, and their conflict precipitating the first world war. In Trump’s imaginarium, he views himself as omnipotent and omniscient. When the world isn’t pliable, he must resort to greater force to reassure himself that the world acknowledges his self-image. The more he meets resistance to his fixed idea, the more pressure he must exert. He finds himself in a vicious cycle. His power hemorrhages, US power dissipates and he spins in a whirlpool. Trump’s Venezuelan paradigm, whose conditions cannot be replicated, have quickly descended into questionable business deals. Failed from the start of his Iran war, his pursuit of “total control” recedes over the horizon. His clash with Canada has been confronted with Carney’s fierce defiance. Trump’s quest for a new field to conquer has landed him in yet another quagmire. “When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” said Carney. In the meantime, Trump’s outlandish exhibitions of triumphalism in the face of rejection and defeat echo the Marx Brothers more than they echo Marx and Lenin: “Hail Freedonia!” Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast

title: First Thing: Nation pauses to remember September 11 on 25th anniversary
author: Martin Belam
summary: Commemoration ceremonies to be held around the world for the nearly 3,000 killed in 2001 terror attack on US. Plus, JD Vance sets out his stall as heir to Donald Trump
body_text: Good morning. It is a sombre day for the nation as people gather to mourn and remember the nearly 3,000 victims of the attacks on September 11 2001, when 19 al-Qaida hijackers seized control of four airliners, slamming two of the planes into the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and the fourth into a field in western Pennsylvania. We have comprehensive coverage of the anniversary, which will be marked by ceremonies around the world. There are stories of the day from people who were there. Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark were two of only four individuals known to have survived above the impact zone in the south tower, and they spoke to our Washington bureau chief David Smith. Anna Sweeney Rossman was five when her mother, Amy Sweeney, a flight attendant, was killed onboard American Airlines flight 11, and she spoke to Ramon Antonio Vargas about how the events of that day have cast a shadow on her life. CIA veterans spoke to Robert Tait about the chaos and confusion in the agency as the unprecedented attacks unfolded, and Guardian readers have told us about how September 11 changed their lives. Jason Burke, our international security correspondent, writes that while al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden may have shaken the world on 9/11, it is clear today his wider plans failed. But we also have to acknowledge that the world’s most powerful country responded to the worst terrorist attack in its history by inflicting terror of its own – around the world, and at home. This read from David Smith outlines how the day saw heroes emerge showing the best of America, and then the response of US governments left a dark legacy – Guantánamo Bay, the Abu Ghraib scandal – which continues to unfold to this day. Those who remember September 11 will never forget the haunting images of that day, including the missing people posters that were put up in the confusing aftermath of the collapse of the towers in New York. Captured by the photographer Phil Buehler, they will form part of a new exhibition, and some can be viewed here. As we look back on a day that reshaped our world, our thoughts remain with the victims, their families, and all those whose lives were irrevocably changed 25 years ago. In other news … Donald Trump’s promise of a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery. With his approval rating at a historic low, Trump brought down the curtain on the Republicans’ first ever midterm convention by pleading with supporters to do him “the biggest favor” and “pretend” they are voting for him in November’s US elections. JD Vance, meanwhile, made a clear pitch that he should be the heir to Trump with a blistering speech that featured exaggerated claims of success, criticism of the Democrats as “lunatics” and an aggressive dismissal of a protester waving a Mexican flag. A US appeals court has rejected Trump’s attempt to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in voting before November’s high-stakes midterm elections, dealing a fresh blow to the president’s attempted crackdown. Anthropic has detailed efforts by bad actors to misuse its AI for the production of bioweapons. More researchers and staff members at the AI startup have posted their own dire warnings about the safety of the technology, but Elon Musk called the chorus of concerns a “setup” and a “psyop”. California has adopted what Gavin Newsom described as “nation-leading” legislation that bans addictive social media features for young users, regulates companion chatbots and implements new safeguards around AI. Sales of previously occupied US homes declined in August to their slowest annual pace in more than a year as home shoppers grappled with rising mortgage rates and home prices. Stat of the day: $15m fund launched to create ‘unstoppable momentum’ to end FGM worldwide Leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice. Culture pick: Is Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman’s agelessness the real trick of Practical Magic 2? Katie Edwards asks the awkward question about Practical Magic 2, would Hollywood have brought the franchise back from the dead if the intervening 28 years looked more visible on Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman? Don’t miss this: ‘We can’t stop for a second’ – tracking South Korea’s stalkers in real time Raphael Rashid reports from Seoul on an app that has allowed survivors – who are overwhelmingly women – to see exactly where their stalker is. If they come within a kilometre, an alert is passed to police and probation authorities, who can call and notify the victim. … or this: I turned off my algorithm for 24 hours – is this how social media used to be? “There are no more posts from accounts that you follow from the past 30 days” is a message we have long since stopped seeing on Instagram. In the wake of a government decision to insist companies provide algorithm opt-outs, my Australian colleague Caitlin Cassidy tried to turn her social media experience back to 2012. Climate check: English winemakers expect ‘vintage year’ after record-breaking summer heat While drought in France has been bringing predictions of a fall in wine production, English winemakers are benefiting after record-breaking summer heat quickly ripened grapes. It isn’t all good news for British drinkers though – beer sellers have warned of a potential shortage after the high temperatures caused poor yields of barley. Last Thing: Diana’s ‘revenge dress’, worn when Charles revealed infidelity, up for auction Worn by Diana the same night Charles would reveal his infidelity on TV, the black, fitted, off-the-shoulder, skintight and short Christina Stambolian dress was quickly labelled “the revenge dress” by the media. This month it will go on display at Sotheby’s auction house in London, before travelling to Hong Kong, Geneva and New York, where it will be sold. title: Wake up, Britain: Donald Trump’s US is no friend of ours. We must secure our own place in the world
author: Simon Jenkins
summary: The US president is ever more wayward – and has little interest in defending Europe. The constitution may hold him to account, but we can’t wait, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
body_text: If Americans vote for a Republican majority in both houses of Congress in November, “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.” But they must not spend it in Canada or China or anywhere else outside the US. So said Donald Trump in Texas on Wednesday in advance of the forthcoming midterm elections. He further told voters to “Pretend that I’m on the ballot”. It was a climactic moment in an almost two-hour rant. Trump does not have the required trillion dollars in his pocket, and it would be illegal to disperse such a sum without congressional approval. In any case, JD Vance now appears to have rowed back on the promise. Observers from abroad must beware: it is unwise to subject Trump’s populism to the discipline of truth. Trump also said Americans should thank him for attacking Iran since that country was “two, maybe three weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”, which it intended to use against them. It was the old Saddam Hussein gambit. The problem is that almost every one of Trump’s speeches refers back to himself, as if he and the United States were synonymous. He claimed to have won the presidency three times. He says: “If we hadn’t won the last election, I’m not sure that our country right now would even exist.” He added that the arena where he was speaking was packed, with crowds outside clamouring to get in. Pictures show it half empty. Anyone watching can see why there has been much medical debate over whether Trump is exhibiting signs of narcissism disorder. Key symptoms are mendacity and inconsistency. In 2021 members of the House of Representatives called for the constitution’s 25th amendment, by which a president can be declared unfit for office, to be invoked over the Capitol Hill riot. But that has a high constitutional threshold, requiring a majority of his sycophantic cabinet to declare him unfit. As for more conventional checks on a wayward president, they have proved extraordinarily weak. A Congress over which Trump exerts a populist terrorism has been reluctant to use its powers to call him to account. He has flagrantly declared wars without congressional authority, abused executive orders as “emergencies” and frozen federal spending to halt the “advance [of] Marxist equity”. He has even tried to redefine US citizenship, which is unconstitutional. Very gradually some institutions supposed to hold the White House in check are finding muscle. Judges have blocked attempts to limit birthright citizenship. Trump’s blanket firing of public officials is being legally challenged, although the supreme court has often sided with him. Even the Senate Republican leader, John Thune, has balked at Trump’s proposed Save America Act – which would require anyone voting to show documentary proof of US citizenship. Its outrageous gerrymandering would shrink Democrat votes and aid Republicans. It is an echo of the Jim Crow laws of the post-civil war south. Where this president leaves the US’s longstanding allies overseas is less clear. Visitors to the British embassy in Washington are traditionally warned that “we disagree with America about almost everything, but remain the closest of friends”. Britain distanced itself from war in Vietnam but joined the US, inexplicably, in Iraq. But nothing has come near Trump’s sustained abuse of Britain in the past year on everything from defence spending to wind turbines. He sees the UK as “weak” and “on the edge of disaster”. It was “once” the US’s greatest ally. But by implication, is no more. This opens the central weakness in Anglo-American relations that Trump has made explicit. This is the assumption that the US would honour the principle of collective defence and go to war with Russia, in the event that Russia declared war on Europe. This held during the cold war, with the US’s guarantee of Europe’s security taken as axiomatic. Since the end of the cold war, that guarantee has become ever more flimsy. Despite events in Ukraine, it has long seemed implausible that Russia would declare nuclear war on the west, let alone on America itself. It is therefore equally implausible that the US could threaten Russia with nuclear retaliation. At which point a central essence of the Nato alliance starts to crumble. European governments have seen a president ready to annex foreign countries, invade others, disrupt world trade with aggressive tariffs and defy international law. Can such a wayward and egocentric man, devoid of domestic constraints, really be relied on to exercise extreme caution and dependability in circumstances where nuclear weapons are at issue – whether or not the end of the cold war has diminished the threat of east-west confrontation? In other words, nations should start looking realistically at the defence of their own continent and their own borders. There is no new world order any longer. That balloon has been punctured. Friends of the US have always relied on its constitution to hold autocratic presidents to the straight and narrow. But not since Andrew Jackson in the 1830s has there been one who flouts law and convention as brazenly as Trump. Over the next two years his nation’s political institutions are to be sorely tested. But then he will be gone. Perhaps only then will Britain learn his legacy. Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

title: US consumers faced more high prices in August as Iran war raised energy costs
author: Gaya Gupta
summary: Annualized inflation rate was 3.4%, same as July, and core inflation, which omits energy and food prices, rose to 2.4%
body_text: US consumer prices remained stubbornly high in August as the end of the ceasefire between the US and Iran pushed energy prices up, according to data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics released on Friday. The annualized inflation rate was 3.4%, the same as it was in July. The most recent peak was seen in May, when the inflation rate hit a three-year high at 4.2%. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, increased 0.3% from the month before and 2.4% annually. Gasoline increased 27.4% compared with the year before, accounting for more than one-third of the overall monthly increase in prices. Fuel , which is used to power and heat homes, increased annually at a staggering 52%. Prices of common grocery store essentials, such as meat, poultry, eggs and dairy, increased slightly, from 0.1% to 0.3%. Lettuce prices continued to fall, probably continued fallout from the cyclosporiasis outbreak. Despite dipping from its most recent peak, inflation remained above levels that were seen before the war in Iran, largely because of higher energy prices. On Friday, the cost of diesel, used for trucks, buses and trains, rose past $6 a gallon for the first time ever. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, also surpassed $108 on Friday, its highest level since May. Meanwhile, gas prices at the pump sat at an average of $4.29 a gallon, $1.10 higher than the average a year ago, according to AAA. It’s a worrying sign for Republicans, who are on the ballot at a time when consumer sentiment has hit record lows and Americans say they are struggling to afford gas and groceries. Concerns over inflation have also bled into the US bond market, where the yields on some US treasurys have reached their highest points since the 2008 recession. Yet it’s unclear when relief will come. The White House is aware of what this could mean for the upcoming elections. On Wednesday night, Trump said Americans would get a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans win a majority in the midterms, which critics said was akin to bribery. One of the most direct ways the federal government can affect prices comes from the power of the US Federal Reserve, which sets the interest rates that have an effect on the price of loans, including mortgages, car payments and student debt. With prices remaining stubbornly high and core inflation rising, Friday’s report bolsters the likelihood that the Fed will vote to increase rates at its board meeting next week.. Either move could have heavy implications for the US economy. In a social media post last week, Trump said the central bank “must get smart” and lower rates. “A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE,” he declared. But pressure to increase rates has been growing. At the Fed’s last board meeting in July, it voted 9-3 to maintain rates – the first time in a decade that three board members shared dissent over a policy decision. Historically, raising interest rates helps to lower inflation – making investments more expensive slows the economy. Inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high, in 2022. After the Fed spent the next few years increasing interest rates, up to a range of 5.25%-5.5%, inflation went down to 2.3% in April 2025. Interest rates now sit at a range of 3.5%-3.75%, two percentage points lower than where they were two years ago. With inflation back up, some Fed economists have said it might be time for higher interest rates. Last week, the Fed governor Christopher Waller said there was “considerable uncertainty about how military conflicts, trade policy, and artificial intelligence will affect prices and economic activity” and it might be appropriate to raise rates if inflation showed no signs of easing. “If there is continued progress toward our 2% goal, then I am willing to support holding the policy rate at its current level,” he said at a Reuters event. “But if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike.” The Fed’s new chair, Kevin Warsh, has made it clear the central bank will combat inflation during his tenure and achieve price stability. During a closely watched speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, last month, Warsh said that underlying inflation trends had not “meaningfully improved” over the summer. “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do,” Warsh said.

title: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s midterm convention: ‘That arena was as empty as a Waymo’
author: Guardian staff
summary: Late-night hosts discussed Trump’s ‘promise’ to send $5,000 to every US adult should the Republicans win
body_text: Late-night hosts recapped the second day of Donald Trump’s underattended and unusual “midterm convention” in which he promised $5,000 for every adult US citizen if the Republicans win. Jimmy Kimmel Jimmy Kimmel opened Thursday’s monologue with a report from the second day of the Republican National Committee’s “midterm convention” in Dallas, held at the request of Donald Trump. “He demanded a midterm convention, which is something that had never been done before, because there’s no reason to do that,” Kimmel explained. “And of course he got it. They do whatever he wants.” Trump spent the previous night posting on Truth Social, disputing all evidence that the Dallas arena was less than crowded. “He is so embarrassingly desperate to convince us that the place was packed. He even tried to convince the people in the place that it was packed,” Kimmel laughed before a montage of Trump saying “the place is packed” or “nobody has left”, among numerous other comments about his audience size, including “please, if you don’t mind, don’t anybody go to the bathroom”, lest the media take a picture of an empty seat. “Easy for you to say, you’re the only one wearing a diaper,” Kimmel retorted. The host then played a clip of the half-empty arena itself, at the moment Trump asserted that it was still jam-packed. “Could there be a better metaphor for this presidency than him bragging about the size of his crowd to a bunch of empty seats? I don’t think so! “That arena was as empty as a Waymo,” he added. “But his must be high-ness has so many trembling flunkies around him willing to corroborate his constant bullshit, why would he even bother to tell the truth?” Later in his hour-plus speech, Trump promised to send $5,000 to every adult US citizen should the Republican party win the US House and Senate in November. “I spent all day today trying to decide whether that was a bribe or a lie,” said Kimmel, “and I think it might be both things? I think Donald Trump just invented the libe. “How nice of the president to offer us our own money. This is like if I went in your bathroom and unplugged your electric toothbrush, put it in a box and gave it to you for Christmas.” If such a scheme were to take place, Kimmel noted, it would add $1.3tn to the US federal deficit. “How is he going to pay for that?” he wondered. “Is Ivanka going to sell girl scout cookies to pay for that? No! We will have to pay it back with more taxes, and the best part is he wouldn’t send us the checks anyway. “If you believe Donald Trump is going to give you $5,000 if the Republicans win, I have a Mexican-paid wall, a privately funded ballroom and a three-day-long Iran war to sell you.” The Daily Show Trump may be unpopular, said Michael Kosta on The Daily Show, but “he has a secret weapon” for the midterms, “and it’s called a bribe”. As Trump claimed on Thursday, should Republicans win in November, he would send “a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000”. “That’s two trips to the grocery store! Or one, if you buy raspberries, Kosta quipped. “I like how Trump calls this a dividend. Do you know when businesses hand out dividends? When they’re raking in money. The last time I checked, we, as a country, have a negative $40tn of money. America should not be handing out dividends. We should be faking our own death and starting a new life in Thailand.” Even Trump’s supporters seemed confused by the untenable offer. Brian Kilmeade, host of Fox & Friends, could only offer: “Not bad … I’m not sure that’s OK but I think it’s kinda fun.” “And that’s what being president is all about! Having fun,” Kosta joked. “Even Brian Kilmeade didn’t know what to make of this … He sounds like Trump just asked him to throw rocks off the overpass. “But this is just the latest in a cycle of Trump’s behavior with the American people,” Kosta conclude. “He promises a huge payout; that never happens. And then he promises an even bigger payout, and then that never happens. This spiral is exhausting, poisonous, and it makes you question the very health of our democracy. And look, I’m not sure that’s OK, but … it is kinda fun.”

title: The ‘war on terror’ weakened the first amendment. Now we desperately need it
author: Jameel Jaffer
summary: Over the past quarter-century, the US supreme court has repeatedly failed to protect first amendment rights. We are suffering the consequences
body_text: Congress ratified the first amendment in 1791 but the supreme court didn’t breathe life into it until after the first world war, when prosecutions of antiwar protesters led the justices Oliver Wendell Holmes and Louis Brandeis – and then, fortunately, other justices as well – to realize that US democracy would be undermined, not strengthened, by allowing the government to suppress disfavored political opinions. Repression during the cold war led the court to better protect the freedom of association, and government efforts to cover up official ineptitude and criminality during the Vietnam war spurred the court to better protect the freedom of the press. It took time, but in each of these instances the court responded to wartime repression by developing new legal doctrine that more robustly protected first amendment freedoms. Unfortunately, the supreme court hasn’t thus far responded the same way to repressive policies introduced in connection with the “war on terror”. After the September 2001 terrorist attacks, our information ecosystem was restructured to protect what the government said were urgent national security imperatives. Both the executive branch and Congress introduced myriad new forms of censorship, surveillance and secrecy, all purportedly intended to keep Americans safe. Many of these policies were in deep tension with freedoms that the first amendment had long been understood to protect – but rather than limit these policies, the court accommodated them. The result is that today we find ourselves with a weakened first amendment at a time when we desperately need its protections. The war on terror began testing the first amendment from its very beginning. The government barred the press from immigration hearings in the first weeks after 9/11. The intelligence agencies began relying heavily on national security arguments to keep crucial information about their policies from the public, and the justice department invoked the same arguments to withhold legal opinions that had far-reaching implications for individual rights, including ones about torture and extrajudicial killing. The Bush administration revived a cold war-era practice of denying visas to foreign scholars, writers and artists critical of US foreign policy. Congress expanded the law prohibiting the provision of “material support” to blacklisted groups, extending the statute so far that it reached some forms of speech. Congress also amped up government surveillance, reviving old programs and inaugurating new ones, many massive in scale. The Patriot Act, which Congress passed just weeks after the attacks, dramatically expanded the government’s surveillance authorities, and Congress extended those powers repeatedly in subsequent years. The FBI exploited new communications technologies to track journalists’ emails and phone calls, and the justice department began using the Espionage Act to prosecute journalists’ sources. Not all of these issues were presented to the supreme court, but the court batted away almost all of the ones that were. It declined multiple opportunities to consider the constitutionality of national security surveillance. It refused multiple chances to consider the constitutionality of gag orders imposed on the recipients of national security letters – administrative subpoenas issued in foreign-intelligence investigations. It also declined an opportunity to consider whether the first amendment guarantees the public a right of access to opinions issued by the foreign intelligence surveillance court – a question that the Knight First Amendment Institute (which I lead), the ACLU, the former solicitor general Ted Olson, and many former intelligence officials all urged the court to take up. (The justices Neil Gorsuch and Sonia Sotomayor dissented from the denial of certiorari, asking: “If these matters are not worthy of our time, what is?”) Over the course of the quarter century that followed 9/11 – a period during which the court heard about a dozen cases involving the second amendment and about 70 involving intellectual property law – the court agreed to hear only three cases involving conflicts between the government’s counter-terrorism policies and free speech. In each of those cases, it narrowed or weakened first amendment rights. In Humanitarian Law Project v Holder, a challenge to the material support law, the court held that the government could make it a crime for a human rights organization to provide training in human rights law to groups that the government had designated as terrorist organizations. In Clapper v Amnesty, which I argued, the court decided that human rights groups lacked standing to challenge a mass surveillance law because they couldn’t prove that their own communications would be collected; the decision had the effect of shielding most national security surveillance from ordinary constitutional review. More recently, in TikTok v Garland, the court rejected a first amendment challenge to a law that banned Americans from accessing the short-form video app, crediting national security arguments that even the NSA’s general counsel had rejected. That decision purported to be a narrow one but it significantly undermined Americans’ right to access information and media from abroad. The supreme court’s failure to defend the first amendment against the considerable encroachments of the war on terror has handed the Trump administration a broad set of tools it can use in its assault on democratic institutions and freedoms. Government whistleblowers who inform the public about abuse or criminality in the military or intelligence agencies – and journalists and publishers who report on those abuses – risk prosecution under the Espionage Act. Those who participate in anti-ICE or pro-Palestinian demonstrations do so under the shadow of the expanded material support laws. Government secrecy about matters relating to war and foreign policy, such as government surveillance in the national security sphere, has become all but unchallengeable. It’s not surprising that 9/11 and the war on terror would test the protections of the first amendment, as they were tested repeatedly by crises and conflicts in the last century. What is surprising and noteworthy is the extent to which the supreme court has failed to rise to the challenge, as its predecessors did, to ensure that the freedoms of speech and the press emerged from these stresses not just intact but fortified against future pressures. We’re suffering the consequences of the court’s failure now. We’ll preserve our democracy against Trump’s assault – but there’s no question that the court’s record during the war on terror has strengthened the hand of our authoritarian president and weakened our own. Jameel Jaffer directs the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University

title: US lettuce prices wilt as costs for other goods remain stubbornly high
author: Lauren Aratani
summary: Price for the crop dropped dramatically this summer after the cyclospora outbreak chopped demand for greens
body_text: At the Republicans’ midterm convention held earlier this week, Donald Trump said that “food prices and almost every other item are rapidly going down”. Fresh inflation data on Friday told a different story – but in one specific case, costs have been chopped. The price of lettuce dropped dramatically this summer after the cyclospora outbreak caused demand to wilt, with prices dropping even further in August, according to new data released on Friday. The crop was closely linked to the diarrhea-causing parasite that has seen more than 19,500 confirmed cases in the US since May – 16 times the cases that were seen in the same period in 2025. The outbreak spread to 20 states, with just more than 1,000 hospitalizations and two deaths, according to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The spread was linked to iceberg lettuce that has since been recalled, and the agency said that it “remains confident that all recalled iceberg lettuce related to this specific Cyclospora outbreak is off the market”. There’s no dressing up the hit the lettuce industry has taken. New price data released on Friday showed that lettuce prices dropped another 6.2% from July to August. Prices had already gone down 16.4% the month prior, the largest decrease in recent history. The economics behind food prices are often a mixed bag, but experts say there is a strong connection between lower lettuce prices and the cyclospora outbreak. As consumers learned about reports linking the parasite to iceberg lettuce, they stopped eating all types of greens. “That’s a very consistent case here,” said David Ortega, a food economics and policy professor at Michigan State University. “People cut back on not just all lettuce, or a lot of lettuce, but even other produce just out of fear.” This put many food chains in a crunch. Though Sweetgreen wasn’t linked to the outbreak, the salad chain cut its outlook for the year in August, citing a fall in foot traffic. Chipotle reported sales were down 2% in the second half of July, though the chain “maintains a very robust food safety program”. Taco Bell, which was directly linked to the outbreak, said it experienced a “meaningful” short-term impact on sales, though that had been “steadily improving”. Before the outbreak, lettuce prices were increasing due to other supply constraints, including adverse weather and disease that were affecting harvests, Ortega said. The drop in demand seems to have somewhat stabilized lettuce prices to where they were a year ago: from August 2025 to August 2026, prices dropped just 2.2%. It’s a tossup as to whether the drop in lettuce prices will alleviate any of the pain Americans have been feeling over higher prices. The ongoing war in Iran has boosted energy prices, with the US cost of diesel, which is essential for transportation within the supply chain, breaching $6 a gallon for the first time ever. Gas prices on average are $1.10 a gallon more expensive than last year, and fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, was up 52% for the year in August. Trump’s trade war with Canada, one of the US’s closest trading partners, is also expected to affect prices, with tariffs expected to affect everything from liquor to toilet paper. Canada is also a major agricultural trading partner with the US. Imports from Canada made up a total of 18.5% of the US’s total agricultural imports in 2025, according to the US Department of Agriculture. The US is Canada’s largest agricultural trading partner, buying up 60.3% of the country’s total agricultural exports. Over the last few days, Trump – who last month said that “prices are coming down very rapidly” – has started to acknowledge that the economy for US consumers isn’t as rosy as he has portrayed. He voiced his prediction that oil prices will go “tumbling downward” after the election, as Iran is “desperate to try and affect the election”. At the Republican convention, Trump said that he would give Americans a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans keep control of Congress after the midterms, a move critics said was a blatant bribe, and blamed Democrats for the higher prices.“I’m asking you to let us finish the job we began,” he said.

title: US lawmakers urge secretive British court to open up about Apple case
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Democrat Ron Wyden and Republican Warren Davidson tell investigatory powers tribunal that secrecy over encrypted data case is ‘needlessly’ straining US-UK relations
body_text: A bipartisan pair of American politicians is telling Britain’s most secretive court to stop hiding its handling of Apple’s legal fight against a government demand to break into its customers’ encrypted data, warning that Whitehall’s taste for secrecy is “needlessly” straining relations between the two allies. The letter, shared with the Guardian ahead of being sent to the investigatory powers tribunal (IPT) on Friday, is signed by the Democratic senator Ron Wyden of Oregon and the Republican congressman Warren Davidson of Ohio. The row dates back to January 2025, when the Home Office served Apple with a technical capability notice under the Investigatory Powers Act, which requires companies to assist law enforcement in providing evidence. The UK government demanded that Apple provide a mechanism to access encrypted iCloud backups worldwide, a call the company met by withdrawing its advanced data protection encryption feature from UK users the following month. Apple’s challenge to that order at the IPT was later thrown out after the Home Office withdrew the original notice and issued a narrower one targeting only British users’ data. “It is wholly inappropriate for a foreign executive body to attempt to dictate the distribution of powers within the US government, nor should it be permitted to use secrecy directives under the Investigatory Powers Act to frustrate article I powers under the US constitution,” the pair wrote. The Home Office has been approached for comment. In August this year, Apple lodged a fresh complaint at the tribunal challenging the government’s power to issue such notices at all, with a case-management hearing on how that claim will proceed now listed for this month – the very hearing the new letter is aimed at. Wyden and Davidson also signed an earlier letter to the tribunal in March 2025, alongside other lawmakers, pressing for the case to be heard in public. That intervention appears to have had an effect: weeks later the IPT rejected the government’s attempt to keep the case entirely secret, ruling that the “bare details” of Apple’s claim, including the identities of the parties, could be made public after receiving representations that, the tribunal noted, “strongly argued in favour of open justice and against the proceedings taking place in secret”. In the new letter, Wyden and Davidson write that Congress “is not only a co-equal branch of government, it is the First Branch”, and argue that no government can be allowed to place “its demands beyond the reach of legislative inquiry”. They accuse the Home Office of trying to use a foreign secrecy order to override the constitutional powers of the US legislature, after Apple told Congress it had been permitted to brief only the attorney general, the vice-president and their staff – but not lawmakers – about the dispute. They argue that Britain’s own constitutional traditions hold that no government can place its actions beyond the reach of legislative scrutiny – the same principle, they say, the Home Office is now violating. “The UK government,” they write, “cannot champion legislative oversight at home while using administrative gag orders to kneecap the constitutional authority of the US Congress.”

title: Republican seeking to implicate Abdul El-Sayed over 9/11 voted twice against benefits for first responders
author: Tom Perkins
summary: Mike Rogers has also helped kill other bills that would have provided healthcare to responders and survivors
body_text: Mike Rogers, a Michigan Republican US Senate candidate, has sought in recent weeks to create controversy over old tweets his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed posted about 9/11. He has for example, falsely suggested El-Sayed, who is Muslim, said the US deserved the attack. But, as critics have noted, Rogers has twice voted against healthcare and other benefits for 9/11 first responders and survivors, congressional records show. He has also helped kill other bills that would have provided benefits and healthcare to first responders nationwide. Rogers, a former member of Congress, is vying for Michigan’s open US Senate seat in a tight race that could decide control of Congress during the next session. Rogers was among Republicans who voted against the 2010 James Zadroga Act to fund healthcare for 9/11 first responders and survivors, which was used in part to treat and monitor 40,000 people who worked in toxic conditions in the attack’s aftermath. The bills’ funding also helped treat responders for more than 50 types of cancer linked to exposures at Ground Zero. In committee, Rogers argued it “jeopardizes the financial health of the United States”. Rogers was joined by 156 other Republicans who voted against it, largely over its $5.1bn price tag, but 17 GOP members broke from the party and supported it. The final package passed the House over Rogers’ vote. That drew sharp criticism this week from John Feal, a 9/11 first responder who has advocated and lobbied for legislation supporting benefit programs, and who spent 11 weeks in the hospital after a steel beam fell on his foot at ground zero. Part of his foot was amputated. Feal told the Guardian he personally discussed the Zadroga legislation with Rogers on Congress’s floor during committee debate in which Feal testified. Feal said Rogers told him first responders’ health issues were a “New York problem” and asked: “Where is the money to help them going to come from?” He called Rogers’ opposition to 9/11 first responder benefits “a betrayal”. “Here’s the thing: Republicans like Mike Rogers love cops and firefighters until one gets shot or burned in a fire and can’t do his job,” Feal said. “That’s their playbook. They say: ‘You’re a hero. Oh, wait, you’re sick? You’re a drain on the municipality and the federal government. Get out of here.’” In response to the Guardian, the Rogers campaign said: “Any attempt to distract from Abdul making Hasan [Piker] the centerpiece of his campaign is incredibly disrespectful to the thousands of Americans who lost their lives that day.” Alyssa Brouillet, a spokesperson for the Rogers campaign, pointed to a 2019 comment the popular Twitch streamer made in which he said “America deserved 9/11”. (Piker has since apologized and walked back the comments soon after, stating that they were a poor attempt at satire. El-Sayed called the comments “dumb” and disavowed them. ) The revelation comes after Rogers sent an email to supporters criticizing El-Sayed over his 9/11 comments, and appeared to lie about seeing Osama bin Laden’s body. In a bold-typed section of the email, Rogers wrote: “I saw the dead body of Osama bin Laden with my own eyes, knowing that together, we had delivered justice for America.” But Rogers was not in Pakistan when Bin Laden was killed by US special forces, nor was he in the White House Situation Room, where then president Barack Obama and senior administration officials followed the raid. Republicans faced enormous backlash in 2010 for their votes against the Zagroda legislation. Feal at the time told CBS News: “Whatever member of Congress voted against this bill, whether Republican or Democrat, should go to jail for manslaughter.” In 2002, Rogers voted against adding additional funding for veterans’ healthcare and first responders to a bill that compensated NYC schools for 9/11-related expenses. In 2011, Rogers voted for a homeland security appropriations bill that was controversial over its deep cuts to funding for state and local first responders, as well as terrorism prevention funding. Several Republicans voted against it because of those issues. In 2013 and 2014, Rogers voted against amendments for budget legislation that included billions in funding for first responders. And in 2013 he voted against a proposal to protect pensions for first responders. Henry Yanez, a retired Michigan firefighter, now a city council member in Sterling Heights, a suburb of Detroit, who has endorsed El-Sayed, was among those who went to New York City to support their fire departments in the 9/11 attack’s wake. He criticized Rogers for his votes. “When you’re talking about the health and safety of our first responders, and now you’re going to kick the can down the road, you know – that’s a problem as far as I’m concerned,” Yanez said. “Mike Rogers – shame on him.” Yanez said he was especially surprised because other Republicans in Michigan have supported first responders, and Rogers was an FBI agent. “He should get it,” Yanez said. Feal said he believes Rogers’ opposition to the bills is disqualifying. “Many members of Congress think they’re untouchable until they get humbled and get beat in an election,” Feal said. “Rogers is not invincible, and he’s just in this for himself.”

title: Corrections and clarifications
author: Corrections and clarifications column editor
summary: Verbatim Investigations | Francois Pienaar | Ian Charleson
body_text: • Verbatim Investigations, which was behind the recent undercover sting on Reform UK, was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, not the “US Center for Climate Reporting” as an editorial said (5 September, Journal, p2). • It was Francois Pienaar, not Joel Stransky, who captained South Africa’s Rugby World Cup-winning side in 1995 (All Blacks brace for Bok-lash as Erasmus throws in plot twist, 29 August, Sport, p12). • The Scottish actor Ian Charleson, star of Chariots of Fire, did not train at Bristol Old Vic but the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art, before joining London’s Young Vic (Late actor’s final role inspires film encore, 5 September, p15). Other recently amended articles include: US citizens will receive $5,000 if Republicans win midterms, Trump claims in lengthy convention speech Woolworths increased prices of at least four ‘family staples’ during ‘Price Freeze’ promotion Francophiles, Norman outfits and broken threads: visitors see Bayeux tapestry in UK for first time Editorial complaints and correction requests can be sent to: guardian.readers@theguardian.com. title: Republican senator fires aide who used Nazi soldiers as Facebook profile picture
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: Washington Post report also reveals Jon Husted staffer Stephen Woytek created pro-Rhodesia playlist on Spotify
body_text: The Republican senator for Ohio, Jon Husted, has fired an aide who was discovered to have used a photo of Nazi SS soldiers as his Facebook profile photo. Stephen Woytek was appointed as Husted’s political director last month in the senator’s knife-edge re-election contest against former Democrat senator Sherrod Brown. According to the Washington Post, Husted had decided to “part ways” with Woytek, 25, after learning that his Facebook profile showed he followed a military re-enactment group called LAH Living History Unit, which portrays the 1st SS Panzer division. The group’s website says its members dress up as the Leibstandarte, a Waffen-SS armored division that began as Adolf Hitler’s bodyguards. LAH says the Leibstandarte “came to symbolize the highest dedication to duty and individual as well as collective loyalty”. The group claims to be “non-political” and insists is disavows “political and religious persecution” that happened the second world war. A Spotify playlist recently created by an account bearing Woytek’s name hailed the former racist white-minority regime of Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe, seen as a symbol of white supremacy by some racist groups. In a statement, a spokesperson for Husted said the campaign had ended its relationship with Woytek. “While he denies negative intent, his social media activity displays a complete lack of judgement and disregard for its impact on others,” the spokesperson said. “Senator Husted demands better of those who represent him. Upon learning about the social media posts today, Senator Husted made the immediate decision to part ways.” The campaign did not respond to the Post’s questions about whether and how Woytek’s social media activity had been vetted before his appointment, the newspaper reported. Woytek’s departure follows a series of damaging episodes in which young Republicans groups have been discovered expressing pro-Nazi sympathies in group chats and internet forums. And in Georgia, Republican congressman Mike Collins’s campaign for Senate has been shaken by controversies involving his staff’s online activity. This summer, Collins replaced top aide, Kip Talley, after Slate revealed he had been part of a group chat with white supremacists. Woytek, who serves in the national guard and was a graduate of the Citadel, a military academy based in Charleston, South Carolina, issued a statement of regret, saying he wished he had “exercised better judgment when posting about my activities online”. “I want to be unequivocal: I reject the racist and antisemitic ideology the SS and Nazi Germany represented. I believe it is important to educate our younger generations, which is why I participate in historical reenactments,” he said. LAH shared a photo on a Flickr account that showed Woytek in 2018 – when he was 16 – wearing an SS uniform and marching in an area adorned with Nazi flags. Woytek follows several suppliers of SS uniforms on his Facebook page. On a Quora account bearing his name, Woytek also answered a question on whether anything good had occurred under Hitler, writing in 2017 “that Hitler started an anti-smoking campaign”. More recently, he created a public playlist of pro-Rhodesia songs on Spotify called “Tales from Rhodesia”, which is captioned: “Homesick for a place that no longer exists.” One of the songs uses a slur to refer to African troops. The former British colony’s white minority government fought a long war against guerrilla groups after issuing a unilateral declaration of independence in 1965. The country was officially recognized as Zimbabwe under black majority rule in 1980, a year after the minority government accepted its rule was unsustainable and entered peace negotiations. Rhodesia has been used by white supremacists as a symbol of the supposed superiority of white rule.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian developers used AI to build ‘kamikaze’ attack drone software, Anthropic says
author: Guardian staff and agencies
summary: Anthropic also found that hackers used AI in attacks against targets in Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic sectors.
body_text: A small team of likely freelance developers in Russia used AI chatbot Claude to develop software for an autonomous swarm of first-person-view “kamikaze” attack drones, including terminal guidance, target selection and coordination between multiple aircraft, according to Anthropic, the company that developed Claude. In a 154-page report describing how bad actors used its Claude AI system for state-sponsored surveillance and propaganda operations, Anthropic said the drone swarm was programmed to pick its own targets and crash into them to detonate, without a human making the final call. In their programming, the freelance team repeatedly picked a location in Ukraine’s Donetsk region as their target and used VPNs to circumvent Anthropic’s geographic blocks. Small drones have become a ‌central weapon in the war in Ukraine. Anthropic ‌also found that cybercriminals and state-backed hackers are increasingly using AI to orchestrate and execute large portions of cyber-attacks, including in attacks targeting officials in Ukraine. One hacking group allegedly ran phishing, hotel wifi hijacking and WhatsApp-takeover operations against targets in the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic sectors, using AI at nearly every stage, Anthropic said. The group’s tradecraft was consistent with Russia-based threat actor Midnight Blizzard, which the US government has previously linked to Russia’s SVR foreign intelligence service, Reuters reported. The Russian embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The group allegedly used AI to build a system that automatically detected when its malware was flagged by security defences and rewrote the code until it evaded detection. The Anthropic report comes as petrol stations in Kyiv have been hit by jet-powered drones in a wave of targeted Russian attacks as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity. At least two people were killed and 12 injured in strikes on two petrol stations on Friday morning, according to the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. The rush-hour strikes follow a similar attack on a petrol station on Thursday. All three strikes targeted petrol stations operated by Ukrnafta, a state-owned oil and natural gas extraction company. A list of 18 petrol stations in Kyiv expected to be hit by Russian drones started circulating on Telegram on Wednesday. The three struck so far were on the list. Russian president Vladimir Putin has blamed the west for the conflict in Ukraine because of what he said was its constant pressure on Moscow and its attempts to “drag” Ukraine into the Nato alliance. Speaking to reporters before the BRICS summit in India, Putin said “everything happening in Europe right now is basically ‌the result of system errors by … the western globalists in politics, security, and economics”. After a Russia-friendly president was forced to flee Ukraine in 2014, he said the West “immediately set the goal of dragging Ukraine into Nato. And this ‌ultimately turned out to be the main reason for today’s tragic events in Ukraine”. He said people in Europe understood what was going on, which explained why they were voting for far-right parties such as the AfD in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt. A Russian official will attend a G20 energy meeting in Houston next week, a White House official said on Friday. Last month, the US welcomed ⁠Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov to a meeting of G20 countries in North Carolina, upsetting European officials because it was the first time Russia’s finance ⁠minister had attended the forum in person since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. The meeting comes as European Union efforts to become independent from Russian oil and gas are faltering, as it heads into winter with low gas stocks, its auditors said this month. The US House of Representatives is expected to take up a tough Russian sanctions package next week, although prospects of passage are uncertain despite the bill receiving overwhelming support in the Senate. The bill is designed to add pressure on Putin to negotiate an end to Russia’s war with Ukraine. However, several top Democratic lawmakers are worried the measure dramatically expands president Donald Trump’s tariff authority, and he would use that new power to go after US allies. Three people were killed in Russian ⁠strikes in southeastern Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia ⁠regions and in Kharkiv in the northeast, according to the governors of those regions. Russia has for two weeks been carrying out almost constant attacks with faster jet-powered drones that have killed a number of ⁠Kyiv residents and disrupted daily life in Ukraine’s capital. Ukraine also carried out drone attacks on Russia, killing two people in the Tula region overnight and one on Friday in the Kursk region, local officials said.
