title: Naomi Klein: ‘Extreme wealth has a deranging effect. It turns you into a supremacist’
author: Zoe Williams
summary: She’s tackled neoliberalism and the digital world, now the writer and activist is taking on tech billionaires. She explains how the super-rich are capitalising on climate and financial chaos in pursuit of power
body_text: Naomi Klein’s new book starts on a mountaintop with two “faithful men gathering an audience to share their vision”. It’s a vision of a paradise city, gated at every entrance, no need for weapons there, everyone in it rich. One of the men has tears in his eyes as he describes its beauty. The opening scene of End Times Fascism, co-written with Astra Taylor, is not a metaphor, however. The men are Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. The year is 2026, the mountain is Davos. The paradise city will be called New Gaza. The World Economic Forum get-together in Davos, Switzerland, has always had a twin purpose – to provide a platform for the super-rich to describe all the good they are doing on poverty and climate, and to give us a glimpse into their enviable lives. This year what we witnessed was, quite brazenly, the world’s richest men gathering to discuss the real estate possibilities of a mass grave. At that same Davos, Donald Trump announced his Board of Peace for the reconstruction of Gaza – it has delivered nothing substantial in the seven months since, but more significantly, Klein says, “we’re being hit with so many extraordinary events that it’s hard to hold on to what a big deal it is: they have announced a privatised United Nations”. “I think we understand that wealth compounds, right? Certainly rich people understand that wealth compounds,” Klein continues, speaking to me from her peaceful, roomy study in British Columbia. “But I don’t feel like we spend a lot of time really thinking about the implications of what it means for that much wealth to be compounded, and what that does psychologically. Part of the new shamelessness we’re seeing is just what happens when this amount of financial, mediagenic, technological and military weaponry is concentrated in the hands of this very small, unaccountable group of people. They stop trying to seduce us in any way.” Klein looks calm and curious as she delivers this message. She has a ready laugh. But then, she had the same unruffled, buoyant delivery when I interviewed her on stage in Manchester for Doppelgänger, her 2023 book in which she described how the digital world is destroying our connection to reality, and one another. In 1999, when her breakthrough work No Logo was published, she seemed exhilaratingly certain, at 29, that neoliberalism was bringing harm that we couldn’t yet even see the extent of, and nonetheless appeared centred and happy in the world. Somehow she manages to maintain this attitude, even though the news she delivers is always so convincingly, unbelievably bad. End Times Fascism describes the world we’re in, where the components of authoritarianism are modelled everywhere you look: anarcho-libertarian economics in Argentina, the destruction of a free press in Russia, the erosion of democratic institutions in Hungary (until Viktor Orbán was deposed), “anti-immigrant neofascism” in Italy, the weaponisation of trans identity by Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil, Islamophobia in Modi’s India. But this is fascism with a difference. Its proponents are actively willing an apocalypse, or a wave of interconnected apocalypses brought forth by climate change and financial chaos, to hasten us towards a post-democratic world in which only a rich few survive to prosper. This book started as an article in the Guardian, “which went totally viral,” Klein says. “Astra and I knew there was a lot more reporting to do, but on a personal level, did we want to spend the next year in the minds of these people, in these cultures? Then Astra said, ‘I’m down the rabbit hole, I’m gonna be listening to these guys anyway. So I may as well feel like I’m doing something about it.’ This is the reason it’s the first book I’ve co-written. When you go to dark, scary places, it’s nice to bring a friend.” Astra Taylor is also a writer, activist and documentary maker, and founded the Debt Collective, a fascinating experiment in building structured, quasi-unionised solidarity around personal debt, with the long term goals of abolishing student tuition fees, nationalising healthcare and building tenant power. In the book, Klein and Taylor introduce us to the religious fundamentalists, Christian Zionists and Christian Nationalists in the US, readying themselves for the second coming. Describing a “bunkered state”, the authors connect climate-related disasters, a rabid anti-immigrant standing army in the form of ICE and a politics built on false promises and misinformation to depict a febrile, riven society that doesn’t know what to believe. But the truly terrifying bit is the bridging section, on tech billionaires. The super-rich have apocalypse fantasies of their own, built not on faith or ideology but on a calm and rational evaluation of how best to maintain their position; they would genuinely rather reign in hell than share in heaven. And they have all the money to make sure they get there. “These are trends I’ve been following for a long time,” Klein says. “The privatised enclave born of shock, of disaster, I saw when I was reporting from Iraq. There’s the image of the Green Zone, this Emerald City run by the US in the middle of Baghdad, built by Halliburton and all of these private contractors, with the power to appoint a viceroy. In the final parts of The Shock Doctrine [2007], I talk about how these contractors migrated [from Iraq] to Hurricane Katrina, and the idea that these climate disasters are their next growth frontier. Reporters started calling New Orleans ‘Baghdad on the Bayou’. The gang’s all here, there’s Halliburton, there’s Bechtel, there’s Blackwater.” But, and she cannot stress this enough, as useful as it is to know the recent history of these trends, you should not take comfort from the idea that you’ve seen it all before. “I have found the image of a spiral really useful, in terms of how to make sense of the fact that our era is both familiar and different,” Klein says. “The thing about a spiral is that you’re going round, but you’re not going to the same place. If the spiral is pointing down, it’s deeper, it’s tighter, it’s carrying more velocity, it’s carrying more force, it’s carrying more heat, it’s carrying more violence.” The image is at once poetic and extremely sobering. She proffers a brief morale boost, like someone handing you a slice of orange on your way into a war zone. “You can flip a spiral – it goes outwards, it’s the spiral of the universe.” At the moment we’re in now, when crises and disasters hit so frequently that we’re in a constant state of disorientation and shock, the status quo isn’t static, it’s always getting worse. “There’s this impulse to read history,” Klein says. “We’ve seen it again and again. After 9/11, people were suddenly reading history books about Afghanistan and Iraq, Chomsky, trying to find their bearings. We saw it again during the pandemic, people were reading about the plagues of the past. But there’s a trap in believing that everything has happened before, that there is not a compounding effect of history. After Donald Trump was re-elected, I’ll be honest with you, Shock Doctrine sales went crazy. People were saying, ‘It’s exactly like you said,’ and I was thinking, ‘I don’t think it is’.” The neoliberal age – for brevity let’s call it the period between the end of the cold war and Covid – was “capitalism lying on the couch in its underwear, going ‘what are you gonna do, leave me?’ In the cold war, a little competition went a long way – after the collapse of the Soviet Union, that competition is lost, capitalism stopped trying.” But there was a vulnerability to being super-rich in those days, because whether you’d come by your wealth through privatisation politics in the US or Europe, or by hastier, more kleptocratic means in ex-communist states, it was plainly public wealth that you’d captured. “So they would stage these seduction rituals, whether it was at Davos or Aspen, or at Ted, or the Clinton Global Initiative. They’d say, ‘We are going to cure the sick, and we are going to fund your schools in this new and exciting way, don’t worry about us. Don’t be afraid of our wealth. This is actually a new way of redistributing for the public good.’” I distinctly remember that world: huge conferences like the Skoll foundation awards, where journalists would be wined and dined while watching immensely rich people hand out £20,000 prizes to grassroots clean water initiatives in Kenya. To be fair, in the era before and directly after the financial crash, there were plenty of dissenting voices about capitalist benevolence solving intractable problems like inequality. Many people, Klein at their vanguard, pointed out that it smelled like a scam. But while we were having that discussion, the wealth agenda moved on. In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, at the Faena Hotel in Miami, Peter Thiel hosted panel discussions titled “the enemy”, naming sustainable development goals, “precautionary principles” and “social responsibility” as those foes, rounded off with an “apocalypse ball”-themed fancy dress party . Some of the costumes, Klein and Taylor write, were “a doctor of eugenics’’; a “Haitian chef with a bloodied cat toy hanging out of his apron [a reference to the Springfield immigrant pet‑eating hoax, which spread in 2024, repeated by both Trump and JD Vance]; a couple wearing pagers as a ha-ha reference to Israel’s murderous attack in Lebanon.” Thiel has been explicitly anti-democracy for years, writing in 2009, “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” But other tech billionaires have had a complete volte face. “Jeff Bezos renamed a stadium in Seattle the Climate Pledge Arena, and gave out Earth prizes,” Klein points out. Elon Musk invested in electric cars and once saw himself as a saviour figure. “Any time anyone was in trouble, Musk would rush in to save them, ‘I shall save Puerto Rico’, ‘I shall save the children stuck down the mine’. It’s fun to be a superhero, right? But if you’re going to be a superhero, you should be worshipped. And people stopped worshiping them.” Now, the climate pledges are gone, replaced by a performed nihilism around averting climate crisis, coupled with a determination to build ever more data centres. “We’re not dealing with stupid people who don’t understand climate change,” Klein says. “We’re dealing with people who know very clearly what it means to wire together 35 gas turbines in Memphis.” (It means gargantuan energy and water use, as well as the destruction of air and sound quality in the vicinity, all for Musk to power Grok, his intermittently Nazi large language model.) The speed with which previously Democrat-leaning billionaires fell in behind Trump in 2024 was jaw-dropping. “I don’t think that Mark Zuckerberg’s phase of seeming to care deeply about democracy and climate change was real,” Klein says. “He reincarnates as whatever is good for his business. Figures like Thiel and Musk, where there is real ideology there, are easier to understand than figures like Bezos and Zuckerberg, where it really does feel like there’s no there there, they’re just uninteresting guys that ended up massively rich.” She’s passingly interested in what combination of events created these men, many of whom were forged in the dotcom boom, when they were worshipped as gods, pictured on the cover of Time magazine in gold thrones. There’s an element of ego rage, that we just aren’t grateful enough. Ultimately, though, “we end the book concluding that wealth has its own deranging effects. It almost inevitably turns you into a supremacist because humans are creatures of story and you need a story to rationalise, why you? Why do you have so much in a time of so much want and need? And the only possible story that’s available is that there’s something about you that justifies it.” There’s a new goading quality to the talking points of the super-rich – explicit eugenicism and Islamophobia, raw delight in the prospect of AI wiping out our jobs. It almost feels as though they’re daring us to rebel, just so that they can prove that rebellion is fruitless. On that, though, Klein would disagree. It is not beyond our collective means to build a wealth disarmament movement, or a tech disarmament movement. She points to the Pearson brothers, KeShaun and Justin, fighting Musk’s Colossus 2 data centre in Memphis: “the way they so consciously root their struggle in the history of the civil rights movement, and the environmental justice movement in Memphis, going back to the formerly enslaved people who built Boxtown. This is where MLK was murdered, assassinated after marching with the sanitation workers in Memphis.” KeShaun Pearson leads Memphis Community Against Pollution, which has had major wins against oil pipelines, the industrial release of carcinogenic chemicals, and is now mobilising against data centres. Justin is running for Congress. In End Times Fascism, Klein and Taylor raise Walter Benjamin’s concept “jetztzeit”, literally “now time”, a moment so pregnant with the spirit, the urgency of revolution that it marshals the energy of all movements that went before it. Again, it’s poetic, but it’s also literal, observable. If we want to oppose this new fascist strain, we really have to get a move on. “I don’t tend to use this language, I try to be measured, but I think I’ve earned the right to escalate,” she says. “The moment we’re in, people are really mad and however mad you are, it’s not enough. Because there is something so profound about no longer believing in the future, about seeing no value in our shared home, in the natural world. They’re traitors to creation.” Klein doesn’t want for reasons to fight. “I’ve made a choice to live very close to nature in a pretty wild part of British Columbia,” she says. “On a dark night, it’s a blanket of stars. And now we see so many of what I call Elon’s space bugs [Starlink satellites] just crawling through the sky. He wants to increase that a hundredfold. Who said he could? Who gave him that right? That’s a place where I find my anger. I get really angry about the stars. I get really angry about the orcas. I get really angry about Gaza. Other people will find their anger somewhere else. We have to find our places of deepest love and fight like hell.” • End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor is published by Allen Lane on 15 September. title: Tensions simmer on US-Canada border for two towns relying on each other
author: Rachel Leingang in International Falls, Minnesota
summary: Canadians ‘angry’ at Trump for suggesting Canada should become 51st state, says mayor, as US businesses see sales fall amid trade war
body_text: Like many Canadians, Tom Reid isn’t crossing the US-Canada border as often these days. But he needed a haircut. The woman who cuts his hair lives in International Falls, Minnesota – her “sister is married to my wife’s cousin”, he explained – and so Reid, whose duty free shop in Fort Frances, Ontario, has to travel to her. That’s how it goes for the residents of the two towns, divided by the Rainy River and an international border. They’re longtime friends and, in many cases, family. People cross the border frequently to shop, dine, go bowling, take their kids to sports and visit each other. But Trump’s trade war against the US’s northern neighbor, and his derogatory comments about their country, has Canadians – known for their politeness – angry. Furious, actually. They’re shopping less at US businesses, and, in an unusual show of patriotism, encouraging consumers to “buy Canadian instead”. Reid is buying Canadian more and more, he said at the register in his shop, with the Canadian flag on the wall behind him. “I don’t have that much choice, eh?” he said. *** American business owners have seen declines in Canadian sales, while grappling with the uncertainty and costs associated with tariffs on their products. With tourist season winding down, and the leaves starting to change into yellows and oranges, the two towns are quieter. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs went into force this week, though no one who lived in the towns had seen that directly reflected in prices yet. It was the latest heated battle between the two countries in the last nearly two years. The mayors of the two towns call each other friends, and signed a joint declaration in 2025 affirming that friendship after Trump retook the White House. The flags of Minnesota, Ontario, both towns, and both countries fly outside the town offices in Fort Frances. But there’s only so much – and really, nothing – that a local official can do to blunt the economic effects of slipshod tariffs put in place by one man, more than a thousand miles away in Washington. Hoping for the best Most Canadians recognize this, according to Andrew Hallikas, the mayor of Fort Frances. They like Americans, and Fort Frances residents can relate to Minnesotans a lot: they share similar interests, in the outdoors and in community, he said. But they’re “irate” at Trump – for bullying their country, for going against an ally – and for suggesting Canada should become the 51st US state. “You cannot imagine how angry that makes us,” Hallikas said. “Please quote me on this. I cannot make this clear enough: we will never become the 51st state. We consider ourselves to probably be the best country in the world in which to live, and we’re quite content to remain that way, thank you very much.” For two towns that rely on each other, the tension of the trade war simmers underneath the surface. They all want it to end. They don’t know how, or when, it will. As the Guardian interviewed the mayor of International Falls at a coffee shop on the town’s main drag, a Fort Frances resident interjected angrily to tell the mayor that Canadians are “so pissed off” at Trump for how he’s attacked their country and that International Falls needed Canadians to survive. Their town was suffering, and their businesses losing longtime customers from Canada, because of it, he said. “I’m originally from the Falls, but I’m an American living in Canada,” the man said. “I’m scared to put that American flag on my shirt, what he’s done.” Residents, and the leaders of the towns, are worried about how they will rebuild the relationship between their two countries if this continues for much longer. Businesses will find other suppliers. Shoppers will replace their favorites with homegrown options. The sense of nationalism hardens. “We just hope for the best at this point,” said the International Falls mayor, Drake Dill. *** Grant Hauschild, a Democratic Minnesota state senator who represents 65% of the state’s border with Canada, said he’s heard from businesses that have lost up to 30% of their revenue from Canadians. With people already struggling with inflation and high costs, he said a hit like that goes from “a concern to devastation”. “My hope is, of course, that the relationship goes back to normal once we pass these chaotic times,” Hauschild said. “I think that’s what really scares me most … Even if people want to go back to the way things were, they might have unfortunately kind of moved on – and moved beyond – the relationship.” Two towns, one community To cross the Rainy River into either side, people use a toll bridge, with the cost for an average car now $10. They present documents to customs agents on whichever side they’re entering, and answer questions about their purpose in town. People who cross regularly recognize the agents and ask after their families. The main parts of each respective town sit on either side of the crossing, with both towns initially growing around paper mills. Fort Frances’ mill has since closed; International Falls’ is still running. Fort Frances is larger than International Falls, and because Canada is more sparse, Fort Frances serves as a regional hub. Its hospital will soon be getting an MRI machine – a huge boon for its aging population. The shops on either side carry gifts from both countries, catering to tourists who fly in to fish, mostly for walleye, and largely on the Canadian side. In a Fort Frances store, kids books called “Little Minnesota” and “Little Canada” sat right beside each other on a shelf. In International Falls, shelves of souvenir cups carried designs for International Falls and Canada. While Canadian flags line the shop windows and fly throughout downtown Fort Frances, Hallikas said this is not a reflection of increased patriotism, but just a border town welcoming visitors to their country. The two towns are “neighbors by geography, but we are friends by choice”, he said. “The bridge is over 100 years old, and we’ve been going back and forth it for over 100 years,” Hallikas said. “Before that, there was a ferry. But our friendship is still going to exist when Trump is long gone.” *** Dill, the International Falls mayor, owned a business and lived in Canada for 11 years. Many of his friends are Canadian. This fall, he will go up to an island in Canada to meet up with friends. “There’s no politics in that. There’s no thought of exchange rate, or trade war, or tariffs. It’s just – we’re friends,” he said. “But then you come home and you talk and you watch the news. … I would be really disappointed if it gets to a point where we can’t work through it, and there’s a fundamental change that will hurt International Falls significantly.” Residents on both sides have favorite products they grab whenever they cross. For Heather Johnson, executive director of the Fort Frances chamber of commerce, it’s Top the Tater, an iconic Minnesota chive and onion dip. She also checks prices on cheeses, and peruses the wider variety of pastas for sale in US stores. Johnson bowls weekly in a league in International Falls, made up of both Americans and Canadians. Leanne Guba, a Canadian who owns Hometown Hobby and Crafts in International Falls, crosses back into her home country once or twice a month, usually walking across the bridge, to buy ketchup chips, chocolate bars and Dad’s brand oatmeal chocolate chip cookies. American liquor is no longer on the shelves at government-run Ontario liquor stores, by order of Premier Doug Ford. The push to buy Canadian is “pretty well elbows-up”, Johnson said. “I’m drinking Canadian red wine now.” ‘Mr T took care of that’ Reid, the duty-free shop owner, said the tourist season was about average for him, with no noticeable decline in sales. He has seen some change in his customers. A couple of years ago, they’d come in with the signature red Maga (Make America Great Again) hats. Last year, not as many. This year, he didn’t see any red hats, and customers would tell him they didn’t vote for Trump. They’ll ask about the missing American bourbon from his shelves, and he’ll tell them, “Mr T took care of that”. He used to cross the border to go to a show, or the grocery store, or Menard’s, a hardware store, but not anymore. His daughter and her husband used to cross weekly for a date night and shopping, but no longer. People over here are “really upset” with Trump, he said. It has renewed his sense of Canadian pride, but “I’ve always had good pride”. Johnson, whose kids are now grown, said: “I’m glad that my kids grew up knowing both countries, and they know that there really isn’t a difference in people.” *** Across the border in International Falls, craft store owner Guba said she was seeing fewer Canadians, for several reasons. They’re dealing with rising costs, too, and the exchange rate is unfavorable. Some of it is politics, she said. Canadian regulars are coming less frequently. “They’re definitely being a little more picky about when they come over or being more careful about what they buy,” she said. The decline, while dealing with unpredictable tariffs on goods she brings in from overseas, has had an impact on her business. She’s adapted by seeking out new suppliers, bringing in new merchandise lines, and trying to reduce costs. She has a few companies she orders from in Canada – including a toy brand and a puzzle company – and expects the new tariffs will likely increase costs on those products. People are upset about the political dynamics, but they don’t tend to vent their political frustrations openly, she said. There may be the odd joke here and there, but not usually full-blown political debate. “We tend to try to stay friendly,” she said. The latest tourist season was “decent”, she said. “Overall, we’re still surviving … You can’t really control it.” ‘We remain neutral’ It’s tough to gauge the full impact of declining Canadian spending in the border town, though anecdotally, people are noticing it. The International Falls chamber of commerce would not comment on the impact of the tariffs on the town, or the deteriorating relationship between the two countries. “We remain neutral on political matters so that we can best serve our diverse membership, which includes individuals and organizations with a wide range of views. Because of that, the Chamber does not have an official comment on the political issues surrounding the US-Canada relationship,” the chamber said in an email. Isaac Johnson, who owns the Coffee Landing café in International Falls and lives above it with his wife, said he still sees a lot of Canadians who come over to grab espresso and breakfast. He loves his Canadian customers, including the couple he watched meet up at the coffee shop from across the border. They later married. The locals are caught in the middle of political games, said Johnson, who tries to just focus on himself, his family, and his faith. But people do get emotional about it at times, and “if you definitely bring up politics, for sure,” he said – just as the man who confronted Dill, the mayor, did. The man, who didn’t share his name or want to have a longer conversation with a reporter, said he’s noticed far fewer Canadians around town, nothing like it used to be. He described Canadians as “very pissed off” and said snowbirds were selling their houses in the US. International Falls voters went for Trump in 2024. These broader issues, like the trade war, “pit us against each other”, Johnson said, noting that the man got mad at the mayor “over a guy that’s making billions off us all”. “I love the Canadians, I love Americans, and I love them coming over here and enjoying what we have here, and we can go and enjoy what they have,” Johnson said. *** Dill, the town’s mayor, said Canadians are “definitely” not coming to International Falls as much as they were, though he thinks it has more to do with the exchange rate. Still, he said later, “we need all the Canadian commerce we can get, and I would like to think they feel the same way”. Local officials are in a tough position. They have no control over the tariffs, though with their communities at the center of the impact, they are expected to answer questions and concerns over levies. They have no direct line to the Trump administration, if that would even make a difference. And their communities are suffering. Hope springs eternal Hauschild, the Minnesota state senator, said he meets regularly with the Canadian consulate in St Paul, and reiterates his belief in a strong relationship with Canada. But as a state lawmaker, he has little to no control over any of it, beyond using his bully pulpit. Hallikas, the Fort Frances mayor, said most Canadians have “no rancor for individual Americans” and treat them kindly when they visit, largely avoiding talking about Trump or American politics. Americans will have to work to undo the damage Trump has done to the relationship between the two countries, and that will take time, even after the trade war simmers down or ends, he said. “But we’ll still be friends with the folks in Minnesota and International Falls,” Hallikas said. Dill said he doesn’t often run into the frustrations directed at him by the man in the coffee shop, though it happens. He doesn’t have any way he can directly fix the issue. “The US elected our current president and he has his own agenda and I don’t see that I can stop it,” he said. “I don’t want it to affect us locally. We’ll see. Hope springs eternal. I mean, I thought that everything was going along fine, but apparently it wasn’t.” The uncertainty of it all is “frustrating”, and he’s most curious about where it all lands, when a truce could be signed so that businesses can have a sense of comfort in planning for their futures. The two countries are engaged in a heated dispute – or a “donnybrook,” as they would say in Canada, noted Dill. He likened the current situation to two longtime best friends, who hunted and fished and vacationed together for years – until one of them said, you’ve been taking advantage of me for years. “That’s like driving a nail in a fence,” he said, “and then you pull it out, and even if the fence still stands, there’s a hole where the nail was.”

title: Trump personality cult alive and well in Dallas – will it power Republican midterm success?
author: David Smith in Dallas
summary: President the star of the show at two-day convention, but party’s plan to treat November elections as referendum on Trump himself poses grave risks
body_text: “We’re going to have a good time listening to music,” Donald Trump told thousands of supporters in downtown Dallas before handing the mic to an opera singer, “because I’m getting a little bit tired of politics now.” Millions of Americans seem tired of politics after a decade dominated by Trump. So the US president’s decision to close out this week’s first ever Republican midterm convention with a plea – treat November’s congressional elections as a referendum on Trump himself – was received by his Democratic opponents with glee. They saw the president’s core pitch as a combination of begging and bribery. First he urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot”. Then he promised $5,000 payouts to every US adult if Republicans retain control of the House of Representatives and Senate in November. Andy Beshear, the Democratic governor of Kentucky, told reporters on Thursday: “If Donald Trump wants to hold a convention saying this election is about him, I fully support his decision. He’s telling me to pretend that he is on the ballot – I want people to pretend that he is on the ballot.” But with hundreds of members of Congress and candidates staying away from the convention, most seats in the upper tier remained empty both nights. Trump’s keynote speech drew a modest 2.5 million viewers on Fox News, ⁠according to ⁠Nielsen data. Some attendees expressed discontent over the cost of living and Iran war while starting to look beyond the president to potential successors in 2028. With Trump’s approval rating at a historic low, it was far from certain that the two-day “Trump-a-palooza” will have the desired effect of galvanising the party’s base and recreating the turnout that powered his 2016 and 2024 presidential election victories. Holding a convention in a midterm year was an attempt to make history in order to defy history. The party that holds the White House typically suffers midterm losses: George W Bush’s Republicans took a “thumping” in 2006, while Barack Obama’s Democrats endured a “shellacking” in 2010. The omens this year are no less foreboding: the Decision Desk HQ website projects that Democrats are poised to capture the House of Representatives 229-206, with the Senate hanging on a knife-edge at 50-50. The spectacle in Dallas was rapidly pulled together at Trump’s behest after the host committee raised $45m in three weeks. It had some familiar trappings, including tall state delegations on the convention floor, fiery speeches and a celebratory balloon drop at the end, but no nominations or formal business. And there was no doubt who was the star of the show. Trump’s image was everywhere in the corridors of the American Airlines Center. Attendees wore clothes with phrases such as “Trump tribe”, “Trump has our back” and “Proud deplorable”. Speaker after speaker lavished him with effusive praise. Among them was Robert Kennedy Jr, the health secretary, who recalled their meeting soon after Trump survived a shooting in Butler, Pennsylvania: “I discovered a self-effacing man of superior intelligence, of empathy and compassion, with an encyclopedic grasp of the issues in molecular detail. And most of all, a near reckless courage to challenge vested interests and official orthodoxies.” But while the Trump personality cult was alive and well, another theme was just as prominent. Unable to point to falling grocery bills or peace in the Middle East, the convention leaned heavily into fear, painting a nightmarish portrait of what the US would look like with the Democrats back in charge. Images of the influencer Hasan Piker and other leftwing figures loomed ominously on giant video screens. A narrator’s voice boomed: “Today’s extreme left hasn’t simply moved away from Republicans. It has moved away from Democrats in its own party. Far beyond the common sense of the American people. This is no longer simply Republican versus Democrat or conservative versus liberal. Today, the choice is unmistakable. Extreme versus mainstream.” Numerous speeches sought to whip up a new red scare. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent warned that Democrats wanted to transform the US into a “socialist hellscape” while House Speaker Mike Johnson framed the midterms as a simple choice between “common sense and crazy”. Many speakers emphasised their own Christian faith while stressing the godlessness of communism and conflating it with threats from outside America’s borders, at times invoking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas said: “We are witnessing a new and dangerous red-green alliance – communists and Islamists coming together and sweeping over the Democrat party. They are united because they share the same enemies. They hate Christians, they hate Jews, they hate capitalism, they hate the constitution, and they hate America!” There were shouts in the arena of “He should be shot!” as Cruz singled out some leading progressives by name: “When people tell you who they are, believe them. When Hasan Piker says, America deserved 9/11, believe him. When Mamdani says he wants to seize the means of production, he means it. When Abdul El-Sayed says he has an ‘obligation’ to comply with Sharia law, he means it. And when James Talarico says he wants to dismantle capitalism, he means this.” On the convention floor, Republicans echoed Cruz’s apocalyptic framing. Pavel Sokolov, 33, vice-chair of the New Jersey Republican party, drew on his personal background to reinforce the point. “I was born in the former Soviet Union; my parents and I fled that exact rhetoric,” Sokolov said. “It always starts nice and friendly, saying everyone must pay their fair share. But it inevitably ends up the same. In the Soviet Union, ostensibly everyone was equal, yet somehow the party bosses ate caviar every day.” Conversely, most speakers swerved past voters’ everyday concerns about the cost of living and Trump’s war of choice in Iran. Trump himself claimed that concerns about ‌inflation were exaggerated and the word “affordable” was “fake”. Interviews with more than a dozen attendees found staunch support for him – but with some reservations beneath the surface. Gregorio Heise, 59, a disabled army veteran from Texas, described Trump’s second term as “friggin’ awesome”, explaining: “I prefer to pay $5 a gallon [of gas] and put my head on a pillow and wake up knowing this country is still here than watching it go boom with a nuke. No, thank you. I’m a vet and I didn’t serve this country to watch it go to crap.” Joseph Ditto, a 50-year-old statistician from suburban Minneapolis wearing an elephant-patterned Republican tie, admitted his frustration with the administration’s foreign policy. “I’m not a fan of the war in Iran. I hope it’s over quickly,” he said. “I voted for the anti-war Trump, so that’s frustrating.” Democrats, who held three midterm conventions in 1974, 1978 and 1982 with mixed results, have no plans for a rival event this time. But some travelled to Dallas to counter the Republican messaging. Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a congresswoman from California, highlighted what she saw as the fundamental disconnect of Trump’s second term. “Last night, Donald Trump was talking about how he wanted to build a big ballroom like they have in China,” she said. “The average American family can’t afford groceries or gas, and he’s fantasising about a ballroom in the people’s house. This entire event is built around one man who likes to hear himself talk.” To many political strategists, turning a midterm election into a direct referendum on an incumbent president whose national approval rating languishes in the low-to-mid 30s looks like a huge own goal. But Trump’s energetic performance on Wednesday night buoyed Republicans who believe he retains a unique ability to galvanise people who might not otherwise vote at all. David Hopkins, a professor of political science at Boston College, said: “There’s been a lot of journalistic dunking on Trump saying that making the election more about him is an ego trip winning out over smart strategy. That’s not an unreasonable take but there’s another way to look at it. The worst-case scenario for Republicans is that Republican voters stay home.” Hopkins pointed out that Trump commands a unique, low-propensity “Make America great again” (Maga) electorate that turns out passionately for him but frequently ignores down-ballot congressional races when his name is absent. “If they can’t get those people out, it looks like a real national wipeout.” The midterm convention also offered an intriguing subplot: the question of who inherits the Maga movement when Trump, the 45th and 47th president, is gone. Vice-President JD Vance was greeted by chants of “JD 48!” as he delivered Thursday night’s keynote address. He spoke at length about his family while describing Democrats as “the party that despises America and the people who built it”. When a protester waving a Mexican flag briefly interrupted his speech, Vance drew thunderous applause with a sharp put-down: “Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket.” In the concourses, delegates were actively sizing up the potential 2028 field. While Vance commands a substantial lead in early polling among Republican primary voters, several other names – most notably secretary of state Marco Rubio and Florida governor Ron DeSantis – were frequently cited. Heise said: “Marco Rubio is doing everything. He’s building on the foundations this country was created on in 1776.” Chris Daniel, 44, from Houston, who has been a delegate at every Republican convention since 2004, echoed that sentiment. “I prefer Marco Rubio over Vance if I had to pick one today. He has proven his ability to lead in any capacity.” Rusat Ramgopal, 26, executive director of the Queens county Republican party in New York, envisioned a pragmatic resolution to avoid a damaging primary battle. “Instead of a divisive primary between Vance and Rubio, I think the two of them and the president will sit down in a room and decide the ticket,” he predicted. “It just depends on who is top of the ticket and who is vice president.” Republicans declared the convention a triumph. Outside the arena, the verdict was rather less enthusiastic. Veteran pollster John Zogby described the two-day gathering as an “act of desperation” that highlighted internal vulnerabilities rather than strength. “The president promised that the war in Iran would end by August, inflation would be down by August, fuel prices would be low again by August,” Zogby noted. “None of those have been achieved. We have moved from the politics of anger into the politics of disappointment.”

title: Why is Trump’s $5,000 offer to voters ‘like a woman’? Ask Fox News
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: Host Jesse Watters says Trump’s offer to Americans if Republicans retain Congress is ‘an enticement’, not a bribe
body_text: I think I finally understand why Fox News pays Jesse Watters the big bucks. The network star, famous for hot takes like men shouldn’t “eat soup in public”, has an incredible talent for inserting misogyny into absolutely any news story. Take, for example, Donald Trump’s ludicrous announcement on Wednesday night that he will give every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm election. That’s a story about apparent bribery, right? A story about fiscal recklessness and empty promises. A story about how the president, whose popularity is plummeting, is so out of ideas that he’s resorted (yet again) to dangling cash in front of voters. Actually, says Watters, it’s none of the above; it’s just Trump behaving like a woman. “That $5,000 check, Dana, that’s not a bribe,” Watters told Fox anchor Dana Perino on Thursday. “We’re calling it an enticement … It’s like a woman. Sometimes a woman can entice you, OK? Maybe – it doesn’t mean you’re going home with her, but it keeps you interested. It keeps you intrigued and wanting more. That’s what this is about.” Perhaps the Fox News host isn’t completely wrong. After all, I am a woman and I am about to entice you to look up the story about how Watters courted his much younger second wife. It’s very intriguing. But back to this definitely-not-a-bribe $5,000 payment which the president calls a Trump “dividend”. I wouldn’t start spending it now, if I were you. The president, like his right-hand man Elon Musk, has a habit of making grandiose promises he doesn’t keep. Remember the Doge dividends floated last February? Those haven’t materialized. Nor have the tariff dividends that Trump made so much noise about. “People that are against Tariffs are FOOLS!” Trump said in a Truth Social post last year. “We are taking in Trillions of Dollars and … A dividend of at least $2000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.” Almost a year after that post, nobody has received a tariff dividend. However, it has been estimated by the Joint Economic Committee – Minority that the average American family will pay more than $2,500 in tariff costs this year. I feel pretty confident saying there is a 0.00001% chance that anyone is going to get a $5,000 Republican celebration check. But let’s just play along for a minute and pretend that Trump isn’t a fabulist. Let’s pretend that the president is a serious man who makes thoughtful policy proposals, rather than an opportunist who says whatever inane thing happens to pop into his brain in the moment. Isn’t it a bit reckless to be giving all this money away, a total that exceeds $1tn, when the US national debt recently surpassed $40tn for the first time? As Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, said in a statement, that debt “doesn’t exist solely on the government’s ledgers”, it is shouldered by everyone. “The more we borrow, the more we exacerbate inflation, squeeze out other priorities in the budget, and leave ourselves vulnerable to emergencies at home and turmoil abroad.” Don’t worry about all that, says the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick. “It’s not tax money,” Lutnick told NBC News on Thursday. The Trump administration is going to earn that money from various moneymaking endeavours like the Trump Platinum Card, which allows wealthy people to pay up to $5m to extend their US visas. JD Vance, meanwhile, has suggested that the money might come from US tariff revenues, even though economists have pointed out the $125bn in tariff revenues wouldn’t come close to covering the costs. The president himself, meanwhile, doesn’t seem keen to elaborate on his cunning plan to win friends and influence voters. When the ABC reporter Rachel Scott asked him about the rationale behind the $5,000 checks on Thursday night, he said it was a reward to Americans for putting up with Joe Biden. After Scott tried to ask a follow-up question, Trump lunged at her and said: “Your network … you’re the worst.” Which is very on-brand for the president. He can’t seem to handle being asked tough questions by anyone, but gets particularly nasty when those questions are posed by a woman. While Trump doesn’t want to get into the details of his dividend, the proposal reflects how the president is looking at some very unconventional ways to sway the midterms. He may not end up issuing people celebration checks, but he has already gutted election security programs and attempted to limit voting access. The real story here isn’t $5,000 cheques, it’s the fact that America’s self-styled king seems intent on meddling with the election, and no meaningful checks and balances are stopping him. Ectopic pregnancy deaths in the US have nearly doubled A ProPublica analysis found almost 200 women died after an ectopic pregnancy from 2020 to 2025. That’s compared to about 100 in the previous six years. To nobody’s surprise, mortality is worse in states with strict abortion bans. “While they cautioned that abortion bans alone can’t explain the national rise, maternal health experts said any examination of the spike should include the documented delays in care caused by the laws, including for ectopic pregnancies,” ProPublica notes. Sudanese refugees are being forced into sex work Sudan’s civil war, which started in 2023, has created the world’s worst displacement crisis. Now, many of the women who fled to Egypt are being sexually exploited. What’s happened to Pete Hegseth’s testosterone screening guidance? The Pentagon published a guidance document on 2 September outlining a new mandatory testosterone screening process to create a “High-T military”. However, the very next day it was withdrawn from the public domain for reasons that remain unclear. Maybe someone in the Pentagon came to their senses. Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed Naza, a highly-feted new film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, reveals the secret systems used in mass killings of civilians in Gaza. “Several interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu,” the Guardian writes. “[O]ne said their mission was to ‘thwart peace’.” Why does the hard right shrug off domestic abusers in their midst? The short answer is because they are misogynists who cynically weaponize women’s rights to advance their agenda. But do read Zoe Williams, who has a longer and more eloquent answer, following on from the attack on a female protester at the Reform UK conference. The Republican convention showed an image of Hasan Piker in his underwear They seem to think showing photos of a buff podcaster in his underwear demonstrates that the left are scary “radicals”. The rise of hairy young women Phoebe Bridgers’ unshaven legs at her Venice film festival debut sparked a flurry of headlines. But, says Leah Harper, Bridgers’ “au naturel look may signal that attitudes are changing – particularly among younger generations”. Emma Bonino, feminist Italian politician, dies aged 78 Bonino got involved in politics after she had an abortion (then illegal) at age 26 and said she decided that “never, never, never again should anyone have to suffer this humiliation”. She handed herself in to the police as an act of protest, leading a campaign to eventually legalize abortion in 1978. Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ is going up for auction Diana famously wore the fitted black dress on the same night that Charles admitted to his infidelity on TV in 1994. It will be auctioned off in December. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: Calls for Democrats to be shot go unchallenged at Republican convention
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Crowd member repeatedly said some Democrats ‘should be shot’ during Ted Cruz’s speech, without senator responding
body_text: On the night Republicans gathered to mourn the killing of Charlie Kirk and warn against the dangers of violent rhetoric, a crowd at the party’s irregular midterm convention in Dallas repeatedly called for a sitting Senate candidate to be shot, while the Republican senator at the podium never denounced or even noted the outbursts. The outbursts came repeatedly during Ted Cruz’s Thursday night address at the American Airlines center, when he named a Democrat he accused of holding radical views. After the senator mentioned the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, video footage depicts at least one audience member shouting: “He should be shot!” The same cry followed when Cruz named Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and again after he named Texas Senate candidate James Talarico. Cruz did not pause or respond to the shouting, and it remains unclear whether he heard it from the stage. Cruz did not respond to a request for comment. Cruz had accused Mamdani of wanting to seize the means of production, said El-Sayed felt an “obligation” to follow Sharia law and claimed Talarico wanted to dismantle capitalism. Each characterization stretched past remarks the three men had actually made in other contexts. Asked about the moment on CNN’s The Source With Kaitlan Collins, El-Sayed said such rhetoric had become dangerously normalized and that it should unsettle anyone who heard it. He called on Republicans to name the chant for what it was: incitement that both parties ought to reject, and appealed for a return to a politics centered on people’s basic needs and dignity. “Look, I’m a dad with two daughters, and I hope those daughters get to grow up and live with their dad. This is what has become the norm in our politics … literally calls to violence and the inability for anybody to actually call it out,” El-Sayed said. “We can learn to disagree agreeably, and when you hear that kind of call to violence, it should be shuddering to all of us,” he added. A spokesperson for Mike Rogers, the Republican former congressman challenging El-Sayed for Michigan’s open Senate seat who was in Dallas for the convention, said Rogers condemned the remarks and “all political violence”. The convention fell on the first anniversary of the assassination of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk, an occasion Republican speakers repeatedly invoked, including the vice-president, JD Vance, who spoke of his friendship with Kirk during a headlining address. El-Sayed is locked in one of the cycle’s most closely watched Senate races. A CNN poll released on Wednesday showed him leading Rogers 47% to 44% in the contest to succeed the retiring Democratic senator Gary Peters, as both parties fight for control of the chamber.

title: Taxes wouldn’t fund $5,000 Trump ‘dividend’ if Republicans win midterms, says commerce secretary
author: Edward Helmore
summary: Lutnick said $500bn of estimated $1tn needed to fund checks to all US adults could come from new visa program
body_text: Donald Trump’s controversial proposal to give a $5,000 “dividend” to all US adults if Republicans maintain control of Congress in November’s elections would not be paid out from US tax revenues, according to the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick. “It’s not tax money,” Lutnick said in an interview with NBC News, adding that the administration could “earn the money that Donald Trump wants to pay out, not from the deficit and not from taxpayers”. In a speech at the Republican midterm convention rally in Dallas, Texas, on Wednesday, Trump said he would issue the dividends “because of our tremendous strength and success economically” and likened the payment to a one-time, tax-free $1,776 “Warrior Dividend” approved for about 1.45 million US military service members last year. Trump suggested the dividend, which could cost as much as $1tn if paid out to all Americans, could come in part from tariff revenue. “If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” he said, adding that it would be called “the Trump dividend”. But the proposal has been widely criticized, in part because the US national debt recently surpassed $40tn, up from $10tn in 2008, marking a near 300% increase over 18 years. Lutnick told NBC that some of the dividend money could come from a planned commerce department program to charge wealthy visitors to the US to pay up to $5m to extend their visas. “We have a waitlist of more than 100,000 people who want to come,” he said, and calculated that this could raise $500bn. He also cited the government’s $8.9bn investment in chipmaker Intel, which has since appreciated in market value, from $20 per share to $100. In his comments, Lutnick joined with other administration officials in floating ideas on where the $5,000 checks might come from. Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, told Bloomberg TV that the White House is considering a “reconciliation process” in Congress to fund the program. “We can do it in a fiscally responsible way,” Hassett said. “The bottom line is there are multiple paths to getting it done – don’t underestimate President Trump.” JD Vance has also suggested tariff revenues would cover the cost and that the payments would not go to wealthy Americans. However, the supreme court has ruled that revenue raised by Trump’s “liberation day” 2025 import tariffs must be returned, and an earlier proposal to return $2,000 to US taxpayers from tariff receipts was more than the revenue that had been raised, according to the nonpartisan Tax Foundation. Trump’s $5,000 dividend proposal comes as a recent Associated Press poll found that only about three in 10 US adults, or 32%, approve of how the president is handling the economy, down from 40% at the start of his second term.

title: Saudi Arabia shuts down key oil pipeline, blaming drones from Iraq
author: Oliver Holmes and agencies
summary: Riyadh has increased use of East-West pipeline since start of war on Iran to bypass closure of strait of Hormuz
body_text: Saudi Arabia has shut down a critical oil pipeline, accusing militants in Iraq of launching drone attacks on the export route being used to bypass the lockdown of the strait of Hormuz. The world’s largest ⁠crude oil exporter has increased its use of the 745-mile (1,200km) pipeline running across the Arabian peninsula, which links Abqaiq, near the Gulf, to the port of Yanbu, on the Red Sea, since the US-Israeli war against Iran began. The Saudi foreign ministry condemned “the targeting of the East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions by several drones coming from Iraq, which caused human injuries and damage”. An energy ministry official told the SPA news agency earlier that the pipeline was “stopped as a precaution”. Baghdad is under mounting pressure to prevent militant groups, including those backed by Saudi Arabia’s regional rival Iran, from launching attacks on Gulf countries from Iraqi soil. The US president, Donald Trump, said he believed Tehran was responsible for the aerial attack. “I ‌think they ‌are, probably they are,” Trump told reporters in ‌Dublin during a visit to Ireland. On Saturday, Iraq’s government confirmed the attacks were launched from its territory and ordered an investigation. It condemned “the attacks targeting our brethren in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”, and the office of the Iraqi prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, said the commander in charge of the southern province of Maysan had been dismissed. Satellite images from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Thursday showed black smoke billowing near Medina, along the general route of the East-West pipeline. According to the International Energy Agency, Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea port at the pipeline’s end have more than doubled since the war began. The news comes as Yemen’s Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the world’s vital shipping routes linking Europe and Asia. Oil prices climbed past $100 (£74) a barrel this week, while average US diesel prices topped $6 for the first time on Friday – a potential headache for Trump before midterm elections in November. A failed attempt by the US and Israel to overthrow the Iranian regime this year has destabilised the Gulf, and Iran and its proxies have now tightened their grip over two crucial shipping routes – the strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Trump said ⁠on Saturday ⁠that everything would “work out ⁠just fine” when asked whether he ⁠could help move ‌traffic ‌through the strait ‌of Hormuz in light of fresh concerns about Saudi ‌Arabia. “Everything will work out just fine,” Trump said, speaking in Dublin ⁠after meeting the Irish president, Catherine Connolly. But Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, speaking on the sidelines of a developing nations Brics summit in India, said the Middle East did not need the US to be a “regional policeman”. Saudi Arabia has previously accused Tehran-backed Iraqi militias of targeting its oil infrastructure. It said the kingdom “reserves the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, its security, its facilities” and its people. Bahrain, Jordan and Qatar also condemned the attack on the Saudi pipeline, while the Gulf Cooperation Council denounced “a dangerous escalation and an unacceptable threat to the security of the kingdom”. Ed Miliband, the British ⁠foreign secretary, said ⁠on ⁠Saturday that he had spoken ⁠with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin ⁠Farhan Al ‌Saud, and ‌discussed the attacks. He added that the UK “stands firmly with ⁠Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised government of Yemen against ‌these attacks”. Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced a maritime blockade in July against Saudi Arabia – which supports the Yemeni government – and attacked its oil tankers in the Red Sea. After taking control of the Yemeni Red Sea coast on Friday, the Houthis said navigation through the Bab al-Mandab strait was “safe” for all but Saudi Arabia.

title: Donald Trump says he would ‘love’ to see united Ireland
author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
summary: US president says on visit to republic that unification will happen eventually so ‘may as well happen now’
body_text: Donald Trump has said he would “love” to see a united Ireland and that it “may as well happen now”. The US president appeared to endorse the push for constitutional change on the island at the start of a two-day visit to Ireland on Saturday. The unexpected intervention prompted a swift rebuttal from the UK government and Northern Ireland’s unionist leaders. “I don’t want ⁠to cause any problems, but ‌I will ‌tell you, I’d love ‌to see it unified,” Trump told reporters at joint press conference with the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, in Dublin. “I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.” The unification of Northern Ireland with the republic of Ireland would be “fantastic”, Trump said. “The UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?” The intervention jolted his hosts and came two weeks after Andy Burnham said a referendum on unification was “off the table”, which angered Sinn Féin and other Irish nationalists. Speaking later on Saturday, Trump acknowledged that his comments on unification, made in response to a reporter’s question, would be controversial. “No matter what you say or how you say it, there’s no good answer,” he said. “I gave a nice answer, I think. We’ll worry about it tomorrow.” Unification, he added, would be a “very cool thing”. A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister still believed there was not the required support for unification to trigger a referendum, as set out in the Good Friday agreement. Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, said Northern Ireland’s constitutional future would be decided by its people, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington. “Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people. I am confident Northern Ireland will continue to choose the UK and the security it offers. As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish republic.” Colum Eastwood, an MP and former leader of the Social Democratic and Labour party (SDLP), and frequent critic of Trump, posted a clip of the president’s remarks on social media and wrote: “Always liked him.” The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said: “President Trump is shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state. This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension.” Trump’s comments strayed from predecessors who sought to keep the White House neutral on Ireland’s constitutional future, but the off-the-cuff nature of the remarks suggested there was no change in US policy. Trump’s unofficial visit is centred on golf – he flew on Saturday afternoon to his resort in Doonbeg, County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open – but started with a courtesy call in Dublin to Áras an Uachtaráin, the official residence and workplace of the Irish president, Catherine Connolly. Before her election to the ceremonial post last year, Connolly called Trump a bully and criticised his policies in Gaza and Iran. Their brief encounter, behind closed doors, appeared to go smoothly despite a coded critique of White House policies. Connolly said in a statement afterwards that she “conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted” and stressed the importance of the United Nations – an organisation Trump has disparaged. Trump said they had a wide-ranging discussion, including about energy and water, and that Connolly was “terrific”. Trump held a separate meeting with Martin at the Phoenix Park, where he told the press that Iran would seek peace after the US midterm elections and repeated his claim that his war had prevented Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon. Asked about protests against his visit – a large crowd was gathering in central Dublin, 5 miles away, as well as at Doonbeg – the president said he had not seen any protests. Addressing guests as at the US ambassador’s residence, Trump assailed US Democrats as extremists and criticised Europe’s approach to immigration. He lauded US-Irish relations but reiterated a complaint about the American pharma giants in Ireland. “You took all our medical companies, we’ve got to get a couple of them back. You fleeced us but that’s OK.” Thousands of protesters marched through central Dublin and held a rally outside parliament. Speakers accused Trump of facilitating genocide in Gaza and led chants of “Donald Trump, can you hear? We don’t want you here.” Others in the crowd accused the president of misogyny, sexual assault, racism and xenophobia. “Donald Trump is utterly immoral and he’s wrecking the world,” said Anne McGuinness, 70, who held a banner that said “unwelcome”. Emily Hamilton, whose daughter held a banner saying “Get rid of the evil orange”, said the Irish government should have shunned him. “We can’t stop him going to Doonbeg but we should not be welcoming him.” Mick Brennan, 70, said he and his wife Helen do not normally attend protests but made an exception for the US president. “We can’t stand that Trump fella, from his toes to his nose.” A smaller protest was held at Doonbeg. Trump is to stay overnight at his resort and present the Irish Open trophy to the winner on Sunday before returning to Washington.

title: ‘Trump accounts’ promise to mint child millionaires. Experts have their doubts
author: Steven Greenhouse
summary: President has hyped growth of federal investment accounts to help US children – for his own political gain
body_text: Since returning to the White House, Donald Trump has scrapped rules that made childcare more affordable and pushed to cut funding for the nation’s public schools. But with midterm elections fast approaching and his approval ratings very low, the US president has repeatedly trumpeted a two-month-old program designed to help the nation’s children. That program, unhumbly named “Trump accounts”, calls for the federal government to give a one-time $1,000 seed deposit to every newborn whose family applies. In campaign speeches this summer, Trump has sought to milk these accounts for maximum political advantage, making big promises about how much these accounts will help the nation’s children. In a speech in Las Vegas last month, Trump hailed the program, saying: “It’s really giving [children] a head start on the American dream… They start off with $1,000 … and they can end up with $100,000, $200,000, $300,000” and if the stock market booms, “you’d end up with $1m”. With these accounts, Trump seems to want to come across as a Santa Claus stuffing $1,000 into every newborn’s stocking (although that money comes from the federal government). He and other Republicans boast that these accounts will significantly lift up all children, including children from low-income families, and also narrow the wealth gap between rich and poor. When Trump kicked off these accounts in early July, the treasury department said: “Trump Accounts level the playing field by allowing every parent to invest in their children’s future, not just wealthy families with trust funds.” A big problem, however, is that many economists say Trump’s claims about these accounts are vastly exaggerated or false. As Trump seeks to excite voters about these accounts, he has hyped how much they will grow, especially with regard to non-affluent families who don’t have the wherewithal to deposit money into these tax-deferred accounts to help their children. In his speeches, Trump sometimes gives the inaccurate impression that a newborn’s account with a $1,000 seed deposit will mushroom to $200,000 or $300,000 by the time the child turns 18, even when that child’s family doesn’t have money to make subsequent deposits. What’s more, “Trump accounts” are likely to increase, not decrease, the wealth gap between rich and poor. These accounts have definite tax advantages for wealthier families, who, unlike most low-income or working-class families, are able to make the maximum $5,000 deposit allowed each year into these tax-deferred accounts. It’s the families rich enough to contribute $5,000 a year who could see their children’s accounts grow to $200,000 or $300,000, far outstripping the accounts of children from poorer families. “This policy is not about giving poor kids a leg up. It’s more likely to widen the gap between rich and poor,” said Justin Wolfers, an economics professor at the University of Michigan, in a video. Kush Desai, a White House spokesperson, said in an email: “Trump Accounts are already shaping up to make a generational difference for working-class children who have not historically benefitted from traditional tax advantaged accounts.” He noted that the billionaires Michael Dell and Ray Dalio, as well as multinational corporations, have “pledged to donate billions of dollars of their wealth to the Trump Accounts of working-class children”. Desai rejected any assertions that the program would increase inequality, saying: “High income parents have always had an array of tools to grow wealth for their kids, but Trump Accounts are giving middle class parents the same opportunity – with billionaires chipping in to help. Only a moron would argue billionaires giving money away to working-class kids will worsen inequality.” The Trump administration has hyped the accounts with extremely optimistic claims. A White House website forecasts that many children with “Trump accounts” will have $271,000 in their account by age 18 and $13m by age 55. That sounds fabulous, but according to Wolfers, those big numbers are based on an impressive 10% annual rate of return for decades – a rate of return that is extraordinarily hard to achieve year after year. Moreover, those higher numbers are for children whose parents put in $5,000 annually until age 18, and then $7,000 a year when their children are in their 20s. Wolfers derided these White House estimates, saying in his video: “They’re ridiculous, they’re dishonest and they’re misleading.” Administration officials defended their estimates of how much the accounts would grow, saying those estimates are “not dissimilar to similar projections issued by retirement account providers”. In his speeches, Trump omits something important: he fails to note that for families unable to contribute beyond the initial $1,000 seed deposit, that amount would, according to White House estimates, grow to $6,000 by age 18. (That too is also based an optimistic 10% annual return.) No one should pooh-pooh a government-given deposit of $1,000 or a possible $6,000 at age 18. But Darrick Hamilton, a New School economics professor and one of the inventors of the baby bonds idea, said those amounts are too small to change the life of a child in need – too small to make college affordable or to buy a house. “It’s really an income transfer, not a wealth-building tool,” Hamilton said. He said it is the wealthiest 20%, especially the top 10%, who save money, while “people in the bottom 80% are usually dis-savers, they’re usually borrowers.” In other words, he said, the richest 20% will benefit from the tax breaks by depositing $5,000 a year into Trump accounts for their children. “The main mechanism for these accounts is active savings by parents, and that’s by nature regressive,” Hamilton said. “These accounts will actually increase wealth inequality because they favor people wealthy enough to have money to put into savings.” As part of the program, employers can contribute $2,500 a year to the account of an employee’s child. That $2,500 becomes a nice tax break for well-paid employees – the $2,500 contribution won’t be counted as taxable income. As a result, high-income workers in higher tax brackets will receive bigger tax breaks than lower-paid workers. The $1,000 seed deposits for newborns – the main part of the program helping the non-affluent – are to expire when Trump’s second term ends. But the parts of the program that help the wealthy most – the tax deferrals and tax breaks – are to continue indefinitely. Many Republicans and business executives have hailed “Trump accounts” as a way to make American children participants in the capitalist system. Senator Ted Cruz said: “Trump accounts are, in many ways, Donald Trump’s New Deal – but instead of having government taking care of everyone, Trump accounts are about making every child and every American a capitalist.” Hamilton sees things differently. Noting that Trump accounts are invested in the stock market, he said: “This is part of their larger plan to privatize our social safety net. This is in line with Republican plans to dismantle social security.” Senator Cory Booker and Representative Ayanna Pressley introduced a never-enacted baby bonds bill in 2019 under which children would receive $1,000 in their birth year and up to $2,000 more every year to age 18. Under their proposal, based on ideas from Hamilton and the Duke professor William Darity, lower-income families would receive larger government contributions than affluent ones. Children from families at the poverty level would see their accounts rise to an estimated $46,000 by age 18, about three times as much as children from families making twice the poverty line and more than 20 times as much as children from wealthy families. Hamilton said giving larger deposits to children from poorer families would give those kids more of a leg up. But that’s not the program that Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress approved. Like so much that Trump and GOP lawmakers have done, Trump accounts will help the rich far more than the non-rich.

title: Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce stayed at Gina Rinehart’s $20m mansion after One Nation fundraisers
author: Sarah Martin Senior correspondent
summary: Exclusive: New details underscoring depth of relationship between billionaire and party revealed in first episode of Guardian podcast The Populist
body_text: Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce stayed overnight at Gina Rinehart’s $20m Brisbane mansion after fundraising events held for One Nation, Guardian Australia can reveal. On one occasion, Joyce conducted a live television interview with Channel Seven’s Sunrise program from a room that appears to be a bedroom in Rinehart’s home. The interview took place on Monday 13 April, the morning after a fundraising event at the mining magnate’s house on the banks of the Brisbane River in Hawthorne. The new details underscoring the depth of the relationship between Australia’s richest person and One Nation have been revealed in the first episode of the Guardian’s new podcast about the party, The Populist, released on Monday. Parliamentary expenditure records show that Hanson and Joyce declared flights on 13 April courtesy of Hancock Prospecting, with flight-tracking data showing that the pair flew on Rinehart’s luxury Gulfstream jet from Brisbane to Sydney that afternoon. The accommodation at Rinehart’s home has not been declared to the parliament, which has rules in place mandating that gifts or hospitality valued at more than $300 – or any interest “where a conflict of interest with a [parliamentarian]’s public duties could foreseeably arise or be seen to arise” – should be declared. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here The guidelines state that “hospitality” refers to “free or concessional accommodation” provided to the MP, the MP’s spouse or partner or dependent children “wholly or partly by any person, organisation, business or interest group or foreign government or its representative”. The provision of meals or accommodation excludes “hospitality provided in a purely social way by friends or colleagues”, but the guidelines are designed to place on the public record interests that may conflict, or be seen to conflict, with an MP’s public duty. Joyce told Guardian Australia that Rinehart “was a long-term friend over decades not a motel”. “When I stay with family or friends they don’t charge me, nor do I see it as work,” he said. “I will never be ashamed of doing the research to do a better job.” Guardian Australia can also reveal that Hanson has been using one of Rinehart’s bodyguards for her personal security. The man, who has been seen escorting Hanson in Perth and Canberra, has been one of Rinehart’s closest bodyguards for more than a decade. The New South Wales supreme court heard in 2013 that Rinehart had asked the bodyguard to offer one of her daughters, Bianca Rinehart, a $25m loan to pull out of a court battle contesting the family trust. The offer was rejected. According to his LinkedIn, the man works as a security manager with an undeclared company but a post from 2023 shows him listed as an employee of Hancock Energy. It is unclear if he remains employed by Hancock Prospecting. Guardian Australia has previously reported multiple breaches of Senate rules, with One Nation failing to declare flights gifted by Hancock Prospecting to Hanson going back to August last year. The fresh details of the company’s financial support for One Nation come despite Hanson telling reporters in February she was not being funded by Rinehart, and after the party’s national director, James Ashby, said in December last year: “We have not seen any money from her.” The Labor senator Murray Watt criticised Hanson for failing to disclose the links between her party and Rinehart, including the undeclared flights. “I think that the lengths that she and her colleagues have gone repeatedly to conceal donations, staffing matters, all sorts of other things about their operations, it does make you think that there’s something to hide,” Watt told the Guardian. “In a democratic system like Australia, there is a responsibility of politicians to be transparent about decision making, about their operations, and again Pauline Hanson seems to want to get all the benefits of power without any of the responsibilities of power. “The level of concealment that goes on suggests a guilty conscience. “I think that one of the reasons that One Nation goes to such efforts to conceal their financial gain from Gina Rinehart and her companies is because there is such a close alignment between what Gina Rinehart and Hancock want to see happen and One Nation’s policies.” One Nation did not respond to questions from Guardian Australia. A spokesperson for Hancock Prospecting said: “Donations will be disclosed in accordance with applicable laws and reporting requirements.” Listen to the Guardian’s podcast The Populist here
