title: Trump reiterates $5,000 ‘dividend’ pledge if Republicans win midterms
author: Guardian staff
summary: Plan to give US adults $5,000 has been greeted with incredulity across the political spectrum as well as outrage
body_text: Donald Trump has doubled down on his controversial pledge to give US adults a $5,000 “dividend” if his Republican ⁠party keeps control of Congress after November’s midterm elections. The plan has been greeted with expressions of incredulity across the US political spectrum as well as outraged accusations of seeking to bribe voters. The proposal – which would cost more than a trillion dollars – also comes amid huge concern over the US national debt, which topped $40tn for the first time in August. “I don’t ‌know but ‌it’s easy if the ‌Republicans win. $5,000 to all adults in the country and we can easily handle that because we’re taking in ‌so much money,” Trump told reporters in Ireland, where he is on a visit to his golf course in Doonbeg. Trump had been asked if Congress would need to approve the $5,000 pledge. He said: “The Democrats can’t make that pledge ⁠because it would all go to hell right away, we’d go into a depression … ‌I made that pledge, I always keep my pledge.” The US has roughly 240 million adult citizens, suggesting a cost of $1.2tn. The federal government spent about $7tn in fiscal year 2025, with about $2tn taken on as debt. When the plan was first touted by Trump last week at a rally in Texas, Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget wrote on X: “The result would be a huge spike in the deficit, and almost certainly in the inflation rate.” Democratic political leaders also reacted with a mix of outrage, disbelief and condemnation to the remarkable suggestion, which comes at a time when Trump is struggling with low poll numbers and a disastrous conflict in Iran, which is having an impact on the health of the US economy. “After making you sicker and poorer with his war, Donald Trump now wants to buy your vote with $5,000 in taxpayer-funded blood money,” said California governor Gavin Newsom. “The most corrupt man ever to occupy the Oval Office.” Some Republicans have backed the idea. “I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” said US senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, in a social media post on X. Any such payment would have ‌to be approved by Congress. On Sunday Mike Johnson, the House speaker and a Louisiana Republican, told CNN: “Of course, the devil’s in the ‌details. We have to figure all that out.” But Democratic politicians on Sunday morning talkshows in the US dismissed the idea. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, told ABC’s This Week that the plan was not a “serious proposal”. Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

title: ‘It’s just straight bigotry’: wave of Islamophobic rhetoric looms over US midterm elections
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: As Muslims win historic victories, experts describe rise in anti-Islamic sentiment that rivals post-9/11 climate
body_text: Within hours of Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic US Senate primary, Republican senator Tommy Tuberville of Alabama declared that the party had “just voted to send a TERRORIST” to Washington. El-Sayed – or “Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed”, as Tuberville called him on X – was a “RADICAL ISLAMIST” who would “do everything he can to destroy America”, he claimed. It was the opening shot in what researchers who track anti-Muslim sentiment describe as the most concentrated wave of Islamophobic rhetoric in US electoral politics since the 9/11 attacks, arriving at the exact moment Muslim candidates are winning office in unprecedented numbers. “It’s probably the worst of what we’ve seen,” said Saher Selod, director of research at the non-partisan Institute for Social Policy and Understanding (ISPU), which has tracked anti-Muslim sentiment nationally for a decade. “We’re certainly seeing in 2025 and 2026, ahead of these midterms, really very Islamophobic ads – more so than what we saw after 9/11.” ISPU’s 2025 Islamophobia Index, a 100-point scale built using common anti-Muslim stereotypes, rose from 25 in 2022 to 33 among the general public in 2025, with the sharpest increases among white and Hispanic Americans. The Pew Research Center found in a survey this spring that 51% of US adults now say Islam is more likely than other religions to encourage violence, up from just 25% six months after the 2001 attacks. The partisan gap on that question has widened sharply. Back in 2002, 32% of likely Republican voters and 23% of Democrats said Islam was more likely than other religions to encourage violence, according to the Pew survey. Today, 76% of Republicans say the same, and 29% of Democrats. Anti-Muslim hate crimes reported to the FBI, which spiked to 481 in 2001 from 28 the year before, have never returned to pre-2001 levels, according to Pew’s research. The ISPU separately found that 63% of Muslims reported experiencing religious discrimination in the past year, the highest share of any faith group it measures. Set against that backdrop is a wave of Muslim electoral success. There are four Muslim members of US Congress, with a fifth likely on the way, compared with zero in 2001. Ghazala Hashmi became Virginia’s first Muslim woman elected to statewide office this year, as lieutenant governor. Zohran Mamdani was inaugurated as New York’s first Muslim mayor in January 2025, and El-Sayed’s primary win put him on track to potentially become the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate. The reaction to El-Sayed’s victory showed how quickly the rhetoric escalates. The Center for the Study of Organized Hate found Islamophobic posts naming El-Sayed rose by nearly 1,900% in the week after his win, from an average of 155 to more than 3,000 a day. The attacks are also coming from the very top of the Republican party. Donald Trump infamously called in 2015 for a “total and complete shutdown” on Muslims entering the US when he was running for president, and attempted to enact one via executive order in early 2017. After years of legal wrangling, the supreme court did allow Trump to implement a limited version of his travel restrictions for majority Muslim countries. This year, Trump called El-Sayed a “jihadist” from the Oval Office, and separately claimed – without naming anyone – that “jihadists” were being elected to office “all over the place”. Vice-president JD Vance, meanwhile, called El-Sayed “very, very evil” at a Michigan rally and, separately, invoked his own late grandfather to attack comments El-Sayed made in 2022 defending a legal challenge to an Oklahoma anti-Sharia ballot measure. The attacks go beyond one candidate, however. Senator Ted Cruz told Fox News that El-Sayed and Mamdani were “Islamists” who “want Sharia law” and “hate Jews, they hate Christians, they hate capitalism, they hate America”. Representative Nancy Mace posted that “every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic”, and followed up by writing that Islam “must be removed from civil society in the US”. In March, Representative Randy Fine of Florida wrote on X, “We need more Islamophobia, not less. Fear of Islam is rational,” while Representative Andy Ogles of Tennessee posted that “Muslims don’t belong in American society”. Republican leadership has been mostly silent. For Mobashra Tazamal, associate director of Georgetown University’s Bridge Initiative, which studies Islamophobia globally, the shift is shockingly noticeable. “It is almost as if the veil has been lifted,” she said. “It is so bigoted, and it’s so crude, and there is no red line. It’s just straight bigotry.” *** The rhetoric has also extended beyond individual candidates into policy fights. In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott has spent much of the summer campaigning against what he calls the imposition of Islamic law, ordering a review of state grants to two major airports and referring both to federal regulators over privately funded wudu stations, ritual washing facilities Muslims use before prayer, which he called illegal religious favoritism. Abbott has separately fought a proposed mosque-anchored housing development outside Dallas. Nationally, the Center for the Study of Organized Hate documented a coordinated campaign among 89 elected officials over 13 months, including 1,111 social media posts and eight bills, tied to a “Sharia Free America Caucus” that has grown to 65 members. The anti-Sharia campaigns are not new: close to two dozen states passed largely symbolic anti-Sharia laws in the early 2010s. “This isn’t an issue. It’s not something that’s real,” said Tazamal. “It’s constructed, and then these politicians claim to be tackling this constructed problem that they create.” The picture is complicated, though. Researchers caution against treating every attack on El-Sayed or Mamdani as bigotry. El-Sayed drew criticism – including from Vance – after he responded to a March attack on a suburban Detroit synagogue by saying “hurt people hurt people”, noting that relatives of the attacker in Lebanon had recently been killed in an Israeli airstrike. El-Sayed eventually apologized, and said the remarks may have been misconstrued. He has also faced scrutiny over his public association with the hyper-popular leftwing streamer Hasan Piker, who mainstream Democrats and Republicans have attacked for past comments minimizing the 11 September attacks. Mamdani has faced sustained criticism, including from rivals in his own mayoral race, over his refusal to unequivocally condemn the phrase “globalize the intifada”, a phrase Jewish groups say amounts to a call for violence against Jews, but one that he has never personally used. Mamdani subsequently said he would discourage the term after a rabbi told him it evokes memories of bus bombings and restaurant attacks for many Jewish New Yorkers. The controversy among Jewish organizations, rival campaigns and national Democrats, was not, in the end, disqualifying in the eyes of voters who ultimately decided the race. The devastation in Gaza, mass settler violence in the West Bank and the suppression of pro-Palestine speech in the US has brought an additional dimension to this discourse. US opinion on Israel has soured immensely in recent years, especially among Democrats, and criticism of Israeli policy by the likes of El-Sayed and Mamdani is cited by those describing Muslim politicians “jihadists”. Mahmoud Khalil, Rümeysa Öztürk and other Muslim residents in the US were among the first swept up for pro-Palestinian campus advocacy, even though most of the students protesting were not Muslim. That pattern, criticism aimed at religious identity rather than positions or votes, is consistent with what researchers have documented since well before this election cycle. And the point, Selod and Tazamal say, is whether that criticism is being used as cover for a broader claim – that Muslim identity itself, not any specific position on issue or another, is disqualifying from US public life. “With Abdul El-Sayed, we’re seeing these kinds of intense Islamophobic attacks against him, as opposed to attacking his platform or critiquing his policies,” Selod said. “It’s a playbook. They’re going to attack him for his religious identity to see if this will help pull voters away from him.” That playbook resurfaced this week in New York, where Mamdani attended the ceremony marking Friday’s 25th anniversary of 9/11 at Ground Zero, as his predecessors have every year. A petition with more than 100,000 signatures, riddled with attacks, unashamedly asked him not to. Rudy Giuliani, mayor of New York City at the time of the attacks, who is now closely aligned to Trump, claimed from thin air that Mamdani “doesn’t agree that September 11 was an Islamic terrorist attack”, and that his attendance “offends” him, adding even more venom against Muslims generally: “They have every desire to take us over … they want to dominate us. Mamdani is a clear supporter of that.” Giuliani offered no evidence for either claim. Cheri Sparacio, one of the petition’s organizers, whose husband died in the attacks, has said her objection is “not about the mayor’s background or faith, but his public actions”. Mamdani attended anyway, and on Friday morning, Mamdani and Giuliani shook hands at the ceremony. *** Yet the current moment cannot be separated from the infrastructure built after 9/11, Selod said. “All of the surveillance programs that were put into place, your no-fly list, ICE – these are a product of 9/11,” she said. “We didn’t have Immigration and Customs Enforcement. We didn’t have the TSA, the Transportation Security Administration. These were all put into place to protect the nation against threats of terrorism.” That architecture has since been extended well past its original target, Selod argued, pointing to the Boston Regional Intelligence Center, a post-9/11 “fusion center” built to detect terrorist plots. Local reporting and ACLU of Massachusetts records show the center has also been used to monitor Black Lives Matter demonstrators. “It’s expanding beyond a Muslim population to target others,” she said. “Muslims are one to two percent of the US population. My hope is when people start to see how it’s expanding beyond that population, maybe they’ll start really critiquing these programs.” ISPU polling suggests the sentiment tracks politics rather than faith. Americans who identify as somewhat or very conservative are 13 percentage points more likely than others to endorse anti-Muslim stereotypes, the ISPU found, while religiosity shows no correlation. Tazamal ties the current spike partly to political calculation. “Polling for Trump is low, and the GOP is the sitting party, and they haven’t delivered on their promises,” she said. “So instead of focusing on institutional failures and policies they haven’t been able to put into place, they’re stirring up hate and bigotry towards a certain group, which is a routine tactic that they do.” Caleb Elfenbein, a Grinnell College professor who has mapped Islamophobic rhetoric for years, sees a small, organized network reactivating on a predictable schedule. “It really looks, and feels, like a very cynical effort to take advantage of a general sense of fear that can be activated at any given time,” he said. Whether it works for a GOP that polling indicates is likely to face heavy losses in November’s midterm elections is the open question hanging over this campaign. Republicans are simultaneously contending with an unpopular war with Iran and rising costs that have squeezed their approval ratings. Whatever happens, amid growing political mobilization among Muslim Americans and other groups, Tazamal does not expect the party to abandon this effort, or the Islamophobic rhetoric at the center of it. “I don’t think the GOP is going to do away with it,” she said. • This article was amended on 15 September 2026 to clarify the date of polling carried out by the Pew Research Center.

title: Obama reportedly urges Democrats to prioritize safety plan for AI
author: Jessica Glenza
summary: Ex-president urged party at closed-door fundraiser to create sweeping framework, from safety ‘slow-down’ to job losses
body_text: Barack Obama urged Democrats to prioritize a “public conversation” about AI management and safety in a closed-door Manhattan fundraiser last week. The comments by the former US president reportedly urged the party to create a sweeping framework for everything from a safety “slow-down” to domestic job losses and children’s wellbeing. Obama’s comments follow a summer in which a band of rogue OpenAI chatbots hacked the company Hugging Face, towns across the country opposed datacenters and an AI researcher resigned in a viral social media post warning: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” AI leaders have recently expressed agreement that the race for technological superiority should slow, but have also sought to appease investors, whose stake in the technology is predicted to exceed $1tn in 2026 alone. “Once you are speaker,” Obama said to US House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York-Democrat, at the fundraiser Thursday. “I would strongly urge that the Democrats put together a framework for a very public conversation,” according to a transcript first reported by the New York Times. “This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous,” Obama said. “If we do get on top of it, I do think it’s beneficial. I genuinely think it’s going to accelerate, for example, drug development in ways that can help us cure diseases. I do think that this can help us figure out pathways for a clean energy future.” Obama later added: “I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety. Here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this,’” he said according to the Times. Obama made the remarks as the US closes in on the midterm elections and Congress has taken little action on AI. While prominent Democratic lawmakers, and some Republicans, have called to regulate the technology, Trump has attempted to aid the AI industry by introducing legislation that would ban state regulations (the bill did not move forward). Democrats face an open presidential field in 2028. One major flashpoint for the midterm elections is datacenters that power AI companies. Both parties have since begun running ads that oppose them, as one of the few issues, “Maga Republicans and liberal Democrats” agree on, according to an NPR analysis. On Sunday, while on a trip to his Irish golf course, Trump told reporters that a lot of “very negative forces” are ⁠bringing up concerns ⁠about AI that “won’t happen”, and that his main concern was that the US remain the industry leader, according to Reuters. “We’re leading China in AI. ‌We’re the ‌most sophisticated country in the world, ‌and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” Trump told reporters when asked if ‌the AI industry should slow down or be more regulated. In the past, Trump has said on social media that anyone who opposes AI datacenters is likely “backwards and poor”. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” he said on TruthSocial two weeks ago.

summary: Brief letters: Trump’s toga | Reform UK donations | Ben Delo | Word watch | Andy Burnham | The name game
body_text: Octavian (later Emperor Augustus), following his victorious battles of Illyricum and Actium, announced he would give 400 sesterces to adult male citizens. Will we see the US president wearing an emperor’s purple and gold toga soon (Trump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’, 10 September)? David Shannon Ashton under Hill, Worcestershire • Can we assume that the donations to Reform UK from the billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo (Report, 12 September) will be followed by some sort of cash offer for every adult in the UK should Mr Farage win the next election? title: Trade unions, MPs and donors urge Burnham to revisit party funding rules
author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
summary: PM has so far declined to insert curbs on UK-based donors, despite £72m donations from billionaires to Reform UK
body_text: Trade unions, MPs and donors have urged the government to look again at party funding rules, after Reform UK insisted £72m in donations from two crypto billionaires was within the law. Andy Burnham, a previous backer of caps on domestic donations, has so far declined to insert any curbs in the elections bill that would apply to UK-based donors. Labour MPs have voiced anger on internal WhatsApp groups that the government did not act last week when the elections bill was in the Commons to restrict domestic donations after two donors – Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo – gave Reform UK a total of £72m over the weekend. The bill returns to the House of Lords next week where peers told the Guardian they would ask the government to look again at the issue. The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, suggested on Sunday that the donations could be caught in a new bill which would apply retrospectively on donors from outside the UK. The two donors who gave Reform £36m each have both previously been based outside the UK. Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong. It is unclear when Delo returned to live in the UK and whether Harborne remains a resident of Thailand. Reform said both donations were within the rules. Senior government sources indicated the government was prepared to look again at the issue of domestic donations once it receives advice from a newly commissioned taskforce and from the Electoral Commission. One No 10 source said they did not want to delay the elections bill – which gives votes to 16-year-olds and puts new curbs on foreign donors – but said the bill was “not the right vehicle but this is not the end of the story”. Several Labour MPs said they had been assured by ministers that further legislation could still come before the general election. Trade unions are also understood to be wavering on the issue and a possible donations cap is expected to be part of discussions at the TUC congress next week, where Rayner and Burnham will speak. Unions have been central to the decision not to impose a domestic donations cap after several, especially GMB, argued it would be a slippery slope towards future rightwing governments curbing union donations. On Sunday the Unite trade union said it was in favour of a cap – and the largest trade union, Unison, said it would fight attempts by billionaires to influence politics. “For individual donors there must be a cap,” said Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary. “I think at some point it gets beyond what people think as normal.” Andrea Egan, Unison’s general secretary, said: “As his support dwindles in this country, Farage is turning to crypto billionaires in an attempt to undermine our democracy. The trade union movement will oppose him every step of the way.” Stella Creasy, the Labour MP whose amendment on donations caps attracted support in the Commons, is liaising with peers about how they can raise the issue when the bill returns to the House of Lords this week. The Labour peer Michael Wills said: “The government has already committed to urgently reviewing the questions of caps on donations. Now the bill is in the Lords, it offers an unmissable opportunity to say when that review will complete its work, and what its remit will be.” Creasy said the Reform donations had “concentrated people’s minds about what is now happening in our politics and what it will do to the voices of working people if it’s not stopped – we have the chance with the Lords to amend this bill with a cap”. Her amendment proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. It was not put to a vote after the government said it would ask a taskforce to look at the proposal. The former shadow chancellor John McDonnell said it was time for the government to move faster and for unions to get onboard. “It’s clear now to the trade unions meeting in congress this week that action is needed to protect our democracy and there’s a growing expectation the government will respond with urgency,” he said. Two influential big party donors also called for a cap on Sunday. The billionaire businessman and Phones 4U founder, John Caudwell, who previously donated to the Conservative party in 2019, told BBC Radio 4’s Broadcasting House: “There should be a definite change in law. We should not have very wealthy people making undue influence.” Dale Vince, the Ecotricity founder who has given donations to the Labour party, said it was “urgent” the government dealt with donations rules. “Ridiculous sums of money don’t level the playing field – they distort it. “Our current system of funding is anti-democratic – those with big money have more say than the simple vote we all have. A cap on donations would be a step in the right direction – the end game should be publicly funded politics.” The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, suggested he was sympathetic to further action. Speaking before the opening of the TUC congress, he said: “No one wants the UK to become a country for hire in the way Reform is clearly a party for hire. Without a doubt, we are going to need to restrict the ability of billionaires like Delo to buy and sell our politics. But we’ll have to do that in a way that doesn’t cut across workers having their voice heard politically.” Reform has said it is confident that its two donors will not be caught in a retrospective cap on donations from Britons living abroad. “We are 100% confident both are legal and won’t ever have to be handed back,” a spokesperson said, suggesting both men would meet the criteria on residency even within the rules of the new bill. As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March. Rayner – the minister responsible for the bill – said it was not targeted at individual donors or parties. “We didn’t know that donors were going to be putting that money in, and this isn’t about individual donors to a political party. This is an issue that has been raised about protecting our democracy from foreign interference, and the government is taking action on that,” she told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme. Reform’s economy spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said the two donors were well aware of the law. He said: “It’s a breakthrough moment, really, for the party. It means that we will be battle ready if Andy Burnham calls an election, and we can compete now finally on a fair, even playing field with the two old parties.”

title: Morning Mail: One Nation sleepovers at Rinehart’s revealed, Japan trips getting more expensive, and more AI alarm
author: Paul Gallagher
summary: New podcast looks at who One Nation really stands for; scrutiny over Australia’s military exports; AI bosses back calls to slow development
body_text: Good morning. Today we launch The Populist: a podcast about how One Nation is gaining ground in Australia. The four-part series follows senior correspondent Sarah Martin as she uncovers the inner workings of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation – a party that has imported the modus operandi of the global populist right, including Trump-style attacks on the media. The Populist asks who One Nation really stands for and what influence its billionaire benefactor Gina Rinehart has over the party. Elsewhere there’s speculation over the intended target of a Russian drone strike near the Ukraine-Poland border. And tech titans, including Elon Musk, say they’ll back calls to pump the brakes on AI development. Australia ‘Red lines’ legislation | David Pocock is among crossbench MPs who will pressure Labor to ban Australian goods from being used by the Israeli military. Sleepover at Rinehart’s | One Nation’s Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce stayed overnight at Gina Rinehart’s Brisbane mansion after fundraising events, with Joyce conducting a live television interview about politics from the $20m home. He did not declare the hospitality to parliament because the billionaire is a “long-term friend”. End of the road? | The Japanese yen has now reached its highest level against the US and Australian dollars in six months. Is the era of budget-friendly trips coming to an end for Australian travellers? ‘They can get to incredible numbers’ | Rabbits are the biggest threat to Australia’s native species. And due to good rainfall and growing resistance to viruses, rabbit populations are booming. Sea lion death | South Australia has recorded the first death of an endangered Australian sea lion from H5 bird flu, amid fears for the protected species of which less than 12,000 remain nationwide. World Russia-Ukraine war | A train carrying former UK PM Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief David Petraeus may have been the intended target of a drone strike near the Poland-Ukraine border, officials say. AI alarm | Sam Altman and Elon Musk have backed a call from the head of Anthropic to “slow the pace” of AI development in a rare show of unity from rival developers. “Too little, too late”: critics remain suspicious of AI leaders’ call for a slowdown. Middle East crisis | A pregnant woman was among more than 10 killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza; Iran-allied Houthis have said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in Saudi Arabia. Buying votes? | Donald Trump has doubled down on his controversial pledge to give US adults a “dividend” if his Republican ⁠party keeps control of Congress after November’s midterm elections. Sweden votes | Results are too close to call in Sweden’s high-stakes election, with projections narrowing after exit polls initially showed the centre-left bloc was set to take power over the incumbent centre-right coalition. Follow updates on our live blog. Full Story The Populist: Aeroplanes and bulldozers | Episode 1 “If you’re trying to say I’m being funded by Gina Rinehart, the answer is no.” That’s what One Nation leader Pauline Hanson told the Guardian’s senior correspondent Sarah Martin in February. We now know that’s not true. Over months, Martin pieced together flight tracking data and expense records to uncover the true extent of financial support flowing from Australia’s richest person to the country’s fastest growing political force. Episode one of the Populist podcast, launched today, tells the inside story, from the Farrer byelection to the National Press Club – including exclusive new reporting. In-depth As peer-on-peer violence continues to rise, many girls, who make up the majority of school-age sexual assault victims, have no choice but to return to school. And in many cases, they must continue to share a campus with their assailant. When schools must balance a duty of care to both victims and perpetrators, where does this leave girls who have to pursue their education in the shadow of sexual assault? Not the news With a busy touring schedule of Brisbane, Melbourne and Sydney ahead, the Fijian Flying Circus is a lo-fi, high energy mix that teaches its performers a valuable grab-bag of theatre and life skills even as they charm the crowds. The most important thing for the performers, however, is what is happening back at home. Once salaries are paid, every extra dollar goes into funding the next generation of Fijian circus performers. Sport Tennis | Alexander Zverev is facing Ben Shelton in this year’s US Open men’s singles final; Elena Rybakina rode the “ups and downs” to transform her status among tennis elite, Tumaini Carayol writes. AFL | The Lions have been rewarded for embracing risk as “good Brisbane” keeps the AFL flag dream alive, Jonathan Horn writes. Football | Manchester City recovered from Phil Foden red card as Erling Haaland won the derby at United; Lewis Dunk’s showstopper helped five-star Brighton to rout 10-man Coventry in the Premier League. Motorsport | Kimi Antonelli held off Max Verstappen during his Madring debut to win the F1 Spanish Grand Prix. Cycling | Enric Mas reigns supreme at last in the Vuelta a España to delight Spanish fans. Rugby union | Greatest Rivalry swagger showed South Africa will take some beating at the World Cup, Gerard Meagher writes. Media roundup Australia is spending $27bn to build three warships to replace the aging Anzac-class ships. Will the project be worth it?, asks ABC News. Australians paid more than five times the benchmark price for a visit to a specialist doctor on more than a million occasions last year, the SMH reports. Documents have revealed how Labor supercharged the use of contingency funding for major infrastructure projects in Victoria, the Age reports. What’s happening today ACT | Federal parliament is sitting in Canberra. NSW | The trial of former broadcaster Alan Jones continues in Sydney. You can follow the latest in US politics by signing up for This Week in Trumpland. Brain teaser And finally, here are the Guardian’s crosswords to keep you entertained throughout the day. title: The US right still paints Muslims as the ‘enemy’. But they are fighting for a brighter future for Americans
author: Nesrine Malik
summary: Progressive politicians such as Zohran Mamdani offer answers to the bitter post-9/11 legacy of failures at home and abroad, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
body_text: Twenty-five years after 9/11, two pieces of journalism, describing two different phenomena in contemporary New York, tell us a great deal about a city, and indeed a world, caught between two eras. In one, New York Magazine dives into “Habibi City”, a New York where a “cultural shift is underway, led by a generation of New Yorkers coming into its own”. This new generation is labelled as originating in “SWANA” – south-west Asia and north Africa, a region that “includes countries from Palestine to Iran to Sudan”. In the other, Vanity Fair describes calls for Zohran Mamdani to not attend the 9/11 memorial ceremony as partly founded in “inchoate, emotional” impulses, that see “the city’s first Muslim mayor as a stand-in for the 19 Muslims who hijacked four planes and turned them into deadly weapons, part of the ‘them’ who attacked ‘us’.” Together they capture what has changed over a generation, and what remains stubbornly the same. Members of a diaspora of Muslim background are indeed breaking through and accumulating, as New York Magazine says, “clout”. They are no longer simply a fixture of bodegas and halal carts, but of Saturday Night Live, upmarket dining, entertainment and politics too. Mamdani is both the expression of that cohort and the catalyst of its recognition as an emerging force. They care deeply for their local communities but also for those in Gaza and beyond. I use the descriptor “of Muslim background” rather than “Muslim” because this diasporic identity is a diverse one that is rooted in a religion but expands to encompass everyone from the practising to those for whom Islam is a cultural totem.The capaciousness of this heritage is demonstrable in its integration – without compromise – into mainstream American society. Mamdani and the Democratic Senate nominee for Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, recuse themselves from the rote fealty to American glory and dare to point out both US support for Israel and the calamitous outcomes of the “war on terror” in the Middle East. This is the result of this new generation of Americans coming from an immigrant background that has cultivated a less parochial and supremacist view of the US. There is something historically inevitable in this. Immigration from countries and backgrounds against which the US has waged military and ideological war eventually yields not a cowed assimilation, but a sort of political cosmopolitanism – kryptonite for American exceptionalism. Growing up in the shadow of Islamophobia is another formative experience that ironically forced many to identify in terms of religious background rather than race or national origin. “In a way,” said American comedian Ramy Youssef, in a now legendary standup comedy segment, “9/11 made me more Muslim. Cos I was told it was my fault.” This is a profoundly recognisable story for many, including myself, for whom a casual religious identity became a sharp political one during the “war on terror” years. At the same time as this new generation found their political and social power, the Islamophobia that began in 2001 has only further burrowed into the fabric of American society. Pew research found that, a quarter of a century after 9/11, “public attitudes toward Islam have become more ‘negative’ and more ‘partisan’” than they were in the wake of the attack. In March 2002, 25% of US adults believed that Islam “is more likely than other religions to encourage violence”. Today that figure has doubled to 51%. That is why Mamdani can be seen as a representative of hijackers (despite the fact that he was nine years old on 9/11) and El-Sayed can be called a “terrorist” by Senator Tommy Tuberville. Congresswoman Nancy Mace said that “every single Muslim holding public office in America” is a “threat to both national security and our republic”. “Jihadists”, said Donald Trump, were “being elected all over the place”. Rozina Ali, the author of Seasons of Fury, a study of the history of Islamophobia in the US, tells me that contemporary Islamophobia cannot be separated from a wider failure of American politics at home and abroad. The “war on terror” turned into a foreign quagmire. At home, a financial crisis saw millions of people lose their homes and savings. One of the reasons Islamophobia has been used by the right is that “a lot of these things can be explained by so called invasions from foreigners or a foreign culture like Islam”. The right, she said, simply “doesn’t have an effective vision for this country that can actually solve a lot of the ills”. The problem for this approach is not only that Muslims are no longer keeping their heads down, but that they represent a broader progressive politics. Political candidates as well as cultural figures are mobilising large blocks of voters and backers because their worldview has been informed by profound marginalisation. They can root their politics in material concerns about standards of living as well as unpopular foreign policy, in addition to humanising the toll of the political backlash against Muslims and making it a part of the American story. They can unite a broad coalition of people because they too experience being on the losing side against a political establishment. Despite all the vitriol from the right, anti-Muslim propaganda has not prevented these connections being formed. At the 9/11 commemorative ceremony this past weekend, Mamdani soberly and graciously shook the hand of Rudy Giuliani, the man who was mayor of New York on 9/11, and who had called for Mamdani not to attend. One man was the past, and the other was the future. Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: AI CEOs say they need to slow the pace of development. But will they?
author: Nick Robins-Early
summary: After apocalyptic warnings about the the threats posed by AI, leaders like Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s calls to ‘slow the pace’
body_text: Facing a public uproar over Anthropic researchers’ repeated warnings that artificial intelligence could kill all of humanity by 2030, the AI company’s CEO, Dario Amodei, issued a proposal at the weekend to slow down the technology’s advancement to ensure public safety. In a rare display of unity, the heads of the largest US artificial intelligence companies all agreed immediately. The OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis and xAI owner Elon Musk posted support for Amodei’s proposal for slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”, with Altman stating he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices. “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman posted Saturday on X. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same.” “Dario’s essay points towards the right path forward,” said Hassabis. Musk simply wrote: “Dario is right.” The AI CEOs’ warnings and promises open up a host of questions about how AI might be regulated, what risks it poses and whether the industry will actually slow down the fevered race to advance its technology. While lawmakers and the tech industry consider how to address growing fear and distrust of AI, many of the hurdles impeding comprehensive AI regulation remain the same as before last week’s apocalyptic declarations from a young Anthropic researcher. The US federal government is committed to a global AI arms race. Previous proposed AI legislation has wilted under intense, well-financed corporate lobbying. AI startups face the enormous pressures to release new, more powerful products ahead of upcoming trillion-dollar public offerings. Amodei’s pacing proposal has drawn heavy skepticism from critics and researchers who allege that AI firms are attempting to preempt more stringent government regulation and retain the status quo of power within the industry. Anthropic and OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Amodei’s proposal focuses on three main pillars. First, a commitment to outside evaluators given employee-level access to monitor risk. Second, agreements between democratic states on AI safety standards. Finally, global coordination with authoritarian governments such as China on security issues. Amodei and others in the industry have made similar calls for global coordination in the past, even before the industry’s recent warnings over models becoming too advanced and gaining autonomy. The AI industry, especially the factions within it that focus on whether the technology is aligned with humanity’s interests, has also long warned about its existential threats. Rahm Emanuel, former congressman and chief of staff to Barack Obama, tweeted: “I can tell you when the last time a CEO or an industry at large asked to be regulated: never. That’s what makes Dario’s letter so striking – it’s an admission that we’re driving down a dark, winding road on wet pavement with the headlights off. And where’s President Trump? Looks like he nodded off again.” AI firms have fluctuated on their emphasis on communicating the potential harm from their products, however, at times warning about apocalyptic effects of AI and at others promising it will bring about utopian prosperity. OpenAI, for instance, shut down a “superalignment” team in 2024 dedicated to studying long term AI risks and earlier this year disbanded another team intended to communicate how OpenAI would benefit humanity. While AI companies have made grandiose claims about the threats and benefits from their technology, they have also historically provided little transparency or oversight into how their models operate and spent millions in lobbying efforts to shape favorable legislation. The result of the AI industry’s narrative that it is too powerful, complex and lucrative of a technology to regulate, critics say, is that it has been allowed to essentially govern itself. “AI exceptionalism has led to a total failure to uphold our standards for what products are deemed safe for use,” Sarah Myers West, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute, posted Sunday on X. Critics similarly see Amodei’s proposal as another instance in which the industry is seeking to set its own rules, in this case picking its own evaluators to monitor safety risks, instead of facing the scrutiny of more intensive government regulators. Alex Bores, a proponent of AI regulation whose failed bid for Congress spurred $24m in spending both for and against his campaign from AI-linked political action committees, warned that the AI lobby often seeks to undermine legislation while claiming to support regulation. “To everyone who genuinely wants real AI regulation, please don’t fall for their games,” Bores posted Sunday on X. Several critics of the AI pacing proposal from across the political spectrum expressed concern around Amodei’s proposal’s suggestion that the government could grant some form of antitrust waiver or exemption to allow industry coordination. Former officials, including Trump’s former “AI czar” David Sacks and Biden-era head of the Federal Trade Commission Alvaro Bedoya, suggested that the proposal amounted to an attempt at regulatory capture, which would benefit current industry leaders. “Antitrust law does not prevent AI companies from coordinating to make sure AI does not hurt people,” Bedoya posted on X, adding: “Antitrust law does absolutely prevent AI companies from organizing to prevent the entry of cheaper, upstart rivals because the bigger companies are burning cash and failing to achieve sufficient profitability.” The proposal’s calls for international coordination around AI and federal intervention also run up against president Donald Trump and his administration’s vows to turn the US into the dominant AI superpower regardless of safety concerns. The Trump administration has often framed AI development as a zero-sum contest against China for technological supremacy, an argument the AI industry itself has also promoted in the face of proposed government regulation. Vice-president JD Vance declared in a speech last year that the future of AI was “not going to be won by hand-wringing about safety”. On Sunday, Trump once again rejected calls for slowing down AI development while citing competition from China and telling reporters “whoever wins AI, wins”. “We could put guardrails. We can do this and that,” Trump told reporters while on a visit to Ireland. “But I think you have a lot of very negative ⁠forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen”. House speaker Mike Johnson likewise said Congress would not lead the charge on regulating AI safety, laying the responsibility at the feet of AI companies.

title: The situation in Iran is dangerously escalating – but whatever you do, don’t call it a war
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: Forget the bombing: the Trump administration keeps insisting this isn’t a war. But it’s not just a matter of semantics
body_text: “I will not send you to fight and die in stupid foreign wars that never end,” Donald Trump promised a crowd in Pennsylvania in 2024. While the disastrous conflict in Iran, which has escalated in recent days, may make it seem like the president has reneged on that promise, that’s inaccurate. It would be wrong to say that the president has dragged the US into yet another disastrous forever war in the Middle East because, as government officials keep insisting, what’s happening in Iran isn’t actually a war. “I wouldn’t call it a war,” JD Vance told reporters early this month, for example, after being asked whether the fighting in Iran might be over by the November midterms. “Right now, there is no active shooting.” Maybe not, but there has been quite a bit of active bombing. Earlier this month, a US missile strike hit a wedding at a private home in southern Iran, killing at least four people, including a four-year-old child and a 16-year-old. That’s fairly restrained compared to the massacre in March when a US precision-guided missile hit an elementary school in Iran, killing 150 people, including 120 children, but it’s still something I would personally file under “possible war crimes”. But not only does the Trump administration keep insisting this isn’t a real war, they’re also adamant there aren’t any real crimes being committed: the vice-president would like to stress that you shouldn’t believe your eyes or ears when it comes to the civilian deaths being reported. Despite a weapons expert and a visual analysis by the New York Times concluding that the bomb that hit the wedding party in a residential area of the country was American, Vance has a hunch the whole thing might have been made up by some untrustworthy brown people. “The Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far,” Vance said at that same press briefing, in relation to the wedding massacre. “So I’m extremely skeptical of this.” The vice-president may be skeptical, but I’m confused. If this isn’t a war, what is it? A little skirmish? An interminable series of special military operations? A very bloody screw-up? Trump himself has called it a war on several occasions. Last Wednesday, for example, he said: “The war is going to end immediately after the election.” However, rather confusing matters, he also recently suggested he agreed with Vance that it wasn’t a full-fledged war. “I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us,” Trump said last month. Those are some very expensive potatoes: the not-a-war already has a price tag of tens of billions. Mark Zandi, the chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, has roughly estimated that it has cost the typical US household $1,200. And then of course there’s the human cost: the thousands of lives that have been lost. What we call this “military conflict” isn’t just semantics, it matters greatly. Not least because the constitution is very clear that a president can’t unilaterally start an official war on a whim; only Congress has the power to declare a war. Trump isn’t the first president to launch major military action without going to Congress for a declaration: Harry Truman classified the Korean conflict as a “police action” to bypass Congress and presidents since have engaged in similar semantic sleights-of-hand. But, as the historian and foreign relations expert Fredrik Logevall noted in an interview with the Harvard Kennedy School: “What’s extraordinary about President Trump in the current context is that he has not really bothered to even consult with Congress, never mind seek the approval of Congress.” In other words, he’s acting like a dictator. Trump, to be fair, has been clear that he’s exploiting the Truman Playbook. “I won’t use the word ‘war’ because they say if you use the word ‘war,’ that’s maybe not a good thing to do,” Trump said at a fundraising dinner in March. “They don’t like the word ‘war’ because you’re supposed to get approval. So, I’ll use the word ‘military operation’, which is really what it is. It’s a military decimation.” Avoiding a formal declaration of war might also help the US government bypass certain “wartime” obligations to its service members and their families. Libby Klinner, the widow of an airman killed in combat operations against Iran in March, recently posted on Instagram that she wasn’t receiving certain benefits because the US wasn’t technically at war. “The Air Force recently told me that because we haven’t officially declared war, my kids and I aren’t eligible for some benefits,” Klinner wrote. “So not only was my husband killed in a war he never wanted to participate in, but now the benefits we’re left with are being dictated by semantics and public perceptions.” After this post went viral, it seems the government has stepped in smooth things over. Vance recently said the administration would ensure Klinner receives “what she is entitled to.” He added: “We will certainly work that on the back end.” The government might be able to fix Klinner’s benefits, but they’re going to have a hard time remedying the economic and political damage this not-a-war is inflicting. Trump’s popularity is plummeting, and a majority of Americans are fed up with this “small potatoes” conflict that has been going on for six months and making everyday life more dangerous and expensive. According to an estimate from Brown University last week, the conflict has cost Americans $100bn in extra energy costs. That bill is going up by $1m every two minutes. This week oil prices also climbed over $100 a barrel for the first time since July. Meanwhile, with hostilities escalating and no off-ramp in sight, it looks like Trump is out of options. All he has left is empty promises. The president has insisted that energy prices will tumble “right after the election” and, in a sign he is completely desperate, promised every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of both chambers of Congress in November. The Trump administration can call the war whatever they like, but future generations will define it as a disastrous act of hubris. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

title: Democrats to train tens of thousands to monitor polls amid election interference fears
author: Rachel Leingang
summary: Project will prepare volunteers across US to monitor polls, encourage early voting and respond to disinformation
body_text: The Democrats intend to train tens of thousands of volunteers to monitor the polls and counter possible voter intimidation under a new plan to protect November’s US midterm elections from anticipated interference from Donald Trump and his allies. The nationwide initiative, dubbed the New Battlefield Project, will help state Democratic committees build up a vast coalition of volunteers to monitor the polls, push voters to cast their ballots early and create a network to respond to disinformation. The Association of State Democratic Committees (ASDC), an arm of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), plans to train volunteers across 57 states and territories. It hopes to train volunteers for 25% of the nation’s 95,000 election day polling places, focusing on districts with competitive races. These volunteers will wear blue vests to provide a visible presence intended to counter any voter intimidation, including by federal agents. Thirty state parties have a trained election protection director, with the goal of all states having one in place. The Trump administration has not explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to cities during the election, and some of the president’s allies have called on him to send immigration agents to the polls. The homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, previously said immigration agents’ job isn’t to patrol polling places, but they could go to polling places if there was a threat or to serve a warrant. The president has personally made a series of interventions that have fanned fears that he could meddle in the upcoming elections, and even declare a national emergency in a bid to exert greater control over the process. Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic party and president of the ASDC, said the project is much more extensive and coordinated than the party has been in the past on election protection. “We didn’t want to be caught flat-footed on election day or leading up to election day,” she said. These volunteers will be trained to “be happy” and respond to any voter needs, including helping them find a polling location if they’re in the wrong place, or informing them they can cast provisional ballots if they need to, Kleeb said. They will also document whether others at the polls are hindering voters. “We don’t know if there are going to be a bunch of insurrectionist types out there trying to intimidate voters, but we’re going to be there happy with information, but we’re also going to be there trained to document if the other side is doing things that are violating the law,” she said. The party will additionally push out its first national early-vote campaign, telling voters to “bank their vote” by casting ballots early by mail or in person. This will include ad campaigns focused on communities at risk of Republican election interference. The state parties and the DNC typically run get-out-the-vote programs, but this year’s will include more explicit directions to voters – telling them to vote early, and not let a mail ballot sit on their kitchen counter for weeks before turning it in, Kleeb said. The party will also push for people to vote early in person. “We don’t know what Donald Trump is going to do. We’ve heard some of the things that he may do, but none of us can predict his behavior,” she said. “He’s so chaotic. All of us have witnessed certainly that. So the earlier you can vote, the better.” The third part of the project will spin up a “democracy defense network”, led by Democratic strategist Simon Rosenberg, designed to identify and counter tactics that can sway elections, including disinformation, dark money, manipulation via artificial intelligence and election subversion. The network will allow state parties to communicate with each other about these threats to share knowledge, with a goal to get ahead of such tactics before they gain traction.

title: What is the Register of British Slave Traders and whom does it identify?
author: David Conn Investigations correspondent
summary: Three years of research has uncovered 13,000 people who invested in Britain’s trafficking of enslaved Africans
body_text: The Register of British Slave Traders is the product of three years of research by a team of historians into all known investors in Britain’s near 250 years of trafficking enslaved African people, from the 16th to 19th centuries. It provides profiles and biographical details of thousands of people who financed the British slave trade, which violently trafficked approximately 3 million African men, women and children across the Atlantic. The register defines slave traders as individuals who invested in directly financing a ship’s transportation of enslaved African people in expectation of a profit share. The project builds on research over recent decades documenting European countries’ trafficking of an estimated 12 million enslaved African people. Its starting point was the Slave Voyages database, a collaboration between universities launched in 2008, which documents enslaving ships, how many people were trafficked and how many died on the notorious Atlantic crossings, as well as the owners and investors. The earliest slave traders were privateers and piratical ship captains and owners such as John Hawkins, whose voyages in the 1560s were backed by Queen Elizabeth I, her chief minister William Cecil, leading courtier Robert Dudley and Sir Thomas Lodge, the lord mayor of London. The register documents the investment that followed by people from across society. The monarchy’s involvement became more institutional from 1660, with three royally chartered companies formed: The Company of Royal Adventurers into Africa, founded in 1660; The Company of Royal Adventurers Trading to Africa, founded in 1663; The Royal African Company, founded 1672, which trafficked about 150,000 enslaved African people. The South Sea Company, founded in 1711, trafficked close to 45,000 enslaved African people. As a crown- and state-backed mass-subscription company, the register documents its directors rather than all its investors. The Royal African Company’s monopoly on the trafficking of enslaved people from Africa was removed in stages from 1689, under pressure from individual “separate traders” who lobbied parliament because they wanted to participate in the trafficking themselves. The register then traces investors beyond London to Bristol, Liverpool and other port towns and cities as Britain’s trafficking of enslaved people increased dramatically. In total, the historians identified 13,000 people who were investors in the British slave trade, from Hawkins’s first voyage in 1562 to parliament’s abolition of the slave trade in 1807. Of these, about 2,500 were shareholders in the South Sea Company, a mass public subscription, who are not part of the register. Of the other 10,500 investors, the historians found identifying information and records for about 6,000. The register also includes details on the directors of the South Sea Company. The researchers examined those individuals’ dates of birth and death, marriages and political participation, identifying dozens from Tory and Whig parties – forerunners of today’s Conservatives and Liberal Democrats – as well as local mayors and aldermen (councillors). They also examined wider biographical information and wills, which showed that many slave traders bequeathed money to hospitals, schools and other welfare organisations, including hundreds who donated to the poor through their local churches and parishes across Britain. About 1,000 of the investors were women. According to the register’s lead historian, Prof William Pettigrew, the aim was to compile “the most comprehensive examination of a nation’s slave traders ever attempted” . The Register of British Slave Traders is a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council. It was led by the principal investigator and editor Prof William Pettigrew, now of King’s College London and co-investigators Dr Nicholas Radburn, Prof Edmond Smith and Dr Nicholas Draper. The research team included Dr Michael Bennett, Dr Lila O’Leary Chambers, Dr James Dawkins, Dr Charmian Mansell, and Dr Kimberley Thomas. The advisory board included Dr Miranda Kaufmann, Dr Omar Khan, Dr Aidan McQuade, Prof David Olusoga and Arthur Torrington.

title: Disaster insurance, datacenters, right to repair: meet the midterm candidates running on green policies
author: Dharna Noor
summary: Some of the everyday struggles animating voters have a climate link lurking in the background
body_text: When Florida governor Ron DeSantis signed a law erasing the words “climate change” from state statutes in May 2024 – colloquially known as the “don’t say climate change” law – Democrats were outraged. Just six months later, many liberal politicians began to go quiet on the issue themselves. After Donald Trump won the 2024 election, mentions of the climate crisis started to disappear from Democrats’ rhetoric. As the 2026 midterms approach, that retreat is still shaping how some candidates talk about climate on the campaign trail. The trend, known as “climate-hushing”, may reflect the limitations of Joe Biden’s climate policies, said Daniel Aldana Cohen, assistant sociology professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who studies climate politics and inequality. Green jobs and housing investments fell short of the climate movement’s desires, consumer incentives disproportionately benefited wealthier households, and Democrats struggled to effectively communicate their accomplishments. The president has since rolled back many Biden-era clean energy incentives and regulations. The climate crisis, however, is still rearing its head around the country, fueling the heatwaves, wildfires and floods plaguing communities around the US. It also lurks behind issues animating voters, from datacenter expansion to rising home insurance rates. And while some pundits have concluded from their polling and research that Americans don’t want to hear about global warming, other surveys directly contradict those findings. “Maybe people don’t rank climate as their main or top issue … but nobody really experiences everyday life like walking around the world rank-ordering the things that they care about,” said Aldana Cohen, who is also founding co-director of the thinktank Climate and Community Institute that calls for “green economic populism”. “What’s important is to learn how to embed the climate issue organically amidst the other issues that people care most about.” Some progressive and populist candidates in the US midterms are pushing back against climate-hushing, linking the issue to economic concerns and everyday struggles. Others aren’t speaking about it directly, but pushing for policies that could curb emissions. Such efforts could help build a mass base for climate policies, said Aldana Cohen. “If we want to decarbonize fast enough and adapt to the impacts that are already here, we’re going to need a robust majority that backs those policies,” he said. “Elite consensus alone will not suffice … we’re going to need like large numbers of people really enthusiastic about climate policies.” The Guardian spoke with three midterm candidates about how three issues with major environmental implications are shaping their campaigns. Single-payer disaster insurance Jane Kim, state director of the Working Families Party and a former San Francisco county supervisor, is running to become California’s next insurance commissioner. The little-noticed but highly influential position oversees the state’s home, auto and business insurance markets. The frontrunner in the race, she received 27% of votes in the June primary. Among her key proposals is a single-payer system for disaster insurance, which she began developing as climate-fueled wildfires ravaged the state. California wildfires have catalyzed homeowners’ insurance crisis. Companies have stopped writing new policies and non-renewed thousands of homeowners in high-risk areas, making coverage increasingly difficult to find. Homeowners can turn to the California Fair Plan, the insurer of last resort, but it provides limited fire coverage rather than the broader protection of a typical homeowners policy. Kim argues that climate-fueled disasters are making catastrophic risk too large and socially consequential to leave to the private sector. “The biggest change in the insurance industry in the past four years is the increase of climate disasters,” she said. “We used to have a billion-dollar storm every three to four months, and it seems like we now have one every three weeks, so the price of risk has truly gone up.” The scheme would create a public, government-run insurance program to cover wildfire damage for all homes, modeled on government-backed programs in New Zealand, France and Spain. Homes would be automatically enrolled regardless of their condition, and owners would pay premiums based on property values, risk, and other factors. Some aspects of the plan would require legislative approval. Since the nonprofit program would not have to generate shareholder profits, Kim said investment returns could build a pool of money for future claims. It could also be designed to mitigate climate risk rather than simply avoid it, she added. “In New Zealand, they actually use a portion of premiums for fire-proofing and flood-proofing, because they guarantee home disaster insurance to everyone,” she said. Private insurers are also major institutional investors in oil and gas, which are fueling the climate crisis, said Kim – an issue she would uplift in office, though it is outside the direct purview of the role. Critics of the single-payer disaster scheme argue that shifting financial risk to the state could further destabilize California’s insurance market and leave taxpayers bearing a greater burden, and fear pricing risk either too high or too low could both cause major challenges. Kim argues consumers are already paying too much for insurance. She says revenues could be raised from a variety of places, including potentially by forcing state insurers to pay an “exit fee”. She also says she does not aim to eliminate the private insurance market, but to bring in government where it falls short. “The current insurance system is a failure,” she said. “Voters know that.” “Insurance was invented centuries ago as a form of mutual aid,” she said, pointing to ancient Roman practices where soldiers used communal funds to cover funeral expenses. “It was always meant to be a way to distribute risk collectively, so that no one would be left out.” Democrats may be moving away from tackling climate issues head-on, but in California, “climate is unavoidable,” Kim said. “It’s a crisis that’s reshaping the way so many people are living,” she said. “Losing your home, your community, your neighborhood, your schools, and then not knowing if you’re going to get insured for the very thing that you paid for? That’s unconscionable.” AI datacenters In Michigan, William Lawrence, a progressive Democrat running for Congress, has placed his opposition to unchecked datacenter expansion at the center of his campaign. He is calling for a statewide moratorium on new datacenters and backing a federal moratorium, arguing that the facilities can strain local infrastructure and drive up energy demand. Lawrence co-founded the youth-led environmental justice group the Sunrise Movement, which mainstreamed calls for the Green New Deal in 2018. He won his primary race earlier this year and will face Republican incumbent Tom Barrett in November. In his race for the state’s hotly contested purple seventh district, Lawrence has featured the datacenter issue prominently, including in multiple television ads and speeches. At least 11 datacenters are planned throughout Michigan, and three hyperscaler-size ones are proposed in district 7 alone, with another recently struck down by Lansing’s city council. The climate ramifications of datacenter buildout are important to the longtime climate organizer. The facilities consume enormous amounts of electricity, much of which is still generated by burning fossil fuels, and their rapid expansion is driving efforts to keep gas, oil, and even coal online, potentially locking in emissions for decades. Recent research found AI could increase fossil fuel production enough to generate at least three times the emissions associated with today’s datacenters. But climate concerns are far from the only reason Michigan voters are worried about the buildout of the facilities, Lawrence said. Some fear water contamination, noise pollution, higher energy bills or falling home values. Others are most concerned about the impact AI will have on the job market and society at large. “You think you know the place you live and you can envision a future there, but then you have to imagine a behemoth datacenter that … potentially driving you and your neighbors out of town,” he said. “That is all so deeply destabilizing.” The “most uniting frame”, he said, is a sense that AI companies have too much power to push projects through small communities. “That all really calls our democracy into question,” he said. Barrett does not support a national datacenter moratorium. This month he put out an ad calling for local control of datacenter development, and put forth legislation he says would stop federal agencies from overriding local land-use, zoning, siting, or permitting rules for the facilities. He had previously backed legislation which included billions in tax breaks for AI developers, and another bill aiming to limit federal environmental reviews for datacenters and other projects, the American Prospect recently reported. In Michigan, some unions and local officials have backed datacenter proposals that promise to bring jobs and revenue. Lawrence says he understands their concerns but fears AI will undermine employment in the longer term. Temporary bans, he said, would allow officials to develop stringent regulations around datacenters before their rapid buildout. A Data For Progress poll indicates that more than 40% of residents were “much more likely” to vote for a candidate who opposed the buildout of datacenters – a dynamic that helped Lawrence win 49% of the vote in Mason, site of a planned facility. Lawrence said climate-hushing is an understandable trend. “There are so many acute crises in our world,” he said. “It is challenging to name them all in a five-minute stump speech and weave it all together into one story.” Still, when he talks about the climate crisis and environmental issues more broadly with voters, particularly when discussing his own background, he said many of them are receptive. They understand that “we live on a living planet and we depend on it,” he said. Right to repair In Nebraska, Dan Osborn, the Independent former labor leader running for Senate, has made “right to repair” a part of his platform, even featuring the issue in a video ad. The policy would make it easier for people to repair and maintain their cars, farm equipment and other products, reducing waste and extending the life of goods. It’s a concept built on a simple idea: if you buy something, you should be able to fix it yourself or hire someone to do so. The candidate became passionate about the proposal after an experience at work. Osborn spent two decades as a mechanic at Kellogg’s, where he helped lead a successful 77-day strike in 2021. One day on the job, he was working with a ball valve used to flavor Fruit Loops. (“All those Fruit Loops are all the same flavors, even though they’re different colors,” he said.) He asked a co-worker in the storeroom how much replacing the valve would cost, and found the answer was between $500 and $600. Only a Teflon seal inside the valve needed replacing – a fix he said he could have made himself for about $80. But the company didn’t stock the necessary rebuild kits, meaning the entire valve would have to be thrown away and replaced. “I said, ‘that’s the dumbest thing I’ve ever heard,’” he said. “I had no choice at that point but to throw that thing in the garbage.” Osborn sees the same problem playing out with farm machinery, cars and other products, where manufacturers’ restrictions can leave workers and consumers waiting for authorized technicians or paying for expensive repairs they could otherwise handle themselves. Defense contractors run “the same monopoly repair scam”, Osborn says, forcing the military to pay contractors taxpayer money for repairs. Though he frames it mainly as an economic justice issue, he also sees an environmental benefit: repair generally uses fewer resources than making and transporting replacements and keeps usable equipment out of the waste stream. “It’s a waste for the environment,” he said. “It’s just a waste all around.” The issue has gained prominence in recent months. In July, the manufacturing company John Deere reached a major settlement with the Federal Trade Commission and five states, requiring the company to give farmers and independent repair shops access to diagnostic software and tools needed to fix up equipment. Federal and state lawmakers across the US have also proposed dozens of right to repair bills across the country. Trump has also backed some right-to-repair measures, signing a June memo directing regulators to clarify what car repairs Americans can legally perform and consider easing enforcement against people who fix their own cars. “Talking about the issue is good,” said Osborn. “But there needs to be actual laws around this, and they need to have some teeth.” Opponents, including the Cato Institute, have argued that right-to-repair laws could expose companies’ intellectual property or that improper repairs could increase emissions. But proponents say the proposals could massively benefit the environment. Planet-warming pollution from electronic waste rose by 53% from 2014 to 2020; green groups say right to repair could help reverse those projections. “I usually really talk about it as a consumer protection issue … but certainly the environment plays into it for people that are concerned about that; it gets brought up,” he said. As a candidate in an agricultural region, Osborn said many voters intrinsically understand the importance of a healthy climate and an uncontaminated landscape. “We only get one planet, and we can’t screw it up,” he said.
