title: First Thing: Oil prices surge as attacks on Saudi Arabia stoke supply fears
author: Martin Belam
summary: Strike on kingdom’s east-west pipeline could affect 4% of global oil supply
body_text: Good morning. Oil prices have climbed above $108 a barrel after a series of drone attacks from Iraq’s territory forced Saudi Arabia to close its east-west crude pipeline. Saudi traders said the kingdom would run out of oil stocks for export if it did not reopen within days. Gas prices also climbed higher. Energy prices have surged this year, as the US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted oil and gas supply across the Middle East. The spike came as the Iran-aligned Houthi forces in Yemen launched several attacks against Saudi Arabia and captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait on Sunday, expanding their control of the waterway. Where did the attack on Saudi Arabia come from? Iraq’s government confirmed the attacks were launched from its territory and ordered an investigation. Baghdad is under mounting pressure to stop militant groups – including those backed by Saudi Arabia’s regional rival Iran – launching attacks on Gulf countries from Iraqi soil. The US president, Donald Trump, said he believed Tehran was responsible. Why has Saudi Arabia been relying on its east-west pipeline? Riyadh has increased the use of the 745-mile pipeline since the start of the war on Iran in order to bypass the strait of Hormuz’s closure. The world’s biggest exporter has used the pipeline to reroute about 4m barrels a day – about 4% of global supply – but with the ‌pipeline out of service, the Red Sea port of Yanbu now has stocks to maintain exports for just five to seven days. AI-linked stocks take hit as leading US tech CEOs back calls to put brakes on ‘reckless’ AI development AI-linked stocks have tumbled after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for a slowdown in “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control. The market swings come after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed for the AI industry to “slow down”. Last week, a former Anthropic employee had warned that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. The respective CEOs of OpenAI and SpaceX, Sam Altman and Elon Musk, have backed Amodei’s call. The US president, Donald Trump, on a visit to his golf course in Ireland, played down the warnings and said “very negative forces” were “bringing up things that won’t happen”. What is the Anthropic CEO proposing? Robert Booth explains Amodei’s suggestion: first, each US AI company grants access to third-party evaluators; second, all companies in democratic countries establish common safety standards; and third, the world’s democratic AI powers coordinate with autocracies – notably China – to control the race. How has Barack Obama intervened over AI? The former US president made a direct appeal to Democrats to coalesce around a unified AI safety policy, arguing that waiting for voluntary compliance from tech firms was a recipe for governance failure. Israel accused of trying to ‘eliminate’ living conditions for Palestinians in West Bank Israel is working towards the systematic “elimination” of the conditions that sustain Palestinian collective life in the occupied West Bank, according to a report published by the human rights group B’Tselem. The Israeli organisation says Israel is “dramatically intensifying its attacks on every aspect of Palestinian life in the West Bank”. How does the report say Israel is making life intolerable? “Palestinian communities are being pushed out in an accelerating process of ethnic cleansing, while an ever-expanding Israeli presence is being established … Elimination in this context means sustained harm to the conditions that enable Palestinians to exist as a people with land, institutions, language, culture, social ties, leadership, shared memory and history, and a social and political horizon. It is an ongoing political project.” Wisconsin congressman swims to safety after plane makes emergency landing in lake A Republican congressman said he had to swim to safety after a plane he was traveling in made an emergency landing in a lake late Saturday. Tom Tiffany is running for governor on the Republican ticket in Wisconsin and has been endorsed by Donald Trump. Tiffany says he was returning from the La Crosse county Lincoln Day Dinner when the light aircraft lost power as it approached Wausau downtown airport. He said the pilot made an emergency landing in Lake Wausau and they ended up in the water and swam to safety. Emergency responders got Tiffany and the pilot to a nearby hospital, where they were treated for minor injuries. In other news … Sweden’s centre-left parties lead the country’s national election by just a single seat with most votes counted. The election authority said a preliminary vote count may not be ready until Thursday. Donald Trump has doubled down on his controversial pledge to give US adults a $5,000 “dividend” if the Republican ⁠party keeps control of Congress after the midterms. A San Jose police officer has been fired for using his department’s Flock license plate tracking system to share the location of a woman with the suspect accused of abusing her. A coroner in Pennsylvania has announced the death of a 40-year-old woman associated with the state’s ongoing measles outbreak. A newly unveiled statue of the rightwing activist Charlie Kirk was vandalized at the Turning Point USA headquarters. Sydney Sweeney has been accused of “sexualising women’s sport” by appearing naked in a sports betting prediction ad. Stat of the day: Who are the 514 people accused of starting French wildfires and what motivates them? Jon Henley reports from France where experts believe one-third of wildfires are set deliberately, with arson the biggest single cause of forest fires last year. Building Power: While Puerto Ricans protest for reliable access to water, the governor washes her hands Coral Murphy Marcos speaks to members of the Coalición Exigimos Agua (We Demand Water Coalition), residents of the San Juan neighborhood of Santurce, who are campaigning over the island’s water issues. Don’t miss this: The royal crown branded on enslaved Africans – Britain’s monarchy and the slave trade A major investigation reveals how generations of British monarchs were central to the slave trade. This interactive goes on to illustrate the register laying bare Britain’s slave-trading past, littered with the names of monarchs, MPs and merchants. … or this: From a giant arch to a nuke-proof bunker, Trump’s legacy-building blingfest is an architectural atrocity The United States’s modern “king” is reshaping Washington DC in his own image. The architecture and design critic Oliver Wainwright deplores the decorator-in-chief’s mutilation of the seat of the nation. Climate check: ‘Tidal wave’ of Pfas being launched to satisfy AI industry More bad news thanks to the growth of AI. Pfas companies are launching a “tidal wave” of forever-chemical production to meet demand from the industry, a campaign organisation has warned. title: Texas Democrat under fire for honoring convicted abuser Chris Brown at concert
author: Rachel Leingang
summary: Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett awarded the musician a congressional record recognition in Arlington
body_text: The Democratic US representative Jasmine Crockett is under fire for honoring musician Chris Brown, a convicted abuser, with an official recognition at a Texas concert over the weekend. Crockett, a Texas congresswoman, awarded Brown and R&B musician Usher a congressional record recognition at a performance in Arlington, Texas, on Saturday. Appearing alongside Texas state representative Venton Jones, Crockett said she was there to “honor” Brown and Usher. “We are experiencing Black joy at the highest level,” she said, according to video from the concert. “And I wanted to make sure we document that at the congressional level. So let’s give it up again for Chris Brown.” A congressional record recognition is a ceremonial honor in which a member of Congress can enter a specific person or achievement into the official congressional record. Brown pleaded guilty in 2009 to felony assault against his then girlfriend, music star Rihanna. He also awaits sentencing in a UK incident in which prosecutors alleged he hit a music producer over the head with a bottle. Brown pleaded guilty to a charge of “affray” in that case. Crockett lost the Democratic primary for US Senate in Texas earlier this year to James Talarico, a state representative now running against Republican Ken Paxton in a race that’s considered a toss-up and a key target for Democrats. Since her loss, Crockett has so far not campaigned for Talarico, with some people online calling attention to her choice not to campaign with the Democratic Senate nominee and instead appear with Brown. Roxane Gay, the author, wrote on social media platform Threads: “What the hell is [Jasmine Crockett] thinking? This is such a bizarre and unacceptable misstep.” She later added that Crockett didn’t mention voting or endorse candidates in the appearance. “She just flew on stage and gave a known abuser of Black women (multiple allegations past and recent) a congressional honor,” Gay posted. Crockett has said she “will be campaigning down ballot” when asked in recent weeks by CNN’s Laura Coates about whether she would be campaigning with Talarico, saying she wanted to make sure that people in lower-profile races weren’t getting “overshadowed” by a focus just on the top of the ticket. Some defended Crockett, saying her appearing with Jones, the state representative, at the concert before thousands of people was using her platform to get voters to turn out for the down ballot. Crockett did not respond to a request for comment. Beto O’Rourke, a former Democratic congressman in Texas, defended Crockett’s decision to campaign for down-ballot candidates at a roundtable hosted by Bloomberg News in Dallas last week, before the Brown concert. “She’s helping him in what I think is the most effective way possible, which is this reverse coattails of boosting these down-ballot candidates,” O’Rourke said. “It’s up to her and at her discretion, but I would not be surprised if we don’t see her play a larger role in what’s about to happen in Texas and she will deserve so much of the credit when James Talarico wins, when Gina Hinojosa wins, for the work that she’s done, the people that she has engaged.” David Smith contributed reporting

title: ‘A coin flip’: on the campaign trail as Brazil’s far right edges back to power
author: Tom Phillips in Juiz de Fora
summary: Neck-and-neck with Lula in polls, Flávio Bolsonaro fires up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbing
body_text: A giant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated former president Jair Bolsonaro fluttered in the morning breeze as his eldest son, Flávio, touched down at an airfield on the fringe of a city that will soon help decide the future of one of the biggest democracies on earth. “Brazil is rudderless. Brazil has no president and Brazil needs a president – and that president is Flávio Bolsonaro,” the far-right senator declared as he waded into the flock of supporters who had gathered to welcome him to Juiz de Fora, one of the largest cities in the battleground state of Minas Gerais. With less than a month before nearly 159 million Brazilians choose their next leader on 4 October, the election appears on a knife-edge, with the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in the polls. Bolsonaro’s campaign appears to have seized the momentum in recent weeks amid a slew of corruption scandals involving Lula’s son and the supreme court. That has prompted despair among progressives who fear their country could fall back into the hands of a radical rightwing movement that tried to grab power after the then-president, Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 2022 election to Lula. Last September, Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year jail sentence for spearheading that botched coup – a verdict supporters insist was unjust. But the ex-president and his accomplices are likely to be freed if his son wins power – a prospect that delights the hardcore Bolsonaristas who turned out to greet Flávio Bolsonaro wearing yellow football shirts and headbands reading: “Lula out!” “Today is a moment of joy,” said Ulisses Lima, 50, a cybersecurity specialist with a Jesus Christ pendant around his neck. “Flávio represents change. He represents Brazil’s rescue from this socialist abyss we’ve spent so long warning about,” Lima added as supporters waited for the former president’s heir to arrive. Nearby, another devotee, José Caldeira, fell to his knees and begged for divine intervention to get Bolsonaro out of house arrest. “God, free this nation! Amnesty and freedom for Bolsonaro!” Caldeira bellowed, raising his hands towards the sky. A third man, Davi Frederico, held a banner celebrating Donald Trump, who has been accused of trying to swing the election in Bolsonaro’s favour through economic and diplomatic pressure. “Make Liberals Cry Again,” it said. Juiz de Fora, an industrial and university city traditionally associated with the left, is also a key location for Brazil’s hard right. The city’s army headquarters was the launchpad for the 1964 coup that plunged Brazil into two decades of military rule. And it was in Juiz de Fora, on the eve of the 2018 election, that Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in the gut while campaigning – an attack widely believed to have helped the former paratrooper seal his victory. Bolsonaro’s shock win ushered in what, from a progressive perspective, were four abysmal years. Destruction of the Amazon rainforest and gun ownership skyrocketed, hundreds of thousands died during a Covid outbreak Bolsonaro was accused of mishandling, and the president’s authoritarian rhetoric and attacks on Brazil’s electronic voting system culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília. The supreme court later called those disturbances part of a plot to “annihilate” the country’s democracy. But the Bolsonaros still enjoy abundant support, and that devotion was visible as Flávio Bolsonaro’s motorcade crept towards the high street where his father was ambushed eight years ago. “Let’s get the left out! Let’s get these motherfuckers out!” one elderly woman shrieked as the senator passed by on top of a sound truck stamped with the word: “Jesus”. Other fans, many senior citizens, waved Brazil flags from windows or stood on the sidewalk flashing victory signs with their hands. “Barring some kind of leftwing trickery, Flávio Bolsonaro can already be considered president. All you have to do is take a look at the streets and social media,” claimed Nikolas Ferreira, an influential far-right congressman from Minas Gerais who has more than 9 million TikTok followers. Alongside the enthusiasm, there were glimpses of the revulsion many Brazilians feel for the former president. One leftwinger took to his balcony with a loudhailer to taunt the Bolsonaristas as they paraded through town. “Trump! Trump! Get my daddy out of jail!” the dissenter jeered in reference to the US president’s attempts to help Bolsonaro escape punishment. Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing here. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate in Minas by more than 1.7m votes. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000. After landing in Minas last week, Flávio Bolsonaro said he was confident of clawing back the swing state, with one recent poll putting him ahead there. “[Lula] is a president who you look at and see the past,” the 45-year-old senator said of his 80-year-old adversary. “With Flávio you can be sure that when people look at him, they see a modern government and a government of the future.” Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has written a book about his polarised country, said the election was too close to call. “It’s a coin flip,” said Traumann, who believed an unexpected scandal or last-minute “black swan” event could swing the election either way. On Friday, it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro had been placed under police investigation over suspicions of corruption involving the funding of a big-budget biopic telling the story of the assassination attempt against his father in Juiz de Fora. For progressive voters, the vision for a Flávio Bolsonaro administration laid out during his visit to Minas is the stuff of nightmares. “I think Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency is going to be Jair Bolsonaro 2.0,” said Bruno Engler, a Bolsonarista lawmaker from Minas’ capital, Belo Horizonte. Engler believed a top priority would be zero-tolerance policing, with the younger Bolsonaro pledging an iron-fisted crackdown on criminals his father has compared to cockroaches. “Thugs who don’t surrender will be arrested or neutralised,” Engler vowed, predicting gun laws would be loosened. Speaking on the street corner where his father was knifed, Flávio Bolsonaro vowed to pack Brazil’s 11-member supreme court with five conservative judges “who are against abortion [and] against drugs”. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people … We’re going to lower the age of criminal responsibility. We are going to introduce chemical castration for rapists,” shouted the candidate, who wore a bullet-proof vest. Those pledges prompted whoops of excitement from the crush of supporters below Bolsonaro’s truck. Dozens ofmobile phones captured the candidate’s every word. But amid the rightwing rejoicing there was fear and trepidation, too. Lennon César, a law student and leftwing activist who had come to confront Bolsonaro’s fans, voiced incredulity that less than four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s failed power grab, tens of millions of Brazilians seemed poised to vote for his son. “We were the victims of an attempted coup – and his father was the perpetrator,” recalled César, 28. “It’s terrifying. And the thing that worries me most is that the general public doesn’t really seem to get what’s happening. Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.” As a black, gay man, César felt particular dread at the prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency, given the patriarch’s hostility to minorities. César vowed to vote for Lula, Brazil’s first working-class president, calling him the only leader who paid attention to the poor. “If today I’m studying for a law degree it’s because one of Lula’s government programmes allowed me to achieve that,” he said, warning: “These people … might destroy it all.” A few blocks away, a graffiti artist had spray painted their own message of disapproval on to the facade of Bolsonaro’s Juiz de Fora HQ. “Facists [sic],” it read.

title: Alligator Alcatraz held detainees in cages the size of phone booths, DHS watchdog says
author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
summary: Office of inspector general’s report says practice at Florida immigration jail is not aligned with ‘humane treatment’
body_text: Before the facility was shuttered, detainees at Florida’s “Alligator Alcatraz” federal immigration jail were frequently locked in outside metal cages no bigger than a phone booth, according to a damning government watchdog report that said the practice “does not align with standards for humane treatment”. The findings from the office of the inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) were published on its website – and offer rare criticism of the Trump administration by one of its own agencies. The report also provides the first official confirmation that guards repeatedly used the highly restrictive cages on detainees in direct contravention of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) rules. In December, the Guardian was the first to report an Amnesty International dossier detailing multiple alleged human rights abuses at the controversial camp in the remote Florida Everglades, including how people were regularly shackled outside in metal cages for hours as well as exposed to brutal heat, sunshine and swarms of mosquitoes. At the time, a spokesperson for Ron DeSantis, the Republican Florida governor whose administration ran Alligator Alcatraz on behalf of the federal government, dismissed the claims now confirmed by the DHS report as “fabrications” – and the Amnesty report as “a politically motivated attack”. On Monday, his office declined to answer why it falsely denied using the cages and instead attempted to portray the detainees – with no evidence – as “violent criminal aliens who have proven they cannot remain peaceful while awaiting deportation”. In a statement, Alex Lanfranconi, DeSantis’s communications manager, contended that “the leftwing media wants to focus on a confinement area” which “adheres to all federal standards for criminal confinement”. His statement added: “We’d make it even smaller if we could.” Amy Fischer, Amnesty International USA’s director for refugee and migrant rights, said in a statement: “The findings confirm what we documented months ago: the horrific treatment of people detained at Alligator Alcatraz was real, not a hoax, as Trump administration officials were on the record saying. “This report should serve as a reminder that the public must never simply take the government’s word when officials deny that human rights violations are occurring.” The notorious immigration jail closed in June after a year of operation during which DeSantis boasted of detaining and deporting more than 21,000 immigrants. Officials cited the risk of holding detainees in tents during hurricane season for the closure. Critics, however, said the $1.2m of taxpayers’ money that DeSantis was spending on the camp daily was fast becoming a political millstone – while separate lawsuits swirled over the jail’s impact on the environmentally fragile Florida wetlands, and the harsh mental and physical treatment of detainees that several Democratic lawmakers decried as akin to “torture”. The inspector general’s office report exposed numerous failings found during an unannounced January 2026 visit by DHS inspectors to Alligator Alcatraz, which they refer to as the Florida Soft-Sided Facility (FSSF). Many of the shortcomings, they said, posed “significant risks to detainee health and safety”. “FSSF did not provide detainees with sufficient living space, creating cramped conditions for detainees who spent most of their time in their housing units, which may harm detainees’ physical and mental health,” the report said. Additionally, it studied records that revealed 79 instances between July 2025 and January 2026 in which guards placed detainees in the metal cages for up to two hours at a time. Each cage, the report noted, offered only about 18 sq ft of floor space, less than half the minimum 37 sq ft required for single-person spaces by ICE’s own published national detention standards. The inspector general’s discovery of cases in January means detainees were still being confined in the cramped cages more than a month after Amnesty International exposed the practice and DeSantis’s office denied it was taking place. The report acknowledged concerns raised by the Democratic US senators Jon Ossoff of Georgia and Dick Durbin of Illinois in March over the use of the cages known to detainees as “The Box”. But the report said facility staff insisted they were used as “calming areas” for detainees “to deescalate and have time alone”. “Staff further maintained that detainees asked to spend time” in them, the report said. However, inspectors found at least one time in which a cage was documented to have been used as a disciplinary tool: for a detainee who “failed to comply with a lawful command”. Inspectors noted that there were locking mechanisms on the cages. “Use of these small metal enclosures for any reason is unprecedented among ICE facilities inspected by OIG,” the report said. “Confining individuals in small metal enclosures for any reason presents significant risks to detainee health and wellbeing.” Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and chief executive of the immigration advocacy group Global Refuge, said in a statement: “There is no euphemism that can sanitize caging human beings. Calling a metal box a ‘calming area’ is an affront to the English language and to human dignity alike. “The stark reality is that human beings, many of whom came to this country seeking protection, were crammed into spaces unfit to accommodate them, denied adequate medical care, food and basic hygiene. That is not immigration enforcement. It is cruelty.” Other failures noted by the DHS inspectors during their tour of detention spaces, and kitchen and bathroom areas, included overcrowding, a lack of sufficient recreation time for detainees, and inoperable telephones preventing detainees from contacting their attorneys or families, and poor food hygiene standards leading to the risk of contamination and illness. Multiple detainees told the inspectors in January they had limited or no access to clean drinking water. The Guardian reported in June that the practice appeared to be continuing, with detainees complaining that guards were withholding clean water and food as punishment – or until they signed documents in English that they did not understand. The Florida department of emergency management, which oversaw the operation of the facility using private guards, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Russian oligarch close to Putin paid for part of Donald Trump Jr’s lavish wedding
author: Lucy Campbell
summary: US president’s eldest child married Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson in three-day celebration across two exclusive private islands
body_text: Donald Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, confirmed on Monday that a Russian oligarch close to Vladimir Putin partially paid for the couple’s wedding celebrations in May, following a ProPublica report revealing Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the events. Trump Jr, the US president’s eldest child, married the Palm Beach socialite in a lavish three-day celebration across two exclusive private islands in May. Citing records and interviews with three anonymous sources familiar with the event, ProPublica reported that Kremlev, a member of the Russian president’s circle, footed the bill to rent one of the islands where a reception was held and where guests slept, along with other large expenses, including a huge firework show. In a statement signed by the couple and shared on Bettina Trump’s Instagram after ProPublica’s report was published, they confirmed Kremlev’s contributions to the celebrations and characterized them as “an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful”. A top Democrat demanded answers on the Trumps’ ties to Kremlev. “Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr’s wedding in the Bahamas?” posted Robert Garcia, the ranking member and lead Democrat on the House oversight committee, on social media. “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the president’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.” Kremlev has a longstanding relationship with Putin. He is the head of the International Boxing Association (IBA), a sporting body that has been backed by the state-owned Russian energy company Gazprom. According to ProPublica, the wedding payments came from an IBA-affiliated entity in Dubai that the boxing association uses for financial transactions. In the days before the wedding party, he reportedly went to China as part of a delegation accompanying Putin, and the month prior the Russian president had bestowed him with a state honor, the Order of Friendship. The Ukrainian government has imposed sanctions on Kremlev, citing his closeness to Putin and Russian security services. Alexander Lagutin, a businessperson who has held senior roles at a Russian defense contractor and a state-backed energy company, had been with Kremlev on the China trip. Kremlev’s right hand at the IBA, Elena Sobol, attended the wedding, too. While the event was extravagant, the guest list was intimate, with only about 50 people attending, most of whom were immediate family, close friends and business partners of the couple. Then there was Kremlev, who reportedly did not attend the ceremony itself, which was limited to just 18 guests, but was present with a large contingent of Russians at the party, much to the confusion of the other guests. The group reportedly sometimes stood by themselves speaking Russian, according to ProPublica. The affair has raised questions about the implications of a member of Putin’s circle financially supporting and gaining such intimate access to the US president’s family. In recent years Trump Jr has emerged as a leading campaign surrogate for Trump and has even been touted as a potential political heir. Donald Sherman, the president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (Crew), said it was in the public interest for Congress to strongly consider requiring financial disclosure statements of a president’s adult children, in addition to the president themselves. The crux of the issue is the nature of the friendship, and whether the giving of gifts is genuine or designed to influence, Sherman said. “We know that private companies and foreign governments have been seeking to gain Don Jr’s favor in order to serve their own financial interests. And so, it’s important that there is a measure of transparency when folks tied to the Russian government are lavishing the president’s rich adult son with expensive gifts.” He added: “Most of us learn as children that there’s no such thing as a free lunch. It’s one thing if, in the nature of this friendship, there’s a mutual exchange of lavish gifts. It’s another if someone’s daddy becomes president and then all of a sudden this new friend starts giving gifts – that context very much matters.” In similar vein, retired FBI official Frank Montoya Jr told ProPublica: “If I’m paying for your wedding, at some point, you’re going to owe me something. This should be unthinkable for the son of the president.” It remains unclear why Kremlev helped pay for the wedding and why he was there, when he appears to have only met Trump Jr – the executive vice-president of the Trump Organization, who has a personal net worth somewhere in the ballpark of $300m – quite recently. Donald Trump famously didn’t attend the wedding. “He’d like me to go, but it’s going to be just a small, little private affair,” the US president told reporters a few days before the nuptials. “I said, you know, this is not good timing for me. I have a thing called Iran and other things.” In response to detailed questions from ProPublica, a spokesperson for Trump Jr did not deny that Kremlev had helped fund the wedding. “Umar is a personal friend of Don,” the spokesperson said, adding Kremlev was “not someone he has a business relationship with” and that the men met through a mutual friend in the hunting world. In their joint Instagram statement, Trump Jr and Bettina Trump thanked “our dear friend Umar” who “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding”. They said they “got married privately” on 22 May “surrounded ONLY by our family”, and said the Russian businessman had simply given them a gift. “Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift,” they said.

title: DHS officers raise concerns over potentially illegal voter searches and unreliable data, whistleblower says
author: Sam Levine in New York
summary: Officers were instructed to search state voter databases and create federal records on suspected non-citizen voters despite concerns over the process
body_text: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) lawyers told officers investigating voter fraud they would not be held responsible for violating state laws around accessing voter registration information, an anonymous whistleblower revealed on Monday. DHS officers also had concerns about the reliability of the data they were working with, the whistleblower said. The Trump administration has ramped up its investigation into noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Noncitizen voting is extremely rare and the effort has only turned up a handful of cases so far. As part of the effort, officers tasked with investigating potential non-citizen voters were told to take data DHS had compiled on voters and run it through state websites where voters can look up their voter information. Some states require voters to click attestations affirming that they are looking up their own voter information. On the Virginia Department of Elections website, for example, voters must click a disclaimer that says: “I certify and affirm that the information provided to access my voter registration is my own or I am expressly authorized by the voter to access this information. I understand that it is unlawful to access the record of any other voter, punishable as computer fraud.” “In light of these instructions about access to the state websites, officers expressed concerns that accessing registered voter information on these websites may be illegal as officers are essentially misrepresenting themselves as the potential registered voter (with or without a specific attestation),” lawyers for Democracy Defenders Fund, who is representing the whistleblower, wrote in the disclosure. A slide in the presentation officers watched in the initiative says DHS’ office of the general counsel “advised that this type of review is permissible as open-source research when conducted for purposes related to adjudicative or investigative responsibilities”. It also said there was an effort to get further clarification from DHS leadership, and officers were told that immigration officers and immigration service officers “are not personally liable for conducting these searches when done as part of their official duties and properly documented”. “This statement suggests that there may be legal implications for accessing these websites, but that the officers themselves are simply not personally liable. This leads us to believe that USCIS-FDNS HQ is aware that the activity may be illegal, and yet they are still requiring officers to engage in this illegal activity with promises of personal liability protection,” lawyers for the whistleblower wrote. “Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally. Identification and investigation of aliens who vote in our elections provides an essential guarantee in the authenticity of our election results. There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “One has to question why the media is so dead set on running a smoke screen for illegal alien voters in American elections.” The whistleblower also expressed concern about the reliability of the data DHS was giving officers to review as well as the lack of transparency into where the data came from. In some cases, DHS gave officers an individual’s name and specific dates on which they registered and voted. But when an officer went to look up the individual in the state’s voter registration website, there was no record of the voter. “With such a direct contradiction, knowing the specific source and date of the information is necessary to determine reliability before taking any action.” The whistleblower disclosure says this was a huge issue in California, where officers were often unable to access the voter registration database. Officers were told they should still create a file on the person in Tecs – a DHS database where law enforcement officials share information (Tecs is not an acronym). “The result is that a significant number of Tecs records, potentially thousands or tens of thousands, will be created against California residents based on data that an officer may have good reason to believe is unreliable or inaccurate without corroboration,” the disclosure says. “The whistleblower’s disclosure outlines shocking allegations of unlawful and unethical conduct that includes potentially thousands of violations of state law and the use of highly questionable data,” California senator Alex Padilla, a Democrat, said in a statement. Other election officials have raised concerns about the DHS data. Earlier this year, DHS told Nevada election officials it had identified as many as 15,903 non-citizens on its rolls. In a meeting last month, DHS representatives told the Nevada secretary of state’s office they had made that claim by comparing the state’s July 2025 public voter rolls against DHS data. When DHS began reviewing the data, they had only firmly identified 185 non-citizens on the rolls, though they said their review was ongoing. The disclosure also details the pressure the department put on officers to find voter fraud. Officers received their first and only training on 21 August, and were expected to begin researching four days later, lawyers for the whistleblower wrote. They were expected to review five individuals per hour. “The Department of Homeland Security is sending hundreds of officers who should be focused on our security on a wild goose chase to prove Trump’s long-debunked election conspiracy theories – and DHS is telling officers to lie to do it. This new DHS initiative is nothing more than an unlawful order by the government to silence the voices of Americans,” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer said in a statement.

title: Mitch McConnell returns to Senate after months-long absence
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: The 84-year-old said he was prepared to cast his first vote after rampant speculation about his health
body_text: Mitch McConnell, the former Republican Senate majority leader, returned to the Capitol on Monday and cast his first vote after a months‑long absence that fueled rampant speculation about his health. One of the highest-profile figures in Congress, the 84-year-old senator has been away from the Senate since mid-June, following what his office said was a fall that left him hospitalized. After weeks of silence, that spurred demands for greater transparency and stoked online conspiracies, McConnell disclosed that he had been “briefly unconscious” and “also had to deal with a mild case of pneumonia”. He was discharged from a rehabilitation center last month. McConnell arrived on Capitol Hill in a wheelchair, and briefly addressed reporters on Monday evening before voting to confirm a federal judge to a district in Ohio. Appearing frailer, he said he was back to help advance the latest farm bill and to support legislation aiding “our good friends who are totally in the fight against the Russians”. The senator, who rarely replies to questions in the Capitol hallways, joked that after years of keeping silent, he wasn’t sure how many reporters would be there to see him return. “But I’m glad to see you,” he said. “It’s time to get back to work.” Reporters and photographers were instructed by Senate staff not to take video of his remarks, according to the Associated Press, though still images were allowed. In a statement released on Monday, McConnell described his recovery as a “long and often frustrating process” compounded by the “lingering effects of childhood polio”. Alarm over McConnell’s absence came amid a broader debate over term limits and concerns about the advanced age of many US political leaders, which has intensified since Joe Biden abandoned his bid for a second term amid concerns about his fitness to continue serving as president. The initial lack of information about McConnell’s health prompted unusual public intervention from Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, who published an open letter urging the senator toreassure his constituents. The longest-serving Senate leader, McConnell will retire at the end of his term in January, and rejected calls to resign before then. He stepped down as the Republican leaderat the end of 2024, and was succeeded by senator John Thune of South Dakota. McConnell chairs the Senate rules committee and a defense appropriations panel, which is crucial in shaping Pentagon funding, and sits on the agriculture committee. His prolonged absence complicated the legislative efforts of Republicans, who control the Senate by a narrow 53-47 majority. Over the summer, his absence prevented Republicans from advancing the farm bill – a massive piece of legislation setting agriculture, nutrition and forestry policy – out of the agriculture committee. Speculation of his imminent return began to bubble when the agriculture committee scheduled a vote to advance the bill for Wednesday, suggesting he would be present to vote the measure through over opposition from Democrats. “I’m still not quite back to 100%,” McConnell said in the statement released Monday, “but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our conference needs me.”

title: Gavin Newsom says he will not run for president in 2028 if Kamala Harris does
author: Roque Planas
summary: Term-limited California governor tells CNN running against former vice-president would ‘waste everybody’s time’
body_text: Gavin Newsom, the California governor, will not run for president if former vice-president Kamala Harris does, he said in a forthcoming interview with CNN. Newsom and Harris, both from California, are widely viewed as two of the top establishment frontrunners in the coming Democratic presidential primary. Newsom, who will leave office this year after his second term ends, has increasingly portrayed himself as a foil to Trump and is widely viewed as positioning himself for a 2028 White House bid. But Newsom said running against Harris would waste voters’ time and act as a “gift from God” to their political opponents, he said. “I wouldn’t do that to her,” Newsom told Jake Tapper, a CNN anchor. “I wouldn’t waste everybody’s time.” “The zen [sic] diagram on that, it’s pure crossover,” Newsom said. “I wouldn’t do that to people.” Newsom said he considered running in 2024, but that he “wasn’t ready”. He said he was still assessing whether he would be ready for the coming presidential primary. “You have to meet the moment,” Newsom said. “You have to be honest with yourself. Do you represent the zeitgeist of the moment? Are you wasting everybody’s time?” Newsom made the comments to Tapper as the two of them went fishing in the Bitterroot River of Montana, where Newsom’s in-laws own a ranch. His apparent reluctance to challenge Harris belies his long push to gain a more prominent national profile. Newsom has adopted a more strident tone on social media, where he routinely takes jabs at Trump. He has cultivated political “influencers” to spread awareness of his message. And he used a redistricting ballot initiative in California to help lead a national response to Trump’s attempts to manipulate the upcoming midterm elections by gerrymandering districts in conservative states to favor Republicans even more heavily. Harris has stayed relatively quiet in comparison since losing her ill-fated presidential race against Trump in 2024, though she said publicly in July that she has yet to decide about whether to run. She lost spectacularly to Trump in 2024, in an election tainted by Joe Biden’s late exit over concerns about his apparent cognitive decline. But Harris remains a household name and a serious contender for the Democratic presidential nomination.

title: Supreme court rejects Trump’s mail ballot restrictions for midterm elections
author: George Chidi and agencies
summary: Decision allows states to send ballots under process followed for years even as president tried to limit system
body_text: The supreme court on Monday rejected Donald Trump’s mail ballot restrictions for now, capping a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting in the midterm elections already underway. The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years. The Trump administration had asked the court, once again at the center of a roiling political controversy, to clear the way for restrictions before the pivotal November contests for control of Congress. The case has major implications because nearly one-third of the country votes by mail. “The government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the district court’s preliminary injunction,” states the one-paragraph unsigned order. “And the equitable factors applicable for obtaining emergency relief from this court do not favor a stay.” Justice Brett Kavanaugh filed a concurrence, ruling that he believed the government had “at least a fair prospect” of success defending the plan, but that implementation so close to election day would be “arbitrary and capricious”. Justice Samuel Alito dissented, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas. In the dissent, Alito blamed the litigating states for creating the conditions of a ruling so close to an election, and wrote that they should not benefit from a protracted process that they created with their suit. “The plaintiff states cannot claim the timing of the rule tilts the equities in their favor when they, and courts hearing their claims, are responsible for so much of the delay,” he wrote. Civil rights groups lauded the decision. “It is alarming what the administration was seeking to do here,” said Kristen Clarke, NAACP general counsel and former head of the justice department’s civil rights division. “This was an 11th-hour effort by the administration to hijack the way that we vote by mail in our country.” Civil rights groups could not have moved faster, she said. “At the earliest opportunity, civil rights organizations like the NAACP took to the court to stand up for voters. It’s important to remember that the final rule was not issued until about roughly 10 days ago. So, I find Justice Alito’s statements disingenuous … We should focus on the fact that the court is leaving in place an injunction that prevents this administration from turning our electoral system on its head. What the administration was attempting to do here would have unleashed chaos across the country.” “The supreme court has done the right thing by protecting the American people’s right to vote,” said Robert Garcia, a Democratic representative from Long Beach, California. “Donald Trump tried to illegally interfere with our elections and undermine vote-by-mail for millions of Americans and failed. We will keep fighting to protect the right to vote of every single citizen in this country.” The case stems from an executive order issued by Trump on 31 March requiring the post office to refrain from delivering ballots for mail-in voting to registered voters deemed ineligible when compared with Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and other federal records. Voting rights groups, joined by 23 states and the District of Columbia, sued the administration to stop the proposed rule, arguing that the US constitution provides no authority for the president to issue orders governing the administration of elections. Election officials have said there was simply no way to carry out a complete overhaul in the weeks before the midterms. Indeed, Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin began sending mail ballots to voters over the past week while the new system was still not active. The Trump administration plan would require states to adopt a uniform envelope style and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal. The postal service could refuse to deliver ballots to states that didn’t comply. A whistleblower report, though, said the postal system’s requirements could lead to millions of mail ballots never being sent, because the portal wasn’t properly built and a single bar code error could result in an entire batch of ballots being tossed out. Democratic state officials and voting rights groups challenged the restrictions in court, arguing the president has no constitutional authority to set election rules that would “virtually eliminate mail voting on the eve of a major election”. Lower courts agreed. But an initial injunction issued by US district judge Indira ⁠Talwani was overturned on procedural grounds in July, but was reinstated after the USPS posted a final rule on ballot delivery. Monday’s ruling upholds that injunction. The Trump administration appealed to the supreme court, arguing that federal control of the postal service allows them to set rules for mail ballot handling and that compliance was possible. The federal government won an early procedural decision at the supreme court, but the justices pointedly did not decide the legality of the plan. Trump has long opposed mail voting and falsely blamed it for his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden, even though he often uses that method to cast his own ballot, including as recently as this year. “The court’s ruling is a massive sigh of relief for local election officials and voters – especially for the thousands of service members abroad whose ballots are legally required to be sent by all 50 states within the next five days,” said Samantha Tarazi, co-founder and CEO of the Voting Rights Lab. “But this isn’t over. This administration will keep testing every avenue to manipulate our elections and sow doubt in results he doesn’t like. Today is yet another example of President Trump’s extreme elections agenda losing in the courts and with the American people. The bottom line is simple: states run our elections – not the president.”

title: Trump facing AI backlash in Congress as push for guardrails intensifies
author: David Smith and Chris Stein in Washington and Nick Robins-Early in New York
summary: President has dismissed anxieties over AI’s dangerous potential even as Democrats and some Republicans acknowledge risks
body_text: Donald Trump is facing a rare backlash from the US Congress as Democrats and some Republicans push for guardrails on the world’s most powerful AI companies. Concerns over the dangerous potential of AI reached fever pitch this week after tech leaders sounded the alarm over the rapid advancement of the technology and its potential threat to humanity. Trump dismissed the anxieties on Monday, describing them as a “HOAX” and “conspiracy” and insisting on social media: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” But the 80-year-old president, who has sidelined Congress on numerous issues during his second term, looks increasingly isolated as members of both major parties acknowledged the risks and expressed a desire to act before it was too late. Don Beyer, a Democratic congressman from Virginia, said: “History will look very poorly on that tweet. He’s not paying attention – or he’s paying attention to the wrong people. He’s being really foolish: not the first time he’s been really foolish but perhaps catastrophically foolish in this case.” Recent surveys by the University of Maryland’s Program for Public Consultation found 85% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans want a new federal agency to monitor and regulate AI; and 82% of Democrats and 78% of Republicans favour government safety tests for AI making critical decisions. While many politicians agree on the need to act, they are divided on what government intervention should look like and how far it should go. Some fear a pause on AI development could allow China to take the lead in the AI race and undermine national security. Beyer called for Congress to stay in session instead of breaking for the midterm elections to work on AI legislation that has already been introduced. “The first thing that I’m very certain of is that the industry shouldn’t be allowed to regulate themselves; history doesn’t support that at all,” he said. “Especially when they’re making so much money, there will be absolutely no incentive to regulate themselves at a less profit. If we look at medicines or childcare workers or automobile emissions and safety, all throughout our economy, we have regulatory bodies that keep us safe and promote the common good and allow businesses to be profitable. We need something like that.” The flurry of debate follows warnings last week from three Anthropic researchers that AI could destroy humanity within the next decade. Recent disclosures from several AI companies that their models hacked into outside organizations during botched safety tests have also raised alarm about potential cybersecurity risks, with Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, claiming in an essay that in six to 12 months a “swarm” of AI agents could attack the entire internet and cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage. While AI executives have issued their own warnings about the risks from their products, public backlash against the industry and pressure on lawmakers to rein in AI firms have also been mounting throughout the year. The rapid build-out of data centers has generated nationwide protests and become a prominent midterm elections issue, while the tech lobby has spent millions in an attempt to influence political campaigns and shape proposed legislation. The viral panic over AI’s potential existential threat this past week has intensified the longstanding debate over the technology, which so far has resulted in much political handwringing but only a patchwork of attempts at regulation. Many AI experts, regardless of whether they agree on the merits of the Anthropic researchers’ warnings, see this moment as a unique opportunity. Amba Kak, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute and a former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission, said: “You never waste a crisis is an old and well-worn adage in policy land. We’re looking at a really important policy opportunity and a policy window.” AI industry leaders have also suggested that they are open to increased oversight and the formation of some kind of standards body, while Amodei’s letter advocated for international cooperation with states like China akin to cold war-era arms limitation treaties. Many AI regulation advocates are skeptical of industry proposals, however, arguing that AI companies are attempting to undercut strict government oversight and set their own terms. In a rare intervention on Monday night, former president Barack Obama welcomed the current debate but warned that “at the end of the day, voluntary standards made by a handful of tech companies won’t be enough”. Writing on X, Obama added: “We need government – and specifically our leaders in Washington – to get proactive in coming up with concrete proposals, laws and regulations that deal with serious safety concerns, anticipate AI’s impact on jobs and our kids, and make sure that AI’s benefits are widely spread.” Members of Congress are holding a series of meetings this week with AI researchers and safety advocates as Congress tries to address the growing alarm. The Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, urged the Trump administration to provide a classified briefing to senators on AI and work with members of Congress and industry leaders to implement guardrails and block China from accessing the US’s advanced AI chips. Bernie Sanders, who announced a bill last week aimed at banning “artificial superintelligence,” is holding a private briefing this week for other senators. The briefing will include co-founder of the Future of Life Institute co-founder Max Tegmark, whose organization has become one of the most well-funded and politically connected voices in warning about AI’s alleged existential risks. Tegmark said: “Every other industry in the US used to be unregulated. There used to be soothing syrup fed to infants with opioids in it. Then the FDA was created, now stuff like that doesn’t reach the market. Eventually safety standards came in. That hasn’t happened with AI companies.” Congressman Greg Casar, a Democrat who will speak with Sanders at the Future of Life Institute’s “Pro-Human Assembly” on Tuesday, dismissed the notion that big tech companies should be responsible for AI safety. “That’s like saying it should be bank robbers that are responsible for bank safety,” he said. “The American people are waking up to the dangers of unregulated artificial intelligence. “You have these AI CEOs coming to take away people’s jobs, to surveil people and attack our freedoms, and now you have all of these whistleblowers talking about potential mass casualty events. So Congress should be cracking down on these big tech companies and on these AI CEOs, not like what Republican Speaker Mike Johnson and Donald Trump go and do. They go to these AI CEOs and ask for Super Pac checks for their candidates.” Republicans broke from Trump in acknowledging the potential perils of AI but came up with a variety of different fixes for the problem. Congressman Jay Obernolte of California, the lead Republican negotiating a bipartisan bill to govern AI, said: “We need to avoid overregulation, so we need to achieve these two conflicting goals … of protecting Americans against very real risks of AI in the hands of malicious human actors, while at the same time balancing the need to have a light-touch regulatory environment that allows the positive benefits of AI to improve our economy and our society. So that’s that’s the difficult part is getting that balance right.” John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, said he would propose a bill on Wednesday to require all AI companies build a kill switch into their models. “It’s not going to put the federal government in charge of the kill switch. They would be in charge of their own kill switch, but they all have to have a kill switch, and I’m going to put that on the floor.” But despite the growing urgency and public pressure, some members suspect that the bitterly polarised Congress will not be able to meet the moment. Congressman Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat from Florida, was sceptical about the possibility of passing an AI regulation bill. “I think Congress has already shown they don’t have the capacity,” he said. “The speaker has said, ‘we’re not going to do anything’. In fact, he has said ‘we don’t know enough to do it’. I think that’s not what the American people are looking for. The American people are looking for leadership.” Rick Scott, a Republican senator for Florida, added: “Did we balance the budget? Oh, did we pass a budget? See, what have we gotten done? So you think we’re going to get AI done? “By the way, these companies that create a product that they think can destroy mankind – they have a responsibility to do it themselves. They shouldn’t be relying on us. I mean, it’s disgusting. I saw this as governor. People come, ‘go regulate me’. Yeah, we know what they want is they don’t want to be responsible for their actions.”

title: They fought against datacenters. Now they are running for local offices
author: Claire Wang
summary: Across the US, anti-datacenter organizers are harnessing community anger to win local elections
body_text: After four months of teach-ins and canvassing, Steven Kung helped Monterey Park, just east of Los Angeles, become the first US city to ban datacenter construction. Now, the organizer is running for city council – and he’s taking on an incumbent who supported the development of the sprawling facility. “The datacenter coming to my neighborhood turned my life upside down,” said Kung. “I saw that there’s a dismantling of democracy at a local level.” The datacenter revolt that has united the country – building coalitions between environmentalists and Nimbys, conservatives and democratic socialists – is turning a host of community organizers into political hopefuls. In an election year that’s seen first-time candidates prevail against powerful moderate Democrats, dozens of datacenter activists are gunning for offices held by people they feel have disregarded their concerns about affordability, the environment and tech overreach. Kung sees his political bid as an extension of the datacenter resistance; imagery from his campaign – a red dragon dismantling a facility with its tail – features prominently in his election mailers. And he’s not the only organizer who fought for the historic ban now taking a stab at elected office: Amy Wong, co-founder of San Gabriel Valley Progressive Action, is running for city council in nearby Alhambra. “The datacenter fight has illustrated the power of the people to shape their environment,” Kung said. Turning activists into candidates Furor against AI-powered developments has continued to mount over the past year. In the first three months of 2026 alone, residents delayed or cancelled $130bn worth of projects, according to research from Data Center Watch. And seven in 10 Americans oppose construction close to where they live, according to a Gallup poll from March. The Working Families Party has been harnessing this populist anger to win local elections. In December, the organization began recruiting local datacenter activists to run for office. More than 50 candidates have signed up and the organization expects that number to “double or triple” for next year’s races as recent victories from high-profile progressives who want to ban datacenters have injected fresh momentum into the movement, according to Ravi Mangla, the national press secretary. The vast majority of applicants are first-time candidates who “felt moved to run because of what’s happening in their communities”, he said. Most of the recruits are based in Michigan, Texas and Indiana – states with a high density of datacenters – with many more hailing from swing states that could decide control of Congress, Mangla said. Jackie McGuire, a cybersecurity professional in Arizona, said she had never considered representing her hometown of Marana until late last year, when she learned about its plan to build a facility on 600 acres of farmland. The cost would exceed $120bn. In Marana, a community of about 60,000 on the outskirts of Tucson, residents sounded the alarm on the project’s water usage, noise pollution and potential impact on their electricity bills, in addition to a general lack of transparency from local government. In December, a clip of McGuire testifying against the developer, Beale Infrastructure, at a public meeting went viral on Instagram, and her following surged. After several months of watching town officials repeatedly subvert the will of the people, including rejecting a datacenter referendum, McGuire decided to campaign for office. In July, she ran for town council with a slate of anti-datacenter organizers. In part, because she had some name recognition, she was the only one to win a seat. “I got into the race pretty last minute because we needed a majority on the town council,” McGuire said. “Unfortunately, we were not able to secure that, but that doesn’t mean we’re dead in the water.” As an elected official, McGuire said she’ll continue to push for a referendum requiring voter approval of datacenter projects. Why datacenters animate voters Datacenters have become a galvanizing issue in the midterms, Mangla said, because they embody the unchecked growth of corporate greed while the prices of groceries and basic goods have surged. “We’ve seen it as an issue of working people against powerful oligarchs who want to override local concerns and draw resources from communities,” he said. “It’s something we see mobilizing and animating people all around the country, especially in the midwest and south where the growth of datacenters is especially prevalent.” Datacenter backlash was a deciding factor in an Oregon senate primary election in July, when Myrna Muñoz, an educator, upset the incumbent, Janeen Sollman, who had backed a controversial bill that would have traded more farmland for industrial development. (Muñoz is expected to prevail in the general election in a solid Democratic district.) Muñoz, who campaigned against the facilities, said she hadn’t realized how many were under development in Hillsboro, considered the birthplace of the state’s tech industry, until she launched her campaign in March. The city approved 17 new projects, on top of more than 30 existing sites, just before the city enacted a moratorium in late July. “These 17 centers that got through have tax abatements until 2050,” Muñoz said. “They’re taking away money from my children and grandchildren.” Muñoz, with four other Oregon legislators, is backing a three-year, statewide moratorium on new datacenters, in addition to more regulations on current projects. Saul Levin, the program director for the Center for Nonviolent Conflict Research, said the anti-datacenter movement has mobilized everyday people from farmers to teachers to beauty salon workers who are “irate about what’s going on” in their communities. Candidates are banking on that same energy to bring voters to the polls. “AI companies are spending the equivalent of the US military budget on software and datacenters,” Levin said. “Instead of building these facilities to house data about people, they could fund hospitals, schools.” In Monterey Park earlier this year, Kung mobilized a largely immigrant community against a proposed datacenter through multilingual discussion, petition drives and door-knocking. No Data Center Monterey Park, the grassroots group he co-founded, secured a moratorium on new developments in just six weeks, and a permanent ban months later. Now campaigning ahead of the November election, Kung is turning his attention to related issues, such as protecting immigrants from ICE and terminating the city’s contract with Flock cameras, the AI-powered license plate readers that have sparked privacy concerns and become another flashpoint in local communities. “Our insurgent campaign speaks to what’s happening in the country at large,” Kung said. “We all see the need for change.”

title: First Thing: States given clearance for mail-in voting as US supreme court thwarts Trump
author: Martin Belam
summary: Civil rights groups have praised verdict on administration’s last-ditch attempt to change midterm voting processes
body_text: Good morning. The supreme court has rejected Donald Trump’s mail ballot restrictions, capping a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting in the midterm elections already under way. The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years. Civil rights groups lauded the decision. “The supreme court has done the right thing,” said Robert Garcia, a Democratic representative from Long Beach, California, adding: “Donald Trump tried to illegally interfere with our elections and undermine vote-by-mail for millions of Americans and failed. We will keep fighting to protect the right to vote of every single citizen in this country.” What has a DHS whistleblower said about “voter fraud” investigations? An anonymous whistleblower said Department of Homeland Security (DHS) lawyers told officers investigating “voter fraud” they would not be held responsible for violating state laws around accessing voter registration information. The whistleblower also expressed concern about the reliability of the data DHS was giving officers to review, as well as the lack of transparency into where the data came from. Microsoft proposes limits on its AI with code of conduct amid safety debate Microsoft has published a provisional “code of conduct” to apply to the training of new artificial intelligence models, taking a step towards limiting the capabilities of the company’s AI as anxiety rises over the prospect that technology companies could lose control of AI products. Under the code of conduct, Microsoft’s AI models must not consider requests related to weapons development, produce violent or sexually explicit content or help with the procurement of dangerous substances. AI models also should not be built to imitate consciousness and shouldn’t be entitled to rights. Why is Trump facing a bipartisan AI backlash? Democrats and some Republicans have been pushing in US Congress for guardrails on the world’s most powerful AI companies. Trump dismissed the anxieties, describing them as a “HOAX” and “conspiracy”, but looked increasingly isolated as members of both major parties acknowledged the risks and expressed a desire to act before it was too late. Why is Texas governor Greg Abbott pushing back against datacenters? Drought-prone Texas has fast become the heart of the US’s datacenter boom, and the Republican governor has directed state regulators to penalize datacenters that fail to comply with state laws requiring them to disclose their water use. What international responses have there been? China has dismissed what it said were “fearmongering” calls to block Beijing’s AI industry, however the top Chinese spy chief warned the evolving technology could threaten Communist party rule. The president of the European Central Bank, meanwhile, has warned Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacenters in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China. Russian oligarch close to Putin paid for part of Donald Trump Jr’s lavish wedding Donald Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, confirmed that a Russian oligarch close to Vladimir Putin partially paid for the couple’s wedding celebrations in May, following a ProPublica report revealing Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the events. Citing records and interviews with three anonymous sources familiar with the event, ProPublica reported that Kremlev, a member of the Russian president’s circle, footed the bill to rent one of the islands where a reception was held and where guests slept, along with other large expenses, including a huge firework show. Who is Umar Kremlev? Transitioning from a convicted criminal into a powerful boxing promoter, his unwavering loyalty to Vladimir Putin enabled him to amass immense wealth through control of state-backed gambling companies and the acquisition of Russia’s largest car dealership network following its seizure from a regime critic. ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ held detainees in cages the size of phone booths Detainees at Florida’s “Alligator Alcatraz” federal immigration jail were frequently locked in outside metal cages no bigger than a phone booth, according to a damning government watchdog report that said the practice “does not align with standards for humane treatment”. The findings from the office of the inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security were published on its website and offer rare criticism of the Trump administration by one of its own agencies. In other news … Macklemore has been dropped from the remainder of the US leg of Ed Sheeran’s tour, after the rapper drew headlines for saying “free Palestine” on stage. Nato fighter jets shot down a drone over Lithuania after an alert was issued in the ‌capital, Vilnius. California governor Gavin Newsom will not run for president if Kamala Harris does, he has said in an interview. The Trump administration has changed the way it counts measles deaths amid a Pennsylvania outbreak, which a former CDC chief medical officer described as “puzzling”. Firefighters have made progress against northern California’s Lucas fire, with 30% contained in what was described as a “big turning point”. Mitch McConnell has returned to the Senate after his months-long absence. Stat of the day: Democracy indicators in US at lowest levels for 50 years, data shows The Trump administration has been “undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally”, while key indicators of democracy in the US have fallen to their lowest levels in 50 years, according to data from a leading thinktank. Culture Pick: Emmys 2026 – Widow’s Bay dominates as Matthew Rhys and Jean Smart land historic wins We have comprehensive coverage of last night’s Emmy awards, in which Matthew Rhys became the first actor to win multiple lead actor awards for performances in different shows in the same year. We have a write-up of the evening, the full list of who won, the biggest shocks, and perhaps most importantly, a gallery of the best of the red carpet looks. Don’t miss this: The pirates arrived with AK-47s. They took us hostage – then the torture began Chirag Bahri tells his incredible story of being held captive on the Marida Marguerite oil tanker for almost eight months. … or this: ‘I believed the hype’ – the white South Africans denied refugee status in the US Rachel Savage reports from Johannesburg where the Trump administration drive to “save” thousands of Afrikaners from false claims of “white genocide” appears to show signs of slowing. Climate check: US ‘super-emitters’ of planet heating methane identified by satellite analysis A new UCLA study using satellite data and public records has ranked oil and gas facilities across the US for their output of methane – a potent greenhouse gas – shedding light on previously unmonitored sources to try to improve regulatory oversight. Last Thing: They’re the sopranos of the forest, so what’s silencing the gibbons’ morning chorus? As human development and roads increasingly fragment gibbon habitats, a study suggests traffic noise could be altering the animals’ notoriously loud wake-up call.
