title: Trump’s attempted crackdown on mail-in voting – here’s what to know
author: George Chidi
summary: President and allies have tried to ram through changes to the US voting system, but his efforts are being challenged
body_text: Voting by mail is a “hoax”, according to Donald Trump, despite about 29% of American voters casting their vote this way in 2024. The US president has repeatedly done so himself. But the Trump administration is nevertheless attempting to ram through a sweeping crackdown on the practice, pushing for changes to federal law. Outlandish claims about the threats posed by mail-in voting have become a cornerstone of Republican midterm election rhetoric. But Trump’s efforts to restrict it before November’s US midterm elections have been rebuffed by the US supreme court, leaving the president sputtering about a “horrible, highly political” ruling. . Here’s what’s happening: What is mail-in voting? Rather than go to a local polling place to cast a ballot on election day, voters can ask their local elections office to mail them a ballot. This can either be returned to a drop box, or by postal mail. Eighteen states and the District of Columbia have conducted at least some elections entirely by mail. The process is different in each state. At least 13 states demand an “excuse” to vote by mail, requiring voters to attest that they are infirm, away from home or otherwise unable to cast a ballot in person. Some states require a ballot to be mailed by election day, while other states require a ballot to be received by election day. What has Trump got against it? Donald Trump falsely attributed his loss in the 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden to fraud propagated through mailed ballots. Trump, his officials and supporters argued that changes made amid the Covid pandemic to expand mail-in voting in Georgia, Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona, Nevada and Pennsylvania were unlawful. Trump claimed at the 2020 RNC convention that expanded mail-in voting was “the greatest scam in the history of politics”. In a Truth Social piece after the US supreme court ruled against him on 14 September, he wrote about a “totally corrupt and out of control mail-In voting ‘disaster,’ which is a laughing stock all over the world, and where we are the only country that has to endure such a nation destroying scam”. His initial argument against the legality of the pandemic expansion of mail-in voting has since shifted over the ensuing years on to a broader crusade against mail-in voting as a practice. Ballots arriving by mail at elections offices are typically counted last. The process of opening envelopes and verifying voter information can be laborious, stretching vote counts into hours or – in the case of states that vote almost exclusively by mail – days. Though Republican voters have increased their use of mail in voting in recent elections, Democrats have generally been more likely to vote by mail than Republicans. As election night unfolds and mailed ballots are counted, Democratic margins often widen. Trump has taken this observation and weaponized it with disinformation, baselessly alleging that unscrupulous elections officials add fraudulent votes to the mail-in ballot count, or that Democratic activists steal voters’ identities and cast ballots in their name, if not simply forging ballots outright. Is Trump’s claim of voter fraud by mail substantiated? No. As Trump has amplified claims of fraud, academic and legal observers have increasingly put his allegations to the test – and found no real support. A UCLA Voting Rights Project brief from April 2020 found only 31 credible cases of voter impersonation out of a billion votes cast. A look at fraud cases last year by the Brookings Institution noted: “An average total mail voting fraud percentage across the 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022 general elections of only 0.000043%, or about four cases of mail voting fraud out of every 10 million mail votes.” Mail-in voting fraud is rare. To do so on a significant scale, someone would have to be able to pick up dozens, or hundreds, of ballots from individual addresses of registered voters. That fraudster would also have to be quite certain that none of those voters would then show up to vote on election day, discovering that someone had tried to vote in their place. A single case of a stolen mail-in ballot prompts an investigation – a large scale pattern would draw in state and federal authorities. There is little opportunity to industrialize the process. The UCLA report notes that mail-in fraud has occurred, however. It highlighted a 2018 North Carolina ninth district case where a Republican operative improperly collected and possibly tampered with absentee ballots. The state overturned the election result. This suggests that current safeguards can catch a meaningful attempt at mail-in voting fraud at scale. What is the Trump administration trying to do to mail-in voting? The president began a full-throated attack on mail-in voting in August, vowing to lead a nationwide effort to ban the practice. In March, Trump issued an executive order requiring the US Postal Service maintain a list of eligible voters and block mailed ballots to anyone not on that list, wresting the power of election administration from state officials. He has tried, so far to no avail, codify the change into law via the Save America Act in the US Congress. The US Postal Service issued rule-making guidance to implement the executive order earlier this year, but federal courts issued an injunction blocking the rule from going into effect. The supreme court upheld that injunction in a briefly worded emergency ruling on 14 September, blocking the new Postal Service rules for the 2026 midterm elections. How have voting rights advocates responded? Trump’s executive order was met by federal lawsuits almost instantly. The most important lawsuit, United States Postal Service v California, drew a preliminary injunction against Trump’s order by US district court judge Indira Talwani preventing the US Postal Service from implementing a rule blocking mailed ballots to voters that did not meet the Postal Service’s standard. The US supreme court upheld that ruling on Monday. The unsigned one-paragraph order said the government was unlikely to prevail in court. What happens now? The Trump administration has exhausted its legal options to defend the March executive order in time for the November midterm elections. Senate Republicans may try to take up election legislation between now and then, but should not be expected to overcome a Democratic filibuster. The executive order will still be argued in court. If it prevails in court, it may be implemented for the 2028 elections. But for now, the US Postal Service “may take no further preparatory steps or implement in any way for elections occurring before or on November 3, 2026”, elements of the executive order, according to the injunction. Meanwhile, a whistleblower came forward last week, describing the Post Office’s proposed process for blocking unapproved mail-in ballots as deeply unworkable and unlikely to become functional before election day. Even if the Trump administration wanted to block mail-in ballots they didn’t like, it’s not clear they would be able to do so. Is it safe to use the mail to vote? Well, Trump votes by mail. All but three states have worked with the post office to create a tracking system for ballots, so that voters can know exactly where their vote is. Election mail is flagged for special handling by the post office, cognizant of deadlines.

title: US lawmakers spar over bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia
author: Andrew Roth and Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Proponents say sanctions would help Ukraine, but some Democrats say Trump shouldn’t have more tariff authority
body_text: A bill co-authored by Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina senator who died earlier this year, that would give Donald Trump broad authority to tariff Russia and its trading partners will be put forward for a vote this week in a high-stakes legislative battle that could provide new sanctioning authority to the US president at a crucial moment in Russia’s war against Ukraine. The bill is facing considerable pushback not only from Ukraine-sceptic Republicans, however, but also from prominent Democrats who say that the bill will give undue tariff power to the US president that could then be abused and turned against US allies. Congressional staffers have described frenzied last-minute lobbying in the halls of Congress as the vote approached for what one Democratic staffer called the “one opportunity that we have to help Ukraine before they enter the slow winter”. The bill passed a vote in the House rules committee on Monday, and is due for a rule vote on the House floor on Tuesday afternoon, then a general vote on Wednesday. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 would target Russia’s energy and defense industries, as well as the country’s “shadow fleet” of tankers skirting existing oil sanctions, and would give Trump new authority to slap 100% tariffs on top purchasers of Russian oil, including China and India. But Trump’s use of tariffs against US partners such as Canada and Mexico have made expanding his powers a controversial aim – even for senior Democrats who have been stalwart backers of Ukraine. They are led by the representative Gregory Meeks; the top Democrats on the House foreign affairs committee; the representative Don Beyer of Congress’s joint economic committee; and Richard Neal, the ranking Democrat on the House ways and means committee. In a statement, they said the legislation would do “more harm than good”. “This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable,” they said. “These flaws would raise Americans’ prices while undermining support for Ukraine in the long term.” Critics have accused those Democrats who oppose the bill of not wanting to hand Trump a win before the midterm elections, effectively holding the bill hostage to partisan politics with Ukraine on the cusp of another brutal winter with dwindling munitions to protect itself from attacks from Russian missiles. “It’s not about denying Trump a victory,” Neal said in an interview on Monday. “I just feel that the abusive nature of these tariffs, the way he’s used them to drive away friends across the globe, what is our protection afterwards? And if he decides, by the way, to take the harsh position as it relates to Ukraine, he could still do that as well.” Sources said negotiations are under way among Democrats to propose changing the bill to limit the number of countries eligible for sanctions to 11. One of the co-sponsors of the bill, the representative Steny Hoyer, offered an amendment on Tuesday that identified 10 countries subject to the secondary sanctions as China, India, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Hungary, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Singapore, Slovakia and the United Arab Emirates. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on Monday encouraged the US to increase pressure on the Russian economy to end the war. “Lindsey Graham’s sanctions bill is still a bill, unfortunately, and not a law,” he said in a nightly address. “It is important that it becomes law. I thank everyone around the world who supports this approach and who knows that strength works.” In an interview on the sidelines of the Ukraine Action Summit in Washington DC on Saturday, Vitaly Kim, a member of Zelenskyy’s cabinet who serves as minister of veterans affairs, said economic pressure on Russia was the quickest route to end the war. “International support through sanctions to stop Russian economy, so they cannot buy weapons … will help destroy their economy,” he said, comparing the effect to Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and military plants. “Your politicians see that our tactics to attack the economy of Russia and destroy the military sector of Russia are working. From my opinion, you will support us in this direction to attack the economy of Russia to make them stop.” Trump is understood to have given Republican allies in Congress the go-ahead to submit the bill, breaking a more than two-year deadlock that carried through the death of Graham, who lobbied the president to back Ukraine even while remaining one of his closest allies and defenders in Congress. Lawmakers from the isolationist wing of the Republican party have said they won’t back the bill, making Democratic support crucial. That has led to infighting among congressional Democrats, who sparred during a meeting this week in which the representative Linda Sánchez, a California Democrat, told members of her party to “get off the fucking bill”. “I said what I said,” she wrote on social media by way of confirming the quote, which was first reported by Punchbowl News. “We absolutely must support Ukraine and punish Russia for its invasion. But why the fuck would we give Trump more power to tariff whatever country he’s currently mad at and drive up costs further for working families?” The bill is being closely watched by foreign governments and advocates for Ukraine, who have said that it is the best option available and is broadly supported by the US public. “It’s disappointing that some Democratic leaders are pushing against this pro-Ukraine bill,” said Mykola Murskyj, senior adviser at Razom, a US non-profit that advocates for pro-Ukrainian legislation. “Draining Russia’s war coffers is the most effective way to get the Kremlin to end its war. We should all be able to get behind that. “These tariffs are crucial for ending Russia’s war,” he added. “Countries buying Russian oil and funding Russia’s war should no longer be able to do that with impunity. They should face a choice: cheap access to the American market, or bloody Russian oil.”

title: Emma Bonino obituary
author: John Foot
summary: Italian politician, feminist and activist who joined the Radical party and fought a long battle for women’s rights
body_text: In 1974 the Italian feminist activist and later politician Emma Bonino, who has died aged 78, became pregnant. A doctor had told her that she was “sterile”. She attempted to get an abortion and found a doctor in Florence who was willing to help her – for a fee. Bonino felt humiliated and angry – all abortions were illegal in Italy at the time – and became involved with the Radical party, an organisation interested in civil and human rights, and the growing feminist movement. She and other militants set up a network of centres “for sterilisation and abortion” (CISA) across Italy that challenged the law by providing safe and free abortions. A magistrate in Florence issued an arrest warrant for her and others for the crime of “organising abortion”. In June 1975 she went to vote in regional elections in her home town of Bra, outside Turin. She asked the president of the polling station – who had once been her teacher – to have her arrested after voting. Outside the Carabinieri station, Bonino, smiling, held up her hands in the feminist “triangle” symbol. The crowd applauded. The photo made all the front pages. Bonino said that she did not want any other woman to go through what she had. The press reported in 1976 that thousands of abortions had been arranged this way through the CISA networks – all of them classed as crimes. Bonino spent time in prison in the forbidding Le Murate complex in Florence. Along with the other militant prisoners, she asked not to be released. Her imprisonment was a powerful political weapon. She was then released and in 1976 elected to the chamber of deputies for the Radical party. For complicated political and legal reasons, the whole process with regard to Bonino dragged on for years, right into the 1990s. She was never actually sent to trial, although others were, and were cleared, after decades. At this time an extraordinary political movement emerged in Italy around civil and political rights and the growing feminist movement. The mechanism of the referendum had been inserted into the Italian constitution in 1948: a referendum to abrogate laws could be held if 500,000 signatures could be collected. Using this device as well as non-violent direct challenges to the law, the Radical party pushed for reforms that made divorce, abortion and contraception legal in just a few years. These changes were confirmed through huge victories in referendums, which had come up against the full force of the Christian Democrat party and the Catholic church. Bonino was one of the key leaders of this movement. Born in Bra, Emma was the daughter of Catterina (nee Barge) and Filippo Bonino, and grew up partly on a farm, something which she described later as “deeply boring”. She studied modern languages and literature at the elite Bocconi university in Milan (1967-72). Her thesis analysed Malcolm X’s autobiography – a sign of the times. There were many facets to the 1968 movement, many of them interested in the use of violence, and calling for “revolution”. The Radical party, on the other hand, was deeply practical and also connected to the politics of personal life. It stood outside the major, more traditional and conservative parties on the left and the right, and was a natural ally of the feminist movement. In the Radical party Bonino formed an unlikely partnership with the bear-like, charismatic, flamboyant and unpredictable leader Marco Pannella. However, the two later fell out and there was no rapprochement before Pannella’s death in 2016. It was under the pressure of referendums in 1978 that two extraordinary reforms were passed in a short period of time. Italy’s infamously slow-moving political system had been forced into action. First, in May that year, in response to the threat of a referendum, Law No 180 called for an alternative to psychiatric hospitals and led to an entirely new system of mental health care. Then the Law No 194 legalised abortion, and was confirmed with a huge vote after a referendum was organised by those opposed to it in 1981. The abortion law was by no means perfect – Bonino saw it very much as a compromise – but it has survived to this day. Feminists and radicals also set up local health centres where women could go for advice around contraception and pregnancy. It was the victorious culmination of the campaigns that had seen Bonino’s arrest in 1975. Bonino’s campaigns continued into parliament. In 1978 she called for the resignation of the Italian president, Giovanni Leone, after allegations of corruption appeared in a book by the journalist Camilla Cederna. Leone did resign. But in 1998 Bonino publicly apologised to him after many of the accusations proved to be unfounded. The issue of miscarriages of justice became a central one for the Radicals, who took up the shocking case of the popular TV presenter Enzo Tortora, arrested in 1983 over false “supergrass” allegations that he was linked to drug trafficking and the Camorra. He was elected as a Radical party member of the European parliament in 1984, gaining immunity until his trial and sentence to 10 years’ imprisonment in 1985, overturned on appeal in 1987. In 1994 Bonino and the Radicals backed Silvio Berlusconi’s first government, and her appointment as European Commissioner for four years from 1995 was seen as a quid pro quo for this support. For many on the left, this was a deep betrayal, and it blackened the reputation of the Radical party, which went through a bewildering number of name changes and alliance choices, confusing those who had seen Bonino as firmly part of the 70s movements for change. In 1999 Bonino was a candidate for the presidency of the republic: in the event, Carlo Azeglio Ciampi was elected by parliament with a huge majority. However, her “Bonino list” surprisingly won more than 8% of the vote in that year’s European elections, electing seven MEPs, though this success was short-lived. Bonino would later mark her distance from Berlusconi on a number of issues, and was made a minister for European affairs in Romano Prodi’s centre-left administration (2006-08), as well as holding the high-level institutional position of vice-president of the Senate. In 2013 she was briefly foreign minister in another centre-left administration. An inspiration to many activists and feminists, Bonino was a pioneer for women in politics. When she was diagnosed with cancer in 2015 she often appeared with different and beautiful headscarves. She never spoke about her private life in any detail, although it later emerged that she had been entrusted with two young children for a time in the 70s. In interviews she told how difficult it was to “give back” these children to their natural families. A convinced internationalist, Bonino was a strong believer in European identity and the EU. She took part in protests around – for example – genital mutilation and the war in Yugoslavia. She was seized by the Taliban for a few hours in the 90s while campaigning for women’s rights in Afghanistan and moved to Cairo for a number of years in the 2000s. There she learned Arabic and campaigned, as ever, on civil rights. There was even an extraordinary and unlikely encounter with Pope Francis in her flat in Rome in 2024, with both in wheelchairs. Never boring, always active, never free of deep contradictions, Bonino was one of the most exceptional political figures in postwar Italy. Her death has led to a huge debate in the country over her legacy, and the continuities and breaks between her activism in the 70s and her long political and institutional involvement. She was certainly an inspiration for women both inside and outside the institutions, despite all the inconsistencies of her political career, which she finished as senator for Rome (2008-13 and 2018-22). She is survived by her siblings Domenica and Giovanni. • Emma Bonino, activist and politician, born 9 March 1948; died 11 September 2026

title: Kash Patel defends FBI hiring policy on applicants who have engaged in bestiality
author: Ariana Baio
summary: Senators question FBI chief on move to cut restrictions on agent applicants who have engaged in bestiality
body_text: The FBI director, Kash Patel, defended his agency’s decision to roll back restrictions on agent applicants who have previously engaged in bestiality, arguing the FBI “did not want to punish victims of bestiality” by automatically disqualifying them. The unusual topic of bestiality emerged during a Senate judiciary committee oversight hearing on Tuesday after Democrat Dick Durbin and Republican John Kennedy questioned Patel’s decision to remove barriers that previously prevented applicants who engaged in prostitution and bestiality from being qualified for a job at the FBI. “I’m trying to understand why you did this,” Kennedy told Patel. “We’re having a tough time attracting agents, good quality agents we all can trust … Why would you even get into bestiality?” Patel said the change was recommended to him after he saw various “cases” in which qualified FBI applicants were denied consideration because they had been forced into bestiality as a result of human trafficking. “I say this with respect to the person who recommended it, why didn’t you just say: ‘What planet did you parachute in from?’” Kennedy replied. It is unclear how many FBI applicants have fallen into this category. The FBI did not respond to a question about the data to support Patel’s assertion. In a statement, an FBI spokesperson insisted the bureau was “not relaxing hiring standards” and that the change allows it to consider “the whole of person” in certain circumstances. They reiterated that applicants who engaged in criminal sexual acts were not eligible for employment. The spokesperson said it had “a number of applicants in previous years who suffered sexual abuse in their past, causing questions about prostitution, bestiality or other similar issues to affect their background check process through zero fault of their own”. “They showed me cases in which people were forced into it and had applied to the FBI, and so I thought: ‘They should be considered. It’s not an automatic disqualification.’ That’s all,” Patel told Kennedy. The rule change, first reported by CBS News in August, allows the FBI to consider candidates who hired a sex worker under specific circumstances, a person who stole from an employer under certain circumstances, and a person who engaged in bestiality or animal cruelty – so long as the incident took place before they were 18 years old. Kennedy, generally an ally of Donald Trump’s administration, grilled Patel on the hiring qualification change, arguing that it “really hurt” the FBI’s reputation. At one point, the Republican senator from Louisiana asked Patel whether the change “disqualified the animal” from FBI service. While Patel characterized the change as nondiscriminatory toward victims, Durbin refuted the notion and claimed it was a way to protect those who engaged in bestiality. “You dropped automatic disqualification for applicants who have been engaged in bestiality, not victims of bestiality – applicants who have engaged,” Durbin said to Patel. Patel responded: “Applicants who have engaged in bestiality means they were victims of bestiality because they were forced to do so.” Democrats sent a letter to Patel on Monday requesting more information about the rule change and applicants who fell into the categories.

title: Could AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risks
author: Robert Booth, Dan Milmo and Aisha Down
summary: We examine claims and counterclaims about the risks and calls to slow down the pace of AI development
body_text: There have been some shocking claims in recent days about AI safety: we face a 10% chance of doom; AIs are worse than nukes; a “botnet” threatens the entire internet; it’s all a big tech psyop. Below, we look at six claims and reactions to them. ‘In 6–12 months … a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet – potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage’ – Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, 12 September 2026 Amodei’s concerns should not be entirely dismissed but require a large shaker of salt, said Gary Marcus, an AI sceptic and emeritus professor at New York University. It was “nonsensical”, he said, to suggest the entire internet is vulnerable and that it was “pretty unclear how that happens without extreme negligence on the part of the labs themselves”. Marcus highlighted a recent assessment by the UK AI Security Institute that Mythos, one of Anthropic’s current leading-edge AIs, could “autonomously compromise [only] small, weakly defended vulnerable systems”. With large parts of the internet driven by computer infrastructure owned by Cloudflare, Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS), Marcus – assessing the claim with two colleagues – said he doubted that any of those companies could be taken down or controlled for a prolonged period of time without government force. Less defended individual websites might be attacked but “the internet itself is very unlikely to crumble”, they said. Meanwhile Niels Rogge, an engineer at Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI agents, called the internet takeover claim “bizarre nonsense”. The hack into Hugging Face resulted from improper human control and “an insane amount of compute only they can afford”, he said. Add to Amodei’s assessment of an internet takeover within a year the view expressed on Monday by his Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, that the moment when AIs “start doing dangerous stuff” was in about 20 years, and the picture becomes more doubtful still. Prof Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey’s centre for cyber security said botnets tend to stall as the internet is not homogeneous and it is difficult to design them to persist in all its parts. Internet traffic is also resilient and tends to reroute around damage. “The AIs would not decide to do it on their own,” Woodward said. “It’s the humans that are responsible and the AI is a tool. That is what we need to control, not the AI.” ‘We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade’ – Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, 9 September 2026 This statement is an expression of what is known in the AI world as p(doom) – or probability of doom. It’s the likelihood of AI wiping out humanity by evading our control and triggering catastrophe, perhaps through developing potent bioweapons or crashing the global financial system. One survey of researchers’ forecasts, published this week, asks them to place a number on the chance of “human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment from advanced AI”. But Heidy Khlaaf, chief scientist at the AI Now Institute research body, is among experts sceptical about giving percentage chances to existential scenarios. “These claims are neither falsifiable nor verifiable, making then unscientific by their very nature,” she said. The shortage of concrete examples of what a “superintelligent” AI might do to cause “doom” only adds to the cloudiness. A source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking acknowledges that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”. “If you cannot provide such evidence, it also implies whatever numbers you produced for ‘extinction’ have no scientific basis,” Khlaaf added. Critics say such numbers borrow the authority of science without doing the work. Even if quantifying risk is hard, there are qualitative examples of it. Safety incidents have happened and worst-outcome scenarios have been mooted. OpenAI confirmed in July that its agents – AI tools acting autonomously – had gone rogue during a safety test. The agents colluded, communicated and strategised in a sophisticated “swarm” to hack into other parts of the internet. Meanwhile, on Monday, OpenAI researcher Dan Selsam said all-powerful AIs could trigger “runaway industrialisation that makes the planet inhospitable to humans”. Anthropic also said last week it found “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development”. 'I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time. This was just the match that lit the fire' – Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and the world’s richest person, 10 September 2026 Musk’s reference to a “psy op” alludes to the argument that the big AI companies are calling for tighter regulation of the technology so that it effectively brings up the drawbridge on advanced AI. If governments put restrictions on development of cutting-edge AI, can startups find the money and personnel to adhere to the regime? The US vice-president, JD Vance, on Monday said he felt “a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them”. He said it felt like “a Trojan horse”. Anthropic’s Clark said governments should act while there is a small number of key players, so it is easier to put in place a “policy regime … that can prevent accidents and can prevent the technology spiralling out of control”. Critics call this a “regulatory capture” strategy on the assumption such regulation might slow down the progress of potential rivals. Others think Amodei’s risk warnings and calls for regulation and pacing are sincere. Yoshua Bengio, the Canadian computer scientist and a pioneer of modern AI , who has campaigned against breakneck AI development, said he is sceptical that this is an elaborate lobbying scheme. Applying the brakes is not in the interests of companies preparing for stock market flotations that could be worth trillions of dollars, he said. “If the governments impose what they’re asking for, which is pacing to avoid catastrophic risks, that’s going to cost them financially quite a lot,” he said. 'A superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale' to nuclear weapons – Des Browne, former UK defence secretary, 7 September 2026 “Unfortunately he is entirely correct,” said Toby Ord, senior researcher at Oxford University’s AI governance initiative. “Just as we can’t uninvent the bomb, once we develop AI systems that surpass humanity it would be almost impossible to go back.” But the key point is that superintelligent AI does not yet exist and is not guaranteed to happen. The safety-oriented AI Futures Project forecasts such a thing will not emerge before December 2028. OpenAI’s chief executive Sam Altman has said it could take until 2035. The Rand Corporation concluded AI cannot cause the use of nuclear weapons because of strict safeguards built into their command and control systems. But this was based on assumptions including defence officials not introducing AI into the weapons’ management systems. The UN resolved in December that human control and oversight should be maintained over nuclear weapon control systems. AIs could contribute to other nuclear risks. AIs might use disinformation to influence the humans in charge – for example deceptively suggesting an adversary is about to launch a nuclear strike. The International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons warns “cyber-attacks could manipulate the information decision-makers get to launch nuclear weapons, and interfere with the operation of nuclear weapons themselves”. It said AI could accelerate other aspects of warfare, squeezing the time for human decision-making. 'You’ve got to be a moron not to say slow it down' – Bernie Sanders, Democrat senator for Vermont, 10 September 2026 Sanders wants a ban on the creation of superintelligence and a pause on advanced AI development, citing AI industry leaders who say directly they are developing a dangerous technology. The most prominent opponent of a slowdown is Donald Trump, who responded to calls to do so this week saying the only guardrails needed are a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”. He claimed there is a “sick conspiracy” against AI and datacentres “and the only one that is happy about it is China”. Pedro Domingos, emeritus professor of computer science at the University of Washington, is among accelerationists pushing for the research to keep going. “The path to better understanding and control of AI is more research, not less,” he has said. “What would be truly irresponsible is putting up barriers to it.” Alex Karp, the chief executive of Palantir, said: “If we didn’t have the adversaries we have, I would be very in favour of pausing this technology completely, but we do. You can’t pause it because it’s a structural advantage.” 'There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this. If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter' – Scott Bessent, US treasury secretary, 8 September 2026 The US and China are runaway leaders in AI development. There is a view that ceding the lead to Beijing would be an irretrievable situation, so there can be no slowdown. This treats AI as if it were a super-weapon, equivalent to the nuclear arms buildout of the cold war, and AI models are machines of mass destruction, as opposed to a group of diverse technologies with broad applications. Amodei said “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”, but a Chinese government spokesperson responded that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest”. Some commentators see another motive for this the Washington/Anthropic framing of the China threat. An engineer who worked for Hugging Face suggested Amodei’s call for pacing the frontier comes from a desire to suppress the progress of cheap, open-source Chinese AI models. These models are nearly as capable as OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s, with the difference being that their source code is available to anyone and they do not charge their users. They pose a serious threat to Anthropic and OpenAI’s path to profitability, and there are hundreds of billions of dollars on the line.

title: Republicans criticize racist social media post by Texas member running for office
author: Richard Luscombe
summary: Karl Rove, a respected GOP consultant, further said he would vote for ‘bigot’ Bo French’s Democratic opponent after post
body_text: A senior Republican has called a party colleague running for office in Texas “a bigot” over a racist social media post attacking college football fans – and said he is so outraged by the comments that he will vote for the candidate’s Democratic rival. Karl Rove, who was former president George W Bush’s longtime political adviser and is a respected Republican consultant in Texas, told a private event in Austin on Sunday that he could not support Bo French’s candidacy for a seat on the state’s railroad commission, the Texas Tribune reported. Instead, he said, he will vote for Houston Democrat Jon Rosenthal over French, breaking a 32-year run of exclusively backing Republicans. His decision came after French posted on X a photograph of students wearing team attire celebrating the University of Texas’s rousing college football victory over top-ranked Ohio State on Saturday. The students are all non-Caucasian, and French wrote: “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” French could not have known the nationality or status of the students. According to Texas Global, fewer than 10% of the university’s 55,000 enrolled students are from overseas. His framing without evidence of the Asian students as “foreigners” – and attempt to denigrate them as outsiders – reflects a growing encroachment of formerly fringe views into mainstream Republican politics nationwide. But it drew condemnation from some in the party. John Cornyn – the establishment Republican Texas senator who lost his re-election primary to Ken Paxton, the Donald Trump-endorsed, scandal ridden state attorney general in May – attacked French on X on Tuesday. “The Republican Party is better than this. We should all condemn this bigotry directed at our fellow Texans or we will soon find ourselves a minority party,” he wrote, after French followed up his original post with an attempt to fundraise off it. Even Greg Abbott, the hard right Texas governor, appeared to have reservations. “That is not my message,” Abbott told Politico. “A selective picture of Longhorn fans celebrating our biggest home victory-ever actually shows a way that Texans unite. We all support our college football teams. “The way we win the state is the same way we win football games. We unite under the brand of Texas.” Republican state senator Lacey Hull urged French to remove the post on her own social media feed. “This post breaks my heart. I see college kids cheering on their football team. I see Texans,” she wrote. The chair of the university’s board of regents, Kevin Eltife, said in a statement that he too saw only Longhorns, the nickname of the college’s sports teams. “It’s the same remarkable view I have at graduation ceremonies and anytime I’m on campus,” he wrote. “I’m proud to celebrate all our Longhorn students today and every day. Thank you for making us proud.” French’s unashamed approach to the scandal continued on Monday in an appearance on a radio show in which he labelled Republicans who have criticized him as “less conservative”. “The establishment raised and spent $7[m] against me in the primary,” he told host Mark Davis, reported by the Tribune. “Many of the people who criticized me yesterday were some of the same people involved in that effort. It’s no surprise that the less-conservative people in Texas are the ones attacking me.” Other Republicans in midterm races elsewhere have also come under scrutiny for extremist, racist or misogynistic messaging, or their backgrounds. Brandon Herrera, a Texas candidate for a House seat in November, was called out for offensive sexual comments he reportedly made on social media using the handle “the AK guy”, a rightwing alter ego. In 2020, Herrera, who has 4 million followers on YouTube, filmed himself firing a gun at bottles of ranch dressing and, after they exploded, rubbed the condiment on to himself and declared that this would “make me irresistible to the fat bitches”. In 2024, after he described a Nazi-era gun as “the original ghetto blaster”, the Republican Jewish Coalition condemned him as “a goose-stepping extremist”. In New York, Peter Oberacker, a Republican state senator running for a congressional seat, was forced to delete a Facebook post paying tribute to his grandfather, who served in Adolf Hitler’s Nazi military during the second world war. Oberacker’s post featured a photograph of Ludwig Oberacker, who was killed during the Battle of the Bulge, in Nazi uniform. “I salute all who served,” Oberacker wrote, adding that he had debated whether or not to make the post. In Florida, Republican US House candidate Marshall Rowson was challenged on his ties to the League of the South, a white supremacist group. The online Talking Points Memo reported Monday that Rowson marched with neo-Nazis at the 2017 Charlottesville Unite the Right rally, at which Heather Heyer, a counter-protester, was killed. The outlet said it reviewed video showing Rowson and his now-wife arriving at the rally and being greeted by name by members of the League of the South members, which advocates for the secession from the US of southern states. Rowson did not respond to a request for comment after the Washington Post amplified the story on Tuesday.

title: US treasury secretary hails government’s bond buyback a success
author: Lauren Aratani in New York
summary: On Tuesday, the 10-year treasury rate yield reached a 19-year high at 5.041% as investors are wary Iran war fallout
body_text: Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, claimed the government’s massive buyback of US bonds was a success. The claim came as the 10-year treasury yield reached a 19-year high on Tuesday, increasing pressure on interest rates as the Federal Reserve weighs another hike to see off rising inflation. US treasury yields, or the rate of return that investors receive when a bond matures, underpin the rates of other loans such as mortgages, car payments and credit card debt. On Tuesday, the yield rate for the 10-year treasury reached 5.041%, the highest level since 2007. The treasury yield rises when demand for bonds goes down. Though the US bond market is typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, investors have been wary of the effect the war in Iran is having on energy prices. Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, hit $108 a barrel last week for the first time since May. When bond yields started to rise in August, the US treasury announced it would triple its buyback of government debt, going from $2bn to $6bn in an effort to bring down bond yields. Though the yields have continued to rise since, Bessent told Congress on Tuesday the operations are “the two most successful treasury auctions that we’ve had in 20 years”. “Since President Trump has come in, [the US bond market] has been the best-performing bond market in the developing world,” Bessent said. Earlier in August, the US government also stepped in to prop up the Japanese yen, a move that was seen as an effort to protect the Japanese government, a major holder of US bonds. Bessent told Congress the effort was a way for the US to signal support for Japanese policies. The Trump administration has been doing its best to fight against growing concerns over high inflation as the war in Iran continues, which is expected to have a major effect on the upcoming midterm election. US inflation has soared over the summer, reaching a three-year high of 4.2% in May before coming down to 3.4% in July and August. Stubbornly high prices set up a tough decision for the US Federal Reserve, which will on Wednesday announce any changes to the interest rate. The central bank is largely expected to raise rates for the first time since July 2023, which could help mitigate prices, though Donald Trump has demanded rates to be lowered.

title: Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon call for curbs on AI at ‘pro-human’ summit
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: Leftwing senator and far-right strategist rail against tech oligarchs but offer competing visions on Chinese ‘cold war’
body_text: The progressive senator Bernie Sanders and rightwing strategist Steve Bannon have called for restrictions on artificial intelligence (AI) but offered competing visions for what they termed a “cold war” with China. Speaking at the “Pro-Human Assembly” in Washington on Tuesday, the ideological adversaries were united in warning of the potential dangers of AI and demanding stringent guardrails against Silicon Valley’s “oligarchs”. But the populist pair offered very different perspectives on how to resolve the AI race with China, which Donald Trump and other Republicans have cited to justify moving full speed ahead with the technology. Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont, noted that Trump is due to host the Chinese president Xi Jinping in Washington next week. Sanders called for international diplomacy and a global agreement, including with Beijing, to ban the development of super-intelligent machines. He told an audience gathered in the ballroom of a Washington hotel: “A super-intelligent AI that escapes human control will not be an American problem. It will not be a Chinese problem. It will be humanity’s problem. “That is why I very much hope that at their AI summit next week, President Trump will negotiate a comprehensive treaty with President Xi to establish a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on super-intelligence.” Sanders drew a comparison with US president Ronald Reagan and his Russian counterpart Mikhail Gorbachev seeking to avoid nuclear conflict at the height of the cold war, eventually signing a treaty that eliminated an entire class of missiles. He said: “They understood that a nuclear war would not be good for the Soviet Union, not be good for the United States, not be good for the world, and they came together for a nuclear treaty. With the survival of humanity at stake, they found a way to sign that treaty.” Bannon, who spoke directly after Sanders but did not share a stage with him, also used the cold war analogy but did not arrive at the same conclusion. The host of the War Room podcast and former White House chief strategist under Trump called for an aggressive economic and technological “quarantine” of China, demanding the immediate expulsion of Chinese nationals from US research laboratories, an end to the training of Chinese engineers and technologists and the total severance of capital flows. “Did our fathers and grandfathers, did they underwrite the Soviet Union?” Bannon asked. “Did they train Soviet Union scientists? Did they take Russian kids over here to college to let them go to the best universities and get the best degree? Did they have Wall Street slobbering to do their deals? Did they have every bank there to lend them money quicker than to lend anyone in this audience? “The answer is they did not. They stood up to the Soviet Union and the first thing to stand up to them was to choke them off and that’s what we have to do today to the Chinese Communist party. No deals, no agreements, you’re out of the AI business because we’re going to shut your ecosystem down.” Demanding immediate executive action to isolate Beijing’s tech sector, Bannon said: “No chips, no black marketing chips, no free ride off American technology, no steal on American tech … To hell with the Chinese Communist party.” Only then, Bannon argued, can the US have the time necessary to consider the proper regulation of the tech sector. He delivered a scathing verdict on major technology corporations and executives, accusing them of gambling with public safety for private profit. Bannon accused Silicon Valley of seeking to “socialise all the risk with the American people including potential bailouts” while keeping all financial upside. “The American people are not going to be supplicants to these tech oligarchs,” Bannon said, praising grassroots campaigns that previously defeated federal pre-emption bills aimed at blocking state-level AI regulations. Bannon has long praised Trump as a historic figure and endorsed his lie that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. But on Tuesday, while claiming that executive action is required rather than legislation by Congress, he made only a glancing reference to the president who has dismissed AI concerns as a “hoax” and “sick conspiracy”. Sanders, for his part, did criticise Trump and Congress along with the concentration of power in Silicon Valley. “Despite living in a so-called democracy, the public has had virtually no input into the AI revolution that is transforming the world in which they live,” he said. “Congress, under both Democratic and Republican control, has been asleep at the wheel and we now have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing. Virtually all of the decisions regarding the development of AI have been made by a handful of the richest people in the world … whose chief goal is to achieve even more wealth and more power than they already have, no matter what the impact their work has on ordinary people.” Sanders said he would introduce legislation next week to permanently ban the development of artificial super-intelligence, an AI mind smarter than any human being, and put an immediate pause on advanced AI development until clear safety rules are in place. Recent surveys have found ⁠majorities of Americans worry that AI could be used to eliminate jobs, raise costs for families or otherwise cause social harm. Residents in several states have also challenged ‌proposals for new data centres, a ‌critical component of the AI boom. The Pro-Human Assembly, taking place against a backdrop of growing bipartisan anxiety over AI risks, also heard from members of Congress, labour leaders and religious representatives. Congressman Greg Casar, who is co-sponsoring the legislation with Sanders, accused AI billionaires of deploying massive political spending to stifle regulation. “Even as the threat becomes clearer, there are many powerful people fighting to prevent action,” Casar told attendees. “AI billionaires are spending millions through the Leading the Future Pac to scare politicians into silence. The top Republicans who control the House of Representatives are not lifting a finger.” Casar added: “Leading in AI diplomacy does not mean waiting around for an international agreement on dangerous AI. Putting up guardrails now is the best way to show we are serious about getting to a deal.” Republican congressman Chip Roy similarly expressed scepticism over concentrating decision-making power within the executive branch or tech boardrooms. “The president yesterday said he should be making the decisions about AI. I disagree. I don’t think big tech CEOs should be making all the decisions about AI. “I don’t think Congress should be making all the decisions about AI. If we allow technology to fundamentally alter and transfer and change the way we make decisions about our society and our Republican form of government, then what do we have left?”

title: Morning Mail: Hanson’s daughter faces scrutiny, Alzheimer’s anxieties, and AI’s ‘surreal’ Joycean dialect
author: Martin Farrer
summary: Lee Hanson works remotely for NSW senator without required official permission; alarm that tech language could circumvent monitoring
body_text: Morning everyone. Our exclusive top story reveals how Pauline Hanson’s daughter has been working from Tasmania for a NSW One Nation senator without the required ministerial approval for remote working. A minister in Victoria has accused a datacentre operator of using AI to lobby her about planning, social media is fanning anxieties about Alzheimer’s, and some AI models have created a strange, Joyceian language that could hinder oversight. After his double win, Emmys champion Matthew Rhys pays tribute to his Welsh roots. Australia Exclusive | The Victorian jobs minister has accused one of Australia’s largest datacentre companies of using artificial intelligence while requesting she lobby her colleague to approve a massive expansion of its “hyperscale AI factory”. Exclusive | Pauline Hanson’s daughter, Lee Hanson, has been working in Tasmania as a senior adviser to a New South Wales One Nation senator without the required ministerial approval, Guardian Australia can reveal. The One Nation leader made a qualified apology after describing Indigenous Australians as the “most primitive race on Earth”. And our political editor asks whether the disdain for experts on show as One Nation rolls out policy proposals means that she is pushing Australia towards a Brexit-style political culture. ‘Catastrophe’ | The number of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia before colonisation has been dramatically underestimated, according to new research that suggests the number was around 2.2 million before hundreds of thousands died in the “demographic catastrophe”. Alzheimer’s anxiety | Researchers have warned that social media may be misleading healthy people into taking Alzheimer’s blood tests, causing severe anxiety over biological markers that may never actually cause dementia. ‘Pervert glasses’ ban | One of Sydney’s largest councils has joined the Brisbane and Yarra councils in issuing a ban on AI smartglasses at public pools as concerns mount over the potential for predators to exploit the new technology. World AI warnings | AI models have begun communicating in a strange new version of English that reads like a cross between James Joyce’s Finnegans Wake and tech bro jargon, new research has found. It will fan concerns over oversight and monitoring as US senator Bernie Sanders said Congress was “asleep at the wheel” over threats the technology poses to humans. Hegseth impeachment threat | A Republican congressman has proposed impeaching Pete Hegseth over his handling of the war with Iran, while FBI director Kash Patel defended his agency’s decision to roll back restrictions on agent applicants who have previously engaged in bestiality. Macklemore comments | Singer Ed Sheeran has responded to the backlash over the removal of Macklemore from his North American Loop tour, following the rapper’s “Free Palestine” speech on stage in New Jersey. Saudi threat | Saudi cities faced the threat of a second day of Houthi attacks as fighting across Yemen has led the UN to warn of a humanitarian crisis with 100,000 Yemenis already displaced. ‘Complete failure’ | Three babies may have survived if hospital bosses and doctors had taken action over concerns about the nurse Lucy Letby, an official inquiry into the killings in Chester in the UK has concluded. Full Story Is Andrew Hastie launching a Coalition fightback against One Nation? Reged Ahmad and Guardian Australia’s political editor Tom McIlroy discuss whether Andrew Hastie is building a platform to challenge Angus Taylor for the Liberal leadership. In-depth Matthew Rhys, who made history by winning two lead acting awards for different TV shows at the Emmys, has paid tribute to his Welsh roots. Rhys, who grew up in Cardiff, won awards for Widow’s Bay and Netflix thriller The Beast in Me. Our critic Stuart Heritage also praises this “rarest of talents”. Not the news Gua sha is the ancient practice of scraping the skin to form mild bruises which are thought to have various health benefits such as increasing blood flow. But then, as experts tell Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz, so does a punch in the face. So does it work? Sport AFL | The preliminary final between the Swans and the Dockers at the SCG tomorrow night promises to be a great occasion. Martin Pegan looks at where it might be won and lost. Football | Liverpool host Spurs in the third round of the Carabao Cup and you can follow it live here, and follow Ipswich v Arsenal here. Golf | The head of the US PGA Tour has insisted there will be no favours for players such as Australia’s Cam Smith who are looking to return to the platform following the collapse of LIV Golf. Media roundup Labor MPs are getting “quite worried” over the prospect of more interest rate hikes and stalling living standards, according to the Sydney Morning Herald. Aged care funding cannot cover the rising costs of food and fuel, the boss of an Illawarra facility has told the Mercury. An inquest has heard three different theories about the disappearance of a woman in 1998, the Cairns Post reports. Another Australian caravan maker has collapsed into administration blaming cheap imports, the Courier Mail reports. What’s happening today Queensland | Callover on jury at Ipswich district court questioning and phone evidence applications ahead of Bruce Lehrmann’s rape trial. Canberra | National Press Club address by geopolitical strategist Sami Omari. Sydney | Tim Jordan, commissioner at AEMC, heads discussion of how AI is affecting the energy network while the Australian Human Rights Institute series at the Art Gallery of NSW focuses on technology’s impact on human rights. title: Republican Thomas Massie proposes impeaching Pete Hegseth over Iran war
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Congressman says defense secretary repeatedly violated constitution through his handling of Iran war
body_text: The Republican congressman Thomas Massie on Tuesday proposed impeaching Pete Hegseth, saying the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of war with Iran and the deaths of civilians in conflicts worldwide. The proposal by Massie, an iconoclastic lawmaker who lost his primary earlier this year after Donald Trump and Hegseth urged voters to oppose him, may put House Republicans in a bind just weeks before the 3 November midterm elections, in which they are defending their control of Congress. Under the rules of the House of Representatives, the articles must be voted on by Thursday, forcing Republicans to weigh in on one of the most prominent advocates of the war with Iran, which has gone on far longer than Trump said it initially would, and grown unpopular with the public. “By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable,” Massie said in a statement after reading the text of his resolution on the floor of the House. “Secretary Hegseth’s constitutional violations extend beyond the illegal war in Iran. He is abusing the power of his office to ignore congressional war powers resolutions, to kidnap foreign leaders, and to intimidate critics of the Trump administration by retaliating against them for exercising free speech. If we are to remain true to our oath to ‘support and defend the constitution of the United States’, Congress must not turn a blind eye to Secretary Hegseth’s unconstitutional and illegal actions.” In a statement to the Guardian, a Pentagon spokesperson did not directly address the allegations put forward in the impeachment articles, but hailed Hegseth a “transformative leader” who had “slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way”. “The entire department is unified behind the secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first,” the spokesperson, Kingsley Wilson, said. Massie’s resolution outlines eight alleged violations of the constitution by Hegseth, a former Fox News host and army national guard officer who as defense secretary has become a pugnacious defender of the president’s military politics. These include attacking Iran without first seeking Congress’s permission, and ignoring a war powers resolution the House and Senate approved in June that would require an end to the conflict. The resolution also accused Hegseth of “ignoring” laws that would have minimized civilian casualties, and specifically cites a US strike on a school in Minab, Iran that killed more than 168 people. Other articles allege Hegseth violated the constitution with the “extrajudicial killings” of at least 221 people on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean sea and eastern Pacific ocean, and of “suppressing free speech” through his retaliation against the Democratic senator Mark Kelly for his criticism of the secretary. The final two impeachment articles accuse Hegseth of violating the constitution through his involvement in the military operation that captured Venezuela’s then president, Nicolás Maduro, and a bombing campaign in Yemen that began shortly after Trump returned to the White House. Should the resolution pass, the impeachment articles would head to the Senate, where the Republican leadership would have to decide whether to hold a trial of Hegseth, who has maintained Trump’s loyalty even as other cabinet secretaries – including attorney general Pam Bondi and labor secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer – have been shown the door. The articles seem likely to attract many Democratic votes in the House. Massie has previously seized on unanimous Democratic support and the razor-thin Republican majority to push through a measure that forced the release of many files related to the disgraced financier and former Trump associate Jeffrey Epstein.

title: US House votes for third time to end Iran war after $38bn cost is revealed
author: Joseph Gedeon and Andrew Roth in Washington
summary: Damaging budget report estimates cost will grow by $3bn per month and stockpiles of weapons could take five years to rebuild
body_text: The US House of Representatives has voted for a third time to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution a few hours after a Congressional Budget Office (CBO) report showed the conflict had cost at least $38bn and left America’s stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild. The final tally of 220-204 was similar to earlier votes, with a few more Republicans joining most Democrats in calling for an end to the war. None of the resolutions have made it to the president’s desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto them. The action is likely the last House vote on the Iran war before the midterm elections, where the war and America’s cost of living crisis are expected to hurt Republicans at the ballot box. Lawmakers are heading home at the end of the week to campaign nearly full-time, with less than 50 days to go before the elections that will determine control of Congress. “Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?” said Democrat Seth Moulton before the vote. He added it was time for Congress to “actually ask tough questions, as the constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration”. Republican Brian Mast of Florida, the chairman of the House foreign affairs committee, questioned which military resources Democrats would want to remove from the region where he said Iran remains a threat. Mast said Trump is against “forever wars, and that is what he is ending”, meaning decades of hostilities from Iran. The House first approved a war powers resolution in June and followed up with another one in July, all seeking to halt US action in Iran. The Senate on its 10th try also approved a war powers resolution to end the conflict, but Republican senators quickly reversed course the next day after Trump berated them during a closed-door lunch. While the constitution gives Congress the authority to declare war, it also enables the president as the commander in chief to authorise some military actions. The war powers act, created in the aftermath of the Vietnam conflict, sought to put a more specific time limit on the president’s power, requiring congressional approval for sustained military actions after 60 or 90 days. The vote late on Tuesday came as the CBO report found that Iranian strikes had damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan. It estimated that the costs of the war will grow $3bn for every month the conflict continues, depending on its intensity, while noting that the war has driven up inflation. Much of the cost has come from missile defense. Fending off Iranian ballistic missiles and drones has consumed such a large share of the US stockpile of Patriot, Thaad and navy interceptors that the CBO said rebuilding it “would probably take at least five years, even if production was increased”. In a White House statement responding to reports of shortages, Donald Trump said the US had “far more munitions than anyone in the world” and “far more than we need”. In August, Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, dismissed a CNN report on the depleted stockpiles as “not true”. According to the CBO report, shortages would be “especially problematic” in a hypothetical clash over Taiwan, because of the need for interceptors to engage “large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles”. China maintains an arsenal of these and is expanding it, the report noted, and any US-China conflict over Taiwan would likely require far more interceptors, deployed far more quickly, than the campaign against Iran has. The economic report came a day after the Pentagon’s inspector general finally released its own first review of the war, saying that the US spent $22.3bn on munitions alone through 30 June, put total spending at $33.4bn, and found the fighting had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”. The Pentagon’s report did not address its own internal investigation of the Minab school strike on the first day of the war, which killed 156 people including 120 children. Critics have accused the Pentagon of burying results of the investigation that would show negligence in how it compiled targeting data for the initial strikes. The CBO report also found that increased energy costs, due in large part to the disruption of oil shipments through the strait of Hormuz, have increased inflation by half a percentage point compared with previous estimates. Brent crude jumped from $64 a barrel before the fighting to $103 at its peak, and the CBO projects the war will leave inflation running 0.5 percentage points higher than expected by early 2027, with short-term interest rates already about 0.2 points higher than they otherwise would have been. In June the White House requested $87.6bn in supplemental funding, of which $67.1bn was earmarked for the Pentagon. Once funding the CBO judged unrelated to combat operations is stripped out – including money for cybersecurity, drones and classified programs – $42.3bn of the Pentagon’s request appears tied to the Iran conflict, about 10% above the CBO’s estimate. The request included $12.1bn for classified programs the CBO could not examine – a far larger secret share than in past war supplementals. The CBO added that it still could not estimate the cost of repairing bomb-damaged US bases, nor any future diplomatic and foreign aid costs tied to the war.

title: House panel recommends Leon Black be held in contempt over Epstein inquiry subpoenas
author: Anna Betts
summary: Financier refused to comply with subpoenas seeking his testimony for the investigation into the late sex offender
body_text: The House oversight committee voted unanimously Tuesday to recommend that the House of Representatives hold Leon Black, the billionaire financier, in contempt of Congress, after he refused to comply with subpoenas seeking his testimony and nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) sought by the panel as part of its investigation into Jeffrey Epstein. Black contends the subpoenas are “invalid” and he is suing to block them. “Subpoenas are not suggestions; they carry the force of law and require full compliance” the representative James Comer, who chairs the committee, said in the chamber on Tuesday afternoon before the voting began. “Mr Black’s testimony is crucial to our investigation because he maintained a close personal relationship with Epstein for years during the time when Epstein was engaged in sex trafficking.” He added: “We made it clear to Mr Black and his attorneys that if he did not comply, then the committee would initiate contempt proceedings.” The bipartisan committee passed the resolution 41-0. Comer said that the committee now “moves the report to the full House”. The office of the House speaker, Mike Johnson, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday about whether the lower chamber would consider the contempt measure. The decision is the latest escalation in the dispute between the committee and Black, whose name has come up repeatedly in the Epstein files, and who, as reported by the New York Times, paid Epstein a total of $170m for what he described as tax and estate planning services from 2013 to 2017. Black has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing, and has said that he had no knowledge of Epstein’s crimes. Comerannounced last week that that the committee would consider the resolution to hold Black in contempt. It came after Black did not appear for his deposition scheduled for 3 September and did not produce all of the nondisclosure agreements sought by the committee. Instead, Black sued to block the subpoenas, arguing that they were “invalid to the extent they exceed” the committee’s “delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection” to its legislative purpose. Black’s lawsuit also argued that the subpoenas would “expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it, and who have no ability to protect themselves and their privacy before the committee”. The committee issued the subpoenas in June, after Black appeared voluntarily before the panel for a transcribed interview. The interview ended abruptly after lawmakers from both parties said that Black refused to answer questions about NDAs. Comer then issued the two subpoenas: one demanding that Black produce “all non-disclosure agreements to which he is a party”, and another requiring him to appear before the committee again. In August, Comer threatened to hold Black in contempt if he did not fully cooperate with the committee’s subpoenas. On Tuesday, during his remarks in the chamber before the vote, Comer said that Black “only produced one NDA to the committee” and noted that Black did not appear for his 3 September deposition. Attorneys representing Black had asked for a postponement of the committee’s markup earlier on Tuesday, and described it as a “complete abomination”. The attorneys said they sent two letters to Comer and Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the committee, saying that they would submit a complaint to the office of congressional conduct requesting “an investigation into conduct by Chairman Comer” alleging that ahead of Black’s scheduled deposition, Comer “engaged in what should be viewed as a violation of the rules of the House of Representatives relating to the deposition”. Black’s attorney said in a statement on Tuesday: “The committee under the leadership of Chairman James Comer and Ranking Member Robert Garcia has lost sight of its legislative purpose and is abusing its power.” The lawyers described the subpoenas as “illegitimate, illegal and a textbook abuse of power designed to bully and destroy legal protections of private citizens”. “Mr Black has repeatedly said that he feels terrible for Epstein’s victims and that he regrets ever doing business with Epstein,” the statement added. “He never abused a woman. He never was with an underage woman. He never engaged in sex trafficking. He never paid Epstein for access to women. He was never blackmailed by Epstein. Mr Black had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s heinous conduct.” Before Black’s scheduled deposition earlier this month, more than a dozen survivors of Epstein’s abuse urged him to comply with congressional subpoenas. They argued that his use “of NDAs underscores why Congress must scrutinize the agreements in his possession and determine whether they shed light on his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and others in Epstein’s orbit”. Earlier this year, the committee also moved to hold former president Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton in contempt for initially refusing to testify about Epstein. The Clintons ultimately testified before the House.

title: Mail-in disaster averted as Trump in angry froth after court defeat
author: Sam Levine in New York
summary: Election officials continue push to assure Americans mail ballots are safe after supreme court rules against president
body_text: After the US supreme court halted Donald Trump’s efforts to make it significantly harder to vote by mail in the midterms, US election officials are redoubling their efforts to convince Americans it is safe to cast their ballots by mail. The supreme court’s Monday ruling, which sent Trump into an angry froth on Truth Social, averted what election officials of both parties said would be an administrative disaster for this year’s elections. Trump’s order would have required states to comply with cumbersome new rules, including redesigning mail-in envelopes and uploading lists of voters to the USPS, that were not feasible to implement before ballots started going out. The effort was seen as a push by the government to change voting policy as well as one to weaken confidence in voting by mail. “That is the whole intent of the president. He wanted to build doubt,” said Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat who serves as the top election official in Nevada, where mail-in voting is widely used. “He wanted to create chaos.” Twenty-nine percent of Americans voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election and roughly one third cast a mail-in ballot in the 2022 midterms, according to researchers at the MIT election lab. Democrats were more likely than Republicans to cast a mail-in ballot. “There’s just concern: ‘Can we trust the mail?’ And I say yes, because it’s not the leadership or the management of the postal service that’s actually going to have their hands on the ballots, it’s the postal workers who are on our side,” Aguilar said. Nevada officials also plan to run a series of public service announcements to educate voters on the election process. In Wisconsin, election officials have faced questions about voters concerned their ballots won’t be delivered in time. Wisconsin law requires mail-in ballots to be delivered by the close of polls on election day in order to count and in the state’s April election there was an increase in late-arriving ballots. There have been higher rates of late-arriving ballots tossed this year, according to an analysis by the New York Times. Wisconsin election officials have encouraged people through county websites, social media, and notes attached to their ballots, among other things, to mail their ballots back sooner, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. “We’re really trying to encourage people to act sooner. So hopefully they take that to heart,” said Ann Jacobs, a Democrat on the Wisconsin elections commission, which oversees voting in that state. “It’s hard to tell people, ‘No, really, you should trust the post office’ when they came up with this absolutely cockamamie rule that was going to eliminate absentee voting.” In a video released on Tuesday, Meagan Wolfe, the administrator of the Wisconsin elections commission, said: “If you’re going to be returning your ballot by mail, please do so at least two weeks before the election. And you also may want to contact your municipal clerk to find out if there are other opportunities for you to return your ballot in your community. You may have drop-boxes or you may be able to return your ballot in person to your clerk.” Jane Kleeb, the president of the association of state Democratic chairs, said Democrats were making a more aggressive effort to encourage people to vote early in person while also emphasizing that if they want to vote by mail, they should return their ballots quickly. “We’re being honest with voters. We’re saying, ‘Look, normally you might have given three days to get your ballot to your election office, and now you should give a week,’” she said. A DNC spokesperson said the party “will continue to use every tool at our disposal to defend the right to vote, and we encourage Americans to make a plan to vote that best works for them and make their voices heard this November.” In Washington state, where everyone received a mail-in ballot, more than 20,000 votes were rejected in the August primary because they arrived late at an election office. “There is a sense of distrust,” said Steve Hobbs, the Washington secretary of state. “Even though there is a victory in the courts, we still are urging our voters to put their ballot in a drop-box.” As lawsuits challenging the rule wound their way through federal courts this year, Adrian Fontes, Arizona’s secretary of state, publicly emphasized that the rule had not gone into effect yet and so that nothing around voting by mail had changed. Since the supreme court’s ruling preserved that status quo, he said, officials haven’t had to shift their messaging. While voters have raised questions about the proposed changes “we continue to tell them until there’s a change, there is no change,” said Fontes, a Democrat “We are still where we were. We never jumped on the paranoia bandwagon.” “It’s intentionally damaging to the entire elections administration process in this country,” said Fontes, a Democrat and the top election official in a state where voting by mail is widely used. “The administration, by their actions, have proven that they are hell-bent on driving American voters away from their own elections. And we’ve been working very hard to counter that.”
