title: Kennedy Center to close as Trump threatens to block repairs over name dispute
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: President says he will block renovation project unless court decision to bar his name from being added is overturned
body_text: Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the Kennedy Center would close “immediately” and threatened to cancel a planned renovation of the institution if federal courts did not allow his name to be placed on the front of the building. Trump’s ultimatum came shortly after the president’s handpicked board voted, again, to close the institution’s performing arts building in Washington, citing safety and financial concerns. In a Truth Social post, Trump said the board voted “almost unanimously” to close the riverside landmark “for Safety reasons, and so that I can begin the process of Reconstruction”. He then said he would block a $257m renovation project that Trump had previously touted to address what the center has described as “decades of deferred maintenance and critical infrastructure needs”. “The Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board’s approved name,” Trump wrote. “If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place.” The performing arts center, built as a memorial to President John F Kennedy, has been embroiled in a dizzying legal dispute over Trump’s desire to put his name on the building. Prior to the Tuesday meeting, a federal judge blocked the center’s board from adding Trump’s name to the venue, writing that it would violate his previous ruling ordering it to be removed. “Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” US district judge Christopher Cooper wrote. “The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted.” Democratic congresswoman Joyce Beatty, an ex officio board member and trustee of the center, who brought the legal challenge, said Trump’s efforts to rebrand the institution in his name was a reflection of the president’s “vanity” and a “ breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee”. “The board’s latest shutdown vote is more of the same failure and abuse that has characterized this administration’s treatment of the Kennedy Center,” Beatty said in a joint statement with attorneys Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky. “The unlawful renaming drove audiences and artists away. Now the board has voted to shut down yet again to hide the terrible mismanagement under its current leadership. We’ll see the defendants in court.” Beatty told MS Now on Tuesday that the president had thrown “a tantrum” in a phone call to the board when he learned that she had prevailed in court. “It was the most unprofessional thing that I’ve ever witnessed or been a part of it,” Beatty said. “He went into name calling,” she added, saying that Trump had called her dumb. “He said, ‘I think you’re incompetent,’ and I said, ‘I know you’re incompetent,’” the congresswoman recalled. “He said he was going to hold me responsible if something fell out of the ceiling and killed someone,” she added. “And I told him, I said, ‘You’re already killing people, we’re at war.’ “Then he wanted to talk about how great he was with developing and he didn’t know anything about me, but I had never done anything. This was the biggest thing I had done. So I reminded him that he had more bankruptcies than anybody in the room.” The board’s vote followed a weekend of dueling court filings. The board’s proposal called for closing the main building on safety grounds, describing it as unsafe for continued occupancy. Beatty’s lawyers disputed that characterization, arguing in a court filing that the safety consultants cited, Delta Consulting Group, “expressly disclaimed” reaching any such opinion. Eisencalled the board’s weekend document dump “an outrageous act of hostage taking”, writing on X: “Pay up or the Kennedy Center closes, and the price is Trump’s name on the building.” The board had also been expected to vote on a proposal related to adding Trump’s name. But in a notice filed on Monday in the US district court for the District of Columbia, government lawyers disclosed that Joe LaFauci, the center’s vice-president of board relations, told the board that Tuesday’s meeting was “now focused exclusively on the necessary closure of the center”, citing “recently exacerbated structural emergencies”. However, in the filing, the board said trustees “stand by the recognition resolution proposed and passed by the board on August 13 2026”. The now-shelved second resolution had listed 10 options for inscribing Trump’s name and the “Trump Kennedy Center Fund” beneath the center’s name on the exterior marble, tying various forms of credit to renovation, endowment or oversight of the building. After Trump’s name was added to the exterior of the building above Kennedy’s, Cooper ordered the president’s name removed, ruling in May that only Congress has authority to rename it, and the lettering came down in June. The board voted in August to reinstate an inscription and proceed with the closure. Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary, posted a security video on Monday appearing to show debris falling in the center’s grand foyer, saying “the entire building is in this kind of shape” and that only Trump “can deliver the renovation on time and on budget”. Trump then shared the post on Truth Social. Lutnick’s wife, Allison, is a member of the president’s appointed board. Tuesday’s vote is the latest turn in a financial and legal fight that has dogged the center since Trump installed himself as chair in February 2025, firing the board and its longtime president, Deborah Rutter. Current leadership has blamed the crisis on mismanagement by Rutter’s team, alleging a “falsified” budget with $26m in “phantom revenue”, a claim Rutter and former board chair David Rubenstein have both denied, noting the center’s finances were independently audited.

title: ‘We need to get it right’: union gusto for Burnham will face make-or-break tests
author: Heather Stewart
summary: TUC conference rings with praise for new No 10 team, but battles loom over workers’ rights and north sea drilling
body_text: Louise Haigh, the UK first secretary, got a standing ovation from trade union members in Brighton this week, as she acknowledged what she called “the necessity to be bolder in this second chance that we’ve been allowed”. Haigh was the stand-in at the annual TUC congress for Andy Burnham, absent because of his father’s death. The headlines from the seaside gathering were dominated by party funding, after Reform announced £72m of donations in a single weekend and Unite called for a cap on donations by individuals in response. But as they gathered to swap gossip in Brighton’s pubs and hotel bars, senior union figures seemed reinvigorated for the moment by the “Burnham bounce”. Relations between the new No 10 team and the unions – including those less than popular with Keir Starmer’s regime – have improved significantly; general secretaries speak warmly of recent chats with “Andy”. Yet there is a clear sense that the real tests are to come – on the implementation of improved workers’ rights; on oil and gas licences, of particular concern to Unite and the GMB; and on John Healey’s crucial autumn budget. TUC delegates voted through policy statements on a slew of tricky issues in Burnham’s prime ministerial in-tray, from the future relationship with the EU – unions want him to drop Labour’s “red lines” – to Shabana Mahmood’s migration reforms. And senior union figures were keen to point to issues they see as make-or-break. Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, said she was pleased to see her former schoolmate Jonathan Reynolds back in cabinet as business secretary – but would judge him by results. In particular, she hopes to see the provisions in the Employment Rights Act on abolishing zero-hours contracts implemented in a way that embraces all workers in the retail and hospitality sectors she represents. “A lot of people think, job done – but the implementation means everything,” she said. “For this to make a real difference to people’s lives, we need to get it right. We want everybody to have a contract that reflects the hours they work.” The TUC is also gearing up to campaign on the issue in the coming weeks and months. “We will be getting our message out loud and clear, to Johnny Reynolds in particular,” she said. “It’s about reducing that one-sided flexibility, which employers have got in abundance.” Thomas also echoed a concern shared by several other senior union figures, about whether Reynolds’s newly expanded Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST), would end up lacking focus. “I would like to see a minister for work. BIST has so much to do, I worry that the labour stuff gets lost,” she warned. Mike Clancy, general secretary of Prospect, whose members include scientists and engineers – and which is not affiliated to Labour – expresses a similar concern, from a different perspective. Prospect is campaigning against real-terms cuts to science budgets by the taxpayer-backed UK Research and Innovation agency. Clancy frets that folding science into the department may lead to it being seen primarily through a business lens. “This is the first test of BIST … and whether this department’s really going to understand science culture,” he said. The GMB and Unite are waiting anxiously for the government’s ruling on the controversial question of whether to allow drilling in the Jackdaw gas and Rosebank oilfields. A decision had previously been expected this week, but appears to have been postponed until after the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in early October, in which the Green party’s leader in England, Zack Polanski, is standing. The two unions’ leaders are such ardent champions of continuing to exploit the North Sea’s declining fields, that Unite’s Sharon Graham and the GMB’s Gary Smith raised concerns about the idea that former energy secretary Ed Miliband would be Burnham’s chancellor. “What that gives us is time,” Graham said of the idea of exploiting Jackdaw and Rosebank. “It gives time for someone to get their backside into gear and realise we have to create an industry over the other side of this, whether it’s green fuel, whether it’s something else. All of that has to be done before you start saying you’re going to choke off what’s going on over here.” But the apparent delay until after a tricky London byelection underlines the fact that other parts of Labour’s electoral coalition are unlikely to welcome a “yes” to future drilling. Meanwhile Graham, who was an outspoken critic of Starmer, said she hoped the first Burnham budget would contain what she characterises as “winter fuel in reverse”. Rachel Reeves’s early decision to severely limit winter fuel payments to pensioners – eventually reversed – came to symbolise the last government’s missteps. “The abhorrence of that: do something as good as that,” Graham said. Unite’s (costly) suggestion is for the government to unfreeze the income tax thresholds that have seen a growing number of workers dragged into paying the basic or higher rates, and take fresh action on household bills. Healey has hinted he would like to do more to give the public a “breathing space” in the face of rising energy costs. But the shaky global backdrop, with oil prices rocketing and febrile markets driving up interest rates on government bonds, means he is likely to be left with little room for manoeuvre against Labour’s fiscal rules. For Graham, the answer is obvious: tax the wealthy more, and tax the banks. She rejects the idea that bond market turbulence is a reason for caution. “We cannot keep being told that we cannot do anything because of the markets. Because if that is the case, what is the point of us electing politicians?” she asked delegates in a fiery speech on Monday afternoon. The TUC has also called for a bank windfall tax to fund energy support. Judging by the mood music emerging from the Treasury of a “focused” budget with big spending decisions kicked into next year, Graham looks set to be disappointed. And as Farage’s lavishly funded Reform gears up for the next general election, the pervasive anxiety in Brighton this week was the same one that preoccupies even senior figures in the new government. The radical rhetoric of Burnham’s early weeks in power seems to have won him a fresh hearing with voters – but in straitened times, can he match them with action?

title: Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe
author: Steven Greenhouse
summary: Not only would the plan do vast economic damage – it assumes that Americans are easily bamboozled
body_text: Whenever Donald Trump gives a speech, it’s filled with so many lies and self-serving exaggerations that when he does utter something true, I see that as a sort of marvel. That’s what happened nearly an hour into Trump’s marathon speech last Wednesday at the Republican midterm convention, when he declared: “Only I can make this promise to you.” Trump said that just before he made a promise that was so shameless and irresponsible that what he said was indeed true: only Trump could make such a preposterous promise. Feeling very generous with other people’s money, the president promised to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in November. It certainly looked and smelled like a bribe. I guess that when you’re fearing an electoral debacle because your public approval ratings are in the toilet, because people are furious about your disastrous war of choice against Iran and because so many Americans are hopping mad that inflation has risen even though you promised to cut prices, then you might feel the need to take desperate measures, and that’s what Trump did by offering to stuff $5,000 in every adult’s pocket to help sway them to vote Republican. Since there are an estimated 240 million adults in the US, Trump’s plan would cost a colossal $1.2tn – that’s more than the Pentagon’s budget and nearly what the US will spend on Medicare this year. Many Republicans and Trump donors rushed to criticize Trump’s $5,000 plan. Joe Lonsdale, a tech billionaire and Republican donor, said he was “strongly against bread and circus bribes”, while Representative Bob Good of Virginia, former chair of the House Freedom caucus, called Trump’s promise a “socialist vote-buying scheme”. What angers me most about Trump’s promise isn’t that it would increase the enormous $40tn federal debt even though the president once promised to eliminate the entire federal debt. Nor am I angriest about the fact that Trump is essentially seeking to bribe the nation’s entire adult population for short-term political gain while in effect passing the cost on to our children and grandchildren. Trump is unconscionably seeking to finance his bribery by borrowing from future generations. But here is what makes me angriest: Trump evidently believes that millions and millions of Americans are such rubes that he can bamboozle them into voting Republican because they would want to get their hands on $5,000. I like to think that Americans are smarter than that and won’t be fooled. When the president made such a shameless proposal, I couldn’t help but wonder: are there no adults in the room with Trump? Is there no one with a sense of shame or fiscal responsibility who will tell him, “Don’t offer this $5,000 bribe. It stinks to high hell, and it’s grossly irresponsible.” Some brutal mockery came from Trump’s one-time ally Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former House member from Georgia. She hasn’t forgotten that Trump promised last fall that, thanks to his tariffs, every American, except for high-income people, would receive “a dividend of at least $2,000”. That didn’t happen. Greene also remembers that when Elon Musk said that Doge would chop the federal budget by $2tn, Trump suggested that a sizable chunk of those savings could go directly to Americans. That didn’t happen either. Greene taunted Trump by writing on X, “$5,000 for the peasants will be in the mail after the election only if you vote Republican, along with those DOGE and tariff money checks.” Trump egomaniacally called the $5,000 payments a “Trump dividend”, saying the money was available “because of our tremendous strength and success economically”. But Trump is embellishing big time here; there really hasn’t been economic success during Trump’s second term, other than the much-detested datacenter boom and the stock market hitting repeated records. Inflation is higher than when Joe Biden left office, GDP growth is slower, the trade deficit has jumped over 60% since April, the nation has lost 35,000 factory jobs since Trump’s inauguration and average monthly job growth is less than one-third what it was during Biden’s last two years in office. So, no, this $5,000 bribe is not a dividend resulting from economic success; it’s a loan from future generations. After Trump’s plan faced an avalanche of criticism, administration officials rushed to insist that the $1.2tn wouldn’t come from taxpayers or deficit spending. JD Vance claimed that much of the money would come from tariff revenues, while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick said something even more far-fetched: that lots of the money would come from charging wealthy foreigners for visas and from the administration’s investments in Intel and other companies. If you believe that, I own a club in Mar-a-Lago that I’d be happy to sell you. Unfortunately for Trump and every American, Trump’s promise to stuff $5,000 in every adult’s stocking will clash with one of his main promises – the $5,000 payments will increase consumer demand and that will inevitably push up inflation even though Trump repeatedly promised to cut prices. Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, issued a stern warning about Trump’s $5,000. “Debt is now as large as our entire economy, deficits are running $2tn per year, inflation is about 3.5%, and the 10-year treasury yield is approaching 5%,” MacGuineas said. “This half-baked political scheme would make this all worse – exploding the deficit, ginning up inflation and further driving up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy.” Kenneth Rogoff, a Harvard economics professor and former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, voiced even more alarm, telling PBS, “The US is already running an unsustainable deficit. This would only blow [it] up even more and increase the already high odds of a debt crisis over next five years.” With his $5,000 “dividend”, Trump is being his impulsive, myopic and reckless self, just like he was in plunging the US into war against Iran, leaving the nation’s economy and global relations in considerably worse shape than before the war. Trump’s $5,000 promise also risks spooking financial markets and nudging up interest rates. Every American – Republican, independent or Democrat – should see through Trump’s shamelessness. If his plan comes to pass, it might be a nice sugar high for many Americans, but it will do real economic damage – to inflation, interest rates and the nation’s debt – and it will also impose an unfair burden on our children and grandchildren. Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

title: Why is the White House being so weird about Natalie Harp again?
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: The president’s assistant travelled with him to Ireland – which really shouldn’t be much of a story. But his comms team seems determined to make it one, writes Arwa Mahdawi
body_text: Passport, money, emotional support human: Donald Trump had all the travel essentials on his recent trip to Ireland. The president flew into Dublin on Saturday morning to play golf, meet the country’s leaders and make provocative comments about unification. Melania didn’t accompany her husband on the trip (“Uh, she sends her regards,” Trump said), but his devoted aide Natalie Harp was obviously at his side. You’ll know Harp: the 35-year-old assistant was headline news last month after Democratic senator Jon Ossoff quipped that Trump didn’t want to do his job; he just wanted to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie”. That comment would have been quickly forgotten were it not for the Trump administration’s unhinged response (sample: “Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics”), which sparked a media frenzy. There was suddenly a spotlight on Harp, who is nicknamed the “human printer” because she trails the president with a portable printer, ready to hand him hard copies of flattering coverage. She appears to be disturbingly obsessed with her boss and he seems to appreciate the attention: it was recently revealed that Trump gave her (and two other female aides) a cash gift of $45,000 (£33,000) for a nice holiday. Harp may be a subject of intrigue, but the news cycle is frenetic. The human printer’s recent business trip to Ireland would not have been particularly noteworthy were it not for the fact that the White House is once again being extremely weird about it. On Saturday, the independent journalist Aaron Rupar posted a photo of the aide with the comment: “Look who made the trip to Ireland! #TravelWithNatalie.” This appeared to incense the White House’s Rapid Response 47 X account, which issued a personal attack in reply. “President Trump does, in fact, travel with staff,” they wrote. “Aaron, on the other hand, is a sick, deluded freak (in his 40s) who sits behind a keyboard and posts creepy things like this.” Sick deluded freaks in glass houses probably shouldn’t throw stones. And while we’re on the subject of best practices: anyone working in a professional comms capacity should probably understand that ignoring Rupar’s tweet would have been the sensible thing to do. Instead, they chose to amplify it and get people talking about the Harp-Trump relationship again. Which leads us to a question that comes up frequently in the Trump era: is all this some sort of cunning distraction technique? Does Team Trump prefer it if people are focused on Harp rather than Iran or the Epstein files or the economy? Or, alternatively, does the president just surround himself with idiots? My money is on the latter. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The US government is failing Americans on AI
author: Shakeel Hashim
summary: Trump and Republicans want companies to regulate themselves. It’s a dereliction of duty that will make AI less safe
body_text: It is hard to get Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei to agree on much. But over the weekend, all three AI company CEOs called for AI development to slow down in the face of growing, alarming risks. Their employees are sounding the siren too, with one researcher publicly quitting and accusing OpenAI and Anthropic of “gambling with our lives”. The combination of dire warnings from insiders and growing real-world evidence of rogue AIs should, in a sane world, lead to government action. Instead, Donald Trump and the Republican leadership have their heads in the sand. On Sunday, Trump dismissed industry concerns, accusing “very negative forces” of “raising exaggerated concerns”. House Speaker Mike Johnson, meanwhile, made it clear that Congress won’t be acting anytime soon. “They can self-police. They can self-regulate,” he said, never mind the fact that those pushing the frontier are the ones begging for legislation. In failing to act, the Trump administration and Republicans are failing the American people. The risks of AI are real: many of those developing the technology believe it is advancing far faster than their ability to control it or manage the risks. A wave of “rogue AI” incidents this summer, in which AI agents broke out of their testing environments, started collaborating with each other and ran rampage across the internet, has made fears once dismissed as “science fiction” much harder to ignore. Inside AI companies, worries of catastrophic cyberattacks, AI-enhanced bioweapons and mass unemployment are now all too commonplace. Meanwhile, companies find themselves in a classic prisoner’s dilemma. It is collectively in everyone’s interest to slow down AI development until we have a better handle on the technology. But each participant in the “AI race” has a strong incentive to defect. Collective action problems like this are nothing new. We have seen exactly the same thing with the climate crisis, where companies are not adequately incentivized to do the right thing, even though no one really wants the planet to burn. That analogy makes Trump and Johnson’s call for self-regulation all the more absurd. They are right that companies should do what’s right even without binding legislation to force them to. (Both OpenAI and Anthropic, to their credit, have indicated that they are willing to voluntarily slow down.) But relying on companies’ good intentions is a fool’s errand. The profit incentive to defect is substantial and ignoring shareholders is easier said than done. While some companies might behave themselves, not everyone will. It just takes one irresponsible actor to charge ahead and develop dangerous AI, and then we’re all in trouble. Moreover, we already have evidence that self-regulation is not working. OpenAI reportedly covered up several incidents of its models breaking out, disclosing them only after independent investigators discovered them. It freely admits that its latest model, GPT-6 Astra, is hard to monitor and control, warning users that the model might “[act] outside the user’s intended instructions” and take “harmful actions”. Anthropic, meanwhile, downplayed reports of its own AI’s problems when asked about it by a congressmember. Situations like this are exactly why government exists: to set a floor on acceptable corporate behavior. And that is why Trump and Johnson ought to use this sudden interest in AI safety to pass concrete laws. The US government should require independent audits of the largest AI companies’ practices. It should force companies to disclose safety incidents to prevent cover ups. It should set minimum safety standards for new AI models. And the government should have the power to block the deployment of a model that does not meet those standards. Putting all this into legislation is much easier said than done, but we need not start from scratch. Good bills already exist, most notably representatives Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan’s Frontier act. If the government was serious in its duties to protect Americans, it would make passing that bill – or a version of it – a priority in the coming weeks. Trump’s argument against doing any of this is that the US is in a race with China on AI, and it must not lose. But China does not want its citizens to have their bank accounts hacked by rogue AIs, either. Rather than throw his hands up, the feted dealmaker should do what he does best: make a deal. An international treaty on minimum safety standards will not be easy – but it is still worth trying, and doing so should be the president’s highest priority at his talks with Xi Jinping this month. No company – or country – wants to cause an AI-driven catastrophe. Despite what Trump may think, it’s the government’s job to make sure they can’t.

title: How Jon Ossoff won the algorithm – and garnered Obama comparisons ahead of 2028
author: George Chidi
summary: Pictures of Georgia Democrat looking into middle distance proliferate – and social media skills have boosted his profile
body_text: Delivering a speech in Atlanta last month, Jon Ossoff accused Donald Trump of corruption, incompetence and fecklessness, and peppered his remarks with substantive observations of dates and times and places. But the comment that ricocheted across the internet – a clip of just a few seconds – was an almost-throwaway reference about how the US president wants to “travel with Natalie” onboard Air Force One. The crowd cheered the US senator, who is running for re-election in battleground Georgia and is increasingly seen as a potential Democratic candidate for president in 2028. But his target audience that day – and this year – spanned far beyond the concert hall. After his remark went viral, stories about Trump’s young, exceptionally devoted, presidential aide Natalie Harp rippled through social and established media. Often enough, they were accompanied by an image of Ossoff, his sharp jawline captured from below as he looks into the middle distance. This photographic framing has increasingly been referred to as the “Ossoff angle”, perhaps in a disservice to myriad politicians from John F Kennedy to Barack Obama who also employed the technique, snapped at a low angle from a camera pit over the past century. While the approach is not new, it has helped the senator for Georgia to reach the social media feeds of users far beyond his state. Kathleen Hall Jamieson, professor of communication at Penn’s Annenberg School, likened Ossoff to Kennedy. The first millennial senator has mastered the medium of the moment, she suggested, much as Kennedy was the first president who really understood television. “How do you communicate that this is a new generation of leadership?,” Jamieson asked. “And how do you do that rhetorically? Because you can’t just stand up and say, ‘This is a new generation of leadership.’ “You have to have people draw that conclusion about you. And part of the way you do that is you master the media of the time, and you demonstrate that in the process you have leadership capacity and that you have the capacity to deal with the old order.” At 33 years, 11 months and four days, Ossoff was the youngest US senator sworn into the 117th Congress. At 39 today, and ever so slightly gray at the temple, he remains the youngest in a chamber with an average age of 65. The value of good lighting, a good background and a good angle in a social media post is not lost on a film-maker, as Ossoff was before turning to public office. The former documentarian has a knack for winning the algorithm with plain language, surfacing absurdities in an era of absurdities. While Trump is also a master of social media, the effect is different. His audience is generationally different. Trump, who regularly attaches infantile nicknames to his political enemies as a political marketing gimmick, calls Ossoff “Pee-wee Herman”, a tepid sobriquet which hasn’t yet landed. More recently, the Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican-aligned Super Pac, began running ads about Ossoff’s haircare and makeup regime using AI-generated videos of Ossoff in a salon chair. (Ossoff has spent about $1,200 on hair and makeup this election cycle – a drop in the bucket, given a fundraising haul of $81m up to June, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) disclosures.) Georgia elected Ossoff in a nail-biting runoff in January 2021 with control of the Senate on the line, amid the turmoil of Trump’s election dispute. His election, alongside fellow Georgia Democrat Raphael Warnock, secured the Senate majority for Democrats. Rioters stormed the US Capitol the next day. Since taking office, Ossoff has built a high profile as an opponent of Washington corruption, maladministration and the so-called Epstein class. He grilled CIA director John Ratcliffe after Jeffrey Goldberg, the editor-in-chief of the Atlantic, published a report that senior officials had shared sensitive information about future military strikes on Signal with him. He pressed Russ Vought, Trump’s budget director, after massive cuts to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. He questioned former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard on her presence at an FBI raid that seized 2020 ballots in Fulton county. His questioning of such Trump administration officials have proven as likely to reach wide social media audiences as anything he says on the campaign trail. Clips circulated of Ossoff repeatedly pressing intelligence director nominee Jay Clayton during a July 2026 hearing to say plainly whether the 2020 election was legitimate. Ossoff’s questions left Clayton sitting in silence at the hearing table, refusing to speak. “Your answers lack credibility,” Ossoff declared. “Your testimony lacks credibility. You’re being evasive and you’re not being candid or forthright. And everybody across the country is going to watch this and know that.” But outside of the spotlight, Ossoff has held hearings on child welfare and federal prison abuses both in Washington DC and across the state of Georgia. These relatively quiet issues tend to draw little media attention and less financial interest from funders, though they are a vital element of government oversight. “It is clear that Jon Ossoff believes what he is saying, and people – they get it,” said Charlie Bailey, chairman of Georgia’s Democratic party. “And so it not only matches up with their experience and their their anger and their frustration, they know he’s telling the truth. They know he’s saying what he believes, and that’s why he’s saying it, because he thinks it’s the right thing to do.”

title: First Thing: Houthis appear to target Mecca as House votes to end Trump’s war on Iran
author: Martin Belam
summary: Vote comes amid Republican call to impeach defense secretary Pete Hegseth. Plus a catnapped bodega cat in Brooklyn is returned home
body_text: Good morning. Saudi Arabia’s air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ⁠Houthi drone south of Mecca yesterday before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city. A spokesperson for the kingdom, which is fighting the Iran-aligned group in Yemen, said the security of Islam’s two holiest sites and of pilgrims was a “red line”. Mecca, home to shrines sacred to Muslims worldwide, is Islam’s holiest city and the focal point ‌of the annual ‌hajj pilgrimage. Meanwhile, in Washington, the US House of Representatives has voted for a third time to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution a few hours after a Congressional Budget Office (CBO) report showed the conflict had cost at least $38bn and left the US stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild. Why is Pete Hegseth being targeted by lawmakers? Republican congressman Thomas Massie has proposed impeaching Pete Hegseth, saying the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of war with Iran and the deaths of civilians in conflicts worldwide. How is the Trump administration reversing decisions over arming Israel? Congress has been informally notified about a pending deal, with the US planning to deliver powerful 2,000lb bombs to Israel. The weapons prompted such concerns about the possibility of mass casualties in Gaza that the Biden administration paused their delivery two years ago. All supporting acts withdraw from Ed Sheeran’s tour in solidarity with Macklemore All four supporting acts for upcoming dates of Ed Sheeran’s Loop tour of the US and Latin America have withdrawn in solidarity with fellow opening act Macklemore, as backlash grows against his removal from the tour over onstage comments in support of Palestine. Grammy-winning Macklemore had said on stage he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”, along with the words “free Palestine”. The remark prompted a petition calling for Macklemore’s removal from the tour from the Israeli-American Council and the opposition of some venue owners – including Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and a prominent donor to Israel. How has Ed Sheeran responded? In a lengthy Instagram post, the British singer said: “I have always used my platform and music to bring people from all backgrounds and cultures together … I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean that I don’t care. Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine.” NBC helicopter crash in LA kills at least three people, with others injured A news helicopter crash in a Los Angeles neighborhood has killed at least three people, after it hit the ground and burst into flames near the site of a bus crash that occurred hours earlier. The helicopter crashed near a one-storey commercial building in the neighborhood of Chatsworth in the San Fernando valley, as news crews were covering the bus crash that left at least two people dead and six others injured, according the Los Angeles fire department. New report reveals prevalence of physical and sexual violence in US In their lifetime, more than half of US adults have experienced physical violence – and nearly half have experienced sexual violence, according to a new national study. The study, led by researchers from Tulane University’s Newcomb Institute and the University of California, San Diego, examined experiences of physical, sexual and intimate partner violence. The study found that 52% of US adults have experienced physical violence during their lifetime, including cases involving a gun or knife. The rate was the same among women and men: 52% for each. In other news … Nick Reiner will not face the death penalty if convicted of the killings of his parents, Rob and Michele Singer Reiner, the Los Angeles county district attorney’s office announced. The US has confirmed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space, in an announcement analysts warn will accelerate an arms race with Russia and China. Human remains have been discovered near Crystal Rapids in Arizona, over two weeks after a flash flood tore through the Grand Canyon. Russia’s intelligence services are plotting to carry out targeted killings in the US and in European nations supporting Ukraine, the FBI has claimed. The European Commission president has told Canada she wants to open the door for the country to become the EU’s first associate member. Stat of the day: US surgeon general nominee made $270,000 from supplement company Donald Trump’s nominee for US surgeon general, Dr Nicole Saphier, reported more than $200,000 in business income from a company she owns that sells dietary supplements, which some critics allege are akin to “snake oil”. Well Actually: Not glamorous, but common – how to manage dandruff Experts don’t know exactly what causes dandruff, but if you’re seeing light flakes on your scalp, over-the-counter products can help. Keren Landman explains how. Don’t miss this: ICE lost count of miscarriages, while detaining a record number of pregnant women ICE is arresting a record number of pregnant women and teenagers – placing them in detention centers where they say it can be exceedingly difficult to access medical care. At the same time, the agency appears to have lost count of how many suffered a miscarriage. … or this: AI ghosts and deathslop are changing the way we mourn The rise of AI-generated tributes and bots for “talking” to the dead has experts concerned more people will grieve in isolation. Climate check: Firefighters say US government is failing them amid intense wildfire season Firefighters battling enormous wildfires in the US say the federal government is failing them at a time when supercharged blazes have made their jobs exponentially more dangerous. Last Thing: Catnapped bodega cat in Brooklyn reunited with owner The owner of a New York City bodega was reunited with the store’s cat after a couple passing by the establishment five days earlier appeared to abduct the feline in plain view of a surveillance camera and ignited an intense grassroots search effort. title: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s 9/11 remembrance: ‘constantly falling asleep on camera’
author: Guardian staff
summary: Late-night hosts discussed the president dozing off at a 9/11 remembrance event and Mitch McConnell’s unreassuring return to Congress
body_text: Late-night hosts reacted to Donald Trump’s sleepy appearance at a 9/11 remembrance event and a new round of panic over a possible AI doomsday. Jimmy Kimmel The night after the Emmy awards, Jimmy Kimmel returned to the stage in Los Angeles with a recap of the president’s remembrance event last Friday for the 25th anniversary of 9/11. “And while Donald Trump doesn’t typically shine in situations like this, he is a New Yorker,” Kimmel said. “He was there when this happened and he was, I have to admit, surprisingly eloquent.” Kimmel cut to a clip of Trump speaking at the Pentagon event: “We will always remember the victims and the families of September 11, 20-01, a very famous … date … unfortunately.” “He’s at his best when he riffs, you know?” Kimmel quipped. “At the event, Teddy Doze-evelt got in a pretty good nap,” he added. “He was sleeping so much on camera the White House had to put out a statement that said he wasn’t asleep. They said he was just ‘solemnly listening’. Which is the same kind of ‘solemnly listening’ Melania does when he tries to crawl into bed with her.” “It’s so perfect,” he continued. “The guy who spent four years screaming, ‘Sleepy Joe, Sleepy Joe,’ constantly falling asleep on camera.” Kimmel then played a montage of Trump asleep at major events, including his first Board of Peace meeting, his own inauguration, his big fireworks parade, the third game of this year’s NBA finals, his Freedom 250 concert, his Memorial Day remembrance event, the pope’s funeral, Lindsay Graham’s funeral, and too many Oval Office press conferences and cabinet meetings to count. “But I will say this: compared to Mitch McConnell, Trump has more energy than Kevin Hart,” Kimmel joked before a clip of the 84-year-old former Senate majority leader returning to work after a three-month hospitalization and absence, appearing dazed and unresponsive to reporters. “He seems good, right?” Kimmel quipped. “For months, no one was sure if he was even alive. And we still don’t know!” The Daily Show And on The Daily Show, Josh Johnson also touched on McConnell’s return after a prolonged absence that sparked numerous conspiracy theories. The Kentucky senator did not respond to any questions while being wheeled from his apartment to a waiting car on Monday, but he did offer a silent thumbs-up. “That’s not the thumbs-up of a man who’s doing well,” said Johnson. “That is the thumbs-up of a football player on a stretcher that you’re never going to see again. “But maybe Mitch was just overwhelmed by the media circus outside his door,” he continued. “I’m sure after he gave the thumbs-up and got in his car, he seemed totally normal.” Well, once in the car, McConnell appeared frozen in position, still giving a thumbs-up to reporters. “Wait, did he get stuck in thumbs-up?” Johnson laughed. “Quick, tell the Senate to vote on universal healthcare right now! He’s stuck like that, he has to vote yes. Republicans are going to have to flip him upside down to get a no vote.” “I’m sorry, but everything here screams puppet,” he added. “Like there’s just a guy on the floor of the SUV with a fishing line being like, ‘Quick, y’all, I can’t open his mouth and move his thumb at the same time!’” Later in the segment, Johnson responded to much fretting over a tweet by a former Anthropic researcher, who resigned after realizing that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. “End of the decade?!” Johnson marveled. “It’s fall 2026 – that’s just three pumpkin spice seasons away!” The tweet kicked off a new round of speculation and consternation over the existential risks of AI development, including from the builders themselves. In an essay, Anthropic’s head, Dario Amodei, said it was possible that rogue AI agents “could be capable of taking over the entire internet” in six to 12 months; the leadership of OpenAI, Meta and xAI called for more regulation, as they believed the technology was becoming too powerful, too fast. “I know a lot of people are worried that AI is going to kill us all before Shrek 5” – out in 2027 – “can give us closure, mainly because the tech CEOs gave us six months to live,” said Johnson. “But I’m not really sold on their narrative. I think it’s just as likely that these people in a speculative, overblown industry got into a room and were like, ‘So … is everybody out of money?’ And this whole thing about pumping the brakes is actually about taking the pressure off of them to deliver mass returns that we know still aren’t possible. “It’s a lot like if a guy couldn’t get it up,” he added, “but instead of apologizing, he was like, ‘It’s actually, like, too big, you know? That’s the problem, really. I’m really saving your life right now because this thing is too dangerous! It’s not that I can’t perform; it’s that I want you to live.’”

title: Epstein survivors praise House panel over Leon Black contempt vote
author: Anna Betts
summary: Victims hail 41-0 vote in favor of holding billionaire in contempt over refusal to comply with panel’s subpoenas
body_text: More than a dozen survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s abuse praised the House oversight committee for unanimously voting to recommend that billionaire investor Leon Black be held in contempt for refusing to comply with subpoenas by the panel seeking his testimony and nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) as part of its investigation into Epstein. “We commend Chairman Comer for showing real resolve in pursuing accountability in the Epstein investigation,” the survivors said in a statement. They said that the 41-0 vote sends a “clear message that wealth and influence do not put anyone beyond the reach of congressional oversight”. “Survivors have fought for years to bring the truth about Epstein’s network into the open and have helped create this moment of accountability,” they added. “Congress now has an opportunity to build on that work by following the investigative leads contained in the Epstein files wherever they go and demanding answers from the powerful people connected to them.” The vote on Tuesday marked the latest escalation in the dispute between the committee and Black, whose name came up repeatedly in the Epstein files, and who, as reported by the New York Times, paid Epstein a total of $170m for what he described as tax and estate planning services from 2013 to 2017. The contempt resolution now goes to the full House for consideration, if speaker Mike Johnson permits a vote. Black has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and said he had no knowledge of Epstein’s criminal activities. He voluntarily appeared before the committee for a transcribed interview in June, but the session ended abruptly after lawmakers from both parties said that Black refused to answer questions about NDAs. The committee, chaired by Republican representative James Comer, then issued two subpoenas: one demanding that Black produce all NDAs “to which he is a party” and another requiring him to appear before the committee again for a deposition. Black did not appear for his scheduled 3 September deposition and did not produce all of the NDAs sought by the committee. He instead sued Comer and the committee, arguing that the subpoenas were “invalid” and exceeded the committee’s “delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection” to its legislative purpose. He also argued that the subpoenas would “expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein”. Attorneys representing Black had asked for a postponement of the committee’s markup earlier on Tuesday, and described it as a “complete abomination”. Black’s attorneys said on Tuesday that the committee under Comer and representative Robert Garcia, its top Democrat, had “lost sight of its legislative purpose and is abusing its power”. The lawyers also described the subpoenas as “illegitimate, illegal and a textbook abuse of power designed to bully and destroy legal protections of private citizens” and reiterated that Black “never abused a woman”, “was never blackmailed by Epstein” and “had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s heinous conduct”. On Wednesday, a day after the vote, Comer announced the introduction of the Survivor’s Voice Protection Act, legislation his office said would ensure “survivors can speak freely about sexual abuse, even if they signed a nondisclosure agreement”. According to Comer’s office, the bill would also create “accountability for trusted individuals to protect minors by establishing an obligation to report suspected grooming behavior to law enforcement”. The legislation is a “result of the Oversight committee’s review of the federal investigations into Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s crimes”, his office added. In a statement on Wednesday, Comer said: “The federal government for decades failed the survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s crimes. We sadly cannot undue the harm and abuse inflicted upon these women. However, we have an obligation to take action to reform our laws to ensure survivors are protected and abusers can be held accountable.” He added: “During our investigation, we’ve learned how powerful men weaponized nondisclosure agreements to silence survivors of sexual abuse.” Republican representatives Nancy Mace, Virginia Foxx, Lauren Boebert and Anna Paulina Luna joined the bill as original cosponsors. The committee says that it has conducted 19 depositions and transcribed interviews thus far as part of its review of the federal government’s investigation of Epstein and Maxwell, and that it has released around 65,000 pages of documents from the Epstein estate, US Department of Justice, and interview transcripts, and also obtained Epstein’s bank records. Additionally, in June, Comer referred two men to the Department of Justice for further investigation after Sarah Kellen, a former assistant of Epstein’s, alleged that she was sexually assaulted by them in the years that she worked for Epstein. Neither men have been charged with any crime related to Epstein, and both have denied any wrongdoing and the allegations against them. Over the summer, the Guardian asked the DoJ for an update on this, to which a DoJ spokesperson told the Guardian that they had forwarded the letter from Comer about the two individuals to the FBI. “If, during the course of their review, FBI encounters of evidence of a federal crime, they will investigate that matter,” a DoJ spokesperson told the Guardian in July. When asked for an update in late August, the DoJ spokesperson said that the July statement “still stands”. The FBI did not respond to multiple requests for comment from the Guardian this month about the matter.

title: House speaker calls early recess before midterms amid AI regulation frenzy
author: Ariana Baio in New York and Shrai Popat in Washington
summary: Mike Johnson cancels votes on Thursday, meaning House members will avoid voting on impeaching Pete Hegseth
body_text: The Republican speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, announced on Wednesday that he would again cancel votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home one day early ahead of the midterm election recess. The latest change to the legislative schedule means House members will avoid voting on Republican Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and comes amid a frenzied attempt to propose legislation on artificial intelligence. It’s the latest round of cancellations at the hands of Johnson, who had already cut the pre-election session short by two weeks. Democrats have reacted angrily, encouraging Johnson to keep lawmakers on Capitol Hill before the midterm recess beginning on Friday. “I think it shows the cowardice of the Republican party. They are canceling votes to do business for the American people because they are afraid that that impeachment resolution of Pete Hegseth would pass on a bipartisan basis,” the Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal told MediasTouch. Lawmakers also hoped to address regulating AI development after industry executives and whistleblowers expressed a dire need for oversight. Johnson, however, has been reluctant to intervene – aligning himself with Donald Trump. “We ⁠cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI,” Johnson told reporters on Tuesday. “Because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for every American family.” More than 100 House Democrats had urged Johnson, via a letter, to cancel the upcoming recess to allow them to craft legislation on AI safeguards. In a notice on Wednesday, House leadership told members that other votes on EPA regulations, originally planned for Thursday, would instead take place on Wednesday afternoon. A spokesperson for Johnson characterized the House speaker’s latest move as simply moving up scheduled votes, not canceling future votes. Speaking to reporters outside of his office on Wednesday, Johnson said he was modifying the schedule because “the House has done its work”. Johnson said he wanted members to return to their districts to spend time with constituents ahead of the election. “You’ve seen the statistics we’ve been talking about for the last few days. This House has been the second most productive in terms of legislation in the history of the institution since 1789,” Johnson said, repeating a claim he also made earlier this month at the Republican midterm convention. However, so far, the current session has fallen short of passing legislation to surpass the two previous House sessions, according to the fact-checking website Snopes. Johnson also addressed Massie’s impeachment resolution, calling it “a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention”. The House speaker insisted it would be “immediately” postponed and he would not address it before the recess because the US is in the middle of international conflicts. Lawmakers will likely face a busy legislative agenda when they return to Capitol Hill after election day in November. Among their priorities will be addressing Massie’s resolution on impeaching Hegseth because it was filed as privileged, which fast-tracks the resolution.

title: More Republicans are turning on Iran war as midterms come into view
author: Chris Stein
summary: Three more GOP members voted for war powers resolution to force withdrawal from the conflict as election looms
body_text: As the US war with Iran drags on, the ranks of Republicans signaling the conflict is a liability for their party continues to grow. When the House of Representatives on Tuesday evening considered its sixth war powers resolution intended to force Donald Trump to withdraw troops from the conflict, three Republicans who had not supported the previous efforts broke with their party to vote this one to passage. Earlier that day, a Republican who had lost his primary after repeatedly clashing with Trump proposed impeaching the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, alleging a variety of constitutional transgressions including prosecuting the war against Iran without congressional authorization. The rebellions in the GOP are thus far mostly symbolic – Trump has ignored the sole war powers resolution to make it through both the House and Senate, and the prospects of Hegseth’s impeachment are unclear. But they underscore the growing nerves among both the party’s most vulnerable and most disobedient lawmakers over continuing a conflict that appears to have accomplished little other than play into the hands of Democrats, who have spent the entirety of Trump’s second term arguing that only they can be trusted to lower costs for Americans. “I said it in March: the mission had to stay focused and limited, because Americans do not want another forever war. I will not vote to keep our soldiers in an open-ended war, with Iowans paying too much at the pump,” said the congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks, one of the trio of Republicans who for the first time supported a war powers resolution. She was joined by another Iowa Republican, Zach Nunn, who justified his vote by noting his state “has already paid a devastating price” in the conflict, with two Iowans among the US soldiers killed by Iranian attacks as the war began. “Congress owes them, their families, and every American in uniform clear objectives and constitutional oversight. With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” the congressman said. “Having deployed multiple times and flown over 700 combat hours in the Middle East, I will not support another open-ended war. We can defend Americans, pressure Iran and pursue peace while ensuring Congress fulfills its constitutional responsibility.” Since the US joined Israel in attacking Iran at the end of February, Democrats have wielded war powers resolutions as a cudgel to get Republicans on the record about a conflict that polls indicate is not popular with the public. Their first three attempts failed, but in June, the fourth passed with the votes of two libertarian-minded Republicans – Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Warren Davidson of Ohio – along with Tom Barrett of Michigan and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, both of whom occupy battlefield districts. The Senate later approved that measure, but Trump refused to abide by it. In July, the same lineup in the House passed a fifth war powers resolution, before Nunn, Miller-Meeks and Nancy Mace of South Carolina expanded the ranks of Republican objectors to seven in Tuesday’s vote. The two Iowans are among the Republicans considered most at risk of losing re-election in the November midterms, with Miller-Meeks having won her race two years ago by fewer than 800 votes. They also represent areas of a state where the market impacts of the war with Iran are pronounced, as Iowa farmers struggle with higher prices for diesel, gasoline and fertilizer, all of which have been compounded by Trump’s tariff regime. Iowa has drifted consistently to the right over the past decade, but this year, Democrats believe the circumstances are right for them to oust not just Miller-Meeks and Nunn, but also to win a Senate seat, the governor’s mansion and potentially more congressional districts in the state. It’s far from the only state where Democrats are on the offensive. The House vote took place on the same day the New York Times and Siena University released polling that showed likely voters preferred Democrats over Republicans for Congress by nearly nine percentage point, a finding that lines up with other surveys. Democrats are helped in their quest to retake the House by the fact that Republicans control it with a tiny majority that may be exceedingly hard to defend in November, and has also enabled Republicans like Massie to seize on splits within the party to embarrass Trump and his ally the House speaker, Mike Johnson. Last year, Massie banded together with Democrats and a handful of Republican dissidents to force passage of a bill requiring the release of files related to the disgraced financier and former Trump associate Jeffrey Epstein. That intensified the president’s ire towards him, and Massie lost his primary to the Trump-endorsed Republican Ed Gallrein earlier this year. Now with even less to lose, the congressman appears to be trying to seize on splits within the House GOP to retaliate against Hegseth, who campaigned for Gallrein. Massie proposed the resolution on Tuesday, and House rules appear to require it be voted on by Thursday. The chamber was scheduled to be in session that day for the last time before the 3 November midterm elections, but on Wednesday morning, House Republican leaders canceled votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home early to face their constituents.

title: Family of pregnant woman who died sues Ken Paxton for wrongful death
author: Marina Dunbar
summary: Tierra Walker, 37, was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia at 20 weeks, and family says denial of abortion led to death
body_text: A wrongful death lawsuit filed on Tuesday accuses Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, doctors and state health officials of contributing to the death of a pregnant San Antonio woman whose family says she was denied an abortion that could have saved her life. Tierra Walker, 37, died in December 2024 while 20 weeks pregnant after being diagnosed with pre-eclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy-related high blood pressure condition that can be fatal. Attorneys representing Walker’s family filed the lawsuit in Bexar county district court, alleging that Paxton, the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, several doctors and other defendants were responsible for “deliberate indifference, discrimination, and medical mistreatment [that] ultimately caused her horrific and tragic death”, according to CBS News. The lawsuit says Walker and members of her family requested an abortion as her condition reportedly worsened and she faced seizures and blood clots. Her family alleges doctors refused to provide the treatment. The legal action also names the executive director of the Texas Medical Board, Stephen Brint Carlton, the University of Texas health system and individual doctors. The lawsuit further challenges Texas’ abortion ban as unconstitutional, according to ABC7. Walker’s family alleges Paxton and Carlton deprived her of her right to life by enforcing “a merciless blanket prohibition” on abortion and that doctors failed to provide medical treatment that could have saved her life. Paxton, a Republican who is currently running for Senate, has repeatedly defended Texas’ abortion ban. He has also filed lawsuits against doctors and organizations accused of sending abortion pills into Texas from other states. Last year, Paxton arrested eight people linked to a midwife accused of performing illegal abortions. He called the individuals “a cabal of abortion-loving radicals” and “fake doctors” in a press release. Abortion is currently prohibited in Texas with only very limited exceptions and providers can face criminal and civil penalties. Since the state’s near-total abortion ban took effect in 2021, the year before Roe v Wade was overturned, reports started emerging of doctors denying or delaying abortion care even in high-risk or emergency situations. In some cases, patients had to be on the cusp of death before medical staff would intervene.

title: Republican senator blames Trump administration policies for measles deaths in Pennsylvania
author: Marina Dunbar and Shrai Popat
summary: Health committee chair Bill Cassidy said fatal outbreak of disease is a ‘terrible legacy’ for Trump administration
body_text: Senator Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the US Senate health committee, blamed the Trump administration’s vaccine-skeptical approach for ‌recent measles deaths in Pennsylvania and challenged Donald Trump’s pick for surgeon general to directly state that vaccines do not cause autism on Wednesday. Cassidy, a Louisiana physician who chairs the panel, said three people in Pennsylvania had died of measles, with a fourth death under review, because of misinformation and misguided policies. His remarks come as the US grapples with its worst measles outbreak in over three decades. “To suffer from any disease is awful, but to suffer one which is avoidable, that’s even worse,” Cassidy said, adding that the country needs health leaders “who make decisions based on science, not politics or ideology”. The senator said that the outbreak would be “a terrible legacy for this administration”. The committee is currently considering the Trump-picked Chris Klomp for deputy secretary of health and human services, Nicole Saphier for surgeon general and Timothy Westlake to ⁠lead the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. Saphier notably avoided mentioning vaccines directly in her opening remarks, instead expressing her Make America Healthy Again bona fides. “I have long believed that we spend too much time and resources treating chronic disease after it takes hold, and not enough time helping Americans reduce their risk before illness begins. And unfortunately, we’re seeing the consequences of that imbalance right now: rising cancer rates in people under 50, cardiovascular disease that remains the number one killer, but also is largely preventable in lots of cases,” Saphier said. Cassidy pushed Saphier about whether she would tell parents concerned about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine that it does not cause autism. “I’m so sensitive to this because I’ve had wriggle room from people sitting there … who later use that wriggle room to do things which are quite contrary?” Cassidy said, referring to the various promises that Robert F Kennedy Jr made to the top Republican in his confirmation hearing, only for the health secretary to renege on several occasions. “Would you feel comfortable communicating with clarity … Is the MMR vaccine extremely lethal, as the president said?” Cassidy asked Saphier. The nominee for surgeon general said that she “cannot speak to what the president has said” but went on to say: “I do not believe the MMR vaccine to be lethal. I believe the MMR vaccine is our greatest tool for combating measles.” Saphier, a practising radiologist and Fox News contributor, added: “The best tool we have to combat these infections to save the most lives and to also create population herd immunity is vaccination against the MMR. I appreciate the president is trying to reach vaccine-hesitant people who are wanting more answers or who are concerned that there are too many doses.” Cassidy, however, remained unconvinced by the president’s public health strategy. “I’m not sure that you reach people who are vaccine hesitant by feeding into untruths,” he said. Last month, Cassidy denounced Trump’s “crazy, stupid” claims about the safety of the combined MMR vaccine for undermining faith in immunization. Cassidy previously voted to confirm Kennedy as health secretary, despite disagreements over how to combat vaccine skepticism. He said that Kennedy, who has pushed the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism for decades, had promised him that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) “will not remove statements on their website pointing out that vaccines do not cause autism”. After Kennedy became health secretary, however, the Autism and Vaccines page on the CDC website was altered to undermine that scientific consensus. An asterisk was added to the headline “Vaccines do not cause Autism”, which leads to a footnote pointing out that “the root causes of autism” remain unknown.

title: Key House Democrat refuses to clear Trump’s $2.8bn arms sale to Israel
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Pro-Israel Gregory Meeks raises concerns over threat to civilian lives from package of 40,000 one-ton bombs
body_text: The top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee has thrown up a roadblock to one of the largest US arms transfers of Trump’s second term, refusing to clear a $2.8bn sale of 2,000lb bombs to Israel. Gregory Meeks announced the hold on Tuesday on a package of 40,000 of the bombs, among the most destructive conventional munitions in the US arsenal. “The Trump administration has not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with US law and with appropriate protections for civilians,” he said. “I therefore will not clear this sale at this time.” The deal, funded through US Foreign Military Financing, covers 20,000 MK-84 bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 penetrator warheads. Meeks cannot single-handedly veto the $2.8bn arms transfer, but his leverage comes from the informal custom of “tiered review”. Under this practice, the state department submits major weapons packages to top foreign affairs lawmakers for an informal sign-off before triggering a formal notification to Congress. Killing the sale outright would need a veto-proof joint resolution of disapproval in both chambers, a bar Congress has not cleared. A similar push by the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders failed along party lines in April. In 2025, the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, declared a national security emergency to bypass congressional review and fast-track nearly $3bn in weapons, including more than 35,000 heavy bombs and 4,000 bunker-buster warheads. With a separate $6.67bn package in January, the administration has now cleared or expedited over $12bn in arms for Israel since Trump took office. Meeks has said the pace has outrun oversight, accusing officials of skipping briefings and rushing sales while raising alarms over Israeli conduct in the occupied West Bank and Lebanon. The hold also lands amid longstanding accusations that Israel has used American weapons unlawfully. The Leahy laws bar US assistance to foreign military units credibly linked to extrajudicial killings and serious abuse; the state department in 2024 flagged at least five Israeli units on those grounds before the war in Gaza even began, including one battalion tied to the death of a Palestinian American at a West Bank checkpoint. The Geneva conventions, meanwhile, bar arming a party where there is a clear risk of war crimes – a standard a UN commission of inquiry cited last year in finding Israel’s Gaza campaign amounted to genocide and calling on the US and other states to halt weapons transfers. In 2024, Biden administration lawyers, including some at the state department, had concluded it was reasonable to assess that Israel had violated international humanitarian law and Leahy laws by using American weapons in Gaza, even as the administration publicly avoided making that determination. Meeks, long known for his strong pro-Israel views, emphasized that the hold was not a break with the country itself. “This decision does not diminish congressional support for Israel’s legitimate defense needs,” he said. “It reflects Congress’s responsibility to ensure that US-funded weapons are used lawfully, responsibly and with meaningful safeguards for human life.” The state department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: House votes to hold Leon Black in contempt over Epstein subpoenas refusal
author: Anna Betts
summary: Billionaire has refused to comply with subpoenas from House oversight committee as part of Epstein inquiry
body_text: The House of Representatives voted on Wednesday to hold billionaire investor Leon Black in contempt of Congress over his refusal to comply with subpoenas issued to him by the House oversight committee as part of its investigation into Jeffrey Epstein. The action came a day after the committee voted unanimously to recommend that the House hold Black in contempt. Wednesday’s House vote passed under unanimous consent, meaning there was not a formal roll call, but no member objected to the contempt resolution. The Department of Justice will now decide whether to take action on the resolution, though it is not required to. Congress held former attorney general Merrick Garland in contempt in 2024, but the justice department did not act on it. But it did prosecute Trump advisers Peter Navarro and Steve Bannon after congressional referrals for contempt, and both men served prison time. In a statement on Wednesday, a justice department spokesperson said: “The Department of Justice is expecting to receive the referral from House oversight committee and takes allegations of contempt of Congress seriously. “For the past 18 months, the department has repeatedly said it will follow additional investigative leads in all matters relating to Jeffrey Epstein,” they added. “The US attorney’s office for the District of Columbia will review the referral of Mr Black carefully and will not hesitate to pursue additional cases where the evidence supports.” Black, whose name came up repeatedly in the Epstein files, and who, as reported by the New York Times, paid Epstein a total of $170m for what he described as tax and estate planning services from 2013 to 2017, first voluntarily appeared before the committee for a transcribed interview as part of its investigation in June, but the session ended abruptly after lawmakers from both parties said that Black refused to answer questions about NDAs. Black has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and said he had no knowledge of Epstein’s criminal activities. His lawyers criticized the contempt resolution shortly after it passed Wednesday. “This an outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr Black. The House of Representatives has rushed through every stage of this inquiry,” they said. “We intend to pursue our litigation challenging this action and will hold the committee and Chairman Comer accountable in the courts.” The committee, chaired by Republican James Comer, then issued two subpoenas: one demanding that Black produce all NDAs “to which he is a party” and another requiring him to appear before the committee again for a deposition. Black did not appear for his scheduled 3 September deposition and did not produce all of the NDAs sought by the committee. He instead sued Comer and the committee, arguing that the subpoenas were “invalid” and exceeded the committee’s “delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection” to its legislative purpose. He also argued that the subpoenas would “expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein”. On Tuesday, Black’s attorneys said that the committee under Comer and the representative Robert Garcia, its top Democrat, had “lost sight of its legislative purpose and is abusing its power”. They described the subpoenas as “illegitimate, illegal and a textbook abuse of power designed to bully and destroy legal protections of private citizens” and reiterated that Black “never abused a woman”, “was never blackmailed by Epstein” and “had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s heinous conduct”. On Wednesday morning, more than a dozen survivors of Epstein’s abuse praised the House oversight committee for their vote. “Survivors have fought for years to bring the truth about Epstein’s network into the open and have helped create this moment of accountability,” they said on Wednesday morning before the House vote. “Congress now has an opportunity to build on that work by following the investigative leads contained in the Epstein files wherever they go and demanding answers from the powerful people connected to them.”
