title: Friday briefing: After two months as PM, is Andy Burnham passing his own test?
summary: In today’s newsletter: The Labour leader said he would assess his success by how his policies affected his constituency. From the cost of living to immigration, we look at how Makerfield voters feel about their MP’s choices
body_text: Good morning. Remember the Makerfield test? When Andy Burnham was elected as an MP back in June, he reassured wary voters that the constituency was not a “stepping stone” (to be fair, it was a bit) but a “touchstone”. He meant that the policies his government devised would have to matter on the high streets of Ashton and Hindley Green. “A Makerfield test at the heart of British politics will make sure that the places Westminster has neglected will now get fairness,” he said. As the Commons breaks for the jamboree of high ideas, low gossip and crap karaoke that is party conference season, it’s a good moment to ask how Burnham’s early decisions as prime minister – he’s been at it under two months, right enough – meet that test and what it tells us about his government. I spoke to someone who, since that byelection, has immersed himself in the opinions of Makerfield voters, and those living in constituencies like it, Luke Tryl, UK director of the research agency More in Common. But first the headlines. Five big stories UK news | Shabana Mahmood has described the anti-asylum activist Daniel Thomas as “a far-right and outright racist” who will feel “the full force of the law” if his organisation commits crimes near contested asylum sites such as Piddington. Russia | Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma in a tightly controlled vote stripped of meaningful competition and with little doubt about the result. UK politics | Andy Burnham is under further pressure to take control of ailing Thames Water from a cross-party group of MPs who are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds who are effectively running the company. Royal family | The brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed in published extracts of his new memoir that King Charles sounded “giddily elated – like a lottery winner” in a phone call to him immediately after her death. Nature | A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s ⁠cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living feline species has been formally named and described in more than a century. In depth: ‘The top thing for people in Makerfield was that life was a struggle’ “Who cares what Makerfield man or woman thinks? I’m a Holborn and St Pancras via Caerphilly gal myself,” you might be muttering into your overnight oats. But here’s why it matters: Makerfield, like dozens of similar post-industrial seats in the north of England, is the sort of seat Labour used to win so easily they could put up a ham sandwich as a candidate. Things have since changed. The area voted to leave by 65% in the Brexit referendum, and in the May council elections, Reform won all eight council wards in the constituency with about 50% of the vote. In his byelection dispatches from Makerfield, Luke Tryl found a pervasive sense of being left behind and forgotten – despite being “at the centre of the universe”, as one constituent put it, for one frantic month of campaigning. According to the voters Tryl spoke to, the Makerfield test should consist of three elements: Burnham showing that he “gets it”; a record of delivery; and a national plan to address the issues that Makerfield residents share with people across the country. So how has Burnham fared on some of the early challenges he’s faced? Cost of living measures “The top thing we heard in Makerfield was a sense that too much of life was a struggle,” Tryl tells me. And More in Common’s polling has found that, so far, Burnham’s early cost of living measures are very popular across the country: 86% of Britons had heard about the bus fare cap, seven in 10 thought it reflected well on the government; about 8 in 10 had heard about the VAT cut on household electricity bills (amounting to an average of about £45 a year per household), and 67% said that it landed well. Voters in Makerfield-like areas are realistic, says Tryl: “They say: ‘£45 is not going to change my life’, but they see it as a statement of intent”. People who are slightly more engaged with politics specifically mention the budget as a test point: earlier this week Burnham warned of “difficult choices” ahead. The cut-through of these measures to voters is striking: “Part of it is just the ubiquity of Andy Burnham,” says Tryl. Most recent More in Common polling shows people are more likely to have seen him on social media than any of the other party leaders. A fifth of Britons (22%) have seen “Cool Dad” Burnham on social media in the past week, compared to 20% for Reform leader Nigel Farage. I’m fascinated to see that for under-25s that rises to 35%, compared with 13% for Green leader Zack Polanski, who is often touted as catnip for younger voters. Immigration More in Common polling in June estimated that 62% of Makerfield residents consider immigration to be a top issue, making it one of the most concerned constituencies in the country about that issue. Here, Burnham gets a mixed review. The idea of taking in refugees through capped, controlled routes is popular in Makerfield, where voters worry over a lack of control. That’s why Tryl argues that one policy that really does pass the Makerfield test is the community sponsorship scheme, part of Shabana Mahmood’s controversial asylum reforms. But while Burnham has won back Labour-Green switchers over the summer, he’s not been so successful with Labour to Reform defectors – and Tryl believes that’s because he has yet to move the dial on migration. Take, for example, the shift in people’s perceptions: 52% of Britons now cite concern that local women and girls would be at risk of sexual violence as the top reason why they’d oppose asylum accommodation in their area (previously, they were more likely to refer to pressure on services). In socially conservative areas such as Makerfield, voters feel this “much more strongly”. “I think this is an achilles heel”, says Tryl. Prisoner release It’s not just constituencies such as Makerfield where voters think the criminal justice system isn’t tough enough: across the country, nearly two-thirds of Britons think prison sentences are too lenient. “The case of Andrew Harper outrages people across the board,” Tryl tells me, “but particularly in somewhere like Makerfield.” So Burnham played a bad hand well, by explaining the competing priorities to the public, and taking time to examine options before finding a partial solution. “Taking the public on that journey – especially in Makerfield where people are very distrustful of politicians – was important,” says Tryl. Climate Burnham, who is now facing intense pressure over whether to approve oil and gasfields in the North Sea, wrote in the Guardian yesterday that the UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050. While Labour-Reform switchers in places like Makerfield are often deeply worried about climate change, there’s also concern that net zero policies will unfairly punish ordinary people. For many, the issue of climate change falls below more pressing daily concerns like the cost of living crisis. In this context, More in Common’s polling suggests the main test for Britain’s energy policies will be whether they can lower household bills. Party donations Tryl’s fieldwork has found that the public aren’t deeply engrossed in the minutiae of donations limits, although they do want the system to be fair. So Burnham’s early failure to support a domestic cap on donations is unlikely to be a decisive factor when constituents in Makerfield next head to the ballot box. But for the recipient of those crypto-millions, the damage has been done: more than one in three voters now name Farage’s “sleaziness and corruption” as a barrier to them voting Reform. Rather than the party’s core voters, who seem unmoved by the continuing financial scandals, it is Labour-Reform switchers in seats such as Makerfield whose faith has been shaken. But Tryl cautions against over-stressing the issue. “At the next election, if the status quo on cost of living, core public services, andimmigration still feels pretty bad, I don’t think donations in themselves will be an issue” he says. We want to hear from you What do you want to know about the US midterms, and how the Guardian plans to report them? I’ll be putting your questions to our Washington bureau in the coming weeks, so send them in by hitting reply or emailing first.edition@theguardian.com What else we’ve been enjoying I loved our pics gallery of eastern Europe’s socialist hotels, which I hadn’t read about until now. Poppy Noor, newsletters team Cracker of a You be the judge this week: Ayaan lent her brother Ahmed some money thinking it was for something important … then he spent it on a holiday. But does it matter what he did with the cash? Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team I found Zoe Williams’s interview with academic/author/policymaker Camilla Cavendish, on all the reasons we’ve stopped having babies, utterly fascinating. Poppy In case you missed it, make sure you read this viral essay from The Cut (£) on friendless husbands and the wives who try desperately to build social lives for them. Charlie The photos in our piece on the Tate’s Edward Enninful-curated show, c, about how the 90s art and fashion changed British culture, are beautiful and nostalgic. Poppy Sport Cricket | England extended their extraordinary hex over Sri Lanka to a 14th game, Tom Banton and Harry Brook leading them to a six-wicket victory with 47 balls to spare in the second T20 international. Football | Two first-half goals inspired Bournemouth, playing in their first European match, to a 2-1 win against Real Sociedad in the Europa League, while Crystal Palace had a comfortable 4-0 win over Lech Poznan. Athletics | Keely Hodgkinson has lifted the lid on how plans to chase the 800m world record this summer were ruined by a freak accident that her team has likened to whiplash. Something for the weekend Our critics’ roundup of the best things to watch, read, play and listen to right now Music Beabadoobee: Pylon | ★★★★☆ The Filipino-British songwriter’s fourth album sprinkles 90s alt fuzz with disarmingly sweet melodies and an impressive host of guests including Paramore’s Hayley Williams and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates. Read Alexis Petridis’s full review. Film Resident Evil (in cinemas now) | ★★★★☆ Weapons director Zach Cregger delivers a seat-edge thriller with a standout lead performance from Austin Abrams as an everyman navigating chaos. Read Jesse Hassenger’s full review. TV 70 Up (ITVX) | ★★★★☆ The landmark documentary series looked like it was done for good – until one participant was diagnosed with terminal cancer. Asif Kapadia takes the helm for its most elegiac, thoughtful outing ever. Read Lucy Mangan’s full review. Games Marvel’s Wolverine | ★★★☆☆ Logan is well realised by Liam McIntyre and some exquisite character art, but there are lapses in narrative and emotional arcs and some of the combat feels like a chore. Read Keith Stuart’s full review. The front pages “UK must fully commit to hitting net zero by 2050, says Burnham”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Telegraph has “Labour’s tax raid on holiday cottages”, and the FT writes “BoE warns of higher rates ahead to tackle rising inflation”. On Earl Spencer’s claims, the Times leads with “Charles was elated after Diana died, earl claims”, the Mail splashes “Queen offered to restore Diana’s HRH … after she died”, the Mirror says “War of words”, and the Sun asks “Why is he doing this to the King now?”. The i Paper runs with “Palace on the defensive after Earl’s new claims against King”, and the Express has “Charles was ‘emphatic we respect Diana’s memory’”. Lastly, Metro says “A royal crisis? What crisis?”. The Latest Taking on Trump? Canada and EU forge closer ties Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, has welcomed the EU’s proposal for Canada to become the bloc’s first ‘associate member’, despite threats from Donald Trump over the plan. The US president said Washington could impose ‘very serious tariffs’ or halt trade if the EU went ahead with the plan. But in a defiant speech to the European parliament, Carney called for ‘deep cooperation’ and said polling showed the overwhelming majority of Canadians supported closer ties with Europe. Lucy Hough speaks to Europe correspondent Jon Henley. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad West Yorkshire’s moors include beautiful pinks and purples; boast rich biodiversity and a variety of flora and fauna, and play an important part in tackling the climate crisis. But, before now, much of the area’s rural beauty might have gone unnoticed by the wider public. But, on Saturday morning, the Bradford Pennine Gateway Trail will open, the first reserve of its kind in West Yorkshire. title: After four killings and a revealing autopsy, Memphis is fed up with the national guard takeover
author: George Chidi
summary: Although state officials laud a reduction in violent crime, a report claims it would have happened without the taskforce
body_text: National guard troops began walking the streets of Memphis a year ago this week, as part of a federal surge of law enforcement agents sent into the city at the behest of the Trump administration to reduce violent crime. Fewer soldiers are on the street today, as the city’s grudging initial acceptance of the president’s deployment has given way to doubts about their effectiveness, focus and respect for civil rights – particularly after four men were killed in gunfire by federal agents working with the taskforce, with a recent autopsy showing that one was shot in the back. Donald Trump signed an executive order last September directing a surge of federal law enforcement agents from the ATF, FBI, Department of Homeland Security and other agencies into Memphis. A month later, Tennessee’s Republican governor, Bill Lee, paired that with additional state patrol officers and the activation of 1,500 Tennessee national guard members to patrol the streets of downtown Memphis. The Memphis Safe Task Force claims credit for deep reductions in the violent crime rate. And while the city is on track for the lowest rate of homicides in decades, independent analysis argues the deployment of the national guard has had no statistically measurable impact on violent crime and that violence would have fallen in Memphis much like it has across the country in cities without similar interventions. Memphis’s headline-driving homicide rate has fallen about 35% since the start of the taskforce. Murders in the city’s second quarter decreased by 60% year over year, according to reports from the Memphis police department. But Memphis had a 26% decrease from 249 murders reported in 2024 to 184 in 2025, before the taskforce was deployed. A year to the day from the start of the Memphis Safe Task Force, Memphis reported 96 murders, compared with 149 the previous year. The city is on pace for 135 murders for 2026, a rate of about 22.2 per 100,000 residents. “The taskforce has been very successful and we appreciate the work the Tennessee national guard has done in helping us reduce crime,” said Brady McCarron, a United States Marshals Service spokeperson who fields media requests for the taskforce. “Overall crime in Memphis is down significantly, dropping nearly 36% year-to-date in 2026 compared to the previous year, according to Memphis police department’s own statistics.” A report by the Center for American Progress, a Washington DC-based thinktank, however, picked apart claims that large reductions in violence could be attributed to national guard patrols in New Orleans, Memphis and Washington DC, where the presence of troops on the tourist-heavy National Mall and the streets around the White House have become ubiquitous. Trump reacted to the center’s report by threatening a personal defamation lawsuit against the authors for $5bn unless they retracted the report and issued an apology. Describing the deployments as a “political charade”, the CAP report used statistical regression to measure changes in violent crime against historical patterns and the double-digit drops in crime in other large cities. “The findings of this analysis confirm what many already suspected: At the time of the administration’s federal law enforcement and National Guard deployments, the primary goal was never to stop crime,” the report said. “Despite multiple tests using multiple data sources, measures, and windows of time, there is no compelling evidence that these deployments reduced homicides, violent crime, or gun violence.” *** In Memphis, a brief initial decrease in violence when national guard troops began patrolling was actually followed by a brief increase in violent crime. The rate eventually smoothed out as crime continued to fall overall, both in Memphis and across the country. Fewer national guard troops are patrolling the streets of downtown Memphis today. The taskforce attributes that to a unit rotation. But the pullback also coincides with an autopsy report released by the family of Tyrin Johnson, who was shot dead by two national guard soldiers on Fourth of July weekend. The taskforce said they were chasing an armed robbery suspect. The autopsy said Johnson was shot in the back. “The timing is suspicious,” said community organizer Lucci Chambless, who has been in close contact with the Johnson family following the shooting. The Tennessee national guard and the governor’s office have not yet responded to requests for comment. Public sentiment in Memphis began to shift after the shooting. Tamboli’s, a pizza place in midtown Memphis, went viral for refusing to seat national guard troops in protest of the deployment. A call by conservatives to boycott the restaurant instead packed it with supporters. More than 50 other businesses have signed on to a “buy-cott” with Tamboli’s affirming their stance. “I think we’re seeing more and more every day that people are coming to the side that they don’t agree with them being here, seeing how they’re harming our community so much,” said Taylor Herndon, owner of Board to Beers, a board-gaming bar near the University of Memphis. Her bar is participating in the national guard lockout, which she says has had a positive impact on business, similar to Tamboli’s. “We have a lot of customers that we have started seeing because of the boycott,” she said. “We already had a large following, but the boycott has definitely helped us reach even more of our community, and we’ve had a lot of people reach out and thank us for being on the right side of history, and that they feel comfortable coming because of it and that they feel support because of it, which has been amazing.” She said she was disappointed that formal resistance by Memphis’s elected leaders has been comparably tepid. “It’s been hard, because I keep fighting and I keep fighting, and it seems like things just keep getting worse. Despite thinking: ‘Oh, it can’t get any worse,’ but it does,” she said. Democratic-led cities like Portland and Chicago strenuously resisted national guard deployments – rhetorically, in court and in the street. But the Memphis city council rejected a resolution condemning the federal surge when it first arrived, and public reaction had largely been muted until recently. The activities of the national guard have been as “transparent as mud”, and an immigration raid on the El Corralón nightclub earlier this month by the taskforce – resulting in 120 arrests, the most in one operation in state history – is exacerbating the change in public sentiment, Chambless said. Many of the people arrested in the raid have already been deported. The children of deportees presented themselves at the Memphis city council hearing Tuesday, to a chamber that has become more receptive to resistance after elections earlier this year. A new crop of county commissioners may restart legal action, she added. “We’re hopeful that maybe they will take up that cause. Especially now that the damages have been shown,” Chambless said. “Tyrin Johnson certainly would still be alive if the national guard had been stopped.”

title: What Trump’s attacks on mail-in voting mean for the midterms
author: George Zornick
summary: The extraordinary danger is that a president who believes he is the law, and the law is him, remains intent on disrupting the electoral process
body_text: For the millions of Americans who vote by mail – almost a third of the country – the week began with significant uncertainty that they would be able to easily submit their ballot this fall, thanks to a March executive order from Donald Trump that aimed to restrict mail-in ballots. By Monday night, the supreme court restored a measure of order by rebuking the president and rejecting his plan – but Trump’s frothing response portends more danger for the rapidly approaching midterms. Trump’s March order forbade the US Postal Service from delivering mailed ballots to anyone the administration deemed ineligible. The Department of Homeland Security, working with the Social Security Administration, would have devised that list of supposedly ineligible, noncitizen voters. On its face, the move appeared plainly illegal. One expert told the Guardian’s Sam Levine, “This is a wholly unconstitutional EO,” because ultimately the federal government cannot set election rules; only states can. The plan was full of logistical problems, too. A whistleblower told Congress earlier this month that the Postal Service simply didn’t have the ability to implement the system safely, and that the whole plan was “perilously rushed and potentially unlawful”, according to Richard Blumenthal, the senator who handled the whistleblower complaint. State election officials also complained they would be unable to implement Trump’s restrictions this close to an election, even if they were deemed lawful. Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin had already begun mailing out ballots before the supreme court ruled, and chaos would have reigned there and across the country had the court blessed Trump’s plan. But it didn’t – and that sent Trump into a furor. In a lengthy post on Truth Social, in which he called mailed ballots “corrupt and out of control”, he singled out the conservative justices who had gone against him on that issue and this year’s ruling on tariffs. (Only the justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented from the mailed ballot ruling; Amy Coney Barrett and Neil Gorsuch, both nominated by Trump, did not.) “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves,” the president fulminated. His position is clear: the federal courts, the states that administer elections, the USPS – all of them should bow to his whims, regardless of what the constitution says. Trump has already shattered legal norms by appointing his former personal lawyer to head the Department of Justice and then continuing to treat him as a personal attorney. Just this week, in a remarkable scene at the White House, the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, served the role of White House press secretary, answering a wide range of questions from reporters on behalf of the president. A day later, a smiling Blanche attended a Trump rally for the GOP Senate candidate Michael Whatley in North Carolina, flashing an enthusiastic thumbs-up from the crowd. The extraordinary danger of this moment is that a president who believes he is the law, and the law is him, remains intent on disrupting the electoral process. Trump’s claims about mail-in voting are false, as the Guardian’s George Chidi explained. The Brookings Institution has found: “An average total mail voting fraud percentage across the 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022 general elections of only 0.000043%, or about four cases of mail voting fraud out of every 10 million mail votes.” But Trump has been obsessed with the issue since 2020, when mailed ballots – which are typically counted last – evaporated his slim lead in some key states on election night. (Incidentally, Trump has voted by mail at least three times since then.) And more Democrats than Republicans vote by mail, so restricting mailed ballots also tilts the playing field towards the GOP. State election officials are now working to assure voters that they can safely vote by mail this year, as Levine reported this week. But one can safely assume Trump will not stop pushing democracy to the brink. Watch this race: Florida’s 27th congressional district Trump won this Miami district by 15 points in 2024, when he aggressively promised a campaign of “mass deportations”. María Elvira Salazar, a Republican representative, easily held the seat, vanquishing her Democratic opponent by 20 points. But Salazar is distancing herself from Trump this time around. “Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she says to the camera in a remarkable ad released on Thursday. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy.” She is facing a significant challenge this year from Eliott Rodriguez, a Democrat and former news anchor. Fact check During Trump’s speech address at a rally in North Carolina on Wednesday, which the Charlotte Observer described in an op-ed as a “dark, divisive” speech, he painted the Tar Heel state as a crime-ridden hellhole. “So nobody used to think of North Carolina as a dangerous state, criminally dangerous,” Trump said. “It was like North Carolina, it was beautiful, it was apple pie, right? And now it’s one of the most violent and one of the worst in the whole nation.” (An interesting pitch to voters: your state is the worst.) But crime has fallen dramatically in North Carolina. Don’t take our word for it: only hours before Trump’s arrival in Gastonia, North Carolina, the White House blasted out a press release correctly noting: “In North Carolina, crime fell across all four major categories in the first half of this year compared with the same period last year, including a 12.4% drop in murders, an 18% drop in robberies and a 23% drop in motor vehicle thefts.” George Zornick is the Guardian’s US political enterprise editor

title: To protect democracy, Democrats should talk about corruption – not authoritarianism
author: Jared Abbott and Joan C Williams
summary: The party needs to thread the needle between college-educated and working-class voters. Our survey offers a way
body_text: Resisting authoritarianism is the second-highest priority for Democrats’ college-educated base. But for working-class Americans, it’s only the 19th priority (out of 20), we found in a new survey. The gap between these two groups was larger than on any other issues: elites prioritized resisting authoritarianism an astonishing 33 percentage points more than non-elites did. Democrats’ dilemma is that their college-educated base insists they stand up to Donald Trump’s attacks on democracy, but they also need to win working-class votes. The way to thread that needle is to recognize that what’s needed to defend democracy in the short term is different from what’s needed to defend it in the long term. In the short term, Democrats’ base is right: immediate action is needed in the courts, exemplified by the more than 150 lawsuits that Democracy Forward has filed against the Trump administration and the 82 filed by California attorney general Rob Bonta, contesting alleged corruption, funding cuts, election interference and more. Action in the streets is powerful, too, from the protests in Minnesota to the mobilization of more than 8 million people (chiefly highly-educated women) at No Kings rallies across the country. But while #resistance is necessary, it’s not enough. Democrats also need to take two additional steps. The first is to talk about defending democracy in ways that connect with working-class voters, which our survey defines as those without college degrees in the middle 50% of US income distribution. While “resisting authoritarianism” was a low priority for working-class voters of any race, “reducing corruption in government” was the third highest priority for white working-class respondents, fourth for working-class Latinos, and sixth for working-class African Americans, our survey found. In fact, reducing corruption was one of only two top working-class priorities we identified that wasn’t economic. A study out of the UK explains why. It found that working-class Britons use “corruption” not in a narrow legal sense but to express “deeply rooted feelings of injustice and unfairness”. “The whole system needs [to be] seriously looked at and reformed,” said one man, protesting MPs at the Parliament bar with their taxpayer-subsidized gin and tonics. “The government don’t care about me, they don’t care about my children,” said a working-class woman. Corruption talk is how working-class people protest against a political system that doesn’t seem to represent them – a political system that has become anti-democratic. One prominent Democrat provides the template for how to respond: Jon Ossoff, the US Senator up for re-election in Georgia. “American politics is coin operated,” he said. “Money comes in, favors come out.” A former documentary film-maker, Ossoff knows how to communicate. First he adopts a catchy phrase–the “Mar-a-Lago mafia” – to describe the alliance of the Trump family and the ultra-rich that “has taken American corruption to spectacular new heights”. Then he ties corruption directly to negative impacts on ordinary people’s lives: “One point six billion of your tax dollars to fund and finance [Donald Trump’s sons’] mining project in Kazakhstan. All this, while you pay for more gas, for groceries, for healthcare.” Then, Ossoff pivots from political to economic elites: “Members of Congress live in fear of these Super Pacs. And that corruption is why insurance companies get away with denying your claim for a procedure you needed to save your life … It’s why the ultra-rich get a tax break while you pay more for everything.” Republicans have been harnessing anger against economic elites and redirecting it against political elites for decades; with an approach like Ossoff’s, Democrats can reverse the process, redirecting anger against political elites on to economic elites benefitting from a corrupt system. If the first step for Democrats is to talk about corruption, not authoritarianism, the second step is to respect working-class priorities. Eight out of the top 10 working-class priorities are economic, our survey found, and while elites’ economic priorities focus tightly on prices, the working class also prioritizes higher wages and economic opportunity. Many working-class voters don’t rush to defend democracy because they feel it’s failed them for the last 40 years. American workers used to get 70% of GDP but today their share is only 54%. That helps explain why virtually all Americans earned more than their parents in the decades immediately after second world war, but only half those born in 1980 will. The only way to defend democracy in the long run is to prioritize creating an economy that delivers a stable, middle-class life for working-class Americans. Donald Trump is busy alienating the working-class voters who swept him into office, but Democrats are also unpopular. If they want to win elections consistently enough to build a progressive, democratic future, they first need to respect that working-class top priorities are economic – not Palestine, not ICE, not trans rights. Democrats also need to talk about “defending democracy” in ways that connect with working-class voters. Anger at corruption offers a powerful entry point when linked to the widely held view that the economic system is rigged. This approach has worked in countries as diverse as Hungary, the Philippines, Guatemala and Malaysia. It can work here, too. Jared Abbott is the director of the Center for Working-Class Politics Joan C Williams is distinguished professor of law and Hastings Foundation chair (emerita) at University of California College of the Law San Francisco. She is the author of Outclassed: How the Left Lost the Working Class and How to Win Them Back

title: No more book bans: how Florida students are pushing rightwingers out of school boards
author: Anna North
summary: Local communities are fighting back against the influence of conservative groups like Moms for Liberty in education
body_text: Jimmy Glover’s youngest children were in high school when he noticed their Florida school district taking an unsettling turn. Beloved books were being pulled from shelves. Teachers were scared of being targeted. “There was this culture of fear that was permeating throughout the district,” Glover said of Sarasota county. By channeling anger against mask mandates in schools, the rightwing group Moms for Liberty, founded in Florida, built an outsized influence on school boards across the country in 2022. Soon, members began pressuring schools to remake their curricula along conservative ideological lines, erasing mentions of LGBTQ+ Americans, slavery, racism and more. As a Black dad living in a historically Black part of Sarasota, Glover said he was especially disturbed by governor Ron DeSantis’s announcement that Florida schools would begin teaching students that some Black people benefited from slavery. “Now my children and the students in my community weren’t going to be learning about the true history of this country,” Glover said. So the father of four decided to run for Sarasota’s school board this year. He is part of a larger movement of students, parents, teachers and concerned community members pushing back against the influence of groups like Moms for Liberty in Florida public education. They wanted schools that were safe and welcoming for all students, and that focused on learning rather than scoring points on the national political scene. And last month, they won. Progressive candidates beat opponents backed by or aligned with Moms for Liberty in school board races across the state – in many cases reversing gains made by the group in 2022. Of the 30 candidates the group supported that year, 20 have declined to seek re-election, have been defeated or will face runoffs in November, according to the LGBTQ+ rights group Equality Florida. In Sarasota, home to Moms for Liberty’s cofounder Bridget Ziegler, progressives flipped the school board, with liberal candidates Megan Tennimon and Beth Mayberry replacing more conservative members (school board races in Florida are technically nonpartisan). Glover got more votes than either of his conservative opponents, but his race will go to a runoff in November since no candidate won a majority. When reached for comment, Moms for Liberty referred the Guardian to a public statement disputing the notion that the recent Florida election represented a loss for the group: “Moms for Liberty-endorsed school board candidates won or advanced in 11 of 15 races across Florida.” But the group had issued fewer endorsements than in past elections and declined to endorse any candidate in several counties. That included Sarasota county, where board chair Ziegler, who has been plagued by scandal, was not running for re-election. Meanwhile, organizers for Glover’s campaign and others say the elections in Florida mark a turning point, a rejection of rightwing educational ideology in a deep-red part of a deep-red state. And, they say, the victories hold lessons for progressives campaigning on the national stage in the midterms and beyond. “We know that a better future is possible,” said Sebastian Martinez, president of the Sarasota Next Gen Democrats, a youth organizing group that helped campaign for the county’s progressive slate. “We’ll work every day to get there.” Students step up and organize Glover wasn’t the only Florida parent concerned about the influence of Moms for Liberty over his children’s education. The group had success in 2022 by appealing to voters angry about pandemic school closures, and by joining the larger rightwing campaign against “critical race theory”. But Moms for Liberty’s popularity has waned since then, said Liv Coleman, a professor of political science and international studies at the University of Tampa. By the time Stephanie Vanos ran for Orange county’s school board in 2024, the top question voters asked her was: “Are you the one who wants to ban books?” “It speaks to the outrage at state censorship in our schools and the complete disrespect for the first amendment,” said Vanos, who won her seat that year. But that outrage had yet to be fully harnessed. Martinez, now 22, has been active in school board organizing since he was 16. He started Next Gen Democrats last year as a way to expand young Sarasotans’ role in Democratic politics. “I really wanted to see young people not just get involved in organizing, but to become part of the party,” he said. For youth, one barrier to political participation is money, Martinez said – they can’t afford to volunteer their time when they could be working a paid job. So to help recruit and retain young canvassers, the group offered $20 an hour. “The Democratic party is supposed to be a party of working-class people supporting working-class people, and so it only makes sense to then pay people to work,” Martinez said. Sarasota Next Gen Democrats recruited about 20 high school students to phone bank, knock on doors and distribute yard signs around the county, said Kennedy Cole, the group’s political director. They also helped decorate a school bus that drove around Sarasota on Election Day, getting the word out about progressive candidates. Students “were sick of what we’ve seen from our school board, and we knew that Megan, Beth and Jimmy would help return normalcy to it”, said Cole, a 17-year-old high school senior. “Students really worked their butts off to get those results.” It wasn’t just students. Youth organizers met regularly with other community activists, including a group of retired women who sent 7,000 handwritten postcards to Sarasota voters. A parents’ group invited candidates to a local park to meet voters while their kids played. Equality Florida spent $250,000 on mailers in support of candidates around the state who were facing opponents aligned with Moms for Liberty. “In order to do something like this, it takes a web of people,” Cole said. “It’s a lot of different people operating in their own ways.” ‘Tired of the chaos’ Whether they were knocking on doors or meeting families at the playground, winning candidates spread a back-to-basics message that resonated with voters across political lines. Cole likes to tell the story of a close friend whose conservative parents voted for liberal school board candidates “because they were tired of the chaos” that Moms for Liberty had brought. Sarasota schools’ statewide ranking had slipped since conservative activists took control of the school board, said Mayberry, a former teacher who won a seat representing Sarasota’s fifth district. “The focus came off of academic performance,” Mayberry said. She and other successful candidates campaigned to restore that focus. They ran on issues like school funding, academic achievement and support for teachers and students, Coleman said. “They really just focused on things that affected people’s everyday lives.” That approach could be instructive for candidates around the country, in November and beyond. Sarasota Next Gen Democrats and their allies built a movement that was “not right v left, not parents v students, not students v teachers”, Cole said. “We were able to organize as a community coalition of people who were sick and tired of political games being played with our students and our education, and want a better change for the future.” That future includes continuing to campaign for Glover, who will face Republican-backed candidate Heidi Brandt in a runoff election in November. If Glover wins, he would be the first person of color ever to serve on the Sarasota county school board. He’ll also have his work cut out for him in a district reeling from book ban battles and facing funding cuts as a statewide school voucher program pulls money from public schools. “We have a big challenge coming up,” he said. “We’re coming out of a time when culture wars and personal agendas dominated the headlines, so we have a lot of work to do.” But he and the organizers behind him are optimistic – not just about Sarasota, but about the country as a whole. “If it can happen here,” Martinez said of the victories this August, “it can happen anywhere.”

title: Trump’s authoritarian mindset can’t handle dissent from his appointees
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: Defiance from the supreme court and the Federal Reserve chair in one week ... how ever will the US president cope?
body_text: “It’s not personal, Sonny. It’s strictly business,” Michael Corleone tells his brother, Sonny, in The Godfather. But for Donald Trump, it’s always personal. And he leaves this week feeling betrayed. First, the US supreme court rejected his effort to restrict mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections. “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” the president wrote on his Truth Social platform. “They are merely a shell of their original selves.” Then the Federal Reserve defied Trump by raising its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%, marking its first rate hike in three years. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, described it as “a sober decision, serious decision, responsible decision”. The president lashed out again but was careful to blame the board rather than Warsh. Trump told reporters he had spoken to the chair. “I said you might ⁠as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They’re very political.” It was an effort to rationalise a shock to the system for Trump, who instinctively assumes that anyone he appoints to high office will be eternally in his debt and automatically do his bidding. It is a view constantly reinforced by his cartoonishly loyal cabinet, from defence secretary Pete Hegseth to attorney general Todd Blanche, who was previously Trump’s personal lawyer. Blanche held a press conference in the White House Rose Garden on Tuesday and staunchly defended Trump. He was rewarded two days later when he attended a campaign rally in Gastonia, North Carolina, and heard Trump say of him: “He’ll go down as the greatest attorney general in the history of our country.” But the supreme court is a different matter. Its conservative majority includes three justices appointed by Trump during his first term. It has certainly given him plenty of wins in emergency appeals during his second term, lifting lower court orders that had blocked his crackdown on immigration, ban on transgender people serving in the military and dismantling of the education department. Perhaps that is why the defeats rankle and, to him, appear inexplicable. The justices struck down his far-reaching tariffs on nearly every other country and his restrictions on birthright citizenship while blocking his attempt to immediately fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook. Last week, the court refused to allow Missouri to use new elections maps redrawn at Trump’s urging to help Republicans gain an extra seat in the House of Representatives. Then came this week’s knockback of his administration’s planned restrictions on mail-in voting, which Trump has long condemned as fraudulent while continuing to vote by mail himself. Of the nine-member court, only justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented. For the authoritarian mindset, this does not compute. Trump has become accustomed to snuffing out the first sparks of dissent among Republicans in Congress before the flames of rebellion can spread. He has taken a scythe to government departments and entities such as the Kennedy Center, which he is now threatening to demolish. But not even he can control his own appointments when they serve in institutions protected by America’s system of checks and balances. The irony is that they might be saving Trump from his own worst impulses. The Fed’s intervention, for example, is aimed at curbing the rising prices that are hurting Trump politically. Warsh explained: “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long.” It may only be a matter of time before Warsh’s honeymoon period ends and he feels the president’s wrath. But the Fed chair may also be aware that time is be on his side: every day brings Trump closer to the point at which Republicans begin looking beyond him to 2028. Last weekend, Mike Johnson, the House speaker, said only that Congress will “debate and discuss” Trump’s promise to give Americans $5,000 if Republicans retain control. On Thursday Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican congresswoman from Florida, forcefully criticised the president’s deportation agenda in a campaign ad. Larry Jacobs, director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, says: “We’re starting to see institutions like the supreme court and the Republicans in the Senate more consistently resisting him. This is the beginning of the lame duck session for Trump. This is the entry point for where it’s going to be: a sour grapes moment in Trump’s political career.”

title: Trump administration sued over threat to deploy federal law enforcement at voting sites
author: Ariana Baio
summary: Civil rights groups say plan will make people ‘afraid to vote’ and violates the Voting Rights Act
body_text: A coalition of civil rights groups filed a lawsuit against Trump administration officials on Friday, seeking to stop them from threatening to deploy federal law enforcement officers to polling stations in the US midterm elections. The suit, led by the NAACP, alleges that by threatening to deploy law enforcement to survey elections and initiating new voter roll oversight, the Trump administration has violated a section of the Voting Rights Act which prohibits voter intimidation. “The result is predictable: voters across the country – particularly Black, Latino, and Asian voters, naturalized citizens and members of mixed-status families – are afraid to vote, help others vote and participate in civic life,” the plaintiffs wrote in the complaint. Plaintiffs cited other examples of voter intimidation, such as Donald Trump giving a primetime address to exaggerate claims of noncitizen voting, the administration’s sweeping immigration enforcement operations in communities of color, and the president’s efforts to create a national voter eligibility list. Friday’s lawsuit is the latest attempt by groups to stop Trump from asserting more control over US elections as the country heads into what is expected to be a competitive midterm in November. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said “those who are here legally and not breaking other laws have nothing to fear” and denied that ICE was planning operations targeting polling locations. “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action,” the spokesperson added. DHS denied allegations of law enforcement engaging in racial profiling, calling the accusations “categorically FALSE” and insisting that targets of immigration enforcement were whether a person was in the US illegally, not by skin color, race or ethnicity. The FBI declined to comment for this story. ICE referred the Guardian to DHS. A White House official pointed to the administration’s past remarks denying any plan to deploy ICE agents to polls in November. Karoline Leavitt, the former White House press secretary, told reporters in February it was “not something I’ve ever heard the president consider”. Kiersten Pels, a justice department spokesperson, said in a statement: “The DOJ has never said it would send federal law enforcement to polling locations. Any suggestion otherwise is fearmongering.” Federal law states that no armed federal officers or members of the armed forces may be placed at a location where an election is being held. So far, the administration has not sent any armed officers or military members to polling locations. But recent mixed-messaging from top administration officials has raised concerns among election integrity advocates. In May, Trump did not rule out the possibility of sending the National Guard or ICE officers to polling locations. Kash Patel, the FBI director, told lawmakers this week that the FBI “will not shy away” from its efforts to ensure elections are safe and honest when asked whether he planned to send FBI agents the polls. “If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation, we will, otherwise we won’t,” he added, noting that “we’re going to house our agents and intel analysts in our field offices”. Earlier this month, Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, told reporters ICE would not be at polling locations to patrol but could be present if there was a threat or if they were serving a warrant to someone. “As a nation, we have no need for armed presence at polling locations – our elections are safe and transparent, which has been the hallmark of our democracy,” said Kristen Clarke, general counsel at the NAACP, in a statement after the lawsuit was filed. “Turning the fundamental right of exercising our vote into a high-stakes encounter with the militarized strong arm of the current administration isn’t protection and it isn’t oversight; it’s disenfranchisement, period,” Clarke added. Friday’s lawsuit is at least the second of its kind. Last week a coalition of groups, led by the League of United Latin American Citizens, also sued the administration seeking to stop it from deploying ICE officers to polling locations.

title: Latvia’s president warns that Europe is not up to date with drone and aerial warfare in Ukraine
author: Andrew Roth in Washington
summary: Edgars Rinkēvičs says drone warfare in Ukraine is moving at ‘lightning speed’ and efforts to prepare for an aerial war could be obsolete by next year
body_text: Latvia’s president has warned that Europe is not keeping up with developments of drone and aerial warfare in Ukraine and that most countries in Nato could not repulse an attack by Russian missiles if the conflict expands. The remarks came during a Guardian interview in Washington DC in which Edgars Rinkēvičs said that the technological developments in drone warfare in Ukraine are moving at “lightning speed” and that current efforts to prepare for an aerial war could be obsolete by the middle of next year. “What we see is that air defence, drone defence, anti-ballistic defence has serious problems,” he said. “And let’s be frank. Ukraine has it. The whole of Europe and Nato has it. “Because if Russia decides to use a couple of missiles in that territory, I think that would be a serious challenge today for many countries to cope with that,” he added. Ukraine and European allies are now facing a delay in supplies of crucial Patriot and other air-defence missiles. The US has expended nearly two-thirds of its stocks of critical interceptors in the war in Iran, according to analysis of a Congressional Budget Office assessment, and it could take at least five years to replenish stocks. The US has considered outsourcing Patriot production to Ukraine and Europe but so far an agreement has not been made. “It’s up to the United States government, it’s up to the company,” Rinkēvičs said, noting that discussions were continuing and acknowledging the difficulties of some technical issues with licensing. “We have some capacities in Europe, but let’s face it: Patriots are still one of the best, if not the best, to tackle this.” At next week’s UN general assembly in New York City, Donald Trump is expected to hold meetings with senior European leaders, and as Nato allies have stepped up their warnings about the risk of Russia escalating the war in Ukraine. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned in a speech on Thursday that Russia could launch drone or missile strikes against Nato countries supporting Ukraine in the coming months in an effort to test the alliance’s commitment to collective defence under article 5 of its charter. Tusk said that Russia would seek to “weaken Nato’s integrity” and show that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”, adding that Russia would seek to play off the incidents as accidents. Asked about Tusk’s concerns about Russia attacking Ukrainian allies in Europe, Trump said: “I think they already have attacked Ukrainian allies. They’ve been attacking Ukrainian allies for approximately five years.” He then pivoted to throw his support behind the Polish president, Karol Nawrocki, who is supported by the conservative Law and Justice party, saying: “You have a great president, he was a big Trump fan … he’s doing a fantastic job, and he’s got it under control.” The Baltic nations, which are on Europe’s eastern flank, have tempered their warnings, saying that there was no indication that Moscow sought to launch a conventional war to retake territory that it once held under the Soviet Union. But Russia would increase mobilisation in the coming months after local elections, Rinkēvičs said, then use the winter to “push” in Ukraine, and also to “do whatever it takes to dissuade nations that are supportive of Ukraine to continue”. Acts of sabotage, cyber-attacks and drone and missile incidents all indicated Russia testing European resolve to support Ukraine, he said. “I would rule out a conventional military incursion but we should be very vigilant when it comes to all kinds of other possibilities,” he said. A Nato jet shot down a Russian drone over Lithuania on Tuesday. Poland scrambled fighter jets and closed Lublin and Rzeszów-Jasionka airports on Thursday due to a Russian strike on western Ukraine. Rinkēvičs also expressed concern about whether European allies were on track to hit a goal of spending 5% of GDP on defence that has become a White House benchmark for the Trump administration’s continued support for Nato. He also said that discussions over Europe bearing a great burden for its own defence were growing “more constructive”, but added that when it comes to “real capabilities … you need time”. “Our message is also to do that, we need time,” he said. “It cannot happen in a month, or in a year.” • This article was amended on 22 September 2026. An earlier version said the Baltic nations were on Russia’s eastern flank; this should have said on Europe’s eastern flank.

title: Trump signs bill imposing sanctions on Russia and giving him more power to levy tariffs
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act signed into law two days after House passed it in bipartisan vote
body_text: Donald Trump on Friday signed legislation enabling sweeping sanctions on Russia aimed at pressing it into ending its war with Ukraine, and also giving him the power to impose additional tariffs on countries breaking the embargo. The US president signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law two days after it passed the House of Representatives in a bipartisan 262-159 vote, amid concerns the legislation gives him too much power. The Trump administration has previously been doubtful about imposing additional sanctions on Moscow but changed its stance after repeated attempts to end its four and a half year war against Ukraine have stalled. The bill named after the hawkish Republican senator, Lindsey Graham, who died in July, is aimed at depleting Russia’s ability to continue funding the war by targeting its natural gas and oil revenues, as well as countries that continue to buy Russian energy. The legislation imposes new sanctions on Russian political and military officials and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. In addition, it targets Russia’s fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite existing sanctions on its energy exports. But it also gives Trump wide leeway over its implementation, including which countries could face tariffs, and which tariff rates could be imposed. It also gives the president sweeping discretion over whether sanctions provisions can be waived against certain countries. Controversially, it allows Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian energy, including China, and on other countries that help Moscow to evade sanctions. The bill’s broad provisions were criticized by many Democrats, who complained that it gave Trump excessive authority to resort to tariffs, which he has already imposed on multiple countries despite a US supreme court ruling prohibiting him from doing so under the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

title: Trump bans CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House
author: Lucy Campbell and Robert Mackey
summary: President has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major news media since start of second term
body_text: In his latest attack on the US constitution’s first amendment and the press, Donald Trump abruptly announced that he is banning outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House over their coverage. In a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday, the US president said he was expelling the news outlets “effective immediately” over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and threatened that bans for others outlets could follow. He went on: “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.” Trump defended the ban at an Oval Office event to promote his administration’s healthcare policies. “I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart. I get it from a little bit from Fox,” Trump told reporters, referring to friendly media outlets. “But what I do ask is just a semblance of truth.” Reminded by one reporter that every president takes an oath to uphold the constitution, including the first amendment right to free speech, Trump said: “You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news.” He added: “I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day. I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they’re going to write false stories all the time.” Towards the end of a chaotic news conference, when a reporter asked Trump to explain how his ban on the three outlets would work, the president expressed confusion. “When you say ‘the ban’, which ban? Do you know how many bans I’m involved in?” Trump asked, seeming confused. After another correspondent rephrased the question, asking, “What do you envision the bans would look like on the media outlets?” Trump said: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?” On Friday, the Washington Post reported that more American service members have died in the war on Iran than the Pentagon has publicly disclosed; CNN revealed that an “entirely false” intelligence report about a Chinese ship in the Middle East generated with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) had “almost started a war”; while a Politico report uncovered a Hill investigation after sensitive F-35 fighter jet technology unexpectedly made its way to Hong Kong, possibly giving China access to them. Trump said his decision to ban the three outlets was unrelated to the stories. “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years,” he said, before threatening more media prohibitions could follow. “There may be others to join them,” Trump said. In a statement, a spokesperson for CNN said the network “stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting”. “We have a right under the US constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally protected right,” the spokesperson said. Politico said its reporters would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones”. “We will vigorously defend our first amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” it added. Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA), said the organization “stands in defense” of the banned reporters “who are being singled out for doing their jobs”. “This is about more than the rights of journalists,” Henrich wrote in a statement. “It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.” A spokesperson for MS Now declined to comment. Trump’s move drew swift condemnation from Democrats and free speech groups. Chris Coons, a Democratic senator, wrote on social media: “Trump is once again trying to use the power of the presidency to punish a free press, now banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House. That is the behavior of an authoritarian, and we must defend the press’ right to hold those in power accountable.” The White House press pool is a “public forum” under the first amendment, so the president cannot expel journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints, said Jameel Jaffer, executive director at Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University. To do so, would be “doubly unconstitutional”. “The first amendment prohibits the president from punishing journalists because he doesn’t like their coverage, just as it prohibits him from punishing universities because he doesn’t like the courses they offer, or from punishing law firms because he doesn’t like the clients they represent,” said Jaffer. “With so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you’d think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now.” Similarly, Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, said: “It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the first amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the ‘People’s House’ for criticizing the government. It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move. “The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him. The press keeps exposing his corruption and his failures. These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public.” Since returning to office, Trump has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major traditional news media at the White House, including the Associated Press, which was banned from press pool events in the Oval Office and on Air Force One after it continued to use Gulf of Mexico instead of Gulf of America in its coverage. The AP sued, and that case remains in litigation. Trump’s White House also seized control over the organization of the presidential press pool, a rotation that determines which news organizations and reporters are allowed to follow – and question – the president in places such as the Oval Office and aboard Air Force One. The WHCA, an independent association made up of members of the media, traditionally coordinated rotating pool coverage of more than a dozen journalists allowed access to the president in smaller settings. The Pentagon also attempted to introduce a new press policy to restrict the ability of journalists to gather and report on sensitive information, which culminated in a mass walkout of news media outlets who refused to sign the pledge. A federal judge later ruled the policy was unconstitutional. The president has also launched high-profile legal battles with major outlets including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, CNN, ABC News and the BBC.

title: Trump administration pushes on with construction of controversial Big Bend border wall
author: Roque Planas
summary: Customs and Border Protection faces bipartisan backlash from locals for 30ft border wall through west Texas
body_text: The Trump administration is pressing forward with construction on the controversial border wall in the Big Bend region of west Texas, even as Customs and Border Protection (CBP) faces furious backlash from local leaders and landowners for its fast-moving plans. Construction began this week in Hudspeth county, which lies just east of the city of El Paso. CBP has been pressing landowners there to grant permission to allow the agency to erect a 30ft steel bollard border wall in that area, offering them signing bonuses as an incentive to avoid eminent domain disputes. CBP did not announce the construction ahead of time, but a spokesperson confirmed by email that installation of the first “panels” in Hudspeth county started on 15 September. The news was first reported by the Associated Press. A panel refers to a section of steel bollard fencing. Images of the construction obtained by the No Big Bend Wall coalition show a towering fence standing in isolation, that anyone could easily walk around on either side. Isolated fencing is likely to remain the norm in much of the area if construction proceeds, said Clara Bensen, the communications director for No Big Bend Wall. Her group estimates that some 400 landowners hold title to properties with Rio Grande frontage where CBP is trying to obtain rights to construct more wall. More than half of those landowners, however, have joined the coalition, and aim to dispute the federal government’s assertion of eminent domain. Those disputes have left the federal government with an uneven patchwork of permissions, leaving CBP unable for the moment to complete work on a contiguous wall. “It’s not about logic,” Bensen said. “They’re moving forward even if the plan is not fully baked, then trying to do busy work because they don’t have the land they need yet.” “They’re just grasping on to whatever little plots of land they’ve managed to get so far,” she added. Republicans in Congress added a whopping $46.5bn for border wall expansion into the so-called “big, beautiful” spending bill last year. Armed with that massive war chest, CBP has barreled forward with unpopular plans to expand its so-called “smart wall” – a mix of 30ft fencing, vehicle barriers, patrol roads and detection sensors – into the remote Big Bend region. The area has remained unwalled until now largely because its towering cliffs, desert geography and lack of towns and cities on the Mexican side already act as natural impediments to unlawful migration. The roughly 500-mile (800km) stretch that CBP refers to as the “Big Bend” region has historically accounted for less than 2% of apprehensions for illegal crossings. Unauthorized crossing there has plummeted still further since Trump returned to office and imposed a major crackdown on the border. CBP’s plans for west Texas beyond Hudspeth county currently include erecting vehicle barrier and other security infrastructure in Big Bend national park, widely viewed as the state’s most beloved wilderness. The possibility of construction at the park, however, has sparked major protests and drawn increasingly bipartisan criticism from Texas lawmakers. Rodney Scott, the CBP commissioner, temporarily paused construction last month, after images of bulldozers clearly brush for new road construction sparked a furious backlash from public land lovers across the country. Bob Krumenaker, a former Big Bend national park superintendent who now chairs an advocacy group called Keep Big Bend Wild, said he and other supporters planned to travel to Washington DC next week to urge lawmakers to shield the park from damage and the unpopular border security infrastructure. “I’m very optimistic that there is a lot of support for Big Bend,” Krumenaker said. “This is a nonpartisan issue.” But while the park has drawn the most attention, CBP’s plans to expand its smart wall would have massive and sprawling effects across the Big Bend region. Private landowners are concerned about the eyesore tanking their property values, obstructing their access to the river, or disrupting their grazing operations. The border barrier expansion would also mar Big Bend Ranch state park, Black Gap wildlife management area and Amistad national recreation area. Blasting from construction threatens to damage or destroy dozens of millennia-old rock art murals that dot the river valley. “It’s all connected,” Bensen said. “It’s all part of the river.”

title: US and Denmark reach security deal after Trump’s threats to take over Greenland
author: Robert Mackey
summary: The agreement would allow the US to expand its military presence, while Denmark and Greenland say it preserves their sovereignty and right to self-determination
body_text: Donald Trump announced on Friday that the US had struck an Arctic security pact with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, after threatening for much of his second term to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory by force. The full scope of the deal Trump described as “very important, historic, and special” was not immediately clear. But soon after his announcement in a post on Truth Social, the leaders of Denmark and Greenland issued statements indicating the deal would be signed by the three governments on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York City next week. In his social media post, Trump cast the deal as a personal triumph, claiming that the agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns”. “We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” Trump added. The US already has a presence on the island, and the right to expand bases, through Nato. The announcement comes just weeks before November’s midterms, giving the president a foreign policy accomplishment he can tout to voters as the deeply unpopular war with Iran becomes an increasing political liability for Republicans vying to hang on to their narrow majorities in the House and Senate. The US has long had a military presence in Greenland – a self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, a fellow Nato member – and has had a military base at Pituffik since the cold war. In his post, Trump said that the agreement means “no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval”. Statements from Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, and the leader of Greenland’s government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, posted online late on Friday, emphasized that the agreement would fall far short of Trump’s previously stated desire for “the acquisition of Greenland by the United States”. Frederiksen said that what she called “a great agreement” for all three parties “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination”. Nielsen said it was “joyous” that the agreement “ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western Alliance”, suggesting that the deal might possibly just reiterate the existing US rights through Nato to use the island as a security base. Once agreed to, the pact would need to go through parliamentary procedures to be enacted, the Danish and Greenlandic statements said. Earlier in his term, Trump argued that the US needed control of Greenland for “economic security”, and has described ownership and control of the territory as an “absolute necessity”. The island had long been on the president’s radar as a target for purchase, and during his first term, in 2019, Trump confirmed reports he had been urging aides to find out how the US could buy Greenland, describing any sale as “essentially a large real estate deal”. Trump’s claims deepened divisions among the western alliance, with the Danish government repeatedly stating that Greenland was “not for sale”. When concerns over Trump’s annexation threats reached a fever pitch last year, the Guardian reported that the Danish government set up a “night watch” in the foreign ministry to monitor the US president’s pronouncements while Copenhagen sleeps. At a Nato summit in Ankara earlier this year, Trump renewed his bid for the US to acquire Greenland. He threatened to pull all American armed forces out of Europe after the continent repeatedly pushed back. Strategically positioned between the US and Russia, Greenland is viewed as increasingly important for defense and is emerging as a geopolitical battleground as Arctic ice melts. The US vice-president, JD Vance, and his wife Usha, received a frosty reception when they visited US troops stationed at Pituffik space base last year, amid the White House’s aggressive campaign to take the mineral-rich island with roughly 56,000 inhabitants. Polling has found Greenlanders strongly oppose any effort to make Greenland a part of the US. Even so, a Trump administration insider dropped a hint online that the US side intends to present whatever the deal actually is as an American triumph. Katie Miller, a former White House aide whose husband is Trump’s closest adviser, posted a map of Greenland covered in the American flag, with the caption: “ITS [sic] HAPPENING”. Miranda Bryant contributed reporting

title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy reaches out to eastern Europe for new trade and security partnership
author: Guardian staff and agencies
summary: The leaders of Poland, Serbia and Romania were among those at the inaugural Carpathian 8 Summit in western Ukraine. What we know on day 1,669
body_text: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy launched on Friday a ⁠new trade and security scheme with a group of eight countries from the Carpathian region of central and eastern Europe. In a comment summing up the outcome of the meeting, Zelenskyy said on ⁠Telegram that 50 agreements had been signed for a total value of more than €1bn ($1.15bn). ‌He gave few details, but ‌said more than half the accords dealt with energy, particularly solar and ‌wind power, with the aim of energy independence from Russia. The group includes Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary, and the European Union. At the meeting in western Ukraine, Zelenskyy thanked regional allies for keeping trade and transport ⁠links open following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Polish ‌prime minister Donald Tusk, Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vucic and Romania’s President Nicusor Dan attended the inaugural event, which is expected to last until Sunday. “This marks the start of a movement that should bring our countries even closer together and create another strong framework for cooperation at the EU level,” Zelenskyy said. Donald Trump on Friday signed legislation enabling sweeping sanctions on Russia aimed at pressing it to end its war with Ukraine, and also giving him the power to impose additional tariffs on countries breaking the embargo. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, named after the hawkish Republican senator, Lindsey Graham, who died in July, aims to deplete Russia’s ability to continue funding the war by targeting its natural gas and oil revenues, as well as countries that continue to buy Russian energy. The legislation imposes new sanctions on Russian political and military officials and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma against a backdrop of intensifying conflict between Russia and Ukraine. There is little doubt that Vladimir Putin’s United Russia will extend its grip on parliament thanks to a tightly controlled vote. The three-day vote began Friday, with results expected after polls close on Sunday. It is the first Duma election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Swarms of Ukrainian drones have struck oil refineries, factories and logistics hubs across Russia over the summer, while polling has pointed to growing anxiety about the course of the fighting and what may still lie ahead. Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Friday that Ukraine was deliberately hindering talks aimed at ending the war and accused Kyiv ⁠of interfering in Russia’s parliamentary ⁠election. Putin, in comments to Russia’s Military-Industrial commission, also reasserted Moscow’s main defence aim of relying on its “nuclear triad” of weapons and said Moscow needed to improve its anti-missile defences. In comments reported by Russian news agencies, Putin said Ukraine had “long degenerated into a dictatorship,” referring to the country not holding a new presidential election ⁠despite the expiry of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s mandate. Latvia’s president has warned that Europe is not keeping up with developments of drone and aerial warfare in Ukraine and that most countries in Nato could not repulse an attack by Russian missiles if the conflict expands. The remarks came during a Guardian interview in Washington DC in which Edgars Rinkēvičs said that the technological developments in drone warfare in Ukraine were moving at “lightning speed”. “What we see is that air defence, drone defence, anti-ballistic defence has serious problems,” he said. “Because if Russia decides to use a couple of missiles in that territory, I think that would be a serious challenge today for many countries to cope with that,” he added. A Russian ⁠glide bomb hit an apartment building in the northern Ukrainian city of Sumy on Friday, killing two people and injuring ⁠seven, leaving three of them ⁠in a serious condition. Writing on the Telegram messaging app, President Zelenskyy said ⁠emergency crews had rescued four people after the attack and said others could still be trapped under rubble. The head of Sumy city council said the two dead were city employees. Regional Governor Oleh Hryhorov said three of the seven injured were in a serious condition. Among the injured was a 13-year-old girl.
