title: As White House shields the AI gold rush, Trump family and other allies strike it rich – with few guardrails
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: It’s not clear that financial interests are driving White House policy, but they run parallel even as resistance mounts
body_text: Donald Trump’s sons, through a series of AI-linked defense and technology ventures, have picked up a $620m Pentagon loan, a Marine Corps robotics contract and an undisclosed air force drone deal in the past year. His longtime friend Michael Dell won a Pentagon contract worth nearly $9bn. And this week, as public support for artificial intelligence sinks to some of the lowest levels ever recorded, the president went to bat for the industry. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” he posted on Truth Social Monday. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers.” It was the first of many aggressively pro-AI posts he would make this week. Trump is resisting new restrictions on AI at a moment when his family and some of his closest allies have accumulated financial interests in the infrastructure and defense-technology ecosystem expanding alongside the AI boom, an overlap that has now drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, government ethics watchdogs and, by some accounts, his own senior aides. It’s not clear that financial interests are driving Trump’s policy, but the two have moved in close parallel. The administration frames its resistance chiefly as a matter of competitiveness. Trump and officials including David Sacks, who co-chairs his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, have repeatedly argued that new rules could slow US AI development when the country is racing China for dominance of the technology. Sacks said at a Politico summit on Wednesday that recent warnings from Anthropic and OpenAI about the technology’s risks amounted to political theater, manufactured by advocacy groups and the press, and said existing laws were largely sufficient. But many concerns are coming from inside the industry itself. In early September, Jacob Coxon – a researcher who spent three years working on the foundational training of AI models at both OpenAI and Anthropic – resigned and published a stark warning. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” He said colleagues privately believe the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Anthropic’s head of AI safety, Mrinank Sharma, separately resigned the same week, writing that “the world is in peril.” Those warnings coincided with a concrete demonstration of AI-enabled risk. A California cybersecurity firm disclosed this month that it had used artificial intelligence to build a self-spreading worm capable of hijacking WeChat accounts through a single unanswered call, and then automatically spreading through the victim’s contact list. The firm estimated the technology could compromise more than a billion devices within hours. Tencent, the Chinese tech giant that owns WeChat, patched the vulnerability before it was deployed and said no accounts were affected, but the firm noted that building the exploit, work it said would once have taken a larger team months, took roughly 10 days with AI assistance. Around the same time, JD Vance, speaking on a Christian podcast, described certain uses of AI as carrying “really, really weird spiritual dark energy” and said there are “things about the world” that leave him “not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us”. Polling shows how far out of step Trump’s posture is with the public, particularly once AI’s costs become tangible. A poll released on Wednesday found just 11% of Americans support an AI datacenter being built in their own community, while 65% oppose one – including 52% of Republicans – and 57% say Trump has handled the issue of AI poorly, up seven points since March. The same day, the House voted 417-3 to require datacenters to bear the costs of the electricity-grid upgrades their operations demand, underscoring how concerns about AI’s infrastructure costs have moved from polling into Congress. If the federal government did enact regulations that ultimately damaged AI profits, it’s possible some members of the Trump family would feel the pain. Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump joined the investment firm Dominari Holdings last year and helped launch American Data Centers Inc, an AI infrastructure venture in which Dominari holds a minority stake. The deal came weeks after their father unveiled an expected $20bn datacenter pledge from Emirati billionaire Hussain Sajwani, and $500 bn in planned private sector AI investment, alongside an executive order unwinding Biden-era AI safeguards. Since then, the brothers have moved from infrastructure into defense contracting, most notably through Vulcan Elements, a rare-earth magnet startup whose products are used in AI datacenters, drones and defense systems. Three months before the Pentagon announced its $620m loan to Vulcan in December – the largest the defense department’s office of strategic capital has ever issued – 1789 Capital, the venture firm where Trump Jr is a partner, quietly took a stake in the company. A ProPublica investigation found the loan request came not from Vulcan or the Pentagon but from Peter Navarro, a senior White House adviser and close friend of Trump Jr’s, and that Pentagon staff were told to move at an “unusually rapid pace”. “The call came from the White House: We have to get this done,” one person involved in the deal told the outlet. Trump Jr’s spokesman, the Pentagon and Vulcan have all said he played no role in the deal and that the company received no political favoritism. Eric Trump, separately, serves as chief strategy adviser to Foundation Future Industries, the robotics startup behind the $24m Marine Corps contract; senator Elizabeth Warren called that award “corruption in plain sight”. A third venture, the drone maker Powerus backed by both brothers and having signed a new agreement with Pakistan’s army, also holds a $90m air force contract, and has separately pitched its technology to Gulf states amid Iran’s striking of US bases across the region. Drones are widely expected to increasingly utilize AI technology in the coming years. A Washington Post analysis in July found 15 companies tied to the brothers’ investment funds have generated at least $3.2bn in direct federal business since they got involved, but SpaceX and Anduril, the latter an AI-powered defense technology firm behind Lattice account for 97% of that figure, and 10 of the 15 companies already had government business before the Trump sons invested. Excluding SpaceX and Anduril, the remaining 13 companies had received $103m in direct federal funding and nearly $1.8bn in long-term commitments after the brothers’ investments. The pattern extends beyond Trump’s family to some of his closest technology allies. Sacks’s influence over Trump’s regulatory decisions has been substantial: in May, he reportedly persuaded the president in a last-minute call to scrap a planned executive order that would have subjected AI models to extended government review, overriding the chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, who had spent months negotiating the stronger version. His own financial position has drawn scrutiny inside the administration as a result. Sacks’s venture firm holds stakes in SpaceX and a range of AI startups, along with earlier investments in Meta, Palantir and Airbnb; federal ethics rules required him to divest only some of those holdings while he served as the White House’s AI and crypto czar, a post he left in March. Some administration officials have privately looked into whether Sacks could personally benefit from blocking new AI rules, the Wall Street Journal reported. The outlet reported that Musk pushed in the same direction, joining Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang last month in personally lobbying Trump against a proposed industry-funded AI oversight body, helping shelve the plan. Dell, a member of Trump’s science and technology advisory council and a longtime friend and donor to the president, saw his company win the nearly $9bn Pentagon contract in May, prompting ethics watchdogs to question whether his advisory role created an unaddressed conflict. The technology industry is not uniformly aligned behind Trump. Federal filings on OpenSecrets show the broader communications and electronics sector still sends roughly two-thirds of its political money to Democratic candidates and committees this cycle. Trump’s support among industry figures has come instead from a narrower group: OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman have given tens of millions of dollars to a pro-Trump super Pac and Trump’s inaugural committee, though have also donated to Democrats in the past. The Pentagon’s own account of its safeguards makes no distinction between a routine contractor and a company whose investors include the president’s son, which is a gap Democratic lawmakers asked the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate last month. Next week, Trump is set to host the leaders of the country’s leading AI companies at the White House, a meeting arranged with the House speaker, Mike Johnson, that will coincide with a visit from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping. In the meantime, the investments continue.

title: Leftists make waves and Trump flexes muscles: US primary season takeaways
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Candidates have been selected for November’s midterms – have Republicans and Democrats made the right choices?
body_text: Primary season has officially concluded in the United States, with Democrats leading the polls among voters amid widespread economic anxieties, a war with Iran and Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda continuing into the end of the year. Democratic and Republican voters have selected contenders for key races in the 3 November midterms that will decide the balance of power in Congress, and the future of both parties. Democrats have been rocked by the primary victories of leftwing candidates. Republicans have doubled down on backing the president’s policies, despite his low approval ratings. And both parties are navigating the fallout from a series of scandals that have forced some candidates from the race, while others decided to press on. Here’s a look back at what we learned over the past six months of primaries: Lawmakers fled the House in droves, ensuring a reshaped Congress in 2027 Viewed as the chamber of Congress most likely to change hands in the midterms, the House saw significant turnover this cycle, with 74 members departing, the most since 1992, according to a tally from the Pew Research Center. Some outgoing lawmakers retired, while others ran for other offices, but generally didn’t fare particularly well – only 13 made it through primaries for governorships, the Senate or other offices, with the remaining 15 were rejected by voters. Among representatives who sought re-election to the House, 11 lost their primaries, the second-highest total since 2022. Seven of these were Democrats, two of whom – Julie Johnson and Al Green – were unseated by other Democratic incumbents after they were redistricted by Texas Republicans to compete against each other. Leftists, especially Democratic socialists, rocked the party ... Of the five House Democrats who lost their primaries to newcomers, four were booted by leftist candidates with ties to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). In New York, Congressional Hispanic Caucus chair Adriano Espaillat fell to DSA member Darializa Avila Chevalier and congressman Dan Goldman was ousted by former DSA member Brad Lander, while DSA member Claire Valdez also won the primary to replace retiring congresswoman Nydia Velazquez. In Colorado, DSA member Melat Kiros unseated 30-year incumbent Diana DeGette, and in Michigan, the DSA-endorsed Donovan McKinney beat congressman Shri Thanedar. All are expected to win their seats in the midterms, as their districts are heavily Democratic. “A lot of people were hoping that it was a blip, like oh well, this is a special case,” said the DSA-endorsed Chris Rabb, who is expected to be elected to the House after winning the Democratic primary in deep-blue Philadelphia. “We showed them a different way. So I think all of those things make this election cycle uniquely powerful in ways that most people could not anticipate, myself included.” The fifth sitting Democrat to lose renomination was John Larson. His challenger, Luke Bronin, 47, successfully argued to voters that it was time to replace the 78-year-old incumbent with a younger candidate. ... but centrists are on the frontlines The battle for the House will not be decided in safe blue seats, but rather the 21 districts that the Cook Political Report considers to be toss-ups. In those districts, the nominees are almost entirely backed by the Pacs of either the center-left New Democrat Coalition, or the moderate Blue Dogs, which centrists say bolsters their arguments that their policies most closely align with the voters who determine control of Congress. “If Democrats are to win the majority in the House and/or the Senate, it will be because moderates flip seats from red to blue,” said Matt Bennett, an executive vice-president at the thinktank Third Way. There are exceptions to the trend: former DSA member William Lawrence won the Democratic nomination to take on Republican incumbent Tom Barrett in a swing Michigan congressional district, while in that state’s Democratic Senate primary, Abdul El-Sayed beat congresswoman Haley Stevens, who was backed by much of the party establishment. Anti-incumbent sentiment among Democrats had its limits The DSA’s wins reintensified debate among Democrats over the political direction of the party, but the left-wing movement’s momentum was not absolute. In Missouri, DSA member Cori Bush failed in her primary challenge against congressman Wesley Bell, who had unseated her two years ago. Hawaii congressman Ed Case fended off state senator Jarrett Keohokalole, who had challenged him from the left and argued it was time for generational change. In Massachusetts, congressman Seth Moulton made a similar argument about the Democratic senator Ed Markey, though in this case Moulton was the moderate candidate and Markey the progressive. It didn’t work, and Markey won renomination, as did other congressional Democrats in the state who faced primary challenges. In Colorado, state senator Julie Gonzales mounted an unsuccessful left-wing challenge to Democratic US senator John Hickenlooper, while in Washington, moderate congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez again won the Democratic nomination in her right-leaning district against several challengers. Trump flexed his muscles, with much success As always, Trump sought to play kingmaker in the primaries, endorsing candidates who hewed to his agenda and seeking revenge against those who had broken with him, however small their transgressions. Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie lost his primary after the president campaigned against him, and the president’s decision not to make an endorsement in Texas representative Dan Crenshaw’s primary was likely a factor in him losing the Republican nomination. Trump successfully ousted Louisiana senator Bill Cassidy – who voted to convict him after January 6 – as well as Texas senator John Cornyn, for comparatively murkier reasons. The president may rue the latter decision – recent polls have shown the Democratic nominee James Talarico with a slight lead over Trump’s preferred candidate, Ken Paxton. All told, it was a successful primary for Trump – an analysis of his record by USA Today shows nearly 97% of the candidates he backed in congressional and gubernatorial races won their primaries. There were a handful of misses – five gubernatorial candidates won their primaries without Trump’s endorsement, along with four House aspirants. Aipac spent, for better or worse The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) waded into some primaries at a particularly fraught moment for supporters of the Middle Eastern ally. Surveys show that some Republicans and many Democrats now hold negative views of Israel, amid accusations it carried out a genocide in Gaza, and many of the left-wing candidates who ousted Democratic House incumbents did so after attacking their ties to Aipac. Through its United Democracy Project Super Pac, the group nonetheless scored some wins, including Ed Gallrein’s defeat of Massie in Kentucky, Adrian Boafo’s victory in the Maryland primary to replace veteran House Democrat Steny Hoyer, and Bell’s defense against Bush’s primary challenge in Missouri. But the group failed to keep El-Sayed from defeating Rogers in the Michigan Senate primary, despite spending more than $30m in that race, or prevent progressive Aisha Wahab from winning a special election to replace former congressman Eric Swalwell in California. Some candidates fell to scandals, others pressed on Several candidates who ran for office were derailed by scandals. Graham Platner won the Democratic primary to take on veteran Republican senator Susan Collins in Maine, but dropped out amid accusations of sexual assault and misconduct. Swalwell ran for governor of California but exited that race and resigned his US House seat after he, too, was accused of sexual assault. North Carolina Republican congressman Chuck Edwards won his primary but ended his re-election campaign after the House ethics committee said he likely broke rules against sexual harassment, but Republican congressman Max Miller remains in the race amid accusations of domestic violence against his ex-wife. In other instances, the GOP used the primaries to dispose of problematic lawmakers in their ranks. Andy Ogles, a congressman with a history of homophobic and Islamophobic statements, lost in Tennessee after the Republican governor endorsed his challenger and a Super Pac backed by the renewable energy industry spent against him, and scandal-plagued congressman Cory Mills was defeated after other Florida Republicans endorsed his challenger.

title: ‘Do you have to be dead?’: US coalminers plead for benefits as black-lung disease cases surge
author: Michael Sainato
summary: Trump says he digs coal – but pneumoconiosis cases are at a 50-year high, and sick miners are mired in benefit delays
body_text: For 38 years, Josh Armes worked as a coal miner in West Virginia and Virginia. After retirement, Armes, 74, of Grundy, Virginia, was diagnosed with black lung disease, medically known as coal workers’ pneumoconiosis (CWP), caused by breathing in coal dust over long periods, which irreversibly damages the lungs. Armes has required an oxygen tank to breathe for the past four years or so, along with regular doctor visits and an albuterol inhaler to help when he has trouble breathing. Even with the supplemental oxygen, he’s severely limited in what he can physically do. In 2014, Armes received notice that the federal black lung benefits he had been receiving for more than three years were being appealed against by a coal operator. For the last 12 years, he and his family have been in an appeals process limbo, trying to regain their benefits while Armes’s condition progresses. The federal black lung program was created in 1969 to provide coal miners disabled by black lung with monetary compensation and medical benefits. But the Armes family is just one of many who have struggled with appeals and long delays in obtaining federal black lung benefits. Those delays come as the Trump administration moves to boost the coal industry and as cases of black lung are surging – reaching a nearly 50-year high, according to data published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine last month. According to a May report by the government accountability office (GAO), 7,709 miner beneficiaries were receiving black lung benefits in 2024. The report was requested in 2023 by Democratic senators Mark Warner, John Hickenlooper, Tim Kaine, and John Fetterman, who have also introduced legislation to improve the black-lung benefits system. In the fiscal year 2025, about 22,500 beneficiaries, including dependents, survivors, and miners, were receiving black lung benefits. Between 2013 to 2024, 40% of approved claims by the Department of Labor were disputed, generally by coal operators. The May report said miners have expressed problems with obtaining black-lung benefits. It said miners have been forced to wait several years for their claims to be approved, and raised issues with coal operators filing appeals. “I can’t figure out one thing. They sent me a paper that said I got first- and second-stage black lung. That ought to be enough, or do you have to be dead?” Armes said. His daughter, Crystal Armes, said obtaining the black lung benefits is an arduous process, involving paying out of pocket for medical tests and finding a lawyer to take on the case. She also argued that the law should change so that coal companies shouldn’t be able to appeal after benefits are awarded. “The burden of proof lies on the coalminer to prove that he has black lung,” she said. “We have appealed it and appealed it and appealed it. Still appealing it. He [Josh] does have black lung. Hopefully, soon we will be awarded the black lung benefits again. But I’m not holding my breath on that one.” The GAO report said: “Miners in all six groups expressed their belief that mine operators were either ‘waiting for them to die’ or ‘waiting for them to give up’ so they could avoid paying benefit.” It noted between January 2013 to mid-August 2024, 390 beneficiaries whose claims were initially approved had their claims denied after appeal, leaving them responsible for paying back the benefits. According to the report, the median length of an appealed claim was three years or more. Among 53,000 closed claims between January 2013 and August 2024, 11 claims took longer than 10 years to close. The report did not state how many open cases have surpassed 10 years. The Armes family are still waiting for their black lungs benefits appeals process to complete, while not receiving benefits. “When you’re awarded it, they can appeal it, get a different judge, and it’s stripped away from you, which I find absolutely insane,” added Crystal Armes. “They fight you at every single step of the way. They’ll send you from one doctor to another doctor to go do another test and another test. You got to go to this doctor. You got to travel over here, and it’s very costly. And some people don’t have the means to be able to do that. I don’t feel like the process should be this difficult.” According to data published in August in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, researchers at the National Institute for Safety and Occupational Health (Niosh) found 32.5% of veteran underground coalminers in central Appalachia are suffering from black lung disease, a rate unseen since 1978. Between 2020 and 2023, more than 1,700 coal miners in the US died from black lung disease. The rise in cases has been attributed to silica dust that is more common in the coal seams being mined today. In April, E&E Greenwire reported that the Trump administration’s Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) would “indefinitely delay” a federal silica dust rule, “pending judicial review” – but any judicial review is on pause due to the agency requesting an abeyance on court action. Rebecca Shelton, Director of Policy for Appalachian Citizens’ Law Center, in a statement on the agency’s freeze on enforcing the rule, said: “If the Trump administration actually cared about protecting coal miners from black lung, we’d have a strong silica rule in place right now. Instead, they are hiding behind a ridiculous legal process to delay action while miners get sick and die.” The United Mine Workers of America has pushed to unfreeze the federal silica dust rule, which would mandate engineering and ventilation controls to protect miners on the job. It was passed in April 2024, but funding for the rule was blocked by Republicans in Congress in June 2024, and the MSHA under the Trump administration indicated to the union it has no plans to enforce the rule. “Every day [that] federal regulators drag their feet and sit on this rule, another working father, mother, husband, wife, sister or brother contracts an incurable, fatal disease,” Brian Sanson, president of UMWA International, in a statement. “Someone’s life is forever changed. A company’s profit margin cannot take precedence over a miner’s right to draw a breath.” Meanwhile, miners already dealing with black lung disease are still facing difficulties in trying to obtain federal benefits. “These people, like my dad, he gave his life to mining to support his family, and now you know we’ve been fighting this fight for over 10 plus years now. Everyone should be outraged by this,” added Crystal Armes. “We’re hardworking, everyday Americans who go to work every day, pay our taxes, try to do the right thing, and then, we can’t get what was promised us.” The White House deferred comment to the Department of Labor. Niosh did not respond to multiple requests for comment. A spokesperson for the MSHA at the Department of Labor said in an email: “Until pending litigation and limited rulemaking on respirable crystalline silica are resolved, MSHA continues to vigorously enforce the permissible exposure limit of 100 micrograms per cubic meter.”

title: Trump claims triumphal arch will serve as a ‘top grade military complex’ to store weapons
author: Ed Pilkington in New York
summary: US president on Truth Social claims his new plan for the 250ft arch comes at the ‘strong request’ of the US military
body_text: Donald Trump is proffering a new argument for building his triumphal arch in Washington DC: it will be converted into a “top grade military complex” replete with drone and ammunition storage space and customised sniper facilities on the roof and plaza. In a post on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning, Trump claimed that his new plan came at the “strong request” of the US military. He said the 250ft structure would be able to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage”. With the hyperbole that is his trademark, the president added that the arch would be unique. “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the world.” The triumphal arch project has come under widespread criticism for its potential impact on the historic area of downtown Washington DC. Its intended location in a circle close to the Memorial Bridge could interrupt the sight lines of several of the most resonant structures, including the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery which would flank it. The siting of the structure close to the Ronald Reagan Washington international airport has also prompted questions from Democratic Congress members. Last week, the National Park Service warned that it could have “adverse effects to historic properties” and called for additional planning before the building work went ahead. The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has initiated which he claims are necessary to elevate the visual greatness of the US capital but which critics have slammed as thinly veiled efforts to promote his own legacy. They include the creation of a White House ballroom, the refurbishment of the reflecting pool at the Lincoln Memorial and the renovation of the Kennedy Center. All those projects have run into big problems, ranging from criticism of their aesthetic qualities, structural difficulties and legal challenges. In the case of the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, one of the world’s pre-eminent cultural venues, Trump has hinted that he might demolish the property altogether in a fit of pique at the courts blocking the addition of his name to its title. The White House ballroom, which Trump has also been calling a “military complex”, was beset by legal wrangling until the US supreme court last month said the project could go ahead. The ground breaking that will kick off construction of the arch is expected to begin this month. Trump has linked it to the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, and said in Sunday’s post that it would be “by far the greatest” triumphal arch in any of the world’s top cities and capitals. It will be clad in granite, with three golden statues on top.

title: ‘An out-of-touch Silicon Valley radical’: meet Trump’s AI whisperer pushing for limited regulation
author: Dara Kerr
summary: David Sacks convinced Trump against any restrictions on AI – putting the White House out of step with its own party
body_text: As lawmakers from both sides of the aisle in the US have joined together calling for the regulation of powerful artificial intelligence models, one of the few vocal naysayers has been Donald Trump. He’s called the perceived dangers of the technology a “hoax” and a “scam”, arguing that the government already has “tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies”. It’s a starkly different stance from those of his former adviser Steve Bannon, the Republican Texas senator Ted Cruz and even the heads of the world’s leading AI companies. But it’s directly in line with the opinion of David Sacks – a prominent billionaire venture capitalist and Trump’s onetime AI and crypto czar, who has pushed back publicly and forcefully against recent claims of an impending AI apocalypse. Sacks, who believes regulation will erase the US lead in the global AI race, is seen as Trump’s AI whisperer – the adviser with the greatest influence in the White House on the topic. Time and again, he’s counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology. He also maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies. On Friday, more than 100 AI researchers, professors and technologists signed a public letter urging third-party evaluations of AI models and outlining how that should be done. The signatories included some of the most notable experts in the field, such as Geoffrey Hinton, the “godfather of AI”, and Stuart Russell, a renowned AI computer scientist. Sacks, in characteristic form, dismissed the letter on social media, calling third-party evaluations “pseudoscience” and “censorship and control”. “The last time we had media-generated panics like this (with Russiagate and Covid), social media companies created ‘trust & safety’ teams to censor conservative and dissident voices,” Sacks wrote. “These groups haven’t earned our trust, and their agenda is not our safety.” The next day, Trump proclaimed he would soon create an “AI Force” headed by an AI czar, Sacks’ previous title. It’s not clear if the venture capitalist will assume the mantle again, but he was quick to respond on X, praising Trump’s efforts and deriding a potential pause on AI once again. Derailing AI safety efforts Last December, Trump signed an executive order to halt state laws that limited AI. It was one of the first of several actions by the president that put his alignment with Sacks on full display. The proclamation assigned a federal taskforce to have the “sole responsibility” of challenging states that attempt to pass laws restricting the technology. The order spelled out an influential role for Sacks to direct the taskforce’s litigation against states. Then, just four months later, in March, the White House unveiled an AI policy for Congress that encouraged lawmakers to pre-empt state rules. Again, Sacks was seen as working behind the scenes to make this happen. This pattern has continued throughout the year. In July, Trump and Sacks hosted a fanfare-filled AI summit in Washington. And just this week, Trump called Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, to discuss AI regulation. In a live demonstration of Sacks’ proximity to the most powerful people in the US, the call came in while Sacks was interviewing Huang at an event on stage. Next week, Trump is hosting China’s leader, Xi Jinping, at the White House and is expected to invite several AI CEOs to be present. Sacks is also slated to be one of the guests in attendance, according to NBC News. Isabel Sunderland, the policy lead for technology reform at the non-profit Issue One, said that Sacks’ relationship with the president shows what happens when money can buy a direct line to power. “David Sacks advising President Trump on AI shows exactly how our political system serves the wealthy and well-connected instead of everyday Americans,” Sunderland said. “This is about more than just AI regulation – it’s about who’s allowed to write the rules.” Trump’s most recent full-throated opposition to AI regulation comes after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, announced on social media last week that he was resigning from the company, saying AI would soon become “superhuman systems” that could cause human extinction by 2030. After Coxon’s post, other Anthropic employees backed these predictions, with one saying: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” The end-of-the-world prognostications whipped up a frenzy of media and lawmakers’ attention over the past two weeks, with US politicians, heads of state and international bodies calling for the tech to be reined in. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, issued a proposal to slow down the technology’s advancement and ensure public safety by regulating the industry. In a rare public display of unity, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis and xAI owner Elon Musk agreed. Sacks, however, pushed back on any regulatory action, instead indicating the proposal was an “election-season psyop” and a bid for “regulatory capture”. In a lengthy social media post responding to Amodei’s proposal, Sacks said: “If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible. But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission.” Sacks’ political evolution Sacks, like his tech contemporaries Elon Musk and Peter Thiel, hails from South Africa. He was born in Cape Town in 1972 and then emigrated with his family to the US in the late 1970s. Sacks spent his college career majoring in economics at Stanford, where he met Thiel and worked with him at the conservative student-run newspaper the Stanford Review. The two men also collaborated after graduating, co-authoring in 1995 the book The Diversity Myth: Multiculturalism and the Politics of Intolerance at Stanford, an early glimpse into Sacks’ political ideology. The book rails against “multiculturalism”, “diversity” and the “politically correct” decline of higher education. By the late 90s and early 2000s, Sacks, Thiel, Musk and others worked together at PayPal, becoming members of what’s now known as the PayPal Mafia – an elite group of influential and wealthy tech investors and founders. After founding and working at various startups over the years, Sacks co-founded Craft Ventures in 2017. The fund has raised hundreds of millions for tech companies and has investments in an array of businesses, including SpaceX, Anduril, Palantir, Meta, Airbnb, Lyft and dozens of AI startups. As of 2023, Sacks said the firm’s assets under management totaled $3.3bn. Around the same time as founding Craft Ventures, Sacks started to get more into politics. While he donated to Hillary Clinton’s 2016 bid for president, he quickly pivoted to backing mostly Republican candidates and causes. In March 2020, Sacks launched the popular and influential All-In tech podcast with three other Silicon Valley investors who lean conservative and trumpet capitalist values. Vanity Fair profiled their annual All-In summit in 2025, calling the gathering a “fever-dream capitalist bacchanal where the faithful can stop being ‘guilt-tripped by this woke mind virus’ and get into ‘founder mode’”. Since then, Sacks’ rightward stances and political giving have deepened, according to a profile in the Atlantic. He donated to JD Vance, Blake Masters, Ron DeSantis and Robert F Kennedy Jr, campaign finance filings show. In June 2024, Sacks threw a fundraiser for Trump at his $45m French-limestone mansion in San Francisco’s Pacific Heights. Tickets went for $500,000 per couple. “President Trump is relaxed, happy, and cracking jokes about AI,” Harmeet Dhillon, assistant attorney general at Trump’s Department of Justice, posted on social media from the event. The AI czar’s time in the White House After Trump won the presidency, he named Sacks his AI and crypto czar, a newly created role. The position, as a “special government employee”, only allowed Sacks to work for the administration for a maximum of 130 days a year, but exempted him from confirmation hearings or financial disclosure requirements. The office of government ethics did require Craft Ventures to divest in some of its AI holdings, though. In March, Sacks said he was leaving the position, but he’s since maintained close ties with the president. In May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would’ve subjected AI models to government review. And in July, the two men hosted the AI summit in Washington. At the event, the president delivered an “AI action plan”, once again aimed at relaxing restrictions on the development and deployment of the technology. Sacks’ influence on Trump has rankled other senior administration officials, according to the Wall Street Journal. Scott Bessent and Susie Wiles have both voiced concerns about the effects of AI on the country and have advised Trump to mandate increased oversight on the technology. But the president has consistently sided with Sacks on the issue. Critics say that Trump and Sacks are out of step with the American public on safeguarding AI, even among Republicans. A May poll by Bryson Gillette Insights for the AI safety group Future of Life Institute, found that 85% of Republicans say they support Trump taking strong action to ensure AI is developed and deployed safely. “Running the David Sacks playbook on AI might be the biggest miscalculation the Trump administration has made,” Sacha Haworth, the executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, said. “He is an out-of-touch Silicon Valley radical who wants to replace humans with machines. You cannot put this guy in charge and not expect to pay a political price. Republicans are going to follow big tech executives right over a cliff.” Sacks and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.

title: House Republican doubles down on jab at Trump’s immigration enforcement
author: Ed Pilkington
summary: Florida’s María Elvira Salazar warns Trump that advisers are ‘compromising his legacy’ and not showing ‘whole picture’
body_text: María Elvira Salazar, the Republican congresswoman who has accused the president of going too far on immigration enforcement, doubled down on her criticism of the administration on Sunday, warning Donald Trump that some of his advisers were “compromising his legacy”. In an interview with CBS News’s Face the Nation, the Florida representative who is locked in a tight race for re-election pleaded with the US president not to “squander” his relationship with Hispanic voters. Though she couched her remarks as criticism of top administration advisers, it was clear that her focus was on Trump’s much-vaunted ambition to carry out the largest mass deportation of undocumented immigrants in US history. “I’m forewarning him and advising him as a member of Congress from the south Florida area that some of his advisers are just not presenting the whole picture,” she said. Asked by Face the Nation whether she were referring to Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, or Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff who has spearheaded the removal of undocumented children, Salazar placed the onus on Trump. “He is the only elected official in the White House. He is the one who has to determine who he listens and who he does not listen to. He is the president.” Last week Salazar became a rare voice of internal criticism within the Republican party towards Trump when she released a 30-second advert pointing out that even law-abiding undocumented immigrants were getting caught up in the aggressive federal sweep. The ad said: “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy … The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.” Salazar’s warning has been backed up by a slew of recent opinion polls that show many Hispanic voters who helped re-elect Trump in 2024 are now turning away from him. They are being repulsed by the rising cost of living and concern about his handling of the economy, as well as by the hardline immigration drive that has led to many hardworking, taxpaying undocumented immigrants being rounded up, detained and deported. In her CBS News interview, Salazar described herself as “a proud Republican”. “I’m first-generation American, and I want to preserve the American values that are entrenched in the [Republican party] and that the Hispanics share”. She is currently facing a tough re-election battle in her Miami-area district against her Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, despite having won in 2024 by 20 points. Trump also won the district by 15 points that year. Salazar told CBS News that 70% of Americans wanted to see some type of immigration reform. She also pushed back on the administration’s deportation of all undocumented immigrants irrespective of their criminal status. “The average America understands the difference between the narco and the nanny, and the gangster and the gardener.” On Saturday, Trump responded to Salazar’s criticisms, saying: “She obviously doesn’t have a very strong feeling about the border. I do.” He added: “Without me, she wouldn’t have gotten elected.” By breaking her silence on immigration, Salazar has put a spotlight on rising fears within Republican circles that the displeasure of Hispanic voters towards the administration’s policies could cost the party dear in November’s midterm elections. Several House seats in Colorado, Florida, Texas, Nevada and other states could be tipped in the Democrats’ favor as a result. Steve Scalise, the second-most powerful Republican in the US House, acknowledged on ABC News’s This Week that immigration was creating divisions within his party. Asked what he thought of Salazar’s comment that many Hispanic voters feel betrayed, he said: “I don’t necessarily agree with that statement.” He added: “When you look at what María said, obviously we have a lot of disagreements in Congress … Even among Republicans we have disagreements on how to actually get to the secure border that we have.”

title: Morning Mail: Pauline Hanson’s right-hand man, warnings Moscow may target Nato, and the end of card surcharges
author: Paul Gallagher
summary: Australians to no longer be hit with card surcharges; James Ashby’s rise in One Nation; Beijing believes AI slowdown would favour US
body_text: Good morning. Episode two of The Populist, out today, tracks the rise and influence of Pauline Hanson’s right-hand man: James Ashby. Overseas, there are warnings from intelligence chiefs that Russia may soon test the resolve of the Nato military alliance. Meanwhile, China is taking a dim view of US warnings over the breakneck speed of AI development. Australia Explainer | Debit and credit card surcharges will be eliminated from 1 October, as part of Reserve Bank reforms that will do away with extra checkout fees on Visa, Mastercard, and Eftpos payments. Exclusive | One Nation’s national director, James Ashby, is enjoying generous benefits as a result of his role working for One Nation, with documents showing that a company linked to the party built a $56,000 shed on his central Queensland property. The road ahead | Australian households will shrink but more people can expect to live well into their 90s, according to the Treasury’s latest intergenerational report looking ahead 40 years into the future. Valley Heights stabbings | A child has died in a stabbing attack in the Blue Mountains, with two other children and a woman being treated in hospital in a critical condition, NSW police say. Outfoxed? | Most people can identify wombats and kangaroos as Australian animals, but one in six people surveyed in Queensland, NSW and Victoria think red foxes are native wildlife. World Russia-Ukraine war | Baltic spy chiefs warn Moscow is preparing for more decisive action in Europe; Ukraine has targeted Moscow and the surrounding region in a large-scale attack involving hundreds of drones on the final day of Russia’s parliamentary elections. Analysis | China is pushing back against US warnings over rapid AI development, as Beijing views calls for a slowdown as a mechanism to lock in advantages enjoyed by American tech companies. Middle East crisis | Nations across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign. ‘Profound upheaval’ | Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office despite his party’s heavy losses in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party. Back on stage | Amid continued calls for a fan boycott, Ed Sheeran says the situation in Gaza is “catastrophic and unjustifiable” in his first show since his tour plunged into turmoil. Triumphal arch | Donald Trump claims the triumphal arch he is planning for Washington DC will serve as a “top grade military complex” replete with drone and ammunition storage space. Podcast The Populist: The favourite son | Episode 2 Most Australians know the story of Pauline Hanson: the fish and chip shop, the maiden speech, the “please explain”. But Hanson’s top adviser, James Ashby, wields as much – if not more – power over One Nation as Hanson herself. When the party bars media from press conferences, it’s Ashby who makes the call. To understand how One Nation operates, it’s important to understand Ashby’s story, from his beginnings as a PR flack, through a massive political scandal, to his ascent to power as One Nation’s popularity soars. In-depth The frustrations of American voters are many and varied: grifters, liars, the two-party system, money influencing elections, the US’s standing in the world, growing national debt and a fixation on cultural issues, not just the larger problems plaguing the country. Voters rage is reshaping US politics – and the looming midterms are starting to be framed not as right versus left but instead the “well-fed versus the fed-up”. Not the news It’s been a huge couple of years for Way Dynamic, the Melbourne multi-instrumentalist whose real name is Dylan Young. His 2025 album Massive Shoe is about to be re-released internationally after he signed with the indie giant Jagjaguwar. With subtle yet lush layers, gentle vocals and pensive lyricism, Way Dynamic’s thoughtful, sunny folk is both contemporary and timeless – and it’s not hard to understand his success. Sport AFL | Was Hawthorn v Brisbane the best game of Australian rules football ever played, Jonathan Horn asks. Cricket | Australia deny Zimbabwe a consolation ODI win after Nathan Ellis pulls off last-over heist in Harare; Brendon McCullum hails Harry Brook’s captaincy as England move top of T20 world rankings. Football | Alexander Isak pounces to give Liverpool victory on Iraola’s return to Bournemouth; Antoine Semenyo helps chaotic Manchester City beat Sunderland 5-3 despite Brian Brobbey hat-trick; Matheus Cunha strikes late to deny Fulham and salvage point for Manchester United. Tennis | Alex de Minaur finds top gear to seal Australia’s Davis Cup progression over Poland. Rugby union | Wallaroos give up big lead as France make miracle comeback in match delayed by burning bus. Media roundup A survey has revealed that Australians are waiting years for dementia diagnoses with early warning signs sometimes overlooked by health professionals, ABC News reports. Disposable vapes, toys, singing birthday cards and rechargeable tools are among the devices causing thousands of fires in waste and recycling centres across Australia, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. What’s happening today Politics | Treasurer Jim Chalmers is set to release the latest intergenerational report this morning. SA | A coronial inquest is scheduled in Adelaide into the death of a woman who was approved for NDIS support but did not receive care. ACT | A public hearing is scheduled in the inquiry into defence amendment (sexual assault prevention, intervention and response commission) bill. Sign up Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email If you would like to receive this Morning Mail update to your email inbox every weekday, sign up here, or finish your day with our Politics, really newsletter. You can follow the latest in US politics by signing up for This Week in Trumpland. Brain teaser And finally, here are the Guardian’s crosswords to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword

title: ‘Brown men are fearless, funny and sexy’: Salman Toor on clubbing, queerness and New York’s Muslim moment
author: Malik Meer
summary: Toor’s electrifying pictures have made him a global star – and he’s even painted Zohran Mamdani. As the artist hits London’s prestigious Courtauld Gallery, he talks about Manet, mullahs and the mayor
body_text: In Salman Toor’s paintings, queer south Asian men hang out in bars, twerk at trippy gatherings and lose themselves in phone screens. Sometimes they huddle in the back of taxis or pillow-fight on beds. In one portrait, a brown man stares apprehensively while facing customs officials. For the 43-year-old Pakistani American artist, it’s crucial that these figures take centre stage, after years of being demonised and erased. “It excites me that the cuteness and sexiness of brown protagonists can become familiar,” says Toor when we meet at his sun-drenched Brooklyn studio, a few weeks before his first solo show in Europe. “Their stories are not a gay side story in a family saga. It’s the main story. And everyone else is in the background.” Over the last decade, Toor has been helping to redraw the narratives around immigrants, desire, power and sex. His artwork – rich, figurative oil paintings that echo and subvert European old masters and Indian Mughal miniatures – has confirmed his status as an “international art star” (the New Yorker) and “one of the most fascinating painters of his generation” (the New York Times). Solo museum exhibitions in New York, Baltimore and Beijing have earned universal praise, while in November 2022, his painting Four Friends sold for $1.2m at Sotheby’s. Time recently included him in its most influential art people list. Next month, London’s Courtauld Gallery presents Someone Like You, a greatest hits of Toor’s paintings and drawings that he selected with the curator Elena Crippa. As it’s home to many of his favourite baroque and impressionist artists, he couldn’t be more thrilled. The Courtauld was one of the galleries he visited on his first trip to London from Pakistan. “It’s the most exciting thing that could happen,” he says, looking genuinely humbled. Dressed in black parachute trousers, a grey sleeveless T-shirt and chunky fashion trainers, Toor is friendly and eager to talk about his art, armed with a printout of images from the show. Like the themes in his work, our conversation moves from pop culture (no, this show is “absolutely not named after an Adele song”) to global politics (he regularly questions his “westernisation”) to family relationships (good, but they’d like to see fewer “willies” in his paintings). As an art student, Toor searched for inspiration at the Courtauld during his many “obsessive” periods. “I was looking at a lot of Rubens and Van Dyck,” he explains. He became particularly obsessed with Édouard Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère. “I stood in front of it and I thought, ‘Oh my God, this has all the solutions to my problems’,” he laughs. In his 2019 painting The Bar on East 13th, Toor pays tribute to Manet’s masterpiece, relocating it to New York’s East Village, where hipster queer couples make out and a brown barman wearing nail polish and braided hair takes the place of the melancholy French barmaid and partying bourgeoisie. Looking at that image now, Toor has mixed feelings: “I had just come out through painting so it was exciting because I felt free. It was a time of well-deserved self-love. But I also felt in danger: I was getting a lot of negative, threatening messages online. I’m from a country which is very conservative. Those are very specific feelings from that time.” Toor was born in Lahore, Pakistan, into a middle-class Muslim family. To avoid his sporty schoolmates, the young artist sought refuge in the art department of the city’s elite Aitchison College and honed his talent. He moved to the US in 2002 to study art in Columbus, Ohio, where he felt isolated until he moved into a hippy commune with “the dreadlocked, blue-haired art kids”. In 2009, he graduated with a master’s in fine arts from New York’s Pratt Institute. Within a few years, Toor landed on his signature style: emerald green compositions with explicit gay themes based on his and his friends’ experiences navigating culture and belonging in New York City. In previous interviews, he’s explained that he chose green because it is simultaneously glamorous and poisonous. Today, Toor adds that it has an “atmospheric aspect that you can go deeper inside, an outdoor or nocturnal forest-like place beckoning you”. Most of the artworks in Someone Like You were produced in the last seven years, during which Toor gained US citizenship. “They’re images about immigration and people on the verge of … the threshold of the free world or whatever.” He pauses, reflecting on the reality of US politics. “Or maybe not.” Toor is excited to be in London for the exhibition. He has fond memories of visiting friends in the city in the early 00s, going to Soho bars and the trashy pop club G-A-Y before taking a night bus home to Streatham – “shades on, getting a doner kebab,” he says. “We were just kids. London was a city that opened me up to gay nightlife and art history.” The city also provides a setting in one image. Cross Street grew out of a scene he glimpsed from the window of a favourite London restaurant: Tayyabs in Whitechapel. It shows a group of buff skaters hanging by a street sign as a mullah passes by. Toor was struck by “the proximity of two kinds of people” and wanted to capture the different threads of masculinity that were intimidating to him growing up: the school bullies on one hand and the religious figure on the other. Right now, Toor lives in New York with his partner, the musician Ali Sethi, in a thrilling moment for the city’s south Asian and Middle Eastern communities. Across politics, culture and arts, New York is witnessing a historic surge of energy and creativity that’s been given a confidence boost by the election of mayor Zohran Mamdani. Earlier this year, the Guardian profiled many of Muslim New York’s artists, organisers and thinkers while New York magazine devoted a special issue to mark the shifting sands of “Habibi City”. “It’s Mamdani’s New York,” Toor beams. “What I love about this city is that there’s a wonderful connection of artists and creative people who are part of our circle.” As a first-generation immigrant he’s excited to see new worlds unfolding around him, the classic New York story, concrete jungle where dreams are made: “People are brilliant at finding new solutions to being from traditional backgrounds, and choosing and shedding things to be part of the future.” Not long after Mamdani won the Democratic nomination for mayor, a portrait by Toor of the future leader surfaced on Instagram. Toor was asked by his friend, the film director Mira Nair, Zohran’s mother, to paint the family in 2007. “The group portrait didn’t come out that well. Mira has it locked up and I hope it remains in storage,” he laughs. “But I knew this [individual portrait of Zohran] was good. She was thrilled and it’s in their home. I saw it there recently.” How does he feel about the image now? “It’s more delicate and smaller than I remember. It’s more finely painted than I thought – at the time it was my idea of rough. Maybe I’ve become freer or grungy.” He won’t be drawn on Mamdani’s first nine months in office but he recently curated the low key exhibition In a Free State, with his friend, the Israeli American artist Doron Langberg. It was an attempt to deal with the global political horrors that left him creatively crippled and unable to paint figures for a five-month period. Showcasing their friends and others, including many Middle Eastern artists, it aimed to “visualise and contend with a chaotic and alienating time”. Toor says also he wanted to address the cynicism people have about art and politics. After Someone Like You opens, Toor will return to his artwork. The studio walls are covered with sketches and ideas; unfinished pieces include an experiment in painting an erect penis, a large image of workmen fixing a phallic air vent and some attempts at drawing dogs. There is also a portrait of Mahmoud Khalil, the Columbia University student who was detained for more than three months and became the face of the Trump administration’s crackdown on pro-Palestine speech. Toor was inspired to capture him after seeing Khalil give a powerful speech, he says, returning to the theme of the “brown protagonist”. Earlier in the interview we discussed the rise of a new generation of US politicians, including the Michigan senate candidate, Abdul El-Sayed. “The great thing about the new brown men that are so visible now is that they’re fearless,” he says. “They’re funny and they’re sexy. I would love to see the west deal with that.” Judging by the hysterical reaction to El-Sayed’s recent win and the bad faith attacks on Zohran Mamdani, they don’t seem to be dealing with it very well, I suggest. “We’ll see,” he says firmly. “They should get used to it.” Salman Toor: Someone Like You is at the Courtauld, London, 2 October to 10 January

title: Whiplashed middle powers seek new alliances as Trump rages on world stage
author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
summary: While world leaders prepare for annual UN gathering, shifts in the global order continue in the face of a disruptive American president
body_text: In the event of a midterms election battering, it is possible that a deflated Donald Trump, constrained by a Democrat-controlled Congress, will gradually have to face up to the indignity of irrelevance. While continuing to sign off Truth Social posts with his usual, “Thank you for your attention to this matter”, no one will actually be paying much attention. His meandering press conferences will no longer be carried live by TV networks. The Republican party will move on to the question of his successor. Trump could announce he had changed the name of the Champs-Élysées to Sunset Boulevard and even Google Maps will stifle a yawn. He would become that most pitied of political animals, the lame duck. Yet somehow this scenario does not seem to fit the Trump personality, the US media landscape or indeed the recent history of other presidential endings. Just before completing their own terms in office, George W Bush launched the Iraq war “surge”, Bill Clinton got China into the World Trade Organization and Ronald Reagan helped end the cold war. Trump will also surely rage against the dying of the light. Many observers, including the former US secretary of state Hillary Clinton and the former UK foreign secretary David Lammy, predict Trump will concentrate even more on his disruptive foreign policy after November’s midterms, seeking to go even further and faster. Potential legislative gridlock in Congress would block him off from domestic initiatives, so the thinking goes, but much less so foreign policy. The likes of António Guterres, attending his final UN general assembly as secretary general this week, who have tried to impress on Trump that the US could achieve more in alliance with others than alone, are likely to receive short shrift. Those hoping for a return from the orderless world to one of order, loosely built around a set of recognisable values, are likely to be disappointed. In short, there is more to come. *** That assessment is accelerating a trend across the world of countries forming a complex web of diplomatic, military and trading alliances designed to act as protective shields from an unpredictable and predatory US president. These hedging alliances, born out of fear of entrapment or of abandonment, are springing up across the globe, changing the matrix of diplomacy, often but not always in favour of the other superpower of the age, China. John Bew, a foreign policy adviser to four former British prime ministers, describes the process as the creation of “a sub-threshold international order”. As Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, urged in a speech at Davos in January, the middle powers are reorganising. The trend is most obvious among former US allies. Mark Leonard, the director of the European Council of Foreign Relations, said: “The world is moving from a situation where countries saw themselves within the context of an alliance system – ‘How do we plug and play and make it all about interoperability with American grand strategy?’ – towards one where the primary goal is: ’How do we hedge and how do we make sure that we can defend ourselves if America isn’t there?’” Wherever one looks it is the alliances in which the US does not feature – from Brics to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) – that are thriving and deepening. The recent Brics summit in Delhi ended with a declaration 140 dense paragraphs long that centred on how sovereign states can insulate their economies, supply lines, and payment infrastructures from weaponised western financial networks. The aim was to show that the “global south” can shape rules without turning into an anti-American alliance. “The operational strategy does not aim to eradicate the dollar overnight,” the Indian commentator Navroop Singh explained, “but to construct a parallel, non-dollar pipeline through which bilateral commerce, especially in strategic commodities like oil, gas, agriculture, and critical minerals can flow unhindered by extraterritorial oversight of the United States.” At this month’s SCO meeting at Bishkek in Kyrgyzstan, China’s president, Xi Jinping, said: “The overwhelming majority of countries do not subscribe to power politics, do not want conflict and confrontation, and do not wish to remain closed off and left behind. Instead, they aspire to secure an equal place on the world stage through their own development and international cooperation.” Formed to manage border disputes among former Soviet states, the SCO’s activities long ago expanded to include an economic dimension fostering connectivity, trade and investment. By contrast, in the groupings that the US dominates, such as the G7 and Nato, the recent key ambition has been to shape an agenda that avoids a Trump walkout. Success is measured according to whether the west avoids public disintegration. Sometimes these new ad hoc alliances are relatively mundane. Some operate inside existing institutions, others involve the creation of specific new cooperation trading mechanisms such as memorandums of understanding on trade in critical minerals or the development of new overlapping institutions. In the case of the UK, the Chatham House thinktank suggests as many as six different mini-alliances could be formed to build submarines and air engines, share critical minerals, or promote free trade. *** The biggest and most striking recent manifestation of this new order came in the Middle East on 7 August, when Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca pact – a defensive military alliance that for some is about ending the dependency on the US military umbrella, and for others combatting Iran. Either way, it is likely to rewrite the Middle East’s security architecture. Trita Parsi, from the US foreign policy thinktank the Quincy Institute For Responsible Statecraft, said: “If you sit in the Gulf Cooperation Council countries right now, you must feel tremendously vulnerable because you have put all your eggs in the American security basket and it turned out not only not to work, but it was supposed to be a guarantee that others would be deterred from attacking you. Instead, the US started a war against the wishes of most Gulf countries and within that war, the entire infrastructure of the US bases turned out not to be a deterrent, but a magnet.” Not only were exposed bases pummelled by Iranian missiles and drones to the point, in the words of Gen David Petraeus, that they became “no longer viable”, the Gulf states also discovered the US was prepared to allow Israel to bomb Qatar’s capital, Doha, in the hope of assassinating the Hamas leadership. It was the first such attack on a GCC state, and changed the GCC’s security calculations as to whether Iran or Israel ultimately was the primary threat in the region. The US insists in public it will reinvest in better-protected bases and will shortly lay out a postwar vision in which the US remains indispensable to the Gulf’s security. But Majed al-Ansari, Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson, said: “Gulf nations cannot rely solely on the US and other international alliances for their security. Self-sufficiency when it comes to security is the only way forward.” Parsi admitted it was not clear what kind of tree would grow out of the seed sown in Mecca. “Is it another bloc formation that at its core divides the region, leading to rivalry and confrontation, or is it, as the Turks insist, an open constellation that is not targeting anyone but based on collective security?” Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, meanwhile, requires foreign investment, tourism and reliable energy routes. Endless wars promoted by Israel and not constrained by the US for purposes not in Saudi Arabia’s long-term interest are a ball and chain on the Saudi economy. In all this, there are deep implications for India, a country dependent on the Middle East for nearly 60% of its crude oil and about 70% of its liquefied natural gas requirements. It may need to form its own hard power security partnerships in the region. Writing in Foreign Affairs magazine, Marc Lynch, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University, asked recently: “If Washington could not even be counted on to consult its allies, defeat its adversaries, or protect its partners from the fallout of its regional misadventures, then what good were its promises? The fundamental bargain the United States offered has crumbled, and it will not be easily rebuilt”. The same set of questions has been posed in Europe, leading to calls for a more Europeanised Nato, most often perceived as an alliance of its five main military powers, a constellation that conveniently bypasses Brexit and would allow Germany, France, Italy, Poland and the UK to work together to face the Russian threat, assuming these democracies next year remain led by forces opposed to Putin’s authoritarianism. Debate about this alliance, promoted at the Munich Security Conference, is driven by the twin fears of the hybrid war conducted by Moscow and the US plan to leave the conventional defence of Europe to the Europeans. Trumpites treat Europeans primarily as trade competitors and sometimes a civilisational threat, not allies. No one can assume that the US would come to Europe’s defence in the event of a Russian attack. Not surprisingly, Poland, the Baltics and Scandinavia have since 2022 increased their defence spending by 71%, 134% and 126% respectively. The call to buy European arms is growing. Such is the concern about where Trump could go next after his threats to Greenland, that some European diplomats privately express relief that the US was unable to repeat the success of Venezuela in Iran. There is no love for the Iranian government, save for its ability to remind Europe of the risks inherent in relying on US military and technological supremacy. *** The country that most acutely faces the American dilemma is of course Canada. Now entering an asymmetric trade war with the largest and most powerful country in the world, it has little doubt about the rupture it is confronting. Bob Rae, a former Canadian ambassador to the UN, recently wrote: “Canada’s nextdoor neighbour is a predatory hegemon [that] tears up treaties, makes a mockery of international law and clearly has a different concept of the relationships between might and right, and between law, morality and self-interest.” But there was an ambiguity deep in Carney’s Davos message. Was he seeking simply to locate new markets blocked by US tariffs, or was he trying to build a network of countries – a third bloc – with like-minded liberal values? Rae argued that for the middle nations alliance to thrive, Carney needed to be clearer about what values Canada stands for, including upholding international law. He wrote: “We can succeed in defeating such aggression only if we are willing to extend economic, political and military support to other countries and jurisdictions facing similar attacks and threats.” In his speech to the European parliament this week while trying to provide the cure to the harsh realities his Davos speech diagnosed, Carney argued that associate membership of the EU would not just be about economics, but an affinity of deep-rooted shared values that implicitly Canada no longer shared with the US. But the rules-based EU does not give access to its markets readily, and the big vision could soon become entangled in the small print Brussels adores. Sometimes this crisis of the west is seen as an exclusively European phenomenon. But South Korea finds itself in a similar place to Canada. Ulchi Freedom Shield, the annual joint military exercise that the US and South Korea held to counter the North Korean threat, was abruptly scaled back by Washington just before it was due to begin in August. Trump ordered the drills cut from 11 days to five, citing costs, his desire to improve relations with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, and South Korea’s reluctance to support his war on Iran. The decline in US military stocks due to the Iran war has hardly helped. It has intensified a debate in South Korea, and in Japan, about pursuing independent nuclear weapons, especially given the apparent indifference of the US and the international community to North Korea’s programme. The friction has given Xi a golden opportunity to promote China to South Korea and Asia as the more reliable ally. Optimists such as Kurt Campbell, who under Joe Biden’s presidency latterly as deputy secretary of state did more than anyone to reconstruct American alliances across Asia after the Trump first term, insists his task can be repeated. There is no need to panic, he said, arguing that “by the winter there will be a dramatic resurgence in discussion, debate, hope and, frankly, optimism about what comes next”. The old centrifugal forces including European aversion to Chinese protectionism and US dominance in artificial intelligence, will resurface. The counterview is that something fundamental has changed. Once bitten, twice shy, the old transatlantic order will not be restored, and something new, less predictable, more fragmented is already taking shape.
