title: Venezuelan shot by ICE seeks medical care as lawyer says bullet lodged in back
author: Emiliano Tahui Gomez in Austin
summary: Sshooting of Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez comes months after increased federal immigration enforcement in Austin
body_text: The Venezuelan man who was shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday spoke out from detention on Monday afternoon when he was able to call his lawyer, in the middle of a press conference, and plead for better medical care. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital in Austin into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine and is in much discomfort. “I haven’t received any medical attention. I’m in a lot of pain,” Garcés Pérez said, in a phone call to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. “I have expressed my pain [to the guards].” He recounted that he had spent the night sleeping on the floor of a cold room in a detention center about 140 miles from Austin, where he was taken hours after being shot by an ICE officer after a traffic stop on Sunday afternoon. Lincoln-Goldfinch had told the Guardian earlier on Monday that the federal officer’s bullet was still inside her client. Garcés Pérez said he had been told it is too close to his spine to operate on to remove at this time. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, has not responded to requests for more information and comment. In an initial statement issued shortly before midnight on Sunday night, DHS said Garcés Pérez was in stable condition and that he was “in federal custody pending removal” out of the US. The shooting did not come out of the blue, amid an immigration enforcement surge in Austin. ICE had already been active in the Texas capital of late, but then matters escalated dramatically on Sunday as shots rang out. Garcés Pérez was in the process of delivering a DoorDash food order on the city’s north side when ICE encountered him shortly before 1pm on Sunday. Video posted online appears to show an ICE officer getting out of his car and shooting at Garcés Pérez’s car three times. His car, as later visible at the scene, had a large dent on the front passenger side. Garcés Pérez, who was hit once in the back between his shoulder blades, is a Venezuelan national who has lived in the United States for two years, according to his lawyer, but had been ordered removed from the US. Garcés Pérez told onlookers who rushed to the scene that he had been shot because he hadn’t stopped. Garcés Pérez was taken to a downtown hospital for treatment but, according to lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, was whisked away from there by ICE late Sunday afternoon. For a few hours, his partner and the lawyer could not locate him, then on Monday morning Lincoln-Goldfinch told the Guardian he’d been located at the South Texas ICE Processing Center, in Pearsall. “Bullet still lodged in his back. No pain meds,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said by text on Monday. Garcés Pérez said when he called the attorney on Monday that what appeared to be a normal car had pulled up next to him before veering in his direction. When he eventually stopped and spoke to what turned out to be an ICE officer, he said he asked to move his vehicle to a nearby parking lot because he wanted his car to be there if he was arrested. He was told he could not and when he drove further the ICE vehicle crashed into him and then he was shot, he said. Austin, the politically liberal capital city of conservative Texas, has repeatedly found itself at the crossfire of the immigration debate. The state’s Republican leadership has often sought to make an example out of the city, forcing local leaders to weaken Austin’s policy of not collaborating with ICE. Local leaders said this summer has marked a low-profile but aggressive surge in immigration enforcement in the region, spurred by a jump in ICE acting alone, relying less on state troopers to stop people and hand them over. “As mayor of the city of Austin, I’m very angry about this,” Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said on Sunday. “A person being shot on the streets of Austin by someone purporting to be law enforcement, particularly when it’s ICE, is something that causes me to be unhappy and angry..” TDHS said that it was leading the investigation into the shooting, alongside the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). However Austin leaders have called for local and state involvement, citing public distrust of ICE. The exact details leading up to the shooting remained unclear on Monday. Video posted on social media shows a man running out of the black SUV and shooting at Garcés Pérez’s almost stationary blue sedan from behind it. Three gunshots ring out. A witness, Nedavia Bolaños, got closest to the scene and shared video with the Guardian of ICE officers standing next to the car as the man clutched his chest, before Austin police officers arrived and were the ones to render first aid. Within an hour, more than a hundred protesters had gathered at the site, chanting expletives against ICE and waving Mexican, American and Guatemalan flags. Several protesters could be seen washing their eyes and mouths in pain, after they were sprayed with what they said was teargas or chemical spray. The shooting came after several months of increased immigration enforcement, particularly in immigrant-heavy neighborhoods, suburbs and exurbs. Austin city council member José “Chito” Vela, who represents the neighborhood where Garcés Pérez was shot, said that he has heard constituents describe an enforcement bump driven by a rise in unilateral action by ICE. While ICE was largely seen making immigration arrests after Texas Department of Public Safety traffic stops for the first year or so of the second Trump administration, they have begun to act increasingly on their own, Vela said. City leaders had previously raised concerns over the increased action. Congressman Greg Casar, an Austin Democrat who leads the Congressional Progressive Caucus, has sent a letter to DHS demanding cooperation in an “immediate, independent investigation” into the shooting, the full release of any footage the federal authorities have of the shooting, and “accountability for any wrongdoing by the agent responsible”. Later on Monday, lawyers representing Garcés Pérez filed both a writ of habeas corpus and an injunction motion in court, hoping to stave off any attempt to deport him before an investigation is complete. In the application for the habeas petition requesting his release, Garcés Pérez’s lawyers argued that he qualified for a type of visa given to victims of crimes.

title: Trump and Mamdani appear friendly after ‘wide-ranging’ meeting at Gracie Mansion
author: José Olivares in New York and David Smith in Washington
summary: Republican president said he hoped the democratic socialist would be a ‘great mayor’ for New York City
body_text: Donald Trump said on Monday that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader whom the president and his Republican allies have spent months holding up as a symbol of the Democratic party’s alleged embrace of “communism” ahead of the November midterms. At a news conference following their closed-door meeting at Gracie Mansion, Trump and Mamdani appeared friendly as they have in previous meetings. Mamdani said he and Trump held a “wide-ranging” discussion, which touched on affordable housing and immigration, but did not offer extensive details regarding any disagreements between them. Asked whether he challenged Trump over his decision to ban CNN, MS Now, and Politico from White House grounds, Mamdani said: “I told the president that we’re going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn, and that is something that I believe in.” “It’s interesting because they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn’t very worried about that,” Trump chimed in, pointing to the large assembly of press on the lawn. The visit to Gracie Mansion, ahead of the president’s speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday, was a measure of Trump’s apparent respect for the 34-year-old mayor of his native New York. It was the first presidential visit to the historic riverside residence in 45 years, following Ronald Reagan, who met there with Ed Koch in 1981. Pressed on why he had invited Trump, Mamdani said he was willing to work with anybody who could “deliver” for New Yorkers, and highlighted their shared interest in building thousands of new housing units at Sunnyside Yard in Queens. For his part, Trump said he believed Mamdani had “great potential”. It was the latest unlikely meeting between Trump, a rightwing populist who has targeted immigrants and Muslims, and Mamdani, a democratic socialist who was born in Uganda and is New York’s first Muslim mayor. Trump has focused his midterm election campaign on denouncing Democrats as “godless communists” who seek to abolish borders and prisons and pose the greatest threat that the US has ever faced. Yet on Monday he said of Mamdani, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America: “I certainly hope he will be a great mayor. You have to understand – I want what’s good for New York. I want what’s good for the country ... I want him to be a great mayor.” The body language again seemed amicable. Trump deferentially stood aside as Mamdani spoke from the lectern and, when the press conference finished, gave him an affectionate double tap on the arm. Trump, Mamdani, Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles and Mamdani’s chief of staff Elle Bisgaard-Church were all in attendance during Monday’s meeting. Mamdani said that they discussed the Trump administration’s stripping of protections for Haitian immigrants. “I shared my very strong opinions about how we can keep New Yorkers safe, how we can keep immigrant New Yorker safe, and how important immigrant New Yorkers, especially Haitian New Yorkers, are – not only to the fabric of our city, but also to our city’s economy,” Mamdani said. “The president and I have been very frank about the many disagreements we have,” he added. The meeting came one day after Mamdani, and Clara Brugada, the mayor of Mexico City, met with migrant delivery workers in New York City, who expressed precarity and fear surrounding the increase in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests. Earlier this month, Mamdani helped initiate a lawsuit against the Trump administration for its “public charge” rule change targeting immigrant communities. The lawsuit was filed by the State of New York and 21 other states against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and various of its agencies. It is unclear if they discussed the lawsuit during the meeting.

title: Trump’s bizarre social media blitz leaves world guessing ahead of UN address
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: President has been posting on Washington arch, AI and his ‘25 top achievements’ – the chances of an uplifting speech appear slim
body_text: The annual gathering of the United Nations general assembly has historically been a platform for US presidents to display their most serious face and a positive vision to the world. From Harry Truman and Dwight Eisenhower to John F Kennedy and Barack Obama, over eight decades US leaders have used the setting to expound on grand themes before a global audience at pivotal moments in international affairs. As world leaders and officials gather in New York for the yearly event, and Donald Trump prepares to address them on Tuesday, how he will contribute to this historic catalog of remarks is a matter of speculation. The US president has spent recent days blitzing social media on a variety of topics, from his planned triumphal arch in Washington to a bid to rebrand artificial intelligence, as he contends with an unpopular war and low approval ratings that threaten to drag down his party in November’s US midterm elections. His previous addresses to the assembly suggest that the chances of a non-divisive and uplifting message are low. Last year, Trump shocked the august gathering in his first appearance since returning to the White House the previous January by declaring to those present that their countries were “going to hell” while launching a full-frontal assault on the UN and the concept of open borders. In 2018, during his first presidency, Trump drew laughter from fellow leaders when he opened his address by claiming: “In less than two years, my administration has accomplished almost more than any other administration in the history of our country.” The previous year, he had attacked longstanding allies, singling out Germany for its energy policy, and declaring that the US “can no longer be taken advantage of, or enter into a one-sided deal where the United States gets nothing in return”. This time around, Trump’s recent social media activities hinted at an even more volatile than usual state of mind from a leader who can be erratic at the best of times. Arguably the most eye-catching was his declaration in an early Sunday morning post that he intended to turn his highly controversial planned arch in Washington DC into a military storage facility, claiming – without providing evidence – that the move was requested by the US military. There was a surfeit of others. A post headlined “His Hemisphere” and depicting Trump gazing at a map of the globe ominously hinted at an imperious tone he could strike, less than nine months after US forces seized the former Venezuelan leader, Nicolás Maduro, in his compound in Caracas and spirited him and his wife to New York. The Trump administration has since trumpeted a deal giving it control over a significant segment of Venezuelan oil reserves. In another post, Trump postures as the defender of AI – denouncing recent fears that its rapid development could presage the destruction of the human race. Instead, he painted it as the latest target of “many hoaxes, all generated by the radical left dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our country” and announced his plans for an “AI force”– headed by an “AI Czar” – in the image of the space force, established during his first presidency. “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our country’s GDP,” he wrote. “We are leading China, and the rest of the world, and I intend to keep it that way.” There is every chance Trump returns to previous themes at the UN on Tuesday. In an echo of his 2018 speech, on Friday he posted a list of his “Top 25 Trump Achievements” since returning to office. Trump’s appearance before the general assembly will be his first since his fateful decision to launch, in tandem with Israel, a war against Iran in February. The conflict – despite his predictions that it would last a few days, and result in the collapse of Tehran’s Islamic regime – shows no signs of ending. The regime still stands. Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway that was a conduit to one-fifth of the world’s oil exports before hostilities began, has sent global energy prices soaring and stoked inflation in the US, challenging the prospects of Trump’s Republican party in November’s midterms. Polls show a majority of Americans oppose the war, which has further deflated his approval ratings. Further piquancy to Trump’s political dilemma is likely to be added by the presence of Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, at the UN. While Trump has signaled a willingness to meet his Iranian counterpart, Pezeshkian – a relative pragmatist, under pressure from regime hardliners to stand firm and avoid compromise with an enemy still branded by Tehran as “the great Satan” – is thought unlikely to agree to such an encounter. The sting of being snubbed by an Iranian leadership he likes to depict as “dying to make a deal” could add further fuel to a fiery speech before the general assembly and witnessed by a global audience. Traditionally, US presidential speeches to the UN go through a long drafting process and are subject to reviews by the state department, the Pentagon and the intelligence community, as well as fevered last-minute rehearsals. That all may still hold true for this address. Yet equally likely is a no-holds-barred, scattergun diatribe, rehashing the themes of Trump’s recent social media output.

title: AI is generating a new wave of economic populism. It could be a tipping point
author: Robert Reich
summary: It’s becoming obvious to many Americans that corporations have been raking it in while workers take it on the chin
body_text: Last week, the unlikely duo of Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon spoke before a Washington group demanding a stop to AI and its datacenters. Notably, both lambasted the corporate oligarchs behind AI. The most potent force in US politics is anti-establishment fury at a system seen as rigged against average working people. AI has become exhibit A. Until recently, both parties largely avoided criticizing the wealthy corporate elites that funded their campaigns. In politics as in nature, one does not bite the hands that feed. Trump Republicans have instead aimed populist fury at immigrants, LGBTQ+ people, Black and Latino people, “communists”, Muslims, so-called “woke” leaders, “coastal elites”, “childless cat ladies” and other scapegoats. Democrats – with the exceptions of Sanders, AOC and a few others – have also avoided criticizing wealthy corporate elites, aiming their populist fury at Trump. This may be changing. It’s becoming obvious to much of the US that giant corporations have been raking it in while workers have been taking it on the chin. As of mid-2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the percentage of the total economy going to workers as wages had fallen to a record low of 52.9% (down from above 65% when tracking began in 1947) – leaving the rest to investors, business owners, and corporate profits. AI is on the way to causing far more inequality – generating billions for its backers while reducing the number of jobs and real wages. Trump and his regime, meanwhile, have exposed the greed, venality, cupidity and corruption of the US’s wealthy corporate elites by allowing them to do anything they wish – including create energy-guzzling, water-depleting AI datacenters – as long as they kiss his assets by funding his Pac, paying for his ballroom and singing his praises. Trump has thereby revealed the truth about corporate America that for years had been hidden behind corporate PR about “corporate social responsibility”, corporate charity and “trickle-down” economics: the captains of corporate America are willing to throw average working Americans under the bus to make billions more. Corporate avarice under Trump has become so blatant and corporate America’s contempt for the needs of average Americans so flagrant that most Americans are now catching on. In a recent NBC poll, 54% of Americans agreed that “when it comes to politics and society, nothing really matters because powerful people will always do whatever they want.” AI may well be the final tipping point. Data centers are unpopular – about 70% of the public opposes them. And Americans harbor deep suspicions of AI. More than 60% believe AI could destroy humanity (this includes 60% of Trump supporters). Fears about AI are provoking larger concerns about wealthy corporate elites bribing politicians – not just to get generous subsidies for AI but also to reduce the corporate elite’s tax bills, kill off unions, slash social safety nets, deregulate Wall Street, attain no-bid government contracts, receive exclusive licenses, open tax loopholes, get tariff exemptions, use public lands, and become even bigger monopolies. Because of Trump, Americans are coming to view those wealthy corporate elites as more aligned with Republicans than with Democrats. According to last week’s Times-Sienna poll, when likely voters were asked which party the word “elitist” describes, a remarkable 43% said Republicans while 33% said Democrats. This is something of a return to how the US’s two major political parties used to be seen. Ninety years ago, Democrats were assumed to be on the side of working people against wealthy corporate elites. On the eve of his 1936 re-election, Franklin D Roosevelt told the American people they were fighting “business and financial monopoly, speculation, reckless banking, class antagonism, war profiteering … We now know that government by organized money is just as dangerous as government organized by the mob.” Will Democrats seize the moment and embrace the new AI-fueled economic populism? Or will they continue to succumb to the siren songs of big money? According to Politico, some Democratic political consultants are quietly urging candidates in the toughest battleground races to stay mum on AI “over fears that powerful and well-resourced pro-AI interest groups could spend money pummeling them in the final weeks of the midterms”. It’s not just the future of the Democratic party that’s at stake; it’s the future of America. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

title: Democrat says ICE restricted her oversight visit to country’s largest detention camp
author: José Olivares
summary: Veronica Escobar tells Guardian she was prevented from speaking to detainees at much-criticized Texas facility
body_text: Federal immigration officials in Texas prevented US representative Veronica Escobar from fully conducting her congressional oversight duties at a controversial Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center, the lawmaker said in an interview with the Guardian. Escobar, a Democrat who represents El Paso and surrounding areas on the US-Mexico border in west Texas, conducted an oversight visit last month at the Camp East Montana ICE tent facility housed in the Fort Bliss military base, after two separate “disturbances” had been reported there in recent weeks. But when she arrived to scrutinize conditions at the camp, the largest ICE detention center in the country, she said she was not allowed to speak with any of the detained immigrants. She also requested surveillance footage of the reported incidents but said she has not received it. “The administration obviously has attempted to block congressional oversight,” Escobar said in a telephone interview with the Guardian. “It’s been very challenging at times. And that has depended on, to a large extent, what the directive has been from the administration.” The constraints placed on Escobar is one of the latest instances in which the Trump administration has limited members of Congress’s ability to conduct oversight visits into federal immigration detention centers. Escobar and other federal lawmakers sued the Trump administration last year for blocking such access. Despite a federal judge ruling in favor of the lawmakers last December, there have been subsequent reports of ICE officials placing limits on or turning away members of congress when attempting to conduct oversight visits. “Oversight, during the second Trump administration, has certainly been significantly more challenging than during the first Trump administration,” Escobar added. Camp East Montana was hastily constructed last summer at the huge army base in El Paso. Unlike other ICE detention centers housed in buildings, this facility is a sprawling “soft-sided” tent camp. It has the capacity to hold up to 5,000 people and has drawn complaints and demands for its closure from the time it opened. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, reported two separate “disturbances” within one week there in early September. On 1 September, it alleged that detained immigrants assaulted security staff by striking, kicking and throwing tablets at them. On 7 September, a larger group of around 130 detained immigrants allegedly threw items, flipped furniture and disabled security cameras. The detainees also knocked down partitions between the tented living quarters, known as pods, at the detention camp, Escobar said. An ICE official at the facility called 911 during the incident, according to reporting by the El Paso Times. The newspaper’s revelation contradicted what ICE officials apparently told Escobar during her visit. “While there absolutely have been serious issues and mismanagement, fraud, deaths, and a homicide, there had never been a riot,” Escobar said. “There had never been, especially in two weeks in a row, situations where the contractor lost control of the population in their custody.” Escobar said that when she spoke with an ICE official about incidents, the official pointed to the detained immigrants’ nationality as the cause. “The deputy was very quick to blame the nationality of the detainees, saying that the Venezuelans are a difficult population,” Escobar said. It is still unclear what exactly happened during the two incidents. Members of Congress have the legal power to conduct oversight visits into ICE detention facilities nationwide, by visiting the sites without prior notice and speaking with detained immigrants. Lawmakers have claimed that the Trump administration has limited those oversight visits by requiring lawmakers to submit the names and personal information of detainees they want to speak with beforehand. The homeland security department disputed Escobar’s claims in an email to the Guardian, while adding that it considers many oversight visits “a media act”, and also denied that there has been an official request for data and footage. “Any member of Congress can still request to speak with any illegal alien in ICE custody,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “If an illegal alien and a member of Congress agree to meet with one another, ICE will facilitate the meeting. We are not stopping members of Congress from meeting with illegal aliens, including many with criminal histories in ICE custody, or touring ICE facilities.” Since Camp East Montana opened last summer, it has been plagued with accusations of abuse, mismanagement and dire conditions. Immigrants and human rights groups have repeatedly alleged human rights and constitutional violations at the site, including physical abuse, sexual harassment, inedible food and medical neglect. ICE was sued over alleged “dire” conditions earlier this year. At least three people detained at the site have died in ICE custody, including a 55-year-old man whose January death was ruled a homicide after security guards beat him. This year, an internal ICE inspection found a number of deficiencies at the site, including with guards’ use of force. A US government accountability office report also found a series of problems with the facility’s contract, its construction and the conditions. The office made four recommendations to DHS, ICE and the US army. Those recommendations remain “open”, meaning they have not been resolved. “That facility, from my perspective, should not be operational,” Escobar said. “It should have been shut down a long time ago.” During her recent Camp East Montana oversight visit, Escobar pressed for the private contractor running the facility to be held accountable for the recent incidents, not just the detained immigrants deemed responsible. Earlier this year, ICE gave the multi-million-dollar contract for running the facility on its behalf to a new private security company. “The contractor needs to eat those costs [of the damage]. If they were not prepared, if they were unable to control the situation, the American taxpayer should not pay for their incompetence,” Escobar said. “These private contractors are making enormous sums of money. And frankly, there needed to be accountability with this contractor.” The DHS spokesman said that far from closing, Camp East Montana “is upgrading” and claimed that the contractor now running the site was providing more services and “precise quality assurance”. “ICE is always looking at ways to improve our detention facilities to ensure we are providing the best care to illegal aliens in our custody,” the spokesperson said. Amentum Services, a Maryland-based contractor now running the Camp East Montana facility, did not respond to a request for comment. Acquisition Logistics, a small and relatively-unknown company based in Virginia first secured a nearly $1.3bn contract to run the site. Amentum took over this April after previously working as a subcontractor at the site. Meanwhile, there have been further accusations of alleged rights violations at other detention facilities. The Guardian has reported exclusively on a series of force feedings in ICE facilities, including inside two detention centers in Texas. During the first Trump administration, Escobar criticized and investigated ICE’s use of force feeding on hunger strikers in 2019. “It’s a very barbaric practice,” Escobar said. “The rapid expansion of immigration detention, under the [second] Trump administration– and fueled by Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill – it is allowing more and more of this absolutely unacceptable behavior by the federal government to continue.”

title: In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed’s candidacy has split the Jewish community
author: Stephen Starr in Detroit
summary: The Democratic Senate nominee’s views on Israel and comments after a synagogue attack prompted a public debate among Jewish voters
body_text: When Jess Newman heard that Temple Israel in Detroit was attacked last March, her first thoughts went to her extended family. “I grew up going to services there,” she said. “The attack was awful. My Jewish identity is very important to me.” On 12 March, Ayman Ghazali, a naturalized US citizen from Lebanon, drove his truck into the Temple Israel, causing a fire and injuring a security guard. But even amid her anxiety for her family, Newman was startled by the response from some community members. “The reaction to it from people close to it that I know in my family is: ‘We need AK-47s under our beds,’” she recalled. Today Newman, a political organizer who sits on the Ferndale school board, spends about 10 hours a week volunteering for the campaign of Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel who is the Democratic party’s candidate to become US senator for Michigan in November’s midterm elections. “There is a problem with antisemitism,” she says. “I think it is made all that much harder to deal with when you can’t have a sensible conversation about why violence is happening … you cannot divorce violence invited upon people from violence being done around the world.” Newman’s experiences reflect the broader disagreements facing Michigan’s diverse Jewish communities this year. An estimated 130,000 Jewish Americans live in Michigan, where a 2021 study reported that 61% identified with or leaned Democrat and that Jewish adults are less likely to identify or lean Republican (31%) than all Michigan adults (42%). El-Sayed won the Democratic party’s Senate primary last month by just 15,000 votes. In a battleground state, El-Sayed’s unapologetically progressive campaign focuses on affordability rather than conflict in the Middle East, which has drawn ire from Republicans. But his positions on Israel-Palestine, including calling for an end to offensive and defensive military aid from the US, have become the focus of an active campaign to urge Jewish Michiganders to vote for his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers – as well as a counter-effort on El-Sayed’s behalf. *** Just six miles north-west of Newman’s progressive Ferndale neighborhood, Oak Park is the heartbeat of Michigan’s Orthodox Jewish community, home to Jewish retirement homes, synagogues and kosher bakeries. On the eve of the recent Rosh Hashanah holiday, there was a steady stream of customers buying bread and sweet treats from kosher stores as children furiously cycled from the stores to a nearby synagogue. It was here, last April, that antisemitic graffiti was sprayed on the outside a synagogue. “In the Jewish community, I think we have an awareness that it’s not if something is going to happen, it’s when something is going to happen. This isn’t the first incident we’ve had here,” Rabbi Robert Gamer of the Congregation Beth Shalom told CBS Detroit in April. El-Sayid was criticized for comments he made in March about the Temple Israel attack, saying, in part, that “hurt people hurt people”, referring to the Temple Israel attacker. An FBI investigation concluded that the attacker was inspired by Hezbollah. Ghazali’s two brothers, a niece and a nephew, had been killed in an Israeli airstrike in southern Lebanon days before. The Democratic candidate has also drawn criticism for links to Hasan Piker, the leftwing streamer who has become a target for attacks from Republicans and centrist Democrats. In the Democratic primary, El-Sayed lost Oak Park’s Oakland county to Haley Stevens by nearly 20,000 votes – a number larger than his final winning margin. El-Sayed later apologized for those comments, saying that he had jumped too quickly to provide “context” for the attack, “but it wasn’t the time for context”. Still, El-Sayed’s message has particularly resonated with young Jewish Michiganders angered by the variety of challenges facing working people, and aligned with his positions on Israel. Since his primary win, he has made a concerted effort to meet with Jewish leaders, including the Michigan Democratic Jewish caucus, which has not yet endorsed him. Several campaign initiatives reflect divisions among Jewish communities. An open letter supporting El Sayed, signed by Michigan Jews for Democracy, has about 1,000 signatures. Other rabbis and Jewish leaders have formed the Nonnegotiable Michigan campaign, a petition that demands, among other things, that candidates for office support “Jewish sovereignty in Israel”. (El-Sayed has said he supports “equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination” for both Israeli and Palestinians, through whatever political system both peoples choose.) A third initiative is openly calling for Jewish Democrats and independents to back Rogers, claiming: “All of us have felt threatened and alienated by the politics and allies embraced by Abdul El-Sayed.” In June, Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP), a pro-Palestine organization that represents about 750,000 members and supporters nationwide, endorsed El-Sayed in a first for the organization, helping him defeat Stevens, who received tens of millions of dollars from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), the pro-Israel Super Pac. Others joined after the primary results were settled. “After the primary, some of the members of our [T’chiyah] congregation who voted for Stevens started showing up to the Jews for Abdul meetings because they were just like: ‘We don’t totally align with him on [Israel], but we are very clear that the alternative is really bad,’” says Jackson Koeppel, a 33-year-old Detroit-based volunteer with Jews for Abdul, a group critical of Israel, citing El-Sayed’s platform on universal healthcare and getting money out of politics. Last month, Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, asked Aipac not to publicly spend advertising money on his own behalf, acknowledging a growing concern Michigan voters have with the powerful pro-Israel lobbying organization. Polls have put El-Sayed and Rogers in a dead heat. For Josh Whinston, a rabbi at Temple Beth Emeth in Ann Arbor, a reform congregation, it was comments El-Sayed made the morning after his primary win last month that prompted significant concern. “When I hear Dr El-Sayed, the morning after the primary, talk about Israel as bloodthirsty and then in the evening tell me that he cared about my security, that really created such a dissonance in my head,” said Whinston, who has joined the “Nonnegotiable” initiative. He said he viewed the term “bloodthirsty” as playing into an antisemitic trope. At the same time, Whinston, who has met El-Sayed in a one-on-one meeting, says his door is not closed to the idea of voting for the Democrat. “He is an inspiring leader I think he has the potential to do amazing things in our country,” he says. “He is moving in the right direction; he has not moved far enough.” Meanwhile, Republicans and rightwing media have seized on his platform. Last month, vice-president JD Vance spoke personally with a rabbi and a security guard from Temple Israel, who also attended a rally Vance held in nearby Sterling Heights in which the vice-president claimed El-Sayed is “very, very evil”. (Temple Israel declined an interview request from the Guardian.) El-Sayed’s campaign also faces a formidable challenge in the shape of big sums of out-of-state campaign spending. “In Detroit, we have a lot of work to do in terms of getting people excited,” says Newman. Elon Musk has already spent $1m in Michigan on online ads targeting El-Sayed. For his part, Newman, who went on a birthright trip to Israel when she was 18, says the contrast between El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, and Rogers, who with his wife has a net worth of between $7m and $14m, is clear. “He’s principled; he believes in and has actually done work to build better conditions for people in the [Michigan] health departments,” she says. “He’s running a campaign that I can respect; he’s not taking any corporate money, which is a huge piece of this.” • This article was amended on 23 September 2026 to clarify that Abdul El-Sayed is the Democratic party’s candidate to represent Michigan in the US Senate in the midterm elections, rather than a candidate for the Michigan senate.

title: The world freaked out about AI doomsday. Now what?
author: Blake Montgomery
summary: Donald Trump and Xi Jinping will meet each other next week, but it’s unlikely they’ll agree to AI regulation
body_text: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while reading and disagreeing with Jenny Odell’s 2019 book How to Do Nothing. I’m pro-screen time. Today in tech, we’re discussing the upcoming meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, in which AI will likely feature prominently. Trump, Xi, AI Last week, the world freaked out about an AI apocalypse. Now the two most powerful men, running the countries with the two most advanced AI industries, are going to discuss that possible doomsday. Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are set to greet one another on Wednesday and meet for talks in Washington DC, and artificial intelligence will be high on the agenda. Though their meeting reflects concern for AI at the highest levels of government, which is a generally positive sign, early indicators are not signalling that either nation is willing to put regulatory checks on the technology. The US and Chinese leaders have stressed in recent days that a slowdown of AI development is unnecessary. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.” “Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance,” China’s foreign ministry said last week, in a statement that seemingly rejected the possibility of any US-led slowdown. Any AI slowdown would need buy-in from the US and China, but the rival nations see each other as the strongest argument against such a pause. Trump wants AI to go full steam ahead, fortified in that conviction by Silicon Valley leaders who’ve long been wary of Chinese ambitions. Even Dario Amodei, while calling for a global coordinated pause, repeatedly called China a threat. China, meanwhile, sees appeals for a slowdown as a way for the US to solidify American companies’ lead. Would you accept a hobbling proposal from your first-place opponent? That doesn’t mean Beijing shares none of Anthropic’s concerns. Last week, China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework. Included in the updates are risks posed by agents, cybersecurity threats from frontier models and the issue of self-improving AI. Amodei has, likewise, highlighted risks on all three fronts. The combative stance between the trans-Pacific rivals doesn’t mean nothing will happen, Trump’s administration is putting on a positive face in the lead-up to the meeting. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has already met with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, to discuss the threat of powerful AI. He called the talks “very successful”. Bessent and He mulled over an international alert system for AI incidents in the same fashion as nuclear alert systems. The two delegations are set to meet again in two months. “The US has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries, and we want a shared vision of common goals and common threats,” Bessent said. Read more: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario The present recalls past inaction If the US and China can’t agree on AI regulation, it’s unlikely any AI regulation at all will come. A decade of dire warnings have failed to slow the pace of the AI industry. As today’s freak-out cools, the political response seems to be moving the same way. Trump is calling AI doomsday warnings “a HOAX”. Should a safety bill arrive on his desk, it seems unlikely he would sign it. Read more: ‘Godfather of AI’ says tech regulation is nearing Covid-style pivot moment Though the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders has promised to propose a prohibition on extremely capable AI, no bill will pass both chambers of the US Congress in the near future. Last week, the House speaker, Mike Johnson, dismissed the chamber early for its seven-week midterm campaigning recess, likely preventing meaningful progress on AI safety legislation while the nation is focused on the issue. “It is just beyond the pale that Mike Johnson has called off Congress,” said the representative Yassamin Ansari, a Democrat from Arizona, on CNN. “We’re going home for seven weeks. And during that time, we’re going to see this frontier AI technology continue to evolve, continue to cause damage. And it’s going to get to a point where it will be impossible to go backward if we don’t move quickly now.” Read more: Why a decade of doomsday warnings failed to slow the AI race The AI industry is not united in its calls for regulation, dampening the possibility further. Though Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have invited new restrictions, and they nearly came to a joint legally binding safety testing agreement, they are but one powerful faction within their business. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has Trump’s ear, as does the influential adviser David Sacks; both are in favor of accelerating AI development. Huang said on Sunday that “2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that’s going to be the end of the world. Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible.” Read more: ‘An out-of-touch Silicon Valley radical’: meet Trump’s AI whisperer pushing for limited regulation Europe, which has played the role of global tech regulator, has little leverage in the debate despite its high concern for safety. Ursula Von der Leyen invited frontier labs to discussions in Europe about pacing the frontier of development, which garnered little response. Read more: Why Europe has been absent from the great AI safety debate In 2023, Geoffrey Hinton, a so-called “godfather of AI” and a Nobel laureate, left Google over his own fears of the risks that AI could be used by bad actors and one day harm humanity. Unlike many whistleblowers, Hinton’s resignation inspired a significant response from lawmakers: an executive order in the US, a congressional hearing and the passage of the EU’s AI Act. Yoshua Bengio, another godfather of AI, told the Guardian much the same last week. Bengio said governments are nearing a Covid-esque moment of rapid action. He’s “more optimistic than many observers because I see the public moving”, he said. Bengio preached his optimism after the Canadian and German governments announced funding of up to £160m for his non-profit organisation, which is dedicated to creating an “honest AI” that will act as a guardrail against rogue agents. I would be optimistic if I were handed £160m. Without such a payout, I am not. The wider TechScape Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘What, if anything, can people like me do about it?’ ‘Just cut the wires’: why UK conspiracy theorists are destroying traffic scanners Trump to create ‘AI Force’ to monitor technology as fears over out-of-control agents grow Google says its Gemini AI model hacked three other companies Meta ordered to remove UK deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguards Feeling overwhelmed by the AI doom loop? Here’s the essential reading list to make sense of it all ‘RAMageddon’: tech crunch hikes the price of your next iPhone by £100

title: Republican calls for Senate investigation of Trump Jr wedding paid for by Russian oligarch
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Putin ally helped cover cost of renting private island in the Bahamas for wedding of Trump Jr and Bettina Anderson
body_text: A Republican senator has accused Donald Trump Jr of corruption and demanded a Senate investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of his recent wedding in the Bahamas. John Curtis, of Utah, wrote to the leaders of the US Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday, urging them to subpoena Trump Jr over his business dealings, his relationships with foreign individuals, gifts he has received – and any occasions where his connection to his father, Donald Trump, “was invoked or understood to provide value”. Trump Jr’s wedding warrants the kind of scrutiny Republicans once trained on Hunter Biden, the son of Joe Biden, Curtis said. “A toaster is a wedding gift. A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else,” he wrote in a social media post accompanying the letter to the committee. “Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden’s foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now.” The push follows reporting by ProPublica that Umar Kremlev, the Russian boxing official with close ties to Vladimir Putin, helped cover the cost of renting a private island and staging a fireworks display for the wedding of Trump Jr and Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas in May. Bettina Trump later described Kremlev on Instagram as a “dear friend” who had generously hosted two nights of post-wedding celebrations. Donald Trump, who did not attend the ceremony, defended Kremlev’s involvement but said he was told by Trump Jr that the money would eventually be reimbursed, though explained that giving a wedding party as a gift is “totally allowed” and is also “very common”. It is not the first time Trump Jr’s conduct has drawn scrutiny over ties to Russia. He was a central figure in the Robert Mueller investigation that followed the 2016 election, after it emerged he had attended a Trump Tower meeting with a Russian lawyer who had promised damaging material on Hillary Clinton. The call for a formal committee inquiry marks one of the sharper breaks with the president by a sitting Republican senator. Curtis first flagged the wedding payment as problematic on Friday, calling it “corruption” in a video posted online and promising further comment. He was elected to the Senate in 2024, pledging not to shy away from disagreements with Trump. His letter, addressed to the committee chair, Chuck Grassley of Iowa, and its top Democrat, Dick Durbin of Illinois, lands amid signs of broader unease among Republicans over Trump’s standing heading into November’s US midterm elections, with the party facing pressure over the war in Iran, high gas prices and slipping poll numbers. Republicans in the House of Representatives spent much of 2023 and 2024 investigating whether Hunter Biden traded on his father’s name in his overseas business dealings, an effort that produced a report alleging a conspiracy to enrich the Biden family, but never resulted in impeachment articles reaching a House vote. The Bidens denied wrongdoing throughout. “‘Trust us’ was not enough then,” wrote Curtis, “and it is not enough now.”

title: AOC refuses to rule out run against Senate leader Chuck Schumer
author: Ariana Baio
summary: ‘I’ll cross that bridge when I get to it,’ the progressive US representative says
body_text: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive Democratic congresswoman, has refused to rule out a potential run against the party’s Senate leader Chuck Schumer amid mounting speculation around her political ambitions. When asked by the New York Times whether she would challenge Schumer in 2028, when his current term is up, Ocasio-Cortez declined to exclude the possibility – even if Democrats win back the Senate majority. “We’re working hard to have that problem,”, Ocasio-Cortez, 36, told the newspaper of a Democratic majority in the Senate, which she called called “the best possible problem we could have as a country”, adding: “And I’ll cross that bridge when I get to it.” The New York congresswoman emphasized that any decision she makes would be personal, saying: “I don’t think that my decisions would come down to deference.” Ocasio-Cortez has been repeatedly cited as a potential challenger to Schumer, 75, and possibly a Democratic presidential candidate in 2028. She has built a significant profile since defeating a top incumbent Democrat to win her seat in the House of Representatives, representing an area of New York City, in 2018. Her progressive policies have resonated with younger Democrats, women and Hispanic voters, according to recent polling from the New York Times/Siena University. She has become a leading figure in rallying anti-Trump voters. She has also raised more money than many of her House colleagues, securing more than $32m since 2025. As of June, Ocasio-Cortez had more than $15m in cash, according to Federal Election Commission data. But Ocasio-Cortez is also polarizing, with roughly 41% of likely voters and 75% of Republicans finding her unfavorable. That combination has made her an easy target for Republican attacks, particularly from the US president. Though her name is floated as a potential 2028 presidential contender, Ocasio-Cortez has been elusive about her plans, often leaving the door open to a run while acknowledging the hurdles she faces. “I’m not naive to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina,” Ocasio-Cortez told the New York Times. “And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities.” Taking on Schumer could be Ocasio-Cortez’s first step to fulfilling greater political ambitions. Earlier this year, a survey from the liberal firm Data for Progress found that 55% of likely Democratic voters said they would support or lean toward supporting Ocasio-Cortez, while only 36% would back Schumer.

title: Trump calls on allies to enforce ‘complete economic isolation of Iran’ in UN speech
author: Andrew Roth in New York
summary: US president threatens to ‘annihilate’ Tehran and dismisses threat from AI as a ‘hoax’ in bellicose address
body_text: Donald Trump has called on nations to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices, as he gave a bellicose defence of his administration’s foreign policy and decision to strike Iran. “I call on all nations to help to enforce the complete economic isolation of Iran,” Trump said in a speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday. “If we stand united, we will soon see a world free of the last 51-year menace of Iranian terror … and oil prices will come plummeting down even lower than they were at the start of the conflict.” Trump’s call for international unity on Iran – he also said he may “annihilate” the country – comes as numerous US allies have complained about soaring energy prices and growing international instability during his US administration. On the first day of the high-level week of the UN general assembly in New York, Trump also reiterated that the US would not seek to rein in the development of artificial intelligence, seeking to rebrand it as “superintelligence” and saying warnings about the threats from out-of-control AI development were a “hoax”. “I’m ⁠not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than ‌the Industrial Revolution,” he said. In an address that mostly rehashed his stump speech talking points, Trump announced that the US would build two new military bases in Greenland as part of an agreement with the government of Denmark, after a year of geopolitical haggling that has unsettled the Nato alliance. “We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent, and also Europe and other places,” Trump said in announcing the two “major” military bases. “No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland any more, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval.” He denied that the US was running short of critical munitions (“we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using”), attacked the international criminal court as a “rogue organisation” and claimed once again that he was close to settling the war in Ukraine. But this was a less bellicose speech than the one he gave last year, when he excoriated the UN and told European allies that their countries were “going to hell” because of their migration policies. At one point on Tuesday, he stopped and turned around to thank the UN security council for condemning Iranian attacks on shipping in the strait of Hormuz. During the speech, he repeated a threat to destroy Iran, which he has made dozens of times since the US and Israel launched joint strikes in February. “I have a big decision to make: will a deal be made with Iran that let them rebuild and create a far greater country than ever was before,” he said. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill or destroy people and continents?” Trump denied that he was under political pressure to end the war and said the midterm elections would have absolutely no influence on his decision-making around the conflict. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realise is that I’m not running,” he said. “It doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.” Iran has maintained a stranglehold over energy shipping through the strait of Hormuz since early in the war, and global oil prices have also been driven up by the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, where Kyiv has successfully targeted Moscow’s refining capacity. Trump used the speech to take a pot shot at Cuba, calling the country “an absolutely failed state” – prompting the Cuban delegation to walk out of the hall as the president continued to criticise the US’s neighbour. Trump went on to say his administration was seeking “a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba”. Cuba’s delegation head, Bruno Rodríguez, later rejected Trump’s remarks as “falsehoods” and “slander”. Trump defended the US move to arrest the former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro in a midnight raid, and the subsequent oil deal he struck with Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro’s successor, who has proved much more amenable to US demands and agreed to a deal sharing the country’s vast oil wealth with the US. “To the victor belong the spoils,” Trump said. Trump’s New York itinerary is a crib sheet of the ways that his presidency has upended global politics in the last two years. After his speech, Trump signed an agreement with Denmark over the future of Greenland, which Trump has claimed could be dominated by Russia and China despite few signs that was the case. Later, he is expected to meet the Ukrainian leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom he is expected to press along with Russia to conclude an energy truce to help assuage soaring prices on diesel mainly prompted by Tehran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz. Trump will also meet Gulf leaders, who have been affected by Iran’s retaliation to the joint US-Israeli attack, and then will have a pull-aside with the US-backed Rodríguez of Venezuela, another major oil exporter.

title: Will anyone topple Infantino? How Fifa president is trying to cling on after World Cup sell-off debacle
author: Matt Hughes
summary: Fifa president continues to lobby for re-election despite no other candidates coming forward to challenge him
body_text: For Gianni Infantino there is no international break. The Fifa president is widely expected to make an appearance at the United Nations general assembly this week in New York, where he will lobby heads of state for their federations’ support as he continues his campaign to be re-elected next year. Infantino has not been idle during the lull since Fifa abandoned its World Cup sell-off plan last month, instead crisscrossing the globe on a private jet provided by Qatar Airways as part of its sponsorship deal with world football’s governing body. From his strongholds in Doha, Rabat and Miami, Infantino has also visited Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Kyrgyzstan and various other countries, his trips often coinciding with the approval of funding for development projects worth millions of dollars. His would-be opponents have been conspicuous by their silence. Whether Qatar Airways facilitating Infantino’s re-election campaign should be considered legitimate Fifa presidential business is a moot point, which neatly encapsulates the huge incumbency bias that will benefit Infantino if a vote takes place at the Fifa congress in March. That ballot appears to be in doubt, with multiple sources involved in the push to remove Infantino telling the Guardian they are running out of hope of finding a candidate to beat him. Although dozens of the 200 member associations that had submitted letters of endorsement for Infantino withdrew them after the emergence of his Fifa Forward Enterprise sale plan in July, the prevailing view is that the silent majority remain steadfastly behind him. A meeting with the Caribbean Football Union, where funding projects were approved, may have splintered the vote at Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – and there are increasing concerns that the European alliance may not be watertight. “As long as Gianni is running, I don’t think anyone else will raise their hand,” one source said. “They would effectively be running against Fifa the institution. Fifa declared his candidacy, provides staff, aeroplanes and cars, even a personal video team. “If he doesn’t step down before March, the election will not be contested. Uefa and others could stage a boycott so the victory would be tainted, but Gianni will win a clear majority of whoever shows up.” Infantino first declared at the April congress in Vancouver his intention to seek a fourth and final term of office. Fifa statutes limit presidents to three full terms but under a recent change he will be permitted a fourth because his first term lasted three years, rather than the usual four, after his 2016 election to replace the disgraced Sepp Blatter. The 56-year-old reasserted his intention to stand after attending the first match of the Under-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland a fortnight ago. That came via a statement issued by Fifa’s media team. As it stands Infantino does not have an opponent, despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to go. Beyond the obvious difficulties of taking on an incumbent who controls the machinery of office and funding budgets – the last Fifa president beaten at the ballot box was Sir Stanley Rous in 1974 – there are specific reasons why none of the would-be candidates have declared. The most credible challenger is regarded as Concacaf’s president, Victor Montagliani, but the Canadian is committed to standing for re-election at his confederation, and the vote is due to take place in February. Standing in both elections is not regarded as feasible, and Montagliani is understandably reluctant to walk away from Concacaf in favour of fighting a potentially losing battle against Infantino. The AFC president, Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, was beaten by Infantino in the 2016 election, the only time Infantino has faced an electoral opponent, and is further hamstrung by the fact that his confederation’s main powers, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, are backing Infantino. Qatar’s position would also appear to rule out a challenge from Nasser al-Khelaifi, the chair of European Football Clubs, and an openly European move led by Uefa’s president, Aleksander Ceferin, would have no chance of success. Ceferin, in any case, has his own presidential contest in March to focus on. To compound the difficulties for Infantino’s would-be challengers, any election would be a secret ballot, making any promises from member associations during the campaign period all but worthless. As a result, Uefa is focusing most of its efforts on legal avenues to remove Infantino, accusing him of “criminal mismanagement” in a 56-page document lodged with US state courts in New York, Miami and Colorado last month seeking the disclosure of all documents relating to FFE. Fifa responded strongly the week after Uefa made its legal complaint, filing a response in New York in which it sought to block the discovery process. Its submission accused Uefa of mounting a smear campaign against Infantino in the absence of any evidence of wrongdoing. Fifa’s submission said: “Uefa’s application suffers from a fundamental defect: Uefa seeks discovery in aid of a foreign criminal proceeding that does not exist and that Uefa admittedly lacks the authority to initiate. “While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of Uefa’s smear campaign against Fifa and its leadership.” Although there is widespread confidence that at least one of the three jurisdictions will grant discovery, the process grants Fifa the right of appeal, so there is little prospect of new material being made public before the 18 November deadline for presidential candidates to come forward. An initial decision from the courts is expected next month, but an appeal from the losing party appears inevitable whatever the outcome. “The issue with discovery is that it takes a long time,” a source said. “It’s likely to run beyond the date of the election in March. If the process is under way by then, Fifa congress could decide to wait until we find out what the courts discover and postpone the election. But there would still have to be a vote on that.” Uefa’s not-so-secret hope is that the discovery process finds evidence that FFE was deliberately undervalued at $20bn (£15bn) to provide a guaranteed future windfall for Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital, which had seemingly agreed to pay $4.2bn for 21% of the new commercial venture, giving it a significant share of future Fifa revenues. Thrive subsequently bought 20% of the LA Lakers last month as part of a larger transaction with the former Disney chief executive Bob Iger that valued the NBA franchise at $12.5bn, a deal that has further highlighted Infantino’s valuation of the World Cup. Fifa’s revenues for the four years to 2026 were $15bn, a figure projected to grow to $18bn over the next four-year cycle owing to larger broadcast deals, without accounting for any expansion of the World Cup and Club World Cup, which remains on the agenda. A corporate fraud lawyer said that undervaluing FFE could potentially constitute a criminal offence by Fifa, a case Uefa would take to the Swiss courts. “If you’re doing a deal that is way off market then you are deceiving the stakeholders, in this case the member associations,” the legal source said. “That is criminal. If Uefa has a criminal case that’s where it will be. It’s about how the valuation was done, by whom, and what conflicts were there. “All of that should come out during disclosure. If beyond that there were personal deals being struck on the side, that could also be criminal. All those details should be disclosed.” Beyond the $20bn valuation, the identity of the would-be investors and Fifa’s claim that it would retain control over governance, very little has been made public about the development of FFE, with a sales deck produced by the US bank JP Morgan containing no details of a tender process, voting rights or future exit terms. A senior investment banker who has been involved in similar deals said it is inconceivable such details were not agreed before Thrive agreed to commit $4bn, albeit much of the funding was due from other investors. “I don’t think Thrive was going to be involved with Fifa for the next 25 years,” they said. “This looks like a quick in-and-out play. The plan would have been to buy it low and sell it high. I think the investors saw an amazing deal.” There is no evidence of any wrongdoing or criminality on the part of the any of the parties involved in the proposed FFE deal. Thrive has revealed little about its intentions beyond a statement issued last month in which it presented FFE as a proposal to be voted on by Fifa’s members, rather than a done deal. Significantly, however, it also expressed an element of regret at getting involved given the political backlash, which many within football have interpreted as an attempt to distance the firm from Infantino. “It was an idea that every member association would vote on, not an obligation or determination,” Thrive said. “While we stand behind the motivations of FFE, we failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football, and the lengths some would go to. Thrive has a long track record of being a partner to all constituents. Had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved.” Uefa and Concacaf, in particular, appear prepared to dig in for the long haul, despite concerns that Infantino will be re-elected. The two confederations are continuing to work together to develop a unified Nations League competition, revealed by the Guardian last month, and last week wrote a joint letter to Fifa demanding that it release funds from its $6bn reserves to fund an additional payment of at least $10m to each of its 211 member associations during the next four-year cycle. Some sort of payment appears inevitable given Infantino promised to provide $20m more to the member associations via FFE, but Uefa and Concacaf are hoping Infantino does not accrue political and electoral credit for it. Ceferin and Montagliani are expected to meet at next week’s general assembly of the European Football Clubs in Copenhagen, where Infantino may also make an appearance. Infantino addressed the EFC’s 900 members at last year’s EFC meeting in Rome, where his suggestion that more international tournaments should take place during European winters to accommodate the global south caused controversy, although that pales compared with his pronouncements and plans since. Uefa has made one accommodation with Fifa by withdrawing its threat to boycott the Under-20 Women’s World Cup that finishes on Sunday, and Infantino has agreed to its demand to commission an external governance review, which he communicated in a letter to the member associations this week. Suggestions that this move could lead to a truce with Uefa are given short shrift by those close to the leadership. Despite the electoral gloom, those agitating for change are also clinging to memories of the fate of Infantino’s predecessor, Blatter, who was forced to resign in 2015 amid an FBI corruption investigation days after winning a fifth term against Prince Ali bin Al Hussein of Jordan. Blatter himself has never been charged in relation to the investigation. For those looking to remove Infantino, the presidential election is not necessarily the end of the process. “This is a fight to the death now and we have to keep going,” one source said. “The fact that Gianni is the only guy running at the moment does not mean it’s over. Look what happened to Blatter. He was re-elected in May 2015, but was gone in June. Eventually the truth will come out.”

title: Call it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King Baby
author: John Crace
summary: Meeting at the UN in New York, the UK prime minister showed signs he can handle trash-talking President Trump
body_text: How do you deal with a problem like The Donald? The simple answer is that you don’t. You can’t. The normal rules of political engagement don’t apply. The US president is like a five-year-old child with the world as his set of toys: a King Baby. Nothing is ever constant or predictable. What’s agreed one day can be forgotten the next. Any deal can be interrupted with a temper tantrum at any time. Trying to second-guess Donald Trump is a fool’s errand. So the primary aim of Andy Burnham’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump was to get out alive with his – and the UK’s – self-respect intact. To take no incoming damage. And whatever he did, not to offer the president a third state visit. Keir Starmer never really lived that one down. Putting out on the first date only encourages the other person to think you’re a pushover. The hoped-for result was a pleasant and almost forgettable bilateral meeting at the United Nations general assembly in New York. It was only scheduled to last 30 minutes, so more like speed dating – one step up from two world leaders shooting the breeze while getting to know each other. Where differences could be acknowledged without causing a major diplomatic incident. All of which falls pretty comfortably within Burnham’s skill set. Andy’s stock in trade is an easy-going self-confidence. He’s comfortable in his skin in a way that Keir never was. Or maybe the artifice is just better concealed. He understands that trash-talking is all in a day’s work for most politicians. In the past, he may have called Trump all sorts of things. Poisoned politics. Someone who would be unwelcome in Manchester. Well, that was then, this is now. Things change. Just like Trump. Now he would be welcoming the US president to the G20 in Manchester next year. Who would have guessed? And it all looked to have gone pretty much to plan. Maybe Trump also wanted this meeting to go well. His poll ratings in the US are dire, the midterm elections look like trouble and The Donald needs all the friends he can get – even if he had just tried to lose a few more of them in his speech to the UN earlier. A speech that had been even wilder and madder than many of his previous ones. Still, at least he hadn’t threatened to invade a Nato country this time. And it’s always good to learn of countries you never knew existed. Anyone for “Kazakhistan”? Taking questions with Trump afterwards, Andy didn’t look quite as self-assured as usual – he seemed very much on edge – but who could blame him for that? This was his first time as prime minister at the UN and The Donald always has it in him to blow any meeting out of the water. It was Andy who went first, trying to remember what they had just talked about. It had all been a bit of a blur. That was it – they had talked about Iran. In his earlier speech, The Donald had suggested it was a toss-up whether he came to a deal with Iran or whether he annihilated it. On the whole, Andy was in favour of a deal. Quickly if possible. The war was causing a massive hit to the cost of living. He chose not to highlight the irony of Trump calling on Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop bombing Russian refineries as it was playing havoc with the cost of oil. Pots and kettles and all that. Burnham then bigged up the deal with Saudi Arabia. The one where we send one plane to refuel Saudi fighters that don’t need refuelling because their targets are only a few hundred miles away. Finally, he mentioned the Falklands. By now The Donald was looking a wee bit bored. Unsure where the Falklands are or why they had been talking about them. Perhaps he was wondering why he was looking even more orange than usual. Then came the actual questions. Was Andy a man with whom Trump could do business? Sure he was, said The Donald. Andy was a “great businessperson”. Really? And by the way he was a lot nicer and a lot more talented than his predecessor. Poor Keir. Not only is he no longer prime minister, but he’s still getting rubbished at meetings he would have been attending. He really can’t buy a break. But that’s Trump for you. Andy shouldn’t relax too much. That will be him getting trashed one day. On we went. Immigration. Burnham deftly trying to give credit to the immigrants working in the NHS while going on to condemn illegal immigration. Trump was just dreaming of walls and border guards. What about patriotism? Which did the prime minister prefer: Manchester or Manhattan? By now Andy was feeling a bit more self-assured that the whole thing wasn’t about to go tits up, so he joked about the president calling Manchester “some town”. Trump just shrugged. It still is just some town to him, but he wasn’t going to labour the point. He was trying to be on his best behaviour. For a five-year-old. Then a question on the sanctions imposed on illegal settlements in the West Bank. Trump looked bewildered. Had never heard of them. Andy insisted he had personally called the White House to inform the president of the UK’s intentions. It had been done to maintain the possibility of a two-state solution and to restore trust in politics. This was more like the authentic Burnham. Standing up for what he believed. Trump said nothing. Maybe he actually did recognise the prime minister as an equal. There was just time for a mention of the proposed handover of the Chagos Islands – It’s a terrible idea,” said Trump unhelpfully, to which Andy gulped “We’re looking at it” – before we closed with Trump insisting relations with the UK had never been better and that Britain was a country on the up. Some of us could distinctly remember The Donald saying the UK was on the slide only last week. But who’s counting? Then a minder called the impromptu presser to a close and kicked everyone out of the room. Trump looked blank. He often does. Burnham looked relieved. He had got out of his first encounter with the president alive. Both he and the UK were still intact. Chalk this one up as a win.

title: Trump says he backs diesel export ban to curb soaring energy costs
author: Guardian staff and agencies
summary: But industry trade group says plan would backfire and lead to even higher prices for gasoline
body_text: Donald Trump on Tuesday said he backed ⁠the idea of a ban on diesel exports, which some US politicians are calling for ⁠as a way ⁠to curb the soaring cost of energy. Diesel prices have rallied in Europe and the US to ⁠record highs as wars in Iran and Ukraine sharply cut exports from some of the biggest producers ⁠such as Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. A gallon of diesel fuel in the US was $6.53 on Tuesday, the highest average on record and more than 75% higher than a year ago. “I’ve said let’s not send ‌out the diesel. ‌We make a lot of diesel … I’ve called for it. ‌I’ve called for it within my people,” Trump told reporters before a meeting with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, speaking at the same meeting, said: “We’re examining whether it’s feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work.” On Sunday, Trump urged Zelenskyy to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries over concerns that they could further push up prices, the Financial Times reported. On social media, Trump wrote that Russia “unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry”. Some Republican Senate candidates in the most competitive midterm races called for the administration to implement the export ban to try to alleviate high costs for Americans. “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” wrote the US representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican who is in a competitive Senate race in Iowa, on X. “We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices.” In a statement, the American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers trade group said that an export ban would “backfire”, noting that domestic refiners would have to reduce production and “producing less diesel also means producing less gasoline”. Trump said he and Zelenskiy would ⁠discuss Ukrainian attacks on refining sites in Russia. “It is a serious hit on the Russians. It’s also a serious hit on the price of diesel,” said ‌Trump, who also told reporters the two leaders would discuss working out a solution to end Russia’s war in Ukraine. “I think it’s going to happen,” Trump said, of a potential solution to the war. Reuters contributed reporting
