title: Nazi jokes and ‘cum trophies’: meet the Texas gunfluencer who could soon represent Uvalde
author: Ed Pilkington
summary: Brandon Herrera, a YouTuber known for making outrageous pro-gun statements, is the frontrunner to represent a district devastated by mass shootings
body_text: The video begins with Brandon Herrera staring intently into the camera. He is filming himself in a hotel room seated between twin beds, his black hair slicked back and beard neatly trimmed. He is wearing a T-shirt branded with his trademark nickname, “The AK Guy”, above the image of a semi-automatic rifle primed for action. Three days earlier, on 3 August 2019, a white nationalist armed with a semi-automatic firearm not dissimilar to the one stamped across Herrera’s chest entered a busy Walmart store in the Texas border city of El Paso and opened fire. Within minutes the shooter had unloaded about 90 rounds, killing 23 people and injuring 22 more. With the massacre still dominating headlines, most public figures were limiting themselves to vanilla expressions of “thoughts and prayers”. Not so Herrera. He opened his video with a warning: what viewers were about to hear might sound “a little harsh”. But, he assured them, it was “data driven” and came from “a place of empathy”. Then he said: “With these terrible mass shootings, you should be really glad that some of these people are using guns to do this … I think we are fortunate that these people are using guns.” Had the perpetrator of the El Paso massacre used a truck, or a fertiliser bomb, the death toll might have been much higher, Herrera opined. He then attempted to back up the argument with statistics: the average victim count in mass shootings is 15; the Oklahoma City bombing killed 168. Such sophistry could not disguise his core argument, however. With the blood barely dry on the Walmart floor, Herrera was urging his viewers to celebrate the choice of weapon used in the carnage – a military-style AR-15 semi-automatic rifle. Herrera, 30, has made a name for himself producing such extreme out-of-the-box pro-gun statements. It is what launched him as a prominent “gunfluencer” with 4.27m subscribers to his YouTube channel, where his videos have been viewed almost 860m times. And now, he is the frontrunner in the race to represent the border district of south-west Texas in November’s midterm elections. Texas’s congressional district 23 is being closely watched as potentially decisive in the battle to control the House of Representatives through Donald Trump’s final two years in the White House. Democrats are hoping that such an extreme candidate, even by Texas’s standards, could be vulnerable at the ballot box. They aim to flip the seat that has been in Republican hands since 2015. Should he win the midterm election in Texas’s congressional district 23, Herrera will take what he calls his “second amendment absolutism” to Washington, with possible ramifications for nationwide gun laws and debate. Locally, the implications are even more poignant. It would mean that a Republican committed to loosening America’s already lax gun laws would become the voice in Congress for those who live in the outskirts of El Paso, the city left devastated by that 2019 Walmart mass shooting. More chillingly still, Herrera would also represent the town of Uvalde where, in May 2022, an 18-year-old former student killed 19 children and two teachers. Shannon Watts, the founder of the gun safety group Moms Demand Action, has been a target of Herrera’s aggressive use of social media. Should he win, she says, there could be long-lasting consequences. “His idea that somehow we should be grateful that firearms are being used in mass killings is a very cynical ploy to numb people to gun violence, to make them expect it and even accept it. The more Brandon Herreras we elect to Congress, the more likely that will be our destiny.” *** Herrera has been presenting himself on the campaign trail as a Trump-endorsed “America First” Republican. He has promised the more than half a million voters scattered across the sprawling, majority-Latino district that he will impose no new taxes, double down on the border crackdown and oppose government funding for abortion. But it was guns – and specifically the Uvalde school shooting – that brought him into politics. Herrera grew up in a military family in Fayetteville, North Carolina, and dropped out of college to build his own firearms manufacturing business, focusing on the growing market for semi-automatic rifles. He spent years developing his own spin on the Soviet Kalashnikov rifle, the AK-47. He scaled up the weapon so that it was capable of taking huge 0.50-caliber cartridges, ammunition developed for Browning heavy machine guns more than a century ago. He called his invention the AK-50, and began marketing it through his company, The AK Guy Inc. Citing frustrations with state-wide Covid restrictions, Herrera relocated the company to San Antonio, Texas, in 2020. Two years later, Uvalde became the site of one of the worst school shootings in American history. The massacre lasted 77 minutes, the shooter killing his victims at close range as police held back for more than an hour before they finally broke into the classroom and killed him. Riding the ensuing wave of revulsion, Joe Biden signed into law the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, which strengthened background checks for buyers under 21 and tightened restrictions on firearm possession for some domestic-abuse offenders. Eric Ruben, an expert on gun policy at the SMU Dedman school of law in Dallas, Texas, says that Uvalde “jolted Congress into passing its first major piece of gun safety legislation in a quarter of a century”. Herrera had a starkly different response. Furious that Tony Gonzales, the Republican congressman representing Uvalde, had backed Biden’s Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, Herrera decided to challenge him for his seat. “If you vote against our interests, if you vote against gun rights,” he warned Gonzales in 2024, “we will primary you, and we will take your fucking job.” He did challenge Gonzales that year, losing to the incumbent narrowly, and was repeating the effort this April when Gonzales abruptly resigned from Congress in a sex scandal. His departure has cleared the way for Herrera to claim the Republican nomination. He is now free to blast his extreme view of gun rights across Uvalde, across the district, through the state of Texas and, should he be successful, nationwide. Energised by his vast YouTube following and the large sums it passes his way, Herrera is in a position to weaponise his gun rights absolutism. He has vowed to resolutely oppose any new gun safety laws, including raising the age of ownership of an AR-15-style weapon from 18 to 21 or introducing so-called “red flag” laws that allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people who pose a threat to themselves or others. Both measures have been championed by families of Uvalde victims, some of whom have devoted themselves to pushing for stricter gun laws in the hope of preventing other mass shootings. Veronica Mata, a founder of the gun safety group Lives Robbed who lost her 10-year-old daughter, Tess, in Uvalde, has put it this way: “Just like we can never turn around and see our daughters again, we’re not going to turn around and walk away.” *** To people outside Texas, and beyond America, one of the state’s enduring mysteries is its fierce loyalty to the most extreme form of gun rights, especially in the wake of such human suffering. There are more than 1m gun licenses in Texas – twice as much as the next state, Florida – with about half of all households in possession of at least one weapon. But as Ruben, the law professor, points out, until the 1990s Texas was relatively restrictive in its gun laws. In 1995, George W Bush, then governor, signed a law allowing licensed Texans to carry concealed handguns in public. He said it would make Texas a “safer place”, an argument that meshed well with the state’s culture of rugged individualism. Herrera’s position echoes that logic: he has argued that the way to protect children is to hire more armed security officers and turn schools into “hard targets”. Since then, Texas’s policies have taken a pro-gun turn in lock step with the tightening grip of an increasingly hard-right Republican party. “Texas has largely tracked the broader effort of the gun rights movement to relax policies on firearms,” Ruben said. And yet, Texans are not universally wedded to the idea of firearms supremacy. A 2025 opinion survey by the Hobby school of public affairs at the University of Houston found that 85% of Texans support raising the age of buying an AR-15-style rifle from 18 to 21. The reform is especially relevant to Uvalde, given that the shooter legally bought two AR-style rifles with 30-round magazines just days after his 18th birthday. The same survey showed a clear majority of Texans wanting firmer background checks on gun buyers, a ban on all AR-15 style rifles, and supporting red flag laws. After the El Paso mass shooting, Republican lawmakers introduced permitless carry, allowing anyone to pack a concealed, loaded handgun in public without a licence or training. It was the polar opposite of the gun safety measures they had promised immediately after the massacre. The law was the end result of an intense lobbying campaign from hard-right gun activists. When he signed permitless carry into law in June 2021, the Republican governor Greg Abbott did not refer to the El Paso shooting. Rather, he presented it as a defiant act to stop the federal government taking Texans’ guns, arguing that arming yourself was a form of self-defense “against attacks by others”. Herrera wants a similar law to be imposed across the country. He wants what he calls “concealed carry reciprocity”. It would override regulations in states that take a more stringent approach to gun safety. Watts, the Moms Demand Action founder, described the end result Herrera is seeking: “His goal is that if you can carry a gun in Texas, no questions asked, then you should be able to carry that firearm down into the New York City subway.” *** Shannon Watts had already experienced Herrera’s particular style of political combat first-hand. He unloaded a stream of obscene invective at her on X in January 2023. Speaking directly to her in a video posted on the platform, he ridiculed the group she had founded. Rather than debate her on gun policy, he opted for vulgar phrases drawn from the pornography industry. “Just because you let somebody creampie you doesn’t mean I have to give a shit about your political opinions,” he said. Referring to her role as a mother and an activist, he continued: “The fact that you kept your cum trophy doesn’t make you any less wrong about the dumb shit that you say.” Watts told the Guardian that she was unsurprised by his virulent attack, as she has been frequently assailed over the years by male gun rights activists. “It has always been about misogyny. How dare a woman and a mother use her voice. That strikes at the heart of every gun extremist, that women could take away their manhood.” Herrera’s ascent and its impact on the gun discourse bears comparison to what Trump has done to the Republican establishment. Herrera and other “guntubers” have filled the void left by the self-implosion of the once almost monopolistic National Rifle Association (NRA), the gun rights group that held an iron grip on Republican politicians and used that power to resist public safety measures. Over the past few years, the NRA has been badly weakened by financial scandals and internal disputes. Into that vacuum has stepped a plethora of even harder-line gun-rights groups and social media influencers: louder, more brazen and pushing at the boundaries of a second-amendment free-for-all. The Guardian repeatedly asked the Herrera campaign whether the candidate would explain his policy stance in an interview, but received no reply. We followed up with a list of detailed questions about his past comments and current positions, including his reductivist view of a child as a “cum trophy”, but that also went unanswered. He did agree to talk to the New York Times recently, swatting away criticism of the base language he uses on the videos and in social media posts by presenting it as a “comedy performance”. Then there’s the company that Herrera keeps. He has been endorsed by Kyle Rittenhouse, the gun rights activist who, then 17, shot dead two men and injured another amid 2020 street protests in Kenosha, Wisconsin. (He was later acquitted of homicide.) Days after the Kenosha incident, Herrera had made another of his “jokes” on video – this time about the death of Rittenhouse’s victims. “Good luck, kid. You minted some good commies,” he said, adding that he was not encouraging anybody to go “get themselves into some shit … it’s not worth it.” The duo have now campaigned together and fired a machine gun in unison out of a helicopter. But sometimes, even some of his followers recoil from the “edgy” humour. One of the remarks that has drawn the strongest condemnation came on the Unsubscribe podcast, when he said he often thought about “putting a gun in my mouth, so I’m basically an honorary veteran”. In 2023, the latest year for which records are available, 4,690 US military veterans died by suicide using a gun. In 2025, more than 28,000 people in the wider US population died by firearm suicide. Another disturbing “joke” he has made relate to the Nazis and the Holocaust. In a 2022 video viewed 2.3m times, he calls the MP 40, the submachine gun used by the Germans in the second world war, “the original ghetto blaster”. Later in the video, he and an associate goosestep to the sound of Ericka, the military marching song adopted by the Waffen SS. The Nazi references were not the only evidence of Herrera’s flirtation with far-right historical imagery. The news outlet Jewish Insider uncovered private videos produced by a younger Herrera in North Carolina on behalf of the Fayetteville chapter of the Sons of Confederate Veterans. The group has promoted the “Lost Cause” narrative which reframes the civil war as a struggle over states’ rights rather than slavery. Herrera described SCV as an “historical honor society dedicated to preserving confederate heritage”, without mentioning its longstanding links with white supremacist groups. His involvement with neo-Confederacy activity continued until at least 2019, the newspaper reported. Such an unsettling back catalogue has provoked objections to his candidacy even from within Texas conservative circles. Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist based in Austin, challenged Herrera by saying there should be zero tolerance for making light about Nazi Germany. “I don’t think the Holocaust is something we should be joking about,” he said. “I don’t think we should be singing the song of the stormtroopers.” Steinhauser told the Guardian that anything perceived as antisemitic was likely to play negatively with Texas Republicans and independent voters, both of whom tend to be strongly pro-Israel. True to form, Herrera lashed back at Steinhauser, posting on social media: “When did conservatives become pearl clutching virtue signalers?” *** Could this toxic screed prove to be Herrera’s political undoing?Nationally, the Democratic party has begun to wake up to the possibilities. In August, the Democratic congressional campaign committee added Texas 23 to its target list, denoting a shift in strategy from previous assumptions that the district was irredeemably Republican. Opinion polls have been few and far between, and those that have been conducted came from partisan sources. A survey back in March was carried out by the House Majority Pac sponsored by the Democratic party. It put Herrera’s Democratic rival, Katy Padilla Stout, two points up. A poll conducted from the other side of the aisle last month put Herrera ahead by six points. That came from the Remington research group, on behalf of the rightwing website Breitbart. On the ground, his opponent Padilla Stout sees his most egregious outbursts as a turn-off for many voters, especially his depiction of children in the wake of the Uvalde massacre at Robb elementary school. “So many children in Uvalde were affected by the shooting. When people hear the way he describes children, their jaws are on the floor,” she said. And yet, Padilla Stout has a palatability problem. How do you talk about “creampies” and “cum trophies” without offending voters anew? “As a mother myself, that’s a hard thing for me to put on thousands of doors.” Texas 23 is a deeply rural and relatively sparsely populated district that has hunting and shooting in its DNA. Padilla Stout herself grew up within that culture. “My dad bought a ranch shortly before I was born, it was part of his American dream,” she said. “And that aspect of gun culture, the hunting and ranching part, I’ve been part of it all my life. I have cousins who would get their first shotgun on their 12th birthday, that’s our family tradition.” Given the prevalence of guns in the local way of life, she hasn’t made Herrera’s gun rights policy front and centre of her campaign. Voters, she said, rarely raise it. Her first campaign ad focused on the cost of childcare and groceries, and the prolonged drag of the Iran war. But she told the Guardian that she would continue to sound the alarm whenever she is able. “Herrera is a gun manufacturer who makes money off his gun absolutism. That’s his end goal. He wants to remove all boundaries on the second amendment, and dismantle public safety piece by piece.”

title: Stung by Trump, machinists union campaigns for affordability in midterms
author: Michael Sainato
summary: One of the largest labor unions in the US targets eight battleground states in ‘workers v billionaires’ campaign
body_text: The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM), one of the largest labor unions in the US, has launched a “workers v billionaires” political campaign tour targeting members in eight battleground states and encouraging them to support pro-worker candidates in the midterms. IAM has nearly 700,000 active and retired members in North America, covering workers at corporations that include Boeing, Lockheed Martin, United Airlines and Harley-Davidson. The union is targeting members and voters in Maine, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Arizona, Nevada and Illinois. “We made a strategic commitment that we’re going to be the most engaged that we have ever been in the history of our union in working,” said Brian Bryant, international president of IAM. “We’re living in an economy that only favors billionaires and does not favor working people, and it’s time that Congress and this administration realize who they should be looking out for.” Bryant emphasized that several union members, including those with IAM, voted for Trump in 2024 because of promises that he would fix the economy and make things more affordable. Throughout his 2024 presidential campaign, Trump repeatedly claimed: “When I win, I will immediately bring prices down, starting on day one.” Yet since Trump took office, inflation has increased from 3.0% in January 2025 to 3.4% in August 2026, health insurance costs are soaring due to the expiration of Affordable Care Act subsidies and gas prices are on average $1 a gallon higher due to Trump’s war with Iran. The union will “send a message to this administration that what the status quo is right now is not acceptable, and they’re going to have to stand up and pay attention to working people”, Bryant said. Jason Gayler, president of IAM local 776A in Fort Worth, Texas, said his state “is more purple than what people put out to be”. As Democrats are seeking to flip several seats, polls are showing that races are the most competitive they’ve been in decades. “The price of just the cost of living in north Texas now has absolutely skyrocketed, and it’s starting to really affect a lot of our members, which is motivating them to back candidates that focus primarily on the working class,” Gayler said. He also noted that the machinists recently elected their first rank-and-file member to the Texas senate; Taylor Rehmet, president of the IAM’s Texas state council, won a special election in January, flipping a state senate district that Trump won in 2024 by 17%. Shay Blodgett, an Alaska Airlines worker in Phoenix who is helping to lead IAM’s political program in Arizona, said the union has worked to oppose Republican-led state legislation that would have restricted public sector workers’ ability to organize and supported the Arizona AFL-CIO “labor 2026 blitz” campaign. “We’ve been conducting member-to-member engagement this summer, reaching out, asking members what matters to them,” Blodgett said. “We heard them loud and clear. The No 1 thing was the economy, cost of living, fuel prices, healthcare and food costs.” Co-workers have expressed regret over voting for Republicans in the last election, especially since transportation workers are exempt from the temporary no-tax-on-overtime deduction that was passed as part of Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act that was passed last summer. “The majority of our airline workers in the state will be entering contract negotiations in early 2027, and we need elected officials that will fix the economy and allow airline workers to fulfill the American dream of home ownership and raising families in Arizona,” Blodgett said. Rich Howell, former president of IAM local 1776, a longtime member of the union and worker at Philadelphia international airport, said the union is supporting Democrats in Pennsylvania who are trying to flip four congressional districts and the state senate while maintaining control of the governorship and statehouse. Trump “said he was going to bring down the prices a year and a half ago. That was his campaign message. If you go back and see all the promises, there wasn’t one that he held,” Howell said. He noted this is a difficult election year due to the amount of money billionaires are pouring into politics – more than $1.6bn in the 2026 midterm elections so far – but noted that “money doesn’t buy a race”. “Trump put the tariffs on, cutting more jobs, hurting more people in our industry,” Howell added. “It’s billionaires versus the workers, and that’s the stance we’re making. They are getting rich and we’re paying for it. We’re paying for it out of our pockets.” • This article was amended on 23 September 2026. It is $1.6bn that has been poured into the 2026 midterm elections so far. An earlier version incorrectly stated it was $1.6tn.

title: First Thing: Trump addresses UN with mixture of boasts, threats and jibes
author: Martin Belam
summary: US-Iran meeting takes place on sidelines despite president’s threat to ‘annihilate’ Tehran regime. Plus, one man’s month-long pilates odyssey
body_text: Good morning. Donald Trump has used the platform of the UN general assembly in New York to threaten to “annihilate the Islamic republic” of Iran, “and do it quickly”. He called on countries to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices. Despite his bombastic rhetoric, Trump also said Iranian officials held three hours of talks with the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the meeting. Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation in Switzerland in June. A senior Iranian official also indicated that Iran was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week. What else did Trump say at the UN? The president doubled down on his defence of AI development, saying warnings about runaway agents were a “hoax”; announced the US would build new military bases in Greenland; attacked the international criminal court as a “rogue organisation”; and prompted the Cuba’s delegation to stage a walkout when he described the country as a “failed state”. Did he continue his attacks on US media networks? Trump scolded a CNN anchor for covering him at the UN, saying “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Last week, the president announced he was banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House. Follow UN proceedings live today here. Republican calls for Senate investigation of Trump Jr wedding paid for by Russian oligarch A Republican senator has accused Donald Trump Jr of corruption and demanded a Senate investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of his recent wedding in the Bahamas. John Curtis, of Utah, wrote to the leaders of the US Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday, urging them to subpoena Trump Jr over his business dealings, his relationships with foreign individuals, gifts he has received – and any occasions where his connection to his father, Donald Trump, “was invoked or understood to provide value”. Where else is the president seeing dissent from Republicans? Another prominent Florida Republican has publicly distanced himself from Trump, days after María Elvira Salazar called out the president’s immigration-enforcement policy targeting law-abiding undocumented immigrants. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in November’s midterm elections, launched an updated campaign website on Tuesday that was stripped of almost every mention of Trump. Mississippi grand jury decides not to charge anyone in death of Nolan Wells A grand jury made a unanimous decision to not bring criminal charges against anyone in the mysterious death of Nolan Wells, a Mississippi teenager who died after a boat outing with friends on 4 July. Wells’s case drew national attention, with many speculating about what happened and suspecting that the 18-year-old’s disappearance and death may have been racially motivated. Wells, who was Black while the friends with whom he was last seen were white, was also the only friend in the group who did not return from the trip that day. Hayden Panettiere’s cause of death confirmed as fentanyl overdose Hayden Panettiere died from a fentanyl overdose, according to the Greenville county coroner’s office. Medical examiners said there were “no signs of trauma” and “the manner of death has been ruled accident”. Panettiere was in her South Carolina apartment with her boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, and his brother Zach when she died on August 16. Panettiere, known for her roles in television series including Heroes and Nashville, began acting at just 11 months old. After her death, her father released a statement, saying: “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her – and to the millions who watched her onscreen.” In other news … Ella Langley’s hit song Choosin’ Texas has set a new record, spending 23 weeks at the top of the Billboard Hot 100, unseating Mariah Carey’s All I Want for Christmas Is You, which topped the charts for 22 weeks. An US F-16 fighter jet ⁠in western Germany crashed on Tuesday, the US military said, ⁠adding that one pilot had ejected safely. DoorDash said it would pay $131.5m ⁠to settle a New York City government investigation that found the food delivery company underpaid or waited too long to pay workers. ‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular has been charged with rape and drug offenses in Massachusetts. The 20-year-old, whose real name is Braden Eric Peters, has been scheduled for a 14 October arraignment. Qantas says travellers will be able to fly between Sydney and New York in just 18 hours from mid-2028 when the airline launches its second ultra long-haul route. Stat of the day: Trump made more than 1,000 stock trades in July worth up to $270m The president made more than 440 purchases and 700 sales despite voter anger over elected officials trading stocks. Well Actually: Get tested and talk to your partner – how to have safer sex after age 50 We are long past the era when sex was for young married couples trying for children and nobody else. Amanda Zuckerman Klarsfeld has compiled this thoughtful selection of advice for older lovers. Don’t miss this: Why public transport in global cities is slowing to a crawl – visualised The UK capital’s iconic red buses have a problem: they are getting slower. And it isn’t just an issue in London, but a growing worldwide problem for transit networks, with worrying implications for the poorest in society. Our visuals team have put together this rich explainer to explore why. … or this: Will anyone topple soccer boss Infantino? Since Fifa abandoned its controversial World Cup sell-off plan last month, causing deep divisions among the global administrators of soccer, the governing body’s president, Gianni Infantino, has continued to lobby for re-election. Matt Hughes analyses how he is trying to cling on after the debacle. Climate check: Huge El Niño projected to cause 450,000 deaths in next six months More than 450,000 people are projected to die from the additional heat brought by the super El Niño in the next six months, according to estimates by climate scientists. The toll is on top of the early deaths resulting from temperatures already driven up by the climate crisis. It will strike across the globe, including the US. Many further deaths are expected from the droughts, wildfires and flooding that El Niños bring. Last Thing: My perilous, painful, perfect month of pilates My colleague Sammy Gecsoyler has taken up pilates, and has written this very funny account of his month’s journey to better fitness and health. title: Nike co-founder gives $1bn to University of Oregon in historic donation
author: Anna Betts
summary: Phil Knight and wife, Penny, make largest known donation to a public university to fund a new engineering school
body_text: Nike co-founder Phil Knight, and his wife, Penny, have donated $1bn to the University of Oregon in what the institution described as the “largest gift ever made to a comprehensive public university”. The donation is intended to be used to establish a new engineering school in Eugene. In a news release seen by the Guardian, the university said the new school would “educate engineers and applied scientists in bioengineering and other high-demand disciplines, attract faculty and researchers to a growing campus, and accelerate the university’s ability to move discoveries out of the laboratory and into products, therapies, technologies and companies”. The University of Oregon president, Karl Scholz, said in a statement that the Knights have “a long history of believing in things before they exist” and that “they did it in 2016, and they are doing it again now, at a scale that is genuinely hard to take in. I am grateful to them, and I am grateful to be here for it.” Knight, 88, is a graduate of the university. The latest donation brings the Knight family’s known total giving to the University of Oregon to more than $2bn, according to the New York Times. The school said in the news release on Wednesday that the gift is the third commitment the Knights have made at this scale in 10 years, following $500m in 2016 and $500m in 2021 that created and expanded the Knight Campus. The school also said the new engineering school will be located at the Phil and Penny Knight Campus for Accelerating Scientific Impact. In the announcement, Knight also shared a statement noting that “to make an audacious dream a reality requires more than a vivid imagination”. “It also requires the sort of opportunity that our great American universities, both public and private, have historically provided,” he said. “This is no time to abandon them.” He added: “Penny and I are grateful for the chance to invest in our most promising young people’s future in this important way.” Bob Guldberg, vice-president and Robert and Leona DeArmond executive director of the Knight Campus, said in a statement that the creation of a college of engineering “builds on the original vision put forward by UO faculty who inspired Phil and Penny to invest in the idea that we can do better translating the great work we do out into the real world”. “The Knight Campus stands on the foundation of a remarkable Oregon legacy: the belief that bold innovation can unlock human potential,” Guldberg said. “Today, we carry that same belief forward, applying it to science, technology, and human health.” Scholz, the university president, said in an interview with the New York Times about the donation that “one of the most successful businesspeople in the history of humanity, and one of the most generous philanthropists in the history of humanity, has said higher education is worth an investment of this magnitude. “At a time when we’re all feeling a little bit under siege, this is tremendous news,” he said, adding that the gift amounted to “a screaming endorsement of the importance of what we’re doing”. Senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, said in a statement: “This groundbreaking gift from Phil and Penny Knight stands out for its extraordinary generosity and monumental impact at a public university. “As a proud University of Oregon alumnus, I know my alma mater will put this massive investment to great use by educating students who will meet the ongoing need for engineers so essential to the economy in our state and nationwide.” The news on Wednesday comes as earlier this month it was announced that the Knights were committing $1.1bn to Providence St Vincent Medical Center and to Providence Heart Institute to create Oregon’s first hospital dedicated exclusively to women’s health. “Penny and I have always believed that real breakthroughs come from people willing to take on the toughest challenges,” Knight said in a statement earlier this month. “Providence has shown that kind of ambition in cardiovascular care, and we see the same opportunity to do something truly distinctive for women’s health. We’re proud to invest in teams that will change what’s possible for communities across Oregon and beyond.” Last year, Oregon Health & Science University announced that it had received a $2bn commitment from the Knights to its cancer institute, which the university said would “transform the future of cancer care and set a new standard globally”.

title: Trump’s UN speech was delusional and dangerous
author: Kenneth Roth
summary: It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president like Trump
body_text: Donald Trump’s speech on Tuesday to the United Nations general assembly was an object lesson in his lawless rule and remarkable capacity for self-delusion. Disregarding the UN charter’s emphasis on the peaceful resolution of disputes, he doubled down on his violent unilateralism while denigrating the global issues that the UN is designed to address. For many, the headline remark was his musing about whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” of Iran. “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” But it was probably less a genuine threat than a clumsy effort to influence negotiations where he has little leverage. Trump is in desperate quest of some face-saving gesture that will allow him to feign “victory” and extract himself from his disastrous war of choice. He spoke of destroying the “Islamic Republic”, which might imply the Iranian military, a legitimate military target. But his reference to precluding future generations suggests he meant to threaten the Iranian people. Attacking them would be a blatant war crime. In July, he already vowed to destroy Iran’s bridges or power plants – itself a threat to commit war crimes. The international criminal court (ICC) has charged four Russian military commanders for doing precisely that in Ukraine. Trump didn’t even bother to offer a coherent rationale for his threat. Once more, he proclaimed: “I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” But Tehran has long disavowed that goal. He claimed that other American presidents “just wanted to ignore” the issue. But Barack Obama negotiated a deal to constrain Iran’s ability to build a nuclear weapon. Trump ripped it up, preferring his utterly counterproductive military solution, which has brought Iran far closer to a nuclear weapon than ever before. Preposterously, Trump claimed, “when it comes to Iran,” the midterm election “doesn’t even enter my mind.” No one believes that. If the Republicans face the disastrous showing that the polls now predict, he knows the election will be seen as a repudiation of his arbitrary tariffs and Iran war which have fueled inflation and aggravated the affordability crisis that he belittles. Trump also spotlighted his other acts of aggression. He celebrated the seizure of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro, emphasizing how some political prisoners have now been freed, although hundreds remain. But while Trump lauded his coerced deal with Venezuela’s remaining autocratic leaders to take a large chunk of the country’s oil, he said nothing about a democratic future. Instead, touting his might-makes-right beliefs, he proclaimed: “To the victor belong the spoils.” He noted the new agreement on Greenland without mentioning his earlier threat to seize the territory by force even though it has long been administered by Denmark, a fellow Nato member. He raved about slaughtering drug suspects at sea, claiming they are “at war with civilization” and “should be killed … as enemy combatants”. But there is no real war, only a rhetorical one. Drug traffickers form a criminal cartel, not an organized force in armed conflict with the United States. They should be arrested and prosecuted, not summarily executed by drone. The killings are murders and arguably crimes against humanity. Many of the victims were on boats registered in Columbia or Venezuela – both at the time members of the ICC. That would give the court jurisdiction over these crimes, which may be why Trump reprised his attack on this important institution of justice. Trump wants to be restrained only by his own warped “morality”. It has been reported that Trump may soon supplement his sanctions against 13 ICC personnel – judges and prosecutors – with sanctions against the court as a whole. But that would only compound the criminality of his conduct, because retaliation against court personnel for the performance of their official duties is obstructing justice under article 70 of the court’s statute. Trump emphasized his role as a peacemaker. “I have made peace,” he declared, as he claimed to have “settle[d] eight wars”. Yet the reality is more complicated. He said he had “ended the war in Gaza”. In fact, despite the “ceasefire”, Israel’s continuing attacks continue to raise the death toll. Trump mentioned his 20-point peace plan for Gaza without noting that virtually none of it has been implemented. Israel continues to kill Palestinians and block needed supplies, while Hamas has not disarmed. He didn’t even bother to mouth the word “Palestinian”. Indeed, the Trump administration has rejected a leading candidate for the next UN secretary general because she has publicly recognized that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, suggesting that Trump will accept only future UN leaders who are willing to deny this reality. He claimed to have “contribute[d] to peace” between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, without noting that Rwanda’s M23 militia continues to occupy large swathes of eastern DRC. Trump seems fine with that, so long as the murderous M23 brings the region’s mineral riches to the western market. He claimed to be making progress in securing peace in Ukraine, without acknowledging his prior suggestion to reward Vladimir Putin’s aggression by having Ukraine not only cede territory already illegally occupied by Russia but to hand over additional chunks of its territory as well. Meanwhile, Trump belittled the problems that the UN, able to convene the world’s nations, is ideally suited to address. He called the existential threat of climate change a “hoax”. Ignoring the enormous risks posed by artificial intelligence, he attempted to relabel AI as “superintelligence” and derided efforts to regulate it as “globalist.” This week Trump meets with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping. Yet rather than outline the important issues to be addressed, Trump chose to self-promote: “We’re leading now over China by a lot”. Most would say only that Trump is leading in national embarrassment. It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president who excels mainly in disseminating self-promoting fantasies while flouting the most basic rules of decency. His UN speech put that all on painful display. Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

title: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
author: Patrick Wintour in New York
summary: Masoud Pezeshkian says Tehran is ready for dialogue and diplomacy ‘but without the language of force’
body_text: Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table. In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US. But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.” On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators. A surprise three-hour meeting between Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech. The Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on winning the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for the future of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway that has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to soar. He made it clear Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests the Islamic republic will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently. Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating the supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war. “We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.” He said Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme and it did not want to build nuclear weapons. He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security. “In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added. Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war. Insisting Iran was the true victim of terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.” Pezeshkian’s speech received domestic praise, but the hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, refused to describe the talks with the Americans as negotiations. He said: “Mr Araghchi [Iran’s foreign minister] has announced Iran’s conditions, and until Iran’s conditions are implemented, the strait of Hormuz will not be opened nor will there be any negotiation.” He warned Iran’s neighbours implementing a US-induced ban on Iranian travel: “If you stand alongside the United States, we will not stand by and watch.” He cautioned that should Iranian flights face bans through regional cooperation with Washington, “their airports will have no flights either”. Pezeshkian’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa. Ultimately, Washington granted the permit but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage. In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position. He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.” Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed. Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours it said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met. It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control. The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day. The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iran-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport choke point, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean. There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing. Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet. Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.

title: ‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club
author: Andrew Roth in New York
summary: Invitation announced by Marco Rubio is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and EU countries
body_text: The United States has invited Vladimir Putin to take part in the meeting of the G20 scheduled in Miami in December in what would be the first major summit with the Russian leader present since he launched his invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The invitation, which marks a significant reversal by the Trump administration of Russia’s international isolation, was announced by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, during a press conference on the sidelines of the United Nations conference in New York. “We’ve invited President Putin to the G20,” Rubio said in a televised press conference following a meeting with Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with [Trump] but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.” The Kremlin has not yet responded publicly to the invitation, which is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and other European leaders who have recently accused Russia of launching hybrid attacks to disrupt logistics and spread political uncertainty among Kyiv’s allies. Russia remains a member of the G20 but Putin has not attended a summit of the body since 2019. He did attend one session virtually in 2023. The December summit is set to take place at the Trump National Doral golf club. Rubio framed the invitation by saying that Trump was willing to meet with “virtually anyone” and that “in order to solve problems, you have to meet with people you disagree with”. He said Trump remained open to meeting with Putin one-on-one in other forums, if “there’s a purpose behind the meeting”. The G20 is a forum of the world’s largest economies and includes the European Union, China, India, the United States, the United Kingdom, and other major countries. European officials were upset by a decision to invite Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov to a meeting of the group’s top economic officials in August and refused to pose in a “family photo” with him at the summit. Zelenskyy had said earlier this month that he would be ready to travel to the summit and would meet with Putin if he attended. “We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions,” he told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle in an interview. “It’s not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. [...] Results matter. That’s it.” On Wednesday, Zelenskyy addressed the United Nations, urging world leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war effort. “Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us,” said Zelenskyy. “In response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too.” Zelenskyy also warned that the war could spread beyond Ukraine if Putin was not stopped. Rubio on Wednesday also indicated that he had spoken with Lavrov about the accusations of “hybrid attacks” in Europe, saying that one concern about the war was that “it could metastasize and spread into other places”. Trump is currently seeking to negotiate a partial ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that would include attacks on Russian oil refineries in order to take pressure off global energy prices. In particular, Trump has called on Zelenskyy to halt attacks against Russian oil in order to reduce prices on diesel fuel, which have spiked to almost double their price last year in the United States before midterm elections for Congress. Trump and Zelenskyy met on the sidelines of the United Nations on Tuesday for a rare face-to-face discussion of measures to end the war. Zelenskyy called for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin to end the war, but the Kremlin has declined past attempts for direct meetings with Zelenskyy. “President Trump, our teams, and I spoke about how to end the war. This is the priority. We are ready. I’m not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday. Despite efforts to broker a ceasefire, however, Russia has continued to pummel Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities with drone and missile attacks. Kyiv hit a major Russian oil refinery over the weekend in its largest attack on Russia’s capital yet. For the past two days, Kyiv has come under particularly severe attack from jet-powered Shahed drones – swifter and harder to intercept than their predecessors. As has been the case since mid-August, the drone attacks have come in the daytime as well as at night, disrupting ordinary life, schools and kindergartens. On Wednesday morning an acrid stench of burning filled the city centre after multiple explosions, and the clear autumnal sky was clouded with plumes of black smoke. A petrol station, warehouses, a business centre and a transport infrastructure building were hit, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. As of mid-morning, one person had died and eight had been injured. Explosions were seen near the capital’s main railway station. Congress last week passed a sweeping sanctions bill against Russia that would also give Trump the authority to levy 100% tariffs against top purchasers of Russian energy exports, including China and India. Democrats, who mostly opposed the bill, said that it gave Trump too much power to levy tariffs and that they could be used against US allies as well. In response to what has happened, the Democratic members of the House foreign affairs committee posted on X: “Trump signed the Russia sanctions bill 5 days ago. Today Rubio makes clear the administration has no intention of isolating Russia for its war of aggression in Ukraine.” Charlotte Higgins contributed reporting from Kyiv • This article was amended on 27 September 2026 to clarify that the Democrats on the House foreign affairs committee posted the X comment on the Russia sanctions bill.

title: Morning Mail: Albanese embraces Zelenskyy at UN; grocery prices climb; and ‘getting weird’ with spring fashion
author: Martin Farrer
summary: President says Tehran will ‘never bow’ to US in defiant speech at UN; basket of typical items increases by an average of 7%
body_text: Morning everyone. Anthony Albanese has crowned a busy day of international diplomacy by pledging another $60m in support for Ukraine at an emotional meeting in New York with the man he described fondly as “my friend” – Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy. It was no less busy elsewhere in New York as Tehran’s president ripped into Donald Trump with a defiant speech to the UN, and Argentina’s president said he would be “taking matters into his own hands” over the Falklands. None of which will help the cost of living, which a survey of typical Australian supermarket items shows is rising fast. We also report on how more young people are living with their parents, Victoria is planning more access to medical abortion, and how to dress for spring. Albanese will also use a speech to say that the world order is no longer fit for purpose. Grocery pain | Groceries have become more expensive at four of Australia’s major supermarket chains, with the average price of a basket of essentials increasing by 7% between March and June, analysis has found. Tax gain | Most property investors may end up paying less capital gains tax after Labor’s budget reforms, research suggests. Exclusive | The gas industry has been accused of unleashing a “scare campaign” before the Victorian election as it pressures the state government to reverse a ban on gas in new homes. Coogee rank | Coogee has once again ranked as the Sydney ocean beach most polluted with faecal matter in a survey of 245 sites across New South Wales. World Iran’s defiance | Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing America as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while also insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table. The US delegation responded by walking out. The price of oil went back over $100. Donald Trump is due to welcome China’s president, Xi Jinping, and his wife for an official visit later this morning. Here’s what’s at stake when the two superpowers get down to talking. Javier Milei has condemned the UN as the Argentinian president warned that his country would take “matters into our own hands” in its dispute with Britain over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands. You can follow it live here. Follow the UN meeting live. The burger chain is targeting an extra 1.5 percentage point share of the market. Midterm threat | Republican leaders are getting nervous as they fear Trump’s unpopularity will result in disaster at the midterms in November. Patrick Commins digests the key takeaways, such as that half of Australians under 30 are living with their parents, poorly educated men aged 25-44 are being left behind, and household incomes are up but people feel less well-off. title: Democrats accuse Susan Collins of corruption after bombshell ‘pay-to-play’ report
author: Chris Stein
summary: Republican senator calls bribery allegation ‘categorically false’ as ProPublica reports Trump derailed FBI inquiry
body_text: Democrats in Maine on Wednesday accused Republican senator Susan Collins of corruption after a major media outlet reported that the FBI had proposed investigating her for allegedly accepting bribes – before Donald Trump derailed the inquiry. The article from the investigative newsroom ProPublica rocked the race for Collins’s Senate seat, which is crucial to Democrats’ hopes of winning control of the chamber in the 3 November midterm election. The outlet reported that in the run-up to Collins’s successful bid for a fifth term in 2020, the head of her Super Pac had solicited a campaign donation from contracting firm Navatek, which demanded assurances of business from the government in return. Using a shell company, Navatek CEO Martin Kao later sent $150,000 to the Super Pac, then told other executives he had been informed Collins would ensure the firm won $32m in federal contracts. In late 2024, the FBI was moving towards investigating the arrangement, in what would have been a large-scale political bribery inquiry, but the agents leading the case were pushed out amid a wider purge of the bureau Trump ordered after returning to power last year, while a justice department office that oversees investigations of politicians was gutted. Collins has disputed the report, which her deputy chief of staff Annie Clark called “categorically false” and noted that Kao is currently in federal prison after pleading guilty to fraud charges. But it served as grist for Maine Democrats who hope they can finally convince voters to unseat Collins, who has represented the state since 1997 and survived repeated re-election challenges. “This is corruption of the highest order,” said Troy Jackson, the former state senate president and the Democratic nominee to take on Collins this year. “We deserve answers about every contract and every conversation that Collins and her team facilitated on the backs of taxpayers. The jig is up.” Collins is the only Republican running for re-election in a state Kamala Harris won in 2024, but has a history of being a tenacious opponent. The last time Collins was on the ballot, in 2020, she beat her Democratic opponent Sara Gideon by eight percentage points, even as Joe Biden carried the state in the presidential race. Political forecasters consider her re-election campaign to be a toss-up, though recent polls have shown Jackson narrowly ahead. At a Wednesday press conference in Portland, the largest city, state Democratic party executive director Devon Murphy-Anderson accused the senator of misconduct as chair of the Senate appropriations committee, a powerful role that oversees federal spending and which Collins has used to channel significant investment to her state. “We sent Susan Collins to Washington to fight for us. Instead, it appears that she has sold us out yet again and gotten bailed out of trouble by the president of the United States,” Murphy-Anderson said. “It is not the first time that she has betrayed us. However, this November we have the opportunity to ensure that it is one of the last.” Addressing reporters separately, Collins’s campaign manager, Steve Abbott, denounced ProPublica’s reporting as based on “allegations from a guy who was awaiting sentencing for a significant federal offense who was trying to get his sentence reduced, as the article states directly”. He said that the justice department under Joe Biden had absolved the senator of the “pay-to-play” scheme that Democrats accuse her of. “In order for that claim to be true, you would have to disbelieve the Biden-led Department of Justice and the Biden-led FBI, who both investigated those contributions and the claims against Senator Collins, her campaign, and her federal staff, thoroughly, and found no basis to charge them,” Abbott said. Maine lies at the center of Democrats’ plans for retaking control of the Senate from Republicans, who won a 53-seat majority in the 2024 election. Beyond Maine, Democrats hope to win in at least three other states currently held by Republicans that voted for Trump two years ago, while also defending seats in Georgia, Michigan, and New Hampshire. Lance Dutson, a strategist who worked on Collins’s three most recent re-election campaigns, said the senator’s campaign in 2020 was so well-funded he found it “obviously absurd” that $150,000 would be viewed as a meaningful donation to her Super Pac. “In 2020, by the end of that race, campaigns were struggling to find places to spend money,” said Dutson, who is not involved with Collins’s re-election effort this year. He condemned ProPublica’s story as “a partisan hit piece” but said: “It’s definitely not helpful to have a story implying corruption show up in the newspaper in late September of an election year.” While Dutson argued the report is not a “silver bullet” for Collins’s foes, he warned that Trump’s low approval ratings – which have unnerved Republicans nationwide – present a significant complication for the senator’s re-election. “The headwind from Trump is very strong, as you know, and people are very upset about it,” he said. “This race is going to come down to Maine voters deciding whether that national argument is more important than the the direct relationship and the positive impact that Collins has had over the state.”

title: Eight USS Lincoln personnel have attempted suicide, US navy confirms
author: Robert Mackey and Uwa Ede-Osifo
summary: Hung Cao, acting US navy secretary, answered questions from US senator Kirsten Gillibrand in a letter
body_text: Eight US navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group have attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran, Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, revealed in a letter to the US senator Kirsten Gillibrand on Tuesday. “Since the beginning of Lincoln’s deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group,” Cao wrote, responding on behalf of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth to Gillibrand’s inquiry about the quality of life aboard the fleet. “This number includes the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons.” CNN first reported on Cao’s response to Gillibrand. The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days, disembarked on 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid the unresolved war. In August, two military newspapers reported on sailors’ deteriorating mental health, including multiple attempts to jump overboard. The reports prompted outcry from Democrats, who called for an investigation of the conditions onboard. In March, one sailor’s attempt to go overboard was thwarted by shipmates, according to Cao. In August, one sailor did go overboard. The individual was rescued and received medical treatment, before being “transferred off-ship for follow-up care”, Cao wrote. MS Now also reported in August on alarming allegations of mold in the ship’s showers and dwindling supplies of food and soap, among other basic necessities. The number of entrée options was temporarily reduced from two to one, Cao wrote in his letter, a measure “implemented to optimize endurance and ensure sustained time on station”. He said four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily. He acknowledged certain delays in replenishing crew supplies. As details of low morale trickled out of the Lincoln, Hegseth downplayed the media coverage, saying news outlets “completely misrepresented” the situation. “We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” he told reporters in August. “What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members,” Gillibrand said in a Wednesday statement to the Guardian. “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect. That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.” “The Navy and the Navy secretary are very committed to sailor health, wellbeing and morale,” a US navy official told the Guardian on Wednesday. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: Elif Eralp: ‘Germany’s Zohran Mamdani’ who vows to be a mayor for all Berliners
author: Kate Connolly in Berlin
summary: Die Linke candidate, a lawyer affected by her experiences as the child of political migrants from Turkey, poised to head Berlin coalition government
body_text: Elif Eralp launched her election bid last autumn with the blunt statement: “People like me are actually not supposed to become mayor in this country.” So the fact that the 45-year-old lawyer and daughter of political migrants from Turkey is on the verge of becoming Berlin’s next mayor and the capital’s first leader of Turkish origin is quite the moment in German politics. After last weekend’s city state election, in which her far-left party, Die Linke, came first with more than a quarter of the votes, Eralp has become a household name. The mood at Die Linke’s election celebrations on Sunday night was electric. Eralp, whose candidacy has helped propel the party from the doldrums to the brink of heading a coalition government in Berlin for the first time, was feted as a star. Some commentators suggested Germany was “having a [Zohran] Mamdani moment”, in reference to the democratic socialist mayor of New York. (One of his advisers was summoned to Berlin to help Eralp weeks before the poll. Her campaign was modelled on that of the veteran US senator Bernie Sanders.) “In our city, love and justice won over hate … this signal goes out into the world,” Eralp said at her victory party, the “hate” a pointed reference to the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, which was celebrating coming first in another regional election. Even in liberal Berlin, the populist party made considerable gains. It was Die Linke, however, that came out on top. With about 26% of the vote, the party not only outperformed the centre-left Social Democrats, whose presence has dominated Berlin politics for decades, and the Greens. It was also well ahead of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the conservative party of the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, which had previously held the mayoral position. A lot is now at stake for Eralp, who has promised to be “a mayor for all Berliners”. Eralp, who was chosen in particular by the young (47% of whom voted for her) and who mobilised thousands of otherwise non-voters thanks in part to intensive door-to-door campaigning and social media, generated most interest with her ambitious promise to take on corporate giants over unaffordable housing in the German capital. Once described as “poor but sexy” by a former mayor for its low cost of living, Berlin’s rents have soared in recent years. In her nomination speech, the lawyer said: “I’m running so that our city becomes affordable again, so that real estate speculators don’t decide what happens to our city, but rather we do together.” She called sky-high rents a defining social issue, saying: “This city belongs to all of us, not to the speculators.” Merz has led the charge against Eralp’s plans to expropriate more than 200,000 Berlin flats from their corporate landlords, saying her policy – decried by some as “socialism on speed” – would have “calamitous effects” on the economy. The chancellor has said he will push for laws to prevent her plans. Eralp has pledged to plough on. It is not a given that Die Linke will take control of Berlin’s towering Rotes Rathaus, or red city hall, named after its red brick and not its association with leftwing politics. Eralp’s victory has been overshadowed by accusations that Die Linke has failed to tackle antisemitism within its own ranks as well as charges that the party has tolerated – and at worst courted – the support of criminal gangs. The Social Democrats and the Greens, potential coalition partners, have said they need urgent clarification on these alleged affiliations before they agree to be associated with Die Linke. Die Linke’s leadership has repeatedly denied the accusations while vowing to clampdown on any antisemitism in its ranks. On Tuesday it announced that one of its Berlin MPs, who is alleged to have connections both to criminal gangs and a terrorist-related, pro-Hamas organisation, would “suspend his parliamentary duties until further notice”. On Monday, Eralp sought to reassure critics. “Any form of glorification or trivialisation of violence or terror is completely out of the question,” she said. “I stand by that, and for me the promise of protection applies unequivocally to Jewish people just as it does to Muslims, Christians and all people in our city.” Eralp has been keen to stress the ordinariness of her life. She lives with her husband and two children in a rental flat in her own constituency of Kreuzberg, in south-central Berlin, one of the city’s most diverse quarters and home to one of Germany’s liveliest Turkish communities. Her children attend a state school in her kiez, or neighbourhood, and she has kept her family away from the cameras “for their own safety”, she says. Much of her campaigning in the district was carried out in Turkish. Unlike most Turkish migrants, Eralp’s parents did not come to Germany as Gastarbeiter, or guest workers, from Eastern Anatolia but were trade unionists and socialists from Istanbul who were imprisoned after a military coup for their political beliefs. Her mother, Hülya, a well-known feminist in Turkey, was only allowed out of jail because she was heavily pregnant with Eralp. She and Eralp’s father, Selçuk, a doctor, fled to Germany, where their daughter was born in Munich in 1981. The family experienced a complicated asylum process, which Eralp has said helped shape her view of the world. “I’ve experienced a lot about what it means when authorities make decisions you don’t understand. I’ve also felt racism and discrimination first-hand, so my life story has a lot to do with where I’ve ended up now,” she has said. She recalls how her parents often put up asylum seekers in their home over many years, and the 15 years of struggle that her mother, a trainer for nurses, faced before her qualifications were recognised in Germany. At the age of 10, Eralp founded a conservation club with friends in her parents’ garage, and later she went into the anti-nuclear movement. After studying law at the University of Hamburg, she moved to Berlin for two years of obligatory practical legal training, ending up working in the parliamentary group of Die Linke and later switching to the Berlin state parliament. She said she was inspired to join Die Linke in 2017 in direct response to the entry of AfD, an anti-immigration party, into the Bundestag for the first time. In 2019, with fellow members and supporters of Die Linke who had refugee and migrant backgrounds, she co-founded Links*kanax, an alliance that aimed to increase the visibility of the migrant-progressive voice within the party and beyond. When she was 12, Eralp says, she wanted to become a human rights lawyer “to fight against all these injustices I’d seen”. Now, she says, “I’m doing what I set out to do, not in a courtroom, but in the political sphere”.

title: Diesel prices across Australia could surge beyond $3 a litre as Trump eyes cut to US fuel exports
author: Luca Ittimani
summary: Fuel costs have risen to levels not seen since early April, adding to risk of inflation and interest rate hike
body_text: Australian diesel prices could surge above $3 a litre if Donald Trump cuts off US diesel exports amid floundering negotiations with Iran. Fuel costs have risen to levels not seen since early April, adding to inflation risks and making another hike in interest rates all but certain. Canberra is recording the highest prices out of the capital cities, with diesel at 298.7c per litre and unleaded at 250c per litre on Thursday. Other cities’ prices were not far behind. Prices have risen nearly 40c a litre since the start of the month, adding $22 to the cost of filling up a vehicle with a 55-litre tank. Service stations have passed on steady increases from international refineries, which have struggled to secure cheap oil as ongoing hostilities in the Middle East prevent supply reaching global markets. The Brent crude oil benchmark price has held above US$100 per barrel for most of the last fortnight, reaching its highest point since May. Gulf countries’ exports of diesel have fallen to just a quarter of their prewar levels with the ongoing conflict preventing transit of fuel tankers through the strait of Hormuz and the smaller Bab al-Mandab chokepoint. Ukrainian attacks have cut off Russian supply, further restricting global oil flow. Shortages would worsen if the Trump administration banned US exports of diesel, which it is actively considering as a measure to suppress local service station prices ahead of the November midterm elections. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email ANZ bank analysts said limits would be especially disruptive as the US had stepped up its global diesel supply since the war began, now exporting more than 1.5m barrels a day. Australia almost entirely relies on overseas imports of diesel, with government data showing it brought in more than 18,400m litres from January to July 2026. Just 510.9m of the total came from the US, most of which arrived in April. Saul Kavonic, an analyst at MST Financial, predicted Australia would have to ration diesel and face prices of over $4 a litre within weeks of a US export ban, in comments to the ABC on Thursday. But Dr Lurion De Mello, from Macquarie University’s Transforming Energy Markets Research Centre, said Australia’s supply was still healthy. Australia’s stockpiles of diesel have fallen to 31 days’ worth of supply, where they were in March, down from 39 days’ worth in July. The energy minister, Chris Bowen, has said government-backed fuel purchases had slowed as existing storage facilities were full. De Mello said a US ban would push up prices as Europe, which relies on American diesel, would start competing with Australia for shipments from South Korea and other Asian refiners. “If you take any supplier out, globally, it puts pressure on prices to go up,” De Mello said. De Mello said Australia’s diesel prices could surpass $3.10 a litre but would be unlikely to reach $3.50 as long as Asian refiners continued to access oil. The Albanese government temporarily lowered the fuel excise in March when diesel prices surpassed $3.10 a litre but has not offered a second excise cut. High fuel costs would threaten industries that rely heavily on imported diesel, including farming and mining, and push up prices in food, manufacturing and transport industries. The Reserve Bank is expected to raise interest rates on Tuesday to 4.6%, a 14-year-high, in part due to upward pressure from fuel costs.
