title: Benjamin Netanyahu to deliver defiant UN speech while facing protests and political isolation
author: Andrew Roth and Alice Speri in New York
summary: Prime minister will ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’ as he heads towards his toughest re-election challenge
body_text: When he takes the stage at the UN on Thursday, Benjamin Netanyahu will deliver a familiar message of defiance even as protests and international condemnation leave the Israeli leader in growing isolation. Netanyahu is facing his toughest re-election challenge in a political career spanning decades with three ongoing conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, and a growing campaign of violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank. Internationally, Israel is facing growing condemnation. The UK, France and Canada are planning to sanction Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has accused Israeli settlers of committing ethnic cleansing of Palestinian communities. And the US is in the midst of a historic shift in public opinion against Israel, with 62% of respondents telling Pew in July they had a negative opinion of Netanyahu’s government, and 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week hoping he is voted out in October. Protests are expected both in the UN’s general assembly hall and on the streets of New York City, where mayor Zohran Mamdani has tempered his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal to assure demonstrators this week that he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city”. Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, defended Netanyahu’s government in a telephone interview before this week’s speech seeking to cast criticism of Israel’s actions as the product of misinformation and bias. “We are aware of the fact that we had a very challenging three years since October 7,” said Danon. “We accomplished a lot, but we were criticised. We were under the spotlight, and for us, I think, we are proud of our achievements.” “At the same time, we will work harder to improve the image of Israel, and we know there’s a campaign against us,” he added. Anger at Netanyahu will be on full display in New York City on Thursday, where several protests have been scheduled, including one from Bryant Park in midtown Manhattan to the UN headquarters in Turtle Bay to “reject war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu and the genocidal Zionist project”. “Netanyahu is coming to New York amid a political environment that has made it crystal clear that he is not welcome here,” said Beth Miller, the political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action. She described a “mainstreaming” of public opinion that “Americans do not want to be supporting Israel’s genocide. We do not want to be supporting Israel’s apartheid. We do not want to be arming Israel or supporting Israel.” And Palestinian representatives are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”. But in Danon’s telling, Israel’s problem was largely one of public relations rather than of policy, and he cited a “wave of misinformation” as the reason for the precipitous shift in polling. Netanyahu would use his speech to “highlight Israel’s achievements”, he said, and to lay out “what still should be done, and how should we verify that we actually achieve the goals of the war?” He did not elaborate on those specific measures before the speech, but the White House and US policymakers will be listening as they calibrate their message to voters – as well as the backlash of public anger – ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. Netanyahu is expected to deliver a hardline message aimed not just at world leaders, but also to his own electorate in Israel ahead of the October elections. “I think that he is trying to demonstrate to the Israeli populace that he still maintains some level of control over the situation,” said Miller. “And I think that he is trying to speak to a rightwing audience and a Trump-Maga audience in this country to try to rile up the hatred and Islamophobia.” Donald Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet with Netanyahu, however, during a visit expected to last less than 24 hours. Trump will be in Washington DC to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, and Netanyahu has cited Israel’s electoral campaign and the holiday of Sukkot as his reason to head home quickly after the speech. A Trump administration official said Netanyahu’s delegation had sought a high-level meeting during the visit but none was organised. There are also no plans to meet congressional leaders, Danon said. With criticism from top Republicans, including the vice-president, JD Vance, and leading democratic presidential contenders, Israel could face a 2028 campaign with two candidates who no longer support arms sales to Israel or the broad diplomatic support that it has enjoyed in the past. Even within the Maga base there are fractures, Miller noted, with “more and more people who don’t really want to be sending our tax dollars to support the Israeli government”. Danon said of a potential shift in the US-Israeli security relationship: “I think that we are still sharing the same values, and that’s why I’m sure that we will continue to have the support from the US.” But there are multiple flashpoints now for anger from both US political parties, as well as the international community, including dire humanitarian concerns and the lack of reconstruction in Gaza, the expansion of settlements in the West Bank, and continued conflicts in Lebanon and Iran, where the US has found itself mired in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices. Asked if a controversial $2.8bn (£2.1bn) arms sale indicated that Israel is preparing to resume its offensive in Gaza, Danon said Israel “hopes that we will see [Hamas’s] disarmament without our involvement”, nodding to efforts by the Trump-backed Board of Peace. But he said Israel “will do it ourselves” if that does not change, adding: “We can not leave it forever like that.” He was equally resolute on the West Bank, saying that Israel would not be swayed by recent criticism led by the UK over plans to expand settlements including E1, the planned construction which would sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank. Senate Democrats are also introducing a bill on Wednesday to sanction facilitators of the new settlement, and Senator Chris Coons, a co-sponsor, said in a statement that “as Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behaviour is unacceptable”. The protests began even before Netanyahu arrived in New York. Already on Wednesday, several members of the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter rallied at the city’s John F Kennedy international airport in protest at weapons and explosive materials destined for the Israeli military being flown out of the airport on commercial aircraft. Aber Kawas, who in November is slated to become the first Palestinian-American elected official in New York state, spoke at the event and later told the Guardian she plans to join many other New Yorkers protesting Nethanyahu’s UN speech on Thursday. “Thousands of people are against his presence in our city,” she said. Even though some had hailed Netanyahu’s decision to cut his visit short as a victory, she added, “the fact that he is coming shows he continues to have a sense of entitlement to be centred on the world stage while being the head architect of a genocide”.

title: Trump administration faces fresh scrutiny after DoJ drops bribery case against Indian billionaire
author: Ariana Baio
summary: Warren and Blumenthal raise concerns about case against Gautam Adani, who promised to invest $10bn in US
body_text: The Trump administration is facing growing questions over its decision to abandon a fraud and bribery case against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after he promised to invest $10bn in the US. For the second time this year, two Democratic senators have demanded that the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, answer questions about the Department of Justice’s handling of the case – and raised concerns over its judgment under Donald Trump. In August, a federal judge in New York agreed to drop the fraud case against Adani, one of the richest people in the world, at the request of prosecutors, despite having concerns about “irregularities” in the “highly unusual” decision. It has become the latest example of judges raising eyebrows at Trump administration prosecutors for pushing to dismiss criminal cases. Now, more than a month later, the senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal are asking Blanche to clarify whether people close to Donald Trump were involved in that decision. It comes after a New York Times report revealed that Adani, represented by one of Trump’s personal lawyers, admitted to offering a $10bn investment in the US to resolve the criminal case. The federal judge overseeing the case determined the investment played no role in the justice department’s decision to abandon the case. “These fresh details continue to raise concerns about the judgment of the DoJ, and the extent to which the DoJ is willing and able to prosecute white-collar criminals under President Trump,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in a letter sent on Wednesday, and seen by the Guardian. Adani was indicted in 2024 in New York for allegedly participating in a bribery and fraud scheme in which he paid Indian officials to secure a contract for one of his companies. He denied the allegations. Prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the case against Adani in May after he hired a new legal team, led by Robert Giuffra Jr, and offered to invest $10bn in the US. Following the news, Warren and Blumenthal sent a letter to Blanche in June requesting information about the fraud case and raising concerns about whether the justice department dismissed the case in exchange for Adani’s investment. However, the senators did not receive a response. Since then, new details about the case have emerged, including allegations that Boris Epshteyn, a member of Trump’s personal legal team who also served as an informal adviser, helped Adani. Another report claimed Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, met with Adani in November 2025, before the case was dropped. A spokesperson for Trump Jr said earlier this year that the conversation “had zero to do with DoJ’s actions in this case”. A spokesperson for Epshteyn denied being involved in Adani’s “arguments, advocacy or efforts” to the Wall Street Journal in June. Epshteyn was never hired by Adani or his company, the Adani Group, nor did he maintain a relationship with Adani, the spokesperson added. The Guardian has asked Epshteyn for comment. The Democratic lawmakers are now asking the justice department for more information about Adani’s alleged investment offer, including a list of employees who were present when the offer was made, the terms of the offer, when the offer was made and where. They also want to know whether the justice department employees knew Epshteyn was allegedly working on behalf of Adani, or if Epshteyn had any contact with justice department employees regarding Adani, among other questions. “We are also concerned about the involvement of two of President Trump’s personal lawyers in this case, and the extent to which they reveal potential political influence and special treatment for well-connected insiders at the DoJ,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in their letter. The Democrats also want to know if Trump Jr, or any person working on behalf of Trump Jr, had contact with a justice department employee regarding Adani. Warren and Blumenthal requested responses no later than 5 October. The Guardian has asked Blanche’s office for comment.

title: Oil price rise creates more pressure on UK policymakers before budget
author: Heather Stewart and Graeme Wearden
summary: Treasury sources concede ‘less room’ for manoeuvre as global bond selloff also hikes government’s borrowing costs
body_text: Oil prices lurched upwards again on Thursday, creating a growing headache for UK policymakers ahead of John Healey’s budget next month. While Healey has been keen to present an upbeat picture of the UK’s economic prospects, Treasury sources concede the sharp jump in oil and gas prices means they have “less room” than a month ago. Officials are working “at pace” on a range of possible options for supporting consumers, particularly if high prices persist, feeding through into a sharp rise in the quarterly energy price cap in January. But any package is expected to fall far short of the costly across-the-board subsidies announced by Liz Truss in 2022, with the Treasury mindful of the measures already taken, including Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on electricity bills. Options are believed to include shifting more green subsidies into general taxation, echoing the approach taken by Rachel Reeves, or targeting help at the poorest households – though some officials are sceptical about how effectively this can be achieved. The price of a barrel of Brent crude was up almost 5% at $108 on Thursday after reports of more military clashes between Saudi Arabia and Houthi forces. Donald Trump has given little indication of how, or when, the wider US-Israeli war on Iran could be brought to a close, despite the impact on gasoline prices in the US before crucial midterm elections. Senior UK government figures are also increasingly concerned about the prospect of interest rate rises, which could push up the cost of a mortgage just as Burnham has promised voters “breathing space”. After leaving interest rates on hold at 3.75% last week, the Bank of England said it expected the energy price cap to rise by as much as 24% in the new year. The Bank’s chief economist, Clare Lombardelli, said in a speech on Thursday that the longer oil prices remained elevated as a result of the war, the more likely it was that rates would have to rise. “The longer higher energy prices persist, the greater the risk that indirect effects build and that inflation expectations, wage bargaining and price-setting behaviour begin to adjust in response,” she told an economic conference in Warsaw, Poland. “On that basis, policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity.” Lombardelli’s warning was echoed by another member of the Bank’s monetary policy committee, the deputy governor Sarah Breeden, who told a conference at Imperial College London: “The larger and longer the shock, the more likely it is that we’ll see the material second-round effects that policy needs to respond [to].” Expectations of higher inflation and interest rates caused by rising energy prices are a key factor driving the global selloff in government bond markets – raising the cost of borrowing for the UK, alongside other economies. The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds, known as gilts, rose to 5.39% on Thursday, approaching the 19-year high set last week. Higher interest rates raise the upfront cost of government investment and feed through into Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts of whether the chancellor is on course to meet Labour’s fiscal rules. Analysts believe recent increases in yields have wiped out more than half of the £24bn “headroom” against the rules that Reeves had built up at the time of the spring statement in March. Healey has repeatedly promised to meet the rules with a “buffer against uncertainty” but this is widely expected to be significantly lower than £24bn. Rebuilding it to that level would be likely to require large tax increases or spending cuts, but Treasury sources insist the budget will be narrowly focused. Investors across the main markets have been ditching bonds in recent weeks in a wave of selling, as the conflict in the Middle East rumbles on. As the bond sell-off continued to worsen on Thursday, yields on 10-year US treasury bonds surged to 5.17%, the highest level since 2007. Alongside higher inflation, investors appear to be concerned about the risks of uncontrolled US government spending. Some analysts also suggest large-scale bond issuance by AI firms is undermining demand for treasuries.

title: First Thing: Trump welcomes Xi to Washington amid tensions over trade, AI and Taiwan
author: Martin Belam
summary: State visit takes place at same time as UN general assembly, which Chinese leader has avoided
body_text: Good morning. Donald Trump has welcomed Xi Jinping to the US, greeting the Chinese leader on the asphalt at Joint Base Andrews at the start of his state visit. Xi’s trip coincides with the UN general assembly in New York, but he is not attending the gathering. The pageantry will continue with a formal welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events. The White House also invited major tech leaders to a state dinner being held for Xi. What will the two leaders discuss? Amy Hawkins notes in this explainer that topics are likely to include the development of AI technology, frosty trade relations and Taiwan. What developments have there been in US-China relations? The US treasury secretary, Scott ⁠Bessent, announced that the US ⁠and China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called Busan ⁠agreement, a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies. Who else has been invited to the US? The US has invited Vladimir Putin to take part in the G20 meeting scheduled to take place in Miami in December, in what would be the Russian leader’s first attendance at such a summit since he launched his invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.” Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian described the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table. But he balanced that with a willingness to talk, saying: “We are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.” Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating the country’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, at the start of the US-Israeli war. He held up photographs of the ayatollah and some of the more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict. He also insisted that Tehran had never started a war. Why is Israel facing a water supply crisis? Israel is facing weeks of water shortages after an exceptional algae bloom crippled much of its desalination capacity, in a crisis scientists say was triggered when Israeli attacks destroyed much of Gaza’s wastewater infrastructure, causing a huge discharge of untreated sewage. Judge orders White House to restore access to CNN, MS Now and Politico In a blow for the administration and Donald Trump’s repeated attacks on US media outlets, a federal judge has ordered the White House to temporarily restore ⁠access to journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico. The US district judge Tim Kelly said the ban on the three media outlets was ⁠likely to be unconstitutional. A lawyer for the Department of Justice told Kelly the administration had provided enough explanation for the revocation of the press passes, but the judge signaled skepticism of that argument, noting that the letters were sent after the revocation occurred and the lawsuit was filed. Where else has Trump suffered a legal setback over media coverage? A judge has also dismissed Trump’s lawsuit accusing the Des Moines Register and its former pollster of misrepresenting the state of the 2024 presidential race, rejecting the president’s claim that the newspaper’s poll coverage violated Iowa’s consumer fraud law. Eight USS Lincoln personnel have attempted suicide, US navy confirms Eight US navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group have attempted to take their own lives since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran, the acting US navy secretary, Hung Cao, revealed in a letter to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand. Donald Trump described reports of poor conditions on the ship as fake news in August. • In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. International helplines can be found at befrienders.org In other news … Democrats accused the Republican senator Susan Collins of corruption after the media outlet ProPublica reported that the FBI had proposed investigating her for allegedly accepting bribes. Collins has disputed the report. The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its jobs website after a criminal hacking group claimed to have accessed “very sensitive data” on nearly all agents and job applicants. Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years after being convicted of sexually assaulting the former TV production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006 at his Manhattan apartment. The former NFL star Antonio Brown plans to accept a plea deal on an attempted murder charge. Doing so will mean the former wide receiver avoids prison. Meta announced a new set of virtual reality glasses and a collection of new smart glasses, including an audio-only version without a camera. Stat of the day: RFK Jr received $4m in book advances from Maha allies over past year The US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, received $4m in book advances over the last year from allies in the Make America Healthy Again movement. According to a 2024 ethics filing, however, he had pledged: “I will not engage in writing, editing, marketing or promotional services for any of these books during government service.” A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services said Kennedy Jr “complies with all applicable federal ethics laws, regulations and financial disclosure requirements”. The Filter recommends: The best THC drinks – these are more than ‘liquid weed’ The market for THC-infused seltzers and spirits has never been more full. Here are seven standouts. Don’t miss this: Meet the real-life Pokémon ‘professors’, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling Ana Diaz spoke to the volunteers who help to organise the game’s competitive communities around the world at the 2026 Pokémon world championships in San Francisco. … or this: ‘I miss old Google’ – readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI I am old enough to remember the 1990s when internet search was mostly haphazard guesswork, then Google came along and you could actually find things. Now you can’t again. Google’s insertion of AI overviews has profoundly changed the browsing habits of billions of people. Guardian readers explain their new search strategies. Climate check: 20 years after An Inconvenient Truth, Al Gore still believes Oliver Milman reports on how the former US vice-president is still optimistic about climate advocacy two decades after the groundbreaking documentary. Last Thing: In historic first, tropical turtles spotted nesting on California beaches “This is the first documented case of a turtle nesting on the west coast,” Justin Viezbicke, the California stranding coordinator for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (Noaa), said. What caused the turtles to begin nesting farther north than usual remains an open question. Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. title: Fossil-fuel firms in line for billions in benefits after answering Trump’s donation call
author: Maya Yang
summary: Senators’ report says taxpayers face higher bills after ‘bargain’ between president and major polluters
body_text: The fossil fuel industry secured an estimated $190bn in tax breaks and subsidies over the next decade after responding to Donald Trump’s pre-election call for major campaign donations, leaving American taxpayers to shoulder higher bills and public health costs associated with pollution, according to a new report. Released on Thursday by Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, ranking member of the Senate environment and public works committee, and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, the report details what the senators describe as the fossil fuel industry’s expansive influence over the Trump administration. Pointing to Trump’s April 2024 fundraiser at Mar-a-Lago, Florida where he reportedly asked industry executives for $1bn in campaign contributions, in exchange for tax breaks and deregulations, the report said: “Big oil delivered in the hundreds of millions.” The senators said: “The Trump administration has delivered right back, handing polluters benefits worth hundreds of billions of dollars. That bargain came at a price, and American families are the ones paying it: higher energy bills and higher costs associated with increased damages from climate change and air and water pollution.” The senators also cited the Trump administration’s “near-total refusal to cooperate with legitimate congressional oversight”, saying it “complicated” their investigation. The estimate of $190bn savings for industry is calculated from existing tax breaks and subsidies over the next 10 years plus new benefits delivered by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to an analysis by Senator Bernie Sanders for legislation he proposed with Congresswoman Ilhan Omar to eliminate “handouts” for industry. In addition to an estimated $201m investment in Trump’s re-election campaign, industry executives contributed $19m to his inaugural fund, which the report described as “the largest political investment the industry has ever made”. In exchange, the report said Trump appointed 26 senior officials – all of whom had previously worked for fossil fuel, chemical, or other polluting industries – across various government agencies including the Environmental Protection Agency, as well as the energy and interior departments. The report also noted that the fossil-fuel industry secured various policies that would curb competition from clean energy, increase gas and coal consumption and “force Americans to spend at least $580bn in added fuel costs alone over the next three decades”. As part of Trump’s “big, beautiful” domestic spending bill, signed last July, the government created a $1bn direct subsidy fund for fossil fuels, using the Defense Production Act authority to “funnel taxpayer money into propping up fossil fuel projects” considered economically risky by private capital markets. The act also provides a permanent 20% business income deduction for oil and gas companies, which the report said would cost the government an estimated $737bn overall. The report further accuses the Trump administration of exempting companies from pollution controls, saying Trump “abused” the Clean Air Act by exempting more than 180 polluting facilities. The senators noted that “the rules at issue were designed to limit emissions of known neurotoxin and carcinogens”. It also highlighted that the Trump administration repealed federal vehicle greenhouse gas standards and moved to roll back emissions rules for power plants and oil and gas facilities. While the Trump administration estimated the changes would save Americans $1.3tn, the report cites an EPA estimate of $1.5tn in additional fuel, repair and maintenance costs for consumers. Separately, the EPA estimated that the repeal would result in at least $580bn in additional fuel costs over the next three decades. The report describes the policy as potentially the “single largest payback” the Trump administration has provided the fossil fuel industry. Moreover, the report found that the Trump administration’s attacks on fossil fuel competitors include paying companies $1.8bn in taxpayer funds to cancel wind projects across the country. As of May, more than 160 projects – all proposed on private land – had been frozen. According to the report, the stalled projects represent approximately 30 gigawatts of generating capacity, $54bn in capital investment, and enough electricity to power more than 8.5m homes. The report also pointed to Trump’s own pledge earlier this year: “My goal is to not let any windmill be built.” The report said: “The buyouts follow the same structure: taxpayer money is used to buy off fossil fuel’s low-cost clean energy competition – a double hit, first to the public treasury, then to the electric rates.” In the second Trump administration, environmental enforcement has also weakened. The report found that the justice department has brought 76% fewer civil environmental enforcement cases than during Joe Biden’s first year in office, and 81% fewer than during Trump’s first term. Highlighting the impact of the fossil fuel industry’s influence on Trump and its consequences for the American public, the report stated that Trump’s “polluter-first agenda exposed Americans to price shocks on fossil fuels, heating, food production, and electricity; increased the cost of trucking food to grocery stores; and raised fertilizer prices for farmers”. One modeling estimate cited in the report found that average household energy bills could be $78 to $192 higher per year by 2035. Industrial energy costs, meanwhile, are projected to rise by between $7bn and $11bn over the same period. In response to the report, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told the Guardian: “These Democrat senators should do some self-reflection on their ties to the so-called ‘green’ energy industry. They wasted billions of American taxpayer dollars in the name of the Green New Scam. “While they are focused on a useless partisan report, the Trump administration is actively working to pass historic permitting reform to help improve energy infrastructure and lower costs.” The administration has hailed its “energy dominance” agenda as delivering for industry, energy workers and saving the US public money in energy costs. The report, however, said the sharpest increases could ironically fall on Republican-led states that lack state-level policies supporting renewable energy development. In addition to rising energy costs, the report pointed to the public health costs associated with Trump’s policies, noting that fossil fuel-related air pollution and climate-related harms cost approximately $820bn annually, or roughly $2,500 per person in additional health costs each year. “Even if Americans do not suffer from polluter-driven heart or respiratory disease, they pay more as health insurance companies spread around those costs,” the report said. Homeowner insurance costs are also rising as climate-driven disasters become more frequent and severe. The report noted that the average American homeowner now pays “about $2,948 per year in insurance premiums, nearly 12% higher than just one year ago”. The report also found that in 2025, fossil fuel companies paid more to shareholders than the direct damages attributable to extreme weather in the US, despite surges in hurricanes, wildfires, floods, heatwaves and droughts. Several environmental advocacy organizations have criticized the Trump administration in response to the report. Climate Power spokesperson Alex Glass told the Guardian: “This report lays it out in black and white. The Trump administration isn’t setting energy policy; the fossil fuel industry is writing it for them. Fossil fuel money bought access, and fossil fuel executives got the keys to the agencies meant to regulate.” Similarly, Mahyar Sorour, the director of beyond fossil fuels policy at the Sierra Club, said: “This report elevates a troubling reality: while fossil fuel companies throw money at politicians to fulfill polluters’ wishlists, American families are left paying for an energy system that puts corporate profits ahead of public health. “It’s time to make polluters pay.” Meanwhile, David Arkush, director of Public Citizen’s climate program, told the Guardian: “The campaign contributions to Donald Trump by big oil have paid dividends, and have allowed the fossil fuel industry to continue to pollute our communities … Every American family struggling with high costs is suffering because of the corrupt relationship between Donald Trump and the fossil fuel industry.”

title: After so long in Trump’s sights, hopeful Greenlanders breathe a collective sigh of relief
author: Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent
summary: Locals hope agreement signed this week is step towards independence and end to US threats to annex island
body_text: Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and Múte B Egede, the foreign minister, received a hero’s welcome when they landed back in Nuuk from New York on Wednesday night – and a nation took a collective sigh of relief. Colleagues, friends and members of the public turned out to greet them at an airport where, just 20 months ago, the landing of a Trump-branded plane containing Donald Trump Jr had kickstarted a geopolitical crisis that the people of Greenland now hope is over. To cheers and applause, and waving red and white Erfalasorput flags, the politicians were credited with saving the nation thanks to a new defence agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the US signed this week at the UN in New York. It comes after an unprecedented period of turbulence in which Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to invade the Arctic island and almost tore apart Nato in the process. “Welcome home,” the speaker of Inatsisartut, the Greenlandic parliament, Kim Kielsen, said. “Welcome to a country that we were about to lose. You have ensured that we have a future here.” Like many Greenlanders, for the last year-and-a-half he said he had been holding his breath. Nielsen, who became prime minister last year in the middle of the crisis, told the crowd: “We can be calm. Our land will not be taken. Our land will not be bought. The road has been long, and it has been very difficult and dangerous.” Hundreds then attended a celebratory coffee party at Katuaq, the Greenlandic capital’s cultural centre. Aqqalukkuluk Fontain, 38, who was there with his girlfriend, Stella, and their youngest daughter, Aura, who is three, said the collective release of tension was palpable. “It was a joyous moment. It’s going to linger for a while,” said the IT manager, who earlier this year organised a protest outside the new US embassy in Nuuk. He cautioned he could not entirely relax – concerned that, after the midterms, Trump could change his mind and relations could “take a turn for the worse” – but hailed the deal with the US as a moment of pride for Greenland and a stroke of “strategy genius” from Greenlandic and Danish negotiators. “Trump is trying to angle it that he made a great deal. But he wanted total control, ownership of Greenland. He didn’t get that,” he said. Its full text contains some key differences from the 1951 defence agreement it is intended to update – for example, the US gets underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system – but is a far cry from Donald Trump’s original threat to annex the Arctic island. And in terms of tangible outcomes, the biggest winner is arguably Greenland, where it is seen as a potential stepping stone to future independence. When the 1951 agreement was signed, Greenland was still a colony of Denmark. Now, it is a largely autonomous territory that has signed an agreement alongside Denmark with the US that it played a central role in negotiating. A big question hanging over Greenland independence was what would happen to its status within Nato and relationship with the US. The new agreement answers that question. It stipulates that if it did become independent, the governments of Greenland and Denmark would “together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will agree to remain in Nato, including by applying to become a member if necessary”. The centrality of Nato to the agreement is also seen as a boost for an alliance that was creaking under US claims against one of its fellow members’ territory. Greenlandic politician Qarsoq Høegh-Dam, who earlier this year became the first member of the pro-independence party Naleraq to be elected to the Danish parliament, said there was still considerable work to do in terms of gaining independence but that “a lot of what ifs” have now gone. “It’s a point of relief for Greenlanders,” he said. “They can lower their shoulders a bit, so we can talk about domestic issues, the road to independence more freely, instead of the search of what if?” Much of the agreement already existed in practice, he said, but now “it is written in ink” with Greenland’s explicit involvement. “It’s a continuation of an agreement since the 1950s. The difference is now that Greenland has some say in it. They want to agree for themselves instead of a country overseas agreeing on behalf of them,” he said. “That’s the difference first and foremost and it is significant.” He said, however, there were still questions about what the words will equate to in practice, for example on investment. “It’s a good foundation, but the details are missing,” he said. Given that just a few months ago Trump was threatening to invade Greenland, and a few weeks since he posted a map of Greenland covered with the US flag to social media, in many ways the very fact that a diplomatic agreement has been reached is a victory in itself. Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS), said: “For Danes and Greenlanders, it’s a win to be able to force Trump into doing something diplomatically. And if this actually puts the Greenland crisis to rest, it will be felt as a win for Greenland, Denmark and Europe because then we can concentrate on real problems and trying to find ways to work with the US on that.” Aviaja Fontain, 41, a student from Nuuk, said the agreement puts to rest months of anxiety. At one point, amid government warnings about preparedness, she thought Nuuk was being attacked by the US during what turned out to be a power cut caused by a storm. “Many of us have been afraid that Trump will use force, but now I can feel relief,” she said. Now she feels she can finally relax. “We don’t have to think about getting attacked and just live our peaceful life again.”

title: EU says Trump’s plan to ban US diesel exports would ‘negatively impact both sides’
author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
summary: US president’s suggested 90-day export ban before midterm elections could bring even higher fuel prices across Europe
body_text: The EU has warned Donald Trump against plans to ban US diesel exports to the global market, saying the move would negatively affect Europe and the US. The European Commission has reacted with “concern” to reports this week that the US president could prevent diesel from reaching the global market. Trump is reportedly considering a 90-day export ban to provide a temporary respite from high pump prices for US households before the midterm elections, after US diesel reached a record average of $6.52 (£4.93) a gallon. “I’ve said let’s not send ‌out the diesel. ‌We make a lot of diesel … I’ve called for it. ‌I’ve called for it within my people,” he said. Olof Gill, a spokesperson for the EU’s executive arm, said on Thursday “any disruption would risk negatively impacting both sides” and the EU expected “close partners to consult each other before taking measures that affect shared markets”. The EU made the diplomatic intervention as experts said that the potential export ban could be “devastating” for Europe, and traders scrambled to assess the continent’s reliance on imports from the US. The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has warned at an Economist event in New York that banning exports was a “blunt tool” that could harm US fuel supplies in the long term. For Europe, the ban could be far more damaging. US diesel exports have made up a third of the continent’s imports this year, as supplies from war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia have plummeted. By August, the US supplied about half of Europe’s diesel imports. Pump prices have already climbed to record highs across Germany and the Netherlands, leading to calls for political leaders to protect households from rising costs. In the UK, motorists may be only days away from fresh all-time highs, raising concerns over the economic impact of further price hikes for hard-pressed households. The RAC said the average cost of diesel was 197.75p a litre on Thursday, up from 142.38p before the start of the Iran war. “A US export ban would be devastating for diesel supply in Europe, which would struggle to replace supply,” said Josh Michalowski, the head of European diesel pricing at Argus Media, a commodities data provider. Fuel stations across Europe are unlikely to run dry, because Europe produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries. It also stores fuels in reserve. But experts fear that competing for cargoes on the global market would lead to higher market prices. So far the market for diesel cargoes has remained relatively quiet since reports of a potential US diesel ban emerged this week, according to Benedict George, the head of European products at Argus. He said traders were still weighing up the degree to which the White House might limit US exports. “If this prospect became even relatively serious [in the White House], it would be very serious for European markets. There would be some degree of panic given how reliant buyers have become on US cargoes,” George said. “There’s enough European diesel production to ensure that we wouldn’t run out, but losing US cargoes would mean buyers would have to compete with buyers in Asia for the few available cargoes from the Middle East and India, in what is already a very competitive global market.” The price of diesel has outpaced the rising price of global oil markets due to severe disruption to refineries in the Gulf and in Russia. The price difference – known as the “crack spread” – reached a record high earlier this month and could climb further still. “A US ban on diesel exports would pose a significant challenge for the UK, given the country’s growing reliance on American refined fuel,” said Thomas Pugh, the chief economist at the audit, tax and consulting firm RSM UK. The UK has only four operating oil refineries after the closures of Grangemouth and Lindsey last year. Both produced diesel for the UK market. Pugh warned that losing almost 90,000 barrels a day of US distillate, or 18% of the country’s total consumption, would leave the UK even more exposed to global diesel prices. He added that, while shortages of fuel were unlikely immediately, a longer-term ban would make them a “real possibility”. Although the number of motorists driving diesel passenger vehicles has fallen, it remains the lifeblood of the UK’s agricultural and logistics sectors by fuelling heavy machinery, lorries and vans. The European Commission spokesperson said: “High-level contacts between the European Union and the US administration are ongoing.” A UK government spokesperson said: “Forecourts in the UK are being supplied with petrol and diesel as normal and we have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”

title: Seth Meyers on Trump’s praise of Xi Jinping: ‘Not even Chinese citizens gush this much about Xi’
author: Guardian staff
summary: Late-night hosts discussed Donald Trump’s unusually lavish state reception for the visiting Chinese leader
body_text: Late-night hosts reacted to Donald Trump’s lavish praise for visiting Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Republicans’ desperate efforts to save their chances in the midterms. Seth Meyers On Late Night, Seth Meyers mocked Donald Trump’s excessive praise for Xi Jinping, the visiting Chinese leader whom the US president has referred to as a “fierce person” “strong, smart, tough” and “a piece of granite … an amazing man,” among many other compliments. “Not even Chinese citizens gush this much about Xi,” said Meyers, noting that the Chinese government had to crack down on social media posts comparing Xi to Winnie the Pooh. “That’s real. Trump thinks Xi is a piece of granite, and meanwhile Xi’s own citizens think he’s a cartoon bear – news that is going to make Trump so sad he will continue to have Eeyore’s posture.” “In fact, Trump has been so excited for Xi’s visit, he’s even been making excuses for China’s behavior toward the US,” the host continued. As Trump told Fox News’s Laura Ingraham: “People say, oh, he spies on us. Well, we spy on him, too.” “Now, this might be an old-fashioned take on things,” Meyers said, “but I think when you’re spying on someone, you’re not supposed to tell them that. That’s why The Americans lasted six years, and not 10 minutes.” Trump’s unusually friendly relations with Xi have drawn condemnation from members of his own party. Roger Wicker, Republican senator from Mississippi, gave a speech on the Senate floor blasting Trump for the invitation, celebrating a rare US-China trade truce instead of inquiring “about the purposes of China’s massive military buildup, or about China’s clear support for Iran”. “I’m sure he’ll get to all that, right after he grills Xi on his fitness regimen,” Meyers joked. Jimmy Kimmel “We’re now less than six weeks out from the midterms, and Republicans are panicking,” said Jimmy Kimmel on Wednesday evening. “They’re scraping the bottom of the cracker barrel looking for something to pull them out of the hole Donald Trump dumped them in.” “Just to give you an idea of how desperate they are for anything,” Kimmel added, Matt Gaetz, the disgraced congressman from Florida, responded to a video on X from a regular Republican voter expressing disappointment in Trump’s war in Iran, with: “Bro we need your vote. I hate the war too. But the Democrats want to trans your kids.” “Yeah, they’re driving around in trans vans, just grabbing children,” Kimmel deadpanned. “They’re eating the dogs and trans-ing your kids.” The host then turned to Xi Jinping’s three-day state visit to the US. “It’s a rare opportunity for Trump to thank the leader of the country where his God Bless the USA bibles are made in person,” he quipped. The Chinese president was greeted at the airport with “a flyover and a combover”, followed by a reception. “Trump was planning to give Xi an exclusive tour of the White House,” Kimmel added, “and he’s even going to let him pick one room of the White House to demolish, which is fun.”

title: Trump’s FDA nominee says MMR shot is ‘safe and effective’ at Senate hearing
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Dr Heidi Overton faces confirmation hearing weeks after standing behind Trump as he suggested shot could be ‘quite lethal’
body_text: Dr Heidi Overton, Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), has told senators the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is “safe and effective”, weeks after standing behind the president as he suggested the shot could be “quite lethal”. At a confirmation hearing on Thursday, Overton described the MMR vaccine as “safe and effective”, adding: “It is our best tool right now in the public health response to the measles outbreak.” Asked whether any vaccine on the US market was unsafe, she said: “Every vaccine on the US market right now is safe and effective, according to the FDA.” Overton faced questions from Bill Cassidy, the Louisiana Republican and physician who chairs the Senate health committee, whose vote is seen as pivotal. He had called her role in Trump’s August vaccine executive order “almost disqualifying”. The hearing comes as the US records its highest number of measles cases since 1991. When Cassidy asked what Overton would do if the president asked her to break those assurances on vaccine safety, she replied: “I would give him my best advice, and I would follow the statutory requirements for the role of FDA commissioner regarding individual product determinations for safety and efficacy.” When Bernie Sanders, the independent Vermont senator, asked whether she would have “the courage to stand up to” a president who he said “lies all of the time”, Overton did not answer directly. “I have worked for the president for a long time now, and earned his trust because I have been part of robust discussions to bring him the best advice,” she said. In her opening statement, Overton framed her agenda around speeding up drug development to protect US leadership in biotechnology. “We can protect America’s global leadership in biotechnology, but we have to act fast,” she said, pledging to make the FDA “the agency of the possible, rather than the impossible”. Overton, whose father leads a church in her home town of Gallup, New Mexico, has described Colossians 3:23 (“Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters”) as one of her life verses since childhood. Susan Collins, the Maine Republican senator, challenged her over the FDA’s August authorization of flavored vapes and nicotine pouches, including blueberry, mango and cappuccino. Collins said nearly 90% of young e-cigarette users choose flavored products. Overton said there was “100% agreement from this administration that we must protect kids”, but defended the decision as recommended by career staff because “so many adults are using flavors preferentially”. She added: “If that standard is not appropriate, we should work on statutes to fix that.” If confirmed, Overton, 37, would be the youngest ever FDA commissioner. A surgeon by training, she is now deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy, and served as a White House fellow during Trump’s first term. In a February 2023 issue brief for the conservative America First Policy Institute, where she was chief policy officer, she criticized federal policies that allowed abortion pills to be sent through the mail, writing that abortion “is corrosive to children, women, and society broadly”. She would replace Marty Makary, who resigned in May, and take over an agency still recovering from 2025 layoffs that cut its workforce by nearly 20%.

title: US mortgage rates top 7% for first time in 20 months
author: Gaya Gupta
summary: Increase comes after Fed decision to raise interest rates, as Americans struggle with high prices and stagnant wages
body_text: US mortgage rates surpassed 7% for the first time since January 2025, according to federal lender Freddie Mac, aggravating a housing market that has endured years of high interest rates and low supply. The increase comes after the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates, which directly affect mortgage rates, for the first time since 2023, citing high inflation. Rates on 16 September went up by a quarter of a point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%. In new projections, a majority of the Fed’s rate-setting committee predicted at least one additional rate hike before the end of this year. Last year, the Freddie Mac 30-year-mortgage rate, commonly used on home loans across the country, had been trending down from 7.79% – a generational high reached in late 2023. But rates have been creeping back up since late February, when the US and Israel launched its war with Iran. The conflict drove inflation to its highest levels in three years and sharply increased energy prices. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, topped $105 earlier on Thursday. On Thursday, the 10-year US treasury yield – which underpins the 30-year mortgage rate and other borrowing costs – also reached its highest level since July 2007 and the 30-year Treasury yield hitting its peak since 2004 as investors raised expectations for another Fed rate hike next month. Earlier in September, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced the Treasury would triple its buyback of government debt, but yields have continued to rise. The housing market has long been in a slowdown, said Anthony Smith, a senior economist at Realtor.com, with existing home sales hitting their 2026 low so far in August and pending sales that have turned negative year over year. “A 7% handle is as much psychological as mathematical, and it arrives at the point in the season when leverage usually shifts toward buyers,” said Smith. High mortgage rates are just one of the many reasons why Americans are struggling to attain home ownership. Wages have not kept pace with higher inflation, and everyday costs are higher. The frustration is expected to show up in November’s midterm elections as Republicans struggle to maintain control of Congress. Nearly three-quarters of Americans disapprove of Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, according to a recent CNN poll conducted by SSRS, and two-thirds of registered voters rate the economy as “extremely important” to their vote.

title: Americans living in Britain should vote – control of Congress is at stake
summary: Letter: John Scardino says US citizens abroad could tip the balance in favour of the Democrats, in response to an article by Kathryn Sikkink
body_text: Americans in the UK should definitely ask for their US ballots and vote. As Kathryn Sikkink writes (Many Americans live in the UK – but few vote back home. This year, that must change, 22 September), it’s easier than they may think and there are several compelling reasons to vote. One helpful website that wasn’t mentioned is votefromabroad.org. This nonpartisan website was launched 20 years ago, never keeps your data and provides 24/7 voter help that’s provided in person in 50 countries or via Zoom or email. Depending on the state in which they last lived, voters may be able to receive and return their ballot electronically. Control of Congress is at stake. Today, Republicans have a razor-thin majority in the House: 218 to 214. Many of these seats were determined by just a few hundred votes. Think of that in the context of the 298,268 voting-age US citizens in the UK that Sikkink references. Congress writes the laws and decides spending. It also investigates corruption, abuse and mismanagement in government. Even if the Democrats regain only the House of Representatives, they’ll have the power to stop some of the self-dealing and destruction of basic services. Decisions made in Washington affect Americans abroad, their families and their communities, and their votes help determine who makes those decisions. John Scardino Former vice-chair, Democrats Abroad UK

title: Democratic lawmakers accuse Trump administration of interference in Brazilian elections
author: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
summary: Legislators sent letter to Marco Rubio saying US interference is weakening Brazil’s democratic institutions
body_text: A group of 31 Democratic members of the US Congress has sent a letter to the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, criticising the Trump administration over “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s elections. Latin America’s largest country will hold the first round of its presidential election on 4 October, with polls showing a technical tie between the incumbent leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro. In the letter sent to Rubio on Thursday, 30 members of the House of Representatives and the senator Bernie Sanders listed a series of measures the US government took that they interpret as attempts to secure a victory for Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. They wrote that those actions “reflect a broader and deeply troubling pattern of interference by the Trump administration in recent electoral processes across Latin America”, citing the recent midterm elections in Argentina and presidential elections in Honduras and Colombia. In July, a group of 11 Democratic members of Congress sent a similar letter arguing that Trump was trying to interfere in Colombia’s election in favour of the far-right millionaire and former lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who went on to win the second round. In Thursday’s letter, the lawmakers wrote that US officials under Trump have engaged in a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil”. They noted that when Trump imposed his first tariffs on Brazil last year, he made clear that one reason was Bolsonaro’s trial over his attempt to stage a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. The former president was ultimately convicted and, unable to run because he is under house arrest, named his son to take his place. They also cited new tariffs that Trump imposed on Brazil in July under section 301 of US trade law, as well as plans by the US government to send two officials to Brazil to “cast doubt on the integrity of the country’s voting system, considered by many experts to be among the most reliable in the world”. The Lula administration ultimately denied the US delegation visas. The Brazilian president has repeatedly complained that Trump is trying to interfere in Brazil’s elections and, in his speech opening the UN general assembly this week, said, without naming anyone: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy, internal or external, to act against the will of the people.” In the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US is “acting as an agent of interference and destabilization – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”. They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October. The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.

title: ICE has wasted tens of millions to carry out Trump’s mass detention agenda – report
author: Guardian staff and agency
summary: GAO documents array of costly problems as ICE pursues controversial plans to rapidly increase detention capacity
body_text: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and other federal agencies have wasted tens of millions of dollars pursuing controversial plans to rapidly increase detention capacity – and the total will likely rise due to continuing mismanagement, congressional investigators warned on Thursday. The US government accountability office (GAO) documented costly problems in several initiatives ICE has pursued since Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025 and ordered the mass arrest and deportation of people his administration has deemed should be forced out of the country. Among the misspending was nearly $3m to erect tents at the Guantánamo Bay US naval base in Cuba that were never used; $20m to maintain bought warehouses that are now being sold without having housed a single detainee; and excessive rates paid to hold detainees at the deficient and now-shuttered Florida lockup known as “Alligator Alcatraz”. Congress gave ICE an unprecedented $45bn to expand detention capacity last year as part of the Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, but the agency has no comprehensive strategic plan for how to spend it wisely, the report warned. The detainee population has increased from 39,000 in January 2025 to 67,000 as of 30 July. “Without taking action to manage detention investments in accordance with program and project management practices, ICE will likely continue to make uninformed decisions and risk further inefficiency and wasted resources,” warned the GAO, a nonpartisan agency that investigated at the request of congressional Democrats. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE’s parent agency, told the GAO it would develop a plan to guide its detention expansion by 31 August 2027, but that may be too late to prevent more waste, the report said. ICE and DHS offered no immediate additional comment on the report. Shortly after Trump returned to the White House, the government began blowing money by hastily pursuing plans to detain more people who, by the administration’s reckoning, were in the US illegally, the report found. Often, the government has pursued people with temporary legal status or an asylum application, or some who have a green card but have used protest speech the administration deems dangerous. In many other cases, despite saying it wanted to focus on “the worst of the worst” criminals, the Trump administration has spent resources on seeking, detaining and removing people with no criminal history who have violated civil immigration law yet lived, worked and paid taxes in the US for decades. After spending much on warehouses to use for detention, that initiative has faltered, the report found. It has sold a lot of the property it bought but ICE has also “incurred significant costs” for the four warehouses that it plans to keep, including a $426m million outlay to renovate facilities in Arizona and Maryland that is on hold due to legal challenges. ICE launched a plan to purchase facilities owned by private contractors that were already housing detainees, saying it would give more control over infrastructure and limit local governments’ ability to restrict their use. The agency spent $1.5bn to buy two of them in July and could buy more, even though ICE has “not assessed the long-term affordability of owning these facilities”, the report said. The report found fault with other initiatives. ICE never reached a contract with the state of Florida to operate Alligator Alcatraz in the Everglades, which housed detainees for a year until it was closed in June after reports of substandard and abusive conditions. Instead, the DHS agreed to reimburse the state through a special $608m Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) grant that authorizes a charge of $249 per detainee per day – 171% higher than ICE’s normal rate of $92, the report found. DHS is also paying the state the higher rate for a second facility that is still open in Sanderson, Florida. ICE is also facing high costs under an agreement in which the Bureau of Prisons is housing detainees at eight facilities. The agreement requires ICE to reimburse the full cost, which has ballooned because of overtime and other staffing assignments, and pay a rate of $182 per detainee per day, the report said. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Texas woman triumphs as court upholds acquittal in voting error case
author: Sam Levine
summary: Crystal Mason has spent nearly a decade fighting conviction for casting provisional ballot that ultimately wasn’t counted
body_text: The nearly decade-long case of a Black Texas woman who was sentenced to five years in prison in a controversial illegal voting case will end with an acquittal, the state’s highest criminal court said in a 5-4 decision on Thursday. The woman, Crystal Mason, has been appealing against the case ever since her 2018 conviction for casting a provisional ballot that ultimately wasn’t counted. In 2024, the Texas court of criminal appeals acquitted her in the case. The local prosecutor handling the case appealed that ruling to Texas’s highest criminal court, which initially agreed to hear it. But on Thursday, the court reversed itself, and said it would not hear an appeal, letting the acquittal stand. It did not offer any explanation for why. “After 10 long years of fighting, I am overwhelmed with joy and gratitude. It’s hard to put into words how excited I am right now. This journey has been long, exhausting, and emotional, but God has carried me through it all,” Mason, 51, said in a text message. Phil Sorrells, the Tarrant county district attorney, said in a statement: “Illegal voting remains a crime in Texas. “If there is evidence that someone knowingly violates our election laws in Tarrant County, we will investigate it and, when the evidence supports it, prosecute it,” he said. Mason was on supervised release – which is like probation – for a federal tax felony when she went to her polling place on election day in the 2016 presidential election. When she arrived, officials could not find her on the list of registered voters and offered her a provisional ballot, a safeguard required by federal law, to cast her vote. Mason decided to do so. Poll workers testified that they had Mason swear everything in the affidavit was true, though Mason has always disputed this occurred. Texas, like many US states, prohibits people with a felony conviction from voting if they are on probation. Even though Mason signed an affidavit saying she was eligible to vote, she maintained she did not actually read the language on it and was never told she could not cast a ballot. Federal probation officials testified at her 2018 trial they never told her she couldn’t vote. Prosecutors nonetheless argued Mason knew she was ineligible because she signed the affidavit and had sworn to poll workers that the information in the ballot was true. Mason has always maintained that testimony poll workers gave at her trial was not true. A judge found her guilty and sentenced her to five years in prison. The case triggered outrage because Mason consistently maintained it was an innocent mistake and the severity of her sentence. As Donald Trump sought to escalate claims about voter fraud after the 2016 race, many also saw the case as a local effort to make an example of Mason. “Civic participation without fear of imprisonment is a cherished right that is critical to our system of democracy. The highest criminal court in Texas affirmed that right by letting the lower court’s acquittal stand,” said Thomas Buser-Clancy, an attorney with the Texas chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union, which helped to represent Mason. “Ms. Mason has spent nearly a decade defending her rights in Texas and today we see that her efforts have been successful not only in defending her own freedom, but also in protecting the ability of Texans across the state to participate in our democracy without fear.” Alison Grinter, another one of Mason’s attorneys, said the ruling was important given the upcoming midterm elections. “This really is a great day for Texas voters who can finally celebrate their right to go to the polls unafraid and undeterred by partisan intimidation and scare tactics,” she said. Because Mason was convicted of a criminal offense while on supervised release, she returned to federal prison for 10 months. During that period, she nearly lost her home to foreclosure and her teenage daughter was entrusted with running her household. Her college-age son left a football scholarship to return home and help with costs around the home. Mason has three children and also raised four of her brother’s children. She has 10 grandchildren. Four of the justices on the court wrote dissenting opinions, saying they believed there was sufficient evidence Mason knew she was ineligible when she cast a ballot. “The evidence presented by the State at Appellant’s trial for illegal voting was sufficient to show that Appellant ‘actually knew’ that she was ineligible to vote,” judge Lee Finley wrote in a dissent that was joined by judge Gina Parker. “The provisional voter affidavit, corroborated by the additional evidence presented by the State, leaves no doubt whatsoever that the trier of fact was presented with sufficient evidence to sustain Appellant’s conviction. This is not a close case.” Mason was not particularly political before 2016, but since her conviction, she has become much more politically engaged. In 2022, she opened a rally for Beto O’Rourke and worked to educate voters about their rights. Recently, she said, the wife of the current district attorney, Phil Sorrells, knocked on her door and asked her if she would consider voting for him this year. “The irony of that moment is something I will never forget,” she said. • This article was amended on 25 September 2026. An earlier version said prosecutors argued that Crystal Mason knew she was eligible to vote; this should have said ineligible.

title: Senate Republicans block Democratic effort to end US war with Iran
author: Joseph Gedeon and Chris Stein in Washington
summary: GOP stymies House-passed war powers resolution as conflict passes 200-day mark with 19 US service members killed
body_text: Senate Republicans on Thursday blocked a Democratic effort to end the US war with Iran, voting down a House-passed war powers resolution as the conflict that has killed 19 American service members passed the 200-day mark. The measure, which passed the House last week with bipartisan support, failed in the Senate by a 49-50 vote. Senate Democrats, led by the minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and the senator Andy Kim of New Jersey, forced the vote under the War Powers Resolution, which allows lawmakers to bring such measures to the floor. The proposal attracted some Republican support, but not enough to pass. For the first time, Thom Tillis of North Carolina voted for the resolution, as did Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Susan Collins of Maine, who had backed previous efforts. But Bill Cassidy of Louisiana – whose vote was key to passage of a resolution in June – voted no, as did John Fetterman a Democratic senator of Pennsylvania, ensuring the measure’s defeat. Ron Wyden, the Democratic senator from Oregon, acknowledged the uphill fight for the minority. “We’re going to stay at it until we win,” he said. Democrats have kept up a steady pace of war powers resolutions ever since Trump ordered the US military to attack Iran in conjunction with Israel at the end of February. While one proposal passed in June, support for others has oscillated – in July, after a ceasefire in the conflict collapsed, the Senate voted 47-49 against advancing a war powers resolution, with Collins the only Republican in support. Tim Kaine, a Democratic senator from Virginia, who has been a leader of the war powers push in the Senate, said: “We’re going to keep doing them every week because we see Republican candidates out in the field now starting to change their position.” In recent days, Republicans running for key congressional and gubernatorial races in the 3 November midterm elections have called for an end to the conflict, which has worsened the inflation that Trump campaigned on ending. “They recognize how bad this is,” Kaine said of the Republicans. Yet most congressional Republicans remain unconvinced by the campaign to end the war. Dan Sullivan, the Republican senatorfacing a tough re-election contest in Alaska, said: “The war powers vote is about removing American forces from the region, and when there are troops in contact, I don’t believe in doing it.” Speaking before the vote, Kim, a former state department official who served in the Middle East, said Americans were “sick and tired of this reckless and expensive war”. “Democrats have taken action. We’ve come to this chamber 11 times in the past 208 days to try to bring this war to an end,” Kim said. He cited a congressional budget office report estimating the war cost nearly $40bn in its first four months, and said at least 19 US service members had been killed and more than 750 injured. Kim also said estimates showed higher petrol prices had cost American households about $900 each since the war began. “Chaos is not a negotiating tactic,” Kim said. “Trump is simply over his head here.”

title: California sheriff ordered to return ballots he confiscated in voter ‘fraud’ inquiry
author: Uwa Ede-Osifo and agency
summary: Court says Chad Bianco’s conduct unlawful and seizure of ballots ‘creates substantial risk to election integrity’
body_text: California Republican sheriff Chad Bianco must return more than 650,000 ballots his department confiscated earlier this year in an unprecedented move that violated election law, a state supreme court ruled on Thursday. “Allowing law enforcement unfettered access to ballots, or the ability to handle and count them in secret, based on unregulated protocols, itself creates a substantial risk to election integrity,” the chief justice, Patricia Guerrero, wrote in a Thursday opinion. During a November 2025 special election, California voters passed Proposition 50, a redistricting amendment designed to counteract Republican-led gerrymandering in Texas. The measure easily passed statewide, and won in Bianco’s Riverside county by roughly 80,000 votes. After the election, a county citizen activist group claimed there was a discrepancy in the total vote count. Local election officials have said the complaint was unfounded. The Riverside county sheriff’s department launched an inquiry into the fraud claims, obtaining search warrants to assume custody of the ballots and other election materials. The Democratic attorney general of California, Rob Bonta, immediately launched a legal challenge, arguing Bianco had no authority over election materials and warning the seizure was designed to sow distrust in elections. He ordered Bianco to return the ballots, but Bianco did not. In court, Bianco’s attorneys argued the top prosecutor could not give directions to a sheriff about an active investigation. “Respondents’ arguments all boil down to the unsustainable view that the state’s chief law enforcement officer … must remain a mere bystander to an unprecedented sheriff’s investigation of undeniable statewide significance. As we have explained, that is not the case,” Guerrero wrote in a separate Thursday ruling. California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, praised the court’s decision. “Today’s ruling affirms that in California we will defend democracy – using every branch of government,” he said in a statement. “People deserve to know their ballot is counted and secure, and in California we will do everything we can to protect that constitutional right – this year, and beyond.” Newsom on Saturday signed a bill that would prevent anyone from seizing ballots, as Bianco did. “The new laws I signed just last week add new protections so attacks like this cannot happen again,” Newsom said on Thursday. Bianco’s ballot investigation came as Donald Trump has repeatedly disputed the results of the 2020 election, citing unsubstantiated instances of fraud. His administration in January seized ballots and other documents from an election office in Georgia. Some Republicans have mirrored Trump’s rhetoric on voting in their states. Election officials and civil rights groups have been following the Bianco case carefully as they brace for the possibility that Trump or his allies may try to seize ballots in November.

title: Mary Peltola’s campaign says reports of her using slurs and shoving staffer are exaggerated
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Alaska Democratic nominee in pivotal Senate race ‘struggled to deal with her grief’ after death of husband and mother, spokesperson said
body_text: Mary Peltola’s campaign on Thursday downplayed a report that the Democratic nominee in Alaska’s pivotal Senate race shoved a staffer and used slurs, saying the article exaggerated her behavior, but acknowledging she struggled following the deaths of her husband and mother. The New York Times article published on Wednesday is based on text messages and interviews with nine former employees of Peltola, who served in the House of Representatives from 2022 till the beginning of last year and is now set to face the Republican senator Dan Sullivan in the 3 November midterm elections. In a statement, Harry Child, a spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign, said her behavior was affected by the stress of working in the House together with the death of her husband in a 2023 plane crash as well as her mother around the same time. “At the time of their passing, Mary was parenting kids through their own grief, serving full-time in the US House of Representatives thousands of miles from home, and running a competitive re-election campaign – all while shouldering the enormous burden of grief,” Child said. “Like any person who has gone through multiple personal tragedies in the span of a few months, Mary sometimes struggled to deal with her grief. But she treats her staff with respect and care, and she maintains close positive relationships with her staff spanning her nearly 30 years in public service.” He added that “exaggerating and outright lying about moments from the hardest period of her life, and falsely presenting them as a pattern of behavior, is wrong”. The contest between the two-term senator Sullivan and Peltola, who lost re-election to the House in 2024, is seen as crucial to Democrats’s hopes of retaking the Senate in the midterms. Democrats must win at least four seats to gain a majority in the chamber, and have named Alaska as a top priority, in addition to Maine, North Carolina and Ohio. Sullivan called the behavior reported by the Times “sad” and “disturbing”. “Young Alaskans went through a lot of abuse and I’m sure there’s a hell of a lot more than was just reported in that story,” he told reporters at the US Capitol. Other former aides to Peltola who spoke to the Times stood by her conduct. “Mary Peltola is one of the finest human beings that I’ve ever worked for,” said Paul Horner, Peltola’s finance director in 2022, when she won both a special election to represent Alaska in the House and then a general election that year. Tyson Fick, a special assistant who had advised Peltola on fishing policy during her time in the House, called her “awesome and demanding”, but acknowledged she occasionally “raised her voice”. He said Peltola was dealing with grief during her time in Congress, and noted since she had previously worked on a commercial fishing boat, staffers who are not familiar with how people act in environments like that may have been misinterpreting her demeanor, the Times reported.
