title: Iran awaiting response from Trump on proposal to open strait of Hormuz in six days
author: Patrick Wintour in New York
summary: Country says US must lift sanctions on its oil exports and end the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon
body_text: Iran said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets. The proposal is designed to accelerate the steps first laid down in the memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June, particularly by helping the talks on Iran’s nuclear program start much more quickly than previously agreed. Iran says a deal on the temporary route through the strait of Hormuz has been agreed with Oman, describing it as a done deal, and is ready to register the details with the International Maritime Organisation. Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, said he was waiting to hear a response from the Americans to the proposal. He added that he had consulted on the plan with China, which fully supported the proposal. Saudi Arabia had been expected to endorse the Oman-Iran route through the strait last week, but pulled back partly due to anger that Iranian-backed Houthis had started attacking Saudi Arabia as part of their dispute over the future of Yemen. Iran claims it has urged the Houthis to cease the attacks on Saudi Arabia but that it does not have control over Houthi decision-making. Araghchi, speaking to reporters in New York, said: “We have introduced a plan to the US through the mediators that if certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start.” He said the Iranian preconditions were not new, and were contained in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding that was signed by Trump. The advantage of the proposal, apart from opening the strait and lifting the chokehold on the world economy, would be bringing the US to the talks on Iran’s nuclear program much more quickly. Talks on the nuclear program under the MoU would not have started for 60 days. Araghchi said he was staying in New York over the weekend to await an American response, but added he was not in a hurry. Privately, Iranian officials believe they could reach a deal with the Americans, and the Saudi hurdle over aspects of the route could be overcome, but fear Israel will use its influence to pull the US president away from the proposal. Araghchi added he would like the deal to go through before the midterm elections, by which he meant that the strait of Hormuz could be opened and energy prices thereby reduced, something Trump badly needs for the Republican party to survive a political mauling. For the US, there are difficulties in the plan related to forcing Israel to end the war in Lebanon. Israel may object to giving Iran such clear control over the route through which ships would travel through the strait of Hormuz. Iran also wants to retain control of shipping to prevent some US military shipping going through the strait. Issues such as whether tolls or navigational fees could be imposed by the littoral states Oman and Iran would be settled later in the process. Earlier in the day, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, met Araghchi, his Iranian counterpart, for the first time in New York. It was also the first meeting between UK and Iranian ministers for a year, and the first exchange since the UK in July proscribed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organisation, a move that has worsened the already sour relations between the two countries. Miliband made clear that the UK was committed to freedom of navigation in the strait and wanted a diplomatic solution, also stressing support for Saudi Arabia, a UK ally in Yemen. He warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, including threats to Jewish communities, and called for the UK to be given consular access to the British couple sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment in Tehran. Araghchi and the US’s special envoy Steve Witkoff also met earlier this week on the sidelines of the general assembly to discuss Iran’s terms for reopening the strait and the speed at which that may happen, as well as the time the US had been given to respond. A faction inside Iran is arguing that Tehran should seek to escalate the conflict with a vulnerable US president, rather than let the crisis drift in its current deadlock. Brent crude was trading at about $107 (£81) a barrel on Thursday. Some IRGC officers have also linked the strait of Hormuz issue to the closure of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway close to the south-west of Yemen now under control of Iranian-backed Houthis. Maj Gen Rahim Safavi, a senior Iranian military figure, said: “If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait may open before their eyes. Are they ready to enter the battle on this front? This is a question that they should pay more attention to.” Domestically, Pezeshkian’s defiant message to the UN general assembly on Wednesday was deemed a success overall in that it balanced a refusal to bend the knee to “the US bully” with a willingness to seek diplomatic talks. He also proposed a new security architecture for the future in partnership with Gulf states, including those it has been bombarding in an effort to dislodge the US from its military bases. Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, praised Pezeshkian’s speech, saying: “We are not afraid of war. It is the loud and firm call of the Iranian nation – a call that resonated from the United Nations podium, through the words of the esteemed president, and reached the ears of the world.”

title: Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder arrested at anti-Netanyahu protest in New York
author: Guardian staff and agencies
summary: Actors detained at Jewish Voice for Peace demonstration against Israeli prime minister’s address to the UN general assembly
body_text: Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon and Hacks star Hannah Einbinder were among people detained by police in New York on Thursday as they moved in to break up a protest against Benjamin Netanyahu. Agence France-Presse footage shows NYPD officers cuffing Thelma & Louise star Sarandon at the demo in the city as the Israeli prime minister was readying to address the United Nations general assembly. The New York Post reported Einbinder had also been marched away from the demonstration organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, where protesters held banners that read “Stop Arming Israel” and “End the Genocide.” A spokesperson for the NYPD said officers had responded to reports of an “unscheduled demonstration” where people were blocking an intersection. “Members of the NYPD Community Affairs Bureau issued … warnings, advising participants that they should leave,” the spokesperson said. “They continued to block the intersection. Multiple individuals who didn’t comply were taken into custody,” she said, without providing the number of people arrested. Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and New York ⁠City council member Chi Ossé were also among those arrested. Inside the general assembly, dozens of envoys from across the world walked out as Netanyahu began his speech, where he assailed both enemies and allies that have crossed him in recent months, including Britain and France, which have recently moved to recognise the state of Palestine. “They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism – some colonialism. And who’s accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God’s sakes, they invented the term,” he told the assembly. Sarandon, whose movie hits also include The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Dead Man Walking and The Witches of Eastwick, is no stranger to protests over Israel’s war in Gaza. The US actor told journalists at the Venice film festival this month she was losing work because of her outspoken views. “I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still. But that’s the power structure,” she said. “I think there has been a change in terms of the understanding of the situation and the general public, but there are still very strongly held positions within my industry that are held by Zionists and who have not relaxed their feelings towards me. “But I found my family, I found my people, and I’m OK,” she added. Einbinder has previously said the cost of not speaking up about Palestine is greater than losing her Hollywood career, citing industry backlash to actors such as Sarandon and Melissa Barrera. “I think what they know is what I know, which is that the cost of not speaking is higher,” she told Cannes film festival earlier this year. “There is a greater toll in not speaking and you’ve just got to have your priorities straight. I am under no impression that my small career could ever measure up in comparison to even one human life. It’s an obligation and I will always do it.” Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

title: Diplomacy or ‘diplotainment’? Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
author: Mark Saunokonoko with agencies
summary: Xi Jinping’s visit heavy on symbolism but no sign closed-door meeting yielded breakthroughs on thorny issues such as AI, trade, Taiwan and Iran
body_text: Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday, with talks on AI, trade and a growing US-China strategic rivalry expected to feature on an elaborate state visit that critics say went big on style but lacked substance. Here are the key takeaways from Xi’s first visit to Washington in more than a decade. Diplomacy or ‘diplotainment’? Senate Democrats criticised Trump’s summit with Xi, saying it prioritised pageantry over substance on the major issues. There was no sign a brief closed-door meeting yielded breakthroughs on the thorny issues of AI, trade, Taiwan and the war with Iran. Both countries agreed to extend until 10 January an agreement pausing their trade war, but experts said there were few other obvious tangible outcomes. Xi once again invoked the “Thucydides Trap”, an academic theory that competition between a rising power and an established one often results in war. Xi said the risk “can be overcome” and urged cooperation. After their meeting, Trump gave Xi a tour of the new helipad he had recently constructed on the White House’s South Lawn. “He loves good granite,” Trump told reporters, adding the two men had a “great meeting” without elaborating. Danny Russel, a former US diplomat serving in the Obama administration, expressed concern that the two leaders spent more time on social and ceremonial events than the actual meeting, which was about 90 minutes. “Pageantry and protocol don’t add up to progress. Pandas are cute, but what America needs are rare earths,” said Russel. “What we’re seeing isn’t diplomacy so much as ‘diplotainment,’ which won’t do much to solve the serious problems in the US-China relationship.” AI unchecked AI analysts were forced to read between the lines to gauge the outcome of AI discussions between the pair. Trump had written in a Truth Social post on Thursday morning that he and Xi would discuss “super intelligence” (Trump’s newly coined term for AI) but suggested he had little interest in new regulations, despite concerns from industry leaders that AI could eventually pose a threat to humans. “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of ⁠discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is,” Trump wrote. “That is China’s position also.” During his comments on Thursday, Xi said both countries must “ensure that the development of AI is always under human control”. Analysts say intense competition between the two powers in AI is likely to limit the scope for anything beyond symbolic agreements. Taiwan and stalled $14bn arms deal During the afternoon discussion, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence,” according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua. The White House did not immediately provide its own summary. Xi was expected to press Trump to halt arms sales to Taiwan. After his visit to China in May, Trump said he was holding in ⁠abeyance an arms package to Taiwan worth about $14bn and called it a “very good negotiating chip” – rattling some US allies in Asia. In a statement signed by at least 19 ⁠of 47 members of the Senate Democrats caucus, seen by Reuters, Democrats on Thursday called on Trump to ‌immediately deliver the security assistance package Congress has approved – $1.3bn in funds and the $14bn arms sale. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out using force to gain control over the island. Unusual airport greeting Trump greeted Xi on arrival with a red carpet on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, the ‌first time a US president has welcomed a foreign leader there since Barack Obama met Pope Francis in 2015. Normally, presidents wait for state visit guests to arrive at the White House before offering a formal welcome. For months, Trump has derided Democrats as “communists”, but the president’s welcome for Xi included Chinese flags adorning the roof above the Oval Office alongside US flags. Despite the fanfare, Trump and Xi’s remarks during the trip were not carried live by any US television networks, which refused to provide footage in protest of the White House’s ban of CNN, MS Now and Politico. Tech billionaires dine out at state dinner Thursday’s state dinner for Xi featured Washington powerbrokers and a cavalcade of billionaires, including: Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Alphabet’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Tesla’s Elon Musk and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. First lady Melania Trump’s menu featured yellow squash velouté, sesame-crusted sea bass and a vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit. In a continuation of Trump’s beef with certain media outlets, CNN and MS Now reporters were barred from attending. While outside the gate, a group of loud protesters shouted slogans like “China out ⁠of Hong Kong” that were clearly audible to the leaders ⁠as they posed for pictures on the red-carpeted White House steps. Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this report

title: First Thing: Netanyahu lambasts Israel’s critics at UN as New York protesters detained
author: Martin Belam
summary: More than 100 people arrested while Israeli PM claims war on Gaza is ‘the opposite of genocide’
body_text: Good morning. Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, delivered an inflammatory address to the UN in New York, decrying what he said was a global anti-Jewish conspiracy and taking aim at critics of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. He branded Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a “tyrant”, described Zohran Mamdani as the “antisemitic mayor of New York”, and declared that Israel’s war in Gaza was not a genocide, “it’s the opposite of genocide”. Netanyahu delivered his address just hours after the Palestinian leader, Mahmoud Abbas, said his delegation was “unlawfully” denied visas by the Trump administration to attend the meeting. Dozens of delegates, inspired by a Palestinian call, walked out of the General Assembly Hall of the UN headquarters as Netanyahu took the stage. What was the reaction on the streets of New York? More than 100 people were arrested outside the UN headquarters as hundreds of Jewish, Palestinian, Iranian and Lebanese New Yorkers, among others, protested during Netanyahu’s address. Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder were among those detained. What has rapper Macklemore announced? The US rapper, removed from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after voicing his support of Palestine, has convened a Free Palestine tour to benefit humanitarian aid organisations. The charity show will visit Dublin, Paris and London, with a North American run to be announced. Iran awaiting response from Trump on proposal to open strait of Hormuz in six days Iran has said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets. Privately, Iranian officials believe they could reach a deal with the Americans, but fear Israel will use its influence to pull the US president away from the proposal due to the inclusion of demands over Lebanon. What happened in the Senate about the war? Senate Republicans have blocked a Democratic effort to end the US war against Iran, voting down a House-passed war powers resolution. The measure, which passed the House last week with bipartisan support, failed in the Senate by a 49-50 vote, attracting some Republican support, but not enough to pass. What other developments have there been in the Middle East? Saudi Arabia says it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, with the latest attacks pushing oil prices ⁠to a one-week high over fears of spiralling supply disruptions. Texas woman triumphs as court upholds acquittal in voting error case The nearly decade-long case of a Black Texas woman who was sentenced to five years in prison in a controversial illegal voting case will end with an acquittal, the state’s highest criminal court has ruled in a 5-4 decision. Crystal Mason has been appealing ever since her 2018 conviction for casting a provisional ballot that ultimately was not counted. What is the latest voting controversy in Nevada? The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) wrongly identified 185 people on Nevada’s voter rolls as non-citizens, state officials said this week, escalating concerns over the shoddy methodology the government is using to raise fear about non-citizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Why is there backlash against a sheriff in California over voting? The Republican sheriff Chad Bianco must return more than 650,000 ballots his department confiscated earlier this year in an unprecedented move that violated election law, a state supreme court has ruled. Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid a trap that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan. Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said. Mark Saunokonoko has this list of key takeaways from the summit. In other news … Mary Peltola’s campaign says reports of her using slurs and shoving a staffer are exaggerated, but acknowledges the Democratic nominee in Alaska’s pivotal Senate race struggled after the deaths of her husband and mother. Trump’s Food and Drug Administration commissioner nominee, Dr Heidi Overton, has said the MMR vaccine shot is “safe and effective”, weeks after standing behind Trump as he suggested the shot could be “quite lethal”. US mortgage rates passed 7% for the first time since January 2025, according to federal lender Freddie Mac. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s presidential campaign has accused Donald Trump of wanting to “colonise” Brazil in order to capture its natural resources by meddling in next month’s election there. Stat of the day: ICE has wasted tens of millions to carry out Trump’s mass detention agenda US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and other federal agencies have wasted tens of millions of dollars pursuing controversial plans to rapidly increase detention capacity – and the total will likely rise due to continuing mismanagement, congressional investigators have warned. Culture Pick: My dad was a monster! Sara Karloff on reviving Frankenstein, 95 years on Boris Karloff’s daughter and the composer Michael Shapiro, who has written a 21st-century musical score for the 1931 classic, talk to Pamela Hutchinson about how it became so loved – and the strange experience of watching your father be Dr Frankenstein’s creation as a teenager. Don’t miss this: Gavin Newsom condemns Democrats’ ‘climate hushing’, predicts Trump’s downfall and expects AOC to run in 2028 Mark Hertsgaard interviews the governor of California, a man who may still – if the circumstances are right for him – run for US president in 2028. … or this: Amid soaring living costs, America’s biggest convenience-store chains quietly overcharge consumers A Guardian investigation has revealed that 7-Eleven and Circle K stores often fail to honor advertised prices – charging more at the pump and register for gas, snacks and other items. Climate check: ‘We wanted to prove we didn’t need air conditioning’ – the airport cooled by natural ventilation Avoiding a planet-heating disaster will take innovative approaches, and at Roland Garros airport on Réunion island, a unique ceiling design funnels a light tropical breeze into the terminal, ending the need to run air conditioning. Last Thing: 55,000 fans and nowhere to hide – what it’s like to play in basketball’s biggest arena I still have nightmares about just a handful of people watching me flounder at sport in my younger years, so appearing at the sprawling Philippine Arena sounds terrifying. title: ‘Your body fights to stay cool’: workers toil in record heat as federal rule frozen
author: Michael Sainato
summary: Trump officials and Republicans are rolling back protections against heat-related illnesses and deaths
body_text: When it’s 90F on a hot summer day, Esther Minton wears a long-sleeved shirt to work. “Working outside, you don’t have cover. There’s nowhere for you to really go if you’re on a roof or if you’re on the side of a building,” said Minton, a member of the Sheet Metal Workers Local Union 28 in New York City. “Having the sun beaming on your skin all day long, you’ll never make it through, so what you wear makes a difference.” Working outside during the brutal summer months means learning how to stay properly hydrated, dealing with port-a-potties that get much hotter than outside temperatures and handling heated copper metals exposed to direct sunlight. “Before the day is over, by the time you’re at break at lunchtime – say 12pm, when the sun is really out and doing its thing – you are drained,” Minton said. “Your body fights hardcore to stay cool, your body fights hard to not be dehydrated.” This summer was the hottest on record in the US, and workers are caught on the frontlines of a heat crisis that is expected to drive up heat-related illnesses and deaths. The rising temperatures come as the Trump administration and Republicans in Congress are rolling back federal rules meant to protect workers from heat injury and illnesses. In January 2025, the White House indefinitely froze Biden-era heat safety regulations that would have mandated water, shade, breaks, training and prevent plans for workers. House Republicans have also been pushing legislation that would prohibit the Department of Labor from enacting any workplace protections for heat exposure. Republicans in Florida and Texas have passed similar legislation prohibiting local city and county governments from passing heat protections. Big business groups and lobbyists, including from the agricultural and construction industries, have strongly opposed heat protection standards for workers, claiming employers already do what would be mandated and claim the rule would be a burden on employers. Workers at a recent Climate Week roundtable in New York City strongly disagreed employers are doing enough to protect workers from heat. Donald Nesbit, executive vice-president of Local 372 and former school cafeteria worker, recalled working in an old school building every summer in a kitchen basement as he prepared meals for students. “It was torture. We clocked temperatures at 130F to 140F in school kitchens during these summer conditions,” said Nesbit during the roundtable. “If we were to lock our animals in a car with those same conditions, we would be arrested, right? And yet, workers are working in those conditions, right, so there [have] to be protections. We have to push as a society to make protections better.” Currently, only seven states have enforceable heat prevention standards in place for workers. A December 2025 a study published in the journal Health Affairs found California’s outdoor heat protections had resulted in at least a 33% reduction in heat-related workplace fatalities since 2010. “We need a federal heat standard in this country,” said Julie Su, deputy mayor of New York City for economic justice and former secretary of labor under Biden. In June, Su and Zohran Mamdani, New York City mayor, issued heat protections for New York City workers, citing the White House’s pullback. “We had one proposed and the administration is not moving on it. There are also lots of states that have a standard, and New York does not have one,” Su said. “In the city, we are doing everything we can with the powers that we have.” The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) estimates over 550 US workers die and nearly 28,000 are injured annually from heat exposure. Heat has caused more than 2,300 deaths in the US in 2023 and 2024 combined, the highest numbers in 45 years of records, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. A spokesperson for the Department of Labor said in an email: “OSHA is currently reviewing comments from the public hearings on the proposed rule ‘Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings.’ OSHA provides compliance assistance to employers regarding potential workplace hazards, including guidance on how to keep employees safe in the heat.”

title: When Trump’s narrative meets voters’ realities
author: Callum Jones
summary: By Donald Trump’s telling, we’re in a US ‘golden age’. Americans may feel differently. Plus: Anger at the elite and a gunfluencer runs in Texas
body_text: One of Donald Trump’s greatest talents – deployed during his time as a real estate tycoon, source and subject of tabloid gossip, reality TV protagonist, and president of the United States – is his ability to tell stories. With six weeks until the US midterm elections, he is likely to lean on this instinct more than ever. Rarely does the US president appear more comfortable than when behind a microphone, speaking without interruption, sometimes for multiple hours. Long before entering the White House, he wholeheartedly embraced social media as a means of crafting his narrative, going so far as to launch his own social network when booted off others. Earlier this week, his administration launched a YouTube channel, which critics quickly dismissed as a “state-run” TV network. Such platforms give Trump the ability to deliver his unfiltered narrative – unencumbered by open discussion, or its often tenuous relationship with the truth. Only when his stories leave the spaces where he has complete control, and enter the real world, do challenges arise. The president has long both courted and criticized the media, seeing the very publications and outlets he claims to loathe as opportunities to amplify his message. He bristles when they fail to do so. Last Friday, Trump abruptly announced a ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House over their coverage. The outlets swiftly sued over the move, setting up an acrimonious legal battle over press access. In the early hours of this morning, a federal judge ordered Trump to restore their ⁠access. “You said you weren’t going to cover me,” Trump told CNN, which had said no such thing, upon his arrival at the United Nations this week. “You shouldn’t be covering me.” *** Americans don’t need to tune in to Trump TV or log in to Truth Social to find out how much it costs to buy a home, feed their families or fill up their cars – factors that, time and again, have influenced which way they vote in elections. By the president’s telling, his controversial war on Iran has been about to end since not long after he launched it in February. Tariffs are meanwhile enriching the US economy. A new “golden age” is under way. When news outlets report otherwise, the president – a voracious media consumer – has a choice. He can engage with the message. The Iran war, more than 200 days since it started, is not over. The US economy is under pressure, despite a boost from vast investment into AI. And while the president and his allies seem to be doing OK, millions of Americans have yet to see tangible evidence that a “golden age” is under way. Or he can blame the messenger. Railing at all hours against the “Fake News Media”, Trump has filed lawsuits against the Wall Street Journal, the BBC and CBS, among others, over their coverage. “I believe in the free press more than anyone in this room does,” Trump claimed at July’s White House correspondents’ dinner. “Hmm,” he added. “Maybe not quite.” *** None of this marks a dramatic departure from the past 11 years, of course. But with Trump’s party facing a crucial electoral test in November, and Republicans increasingly nervous of an impending “bloodbath”, his hunger to control the narrative is set to grow. In this final stretch of the campaign, we can expect to see the president intensify efforts to hammer his narrative – from a purported “communist” infiltration of the Democratic party to a supposed economic boom across the nation – and attack those who dare to question it. This remarkably volatile president has shown a striking ability to stick to a message like glue in the final stages of an election. In 2024, this included relentlessly blaming Joe Biden for a surge in consumer prices, and promising Americans that he would fix it. We have a good sense of what it will include in 2026. After summoning Republicans for the party’s first ever midterm convention in Dallas this month – another chance to get behind a microphone, uninterrupted by reporters, or reality – Trump asked supporters to do him “the biggest favor” and “pretend” they were voting for him. In truth, his name will not appear on a single ballot paper. As polling day edges closer, the president is escalating his fights with the media. My colleague Chris Stein noted earlier this week that polls continue to show Democrats with an edge on the generic ballot, a key indicator of voter sentiment in congressional races, as well as in some key Senate contests. Once all votes are cast and counted, there is a world in which the president and his party retain control of Congress – defying frustration over the Iran war, concern over their handling of the economy and broader anger over the status quo – in an extraordinary display of political resilience. There is also a world in which they endure a painful rejection by voters and lose control of both congressional chambers, leaving Trump to serve out his second term as a lame duck in the White House. The president’s version of events is only likely to accept one of these outcomes. Quoted “Most people around the country, many of whom don’t even identify as Democrat or Republican or whatever, are 10 out of 10 pissed off, angry and willing to take that anger into action against the status quo.” – Maurice Mitchell, the national director of the Working Families party, a progressive third political party that has seen its endorsees winning bigger than ever this year Read more: ‘People are pissed off’: anger at the elite and the establishment is fueling this year’s midterms Meet the candidate: Brandon Herrera Brandon Herrera, a 30-year-old YouTuber with more than 4 million subscribers, has made a name for himself making outrageous pro-gun statements. He’s also the frontrunner in a race to represent Texas’s 23rd congressional district, where 23 people were killed in a mass shooting at a Walmart in 2019 and an 18-year-old former student killed 19 children and two teachers in the Uvalde school shooting. Democrats are hoping that such an extreme candidate, even by Texas’s standards, could be vulnerable at the ballot box. They aim to flip the seat that has been in Republican hands since 2015. Should he win the midterm election, Herrera will take what he calls his “second amendment absolutism” to Washington, with possible ramifications for nationwide gun laws and debate. title: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China
author: Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent
summary: While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
body_text: If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “stalemate summit”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs. Instead, it was described as a celebration of “diplotainment” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo. Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”. “The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration. But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short. One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China. To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year. With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year. That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029. On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society. William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”. China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China. Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.” Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights. On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”. For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely. On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.” For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

title: It’s going to take more than an email to a public inbox to protect Australians from potential AI doom
author: Tom McIlroy
summary: OpenAI’s hack of Medicare suggests safeguarding civilisation is the task facing leaders in this extraordinary new era
body_text: More than 130 world leaders descended on the United Nations headquarters in New York this week, joining the pageantry and speechmaking of the annual general assembly. Many of the visiting presidents and prime ministers delivered their set-piece addresses to a sparsely populated hall, but contributions from two unlikely visitors in the nearby security council chamber stood out. OpenAI boss Sam Altman and Dario Amodei of Anthropic gave briefings on the safety of artificial intelligence on Wednesday, as a nervous world watched on. Speaking in the room where some of the biggest questions to face humanity have been deliberated on since the end of the second world war, Altman said the world faced a choice. AI could be like a renaissance of creativity and discovery, he said, or more like a new Industrial Revolution bringing upheaval and disarray. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The words rang hollow less than 24 hours later, when Altman was the subject of an angry phone call from Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, after revelations a rogue OpenAI agent had hacked into sensitive Medicare systems in Australia. Altman and his colleagues had kept the incident secret for two months. As people become more anxious about the risk posed by AI to civilisation, Albanese grasped the company’s transgression as proof that democratically elected governments need to impose guardrails on the technology. Already, many believe the risk of AI slipping out of human control is a threat akin to the Covid-19 pandemic or a nuclear arms race. Like his government’s moves to ban children under 16 from using social media, and forcing platforms to give users the ability to opt out of powerful algorithms, Albanese wants to use new AI laws as a way to curb the creeping sense of helplessness so many people feel in the face of big tech. But Thursday’s announcement that government websites had been compromised by OpenAI showed that serious vulnerabilities and failures of process exist within both the company and the federal government. The hack happened in June, but it took OpenAI executives until September to alert Services Australia that statistical data on Medicare use had been accessed. Despite the company’s corporate might – and an army of well-paid government relations executives and lobbyists – OpenAI deemed it appropriate to send an email to a public-facing Australian government address to raise the alarm, months after the hack. It’s incredible the email wasn’t mistaken for spam. Wholly inadequate to the point of recklessness, the company’s actions show contempt for the Australian government and its citizens, whose healthcare data had been stolen. Worse, Altman met with Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, in early September but did not tell him about the hack. It took time for the public service to react to OpenAI’s email. Because the public inbox is checked routinely only once a day, the email was first read by staff within Services Australia on 11 September. It was not until 15 September that the intelligence agency the Australian Signals Directorate was informed, and two more days before the relevant minister, Katy Gallagher, was alerted. Then on 22 September, public servants asked OpenAI for more information about the scale of the hack. An investigation was quickly launched and the public finally informed. Albanese himself was only told after leaving for New York. The government’s planned AI legislation – expected to be finalised before Christmas and considered by parliament next year – must surely include mandatory reporting requirements for AI companies. Future notifications must come from senior officials within the responsible entity to ensure they are taken seriously. Sending an alert to a public email inbox will not cut it. On Friday, the assistant technology and digital economy minister, Andrew Charlton, said the government would take advice on possible referrals for criminal investigation, and that any legal liability would have to be traced back to the intent of a person or a company that created or directed an AI agent to hack. The terms of reference for a rapid investigation, released by the prime minister’s department on Thursday, cover reporting requirements for AI-driven cyber-incidents and vulnerabilities; governance and information sharing responsibilities for federal officials; obligations on AI firms for timely disclosure of breaches; gaps in existing laws; and mechanisms to boost protection against hacking that targets the federal government. Before leaving the US on Friday, Albanese floated the idea of creating an international authority with governance and investigative powers to help governments protect their people. The general sense of vulnerability to AI comes after a top safety researcher at Anthropic this month warned AI is advancing so quickly there is a greater than 10% chance it “could kill all humans” within the next decade. Not helping is the spectacle of Donald Trump and Xi Jinping dining with Altman and other tech bosses at a White House state dinner. Trump has resisted pressing the breaks on AI for fear China will develop a new strategic advantage over the US. Behind closed doors Xi apparently proposed continuing a dialogue with Trump to prevent AI “misuse and abuse”, while ahead of an expected drubbing in the November midterm elections, Trump said AI “concerns the future of humanity”. The latest revelations from OpenAI will have done little to reassure anyone in Australia. In this extraordinary new era, world leaders must address our creeping sense of helplessness and start protecting civilisation. Tom McIlroy is Guardian Australia’s political editor

title: Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms
author: Patrick Wintour in New York
summary: Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?
body_text: Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions. In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”. Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver. Iran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board. The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU. “The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed. In the first four to five days under this timetable, the US would have to lift the naval blockade on Iran’s oil ports, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, end the war on all fronts and permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets. On the sixth day, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened by Iran, with ships using a new route designated by Oman and Iran. And on the next day, negotiations would start on the future of Iran’s civil nuclear programme, including a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. This accelerates the point at which nuclear talks would begin, from 60 days in the June agreement to seven. Those talks could, of course, take a long time, but from Trump’s perspective, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened before the midterm elections, a point in the political calendar that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says has never been a factor in Iranian thinking. Trump had claimed Iran was waiting until after the vote to offer a deal. Iran, Araghchi argued at a largely off-the-record briefing with reporters – at which Pezeshkian was also present – had every reason not to negotiate with the US. In particular, he admitted to being sceptical that Witkoff could deliver. He recounted how he had twice held talks with Trump’s special envoy, after which Witkoff had described them as “productive and good”, only for the US to bomb Iran the next day. Other Iranian diplomats say Trump’s willingness to rein in Netanyahu in Lebanon remains key. If he could do that, a deal would be feasible. It is a difficult deal for Trump to swallow since the strait would reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories. Trump says he has a choice to make between the annihilation of Iran and engagement – an engagement that, he says with typical hyperbole, could make Iran one of the great countries of the world. In reality, the judgment he has to make is more prosaic. Is he prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterms and, if not, does he believe the US can squeeze the Iranian economy so hard that the leadership will succumb. Pezeshkian, who handed all questions about the talks to Araghchi, admitted Iranians wanted the war to end and did not deny the economic pressure, but said the public had withstood sanctions for 45 years. He also insisted Iran’s decision-making machinery was functioning. The reclusive supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, was completely healthy, he claimed, a testimony based on spending seven hours in his presence. He did not explain why, apart from security, Khamenei had not issued a voice recording, photograph or video as proof of life.

title: US supreme court lifts restrictions on controversial voter database
author: George Chidi
summary: Trump and officials claimed database combats noncitizen voting but critics said it could disenfranchise eligible voters
body_text: The US supreme court has lifted restrictions on a controversial federal database of voters as Donald Trump seeks to impose tougher restrictions on voting ahead of November’s midterm elections. The ruling issued Friday by the chief justice, John Roberts, in the name of the court temporarily sets aside an injunction issued by US district judge Sparkle L Sooknanan, who ruled on 22 June against the Trump administration’s plan to use the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements – Save – database to vet voter registration eligibility. A federal appeals court later declined to pause that ruling. The ruling sends the case back to the DC circuit court of appeals to be heard. “Today’s decision is profoundly disappointing, as it puts millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections,” the League of Women Voters said in a prepared statement. “However, this case is not over. The D.C. district court ruled that the expanded SAVE program violated multiple laws. We will be doing everything in our power to protect Americans’ voting and privacy rights by ensuring that the district court decision stands.” The case stems from an executive order issued in March 2025 with the stated purpose of improving enforcement of laws barring noncitizens from voting in US elections. Among its provisions, the order directed the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and other agencies to make federal databases of citizenship information available to state elections directors. Other provisions of that executive order, like its demand to states to turn over their voter rolls to the federal goverment, remain bottled up in court. The League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center and other groups sued to block the use of the Save database, arguing that it was riddled with inaccuracies, and that taking social security numbers from the Social Security Administration violation of the Privacy Act, Social Security Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act. State officials had used social security numbers and other information obtained by DHS to conduct sweeping checks of the citizenship status of registered voters against federal records. Federal law prevents state election administrators from systematically striking people from the voter rolls within 90 days of an election, with or without the use of the Save database. However, the Friday ruling notes that “all agree that the order prevents the Federal Government from using the modified SAVE program to conduct individualized inquiries, which are permitted under federal law during this period.” That distinction matters in light of a DHS whistleblower’s allegations that the department has as part of its “Unlawful Voter Initiative” directed federal agents to impersonate voters in violation of state laws, using social security numbers and other information to look up voter history on state websites. US senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, both California Democrats, sent a letter Monday to the state’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, asking for an investigation. “As you know, the U.S. Department of Justice has been unsuccessful in its attempt to compel California to provide its voter information to the Trump Administration, raising serious questions about what this data is, how DHS obtained it, and whether they complied with the law in collecting and using this data,” the letter said. “The fact that the DHS data was compiled with something called ‘supplemental magic’ does not provide reassurance.”

title: US senators propose legislation to limit ICE arrests and indefinite detention
author: Maanvi Singh
summary: Exclusive: Democrats Dick Durbin of Illinois and Alex Padilla of California seek to prevent unlawful arrests
body_text: US senators have introduced legislation aimed at cutting down warrantless or specious ICE arrests, and curbing the agency’s ability to indefinitely detain immigrants who do not pose any danger to their communities. The new legislation, shared exclusively with the Guardian, would require immigration officers to obtain an administrative warrant from a supervisor outlining a probable cause for detaining someone. Such a warrant must also be presented to each person who is detained, the bill says, alongside notice of when the detainee must appear in immigration court. The bill would require a bond hearing within 24 hours of any warrantless arrests, and custody review of every noncitizen in immigration detention every 60 days by an immigration judge or US district judge – ideally ensuring that detainees are not held in ICE custody indefinitely without clear cause. The Democratic senators Dick Durbin of Illinois and Alex Padilla of California – – said they are introducing the “Immigration Warrant Reform Act” to prevent unlawful arrests and detentions following reports that US citizens and immigrants with legal status were being apprehended. By clarifying how and when ICE can make arrests and detain individuals, the senators said, they also hope to stop the agency from racial profiling or detaining people for arbitrary reasoning. “This bill would establish stronger accountability and oversight,” Padilla said, referring to Americans and noncitizens alike. “The disturbing reality today is that many American citizens and immigrants with lawful status have been caught in the Trump administration’s indiscriminate and violent immigration enforcement dragnet across the country,” said Durbin. “[The legislation] is commonsense, and I encourage my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to support it.” With Republicans in the majority in both chambers of Congress, there isn’t an easy path for the the bill to become law. But Durbin said he was compelled to do something after seeing civil rights abuses during the Trump administration’s Operation Midway Blitz – the militarized immigration raid in Chicago last fall and winter. Immigration advocates and attorneys who reviewed the legislation were concerned that it still left several groups of immigrants vulnerable to arbitrary arrest and detention by granting ICE officers broad leeway in deciding when to conduct a warrantless arrest. The proposed law states, for example, that a warrant isn’t required when someone poses an “imminent danger to the community” – but doesn’t clarify what that means. “The framework neglects how the current administration routinely weaponizes unsubstantiated national security allegations to advance its anti-immigrant agenda,” said Faisal Al-Juburi, the co-chief executive of Raíces, a Texas-based humanitarian aid and immigration services non-profit. Donald Trump and his administration have specifically claimed that Venezuelan asylum seekers without criminal records pose a national security threat, or arbitrarily proclaimed that families who have lived in the US with temporary legal status for years are dangerous criminals. It is also unclear, advocates said, how the bill would hold ICE accountable for violating these standards. Durbin’s office said the bill codifies constitutional safeguards, by requiring immigration agents to prove they have a probable cause to detain someone – and if not, release them within 24 hours. Requiring that detainees get a hearing every 60 days would also force the government to justify its reasoning for the continued detention. The bill would “help prevent these due process violations while ensuring noncitizens who present a threat to public safety are not released”, Durbin said. Al-Juburi said he was skeptical the bill meets the moment. And a bigger question raised by the bill is whether immigrants should be detained at all for civil violations such as entering the US without authorization, he added.. “My concern here is that this approach fails to reject the inhumane notion that people should face detention, and loss of liberty, for non-criminal matters,” said Al-Juburi. “Detaining people for civil immigration enforcement stands in direct conflict with what are ostensibly core constitutional protections.”

title: In latest blow to Obamacare, Trump is threatening the entire US health system
author: Melody Schreiber
summary: The Trump administration is removing 760,000 people enrolled in the Affordable Care Act marketplace
body_text: The Trump administration is removing 760,000 people enrolled in the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace on allegations of fraud, officials said on Tuesday – adding to previous efforts to chip away at federally subsidized insurance programs and likely causing some of the lowest-income Americans to forego healthcare, experts said. The US government is also investigating about 420,000 people whom they suspect of fraud, and they are putting a six-month enrollment moratorium on new agents and brokers selling Obamacare policies, officials said at a press conference. The removed enrollees are a mixture of “phantoms” and “ghosts” as well as people who don’t meet the eligibility requirements of Obamacare, said Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS). “These are not real people,” he said, claiming that expelling them from the ACA marketplace would save the federal government $2.2bn. JD Vance, who is leading a federal taskforce on fraud, claimed: “We’re actually making sure that the people receiving Obamacare subsidies are actually entitled to receive them.” No details were provided about how many enrollees were fictional, enrolled by fraudulent brokers without their knowledge or expelled because of income restrictions. “There’s no transparency about who these people are and why they’re being disenrolled, but I think it’s a reasonable concern that some number are being disenrolled inappropriately,” said Edwin Park, a research professor at the Center for Children and Families at Georgetown University’s McCourt School of Public Policy. “A common theme here is to make it incredibly burdensome for individuals to enroll and stay enrolled in their health coverage.” Without more information, “there is no way to know how many legitimately enrolled people had their plans canceled”, said Cynthia Cox, senior vice-president and director of the Program on the ACA at KFF, an independent health policy organization. The move follows recent rules and legislation to reduce enrollment in Medicaid, Medicare and the ACA, said Park, who added: “A lot of these actions are intended to sharply undercut the success of and the long-term viability of the ACA’s coverage expansions, which have been an incredible success in terms of reducing the number of people without health insurance.” About 19.2 million Americans are enrolled in the ACA marketplace, but nearly 3 million people lost their coverage between February 2025 and February 2026, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. The fraud taskforce has also withheld $2.2bn in Medicaid payments from California and Minnesota over alleged fraud – primarily in home health aide programs, which disability advocates say are a lifeline. Officials followed an unusual path to verify ACA enrollment, experts said. The administration sent to insurers a list of more than a million people suspected of being fraudulently enrolled in the ACA marketplace, also known as Obamacare. Officials said on Tuesday that they used AI tools to identify the enrollees. The people were identified by three factors: they’d been enrolled by a broker or agent, had all of their ACA premium paid by the tax credit, and they had not supplied social security numbers or immigration documents. Insurers were asked to try to make contact with those enrollees; they were permitted to filter out people who had a previous claim or had communicated with the insurer. The enrollees had 30 days to respond, or their coverage was canceled. “It is entirely possible that many of these people were enrolled without their knowledge or were so-called phantom enrollees,” Cox said. “It is also entirely possible that many of these people were legitimately enrolled and simply did not respond in time.” People can appeal and be reinstated once they prove their identities – but this will likely function as an additional hurdle making it harder for people to stay enrolled, Park said. “We know that when you add a lot of red tape, increase the amount of complexity and the requirements for paperwork,” Park said, that “leads to eligible people being disenrolled.” Vance spoke of two fraudulent brokers who were convicted of quietly enrolling people to collect commissions from insurance companies, acknowledging that “some of those people were probably legitimate”, but he did not speak of the steps necessary to reinstate them or to prevent future disenrollments. Ending unscrupulous broker practices has been a bipartisan issue, and the Biden administration was the first to act, finalizing a rule to crack down on shady brokers. Officials under Biden decertified about 200 such brokers – but Trump administration officials recertified them last year. About 35% of ACA enrollees have never used their health insurance, Oz said. “That’s just not possible,” he said, adding, “So we know there is fraud.” But it’s not unusual for healthy people to be enrolled in insurance and not need to use it, Park noted: “You can expect in any insurance risk pool that there’s going to be a lot of people who don’t use much healthcare or use healthcare at all.” By removing lower-risk enrollees, insurance premiums could increase or insurers could decide to leave markets entirely, he said. Some enrollees also appear to have been cut because they are low-income. The Affordable Care Act was intended to include a Medicaid expansion for those living under the poverty line, but a supreme court decision made the expansion optional. In states that chose not to expand Medicaid, there is a group of low-income people who make too much money to qualify for Medicaid – earning between $16,000 and $22,000 per year – but don’t make enough to qualify for the ACA. “We’re going to make sure that they actually meet the income threshold requirements in order to receive these Obamacare benefits,” Vance said of this group. Oz called their disenrollment “a little bit painful”. Park said that there have been a series of “at best misleading” allegations arguing that a large share of current marketplace plan enrollees are fraudulently or inappropriately enrolled. Reports from the Paragon Institute and the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) have indicated millions of fraudulent enrollees – but those analyses are “flawed”, Park said. These reports directly compare administrative data and unadjusted census data, but income and household sizes are calculated differently in these two measures. The census counts all individuals living in the household, while Medicaid and the ACA marketplace exclude non-dependent relatives. “That has a big effect on the number of people who appear to be in certain income ranges,” Park said. “That has been used to say a huge percent of people don’t look like they have incomes in the right eligibility range.” These disenrollments are happening in the context of major cuts to the marketplace. Premiums skyrocketed, doubling or tripling for some enrollees, after Republicans opposed extending the enhanced tax credits at the end of last year. Alongside other financial pressures, like higher energy and food costs, “there’s going to be an increasing number of people who can no longer afford their share of the premium”, Park said. The healthcare cuts of the budget reconciliation law HR1 “in many ways were designed to undermine the Affordable Care Act coverage expansions” without explicitly repealing it – a longtime Trump promise, Park said. The Trump administration has also created new regulations to restrict marketplace enrollment, he noted, adding: “You add it all together, and you’re going to have certainly significant reductions in enrollment – with those enrollment losses increasing over time.” When people lose their health insurance, it has ripple effects – including added pressure on health systems that affect all patients. “Providers, particularly safety net providers, operate under thinner operating margins. If they’re facing payment cuts, they’re facing higher uncompensated care costs, as a result of more uninsured [patients],” Park said, which may lead hospitals to cut services or staff, or close their doors entirely. “And that makes it harder for everyone to access the care they need.”

title: New Jersey lieutenant governor resigns after sexual harassment accusation
author: Ariana Baio
summary: Investigation determined Dale Caldwell violated state ethics rules and engaged in harassing behavior
body_text: Dale Caldwell, the lieutenant governor of New Jersey, resigned from his position on Friday, after the release of a report accusing him of sexually harassing a female staffer, among other ethics violations. New Jersey’s governor, Mikie Sherrill, announced on Friday afternoon that Caldwell had submitted his resignation to her earlier in the day. The decision by Caldwell, 66, came one day after Sherrill called on him to step down after an investigation determined he violated state ethics rules and engaged in behavior that constituted sexual harassment. The 61-page report said it found credible evidence that Caldwell made romantic advances toward a female staffer’s friend, tried to secure a promotion for his girlfriend and gave tickets to personal guests without reimbursement. The New Jersey Globe was the first to report on Caldwell’s resignation. Thomas Calcagni, a lawyer for Caldwell, said in a statement they would “continue to forcefully challenge the report”. “Dr Caldwell’s resignation, submitted to put an end to the targeted campaign to discredit his character, does not in any way diminish our outrage concerning the investigative process and its specious findings,” Calcagni said. “Counsel is fully exploring all legal remedies to ensure a true, balanced, and unbiased record.” Sherrill, a Democrat, said she would appoint the state’s acting comptroller, Shirley Emehelu, as the acting secretary of state. “We can no longer tolerate the culture of silence, sweeping things under the rug or kicking cans down the road,” Sherrill said Friday at press conference in Trenton, the state capital. “New Jerseyans deserve fairness and they deserve accountability.” The change-up comes just weeks before midterm elections, which the lieutenant governor is responsible for overseeing. The New Jersey governor initiated an investigation into Caldwell in May after receiving an anonymous letter that accused him of “bringing uninvited female guests to events while traveling using taxpayer funds” and “hitting on women at functions”. Ultimately, investigators concluded that aspects of the allegations were credible. In one instance, investigators said Caldwell made a romantic advance toward a female staffer’s friend and then made a “derogatory or demeaning reference” about women after his advances were rebuffed. Caldwell allegedly told the staffer that women like them were ambitious and successful and needed a man in a position to help them, “but you young women are looking for young sperm”. Investigators also found that Caldwell advocated for the promotion of his girlfriend, a state employee, to a “senior leadership position”. Caldwell acknowledged that he did not disclose the nature of his relationship with the state employee until he was confronted. Caldwell had pushed for his girlfriend’s promotion, even after being informed he was under investigation. Ultimately, she did not get the promotion and no longer works in state government. Credible evidence also determined Caldwell brought at least three personal guests, including his girlfriend, to ticketed events, in his capacity as lieutenant governor, without advance authorization or payment. After Sherrill announced the report’s findings and called for Caldwell to resign, it was unclear whether or not he would step down. As lieutenant governor, Caldwell was also serving as New Jersey’s secretary of state, who is the chief elections officer. With just 39 days until the midterm elections, Sherrill said she was tapping Emehelu to ensure “all eligible New Jerseyans can make their voices heard”. “Shirley is a veteran of the US Department of Justice and the New Jersey attorney general’s office. She has the judgment to run these elections and the strength to stand up to Trump’s attacks on voting,” Sherrill added. Sherrill has 45 days to name a permanent replacement for Caldwell. • This story was amended on 26 September 2026. New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill said she would appoint the state’s acting comptroller, Shirley Emehelu, as the acting secretary of state, not as lieutenant governor as a previous version stated.

title: Nearly 200 people wrongly identified on Nevada’s voter rolls as non-citizens
author: Sam Levine
summary: State election officials said they reviewed 185 records homeland security sent them and confirmed they were US citizens
body_text: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) wrongly identified 185 people on Nevada’s voter rolls as non-citizens, state officials said this week, escalating concerns over the shoddy methodology the government is using to raise fear about non-citizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. In July, Donald Trump gave a speech saying DHS had found a combined 278,000 non-citizens on the rolls in Nevada, California, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Follow-up letters to each of those states weakened the claim, saying there only could be as many as 278,000 non-citizens on the rolls, including up to 15,903 in Nevada. In August, DHS officials told staffers in the Nevada secretary of state’s office that they had reviewed the numbers and confirmed only 185 were non-citizens. DHS officials said they still needed to review more than 14,000 records. But on Wednesday, Nevada election officials said they had reviewed the 185 records DHS sent them and confirmed they were US citizens. “As for the 185 individuals, our records indicate that they were citizens. You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise,” Greg Ott, a deputy attorney general, wrote to DHS this week in an email obtained by the Guardian through a public records request. The message was first reported by the New York Times and Nevada Independent. In a statement on Friday, a DHS spokesperson did not address whether the department still believed the 185 were non-citizens. The spokesperson said the agency “is providing a service to the citizens of Nevada”. “The list of 185 were simply a subset of individuals that had gone through a rigorous manual review process at that time of the call. The list shared with Nevada last month also included 6,218 individuals with the highest number of matching attributes to an alien in DHS records,” the spokesperson said. In his email, Ott lamented DHS had not been transparent about the methodology DHS had used to flag alleged non-citizens nor had it shared adequate information. When Nevada officials requested DHS provide the first name, last name, address, and any other data point DHS officials matched, the department said they were only going to provide the voter ID number. In Nevada, a voter registration number can belong to multiple people, he wrote. Each of Nevada’s counties used to maintain their own registration system, but Nevada recently transitioned to a single statewide voter registration system and gave voters new state voter identification numbers. “As a result, the same number may appear at different points in time in connection with different voter records,” he wrote. “The number also doesn’t tell us whether an individual was born in the United States, naturalized, derived citizenship through a parent, or holds any particular immigration status. Election records commonly reflect the information supplied during registration,” he added. “For example, if someone registered to vote in 1970, the registration record may be incomplete; the name, address, and date of birth may be incomplete, changed, entered differently, or shared by more than one person. A number that matches a voter record thus establishes only that a number exists in, or once existed in, a voter registration system.” The news outlet Votebeat also reported earlier this month that election officials in Pennsylvania have also pushed DHS for information on its basis for claiming there were as many as 14,576 non-citizens on its rolls. In an August letter obtained by Votebeat, Al Schmidt, Pennsylvania’s top election official, said DHS representatives had indicated they did not have “high confidence” in that number.
