title: As the US midterms approach, Trump’s boasts on the economy fall flat with voters
author: Steven Greenhouse
summary: Trump’s tariffs and his war against Iran caused prices to to rise, but the US president continues to claim it’s ‘the greatest economy in history’
body_text: Donald Trump has taken to repeating a familiar boast: “We have the greatest economy in history,” Trump said recently at a White House press gaggle. The boast comes even though inflation is higher and economic growth lower than when Joe Biden left office, even though gas prices have jumped about 50% since the war against Iran started, and even though 73% of Americans think the economy is in fair or poor shape (48% say it’s in poor shape). What’s more, the Federal Reserve is so worried about inflation that it just raised interest rates. “It’s bluster, it’s gaslighting for him to say the economy is the greatest ever,” said Darrick Hamilton, chief economist for the AFL-CIO, the nation’s main union federation. “The economy is trending down by many measures. A lot of that has been caused by Trump’s unforced errors.” Hamilton said those errors include Trump’s tariffs and his war against Iran, both of which have pushed up prices – inflation is running at 3.4%, up from 3.0% when Biden left office. One unfortunate result is that prices have been rising faster than wages, worsening Americans’ affordability problems. A New York Times/Siena Poll found that 71% of voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living. Over the past 12 months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, fuel oil prices have soared 52%, while ground beef is up 7.2%, fish and seafood up 6.5%, coffee 6.1%, sugar and sweets 6.1% and electricity up 3.8%. The administration boasts that egg prices are down 23%, even as gas has soared to an average of $4.47 per gallon nationwide. With the economy growing at a modest 1.5% rate in the second quarter, Trump stretches the truth when he boasts of a great economy, considering that under John F Kennedy, Lyndon Johnson and Ronald Reagan, there were full years when GDP growth – the broadest measure of the nation’s economy – averaged over 6%. (The economy grew at a 2.7% annual rate during Biden’s last six months in office.) Consumer sentiment has slid sharply in light of today’s stubborn inflation, mixed with slower economic growth, high interest rates and huge economic uncertainty about trade wars and AI. According to a University of Michigan poll, consumer sentiment fell in September to its second lowest level ever in the poll’s 74-year history. Only this past May was lower. Kush Desai, a White House spokesman, said: “President Trump has always been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict, but the Trump administration has remained laser-focused delivering on the president’s long-term economic agenda on the home front.” As good news, Desai cited “continued private-sector job growth” and “booming investments”. The unemployment rate has been fairly low during Trump’s second term – at 4.1%, it’s about the same rate as in Biden’s last year. But the jobless rate has been lower under several previous presidents; it sank to 2.5 % at one point under Dwight Eisenhower and below 4% at times under Bill Clinton, Richard Nixon and Johnson. But in a not-so-great statistic, job growth has been mediocre since Trump returned to office – just 43,000 a month on average, less than one-third the 145,000 average during Biden’s last two years in office. Although Trump said his tariffs were aimed at revving up manufacturing, the US has lost 35,000 factory jobs since he returned to office. Last month, however, there was good news on job growth – the nation added an impressive 162,000 jobs. Desai said the Biden administration “padded employment growth” by “adding hundreds of thousands of government or government-adjacent jobs that relied on runaway federal spending”. He added, “President Trump is slashing regulations and taxes to create sustainable private-sector jobs – not juking the statistics by drumming up government spending.” Michael Strain, director of economic policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute, a center-right thinktank, had an upbeat view, saying: “The economy is strong.” Strain added, “the unemployment rate is very low,” and “the economy is very resilient in the face of high energy prices, and consumers are resilient in the face of the trade war.” He noted that “investment spending is very strong”. “Where we’re not doing well is inflation,” Strain added. “It’s eroding wages and income. Inflation is a headwind that households are facing.” Responding to the widespread concerns about inflation, Desai said: “The last two inflation reports [show] dramatic month-over-month price reductions in beef, prescription drugs, and auto insurance.” He said this was “proof that the administration’s targeted policy interventions to lower costs are delivering”. Responding to concerns about inflation, Desai said: “President Trump had always been clear about market disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict, but the last two inflation reports showing dramatic month-over-month price reductions in beef, prescription drugs, and auto insurance are proof that the administration’s targeted policy interventions to lower costs for American families are delivering.” Lindsay Owens, president of the Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive thinktank, was far more downbeat about the economy. “I think it’s going pretty poorly,” she said. “The Federal Reserve just raised interest rates, when Americans were already concerned about high interest rates. That’s not going to do anything to help people who want to buy houses when mortgage rates are already high. Americans are feeling that things are pretty grim. “Trump’s approval rating on the economy was his superpower in his first term,” she continued. “But now it’s absolutely in the toilet.” Just 28% of Americans approve of how Trump has handled the economy, according to a new Marquette Law School poll. Just 29% of Republicans say the economy is better than a year ago, down from last January when 72% of Republicans said the economy was better than a year earlier, Owens said AI has been crucial for Trump’s economy, helping fuel GDP growth, business investment and repeated stock market records. “The pieces of the economy that are doing well are completely propped up by AI investment,” Owens said. “That’s the whole story. That’s what Trump has going for him. “But,” she continued, “that’s an increasingly precarious place for him to be right now,” considering the fast-growing worries about AI, including the fierce opposition to datacenters in many communities, the recent calls to slow AI development for safety reasons, and Wall Street’s increasing skittishness about AI stocks. Owens pointed to a second factor that’s sustained the economy: the vast spending power of the richest 10% of Americans. She said they account for nearly 50% of consumer spending, and while the bottom 50% by income are feeling squeezed, it’s the top 10%’s buying power – whether on new cars, airline tickets, or home renovations – that has kept consumer spending and the economy from faltering. “It seems to me the president doesn’t care about how average Americans are doing,” Owens said, pointing to such Trump statements as “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation,” which Trump said last May when asked about how the Iran war was affecting Americans. And last week, he downplayed consumers’ dismay about the surge in gasoline prices, saying, it was “a little higher” and “it’s a very inexpensive price”. Owens said responsibility for high gas prices and higher inflation rests squarely with Trump. “This is not a situation where the economic conditions are beyond his control,” she said. “He has made a deliberate series of choices that cut against his promises to reduce prices.” According to the Yale Budget Lab, the average American household will spend $1,100 more this year due to Trump’s tariffs, while Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, says the average household will have to spend $1,000 more this year because of higher fuel, food and other prices caused by the Iran war. “The biggest drivers of inflation are his tariffs and the war against Iran,” Owens said. “These are policy-driven price hikes,” The White House sees it differently. “The hard data of actual consumer spending and retail sales has remained robust throughout President Trump’s term so far. American consumers remain resilient and are voting with their dollars,” said Desai. How consumers really feel will become clear in November, when the real voting takes place.

title: Gouged: why Americans are being ripped off – and what to do about it
author: Heather Timmons
summary: How can we fix our pricing crisis? Economic sociologist Lindsay Owens urges tough new rules – and a consumer uprising
body_text: “Repeat after me: it’s not my fault, it’s not my fault, it’s not my fault.” That’s the message to frustrated US shoppers in Gouged: The End of a Fair Price – and What That Means for Your Wallet by Lindsay Owens, economic sociologist and head of the Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive Washington thinktank. Consumer rage is rising and no wonder – we are all living through the “reinvention of the rip-off”, Owens told the Guardian, an experience that is undermining Americans’ trust in the economy. Nothing short of a consumer uprising and a slate of tough new rules is going to fix the problem, she believes. The book concludes with a “shoppers’ bill of rights” that lays out how local and federal governments could write rules to fix the problem: ban companies from using shared software to coordinate prices, it urges, and require AI “shopping assistants” to act in consumers’ best interest, not steer them to higher-price items, among other moves. “A cost of living crisis is the right time to build the constituency for a revived consumer movement in this country,” Owens says. The following interview was compiled from several conversations and edited and condensed for clarity. Why did you write Gouged? Right around the time that America started experiencing rising inflation and cost of living in 2021, I started to realize that there was something else going on besides just high prices. The way companies were talking about pricing was starting to shift. Their costs were going up but they weren’t too worried about it. They were planning to pass all of their rising costs along to us, and they were pretty bullish about gilding the lily and going for more. In an economy with competitive pricing, that shouldn’t happen, right? I started to see a little bit of a breadcrumb trail: “Oh, these companies are bullish because they have a plan for this, right?” They have some new techniques and technologies they’re planning to deploy, they have some new partnerships, they’ve been buying up AI pricing companies … they were ready for this moment. What actually changed inside corporate boardrooms? Cost-cutting hit bone. I cut my teeth in academia and the Senate studying the ruthless form of American capitalism that’s centered around it: bust unions and keep wages down, pass Nafta and outsource labor, bring in the bean counters from the big four accounting firms and ask: “How do we limit our regulatory costs?” Low prices were part of that part of capitalism. But there’s been a shift toward the revenue side of the ledger that includes getting better on price hiking. That’s easier to do when there’s less competition, but it’s also the result of new technologies. Gouged details data-mining companies unknown to the average consumer, like EverSight, Kronos, Plexure. How important have they been to the “gouging” problem US consumers are facing? Hugely important. Their dossiers contain thousands of data points and inferences about consumers, including their age, income, health, religion and even partisan affiliation. Virtually no one evades data brokers’ grasp. One data broker claims to have data profiles on roughly 95% of adults. With these troves of personal data in hand, retailers increasingly rely on outside consultants and AI startups who specialize in the “art and science behind pricing decisions”. They run experiments on consumers – and even personalize prices to each consumer’s pain point. Should these companies exist in an economy that’s also fair to workers and consumers? Profit maximization is not intrinsically problematic. In a competitive marketplace, companies would have to compete on price and quality in order to win over consumers, resulting in better products and better deals. However, as competition disappears and the law struggles to keep pace, new technologies and newer, more brazen methods of corporate profiteering erode the basic social contract between shoppers and retailers. Companies whose sole purpose is to harvest consumer data would probably cease to exist if Congress had passed adequate privacy protections. Companies should not get a gold star for refusing to gouge customers; they should be required not to. There’s a lot of telling history in this book, like the lightbulb that has been burning in California for 120 years, and how manufacturers banded together to make sure they never lasted that long again. Yet we’re still surprised by “planned obsolescence”. Have modern US consumers just been too naive? I think we all have a sense that this is going on and something has shifted, but we don’t fully appreciate how systematic and how purposeful this is. Whether it’s making the jar of Skippy peanut butter concave, degrading product quality, locking you out of something you bought, forcing you to pay top dollar for parts and repair – all of that is really baked into how companies operate these days. I don’t think Americans are naive. But every 10 or 20 years we need to have a conversation about what we’re owed as consumers and shoppers. It’s time to update the rules. How are American shoppers doing right now? I think American shoppers are exhausted. High prices make shopping pretty treacherous. The amount of basics Americans are putting on credit cards, the amount of Americans who are using things like “buy now, pay later” shows how difficult it is. Adding insult to injury is the increasingly opaque manipulative and volatile way that corporate America does pricing. This reinvention of the rip-off that we’re all living through has undermined trust in one of the major ways we participate in the economy. Comparison shopping is almost impossible now. Trying to get a refund is a three-day battle with a chatbot, and even if you think you won, you’d better remember to check with your bank to make sure they actually follow through. Where are we in the current inflation and rising cost cycle? I don’t even think we’re even at the halfway point. This is something I’ve been saying since 2022. Every time I was on the Hill, I was screaming at the Biden administration to focus more on prices and cost of living. This is a once-in-50-year period of high inflation. Something has completely changed in our culture and our economy, in our politics, and you have to be responsive to it. You wrote Gouged before the US and Israel attacks on Iran, which have ramped up inflation. Yes. I do talk in the book about Trump’s trade war, and its impact on prices. The Iran war is similar. Most Americans do understand how gas prices ripple through the whole economy. The fog of war, the fog of crisis, is really powerful. It makes it so that Americans have a hard time discerning which piece of the price increase is indeed because of import costs, and which is companies gilding the lily. Buckle up. You expect companies to take advantage of the war? Absolutely. What about your personal shopping? How are you and your family navigating this situation? The first thing I will say is I am not the “points guy” for e-commerce. I, like you, am being screwed by these companies. Most Americans are balancing trying to get a good deal with figuring out how much time they could possibly spend on not getting ripped off. So I updated how I comparison-shop. I look at brick and mortar, on the app, logged in, logged out. I try not to buy in-app. I run experiments. Call your friends and say: “What price are you seeing?” My husband and I sit in bed with our laptops open, figuring out which of us gets the better deal. Whoever gets the better deal buys the plane tickets. One thing I often hear from readers is “nothing is ever going to change” – a sort of pessimism about reforming the system. I do think the deck is stacked against us and we have our work cut out. It feels like Whac-A-Mole – you get a win in one city, you find out your bill is vetoed in another. [Colorado governor] Jared Polis vetoed surveillance pricing legislation. We’re still waiting for [New York governor] Kathy Hochul to sign a bill that passed there. But when Americans find out that companies are partnering with AI companies to spy on you and figure out how to take your last three pennies for every item in your grocery cart, they get pretty ticked off. I think the optimism I have is the sort of public anger, and, frankly, the groundswell of public conversation around this. The Federal Trade Commission is sorting through about 1,000 comments from Americans about surveillance pricing regulation. Wendy’s had to cry “uncle” and say they wouldn’t do surge pricing on their electronic menu board. Delta cried “uncle”, and so did Instacart two weeks after Groundwork exposed their algorithmic pricing experiments. I think all of that is a really important part about how we stick the genie back in the bottle, combined with legislative activity. If Democrats take the House and Senate, there’s a long list of things they are expected to address related to the Trump administration, national security et cetera. Where should this be on the priority list? The top issue for the American people, and it has been this way since 2022, is prices and the cost of living. Anything that takes on the economy is going to be top of the list. The only that could shift could be rising concern about AI – and a lot of the most sinister nefarious and opaque pricing practices that corporate America is using are powered by AI. We’re seeing interest from Republicans as well. I testified in front of [Missouri senator] Josh Hawley on this a couple weeks ago, at his request, as a majority witness, which has never happened to me before. You ask readers to repeat “It’s not your fault” three times before they try to confront this new landscape. Why? From the bottom of my heart, I don’t believe it should be Americans’ job to duck and dodge and beat the machine. The most dystopian version of this world is one in which there’s a “points guy” for everything. Outsmarting price-gouging on your own is like trying to solve climate change by yourself. Gougers are always reinventing themselves, always figuring out newer, more cunning ways to stay one step ahead. And all that effort eats up one of your most precious resources: time. Companies know this – and they are banking on it. What are you hoping to change, near term? It’s been a really long time since the consumer laws have been updated. I do think e-commerce and agentic commerce begs a new type of policy regime. This year alone, there are 90 pieces of legislation throughout the country, in states and cities to try to curtail algorithmic price fixing. A cost of living crisis is the right time to build the constituency for a revived consumer movement in this country.

title: First Thing: ‘Counting window’ seen as high-risk time for Trump to cast doubt on midterm results
author: Martin Belam
summary: Experts warn Republicans may try and sow distrust and claim ‘foreign interference’ in crucial hours after counting begins
body_text: Good morning. Election experts have warned that Donald Trump’s administration could use the crucial hours and days after November’s midterm elections to disrupt the results after struggling to enforce the crackdown it wanted on voting. After a succession of court setbacks to plans to restrict voting access, and with less than six weeks remaining until polls close, the post-election “counting window” is being seen as a particularly vulnerable moment by former US federal government officials. How might Republicans cause doubt over results? Caitlin Durkovich, a former deputy homeland security adviser, said: “I think because the administration has lost so many of their attempts to disrupt the normal process in court, that they are going to use the claim of foreign interference at the end of voting days to either seize equipment or to seize ballots, whether they’re legally justified to do so or not.” What are Democratic prospects for the midterms looking like? With control of the US Congress in the balance, Shrai Popat has interviewed Yasmin Radjy, a grassroots organizer, about what Democrats are getting right – and wrong – in the election run-up. UK counter-terror police investigate Iran link over suspected bomb plot at English base used by US forces British counter-terrorism police are investigating whether Iran is behind a suspected bomb plot after armed officers found explosives in three vans parked minutes from an RAF base used by the US military. After five men were arrested on terrorism charges, investigators were examining materials found in the vans near RAF Fairford, with an initial view being that they were consistent with improvised explosive devices. What have authorities said about the plot? Counter-terrorism police said: “At around 12.45am Sunday, police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the airbase. Armed officers responded and five men were arrested.” How did the arrests unfold? A resident of the village of Whelford was driving home from a party when she saw three white vans parked on a country road. She was immediately suspicious, she said, and became all the more so when she spotted a “large group of hooded and balaclavaed” men. She called emergency services and police arrived on the scene 15 minutes later. You can follow the latest developments in this story in our live blog. What has the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, said about attempts to end the US-Iran war? “They were asking for everything upfront with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz told CNN. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.” Republican senator criticizes White House for taxpayer-funded Trump ads The US senator John Kennedy told CBS News on Sunday “there ought to be a rule” against the White House expanding a taxpayer-funded advertising campaign to promote Donald Trump’s political agenda before the November midterm elections – before tacitly admitting such spending is “probably” illegal. Kennedy appeared to also be acknowledging the argument made by Jamie Raskin, a Democratic congressman, that any government employees who worked on the pro-Trump ads may have committed a felony violation of the Hatch Act, a law that bars government workers from partisan campaign activities. US attorney general defends Trump’s White House media ban Donald Trump’s attorney general, Todd Blanche, argued that the administration was permitted to ban three news outlets from the White House because “it is a privilege and not a right to be there”. On Thursday, a judge issued a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to temporarily restore the credentials of affected journalists at CNN, MS Now and Politico, and they were allowed entry to the executive complex. However, on Saturday CNN said its journalists were barred from joining the press pool traveling with the president on Air Force One. Pressed to point to a specific report the administration objected to, Blanche seemed to suggest that any negative reporting about Trump must be inaccurate, saying: “The information coming out of CNN and some of these other networks is wholly and completely, almost 100% negative toward the president.” Without providing any evidence, Blanche repeated the administration’s position that the affected three outlets’ reporting amounted to a “national security problem”. In other news … Madonna and Taylor Swift triumphed at the 2026 MTV Video Music awards, with the former winning three trophies and the latter winning the night’s top honor, extending her run as the most-awarded artist in VMAs history. Bill Gates has called on the US to regulate the development of artificial intelligence, saying that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths”. Datacenter developers are manipulating the EPA’s air pollution permitting process to avoid emission controls and scrutiny of their projects, environmental advocates allege. France’s far-right National Rally has surged in senate elections, with Marine Le Pen hailing a “historic victory”. Stat of the day: 61m tonnes of rubble – Gaza aid workers face delicate task of clearing ruins concealing up to 10,000 bodies The removal of the war debris, in which lives, memories and unexploded Israeli bombs lie buried, is one of largest clearance operations in modern history. Seham Tantesh reports from Gaza City for the Guardian. Building Power: Climate protesters call out big tech’s disconnect from reality In New York City activists gathered outside the OpenAI offices during climate week as figures showed that from 2024 to 2026 at least $64bn in proposed datacenter buildout was blocked by local organizing. Don’t miss this: US states grapple with uptick in encounters between bears and humans Experts largely attribute the increase in human-bear encounters – up in 15 states – to the impact of unusual weather on the animals’ food sources and a rebound in recent decades in black, brown and grizzly bear populations. … or this: A new museum coaxes Austrians to embrace The Sound of Music It is a beloved classic all over the world – except where it was filmed. Now a new museum aims to lift the profile of The Sound of Music in the beautiful Austrian city of Salzburg, where much of it was made. Climate check: Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as nor’easter storm batters US east coast Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but the threat of heavy rain, flash flooding and strong winds persisted. Mexico’s National Meteorological Service said Polo was expected to make a Baja landfall on Monday. Meanwhile, a nor’easter storm was battering the US east coast with heavy winds causing power outages. Last Thing: Two giant pandas arrive after Xi-Trump summit A longstanding diplomatic soft-power move by China has been the loan of endangered giant pandas to zoos, and after Xi Jinping’s trip to Washington, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will be settling in to Atlanta zoo. It is certainly softer diplomacy than the reports that Trump asked Xi if China would like to buy US weapons. Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. title: Larissa Waters steps down as Greens leader due to ill health
author: Tom McIlroy Political editor
summary: Ballot for new leader expected next week after Waters quits to manage pre-existing kidney disease that has ‘declined significantly’
body_text: Greens leader Larissa Waters has announced she will step down due to ill health, with a party room meeting expected within days to choose her successor. Waters revealed on Monday night she has been managing a pre-existing kidney disease, but that her health had “declined significantly over the course of recent months”. She said while her prognosis for recovery was positive, the pressure of the party’s leadership, including additional travel demands, was detracting from a focus on her health. Waters replaced Adam Bandt as Greens leader after the 2025 election, in which Bandt lost his lower house seat in a shock result. But some Greens members have expressed frustration with the party’s position under Waters, including its cut-through with voters as the major parties haemorrhage support to One Nation. Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast Waters said in a statement she would take a period of medical leave, before returning to parliament to represent Queensland in the Senate. “It has been a tremendous honour to be leader of the Greens, fighting for people and the planet,” she said. “I’m really sad that illness means my time as leader has been cut short, but our movement needs a leader in good health to lead us to success at the next election. “Passing the torch on to the next leader of the party will put them in the best position to take the Greens to the next election, fighting for people, not the corporate interests that run Labor, Liberals and One Nation. “Our fight is too important, and it needs more time and energy than I am able to give while I focus on my recovery.” She thanked her colleagues and doctors for their support, citing successes including negotiations with Labor on environmental law reforms and tougher gun laws introduced after last year’s Bondi Beach terror attack. “I will keep working for the people of Queensland, for women’s safety and for climate action when I am able to return to parliament.” Deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi, and high profile senators Sarah Hanson-Young, David Shoebridge and Nick McKim could contest the leadership ballot. Waters was first elected to the Senate in 2011 but was forced to resign in July 2017 after discovering she held duel Canadian citizenship during parliament’s eligibility crisis. After renouncing her citizenship, she returned to the upper house in September 2018 to fill a vacancy. Waters was a co-deputy leader to Bandt, and to former leader Richard Di Natale at various times between 2015 and 2022. As the party’s spokesperson for women, Waters played a role in shaping the independent parliamentary workplace watchdog based on recommendations from Kate Jenkins’ report into the culture in Parliament House. The Greens have been reduced to a single lower house MP – Ryan’s Elizabeth Watson-Brown – after the May election, with minor primary vote swings against Bandt and two Queensland incumbents, Max Chandler-Mather and Stephen Bates. The party maintains the losses were due to a drop in votes for the Liberal party favouring Labor candidates, as well as a reduction in favourable preference flows.

title: Why has abortion faded from America’s national conversation?
author: Moira Donegan
summary: The US has already grown used to the horror caused by abortion bans. And Republicans have sought to quash the stories
body_text: Abortion has faded from the headlines since the Dobbs decision of 2022, and Republicans like it that way. In the immediate aftermath of the supreme court’s overturning of Roe v Wade, as millions of women lost access to the dignity and self-determination that abortion provided them, clinics shut their doors, and the extent of Dobbs’s horrendously adverse public health implications started to become clear, abortion was always, it seemed, in the headlines. There were plenty of stories. There was the first known woman to die as the result of an abortion ban; and then the second; and then the third. There were the various lawsuits and ballot initiatives that for a while turned access off and on and then off again in various states; then there were the state supreme court elections, races that were newly transformed by the abortion debate and on which the health and status of a state’s women now relied. There were the clinics that shut their doors in Republican-controlled states, many of which had provided the essential, stigmatized care for decades, under hostile conditions, with persistence and innovation and determination that were staggering. But the stories have faded from the headlines as the years have gone by. Feminism has gone dramatically out of style, with the big women’s rights NGOs wounded enough by Dobbs and attacks from the Trump administration that they have been largely unable to push their agenda in either media or policy, and algorithmic social media driving a rise in gender conservatism and politicized misogyny, particularly among young men. But maybe more importantly, abortion has ceased to be a story because the horrors of abortion bans have ceased to be news: the US has grown used to the swift and dramatic erosion of women’s health and status that has followed Dobbs, grown used to the horror stories and upward ticking body counts, grown into ease, and even a kind of compliant boredom, with women’s death and indignity. But lately, there have been efforts to change that. Pro-choice activists and health researchers have advanced stories about the extent of Dobbs’s impact on women’s health, looking to advance new studies, particular stories and illuminating statistics that reveal the extent of the danger and damaged posed to women by Republican governance. And Republicans, in turn, have looked to quash stories about the impact of abortion bans and suppress data that illustrates their impact, fearing, it seems, that being reminded of what abortion bans mean in practice will further dampen their party’s odds in the coming midterms. First, there’s Texas. The Lone Star state was the first to implement a near-total abortion ban in September 2021, about nine months before Roe was struck down, after the supreme court used its controversial shadow docket to allow Texas to ban abortion without full briefing or argument. That means that Texas has an unusually large amount of data on how abortion bans affect women’s health and status: no other state has had an abortion ban in place for as long. But state health officials in Texas, most of them appointed by the solidly Republican state government, have dragged their feet on studying the impact of abortion on maternal health outcomes – maybe because they don’t think they’ll like what they find. After the state committee refused to expand the purview of its longstanding maternal mortality data collection to include adverse health outcomes caused by delayed or denied abortion care, investigators at ProPublica did so themselves, finding that in 2022 and 2023, the first two full calendar years that the state’s abortion ban was in effect, that the rate of sepsis in Texas patients who experienced miscarriages in the second trimester increased by more than 50% – probably because doctors, fearing sanction and prosecution under the new laws, delayed administering the very simple dilation and curettage procedure that would have spared the patients’ lives until the women’s condition worsened to the point of death. The new law, in short, forces healthcare providers to play chicken with women’s lives, like daredevil teenagers standing in the path of oncoming headlights and daring themselves to stand still before leaping out of the roadway at the last available minute. Predictably, this has had fatal results. The same ProPublica study found that in the first two years after the ban went into effect, 120 pregnant or postpartum women died in Texas hospitals – a dramatic increase over previous years. But despite the growing body count, Texas health authorities evidently remain determined to cover up the fatal results of the abortion ban. Every year in early September, an official medical body in the state issues a report on the maternal and infant death rate in Texas – data that is essential for health researchers, even as the methods of its collection have become disputed and politicized in the post-Dobbs era. But this year, in an unprecedented move, the release of the report was postponed – pushed back from its longstanding date of 1 September, all the way to 1 December. The delay means that whatever the report says about the state of pregnant women suffering, sickening and dying in Texas, that information will be kept confidential until after the midterms. Voters will be deprived of it as they make their choices in November. It’s easier to understand why Republicans want to hide data on the health effects of abortion bans when you realize just how profound those impacts are. New studies show they are quite profound indeed. An analysis of CDC data reveals that since Dobbs, women are dying at alarmingly high rates from ectopic pregnancies – in which an embryo implants in the fallopian tube, rather than the wall of the uterus, a condition which has no possibility of leading to a live birth and which is fatal if left untreated. Ectopic pregnancies are easily detectible using ultrasounds, and simply terminated with a shot; there is no reason, medical or moral, why they should be fatal. And yet, between 2020 and 2025, they killed nearly 200 women in the US – almost doubling the number who died in the previous six years. The culprit? Probably the same phenomenon that is driving the increase in sepsis among pregnant women in Texas: doctors, scared to do their duty by their patients because of sadistic, punitive and misogynist abortion bans, are forced to subordinate medical best practices to the incoherent demands of the law. The rate of ectopic pregnancy deaths in states with abortion bans is nearly double that in states where abortion is legal. Neither Democrats nor the media seems interested in making abortion a centerpiece of the midterm campaign cycle, and so Republican efforts to bury this data have been largely successful. But there are still those struggling to assert the value of women’s lives. This month, the family of Tierra Walker, a 37-year-old mother who died at 20 weeks pregnant in a Texas hospital in 2024, after doctors had repeatedly denied her an abortion to treat her worsening pre-eclampsia, sued the Texas attorney general and Republican Senate nominee, Ken Paxton, and others for wrongful death. They allege that Walker, who had suffered multiple seizures and had become unable to work due to her condition, was subjected to neglect and indifference by a Texas medical and legal system that cares more about enforcing pregnancies than it does about civil rights, personal dignity, public health or human life. When she died, her son, then 14, lost his mother. Ken Paxton, and all the other abortion-ban supporting Republicans on the ticket in November, should have to answer to him. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

title: Boston sues Trump administration over infrastructure grant withdrawal
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: City challenges transportation department’s decision to cancel funding that included money for EV charging
body_text: Boston has sued Donald Trump’s administration over the withdrawal of a $20m grant for infrastructure improvements in the latest example of cities across the country mobilising against the federal government. Boston is challenging a decision by the transportation department to cancel funding for a project on the basis that it included a small allocation for electric vehicle charging. The grant was awarded to Boston during Democrat Joe Biden’s presidency under the Rebuilding American Infrastructure with Sustainability and Equity (Raise) programme. The city argues the Roxbury Resilient Corridors project would improve safety, public transport, accessibility and traffic flow. Three streets identified for improvements are in the top 3% of Boston’s streets in terms of concentration of traffic injuries and fatalities. They are in an area classified by the transportation department as one of “persistent poverty” and a “historically disadvantaged community”. Boston says the department gave a single reason for withdrawing the grant in September last year: it included electric vehicle charging infrastructure. However, the city contends this accounted for less than 1% of the project’s costs. The lawsuit argues that the decision was unlawful and overtly political and contradicted the purpose of the Raise programme, which Congress established to support infrastructure projects promoting sustainability, safety and technological innovation, including in underserved communities. Michelle Wu, the mayor of Boston, said: “We’re fighting for every dollar of investment to improve quality of life for Roxbury residents, commuters and businesses. “Boston earned this competitive grant to meet community needs and address long-needed infrastructure upgrades. The City of Boston will continue to fight back against lawless federal attacks, and we urge the court to reverse the Trump administration’s illegal actions and restore these critical funds for Roxbury.” The Democratic congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, whose Massachusetts district includes Roxbury, said: “These funds are an essential investment in Roxbury and the unlawful cancellation of this grant is more evidence of Sean Duffy and Donald Trump’s contempt for the people we serve.” She added: “There was no good reason to rescind these funds – DOT should reverse course so we can move this project forward, improve the daily lives of commuters, and enhance the climate resilience of at-risk communities—just as Congress intended.” The lawsuit argues that federal agencies cannot change the terms of a programme established by Congress to reflect changing political priorities. The case, City of Boston v Duffy, names the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, and was filed in the US district court for the district of Massachusetts. Boston city says it will have filed nine lawsuits against the administration once the latest case is included, eight of them in partnership with the Public Rights Project. Toby Merrill, litigation director at the Public Rights Project, which is providing pro bono legal counsel to Boston, said: “Boston lost a $20m infrastructure grant over electric vehicle chargers that represented a fraction of 1% of the funding – infrastructure the federal government itself encouraged.” Cities including Chicago, New York and Los Angeles and states across the US have brought a series of lawsuits against the administration over federal funding decisions and other policies since Trump returned to the White House.

title: False claims about Aboriginal rock art and aliens were once fringe. Researchers fear AI could push them mainstream
author: Tory Shepherd
summary: Archeologists warn AI summaries can repeat false claims about 12,000-year-old rock art from Western Australia’s Kimberley region being painted by aliens
body_text: Traditional owner Warren Barunga says he is angry that people are misusing his people’s sacred rock paintings. The ancient Gwion Gwion and Wandjina figures, found in the Kimberley in Western Australia, have long been used in false claims that they were created by aliens or vanished civilisations. Now the old tropes about the sacred rock art, born in the 19th century, have been supercharged by social media. In the latest issue of Australian Archaeology, researchers have analysed the “extent to which popularised fringe narratives are displacing science-based and Indigenous knowledge-informed archaeology online” and the further dangers posed by AI summaries absorbing those narratives. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Countless social media accounts, some with tens of thousands of followers, falsely claim that the figures in Kimberley rock art were painted by a different or “superior” race, and possibly aliens. The researchers, from various Australian universities, looked at examples in the Pacific as well as the Gwion Gwion paintings. These examples “have all been subject to fringe ideas about a ‘superior race’ that dissociates descendant Indigenous peoples from their pasts”, they wrote. The Gwion Gwion paintings, which feature tall, thin people with intricate details such as complex headdresses, were introduced to Europeans by the pastoralist Joseph Bradshaw in the 1890s. They are about 12,000 years old, and are often flanked by Wandjina, which are up to 5,000 years old. Both are used in the false claims. Barunga is a Worrorra man and a Dambimangari Aboriginal Corporation director. Worrorra people are part of the Wanjina Wunggurr community, which includes the Wunambal, Gaambera and Ngarinyin people. Barunga says the Wandjinas are the core of his people’s existence, from the Lalai or Dreaming. “It is our kinship system … our cultural heritage … our way of life,” he says. “We garden this country, we look after Wandjina. “When I hear about these misinterpretations, it not only saddens but it angers me.” Of the Gwion Gwion, he says they are “the first people, our ancestors. They were here; we are the children that belong to them.” Competing with make-believe The use of “pseudoarchaeology” to make false claims about the paintings and other ancient artefacts has a long history. The “‘lunatic fringe’ of prehistoric archaeology rose in Germany in the 1920s and 30s, essentially as an “ideologically motivated misinformation scheme”, the researchers write. “Pseudoarchaeology often favours white nationalist imaginings of the world and therefore disempowers Indigenous histories.” The Swiss author Erich von Däniken’s 1968 bestseller Chariots of the Gods? suggested we were all the descendants of aliens who visited Earth in the distant past. Cave paintings, Egypt’s pyramids and the Easter Island statues were proof of their visit, he wrote, arguing the people who lived there would not have been capable of creating them. Speculation about a “non-Aboriginal origin” of the Kimberley figures started in the 19th century and re-emerged in the 1990s, in the context of Mabo and native title. The myth was spurred by an amateur archaeologist Grahame Walsh, who claimed they were painted by a pre-Aboriginal group. In 2015, then Liberal Democratic party senator David Leyonhjelm cited the Gwion Gwion paintings when he claimed there might have been a “previous culture” before Aboriginal people occupied Australia. He used that false claim to argue it was “not necessarily a good thing” to recognise Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the constitution. Last year, online images circulating with posts claiming to feature the Gwion Gwion were thoroughly debunked by experts. The same picture had been previously posted with the claim it was an ancient Indian cave painting depicting the “groundbreaking revelation of prehistoric extraterrestrial encounters”. A search today of social media shows multiple accounts posting false claims about the origin of Kimberley paintings, often featuring Wandjina figures, alongside the Gwion Gwion, with speculation that with their large heads and eyes they might be alien “greys”. The researchers say the rise of social media and AI as primary sources of information for many raises concerns about “how the outputs will influence how the past is written for mainstream audiences”. The paper’s lead author, Dr Michelle Richards, a University of Melbourne archaeologist, says academic research struggles to get into the public realm and has to compete with “fringe narratives, pseudoscience, even just made-up stories … they have that promise of mystery, dramatic revelations”. The researchers found ChatGPT gave “largely non-harmful answers” when asked about the origin of the Gwion Gwion figures. The OpenAI chatbot said definitively they were painted by Aboriginal Australians and reflected a “long, continuous cultural tradition”. But Richards says she is worried that could change, and it’s important to “keep on top of it”. When Guardian Australia asked ChatGPT about them, it said they were “most likely” painted by the ancestors of Aboriginal people and that there had been “considerable debate about their origins”, but that answer varied when different variations of the question were asked. Richards says: “I think we still have a chance to stay on top of it, but we do have to pay attention.”

title: John Oliver on Brazil’s Flávio Bolsonaro: ‘Fearmongering and flagrant daddy issues’
author: Guardian staff
summary: The Last Week Tonight host digs into Brazil’s election, with current leader Lula faces a disgraced former president’s son
body_text: On the latest Last Week Tonight, John Oliver looked ahead to Sunday’s major election in Brazil, where 160 million people will vote to determine the country’s president, as well as state governors, two-thirds of the senate and every member of the lower house. “Yet again, Brazil finds itself having to choose between Lula and a guy named Bolsonaro for president, and many do not seem thrilled that those are their main choices,” the host explained of the two candidates for president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, and Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the disgraced former rightwing president Jair Bolsonaro. All signs are pointing toward an extremely close race, “which is worrying, because that means the world’s fourth-largest democracy and the home to, not insignificantly, the rainforest that is key to meeting the world’s climate goals, could yet again be run by a dangerous dipshit named Bolsonaro,” said Oliver. The host then traced how we got to this moment, after Lula defeated Jair Bolsonaro by two percentage points in 2022, the smallest margin for a Brazilian presidential election since the fall of the military dictatorship in 1985. Bolsonaro fled to Florida, but months later, violent rioters clashed with police as they vandalized government buildings, claiming Bolsonaro did not actually lose the election. “It turns out history doesn’t repeat itself,” said Oliver over footage of January 6, 2021 in the US, “but sometimes, it does get dubbed in Portuguese.” After collecting significant evidence that he was planning to stage a military coup, Bolsonaro was convicted and sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison, and barred from ever running for president again. He was released from prison after four months, however, to serve the remainder of his sentence on “humanitarian house arrest”, owing to his failing health. “If you’re seeing a lot of parallels to Trump here – an authoritarian leader who lost an election, only to then go sulk in Florida and plot his revenge – you’re not alone in that,” said Oliver. “Trump clearly sees a reflection of his own experiences in all this, and during Bolsonaro’s trial, he even seemed to try to sway the outcome.” Trump called the trial “a witch-hunt that should end immediately” as he threatened Brazil with 50% tariffs. “Of course he called it that!” said Oliver. “Trump overuses the term ‘witch-hunt’ the way the internet overuses the word ‘iconic’.” Trump’s attempted meddling in Brazilian affairs may backfire; Lula has seen a boost in popularity whenever he denounces Trump’s tariffs as infringements on Brazilian sovereignty. “And to be honest, he could do with the help,” said Oliver. “Because if Bolsonaro is reminiscent of Trump, Lula can unfortunately be pretty reminiscent of Joe Biden, and not just because they both have big ‘I have a Werther’s original in my pocket’ energy.” Like Biden, Lula is a career politician who has generally governed as a center-left pragmatist, prioritizing social programs and supporting oil drilling in the Amazon while still attempting to curb deforestation. The 80-year-old has also combatted concerns about his age via a steady stream of workout videos posted to social media. “I think I speak for everyone when I say that that is truly inspiring,” said Oliver. “Specifically, it has inspired me to stay the fuck off of Instagram, so I don’t risk witnessing an 80-year-old with his pits out filming geriatric thirst traps.” “The problem for Lula is that many voters see him as an establishment candidate,” he added, and even though unemployment in Brazil is currently at its lowest level since 2012, affordability remains a major concern. He also faces a candidate half his age in Flávio Bolsonaro, who has tried to paint himself as a newer, “vaccinated” version of his father without some of the baggage. But Flávio shares many characteristics with his father, whom he has invoked at his rallies via AI-generated videos skirting around rules that Jair Bolsonaro not address the public. Like his father, Flávio has a history of homophobic statements and a penchant for defending Brazil’s military dictatorship, which killed and tortured its political rivals. He has also aligned himself with rightwing world leaders such as Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu and Argentina’s Javier Milei. “But maybe the biggest similarity between Flávio and his dad concerns their rich history of being connected to scandals,” said Oliver, turning to the huge scandal around shady financing for a movie called Dark Horse. The English-language movie starring Jim Caviezel paints Jair Bolsonaro as the victim of a conspiracy of elites, and is now at the center of a corruption scandal after documents revealed that Flávio received 61m reais ($12m) from a disgraced banker to finance the less than expensive-looking film. “This suspiciously expensive movie was pretty clearly designed to reset Jair Bolsonaro’s image among Brazilians and in doing so, boost Flávio’s campaign,” Oliver explained. “Which is what makes it so funny that amid all of the controversy, the film’s distributor decided to postpone the release until after the election. So Flávio’s not going to get any of the propaganda benefits of Dark Horse, but he’s still having to deal with the scandal surrounding its financing,” which has become a major headline in Brazil. But Flávio Bolsonaro still has a very real chance of winning the election, which is “not good”, said Oliver, noting that the son has already promised to pardon the father if elected. “There is clearly a lot at stake in Brazil right now,” he continued, “and I’m not just saying that because I’m not a big fan of the Bolsonaros, which is about as much of an understatement as me saying ‘the movie Dark Horse probably won’t win an Oscar.’” Oliver conceded that “the only thing more annoying than me ending a story telling you to go vote is telling you to go vote if you’re in Brazil,” where voting is mandatory. “So all I’ll say is that hopefully next Sunday, Lula’s message of defiance and gym lunges will end up gaining a lot more traction that Flávio’s fearmongering and flagrant daddy issues.”

title: Texas Republican called for public execution of Democratic leaders – report
author: Ariana Baio
summary: Bo French, who is running to lead a state agency, has in the past posted controversial and racist statements online
body_text: Bo French, a Texas Republican running to lead a powerful state agency, has a history of making controversial social media posts, including calling for the public execution of Democratic leaders, according to a recent investigation from CNN’s KFile team. French, who is running to lead Texas’s railroad commission, has recently faced criticism from members of his own party after making a racist post on social media. Powerful Republicans, including the Texas senator John Cornyn, said they would not support French in the upcoming election. But the latest spat over French’s social media has led to a deeper look at his online history. In a review of old posts from social media accounts that seemingly belonged to French, CNN’s KFile team found that the Texas Republican repeatedly called for public executions of opponents. In 2020, French used a now-suspended X account to seemingly call for the execution of former president Barack Obama and other Obama administration officials that he believed had disseminated false information about Russia’s involvement in the 2016 presidential election. In February 2025, French used his X account, under a former handle, to call for other public executions, including Senator Adam Schiff. The Guardian has asked French’s campaign for comment. French is no stranger to posting controversial statements online. Over the last year, he has used his platform to assert that the entire religion of Islam should be banned; claim childless women were “selfish” and “responsible for the demise of our culture”; and posted a poll to ask whether “Jews” or “Muslims” posed a bigger threat. According to CNN/KFile’s investigation, in May 2020 French used an account under the name “rwbofrench”, which has since been suspended, to encourage Donald Trump to “hang” Obama-era officials believed to be part of the “Russia hoax”. The posts came after Trump accused Obama administration officials of “treason” to dismiss reports that Russia tried to interfere with the 2016 presidential election to assist Trump. In response to Trump’s “Drain the Swamp” post, French wrote: “I agree. But you can not do that until your DOJ charges and prosecutes the treasonous bastards who spearheaded the Russia hoax. The death penalty for the Obama conspirators will be the only thing that pulls the stopper out of the drain. #HangEmHigh.” Minutes later, French responded to another social media user who accused Obama of running the Russia interference, seemingly promoting the death penalty for the former president. “The penalty for treason used to be death. Even for a former president. #HangEmHigh,” French wrote. It was unclear why the account was suspended. In another instance of calling for public executions, French used his current social media account, under the former handle “Bo_French_TX”, to call for the death of government officials identified by Elon Musk’s Doge team. “I want more than perp walks. I want public executions,” French wrote in a now-deleted post from February 2025. In another post, French called for the public execution of Schiff, who led the House committee that released the report on Russia’s interference in the 2016 election. It was unclear whether the latest social media posts were deleted by French or a member of his team.

title: Marine Le Pen hails RN senate surge as ‘milestone’ towards French presidency
author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
summary: National Rally and allies gain record 14 seats and can form senate group for first time after indirect vote by local officials
body_text: The French far-right leader Marine Le Pen has said her 2027 presidential campaign will be boosted after her anti-immigration party, the National Rally (RN), and its allies improved to a record 14 seats in partial senate elections this weekend. Le Pen called the results a “historic victory” and a “major milestone” after her party cleared the 10-seat threshold to be able to form a senate group for the first time, after an indirect vote by local officials including mayors and councillors. The party’s progress in the senate will allow it higher visibility and more funding in the second house of parliament before next spring’s presidential election. Le Pen is polling high as Emmanuel Macron prepares to step down after 10 years in office. The French investigative website Mediapart reported on Monday that the RN party president, Jordan Bardella, allegedly made antisemitic comments in writing in 2013, when he was a young party member. The alleged comments in a chat, which Mediapart said it had authenticated, included: “The Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so.” He was also alleged to have written “all the banks are owned by Jews”. Bardella responded on X that he “formally” rejected the allegations, which he described as “crude forgeries”, saying he would take legal action. The RN MP Sébastien Chenu called the senate gains “a boost for the presidential campaign” and said there was “no more glass ceiling” for the party. Edwige Diaz, who secured a large senate win for the RN in Gironde outside Bordeaux, told Le Parisien: “This will be very useful for us before the presidential election.” The 348-seat senate is France’s second chamber of parliament alongside the national assembly. Final results on Monday morning showed the senate remained dominated by the traditional right and centre right. The upper chamber’s president of more than a decade, Gerard Larcher, 77, from the rightwing party Les Républicains, is expected to be re-elected next week. Although the RN is now the biggest single opposition party in the national assembly and has the largest number of French members of the European parliament, it has until now never had a grouping in the senate, where its presence has been small. Nine RN senators were elected on Sunday, in addition to the three who won seats in 2023. The RN ally, Éric Ciotti’s Union of the Right for the Republic party, won two seats. The RN had entered the senate for the first time with two seats in 2014, when it was known as the Front National. The senate has an indirect voting system, with local elected officials choosing new senators for half the upper chamber every three years, each to serve a six-year term. Sunday’s vote by local mayors and councillors reflected the RN’s growth in support in medium towns at the last local elections in March. It also showed the party has support among independent rural mayors. Bardella called on politicians on the traditional right to join forces with his party. The Socialist senator Laurence Rossignol said a crucial question would be whether the right and centre right in the senate now moved closer to the RN and hardened their own stance on issues such as immigration and welfare benefits. She told Public Sénat TV: “Will there be a republican barrier against RN ideas? That will be key.” The right, the centre and the left’s Socialists remain the three major forces in the upper house. The radical left party La France Insoumise won a senate seat for the first time, with Gabriel Amard elected in the Rhône. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the party’s leader, who is the highest-polling left candidate for the presidency, said Amard’s win was a “good omen” for his own 2027 presidential campaign.

title: Trump announces $15bn Iowa steel plant as he bids to boost flagging midterm hopes
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: President says plant will be built by Indian-owned company and calls it largest such facility in American history
body_text: Donald Trump on Monday announced what he called the largest steel plant in American history to be built in Iowa, giving Republicans a jobs message to take to voters in a state that could help decide control of the Senate in November. “Using advanced steelmaking technology, the plant will produce some of the highest quality, most affordable steel anywhere in the world,” Trump said in the Oval Office, flanked by Iowa’s top Republicans. The plant, which “they’ve already started building”, Trump said, will be built in eastern Iowa by the foreign-owned steelmaker Mesabi Metallics and is expected to cost about $15bn, according to a White House official. It aims to begin production in 2030, years after voters go to the polls in November. In his announcement, Trump singled out Iowa’s Ashley Hinson, the Republican congresswoman who was in the Oval Office and who is running for the Senate seat being vacated by Joni Ernst, also in the room. “I saw some good polls just recently,” he told her. “Looks like you’re doing well.” But the polls for that race are less rosy than Trump suggested. A Marist survey published last week found Hinson trailing Democrat Josh Turek by eight points in the conservative state, while an earlier Emerson College poll had Hinson narrowly ahead but found voters worried about tariffs. Democrats see the seat as one of four they need to retake the Senate. Trump said the plant would run on iron ore from the company’s mine in Minnesota, which accounted for roughly 60% of iron ore production in the US in the 20th century. The president took the chance to attack that state’s Democratic governor, Tim Walz. “They have one of the worst governors in history, a real stupid guy, but they do have good iron ore, which is more important, I guess,” Trump said. The two men have clashed over mining in the state, most recently over Walz’s August order halting permitting for mining projects near the Boundary Waters wilderness. The Mesabi Metallics company itself, however, is owned by the India-based Essar Group, and US taxpayers are helping to pay for the expansion: the Export-Import Bank, a federal agency, will provide up to $10bn in financing. When asked whether global outsourcing would be needed to build the plant, the chairman of Mesabi Metallics, Rewant Ruia, said “most of the critical materials” would come from the US but added “there are some materials that might be used that need to be imported for making and refining the highest quality steels”. Still, the president credited his tariffs – the taxes the US charges consumers on imported goods – for the investment. “Everyone’s building their plant here because they don’t want to pay tariffs,” he said. “It’s really not that complicated. A lot of people say they don’t understand it, but they do. They just don’t like to give us credit.” Trump said the project was “expected to create up to 6,000 new construction jobs, nearly 2,000 manufacturing and mining jobs, and add another $95bn to the US economy”.

title: Morning Mail: Larissa Waters quits as Greens leader; Sydney datacentre scrapped; and SpaceX rocket blasts off
author: Martin Farrer
summary: Ill health forces resignation with leadership ballot set for next week; Reserve Bank expected to hike again today
body_text: Morning everyone. The Greens will choose a new leader next week after Larissa Waters shocked Australian politics last night by announcing she was standing down due to ill health. There will also be intense focus on the Reserve Bank at 2.30pm this afternoon when it is expected that interest rates will be lifted again to curb inflation. Our research reveals the huge turnover in One Nation MPs, AI godfathers warn governments to prepare for an “explosion” in the technology, the huge wave menacing the coast of California, and Magda Szubanski’s “elegant, insightful” new book. Australia Leaving party | More than half of the One Nation MPs elected to state or federal parliaments have left the party before the end of their term, according to Guardian analysis, with 28 of the 51 people elected under Pauline Hanson’s banner either resigning midterm or being expelled. Rate risk | Two or even three more Reserve Bank interest rate hikes would be “devastating” for the property market but still leave housing more unaffordable than ever as higher borrowing costs trump lower prices, experts say. Waters quits | The Greens leader, Larissa Waters, has announced she will step down due to ill health, with a party room meeting scheduled for next week to choose her successor. Deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi, and senators Sarah Hanson-Young, David Shoebridge and Nick McKim are contenders to take over. Off centre | Plans for a controversial $1.2bn datacentre in Lane Cove in Sydney’s north have been withdrawn, with the developer blaming “emerging” regulations from the state and federal governments. Corruption questions | Queensland’s anti-corruption commission has investigated just 20 of more than 6,000 complaints in the past year. World ‘Kelvin wave’ | Concerns are mounting about an ocean phenomenon known as a Kelvin wave that could raise sea levels along the California coastline by up to 30cm, as scientists say El Niño is supercharging the threat of storm surges and flooding in the coming months. AI ‘explosion’ | Two of the “godfathers” of modern AI and senior executives at OpenAI and Anthropic have warned governments to prepare for an AI “intelligence explosion”, which they say could be the most consequential technological development in history. They did so as Nvidia unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop AI agents from going rogue. Base arrests | Five British nationals have been released on bail after being arrested on suspicion of terror offences at an air force base in south-west England, police have said. Questions remain over whether Iran was involved in the suspected plot. Screen study | The effect of high screen time on children is as significant as parental behaviour and premature birth, if not greater, a global study has found. SpaceX liftoff | SpaceX has sent its enormous Starship rocket into Earth’s orbit for the first time on a milestone flight intended to pave the way for future missions to the moon and Mars. Full Story From fuel wars to AI: the forces driving the RBA rate decision With inflation proving stubborn and global economic pressures mounting, Australians are bracing for another potential interest rate rise. Could pushing the cash rate to its highest level since 2011 send struggling households over the edge? Economics editor Patrick Commins joins Reged Ahmad to unpack what’s driving today’s decision and what it means for the broader economic outlook. In-depth As the debate around migration becomes more intense, our reporter Achol Arok has been talking to immigrants such as Shamsullah Sadey. The 19-year-old year 12 student fled Afghanistan for a new life in Australia and wants to be a doctor, but feels he is now seen as more of a problem than a contributor to society. Not the news Tim Byrne welcomes Magda Szubanski’s latest book, I Can’t Tell You But I Will, which combines the story of the life and decline of Szubanski’s mother and the author’s public activism in the fight for marriage equality to produce an insightful and deeply elegant anti-celebrity memoir. Sport NRL | Nathan Cleary has told fans “I’ll be back” in a social media post from his hospital bed after the Penrith star underwent emergency surgery on a horrific ankle injury. He also urged fans not to blame Knights’ hooker Phoenix Crossland for the tackle that caused the injury. Football | Israel captain Manor Solomon claimed his country was “10 times better” than Ireland as fallout intensified from their Nations League match and stated bluntly: “They hate us and we don’t like them.” Cricket | A Cambridge professor is working on a prototype bamboo bat to replace willow. Media roundup The Telegraph says 1,500 workers fear for their future as a critical Hunter Valley mine ruling nears. Jake Kolodjashnij of the Geelong Cats is retiring from the AFL following fresh neuropsychology scans and tests after his concussion injury, the Advertiser reports. title: How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools
author: Nathan Sanders and Bruce Schneier
summary: Though politicians are quiet about how they use AI, the book Rewiring Democracy examines how AI is starting to influence American politics
body_text: New campaign finance disclosure data shines a light on which US political campaigns are using AI tools and how much they are spending on them. Candidates’, parties’ and committees’ spending reveals that AI is fast becoming an essential tool of politics. The candidates themselves are quiet about how they are using the technology in their own campaigns. It’s a sensitive issue that we have been tracking closely since we started writing our book, Rewiring Democracy, which examined how AI is beginning to influence politics. A September 2025 Pew survey of Americans found that more than 70% would think less of a candidate if they used AI to help write a speech. Itemized expenditure disclosure data from the US Federal Election Commission, dating back to 2020, reveals at least $17m in disclosed spending on AI technology vendors across 523 federal candidates and campaigns. Data from four states, California, Colorado, Massachusetts and Washington, provides a more localized picture going back to 2022. Beginning with the AI behemoths, at least 80 federal campaigns and committees have reported spending with OpenAI since 2024. The total spending is not huge: only about $50,000 reported, skewing slightly more Republican than Democratic. The Republican National Committee is the largest overall buyer, with nearly $10,000 in reported expenses. Top individual users include the campaigns of Republicans Mike Lawler, John Kennedy and Bill Cassidy, as well as the California Democrats Ro Khanna and Ted Lieu. Most of these expenses are listed as office expenses, subscriptions to ChatGPT for staff, or research tools, rather than as specific political services. The company’s policies prohibit some political uses of their ChatGPT tool. OpenAI’s biggest competitor, Anthropic, has rapidly built a similar level of usage, but with a different split. At least 65 candidates or committees now report paying the Claude maker in 2026, up from essentially zero in previous years, with a nearly two-to-one Democrat-to-Republican ratio. However, the largest individual user is the campaign of Tom Cotton, a Republican senator from Arkansas, who reported more than $4,000 in spend on Anthropic software in his June filing. Other major users are the Montana independent Senate candidate Seth Bodnar and Jason Knapp, who lost a Democratic House primary in Virginia, and the Democratic Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola. Candidates use either Claude or ChatGPT, rarely both, according to the disclosures. Only about 12% of campaigns or committees using either tool reported expenditures to both vendors. The Democratic lean of Anthropic usage may reflect the company’s alleged liberal skew and clashes with the Trump administration. In contrast, Elon Musk’s xAI caters to Republican interests and, accordingly, its meager usage comes almost entirely from the political right. Just seven federal and two state-level candidates or committees have reported paying xAI, a total of about $5,000, the majority of which was spent by the presidential campaign of RFK Jr in 2024, but also includes Republicans Dave McCormick and Thomas Massie. More dollars go to the vendors specializing in political campaign applications of AI. For years, AmplifAI, which provides automated text messaging, essentially a new iteration on robocalling technology, was a dominant target of spending, soaking up $4.7m in campaign spending in the 2022 cycle alone. It was used heavily by Democratic candidates including Mark Kelly, Joe Biden, Bernie Sanders and Adam Schiff. Spending on AmplifAI, now owned by the troubled media conglomerate Triller, seems to have tapered off in the years since 2022. The new rising Democratic solution for AI-powered text messaging is Daisychain, which has so far garnered about $300,000 in reported candidate spend in the 2026 cycle – up from only about $50,000 reported in 2024. More than half of this year’s spending comes from the Senate campaign of Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. The closest equivalent on the Republican side has been Campaign Nucleus, associated with former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale. The AI-powered voter engagement tool has attracted six-figure spending from the Republican National Committee, multiple Pacs aligned with Donald Trump, and five-figure investments from Mike Johnson, Kari Lake and other candidates. It is displacing the legacy Republican-serving texting vendor Prompt.io, which has retained about $375,000 in 2026 spending to date, down from more than $500,000 in the 2022 cycle. But it continues to be used: the A More Affordable California Pac sponsored by Uber has single-handedly spent more than $1m on Prompt.io in 2026. The Republican Massachusetts gubernatorial nominee Michael Minogue has been a recurring customer, as has the failed Republican California gubernatorial candidate Ché Ahn and Republican-aligned Super Pac Neighbors for a Better Colorado. At the state level At the state level, the AI spending is smaller but growing fast. Across the four states studied, we found a total of at least $92,000 in spending confidently attributable to modern generative AI vendors since 2022. The spending is spread across at least 108 candidates and committees. The growth has been explosive; there has already been about 10 times the amount of state-level AI spending reported in 2026 as there was in all of 2024. Much of the state spending mirrors federal patterns. Daisychain again has the highest overall spend, and OpenAI and Claude dominate among the general-purpose AI vendors. DonorAtlas – the AI-powered prospect research tool – sticks out for its usage in these states, sitting behind only Daisychain and OpenAI and buoyed up by nearly $4,000 in spending by the California Democratic party. Even though it has dominated so much media conversation, few candidates seem to be reporting spending on AI tools designed specifically to create synthetic audio and video, also known as “deepfakes”. We found just six federal candidates or committees reporting spending on the popular AI audio generator tool from ElevenLabs, with total spending of about $1,400 led by independent candidate for Colorado’s sixth congressional district Samir Witta. The AI image generator service Midjourney has five reported federal campaign or committee users reporting about $1,600, led by Sholdon Daniels, the Republican primary runner-up in the Texas 30th district. Combined, those two firms had less than $100 in reported spend across the four states. However, recent data from the Wesleyan Media Project shows that at least 164 political ads in this cycle have included AI-generated media, supported by at least $80m in ad spending. What this illustrates is that candidate and committee disclosure reports are just the tip of the iceberg. They don’t cover spending on AI by political consultants, media firms and other vendors hired by the campaigns or by Pacs, or independent committees raising and spending money aimed at boosting candidates’ campaigns. Those entities aren’t required to disclose detailed expenditure reports, and are very likely where the bulk of campaign AI usage is happening. Since a large fraction of all spending in the campaign cycle will happen in the final weeks leading to November, much remains to be seen about the totality of how campaigns will leverage AI and what impact its use will have on voters’ decisions.
