title: Stop shaming people for using AI. Start organizing to prevent our obsolescence
author: Garrison Lovely
summary: The industry is engaged in a perverse quest to replace humans. We cannot cede the best tools available to the other side
body_text: I don’t need to tell you that people hate AI. The list of grievances is long: slop, cheating, bias, enfeeblement, electricity bills, environmental destruction, exploitation, theft, cybercrime, doom. But resistance to the technology has often taken the form of shaming people for personally using it, with precious little organizing against the companies building the machines. This is perplexing, given that those companies are attempting to render us obsolete. The executives may contest this framing, offering some bromides about how AI will augment human work or how we’ll simply find new jobs to do. But their clear goals are to create systems that so clearly surpass our abilities that we will have little hope of competing. OpenAI defines its north star of artificial general intelligence (AGI) as “a highly autonomous system that outperforms humans at most economically valuable work”. And the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, writes: “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans.” The industry’s ultimate ambition, what it calls AGI, is better understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. These systems would be able to do any work a human could do from a remote desk – leaving livelihoods safe to the extent a human touch is preferred, a physical presence is required, or the jobs themselves are legally protected. You may doubt that the industry will ever succeed in its perverse quest, but we should agree that it shouldn’t even be allowed to try. We should freeze frontier AI development – that is, the effort to build AGI, and only resume the work when there is strong public buy-in and broad scientific consensus that it will be done safely and controllably. But realizing this commonsense ideal will require us to get organized enough to overcome the richest industry in history. And that means changing the way we think about AI. In many corners of the internet, especially on the left, people pride themselves on never touching the stuff – while simultaneously making bold, deeply mistaken claims about its nature and capabilities. I understand the reluctance to give these companies your money, your data, your attention. But using what is increasingly an indispensable technology is not an endorsement of the industry building it, any more so than using Instagram to advocate for aggressive regulations on social media would be an endorsement of Mark Zuckerberg’s toxic empire. Moreover, the people using AI are going to outcompete the ones who don’t, bending the world in their preferred direction, while forming a deeper understanding of the technology itself. Bosses will use Claude Code to replace workers, while the leftist policy analyst Matt Bruenig is having it build a publicly accessible, automatically updating database of National Labor Relations Board decisions. If you’re serious about your mission, you should use whichever tools work best. Most importantly, anyone not seriously engaging with what the technology can already do – and might soon do – is ceding their seat at the table. Sixty-nine active members of Congress have publicly used terms like artificial superintelligence, the Singularity and AI existential risk. If certain techies are the only people willing to acknowledge that the technology’s capabilities have dramatically improved and could pose a species-level threat in the future, that’s who concerned policymakers will disproportionately listen to. The left’s lack of engagement here is a real loss. Even non-leftists recognize it. Joshua Achiam, then OpenAI’s chief futurist, declared: “The left has completely abdicated their role in this discussion. A decade from now, this will be understood on the left to have been a generational mistake; perhaps even more than merely generational.” Dean Ball, who led the authorship of Trump’s AI action plan before becoming an executive at OpenAI, declared: “Joshua is right.” You may be suspicious of political adversaries wishing you were more present in the arena, but they recognize that – on the technology’s current course – this is an all-hands-on-deck situation. Indeed, we all need to reckon with the industry’s race to replace us, but we especially need – and especially don’t have – the left. We need organizers. We need people who can’t help but think about power to teach the ones who never learned to. We need ambition. We need people who believe that better worlds are possible. The popularity of stigmatizing individual AI usage has been a gift to the industry, fracturing would-be opponents and activating our identities as consumers. BP had to pay an ad agency to popularize the “carbon footprint” to shift the blame for climate change to individuals. When we think as consumers, the goal becomes minimizing our own complicity. We should instead think as citizens: how do we democratically govern this technology in the public interest? Right now, AI is being governed by unelected, unaccountable tech billionaires, subject to intense pressures from shareholders and the Trump administration. To have any hope of changing this intolerable status quo, we’ll need to build a movement powerful enough to defeat the richest industry in history. In March, when I finished writing Obsolete, the book this piece draws from, I predicted: It won’t be easy, but the ingredients are there for a mass movement unlike any the world has ever seen. Everyone has a stake in how AI develops – a reality that will become increasingly indisputable as the technology eats ever more of the world. Since then, the dangers have appeared faster than I expected, but public awareness has grown even faster – making me feel more optimistic than ever. The AI story was never going to have a happy ending without deep and sustained engagement from the world, not just the tiny handful of people racing to build our replacements. The big question is whether we can channel this new wave of concern into effective advocacy. Personally, I think the most promising place to start is at Irreplaceable.org. (I serve on the non-profit board and am donating my share of the book’s royalties to Irreplaceable.) Founded by veterans of the climate movement, Irreplaceable aims to meet people where they are, organize their anger into political power, and build a coalition strong enough to win democratic control over AI. The non-profit is organizing a national walkout to Freeze AI on 20 October. Anyone can join one near them or host their own. I have no illusions that a day of walkouts will solve our AI problems. But it will bring together people with shared concerns, and some of them will become the friendships that sustain successful movements. Most of all, we’ll need to keep our eye on the ball: the companies trying to render us obsolete, not the friends and neighbors using their products. Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist, the author of Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – and How to Stop It (Nation Books, 29 September), and the co-host of the podcast Organize Against the Machine

title: ‘It takes a lot of work’: Deb Haaland puts addiction struggles at center of New Mexico governor bid
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: First Native American woman to serve as US cabinet secretary candid about history with alcohol as she seeks to tackle billowing public health crisis
body_text: “It clouds your mind,” recalls Deb Haaland, the trailblazing US cabinet secretary now running to be New Mexico’s next governor. “They say that, after the first drink, you lose your judgment.” Haaland developed a drinking problem after leaving high school and was twice arrested for driving under the influence. But in her 20s she decided to get sober, a battle that required personal commitment and critical external support. She went on to become a member of Congress, one of the first two Native American women ever elected to the House, and then to become the first Native American to serve as a US cabinet secretary. Now Haaland is writing her next chapter. The Democrat is taking the unusual step of putting her own 35 years of sobriety and her past struggles with alcoholism at the center of her campaign for governor in November’s midterm elections. In a statewide six-figure broadcast and digital ad buy launching ahead of the election, Haaland links her intimate experience with addiction directly to the public health crisis ravaging local communities. “I guess I’m like so many New Mexicans,” she told the Guardian by phone on Monday. “I started abusing alcohol at a young age and I was very fortunate that, at the age of 23, I recognised that I wanted to live a sober life and so I went on that journey and worked on myself for quite a while. It’s a lot of hard work to pay attention to yourself. I recognised there were so many things in my life that I needed to change.” She added: “I was fortunate to have the help of an inpatient treatment programme way back then, and so that helped me to get sober initially, but it takes a lot of work even after your head clears. I went to meetings and therapy and all of those things. I found the help that I needed and thankfully I’ve been sober for 35 years now.” Haaland, a member of the Pueblo of Laguna tribe who grew up in a military family, served in Congress from 2019 to 2021 then as interior secretary in Joe Biden’s cabinet from 2021 to 2025. She is now taking on Republican Gregg Hull, the former mayor of Rio Rancho, in the election for governor of New Mexico. In a political era in which personal vulnerability is often weaponised, her campaign is betting that voters in The Land of Enchantment – where the deadly fentanyl crisis has touched families in every corner of the state – will appreciate her candid treatment of a subject once regarded as taboo. “I look at this as a public health issue,” she emphasised. “I look at this as not somebody with a moral failing but essentially a victim of this terrible disease. We want to make sure that this is looked at as a public health issue, that we move some behavioural health dollars to this area so that people can get the help they need.” She notes that the pervasive stigma surrounding substance use disorder frequently prevents families from seeking life-saving care. “For a lot of folks it’s hard not to feel remorse and shame and all of those things,” Haaland said. But attitudes are changing. “This fentanyl crisis in our state affects even our smallest rural communities here in New Mexico. It’s hitting us in the face. People are dying from this drug, and so I feel like any shame or remorse that anyone might feel about a family member in facing this type of substance use disorder, we would put that aside and say we want people to find the help they need.” The campaign’s political ad brings these human stories into sharp focus. The spot features Jorge, a local father who announces on screen: “I am one year and one month sober.” Jorge tells viewers that while addiction leaves individuals feeling isolated, “there’s a community of people that understand completely.” The commercial also features David, a behavioural health psychologist, who highlights Haaland’s plan to force insurance providers to cover comprehensive treatment and crack down on drug-trafficking networks. Jorge closes: “With Deb, I have hope.” Haaland frames her recovery experience as the foundation for reforming New Mexico’s fractured health infrastructure. She offers sharp criticism of former Republican governor Susana Martinez, whose administration dismantled local treatment networks through unproven fraud allegations against providers. Haaland said: “She essentially destroyed our behavioural health system. She accused a lot of behavioural health professionals of fraud and so many of them went out of business and it took years for the attorney general to clear them all of any wrongdoing. It’s easy to demolish something; it’s difficult to build something back, so we’re still building back from that and I feel committed to helping people live better lives.” She proposes a structural redesign to prevent addiction being funneled into the criminal justice system. Haaland proposes creating a state office of community safety that would deploy behavioural health specialists to non-criminal emergency calls on street corners, allowing police officers to focus their resources on violent crime and drug traffickers. “A lot of these issues with substance use are not criminal in nature and so my office of community safety would ensure that we can help law enforcement to focus on crime. Drug traffickers are part of crime and then we can focus on the people who are suffering.” Haaland’s campaign trail stops have included visits to extended residential care facilities such as Grand Summit, in Albuquerque, which provides long-term housing, job assistance and financial support for recovering residents. During a recent stop, Haaland invited programme residents to walk across the street and cast their ballots alongside her. “They felt empowered and they felt like they were part of something larger than themselves,” she reflected. Haaland’s focus on community health coincides with looming federal challenges. She raised alarm over impending Medicaid rollbacks under the Trump administration, scheduled to begin on 1 January, that could strip addiction treatment coverage from vulnerable state residents. In response, New Mexico has established a Medicaid trust fund intended to provide longer-term support for the programme. She also voiced opposition to aggressive federal enforcement actions in New Mexico, calling recent ICE raids “untenable” “cruel” and “ruthless”, referencing an incident where an individual was detained in front of his 11-year-old child outside a medical clinic. “They wear masks, they don’t identify themselves.” Haaland also linked voter discontent to economic pressures such as tariffs and rising fuel costs, which hit rural New Mexicans commuting up to 100 miles round-trip for work. “I can’t say why people are coming out to vote and why people want to build this momentum in New Mexico for Democrats,” she said, “but it’s happening.”

title: ‘It’s just cruel’: US households hit by surge in electricity shutoffs amid record hot summer
author: Oliver Milman, with data visuals by Aliya Uteuova
summary: Utility disconnections were up 28% in 10 states in July 2026 – the hottest month ever recorded in the US – compared with July 2024, data shows
body_text: A record hot summer collided unhappily with rising energy costs for households across the US that struggled to the point where many were disconnected from their electricity supply, even as dangerous heat baked their communities. In July, the hottest month ever recorded in the US, 173,598 households were shut off from their electric supply by utilities across 10 states, figures provided to the Guardian show. This snapshot of American life points to a worsening problem, with the rate of electricity disconnections surging 28% compared to July 2024. Even as three separate “heat dome” events scorched the US in July, probably worsened by global heating caused by the burning of fossil fuels, many people were rationing their use of air conditioning and other appliances or lost use of them entirely by being cut off for non-payment. “We have been hearing from so many people angry and desperate because their bills have doubled – temperatures are going up and so are the costs,” said Mark Wolfe, executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), which represents the state and tribal bodies tasked with helping low-income people afford their energy bills. “People now are cutting back on food or medicine or resorting to payday lenders because you need to get the power back on. The protections in place aren’t working, it’s just cruel. Poorer people and older people aren’t turning on the AC because of the cost and when you get back-to-back heatwaves they may die because of that.” Not all states require utilities to report shut-off figures, but NEADA was able to compile data from 10 states, including New York, Georgia, California and Illinois. The true level of disconnections nationally is far higher – the federal government reported 13.4m household shut-offs in 2024, with rates particularly high in southern states including Texas, Florida, Oklahoma and Louisiana. About one in six US households are now behind on their energy bills, putting them at potential risk of being cut off, NEADA estimates. This risk varies by state – 23 states and Washington DC have rules preventing electricity disconnections when the heat rises above a certain threshold, meaning the remaining 27 states allow shut-offs regardless of the weather. “Most people do manage to find some way to pay the bill and get reconnected, but the core problem is that electricity prices are continuing to rise faster than overall inflation,” said Wolfe. The crunch of extreme heat and ballooning bills resulted in a fraught summer for many Americans. Carol Norman, 70, who lives in the town of Tom Bean, Texas, said her utility bills soared to about $600 a month, mostly due to air conditioning. She now just uses bursts of air conditioning in one room despite barely venturing outside over summer because of the heat. “A couple of times I walked to the grocery store before it got too hot but once it gets to 100F [37C] you can’t go out,” said Norman, who has custody of her grandson, aged 18. “It’s very isolating, it’s depressing. I’ve had panic attacks worrying about my electricity bill. If my daughter didn’t help out I would probably have ended up homeless or close to it.” Others asked to recount their experiences of this summer also felt life was altered because of the heat. “It’s sad because I usually love being out and about in the summer and I want to share that joy with my child but I’m scared of her overheating and suffering a heat injury,” said one man, who wished to remain anonymous, from North Carolina. Nina Johnson, from Austin, Texas, said electric bills of more than $200 take up a large portion of her monthly income of $550, meaning she has cut out pleasures such as ice-cream and lunch out with friends. “I’m eating a lot of peanut butter sandwiches,” she said. “There are food banks, but I don’t have transportation and taking the bus and walking in the heat for blocks is too much for me.” Some said their health, as well as their wallets, had suffered. Erin Hutchins, who lives in Biddeford, Maine, has previously suffered heatstroke and found this summer “unbearably hot” as her air conditioning doesn’t adequately cool her older building. “I pay over $100 a month in electricity bills, and have had to go without other necessities to do so, because I live on a fixed income,” she said. “I think having heatstroke multiple times has permanently done damage, but it’s too soon to say. I don’t feel like the same person any more though.” Electricity bills have been climbing in the US since 2021, spurred by the power demands of artificial intelligence datacenters and the cost of utilities’ grid upgrades. The severe global energy disruption caused by the US and Israeli attack on Iran earlier this year has accelerated this trend, raising power bills and adding $100bn in extra gasoline costs for Americans’ cars and trucks. Donald Trump, who has dismissed both established climate science and concerns over soaring bills as a “hoax”, has consistently rejected criticism that the ongoing Iran war has hurt Americans by pushing up the cost of oil and gas. “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation, I don’t think about anybody,” Trump said in May. “We cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon, that’s all. That’s the only thing that motivates me.” At a recent rally in North Carolina, Trump acknowledged that Americans were facing higher gasoline costs but that was a “very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done”. To compound matters, the Trump administration has also sought to completely axe the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (Liheap), which gives states money to assist people struggling with power bills. While Congress has not agreed to the scheme’s demise, the administration has been accused of freezing obligated funds. “Americans are very concerned about affordability and getting rid of low-income energy aid is a step in the wrong direction, especially since the administration has made decisions that have increased many people’s costs around energy,” said Kate Gallego, mayor of Phoenix, which has just had its second hottest summer on record. Speaking to the Guardian at New York climate week, Gallego, a Democrat, said that the Trump administration’s attempts to strangle solar and wind energy, typically the cheapest sources of new power, and prop up more expensive, and dirtier, coal has also been harmful. The Trump administration insists it is focused on cutting energy costs. “Lowering electricity prices is a top priority for President Trump, and he is aggressively unleashing reliable energy sources like coal and natural gas to reverse the catastrophic damage that Joe Biden and the Democrats did to our power grid,” said Taylor Rogers, a White House spokesperson. “Joe Biden created a grid crisis, President Trump is fixing it. If the Democrats had their way, these costly and unreliable renewable energy projects would still be failing our grid and our communities.” Yet successive presidencies have floundered in updating policies to align with a much hotter world. Even if the Liheap is saved, the program still allocates about 80% of its funding for heating assistance in winter, rather than for cooling in summer. “That’s been a problem across multiple administrations when we’re seeing so much of the country have challenges with heat,” said Gallego. “When I think about the mayors I know throughout the world, most of them have a heatwave to contend with. This is a growing and global challenge.” Some cities and states have sought to provide financial assistance to households caught in the crunch of extreme weather and rising bills. Shade from extra trees, new water features in parks and playgrounds, cooling centers and early warning systems have all also become priorities for municipalities as hazards such as heatwaves have got fiercer. “I have never known more about the weather than I do now,” admitted Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, last week as he recounted how the city has been repeatedly battered by floods since he took office. Another mayor, Michelle Wu of Boston, said this summer’s roasting temperatures were particularly challenging due to an influx of people drawn to the city for the World Cup, America’s 250th anniversary celebrations and a tall ships event. “We are past warning signs at this point, we are seeing increasing impacts from heat, flooding, air quality and livability and at the same time it has become more and more a political flashpoint to avoid talking about certain issues or words,” Wu said. “At the city level, it doesn’t matter what words are said. We just have to take action and respond to the reality our residents are living.” With a record hot summer now passed, NEADA’s attention is now turning to how the elevated costs of oil and gas will affect Americans heating their homes in the colder months. On Monday, the organization estimated that homes heated by oil, most common in the US north-east, will face bills 50% higher than last year. “Winter is just around the bend, and we are very concerned about what this means for low-income families that use heating oil,” said Wolfe, who has requested that Congress provide a further $3bn for Liheap to help defray this burden.

title: US senator blocks bill to ban Trump from demolishing Kennedy Center without Congress’s approval
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Mike Lee objected to the safeguard against the demolition of any presidential memorial Congress designates
body_text: A Republican senator has blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prevented Donald Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center without the approval of Congress. Mike Lee, of Utah, objected on Monday night when the Oregon Democrat Jeff Merkley asked the Senate to pass the Protecting Presidential Memorials Act by unanimous consent. The bill, co-written with the Alaska Republican Lisa Murkowski, would have banned the demolition of any presidential memorial designated by Congress, including the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials, unless lawmakers explicitly approved it. “First, he destroyed its programming, and now, he wants to destroy the building itself,” Merkley wrote in a statement. “All because the law says Trump can’t put his name on the building.” He called the president’s threats “straight out of the authoritarian playbook”. Murkowski, who chairs the appropriations subcommittee that funds the center, said last week that lawmakers had authorized and funded substantial renovation work, but “what was not authorized is a demolition of the Kennedy Center”. The fight over the Kennedy Center has been one of the longest legal dramas of Trump’s second term. It started when the president seized control of the center shortly after returning to office, clearing out the board and installing allies while attacking what he called “woke” programming. Trump’s handpicked board voted last December to rename the venue the Trump-Kennedy Center, but in May, federal judge Christopher Cooper ruled the change illegal and halted a planned two-year closure. On 15 September, Cooper rejected a second attempt to put Trump’s name on the building, and Trump said the $257m renovation would not go ahead unless the decision was reversed. In August, justice department lawyers warned in court that the building could decay until it had to come down, and floated an outdoor amphitheater as a replacement. A judge has since ordered 30 days’ notice of any demolition plans, and the center’s leader has told the court the building will stay standing. Lee has been closely aligned with Trump since 2020, and supported his efforts to overturn that year’s election result. More recently, he has repeatedly brought the Trump-backed Save act, which would impose voter ID and citizenship-proof requirements, to the Senate floor, and in April urged Trump to force lawmakers back to Washington to end a partial shutdown and pass it. “Democrats should join us in lowering the cost of living and securing American elections instead of wasting the Senate’s time with partisan scaremongering they haven’t even tried to run through the appropriate committee process,” Lee told the Guardian.

title: National Rally’s Jordan Bardella rails at ‘war’ on party after antisemitism claims
author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
summary: President of Marine Le Pen’s far-right party faces calls to resign over comments he allegedly wrote as a teenager
body_text: Jordan Bardella, the head of Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN), has claimed a “total war” is being waged against his party as he faces a political storm after the publication of antisemitic comments he allegedly wrote as a young party member. Bardella, who is facing calls from political opponents to resign, said on Tuesday that the report by the investigative website Mediapart was false. To a standing ovation from his party’s lawmakers and senators at a meeting in parliament, he said the report was an attempt to damage his party as Le Pen tops the polls before the 2027 presidential election. “We are seeing the beginnings of a total war, an attempt to destabilise the presidential campaign,” Bardella said. He accused Mediapart of wanting “to kill my political career” and said he would take legal action for defamation. Le Pen, at Bardella’s side, said she had “absolute confidence” in him. Journalists at Mediapart said they had independently authenticated the comments allegedly written between 2013 and 2015, including in email groups and on messaging services. Bardella was aged 17 to 18 at the time and was a member of the party that was then called the Front National. The alleged comments included “the Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so”. He is also alleged to have written “all the banks are owned by Jews”. Mediapart’s investigation has shaken Le Pen’s presidential campaign. Since Le Pen took over the party leadership in 2011, she has sought to detoxify the party image and move it away from its antisemitic past in order to increase its electoral reach. When Le Pen’s father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, co-founded the party in 1972, its ranks included former members of a Waffen SS military unit under Nazi command during the second world war. Pierre Bousquet, a former member of the Waffen SS Charlemagne division, was the party’s treasurer for its first nine years. Another early member had been in the paramilitary militia under Philippe Pétain, the leader of the puppet Vichy regime that collaborated with the Nazis and ensured the deportation of one-quarter of France’s Jewish population to concentration camps, about 76,000 people. In 1987, Jean-Marie Le Pen described the Holocaust as a “mere detail” of the second world war. In the decades that followed he was convicted more than 15 times for hate speech and contesting crimes against humanity as he repeated negationist comments, including saying the Nazi occupation was “not particularly inhumane”. Marine Le Pen, who expelled her father from the party in 2015 after he repeated antisemitic comments, has in recent years directly appealed to French Jewish voters. She said her party would protect them, describing the RN as “the best shield for our fellow French citizens of Jewish faith”. Bardella made an unprecedented visit to Israel in 2025, the first by a French far-right leader, in an attempt to demonstrate the RN’s new credentials. In 2023, Bardella told a TV interviewer he did not think Jean-Marie Le Pen was antisemitic, before backtracking on his comments after criticism. The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, responding to the Mediapart investigation, wrote on social media: “To all those with a short memory: antisemitism isn’t an accident in the RN, it’s that party’s history. That’s the real face of the far right.” Aurore Bergé, the minister for equality and against discrimination, said the “antisemitic and conspiracy theory” content of the alleged messages “reminds those who might have forgotten the nature of the far right”. Raphaël Glucksmann, a candidate in the Socialist presidential primary, wrote on social media that no public relations exercise would fundamentally change the RN. “Let us never forget that they all joined a party founded by antisemitic fanatics and out-and-out racists,” he said. Yonathan Arfi, of the CRIF, the umbrella group of French Jewish organisations, told France Culture radio he was “stupefied by the virulence of the antisemitic comments” allegedly made by Bardella. He said that if true, the comments undermined the RN’s claims to have detoxified its image. He asked: “How could a political party leader, having made such sickening comments, reach such a high position in a party that claims to have changed and now fights against the hatred of Jews?” The Green leader, Marine Tondelier, said Bardella, an MEP, should resign from all his political positions. She said: “The man who presents himself today as the biggest defender of Jews … is in reality an obsessional antisemite.”

title: The Maga cult is finally crumbling
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: With the midterms looming, and after the Epstein files and the war on Iran, Trump superfans are losing faith in their lame duck president, writes Arwa Mahdawi
body_text: It took a dead child sex offender and a disastrous war to do it, but it looks as though the Maga faithful are slowly beginning to lose confidence in their dear leader. As Donald Trump’s approval ratings drop to record lows, some of his most fervent supporters are turning on him. See, as exhibit one, Trisha Hope, who was once a proud member of the Front Row Joes, a group of Trump superfans who follow the president to rallies around the country. They have custom-made T-shirts! They have branded baseball caps! They even have the attention of Trump himself, who frequently shouts out the group. He did once accidentally call them the “front row Jacks and Joes”, but who can expect a man of his calibre to pay attention to the plebs, eh? During Trump’s first impeachment, in 2019, Hope stationed herself in Washington DC for weeks, trying to drum up support for the president. But she’s not doing that again. In an interview with Politico published on Monday, Hope declared: “If we do lose the midterms and [Trump] is impeached again, I will be walking the halls of Congress in support of that impeachment.” What caused this change of heart? Hope cites the Iran war and the Epstein files as significant factors. So too does Rick Frazier, another defector from the Front Row Joes interviewed by Politico. “Epstein crimes and feeding the industrial military complex … those are big nos for me,” Frazier said. Hope and Frazier are just two people with limited influence, but there’s another, much more powerful, Joe who has soured on Trump. Earlier this month the podcaster Joe Rogan, whose endorsement of Trump in 2024 is widely credited with helping him win the election, distanced himself from the president and his “rabid” supporters. “Trump supporters are fucking nuts, man,” Rogan said on his podcast. In the same episode, Rogan admitted that “I did kind of help Trump”, but insisted it was because he thought he’d drain the swamp. “Obviously, it’s not been ideal in that regard,” Rogan added. It’s very satisfying to watch people wake up to the fact that the convicted felon in the White House is out for himself and nobody else. But Trump is a lame duck now. With the end of his very lucrative reign in sight, does it really matter that people like Hope are calling him “a fraud and liar”? In the long term, the answer to that question is complicated. But growing disgust with the president certainly matters for the November midterm elections. Trump has asked voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and many have taken that advice to heart. A recent PBS News/NPR/Marist poll found that 45% of voters overall said their largest motivating factor for the midterms was voting against Trump. While he still has a loyal following, the midterms are likely to be a rebuke to his presidency, with Democrats now on a path to flipping the Senate as well as retaking the House. Trump’s desperate gimmicks and grandiose assurances aren’t landing the way they used to. This month, the president promised a $5,000 (£3,775) “Trump dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress after the midterms. According to one poll, only 13% of voters believed him. If Trump is worried about the midterms – and the possibility of a third impeachment that comes with a Democratic victory – he’s not letting it show. But Republicans more broadly are clearly stressed, not just about the midterms, but also about what sort of trouble they may be in when Trump 2.0 comes to an end. “After the first Trump administration, my family spent money we did not have on lawyers because of multiple partisan Democrat-led investigations into President Trump,” Katie Miller, the podcasting wife of Trump’s right-hand man, Stephen Miller, tweeted earlier this month. “You can’t convince me Democrats won’t do this again.” I hope they do. And this time I hope they do it properly, so that Trump and his enablers are at last held accountable. People who are finally leaving the Maga cult are angry at Trump, certainly, but they’re also angry at a world in which the powerful seem to get away with everything. To stop that anger from propelling another Trump-like figure into the White House, there needs to be a reckoning with the systems that created him. Let’s make Maga’s legal bills high again. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘You make me want to throw up’: Republicans attack ex-special counsel Jack Smith at Senate hearing
author: Ariana Baio
summary: GOP senators lash out on Smith, who led criminal cases against Trump, with invective and inaccurate information
body_text: Jack Smith, the former special counsel who led two criminal cases against Donald Trump in 2023, faced attacks from Republicans in a wide-ranging hearing on Tuesday that included a basketball mix-up, a reference to the tooth fairy and accusations of perjury. In the Senate judiciary committee hearing on Tuesday, the Republican senator Eric Schmitt, of Missouri, raised perjury allegations against Smith, seemingly over a mix-up about the Atlanta Hawks and University of Iowa Hawkeyes basketball teams. Schmitt, who called Smith a “dirtbag”, claimed the prosecutor went to Atlanta to attend a Hawks game on 3 February 2024, and insinuated Smith may have met with Fani Willis, the former Fulton county district attorney who brought state charges against Trump. But Smith denied ever attending an Atlanta Hawks game. He later clarified that he attended a University of Iowa Hawkeyes game in Maryland to watch Caitlin Clark play. Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic senator of Minnesota, admonished Schmitt for presenting the claim as evidence and accusing Schmitt of lying. “I would just say, for a US senator to have false information, and imply, based on a confusion about the name of a team … that you were in another city, that you were somehow involved, that day, in what was happening in Georgia, and then call you a ‘dirtbag’, is something that deserves an apology,” Klobuchar said. The Guardian has asked Schmitt’s office for comment. The unusual exchange between Schmitt and Smith became a highlight of the hearing on social media. Smith also testified to the Senate judiciary committee to defend his handling of two federal investigations into Trump – one related to efforts to overturn the 2020 election and the other regarding Trump’s mishandling of classified documents. Both cases were dismissed before going to trial. Republicans have accused Smith of bringing the investigations to undermine Trump and targeting Republicans in the process – including by subpoenaing phone records from members of Congress. Smith has defended his practices, saying the subpoenas were necessary to collect evidence that Trump called members of Congress to try to delay the certification of the 2020 presidential election. But Tuesday’s hearing was also defined by other tense exchanges between Republican senators and Smith. The Republican John Kennedy, of Louisiana, appeared frustrated after raising accusations that Joe Biden or his White House staff told Merrick Garland, the then attorney general, to prosecute Trump – an allegation with no public evidence. Smith said he did not know about conversations between Biden and Garland regarding the subject. “Do you believe in the Tooth Fairy?” Kennedy asked Smith. “How about the Easter Bunny?” The question elicited a response from Smith: “I no longer believe in the Easter Bunny.” At one point, Kennedy told Smith: “You make me want to throw up in my mouth.” Ted Cruz, a Republican senator from Texas who became increasingly angry while talking about Smith subpoenaing congressional members’ phone records, told Smith: “Javert from Les Mis would look at you with astonishment.” Cruz insinuated that Smith used his position as a special counsel to target Republicans by requesting records from the Republican National Committee and other conservative lawmakers. Darline Graham, the senator from South Carolina, used her time during the hearing to accuse Smith of “trying to bully” her brother, the late senator Lindsey Graham, and causing him stress with subpoenas. But Smith pushed back on Darline Graham’s assertion. “I believe your brother was a patriotic public servant. He was not a target of our investigation, and in fact he likely would have been a witness in our case,” Smith replied, adding that Lindsey Graham did not believe the 2020 election was stolen. Democrats, meanwhile, used Tuesday’s hearing to highlight the 6 January 2021 attack on the US Capitol and accused Trump of inciting the violent mob with false claims of election fraud during the 2020 presidential election. Cory Booker, the senator from New Jersey, declared the hearing “a farce”. Booker and Delaware’s Chris Coons highlighted that the current administration had fired justice department staffers who worked on Smith’s team. Despite the partisan divide over Smith’s appointment and prosecutions, Smith said he maintained a nonpartisan approach to the investigations into Trump and that his team had compiled enough evidence to prosecute the president. “If asked whether to prosecute a former president today, based on the same facts, I would do so regardless of whether that president was a Republican or a Democrat,” Smith said in his opening statement.

title: Morning Mail: Coalition’s lowest-ever poll rating; homeowners reel after rate hike; and a Socceroos thriller
author: Martin Farrer
summary: Our latest Essential poll shows slump to 22% of primary vote amid immigration debate; mortgage holders fear mounting costs after RBA hike
body_text: Morning everyone. Weeks of discussion about tougher immigration rules appears to have damaged rather than benefited the opposition as our latest Essential poll shows Angus Taylor’s Coalition languishing on its lowest-ever primary vote. Senior Greens figures say the party’s new leader will have to take the fight to the government on fossil fuel expansion, we talk to homeowners who fear being squeezed by the latest interest rate hike, the Socceroos go down fighting against Brazil, and Thunderbirds are go, again. Australia Greens gambit | The former Greens leader Adam Bandt says the party’s new leadership team, which could be chosen as early as today, will face mounting pressure from grassroots members to block the Labor government from approving any new coal and gas projects “by whatever means”. Exclusive | The Coalition has failed to capitalise on growing criticism of the Albanese Labor government, with the opposition stuck at its lowest-ever primary vote of 22% in the Guardian Essential poll – down four points from last month despite a tough few weeks for the prime minister. Imam ‘concerns’ | Australia’s peak body for imams says it is “deeply concerned” about reports a Melbourne-based Islamic preacher called for followers to “take up arms against his enemies” and not take “Jews and the Christians for friends”. ‘Credible risks’ | The government has conceded it implemented the “world-leading” under-16s social media ban before there was scientific consensus on the link between mental health harms and social media use, but argued the “credible risks” about addictive behaviours and anxiety justify the policy. ‘Theatre of the absurd’ | After 10 weeks and allegations likened to a “three-tentacled octopus”, the NSW anti-corruption hearings into political donations have finished. Penry Buckley looks at what has been achieved. World Burnham pledge | Andy Burnham has promised a new “long-term” relationship with the EU in an emotional UK Labour conference speech in which he also confirmed the end of guaranteed above-inflation increases for state pensions and floated the possibility of electoral reform. French clashes | French teenagers blockading their schools in protest at class sizes, teacher shortages and long timetables have clashed with police, as politicians traded verbal blows over how to respond. Saudi price | Saudi Arabia is being urged to reconcile with the United Arab Emirates over Yemen as the price Riyadh must pay to form a military alliance capable of driving the Houthis back. Bill blocker | A Republican senator has blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prevented Donald Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center without the approval of Congress. ‘Love letter’ | A JMW Turner painting of Rome that has been described as his “great love letter” to the city and has fleetingly returned there after almost 200 years is expected to set a new record when it goes up for sale in December. Full Story Inside the trial of former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon Matilda Boseley speaks to reporter Kat Wong to unpack the evidence so far in the murder trial of former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon. In-depth The latest increase in interest rates will pile financial pressure on households across Australia. Sydney man Shane McClymont tells Achol Arok he’s worried he can’t afford his son’s upcoming birthday dinner, while Ann Mureithi, a mother of two from Pakenham, south-east of Melbourne, says she feels like “there’s a threat waiting for me”. Not the news More than 60 years after the first episodes were made, Thunderbirds remains an incomparable piece of TV, writes Paul F Verhoeven, with the Tracy brothers’ famous futuristic vehicles, Parker and Lady Penelope, and a bewildering array of sets and plots. Sport Football | Australia lost its second friendly against Brazil 4-2 in Brisbane last night but the scoreline masks the ups and downs of an open and often fiery encounter that saw the Socceroos leading 2-1 before being pegged back. There’s Nations League action under way in Europe, including Czechia v England and Spain v Croatia. NRL | Newcastle’s run to the grand final is a great moment for their veterans like Tyson Frizell and youngsters like Fletcher Sharpe, writes Jack Snape. Premier League | Manchester City’s chief executive has said the guilty verdicts against the club for breaches of financial rules – confirmed overnight – are based on a “conspiracy theory”. Wayne Rooney says City should not be stripped of its titles, but Jonathan Liew thinks the case shows how the mega-rich think they can act with impunity. Media roundup The Sydney Morning Herald claims researchers at Monash was discovered a new form of antibiotic resistance which could be the “ultimate superbug”. Closed theatres and empty beds are among the problems plaguing Melbourne’s new $1.5bn hospital in Footscray, according to the Age. A Knights rookie, Diesel Hagan, could become the first player in NRL history to make his debut in a grand final, the Newcastle Herald claims. Grampians Health doctors will strike again tomorrow over unsustainable working hours, fatigue and threat to patient safety, the Ballarat Courier reports. title: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Nine American citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in occupied West Bank since 2022
body_text: The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years. The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children. The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor. Van Hollen was able to force the vote under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, a law that lets senators demand human rights reports on countries receiving US military aid. The measure drew 24 Democratic sponsors, including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Tim Kaine of Virginia and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee. “While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” Van Hollen said in a statement after the vote. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.” Nine Americans have been killed in the occupied West Bank since 2022. The most recent include Sayfollah Musallet, a 20-year-old from Tampa, Florida, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025 while visiting family in the village of Sinjil. His family said the settlers surrounded him for more than three hours and blocked an ambulance from reaching him as he tried to protect their land. Weeks later, Khamis Ayyad, a 40-year-old father of five from Cicero, Illinois, died of smoke inhalation after settlers set fire to cars and homes in the village of Silwad. Two other Americans, both 17, Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Khdour, were shot dead in separate incidents in early 2024. Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi, a 26-year-old raised in Seattle, was shot in the head by Israeli troops, and Amer Rabee, a 14-year-old from New Jersey, was shot 11 times, according to Van Hollen. The victim list also includes the journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, killed in 2022, and Omar Assad, an elderly man who died after Israeli soldiers bound and gagged him. Van Hollen said none of the cases has ended in accountability, from either the Israeli or US government, and he places the blame largely on Republican senators who continue to vote against it. “If the killing of nine Americans does not justify a report from our own state department, I would ask my colleagues: what would?” the Maryland Democrat said in a floor speech. “How many more Americans must be killed before the executive branch does its job? These families deserve answers.” In August, 45 Democratic senators signed a letter to Benjamin Netanyahu urging him to act to protect Americans in the West Bank. The vote comes amid what human rights groups describe as rising settler violence. Human Rights Watch in August reported that settler attacks, together with a rapid expansion of settlements, had fully or partly displaced 107 Palestinian communities, about 5,900 people, since January 2023. The group cited UN figures showing more Palestinians were displaced in the first four months of 2026 than in all of 2025. A UN report from March covering the 12 months up to October 2025 documented 1,732 settler attacks causing injuries or property damage, and determined that Israel’s settlement expansion had forced more than 36,000 Palestinians from their homes. Many of the Democrats, who have historically been in lockstep with Israel, have now shifted over the last few years. When Sanders first forced a Senate vote on blocking arms sales to Israel in November 2024, 18 senators backed him. Then, in April of this year, 40 of the 47 Democrats voted to block a $295m sale of bulldozers to Israel, which Sanders argued would be used to demolish homes in the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon. Another 36 voted to block a $152m sale of 1,000lb bombs. The measures failed because every Republican voted against them.

title: David Shoebridge says ‘we’re here to replace Labor’ in first remarks after being elected new Greens leader
author: Krishani Dhanji, Tom McIlroy and Josh Butler
summary: Shoebridge, a senator from New South Wales and former upper house state MP, won the role over Mehreen Faruqi and Sarah Hanson-Young
body_text: David Shoebridge has declared he wants the Greens to replace Labor and has accused the government of creating the circumstances for One Nation’s rise in his first remarks after being elected the Greens’ federal leader. The party’s 10 senators and lone MP met to decide the new leadership team during a pre-planned two-day retreat in Sydney, after the shock resignation of Larissa Waters on Monday due to ill health. The leadership became a three-way race after Shoebridge announced his run on Wednesday morning. The South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Young had declared her candidacy on Tuesday, followed by a joint ticket of New South Wales senator and former deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi and Tasmanian senator Nick McKim. Shoebridge was announced as leader with Steph Hodgins-May as his deputy on Wednesday. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Speaking to reporters, Shoebridge paid tribute to Waters, and said she rose to the occasion after taking the leadership in challenging circumstances. “This is an extraordinary moment in politics and we can all feel it. We can feel that politics as usual is not providing the answers that people are desperately calling for now,” Shoebridge said. “We know the Greens need to seize this moment because politics demands it of us … Labor has created the circumstances for One Nation, and Labor is not the answer. The Greens, the progressive alternative, we’re here to beat down One Nation, and we’re here to replace Labor and return hope and faith to politics.” Shoebridge won the leadership on primaries with six votes, with Faruqi receiving three votes and Hanson-Young receiving two. After preferences, Shoebridge won seven votes to four. The deputy leadership was also contested. Hodgins-May won six votes on primaries, while Tasmanian senator Vanessa Bleyer, who recently replaced Peter Whish-Wilson, received three votes, and Jordon Steele-John received two. Hanson-Young was elected uncontested as Greens manager of business while Penny Allman-Payne was elected uncontested as party chair. Shoebridge entered federal parliament in 2022, after more than a decade in NSW state politics. He holds the Greens’ defence and foreign affairs portfolios, and is a forceful presence in parliamentary debates, on social media and in Senate estimates hearings. Before politics, he was a corporate lawyer and then became a barrister specialising in employment law, and at one point was a Labor branch member in Sydney’s inner west. In the early 2000s he met the hard-left Greens MP Lee Rhiannon, who went on to become his mentor. ‘People are desperate for material change’ Shoebridge said voters wanted to see some drastic political changes, rather than gradual reform. “That is the dead politics of Labor, it’s the dead politics of the Coalition, and when you really test it, it’s the dead politics of One Nation,” he said. “People are desperate for material change. They don’t want another meaningless message being delivered by some Labor hack that they know isn’t going to change their lives. They want to take on the vested interests.” Hodgins-May is one of the Greens’ newest members, and entered parliament in May 2024, filling a casual vacancy created by Janet Rice’s retirement. In a statement on social media, Faruqi said she was disappointed by the result. “Globally, people are struggling against genocide, wars, surging fascism and the twin crises of capitalism making working life too expensive and climate breakdown threatening our future,” she said. “This struggle calls for bold politics and radical action. I did not stand again for deputy leader today because, on reflection, I believe I can best play my part in that action outside the constraints of the leadership team.” Under Waters, the Greens supported the government to pass nature laws, including the establishment of a federal environment watchdog, and more recently supported Labor’s changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax. The Greens also teamed up with the Coalition and crossbench in the Senate to force Labor to drop a controversial $5,000 cap for veterans to access allied health services, and compelled the government to bring forward 20,000 aged care beds. Waters said she would take some medical leave before returning to the Senate. “It’s with great sadness that I’m not able to continue in that role due to my health getting worse. I hope to be OK but I need to look after myself to do that. I’m proud that the party is polling higher than ever before amidst the surge to the rightwing forces of politics,” Waters said. Shoebridge will come under pressure to bring a more forceful approach to the job, amid frustrations with Waters’ more moderate style, and the party’s inability to exploit growing moves by voters away from Labor and the Coalition. The former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather on Tuesday called for the party’s membership to get a vote in the leadership race. In her statement, Faruqi said she had also long advocated for a membership vote.

title: Economic growth and democratic decline: the ‘cotton king’ who reshaped Benin
author: Eromo Egbejule in Cotonou and Porto Novo
summary: Patrice Talon has transformed the west African country’s economy and infrastructure at the expense of political freedom
body_text: In recent years, a building boom has reshaped Benin’s largest city, Cotonou, and a shiny new coastal road has reduced journey times to Ouidah, the west African country’s spiritual and cultural capital. In the last decade, Benin’s annual GDP has grown from 3% to 6%, a regional high, and an industrial zone has been launched north-west of Cotonou to help industrialise the relatively small nation’s largely informal economy. “Benin is now looking like a paradise,” said Savossou Stanislas, a 40-year-old tyre repairer in the official capital, Porto-Novo. The rapid infrastructural development has been overseen by Patrice Talon, the president from 2016 till this May. For years, Benin was so content being in the shadow of Nigeria, a neighbour about eight times its size and with about 16 times its population, that Talon’s predecessor, Thomas Boni Yayi, once quipped during a visit to Abuja that “Benin is the 37th state of Nigeria”. Talon, who also enjoys good relations with Nigeria and called on it to help quell an attempted coup d’etat in December, chose a different path: to engineer enough growth for Benin to be recognised in its own right. The Kagame model Widely believed to be Benin’s richest person, Talon, known as “the cotton king”, made his name in agriculture but diversified into banking and hospitality. Before becoming president, he had financed the campaigns of Yayi and Yayi’s predecessor, Mathieu Kérékou. Critics say his development agenda has come at a severe cost: once held up as a poster child for democratic transition in west Africa, Benin has also undergone democratic decline since Talon took power. In many respects, Talon modelled his governance style on the leader of another relatively small African country: Paul Kagame. The archetypal “benevolent strongman”, Rwanda’s de facto leader since 1994 has also combined repression with policies aimed at economic and social transformation. In time, the two men became allies and Talon even appointed two former Rwandan officials to head sensitive Beninese government agencies. Benin has also sought the east African nation’s help in countering a growing insurgency along the border with Nigeria. By the end of Talon’s first term, strict new election laws and heavy registration fees had purged a lot of the opposition from parliament. In 2019, the government shut down the internet during a parliamentary election as people protested against the changes. The judiciary was co-opted to muzzle dissent, resulting in the targeting of several dozen former allies and dissidents, including the opposition leader Reckya Madougou, who is in prison on charges of “undermining the state”, and the journalist Hugues Comlan Sossoukpé. In April 2021, a month after Madougou’s arrest, Essowé Batamoussi, a judge at the court for the repression of economic offences and terrorism, resigned his post and fled to France to seek asylum. “There was no justice in her [Madougou’s] case,” Batamoussi said. “We received an empty file and a threat: if we did not put her in jail, we were in danger.” Last November, it became apparent how deeply Talon had control of every major aspect of life in Benin. A controversial constitutional amendment, the second of his tenure, elongated the presidential term from five years to seven and introduced thresholds that kept opposition parties outside parliament. It also created a new senate, whose members are all appointed by government rather than elected. Within a month of parliament approving the amendment, mutineers led by a former commander of the national guard attempted a coup, citing Talon’s authoritarianism and inability to tackle rising insecurity. Only one opposition candidate was approved to stand in April’s presidential election, which was won by Talon’s hand-picked successor, Romuald Wadagni, with more than 94% of the vote. In August, Talon himself returned to centre stage as president of the senate. Morgan Assogba, a Cotonou-based geopolitical analyst, described Talon as a “gigantic political actor with a good understanding of how politics works in Benin”, who had reshaped the political arena to suit his economic development drive. For Guillaume Moumouni, a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Abomey-Calavi, Talon’s dual policies of constitutional change and development constituted a “carrot and stick” approach to governing, aimed at ensuring the political environment did not jeopardise his economic objectives. In time, however, he added, there was “less carrot and more stick” as freedoms were increasingly suppressed. What price progress? During his campaign for the April election, Wadagni vowed to tackle extreme poverty, a tacit admission that economic growth had not been to the benefit of all Beninese. The minimum monthly wage increased from 40,000 CFA francs to 52,000 CFA francs (£52-£68) in January 2023, but many still earn far less. In recent years, rent and electricity tariffs have also risen by at least 15%, while the price of fuel has almost doubled. “With the upcoming school term, we don’t know how we’ll manage,” said Stanislas, the tyre repairer, who has four children of school age. Most of the development has been in Cotonou and Ouidah, Talon’s home town. Opposition figures have said there has been a lack of transparency in some of those projects, while civil society groups said some were awarded to entities linked to Talon’s political allies and business network. According to a 2023 report by Amnesty International, four development projects resulted in mass forced evictions that affected at least 6,000 people. The communication ministry was approached for comment. Moumouni said economically Talon’s vision had brought net progress. “People are not gaining or enjoying much more in terms of cash, but they are enjoying [progress] in terms of social infrastructure,” he said. “There’s room for improvement for sure but compared to 10 or 15 years ago, there is quite a huge difference.” Eugène Azatassou, the vice-president of the opposition Democrats party, feels differently. “Development cannot be limited to roads and buildings,” he said. “It must also be measured by the quality of democracy, purchasing power, employment, security, improvement of living conditions … when a power continuously modifies political and electoral rules in order to conserve control of institutions, we have the right to ask ourselves if we are facing [only] a facade of development.”

title: ‘We’re afraid of dying’: Brazilian news site will not cover upcoming elections after threats
author: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
summary: Co-founder of independent website Tapajós de Fato said decision was made to protect journalists and their families
body_text: Four years ago, during Brazil’s last presidential election, the tyres were slashed on the pickup truck used for reporting by Tapajós de Fato, an independent journalism website in the Brazilian Amazon. Days later, a cat’s severed head was left next to the car park, alongside a note bearing the name of one of the site’s founders, Marcos Wesley Pedroso, and a warning that he would be next. Last July, security cameras outside Pedroso’s house showed cyclists circling the block, whistling and filming his car until, minutes later, another car crashed into it. “I believe they wanted me to come outside so they could ambush me,” said Pedroso. Police have not identified those responsible or established whether the cases are connected, but Pedroso sees them as part of a wider series of threats linked to Tapajós de Fato’s reporting on environmental and Indigenous rights violations, land disputes, and pesticide contamination in the Amazonian state of Pará. As a result, the site’s team decided not to cover this year’s elections – which will choose the next president, state governors, members of the lower house and part of the senate, with the first round on 4 October. “We’re afraid of dying and of putting our families’ safety at risk,” said Pedroso. He added that the site, whose name refers to the 1,238-mile-long (1,992km) Tapajós River, would remain online and continue covering environmental issues, but would avoid stories about the election. News of violence around election time is not uncommon: in 2022 a man was struck on the head with a piece of wood after saying he did not support the far-right incumbent Jair Bolsonaro’s re-election bid. Journalism and free-expression organisations in Brazil see Tapajós de Fato’s decision, first reported by a network of independent Amazonian media outlets, as a serious example of the consequences of attacks against journalists during the electoral period. “It reflects the different forms of attempted censorship and silencing that journalists have to face in Brazil,” said Letícia Kleim, legal coordinator at the Brazilian Association of Investigative Journalism. “Silencing the message by silencing the messenger affects not just their community, but democracy as a whole, which will no longer receive the valuable information they were providing by reporting on the Amazon from within the region.” Her association is part of a coalition that recorded 4,400 online attacks against journalists, media outlets and the press on X and Instagram between 30 August and 12 September alone, an increase of 67% compared with the previous two weeks. Because the election campaign was still under way, Kleim said it was not yet possible to know whether there had been more attacks than in the previous election, although she stressed that the context four years ago was particularly hostile because of the then president Bolsonaro, who routinely attacked the media and made threatening remarks to reporters such as: “I’d like to smash your mouth.” Kleim said: “His government made discrediting the press a priority at times; his family, supporters and politicians close to him embraced that agenda, and many continue with it.” Bolsonaro is now unable to run because he is under house arrest serving a sentence for attempting a coup after losing the 2022 election, but one of his sons, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, is in a technical tie in the polls with the incumbent, the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. “The possibility of Flávio being elected worries me enormously,” said Pedroso. He said reporting was even more dangerous four years ago, particularly in the Amazon – where Bolsonaro’s anti-environmental and anti-Indigenous policies led to soaring deforestation, a gold rush into Indigenous lands and increased criminal activity. In 2022, the British journalist Dom Phillips, who reported for the Guardian from Brazil, and the Brazilian Indigenous expert Bruno Pereira were ambushed and killed in the Amazon by men accused of links to a transnational criminal network exploiting an Indigenous territory. The Amazon-based NGO Comitê Chico Mendes, named after the environmentalist murdered in 1988, issued a statement deploring the threats against Tapajós de Fato: “We cannot normalise an Amazon where fear determines what can and cannot be reported.” Pedroso said that Tapajós de Fato had decided to make the threats public after years of reporting them to the authorities without any investigation producing results. “Deciding not to cover the elections was not easy,” he said. “With a great deal of humility and responsibility, I know the role we play in educating and informing many people in the communities around us, but there was no other way. In the end, those are the people who lose out.”

title: A fake image of a Georgia mayor kissing a person went viral. Can US voters trust everything they see?
author: George Chidi
summary: Deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence have become a point of deep concern for legislators, advocates and the public
body_text: An image of Bianca Motley Broom, the mayor of College Park, Georgia, kissing a man who was not her husband in a bar spread far and wide on Facebook. The fact that it was fake is spreading faster, now, but only after it had been seen by thousands of people. “I think this is a sad commentary about where we are in our democracy, and where we are in our political discourse,” Motley Broom said. “It also seeks to reinforce really tired stereotypes about women in leadership.” Six years ago, when Motley Broom first took office in the Atlanta suburb, a political enemy might have needed at least rudimentary skill with image-editing software to forge an image of a politician in a compromising position. Today, all that is required is a computer and a prompt for an AI image generator. The threat of deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence has become a point of deep concern for legislators, advocates and the public. A poll taken in mid-June by Rad Campaign, a digital marketing agency, and Women Who Tech, an advocacy organization for female entrepreneurs, showed that about 71% of respondents worry about AI-generated deepfakes and disinformation affecting elections, while two in three respondents said they were concerned about AI being used to sexualize women. “The findings show that Americans are more concerned about AI’s use in deepfakes, election disinformation, and the sexualization of women and children than its impact on jobs or the economy,” said Allyson Kapin, founder of the Rad Campaign and co-founder of Women Who Tech. The Trump administration has a penchant for deploying AI imagery. In January, the White House’s official account on the social media platform X posted a digitally altered image of Nekima Levy Armstrong, who had been arrested in connection with a demonstration that disrupted church services in St Paul, Minnesota. A picture of her calmly being escorted by a DHS agent was altered so that she appeared to be crying, and her skin had been darkened. Kaelan Dorr, the White House deputy communications director, later described the image as a “meme”. Fake images of Zohran Mamdami, New York’s mayor, also began circulating from a “parody” account on X in February, falsely depicting him and his mother in the company of the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. Using Google’s SynthID tool, Reuters debunked the images, but not before other accounts had recirculated them as authentic, fueling conspiracy theories. Despite significant apprehension around the potential economic consequences of AI, concern about deepfake images being used to sexualize women or children, or to influence elections, outstrips concern about AI affecting jobs by about three to one, Kapin said. “The public is deeply concerned,” she said. Fact from fiction Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democratic senator, said in a video posted to Facebook that deepfake images had been circulating online falsely depicting him with health problems, with an armful of grandchildren he does not have – and with a full head of hair, which he said was funny, if problematic. “As these tools become increasingly powerful, it will get harder and harder to distinguish fact from fiction, and there are already bad actors out there, who are doing everything they can to divide us and confuse us,” Warnock said. “This has huge implications for our democracy. What if hours before an election, someone created a page with AI-generated images, fake stories about the candidates – how will voters know what’s true, and what’s not true?” Warnock is among a group of Senate Democrats who have been war-gaming political responses to possible election interference scenarios. Chief among those scenarios: disinformation driven by fabricated images or videos circulated through social media. The outgoing US senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, offered a bill last week requiring AI firms to install a “kill switch” for rogue AI. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky blocked Kennedy’s bill, describing the effort as premature without additional industry input. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic House minority leader, said in an interview earlier this month on SiriusXM that government should move “urgently” on AI regulations, broadly, calling for “guardrails to protect the American people from bad actors and bad behavior”, adding: “It should be a high priority.” Jeffries noted that Republicans attempted to pass legislation pre-empting states from regulating AI last year, as part of the omnibus One Big Beautiful Bill. The amendment failed on a 99-1 vote in the Senate. State legislatures are also wrestling with AI regulation amid a widespread, bipartisan public backlash. Some states have legislation like Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act – the Elvis Act – which protects politicians and residents alike from AI voice cloning and digital likeness replication, using the state’s robust right-of-publicity protections that are a product of Nashville’s recording industry. Clear disclaimers are legally required in most states when a political campaign uses AI to manipulate the speeches, appearances or actions of officials or candidates. Georgia is not one of them. While legislators in Georgia began debating deepfake protections in bills proposed in 2024 and 2025, they have not yet enacted legislation. Motley Broom said she believed she was targeted by political opponents who objected to her role as a past president of the Georgia Municipal Association. “I have worked for my city to try to be the best advocate I can be on behalf of College Park,” Motley Broom said. “And I certainly won’t be deterred by internet trolls who think this carries weight.” While she could consider legal action under existing defamation law in Georgia, Motley Broom paused for a moment when asked what legislators should be doing about this. The first amendment protection for speech has to be considered, she said. “These types of attacks should not be without consequences,” she said. “I hope that lawmakers can address this in a way that balances not only first amendment protections, but the right of an individual not to have completely false accusations being levied. And I’m really hopeful that … lawmakers on the state and federal level can think about that and think about it carefully, because this is the tip of the iceberg.”
