title: Clay Travis: inside the Maga permadad’s world of sports bros, trans panic and mortgages
author: Aaron Timms
summary: The rightwing media mogul has lost ground to the likes of Pat McAfee and Joe Rogan. He’s hoping his new venture can recapture some headway
body_text: When Maga media blowhard Clay Travis offered $2m to Colin Kaepernick last week to appear on the daily talkshow he hosts with former CIA analyst Buck Sexton, it represented the culmination of a years-long obsession on the right with the onetime NFL star. In Travis’s telling of history, Kaepernick taking a knee during the 2016 NFL season was the event that catalyzed professional sports into the era of “woke” excess from which, he claims, it has been struggling to recover ever since. But more than simply confirming the right’s longstanding villainization of Kaepernick, Travis’s offer was also a smarmy bid for publicity for his new media venture, Sport & State. Sport & State, which launched in August, is Travis’s bid to get back to his roots as a media mogul who sold the wildly popular Outkick to Fox Sports for a rumored $100m, and reclaim some of the cultural territory lost to fellow sports bros and Magagitators like Pat McAfee, Joe Rogan, Tucker Carlson and Ben Shapiro. But if there’s one thing Sport & State won’t be doing, it’s engaging with anyone beyond the Magaverse. There has been no response from Kaepernick since Travis made his “offer” of $2m to charity in exchange for an interview, which suggests he understands that it was extended more in a spirit of trolling buffoonery than sincerity. No one associated with the left or progressive politics ever appears on Travis’s shows, for the simple reason that they are designed purely for the right to talk to itself. (Some would say the same could be said of the left, although the disregard for dissenting perspectives in the Magasphere seems way more extreme.) More than it heralds a renewal of Travis’s career or an injection of fresh energy into the Trumpist mediasphere, Sport & State is a case study in the stagnation that has taken hold on the right as Donald Trump stares down the barrel of defeat in November’s midterm elections. Having spent the better part of the past two months listening to the Clay Travis & Buck Sexton Show (which runs from noon to 3pm ET every weekday) and the Clay Travis Show (3-4pm), I can say with confidence that there are, in essence, only 11 topics a given day’s programming on Sport & State will cover: college football gambling picks; Trumpworld figures who are friends with Travis and Sexton; the wonderful job that these figures are doing in power (sometimes mixed with the preceding theme: “Our friend Kash, who is truly our friend, Clay and I are both buddies with him, he’s a good man,” Sexton affirmed on a recent episode); the low levels of testosterone apparently common among white males who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 (“white dudes for Kamala” is perhaps the gravest slur on the Clay Travis Show); trans women in professional sport (I haven’t calculated this precisely but at a guess I’d say this accounts for 20% to 50% of the discussion on any show that Travis hosts, even as the number of actual trans women competing in professional American sports remains exactly zero and there are probably fewer than 10 trans athletes in total in college sports); crime in America’s cities (in recent weeks the fixation has been Lindsay Clancy, but it’s liable to switch at any moment to Iryna Zarutska, Luigi Mangione, Charlie Kirk, Iryna Zarutska, or whatever murder happens to have taken place on that particular day in New York City); the problem with women (in summary: they are women); the fact that Travis and Sexton are both family men with wives and children; the fact that Travis has a law degree from Vanderbilt University; the fact that Travis studied law at Vanderbilt after he was rejected by Stanford (“I wanted to go to Stanford Law School, they didn’t want me, I went to Vanderbilt instead – I’ve now made a $10m donation to Vanderbilt Law School”); and the fact that Travis appeared on Fox News last night and will appear on Fox News again later today. Sprinkled throughout all of this are plugs for Hard Rock Bet (“Bet $5, get $100 in bonus bets”), which is the official gambling partner of Sport & State and holds equity in Travis’s upstart media concern, and companies such as Perfect 10 Mortgage, Crockett Coffee, XX-XY Athletics and Clay Travis Law, all of which – it should come as no surprise – Travis either outright owns or holds a stake in. The recursiveness and self-referentiality of the advertising and content on Sport & State are all part of the site’s commercial strategy, according to Travis’s lengthy mission statement. The onshoring of all the advertising will, Travis claims, insulate his new venture from the vagaries of media’s traditional dependence on subscriptions and external advertisers. Gambling is the key revenue driver: Outkick became an affiliate of FanDuel after sports betting was legalized in 2018 and eventually made $350 for every new gambling account it helped set up, netting $2m in affiliate betting revenue on Super Bowl Sunday in 2021 alone, and Sport & State is set up to reap similar rewards through its partnership with Hard Rock Bet. But Travis’s expectation is that his home loan business, say, will also prosper as viewers stay online to hear his views on Ole Miss v LSU, Lane Kiffin or the apparent attempted hijacking of the Israel-bound passenger jet and what it means for the future of DEI in America. Inadvertently, perhaps, Travis’s sidequest companies offer a sense of what Sport & State’s ideal audience member looks like: a patriotic American male with a habit of deploying the phrase “perfect 10” unironically whose life revolves around mortgages, coffee, litigation, gambling and moaning about trans women. On the Crockett Coffee blog, recent posts include “American Coffee Origins and Brewing Techniques”, “Discovering American Coffee’s Unique Flavors”, and “The Americano: A Complete History” (do I detect a theme here?); Travis sips throughout the day on Sport & State from a black spillproof coffee container, emphasizing his own commitment to the cause of caffeine and country. If there’s a persistent “Spider-Men pointing at each other” quality to the advertising on Sport & State, that extends to the content as well. Travis’s big idea is that in the age of AI and commodified writing, it’s better to go deep than big, that depth of audience commitment matters more than the old traffic era’s scale-focused contest for clicks. There may be some wisdom in the strategy, but that approach – drumming down and appeasing an already loyal base – seems to have become the media-obsessed Trump White House’s guiding political strategy too, a choice that risks self-sabotage as the midterms loom. Travis’s theory of media is second-term Trump’s theory of power: instead of growing the audience, the electorate, the constituency, the sole purpose of having attention is to give those listening more of the same. Discussion on Sport & State this week included a summary of Travis and Sexton’s Monday meeting with Trump in the Oval Office. Their main point was to emphasize that “President Trump says he loves the show, says we’re doing a great job” and that various Trumpworld figures greeted them during their half-hour in front of the Resolute Desk. “We saw Karoline Leavitt, our very good friend”; “We also saw Susie Wiles – she said she is cancer-free now”; “We got a little quick high-five from Stephen Miller”. Over a chyron announcing THE VOICE OF SEAN HANNITY, the longtime Fox News host then called in to discuss: sports betting (what else?); the border collie he’s about to take delivery of at the conclusion of nine months of dog training (if this is what it takes to survive domestic cohabitation with Hannity as an animal, imagine how things must be for the humans in his house); Gavin Newsom and Kathy Hochul as the highest-taxing, and therefore worst, governors in America; and potential Democratic candidates for 2028 (Hannity thinks AOC will be the nominee, Travis thinks it will be Kamala Harris; they agreed to bet on the outcome, with the loser to buy the winner a steak dinner in a demonstration of red-blooded American masculinity). The segment concluded with Hannity, Sexton and Travis all saying “we had an awesome time” after five minutes of meandering conversation about nothing, and the welcome announcement that Travis would be on Hannity’s show on Fox the following day for more of the same. On the right, the Spider-Men are always pointing at each other, and they’re all the audience each other needs. Watching Sport & State’s live programming and reading its endless churn of tiresome posts about how sports and the world suck now because of Joe Biden and woke, it’s difficult to figure out what, exactly, the appeal of Travis as a right-wing media personality is. Rogan has the vague charisma of a lifelong stoner; McAfee has that dog in him, a kind of American mongrel who forever puts himself next to a gas pump or under the chassis of a hoisted car; Carlson has a habit of Mozart-laughing at his own jokes, which is at the very least engagingly bizarre; Shapiro … well, Shapiro doesn’t have much going for him, but he does talk quickly. Travis, by contrast, has neither a sense of personal style nor any real sense of humor; he’s a boring dad who drones on endlessly about mortgages and failed sports bets and his law degree. He also frequently looks exhausted on air, as does Sexton; together they form perhaps the puffiest-looking duo in American media. Who knows? Perhaps a pair of hungover-looking permadads sipping mournfully from their coffee canisters while they bemoan the latest poll numbers out of Ohio is exactly the new groove the right needs to salvage a listing presidency. But it seems unlikely. Travis claims he’s working “20 hours a day” to produce material for Sport & State, and perhaps it really does take that long to package up clips from the previous 24 hours’ appearances on the Sean Hannity Show and Jesse Watters Primetime and Titans on Tomorrow with Ben Shapiro, brew the Crockett Coffee and get it into the spillproof containers, go on air, play the clips, then restate their substance using different words 500 times in a row. But if this is the right’s idea of a bold new intervention in sports and media, it’s hard not to feel that as a cultural force, the Magaverse is now well and truly running on fumes.

title: Drumcree talks break up without agreement on fifth day of standoff
author: Lisa O’Carroll
summary: Dispute over march will go to legal appeal on Monday after talks hosted by Northern Ireland secretary end
body_text: Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement, with the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, describing the situation as being between a “rock and a hard place”. Speaking on Thursday night after the latest talks with the Orange Order and residents of Garvaghy Road broke up, Bryant said: “I think this is the end of these conversations. We haven’t come to a settled agreement, and it’s a shame, but my door remains open.” Last Friday’s Parades Commission decision to grant the Orange Order the right to hold a procession down the nationalist Garvaghy Road plunged Northern Ireland into one of its most perilous periods since the 1998 peace deal. A legal appeal by the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition originally scheduled for Friday has been pushed back to Monday to facilitate any further talks. “Obviously we’ll have to see how that plays out,” Bryant said, indicating he would not be intervening unilaterally. “I would say that the law, in the end, is the law.” Five days of talks ended in deadlock, he said, outlining the compromises on the table for the first time. “We’ve discussed a wide range of options, including mediation, including an option where the right to march was respected but wasn’t exercised, including an option where there was a final march and no further applications for marches into the future, and we’ve not managed to come to agreement on any of all that.” Earlier in the week, reports suggested one option was a “one and done” parade involving just a dozen people without insignia in October. This would have been on condition the Orange Order would never apply for permit for that parade route again. Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition said “the reality is” there was “no such thing as half a march”. “There’s a march or there’s not a march – simply that,” he said. Jamie Bryson, a legal adviser to the Orange Order, who earlier this week said he would “not surrender” said he would accept Monday’s ruling. “The challenge that we would put down to the Garvaghy Road residents – they’re going to the court of appeal on Monday – if the court of appeal upholds this determination, commit to accepting the law and walk away, and we’ll do the same,” he said. “Abide by the law, and if the court of appeal upholds the determination, get off the road, stop breaking the law and allow the parade to go ahead. If we lose, we’ll accept that.” The dispute began last week after the march along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road was given the go-ahead by the Parades Commission for the first time since 1998, a decision denounced by Sinn Féin as “madness” and by the taoiseach as “incomprehensible and wrong”. The dispute, which threatened to collapse Stormont and has returned Northern Ireland to bleak days of the past, has also revived the interest of key US Democrats. Richie Neal, the US representative for Massachussetts’ 1st congressional district, described the parade as “needlessly provocative”. The Congressional Friends of Ireland Caucus, which Neal sits on, wrote to Bryant urging him to use his powers to reverse the Parades Commission decision. “Over the last three decades, the progress made on the island of Ireland has been nothing short of extraordinary. Twenty-eight years have passed since the signing of the Good Friday agreement, and a generation has grown without a single memory of the Troubles,” the lawmakers wrote. “Without decisive action, we risk reopening one of the most painful chapters of Northern Ireland’s history and undermining nearly three decades of peace, stability and reconciliation made possible by the Good Friday agreement.” The Northern Ireland Policing Board has been told that the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) operation around the parading dispute has topped £3m.

title: First Thing: Christa Pike in ‘critical condition’ as Tennessee halts all executions
author: Martin Belam
summary: Failed attempt to execute 50-year-old prompts review of state’s execution practices amid distressing witness accounts
body_text: Good morning. Tennessee’s governor has suspended executions as Christa Pike’s lawyer says the state’s failed lethal injection execution attempt has left her in a critical condition. Bill Lee, the Republican state governor, has suspended all executions in the state until at least the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry. Leading voices on the death penalty in the US have told the Guardian that the failed execution was such a violation of the constitutional prohibition on “cruel and unusual punishment” that all judicial killings should be halted nationwide. What have Pike’s lawyers said about her condition? Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said: “We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now and receiving life-saving medical care. She is in a critical condition.” What did witnesses say took place during the execution attempt? Catherine Sweeney, a reporter at the Nashville Public Radio WPLN, said: “They went through two rounds, and she was still breathing at the end. She was very ragged. She lifted her head up and was looking around. At one point, she said … there was a spot that was burning and hurting, and asked if that was normal. None of it was normal.” What was Pike convicted of? She was convicted of the brutal 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, alongside her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp. Lee said he had not yet spoken to Slemmer’s family after the failed execution. Family of Renee Good sues administration officials and the ICE agent who shot her The family of Renee Good, the woman killed by immigration agents in January in Minneapolis, filed two federal lawsuits against the agent who shot her and several top officials in the Trump administration on Thursday. In the lawsuits, Good’s partner, Becca Good, and her brother, Brent Ganger, alleged wrongful death and other violations of federal law, according to a press release issued by their lawyers. Why has the DNC issued a lawsuit against the administration? The Trump administration broke the law when it pushed through a last-minute change to the form overseas citizens use to register and request absentee ballots, the Democratic National Committee (DNC) said in a lawsuit filed on Thursday. “Trump and Republicans are so desperate to hang on to power that they are trying to eliminate the way some American citizens abroad register to vote and request mail ballots,” said Ken Martin, the chair of the DNC. Which states are leading the resistance to the Trump EPA’s repeal of emissions rules? Twenty-one states, led by New York, are challenging the Environmental Protection Agency’s power plant rule. The New York attorney general, Letitia James, said the federal government was showing “callous disregard” for Americans’ health and the environment, and future generations would pay the price. Power plants that burn fossil fuels are a major source of planet-warming pollution. Hegseth puts the future of warfare in the hands of major Maga donors By installing the tech billionaires Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to advisory roles in a Pentagon project about the future of warfare, the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has given extraordinary influence to two of Maga’s most significant campaign donors – and both men own companies that benefit from federal defense contracting. Luckey, 34, whose company is backed by Joshua Kushner’s equity fund, has acquired manufacturers of underwater drones, unmanned aerial vehicles, and space technology, and has already been voluble about his philosophy on warfare, saying he thought warfare in the second half of this century would involve “subterranean” conflict, with vehicles that can “move through the crust of the Earth the same way that submarines move through the water”. What have been the latest developments with US forces in the Middle East? The US military is dispatching a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, as Donald Trump warned new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon. Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the US naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines as well as hundreds of aircraft. Letitia James appointed special prosecutor in alleged gang-rape at Cornell Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang-rape at Cornell University. “The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Hochul said in a statement. “This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands.” In other news … Google has rolled out a new Gemini AI model – but has restricted access over safety concerns. California’s attorney general, meanwhile, has issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI over reports of rogue agents’ hacking. SpaceX launched a crew to the ISS successfully, with Jessica Watkins, the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit, making her second trip to the space station. Lawmakers have called for action on what they say are “plainly illegal” taxpayer-funded ads to promote Donald Trump in the run-up to the midterms. The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case on Thursday refused to declare her not guilty, turning down a defense motion. Kanye West’s sold-out Russia concerts have been cancelled, organisers have confirmed. Russia’s foreign ministry had called the planned shows unacceptable due to the rapper’s “glorification” of Adolf Hitler. Stat of the day: Lyft agrees to pay California $272.5m in largest-ever wage theft settlement Lyft agreed to pay the state of California $272.5m to ⁠settle claims that it stole drivers’ wages by mislabeling them as independent contractors rather than employees. Culture pick: The 20 best making-of documentaries – ranked! From tropical disasters and doomed sci-fi epics to bribing Orson Welles and fending off a puma, Ryan Gilbey rates cinema’s most revealing glimpses behind the scenes. Don’t miss this: I’m allergic to the cold California’s Shauna Castaner recounts her extraordinary experience of gradually coming to realise that her condition was getting so severe she has to a keep a close watch on her body temperature and can’t eat chilled foods. … or this: Erasure on how 40 years of friendship got them through grief – and why Vince Clarke has quit touring Erasure were regulars on the Billboard chart in the 1980s and 90s with hits like Chains of Love, A Little Respect and Always. They return with their 20th – TWENTIETH! – studio album. Tim Jonze speaks to the iconic British synthpop duo. Climate check: Think more rain means more river water? Not necessarily More rain and snow equals more water in rivers, right? Not necessarily. A new study shows that, despite receiving more rainfall than they used to, river water levels are falling because of changes in climate. Last Thing: Bear treats itself to baked goods at Colorado farmers’ market One animal in Aspen, Colorado, seemed to decide to make a late bid to win Fat Bear Week, as it rocked up to a farmers’ market and started devouring fresh bread and pastries at one of the stalls. title: ‘A persistent crisis’: the 16 children removed from an Ohio family are part of a statewide issue
author: Stephen Starr in Dayton, Ohio
summary: The case of the Siders family illustrates major shortcomings among Ohio’s political and administrative authorities
body_text: In June 2025, Jody Walker stood in front of Ohio lawmakers at a senate finance committee meeting in Columbus. As the head of South Central Ohio Job and Family Services, he was desperate for help. “I have been a county director since 1999, yet I have not seen such a challenging time in the child welfare system as I do today,” he said, “specifically in terms of the needs of our children.” His agency, which oversees three rural counties in southern Ohio, frequently saw children sleeping at the organization’s office because they had no other safe place to go. Twelve months later, Walker’s fears were realized right in his own backyard. On 30 June, 16 children were found in a dilapidated home in Hamden, a short drive from where Walker works. Several were found near death; two children were flown to a level one trauma medical facility, where one was placed in an intensive care unit, according to reports. Gary Siders and Christina Siders, the children’s grandparents, and Gary Siders II and Elizabeth Siders, their parents, were charged with 16 counts of child endangerment. In August, Gary Siders II and Elizabeth Siders were additionally charged on separate counts of sexual battery and unlawful sexual conduct with a minor, who was not their own child. All four have pleaded not guilty to the charges. The Siders case illustrates major shortcomings among Ohio’s political and administrative authorities when it comes to supporting the most at-risk in society, say experts. “Our biggest challenge is a persistent crisis in identifying appropriate, affordable and accessible placements … Paid placement costs have increased 41% since 2020, far outpacing inflation, with the cost for residential and group home care skyrocketing by more than 65%,” said Angela Sausser of the Public Children Services Association of Ohio, which represents public children services agencies in the state. “While the state share [of spending on children services] has been rising over the last eight years, from 10% to 20%, it still falls below the national average of 42%.” Today, the family services department in Vinton county is drowning in the estimated $200 per child per day expense of caring for the 16 Siders children, who are now in foster care; six of the children are twins aged four or younger. A rural region with fewer than 13,000 residents, Vinton county is the least populous county in Ohio. Property tax levies in the area fail to come close to covering the costs of caring for at-risk children, which for South Central Ohio Job and Family Services rose from less than $4m in 2015 to more than $10m in 2024. In fact, the conditions facing the children were discovered by accident. Law enforcement officers went to the property to serve arrest warrants on Gary Siders II and Elizabeth Siders on charges unrelated to the neglect of their children. “County leaders should not have to choose among services for vulnerable children, public safety, seniors and those with behavioral health needs or developmental disabilities,” said Sausser. For more than 30 years, Republicans have broadly controlled governing and lawmaking in Ohio, regularly holding a supermajority in the state legislature. According to the Annie E Casey Foundation, a private philanthropic organization focusing on children’s needs, while the percentage of children in Ohio living in high-poverty areas has fallen in recent years, figures for child deaths, children without health insurance and children aged three and four who are not in school all have risen. Financial disclosure information from the Siders family published by Los Angeles magazine found that Elizabeth Siders had no income and her husband’s salary amounted to $1,500 per month in 2021. Ohio isn’t alone in struggling to fund care for vulnerable children. Nationally, a swathe of cuts including supports such as food benefits for 1 million children are under way. For the 2027 federal budget, the Trump administration is proposing cuts to nutrition programs for women and children, home energy assistance for low-income families, a $6bn cut to the budget of the National Institutes of Health and the elimination of a federal preschool development grant program. Data and research overwhelmingly show that children in states governed by Republican leadership face higher risk factors than those run by Democrats or members of both parties. The infant mortality rates in Tennessee, Mississippi and Arkansas are more than 50% higher than in states such as New York and California. In Ohio, a case worker reported in 2020 that the Siders children suffered from high levels of lead; last year, Republican lawmakers in Ohio cut funding for a lead abatement program from $7.5m to $250,000 a year. The office of Andy Wilson, Ohio’s Republican attorney general, declined to comment on questions from the Guardian asking, among other things, whether he believed the state of Ohio had failed the Siders children. Search warrant materials have been sealed by a judge, and a gag order has been issued by another, meaning attorneys for the accused and others involved, including law enforcement officials, cannot speak publicly on the matter. Wilson has claimed that the adults in the Siders household “[w]ere pretty adept at keeping these kids out of sight and out of the eyes of investigators” and called the family members responsible for the abuse “pure evil”. State authorities through the Ohio department of children and youth have initiated a review of the Siders case, “to determine how the county public children services agency followed federal and state requirements and to provide technical assistance on best practice”, said Jodi Norton Trimble of the Ohio DCY. However, reports show that child and family services at the county and regional levels made significant efforts to highlight the conditions the Siders children faced. When the family lived in neighboring Gallia county in 2020, a staff member from its department of jobs and family services visiting the children reported finding them living in desperate conditions, prompting court-ordered protective supervision for the children. But by May 2021, the supervision requirement was terminated and the family moved out of Gallia county. The same year, school officials in Gallia county filed a complaint in a juvenile court reporting that several of the Siders children had become habitually truant. But local authorities were unable to keep up with the family’s movements. “I believe the school made contact with the appropriate school district where the family was living in West Virginia. However, before authorities could take action, the family moved again,” a representative of Gallia juvenile court said. At 34 years old, Elizabeth Siders, the mother of all 16 children, was pregnant every 15 months. She was 15 years old when she was married in West Virginia, (before 2023, a child of any age in the state could legally be married with permission of a judge) and, shortly after, gave birth to her first child at the Holzer health system outside Gallipolis, Ohio. She would give birth to nine children at the facility, according to reports. Her attorneys have called for a mental health evaluation to see whether she is competent to stand trial. The Ohio department of children and youth report on the incident is expected to be completed by the end of the year, “but it must be conducted without interfering with the criminal investigations that are ongoing”, said Norton Trimble.

title: A small Texas town stopped Trump’s border wall construction – for now
author: Shilpi Chhotray
summary: As they had in the past, San Ygnacio residents banded together to stop a development threatening their town
body_text: This story was co-published and supported by the journalism non-profit the Economic Hardship Reporting Project. Joel Ruiz pointed his cane toward a long piece of metal lying in the dirt. Unwanted construction crews had left it behind on his riverfront property where he has lived and run a small fishing business for decades in San Ygnacio, Texas. At 90, Ruiz still tends the land. But in July, heavy machinery gouged the earth where mesquite and dense brush once grew. A steel barricade of 30ft-high bars was erected across the riverfront, including on his property just across the Rio Grande from Mexico. For months, Ruiz and a handful of other San Ygnacio residents have been trying to halt the construction of a federal border wall in their Mexican American town of roughly 400 people. They’ve blocked bulldozers, been arrested, unearthed 75-year-old land records and filed lawsuits challenging the federal government’s authority to build here. Even though residents say nearly all the riverfront land in the county is privately owned, the government is building on it anyway, claiming a decades-old right. While they have stopped construction on the disputed land for now – a verbal concession, not a court order – the reprieve is precarious: the lawsuits are unresolved, the federal money set aside for construction remains in place and residents know the crews could be back. But they are drawing on the memory of a town that rose up against the government once before. “This little spot is all we have,” said Elsa Hull, who owns property downriver with her two daughters. “But [residents] fought the federal government before and won – and we can do it again.” ‘Life or death for us’ Founded along the Rio Grande in 1830, San Ygnacio grew from a cluster of ranches into a small border town. Today, its plaza is still lined with homes made of sandstone quarried from the riverbank. The town sits in Zapata county, where roughly 38% of residents live below the poverty line and the median household income is about $39,000. Many work in healthcare, schools, food service and ranching. The border patrol is a major regional employer: its sector in Laredo employs about 3,025 people. The construction is part of the Trump administration’s renewed border-wall push – a roughly $46.5bn expansion funded by what is known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. San Ygnacio is located in one of the stretches where that money is now hitting the ground – and it’s going up as the number of border apprehensions is dropping drastically. Ruiz said he rarely sees anyone crossing this stretch of river any more. The Rio Grande is also San Ygnacio’s sole source of drinking water, and the wall is being built in its floodplain. To expedite construction, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) waived 30 federal laws – among them the Clean Water Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, eliminating the environmental review that would normally accompany a project of this scale. (The DHS did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.) To fill that gap, the Laredo-based Rio Grande International Study Center (RGISC) commissioned its own. The assessment warned that the wall and buoy system along and in the Rio Grande would worsen flooding – and, in places, fail outright. “This is life or death for us,” said Tricia Cortez, the center’s executive director. A breach of the wall system, she warned, would be sudden and catastrophic – homes destroyed, lives endangered. “The wall will straitjacket the river, forcing flood waters to rise and move faster.” Construction in San Ygnacio had begun without notice. Residents watched what they called a “man camp” rise at its edge and sensed something was coming. At a June community meeting to discuss other business, word began spreading through the back of the room: contractors were clearing land along the riverbank. Several residents hurried down and confronted the equipment operators, telling them they were on private property. Hull spent 25 years as an environmental investigator for the Texas commission on environmental quality. She recalled how she would watch deer, bobcats, coyotes and sunsets over the river from a bench beneath a tree on the bluff. Border construction has since knocked the tree down and smashed the bench. “Every part of my life is intertwined with the Rio Grande,” Hull said. “To me this river is sacred.” When contractors arrived near Ruiz’s home and RV park in June, he invited Hull and her friend to see the damage done. Crews had razed trees and severed an irrigation line. Before leaving for an appointment, Ruiz signed a paper authorizing Hull and her friend to stay and watch the property. Two contractor trucks slipped through the gate. Hull said one worker repeatedly flashed a card marked “CBP” – presumably Customs and Border Protection. Then she noticed Southwest Valley Constructors identification on his vest. “You’re not CBP,” Hull recalled telling him. When another truck approached, Hull drove her car across the entrance. More trucks arrived, followed by sheriff’s deputies, state troopers and border patrol agents. “We were just surrounded by all these men,” Hull said. Hull pulled up the county appraisal map and argued the crews were on Ruiz’s property. A deputy insisted the land was federal. Finally, Hull put her water bottle on the hood of her car and sat down. “Fuck it,” she said. “Arrest me.” They did. On 14 August, Hull returned, carrying a flag that read “Keep Our River Free” on one side and “Walls and Buoys Kill” on the other. When a sheriff’s deputy called to her from across a fence, she thought he wanted to talk. Instead, she was handcuffed and arrested again. A win from the past San Ygnacio had fought the federal government for this land once before – and won. When government contractors insisted the land was federal, Frank “Chip” Briscoe, an architectural conservator, started digging through county records. The trail led back to the early 1950s, when the government built the Falcon dam. Its reservoir submerged historic ranch communities and Indigenous sites along the river, and San Ygnacio was scheduled to be condemned and cleared for the reservoir, too. But residents refused to accept it. In 1951, more than 200 people signed a petition, organized by local veterans and civic leaders, opposing the measure. It worked: the government carved San Ygnacio out of the condemnation, the one stretch along the river bend spared from the reservoir. Seventy years later, the town is invoking that same exclusion again. Briscoe and attorney Ricardo de Anda searched subsequent property records and still found no evidence that the federal government had later acquired the excluded land. The documents gave De Anda something concrete to act on. In mid-June, he met with the US army corps of engineers on Ruiz’s behalf, arguing the crews had no legal grounds to build on the disputed property. When construction continued, De Anda sent a warning letter and filed two lawsuits against the federal government, alleging it took private property in violation of the fifth amendment. Two more landowners are preparing to sue, and De Anda plans to sue the contractor, Southwest Valley Constructors, in state court. Landowners filed criminal trespass complaints, while about a dozen residents pressed local officials to intervene. About a month later, according to De Anda, the county attorney arranged a meeting with contractors and federal officials. “They agreed to stop,” he said, and the crews pulled back – for now. For De Anda, stopping construction is only part of the plan. “Our strategy is to affect the national consciousness,” he said. The rest is a matter of time. Every day they hold the line – with their bodies, their deeds, their lawsuits – buys more of it. They are looking toward the midterms, hoping a change in Congress could give them another opening. They are betting they can outlast it. At San Ygnacio’s Grito de Septiembre festival, enlarged copies of the 1951 petition and its signature pages were displayed in the plaza. Residents gathered around them, searching for the names of their ancestors. Back on Ruiz’s land, people have stopped coming to fish for white bass and alligator gar; when construction began, it blocked his boat ramp access. The small fishing business he ran here is now, in his words, “kaput”. Still, Ruiz keeps coming to the river. In 1973, he helped establish a bird sanctuary beside his property. “My baby,” he called it. “I built it.” When asked whether his daily walks down to the river had become a way of watching for the crews to return – their equipment still sitting idle on the land – he shook his head. He was here “just to be here”, he said.

title: US added just 29,000 jobs in September in sharp drop from last month’s gains
author: Gaya Gupta
summary: Final jobs report before the midterm elections also shows the US unemployment rate rose slightly to 4.2%
body_text: US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp drop from last month’s gains, and unemployment rose slightly to 4.2%, a sign of a cooling labor market in the final jobs report before the midterm election. The numbers were under half of economists’ expectations of just under 70,000 new jobs. Most job gains were concentrated in the healthcare industry, which added 17,000 new jobs, while the information, financial and professional industries saw losses, according to the latest data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. Earlier jobs figures were also revised down: Initial reports from July and August altogether dropped by 60,000. The labor market contracted by 10,000 jobs in July after revisions, while August saw 133,000 jobs added. Growth in average hourly earnings slumped to 3%, the lowest rate in over five years. The unemployment rate has remained relatively steady since last year, when it hit 4.5% in November. US jobless claims also inched lower for the fourth week in a row, the labor department said on Thursday. But a closer look at the data also reveals how not all Americans are experiencing the same labor market. Unemployment among Black Americans grew an entire percentage point to 7%, double the rate of white Americans. Though job growth slumped over the summer – the labor market unexpectedly contracted in July and figures in June and May were revised sharply down from initial reports – 162,000 jobs were added in August, the highest since March. Job openings and the number of hires have also remained little changed in August, according to the recent data from the labor department, as the “slow-hire, slow-fire” job market continues. Data from private employers released by the payroll firm, ADP, earlier this week had painted a much rosier picture of the labor market. It found that private sector hiring accelerated last month for the first time since May, carried by growth in the healthcare, education and hospitality industries, and private employers added 90,000 new jobs. The labor market has remained largely strong this year even as the US-Israel war on Iran has upped inflation, especially energy prices. Last month, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in three years, citing higher prices. At the time, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, emphasized the strength of the US labor market, which “is basically running consistent with full employment”, but he noted that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”. Though the data still reflects an overall solid jobs market, the September release cools expectations for the US Federal Reserve to increase rates again in its final meeting before the 3 November midterms. Most central bank officials penciled in at least one more rate hike before the year’s end, which is now more likely to come at the Fed’s December conference. But higher prices continue to be the biggest economic pain point for Americans. Mortgage rates accelerated to their highest level in three years on Thursday from 7% to 7.28%, the largest weekly jump since 2022. The 10-year treasury yield, which underpins mortgages and other loans, also reached a 24-year high as the recent global bond sell-off continued. Meanwhile, higher oil prices have cost Americans an estimated $936 per household.

title: Seth Meyers on Trump: ‘Is there anything this grub won’t make us pay for?’
author: Guardian staff
summary: Late-night hosts talked Trump’s use of taxpayer money to fund campaign ads as GOP candidates distance themselves
body_text: Late-night hosts dug into Donald Trump’s unpopularity with GOP midterm candidates and his insistence on having US taxpayers foot the bill for recycled campaign ads. Seth Meyers On Thursday’s Late Night, Seth Meyers noted dissent within the Republican party over Donald Trump’s hugely unpopular war with Iran. In the run-up to the midterms next month, several GOP candidates, including Ken Paxton in Texas and Ashley Hinson in Iowa, have run ads calling the war a mistake, though not directly calling out Trump himself. “I’m sorry, you both supported the war, and now you want it to end? Who is that campaign ad for – you?” Meyers asked. “Also by the way, very cool and not at all cowardly to call for an end to the war while not naming the president who started it,” he continued. “But I get it, you guys are in a tough spot. Trump doesn’t care about anyone but himself. When it comes to Republicans running in competitive races, Trump is thinking ‘maybe I help them,’ or” to quote Trump speaking in the Oval Office this week about Iran, “maybe I blow them up.” Trump had previously endorsed Paxton, but “his endorsement came with some very strange and unusual caveats,” said Meyers. As Trump put it in one of many similar asides on Paxton: “He may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen.” “How would you like to have Trump as your wingman?” Meyers laughed. “‘Excuse me, miss, my friend over there thinks you’re very attractive. He, on the other hand, is not attractive at all.’” Later in the segment, Meyers noted: “Trump’s own lackeys are slamming him, his poll numbers are bad, his TV ratings are worse, which is why he’s found a new and totally legal way to get his message out: just air campaign ads on national television using your taxpayer money.” New ads in support of the midterms aired this week that look suspiciously like Trump’s ads from 2024 yet paid for by the US government, raising concerns from Congress. “They literally took a campaign ad they used in 2024 and re-aired it on TV using taxpayer dollars,” Meyers fumed. “He’s $2bn richer than he was two years ago, just pay for it yourself, you cheapskate! Is there anything this grub won’t make us pay for? If you went out to dinner with Trump, he’d order everything on the menu then say I forgot my wallet, then ask you for 50 bucks, then put it into his wallet in front of you.” Jimmy Kimmel And on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host reacted to a new report finding that consumer confidence is now lower than it was during the pandemic. “Remember the good old days, when we thought our parents were going to die of a highly contagious disease?” he joked. “But don’t worry, the president says our nation is doing really well.” In a post on Truth Social, Trump claimed the US was doing “better than ever before, but the Public just doesn’t know how well we’re doing. The Fake News Media refuses to disseminate our Record Setting Numbers, so I’m doing the best I can to do it myself!” “No way he came up with ‘disseminate’ on his own,” Kimmel quipped. “He thinks disseminate is how he got stuck with Don Jr.” “The president right now is working very hard to right the ship that definitely isn’t sinking,” Kimmel continued. “Trump held an event yesterday to triumphantly announce a $54bn investment in natural gas,” though he appeared to doze off during it. “Only Donald Trump would fall asleep during a press conference with the secretary of energy,” Kimmel quipped.

title: A Democratic upset is brewing in Alaska’s governor’s race as Trump’s popularity craters
author: Brendan Jones in Sitka, Alaska
summary: Support for 37-year-old Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins could upend the governor’s race in the heavily Republican state
body_text: This July, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins spent four days and 450 miles (725km) wending his way down the Yukon River in a 24ft Alweld skiff, a flat-bottomed aluminum boat built for shallow Alaska rivers. Starting in Koyukon Athabascan country, he passed through Indigenous Deg Hit’an communities like Anvik, before ending among the Yup’ik villages of the lower river, Russian Mission and Pilot Station among them. The boat carried him through 11 villages – some only reachable by water or small plane, and most with fewer than 300 residents, and fewer still who could recall the last time they had seen a candidate for Alaska governor, Republican, Democrat or independent. The 37-year-old former state representative is hopping on snowmachines – only people in the lower 48 call them snowmobiles – as well as boats and floatplanes to accomplish what Alaska Democrats have failed to do for nearly a generation: win the governor’s office. “Alaskans are hungry for change,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. “We’ve been running the same campaign since we launched in February, and I don’t take anyone’s vote for granted.” Just two years after Donald Trump carried Alaska by 13 points, his approval rating there has collapsed – a net 21- to 22-point swing, among the steepest drops in any reliably Republican state he won. In August, Kreiss-Tomkins came in first ahead of his Democratic and Republican rivals in the state’s non-partisan primary. Now, “JKT”, as he’s known in his home town of Sitka, is betting that an old-fashioned exercise in retail politics – traveling the vast expanse of a state larger than Texas, California and Montana combined and asking voters for their support in person – will help him do it again in November. But a question looms over the race: how much of his strength is a reflection of the changing national political environment, and Americans’ broad dissatisfaction with Trump, and how much is particular to the candidates, personalities and particular electoral system of the last frontier? Unlike nearly every other US state, Alaska no longer holds a traditional party primary followed by a winner-take-all general election. Under the ranked-choice voting system adopted by voters in 2020, the top four candidates from an open primary advance to the general election. Voters then rank candidates in order of preference, and votes can transfer to their next-ranked candidate as lower-placed contenders are eliminated. Though reliably Republican, the state has a long independent streak. The outgoing governor, Mike Dunleavy, an early supporter of Trump, leaves office deeply unpopular, largely for his unfulfilled promise to increase the amount of oil-dividend money Alaskans are given each year; in 2026, every eligible Alaskan received $1,000, with an additional $200 energy relief payment. This localized frustration coupled with Trump’s sagging approval ratings, particularly on the economy, has created a potential opening for Democrats. A recent bipartisan AARP poll found Kreiss-Tomkins winning 40% of first-choice preferences, compared with a combined 41% for his three Republican opponents, Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor, all of whom will appear on Alaska’s general election ballot. *** Kreiss-Tomkins grew up in Sitka, a fishing town of 8,500 where compromise is required. It’s wedged among the spruce and hemlock of the Tongass national forest and the open swell of the north Pacific, where you can’t escape political opponents in a town with just 14 miles of coastal road, accessible only by water or air. He entered politics in 2012, at the age of 22, winning a statehouse seat by defeating the Republican incumbent by 32 votes. “JKT is the clear frontrunner for governor not because of anything Trump did, but because he’s running a good campaign,” said Larry Persily, who has watched Alaska politics since the 1970s, first as the owner of the Wrangell Sentinel newspaper and later as an editorial page editor at the Anchorage Daily News. “He’s energized a lot of young people. His Republican opponents are just a sorry lot. The Republicans just put up a bunch of political losers.” Wilson, the top-finishing Republican candidate, would disagree. The Anchorage garbage-hauling entrepreneur, who finished third in August’s primary, is a former competitive figure skater and the great-niece of the late Republican governor Wally Hickel. She has secured endorsements from the Arkansas governor, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, one of Trump’s press secretaries during his first term, and Alaska’s own Republican congressman, Nick Begich – along with Byron Donalds, the Florida congressman running to succeed Ron DeSantis as governor there. Wilson casts Kreiss-Tomkins’s decade in elected office, and his elite educational background – he dropped out of Yale University in 2011, one credit short of graduating – as liabilities. “Alaskans are looking for fresh leadership from the private sector,” she said in an emailed statement. “Not another ‘experienced’ politician who will wreck our energy economy, raise taxes, continue to fail us on the PFD [permanent fund dividend], and sell out Alaska to advance their career.” Wilson’s relationship with one of her Republican rivals is tangled: she chaired Bronson’s 2020 campaign for Anchorage mayor. He won, arrived in office as a political newcomer, then spent his single term fighting the assembly over homelessness – at one point floating one-way plane tickets to the lower 48 for people living on the street – before losing re-election to the independent Suzanne LaFrance in 2024. Republican candidate Taylor’s route to the ballot has been stranger still. The former state attorney general was elevated to the final slot after Tom Begich withdrew and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, only to be disqualified four days later over an undeclared rental income disclosure; briefly replaced by his own running mate; then reinstated after a department of law review – conducted by the office he used to run – found trivial but, he claimed, similar issues among dozens of other candidates. The three Republicans’ competing campaigns have prompted efforts to consolidate conservative support behind Wilson. Alaska’s electoral history offers a precedent. In 1994, Democrat Tony Knowles won the governorship by just 536 votes after the conservative vote split between Republican nominee Jim Campbell and Jack Coghill, the sitting lieutenant governor, who ran on the Alaskan independence party ticket. Knowles, the last Democrat elected to the office, went on to serve two terms. *** The governor’s race is unfolding against a national backdrop of declining approval for Trump. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published in September put his approval at 32%, with dissatisfaction over living costs among the principal concerns. But national figures alone cannot explain what is happening in Alaska, where the statewide candidates are also confronting distinctly local issues. Electing a Democrat here is not as surprising as it is in some other red states, said Tom Kizzia, a longtime Anchorage Daily News reporter and Alaska historian. “It’s that Alaska iconoclasm that kicks in – the simmering resentment of big business ripping off our resources.” The common thread, in Kizzia’s telling, is not a particular political party, but rather a distrust of whoever is currently perceived as extracting Alaska’s wealth without giving enough back – a role historically filled by outside oil and mining interests, and one conservatives have often redirected toward the federal government instead. That history helps explain why Trump’s brand of politics has not translated into durable support for his allies on this year’s ballot. “Dunleavy hitched himself to the Maga wagon, which contained elements of that iconoclasm,” Kizzia says. “But Trump was mostly about non-Alaska things that don’t register strongly with Alaska voters.” What does register, he argues, is Dunleavy’s failure to deliver on a hefty permanent fund check, the annual payment that Alaskans receive from the state’s oil-wealth savings each October. Dunleavy promised to up the amount of these checks, and even to pay Alaskans retroactively. None of this has come to pass. This same unresolved grievance now faces all three Republicans running to succeed him. Kreiss-Tomkins argues for a dividend payment that can be maintained without destabilizing the budget. “I want a permanent fund dividend that is meaningful and sustainable. We don’t need an election-year promise that blows a hole in the budget and is mathematically impossible,” he said. His campaign blends the Alaska tradition of “visiting” with people, sometimes onboard his skiff retrofitted with a three-quarter-ply cabin with the amber varnish flaking off, with a volunteer operation nicknamed “Superpod”, built on the premise that someone responding to a campaign text should reach an actual human being rather than a bot. That emphasis on personal contact was apparent to Debbie Moderow, who operates sled dog kennels near Denali national park and in Anchorage. At a meet-and-greet in Anchorage attended by about 30 people, she watched Kreiss-Tomkins climb on to a folding chair to address the crowd. “He was brimming with energy and wisdom, young and bright-eyed, and it was obvious that he had been obsessed with government in a geeky way for a long time,” she said. “I immediately thought, this guy has a vision, and a way to chart the way forward at a time when our state desperately needs it.” Persily, the newspaper publisher, who keeps his 100-year-old Underwood manual typewriter atop a restored lead-type cabinet and pops in CDs for music, sees the campaign’s emphasis on face-to-face campaigning as significant. “Elections are determined by turnout,” he said. “If you can turn out people who wouldn’t otherwise vote, that will make the difference. The public in the state is looking for someone who is going to excite people who wouldn’t otherwise get engaged. On a boat, on a snowmachine, what have you – Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, from what I can see, is making that happen.” It hasn’t been without hiccups. Kreiss-Tomkins’s campaign has attracted criticism over its finances. He outraised the entire field during the primary, drawing substantial contributions from outside Alaska, including six-figure sums from employees of artificial intelligence companies. He has responded by emphasizing his proposed moratorium on new Alaska datacenters and his support for regulations intended to protect Alaskans from harms associated with AI. His position is that the donations reflect support for his proposals rather than an effort to influence them. Asked about his priorities in office, Kreiss-Tomkins returns to two concerns familiar to Alaskans: education and the cost of living. “Our top-of-mind campaign issues are supporting our schools and lowering everyday costs for Alaskans,” he said. Whether dissatisfaction with Trump translates into votes for Democratic candidates remains a separate question from whether Kreiss-Tomkins can assemble a coalition of his own. The governor’s race will test both possibilities, alongside the ability of Alaska’s ranked-choice system to accommodate three Republican candidates competing for many of the same voters. For Moderow, Kreiss-Tomkins’s relative youth is less significant than his years of experience in Juneau. “People frame it as giving a young guy a chance,” she said. “For me, it’s the opposite. It’s giving a professional an opportunity when Alaska needs a leader.”

title: How Trump changed the way US women vote
author: Lauren Gambino
summary: A decade after his infamous Access Hollywood tape, the gender divide is again shaping a pivotal midterm election
body_text: A decade ago, Donald Trump’s improbable presidential campaign was rocked – and nearly derailed – by the now-infamous Access Hollywood tape, a 2005 recording in which the real estate developer turned reality TV star boasted about kissing and grabbing women without their consent. “When you’re a star, they let you do it,” he said, a remark he later downplayed as “locker-room talk” before musing that the tape might be fake. (It wasn’t.) In the moment, it felt fatal – the ignoble end of an explosive campaign for the White House. Back then, Americans hadn’t quite grasped Trump’s capacity to shock but not surprise. Within days, the outrage receded, swallowed by two more “October surprises” – WikiLeaks released the hacked emails of Hillary Clinton’s campaign manager, John Podesta, and then-FBI director James Comey announced the bureau was reviewing new emails related to her private server. That November, voters punished the first woman to be nominated for president by a major party for her emails, among other grievances, real and imagined, and handed the presidency to the man who had boasted that he could “grab em by the pussy”. US women haven’t voted the same since, and next month’s midterm elections offer another test of their tolerance for Trump in the Trump era. Long divided by race and class, Trump’s rise – or perhaps Clinton’s defeat – splintered US women further, along lines of educational achievement and marital status. In 2016, Trump won white women overall, but Clinton prevailed among college-educated white women, a partisan reversal from the presidential election four years earlier. In 2018, suburban women voters “revolted”, propelling Democratic victories and sending a record 102 women to the US House of Representatives in what was hailed as another Year of the Women. A conservative backlash brewed. The Senate confirmed Brett Kavanaugh to the supreme court after Christine Blasey Ford testified that he had sexually assaulted her when they were teens – a claim he vigorously denied. Gen Z grew up in the shadow of that collision. As a cohort, they are marked by a wide ideological gender divide, with gen Z women – many mobilized by the overturning of Roe v Wade – becoming more progressive and politically engaged, while their male peers drifted rightward into Maga and the “manosphere”. Anger over the loss of federal abortion protections helped forestall Democratic losses in the 2022 midterms. But the gender gap wasn’t enough to shatter the glass ceiling in 2024, when Trump defeated Kamala Harris – even after a jury found him liable for sexual abuse and defamation in a civil suit brought by writer E Jean Carroll. A gender divide once again looms over the midterm map that will determine the balance of power in Washington for Trump’s final two years in office. A recent New York Times-Siena poll found 65% of women disapproved of Trump’s handling of his job as president, compared with 52% of men. According to the survey, 57% of women would back the Democratic House candidate in their district, whereas only 45% of men said the same, a dynamic that played out across three key Senate contests surveyed in the poll – Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire. Trump has maintained that he has empowered women throughout his business and political career. His chief of staff, Susie Wiles, is the first woman to ever serve in the role. But polling suggests women are deeply dissatisfied with the president’s second-term performance, including, according to one national poll, one in four women who voted for him. In Maine, Republican senator Susan Collins, long considered untouchable, is facing voters for the first time since Kavanaugh joined four conservative justices to end the constitutional right to abortion. Her Democratic opponent, logger-turned politician Troy Jackson, is working hard to ensure voters don’t forget that their senator cast a decisive vote to put him on the bench. The Times poll shows him leading among women voters by 53% to 44%. Trump has cast the November election as a referendum on his presidency. Will voters cement his power – or turn over control to Democrats, and grind his agenda to a halt? It all may depend on what US women want. Can US voters trust everything they see? Most Americans don’t know Hasan Piker. The rest say he is changing this year’s elections Trump campaign ads paid with public money violate federal law, critics say Trump allies could use midterms ‘counting window’ to disrupt results, experts warn What Democrats are getting right – and wrong – in run-up to midterms: ‘We can’t just be anti-Trump’ Quoted: “This is the beginning of the end. This is the decline. As powerful and transgressive as he’s been, the country does not have a positive outlook right now. In fact, the negativity and pessimism among voters has reached a point that is unparalleled since Jimmy Carter,” Rick Wilson, a longtime Republican strategist, said about Trump’s final years in office. Read more: ‘The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets’: Trump lashes out as his power wanes Watch this race: A Hobbs’ Choice in Arizona A “unity ticket”? In these partisan times? Katie Hobbs, the Democratic governor of Arizona, and John Giles, a former Republican mayor of Mesa, a populous Phoenix suburb, are giving bipartisanship a whirl in the battleground state. Facing a tough re-election, Hobbs tapped Giles – a vocal Trump critic who formally left his party in May to become an independent after endorsing Kamala Harris in 2024 – to be her running mate. Hobbs’ choice of Giles is an overture to the independents and moderate Republicans she will likely need to secure a second term. Once a reliably Republican stronghold, Arizona has elected a string of Democrats statewide since Trump was first elected. In 2020, voters there narrowly backed Joe Biden for president before swinging back to Trump in 2024. This year is the first time Arizonans will elect a lieutenant governor, after voters approved the second-in-command role in 2022. Hobbs faces Republican congressman Andy Biggs, a staunch Trump ally who played a prominent role in the effort to overturn Biden’s 2020 victory. Biggs has chosen Sine Kerr, a dairy farmer and former state senator as his running mate. In an age of political tribalism and populist rage, is the center a viable path to power for the unassuming Hobbs-Giles ticket? *** The US politics team is hosting a series of reader Q&As leading up to the midterms. Our next live conversation will be on 6 October 2026 at 12pm EDT, with a panel of our politics and foreign policy reporters breaking down the war with Iran, the costs that come with it and political consequences for Trump as US voters head to the polls in November. title: G7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves
author: Joanna Partridge, Jillian Ambrose and Mark Sweney
summary: Leaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US supplies
body_text: Leaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel. The French President, Emmanuel Macron, said ministers from some of world’s largest economies had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks on Friday. Macron convened the leaders’ video call to discuss the global surge in diesel prices, and Trump’s threat to cut off US diesel exports unless Europe tapped their own stockpiles to help cool global markets. Under proposals reportedly drawn up by Macron, the current G7 chair, members will release 50m barrels of diesel and 50m of crude oil into the global market to ease prices. The agreement suggests European countries will avoid being cut off from vital supplies of US diesel after coming under pressure from the White House in recent days to release their emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban. Trump said he was considering a ban on diesel exports after the surge in sales to overseas buyers pushed US diesel prices to record highs in a blow to the economy before the US midterm elections in November. Macron said G7 nations – which also includes the US, UK, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan – wanted to “work in a coordinated manner to help bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”. He added that the G7 members and partners would front-load a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days and that ministers would discuss the “possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary” in the coming days. “We have all committed together to releasing these strategic reserves in the proportions I mentioned, with a focus on diesel, and we are all committed to ensuring there are no export bans, and President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point,” Macron said. Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Europe had “agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil” and that the process would start “immediately”. The threat of a US export ban presented a considerable challenge for Europe, which produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries but relies on imports to make up the shortfall. The ongoing disruption to fossil fuel exports from the Middle East has limited output from the region’s refineries as well as those in China, which is a leading buyer of Gulf crude. Meanwhile, Russian refineries have come under attack from Ukraine, causing its fuel output to fall to 20-year lows. In response, the US exported a record high of 1.9m barrels a week to overseas buyers in early August as the slump in global refining squeezed supplies across Europe and Asia. The record exports caused the US’s own distillate stockpiles to fall to their lowest seasonal levels since 1996, causing diesel pump prices to climb above $5.85 a gallon (£1.18 a litre) for the first time in early September. The proposed ban on US exports was expected to fuel greater competition for cargoes on the global market which would push prices in the UK and Europe well beyond current record levels. In the UK, the average price of diesel at the pumps climbed to a record high of £2 a litre on forecourts on Friday, putting more pressure on motorists and the wider economy. The cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, according to the RAC motoring group, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war. UK lorries, vans and farming vehicles are also typically diesel-fuelled, meaning the price rises will be felt in the higher cost of goods across the economy. Brent crude oil was trading at just above $100 (£76) a barrel on Friday, compared with about $72 before the Iran war started. It fell to about $98 a barrel after news of the emergency stockpile release before returning to more than $102 a barrel by the end of the day. Macquarie Group’s Walt Chancellor said a US ban on diesel exports would not address the underlying problem in the US or the global market. “The core issue the US faces is not a diesel problem. Nor is it a refined product problem. It may not even be a petroleum problem. It is a global energy problem,” he said, according to CNBC. “So what is the solution then? In short, more oil through the strait of Hormuz and out of the Middle East. Anything short of that is really just shuffling deck chairs,” he added. The IEA, the world’s energy watchdog, ordered the largest release of government oil reserves in its history in March when it agreed to release 400m barrels of emergency crude, to help calm the oil price shock sparked by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran. The intervention represented a third of the group’s total government stockpiles and was more than double the release of 182m barrels of oil made in 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. • This article was amended on 4 October 2026. Walt Chancellor was speaking in response to the news of a potential US ban on diesel exports, not about the subsequent reaction by some European nations.

title: Georgia holds emergency meeting on AI exposing voters’ secret ballots
author: George Chidi
summary: A Princeton researcher found that publicly available election records could be combined with AI to link voters to their ballots
body_text: When voters cast their ballots, their votes are supposed to remain secret: from their family, their neighbors, and the government. But what if artificial intelligence could make secret votes visible? Last month, Max Springer, a postdoctoral research fellow at Princeton University’s Center for Information Technology Policy, tested the prospect of identifying voters based on their Georgia ballots with a $20 subscription to an AI large language model and data obtained from an Open Records Act request. “Within a couple of hours, I had a pipeline to analyze and identify secret ballots across the state of Georgia and the agent told me exactly what further information it would need to identify real voters’ ballots,” Springer wrote. “At no point did the agent refuse to comply or raise concerns over implementing the exploit.” The issue has raised alarms among Georgia’s election officials less than two weeks before early voting starts in the high-stakes midterm election that will determine control of the US Congress. Ballot secrecy is a democratic safeguard, allowing voters to shield their selection from anyone who might try to influence or intimidate them into voting a certain way. But Springer’s test showed that he could use AI to find out who people voted for, using Georgia’s public election records. Georgia’s state elections board held an emergency meeting on Thursday morning to discuss how artificial intelligence has made it easier to identify voters through their ballot code, leaving people more vulnerable. Georgia’s outgoing secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, locked down the tabulation data that someone might use to identify a voter, ordering any public release to redact the ID numbers after an election, which “substantially address[es] this flaw”, said Ben Adida, an MIT-trained cryptographer and the founder of the election technology non-profit VotingWorks, as he addressed the board on Thursday. Election workers make a record of every voter who comes through a polling place. Voters then choose candidates on a touchscreen, which then prints out a paper ballot. The voter feeds that ballot by hand into a scanner to be tabulated. “When a voter inserts their ballot into a tabulator, a digital record of that ballot is created. Think of it as a row in a spreadsheet. One row is one scanned ballot. It’s often called a cast vote record, or CVR for short. In order to later retrieve the CVR, the tabulator assigns a unique identifier to each CVR at the time of scanning.” The flaw shows up in how the machine records that ballot, Adida said. The identifying is not actually random enough. Using AI, the early-voting list and the cast-vote record file for each county, Springer, the Princeton researcher who says he’s never been to Georgia, could recover the voting order for 1.52m ballots, or 98.9% of in-person ballots in 114 of the 139 counties he examined. “In some of Georgia’s counties, I can determine the exact ballot cast by every voter at the vote centers – ballot secrecy is entirely lost,” he wrote. In places with few voters on any given day, like tiny Heard county, Springer said: “the agent was able to match the majority of the 650 early in-person voters to a specific ballot, and the rest to within a single swap.” About four years ago, election security researchers had discovered a flaw in the software used by Georgia voters that could connect a voter’s identity to their secret ballot. The fact that ballots have an identifying number assigned at all is a product of the political paranoia attending Georgia’s elections. An ID number for each ballot addresses a fear of unscrupulous election workers double-stuffing ballots through tabulator machines. But if the order of ballots can be paired with other information, like sign-in data when a voter checks into the precinct, or perhaps Flock camera imagery that shows when someone entered a building on a slow day, then that ballot can be synched up to a voter’s name. Representatives of the secretary of state’s office say they have been shouting into the wind for help with this problem for three years. Requests for money have been bound up in the long-running political feud between Raffensperger and conservative legislators positioning themselves in the orbit of Donald Trump and 2020 election skeptics. (Raffensperger has remained a top Trump target after refusing to overturn his defeat in the state’s 2020 presidential election.) Spokesperson Robert Sinners sent a litany of emails and phone records showing requests for an appropriation to upgrade Georgia’s voting system, to no avail. The governmental affairs committee secretary, Tim Fleming, now the Republican nominee for secretary of state, was on the receiving end of many of those requests. “We have presented numerous plans to the legislature for this – not, not just a patch, but an entire overhaul of the software to fix up any known vulnerabilities,” Sinners said. “Guess what we were gifted with from the legislature? A big fat goose egg.” Fleming did not respond to a request for comment. Other states use Dominion software for their elections. Every other state has either patched the software or withholds vulnerable voting data from public inspection. Georgia law has two competing imperatives. The Georgia constitution explicitly requires a secret ballot, and the law protecting ballot secrecy in Georgia is among the strongest in the country. However, Georgia law – with revisions driven by the election disputes of 2020 – also demands transparency for election records. Elections board member Salleigh Grubbs raised that latter point as she circulated a draft proposal that would call for poll workers to hold ballots in a tray before voters cast them into the machine, to shuffle the printed pages out of order as a way to defeat the problem. Grubbs said that Raffensperger’s fix – redacting the ID numbers in the cast vote record – violates the law. But county elections officials and other board members – including Janelle King, a conservative Republican – dismissed the proposal as equally problematic. “We are asking our election officials to completely retrain everybody that has been a part of this process up until this point on how to administer the election,” King said. “I also have major concerns about dropping our ballots into a secured box and then having other individuals scan my ballot. How do I know that in the shuffling something doesn’t fall out? I mean, I just have some major concerns about whether or not we are creating more problems while we are trying to address a problem.” With early voting around the corner, changes to processes now are “a day late and about $30m short,” Sinners added.
