title: When is the right time to compare US politics to the Nazi era? This expert on Christian nationalism says: now
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: Robert P Jones argues that declining white Christian influence has fuelled an alliance with Trump, and warns it is reshaping US democracy
body_text: The lawyer Mike Godwin famously came up with the “law” that, as an online discussion grows longer, the probability of a comparison involving Nazis or Hitler approaches one (or 100%). Robert P Jones thought long and hard about whether to go there in his latest book. But the more he studied US demographic numbers, considered the rise of Christian nationalism and heard Donald Trump use the language of racial purity, he found the conclusion inescapable. “This is our 1933,” he writes. So it is that Backslide: Reclaiming a Faith and a Nation After the Christian Turn Against Democracy begins with the rise of the Nazi party and the complicity of the German people, including German Christians and churches. Jones cites Martin Niemöller, a Lutheran pastor imprisoned for opposing Hitler, remembered for the poem First They Came. But for the first four years of Hitler’s reign, he notes, Niemöller did not fully oppose the Nazis. He later regretted that he and the Protestant German church did not speak out sooner. Backslide returns to the analogy in its epilogue. He writes: “Just as God asked Niemoller where he was between 1933 and 1937, God will ask us where we were between 2025 and 2028. Just as Germans who backed Hitler and the Nazi Party after 1933 were fully aware of what they were joining, so Christians who have backed Trump and the MAGA movement a second time know and bear responsibility for what they are now endorsing.” Sitting in his downtown Washington office, the president and founder of the Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI) contends that US democracy is experiencing a severe “backslide” that is directly aided and abetted by an “apostate” white Christianity, including Trump’s language on the campaign trail. “This dehumanising language, talking about immigrants as vermin, and this racial purity language, like they’re ‘poisoning the blood of our country’. What does that mean? If they’re poisoning the blood, what’s the pure blood? We know where that story goes,” he said. Trump has repeatedly used the concept of genetic inheritance. In 2020, addressing a mostly white crowd in Minnesota, he declared: “You have good genes, you know that, right? You have good genes. A lot of it is about the genes, isn’t it, don’t you believe? The racehorse theory, you think we’re so different? You have good genes in Minnesota.” Normalisation is a perennial danger. “If don’t want to live in a place where we have a thuggish police force that’s kidnapping people off the street in masks and killing US citizens in the streets, now’s the time to speak up,” Jones said. Backslide cites historian and philosopher Hannah Arendt’s 1950 The Aftermath of Nazi Rule report for Commentary magazine based on interviews with postwar Berliners: “A great number of Germans, especially among the more educated, apparently are no longer capable of telling the truth even if they want to.” *** Jones grew up a Southern Baptist in Jackson, Mississippi, went to church five times a week and earned a master of divinity degree. His previous books include The End of White Christian America in 2016, White Too Long in 2020 and The Hidden Roots of White Supremacy and the Path to a Shared American Future in 2023. He called this one Backslide very deliberately. In international political science, “democratic backsliding” has become the established academic term for the systematic erosion of democratic norms, judicial independence and voting rights. Yet Jones recognises that the term carries an even older resonance. “In the evangelical world I grew up in, backslide was a word we heard all the time – a theological word about the fear of falling away from the faith,” he says, tracing the word’s history back through the Oxford English Dictionary to the 16th-century Protestant reformer John Knox. In Jones’s diagnosis, white American Christianity has committed a profound act of apostasy by trading its spiritual core for political dominance. By endorsing anti-democratic tactics, white Christian institutions have become the primary engine behind the country’s autocratic slide. To understand how a major religious tradition arrived at this moral impasse, Jones turns to the arithmetic of demographics. When Barack Obama was elected president in 2008, white Christian Americans still constituted 54% of the US population. By 2014, that figure had dropped to 47%. Today, white Christians account for 41% of the country. The decline among white evangelicals, long considered a bedrock of conservative politics, is even steeper. At the turn of the 21st century, white evangelicals represented a quarter of all Americans; today, they make up barely 13%. The Southern Baptist Convention, the country’s biggest evangelical denomination, has lost more than 3 million members since its 2006 peak. Faced with shrinking numbers and cultural marginalisation, white evangelicalism embraced not spiritual renewal, but existential panic – creating fertile ground for Trump’s demagoguery. “Trump loves to talk about the art of the deal and, in many ways, there’s been a massive quid pro quo deal struck between a declining white evangelical population and Trump,” Jones observes. “His big appeal to them was less about policy and more anti-immigrant: I’m going to restore an America that looks like you, and I’m going to restore power to the Christian churches. “He was literally saying on the campaign trail: this is a quid pro quo deal. Give me your votes and you won’t even have to vote again. I’ll fix it so you don’t have to vote again.’” This transactional alliance marks a complete departure from the religious right of the late 20th century, which wrapped its political ambitions in the language of morality. “You don’t hear those words any more,” says Jones, contrasting today’s movement with Jerry Falwell’s Moral Majority or the “Values Voters” summits of the George W Bush era. “What we have now is an overtly anti-democratic Christian nationalism flying under the banner of: ‘We believe this country belongs to us, and we’re going to use the power we can to claim it.’” This Faustian bargain relies purely on power rather than shared theology – a dynamic starkly highlighted by the contrast between Trump and his running mate, JD Vance. While Vance recently discussed the End Times with 22-year-old evangelical podcaster Bryce Crawford, awkwardly reflecting on his evangelical upbringing and subsequent conversion to Catholicism, Trump operates largely without theological pretence. Jones continues: “He makes straight appeals to self-interest: if you’re for me, I’ll be for you. Evangelicals are willing to forgive a whole host of sins for the idea that he is going to bring them back into power as their numbers are dwindling.” The real world manifestation of this transaction plays out every Sunday across thousands of congregations. While high-profile megachurches such as First Baptist church in Dallas make their political allegiance explicit, Jones contends that overt political sermonising is rarely needed. “Once you have churches that are largely segregated by race and increasingly segregated by partisanship, all you really have to do is keep out any critique. It’s reinforced by Fox News, Christian radio and going home to people of like mind. You don’t have to overtly teach Christian nationalism; you just keep it from being critiqued.” PRRI’s extensive empirical data undermines the widespread belief that religious attendance automatically fosters civic tolerance or democratic values. Jones says: “Particularly among white evangelicals, on several measures around Christian nationalism, anti-immigrant views, anti-Black views, and anti-Muslim views, going to church actually makes your views more extreme. It’s not the case that more church is the answer to democracy.” The dangerous potential of this theological radicalisation materialised dramatically during the January 6, 2021 attack on the US Capitol. Christian symbols were displayed prominently throughout the insurrection, including wooden crosses set up on Capitol grounds and rioters holding “Jesus Saves” banners alongside Confederate flags. Yet official investigations largely overlooked this central element, influenced in part by political figures like Congresswoman Liz Cheney on the House select committee. “I was stunned to see very little of it in the House select committee report,” Jones recalls. “It was a huge loss and a huge skewing of public perception that we didn’t take those Christian symbols at the riot seriously.” Today, this blend of Christian nationalism and military authority reaches into the upper echelons of the national security apparatus. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, sports tattoos featuring Crusader iconography – including the medieval battle cry Deus Vult (“God wills it”) next to a Jerusalem cross – while renaming the Department of Defense as the “Department of War”. Hegseth has welcomed vocal Christian nationalists such as Pastor Doug Wilson to lead a worship service at the Pentagon. Jones comments: “I can’t imagine much more dangerous than somebody who thinks, ‘I am the instrument of God, I alone understand how the forces of good and evil are aligned,’ while holding the power to deploy the most powerful military force the world has ever seen. While George W Bush took care after 9/11 to explicitly state that the US was not at war with Islam, today we are making radicalisation propaganda films for extremists by presenting ourselves as a Christian nation at war with Islam.” Behind the public spectacle of rallies and political theatre, ideologues such as Russell Vought, a key architect of Project 2025 and advocate of the “unitary executive” theory, are laying the groundwork for a government rooted in Christian nationalist principles. “They are building an apparatus designed to institutionalise this worldview across the federal government,” Jones warns. “It is an intentional, long-term project to reshape American democracy in their own image.” Despite the alarming trajectory detailed in Backslide, Jones resists total pessimism. The central message of his book is that “backsliding is not irreversible” and that national recovery remains possible through honest confrontation with history and sincere repentance. Across the country, alternative Christian voices are beginning to organise against Christian nationalism. Figures such as James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian running for the US Senate in Texas, and Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas are offering a pro-democracy theological vision. “For a long time, mainline Protestants were taught propriety and politeness, leading to a reticence to speak out,” Jones notes. “If we don’t want the public and future face of Christianity to be only Christian nationalism, we have to present a public version of Christianity that is compatible with democracy – one that leans into care for the orphan, the widow and the immigrant.” Ultimately, Jones argues, neither sacred texts nor historical precedents will dictate the future of US democracy. He hopes his book will make white Christians realise they face a decision similar to the one that confronted the establishment Christian church in Nazi Germany in 1933. “It’s a wake-up call to see the bright lines that are being crossed, to be clear-eyed about how dangerous that is, and for those readers who are Christian – particularly white and Christian – to realise we have a particular responsibility to offer a different version of faith. Because it is our faith that’s been hijacked and used to legitimise this illiberal, anti-democratic, authoritarian movement that’s running rampant and taking over in the US.”

title: A Statement review – outstanding climate change dramedy about a 1980 meeting
author: Adrian Horton
summary: Paul Rudd, Paul Giamatti and Tatiana Maslany lead an excellent ensemble in this dramatization of a failed 1980 conference on climate change
body_text: In late October 1980, days before the election of Ronald Reagan, Congress summoned 20 experts in various fields to a beachfront hotel in Florida. Their mandate was simple: figure out how to address the dire threat posed to the climate by fossil fuel emissions, then deliver their recommendations to Congress in the form of a statement. Every word said during four marathon sessions over the next 36 hours – every disagreement or digression, tirade or truce – was recorded by a stenographer for posterity into a single document, hundreds of pages long, that stands as an artifact from a time when expertise was trusted, before corporate greed and political expediency mired “debate” about rising levels of CO2 in the atmosphere in a haze of misinformation and inaction. The fact that this meeting took place at all – that experts in climate, energy, law, philosophy, politics and more agreed on the fundamental facts, yet struggled to reach consensus on what to do about them – is fascinating, if perhaps not the most natural fit for a movie. This was, after all, a conference room of specialists sharing evidence via overhead projector. Nevertheless, A Statement, a new film from Spotlight director Tom McCarthy that dramatizes the landmark conference, bets on the inherent sparks of watching fractious personalities forced together, as outlined in a 10-page section within Nathaniel Rich’s 2019 book Losing Earth. McCarthy and fellow screenwriters Noé Debré and Thomas Bidegain have embarked on an admirable act of faith: every word said within the conference room walls – roughly half of the movie – is pulled verbatim from the stenographer’s document. That is no mere fun fact within the press notes; though occasional text overlays from the actual transcript suggest some level of verisimilitude, it is in fact helpful to one’s appreciation of the movie, which dives headlong into the weeds and spins out in circular debates, to know that every tedious discussion of semantics, every frustrating spiral of potentials, was not in fact a writerly decision, but a real event – the natural and instructive result of 20 individual humans, each with their own personal feelings and professional responsibilities, confronting an existential problem of global scale. McCarthy, of course, is the writer/director of one of the great so-called competency porn movies of our time; the thrill of Spotlight is in both the successful reveal of a corrupted institution, and the frisson of watching people be unflappably good at their jobs. A Statement puts a misty-eyed spin on that pleasure: its people may be failing their objective – it’s a 46-year-old spoiler to say that no consensus was ever reached, nor a statement ever issued – but they’re at least trying their best, generally respecting each other’s views and, in the speculative bits outside the conference room that thankfully make the movie a treatise on the interminable condition of being human, actually befriending and learning from each other. If there is competency porn to be found, it is in McCarthy’s proficient, no-frills filmmaking, gracefully condensing 36 hours of collective tedium and personal reckonings into a tight 104 minutes. That, as well as a stacked cast of character actors demonstrating their mastery of type. Paul Rudd is awkwardly charming as the conference moderator who just wants everyone to get along. Paul Giamatti is never less than commanding as the curmudgeonly stick-in-the-mud from the Department of Energy with wisdom to spare, should you wait for it. John Turturro provides comic relief as an endearingly serious oddball scientist who has stared down the void. Evan Peters, playing “the Paul Revere of climate change”, can still do boyish live wire while pushing 40, as the film’s moral conscience. Tatiana Maslany disappears so fully into her role as a law professor, nervously holding the room hostage in legalese, that I did not clock her until the credits. The film’s ensemble – including Amy Ryan, Silicon Valley’s Zach Woods and Somebody Somewhere’s Mary Catherine Garrison, among others – are uniformly excellent and calibrated, no one performer running away with things (though Giamatti, perhaps unsurprisingly, has the best go at it, in a fictionalized nighttime scene that satisfyingly pits his hardbitten pragmatism against Peters’s fiery idealism). That is the gristle of the work, the difficult collaborations required to even have a shot of getting out of our human-made bind. For all its commendable historical accuracy – and there is a thrill in seeing, exactly, how we once thought about modernity’s most pressing and intractable problem – it’s the additional stuff, the late nights and vulnerable phone calls, dishy drinks and bruised egos, that makes A Statement a much more effective film about climate change than, say, a smug satire like Don’t Look Up. If we’ve learned anything in the decades since that beachside conference, it’s that the science can say what it will, but emotion will rule the day. The conference may have been a failure, but there is a satisfaction in watching them naively try. A Statement is playing at the New York film festival with a US release later this year and UK and Australian releases to be announced

title: Conservative US supreme court justice Samuel Alito hints at retirement in interview
author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
summary: Alito, 76, delivers comment in rare interview with CBS News scheduled to air on Monday
body_text: Samuel Alito, the conservative US supreme court justice, has said “I think I have to” contemplate retiring every year at his age. Alito, 76, delivered that comment in a rare interview with CBS News scheduled to air on Monday, a little more than six months after a widely publicized hospital visit invited speculation about his potential retirement. In a preview clip circulated online by the network, Alito told Jan Crawford, CBS national correspondent, that “I thought about” retiring at the end of the supreme court term that ended in June, saying: “It’s something that I think someone at my age has to think about.” “But,” Alito continued, “I thought I could still make a valuable contribution – which is why I became a justice and a judge in the first place. So that was basically it.” Crawford then said: “So you’ll be considering this probably every year – rethinking it.” And Alito replied: “Yeah, I think I have to.” Asked whether he was unduly undermining Republicans’ wish to confirm a conservative replacement at a time when their party controlled the US Senate, Alito rejoined: “It’s too hard to predict … how for anybody, and particularly when you reach a certain age, what your situation will be. “A year from now, two years from now and so forth – it’s too hard to predict what the political situation will be and what any president might do with respect to a replacement.” Fox News host Shannon Bream separately asked Alito in an interview broadcast on Sunday whether he had a “calculation” for when he may retire. Alito replied: “I think it would be foolhardy to … make a calculation. I’m going to serve for a certain number of additional years. “I’m grateful for every day when I wake up, and I’m still here – and grateful for every day when I’ll wake up and I am still able to do the job.” Crawford’s and Bream’s conversations with Alito came after he became sick at a Federalist Society dinner in Philadelphia on 20 March and was brought to a hospital. A supreme court spokesperson later said that Alito was treated for dehydration; returned to his Virginia home that night, as had been previously planned; and returned to work by 23 March. Nonetheless, news of the hospital trip prompted commentary across the political spectrum about whether Alito – who secured his supreme court appointment during George W Bush’s presidency in 2006 – may retire. Much of it centered on the possibility that his retirement would give Donald Trump the chance to appoint a fourth justice to the nine-member court, in all likelihood someone both younger and equally or more conservative than Alito. Progressive groups have also been girding themselves for the possibility that Alito’s fellow conservative supreme court justice Clarence Thomas, 78, could retire while Trump is in office. Trump appointed three justices during the first of his two presidencies: Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. They established a conservative supreme court supermajority alongside Alito, Thomas and John Roberts that has frequently – though not always – ruled in favor of Trump’s administration. Alito also spoke to Crawford about how he had endured everything from “the loss of old friendships” to “physical threats and harassment” after writing the 2022 majority opinion that struck down the federal right to an abortion created by the Roe v Wade decision nearly 50 years earlier. He asserted that overturning Roe v Wade – a decision disapproved by nearly six in 10 Americans, according to polling by the Pew Research Center – required “courage” from him and the four justices who joined his opinion: Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, Barrett and Thomas. Lost friendships were “something you have to live with,” Alito said, because it is “part of the job that you are going to displease people by making decisions on controversial matters”. “One side or the other is going to really dislike you because of the decision,” said Alito, who in late September recused himself from a major climate change case amid scrutiny over his stock holdings in oil companies. But, the justice said, threats and harassment were “quite disturbing” as well as “a danger for the courts and … others in public life”. Those remarks echoed rare testimony before the US House in July by Barrett and her liberal colleague Elena Kagan as they made the case for upgraded supreme court security, saying a rise in threats had increasingly affected the justices’ personal and family lives. One notable case was the arrest of a would-be assassin near the home of Kavanaugh with weapons and zip ties in 2022 after word leaked that the supreme court would overturn Roe v Wade. Alito additionally expressed his belief that “very harsh criticism” by Trump as well as his presidential successor and predecessor Joe Biden could be “quite damaging” to the supreme court. And he insisted that the supreme court’s job was to interpret the US constitution “as best we can” and apply it to the cases it handles, while rejecting the notion that it had evolved into a political institution. “We are not part of any political movement,” said Alito, whose memoir – titled So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court and Our Country – was given a Tuesday release date. “And we are not attempting to further any political agenda.”

title: MS Now connects ‘blue dots’ at Texas fan event: ‘I always feel hope when I watch them’
author: Jeremy Barr in Arlington, Texas
summary: Network at receiving end of White House press ban recently chose red state to host fan event as part of broader outreach
body_text: In 2024, Donald Trump and JD Vance carried Tarrant county, Texas, by 42,125 votes. So why, on the afternoon of 26 September, was the arena at the University of Texas-Arlington filled with nearly 5,000 super fans cheering for liberal media darlings Rachel Maddow and Lawrence O’Donnell like they were rock stars? After two years of hosting the network’s annual fan event in dark blue New York City, MS Now (formerly MSNBC) got wind that something was happening in Texas. The state, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate in 37 years, might do so next month, when 37-year-old James Talarico, Texas state representative, goes up against the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton, a well-known but controversial figure who ousted incumbent John Cornyn in the party’s primary with Donald Trump’s backing. “We wanted to be bigger and bolder. We wanted to go to a story that really matters (and this is one of the most important stories of the season), and we wanted to keep growing our live events business,” Marcus Mabry, senior vice-president of content strategy for MS Now, said in an interview. And, he noted, “everything is bigger in Texas”. While MS Now has a relative monopoly on older liberal Americans who still watch linear television, the network sees potential outside of its traditional coastal strongholds – much like the national Democratic party. Several MS Now hosts hinted at that growth opportunity in their onstage remarks throughout the day’s programming. “I will say, in the state of Texas, you might have a lot of neighbors that don’t vote like you, but it doesn’t mean they can’t tomorrow,” Stephanie Ruhle, an MS Now host, told the crowd. “I met so many people today whose eyes were filled with tears, and they said: ‘I’m the sole blue dot in Texas.’ How great that you are outstanding. How great that you are a special voice.” Or, as Mabry put it: “I think right now the opportunity for any journalism in the country is to stop speaking red and blue, and to start speaking to people as individuals.” In a holding room before his onstage interview with Stacey Abrams, a former Georgia state representative, Chris Hayes, an MS Now host, said viewers seem to be more “locked into the news” lately after a period of post-election malaise (and softer television ratings) in late 2024 and early 2025, particularly now that Democrats face good odds in next month’s midterm elections. “There are thousands and thousands of people here – in the middle of Texas,” he said of the event. Comparing the vibes with the months after Trump took office, “it feels like another world … We’ve had the most intense stress test in the American constitutional republic in my lifetime, and I don’t think anything is determined yet, but it certainly feels better than a year and a half ago.” The network is feeling that surge of interest. So far this year, MS Now’s primetime lineup is averaging 1.3 million viewers, up 11% from 2025. The network has seen an even bigger increase among viewers aged 25 to 54, the demographic most prized by advertisers. The event – Together In Texas: We the People 2026 – also served as something of an in-person illustration of the network’s first major direct-to-consumer offering, a membership plan – for $7.99 per month or $79.99 annually – that gives subscribers access to two daily Q&As with top hosts and reporters, a moderated discussion community for members, exclusive content, a curated daily briefing and even a collection of guided meditations. (Those in the Founders tier of the membership program had access to a special lounge at the event space.) “We’re still telling the audience what they need to know, but we’re also asking them, ‘What do you want to know, and how can we actually have a relationship where we actually are more than just delivering news to you as the voice of God,’ which fewer and fewer audience actually wants,” Mabry said. “I hope our business is learning that, because that’s the only way we survive. And we have to survive – it’s important for democracy.” With MS Now leaning into direct-to-customer products, fan service was the name of the game at the event. At one point, Rebecca Kutler, the network president, happily agreed to photograph several attenders who wanted to take photos with Laura Barrón-López, the MS Now White House correspondent, after a panel on the network’s expulsion from the building – seemingly without realizing who their amateur photographer was. “I’ll do any job!” Kutler told the Guardian. Ruhle served as the event’s unofficial “cheerleader”, as one attender said, hyping up the crowd and taking photos with fans. “Those are the people that we work for,” she said in an interview. “When you talk about the media being disconnected from the people, we are no longer – or we shouldn’t be – in the presentation business. No longer should we be sitting in newsrooms deciding here’s what we’re going to make or here’s how it has to look.” “This isn’t a political rally,” Ruhle said of the event. “This is what America is … These people make our shows better. Why wouldn’t you want to be with them?” Ahead of the event, several attenders said it was a no-brainer for MS Now to host the event in Texas – and said they were committed to watching the network as a purveyor of both reliable information and a much-needed sense of optimism. Ronnie Thomas, a 47-year-old Dallas resident who works in automotive sales, said he was “very happy” to be able to see Maddow and his other favorite hosts with only a short drive. “I like getting more of the truth,” his wife Rachael, also 47, said. “And it feels like they are closer to what the true state of things are compared to some of the things we see on other stations.” Former Republican Leslie Lesher, 73, and her spouse Joni Dennis, 68, said they watch MS Now “almost all day” every day. “These are our favorite people,” Lesher said. “I know they have knowledge that we don’t have. I always feel hope when I watch them.” Ruhle shared her sentiments. “A lot of people are scared about the state of the world,” she said. “They’re scared of the state of democracy. And I just think we’re all in this together.”

title: Trump wants control of South America. If Bolsonaro Jr wins in Brazil, that could become a reality
author: Steve Bloomfield
summary: The US president has taken credit for far-right victories across Latin America, but those wins have had more to do with fears of gang crime than his meddling, says journalist Steve Bloomfield
body_text: Donald Trump has enjoyed very few foreign policy victories since returning to power. From failed wars to failed peace processes, his second term in office has been marked by one costly blunder on the world stage after another. In Latin America, though, the US president has a different story to tell. His administration’s national security strategy outlined how the US wanted to “restore American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere”. It was a brazen document, laying out how his government would interfere in the political life of countries it considered part of its sphere of influence, rewarding governments and movements that are “broadly aligned with our principles and strategy”. To this end, Trump bailed out Argentina to the tune of $40bn and threatened to withdraw the funding if President Javier Milei’s party lost the midterm elections. In Colombia, he repeatedly bullied and threatened the leftwing president, Gustavo Petro, hitting him with personal sanctions and accusing him of being an “illegal drug leader”. And most dramatically, he invaded Venezuela and kidnapped its president. The day after Nicolás Maduro was brought to the US, the state department posted a picture of Trump above the slogan “This is OUR hemisphere”. Over the past 18 months, seven rightwing or far-right candidates have won presidential elections across Latin America. In most of them, Trump openly backed the winning candidate. “We’re doing very well in South America,” Trump said last month. “Lots of people that I got elected.” This weekend, he will be hoping to add the greatest prize of all: Brazil, South America’s biggest country and its largest economy. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, is neck and neck with the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. If he wins, Trump wins – and the hemisphere really will be his. The White House has not simply been watching the election from afar. Since Trump returned to power in January 2025, administration officials and Maga-world allies have been doing what they can to damage Lula and boost the Bolsonaros. Initially, the aim of the support was to keep Jair Bolsonaro out of jail. Like Trump, he had not accepted defeat at the ballot box when he lost in the 2022 general election. Like Trump, his supporters stormed government buildings. But there were two crucial differences in Brazil – the seriousness of Bolsonaro’s attempt to hold on to power, and the determination of Brazilians that he should be held to account. Investigators uncovered a sprawling conspiracy led by Bolsonaro and seven of his closest allies to keep him in power. It included an astonishing plot to kill Lula and his running mate, as well as a supreme court judge. A draft decree had been written that would overturn the result. The military would step in and ensure Bolosnaro returned to power. But the plot failed and Bolsonaro and allies, including his defence minister and the navy chief, were arrested and put on trial. In response, Trump threatened in July 2025 to impose a 50% tariff on all imports from Brazil, arguing the case against Bolsonaro was a “witch hunt”. This blatant attempt at interfering in the judicial procedure of another country backfired. Lula made clear he wouldn’t bow to US pressure, the trial went ahead and Bolsonaro was found guilty and sentenced to 27 years in prison. Lula also received a bump in the polls after standing up to Trump. In July, as the election campaign was kicking into gear, Trump tried his tariff trick again, imposing a new 25% rate on some Brazilian goods. The state department then tried to dispatch two officials to Brazil to investigate “electoral integrity” – Brazil denied them visas, accusing the officials of coming to “meddle in Brazil’s elections”. In the final weeks of the campaign, Lula has leaned into those accusations. A recent advert accused Flávio Bolsonaro of being “Trump’s candidate” and said the US president wants “to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust”. What remains unclear is whether the White House’s strategy in Brazil is working. “Some in Brazil joke that Lula’s most effective surrogate is Trump,” Brian Winter, editor in chief of Americas Quarterly, told me. Indeed, while Latin American countries have undoubtedly moved to the right in the past 18 months, US interference, despite Trump’s boasts, has arguably had little direct impact. In Peru and Chile, the Trump-aligned candidates were careful not to seek his endorsement for fear it would cause more trouble than it was worth. In Bolivia, the leftwing Mas government was responsible for its own downfall, winning just 3.16% in last year’s election after 20 years of increasingly chaotic rule. The biggest reason countries have moved to the right has nothing to do with the US and everything to do with safety and security at home. Organised crime gangs, many of them linked to drug trafficking, are increasing in power. As Crisis Group put it in a report last year, while drug-related organised crime has been a problem across the continent for decades, “never has it spread so wide, and rarely has it penetrated so deeply into states and communities”. The failure of leftwing governments to deal with the problem has hurt them more than Trump’s attempts at interference. If there is a foreign president whose policies are having an influence on Latin America, it’s El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. His authoritarian clampdown, which has involved arresting tens of thousands of people, mostly without legal process, has become a model for other rightwing leaders in countries beset by gang and drug cartel-related violence. Democracy has been eroded and human rights trampled upon, but Bukele claims that his strategy – best described as “security populism” – has turned one of the most violent countries in the world into one of the safest. Other rightwing populists have found success in vowing to emulate him. In Brazil, Flávio Bolsonaro has made a crackdown on drug cartels and organised crime gangs the centrepiece of his campaign. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people,” he said at a recent campaign stop, vowing to chemically castrate rapists and reduce the age of criminal responsibility. On this issue, Trump may have an influence. The US decision in May to designate two criminal organisations – the Red Command and First Capital Command (PCC) – as terrorist organisations has put Lula on the back foot. Bolsonaro has campaigned relentlessly on the issue, accusing Lula of weakness. Lula has talked about targeting the crime boss “who lives in a penthouse”, but has been more comfortable campaigning on improvements he wants to make in education and health. Bolsonaro Jr, should he win, will almost certainly sign Brazil up to Trump’s Shield of the Americas, a coalition of 18 rightwing Latin American and Caribbean heads of state that promises to use “lethal military force to destroy the sinister cartels and terrorist networks”. Trump arguably paved the way for this new generation of Latin American political leader. His first victory in 2016 showed that posing as an outsider, using coarse language and embracing authoritarianism could be popular. Jair Bolsonaro was the first to emulate him, embracing the “Trump of the Tropics” tag. If Flávio Bolsonaro wins this month – either on Sunday or in the probable second round on 25 October – Trump’s ideology will dominate the continent. It is likely to outlast the man himself. The rise of organised crime has spread fear across the continent and, at the moment, the security populists are the only ones who voters believe have the answer. As long as that remains, the right’s grip on Latin America will only get stronger, regardless of who is in the White House. Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

title: Republicans say they hate communists. So why do they like Donald Trump?
author: Eduardo Porter
summary: Trump supporters may be surprised to learn the state takeover of means of production is not driven by the left
body_text: Americans will never accept the Democratic party’s slide to the left, or so desperate Republicans are hoping. With the midterm elections fast upon us, Zohran Mamdani’s promise of a few city-run bodegas in New York City will scare the bejeezus out of middle America. Disgust over the democratic socialists’ unicorn-and-puppy promises of a world without capitalism will keep the Republicans in power. Leading the charge against the new reds-under-the-bed is Donald Trump. “Together, we will defeat communism,” Trump promised in his recent TV ads. Trump’s supporters might be surprised to discover that the United States is, indeed, sliding in the direction of a command and control economy. But the state takeover of the means of production is not being driven by the left. The grab for the US’s productive resources is the project of none other than Trump – who, it’s a fair guess, has never read Lenin. The latest evidence comes in data crunched by the V-Dem project in Sweden, which measures the erosion of democracy around the world. It built a scale to gauge “state ownership of the economy”. As noted by Cullen Hendrix from the Peterson Institute for International Economics, from 2002 to 2024, the US ranked among the four countries with the least state control. In 2025, the first year of Trump’s second term, it dropped from second place to 16th. By November of last year, the Trump administration had spent more than $10bn taking stakes in companies he deemed essential for national security, from Intel to a range of ventures mining for critical minerals. It also acquired an option to take a stake in Westinghouse, which makes nuclear reactors. And it blackmailed Nippon Steel into granting Trump’s Washington a “golden share” in exchange for the go-ahead to purchase US Steel. To be fair, Trump’s acquisitiveness notwithstanding, the US is not even close to flirting with the flavor of socialism favored by the Soviet Union and its satellites in the second half of the 20th century. By the V-Dem accounting, Washington’s stake in the economy is still smaller than in 163 countries. Government-run companies are a standard feature in many market economies. The Norwegian government has a majority stake in its massive oil company, which puts the country in 18th place. Even “communist” countries are pretty capitalist: private companies contribute 60% of China’s GDP. And in a geopolitical landscape shaped by competition with China, there is a reasonable case to be made for Washington to take equity stakes in industries that are critical for American leadership and security, and which might not develop autonomously in competition with rivals heavily subsidized by Beijing. Yet Trump’s wanton lunge for private assets lacks the discipline required for this kind of strategic positioning. The president’s statist leanings mark a dramatic break with the market-focused presidencies of his recent predecessors, Democrat and Republican. The question is, what motivates him? His appetites are embedded in a body of thought that is skeptical, if not outright hostile, towards essential building blocks of the global market economy. He has pushed back against globalization since his first term in office, seemingly drawn to the Marxist-inspired dependency theory, which washed across Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s proposing protectionism and state industrial policy as a path to economic development. His lust to control the economy is there for all to see. Though the supreme court already slapped down his attempt to take over trade policy from Congress, he is still threatening to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT”. His promise to give $5,000 to every American if Republicans maintain control of Congress in November’s elections underscores how he views the state’s coffers as his private piggy bank. Even his commie-bashing ads were paid for by taxpayer dollars. Still, he clearly has no interest in the dictatorship of the proletariat, caring little if at all for the fate of the downtrodden. His preferred flavor of redistribution takes from those on the bottom to give to those on the top. If anything, Trump reminds us that socialism is not the only ideological justification for state projects to take control over resources and wealth. Watching the US president bow to Xi Jinping last week, it’s tempting to think that Trump wants to emulate China’s leader. Xi gets to rule unimpeded over more than one billion Chinese. He gets to shape China’s society and economy at will – purging this rival, raising that sycophant to power. But Xi’s China is too disciplined for Trump. The Chinese leader still relies on hordes of technocrats to execute a coherent strategy aimed to achieve technological superiority. The US president doesn’t have the attention span for this kind of thing. Rather, Trump’s model might be Vladimir Putin, who rules Russia like a fiefdom. Or maybe one of those dictators the US used to support in Latin America during the cold war: Haiti’s Papa Doc Duvalier or Anastasio Somoza in Nicaragua, who saw government as a tool to enrich their families and cement dynasties in power. If nothing else, Trump’s dealings with crypto suggest he views his administration as a road to family riches. Karl Marx may not be Trump’s guiding light. But his writings can help understand Trump’s place in history. Marx proposes that his tome The 18th Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, about the 1851 coup that brought Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte to power in France, was meant to “demonstrate how the class struggle in France created circumstances and relationships that made it possible for a grotesque mediocrity to play a hero’s part”. Americans may be grateful that their most recent class struggles didn’t produce a homegrown Lenin. But they did deliver Donald Trump. Perhaps this does not condemn the US to an autocratic future. Hendrix points out that while Trump “clearly wants to be king”, the US’s political economy may not let him. Putin managed to establish autocratic rule over a fairly primitive, oil-based economy. This kind of control “is much harder to achieve in a modern complex economy” such as that of the United States, Hendrix noted. You can’t simply seize the oil to run the place. Though Trump may fail, Americans’ acquiescence as he grabs for power raises a question for those who freak out over Mamdani’s city-run bodegas: why is Trump’s lurch to take over the American economy any better than what they hear from the Democratic Socialists of America? Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

title: Trump sets off on midterm blitz – are his trademark rallies a liability for Republicans?
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: Rallies have been mainstay of president’s brand but even some in his own party fear voters are sick of the sight of him
body_text: “Get your asses in that car.” That was Donald Trump’s order, he later recalled, to his motorcade after foul weather grounded Air Force One in Texas on Thursday. The 85-mile dash to Oklahoma at nearly 100mph was proof that nothing can keep Trump from a Trump rally. Which might not be the good news for Republicans it once was. As the US president embarked on a 32-day campaign blitz aimed at helping them defend narrow congressional majorities in next month’s midterms, some fear that he is driving them towards an electoral wipeout. Trump’s approval rating is at an all-time low. Voters are angry about the cost of living, the Iran war and excessive immigration crackdowns. Some Republicans are moving to distance themselves from a man they now see as more liability than asset. Wherever he turns, the outlook is grim as he sets off on an expected schedule of five to seven rallies a week. “They’ve been a mainstay of his brand, but they’re also the engine of his doom,” Steve Schmidt, a political strategist, said of Trump’s signature campaign rallies. “Everybody knows the obvious, which is that his presence hurts every Republican candidate on the ballot because the race is fundamentally about Trump and the American people are sick and tired of him.” Schmidt added: “He’s surrounded by people who tell him that he’s beloved and that the answer to his problem is to keep talking, to keep performing, to keep doing the rallies, that the answer is more, not less. These rallies have become his lead weight, his proverbial anchor that’s going to drown them all.” Even in a hyper-digital age, Trump’s rallies have shown the enduring power of live performance. The atmosphere, somewhere between cult worship, rock concert and partisan sports event, offers his followers a sense of belonging. Since launching his bid for president in 2015 he has held roughly a thousand of them, though definitions of what counts as a full “rally” can vary. Blake Marnell, a rally regular in a brick-patterned suit resembling Trump’s border wall, was in Oklahoma on Thursday night. He said: “Getting in the motorcade, driving 100 miles an hour to Durant – he’s not gonna let stuff get in his way. He enjoys the rallies. They’re energising for the crowd and for him. It’s a way for him to connect with the grassroots.” Once in Durant, Trump again basked in the adulation of the rally crowd. Having spotted two diehard supporters being interviewed by TV crews outside the venue, he replayed the clip and summoned them on to the main stage. “You can’t miss big, strong, handsome Oklahoma studs,” he said. “Where are you? Come up here!” The pair were white, male and elderly. One, wearing a green Trump cap and grey Trump T-shirt, stepped up to the microphone and said: “Thank you, President Trump, for all you do. Every day you work harder than any American I know.” The other, wearing a red Make America Great Again cap and red T-shirt, said: “Absolute honour of a lifetime to be with the greatest president this country has ever had!” Marnell, from San Diego, California, loved this example of Trump showmanship and dismissed the notion that his rallies are hurting rather than helping Republicans. “That’s ridiculous. How many years now have we heard critics saying that Trump is done, the end is near, the walls are closing in, this is the beginning of the end, he can’t possibly win. “They’ve written him off so many times, I don’t know why people listen when they say things like that. It makes no sense to me. This election is, to an extent larger than normal, going to be swayed by turnout and so turnout is the goal of these rallies.” Yet beneath the carnival atmosphere in Oklahoma lay an undercurrent of anxiety and a new vulnerability. At one point Trump entreated the audience, “Pretend I’m running, please,” and begged them to contact friends and relatives. He openly admitted the Republican party’s precarious footing across the national map. “We’re worried about Michigan, we’re worried about Texas, we’re worried about a few states.” He has cause to be worried. A recent survey by the Associated Press-Norc Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of US adults approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy – a new low. Only about three in 10 approve of how he is handling his job as president. In a striking sign of trouble, a major Republican political action committee has reportedly pulled back its spending in North Carolina, the only battleground state Trump won in all three of his presidential bids, diverting its resources instead to ruby red Kansas. Even among dedicated fans who have followed him around the country and become known as “front-row Joes” at his rallies, doubts are creeping in. Trisha Hope, a “front-row Joe” who once bought an RV and published a book of Trump’s tweets to fund her travel, recently declared him a “fraud and liar”. Speaking to Politico, Hope cited Trump’s abrupt dismissal of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation during a cabinet meeting, as well as his unfulfilled promises regarding the war in Iran. “If we do lose the midterms and he is impeached again, I will be walking the halls of Congress in support of that impeachment,” she said. But when confronted with the negative numbers, the president has sounded like a man in denial, preferring to discuss his architectural projects in Washington including a new White House ballroom. At his stop in Denton, north-west of Dallas, Texas, earlier on Thursday, he insisted that inflation was entirely the fault of Joe Biden as he dismissed concerns about everyday living costs. “We have the greatest numbers of any president in the history of our country, and I can’t get the word out,” Trump lamented to workers at a truck factory. “Maybe we’re doing a bad job selling it.” John Zogby, an author and pollster, said: “It looks as if he’s very out of touch with the reality of most Americans. Of course, he has spent a lifetime being out of touch and creating that kind of lifestyle for himself.” The 80-year-old’s rally performances have noticeably deteriorated, Zogby argues, marked by rambling digressions that fail to speak to the immediate anxieties of ordinary voters. “Number one, he is tending to digress. He’s not on his best form. But secondly, when he does address affordability, it’s, ‘Wait and see, just a little longer, the war will be over.’ It’s not connecting.” The strain between Trump and Republicans was highlighted this week by a secret audio recording from a high-dollar fundraiser. On the tape, obtained by the New York Times, the Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton – whose Senate campaign has been floundering under the weight of scandals – was overheard candidly admitting to donors that Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas damaged Republican prospects. Paxton admitted: “When we did that convention, it dropped our numbers; everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now? Yeah. It’s not good. I wish there was something we could do to turn that around, but obviously nothing.” At the event in Denton, Trump praised Paxton as one of his “most loyal people”, while jokingly adding: “I have to always remember that because he can be a pain in the ass sometimes, I’ll be honest. Is he here, by the way? Oh, there he is – good. I didn’t even know if he’s here. I don’t care!” The president also insisted: “My heart is in it like never before.” Yet his early campaign schedule has raised eyebrows. He is spending the first five days of October in Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska, all reliable Republican strongholds in recent years. Critics say it shows that he is on the defensive. Schmidt, who worked for Republicans George W Bush and John McCain, observed: “The BS stops on the map. When you’re campaigning in October as a Republican in those states, not only does it mean you’re losing, it means you’re losing in a biblical sense, an end-times sense. The reality is that there’s no safe Republican anywhere in the country. That’s why he’s there.” Generic congressional polls show Democrats holding a lead approaching double digits, raising the spectre of a “blue wave” that could sweep away Republican majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. A Republican official said: “We’re not going to send Potus to areas where it would be hurtful to our candidates.” For Democrats, Trump’s tour through safe conservative territory is an open admission of weakness. Michelle Lujan Grisham, the governor of New Mexico, suggested that reminding voters of Trump’s presidency in the final weeks of the campaign is a strategic blunder on his part. “In those places, I would hope that it hurts,” she said. “People are angry and you shouldn’t be reminding them. So, I’m going to say go ahead. Maybe he should spend some more time in Texas.” Lujan Grisham criticised Trump’s second term, pointing to what she described as a litany of broken promises, economic mismanagement and foreign policy overreach. “He promised to deliver for Americans and he did none of the above. He’s in a war that nobody wants in Iran that he can’t get out of. He’s doing nothing for inflation; he’s making it worse. And he certainly isn’t addressing affordability.” She singled out the administration’s aggressive policies under Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which she described as a major moral and political liability for the White House. “ICE of course is a huge liability for the White House and this administration, just given they continue to detain both lawfully present individuals and Americans. We’ve had Americans lose their lives, and we’ve devastated whole communities and families. He’s in real trouble.” Trump hopes the campaign rallies that featured so prominently in his victories in 2016 and 2024 will do the trick again on behalf of Republicans in 2026. They will also feed his appetite for the cheering faithful that have become central to his political identity. Schmidt sees a parallel with the faded Hollywood star from one of Trump’s favourite films, Sunset Boulevard. “He needs attention like Norma Desmond and that’s who he’s become here at the nadir of his presidency as he moves from king of the hill into decrepit lame duck. All of the Führer rallies in the red states don’t change the fact. There’s no amount of money that could be spent on his behalf, no amount of rallies, nothing that can save him from the judgment that’s coming down on his head.”

title: Polls close in first round of Brazil’s high-stakes presidential election
author: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
summary: Leftwing incumbent Lula trying to fight off close rival Flávio Bolsonaro, far-right son of jailed ex-president
body_text: The polls have closed in the first round of Brazil’s highly polarised and high-stakes presidential election that could change not only the direction of Latin America’s largest country but that of the entire region. The election pits the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump and the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election attempt. Late on Sunday Bolsonaro was leading Lula in partial results. With results in from almost 65% of the country, Bolsonaro had 49.8% to Lula’s 42.25%, while several other candidates stood in the single digits. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable. In recent days both have focused on persuading undecided voters in hopes of reaching 50% plus one vote; if neither does, there will be a runoff on 25 October. Brazil is one of the few Latin American countries that still has a leftwing government after a wave of rightwing and far-right electoral victories across the region and the US takeover of Venezuela after the capture of Nicolás Maduro. The 80-year-old Lula has positioned himself as one of the last regional leaders still willing to say no to Trump, and has recently accused the US president of trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour. Like his father, who was Brazil’s president during Trump’s first term, Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, frequently praises the US president and has pledged to join the US-led anti-drug-cartel coalition that has killed dozens of people in airstrikes and carried out military operations across the region. Voting on Sunday morning in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his political career began nearly half a century ago, Lula said: “People will have to choose between strengthening democracy and barbarism.” The incumbent played down polls released on Saturday that showed the race was wide open – they suggested either candidate could finish ahead and force a runoff, or even win outright on Sunday. “The poll that matters will be carried out today,” he said. Flávio Bolsonaro, who voted in Rio de Janeiro’s north zone, urged supporters of other rightwing candidates to switch to him in a “protest vote”. “Our internal polls show people who would have voted for other candidates, who are also against Lula, already voting for Flávio Bolsonaro … I hope it’s enough to give us victory in the first round,” he said. Claudinei Ferreira Viana, 45, a workshop manager in Pinhais in Paraná state, is one of the senator’s supporters. “My first choice would be Jair Bolsonaro but, since he is under house arrest and there is no other rightwing candidate strong enough to take on the current president, I’m going with Flávio,” he said. At the beginning of the year, polls suggested Bolsonaro voters would have preferred a ticket led by the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, or the former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro. But the former president chose his eldest son. The campaign was also marked by a scandal in which the senator was caught on tape asking a banker accused of corruption for $26.8m (£20m) to fund a film about his father, as well as speculation that Bolsonaro might strip the country’s widely cherished patron saint of her status, but he has nevertheless remained highly competitive. For many analysts, that reflects a combination of a straightforward transfer of his father’s voter base – Jair Bolsonaro lost to Lula by less than two percentage points in 2022 – and an anti-Lula vote, with the president still facing high rejection rates despite strong social and economic indicators. The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, as well as a scandal involving supreme court justices, which, despite having no connection to Lula, is seen as fuelling an “anti-system” vote and by extension an anti-incumbent one. Brazilians will also elect 27 state governors, members of state legislatures, all 513 federal congress members and 54 of the country’s 81 senators in Sunday’s vote. AMC, 40, who asked to be identified only by her initials because she fears reprisals from the local conservative government where she works in the interior of Amazonas state, will vote for Lula on Sunday “because of the many programmes he created to support the most vulnerable groups”. “Jair Bolsonaro weakened protections for Indigenous peoples, and everything Lula has done over the past four years to strengthen those protections and protect the Amazon would be seriously threatened if his son came to power,” she said.

title: Medicare for All remains key pressure point for Democrats before midterms
author: Jessica Glenza
summary: The idea of universal health coverage in the US is embraced by party’s left but often considered a liability by centrists
body_text: Last week, 1,500 unionized nurses gathered in a large conference room at the Marriott Marquis in San Francisco to cheer for a cause they’ve championed for years: Medicare for All. Considered a radical and even fringe idea for decades, interest in sweeping healthcare reform has surged as progressive Democrats have won a series of primary victories before November’s crucial midterm elections. Most prominent among its advocates is Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic US Senate nominee from Michigan, who took the lectern before the nurses. “Medicare for who?” asked El-Sayed. “All!” the crowd shouted back. El-Sayed went on to describe why he wrote a book about Medicare for All: to answer questions about “the very simple idea that in the richest, most powerful country in the world you should not have to suffer for your healthcare”. As progressive candidates like El-Sayed prevail in primaries, and the Democratic party stresses unity in the face of its midterm challenge to Republicans, Medicare for All remains a pressure point – embraced by the party’s left but often considered a liability by centrists. “There’s too many unnecessary illnesses and unnecessary costs,” said Michelle Gutierrez Vo, president of the California Nurses Association, the National Nurses Organizing Committee and vice-president of National Nurses United – all unions that represent nurses attending the San Francisco conference. “What are we doing?” These unions have advocated for Medicare for All for years, and watched interest swell as candidates like El-Sayed picked up steam. By contrast, centrist Democrat groups, such as Third Way, consider Medicare for All an unattainable albatross. “Medicare for All has a lot of political and substantive issues,” said Gabe Horwitz, senior vice-president for the economic program at Third Way. The party is unanimous in opposition to the $1tn in healthcare cuts made by Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Democrats have taken to calling the “big, ugly bill”. The legislation is expected to result in an additional 16 million people becoming uninsured by 2034. “We want to get everyone insured, we want to lower costs and want to make care easier to use,” said Horwitz, who also said the party acknowledges that it needs to make reforms for people struggling to afford employer-sponsored health insurance. “I don’t know if there’s one Democrat in the party who wouldn’t agree with that. “There is unanimity in the goals – the ends – there’s just not necessarily unanimity in the means to get there,” said Horwitz. This divide was most recently evident in an 84-page memo sent to Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, from the cost-of-living healthcare working group. “Members of the Democratic Caucus hold a diversity of views on how to achieve universal coverage,” the memo read, “including Medicare for All” and a wide range of other more incremental policies. Centrist Democrats have sought to answer the gnawing question of what to do about soaring healthcare costs and reviled insurance company practices by proposing incremental reform – a strategy that builds off the Affordable Care Act (ACA) passed by the Obama administration. A healthcare bill of rights, more government subsidies to health insurance companies to offset costs to consumers, and some version of a “public option”, or a government-sponsored health insurance plan that people could buy into. For years, the party’s left has offered a proposition at once seen as radical by US standards and typical by many of the world’s industrialized democracies: a single-payer health system sponsored by the government. “All Democrats from 1948 on have been in favor of universal healthcare – that’s been in every democratic platform since literally Harry Truman,” said Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, whose recent analysis of primary victories across the political spectrum found mainstream candidates continue to win. “That’s not the issue – the issue is how do you do it.” What’s more, said Kamarck, the issue is one likely to simmer long past the primaries. US health reform is a virtual nonstarter while Republicans hold the Oval Office. But if Democrats won a “trifecta” in 2028, “then this is going to be a really big issue”. At present, the US health system is a patchwork of different insurers, or “payers”, all of which are subsidized by US taxpayers. Four large programs dominate the mix: employer-sponsored health insurance covers almost half of Americans (48% of the population), Medicare covers people older than 65 (14.8%), Medicaid covers low-income and disabled people (20.4%) and Obamacare allows people to buy private insurance as individuals (6.6%), all according to Kaiser Family Foundation. About 27 million people (8.2%) lack insurance entirely. About one in four Americans are “underinsured”, or have high health costs relative to their incomes. Across these various programs, the US government plans to spend $33.6tn through 2034. This includes subsidies for the private insurance Americans get through their jobs, for which employers receive a tax break. That is equal to 7.4% of gross domestic product. As a point of reference, the United Kingdom spends about 11.9% of GDP to insure everyone in the country, according to the Commonwealth Fund. Total US health spending is 18% of GDP – far more than comparable countries. Although the slogan Medicare for All has a somewhat loose definition, a bill repeatedly introduced in Congress provides for a Medicare-style single-payer system, with universal health coverage. Private insurers would be barred from duplicating services. Because healthcare as an industry represents 18% of US gross domestic product (GDP), and such a dramatic transition would inevitably disrupt thousands of jobs, the bill also provides for temporary worker compensation. But for advocates of Medicare for All, such as Gutierrez Vo, anything else is, “a patch-up – it’s not a fix”. “Just like nurses take care of the whole patient– that’s like taking care of a leg and letting the rest be ill,” he said. “That’s silly.”

title: Before Cornell turmoil, successive US administrations seesawed in attitudes towards campus assaults
author: Eric Berger
summary: Federal government has struggled to affect lasting change in how accusers and accused are treated in higher education
body_text: Amid renewed concerns about sexual assault on US college campuses following allegations that a student was gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity, the Trump administration last week formally reversed measures from recent Democratic presidents concerning how schools should investigate such claims. A federal judge had already in January 2025 struck down Biden-era regulations that expanded Title IX, the federal law prohibiting sex discrimination in education. The Democratic president tried to undo regulations established during Trump’s first term that, contrary to guidance from the Obama administration, required schools to adjudicate sexual misconduct claims through live hearings. The back-and-forth between successive Democratic and Republican administrations, stakeholders on both the left and right say, has created a chaotic situation in the US in which the federal government has struggled to effect lasting change in how accusers and accused are treated in higher education when it comes to sexual assault allegations. “To prevent this kind of ping-ponging between administrations, we need to see a congressional fix,” Shiwali Patel, senior director of education justice at the National Women’s Law Center, who opposes the Trump Title IX rule. “How do we ensure that these protections are made clear in a way that an administration cannot keep going back and forth depending on what their political agenda is?” In 2011, the Department of Education, under Obama, issued what became known as the “Dear Colleague” letter, which stated that the agency was “deeply concerned” about a report stating that one in five women at two universities reported experiencing a completed or attempted sexual assault since entering college. The letter stated that the department was “committed to ensuring that all students feel safe in their school, so that they have the opportunity to benefit fully from the school’s programs and activities” and included guidance on how schools should handle sexual misconduct allegations In 2014, the department provided more specific directions, including that schools should use a “preponderance of evidence” standard, meaning that it was “more likely than not” sexual harassment or violence occurred rather than the stricter “clear and convincing evidence” standard many schools used. The White House also discouraged schools from allowing parties in a hearing to question or cross-examine each other and praised a “single investigator” model that provided one person the authority not just to investigate alleged misconduct but to determine guilt and innocence, according to the Brookings Institution. The Obama administration launched more than 300 investigations into schools over their handling of sexual abuse complaints. Catherine Lhamon, the then head of the education department’s office for civil rights (OCR), threatened to cut off federal funding to the schools but never did, according to R Shep Melnick’s book The Transformation of Title IX. The office and 62 schools reached settlements, which included provisions such as agreeing to move to the “preponderance of evidence” standard. Patel, an attorney who worked in the OCR under Obama, said that the guidance did not “force a specific type of investigatory or hearing procedure. It focused on fairness for both parties.” The directives concerning how schools should handle hearings was intended to show schools that there are “different ways of conducting impartial hearings and investigations and questioning that is not retraumatizing” for the complainants, Patel said. But critics said the administration had overreached. Students filed hundreds of lawsuits alleging that their due process had been violated in campus judicial proceedings, according to the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, a free-speech advocacy group. The single-investigator model is problematic because it empowers just one person “who might have their own biases or blind spots or just might miss things because they are just a single person”, said Tyler Coward, the foundation’s lead counsel of government affairs. “Empowering one person to do all that is an enormous threat to due process, and that is why we don’t tolerate it in our criminal justice system.” When Trump first took office in 2017, his education secretary, Betsy DeVos, rescinded the Obama administration’s guidance and issued a new Title IX rule for how colleges should handle sexual misconduct complaints. The institutions should not use a single-investigator model and should hold a live hearing in which a party adviser, like an attorney, but not the parties themselves, can conduct cross-examinations, the rule stated. The schools could also use either the “preponderance of evidence” or the “clear and convincing evidence” standards. After Biden took office in 2021, his administration tried to reverse many of those measures. Its new rule allowed colleges to use a single-investigator model and no longer required schools to hold live hearings. But courts blocked the rule from taking effect, and in January 2025, days before Trump again took office, a judge struck it down. The Trump administration immediately started using the 2020 rule and this week formally restored it. The rule, as compared with the one from Biden, also narrowed the definition of what is considered sexual harassment. “The Trump rules really fall very short for many students because they really don’t cover the full scope of sexual violence and harassment that students can experience on campus and should deserve to get support around from their schools,” said Emma Grasso Levine, senior manager of Title IX policy and programs at Advocates for Youth, which aims to protect rights to bodily autonomy and sexual health. Melnick, however, argues that the Trump rule prevents universities from “really having kangaroo courts”. “It’s one of the few things from the first Trump administration that I would say they did a pretty thorough job,” said Melnick, a Boston College professor of American politics. This might not be the end of the battle. Like Patel, Robert Eitel, who served as senior counselor to the education secretary during the first Trump administration, said he did not think the back-and-forth will stop until Congress passes a law mandating what institutions must do with such claims. There has never been an opportunity for these “due process provisions to come into full force and effect”, said Eitel, who co-founded the Defense of Freedom Institute. While such conservative groups applaud the measures taken by Trump, much of the public is again questioning whether schools are doing enough to stop sexual assault and hold alleged perpetrators accountable. At Cornell University, seven Chi Phi fraternity members are accused of raping a female student in 2024. “Free pussy upstairs,” a message in a Snapchat group called Chi Phi Actives stated. The district attorney in Ithaca, New York, stated that he did not file charges when the alleged victim reported the event to police in 2024 because she described her drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual. But she has since filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell and the fraternity members over rape allegations, and the district attorney said he is now reopening the investigation. “Individuals who are accused of committing a crime must be prosecuted based upon evidence and not public opinion, especially not public opinion based upon false information,” the district attorney stated in a letter explaining the decision. “However, recognizing that the process of healing from trauma is personal and different for every human, my office has reopened this investigation.” The Ithaca mayor also issued a statement arguing that Cornell had “failed to hold the perpetrators to account” and called for a moratorium on all student activities, including Greek life. The Cornell story “should hopefully raise alarm for anyone who has not been thinking that this is such a huge and gross problem”, Patel said “This is a cultural issue because there needs to be a lot more education. There needs to be a lot more institutional accountability.” Cornell has said it took the reports of assault “very seriously” and “moved promptly to initiate its Title IX process”. • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html
