title: Saturday Night Live: Dakota Johnson struggles through weak episode as Taylor Swift gatecrashes
author: Zach Vasquez
summary: The Verity star’s awkwardness with live comedy is matched with similarly sub-par writing in an episode featuring a surprise cameo from her superstar friend
body_text: Saturday Night Live kicks off the second episode of its new season at RNC headquarters. With the midterms looking bleak for Republicans, strategists bring out some heavy hitters to record TV ads. Marco Rubio (Marcello Hernández) delivers a message in Spanish putting all of the blame on Trump (“Oh my God! He tricked us!”); a comatose Mitch McConnell (Mikey Day) is rolled in to flash the peace sign; and Vice-President JD Vance (Jeremy Culhane) tries to make his pitch for 2028, only to be laughed out of the room. Secretary of war Pete Hegseth (Colin Jost) barges in, chugging “Spider-Man’s new non-alcoholic bitch beer” to demand voters “do the gayest thing ever and vote”. Finally, president Trump (James Austin Johnson) interrupts to deliver a rambling diatribe, promising checks for five grand to voters if they re-elect Republicans (“that’s not a bribe because I have no intention to follow through on that promise”), test out some terrible new slogans (“imagination makes a Maga nation”), and record victory and concession messages, both of which are the same: “We did it, we won!” A much better cold open than last week, if still wanting. The show relied a little too heavily of Jost’s Hegseth last season, but the passage of time makes for a fun return here. Dakota Johnson hosts for the second time. The actor will celebrate her birthday at the stroke of midnight by doing the same thing she does every year: “Stand in midtown in a tight-ass latex dress looking for attention.” She devotes most of her monologue making self-deprecating jokes about her high-profile failed relationships with musicians, before her BFF Taylor Swift joins her on stage, playing reluctant therapist to the romantically-challenged star. Swift’s entrance gets a huge pop from the studio audience, but the jokes elicit little more than chuckles. Then, Johnson plays Elizabeth Banks, host of the game show Press Your Luck. Players spin a digital wheel for prizes, trying to avoid little red trouble maker The Whammy, who erases their points. Overexcited contestant Sherri (Ashley Padilla) immediately scores the million dollar prize, but stupidly continues on, only to land on the Whammy and lose it all. The same thing happens again and again, much to the chagrin of Banks and the other contestants. This is all yelling. Mean Scary Girlfriend is a cruel, icy partner who tells helpless guys the harsh truth, making their lives both easier and way, way more stressful. Not particularly funny, but a good use of Johnson’s sexy ice queen demeanor. At a hospital cafeteria, a trio of nurses spread work gossip until they’re interrupted by nerdy Eric from legal (Culhane), who uses the dish sesh to reveal sad information about himself (“I heard Eric from legal has an AI girlfriend – had, she killed herself”). The premise is promising, but it goes nowhere and quickly sputters out. This is followed by a commercial for the Glunt, the first “gun for women”. It’s a pink sidearm in the shape of a vagina, with a “hard to find” trigger and available “at the opposite of Dick’s Sporting Goods”. This one is over and done with before you even realize it. On a new Game of Thrones spin-off, Johnson and Ben Marshall play members of the royal court, whose attempts to get it on “brother-style” are continually interrupted by her fire breathing dragon, who remains in their bed chamber and likes to watch. There’s some impressive animatronics on display, but every joke falls completely flat. Indie rockers Turnstile bring some much needed energy to the show with their first set of the night, then its on to Weekend Update. Michael Che and Jost take a page from classic Late Night with Conan O’Brian’s playbook, touching on the Cornell rape case by way of Che solemnly chastising men who don’t hold predators accountable while the camera tellingly lingers on a guilty-looking Jost. The segment’s first guests are Jason and Link, the protagonists of the highly-anticipated new Grand Theft Auto and Zelda video games, respectively. The former promises “destruction, chaos, and sex”, while the latter boasts “TMPNG: too many puzzles, no guns.” Day follows up his show-stealing performance last week with another bombastic turn as the dweeby Link, getting his fellow cast members to break at just about every line. Featured player Kam Patterson pretends to be a proud “Gleek”, ecstatic over the news that Glee is coming back to TV, before Che tells him, “You don’t have to say yes to every idea the white writers pitch to you.” Then, Che welcomes on Debbie the Matchmaker (Sarah Sherman), who tries to set him up with other hopeless singles, including a phonebook’s worth of ex-felons, author and transphobe JK Rowling, a ghost, Mrs Potato Head, “the girl who crapped her pants during the Chinese marathon”, and, finally, herself. Sherman is at her bizarre best here, and its fun to see her playing off/tormenting Che instead of Jost for a change, although it feels like a missed opportunity to not include Johnson, considering she recently played a matchmaker in the popular film Materialists. At a middle school girl sleepover, three tweens watch a series of get ready with me videos on TikTok. They land on Colorado Vicky, an unwell influencer who shares insane beauty tips while getting 51/50’d and performing self-lobotomies. Just as unwell is the host girl’s dead-eyed, suicidal father (“he’s just in a funk because mom left, his boss found his Sailor Moon costume, and he just found out Draft Kings is real money”). At first, the sketch seems unfocused, but both threads are tied together satisfactorily. An episode of the TV series Amazing Tales of Truth sees a young girl (Veronika Slowikowska) attempt to bring her dying father out of a coma by singing Somewhere Over the Rainbow. It does not work. Mean and quick, this seems designed to show off Sowikowska’s impressive pipes more than anything else. And with that, the show comes to an abrupt end. Fitting, considered how rushed almost every sketch felt. Johnson is gifted a birthday cake for the curtain call, which is a nice gesture. Unfortunately, the atmosphere more resembles a wake than a party. Johnson, a talented screen actor, just does not have the chops for live comedy, and she was further hampered by the weak writing. With the exception of Day and Sherman’s turn on Update and Turnstile’s performances, this episode was a real energy vacuum.

title: After a deadly paper mill explosion, a community in Washington state looks to a key House race
author: Lok Darjee
summary: In a district shaken by the deaths of 11 workers, Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez faces a stiff challenge to keep her seat
body_text: On a misty morning in May in south-west Washington state, Laura Oltmann, a 41-year-old dietitian, had barely clocked in when an unfamiliar overhead announcement echoed through the hospital. “We get overhead pages for different types of emergencies. But this one, we don’t get very often,” recalled Oltmann. Doctors, nurses and staff began guessing what could have happened. Perhaps it was a train derailment. Maybe a major highway crash. As the speculation grew, so did the uncertainty. Staff started calling one another. The answer shook them all. “Someone mentioned there had been an explosion at this plant, and that we were probably going to be getting some patients from there,” Oltmann said. Forty miles south, in the port city of Longview, residents had awakened to a thunderous boom. At approximately 7.18am, as workers changed shifts at a paper mill company, Nippon Dynawave Packaging, a tank of white liquor, a caustic chemical used in the paper-making process, imploded. Hours passed with no explanation of what had caused it or how it could have happened at all, and suspicion began to brew. With roughly a thousand people working at the mill, thousands more were waiting for a phone call. Parents called children. Wives called husbands. Grandparents called grandchildren. “For those that did not get that response,” said Jeff Wilson, a Republican state senator representing Longview, who also sits as the port commissioner, “all they got was silence.” In the end, 11 people were killed in one of Washington state’s deadliest industrial accidents in nearly a century. Nowhere was that impact felt more deeply than in Longview itself, a working-class city of about 38,000 people whose economy and identity have long been tied to the paper industry, shipping and logging. For generations, families have depended on the mills for their livelihoods. The disaster struck at something the city had long regarded as permanent: the mills where generations had gone to work, and helped many send their children to college or put down a down payment on a home. The implosion rippled through nearly every corner of a community affected by mill closures and economic change. Those concerns will probably have an impact at the ballot box. As summer turned toward fall and the leaves along the Columbia River began to turn yellow, memorial services gave way to campaign rallies. The same communities that had gathered around grieving families were preparing for one of the country’s most closely watched House races in November. Nearly two months after the implosion, on 8 July, Wilson still spoke first about the workers, the funerals he had attended, the families and the co-workers who ran toward danger looking for one another. He recalled brothers Tyler and Brad Covington, 27 and 29; he said: “They went to work together. And then they died together.” Before entering politics, Wilson spent more than 23 years cleaning tanks at the Nippon Dynawave mill. In the aftermath of the tragedy, he worked routinely with Democratic congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez’s office as local, state and federal officials responded to the disaster, his role in Olympia intersecting with hers in Washington. Though he declined to endorse her re-election, Wilson credited the Democratic congresswoman with being “present and accountable” and praised her for asking questions rather than “rubber-stamping anything”. For a community divided by many of the same political forces pulling at the rest of the country, the disaster briefly created a sense of togetherness, as the whole community grieved the deaths of many of their neighbors and family members. “Natural disasters will tend to bring people together,” said Mark Alan Smith, a political science professor at the University of Washington who studies American politics and religion. “It’s something people can unify around … across race and class and other divisions.” *** On 4 August, Gluesenkamp Perez and the Republican state senator John Braun advanced from a field of nine to face off for the district’s congressional seat in November. Braun finished first with about 39.7% of the vote to Gluesenkamp Perez’s 36.4%. Brent Hennrich, the progressive Democrat who argued that Gluesenkamp Perez no longer represented many of her party’s voters, took 16.7%. The results exposed the competing pressures facing Gluesenkamp Perez heading into the general election. Braun, who netted a Trump endorsement in April and millions in pro-Trump money, finished ahead of the incumbent. Meanwhile, Hennrich’s showing demonstrated the size of the progressive bloc she will have to contend with in November. Many of those voters remain angry over parts of her vote on the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (Save) Act (which would require proof of citizenship to vote), ICE funding, and a bill restricting how public schools address gender identity. When asked about those direct criticisms of the congresswoman – whom many on the left feel has drifted from the party – her campaign responded with a written statement to the Guardian that cast her independence as the reason south-west Washington should return her to office. “DC has enough career politicians following national agendas,” said her campaign manager, Timothy Gowen. “Southwest Washington deserves an independent representative who delivers real results. Marie will always be loyal to her district first.” The statement did not address questions about her voting record or the primary result. The race stretches far beyond Longview and the nearby city of Battle Ground. Washington’s third congressional district runs from the Pacific coast through the timber towns of the lower Columbia and inland farm country to Vancouver and the fast-growing suburbs north of Portland. Logging, paper mills, agriculture, shipping and manufacturing still shape daily life across much of it, while its politics pull hard in opposite directions. That geography has forced Gluesenkamp Perez to build an unusual coalition. Her political survival has depended partly on voters who do not ordinarily identify with Democrats, including moderates and conservatives drawn to her emphasis on the trades, guns and independence from her party. But that same positioning has alienated Democrats who believe she has moved too far from them. “Two years ago, people reported having to hold their nose and vote for her, because she was better than [former opponent and one-time counter-intelligence official] Joe Kent,” said LaDonna Kirkpatrick, chair of the 18th Legislative District Democrats, speaking in a personal capacity. “But now we’re in a situation where I’m hearing from so many people that even if she wins the primary, they will not vote for her. And the frustration is real. I’m feeling that personally.” Thea Zaine, chair of the 20th Legislative District Democrats, speaks for the bloc of progressive Democrats whose discontent showed up in the primary returns. Her organization was the only Democratic party body in the district to endorse Hennrich. “We believe in protecting immigrants. She’s voted to give more money to ICE,” Zaine said. “She voted to give funding to wars in Iran. And she takes money from Aipac, and she’s voted to fund the genocide in Gaza.” Gluesenkamp Perez’s record on Iran, however, is more complicated than Zaine suggested. The Democratic representative voted for war powers resolutions directing the removal of US forces from the unauthorized war with Iran, while also breaking with most Democrats to support the broader $1.15tn National Defense Authorization Act. For Zaine, those votes have made the choice straightforward. But not every young, left-leaning voter who shares her frustration has reached the same conclusion. Tanner Manley, 25, an incoming law student who lives near Vancouver and describes himself as left-leaning, shares much of the critique. He plans to vote for Gluesenkamp Perez anyway. “Of course, I wish more progressive candidates were viable here, and that Marie would take a clear moral stand on Israel and reject Aipac funding the way she refuses corporate Pac money,” he said. “In another race with different options, I’d likely support a different candidate.” What keeps Manley with her is closer to home. After the Longview disaster, the US Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, the independent federal agency investigating the tank failure at the Longview paper plant, faced elimination under the administration’s proposed budget. In June, Gluesenkamp Perez backed an amendment restoring $14m for the agency, which passed the House appropriations committee with Republican support. “That might not satisfy progressives watching from the other side of the country,” Manley said, “but try telling people in this district that that kind of fight in Congress doesn’t matter.” Neither candidate’s campaign has made the Longview tragedy a centerpiece of the race. A recent poll underscores how little room both candidates have: the survey, conducted by DHM Research for Oregon Public Broadcasting, found Braun at 48% and Gluesenkamp Perez at 47% after undecided voters were asked which candidate they leaned toward, with 5% still undecided. Smith, of the University of Washington, said events that bring communities together can be difficult to translate into partisan advantage. “In order for something like that to affect how people vote, somebody has to channel it,” Smith said. “It’s hard to channel anything where everybody agrees.” That could change, he said, “if you can somehow link your opponent to some negative aspect” of the event. So far, neither campaign has done so. And Wilson praised Gluesenkamp Perez’s handling of the disaster. “She’s been representing, you know, from the federal angle, well on this,” he said. The response also fit the political identity Gluesenkamp Perez has cultivated in south-west Washington, where she has emphasized the trades and the economic pressures facing rural and working-class communities. In an interview with OPB, she described watching the decline of industries that have long sustained towns across the region. “Mill after mill closed in our region,” she said. “It’s just got people really at high anxiety levels.” About three miles north of Nippon Dynawave, at the Pentecostal church where Ron Peterson is pastor, the disaster remains part of the community’s memory. For Peterson, 38, the tragedy had briefly brought together people who otherwise disagreed about much else. But when I asked him about politics, he drew a distinction. “We don’t win politically,” he said. “We win spiritually.” A few miles south, and across a district where the divisions are not only political, Chydell Armijo, 35, mother of two, was thinking about something more immediate. She had little enthusiasm for either political party. What worried her was whether people like her could still build a stable life: whether a small business could survive, whether her children could find opportunity and whether working people could still move up. “I honestly feel like everybody is struggling,” Armijo said. “There is no such thing as middle class any more.” For all the attention on which party will control this congressional seat after November, Armijo saw a divide that would remain regardless of who won. “Our economic system has become difficult, in many ways, for us to climb,” she said.

title: Trump names intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new White House AI czar
author: Ariana Baio
summary: Clayton had said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but also posed ‘a threat’ during his confirmation hearing
body_text: Donald Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, to also serve as the new White House AI czar. Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies, previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Clayton said AI was a “gamechanger” but it also posed “a threat”. “When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton told lawmakers when asked about AI. CBS News was the first to report that Clayton would be appointed White House AI czar. In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”. Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”. Among those reacting on Sunday to Trump’s invoking the term “super intelligence” was the SpaceX chief, Elon Musk. Musk said on his social media platform X that SI was “better” than AI – and that he was renaming his aerospace company’s AI unit from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat who is vice-chair of the Senate select committee on intelligence, cautiously welcomed the appointment of Clayton, while noting that “the administration has resisted meaningful safeguards without offering a serious alternative for addressing the national security risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems”. “I look forward to working with Director Clayton on ensuring the United States stays ahead of China and other adversaries, strengthening the security and resilience of our most advanced AI systems, and establishing rigorous testing and safeguards so that increasingly powerful systems remain secure, reliable, and under human control,” Warner added. In September, Trump announced he was creating an “AI Force” and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development. The announcement came after tech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidly to control and that it could harm humans. The president has largely brushed aside concerns about AI development and the construction of datacenters, which power the technology. Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race. But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – whom he previously promised would be led by a “high IQ” individual. Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns. On Tuesday, Trump and six executives signed an AI accord at the White House, promising to create internal and external monitors to ensure the technology is used as intended and any safety issues are addressed. Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025. David Sacks, the venture capitalist and tech businessman, served as the administration’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he reached his employment limit under his designation as a “special government employee”. Sacks still co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, telling Axios in September that Clayton was “a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.

title: White House defends new press aide who posed with rifle in ‘Fuck Joe Biden’ shirt
author: Robert Mackey
summary: Beni Rae Harmony, 24, has been ‘a trusted voice for the Maga movement’ as a correspondent, White House says
body_text: The White House has defended a newly hired press aide who posed for a holiday photograph in 2021 wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirt and holding a rifle. Beni Rae Harmony, the new assistant White House press secretary, announced on Friday that she was going to work for Donald Trump just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outlet originally created as a video podcast platform for the US president’s former adviser Steve Bannon. According to a LinkedIn profile, Harmony, 24, previously worked as a producer for Jack Posobiec, the far-right Turning Point USA host – and as a press aide “focusing on crisis management” for two far-right Republicans: Congressman Paul Gosar of Arizona and former congressman Matt Gaetz of Florida. In 2021, when Gosar was censured by the US House for posting an animated video that depicted him killing Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and attacking Joe Biden, Harmony recorded an outraged defense of her boss for his YouTube channel. The photograph of Harmony and an older man posing with rifles in matching anti-Biden shirts, in front of Christmas decorations, was reportedly posted on Instagram in November 2021 by Jarome Bell, a far-right Republican who mounted a failed campaign for Congress in 2022. A screenshot of that post, published by the Daily Mirror, shows that it included the caption: “My campaign Public Affairs Director @beniraeharmony is a beast. This is how we roll.” Harmony appeared to verify the authenticity of the photograph in December 2021, when it was shared on social media by an anti-Maga outlet, PatriotTakes, which also identified her as an aide to Gosar. The next day, Harmony replied to the PatriotTakes post of the image with another image of herself, wearing the same shirt in the same location and grinning into the camera. When another social media user posted a sarcastic question about the relationship between the older man and the young woman seen in the image, asking: “Daughter or date?”, Harmony replied with a one-word answer: “Uncle”. Biden at the time was serving his lone term in the Oval Office, and Trump supporters chanting “Fuck Joe Biden” at a Nascar race that autumn inspired a viral meme featuring a variation of the slogan. Harmony did not reply to requests to comment on the photograph. But the White House press office responded with a statement from a deputy press secretary, Anna Kelly, who praised the new hire for her advocacy of Trump’s “Make America great again” movement, while ostensibly covering the president as a journalist. “Beni Rae Harmony has been a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent,” Kelly wrote. “She will be an outstanding addition to President Trump’s communications team as an Assistant Press Secretary – we look forward to having her on board!” Harmony joins a White House press office that has taken unprecedented steps to ensure that the president is surrounded at all times by correspondents from partisan outlets who shower him with praise, and limit or deny access to reporters from nonpartisan outlets who challenge him. Trump has tried to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House entirely, for what he considers overly negative coverage, and his aides now select which outlets are in place to ask him questions, with frequent slots reserved for correspondents who openly support him. Harmony became the White House correspondent for Real America’s Voice after her predecessor, Brian Glenn, fell out of favor with Trump when his partner, Marjorie Taylor Greene, broke with the president and accused him of betraying the Maga movement. Glenn had previously worked hard to advance Trump’s political agenda when invited by the president to ask questions. In 2025, for instance, Glenn pointedly asked Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, why he refused to wear a suit in the Oval Office, a question that inflamed an already volatile encounter. During a press availability on Air Force One last month, Trump approached reporters with a sheaf of papers in his left hand. Harmony asked Trump a series of friendly questions that seemed designed to help him score political points. As TMZ reported on Friday, Associated Press photographs taken during that exchange showed that Harmony’s name was at the top of the first page in the president’s hand, suggesting that he might have been holding her résumé as he took her questions. Harmony achieved a measure of celebrity in the rightwing media in 2025, when she left her job as an on-air host at a local TV station in Springfield, Illinois, after delivering an on-air tribute to the late Charlie Kirk, describing him as her first boss and mentor. The station’s news director denied that Harmony had been suspended over the tribute, as she claimed, and clarified that she had never been a member of its news team, and instead hosted a program run by the channel’s sales department that featured clients who paid to be interviewed on television.

title: Brazil’s presidential race goes to second round as Flávio Bolsonaro leads incumbent Lula
author: Tom Phillips and Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
summary: Far-right challenger and son of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro put in a stronger than expected showing, with Lula calling the result ‘unexpected’
body_text: Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff. With 99.9% of votes counted, the 45-year-old son of the disgraced former president, Jair Bolsonaro, had won 47%, meaning he will now face a 25 October showdown with his 80-year-old rival. Lula received 45.1%. Bolsonaro received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m. Bolsonaro will go into the second round as strong favourite and is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates, who included Ronaldo Caiado, who secured 2.1%, and Renan Santos, who won 2.2%. Brazil’s far-right put in an even stronger than expected showing, with a succession of Bolsonarista politicians winning congressional or gubernatorial races. They included Jair Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, and his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who both won seats in the senate. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, Jair Renan, was elected to the lower house of congress. Bolsonaro’s former infrastructure minister, Tarcísio de Freitas, was reelected as governor of São Paulo, Brazil’s most populous and economically important state. Of the 54 senators elected, 34 were from the right or far right. Flávio Bolsonaro told supporters in the capital, Brasília, that the result signalled “the end of an era” for Lula’s Workers’ party. “Lula has fought seven presidential elections. He’s worried about power. I am worried about the future of Brazil,” he said. Speaking in Sāo Paulo, Lula put a brave face on a difficult night for the left. “We have just had a lesson in Brazilian democracy,” he said. “The result is often unexpected. We can never get everything we wanted. I confess to you that I was convinced I was going to win the election in the first round … But we have a second round.” Lula said Bolsonaro’s “dark past” would become clearer to voters in the lead-up to that vote. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil.” Earlier, as he cast this vote, Lula said Latin America’s largest democracy faced a stark choice, highlighting his adversary’s well-documented links to members of Rio’s underworld, including once employing close relatives of a notorious contract killer. Lula, who became Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002 and was returned to office in 2006 and 2022, is hoping to secure a historic fourth non-consecutive term in this year’s election. Allies of the veteran leftwinger called the election a crucial battle in the fight against a far-right movement that less than four years ago brought chaos to the capital, Brasília, during an unsuccessful attempt to overturn the result of the 2022 election, when Lula beat the incumbent president, Jair Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro hopes winning the presidency will allow him to free his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after refusing to accept he had lost the last election to Lula. Ahead of the election he also called for tactical voting from conservatives who are not supporters of Bolsonarismo, but want to vote Lula out of power. As well as the president, Brazil’s nearly 159 million voters were choosing state parliamentarians, 27 state governors, 513 members of the lower house and 54 members of the 81-seat senate. Bolsonaro supporters made the senate race a priority because senators are the only lawmakers who can impeach supreme court justices – a demand among Bolsonaristas since the court jailed the former president for attempting a coup. Hundreds of leftwingers had gathered at the heart of Laranjeiras, one of Rio’s most leftwing neighbourhoods, hoping to celebrate a Lula win to the sound of samba. But the mood soured and tears were shed as the hours passed and Bolsonaro’s lead over Lula held. “It’s so sad that the Brazilian people … have opted for so much retrogression,” said Marcelo Mac, one of the owners of Miolo, a leftwing bar in Laranjeiras, as the scale of the rightwing advance was confirmed on Sunday night. Mac, 46, voiced perplexity that the son of the man who tried to stage a coup only four years ago was now in pole position to become Brazil’s next leader. “He’s such an abominable guy that he manages to be even worse than his father,” Mac said of Bolsonaro. Beside the bar a yellow flag stamped with Lula’s face carried the slogan: “Turn left”. But Brazil had voted for a turn to the far right. Bolsonaro seemed to have the wind in his sails in the final days before Sunday’s vote, amid public frustration at a cost of living crisis and urban violence. But opinion polls failed to predict the scale of the rightwing triumph. Shop assistant Italo Andrade dos Santos, a 31-year-old Bolsonaro voter, had to keep his celebrations restrained behind the counter of the pharmacy where he was working a Sunday night shift. “I was a little disappointed because I expected Flávio to win in the first round. But I’m happy he’s ahead,” said Santos, adding that he voted “more to get Lula out than for Flávio himself”. Donald Trump became a key election issue, with Lula accusing the US president of trying to swing the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour in order to “colonise” Brazil and appropriate its natural resources. Bolsonaro has vowed to build a closer relationship with Trump, who hopes a rightwing victory will help him further cement US control over Latin America after the election of pro-Trump leaders in a succession of countries, including Chile, Colombia and Peru.

title: One Nation to establish headquarters in multimillion-dollar Brisbane office bought by Gina Rinehart
author: Sarah Basford Canales
summary: Barnaby Joyce defends move, saying party will lease space from mining billionaire’s company at commercial rates
body_text: Barnaby Joyce has defended One Nation’s plan to move its headquarters to a multimillion-dollar Brisbane office building bought by the mining billionaire Gina Rinehart. The One Nation MP said the party’s national head office would pay the market rate to Rinehart’s company to rent the space, claiming there would be no mate’s rates. “I don’t live in her [Gina’s] pocket,” Joyce told News24. “It’s her building, it’s her lease. We’re leasing it off her at commercial rates. “If … we’ve got an individual who’s got money, they should be allowed to spend it as they see fit.” Rinehart’s property investment company Hanrine finalised the purchase of the three-storey office in the Brisbane suburb of Spring Hill last week, Queensland property titles confirm, and as first reported by The Australian newspaper on Monday. The party’s headquarters will relocate there from its Brisbane airport office once a re-fit is complete. Joyce said One Nation would pay for the office space out of the party’s “wallet”. Under parliamentary business resources rules, the commonwealth only pays for office space for elected officials – not political parties. “We can put on the taxpayers’ ticket but we don’t,” Joyce said. “We always make sure we pay for things ourselves as best we can in One Nation. “I think per-person you’ll find us doing a lot more off our own bat and reaching into our own wallet, of the party, rather than putting it on the on the taxpayers’ ticket.” The office is believed to be valued at about $8m, according to The Australian. Property data shows it was last sold for $2.4m in 2003. A spokesperson for Rinehart’s Hancock Prospecting said: “Hancock Prospecting holds a range of commercial property, and this building is one of them. Hancock is not providing free or discounted space to any outside tenant, political or otherwise.” Guardian Australia has contacted One Nation for a response. The building is described in a real estate listing as having “two upper levels of spacious, light-filled office accommodation, complemented by a stunning top-floor balcony offering expansive views of the city, perfect for corporate gatherings”. The ground level “provides a boutique office, showroom and retail space, all connected via an internal lift and direct access to 10 secure onsite car parks”. The ads reads: “The building provides quick and convenient access to the Brisbane CBD and Golden Triangle, while being perfectly positioned within the rapidly evolving inner-city precinct of Spring Hill, which is undergoing significant gentrification.” Pauline Hanson’s relationship with Rinehart has been the subject of the Guardian’s new podcast about the party, The Populist, which detail numerous instances when the Queensland senator and the party she leads have received gifts or benefits. Guardian Australia revealed last month that Hanson and Joyce stayed overnight at Rinehart’s $20m Brisbane mansion in April after fundraising events held for One Nation. On one occasion, Joyce conducted a live television interview with Channel Seven’s Sunrise program from a room that appears to be a bedroom in Rinehart’s home. Joyce told News24 on Monday he hadn’t spoken to Rinehart in six months. The reporting also revealed that Hanson has been using one of Rinehart’s bodyguards for her personal security. The man, who has been seen escorting Hanson in Perth and Canberra, has been one of Rinehart’s closest bodyguards for more than a decade. One Nation has also committed multiple breaches of Senate rules, with the party failing to declare a number of flights gifted by Hancock Prospecting to Hanson going back to August last year, including flights to attend a Conservative Political Action Conference in Florida and Donald Trump’s Great Gatsby-themed Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago. In April, Rinehart gifted Hanson a “sexy” new private plane, worth more than $1.5m. Hanson has said she considers Rinehart an unofficial policy adviser to her and One Nation. “My policy on pensioners being able to work unlimited hours and without losing their pension or healthcare card came from Mrs Rinehart,” Hanson told ABC radio in Perth in June. “And I think that’s great. I listen to anyone who brings good policy to me. “I consider her a friend and I’m very … grateful for her support. She’s an Australian identity, she’s one of the highest taxpayers in the country.”

title: Monday briefing: You asked, we answered – how will the US midterms go?
author: Libby Brooks
summary: In today’s newsletter: As Americans get ready to vote on whether the Republican party remains in control of Congress, our Washington editor talks about the disconnect between Trump and his supporters
body_text: Good morning. Later today, Donald Trump will be in the state of Nebraska to rev up supporters as he kicks off a campaign blitz of rallies ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November. If his early speeches are anything to go by, cornhuskers can anticipate poll denial, accusations of veganism and an expletive ratio that my nine-year-old would love. And Nebraskans may love it, too: aside from one “blue dot” district in Omaha, Republicans argue their support is steady in the state that has easily backed Trump three times. This campaign is set against the president’s plummeting approval ratings, the unravelling of his Maga movement and an affordability crisis escalated by his unpopular war on Iran. But Trump supporters are also among the most motivated to vote, and Republicans have far deeper coffers to mobilise their base. I asked First Edition readers what you really want to know about the US midterms. Today, in a happy exercise in newsletter cross-pollination, I put your questions to our Washington editor Ankita Rao, who runs our US elections newsletter The Stakes. First, the headlines. Weekend roundup UK politics | The Greens in England and Wales have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. Schools | Lawyers and campaigners have condemned the “horrifying” scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools after a Guardian investigation revealed thousands of sexual offences against under-13s are reported to police each year. Brazil | Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff. Environment | A study of Europe’s summer paints a grim picture for the future, with doctors and climate scientists calling on governments to stop burning fossil fuels, shade buildings, green cities, and install air conditioning in hospitals, schools and care homes. US military | The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base. In depth: ‘We are prepared for anything’ You’d be forgiven, readers, if the state of US politics is perplexing you. On the one hand, there are voters who have little faith in the president’s war in the Middle East and are increasingly angry about his inability to make daily life more affordable at home. On the other, Trump has promised a “big surprise” come 3 November – and polls have predicted the wrong results for previous elections. As Ankita Rao set out in The Stakes in September, her team of reporters across the US are hearing the same things in almost every community they’ve spent time in: • Americans feel their lives are dictated by an elite class that goes beyond political parties – best summed up by Democratic senator Jon Ossoff’s use of the term “Epstein class”. • People are exhausted by an ongoing crisis in affordability of childcare, healthcare, food and gas. • Many have lost trust in institutions, from hospitals to schools. With this deep knowledge of the mood of the country, she is the woman to answer your questions. Over to you. *** Who still believes in Donald Trump? Johanne, Quebec, Canada Ankita’s short answer is that it might be the other way around: a lot of Americans don’t feel they’ve been presented with a better option yet. This was evident during primary season, when both Democrats and Republicans went for candidates “who they felt would actually stick it to the man”, says Ankita, rather than regurgitating established party platforms. After all, that was what so many hoped to get with Trump – but those voters who had flocked to him as the anti-establishment leader, or the man who represented something beyond the two-party system, now see him aligning himself with big tech and other corporate interests, particularly this last term in office. There’s a serious disconnect between Trump and his supporters, Ankita tells me. His previously impressive political instincts have faltered “partly because he can’t see beyond his own fixations” – be that his ballroom, the war in Iran, or the unfettered growth of AI. As one Ohio voter told us at the weekend: “I’m sorry, but I don’t give a shit whose name is on the Kennedy Center.” *** Has Trump got a decisive ‘dirty trick’ up his sleeve? Bron Purkiss, England A big concern for First Edition readers is election interference: how Trump has already restricted voting and what dirty tricks he might still try. Will he try to ignore the election results – and how would the Guardian report that? Ankita joined Guardian US seven years ago as voting rights editor, launching our multiyear democracy project. “We had four reporters on that, but now they’re part of the larger politics team, and election integrity has become essential to our coverage,” she says. In the months leading up to the midterms, Trump signed executive orders seeking to assert more control over voting methods, and in a Time magazine interview last week, he refused to rule out declaring a national emergency around elections to implement them. “So we are prepared for anything,” says Ankita. Legal challenges in individual races are “almost inevitable”, she says. “We know the states where the election systems are fully controlled by Republicans, and we’re ready to move everybody there if we see anything strange happening”. Fear of election rigging is high in the communities Guardian reporters are visiting. “We hear this a lot from Democrats who are worried about making sure their vote counts, and more nervous about using mail-in ballots.” This September edition of The Stakes covers Trump’s attempts to restrict postal voting – which is how almost one-third of Americans vote. Ankita suggests this could result in higher turnout. Early data in the deeply red state of Florida, for example, showed voter registration among Democrats already very high. “There’s a sense that ‘we need to go out in droves and make sure that all of these wins are very decisive, so that nobody can question them’.” *** Would Republican losses limit Trump’s excesses? Peter Alexander, England Ankita tells me she doesn’t make predictions any more – a lot can change in a few short weeks – but if an election was called tomorrow “it looks as if the Democrats will absolutely win the House and most likely win the Senate”. The mechanics of voting mean that it will take a decisive majority in both chambers to act as a genuine bulwark against Trump, says Ankita, before adding the weighty caveat that Trump sidestepped congressional authorisation altogether ahead of the Iran war. Nonetheless, she anticipates a slew of investigations after the midterms, launched in the House and then requiring the Senate to move them forward. For example, there are already calls for an investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of Donald Trump Jr’s recent wedding in the Bahamas. *** How will democratic socialists influence policy decisions after the midterms? Feride Hekimgil, Turkey This is a “huge question”, Ankita agrees, as progressive candidates capture the enthusiasm of voters desperate for radical change. While the number of Democratic Socialists actually elected is likely to only be a handful, it could become a “very vocal group”. What’s not clear yet is how they will act once in the Congress. Ankita points to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, one of the country’s most prominent democratic socialists: “She was very clear about her affiliation when she ran, but she hasn’t been that type of lawmaker where she exists to stop the party from doing certain things. She has been much more strategic and collaborative with establishment Democrats.” It remains to be seen whether an augmented group after 3 November takes a similar route or choses a more hardline stance, in particular on Israel’s decimation of Gaza, which has already created gaping divisions in the Democratic party. *** One more thing In an early edition of The Stakes, Ankita described her morning bike ride to the Guardian’s Washington office, navigating National Guard trucks and reflecting on the militarisation of her city since the last election. I wanted to ask her, as a citizen as well as a journalist, how that influences the way she approaches this election. It can’t be overstated, she tells me, how it changes your day-to-day life: “It adds a layer of subtle fear. I’m not actively scared about walking around DC, but it feels as if things could escalate really quickly.” Will it hold people back from voting, or at least displaying their preferences? Quite the opposite, she tells me. “Places where we see this military presence – in Minneapolis, or LA, or DC – are such vocal, largely Democratic cities that people are undeterred.” “There are double the number of lawn signs,” she says. “It’s defiant.” • For more from Ankita and the Guardian US politics in the run-up to the midterms, sign up to The Stakes 2026 here The week to come Tuesday | ABC News is suing the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) over its licence review, and on Thursday its hearing will take place. The broadcaster claims the review, ordered by Donald Trump in April over comedian Jimmy Kimmel’s comments about the US president, is a “retaliatory campaign” in violation of its first amendment rights. Wednesday | Kemi Badenoch is to speak at the Conservative party conference in Birmingham. This day also marks the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks by Hamas. In London, the Met are asking organisers of a pro-Palestinian student march to move the event. Thursday | Holborn and St Pancras will hold its byelection. The seat belongs to former prime minister and Labour party leader Keir Starmer, who held it from 2015 until his resignation in September. What else we’ve been enjoying Helena Horton’s sweeping interview with the Royal Horticultural Society boss Clare Matterson is an absorbing conversation about everything from her high hopes for Andy Burnham, the roles of gardens in public health and the RHS’s £2.3m roadworks compensation. “Who is gardening for in the 21st century?” Matterson asks. “Is it for a small elite band of people, or is it for everybody?” Craille Maguire Gillies, newsletters team If you didn’t catch it yesterday, our interview with the actor John Boyega, recounting the impact of seeing his close friend Damilola Taylor die when he was a child, is deeply moving. Poppy Noor, newsletters team Who doesn’t love images of funny animals? This photo gallery of laughing bears, a sexy mantis and a truly angry bird is worth a look and chuckle. Craille Sport Football | Manchester City came from behind on two occasions to beat Arsenal 4-2 ⁠in the Women’s Super League on Sunday, keeping the champions top of the table. Racing | Formula One drivers have issued a damning condemnation of the sport’s engine regulations that caused the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to open with scenes of cars stopping on track and unable to accelerate because of software problems. Max Verstappen got his first win of the season at the chaotic race. Football | The Republic of Ireland’s manager Heimir Hallgrímsson has called on Uefa to keep his side away from Israel in future draws after a pair of fixtures he admitted “has been tough on us all”. The front pages The Guardian leads with “Horryfying scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools revealed”. The Times splashes with “Badenoch to pledge a bonfire of green laws” and the Mail has “Kemi’s common sense blueprint”. The Mirror, on Badenoch’s pledges to cut benefits, goes with “Bad to the future”. The Telegraph has “Andrew takes police to court over arrest” and The Financial Times says “Hopes for record year in dealmaking punctured by interest rate increases”. The i Paper runs with “Man City owners’ link to Burnham’s No 10 North site after ‘sweetheart deal’ with UAE firm”. And the Sun leads with a story on the romance between Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates, headlined “Love match of the day”. Today in Focus Colonialism for clicks? The influencers targeting uncontacted tribes Features writer Elle Hunt and Indigenous activist María José Andrade Cerda on the growing phenomenon of influencers around the world trying to reach uncontacted tribes. Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Five years ago, Barbara Scully sat in her car crying. Trying to find work after taking time to raise her children, she found herself facing closed doors. “I presume it was the fact that I was 50 and had a 10-year gap where my career used to live [while she was raising children],” she says. “I sat in the car on the driveway in tears, thinking: that’s it, I’m washed up, I’m done.” Then something changed. “Once I pulled myself together, I thought: OK, if this were one of my kids, what would I tell them? … Look at what it is you enjoy doing and try to make that work for you.” Scully relaunched her career for the sixth time, as a broadcaster and comedian, and feels happier than ever. “I am on a mission to try to tell women in particular not to fear getting older; to embrace it, to push back against all the bullshit about how you should be fighting ageing,” she says. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. title: Trump’s recent statements on the economy are even more bonkers than usual
author: Steven Greenhouse
summary: Our ‘genius’ president is revealing his ignorance of economics, fueling concerns about the threat he poses to the world
body_text: Donald Trump recently made a bold claim about his abilities, writing on Truth Social: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” But in the days before and after that post, Trump made one mind-boggling statement after another, including one that raised the possibility of cutting off all trade with dozens of the US’s trading partners. The president’s statements had many experts questioning not just his intelligence, but also whether he – and the outlandish policies he was proposing – were a clear and present danger to both the US economy and the world economy. Public respect for Trump’s economic sense has fallen so low that just 7% of Americans think he should take the lead in regulating AI, according to a recent WSJ poll. Responding to Trump’s reckless statements, one prominent advocacy group, Republicans Against Trump, derided him as “Dumbest. President. Ever.” Economists and corporate executives were especially alarmed by two Trump statements. First, he wrote on Truth Social: “I’ll stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit” if the Federal Reserve doesn’t cut interest rates. The second disconcerting statement was: “If we stopped Trading with every country that we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year.” Not only is Trump’s arithmetic childishly silly here, but any college student who took Econ 101 knows that if a trade-dependent nation like the US suddenly ended all trade with dozens of countries, that would lead to economic disaster. What’s more, it was worrisome that Trump views himself as almighty emperor with the power to singlehandedly halt hundreds of billions of dollars in trade. If Trump ordered the US to terminate all trade with every place with which it has a trade deficit – that includes China, Mexico, Taiwan and the European Union – many US manufacturers would quickly find themselves in desperate straits, unable to obtain critically needed computer chips, rare earths, auto parts, aluminum and much more. As a result, many factories would be forced to close. Not only that, many farmers would be crippled because they couldn’t import the fertilizer they need, while many homebuilders would have to stop work because they couldn’t import needed lumber. Those were by no means Trump’s only recent mind-boggling statements. Two days before the Federal Reserve raised its short-term interest rates to 3.75% to 4% to combat inflation, Trump was on a tear, badgering and bullying the Fed, telling it not only not to raise interest rates, but to cut rates sharply. “We should be at 1% or half a percent,” Trump said. Again, anyone who took Econ 101 knows that cutting rates so sharply and so low will push prices skyward at a time when the Fed and consumers already think inflation is too high. And let’s not forget that Trump was the guy who promised to reduce prices on day one as president. With that statement, the self-described “stable genius” president showed his utter failure to understand one of the most basic teachings of Econ 101 – when interest rates are extremely low, like 1%, that heats up the economy and that revved-up economic activity fuels inflation. The University of Michigan economist Justin Wolfers called Trump’s demand for a 1% interest rate “the dumbest thing ever said by a president”. Then there was this whopper. Trump said that if the Fed bowed to his demands and slashed interest rates, “we could have a GDP [growth] of 14, 15, 16 and 20.” Those numbers are absurd, fantastical. Considering that the US economy grew at a moderate 2.2% rate in this year’s second quarter and rarely grows faster than 5%, talk of 20% growth is delusional. Since the second world war, the US economy has grown at a rate at 20% or higher just once. That happened in the third quarter of 2020 due to extraordinary circumstances – in that quarter, myriad businesses rushed to reopen after the worst pandemic in a century caused many to suddenly shut down during the previous quarter. (GDP plunged at a 28% rate that quarter.) Then there was this colossally wrong-headed statement about trade: “The word ‘Deficit’ is nothing more than a fancy word for LOSS.” Trump coupled that assertion with his misbegotten statement that the US would magically be $1.5tn richer if it terminated all trade with every nation with which it has a deficit. This shows an infantile understanding of trade – and a stunning blindness to its mutual benefits. To explain how inane Trump is being here, let’s hypothesize for a second that in the US-France trade relationship, the only goods traded are wine and bourbon. Under Trump’s ludicrous logic, if the US buys $2bn of wine from France, and the French import $1bn worth of Kentucky bourbon, the resulting $1bn trade deficit means the US is simply giving away $1bn to France. Trump bafflingly sees that as an outright $1bn loss. Blinded by ignorance, ideology or an idée fixe, Trump fails to see that that’s not a harmful $1bn “loss” – rather, Americans are getting $1bn worth of fine wine to enjoy. No doubt wine lovers across the US see that as a gain and certainly not as a $1bn loss. Bottom line, Trump’s delusional statements on the economy show that he is becoming more detached from reality and from rational understanding of how the world works. One can’t help but wonder why his economic advisers don’t stop him from making such ridiculous and at times dangerous statements. If Trump turns his absurd economic notions into reality, as he has done in his ugly, unnecessary trade war with Canada, that will be more bad news for Americans. Voters should realize that Trump, with his failure to grasp basic economics, is a danger to the economy. He has brought us higher prices, slower GDP growth, and constant economic chaos and uncertainty. His tariffs and disastrous war against Iran have hit the great majority of Americans in their wallets and pocketbooks. Tragically, Trump’s Republican supporters in Congress either cheer him on or remain dismayingly silent while Trump does serious damage to the economy and to the finances of millions of struggling families. Americans shouldn’t forget this when they vote in November’s midterm elections. Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

title: First Thing: Son of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro takes election lead in Brazil
author: Martin Belam
summary: Flávio Bolsonaro is favorite to win 25 October runoff against 80-year-old incumbent leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva
body_text: Good morning. Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff. The 45-year-old son of the disgraced former president Jair Bolsonaro will go into the second round as strong favourite, likely to pick up votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates, including Ronaldo Caiado, who secured 2.1%, and Renan Santos, who won 2.2%. The second round will take place on 25 October. How have Bolsonarista politicians taken a grip on Brazil? Brazil’s far right put in an even stronger than expected showing, with a succession of Bolsonarista politicians winning congressional or gubernatorial races. They included Jair Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, and his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who both won seats in the senate. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, Jair Renan Bolsonaro, was elected to the lower house of congress. Woman in Cornell rape allegations case targeted with threats, her lawyer says The woman who has alleged that ⁠she was drugged ⁠and raped by Cornell University students has been the target of threats, her lawyer said. Thomas Giuffra told CNN that people had threatened to silence or harm her if she did not withdraw her civil lawsuit ⁠alleging that several members of a Cornell fraternity had drugged and raped her in 2024. Giuffra ‌said he had also been threatened. “I’m not afraid of these people,” he ‌said. “But the threats, the abuse to protect what’s going on, the status quo – these guys are disgusting. They should stay in their mother’s basement and stay out of the world.” What has been the latest response from Cornell University? In a video message, the Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff, said the school would take “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, adding: “At their best, these organisations can provide ‌students with friendship, belonging, mentorship ‌and a powerful sense of community. But being part of a group can never diminish ‌individual responsibility.” White House defends new press aide who posed with rifle in ‘Fuck Joe Biden’ shirt Beni Rae Harmony revealed on Friday she was going to work for Donald Trump, just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outlet originally created as a video podcast platform for the president’s former adviser Steve Bannon. It then emerged she had posed for a holiday photograph in 2021 wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirt and holding a rifle. The White House deputy press secretary, Anna Kelly, defended the appointment, saying: “Beni Rae Harmony has been a trusted voice for the Maga movement as a White House correspondent. She will be an outstanding addition to President Trump’s communications team as an assistant press secretary – we look forward to having her onboard!” US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot The US air force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford in England following an investigation into an alleged planned terrorist attack at the base. At least 10 B-1 bombers out of 12 flew out of the base on Sunday, including some that arrived on rotation less than a week ago, underlining the haste of the departure. According to reporting by US media, the withdrawal appears to be in response to fresh or renewed security concerns about safety on the base. Five British nationals were initially detained on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism last weekend after three vans were found near the base. They were later released on bail. What are the latest developments in the Middle East? Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis. The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden. Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to hold off Houthi territorial gains, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia. In other news … The former prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched legal action against British police over their raids on his property in connection with the Epstein files. It represents the first time a member of the British royal family has challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649. He was executed. Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, a frequent target of criticism from Trump and from Israel, has announced a snap general election three days after rightwing parties torpedoed the emergency legislation his minority government had put forward in response to growing public anger over the country’s housing crisis. A US marine stationed on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa is accused of murdering a Japanese woman and has been arrested, police said. Donald Trump has named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, to also serve as the new White House AI czar. Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”. More than 400 schools in France will be closed or partly closed on Monday as authorities brace for another week of student protests. A minister said 24 schools had been burnt or ransacked and 78 education staff members injured. Stat of the day: Digger may lose $150m after Tom Cruise film bombs at the box office Tom Cruise is used to success, but his appearance in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s critically panned satire doesn’t seem to have pulled in an audience. It took just $20m globally in its opening weekend, against a reported $150m production budget and $100m marketing spend. Don’t miss this: Are rumors of lost gold spurring clandestine excursions into New York sewers? Can it really be true that underground invaders of the city’s sewer system are lured by the promise of lost valuables? Adam Gabbatt investigates. … or this: My sister Nicole married OJ Simpson – this is what I wish I had known Since Nicole Brown Simpson’s murder in 1994, Denise Brown has devoted herself to the cause of ending domestic violence. Emine Saner interviews her. Climate check: Extreme heat warnings issued for parts of southern California The National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings for parts of southern California, including Los Angeles, until Thursday. Burbank, a suburb north of Los Angeles, recorded 102F on Saturday, a few degrees shy of the October record for the region set in 1987. Last Thing: Mexico debuts tiniest national guard recruit – Comando the chihuahua Diminutive Comando stands just 8in tall and looks nothing like the ⁠powerful dogs usually associated with military or police units. However, the 13-month-old pup is being trained not ⁠just as a crowd-pleasing mascot but for search-and-rescue work as well. Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. title: Vance wants voters to ‘give us another chance’. But he is cornered
author: Sidney Blumenthal
summary: The vice-president’s recent remarks seek to maintain a posture of strength while they inadvertently expose political realities
body_text: JD Vance has parachuted into the midterm election campaign on a rescue mission in a new guise: a risk management consultant. Speaking in the flat language of the expert hired to identify threats, weaknesses and losses affecting a business’s reputation, he has presented his executive summary for limiting vulnerabilities and a scenario for averting disaster. “There’s a lot of good that’s been done, but there’s a lot of work left to do,” he informed his clients on 15 September about the words to use. “Give us another chance, or give us another couple of years, to continue to work on the amazing things that we’ve been doing for the past two years.” He turned the focus to harm reduction rather than total agreement and then shifted the equation to a negative binary choice. “Even if you don’t agree with us on every issue, the other party is consumed by craziness.” His proposal for a “another chance”, however, did not acknowledge harm, express remorse or offer any pledge to change. Skipping the apology avoided admitting error, wrongdoing or enlightenment. The lack of an apology allowed Vance – and Donald Trump – to maintain a posture of unwavering strength, to demand continued fealty and to maintain their pretenses. Vance’s strategy does double duty by firmly establishing his stake to become the prospective successor to Trump as the Republican presidential candidate in 2028. He himself embodies “another chance”. But his implicit self-characterization creates an indelible political identity that the man of many identities must carry forward through this campaign and the next. Every vice-president seeking to become president is inevitably “another chance”. Vance carries the burden of one of the most unpopular presidents of modern times. His gameplan depends upon more than calculated forgetfulness. Abject failure should be seen as “amazing” success. Explaining away Trump means never having to say you’re sorry. Vance’s plea for “another chance”, however, has not produced the desired effect. Instead of Maga minions aroused to march in a phalanx through Trump’s Arch of Triumph, Vance’s defensive positioning has dampened fervor while opening the door to criticism within his party. Beleaguered Republican Senate candidates who had been in lockstep with Trump have suddenly started to flake off. Yet even as they edge away, they still take timid steps. Mike Rogers in Michigan had previously argued that congressional efforts to limit Trump’s authority in the Iran war would “not be good for America” and dismissed concerns about rising fuel costs. “We’re going to be fine, we got plenty of oil,” he said. Senator Ashley Hinson in Iowa insisted that the US needed to “finish the job”, voting numerous times against invoking the War Powers Resolution to force an end to US involvement or curb executive authority without congressional approval. Then Rogers reversed himself, “I think the best option now is to wind it down … The time is now.” Hinson followed suit, pleading that “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.” The panicked Republicans are not really defectors. None of them has offered a single reason why any Trump policy has been flawed, damaging or counterproductive. But now they want out, somehow to reduce their vulnerabilities. They demand an export ban on diesel as a panacea, which the Financial Times reports “wouldn’t be workable” and would have unintended consequences that would lead eventually to fuel price spikes. The Republicans without a cause are seeking “another chance” without being able to articulate a difference from the past. They are pivoting into a void. Having supported Trump down the line they would prefer not to be held responsible for the consequences. But their fracturing underscores that the president and the policies they supported are the source of their quandary. The Republican freak-out validates voters’ anxieties that continuing the Trump status quo carries unacceptable risk. Rogers, Hinson and others cannot be dismissed as Democratic complainers. Their attempt to distance themselves grounds the Democratic criticism in more than partisanship and undermines the simple choice of rejecting the Democrats as the radicals. Intra-party disintegration makes the Trump administration, not the opposition, appear more unpredictable and untrustworthy. The uneasy Republicans’ bid for “another chance” subverts Vance’s framing of the midterms as a judgment about who flew over the cuckoo’s nest. “So, to the American people, I’d say, send these people packing, put them in the mental hospital, do not put them in Congress, because even if you don’t agree with us on every policy issue, at least we’re motivated by common sense and American interest.” Vance’s pitch relies on vapid “common sense”, but when Republicans turn tail the illusion of irresistible power is shattered and the dogma loses its magnetism. It is the Republicans above all who are neutralizing Vance’s damage control. His request for “another chance” to manage voter dissatisfaction through relative comparison places a marker against which the uncertainty, doubt and fear of Republicans is gauged. At a pep talk to House Republicans, Vance suggested what he thought was a clever pointer about how to demonize Democrats. “And if you are one of the few Republicans who’s running against a Democrat who’s not that crazy, then just talk about Abdul El-Sayed,” he said. But Vance’s advice overstretched his less-than-crazy defense, not least with El-Sayed polling ahead of Rogers. Vance disclosed the hollowness and falsity of his strategy by acknowledging that Democrats are “not that crazy” and that the insinuation must be contrived, a trick he has done before. Vance’s insistence on making the election into a contest of who is crazier is his most self-defeating idea. In that competition, Trump will always be the winner. The Economist/YouGov poll, taken at the same moment Vance delivered his advice, showed that 51% of registered voters selected the word “dangerous” to describe Trump, alongside 53% choosing “corrupt” and 47% “out-of-touch”. Only 18% called him “steady”. Vance’s simplification discards the cult of personality in which the leader can do no wrong and ideology brooks no debate. The leader must always be uniquely capable, his words unassailable and the movement always winning, so much you’ll get tired of it. Vance’s imploring introduces an element of skepticism. He shifts the basis for support from zealotry to a cold calculation. Ideology is unmasked, vision lost, the leader becomes fallible. Without unquestioning belief, the cult of personality no longer is attributed magic but depends on risk management. When Vance confesses that it is the Trump administration that is the incumbent regime that must be defended and Republicans are banging to get out of Trump’s Iran war, resentment cannot be easily mobilized against “the deep state”, “the establishment” or “globalist elites”. When Trump rolled out the red carpet for the Chinese communist leader, Xi Jinping, he rolled it over the trope against Democrats as “communists”. Once again, “another chance” Vance has inverted his personal identity, contradicting the character he projected in Hillbilly Elegy, his foundation myth. Scourged by his dysfunctional upbringing he rejected the endless excuses of his alcoholic and drug-addicted mother and accepted the raw honesty and moral clarity of his “Mamaw” and “Papaw”, and found the road to redemption. Vance wrote urgently about the danger of false messiahs blaming scapegoats such as immigrants instead of offering hard truths of responsibility to working-class people. He depicted himself as a “cultural emigrant”, bearing authentic Appalachian values among the “elite” toward whom he had an “almost primal scorn”. In 2016, Vance referred to Trump as “reprehensible”, “an idiot”, and wondered to a friend if he was “America’s Hitler”. Vance wrote in the Atlantic that Trump was like “cultural heroin” and offered private advice to Hillary Clinton’s campaign, according to Chris Whipple’s profile of him in Vanity Fair. Vance was recruited to Silicon Valley as a venture capitalist set up by Peter Thiel of the Paypal mafia and co-founder of Palantir, who had notoriously stated: “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” When Vance ran for the US Senate from Ohio in 2022, Thiel bankrolled his campaign to the tune of $15m. Vance transformed himself into the stalwart Trump supporter. “I regret being wrong about the guy,” he said. But he didn’t explain the inner process of his Damascene conversion. After barely serving in the Senate, his new best friends, Tucker Carlson and Donald Trump Jr, promoted him to Trump into the vice-presidency. During the 2024 campaign, Vance cemented his latest new identity by scapegoating Haitian immigrants for supposedly eating pets. He confessed he made it up. “If I have to create stories so that the American media actually pays attention to the suffering of the American people, then that’s what I’m going to do,” he admitted. Vance announced he had converted from evangelical Protestantism to Catholicism, and he has clashed with Pope Leo. “I think it’s very, very important for the pope to be careful when he talks about matters of theology,” Vance said in April about Leo, channeling Trump’s spirit of retribution. Leo replied that he had “no fear” of the Trump administration for “speaking out loudly of the message of the Gospel, which is what I believe I am here to do”. In June, Vance published another memoir, Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith, in which he credits Thiel – “possibly the smartest person I ever met” – for his conversion, but mentions Leo only in passing, avoiding reference to his feud. Vance identifies himself with a narrow “postliberal” rightwing movement. The Catholic theological historians James M Patterson and Thomas D Howes, in their new book, Why Postliberalism Failed, explicitly describe Vance’s newfound faith as “an ideology that failed”. Vance’s ritualistic non-apology, “another chance”, is a sheer power play that repudiates his original transformation as described in Hillbilly Elegy in which he achieves mature reflection by the grace of accepting personal responsibility. More dangerously to him, his opportunism may have closed off his opportunity. Vance has cornered himself into perhaps not simply his latest but his last political identity – the unapologetic apologist – from which he cannot escape through the election of 2028. In calling for “another chance”, Vance may have run himself out of identities. Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast
