title: Spain’s PM Pedro Sánchez calls snap election after housing law fails to pass
author: Sam Jones and Ashifa Kassam in Madrid
summary: Election called after rightwing parties voted down emergency legislation aimed at tackling housing crisis
body_text: Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has once again staked his political future on a snap general election called after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency legislation to tackle the housing crisis. Sánchez, who has been in office since 2018, used a televised address to communicate his decision, which had been widely expected. The next general election had been due before the end of next summer. Announcing on Monday morning that an early general election would be held on 29 November, the prime minister defended his government’s social, environmental and humanitarian record – and admitted it had made mistakes – but said it was time to let the Spanish people have their say. “It’s up to you now,” he said. “A glance at the horizon shows us that the world is in a very complex era of transformation and transition. It’s a time of great tension, of climate emergency, and of social and technological changes – including highly disruptive advances in artificial intelligence. It is, therefore, a time of great dangers, but also – if we know how to seize the moment – of great opportunities. You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you wish to play in this era, and what role you want Spain to play as well.” Sánchez’s gamble is being seen as a pragmatic move from a seasoned political risk-taker. His minority coalition government with the small, leftwing Sumar alliance has faced a turbulent time in parliament since the prime minister secured his return to office by striking a controversial deal with Catalan pro-independence parties in the aftermath of the inconclusive snap general election he called three years ago. Unable to pass a budget since 2023, with his party and inner circle beset by corruption allegations and his government facing enduring pressure over its handling of the mass crossing into Spain’s north African enclave of Ceuta over the summer, he appears to have decided another snap vote is his best chance of survival. Sánchez repeated his familiar assertion in Monday’s address that the choice was between his progressive government and a Spanish right that would curtail freedoms and turn back the clock on hard-won advances. “You, the men and women of Spain, must decide whether you want to join the far-right wave that rolls back progress wherever it governs, or to ensure that Spain remains a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility,” he said. “You must decide whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forwards, and whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society.” The government’s efforts to tackle the housing crisis were set out in two decrees that contained a range of measures – from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room – but were voted down in congress last Friday by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence party Junts. The PP, which is leading the polls but which may need to rely on Vox’s support to form a national government, said it believed construction, and not regulation, was the best way to tackle the crisis. The votes were met with an angry response from the crowds who had gathered outside congress, eliciting boos and cries of “Shame” and “Your profits, our misery”. The PP welcomed news of the snap election. “At last, the Spanish people will decide,” said the party’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo. “This isn’t an election like previous ones. This is about Spain beating Sánchez.” Vox, which already governs with the PP in four Spanish regions, hailed the decision. The party’s leader, Santiago Abascal, said Vox would fight to ensure that Spaniards “are not discriminated against in their own homeland” when it came to housing and benefits. He also said his party would focus on “remigration” in order to reverse what he called “the migrant invasion”. Long-brewing fury over the high cost of renting and the precarious nature of many tenancies exploded late last month following the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was removed from the home in Madrid where she had lived for 70 years. Abascal said she could not possibly afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment. Her plight prompted tens of thousands of people to take to the streets to protest, and saw a huge tent camp reminiscent of the 2011 indignados movement spring up in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square. Over the weekend, large demonstrations were held across the country as protesters stepped up their demands for urgent action on the housing crisis. Authorities said 70,000 people had taken part in a protest in Madrid on Saturday, while organisers put the figure at 500,000. Sánchez will be hoping that the focus on housing, and the right’s rejection of his government’s plans to address the crisis, will mobilise voters. The housing issue has served to deflect attention from the government’s much-criticised handling of the continuing crisis in Ceuta, which was sparked when about 70,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours. Members of Sánchez’s administration, his party and his inner circle have also been battling a series of corruption allegations over the past two years. In July this year, the prime minister’s brother, David Sánchez, was banned from holding public office for nine years after being found guilty of administrative misconduct relating to his hiring by a socialist-led council in the south-western region of Extremadura. Meanwhile, Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gomez, is due to face trial after a judge charged her with embezzlement, influence peddling, corruption in business dealings and misappropriation of funds at the end of a two-year investigation. David Sánchez and Begoña Gómez have both denied any wrongdoing, and the prime minister has previously accused his political and media enemies of launching a “harassment and bullying operation” against his family.

title: Trump’s former press secretary Karoline Leavitt to join Fox News
author: Shrai Popat and Jeremy Barr in Washington
summary: Youngest press secretary in White House history left earlier this year after the birth of her second child
body_text: Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down as White House press secretary in August, is joining her former boss’s favorite network, Fox News, as an on-air contributor, the channel announced on Monday. Considering that two of her predecessors from Donald Trump’s first administration, Sarah Huckabee Sanders and Kayleigh McEnany, had also joined Fox after leaving office, Leavitt was seen as a logical fit for Fox, on which she will begin providing commentary on 1 November. In the announcement, the Fox News chief executive, Suzanne Scott, praised Leavitt’s “authentic and sharp insight” and said her “first-hand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today’s political landscape”. In her own statement, Leavitt said she was “grateful for the opportunity”, adding, “I look forward to bringing my unique perspective from my experience as White House Press Secretary, along with the same energy and candor that defined my tenure, to Fox’s millions of viewers across their many platforms.” Leavitt, 29, who was the youngest press secretary in White House history, left the administration after the birth of her second child earlier this year. She said at the time that she planned to spend more time with her family and take a role with the Trump-aligned Super Pac Maga Inc. When she announced her pregnancy in December, she became the first sitting White House press secretary to do so. During her tenure, Leavitt sought to reshape the White House media landscape. She moved to exert greater control over the press pool, the small group of journalists who closely track the president’s daily activities; created a “new media” briefing room seat, often filled by conservative commentators and pro-Trump personalities; and frequently clashed with reporters. One of Trump’s most steadfast defenders, Leavitt emerged as a key ally for the president and regularly drew praise from him during her time in the West Wing. Despite his long-term relationship with the network, which helped launch his political career, Trump still regularly criticizes Fox News for being insufficiently loyal, including a lengthy Truth Social post on Sunday criticizing the network’s morning show Fox & Friends for not airing his recent rallies. “Our people want to see our Rallies, and reports on our Rallies, on FoxNews, or they will very quickly stop watching (like I am doing right now!). Fox spends more time talking to Communists, Socialists, and Dumocrats, often without rebuttal, and MAGA is not, to put it mildly, happy.” He also repeated his familiar attacks on the left-leaning Fox News commentator Jessica Tarlov and criticized the network for cutting ties with longtime host Maria Bartiromo. But many of Trump’s former associates – and even his daughter-in-law Lara – remain Fox News regulars. Larry Kudlow, who served as his director of the national economic council during his first administration, was recently tapped by Fox to replace Bartiromo on Fox News’ Sunday morning lineup through the midterm elections next month.

title: Relatives of Epstein victim appear in attack ad targeting Republican congressman
author: Edward Helmore
summary: Family of Virginia Giuffre criticizes Colorado’s Jeff Crank for voting to block a vote to release the Epstein files
body_text: Two relatives of Virginia Giuffre, one of the most prominent Jeffrey Epstein victims who died last year, appeared in a political attack ad targeting the Colorado Republican congressman Jeff Crank, accusing him of refusing to meet with them. Sky Roberts, Giuffre’s brother, and his wife, Amanda Roberts, expressed disappointment that Crank had voted to block a vote to release the federal investigative files relating to Epstein. The couple claimed that Crank, who later supported the Epstein Files Transparency Act which authorized the release of a tranche of documents in a near-unanimous vote, refused to meet with them in Washington. “My sister Virginia was one of Jeffrey Epstein’s victims. She spent her life trying to expose the truth. After she died, we promised to carry on her fight,” Sky Roberts said in the ad backing Crank’s opponent, Democrat Jessica Killin. “But our own congressman Jeff Crank refused to meet with us,” Amanda Roberts continued. “Then, when he had the chance to expose the truth and release the Epstein files, he repeatedly voted to cover them up.” The couple have become increasingly politically active. Over the summer they urged senators on the Senate judiciary committee to block the confirmation of Todd Blanche as attorney general. They also criticized a decision by the Department of Justice to restrict the release of unredacted files to Epstein investigators in New Mexico. They also appeared at Donald Trump’s State of the Union address in February as guests of the Maryland congressman Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee. Epstein has become a major issue for Donald Trump amid public unhappiness over the presidential administration’s handling of the issue. While Democrats are largely focusing on economic issues ahead of the midterm elections, the Epstein issue has cropped up in some races, though the Colorado ad is the first to feature family members of an Epstein victim. An ad funded by a Democratic group in Maine accused the Republican senator Susan Collins of voting “with Trump to cover up the Epstein files” and “protecting child predators” and another political ad in Iowa accused the Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson of accepting donations from people named in the files. They have not been accused of wrongdoing. “I would like to tell Ashley Hinson that I don’t trust you. If you can’t stand up for girls and women in Iowa and the rest of this country, why should I ever vote for you?” a woman says in the voiceover of the ad. The New York Times has identified 35 congressional races with ads that mention Epstein, though most appear to reference the financier in the context of the “Epstein class”, a phrase used to assemble opposition to an idea of unaccountable or excessive wealth in the US. The outlet noted that attack ads deploying “Epstein” lack reference to the reversals of the lawmakers positions on the document release. Sky and Amanda Roberts told the New York Times that they met with Crank’s district director after joining protests against his re-election in the district. “At the end of the day, the bare minimum of this job in this role is to hear your constituents,” Sky Roberts said, relaying his conversation with Crank’s aide. “How can you stay with your constituents and vote according to their needs if you have no idea what their needs are?” Simon Andriesz, a whistleblower and former Wall Street banker who alerted Congress to commerce secretary Howard Lutnick’s ties to Epstein, died by suicide last week.

title: Republican Ken Paxton admits forces in DC control his Texas Senate campaign
author: Ariana Baio
summary: ‘I don’t control message or what we’re doing,’ scandal-hit state attorney general reportedly says at private event
body_text: Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general chosen by Donald Trump to run as the Republican candidate for a Senate seat, admitted in private that his campaign was being controlled by outside forces in Washington DC. Paxton, who is locked in a competitive race with the progressive Democrat James Talarico, told people at a fundraising event in September that he had never felt such little control over his campaign because of outside influence. “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming – you know – from DC,” Paxton said, according to an audio recording obtained by Politico. “I don’t control message or what we’re doing,” Paxton said. An unnamed attender told Politico that Paxton never explicitly said he was referring to Trump’s team controlling his campaign messaging but that Paxton’s comments arose during a conversation about the national political environment. Paxton’s campaign adviser Nick Maddux said in a statement: “Campaigns don’t coordinate with Super Pacs, and that’s obviously what AG Paxton was referring to. “AG Paxton is thankful for the support and knows how important Texas is to keeping the majority which is why he’s on the ground every day talking to Texas, raising money, and taking his message directly to the people including with his statewide television buy that started over this past weekend,” Maddux added. Earlier this year, Trump chose Paxton to run against Talarico, a political newcomer who Democrats hope will flip Texas’s longtime red Senate seat to blue in the midterm elections next month. Though Paxton has been a well-known conservative figure in Texas for years, he has also been embroiled in a series of scandals. He was impeached in 2023 on allegations including bribery and abuse of public trust – though he was later acquitted. Paxton’s wife, Angela Paxton, also divorced him on “biblical grounds”, citing adultery. Polls show Paxton and Talarico neck-and-neck, with Talarico having a small lead over the Texas attorney general. A Fox News survey found Talarico at 51% and Paxton at 49% among likely voters. A New York Times/Siena College poll found Talarico at 51% and Paxton at 45% among likely Texas voters. A Marist University poll indicated Talarico had 50% while Paxton had 44% among registered voters. Paxton’s latest comments are the second reported set of critical remarks the Texas attorney general has made about outside involvement in his campaign. Last week, the New York Times reported that Paxton admitted that Trump’s Republican midterm convention “dropped” his polling numbers. Asked whether the convention had negative consequences, Paxton replied: “So to be honest with you, the numbers – when we did that convention – it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.” Maddux told the New York Times that Paxton’s reported comment was “manipulated nonsense from the New York Times to create a story that doesn’t exist”.

title: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws its bombers from base
author: Dan Sabbagh and Aletha Adu
summary: A dozen B-1s stationed at Gloucestershire base redeployed over concerns about possible threat from Iran
body_text: Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is secure a day after the US air force suddenly withdrew a dozen B-1 bombers from the Gloucestershire base over security concerns about a possible threat from Iran. The prime minister’s spokesperson, speaking during a scheduled briefing, said “yes” when asked if the military site was safe – contrasting with the concern the US military revealed during the hasty redeployment the day before. Pointing to comments made last week by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, the official said there were “tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world”. Aircraft trackers reported that an entire squadron of 12 B-1 bombers based at Fairford had redeployed from the British base to the US on Sunday, a rapid movement that the Pentagon confirmed on Sunday evening. US officials told the New York Times commanders had received new information about an Iran-backed plot against the base, which has been on high alert for more than a week. Some of the bombers left so quickly that refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled to support their flights to the US. A report on ITV News said the US feared a multiple drone attack, similar to Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb, in which cheap small drones launched from trucks destroyed 10 Russian bombers in a coordinated attack in June last year. But UK sources cast doubt on whether Iran had the capability to launch such a complex operation 2,700 miles away. The Ukrainian operation took about 18 months to plan. Donald Trump said on Monday that the US had withdrawn the bombers from the base because of “some threats”, without saying what they were. “There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy – we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit, not very far,” Trump said. UK sources indicated they were not aware of a new terrorism threat to the base and that they would be surprised if Iran could orchestrate a fresh attack, a week after five men from London were arrested late at night having driven to a village near the base in white vans with an unclear purpose. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Monday that the redeployment of the bombers was not tied to the arrests and tried to downplay any discrepancies with the UK. He said the US was confident in the security of all its bases and “with the Brits, we’ve worked very closely for a long time, including on this investigation, and they couldn’t be more cooperative”. Downing Street’s comments were the first made by the UK in the light of the US withdrawal. Neither the Ministry of Defence nor Gloucestershire police commented when asked if there was any additional threat to residents near the base. Other UK officials indicated they had not been briefed on US thinking. RAF Fairford has already been on high alert for several weeks amid heightened US concern that Tehran could try to instigate an attack on the base, which was used for US air force bombing runs against Iran earlier this year. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that the base was a legitimate military target. The hasty redeployment arguably represents a victory for Iran, forcing US bombers to retreat without any kind of attack taking place, though some experts said Washington was engaging in a wider redeployment that could lead to a scaling up of operations against Iran after the US midterm elections in November. It is unclear what level of threat Tehran could pose to a base in the heart of the UK, though Iran destroyed a US Awacs radar plane on the tarmac during fighting in March. Missiles fired from Iran may be able to reach the UK but would be likely to be shot down first, and a drone attack would be a high-risk operation close to the base. Experts cautioned there remained a lack of information. “Airfields are hard to defend, but the US could be making a point or just being very cautious,” said Matthew Savill, an expert with the Royal United Services Institute. Developments in the UK have not so far matched the apparent level of US concern. The five men from London were arrested in Whelford, next to the base, on suspicion of carrying explosives, but they were not charged. No explosive devices were found in the search of the vans or the men, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. All five were released on bail a day later. Trump said afterwards that he was surprised they had been allowed out on bail. “We know everything about them, we would not have released them,” he said. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been more muted. He said last week that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, but developments in the British investigation, led by counter-terrorism police, have been limited. A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparing acts of terrorism, but he was also released on bail on Saturday. Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the events in Gloucestershire were continuing, counter-terrorism police said.

title: Far right on the march and Lula’s failures: key drivers of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Brazil surge
author: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro
summary: Experts say strength of evangelical church and stubbornness of Lula, 80, also helped propel Jair Bolsonaro’s son to first-round election win
body_text: On Sunday night, as the scale of the far-right triumph in Brazil sank in, an adapted football chant rang out in one of Rio’s most leftwing areas. “Let’s turn this around, Lu-laaaaa! Let’s turn this around, Lu-laaaaa! Let’s turn this around, Lu-laaaaa!” crestfallen progressives bellowed while drowning their sorrows after witnessing an excruciating election setback for their leader, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. But the scale of the challenge facing the veteran leftist looks immense after Flávio Bolsonaro’s shock first-round win, which analysts attribute to a complex lattice of social, political and religious phenomena. “Flávio Bolsonaro’s result shows that Bolsonarismo is a far-right movement … that has put down deep roots in Brazilian society,” said Bernardo Mello Franco, a political columnist for the Rio broadsheet O Globo. “His father [Jair Bolsonaro] was convicted and jailed for attempting a coup d’état [in 2022-23] yet despite this, his allies won elections across the country, and his son is the frontrunner in the second round of the presidential election.” Among the main drivers behind Bolsonaro’s strong showing: The evangelical church Brazil’s evangelical church has expanded dramatically since the 1980s, with evangelical Christians now making up nearly a third of the population. Many evangelical voters – often influenced by church leaders – have thrown their weight behind the radical populist movement built by Jair Bolsonaro, and now spearheaded by his evangelical eldest son. As president from 2018 to 2022, Bolsonaro’s ultra-conservative policies helped him cement a lasting alliance with powerful megachurch leaders such as the televangelist Silas Malafaia. “This religious machine … was put at the service of Bolsonarismo: starting with these pastors who have millions of followers on social media, who buy airtime on TV, who lead churches with millions of members, and who turned themselves into canvassers for the Bolsonaro family,” said Mello Franco. Urban violence Mello Franco believed urban violence was another factor that had turbocharged the “far-right windstorm” sweeping Brazil. Rightwing populists such as the pro-gun Bolsonaros were offering voters “misguided but easy-to-understand solutions” to high crime rates, such as increased police violence, mass incarceration and lowering the age of criminal responsibility. “This appeals to an electorate that is scared of violence and crime,” Mello Franco said. The leading light of such “security populism” in Latin America is El Salvador’s authoritarian president, Nayib Bukele, who has jailed thousands of people, often without due process, in his successful bid to cut murder rates. Mello Franco said El Salvador’s “proto-dictator” and his supposedly “magic solutions” had been held up as an inspiration by Bolsonarista politicians during the 2026 campaign. Such hardline proposals have also been boosted by Donald Trump’s decision to designate Brazil’s two biggest crime groups, Rio’s Red Command and São Paulo’s PCC, as foreign terrorist organizations. On the campaign trail, Bolsonaro and his allies have vowed to “neutralize narco-terrorists” and chemically castrate rapists – promises that appear to have won over many violence-weary voters. Lula’s campaign Analysts say Lula’s failure to focus on day-to-day issues such as crime may have hurt his prospects. The leftwing veteran spent much of the campaign vowing to defend Brazil’s sovereignty from Donald Trump’s “colonial” designs and protect its rare earth reserves. “Meanwhile, what voters wanted were solutions to more immediate problems such as bank debts, the cost of food, and insecurity,” Mello Franco said. During one recent rally in suburban Rio, some Lula supporters visibly zoned out as the president waxed lyrical about critical minerals and artificial intelligence. Political analyst Thomas Traumann, who was spokesperson for the former leftwing president Dilma Rousseff, believed Lula’s third administration had ignored a large chunk of society that was unsatisfied over economic issues or because of controversies involving the supreme court. “The government treated any kind of criticism … as a display of fascism – which undoubtedly exists in Brazil – and elitism, which also exists,” he said. “But what also exists is a group of voters who expected more from the government and who are neither fascists, nor elitists. They are simply people who didn’t like the government and decided to punish it.” A Brazilian Biden? Some critics have also pointed to Lula’s age as his achilles heel and blame him for failing to produce an obvious successor. He will turn 81 two days after the election’s 25 October second round. One recent story in the Economist called Lula “a doddering leftie” and compared him to the “geriatric leader” Joe Biden, who was forced to abandon his 2024 re-election campaign after a disastrous debate performance against Trump. Traumann called questions over Lula’s physical or mental state “ridiculous”. “When you see him speak, you can tell it’s not about this,” he said of the gym-going octogenarian. Mello Franco agreed: “Unlike Biden, Lula has at no point shown any kind of physical frailty or cognitive impairment. I don’t think this was an issue.” But Traumann did see one parallel with the former US president: like Biden, Lula was stubborn, had not listened enough to others, and appeared to have thought decent economic indicators were enough to ensure re-election. “This disconnection from reality reminds me of Biden,” he said, attributing it to “the stubbornness of age”. From the start of the campaign, Lula seemed to believe “the election was in the bag”. “And it wasn’t,” Traumann said. The global far right Many observers saw Sunday’s rightwing victory as another chapter in the global advance of the social media-savvy far right. “We’re seeing this revolution in many other parts of the world. We’re seeing this in the US, we’re seeing it in parts of Latin America, we’re see this in a different way in Europe,” said Miguel Lagos, a political scientist. Lagos believed that in Brazil, the movement was driven by a deep “rage against the classical political elites” including journalists, traditional politicians and intellectuals. Jair Bolsonaro and his son Flávio are career politicians. Between them, they have spent half a century working in Rio’s state legislature or the Brazilian congress. Even so, father and son have managed to portray themselves as Trump-style anti-establishment outsiders who have come to drain a swamp of which they, too, are part. Mello Franco believed Bolsonaro was now the favourite to become president. “But I don’t think the contest is over,” he cautioned. “Brazil is always showing us that plot twists aren’t just possible – they’re practically part of the landscape.”

title: Republicans criticize Steve Hilton for ‘creepy’ innuendo-filled campaign ad
author: Dani Anguiano
summary: Hilton faces heavy backlash from within his own party for ‘Just Try It’ ad amid his longshot bid for California governor
body_text: Steve Hilton, the Republican candidate for California governor, is receiving heavy criticism from members of his own party over a controversial, sexual innuendo-filled campaign ad that has been described as “creepy”. The video entitled “Just Try It, California” was released last week and depicts two young women with brightly colored hair, sitting on a bed in front of a pride flag in low lighting. One nervously says “I can’t believe I’m doing this”, while another strokes her hair and coaxes “don’t be nervous, it’s not that bad” before guiding her to fill out a ballot for Hilton and aggressively commanding “lick it”. The controversy comes as Hilton, a British former political adviser to David Cameron and Fox News host, is fighting to advance his longshot bid against Xavier Becerra, the former health secretary. With just a few weeks to go before the November midterm elections, Hilton is trailing in the polls. Sonja Shaw, the Republican nominee for California superintendent of public instruction, called the new campaign ad “creepy, weird, disturbing garbage”. “This is a clear example of exactly why good people are walking away from the Republican party. As a mother and someone who has fought to protect the innocence of children, this crosses a line. We have lost our way,” she wrote on social media. Michael Gates, the party’s nominee for state attorney general, also condemned the advertisement, stating that he “emphatically [denounced] the use of young women as a political tool”. Hilton faces tough odds in the deep blue state, where voters haven’t elected a Republican to lead since 2004. Polls have consistently shown Becerra with a significant lead over Hilton. Hilton is trying to rally California’s Republicans while converting Democrats and independents frustrated with the ever-increasing cost of living in California. In a video posted shortly after the ad was launched, Hilton said it had largely been positively received but that he recognized that people were offended, and that was not his campaign’s intention. “We were trying to make a point in a provocative way, in satirical way,” he said. “It grieves me that you’ve been upset by this. But I also want to ask you to understand what we are doing, why we’re doing it and to ask for some grace as well as understanding as we fight this campaign.” Becerra was quick to jump on the controversy, posting an article about his own support for Medicare for All with a line directed at his rival: “Steve, just try it!”

title: Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory
author: Tom Phillips and Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
summary: Progressive voters and supporters of incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva left reeling after far-right surge
body_text: Flávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, leaving progressive voters reeling. The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot. “Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now.” Speaking outside the White House on Monday, Donald Trump told reporters: “Well, it’s a big victory: close but a very, very big victory. Amazing, actually.” Trump, who is a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, predicted the runoff would be “a very close election”. The far-right surge was a triumph – albeit an incomplete one – for the Bolsonaro clan and its 71-year-old patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro. The disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, saw four relatives elected to congress. His 44-year-old wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won a seat in the senate, as did his second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, who is 43. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, 28-year-old Jair Renan Bolsonaro, and the ex-president’s 62-year-old brother, Renato Bolsonaro, both won seats in the lower house of congress. Across Latin America’s biggest democracy, key congressional and gubernatorial races were also won by staunch Bolsonaristas including Tarcísio de Freitas, who was re-elected as the governor of São Paulo state, and Sérgio Moro, who was elected governor of the southern state of Paraná. Both men were ministers during Bolsonaro’s 2018-22 government. Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) will now boast the largest caucus in the senate with 28 of its 81 seats. Combined with the seats of other hard-right parties, that number rises to 43, giving the movement an upper house majority. Meanwhile, pro-Lula senate candidates, including the former environment minister Marina Silva, the leftwing veteran Benedita da Silva, and the centrist former planning minister Simone Tebet, suffered bitter defeats. Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, two young Bolsonarista social media warriors, became the best-voted congresspeople in Brazilian history, securing more than 3m votes. “We are experiencing a revolution … The far right is growing in a very consistent way, election after election,” said Lago, calling the election the worst for progressive and moderate centrist parties since the late 80s. Lago believed Lula had managed to interrupt the advance of Bolsonaro’s populist movement in 2022, thanks to positive voter memories of his first two terms, from 2002 to 2010. Back then, a global commodities boom allowed Brazil’s first working-class president to fund major social welfare programmes that helped millions escape poverty. “But it was just an interregnum,” Lago said. Control of the senate should allow pro-Bolsonaro politicians to approve an amnesty for their movement’s charismatic leader, allowing the former president to emerge from the Brasília mansion where he is living under house arrest and reassert his leadership of the far right. “I think he will be freed and I think he will be very important during Flávio Bolsonaro’s [presidency],” said Lago. “Flávio will be running the country and [Jair] Bolsonaro will be doing what he has always done: leading the revolution.” The senate majority may also help Bolsonaro’s third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, return from self-imposed exile in the US. The 42-year-old, who has close ties to Donald Trump’s Maga movement, was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison earlier this year for coercion – the result of his lobbying the Trump administration to interfere in his father’s coup trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency. The result is good news for Trump, who has been accused of trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour, and his attempt to expand the conservative “orange wave” sweeping Latin America to its biggest democracy and economy. Recent years have seen a succession of pro-Trump presidents win power in the region, from Costa Rica, Honduras and El Salvador to Chile and Colombia. One of Trump’s most enthusiastic regional cheerleaders, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, celebrated Bolsonaro’s “historic” victory against “the communist Lula”. “The American continent belongs to citizens who want to live in freedom,” Milei wrote on X. The prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, wished Bolsonaro “good luck in the final” and celebrated his “great victory”. He wrote on X: “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.” Speaking after Sunday’s result was confirmed, Lula put a brave face on what analysts called a catastrophic night for the left. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil,” he said, vowing to expose his rival’s “dark past”, which involves well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld and corruption allegations, which Bolsonaro has denied. But the mood at Lula’s post-election event was reportedly funereal and Bolsonaro goes into the second round as the firm favourite. He is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates – Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema – who, between them, won more than 5.5m votes. Santos quickly announced he would endorse neither candidate, considering both Lula and Bolsonaro to be “crooks”. Zema has vowed to vote against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) in the runoff, while Caiado has yet to declare his intentions. Lula’s best hope may be convincing some of the record 33 million Brazilians who did not vote to turn out next time. “He will need to mobilise these apathetic voters who, in a sense, have already abandoned politics, which will be an extremely difficult task,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right. Rocha has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters and identified “a great deal of voter apathy, especially among those who are not aligned with Bolsonarismo, and who could potentially vote for Lula”. Although Flávio Bolsonaro has held political office for more than 20 years, “for undecided voters, his main positive characteristic is this idea of ‘renewal’, despite his possible involvement in corruption and with paramilitary groups,” Rocha added. Lago believed only a dramatic shift from Lula’s campaign – such as changing the candidate, or a severe scandal involving Bolsonaro – could change the election’s outcome. But he was doubtful that would occur.

title: Obama to appear at Abdul El-Sayed rally in critical Michigan Senate race
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Former president to visit 10 days before election day as victory for progressive challenger could tip Senate balance
body_text: Barack Obama will head to Detroit this month to rally with Abdul El-Sayed, a show of establishment support for a progressive insurgent in Michigan, one of the most consequential Senate races in the country. The former US president will appear with El-Sayed and the gubernatorial nominee, Jocelyn Benson, on 24 October, the state’s Democratic party announced on Monday. The rally falls on the first day of the state’s in-person early voting period and 10 days before election day. “Get. Ready,” El-Sayed wrote on social media as he confirmed the appearance. The event is a significant endorsement for a candidate who survived tens of millions in an out-of-state ad blitz to beat the congresswoman Haley Stevens by less than a percentage point in August, making the contest a national proxy battle over the party’s direction. El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health director, ran on Medicare for All and a refusal to take corporate Pac money, and was backed by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. He made opposition to US military aid to Israel and criticism of its conduct in Gaza central to his campaign, and has described Israel’s actions there as genocide. Aipac and its allies as a result spent a record-breaking $30m trying to stop him, and in total Stevens and her allies outspent El-Sayed’s side nearly nine to one on advertising, according to AdImpact. Stevens, a moderate, was backed by the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, incumbent senator Gary Peters, and the party establishment. Obama’s presence matters most in Detroit, where Black residents make up more than three-quarters of the population and where he is still highly popular. Stevens won Wayne county, which includes the city, with about 51% of the Democratic primary vote to El-Sayed’s 45%. Some ads backing her used old footage of Obama praising her, which critics called misleading because he had not endorsed in the race. Kamala Harris, the first Black and south Asian vice-president, campaigned with El-Sayed last month, and Obama phoned him after the primary. El-Sayed is running for the seat being vacated by the retiring Democrat Peters, against the Republican former congressman Mike Rogers, and the contest is one of a handful that will determine Senate control next year. Rogers was the Republican nominee in 2024, and lost that race against Elissa Slotkin, despite Donald Trump winning the state. A Marist poll of registered voters from late September had El-Sayed ahead 51% to 44%. Still, El-Sayed, who has sworn off corporate donations and made his opposition to big money in politics a theme of his campaign, traveled to New York for a fundraiser where top “all-star” donors were asked to give $57,800, split among his campaign, the Michigan Democratic party and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, with Ocasio-Cortez and the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, expected to attend, the New York Times reported. Obama has kept a relatively low profile this cycle, but is preparing a broader push. He has recorded about two dozen advertisements for Democratic candidates for governor and Senate, to be released in the coming weeks, and further stops are to be announced. Earlier this year he campaigned in Texas with the Senate nominee James Talarico and the gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa, and featured in an ad for Josh Turek, the Iowa Senate candidate. This week he will headline a Washington fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, his first with the group this cycle.

title: Trump approval ratings plummet to new low, polls show
author: Cecilia Nowell and Guardian staff
summary: President says ‘I’m doing great’ despite polls showing 32% approval rating and loss of support from 2024 voters
body_text: Donald Trump’s approval ratings reached a record low on Monday, according to new opinion polls. A new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Trump’s approval rating at a record-low 32%. That polling included the president losing support among independent voters and Latinos, who had backed him in 2024. The dip could prove dire for the Republican party a month before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. Before boarding a flight to Nebraska on Monday, Trump shrugged off questions about his approval ratings. “I’m doing great,” Trump told a reporter, who had asked about recent polls showing the president losing support among Latino voters, before blaming CNN and the media. But according to a NBC News/Telemundo poll release Sunday, 59% of Latino voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress, double the number that supported the party two years ago. According to that poll, just 24% of Hispanic Americans approve of Trump’s performance. Trump has spent the past few days campaigning across the country for Republican candidates, despite even conservative states starting to show the loss of support. Some Republicans have also started to distance themselves from the president over issues such as immigration as they attempt to hold on to local support. With Americans souring on the economy, the war with Iran, and other key issues they attribute to the administration, the impact of the negative sentiments could reach far and wide.

title: Trump says Super Pac will pay for taxpayer-funded ads that sparked outcry
author: Cecilia Nowell and agencies
summary: President’s U-turn comes after Democrats and Republicans condemned use of tax dollars for pro-Trump ads
body_text: Donald Trump said on Monday he would pay for taxpayer-funded, pro-Trump ads “with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”, a political action committee, after the television advertisements glorifying himself sparked a major backlash. In a social media post, Trump characterized the ads, which cost at least $1.5m in federal funds, as “a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.” and called them “a rather standard thing to do”. Maga Inc is Trump’s political war chest, which had amassed more than $400m by the end of July. Trump has begun to tap it to boost Republican candidates across the US ahead of midterm elections. Trump provided no details on reimbursing taxpayers for ads that already aired, nor how he would go about having his political organization pay for such advertising. The White House – which had fiercely defended using taxpayer money on spots meant to promote the president – said on Monday night Maga Inc would pay for such ads in the future. It did not answer questions on how it or Trump might prove that his political funds were being used on any ads. The California senator Adam Schiff called for the White House to show proof it had stopped using taxpayer dollars to fund the ads. “Let’s see the proof this illegal waste of your taxes is over for good. And that he pays the money back. We don’t want the U.S. taxpayers to be the latest contractors to get stiffed,” Schiff said in a social media post. Trump’s abrupt about-face came after leaders from both parties criticized using taxpayer funds. Last week, two congressional Democrats asked federal watchdogs to investigate whether the Trump administration illegally used taxpayer money to air the television spots that began airing in late September. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, and the California congressman George Whitesides wrote to the government accountability office (GAO) and the office of special counsel (OSC), describing the commercials as “desperate pre-election propaganda”. Legal experts said the ads might even violate federal statutes, including a law against congressionally appropriated funds being used for “publicity or propaganda” and one limiting the partisan political activities of government employees. The first ad featured clips of Trump talking about defeating communism interspersed with onscreen text promoting the “largest tax cuts in history”, “reigniting American manufacturing” and a call to “defend law and order and police”. Later the same week, a second ad began running. It showed scenic videos of Mount Rushmore with quotes and clips from Trump’s Fourth of July weekend speech there honoring the country’s 250th anniversary. A third, more recent one was virtually identical to an ad for Trump’s Republican re-election campaign in 2024 and showed him walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers”. All ended with a message: “Paid for by the US government.” According to AdImpact, which tracks media spending, the spots had cost at least $1.4m by the end of September. The actual amount spent could be far more, depending on whether networks classified the ad as a political ad.

title: Flávio’s surprise first-round election win highlights rapid rise of Brazil’s House of Bolsonaro
author: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
summary: Four members of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro’s family have been elected to office, most notably his wife and son Flávio, who won the first round of voting to be Brazil’s new president
body_text: The weekend’s elections in Brazil not only put Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the lead in the presidential race, but also underscored how far the former president has come in building a political dynasty. As his far-right senator son heads into a runoff against the leftist incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a sweeping far-right victory in congressional races also secured seats for Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, two of his sons and one of his brothers. Few in the family have spent much time working outside politics since the patriarch led the way four decades ago, but the offices they now hold have had a significant upgrade. Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro, 44, who divided her campaign with caring for her husband as he serves a sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup, ran for public office for the first time and was elected senator. Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, regarded as the most radical of the siblings – he ran his father’s social media accounts and was indicted by federal police for leading a so-called hate cabinet that spread fake news and attacks on opponents – was also elected senator for the first time. His previous political career amounted to 25 years as a city councillor in Rio de Janeiro – starting at the age of 17, when his father put him up for a seat against his own mother, Rogéria Bolsonaro, who had divorced Jair. Carlos won. (Rogéria also ran last Sunday for a seat in the state legislature, still using the Bolsonaro surname, but lost.) The patriarch’s fourth son, Jair Renan Valle Bolsonaro, 28, who dropped his two middle names on the ballot to run simply as Jair Bolsonaro, jumped from city councillor to federal congressman. Of Bolsonaro’s five children, only his 15-year-old daughter has never held political office. Even the former president’s younger brother, Renato Bolsonaro, 62, nicknamed the “brother who can’t win” after losing seven consecutive elections for lower-level offices, was elected. He went from fewer than 10,000 votes in a mayoral race two years ago to 380,000 votes for congress. During the campaign, Renato caused some friction within the family by saying that “Flávio is not Jair. He doesn’t draw crowds”. At the polls, however, Flávio ended up winning more votes than his father did in 2018 and 2022, although the result is seen by some as more of an anti-Lula vote than a strong preference for the senator. The number of Bolsonaros in office could have been even higher had “son 03”, Eduardo Bolsonaro, 42, not abandoned his seat in congress and gone into self-imposed exile in the US, where for more than a year he has lobbied for what Lula and many others see as Donald Trump’s attempts to interfere in Brazil’s elections. Although Michelle is the most recent member of the family to enter politics, it is she who is often considered to be the leading figure among the Bolsonaros. In a July poll, she was named the most powerful woman in Brazilian politics, well ahead of the current first lady, Janja Lula da Silva, in addition to a supreme court justice and many members of congress. “She is a phenomenon,” said Camila Rocha, a researcher at the Brazilian Center for Analysis and Planning, who has interviewed voters and studied the Brazilian right for a decade. “Even Bolsonaro voters don’t like his sons very much, but many of them like Michelle, who is very charismatic.” The daughter of a housewife and a retired bus driver from the metropolitan region around Brasília, Michelle was working as a parliamentary secretary for another politician when, at 25, she met Bolsonaro, then a 52-year-old congressman. She is his third wife. When he took office as president in 2019, Michelle made history by becoming the first and only Brazilian first lady to deliver a speech at an inauguration. She did so in Brazilian Sign Language, which she had mastered while working as an interpreter at evangelical church services – her religiosity is seen as one of the main assets behind Bolsonaro’s close relationship with evangelical voters. Despite playing by Bolsonaro’s party’s rules, Michelle was at the centre of one of the most contentious moments of Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign, when she said that she had been “humiliated”, “disrespected” and “mistreated” by the senator. Reports of friction between her and her stepsons are frequent. Given her popularity, Flávio had to apologise publicly – although Michelle accepted it, the two did not campaign together. Polls suggested Bolsonaro supporters would have preferred the former first lady as the presidential candidate, but the patriarch opted for his eldest son, and gave her the senate mission instead. “That was the mission my husband entrusted to me, and I will represent him, God willing,” she said in August. Michelle and Bolsonaro’s sons were also widely seen as helping secure victories for other far-right candidates from Bolsonaro’s party, which will have by far the largest bloc in the next congress. “Although the family has been in politics for a long time, many voters still see the Bolsonaros as representing ‘renewal’ and an anti-system vote,” said Rocha. “So, to change everything, these voters want to throw a ‘bomb’ that blows up congress and Lula. And that bomb is the Bolsonaro family,” she added.

title: Trump suggests Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego
author: Lauren Gambino in Los Angeles
summary: Gavin Newsom calls comments ‘deranged and dangerous’ after president tells Nebraska rally: ‘They can take out a city’
body_text: Leaders in California have denounced Donald Trump as “reckless” and “deranged” after the US president suggested Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego – two liberal cities in the blue state that has been a frequent target of his administration. At a rally in ruby red Nebraska on Monday night, Trump told supporters that he hoped to see a “tremendous victory” in the fast-approaching November midterm elections. He then suggested high prices due to the war with Iran were a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”. “They can take out a city,” Trump said in Grand Island. “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” The crowd applauded. “It’ll be over very soon,” Trump said of the war. The governor and the cities’ mayors quickly condemned the comments. “After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said on X. “He is deranged and dangerous.” Newsom, a Democrat who has repeatedly clashed with Trump over his two terms, said from his press office account: “Let’s be clear: The President is advocating for an attack on 10+ million U.S. residents in two of America’s largest cities. This is not normal. None of this is. And we will continue to remind folks of that every day.” Karen Bass, the mayor of Los Angeles, assailed the president for making what she called “irresponsible threats” that “could potentially compromise” the safety of America’s second-largest city. “The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” she said in a statement. Todd Gloria, the mayor of San Diego, said his city was “not collateral damage” in the president’s war. “We are not expendable. And we are never a “small price to pay,” he wrote on X “Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.” San Diego, the nation’s eighth-largest city, is home to critical US military infrastructure. Online, the comments – part of a rambling, nearly hour-and-a-half speech – set off a debate about what the president actually meant. Was it a crude joke about two blue cities or had he, accidentally perhaps, disclosed confidential intelligence about potential Iranian targets? Some conservative activists argued that Trump, in his elliptical way of speaking, was referring to high gas prices when he argued that it was a “small price to pay”, and not the capacity of Iran to “take out” a US city. The White House on Tuesday sought to downplay the remark, calling the backlash a “media freakout” and “not rooted in reality”. In a social media post, the White House communications director, Steven Cheung, said the president was “clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped”. “America is safer because of the President,” he added. “Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.” US defence officials have previously stated that Iran currently lacks the capability to launch a direct missile attack on the US mainland. Trump has argued in previous speeches that allowing Iran to develop a nuclear weapon would threaten US cities. In his last state of the union speech he claimed that Iran was working to build missiles that would “soon” reach US soil. In Nebraska, where an unexpectedly close Senate race has rattled Republicans, Trump insisted that he was “doing great” and urged supporters to pretend like his name was on the ballot when they vote in November. But in California, where Steve Hilton, the Republican gubernatorial candidate endorsed by Trump, is seeking an upset, the president’s comments were met with furious denunciations. “Thirteen million Californians call LA and San Diego counties home,” said Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor who has sought to take up the anti-Trump mantle carried by the outgoing Newsom. “Their lives are not a ‘small price to pay’ or a punchline for Donald Trump.” • This article was amended on 6 October 2026. Trump suggested that Iran could “take out” the two cities, but did not suggest that it do so, as the original headline indicated.

title: ‘Spit on our sacrifice’: Canadian veterans fume after Trump and allies take jibes at military
author: John Semley
summary: Military families say Trump officials ‘owe us an apology’ after disparaging remarks by JD Vance, Pete Hegseth and others
body_text: On the morning of 11 September 2001, Perry Chalmers was running drills for the Royal Canadian Regiment’s specialised mortar platoon in New Brunswick when he heard the news: America was under attack. Word quickly spread across the base. “I went inside to watch the news,” the former corporal recalls. “And there was a huge feeling of – and you’re going to have to excuse me – holy shit. What the fuck just happened?” Chalmers called his wife, who informed him that, just before 10.30am, the second of the World Trade Center towers had fallen. With that, his battalion was put on notice: dispatched to nearby airports to assist in the forced landings of commercial aircraft after the shutdown of North American airspace. The Canadian troops went to retrieve their rucksacks and any other necessities, should they need to spring into action at a moment’s notice. As Chalmers recalls: “Things started to happen really quickly.” Chalmers would deploy to Afghanistan, on a nine-month tour of combat duty, where he saw combat alongside US troops. He put his mortar platoon training to good use, as a counter-IED engineer, dealing with the threat of improvised explosives in conjunction with the US army’s 10th Mountain Division. He was one of more than 40,000 members of the Canadian armed forces who served in Afghanistan, supporting US and Nato operations. The Canadians lost 158 lives. In 2007, a stretch of Ontario’s highway 401 was rechristened the “Highway of Heroes” to commemorate the convoys of fallen soldiers ferried between the military base in Trenton, Ontario, and the coroner’s office in Toronto. This response to 9/11 was consistent with the longer history of Canadian-US military cooperation. About 14,000 Canadians landed on Juno Beach in Normandy on D-day during the second world war. More than 26,000 Canadians served in the Korean war. While Canada did not officially participate in the Vietnam war, an estimated 30,000 Canadians headed across the border to volunteer for the US military. Over the course of the war in Afghanistan, Chalmers can count 35 fellow Canadian troops who lost their lives. But he never really brooked any regrets, or bad feelings, about his role in the US-led war. “My experience was that we were participating in an operation to help our brothers and sisters in the United States,” he says. “None of them ever snubbed their noses at us. We were treated as equals, and respected, for what we brought to the table.” But no longer. While calling Canada “a state”, the US vice-president, JD Vance, recently commented that it “had underinvested in its military that quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America”. Going one step further, Donald Trump’s transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, told Fox News that Canada “doesn’t have a military”. Self-styled “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth has spent time on X, mocking Canadian cadets and criticising a Canadian coast guard detachment for taking part in a Pride celebration. Trump himself was criticised earlier this year for claiming that Canadian and other Nato forces in Afghanistan were “never needed”, claiming these allies “stayed a little back, a little off the frontlines”. The remarks have been condemned at the highest level of the Canadian government. The defence minister, David McGuinty, described Hegseth’s social media posts as “below the dignity of the office he holds”. Amid a serious diplomatic dispute between the two countries, the prime minister, Mark Carney, accused Trump and Hegseth of “doing memes”. “It’s disrespect and betrayal,” Chalmers says. “It makes me very angry.” “It’s really hard to hear how ungrateful they are, especially Vance, who served,” said Chris Banks, a retired Canadian army sergeant with nearly two decades of experience. “To hear him spit on our sacrifice is insulting, it’s hurtful, and it’s disrespectful to the dead. On the other hand, these men have proven themselves nothing more than children. So when I heard JD Vance say it, it’s like, ‘Oh, good. Dumbass said something else.’” Banks deployed to Afghanistan in 2008, where he was part of a Canadian platoon that laid down cover fire for Americans under attack from the Taliban. To this day, he still has vivid memories of taking cover in a ditch near Pashmul, alongside an American platoon, looking up as the trees overhead were shredded by shrapnel. He says he was proud to serve. But when he came home to Ontario in 2009, he felt something had changed. He began drinking heavily – sometimes as much as a litre of vodka a day – and struggling with suicidal thoughts. All hallmarks of PTSD. He received treatment, and now advocates for the mental health and wellbeing of other Canadian veterans. Still, a tinge of bitterness remains, when he thinks back on fighting on behalf of the US. “I lost a part of myself,” he says. “In that war we fought, for them.” *** Nancy Payne still remembers exactly where she was when she found out her son had died. Cpl Randy Payne served with a military police unit, stationed in Wainwright, Alberta. He was part of a specialised close protection team, charged with safeguarding high-ranking officers, government officials and other VIPs, in war zones. On 22 April 2006, an armoured vehicle triggered a roadside bomb outside Kandahar airbase, killing Payne and three other Canadian soldiers. It was the deadliest attack on Canadian forces since 2002 – when four Canadian soldiers were killed by a US bomb after a disastrous friendly fire incident at the Tarnak Farms training facility in Afghanistan. Nancy was at home, alone, when the phone rang in the dead of the night. It was her son’s commanding officer. “When you get a call at three in the morning from Randy’s boss, you know it’s not good news,” she recalls, speaking over the phone from her home in Lansdowne, Ontario. “I just kept saying ‘Not my Randy … not my Randy’.” In 2025, the Canadian government awarded Nancy a Silver Cross, a commendation for Canadian military mothers. She laid a wreath at the national war memorial during the Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa. More locally, she has commemorated her son with a prize – “the Captain’s Award” – bestowed to students who distinguish themselves in athletics and leadership at his former high school. She, too, is unnerved by the US attacks on the Canadian military and veterans like her son. “What they’re saying is not right,” she says. “We were neighbours for so long. That’s all changed, now.” Nancy is not the only military mother who feels this way. Earlier this year, Jane McKay, mother of deceased Master Cpl Tim Wilson, penned an op-ed for the Toronto Sun newspaper taking aim at the Trump administration. “Trump has no respect for any soldier – American, or Canadian, or those from the Nato alliance,” she wrote. “He owes them all an apology.” Some US politicians have tried to make amends. On 1 September, the Arizona Democratic senator Ruben Gallego travelled to Ottawa on an official congressional trip. The goal was to strengthen the weakening trade relations between the two countries. But Gallego made a point of singling out Hegseth’s anti-Canadian military tweets as “deeply disrespectful to the men and women of Canada that have died fighting with us”. For veterans like Chalmers, such words may be too little, too late. He used to play tabletop strategy games with a group of civilian friends in the US, via the online social platform Discord. That all ended when they laughed off his concerns about Trump’s talk of Canada becoming the “51st state”. Banks used to routinely take his family across the border for vacations and stateside shopping trips. No more. “I loved working with Americans, I loved training with them,” he says. “But now it’s hard to have that same level of empathy.” Would he eagerly enlist to help the US again? “What would happen if there was another hypothetical 9/11?” he says. “I hate to say it, but why would any nation, ever again, partner with the United States, if this is how they treat their closest neighbour and ally?” • This article was amended on 7 October 2026. The Silver Cross is awarded by the Canadian government, not by the Royal Canadian Legion.

title: ‘Using the presidency to line his pockets’: could claims of corruption fuel backlash against Trump?
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: Experts say president is vulnerable amid discontent over rising prices
body_text: In Donald Trump’s telling, he’s a model of incorruptible self-sacrifice. “I’m the only president that donated his salary,” he told a group of cheering supporters at a Hispanic heritage month celebration in the White House last week, before conceding that George Washington – “a very wealthy person” – might have beaten him to the punch. “They pay me $550,000 a year, and in my first term, I donated it,” he continued. “In my second term I donated it too. I donated it to fixing the White House. I donated the salary into the White House preservation.” Trump’s ethical self-depiction was undercut in startling fashion a day later when the crypto company that runs his memecoin offered “the most exclusive dinner in the world” at the president’s members-only Trump National club in Washington. “Join three legends and featured speaker Donald J Trump,” gushed the invite to the 185 biggest investors in the Trump coin. The top 29 buyers were promised an invitation to an additional “VIP reception with your favourite president and one of the legends”. For the top four donors, a Trump 18-karat gold watch lay in store. The aim appeared to be to boost sales of the memecoin – called $Trump – over the next two months. Trump personally profits from the coin, and disclosures show he made about $636m from it last year. With just over a month to go before November’s midterm elections, Democrats seized on the dinner invitation as a political gift as they try to convert concerns over Trump’s perceived corruption into a groundswell of outrage. They theorize it will power a “blue wave” that could enable the party to retake control of the House of Representatives and the Senate on 3 November. “Donald Trump is vying to become the most corrupt person to ever walk the face of the earth,” posted Chuck Schumer, the Democrats’ leader in the US Senate. With the US president’s approval ratings already at record lows amid discontent over rising living costs fueled by the unpopular war with Iran, ethics experts say “unprecedented” levels of corruption engaged in by Trump, his family and close associates are sufficiently serious to make him vulnerable to a popular backlash. The question is whether the myriad of accusations – many of them technical in nature – are straightforward enough to carry popular resonance. The administration vigorously rejects the assertions, which a White House spokesman, Davis Ingle, called “irresponsible” and likely to “reinforce the public’s distrust in what they read”. “President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses,” he said in a statement. “There are no conflicts of interest. “The only special interest guiding President Trump’s decision-making is the best interest of the American people. President Trump has taken on a broad swath of entrenched special interests: negotiating most-favored-nation pricing deals with major pharmaceutical companies, launching TrumpRx.gov to lower drug prices, ending unfair trade practices that international corporations have exploited to offshore jobs, and implementing schedule F to fire unelected bureaucrats who actively subvert a democratically-elected president’s agenda. “Through these actions, President Trump is delivering on his promise to empower the forgotten men and women of our country by finally putting their interests first.” Recent surveys, however, indicate American voters are more concerned than ever before about government corruption. A Gallup poll published in September recorded 89% of both all adults as saying the problem was widespread. Only Lebanon, Peru, Ghana and Nigeria have registered higher levels of public concern in the past three years. Analysts insist the US public has ample cause for complaint. “We’re facing an ethics crisis which starts and ends with a president who is constantly using his office to find new ways to personally profit,” said Jordan Libowitz, communications vice-president with Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a non-partisan watchdog. “With a new story every day about Donald Trump using the presidency to line his pockets, it’s no surprise that Americans are losing faith in their government.” Trump’s own filings show he earned $2.2bn from his various business dealings in his first year back in the White House – including $1.4bn from his family’s cryptocurrency enterprise, World Liberty Financial. Observers identify at least three main areas of potential abuse; crypto, a venture which Trump denounced as a “fraud” just five years ago; stock trading by government officials, including the president himself; and the predictions markets, represented by companies such as Kalshi and Polymarket, both of which have links to Donald Trump Jr, and which have raised concerns about well-connected figures profiting through putting bets on government decisions and the content of official speeches. There are also concerns about the growth of “pay to play” practices that have seen wealthy donors being granted special access and favorable decisions, including dropped criminal investigations, in exchange for donations to Trump’s campaign and political Super Pac. Presidential pardons and sentence commutations have been doled out to those who have contributed to the president’s re-election effort. As Schumer’s post indicates, Democrats have increasingly tried to make corruption a campaign issue. A 30-second advertisement from Chris Pappas, a New Hampshire representative running for re-election, reflects a more widespread mood in favor of putting it center stage. The question is whether the message on rampant graft is cutting through with an electorate that may find inflation and higher living costs easier issues to grapple with. Dylan Hedtler-Gaudette, director of government affairs at the Project on Government Oversight, another watchdog group, acknowledged that many voters were confused by the complexity of the accusations leveled at Trump. “Support for the Trump administration and for President Trump himself is declining pretty rapidly,” he said. “But it’s hard to disentangle. Is it about the corruption? Or is it about the affordability crisis continuing and in some ways getting worse? “Corruption tends to be in the eye of the beholder. And if you ask different people about the word corruption, they say, ‘Yeah, it’s a problem.’ But if you ask them to define what they mean by corruption, it can diverge wildly depending on how they affiliate and how they identify in terms of their partisanship and their political identity.” Brendan Fischer, director of strategic investigation at the Campaign Legal Center, said the public had been overwhelmed and “numbed” by a “fire hose” of corruption emanating from Trump’s second presidency which, experts agree, has greatly exceeded that of his first administration. “It can become overwhelming trying to keep up with each of the latest examples,” said Fischer. “I think the Trump’s crypto dealings are incredibly concerning. His investments in the crypto industry open up new avenues for wealthy special interests to channel money to the president. But It’s potentially harder for the public to grasp. So it hasn’t broken through in the way that it that it probably should.” Easier to grasp, he believed, was Trump’s acceptance of a $400m plane from Qatar, which the president has said he will use in place of the existing Air Force One. The scale and brazenness of Trump’s cavalier disregard for ethical considerations creates a danger of apathy among voters, who may feel they are powerless to change the situation as they grapple with more quotidian cost issues. “It’s easy to just throw your hands up and say, ‘Everybody’s corrupt, nobody’s representing my interests, and my life is just not getting any better,’” Fischer said. “That is a dangerous situation for democracy. We need voters to cast their ballots and then remain engaged in the political process to make sure our elected officials are representing the interests of voters and not just their own or the interests of their donors.” Richard Painter, a former White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, said Trump’s decision to go war with Iran opened up further corruption avenues – citing reports that both Donald Trump Jr and his brother, Eric Trump, have invested in drone manufacturers that have secured government contracts. “Whenever there’s a war, there’s an enormous amount of money to be made. People say there are those who die in a war, and those who become millionaires, or maybe in this case billionaires,” said Painter, now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota. “This is what President Eisenhower talked about with the military-industrial complex back in 1961, but we’ve never had a president whose family actually made money from the military-industrial complex.” Painter predicted that conditions were ripe for “an enormous public backlash” but said the Democrats had to adopt a credible anti-corruption message after losing the public’s confidence by failing to speak out against Hunter Biden’s attempts to leverage his White House access when his father Joe Biden was president. “The Democrats had their chance in 2021 when Biden took office, when we should have had our reawakening on ethics, and they failed,” he said. “If they want to win races not only in 2026, but in 2028, they’d better get their act together and focus on ethics.” One historical model, Painter suggested, was the anti-corruption crusade championed by Jimmy Carter in his successful 1976 presidential campaign, which took place amid lingering anger at Richard Nixon over the Watergate scandal that drove him from office and his failure to quickly end the war in Vietnam. Democrats have invoked a more recent inspiration: Hungary’s recently elected prime minister, Peter Magyar, who mobilized rising resentment over government corruption in April this year to unseat the incumbent, Viktor Orbán – a close ally of Trump – in an election landslide. Steven Levitsky, a political scientist at Harvard University and co-author, with Daniel Ziblatt, of How Democracies Die, said the key similarity between the US and Hungarian circumstances was the sense of corruption further undermining an already failing government. “Orbán was successful in part because the economy was pretty good for much of his period in office,” Levitsky said. “But eventually it slowed down, and corruption became a major factor. “It’s sad but true that in many, many cases in democracies around the world, if incumbents are perceived to be delivering – if the economy is going well, if they brought down inflation, etc – voters will turn a blind eye to corruption. It’s only when you combine poor performance with corruption that it becomes salient. “Unfortunately, in the United States, one of the things that’s benefited Trump is the perception that all of politics is corrupt, mainly because of the extraordinarily outsized role of money in politics. “There are a lot of reasons why Trump is unpopular now. Corruption is one of them but I don’t think it’s the principal one.”
