title: Trump is fueling a culture of misogynistic impunity
author: Robert Reich
summary: The allegations against seven men at Cornell University come amid a climate of belligerent sexism
body_text: Last month, a young woman filed a lawsuit against Cornell University, alleging that two years ago the university had failed to protect her from being raped by seven men at a fraternity house near the university campus. She also sued the fraternity. The lawsuit has plunged the university into a crisis and invited criticism of the district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, who decided there wasn’t enough evidence to bring criminal charges against the seven men. At this point, we can only guess why neither Cornell nor Van Houten did more in response to the young woman’s allegations. But there’s little question that we’re living through a time when men feel some impunity when it comes to attacking women. Violence against women is hardly new. Nor is the impunity that some men feel in attacking them. But the man now occupying the White House has contributed to a lower and more dangerous standard for what men can do to women with impunity. Trump was found in civil court to have sexually abused the writer E Jean Carroll. He has repeatedly insulted the physical appearance of female journalists, politicians and public figures. He was caught on a hot microphone boasting about using his fame to forcefully kiss and grope women without consent, stating that being a star allows men to “do anything” and “grab ’em by the pussy”. When women have spoken out against him, Trump has resorted to smear campaigns, as he did with Carroll, Stormy Daniels and Hillary Clinton. When women have stood up to him, he has exploded in anger against them, as he did with Megyn Kelly, Rosie O’Donnell, Kamala Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. His administration is the most belligerently misogynistic of any in memory. It has openly equated testosterone levels to strength, conducted a cage match on the White House lawn as part of its celebration of America’s 250th anniversary, fired senior female officials, and accused the Democratic party of being run by “a bunch of childless cat ladies”. Nor do I think it irrelevant that Trump, JD Vance and Trump’s erstwhile pal Elon Musk inhabit what’s been termed the “manosphere” – a place where the main events are dominance and submission. The whole point is to humiliate weak men and to subjugate women. An implicit promise of the 2024 Trump campaign was to restore patriarchy to America. Fifty-four per cent of men supported Trump in that year’s election. After Trump’s re-election, sexist and abusive attacks on women – such as “your body, my choice” and “get back in the kitchen” – surged across social media, according to an analysis from the Institute for Strategic Dialogue. A remarkable number of Trump’s cronies are sexual harassers and predators. Trump was introduced at the Republican national convention by Dana White, chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, who was once caught on tape slapping his wife in a nightclub. JD Vance has claimed men in America are “suppressed” in their masculinity. Before becoming Trump’s defense secretary, Pete Hegseth paid off a woman who accused him of sexual assault. (Hegseth’s own mother accused him of abusing women, though she later disavowed her words. He has denied the claims.) And as secretary, Hegseth has championed “high-T” men and blocked promotions of female officers. One of Elon Musk’s companies, SpaceX, reportedly paid $250,000 to a flight attendant who said Musk had exposed himself to her, though he denies the allegation. In a lawsuit filed last year, former employees accused him of “treating women as sexual objects to be evaluated on their bra size”. After kissing Trump’s derriere, Mark Zuckerberg, the third-richest person in the US, called for more “masculine energy” because the corporate world was becoming “culturally neutered”. He told Joe Rogan: “Having a culture that celebrates the aggression a bit more has its own merits that are really positive.” The Trump regime celebrated toxic masculinity by smoothing the way for Andrew and Tristan Tate to be released from Romania to the United States. The Tate brothers had been accused of luring women to Romania and then forcing them to work as pornographic webcam performers. Britain is also investigating the Tate brothers for rape and human trafficking. (US marshals arrested the Tate brothers in Miami on 18 July, following an extradition request from the United Kingdom. They’ve denied all charges.) “I’m a Trump fan because I’m a man,” Tate has said. “You have to support Trump if you’re a man.” Trump’s authoritarian manosphere is organized around a hierarchy topped by heroic male warriors. Winning is all about getting other males to submit to the dominant male. Women are relegated to subservient roles. Anything that challenges the traditional heroic male roles of protector, provider and controller of the family is considered a threat to the social order. LGBTQ+ people are believed to weaken the heroic male. Hence, Trump’s executive order declaring that the US government will recognize only a person’s sex assigned at birth, limit the definition of a “male” or “female” to their reproductive cells, and potentially withhold federal funding from programs that acknowledge transgender people or “gender ideology”. I don’t want to oversimplify a complex social phenomenon or engage in the same kind of gender stereotypes that the manosphere promotes. Male domination is hardly the only characteristic that unites Trump, Vance, Hegseth, Kennedy, Musk and the tech bros. Misogyny is not unique to authoritarian men. Nor do I presume to know what happened at the Cornell fraternity house two years ago. But I don’t think it unreasonable to see it related to a climate of distrust bordering on hate, fostered by Trump and his administration against people who seem weak or feminine. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

title: New Jersey congresswoman faces deadline in Trump case days after giving birth
author: Rachel Leingang
summary: LaMonica McIver is only the 15th member of Congress have a baby while serving, and also the only member indicted for visiting ICE facility
body_text: A US congresswoman who just gave birth to a baby girl faces a deadline this week on whether to seek a rehearing of a federal case against her by the Trump administration after an oversight visit to an immigration detention facility. LaMonica McIver, 40, represents New Jersey’s 10th congressional district. She gave birth to her second child last Thursday – a rarity for a sitting member of Congress. She is only the 15th member of Congress to give birth while serving and part of a small subset of congresswomen who have school-age children. McIver first won her seat during a special election in mid-2024, then won a full term later that year. She is also running for re-election this year. In announcing the birth of her second child after publicly discussing fertility struggles, McIver called being a mom “one of the greatest joys of my life”. “Getting the chance to raise a family is a priority and a delight for me, something I hope everyone who wants to, gets the chance to do,” she said in a statement last week. “Bringing a child into the world is a reminder not only of why we fight for maternal healthcare and reproductive rights, but of why we fight for the rights and freedoms of our most vulnerable – they are someone’s babies too.” In late August, a federal appeals court declined to dismiss criminal charges against McIver, who is charged with interfering with an arrest in May 2025 outside Delaney Hall, an immigration detention facility that has drawn protests over poor conditions inside. She is the only member of Congress whom the Department of Justice has indicted, and the charges carry a potential 17 years in prison. She has pleaded not guilty to the charges and sought to get them dismissed, arguing that she is immune from prosecution under the US constitution’s speech and debate clause because she was doing her job and that she has been selectively prosecuted by the Trump administration. McIver and her legal team will need to decide by 9 October whether to seek a rehearing or en banc hearing before the third circuit court of appeals in New Jersey in the case, basically a further review of the case by the full appellate court. She could also ask the US supreme court to consider the appellate court’s decision, or let the case go to trial. McIver previously told the Guardian that the case against her was part of a pattern of intimidation and retaliation by the Trump administration against those who disagree with the president or try to hold him accountable. “This is about intimidation. It’s about bullying,” McIver said last year. “It’s about trying to stop our level of government from having oversight and holding this administration accountable.” Charging documents in the case noted that people, including members of Congress, surrounded the Newark mayor, Ras Baraka, outside Delaney Hall to prevent his arrest and alleged that McIver shouted “hell no” repeatedly. The Washington Post, after analyzing video from many angles, said McIver “made contact with at least two agents” in the scuffle, but that it was “difficult to discern the force of the contact and to what extent it was intentional or the result of the chaotic moment”. In a radio interview in September, McIver described the situation outside Delaney Hall that day as “very chaotic, very scary”, noting that armed federal agents were surrounding her and her congressional colleagues. She called the charges “dangerous for all members of Congress on both sides of the aisle, not just for me”. McIver has spoken about the challenge of doing her job, managing the case and fundraising to pay for legal fees as a relatively new member of Congress, especially while pregnant and caring for her older daughter, who is 10. In a profile with Elle magazine, McIver said that she “couldn’t put the world on pause” while contending with her legal case and her dream of another child. “Now, instead of just running for reelection – which, to be fair, I am also doing – I spend my days writing bills about bringing down energy costs and protecting food stamps, and my nights talking to lawyers about how to keep standing up to ICE without being sent to prison,” she told Elle. Members of Congress do not get paid parental leave, McIver noted in her announcement, adding that she plans to return to voting in November after taking October to heal and spend time with her new baby.

title: Democrats upbeat as unpopular Trump imperils Republican midterm hopes
author: Chris Stein in Washington
summary: Polls show GOP candidates trailing Democrats in Senate races, and Republicans also struggling in House contests
body_text: Thirty days remain until the midterm elections, and Donald Trump and his Republican allies are pulling out all the stops to maintain control of Congress. Super Pacs aligned with the GOP have already spent hundreds of millions of dollars on advertising and voter outreach in races expected to decide the majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, and plan to spend even more before the election is over. The president, Vice-President JD Vance, and other top Republicans are fanning out across the country to stump for vulnerable lawmakers. So far, there are no signs the money or the rallies have improved what appears to be a grim state of affairs for Republicans, less than two years after their resounding victories in the 2024 election. Recently released polls continue to show the party’s candidates trailing their Democratic challengers in the Senate races that will decide the majority and control of the chamber. “Candidate quality is beating gobs of Republican money,” the Senate’s Democratic minority leader, Chuck Schumer, quipped over the weekend, when the New York Times released the latest in a series of closely watched polls that confirmed the momentum behind their bid to retake the Senate. The surveys, conducted with Siena University, found Democratic Senate candidates leading in Alaska, Ohio and Texas – all states Trump won by double digits two years ago. In Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years, the party’s candidate Adam Hamilton was neck-and-neck with the Republican senator Roger Marshall, while in Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek is narrowly trailing the Republican candidate, Ashley Hinson. Democratic candidates for governor were also leading in many traditionally Republican states, the Times and Siena found. “If the election were held tomorrow, all state wide races [would] go blue,” Briscoe Cain, a Republican state representative in Texas wrote on X Monday. The Democrats’ Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa were both leading in the Times and Siena survey. “Republican voters feel too comfortable and are not as intense about this election as they should be. We have more voters than the left in Texas, but we have to vote,” Cain added. Last Friday, the news outlet Semafor reported that the Senate Leadership Fund, a major GOP Super Pac, planned to pull money from the campaign of its candidate Michael Whatley in North Carolina, in favor of upping support for Marshall in Kansas. No Democrat has won a US Senate election in North Carolina since 2008, but Whatley has trailed in polls for months. Democrats need to win at least four seats in the chamber to regain the majority they lost in the 2024 election. The situation for Democrats appears to be similarly positive in their campaign to retake the House, which Republicans control only narrowly. A CBS News and YouGov poll released on Sunday found Democrats with a nine percentage point lead on the generic ballot, an important indicator of voter intention in congressional races. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday found Trump’s approval ratings remained at the lowest point of his career, with only 32% of adult respondents approving of his performance as president. Independent voters – whose views often make the difference in close races – planned to back Democrats by a 16-percentage-point margin, though many remained undecided. The president’s poor marks are believed to be a major cause of the Republican candidates’ struggles nationwide, but are far from the only one. Discontent over the state of the economy – particularly the price of gasoline and other consumer staples – is another reason, as is the on-again, off-again conflict with Iran, and concern over Trump’s hardline approach to enforcing immigration laws. Republicans maintain they have avenues to victory in both chambers of Congress. Eight House Republicans represent districts that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, as opposed to 22 House Democrats representing districts Trump won – a number that has grown larger thanks to the unprecedented redistricting war Trump instigated. Many polls show voters have an unfavorable perception of the Democratic party, though views of Republicans are similarly negative. And despite strong fundraising by some Democratic candidates, Republicans and groups allied with their agenda have an edge in cash to spend on this election. It may not be enough to halt the disintegration that appears to be occurring in the coalition that elected Trump two years ago. Only 26% of Hispanic voters – who swung towards Trump after years of leaning Democratic – plan to vote for Republicans this year, while 52% prefer the Democrats, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found. “We’ve been seeing among Latino voters, as we’ve been seeing kind of in the electorate as a whole, a real strong rejection of the Trump administration, and that has inflated into an increase in support for Democratic candidates,” said Maria Isabel Di Franco Quinonez, a senior research director at Equis Research, a progressive firm that focuses on the community. Should the trend hold, it could bode well for Democrats’ hopes in states and districts with large Latino populations. The effect may be pronounced in Texas, where the Republican leaders drew new congressional maps to favor their candidates, but only if Latino voters continue voting the way they did in 2024. “If we see those levels continue to rise and see those districts look more like the kinds of support levels for Democrats that we had seen back in 2018, then that would result in maybe Republicans get one more seat after redrawing all the lines, as opposed to getting four or five more seats,” Quinonez said.

title: First Thing: ‘Deranged’ and ‘dangerous’ Trump calls for Iran to strike US cities amid historic ratings low
author: Martin Belam
summary: California’s leaders attack president after he suggests Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego
body_text: Good morning. Donald Trump has suggested Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego, in comments described as “reckless” and “deranged” by California officials. At a rally in Nebraska on Monday, the crowd applauded when the US president said high prices owing to the war with Iran were a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”. He added: “They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” Gavin Newsom, the governor of California and a Democrat who has repeatedly clashed with Trump during his two terms, said from his press office account: “Let’s be clear: the president is advocating for an attack on 10+ million US residents in two of America’s largest cities. This is not normal … He is deranged and dangerous.” What is happening with Trump’s approval rating? A new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Trump’s approval rating at a record low of 32% and the president losing support among independent voters and Latinos, who had backed him in 2024. The dip comes before the crucial midterm elections in November that will determine control of Congress. What is the latest with taxpayer-funded Trump ads? After repeated criticism, Trump said on Monday he would pay for the hitherto taxpayer-funded ads from Maga Inc, his political war chest. He provided no details on reimbursing taxpayers for ads that had already aired, nor how he would go about having his political organization pay for such advertising. Saudi-backed forces recapture key areas around strait from Houthis in Yemen Forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen have recaptured several key areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait from Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said. The push by Yemen’s internationally recognized government was part of a large offensive launched early Monday under an air cover by a Saudi military coalition, which aimed to retake all territory held by the Houthis. Asked if the Saudi-led coalition coordinated the action with the United States, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said Saudi Arabia and the US had a defense agreement but would not give more details. Why has Iran’s oil minister resigned? Mohsen Paknejad has resigned days after allegations that an intermediary trust selling Iranian oil abroad owed millions of dollars-worth of export receipts to the state. Iran is grappling with a dire economic situation, including inflation running at 85%. What is behind the latest disagreement between Israel and the UK? It stems from the UK’s decision to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank – a move that Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, labelled “morally distorted”. Israel has threatened to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, prompting the UK to warn it will expel one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat forced out. Why has the Green party in England and Wales been condemned over its Zionism policy? The English and Welsh Greens are facing international ostracism after adopting a policy declaring Zionism as a form of racism, which has drawn dismay from the group representing European Greens. The co-leader of the German Greens separately said the policy was “intolerable and unacceptable”. Student protests erupt at Cornell over mishandling of gang-rape allegations Mass protests erupted at Cornell University on Monday, with students criticising officials’ handling of gang-rape allegations, demanding the president’s resignation and painting “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” on an administration building. Thousands of students and faculty gathered for a demonstration over the high-profile case of a former student known as Jane Doe, who said in a recent lawsuit that she was plied with drugs and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. US supreme court hears big oil’s attempt to block climate damage lawsuits The US supreme court began its new nine-month term hearing arguments on Monday in a major case in which big oil companies attempted to strike a fatal blow against lawsuits seeking to hold them accountable for the climate crisis. In Suncor Energy Inc v County Commissioners of Boulder County, local officials in Boulder are suing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil in state court to force the companies to share a portion of the costs that the climate crisis has imposed on local taxpayers. However, Exxon and Suncor, which is based in Canada, are arguing that federal law prevents state courts from hearing Boulder’s climate change lawsuit. In other news … Televangelist Jim Bakker has died aged 86. He built a multimillion-dollar empire and lived ⁠in opulence before being disgraced by a sex scandal and a conviction for defrauding followers. The US is closely monitoring the case of a Russian laboratory worker who died last week after a reported accident at a plague research institute in Siberia, Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, has said. Separatists Parti Québécois have won Quebec’s provincial election but fell short of enough seats to govern alone. They have promised to hold another referendum on independence from Canada. Norway is planning a temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places amid rising global concern at the spread of the AI-enabled recording devices. Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final after hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd that struck a spectator in the eye. Stat of the day: US book bans in public schools reach record annual high of 12,000 Texas tops list with 8,100 bans and Stephen King is again the most-banned author, Pen America finds. Culture pick: Jaclyn Smith on the fun, friendship and frustration of Charlie’s Angels The only original Charlie’s Angel to make it to the end of the show’s five-year run, Jaclyn Smith talks to Emine Saner about the love she found on set, the harassment she endured off it and the drug-taking she did her best to ignore. Don’t miss this: the mum fighting for social media reform after her son’s suicide Vivian Ho speaks to Kristin Bride, who appears in a new documentary taking on Congress after the death of her 16-year-old son, who was cyberbullied. … or this: ‘It could knock a whole street down’ – the art of defusing a second world war bomb Incredibly, more than eight decades since the second world war began, unexploded bombs from the era can still be a problem. Samira Shackle has a gripping tale of how two were discovered close together in January in southern England. Climate check: US households pay 62% more for water than they did a decade ago, study finds For-profit water corporations, federal cuts and the climate crisis are “supercharging water rate hikes”, the study’s co-author says. Last thing: personal props auction from ‘enigmatic, obsessive and dictatorial’ director Stanley Kubrick Have you ever fancied owning the axe that Jack Nicholson menaced Shelley Duvall with in The Shining? Now is your chance. It is one of hundreds of items to be sold as part of an auction of the influential late director Stanley Kubrick’s personal archive. title: JD Vance and Ted Cruz are fighting for control of the GOP. The problem? Neither is called Trump
author: Arwa Mahdawi
summary: Having seemingly written off the midterms, the Republican bigwigs are making their pitches for 2028. But the current commander-in-chief could be looking closer to home, writes Arwa Mahdawi
body_text: The US midterm elections are a month away and it’s looking rough for the Republicans. I wouldn’t discount devious schemes behind the scenes, but, on the face of it, the president and his entourage seem to be flailing. Donald Trump is desperately dangling money in front of voters and promising “a big surprise”. Meanwhile, the vice-president, JD Vance, and the GOP senator Ted Cruz seem more concerned with fighting over who will be Trump’s heir than with the midterms. If the polls are to be believed, Vance is the frontrunner for the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. But while he may have great name recognition, Vance is also unlikable. According to the CNN analyst Harry Enten, he is one of the least popular vice-presidents in history. He’s also apparently made enemies within his own party, largely because of his scepticism about the Iran war. His detractors include Cruz, who told MS Now in August that Vance wasn’t a shoo-in for the nomination. The party, Cruz said, was still figuring out the best candidate and needed “to decide who we are, what do we believe”. These remarks did not go unnoticed by the ever-observant vice-president. “It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance said in an interview with NBC News on Friday. “At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans.” Cruz, in turn, denied he was thinking about 2028 yet and suggested Vance may have a chip on his shoulder. “In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure,” Cruz told Politico on Saturday. “So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes.” Yes, please continue making whatever comments you like, JD! In fact, I’d strongly suggest you take it up a notch and remind people of Cruz’s greatest hits. There was the time he fled to Cancún on holiday when his state, Texas, was facing deadly, record-breaking freezing temperatures, for example. And the time his official Twitter account “liked” a pornographic tweet (apparently it was “a staffing issue, and it was inadvertent”). And there’s the longstanding joke, which started with a meme in 2013, that Cruz is the Zodiac killer. Obviously, this was baseless, but it went viral because apparently it is believable. Indeed, a 2016 poll found that 10% of voters in Florida thought Cruz was the Zodiac killer and an additional 28% said they were not sure. That said, Vance should be careful about what he dishes out: he’s been the subject of a few memes himself. Who can forget the (completely unfounded) viral rumours about the vice-president having sexual relations with a couch? While Vance and Cruz may be butting heads now, I suspect they’ll eventually kiss and make up. They are pragmatists, which is a polite way to say soulless opportunists. They had similar journeys when it comes to Trump, for example. In 2016, Cruz called Trump, who nicknamed him Lyin’ Ted, a “serial philanderer” and a “pathological liar”. Around the same time, Vance wondered if Trump was “America’s Hitler” and called him “the most-raw expression of a massive finger pointed at other people”. Now, of course, it’s a very different story. Vance is veep and Cruz has become such a staunch Trump ally that the president calls him Beautiful Ted. With the news as grim as it is, you’ve got to find satisfaction where you can. And it’s certainly satisfying to watch Vance (who absolutely does not fornicate with furniture) and Cruz (who is definitely not the Zodiac killer) feud. Ultimately, though, it may turn out that we don’t have to worry about either man come 2028. MS Now’s Rachel Maddow thinks the president may follow the authoritarian playbook and install a family member as his successor. “If he wants [his family] to not end up in jail or prosecuted or having their … gains investigated … he’s got to make sure that the next president is also a Trump,” Maddow opined on a recent podcast. Potus himself has said “there could be” a Trump dynasty and seemed to suggest his daughter-in-law Lara may be his successor. Take a seat on a comfy couch for this one, JD: you’re going to have a tough time trumping a Trump. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Pedro Sánchez is a master of the political comeback. But calling a snap election in Spain may be a gamble too far
author: Paolo Gerbaudo
summary: A thriving economy, a model green transition, social advances – Spain’s PM shouldn’t be in trouble. Yet he is, and it’s a lesson for progressives everywhere, says sociologist Paolo Gerbaudo
body_text: To progressives across the west, Spain has been a rare glimmer of hope in a world where far-right parties are increasingly entering government. Under Pedro Sánchez, who became prime minister in 2018, the country has combined a post-Covid economic boom with a bold green energy transition programme, and a pro-immigration stance with a principled opposition to the war agenda of Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu. Yet, at the end of next month, this rare beacon of democratic progress could fall. On Monday Sánchez called a snap general election, set for 29 November, after two decrees to address the country’s housing crisis were voted down in the lower chamber by politicians from rightwing parties. Speaking from the staircase of the Moncloa palace, Sánchez admitted that his government had not achieved all it had set out to do. “Many injustices remain to be corrected … particularly regarding inequality in public services and access to housing,” he said, adding: “To do more, we need to renew and expand public support.” Sánchez attempted to pass the legislation after tens of thousands took to the streets to protest against the housing crisis, setting up camps reminiscent of the country’s 15-M anti-austerity movement and the global Occupy movement of 2011. But this explosion of popular anger has been long in the making. According to Spain’s national public opinion research institute Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS), housing has been the country’s top preoccupation since the end of 2024, as a growing number of people struggle to pay rent. In the latest gamble of his long career as master of the political comeback, Sánchez hopes to ride the wave of popular mobilisation to turn public attention away from the Ceuta immigration crisis of July, which rightwing opponents exploited as a demonstration of the government’s failures, and focus attention on the housing crisis, an issue where the left holds stronger political ground. But this time it will be hard to convince Spaniards that with a new lease of life, the progressive coalition government will solve an issue it had promised to address a long time ago. Sánchez’s troubles provide useful lessons for progressives all over the world about the difficulties of translating policy achievements into a solid base of political support. They are also a reminder that – as championed by New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani – addressing the affordability crisis rather than promising abstract economic growth is of more significance to voters. In the US midterm election campaign, Republicans are struggling because of rising prices at the gas pump, while in Brazil, rightwing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro just rode to an impressive result in the first round of the presidential elections partly due to discontent with living conditions and household pressures. In Spain, Sánchez’s government is facing similar concerns about affordability, which are obfuscating an otherwise impressive macro-economic performance. Indeed, seen from the outside, Sánchez’s Spain may appear to be a dazzling political success. The country, which in the 2010s was derided as part of the European Piigs – a term coined to mock Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Greece and Spain as the eurozone’s weakest economies – has become an economic powerhouse. In the years after the Covid pandemic, Spain’s GDP grew at a rate of around 3%, while France, Germany, the UK and Italy grew at a miserly 1% or less. Spain is also held up as a model of successful green transition, with renewables now generating close to 60% of the country’s power, which has also kept energy bills low and helped insulate the country from the energy shocks caused by international crises. Spain, enabled by significant Chinese investment, is also surprisingly becoming the leading European hub for electric car production, to the dismay of some of the country’s traditional allies. To these economic and environmental achievements add the significant social improvements achieved under Sánchez, exemplified by the rise in the minimum wage from €736 to €1,184 per month since 2018. Yet despite these measurable successes, Sánchez’s centre-left coalition is now trailing the right by about 7 percentage points in national polling. That’s partly because while minimum wages have increased, median wages have remained relatively stagnant. But it is real estate that Sánchez’s government has been judged as failing to deliver: during its eight years in power, house prices have risen by an estimated 50%, with rents rising by over 40%. As climbing the housing ladder becomes prohibitive, a growing number of young people in Spain are forced to pay extortionate rents. This is acutely felt in large urban areas, where the presence of tourists and digital nomads further increases rents, forcing out local residents; this is enabled by private equity firms, who purchase entire blocks to expel local inhabitants in order to create Airbnbs. Sánchez’s government has repeatedly promised to take action on these issues, but its measures have been thwarted by political gridlock or otherwise proven indecisive, partly due to fear of alienating homeowners and antagonising international finance. If Spain’s centre-left coalition falls, the country could be left with an alliance of the mainstream conservative Partido Popular and the far-right party Vox. It would be the most rightwing Spanish government since Francisco Franco’s dictatorship. The lesson for progressives everywhere is clear: economic growth and ambitious reform will count for little unless working people feel the benefits in their daily lives. Paolo Gerbaudo is a senior researcher at the faculty of political science and sociology of Complutense University in Madrid and a lead researcher at the Alameda Institute

title: California to ‘actively monitor’ for possible threats after Trump said Iran could ‘take out’ LA and San Diego
author: Shrai Popat and David Smith in Washington, Lauren Gambino and Dani Anguiano in Los Angeles
summary: Gavin Newsom said state’s threat-assessment center would be on heightened alert after president’s remarks
body_text: California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, on Tuesday directed the state’s emergency preparedness center to “actively monitor” possible threats to the state after Donald Trump suggested Iran could “take out” the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego. Trump has faced a chorus of condemnation from Democratic leaders in California after his comments at a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, which the White House has suggested were being taken out of context. At the president’s rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, Trump claimed that high prices due to the war with Iran are a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”. He went on: “They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” The crowd applauded the line. “Donald Trump’s remarks were dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs,” Newsom said in a post on X, adding that the state’s threat-assessment center would be on heightened alert “in the event that foreign actors interpret the President’s remarks as an invitation to target California”. From the governor’s press office account, he taunted California Republicans for their “radio silence” in response the president’s bombastic remark. But one Republican House candidate, Jim Desmond, who is running in a competitive San Diego-based seat, pushed back. “America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our commander in chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” Desmond, a former mayor of San Marcos, said in a statement. It is a notable rebuke from a Republican in a closely watched contest that could help the party retain their razor-thin majority in the lower chamber. Desmond is set to face Marni Von Wilpert, a lawyer and member of San Diego’s city council, for the state’s 48th congressional district – which was redrawn in response to Proposition 50. Desmond, also a navy veteran, said that he “served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war”. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage,” he added. He joined a string of prominent Democrats who called out the comments. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, said: “The nuclear annihilation of an American city is no laughing matter.” Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor vying to succeed Newsom, said he wasn’t surprised by the president’s comments. “Donald Trump is a known commodity – you know how he acts, you know how he behaves,” Becerra told reporters at a campaign event in Los Angeles on Tuesday. But he took a jab at Republicans who “profess that they should be the leaders of our state” but were. not willing to “stand up to Donald Trump”. Becerra’s Republican rival, Steve Hilton, did not return a request for comment. But many Trump supporters dismissed the uproar. Blake Marnell, who wears a brick-patterned suit to resemble Trump’s border wall, lives in San Diego and was at the rally in Nebraska. He said by phone on Tuesday: “I defend his comments absolutely. It is not inappropriate to mention something like that now because you have to take it in the context in which it is spoken. If you look at that context, it’s appropriate for a rally in which the president is addressing his base.” Marnell added: “The Democrats have a long and storied history of flying off the handle at any remark that President Trump makes, and this is just another chapter in that history, and I ascribe no significance to it, and in two days no one will be talking about it.” Darrell Issa, a Republican congressman who represents parts of southern California, did not directly respond to an inquiry about Trump’s remarks, but defended the president in a statement, saying he had “taken historic and concrete action to eliminate the nuclear threat, protect every inch of our homeland, and ensure Iran never threatens America or her allies ever again”. Paula Whitsell, chair of the Republican party of San Diego county, criticized what she called the “biased media” for taking the president’s remarks “completely out of context”. “No one should believe for a single moment that he wants ANY American city attacked,” Whitsell said in a statement. “The president was simply speaking to his belief that confronting Iran is worth it to eliminate the threat to our country and named two cities as an example of what could happen if we don’t act, not as an invitation for them to be attacked.” The White House also insisted that Trump was being willfully misinterpreted. Steven Cheung, its director of communications, posted on X: “The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality. He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.” The White House’s “Rapid Response 47” account called the Los Angeles Times newspaper “buffoons” and insisted that Trump was saying the US is “fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon – which they would if they had the chance.” • This article was amended on 6 October 2026. A previous headline implied it was Trump’s suggestion to “take out” LA or San Diego. Trump suggested that Iran could do so.

title: Jon Stewart on Trump and AI tech bros: ‘Stop lying to us’
author: Guardian staff
summary: Late-night hosts discussed the frightening rise of AI and how Trump is choosing to target voters for the midterms
body_text: Late-night hosts took aim at Donald Trump’s close ties to the AI industry and his flailing attempts to lure midterm voters. Jon Stewart On The Daily Show, Jon Stewart spoke about how AI had been a “great concern lately” and how the biggest AI leaders meeting at the White House seemed to suggest that something important was being done about it. But instead, the president went against many of his previous statements against tech bros to announce that they would be self-policing their actions. “They’re tyrants!” Stewart said in response. “I thought you hated these guys?” He asked “how can you justify letting the tech giants police themselves?” as well as “why can’t we just fucking slow this down rather than let people regulate something they have a clear conflict of interest in regulating?” When asked about the positive impact of AI, many of the key figures said that it would be used for the greater good but Stewart spoke instead about how it’s mostly being used at this moment. “So in the future we will use AI to cure diseases but right now it’s mostly murder, surveillance and surge pricing for the McRib,” he said. He added: “I’m getting the sense that you guys might be full of shit” before moving on to the topic of jobs and how they will be affected by the rise of AI. Many key tech figures have found themselves unable to fully answer how employment will be affected while also suggesting it won’t be a problem. “They can’t answer the jobs question in a straightforward manner,” he said, Stewart added: “My guess is that they’ll still have jobs when this is done”. He played a clip of Elon Musk claiming that AI will actually lead to a universal high income for us all. “If we let them do enough unfettered capitalism, we can apparently capitalism our way to socialism,” Stewart said. But he questioned why that money isn’t coming to us now. “Don’t call us welfare queens, just call us early adopters,” he joked. “Stop lying to us,” he added. Jimmy Kimmel On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host spoke about flu season being more dangerous than ever, with a rise in other diseases, including the plague in Russia. “No worries, the gang who brought polio back is on the case,” he joked after showing a clip of Trump speaking about the story. Kimmel reminded viewers that the president is “a doctor but also Jesus” in reference to his AI social media posts. The host reminded viewers that the midterms are close and “you’d better be registered to vote” as Trump is trying to “save the Republican majority and his marriage”. Polls suggest his party won’t do well but if he can’t inspire the vote, “he’s gonna buy it from you” with the president repeating his claim that every American will receive $5,000 if Republicans win. “Why not make it five million dollars?” Kimmel asked before saying that Trump is “more likely to run a 5K than give it to us”. Trump has also been trying to tank Democrat James Talarico’s campaign as he is “one of the strongest candidates we’ve seen in a long time”. He is also still trying to make “dumocrat” happen even though “not one time has it gotten a laugh”. Taxpayer money has also been used for Trump ads and the FCC chair, Brendan Carr, has not found that to be a problem. Kimmel said it was “hard to see anything when your head is that far up the president’s ass”. Seth Meyers On Late Night, Seth Meyers spoke about Trump claiming he is a “high IQ person” at a recent rally. “This dude thinks he’s a genius because he passed a dementia test,” he said. Trump, who is “obsessed with his own intelligence”, has recently spent time attacking Senator Tom Cotton as he has opposed a bill to establish year-round daylight savings time. The president raged against it to the press, complaining about the annoyance of changing clocks. “Nobody changes their clock any more!” Meyers countered before saying that Trump must be using his “stove as an alarm clock”. “We don’t just decide to make it dark earlier for no reason,” he said before suggesting Trump’s talk of light and dark made him sound like a Neanderthal. But Trump “desperately needs a win no matter how small” and recently gave out Cotton’s cell number on social media. “Never give Donald Trump your cell, you gotta be more careful with that,” Meyers said. Meyers said that Trump’s circle was now just “weirdos and losers”, which is what happened when you spend “a decade devoting yourself to someone with no fixed principles, allegiances and loyalties”.

title: Election deniers stoke Trump-driven ballot security fears before midterms
author: Ariana Baio
summary: Former and current officials who bolstered claims of voter fraud in 2020 make fresh allegations of vulnerabilities
body_text: Prominent election deniers have spent recent weeks stoking fears over US election security before next month’s midterms, echoing claims pushed by Donald Trump to justify asserting more control over voting. On conservative-friendly media outlets, former or current officials who tried to bolster the US president’s false claims of mass voter fraud in 2020 have in recent weeks made fresh allegations of election vulnerabilities. Cleta Mitchell, a former politician who tried to help Trump overturn the 2020 election results, capitalized on recent reports that voting machines in Georgia had a privacy vulnerability to assert the state was not doing enough to secure voters’ ballots. “The problem in Georgia is that they use a version of these machines where … the machine doesn’t count the choices. The machine actually counts a QR code,” Mitchell told the conservative strategist and longtime ally Steve Bannon in an interview on Friday. Ed Martin, the controversial former US pardon attorney, repeated claims from top administration officials that voting machines, which used parts manufactured in China and other countries, were “compromised”. Other election deniers have planted seeds of doubt about the predicted outcome of the 2026 midterm elections. Kevin Roberts, president of the Heritage Foundation, which established and published Project 2025, told Fox Business in September that predictions Democrats could flip the Senate were “a psyop” – a term popularized by online theorists to describe something they believe authorities are doing to influence people covertly. “I think that this prognosticating is a psyop by so many of these polling firms. In order to do what? To depress conservative turnout,” Roberts said. In conducting media hits about election integrity, some prominent election deniers also revealed that the Trump administration was continuing its effort to assert greater power over states, which are responsible for running elections. Martin told Eric Bolling of Real America’s Voice on Monday that Trump had met with Tina Peters, a politician convicted of crimes related to her efforts to interfere with 2020 election results. “Just hours ago, maybe two hours ago, Tina Peters, you know, from Colorado, was in the Oval Office meeting with the president on election integrity, and they were talking about the plans,” Martin said. “The president is taking it seriously. If the Congress won’t pass the Save America Act, and they won’t, then the president’s going to have to do what he’s going to do,” Martin added. Trump has sought to undermine public confidence in US elections by promoting false claims of election fraud and making unverified claims of election insecurity. Earlier this year, the president tried to heighten those claims in a prime-time address. The president has attempted to crack down on voting, ostensibly to secure elections – despite experts assuring voters that elections are already secure. That includes directing his administration to implement new rules to restrict mail-in ballot voting, a method of voting Trump has criticized despite using it himself, create a federal database of eligible citizens, and force voters to provide proof of citizenship when voting in federal elections. Most of those actions have been stalled by court challenges. The supreme court has allowed the administration to move forward with compiling a federal database of eligible voters. Mitchell told Bannon she had “on good authority, from some of the highest levels in the Trump administration”, that the justice department was inquiring with the Georgia secretary of state about voter data it shares with two non-profit groups. She accused the states, including Georgia, of being “hypocrites” for refusing to share voter data with the federal government.

title: Disney accuses Trump officials of ‘blatant violations’ of constitution amid FCC battle
author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
summary: Lawyers tell judge ABC being unfairly targeted as US regulator seeks review of network’s local TV station licenses
body_text: Lawyers for Disney accused the Trump administration of “blatant violations of the US constitution” and censorship on Tuesday in the first court hearing over the Federal Communications Commission’s early review of the media giant’s eight local television station licenses. District judge Loren AliKhan seemed unswayed by government arguments that the order to force Disney’s ABC to apply years early to renew local television station licenses was tied to an investigation into parent company Disney’s hiring practices. ABC, Disney and its station group filed suit against the FCC in August, seeking to block the US media regulator from taking any further steps to punish or pressure the network in connection to the order. In its lawsuit, ABC argued that the FCC’s actions – taken at the behest of the Donald Trump-appointed chair, Brendan Carr – were actually intended to chill the network’s speech, which the president and Carr have argued is tilted against the administration. In legal filings and during Tuesday’s hearing, the network cited past threats by the president and the FCC chairman that jeopardized the licenses of television networks, including ABC on several occasions, for editorial purposes. “These are blatant violations of the US constitution,” the prominent trial lawyer Beth Wilkinson, arguing on behalf of ABC, told the judge during the approximately two-hour hearing. She said ABC faced a “chilling effect” that has affected – and will continue to impact – its editorial decision-making, as the network steers clear of political bookings and any other programming decisions that could spark further ire from the Trump administration and Carr. “That chilling effect has been happening and will happen every day,” she said, causing “irreparable harm” to the network and its ability to broadcast independent news for the benefit of the American people. ABC has said it has stopped booking politicians on the daytime talkshow The View and chose to air a July speech by Trump on its streaming platform so as not to antagonize the president. “Our editorial decisions are being affected right now,” Wilkinson said, noting the significance of decisions about how to cover next month’s pivotal midterm elections. “We are watching everything we do … We have already altered our conduct because of the fear of retaliation.” She also noted that ABC recently chose to air a Jimmy Kimmel-conducted interview with Texas US Senate candidate James Talarico on YouTube, rather than television, “because the FCC has no control over YouTube”. Dimitar P Georgiev, representing the FCC defendants, argued that “there is no reason to believe the early renewal order has prompted changes to the plaintiffs’ editorial decisions”. He also argued that the US district court for the District of Columbia was not the proper jurisdiction for the case, saying that ABC could instead appeal any adverse decision to the US court of appeals for the District of Columbia. ABC is seeking a decision from the judge to enjoin the FCC from taking any further actions against the network’s licenses. “We are asking to stop pure retaliation, putting us in a process that we should never have to be in,” Wilkinson said. In what Wilkinson called a “fatal admission”, Georgiev said the license renewal process “is not about the licenses”, but is instead a “tool” to expedite the commission’s review of ABC for potential violations of federal equal opportunities regulations. The lawyer also said the FCC could choose to end the license review process early if ABC is able to satisfy its document requests. Considering that the FCC opened its employment practice investigation into Disney last year, with requests for documents ongoing since then, the judge asked: “Why is it only in the summer that you determined that their responses were woefully inadequate?” She also questioned why the commission required the company to submit renewal applications for all eight of its stations simultaneously. And she noted past comments by Carr about the network’s licenses, including a remark in July, when he had said ABC’s decision not to carry the president’s speech that month on its linear channel could factor into the license investigation. “It strikes me with all the comments that this was merely over a discovery dispute, what made this so different that you needed to call for an early license renewal?” Judge AliKhan asked lawyers for the FCC, whom she asked for a list of some of the other enforcement actions the commission could have taken short of calling up the network’s licenses early. And she noted that there was “some daylight” in the FCC’s arguments, considering that the diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) inquiry was handled by the commission’s enforcement bureau, while the license order was made by the media bureau. The judge ended the hearing without issuing an order, saying she would take the matter “under advisement”.

title: Morning Mail: Mourning on 7 October anniversary; Coalition policy may risk India relations; and vale Richard Morecroft
author: Martin Farrer
summary: Israelis who lost friends or were held captive tell of their grief and rebuilding; trade fears over proposed immigration crackdown
body_text: Morning everyone. Three years on from the Hamas attack on Israel that set off a spiral of violence in the Middle East, our reporters have been talking to Israelis who survived the attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals. At home, there are concerns that the Coalition’s plan to severely limit immigration would cause havoc with trade agreements, there are calls for Anthony Albanese to act on the unmarked graves scandal we exposed yesterday, and the media world mourns ABC newsreader Richard Morecroft. Australia ‘A lovely man’ | Michael Rowland and Leigh Sales have led tributes to the veteran ABC newsreader Richard Morecroft, who has died aged 70. Migration risk | The Coalition’s plan to slash immigration risks breaching Australia’s free trade agreement with India, signed by the former Morrison government, allowing Indian students to stay and work for up to four years after completing their studies. It also seems certain to drag politics to the right, says our political editor. Climate crisis | Anthony Albanese has told delegates at the pre-Cop meeting in Tuvalu and Fiji that a rising “super El Niño” means Australia faces a hazardous summer, likely including floods, cyclones and extreme heat, and that it shows climate change is “here right now”. Unmarked graves | Albanese has been urged to use national cabinet to stop the use of unmarked communal graves to bury impoverished Australians and address failings that are leaving family and friends blindsided. Our revelations about the use of such graves prompted widespread condemnation from federal Liberal MPs, state Labor ministers and the Greens, and calls for federal action. Body found | A partially submerged body believed to be a woman has been discovered in a remote stockyard in northern New South Wales with the death being treated as suspicious. World ‘My life project’ | Shlomo Margalit, 89, embodies the loss felt by Israelis on 7 October 2023. He is the caretaker of the cemetery at kibbutz Nir Oz and shows our reporters the graves of three of his oldest friends, founding members of the kibbutz in the 1950s. “This is my life project, as well as my home,” he says. Israelis taken prisoner that day three years ago explain how they have tried to piece their lives back together despite witnessing the horrific violence. In Australia, Israel’s ambassador says the third anniversary of 7 October is an opportunity for both countries to return to “traditional friendship”. French unrest | Nearly 90,000 students, staff and parents have taken to the streets in cities across France as protesters blockaded hundreds of high schools in a nationwide day of action against long hours, missing teachers and crumbling classrooms. Iran plot | Three alleged Iranian spies carried out surveillance and reconnaissance to target journalists in the UK as part of a plan to commit “serious violence”, a UK court heard Election fears | Prominent US election deniers have spent recent weeks stoking fears over election security before next month’s midterms, echoing claims pushed by Donald Trump – whose Republican party is on track to lose heavily – to justify asserting more control over voting. Royal ‘betrayal’ | The Norwegian princess Märtha Louise and her husband, the American businessman Durek Verrett, are suing several former members of their inner circle for defamation over what they described as a “calculated betrayal of trust”. Full Story Is Australia ready for a datacentre boom? Josh Taylor joins Reged Ahmad to unpack why Australians are becoming so uneasy about datacentres, and whether government regulation can address their fears. In-depth As OpenAI’s representative on hostile ground and under pressure, Jason Kwon delivered a mea culpa for the company’s breach of government data in a helpful, quiet and calm manner. In fact, as Josh Butler observes, a bit like ChatGPT and leaving no one any the wiser. Not the news Traditionalists might object, but Alice Zaslavsky’s shortcut beetroot baked risotto – where the ingredients are baked with no need for constant stirring – looks like a perfect quick dinner for weeknights. Sport Tennis | Alex de Minaur was forced to retire injured after only one game of the second set of the China Open final, handing the title to his opponent Novak Djokovic. Coco Gauff alleged she received an “insane” amount of racist comments on social media following a controversial point in her win over Sun Xinran. Olympics | South Africa is in the hunt to stage Africa’s first Olympics after it was named as one of seven countries that will formally present its case to host the 2036 Games. Football | There are more Nations League matches this morning including England v Czechia, plus Croatia v Spain, and Scotland v Slovenia. title: S&P 500 and Nasdaq surge to record highs after AI chipmaker rally
author: Lauren Aratani
summary: S&P tops 7,800 for first time in history as investors optimistic despite signs of instability in US economy
body_text: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed at a record high after a rally around AI chipmakers and a dip in US treasury yields. At market’s close, the S&P 500 was up 0.58%, topping 7,800 for the first time in its history. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index rose 0.45%, while the Dow, which is slightly down from its record high in August, climbed 0.49%. Investors appeared optimistic after recent developments for chipmakers including Marvell Technology, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom that showed growth in the markets for the chips used to power AI. Wall Street has also grown more optimistic that the US Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its next board meeting in October. Job figures from September showed underwhelming growth in the labor market, and multiple Fed officials have said the next interest rate increase can probably wait. The optimism in the stock market, largely coming from continuing investment in AI, has defied other signs of instability in the US economy and global politics. The US bond market, typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, has been in turmoil in recent weeks. US bond yields, or the return an investor receives when a bond matures, reached recent highs amid concerns over high inflation and interest rates. The yield for 10-year US treasury bonds on Monday reached 5.349%, the highest since April 2022, before dipping back down on Tuesday. For American consumers, higher energy prices continue to be a major pain point. While gas prices have dipped over the last week, prices are still about $1.20 a gallon on average higher than a year ago. Diesel, which is used to fuel trucks, buses and trains, has also gone down from record high but is still over 40% higher than a year ago. The economy is expected to be a top issue in the upcoming midterm elections, with many voters expressing frustration over high prices. Donald Trump, who has been stumping for Republican candidates across the country, has been trying to paint a different picture for voters. At a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, Trump said that “our nation is doing better now than it’s ever done” and that gas prices would fall below $1.85 a gallon “in no time”.

title: Whistleblower report alleges Trump ordered FBI investigation on LA anti-ICE protesters
author: Shrai Popat in Washington
summary: White House denies the allegations as ‘false’ and says ‘first amendment does not protect violent rioting’
body_text: Donald Trump ordered the FBI to investigate protesters in Los Angeles who were demonstrating against the president’s immigration crackdown, according to a whistleblower complaint. Alex Padilla, a Democratic senator who represents California and serves on the Senate judiciary committee, said his office had received a copy of the complaint, which makes sweeping allegations about the Trump administration’s response to protests in LA in early 2025. Demonstrators had been protesting against Trump’s deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to push the president’s agenda. “These allegations are deeply alarming,” Padilla, who also serves as the top Democrat on the border security and immigration subcommittee, said in a statement. “Using the FBI to target Americans for exercising their first amendment rights directly undermines our nation’s foundational values. I won’t rest until we get answers.” NBC first reported on the allegations after viewing a copy of the disclosure, which identifies the whistleblower as Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles field office, who made the complaint following the federal response to anti-ICE protests around the city’s federal buildings, and in residential area, in February last year. Fields alleges that Emil Bove, then the acting deputy attorney general, told Akil Davis, the head of the field office, to open an investigation into protesters’ activities outside federal buildings, even though Fields says the demonstrations were protected free speech, and several FBI employees expressed concern with the legality of these requests. Fields, who joined the FBI in May 2016, also alleges that Trump reportedly viewed a TikTok video of protesters in Alhambra, California, that alerted neighbors about the presence of federal immigration officers and advised them of their legal rights. The White House, Fields says, then instructed Patel to direct the Los Angeles field office to initiate an investigation into those demonstrating in the video, because the president “was angry about the incident”. Despite the fact that member of Fields’s team determined that the protesters’ actions were constitutionally protected and there was insufficient evidence, Fields was told by a colleague – whose name is redacted – that “the president wants this investigation”. Fields says that even though her supervisor acknowledged the investigation was unconstitutional, the directive still had to be followed. Fields alleges that a “dedicated immigration squad” was created, comprising 10 agents, some of whom were taken off active cartel cases to carry out the White House’s requests. Fields says that she questioned the directive’s “operational logic” but her supervisor – whose name is also redacted in the complaint – described the move as “optics” designed to “make a show for the president”. Fields says, however, she was not aware of any “actual or potential national security threat, federal criminal activity, or vulnerability” that would have warranted conducting assessments or opening investigations into anti-ICE and CBP protesters at the time. She ultimately resigned from the bureau last year after she was removed from overseeing several programs, and believes that her diminished role was the result of objecting to protest-related investigations, according to the complaint. A White House spokesperson, Lauren Bis, called the allegations “false” in a statement to the Guardian. “The first amendment does not protect violent rioting, obstructing law enforcement, and assaulting law enforcement,” she said. “Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime. This administration has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be arrested and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” Meanwhile, the FBI and justice department said in a joint statement they would “continue to vigorously uphold the First Amendment rights of all Americans and restore the rule of law”. “The DoJ and FBI have a responsibility to investigate any potential violations of federal law, and conspiracies to impede federal law enforcement and assaults on federal officers are against the law. Violence is not protected by the First Amendment. Politically motivated attacks will not deter us from doing our job,” they added. In a letter to attorney general Todd Blanche and Patel, Padilla outlined Fields’s allegations and asked the officials dozens of questions about the reported investigations – including whether they resulted in arrests, how many directives of this kind the justice department has received from the president and the number of investigations that are still open.

title: Trump says he is weighing suspension of federal gas tax
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: President floats idea as voter anger over rising costs threatens Republican hopes in November midterms
body_text: Donald Trump said on Tuesday his administration was considering suspending the federal gasoline tax, a sign the president is noticing voter anger over fuel costs a month before the midterm elections. “We’re thinking about that,” Trump said when asked whether the tax should be suspended. Any suspension would require an act of Congress. The president cannot unilaterally suspend the federal tax. Trump first raised the idea in May, as the Iran war pushed fuel prices sharply higher. Pump prices have stayed high since. The national average for regular was $4.3685 a gallon on Tuesday, according to AAA, more than a dollar above where it stood a year ago. The federal tax is 18.4¢ a gallon on gasoline and 24.4¢ on diesel. Dropping it would cut about 4% from the price of a gallon of regular. The tax also brings in more than $23bn a year for highways and public transit. Asked about the midterms, Trump said he expected Republicans to “do very well”. He said his rallies, were “changing things around” because voters were hearing “what the Republicans have done”. “Prices are now coming way down,” he said. “And oil, as soon as the war is over, which will be soon, will be coming way down.” He gave no date for the end of the war and did not say how a tax suspension would pass Congress.

title: LA and San Diego residents ‘horrified’ by Trump suggesting Iran bomb them
author: Roque Planas and Sam Levin in Los Angeles
summary: As Angelenos bemoan ‘sad situation’, those in San Diego say remark a ‘disservice’ to town with multiple naval bases
body_text: Donald Trump’s extraordinary implication that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego have sparked condemnation across the political spectrum. As residents of the two major west coast cities awoke on Tuesday to another sweltering day in a record-breaking heatwave, the president’s comments sent blood boiling even higher. Jessica, a 28-year-old Los Angeles hair stylist, was scrolling through social media early on Tuesday morning and was shocked to see that Trump had just suggested Iran should decimate her home town. For Jessica, who declined to be identified by her full name because she fears for the safety of her Mexican-born parents, the comments marked a new low for a president who had already spent years attacking immigrant families like hers. “I was just thinking what the fuck is wrong with him?” she said while waiting for a Waymo outside grocery store in LA’s Koreatown neighborhood. “He hates us. He hates LA. He hates any Democratic state ... It’s just a really sad situation.” In southern California, Trump’s unprecedented musing before a cheering crowd at a Nebraska rally on Monday night – that perhaps a foreign power should decimate two of the country’s best-known cities – has been met with reactions ranging from deep hostility to dismissive incredulity. Gavin Newsom, the state’s governor, called the remarks “dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs”. Perhaps most of all, California residents see it as a sign of the president’s fixation on tearing down west coast progressivism and diversity, most visibly through the deployment of national guard troops in Los Angeles during a series of brutal ICE raids in 2025. During a bustling lunch service at Grand Central Market, a food hall in downtown LA, tourists and residents milled between taco stands and dumpling stalls. Many had yet to hear of the president’s threats, until asked by a reporter. One of those who had was Jens Midthun, a downtown resident who often stops at the market for coffee. “Trump has tried to paint Los Angeles as a dystopia despite it being a wonderful place,” said Midthun, sipping an iced coffee under a shaded outdoor table as the temperature approached the triple digits. (Midthun serves as the president of the downtown LA neighborhood council, but was speaking in a personal capacity.) “It reminded me that the president is obsessed with us – obsessed with California, obsessed with Los Angeles,” Midthun said. “We try not to think about him and yet, here he is with Los Angeles’s name right there in his mouth.” Trump’s remarks have sparked a particularly strong reaction in San Diego, which is home to roughly a quarter-million veterans and has one of the largest concentrations of military personnel in the US. “His statement was so irrational, it’s hard to explain exactly what he was saying, but it sounded like he was willing to give us up,” said Gil Field, communications director for San Diego Veterans for Peace, a group that opposes the war. “It’s horrible and we’re horrified.” The military supports nearly 357,000 local jobs in the region, representing $61.3bn of San Diego county’s economy, according to a report released last year. Defense spending accounts for 22% of San Diego’s gross regional product and the area is home to multiple naval bases and Marine Corps stations, with one out of four active-duty marines based in San Diego. “This is a military town, so you’ve got bipartisan objections to his comments,” said Field, who noted that there were always concerns that San Diego could be targeted in war due to the heavy military presence. “So for him to say this about San Diego is particularly galling. He did San Diego a disservice.” Jim Desmond, a Republican naval veteran running for a congressional seat in San Diego, also offered a pointed rebuke. “I served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war. Our job is to keep Americans safe, stand up to our enemies, and make sure a threat like that never becomes reality,” Desmond said on X. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.” Back in Los Angeles, far from the negative fantasies that Trump spins in his speeches, Midthun sees an economic powerhouse and vibrant cultural center sandwiched between the beach and the mountains, and enriched by some of the largest diaspora communities from across the world – South Korea, Mexico, El Salvador, Armenia and even Iran. “The president keeps talking about us, and talking about us,” Midthun said. “He’s got a lot of issues to solve. He should work on those issues instead of obsessing over the beautiful, great people of Los Angeles.”

title: David Ellison denies he has ‘politicized’ Skydance despite close Trump links
author: Jeremy Barr
summary: Ellison admits ‘good relationship’ with administration in remarks to reporters about newly merged media company
body_text: David Ellison, the chief executive of the newly formed media conglomerate Skydance, denied that he had “politicized” the company despite the close connection he has forged with Donald Trump’s White House over the 20 months of his administration. “We have a good relationship with this administration,” Ellison acknowledged to reporters at a Tuesday press briefing focused on the now-consummated merger of Paramount Skydance and CNN parent company Warner Bros Discovery. “I also had a really good relationship with President Biden. I have a good relationship with [Republican South Carolina senator] Tim Scott, and I have a good relationship with Governor Gavin Newsom. I think it is important to talk to everybody on both sides of the aisle … When you’re operating within a business-friendly administration, you should always have those relationships. “We want to speak to everybody,” Ellison added. “We do not want to politicize the company.” Asked about his conversations with Trump about CNN, Ellison did not directly discuss his communications with the president, the network’s most prominent critic. But he said he wanted to clarify that “we have not talked to any political leader of any party about news, other than to say that we want to be in the truth business and we want to be in the trust business. And we believe in complete editorial independence.” Amid concerns about whether Ellison might move CNN in a more rightward editorial direction, he said that both the cable news network and CBS News would be “completely editorially independent”, echoing a message he delivered earlier in the day during a town hall meeting with company employees. Ellison also gave an endorsement to the two leaders he has tapped to continue running the two news networks networks he now controls, the CNN chief executive, Mark Thompson, and CBS News editor-in-chief, Bari Weiss. On Monday, Thompson told staffers in a memo that he would remain at the merged company, while Skydance also confirmed that Weiss would remain in her role. “We’re thrilled, obviously, with Mark,” Ellison said. “We’re thrilled with Bari.” Asked about a potential merging of CBS News and CNN and any cuts – or “synergies” – that might stem from that, Ellison said he and his leadership team would spend the next several months “basically getting under the hood on all of that”. Most of the $6bn in expected savings from the merger would not come from job losses, he said. Ellison was not asked about Weiss’s performance as the editorial leader of CBS News. When asked specifically about Weiss’s performance by a Guardian reporter in June, Ellison ignored the question.

title: ‘Not exactly his favorite senator’: Susan Collins distances herself from Trump in Maine debate
author: Robert Tait in Washington
summary: Republican challenged by Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Senate race says she opposes Iran war and Canada tariffs
body_text: Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine, pointedly distanced herself from Donald Trump in a televised debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, as she sought to present an image of independence in a state that has voted against Trump three times. Proclaiming herself as not the US president’s “favorite senator”, Collins made the highly unusual boast for a Republican that she had voted with Joe Biden, a Democrat, more than 90% of the time when he was president. She also emphasized her differences with her fellow Republicans, saying she voted against her own party more than any other senator. Collins’s defensiveness came amid a determined onslaught from Jackson, 58, a veteran former state legislator who was getting his first chance to present himself to a broad audience since replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic candidate in a contest that could be vital to the party’s hopes of winning the Senate. Platner, a former harbor master, was forced to withdraw from the race in July after facing sexual assault allegations, which he denied, leaving Democrats racing against the clock to replace a candidate who had built up momentum campaigning on a populist progressive platform. Jackson painted Collins as a Trump loyalist, saying she voted with the president 96% of the time. He also doggedly focused on her 2018 vote for the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, tying it to the court’s subsequent overturning of Roe v Wade, which had for half a century guaranteed the national right to abortion. “Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in a pithy opening statement. “Eight years ago today, Maine women went to DC and begged Senator Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but she did it anyways. “He helped overturn Roe v Wade, and today she says she has no regrets. Would you trust her to pick the next supreme court justice?” Collins, 73, who has been a senator since 1996, has frequently presented herself as a moderate who stands against more radical trends in her own party. The posture is in line with Maine’s profile as a more Democratic-leaning state, which Trump has not won in any of his three presidential campaigns and which has voted for Democratic presidential candidates in every election since 1992. Nevertheless, Collins went to unusual lengths to differentiate herself from Trump on a range of issues, including the war with Iran, which she said she voted to end nine times, calling it “not well thought out”. Collins reacted with something close to alarm when the moderator, Gregg Lagerquist, said Trump had suggested that the president might pay a campaign visit to Maine. “I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” she said. “He’s talking about going to a lot of different states. I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator.” Collins stressed her differences with the president on specific issues pertinent to the Maine economy, including rural healthcare and tariffs against Canada, with which the state shares a border. “I have been the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada,” she said. “Canada is not China. It’s our neighbor and our friends.” Polls show the two candidates running neck and neck.
