title: British billionaire warned Epstein was a ‘sexual deviant’ decades before FBI closed in on the abuser
author: Marilyn W Thompson
summary: Sir James Goldsmith’s links to Hilton Head, South Carolina, add to mystery of Jane Doe 4, who claimed she was abused by Epstein in the 1980s
body_text: For Jeffrey Epstein, the billionaire Goldsmith family was a gateway to elite society and he wanted to be in their circle. The disgraced financier, who died in prison in 2019 facing sex-trafficking charges, longed for a billionaire’s lifestyle and cultivated the family’s friends, bankers, business associates and advisers. But Sir James Goldsmith, who was knighted by the Queen in 1976 and became a prominent British politician, remained wary of the American financier and even “despised” him, his daughter Jemima recently told the Guardian. Two decades before Epstein came under federal investigation, Goldsmith – who died in 1997 – told a confidant that Epstein was a “sexual deviant” who was recruiting children for illicit activities. Goldsmith “told me not to have anything to do with him, that he was a pervert, and he didn’t want him near any of us. He had four daughters to protect,” recalled the famous French architect Robert Couturier, who designed opulent homes for Goldsmith in New York and Mexico. Goldsmith’s alleged warning came around 1987, years before complaints about Epstein’s solicitation of young girls for sex began filtering into federal law enforcement. Epstein’s network of pretty “girls” evolved into what authorities describe as a global sex-trafficking ring that catered to the ultra-rich and powerful. It would become a scandal that touched royals, politicians, businessmen, academics, foreign diplomats and celebrities around the world, and left more than 1,000 victims in its wake. “That is the pity of it all. It was all preventable,” Couturier told the Guardian. Epstein, born on Coney Island, had been on the radar of New York’s elite since he first surfaced at society events, often on the arm of heiresses, Couturier said. “He was a charmer and a talker. Lots of rich people are deeply gullible, as protected as they are from reality. No one did anything about it.” In the mid-1980s, Sir James Goldsmith – known as “Jimmy” – announced he was making a shift in his US business operations. Goldsmith had hired a new chief executive who would open an office for him in Hilton Head, South Carolina, an emerging luxury resort. Goldsmith’s Hilton Head office is rarely mentioned in writings about his reign as the “lucky gambler”, as Time Magazine called him, an adviser to US presidents who became one of the world’s richest men by betting on undervalued companies. His conglomerate, with command centers in Paris and London, had its US headquarters in New York, close to his elegant Manhattan townhouse where Goldsmith entertained and where the young Epstein trolled for wealthy clients. Hilton Head at the time was undergoing a chaotic development boom that brought in a rush of speculators, shady operators and vacationers lured by star-studded golf tournaments and tennis matches. Its population, 11,000 in 1980, doubled in a decade. Its tiny airport was suddenly a busy landing strip for private jets, including a $10m Gulfstream owned by Goldsmith’s company that was parked there for quick hops. Epstein developed a lifelong fascination with Goldsmith, his family and fortune, an investigation by the Guardian found. Epstein’s connection to Goldsmith, and the presence of the billionaire’s company and his associates on a South Carolina sea island – which was attracting an infusion of investors – is potentially relevant because of an alleged sexual assault that is said to have occurred there in the 1980s. A woman known only as Jane Doe 4 claimed in four FBI interviews after Epstein’s 2019 arrest that he had assaulted her during his visits to the island in the 1980s, when she was still a teenager. She has also claimed the man she only knew as “Jeff” trafficked her to other men, including Donald Trump. The White House has vehemently denied the allegation about the US president, calling it “completely baseless” and “backed by zero credible evidence”. The Guardian has been examining records, digging into archives and conducting interviews to explore intersections of Goldsmith and Epstein and try to understand if Epstein, with decades of secretive movements and a web of global financial ties, might have had reason to be on Hilton Head in the 1980s when those alleged assaults by Epstein occurred. This remains a mystery, but Epstein’s relationship with Goldsmith provides some additional clues. Those who dismiss the claim of Jane Doe 4 – including Epstein’s brother Mark – have cited the lack of a public record of his presence on the island as proof that her story is untrue. Mark Epstein told the Guardian he has “no knowledge of him being in Hilton Head”. * * * Understanding how Epstein won and retained access to power and privilege throughout his life is important as criminal investigations of his sexual abuse and financial crimes continue around the globe. Federal prosecutors in New York have opened an investigation into the two overseers – Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn – of Epstein’s $577m estate, according to the Wall Street Journal. Both have denied they knew of Epstein’s criminal behavior. The Department of Justice has said that Epstein “harmed” over 1,000 people, including minors who were sexually abused. The justice department has released about 3.5m documents under the Epstein Disclosure Act, including reams of emails, letters and bank transactions. But the trove includes almost no records from the 1980s, leaving a large gap in the public’s understanding. Epstein’s alleged victims continue to accuse the justice department of a cover-up for holding back documents that might implicate Trump and other powerful men in Epstein’s exclusive circle. Trump has said he ended their friendship in 2004 after a real estate dispute and kicked Epstein out of his Mar-A-Lago club in 2007 for poaching employees. It is unclear whether Goldsmith’s concerns about Epstein stemmed from specific encounters, and there is no indication that Goldsmith ever reported his concerns to local or federal law enforcement. It took decades for the FBI to catch up with Epstein’s crimes. Federal investigators in Florida charged him in 2008 with soliciting sex from minors after a two-year investigation in which they interviewed young women, including some minors, who he paid for sexual encounters in his Palm Beach mansion. He served 13 months in jail under a lenient deal cut with federal prosecutors. Until now, the earliest warning about Epstein’s criminal behavior is believed to have come in 1996, when one alleged victim – an artist named Maria Farmer – claims she alerted authorities that she was sexually assaulted by Epstein, according to a lawsuit she has brought against the FBI. Farmer has also claimed that Epstein stole nude images she had of her two minor siblings, which she kept for her personal use in her artwork. The FBI has said in response to the ongoing litigation, which now includes 34 alleged victims, that agents do not have a duty to investigate “every single tip that comes across their desk”. A fascination with ‘Sir James’ Since Epstein’s death, Goldsmith has been portrayed as an important influence in his early career. The New York Times last year described Sir James as a connection Epstein shrewdly calculated was “worth nurturing for the long haul”. It recounted a party scene at Goldsmith’s Upper East Side mansion where Epstein, trained in classical piano, serenaded guests with a piano solo from the grand entry hall. Goldsmith’s warnings about Epstein came just as Epstein signed one of his biggest clients, the Ohio retail magnate Les Wexner, the founder of Victoria’s Secret, who was then ranked by Forbes as the 10th richest person in the US. Wexner says he severed the relationship with Epstein in 2007 after discovering he had stolen funds from Wexner. Some questions about Epstein and Goldsmith may never be answered given the secrecy surrounding these events and the refusal of key sources to answer questions. Meanwhile, the debate over the government’s release of the Epstein files rages on. Attorney general Todd Blanche has declined to release about 2.5m Epstein documents he deemed duplicative. An independent journalist, Katie Phang, is suing Blanche to try to force their release, and Blanche recently quietly turned over some of the documents related to Jane Doe 4 to a federal judge, who is reviewing the documents in his chambers. Prominent figures caught up in the Epstein controversy include former US president Bill Clinton, former Prince Andrew, former Harvard president Larry Summers and billionaire investor Leon Black. Black was recently held in contempt of Congress for his refusal to comply with subpoenas issued to him by the House oversight committee in connection to its Epstein investigation. Epstein’s emails about the Goldsmiths sometimes suggested bruised feelings and revealed he was watching the family from afar. He was not among the dozens of invited guests in 1997 to Jemima Goldsmith’s grand wedding party to the cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan, who served as Pakistani prime minister, according to the guest list. Just before he finished his lenient 2008 sentence for sex crimes in Palm Beach, Epstein scolded a young Romanian admirer for turning down her exclusive invite to a swanky dinner at Jemima’s Oxfordshire estate. “That was a BIG mistake,” he wrote in an angry 2010 email. Epstein criticized daughter Jemima’s choice of husband, calling Khan – who is now divorced from Goldsmith and in jail on corruption charges – a “whacko”. In a 2018 text, Epstein wrote of Imran Khan: “makes donald look like einstein. incapable of truth. , devout islamisist . many nuclear weapons. ( not erdogan or khomeni). he was married to two friends of mine. one daughter of jimmy goldsmith.” After the family distanced itself from him, Epstein gathered gossip about James’s daughter Isabel’s haughty behavior and joked when a hurricane seemed destined to damage Las Alamandas, her posh Mexican resort. “hurricane will hit isabel goldsmith resort and bye bye,” he wrote to a friend in 2015. Epstein elevated his access to the British elite when, in 1990, he started dating Ghislaine Maxwell, the daughter of a British media baron, who hobnobbed with British royals and enhanced Epstein’s standing among upper-crust families like the Goldsmiths. Maxwell became Epstein’s closest partner in recruiting young women, according to her federal indictment. She is serving a 20-year sentence. Three Goldsmith heirs told the Guardian in emails they never met Epstein and doubted their father had any business dealings with him. Isabel Goldsmith did not respond to messages. “I’m not sure I had ever heard of Jeffrey Epstein before he hit the news for the first time. So I’m presuming my father did not know him,” said Ben Goldsmith, an environmentalist and investor who was 16 when his father died. Zac Goldsmith, a conservative member of the House of Lords, said he never met Epstein and was not aware of his fascination with the family. Jemima Goldsmith Khan, who owns a London-based film production company, said she never met Epstein. “I heard that my father despised him – he was certainly not a friend of his,” she said. Sir James was a king of US corporate takeovers in a frenetic era of Wall Street deal-making, earning hundreds of millions by seizing control of vulnerable companies and cutting thousands of American jobs. Goldsmith sold his New York investments in 1987 and made a hasty exit back to London after correctly predicting the Black Monday stock market crash. Epstein was a takeover amateur who concocted his own deals while working as a consultant to a shady Manhattan debt collection company, Towers Financial, whose chief executive, Steven Hoffenberg, was later convicted of running a $450m Ponzi scheme. Before his death, Hoffenberg accused Epstein of masterminding the scheme. Epstein was never charged. Hoffenberg’s most ambitious effort was an attempted takeover of troubled Pan Am Airlines, the prestigious international carrier Epstein had fantasized as a boy about one day owning, according to an email from one of his friends. Working from its Hilton Head office, Goldsmith’s takeover team had already analyzed Pan Am’s books and backed off from making an offer. Developer Donald Trump also flirted with a takeover bid but never made it, media reports show. *** Couturier met Epstein through Isabel Goldsmith, the titan’s oldest daughter. Jet-setting Isabel became friendly – but not romantically involved – with Epstein, he said, and Isabel and Epstein both socialized in New York City’s nightlife scene. Epstein kept Isabel’s phone contacts at several addresses in his “little black book” later seized by the FBI as evidence. Couturier had grown close to James Goldsmith and his long-term girlfriend, who hired him in 1981 to renovate a mansion on East 80th Street. Goldsmith cut famous takeover deals around the dining room table, and his catered parties attracted the cream of Manhattan society. Isabel told Couturier that Epstein wanted to discuss hiring him for another renovation at a huge Upper East Side brownstone purchased by Wexner, he said. Epstein later moved into the restored mansion at 9 East 71st Street, about a half mile from Goldsmith’s, and decorated its dark wooded interior with his private art collection and gaudy fabrics. It became a center of his sexual misconduct, an address where the FBI in 2019 carried out boxes of photographs of alleged victims, massage tables and sex toys. Wexner also owned a dilapidated historic townhome next door at 11 East 71st Street that needed total renovation. The house was eventually bought through a trust by Trump’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, who has said he hardly knew Epstein, his nextdoor neighbor. Under questioning by House investigators, Lutnick acknowledged visiting Epstein for lunch at the predator’s Caribbean island, Little Saint James. Couturier was approached and interviewed by the FBI in 2010, after Epstein’s first arrest. A record of the interview, which is included in the Epstein files, indicates that Epstein had approached Couturier for a high-paying project on Little Saint James Island, where he was asked to provide “decor and furniture appropriate for teenage girls, with pink furnishings and bunk beds”. Couturier told the Guardian he remembered Sir Jimmy’s earlier warning. He withdrew from the contract, leading to a legal dispute. Goldsmith was hardly a prude, Couturier said, but he had no tolerance for inappropriate behavior with children. Goldsmith’s own domestic life was what his daughter Alix once described as “unconventional”, with three wives, numerous girlfriends and eight children. Two children were born in New York to his longtime girlfriend, a French journalist who moved with him to the city. Another link between Epstein and Goldsmith was Bear Stearns, where Epstein was a junior broker until he was targeted in an internal investigation of his trading practices. He quit in 1981 with an indignant resignation letter that was included in the Epstein files. Goldsmith remained a major Bear Stearns client, and Epstein, who somehow remained on good terms with the brokerage top brass, invested his own and his clients’ money into the firm, which collapsed in 2008. Epstein always kept an air of mystery around his business deals. In the 1980s, he described himself to friends as a “bounty hunter” who traveled the world to recover stolen money for rich clients. He and Goldsmith knew many of the same influential people. The Saudi billionaire Adnan Khashoggi, an international arms dealer, hired Epstein in the 1980s for unspecified work, according to published reports. Khashoggi and Goldsmith were both trusted advisers to President Richard Nixon, who met with them after his 1974 resignation to discuss overseas income opportunities, according to a Nixon biographer. Epstein became friendly with a wealthy international investor, Jean “Johnny” Pigozzi, who was in Goldsmith’s circle of advisers and is one of the trustees of Goldsmith’s estate, according to published reports. At one point, Epstein’s girlfriend Maxwell emailed Pigozzi to get price estimates for his French estate and nature preserve in Panama, saying she had an interested potential buyer, the emails show. Pigozzi, an art collector and heir to an auto fortune, is best known in popular culture as the inventor of the “selfie” because of his candid photographs of the rich and famous, including Goldsmith. He did not respond to messages. *** Goldsmith’s massive holding company, GOSL, had operations around the world and a corporate office in Manhattan run by his trusted team. But in 1985, GOSL filed papers with the state of South Carolina seeking authorization to do business in the state, the Guardian found. It opened an office in Hilton Head, the home of Al Dunlap, a notorious corporate raider Goldsmith was hiring to run his US operations. Dunlap had been living part-time on Hilton Head since the early 1980s when he was running a company that made paper cups. He was among the many corporate bigwigs who had discovered Hilton Head as a sanctuary for executives and government officials who needed privacy. Most exclusive neighborhoods were gated and developed on former rice plantations. Dunlap – who died in 2019 – had the Wall Street clout to ask investors to come to him. A newspaper account describes one session in 1985 at a new Marriott waterfront resort in Hilton Head where Dunlap pitched a Lily-Tulip stock offering backed by Wall Street firms to 70 out-of-town investors before leaving on a global capital-raising tour. Some locals say the atmosphere on the island was so frenetic, with investors and deal makers arriving for meetings, that anyone could slip in and out without notice. Goldsmith’s office in Hilton Head was tasked with selling millions of acres of forest land the company had acquired in takeovers of US paper companies. Its vast new holdings stretched from the Pacific north-west to the Adirondacks, making Goldsmith’s company one of the largest owners of undeveloped US land. The Guardian tracked down former GOSL executive Phil Lader, who was in charge of land sales, to ask if he recalled seeing Epstein in Hilton Head during the time GOSL had an office there. The short answer was “no”. Lader was a Hilton Head resident and former chief executive at Sea Pines. In 1981, he founded the prestigious Renaissance Weekends, which drew luminaries to the island for private invitation-only retreats. He was especially close to Bill Clinton, who was governor of Arkansas when he and his wife, Hillary, began coming to Lader’s exclusive gatherings. Other featured guests included Wall Street executives, university and government officials and leaders in the arts and sciences. Goldsmith hired Lader as a GOSL vice-president in 1986, just after he lost a Democratic party bid for the South Carolina governorship. Lader was appointed Clinton’s deputy White House chief of staff in 1993 and moved to London four years later when he was appointed ambassador to the court of Saint James’s. Lader said he never met Epstein and “never heard the name Jeffrey Epstein in my years on Hilton Head”. Epstein reportedly made 17 visits to the Clinton White House and later flew Clinton on his private jet. A partially redacted 2011 exchange in Epstein’s emails shows he was aware of Renaissance Weekends, which are promoted on social media as gathering places for “thought-leaders”. An unnamed friend asked if Epstein had heard of the gatherings. “Of course,” Epstein wrote. Asked if it was “something i should do?”, Epstein wrote “yes”. Renaissance Weekends were held in Hilton Head for 20 years, then moved to Charleston. Similar programs are also held in other cities. *** The woman who would come to be known as Jane Doe 4 first called an FBI victim hotline to report her alleged abuse on 10 July 2019. It was four days after Epstein’s arrest at a New Jersey airport. The agent manning the phones recommended that she be interviewed in person, near her home in Vancouver, Washington. One of her close friends made a separate call to anonymously report Jane Doe 4’s abuse. Jane Doe 4’s federal class-action lawsuit, filed later in New York against the Epstein estate, alleges she met Epstein around 1984, when she was a teenager, and had sex with him for several years when he visited the island. She said he rented properties, including a villa at Sea Pines, from her mother’s realty firm. In four FBI interviews in 2019 she described her abuser’s specific sexual quirks – including his use of butt plugs. Several were seized when the FBI gathered evidence in Epstein’s home in 2019. Some details squared with accounts given by other young victims who came forward during the previous Florida investigation. She described how he allegedly asked her to recruit friends and took nude photographs of her, also part of a pattern, and repeatedly plied her with drugs and alcohol. The FBI seized thousands of photographs and videos depicting victims when it searched his various properties. The Marriott hotel on Hilton Head figures heavily in her allegations. She told the FBI about a pool party there with local teenage girls and older males. She claimed the older man she knew as “Jeff” made a brief appearance at the pool before taking her back to his rented villa. She also mentioned a neighbor she had talked with during the period of alleged abuse. Her local attorney told the Guardian he sat in on the FBI interview and interrupted when she began describing telling other girls about “Jeff”. The lawyer said he feared the FBI might accuse her of aiding her abuser in soliciting other minors. FBI notes in the case, which were first reported by the Post and Courier in Charleston, South Carolina, repeat the woman’s allegation that at one point, Epstein transported her to New York or New Jersey where she claims he introduced her to Trump, who forced her into a sex act. She estimated she was about 13-15 years old, which would place the dates between 1983 and 1985, but she acknowledged a fuzzy memory. Trump said in a 2002 interview with New York magazine that he had known Epstein for 15 years, which would date their relationship to 1987. The White House has denied Jane Doe 4’s allegations. Jane Doe 4 also offered names of some of her high school friends who might have seen her with Epstein. But there is no evidence the FBI ever followed up on the leads Jane Doe 4 gave investigators. Its interest in her case appears to have died abruptly when she asked agents what the point was of her continued cooperation and told them she intended to join a class-action lawsuit, filed by the Bloom Law Firm in December 2019. A relative of Jane Doe 4 told the Guardian that she had been scarred by “layers of trauma” as a young girl from family tragedies and upheavals. She had spent time in foster care and had just finished elementary school when the family made its way south. Jane Doe 4 declined to answer questions from the Guardian relayed through the relative, who considers her account “plausible” because she was often unsupervised in her early teens. Three friends contacted by the Guardian did not respond to messages. Jane Doe 4’s attorney at the Bloom Law Firm told the Post and Courier she ultimately reached a settlement with Epstein’s estate but declined to give an amount. Court records show a claim she filed with the Epstein victims’ compensation fund, a formal review panel funded by the estate, was denied. The dates of her alleged abuse are much earlier than most other victims who have come forward with claims. In response to lawmakers’ questions about whether Jane Doe 4 had received a settlement from the estate, an attorney for Epstein’s accountant, Richard Kahn, said he could not recall details of all 60 women who settled with the estate outside of the compensation fund. The record is far from definitive about whether Epstein ever visited Hilton Head during this time. He did not own a private plane in the 1980s, so no travel logs are available. Epstein did have other real estate development interests at that time, including a long friendship with a developer who was building an oceanfront golf course on nearby Kiawah Island. Later records in the Epstein files show his plane landing at the nearby Savannah airport several times from 2013 to 2019, for unknown reasons. The emails show a redacted exchange in 2014 suggesting he was on Hilton Head for a March visit. Kenneth Lannon, a retired FBI expert in child sexual victimization who has trained hundreds of law enforcement agents to investigate abusers, said it was “highly likely” Epstein had victims pre-dating his Florida arrest and that he probably “started out slowly and just got better and better at it as time went on. The typical child sex abuser, he said, begins targeting and grooming potential victims soon after puberty, although they may come across as “nice guys” in regular social interactions. Money and the ability to travel freely make the crimes easier to pull off, he said. Child victims are often so starved for attention they become compliant and have more than one encounter with the abuser. Jane Doe 4 had a troubled life after leaving Hilton Head. She married several times and moved to the west coast. She returned to be with family in Georgia and was arrested in 2023 for stealing money from a dying man. She pleaded guilty and spent a year in jail. Her brothers were well educated; one worked for a few years as a Bear Stearns trader before the brokerage collapsed in 2008. A family member told the Guardian in June that Jane Doe 4 was “staying off the grid” and lived in fear of retaliation from the Trump administration amid the ongoing controversy over the handling of the case. Additional research by Sophie Sullivan

title: ‘Another coup d’état’: fears grow as Flávio Bolsonaro vows to ‘re-democratise’ Brazil
author: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro
summary: After a surprise first-round victory, critics suggest son of disgraced ex-president could seek to continue his father’s authoritarian project
body_text: Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right frontrunner to become Brazil’s next president, has vowed to “re-democratise” the South American country, increasing fears about a move into authoritarian rule if he wins power. Brazil was re-democratised in the 1980s after a brutal 21-year dictatorship that Flávio’s father, the disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, has long praised. Last year, Jair Bolsonaro, a former soldier who served under that military regime, was jailed for 27 years for trying to engineer a coup after he lost the 2022 election to the current leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Flávio, 45, beat Lula, 80, in Sunday’s presidential election first round and goes into the runoff on 25 October as favourite. On Tuesday, the rightwinger vowed to capitalise on the hugely increased far-right presence in congress after the election to change the constitution and “re-democratise this country”. “The only thing standing in the way of Brazil becoming a barbarity is called Flávio Bolsonaro as president,” he claimed at a campaign event in Goiânia, a city near the capital, Brasília. The incendiary comments caused outrage among historians and opponents of Bolsonaro’s radical populist movement, who have accused him of co-opting the language of democracy to disguise an illiberal shift. Talíria Petrone, the leftwing congresswoman, wrote on X: “This is the announcement of a coup.” Marcelo Freixo, a newly elected congressman from Lula’s Workers’ party (PT), said: “Brazil was re-democratised in 1988. The person who tried to undo this was his father, who was convicted of an attempted coup. What they want, once again, is a coup.” Bolsonaro did not spell out what he meant by “re-democratising” Brazil, a vibrant if polarised multiparty democracy that the Sweden-based V-Dem institute ranks 28th on its liberal democracy index, two places ahead of the UK and 23 ahead of the US. But Jair Bolsonaro, who has praised authoritarian leaders including Chile’s former dictator Augusto Pinochet, has long hankered for a return to military rule. Last September, the supreme court found Jair Bolsonaro guilty of trying to convince military chiefs to help him cling to power at the end of his 2018-22 presidency. The conspiracy culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília, a far-right insurrection seemingly inspired by the 6 January 2021 storming of the US Capitol. Writing in O Globo newspaper, Míriam Leitão, a prominent political and economic journalist, warned that if Bolsonaro won, Brazil faced “the extreme and concrete danger of … another coup d’état attempt”. “Flávio follows the same ideas as his father and has already said that an intervention in the institutions is necessary,” Leitão wrote. “If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, he will have more tools at his disposal to carry out his father’s authoritarian project: robust caucuses in the lower house and senate, a weakened supreme court, and the support of the Donald Trump administration. “Political science shows that it’s in the second term that an autocrat doubles down on their plan. Look at the case of Donald Trump. The risk isn’t of the son repeating the father, it’s that he surpasses him.” Miguel Lago, a political scientist, said Sunday’s far-right election triumph – in which Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) secured the senate’s largest caucus, with 28 of its 81 seats – would permit radical changes, including the impeachment of supreme court ministers considered enemies of the Bolsonarismo movement. Jair Bolsonaro and his jailed co-conspirators are likely to be freed if his son wins, with the former president expected to become an influential minister able to select the new heads of the armed forces. “It’s better than a coup d’état … it’s almost like a coup d’état with the support of the majority of the population,” Lago said. Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s authoritarian president, has been accused of “killing” democracy by using control over the country’s congress and institutions to approve sweeping constitutional changes, including scrapping presidential term limits so he can seek indefinite re-election. Flávio Bolsonaro recently met Bukele’s security minister, Gustavo Villatoro, in São Paulo, hailing the Central American country’s hardline security policies under which thousands have been jailed during a state of exception that has lasted nearly five years. Bolsonaro told reporters that during their conversation, Villatoro “stressed the importance” of using control of congress to make the “necessary legal changes”. Celso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist, said he believed that by using the word “re-democratise”, Flávio Bolsonaro sought “to smuggle his authoritarian purposes into acceptable language”. Barros said Bolsonaro, unlike his father who always seemed to favour an “old school barracks uprising” to seize power, appeared to be part of “a new generation of authoritarians” who sought to dismantle democracy from within by undermining and occupying the institutions. “Then you don’t need to break any laws to achieve authoritarianism … because you are the law,” Barros added, citing Hungary’s former far-right prime minister Viktor Orbán as an example. “Clearly, Flávio’s plan is a corrosion of democracy so [Brazil] becomes a Hungary or Bukele-style system.” Danilo Araújo Marques, a historian, said the word “democracy” had been co-opted before in Brazil by undemocratic forces, when the military men and politicians behind the 1964 coup called their actions “an intervention to democratise the country”. “They all talked about democracy … [but] democracy has a different meaning in the mouth of a coup-monger,” said Marques, who is from a research unit at the Federal University of Minas Gerais called Projeto República. Marques noted that during the campaign, Bolsonaro had claimed his octogenarian opponent, Lula, represented the past while he was selling the future. “But this future means going back to what [Brazil] was before,” Marques said. “It’s a ‘future’ that is based on the order prior to the 1988 constitution, which is precisely the military dictatorship.” Asked to clarify his plans on Wednesday, Bolsonaro rejected speculation he was seeking to finish “what his father didn’t do”. “Let’s stop lying. Let’s touch down in the real world,” he told reporters, adding: “Brazil needs to go back to normal, that’s all.”

title: Paxton admits Trump’s Iran war and US gas prices are plaguing Republicans in leaked audio
author: Ariana Baio
summary: Texas attorney general acknowledged affordability was his party’s ‘biggest problem’ heading into the midterms
body_text: Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general running as the Republican candidate in a competitive Senate race, admitted privately that rising fuel prices as a result of Donald Trump’s Iran war were hurting his party before the midterms in the latest leaked audio recording. Asked what issues were “dragging” his campaign at a closed-door fundraising event, Paxton replied, “It’s not tariffs … it’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel,” according to an audio recording shared with Axios. “When it’s over $6 per gallon for diesel … people are feeling the pinch,” Paxton said. Paxton acknowledged affordability was Republicans’ “biggest problem” heading into next month’s election, citing polling numbers that indicate Democrats are ahead in many competitive races – including his own. Trump has tried to change the narrative around affordability, insisting his administration has done more to lower everyday prices for Americans than Democrats. Trump, who picked Paxton to run as the Republican in the Texas Senate race, will join Paxton at a rally in San Antonio on Wednesday evening. But Paxton appeared to recognize the uphill battle facing Republicans, telling people at the closed-door events that “so many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable”. “I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t, you know, I don’t know what’s behind some of the decisions,” Paxton said. The Guardian has asked Paxton’s campaign for comment. Madison Cercy, a spokesperson for Paxton’s campaign, said in a statement that the Texas attorney general’s comments were “a non-story”. “The attorney general said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store,” Cercy said. “President Trump is doing everything he can to bring prices down, and Ken Paxton is going to Washington to help him by putting money back in families’ pockets with a bigger child tax credit and larger deductions for health care and buying a home. Texans need immediate relief, and everyone knows James Talarico will raise your taxes,” Cercy added. Recent polling from the Associated Press/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research indicates most adults blame Trump for poor economic conditions. Approximately 74% of Americans said the economy was leaning poorly. Another 65% of survey respondents said they blame Trump’s policies directly for higher costs. In the audio recording, obtained by Axios, Paxton said he was trying to help lower costs in ways that he could, such as through his proposed tax cut plan that includes healthcare and housing write-offs. Axios’s reporting is just the latest leaked audio clip of Paxton being critical of his own party. Earlier this week, Politico reported that Paxton privately admitted to people at a closed-door event that outside forces in Washington DC were controlling much of his campaign messaging. “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming – you know – from DC,” Paxton said, according to an audio recording obtained by Politico. Last week, the New York Times reported that Paxton admitted that Trump’s Republican midterm convention “dropped” his polling numbers. Paxton is locked in a competitive race with the progressive Democrat James Talarico. Polls show Paxton and Talarico are neck-and-neck, but Talarico has a small lead over the Texas attorney general.

title: Will Trump’s rallies lift the Republicans?
author: Isobel Montgomery
summary: The US midterms in focus. Plus: porn’s big players
body_text: With fewer than 30 days until the US midterm elections, Donald Trump seems determined to still be centre stage despite poll fears that after 3 November he may end up a lame-duck president as a Democratic blue wave sweeps the country. Our Washington bureau chief, David Smith, has been watching how the president is playing to Republican voters at the start of a blitz of cross-country rallies. It’s, at best, a mixed picture. As David reports, Trump’s self-belief and message to voters to “pretend” his name is on the ballot reveal a man out of touch with ordinary Americans’ worries about the cost of living and whose promises that the war with Iran will soon be over ring ever more hollow. And then there are the candidates, more of whom are shying away from their earlier allegiances to a president whose approval ratings continue to slide. Republican analysts view Trump’s contribution to the midterm campaign as more of a hindrance than help, David discovers. And it’s a view shared by some voters Stephen Starr spoke to in Ohio. All of which bodes ill for JD Vance, whose “one more chance” messaging is unpicked by columnist Sidney Blumenthal as a strategy that only underlines the view of voters, like the ones in Stephen’s piece, who will vote for change and an America that is not like it is now. I hope that this week’s cover story primes you to make sense of the midterms. And it comes with an early reminder that due to our printing deadlines, Guardian Weekly won’t carry news of the results immediately but we will provide in-depth analysis of what they mean in our 13 November issue. title: The most shocking part of Trump’s comments is what our reaction says about us
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: Listening to the president at a rally these days is a mix of deja vu and word salad, but his decade-long project of division remains abnormal and dangerous
body_text: Donald Trump’s campaign rallies can be repetitive. Very repetitive. He calls himself the “greatest” president leading the “greatest” movement inside the “greatest” economy. He rails against “Dumocrats” for the “transgender mutilization” of children. He lambasts the “fake news” and reheats election lies. He describes illegal immigration as an “invasion” and recites the poem The Snake. If we were all frogs being slowly boiled alive, we’ve now reached the stage of blackened toad. After a decade of this, presidential utterances that would once have caused outrage are met with a shrug. We are no longer shockable. Or so we thought. On Monday, speaking at a rally in Nebraska, Trump seemingly suggested that Iran, which he long accused of pursuing nuclear weapons, could “take out” the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego. “I want to see a tremendous victory,” the US president told supporters of his war on Iran, launched almost eight months ago. “You want to see a tremendous victory because it verifies all the things we did. “And again, remember, with the war, it’s just artificial,” he added, in an apparent reference to higher prices. “It’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.” Trump went on: “They can take out a city. Let them take – let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s – this is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon. It’s essentially almost over with.” Perhaps the only thing more chilling than a commander-in-chief musing about the deaths of millions of Americans under mushroom clouds was the sound of his supporters cheering at the line “let them take out”. After all, the question of the Trump era has always been: what does this say about us? Democrats had a field day. The Democratic senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut called it “such a sick, evil thing to say”. The independent senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont accused Trump of saying the small price to pay was the “annihilation of two major American cities”. California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, called Trump “deranged and dangerous” and put the state’s threat-assessment centre on alert. Forty-three members of Congress from California jointly called on the president to apologise. Even a group called Astronauts for America felt compelled to issue a statement of condemnation. But most Republicans remained silent (a sentence written countless times in recent years). The White House communications director, Steven Cheung, claimed that Trump “was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped”. Some of Trump’s critics allowed that perhaps this time he had merely spoken clumsily, rather than diabolically. Aaron Blake of CNN argued that the comment was “incoherent, not malicious”. Yet the central formulation was undeniable: “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” All you have to do is imagine another president uttering those words and imagine the response. Obama would have faced accusations of treason and potential impeachment; Biden would have been written off as an old man suffering dementia. But what to make of Trump? The comments were a jumbled word salad that raises familiar questions about the 80-year-old’s mental acuity. Last week, for example, inviting attenders of a Hispanic Heritage Month celebration to walk the floor of the new White House ballroom, he warned: “Don’t fall over the edge because it’s a long way down. And only a Hispanic could survive that fall.” Listening to Trump at a rally these days is akin to listening to Lucky in Samuel Beckett’s absurdist play Waiting for Godot: “Given the existence as uttered forth in the public works of Puncher and Wattmann of a personal God quaquaquaqua with white beard quaquaquaqua outside time without extension who from the heights of divine apathia divine athambia divine aphasia loves us dearly with some exceptions for reasons unknown but time will tell …” The way in which the president singled out Los Angeles and San Diego underlined his decade-long project of division. Indeed, for years California has been Republicans’ idea of the bastion of woke decadence, the quintessential “enemy within”. We’ve grown used to the president’s campaigns of retribution against Democratic power centres, but such othering is dangerous in any society. Trump has a willing accomplice in JD Vance, who is quietly pursuing a rally schedule of his own. Speaking in Lakeland, Florida, the vice-president responded to the Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon, who is Black, after she called herself a socialist, saying: “Then get the hell out of here. You don’t belong in America if those are your views.” Vance, who is 42 and potentially rehearsing for a White House bid, speaks less incoherently than his boss. He has also shown more willingness to acknowledge voters’ struggles and plead with them to give Republicans more time to get the job done. But history will remember that, even as Trump unravelled before the world’s gaze, Vance remained loyal, and was among his chief enablers. It is their task to normalise Trump, whose approval ratings continue to test fresh lows, and sanewash his statements so that Americans forget what a catastrophically abnormal chapter this is. The worst horror of all in Nebraska was not what the president said, but what Republicans and others failed to say in response. Lawrence O’Donnell, a host on the MS Now network, warned viewers on Tuesday: “You live in a country, you live in a world tonight, where it is no longer news that the president of the United States appears to be insane. It remains the single most important ongoing news story of this era.”

title: The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy too
author: Editorial
summary: Editorial: Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the economic struggles of voters have boosted Democrats. But with less than a month to go, there is no complacency
body_text: For once, Democrats and Donald Trump might be in agreement: “Pretend I’m on the ticket,” the historically unpopular president has instructed supporters. Midterms are in large part a referendum on the incumbent, and Trump’s war on Iran and its impact on the cost of living have boosted support for Democrats. With less than a month to go, they have reason to be upbeat. The party has a mountain to climb after the devastating defeats of 2024, and the gerrymandering of Republicans, but surveys give it a lead of about nine points on the generic ballot, which measures preference for parties rather than specific candidates. Attention has turned from the prospects of seizing the House, where Democrats are forecast a clear majority, to what once seemed like the highly optimistic possibility of taking the Senate too. That would require flipping four seats, with 35 in play. Remarkably, Democrats are prospering in red states from Texas to Alaska. In Kansas – which Mr Trump carried by 16 points, and which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932 – the race is neck and neck. Even putting aside the ongoing questions about polling accuracy, there are very good reasons for caution. The first and most glaring is that the Democrats remain unpopular. Voters are being turned off the Republicans rather than drawn towards their rivals; pundits talk of a red undertow rather than a blue wave. Second, the picture is extremely patchy. Democrats’ striking progress in key races where few had favoured them is tied to standout candidates and especially unpopular opponents – notably in Texas, where the Christian pastor and economic populist James Talarico is leading Ken Paxton, viewed unfavourably by a third of his own party’s supporters. Yet Democrats are struggling in some places where they initially had good reason for optimism, such as Maine. Third, the huge Republican spending advantage is now materialising – with $700m of advertising booked since the start of September. Mr Trump, who has fared better than his party in elections, is hitting the campaign trail. He may make sure his base turns out. But candidates – including those who benefited from his endorsement – are increasingly distancing themselves from the president because he alienates others. He is visibly more energised by his construction projects than how his voters can pay their bills. His war on Iran looks not only reckless and ineffectual, but is pushing up prices. Strikingly, voters are now more likely to identify Republicans than Democrats as “elitist”. Latino voters who swung to him are changing their minds, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement excesses contributing. Outrageously, Mr Trump has used taxpayer-funded adverts to laud his presidency. It goes without saying that he cannot be expected to respect the midterm results. The supreme court rejected his efforts to restrict mail-in voting – used by almost a third of the electorate – but he continues to smear it. Just as he disrupts the electoral process, in office he rejects the norms and restraints that his predecessors recognised, and relies more and more on executive orders – seeking to avoid checks on issues ranging from war to vaccines. But should Democrats manage to take both House and Senate, they would regain both legislative control and investigative powers. In these elections, most votes will be driven by economic stress rather than democratic peril. But their outcome will be critical to the defence of American democracy – or its continued erosion.

title: Flávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaigners
author: Jonathan Watts
summary: Inquest under way into why President Lula’s success in curbing Amazon deforestation has not led to success at polls
body_text: More fire, more ash, more crime, more death. And a globally important ecosystem driven ever more rapidly towards a point of no return. That is the prospect for the Amazon rainforest for at least the next four years if Flávio Bolsonaro holds on to the lead he established this week in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election. This appears to be of far more concern to the outside world than to voters in Latin America’s biggest, richest and most biodiverse nation. The far-right son of the former president and jailed coup-monger Jair Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote, putting him in pole position before the 25 October runoff with the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who was backed by 44.2%. The result is an unnerving jolt to climate and nature campaigners. Taken out of context, this appears to be a vote against the forest. The current administration of Lula (as the veteran Brazilian president is best known) has reduced deforestation in the Amazon by almost 50%. But that success secured little noticeable electoral traction for either Lula or pro-forest candidates in other polls held the same day. The former environment minister Marina Silva lost a bid for the Senate and Joenia Wapichana, a former head of Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, failed to win a seat in Congress. Out of 57 Indigenous candidates, only two won. Flávio Bolsonaro is the heir to the political legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, a former army captain whose four years in power resulted in a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying 2bn trees. If he wins, Bolsonaro has promised to free his father, who was imprisoned for plotting a military coup and attempting to annihilate democracy in Brazil. He has said that his father could have any position he wants in his administration. Flávio Bolsonaro has shown that he will be just as willing as his father to dismantle protections for climate and nature and allow illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers to invade Indigenous territories. As a lawmaker, he backed a 2019 bill to eliminate requirements for landowners in the Amazon to conserve a proportion of native vegetation. In his manifesto, he completely ignored the climate crisis. And he has courted support from some of the most predatory landowners in the rainforest. He is also part of a movement – Bolsonarism – that is geared towards maximising profits for extractive industries regardless of the environmental cost. Take its victorious candidate for the Amazonian state of Pará, Daniel Santos, who was fined $275,000 (£208,000) for deforestating 280 hectares (690 acres) of his land without authorisation and is now promising to waive such penalties. As a result of Sunday’s election, Bolsonarists now control seven of the nine states in the Brazilian Amazon, and could win an eighth in the runoffs. Bolsonarist influence in the legislature, which is dominated by agribusiness interests, is also growing. Flávio’s brother, Carlos, and stepmother, Michelle, were elected to the Senate, while an uncle and brother won seats in the lower house of deputies. Even before the election, Congress had been pushing hard to weaken environmental protections. Now it will be almost impossible to stop, particularly given the current chaos in the supreme court, which has been a partial check on untrammelled expansion by miners, ranchers and monoculturalists. Against these forces, Lula would struggle to govern even if he wins the runoff. As a result, it is not just the Amazon that is in peril, but all of Brazil’s biomes, its traditional peoples and the stability of the global climate. The question now is why voters paid so little heed to these concerns. That inquest is already under way. Many focus on the influence of social media, which has been used far more effectively by the far right. During the Bolsonaro administration, his sons were part of the “hate cabinet” that spread fear and disinformation via WhatsApp groups and other online channels – Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos, was indicted by federal police for leading the group. Environmentalists were often the target. Another factor is the expansion of US-style Pentecostalism, which is steadily supplanting Catholicism across Brazil, particularly in the Amazon. The political and environmental consequences of that religious shift can be seen by comparing the pro-nature treatise of the past two popes with the sermons of many evangelical preachers who encourage followers to seek wealth today as much as, if not more, than following moral creeds to ensure a good afterlife. Lula, 80, has been slow to adapt. Although he is arguably the most iconic and successful Latin American politician of the 21st century, his messaging seems less attuned to the people than it was in his heyday. The Workers party has struggled in an era of weaker unions and in some ways been the victim of its own success – with education and social policies that raised millions out of poverty and created greater expectations for consumption and entrepreneurism; and huge subsidies to farmers, who now support the right wing because they chafe at environmental limits. Tied into those explanations are the geopolitics of the climate and nature crisis, which is exacerbating great power rivalry between the US and China and amplifying extreme ideologies as much as extreme weather. In this light, the Brazil election is just the latest in a broader pattern of the far right taking control to expand extractivism despite growing evidence that the capitalist economy is breaking planetary boundaries. In the past two years, Donald Trump has ripped apart environmental regulations in the US and treated the rest of the Americas as his sphere of influence. Argentina was already onboard. Venezuela has been invaded for its resources, while in Colombia, Peru and Chile there has been a sharp shift to the right. Will Brazil be the next domino to fall to Trumpism and its bonfire approach to nature? The Bolsonaro family certainly hope so. Jair went so far as to salute the US flag. His son Eduardo urged the US to apply tariffs on Brazilian people to “punish” the government for imprisoning his father. The Brazilian intelligence agency has warned that the US was trying to interfere in the election. That election isn’t over yet. Lula stands a small chance if he can win over the many millions of voters who chose not to mark their ballots for either candidate. But the odds are stacked against him. Most of the eliminated candidates were on the right so their supporters are more likely to switch to Bolsonaro. No first round leader has ever failed to win the runoff of a Brazilian presidential election. Voters, of course, are allowed to change their minds. Either on 25 October or, constitutionally, in four years’ time. But for how much longer will that be possible? If Bolsonaro wins, it won’t just be Lula that is finished, it could also be the Amazon and democracy itself. • This article was amended on 7 October 2026. An earlier version incorrectly said that Jair Bolsonaro’s brother, Eduardo, and mother-in-law, Michelle, were elected to the Senate. It was Flávio Bolsonaro’s brother, Carlos, and his stepmother, Michelle, who were elected.

title: Hegseth tells USS Lincoln sailors controversial deployment ‘wasn’t easy’
author: Anna Betts
summary: Pentagon chief tries to play down problems onboard carrier as it returns to dock after 260 days at sea without port call
body_text: Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, told service members on the USS Abraham Lincoln on Wednesday that their deployment “wasn’t easy” as the carrier prepares to dock after spending over 260 consecutive days at sea without a port call, setting a navy record. For months, there have been widespread concerns since reports first emerged of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health onboard. In his remarks on Wednesday, however, Hegseth again sought to play down the issues. Instead, he condemned “a few folks in the media” who he accused of trying to “turn” the Lincoln’s deployment “into some sort of symbol of dysfunction, or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission”. “I never say this lightly, but I’m the one who signed that orders go twice to extend you,” Hegseth, who has pledged to restore the “warrior ethos” to the US military, told the service members on Wednesday. “I plead guilty.” Hegseth announced that those onboard the vessel, which is set to arrive in San Diego later this week, would be awarded the presidential unit citation, which, according to the US military is conferred on units of the armed forces “for extraordinary heroism in action against an armed enemy”. The USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group “did what no other carrier strike group has ever done”, he declared on Wednesday. “We asked you to do more, and you know what you did? You did more. And it wasn’t easy, and there wasn’t easy resupply.” The US carrier, with roughly 5,000 sailors and marines onboard, left San Diego in November 2025, initially bound for the Pacific and expected to return in the spring. But after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in late February, the Lincoln was redirected to the Middle East, to support US operations in the region. Its deployment was extended, and the carrier spent over 250 consecutive days at sea without a port visit, setting a navy record, as the war disrupted regional resupply routes and traditional hubs. The deployment was described as “one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era” by Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command. As Donald Trump struggled to end the war with Iran, and the Lincoln’s deployment dragged on, reports emerged over the summer of shortages of food and basic supplies, and deteriorating mental health and morale among some crew members, including that two crew members had attempted to jump overboard. At the time, senior Trump administration officials dismissed the reports. Hegseth claimed they “completely misrepresented” the reality, while Trump, when asked in August whether the deployment had gone on too long, responded, “Not nearly long enough” – a remark that upset some naval families. The reports about the conditions on the Lincoln caused concern among some military health experts, veterans and families of sailors onboard, and drew outrage from Democratic lawmakers, including several who demanded more information from the Pentagon. The Lincoln was relieved from its deployment later in August, as the USS George Washington aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East to take its place. But in recent weeks, as the Lincoln has headed back to San Diego, a new disclosure about the carrier has renewed scrutiny. Acting navy secretary Hung Cao acknowledged last month that eight service members from the Lincoln and its strike group had attempted suicide during the deployment. He was responding to questions from Kirsten Gillibrand, the the Democratic senator. As Hegseth delivered his remarks on the Lincoln, Gillibrand criticized him, stating that “our service members deserve better than a photo-op. They deserve real accountability for this administration’s failures”. Other Democratic lawmakers have requested that navy leaders provide an accounting of the eight suicide attempts, and have also asked navy leaders to detail the steps they will take to “protect sailors’ mental health and wellbeing during future extended deployments”. As the Lincoln returns home this week, another aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, was recently dispatched to the Middle East. Navy officials have said they are taking steps to prevent similar problems during future deployments, including loading up the vessel with additional supplies, and improving communication with families.

title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while trying to repair campaign sign
author: Sam Levin in Los Angeles
summary: Bernadette Greene-Placentia says she is sharing her story in order to fight for victims of sexual assault
body_text: This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual assault. A congressional candidate in Arizona says she was attacked and raped in August while trying to repair one of her damaged campaign signs. Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a trucker and small-business owner, shared her account with the Phoenix New Times, a local publication. The assault took place on 14 August, according to the campaign. The Democratic candidate, running in a district that includes parts of Phoenix, told the newspaper that she was walking across a parking lot just after 2am to fix a campaign sign when an attacker smashed her over the head, causing her to black out. Greene-Placentia told the newspaper that she awoke to find a man on top of her and discovered he was raping her. She recalled another man coming over and pushing her leg, at which point she said she swung her foot at him. The man said, “Not even worth it”, and the two attackers left, leaving her face down in the parking lot, she recalled. The candidate said her memory of the incident and its aftermath was hazy, telling the newspaper she did not remember picking herself off the pavement or returning home. “It’s just these little tiny flashes of things that I do remember,” Greene-Placentia told the Phoenix New Times. “As much as I don’t want to remember, I’ve tried very, very hard to remember more stuff. But that’s where I’m at.” She said she may have had a concussion as a result of the attack and that her body was covered in bruises. She said she initially wanted to forget what had happened and felt “embarrassed”, at first choosing not to report the assault. But she told the paper that on the campaign trail, she often spoke about fighting for Arizonans, “and I didn’t feel like I could keep saying that if I weren’t also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault”. Greene-Placentia told her campaign staff and husband about the assault days after it happened and reported it to the Maricopa county sheriff’s office two weeks later, according to the Phoenix New Times. The newspaper interviewed Greene-Placentia’s relatives, friends, campaign staff and landlord about the aftermath of the assault. “Speaking publicly about what happened has been incredibly difficult for Bernadette,” a campaign spokesperson told the Guardian on Wednesday after the Phoenix New Times story was published. “She chose to share her story because she knows many survivors struggle in silence, and she hopes that by speaking about her experience, others will know they are not alone.” The spokesperson added: “She hopes the focus remains on supporting survivors and making sure people who have experienced sexual violence know they are seen, heard and supported.” “I need to let women know that it’s OK to talk about it,” Greene-Placentia told the newspaper. Stephanie Simacek, a state representative and friend of Greene-Placentia, said the congressional candidate told her of the assault in early September, telling the Phoenix New Times, “I felt sick to my stomach, and it was extremely disturbing. It was a big wake-up call for me. I think oftentimes, as candidates and electeds, we think that it’s not going to happen to us.” A Maricopa county sheriff’s spokesperson declined to comment, saying the investigation was ongoing. Greene-Placentia is running against an incumbent Republican member of Congress, Abraham Hamadeh. Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: Morning Mail: Pauper’s grave for ‘king of town hall’; Antarctic penguin numbers decline; and The Castle in real life
author: Martin Farrer
summary: Our investigation reveals shock of homelessness workers at fate of rough sleeper; Hunter Valley couple’s high court victory mimics film’s storyline
body_text: Morning everyone. Our exclusive top story reveals that a well-known Sydney rough sleeper was buried in an unmarked communal grave without the knowledge of his support workers as we continue our investigations into the scandal. Elsewhere, the story of the couple who led the fight against a coalmine expansion in the Hunter Valley has been called a real life version of The Castle, and a British billionaire is revealed to have warned as early as the 1980s that Jeffrey Epstein was a “sexual deviant”. Australia Pill boom | The number of pharmacies stocking an abortion pill increased by almost 50% when restrictions were relaxed, with researchers saying the findings suggest deregulation of abortion promotes safer and faster healthcare. Exclusive | Homelessness support workers say they are shocked that they did not know that a Sydney rough sleeper known as the “king of town hall” for his constant presence on the steps of the building was one of the people “without means” who ended up being buried in unmarked graves. ‘Catastrophic loop’ | The drastic land use changes wreaked by colonisation created a “catastrophic wildfire loop” that rendered south-east Australia more susceptible to climate-fuelled bushfires, experts say. Policy problem | What is the right level of immigration into Australia? The main political parties all have different proposals for this key issue, but what exactly are they all suggesting? World ‘All preventable’ | Two decades before Jeffrey Epstein came under federal investigation, the British billionaire Sir James Goldsmith – who died in 1997 – told a confidante that Epstein was a “sexual deviant” who was recruiting children for illicit activities. “It was all preventable,” the confidante has told the Guardian. Penguin fears | The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed. Paxton pain | Ken Paxton, the Trump-backed Republican in a tight Senate race in Texas, has admitted privately that rising fuel prices as a result of the president’s Iran war are hurting his party ahead of the midterms. Why are the midterms so important? Birthday bombing | Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia’s military of deliberately killing civilians and bombing residential buildings as a macabre gift for Vladimir Putin, who celebrates his 74th birthday on Wednesday. Brazil coup fears | Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right frontrunner to become Brazil’s next president, has vowed to “re-democratise” the South American country, increasing fears about a move into authoritarian rule if he wins power. Full Story The Coalition’s race to the bottom on migration Tom McIlroy joins Matilda Boseley to discuss whether being more extreme on immigration than One Nation is a vote winner, and why the most vulnerable will be hit hardest by the Coalition’s plan. In-depth The successful attempt by two retired teachers in the Hunter Valley to prevent the expansion of a coalmine next to their farm has been likened, writes Lisa Cox, to “a real-life moment from The Castle”. Our environment editor Adam Morton notes that critics were quick to point out Anthony Albanese’s language opposing legal action to stop a coalmine sat in contrast with the message he delivered over the past three days at a climate conference in Fiji. Not the news The Melbourne singer-songwriter Gretta Ray talks to Katie Cunningham about suffering a serious illness while on the brink of her big breakthrough, rebuilding her life, and her new album Heartsong out later this month. Sport Football | After Lionel Messi played his final match for Argentina, Marcela Mora y Araujo reflects on how the legendary player turned football into a sacred mystery. Tennis | Coco Gauff said she had been left drained by the racist abuse she experienced during the China Open after losing in the last 16 to Elise Mertens. Rugby union | Demand for South Africa and New Zealand tickets for the Nations Championship finals weekend has been greater than those for England despite Twickenham hosting the inaugural competition’s finale. title: Trump backs away from top aides who reportedly advised pro-Russia government
author: Ariana Baio
summary: President floats firing Chris LaCivita and James Blair over any ‘conflict’ after reports of work in Republika Srpska
body_text: Donald Trump distanced himself from two top advisers on Wednesday, claiming he did not have “any idea who else they work for”, after it was reported they spent the weekend assisting a pro-Russia government in the Balkans. On Truth Social, Trump wrote that Chris LaCivita, the co-manager of his 2024 presidential campaign, and James Blair, a campaign adviser and White House deputy chief of staff on leave of absence, “are outside consultants” and “do not work for me other than as outside consultants”. “They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C.,” Trump wrote. “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” The president’s comments came after the New York Times reported that LaCivita and Blair traveled to Republika Srpska, an autonomous entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to assist the government ahead of elections over the weekend. Sources told the newspaper that each adviser was paid hundreds of thousands of dollars. LaCivita and Blair are meanwhile working with Maga Inc, the Trump-backed SuperPac assisting Republican candidates in November’s US midterm elections. Both men have long histories with Trump, and the US president has praised them separately on social media. LaCivita joined Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign in 2022, after leading a pro-Trump Super Pac called Preserve America. In 2024, Trump wrote on Truth Social that LaCivita was “THE BEST” co-campaign manager alongside Susie Wiles, who now serves as the White House chief of staff. Blair worked for Trump’s 2020 campaign in Florida and was the political director of Trump’s 2024 campaign. He joined the president at the White House as deputy chief of staff for legislative, political and public affairs. In April, Trump called Blair “one of the brightest political minds” while announcing that Blair would leave his White House position, briefly, to join Maga Inc and assist Republicans in the midterms. Trump said Blair would return to the White House after the midterms. Trump’s statement distancing himself from the two advisers comes as Maga Inc prepares to ramp up efforts to assist Republican candidates in next month’s elections. Public polls indicate Democrats are leading Republicans in several key competitive races. That is largely attributed to widespread disapproval over Trump’s handling of the economy and cost of living. A spokesperson for Maga Inc told the New York Times that Blair and LaCivita remained engaged with midterm efforts while traveling, saying the two “hosted a team call with race captains on Saturday morning to go over recent survey data”. The Guardian has contacted Maga Inc for comment. Despite polling showing waning voter enthusiasm for Republicans, the party has a cash advantage over Democrats. At the end of August, Maga Inc had more than $415m cash on hand. Several Super Pacs tied to Maga Inc have begun launching multimillion-dollar ad blitzes.

title: Democrats sue to stop Trump from using taxpayer funds for self-promoting ads
author: Robert Mackey
summary: Ads promoting the president have cost more than $12m so far and Trump’s Super Pac has refused to reimburse taxpayers
body_text: The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration in federal court on Wednesday, asking a judge in Washington DC to stop the president from using taxpayer funds to air a series of ads promoting himself, arguing that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda. The ads promoting Donald Trump, including one recycled from his 2024 presidential campaign, have cost taxpayers more than $12m so far, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. Ken Martin, the DNC chair, said in a statement that Trump was misusing taxpayer dollars in “a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November. Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes.” After a bipartisan backlash to the use of public money to promote himself during the final month of the midterm campaign season, Trump claimed on Monday that he would direct the Maga Inc Super Pac he controls to pay for the ads instead. The next day, however, the White House said Trump’s political action committee would not reimburse taxpayers for the money it had already spent on the ads. Then, when the government unveiled a fifth ad in the series, celebrating Trump’s military intervention in Venezuela, it was also paid for by the US government. The DNC complaint, filed in the US district court for the District of Columbia, alleges the ads violate federal law, including a ban on congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda”. “President Trump personally directed this illegal activity. The White House office crafted the partisan campaign. The office of management and budget shifted $20m to pay for it. And US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has carried it out. These unlawful actions are ultra vires and violate the Administrative Procedure Act (APA),” the complaint states. The suit also notes the first ad in the series features an image of Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, awarding Trump the so-called “Fifa peace prize” to support its case that the ads all violate a prohibition on the use of taxpayer funds for “self-aggrandizement”. The complaint also references new polling from Reuters/Ipsos released on Tuesday which found that an overwhelming majority of Americans, 86%, called it inappropriate to use taxpayer funds for TV ads featuring the president around an election. The survey reported that about 80% of Republicans called the ads inappropriate, with only 17% of the president’s party approving of them. According to the suit, the ads have been broadcast on ABC, NBC, MS Now, CBS, CNN, Fox News and Newsmax, and appeared during popular NFL and college football games, and news and entertainment shows in which the president has been criticized, including Meet the Press, Jimmy Kimmel Live! and Saturday Night Live. The federal lawsuit also includes details of another eight ads that have already been prepared for broadcast and were found “in a Dropbox account controlled by LMD Agency Inc, the government contractor bringing the ads to air”. The ads ready to be broadcast include: one that celebrates the UFC fights staged at the White House on Trump’s birthday in June; one titled “God Made Trump”, a fan-created hymn of praise to Trump that was shown during the Republican midterm convention; one titled “Resilience”, which includes images of Trump announcing his candidacy for the presidency in 2015, then being charged in Fulton county, Georgia, in 2023 for conspiring to overturn the results of the 2020 election, and video of the assassination attempt on him during the 2024 election campaign; one titled “King of the Jungle”, which shows a lion hunting in the wild and disparages Trump’s political enemies, including former president Barack Obama. In February, Trump shared a racist video on social media that portrayed him as a lion and Barack and Michelle Obama as apes. According to CNN, which gained access to the Dropbox last week, another ad in the series features attacks on Joe Biden, including the mocking image of the former president as an autopen installed by Trump on an exterior wall of the White House.
