title: Leon Botstein resigns from Bard roles as key Democrat demands investigation into Epstein links
author: Stephanie Kirchgaessner
summary: Jamie Raskin says ‘startling’ email asked whether young woman was ‘for me, or are you keeping her for yourself’
body_text: A powerful Democratic lawmaker has called for a criminal investigation into the former Bard College president Leon Botstein after congressional investigators uncovered an email from Botstein to the accused sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein in which he says Botstein asked if a young woman was “for me, or are you keeping her for yourself”. The latest development appears to have triggered the immediate resignation of Botstein from all Bard-affiliated positions, including his professorship and roles in Bard’s music programs. Botstein had led the college for 50 years and only recently stepped down as president. Brandon Weber, the chair of Bard College’s board of trustees, said in a statement on Wednesday evening that the college had received additional communications from Congressman Jamie Raskin, who is the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee and is leading a congressional investigation into Botstein’s relationship with Epstein. Weber said Bard was undertaking “a full review” of the allegations that have been made in Raskin’s letter, and was cooperating with the committee’s investigation. Weber also said members of the executive committee of Bard’s board of trustees voted unanimously to accept Botstein’s resignation. Botstein said in a statement that “any assertion that I knew of or was involved in Epstein’s criminal behavior is wrong”. “But I do not want to see even false allegations about me put the institution I have served for more than half a century put at any risk,” he said, saying he had submitted his resignation to protect Bard from any distraction. Botstein has faced intense scrutiny since the release earlier this year of the Epstein files, which revealed a friendly relationship between the then longtime college president and Epstein, who died in prison in 2019 while facing sex-trafficking charges. The revelations, including that Botstein had once been on Epstein’s island for a visit, contributed to his decision to step down as president. The latest controversy centers on an email that the Democratic committee members – who have access to unredacted emails in the Epstein files – said was sent by Botstein to Epstein in connection to a young foreign model and aspiring vocalist who they say was being “groomed” by Epstein throughout 2014. According to a letter sent by Democrats Jamie Raskin and Madeleine Dean to the attorney general, Todd Blanche, and FBI director, Kash Patel, records in the Epstein files indicate that Epstein was offering the young woman – referred to as Jane Doe – advice and help with her plans to attend school and develop her career in the US. But instead of helping her pursue her career, the lawmakers said in their letter, Epstein pressured her to take sex education and massage courses, and “employed” her while he was sexually abusing her. “By all appearances, Epstein was trafficking this young woman across state and international lines by mid-2014,” the Democrats’ letter said. Jane Doe, they said, was sent to Europe, Canada and multiple destinations in the US. The Democrats’ letter further alleges that the files indicate that Epstein “used his relationship with Leon Botstein to convince Jane Doe that she could have a successful musical career after modeling”. In May 2014, Epstein sent Jane Doe to meet Botstein, ostensibly for him to assess her musical talents. The Democratic lawmakers say they have reviewed one “startling” email – which had been redacted by the Department of Justice – that they said was sent from Botstein’s then Bard account, president@bard.edu. It reads: “Is [Jane Doe] for me, or are you keeping her for yourself.” The lawmakers wrote: “The evidence meets the federal standard for opening a criminal investigation, yet [the] DoJ and FBI apparently had it for at least 18 months without investigating Botstein. We are demanding they investigate Botstein and other potential co-conspirators.” In a statement, Botstein denied the Democrats’ allegations, including that he had sent the email in question. “The allegations in this letter are untrue, including an email that I did not author or send,” he said. The lawmakers said they have also heard from more than a dozen whistleblowers who have provided the committee with allegations of “decades of unpunished sexual misconduct at Bard”. In his statement, the Bard board of trustees chairman said: “When a formal complaint alleging sexual harassment or assault is filed, an independent external investigator conducts the review and submits a report to an impartial hearing chair. The college president has not had unilateral decision-making authority over title IX investigations or adjudications since the 2015-16 school year.” The Guardian reported in April, before Botstein’s resignation, that the then president told staff there was no way he could have known that Epstein – who was a convicted sex offender during their interactions – was actually “reprehensible”. At the time, he predicted he would be cleared of any hint of impropriety. The Guardian asked Bard at that time about the May 2014 email, which appeared in the redacted Epstein files as an email that Epstein appeared to have forwarded to himself, and was originally sent by an email address that only contained the name “President”. A spokesperson for Bard College told the Guardian at the time that the May 2014 message “has absolutely nothing to do with Bard College or President Botstein”. Botstein announced he was stepping down as president in May, after an independent review of his contacts with Jeffrey Epstein found the college president’s frequent interactions with Epstein “could have alerted” him to the possibility that he and Bard would be facilitating Epstein’s abuse of women. An investigation by the WilmerHale law firm, which had been commissioned by Bard’s board of trustees earlier this year to review Botstein’s interactions with Epstein, found the Bard president – who had previously claimed he was not friends with Epstein – made about 25 visits to Epstein’s townhouse, a two-day visit to Epstein’s Little St James Island, and that there were two visits by Epstein to Bard. These visits, WilmerHale reported, included “multiple women” who have since been identified as victims of Epstein. Botstein has not been charged with wrongdoing in connection with his relationship with the accused sex trafficker. They were in contact from 2012 to 2019. The Times Union first reported Raskin’s letter.

title: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage
body_text: Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back the embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton. At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena. Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. “He’s going back home to mom,” the president said after the man was removed. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.” Supporters waving cowboy hats and chanting “USA” drowned out some of the protesters, while Trump told demonstrators to “get the hell out of here”. He mocked their appearance and claimed without evidence that “they’re paid by enemies of our nation”. The president also used Wednesday’s rally to address recent comments in which he appeared to suggest that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego, earning widespread condemnation from Democrats. In remarks that were again less than crystal clear, Trump said: “I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit – you want to see a horror show? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles and you want to see some bad things happen. “You want to see a country that would be in freefall. We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities, we protect our country, we’re not letting that happen. And they’d use it, too. They’d use it.” Trump was making his third trip to Texas in less than a month as Republicans pour money into races they had expected to win comfortably in November’s midterm elections. Paxton, whom Trump endorsed during the Republican primary after turning against the incumbent senator John Cornyn, was called on stage by the president and thanked him for his support. “Mr President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas,” Paxton said. “We are going to win this race.” Trump described Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America”, and said: “He was tough and he was with us all the way. He’s a fantastic man.” The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat. A New York Times/Siena College poll released last weekend showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. Trump won the state by almost 14 percentage points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen sharply. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday put his approval rating at 32%, while registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans 44%-37%. Trump’s relationship with Paxton has sometimes appeared uneasy. Trump called Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week, but on Wednesday did not discuss a leaked recording of Paxton in which the Senate candidate reportedly complained about the war in Iran, rising fuel prices and the way his campaign was being run. Instead he spent much of the rally attacking Talarico, whom he repeatedly referred to as “Tala-freako”. He claimed without evidence that Talarico is vegan and recently disappeared: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.” Trump insisted: “The people of Texas are not going to let weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak shows destroy everything that we’ve built.” The president’s political difficulties in Texas were underlined by the absence of the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is himself facing a competitive re-election race against the Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa. Abbott was instead due to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on his decision not to appear with Trump. Republicans have now devoted more than $300m to elections in Texas, according to the Associated Press, while Trump’s broader 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through several Republican-leaning states, including Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska.

title: Tanker attacked off Qatar as Iran claims route transporting oil through strait of Hormuz will be ‘closed’
author: Mark Saunokonoko
summary: Oil rises above $100 as attacks on ships hit new high, amid reports Trump is discussing launching strikes before the US midterms
body_text: A tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar has been attacked, causing an unknown number of casualties, a British maritime security agency said. The attack came as Iran declared it would close a route in the strait of Hormuz being used to circumvent Tehran’s blockade of traffic. The vessel was in the Gulf, about 500km (300 miles) west of the strait of Hormuz, when it reported being struck “by multiple projectiles”, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said on Wednesday. The UK authority did not specify the origin of the ship. Wednesday’s attack comes as strikes on tankers sailing through the strait of Hormuz hit their ⁠highest weekly level since the Iran war began, according to maritime security firms, as oil prices climbed above $100 per barrel. In the ‌week to 5 October, there were at least 12 attacks ‌on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the strait, according to data from three security sources. On Tuesday, India’s foreign ministry said 12 crew members were injured after an attack on a Panama-flagged oil tanker passing through the strait of Hormuz. Attacks, attempted attacks and harassment activity including drone overflights and surveillanceby Iran’s Revolutionary ⁠Guards have persisted in the strait, a US Navy-led agency said on Sunday. “These actions ⁠continue to demonstrate Iran’s intent to assert presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels,” ‌the Joint Maritime Information Center said. Ships in the Gulf and those attempting to transit the strait, the only way in or out of the oil-rich region for vessels, have come under repeated attack since the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February. On Wednesday, Tehran said it would further choke Hormuz, declaring transit routes in the strait deemed illegal by Iran ⁠would soon be closed, in reference to a southern pathway hugging Oman’s coast. Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the Revolutionary Guards’ Commander, said these “few routes” had been created by blasting and damaging ⁠some of the rocky passages and were used by “small boats smuggling oil and transferring ⁠it to tankers”, despite evidence Gulf oil exports are regaining prewar levels. “The strait of ‌Hormuz is closed, ‌and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have ‌full control over it,” he told the Fars news agency. The IRGC has consistently denied that seaborne crude flows in the strait are rebounding thanks to US Navy help. IRGC adviser Majid Mirahmadi said on ⁠Thursday that a daily average of 10 ships were transiting the waterway against an average of 125 before the war. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, disputed that account on Wednesday, saying Iran had “lost complete control” of the strait. “There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began.” Amid mixed messaging and supply concerns, the price of oil rose on Wednesday, with Brent crude topping $100 per barrel. The continuing stalemate in the war is heaping pressure on Donald Trump. On Thursday, the US president announced he would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, contrary to recent reports in US media that he was considering resuming military operations against Iran in the coming weeks. On social media he wrote that “while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait (22 Million Barrels, last night alone, with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran!), we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections”. Last week, a third US aircraft carrier set sail for the region. It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October. As a result of Trump’s war with Iran, Americans have been grappling with high gas prices and soaring diesel costs. The US has set up its own counter blockade of Iranian ports and occasionally fires on vessels linked to Tehran. It has also bombed Iranian targets in retaliation for Tehran’s attacks on ships, although there have been no such reported strikes since 1 September. Hormuz is vital to the world economy, with around a fifth of the planet’s oil and liquefied natural gas passing through the strait before the war began. With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

title: Indiana Fever and the Magasphere: a WNBA team’s dangerous path to popularity
author: Howard Bryant
summary: Teams have always symbolized division within America. And the Fever have come to prominence during a time of dark political intensity
body_text: It’s over for now, but no professional sports team spent more time receiving and drawing attention to itself than did the Indiana Fever this season. The Fever has broken, the team eliminated by the defending champion Las Vegas Aces for the second straight season, but Indiana succeeded in being the WNBA’s canary in the coal mine, embodying both the obvious and unintended consequences of rapid growth, while also allowing themselves to be a season-long distraction: part-time professional basketball team, part-time right-wing culture war centerpiece. Less than a decade ago, Atlanta and Minneapolis were praised for their unified political stances. Today, Trumpism has replaced social justice as the defining characteristic of the league – and as the curtain closed on the 2026 WNBA regular season, Indiana stood at its epicenter. The Fever were the most polarizing team in professional sports, known less for their basketball than their culpability in pulling the league from its old cultural identity as a Black/queer league into its current climate of political divisiveness – a calculated and dangerous path to popularity. This season, there was the basketball of the WNBA, and then there was the Indiana Fever, the league’s Maga-friendly option. Their two most recognizable players, Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham, were in a constant state of churn, always in the news, always embroiled against an other, symbolizing and pandering to America’s fractures. Their best and longest-tenured player, Kelsey Mitchell, hasn’t been able to concentrate fully on basketball the past two seasons as the Clark-Cunningham sideshow devours the oxygen and may end her time in Indiana that began as the second overall pick in 2018. Clark remains the league’s biggest name and its chief avatar – mildly reluctant or willing pawn, but an avatar nevertheless. She is an avatar for the money at a time when broadcasters and venture capitalists are making their bets on women’s sports. She represented a certain type of hope, that the day had arrived where women’s team sports would enjoy the same visibility as female stars such as Serena Williams and Lindsey Vonn. She was an avatar of weaponization, the speculator’s proof that the WNBA is doomed by its own hand for not recognizing her overall importance to its future, a future bizarrely framed as bright only if Clark succeeds – an odd framework for sports, where the final score and holders of the trophies determines who wins. Most obviously and explosively, Clark was an avatar for whiteness, a Christian, hetero whiteness that holds the pervasive belief that it is straight, white America – already the overwhelming and unchallenged dominant cultural and financial force in this country – that is under assault. Any struggle Clark showed on the court – a foul call, a non-call – was treated as if it were an urban crime statistic, unmistakable proof that Black people had even turned basketball lawless. The opportunistic and racist White House and the Trump administration repeated this fiction. Republican members of Congress earlier this season insinuated Clark was being discriminated against by the league because she is white. The Congressmen threatened the WNBA with a Department of Justice investigation if the league did not take steps to protect her. Clark and the Fever did little to dispel the notion. Whenever Clark did succeed, her partisans saw it as proof of how much better the league would be if only it stopped persecuting her. Through Clark, and how she navigated playing basketball in a league largely comprised of Black women – even as Breanna Stewart, Paige Bueckers and a host of other white women thrive without incident – was how the government (as well as many fans and journalists) framed the state of women’s professional basketball. She is half of what all the fuss has been about. The other half is Cunningham, who spent much of the season building the scaffolding for her second act by driving a wedge into heart of the league, positioning herself at the center of the attention-fueled culture war against trans women, being the blonde, blue-eyed foil to the league’s unruly Black women, and providing an entry point for the bros, their money and misogyny to show up, for men such an Enes Kanter Freedom to do what they have always done to women’s sport – find a way to denigrate it and be rewarded with attention. While it was all very tired and calculating, framed as speaking her truth, designed to reach the very group of white male sports fans that have either criticized or ignored women’s sports but are now bringing their toxicity to the tent under the guise of “growth,” Cunningham has been the subject of more attention than she’s ever had in her decade-long career, with public appearances and lengthy profiles. She knows exactly to whom she is talking, and why. The Fever carrying these burdens – or wearing them proudly until having to answer for them – is how Clark’s career has shifted from starting her first season a phenom joining a team that hadn’t had a winning season in seven years to ending her third in daily controversy, with her as the signature, aggrieved face of Maga’s team. With the avatars mercifully tabled, Clark emerged as an excellent player with enormous upside and serious deficiencies. She is a volume scorer but not yet a great one – her career field-goal percentage is just 42.3, below the league average, and for all her dazzle, her career three-point percentage is a below-average 34.2. She shot 36.1% from three this season, below the Fever team average of 38.6%. She is an adept playmaker whose true skill may be less in creating offense for herself and more in controlling the tempo of the game and involving her teammates. She was second in the league in assists and first in turnovers, fitting considering she constantly has the ball – similar to James Harden in a way. She is an apathetic defender. As a basketball presence, she is wholly unlikeable. She does not play the game with her teammates as much as beyond them – a common affliction of many superstars that in victory is touted as a virtue but looks selfish following first-round defeats. She does not appear to play the game with joy or intensity, but carries a childish outrage, not only confronting officials on virtually every trip downcourt, but sprinting to berate them in dead-ball situations. Clark plays with grievance, an entitled grievance that recalls the White House grievance, the same grievance shared by much of the white electorate that uncoincidentally claims her as their champion – they’re all unfairly under attack. For all the criticism, WNBA officials have actually shown remarkable restraint toward her. She exaggerates most calls and outwardly flops on others to steal calls – call it European gamesmanship, but the true nature of flopping is to receive something undeserved and is the worst example of immoral basketball. Even during timeouts Clark finds a way to spar with someone, be it a cameraman or an assistant coach. Like Cunningham, however, Clark has mastered the key component of the so-called attention economy – she sees to it the camera is always on her. A more professional Clark, with fewer outbursts and deeper concentration on basketball would lower the temperature on the league, her team, herself, and would probably win her more trips to the foul line – but there was virtually no evidence this season that is what she wants. Superstar petulance is nothing new, and if Stephanie White doesn’t return as coach, it won’t be the first time a star player will be accused of getting the coach fired. Nor is it the first time a sports team has reflected a national political mood or been pulled into its vortex. Usually reflection marks triumph – Black and Jewish America loved the Dodgers because of Jackie Robinson and Sandy Koufax just as the Yankee teams of Tony Lazzeri, Frankie Crosetti, Joe DiMaggio, and Phil Rizzuto made them beloved in Italian-American homes. Teams have also symbolized division. In the 1980s, the Boston Celtics were often considered white America’s team because of Larry Bird, the high number of white players the Celtics routinely signed, and the perception that the Celtics did not play with the flamboyant Blackness that defined the rest of the league, which allowed white fans to see themselves in their no-nonsense, blue-collar ethic. Despite the presence of James White, Dont’a Hightower, the McCourty twins and Stephon Gilmore, the late-stage Brady/Belichick Patriots were adopted by certain white supremacists because the Patriots were led offensively by a handful of white players – Tom Brady, Rob Gronkowski and Julian Edelman. The supposedly colorblind whites had found their ideal. None of those examples, however, have existed within the combination of today’s dark political intensity where the federal government has positioned itself as the legal guardian of whiteness and the precarious political footing of the league. The nation has effectively closed its borders to everyone except white South Africans, while Cunningham encourages the right to use the WNBA for anti-trans fodder and the DOJ believes Clark needs its protection. In a feeble attempt to distance itself from the obvious racism, the Fever periodically made bland, unconvincing statements – there’s no room for hate in the game – but their actions undermined their sentiments. Cunningham knows exactly who her fans view as the enemy, which fires to stoke on her podcasts, which dog whistles to sound. As does Clark, for her constant on-court histrionics elicit the right sympathy from the right people. They both know exactly what they’re doing. The season over, the Fever closed 2026 not by celebrating their best record since 2015, or by marking the first time since the 2009-2012 season the franchise posted three-straight 20-win seasons and have momentum as a potential title contender, but with more grievance. General manager Amber Cox read a ridiculous, gaslighting statement blaming outside media for the odious reputation of Fever fans. “The attacks on our fan base have no basis in reality, and must stop,” she read from the podium. Mitchell’s own words painfully contradicted Cox, as did rival players around the league. Maybe they just want it this way. This article originally appeared on Howard Bryant’s Substack. title: Trump’s latest attacks on the press exude desperation
author: Margaret Sullivan
summary: Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day
body_text: When you hate the mainstream press as much as Donald Trump does, nothing gets in the way of the punishment fantasy. Not court rulings. Not public opinion. Not even the dreadful consequence of less media coverage. And certainly not any awareness of how the first amendment is supposed to function in American democracy. This week, his revenge tour took yet another turn. He barred one of his most disfavored media organizations – Politico – from boarding Air Force One, where it was supposed to provide “pool coverage” to the rest of the press corps as Trump traveled to Nebraska for a campaign stop on Monday afternoon. That move was met with a strong show of solidarity by several media outlets, who decided not to fill the Politico spot. And the White House was defiantly delusional, claiming that Trump will “continue to grant an unprecedented level of access to the press”. This latest chapter came with the usual blast of venom at the mainstream media, though not specifically aimed at Politico. “The New York Times and many other Artificial Media Outlets should be arrested for their dishonesty and disservice to our Country,” he posted on Truth Social. The episode follows Trump’s effort in mid-September to ban Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House. Those organizations quickly sued, charging that Trump’s action was unconstitutional. Trump-appointed judge Timothy Kelly came down on the side of the media, issuing a temporary restraining order that ordered the White House to reinstate the press badges that had been taken away. And since then, CNN has been kept off Air Force One repeatedly, using the rationale that access to the White House is one thing, but access to the president’s plane is another. “The law is absolutely clear,” Ted Boutrous, the first amendment lawyer who is representing the three news organizations said in a statement. “The harm to our clients, the first amendment and the public as a whole is profound.” The Trump administration’s position is that traveling with the president is a privilege not a right. The fight is not over, since Kelly will conduct a hearing later this week over the media outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction – a stopgap measure to protect press access in advance of a possible trial. Trump, of course, has been picking fights with individual journalists and entire news outlets for years. At this very moment, there are court fights involving the Associated Press, the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and Disney, which owns ABC News and a number of local ABC affiliates. So far, there’s been a rare display of support among news organizations that are normally each other’s competition. Columbia Journalism Review called it “a striking and heartening show of solidarity from the White House Press Corps”. When the three outlets were kicked out of the White House last month, the other networks in the press pool decided not to replace CNN in the rotation, thus suspending coverage for a time. Peter Baker of the New York Times noted that for the first time in his 30 years covering the White House, “the president will not have a network TV camera covering his everyday official actions and travels”. What’s more, about 50 media organizations backed up the lawsuit by the three who had been singled out by filing an amicus brief. It’s hard to understand exactly how less coverage and this constant squabbling benefits Trump, but apparently, he is making a different calculation. His anti-press actions get a lot of attention, which is the very oxygen he requires to breathe. It doesn’t matter that much of the attention is negative. Meanwhile, he has entered a phase of saying and doing ever more outrageous things, like his statement this week at a rally that his war in Iran was necessary to protect the world. Trump appeared to suggest that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if it develops a nuclear weapon which prompted California’s Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, to call the president “deranged and dangerous”. Trump exudes a sense of desperation these days, with the midterm elections only weeks away and his approval ratings underwater. His war against the press is something of a reflex for him – it’s what comes naturally, especially when he doesn’t like the shape of reality. The press corps’ newfound solidarity is encouraging. It’s been a long time coming from a group that, in the past, has responded to this president’s constant abuse with deference and dinner invitations. Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day. Standing together will be a necessity in the weeks and months ahead. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

title: ‘System is rigged’: Democrat Sherrod Brown puts datacenter danger at heart of populist Senate bid
author: Chris Stein in Lima, Ohio
summary: Ohio former senator attacks Republican rival as the ‘face of datacenters’ as he wraps AI concerns into pro-worker message
body_text: Sherrod Brown, the Democratic former senator from Ohio hoping to return to office in November’s midterm elections, has spent the past year traveling across his home state explaining to voters about all the ways the “system is rigged” against them. Recently, he’s been telling people about a trip he took across the north-west Ohio countryside. “You’re driving on what looks like really good farmland, driving past fields, driving past barns, driving past milking parlors, and you see, all of a sudden, you see these huge cranes and you see these trucks coming,” Brown told a crowd of dozens at a coffee shop in the city of Lima earlier this month. The construction site was for a datacenter, Brown said, a component of the AI boom in which Ohio is a national leader. Brown believes the massive installations that pop up without warning do little good for the people around them. “Nobody knows they’re there,” Brown, speaking in shirtsleeves and without notes, said in his gravelly voice, as the crowd murmurs in agreement. “They eat up our land. They swallow up our water … then once they’re built, our electricity prices go up.” It was the latest iteration of an argument that Brown has been making his whole political career: that the most powerful people in the United States do not have the interests of Ohioans at heart. That message helped him win seven terms in the US House of Representatives and then three in the Senate, even as Ohio grew increasingly dominated by Republicans, and the working-class voters Democrats once relied upon deserted the party. In 2024, Brown lost his bid for a fourth term in an election in which Ohio voters backed Trump by an 11-percentage-point margin. “It’s not, I promise you, the last time you’ll hear from me,” he said in his final speech on the Senate floor, and months later, he announced another run for the Senate. Now 73, Brown has made standing up to datacenter developers a centerpiece of this campaign, calling his Republican opponent, Senator Jon Husted, “the face of datacenters”. A report from Ohio’s chamber of commerce found the state gave $2.5bn in tax breaks for the facilities from 2017 to 2024, a period during which Husted was lieutenant governor. “John Husted, I mean, he’s the guy that – he’s talking like he didn’t know – but he’s the reason these datacenters are here – 200 of them,” Brown said. Whether the former senator’s message lands with voters is central to Democrats’ hopes of retaking the Senate and blunting Trump’s abilities to get bills passed and judges confirmed for the final two years of his presidency. Democrats must win at least four Senate seats to return to the majority, most of which will come from states that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024 – like Ohio. ‘The anchor hanging around Husted’s neck’ Brown has wrapped concerns over datacenters’ impacts into the broad message of affordability that many congressional Democrats are campaigning on nationwide. He peppers his speeches with references to the Iran war, tariffs, Medicaid cuts approved by the Republican Congress and rising prices for Affordable Care Act plans brought on by their inaction. Asked in Lima to name an idea to lowercosts if he wins, Brown proposed a new expansion of the child tax credit, which reduced the poverty rate among children during its single year of enactment under Joe Biden. As the election has drawn closer, Brown has intensified his efforts to tie datacenters to Husted, who the Republican governor, Mike DeWine, appointed in 2025 to the seat JD Vance vacated when he became vice-president. Whichever candidate wins will serve out the remainder of his term, which expires at the end of 2028. This week, Brown’s campaign announced a volley of billboards reading “See that datacenter? Jon Husted did that” and a website critical of the senator that offers voters a map of the facilities in the state. Amy Natoce, a campaign spokesperson for Husted, accused Brown of lying, saying that while serving as lieutenant governor under DeWine from 2019 to 2025, Husted “did not have the authority to grant tax breaks”. She also noted his championing of the Ratepayer Protection Act in the Senate, which would have required electric utilities to consider standards that would make datacenters pay for their impacts on the grid. Though it passed the House with wide, bipartisan support, Senate Democrats called the proposal ineffective, and last month blocked its advancement. “Sherrod Brown and his friends like to talk about affordability, but when the rubber meets the road, they’d rather play politics than actually lower Ohioans’ energy bills. It’s disgusting,” Natoce said. There’s evidence that Brown’s attacks could be effective. Last week, the New York Times and Siena University released polling that found voters believed Brown would do a better job than Husted would managing the development of datacenters, by an 11-percentage-point margin. The race otherwise remains tight, with the Democrat leading the incumbent by three percentage points, within the survey’s margin of error. In August, a memo emerged from the GOP’s Senate campaign arm, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, warning that the issue could sink Husted. “More than any other thing in this race, datacenters are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” the memo read. “If he loses and datacenters get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice – and they will not go near the next one.” DeWine and his predecessor have sought to encourage the development of datacenters. But political winds have shifted rapidly on the issue – nearly 140 communities in the state have put moratoriums on new constructions, according to the Ohio Capital Journal, and in May, DeWine announced a pause on tax exemptions for the buildings. Last year, Democrats campaigned against datacenters to gain power in elections in Virginia, New Jersey and elsewhere, and are this year lumping their perceived impacts on electricity prices with the Iran war’s upward pressure on gas prices to argue that Republicans have failed to accomplish Trump’s promise of fighting inflation. “Husted has been involved in datacenters prior to this election year, and … he’s just more exposed,” said Dan Birdsong, a senior lecturer in political science at the University of Dayton. It also offers Brown a way to appeal to rural voters who typically do not vote for Democrats, but are sensitive to the possibility of the datacenters being built nearby. “He has a bipartisan voting base that he can appeal to with this issue that’s different than other issues in the state,” Birdson said of Brown. Powerful enemies An Ohio native who received a bachelor’s degree from Yale University, Brown had been in office almost without interruption from 1975 until he lost in 2024 to Republican Bernie Moreno. By the end of his time in the chamber, he was something of an outlier – the last Democrat holding statewide elected office in Ohio and still describing himself as a champion for workers even amid abundant evidence that they had soured on his party. Brown argues that he has the accomplishments to back up his record. As a House member, he voted against implementing the North American Free Trade Agreement, concerned about its impact on Ohio manufacturers, and one of his last votes in the Senate was to pass legislation that boosts social security payments to public employees. Brown has been in politics so long that when Bowling Green State University polled the Senate race last month, a quarter of respondents incorrectly thought Brown was the incumbent. He has long courted the alliance of unions, many of whom have backed his comeback attempt this year, though some who supported him in 2024 are now behind Husted. His stances have also earned him deep-pocketed enemies: as chair of the Senate banking committee, he was an adversary of cryptocurrency, and this year, Fairshake, a Super Pac linked to that industry, plans to spend $30m against him, after helping Moreno to victory in 2024. “We will be outspent for sure,” Brown acknowledged to reporters in Lima, echoing a reality for many Democratic campaigns in a year when Republicans are generally seen as having the fundraising advantage. His campaign against datacenters also runs up against their own benefits to building trade unions, for which they have provided significant employment opportunities. Lee Daher, the senior business representative at north-west Ohio’s Carpenters Local Union 351, said datacenters were “a really good source of employment for us”. “It means a lot of work for our members, not only today, tomorrow, but for the years to come,” he said. His local is backing Brown this year, as they did in 2024, and Daher said his comments about datacenters had not dampened that support. “They’re coming one way or another, and is there some regulation that’s needed? I think so, but I think big tech is hearing what is being asked of them,” he said. Asked to reconcile this tension, Brown insisted it was his emphasis on costs that would convince some of the same workers who turned their backs on him two years ago to give him another chance. “Those unions support me in large part because their members don’t like higher electric bills. Their members don’t like having no say on these datacenters coming to their towns,” Brown said. “I don’t think very many union members want the state to give these huge tax breaks to these out-of-state billionaires that are building these datacenters.”

title: I’m the attorney general of Washington state. Here’s how we’re protecting the midterm elections
author: Nick Brown
summary: A coalition of Democratic attorneys general is working to make sure voters across the spectrum have their voices heard
body_text: Elections have consequences. So do the Trump administration’s exhaustive efforts to undermine them. Voters will be confident in their choices, but less certain whose voice will count in the face of myriad intrusions by the executive branch. A coalition of Democratic attorneys general are working to make sure voters across the political spectrum have their say. Led by the attorneys general of Washington, California, Massachusetts and Nevada, 24 states sued to block President Donald Trump’s US Postal Service plot to interfere with voting by mail. Last month, the supreme court upheld our lower court victories and blocked the administration’s unconstitutional power grab, at least for this election. The law says states decide who receives a mail ballot. The USPS has never had the final say and, according to the American Postal Workers Union, until this year had never in its 250-year history tried to put such arbitrary restrictions on what mail it will deliver. The case we brought was an important victory in every state, and particularly Washington, where more than 99% of voters cast their ballot by mail. States such as Colorado, Hawaii and Oregon have similarly high mail voting rates. But mail voting is not confined to blue states; it is widely used in red states as well, particularly those like Nebraska and the Dakotas, with large rural populations. It’s also the president’s preferred way to cast his own ballot. The case of the postal service is just part of the multi-pronged federal attack states are pushing back against. The administration has abandoned the federal government’s traditional role of supporting election security and defending voting rights, work I participated in first-hand as a US attorney. Recall, in 2020, Trump’s own administration – and particularly the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency – worked to protect the vote and defend the election. Then, efforts to misuse the Department of Justice were thwarted, and Trump relied on insurrectionists to do his bidding. In return for serving honorably, many public servants were sent packing upon Trump’s return to office, and the convicted insurrectionists were pardoned. Now we have a US solicitor general who described the postal service’s attempt to deprive the rights of millions of eligible voters as only a “modest” use of federal authority. The Trump administration is not known for its discretion or consistency. While the administration was in court purportedly concerned about election integrity, the president publicly demanded his supporters “cheat like hell” in midterm voting. I don’t think Republican voters want that any more than Democrats do. We don’t doubt the administration will continue its lawless blitz against voters. Democratic state attorneys general are prepared, and have undertaken the largest multi-state effort to protect the vote in modern American history. Recent rulings keep state elections on track and show the law is on our side. If Trump attempts to intimidate or discourage eligible voters, or to obstruct the counting of votes or certification of the election, Democratic state attorneys general will take swift action. States have decades of experience countering these threats when lodged by private actors, and they are just as illegal when attempted by the federal government. Voters can do their part by exercising the right to elect their representatives. The president’s scheming benefits from public doubt and uncertainty. Democracy depends on the participation of its citizens, and every eligible voter should have the opportunity to render a verdict on their elected representatives. That verdict is unlikely to favor President Trump, who ran on lowering costs, preserving peace, and economic stability, but instead delivered higher prices, hollowed out critical public services, engaged in unprecedented self-dealing, and began a globally destabilizing war with no end in sight. Presidents don’t decide elections. State attorneys general and the millions of eligible voters we represent will exercise our constitutional powers to help keep it that way. Nick Brown is the attorney general of the state of Washington

title: Oil prices jump 5% on Middle East tensions and US hurricane threat
author: Lauren Almeida
summary: Global bond market sell-off continues and stocks fall amid reports White House has asked to see options for more strikes against Iran
body_text: Oil prices have risen sharply amid fears about escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast. Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 5% to $105.3 a barrel on Thursday, triggering a wave of selling in the global bond and stock markets. In the UK, the yield – or interest rate – on the 10-year government bond hit its highest level since July 2007, rising by six basis points to 5.515%. Investors appear concerned that rising oil prices could stoke higher inflation. The yield on the 30-year bond – the UK’s benchmark cost for its long-term borrowing – rose by three basis points to 6.0117%, after touching 6.036% on Wednesday, the highest since January 1998. The climbing cost of government borrowing places further pressure on John Healey, as he prepares to deliver his first budget, on 28 October. The market swings came after the Atlantic reported that the White House had asked the Pentagon to draw up options for strikes against Iran before the US midterm elections. The report cited unnamed officials in Donald Trump’s administration who said the size and targets of potential strikes, and whether they would go ahead, were still being debated. The report has weakened hopes that Trump will refrain from escalating the conflict with Iran before the midterm polls next month. A “limited operation” could be followed up with more substantial action after the midterms, it states. Another wave of strikes against Iran represents further risk to oil supply from the Middle East, with the US-Israeli war against Tehran now entering its eighth month. Attacks on tankers in the strait of Hormuz have reached their highest levels of ⁠the war, ⁠cutting traffic through the waterway and deepening fears about supply. The latest attack came ⁠on Wednesday, when a tanker was hit by projectiles off the north coast of Qatar, causing casualties, according to United Kingdom Maritime ‌Trade Operations. Oil prices also rose in response to a squeeze on production in the Gulf of Mexico, after Tropical Storm Isaias strengthened to become the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. Shell and Chevron said they were shutting down production as the storm approached the region, forecast to make landfall on Friday or Saturday. The Danish shipping group Maersk added to worries around rising energy prices on Thursday after it said it was increasing its emergency fuel surcharge on all its export collections and import deliveries. The rise in energy prices has fed fears about inflation, reinforcing expectations that central banks will have to raise their interest rates in order to control rising prices. A sell-off in global bond markets continued on Thursday. In France, which has been hit particularly hard over worries about its rising debt and growing spending, the 10-year yield rose by six basis points to 4.931%, just behind the 24-year high of 4.994% it hit last week. Yields rise when prices fall. The German 10-year yield, the benchmark for European debt, rose by two basis points to 3.504%. The yield on the US 10-year treasury, which is widely considered the best quality government debt on the market, rose by five basis points to 5.331%. Global stocks also fell, with Japan’s Nikkei share index falling 1.4% and the South Korean Kospi down 2.6%. In Europe, the Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, dropped 0.9%. The UK’s FTSE 100 slipped by 0.4% in early trading on Thursday.

title: First Thing: Trump endures protests in Texas as DNC sues over adverts
author: Martin Belam
summary: The president was repeatedly interrupted at a rally, and faces a legal challenge over taxpayer-funded adverts. Plus Jonathan the giant tortoise, who may have the secret to longevity
body_text: Good morning. Donald Trump suffered a torrid night at a rally in Texas that was rocked by repeated protests. The US president briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted Trump during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena. What is the latest development in the saga over taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads? The Democratic National Committee has sued the Trump administration in federal court, asking a judge in Washington to stop the president from using taxpayer funds to air a series of ads promoting himself. The ads have cost taxpayers more than $12m so far, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. Why has Trump been forced to distance himself from two top aides? Trump claimed he did not have “any idea who else they work for” after it was reported that Chris LaCivita, the co-manager of his 2024 presidential campaign, and James Blair, a campaign adviser and White House deputy chief of staff on leave of absence, spent the weekend assisting the pro-Russia government in Republika Srpska in the Balkans. Trump said: “I will terminate them, immediately” if he determined there was a conflict of interest. Tanker attacked off Qatar as Ken Paxton admits Iran war and gas prices are plaguing Republicans A tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar has been attacked, causing an unknown number of casualties. It came as Iran declared it would close a route in the strait of Hormuz being used to circumvent Tehran’s blockade of traffic. Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general running as the Republican candidate in a competitive Senate race, admitted in a leaked audio recording that rising fuel prices as a result of Trump’s Iran war were hurting his party before the midterms. The Guardian has asked Paxton’s campaign for comment. What is the latest in the diplomatic dispute between the UK and Israel? Britain is rebranding its East Jerusalem consulate as a UK mission. The move was forced by the Israeli government as punishment for Britain’s decision to ban trade with illegal settlements. There has been some dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures at this time against Israel could help Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election prospects this month. WHO says it does not have ‘full picture’ from Russia after suspected plague death The World Health Organization has said it does not have the “full picture” from Russia after the suspected death from plague last week of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia. Russian authorities have denied a connection with the anti-plague research institute and say Darya Shipilova died from “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. They insist there is no danger of a plague outbreak and have described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the region as stable. What did the WHO director general say? At a press conference, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said: “We don’t yet have the full picture of this event. Timely, complete and transparent information-sharing is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public risks.” What action has Russia appeared to have taken? Officials have imposed sweeping quarantine restrictions at the lab where Shipilova worked and in nearby hospitals. Staff were locked down inside the institute for three days, sleeping on the floors and on chairs, while tests were conducted. Christa Pike ‘angry, confused’ and unable to move arms after failed execution, lawyers say Christa Pike had woken up “angry and confused” after surviving two lethal injections, her attorneys said. Pike remains hospitalized and shackled to her bed. She has pneumonia and a blood clot, and is unable to move either of her badly injured arms. Randy Spivey, one of her lawyers, said her first words were: “Where am I?”, adding: “I think she is angry and confused about everything right now.” A judge has ordered Tennessee state officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution. Pike was convicted for her part in the 1995 brutal murder of Colleen Slemmer. In other news … Margaret Hamilton, whose software powered the Apollo 11 moon landing, has died aged 90. Reflecting on the historic mission, she once said: “We were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.” The FBI says it thwarted a terrorist attack on a Minnesota shopping mall by an 18-year-old it had supplied with an AK-47. An Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while trying to repair a campaign sign. Bernadette Greene-Placentia says she is sharing her story to fight for victims of sexual assault. OpenAI’s release of mathematical findings has drawn concerns from experts, who say the company is not doing due diligence to vet results. María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction in Madrid set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died. Stat of the day: Golden State Valkyries become first women’s sports team to top $100m in annual revenue The Golden State Valkyries are pursuing their first WNBA championship, but the second-year franchise has already achieved a historic financial milestone. The Filter Recommends: The first step of caring for your makeup is storing it right Lauren Gould speaks to three experts for their best advice on preserving the life of makeup and reducing the chance of it ending up in landfill. Don’t miss this: ‘Neither war nor peace’ – Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins People tell Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Jason Burke, our international security correspondent, how their lives have been changed beyond recognition after the 7 October attacks by Hamas three years ago and the subsequent devastating Israeli offensive. … or this: Why Arturo Béjar left Meta – and blew the whistle Arturo Béjar’s daughter was 14 when she told him Instagram was failing to keep her safe, and he has subsequently testified repeatedly against his former employer Meta. Steve Rose interviews him. Climate check: Landslides, flash floods and raging seas – is California ready for the ravages of El Niño? A mix of natural disasters could all befall the state at once as it finds itself in the crosshairs of the climate phenomenon, as Gabrielle Canon reports. In other climate developments, the Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires, and the Norwegian government has given a permit to a mining company to release waste into one of Norway’s most pristine fjords. Last Thing: Jonathan the giant tortoise, 194, offers up insight into secrets of longevity Alas, it is the animal’s DNA that has revealed a host of genetic variants in most of the biological pathways for ageing, not that he has learned to talk and started giving his opinion on things. Still a fascinating development though. Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. If you’re not already signed up, subscribe now. title: Victor Montagliani eyes re-election at Concacaf that would rule out Fifa presidency run
author: Exclusive by Matt Hughes and Nick Ames
summary: Concacaf president Victor Montagliani has clarified his intentions to staff at the confederation after he was touted as a potential rival to Gianni Infantino at Fifa
body_text: Victor Montagliani has told Concacaf staff he intends to stand for re-election as the confederation’s presidentnext year, which will rule him out of going up against Gianni Infantino for the top job at Fifa. The Canadian businessman is understood to have relayed the message to most of the 41 members of Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation. Montagliani has been widely touted as a potential candidate to take on Infantino for the Fifa presidency, particularly among Uefa member associations, who are conscious a European candidate would have no chance of beating Infantino in a ballot of Fifa’s 211 members. At a town hall meeting of Concacaf staff late last month, however, Montagliani is understood to have said that despite the Fifa governance crisis and calls for him to stand, he wants to continue serving members in the region. Concacaf’s presidential election will take place in the first quarter of next year before the Fifa vote on 18 March in Rabat, with the similar timelines leading Montagliani to clarify his intentions to staff. The 61-year-old was elected president on a reforming mandate 10 years ago after the corruption scandal that culminated in the arrest of then Concacaf president, Jeffrey Webb, after an FBI investigation. Webb admitted he had taken “bribes and kickbacks”. Uefa will also hold presidential elections next year, with Aleksander Ceferin confirming his intention to stand at a meeting of Uefa’s 55 member associations in Berlin on Thursday. Ceferin had said in February 2024 that he would not run for a fourth term at the helm but the likelihood that he would, after all, continue had long been an open secret. Previously, changes to the Uefa statutes had been passed that meant his first term, which began midway through the standard four-year cycle, did not count towards the standard three-term limit. It raises the prospect of Ceferin, who took the presidency in September 2016, holding power for more than 15 years in total. That is seen among most European FAs as a positive amid the turmoil engulfing football’s governance while putting to bed any perception that Ceferin, who would have had a number of proponents, might be tempted to challenge Infantino for the Fifa role Montagliani and Ceferin are expected to continue working together to bring about governance reform at Fifa after the World Cup sell-off scandal, which will be on the agenda at next Thursday’s Fifa council meeting in Zurich. Fifa’s council has not met since Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan was exposed in July despite repeated calls from members for an extraordinary general meeting, with the summit their first meeting since Fifa congress in Vancouver last March. Montagliani, Ceferin and the Asian Football Confederation president, Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, are expected to use the council meeting to demand an independent review of FFE and call for broader governance reforms of Fifa, which would give a greater voice to stakeholders and formalise the council’s role in decision-making. Previous calls from the trio, expressed in letters sent to Infantino last month, for Fifa to allocate a portion of its $6bn (£4.5bn) cash reserves to members will also be discussed. Delegates at Uefa’s Berlin meeting discussed a framework for Fifa reform, whose key points were made public during the afternoon. Among the points listed were the need for “a president who leads, not manages”, “stronger ethics, disciplinary, audit and compliance”, and “a clear process for major decisions”. Azerbaijan was an outlier in refusing to back Uefa’s reform proposals. The Azeri FA’s former general secretary, Elkhan Mammadov, now plays a key role at Fifa as its chief member associations officer and has been instrumental in Infantino’s attempts to keep wavering nations onside during the FFE crisis. Later this month, Azerbaijan will hold the first Fifa Under-15 World Cup, whose contestants will include Russia.

title: Trump promises not to attack Iran before November’s US midterms
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Statement outlines pause on protracted war US president has struggled to end after almost eight months
body_text: Donald Trump has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections, outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months. In a Truth Social post on Thursday, the US president said Washington was “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran”, which he claimed was “in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily”. The strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passed through before the war, was all but closed after the US and Israel struck Iran in late February. On Thursday, however, Trump suggested that oil was moving through the strait in record volumes: “22 Million Barrels, last night alone”, he claimed, “with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran”. The figure could not be independently verified. “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump wrote. “IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!” The US first imposed a blockade on the strait of Hormuz in April after talks in Islamabad collapsed, and reinstated it in July after a short-lived June deal to end the fighting. Fighting flared again in early September, when US forces struck rocket launchers on Iran’s Larak Island and Tehran responded with missiles aimed at American military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. Trump’s public position on the elections has shifted over the past month. On 2 September, as the US exchanged fire with Iran for the first time in weeks, he told reporters he was “not affected by the election”, adding that he was not on the ballot himself but intended to help his party. A week later, before heading to the Republican “midterm convention” in Dallas, he said he expected the war to end almost as soon as the voting was over, and accused Tehran of holding out in the hope that a change of power in Congress would leave it free to pursue a nuclear weapon. He also conceded that US oil prices were unlikely to fall before polling day. A Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September found that only about a third of Americans approved of the strikes on Iran, while more than four in five expected the conflict to last for an extended period, and that approval for Trump among Republicans had fallen from 82% to 73% in a week. Polling averages now show Democrats leading Republicans by roughly nine points on the generic congressional ballot, according to forecaster Nate Silver, the widest margin of this election cycle. The Wall Street Journal reported in September that JD Vance, the US vice-president, and secretary of state Marco Rubio had privately warned Trump the conflict could extend through the remainder of his presidency. Trump’s post did not say what the US would do after 3 November.

title: Nicolás Maduro and his wife indicted for alleged torture of US citizens
author: Victoria Bekiempis
summary: Ousted Venezuelan president and Cilia Flores have been in jail in New York since early January
body_text: The deposed Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been indicted for alleged conspiracy to commit torture, according to Manhattan federal court papers unsealed on Thursday. The superseding indictment was unsealed shortly before Flores appeared at court in her ongoing push for pretrial release – which was denied by Judge Alvin Hellerstein. Maduro and Flores have been jailed in New York City since early January. They were captured by US special forces during a shocking predawn assault on Caracas and transported to New York to face “narcoterrorism”-related charges in a move that sparked widespread international outrage. Charging documents at the time alleged that Maduro spearheaded a “corrupt, illegitimate government that, for decades, has leveraged government power to protect and promote illegal activity, including drug trafficking”. Maduro and Flores have previously pleaded not guilty in the criminal case against them. CNN on Wednesday first reported that a new indictment was expected. The new charging document described how Maduro and his wife allegedly wielded untold horrors to suppress opposition and maintain their control. Maduro, Flores and other Venezuelan leaders “presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens”, the just-released charging document said. Maduro and Flores, the superseding indictment alleged, “sat atop that violent power structure”. They allegedly “developed and facilitated the systems which they and their co-conspirators used corruptly to amass immense wealth and power, rewarding allies with ill-gotten funds and terrorizing perceived opponents through persecution and violence”. Flores was integral to this effort, authorities claimed, saying she “helped develop this system of repression and ordered that individuals be tortured to protect her family members’ illegal activities”. The victims of their torture included US citizens “who were believed to pose a threat” to Maduro’s power. “One particular United States citizen was detained in Venezuela and subjected to, among other things, deprivation of food and water, simulated drowning, repeated beatings, electric shock to his testicles, and forced injections.” Maduro and Flores also put pressure on Venezuela’s judiciary to make legal decisions that supported their efforts to thwart opposition, charging papers alleged. When one official resisted, Venezuelan intelligence agents arrested and tortured their family members, charging papers stated. “For example, one family member … was forced to drink latrine water; assaulted with tear gas in Victim-1’s cell; threatened that Victim-1 would be killed at gunpoint; and placed in a cold room known as the ‘Freezer’ in which a bright light was left on at all times of day and night and music was blared on repeat,” the superseding indictment said. This official “ultimately … relented and blocked the opposition figures from running for political office”. During another alleged torture incident, authorities allegedly abused the friend of a suspected opponent by “asphyxiating him with a bag, applying electric shocks to his testicles and knees, and kicking and beating him with a blunt object”, court papers said. One torture victim, who was repeatedly interrogated, endured numerous threats “including that his daughter would be kidnapped and raped if he did not confess and name his supposed confederates”, court papers state. “On one occasion, interrogators produced women’s underwear, claiming it belonged to his daughter.” Shortly after this indictment surfaced, Flores’s attorneys argued for her release in an already scheduled proceeding, pitching house arrest guarded by 24-hour private security. In doing so, they invoked chronic health issues, including cardiac infirmities. Hellerstein pushed back on this claim, noting that Flores was refusing to have catheterization while detained in general population. “I’ve undergone it, so I know what it is,” Hellerstein said, noting that it was generally an outpatient procedure. “There’s no pain. There’s no general anesthesia.” Flores’s attorney then pointed to her high blood pressure. “It’s controllable by pills,” Hellerstein said. Her team also said in court that Flores dropped more than 25lbs and lost two teeth since her detention. “For whatever it’s worth, her appearance today is no worse than, and perhaps a little better, than when I first met with her [at] her arraignment,” Hellerstein said. Flores’s lawyer said that during her arraignment she was “still bandaged up” from her rough arrest. Flores wore dark jail scrubs during her court appearance. She listened to the proceedings with headphones through a Spanish-language interpreter. The US attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, which is prosecuting this case, opposed Flores’s now-failed bail request. Prosecutors have argued that Flores was a flight risk. Prosecutors also maintained that she had received appropriate medical care. Donald Trump has defended the controversial raid on Maduro, insisting it was a “surgical law enforcement operation”. At Maduro’s first US court appearance, he said: “I’m a kidnapped president – a prisoner of war!” After Maduro’s forced ouster, Trump worked swiftly to gain access to Venezuela’s expansive oil reserves. In August, Trump announced a new oil agreement with Venezuela – claiming that the US would have “majority” control over 65bn barrels of proven reserves. Venezuela boasts approximately 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves – the largest in the world. The White House has tried establishing a consistent flow of Venezuelan crude oil to US refineries while boosting US investment into the country’s flagging petroleum industry. Trump has faced mounting pressure over skyrocketing gas prices in advance of November’s midterm elections. Greater access to cheaper oil and broadened output could help lower costs. A Guardian investigation found, however, that Trump’s proclaimed “biggest oil deal in world history” is likely to fail due to legal and logistical problems.

title: Billionaires fund California ballot measure to make voters show ID at polls
author: Dani Anguiano
summary: Various out-of-state conservative donors have given millions of dollars to support California’s Proposition 39
body_text: Billionaires across the US are spending vast sums to support California’s Proposition 39, a measure that would require voters to show identification before casting their ballots. The measure is being promoted as a way to “[increase] trust and confidence in our elections”, and comes amid a nationwide push by the Trump administration to restrict voting. California Republicans have long sought to advance a voter ID initiative in the state. The campaign has received more than $36m, according to a report from CalMatters, including $17m from Richard Uihlein, a prominent conservative donor and owner of a shipping supply company. Joe Gebbia, a co-founder of Airbnb and Trump administration official, has given $8m, and Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss and Nicole Shanahan have also made significant donations. The yes campaign has far outraised its opponents by as much as $13m, according to CalMatters. California voters do not currently have to show identification at the polls, but are required to provide a driver’s license or state identification number or their partial social security number when registering to vote. In addition to requiring ID at the polls, Prop 39 would also mandate that mail ballots include the last four digits of a government-issued ID number on an envelope. The Republican lawmaker Carl DeMaio authored the proposition after unsuccessfully fighting in California’s Democratic-dominated statehouse to advance legislation implementing voter ID requirements in response to a demand from Trump. He has argued the initiative could be a bright spot for Republicans in an election where the party is expected to see significant losses. “It’s not the same as the Trump Save Act. It is a more nuanced, balanced approach customized for California. It keeps mail-in ballots, but requires citizenship verification, requires voter ID,” DeMaio recently said. “This is a gamechanger.” The state Democratic party, the ACLU and the League of Women Voters oppose the measure. Supporters have said the proposition has bipartisan support. A recent poll from the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies found that Prop 39 was losing some of the support it had attracted in late summer and was trailing by a 13-point margin. But other polls from late September showed it with a lead. A bilingual statewide survey of 600 Latino likely voters in early August found they were evenly divided on the measure.

title: DoJ seeks to charge ex-Trump aide who gave key testimony on January 6 attack
author: Sam Levine
summary: Cassidy Hutchinson told panel she had been told Trump lunged for wheel of SUV to try to join mob at Capitol
body_text: Prosecutors in the justice department’s civil rights division are seeking criminal charges against Cassidy Hutchinson, a former top Trump White House aide who gave explosive testimony to the committee that investigated the US attack on the Capitol, according to a person familiar with the matter. The potential charges involve lying to Congress, the person said. Hutchinson, a former top aide to the White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, told the panel among other things that the deputy chief of staff for operations told her that Trump did not want to return to the White House on January 6 and at one point grabbed the wheel of his SUV to try to join supporters at the Capitol. Republicans have long disputed this account. The justice department’s efforts to indict Hutchinson were first reported by Punchbowl News on Thursday. “The department does not confirm or deny the existence of investigations, or the lack thereof,” a department spokesperson said in a statement. In April, the New York Times reported that prosecutors in the justice department’s civil rights division, which handles investigations into civil rights crimes, had been tapped to investigate Hutchinson. It was seen as a highly unusual move at the time since the investigation would typically be handled by the US attorney for the district of Columbia. Hutchinson also said she was under investigation by the Department of Justice in filings in an unrelated case. The case is the latest example of how Trump has used the justice department to prosecute his enemies. Last year, the justice department indicted former FBI director James Comey on charges of lying to Congress and Letitia James on mortgage fraud. Both indictments were dismissed after a judge ruled the prosecutor overseeing them had been unlawfully appointed. The department has since filed a new indictment against Comey for posting a picture of seashells arranged in a formation that said “8647.” The Trump justice department has also filed charges against the non-profit Southern Poverty Law Center and the journalist Don Lemon.
