title: Morning Mail: the rise and fall of Sam Wood; a 16-year grave quest; and a 10bn-year-old burst of energy
author: Martin Farrer
summary: How it all went wrong for the dashing star of The Bachelor; scientists detect what they believe to be the most distant fast radio burst ever recorded
body_text: Morning everyone. Sam Wood once seemed to represent the exception that proved the rule that there weren’t many “nice guys” on reality TV. But after being charged with domestic violence, we report on how Sam Wood’s image – and business empire – has crashed. Elsewhere, our latest Unmarked graves investigation reveals how a woman’s quest for her family ended in a swampy cemetery; astronomers think an energy flash has travelled through “80% of cosmic history”; Anne Carson wins the Nobel prize for literature; and an Australian Olympian’s unusual advice for her F1 driver boyfriend. Australia ‘Unambiguously Queensland’ | A “stunning” debut novel by Meriam and Wagedagam author Lenora Thaker has won the premier’s award at the Queensland literary awards for her historical novel The Pearl of Tagai Town, described as “unambiguously and distinctively Queensland”. Exclusive | A woman’s years-long search for her family ended in shock and fury in a swampy corner of Rookwood cemetery in Sydney, and sparked a 16-year quest to stop people being buried in unmarked graves. Political ‘slop’ | One Nation’s latest AI-generated campaign videos featuring a series of racist tropes represents the “ensloppification” of Australian politics, argues Josh Butler. 10bn years | Astronomers have detected a mysterious burst of energy emitted in some far-flung part of the universe more than 10bn years ago and which they estimate has travelled through “approximately 80% of cosmic history” to reach Earth. Payment pressure | Labor is putting pressure on the tax office to reverse its decision not to accept credit card payments amid a growing backlash, insisting the ATO help small business operators manage critical cashflow after a ban on surcharges. World Drowning tragedy | Three sisters who drowned in the sea off Brighton in the UK collectively decided to end their own lives, a coroner has ruled, after making a trip to Birmingham where they visited the lake where their mother died by drowning in 2010. Bus strike | A Russian missile strike on a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people, officials have said, in one of the worst attacks by Moscow on Ukrainian civilians this year. Survival story | Christa Pike is “up and walking” in hospital, her lawyer said, more than a week after she survived two lethal injections during a botched execution in Tennessee. Oil surge | Donald Trump has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections, outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months. Oil prices have risen sharply amid fears about escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast. ‘Bold and inventive’ | The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded to the Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson, with the Swedish Academy citing the author’s “bold and inventive oeuvre”. Full Story Back to Back Barries: How Labor should fight One Nation Tony Barry and Jessie McCrone examine the latest Redbridge poll showing support for the prime minister and Labor is slipping significantly and give their thoughts on the upcoming Victorian election. In-depth Sam Wood built his post-Bachelor fitness empire off his family-friendly, women-friendly image. He seemed to be the robust exception that proved the rule about “nice guys” on reality TV, writes Stephanie Convery, but this week his image – and business – came crashing down amid a charge of domestic violence. Wood’s lawyer told media that he intended to “defend the charges”. Not the news Cassie Tongue gives five stars to Grace Chapple’s “vibrant, clever” adaptation of EM Forster’s 1908 coming-of-age novel, Room With A View, at the Belvoir Street theatre in Sydney. “This play is alive,” she writes, “and it’s a gift: it reminds you, with well-earned wonder, that you too are alive.” Sport Formula One | After a suggestion from his girlfriend, the Australian Olympic cyclist Tiffany Cromwell, Cadillac team driver Valtteri Bottas has cycled 418km from Malaysia to Singapore to acclimatise for this weekend’s grand prix. Football | The former Manchester City coach Pep Guardiola is expected at the club’s home Champions League match against PSG next week as a show of support for his old bosses amid the financial rules verdict. We also profile Khaldoon al-Mubarak, the driving force behind the City project but whose next move might be the sale of the club. Basketball | Owners of leading European football clubs such as Barcelona, Paris Saint-Germain and Bayern Munich could bid for franchises in NBA’s US$10bn plan to set up a league in Europe. Media roundup The federal police chief, Krissy Barrett, has warned in the Telegraph that police are grappling with the “diabolical reality” of hostile governments teaming up with local organised crime networks to cause chaos. The Gold Coast mayor, Tom Tate, admits to the Bulletin that the region’s preparedness for the storm season is “not good enough”. And after waiting weeks for the council to fix a pothole, a Mornington Peninsula tradie did it himself with 100kg of asphalt and cement, the Herald Sun reports. What’s happening today Games | The PAX Aus gaming convention begins in Melbourne. Sydney | There is a hearing at Parramatta district court for four teenagers charged over the alleged gang rape of a 17-year-old girl. Film | Tropfest season launches in Sydney at 10.30am. You can follow the latest in US politics by signing up for This Week in Trumpland. Brain teaser And finally, here are the Guardian’s crosswords to keep you entertained throughout the day. title: Trump donor accuses ‘grifter’ Kimberly Guilfoyle of $100,000 quid pro quo
author: Ariana Baio
summary: Eric Deters says US ambassador to Greece asked him to pay off American Express credit card bill in return for access
body_text: A Trump donor accused Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece and Trump family ally, of engaging in a “quid pro quo” by asking him to pay off her $100,000 debt in exchange for access to administration officials. Eric Deters, a former congressional candidate and lawyer, told MS Now on Thursday that Guilfoyle had “ambushed” him last year with an offer to provide access to government officials if he paid her American Express credit card bill, before her US Senate confirmation hearing as ambassador to Greece. “It absolutely was a quid pro quo,” Deters told the network in response to a Wall Street Journal report that she had pushed him for the money. “Kimberly Guilfoyle is a grifter,” he added. The Guardian has asked Guilfoyle’s lawyer for comment. Jesse Binnall, a lawyer for Guilfoyle, told the Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages, but that she was “owed a balance” for travel and speaking at events before her nomination. Deters told the Journal that he did not owe Guilfoyle any balance. The report is the latest allegation about Guilfoyle’s conduct as a US official. Deters shared messages he and Guilfoyle exchanged in which the US ambassador to Greece promised him “ride or die” access to Trump administration officials if he wired American Express $100,000. Asked about the report during a press conference in Athens on Wednesday, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said he would not address the allegations. He reaffirmed his support for the US embassy in Greece adding, “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.” Asked again about the reports on Thursday, Rubio refused to comment. The top Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees have asked Rubio to open an investigation into Guilfoyle’s conduct as an ambassador. A spokesperson for the Democratic staff of the Senate foreign relations committee confirmed to the Guardian that they were requesting further information and continuing to investigate. JD Vance similarly expressed hesitation, similar to Rubio, on Thursday when asked to respond to a US ambassador offering access to government officials in exchange for money to pay off debts. “With that hypothetical, Jen, obviously I don’t love that,” the vice-president replied. “But I don’t know exactly who you’re talking about. I don’t know the full details. What I find with these stories is you never want to comment in a purely abstract way because a lot of times the details really matter,” he added. Concerns about Guilfoyle’s conduct were first raised in September when the Wall Street Journal reported she had used her position to invite Greek lobbyists to sit in on official diplomatic meetings and promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company. Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee, sent a letter to Rubio on Tuesday, asking him to look into the allegations against Guilfoyle. “Such actions do not serve US credibility overseas and risk undermining US diplomacy,” Shaheen wrote. “In advance of your upcoming travel to Greece, I request an immediate review of Ambassador Guilfoyle’s actions and a clarification of what steps have and will be taken to avoid undue influence and even the appearance of a conflict of interest.” Separately, Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, sent a letter to Rubio in September, requesting more information about Guilfoyle’s conduct, her relationship with the Greek construction and energy company and her relationship with the lobbyist. “If these reports are accurate, Ambassador Guilfoyle is unfit to represent the United States abroad and should be removed from her position,” Meeks wrote. Guilfoyle, 57, was once a member of the Trump family’s inner circle, having been engaged to Donald Trump Jr, the US president’s eldest son, for roughly three years. The couple ended their engagement in 2024, and shortly after taking office, Donald Trump nominated Guilfoyle to be ambassador to Greece. But now further allegations accuse Guilfoyle of promising a Trump donor, Eric Deters, access to the Trump administration in exchange for a $100,000 payment to American Express. Deters shared messages exchanged between himself and Guilfoyle with the Wall Street Journal in which she reportedly pleaded: “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.” Deters said Guilfoyle had promised him thatshe would “be your Trump ride or die, forever and ever” if he made the American Express balance. Deters said he never made the payment. In other messages, Guilfoyle reportedly raised concerns about her communications with Deters becoming public and reprimanded him for not being discreet. “Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things. It’s really dangerous and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on Signal,” she is said to have written in one message. “What a nightmare, you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” Guilfoyle reportedly wrote in another message. A lawyer for Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of messages Deters shared with the Wall Street Journal. It is unclear whether Shaheen or Meeks will ask Rubio for further information about the latest report. The Guardian has asked Meeks and Shaheen for comment.

title: Democratic senator says Hegseth trying to hide costs of Iran war from US public
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Chris Murphy says Pentagon blocked him from military base in Qatar and Iran strike on US embassy in Riyadh far worse than public led to believe
body_text: Senator Chris Murphy said the Pentagon blocked him from a major US base in Qatar, yet saw enough damage on the US embassy in Saudi Arabia to conclude that an Iranian strike would have been deadly had it happened during the day. The Connecticut Democrat, who sits on the Senate foreign relations and appropriations committees, described the destruction he witnessed in Riyadh as “extraordinary” and much more damaging than the public has been led to believe. “Had that attack happened during the daytime, there’s no doubt that there would have been many, many Americans killed,” he told reporters on a call after returning from Qatar and Saudi Arabia. He also accused the Pentagon of trying to prevent Congress from seeing the costs of the war first-hand, saying the Pentagon secretary, Pete Hegseth, was “determined to hide the cost and the consequences of this war from the American public”. Two drones hit the compound in the early hours of 3 March, days after the US and Israel launched the war on 28 February, setting off a fire and sending black smoke over the district. The building was reportedly empty at the time and no injuries were reported. Saudi Arabia’s defense ministry initially described the damage as minor. But, according to Murphy, the drones caused extensive damage across several floors. The strike, he explained, hit “an area of the embassy in which there are a lot of people” and said that “part of that space is uninhabitable and will likely remain uninhabitable”. Murphy said some of it would not be repaired because the embassy is moving soon. In Qatar, the senator visited Ras Laffan, the gas complex where Iranian drone strikes halted LNG (liquefied natural gas) production early in the war. Murphy said 17% of Qatar’s exports had been eliminated, probably for at least three years of repairs. He also said he saw just one LNG tanker in port, compared with the usual six, and about one a day leaving rather than 10. Murphy said the Pentagon blocked him from seeing more. He said he gave notice of his visit weeks in advance and submitted a written request for access to Al Udeid air base, the largest US military installation in the region. He also said he raised it with Adm Brad Cooper, the commander of the US Central Command, who appeared surprised that military leaders had also been barred from speaking to him. On arrival, Murphy said, he was told he would not have access to the base and no contact with military leadership. In response, a senior Pentagon official told the Guardian that Murphy’s office “was informed before his trip” that he would not receive department support to access Al Udeid air base, as per Hegseth’s 3 March directive on travel restrictions in the region. “That decision was communicated in advance by the office of the secretary of war for legislative affairs,” the official said in a statement. “The department applies the secretary’s guidance evenly.” Murphy said he would draft language in the coming days requiring the Pentagon to give members of Congress access to overseas bases, which he would seek to include in next year’s appropriations and defense authorization bills. If the war is still going by early next year, he said Congress should withhold defense funding unless it includes a provision to end the conflict, and vowed accountability and investigations if Democrats win one or both chambers in next month’s midterm elections. The administration, he said, was “giving its middle finger to the Congress, pretending as if we are totally irrelevant”. “We will potentially have power of both the House and the Senate,” Murphy said of Democrats, “and we should make the end of the war a priority.”

title: Trump hosts awards party for tech billionaires, almost as if he doesn’t care about ordinary Americans
author: David Smith in Washington
summary: Amid a cost-of-living crisis, with US midterms a month away, the president held a ceremony to celebrate our tech overlords – again
body_text: He stands accused of being out of touch, enriching himself and his family, building a lavish White House ballroom and, with elections looming, neglecting the hardships of the voters who brought him to power. Time for Donald Trump to show he still has the common touch? Nope. On Thursday, the US president went to a building he named after himself, dished out awards to the world’s richest person – his old frenemy Elon Musk – and other tech billionaires and even received an award that belonged to his late uncle. Given Trump’s gold fetish, the event was naturally entitled the Golden Age of American Innovation summit, which will be news to the many agencies and academies suffering billions of dollars in cuts to scientific research on his watch. “We have an extremely high-IQ audience for a change,” the president told about 300 invited guests at the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington, a compliment he never pays to the crowds who line up for hours to attend his campaign rallies. Standing on a podium with a white backdrop and series of US flags, the president gave a perfunctory speech, sticking unusually close to his teleprompter. He made references to artificial super intelligence but steered clear of the datacentres these tech overlords are erecting all over the country and, in the process, achieving the unique feat of getting Democrats and Republicans to agree on how much they hate them. Michael Kratsios, director of the White House office of science and technology policy, then treated Trump to a video about his uncle, Dr John Trump, an electrical engineer and professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who received the National Medal of Science in 1983. The short film’s claims that John Trump’s research produced X-ray generators “used for the first radiation treatments for cancer” and that “his radars jammed German defences” on D-day in 1944 owe something to his nephew’s fondness for “truthful hyperbole”. Six years ago, the president, who believes in “good genes” and “racehorse theory”, suggested that his uncle’s legacy would help him fight the Covid-19 pandemic: “He was a great super genius. Dr John Trump. I like this stuff. I really get it. People are surprised that I understand it. Every one of these doctors said: ‘How do you know so much about this?’ Maybe I have a natural ability. Maybe I should have done that instead of running for president.” Kratsios had a surprise for the boss. He presented Trump with his uncle’s National Medal of Science in a handsome frame as the audience clapped. He looked happy enough, though it was clear this won’t displace the gaudy Fifa peace prize from his trophy cabinet. Among the six tech leaders who came up on stage to receive an award for scientific and technological achievement, five were immigrants. The “America first” president gave the National Medal of Science to SpaceX chief executive Musk (born in South Africa); Google co-founder Sergey Brin (Russia); Jensen Huang (Taiwan), whose AI chip maker Nvidia is the world’s most valuable company; and Lisa Su (Taiwan), head of the semiconductor company Advanced Micro Devices. Trump also handed the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft supremo Satya Nadella (India) and Dell Technologies chief executive Michael Dell (Texas). Hours earlier, JD Vance had announced Microsoft’s suspension from a programme allowing companies to sponsor foreign workers for green cards. The trillionaire Musk was wearing a dark suit, white shirt and white tie. Trump gave him a pat on the back, handed him the medal and gave him another pat, then showed him a certificate and patted him once more. In earlier remarks, the president called Musk an “industrial titan”, “brilliant engineer”, “national treasure” and “modern-day Thomas Edison”. He observed: “It all works out well for Elon, right?” These guys’ relationship is more complicated than Rhett Butler and Scarlett O’Hara. Musk helped buy the 2024 election for Trump and found Doge a useful vehicle to gut the federal agencies investigating his companies. The president considered Musk’s Grok chatbot ingenious after it accurately predicted that ordinary Venezuelans would celebrate the removal of leader Nicolás Maduro, according to Time magazine. Then came their explosive falling out, with Musk tweeting on his own X platform: “Time to drop the really big bomb: [Trump] is in the Epstein files. That is the real reason they have not been made public.” It turned out both men were in the files. Vance reportedly brokered a truce between the two titanic egos. The bromance has never been fully rekindled, but Thursday was proof that power and wealth can’t live without each other – especially with elections less than a month away and Trump’s approval rating in the doldrums. When the ceremony was over, however, it was AI king Huang who remained on stage alongside Trump as the familiar strains of the Village People’s YMCA blasted from loudspeakers (“Young man, when you’re short on your dough,” did not resonate with this crowd). The pair were pointing and directing people, presumably for a photo op, and looking pleased with themselves. It was a fitting closing image of two men who rule the world and may yet find a artificial super intelligent way to destroy it.

title: US midterms: key takeaways from Senate debates in Michigan, Georgia and Maine
author: Rachel Leingang, George Chidi and Auzzy Byrdsell
summary: Candidates traded personal attacks, sparred over affordability, the economy and abortion win three closely watched US Senate debates on Thursday
body_text: With just weeks left in the contentious midterm election campaign, candidates in a trio of highly-competitive Senate races debated Thursday night, clashing over the economy, tariffs, the Iran war and abortion rights, with control of the upper chamber at stake. In Georgia, incumbent Democratic senator Jon Ossoff faced GOP representative Mike Collins. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul Al-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers debated over the state’s open Senate seat. And in Maine, longtime senator Susan Collins met Democratic challenger Troy Jackson. Democrats need to flip four Republican-held Senate seats to win the majority. Here are the key takeaways from the battleground state debates. Affordability, affordability, affordability Affordability was a major topic across all three debates on Thursday night, as voters consistently name the cost of goods, gas, housing and healthcare as their top concerns in this year’s midterms. “Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries under this guy who’s going to rubber stamp everything Donald Trump tells him to rubber stamp?” El-Sayed asked during the Michigan debate, the first of two in one of this cycle’s most fiercely contested races. Both Rogers and El-Sayed said they support suspending a fuel tax to alleviate costs, while El-Sayed argued that the Iran war, which was driving up gas prices, needs to end. El-Sayed attacked Rogers for growing his personal wealth while in office as a US representative. Rogers called El-Sayed “bought off” by billionaire George Soros, Hamas and Hezbollah. “We cannot afford Abdul, and we cannot risk his ideology,” Rogers said. In Georgia, Ossoff repeatedly asked Collins to justify his support for Trump’s global tariff policies, which the senator said have “crushed Georgia families” and “strangled” economic growth. “Let’s see if he has the courage to explain his votes,” Ossoff said, adding later: “Still have not heard an explanation for the tariffs.” Collins, who is trying to cut into Ossoff’s lead, blamed inflation on Biden administration policies, singling out spending measures that his opponent had supported. Later in Maine, where polls show a tight race, Jackson focused his remarks on pocketbook issues, including the sharp spike in heating oil costs and high energy prices. Collins defended her record and argued that Maine had benefited from the $50bn rural health transformation fund that was appended to Trump’s signature tax cut and spending bill, the so-called Big Beautiful bill. It gets personal in Georgia In the Georgia debate, a question about data centers erupted into a pointed, personal exchange between Ossoff and Collins. “Mike Collins voted to take that money out of your pocket and out of your community and give it instead to data center developers,” Ossoff said. He then accused Collins of being a “bigot” who has “hired half the Third Reich” – a reference to the congressman’s history of employing staffers who have expressed white nationalist, antisemitic, and extremist views online. “If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery,” Ossoff said of the late civil rights icon and long-serving Georgia congressman, “Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club. His office has been in cahoots with some of the most notorious white supremacists on the country.” Collins was asked directly about his son-in-law’s social media posts promoting white nationalist and antisemitic views. “You know, Rick, that’s my family,” Collins replied. “That’s the craziness that Jon Ossoff has been spewing out there.” Collins noted that a New York man had recently been charged after threatening to kill him, and added: “I’ve condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don’t care where the source is. And I tell him that too, it’s wrong. We have no place in this world for that.” Collins, meanwhile, sought to cast Ossoff as “radical” and an “extremist” whose record in the Senate had left the state “less safe, more expensive and worse off”. Labatt and Red Wings in Michigan Tariffs were also a topic of heated debate in Michigan, which shares hundreds of miles of border with Canada. This week, Rogers publicly backtracked on previous support for Trump’s tariffs on the US’s northern neighbor, saying in a campaign ad that “Canada is not our enemy” and that the “tariff war” needed to end now. During Thursday night’s debate, Rogers said he had spoken to the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, this week to advocate for a deal between the two countries. There are tariffs in place that are “too high and not helpful for us”, Rogers said. El-Sayed said he supports targeted, logical tariffs that protect Michigan manufacturing, but nothing like the “ham-fisted, chaotic, self-serving” tariffs Trump put in place. He called out Rogers for “flip-flopping” on the issue, saying he was only reversing his stance because of “sagging poll numbers”. “He’s doing an ad drinking a Labatt and talking about the Red Wings, pretending like he was not for this the entire time,” El-Sayed said. “Be serious, my guy.” Accusations fly in Maine In Maine, discussions about gas prices and the war in Iran raised notable tension in the second debate between Jackson and Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in her seat. “She’s the Chairman of Appropriations,” Jackson said. “Money has to come through them for these wars – she still can do something.” Collins, who plans to continue leading the Appropriations committee if re-elected, said she had repeatedly supported war powers resolutions to halt Trump’s military action in Iran. But Jackson pushed further, accusing the senator and her husband of profiting from the war. She could use her leverage to stop this war, but instead they’re making money,” he said, prompting a furious response from Collins, who called the allegation “absolutely outrageous”. “You owe me an apology,” she said. Reproductive rights under the spotlight in Maine In Maine, both candidates were also pressed to address inconsistencies in their positions on reproductive rights, a crucial issue for voters in the state. “Our records have changed,” Jackson said. “Mine has gotten better – hers has gotten worse.” He pointed to Collins’ vote to confirm supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, who helped overturn Roe v Wade in 2022. Collins, one of just two Republican senators who supports abortion rights, has said she does not regret her vote for Kavanaugh, even though she believed he had given her private assurances before his 2018 confirmation that he would not overturn the landmark ruling. Collins sought to turn the issue back on her opponent, noting his past stances on abortion that have left many voters wary. “From 2000 until he ran for the house seat in 2013 was very anti-choice,” she said, accusing Jackson of having held “extremist” views on abortion. “He was for a bill that would not allow abortion when the mother’s life was at risk.” She also pointed to legislation she helped write that sought to “codify Roe v Wade nationwide,” but the bill never made it passed the Senate. Mittens off in Michigan In Michigan, Rogers repeatedly attacked El-Sayed by attempting to tie him to Muslim terrorist groups, including Hamas, and suggested government surveillance would only bother someone if he or his family had something to hide. Rogers brought up El-Sayed’s mom and sister, prompting El-Sayed to say at one point that Rogers should just come out and say what he’s been dancing around all night, after Rogers’ repeated references to terrorist groups. “He wants this to be about anything but his own record,” El-Sayed said. Rogers claimed El-Sayed refused to condemn a terrorist attack in Michigan earlier this year and the 7 October Hamas terrorist attacks in Gaza, although El-Sayed said he had condemned both. But, El-Sayed added: “I’m not somebody who tries to make political theater out of other people’s pain.” He also retorted to Rogers: “Did you sell your yachts?” Rogers responded: “I never owned a yacht in Florida, brother.” After a 30-second commercial break, moderator Rick Albin said that in his 30 years of hosting debates, he’d never seen the sparring continue during the break, but tonight, it had.

title: OpenAI projected to bring in $20bn less in revenue than expected
author: Mark Sweney
summary: Questions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled before
body_text: OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI. The ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September. However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported. Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment. OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn. News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%. The discrepancy arose from attempts by OpenAI investors to provide a more direct comparison with how projected revenue is measured by Anthropic, which hit $65bn in forecast revenue by the end of July. Anthropic includes the revenue from sales via cloud partners, such as Amazon’s AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI does not. Last month, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said that the company would not float on the stock market this year as had been expected, citing safety concerns over AI. Altman’s decision followed cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks. Democrat and Republican politicians are calling for new rules to govern AI systems, after two researchers from Anthropic warned that the lightning pace of development of AI without safeguards could lead to the extinction of the human race. Anthropic is expected to push ahead with plans for an initial public offering (IPO) as soon as next month. OpenAI’s most recent fundraising was in March when it closed a $122bn round of finance at a valuation of $852bn. Two months later Anthropic announced it had raised $65bn, valuing the company at $965bn. On Friday, it emerged that Masayoshi Son, the founder of Japanese investment company SoftBank, is seeking to raise up to $100bn from Gulf states as he scales up his already mammoth investments in AI. SoftBank has aggressively pivoted towards AI, including making a $65bn investment in OpenAI, and discussions have been held with Gulf investors including the United Arab Emirates, the Financial Times reported. Last month, SoftBank raised $11.1bn in the largest high-yield corporate bond sale globally on record, paying investors yields as high as 9.75%, to fund its bets on AI and semiconductor assets.

title: First Thing: Hegseth promises execution live stream as Trump appears to ‘pause’ war on Iran
author: Martin Belam
summary: US president says US will not attack Iran before midterms, while defense secretary says Nidal Hasan will face a firing squad next month
body_text: Good morning. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has said the execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad will be livestreamed next month, in a radical departure from the previous norm. Hegseth said: “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center at Fort Hood, Texas, on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013 and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was in November 1945. Why is Hegseth being criticised over the Iran war? The Democratic senator Chris Murphy said Hegseth was “determined to hide the cost and the consequences of this war from the American public”. Murphy claimed the Pentagon blocked him from visiting a military base in Qatar and that an Iranian strike on the US embassy in Riyadh was far worse than the public were led to believe. What has Donald Trump said about the US war on Iran? The US president has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections, outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months. A Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September found that only about a third of Americans approved of the strikes on Iran. Billionaires fund California ballot measure to make voters show ID at polls Billionaires across the US are spending vast sums to support California’s Proposition 39, a measure that would require voters to show identification before casting their ballots. The measure is being promoted amid a nationwide push by the Trump administration to restrict voting. California Republicans have long sought to advance a voter ID initiative in the state. Various out-of-state conservative donors have given millions of dollars in support. Why are some voters calling Missouri’s elections ‘dizzying and embarrassing’? Thanks to a protracted legal battle over an effort by Republicans to redraw the state’s congressional map, some voters are no longer sure which congressional district they live in or who will be on their ballot paper for the midterms. What happened in last night’s crucial midterm debates? Rachel Leingang, George Chidi and Auzzy Byrdsell have rounded up the key takeaways from debates in the battleground states of Michigan, Georgia and Maine. Trump made clear that media ban was due to critical coverage, court told A lawyer who has represented numerous media companies that have sued the Trump administration over access issues has told a court that Donald Trump’s own words are one of the strongest parts of their case, after the US president made clear in a recent interview with Time magazine that he chose to bar three news organizations because of their critical coverage of him. CNN, MS Now and Politico were asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. The district court judge Timothy Kelly – a Trump appointee – said he would extend it until next Tuesday. That means the White House will be forced to allow journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to continue accessing the building until then. Film shoot appearing to echo Renee Good killing roils Montana town A Daily Wire film production that appears to re-enact elements of Renee Good’s killing has been allowed to continue filming in a rural Montana town. The project, which reportedly stars Danny Trejo and Harvey Keitel, follows an ICE agent’s effort to escape a mob seeking to free an immigrant he has detained, according to its logline. In one video of the shoot that surfaced online, a female actor portraying a protester can be seen driving a beat-up car into a flock of law enforcement agents, knocking one officer down as another fires his weapon. Then, the car abruptly lurches back. That scene drew backlash – and real protesters – over its resemblance to an ICE agent’s fatal shooting of Good in January. In other news … Four astronauts have returned to Earth from the International Space Station after a medical relief mission. The crew hurried to the ISS eight months ago after an astronaut fell ill in space. The DoJ is seeking to charge the ex-Trump aide Cassidy Hutchinson, who gave key testimony on the January 6 attack on the Capitol. She said she had been told that Trump lunged for the wheel of an SUV to try to join the mob. An ICE agent shot and injured a man in New York City during an enforcement operation, federal officials said. Trump says he is considering asking the FBI to investigate the death of Nolan Wells. Wells’s cause and manner of death are still undetermined, and a Jackson County grand jury declined to indict anyone in his case. Stat of the day: Thousands turn out to welcome weary USS Lincoln sailors after grueling deployment Thousands of people flooded to greet the USS Lincoln’s long-awaited return. It left San Diego last November, expected to return in the spring, until the US and Israel launched the war with Iran. Culture pick: As pointless as a film based on a toy car could be … Enjoy a review that gives something an absolute battering? I can recommend Benjamin Lee on Matchbox, who says “John Cena and Jessica Biel collect paychecks in a soulless and synthetic slab of corporate product”. Elsewhere, Rich Pelley speaks to someone who has been behind films with a lot more soul. Sofia Coppola is, as you’d expect, a compelling read. Don’t miss this: ‘Delights await!’ – Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne Carson The Handmaid’s Tale author is joined by Emily Wilson, Ocean Vuong and the Booker-shortlisted writer Rebecca Perry in celebrating the newly announced Nobel laureate. … or this: How a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find The species, with leaves large enough to be seen from space, is already considered critically endangered – but plans are afoot to protect it. Climate check: Millions on alert as Hurricane Isaias set to bring dangerous storm surge Millions of people from Louisiana to Florida were under hurricane warnings as Hurricane Isaias heads toward the US Gulf coast, with weather officials warning of hurricane-force winds, heavy rainfall and flooding. Storm surge warnings are already in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwanee River in Florida. When it makes its expected landfall, experts say it will be the biggest test for Fema since the Trump-imposed cuts on the agency. Last Thing: Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away I love a space mystery, and scientists have detected a fast radio burst that traveled for more than 10bn years before reaching Earth. The burst is believed to be the farthest yet detected, more than double the previous distance record. And nobody knows what they are. title: AI and the climate crisis pose existential risks. The law offers a way to reduce them
author: Robert Reich
summary: Liability lawsuits have held tobacco, oil and pharma companies to account in the past. AI investors won’t ignore this threat
body_text: The most basic function of government is to protect people from harm. Two growing phenomena – the climate crisis and AI – pose escalating risks of extraordinary harm. The climate crisis is already causing floods, wildfires, drought and record heat. AI agents are already escaping super-secure environments to hack into systems they’re supposed to avoid. Yet Donald Trump and his Republican enablers, backed by big money from big oil and big AI, refuse to do a thing about either risk. In many ways, they’re worsening both. But there’s another way to reduce these risks: through liability law. I have no more faith in the supreme court than you do, but I was struck by the responses of at least half the justices who will be considering an important case that opened the supreme court’s new term, Suncor v Boulder. The case was brought by several Colorado localities against Suncor and ExxonMobil – one of about three dozen filed around the country in which cities and states are demanding that big oil reimburse them for the escalating costs of climate disasters brought on by the burning of fossil fuels. On Monday, at least four justices (Samuel Alito has recused himself) expressed skepticism about big oil’s argument that the Clean Air Act explicitly prevents such lawsuits against polluters. “It’s like, wow, like, where is the text for that? Where’s the support for that? Where’s the precedent for that? Where’s the anything for that?” asked Justice Elena Kagan. Chief Justice John Roberts drew parallels between Boulder’s claim and prior lawsuits against the tobacco and opioid industries in which states and localities won significant damages. “I’m not quite sure what makes this situation different from all those other ones where we’ve allowed them to proceed in state court,” said Roberts. In 1998, the leading US tobacco companies agreed to pay $206bn to cover public health costs and smoking-related expenses. When translated into current dollars, this is more than $423bn. And recall the $20bn paid by BP in 2010 to cover environmental and economic damage to the Gulf coast after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. Or the $7.4bn paid by the Sackler family and Purdue Pharma to resolve liability for the opioid crisis. Such liability lawsuits – the last resort when the public is harmed by corporate malfeasance or nonfeasance – are also relevant to the risks posed by AI. If AI agents escape super-secure environments to release dangerous toxins, or destroy critical water, electricity, transportation, or health infrastructure, AI companies and the tech giants behind them could be on the hook for tens if not hundreds of billions of dollars in payments to those who are harmed. No way major investors in AI – or the insurance companies backstopping AI – are going to ignore this potential liability. The current dollar value of the tobacco settlement – as I said, $423bn – is comparable to what the tech giants spent on AI chips, servers, and datacenters last year. This gigantic financial risk will weigh on the values of AI companies and the tech companies unless or until they become far more serious about protecting the public against such harms. I expect political demands from the AI industry to limit such liability through federal laws that set caps on it and that establish industry-funded “trust funds” to pay for big liability judgments. A sane Congress (we may yet have one) wouldn’t agree without specific industry steps to dramatically increase safety. In all likelihood, the AI industry will also seek government regulations it could use as partial defenses against such massive liability, just as pharmaceutical companies use certification by the Food and Drug Administration that their drugs are safe and effective to defend against lawsuits claiming their drugs cause harm. The big AI investors and insurers will force this issue. More than 200 cases already in the courts involve cyber-liability and AI-related product liability. Follow the money. Insurers are already demanding more effective means of controlling AI risks, and big investors are demanding better means of limiting them. Both the climate crisis and AI pose existential risks to human life on this planet. Liability law is hardly an easy or perfect fix, but it’s an important start. The fact that liability for the climate crisis is already in the supreme court and that four justices seem sympathetic suggests how significant a role liability can play as an incentive for both fossil fuel and AI giants – and their insurers and major investors – to clean up their acts. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

title: Stop talking about the US ‘Jewish vote’. It’s not that simple
author: Judith Levine
summary: Political parties vie for Jewish support based on false assumptions that boil down to one issue: Israel
body_text: Everybody wants the Jewish vote. As if there were one. Jews are educated, generally liberal. Although they comprise only about 2% of the electorate, they vote in high numbers, overwhelmingly for Democrats. In 2024, 79% chose Kamala Harris. They are also assumed to be steadfast friends of Israel, no matter what it does. Republicans, waging a fake war on antisemitism while courting white supremacists, consider Jews increasingly up for grabs. Nationally, Jewish Americans are concentrated in a few bright blue spots. A 2020 map from the Jewish Electorate Institute showed a third of Jews living in 20 congressional districts – out of 435 – most of them in New York, New Jersey, California and (purple) Florida. Of these, only one sent a Republican to Washington. Today, it’s two. Florida’s 21st district switched parties only after falling victim to redistricting in 2022. The other outlier has elected the pro-Israel, anti-immigration Republican Chris Smith every term since 1981. Why? The mapmakers’ explanation: New Jersey fourth district includes Lakewood, where half the residents are ultra-Orthodox – scrupulously, ceaselessly observant. Unsurprisingly, among white voters, regular religious service attendance is a big predictor of conservatism. In other words, in Lakewood, Orthodox may be more salient that Jewish. In fact, if pro-Israel candidates are looking for votes, even Jewish is no longer salient. White Evangelical Christians are more firmly supportive of Israel than American Jews. The US is home to the largest population of Christian Zionists in the world, numbering more than 30 million, a third of whom belong to Christians United for Israel, the largest Zionist organization is the US. The Bible belt churches these people attend preach that the founding of Israel in 1948 was part of God’s plan to bring about the End Times, and the ongoing hostilities in the Middle East are the mayhem and destruction preceding the second coming of Christ (when nonbelievers – including Jews – will drown in the Lake of Fire). While the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) spends far more on political campaigns, Christians United for Israel is busy mobilizing its millions to grassroots action. Meanwhile, a minority of American Jews now call themselves Zionists. A late-2025 Washington Post poll found that six in 10 believed Israel was committing war crimes in Gaza; four in 10 said the assault was genocide. And aside from the fiercest partisans, for many young Jews, Israel just isn’t that important. The Gaza war figured large in the 2024 presidential elections, as the civilian death toll mounted and the Biden-Harris administration stood unwaveringly beside Israel. Now, even as the killing spreads to the West Bank and southern Lebanon, US voters are moving on. Affordability is the winning buzzword this cycle, at least for Democrats. Almost no one is thinking about foreign policy. What about abortion? Climate change? Voting rights? The press, the pundits, and the mainstream party strategists keep behaving as if every Jew cares about Israel – and all Jews care about is Israel – and a candidate must be pro-Zionist or lose the elusive Jewish vote. We saw this during the campaign of the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani. Forthright support for Palestinian self-determination had long been central to his politics, and to his appeal to progressives. But Mamdani was running for mayor, not president. His brilliant stroke was affordability – a theme that is easily understandable, widely relatable, and capable of making socialist solutions sound reasonable. Nevertheless, from the moment he appeared, the press, from the New York Times op-ed page to college newspapers to the international Jewish press, made the election a referendum on Israel – and, more perniciously, on Islam. Mamdani’s Democratic primary opponent, former governor Andrew Cuomo, attacked him with flagrant Islamophobia, conflating his critique of Israel with antisemitism and signalling that his faith was a danger to Jews. The fearmongering did not defeat Mamdani. In the end, only a third of Jews voted for him; in Hasidic neighborhoods, 90% went for Cuomo. But progressive Jewish organizations including Jewish Voice for Peace and Jews for Racial and Economic Justice endorsed him. He won in almost every racial and class demographic and pulled in three-quarters of voters under 30. What’s the lesson here? The youth vote – plus the Black vote, the Hispanic vote, the working-class vote, etc – plus good ideas and a great campaign put Mamdani over the top. Furthermore, an analysis by Good Authority concludes that no position on Israel, pro or con, is driving Jews out of the Democratic party. Now Abdul El-Sayed, the Muslim Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, is shlepping the burden of this vaguely defined, perpetually disgruntled “Jewish vote”. After narrowly winning the primary, he apologized to members of the Jewish community for a statement he made after a Lebanese-born naturalized citizen rammed his truck into a large synagogue, injuring a guard. The apology came after El-Sayed clumsily linked the man’s antisemitism to Israeli violence in Lebanon, saying: “Hurt people hurt people.” It was an inoffensive adage among, say, prison abolitionists. But to some Jews, it sounded as if El-Sayed felt more sympathy for the perpetrator than for his targeted victims. The Republicans have taken advantage of these fissures, attacking El-Sayed with a combination of Islamophobia and the usual hypocritical condemnations of antisemitism. At their midterm “convention”, El-Sayed’s opponent Mike Rogers claimed, falsely, that the Democrat had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. And while El-Sayed definitively distanced himself from the leftwing Israel critic Hasan Piker – a Twitch streamer the press began to cover obsessively – speaker after speaker hammered on the connection between the two men. These tactics appear to be falling flat. A recent New York Times/Siena poll found that most Michiganders have never heard of Piker. The poll found that El-Sayed leads his opponent by 39 points among voters 44 and younger, who are far more critical of Israel’s policies than their elders. That generational split is also pronounced among Jews. El-Sayed has the endorsements of JVP and IfNotNow, an organization that attracts many young Jews who are painfully rejecting their parents’ Zionism, as well as Vermont’s Jewish senator, Bernie Sanders. While Rogers has been collecting pledges of votes from Jewish Michiganders, more than 600 “Michigan Jews for Democracy”, including elected officials and rabbis, have signed a letter in support of El-Sayed. Recently, Mamdani repeated his condemnation of Benjamin Netanyahu as a war criminal who should be arrested in advance of the Israeli prime minister’s visit to New York to address the UN. That revived Zionist fury toward the mayor, but Jews both supportive and critical of Israel – and Mamdani – held noisy rallies. The reason for Mamdani to keep trying to speak to both sides is not to win the mythical Jewish vote. It is to make common cause with people who don’t want Israel swept into the sea but also cannot abide a Jewish ethnostate whose survival depends on occupation and apartheid. That said, if El-Sayed were the Islamist Jew-hater his enemies claim he is, it should be obvious to a lot more Jews. If it were obvious to a lot more Jews, Aipac would not have had to pour $32m – unsuccessfully – into Stevens’ campaign or contemplate pouring more into supporting Rogers in the general election. And of course, the “Arab American” or “Muslim vote” is no more unanimous than the hypothetical Jewish vote. To be frank, the whole discourse stinks. It boils down to “support the Muslim” or “support the Jew”, as if this were some ancient racial animosity – natural enemies “fighting”, as Trump said of the Palestinians and Israeli Jews, “for a thousand years”. Not only is this contention untrue. Such thinking obviates politics, the effort to understand a problem and convince others that your solution is best. It is not good for the Jews – or for anyone. And it is deadly for a secular, pluralistic democracy. Judith Levine is a frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

title: Targeting Trump: how Democrats plan to investigate the president if they win Congress
author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
summary: Control of Congress after the 2026 midterm elections would give Democrats power to subpoena documents and testimony
body_text: In August, Jamie Raskin renewed his demand that Jared Kushner hand over documents about the overlap between his informal role advising Donald Trump on foreign policy and the private equity firm he runs after an earlier request was ignored. Five of the 11 companies that Elizabeth Warren, Chuck Schumer and Ron Wyden wrote to about Donald Trump’s IRS settlement – including the Trump Organization and World Liberty Financial – never answered at all. Of course, none of them had to. That all changes if Democrats win the House and Senate in November. Control of the chamber would not only give Democrats the gavels, but they would be handed bigger staffs and the power to subpoena documents and testimony – and they have been unusually candid about how they plan to use it. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, has ranked his priorities in September: the Trump family’s businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, corporate profiteering and Robert F Kennedy Jr’s handling of vaccines. Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee and its likely chair, calls the potential scope of the work “gargantuan”. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, has promised to “hold the crooks accountable”. Here are eight of the most consequential investigations, what Democrats have already demanded, and where they could hit a wall. The family business Garcia ranks Trump family corruption first on his list for the oversight committee, while Raskin has requested information on the business dealings of Kushner and Trump Jr. On 25 August, Raskin wrote to Kushner, renewing a demand for documents on his dual roles as an informal foreign policy adviser to Trump and the head of a private equity firm that does business with foreign governments. He has been chasing Kushner’s firm, Affinity Partners, since 2023, when he said it took $2bn from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund after Kushner left the White House. There is also the $400m plane that Qatar gifted Trump, a Trump Jr wedding party that was partly funded by a Russian oligarch, and several multimillion-dollar defense contracts won by the extended Trump family that will draw more scrutiny. The IRS settlement In May, the Department of Justice settled the president’s $10bn lawsuit against the IRS with an order barring the agency from auditing past returns of Trump, his family and related companies. Richard Neal, the top Democrat on the House ways and means committee, and Raskin demanded documents on the negotiations, the roles of the justice department and treasury officials, and safeguards against fraud, with a 27 May deadline ahead of the appearance of the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, before Neal’s committee. In the Senate, Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the finance committee, and 12 other finance Democrats on 22 May called for a bipartisan investigation into the settlement and the administration’s decision to bar the IRS from auditing Trump, his family and businesses. At a hearing, Wyden pressed Bessent on whether the audit immunity remained in effect, which he declined to answer. On 7 July, Wyden, Warren and Schumer wrote to 11 companies, including Kalshi and Polymarket, asking whether they intend to rely on the settlement as protection against audits, given Trump Jr’s financial ties with the companies. Raskin and Garcia, meanwhile, demanded correspondence between Trump’s lawyers and the justice department over his reported $230m claim for past investigations. A federal judge has said the order conflicts with federal law, according to Warren’s office, and the legal fight is unresolved. Crypto and betting markets Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Senate’s permanent subcommittee on investigations, opened a preliminary inquiry and wrote to executives behind the $Trump memecoin and World Liberty Financial, asking about ownership and investment structure. Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate banking committee, asked the Office of Government Ethics to review a reported deal involving World Liberty, Binance and a UAE state-backed fund. Warren, Blumenthal, Gary Peters, Dick Durbin and Wyden demanded hearings after disclosures showed Trump earned more than $1.2bn from crypto ventures, including about $588m tied to World Liberty token sales. In the House, Maxine Waters, the top Democrat on the financial services committee, has called for legislation to “end the President’s crypto profiteering and recoup his ill-gotten gains”. On prediction markets, the July letter to Kalshi’s chief executive noted that Trump Jr was a “strategic advisor” to the company, and seven House Democrats asked the oversight chair, James Comer, to subpoena the markets over suspicious trades tied to the Iran war. This one has the most bipartisan appeal: the Republican senator John Curtis asked the Senate judiciary committee to subpoena Trump Jr over his Kalshi and Polymarket ties, and Comer opened his own insider-trading investigation. Epstein and the emails Thanks to a tag-team effort by representatives Ro Khanna and Thomas Massie, the Department of Justice was forced to release millions of files related to Jeffrey Epstein last year. But off the bat, the justice department blew the legally mandated deadline to disclose the files. Then it released only about 3.5m pages of the 6m in its possession; it said it has deemed the rest duplicates. And there has been bipartisan consternation about heavy redactions in some places, and the apparently accidental disclosure of the names of victims in other places. The justice department is now facing a lawsuit from journalist Katie Phang over many of these issues. Even under a Republican-controlled Congress, the oversight committee under its GOP chair, James Comer, has been a rare spot of bipartisan comity, with members of both sides routinely (but not always) acting in concert to subpoena witnesses and hold them in contempt when they don’t cooperate. Expect that to continue in any new Democratic Congress. The Pentagon and the wars Jason Crow, a Colorado congressman who sits on the armed services and intelligence committees and co-chairs the House end corruption caucus, says he will start with the Pentagon, citing reports of defense money steered toward companies linked to the Trump family. The sharpest look so far is a January letter from Warren, Blumenthal and Andy Kim. It lists companies backed by 1789 Capital, the venture firm Trump Jr joined as a partner: Cerberus ($45m), PsiQuantum ($10.8m), Firehawk Aerospace ($4.9m) and Vulcan Elements ($10m, plus a reported $620m loan). It also cites a $12.8m contract to Unusual Machines, a drone company in which Trump Jr holds a stake. The senators asked whether the Vulcan loan was competitive, which officials Trump Jr screened for Pentagon jobs, and for every contact between defense department officials and Trump Jr since 5 November 2024. A later Pentagon reply, they wrote, showed no safeguards against such conflicts. Vulcan and the Pentagon have denied Trump Jr had any involvement in the loan. On the war, Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, led his colleagues in demanding that Marco Rubio, Pete Hegseth, Steve Witkoff and Kushner testify on the Iran war, and forced a vote to subpoena them. He also demanded documents on Venezuelan oil revenue routed into a Qatar account. In 2025, Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate armed services committee, pressed for an expanded inspector general investigation of the defense secretary’s use of Signal. He and Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House armed services committee, objected to a Hegseth memo routing Pentagon communications with Congress through his office. Immigration enforcement and who profits In March, Raskin and Warren led 52 lawmakers in writing to six companies tied to ICE’s warehouse detention plan: CoreCivic, Geo Group, GardaWorld Federal, Gosin Group, KVG LLC and PNK Group. They asked for expected profit margins, lobbying efforts and donations to Trump’s campaign or cabinet officials, by 13 April. The plan carries a $38.3bn price tag and aims to hold nearly 100,000 people by November. The lawmakers flagged ICE paying $129m for a Georgia facility, nearly five times its assessed value, and a contracting official who came from Geo. Garcia’s oversight Democrats wrote separately to Geo about Corey Lewandowski’s dealings, after reports he sought personal payments from contractors. Peters, the retiring top Democrat on the Senate homeland security committee, led a letter seeking every DHS contract that the border czar, Tom Homan, may have influenced, after reports of a bribery investigation. Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the House homeland security committee, would take the matter up there. Warren’s Wall Street If Democrats flip the Senate, now-ranking member Elizabeth Warren would be positioned to chair the banking committee, and private credit is her likeliest target. On 13 May, she wrote to Bessent and the SEC chair, Paul Atkins, on how deregulation has increased private credit risks, with responses due by 26 May. In July 2025 she asked Bessent to run a stress test of the market, which he did not do. She has also written to ratings agencies including S&P, Moody’s and Fitch over reportedly inflated private credit ratings. When Blue Owl restricted withdrawals from a fund, she called for higher bank capital requirements for private credit exposures, transparent data from the firms and a stress test. The wildcard Impeachment hangs over all of it. Trump was impeached twice in his first term and acquitted both times. Jeffries says Democrats have ruled nothing in and nothing out, while the Republican House majority leader, Steve Scalise, predicts an attempt on “Day 1”. Even if Jeffries does not ultimately pursue impeachment, Trump could force his hand. Nancy Pelosi held off leftwing calls for impeachment for months after she became speaker of the House after the 2018 midterms, but when Trump tried to get Ukrainian leaders to pursue an investigation of Joe Biden – and then incited the January 6 attack on the Capitol – Pelosi relented and oversaw two different impeachments.

title: Tory tax break for banks has cost UK public purse £6bn, says TUC
author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
summary: Exclusive: Chancellor urged to reverse Jeremy Hunt’s tax surcharge cuts to claw back billions in lost revenue
body_text: Tax cuts for big banks have deprived the UK government of £6bn in revenues, according to campaigners, who are calling on the chancellor, John Healey, to increase taxes and force lenders to pay their “fair share” in the budget. Calculations by the Trades Union Congress (TUC), which represents unions with more than 5.3 million members across England and Wales, shows that the public purse is billions of pounds worse off as a result of tax cuts introduced under the Tory chancellor Jeremy Hunt in 2023. The then government agreed to slash the bank surcharge – an additional levy on lenders’ profits – from 8% to 3% that year. The move was meant to offset a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%, after the industry argued higher taxes would put them at a competitive disadvantage compared with other big financial centres such as New York. However, the cuts came just as lenders started reaping handsome earnings, thanks to rising interest rates. The UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group – have now generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years. The TUC says the 2023 cuts ultimately robbed the UK purse of tax revenues. Its analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the UK public lost out £2.3bn in 2023-24, a further £1.7bn in 2024-25, and £2bn in 2025-26 – totalling £6bn over three years. With banks pocketing record profits, the TUC said the surcharge should now be increased beyond its pre-2023 level at the 28 October budget. That could raise up to £60bn, which could be used to cover rising household bills as part of prime minister Andy Burnham’s drive to tackle the cost of living. “The Tories’ tax break for banks has cost the UK public purse £6bn and counting. It’s time to end it and to make sure banks pay their fair share,” the TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, said. “At a time when families are struggling with soaring energy costs, taxing banks’ booming profits to cut bills is just plain common sense. There is a mountain of evidence to suggest that banks can afford to pay more tax – not least the record £25bn bonus pool they paid out last year. “This month’s budget is an opportunity to put things right.” Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against bank tax rises, after narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget. Jamie Dimon, chief executive of the largest US bank, JP Morgan, warned Burnham and Healey against further levies during a meeting last month, saying it could put investment and jobs at risk. Earlier this year, Dimon warned that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile to banks. The TUC has said raising the surcharge to 16% – double the rate prior to Conservative cuts – could raise £24bn in tax revenues over the next four years. Meanwhile, a 35% bank surcharge, which would match the windfall tax rate that Conservatives imposed on energy companies, would deliver £60bn over four years. Even reversing the surcharge cuts and setting it at 8% would raise £9bn over that same period, the union body said. “Reversing the last government’s tax cuts is the very least this government can do to claw back some of the lost billions it’s handed to banks in recent years,” said a spokesperson for campaign group Positive Money, which has also been pushing for bank tax rises at the budget. “Banks are making record profits without lifting a finger, thanks to the higher rates being paid to them, by both customers and the Bank of England.” David Postings, the chief executive of banking lobby group UK Finance said that a strong banking sector was essential for a strong UK economy and that profitable lenders would be able to invest in better services for customers, issue more loans, and deliver “returns” – such as shareholder dividends – that supported people’s savings and pensions. “Banks also make a major contribution to the public finances and already face a materially higher total tax rate in the UK than in other leading financial centres,” he said. “Further tax increases would weaken the UK’s competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government’s ambition to deliver growth in every postcode.” The Treasury was contacted for comment.

title: Democratic Senate candidate responds to anti-trans attacks pushed by Republicans
author: Ariana Baio
summary: Dr Annie Andrews voices opposition to ‘biological men … in women’s sports’ in response to Republican attacks
body_text: Dr Annie Andrews, a Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina, has responded to persistent efforts by Republicans to make trans athletes in women’s sports a wedge issue in the race. In a restrained direct-to-camera statement, Andrews – a pediatrician – outlined her opposition to “biological men playing in women’s sports”, as her party pushes back against Republican attacks. “I want you to hear me loud and clear: I don’t support biological men playing in women’s sports, and I don’t support and haven’t ever performed gender surgery for minors,” Andrews said in a new ad. Andrews’ video, in which she wears a white lab coat with a stethoscope around her neck, was in response to recent attacks from Donald Trump and an aggressive ad, paid for by a super political action committee (Super Pac) supporting her Republican opponent in South Carolina, Darline Graham. The ad claims Andrews “is for they/them” and frames a transgender person as predatory toward a child. Republicans are using anti-trans issues, such as keeping trans women off women’s and girls’ sports teams, to try to thwart Democrats in the upcoming midterms. Trump has pushed the issue for years. A landmark supreme court ruling earlier this year handed Trump a key “culture war” victory by upholding laws in two conservative states excluding transgender girls and women from competing in female sports. Andrews, who has previously been vocal in her support of trans people, used her response ad to directly address Republican criticisms and claims as the party pushes anti-trans attacks against Democrats nationwide. Some Democrats running in competitive districts have shifted their tone on the issue of trans rights, particularly on the issue of trans athletes in women’s sports. Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, seeking re-election in a district that voted for Trump in 2024, recently aired an ad touting that she “voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools” and “boys should not play in girls’ sports”. Congressman Don Davis of North Carolina, running for re-election in a district that also backed the president in 2024, released an ad saying: “There’s real concerns about fairness and safety; that’s what I believe states should decide what’s right for protecting women and girls.” Blake Gendebien, the Democratic candidate running in a primarily Republican district in New York, released an ad stating that “boys shouldn’t play on girls’ sports teams” while also highlighting that the topic was a non-issue in the district. “The thing is, in 20 years raising a family here, I haven’t heard this issue come up. Not once,” Gendebien said. “But internet trolls like [the Republican candidate] Anthony Constantino use it to rile people up.” In 2024, pro-Trump groups seized on conservative opposition to the Biden administration’s trans inclusive policies to attack former vice-president Kamala Harris, the then Democratic presidential candidate. “Kamala’s agenda is they/them, not you,” a voiceover said in one widely seen pro-Trump ad. The ad attacking Andrews in South Carolina uses nearly identical language as the pro-Trump one two years ago. How Democrats should respond to Republicans’ anti-trans attacks has divided some. Equality Pac, the fundraising arm of the congressional equality caucus focusing on electing LGBTQ+ people, told Axios it disapproved of Kaptur’s handling of her response to the anti-trans attacks. The Pac called Kaptur’s language “unacceptable” and said it was “absolutely not supporting her campaign at this time”, referring to her ad in which she called transgender girls “boys”. Last month, the Human Rights Campaign – an LGBTQ+ advocacy group – wrote a Substack article to help guide Democrats on how to best respond to anti-trans rights attacks. “Turning on a vulnerable community is not a winning political strategy – and it’s exactly what Trump, [Elon] Musk, and MAGA want,” it wrote. “It legitimizes their side and weakens ours. And it harms transgender people.” The group pointed to the Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown’s response to anti-trans attacks as a good example of how to handle those attacks. Brown released an ad last month featuring voters who dismiss the anti-trans issues, and instead redirected attention to affordability issues under Brown’s competitor, and the incumbent senator, Jon Husted. “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?” one voter said in Brown’s advertisement. The Human Rights Campaign said Brown “didn’t play into MAGA’s hands” and “let voters do the talking” in the video.
