title: The fight over using super for housing has deep roots in Australian politics. But would it actually work?
author: Emily Millane
summary: Ultimately, the debate is a battle for power over Australians’ savings pool of $4.8tn dating back to the scheme’s inception
body_text: Should you be able to take money out of your super to pay for housing? One Nation has recently suggested you should. Liberal senator Andrew Bragg has also revived the idea. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, tells us the Coalition and One Nation are “coming after super” and want to “vandalise” the retirement savings scheme. He also predicts the next federal election will be a referendum on super. In the midst of a national cost of living crisis and housing shortage, it would seem reasonable to ask about the balance between how much money we are saving for retirement and how much money we have to use now. It would also seem uncontroversial to discuss whether altering that balance will assist with cost-of-living pressures or add to them. The idea of using super for housing is hotly contested. Why is this the case? The answer resides in the history of Australia’s private retirement saving system, the battles over its design and, ultimately, for power over a $4.8tn savings pool. The national system of compulsory superannuation was legislated in 1992 by the Keating Labor government. Paul Keating and former ACTU secretary Bill Kelty are regarded as the founders of the system and continue to be active voices in the debate more than 30 years after superannuation was introduced. The 1992 legislation grew out of industrial campaigns by trade unions for a “right” to superannuation. Before the superannuation reforms, most workers received only the government age pension in retirement. Those who also had superannuation were limited to some white-collar workers and government employees, and mostly to men. As Kelty put it in an interview with me for my book, “before superannuation, when you got the sack, you got nothing”. When super was introduced, Kelty recalled there was a sense that “never again can you leave workers in a position where they’ve got nothing.” For these reasons the Labor party and the broader labour movement regard themselves as proprietors and custodians of superannuation as a social justice measure. The Liberal party originally opposed universal superannuation for ideological and political reasons. Forcing workers to hand over a portion of their wages was anathema to a party of free enterprise. Hence the reminder today by people like Liberal MP Tim Wilson that superannuation is “your money”, compulsorily acquired by government mandate. There was – and still remains – a deep suspicion within the Coalition about the links between industry superannuation funds, the unions and Labor. In the late 1980s, then shadow treasurer John Howard characterised the industrial precursor to the superannuation legislation as the “Keating/Kelty accord”, creating a “union slush fund which would be controlled by union bosses”. He later labelled national superannuation legislation as “nothing short of parliamentary confiscation of the assets of employers”. After the Superannuation Guarantee was legislated, the Liberal party would come to accept that superannuation was here to stay, but it sought to refashion the policy in their philosophical mould. In 2005, Howard and then treasurer Peter Costello introduced choice-of-fund legislation. The choice changes meant that employees would no longer be defaulted into a superannuation fund because of their industrial award or agreement but instead have the option of choosing where their savings went. This was an effort to divert savings away from industry superannuation funds with union ties and an attempt to open superannuation to the private market. There have been earlier proposals by the Liberal party to use super for housing, too. Indeed, as some have pointed out, there already exists a means to use superannuation for a first home deposit. The Turnbull government introduced the First Home Super Saver Scheme in 2017, allowing individuals to make up to $15,000 in voluntary superannuation contributions per year, to a maximum of $30,000 in total, which could be withdrawn to help fund a first home deposit. Labor opposed the scheme, with then shadow treasurer Chris Bowen characterising it as a “fundamental undermining of Australia’s superannuation system” and one that will “make housing affordability worse, not better, by pushing up demand and overinflating prices”. Keating described the earlier proposal for the scheme as “not responsible enough even to be considered a thought bubble”. The Morrison government went to the 2022 election with the Super Home Buyer policy, under which first home buyers would be able to use 40% of their super, up to $50,000, towards buying a home. These same arguments have been used to advance the current proposals by politicians as well as superannuation interest groups who have their own links to different actors in the system. Some groups have ties to not-for-profit and industry funds, which have equal representatives of employers and employees on their boards. Others have members from the for-profit retail sector. Super Members Council (SMC) was created after a merger of two former peak bodies, including Industry Super Australia, with its famous “compare the pair” ads. SMC found that the Morrison government’s Covid-19 early release scheme saw about 725,000 Australians effectively wipe out their superannuation accounts. This was a measure legislated in the early days of the pandemic to allow people to access ‘their own money’ when many lost their incomes. It was only afterwards that the jobkeeper reforms took place. Recently, Senator Bragg reignited the super-for-housing debate in an address to the retail fund-aligned Financial Services Council. He pointed out that Keating himself floated the idea of using up to $10,000 for housing in 1993. Housing is an unofficial pillar of the retirement system. Those who rent in retirement, especially single people, are more likely to be living in poverty. There are other measures to address this issue, namely the tax and transfer system or potentially boosting commonwealth rent assistance to retirees. Superannuation is a complex system that many find hard to understand, especially with so many actors who have a dog in the fight over how the savings pool should be used. Super was created to address a genuine social problem: ensuring Australians could retire with more than the age pension and avoid poverty in old age. But housing is also a social problem, and for many younger Australians, the prospect of ever owning a home is becoming increasingly remote. Considering the history of superannuation and the scale of Australia’s housing crisis helps us understand why proposals such as using super for housing have arisen and why the debate over their merits is ongoing. • Emily Millane is a lawyer, policy analyst and researcher. She is a member of the Australian Historical Association. Her book, Super: The Policy History of Australia’s Retirement Savings Scheme, is out on Tuesday through Melbourne University Publishing

title: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s government: ‘There’s just so much lying and stealing’
author: Guardian staff
summary: Late-night hosts looked at Trump’s latest lies and bizarre comments on Iran destroying Los Angeles and San Diego
body_text: Late-night hosts poked fun at Donald Trump’s attempts to lie about crowd size once again as his administration continues to show signs of corruption. Jimmy Kimmel On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host reminded viewers that it was the “magical time of the year” when Trump thinks he deserves the Nobel peace prize and “cries like a newborn baby” when he doesn’t get it. Kimmel said the president would once again be “mortified” to not receive it “seven months after starting a war for no reason”. This week also saw Trump award the National Medal of Science to Elon Musk, which Kimmel said was deserved as “no one has meddled more with our nation’s scientists” than him. Kimmel added: “It’s so nice when two terrible people can put their differences aside for the greater bad.” Trump has continued to defend his comments that Iran could “take out” San Diego and Los Angeles – yet Kimmel said if he wanted to explain himself then “try mixing the cities up a little bit”. Given that Iran doesn’t possess weaponry that could make it all the way to the west coast, “he might as well be protecting us from the chupacabra”. This week has also seen Trump continuing to panic over James Talarico, the Democratic Texas Senate candidate, claiming that if Texans vote for him then everything will have a “bad smell” but Kimmel said that’s “mostly from your diapers”. Talarico has been virtually “begging” his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, to debate him but the Republican has been “running from him like Ted Cruz to Cancún during an ice storm”. Trump has also claimed that he never lies and always keeps his promises despite recently lying about giving back taxpayer money that had been spent on political ads. “There’s just so much lying and stealing it gives you a headache,” Kimmel said. He then moved on to Kimberly Guilfoyle who was once “a Fox News something” before being dumped by Trump’s son and then being sent to Greece to became the US ambassador, which Kimmel said was “a funny thing to do”. This week showed that she asked a Trump donor, who owns a pizza chain called Snappy Tomato, to pay her personal Amex bill. “We finally made America great,” he said, before saying she needs “$30k a month just in eyeliner alone”. Seth Meyers On Late Night, Seth Meyers played footage of Trump claiming he had filled up an arena for a new rally, yet the camera showed empty seats. There’s no way to use this as a measure of success compared with previous presidents as “most presidents stop doing fucking rallies” as they are “too busy being president”. Meyers said people probably sick of hearing the “same material for 10 years straight”. He added that “Republicans in close races don’t want him around” so he has been “soothing himself with lies about his crowds in deep red states”. Meyers also played bizarre footage of Trump talking about meeting strapping male “studs” who were fans of his, repeatedly referring to their looks and physique. “If any of us behaved like Donald Trump we would never hear the end of it from Donald Trump,” he said. Meyers also spoke about Trump’s strange comments suggesting Iran could destroy Los Angeles and San Diego, and said that “throwing in San Diego makes it weirdly specific”. Meyers added that “even Republicans had to come out and denounce” what Trump had said.

title: Mike Ditka, legendary Chicago Bears head coach, dies aged 86
author: Associated Press
summary: The Hall of Famer who led the 1985 Bears to the Super Bowl title was one of two people in NFL history to win league titles as a player, assistant and head coach
body_text: Mike Ditka, who won NFL titles as a player and coach with the Chicago Bears, has died at 86, his family announced Friday. “It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka,” the family said. “While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears’ Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever.” Nicknamed “Iron Mike” as a player, Ditka helped revolutionize the tight end position, then moved to the sidelines and took over as Chicago’s coach. His 1985 Bears team featured one of football’s most dominant defenses ever. It also had enough outsized personalities to record a rap video, The Super Bowl Shuffle, and back up their boasting in the championship game three months later. After retiring as a coach, Ditka became a restaurateur, pitchman and TV personality, as well as an advocate for improved medical and retirement benefits for former players. Ditka was tough and gruff, the quintessential Chicago Bear nicknamed “Da Coach”. He did everything from order off the menu to knock defensive backs on their butts with a growl, and his adopted home town reveled in every minute. He was enshrined in the College and Pro Football Halls of Fame, and the Bears said during a ceremony in 2013 that his “No 89” jersey will be the last one retired by the team. He was born in Carnegie, Pennsylvania, the son of a welder who changed the family name from Dyczko. He grew up in nearby Aliquippa, close to the coal-mining and steel-manufacturing plants that dotted the western part of the state, a big, talented, three-sport athlete and All-American at Pitt whose bruising style made his first nickname, “Iron Mike” a good fit. Selected fifth overall by flinty Chicago owner George Halas in the 1961 draft, Ditka went on to Rookie of the Year honors, multiple Pro Bowl trips and the 1963 NFL championship. He left Chicago in 1966, playing briefly for Philadelphia and Dallas. He moved to the sideline in 1973 as an assistant to the revered Tom Landry and stayed with the Cowboys for eight seasons, before returning to a hero’s welcome in Chicago as head coach in 1982. Ditka’s return to the Bears lasted 10 tumultuous years, including five straight NFC Central titles, the Super Bowl win, a DUI conviction, a heart attack, a long-running feud with defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan and a new nickname – “Da Coach.” The public beefs with Ryan mirrored the behind-the-scenes battles Ditka waged trying to contain a team bristling with outsized personalities. “It was more than a team,” Ditka once said. “It was a team of characters that had character that played for a crazy man, who let him be crazy and had fun doing it and don’t apologize for it ever. I wouldn’t want to be one of these suits walking around on the sideline today. I have no desire to be that. I was what I was and they were what they were and, damn, it was fun.” It wasn’t until two dozen players recorded The Super Bowl Shuffle – an audacious rap-styled video released three months ahead of the 1986 title game – that the rest of the football world wondered whether Ditka was losing his grip. His players never did. “We call him ‘Sybil’ after that girl in the movie,” quarterback Jim McMahon once explained. “You know, the one that had all those personalities. Mike will be calm one minute, then throw a clipboard the next. People don’t understand that, but we do.” The Bears demolished the New England Patriots 46-10 in the Super Bowl, but Ditka often said he regretted having McMahon and defensive tackle William “The Refrigerator” Perry run for touchdowns instead of Walter Payton, Chicago’s loyal and longsuffering running back. Ryan departed for a head coaching job in Philadelphia soon after. While the Bears continued to be a contender for most of the next five years, a 5-11 season prompted Ditka’s departure in 1992. After a five-year absence, he returned to coaching with the New Orleans Saints, but failed to revive the franchise. After a miserable 1999 season ended with a 3-13 record- his worst as either a player or coach – he left the sidelines for good. His face and demeanor were so familiar by then that a second act became an easy segue. Ditka began building a stable of restaurants and appeared as himself in TV sitcoms from Cheers to Third Rock from the Sun, as well as shows such as LA Law and Saturday Night Live. He also stayed close to the game as an NFL analyst and game-day show personality at ESPN. Ditka’s high-profile status also made him an effective advocate to secure improved health and retirement benefits for former players. His name also circulated for years in Illinois political circles. Though he never ran for office, Ditka described himself as a staunch conservative and was mentioned several times as a possible Republican candidate, including a congressional race against then state representative Barack Obama for the US Senate.

title: ‘Medieval’ and ‘disturbing’: US plan to livestream execution elicits global condemnation
author: David Smith in Washington and Ariana Baio in New York
summary: Pentagon said execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, would be broadcast live
body_text: The US is facing worldwide condemnation over a “barbaric” plan to execute a disabled man by firing squad and livestream it to the public, with critics comparing the Trump administration to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan. The Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, would be livestreamed on 3 December. The United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned on Friday that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”. The plan also drew opprobrium from politicians, religious leaders and human rights advocates in the US and abroad. Hillary Clinton, the former US secretary of state, wrote on social media: “A barbaric idea, beneath our dignity as a country. Push back on this.” Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, posted: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.” Britain, which abolished the death penalty in the 1960s, moved to distance itself from the execution. Bridget Phillipson, the UK’s equalities minister and Labour party chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that she found the concept “rather disturbing”. Phillipson stressed that the decision was a matter for the US government, adding: “They are a close ally. Does that mean that we support everything the US government does? No.” Under US military law, a president must approve an execution by firing squad. Trump did so on the recommendation of his defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, according to the Pentagon. JD Vance – a practicing Catholic – told reporters on Friday he wouldn’t watch the livestreamed execution of Hasan, but stopped short of criticizing the administration’s decision. When asked how his Christian beliefs influence his view of the public execution, Vance dismissed controversy about the manner of execution and appeared to question whether the livestream will happen. “Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope the people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” the US vice-president told reporters. “That said, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.” Hegseth gleefully confirmed the livestream plan after previously saying that the execution would be public. Speaking to the conservative broadcaster Real America’s Voice, he said people should be able to watch because they need to understand that there were “serious consequences” for such crimes. Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.” Now 56, Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 after being convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. Twelve of those killed and 30 of the wounded were soldiers. The former army psychiatrist opened fire with a handgun at a medical facility at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009 as soldiers waited for medical checks before deployment. He was shot by a police officer during his arrest and left partly paralysed, and now uses a wheelchair. The execution is expected to be the first by firing squad carried out by the US military since 1945, when army private Eddie Slovik was executed for desertion during the second world war. The last US military execution of any kind took place in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged. Hasan’s case comes amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US following the botched lethal injection of Tennessee death-row prisoner Christa Pike last week. Her lawyers said she awoke in hospital “angry and confused” and remained seriously ill and shackled to her hospital bed. Media have sought to televise US executions ⁠in the past, but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream legal executions, experts said. Indeed, public executions have largely disappeared around the world. Amnesty International recorded at least 17 in 2025, including 11 in Iran and six in Taliban-run Afghanistan. In the US, executions have been conducted privately for about nine decades. The hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky in 1936, witnessed by thousands, is generally regarded as the country’s last public execution, although another hanging took place in Missouri the following year. Experts said there was no known precedent for livestreaming a legal execution. The execution of the Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001 was made available to victims’ relatives through closed-circuit television, but was not broadcast publicly. The proposed live stream has prompted criticism from religious leaders. Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”. Politicians from both sides of the aisle also spoke out. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives armed services committee, said the plan was “disturbing and makes a mockery of our legal system”. The Democratic senator Chris Murphy described public executions as “medieval”. The Republican senator Thom Tillis said Hasan should face the death penalty but that broadcasting his execution was “beyond disgusting”, arguing that public executions were associated with oppressive regimes. Others warned that the spectacle would be counterproductive and act as a recruiting sergeant for US enemies seeking fresh propaganda. Ned Price, a former deputy to the US representative to the United Nations, posted on X: “You can take it from those of us who’ve spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause. “Or take it from [al-Qaida] and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth’s proposal. Either way, it’s hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America’s image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable.” Some experts have raised questions about whether the live stream could be challenged in court. Eugene Fidell, a military law specialist at Yale Law School, said Hasan could seek legal action to block the public display of his death. Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at the University of California, Berkeley, said the announcement raised serious questions about the dignity of the condemned prisoner and the government’s motivation for staging such an unusual spectacle. “This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” she told the Associated Press. Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said: “Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end. “This announcement adds to the display of cruelty that we have just witnessed in the senseless pursuit of the execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee. The US death penalty is irredeemably broken. It is high time that the US authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all.” Other experts argued that public access could increase transparency around capital punishment. Deborah Denno, a death penalty specialist at Fordham University, told the AP that a live stream could make the process more transparent at a time when the botched execution in Tennessee had renewed questions about how the state puts prisoners to death. It remains unclear whether Hasan will seek to challenge his execution in civilian court, a move that could significantly delay the proceedings.

title: Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook
author: Gaya Gupta
summary: US president renews his efforts to oust Cook despite supreme court ruling that her firing was unconstitutional
body_text: Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite a June supreme court ruling that her earlier firing was unconstitutional. Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published. Cook will be able to submit a written statement to present her own evidence and will be subject to examination from White House and her own legal counsel. “As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump said in a statement posted to the White House’s website. Her legal team has maintained that the White House is “cherrypicking” facts and any claims of fraud are based on unrelated clerical errors. In response to the announcement, Cook’s lawyers said that they had “grave doubts” that the White House hearing would be “a legitimate one that would conform to the law”. “But if it is anything close to objective,” they continued, “the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board.” They added that Cook “welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her”. Cook was appointed by Joe Biden in 2022 to a 14-year term, becoming the Fed’s first Black governor. Before her tenure at the central bank, she taught at Harvard University and Stanford University and served on Barack Obama’s council of economic advisers. Cook’s battle with the White House began in August 2025 when she was abruptly fired after Trump said she committed mortgage fraud by listing two properties in Georgia and Michigan as her primary residence and failing to report rental income on her Atlanta property. Cook immediately sued the Trump administration, and the supreme court reinstated her after a 5-4 ruling that she could stay on as governor while fighting the fraud allegations. In June, the court ruled that Trump’s firing was unconstitutional because he did not follow proper procedure and give Cook an opportunity to dispute the allegations before she was fired. Cook was fired just as Trump was launching unprecedented attacks on the Fed’s chair, then Jerome Powell, in his blustering push to get the central bank to lower interest rates. Trump also launched a justice department investigation into Powell, which was dropped in April. Congress created the Fed to be an independent and non-partisan institution. Economists widely agree that a central bank unswayed by politics is essential for the stability of a country’s economy. Kevin Warsh, Powell’s successor, has repeatedly faced questions over how he will maintain the Fed’s independence. Before Trump picked him to lead the world’s most powerful central bank, he had echoed the president’s calls for cutting rates. But because of elevated inflation brought on by the war in the Middle East, the bank ultimately voted to raise rates in its last meeting, which drew the ire of the White House just more than a month before the crucial midterm elections.

title: Federal judge rules against Trump DoJ’s policy of collecting state voter rolls
author: Ariana Baio
summary: Judge says justice department policy of checking state voter rolls against a federal immigration database is unlawful
body_text: A federal judge ruled on Friday that the US justice department’s policy of collecting states’ unredacted voter rolls to check them against a federal immigration database is unlawful. The ruling, by the US district judge Sparkle Sooknanan, was a setback for Donald Trump, who has pushed his administration to ramp up investigations into non-citizen voting ahead of the November midterm elections, with control of Congress at stake. The department’s list maintenance policy, adopted to comply with the president’s election integrity executive order, violated privacy laws and risked disenfranchising voters, Sooknanan said. “The court vacates a policy that has removed United States citizens from the voter rolls in their home states and risks disenfranchising many more – a policy that flies in the face of duly enacted laws designed to protect Americans,” Sooknanan wrote in the 78-page ruling. Sooknanan said the policy not only violated federal laws, but also that the justice department did not have the authority to enact it because Congress gave the states, not the federal government, control over the maintenance of their voter rolls. “Behind all the window dressing, the challenged policy represents the federal government’s attempt to decide who gets to vote,” Sooknanan wrote. “But Congress has left that authority where our constitution has always placed it: with the states.” Sooknanan wrote that her ruling “does not prevent the federal government from taking lawful steps to support states’ efforts to maintain accurate voter rolls” and did not prevent states from maintaining their own. Sooknanan previously ruled against the administration in June, limiting the its ability to create a database of Americans’ information. The US supreme court later temporarily set aside her decision. The justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The lawsuit, brought by the government watchdog group Common Cause, came after the justice department requested voter information from states in May. Roughly 18 states complied, handing over information that included voters’ full names, birth dates, residential addresses, and state driver’s license numbers or the last four digits of their social security numbers. Sooknanan said the department “improperly” disclosed and maintained records. The administration wanted voter roll information to compare with immigration data, to ensure non-citizens are not registered to vote. But Sooknanan said the justice department “failed to consider the risk that its use of citizenship records known to be unreliable would lead the civil rights division to demand that states remove US citizens from their voter rolls”. In her ruling, she cited two people who had been incorrectly removed from their state’s voter roll list because they had been wrongly identified as non-citizens. “This is a victory for voters and yet another loss for the Department of Justice. It’s time the Trump administration stop these desperate attempts to seize voters’ private data and take control of our elections,” said Virginia Kase Solomón, president and CEO of Common Cause.

title: Trump says he picked ‘devoted fan’ Katie Zacharia to be next press secretary
author: Shrai Popat in Washington and Ariana Baio
summary: Zacharia will replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the role at the end of August after giving birth to her second child
body_text: Donald Trump on Friday announced that he had picked Katie Zacharia to be the next White House press secretary, lining up a conservative commentator he called a “devoted fan” to be his most prominent spokesperson. Zacharia will replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the role at the end of August after the birth to her second child. “It is my Great Honor to have just appointed, as Press Secretary, Katie Zacharia,” the president wrote in a social media post on Truth Social. “She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!” Trump added. The New York Times was first to report that Zacharia has been selected for the role. The Guardian has reached out to Zacharia for comment. Zacharia’s selection puts her at the heart of the White House’s efforts to shape the public narrative around Trump’s second term, as his approval rating falls to record lows, and his party fights to maintain control of Congress in next month’s midterm elections. Trump has asked supporters to vote like his name is on the ballot, turning the election into a referendum on his presidency amid widespread economic discontent and an unpopular war with Iran. Zacharia previously worked as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and now serves as a communications adviser for the Trump Media and Technology Group, which owns Truth Social, the president’s social network, on which he made the announcement about her selection official. The appointment came as a something of a surprise in Washington, after weeks of building speculation about who the president might choose to replace Leavitt. Several reports suggested Scott Jennings, the conservative TV pundit was an “an early favorite” for the role, though skeptics noted that his past criticism of the president would likely be an issue. Zacharia, a California native, has been involved in Republican politics for years. She attended Pepperdine University and served as president of her school’s College Republican organization. She interned in the White House’s office of political affairs during the second Bush administration as well as at the Republican National Committee. She obtained her law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011. Prior to joining DHS, Zacharia worked as general counsel at Fix California, a conservative nonprofit focused on “election integrity”. The organization is headed up by Trump ally and diplomat Ric Grenell. Zacharia was a frequent join Fox News commentator, often promoting or defending the US president’s policies while harshly criticizing Democrats. She is married to film producer Tyler Zacharia. They have four children. In his Truth Social post, Trump praised Leavitt, who he said had done a “fantastic job” in the role. On Monday, Fox News announced that Leavitt would join the network as an on-air contributor. “I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration,” Trump wrote, adding: “Good luck Katie!”
